We ſhall have ſome of the Court boys do that Office.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: My Lord we do no more than we are charg'd:
It is the Ladies pleaſure we be thus in grief;
She is forſaken.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: There's a Rogue too,
A young diſſembling ſlave; well, get you in,
I'le have a bout with that boy; 'tis high time
Now to be valiant; I confeſs my youth
Was never prone that way: what, made an Aſs?
A Court ſtale? well I will be valiant,
And beat ſome dozen of theſe Whelps; I will; and there's
Another of 'em, a trim cheating ſouldier,
I'le maul that Raſcal, h'as out-brav'd me twice;
But now I thank the Gods I am valiant;
Go, get you in, I'le take a courſe with all.

sp.speaker: CLE.
sp.p: Your ſiſter is not up yet.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.p: Oh, Brides muſt take their mornings reſt,
The night is troubleſome.

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.p: But not tedious.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.p: What odds, he has not my Siſters maiden head to night?

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.p: No, it's odds againſt any Bridegroom living, he ne're gets it while he lives.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.p: Y'are merry with my Siſter, you'l pleaſe to allow me the ſame freedom with your Mother.

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.p: She's at your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.p: Then ſhe's merry enough of her ſelf, ſhe needs no tickling; knock at the door.

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.p: We ſhall interrupt them.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.p: No matter, they have the year before them.
Good morrow Siſter; ſpare your ſelf to day, the night will come again. Enter Amintor.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.p: Who's there, my Brother? I am no readier yet, your Siſter is but now up.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.p: You look as you had loſt your eyes to night; I think you ha' not ſlept.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.p: I faith I have not.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.p: You have done better then.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: We ventured for a Boy; when he is Twelve,
He ſhall command againſt the foes of Rhodes.

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.l: You cannot, you want ſleep. Aſide.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: 'Tis true; but ſhe
As if ſhe had drunk Lethe, or had made
Even with Heaven, did fetch ſo ſtill a ſleep,
So ſweet and ſound.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.p: Your Siſter frets this morning, and does turn her eyes upon me, as people on their headſman; ſhe does chafe, and kiſs, and chaſe again, and clap my cheeks; ſhe's in another world.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: Then I had loſt; I was about to lay, you had not got her Maiden-head to night.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Ha! he does not mock me; y'ad loſt indeed;
I do not uſe to bungle.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: You do deſerve her.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I laid my lips to hers, and what wild breath
That was rude and rough to me, laſt night Aſide.
Was ſweet as April; I'le be guilty too,
If theſe be the effects. Enter Melantius.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Good day Amintor, for to me the name
Of Brother is too diſtant; we are friends,
And that is nearer.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Dear Melantius!
Let me behold thee; is it poſſible?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: What ſudden gaze is this?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: 'Tis wonderous ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Why does thine eye deſire ſo ſtrict a view
Of that it knows ſo well?
There's nothing here that is not thine.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I wonder much Melantius,
To ſee thoſe noble looks that make me think
How vertuous thou art; and on the ſudden
'Tis ſtrange to me, thou ſhouldſt have worth and honour,
Or not be baſe, and falſe, and treacherous,
And every ill. But—

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Stay, ſtay my Friend,
I fear this ſound will not become our loves; no more, embrace me.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Oh miſtake me not;
I know thee to be full of all thoſe deeds
That we frail men call good: but by the courſe
Of nature thou ſhouldſt be as quickly chang'd
As are the winds, diſſembling as the Sea,
That now wears brows as ſmooth as Virgins be,
Tempting the Merchant to invade his face,
And in an hour calls his billows up,
And ſhoots 'em at the Sun, deſtroying all
He carries on him. O how near am I Aſide.
To utter my ſick thoughts!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: But why, my Friend, ſhould I be ſo by Nature?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I have wed thy Siſter, who hath vertuous thoughts
Enough for one whole family, and it is ſtrange
That you ſhould feel no want.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Believe me, this complement's too cunning for me.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: What ſhould I be then by the courſe of nature,
They having both robb'd me of ſo much vertue?

sp.speaker: Strat.
sp.l: O call the Bride, my Lord Amintor, that we may ſee her bluſh, and turn her eyes down; it is the prettieſt ſport.

l.hi: Evadne!

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: My Lord! Within.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Come forth my Love,
Your Brothers do attend to wiſh you joy.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I am not ready yet.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Enough, enough.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: They'l mock me.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Faith thou ſhalt come in. Enter Evadne.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Good morrow Siſter; he that underſtands
Whom you have wed, need not to wiſh you joy.
You have enough, take heed you be not proud.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: O Siſter, what have you done!

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I done! why, what have I done?

sp.speaker: Strat.
sp.l: My Lord Amintor ſwears you are no Maid now,

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Puſh!

sp.speaker: Strat.
sp.l: I faith he does.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I knew I ſhould be mockt.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: With a truth.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: If 'twere to do again, in faith I would not marry.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Not I by Heaven. Aſide.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: Siſter, Dula ſwears ſhe heard you cry two rooms off.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Fie how you talk!

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: Let's ſee you walk.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: By my troth y'are ſpoil'd.

l.hi: Amintor!

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Ha!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Thou art ſad.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Who I? I thank you for that, ſhall Diphilus, thou and I ſing a catch?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: How!

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Prethee let's.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Nay, that's too much the other way.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I am ſo lightned with my happineſs: how doſt thou Love? kiſs me.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I cannot love you, you tell tales of me.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Nothing but what becomes us: Gentlemen,
Would you had all ſuch Wives, and all the world,
That I might be no wonder; y'are all ſad;
What, do you envie me? I walk methinks
On water, and ne're ſink, I am ſo light.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: 'Tis well you are ſo.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Well? how can I be other, when ſhe looks thus?
Is there no muſick there? let's dance.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Why? this is ſtrange, Amintor!

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I do not know my ſelf;
Yet I could wiſh my joy were leſs.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: I'le marry too, if it will make one thus.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Amintor, hark. Aſide.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: What ſays my Love? I muſt obey.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: You do it ſcurvily, 'twill be perceiv'd.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: My Lord the King is here. Enter King and Lyſi.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.l: And his Brother.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Good morrow all.
Amintor, joy on, joy fall thick upon thee!
And Madam, you are alter'd ſince I ſaw you,
I muſt ſalute you; you are now anothers;
How lik't you your nights reſt?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Ill Sir.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I! 'deed ſhe took but little.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: You'l let her take more, and thank her too ſhortly.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Amintor, wert thou truly honeſt
Till thou wert Married?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Tell me then, how ſhews the ſport unto thee?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Why well.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What did you do?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: No more nor leſs than other couples uſe;
You know what 'tis; it has but a courſe name.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: But prethee, I ſhould think by her black eye,
And her red cheek, ſhe ſhould be quick and ſtirring
In this ſame buſineſs, ha?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I cannot tell, I ne're try'd other Sir, but I perceive
She is as quick as you delivered.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Well, you'l truſt me then Amintor,
To chooſe a Wife for you agen?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: No never Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Why? like you this ſo ill?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: So well I like her.
For this I bow my knee in thanks to you,
And unto Heaven will pay my grateful tribute
Hourly, and to hope we ſhall draw out
A long contented life together here,
And die both full of gray hairs in one day;
For which the thanks is yours; but if the powers
That rule us, pleaſe to call her firſt away,
Without pride ſpoke, this World holds not a Wiſe
Worthy to take her room.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I do not like this; all forbear the room
But you Amintor and your Lady. I have ſome ſpeech with
You, that may concern your after living well.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: He will not tell me that he lies with her: if he do,
Something Heavenly ſtay my heart, for I ſhall be apt
To thruſt this arm of mine to acts unlawful.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: You will ſuffer me to talk with her Amintor,
And not have a jealous pang!

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Sir, I dare truſt my Wiſe
With whom ſhe dares to talk, and not be jealous.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How do you like Amintor?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: As I did Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How's that!

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: As one that to fulfil your will and pleaſure,
I have given leave to call me Wife and Love.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I ſee there is no laſting Faith in Sin;
They that break word with Heaven, will break again
With all the World, and ſo doſt thou with me.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: How Sir?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: This ſubtile Womans ignorance
Will not excuſe you; thou haſt taken Oaths
So great, methought they did not well become
A Womans mouth, that thou wouldſt ne're enjoy
A man but me.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I never did ſwear ſo; you do me wrong.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Day and night have heard it.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I ſwore indeed that I would never love
A man of lower place; but if your fortune
Should throw you from this height, I bade you truſt
I would forſake you, and would bend to him
That won your Throne; I love with my ambition,
Not with mine eyes; but if I ever yet
Toucht any other, Leproſie light here
Upon my face, which for your Royalty I would not ſtain.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Why thou diſſembleſt, and it is in me to puniſh thee.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Why, it is in me then not to love you, which will
More afflict your body, than your puniſhment can mine.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: But thou haſt let Amintor lie with thee.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I ha'not.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Impudence! he ſaies himſelf ſo.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: He lyes.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: He does not.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: By this light he does, ſtrangely and baſely, and
I'le prove it ſo; I did not ſhun him for a night,
But told him I would never cloſe with him.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Speak lower, 'tis falſe.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I'm no man to anſwer with a blow;
Or if I were, you are the King; but urge me not, 'tis moſt true.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Do not I know the uncontrouled thoughts
That youth brings with him, when his bloud is high
With expectation and deſires of that
He long hath waited for? is not his ſpirit,
Though he be temperate, of a valiant ſtrain,
As this our age hath known? what could he do,
If ſuch a ſudden ſpeech had met his blood,
But ruine thee for ever? if he had not kill'd thee,
He could not bear it thus; he is as we,
Or any other wrong'd man.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: It is diſſembling.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Take him; farewel; henceforth I am thy foe;
And what diſgraces I can blot thee, look for.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Stay Sir; Amintor, you ſhall hear, Amintor.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: What my Love?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Amintor, thou haſt an ingenious look,
And ſhouldſt be vertuous; it amazeth me,
That thou canſt make ſuch baſe malicious lyes.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: What my dear Wife?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Dear Wife! I do deſpiſe thee;
Why, nothing can be baſer, than to ſow
Diſſention amongſt Lovers.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Lovers! who?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: The King and me.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: O Heaven!

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Who ſhould live long, and love without diſtaſte,
Were it not for ſuch pickthanks as thy ſelf!
Did you lie with me? ſwear now, and be puniſht in hell
For this.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: The ſaithleſs Sin I made
To fair Aſpatia, is not yet reveng'd,
It follows me; I will not loſe a word
To this wild Woman; but to you my King,
The anguiſh of my ſoul thruſts out this truth,
Y'are a Tyrant; and not ſo much to wrong
An honeſt man thus, as to take a pride
In talking with him of it.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Now Sir, ſee how loud this fellow lyed.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: You that can know to wrong, ſhould know how
Men muſt right themſelves: what puniſhment is due
From me to him that ſhall abuſe my bed!
It is not death; nor can that ſatisfie,
Unleſs I ſend your lives through all the Land,
To ſhew how nobly I have freed my ſelf.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Draw not thy Sword, thou knoweſt I cannot fear
A ſubjects hand; but thou ſhalt feel the weight of this
If thou doſt rage.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: The weight of that?
If you have any worth, for Heavens ſake think
I fear not Swords; for as you are meer man,
I dare as eaſily kill you for this deed,
As you dare think to do it; but there is
Divinity about you, that ſtrikes dead
My riſing paſſions, as you are my King,
I fall before you, and preſent my Sword
To cut mine own fleſh, if it be your will.
Alas! I am nothing but a multitude
Of walking griefs; yet ſhould I murther you,
I might before the world take the excuſe
Of madneſs: for compare my injuries,
And they will well appear too ſad a weight
For reaſon to endure; but fall I firſt
Amongſt my ſorrows, ere my treacherous hand
Touch holy things: but why? I know not what
I have to ſay; why did you chooſe out me
To make thus wretched? there were thouſand fools
Eaſie to work on, and of ſtate enough within the Iſland.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I would not have a fool, it were no credit for me.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Worſe and worſe!
Thou that dar'ſt talk unto thy Husband thus,
Profeſs thy ſelf a Whore; and more than ſo,
Reſolve to be ſo ſtill; it is my fate
To bear and bow beneath a thouſand griefs,
To keep that little credit with the World.
But there were wiſe ones too, you might have ta'ne another.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No; for I believe thee honeſt, as thou wert valiant.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: All the happineſs
Beſtow'd upon me, turns into diſgrace;
Gods take your honeſty again, for I
Am loaden with it; good my Lord the King, be private in it.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Thou may'ſt live Amintor,
Free as thy King, if thou wilt wink at this,
And be a means that we may meet in ſecret.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: A Baud! hold my breaſt, a bitter curſe
Seize me, if I forget not all reſpects
That are Religious, on another word
Sounded like that, and through a Sea of ſins
Will wade to my revenge, though I ſhould call
Pains here, and after life upon my ſoul.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Well I am reſolute you lay not with her,
And ſo leave you. Exit King.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: You muſt be prating, and ſee what follows.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Prethee vex me not.
Leave me, I am afraid ſome ſudden ſtart
Will pull a murther on me.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I am gone; I love my life well. Exit Evadne.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I hate mine as much.
This 'tis to break a troth; I ſhould be glad
If all this tide of grief would make me mad. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I'le know the cauſe of all Amintors griefs,
Or friendſhip ſhall be idle. Enter Calianax.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: O Melantius, my Daughter will die.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Truſt me, I am ſorry; would thou hadſt ta'ne her room.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Thou art a ſlave, a cut-throat ſlave, a bloody treacherous ſlave.

sp.speaker: Melan.
sp.l: Take heed old man, thou wilt be heard to rave,
And loſe thine Offices.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am valiant grown
At all theſe years, and thou art but a ſlave.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Leave, ſome company will come, and I reſpect
Thy years, not thee ſo much, that I could wiſh
To laugh at thee alone.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I'le ſpoil your mirth, I mean to ſight with thee;
There lie my Cloak, this was my Fathers Sword,
And he durſt ſight; are you prepar'd?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Why? wilt thou doat thy ſelf out of thy life?
Hence get thee to bed, have careful looking to, and eat warm things, and trouble not me: my head is full of thoughts more weighty than thy life or death can be.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: You have a name in War, when you ſtand ſafe
Amongſt a multitude; but I will try
What you dare do unto a weak old man
In ſingle ſight; you'l ground I fear: Come draw.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I will not draw, unleſs thou pul'ſt thy death
Upon thee with a ſtroke; there's no one blow
That thou canſt give, hath ſtrength enough to kill me.
Tempt me not ſo far then; the power of earth
Shall not redeem thee.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I muſt let him alone,
He's ſtout and able; and to ſay the truth,
However I may ſet a face, and talk,
I am not valiant: when I was a youth,
I kept my credit with a teſtie trick I had,
Amongſt cowards, but durſt never ſight.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I will not promiſe to preſerve your life if you do ſtay.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I would give half my Land that I durſt ſight with that proud man a little: if I had men to hold, I would beat him, till he ask me mercy.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Sir, will you be gone?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I dare not ſtay, but I will go home, and beat my ſervants all over for this. Exit Calianax.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: This old fellow haunts me,
But the diſtracted carriage of mine Amintor
Takes deeply on me, I will find the cauſe;
I fear his Conſcience cries, he wrong'd Aſpatia.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Mens eyes are not ſo ſubtil to perceive
My inward miſery; I bear my grief
Hid from the World; how art thou wretched then?
For ought I know, all Husbands are like me;
And every one I talk with of his Wife,
Is but a well diſſembler of his woes
As I am; would I knew it, for the rareneſs afflicts me now.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Amintor, We have not enjoy'd our friendſhip of late, for we were wont to charge our ſouls in talk.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Melantius, I can tell thee a good jeſt of Strato and a Lady the laſt day.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: How waſt?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Why ſuch an odd one.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I have long'd to ſpeak with you, not of an idle jeſt that's forc'd, but of matter you are bound to utter to me.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: What is that my friend?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I have obſerv'd, your words ſall from your tongue
Wildly; and all your carriage,
L • ke one that ſtrove to ſhew his merry mood,
When he were ill diſpos'd: you were not wont
To put ſuch ſcorn into your ſpeech, or wear
Upon your face ridiculous jollity:
Some ſadneſs ſits here, which your cunning would
Cover o're with ſmiles, and 'twill not be. What is it?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: A ſadneſs here! what cauſe
Can ſate provide for me, to make me ſo?
Am I not lov'd through all this Iſle? the King
Rains greatneſs on me: have I not received
A Lady to my bed, that in her eye
Keeps mounting fire, and on her tender cheeks
Inevitable colour, in her heart
A priſon for all vertue? are not you,
Which is above all joyes, my conſtant friend?
What ſadneſs can I have? no, I am light,
And feel the courſes of my blood more warm
And ſtirring than they were; faith marry too,
And you will feel ſo unexpreſt a joy
In chaſt embraces, that you will indeed appear another.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: You may ſhape, Amintor,
Cauſes to cozen the whole world withal,
And your ſelf too; but 'tis not like a friend,
To hide your ſoul from me; 'tis not your nature
To be thus idle; I have ſeen you ſtand
As you were blaſted; midſt of all your mirth,
Call thrice aloud, and then ſtart, feigning joy
So coldly: World! what do I here? a friend
Is nothing, Heaven! I would ha' told that man
My ſecret ſins; I'le ſearch an unknown Land,
And there plant friendſhip, all is withered here;
Come with a complement, I would have fought,
Or told my friend he ly'd, ere ſooth'd him ſo;
Out of my boſom.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: But there is nothing.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Worſe and worſe; farewel;
From this time have acquaintance, but no friend.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Melantius, ſtay, you ſhall know what that is.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: See how you play'd with friendſhip; be advis'd
How you give cauſe unto your ſelf to ſay, You ha'loſt a friend.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Forgive what I have done;
For I am ſo ore-gone with injuries
Unheard of, that I loſe conſideration
Of what I ought to do—oh—oh.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Do not weep; what is't?
May I once but know the man
Hath turn'd my friend thus?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I had ſpoke at firſt, but that.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: But what?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I held it moſt unfit
For you to know; ſaith do not know it yet.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Thou feeſt my love, that will keep company
With thee in tears; hide nothing then from me;
For when I know the cauſe of thy diſtemper,
With mine own armour I'le adorn my ſelf,
My reſolution, and cut through thy foes,
Unto thy quiet, till I place thy heart
As peaceable as ſpotleſs innocence. What is it?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Why, 'tis this—it is too big
To get out, let my tears make way a while.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Puniſh me ſtrangely heaven, if he eſcape
Of life or ſame, that brought this youth to this.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Your Siſter.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Well ſaid.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: You'l wiſh't unknown, when you have heard it.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Is much to blame,
And to the King has given her honour up,
And lives in Whoredom with him.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: How, this!
Thou art run mad with injury indeed,
Thou couldſt not utter this elſe; ſpeak again,
For I forgive it freely; tell thy griefs.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: She's wanton; I am loth to ſay a Whore,
Though it be true.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Speak yet again, before mine anger grow
Up beyond throwing down; what are thy griefs?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: By all our friendſhip, theſe.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: What? am I tame?
After mine actions, ſhall the name of friend
Blot all our family, and ſtrike the brand
Of Whore upon my Siſter unreveng'd?
My ſhaking fleſh be thou a Witneſs for me,
With what unwillingneſs I go to ſcourge
This Rayler, whom my folly hath call'd Friend;
I will not take thee baſely; thy ſword
Hangs near thy hand, draw it, that I may whip
Thy raſhneſs to repentance; draw thy ſword.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Not on thee, did thine anger ſwell as high
As the wild ſurges; thou ſhouldſt do me eaſe
Here, and Eternally, if thy noble hand
Would cut me from my ſorrows.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: This is baſe and fearful! they that uſe to utter lyes,
Provide not blows, but words to qualifie
The men they wrong'd; thou haſt a guilty cauſe.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Thou pleaſeſt me; for ſo much more like this,
Will raiſe my anger up above my griefs,
Which is a paſſion eaſier to be born,
And I ſhall then be happy.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Take then more to raiſe thine anger. 'Tis meer
Cowardize makes thee not draw; and I will leave thee dead
However; but if thou art ſo much preſt
With guilt and fear, as not to dare to fight,
I'le make thy memory loath'd, and ſix a ſcandal
Upon thy name for ever.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Then I draw,
As juſtly as our Magiſtrates their Swords,
To cut offenders off; I knew before
'Twould grate your ears; but it was baſe in you
To urge a weighty ſecret from your friend,
And then rage at it; I ſhall be at eaſe
If I be kill'd; and if you fall by me,
I ſhall not long out-live you.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Stay a while.
The name of friend is more than family,
Or all the world beſides; I was a fool.
Thou ſearching humane nature, that didſt wake
To do me wrong, thou art inquiſitive,
And thruſts me upon queſtions that will take
My ſleep away; would I had died ere known
This ſad diſhonour; pardon me my friend;
If thou wilt ſtrike, here is a faithful heart,
Pierce it, for I will never heave my hand
To thine; behold the power thou haſt in me!
I do believe my Siſter is a Whore,
A Leprous one, put up thy ſword young man.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: How ſhould I bear it then, ſhe being ſo?
I fear my friend that you will loſe me ſhortly;
And I ſhall do a foul action my ſelf
Through theſe diſgraces.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Better half the Land
Were buried quick together; no, Amintor,
Thou ſhalt have eaſe: O this Adulterous King
That drew her to't! where got he the ſpirit
To wrong me ſo?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: What is it then to me,
If it be wrong to you!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Why, not ſo much: the credit of our houſe
Is thrown away;
But from his Iron Den I'le waken death,
And hurle him on this King; my honeſty
Shall ſteel my ſword, and on its horrid point
I'le wear my cauſe, that ſhall amaze the eyes
Of this proud man, and be too glittering
For him to look on.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I have quite undone my ſame.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Dry up thy watry eyes,
And caſt a manly look upon my face;
For nothing is ſo wild as I thy friend
Till I have freed thee; ſtill this ſwelling breaſt;
I go thus from thee, and will never ceaſe
My vengeance, till I find my heart at peace.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: It muſt not be ſo; ſtay, mine eyes would tell
How loth I am to this; but love and tears
Leave me a while, for I have hazarded
All this world calls happy; thou haſt wrought
A ſecret from me under name of Friend,
Which Art could ne're have found, nor torture wrung
From out my boſom; give it me agen,
For I will find it, whereſoe're it lies
Hid in the mortal'ſt part; invent a way to give it back.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Why, would you have it back?
I will to death purſue him with revenge.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Therefore I call it back from thee; for I know
Thy blood ſo high, that thou wilt ſtir in this, and ſhame me
To poſterity: take to thy Weapon.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Hear thy friend, that bears more years than thou.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I will not hear: but draw, or I—

l.hi: Amintor.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Draw then, for I am full as reſolute
As fame and honour can inforce me be;
I cannot linger, draw.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I do— but is not
My ſhare of credit equal with thine if I do ſtir?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: No; for it will be cal'd
Honour in thee to ſpill thy Siſters blood,
If ſhe her birth abuſe, and on the King
A brave revenge: but on me that have walkt
With patience in it, it will fix the name
Of fearful Cuckold—O that word! be quick.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Then joyn with me.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I dare not do a ſin, or elſe I would: be ſpeedy.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Then dare not fight with me, for that's a ſin.
His grief diſtracts him; call thy thoughts agen,
And to thy ſelf pronounce the name of friend,
And ſee what that will work; I will not fight.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: You muſt.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I will be kill'd firſt, though my paſſions
Offred the like to you; 'tis not this earth
Shall buy my reaſon to it; think a while,
For you are (I muſt weep when I ſpeak that)
Almoſt beſides your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Oh my ſoft temper!
So many ſweet words from thy Siſters mouth,
I am afraid would make me take her
To embrace, and pardon her. I am mad indeed,
And know not what I do; yet have a care
Of me in what thou doeſt.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Why thinks my friend I will forget his honour, or to ſave
The bravery of our houſe, will loſe his fame,
And fear to touch the Throne of Majeſty?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: A curſe will follow that, but rather live
And ſuffer with me.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I will do what worth ſhall bid me, and no more.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Faith I am ſick, and deſperately I hope,
Yet leaning thus, I feel a kind of eaſe.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Come take agen your mirth about you.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I ſhall never do't.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I warrant you, look up, wee'l walk together,
Put thine arm here, all ſhall be well agen.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Thy Love, O wretched, I thy Love, Melantius; why,
I have nothing elſe.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Be merry then. Exeunt. Enter Melantius agen.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: This worthy young man may do violence
Upon himſelf, but I have cheriſht him
To my beſt power, and ſent him ſmiling from me
To counterfeit again; Sword hold thine edge,
My heart will never fail me: Diphilus,
Thou com'ſt as ſent. Enter Diphilus.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: Yonder has been ſuch laughing.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Betwixt whom?

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: Why, our Siſter and the King,
I thought their ſpleens would break,
They laught us all out of the room.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: They muſt weep, Diphilus.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: Muſt they?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: They muſt: thou art my Brother, and if I did believe
Thou hadſt a baſe thought, I would rip it out,
Lie where it durſt.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: You ſhould not, I would firſt mangle my ſelf and find it.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: That was ſpoke according to our ſtrain; come
Joyn thy hands to mine,
And ſwear a firmneſs to what project I ſhall lay before thee.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: You do wrong us both;
People hereafter ſhall not ſay there paſt
A bond more than our loves, to tie our lives
And deaths together.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: It is as nobly ſaid as I would wiſh;
Anon I'le tell you wonders; we are wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: But I will tell you now, wee'l right our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Stay not, prepare the armour in my houſe;
And what friends you can draw unto our ſide,
Not knowing of the cauſe, make ready too;
Haſte Diphilus, the time requires it, haſte. Exit Diphilus.
I hope my cauſe is juſt, I know my blood
Tells me it is, and I will credit it:
To take revenge, and loſe my ſelf withal,
Were idle; and to ſcape impoſſible,
Without I had the ſort, which miſery
Remaining in the hands of my old enemy
Calianax, but I muſt have it, ſee Enter Calianax.
Where he comes ſhaking by me: good my Lord,
Forget your ſpleen to me, I never wrong'd you,
But would have peace with every man.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: 'Tis well;
If I durſt ſight, your tongue would lie at quiet.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Y'are touchie without all cauſe.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Do, mock me.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: By mine honour I ſpeak truth.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Honour? where is't?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: See what ſtarts you make into your hatred to my love and freedom to you.—
I come with reſolution to obtain a ſuit of you.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: A ſuit of me! 'tis very like it ſhould be granted, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Nay, go not hence;
'Tis this; you have the keeping of the Fort,
And I would wiſh you by the love you ought
To bear unto me, to deliver it into my hands.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am in hope that thou art mad, to talk to me thus.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: But there is a reaſon to move you to it. I would kill the King that wrong'd you and your daughter.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Out Traytor!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Nay but ſtay; I cannot ſcape, the deed once done,
Without I have this fort.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: And ſhould I help thee? now thy treacherous mind betrays it ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Come, delay me not;
Give me a ſudden anſwer, or already
Thy laſt is ſpoke; refuſe not offered love,
When it comes clad in ſecrets.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: If I ſay I will not, he will kill me, I do ſee't writ
In his looks; and ſhould I ſay I will, he'l run and tell the
King: I do not ſhun your friendſhip dear Melantius,
But this cauſe is weighty, give me but an hour to think.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Take it—I know this goes unto the King,
But I am arm'd. Ex. Melant.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Me thinks I feel my ſelf
But twenty now agen; this fighting fool
Wants Policy; I ſhall revenge my Girl,
And make her red again; I pray, my legs
Will laſt that pace that I will carry them,
I ſhall want breath before I find the King.

div.head: Actus Quartus.
div.stage: Enter Melantius, Evadne, and a Lady.

sp.speaker: MEL.
sp.l: Save you.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Save you ſweet Brother.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: In my blunt eye methinks you look Evadne.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Come, you would make me bluſh.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I would Evadne, I ſhall diſpleaſe my ends elſe.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: You ſhall if you command me; I am baſhful;
Come Sir, how do I look?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I would not have your women hear me
Break into commendation of you, 'tis not ſeemly.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Go walt me in the Gallery—now ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I'le lock the door firſt. Exeunt Ladies.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I will not have your guilded things that dance in viſitation with their Millan skins choke up my buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: You are ſtrangely diſpos'd Sir.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Good Madam, not to make you merry.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: No, if you praiſe me, 'twill make me ſad.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Such a ſad commendation I have for you.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Brother, the Court hath made you witty,
And learn to riddle.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I praiſe the Court for't; has it learned you nothing?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Me?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I Evadne, thou art young and handſom,
A Lady of a ſweet complexion,
And ſuch a flowing carriage, that it cannot
Chuſe but inflame a Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Gentle Brother!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: 'Tis yet in thy remembrance, fooliſh woman,
To make me gentle.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: How is this?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: 'Tis baſe,
And I could bluſh at theſe years, thorough all
My honour'd ſcars, to come to ſuch a parly.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I underſtand you not.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: You dare not, Fool;
They that commit thy faults, fly the remembrance.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: My faults, Sir! I would have you know I care not
If they were written here, here in my forehead.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Thy body is too little for the ſtory,
The luſts of which would fill another woman,
Though ſhe had Twins within her.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: This is ſaucy;
Look you intrude no more, there lies your way.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Thou art my way, and I will tread upon thee,
Till I find truth out.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: What truth is that you look for?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Thy long-loſt honour: would the Gods had ſet me
One of their loudeſt bolts; come tell me quickly,
Do it without enforcement, and take heed
You ſwell me not above my temper.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: How Sir? where got you this report?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Where there was people in every place.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: They and the ſeconds of it are baſe people;
Believe them not, they lyed.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Do not play with mine anger, do not Wretch,
I come to know that deſperate Fool that drew thee
From thy fair life; be wiſe, and lay him open.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Unhand me, and learn manners, ſuch another
Forgetfulneſs forfeits your life.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Quench me this mighty humour, and then tell me
Whoſe Whore you are, for you are one, I know it.
Let all mine honours periſh but I'le find him,
Though he lie lockt up in thy blood; be ſudden;
There is no facing it, and be not flattered;
The burnt air, when the Dog raigns, is not fouler
Than thy contagious name, till thy repentance
(If the Gods grant thee any) purge thy ſickneſs.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Be gone, you are my Brother, that's your ſafety.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I'le be a Wolf firſt; 'tis to be thy Brother
An infamy below the ſin of a Coward:
I am as far from being part of thee,
As thou art from thy vertue: ſeek a kindred
'Mongſt ſenſual beaſts, and make a Goat thy Brother,
A Goat is cooler; will you tell me yet?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: If you ſtay here and rail thus, I ſhall tell you,
I'le ha' you whipt; get you to your command,
And there preach to your Sentinels,
And tell them what a brave man you are; I ſhall laugh at you.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Y'are grown a glorious Whore; where be your
Fighters? what mortal Fool durſt raiſe thee to this daring,
And I alive? by my juſt Sword, h'ad ſafer
Beſtride a Billow when the angry North
Plows up the Sea, or made Heavens fire his food;
Work me no higher; will you diſcover yet?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: The Fellow's mad, ſleep and ſpeak ſenſe.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.p: Force my ſwollen heart no further; I would ſave thee; your great maintainers are not here, they dare not, would they were all, and armed, I would ſpeak loud; here's one ſhould thunder to'em: will you tell me? thou haſt no hope to ſcape; he that dares moſt, and damns away his ſoul to do thee ſervice, will ſooner fetch meat from a hungry Lion, than come to reſcue thee; thou haſt death about thee: h'as undone thine honour, poyſon'd thy vertue, and of a lovely roſe, left thee a canker.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Let me conſider.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Do, whoſe child thou wert,
Whoſe honour thou haſt murdered, whoſe grave open'd,
And ſo pull'd on the Gods, that in their juſtice
They muſt reſtore him fleſh again and life,
And raiſe his dry bones to revenge his ſcandal.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: The gods are not of my mind; they had better let 'em lie ſweet ſtill in the earth; they'l ſtink here.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Do you raiſe mirth out of my eaſineſs?
Forſake me then all weakneſſes of Nature,
That make men women: Speak you whore, ſpeak truth,
Or by the dear ſoul of thy ſleeping Father,
This ſword ſhall be thy lover: tell, or I'le kill thee:
And when thou haſt told all, thou wilt deſerve it.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: You will not murder me!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: No, 'tis a juſtice, and a noble one,
To put the light out of ſuch baſe offenders.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Help!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: By thy foul ſelf, no humane help ſhall help thee,
If thou crieſt: when I have kill'd thee, as I have
Vow'd to do, if thou confeſs not, naked as thou haſt left
Thine honour, will I leave thee,
That on thy branded fleſh the world may read
Thy black ſhame, and my juſtice; wilt thou bend yet?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Up and begin your ſtory.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Oh I am miſerable.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: 'Tis true, thou art, ſpeak truth ſtill.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I have offended, noble Sir: forgive me.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: With what ſecure ſlave?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Do not ask me Sir.
Mine own remembrance is a miſery too mightie for me.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Do not fall back again; my ſword's unſheath'd yet.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: What ſhall I do?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Be true, and make your fault leſs.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I dare not tell.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Tell, or I'le be this day a killing thee.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Will you forgive me then?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Stay, I muſt ask mine honour firſt, I have too much fooliſh nature in me; ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Is there none elſe here?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: None but a fearful conſcience, that's too many. Who is't?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: O hear me gently; it was the King.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: No more. My worthy father's and my ſervices
Are liberally rewarded! King, I thank thee,
For all my dangers and my wounds, thou haſt paid me
In my own metal: Theſe are Souldiers thanks.
How long have you liv'd thus Evadne?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Too long.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Too late you find it: can you be ſorry?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Would I were half as blameleſs.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Evadne, thou wilt to thy trade again.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Firſt to my grave.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Would gods th'hadſt been ſo bleſt:
Doſt thou not hate this King now? prethee hate him:
Couldſt thou not curſe him? I command thee curſe him,
Curſe till the gods hear, and deliver him
To thy juſt wiſhes: yet I fear Evadne,
You had rather play your game out.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: No, I feel
Too many ſad confuſions here to let in any looſe flame hereafter.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Doſt thou not feel amongſt all thoſe one brave anger
That breaks out nobly, and directs thine arm to kill this baſe King?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: All the gods forbid it.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: No, all the gods require it, they are diſhonoured in him.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: 'Tis too fearful.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Y'are valiant in his bed, and bold enough
To be a ſtale whore, and have your Madams name
Diſcourſe for Grooms and Pages, and hereafter
When his cool Majeſtie hath laid you by,
To be at penſion with ſome needy Sir
For meat and courſer clothes, thus far you know no fear.
Come, you ſhall kill him.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Good Sir!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: And 'twere to kiſs him dead, thou'd ſmother him;
Be wiſe and kill him: Canſt thou live and know
What noble minds ſhall make thee ſee thy ſelf
Found out with every finger, made the ſhame
Of all ſucceſſions, and in this great ruine
Thy brother and thy noble husband broken?
Thou ſhalt not live thus; kneel and ſwear to help me
When I ſhall call thee to it, or by all
Holy in heaven and earth, thou ſhalt not live
To breath a full hour longer, not a thought:
Come 'tis a righteous oath; give me thy hand,
And both to heaven held up, ſwear by that wealth
This luſtful thief ſtole from thee, when I ſay it,
To let his foul ſoul out.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Here I ſwear it,
And all you ſpirits of abuſed Ladies
Help me in this performance.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Enough; this muſt be known to none
But you and I Evadne; not to your Lord,
Though he be wiſe and noble, and a fellow
Dares ſtep as far into a worthy action,
As the moſt daring, I as far as Juſtice.
Ask me not why. Farewell. Exit. Mel.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Would I could ſay ſo to my black diſgrace.
Oh where have I been all this time! how friended,
That I ſhould loſe my ſelf thus deſperately,
And none for pity ſhew me how I wandred?
There is not in the compaſs of the light
A more unhappy creature: ſure I am monſtrous,
For I have done thoſe follies, thoſe mad miſchiefs,
Would dare a woman. O my loaden ſoul,
Be not ſo cruel to me, choak not up Enter Amintor.
The way to my repentance. O my Lord.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: How now?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: My much abuſed Lord! Kneels.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: This cannot be.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I do not kneel to live, I dare not hope it;
The wrongs I did are greater; look upon me
Though I appear with all my faults.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Stand up.
This is no new way to beget more ſorrow;
Heaven knows I have too many; do not mock me;
Though I am tame and bred up with my wrongs,
Which are my foſter-brothers, I may leap
Like a hand-wolf into my natural wilderneſs,
And do an out-rage: pray thee do not mock me.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: My whole life is ſo leprous, it infects
All my repentance: I would buy your pardon
Though at the higheſt ſet, even with my life:
That ſlight contrition, that's no ſacrifice
For what I have committed.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Sure I dazle:
There cannot be a faith in that ſoul woman
That knows no God more mighty than her miſchiefs:
Thou doſt ſtill worſt, ſtill number on thy faults,
To preſs my poor heart thus. Can I believe
There's any ſeed of Vertue in that woman
Left to ſhoot up, that dares go on in ſin
Known, and ſo known as thine is, O Evadne!
Would there were any ſafety in thy ſex,
That I might put a thouſand ſorrows off,
And credit thy repentance: but I muſt not;
Thou haſt brought me to the dull calamity,
To that ſtrange misbelief of all the world,
And all things that are in it, that I fear
I ſhall fall like a tree, and find my grave,
Only remembring that I grieve.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: My Lord,
Give me your griefs: you are an innocent,
A ſoul as white as heaven: let not my ſins
Periſh your noble youth: I do not fall here
To ſhadow by diſſembling with my tears,
As all ſay women can, or to make leſs
What my hot will hath done, which heaven and you
Knows to be tougher than the hand of time
Can cut from mans remembrance; no I do not;
I do appear the ſame, the ſame Evadne,
Dreſt in the ſhames I liv'd in, the ſame monſter.
But theſe are names of honour, to what I am;
I do preſent my ſelf the fouleſt creature,
Moſt poyſonous, dangerous, and deſpis'd of men,
Lerna e're bred, or Nilus; I am hell,
Till you, my dear Lord, ſhoot your light into me,
The beams of your forgiveneſs: I am ſoul-ſick,
And whither with the fear of one condemn'd,
Till I have got your pardon.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Riſe Evadne.
Theſe heavenly powers that put this good into thee,
Grant a continuance of it: I forgive thee;
Make thy ſelf worthy of it, and take heed,
Take heed Evadne this be ſerious;
Mock not the powers above, that can and dare
Give thee a great example of their juſtice
To all enſuing eyes, if thou plai'ſt
With thy repentance, the beſt ſacrifice.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I have done nothing good to win belief,
My life hath been ſo faithleſs; all the creatures
Made for heavens honours have their ends, and good ones,
All but the couſening Crocodiles, falſe women;
They reign here like thoſe plagues, thoſe killing ſores
Men pray againſt; and when they die, like tales
Ill told, and unbeliev'd, they paſs away,
And go to duſt forgotten: But my Lord,
Thoſe ſhort dayes I ſhall number to my reſt,
(As many muſt not ſee me) ſhall though too late,
Though in my evening, yet perceive a will,
Since I can do no good becauſe a woman,
Reach conſtantly at ſome thing that is near it;
I w ll redeem one minute of my age,
Or like another Njobe I'le weep till I am water.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I am now diſſolved:
My frozen ſoul melts: may each ſin thou haſt,
Find a new mercy: Riſe, I am at peace:
Hadſt thou been thus, thus excellently good,
Before that devil King tempted thy frailty,
Sure thou hadſt made a ſtar: give me thy hand;
From this time I will know thee, and as far
As honour gives me leave, be thy Amintor:
When we meet next, I will ſalute thee fairly,
And pray the gods to give thee happy dayes:
My charity ſhall go along with thee,
Though my embraces muſt be far from thee.
I ſhould ha • kill'd thee, but this ſweet repentance
Looks up my vengeance, for which thus I kiſs thee,
The laſt kiſs we muſt take; and would to heaven
The holy Prieſt that gave our hands together,
Had given us equal Vertues: go, Evadne,
The gods thus part our bodies, have a care
My honour falls no farther, I am well then.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: All the dear joyes here, and above hereafter
Crown thy fair ſoul: thus I take leave my Lord,
And never ſhall you ſee the ſoul Evadne
Till ſh'ave tryed all honoured means that may
Set her in reſt, and waſh her ſtains away. Exeunt.

div.stage: Banquet, Enter King, Calianax. Hoboyes play within.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I cannot tell how I ſhould credit this
From you that are his enemy.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am ſure he ſaid it to me, and I'le juſtifie it
What way he dares oppoſe, but with my ſword.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: But did he break without all circumſtance
To you his foe, that he would have the Fort
To kill me, and then eſcape?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: If he deny it, I'le make him bluſh.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: It ſounds incredibly.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I, ſo does every thing I ſay of late.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Not ſo Calianax.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Yes, I ſhould fit
Mute, whilſt a Rogue with ſtrong arms cuts your throat.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Well, I will try him, and if this be true
I'le pawn my life I'le find it; if 't be falſe,
And that you clothe your hate in ſuch a lie,
You ſhall hereafter doat in your own houſe, not in the Court.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why if it be a lie,
Mine ears are falſe; for I'le be ſworn I heard it:
Old men are good for nothing; you were beſt
Put me to death for hearing, and free him
For meaning of it; you would ha' truſted me
Once, but the time is altered.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: And will ſtill where I may do with juſtice to the world;
You have no witneſs.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Yes, my ſelf.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No more I mean there were that heard it.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: How no more? would you have more? why am
Not I enough to hang a thouſand Rogues?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: But ſo you may hang honeſt men too if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I may, 'tis like I will do ſo; there are a hundred will ſwear it for a need too, if I ſay it.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Such witneſſes we need not.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: And 'tis hard if my Word cannot hang a boyſterous knave.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Enough; where's Strato?

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.l: Sir!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Why where's all the company? call Amintor in.
Evadne, where's my Brother, and Melantius?
Bid him come too, and Diphilus; call all Exit Strato.
That are without there: if he ſhould deſire
The combat of you, 'tis not in the power
Of all our Laws to hinder it, unleſs we mean to quit 'em.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why if you do think
'Tis ſit an old Man and a Counſellor,
To ſight for what he ſayes, then you may grant it.

div.stage: Enter Amin. Evad. Mel. Diph. Lipſi. Cle. Stra. Diag.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Come Sirs, Amintor thou art yet a Bridegroom,
And I will uſe thee ſo: thou ſhalt ſit down;
Evadne ſit, and you Amintor too;
This Banquet is for you, ſir: Who has brought
A merry Tale about him, to raiſe a laughter
Amongſt our wine? why Strato, where art thou?
Thou wilt chop out with them unſeaſonably
When I deſire 'em not.

sp.speaker: Strato.
sp.l: 'Tis my ill luck Sir, ſo to ſpend them then.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Reach me a boul of wine: Melantius, thou art ſad.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I ſhould be Sir the merrieſt here,
But I ha' ne're a ſtory of mine own
Worth telling at this time.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Give me the Wine.
Melantius, I am now conſidering
How eaſie 'twere for any man we truſt
To poyſon one of us in ſuch a boul.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I think it were not hard Sir, for a Knave.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Such as you are.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I' faith 'twere eaſie, it becomes us well
To get plain dealing men about our ſelves,
Such as you all are here: Amintor, to thee
And to thy fair Evadne.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Have you thought of this Calianax? Aſide.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Yes marry have I.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: And what's your reſolution?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have it ſoundly?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Reach to Amintor, Strato.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Here my love,
This Wine will do thee wrong, for it will ſet
Bluſhes upon thy cheeks, and till thou doſt a fault, 'twere pity.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Yet I wonder much
Of the ſtrange deſperation of theſe men,
That dare attempt ſuch acts here in our State;
He could not eſcape that did it.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Were he known, unpoſſible.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: It would be known, Melantius.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: It ought to be, if he got then away
He muſt wear all our lives upon his ſword,
He need not fly the Iſland, he muſt leave no one alive.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No, I ſhould think no man
Could kill me and ſcape clear, but that old man.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: But I! heaven bleſs me: I, ſhould I my Liege?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I do not think thou wouldſt, but yet thou might'ſt,
For thou haſt in thy hands the means to ſcape,
By keeping of the Fort; he has, Melantius, and he has kept it well.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: From cobwebs Sir,
'Tis clean ſwept: I can find no other Art
In keeping of it now, 'twas ne're beſieg'd ſince he commanded.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I ſhall be ſure of your good word,
But I have kept it ſafe from ſuch as you.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Keep your ill temper in,
I ſpeak no malice; had my brother kept it I ſhould ha' ſaid as much.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: You are not merry, brother; drink wine,
Sit you all ſtill! Calianax, Aſide.
I cannot truſt thus: I have thrown out words
That would have fetcht warm blood upon the cheeks
Of guilty men, and he is never mov'd, he knows no ſuch thing.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Impudence may ſcape, when feeble vertue is accus'd.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: He muſt, if he were guilty, feel an alteration
At this our whiſper, whilſt we point at him,
You ſee he does not.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Let him hang himſelf,
What care I what he does; this he did ſay.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Melantius, you cannot eaſily conceive
What I have meant; for men that are in fault
Can ſubtly apprehend when others aime
At what they do amiſs; but I forgive
Freely before this man; heaven do ſo too:
I will not touch thee ſo much as with ſhame
Of telling it, let it be ſo no more.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why this is very ſine.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I cannot tell
What 'tis you mean, but I am apt enough
Rudely to thruſt into ignorant fault,
But let me know it; happily 'tis nought
But miſconſtruction, and where I am clear
I will not take forgiveneſs of the gods, much leſs of you.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Nay if you ſtand ſo ſtiff, I ſhall call back my mercy.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I want ſmoothneſs
To thank a man for pardoning of a crime I never knew.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Not to inſtruct your knowledge, but to ſhew you my ears are every where, you meant to kill me, and get the Fort to ſcape.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Pardon me Sir; my bluntneſs will be pardoned:
You preſerve
A race of idle people here about you,
Eaters, and talkers, to defame the worth
Of thoſe that do things worthy; the man that uttered this
Had pe •• ſht without food, be't who it will,
But for •• is arm that ſene't him from the ſoe.
And if I thought you gave a faith to this,
The plainneſs of my nature would ſpeak more;
• ive me a pardon (for you ought to do't)
To kill him that ſpake this.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I, that will be the end of all,
Then I am fairly paid for all my care and ſervice.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: That old man who calls me enemy, and of whom I
(Though I will never match my hate ſo low)
Have no good thought, would yet I think excuſe me,
And ſwear he thought me wrong'd in this.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Who I, thou ſhameleſs fellow! didſt thou not ſpeak to me of it thy ſelf?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: O then it came from him.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: From me! who ſhould it come from but from me?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Nay, I believe your malice is enough,
But I ha' loſt my anger. Sir, I hope you are well ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Liſip. Chear Amintor and his Lady; there's no ſound
Comes from you; I will come and do't my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: You have done already Sir for me, I thank you.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Melantius, I do credit this from him,
How ſlight ſo e're you mak't.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange you ſhould.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange he ſhould believe an old mans word,
That never lied in his life.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I talk not to thee;
Shall the wild words of this diſtempered man,
Frantick with age and ſorrow, make a breach
Betwixt your Majeſty and me? 'twas wrong
To hearken to him; but to credit him
As much, at leaſt, as I have power to bear.
But pardon me, whilſt I ſpeak only truth,
I may commend my ſelf—I have beſtow'd
My careleſs blood with you, and ſhould be loth
To think an action that would make me loſe
That, and my thanks too: when I was a boy,
I thruſt my ſelf into my Countries cauſe,
And did a deed that pluckt five years from time,
And ſtil'd me man then: And for you my King,
Your ſubjects all have fed by vertue of my arm.
This ſword of mine hath plow'd the ground,
And reapt the fruit in peace;
And your ſelf have liv'd at home in eaſe:
So terrible I grew, that without ſwords
My name hath fetcht you conqueſt, and my heart
And limbs are ſtill the ſame; my will is great
To do you ſervice: let me not be paid
With ſuch a ſtrange diſtruſt.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Melantius, I held it great injuſtice to believe
Thine Enemy, and did not; if I did,
I do not, let that ſatisfie: what ſtruck
With ſadneſs all? More Wine!

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: A few fine words have overthrown my truth:
Ah th'art a Villain.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Why thou wert better let me have the Fort,
Dotard, I will diſgrace thee thus for ever; Aſide.
There ſhall no credit lie upon thy words;
Think better and deliver it.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: My Liege, he's at me now agen to do it; ſpeak,
Deny it if thou canſt; examine him
Whilſt he's hot, for he'l cool agen, he will forſwear it.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: This is lunacy I hope, Melantius.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: He hath loſt himſelf
Much ſince his Daughter miſt the happineſs
My Siſter gain'd; and though he call me Foe, I pity him.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Pity! a pox upon you.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Mark his diſordered words, and at the Mask.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Diagoras knows he raged, and rail'd at me,
And cal'd a Lady Whore, ſo innocent
She underſtood him not; but it becomes
Both you and me too, to forgive diſtraction,
Pardon him as I do.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.p: I'le not ſpeak for thee, for all thy cunning, if you will be ſafe chop off his head, for there was never known ſo impudent a Raſcal.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Some that love him, get him to bed: Why, pity ſhould not let age make it ſelf contemptible; we muſt be all old, have him away.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Calianax, the King believes you; come, you ſhall go
Home, and reſt; you ha' done well; you'l give it up
When I have us'd you thus a moneth I hope.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Now, now, 'tis plain Sir, he does move me ſtill;
He ſayes he knows I'le give him up the Fort,
When he had us'd me thus a moneth: I am mad,
Am I not ſtill?

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I ſhall be mad indeed, if you do thus;
Why would you truſt a ſturdy fellow there
(That has no vertue in him, all's in his ſword)
Before me? do but take his weapons from him,
And he's an Aſs, and I am a very fool,
Both with him, and without him, as you uſe me.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: 'Tis well Calianax; but if you uſe
This once again, I ſhall intreat ſome other
To ſee your Offices be well diſcharg'd.
Be merry Gentlemen, it grows ſomewhat late.
Amintor, thou wouldeſt be abed again.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: And you Evadne; let me take thee in my arms, Melantius, and believe thou art as thou deſerveſt to be, my friend ſtill, and for ever. Good Calianax,
sp.l: Sleep ſoundly, it will bring thee to thy ſelf.

div.stage: Exeunt omnes. Manent Mel. and Cal.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Sleep ſoundly! I ſleep ſoundly now I hope,
I could not be thus elſe. How dar'ſt thou ſtay
Alone with me, knowing how thou haſt uſed me?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: You cannot blaſt me with your tongue,
And that's the ſtrongeſt part you have about you.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I do look for ſome great puniſhment for this,
For I begin to forget all my hate,
And tak't unkindly that mine enemy
Should uſe me ſo extraordinarily ſcurvily.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I ſhall melt too, if you begin to take
Unkindneſſes: I never meant you hurt.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Thou'lt anger me again; thou wretched rogue,
Meant me no hurt! diſgrace me with the King;
Loſe all my Offices! this is no hurt.
Is it? I prethee what doſt thou call hurt?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: To poyſon men becauſe they love me not;
To call the credit of mens Wives in queſtion;
To murder children betwixt me and land; this is all hurt.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: All this thou think'ſt is ſport;
For mine is worſe: but uſe thy will with me;
For betwixt grief and anger I could cry.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Be wiſe then, and be ſafe; thou may'ſt revenge.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I o'th'King? I would revenge of thee.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: That you muſt plot your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am a fine plotter.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: The ſhort is, I will hold thee with the King
In this perplexity, till peeviſhneſs
And thy diſgrace have laid thee in thy grave:
But if thou wilt deliver up the Fort,
I'le take thy trembling body in my arms,
And bear thee over dangers; thou ſhalt hold thy wonted ſtate.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: If I ſhould tell the King, can'ſt thou deny't again?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Try and believe.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Nay then, thou can'ſt bring any thing about:
Thou ſhalt have the Fort.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Why well, here let our hate be buried, and
This hand ſhall right us both; give me thy aged breaſt to compaſs.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Nay, I do not love thee yet
I cannot well endure to look on thee:
And if I thought it were a courteſie,
Thou ſhould'ſt not have it: but I am diſgrac'd;
My Offices are to be ta'ne away;
And if I did but hold this Fort a day,
I do believe the King would take it from me,
And give it thee, things are ſo ſtrangely carried;
Nere thank me for't; but yet the King ſhall know
There was ſome ſuch thing in't I told him of;
And that I was an honeſt man.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Hee'l buy that knowledge very dearly.
What news with thee?

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: This were a night indeed to do it in;
The King hath ſent for her.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: She ſhall perform it then; go Diphilus,
And take from this good man, my worthy friend,
The Fort; he'l give it thee.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: Ha' you got that?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Art thou of the ſame breed? canſt thou deny
This to the King too?

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: With a confidence as great as his.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Faith, like enough.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Away, and uſe him kindly.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.p: Touch not me, I hate the whole ſtrain: if thou follow me a great way off, I'le give thee up the Fort; and hang your ſelves.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Be gone.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: He's finely wrought. Exeunt Cal. Diph.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: This is a night in ſpite of Aſtronomers
To do the deed in; I will waſh the ſlain
That teſts upon our Houſe, off with his blood.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Melantius, now aſſiſt me if thou beeſt
That which thou ſay'ſt, aſſiſt me: I have loſt
All my diſtempers, and have found a rage ſo pleaſing; help me.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Who can ſee him thus,
And not ſwear vengeance? what's the matter friend?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Out with thy ſword; and hand in hand with me
Ruſh to the Chamber of this hated King,
And ſink him with the weight of all his ſins to hell for ever.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: 'Twere a • aſh attempt,
Not to be done with ſafety: let your reaſon
Plot your revenge, and not your paſſion.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: If thou refuſeſt me in theſe extreams,
Thou art no friend: he ſent for her to me;
By Heaven to me; my ſelf; and I muſt tell ye
I love her as a ſtranger; there is worth
In that vile woman, worthy things, Melantius;
And ſhe repents. I'le do't my ſelf alone,
Though I be ſlain. Farewell.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: He'l overthrow my whole deſign with madneſs:
Amintor, think what thou doeſt; I dare as much as valour;
But 'tis the King, the King, the King, Amintor,
With whom thou fighteſt; I know he's honeſt, Aſide.
And this will work with him.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I cannot tell
What thou haſt ſaid; but thou haſt charm'd my ſword
Out of my hand, and left me ſhaking here defenceleſs.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I will take it up for thee.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: What a wild beaſt is uncollected man!
The thing that we call Honour, bears us all
Headlong unto ſin, and yet it ſelf is nothing.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Alas, how variable are thy thoughts!

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Juſt like my fortunes: I was run to that
I purpos'd to have chid thee for.
Some Plot I did diſtruſt thou hadſt againſt the King
By that old fellows carriage: but take heed,
There is not the leaſt limb growing to a King,
But carries thunder in it.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I have none againſt him.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Why? come then, and ſtill remember we may not think revenge.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I will remember.

div.head: Actus Quintus.

sp.speaker: EVAD.
sp.l: Sir, is the King abed?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Madam, an hour ago.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Give me the key then, and let none be near;
'Tis the Kings pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I underſtand you Madam, would 'twere mine.
I muſt not wiſh good reſt unto your Ladiſhip.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: You talk, you talk.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis all I dare do, Madam; but the King will wake, and then.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Saving your imagination, pray good night Sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: A good night be it then, and a long one Madam;
I am gone.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: The night grows horrible, and all about me
Like my black purpoſe: O the Conſcience King abed.
Of a loſt Virgin; whither wilt thou pull me?
To what things diſmal, as the depth of Hell,
Wilt thou provoke me? Let no man dare
From this hour be diſloyal: if her heart
Be fleſh, if ſhe have blood, and can fear, 'tis a daring
Above that deſperate fool that left his peace,
And went to Sea to fight: 'tis ſo many ſins
An age cannot prevent 'em: and ſo great,
The gods want mercy for: yet I muſt through 'em.
I have begun a ſlaughter on my honour,
And I muſt end it there: he ſleeps, good heavens!
Why give you peace to this untemperate beaſt
That hath ſo long tranſgreſſed you? I muſt kill him,
And I will do't bravely: the meer joy
Tells me I merit in it: yet I muſt not
Thus tamely do it as he ſleeps: that were
To rock him to another world: my vengeance
Shall take him waking, and then lay before him
The number of his wrongs and puniſhments.
I'le ſhake his ſins like furies, till I waken
His evil Angel, his ſick Conſcience:
And then I'le ſtrike him dead: King, by your leave: Ties his armes to the bed.
I dare not truſt your ſtrength: your Grace and I
Muſt grapple upon even terms no more:
So, if he rail me not from my reſolution,
I ſhall be ſtrong enough.
My Lord the King, my Lord; he ſleeps
As if he meant to wake no more, my Lord;
Is he not dead already? Sir, my Lord.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: O you ſleep ſoundly Sir!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: My dear Evadne,
I have been dreaming of thee; come to bed.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I am come at length Sir, but how welcome?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What pretty new device is this Evadne?
What do you tie me to you by my love?
This is a quaint one: Come my dear and kiſs me;
I'le be thy Mars to bed my Queen of Love:
Let us be caught together, that the Gods may ſee,
And envy our embraces.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Stay Sir, ſtay,
You are too hot, and I have brought you Phyſick
To temper your high veins.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Prethee to bed then; let me take it warm,
There you ſhall know the ſtate of my body better.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I know you have a ſurfeited ſoul body,
And you muſt bleed.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Bleed!

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I, you ſhall bleed: lie ſtill, and if the Devil,
Your luſt will give you leave, repent: this ſteel
Comes to redeem the honour that you ſtole,
King, my fair name, which nothing but thy death
Can anſwer to the world.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How's this Evadne?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I am not ſhe: nor bear I in this breaſt
So much cold Spirit to be call'd a Woman:
I am a Tyger: I am any thing
That knows not pity: ſtir not, if thou doſt,
I'le take thee unprepar'd; thy fears upon thee,
That make thy ſins look double, and ſo ſend thee
(By my revenge I will) to look thoſe torments
Prepar'd for ſuch black ſouls.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Thou doſt not mean this; 'tis impoſſible:
Thou art too ſweet and gentle.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: No, I am not:
I am as foul as thou art, and can number
As many ſuch hells here: I was once fair,
Once I was lovely, not a blowing Roſe
More chaſtly ſweet, till thou, thou, thou, ſoul Canker,
(Stir not) didſt poyſon me: I was a world of vertue,
Till your curſt Court and you (hell bleſs you ſor't)
With your temptations on temptations
Made me give up mine honour; for which (King)
I am come to kill thee.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I am.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Thou art not.
I prethee ſpeak not theſe things; thou art gentle,
And wert not meant thus rugged.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Peace and hear me.
Stir nothing but your tongue, and that for mercy
To thoſe above us; by whoſe lights I vow,
Thoſe bleſſed fires that ſhot to ſee our ſin,
If thy hot ſoul had ſubſtance with thy blood,
I would kill that too, which being paſt my ſteel,
My tongue ſhall • each: Thou art a ſhameleſs Villain,
A thing out of the overchange of Nature;
Sent like a thick cloud to diſperſe a plague
Upon weak catching women; ſuch a tyrant
That for his Luſt would ſell away his Subjects,
I, all his heaven hereafter.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Hear Evadne,
Thou ſoul of ſweetneſs! hear, I am thy King.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Thou art my ſhame; lie ſtill, there's none about you,
Within your cries; all promiſes of ſafety
Are but deluding dreams: thus, thus, thou ſoul man,
Thus I begin my vengeance. Stabs him.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Hold Evadne!
I do command thee hold.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: I do not mean Sir,
To part ſo fairly with you; we muſt change
More of theſe love-tricks yet.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What bloody villain
Provok't thee to this murther?

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Thou, thou monſter.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Thou kept'ſt me brave at Court, and Whor'd me;
Then married me to a young noble Gentleman;
And Whor'd me ſtill.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Evadne, pity me.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Hell take me then; this for my Lord Amintor;
This for my noble brother: and this ſtroke
For the moſt wrong'd of women. Kills him.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Oh! I die.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Die all our faults together; I forgive thee. Exit.
Come now ſhe's gone, let's enter, the King expects it, and will be angry.
'Tis a fine wench, we'l have a ſnap at her one of theſe nights as ſhe goes from him.
Content: how quickly he had done with her! I ſee
Kings can do no more that way than other mortal people.
How faſt he is! I cannot hear him breathe.
Either the Tapers give a feeble light, or he looks very pale.
And ſo he does, pray Heaven he be well.
Let's look: Alas! he's ſtiffe, wounded and dead:
Treaſon, Treaſon!
Run forth and call. Exit Gent.
Treaſon, Treaſon!
This will be laid on us: who can believe
A Woman could do this?

sp.speaker: Cleon.
sp.l: How now, where's the Traytor?
Fled, fled away; but there her woful act lies ſtill.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Her act! a Woman!

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Where's the body?
There.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Farewel thou worthy man; there were two bonds
That tyed our loves, a Brother and a King;
The leaſt of which might fetch a ſtood of tears:
But ſuch the miſery of greatneſs is,
They have no time to mourn; then pardon me.

Sirs, which way went ſhe?
〈…〉 .

sp.speaker: Strat.
sp.l: Never follow her,
For ſhe alas! was but the inſtrument.
News is now brought in, that Melantius
Has got the Fort, and ſtands upon the wall;
And with a loud voice calls thoſe few that paſs
At this dead time of night, delivering
The innocent of this act.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Gentlemen, I am your King.

sp.speaker: Strat.
sp.l: We do acknowledge it.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I would I were not: follow all; for this muſt have a ſudden ſtop. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Melant. Diph. and Cal. on the wall.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: If the dull people can believe I am arm'd,
Be conſtant Diphilus; now we have time,
Either to bring our baniſht honours home,
Or create new ones in our ends.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: I fear not;
My ſpirit lies not that way. Courage Calianax.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Would I had any, you ſhould quickly know it.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Speak to the people; thou art eloquent.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: You were born to be my end; the Devil take you.
Now muſt I hang for company; 'tis ſtrange
I ſhould be old, and neither wiſe nor valiant.

div.stage: Enter Liſip. Diag. Cleon, Strat. Guard.

sp.speaker: Liſip.
sp.l: See where he ſtands as boldly confident,
As if he had his full command about him.

sp.speaker: Strat.
sp.l: He looks as if he had the beter cauſe; Sir,
•• der your gracious pardon let me ſpeak it;
• hough he be mighty-ſpirited and forward
To all great things; to all things of that danger
Worſe men ſhake at the telling of; yet certainly
I do believe him noble, and this action
Rather pull'd on than ſought; his mind was ever
As worthy as his hand.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: 'Tis my fear too;
Heaven forgive all: ſummon him Lord Cleon.

sp.speaker: Cleon.
sp.l: Ho from the walls there.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Worthy Cleon, welcome;
We could have wiſht you here Lord; you are honeſt.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.p: Well, thou art as flattering a knave, though I dare not tell you ſo. Aſide.

l.hi: Melantius!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I am ſorry that we meet thus; our old love
Never requir'd ſuch diſtance; pray Heaven
You have not left your ſelf, and ſought this ſafety
More out of fear than honour; you have loſt
A noble Maſter, which your faith Melantius,
Some think might have preſerv'd; yet you know beſt.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: When time was I was mad; ſome that dares
Fight I hope will pay this Raſcal.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Royal young man, whoſe tears look lovely on thee;
Had they been ſhed for a deſerving one,
They had been laſting monuments. Thy Brother,
Whil'ſt he was good, I call'd him King, and ſerv'd him
With that ſtrong faith, that moſt unwearied valour;
Pul'd people from the fartheſt Sun to ſeek him;
And by his friendſhip, I was then his ſouldier;
But ſince his hot pride drew him to diſgrace me,
And brand my noble actions with his luſt,
(That never cur'd diſhonour of my Siſter,
Baſe ſtain of Whore; and which is worſe,
The joy to make it ſtill ſo) like my ſelf;
Thus have I ſlung him off with my allegiance,
And ſtand here mine own juſtice to revenge
What I have ſuffered in him; and this old man
Wrong'd almoſt to lunacy.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Who I? you'd draw me in: I have had no wrong,
I do diſclaim ye all.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: The ſhort is this;
'Tis no ambition to lift up my ſelf,
Urgeth me thus; I do deſire again
To be a ſubject, ſo I may be freed;
If not, I know my ſtrength, and will unbuild
This goodly Town; be ſpeedy, and be wiſe, in a reply.

sp.speaker: Strat.
sp.l: Be ſudden Sir to tie
All again; what's done is paſt recal,
And paſt you to revenge; and there are thouſands
That wait for ſuch a troubled hour as this;
Throw him the blank.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Melantius, write in that thy choice,
My Seal is at it.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: It was our honour drew us to this act,
Not gain; and we will only work our pardon.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Put my name in too.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: You diſclaim'd us but now, Calianax.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: That's all one;
I'le not be hanged hereafter by a trick;
I'le have it in.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: You ſhall, you ſhall;
Come to the back gate, and we'l call you King,
And give you up the Fort.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Away, away. Exeunt Omnes.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: This is my fatal hour; heaven may forgive
My • aſh attempt, that cauſeleſly hath laid
Griefs on me that will never let me reſt:
And put a Womans heart into my breſt;
It is more honour for you that I die;
For ſhe that can endure the miſery
That I have on me, and be patient too,
May live, and laugh at all that you can do.
God ſave you Sir. Enter Servant.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: And you Sir; what's your buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: With you Sir now, to do me the Office
To help me to you Lord.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: What, would you ſerve him?

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: I'le do him any ſervice; but to haſte,
For my affairs are earneſt, I deſire to ſpeak with him.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Sir, becauſe you are in ſuch haſte, I would be loth delay you any longer: you cannot.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: It ſhall become you tho' to tell your Lord.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sir, he will ſpeak with no body.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.p: This is moſt ſtrange: art thou gold proof? there's for thee; help me to him.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Pray be not angry Sir, I'le do my beſt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: How ſtubbornly this fellow anſwer'd me!
There is a vile diſhoneſt trick in man,
More than in women: all the men I meet
Appear thus to me, are harſh and rude,
And have a ſubtilty in every thing,
Which love could never know; but we fond women
Harbor the eaſieſt and ſmootheſt thoughts,
And think all ſhall go ſo; it is unjuſt
That men and women ſhould be matcht together.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Where is he!

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: There my Lord.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: What would you Sir?

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: Pleaſe it your Lordſhip to command your man
Out of the room; I ſhall deliver things
Worthy your hearing.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Leave us.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: O that that ſhape ſhould bury falſhood in it. Aſide.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Now your will Sir.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: When you know me, my Lord, you needs muſt gueſs
My buſineſs! and I am not hard to know;
For till the change of War mark'd this ſmooth face
With theſe few blemiſhes, people would call me
My Siſters Picture, and her mine; in ſhort,
I am the brother to the wrong'd Aſpatia.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: The wrong'd Aſpatia! would thou wert ſo too
Unto the wrong'd Amintor; let me kiſs
That hand of thine in honour that I bear
Unto the wrong'd Aſpatia: here I ſtand
That did it; would he could not; gentle youth,
Leave me, for there is ſomething in thy looks
That calls my ſins in a moſt hideous form
Into my mind; and I have grief enough
Without thy help.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: I would I could with credit:
Since I was twelve years old I had not ſeen
My Siſter till this hour; I now arriv'd;
She ſent for me to ſee her Marriage,
A woſul one: but they that are above,
Have ends in every thing; ſhe us'd few words,
But yet enough to make me underſtand
The baſeneſs of the injury you did her;
That little training I have had, is War;
I may behave my ſelf rudely in Peace;
I would not though; I ſhall not need to tell you
I am but young; and you would be loth to loſe
Honour that is not eaſily gain'd again;
Fairly I mean to deal; the age is ſtrict
For ſingle combats, and we ſhall be ſtopt
If it be publiſh't: if you like your ſword,
Uſe it; if mine appear a better to you,
Change; for the ground is this, and this the time
To end our difference.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Charitable youth,
If thou be'ſt ſuch, think not I will maintain
So ſtrange a wrong; and for thy Siſters ſake,
Know that I could not think that deſperate thing
〈◊〉 durſt not do; yet to enjoy this world
〈◊〉 would not ſee her; for beholding thee,
〈◊〉 am I know not what; if I have ought
• hat may content thee, take it and be gone;
For death is not ſo terrible as thou;
Thine eyes ſhoot guilt into me.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: Thus ſhe ſwore
Thou would'ſt behave thy ſelf, and give me words
That would fetch tears into mine eyes, and ſo
Thou doſt indeed; but yet ſhe bade me watch,
Leſt I were corſen'd, and be ſure to ſight ere I return'd.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: That muſt not be with me;
For her I'le die directly, but againſt her will never hazard it.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: You muſt be urg'd; I do not deal uncivilly with thoſe that
Dare to fight; but ſuch a one as you
Muſt be us'd thus. She ſtrikes him.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Prethee youth take heed;
Thy Siſter is a thing to me ſo much
Above mine honour, that I can endute
All this; good gods— a blow I can endure;
