But ſtay not, leſt thou draw a timely death upon thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: Thou art ſome prating fellow,
One that hath ſtudyed out a trick to talk
And move ſoft-hearted people; to be kickt, She kicks him.
Thus to be kickt— why ſhould he be ſo ſlow Aſide.
In giving me my death?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: A man can bear
No more and keep his fleſh; forgive me then;
I would endure yet if I could; now ſhew
The ſpirit thou pretendeſt, and underſtand
Thou haſt no honour to live: They ſight.
What doſt thou mean? thou canſt not fight:
The blows thou mak'ſt at me are quite beſides;
And thoſe I offer at thee, thou ſpread'ſt thine arms,
And tak'ſt upon thy breaſt, Alas! defenceleſs.

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: I have got enough,
And my deſire; there's no place ſo fit for me to die as here.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Amintor; I am loaden with events
That flie to make thee happy; I have joyes Her hands bloody with a knife.
That in a moment can call back thy wrongs,
And ſettle thee in thy free ſtate again;
It is Evadne ſtill that follows thee, but not her miſchiefs.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Thou canſt not fool me to believe agen;
But thou haſt looks and things ſo full of news that I am ſtaid.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Noble Amintor, put off thy amaze;
Let thine eyes looſe, and ſpeak, am I not fair?
Looks not Evadne beauteous with theſe rites now?
Were thoſe hours half ſo lovely in thine eyes,
When our hands met before the holy man?
I was too foul within to look fair then;
Since I knew ill, I was not free till now.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: There is preſage of ſome important thing
About thee, which it ſeems thy tongue hath loſt:
Thy hands are bloody, and thou haſt a knife.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: In this conſiſts thy happineſs and mine;
Joy to Amintor, for the King is dead.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Thoſe have moſt power to hurt us that we love,
We lay our ſleeping lives within their arms.
Why thou haſt rais'd up miſchief to this height,
And found out one to out-name thy other faults;
Thou haſt no intermiſſion of thy ſins,
But all thy life is a continuall ill;
Black is thy colour now, diſeaſe thy nature.
Joy to Amintor! thou haſt touch't a life,
The very name of which had power to chain
Up all my rage, and calm my wildeſt wrongs.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: 'Tis done; and ſince I could not find a way
To meet thy love ſo clear, as through his life,
I cannot now repent it.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Could'ſt thou procure the Gods to ſpeak to me,
To bid me love this woman, and forgive,
I think I ſhould fall out with them; behold
Here lies a youth whoſe wounds bleed in my breſt,
Sent by his violent Fate to fetch his death
From my ſlow hand: and to augment my woe,
You now are preſent ſtain'd with a Kings blood
Violently ſhed: this keeps night here,
And throws an unknown wilderneſs about me.

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: Oh, oh, oh!

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: No more, purſue me not.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Forgive me then, and take me to thy bed.
We may not part.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Forbear, be wiſe, and let my rage go this way.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: 'Tis you that I would ſtay, not it.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Take heed, it will return with me.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: If it muſt be, I ſhall not fear to meet it; take me home.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Thou monſter of cruelty, forbear.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: For heavens ſake look more calm;
Thine eyes are ſharper than thou canſt m ••• thy ſword.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Away, away, thy knees are more to me than violence.
I am worſe than ſick to ſee knees follow me
For that I muſt not grant; for heavens ſake ſtand.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Receive me then.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I dare not ſtay thy language;
In midſt of all my anger and my grief,
Thou doſt awake ſomething that troubles me,
And ſayes I lov'd thee once; I dare not ſtay;
There is no end of womens reaſoning. Leaves her.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Amintor, thou ſhalt love me once again;
Go, I am calm; farewell; and peace for ever.
Evadne whom thou hat'ſt will die for thee. Kills her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I have a little humane nature yet
That's leſt for thee, that bids me ſtay thy hand. Returns.

sp.speaker: Evad.
sp.l: Thy hand was welcome, but came too late;
Oh I am loſt! the heavy ſleep makes haſte. She dies.

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: Oh, oh, oh!

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: This earth of mine doth tremble, and I feel
A ſtark affrighted motion in my blood;
My ſoul grows weary of her houſe, and I
All over am a trouble to my ſelf;
There is ſome hidden power in theſe dead things
That calls my fleſh into'em; I am cold;
Be reſolute, and bear'em company:
There's ſomething yet which I am loth to leave.
There's man enough in me to meet the fears
That death can bring, and yet would it were done;
I can find nothing in the whole diſcourſe
Of death, I durſt not meet the boldeſt way;
Yet ſtill betwixt the reaſon and the act,
The wrong I to Aspatia did ſtands up,
I have not ſuch a fault to anſwer,
Though ſhe may juſtly arm with ſcorn
And hate of me, my ſoul will part leſs troubled,
When I have paid to her in tears my ſorrow:
I will not leave this act unſatisfied,
If all that's left in me can anſwer it.

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: Was it a dream? there ſtands Amintor ſtill:
Or I dream ſtill.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: How doſt thou? ſpeak, receive my love, and help:
Thy blood climbs up to his old place again:
There's hope of thy recovery.

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: Did you not name Aspatia?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I did.

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: And talkt of tears and ſorrow unto her?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: 'Tis true, and till theſe happy ſigns in thee
Did ſtay my courſe, 'twas thither I was going.

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: Th'art there already, and theſe wounds are hers:
Thoſe threats I brought with me, ſought not revenge,
But came to fetch this bleſſing from thy hand, I am Aspatia yet.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Dare my ſoul ever look abroad agen?

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: I ſhall live Amintor; I am well:
A kind of healthful joy wanders within me.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: The world wants lines to excuſe thy loſs:
Come let me bear thee to ſome place of help.

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: Amintor thou muſt ſtay, I muſt reſt here,
My ſtrength begins to diſobey my will.
How doſt thou my beſt ſoul? I would fain live,
Now if I could: would'ſt thou have loved me then?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Alas! all that I am's not worth a hair from thee.

sp.speaker: Aſp.
sp.l: Give me thy hand, mine hands grope up and down,
And cannot find thee; I am wondrous ſick:
Have I thy hand Amintor?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Thou greateſt bleſſing of the world, thou haſt.

sp.speaker: Asp.
sp.l: I do believe thee better than my ſenſe.
Oh! I muſt go, farewell.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: She ſwounds: Aſpatia help, for Heavens ſake water;
Such as may chain life for ever to this frame.
Aspatia, ſpeak: what no help? yet I fool,
I'le chaſe her temples, yet there's nothing ſtirs;
Some hidden Power tell her that Amintor calls,
A •• let her anſwer me: Aſpatia, ſpeak.
I ha • e heard, if there be life, but bow
The body thus, and it will ſhew it ſelf.
Oh ſhe is gone! I will not leave her yet.
Since out of juſtice we muſt challenge nothing;
I'le call it mercy if you'l pity me,
You heavenly powers, and lend for ſome few years,
The bleſſed ſoul to this fair ſeat agen.
No comfort comes, the gods deny me too.
I'le bow the body once agen: Aſpatia!
The ſoul is fled for ever, and I wrong
My ſelf, ſo long to loſe her company.
Muſt I talk now? Here's to be with thee love. Kills himſelf.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: This is a great grace to my Lord, to have the new King come to him; I muſt tell him, he is entring. O Heaven help, help;

div.stage: Enter Lyſip. Melant. Cal. Cleon. Diph. Strato.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: Where's Amintor?

sp.speaker: Sirat.
sp.l: O there, there.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: How ſtrange is this!

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: What ſhould we do here?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Theſe deaths are ſuch acquainted things with me,
That yet my heart diſſolves not. May I ſtand
Stiff here for ever; eyes, call up your tears;
This is Amintor: heart he was my friend;
Melt, now it flows; Amintor, give a word
To call me to thee.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Melantius calls his friend Amintor; Oh thy arms
Are kinder to me than thy tongue;
Speak, ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: That little word was worth all the ſounds
That ever I ſhall hear agen.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: O brother! here lies your Siſter ſlain,
You loſe your ſelf in ſorrow there.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Why Diphilus, it is
A thing to laugh at in reſpect of this;
Here was my Siſter, Father, Brother, Son;
All that I had; ſpeak once again;
What youth lies ſlain there by thee?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: 'Tis Aſpatia.
My ſenſes fade, let me give up my ſoul
Into thy boſom.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: What's that? what's that? Aſpatia!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I never did repent the greatneſs of my heart till now,
It will not burſt at need.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: My daughter dead here too! and you have all fine new tricks to grieve, but I ne're knew any but direct crying.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: I am a pratler, but no more.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: Hold Brother.

sp.speaker: Lyſip.
sp.l: Stop him.

sp.speaker: Diph.
sp.l: Fie; how unmanly was this offer in you!
Does this become our ſtrain?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I know not what the mater is, but I am
Grown very kind, and am friends with you;
You have given me that among you will kill me
Quickly; but I'le go home, and live as long as I can.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: His ſpirit is but poor that can be kept
From death for want of weapons.
Is not my hand a weapon good enough
To ſtop my breath? or if you tie down thoſe,
I vow Amintor I will never eat,
Or drink, or ſleep, or have to do with that
That may preſerve life; this I ſwear to keep.

sp.speaker: Lyſip.
sp.l: Look to him tho', and bear thoſe bodies in.
May this a fair example be to me,
To rule with temper: for on luſtful Kings
Unlookt for ſudden deaths from heaven are ſent!
But curſt is he that is their inſtrument.

div.head: PHILASTER OR, Love lies a Bleeding.

list.item: Galatea, a wiſe modeſt Lady attending the Princeſs.
An old wanton Lady, or Croan.
Eufraſia, Daughter of Dion, but diſguiſed like a Page, and called Bellario.

div.head: Scena prima.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.p: HEre's not Lords nor Ladies.

sp.speaker: Dion.
sp.p: Credit me Gentlemen, I wonder at it. They receiv'd ſtrict charge from the King to attend here: Beſides it was boldly publiſhed, that no Officer ſhould forbid any Gentlemen that deſire to attend and hear.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: Can you gheſs the cauſe?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Sir, it is plain about the Spaniſh Prince, that's come to marry our Kingdoms Heir, and be our Soveraign.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.p: Many (that will ſeem to know much) ſay, ſhe looks not on him like a Maid in Love.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: O Sir, the multitude (that ſeldom know any thing but their own opinions) ſpeak that they would have; but the Prince, before his own approach, receiv'd ſo many confident meſſages from the State, that I think ſhe's reſolv'd to be rul'd.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: Sir, it is thought, with her he ſhall enjoy both theſe Kingdoms of Cicilie and Calabria.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Sir, it is (without controverſie) ſo meant. But 'twill be a troubleſome labour for him to enjoy both theſe Kingdoms, with ſafetie, the right Heir to one of them living, and living ſo vertuouſly, eſpecially the people admiring the bravery of his mind, and lamenting his injuries.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: Who, Philaſter?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Yes, whoſe Father we all know, was by our late King of Calabria, unrighteouſly depoſed from his fruitful Cicilie. My ſelf drew ſome blood in thoſe Wars, which I would give my hand to be waſhed from.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: Sir, my ignorance in State-policy, will not let me know why Philaſter being Heir to one of theſe Kingdoms, the King ſhould ſuffer him to walk abroad with ſuch free liberty.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Sir, it ſeems your nature is more conſtant than to enquire after State news. But the King (of late) made a hazard of both the Kingdoms, of Cicilie and his own, with offering but to impriſon Philaſter. At which the City was in arms, not to be charm'd down by any State order or Proclamation, till they ſaw Philaſter ride through the ſtreets pleas'd, and without a guard; at which they threw their Hats, and their arms from them; ſome to make bonefires, ſome to drink, all for his deliverance. Which (wiſe men ſay) is the cauſe, the King labours to bring in the power of a Foreign Nation, to aw his own with.

div.stage: Enter Galatea, Megra, and a Lady.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.p: See, the Ladies, what's the firſt?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: A wife and modeſt Gentlwoman that attends the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: The ſecond?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: She is one that may ſtand ſtill diſcreetly enough, and ill ſavour'dly Dance her Meaſure; ſimper when ſhe is Courted by her Friend, and ſlight her Husband.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: The laſt?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Marry I think ſhe is one whom the State keeps for the Agents of our confederate Princes: ſhe'll cog and lie with a whole Army before the League ſhall break: her name is common through the Kingdom, and the Trophies of her diſhonour, advanced beyond Hercules-pillars. She loves to try the ſeveral conſtitutions of mens bodies; and indeed has deſtroyed the worth of her own body, by making experiment upon it, for the good of the Common-wealth.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: She's a profitable member.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Peace, if you love me: you ſhall ſee theſe Gentlemen ſtand their ground, and not Court us.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: What if they ſhould?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: What if they ſhould?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p:
Nay, let her alone; what if they ſhould? why, if they ſhould, I ſay, they were never abroad: what Foreigner
would do ſo? it writes them directly untravel'd.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: Why, what if they be?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: What if they be?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Good Madam let her go on; what if they be? Why if they be I will juſtifie, they cannot maintain diſcourſe with a judicious Lady, nor make a Leg, nor ſay Excuſe me.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Do you laugh Madam?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Your deſires upon you Ladies.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Then you muſt ſit beſide us.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: I ſhall ſit near you then Lady.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Near me perhaps: But there's a Lady indures no ſtranger; and to me you appear a very ſtrange fellow.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: Me thinks he's not ſo ſtrange, he would quickly be acquainted.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.p: Peace, the King.

div.stage: Enter King, Pharamond, Arethuſa, and Train.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: To give a ſtranger teſtimony of love
Than fickly promiſes (which commonly
In Princes find both birth and burial
In one breath) we have drawn you worthy Sir,
To make your lair indearments to your daughter,
And worthy ſervices known to our ſubjects,
Now lov'd and wondered at. Next, our intent,
To plant you deeply, our immediate Heir,
Both to our Blood and Kingdoms. For this Lady,
(The beſt part of your life, as you confirm me,
And I believe) though her few years and ſex
Yet teach her nothing but her fears and bluſhes,
Deſires without deſire, diſcourſe and knowledge
Only of what her ſell is to her ſell,
Make her feel moderate health: and when ſhe ſleeps,
In making no ill day, knows no ill dreams.
Think not (dear Sir) theſe undivided parts,
That muſt mould up a Virgin, are put on
To ſhew her ſo, as borrowed ornaments,
To ſpeak her perfect love to you, or add
An Artificial ſhadow to her nature:
No Sir; I boldly dare proclaim her, yet
No Woman. But woo her ſtill, and think her modeſty
A ſweeter miſtreſs than the offer'd Language
Of any Dame, were ſhe a Queen whoſe eye
Speaks common loves and comforts to her ſervants.
Laſt, noble ſon, (for ſo I now muſt call you)
What I have done thus publick, is not only
To add a comfort in particular
To you or me, but all; and to confirm
The Nobles, and the Gentry of theſe Kingdoms,
By oath to your ſucceſſion, which ſhall be
Within this month at moſt.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: This will be hardly done.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: It muſt be ill done, if it be done.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: When 'tis at beſt, 't will be but half done,
Whilſt ſo brave a Gentleman's wrong'd and ſtung off.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: I fear.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Who does not?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I fear not for my ſelf, and yet I fear too:
Well, we ſhall ſee, we ſhall ſee: no more.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Kiſſing your white hand (Miſtreſs) I take leave,
To thank your Royal Father: and thus far,
To be my own free Trumpet. Underſtand
Great King, and theſe your ſubjects, mine that muſt be,
(For ſo deſerving you have ſpoke me Sir,
And ſo deſerving I da • e ſpeak my ſelf)
To what a perſon, of what eminence,
Ripe expectation of what faculties,
Manners and vertues you would wed your Kingdoms?
You in me have your wiſhes. Oh this Country,
By more than all my hopes I hold it
Happy, in their dear memories that have been
Kings great and good, happy in yours, that is,
And from you (as a Chronicle to keep
Your Noble name from eating age) do I
Opine my ſelf moſt happy. Gentlemen,
Believe me in a word, a Princes word,
There ſhall be nothing to make up a Kingdom
Mighty, and flouriſhing, defenced, fear'd,
Equall to be commanded and obey'd,
But through the travels of my life I'le find it,
And tye it to this Country. And I vow
My reign ſhall be ſo eaſie to the ſubject,
That every man ſhall be his Prince himſelf,
And his own law (yet I his Prince and law.)
And deareſt Lady, to your deareſt ſelf
(Dear, in the choice of him, whoſe name and luſtre
Muſt make you more and mightier) let me ſay,
You are the bleſſed'ſt living; for ſweet Princeſs,
You ſhall enjoy a man of men, to be
Your ſervant; you ſhall make him yours, for whom
Great Queens muſt die.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: Miraculous.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: This ſpeech calls him Spaniard, being nothing but
A large inventory of his own commendations.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: I wonder what's his price? For certainly he'll tell himſelf he has ſo prais'd his ſhape: But here comes one more worthy thoſe large ſpeeches, than the large ſpeaker of them? let me be ſwallowed quick, if I can find, in all the Anatomy of yon mans vertues, one ſinew ſound enough to promiſe for him, he ſhall be Conſtable. By this Sun, he'll ne're make King unleſs it be for trifles, in my poor judgment.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Right Noble Sir, as low as my obedience,
And with a heart as Loyal as my knee,
I beg your favour.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Riſe, you have it Sir.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Mark but the King how pale he looks with fear.
Oh! this ſame whorſon Conſcience, how it jades us!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Speak your intents Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Shall I ſpeak 'um freely?
Be ſtill my royal Soveraign.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: As a ſubject
We give you freedom.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Now it heats.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Then thus I turn
My language to you Prince, you foreign man.
Ne're ſtare nor put on wonder, for you muſt
Indure me, and you ſhall. This earth you tread upon
(A dowry as you hope with this fair Princeſs,
Whoſe memory I bow to) was not left
By my dead Father (Oh, I had a Father)
To your inheritance, and I up and living,
Having my ſelf about me and my ſword,
The ſouls of all my name, and memories,
Theſe arms and ſome few friends, beſides the gods,
To part ſo calmly with it, and ſit ſtill,
And ſay I might have been! I tell thee Pharamond,
When thou art King, look I be dead and rotten,
And my name aſhes; For, hear me Pharamond,
This very ground thou goeſt on, this fat earth,
My Fathers friends made fertile with their faiths,
Before that day of ſhame, ſhall gape and ſwallow
Thee and thy Nation, like a hungry grave,
Into her hidden bowels: Prince, it ſhall;
By Nemeſis it ſhall.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: He's mad beyond cure, mad.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Here's a fellow has ſome fire in's veins:
The outlandiſh Prince looks like a Tooth drawer.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Sir, Prince of Popping jayes, I'le make it well appear
To you I am not mad.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: You diſpleaſe us.
You are too bold.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: No Sir, I am too tame,
Too much a Turtle, a thing born without paſſion,
A faint ſhadow, that every drunken cloud ſails over,
And makes nothing.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I do not fancy this,
Call our Phyſicians: ſure he is ſomewhat tainted.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: I do not think 'twill prove ſo.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: H'as given him a general purge already, for all the right he has, and now he means to let him blood: Be conſtant Gentlemen; by theſe hilts I'le run his hazard, although I run my name out of the Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Peace, we are one ſoul.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: What you have ſeen in me, to ſtir offence,
I cannot find, unleſs it be this Lady
Offer'd into mine arms, with the ſucceſſion,
Which I muſt keep though it hath pleas'd your fury
To mutiny within you; without diſputing
Your Genealogies, or taking knowledge
Whoſe branch you are. The King will leave it me;
And I dare make it mine; you have your anſwer.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: If thou wert ſole inheritor to him,
That made the world his; and couldſt ſee no ſun
Shine upon any but thine: were Pharamond
As truly valiant, as I feel him cold,
And ring'd among the choiceſt of his friends,
Such as would bluſh to talk ſuch ſerious follies,
Or back ſuch bellied commendations,
And from this preſent, ſpight of all theſe bugs,
You ſhould hear further from me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Sir, you wrong the Prince:
I gave you not this freedom to brave our beſt friends,
You deſerve our frown: go to, be better temper'd.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: It muſt be Sir, when I am nobler us'd.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: Ladyes,
This would have been a pattern of ſucceſſion,
Had he ne're met this miſchief. By my life,
He is the worthieſt the true name of man
This day within my knowledge.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: I cannot tell what you may call your knowledge,
But the other is the man ſet in mine eye;
Oh! 'tis a Prince of wax.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: A Dog it is.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Philaſter, tell me,
The injuries you aim at in your riddles.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: If you had my eyes Sir, and ſufferance,
My griefs upon you and my broken fortunes,
My want's great, and now nought but hopes and fears,
My wrongs would make ill riddles to be laught at.
Dare you be ſtill my King and right me not?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Give me your wrongs in private. They whiſper.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Take them, and eaſe me of a load would bow ſtrong

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: He dares not ſtand the ſhock. Atlas.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: I cannot blame him, there's danger in't. Every man in this age, has not a ſoul of Cryſtal for all men to read their actions through: mens hearts and faces are ſo far aſunder, that they hold no intelligence. Do but view yon ſtranger well, and you ſhall ſee a Feaver through all his bravery, and feel him ſhake like a true Tenant; if he give not back his Crown again, upon the report of an Elder Gun, I have no augury.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Go to:
Be more your ſelf, as you reſpect our favour:
You'l ſtir us elſe: Sir, I muſt have you know
That y'are and ſhall be at our pleaſure, what faſhion we
Will put upon you: ſmooth your brow, or by the gods.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I am dead Sir, y'are my fate: it was not I
Said I was 〈◊〉 wrong'd: I carry all about me,
My weak ſtars led me to all my weak fortunes.
Who dares in all this preſence ſpeak (that is
But man of fleſh and may be mortal) tell me
I do not moſt intirely love this Prince,
And honour his full vertues!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Sure he's poſſeſt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Yes, with my Fathers ſpirit: It's here O King!
A dangerous ſpirit; now he tells me King,
I was a Kings heir, bids me be a King,
And whiſpers to me, theſe be all my Subjects.
'Tis ſtrange, he will not let me ſleep, but dives
Into my fancy, and there gives me ſhapes
That kneel, and do me ſervice, cry me King:
But I'le ſuppreſs him, he's a factious ſpirit,
And will undo me: noble Sir, • our hand, I am your ſervant.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Away, I do not like this:
I'le make you tamer, or I'le diſpoſſeſs you
Both of life and ſpirit: For this time
I pardon your wild ſpeech, without ſo much

As your impriſonment.
Ex. King, Pha. and Are.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I thank you Sir, you dare not for the people.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: Ladies, what think you now of this brave fellow?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: A pretty talking fellow, hot at hand; but eye yon ſtranger, is not he a fine compleat Gentleman? O theſe ſtrangers, I do affect them ſtrangely: they do the rareſt home things, and pleaſe the fulleſt! as I live, could love all the Nation over and over for his ſake,

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: Pride comfort your poor head-piece Lady: 'tis a weak one, and had need of a Night-cap.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: See how his fancy labours, has he not ſpoke
Home, and bravely? what a dangerous train
Did he give fire to! How he ſhook the King,
Made his ſoul melt within him, and his blood
Run into whay! it ſtood upon his brow,
Like a cold winter dew.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Gentlemen,
You have no ſuit to me? I am no minion:
You ſtand (methinks) like men that would be Courtiers,
If you could well be flatter'd at a price,
Not to undo your Children: y'are all honeſt:
Go get you home again, and make your Country
A vertuous Court, to which your great ones may,
In their Diſeaſed age, retire, and live recluſe.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: How do you worthy Sir?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Well, very well;
And ſo well, that if the King pleaſe, I find
I may live many years.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: The King muſt pleaſe,
Whilſt we know what you are, and who you are,
Your wrongs and juiuries: ſhrink not, worthy Sir,
But add your Father to you: in whoſe name,
We'll waken all the gods, and conjure up
The rods of vengeance, the abuſed people,
Who like to raging torrents ſhall ſwell high,
And ſo begirt the dens of theſe Male-dragons,
That through the ſtrongeſt ſafety, they ſhall beg
For mercy at your ſwords point.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Friends, no more,
Our years may be corrupted: 'Tis an age
We dare not truſt our wills to: do you love me?

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: Do we love Heaven and honour?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: My Lord Dion, you had
A vertuous Gentlewoman, call'd you Father;
Is ſhe yet alive?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Moſt honour'd Sir, ſhe is:
And for the penance but of an idle dream,
Has undertook a tedious Pilgrimage.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Is it to me, or any of theſe Gentlemen you come?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: To you, brave Lord; the Princeſs would intreat
Your preſent company.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: The Princeſs ſend for me! y'are miſtaken.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: If you be call'd Philaſter, 'tis to you.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Kiſs her hand, and ſay I will attend her.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Do you know what you do?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Yes, go to ſee a woman.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: But do you weigh the danger you are in?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Danger in a ſweet face?
By Jupiter I muſt not fear a woman.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: But are you ſure it was the Princeſs ſent?
It may be ſome ſoul train to catch your life.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I do not think it Gentlemen: ſhe's noble,
Her eye may ſhoot me dead, or thoſe true red
And white friends in her face may ſteal my ſoul out:

There's all the danger in't: but be what may,
Ex. Phil.
Her ſingle name hath arm'd me.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Go on:
And be as truly happy as thou art fearleſs:
Come Gentlemen, let's make our friends acquainted,
Leſt the King prove falſe. Ex. Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Comes he not?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Madam?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Will Philaſter come?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Dear Madam, you were wont
To credit me at firſt.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: But didſt thou tell me ſo?
I am forgetful, and my womans ſtrength
Is ſo o'recharg'd with danger like to grow
About my Marriage that theſe under-things
Dare not abide in ſuch a troubled ſea:
How look't he, when he told thee he would come?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Why, well.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: And not a little fearful?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Fear Madam? ſure he knows not what it is.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: You are all of his Faction; the whole Court
Is bold in praiſe of him, whilſt I
May live neglected: and do noble things,
As fools in ſtrife throw gold into the Sea,
Drown'd in the doing: but I know he fears.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Fear? Madam (me thought) his looks hid more
Of love than fear.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Of love? To whom? to you?
Did you deliver thoſe plain words I ſent,
With ſuch a winning geſture, and quick look
That you have caught him?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Madam, I mean to you.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Of love to me? Alas! thy ignorance
Lets thee not ſee the croſſes of our births:
Nature, that loves not to be queſtioned
Why ſhe did this, or that, but has her ends,
And knows ſhe does well; never gave the world
Two things ſo oppoſite, ſo contrary,
As he and I am: If a bowl of blood
Drawn from this arm of mine, would poyſon thee,
A draught of his would cure thee. Of love to me?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Madam, I think I hear him.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Bring him in:
You gods that would not have your dooms withſtood,
Whoſe holy wiſdoms at this time it is,
To make the paſſion of a feeble maid

The way unto your juſtice, I obey.
Enter Phil.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Here is my Lord Philaſter.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Oh! 'tis well:
Withdraw your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Madam, your meſſenger
Made me believe, you wiſht to ſpeak with me.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: 'Tis true Philaſter, but the words are ſuch,
I have to ſay, and do ſo ill beſeem
The mouth of woman, that I wiſh them ſaid,
And yet am loth to ſpeak them. Have you known
That I have ought detracted from your worth?
Have I in perſon wrong'd you? or have ſet
My baſer inſtruments to throw diſgrace
Upon your vertues?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Never Madam you.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Why then ſhould you in ſuch a publick place,
Injure a Princeſs and a ſcandal lay
Upon my fortunes, ſam'd to be ſo great:
Calling a great part of my dowry in queſtion.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Madam, this truth which I ſhall ſpeak, will be
Fooliſh: but for your fair and vertuous ſelf,
I could afford my ſelf to have no right
To any thing you wiſh'd.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Philaſter, know
I muſt enjoy theſe Kingdoms,

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Madam, both?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Both or I die: by Fate I die Philaſter,
If I not calmly may enjoy them both.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I would do much to ſave that Noble life:
Yet would be loth to have poſterity
Find in our ſtories, that Philaſter gave
His right unto a Scepter, and a Crown,
To ſave a Ladies longing.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Nay then hear:
I muſt, and will have them, and more.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What more?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Or loſe that little life the gods prepared,
To trouble this poor piece of earth withall.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Madam, what more?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Turn then away thy face.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Do.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I cannot endure it: turn away my face?
I never yet ſaw enemy that lookt
So dreadful, but that I thought my ſelf
As great a Baſilisk as he; or ſpake
So horribly, but that I thought my tongue
Bore Thunder underneath, as much as his:
Nor beaſt that I could turn from: ſhall I then
Begin to fear ſweet ſounds? a Ladies voice,
Whom I do love? Say you would have my life,
Why, I will give it you; for it is of me
A thing ſo loath'd, and unto you that ask
Of ſo poor uſe, that I ſhall make no price
If you intreat, I will unmov'dly hear.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Yet for my ſake a little bend thy looks.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I do.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Then know I muſt have them and thee.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And me?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Thy love: without which, all the Land
Diſcovered yet, will ſerve me for no uſe,
But to be buried in.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: With it, it were too little to beſtow
On thee: Now, though thy breath doth ſtrike me dead
(Which know it may) I have unript my breaſt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Madam, you are too full of noble thoughts,
To lay a train for this contemned life,
Which you may have for asking: to ſuſpect
Were baſe, where I deſerve no ill: love you!
By all my hopes I do, above my life:
But how this paſſion ſhould proceed from you
So violently, would amaze a man, that would be jealous.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Another ſoul into my body ſhot,
Could not have fill'd me with more ſtrength and ſpirit,
Than this thy breath: but ſpend not haſty time,
In ſeeking how I came thus: 'tis the gods,
The gods, that make me ſo; and ſure our love
Will be the nobler, and the better bleſt,
In that the ſecret juſtice of the gods
Is mingled with it. Let us leave and kiſs,
Leſt ſome unwelcome gueſt ſhould fall betwixt us,
And we ſhould part without it.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: 'Twill be ill
I ſhould abide here long.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: 'Tis true, and worſe
You ſhould come often: How ſhall we deviſe
To hold intelligence? That our true lovers,
On any new occaſion may agree, what path is beſt to tread?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I have a boy ſent by the gods, I hope to this intent,
Not yet ſeen in the Court; hunting the Buck,
I found him ſitting by a Fountain ſide,
Of which he borrow'd ſome to quench his thirſt,
And paid the Nymph again as much in tears;
A Garland lay him by, made by himſelf,
Of many ſeveral flowers, bred in the bay,
Stuck in that myſtick order, that the rareneſs
Delighted me: but ever when he turned
His tender eyes upon 'um, he would weep,
As if he meant to make 'um grow again.
Seeing ſuch pretty helpleſs innocence
Dwell in his face, I ask'd him all his ſtory;
He told me that his Parents gentle dyed,
Leaving him to the mercy of the fields,
Which gave him roots; and of the Cryſtal ſprings,
Which did not ſtop their courſes: and the Sun,
Which ſtill, he thank'd him, yielded him his light,
Then took he up his Garland and did ſhew,
What every flower as Country people hold,
Did ſignifie: and how all ordered thus,
Expreſt his grief: and to my thoughts did read
The prettieſt lecture of his Country Art
That could be wiſht: ſo that, me thought, I could
Have ſtudied it. I gladly entertain'd him,
Who was glad to follow; and have got
The truſtleſt, loving'ſt, and the gentleſt boy,
That ever Maſter kept: Him will I ſend
To wait on you, and bear our hidden love.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: 'Tis well, no more.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Madam, the Prince is come to do his ſervice.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: What will you do Philaſter with your ſelf?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why, that which all the gods have appointed out for me.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Dear, hide thy ſelf. Bring in the Prince.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Hide me from Pharamond!
When Thunder ſpeaks, which is the voice of Jove,
Though I do reverence, yet I hide me not;
And ſhall a ſtranger Prince have leave to brag
Unto a forreign Nation, that he made Philaſter hide himſelf?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: He cannot know it.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Though it ſhould ſleep for ever to the world,
It is a ſimple ſin to hide my ſelf,
Which will for ever on my conſcience lie.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Then good Philaſter, give him ſcope and way
In what he ſaies: for he is apt to ſpeak.
What you are loth to hear: for my ſake do.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: My Princely Miſtreſs, as true lovers ought,
I come to kiſs theſe fair hands; and to ſhew
In outward Ceremonies, the dear love
Writ in my heart.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: If I ſhall have an anſwer no directlier,
I am gone.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: To what would he have an anſwer?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: To his claim unto the Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Sirrah, I forbear you before the King.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Good Sir, do ſo ſtill, I would not talk with you.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: But now the time is fitter, do but offer
To make mention of right to any Kingdom,
Though it be ſcarce habitable.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Good Sir, let me go.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: And by my ſword.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Peace Pharamond: if thou—

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Leave us Philaſter.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I have done.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: You are gone, by heaven I'le fetch you back.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: You ſhall not need.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: What now?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Know Pharamond,
I loath to brawl with ſuch a blaſt as thou,
Who art nought but a valiant voice: But if
Thou ſhalt provoke me further, men ſhall ſay
Thou wert, and not lament it.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Do you ſlight
My greatneſs ſo, and in the Chamber of the Princeſs!

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: It is a place to which I muſt confeſs
I owe a reverence: but wer't the Church,
I, at the Altar, there's no place ſo ſafe,
Where thou dar'ſt injure me, but I dare kill thee:
And for your greatneſs; know Sir, I can graſp
You, and your greatneſs thus, thus into nothing:

Give not a word, not a word back: Farewell.
Exit Phi.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: 'Tis an odd fellow Madam, we muſt ſtop
His mouth with ſome Office, when we are married.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: You were beſt make him your Controuler.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I think he would diſcharge it well. But Madam,
I hope our hearts are knit; and yet ſo ſlow
The Ceremonies of State are, that 'twill be long
Before our hands be ſo: If then you pleaſe,
Being agreed in heart, let us not wait
For dreaming for me, but take a little ſtoln
Delights, and ſo prevent our joyes to come.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: If you dare ſpeak ſuch thoughts,

I muſt withdraw in honour.
Exit Are.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l:
The conſtitution of my body will never hold out till the wedding; I muſt ſeek elſewhere.
Exit Pha.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: AND thou ſhalt find her honourable boy,
Full of regard unto thy tendor youth,
For thine own modeſty; and for my ſake,
Apter to give, than thou wilt be to ask, I, or deſerve.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Sir, you did take me up when I was nothing;
And only yet am ſomething, by being yours;
You truſted me unknown; and that which you are apt
To conſter a ſimple innocence in me,
Perhaps, might have been craft; the cunning of a boy
Hardened in lies and theft; yet ventur'd you,
To part my miſeries and me: for which,
I never can expect to ſerve a Lady
That bears more honour in her breaſt than you.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: But boy, it will prefer thee; thou art young,
And beareſt a childiſh overflowing love
To them that clap thy cheeks, and ſpeak thee fair yet:
But when thy judgment comes to rule thoſe paſſions,
Thou wilt remember beſt thoſe careful friends
That plac'd thee in the nobleſt way of life;
She is a Princeſs I prefer thee to.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: In that ſmall time that I have ſeen the world,
I never knew a man haſty to part
With a ſervant he thought truſty; I remember
My Father would prefer the boys he kept
To greater men than he, but did it not,
Till they were grown too ſawcy for himſelf.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why gentle boy, I find no fault at all in thy behaviour.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Sir, if I have made
A fault of ignorance, inſtruct my youth;
I ſhall be willing, if not apt to learn;
Age and experience will adorn my mind
With larger knowledge: And if I have done
A wilful fault, think me not paſt a • hope
For once; what Maſter holds ſo ſtrict a hand
Over his boy, that he will part with him
Without one warning? Let me be corrected
To break my ſtubbornneſs if it be ſo,
Rather than turn me off, and I ſhall mend.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Thy love doth plead ſo prettily to ſtay,
That (truſt me) I could weep to part with thee.
Alas! I do not turn thee off; thou knoweſt
It is my buſineſs that doth call thee hence,
And when thou art with her thou dwel'ſt with me:
Think ſo, and 'tis ſo; and when time is full,
That thou haſt well diſcharged this heavy truſt,
Laid on ſo weak a one, I will again
With joy receive thee; as I live, I will;
Nay weep not, gentle boy; 'Tis more than time
Thou didſt attend the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: I am gone;
But ſince I am to part with you my Lord,
And none knows whether I ſhall live to do
More ſervice for you; take this little prayer;
Heaven bleſs your loves, your ſights, all your deſigns.
May ſick men, if they have your wiſh, be well;
And Heavens hate thoſe you curſe, though I be one. Exit.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: The love of boyes unto their Lords is ſtrange,
I have read wonders of it; yet this boy
For my ſake (if a man may judge by looks,
And ſpeech) would out do ſtory. I may ſee

A day to pay him for his loyalty.
Exit Phi.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Why ſhould theſe Ladies ſtay ſo long? They muſt come this way; I know the Queen imployes 'em not, for the Reverend Mother ſent me word they would all be for the Garden. If they ſhould all prove honeſt now, I were in a fair taking; I was never ſo long without ſport in my life, and in my conſcience 'tis not my fault: Oh, for our Country Ladies! Here's one boulted, I'le hound at her.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: Your Grace!

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Shall I not be a trouble?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: Not to me Sir.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Nay, nay, you are too quick; by this ſweet hand.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: You'l be forſworn Sir, 'tis but an old glove. If you will talk at diſtance, I am for you: but good Prince, be not bawdy, nor do not brag; theſe two I bar, and then I think, I ſhall have ſence enough to anſwer all the weighty Apothegmes your Royal blood ſhall manage.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Dear Lady, can you love?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: Dear, Prince, how dear! I ne're coſt you a Coach yet, nor put you to the dear repentance of a Banquet; here's no Scarlet Sir, to bluſh the ſin out it was given for: This wyer mine own hair covers: and this face has been ſo far from being dear to any, that it ne're coſt penny painting: And for the reſt of my poor Wardrobe, ſuch as you ſee, it leaves no hand behind it, to make the jealous Mercers wife curſe our good doings.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: You miſtake me Lady.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Lord, I do ſo; would you or I could help it.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Do Ladies of this Country uſe to give no more reſpect to men of my full being?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: Full being! I underſtand you not, unleſs your Grace means growing to fatneſs; and then your only remedy (upon my knowledge, Prince) is in a morning a Cup of neat White-wine brew'd with Carduus, then faſt till ſupper, about eight you may eat; uſe exerciſe, and keep a Sparrow-hawk, you can ſhoot in a Tiller; but of all, your Grace muſt flie Phlebotomie, freſh Pork, Conger, and clarified Whay; They are all dullers of the vital ſpirits.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Lady, you talk of nothing all this while.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: 'Tis very true Sir, I talk of you.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: This is a crafty wench, I like her wit well, 'twill be rare to ſtir up a leaden appetite, ſhe's a Danae, and muſt be courted in a ſhowr of gold. Madam, look here, all theſe, and more, than —

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: What have you there, my Lord? Gold? Now, as I live 'tis fair gold; you would have ſilver for it to play with the Pages; you could not have taken me in a worſe time; But if you have preſent uſe my Lord, I'le ſend my man with ſilver and keep your gold for you.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Lady, Lady.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p:
She's coming Sir behind, will take white mony. Yet for all this I'le match ye.
Exit Gal. behind the hangings.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: If there be but two ſuch more in this Kingdom, and near the Court, we may even hang up our Harps: ten ſuch Camphire conſtitutions as this, would call the golden age again in queſtion, and teach the old way for every ill fac't Husband to get his own Children, and what a miſchief that will breed, let all conſider.
Here's another; if ſhe be of the ſame laſt, the Devil ſhall pluck her on. Many fair mornings, Lady.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: As many mornings bring as many dayes,
Fair, ſweet, and hopeful to your Grace.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: She gives good words yet; Sure this wench is free.
If your more ſerious buſineſs do not call you,
Let me hold quarter with you, we'll take an hour
Out quickly.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: What would your Grace talk of?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Of ſome ſuch pretty ſubject as your ſelf.
I'le go no further than your eye, or lip,
There's theme enough for one man for an age.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Sir, they ſtand right, and my lips are yet even,
Smooth, young enough, ripe enough, red enough,
Or my glaſs wrongs me.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: O they are two twin'd Cherries died in bluſhes,
Which thoſe fair ſuns above, with their bright beams
Reflect upon, and ripen: ſweeteſt beauty,
Bow down thoſe branches, that the longing taſte,
Of the faint looker on, may meet thoſe bleſſings,
And taſte and live.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: O delicate ſweet Prince;
She that hath ſnow enough about her heart,
To take the wanton ſpring of ten ſuch lines off,
May be a Nun without probation.
Sir, you have in ſuch neat poetry, gathered a kiſs,
That if I had but five lines of that number,
Such pretty begging blanks, I ſhould commend
Your fore-head, of your cheeks, and kiſs you too.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Do it in proſe; you cannot miſs it Madam.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: I ſhall, I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: By my life you ſhall not.
I'le prompt you firſt: Can you do it now?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Methinks 'tis eaſie, now I ha' don't before;
But yet I ſhould ſtick at it.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Stick till to morrow.
I'le ne'r part you ſweeteſt. But we loſe time,
Can you love me?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: Love you my Lord? How would you have me love you?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: I'le teach you in a ſhort ſentence, cauſe I will not load your memory, this is all: love me, and lie with me.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: Was it lie with you that you ſaid? 'Tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Not to a willing mind, that will endeavour; if I do not teach you to do it as eaſily in one night, as you'l go to bed, I'le loſe my Royal blood ſor't.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: Why Prince, you have a Lady of your own, that yet wants teaching.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: I'le ſooner teach a Mare the old meaſures, than teach her any thing belonging to the function; ſhe's afraid to lie with her ſelf, if ſhe have but any maſculine imaginations about her; I know when we are married, I muſt raviſh her.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: By my honour, that's a foul fault indeed, but time and your good help will wear it out Sir.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: And for any other I ſee, excepting your dear ſelf, deareſt Lady, I had rather be Sir Tim the Schoolmaſter, and leap a Dairy-maid.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: Has your Grace ſeen the Court-ſtar Galatea?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Out upon her; ſhe's as cold of her favour as an apoplex? ſhe ſail'd by but now.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: And how do you hold her wit Sir?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: I hold her wit? The ſtrength of all the Guard cannot hold it, if they were tied to it, ſhe would blow 'em out of the Kingdom, they talk of Jupiter, he's but a ſquib cracker to her: Look well about you, and you may find a tongue-bolt. But ſpeak ſweet Lady, ſhall I be freely welcome?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: Whither?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: To your bed; if you miſtruſt my faith, you do me the unnobleſt wrong.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: I dare not Prince, I dare not.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Make your own conditions, my purſe ſhall ſeal'em, and what you dare imagine you can want, I'le furniſh you withal: give two hours to your thoughts every morning about it. Come, I know you are baſhful, ſpeak in my car, will you be mine? keep this, and with it me: ſoon I will viſit you.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.p: My Lord, my Chamber's moſt unſafe, but when 'tis night I'le find ſome means to ſlip into your lodging: till when—

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Till when, this, and my heart go with thee.

div.stage: Enter Galatea from behind the hangings.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: Oh thou pernicious Petticoat Prince, are theſe your vertues? Well, if I do not lay a train to blow your ſport up, I am no woman; and Lady Towſabel I'le ſit you for't.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Where's the boy?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Within Madam.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Gave you him gold to buy him cloaths?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I did.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: And has he don't?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Yes Madam.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: 'Tis a pretty ſad talking boy, is it not?
Askt you his name?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: No Madam.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.p: O you are welcome, what good news?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: As good as any one can tell your Grace,
That ſaies ſhe hath done that you would have wiſh'd.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.p: Haſt thou diſcovered?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: I have ſtrained a point of modeſty for you.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.p: I prethee how?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.p: In liſtning after bawdery; I ſee, let a Lady live never ſo modeſtly, ſhe ſhall be ſure to find a lawful time, to harken after bawdery; your Prince, brave Pharamond, was ſo hot on't.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: With whom?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: Why, with the Lady I ſuſpect: I can tell the time and place.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: O when, and where?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: To night, his Lodging.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Run thy ſelf into the preſence, mingle there again
With other Ladies, leave the reſt to me:
If deſtiny (to whom we dare not ſay,
Why thou didſt this) have not decreed it ſo
In laſting leaves (whoſe ſmalleſt Characters
Were never altered:) yet, this match ſhall break.
Where's the boy?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Here Madam.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Sir, you are ſad to change your ſervice, is't not ſo?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Madam, I have not chang'd; I wait on you,
To do him ſervice.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Thou diſclaim'ſt in me;
Tell me thy name.

l.hi: Bellario.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Thou canſt ſing, and play?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: If grief will give me leave, Madam, I can.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Alas! what kind of grief can thy years know?
Hadſt thou a curſt maſter, when thou went'ſt to School?
Thou art not capable of other grief;
Thy brows and cheeks are ſmooth as waters be,
When no dreath troubles them: believe me boy,
Care ſeeks out wrinkled brows, and hollow eyes,
And builds himſelf caves to abide in them.
Come Sir, tell me truly, does your Lord love me?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Love Madam? I know not what it is.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Canſt thou know grief, and never yet knew'ſt love?
Thou art deceiv'd boy; does he ſpeak of me
As if he wiſh'd me well?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: If it be love,
To forget all reſpect of his own friends,
In thinking of your face; if it be love
To ſit croſs arm'd and ſigh away the day,
Mingled with ſtarts, crying your name as loud
And haſtily, as men i'the ſtreets do fire:
If it be love to weep himſelf away,
When he but hears of any Lady dead,
Or kill'd, becauſe it might have been your chance;
If when he goes to reſt (which will not be)
'Twixt every prayer he ſaies, to name you once
As others drop a bead, be to be in love;
Then Madam, I dare ſwear he loves you.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: O y'are a cunning boy, and taught to lie,
For your Lords credit; but thou knoweſt, a lie,
That bears this ſound, is welcomer to me,
Than any truth that ſaies he loves me not.
Lead the way Boy: Do you attend me too;
'Tis thy Lords buſineſs haſts me thus; Away. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Dion, Cleremont, Thraſilin, Megra and Galatea.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Come Ladies, ſhall we talk a round? As men
Do walk a mile, women ſhould take an hour
After ſupper: 'Tis their exerciſe.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: 'Tis late.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: 'Tis all
My eyes will do to lead me to my bed.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: I fear they are ſo heavy, you'l ſcarce find
The way to your lodging with 'em to night.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: The Prince.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Not a bed Ladies? y'are good ſitters up;
What think you of a pleaſant dream to laſt
Till morning?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: I ſhould chooſe, my Lord, a pleaſing wake before it.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: 'Tis well my Lord y'are courting of Ladies.
Is't not late Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Yes Madam.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l:
Wait you there.
Exit Arethuſa.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: She's jealous, as I live; look you my Lord,
The Princeſs has a Hilas, an Adonis.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: His form is Angel-like.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Why this is he, muſt, when you are wed,
Sit by your pillow, like young Apollo, with
His hand and voice, binding your thoughts in ſleep;
The Princeſs does provide him for you, and for her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I find no muſick in theſe boys.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Nor I.
They can do little, and that ſmall they do,
They have not wit to hide.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Serves he the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſweet boy, how brave ſhe keeps him!

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Ladies all good reſt; I mean to kill a Buck
To morrow morning, ere y'ave done your dreams.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: All happineſs attend your Grace, Gentlemen good reſt,
Come ſhall we to bed?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l:
Yes, all good night.
Ex. Gal. and Meg.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: May your dreams be true to you;
What ſhall we do Gallants? 'Tis late, the King
Is up ſtill, ſee, he comes, a Guard along
With him.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Look your intelligence be true.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Upon my life it is: and I do hope,
Your Highneſs will not tye me to a man,
That in the heat of wooing throws me off,
And takes another.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: What ſhould this mean?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: If it be true,
That Lady had been better have embrac'd

Cureleſs Diſeaſes; get you to your reſt,
Ex. Are. and Bel.
You ſhall be tighted: Gentlemen draw near,
We ſhall imploy you: Is young Pharamond
Come to his lodging?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I ſaw him enter there.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Haſte ſome of you, and cunningly diſcover,
If Megra be in her lodging.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Sir,
She parted hence but now with other Ladies.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: If ſhe be there, we ſhall not need to make
A vain diſcovery of our ſuſpicion.
You gods I ſee, that who unrighteouſly
Holds wealth or ſtate from others, ſhall be curſt,
In that, which meaner men are bleſt withall:
Ages to come ſhall know no male of him
Leſt to inherit, and his name ſhall be
Blotted from earth; If he have any child,
It ſhall be croſsly matched: the gods themſelves
Shall ſow wild ſtrife betwixt her Lord and her,
Yet, if it be your wills, forgive the ſin
I have committed, let it not fall
Upon this underſtanding child of mine,
She has not broke your Laws; but how can I,
Look to be heard of gods, that muſt be juſt,
Praying upon the ground I hold by wrong?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Sir, I have asked, and her women ſwear ſhe is within, but they I think are bawds; I told 'em I muſt ſpeak with her: they laught, and ſaid their Lady lay ſpeechleſs. I ſaid, my buſineſs was important; they ſaid their Lady was about it: I grew hot, and cryed my buſineſs was a matter that concern'd life and death; they anſwered, ſo was ſleeping, at which their Lady was; I urg'd again, ſhe had ſcarce time to be ſo ſince laſt I ſaw her; they ſmil'd again, and ſeem'd to inſtruct me, that ſleeping was nothing but lying down and winking: Anſwers more direct I could not get: in ſhort Sir, I think ſhe is not there.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: 'Tis then no time to dally: you o'th' Guard,
Wait at the back door of the Princes lodging,
And ſee that none paſs thence upon your lives.
Knock Gentlemen: knock loud: louder yet:
What, has their pleaſure taken off their hearing?
I'le break your meditations? knock again:
Not yet? I do not think he ſleeps, having this
Larum by him; once more, Pharamond, Prince.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: What ſawcy groom knocks at this dead of night?
Where be our waiters? By my vexed ſoul,
He meets his death, that meets me, for this boldneſs.

sp.speaker: K.
sp.l: Prince, you wrong your thoughts, we are your friends,
Come down.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: The King?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: The ſame Sir, come down,
We have cauſe of preſent Counſel with you.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: If your Grace pleaſe to uſe me, I'le attend you
To your Chamber. Pha. below.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No, 'tis too late Prince, I'le make bold with yours.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I have ſome private reaſons to my ſelf,
Makes me unmannerly, and ſay you cannot;
Nay, preſs not forward Gentlemen, he muſt come
Through my life, that comes here. Enter.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Sir be reſolv'd, I muſt and will come.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I will not be diſhonour'd;
He that enters, enters upon his death;
Sir, 'tis a ſign you make no ſtranger of me,
To bring theſe Renegados to my Chamber,
At theſe unſeaſon'd hours.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Why do you
Chaſe your ſelf ſo? you are not wrong'd, nor ſhall be;
Onely I'le ſearch your lodging, for ſome cauſe
To our ſelf known: Enter I ſay.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I ſay no. Meg. Above.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Let 'em enter Prince,
Let 'em enter, I am up, and ready; I know their buſineſs,
'Tis the poor breaking of a Ladies honour,
They hunt ſo hotly after; let 'em enjoy it.
You have your buſineſs Gentlemen, I lay here.
O my Lord the King, this is not noble in you
To make publick the weakneſs of a Woman.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Come down.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: I dare my Lord; your whootings and your clamors,
Your private whiſpers, and your broad ſteerings,
Can no more vex my ſoul, than this baſe carriage;
But I have vengeance yet in ſtore for ſome,
Shall in the moſt contempt you can have of me,
Be joy and nouriſhment.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Will you come down?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Yes, to laugh at your worſt: but I ſhall wrong you,
If my skill fail me not.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Sir, I muſt dearly chide you for this looſeneſs,
You have wrong'd a worthy Lady; but no more,
Conduct him to my lodging, and to bed.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Get him another wench, and you bring him to bed in deed.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange a man cannot ride a Stagg
Or two, to breath himſelf, without a warrant:
If this geer hold, that lodgings be ſearch'd thus,
Pray heaven we may lie with our own wives in ſafety,
That they be not by ſome trick of State miſtaken.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Now Lady of honour, where's your honour now?
No man can fit your palat, but the Prince.
Thou moſt ill ſhrowded rottenneſs; thou piece
Made by a Painter and a Pothecary;
Thou troubled ſea of luſt; thou wilderneſs,
Inhabited by wild thoughts; thou ſwoln cloud
Of Infection; thou ripe Mine of all Diſeaſes;
Thou all Sin, all Hell, and laſt, all Devils, tell me,
Had you none to pull on with your courteſies,
But he that muſt be mine, and wrong my Daughter?
By all the gods, all theſe, and all the Pages,
And all the Court ſhall hoot thee through the Court,
Fling rotten Oranges, make ribald Rimes,
And fear thy name with Candles upon walls:
Do you laugh Lady Venus?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Faith Sir, you muſt pardon me;
I cannot chuſe but laugh to ſee you merry.
If you do this, O King; nay, if you dare do it;
By all theſe gods you ſwore by, and as many
More of my own; I will have fellows, and ſuch
Fellows in it, as ſhall make noble mirth;
The Princeſs, your dear Daughter, ſhall ſtand by me
On walls, and ſung in ballads, any thing:
Urge me no more, I know her, and her haunts,
Her layes, leaps, and out layes, and will diſcover all;
Nay will diſhonour her. I know the boy
She keeps, a handſome boy; about eighteen:
Know what ſhe does with him, where, and when.
Come Sir, you put me to a womans madneſs,
The glory of a fury; and if I do not
Do it to the height?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What boy is this ſhe raves at?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Alas! good minded Prince, you know not theſe things?
I am loth to reveal 'em. Keep this fault
As you would keep your health from the hot air
Of the corrupted people, or by heaven,
I will not fall alone: what I have known,
Shall be as publick as a print: all tongues
Shall ſpeak it as they do the language they
Are born in, as free and commonly; I'le ſet it
Like a prodigious ſtar for all to gaze at,
And ſo high and glowing, that other Kingdoms far and Forreign
Shall read it there, nay travel with it, till they find
No tongue to make it more, nor no more people;
And then behold the fall of your fair Princeſs.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Has ſhe a boy?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: So pleaſe your Grace I have ſeen a boy wait
On her, a fair boy.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Go get you to your quarter:
For this time I'le ſtudy to forget you.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Do you ſtudy to forget me, and I'le ſtudy

To forget you.
Ex. King, Meg. and Guard.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: Why here's a Male ſpirit for Hercules, if ever there be nine worthies of women, this wench ſhall ride aſtride, and be their Captain.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Sure ſhe hath a garriſon of Devils in her tongue, ſhe uttereth ſuch balls of wild-fire. She has ſo netled the King, that all the Doctors in the Country will ſcarce cure him. That boy was a ſtrange found out antidote to cure her infection: that boy, that Princeſs boy: that brave, chaſt, vertuous Ladies boy: and a fair boy, a well ſpoken boy: All theſe conſidered, can make nothing elſe—but there I leave you Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: Nay we'l go wander with you. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: NAY doubtleſs 'tis true.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I, and 'tis the gods
That rais'd this Puniſhment to ſcourge the King
With his own iſſue: Is it not a ſhame
For us, that ſhould write noble in the land;
For us, that ſhould be freemen, to behold
A man, that is the bravery of his age,
Philaſter, preſt down from his Royal right,
By this regardleſs King; and only look,
And ſee the Scepter ready to be caſt
Into the hands of that laſcivious Lady,
That lives in luſt with a ſmooth boy, now to be
Married to yon ſtrange Prince, who, but that people
Pleaſe to let him be a Prince, is born a ſlave,
In that which ſhould be his moſt noble part,
His mind?

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: That man that would not ſtir with you,
To aid Philaſter, let the gods forget,
That ſuch a Creature walks upon the earth.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Philaſter is too backward in't himſelf;
The Gentry do await it, and the people
Againſt their nature are all bent for him,
And like a field of ſtanding Corn, that's mov'd
With a ſtiſſ gale, their heads bow all one way.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: The only cauſe that draws Philaſter back
From this attempt, is the fair Princeſs love,
Which he admires and we can now confute.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: Perhaps he'l not believe it.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Why Gentlemen, 'tis without queſtion ſo.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I 'tis paſt ſpeech, ſhe lives diſhoneſtly.
But how ſhall we, if he be curious, work
Upon his faith?

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: We all are ſatisfied within our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Since it is true, and tends to his own good,
I'le make this new report to be my knowledge,
I'le ſay I know it, nay, I'le ſwear I ſaw it.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: It will be beſt.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: 'Twill move him.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Here he comes. Good morrow to your honour,
We have ſpent ſome time in ſeeking you.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: My worthy friends,
You that can keep your memories to know
Your friend in miſeries, and cannot frown
On men diſgrac'd for vertue: A good day
Attend you all. What ſervice may I do worthy your acceptation?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: My good Lord,
We come to urge that vertue which we know
Lives in your breaſt, forth, riſe, and make a head,
The Nobles, and the people are all dull'd
With this uſurping King: and not a man
That ever heard the word, or knew ſuch a thing
As vertue, but will ſecond your attempts.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: How honourable is this love in you
To me that have deſerv'd none? Know my friends
(You that were born to ſhame your poor Philaſter,
With too much courteſie) I could afford
To melt my ſelf in thanks; but my deſigns
Are not yet ripe, ſuffice it, that ere long
I ſhall imploy your loves: but yet the time is ſhort of what I would

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: The time is fuller Sir, than you expect;
That which hereafter will not perhaps be reach'd
By violence, may now be caught; As for the King,
You know the people have long hated him;
But now the Princeſs, whom they lov'd.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why, what of her?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Is loath'd as much as he.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: By what ſtrange means?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: She's known a Whore.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: My Lord—

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt, Offers to draw and is held.
And thou ſhalt feel it; I had thought thy mind
Had been of honour; thus to rob a Lady
Of her good name, is an infectious ſin,
Not to be pardon'd; be it falſe as hell,
'Twill never be redeem'd, if it be ſown
Amongſt the people, fruitful to increaſe
All evil they ſhall hear. Let me alone,
That I may cut off falſhood, whilſt it ſprings.
Set hills on hills betwixt me and the man
That utters this, and I will ſcale them all,
And from the utmoſt top fall on his neck,
Like Thunder from a Cloud.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: This is moſt ſtrange;
Sure he does love her.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I do love fair truth:
She is my Miſtreſs, and who injures her,
Draws vengeance from me Sirs, let go my arms.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: Nay, good my Lord be patient.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Sir, remember this is your honour'd friend,
That comes to do his ſervice, and will ſhew you
Why he utter'd this.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I ask you pardon Sir,
My zeal to truth made me unmannerly:
Should I have heard diſhonour ſpoke of you,
Behind your back untruly, I had been
As much diſtemper'd, and enrag'd as now.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: But this my Lord is truth.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: O ſay not ſo, good Sir forbear to ſay ſo,
'Tis the truth that all womenkind is falſe;
Urge it no more, it is impoſſible;
Why ſhould you think the Princeſs light?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Why, ſhe was taken at it.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: 'Tis falſe, O Heaven 'tis falſe: it cannot be,
Can it? Speak Gentlemen, for love of truth ſpeak;
Is't poſſible? can women all be damn'd?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Why no, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why then it cannot be.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: And ſhe was taken with her boy.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What boy?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: A Page, a boy that ſerves her.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh good gods, a little boy?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I, know you him my Lord?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Hell and ſin know him? Sir, you are deceiv'd;
I'le reaſon it a little coldly with you;
If ſhe were luſtful, would ſhe take a boy,
That knows not yet deſire? ſhe would have one
Should meet her thoughts and knows the ſin he acts,
Which is the great delight of wickedneſs;
You are abus'd, and ſo is ſhe, and I.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: How you my Lord?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why all the world's abus'd
In an unjuſt report.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Oh noble Sir your vertues
Cannot look into the ſubtil thoughts of woman.
In ſhort my Lord, I took them: I my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Now all the Devils thou didſt ille from my rage,
Would thou • adl • ta' • e devils • nge • dring plagues:
When thou didſt take them, hide thee from my eyes,
Would them hadſt taken Thunder on thy breaſt,
When thou didſt take them, or been ſtrucken dumb
For ever: that this ſoul deed might have ſlept in ſilence.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: Have you known him ſo ill temper'd?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Never before.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: The winds that are l • t looſe,
From the • our ſeveral cor ••• s of the earth,
And ſpread themſ • lves all over ſea and land,
Kiſs 〈◊〉 chaſt • one. What friend bears a ſword
To run me through?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Why, my Lord, are you ſo mov'd at this?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: When any falls from vertue I am diſtract,
I have an intereſt in't.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: But good my Lord recal your ſelf,
And think what's beſt to be done.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I thank you. I will do it;
Pleaſe you to leave me, I'le conſider of it:
To morrow I will find your lodging forth,
And give you anſwer
The readieſt way.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: All the gods direct you.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: He was extream impatient.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: It was his vertue and his noble mind.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I had forgot to ask him where he took them,
I'le follow him. O that I had a ſea
Within my breaſt, to quench the fire I feel;
More circumſtances will but fan this ſire;
It more afflicts me now, to know by whom
This deed is done, than ſimply that 'tis done:
And he that tells me this is honourable,
As far from lies, as ſhe is far from truth.
O that like beaſts, we could not grieve our ſelves,
With that we ſee not; Bulls and Rams will fight,
To keep their Females ſtanding in their fight;
But take 'em from them, and you take at once
Their ſpleens away; and they will fall again
Unto their Paſtures, growing freſh and fat,
And taſte the waters of the ſprings as ſweet,
As 'twas before, finding no ſtart in ſleep.
But miſerable man; See, ſee you gods,
He walks ſtill; and the face you let him wear
When he was innocent, is ſtill the ſame,
Not blaſted; is this juſtice? Do you mean
To intrap mortality, that you allow
Treaſon ſo ſmooth a brow? I cannot now
Think he is guilty.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Health to you my Lord;
The Princeſs doth commend her love, her life,
And this unto you.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh Bellario,
Now I perceive ſhe loves me, ſhe does ſhew it
In loving thee my boy, ſhe has made thee brave.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: My Lord ſhe has attired me paſt my wiſh,
Paſt my deſert, more fit for her attendant,
Though far unfit for me, who do attend.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Thou art grown courtly boy. O let all women
That love black deeds, learn to diſſemble here,
Here, by this paper ſhe does write to me,
As if her heart were Min • s of Adamant
To all the world beſides, but unto me,
A maiden ſnow that melted with my looks.
Tell me my boy how doth the Princeſs uſe thee?
For I ſhall gueſs her love to me by that.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Scarce like her ſervant, but as if I were
Something allied to her; or had preſerv'd
Her life three times by my fidelity.
As mothers fond do uſe their only ſons;
As I'de uſe one, that's lef • unto my truſt,
For whom my life ſhould pay, if he met harm,
So ſhe does uſe me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why, this is wondrous well:
But what kind language does ſhe feed thee with?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Why, ſhe does tell me, ſhe will truſt my youth
With all her loving ſecrets; and does call me
Her pretty ſervant, bids me weep no more
For leaving you: ſhee'l ſee my ſervices
Regarded; and ſuch words of that ſoft ſtrain,
That I am nearer weeping when ſhe ends
Than ere ſhe ſpake.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: This is much better ſtill.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Are you ill my Lord?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Ill? No Bellario.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Me thinks your words
Fall not from off your tongue ſo evenly,
Nor is there in your looks that quietneſs,
That I was wont to ſee.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Thou art deceiv'd boy:
And ſhe ſtroakes thy head?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And ſhe does clap thy cheeks?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: She does my Lord.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And ſhe does kiſs thee boy? ha!

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: How my Lord?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: She kiſſes thee?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Not ſo my Lord.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Come, come, I know ſhe does.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: No by my life.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why then ſhe does not love me; come, ſhe does,
I bad her do it; I charg'd her by all charms
Of love between us, by the hope of peace
We ſhould enjoy, to yield thee all delights
Naked, as to her bed: I took her oath
Thou ſhould'ſt enjoy her: Tell me gentle boy,
Is ſhe not paralleleſs? Is not her breath
Sweet as Arabian winds, when fruits are ripe?
Are not her breaſts two liquid Ivory balls?
Is ſhe not all a laſting Mine of joy?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: I, now I ſee why my diſturbed thoughts
Were ſo perplext, When firſt I went to her,
My heart held augury; you are abus'd,
Some villain has abus'd you; I do ſee
Whereto you tend; fall Rocks upon his head,
That put this to you; 'tis ſome ſubtil train,
To bring that noble frame of yours to nought.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Thou think'ſt I will be angry with thee; Come
Thou ſhalt know all my drift, I hate her more,
Than I love happineſs, and plac'd thee there,
To pry with narrow eyes into her deeds;
Haſt thou diſcover'd? Is ſhe faln 〈◊〉
As I would wiſh her? Speak ſome comfort to me.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: My Lord, you did miſtake the boy you ſent:
Had ſhe a ſin that way, hid from the world,
〈…〉 I would not aid
Her baſe deſires; but what I came to know
As ſervant to her, I would not reveal, to make my life laſt ages

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh my heart; this is a ſalve worſe than the main diſeaſe.
Tell me thy thoughts; for I will know the leaſt
That dwells within thee, or will rip thy heart
To know it; I will ſee thy thoughts as plain,
As I do know thy face.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Why, ſo you do.
She is (for ought I know) by all the gods,
As chaſte as • ee; but were ſhe foul as Hell
And I did know it, thus; the breath of Kings,
The points of Swords, Tortures nor Bulls of Braſs,
Should draw it from me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Then 'tis no time to dally with thee;
I will take thy life, for I do hate thee; I could curſe thee now.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: If you do hate you could not curſe me worſe;
The gods have not a puniſhment in ſtore
Greater for me, than is your hate.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Fie, fie, ſo young and ſo diſſembling;
Tell me when and where thou diſt enjoy her,
Or let plugues fall on me, if I deſtroy thee not,

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Heaven knows I never did: and when I lie
To ſave my life, may I live long and loath'd.
Hew me a ſunder, and whilſt I can think
I'le love thoſe pieces you have cut away,
Better than thoſe that grow: and kiſs theſe limbs,
Becauſe you made 'em ſo.
Feareſt thou not death?
Can boys contemn that?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Oh, what boy is he
Can be content to live to be a man
That ſees the beſt of men thus paſſionate, thus without reaſon?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh, but thou doſt not know what 'tis to die.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Yes, I do know my Lord;
'Tis leſs than to be born; a laſting ſleep,
A quiet reſting from all jealouſie;
A thing we all purſue; I know beſides,
It is but giving over of a game that muſt be loſt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: But there are pains, falſe boy,
For perjur'd ſouls; think but on theſe, and then
Thy heart will melt, and thou wilt utter all.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: May they fall all upon me whilſt I live,
If I be perjur'd, or have ever thought
Of that you charge me with; if I be falſe,
Send me to ſuffer in thoſe puniſhments you ſpeak of; kill me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh, what ſhould I do?
Why, who can but believe him? He does ſwear
So earneſtly, that if it were not true,
The gods would not endure him. Riſe Bellario,
Thy proteſtations are ſo deep; and thou
Doſt look ſo truly, when thou uttereſt them,
That though I known 'em falſe, as were my hopes,
I cannot urge thee further; but thou wert
To blame to injure me, for I muſt love
Thy honeſt looks, and take no revenge upon
Thy tender youth; A love from me to thee
Is firm, what ere thou doſt: It troubles me
That I have call'd the blood out of thy cheeks,
That did ſo well become thee: but good boy
Let me not ſee thee more; ſomething is done,
That will diſtract me, that will make me mad,
If I behold thee: if thou tender'ſt me,
Let me not ſee thee.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: I will fly as far
As there is morning, ere I give diſtaſte
To that moſt honour'd mind. But through theſe tears
Shed at my hopeleſs parting, I can ſee
A world of Treaſon practis'd upon you,
And her and me. Farewel for evermore;
If you ſhall hear, that ſorrow ſtruck me dead,
And after find me Loyal, let there be
A tear ſhed from you in my memorie.

And I ſhall reſt at peace.
Exit Bel.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Bleſſing be with thee,
What ever thou deſerv'ſt. Oh, where ſhall I
Go bath thy body? Nature too unkind,

That made no medicine for a troubled mind!
Ex. Phi.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: I marvel my boy comes not back again;
But that I know my love will queſtion him
Over and over; how I ſlept, wak'd, talk'd;
How I remembred him when his dear name
Was laſt ſpoke, and how, when I ſigh'd, wept, ſung,
And ten thouſand ſuch; I ſhould be angry at his ſtay.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What are your meditations? who attends you?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: None but my ſingle ſelf, I need no Guard,
I do no wrong, nor fear none.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Tell me: have you not a boy?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What kind of boy?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: A Page, a waiting boy.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: A handſome boy?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: I think he be not ugly:
Well qualified, and dutiful, I know him,
I took him not for beauty.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: He ſpeaks, and ſings and plays?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: About Eighteen?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: I never ask'd his age.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Is he full of ſervice?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: By your pardon why do you ask?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Put him away.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Put him away, h'as done you that good ſervice,
Shames me to ſpeak of.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Good Sir let me underſtand you.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: If you fear me, ſhew it in duty; put away that boy.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Let me have reaſon for it Sir, and then
Your will is my command.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Do not you bluſh to ask it? Caſt him off,
Or I ſhall do the ſame to you. Y'are one
Shame with me, and ſo near unto my ſelf,
That by my life, I dare not tell my ſelf,
What you, my ſelf have done.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: What have I done my Lord?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: 'Tis a new language, that all love to learn,
The common people ſpeak it well already,
They need no Grammer; underſtand me well,
There be foul whiſpers ſtirring; caſt him off!

And ſuddenly do it: Farewel.
Exit King.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Where may a Maiden live ſecurely free,
Keeping her Honour ſafe? Not with the living,
They feed upon opinions, errours, dreams,
And make 'em truths: they draw a nouriſhment
Out of defamings, grow upon diſgraces,
And when they ſee a vertue fortified
Strongly above the battery of their tongues;
Oh, how they caſt to ſink it; and deſeated
(Soul ſick with Poyſon) ſtrike the Monuments
Where noble names lie ſleeping: till they ſweat,
And the cold Marble melt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Peace to your faireſt thoughts, deareſt Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Oh, my deareſt ſervant I have a War within me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: He muſt be more than man, that makes theſe Cryſtals
Run into Rivers; ſweeteſt fair, the cauſe;
And as I am your ſlave, tied to your goodneſs,
Your creature made again from what I was,
And newly ſpirited, I'le right your honours.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Oh, my beſt love; that boy!

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What boy?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: The pretty boy you gave me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What of him?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Muſt be no more mine.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: They are jealous of him.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Jealous, who?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: The King.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh, my fortune,
