Then 'tis no idle jealouſie. Let him go.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Oh cruel, are you hard hearted too?
Who ſhall now tell you, how much I lov'd you;
Who ſhall ſwear it to you, and weep the tears I ſend?
Who ſhall now bring you Letters, Rings, Bracelets,
Loſe his health in ſervice? wake tedious nights
In ſtories of your praiſe? Who ſhall ſing
Your crying Elegies? And ſtrike a ſad ſoul
Into ſenſeleſs Pictures, and make them mourn?
Who ſhall take up his Lute, and touch it, till
He crown a ſilent ſleep upon my eye-lid,
Making me dream and cry, Oh my dear, dear Philaſter.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh my heart!
Would he had broken thee, that made thee know
This Lady was not Loyal. Miſtreſs, forget
The boy, I'le get thee a far better.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Oh never, never ſuch a boy again, as my Bellario.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: 'Tis but your fond affection.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: With thee my boy, farewel for ever,
All ſecrecy in ſervants: farewel faith,
And all deſire to do well for it ſelf:
Let all that ſhall ſucceed thee, for thy wrongs,
Sell and betray chaſt love.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And all this paſſion for a boy?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: He was your boy, and you put him to me,
And the loſs of ſuch muſt have a mourning for.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: O thou forgetful woman!

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: How, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Falſe Arethuſa!
Haſt thou a Medicine to reſtore my wits,
When I have loſt 'em? If not, leave to talk, and do thus.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Do what Sir? would you ſleep?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: For ever Arethuſa. Oh you gods,
Give me a worthy patience; Have I ſtood
Naked, alone the ſhock of many fortunes?
Have I ſeen miſchiefs numberleſs, and mighty
Grow live a ſea upon me? Have I taken
Danger as ſtorn as death into my boſom,
And laught upon it, made it but a mirth,
And ſlung it by? Do I live now like him,
Under this Tyrant King, that languiſhing
Hears his ſad Bell, and ſees his Mourners? Do I
Bear all this bravely, and muſt ſink at length
Under a womans falſhood? Oh that boy,
That curſed boy? None but a villain boy, to eaſe your luſt?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Nay, then I am betray'd,
I feel the plot caſt for my overthrow; Oh I am wretched.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Now you may take that little right I have
To this poor Kingdom; give it to your Joy,
For I have no joy in it. Some far place,
Where never womankind durſt ſet her foot,
For burſting with her poiſons, muſt I ſeek,
And live to curſe you;
There dig a Cave, and preach to birds and beaſts,
What woman is, and help to ſave them from you.
How heaven is in your eyes, but in your hearts,
More hell than hell has; how your tongues like Scorpions,
Both heal and poyſon; how your thoughts are woven
With thouſand changes in one ſubtle webb,
And worn ſo by you. How that fooliſh man,
That reads the ſtory of a womans face,
And dies believing it, is loſt for ever.
How all the good you have, is but a ſhadow,
I'th' morning with you, and at night behind you,
Paſt and forgotten. How your vows are froſts,
Faſt for a night, and with the next ſun gone.
How you are, being taken all together,
A meer confuſion, and ſo dead a Chaos,
That love cannot diſtinguiſh. Theſe ſad Texts
Till my laſt hour, I am bound to utter of you.

So farewel all my wo, all my delight.
Exit Phi

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Be merciful ye gods and ſtrike me dead;
What way have I deſerv'd this? make my breaſt
Tranſparent as pure Cryſtal, that the world
Jealous of me, may ſee the fouleſt thought
My heart holds. Where ſhall a woman turn her eyes,

To find out conſtancy? Save me, how black,
Enter Bell.
And guilty (me thinks) that boy looks now?
Oh thou diſſembler, that before thou ſpak'ſt
Wert in thy cradle falſe? ſent to make lies,
And betray Innocents; thy Lord and thou,
May glory in the aſhes of a Maid
Fool'd by her paſſion; but the conqueſt is
Nothing ſo great as wicked. Fly away,
Let my command force thee to that, which ſhame
Would do without it. If thou underſtoodſt
The loathed Office thou haſt undergone,
Why, thou wouldſt hide thee under heaps of hills,
Leſt men ſhould dig and find thee.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Oh what God
Angry with men, hath ſent this ſtrange diſeaſe
Into the nobleſt minds? Madam this grief
You add unto me is no more than drops
To ſeas, for which they are not ſeen to ſwell;
My Lord had ſtruck his anger through my heart,
And let out all the hope of future joyes,
You need not bid me fly, I came to part,
To take my lateſt leave, Farewel for ever;
I durſt not run away in honeſty,
From ſuch a Lady, like a boy that ſtole,
Or made ſome grievous fault; the power of gods
Aſſiſt you in your ſufferings; haſty time
Reveal the truth to your abuſed Lord,
And mine: That he may know your worth: whilſt I

Go ſeek out ſome forgotten place to die.
Exit Bell.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Peace guide thee, th'aſt overthrown me once,
Yet if I had another Troy to loſe,
Thou or another villain with thy looks,
Might talk me out of it, and ſend me naked,
My hair diſhevel'd through the fiery ſtreets.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Madam, the King would hunt, and calls for you
With earneſtneſs.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: I am in tune to hunt!
Diana if thou canſt rage with a maid,
As with a man, let me diſcover thee
Bathing, and turn me to a fearful Hind,
That I may die purſu'd by cruel Hounds,
And have my ſtory written in my wounds. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter King, Pharamond, Arethuſa, Galatea, Megra, Dion, Cleremont, Thraſilin, and Attendants.

sp.speaker: K.
sp.l: WHat, are the Hounds before, and all the woodmen?
Our horſes ready, and our bows bent?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: All Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Y'are cloudy Sir, come we have forgotten
Your venial treſpaſs, let not that ſit heavy
Upon your ſpirit; none dare utter it.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: He looks like an old ſurfeited Stallion after his leaping, dull as a Dormouſe: ſee how he ſinks; the wench has ſhot him between wind and water, and I hope ſprung a leak.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.p: He needs no teaching, he ſtrikes ſure enough; his greateſt fault is, he Hunts too much in the Purlues, would he would leave off Poaching.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: And for his horn, has left it at the Lodge where he lay late; Oh, he's a precious Lime-hound; turn him looſe upon the purſuit of a Lady, and if he loſe her, hang him up i'th' ſlip. When my Fox-bitch Beauty grows proud, I'le borrow him.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Is your Boy turn'd away?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.p: You did command Sir, and I obey you.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: 'Tis well done: Hark ye further.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: Is't poſſible this fellow ſhould repent? Me thinks that were not noble in him: and yet he looks like a mortified member, as if he had a ſick mans Salve in's mouth. If a worſe man had done this fault now, ſome Phyſical Juſtice or other, would preſently (without the help of an Almanack) have opened the obſtructions of his Liver, and let him bloud with a Dog whip.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: See, ſee, how modeſtly your Lady looks, as if ſhe came from Churching with her Neighbour; why, what a Devil can a man ſee in her face, but that ſhe's honeſt?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: Troth no great matter to ſpeak of, a fooliſh twinkling with the eye, that ſpoils her Coat; but he muſt be a cunning Herald that finds it.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: See how they Muſter one another! O there's a Rank Regiment where the Devil carries the Colours, and his Dam D • um major, now the world and the fleſh come behind with the Carriage.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: Sure this Lady has a good turn done her againſt her will: before ſhe was common talk, now none dare ſay, Cantha • ides can ſtir her, her face looks like a Warrant, willing and commanding all Tongues, as they will anſwer it, to be tied up and bolted when this Lady means to let her ſelf looſe. As I live ſhe has got her a goodly protection, and a gracious; and may uſe her body diſcreetly, for her healths ſake, once a week, excepting Lent and Dog-days: Oh if they were to be got for mony, what a great ſum would come out of the City for theſe Licences?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: To horſe, to horſe, we loſe the morning, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1 Wood.
sp.p: What, have you lodged the Deer?

sp.speaker: 2 Wood.
sp.p: Yes, they are ready for the Bow.

sp.speaker: 1 Wood.
sp.p: Who ſhoots?

sp.speaker: 2 Wood.
sp.p: The Princeſs.

sp.speaker: 1 Wood.
sp.p: No ſhe'l Hunt.

sp.speaker: 2 Wood.
sp.p: She'l take a Stand I ſay.

sp.speaker: 1 Wood.
sp.p: Who elſe?

sp.speaker: 2 Wood.
sp.p: Why the young ſtranger Prince.

sp.speaker: 1 Wood.
sp.p: He ſhall Shoot in a Stone-bow for me. I never lov'd his beyond-ſea-ſhip, ſince he forſook the Say, for paying Ten ſhillings: he was there at the fall of a Deer, and would needs (out of his mightineſs) give Ten groats for the Dowcers; marry the Steward would have had the Velvet-head into the bargain, to Turf his Hat withal: I think he ſhould love Venery, he is an old Sir Triſtram; for if you be remembred, he forſook the Stagg once, to ſtrike a Raſcal Milking in a Medow, and her he kill'd in the eye. Who ſhoots elſe?

sp.speaker: 2 Wood.
sp.p: The Lady Galatea.

sp.speaker: 1 Wood.
sp.p: That's a good wench, and ſhe would not chide us for tumbling of her women in the Brakes. She's liberal, and by my Bow they ſay ſhe's honeſt, and whether that be a fault, I have nothing to do. There's all?

sp.speaker: 2 Wood.
sp.p: No, one more, Megra.

sp.speaker: 1 Wood.
sp.p: That's a ſirker I' faith boy; there's a wench will Ride her Haunces as hard after a Kennel of Hounds, as a Hunting-ſaddle; and when ſhe comes home, get 'em clapt, and all is well again. I have known her loſe her ſelf three times in one Afternoon (if the Woods had been anſwerable) and it has been work enough for one man to find her, and he has ſweat for it. She Rides well, and ſhe payes well. Hark, let's go. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh, that I had been nouriſhed in theſe woods
With Milk of Goats, and Acorns, and not known
The right of Crowns, nor the diſſembling Trains
Of Womens looks; but dig'd my ſelf a Cave,
Where I, my Fire, my Cattel, and my Bed
Might have been ſhut together in one ſhed;
And then had taken me ſome Mountain Girl,
Beaten with Winds, chaſt as the hardened Rocks
Whereon ſhe dwells; that might have ſtrewed my Bed
With leaves, and Reeds, and with the Skins of beaſts
Our Neighbours; and have born at her big breaſts
My large courſe iſſue. This had been a life free from vexation.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Oh wicked men!
An innocent man may walk ſafe among beaſts,
Nothing aſſaults me here. See, my griev'd Lord
Sits as his ſoul were ſearching out a way,
To leave his body. Pardon me that muſt
Break thy laſt commandment; For I muſt ſpeak;
You that are griev'd can pity; hear my Lord.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Is there a Creature yet ſo miſerable,
That I can pity?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Oh my Noble Lord,
View my ſtrange fortune, and beſtow on me,
According to your bounty (if my ſervice
Can merit nothing) ſo much as may ſerve
To keep that little piece I hold of life
From cold and hunger.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Is it thou? be gone:
Go ſell thoſe misbeſeeming Cloaths thou wear'ſt,
And feed thy ſelf with them.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Alas! my Lord, I can get nothing for them:
The ſilly Country people think 'tis Treaſon
To touch ſuch gay things.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Now by my life this is
Unkindly done, to vex me with thy ſight,
Th'art faln again to thy diſſembling trade:
How ſhould'ſt thou think to cozen me again?
Remains there yet a plague untri'd for me?
Even ſo thou wept'ſt and ſpok'ſt when firſt
I took thee up; curſe on the time. If thy
Commanding tears can work on any other,
Uſe thy art, I'le not betray it. Which way
Wilt thou take, that I may ſhun thee;
For thine eyes are poyſon to mine; and I
Am loth to grow in rage. This way, or that way?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Any will ſerve. But I will chuſe to have
That path in chaſe that leads unto my grave.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: This is the ſtrangeſt ſudden change! You Woodman.

sp.speaker: 1 Wood.
sp.l: My Lord Dion.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Saw you a Lady come this way on a Sable-horſe ſtubbed with ſtars of white?

sp.speaker: 2 Wood.
sp.l: Was ſhe not young and tall?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Yes; Rode ſhe to the wood, or to the plain?

sp.speaker: 2 Wood.
sp.l:
Faith my Lord we ſaw none.
Exeunt Wood.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Pox of your queſtions then. What, is ſhe found?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Nor will be I think.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Let him ſeek his Daughter himſelf; ſhe cannot ſtray about a little neceſſary natural buſineſs, but the whole Court muſt be in Arms; when ſhe has done, we ſhall have peace.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: There's already a thouſand fatherleſs tales amongſt us; ſome ſay her Horſe run away with her; ſome a Wolf purſued her; others, it was a plot to kill her; and that Armed men were ſeen in the Wood: but queſtionleſs, ſhe rode away willingly.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Sir, I cannot tell.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How is that? Anſwer me ſo again.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Sir, ſhall I lie?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Yes, lie and damn, rather than tell me that;
I ſay again, where is ſhe? Mutter not;
Sir, ſpeak you where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Sir, I do not know.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Speak that again ſo boldly, and by Heaven
It is thy laſt. You fellows anſwer me,
Where is ſhe? Mark me all, I am your King.
I wiſh to ſee my Daughter, ſhew her me;
I do command you all, as you are ſubjects,
To ſhew her me, what am I not your King?
If I, then am I not to be obeyed?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Yes, if you command things poſſible and honeſt.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Things poſſible and honeſt! Hear me, thou,
Thou Traytor, that dareſt confine thy King to things
Poſſible and honeſt, ſhew her me,
Or let me periſh, if I cover not all Cicily with bloud.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Indeed I cannot, unleſs you tell me where ſhe is.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: You have betray'd me, y'have, let me loſe
The Jewel of my life, go; bring her me,
And ſet her before me; 'tis the King
Will have it ſo, whoſe breath can ſtill the winds,
Uncloud the Sun, charm down the ſwelling Sea,
And ſtop the Flouds of Heaven; ſpeak, can it not?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No, cannot the breath of Kings do this?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: No; nor ſmell ſweet it ſelf, if once the Lungs
Be but corrupted.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Is it ſo? Take heed.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Sir, take you heed; how you dare the powers
That muſt be juſt.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Alas! what are we Kings?
Why do you gods place us above the reſt;
To be ſerv'd, flatter'd, and ador'd till we
Believe we hold within our hands your Thunder,
And when we come to try the power we have,
There's not a leaf ſhakes at our threatnings.
I have fin'd 'tis true, and here ſtand to be puniſh'd;
Yet would not thus be puniſh'd; let me chuſe
My way, and lay it on.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: He Articles with the gods; would ſome body would draw bonds, for the performance of Covenants betwixt them.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What, is ſhe found?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: No, we have ta'ne her Horſe.
He gallopt empty by: there's ſome Treaſon;
You Galatea rode with her into the wood; why left you her?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: She did command me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Command! you ſhould not.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: 'Twould ill become my Fortunes and my Birth
To diſobey the Daughter of my King.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Y'are all cunning to obey us for our hurt,
But I will have her.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: If I have her not,
By this hand there ſhall be no more Cicily.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: What will he carry it to Spain in's pocket?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I will not leave one man alive, but the King,
A Cook and a Taylor.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Yet you may do well to ſpare your Ladies Bed-fellow, and her you may keep for a Spawner.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I ſee the injuries I have done muſt be reveng'd.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Sir, this is not the way to find her out.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Run all, diſperſe your ſelves: the man that finds her,
Or (if ſhe be kill'd) the Traytor; I'le may him great.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I know ſome would give five thouſand pounds to find her.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Come let us ſeek.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Each man a ſeveral way, here I my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen we here.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Lady you muſt go ſearch too.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: I had rather be ſearch'd my ſelf. Exeunt omnes.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Where am I now? Feet find me out a way,
Without the counſel of my troubled head,
I'le follow you boldly about theſe woods,
O're mountains, thorow brambles, pits, and flouds:
Heaven I hope will eaſe me. I am ſick.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Yonder's my Lady; Heaven knows I want nothing;
Becauſe I do not wiſh to live, yet I
Will try her Charity. O hear, you that have plenty,
From that flowing ſtore, drop ſome on dry ground; ſee,
The lively red is gone to guard her heart;
I fear ſhe ſaints. Madam look up, ſhe breaths not;
Open once more thoſe roſie twins, and ſend
Unto my Lord, your lateſt farewell; Oh, ſhe ſtirs:
How is it Madam? Speak comfort.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: 'Tis not gently done,
To put me in a miſerable life,
And hold me there; I pray thee let me go,
I ſhall do beſt without thee; I am well.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I am to blame to be ſo much in rage,
I'le tell her coolely, when and where I heard
This killing truth. I will be temperate
In ſpeaking, and as juſt in hearing.
Oh monſtrous! Tempt me not ye gods, good gods
Tempt not a frail man, what's he, that has a heart
But he muſt eaſe it here?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: My Lord, help the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: I am well, forbear.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Let me love lightning, let me be embrac'd
And kiſt by Scorpions, or adore the eyes
Of Baſilisks, rather than truſt to tongues,
And ſhrink theſe veins up; ſtick me here a ſtone
Laſting to ages in the memory
Of this damn'd act. Hear me you wicked ones,
You have put the hills on fire into this breaſt,
Not to be quench'd with tears, for which may guilt
Sit on your boſoms; at your meals, and beds,
Deſpair await you: what, before my face?
Poyſon of Aſpes between your lips; Diſeaſes
Be your beſt iſſues, Nature make a Curſe
And throw it on you.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Dear Philaſter, leave
To be enrag'd, and hear me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I have done;
Forgive my paſſion, not the calm'd ſea,
When AEolus locks up his windy brood,
Is leſs diſturb'd than I, I'le make you know it.
Dear Arethuſa, do but take this ſword,
And ſearch how temperate a heart I have;
Then you and this your boy, may live and raign
In luſt without control; Wilt thou Bellario?
I prethee kill me; thou art poor, and maiſt
Nouriſh ambitious thoughts, when I am dead:
This way were freer; Am I raging now?
If I were mad I ſhould deſire to live;
Sirs, feel my pulſe; whether have you known
A man in a more equal tune to die?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Alas my Lord, your pulſe keeps madmans time,
So does your tongue.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: You will not kill me then?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Kill you?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Not for a world.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I blame not thee,
Bellario; thou haſt done but that, which gods
Would have transform'd themſelves to do; be gone,
Leave me without reply; this is the laſt
Of all our meeting. Kill me with this ſword;
Be wiſe, or worſe will follow: we are two
Earth cannot bear at once. Reſolve to do, or ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: If my fortunes be ſo good to let me fall
Upon thy hand, I ſhall have peace in death.
Yet tell me this, will there be no ſlanders,
No jealouſies in the other world, no ill there?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Shew me then the way.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Then guide
My feeble hand, you that have power to do it,
For I muſt perform a piece of juſtice. If your youth
Have any way offended Heaven, let prayers
Short and effectual reconcile you to it.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: I am prepared.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.p: I'le ſee the King if he be in the Foreſt, I have hunted him theſe two hours, if I ſhould come home and not ſee him my Siſters would laugh at me; I can ſee nothing but people better horſt than my ſelf, that out • ide me; I can hear nothing but ſhouting. Theſe Kings had need of good brains, this whooping is able to put a mean man out of his wits. There's a Courtier with his ſword drawn, by this hand upon a woman, I think.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Are you at peace?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: With Heavens and Earth.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: May they divide thy ſoul and body?

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.p: Hold daſtard, ſtrike a Woman! 'th'art a craven I warrant thee, thou wouldſt be loth to play half a dozen of venies at waſters with a good fellow for a broken head.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Leave us good friend.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: What ill bred man a • t thou, to intrude thy ſelf
Upon our private ſports, our recreations?

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: God 'uds, I underſtand you not, but I know the Rogue has hu • t you.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Purſue thy own affairs: it will be ill
To multiply bloud upon my head; which thou wilt force me to.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.p: I know not your Rhetorick, but I can lay it on if you touch the woman. They fight.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Slave, take what thou deſerveſt.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Heavens guard my Lord.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: Oh do you breath?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I hear the tread of people: I am hurt.
The gods take part againſt me, could this Poor
Have held me thus elſe? I muſt ſhift for life,
Though I do loath it. I would find a courſe,

To loſe it, rather by my will than force.
Exit Phil.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.p: I cannot follow the Rogue. I pray thee wench come and kiſs me now.

div.stage: Enter Pha • a. Dion, Cle. Thra. and Woodmen.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: What art thou?

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: Almoſt kil'd I am for a fooliſh woman; a knave has hurt her.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: The Princeſs Gentlemen! Where's the wound Madam?
Is it dangerous?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: He has not hurt me.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: I'ſaith ſhe lies, has hurt her in the breaſt, look elſe.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: O ſacred ſpring of innocent blood!

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: 'Tis above wonder! who ſhould dare this?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: I felt it not.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Speak villain, who has hurt the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: Is it the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: Then I have ſeen ſomething yet.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: But who has hurt her?

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: I told you a Rogue I ne're ſaw him before, I.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Madam who did it?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Some diſhoneſt wretch, Alas I know him not,
And do forgive him.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.p: He's hurt too, he cannot go far, I made my Fathers old Fox flie about his ears.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: How will you have me kill him?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Not at all, 'tis ſome diſtracted fellow.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: By this hand, I'le leave ne'er a piece of him bigger than a Nut, and bring him all in my Hat.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Nay, good Sir;
If you do take him, bring him quick to me,
And I will ſtudy for a puniſhment,
Great as his fault.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: But ſwear.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.p: By all my love I will: Woodmen conduct the Princeſs to the King, and bear that wounded fellow to dreſſing: Come Gentlemen, we'l follow the chaſe cloſe.

div.stage: Ex. Are. Pha. Di. Cle. Thra. and 1 Woodman

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: I pray you friend let me ſee the King.

sp.speaker: 2 Wood.
sp.l: That you ſhall, and receive thanks. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: If I get clear with this, I'le go ſee no more gay ſights

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: A heavineſs near death ſits on my brow,
And I muſt ſleep: Bear me thou gentle bank,
For ever if thou wilt: you ſweet ones all,
Let me unworthy preſs you: I could wiſh
I rather were a Coarſe ſtrewed o're with you,
Than quick above you. Dulneſs ſhuts mine eyes,
And I am giddy; Oh that I could take
So ſound a ſleep, that I might never wake.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I have done ill, my conſcience calls me falſe,
To ſtrike at her, that would not ſtrike at me:
When I did ſight, me thought I heard her pray
The gods to guard me. She may be abus'd,
And I a loathed villain: if ſhe be,
She will conceal who hurt her; He has wounds,
And cannot follow, neither knows he me.
Who's this; Bellario ſleeping? If thou beeſt
Guilty, there is no juſtice that thy ſleep Cry within.
Should be ſo ſound, and mine, whom thou haſt wrong'd,
So broken: Hark I am purſued: you gods
I'le take this offer'd means of my eſcape:
They have no mark to know me, but my wounds,
If ſhe be true; if falſe, let miſchief light
On all the world at once. Sword, print my wounds
Upon this ſleeping boy: I ha' none I think
Are mortal, nor would I lay greater on thee. Wounds him.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Oh death I hope is come, bleſt be that hand,
It meant me well; again, for pities ſake.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I have caught my ſelf, Phi. falls.
The loſs of bloud hath ſtayed my flight. Here, here,
Is he that ſtroke thee: take thy full revenge,
Uſe me, as I did mean thee, worſe than death:
I'le teach thee to revenge, this luckleſs hand
Wounded the Princeſs, tell my followers
Thou didſt receive theſe hurts in ſtaying me,
And I will ſecond thee: Get a reward.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Fly, fly my Lord and ſave your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: How's this?
Wouldſt thou I ſhould be ſafe?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Elſe it were vain
For me to live. Theſe little wounds I have,
Ha' not bled much, reach me that noble hand,
I'le help to cover you.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Art thou true to me?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Or let me periſh loath'd. Come my good Lord,
Creep in amongſt thoſe buſhes: who does know
But that the gods may ſave your (much lov'd) breath?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Then I ſhall die for grief, if not for this,
That I have wounded thee: what wilt thou do?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Shift for my ſelf well: peace, I hear 'em come.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Follow, follow, follow; that way they went.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: With my own wounds I'le bloudy my own ſword.
I need not counterfeit to fall; Heaven knows,
That I can ſtand no longer.

div.stage: Enter Pha. Dion, Cle. and Thra.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: To this place we have tract him by his bloud.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Yonder, my Lord, creeps one away.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Stay Sir, what are you?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: A wretched creature wounded in theſe Woods
By Beaſts; relieve me, if your names be men,
Or I ſhall periſh.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: This is he my Lord,
Upon my ſoul that hurt her; 'tis the boy,
That wicked boy that ſerv'd her.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: O thou damn'd in thy creation!
What cauſe could'ſt thou ſhape to hurt the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Then I am betrayed.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Betrayed! no, apprehended.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: I confeſs;
Urge it no more, that big with evil thoughts
I ſet upon her, and did take my aim
Her death. For charity let fall at once
The puniſhment you mean, and do not load
This weary fleſh with tortures.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I will know who hir'd thee to this deed?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Mine own revenge.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Revenge, for what?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: It pleas'd her to receive
Me as her Page, and when my fortunes ebb'd,
That men ſtrid o're them careleſly, ſhe did ſhowr
Her welcome graces on me, and did ſwell
My fortunes, till they overflow'd their banks,
Threatning the men that croſt 'em; when as ſwift
As ſtorms ariſe at ſea, ſhe turn'd her eyes
To burning Suns upon me, and did dry
The ſtreams ſhe had beſtowed, leaving me worſe
And more contemn'd than other little brooks,
Becauſe I had been great: In ſhort, I knew
I could not live, and therefore did deſire
To die reveng'd.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: If tortures can be found,
Long as thy natural life, reſolve to feel
The utmoſt rigour. Philaſter creeps out of a buſh.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Help to lead him hence.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Turn back you raviſhers of Innocence,
Know ye the price of that you bear away ſo rudely?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: 'Tis the Lord Philaſter.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: 'Tis not the treaſure of all Kings in one,
The wealth of Tagus, nor the Rocks of Pearl,
That pave the Court of Neptune, can weigh down
That vertue. It was I that hurt the Princeſs.
Place me, ſome god, upon a Piramis,
Higher than hills of earth, and lend a voice
Loud as your Thunder to me, that from thence,
I may diſcourſe to all the under-world,
The worth that dwells in him.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: My Lord, ſome man
Weary of life, that would be glad to die.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Leave theſe untimely courteſies Bellario.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Alas he's mad, come will you lead me on?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: By all the Oaths that men ought moſt to keep:
And Gods do puniſh moſt, when men do break,
He toucht her not. Take heed Bellario,
How thou doſt drown the vertues thou haſt ſhown
With perjury. By all that's good 'twas I:
You know ſhe ſtood betwixt me and my right.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Thy own tongue be thy judge.

sp.speaker: Cle
sp.l: It was Philaſter.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Is 't not a brave boy?
Well Sirs, I fear we were all deceived.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Have I no friend here?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Then ſhew it;
Some good body lend a hand to draw us nearer.
Would you have tears ſhed for you when you die •
Then lay me gentle on his neck that there
I may weep flouds, and breath out my ſpirit:
'Tis not the wealth of Plutus, nor the gold
Lockt in the heart of earth, can buy away
This arm-full from me, this had been a ranſ • m
To have redeem'd the great Auguſtus C • ſar,
Had he been taken: you hard-hearted men,
More ſtony than theſe Mountains, can you ſee
Such clear pure bloud drop, and not cut your fleſh
To ſtop his life? To bind whoſe better woun • s,
Queens ought to tear their hair, and with their tears,
Bath'em. Forgive me, thou that art the wealth of poor Phi. laſter.

div.stage: Enter King, Arethuſa and a Guard.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Is the villain ta'ne?

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Sir, here be two confeſs the deed, but ſay it was Phi. laſter.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Queſtion it no more, it was.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: The fellow that did fight with him will tell us.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Ay me, I know he will.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Did not you know him?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Sir, if it was he, he was diſguiſed.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I was ſo. Oh my ſ • ars! that I ſhould live ſtill.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Thou ambitious fool;
Thou that haſt laid a train for thy own life;
Now I do mean to do, I'le leave to talk, bear him to priſon

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Sir, they did plot together to take hence
This harmleſs life; ſhould it paſs unreveng'd,
I ſhould to earth go weeping: grant me then
(By all the love a Father bears his Child)
Their cuſtodies, and that I may appoint
Their tortures and their death.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Death? ſoft, our Law will not reach that, for this fault.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: 'Tis granted, take 'em to you, with a Guard.
Come Princely Pharamond, this buſineſs paſt,
We may with more ſecurity go on to your intended match.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.p: I pray that this action loſe not Philaſter the hearts of the people.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Fear it not, their overwiſe heads will think it but a trick.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: HAS the King ſent for him to death?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Yes, but the King muſt know, 'tis not in his power to war with Heaven.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: We linger time; the King ſent for Philaſter and the Headſman an hour ago.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: Are all his wounds well?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: All they were but ſcratches; but the loſs of bloud made him faint.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: We dally Gentlem • n.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: Away.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: We'l ſcuffle hard before he periſh. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Nay dear Philaſter grieve not, we are well.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Nay good my Lord forbear, we are wondrous well.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh Arethuſa! O Bellario! leave to be kind:
I ſhall be ſhot from Heaven, as now from Earth,
If you continue ſo; I am a man,
Falſe to a pair of the moſt truſly ones
That ever earth bore, can it bear us all?
Forgive and leave me, but the King hath ſent
To call me to my death, Oh ſhew it me,
And then forget me: And for thee my boy,
I ſhall deliver words will mollifie
The hearts of beaſts, to ſpare thy innocence.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Alas my Lord, my life is not a thing
Worthy your noble thoughts; 'tis not a life,
'Tis but a piece of child-hood thrown away:
Should I out-live, I ſhall then out live
Vertu • and honour. And when that day comes,
If • v •• I ſhould cloſe theſe eyes but once,
May I live ſpotted for my perjury,
And waſ •• my limbs to nothing.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: And I (the woful'ſt maid as ever was,
Fo 〈◊〉 with my hands to bring my Lord to death)
Do b • th honour of a Virgin ſwear,
To t • ll no hours beyond it.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Make me not hated ſo.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Come from this priſon, all joyful to our deaths.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: People will tear me when they find you true
To ſuch a wretch as I; I ſhall die loath'd.
〈◊〉 our Kingdoms peaceably, whil'ſt I

Fo •
〈◊〉
• l • p ſo, gotten with my faults,
I ver • put 〈◊〉 , every maid in love
Will have a piece of me if you be true.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: My dear Lord ſay not ſo.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: A piece of you?
He was not born of women that can out it and look on.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Take me in tears betwixt you,
For my heart will break with ſhame and ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Why 'tis well.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Lament no more.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What would you have done
If you had wrong'd me baſely, and had found
My life no price, compar'd to yours? For love Sirs,
Deal with me truly.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: 'Twas miſtaken, Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why if it were?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Then Sir we would have ask'd you pardon.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And have hope to enjoy it?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Injoy it? I.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Would you indeed? be plain.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: We would my Lord.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Forgive me then.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: So, ſo.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: 'Tis as it ſhould be now.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Lead to my death. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter King, Dion, Cleremont, and Thraſiline.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Gentlemen, who ſaw the Prince?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: So pl ••• you Sir, he's gone to ſee the City,
And t •• new Platform, with ſome Gentlemen
Atten • ing on him.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Is the Princeſs ready,
To bring her priſoner out?

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.l: She waits your Grace.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Tell her we ſtay.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: King, you may be deceiv'd yet:
The head you a m •• coſt more ſetting on
Than to be loſt ſo ſlightly: If it muſt off
Like a wild overflow, that ſoops before him
A golden Stack, and with it ſhakes down Bridges,
Cracks the ſtrong hearts of Pines, whoſe Cable roots
H • ld out a thouſand Storms, a thouſand Thunders,
And ſo made mightier, takes whole Villages
Upon his back, and in that heat of pride,
Charges ſtrong Towns, Towers, Caſtles, Palaces,
And layes them deſolate: ſo ſhall thy head,
Thy noble head, bury the lives of thouſands
That muſt bleed with thee like a ſacrifice,
In thy red ruines.

div.stage: Enter Phil. Are. and Bell. in a Robe and Garland.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How now, what Mask is this?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Right Royal Sir, I ſhould
Sing you an Epithalamium of theſe lovers,
But having loſt my beſt ayres with my fortunes,
And wanting a celeſtial Harp to ſtrike
This bleſſed union on; thus in glad ſtory
I give you all. Theſe two fair Cedar-branches,
The nobleſt of the Mountain, where they grew
Straighteſt and talleſt, under whoſe ſtill ſhades
The worthie • beaſts have made their layers, and ſlept

Free from the
• y •• a •
Sta • , and the fell Thunder-ſtroke,
Free from the Clouds, when they were big with humour,
And delivered in thouſand ſpouts, their iſſues to the earth:
O there was none but ſilent quiet there!
Till never pleas'd fortune ſhot up ſhrubs,
Baſe under brambles to divorce theſe branches;
And for a while they did ſo, and did raign
Over the Mountain, and choakt up his beauty
With Brakes, rude Thornes and Thiſtles, till thy Sun
Scorcht them even to the roots, and dried them there:
And now a gentle gale hath blown again
That made theſe branches meet, and twine together,
Never to be divided: The god that ſings
His holy numbers over marriage beds,
Hath knit their noble hearts, and here they ſtand
Your Children mighty King, and I have done.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How, how?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Sir, if you love it in plain truth,
For there is no Masking in't; This Gentleman
The priſoner that you gave me is become
My keeper, and through all the bitter throws
Your jealouſies and his ill fate have wrought him,
Thus nobly hath he ſtrangled, and at length
Arriv'd here my dear Husband.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Your dear Husband! call in
The Captain of the Cittadel; There you ſhall keep
Your Wedding. I'le provide a Mask ſhall make
Your Hymen turn his Saffron into a ſullen Coat,
And ſing ſad Requiems to your departing ſouls:
Bloud ſhall put out your Torches, and inſtead
Of gaudy flowers about your wanton necks,
An Ax ſhall hang like a prodigious Meteor
Ready to crop your loves ſweets. Hear you gods:
From this time do I ſhake all title off,
Of Father to this woman, this baſe woman,
And what there is of vengeance, in a Lion
Caſt amongſt Dogs, or rob'd of his dear young,
The ſame inforc't more terrible, more mighty,
Expect from me.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Sir,
By that little life I have left to ſwear by,
There's nothing that can ſtir me from my ſelf.
What I have done, I have done without repentance,
For death can be no Bug-bear unto me,
So long as Pharamond is not my headſman.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Sweet peace upon thy ſoul, thou worthy maid
When ere thou dyeſt; for this time I'le excuſe thee,
Or be thy Prologue.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Sir, let me ſpeak next,
And let my dying words be better with you
Than my dull living actions; if you aime
At the dear life of this ſweet Innocent,
Y'are a Tyrant and a ſavage Monſter;
Your memory ſhall be as ſoul behind you
As you are living, all your better deeds
Shall be in water writ, but this in Marble:
No Chronicle ſhall ſpeak you, though your own,
But for the ſhame of men. No Monument
(Though high and big as Pelion) ſhall be able
To cover this baſe murther; make it rich
With Braſs, with pureſt Gold, and ſhining Jaſper,
Like the Pyramids, lay on Epitaphs,
Such as make great men gods; my little marble
(That only cloaths my aſhes, not my faults)
Shall far out ſhine it: And for after iſſues
Think not ſo madly of the heavenly wiſdoms,
That they will give you more, for your mad rage
To cut off, unleſs it be ſome Snake, or ſomething
Like your ſelf, that in his birth ſhall ſtrangle you.
Remember, my Father, King; there was a fault,
But I forgive it: let that ſin perſwade you
To love this Lady. If you have a ſoul,
Think, ſave her, and be ſaved, for my ſelf,
I have ſo long expected this glad hour,
So languiſht under you, and daily withered,
That heaven knows it is my joy to dye,
I find a recreation in't.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: Where's the King?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Here.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: Get you to your ſtrength,
And reſcue the Prince Pharamond from danger,
He's taken priſoner by the Citizens,
Fearing the Lord Philaſter.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Oh brave followers;
Mutiny, my fine dear Country-men, mutiny,
Now my brave valiant foremen, ſhew your weapons
In honour of your Miſtreſſes.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: Arm, arm, arm.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: A thouſand devils take 'em.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: A thouſand bleſſing on 'em.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: Arm O King, the City is in mutiny,
Led by an old Gray Ruffin, who comes on

In reſcue of the Lord Philaſter.
Exit with Are. Phi. Bell.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Away to the Cittadel, I'le ſee them ſafe,
And then cope with theſe Burgers: Let the Guard
And all the Gentlemen give ſtrong attendance. Ex. King.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: The City up! this was above our wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I and the Marriage too; by my life,
sp.p: This noble Lady has deceiv'd us all, a plague upon my ſelf; a thouſand plagues, for having ſuch unworthy thoughts of her dear honour: O I could beat my ſelf, or do you beat me and I'le beat you, for we had all one thought.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: No, no, 'twill but loſe time.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: You ſay true, are your ſwords ſharp? Well my dear Country-men, what ye lack, if you continue and fall not back upon the firſt broken ſhin, I'le have you chronicled, and chronicled, and cut and chronicled and all to be prais'd, and ſung in Sonnets, and bath'd in new brave Ballads, that all tongues ſhall troule you in Saecula Saeculorum my kind Can carriers.

sp.speaker: Thra.
sp.p: What if a toy take 'em i'th' heels now, and they run all away, and cry the Devil take the hindmoſt?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Then the ſame Devil take the foremoſt too, and fowce him for his breakfaſt; if they all prove Cowards, my curſes fly amongſt them and be ſpeeding. May they have Murreins raign to keep the Gentlemen at home unbound in eaſie freez: May the Moths branch their Velvets, and their Silks only be worn before ſore eyes. May their falſe lights undo 'em, and diſcover preſſes, holes, ſtains, and oldneſs in their Stuffs, and make them ſhop-rid: May they keep Whores and Horſes, and break; and live mued up with necks of Beef and Turnips: May they have many children, and none like the Father: May they know no language but that gibberiſh they prattle to their Parcels, unleſs it be the goariſh Latine they write in their bonds, and may they write that falſe, and loſe their debts.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Now the vengeance of all the gods confound them; how they ſwarm together! what a hum they raiſe; Devils choak your wilde throats; If a man had need to uſe their valours, he muſt pay a Brokage for it, and then bring 'em on, they will fight like ſheep. 'Tis Philaſter, none but Philaſter muſt allay this heat: They will not hear me ſpeak, but ſling di • t at me, and call me Tyrant. Oh run dear friend, and bring the Lord Philaſter: ſpeak him fair, call him Prince, do him all the courteſie you can, commend me to him. Oh my wits, my wits!
Exit Cle.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Oh my brave Countrymen! as I live, I will not buy a pin out of your walls for this; Nay, you ſhall cozen me, and I'le thank you; and ſend you Brawn and Bacon, and ſoil you every long vacation a brace of foremen, that at Michaelmas ſhall come up fat and kicking.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: What they will do with this poor Prince, the gods know, and I fear.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.p: Why Sir: they'l flea him, and make Church Buckets on's skin to ſquench rebellion, then clap a rivet in's ſconce, and hang him up for a ſign.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: O worthy Sir forgive me, do not make
Your miſeries and my faults meet together,
To bring a greater danger. Be your ſelf,
Still ſound amongſt Diſeaſes, I have wrong'd you,
And though I find it laſt, and beaten to it,
Let firſt your goodneſs know it. Calm the people,
And be what you were born to: take your love,
And with her my repentance, and my wiſh •
And all my prayers, by the gods my heart ſpeaks this:
And if the l • aſt fall from me not perform'd,
May I be ſt •• ck with Thunder.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Mighty Sir,
I will not do your greatneſs ſo much wrong,
As not to make your word truth; free the Princeſs,
And the poor boy, and let me ſtand the ſhock
Of this mad Sea breach, which I'le either turn
Or periſh with it.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Let your own word free them.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Then thus I take my leave kiſſing your hand,
And hanging on your Royal word: be Kingly,
And be not moved Sir, I ſhall bring your peace,
Or never bring my ſelf back.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: All the gods go with thee. Exeunt Omnes.

div.stage: Enter an old Captain and Citizens with Pharamond.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Come my brave Mirmidons let's fall on, let our caps
Swarm my boys, and you nimble tongues forget your mothers
Gibberiſh, of what do you lack, and ſet your mouths
Up Children, till your Pallats fall frighted hal • a
Fathom, paſt the cure of Bay-ſalt and groſs P • pper.
And then cry Philaſter, brave Philaſter,
Let Philaſter be deeper in requeſt, my ding dongs,
My pairs of dear Indentures, King of Cl •• s,
Than your cold water Chamblets o • your paintings
Spitted with Copper; let not your haſty Silks,
Or your branch'd Cloth of Bodkin, or your Tiſhues,
Dearly belov'd of ſpiced Cake and Cuſtard,
Your Robin-hoods ſcarlets and Johns, tie your affections
In darkneſs to your ſhops; no, dainty Duckers,
Up with your three pil'd ſpirits, your wrought valours.
And let your un-cut Coller make the King feel
The meaſure of your mightineſs Philaſter.
Cry my Roſe nobles, cry.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Philaſter, Philaſter.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: How do you like this my Lord Prince, theſe are mad boys, I tell you, theſe are things that will not ſtrike their top-ſayles to a Foiſt. And let a man of war, an Argoſie hull and cry Cockles.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Why you rude ſlave, do you know what you do?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: My Pretty Prince of Puppets, we do know,
And give your greatneſs warning, that you talk
No more ſuch Bugs-words, or that ſoldred Crown
Shall be ſcratch'd with a Musket: Dear Prince Pippen,
Down with your noble bloud; or as I live,
I'le have you codled: let him loſe my ſpirits,
Make us a round Ring with your Bills my H • ct •• s,
And let us ſee what this trim man dares do.
Now Sir, have at you; here I it,
And with this ſwaſhing blow, do you ſwear Prince;
I could hulk your Grace, and hang you up croſs leg'd,
Like a Hare at a Poulters, and do this with this w • per.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: You will not ſee me murder'd wicked V •• a • s?

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.l: Yes indeed will we Sir, we hav • not ſeen one for a great while.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: He would have weapons would he? give him a Broad-ſide my brave boyes with your pikes, branch in his skin in Flowers like a Satin, and between every Flow • a mortal cut, your Royalty ſhall ravel, jag him Gentlemen. • 'le have him cut to the kell, then down the ſea • es, oh for a whip
sp.l: To make him Galoone-Laces,
I'le have a Coach-whip.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: O ſpare me Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Hold, hold, the man begins to fear and know himſelf
He ſhall for this time only be ſcal'd up
With a Feather through his noſe, that he may only ſee
Heaven, and think whither he's going,
Nay beyond Sea Sir, we will proclaim you, you would be King
Thou tender •• ir apparent to a Church-Ale,
Thou Royal Ring-tail, fit to fly at nothing
But poor mens Poultry, and have every Boy
Beat thee from that too with his Bread and Butter.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Gods keep me from theſe Hell-hounds.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: Shall's g • ld him Captain?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: No, you ſhall ſpare his dowcets my dear Donſels,
As you reſpect the Ladies let them flouriſh;
The curſes of a longing woman kill as ſpeedy as a Plague, Boys.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.l: I'le have a Leg that's certain.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: I'le have an Arm.

sp.speaker: 3 Cit.
sp.p: I'le have his Noſe, and at mine own charge build a Colledge, and clap't upon the Gate.

sp.speaker: 4 Cit.
sp.l: I'le have his little Gut to ſtring a Kit with,
For certainly a Royal Gut will found like ſilver.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Would they were in thy belly, and I paſt my pain once.

sp.speaker: 5 Cit.
sp.l: Good Captain let me have his Liver to ſeed Ferrets.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Who will have parcels elſe? ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Good gods conſider me, I ſhall be tortur'd.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Captain, I'le give you the trimming of your hand-ſword, and let me have his Skin to make falſe Scabbards.

sp.l: He had no horns Sir had he?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: No Sir, he's a Pollard, what would'ſt thou do with horns?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: O if he had, I would have made rare Haſts and Whiſtles of 'em, but his Shin bones if they be ſound ſhall ſerve me.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Long live Philaſter, the brave Prince Philaſter.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I thank you Gentlemen, but why are theſe
Rude weapons brought abroad, to teach your hands
Uncivil Trades?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: My Royal Roſiclear,
We are thy Mirmidons, thy Guard, thy Rorers,
And when thy noble body is in durance,
Thus do we clap our muſty Mutrions on,
And trace the ſtreets in terrour: Is it peace
Thou Mars of men? Is the King ſociable,
And bids thee live? Art thou above thy ſoemen,
And free as Phoebus? Speak, if not, this ſtand
Of Royal blood ſhall be abroach, atilt, and run
Even to the lees of honour.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Hold and be ſatisfied, I am my ſelf
Free as my thoughts are, by the gods I am.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Art thou the dainty darling of the King?
Art thou the Hylas to our Hercules?
Do the Lords bow, and the regarded ſcarlets,
Kiſs their Gumd go's, and cry, we are your ſervants?
Is the Court Navigable, and the preſence ſtruck
With Flags of friendſhip? if not, we are thy Caſtle
And this man ſleeps.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I am what I deſire to be, your friend,
I am what I was born to be, your Prince.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: Sir, there is ſome humanity in you,
You have a noble ſoul, forget my name,
And know my miſery, ſet me ſafe aboard
From theſe wild Cambals, and as I live,
I'le quit this Land for ever: there is nothing,
Perpetual priſonment, cold, hunger, ſickneſs
Of all ſorts, all dangers, and all together
The worſt company of the worſt men, madneſs, age,
To be as many Creatures as a woman,
And do as all they do, nay to deſpair;
But I would rather make it a new Nature,
And live with all thoſe than endure one hour
Amongſt theſe wild Dogs.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I do pity you: Friends diſcharge your fears,
Deliver me the Prince, I'le warrant you
I ſhall be old enough to find my ſafety.

sp.speaker: 3 Cit.
sp.l: Good Si • take heed he does not hurt you,
He's a fierce man I can tell you Sir.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Prince, by your leave I'le have a Surſingle,
And Male you like a Hawke. He ſtirs.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Away, away, there is no danger in him:
Alas he had rather ſleep to ſhake his fit off.
Look you friends, how gently he leads, upon my word
He's tame enough, he need no further watching.
Good my friends go to your houſes and by me have your pardons, and my love,
And know there ſhall be nothing in my power
You may deſerve, but you ſhall have your wiſhes.
To give you more thanks were to ſlatter you,
Continue ſtill your love, and for an earneſt
Drink this.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l:
Long maiſt thou live brave Prince, brave Prince, brave Prince.
Exeunt Phi. and Pha.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Thou art the King of Courteſie:
Fall off again my ſweet youths, come and every man
Trace to his houſe again, and hang his pewter up, then to
The Tavern and bring your wives in Muſſes: we will have
Muſick and the red grape ſhall make us dance, and riſe Boys

div.stage: Enter King, Are. Gal. Meg. Cle. Dion, Thra. Bellario, and Attendants.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Is it appeas'd?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Sir, all is quiet as this dead of night,
As peaceable as ſleep, my Lord Philaſter
Brings on the Prince himſelf.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Kind Gentlemen!
I will not break the leaſt word I have given
In promiſe to him, I have heap'd a world
Of grief upon his head, which yet I hope
To waſh away.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: My Lord is come.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: My Son!
Bleſt be the time that I have leave to call
Such vertue mine; now thou art in mine arms,
Me thinks I have a ſalve unto my breaſt
For all the ſtings that dwell there, ſtreams of grief
That I have wrought thee, and as much of joy
That I repent it, iſſue from mine eyes:
Let them appeaſe thee, take thy right; take her,
She is thy right too, and forget to urge
My vexed ſoul with that I did before.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Sir, is it blotted from my memory,
Paſt and forgotten: For you Prince of Spain,
Whom I have thus redeem'd, you have full leave
To make an honourable voyage home.
And if you would go furniſh'd to your Realm
With fair proviſion, I do ſee a Lady
Me thinks would gladly bear you company.
How like you this piece?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Sir, he likes it well,
For he hath tried it, and found it worth
His princely liking; we were ta'ne a bed,
I know your meaning, I am not the firſt
That Nature taught to ſeek a fellow forth:
Can ſhame remain perpetually in me,
And not in others? or have Princes ſalves
To cure ill names that meaner people want?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What mean you?

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: You muſt get another ſhip
To clear the Princeſs and the boy together.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: How now!

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: Others took me, and I took her and him
At that all women may be ta'ne ſometimes:
Ship us all four my Lord, we can endure
Weather and wind alike.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Clear thou thy ſelf, or know not me for Father.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: This earth, How falſe it is? what means is left for me
To clear my ſelf? It lies in your belief,
My Lords believe me, and let all things elſe
Struggle together to diſhonour me.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: O ſtop your cars great King, that I may ſpeak
As freedom would, then I will call this Lady
As baſe as be her actions, hear me Sir,
Believe hour hated bloud when it rebels
Againſt your reaſon ſooner than this Lady.

sp.speaker: Meg.
sp.l: By this good light he bears it hanſomely.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: This Lady? I will ſooner truſt the wind
With Feathers, or the troubled Sea with Pearl,
Than her with any thing; believe her not!
Why think you, if I did believe her words;
I would outlive 'em: honour cannot take
Revenge on you, then what were to be known
But death?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Forget her Sir, ſince all is knit
Between us: but I muſt requeſt of you
One favour, and will ſadly be denied.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Command what ere it be.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Swear to be true to what you promiſe.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: By the powers above,
Let it not be the death of her or him,
And it is granted.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Bear away the boy
To Torture, I will have her clear'd or buried.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: O let me call my words back, worthy Sir,
Ask ſomething elſe, bury my life and right
In one poor grave, but do not take away my life and fame at once

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Away with him, it ſtands irrevocable.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Turn all your eyes on me, here ſtands a man
The falſeſt and the baſeſt of this world:
Set ſwords againſt this breaſt ſome honeſt man,
For I have liv'd till I am pitied,
My former deeds are hateful, but this laſt
Is pitifull, for I unwillingly
Have given the dear preſerver of my life
Unto his Torture: is it in the power Offers to kill himſelf.
Of fleſh and blood, to carry this and live?

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: Dear Sir be patient yet, or ſtay that hand.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Sirs, ſtrip that boy.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Come Sir, your tender fleſh will try your conſtancie.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: O kill me gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: No, help Sirs.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Will you Torture me?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Haſt there, why ſtay you?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Then I ſhall not break my vow,
You know juſt gods, though I diſcover all.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How's that? Will he confeſs?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Sir, ſo he ſays.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Speak then.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Great King if you command
This Lord to talk with me alone, my tongue
Urg'd by my heart, ſhall utter all the thoughts
My youth hath known, and ſtranger things than theſe
You hear not often.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Walk aſide with him.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Why ſpeak'ſt thou not?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Know you this face my Lord?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Have you not ſeen it, nor the like?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Yes, I have ſeen the like, but readily
I know not where.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: I have been often told
In Court, of one Euphraſia, a Lady
And Daughter to you; betwixt whom and me
(They that would flatter my bad face would ſwear)
There was ſuch ſtrange reſemblance, that we two
Could not be known aſunder, dreſt alike.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: By Heaven and ſo there is.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: For her fair ſake,
Who now doth ſpend the ſpring time of her life
In holy Pilgrimage, move to the King,
That I may ſcape this Torture.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: But thou ſpeak'ſt
As like Euphraſia as thou doſt look,
How came it to thy knowledge that ſhe lives in Pilgrimage?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: I know it not my Lord,
But I have heard it, and do ſcarce believe it.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Oh my ſhame, is't poſſible? Draw near,
That I may gaze upon thee, art thou ſhe?
Or elſe her Murderer? where wert thou born?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: In Siracuſa.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: What's thy name?

l.hi: Euphraſia.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: O'tis juſt, 'tis ſhe now, I do know thee, Oh that thou hadſt died
And I had never ſeen thee nor my ſhame,
How ſhall I own thee? ſhall this tongue of mine
E're call thee Daughter more?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Would I had died indeed, I wiſh it too,
And ſo I muſt have done by vow, e're publiſhed
What I have told, but that there was no means
To hide it longer, yet I joy in this,
The Princeſs is all clear.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What have you done?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: All is diſcovered.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why then hold you me?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: All is diſcovered, pray you let me go.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Stay him.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: What is diſcovered? He offers to ſtab himſelf.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: Why my ſhame, it is a woman, let her ſpeak the reſt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: How! that again.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: It is a woman.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Bleſt be you powers that favour innocence.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Lay hold upon that Lady.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: It is a woman Sir, hark Gentlemen!
It is a woman. Arethuſa take
My ſoul into thy breaſt, that would be gone
With joy: it is a woman, thou art fair,
And vertuous ſtill to ages, in deſpight of malice.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Speak you, where lies his ſhame?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: I am his Daughter.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: The Gods are juſt.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: I dare accuſe none, but before you two
The vertue of our age, I bend my knee
For mercy.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Take it freely; for I know,
Though what thou didſt were undiſcreetly done,
'Twas meant well.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: And for me,
I have a power to pardon ſins as oft
As any man has power to wrong me.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Noble and worthy.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: But Bellario,
(For I muſt call thee ſtill ſo) tell me why
Thou didſt conceal thy Sex, it was a fault,
A fault Bellario, though thy other deeds
Of truth outweigh'd it: All theſe Jealouſies
Had flown to nothing, if thou hadſt diſcovered,
What now we know.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: My Father would oft ſpeak
Your worth and vertue, and as I did grow
More and more apprehenſive, I did thirſt
To ſee the man ſo rais'd, but yet all this
Was but a Maiden longing to be loſt
As ſoon as found, till ſitting in my window,
Printing my thoughts in Lawne, I ſaw a God
I thought (but it was you) enter our Gates,
My bloud flew out, and back again as faſt
As I had puft it forth, and ſuck't it in
Like breath, then was I call'd away in haſt
To entertain you. Never was a man
Heav'd from a Sheep-coat to a Scepter rais'd
So high in thoughts as I, you left a kiſs
Upon theſe lips then, which I mean to keep
From you for ever, I did hear you talk
Far above ſinging; after you were gone,
I grew acquainted with my heart, and ſearch'd
What ſtir'd it ſo, Alas I found it love,
Yet far from 〈◊〉 for could I have but liv'd
In preſence of you, I had had my end,
For this I did delude my noble Father
With a feign'd Pilgrimage, and dreſt my ſelf
In habit of a boy, and, for I knew
My birth no match for you, I was paſt hope
Of having you. And underſtanding well
That when I made diſcovery of my Sex,
I could not ſtay with you, I made a vow
By all the moſt religious things a Maid
Could call together, never to be known,
Whilſt there was hope to hide me from mens eyes,
For other than I ſeem'd; that I might ever
Abide with you, then fate I by the Fount
Where firſt you took me up.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Search out a match
Within our Kingdom where and when thou wilt,
And I will pay thy Dowry, and thy ſelf
Wilt well deſerve him.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Never Sir will I
Ma • ry, it is a thing within my vow,
But if I may have leave to ſerve the Princeſs,
To ſee the vertues of her Lord and her,
I ſhall have hope to live.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: I Philaſter,
Cannot be jealous, though you had a Lady
Dreſt like a Page to ſerve you, nor will I
Suſpect her living here: come live with me,
Live free, as I do, ſhe that loves my Lord,
Curſt be the wife that hates her.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I grieve ſuch vertues ſhould be laid in earth
Without an Heir; hear me my Royal Father,
Wrong not the freedom of our ſouls ſo much,
To think to take revenge of that baſe woman,
Her malice cannot hurt us: ſet her free
As ſhe was born, ſaving from ſhame and ſin.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Set her at liberty, but leave the Court,
This is no place for ſuch: you Pharamond
Shall have free paſſage, and a conduct home
Worthy ſo great a Prince, when you come there,
Remember 'twas your faults that loſt you her,
And not my purpos'd will.

sp.speaker: Pha.
sp.l: I do confeſs,
Renowned Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Laſt joyn your hands in one, enjoy Philaſter
This Kingdom which is yours, and after me
What ever I call mine, my bleſſing on you,
All happy hours be at your Marriage joyes,
That you may grow your ſelves over all Lands,
And live to ſee your plenteous branches ſpring
Where ever there is Sun. Let Princes learn
By this to rule the paſſions of their blood,
For what Heaven wills, can never be withſtood.

list.item: Gobrias, Lord Protector, and Father of Arbaces.
Philip, a ſervant, and two Citizens Wives.
Spaconia, A Lady Daughter of Ligones.
Mandane, A waiting woman, and other attendants.

div.head: Scena prima.
div.stage: Enter Mardonius and Beſſus, two Captains.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: BEſſus, the King has made a fair hand on't, he has ended the Wars at a blow, would my ſword had a cloſe basket hilt to hold Wine, and the blade would make knives, for we ſhall have nothing but eating and drinking.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: We that are Commanders ſhall do well enough.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Faith Beſſus, ſuch Commanders as thou may; I had as lieve ſet thee Perdue for a pudding i'th' dark, as Alexander the Great.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I love theſe jeſts exceedingly.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I think thou lov'ſt'em better than quarrelling Beſſus, I'le ſay ſo much i'thy behalf, and yet thou 'it valiant enough upon a retreat, I think thou wouldſt kill any man that ſtopt thee if thou couldſt.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: But was not this a brave Combate Mardonius?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Why, didſt thou ſee't?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: You ſtood wi'me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I did ſo, but me thought thou wink'dſt every blow they ſtrook.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Well, I believe there are better ſouldiers than I, that never ſaw two Princes fight in liſts.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: By my troth I think ſo too Beſſus, many a thouſand, but certainly all that are worſe than thou have ſeen as much.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: 'Twas bravely done of our King.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes, if he had not ended the wars: I'me glad thou dar'ſt talk of ſuch dangerous buſineſſes.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: To take a Prince priſoner in the heart of's own Country in ſingle combat.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: See how thy blood curdles at this, I think thou couldſt be contented to be beaten i'this paſſion.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Shall I tell you truly?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I could willingly venture for't.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Um, no venture neither Beſſus.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Let me not live, if I do not think 'tis a braver piece of ſervice than that I'me ſo fam'd for.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Why, art thou fam'd for any valour?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Fam'd! I, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: I'me e'en heartily glad on't, I have been with thee e're ſince thou cam'ſt to th'wars, and this is the firſt word that ever I heard on't, prethee who fames thee.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: The Chriſtian world.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p:
'Tis heatheniſhly done of'em in my conſcience, thou
deſerv'ſt it not.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Yes, I ha' don good ſervice.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I do not know how thou mayſt wait of a man in's Chamber, or thy agility of ſhifting of a Trencher, but otherwiſe no ſervice good Beſſus.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: You ſaw me do the ſervice your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Not ſo haſty ſweet Beſſus, where was it, is the place vaniſh'd?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: At Beſſus deſp'rate redemption.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: At Beſſus deſp'rate redemption, where's that?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: There where I redeem'd the day, the place bears my name.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Pray thee, who Chriſtened it?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: The Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: If I were not a very merrily diſpos'd man, what would become of thee? one that had but a grain of choler in the whole compoſition of his body, would ſend thee of an errand to the worms for putting thy name upon that field: did not I beat thee there i'th' head o'th' Troops with a Trunchion, becauſe thou wouldſt needs run away with thy company, when we ſhould charge the enemy?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: True, but I did not run.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Right Beſſus, I beat thee out on't.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: But came I not up when the day was gone, and redeem'd all?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Thou knoweſt, and ſo do I, thou meanedſt to flie, and thy fear making thee miſtake, thou ranſt upon the enemy, and a hot charge thou gav'ſt, as I'le do thee right, thou art furious in running away, and I think, we owe thy fear for our victory; If I were the King, and were ſure thou wouldſt miſtake alwaies and run away upon th' enemy, thou ſhouldſt be General by this light.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: You'l never leave this till I fall foul.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: No more ſuch words dear Beſſus, for though I have ever known thee a coward, and therefore durſt never ſtrike thee, yet if thou proceedeſt, I will allow thee valiant, and beat thee.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Come, our King's a brave fellow.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: He is ſo Beſſus, I wonder how thou cam'ſt to know it. But if thou wer't a man of underſtanding, I would tell thee, he is vain-glorious, and humble, and angry, and patient, and merry and dull, and joyful and ſorrowful in extremity in an hour: Do not think me thy friend for this, for if I car'd who knew it, thou ſhouldſt not hear it Beſſus. Here he is with his prey in his foot.

div.stage: Enter Arbaces and Tigranes, two Kings and two Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Thy ſadneſs brave Tigranes takes away
From my full victory, am I become
Of ſo ſmall fame, that any man ſhould grieve
When I o'recome him? They that plac'd me here,
Intended it an honour large enough,
For the moſt valiant living, but to dare oppoſe me ſingle, though he
Loſt the day. What ſhould afflict you, you are as free as I,
To be my priſoner, is to be more free
Than you were formerly, and never think
The man I held worthy to combate me
Shall be us'd ſervilely: Thy ranſom is
To take my only Siſter to thy Wife.
A heavy one Tigranes, for ſhe is
A Lady, that the neighbour Princes ſend
Blanks to fetch home. I have been too unkind
To her Tigranes, ſhe but nine years old
I left her, and ne're ſaw her ſince, your wars
Have held me long and taught me though a youth,
The way to victory, ſhe was a pretty child,
Then I was little better, but now fame
Cries loudly on her, and my meſſengers
Make me believe ſhe is a miracle;
She'l make you ſhrink, as I did, with a ſtroak
But of her eye Tigranes.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Is't the courſe of Iberia to uſe their priſoners thus?
Had fortune thrown my name above Arbace,
I ſhould not thus have talk'd Sir, in Armenia,
We hold it baſe, you ſhould have kept your temper
Till you ſaw home again, where 'tis the faſhion
Perhaps to brag.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Be you my witneſs earth, need I to brag,
Doth not this captive Prince ſpeak
Me ſufficiently, and all the acts
That I have wrought upon his ſuffering Land;
Should I then boaſt! where lies that foot of ground
Within his whole Realm, that I have not paſt,
Fighting and conquering; Far then from me
Be oſtentation. I could tell the world
How I have laid his Kingdom deſolate
By this ſole Arm prop't by divinity,
Stript him out of his glories, and have ſent
The pride of all his youth to people graves,
And made his Virgins languiſh for their Loves,
If I would brag, ſhould I that have the power
To teach the Neighbour world humility,
Mix with vain-glory?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Indeed this is none.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Tigranes, Nay did I but take delight
To ſtretch my deeds as others do, on words,
I could amaze my hearers.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: So you do.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: But he ſhall wrong his and my modeſty,
That thinks me apt to boaſt after any act
Fit for a good man to do upon his foe.
A little glory in a ſouldiers mouth
Is well-becoming, be it far from vain.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis pity that valour ſhould be thus drunk.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I offer you my Siſter, and you anſwer
I do inſult, a Lady that no ſuite
Nor treaſure, nor thy Crown could purchaſe thee,
But that thou fought'ſt with me.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Though this be worſe
Than that you ſpake before, it ſtrikes me not;
But that you think to overgrace me with
The marriage of your Siſter, troubles me.
I would give worlds for ranſoms were they mine,
Rather than have her.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: See if I inſult
That am the Conquerour, and for a ranſom
Offer rich treaſure to the Conquered,
Which he refuſes, and I bear his ſcorn:
It cannot be ſelf-flattery to ſay,
The Daughters of your Country ſet by her,
Would ſee their ſhame, run home and bluſh to death,
At their own foulneſs; yet ſhe is not fair,
Nor beautiful, thoſe words expreſs her not,
They ſay her looks have ſomething excellent,
That wants a name: yet were ſhe odious,
Her birth deſerves the Empire of the world,
Siſter to ſuch a brother, that hath ta'ne
Victory priſoner, and throughout the earth,
Carries her bound, and ſhould he let her looſe,
She durſt not leave him; Nature did her wrong,
To Print continual conqueſt on her cheeks,
And make no man worthy for her to taſte
But me that am too near her, and as ſtrangely
She did for me, but you will think I brag.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I do I'le be ſworn. Thy valour and thy paſſions ſever'd, would have made two excellent fellows in their kinds: I know not whether I ſhould be ſorry thou art ſo valiant, or ſo paſſionate, wou'd one of 'em were away.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Do I refuſe her that I doubt her worth?
Were ſhe as vertuous as ſhe would be thought,
So perfect that no one of her own ſex
Could find a want, had ſhe ſo tempting fair,
That ſhe could wiſh it off for damning ſouls,
I would pay any ranſom, twenty lives
Rather than mee • her married in my bed.
Perhaps I have a love, where I have ſixt
Mine eyes not to be mov'd, and ſhe on me,
I am not fickle.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Is that all the cauſe?
Think you, you can ſo knit your ſelf in love
To any other, that her ſearching ſight
Cannot diſſolve it? So before you tri'd,
You thought your ſelf a match for me in ſight,
Truſt me Tigranes, ſhe can do as much
In peace, as I in war, ſhe'l conquer too,
You ſhall ſee if you have the power to ſtand
The force of her ſwift looks, if you diſlike,
I'le ſend you home with love, and name your ranſom
Some other way, but if ſhe be your choice,
She frees you: To Iberia you muſt.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Sir, I have learn'd a priſoners ſufferance,
And will obey, but give me leave to talk
In private with ſome friends before I go.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Some to await him forth, and ſee him ſafe,
But let him freely ſend for whom he pleaſe,
And none dare to diſturb his conference,
I will not have him know what bondage is, Exit Tigranes.
Till he be free from me. This Prince, Mardonius,
Is full of wiſdom, valour, all the graces
Man can receive.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And yet you conquer'd him.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: And yet I conquer'd him, and could have don't
Hadſt thou joyn'd with him, though thy name in Arms
Be great; muſt all men that are vertuous
Think ſuddenly to match themſelves with me?
I conquered him and bravely, did I not?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: And pleaſe your Majeſty, I was afraid at firſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: When wert thou other?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Of what?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: That you would not have ſpy'd your beſt advantages, for your Majeſty in my opinion lay too high, methinks, under favour, you ſhould have lain thus.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Like a Taylor at a wake.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: And then, if pleaſe your Majeſty to remember, at one time, by my troth I wiſht my ſelf wi'you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: By my troth thou wouldſt ha' ſtunk 'em both out o'th' Liſts.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: What to do?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: To put your Majeſty in mind of an occaſion; you lay thus, and Tigranes falſified a blow at your Leg, which you by doing thus avoided; but if you had whip'd up your Leg thus, and reach'd him on the ear, you had made the Blood-Royal run down his head.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What Country Fence-ſchool learn'ſt thou at?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Piſh, did not I take him nobly?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why you did, and you have talked enough on't.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Talkt enough?
Will you confine my word? by heaven and earth,
I were much better be a King of beaſts
Than ſuch a people: if I had not patience
Above a God, I ſhould be call'd a Tyrant
Throughout the world. They will offend to death
Each minute: Let me hear thee ſpeak again,
And thou art earth again: why this is like
Tigranes ſpeech that needs would ſay I brag'd.
Beſſus, he ſaid I brag'd.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why doſt thou laugh?
By all the world, I'm grown ridiculous
To my own Subjects: Tie me in a Chair
And jeſt at me, but I ſhall make a ſtart,
And puniſh ſome that others may take heed
How they are haughty; who will anſwer me?
He ſaid I boaſted, ſpeak Mardonius,
Did I? He will not anſwer, O my temper!
I give you thanks above, that taught my heart
Patience, I can endure his ſilence; what will none
Vouchſafe to give me anſwer? am I grown
To ſuch a poor reſpect, or do you mean
To break my wind? Speak, ſpeak, ſome one of you,
Or elſe by heaven.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: So pleaſe your.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Monſtrous,
I cannot be heard out, they cut me off,
As if I were too ſaucy, I will live
In woods, and talk to trees, they will allow me
To end what I begin. The meaneſt Subject
Can find a freedom to diſcharge his ſoul
And not I, now it is a time to ſpeak,
I hearken.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: May it pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I mean not you,
Did not I ſtop you once? but I am grown
To balk, but I defie, let another ſpeak,

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: I hope your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Thou draweſt thy words,
That I muſt wait an hour, where other men
Can hear in inſtants; throw your words away,
Quick, and to purpoſe, I have told you this.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: And pleaſe your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Wilt thou devour me? this is ſuch a rudeneſs
As you never ſhew'd me, and I want
Power to command too, elſe Mardonius
Would ſpeak at my requeſt; were you my King,
I would have anſwered at your word Mardonius,
I pray you ſpeak, and truely, did I boaſt?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Truth will offend you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: You take all great care what will offend me,
When you dare to utter ſuch things as theſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You told Tigranes, you had won his Land,
With that ſole arm propt by Divinity:
Was not that bragging, and a wrong to us,
That daily ventured lives?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: O that thy name
Were as great, as mine, would I had paid my wealth,
It were as great, as I might combate thee,
I would through all the Regions habitable
Search thee, and having found thee, wi'my Sword
Drive thee about the world, till I had met
Some place that yet mans curioſity
Hath miſt of; there, there would I ſtrike thee dead:
Forgotten of mankind, ſuch Funeral rites
As beaſts would give thee, thou ſhouldſt have.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: The King rages extreamly, ſhall we ſlink away?
He'l ſtrike us.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Content.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: There I would make you know 'twas this ſole arm.
I grant you were my inſtruments, and did
As I commanded you, but 'twas this arm
Mov'd you like wheels, it mov'd you as it pleas'd.
Whither ſlip you now? what are you too good
To wait on me (puffe,) I had need have temper
That rule ſuch people; I have nothing left
At my own choice, I would I might be private:
Mean men enjoy themſelves, but 'tis our curſe,
To have a tumult that out of their loves
Will wait on us, whether we will or no;
Go get you gone: Why here they ſtand like death,
My words move nothing.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Muſt we go?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: I know not.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I pray you leave me Sirs, I'me proud of this,
That you will be intreated from my ſight:

Why now the leave me all: Mardonius.
Exeunt all but Arb. and Mar.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Will you leave me quite alone? me thinks
Civility ſhould teach you more than this,
If I were but your friend: Stay here and wait.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir ſhall I ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why, you would now think much
To be denied, but I can ſcare intreat
What I would have: do, ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: But will you hear me out?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: With me you Article to talk thus: well,
I will hear you out.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sir, that I have ever lov'd you, my ſword hath ſpoken for me; that I do, if it be doubted, I dare call an oath, a great one to my witneſs; and were you not my King, from amongſt men, I ſhould have choſe you out to love above the reſt: nor can this challenge thanks, for my own ſake I ſhould have done it, becauſe I would have lov'd the moſt deſerving man, for ſo you are.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Alas Mardonius, riſe you ſhall not kneel,
We all are ſouldiers, and all venture lives:
And where there is no difference in mens worths,
Titles are jeſts, who can outvalue thee?
Mardonius thou haſt lov'd me, and haſt wrong,
Thy love is not rewarded, but believe
• t ſhall be better, more than friend in arms,
My Father, and my Tutor, good Mardonius.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir, you did promiſe you would hear me out.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: And ſo I will; ſpeak freely, for from thee
Nothing can come but worthy things and true.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Though you have all this worth, you hold ſome qualities that do Eclipſe your vertues.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Eclipſe my vertues?

sp.speaker: Mar.
