sp.p: Yes, your paſſions, which are ſo manifold, that they appear even in this: when I commend you, you hug me for that truth: but when I ſpeak your faults, you make a ſtart, and flie the hearing but.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: When you commend me? O that I ſhould live
To need ſuch commendations: If my deeds
Blew not my praiſe themſelves about the earth,
I were moſt wretched: ſpare your idle praiſe:
If thou didſt mean to flatter, and ſhouldſt utter
Words in my praiſe, that thou thoughtſt impudence,
sp.p: My deeds ſhould make 'em modeſt: when you praiſe I hug you? 'tis ſo ſafe, that wert thou worthy thou ſhouldſt receive a death, a glorious death from me: but thou ſhalt underſtand thy lies, for ſhouldſt thou praiſe me into Heaven, and there leave me inthron'd, I would deſpiſe thee though as much as now, which is as much as duſt becauſe I ſee thy envie.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: However you will uſe me after, yet for your own promiſe ſake, hear me the reſt.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I will, and after call unto the winds, for they ſhall lend as large an ear as I to what you utter: ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Would you but leave theſe haſty tempers, which I do not ſay take from you all your worth, but darken 'em, then you will ſhine indeed.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Well.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yet I would have you keep ſome paſſions, leſt men ſhould take you for a God, your vertues are ſuch.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Why now you flatter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I never underſtood the word, were you no King, and free from theſe moods, ſhould I chooſe a companion for wit and pleaſure, it ſhould be you; or for honeſty to enterchange my boſom with, it ſhould be you; or wiſdom to give me counſel, I would pick out you; or valour to defend my reputation, ſtill I ſhould find you out; for you are fit to ſight for all the world, if it could come in queſtion: Now I have ſpoke, conſider to your ſelf, find out a uſe; if ſo, then what ſhall fall to me is not material.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Is not material? more than ten ſuch lives, as mine, Mardonius: it was nobly ſaid, thou haſt ſpoke truth, and boldly ſuch a truth as might offend another. I have been too paſſionate and idle, thou ſhalt ſee a ſwift amendment, but I want thoſe parts you praiſe me for: I fight for all the world? Give me a ſword, and thou wilt go as far beyond me, as thou art beyond in years, I know thou dar'ſt and wilt; it troubles me that I ſhould uſe ſo rough a phraſe to thee, impute it to my folly, what thou wilt, ſo thou wilt paron me: that thou and I ſhould differ thus!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Why 'tis no matter Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Faith but it is, but thou doſt ever take all things I do, thus patiently, for which I never can requite thee, but with love, and that thou ſhalt be ſure of. Thou and I have not been merry lately: pray thee tell me where hadſt thou that ſame jewel in thine ear?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Why at the taking of a Town.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: A wench upon my life, a wench Mardonius gave thee that jewel.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Wench! they reſpect not me, I'm old and rough, and every limb about me, but that which ſhould, grows ſtiffer, I'thoſe buſineſſes I may ſwear I am truly honeſt: for I pay juſtly for what I take, and would be glad to be at a certainty.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Why, do the wenches encroach upon thee?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I by this light do they.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Didſt thou ſit at an old rent with 'em?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes ſaith.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: And do they improve themſelves?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I ten ſhillings to me, every new young fellow they come acquainted with.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: How canſt live on't?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Why I think I muſt petition to you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt take them up at my price.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Your price?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I at the Kings price.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: That may be more than I'me worth.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.p: Is he not merry now?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.p: I think not.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: He is, he is: we'l ſhew our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Beſſus, I thought you had been in Iberia by this, I bad you haſt; Gobrias will want entertainment for me.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: And pleaſe your Majeſty I have a ſute.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Is't not louſie Beſſus, what is't?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I am to carry a Lady with me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Then thou haſt two ſutes.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: And if I can prefer her to the Lady Pentha your Majeſties Siſter, to learn faſhions, as her friends term it, it will be worth ſomething to me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: So many nights lodgings as 'tis thither, wilt not?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I know not that Sir, but gold I ſhall be ſure of.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Why thou ſhalt bid her entertain her from me, ſo thou wilt reſolve me one thing.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: If I can.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Faith 'tis a very diſputable queſtion, and yet I think thou canſt decide it.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Your Majeſty has a good opinion of my underſtanding.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I have ſo good an opinion of it: 'tis whether thou be valiant.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Some body has traduced me to you: do you ſee this ſword Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: If I do not make my back-biters eat it to a knife within this week, ſay I am not valiant.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Health to your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: From Gobrias?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: How does he, is he well?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: In perfect health.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Take that for thy good news. A truſtier ſervant to his Prince there lives not, than is good Gobrias.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.p: The King ſtarts back.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: His blood goes back as faſt.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.p: And now it comes again.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: He alters ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: The hand of Heaven is on me, be it far from me to ſtruggle, if my ſecret ſins have pull'd this curſe upon me, lend me tears now to waſh me white, that I may feel a child-like innocence within my breaſt; which once perform'd, O give me leave to ſtand as fix'd as conſtancy her ſelf, my eyes ſet here unmov'd, regardleſs of the world though thouſand miſeries incompaſs me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: This is ſtrange, Sir, how do you?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Mardonius, my mother.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Is ſhe dead?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Alas ſhe's not ſo happy, thou doſt know how ſhe hath laboured ſince my Father died to take by treaſon hence this loathed life, that would but be to ſerve her, I have pardoned, and pardoned, and by that have made her fit to practiſe new ſins, not repent the old: ſhe now had ſtirr'd a ſlave to come from thence, and ſtrike me here, whom Gobrias ſifting out, took and condemn'd and executed there, the carefulſt ſervant: Heaven let me but live to pay that man; Nature is poor to me, that will not let me have as many deaths as are the times that he hath ſav'd my life, that I might dye 'em over all for him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir let her bear her ſins on her own head,
Vex not your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: What will the world
Conceive of me? with what unnatural ſins
Will they ſuppoſe me loaden, when my life
Is fought by her that gave it to the world?
But yet he writes me comfort here, my Siſter,
He ſaies, is grown in beauty and in grace.
In all the innocent vertues that become
A tender ſpotleſs maid: ſhe ſtains her cheeks
With morning tears to purge her mothers ill,
And 'mongſt that ſacred dew ſhe mingles Prayers
Her pure Oblations for my ſafe return:
If I have loſt the duty of a Son,
If any pomp or vanity of ſtate
Made me forget my natural offices,
Nay farther, if I have not every night
Expoſtulated with my wandring thoughts,
If ought unto my parent they have err'd,
And call'd 'em back: do you direct her arm
Unto this ſoul diſſembling heart of mine:
But if I have been juſt to her, ſend out
Your power to compaſs me, and hold me ſafe
From ſearching treaſon; I will uſe no means
But prayer: for rather ſuffer me to ſee
From mine own veins iſſue a deadly flood,
Than waſh my danger off with mothers blood.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I n'ere ſaw ſuch ſuddain extremities. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Why? wilt thou have me die Spaconia,
What ſhould I do?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Nay let me ſtay alone,
And when you ſee Armenia again,
You ſhall behold a Tomb more worth than I;
Some friend that ever lov'd me or my cauſe,
Will build me ſomething to diſtinguiſh me
From other women, many a weeping verſe
He will lay on, and much lament thoſe maids,
That plac'd their loves unfortunately high,
As I have done, where they can never reach;
But why ſhould you go to Iberia?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Alas, that thou wilt ask me, ask the man
That rages in a Fever why he lies
Diſtempered there, when all the other youths
Are courſing o're the Meadows with their Loves?
Can I reſiſt it? am I not a ſlave
To him that conquer'd me?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: That conquer'd thee Tigranes! he has won
But half of thee, thy body, but thy mind
May be as free as his, his will did never
Combate thine, and take it priſoner.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: But if he by force convey my body hence,
What helps it me or thee to be unwilling?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: O Tigranes, I know you are to ſee a Lady there,
To ſee, and like I fear: perhaps the hope
Of her make you forget me, ere we part,
Be happier than you know to wiſh; farewel.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Spaconia, ſtay and hear me what I ſay:
In ſhort, deſtruction meet me that I may
See it, and not avoid it, when I leave
To be thy faithful lover: part with me
Thou ſhalt not, there are none that know our love,
And I have given gold unto a Captain
That goes unto Iberia from the King,
That he will place a Lady of our Land
With the Kings Siſter that is offered me;
Thither ſhall you, and being once got in
Perſwade her by what ſubtil means you can
To be as backward in her love as I.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Can you imagine that a longing maid
When ſhe beholds you, can be pull'd away
With words from loving you?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Diſpraiſe my health, my honeſty, and tell her I am jealous.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Why, I had rather loſe you: can my heart
Conſent to let my tongue throw out ſuch words,
And I that ever yet ſpoke what I thought,
Shall find it ſuch a thing at firſt to lie?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Yet do thy belt.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: What, is your Majeſty ready?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: There is the Lady, Captain.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Sweet Lady, by your leave, I could wiſh my ſelf more full of Courtſhip for your fair ſake.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: Sir I ſhall feel no want of that.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Lady, you muſt haſt, I have received new letters from the King that require more haſt than I expected, he will follow me ſuddenly himſelf, and begins to call for your Majeſty already.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: He ſhall not do ſo long.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Sweet Lady, ſhall I call you my Charge hereafter?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: I will not take upon me to govern your tongue Sir, you ſhall call me what you pleaſe.

div.head: Actus Secundus.
div.stage: Enter Gobrias, Bacurius, Arane, Panthe, and Mandane, Waiting-women with Attendants.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: MY Lord Bacurius, you muſt have regard unto the Queen, ſhe is your priſoner, 'tis at your peril if ſhe make eſcape.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: My Lord, I know't, ſhe is my priſoner from you committed; yet ſhe is a woman, and ſo I keep her ſafe, you will not urge me to keep her cloſe, I ſhall not ſhame to ſay I ſorrow for her.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: So do I my Lord; I ſorrow for her, that ſo little grace doth govern her: that ſhe ſhould ſtretch her arm againſt her King, ſo little womanhood and natural goodneſs, as to think the death of her own Son.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: Thou knowſt the reaſon why, diſſembling as thou art, and wilt not ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: There is a Lady takes not after you,
Her Father is within her, that good man
Whoſe tears weigh'd down his ſins, mark how ſhe weeps,
How well it does become her, and if you
Can find no diſpoſition in your ſelf
To ſorrow, yet by gracefulneſs in her
Find out the way, and by your reaſon weep:
All this ſhe does for you, and more ſhe needs
When for your ſelf you will not loſe a tear,
Think how this want of grief diſcredits you,
And you will weep, becauſe you cannot weep.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: You talk to me as having got a time fit for your purpoſe; but you know I know you ſpeak not what you think.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I would my heart were Stone, before my ſoftneſs ſhould be urg'd
Againſt my mother, a more troubled thought
No Virgin bears about; ſhould I excuſe
My Mothers fault, I ſhould ſet light a life
In loſing which, a brother and a King
Were taken from me, if I ſeek to ſave
That life ſo lov'd, I loſe another life
That gave me being, I ſhall loſe a Mother,
A word of ſuch a ſound in a childs ears
That it ſtrikes reverence through it; may the will
Of heaven be done, and if one needs muſt fall,
Take a poor Virgins life to anſwer all.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: But Gobrias let us talk, you know this fault
Is not in me as in another Mother.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: I know it is not.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: Yet you make it ſo.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Why, is not all that's paſt beyond your help?

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: I know it is.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Nay ſhould you publiſh it before the world,
Think you 'twould be believ'd?

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: I know it would not.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Nay ſhould I joyn with you, ſhould we not both be torn and yet both die uncredited?

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: I think we ſhould.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Why then take you ſuch violent courſes? As for me I do but right in ſaving of the King from all your plots

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: The King?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: I bad you reſt with patience, and a time
Would come for me to reconcile all to
Your own content, but by this way you take
Away my power, and what was done unknown,
Was not by me but you: your urging being done
I muſt preſerve my own, but time may bring
All this to light, and happily for all.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: Accurſed be this over curious brain
That gave that plot a birth, accurſt this womb
That after did conceive to my diſgrace.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: My Lord Protector, they ſay there are divers Letters come from Armenia, that Beſſus has done good ſervice, and brought again a day, by his particular valour, receiv'd you any to that effect?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Yes, 'tis moſt certain.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I'm ſorry for't, not that the day was won,
But that 'twas won by him: we held him here
A Coward, he did me wrong once, at which I laugh'd,
And ſo did all the world, for nor I,
Nor any other held him worth my ſword.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Health to my Protector; from the King
Theſe Letters; and to your grace Madam, theſe.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: How does his Majeſty?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: As well as conqueſt by his own means and his valiant Cammanders can make him; your letters will tell you all.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I will not open mine till I do know
My Brothers health: good Captain is he well?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: As the reſt of us that fought are.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: But how's that? is he hurt?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: He's a ſtrange ſouldier that gets not a knock.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I do not ask how ſtrange that ſouldier is
That gets no hurt, but whether he have one.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: He had divers.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: And is he well again?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Well again, an't pleaſe your Grace: why I was run twice through the body, and ſhot i'th' head with a croſs-arrow, and yet am well again.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I do not care how thou do'ſt, is he well?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Not care how I do? Let a man out of the mightineſs of his ſpirit, fructifie Foreign Countries with his blood for the good of his own, and thus he ſhall be anſwered: Why I may live to relieve with ſpear and ſhield, ſuch a Lady as you diſtreſſed.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Why, I will care, I'me glad that thou art well,
I prethee is he ſo?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: The King is well and will be here to morrow.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: My prayer is heard, now will I open mine.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Bacurius, I muſt eaſe you of your charge:
Madam, the wonted mercy of the King,
That overtakes your faults, has met with this,
And ſtruck it out, he has forgiven you freely,
Your own will is your law, be where you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: I thank him.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: You will be ready to wait upon his Majeſty to morrow?

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l:
I will.
Exit Arane.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Madam be wiſe hereafter; I am glad I have loſt this Office.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Good Captain Beſſus, tell us the diſcourſe betwixt Tigranes and our King, and how we got the victory.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I prethee do, and if my Brother were
In any danger, let not thy tale make
Him abide there long before thou bring him off,
For all that while my heart will beat.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Madam let what will beat, I muſt tell the truth, and thus it was; they fought ſingle in liſts, but one to one; as for my own part, I was dangerouſly hurt but three days before, elſe, perhaps, we had been two to two, I cannot tell, ſome thought we had, and the occaſion of my hurt was this, the enemy had made Trenches.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Captain, without the manner of your hurt be much material to this buſineſs, we'l hear't ſome other time.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I prethee leave it, and go on with my Brother.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: I will, but 'twould be worth your hearing: To the Liſts they came, and ſingle-ſword and gantlet was their fight.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Alas!

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Without the Liſts there ſtood ſome dozen Captains of either ſide mingled, all which were ſworn, and one of thoſe was I: and 'twas my chance to ſtand next a Captain o'th' enemies ſide, called Tiribaſus; Valiant they ſaid he was; whilſt theſe two Kings were ſtreaching themſelves, this Tiribaſus caſt ſomething a ſcornful look on me, and ask't me who I thought would overcome: I ſmil'd and told him if he would fight with me, he ſhould perceive by the event of that whoſe King would win: ſomething he anſwered, and a ſcuſtle was like to grow, when one Zipetus offered to help him, I—

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: All this is of thy ſelf, I pray thee Beſſus tell ſomething of my Brother, did he nothing?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Why yes, I'le tell your Grace, they were not to ſight till the word given, which for my own part, by my troth I confeſs I was not to give.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: See for his own part.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: I fear yet this fellow's abus'd with a good report.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: But I—

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Still of himſelf.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Cri'd give the word, when as ſome of them ſay, Tigranes was ſtooping, but the word was not given then, yet one Coſroes of the enemies part, held up his finger to me, which is as much with us Martialiſts, as I will ſight with you: I ſaid not a word, nor made ſign during the combate, but that once done.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: He ſlips o're all the fight.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I call'd him to me, Coſroes ſaid I.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: I will hear no more.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: No, no, I lie.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: I dare be ſworn thou doſt.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Captain ſaid I, ſo it was.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: I tell thee, I will hear no further.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: No? Your Grace will wiſh you had.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: I will not wiſh it, what is this the Lady
My brother writes to me to take?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: And pleaſe your Grace this is ſhe: Charge, will you come near the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: You'r welcome from your Country, and this land ſhall ſhew unto you all the kindneſs that I can make it; what's your name?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Y'are very welcome, you have got a letter to put you to me, that has power enough to place mine enemy here; then much more you that are ſo far from being ſo to me that you ne're ſaw me.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Madam, I dare paſs my word for her truth.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: My truth?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Why Captain, do you think I am afraid ſhe'l ſteal?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I cannot tell, ſervants are ſlippery, but I dare give my word for her, and for honeſty, ſhe came along with me, and many favours ſhe did me by the way, but by this light none but what ſhe might do with modeſty, to a man of my rank.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Why Captain, here's no body thinks otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Nay, if you ſhould, your Grace may think your pleaſure; but I am ſure I brought her from Armenia, and in all that way, if ever I touch'd any bare of her above her knee; I pray God I may ſink where I ſtand.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: Above my knee?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: No, you know I did not, and if any man will ſay, I did, this ſword ſhall anſwer; Nay, I'le defend the reputation of my charge whilſt I live, your Grace ſhall underſtand I am ſecret in theſe buſineſſes, and know how to defend a Ladies honour.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: I hope your Grace knows him ſo well already, I ſhall not need to tell you he's vain and fooliſh.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I you may call me what you pleaſe, but I'le defend your good name againſt the world; and ſo I take my leave of your Grace, and of you my Lord Protector; I am likewiſe glad to ſee your Lordſhip well.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: O Captain Beſſus, I thank you, I would ſpeak with you anon.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: When you pleaſe, I will attend your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Madam, I'le take my leave too.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p:
Good Bacurius.
Exeunt Beſ. and Bac.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Madam what writes his Majeſty to you?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: O my Lord, the kindeſt words, I'le keep 'em whilſt I live, here in my boſom, there's no art in 'em, they lie diſordered in this paper, juſt as hearty nature ſpeaks 'em.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: And to me he writes what tears of joy he ſhed to hear how you were grown in every vertues way, and yields all thanks to me, for that dear care which I was bound to have in training you, there is no Princeſs living that enjoys a brother of that worth.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: My Lord, no maid longs more for any thing,
And feels more heat and cold within her breaſt,
Than I do now, in hopes to ſee him.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Yet I wonder much
At this he writes, be brings along with him
A husband for you, that ſame Captive Prince,
And if he loves you as he makes a ſhew,
He will allow you freedom in your choice.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: And ſo he will my Lord, I warrant you, he will but offer and give me the power to take or leave.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Truſt me, were I a Lady, I could not like that man were bargain'd with before I chooſe him.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: But I am not built on ſuch wild humours, if I find him worthy, he is not leſs becauſe he's offer'd.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: 'Tis true, he is not, would he would ſeem leſs.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: I think there's no Lady can affect
Another Prince, your brother ſtanding by;
He doth Eclipſe mens vertues ſo with his.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: I know a Lady may, and more I fear
Another Lady will.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Would I might ſee him.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Why ſo you ſhall, my buſineſſes are great,
I will attend you when it is his pleaſure to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I thank you good my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: You will be ready Madam. Exit Gob.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: I do beſeech you Madam, ſend away
Your other women, and receive from me
A few ſad words, which ſet againſt your joyes
May make 'em ſhine the more.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Sirs, leave me all. Exeunt Women.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: I kneel a ſtranger here to beg a thing
Unfit for me to ask, and you to grant,
'Tis ſuch another ſtrange ill-laid-requeſt,
As if a begger ſhould intreat a King
To leave his Scepter, and his Throne to him
And take his rags to wander o're the world
Hungry and cold.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: That were a ſtrange requeſt.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: As ill is mine.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Then do not utter it.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Alas 'tis of that nature, that it muſt
Be utter'd, I, and granted, or I die:
I am aſham'd to ſpeak it; but where life
Lies at the ſtake, I cannot think her woman
sp.p: That will not take ſomething unreaſonably to hazard ſaying of it: I ſhall ſeem a ſtrange Petitioner, that wiſh all ill to them I beg of, e're they give me ought; yet ſo I muſt: I would you were not fair, nor wiſe, for in your ill conſiſts my good: if you were fooliſh, you would hear my prayer, if foul, you had not power to hinder me: he would not love you.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: What's the meaning of it.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Nay, my requeſt is more without the bounds
Of reaſon yet: for 'tis not in the power
Of you to do, what I would have you grant.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Why then 'tis idle, pray thee ſpeak it out.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Your brother brings a Prince into this land,
Of ſuch a noble ſhape, ſo ſweet a grace,
So full of worth withal, that every maid
That looks upon him, gives away her ſelf
To him for ever; and for you to have
He brings him: and ſo mad is my demand
That I deſire you not to have this man,
This excellent man, for whom you needs muſt die,
If you ſhould miſs him. I do now expect
You ſhould laugh at me.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Truſt me I could weep rather, for I have found
In all thy words a ſtrange disjoynted ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: 'Tis by me his own deſire ſo, that you would not love him.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: His own deſire! why credit me Thaleſtris,
sp.p: I am no common wooer: if he ſhall wooe me, his worth may be ſuch, that I dare not ſwear I will not love him; but if he will ſtay to have me wooe him, I will promiſe thee, he may keep all his graces to himſelf, and fear no raviſhing from me.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: 'Tis yet his own deſire, but when he ſees your face, I fear it will not be; therefore I charge you as you have pity, ſtop theſe tender ears from his enchanting voice, cloſe up thoſe eyes, that you may neither catch a dart from him, nor he from you; I charge you as you hope to live in quiet; for when I am dead, for certain I will walk to viſit him if he break promiſe with me: for as faſt as Oaths without a formal Ceremony can make me, I am to him.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Then be fearleſs;
For if he were a thing 'twixt God and man,
I could gaze on him; if I knew it ſin
To love him without paſſion: Dry your eyes,
I ſwear you ſhall enjoy him ſtill for me,
I will not hinder you; but I perceive
You are not what you ſeem, riſe, riſe Thaleſtris,
If your right name be ſo.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: Indeed it is not, Spaconia is my name; but I deſire not to be known to other.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Why, by me you ſhall not, I will never do you wrong, what good I can, I will, think not my birth or education ſuch, that I ſhould injure a ſtranger Virgin; you are welcome hither, in company you wiſh to be commanded, but when we are alone, I ſhall be ready to be your ſervant.

div.stage: Enter three Men and a Woman.

sp.p: Come, come, run, run, run.
2 We ſhall out-go her.
One were better be hang'd than carry out women ſidling to theſe ſhews.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.p: Is the King hard by?
You heard he with the Bottles ſaid, he thought we ſhould come too late: What abundance of people here is?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.p: But what had he in thoſe Bottles?
I know not.
Why, Ink goodman fool.
Ink, what to do?
Why the King look you, will many times call for theſe Bottles, and break his mind to his friends.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.p: Let's take our places, we ſhall have no room elſe.
The man told us he would walk o' foot through the people.
I marry did he.
Our ſhops are well look't to now.
'Slife, yonder's my Maſter, I think.
No 'tis not he.

div.stage: Enter a man with two Citizens-wives.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Lord how fine the fields be, what ſweet living 'tis in the Country!

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: I poor ſouls, God help 'em; they live as contentedly as one of us.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: My husbands Couſin would have had me gone into the Country laſt year, wert thou ever there?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: I, poor ſouls, I was amongſt 'em once.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: And what kind of creatures are they, for love of God?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Very good people, God help 'em.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Wilt thou go down with me this Summer when I am brought to bed?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Alas, it is no place for us.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Why, pray thee?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Why you can have nothing there, there's no body cryes brooms.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: No truly, nor milk.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Nor milk, how do they?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: They are fain to milk themſelves i'th' Country.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Good Lord! but the people there, I think, will be very dutiful to one of us.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p:
I God knows will they, and yet they do not greatly
care for our husbands.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p:
Do they not? Alas! I'good faith I cannot blame •• em: for we do not greatly care for them our ſelves. Phi
••• , I pray chooſe us a place.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.p: There's the beſt forſooth.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: By your leave good people a little.
What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.p: I pray you my friend, do not thruſt my Miſtreſs ſo, • e's with Child.
Let her look to her ſelf then, has ſhe not had ſhowing •• ough yet? if ſhe ſtay ſhouldring here, ſhe may haps go • ome with a cake in her belly.
How now, goodman ſquitter breech, why do you lean • n me?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.p: Becauſe I will.
Will you Sir ſawce-box?

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p:
Look if one ha' not ſtruck Philip, come hither
• hilip, why did he ſtrike thee?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.p: For leaning on him.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Why didſt thou lean on him?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.p: I did not think he would have ſtruck me.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: As God ſave me la thou'rt as wild as a Buck, there's • o quarel but thou'rt at one end or other on't.
It's at the firſt end then, for he'l ne'r ſtay the laſt.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Well ſlip-ſtring, I ſhall meet with you.
When you will.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: I'le give a crown to meet with you.
At a Bawdy-houſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: I you're full of your Roguery; but if I do meet you ſhall coſt me a fall.
The King, the King, the King. Now, now, now, now.

div.stage: Flouriſh. Enter Arb. Tigr. the two Kings and Mardonius.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: God preſerve your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I thank you all, now are my joyes at full, when I behold you ſafe, my loving Subjects; by you I grow, 'tis your united love that lifts me to this height: all the account • hat I can render you for all the love you have beſtowed on me, all your expences to maintain my war, is but a little word, you will imagine 'tis ſlender paiment, yet 'tis ſuch a word, as is not to be bought but with your bloods, 'tis Peace.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: God preſerve your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Now you may live ſecurely i'your Towns,
Your Children round about you; may ſit
Under your Vines, and make the miſeries
Of other Kingdoms a diſcourſe for you,
And lend them ſorrows; for your ſelves, you may
Safely forget there are ſuch things as tears,
And you may all whoſe good thoughts I have gain'd,
Hold me unworthy, where I think my life
A ſacrifice too great to keep you thus
In ſuch a calm eſtate.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: God bleſs your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: See all good people, I have brought the man whoſe very name you fear'd, a captive home; behold him, 'tis Tigranes; in your heart ſing ſongs of gladneſs, and deliverance.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.l: Out upon him.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: How he looks.

sp.speaker: 3 Wom.
sp.l: Hang him, hang him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Theſe are ſweet people.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: Sir, you do me wrong, to render me a ſcorned ſpectacle to common people.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: It was ſo far from me to mean it ſo: if I have ought deſerv'd, my loving Subjects, let me beg of you, not to revile this Prince, in whom there dwells all worth of which the name of a man is capable, valour beyond compare, the terrour of his name has ſtretcht it ſelf where ever there is ſun; and yet for you I fought with him ſingle, and won him too; I made his valour ſtoop, and brought that name ſoar'd to ſo unbeliev'd a height, to fall beneath mine: this inſpir'd with all your loves, I did perform, and will for your content, be ever ready for a greater work.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: The Lord bleſs your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: So he has made me amends now with a ſpeech in commendation of himſelf: I would not be ſo vain-glorious.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: If there be any thing in which I may
Do good to any creature, here ſpeak out;
For I muſt leave you: and it troubles me,
That my occaſions for the good of you,
Are ſuch as call me from you: elſe, my joy
Would be to ſpend my days among you all.
You ſhew your loves in theſe large multitudes
That come to meet me, I will pray for you,
Heaven proſper you, that you may know old years,
And live to ſee your childrens children ſit
At your boards with plenty: when there is
A want of any thing, let it be known
To me, and I will be a Father to you:
God keep you all.

div.stage: Flouriſh. Exeunt Kings and their Train.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: God bleſs your Majeſty, God bleſs your Majeſty.
Come, ſhall we go? all's done.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.p: I for God ſake, I have not made a fire yet.
Away, away, all's done.
Content, farewel Philip.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Away you halter-ſack you.
Philip will not fight, he's afraid on's face.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.p: I marry am I afraid of my face.

Thou wouldſt be Philip if thou ſawſt it in a glaſs; it looks ſo like a Viſour.
Exeunt 2, 3, and Woman.
Cit. you'l be hang'd ſirra: Come Philip walk before us homewards; did not his Majeſty ſay he had brought us home Peaſe for all our money?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Yes marry did he.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: They're the firſt I heard of this year by my troth, I longed for ſome of 'em: did he not ſay we ſhould have ſome?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Yes, and ſo we ſhall anon I warrant you have every one a peck brought home to our houſes.

div.head: Actus Tertius.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: MY Siſter take it ill?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Not very ill,
Something unkindly ſhe does take it Sir to have
Her Husband choſen to her hands.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Why Gobrias let her, I muſt have her know, my will and not her own muſt govern her: what will ſhe marry with ſome ſlave at home?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: O ſhe is far from any ſtubbornneſs, you much miſtake her, and no doubt will like where you would have her, but when you behold her, you will be loth to part with ſuch a jewel.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: To part with her? why Gobrias, art thou mad? ſhe is my Siſter.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Sir, I know ſhe is: but it were pity to make poor our Land, with ſuch a beauty to enrich another.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Piſh will ſhe have him?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: I do hope ſhe will not, I think ſhe will Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Were ſhe my Father and my Mother too, and all the names for which we think folks friends, ſhe ſhould be forc't to have him when I know 'tis ſit: I will not hear her ſay ſhe's loth.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Heaven bring my purpoſe luckily to paſs, you know 'tis juſt, ſhe will not need conſtraint ſhe loves you ſo.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: How does ſhe love me, ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: She loves you more than people love their health, that live by labour; more than I could love a man that died for me, if he could live again.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: She is not like her mother then.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: O no, when you were in Armenia,
I durſt not let her know when you were hurt:
For at the firſt on every little ſcratch,
She kept he • Chamber, wept, and could not eat,
Till you were well, and many times the news
Was ſo long coming, that before we heard
She was as near her death, as you your health.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Alas poor ſoul, but yet ſhe muſt be rul'd;
I know not how I ſhall requite her well.
I long to ſee her, have you ſent for her,
To tell her I am ready?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Sir I have.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Sir, here is the Armenian King.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: He's welcome.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.p: And the Queen mother, and the Princeſs wait without.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Good Gobrias bring 'em in.
Tigranes, you will think you are arriv'd
In a ſtrange Land, where Mothers caſt to poyſon
Their only Sons; think you you ſhall be ſafe?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Too ſafe I am Sir.

div.stage: Enter Gobrias, Arane, Panthea, Spaconia, Bacurius, Mardonius and Beſſus, and two Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: As low as this I bow to you, and would
As low as is my grave, to ſhew a mind
Thankful for all your mercies.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: O ſtand up,
And let me kneel, the light will be aſham'd
To ſee obſervance done to me by you.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: You are my King.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: You are my Mother, riſe;
As far be all your faults from your own ſoul,
As from my memory; then you ſhall be
As white as innocence her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: I came
Only to ſhew my duty, and acknowledge
My ſorrows for my ſins; longer to ſtay
Were but to draw eyes more attentively
Upon my ſhame, that power that kept you ſafe
From me, preſerve you ſtill.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Your own deſires ſhall be your guide. Exit Arane.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Now let me die, ſince I have ſeen my Lord the King
Return in ſafetie, I have ſeen all good that life
Can ſhew me; I have ne're another wiſh
For Heaven to grant, nor were it ſit I ſhould;
For I am bound to ſpend my age to come,
In giving thanks that this was granted me.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Why does not your Majeſty ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: To whom?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: To the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Alas Sir, I am fearful, you do look
On me, as if I were ſome loathed thing
That you were finding out a way to ſlain.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Sir, you ſhould ſpeak to her.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: I know I am unworthy, yet not ill arm'd, with which innocence here I will kneel, till I am one with earth, but I will gain ſome words and kindneſs from you.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Will you ſpeak Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Speak, am I what I was?
What art thou that doſt creep into my breaſt,
And dar'ſt not ſee my face? ſhew forth thy ſelf:
I feel a pair of fiery wings diſplai'd
Hither, from hence; you ſhall not tarry there,
Up, and be gone, if thou beeſt Love be gone:
Or I will tear thee from my wounded breaſt,
Pull thy lov'd Down away, and with thy Quill
By this right arm drawn from thy wonted wing,
Write to thy laughing Mother i'thy bloud,
That you are powers bely'd, and all your darts
Are to be blown away, by men reſolv'd,
Like duſt; I know thou ſcar'ſt my words, away.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: O miſery! why ſhould he be ſo ſlow?
There can no falſhood come of loving her;
Though I have given my ſaith; ſhe is a thing
Both to be lov'd and ſerv'd beyond my faith:
I would he would preſent me to her quickly.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Will you not ſpeak at all? are you ſo far
From kind words? yet to ſave my modeſty,
That muſt talk till you anſwer, do not ſtand
As you were dumb, ſay ſomething, though it be
Poyſon'd with anger, that it may ſtrike me dead.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Have you no life at all? for man-hood ſake
Let her not kneel, and talk neglected thus;
A tree would find a tongue to anſwer her,
Did ſhe but give it ſuch a lov'd reſpect.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: You mean this Lady: liſt her from the earth; w •• do you let her kneel ſo long? Alas, Madam, your bea •• uſes to command, and not to beg. What is your ſute to me? it ſhall be granted, yet the time is ſhort, and my affairs are great: but where's my Siſter? I bade ſhe ſhould be brought

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What, is he mad?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Gobrias, where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Where is ſhe man?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Who, Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Who, haſt thou forgot my Siſter?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Your Siſter, Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Your Siſter, Sir? ſome one that hath a wit, anſwer, where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Do you not ſee her there?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: There, where?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: S'light, there, are you blind?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Which do you mean, that little one?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: No Sir? why, do you mock me? I can ſee
No other here, but that petitioning Lady.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: That's ſhe.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Away.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Sir, it is ſhe.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: 'Tis falſe.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Is it?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: As hell, by Heaven, as falſe as hell,
My Siſter: is ſhe dead? if it be ſo,
Speak boldly to me; for I am a man,
And dare not quarrel with Divinity;
And do not think to cozen me with this:
I ſee you all are mute and ſtand amaz'd,
Fearful to anſwer me; it is too true,
A decreed inſtant cuts off ev'ry life,
For which to mourn, is to repine; ſhe dy'd
A Virgin, though more innocent than ſheep,
As clear as her own eyes, and bleſſedneſs
Eternal waits upon her where ſhe is:
I know ſhe could not make a wiſh to change
Her ſtate for new, and you ſhall ſee me bear
My croſſes like a man; we all muſt die,
And ſhe hath taught us how.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Do not miſtake,
And vex your ſelf for nothing; for her death
Is a long life off, I hope: 'Tis ſhe,
And if my ſpeech deſerve not faith, lay death
Upon me, and my lateſt words ſhall force
A credit from you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Which, good Gobrias? that Lady doſt thou mean?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: That Lady Sir,
She is your Siſter, and ſhe is your Siſter
That loves you ſo, 'tis ſhe for whom I weep,
To ſee you uſe her thus.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: It cannot be.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Piſh, this is tedious,
I cannot hold, I muſt preſent my ſelf,
And yet the ſight of my Spaconia
Touches me, as a ſudden thunder-clap
Does one that is about to ſin.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Away,
No more of this; here I pronounce him Traytor,
The direct plotter of my death, that names
Or thinks her for my Siſter, 'tis a lie,
The moſt malicious of the world, invented
To mad your King; he that will ſay ſo next,
Let him draw out his ſword and ſheath it here.
It is a ſin fully as pardonable:
She is no kin to me, nor ſhall ſhe be;
If ſhe were ever, I create her none:
And which of you can queſtion this? My power
Is like the Sea, that is to be obey'd,
And not diſputed with: I have decreed her
As far from having part of blood with me,
As the nak'd Indians; come and anſwer me,
He that is boldeſt now; is that my Siſter?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: O this is fine.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: No marry, ſhe is not, an't pleaſe your Majeſty, I never thought ſhe was, ſhe's nothing like you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: No 'tis true, ſhe is not.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thou ſhou'dſt be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Sir, I will ſpeak but once; by the ſame power
You make my blood a ſtranger unto yours,
You may command me dead, and ſo much love
A ſtranger may importune, pray you do;
If this requeſt appear too much to grant,
Adopt me of ſome other Family,
By your unqueſtion'd word; elſe I ſhall live
Like ſinfull iſſues that are left in ſtreets
By their regardleſs Mothers, and no name
Will be found for me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I will hear no more,
Why ſhould there be ſuch muſick in a voyce,
And ſin for me to hear it? All the world
May take delight in this, and 'tis damnation
For me to do ſo: You are fair and wiſe
And vertuous I think, and he is bleſt
That is ſo near you as my brother is;
But you are nought to me but a diſeaſe;
Continual torment without hope of eaſe;
Such an ungodly ſickneſs I have got,
That he that undertakes my cure, muſt firſt
O'rethrow Divinity, all moral Laws,
And leave mankind as unconfin'd as beaſts,
Allowing 'em to do all actions
As freely as they drink when they deſire.
Let me not hear you ſpeak again; yet ſee
I ſhall but langiſh for the want of that,
The having which, would kill me: No man here
Offer to ſpeak for her; for I conſider
As much as you can ſay; I will not toil
My body and my mind too, reſt thou there,
Here's one within will labour for you both.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I would I were paſt ſpeaking.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Fear not Madam,
The King will alter, 'tis ſome ſudden rage,
And you ſhall ſee it end ſome other way.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Pray heaven it do.

sp.speaker: Tig.
sp.l: Though ſhe to whom I ſwore, be here, I cannot
Stifle my paſſion longer; if my father
Should riſe again diſquieted with this,
And charge me to forbear, yet it would out.
Madam, a ſtranger, and a pris'ner begs
To be bid welcome.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: You are welcome, Sir,
I think, but if you be not, 'tis paſt me
To make you ſo: for I am here a ſtranger,
Greater than you; we know from whence you come,
But I appear a loſt thing, and by whom
Is yet uncertain, found here i'th' Court,
And onely ſuffer'd to walk up and down,
As one not worth the owning.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: O, I fear
Tigranes will be caught, he looks, me-thinks,
As he would change his eyes with her; ſome help
There is above for me, I hope.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Why do you turn away, and weep ſo faſt,
And utter things that miſ-become your looks,
Can you want owning?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: O 'tis certain ſo.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Acknowledge your ſelf mine.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: How now?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: And then ſee if you want an owner.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: They are talking.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Nations ſhall owne you for their Queen.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Tigranes, art not thou my priſoner?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: I am.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: And who is this?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: She is your Siſter.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: She is ſo.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Is ſhe ſo again? that's well.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: And then how dare you offer to change words with her?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Dare do it! Why? you brought me hither Sir,
To that intent.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Perhaps I told you ſo,
If I had ſworn it, had you ſo much folly
To credit it? The leaſt word that ſhe ſpeaks
Is worth a life; rule your diſordered tongue,
Or I will temper it.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Bleſt be the breath.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Temper my tongue! ſuch incivilities
As theſe, no barbarous people ever knew:
You break the lawes of Nature, and of Nations,
You talk to me as if I were a priſoner
For theft: my tongue be temper'd? I muſt ſpeak
If thunder check me, and I will.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: You will?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Alas my fortune.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Do not fear his frown, dear Madam, hear me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Fear not my frown? but that 'twere baſe in me
To ſight with one I know I can o'recome,
Again thou ſhouldſt be conquer'd by me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: He has one ranſome with him already; me-thinks
'T were good to fight double, or quit.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Away with him to priſon: Now Sir, ſee
If my frown be regardleſs; Why delay you?
Seiſe him Bacurius, you ſhall know my word
Sweeps like a wind, and all it grapples with,
Are as the chaffe before it.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Touch me not.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Help there.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Away.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: It is in vain to ſtruggle.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: You muſt be forc'd.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Sir, you muſt pardon us, we muſt obey.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why do you dally there? drag him away
By any thing.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Come Sir.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Juſtice, thou ought'ſt to give me ſtrength enough
To ſhake all theſe off; This is tyrannie,
Arbaces, ſutler than the burning Bulls,
Or that fam'd Titans bed. Thou mightſt as well
Search i'th' deep of Winter through the ſnow
For half ſtarv'd people, to bring home with thee,
To ſhew 'em fire, and ſend 'em back again,
As uſe me thus.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l:
Let him be cloſe, Bacurius.
Exeunt Tigr. and Bac.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: I ne're rejoyc'd at any ill to him,
But this impriſonment: what ſhall become
Of me forſaken?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: You will not let your Siſter
Depart thus diſcontented from you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: By no means Gobrias, I have done her wrong,
And made my ſelf believe much of my ſelf,
That is not in me: You did kneel to me,
Whileſt I ſtood ſtubborn and regardleſs by,
And like a god incenſed, gave no ear
To all your prayers: behold, I kneel to you,
Shew a contempt as large as was my own,
And I will ſuffer it, yet at the laſt forgive me.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: O you wrong me more in this,
Than in your rage you did: you mock me now.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Never forgive me then, which is the worſt
Can happen to me.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: If you be in earneſt,
Stand up and give me but a gentle look,
And two kind words, and I ſhall be in heaven.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Riſe you then to hear; I acknowledge thee
My hope, the only jewel of my life,
The beſt of Siſters, dearer than my breath,
A happineſs as high as I could think;
And when my actions call thee otherwiſe,
Perdition light upon me.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: This is better
Than if you had not frown'd, it comes to me,
Like mercie at the block, and when I leave
To ſerve you with my life, your curſe be with me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Then thus I do ſalute thee, and again,
To make this knot the ſtronger, Paradiſe
Is there: It may be you are yet in doubt,
This third kiſs blots it out, I wade in ſin,
And fooliſhly intice my ſelf along;
Take her away, ſee her a priſoner
In her own chamber cloſely, Gobrias.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Alas Sir, why?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I muſt not ſtay the anſwer, doe it.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Good Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: No more, doe it I ſay.

sp.speaker: Mard.
sp.l: This is better and better.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Yet hear me ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I will not hear you ſpeak,
Away with her, let no man think to ſpeak
For ſuch a creature; for ſhe is a witch,
A priſoner, and a Traitor.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Madam, this office grieves me.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis well the king is pleaſed with it.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Beſſus, go you along too with her; I will prove
All this that I have ſaid, if I may live
So long; but I am deſperately ſick,
For ſhe has given me poiſon in a kiſs;
She had't betwixt her lips, and with her eyes
She witches people: go without a word.
sp.stage: Exeunt Gob. Pan. Beſ. and Spaconia.
sp.l: Why ſhould you that have made me ſtand in war
Like ſate it ſelf, cutting what threds I pleas'd,
Decree ſuch an unworthy end of me,
And all my glories? What am I, alas,
That you oppoſe me? if my ſecret thoughts
Have ever harbour'd ſwellings againſt you,
They could not hurt you, and it is in you
To give me ſorrow, that will render me
Apt to receive your mercy; rather ſo,
Let it be rather ſo, than puniſh me
With ſuch unmanly ſins: Inceſt is in me
Dwelling already, and it muſt be holy
That pulls it thence, where art Mardonius

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Here Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I pray thee bear me, if thou canſt,
Am I not grown a ſtrange weight?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: As you were.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: No heavier?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why, my legs
Refuſe to bear my body; O Mardonius,
Thou haſt in field beheld me, when thou knowſt
I could have gone, though I could never run.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And ſo I ſhall again.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: O no, 'tis paſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Pray you go reſt your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Wilt thou hereafter when they talk of me,
As thou ſhalt hear nothing but infamy,
Remember ſome of thoſe things?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes I will.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I pray thee do: for thou ſhalt never ſee me ſo again.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: They talk of fame, I have gotten it in the wars; and will afford any man a reaſonable penny-worth: ſome will ſay, they could be content to have it, but that it is to be atchiev'd with danger; but my opinion is otherwiſe: for if I might ſtand ſtill in Cannon proof, and have ſame fall upon me, I would refuſe it: my reputation came principally by thinking to run away, which no body knows but Mardonius, and I think he conceals it to anger me. Before I went to the warrs, I came to the Town a young fellow, without means or parts to deſerve friends; and my empty guts perſwaded me to lie, and abuſe people for my meat, which I did, and they heat me: then would I faſt two days, till my hunger cri'd out on me, rail ſtill, then me thought I had a monſtrous ſtomach to abuſe 'em again, and did it. I, this ſtate I continu'd till they hung me up by th' heels, and beat me wi' hatle ſticks, as if they would have baked me, and have conſ • n'd ſome body wi'me for Veniſon: After this I rail'd, and • at quietly: for the whole Kingdom took notice of me for a baſtl'd whipt fellow, and what I ſaid was remembred in mirth but never in anger, of which I was glad; I would it were at that paſs again. After this, heaven calls an Aunt of mine, that left two hundred pound in a couſins hand for me, who taking me to be a gallant young ſpirit, raiſed a company for me with the money and ſent me into Armonia with'em: Away I would have run from them, but that I could get no company, and alone I durſt not run. I was never at battail but once, and there I was running, but Mardonius cudgel'd me; yet I got looſe at laſt, but was ſo fraid, that I ſaw no more than my ſhoulders doe, but fled with my whole company amongſt my Enemies, and overthrew'em: Now the report of my valour is come over before me, and they ſay I was a raw young fellow, but now I am improv'd, a Plague on their eloquence, 't will coſt me many a beating; And Mardonius might help this too, if he would; for now they think to get honour on me, and all the men I have abus'd call me freſhly worthily, as they call it by the way of challenge.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.p: Good morrow, Captain Beſſus.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Good morrow Sir.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.p: I come to ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: You're very welcome.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.p: From one that holds himſelf wrong'd by you ſome three years ſince: your worth he ſays is fam'd, and he doth nothing doubt but you will do him right, as beſeems a ſouldier.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: A pox on'em, ſo they cry all.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.p: And a ſlight note I have about me for you, for the delivery of which you muſt excuſe me; it is an office that friendſhip calls upon me to do, and no way offenſive to you; ſince I deſire but right on both ſides.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: 'Tis a challenge Sir, is it not?

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.p: 'Tis an inviting to the field.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: An inviting? O Sir your Mercy, what a Complement he delivers it with? he might as agreeable to my nature preſent me poiſon with ſuch a ſpeech: um um um reputation, um um um call you to account, um um um forc'd to this, um um um with my Sword, um um um like a Gentleman, um um um dear to me, um um um ſatisfaction: 'Tis very well Sir, I do accept it, but he muſt await an anſwer this thirteen weeks.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.p: Why Sir, he would be glad to wipe off his ſtain as ſoon as he could.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Sir upon my credit I am already ingag'd to two hundred, and twelve, all which muſt have their ſtains wip'd off, if that be the word, before him.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.p: Sir, if you be truly ingag'd but to one, he ſhall ſtay a competent time.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Upon my faith Sir, to two hundred and twelve, and I have a ſpent body, too much bruis'd in battel, ſo that I cannot fight, I muſt be plain, above three combats a day: All the kindneſs I can ſhew him, is to ſet him reſolvedly in my rowle, the two hundred and thirteenth man, which is ſomething, for I tell you, I think there will be more after him, than before him, I think ſo; pray you commend me to him, and tell him this.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.p: I will Sir, good morrow to you.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Good morrow good Sir. Certainly my ſafeſt way were to print my ſelf a coward, with a diſcovery how I came by my credit, and clap it upon every poſt; I have received above thirty challenges within this two hours, marry all but the firſt I put off with ingagement, and by good fortune, the firſt is no madder of fighting than I, ſo that that's referred, the place where it muſt be ended, is four days journey off, and our arbitratours are theſe: He has choſen a Gentleman in travel, and I have a ſpecial friend with a quartain ague, like to hold him this five years, for mine: and when his man comes home, we are to expect my friends health: If they would finde me challenges thus thick, as long as I liv'd, I would have no other living; I can make ſeven ſhillings a day o'th' paper to the Grocers: yet I learn nothing by all theſe but a little skill in comparing of ſtiles. I do finde evidently, that there is ſome one Scri • ener in this Town, that has a great hand in writing of Challenges, for they are all of a cut, and ſix of 'em in a hand; and they all end, my reputation is dear to me, and I muſt require ſatisfaction. Who's there? more paper I hope, no, 'tis my Lord Bacurius, I fear all is not well betwixt us.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Now Captain Beſſus, I come about a frivolous matter, caus'd by as idle a report: you know you were a coward.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Very right.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: And wronged me.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: True my Lord.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: But now people will call you valiant, deſertleſly I think, yet for their ſatisfaction, I will have you ſight with me.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: O my good Lord, my deep Engagements.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Tell not me of your Engagements, Captain Beſſus, it is not to be put off with an excuſe: for my own part, I am none of the multitude that believe your converſion from Coward.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: My Lord, I ſeek not Quarrels, and this belongs not to me, I am not to maintain it.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Who then pray?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Beſſus the Coward wrong'd you.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: And ſhall Beſſus the Valiant, maintain what Beſſus the Coward did?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: I pray thee leave theſe cheating tricks, I ſwear thou ſhalt fight with me, or thou ſhalt be beaten extreamly, and kick'd.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Since you provoke me thus far, my Lord, I will fight with you, and by my Sword it ſhall coſt me twenty pound, but I will have my Leg well a week ſooner purpoſely.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Your Leg? Why, what ailes your Leg? i'le do a cure on you, ſtand up.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: My Lord, this is not Noble in you.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: What doſt thou with ſuch a phraſe in thy mouth? I will kick thee out of all good words before I leave thee.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: My Lord, I take this as a puniſhment for the offence I did when I was a Coward.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: When thou wert? Confeſs thy ſelf a Coward ſtill, or by this light, I'le beat thee into Spunge.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Why I am one.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Are you ſo Sir? And why do you wear a Sword then? Come unbuckle.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Unbuckle I ſay, and give it me, or as I live, thy head will ake extreamly.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: It is a pretty Hilt, and if your Lordſhip take an affection to it, with all my heart I preſent it to you for a New-years gift.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: I thank you very heartily, ſweet Captain, farewel.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: One word more, I beſeech your Lordſhip to render me my knife again.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p:
Marry by all means Captain; cheriſh your ſelf with it, and eat hard, good Captain; we cannot tell whether we ſhall have any more ſuch: Adue dear Captain.
Exit Bac.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p:
I will make better uſe of this, than of my Sword: A baſe ſpirit has this vantage of a brave one, it keeps alwayes at a ſtay, nothing brings it down, not beating. I remember I promis'd the King in a great Audience, that I would make my back-biters eat my ſword to a knife; how to get another ſword I know not, nor know any means left for me to maintain my credit, but impudence: therefore I will out-ſwear him and all his followers, that this is all that's left uneaten of my ſword.
Exit Beſſus.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p:
I'le move the King, he is moſt ſtrangely alter'd; I gueſs the cauſe I fear too right, Heaven has ſome ſecret end in't, and 'tis a ſcourge no queſtion juſtly laid upon him: he has followed me through twenty Rooms; and ever when I ſtay to wait his command, he bluſhes like a Girl, and looks upon me, as if modeſty kept in his buſineſs: ſo turns away from me, but if I go on, he follows me again.
Enter Arbaces. See, here he is. I do not uſe this, yet I know not how, I cannot chuſe but weep to ſee him; his very Enemies I think, whoſe wounds have bred his fame, if they ſhould ſee him now, would find tears i'their eyes.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I cannot utter it, why ſhould I keep
A breaſt to harbour thoughts? I dare not ſpeak.
Darkneſs is in my boſom, and there lie
A thouſand thoughts that cannot brook the light:
How wilt thou vex'em when this deed is done,
Conſcience, that art afraid to let me name it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: How do you Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why very well Mardonius, how doſt thou do?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Better than you I fear.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I hope thou art; for to be plain with thee,
Thou art in Hell elſe, ſecret ſcorching flames
That far tranſcend earthly material fires
Are crept into me, and there is no cure.
Is it not ſtrange Mardonius, there's no cure?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir, either I miſtake, or there is ſomething hid That you would utter to me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: So there is, but yet I cannot do it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Out with it Sir, if it be dangerous, I will not ſhrink to do you ſervice, I ſhall not eſteem my life a weightier matter than indeed it is, I know it is ſubject to more chances than it has hours, and I were better loſe it in my Kings cauſe, than with an ague, or a fall, or ſleeping, to a Thief; as all theſe are probable enough: let me but know what I ſhall do for you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: It will not out: were you with Gobrias,
And bad him give my Siſter all content
The place affords, and give her leave to ſend
And ſpeak to whom ſhe pleaſe?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I was.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: And did you to Bacurius ſay as much About Tigranes?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: That's all my buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: O ſay not ſo,
You had an anſwer of this before;
Beſides I think this buſineſs might
Be utter'd more careleſly.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Come thou ſhalt have it out, I do beſeech thee
By all the love thou haſt profeſt to me,
To ſee my Siſter from me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Well, and what?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: That's all.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That's ſtrange, I ſhall ſay nothing to her?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Not a word;
But if thou loveſt me, find ſome ſubtil way
To make her underſtand by ſigns.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: But what ſhall I make her underſtand?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: O Mardonius, for that I muſt be pardon'd.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You may, but I can only ſee her then.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: 'Tis true;
Bear her this Ring then, and
One more advice, thou ſhalt ſpeak to her:
Tell her I do love My kindred all: wilt thou?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Is there no more?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: O yes and her the beſt;
Better than any Brother loves his Siſter: That's all.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Methinks this need not have been delivered with ſuch a caution; I'le do it.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: There is more yet,
Wilt thou be faithul to me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir, if I take upon me to deliver it, after I hear it,
I'le paſs through fire to do it.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I love her better than a Brother ought;
Doſt thou conceive me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I hope you do not Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: No, thou art dull, kneel down before her,
And ne'r riſe again, till ſhe will love me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why, I think ſhe does.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: But better than ſhe does, another way;
As wives love Husbands.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why, I think there are few Wives that love their Husbands better than ſhe does you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Thou wilt not underſtand me: is it ſit
This ſhould be uttered plainly? take it then
Naked as it is: I would deſire her love
Laſciviouſly, lewdly, inceſtuouſly,
To do a ſin that needs muſt damn us both,
And thee too: doſt thou underſtand me now?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, there's your Ring again; what have I done
Diſhoneſtly in my whole life, name it,
That you ſhould put ſo baſe a buſineſs to me?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Didſt thou not tell me thou wouldſt do it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes; if I undertook it, but if all
My hairs were lives, I would not be engag'd
In ſuch a caſe to ſave my laſt life.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: O guilt! ha how poor and weak a thing art thou?
This man that is my ſervant, whom my breath
Might blow upon the world, might beat me here
Having this cauſe, whil'ſt I preſt down with ſin
Could not reſiſt him: hear Mardonius,
It was a motion miſ-beſeeming man,
And I am ſorry for it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Heaven grant you may be ſo: you muſt underſtand, nothing that you can utter, can remove my love and ſervice from my Prince. But otherwiſe, I think I ſhall not love you more. For you are ſinful, and if you do this crime, you ought to have no Laws. For after this, it will be great injuſtice in you to puniſh any offender for any crime. For my ſelf I find my heart too big: I feel I have not patience to look on whilſt you run theſe forbidden courſes. Means I have none but your favour, and I am rather glad that I ſhall loſe 'em both together, than keep 'em with ſuch conditions; I ſhall find a dwelling amongſt ſome people, where though our Garments perhaps be courſ •• , we ſhall be richer far within, and harbour no ſuch vices in 'em: the Gods preſerve you, and mend.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Mardonius, ſtay Mardonius, for though
My preſent ſtate requires nothing but knaves
To be about me, ſuch as are prepar'd
For every wicked act, yet who does know
But that my loathed Fate may turn about,
And I have uſe for honeſt men again?
I hope I may, I prethee leave me not.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Where is the King?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: An't pleaſe your Majeſty, there's the knife.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: What knife?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: The Sword is eaten.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Away you fool, the King is ſerious,
And cannot now admit your vanities.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Vanities! I'me no honeſt man, if my enemies have not brought it to this, what, do you think I lie?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: No, no, 'tis well Beſſus, 'tis very well I'm glad on't.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: If your enemies brought it to this, your enemies are Cutlers, come leave the King.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Why, may not valour approach him?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes, but he has affairs, depart, or I ſhall be ſomething unmannerly with you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: No, let him ſtay Mardonius, let him ſtay,
I have occaſion with him very weighty,
And I can ſpare you now.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why I can ſpare you now.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Mardonius give way to theſe State affairs.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Indeed you are fitter for this preſent purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Beſſus, I ſhould imploy thee, wilt thou do't?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Do't for you? by this Air I will do any thing without exception, be it a good, bad, or indifferent thing.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Do not ſwear.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: By this light but I will, any thing whatſoever.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: But I ſhall name the thing,
Thy Conſcience will not ſuffer thee to do.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: I would fain hear that thing.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why I would have thee get my Siſter for me?
Thou underſtandſt me, in a wicked manner.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: O you would have a bout with her?
I'le do't, I'le do't, I'ſaith.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Wilt thou, do'ſt thou make no more on't?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: More? no, why is there any thing elſe? if there be, it ſhall be done too.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Haſt thou no greater ſenſe of ſuch a ſin?
Thou art too wicked for my company,
Though I have hell within me, thou may'ſt yet
Corrupt me further: pray thee anſwer me,
How do I ſhew to thee after this motion?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Why your Majeſty looks as well in my opinion, as ever you did ſince you were born.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: But thou appear'ſt to me after thy grant,
The uglieſt, loathed deteſtable thing
That I ever met with. Thou haſt eyes
Like the flames of Sulphur, which me thinks do dart
Infection on me, and thou haſt a mouth
Enough to take me in where there do ſtand
Four rows of Iron Teeth.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I feel no ſuch thing, but 'tis no matter how I look, I'le do my buſineſs as well as they that look better, and when this is diſpatch'd, if you have a mind to your Mother, tell me, and you ſhall ſee I'le ſet it hard.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: My Mother! Heaven forgive me to hear this,
I am inſpir'd with horrour: now I hate thee
Worſe than my ſin, which if I could come by
Should ſuffer death Eternal ne're to riſe
In any breaſt again. Know I will die
Languiſhing mad, as I reſolve, I ſhall,
E're I will deal by ſuch an inſtrument:
Thou art too ſinful to imploy in this;
Out of the World, away.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: What do you mean, Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Hung round with Curſes, take thy fearful ſlight
Into the Deſarts, where 'mongſt all the Monſters
If thou find'ſt one ſo beaſtly as thy ſelf,
Thou ſhalt be held as innocent.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Good Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: If there were no ſuch inſtruments as thou,
We Kings could never act ſuch wicked deeds:
Seek out a man that mocks Divinity,
That breaks each precept both of God and man,
And natures too, and does it without luſt,
Meerly becauſe it is a law, and good,
And live with him: for him thou canſt not ſpoil.

Away I ſay, I will not do this ſin.
Exit Beſſus.
I'le preſs it here, till it do break my breaſt,
It heaves to get out, but thou art a ſin,
And ſpight of torture I will keep thee in.

div.head: Actus Quartus.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: HAve you written Madam?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Yes, good Gobrias.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: And with a kindneſs, and ſuch winning words
As may provoke him, at one inſtant feel
His double fault, your wrong, and his own raſhneſs?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I have ſent words enough, if words may win him
From his diſpleaſure; and ſuch words I hope,
As ſhall gain much upon his goodneſs, Gobrias.
Yet fearing they are many, and a womans,
A poor belief may follow, I have woven
As many truths within 'em to ſpeak for me,
That if he be but gracious, and receive 'em—

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Good Lady be not fearful, though he ſhould not
Give you your preſent end in this, believe it,
You ſhall feel, if your vertue can induce you
To labour on't, this tempeſt which I know,
Is but a poor proof 'gainſt your patience:
All thoſe contents, your ſpirit will arrive at,
Newer and ſweeter to you; your Royal brother,
When he ſhall once collect himſelf, and ſee
How far he has been aſunder from himſelf;
What a meer ſtranger to his golden temper:
Muſt from thoſe roots of vertue, never dying,
Though ſomewhat ſtopt with humour, ſhoot again
• nto a thouſand glories, bearing his fair branches
High as our hopes can look at, ſtraight as juſtice,
• oaden with ripe contents; he loves you dearly,
〈◊〉 know it, and I hope I need not farther
Win you to underſtand it.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I believe it.
But howſoever, I am ſure I love him dearly:
So dearly, that if any thing I write
For my enlarging ſhould beget his anger,
Heaven be a witneſs with me and my faith,
〈◊〉 had rather live intomb'd here.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: You ſhall not feel a worſe ſtroke than your grief,
I am ſorry 'tis ſo ſharp, I kiſs your hand,
And this night will deliver this true ſtory,
With this hand to your Brother.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l:
Peace go with you, you are a good man.
Exit Gob.
My Spaconia, why are you ever ſad thus?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: O dear Lady.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Prethee diſcover not a way to ſadneſs,
Nearer than I have in me, our two ſorrows
Work like two eager Hawks, who ſhall get higheſt;
How ſhall I leſſen thine? for mine I fear
Is eaſier known than cur'd.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Heaven comfort both,
And give you happy ends, however I
Fall in my ſtubborn fortunes.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: This but teaches
How to be more familiar with our ſorrows,
That are too much our maſters: good Spaconia
How ſhall I do you ſervice?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Nobleſt Lady,
You make me more a ſlave ſtill to your goodneſs,
And only live to purchaſe thanks to pay you,
For that is all the buſineſs of my life: now
I will be bold, ſince you will have it ſo,
To ask a noble favour of you.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Speak it, 'tis yours, for from ſo ſweet a vertue,
No ill demand has iſſue.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Then ever vertuous, let me beg your will
In helping me to ſee the Prince Tigranes,
With whom I am equal priſoner, if not more.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Reſerve me to a greater end Spaconia;
Bacurius cannot want ſo much good manners
As to deny your gentle viſitation,
Though you came only with your own command.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: I know they will deny me gracious Madam,
Being a ſtranger, and ſo little fam'd,
So utter empty of thoſe excellencies
That tame Authority; but in you ſweet Lady,
All theſe are natural; beſide, a power
Deriv'd immediate from your Royal brother,
Whoſe leaſt word in you may command the Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: More than my word Spaconia, you ſhall carry,
For fear it fail you.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Dare you truſt a Token?
Madam I fear I am grown too bold a begger.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: You are a pretty one, and truſt me Lady
It joyes me, I ſhall do a good to you,
Though to my ſelf I never ſhall be happy:
Here, take this Ring, and from me as a Token
Deliver it; I think they will not ſtay you:
So all your own deſires go with you Lady.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: And ſweet peace to your Grace.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Pray Heaven I find it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Fool that I am, I have undone my ſelf,
And with my own hand turn'd my fortune round,
That was a fair one: I have childiſhly
Plaid with my hope ſo long, till I have broke it,
And now too late I mourn for't; O Spaconia!
Thou haſt found an even way to thy revenge now,
Why didſt thou follow me like a faint ſhadow,
To wither my deſires? But wretched fool,
Why did I plant thee 'twixt the Sun and me,
To make me freeze thus? Why did I prefer her
To the fair Princeſs? O thou fool, thou fool,
Thou family of tools, live like a ſlave ſtill,
And in thee bear thine own hell and thy torment,
Thou haſt deſerv'd: Couldſt thou find no Lady
But ſhe that has thy hopes to put her to,
And hazard all thy peace? None to abuſe,
But ſhe that lov'd thee ever? poor Spaconia,
And ſo much lov'd thee, that in honeſty
And honour thou art bound to meet her vertues:
She that forgot the greatneſs of her grief
And miſeries, that muſt follow ſuch mad paſſions,
Endleſs and wild as women; ſhe that for thee
And with thee leſt her liberty, her name,
And Country, you have paid me equal, Heavens,
And ſent my own rod to correct me with;
A woman: for inconſtancy I'le ſuffer,
Lay it on juſtice, till my ſoul melt in me
For my unmanly, beaſtly, ſudden doting
Upon a new face: after all my oaths
Many and ſtrange ones,
I feel my old fire flame again and burn
So ſtrong and violent, that ſhould I ſee her
Again, the grief and that would kill me.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Lady, your token I acknowledge, you may paſs;
There is the King.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l:
I thank your Lordſhip for it.
Exit Bac.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: She comes, ſhe comes, ſhame hide me ever from her,
Would I were buried, or ſo far remov'd
Light might not find me out, I dare not ſee her.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Nay never hide your ſelf; or were you hid
Where earth hides all her riches, near her Center;
My wrongs without more day would light me to you:
I muſt ſpeak e're I die; were all your greatneſs
Doubled upon you, y'are a perjur'd man,
And only mighty in your wickedneſs
Of wronging women. Thou art falſe, falſe Prince;
I live to ſee it, poor Spaconia lives
To tell thee thou art falſe; and then no more;
She lives to tell thee thou art more unconſtant,
Than all ill women ever were together.
Thy faith is firm as raging over-flowes,
That no bank can command; as laſting
As boyes gay bubbles, blown i'th' Air and broken:
The wind is ſixt to thee: and ſooner ſhall
The beaten Mariner with his ſhrill whiſtle
Calm the loud murmur of the troubled main,
And ſtrike it ſmooth again; than thy ſoul fall
To have peace in love with any: Thou art all
That all good men muſt hate; and if thy ſtory
Shall tell ſucceeeding ages what thou wert,
O let it ſpare me in it, leſt true lovers
In pity of my wrong, burn thy black Legend,
And with their curſes, ſhake thy ſleeping aſhes.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Oh! oh!

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: The deſtinies, I hope, have pointed out
Our ends, that thou maiſt die for love,
Though not for me; for this aſſure thy ſelf,
The Princeſs hates thee deadly, and will ſooner
Be won to marry with a Bull, and ſafer
Than ſuch a beaſt as thou art: I have ſtruck,
I fear, too deep; beſhrow me ſor't; Sir,
This ſorrow works me like a cunning friendſhip,
Into the ſame piece with it; 'tis aſham'd,
Alas, I have been too rugged: Dear my Lord,
I am ſorry I have ſpoken any thing,
Indeed I am, that may add more reſtraint
To that too much you have: good Sir, be pleas'd
To think it was a fault of love, not malice;
And do as I will do, forgive it Prince.
I do, and can forgive the greateſt ſins
To me you can repent of; pray believe.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: O my Spaconia! O thou vertuous woman!

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.l: Nay, more, the King Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Have you been carefull of our noble Priſoner,
That he want nothing ſitting for his greatneſs?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I hope his grace will quit me for my care Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: 'Tis well, royal Tigranes, health.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: More than the ſtrictneſs of this place can give Sir, I offer back again to great Arbaces.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: We thank you worthy Prince, and pray excuſe us,
We have not ſeen you ſince your being here,
I hope your noble uſage has been equall
With your own perſon: your impriſonment,
If it be any, I dare ſay is eaſie,
And ſhall not laſt too dayes.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: I thank you;
My uſage here has been the ſame it was,
Worthy a royal Conqueror. For my reſtraint,
It came unkindly, becauſe much unlook'd for;
But I muſt bear it.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: What Lady's that? Bacurius?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: One of the Princeſs women, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I fear'd it, why comes ſhe hither?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: To ſpeak with the Prince Tigranes.

sp.speaker: Arb.
