sp.l: From whom, Bacurius?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: From the Princeſs, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I knew I had ſeen her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: His ſit begins to take him now again,
'Tis a ſtrange Feaver, and 'twill ſhake us all anon, I fear,
Would he were well cur'd of this raging folly:
Give me the warrs, where men are mad, and may talk what they liſt, and held the braveſt fellows; This pelting prating peace is good for nothing: drinking's a vertue to't.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I ſee there's truth in no man, nor obedience,
But for his own ends, why did you let her in?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: It was your own command to barr none from him,
Beſides, the Princeſs ſent her ring Sir, for my warrant.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: A token to Tigranes, did ſhe not?
Sir tell truth.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I do not uſe to lie Sir,
'Tis no way I eat or live by, and I think,
This is no token Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: This combat has undone him: if he had been well beaten, he had been temperate; I ſhall never ſee him handſome again, till he have a Horſe mans ſtaffe yok'd thorow his ſhoulders, or an arm broken with a bullet.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I am trifled with.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I know it, as I know thee to be falſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now the clap comes.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: You never knew me ſo, Sir I dare ſpeak it,
And durſt a worſe man tell me, though my better—

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis well ſaid, by my ſoul.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Sirra, you anſwer as you had no life.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: That I fear Sir to loſe nobly.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I ſay Sir, once again.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: You may ſay what yon pleaſe, Sir,
Would I might do ſo.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I will, Sir, and ſay openly, this woman carries letters,
By my life I know ſhe carries letters, this woman does it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Would Beſſus were here to take her aſide and ſearch her, He would quickly tell you what ſhe carried Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I have found it out, this woman carries letters.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: If this hold, 'twill be an ill world for Bawdes, Chamber-maids and Poſt-boyes, I thank heaven I have none but his letters patents, things of his own enditing.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Prince, this cunning cannot do't.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Doe, What Sir? I reach you not.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: It ſhall not ſerve your turn, Prince.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Serve my turn Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I Sit, it ſhall not ſerve your turn.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Be plainer, good Sir.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: This woman ſhall carry no more letters back to your Love Pa • thea, by Heaven ſhe ſhall not, I ſay ſhe ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: This would make a Saint ſwear like a ſouldier.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: This beats me more, King, than the blow • you gave me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Take'em away both, and together let them priſoners be, ſtrictly and cloſely kept, or Sirra, your life ſhall anſwe • it, and let no body ſpeak with'em hereafter.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.l: Well, I am ſubject to you,
And muſt indure theſe paſſions:
This is the impriſonment I have look'd for always.
And the dearer place I would chooſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir, you have done well now.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Dare you reprove it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: You muſt be croſſing me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I have no letters Sir to anger you,
But a dry ſonnet of my Corporals
To an old Suttlers wife, and that I'll burn, Sir.
'Tis like to prove a fine age for the Ignorant.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: How darſt thou ſo often forfeit thy life?
Thou know'ſt 'tis in my power to take it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, and I know you wo'not, or if you doe, you'll miſs it quickly.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Who ſhall tell you of theſe childiſh ſollies
When I am dead? who ſhall put to his power
To draw thoſe vertues out of a flood of humors,
When they are drown'd, and make'em ſhine again?
No, cut my head off:
Then you may talk, and be believed, and grow worſe,
And have your too ſelf glorious temper rot
Into a deep ſleep, and the Kingdom with you,
Till forraign ſwords be in your throats, and ſlaughter
Be every where about you like your ſlatterers.
Do, kill me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Prethee be tamer, good Mardonius,
Thou know'ſt I love thee, nay I honour thee,
Believe it good old Souldier, I am thine;
But I am rack'd clean from my ſelf, bear with me,
Woot thou bear with me my Mardonius?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There comes a good man, love him too, he's temperate,
You may live to have need of ſuch a vertue,
Rage is not ſtill in faſhion.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Welcome good Gobrias.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: My ſervice and this letter to your Grace.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: From whom?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: From the rich Mine of vertue and beauty,
Your mournfull Siſter.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: She is in priſon, Gobrias, is ſhe not?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: She is Sir, till your pleaſure to enlarge her,
Which on my knees I beg. Oh 'tis not fit,
That all the ſweetneſs of the world in one,
The youth and vertue that would tame wild Tygers,
And wilder people, that have known no manners,
Should live thus cloiſtred up; for your loves ſake,
If there be any in that noble heart,
To her a wretched Lady, and forlorn,
Or for her love to you, which is as much
As nature and obedience ever gave,
Have pity on her beauties.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Pray thee ſtand up; 'Tis true, ſhe is too fair,
And all theſe commendations but her own,
Would thou had'ſt never ſo commended her,
Or I nere liv'd to have heard it Gobrias;
If thou but know'ſt the wrong her beautie does her,
Thou wouldſt in pity of her be a lyar,
Thy ignorance has drawn me wretched man,
Whither my ſelf nor thou canſt well tell: O my fate!
I think ſhe loves me, but I fear another
Is deeper in her heart: How thinkſt thou Gobrias?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: I do beſeech your Grace believe it not,
For let me periſh if it be not falſe. Good Sir, read her Letter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p:
This Love, or what a devil it is I know not, begets more miſchief than a Wake. I had rather be well beaten, ſtarv'd, or lowſie, than live within the Air on't. He that
had ſeen this brave fellow Charge through a grove of Pikes • ut t'other day, and look upon him now, will ne'r believe • is eyes again: if he continue thus but two days more, a Taylor may beat him with one hand tied behind him.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Alas, ſhe would be at liberty.
And there bo a thouſand reaſons Gobrias,
Thouſands that will deny't:
Which if ſhe knew, ſhe would contentedly
Be where ſhe is: and bleſs her vertues for it,
And me, though ſhe were cloſer, ſhe would, Gobrias,
Good man indeed ſhe would.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Then good Sir, for her ſatisfaction,
Send for her and with reaſon make her know
Why ſhe muſt live thus from you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I will; go bring her to me. Exeunt all.

div.stage: Enter Beſſus, and two Sword-men, and a Boy.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Y'are very welcome both; ſome ſtools boy,
And reach a Table; Gentlemen o'th' Sword,
Pray ſit without more complement; be gone child.
I have been curious in the ſearching of you,
Becauſe I underſtand you wiſe and valiant perſons.
We underſtand our ſelves Sir.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Nay Gentlemen, and dear friends o'th' Sword,
No complement I pray, but to the cauſe
I hang upon, which in few, is my honour.
You cannot hang too much Sir, for your honour,
But to your cauſe.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Be wiſe, and ſpeak truth, my firſt doubt is,
My beating by my Prince.
Stay there a little Sir, do you doubt a beating?
Or have you had a beating by your Prince?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Gentlemen o'th' Sword, my Prince has beaten me.
Brother, what think you of this caſe?
If he has beaten him, the caſe is clear.
If he have beaten him, I grant the caſe;
But how? we cannot be too ſubtil in this buſineſs,
I ſay, but how?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Even with his Royal hand.
Was it a blow of love, or indignation?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: 'Twas twenty blows of indignation, Gentlemen,
Beſides two blows o'th' face.
Thoſe blows o'th' face have made a new cauſe on't,
The reſt were but an horrible rudeneſs.

sp.p: Two blows o'th' face, and given by a worſe man, I muſt confeſs, as the Sword-men ſay, had turn'd the buſineſs: Mark me brother, by a worſe man; but being by his Prince, had they been ten, and thoſe ten drawn teeth, beſides the hazard of his noſe for ever; all this had been but favours: this is my flat opinion, which I'le die in.

The King may do much Captain, believe it; for had he crackt your Scull through, like a bottle, or broke a Rib or two with toſſing of you, yet you had loſt no honour: This is ſtrange you may imagine, but this is truth now Captain.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: I will be glad to embrace it Gentlemen;
But how far may he ſtrike me?

sp.p: There is another: a new cauſe riſing from the time and diſtance, in which I will deliver my opinion: he may ſtrike, beat, or cauſe to be beaten: for theſe are natural to man: your Prince, I ſay, may beat you, ſo far forth as his dominion reacheth, that's for the diſtance; the time, ten miles a day, I take it.

sp.l: Brother, you err, 'tis fifteen miles a day,
His ſtage is ten, his beatings are fifteen.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: 'Tis the longeſt, but we ſubjects muſt—
Be ſubject to it; you are wiſe and vertuous.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Obedience ever makes that noble uſe on't,
To which I dedicate my beaten body;
I muſt trouble you a little further, Gentlemen o'th' Sword.
No trouble at all to us Sir, if we may
Profit your underſtanding, we are bound
By vertue of our calling to utter our opinions,
Shortly, and diſcreetly.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: My foreſt buſineſs is, I have been kick'd.
How far Sir?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Not to flatter my ſelf in it, all over, my ſword forc'd but not loſt; for diſcreetly I rendred it to ſave that imputation.

sp.l: It ſhew'd diſcretion, the beſt part of valour.
Brother, this is a pretty cauſe, pray ponder on't;
Our friend here has been kick'd.
He has ſo, brother.
Sorely he ſaies: Now, had he ſet down here
Upon the meer kick, 't had been Cowardly.
I think it had been Cowardly indeed.
But our friend has redeem'd it in delivering
His ſword without compulſion; and that man
That took it of him, I pronounce a weak one,
And his kicks nullities.
He ſhould have kick'd him after the delivering
Which is the confirmation of a Coward.
Brother, I take it, you miſtake the queſtion;
For; ſay that I were kick'd.
I muſt not ſay ſo;
Nor I muſt not hear it ſpoke by the tongue of man.
You kick'd, dear brother! you're merry.
But put the caſe I were kick'd?

sp.p: Let them put it that are things weary of their lives, and know not honour; put the caſe you were kick'd?

sp.l: I do not ſay I was kickt.
Nor no ſilly creature that wears his head without a Caſe, his ſoul in a Skin-coat: You kickt dear brother?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Nay Gentlemen, let us do what we ſhall do,
Truly and honeſty; good Sirs to the queſtion.
Why then I ſay, ſuppoſe your Boy kick't, Captain?
The Boy may be ſuppos'd is liable.
A fooliſh forward zeal Sir, in my friend;
But to the Boy, ſuppoſe the Boy were kickt.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: I do ſuppoſe it.
Has your Boy a ſword?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Surely no; I pray ſuppoſe a ſword too.
I do ſuppoſe it; you grant your Boy was kick't then.

sp.p: By no means Captain, let it be ſuppoſed ſtill; the word grant, makes not for us.

sp.l: I ſay this muſt be granted.
This muſt be granted brother?
I, this muſt be granted.
Still this muſt?
I ſay this muſt be granted.
I, give me the muſt again, brother, you palter.
I will not hear you, waſp.

sp.p: Brother, I ſay you palter, the muſt three times together; I wear as ſharp Steel as another man, and my Fox bites as deep, muſled, my dear brother.
sp.l: But to the cauſe again.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Nay look you Gentlemen.
In a word, I ha' done.
A tall man but intemperate, 'tis great pity;
Once more ſuppoſe the Boy kick'd.
Forward.
And being thorowly kick'd, laughs at the kicker.
So much for us; proceed.
And in this beaten ſcorn, as I may call it,
Delivers up his weapon; where lies the error?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: It lies i'th' beating Sir, I found it four dayes ſince.
The error, and a ſore one as I take it,
Lies in the thing kicking.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: I underſtand that well, 'tis ſo indeed Sir.
That is according to the man that did it.
There ſprings a new branch, whoſe was the foot?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: A Lords.
The cauſe is mighty, but had it been two Lords,
And both had kick'd you, if you laugh, 'tis clear.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: I did laugh,
But how will that help me, Gentlemen?
Yes, it ſhall help you if you laught aloud.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: As loud as a kick'd man could laugh, I laught Sir.
My reaſon now, the valiant man is known
By ſuffering and contemning; you have
Enough of both, and you are valiant.
If he be ſure he has been kick'd enough:
For that brave ſufferance you ſpeak of brother,
Conſiſts not in a beating and away,
But in a endgell'd body, from eighteen
To eight and thirty; in a head rebuk'd
With pots of all ſize, degrees, ſtools, and bed-ſtaves,
This ſhowes a valiant man.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Then I am valiant, as valiant as the proudeſt,
For theſe are all familiar things to me;
Familiar as my ſleep, or want of money,
All my whole body's but one bruiſe with beating,
I think I have been endgell'd with all nations,
And almoſt all Religions.
Embrace him brother, this man is valiant,
I know it by my ſelf, he's valiant.
Captain, thou art a valiant Gentleman,
To bide upon, a very valiant man.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: My equall friends o'th'Sword, I muſt requeſt your hands to this.

sp.l: 'Tis fit it ſhould be.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Boy, get me ſome wine, and pen and Ink within:
Am I clear, Gentlemen?
Sir, the world has taken notice what we have done,
Make much of your body, for I'll pawn my ſteel,
Men will be cover of their legs hereafter.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: I muſt requeſt you goe along and teſtife to the Lord Bacurius, whoſe foot has ſtruck me, how you find my cauſe.
We will, and tell that Lord he muſt be rul'd,
Or there are thoſe abroad, will rule his Lordſhip. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Arbaces at one door, and Gob. and Panthea at another.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.l: Sir, here's the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Leave us then alone,
For the main cauſe of her impriſonment

Muſt not be heard by any but her ſelf.
Exit Gob.
You're welcome Siſter, and would to heaven
I could ſo bid you by another name:
If you above love not ſuch ſins as theſe,
Circle my heart with thoughts as cold as ſnow
To quench theſe riſing flames that harbour here.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Sir, does it pleaſe you I ſhould ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Pleaſe me?
I, more than all the art of muſick can,
Thy ſpeech doth pleaſe me, for it ever ſounds,
As thou brought'ſt joyfull unexpected news;
And yet it is not fit thou ſhouldſt be heard.
I pray thee think ſo.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Be it ſo, I will.
Am I the firſt that ever had a wrong
So far from being ſit to have redreſs,
That 't was unfit to hear it? I will back
To priſon, rather than diſquiet you,
And wait till it be fit.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: No, do not goe;
For I will hear thee with a ſerious thought:
I have collected all that's man about me
Together ſtrongly, and I am reſolv'd
To hear thee largely, but I do beſeech thee,
Do not come nearer to me, for there is
Something in that, that will undoe us both.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: A • as Sir, am I v • nome?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Yes, to me;
Though of thy ſelf I think thee to be
In equall degree of heat or cold,
As nature can make: yet as unfound men
Convert the ſweeteſt and the nouriſhing'ſt meats
Into diſeaſes, ſo ſhall I diſtemper'd,
Do thee, I pray thee draw no nearer to me.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Sir, this is that I would: I am of late
Shut from the world, and why it ſhould be thus,
Is all I wiſh to know.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why credit me Panthea,
Credit me that am thy brother,
Thy loving brother, that there is a cauſe
Sufficient, yet unſit for thee to know,
That might undoe thee everlaſtingly,
Only to hear, wilt thou but credit this?
By Heaven 'tis true, believe it if thou canſt.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Children and fools are ever credulous,
And I am both, I think, for I believe;
If you diſſemble, be it on your head;
I'le back unto my priſon: yet me-thinks
I might be kept in ſome place where you are;
For in my ſelf, I find I know not what
To call it, but it is a great deſire
To ſee you often.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Fie, you come in a ſtep, what do you mean?
Dear ſiſter, do not ſo: Alas Panthea,
Where I am would you be? Why that's the cauſe
You are impriſon'd, that you may not be
Where I am.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Then I muſt indure it Sir, Heaven keep you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Nay, you ſhall hear the caſe in ſhort Panthea,
And when thou hear'ſt it, thou wilt bluſh for me,
And hang thy head down like a Violet
Full of the mornings dew: There is a way
To gain thy freedome, but 'tis ſuch a one
As puts thee in worſe bondage, and I know,
Thou wouldſt encounter fire, and make a proof
Whether the gods have care of innocence,
Rather than follow it: Know that I have loſt,
The only difference betwixt man and beaſt,
My reaſon.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Heaven forbid.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Nay 'tis gone;
And I am left as far without a bound,
As the wild Ocean, that obeys the winds;
Each ſodain paſſion throwes me where it liſts,
And overwhelms all that oppoſe my will:
I have beheld thee with a luſtfull eye;
My heart is ſet on wickedneſs to act
Such ſins with thee, as I have been afraid
To think of, if thou dar'ſt conſent to this,
Which I beſeech thee do not, thou maiſt gain
Thy liberty, and yield me a content;
If not, thy dwelling muſt be dark and cloſe,
Where I may never ſee thee; For heaven knows
That laid this puniſhment upon my pride,
Thy ſight at ſome time will enforce my madneſs
To make a ſtart e'ne to thy raviſhing;
Now ſpit upon me, and call all reproaches
Thou canſt deviſe together, and at once
Hurle 'em againſt me: for I am a ſickneſs
As killing as the plague, ready to ſeize thee.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Far be it from me to revile the King:
But it is true, that I ſhall rather chooſe
To ſearch out death, that elſe would ſearch out me,
And in a grave ſleep with my innocence,
Than welcome ſuch a ſin: It is my fate,
To theſe croſs accidents I was ordain'd,
And muſt have patience; and but that my eyes
Have more of woman in 'em than my heart,
I would not weep: Peace enter you again.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Farwell, and good Panthea pray for me,
Thy prayers are pure, that I may find a death
However ſoon before my paſſions grow
That they forget what I deſire is ſin;
For thither they are tending: if that happen,
Then I ſhall force thee tho' thou wert a Virgin
By vow to Heaven, and ſhall pull a heap
Of ſtrange yet uninvented ſin upon me.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Sir, I will pray for you, yet you ſhall know
It is a fullen fate that governs us,
For I could wiſh as heartily as you
I were no ſiſter to you, I ſhould then
Imbrace your lawfull love, ſooner than health.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Couldſt thou affect me then?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: So perfectly,
That as it is, I ne're ſhall ſway my heart,
To like another.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Then I curſe my birth,
Muſt this be added to my miſeries
That thou art willing too? is there no ſtop
To our full happineſs, but theſe meer ſounds
Brother and Siſter?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: There is nothing elſe,
But theſe alas will ſeparate us more
Than twenty worlds betwixt us.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I have liv'd
To conquer men and now am overthrown
Only by words Brother and Siſter: where
Have thoſe words dwelling? I will find 'em out,
And utterly deſtroy 'em; but they are
Not to be graſp'd: let 'em be men or beaſts,
And I will cut 'em from the Earth, or Towns,
And I will raze 'em, and them blow 'em up:
Let 'em be Seas, and I will drink 'em off,
And yet have unquencht fire left in my breaſt:
Let 'em be any thing but meerly voice.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: But 'tis not in the power of any force,
Or policy to conquer them.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Panthea, What ſhall we do?
Shall we ſtand firmly here, and gaze our eyes out?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Would I could do ſo,
But I ſhall weep out mine.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Accurſed man,
Thou bought'ſt thy reaſon at too dear a rate,
For thou haſt all thy actions bounded in
With curious rules, when every beaſt is free:
What is there that acknowledges a kindred
But wretched man? Who ever ſaw the Bull
Fearfully leave the Heifer that he lik'd
Becauſe they had one Dam?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Sir, I diſturb you and my ſelf too;
'Twere better I were gone.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: I will not be ſo fooliſh as I was,
Stay, we will love juſt as becomes our births,
No otherwiſe: Brothers and Siſters may
Walk hand in hand together; ſo will we,
Come nearer: is there any hurt in this?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I hope not.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Faith there is none at all:
And tell me truly now, is there not one
You love above me?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: No by Heaven.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: Why yet you ſent unto Tigranes, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: True, but for another: for the truth —

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: No more,
I'le credit thee, thou canſt not lie,
Thou art all truth.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: But is there nothing elſe,
That we may do, but only walk? methinks
Brothers and Siſters lawfully may kiſs.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: And ſo they may Panthea, ſo will we,
And kiſs again too; we were too ſcrupulous,
And fooliſh, but we will be ſo no more.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: If you have any mercy, let me go
To priſon, to my death, to any thing:
I feel a ſin growing upon my blood,
Worſe than all theſe, hotter than yours.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: That is impoſſible, what ſhou'd we do?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Flie Sir, for Heavens ſake.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.l: So we muſt away,
Sin grows upon us more by this delay.

div.head: Actus Quintus.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: SIR, the King has ſeen your Commiſſion, and believes it, and freely by this warrant gives you power to viſit Prince Tigranes, your Noble Maſter.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: I thank his Grace and kiſs his hand.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: But is the main of all you • buſineſs ended in this?

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: I have another, but a worſe, I am aſham'd, it is a buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: You ſerve a worthy perſon, and a ſtranger I am ſure you are; you may imploy me if you pleaſe without your purſe, ſuch Offices ſhould ever be their own rewards.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.l: I am bound to your Nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I may have need of you, and then this courteſie,
If it be any, is not ill beſtowed;
But may I civilly deſire the reſt?
I ſhall not be a hurter if no helper.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.l: Sir you ſhall know I have loſt a fooliſh Daughter,
And with her all my patience, pilfer'd away
By a mean Captain of your Kings.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay there Sir:
If he have reacht the Noble worth of Captain,
He may well claim a worthy Gentlewoman,
Though ſhe were yours, and Noble.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.l: I grant all that too: but this wretched fellow
Reaches no further than the empty name
That ſerves to ſeed him; were he valiant,
Or had but in him any noble nature
That might hereafter promiſe him a good man,
My cares were ſo much lighter, and my grave
A ſpan yet from me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I confeſs ſuch fellows
Be in all Royal Camps, and have and muſt be,
To make the ſin of Coward more deteſted
In the mean ſouldier that with ſuch a foil
Sets off much valour. By deſcription
I ſhould now gueſs him to you, it was Beſſus,
I dare almoſt with confidence pronounce it.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.l: 'Tis ſuch a ſcurvie name as Beſſus, and now I think 'tis he

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Captain do you call him?
Believe me Sir, you have a miſery
Too mighty for your age: A pox upon him,
For that muſt be the end of all his ſervice:
Your Daughter was not mad Sir?

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.l: No, would ſhe had been,
The fault had had more credit: I would do ſomething.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I would fain counſel you, but to what I know not, he's ſo below a beating, that the Women find him not worthy of their Diſlaves, and to hang him were to caſt away a Rope; he's ſuch an Airie, thin unbodyed Coward, that no revenge can catch him: I'le tell you Sir, and tell you truth; this Raſcal fears neither God nor man, he has been ſo beaten: ſufferance has made him Wainſcot: he has had ſince he was firſt a ſlave, at leaſt three hundred Daggers ſet in's head, as little boys do new Knives in hot meat, there's not a Rib in's body o' my Conſcience that has not been thrice broken with dry beating: and now his ſides look like two Wicker Targets, every way bended; Children will ſhortly take him for a Wall, and ſet their Stone-bows in his forehead, he is of ſo baſe a ſenſe, I cannot in a week imagine what ſhall be done to him.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.l: Sure I have committed ſome great ſin
That this fellow ſhould be made my Rod,
I would ſee him, but I ſhall have no patience.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p:
'Tis no great matter if you have not: if a Laming of him, or ſuch a toy may do you pleaſure Sir, he has it for you, and I'le help you to him: 'tis no news to him to have a Leg broken, or Shoulder out, with being turn'd o'th'ſtones like a Tanſie: draw not your Sword if you love it; for on my Conſcience his head will break it: we uſe him i'th' Wars like a Ram to ſhake a wall withal. Here comes the very perſon of him, do as you ſhall find your temper, I muſt leave you: but if you do not break him like a Bisket, you are much to blame Sir.
Exit Mar.

div.stage: Enter Beſſus and the Sword men.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.l: Is your name Beſſus?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.l: Men call me Captain Beſſus.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p:
Then Catain Beſſus, you are a rank raſcall, without more exordiums, a durty frozen ſlave; and with the
favor of your friends here I will beat you.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.l: Pray uſe your pleaſure Sir,
You ſeem to be a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Thus Captain Beſſus, thus; thus twing your noſe, thus kick, thus tread you.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I do beſeech you yield your cauſe Sir quickly.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Indeed I ſhould have told that firſt.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I take it ſo.

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: Captain, he ſhould indeed, he is miſtaken.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Sir, you ſhall have it quickly, and more beating, you have ſtoln away a Lady, Captain coward, and ſuch an one. beats him.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Hold, I beſeech you, hold Sir, I never yet ſtole any living thing that had a tooth about it.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: I know you dare lie.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: With none but Summer Whores upon my life Sir, my means and manners never could attempt above a hedge or hay cock.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Sirra, that quits not me, where is this Lady? do that you do not uſe to do; tell truth, or by my hand, I'le beat your Captains brains out, waſh'em, and put 'em in again, that will I.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: There was a Lady Sir, I muſt confeſs, once in my charge: the Prince Tigranes gave her to my guard for her ſafety, how I us'd her, ſhe may her ſelf report, ſhe's with the Prince now: I did but wait upon her like a groom, which ſhe will teſtife I am ſure: if not, my brains are at your ſervice when you pleaſe Sir, and glad I have 'em for you.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: This is moſt likely, Sir, I ask you pardon, and am ſorry I was ſo intemperate.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Well I can ask no more, you will think it ſtrange not to have me beat you at firſt ſight.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Indeed I would, but I know your goodneſs can forget twenty beatings, you muſt forgive me.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Yes there's my hand, go where you will, I ſhall think you a valiant fellow for all this.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p:
My daughter is a Whore, I feel it now too ſenſible; yet I will ſee her, diſcharge my ſelf from being father to her, and then back to my Country, and there die, farwell Captain.
Exit Lygo.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Farwell Sir, farwell, commend me to the gentlewoman I pray.

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: How now Captain? bear up man.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Gentlemen o'th'ſword, your hands once more; I have been kickt agen, but the fooliſh fellow is penitent, has askt me Mercy, and my honour's ſafe.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: We knew that, or the fooliſh fellow had better have kickt his grandſir.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Confirm, confirm I pray.

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: There be our hands agen, now let him come and ſay he was not ſorry, and he ſleeps for it.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Alas good ignorant old man, let him go, let him go, theſe courſes will undo him. Exeunt clear.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: My Lord, your authority is good, and I am glad it is ſo, for my conſent would never hinder you from ſeeing your own King, I am a Miniſter, but not a governor of this State, yonder is your King, I'le leave you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: There he is indeed, and with him my diſloyal child.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: I do perceive my fault ſo much, that yet me thinks thou ſhouldſt not have forgiven me.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Health to your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: What? good Lygones welcome, what buſineſs brought thee hither?

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Several buſineſſes. My publick buſineſſes will appear by this, I have a meſſage to deliver, which if it pleaſe you ſo to authorize, is an embaſſage from the Armenian State, unto Arbaces for your liberty: the offer's there ſet down, pleaſe you to read it.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: There is no alteration happened ſince I came thence?

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: None Sir, all is as it was.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: And all our friends are well?

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: All very well.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: Though I have done nothing but what was good, I dare not ſee my Father, it was fault enough not to acquai •• him with that good.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Madam I ſhould have ſeen you.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: O good Sir forgive me.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Forgive you, why? I am no kin to you, am I?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: Should it be meaſur'd by my mean deſerts, indeed you are not.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Thou couldeſt prate unhappily ere thou couldſt go, would thou couldſt do as well, and how does your cuſtome hold out here?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: Sir?

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Are you in private ſtill, or how?

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Do you take mony? are you come to ſell ſin yet perhaps I can help you to liberal Clients: or has not the King caſt you off yet? O thou vile creature, whoſe beſt commendation is, that thou art a young whore, I would thy Mother had liv'd to ſee this, or rather that I had died ere I had ſeen it; why didſt not make me acquainted when thou wert firſt reſolv'd to be a whore, I would have ſeen thy hot luſt ſatisfied more privately: I would have kept a dancer and a whole conſort of muſicians in my own houſe only to fiddle thee.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: Sir, I was never whore.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: If thou couldſt not ſay ſo much for thy ſelf, thou ſhouldſt be carted.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: Lygones, I have read it, and I like it, you ſhall deliver it.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Well Sir, I will: but I have private buſineſs with you.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: Speak, what is't?

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: How has my age deſerv'd ſo ill of you, that you can pick no ſtrumpets i'th' land, but out of my breed?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: Strumpets, good Lygones?

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Yes, and I wiſh to have you know, I ſcorn to get a whore for any prince alive, and yet ſcorn will not help me-thinks: my Daughter might have been ſpar'd, there were enow beſides.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: May I not proſper but ſhe's innocent as morning light for me, and I dare ſwear for all the world.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Why is ſhe with you then? can ſhe wait on yor better than your man, has ſhe a gift in plucking off your ſtockings, can ſhe make Cawdles well or cut your cornes? Why do you keep her with you? For a Queen I know y •• do contemn her, ſo ſhould I, and every ſubject elſe think much at it.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: Let 'em think much, but 'tis more firm than earth: thou ſee'ſt thy Queen there.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Then have I made a fair hand, I call'd her Whore If I ſhall ſpeak now as her Father, I cannot chuſe but greatly rejoyce that ſhe ſhall be a Queen: but if I ſhall ſpeak to you as a States-man, ſhe were more fit to be your whore.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: Get you about your buſineſs to Arbaces, now you talk idlely.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Yes Sir, I will go, and ſhall ſhe be a Queen? ſhe had more wit than her old Father, when ſhe ran away: ſhall ſhe be Queen? now by my troth 'tis fine, I'le dance out of all meaſure at her wedding: ſhall I not Sir?

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: Yes marry ſhalt thou.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: I'le make theſe withered kexes bear my body two hours together above ground.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: Nay go, my buſineſs requires haſt.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Good Heaven preſerve you, you are an excellent King.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: Farwell good Father.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p:
Farwell ſweet vertuous Daughter, I never was ſo joyfull in all my life, that I remember: ſhall ſhe be a Queen? Now I perceive a man may weep for joy, I had thought they had lyed that ſaid ſo.
Exit Lygones

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: Come my dear love.

sp.speaker: Spa.
sp.p: But you may ſee another may alter that again.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p:
Urge it no more, I have made up a new ſtrong conſtancy, not to be ſhook with eyes: I know I have the paſſions of a man, but if I meet with any ſubject that ſhould hold my
eyes more firmly than is fit, I'le think of thee, and run away from it: let that ſuffice. Exeunt all.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Three Gentlemen without to ſpeak with me?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Let them come in.

div.stage: Enter Beſſus with the two Sword men.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: They are entred Sir already.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Now fellows your buſineſs? are theſe the Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: My Lord, I have made bold to bring theſe Gentlemen, my friends o'th' Sword along with me.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: I am afraid you'l fight then.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: My good Lord, I will not, your Lordſhip is much miſtaken, fear not Lord.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Sir, I am ſorry for't.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I ask no more in honour, Gentlemen you hear my Lord is ſorry.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Not that I have beaten you, but beaten one that will be beaten: one whoſe dull body will require a laming, as Surfeits do the diet, ſpring and fall; now to your Swordmen; what come they for, good Captain Stock-fiſh?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: It ſeems your Lordſhip has forgot my name.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: No, nor your nature neither, though they are things fitter I muſt confeſs for any thing, than my remembrance, or any honeſt mans: what ſhall theſe Billets do; be pil'd up in my wood-yard?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip holds your mirth ſtill, Heaven continue it: but for theſe Gentlemen, they come—

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: To ſwear you are a Coward, ſpare your book, I do believe it.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip ſtill draws wide, they come to vouch under their valiant hands I am no Coward.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: That would be a ſhow indeed worth ſeeing: ſirra be wiſe, and take Mony for this motion, travel with it, and where the name of Beſſus has been known or a good Coward ſtirring, 'twill yield more than a tilting. This will prove more beneficial to you, if you be thriſty, than your Captainſhip, and more natural: men of moſt valiant hands is this true?

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: It is ſo, moſt renowned.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: 'Tis ſomewhat ſtrange.

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: Lord, it is ſtrange, yet true; we have examined from your Lordſhips foot there, to this mans head, the nature of the beatings; and we do find his honour is come off clean and ſufficient: this as our ſwords ſhall help us.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: You are much bound to your Bil-bow-men, I am glad you are ſtraight again Captain; 'twere good you would think on ſome way to gratifie them, they have undergone a labour for you, Beſſus, would have puzl'd Hercules with all his valour.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip muſt underſtand we are no men o'th' Law, that take pay for our opinions: it is ſufficient we have clear'd our friend.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Yet there is ſomething due, which I as toucht in Conſcience will diſcharge Captain; I'le pay this Rent for you.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Spare your ſelf my good Lord; my brave friends aim at nothing but the vertue.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: That's but a cold diſcharge Sir for the pains.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: O Lord, my good Lord.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Be not ſo modeſt, I will give you ſomething.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: They ſhall dine with your Lordſhip, that's ſufficient.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Something in hand the while, you Rogues, you Apple-ſquires: do you come hither with your botled valour, your windy froth, to limit out my beatings?

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: I do beſeech your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: O good Lord.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: S'foot what a beavy of beaten ſlaves are here? get me a Cudgel ſirra, and a tough one.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: More of your foot, I do beſeech your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: You ſhall, you ſhall dog, and your fellow-beagle.

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: O' this ſide good my Lord.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Off with your ſwords, for if you hurt my foot, I'le have you ſlead you Raſcals.

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: Mine's off my Lord.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: I beſeech your Lordſhip ſtay a little, my ſtrap's tied to my Cod piece-point: now when you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Captain theſe are your valiant friends, you long for a little too?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: I am very well, I humbly thank your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: What's that in your pocket, hurts my Toe you Mungril? Thy Buttocks cannot be ſo hard, out with it quickly.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: Here 'tis Sir, a ſmall piece of Artillery, that a Gentleman a dear friend of your Lordſhips ſent me with, to get it mended Sir, for if you mark, the noſe is ſomewhat looſe.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: A friend of mine you Raſcal? I was never wearier of doing any thing, than kicking theſe two Foot-balls.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Here is a good Cudgel Sir.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: It comes too late l'me weary, pray thee do thou beat them.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: My Lord, this is ſoul play i'ſaith, to put a freſh man upon us, men are but men Sir.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p:
That jeſt ſhall ſave your bones; Captain, Rally up your rotten Regiment and be gone: I had rather thraſh than be bound to kick theſe Raſcals, till they cry'd ho; Beſſus you may put your hand to them now, and then you are quit. Farewel, as you like this, pray viſit me again, 'twill keep me in good health.
Exit Bac.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: H'as a deviliſh hard foot, I never felt the like.

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: Nor I, and yet I am ſure I have felt a hundred.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: If he kick thus i'th' Dog-daies, he will be dry foundred: what cure now Captain beſides Oyl of Baies?

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Why well enough I warrant you, you can go.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: Yes, heaven be thanked; but I feel a ſhrowd ach, ſure h'as ſprang my huckle-bone.

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: I ha' loſt a hanch.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: A little butter, friend a little butter, butter and parſeley and a ſoveraign matter: probatum eſt.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: Captain we muſt requeſt your hand now to our honours.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Yes marry ſhall ye, and then let all the world come, we are valiant to our ſelves, and there's an end.

sp.speaker: 1 Sword.
sp.p: Nay then we muſt be valiant; O my ribs.

sp.speaker: 2 Sword.
sp.p: O my ſmall guts, a plague upon theſe ſharptoed ſhooes, they are murtherers. Exeunt clear.

div.stage: Enter Arbaces with his ſword drawn.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: It is reſolv'd, I bare it whilſt I could, I can no more, I muſt begin with murther of my friends, and ſo go on to that inceſtuous raviſhing, and end my life and ſins with a forbidden blow, upon my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: What Tragedy is near? That hand was never wont to draw a ſword, but it cry'd dead to ſomething.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Mardonius, have you bid Gobrias come?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: How do you Sir?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Well, is he coming?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Why Sir, are you thus? why do your hands proclaim a lawleſs War againſt your ſelf?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Thou anſwereſt me one queſtion with an other, is Gobrias coming?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sir he is.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: 'Tis well, I can forbear your queſtions then, be gone.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sir, I have mark't.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Mark leſs, it troubles you and me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: You are more variable than you were.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: It may be ſo.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: To day no Hermit could be humbler than you were to us all.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: And what of this?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: And now you take new rage into your eyes, as you would look us all out of the Land.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I do confeſs it, will that ſatisfie? I prethee get thee gone.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sir, I will ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Will ye?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: It is my duty. I fear you will kill your ſelf: I am a ſubject, and you ſhall do me wrong in't: 'tis my cauſe, and I may ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Thou art not train'd in ſin, it ſeems Mardonius: kill my ſelf! by Heaven I will not do it yet; and when I will, I'le tell thee then: I ſhall be ſuch a creature, that thou wilt give me leave without a word. There is a method in mans wickedneſs, it grows up by degrees: I am not come ſo high as killing of my ſelf, there are a hundred thouſand ſins 'twixt me and it, which I muſt doe, and I ſhall come to't at laſt; but take my oath not now, be ſatisfied, and get thee hence.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I am ſorry 'tis ſo ill.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Be ſorry then, true ſorrow is alone, grieve by thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I pray you let me ſee your Sword put up before I go: I'le leave you then.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Why ſo? what folly is this in thee, is it not as apt to miſchief as it was before? can I not reach it thinkſt thou? theſe are toyes for Children to be pleas'd with, and not men, now I am ſafe you think: I would the book of fate were here, my Sword is not ſo ſure but I would get it out and mangle that, that all the deſtinies ſhould quite forget their ſixt decrees, and haſt to make us new, for other fortunes, mine could not be worſe, wilt thou now leave me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Heaven put into your boſome temperate thoughts, I'le leave you though I fear.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Go, thou art honeſt, why ſhould the haſty error of my youth be ſo unpardonable to draw a ſin helpleſs upon me?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: There is the King, now it is ripe.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Draw near thou guilty man, that art the authour of the loathedſt crime five ages have brought forth, and hear me ſpeak; curſes more incurable, and all the evils mans body or his Spirit can receive be with thee.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Why Sir do you curſe me thus?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Why do I curſe thee? if there be a man ſubtil in curſes, that exceeds the reſt, his worſt wiſh on thee, thou haſt broke my heart.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: How Sir, have I preſerv'd you from a child, from all the arrows, malice, or ambition could ſhoot at you, and have I this for my pay?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: 'Tis true, thou didſt preſerve me, and in that wert crueller than hardned murtherers of infants and their Mothers? thou didſt ſave me only till thou hadſt ſtudied out a way how to deſtroy me cunningly thy ſelf: this was a curious way of torturing.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Thou knowſt the evils thou haſt done to me; doſt thou remember all thoſe witching letters thou ſent'ſt unto me to Armenia, fill'd with the praiſe of my beloved Siſter, where thou extol'ſt her beauty, what had I to do with that? what could her beauty be to me? and thou didſt write how well ſhe lov'd me, doſt thou remember this? ſo that I doted ſomething before I ſaw her.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: This is true.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Is it? and when I was return'd thou knowſt thou didſt purſue it, till thou woundſt me into ſuch a ſtrange and unbeliev'd affection, as good men cannot think on.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: This I grant, I think I was the cauſe.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Wert thou? Nay more, I think thou meant'ſt it.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Sir, I hate to lie, as I love Heaven and honeſty, I did, it was my meaning.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Be thine own ſad judge, a further condemnation will not need, prepare thy ſelf to dy.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Why Sir to dy?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Why ſhouldſt thou live? was ever yet offender ſo impudent, that had a thought of Mercy after confeſſion of a crime like this? get out I cannot where thou hurl'ſt me in, but I can take revenge, that's all the ſweetneſs left for me.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Now is the time, hear me but ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: No, yet I will be far more mercifull than thou wert to me; thou didſt ſteal into me and never gav'ſt me warning: ſo much time as I give thee now, had prevented thee for ever. Notwithſtanding all thy ſins, if thou haſt hope, that there is yet a prayer to ſave thee, turn and ſpeak it to thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Sir, you ſhall know your ſins before you do 'em, if you kill me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I will not ſtay then.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Know you kill your Father.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: You kill your Father.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: My Father? though I know't for a lie, made out of fear to ſave thy ſtained life; the very reverence of the word comes croſs me, and ties mine arm down.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: I will tell you that ſhall heighten you again, I am thy Father, I charge thee hear me.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: If it ſhould be ſo, as 'tis moſt falſe, and that I ſhould be found a Baſtard iſſue, the deſpiſed fruit of lawleſs luſt, I ſhould no more admire all my wild paſſions: but another truth ſhall be wrung from thee: if I could come by the Spirit of pain, it ſhould be poured on thee, till thou allow'ſt thy ſelf more full of lies than he that teaches thee.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: Turn thee about, I come to ſpeak to thee thou wicked man, hear me thou tyrant.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I will turn to thee, hear me thou Strumpet; I have blotted out the name of Mother, as thou haſt thy ſhame.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: My ſhame! thou haſt leſs ſhame than any thing; why doſt thou keep my Daughter in a priſon? why doſt thou call her Siſter, and do this?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Ceaſe thy ſtrange impudence, and anſwer quickly if thou contemneſt me, this will ask an anſwer, and have it.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: Help me Gentle Gobrias.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Guilt d • a • not help guilt though they grow together in doing ill, yet at the puniſhment they ſever, and each flies the noiſe of other, think not of help, anſwer.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: I will, to what?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: To ſuch a thing, as if it be a truth think what a creature thou haſt made thy ſelf, that didſt not ſhame to do, what I muſt bluſh only to ask thee: tell me who I am, whoſe ſon I am without all circumſtance, be thou as haſty as my Sword will be if thou refuſeſt.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: Why, you are his ſon.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: His Son? ſwear, ſwear, thou worſe than woman damn'd.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: By all that's good you are.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Then art thou all that ever was known bad, now is the cauſe of all my ſtrange miſ-fortunes come to light: what reverence expecteſt thou from a child, to bring forth which thou haſt offended heaven, thy husband, and the Land? adulterous witch, I know now why thou wouldſt have poyſon'd me, I was thy luſt which thou wouldſt have forgot: then wicked Mother of my ſins, and me, ſhow me the way to the inheritance I have by thee: which is a ſpacious world of impious acts, that I may ſoon poſſeſs it: plagues rot thee, as thou liv'ſt, and ſuch diſeaſes, as uſe to pay luſt, recompence thy deed.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: You do not know why you curſe thus.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Too well; you are a pair of Vipers; and behold the Serpent you have got; there is no beaſt but if he knew it, has a pedigree as brave as mine, for they have more deſcents, and I am every way as beaſtly got, as far without the compaſs of Law as they.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: You ſpend your rage and words in vain, and rail upon a gueſs; hear us a little.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p:
No, I will never hear, but talk away my breath,
•• d die.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Why, but you are no Baſtard.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: How's that?

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: Nor child of mine.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Still you go on in wonders to me.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Pray you be more patient, I may bring comfort to • ou.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I will kneel, and hear with the obedience of a • hild; good Father ſpeak, I do acknowledge you, ſo you •• ring comfort.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Firſt know, our laſt King, your ſuppoſed Father • as old and feeble when he married her, and almoſt all • he Land thought ſhe was paſt hope of iſſue from him.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Therefore ſhe took leave to play the whore, becauſe • he King was old: is this the comfort?

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: What will you find out to give me ſatisfaction, • hen you find how you have injur'd me? let fire conſume • e, if ever I were a whore.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: For-bear theſe ſtarts, or I will leave you wedded to deſpair, as you are now: if you can find a temper, my breath ſhall be a pleaſant weſtern wind that cools and blaſts not.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Bring it out good Father. I'le lie, and liſten here • s reverently as to an Angel: if I breath too loud, tell me; for I would be as ſtill as night.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Our King I ſay, was old, and this our Queen deſir'd to bring an heir, but yet her husband ſhe thought was paſt • t, and to be diſhoneſt I think ſhe would not: if ſhe would have been, the truth is, ſhe was watcht ſo narrowly, and had ſo ſlender opportunities, ſhe hardly could have been: but yet her cunning found out this way; ſhe feign'd her ſelf with child, and poſts were ſent in haſt throughout the Land, and humble thanks was given in every Church, and prayers were made for her ſafe going and delivery: ſhe feign'd now to grow bigger, and perceiv'd this hope of iſſue made her fear'd, and brought a far more large reſpect from every man, and ſaw her power increaſe, and was reſolv'd, ſince ſhe believ'd, ſhe could not hav't indeed, at leaſt ſhe would be thought to have a child.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Do I not hear it well? nay I will make no noiſe at all; but pray you to the point, quickly as you can.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Now when the time was full, ſhe ſhould be brought to bed, I had a Son born, which was you, this the Queen hearing of mov'd me to let her have you; and ſuch reaſons ſhe ſhewed me, as ſhe knew would tie my ſecrecie, ſhe ſwore you ſhould be King, and to be ſhort, I did deliver you unto her, and pretended you were dead, and in mine own houſe kept a funeral, and had an empty coſſin put in Earth, that night this Queen feign'd haſtily to labour and by a pair of women of her own, which ſhe had charm'd, ſhe made the world believe ſhe was delivered of you. You grew up as the Kings Son, till you were ſix years old; then did the King dye, and did leave to me Protection of the Realm; and contrary to his own expectation, left this Queen truely with child indeed, of the fair Princeſs Panthea: then ſhe could have torn her hair and did alone to me, yet durſt not ſpeak in publick, for ſhe knew ſhe ſhould be found a traytor: and her tale would have been thought madneſs, or any thing rather than truth. This was the only cauſe why ſhe did ſeek to poyſon you, and I to keep you ſafe; and this the reaſon, why I ſought to kindle ſome ſparks of love in you to fair Panthea, that ſhe might get part of her right again.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: And have you made an end now? is this all? if not, I will be ſtill till I be aged, till all my hairs be Silver.

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: This is all.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: And is it true ſay you too Madam?

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.p: Yes heaven knows it is moſt true.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Panthea then is not my Siſter?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: But can you prove this?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: If you will give conſent, elſe who dares go about it?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Give conſent? why I will have 'em all that know it rackt, to get this from 'em, all that wait without come in, what ere you be, come in and be partakers of my joy, O you are welcome.

div.stage: Enter Beſſus, Gentlemen, Mardonius, and other attendants.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: The beſt news, nay draw no nearer, they all ſhall hear it, I am found no King.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Is that ſo good news?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Yes the happieſt news that ere was heard.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Indeed 'twere well for you if you might be a little leſs obey'd.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: One call the Queen.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Why ſhe is there.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: The Queen Mardonius, Panthea is the Queen and I am plain Arbaces; go ſome one, ſhe is in Gobrias houſe, ſince I ſaw you there are a thouſand things delivered to me, you little dream of. Exit a Gent.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: So it ſhould ſeem my Lord, what fury's this?

sp.speaker: Gob.
sp.p: Believe me 'tis no fury, all that he ſaies is truth.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: 'Tis very ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Why do you keep your hats off Gentlemen? is it to me? I ſwear it muſt not be; nay, truſt me, in good faith it muſt not be; I cannot now command you, but I pray you for the reſpect you bare me, when you took me for your King, each man clap on his hat at my deſire.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: We will, you are not found ſo mean a man, but that you may be cover'd as well as we, may you not?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: O not here, you may, but not I, for here is my Father in preſence.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Why there: O the whole ſtory would be a wilderneſs to loſe thy ſelf for ever: O pardon me dear Father for all the idle and unreverent words that I have ſpoke in idle moods to you: I am Arbaces, we all fellow-ſubjects, nor is the Queen Panthea now my Siſter.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Why if you remember fellow-ſubject Arbaces; I told you once ſhe was not your Siſter: I, and ſhe lookt nothing like you.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I think you did, good Captain Beſſus.

sp.speaker: Beſ.
sp.p: Here will ariſe another queſtion now amongſt the Sword-men, whether I be to call him to account for beating me, now he is proved no King.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sir here's Lygones, the agent for the Armenian State.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Where is he? I know your buſineſs good Lygones.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: We muſt have our King again, and will.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I knew that was your buſineſs: you ſhall have your King again, and have him ſo again as never King was had, go one of you and bid Bacurius bring Tigranes hither; and bring the Lady with him, that Panthea, the Queen Panthea ſent me word this morrning, was brave Tigranes miſtreſs. Ex. two Gent.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: 'Tis Spaconia.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I, I, Spaconia.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: She is my Daughter.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: She is ſo: I could now tell any thing I never heard: your King ſhall go ſo home, as never man went.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Shall he go on's head?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: He ſhall have chariots eaſier than air that I will have invented; and ne're think one ſhall pay any ranſome, and thy ſelf that art the meſſenger, ſhalt ride before him on a horſe cut out of an intire Diamond, that ſhall be made to go with golden wheeles, I know not how yet.

sp.speaker: Lyg.
sp.p: Why I ſhall be made for ever? they beli'd this King with us, and ſaid he was unkind.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: And then thy Daughter, ſhe ſhall have ſome ſtrange thing, wee'l have the Kingdom ſold utterly, and put into a toy which ſhe ſhall wear about her careleſly ſome where or other. See the vertuous Queen; behold the humbleſt ſubject that you have kneel here before you.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Why kneel you to me that am your Vaſſal?

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Grant me one requeſt.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Alas what can I grant you? what I can, I will.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: That you will pleaſe to marry me if I can prove it lawfull.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Is that all? more willingly than I would draw this air.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: I'le kiſs this hand in earneſt.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.p: Sir, Tigranes is coming though he made it ſtrange at firſt, to ſee the Princeſs any more.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: The Queen thou meaneſt, O my Tigranes. Pardon me, tread on my neck, I freely offer it, and if thou beeſt in given take revenge, for I have injur'd thee.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: No, I forgive, and rejoyce more that you h ••• found repentance, than I my liberty.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Mayeſt thou be happy in thy fair choice, for th •• art temperate. You owe no ranſom to the ſtate, know th •• I have a thouſand joyes to tell you of, which yet I dare 〈◊〉 utter till I pay my thanks to Heaven for 'em: Will you g • with me and help me? pray you do.

sp.speaker: Tigr.
sp.p: I will.

sp.speaker: Arb.
sp.p: Take then your fair one with you; and you Qu ••• of goodneſs and of us, O give me leave to take you arm in mine: come every one that takes delight i • goodneſs, help to ſing loud thanks for me, that I am prov •• no King.

list.item: Elder Loveleſs, a Sutor to the Lady.
Your glove, or Abigal, a waiting Gentlewoman.
Welford, a Sutor to the Lady.
Sir Roger, Curate to the Lady.

div.head: Scena prima.
div.stage: Enter the two Loveleſſes, Savil the Steward, and a Page.

sp.speaker: Elder Love.
sp.p: BRother, is your laſt hope paſt to mollifie Morecrafts heart about your Morgage?

sp.speaker: Young Love.
sp.p: Hopeleſly paſt: I have preſented the Uſurer with a richer draught than ever Cleopatra ſwallowed; he hath ſuckt in ten thouſand pound worth of my Land, more than he paid for at a grip, without Trumpets.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: I hav • as hard a task to perform in this houſe.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Faith mine was to make an Uſurer honeſt, or to loſe my Land.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: And mine is to perſwade a paſſionate woman, or to leave the La •• . Make the boat ſtay, I fear I ſhall begin my unfortunate journey this night, though the darkneſs of the night and the •• ughneſs of the waters might eaſily diſſwade an unwilling ma • .

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Sir, your Fathers old friends hold it the ſounder courſe for your body and eſtate to ſtay at home and marry, and propagate and govern in our Country, than to Travel and die without iſſue.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Savil, you ſhall gain the opinion of a better ſervant in ſeeking to execute, not alter my will, howſoever my in ••• nts ſucceed.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Yo • le • s Miſtres Younglove, Brother, the grave r •• her of your Miſtreſſes toes.

div.stage: Enter M •• tres Younglove the waiting woman.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Miſtres Younglove.

sp.speaker: Young.
sp.p: M • ſter Loveleſs, truly we thought your ſails had been boiſt: • y Miſtres is perſwaded you are Sea-ſick ere 〈◊〉 .

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p:
Love •
•• e her ill taken up reſolution ſo dearly? 〈◊〉 thou move her from me?
By th •• light that ſhines, there's no removing her, •• ngger a ſtill opinion by the end. I attempted her to day when they ſay a woman can deny nothing.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: What critical minute was that?

sp.speaker: Young.
sp.p: When her ſmock was over her ears: but ſhe was no more pliant than if it hung about her heels.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: I prethee deliver my ſervice, and ſay, I deſire to ſee the dear cauſe of my baniſhment; and then for France.

sp.speaker: Young.
sp.p: I'le do't: hark hither, is that your Brother?

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Yes, have you loſt your memory?

sp.speaker: Young.
sp.p: As I live he's a pretty fellow. Exit.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: O this is a ſweet Brache.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Why ſhe knows not you.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: No, but ſhe offered me once to know her: to this day ſhe loves youth of Eighteen; ſhe heard a tale how Cupid ſtruck her in love with a great Lord in the Tilt-yard, but he never ſaw her; yet ſhe in kindneſs would needs wear a Willow-garland at his Wedding. She lov'd all the Players in the laſt Queens time once over: ſhe was ſtruck when they acted Lovers, and forſook ſome when they plaid Murthers. She has nine Spur-royals, and the ſervants ſay ſhe hoards old gold; and ſhe her ſelf pronounces angerly, that the Farmers eldeſt ſon, or her Miſtres Husbands Clerk ſhall be, that Marries her, ſhall make her a joynture of fourſcore pounds a year; ſhe tells tales of the ſerving-men.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Enough, I know her Brother. I ſhall intreat you only to ſalute my Miſtres, and take leave, we'l part at the Stairs.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Now Sir, this firſt part of your will is performed, what's the reſt?

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Firſt, let me beg your notice for this Gentleman my Brother.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p:
I ſhall take it as a favour done to me, though the Gentleman hath received but an untimely grace from you •
yet my charitable diſpoſition would have been ready to have done him freer courteſies as a ſtranger, than upon thoſe cold commendations.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Lady, my ſalutations crave acquaintance and leave at once.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p:
Sir I hope you are the maſter of your own occaſions.
Exit. Yo. Lo. and Savil.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Would I were ſo. Miſtris, for me to praiſe over again that worth, which all the world, and you your ſelf can ſee.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: It's a cold room this, Servant.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Miſtris.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: What think you if I have a Chimney for't, out here?

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Miſtris, another in my place, that were not tyed to believe all your actions juſt, would apprehend himſelf wrong'd: But I whoſe vertues are conſtancy and obedience.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Younglove, make a good ſire above to warm me after my ſervants Exordium.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: I have heard and ſeen your affability to be ſuch, that the ſervants you give wages to may ſpeak.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: 'Tis true, 'tis true; but they ſpeak toth' purpoſe.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Miſtris, your will leads my ſpeeches from the purpoſe. But as a man—

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: A Simile ſervant? This room was built for honeſt meaners, that deliver themſelves haſtily and plainly, and are gone. Is this a time or place for Exordiums, and Similes and Metaphors? If you have ought to ſay, break into't: my anſwers ſhall very reaſonably meet you.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Miſtris I came to ſee you.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: That's happily diſpatcht, the next.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: To take leave of you.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: To be gone?

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: You need not have deſpair'd of that, nor have us'd ſo many circumſtances to win me to give you leave to perform my command; is there a third?

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Yes, I had a third had you been apt to hear it.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I? Never apter. Faſt (good ſervant) faſt.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: 'Twas to intreat you to hear reaſon.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Moſt willingly, have you brought one can ſpeak it?

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Laſtly, it is to kindle in that barren heart love and forgiveneſs.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: You would ſtay at home?

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Yes Lady.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Why you may, and doubtleſly will, when you have deba •• d that your commander is but your Miſtris, a woman, a weak one, wildly overborn with paſſions: but the thing by her commanded, is to ſee Dovers dreadful cliffe, paſſing in a poor Water-houſe 〈◊〉 the dangers of the mercileſs Channel 'twixt that and Callis, five long hours ſail, with three poor weeks victuals.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: You wrong me.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Then to land dumb, unable to enquire for an Engliſh hoaſt, to remove from City to City, by moſt chargeable Poſt-horſe, like one that rode in queſt of his Mother tongue.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: You wrong me much.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: And all theſe (almoſt invincible labours) performed for your Miſtris, to be in danger to forſake her, and to put on new allegeance to ſome French Lady, who is content to change language with your laughter, and after your whole year ſpent in Tennis and broken ſpeech, to ſtand to the hazard of being laught at, at your return, and have tales made on you by the Chamber-maids.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: You wrong me much.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Louder yet.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: You know your leaſt word is of force to make me ſeek out dangers, move me not with toyes: but in this baniſhment, I muſt take leave to ſay, you are unjuſt: was one kiſs forc't from you in publick by me ſo unpardonable? Why all the hours of day and night have ſeen us kiſs.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: 'Tis true, and ſo you told the company that heard me chide.

sp.speaker: Elder Lov.
sp.p: Your own eyes were not dearer to than I.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: And ſo you told 'em.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I did, yet no ſign of diſgrace need to h •• ſtain'd your cheek: you your ſelf knew your pure 〈◊〉 ſimple heart to be moſt unſpotted, and free from the 〈◊〉 baſeneſs.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I did: But if a Maids heart doth but once th ••• that ſhe is ſuſpected, her own face will write her guilty.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: But where lay this diſgrace? The world the knew us, knew our reſolutions well: And could it be hop • that I ſhould give away my freedom; and vent • e a perpetual bondage with one I never kiſt? or could •• n ſtrict 〈◊〉 doth take too much love upon me, from her that choſe 〈◊〉 for her Husband?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Believe me; if my Wedding-ſmock were on,
Were the Gloves bought and given, the Licence come,
Were the Roſemary-branches dipt, and all
The Hipochriſt and Cakes eat and drunk off,
Were theſe two armes incompaſt with the hands
Of Bachelors to lead me to the Church,
Were my feet in the door, were I John, ſaid,
If John ſhould boaſt a favour done by me,
I would not wed that year: And you I hope,
When you have ſpent this year commodiouſly
In atchieving Languages, will at your return
Acknowledge me more coy of parting with mine eyes,
Than ſuch a friend: More talk I hold not now
If you dare go.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I dare, you know: Firſt let me kiſs.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Farewel ſweet Servant, your task perform'd,
On a new ground as a beginning Sucor,
I ſhall be apt to hear you.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
Farewel cruel Miſtres.
Exit Lady.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Brother you'l hazard the loſing your tide to Graveſend: you have a long half mile by Land to Greenewich?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I go: but Brother, what yet unheard of courſe to live, doth your imagination flatter you with? Your ordinary means are devour'd.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Courſe? why Horſe-courſing I think. Conſume no time in this: I have no Eſtate to be mended by meditation: he that buſies himſelf about my fortunes may properly be ſaid to buſie himſelf about nothing.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Yet ſome courſe you muſt take, which for my ſatisfaction reſolve and open; if you will ſhape none, I muſt inform you that that man but perſwades himſelf he means to live, that imagines not the means.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Why live upon others, as others have lived upon me.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I apprehend not that: you have fed others, and conſequently diſpos'd of 'em: and the ſame meaſure muſt you expect from your maintainers, which will be too heavy an alteration for you to bear.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Why I'le purſe; if that raiſe me not, I'le bet at Bowling-alleyes, or man Whores; I would fain live by others: but I'le live whilſt I am unhang'd, and after the thought's taken.

sp.speaker: Elder Love.
sp.p: I ſee you are ty'd to no particular imp • oiment then?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Faith I may chooſe my co • rſe: they ſay nature brings forth none but ſhe provides for them: I'le try her liberality.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Well, to keep your feet out of baſe and dangerous paths, I have reſolved you ſhall live as Maſter of my Houſe. It ſhall be your care Savil to ſee him fell and cloathed, not according to his preſent Eſtate, but to his birth and former fortunes.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: If it be refer'd to him, if I be not 〈◊〉 Carnation Jearſie-ſtockins, blew devils breeches, • ith the gad • down, and my pocket i'th' ſleeves, I'le n'er lo •• you i'th fa • again.

sp.speaker: Sa.
sp.p: A comelier wear I wuſs it is than thoſe dangling •• ps.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
To keep you readie to do him all ſervice peace
•• ly, and him to command you reaſonably, I leave theſe fur
•• er directions in writing, which at your beſt leaſure toge
•• er open and read.

div.stage: Enter Younglove to them with a Iewell.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Sir, my Miſtreſs commends her love to you in this •• ken, and theſe words; it is a Iewell (ſhe ſayes) which as favour from her ſhe would requeſt you to wear till your • ears travel be performed: which once expired, ſhe will • aſtily expect your happy return.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
Return my ſervice with ſuch thanks, as ſhe may •• agine the heart of a ſuddenly over-joyed man would wil
•• ngly utter; and you I hope I ſhall with ſlender arguments • erſwade to wear this Diamond, that when my Miſtris ſhall •• rough my long abſence, and the approach of new Suitors, •• ffer to forget me; you may caſt your eye down to your • nger, and remember and ſpeak of me: She will hear thee • etter than thoſe allied by birth to her; as we ſee many men • uch ſwayed by the Grooms of their Chambers, not that • hey have a greater part of their love or opinion on them, •• an on others, but for that they know their ſecrets.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: O' my credit I ſwear, I think 'twas made for me: •• ar no other Suitors.

sp.speaker: Elder Love.
sp.p:
I ſhall not need to teach you how to diſcre
• it their beginning, you know how to take exception at • heir ſhirts at waſhing, or to make the maids ſwear they 〈◊〉 and plaſters in their beds.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: I know, I know, and do not you fear the Suitors.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Farewell, be mindfull, and be happie; the night • alls me. Exeunt omnes praeier Younglove.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p:
The Gods of the Winds befriend you Sir; a con
• ant and a liberal Lover thou art, more ſuch God ſend us.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Let 'em not ſtand ſtill, we have rid.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: A ſuitor I know by his riding hard, I'le not be ſeen.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: A prettie Hall this, no Servant in't? I would look • reſhly.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: You have delivered your errand to me then: there's • o danger in a hanſome young fellow: I'le ſhew my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Lady, may it pleaſe you to beſtow upon a ſtranger • he ordinary grace of ſalutation: Are you the Lady of this • ouſe?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Sir, I am worthily proud to be a Servant of hers.

sp.speaker: Wel,
sp.p: Lady, I ſhould be as proud to be a Servant of yours, • id not my ſo late acquaintance make me deſpair.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Sir, it is not ſo hard to atchieve, but nature may • ring it about.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: For theſe comfortable words, I remain your glad Debtor. Is your Lady at home?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: She is no ſtragler Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: May her occaſions admit me to ſpeak with her?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: If you come in the way of a Suitor, No.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p:
I know your affable vertue will be moved to per
• wade her, that a Gentleman benighted and ſtrayed, offers • o be bound to her for a nights lodging.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p:
I will commend this meſſage to her; but if you aim • t her body, you will be deluded: other women of the houſe
• old of good carriage and government; upon any of which • f you can caſt your affection, they will perhaps be found as • aithfull and not ſo coy.
Exit Younglove.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: What a skin full of luſt is this? I thought I had • ome a wooing, and I am the courted partie. This is right Court faſhion: Men, Women, and all woo, catch that catch may. If this ſoft hearted woman have infuſed any of her tenderneſs into her Lady, there is hope ſhe will be plyant. But who's here?

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: Gad ſave you Sir. My Lady lets you know ſhe deſires to be acquainted with your name, before ſhe confer with you?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Sir, my name calls me Welford.

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: Sir, you are a Gentleman of a good name. I'le try his wit.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I will uphold it as good as any of my Anceſtors had this two hundred years Sir.

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: I knew a worſhipfull and a Religious Gentleman of your name in the Biſhoprick of Durham. Call you him Couſen?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I am only allyed to his vertues Sir.

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: It is modeſtly ſaid: I ſhould carry the badge of your Chriſtianity with me too.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: What's that, a Croſs? there's a teſter.

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: I mean the name which your God fathers and God-mothers gave you at the Font.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: 'Tis Harry: but you cannot proceed orderly now in your Catechiſm: for you have told me who gave me that name. Shall I beg your name?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: What room fill you in this houſe?

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: More rooms than one.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: The more the merrier: but may my boldneſs know, why your Lady hath ſent you to decypher my name?

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: Her own words were theſe: To know whether you were a formerly denyed Suitor, diſguiſed in this meſſage: for I can aſſure you ſhe delights not in Thalame: Hymen and ſhe are at variance, I ſhall return with much haſt.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: And much ſpeed Sir, I hope: certainly I am arrived amongſt a Nation of new found fools, on a Land where no Navigator has yet planted wit; if I had foreſeen it, I would have laded my breeches with bells, knives, copper, and glaſſes, to trade with women for their virginities: yet I fear, I ſhould have betrayed my ſelf to a needleſs charge then: here's the walking night cap again.

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: Sir, my Ladies pleaſure is to ſee you: who hath commanded me to acknowledge her ſorrow, that you muſt take the pains to come up for ſo bad entertainment.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I ſhall obey your Lady that ſent it, and acknowledge you that brought it to be your Arts Maſter.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: I am but a Batchelor of Art, Sir; and I have the mending of all under this roof, from my Lady on her down-bed, to the maid in the Peaſe ſtraw.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: A Cobler, Sir?

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: No Sir, I inculcate Divine Service within theſe Walls.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: But the Inhabitants of this houſe do often imploy you on errands without any ſcruple of Conſcience.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Yes, I do take the air many mornings on foot, three or four miles for eggs: but why move you that?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: To know whether it might become your function to bid my man to neglect his horſe a little to attend on me.

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: Moſt properly Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I pray you doe ſo then: the whilſt I will attend your Lady. You direct all this houſe in the true way?

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: I doe Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: And this door I hope conducts to your Lady?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Your underſtanding is ingenious. Ex. ſeverally

div.stage: Enter young Loveleſs and Savil, with a writing.

sp.speaker: Sa.
sp.p: By your favour Sir, you ſhall pardon me?

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: I ſhall bear your favour Sir, croſs me no more, I ſay they ſhall come in.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Sir, you forget who I am?

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Sir, I do not; thou art my Brothers Steward, his caſt off mill-money, his Kitchen Arithmetick.

sp.speaker: Sa.
sp.p: Sir, I hope you will not make ſo little of me?

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: I make thee not ſo little as thou art: for indeed there goes no more to the making of a Steward, but a fair Imprimis, and then a reaſonable Item infus'd into him, and the thing is done.

sp.speaker: Sa.
sp.p: Nay then you ſtir my duty, and I moſt tell you?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: What wouldſt thou tell me, how Hopps grow, or hold ſome rotten diſcourſe of Sheep, or when our Lady-day falls? Prethee farewel, and entertain my friends, be drunk and burn thy Table books: and my dear ſpark of velvet, thou and I.

sp.speaker: Sa.
sp.p: Good Sir remember?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I do remember thee a fooliſh fellow, one that did put his truſt in Almanacks, and Horſe-fairs, and roſe by Hony and Pot-butter. Shall they come in yet?

sp.speaker: Sa.
sp.p: Nay then I muſt unfold your Brothers pleaſure, theſe be the leſſons Sir, he left behind him.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Prethee expound the firſt.

sp.speaker: Sa.
sp.p: I leave to maintain my houſe three hundred pounds a year; and my Brother to diſpoſe of it.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Mark that my wicked Steward, and I diſpoſe of it?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Whileſt he bears himſelf like a Gentleman, and my credit falls not in him. Mark that my good young Sir, mark that.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Nay, if it be no more I ſhall fulfil it, whilſt my Legs will carry me I'le bear my ſelf Gentleman-like, but when I am drunk, let them bear me that can. Forward dear Steward.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Next it is my will, that he be furniſhed (as my Brother) with Attendance, Apparel, and the obedience of my people.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Steward this is as plain as your old Minikinbreeches. Your wiſdom will relent now, will it not? Be mollified or— you underſtand me Sir, proceed?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Next, that my Steward keep his place, and power, and bound my Brother's wildneſs with his care.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I'le hear no more of this Apocrypha, bind it by it ſelf Steward.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: This is your Brothers will, and as I take it, he makes no mention of ſuch company as you would draw unto you. Captains of Gallyſoiſts, ſuch as in a clear day have ſeen Callis, fellows that have no more of God, than their Oaths come to: they wear ſwords to reach fire at a Play, and get there the oyl'd end of a Pipe, for their Guerdon: then the remnant of your Regiment, are wealthy Tobacco-Marchants, that ſet up with one Ounce, and break for three: together with a Forlorn hope of Poets, and all theſe look like Carthuſians, things without linnen: Are theſe fit company for my Maſters Brother?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I will either convert thee (O thou Pagan Steward) or preſently confound thee and thy reckonings, who's there? Call in the Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Good Sir.
