sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Nay, you ſhall know both who I am, and where I am.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Are you my Maſters Brother?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Are you the ſage Maſter Steward, with a face like an old Ephemerides?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Then God help us all I ſay.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I, and 'tis well ſaid my old peer of France: welcome Gentlemen, welcome Gentlemen; mine own dear Lads y'are richly welcome. Know this old Harry Groat.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Sir I will take your love.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Sir, you will take my Purſe.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: And ſtudy to continue it.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: I do believe you.

sp.speaker: Trav.
sp.p: Your honorable friend and Maſters Brother, hath given you to us for a worthy fellow, and ſo we hugg you Sir.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Has given himſelf into the hands of Varlets, not to be curv'd out. Sir, are theſe the pieces?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: They are the Morals of the Age, the vertues, men made of gold.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Of your gold you mean Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: This is a man of War, and cryes go on, and wears his colours.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: In's noſe.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: In the fragrant field. This is a Traveler Sir, knows men and manners, and has plow'd up the S •• ſo far till both the Poles have knockt, has ſeen the Sun 〈◊〉 Coach, and can diſtinguiſh the colour of his Horſes, 〈◊〉 their kinds, and had a Flanders-Mare leapt there.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: 'Tis much.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: I have ſeen more Sir.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: 'Tis even enough o' Conſcience; ſit down, and re •• you, you are at the end of the world already. Would ye had as good a Living Sir, as this fellow could lie you out o • he has a notable gift in't.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: This miniſters the ſmoak, and this the Mu ••

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: And you the Cloaths, and Meat, and Money, yo • have a goodly generation of 'em, pray let them multipl • your Brothers houſe is big enough, and to ſay truth, h •• too much Land, hang it durt.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Why now thou art a loving ſtinkard. Fire of thy Annotations and thy Rent-books, thou haſt a weak brain Savil, and with the next long Bill thou wilt run mad Gentlemen, you are once more welcome to three hundred pounds a year; we will be freely merry, ſhall we not?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Merry as mirth and wine, my lovely Loveleſs.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.p: A ſerious look ſhall be a Jury to excommunicate any man from our company.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: We will not talk wiſely neither?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: What think you Gentlemen by all this Revenue in Drink?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: I am all for Drink.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: I am dry till it be ſo.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.p: He that will not cry Amen to this, let him live ſober, ſeem wiſe, and dye o'th' Coram.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: It ſhall be ſo, we'l have it all in Drink, let Meat and Lodging go, they are tranſitory, and ſhew men meerly mortal: then we'l have Wenches, every one his Wench, and every week a freſh one: we'l keep no powdered fleſh: all theſe we have by warrant, under the title of things neceſſary. Here upon this place I ground it, The obedience of my people, and all neceſſaries: your opinions Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: 'Tis plain and evident that he meant Wenches.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Good Sir let me expound it?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Here be as ſound men, as your ſelf Sir.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.p: This do I hold to be the interpretation of it: In this word Neceſſary, is concluded all that be helps to Man; Woman was made the firſt, and therefore here the chiefeſt.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Believe me 'tis a learned one; and by theſe words, The obedience of my people, you Steward being one, are bound to fetch us Wenches.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: He is, he is.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Steward, attend us for inſtructions?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: But will you keep no houſe Sir?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Nothing but drink Sir, three hundred pounds in drink.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: O miſerable houſe, and miſerable I that live to ſee it! Good Sir keep ſome meat.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Get us good Whores, and for your part, I'le board you in an Alehouſe, you ſhall have Cheeſe and Onions.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: What ſhall become of me, no Chimney ſmoaking? Well Prodigal, your Brother will come home. Exit.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Come Lads, I'le warrant you for Wenches, three hundred pounds in drink. Exeunt omnes.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Lady, her Siſter Martha, Welford, Younglove, and others.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: SIR, now you ſee your bad lodging, I muſt bid you good night.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Lady if there be any want, 'tis in want of you.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: A little ſleep will eaſe that complement. Once more good night.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Once more dear Lady, and then all ſweet nights.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Dear Sir be ſhort and ſweet then.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Shall the morrow prove better to me, ſhall I hope my ſute happier by this nights reſt?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Is your ſute ſo ſickly that reſt will help it? Pray • e let it reſt then till I call for it. Sir as a ſtranger you have had all my welcome: but had I known your errand ere you came, your paſſage had been ſtraiter. Sir, good night.

sp.speaker: Welford.
sp.p: So fair, and cruel, dear unkind good night.
Nay Sir, you ſhall ſtay with me, I'le preſs your zeal ſo far.

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: O Lord Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Do you love Tobacco?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Surely I love it, but it loves not me; yet with your reverence I'le be bold.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Pray light it Sir. How do you like it?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: I promiſe you it is notable ſtinging geer indeed. It is wet Sir, Lord how it brings down Rheum?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Handle it again Sir, you have a warm text of it.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Thanks ever promiſed for it. I promiſe you it is very powerful, and by a Trope, ſpiritual; for certainly it moves in ſundry places.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I, it does ſo Sir, and me eſpecially to ask Sir, why you wear a Night-cap.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Aſſuredly I will ſpeak the truth unto you: you ſhall underſtand Sir, that my head is broken, and by whom; even by that viſible beaſt the Butler.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: The Butler? certainly he had all his drink about him when he did it. Strike one of your grave Caſſock? The offence Sir?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Reproving him at Tra-trip Sir, for ſwearing; you have the total ſurely.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: You told him when his rage was ſet a tilt, and ſo he crackt your Canons. I hope he has not hurt your gentle reading: But ſhall we ſee theſe Gentlewomen to night.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Have patience Sir until our fellow Nicholas be deceaſt, that is, aſleep: for ſo the word is taken: to ſleep to dye, to dye to ſleep, a very figure Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Cannot you caſt another for the Gentlewomen?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Not till the man be in his bed, his grave: his grave, his bed: the very ſame again Sir. Our Comick Poet gives the reaſon ſweetly; Plenus rimarum eſt, he is full of loopeholes, and will diſcover to our Patroneſs.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Your comment Sir has made me underſtand you.

div.stage: Enter Martha the Ladies Siſter, and Younglove, to them with a Poſſet.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Sir be addreſt, the graces do ſalute you with the full bowl of plenty. Is our old enemy entomb'd?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: He's ſafe?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: And does he ſnore out ſupinely with the Poet?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: No, he out-ſnores the Poet.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Gentlewoman, this courteſie ſhall bind a ſtranger to you, ever your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sir, my Siſters ſtrictneſs makes not us forget you are a ſtranger and a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: In ſooth Sir, were I chang'd into my Lady, a Gentleman ſo well indued with parts, ſhould not be loſt.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I thank you Gentlewoman, and reſt bound to you. See how this foul familiar chewes the Cud: From thee, and three and fifty good Love deliver me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Will you ſit down Sir, and take a ſpoon?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I take it kindly, Lady.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: It is our beſt banquet Sir.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Shall we give thanks?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I have to the Gentlewomen already Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Good Sir Roger. keep that breath to cool your part o'th' Poſſet, you may chance have a ſcalding zeal elſe; and you will needs be doing, pray tell your twenty to your ſelf. Would you could like this Sir?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I would your Siſter would like me as well Lady.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sure Sir, ſhe would not eat you: but baniſh that imagination; ſhe's only wedded to her ſelf, lyes with her ſelf, and loves her ſelf; and for another Husband than herſelf, he may knock at the gate, but ne're come in: be wiſe Sir, ſhe's a Woman, and a trouble, and has her many faults, the leaſt of which is, ſhe cannot love you.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: God pardon her, ſhe'l do worſe, would I were worthy his leaſt grief, Miſtris Martha.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Now I muſt over-hear her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Faith would thou hadſt them all with all my heart; I do not think they would make thee a day older.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Sir, will you put in deeper, 'tis the ſweeter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Well ſaid old ſayings.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: She looks like one indeed. Gentlewoman you keep your word, your ſweet ſelf has made the bottom ſweeter.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Sir, I begin a frolick, dare you change Sir?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: My ſelf for you, ſo pleaſe you. That ſmile has turn'd my ſtomach: this is right the old Embleme of the Moyle cropping of Thiſtles: Lord what a hunting head ſhe carries, ſure ſhe has been ridden with a Martingale. Now love deliver me.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Do I dream, or do I wake? ſurely I know not: am I rub'd off? Is this the way of all my morning Prayers? Oh Roger, thou art but graſs, and woman as a flower. Did I for this conſume my quarters in Meditation, Vowes, and wooed her in Heroical Epiſtles? Did I expound the Owl, and undertook with labour and expence the recollection of thoſe thouſand Pieces, conſum'd in Cellars, and Tabacco ſhops of that our honour'd Engliſhman Ni. Br. Have I done this, and am I done thus too? I will end with the wiſe man, and ſay; He that holds a Woman, has an Eel by the tail.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sir 'tis ſo late, and our entertainment (meaning our Poſſet) by this is grown ſo cold, that 'twere an unmannerly part longer to hold you from your reſt: let what the houſe has be at your command Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Sweet reſt be with you Lady; and to you what you deſire too. Exceunt.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: It ſhould be ſome ſuch good thing like your ſelf then.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Heaven keep me from that curſe, and all my iſſue. Good night Antiquity.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Solamen Miſeris ſocios habuiſſe Doloris: but I alone.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Learned Sir, will you bid my man come to me? and requeſting a greater meaſure of your learning, good night, good Maſter Roger.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p:
Good Sir, peace be with you.
Exit Roger.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Adue dear Domine. Half a dozen ſuch in a Kingdom would make a man forſwear confeſſion: for who that had but half his wits about him, would commit the Counſel of a ſerious ſin to ſuch a cruel Night-cap? Why how now ſhall we have an Antick? Enter Servant.
Whoſe head do you carry upon your ſhoulders, that you jole it ſo againſt the Poſt? Is't for your eaſe? Or have you ſeen the Celler? Where are my ſlippers Sir?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Here Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Where Sir? have you got the pot Verdugo? have you ſeen the Horſes Sir?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Have they any meat?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Faith Sir, they have a kind of wholeſome Ruſhes, Hay I cannot call it.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: And no Provender?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Sir, ſo I take it.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: You are merry Sir, and why ſo?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p:
Faith Sir, here are no Oats to be got, unleſs you'l have 'em in Portedge: the people are ſo mainly given to
ſpoon-meat: yonder's a caſt of Coach mares of the Gentlewomans, the ſtrangeſt Cattel.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Why, they are tranſparent Sir, you may ſee through them: and ſuch a houſe!

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Come Sir, the truth of your diſcovery.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Sir, they are in tribes like Jewes: the Kitchin and the Daytie make one tribe, and have their faction and their fornication within themſelves; the Buttery and the Landry are another, and there's no love loſt; the chambers are intire, and what's done there, is ſomewhat higher than my knowledge: but this I am ſure, between theſe copulations, a ſtranger is kept vertuous, that is, faſting. But of all this the drink Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: What of that Sir?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Faith Sir, I will handle it as the time and your patience will give me leave. This drink, or this cooling Julip, of which three ſpoonfuls kills the Calenture, a pint breeds the cold Palſie.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Sir, you bely the houſe.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: I would I did Sir. But as I am a true man, if 'twere but one degree colder, nothing but an Aſſes hoof would hold it.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I am glad on't Sir, for if it had proved ſtronger, you had been tongue •• 'd of theſe commendations. Light me the candle Sir, I'le hear no more. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter young Loveleſs and his Comrades, with wenches, and two Fidlers.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.l: Come my brave man of war, trace out thy darling,
And you my learned Council, 〈◊〉 and turn boyes,
Kiſs till the Cow come home, kiſs cloſe, kiſs cloſe knaves.
My Modern Poet, thou ſhalt kiſs in couplets.
Strike up you merry varlets, and leave your peeping,
This is no pay for Fidlers.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.l: O my dear boy, thy Hercules, thy Captain
Makes thee his Hyla • , his delight, his ſolace.
Love thy brave man of war, and let thy bounty
Clap him in Shamois: Let there be deducted out of our main potation
Five Marks in hatchments to adorn this thigh,
C • ampt with this reſt of peace, and I will ſight
Thy battels.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt hav't boy, and fly in Feather,
Lead on a March you Michers.

sp.speaker: Savill.
sp.p: O my head, O my heart, what a noyſe and change where! would I had been cold i'th' mouth before this day, and ne're have liv'd to ſee this diſſolution. He that lives within a mile of this place, had as good ſleep in the perpetual noyſe of an Iron Mill. There's a dead Sea of drink i'th' S • ller, in which goodly veſſels lye wrackt, and in the middle of this deluge appear the tops of ſlagons and black jacks, like Churches drown'd i'th' marſhes.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: What, art thou come? My ſweet Sir Amias welcome to 〈◊〉 . Come thou ſhalt kiſs my Helen, and court her in a dance.
Good Sir conſider?

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Shall we conſider Gentlemen? How ſay you?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Conſider? that were a ſimple toy i'ſaith, conſider? whoſe moral's that? The man that cryes conſider is our foe: 〈◊〉 my ſt •• l know him.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Stay thy dead doing hand, he muſt not die yet: p • ethee be calm my Hector?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Pea • ant ſlave, thou groom compos'd of grudgings, 〈◊〉 and than • this Gentleman, thou hadſt ſeen Pl • to elſe. The next conſider kills thee.

sp.speaker: Trav.
sp.p: Let him drink down his word again in a gallon of Sack?
Tis but a ſnuſle, make it two gallons, and let him doe it kneeling in repentance.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Nay rather kill me, there's but a lay-man loſt. Good Captain doe your office?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt drink Steward, drink and dance my Steward. Strike him a horn-pipe ſqueakers, take thy ſtriver, and pace her till ſhe ſtew.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Sure Sir, I cannot dance with your Gentlewomen, they are too light for me, pray break my head, and let me goe?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: He ſhall dance, he ſhall dance.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: He ſhall dance, and drink, and be drunk and dance, and be drunk again, and ſhall ſee no meat in a year.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.p: And three quarters?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: And three quarters be it.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Who knocks there? let him in.

sp.speaker: Savill.
sp.p: Some to deliver me I hope.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Gentlemen, God ſave you all, my buſineſs is to one Maſter Loveleſs?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: This is the Gentleman you mean; view him, and take his Inventorie, he's a right one.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: He promiſes no leſs Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Sir, your buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Sir, I ſhould let you know, yet I am loth, yet I am ſworn to't, would ſome other tongue would ſpeak it for me.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Out with it i' Gods name.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: All I deſire Sir is, the patience and ſufferance of a man, and good Sir be not mov'd more.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Then a pottle of ſack will doe, here's my hand, pr • thee thy buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
Good Sir excuſe me, and whatſoever you hear, think muſt have been known unto you, and be your ſelf ••
ſcreet, and bear it nobly.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Prethee diſpatch me?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Your Brother's dead Sir?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Thou doſt not mean dead drunk?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: No, no, dead and drown'd at ſea Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Art ſure he's dead?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Too ſure Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I but art thou very certainly ſure of it?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: As ſure Sir, as I tell it.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: But art thou ſure he came not up again?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: He may come up, but ne're to call you Brother?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: But art ſure he had water enough to drown him?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Sure Sir, he wanted none.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I would not have him want, I lov'd him better; here I forgive thee: and i'faith be plain, how do I bear it?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Very wiſely Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Fill him ſome wine. Thou doſt not ſee me mov'd, theſe tranſitorie toyes ne're trouble me, he's in a better place, my friend I know't. Some fellows would have cryed now, and have curſt thee, and faln out with their meat, and kept a pudder; but all this helps not, he was too good for us, and let God keep him: there's the right uſe on't friend. Off with thy drink, thou haſt a ſpice of ſorrow makes thee dry: fill him another. Savill, your Maſter's dead, and who am I now Savill? Nay, let's all bear it well, wipe Savill wipe, tears are but thrown away: we ſhall have wenches now, ſhall we not Savill?

sp.speaker: Savill.
sp.p: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: And drink innumerable.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Yes forſooth.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: And you'll ſtrain curtſie and be drunk a little?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: I would be glad, Sir, to doe my weak endeavour.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: You may be brought in time to love a wench too.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: In time the ſturdie Oak Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Some more wine for my friend there.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I ſhall be drunk anon for my good news: but I have a loving Brother, that's my comfort.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p:
Here's to you Sir, this is the worſt I wiſh you for your news: and if I had another elder Brother, and ſay it were his chance to feed Haddocks, I ſhould be ſtill the ſame
you ſee me now, a poor contented Gentleman. More wine for my friend there, he's dry again.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I ſhall be if I follow this beginning. Well my dear Brother, if I ſcape this drowning, 'tis your turn next to ſink, you ſhall duck twice before I help you. Sir I cannot drink more; pray let me have your pardon.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: O Lord Sir, 'tis your modeſtie: more wine, give him a bigger glaſs; hug him my Captain, thou ſhalt be my chief mourner.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: And this my pennon: Sir, a full carouſe to you, and to my Lord of Land here.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I feel a buzzing in my brains, pray God they bear this out, and I'le ne're trouble them ſo far again. Here's to you Sir?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: To my dear Steward, down o' your knees you infidel, you Pagan; be drunk and penitent.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Forgive me Sir, and I'le be any thing.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Then be a Baud, I'le have thee a brave Band.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Sir, I muſt take my leave of you, my buſineſs is ſo urgent.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Let's have a bridling caſt before you go. Fill's a new ſtoupe.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I dare not Sir, by no means.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Have you any mind to a wench? I would fain gratifie you for the pains you took Sir.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: As little as to the t'other.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: If you find any ſtirring do but ſay ſo.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Sir, you are too bounteous, when I feel that itching, you ſhall aſſwage it Sir, before another: this only and Farewell Sir. Your Brother when the ſtorm was moſt extream, told all about him, he left a will which lies cloſe behind a Chimney in the matted Chamber: and ſo as well Sir, as you have made me able, I take my leave.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Let us imbrace him all: if you grow drie before you end your buſineſs, pray take a baite here, I have a freſh hogſhead for you.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: You ſhall neither will nor chuſe Sir. My Maſter is a wonderfull fine Gentleman, has a fine ſtate, a very fine ſtate Sir, I am his Steward Sir, and his man.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Would you were your own ſir, as I left you. Well I muſt caſt about, or all ſinks.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Farewell Gentleman, Gentleman, Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: What would you with me ſir?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Farewell Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
O ſleep Sir, ſleep.
Exit Elder Lo.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Well boyes, you ſee what's faln, let's in and drink, and give thanks for it.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Let's give thanks for it.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Drunk as I live.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Drunk as I live boyes.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Why, now thou art able to diſcharge thine office, and caſt up a reckoning of ſome weight; I will be knighted, for my ſtate will bear it, 'tis ſixteen hundred boyes: off with your husks, I'le skin you all in Sattin.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: O ſweet Loveleſs!

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: All in Sattin? O ſweet Loveleſs!

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: March in my noble Compeeres: and this my Counteſs ſhall be led by two: and ſo proceed we to the Will.

div.stage: Enter Morecraft the Uſurer, and Widow.

sp.speaker: Morec.
sp.p: And Widow as I ſay be your own friend: your husband left you wealthy, I and wife, continue ſo ſweet duck, continue ſo. Take heed of young ſmooth Varlets, younger Brothers: they are worms that will eat through your bags: they are very Lightning, that with a flaſh or two will melt your money, and never ſinge your purſeſtrings: they are Colts, wench Colts, heady and dangerous, till we take 'em up, and make 'em ſit for Bonds: look upon me, I have had, and have yet matter of moment girle, matter of moment; you may meet with a worſe back, I'le not commend it.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Nor I neither Sir?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Yet thus far by your favour Widow, 'tis tuſſe.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: And therefore not for my dyet, for I love a tender one.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Sweet Widow leave your frumps, and be edified you know my ſtate, I ſell no Perſpectives, Scarfs, Gloves, nor Hangers, nor put my truſt in Shoe-ties; and where your Husband in an age was riſing by burnt figs, dreg'd with meal and powdered ſugar, ſaunders, and grains, wormeſeed and rotten Raiſins, and ſuch vile Tobacco, that made the footmen mangie; I in a year have put up hundreds inclos'd, my Widow, thoſe pleaſant Meadows, by a forſeit morgage: for which the poor Knight takes a lone chamber, owes for his Ale, and dare not beat his Hoſteſs: nay more —

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Good Sir no more, what ere my Husband was, I know what I am, and if you marry me, you muſt bear it bravely off Sir.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Not with the head, ſweet Widow.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
No ſweet Sir, but with your ſhoulders: I muſt have you dub'd, for under that I will not ſtoop a feather. My husband was a fellow lov'd to toyle, fed ill, made gain his exerciſe, and ſo grew coſtive, which for that I was his wife, I gave way to, and ſpun mine own ſmocks courſe, and ſir, ſo little: but let that paſs, time, that wears all things out, wore out this husband, who in penitence of ſuch fruitleſs five years marriage, left me great with his wealth, which if you'le be a worthie goſſip to, be knighted Sir?
Enter Savil.

sp.speaker: Morec.
sp.p: Now, Sir, from whom come you? whoſe man are you Sir?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Sir, I come from young Maſter Loveleſs.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Be ſilent Sir, I have no money, not a penny for you, he's ſunk, your Maſter's ſunk, a periſht man Sir.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Indeed his Brother's ſunk ſir, God be with him, a periſht man indeed, and drown'd at Sea.

sp.speaker: Morec.
sp.p: How ſaidſt thou, good my friend, his Brother drown'd?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Untimely ſir, at Sea.

sp.speaker: Morec.
sp.p: And thy young Maſter left ſole Heir?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Morec.
sp.p: And he wants money?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Yes, and ſent me to you, for he is now to be knighted.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Widow be wiſe, there's more Land coming, widow be very wiſe, and give thanks for me widow.

sp.speaker: Widow.
sp.p: Be you very wiſe, and be knighted, and then give thanks for me Sir?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: What ſayes your worſhip to this mony?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: I ſay he may have mony if he pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: A thouſand Sir?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: A thouſand Sir, provided any wiſe Sir, his Land lye for the payment, otherwiſe —

div.stage: Enter Young Loveleſs and Comrades to them.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: He's here himſelf Sir, and can better tell you.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: My notable dear friend, and worthy Maſter Loveleſs, and now right worſhipfull, all joy and welcom.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Thanks to my dear incloſer Maſter Morecraft, prethee old Angel gold, ſalute my family, I'le do as much for yours; this, and your own deſires, fair Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: And yours Sir, if you mean well; 'tis a hanſome Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Sirrah, my Brother's dead.

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: Dead?

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Dead, and by this time ſouſt for Ember Week.

sp.speaker: Morecraft.
sp.p: Dead?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Drown'd, drown'd at ſea man, by the next freſh Conger that comes we ſhall hear more.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Now by my faith of my body it moves me much.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: What, wilt thou be an Aſs, and weep for the dead? why I thought nothing but a general inundation would have mov'd thee, prethe be quiet, he hath left his land behind him.

sp.speaker: Morecraft.
sp.p: O has he ſo?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Yes faith, I thank him for't, I have all boy, haſt any ready mony?

sp.speaker: Morecraft.
sp.p: Will you ſell Sir?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: No not out right good Gripe; marry, a morgage or ſuch a ſlight ſecuritie.

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: I have no mony, Sir, for Morgage; if you will ſell, and all or none, I'le work a new Mine for you.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Good Sir look before you, he'l work you out of all elſe: if you ſell all your Land, you have ſold your Country, and then you muſt to Sea, to ſeek your Brother, and there lye p ••• ed in a Powdering tub, and break your teeth with Biskets and hard Beef, that muſt have wat •• ing Sir: and where's your • 00 pounds a year in drink then? If you'l tun up the Straights you may, for you have no calling for drink t •• re, but with a Canon, nor no ſcoring but on your Ships ſides, and then if you ſcape with life, and take a Faggot boat and a bottle of Ʋſquebaugh, come home poor men, like a tip • of Thames ſtreet ſ • inking of Pitch and Poor-John. I cannot tell Sir, I would be loth to ſee it.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p:
Steward, you are an Aſs, a meazel'd mungril, and were • t not again the peace of my ſoveraign friend here, I would br ••• your • ore-caſting Coxcomb, dog I would even with m • ſtaffe of Office there. Thy Pen and Inkhorn Noble 〈◊〉 , the God of gold here has ſed thee well, take mony for th •
〈◊〉 : ha •• and believe, thou art cold of conſtitution, thy 〈◊〉 unhealthful, ſell and be wiſe; we are three that will adorn thee, and live according to thine own heart child; 〈◊〉 all be only ours, and only ours ſhall be the black eyed beauties of the time. Mony makes men Eternal.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.p:
Do what you will, 'tis the nobleſt courſe, then you may live without the charge of people, only we four will make a Family, I and an Age that will beget new An • als, in which I'le write thy life my ſon of pleaſure, equal wit •
Nero and Cal • gula.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: What m • n were they Captain?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Two roaring Boys of Rome, that made all ſplit.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Come Sir, what dare you give?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: You will not fell Sir?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Who told you ſo Sir?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Good Sir have a care.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Peace, or I'le tack your Tongue up to your Roof. What money? ſpeak.

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: Six thouſand pound Sir.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Take it, h'as over bidden by the Sun: bind him to his bargain quickly.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Come ſtrike me luck with earneſt, and draw the writings.

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: There's a Gods peny for thee.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Sir lo • my old Maſters ſake let my Farm be excepted, if I b come his Tenant I am undone, my Children begge • s, and in, Wiſe God knows what: conſider me dear Si • .

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: I'le have all o • none.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: All in, all in • diſpatch the writings.
Go, thou art a pretty forehanded fellow, would thou wert wiſ • .

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p:
Now do I ſenſibly begin to feel my ſelf a Raſcal; would I could teach a School, or beg, or lye well, I am utterly undone; now he that taught thee to deceive and conſen, take thee to his mercy; ſo be it.
Exit Savil.

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: Come Widow come, never ſtand upon a Knight hood, 'tis a meer paper honour, and not proof enough for a Ser • ant. Come, Come, I'le make thee.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: To anſwer in ſhort, 'tis this Sir. No Knight no Widow, if you make me any thing, it muſt be a Lady, and ſo I ta • e my leave.

Farewel ſweet Widow, and think of it.
Ex. Wid.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Sir, I do more than think of it, it makes me dream Sir.

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: She's rich and ſober, if this itch were from her: 〈◊〉 ſay I be at the charge to pay the Footmen, and the Trumpets, I and the Horſemen too, and be a Knight, and ſhe refuſe me thou; then am I horſt into the ſubſidy, and ſo by conſequence ſhould prove a Coxcomb: I'le have a care of that. Six thouſand pound, and then the Land is mine, there's ſome refreſhing yet. Exit.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Abigal, and drops her Glove.

sp.speaker: Abigal.
sp.p: IF he but follow me, as all my hopes tell me, he's man enough, up goes my reſt, and I know I ſhall draw him.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: This is the ſtrangeſt pampered piece of fleſh towards fifty, that ever frailty copt withal, what a trim lennoy here ſhe has put upon me, theſe women are a proud kind of Cattel, and love this whorſon doing ſo directly, that they will not ſtick to make their very skins Bawdes to their fleſh. Here's Dogskin and Storax ſufficient to kill a Hawk: what to do with it, beſides nailing it up amongſt Iriſh heads of Teere, to ſhew the mightineſs of her Palm, I know not: there ſhe is. I muſt enter into Dialogue. Lady you have loſt your Glove.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Not Sir, if you have found it.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: It was my meaning Lady to reſtore it.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: 'Twill be uncivil in me to take back a favour, Fortune hath ſo well beſtowed Sir, pray wear it for me.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I had rather wear a Bell. But hark you Miſtres, what hidden vertue is there in this Glove, that you would have me wear it? Is't good againſt ſore eyes, or will it charm the Toothach? Or theſe red tops; being ſteept in white wine ſoluble, wil't kill the Itch? Or has it ſo conceal'd a providence to keep my hand from Bonds? If it have none of theſe and prove no more but a bare Glove of half a Crown a pair, 'twill be but half a courteſie, I wear two alwayes, faith let's draw cuts, one will do me no pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: The tenderneſs of his years keeps him as yet in ignorance, he's a well moulded fellow, and I wonder his bloud ſhould ſtir no higher; but 'tis his want of company: I muſt grow nearer to him.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: God ſave you both.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: And pardon you Sir; this is ſomewhat rude, how came you hither?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Why through the doors, they are open.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: What are you? And what buſineſs have you here?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: More I believe than you have.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Who would this fellow ſpeak with? Art thou ſober?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Yes, I come not here to ſleep.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Prethee what art thou?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: As much (gay man) as thou art, I am a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Art thou no more?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Yes more than thou dar'ſt be; a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Thou doſt not come to quarrel?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: No, not with women; I come to ſpeak here with a Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Why, I am one.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: But not with one ſo gentle.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: This is a fine fellow.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Sir, I am not fine yet. I am but new come over, direct me with your ticket to your Taylor, and then I ſhall be fine Sir. Lady if there be a better of your Sex within this houſe, ſay I would ſee her.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Why am not I good enough for you Sir?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Your way you'l be too good, pray end my buſineſs. This is another Sutor, O frail Woman!

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: This fellow with his bluntneſs hopes to do more than the long ſutes of a thouſand could; though he be ſowre he's quick, I muſt not truſt him. Sir, this Lady is not to ſpeak with you, ſhe is more ſerious: you ſmell as if you were new calkt; go and be hanſome, and then you may fit with her Servingmen.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: What are you Sir?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Gueſs by my outſide.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
Then I take you Sir, for ſome new ſilken thing wean'd from the Country, that ſhall (when you come to keep good company) be beaten into better manners. Pray
good proud Gentlewoman, help me to your Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.l: How many lives haſt thou, that thou talk'ſt thus rudely?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: But one, one, I am neither Cat nor Woman.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: And will that one life, Sir, maintain you ever in ſuch bold ſawcineſs?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Yes, amongſt a Nation of ſuch men as you are, and be no worſe for wearing, ſhall I ſpeak with this Lady?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.l: No by my troth ſhall you not.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: I muſt ſtay here then?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: That you ſhall not neither.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Good fine thing tell me why?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: Good angry thing I'le tell you:
This is no place for ſuch companions,
Such louſie Gentlemen ſhall find their buſineſs
Better i'th' Suburbs, there your ſtrong pitch perfume,
Mingled with lees of Ale, ſhall reek in faſhion:
This is no Thames-ſtreet, Sir.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.l: This Gentleman informs you truly:
Prethee be ſatisfied, and ſeek the Suburbs,
Good Captain, or what ever title elſe,
The Warlike Eele boats have beſtowed upon thee,
Go and reform thy ſelf, prethee be ſweeter,
And know my Lady ſpeaks with no Swabbers.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: You cannot talk me out with your tradition
Of wit you pick from Plays, go to, I have found ye:
And for you, Sir, whoſe tender gentle blood
Runs in your Noſe, and makes you ſnuff at all,
But three pil'd people, I do let you know,
He that begot your worſhips Sattin-ſute,
Can make no men Sir: I will ſee this Lady,
And with the reverence of your ſilkenſhip,
In theſe old Ornaments.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: You will not ſure?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Sure Sir I ſhall?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.l: You would be beaten out?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Indeed I would not, or if I would be beaten,
Pray who ſhall beat me? this good Gentleman
Looks as he were o'th' peace.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: Sir you ſhall ſee that: will you get you out?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Yes, that, that ſhall correct your boys tongue.
Dare you fight, I will ſtay here ſtill. They draw.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.l: O their things are out, help, help for Gods ſake,
Madam; Jeſus they foin at one another.
Madam, why, who is within there?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Who breeds this rudeneſs?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: This uncivil fellow;
He ſaies he comes from Sea, where I believe,
H'as purg'd away his manners.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Why what of him?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: Why he will rudely without once God bleſs you,
Preſs to your privacies, and no denial
Muſt ſtand betwixt your perſon and his buſineſs;
I let go his ill Language.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Sir, have you buſineſs with me?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Madam ſome I have,
But not ſo ſerious to pawn my life for't:
If you keep this quarter, and maintain about you
Such Knights o'th' Sun as this is, to defie
Men of imployment to ye, you may live,
But in what fame?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Pray ſtay Sir, who has wrong'd you?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Wrong me he cannot, though uncivilly
He flung his wild words at me: but to you
I think he did no honour, to deny
The haſt I come withal, a paſſage to you,
Though I ſeem courſe.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Excuſe me gentle Sir, 'twas from my knowledge,
And ſhall have no protection. And to you Sir,
You have ſhew'd more heat than wit, and from your ſelf
Have borrowed power, I never gave you here,
To do theſe vile unmanly things: my houſe
Is no blind ſtreet to ſwagger in; and my favours
Not doting yet on your unknown deſerts
So far, that I ſhould make you Maſter of my buſineſs,
My credit yet ſtands fairer with the people
Than to be tried with ſwords; and they that come
To do me ſervice, muſt not think to win me
With hazard of a murther; if your love
Conſiſt in fury, carry it to the Camp:
And there in honour of ſome common Miſtreſs,
Shorten your youth, I pray be better temper'd:
And give me leave a while Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l:
You muſt have it.
Exit Welford.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Now Sir, your buſineſs?

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.l: Firſt, I thank you for ſchooling this young fellow,
Whom his own follies, which he's prone enough
Daily to fall into, if you but frown,
Shall level him a way to his repentance:
Next, I ſhould rail at you, but you are a Woman,
And anger's loſt upon you.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Why at me Sir?
I never did you wrong, for to my knowledge
This is the firſt ſight of you.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: You have done that,
I muſt confeſs I have the leaſt curſe in
Becauſe the leaſt acquaintance: But there be
(If there be honour in the minds of men)
Thouſands when they ſhall know what I deliver,
(As all good men muſt ſhare in't) will to ſhame
Blaſt your black memory.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: How is this good Sir?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: 'Tis that, that if you have a ſoul will choak it:
Y'ave kill'd a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: I kill'd a Gentleman!

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: You and your cruelty have kill'd him Woman,
And ſuch a man (let me be angry in't)
Whoſe leaſt worth weighed above all womens vertues
That are; I ſpare you all to come too: gueſs him now?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: I am ſo innocent I cannot Sir.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Repent you mean, you are a perfect Woman,
And as the firſt was, made for mans undoing.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Sir, you have miſt your way, I am not ſhe.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Would he had miſt his way too, though he had
Wandered farther than Women are ill ſpoken of,
So he had miſt this miſery, you Lady.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: How do you do, Sir?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Well enough I hope.
While I can keep my ſelf out from temptations.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Leap into this matter, whither would ye?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: You had a Servant that your peeviſhneſs
Injoined to Travel.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Such a one I have
Still, and ſhall be griev'd 'twere otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.l: Then have your asking, and be griev'd he's dead;
How you will anſwer for his worth, I know not,
But this I am ſure, either he, or you, or both
Were ſtark mad, elſe he might have liv'd
To have given a ſtronger teſtimony to th' world
Of what he might have been. He was a man
I knew but in his evening, ten Suns after,
Forc'd by a Tyrant ſtorm our beaten Bark
Bulg'd under us; in which ſad parting blow,
He call'd upon his Saint, but not for life,
On you unhappy Woman, and whileſt all
Sought to preſerve their Souls, he deſperately
Imbrac'd a Wave, crying to all that ſaw it,
If any live, go to my Fate that forc'd me
To this untimely end, and make her happy:
His name was Loveleſs: And I ſcap't the ſtorm,
And now you have my buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: 'Tis too much.
Would I had been that ſtorm, he had not periſht.
If you'l rail now I will forgive you Sir?
Or if you'l call in more, if any more
Come from this ruine, I ſhall juſtly ſuffer
What they can ſay, I do confeſs my ſelf
A guiltie cauſe in this. I would ſay more,
But grief is grown too great to be delivered.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: I like this well: theſe women are ſtrange things.
Tis ſomewhat of the lateſt now to weep,
You ſhould have wept when he was going from you,
And chain'd him with thoſe tears at home.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Would you had told me then ſo, theſe two arms had been his Sea.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Truſt me you move me much: but ſay he lived, theſe were forgotten things again.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I, ſay you ſo? Sure I ſhould know that voice: this is knavery. I'le fit you for it. Were he living Sir, I would perſwade you to be charitable, I, and confeſs we are not all ſo ill as your opinion holds us. O my friend, what penance ſhall I pull upon my fault, upon my moſt unworthy ſelf for this?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Leave to love others, 'twas ſome jealouſie
That turn'd him deſperate.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I'le be with you ſtraight: are you wrung there?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: This works a main upon her.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I do confeſs there is a Gentleman
Has born me long good will.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I do not like that.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: And vow'd a thouſand ſervices to me; to me, regardleſs of him: But ſince Fate, that no power can withſtand, has taken from me my firſt, and beſt love, and to weep away my youth is a mere folly, I will ſhew you what I determine ſir: you ſhall know all: Call M. Welford there: That Gentleman I mean to make the model of my Fortunes, and in his chaſt imbraces keep alive the memory of my loſt lovely Loveleſs: he is ſomewhat like him too.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Then you can love.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Yes certainly Sir?
Though it pleaſe you to think me hard and cruel,
I hope I ſhall perſwade you otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I have made my ſelf a fine fool.
Would you have ſpoke with me Madam?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Yes M. Welford, and I ask your pardon before this Gentleman for being froward: this kiſs, and henceforth more affection.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: So, 'tis better I were drown'd indeed.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: This is a ſudden paſſion, God hold it.
This fellow out of his fear ſure has
Perſwaded her. I'le give him a new ſuit on't.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: A parting kiſs, and good Sir, let me pray you
To wait me in the Gallerie.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I am in another world, Madam where you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I will to Sea, and 't ſhall goe hard but I'le be drown'd indeed.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Now Sir you ſee I am no ſuch hard creature,
But time may win me.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: You have forgot your loſt Love.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Alas Sir, what would you have me do? I cannot call him back again with ſorrow; I'le love this man as dearly, and beſh • ow me I'le keep him far enough from Sea, and 'twas told me, now I remember me, by an old wiſe woman, that my firſt Love ſhould be drown'd, and ſee 'tis come about.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I would ſhe had told you your ſecond ſhould be hang'd too, and let that come about: but this is very ſtrange.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Faith Sir, conſider all, and then I know you'le be of my mind: if weeping would redeem him, I would weep ſtill.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: But ſay that I were Loveleſs,
And ſcap'd the ſtorm, how would you anſwer this?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why for that Gentleman I would leave all the world.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: This young thing too?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: That young thing too,
〈◊〉 any young thing elſe: why, I would loſe my ſtate.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Why then he lives ſtill, I am he, your Loveleſs.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Alas I knew it Sir, and for that purpoſe prepared this Pageant: get you to your task. And leave theſe Players tricks, or I ſhall leave you, indeed I ſhall. Travel, or know me not.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Will you then marry?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I will not promiſe, take your choice. Farewell.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: There is no other Purgatorie but a Woman.

I muſt doe ſomething.
Exit Loveleſs

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Miſtreſs I am bold.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: You are indeed.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: You ſo overjoyed me Lady.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Take heed you ſurfeit not, pray faſt and welcom.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: By this light you love me extreamly.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: By this, and to morrows light, I care not for you.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Come, come, you cannot hide it.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Indeed I can, where you ſhall never find it.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I like this mirth well Lady.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: You ſhall have more on't.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I muſt kiſs you.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Indeed I muſt.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: What muſt be, muſt be; I'le take my leave, ye • have your parting blow: I pray commend me to thoſe few friends you have, that ſent you hither, and tell them when you travel next, 'twere ſit you brought leſs bravery with you, and more wit, you'le never get a wife elſe.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Are you in earneſt?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Yes faith. Will you eat Sir, your horſes will be readie ſtraight, you ſhall have a napkin laid in the butterie for ye.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Do not you love me then?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Yes, for that face.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: It is a good one Ladie.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Yes, if it were not warpt, the fire in time may mend it.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Me thinks yours is none of the beſt Ladie.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: No by my troth Sir; yet o'my conſcience,
You would make ſhift with it.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Come pray no more of this?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I will not: Fare you well. Ho, who's within there? bring out the Gentlemans horſes, he's in haſte; and ſet ſome cold meat on the Table.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I have too much of that I thank you Ladie: take your Chamber when you pleaſe, there goes a black one with you Ladie.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p:
Farewell young man.
Exit Ladie.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: You have made me one, Farewell: and may the curſe of a great houſe fall upon thee, I mean the Butler. The devil and all his works are in theſe women, would all of my ſex were of my mind, I would make 'em a new Lent, and a long one, that fleſh might be in more reverence with them.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: I am ſorry M. Welford.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: So am I, that you are here.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: How does my Ladie uſe you?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: As I would uſe you, ſcurvilie.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: I ſhould have been more kind Sir?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I ſhould have been undone then. Pray leave me, and look to your ſweet meats; hark, your Ladie calls?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Sir, I ſhall borrow ſo much time without offence.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Y'are nothing but offence, for Gods love leave me.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: 'Tis ſtrange my Ladie ſhould be ſuch a tyrant?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: To ſend you to me, 'Pray goe ſtitch, good doe, y'are more trouble to me than a Term.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: I do not know how my good will, if I ſaid love I lied not, ſhould any way deſerve this?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: A thouſand waies, a thouſand waies; ſweet creature let me depart in peace.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: What Creature Sir? I hope I am a woman.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: A hundred I think by your noiſe.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Since you are angrie Sir, I am bold to tell you that I am a woman, and a rib.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Of a roaſted horſe.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Conſter me that?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: A Dog can doe it better; Farwell Counteſs, and commend me to your Ladie, tell her ſhe's proud, and ſcurvie, and ſo I commit you both to your tempter.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Sweet Mr. Welford.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Avoid old Satanus: Go daub your ruines, your face looks fouler than a ſtorm: the Foot-man ſtayes for you in the Lobby Lady.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: If you were a Gentleman, I ſhould know it by your gentle conditions? are theſe ſit words to give a Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p:
As fit as they were made for ye: Sirrah, my horſes. Farwell old Adage, keep your noſe warm, the Rheum will make it horn elſe—
Exit Welford.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p:
The bleſſings of a Prodigal young heir be thy companions Welford, marry come up my Gentleman, are your gums grown ſo tender they cannot bite? A skittiſh Filly will be your fortune Welford, and fair enough for ſuch a packſaddle. And I doubt not (if my aim hold) to ſee her made to amble to your hand.
Exit Abigal.

div.stage: Enter Young Loveleſs, and Comrades, Morecraft, Widow, Savil, and the reſt.

sp.speaker: Captain.
sp.p: Save thy brave ſhoulder, my young puiſſant Knight, and may thy back Sword bite them to the bone that love thee not, thou art an errant man, go on. The circumcis'd ſhall fall by thee. Let Land and labour fill the man that tills, thy ſword muſt be thy plough, and Jove it ſpeed. Mecha ſhall ſweat, and Mahomet ſhall fall, and thy dear name fill up his monument.

sp.speaker: Yo. L.
sp.p: It ſhall Captain, I mean to be a Worthy.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: One Worthy is too little, thou ſhalt be all.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Captain I ſhall deſerve ſome of your love too.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt have heart and hand too, noble Morecraft, if thou wilt lend me mony. I am a man of Garriſon, be rul'd, and open to me thoſe infernal gates, whence none of thy evil Angels paſs again, and I will ſtile thee noble, nay Don Diego. I'le woo thy Infanta for thee, and my Knight ſhall feaſt her with high meats, and make her apt.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Pardon me Captain, y'are beſide my meaning.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: No Mr. Morecraft, 'tis the Captains meaning I ſhould prepare her for ye.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Or provok her. Speak my modern man, I ſay provoke her.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.p: Captain, I ſay ſo too, or ſtir her to it. So ſay the Criticks.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: But howſoever you expound it ſir, ſhe's very welcom, and this ſhall ſerve for witneſs. And Widow, ſince y'are come ſo happily, you ſhall deliver up the keyes, and free poſſeſſion of this houſe, whilſt I ſtand by to ratifie.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I had rather give it back again believe me,
'Tis a miſerie to ſay you had it. Take heed?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: 'Tis paſt that Widow, come, ſit down, ſome wine there, there is a ſcurvie banquet if we had it. All this fair houſe is yours Sir, Savil?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Are your keyes readie, I muſt eaſe your burden.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: I am readie Sir to be undone, when you ſhall call me to't.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Come come, thou ſhalt live better.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: I ſhall have leſs to doe, that's all, there's half a dozen of my friends i'th' fields ſunning againſt a bank, with half a breech among 'em, I ſhall be with 'em ſhortly. The care and continuall vexation of being rich, eat up this raſcall. What ſhall become of my poor familie, they are no ſheep, and they muſt keep themſelves.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Drink Maſter Morecraft, pray be merrie all:
Nay and you will not drink there's no ſocietie,
Captain ſpeak loud, and drink: widow, a word.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Expound her throughly Knight. Here God o' gold, here's to thy fair poſſeſſions; Be a Baron and a bold one: leave off your tickling of young heirs like Trouts, and let thy Chimnies ſmoke. Feed men of war, live and be honeſt, and be ſaved yet.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: I thank you worthie Captain for your counſel. You keep your Chimnies ſmoking there, your noſtrils, and when you can, you feed a man of War, this makes you not a Baron, but a bare one: and how or when you ſhall be ſaved, let the Clark o'th' companie (you have commanded) have a juſt care of.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.p: The man is much moved. Be not angrie Sir, but as the Poet ſings, let your diſpleaſure be a ſhort furie, and goe out. You have ſpoke home, and bitterly, to me Sir? Captain take truce, the Miſer is a tart and a wittie whorſon—

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Poet, you feign perdie, the wit of this man lies in his ſingers ends, he muſt tell all; his tongue fills his mouth like a neats tongue, and only ſerves to lick his hungrie chaps after a purchaſe: his brains and brimſtone are the devils diet to a fat uſurers head: To her Knight, to her: clap her aboard, and ſlow her. Where's the brave Steward?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Here's your poor friend, and Savil Sir?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Away, th'art rich in ornaments of nature. Firſt in thy face, thou haſt a ſerious face, a betting, bargaining, and ſaving face, a rich face, pawn it to the Uſurer; a face to kindle the compaſſion of the moſt ignorant and frozen Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: 'Tis ſuch I dare not ſhew it ſhortly ſir.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Be blithe and bonny ſteward: Maſter Morecraft, Drink to this man of reckoning?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Here's e'ne to him.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: The Devil guide it downward: would there were in't an acre of the great broom field he bought, to ſweep your durtie Conſcience, or to choak ye, 'tis all one to me, Uſurer.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Conſider what I told you, you are young, unapt for worldly buſineſs: Is it ſit one of ſuch tenderneſs, ſo delicate, ſo contrarie to things of care, ſhould ſtir and break her better meditations, in the bare brokage of a brace of Angels? or a new Kirtel, though it be Satten? eat by the hope of ſurfeits, and lie down only in expectation of a morrow, that may undo ſome eaſie hearted fool, or reach a widows curſes? Let out mony, whoſe uſe returns the principal? and get out of theſe troubles, a conſuming heir: For ſuch a one muſt follow neceſſarily, you ſhall die hated, if not old and miſerable; and that poſſeſt wealth that you got with pining, live to ſee tumbled to anothers hands, that is no more a kin to you, than you to his co • zenage.

sp.speaker: Widow.
sp.p: Sir you ſpeak well, would God that charity had firſt begun here?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: 'Tis yet time, Be merrie, me thinks you want wine there, there's more i'th' houſe. Captain, where reſts the health?

sp.speaker: Captain.
sp.p: It ſhall goe round boy?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Say you can ſuffer this, becauſe the end points at much profit, can you ſo far bow below your blood, below your too much beautie, to be a partner of this fellowes bed, and lie with his diſeaſes? if you can, I will nor preſs you further: yet look upon him: there's nothing in that hide-bound Uſurer, that man of mat, that all decai'd, but aches, for you to love, unleſs his periſht lungs, his drie cough, or his ſcurvie. This is truth, and ſo far I dare ſpeak yet: he has yet paſt cure of Phyſick, ſpaw, or any diet, a primitive pox in his bones; and o' my Knowledge he has been ten times rowell'd: ye may love him; he had a baſtard, his own toward iſſue, whipt, and then cropt for waſhing out the roſes, in three farthings to make 'em pence.

sp.speaker: Widow.
sp.p: I do not like theſe Morals?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: You muſt not like him then?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: By your leave Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p:
By my troth ſir you are welcom, welcom faith: Lord what a ſtranger you are grown; pray know this Gentlewoman, and if you pleaſe theſe friends here: we are merry,
you ſee the worſt on't; your houſe has been kept warm Sir?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I am glad to hear it Brother, pray God you are wiſe too.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Pray Mr Morecraft know my elder Brother, and Captain do you complement. Savil I date ſwear is glad at heart to ſee you; Lord, we heard Sir you were drown'd at Sea, and ſee how luckily things come about?

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: This mony muſt be paid again Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: No Sir, pray keep the Sale, 'twill make good Tailo • s meaſures; I am well I thank you.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: By my troth the Gentleman has ſtew'd him in his own Sawce, I ſhall love him for't.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: I know not where I am, I am ſo glad: your worſhip is the welcom'ſt man alive; upon my knees I bid you welcome home: here has been ſuch a hurry, ſuch a din, ſuch diſmal Drinking, Swearing and Whoring, 'thas almoſt made me mad: we have all liv'd in a continual Turnbal-ſtreet; Sir, bleſt be Heaven, that ſent you ſafe again, now ſhall I eat and go to bed again.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Brother diſmiſs theſe people.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Captain be gone a while, meet me at my old Randevouſe in the evening, take your ſmall Poet with you. Mr Morecraft you were beſt go prattle with your learned Counſel, I ſhall preſerve your mony, I was couzen'd when time was, we are quit Sir.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Better and better ſtill.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: What is this fellow, Brother?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: The thirſty Uſurer that ſupt my Land off.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: What does he tarry for?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Si • to be Landlord of your Houſe and State: I was bold to make a little ſale Sir.

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: Am I overreach'd? if there be Law I'le hamper ye.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: P • ethee be gone, and rave at home, thou art ſo baſe a fool I cannot laugh at thee: Sirrah, this comes of couzening, home and ſpa • e, eat Reddiſh till you raiſe your ſums again. If you ſtir far in this, I'le have you whipt, your ca • s nail'd for intelligencing o'the Pillory, and your goods forfeit: you are a ſtale conzener, leave my houſe: no more.

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: A pox upon your houſe. Come Widow, I ſhall yet hamper this young Gameſter.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Good twelve i'th' hundred keep your way, I am not for your diet, marry in your own Tribe Jew, and get a Broker.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: 'Tis well ſaid Widow: will you jog on Sir?

sp.speaker: More.
sp.p: Yes, I will go, but 'tis no matter whither:
But when I truſt a wild Fool, and a Woman,
May I lend Gratis, and build Hoſpitals.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Nay good Sir, make all even, here's a Widow wants your good word for me, ſhe's rich, and may renew me and my fortunes.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I am glad you look before you. Gentlewoman, here is a poor diſtreſſed younger Brother.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You do him wrong Sir, he's a Knight.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I ask you mercy: yet 'tis no matter, his Knighthood is no inheritance I take it: whatſoever he is, he is your Servant, or would be, Lady. Faith be not mercileſs, but make a man; he's young and handſome, though he b • my Brother, and his obſervances may deſerve your Love: he ſhall not ſail for means.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Sir you ſpeak like a worthy Brother: and ſo much I do credit your fair Language, that I ſhall love your Brother: and ſo love him, but I ſhall bluſh to ſay more.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Stop her mouth. I hope you ſhall not live to know that hour when this ſhall be repented. Now Brother I ſhould chide, but I'le give no diſtaſte to your fair Miſtreſs. I will inſtruct her in't and ſhe ſhall do't: you have been wild and ignorant, pray mend it.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Sir, every day now Spring comes on.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: To you good Mr Savil and your Office, thus much I have to ſay: Y'a •• from my Steward become, firſt your own Drunk •• d, then his Bawd: they ſay y'are excellent grown in both, and perfect: give me your keys Sir Savil?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: Good Sir conſider whom you left me to.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo
sp.p: I left you as a carb for, not to provoke my Brothers follies: where's the beſt drink, now? come, tell me Savil; where's the ſoundeſt Whores? Ye old he Goat, ye dried Ape, ye lame Stallion, muſt you be leading in my houſe your Whores, like Fairies dance their night rounds, without fear either of King or Conſtable, within my walls? Are all my Hangings ſafe; my Sheep unſold yet? I hope my Plate is currant, I ha' too much on't. What ſay you to 300 pounds in drink now?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Good Sir forgive me, and but hear me ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Me thinks thou ſhouldſt be drunk ſtill, and not ſpeak, 'tis the more pardonable.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: I will Sir, if you will have it ſo.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
I thank ye: yes, e'ne purſue it Sir: do yo • hear? get a Whore ſoon for your recreation: go look o •• Captain Broken-breech your fellow, and Quarrel if you dare: I ſhall deliver theſe Keys to one ſhall have more honeſty, though not ſo much fine wit Sir. You may walk and gather Creſſes ſit to cool your Liver; there's ſomething for you to begin a Diet, you'l have the Pox elſe. Speed yo • well, Sir Savil: you may eat at my houſe to preſerve life: but keep no Fornication in the Stables.
Ex. om. pr. Savil.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Now muſt I hang my ſelf, my friends will look ſor't.
Eating and ſleeping, I do deſpiſe you both now:
I will run mad firſt, and if that get not pitty,

I'le drown my ſelf, to a moſt diſmal ditty.
Exit Savil.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Abigal.
sp.p:
ALas poor Gentlewoman, to what a miſery hath Age brought thee: to what a ſcurvy Fortune? Thou that haſt been a Companion for Noblemen, and at the worſt of thoſe times for Gentlemen: now like a broken Servingman, muſt beg for favour to thoſe, that would have crawl'd like Pilgrims to my Chamber but for an Apparition of me. You that be coming on, make much of fifteen, and ſo till five and twenty: uſe your time with reverence, that your profits may ariſe: it will not tarry with you, Ecce ſignum: here was a face, but time that like a furfeit eats our youth, plague of his iron teeth, and draw 'em ſor't, has been a little bolder here than welcome: and now to ſay the truth, I am fit for no man. Old men i'th' houſe of fifty, call me Granum; and when they are drunk, e'ne then, when Jon •
and my Lady are all one, not one will do me reaſon. My little Levite hath forſaken me, his ſilver ſound of Cittern quite aboliſh this doleful hymns under my Chamber window, digeſted into tedious learning: well fool, you leapt a Haddock when you left him: he's a clean man, and a good edifier, and twenty nobles is his ſtate de claro, beſides his pigs in poſſe. To this good Homiliſt I have been ever ſtubborn, which God forgive me for, and mend my manners: and Love, if ever thou hadſt care of forty, of ſuch a piece of lape ground, hear my prayer, and fire his zeal ſo far forth that my faults in this renued impreſſion of my love may ſhew corrected to our gentle reader.

See how negligently he paſſes by me: with what an Equipage Canonical, as though he had broken the heart of Bellarmine, or added ſomething to the ſinging Brethren. 'Tis ſcorn, I know it, and deſerve it, Mr Roger.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Fair Gentlewoman, my name is Roger.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Then gentle Roger?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Ungentle Abigal.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Why Mr Roger will you ſet your wit to a weak womans?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: You are weak indeed: for ſo the Poet ſings.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: I do confeſs my weakneſs, ſweet Sir Roger.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Good my Ladies Gentlewoman, or my good Ladies Gentlewoman (this trope is loſt to you now) leave your prating, you have a ſeaſon of your firſt mother in ye: and ſurely had the Devil been in love, he had been abuſed too: go Dalilah, you make men fools, and wear Fig breeches.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Well, well, hard hearted man; dilate upon the weak infirmities of women: theſe are fit texts, but once there was a time, would I had never ſeen thoſe eyes, thoſe eyes, thoſe orient eyes.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: I they were pearls once with you.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Saving your reverence Sir, ſo they are ſtill.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Nay, nay, I do beſeech you leave your cogging, what they are, they are, they ſerve me without Spectacles I thank 'em.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: O will you kill me?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: I do not think I can,
Y'are like a Copy-hold with nine lives in't.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: You were wont to bear a Chriſtian fear about you: For your own worſhips ſake.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: I was a Chriſtian fool then: Do you remember what a dance you led me? how I grew qualm'd in love, and was a dunce? could expound but once a quarter, and then was out too: and then out of the ſtinking ſtir you put me in, I prayed for my own iſſue. You do remember all this?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: O be as then you were?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: I thank you for it, ſurely I will be wiſer Abigal: and as the Ethnick Poet ſings, I will not loſe my oyl and labour too. Y'are for the worſhipfull I take it Abigal.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: O take it ſo, and then I am for thee?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: I like theſe tears well, and this humbling alſo, they are Symptomes of contrition. If I ſhould fall into my ſit again, would you not ſhake me into a quotidian Coxcombe? Would you not uſe me ſcurvily again, and give me poſſets with purging Confets in't? I tell thee Gentlewoman, thou haſt been harder to me, than a long pedigree.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: O Curate cure me: I will love thee better, dearer, longer: I will do any thing, betray the ſecrets of the main houſe-hold to thy reformation. My Ladie ſhall look lovingly on thy learning, and when true time ſhall point thee for a Parſon, I will convert thy egges to penny cuſtards, and thy tith gooſe ſhall graze and multiply.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: I am mollified, as well ſhall teſtifie this faithfull kiſs, and have a great care Miſtris Abigal how you depreſs the Spirit any more with your rebukes and mocks: for certainly the edge of ſuch a follie cuts it ſelf.

sp.speaker: Abigal.
sp.p: O Sir, you have pierc'd me thorow. Here I vow a recantation to thoſe malicious faults I ever did againſt you. Never more will I deſpiſe your learning, never more pin cards and cony tails upon your Caſſock, never again reproach your reverend nightcap, and call it by the mangie name of murrin, never your reverend perſon more, and ſay, you look like one of Baals Prieſts in a hanging, never again when you ſay grace laugh at you, nor put you out at prayers: never cramp you more, nor when you ride, get Sope and Thiſtles for you. No my Roger, theſe faults ſhall be corrected and amended, as by the tenour of my tears appears.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Now cannot I hold if I ſhould be hang'd, I muſt crie too. Come to thine own beloved, and do even what thou wilt with me ſweet, ſweet Abigal. I am thine own for ever: here's my hand, when Roger proves a recreant, hang him i'th' Bel-ropes.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why how now Maſter Roger, no prayers down with you to night? Did you hear the bell ring? You are courting: your ſlock ſhall ſat well for it.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p:
I humbly ask your pardon: I'le clap up Prayers, but ſtay a little, and be with you again.
Exit Roger.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: How dare you, being ſo unworthie a fellow,
Preſume to come to move me any more?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: What ails the fellow?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: The fellow comes to laugh at you, I tell you Ladie I would not for your Land, be ſuch a Coxcomb, ſuch a whining Aſs, as you decreed me for when I was laſt here.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I joy to hear you are wiſe, 'tis a rare Jewel
In an Elder Brother: pray be wiſer yet?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Me thinks I am very wiſe: I do not come a wooing. Indeed I'le move no more love to your Ladiſhip.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: What makes you here then?

sp.speaker: El er Lo.
sp.p: Only to ſee you and be merry Ladie: that's all my buſineſs. Faith let's be very merry. Where's little Rogers he's a good fellow: an hour or two well ſpent in wholſome mirth, is worth a thouſand of theſe puling paſſions. 'Tis an ill world for Lovers.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: They were never fewer.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I thank God there's one leſs for me Ladie?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: You were never any Sir.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Till now, and now I am the prettieſt fellow.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: You talk like a Tailor Sir.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Me thinks your faces are no ſuch fine things now.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why did you tell me you were wiſe? Lord what a lying age is this, where will you mend theſe faces?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: A Hogs face fouſt is worth a hundred of 'em.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Sure you had a Sow to your Mother.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: She brought ſuch fine white Pigs as you, fit for none but Parſons Ladie?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: 'Tis well you will allow us our Clergie yet.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: That ſhall not ſave you. O that I were in love again with a wiſh.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: By this light you are a ſcurvie fellow, pray be gone.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: You know I am a clean skin'd man.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Do I know it?

sp.speaker: Elder. Lo.
sp.p: Come, come, you would know it; that's as good: but not a ſnap, never long for't, not a ſnap dear Ladie.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Hark ye Sir, hark ye, get ye to the Suburbs, there's horſe fleſh for ſuch hounds: will you goe Sir?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Lord how I lov'd this woman, how I worſhipt this prettie calf with the white face here: as I live, you were the prettieſt fool to play withall, the wittieſt little varlet, it would talk: Lord how it talk't! and when I angred it, it would cry out, and ſcratch, and cat no meat, and it would ſay, goe hang.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: It will ſay ſo ſtill, if you anger it.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: And when I askt it, if it would be married, it ſent me of an errand into France, and would abuſe me, and be glad it did ſo.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Sir this is moſt unmanly, pray by gon.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: And ſwear (even when it twitter'd to be at me) I was unhanſome.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Have you no manners in you?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: And ſay my back was melted, when God he knows, I kept it at a charge: Four Flaunders Mares would have been eaſier to me, and a Fencer.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: You think all this is true now?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Faith whether it be or no, 'tis too good for you. But ſo much for our mirth: Now have at you in earneſt.

sp.speaker: Lo.
sp.p: There is enough Sir, I deſire no more.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Yes faith, wee'l have a caſt at your beſt parts now. And then the Devil take the worſt.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Pray Sir no more, I am not ſo much affected with your commendations, 'tis almoſt dinner, I know they ſtay for you at the Ordinary.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: E'ne a ſhort Grace, and then I am gone; You are a woman, and the proudeſt that ever lov'd a Coach: the ſcornfulleſt, ſcurvieſt, and moſt ſenceleſs woman; the greedieſt to be prais'd, and never mov'd though it be groſs and open; the moſt envious, that at the poor ſame of anothers face, would eat your own, and more than is your own, the paint belonging to it: of ſuch a ſelf opinion, that you think none can deſerve your glove: and for your malice, you are ſo excellent, you might have been your Tempters tutor: nay, never cry.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Your own heart knows you wrong me: I cry for ye?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: You ſhall before I leave you.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Is all this ſpoke in earneſt?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Yes and more as ſoon as I can get it out.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Well out with't.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: You are, let me ſee.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: One that has us'd you with too much reſpect.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: One that hath us'd me (ſince you will have it ſo) the baſeſt, the moſt Foot-boy-like, without reſpect of what I was, or what you might be by me; you have us'd me, as I would uſe a jade, ride him off's legs, then turn him to the Commons; you have us'd me with diſcretion, and I thank ye. If you have many more ſuch pretty Servants, pray build an Hoſpital, and when they are old, pray keep 'em for ſhame.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I cannot think yet this is ſerious.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Will you have more on't?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: No ſaith, there's enough if it be true:
Too much by all my part; you are no Lover then?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: No, I had rather be a Carrier.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why the Gods amend all.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Neither do I think there can be ſuch a fellow found • 'th' world, to be in love with ſuch a froward woman, if there be ſuch, they're mad, Jove comfort 'em. Now you have all, and I as new a man, as light, and ſpirited, that I feel my ſelf clean through another creature. O 'tis brave to be ones own man, I can ſee you now as I would ſee a Picture, ſit all day by you and never kiſs your hand: hear you ſing, and never fall backward: but with as ſet a temper, as I would hear a Fidler, riſe and thank you. I can now keep my mony in my purſe, that ſtill was gadding out for Scarfes and Waſtcoats: and keep my hand from Mercers ſheep skins finely. I can eat mutton now, and feaſt my ſelf with my two ſhillings, and can ſee a play for eighteen pence again: I can my Ladie.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: The carriage of this fellow vexes me. Sir, pray let me ſpeak a little private with you, I muſt not ſuffer this.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, what would you with me?
You will not raviſh me? Now, your ſet ſpeech?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Thou perjur'd man.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, this is a fine exordium.
And why I pray you perjur'd?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Did you not ſwear a thouſand times you lov'd me beſt of all things?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I do confeſs it: make your beſt of that.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why do you ſay you do not then?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Nay I'le ſwear it,
And give ſufficient reaſon, your own uſage.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Do you not love me then?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: No ſaith.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Did you ever think I lov'd you dearly?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Yes, but I ſee but rotten fruits on't.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Do not denie your hand for I muſt kiſs it, and take my laſt farewell, now let me die ſo you be happy.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: I am too fooliſh: Ladie ſpeak dear Ladie.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: No let me die. She ſwounds.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Oh my Siſter!

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: O my Ladie help, help.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Run for ſome Roſalis?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I have plaid the fine aſs: bend her bodie, Lady, beſt, deareſt, worthieſt Ladie, hear your Servant, I am not as I ſhew'd: O wretched fool, to fling away the Jewel of thy life thus. Give her more air, ſee ſhe begins to ſtir, ſweet Miſtris hear me?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Is my Servant well?

sp.speaker: Elder La.
sp.p: In being yours I am ſo.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Then I care not.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: How do ye, reach a chair there; I confeſs my fault not pardonable, in purſuing thus upon ſuch tenderneſs my wilfull error; but had I known it would have wrought thus with ye, thus ſtrangely, not the world had won me to it, and let not (my beſt Ladie) any word ſpoke to my end diſturb your quiet peace: for ſooner ſhall you know a general ruine, than my faith broken. Do not doubt this Miſtris, for by my life I cannot live without you. Come, come, you ſhall not grieve, rather be angrie, and heap infliction upon me: I will ſuffer. O I could curſe my ſelf, pray ſmile upon me. Upon my faith it was but a trick to trie you, knowing you lov'd me dearlie, and yet ſtrangely that you would never ſhew it, though my means was all humilitie.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: How now?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I thank you fine fool for your moſt fine plot; this was a ſubtile one, a ſtiff device to have caught Dottrels with Good ſenceleſs Sir, could you imagine I ſhould ſwound for you, and know your ſelf to be an arrant aſs? I, a diſcovered one. 'Tis quit I thank you Sir. Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Take heed Sir, ſhe may chance to ſwound again?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Step to her Sir, ſee how ſhe changes colour.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I'le goe to hell firſt, and be better welcom.
I am fool'd, I do confeſs it, finely fool'd,
Ladie, fool'd Madam, and I thank you for it.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Faith 'tis not ſo much worth Sir:
But if I knew when you come next a burding,
I'le have a ſtronger nooſe to hold the Woodcock.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I am glad to ſee you merry, pray laugh on.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: H'ad a hard heart that could not laugh at you S •• ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Pray Siſter do not laugh, you'le anger him,
And then hee'l rail like a rude Coſtermonger.
That School-boys had couzened of his Apples,
As loud and ſenceleſs?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I will not rail.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Faith then let's hear him Siſter?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Yes, you ſhall hear me.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Shall we be the better by it then?

sp.speaker: Eld. L.
sp.p: No, he that makes a woman better by his words,
I'le have him Sainted: blows will not doe it.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: By this light hee'll beat us.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: You do deſerve it richly,
And may live to have a Beadle doe it.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Now he rails?
