sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Come ſcornfull Folly,
If this be railing, you ſhall hear me rail.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Pray put it in good words then.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: The worſt are good enough for ſuch a trifle,
Such a proud piece of Cobweblawn.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: You bite Sir?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I would till the bones crackt, and I had my will.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: We had beſt muzzel him, he grows mad.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I would 'twere lawfull in the next great ſickneſs to have the Dogs ſpared, thoſe harmleſs creatures, and knock i'th' head theſe hot continual plagues, women, that are more infectious. I hope the State will think on't.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Are you well Sir?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: He looks as though he had a grievous fit o'th' Colick.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Green-ginger will cure me.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: I'le heat a trencher for him.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Durty December doe, Thou with a face as old as Erra Pater, ſuch a Prognoſticating noſe: thou thing that ten years ſince has leſt to be a woman, outworn the expectation of a Baud; and thy dry bones can reach at nothing now, but gords or ninepins, pray goe fetch a trencher goe.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Let him alone, he's crackt.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: I'le ſee him hang'd firſt, is a beaſtly fellow to uſe a woman of my breeding thus; I marry is he: would I were a man, I'de make him eat his Knaves words?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Tie your ſhe Otter up, good Lady folly, ſhe ſtinks worſe than a Bear-baiting.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why will you be angry now?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Goe paint and purge, call in your kennel with you: you a Lady?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Sirra, look to't againſt the quarter Seſſions, if there be good behaviour in the world, I'le have thee bound to it.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
You muſt not ſeek it in your Ladies houſe then; pray ſend this Ferret home, and ſpi • good Abigal. And Madam, that your Ladiſhip may know, in what •• fe manner you have us'd my ſervice, I do from this hour hate
thee heartily; and though your folly ſhould whip you to repentance, and waken you at length to ſee my wrongs, 'tis not the endeavour of your life ſhall win me; not all the friends you have, interceſſion, nor your ſubmiſſive letters, though they ſpoke as many tears as words; not your knees grown to th'ground in penitence, nor all your ſtate, to kiſs you, nor my pardon, nor will to give you Chriſtian burial, if you dye thus; ſo farewell. When I am married and made ſure, I'le come and viſit you again, and vex you Ladie. By all my hopes I'le be a torment to you, worſe than a tedious winter. I know you will recant and ſue to me, but ſave that labour: I'le rather love a fever and continual thirſt, rather contract my youth to drink and ſacerdote upon quarrels, or take a drawn whore from an Hoſpital, that time, diſeaſes, and Mercury had eaten, than to be drawn to love you.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, pray do, but take heed though.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: From thee, falſe dice, jades, Cowards, and plaguy Summers, good Lord deliver me.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: But hark you Servant, hark ye: is he gon? call him again.

sp.speaker: Abigal.
sp.p: Hang him Paddock.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Art thou here ſtill? flie, flie, and call my Servant, flie o • ne'r ſee me more.

sp.speaker: Abigal.
sp.p:
I had rather knit again than ſee that raſcall, but I muſt doe it.
Exit Abigal.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I would be loth to anger him too much; what fine foolery is this in a woman, to uſe thoſe men moſt frowardly they love moſt? If I ſhould loſe him thus, I were rightly ſerved. I hope he's not ſo much himſelf, to take it to th'heart: how now? will he come back?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Never, he ſwears, whilſt he can hear men ſay there's any woman living: he ſwore he would ha' me firſt.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Didſt thou intreat him wench?

sp.speaker: Abigal.
sp.p: As well as I could Madam. But this is ſtill your way, to love being abſent, and when he's with you, laugh at him and abuſe him. There's another way if you could hit on't.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Thou ſaiſt true, get me paper, pen and ink, I'le write to him, I'de be loth he ſhould ſleep in's anger.
Women are moſt fools when they think th'are wiſeſt.

div.stage: Muſick Enter Young Loveleſs, and Widow, going to be Married, with them his Comrades.

sp.speaker: Widow.
sp.p: Pray Sir caſt off theſe fellows, as unſitting for your bare knowledge, and far more your companie: is't fit ſuch Ragamuſſins as theſe are ſhould bear the name of friends? and furniſh out a civil houſe? ye're to be married now, and men that love you muſt expect a courſe far from your old carrier: if you will keep 'em, turn 'em toth' ſtable, and there make 'em grooms: and yet now conſider it, ſuch beggars once ſet o' horſe back, you have heard will ride, how far you had beſt to look.

sp.speaker: Captain.
sp.p: Hear you, you that muſt be Ladie, pray content your ſelf and think upon your carriage ſoon at night, what dreſſing will beſt take your Knight, what waſtcote, what cordial will do well i'th' morning for him, what triers have you?

sp.speaker: Widow.
sp.p: What do you mean Sir?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: Thoſe that muſt ſwitch him up: if he ſtart well, fear not but cry Saint George, and bear him hard: when you perceive his wind growes hot and wanting, let him a little down, he's fleet, ne're doubt him, and ſtands ſound.

sp.speaker: Widow.
sp.p: Sir, you hear theſe fellows?

sp.speaker: Young Love.
sp.p: Merrie companions, wench, Merry companions.

sp.speaker: Widow.
sp.p: To one another let 'em be companions, but good Sir not to you: you ſhall be civil and ſlip off theſe baſe t • appings.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: He ſhall not need, my moſt ſweed Ladie Grocer, if he be civil, not your powdered Sugar, nor your Raiſins ſhall perſwade the Captain to live a Coxcomb with him; let him be civil and eat i'th' Arches, and ſee what will come on't.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.p: Let him be civil, doe: undo him; I, that's the next way. I will not take (if he be civil once) two hundred pound a year to live with him; be civil? there's a trim perſwaſion.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: If thou beeſt civil Knight, as Jove defends it, get thee another noſe, that will be pull'd off by the angry boyes for thy converſion: the children thou ſhalt get on this Civillian cannot inherit by the law, th'are Ethnicks, and all thy ſport meer Moral leacherie: when they are grown, having but little in 'em, they may prove Haberda • hers, or groſs Grocers, like their dear Damm there: prethee be civil Knig • t, in time thou maiſt read to thy houſhold, and be drunk once a year: this would ſhew finely.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I wonder ſweet heart you will offer this, you do not underſtand theſe Gentlemen: I will be ſhort and pithy: I had rather call you off by the way of charge: theſe are Creatures, that nothing goes to the maintenance of but Corn and Water. I will keep theſe fellows juſt in the competencie of two Hens.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: If you can caſt it ſo Sir, you have my liking? If they eat leſs, I ſhould not be offended: But how theſe Sir, can live upon ſo little as Corn and Water, I am unbelieving.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Why prethee ſweet heart what's your Ale? is not that Corn and Water, my ſweet Widow?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I but my ſweet Knight where's the meat to this, and cloaths that they muſt look for?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: In this ſhort ſentence Ale, is all included: Meat, Drink, and Cloth; Theſe are no ravening Footmen, no fellows, that at Ordinaries dare eat their eighteen pence thrice out before they riſe, and yet goe hungry to play, and crack more nuts than would ſuffice a dozen Squirrels; beſides the din, which is damnable: I had rather rail, and be confin'd to a Boatmaker, than live amongſt ſuch raſcals; theſe are people of ſuch a clean diſcretion in their diet, of ſuch a moderate ſuſtenance, that they ſweat if they but ſmell hot meat. Porredge is poiſon, they hate a Kitchin as they hate a Counter, and ſhow 'em but a Feather-bed they ſwound. Ale is their eating and their drinking ſurely, which keeps their bodies clear, and ſoluble. Bread is a binder, and for that aboliſht even in their Ale, whoſe loſt room fills an apple, which is more airy and of ſubtiler nature. The reſt they take is little, and that little is little eaſie: For like ſtrict men of order, they do correct their bodies with a bench, or a poor ſtubborn table; if a chimny offer it ſelf with ſome few broken ruſhes, they are in down: when they are ſick, that's drunk, they may have freſh ſtraw, elſe they do deſpiſe theſe worldly pamperings. For their poor apparel, 'tis worn out to the diet; new they ſeek none, and if a man ſhould offer, they are angrie, ſcarce to be reconcil'd again with him: you ſhall not hear 'em ask one a caſt doublet once in a year, which is modeſty beſitting my poor friends: you ſee their Wardrobe, though ſlender, competent: For ſhirts I take it, they are things worn out of their remembrance. Louſie they will be when they liſt, and mangie, which ſhows a fine variety: and then to cure 'em, a Tanners lime pit, which is little charge, two dogs, and theſe; theſe two may be cur'd for 3. pence.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You have half perſwaded me, pray uſe your pleaſure: and my good friends ſince I do know your diet, I'le take an order, meat ſhall not offend you, you ſhall have Ale.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.p: We ask no more, let it be mighty Lady: and if we periſh, then our own ſins on us.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Come forward Gentlemen, to Church my boys, when we have done, I'le give you cheer in bowles.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: THis ſenſeleſs woman vexes me to th' heart, ſhe will not from my memory: would ſhe were a man for one two hours, that I might beat her. If I had been unhanſome, old or jealous, 'thad been an even lay ſhe might have ſcorn'd me; but to be young, and by this light I think as proper as the proudeſt; made as clean, as ſtraight, and ſtrong backt; means and manners equal with the beſt cloth of ſilver Sir i'th' kingdom: But theſe are things at ſome time of the Moon, below the cut of Canvas: ſure ſhe has ſome Meeching Raſcal in her houſe, ſome Hind, that ſhe hath ſeen bear (like another Milo) quarters of Malt upon his back, and ſing with't, Thraſh all day, and i'th' evening in his ſtockings, ſtrike up a Hornpipe, and there ſtink two hours, and ne're a whit the worſe man; theſe are they, theſe ſteel chin'd Raſcals that undo us all. Would I had been a Carter, or a Coachman, I had done the deed e're this time.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Sir, there's a Gentleman without would ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Bid him come in.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: By your leave Sir.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: You are welcome, what's your will Sir?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Have you forgotten me?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I do not much remember you.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: You muſt Sir. I am that Gentleman you pleas'd to wrong, in your diſguiſe, I have inquired you out.
I was diſguiſed indeed Sir if I wrong'd you, pray where and when?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: In ſuch a Ladies houſe, I need not name her.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I do remember you, you ſeem'd to be a Sutor to that Lady?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: If you remember this, do not forget how ſ • urvily you us'd me: that was no place to quarrel in, pray you think of it; if you be honeſt you dare fight with me, without more urging, elſe I muſt provoke ye.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Sir I dare fight, but never for a woman, I will not have her in my cauſe, ſhe's mortal, and ſo is not my anger: if you have brought a nobler ſubject for our Swords, I am for you; in this I would be loth to prick my Finger. And where you ſay I wrong'd you, 'tis ſo far from my profeſſion, that amongſt my fears, to do wrong is the greateſt: credit me we have been both abuſed, (not by our ſelves, for that I hold a ſpleen, no ſin of malice, and may with man enough be beſt forgoten,) but by that willfull, ſcornful piece of hatred, that much forgetful Lady: for whoſe ſake, if we ſhould leave our reaſon, and run on upon our ſenſe, like Rams, the little world of good men would laugh at us, and deſpiſe us, fixing upon our deſperate memories the never worn out names of Fools and Fencers. Sir 'tis not fear, but reaſon makes me tell you; in this I had rather help you Sir, than h •• t you, and you ſhall find it, though you throw your ſelf into as many dangers as ſhe offers, though you redeem her loſt name ev • ry day, and find her out new honours with your Sword, you ſhall l • t be her mirth as I have been.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I ask you mercy Sir, you have ta'ne my edge off: yet I would fain be ev • n with this Lady.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: In which I l • be your h •• per: we are two, and they are two: two Siſters, • ich alike, only the elder has the prouder Dow • y: In • roth I pity this diſgrace in you, yet of mine own I am ſen • eleſ • : do but follow my Counſel, and I'le p • wn my ſp ••• t, we'l over reach 'em yet; the means is th •

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Si • there' • a Gentlewoman will needs ſpeak with you, I cannot keep her out, ſhe's entred Sir.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
It is the waiting woman, pray be not ſeen: farre hold her in diſcourſe a while: hark in your ear, go and di •
patch it quickly, when I come in, I'le tell you all the project.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p:
I care not which I have.
Exit Welford

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Away, 'tis done, ſhe muſt not ſee you: no • Lady Guin • ver what news with you?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Pray leave theſe frumps Sir, and receive this letter.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: From whom good vanity?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: 'Tis from my Lady Sir: Alas good ſoul, ſhe cries and takes on!

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p:
Do's ſhe ſo good Soul? wou'd ſhe not have a Cawdle? do's ſhe ſend you with your fine Oratory goo ••
Tully to tye me to believe again? bring out the Cat-hou ••• . I'le make you take a tree Whore, then with my ti ••• bring down your Gibſhip, and then have you caſt, and hung up i'th' Warren.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: I am no beaſt Sir, would you knew it.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Wou'd I did, for I am yet very doubtful; what will you ſay now?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Nothing not I.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Art thou a woman, and ſay nothing?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Unleſs you'l hear me with more moderation, I can ſpeak wiſe enough.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: And loud enough? will your Lady love me?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: It ſeems ſo by her letter, and her lamentations; but you are ſuch another man.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Not ſuch another as I was, Mumps; nor will not be: I'le read her fine Epiſtle: ha, ha, ha, is not thy Miſtreſs mad?

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: For you ſhe will be, 'tis a ſhame you ſhould uſe a poor Gentlewoman ſo untowardly; ſhe loves the ground you tread on; and you (hard heart) becauſe ſhe jeſted with you, mean to kill her; 'tis a fine conqueſt as they ſay.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Haſt thou ſo much moiſture in the Whitleather hide yet, that thou canſt cry? I wou'd have ſworn thou ha •• been touchwood five year ſince; nay let it rain, thy face chops for a ſhower like a dry Dunghil.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: I'le not indure this Ribauldry; farewel i'th' Devils name; if my Lady die, I'le be ſworn before a jury, thou art the cauſe on't.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Do Mankin do, deliver to your Lady from me this: I mean to ſee her, if I have no other buſineſs: which before I'le want to come to her, I mean to go ſeek birds neſts: yet I may come too: but if I come, from this door till I ſee her, will I think how to rail vildly at her; how to vex her, and make her cry ſo much, that the Phyſician if ſhe fall ſick upon't, ſhall find the cauſe to be want of Urine, and ſhe remedileſs dye in her Hereſie: Farewell old Adage, I hope to ſee the Boys make Potguns on thee.

sp.speaker: Abig.
sp.p: Th'art a vile man, God bleſs my iſſue from thee.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Thou haſt but one, and that's in thy left crupper, that makes thee hobble ſo; you muſt be ground i'th' breech like a Top, you'l ne're ſpin well elſe: Farewell Fytchock. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p:
Is it not ſtrange that every womans will ſhould track out new wayes to diſturb her ſelf? if I ſhould call my reaſon to account, it cannot anſwer why I keep my ſelf from mine own wiſh, and ſtop the man I love from his; and every hour repent again, yet ſtill go on: I know 'tis like a man, that wants his natural ſleep, and growing dull would gladly give the remnant of his life fo • two hours reſt; yet through his frowardneſs, will rather chooſe to watch another man, drowſie as he, than take his own repoſe. All this I know: yet a ſtrange peeviſhneſs and anger, not to have the power to do things unexpected, carries me away to mine own ruine: I had rather 〈◊〉 ſometimes than not diſgrace in publick him whom people think I love, and do't with oaths, and am in earneſt the •
O what are we! Men, you muſt anſwer this, that dare obey • uch things as we command. How now? what newes?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Faith Madam none worth hearing.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Is he not come?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: No truly.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Nor has he writ?

sp.speaker: Abigal.
sp.p: Neither. I pray God you have not undone your • elf.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why, but what ſaies he?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Faith he talks ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: How ſtrangely?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Firſt at your Letter he laught extremely?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: What, in contempt?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: He laught monſtrous loud, as he would die, and when you wrote it I think you were in no ſuch merry mood, • o provoke him that way: and having done he cried Alas for her, and violently laught again.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Did he?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Yes, till I was angry.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Angry, why? why wert thou angry? he did doe but well, I did deſerve it, he had been a fool, an unfit man for any one to love, had he not laught thus at me: you were angry, that ſhow'd your folly; I ſhall love him more for that, than all that ere he did before: but ſaid he nothing elſe?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: Many uncertain things: he ſaid though you had mockt him, becauſe you were a woman, he could wiſh to do you ſo much favour as to ſee you: yet he ſaid, he knew you raſh, and was loth to offend you with the ſight of one, whom now he was bound not to leave.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: What one was that?

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: I know not, but truly I do fear there is a making up there: for I heard the ſervants, as I paſt by ſome, whiſper ſuch a thing: and as I came back through the hall, there were two or three Clarks writing great conveyances in haſt, which they ſaid were for their Miſtris joynture.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: 'Tis very like, and fit it ſhould be ſo, for he does think, and reaſonably think, that I ſhould keep him with my idle tricks for ever ere he be married.

sp.speaker: Abi.
sp.p: At laſt he ſaid, it ſhould go hard but he would ſee you for your ſatisfaction.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: All we that are call'd Women, know as well as men, it were a far more noble thing to grace where we are grace't, and give reſpect there where we are reſpected: yet we practiſe a wilder courſe, and never bend our eyes on men with pleaſure, till they find the way to give us a neglect: then we, too late, perceive the loſs of what we might have had, and dote to death.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Siſter, yonder's your Servant, with a Gentlewoman with him.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Cloſe at the door.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Alas I am undone, I fear he is berroth'd,
What kind of woman is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: A moſt ill favoured one, with her Maſque on:
And how her face ſhould mend the reſt I know not.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: But yet her mind was of a milder ſtuff than mine was.

div.stage: Enter Elder Loveleſs, and Welford in Womans apparel.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Now I ſee him, if my heart ſwell not again (away thou womans pride) ſo that I cannot ſpeak a gentle word to him, let me not live.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: By your leave here.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: How now, what new trick invites you hither?
Ha' you a ſine device again?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Faith this is the fineſt device I have now:
How doſt thou ſweet heart?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Why very well, ſo long as I may pleaſe
You my dear Lover. I nor can, nor will
Be ill when you are well, well when you are ill.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: O thy ſweet temper! what would I have given, that Lady had been like thee: ſeeſt thou her? that face (my love) join'd with thy humble mind, had made a wench indeed.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Alas my love, what God hath done, I dare not think to mend. I uſe no paint, nor any drugs of Art, my hands and face will ſhew it.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Why what thing have you brought to ſhew us there? do you take mony for it?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: A Godlike thing, not to be bought for mony: 'tis my Miſtris: in whom there is no paſſion, nor no ſcorn: what I will is for law; pray you ſalute her.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Salute her? by this good light, I would not kiſs her for half my wealth.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Why? why pray you?
You ſhall ſee me do't afore you; look you.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Now ſie upon thee, a beaſt would not have don't. I would not kiſs thee of a month to gain a Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Marry you ſhall not be troubled.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why was there ever ſuch a Meg as this?
Sure thou art mad.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I was mad once, when I lov'd pictures; for what are ſhape and colours elſe, but pictures? in that tawnie hide there lies an endleſs maſs of vertues, when all your red and white ones want it.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: And this is ſhe you are to marry, is't not?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Yes indeed is't.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: God give you joy.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Amen.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I thank you, as unknown for your good wiſh.
The like to you when ever you ſhall wed.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: O gentle Spirit!

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: You thank me? I pray
Keep your breath nearer you, I do not like it.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I would not willingly offend at all,
Much leſs a Lady of your worthie parts.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Sweet, Sweet!

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I do not think this woman can by nature be thus,
Thus ugly; ſure ſhe's ſome common Strumpet,
Deform'd with exerciſe of ſin?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: O Sir believe not this, for Heaven ſo comfort me as I am free from ſoul pollution with any man; my honour ta'ne away, I am no woman.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Ariſe my deareſt Soul; I do not credit it. Alas, I fear her tender heart will break with this reproach; ſie that you know no more civility to a weak Virgin. 'Tis no matter Sweet, let her ſay what ſhe will, thou art not worſe to me, and therefore not at all; be careleſs.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: For all things elſe I would, but for mine honor; Me thinks.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Alas, thine honour is not ſtain'd,
Is this the buſineſs that you ſent for me about?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Faith Siſter you are much to blame, to uſe a woman, whatſoe're ſhe be, thus; I'le ſalute her: You are welcom hither.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I humbly thank you.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Milde yet as the Dove, for all theſe injuries. Come ſhall we goe, I love thee not ſo ill to keep thee here a jeſting ſtock.
Adue to the worlds end.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why whither now?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Nay you ſhall never know, becauſe you ſhall not find me.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I pray let me ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: 'Tis very well: come.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I pray you let me ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Yes for another mock.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: By Heaven I have no mocks: good Sir a word.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Though you deſerve not ſo much at my hands, yet if you be in ſuch earneſt, I'le ſpeak a word with you; but I beſeech you be brief: for in good faith there's a Parſon and a licence ſtay for us i'th' Church all this while: and you know 'tis night.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p:
Sir, give me hearing patiently, and whatſoever I have heretofore ſpoke jeſtingly, forget: for as I hope 〈◊〉 mercy any where, what I ſhall utter now is from my he •
〈◊〉
and as I mean.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Well, well, what do you mean?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Was not I once your Miſtreſs, and you my Servant?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: O 'tis about the old matter.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Nay good Sir ſtay me out; I would but hear you excuſe your ſelf, why you ſhould take this woman, and leave me.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Prethee why not, deſerves ſhe not as much as you?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I think not, if you will look
With an indifferency upon us both.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Upon your faces, 'tis true: but if judiciouſly we ſhall caſt our eyes upon your minds, you are a thouſand women of her in worth: ſhe cannot ſwound in jeſt, nor ſet her lover tasks, to ſhew her peeviſhneſs, and his affection, not croſs what he ſaies, though it be Canonical. She's a good plain wench, that will do as I will have her, and bring me luſty Boys to throw the Sledge, and lift at Pigs of Lead: and for a Wife, ſhe's far beyond you: what can you do in a houſhold to provide for your iſſue, but lye i' bed and get 'em? your buſineſs is to dreſs you, and at idle hours to eat; when ſhe can do a thouſand profitable things: ſhe can do pretty well in the Paſtry, and knows how Pullen ſhould be cram'd, ſhe cuts Cambrick at a thread, weaves Bone-lace, and quilts Balls; and what are you good for?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Admit it true, that ſhe were far beyond me in all reſpects, does that give you a licence to forſwear your ſelf?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Forſwear my ſelf, how?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Perhaps you have forgotten the innumerable oaths you have utter'd in diſclaiming all for Wives but me: I'le not remember you: God give you joy.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Nay but conceive me, the intent of oaths is ever underſtood: Admit I ſhould proteſt to ſuch a friend, to ſee him at his Lodging to morrow: Divines would never hold me perjur'd if I were ſtruck blind, or he hid him where my diligent ſearch could not find him: ſo there were no croſs act of mine own in't. Can it be imagined I mean to force you to Marriage, and to have you whether you will or no?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Alas you need not. I make already tender of my ſelf, and then you are forſworn.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Some ſin I ſee indeed muſt neceſſarily fall upon me, as whoſoever deals with Women ſhall never utterly avoid it; yet I would chuſe the leaſt ill; which is to forſake you, that have done me all the abuſes of a malignant Woman, contemn'd my ſervice, and would have held me prating about Marriage, till I had been paſt getting of Children: then her that hath forſaken her Family, and put her tender body in my hand, upon my word—

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Which of us ſwore you firſt to?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Why to you.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Which oath is to be kept then?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I prethee do not urge my ſins unto me,
Without I could amend 'em.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why you may by wedding me.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: How will that ſatisfie my word to her?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: 'Tis not to be kept, and needs no ſatisfaction,
'Tis an error ſit for repentance only.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Shall I live to wrong that tender hearted Virgin ſo? It may not be.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Why may it not be?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I ſwear I had rather marry thee than her: but yet mine honeſty?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: What honeſty? 'Tis more preſerv'd this way:
Come, by this light, ſervant, thou ſhalt, I'le kiſs thee on't.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: This kiſs indeed is ſweet, pray God no ſin lie under it.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: There is no ſin at all, try but another.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: O my heart!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Help Siſter, this Lady ſwounds.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: How do you?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Why very well, if you be ſo.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Since a quiet mind lives not in any Woman, ſhall do a moſt ungodly thing. Hear me one word more, which by all my hopes I will not alter, I did make a • oath when you delai'd me ſo, that this very night I would be married. Now if you will go without delay, ſuddenly as late as it is, with your own Miniſter to your own Chappel, I'le wed you and to bed.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: A match dear ſervant.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: For if you ſhould forſake me now, I care not ſhe would not though for all her injuries, ſuch is her ſpi •• If I be not aſhamed to kiſs her now I part, may I not live.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I ſee you go, as ſlily as you think to ſteal away yet I will pray for you; all bleſſings of the world light o • you two, that you may live to be an aged pair. All curſes on me if I do not ſpeak what I do wiſh indeed.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: If I can ſpeak to purpoſe to her, I am a villa ••

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Servant away.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Siſter, will you Marry that inconſtant ma • ' think you he will not caſt you off to morrow, to wrong a Lady thus, lookt ſhe like dirt, 'twas baſely done. May you ne're proſper with him.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Now God forbid. Alas I was unworthy, ſo I told him

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: That was your modeſty, too good for him.
I would not ſee your wedding for a world.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Chuſe chuſe, come Younglove.

div.stage: Exit La. Elder Lo. and Young

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Dry up your eyes forſooth, you ſhall not think we are all ſuch uncivil beaſts as theſe. Would I knew how to give you a revenge.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: So would not I: No let me ſuffer truly, that I deſire.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Pray walk in with me, 'tis very late, and you ſha • l ſtay all night: your bed ſhall be no worſe than mine; I wi •• I could but do you right.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: my humble thanks:

God grant I may but live to quit your love.
Exeu • .

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Did your Maſter ſend for me Savil?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Yes, he did ſend for your worſhip Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Do you know the buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Alas Sir, I know nothing, nor am imployed beyond my hours of eating. My dancing days are done Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: What art thou now then?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: If you conſider me in little, I am with your worſhips reverence Sir, a Raſcal: one that upon the next anger of your Brother, muſt raiſe a ſconce by the high way, and ſell ſwitches; my wife is learning now Sir, to weave inkle.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: What doſt thou mean to do with thy Children Savil?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: My eldeſt boy is half a Rogue already, he was born burſten, and your worſhip knows, that is a pretty ſtep to mens compaſſions. My youngeſt boy I purpoſe Sir to bind for ten years to a Goaler, to draw under him, that he may ſhew us mercy in his function.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Your family is quartered with diſcretion: yet are reſolved to Cant then: where Savil ſhall your ſeene lie?

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Beggers muſt be no chuſers.
In every place (I take it) but the ſtocks.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: This is your drinking, and your whoring Savil, I told you of it, but your heart was hardened.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: 'Tis true, you were the firſt that told me of it I do remember yet in tears, you told me you would have Whores, and in that paſſion Sir, you broke out thus; Thou miſerable man, repent, and brew three Strikes more in a Hogſhead. 'Tis noon e're we be drunk now, and the time can tarry for no man.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Y'are grown a bitter Gentleman. I ſee miſery can clear your head better than Muſtard, I'le be a ſutor for your Keys again Sir.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Will you but be ſo gracious to me Sir? I ſhall be bound.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: You ſhall Sir
To your bunch again, or I'le miſs foully.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Save you Gentleman, ſave you.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Now Polecat, what young Rabets neſt have you to draw?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Come, prethee be familiar Knight.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Away Fox, I'le ſend for Terriers for you.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Thou art wide yet: I'le keep thee companie.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I am about ſome buſineſs; Indentures,
If ye follow me I'le beat you: take heed,
A I live I'le cancel your Coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Thou art cozen'd now, I am no uſurer:
What poor fellow's this?

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: I am poor indeed Sir.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Give him mony Knight.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Do you begin the offering.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: There poor fellow, here's an Angel for thee.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Art thou in earneſt Morecraft?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Yes faith Knight, I'le follow thy example: thou hadſt land and thouſands, thou ſpendſt, and flungſt away, and yet it flows in double: I purchaſed, wrung, and wierdraw'd, for my wealth, loſt, and was cozen'd: for which I make a vow, to trie all the waies above ground, but I'le find a conſtant means to riches without curſes.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I am glad of your converſion Maſter Morecraft:
Y'are in a fair courſe, pray purſue it ſtill.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Come, we are all gallants now, I'le keep thee company; Here honeſt fellow, for this Gentlemans ſake, there's two Angels more for thee.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.p: God quite you Sir, and keep you long in this mind.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: Wilt thou perſevere?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Till I have a penny. I have brave cloathes a making, and two horſes; canſt thou not help me to a match Knight, I'le lay a thouſand pound upon my crop-ear.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Foot, this is ſtranger than an Africk monſter,
There will be no more talk of the Cleve wars
Whilſt this laſts, come, I'le put thee into blood.

sp.speaker: Sav.
sp.p: Would all his damn'd tribe were as tender hearted. I beſeech you let this Gentleman join with you in the recovery of my Keyes; I like his good beginning Sir, the whilſt I'le pray for both your worſhips.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: He ſhall Sir.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Shall we goe noble Knight? I would fain be acquainted.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I'le be your ſervant Sir. Excunt.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Faith my ſweet Lady, I have caught you now, maugre your ſubtilties, and fine devices, be coy again now.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Prethee ſweet-heart tell true.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: By this light, by all the pleaſures I have had this night, by your loſt maidenhead, you are cozened meerly. I have caſt beyond your wit. That Gentleman is your retainer Welford.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: It cannot be ſo.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Your Siſter has found it ſo, or I miſtake, mark how ſhe bluſhes when you ſee her next. Ha, ha, ha, I ſhall not travel now, ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Prethee ſweet heart be quiet, thou haſt angred me at heart.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I'le pleaſe you ſoon again.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Welford?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I Welford, hee's a young handſome fellow, well bred and landed, your Siſter can inſtruct you in his good parts, better than I by this time.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Uds foot am I fetcht over thus?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Yes i'faith.
And over ſhall be fetcht again, never fear it.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: I muſt be patient, though it torture me:
You have got the Sun Sir.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: And the Moon too, in which I'le be the man.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: But had I known this, had I but ſurmiz'd it, you ſhould have hunted three trains more, before you had come toth' courſe, you ſhould have hankt o'th' bridle, Sir, i'faith.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: I knew it, and min'd with you, and ſo blew you up.
Now you may ſee the Gentlewoman: ſtand cloſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: For Gods ſake Sir, be private in this buſineſs,
You have undone me elſe. O God, what have I done?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: No harm I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: How ſhall I look upon my friends again?
With what face?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Why e'ne with that: 'tis a good one, thou canſt not find a better: look upon all the faces thou ſhalt ſee there, and you ſhall find 'em ſmooth ſtill, fair ſtill, ſweet ſtill, and to your thinking honeſt; thoſe have done as much as you have yet, or daie doe Miſtris, and yet they keep no ſtir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Good Sir goe in, and put your womans cloaths on:
If you be ſeen thus, I am loſt for ever.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I'le watch you for that Miſtris: I am no fool, here will I tarry till the houſe be up and witneſs with me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Good dear friend goe in.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: To bed again if you pleaſe, elſe I am ſixt here till there be notice taken what I am, and what I have done: if you could juggle me into my woman-hood again, an I ſo cog me out of your company, all this would be forſworn, and I again an aſinego, as your Siſter left me. No, I'le have it known and publiſht; then if you'le be a whore, forſake me and be aſham'd: and when you can hold no longer, marry ſome caſt Cleve Captain, and ſell Bottle-ale.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I dare not ſtay Sir, uſe me modeſtly, I am your wife.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Goe in, I'le make up all.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I'le be a witneſs of your naked truth Sir: this is the Gentlewoman, prethee look upon him, this is he that made me break my ſaith ſweet: but thank your Siſter, ſhe hath ſoder'd it.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: What a dull aſs was I, I could not ſee this wencher from a wench: twenty to one, if I had been but tender like my Siſter, he had ſerved me ſuch a ſlippery trick too.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Twenty to one I had.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: I would have watcht you Sir, by your good patience, for ferreting in my ground.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: You have been with my Siſter.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Yes to bring.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: An heir into the world he means.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: There is no chaſing now.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I have had my part on't: I have been chaft this three hours, that's the leaſt, I am reaſonable cool now.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Cannot you fare well, but you muſt cry to 〈◊〉 meat?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: He that fares well, and will not bleſs the founders, is either ſurfeited, or ill taught, Lady, for mine own part, I have found ſo ſweet a diet, I can commend it, though I cannot ſpare it.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: How like you this diſh, Welford, I made a ſupper on't, and fed ſo heartily, I could not ſleep.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: By this light, had I but ſcented out your t ••• , y e had ſlept with a bare pillow in your arms and kiſt that, or elſe the bed-poſt, for any wiſe ye had got this twelve-month yet: I would have vext you more than a try'd p ſt horſe; and been longer bearing, than ever after game at Iriſh was. Lord, that I were unmarried again.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Lady I would not undertake ye, were you again a Haggard, for the beſt caſt of four Ladys i'th' Kingdom: you were ever tickle-footed, and would not truſs round.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Is ſhe faſt?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: She was all night lockt here boy.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Then you may lure her without fear of loſing: take off her Cranes. You have a delicate Gentlewoman to your Siſter: Lord what a prettie furie ſhe was in, when ſhe perceived I was a man: but I thank God I ſatisfied her ſcruple, without the Parſon o'th' town.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: What did ye?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Madam, can you tell what we did?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: She has a ſhrewd gueſs at it I ſee it by her.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Well you may mock us: but my large Gentlewoman, my Mary Ambre, had I but ſeen into you, you ſhould have had another bed-fellow, fitter a great deal for your itch.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: I thank you Lady, me thought it was well,
You are ſo curious.

div.stage: Enter Young Loveleſs, his Lady, Morecraft, Savil, and two Servingmen.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Get on your doublet, here comes my Brother.

sp.speaker: Yo Lo.
sp.p: Good morrow Brother, and all good to your Lady.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: God ſave you and good morrow to you all.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Good morrow. Here's a poor brother of yours.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Fie how this ſhames me.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: Prethee good fellow help me to a cup of beer.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: I will Sir.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Brother what makes you here? will this Lady do? Will ſhe? is ſhe not nettl'd ſtill?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: No I have em'd her.
Mr. Welford, pray know this Gentleman is my Brother.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.p: Sir I ſhall long to love him.

sp.speaker: Yo Lo.
sp.p: I ſhall not be your debter Sir. But how is't with you?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: As well as may be man: I am married: your new acquaintance hath her Siſter, and all's well.
I am glad on't. Now my prettie Lady Siſter,
How do you find my Brother?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Almoſt as wild as you are.

sp.speaker: Yo Lo.
sp.p: He will make the better husband: you have tried him?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Againſt my will Sir.

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Hee'l make your will amends ſoon, do not doubt it.
But Sir I muſt intreat you to be better known
To this converted Jew here.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Here's Beer for you Sir.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.p: And here's for you an Angel:
Pray buy no Land, 'twill never proſper Sir.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: How's this?

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: Bleſs you, and then I'le tell: He's turn'd Gallant.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.p: Gallant?

sp.speaker: Yo. Lo.
sp.p: I Gallant, and is now called, Cutting Morecraft:
〈◊〉 reaſon I'le inform you at more leiſure.

O 〈…〉
• t me know him preſently.

Y ••
• ll hug one another.
Sir I muſt keep you company.
Cutting Morecraft faces about, I muſt preſent 〈◊〉
As 〈◊〉 as you will Sir, I am for 'em.
〈…〉 you ſervice.
〈◊〉 look for't in good ſaith Sir.
〈…〉 ſweet heart kiſs him.
〈…〉 , f • llow?
〈…〉 will it pleaſe you to remember me: my keys good Sir.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.p: I'le doe it preſently.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.p: Come thou ſhalt kiſs him for our ſport ſake.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Let him come on then; and do you hear, do not inſtruct me in theſe tricks, for you may repent it.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.l: That at my peril. Luſty Mr. Morecraft,
Here is a Lady would ſalute you.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: She ſhall not loſe her longing Sir: what is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: My wiſe Sir.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: She muſt be then my Miſtres.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Muſt I Sir?

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: O yes, you muſt.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: And you muſt take this ring, a poor pawn
Of ſome fiftie pound.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.l: Take it by any means, 'tis lawfull prize.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Sir I ſhall call you ſervant.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I ſhall be proud on't: what fellow's that?

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.l: My Ladies Coachman.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: There's ſomething, (my friend) for you to buy whips,
And for you Sir, and you Sir.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Under a miracle this is the ſtrangeſt
I ever heard of.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: What, ſhall we play, or drink? what ſhall we doe?
Who will hunt with me for a hundred pounds?

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: Stranger and Stranger!
Sir you ſhall find ſport after a day or two.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.l: Sir I have a ſute unto you
Concerning your old ſervant Savil.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: O, for his keys, I know it.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.l: Now Sir, ſtrike in.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Sir I muſt have you grant me.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: 'Tis done Sir, take your keys again:
But hark you Savil, leave off the motions
Of the fleſh, and be honeſt, or elſe you ſhall graze again:
I'le try you once more.

sp.speaker: Savil.
sp.l: If ever I be taken drunk, or whoring,
Take off the biggeſt key i'th' bunch, and open
My head with it Sir: I humbly thank your worſhips.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Nay then I ſee we muſt keep holiday.
Here's the laſt couple in hell.

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.l: Joy be among you all.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Why how now Sir, what is the meaning of this emblem?

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.l: Marriage an't like your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Are you married?

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.l: As well as the next Prieſt could doe it, Madam.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: I think the ſign's in Gemini, here's ſuch coupling.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: Sir Roger, what will you take to lie from your ſweet-heart to night?

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.l: Not the beſt benifice in your worſhips gift Sir.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: A whorſon, how he ſwells.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.l: How many times to night Sir Roger?

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.l: Sir you grow ſcurrilous:
What I ſhall do, I ſhall do: I ſhall not need your help.

sp.speaker: Young Lo.
sp.l: For horſe fleſh Roger.

sp.speaker: Elder Lo.
sp.l: Come prethee be not angry, 'tis a day
Given wholly to our mirth.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: It ſhall be ſo Sir: Sir Roger and his Bride,
We ſhall intreat to be at our charge.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.l: Welford get you to the Church: by this light,
You ſhall not lie with her again, till y'are married.

sp.speaker: Wel.
sp.l: I am gone.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: To every Bride I dedicate this day
Six healths a piece, and it ſhall goe hard,
But every one a jewell: Come be mad boys.

sp.speaker: El. Lo.
sp.l: Th'art in a good beginning: come who leads?
Sir Roger, you ſhall have the Van: lead the way:
Would every dogged wench had ſuch a day. Exeunt.

div.head: Perſons Repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Count Clodio, Governour and a diſhonourable purſuer of Zenocia.
Manuel du Soſa, Governour of Lisbon, and Brother to Guiomar.
Arnoldo, A Gentleman contracted to Zenocia.
Rutilio, A merry Gentleman Brother to Arnoldo.
Duarte, Son to Guiomar, a Gentleman well qualified but vain-glorious.
Alonzo, a young Portugal Gentleman, enemy to Duarte.
Leopold, a Sea Captain Enamour'd on Hippolyta.
Zabulon, a Jew, ſervant to Hippolyta.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Zenocia, Miſtreſs to Arnoldo, and a chaſte Wife.
Guiomar, a vertuous Lady, Mother to Duarte.
Hippolyta, a rich Lady, wantonly in Love with Arnoldo.
Sulpitia, a Bawd, Miſtreſs of the Male Stewes.

div.p: The Scene ſometimes Lisbon, ſometimes Italy.

div.head: Scena prima.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: WHY do you grieve thus ſtill?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: 'Twould melt a Marble,
And tame a Savage man, to feel my fortune.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: What fortune? I have liv'd this thirty years,
And run through all theſe follies you call fortunes,
Yet never fixt on any good and conſtant,
But what I made my ſelf: why ſhould I grieve then
At that I may mould any way?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: You are wide ſtill.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: You love a Gentlewoman, a young handſom woman,
I have lov'd a thoſand, not ſo few.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: You are diſpos'd.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: You hope to Marry her; 'tis a lawful calling
And prettily eſteem'd of, but take heed then,
Take heed dear Brother of a ſtranger fortune
Than e're you felt yet; fortune my ſoe is a friend to it.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: 'Tis true I love, dearly, and truly love,
A noble, vertuous, and moſt beauteous Maid,
And am belov'd again.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: That's too much o' Conſcience,
To love all theſe would run me out o' my wits.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Prethee give ear, I am to Marry her.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Diſpatch it then, and I'le go call the Piper.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: But O the wicked Cuſtom of this Country,
The barbarous, moſt inhumane, damned Cuſtom.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: 'Tis true, to marry is a Cuſtom
l' the world; for look you Brother,
Wou'd any man ſtand plucking for the Ace of Harts,
With one pack of Cards all dayes on's life?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: You do not
Or elſe you purpoſe not to underſtand me.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Proceed, I will give ear.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: They have a Cuſtom
In this moſt beaſtly Country, out upon't.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Let's hear it firſt.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: That when a Maid is contracted
And ready for the tye o'th' Church, the Governour,
He that commands in chief, muſt have her Maiden-head,
Or Ranſom it for mony at his pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: How might a man atchieve that place? a rare Cuſtom!
An admirable rare Cuſtom: and none excepted?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: None, none.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: The ra • er ſtill: how could I lay about me,
In this ra • e Office? are they born to it, or choſen?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Both equal damnable.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Me thinks both excellent,
Would I were the next heir.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: To this mad fortune
Am I now come, my Marriage is proclaim'd,
And nothing can redeem me from this miſchief.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: She s very young.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: And fair I dare proclaim her,
Elſe mine • yes fail.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Fa •• as the • nd unblaſted.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I cannot blame him then, if 'twere mine own caſe,
I would not go an Ace leſs.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: • ye Rutilio,
Why do you make your brothers miſery
Your ſport and game?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: There is no paſtime like it.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I look'd for your advice, your timely Counſel,
How to avoid this blow, not to be mockt at,
And my afflictions jeer'd.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I tell thee Arnoldo,
An thou wert my Father, as thou art but my Brother,
My younger Brother too, I muſt be merry.
And where there is a wench yet can, a young wench,
A handſome wench, and ſooner a good turn too,
An I were to be hang'd, thus muſt I handle it.
But you ſhall ſee Sir, I can change this habit
To do you any ſervice; adviſe what you pleaſe,
And ſee with what Devotion I'le attend it?
But yet me thinks, I am taken with this Cuſtom,
And could pretend to th' place.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Draw off a little;
Here comes my Miſtreſs and her Father.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: A dainty wench!
Wou'd I might farm his Cuſtom.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: My dear Daughter,
Now to bethink your ſelf of new advice
Will be too late, late, this timeleſs ſorrow,
No price, not prayers, can infringe the fate

Your beauty hath 〈…〉
• ou, my beſt Zenocia,
Be rul'd by me, a Fa •••• care directs ye,
Look on the Count, look chearfully and ſweetly;
What though he have th • power to poſſeſs ye,

〈◊〉 pluck your Mai ••
• onour, and then ſlight ye
〈…〉 unreſiſtible to enjoy you;

〈◊〉
••• et Child, ſo much your youth and goodneſs,

〈◊〉
•• auty of your ſoul, and Saint-like Modeſty,
Have won upon his mild mind, ſo much charm'd him,
That all power laid aſide, what Law allows him,
Or ſudden fires, kindled from thoſe bright eyes,
He ſues to be your ſervant, fairly, nobly
For ever to be tyed your faithful Husband:
Conſider my beſt child.

sp.speaker: Zeno.
sp.l: I have conſidered.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: The bleſſedneſs that this breeds too, conſider
Beſides your Fathers Honour, your own peace,
The baniſhment for ever of this Cuſtom,
This baſe and barbarous uſe, for after once
He has ſound the happineſs of holy Marriage,
And what it is to grow up with one Beauty,
How he will ſcorn and kick at ſuch an heritage
Left him by luſt and lewd progenitors.
All Virgins too, ſhall bleſs your name, ſhall Saint it,
And like ſo many Pilgrims go to your ſhrine,
When time has turn'd your beauty into aſhes,
Fill d with your pious memory.

sp.speaker: Zeno.
sp.l: Good Father
Hide not that better Pill I loath to ſwallow
In ſuch ſweet words.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: The Count's a handſome Gentleman,
And having him, y'are certain of a fortune,
A high and noble fortune to attend you:
Where if you fling your Love upon this ſtranger
This young Arnoldo, not knowing from what place
Or honourable ſtrain of blood he is ſprung, you venture
All your own ſweets, and my long cares to nothing,
Nor are you certain of his ſaith; why may not that
Wander as he does, every where?

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: No more Sir;
I muſt not hear, I dare not hear him wrong'd thus,
Vertue is never wounded, but I ſuffer.
'Tis an ill Office in your age, a poor one,
To judge thus weakly: and believe your ſelf too,
A weaker, to betray your innocent Daughter,
To his intemp'rate, rude, and wild embraces,
She hates as Heaven hates falſhood.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: A good wench,
She ſticks cloſe to you Sir,

sp.speaker: Zeno.
sp.l: His faith uncertain?
The nobleneſs his vertue ſprings from, doubted?
D'ye doubt it is day now? or when your body's perfect,
Your ſtomach's well diſpos'd, your pulſe's temperate,
D'ye doubt you are in health? I tell you Father,
One hour of this mans goodneſs, this mans Nobleneſs
Put in the Scale, againſt the Counts whole being,
Forgive his luſts too, which are half his life,
He could no more endure to hold weight with him;
Arnoldo's very looks, are fair examples;
His common and indifferent actions,
Rules and ſtrong ties of vertue: he has my firſt love,
To him in ſacred vow I have given this body,
In him my mind inhabits.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Good wench ſtill.

sp.speaker: Zeno.
sp.l: And till he ſting me off, as undeſerving,
Which I confeſs I am, of ſuch a bleſſing,
But would be loth to find it ſo—

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: O never;
Never my happy Miſtreſs, never, never,
When your poor ſervant lives but in your favour,
One foot i'th' grave the other ſhall not linger.
What ſacrifice of thanks, what age of ſervice,
What danger, of more dreadful look than death,
What willing Martyrdom to crown me conſtant
May merit ſuch a goodneſs, ſuch a ſweetneſs?
A love ſo Nobly great, no power can ruine;
Moſt bleſſed Maid go on, the Gods that gave this,
This pure unſpotted love, the Child of Heaven,
In their own goodneſs, muſt preſerve and ſave it,
And raiſe you a reward beyond our recompence.

sp.speaker: Zeno.
sp.l: I ask but you, a pure Maid to poſſeſs,
And then they have crown'd my wiſhes: If I fall then
Go ſeek ſome better love, mine will debaſe you.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: A pretty innocent fool; well, Governour,
Though I think well of your cuſtom, and could wiſh my ſelf
For this night in your place, heartily wiſh it:
Yet if you play not fair play and above board too,
I have a fooliſh gin here, I ſay no more;
I'le tell you what, and if your honours guts are not inchanted.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I ſhould now chide you Sir, for ſo declining
The goodneſs and the grace you have ever ſhew'd me;
And your own vertue too, in ſeeking raſhly
To violate that love Heaven has appointed,
To wreſt your Daughters thoughts, part that affection
That both our hearts have tyed, and ſeek to give it

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: To a wild fellow, that would weary her;
A Cannibal, that feeds on the heads of Maids,
Then flings their bones and bodies to the Devil,
Would any man of diſcretion venture ſuch a griſtle,
To the rude clawes of ſuch a Cat-a-mountain?
You had better tear her between two Oaks, a Town Bull
Is a meer Stoick to this fellow, a grave Philoſopher,
And a Spaniſh Jennet, a moſt vertuous Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Does this ſeem handſome Sir?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Though I confeſs
Any man would deſire to have her, and by any means,
At any rate too, yet that this common Hangman,
That hath whipt off the heads of a thouſand maids already,
That he ſhould glean the Harveſt, ſticks in my ſtomach:
This Rogue breaks young wenches to the Saddle,
And teaches them to ſtumble ever after;
That he ſhould have her? for my Brother now
That is a handſome young fellow; and well thought on,
And will deal tenderly in the buſineſs;
Or for my ſelf that have a reputation,
And have ſtudied the concluſions of theſe cauſes,
And know the perfect manage, I'le tell you old Sir,
If I ſhould call you wiſe Sir, I ſhould bely you,
This thing, you ſtudy to betray your child to,
This Maiden-monger. When you have done your beſt,
And think you have fixt her in the point of honour,
Who do you think you have tyed her to? a Surgeon,
I muſt confeſs an excellent diſſector,
One that has cut up more young tender Lamb-pies—

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: What I ſpake Gentlemen, was meer compulſion,
No Fathers free-will, nor did I touch your perſon
With any edge of ſpight; or ſtrain your loves
With any baſe, or hir'd perſwaſions;
Witneſs theſe tears, how well I wiſht your fortunes. Exit.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: There's ſome grace in thee yet, you are determined
To marry this Count, Lady.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Marry him Rutilio?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Marry him, and lye with him I mean.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: You cannot mean that,
If you be a true Gentleman, you dare not,
The Brother to this man, and one that loves him;
I'le marry the Devil firſt.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: A better choice
And lay his horns by, a handſomer bed-fellow,
A cooler o' my conſcience.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Pray let me ask you;
And my dear Miſtris, be not angry with me
For what I ſhall propound, I am confident,
No promiſe, nor no power, can force your love,
I mean in way of marriage, never ſtir you,
Nor to forget my faith, no ſtate can wound you.
But for this Cuſtom, which this wretched country
Hath wrought into a law, and muſt be ſatisfied;
Where all the pleas of honour are but laught at,
And modeſty regarded as a may-game,
What ſhall be here conſidered? power we have none,
To make reſiſtance, nor policie to croſs it:
'Tis held Religion too, to pay this duty.

sp.speaker: Zeno.
sp.l: I'le dye an Atheiſt then.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: My nobleſt Miſtris,
Not that I wiſh it ſo, but ſay it were ſo,
Say you did render up part of your honour,
For whilſt your will is clear, all cannot periſh;
Say for one night you entertain'd this monſter,
Should I eſteem you worſe, forc'd to this render?
Your mind I know is pure, and full as beauteous;
After this ſhort eclipſe, you would riſe again,
And ſhaking off that cloud, ſpread all your luſtre.

sp.speaker: Zeno.
sp.l: Who made you witty, to undoe your ſelf, Sir?
Or are you loaden, with the love I bring you,
And fain would fling that burthen on another?
Am I grown common in your eyes Arnoldo?
Old, or unworthy of your fellowſhip?
D'ye think becauſe a woman, I muſt err,
And therefore rather wiſh that fall before-hand
Coloured with Cuſtom, not to be reſiſted?
D'ye love as painters doe, only ſome pieces,
Some certain handſome touches of your Miſtris,
And let the mind paſs by you, unexamined?
Be not abus'd; with what the maiden veſſel
Is ſeaſoned firſt, you underſtand the proverb.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I am afraid, this thing will make me vertuous.

sp.speaker: Zeno.
sp.l: Should you lay by the leaſt part of that love
Y'ave ſworn is mine, your youth and faith has given me,
To entertain another, nay a fairer,
And make the caſe thus deſp'rate, ſhe muſt dy elſe;
D'ye think I would give way, or count this honeſt?
Be not deceiv'd, theſe eyes ſhould never ſee you more,
This tongue forget to name you, and this heart
Hate you, as if you were born, my full Antipathie.
Empire and more imperious love, alone
Rule, and admit no rivals: the pureſt ſprings
When they are courted by laſcivious land-floods,
Their maiden pureneſs, and their coolneſs periſh.
And though they purge again to their firſt beauty,
The ſweetneſs of their taſte is clean departed.
I muſt have all or none; and am not worthy
Longer the noble name of wife, Arnoldo,
Than I can bring a whole heart pure and handſom.

sp.speaker: Arnol.
sp.l: I never ſhall deſerve you: not to thank you;
You are ſo heavenly good, no man can reach you:
I am ſorrie I ſpake ſo raſhly, 't was but to try you.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: You might have tryed a thouſand women ſo,
And 900, fourſcore and 19 ſhould ha' followed your counſel.
Take heed o' clapping ſpurts to ſuch free cattell.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: We muſt bethink us ſuddenly and conſtantly,
And wiſely too, we expect no common danger.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Be moſt aſſur'd, I'le dye firſt.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: An't come to that once,
The Devil pick his bones, that dyes a coward,
I'le jog along with you, here comes the Stallion,
How ſmug he looks upon the imagination
Of what he hopes to act? pox on your kidneys;
How they begin to melt? how big he bears,
Sure he will leap before us all: what a ſweet company
Of rogues and panders wait upon his lewdneſs?
Plague of your chops, you ha' more handſome bitts,
Than a hundred honeſter men, and more deſerving.
How the dogg leers.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: You need not now be jealous,
I ſpeak at diſtance to your wiſe, but when the Prieſt has done,
We ſhall grow nearer, and more familiar.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I'le watch you for that trick, baboon, I'le
Smoke you: the rogue ſweats, as if he had eaten
Grains, he broyles, if I do come to the
Baſting of you.

sp.speaker: Arno.
sp.l: Your Lordſhip
May happily ſpeak this, to fright a ſtranger,
But 'tis not in your honour, to perform it;
The Cuſtom of this place, if ſuch there be,
At beſt moſt damnable, may urge you to it,
But if you be an honeſt man you hate it,
How ever I will preſently prepare
To make her mine, and moſt undoubtedly
Believe you are abus'd, this cuſtome feign'd too,
And what you now pretend, moſt fair and vertuous.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Go and believe, a good belief does well Sir;
And you Sir, clear the place, but leave her here.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Your Lordſhips pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: That anon Arnoldo,
This is but talk.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Shall we goe off?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: By any means,
I know ſhe has pious thoughts enough to guard her:
Beſides, here's nothing due to him till the tye be done,
Nor dare he offer.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Now do I long to worry him:

Pray have a care to the main chance.
Exit. Ar. and Rut.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Pray Sir, fear not

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Now, what ſay you to me?

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Sir it becomes
The modeſtie, that maids are ever born with,
To uſe few words.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Do you ſee nothing in me?
Nothing to catch your eyes, nothing of wonder
The common mould of men, come ſhort, and want in?
Do you read no future fortune for your ſelf here?
And what a happineſs it may be to you,
To have him honour you, all women aim at?
To have him love you Lady, that man love you,
The beſt, and the moſt beauteous have run mad for?
Loo • and be w • ſe, you have a favour offer'd you
〈◊〉 not every day propound to women;
You are a prettie one; and though each hour
I am glutted with the ſacrifice of beautie,
I may be brought, as you may handle it,
To call ſo good a grace and liking on you.
You underſtand, come kiſs me, and be joyfull,
I give you leave.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Faith Sir, 'twill not ſhew handſome;
Our •• x is bluſhing, full of fear, unskil'd too
In theſe alarms.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Learn then and be perfect.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: I do beſeech your honour pardon me,
And take ſome skilfull one can hold you play,
I am a fool.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: I tell thee maid I love thee,
〈◊〉 that word make thee happie, ſo far love thee,
That though I may enjoy thee without ceremony,
I will deſcend ſo low, to marry thee,
Me thinks I ſee the race that ſhall ſpring from us,
Some Princes, ſome great Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: I am afraid
Your honour's couzen'd in this calculation;
For certain, I ſhall ne're have a child by you.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Becauſe I muſt not think to marry you,
I dare not Sir, the ſtep betwixt your honour,
And my poor humble State.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: I will deſcend to thee,
And buo • thee up.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: I'le ſink to th'Center firſt.
Why would your Lordſhip marry, and confine that pleaſure
You ever have had freely caſt upon you?
Take heed my Lord, this marrying is a mad matter,
Lighter a pair of ſhackles will hang on you,
And quiet • r a qua • tane • eaver find you.
If you wed me I muſt enjoy you only,
Your eyes muſt be called home, your thoughts in cages,
To •• ng to no ears then but mine; your heart bound,
The cuſtom, that your youth was ever nurſt in,
Muſt be forgot, I ſhall forget my duty elſe,
And how that will appear

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Wee'l talk of that more.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Beſides I tell ye, I am naturally,
As all young women are, that ſhew like handſome,
Exceeding proud, being commended, monſtrous.
Of an unquiet temper, ſeldom pleas'd,
Unleſs it be with infinite obſervance,
Which you were never bred to; once well angred,
As every croſs in us, provokes that paſſion,
And like a Sea, I • oule, toſs, and chaſe a week after.
And then all miſchief I can think upon,
Abuſing of your bed the leaſt and pooreſt,
I tell you what you're finde, and in theſe fitts,
This little beauty you are pleaſed to honour,
Will be ſo chang'd, ſo alter'd to an uglineſs,
To ſuch a vizard, 〈◊〉 one, I dye too,
Take 't then upon my death you murder'd me.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Away, away fool, why doſt thou proclame theſe
To prevent that in me, thou haſt choſen in another?

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Him I have choſen, I can rule and maſter,
Temp r to what I pleaſe, you me a great one
Of ••• ong will to 〈◊〉 , I • are not venture.
B • wife my ••• d, and ſay you were well counſel'd,
〈…〉 , and forget me,
'Twill b • both 〈◊〉 and noble for your honour,
And 〈…〉 fortunes ſhall conduct me,

So 〈◊〉
•••• ions I ſhall render of you,
So vert •• us and ſo 〈◊〉 .

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: You will not marrie me?

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: I do beſeech your honour, be not angry
At what I ſay, I cannot love ye, dare not;
But ſet a ranſom, for the flowr you covet.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: No mony, nor no prayers, ſhall redeem that,
Not all the art you have.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Set your own price Sir.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Goe to your wedding, never kneel to me,
When that's done, you are mine, I will enjoy you:
Your tears do nothing, I will not loſe my cuſtom

To caſt upon my ſelf an Empires fortune.
Ex •

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: My mind ſhall not pay this cuſtom, cruel man.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l:
Your body will content me: I'le look for you.
E •

div.stage: Enter Charino, and ſervants in blacks. Covering the place with blacks.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Strew all your withered flowers, your Autum • ſweets
By the hot Sun raviſht of bud and beauty
Thus round about her Bride-bed, hang thoſe blacks there
The emblemes of her honour loſt; all joy
That leads a Virgin to receive her lover,
Keep from this place, all fellow maids that bleſs her,
And bluſhing do unlooſe her Zone, keep from her:
No merry noiſe nor luſty ſongs be heard here,
Nor full cups crown'd with wine make the rooms giddy;
This is no maſque of mirth, but murdered honour.
Sing mournfully that ſad Epithalamion
I gave thee now: and prethee let thy lute weep.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: How now, what livery's this? do you call this a wedding?
This is more like a funeral.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: It is one,
And my poor Daughter going to her grave,
To his moſt loath'd embraces that gapes for her.
Make the Earles bed readie, is the marriage done Sir?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Yes they are knit; but muſt this ſlubberdegullion
Have her maiden-head now?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: There's no avoiding it?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: And there's the ſcaffold where ſhe muſt loſe it.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: The bed Sir.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: No way to wipe his mouldy chaps?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: That we know.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: To any honeſt well-deſerving fellow,
And 'twere but to a merry Cobler, I could ſit ſtill now,
I love the game ſo well; but that this puckſiſt,
This univerſal rutter—fare ye well Sir;
And if you have any good prayers, put'em forward,
There may be yet a remedie.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l:
I wiſh it,
Exit Rut.
And all my beſt devotions offer to it.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Now is this tye diſpatch'd?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: I think it be Sir.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l:
And my bed ready?
wi ••

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: There you may quickly find Sir,
Such a loath'd preparation.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Never grumble,
Nor fling a diſcontent upon my pleaſure,
It muſt and ſhall be done: give me ſome wine,
And fill it till it leap upon my lips:
Here's to the fooliſh maidenhead you wot of,
The toy I muſt take pains for.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: I beſeech your Lordſhip
Load not a Fathers love.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Pledge it Charino,
Or by my life I'le make thee pledge thy laſt,
And be ſure ſhe be a maid, a perfect Virgin,
(I will not have my expectation dull'd)
Or your old pate goes off. I am hot and fiery,
And my bloud beats alarms through my body,
And fancie high. You of my guard retire,
And let me hear no noiſe about the lodging
But muſick and ſweet ayres, now fetch your Daughter,
And bid the coy wench put on all her beauties,
All her enticements, out-bluſh damask Roſes,
And dim the breaking Eaſt with her bright Cryſtals.
I am all on fire, away.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: And I am frozen. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Zenocia with Bow and Quiver, an Arrow bent, Arnoldo and Rutilio after her, arm'd.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Come fearleſs on.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Nay an I budge from thee
Beat me with durty ſticks.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: What Maſque is this?
What pretty fancy to provoke me high?
The beauteous Huntreſs, fairer far, and ſweeter;
Diana ſhewes an Ethiop to this beauty
Protected by two Virgin Knights.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: That's a lye,
A loud one, if you knew as much as I do,
The Guard's diſpers'd.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Fortune I hope invites us.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: I can no longer hold, ſhe pulls my heart from me.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Stand, and ſtand fixt, move not a foot, nor ſpeak not,
For if thou doeſt, upon this point thy death fits.
Thou miſerable, baſe, and ſordid lecher,
Thou ſcum of noble blood, repent and ſpeedily,
Repent thy thouſand thefts, from helpleſs Virgins,
Their innocence betrayed to thy embraces.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: The baſe diſhonour, that thou doeſt to ſtrangers,
In glorying to abuſe the Laws of Marriage,
Thy Infamy thou haſt flung upon thy Country,
In nouriſhing this black and barbarous Cuſtom.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: My Guard.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: One word more, and thou dieſt.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: One ſyllable
That tends to any thing, but I beſeech you,
And as y'are Gentlemen tender my caſe,
And I'le thruſt my Javeling down thy throat.
Thou Dog-whelp, thou, pox upon thee, what
Should I call thee, Pompion,
Thou kiſs my Lady? thou ſcour her Chamber-pot:
Thou have a Maiden-head? a mottly Coat,
You great blind fool, farewel and be hang'd to ye,
Loſe no time Lady.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Pray take your pleaſure Sir,
And ſo we'l take our leaves.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: We are determined,
Dye, before yield.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Honour, and a fair grave.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Before a luſtful Bed, ſo for our fortunes.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Du cat awhee, good Count, cry, prethee cry,
O what a wench haſt thou loſt? cry you great booby. Exe.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: And is ſhe gone then, am I diſhonoured thus,
Cozened and baffl'd? my Guard there, no man anſwer?
My Guard I ſay, ſirrah you knew of this plot;
Where are my Guard? I'le have your life you villain,
You politick old Thief.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Heaven ſend her far enough,
And let me pay the ranſom.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Did your honour call us?

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Poſt every way, and preſently recover
The two ſtrange Gentlemen, and the fair Lady.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: This day was Married Sir?

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: The ſame.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: We ſaw 'em
Making with all main ſpeed to th'Port.

sp.speaker: Cod.
sp.l: Away villains. Exit Guard.
Recover her, or I ſhall dye; deal truly,
Didſt not thou know?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: By all that's good I did not.
If your honour mean their ſlight, to ſay I grieve for that,
Will be to lye; you may handle me as you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Be ſure, with all the cruelty, with all the rigor,
For thou haſt rob'd me villain of a treaſure.
How now?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: They're all aboard, a Bark rode ready for 'em,
And now are under Sail, and paſt recovery.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Rig me a Ship with all the ſpeed that may be,
I will not loſe her: thou her moſt falſe Father,
Shalt go along; and if I miſs her, hear me,
A whole day will I ſtudy to deſtroy thee.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: I ſhall be joyful of it; and ſo you'l find me.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Manuel du ſoſa, and Guiomar.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: I Hear and ſee too much of him, and that
Compels me Madam, though unwillingly,
To wiſh I had no Uncles part in him,
And much I fear, the comfort of a Son
You will not long enjoy.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: 'Tis not my fault,
And therefore from his guilt my innocence
Cannot be tainted, ſince his Fathers death,
(Peace to his ſoul) a Mothers prayers and care
Were never wanting, in his education.
His Child-hood I paſs o're, as being brought up
Under my wing; and growing ripe for ſtudy,
I overcame the tenderneſs, and joy
I had to look upon him, and provided
The choiceſt Maſters, and of greateſt name
Of Salamanca, in all liberal Arts.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: To train his youth up.
I muſt witneſs that.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: How there he proſpered to the admiration
Of all that knew him, for a general Scholar,
Being one of note, before he was a man,
Is ſtill remembred in that Academy,
From thence I ſent him to the Emperours Court,
Attended like his Fathers Son, and there
Maintain'd him, in ſuch bravery and height,
As did become a Courtier.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: 'Twas that ſpoil'd him, my Nephew had been happy.
The Court's a School indeed, in which ſome few
Learn vertuous principles, but moſt forget
What ever they brought thither good and honeſt.
Trifling is there in practice, ſerious actions
Are obſolete and out of uſe, my Nephew
Had been a happy man, had he ne're known
What's there in grace and faſhion.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: I have heard yet,
That while he liv'd in Court, the Emperour
Took notice of his carriage and good parts,
The Grandees did not ſcorn his company,
And of the greateſt Ladies he was held
A compleat Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: He indeed Daunc'd well;
A turn o'th'Toe, with a lofty trick or two,
To argue nimbleneſs, and a ſtrong back,
Will go far with a Madam: 'tis moſt true,
That he's an excellent Scholar, and he knows it;
An exact Courtier, and he knows that too;
He has fought thrice, and come off ſtill with honour,
Which he forgets not.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: Nor have I much reaſon,
To grieve his fortune that way.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: You are miſtaken,
Proſperity does ſearch a Gentlemans temper,
More than his adverſe fortune: I have known
Many, and of rare parts from their ſucceſs
In private Duels, rais'd up to ſuch a pride,
And ſo transform'd from what they were, that all
That lov'd them truly, wiſh'd they had fallen in them.
I need not write examples, in your Son
'Tis too apparent; for e're Don Duarte
Made tryal of his valour, he indeed was
Admired for civil courteſie, but now
He's ſwoln ſo high, out of his own aſſurance,
Of what he dares do, that he ſeeks occaſions,
Unjuſt occaſions, grounded on blind paſſion,
Ever to be in quarrels, and this makes him
Shunn'd of all fair Societies.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: Would it were
In my weak power to help it: I will uſe
With my entreaties th' Authority of a Mother,
As you may of an Uncle, and enlarge it
With your command, as being a Governour
To the great King in Lasbon.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Here he comes.
We are unſeen, obſerve him.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Boy.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: What ſaith the Spaniſh Captain that I ſtruck,
To my bold challenge?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: He refus'd to read it.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Why didſt not leave it there?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: I did my Lord,
But to no purpoſe, for he ſeems more willing
To ſit down with the wrongs, than to repair
His honour by the ſword; he knows too well,
That from your Lordſhip nothing can be got
But more blows, and diſgraces.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: He's a wretch,
A miſerable wretch, and all my fury
Is loſt upon him; holds the Mask, appointed
I'th' honour of Hippolyta?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: 'Tis broke off.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: The reaſon?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: This was one, they heard your Lordſhip
Was by the Ladies choice to lead the Dance,
And therefore they, too well aſſur'd how far
You would out ſhine 'em, gave it o're and ſaid,
They would not ſerve for foiles to ſet you off.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: They at their beſt are ſuch, and ever ſhall be
Where I appear.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Do you note his modeſty?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: But was there nothing elſe pretended?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Yes,
Young Don Alonzo, the great Captains Nephew,
Stood on compariſons.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: With whom?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: With you,
And openly profeſs'd that all precedence,
His birth and ſtate conſider'd, was due to him,
Not were your Lordſhip to contend with one
So far above you.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I look down upon him
With ſuch contempt and ſcorn, as on my ſlave,
He's a name only, and all good in him
He muſt derive from his great grandſires Aſhes,
For had not their victorious acts bequeath'd
His titles to him, and wrote on his forehead,
This is a Lord, he had liv'd unobſerv'd
By any man of mark, and died as one
Amongſt the common route. Compare with me?
'Tis Gyant-like ambition, I know him,
And know my ſelf, that man is truly noble,
And he may juſtly call that worth his own,
Which his deſerts have purchas'd, I could wiſh
My hath were more obſerue, my friends and kinſmen
Of leſſer power, or that my provident Father
Had been like to that riotous Emperour
That choſe his belly for his only heir;
For being of no family then, and poor
My vertues whereſoe'r I liv'd, ſhould make
That kingdom my inheritance.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: Strange ſelf Love!

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: For if I ſtudied the Countries Laws,
I ſhould ſo eaſily ſound all their depth,
And riſe up ſuch a wonder, that the pleaders,
That now are in moſt practice and eſteem,
Should ſtarve for want of Clients: if I travell'd,
Like wiſe Ʋlyſſes to ſee men and manners,
I would return in act, more knowing, than
Homer could fancy him; if a Phyſician,
So oft I would reſtore death-wounded men,
That where I liv'd, Galen ſhould not be nam'd,
And he that joyn'd again the ſcatter'd limbs
Of torn Hippolytus ſhould be forgotten.
I could teach Ovid courtſhip, how to win
A Julia, and enjoy her, though her Dower
Were all the Sun gives light to: and for arms
Were the Perſian hoſt that drank up Rivers, added
To the Turks preſent powers, I could direct,
Command, and Marſhal them.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: And yet you know not
To rule your ſelf, you would not to a boy elſe
Like Plautus Braggart boaſt thus.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: All I ſpeak,
In act I can make good.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: Why then being Maſter
Of ſuch and ſo good parts do you deſtroy them,
With ſelf opinion, or like a rich miſer,
Hoard up the treaſures you poſſeſs, imparting
Nor to your ſelf nor others, the uſe of them?
They are to you but like inchanted viands,
On which you ſeem to feed, yet pine with hunger;
And thoſe ſo rare perfections in my Son
Which would make others happy, render me
A wretched Mother.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: You are too inſolent.
And thoſe too many excellencies, that feed
