Your pride, turn to a Pleuriſie, and kill
That which ſhould nouriſh vertue; dare you think
All bleſſings are confer'd on you alone?
Y'are groſly couſen'd; there's no good in you,
Which others have not: are you a Scholar? ſo
Are many, • nd as knowing: are you valiant?
Waſte not that courage then in braules, but ſpend it
In the Wars, in ſervice of your King and Country.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Yes, ſo I might be General, no man lives
That's worthy to command me.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Sir, in Lisbon
I am: and you ſhall know it; every hour
I am troubled with complaints of your behaviour
From men of all conditions, and all ſexes.
And my authority, which you preſume
Will bear you out, in that you are my Nephew,
No longer ſhall protect you, for I vow
Though all that's paſt I pardon, I will puniſh
The next fault with as much ſeverity
As if you were a ſtranger, reſt aſſur'd on't.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: And by that love you ſhould bear, or that duty
You owe a Mother, once more I command you
To caſt this haughtineſs off; which if you do,
All that is mine, is yours, if not, expect
My prayers, and vows, for your converſion only,

But never means nor favour.
Ex. Manuel and Guiomar.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I am Tutor'd
As if I were a child ſtill, the baſe Peaſants
That fear, and envy my great worth, have done this;
But I will find them out, I will o' boord
Get my diſguiſe; I have too long been idle,
Nor will I curb my ſpirit, I was born free,
• d will purſue the courſe beſt liketh me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: Divide the ſpoil amongſt you, this fair Captive
• nly challenge for my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: You have won her
• nd well deſerve her: twenty years I have liv'd
〈◊〉 Burgeſs of the Sea, and have been preſent
〈◊〉 many a deſperate fight, but never ſaw
〈◊〉 ſmall a Bark with ſuch incredible valour
〈◊〉 long defended, and againſt ſuch odds,
• nd by two men ſcarce arm'd too.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: 'Twas a wonder.
• nd yet the courage they expreſt being taken,
• nd their contempt of death wan more upon me
• han all they did, when they were free: me thinks
〈◊〉 ſee them yet when they were brought aboard us,
• iſarm'd and ready to be put in ſetters
• ow on the ſuddain, as if they had ſworn
• ever to taſte the bread of ſervitude,
• oth ſnatching up their ſwords, and from this Virgin,
Taking a farewel only with their eyes,
They leapt into the Sea.

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: Indeed 'twas rare.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: It wrought ſo much on me, that but I fear'd
The great ſhip that purſued us, our own ſafety
Hindring my charitable purpoſe to 'em,
〈◊〉 would have took 'em up, and with their lives
They ſhould have had their liberties.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: O too late,
For they are loſt, for ever loſt.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: Take comfort
'Tis not impoſſible, but that they live yet,
For when they left the ſhips, they were within
A League o'th' ſhore, and with ſuch ſtrength and cunning
They ſwimming, did delude the riſing Billows,
With one hand making way, and with the other,
Their bloudy ſwords advanced, threatning the Sea-gods
With war, unleſs they brought them ſafely off,
That I am almoſt confident they live,
And you again may ſee them.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: In that hope
I brook a wretched being, till I am
Made certain of their fortunes; but they dead,
Death hath ſo many doors to let out life,
I will not long ſurvive them.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: Hope the beſt,
And let the courteous uſage you have found,
Not uſual in men of War perſwade you
To tell me your condition.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: You know it,
A Captive, my fate and your power have made me,
Such I am now, but what I was it skills not:
For they being dead, in whom I only live,
I dare not challenge Family, or Country,
And therefore Sir enquire not, let it ſuffice,
I am your ſervant, and a thankful ſervant
(If you will call that ſo, which is but duty)
I ever will be, and my honour ſafe,
Which nobly hitherto ye have preſerv'd,
No ſlavery can appear in ſuch a form,
Which with a maſculine conſtancy I will not
Boldly look on and ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: You miſtake me:
That you are made my priſoner, may prove
The birth of your good fortune. I do find
A winning language in your tongue and looks;
Nor can a ſuit by you mov'd be deni'd,
And therefore of a priſoner you muſt be
The Victors advocate.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: To whom?

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: A Lady:
In whom all graces that can perfect beauty
Are friendly met. I grant that you are fair:
And had I not ſeen her before, perhaps
I might have ſought to you.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: This I hear gladly.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: To this incomparable Lady I will give you,
(Yet being mine, you are already hers)
And to ſerve her is more than to be free,
At leaſt I think ſo; and when you live with her,
If you will pleaſe to think on him that brought you
To ſuch a happineſs, for ſo her bounty
Will make you think her ſervice, you ſhall ever
Make me at your devotion.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: All I can do,
Reſt you aſſur'd of.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: At night I'le preſent you,
Till when I am your Guard.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Ever your ſervant. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: To what are we reſerv'd?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Troth 'tis uncertain,
Drowning we have ſcap'd miraculouſly, and
Stand fair for ought I know for hanging; mony
We have none, nor e're are like to have,
'Tis to be doubted: beſides we are ſtrangers,
Wondrous hungry ſtrangers; and charity
Growing cold, and miracles ceaſing,
Without a Conjurers help, cannot find
When we ſhall eat again.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Theſe are no wants
If put in ballance with Zenocias loſs;
In that alone all miſeries are ſpoken:
O my Rutilio, when I think on her,
And that which ſhe may ſuffer, being a Captive,
Then I could curſe my ſelf, almoſt thoſe powers
That ſend me from the fury of the Ocean.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: You have loſt a wiſe indeed, a fair and chaſt one,
Two bleſſings, not found often in one woman;
But ſhe may be recovered, queſtionleſs
The ſhip that took us was of Portugal,
And here in Lisbon, by ſome means or other
We may hear of her.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: In that hope I live.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: And ſo do I, but hope is a poor Sallad
To dine and ſup with, after a two dayes faſt too,
Have you no mony left?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Not a Denier.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Nor any thing to pawn? 'tis now in faſhion,
Having a Miſtreſs, ſure you ſhould not be
Without a neat Hiſtorical ſhirt.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: For ſhame
Talk not ſo poorly.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I muſt talk of that
Neceſſity prompts us to, for beg I cannot,
Nor am I made to creep in at a window,
To filch to feed me, ſomething muſt be done,
And ſuddenly reſolve on't.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: What are theſe?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: One by his habit is a Jew.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: No more:
Thou art ſure that's he.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Moſt certain.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: How long is it
Since firſt ſhe ſaw him?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l:
Some two hours.
Exit Ser.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Be gone— let me alone to work him.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: How he eyes you!
Now he moves towards us, in the Devils name
What would he with us?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Innocence is bold:
Nor can I fear.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: That you are poor and ſtrangers,
I eaſily perceive.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: But that you'l help us,
Or any of your tribe, we dare not hope Sir.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Why think you ſo?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Becauſe you are a Jew Sir,
And courteſies come ſooner from the Devil
Than any of your Nation.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: We are men,
And have like you, compaſſion when we find
Fit ſubjects for our bounty, and for proof
That we dare give, and freely, not to you Sir,
Pray ſpare your pains, there's gold, ſtand not amaz'd,
'Tis current I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Take it man,
Sure thy good Angel is a Jew, and comes
In his own ſhape to help thee: I could wiſh now
Mine would appear too like a Turk.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I thank you,
But yet muſt tell you, if this be the Prologue
To any bad act, you would have me practiſe,
I muſt not take it.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: This is but the earneſt
Of what which is to follow, and the bond
Which you muſt ſeal to for't, is your advancement,
Fortune with all that's in her power to give,
Offers her ſelf up to you: entertain her,
And that which Princes have kneel'd for in vain
Preſents it ſelf to you.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: 'Tis above wonder.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: But far beneath the truth, in my relation
Of what you ſhall poſſeſs, if you embace it.
There is an hour in each mans life appointed
To make his happineſs if then he ſeize it,
And this, (in which, beyond all expectation,
You are invited to your good) is yours,
If you dare follow me, ſo, if not, hereafter
Expect not the like offer. Exit.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: 'Tis no viſion.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: 'Tis gold I'm ſure.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: We muſt like brothers ſhare;
There's for you.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: By this light I'm glad I have it:
There are few Gallants, (for men may be ſuch
And yet want gold, yea and ſometimes ſilver)
But would receive ſuch favours from the Devil,
Though he appear'd like a Broker, and demanded
Sixty i'th' hundred.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Wherefore ſhould I fear
Some plot upon my life? 'tis now to me
Not worth the keeping. I will follow him,
Farewel, wiſh me good fortune, we ſhall meet
Again I doubt not.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l:
Or I'le ne're truſt Jew more,
Exit Arnoldo.
Nor Chriſtian for his ſake— plague o' my ſtars,
How long might I have walkt without a Cloak,
Before I ſhould have met with ſuch a fortune?
We elder Brothers, though we are proper men,
Ha' not the luck, ha' too much beard, that ſpoils us;
The ſmooth Chin carries all: what's here to do now?

div.stage: Enter Duarte, Alonzo, and a Page.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I'le take you as I find you.

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: That were baſe — you ſee I am unarm'd.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Out with your Bodkin
Your Pocket-dagger, your Steletto, out with it,
Or by this hand I'le kill you: ſuch as you are
Have ſtudied the undoing of poor Cutlers,
And made all manly weapons out of faſhion:
You carry Poniards to murder men,
Yet dare not wear a ſword to guard your Honour.

sp.speaker: Rut
sp.l: That's true indeed: upon my life this gallant
Is brib'd to repeal baniſht ſwords.

sp.speaker: Dua
sp.l: I'le ſhew you
The difference now between a Spaniſh Rapier
And your pure Piſa.

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: Let me fetch a ſword,
Upon mine honour I'le return.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Not ſo Sir.

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: Or lend me yours I pray you, and take this.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: To be diſgrac'd as you are, no I thank you
Spight of the faſhion, while I live, I am
Inſtructed to go arm'd: what folly 'tis
For you that are a man, to put your ſelf
Into your enemies mercy.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Yield it quickly
Or I'le cut off your hand, and now diſgrace you,
Thus kick and baffle you: as you like this,
You may again prefer complaints againſt me
To my Uncle and my Mother, and then think
To make it good with a Poniard.

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: I am paid
For being of the faſhion.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Get a ſword,
Then if you dare redeem your reputation:
You know I am eaſily found: I'le add this to it
To put you in mind.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: You are too inſolent,
And do inſult too much on the advantage
Of that which your unequal weapon gave you,
More than your valour.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: This to me, you Peaſant?
Thou art not worthy of my foot poor fellow,
'Tis ſcorn, not pity, makes me give thee life:
Kneel down and thank me for't: how, do you ſtare?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I have a ſword Sir, you ſhall find, a good one;
This is no ſtabbing guard.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Wert thou thrice arm'd,
Thus yet I durſt attempt thee.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Then have at you, Fight
I ſcorn to take blows.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l:
O I am ſlain.
Fall • .

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Help! murther, murther!

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: Shift for your ſelf you are dead elſe,
You have kill'd the Governous Nephew.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Raiſe the ſtreets there.

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: If once you are beſet you cannot ſcape,
Will you betray your-ſelf?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l:
Undone for ever.
Exit Rut. and Alonzo.

sp.speaker: 1 Offi.
sp.l: Who makes this out-cry?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: O my Lord is murdered;
This way he took, make after him,

Help help there.
Exit Page.

sp.speaker: 2 Offi.
sp.l: 'Tis Don Duarte.

sp.speaker: 1 Offi.
sp.l: Pride has got a fall,
He was ſtill in quarrels, ſcorn'd us Peace-makers,
And all our Bill-authority, now h'as paid for't.
You ha' met with your match Sir now, bring off his body
And bear it to the Governour. Some purſue
The murderer; yet if he ſcape, it skills not;
Were I a Prince, I would reward him for't,
He has rid the City of a turbulent beaſt,
There's few will pity him: but for his Mother
I truly grieve indeed, ſhe's a good Lady. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: He's not i'th' houſe?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: No Madam.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: Haſte and ſeek him,
Go all and every where, I'le not to bed
Till you return him, take away the lights too,
The Moon lends me too much, to find my fears
And thoſe devotions I am to pay
Are written in my heart, not in this book,

And I ſhall read them there without a Taper.
Ex. Ser. Kneel.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I am purſued; all the Ports are ſtopt too;
Not any hope to eſcape, behind, before me,
On either ſide I am beſet, curſed fortune
My enemie on the Sea, and on the Land too,
Redeem'd from one affliction to another:
Would I had made the greedy waves my tomb
And dyed obſcure, and innocent, not as Nero
Smear'd o're with blood. Whither have my fears brought me?
I am got into a houſe, the doors all open,
This, by the largeneſs of the room, the hangings,
And other rich adornments, gliſtring through
The fable maſque of night, ſayes it belongs
To one of means and rank: no ſervant ſtirring?
Murmur nor whiſper?

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: By the voice,
This is a woman.

sp.speaker: Guio.

l.hi: Stephano, Jaſpe, Julia,

sp.l: Who waits there?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: 'Tis the Lady of the houſe,
I'le flie to her protection.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Speak, what are you?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Of all that ever breath'd, a man moſt wretched.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: I am ſure you are a man of moſt ill manners,
You could not with ſo little reverence elſe
Preſs to my private chamber. Whither would you,
Or what do you ſeek for?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Gracious woman hear me;
I am a ſtranger, and in that I anſwer
All your demands, a moſt unfortunate ſtranger,
That call'd unto it by my enemies pride,
Have left him dead i'th' ſtreets, Juſtice purſues me,
And for that life I took unwillingly,
And in a fair defence, I muſt loſe mine,
Unleſs you in your charity protect me.
Your houſe is now my ſanctuary, and the Altar,
I gladly would take hold of your ſweet mercy.
By all that's dear unto you, by your vertues,
And by your innocence, that needs no forgiveneſs,
Take pity on me.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Are you a Caſtillian?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: No Madam, Italy claims my birth.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: I ask not
With purpoſe to betray you, if you were
Ten thouſand times a Spaniard, the nation
We Portugals moſt hate, I yet would ſave you
If it lay in my power: lift up theſe hangings;
Behind my Beds head there's a hollow place,
Into which enter; ſo, but from this ſtir not
If the Officers come, as you expect they will doe,
I know they owe ſuch reverence to my lodgings,
That they will eaſily give credit to me
And ſearch no further.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: The bleſt Saints pay for me
The infinite debt I owe you.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: How he quakes?
Thus far I feel his heart beat, be of comfort,
Once more I give my promiſe for your ſafety,
All men are ſubject to ſuch accidents,
Eſpecially the valiant; and who knows not,
But that the charity I afford this ſtranger
My only Son elſe-where may ſtand in need of?

div.stage: Enter Officers, and Servants, with the body of Duarte—Page.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: Now Madam, if your wiſedom ever could
Raiſe up defences againſt floods of ſorrow
That haſte to overwhelm you, make true uſe of
Your great diſcretion.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: Your only ſon
My Lord Duart's ſlain.

sp.speaker: 1 Off.
sp.l: His murtherer, purſued by us
Was by a boy diſcovered
Entring your houſe, and that induced us
To preſs into it for his apprehenſion.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Oh?

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: Sure her heart is broke.

sp.speaker: Off.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Stand off.
My ſorrow is ſo dear and pretious to me,
That you muſt not partake it, ſuffer it
Like wounds that do breed inward to diſpatch me.
O my Duart, ſuch an end as this
Thy pride long ſince did propheſie; thou art dead,
And to encreaſe my miſery, thy ſad Mother
Muſt make a wilfull ſhipwrack of her vow
Or thou fall unreveng'd. My Soul's divided,
And piety to a ſon, and true performance
Of hoſpitable duties to my gueſt,
That are to others Angels, are my furies.
Vengeance knocks at my heart, but my word given
Denies the entrance, is no Medium left,
But that I muſt protect the murderer,
Or ſuffer in that faith he made his altar?
Motherly love give place, the fault made this way,
To keep a vow, to which high Heaven is witneſs,
Heaven may be pleas'd to pardon.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: 'Tis too late,
Hee's gone, paſt all recovery: now reproof
Were but unſeaſonable when I ſhould give comfort,
And yet remember Siſter.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: O forbear,
Search for the murtherer, and remove the body,
And as you think ſit, give it burial.
Wretch that I am, uncapable of all comfort,
And therefore I intreat my friends and kinsfolk,
And you my Lord, for ſome ſpace to forbear
Your courteous viſitations.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: We obey you. Exeunt omnes with the body.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: My Spirits come back, and now deſpair reſigns Manet Guiomar.
Her place again to hope.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: What ere thou art
To whom I have given means of life, to witneſs
With what Religion I have kept my promiſe,
Come fearleſs forth, but let thy face be cover'd,
That I hereafter be not forc't to know thee,
For motherly affection may return
My vow once paid to heaven. Thou haſt taken from me
The reſpiration of my heart, the light
Of my ſwoln eyes, in his life that ſuſtain'd me:
Yet my word given to ſave you, I make good,
Becauſe what you did, was not done with malice,
You are not known, there is no mark about you
That can diſcover you; let not fear betray you.
With all convenient ſpeed you can, flie from me
That I may never ſee you; and that want
Of means may be no let unto your journie,
There are a hundred Crownes: you are at the door now,
And ſo Farewell for ever.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Let me firſt fall
Before your feet, and on them pay the duty
I owe your goodneſs; next all bleſſings to you,
And Heaven reſtore the joyes I have bereft you,
With full increaſe hereafter, living be
The Goddeſs ſtil'd of Hoſpitalitie.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: FLing off theſe ſullen clouds, you are enter'd now
Into a houſe of joy and happineſs,
I have prepar'd a bleſſing for ye.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Thank ye, my ſtate would rather ask a curſe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You are peeviſh
And know not when ye are friended, I have us'd thoſe means,
The Lady of this houſe, the noble Lady,
Will take ye as her own, and uſe ye graciouſly:
Make much of what you are, Miſtris of that beautie,
And expoſe it not to ſuch betraying ſorrows,
When ye are old, and all thoſe ſweets hang wither'd,
Then ſit and ſigh.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: My Autumn is not far off.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Have you told your Lady?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I have told her
Both of your noble ſervice, and your preſent,
Which ſhe accepts.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I ſhould be bleſt to ſee her.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: That now you cannot doe: ſhe keeps the Chamber
Not well diſpos'd; and has denied all viſits,
The maid I have in charge to receive from ye,
So pleaſe you render her.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: With all my ſervice,
But • am I would have ſeen.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis but your patience;
No doubt ſhe cannot but remember nobly.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Theſe three years I have lov'd this ſcornfull Lady,
And follow'd her with all the truth of ſervice,
In all which time, but twice ſhe has honour'd me
With ſight of her bleſt beauty: when you pleaſe Sir,
You may receive your charge, and tell your Lady;
A Gentleman whoſe life is only dedicated
To her commands, kiſſes her beauteous hands;
And Faire one, now your help, you may remember
The honeſt courteſies, ſince you are mine,
I ever did your modeſtie: you ſhall be near her,
And if ſometimes you name my ſervice to her,
And tell her with what nobleneſs I love her,
'Twill be a gratitude I ſhall remember.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: What in my poor power lyes, ſo it be honeſt.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I ask no more.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You muſt along with me (Fair.)

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And ſo I leave you two: but a fortune
Too happy for my fate: you ſhall enjoy her.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Be quick, be quick, out with the banquet there,
Theſe ſcents are dull; caſt richer on, and fuller;
Scent every place, where have you plac'd the muſick?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Here they ſtand ready Sir.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: 'Tis well, be ſure
The wines be luſty, high, and full of Spirit,
And Amber'd all.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: They are.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Give fair attendance.
In the beſt trim, and ſtate, make ready all. Banquet ſet forth. Exit.
I ſhall come preſently again.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: We ſhall Si • ,
What preparation's this?
Some new device
My Lady has in hand.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: O, proſper it
As long as it carries good wine in the mouth,
And good meat with it, where are all the reſt?

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: They are ready to attend. Muſick

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: Sure ſome great p •• ſon,
They would not make this hu •• y elſe.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: Hark the Muſick.
It will appear now certain, here it comes.
Now to ou • places

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Whither will he lead me?
What invitation's this? to what new end

Are theſe ſa •• preparations? 〈◊〉
• ich Banquet,
Muſick, and every place ſtuck with adornment,
Fit for a Princes welcome; what new game
Has Fortune now prepar'd to ſhew me happy?
And then again to ſink me? 'tis no illuſion,
Mine eyes are not deceiv'd, all theſe are reall;
What wealth and ſtate!

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Will you ſit down and eat Sir?
Theſe carry little wonder, they are uſual;
But you ſhall ſee, if you be wiſe to obſerve it,
That that will ſtrike dead, ſtrike with amazement,
Then if you be a man: this fair health to you.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: What ſhall I ſee? I pledge ye Sir, I was never
So buried in amazement —

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: You are ſo ſtill:
Drink freely.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: The very wines are admirable:
Good Sir, give me leave to ask this queſtion,
For what great worthy man are theſe prepar'd?
And why do you bring me hither?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: They are for you, Sir;
And under-value not the worth you carry,
You are that worthy man: think well of theſe,
They ſhall be more, and greater.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Well, blind fortune
Thou haſt the prettieſt changes when thou art pleas'd,
To play thy game out wantonly —

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Come be luſty,
And awake your Spirits. Ceaſe Muſick

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Good Sir, do not wake me.
For willingly I would dye in this dream, pray whoſe Servants
Are all theſe that attend here?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: They are yours;
They wait on you.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I never yet remember
I kept ſuch faces, nor that I was ever able
To maintain ſo many.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Now you are, and ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: You'l ſay this houſe is mine too?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Say it? ſwear it.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: And all this wealth?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: This is the leaſt you ſee Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Why, where has this been hid theſe thirtie years?
For certainly I never ſound I was wealthie
Till this hour, never dream'd of houſe, and Servants.
I had thought I had been a younger Brother, a poor Gent.
I may eat boldly then.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: 'Tis prepar'd for ye.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: The taſte is perfect, and moſt delicate:
But why for me? give me ſome wine, I do drink;
I feel it ſenſibly, and I am here,
Here in this glorious place: I am bravely us'd too,
Good Gentle Sir, give me leave to think a little,
For either I am much abus'd —

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Strike Muſick
And ſing that luſty Song. Muſick Song.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Bewitching harmony!
Sure I am turn'd into another Creature.
Happy and bleſt, Arnoldo was unfortunate;
Ha! bleſs mine eyes; what pretious piece of nature
To poſe the world?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: I told you, you would ſee that
Would darken theſe poor preparations;
What think ye now? nay riſe not, 'tis no viſion.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: 'Tis more: 'tis miracle.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: You are welcom Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: It ſpeaks, and entertains me ſtill more glorious;
She is warm, and this is fleſh here: how ſhe ſtirs me!
Bleſs me what ſtars are there?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: May I ſit near ye?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: No, you are too pure an object to behold,
Too excellent to look upon, and live;
I muſt remove.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: She is a woman Sir,
〈◊〉 what faint heart is this?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: The houſe of wonder.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Do not you think your ſelf now truly happy?
• ou have the abſtract of all ſweetneſs by ye,
• he precious wealth youth labours to arrive at;
• or is ſhe leſs in honour, than in beauty,
••• ra's Royal Duke is proud to call her
• is beſt, his Nobleſt, and moſt happy Siſter,
• ortune has made her Miſtreſs of herſelf,
Wealthy, and wiſe, without a power to ſway her,
Wonder of Italy, of all hearts Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: And all this is—

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Hippolyta the beauteous.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: You are a poor relator of my fortunes,
• oo weak a Chronicle to ſpeak my bleſſings,
And leave out that eſſential part of ſtory
I am moſt high and happy in, moſt fortunate,
The acquaintance, and the noble fellowſhip
Of this fair Gentleman: pray ye do not wonder,
Nor hold it ſtrange to hear a handſome Lady.
• peak freely to ye: with your fair leave and courteſie
〈◊〉 will ſit by ye.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I know not what to anſwer,
Nor where I am, nor to what end conſider;
Why do you uſe me thus?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Are ye angry Sir,
Becauſe ye are entertain'd with all humanity?
• reely and nobly us'd?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: No gentle Lady,
That were uncivil, but it much amazes me
A ſtranger, and a man of no deſert
Should find ſuch floods of courteſie.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: I love ye,
〈◊〉 honour ye, the firſt and beſt of all men,
And where that fair opinion leads, 'tis uſual
Theſe trifles that but ſerve to ſet off, follow.
〈◊〉 would not have you proud now, nor diſdainful
Becauſe I ſay I love ye, though I ſwear it,
Nor think it a ſtale favour I ſting on ye,
Though ye be handſome, and the only man
〈◊〉 muſt confeſs I ever fixt mine eye on,
And bring along all promiſes that pleaſe us,
Yet I ſhould hate ye then, deſpiſe ye, ſcorn ye,
And with as much contempt purſue your perſon,
As now I do with love. But you are wiſer,
At leaſt I think, more maſter of your fortune,
And ſo I drink your health.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Hold faſt good honeſty,
I am a loſt man elſe.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Now you may kiſs me,
'Tis the firſt kiſs, I ever askt, I ſwear to ye.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: That I dare do ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: You do it well too;
You are a Maſter Sir, that makes you coy.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Would you would ſend your people off.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Well thought on.

Wait all without.
Exit Zab. and Servants.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: I hope ſhe is pleas'd throughly.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Why ſtand ye ſtill? here's no man to detect ye,
My people are gone off: come, come, leave conjuring,
The Spirit you would raiſe, is here already,
Look boldly on me.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: What would you have me do?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: O moſt unmanly queſtion! have you do?
Is't poſſible your years ſhould want a Tutor?
I'le teach ye: come, embrace me.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Fye ſtand off;
And give me leave, more now than e're, to wonder,
A building of ſo goodly a proportion,
Outwardly all exact, the frame of Heaven,
Should hide within ſo baſe inhabitants?
You are as fair, as if the morning bare ye,
Imagination never made a ſweeter;
Can it be poſſible this frame ſhould ſuffer,
And built on ſlight affections, fright the viewer?
Be excellent in all, as you are outward,
The worthy Miſtreſs of thoſe many bleſſings
Heaven has beſtowed, make 'em appear ſtill nobler,
Becauſe they are truſted to a weaker keeper.
Would ye have me love ye?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Not for your beauty;
Though I confeſs, it blowes the firſt fire in us,
Time as he paſſes by, puts out that ſparkle;
Nor for your wealth, although the world kneel to it.
And make it all addition to a woman,
Fortune that ruines all, makes that his conqueſt;
Be honeſt, and be vertuous, I'le admire ye,
At leaſt be wiſe, and where ye lay theſe nets,
Strow over 'em a little modeſty,
'Twill well become your cauſe, and catch more Fools.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Could any one that lov'd this wholeſome counſel
But love the giver more? you make me fonder:
You have a vertuous mind, I want that ornament;
Is it a ſin I covet to enjoy ye?
If ye imagine I am too free a Lover,
And act that part belongs to you, I am ſilent:
Mine eyes ſhall ſpeak my bluſhes, parly with ye;
I will not touch your hand, but with a tremble
Fitting a Veſtal Nun; not long to kiſs ye,
But gently as the Air, and undiſcern'd too,
I'le ſteal it thus: I'le walk your ſhadow by ye,
So ſtill and ſilent that it ſhall be equal,
To put me off, as that, and when I covet,
To give ſuch toyes as theſe—

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: A new temptation—

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Thus like the lazie minutes will I drop 'em,
Which paſt once are forgotten.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Excellent vice!

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Will ye be won? look ſtedfaſtly upon me,
Look manly, take a mans affections to you;
Young women, in the old world were not wont, Sir,
To hang out gaudy buſhes for their beauties,
To talk themſelves into young mens affections;
How cold and dull you are!

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: How I ſtagger?
She is wiſe, as fair; but 'tis a wicked wiſdom;
I'le choak before I yield.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Who waits within there? Zabulon within.
Make ready the green Chamber.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: It ſhall be Madam.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I am afraid ſhe will injoy me indeed.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: What Muſick do ye love?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: A modeſt tongue.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: We'l have enough of that: ſye, ſye, how lumpiſh?
In a young Ladyes arms thus dull?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: For Heaven ſake
Profeſs a little goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Of what Country?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I am of Rome.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Nay then I know you mock me,
The Italians are not frighted with ſuch bug bears,
Prethee go in.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I am not well.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: I'le make thee,
I'le kiſs thee well.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I am not ſick of that ſore.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Upon my Conſcience, I muſt raviſh thee,
I ſhall be famous for the firſt example:
With this I'le tye ye firſt, then try your ſtrength Sir.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: My ſtrength? away baſe woman, I abhor thee.
I am not caught with ſtales, diſeaſe dwell with thee. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Are ye ſo quick? and have I loſt my wiſhes?
Hoe, Zabulon; my ſervants.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Call'd ye Madam?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Is all that beauty ſcorned, ſo many ſu'd for;
So many Princes? by a ſtranger too?
Muſ • I endure this?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Where's the Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Go preſently, purſue the ſtranger, Zabulon.
He has b • oke from me, Jewels I have given him:
Charge him with theft: he has ſtoln my love, my freedome,
Draw him before the Governour, impriſon him,
Why doſt thou ſtay?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: I'le teach him a new dance,
For pla ••• faſt and looſe with ſuch a Lady.
Come fellows, come: I'le execute your anger,
And to the ſail.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: His ſcorn ſhall feel my vengeance— Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Sul
sp.l: Shall I never ſee a luſty man again?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Faith Miſtreſs
You do ſo over labour 'em when you have 'em,
And ſo d • y ſounder 'em, they cannot laſt.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: Where's the French-man?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Alas, he's all to fitters,
And lyes, taking the height of his fortune with a Syringe.
He's chin'd, he's chin'd good man, he is a mourner.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: What's become of the Dane?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Who? goldy-locks?
He's ſoul i'th' touch-hole; and recoils again,
The main Spring's weaken'd that holds up his co • k,
He lies at the ſign of the Sun, to be new breech'd.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: The Rutter too, is gone.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: O that was a brave Raſcal,
He would labour like a Thraſher: but alas
What thing can ever laſt? he has been ill mew'd,
And drawn too ſoon; I have ſeen him in the Hoſpital.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: There was an Engliſh-man.

sp.speaker: Ja
sp.l: I there was an Engliſh-man;
You'l ſ • ant find any now, to make that name good:
There were thoſe Engliſh that were men indeed,
And would perform like men, but now they are vaniſht:
They are ſo taken up in their own Country,
And ſo heat • n of their ſpeed by their own women,
When they come here, they draw their legs like Hackneys:
Drink, and their own devices have undone 'em.

sp.speaker: Sul
sp.l: I muſt have one that's ſtrong, no life in Lisbon elſe,
Perfect and young: my Cuſtom with young Ladies,
And •• gh ſ • d City dames, will fall, and break elſe.
I want my ſelf too, in mine age to nouriſh me:
They are all ſunk I mantain'd: now what's this buſineſs,
What goodly fellow's that?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Why do you d • ag me?
Pox o' your juſtice; let me looſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Offi.
sp.l: Not ſo Sir.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Cannot a man fall into one of your drunken Collars,
And venture the breaking on's neck, your trap-doors open,
But he muſt be us'd thus raſcally?

sp.speaker: 1 Offi.
sp.l: What made you wandring
So late i'th' night? you know that is impriſonment.

sp.speaker: Rut
sp.l: May be I walk in my ſleep.
May be we'l walk ye.
What made you wandring Sir, into that vault
Where all the City ſtore, and the Munition lay?
I fell into it by chance, I broke my ſhins ſor't:
Your worſhips feel not that. I knockt my head
Againſt a hundred paſts, would you had had it.
Cannot I break my neck in my own defence?

sp.speaker: 2 Offi.
sp.l: This will not ſerve: you cannot put it off ſo,
Your coming thither was to play the villain,
To 〈◊〉 the Powder, to blow up that part o'th' City.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Yes, with my noſe: why were the trap doors open?
M ••• n •• you •• ll, 〈◊〉 you, had you gone that way?
I thought your C • ty had ſunk.

sp.speaker: 1 Offi.
sp.l: You did your bell Sir,
We muſt preſume, to help it into th' Air,
If you call that ſinking: we have told you what's the la •• ,
He that is taken there, unleſs a Magiſtrate,
And have command in that place, preſently
If there be nothing found apparent near him
Worthy his torture, or his preſent death,
Muſt eitheir pay his fine for his preſumption,
(Which is ſix hundred Duckets) or for ſix years
Tug at an Oar i'th' Gallies: will ye walk Sir,
For we preſume you cannot pay the penalty.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Row in the Gallies, after all this miſchief?

sp.speaker: 2 Offi.
sp.l: May be you were drunk, they'l keep you ſober ther •

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Tug at an Oar? you are not arrant raſcals,
To catch me in a pit-fall, and betray me?

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: A luſty minded man.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: A wondrous able.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: Pray Gentlemen, allow me but that liberty
To ſpeak a few words with your priſoner,
And I ſhall thank you.

sp.speaker: 1 Offi.
sp.l: Take your pleaſure Lady.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: What would you give that woman ſhould redeem ye,
Redeem ye from this ſlavery?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Beſides my ſervice
I would give her my whole ſelf, I would be her vaſſal.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: She has reaſon to expect as much, conſidering
The great ſum ſhe pays ſor't, yet take comfort,
What ye ſhall do to merit this, is eaſie,
And I will be the woman ſhall befriend ye,
'Tis but to entertain ſome handſome Ladies,
And young fair Gentlewomen: you gueſs the way:
But giving of your mind—

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I am excellent at it:
You cannot pick out ſuch another living.
I underſtand ye: is't not thus?

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: Ye have it.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Bring me a hundred of'em: I'le diſpatch 'em.
I will be none but yours: ſhould another offer
Another way to redeem me, I ſhould ſcorn it.
What women you ſhall pleaſe: I am monſtrous luſty:
Not to be taken down: would you have Children?
I'le get you thoſe as faſt, and thick as flie-blows.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: I admire him: wonder at him!

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Hark ye Lady,
You may require ſometimes—

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: I by my faith.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: And you ſhall have it by my faith, and handſomly:
This old Cat will ſuck ſhrewdly: you have no Daughters?
I flye at all: now am I in my Kingdom.
Tug at an Oar? no, tug in a Feather-bed,
With good warm Caudles; hang your bread and water,
I'le make you young again, believe that Lady.
I will ſo frubbiſh you.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: Come, follow Officers,
This Gentleman is free: I'le pay the Duckets.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: And when you catch me in your City-powdring-tub
Again, boil me with Cabbidge.

sp.speaker: 1 Offi.
sp.l: You are both warn'd and arm'd Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Will your Ladyſhip wear this Dreſſing?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Leave thy prating:
I care not what I wear.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Yet 'tis my duty
To know your pleaſure, and my worſt affliction
To ſee you diſcontented.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Weeping too?
Prethee forgive me: I am much diſtemper'd,
And ſpeak I know not what: to make thee amends
The Gown that I wore yeſterday, is thine;
Let it alone awhile.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Now you perceive,
And taſte her bounty.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Much above my merit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: But have you not yet ſound a happy time
To move for me.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: I have watched all occaſions,
But hitherto, without ſucceſs: yet doubt not
But I'le embrace the firſt means.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Do, and proſper:
Excellent creature, whoſe perfections make
Even ſorrow lovely, if your frowns thus take me,
What would your ſmiles doe?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Pox o' this ſtale Courtſhip:
If I have any power.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I am commanded,
Obedience is the Lovers ſacrifice
Which I pay gladly.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: To be forc'd to wooe,
Being a woman, could not but torment me,
But bringing for my advocates, youth and beauty,
Set off with wealth, and then to be deni'd too
Do's comprehend all tortures. They flatter'd me,
That ſaid my looks were charms, my touches fetters,
My locks ſoft chains, to bind the arms of Princes,
And make them in that wiſh'd for bondage, happy.
I am like others of a courſer feature,
As weak to allure, but in my dotage, ſtronger:
I am no Carce; he, more than Ʋlyſſes,
Scorns all my offer'd bounties, ſlights my favours,
And, as I were ſome new Egyptian, flyes me,
Leaving no pawn, but my own ſhame behind him.
But he ſhall finde, that in my fell revenge,
I am a woman: one that never pardons
The rude contemner of her proffered ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Madam, 'tis done.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: What's done?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: The uncivill ſtranger
Is at your ſuite arreſted.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: 'Tis well handled.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: And under guard ſent to the Governour,
With whom my teſtimony, and the favour
He bears your Ladiſhip, have ſo prevail'd
That he is ſentenc'd.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: To loſe his head.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Is that the means to quench the ſcorching heat
Of my inrag'd deſires? muſt innocence ſuffer,
Cauſe I am faulty? or is my Love ſo fatall
That of neceſſity it muſt deſtroy
The object it moſt longs for? dull Hippolyta,
To think that injuries could make way for love,
When courteſies were deſpis'd: that by his death
Thou ſhouldſt gain that, which only thou canſt hope for
While he is living: My honour's at the ſtake now,
And cannot be preſerv'd, unleſs he periſh,
The enjoying of the thing I love, I ever
Have priz'd above my fame: why doubt I now then?
One only way is left me, to redeem all:
Make ready my Caroch.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What will you Madam?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: And yet I am impatient of ſuch ſtay:
Bind up my hair: fye, fye, while that is doing
The Law my feiſe his life: thus as I am then,
Not like Hippolyta, but a Bacchanall
My frantique Love tranſports me. Exit

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Sure ſhe's diſtracted.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Pray you follow her: I will along with you:
I more than gueſs the cauſe: women that love
Are moſt uncertain, and one minute crave,
What in another they refuſe to have. Exit.

div.head: Scena Quinta.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Aſſure thy ſelf Charino, I am alter'd
From what I was; the tempeſts we have met with
In our uncertain voyage, were ſmooth gales
Compar'd to thoſe, the memory of my luſts
Rais'd in my Conſcience: and if ere again
I live to ſee Zenocia, I will ſue,
And ſeek to her as a Lover, and a Servant,
And not command affection, like a Tyrant.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: In hearing this, you make me young again,
And Heaven, it ſeems, favouring this good change in you
In ſetting of a period to our dangers
Gives us fair hopes to find that here in Lisbon
Which hitherto in vain we long have ſought for.
I have receiv'd aſſur'd intelligence,
Such ſtrangers have been ſeen here: and though yet
I cannot learn their fortunes, nor the place
Of their abode, I have a Soul preſages
A fortunate event here.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: There have paſs'd
A mutual enterchange of courteſies
Between me, and the Governour; therefore boldly
We may preſume of him, and of his power
If we finde cauſe to uſe them, otherwiſe
I would not be known here, and theſe diſguiſes
Will keep us from diſcovery.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: What are theſe?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: The Governour: with him my Rival, bound.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: For certain 'tis Arnoldo.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Let's attend
What the ſucceſs will be.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Is't poſſible
There ſhould be hope of his recovery,
His wounds ſo many and ſo deadly?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: So they appear'd at firſt, but the blood ſtop'd,
His trance forſook him, and on better ſearch
We found they were not mortal.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Uſe all care
To perfect this unhop'd for cure: that done
Propoſe your own rewards: and till you ſhall
Hear farther from me, for ſome ends I have,
Conceal it from his Mother.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Wee'l not fail Sir. Exit

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: You ſtill ſtand confident on your innocence.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: It is my beſt and laſt guard, which I will not
Leave, to relye on your uncertain mercy.

div.stage: Enter Hippolyta, Zabulon, Leopold, Zenocia, 2 Servants.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Who bad you follow me! Goe home, and you Sir,
As you reſpect me, goe with her.

sp.speaker: Arn.

l.hi: Zenocia!

sp.l: And in her houſe a Servant!

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: 'Tis my Daughter.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: My love? Contain your joy, obſerve the ſequel. Zen. paſſes

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Fye Madam, how undecent 'tis for you,
So far unlike your ſelf to bee ſeen thus
In th'open ſtreets? why do you kneel? pray you riſe,
I am acquainted with the wrong, and loſs
You have ſuſtain'd, and the Delinquent now
Stands ready for his puniſhment.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Let it fall, Sir,
On the offender: he is innocent,
And moſt unworthy of theſe bonds he wears,
But I made up of guilt.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: VVhat ſtrange turn's this?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: This was my priſoner once.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: If chaſtity
In a young man, and tempted to the height too
Did ere deſerve reward, or admiration,
He juſtly may claim both. Love to his perſon
(Or if you pleaſe give it a fouler name)
Compel'd me firſt to train him to my houſe,
All engines I rais'd there to ſhake his vertue,
VVhich in the aſſault were uſeleſs; he unmov'd ſtill
As if he had no part of humane frailty.
Againſt the nature of my Sex, almoſt
I plaid the Raviſher. You might have ſeen
In our contention, young Apollo fly
And love-ſick Daphne follow, all arts failing,
By ſlight he wan the victory, breaking from
My ſcorn'd embraces: the repulſe (in women
Unſufferable) invited me to practiſe
A means to be reveng'd: and from this grew
His Accuſation, and the abuſe
Of your ſtill equall juſtice: My rage ever
Thanks heaven, though wanton, I found not my ſelf
So far engag'd to Hell, to proſecute
To the death what I had plotted, for that love
That made me fall deſire him, then accuſe him,
Commands me with the hazard of my ſelf
Firſt to entreat his pardon, then acquit him.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: VVhat • re you are, ſo much I love your vertue,
That I deſire your friendſhip: do you unlooſe him
From thoſe bon • s, you are worthy of: your repentance
Makes part of ſatisfaction; yet I muſt
Severely reprehend you.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I am made
A ſtale on all parts: But this fellow ſhall
Pay dearly for her favour.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: My life's ſo full
Of various changes, that I now deſpair
Of any certain port; one trouble ending,
A new, and worſe ſucceeds it: what ſhould Zenocia
Do in this womans houſe? Can chaſtity
And hot Luſt dwell together without infection?
I would not be or jealous, or ſecure,
Yet ſomething muſt be done, to found the depth on't:
That ſhe lives is my bliſs, but living there,
A hell of torments; there's no way to her
In whom I live, but by • his door, through which
To me 'tis •• ath to enter, ye • I muſt,
And 〈◊〉 ma • e tryal.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Let me hear no more
Of theſe devices, Lady: this I pard •• ,
And at your interceſſion I forgive
Your inſtrument the Jew too: get you home.
The hundred thouſand crowns you lent the City
Towards the ſetting forth of the laſt Navy
Bound for the Iſlands, was a good then, which
I ballance with your ill now.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Now Sir, to him,
You know my Daughter needs it.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Let me take
A farewell with mine eye, Sir, though my lip
Be barr'd the Ceremonie, courteſie
And Cuſtom too allows of.
Gentle Madam,
I neither am ſo cold, nor ſo ill bred
But that I dare receive it: you are unguarded,
And let me tell you that I am aſham'd
Of my late rudeneſs, and would gladly therefore
If you pleaſe to accept my ready ſervice
Wait on you to your houſe.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Above my hope:
Sir, if an Angel were to be my convoy,

He ſhould not be more welcom.—
Ex. Arn. and Hip.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Now you know me.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and honour you: ever remembring
Your many bounties, being ambitious only
To give you cauſe to ſay by ſome one ſervice
That I am not ungratefull.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: 'Tis now offer'd:
I have a ſuit to you, and an eaſie one,
Which e're long you ſhall know.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: When you think fit Sir,
And then as a command I will receive it,
Till when, moſt welcom: you are welcom too Sir,
'Tis ſpoken from the heart, and therefore needs not
Much proteſtation: at your better leiſure
I will enquire the cauſe that brought you hither:
In the mean time ſerve you.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l:
You out-doe me Sir.
Exe •• t.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: YOU have beſtow'd on me a ſecond life,
For which I live your creature, and have better'd
What nature fram'd unperfect, my firſt being
Inſolent pride made monſtrous; but this later
In learning me to know my ſelf, hath taught me
Not to wrong others.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Then we live indeed,
When we can goe to reſt without alarm
Given every minute to a guilt-ſick conſcience
To keep us waking, and riſe in the morning
Secure in being innocent: but when
In the remembrance of our worſer actions
We ever bear about us whips and furies,
To make the day a night of ſorrow to us,
Even life's a burthen.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I have found and felt it;
But will endeavour having firſt made peace
VVith thoſe inteſtine enemies my rude paſſions,
To be ſo with man-kind: but worthy Doctor,
Pray if you can reſolve me; was the Gentleman
That left me dead, ere brought unto his tryal?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Nor known, nor apprehended.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: That's my grief.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Why, do you wiſh he had been puniſhed?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: No,
The ſtream of my ſwoln ſorrow runs not that way:
For could I find him, as I vow to Heaven
It ſhall be my firſt care to ſeek him out,
I would with thanks acknowledge that his ſword,
In opening my veins, which proud bloud poiſon'd,
Gave the firſt ſymptoms of true health.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: 'Tis in you
A Chriſtian reſolution: that you live
Is 〈◊〉 the Governours, your Uncles charge
As yet conceal'd. And though a ſons loſs never
Was ſolemniz'd with more tears of true ſorrow
Than have been paid by your unequal'd Mother
For your ſuppoſed death, ſhe's not acquainted
With your recovery.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: For ſome few dayes
Pray let her ſo continue: thus diſguis'd
I may abroad unknown.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Without ſuſpicion
Of being diſcovered

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I am confident
No moiſture ſooner dies than womens tears,
And therefore though I know my Mother vertuous,
Yet being one of that frail ſex I purpoſe
Her farther tryal.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: That as you think fit—I'le not betray you.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: To find out this ſtranger
This true Phyſician of my mind and manners
Were ſuch a bleſſing. He ſeem'd poor, and may
Perhaps be now in want; would I could find him.
The Innes I'le ſearch firſt, then the publick Stewes;
He was of Italy, and that Country breeds not
Preciſians that way, but hot Libertines;
And ſuch the moſt are: 'tis but a little travail:
I am unfurniſht too, pray Mr. Doctor,
Can you ſupply me?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: VVith what ſumm you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I will not be long abſent.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: That I wiſh too;
For till you have more ſtrength, I would not have you
To be too bold.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Fear not, I will be carefull. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: I have brought him Sir, a fellow that will do it
• hough Hell ſtood in his way, ever provided
• ou pay him for't.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: He has a ſtrange aſpect,
• nd looks much like the figure of a hang-man
〈◊〉 a table of the Paſſion.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: He tranſcends
• ll precedents, believe it, a fleſh'd ruffian,
• hat hath ſo often taken the Strappado,
• hat 'tis to him but as a lofty trick
〈◊〉 to a tumbler: he hath peruſed too
• ll Dungeons in Portual, thrice ſeven years
• owed in the Galleys for three ſeveral murthers,
• hough I preſume that he has done a hundred,
• nd ſcap't unpuniſht.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: He is much in debt to y ••
• ou ſet him off ſo well. VVhat will y • u take Sir
• o beat a fellow for me, that thus wrong'd me?

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.l: To beat him ſay you?

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: Yes, beat him to lameneſs,
• o cut his lips or noſe off; any thing,
• hat may disfigure him.

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.l: Let me conſider?
• ive hundred piſtolets for ſuch a ſervice
〈◊〉 think were no dear penniworth.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Five hundred!
• Vhy there are of your Brother-hood in the City,
• e undertake, ſhall kill a man for twenty.

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.l: Kill him? I think ſo; I'le kill any man
• or half the mony.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: And will you ask more
• or a ſound beating than a murther?

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.l: I Sir,
• nd with good reaſon, for a dog that's dead,
• he Spaniſh proverb ſays, will never bite:
• ut ſhould I beat or hurt him only, he may
• ecover, and kill me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A good concluſion,
• he obduracie of this raſcal makes me tender.
• le run ſome other courſe, there's your reward
• Vithout the employment.

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.l: For that as you pleaſe Sir;
• hen you have need to kill a man, pray uſe me,
• ut I am out at beating. Exit.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: What's to be done then?

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: I'le tell thee Zabulon, and make thee privy
• o my moſt near deſigns: this ſtranger, which
• ippolyta ſo dotes on, was my priſoner
• hen the laſt Virgin, I beſtowed upon her,
• as made my prize; how he eſcaped, hereafter
• le let thee know; and it may be the love
• e bears the ſervant, makes him ſcorn the Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: 'Tis not unlike; for the firſt time he ſaw her
• is looks expreſt ſo much, and for more proof
•• nce he came to my Ladys houſe, though yet
• e never knew her, he hath practis'd with me
• o help him to a conference, without
• he knowledge of Hippolyta; which I promis'd.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: And by all means perform it for their meeting,
• ut work it ſo, that my diſdainful Miſtris
Whom, notwithſtanding all her injuries,
'Tis my hard fate to love) may ſee and hear them.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: To what end Sir?

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: This Zabulon: when ſhe ſees
• ho is her rival, and her Lovers baſeneſs
• o leave a Princeſs for her bondwoman,
• he fight will make her ſcorn, what now ſhe dotes on,
• le double thy reward.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: You are like to ſpeed then:
• or I confeſs what you will ſoon believe,
• e ſerve them beſt that are moſt apt to give.
For you, I'le place you where you ſhall ſee all, and yet be unobſerv'd.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: That I deſire too. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I cannot ſee her yet, how it afflicts me
The poyſon of this place ſhould mix it ſelf
With her pure thoughts? 'Twas ſhe that was commanded,
Or my eyes failed me groſly; that youth, that face
And all that noble ſweetneſs. May ſhe not live here,
And yet be honeſt ſtill?

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: It is Arnoldo,
From all his dangers free; fortune I bleſs thee.
My noble husband! how my joy ſwells in me,
But why in this place? what buſineſs hath he here?
He cannot hear of me, I am not known here.
I left him vertuous; how I ſhake to think now?
And how that joy I had, cools, and forſakes me?
This Lady is but fair, I have been thought ſo
Without compare admired; She has bewitched 〈◊〉
And he forgot —

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe again, the ſame—the 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: There they are together.—Now 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Peace, let 'em parly.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: That you are well Zenocia, and once 〈◊〉
Bleſs my deſpairing eyes, with your wiſht p •••••
I thank the gods; but that I meet you here—

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: They are acquainted.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: I found that ſecret Madam,
When you comanded her go home: pray hear 'em.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: That you meet me here, ne're bluſn at that Arnol ••
Your coming comes too late: I am a woman,
And one woman with another may be truſted;
Do you fear the houſe?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: More than a fear, I know it,
Know it not good, not honeſt.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: VVhat do you here then?
I'th' name of vertue why do you approach it?
Will you confeſs the doubt and yet purſue it?
Where have your eyes been wandring, my Arnoldo?
What conſtancy, what faith do you call this? Fie,
Aim at one wanton mark, and wound another?
I do confeſs, the Lady fai • , moſt beauteous,
And able to betray a ſtrong mans liberty, Leopold places himſelf •• fe •• below.
But you that have a love, a wife—you do well
To deal thus wiſely with me: yet Arnoldo,
Since you are pleas'd to ſtudy a new beauty,
And think this old and ill, beaten with miſery,
Study a nobler way for ſhame to love me,
VVrong not her honeſty.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: You have confirm'd me.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: VVho though ſhe be your wiſe, will never hinder you,
So much I reſt a ſervant to your wiſhes,
And love your Loves, though they be my deſtructions,
No man ſhall know me, nor the ſhare I have in thee,
No eye ſuſpect I am able to prevent you,
For ſince I am a ſlave to this great Lady,
Whom I perceive you follow,

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Be not blinded.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Fortune ſhall make me uſeful to your ſervice,
I will ſpeak for you.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Speak for me? you wrong me.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: I will endeavour all the wayes I am able
To make her think well of you; will that pleaſe?
To make her dote upon you, dote to madneſs,
So far againſt my ſelf I will obey you.
But when that's done, and I have ſhewed this duty,
This great obedience, few will buy it at m • price,
Thus will I ſhake hands with you, wiſh you well,
But never ſee you more, nor receive comfort
From any thing, Arnoldo.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: You are too tender;
I neither doubt you, nor deſire longer
To be a man, and live, than I am honeſt
And only yours; our infinite affections
Abus'd us both.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: VVhere are your favours now?
The courteſies you ſhew'd this ſtranger, Madam?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Have I now ſound the cauſe?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Attend it further.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Did ſhe invite you, do you ſay?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Moſt cunningly,
And with a preparation of that ſtate
I was brought in and welcom'd.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Seem'd to love you?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Moſt infinitely, at firſt ſight, moſt dotingly.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: She is a goodly Lady.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: VVondrous handſom:
At firſt view, being taken unprepar'd,
Your memory not preſent then to aſſiſt me,
She ſeem'd ſo glorious ſweet, and ſo far ſtir'd me,
Nay be not jealous, there's no harm done.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Prethee—didſt thou not kiſs, Arnoldo?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Yes ſaith did I.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: And then —

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I durſt not, did not —

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: I forgive you,
Come tell the truth.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: May be I lay with her.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: He mocks me too, moſt baſely.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Did ye faith? did ye forget ſo far?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Come, come, no weeping;
I would have lyen firſt in my grave, believe that.
VVhy will you ask thoſe things you would not hear?
She is too untemperate to betray my vertues,
Too openly laſcivious: had ſhe dealt
But with that ſeeming modeſty ſhe might,
And ſtung a little Art upon her ardor,
But 'twas forgot, and I forgot to like her,
And glad I was deceiv'd. No my Zenocia,
My firſt love here begun, reſts here unreapt yet,
And here for ever.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: You have made me happy,
Even in the midſt of bondage bleſt.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: You ſee now
What rubs are in your way.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: And quickly Zabulon
I'le root 'em out.—Be ſure you do this preſently.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Do not you alter then.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l:
I am reſolute.
Exit Zabulon.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: To ſee you only I came hither laſt,
Drawn by no love of hers, nor baſe allurements,
For by this holy light I hate her heartily.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: I am glad of that, you have ſav'd me ſo much vengeance
And ſo much fear,
From this hour fair beſal you.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Some means I ſhall make ſhortly to redeem you,
Till when, obſerve her well, and fit her temper,
Only her luſt contemn.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: When ſhall I ſee you?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I will live hereabouts, and bear her fair ſtill,
Till I can find a ſit hour to redeem you.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Shut all the doors.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: We are betray'd,
The Lady of the houſe has heard our parly,
Seen us, and ſeen our Loves.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: You courteous Gallant,
You that ſcorn all I can beſtow, that laugh at
The afflictions, and the groans I ſuffer for you,
That ſlight and jeer my love, contemn the fortune
My favours can ſting on you, have I caught you?
Have I now ſound the cauſe? ye fool my wiſhes;
Is mine own ſlave, my bane? I nouriſh that
That ſucks up my content. I'le pray no more,
Nor wooe no more; thou ſhalt ſee fooliſh man,
And to thy bitter pain and anguiſh, look on
The vengeance I ſhall take, provok'd and ſlighted;
Redeem her then, and ſteal her hence: ho Zabulon
Now to your work.

div.stage: Enter Zabulon, and Servants, ſome holding Arnoldo, ſome ready with a cord to ſtrangle Zenocia.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Lady, but hear me ſpeak firſt,
As you have pity.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: I have none. You taught me,
When I even hung about your neck, you ſcorn'd me.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Shall we pluck yet?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: No, hold a little Zabulon,
I'le pluck his heart-ſtrings firſt: now am I worthy
A little of your love?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I'le be your Servant,
Command me through what danger you ſhall aime at,
Let it be death.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Be ſure Sir, I ſhall fit you.

sp.speaker: Ara.
sp.l: But ſpare this Virgin.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: I would ſpare that villain firſt,
Had cut my Fathers throat.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Bounteous Lady,
If in your ſex there be that noble ſoftneſs,
That tenderneſs of heart, wom • n are crown'd for —

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Kneel not Arnoldo, doe her not that honour,
She is not worthy ſuch ſubmiſſion,
I ſcorn a life depends upon her pity.
Proud woman do thy worſt, and arm thy anger
With thoughts as black as Hell, as hot and bloody,
I bring a patience here, ſhall make 'em bluſh,
An innocence, ſhall outlook thee, and death too.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Make me your ſlave, I give my freedom to ye,
For ever to be fetter'd to your ſervice;
'Twas I offended, be not ſo unjuſt then,
To ſtrike the innocent, this gentle maid
Never intended fear and doubt againſt you:
She is your Servant, pay not her obſervance
With cruel looks, her duteous faith with death.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Am I fair now? now am I worth your liking?

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Not fair, not to be liked, thou glorious Devil,
Thou verniſht piece of luſt, thou painted fury.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Speak gently ſweet, ſpeak gently.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: I'le ſpeak nobly.
'Tis not the ſaving of a life I aim at,
Mark me laſcivious woman, mark me truly,
And then conſider, how I weigh thy anger.
Life is no longer mine, nor dear unto me,
Than uſefull to his honour I preſerve it.
If thou hadſt ſtudied all the courteſies
Humanity and noble blood are linkt to,
Thou couldſt not have propounded ſuch a benefit,
Nor heapt upon me ſuch unlookt for honour
As dying for his ſake, to be his Martyr,
'Tis ſuch a grace.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: You ſhall not want that ſavour,
Let your bones work miracles.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Dear Lady
By thoſe fair eyes—

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: There is but this way left ye
To ſave her life. —

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Speak it, and I embrace it.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Come to my private chamber preſently,
And there, what love and I command—

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I'le doe it,
Be comforted Zenocia.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Do not do this
To ſave me, do not loſe your ſelf I charge you,
I charge you by your love, that love your bear me;
That love, that conſtant love you have twin'd to me,
By all your promiſes, take heed you keep 'em,
Now is your conſtant tryal. If thou doſt this,
Or mov'ſt one foot, to guide thee to her luſt,
My curſes and eternal hate purſue thee.
Redeem me at the baſe price of diſ-loyalty?
Muſt my undoubted honeſty be thy Bawd too?
Go and intwine thy ſelf about that body;
Tell her, for my life thou haſt loſt thine honour,
Pull'd all thy vows from heaven, baſely, moſt baſely
Stoop'd to the ſervile flames of that foul woman,
To add an hour to me that hate thee for it,
Know thee not again, nor name thee for a Husband.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: What ſhall I do to ſave her?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: How now, what haſt there?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The Governour, attended with ſome Gentlemen,
Are newly entred, to ſpeak with your Ladiſhip.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Pox o' their buſineſs, reprieve her for this hour,
I ſhall have other time.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Now fortune help us.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: I'le meet 'em preſently: retire awhile all. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: You riſe to day upon your right ſide Lady;
You know the danger too, and may prevent it,
And if you ſuffer her to periſh thus,
As ſhe muſt do, and ſuddenly, believe it,
Unleſs you ſtand her friend; you know the way on't,
I gueſs you poorly love her, leſs your fortune.
Let her know nothing, and perform this matter,
There are hours ordained for ſeveral buſineſſes,
You underſtand.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: I underſtand you Bawd Sir,
And ſuch a Counſellour I never car'd for.

div.stage: Enter the Governour, Clodio, Leopold, Charino and Attendants at one door, Hippolyta at the other.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Your Lordſhip does me honour.

sp.speaker: Gover.
sp.l: Fair Hippolyta,
I am come to eaſe you of a charge.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: I keep none
I count a burthen Sir: and yet I lye too.

sp.speaker: Gover.
sp.l: Which is the Maid; is ſhe here?

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Yes Sir,
This is ſhe, this is Zenocia,
The very ſame I ſued to your Lordſhip for.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: Clodio again? more miſery? more ruin?
Under what angry ſtar is my life govern'd?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Gome hither Maid, you are once more a free woman,
Here I diſcharge your bonds.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Another ſmile,
Another trick of fortune to betray us!

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Why does your Lordſhip uſe me ſo unnobly?
Againſt my will to take away my bond-woman?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: She was no lawful prize, therefore no bond-woman:
She's of that Country we hold friendſhip with,
And ever did, and therefore to be uſed
With entertainment, fair and courteous.
The breach of League in us gives foul example,
Therefore you muſt be pleas'd to think this honeſt;
Did you know what ſhe was?

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: Not till this inſtant;
For had I known her, ſhe had been no priſoner.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: There, take the Maid, ſhe is at her own diſpoſe now,
And if there be ought elſe to do your honour
Any poor ſervice in—

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: I am vowed your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Your Father's here too, that's our only comfort,
And in a Country now, we ſtand free people,
Where Clodio has no power, be comforted.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: I fear ſome trick yet.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Be not ſo dejected.

sp.speaker: Gover.
sp.l: You muſt not be diſpleas'd; ſo farewel Lady.
Come Gentlemen; Captain, you muſt with me too,
I have a little buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: I attend your Lordſhip:
Now my way's free, and my hope's Lord again.

div.stage: Exeunt all but Hip. and Zab.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: D'ye jeer me now ye are going?
I may live yet— to make you howl both.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: You might have done; you had power then,
But now the chains are off, the command loſt,
And ſuch a ſtory they will make of this
To laugh out lazie time.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: No means yet left me?
For now I burſt with anger: none to ſatisfie me?
No comfort? no revenge?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: You ſpeak too late;
You might have had all theſe, your uſeful ſervants,
Had you been wiſe, and ſuddain: what power, or will
Over her beauty, have you now? by violence
To conſtrain his love; ſhe is as free as you are,
And no law can impeach her liberty,
And whilſt ſhe is ſo, Arnoldo will deſpiſe you.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Either my love or anger muſt be ſatisfied,
Or I muſt dye.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: I have a way wou'd do it,
Wou'd do it yet, protect me from the Law.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: From any thing; thou knoweſt what power I have,
What mony, and what friends.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: 'Tis a deviliſh one:
But ſuch muſt now be us'd: walk in, I'le tell you;
And if you like it, if the Devil can do any thing—

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Devil, or what thou wilt, ſo I be ſatisfied. Ex.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: This is the rareſt and the luſtieſt fellow,
And ſo beſtirs himſelf—

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Give him breath Miſtreſs,
You'l melt him elſe.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: He does perform ſuch wonders—
The women are mad on him.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Give him breath I ſay;
The man is but a man, he muſt have breath.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: How many had he yeſterday?
And they paid bravely too.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: About fourteen,
But ſtill I cry give breath, ſpare him and have him:

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Five Dames to day; this was a ſmall ſtage,
He may endure five more.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Breath, breath I cry ſtill;
Body o' me give breath, the man's a loſt man elſe.
Feed him and give him breath.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Welcome Gentlewomen,
Y'are very welcome.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: We hear you have a luſty and well complexion'd fellow
That does rare tricks; my Siſter and my ſelf here,
Would trifle out an hour or two, ſo pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Jaques, conduct 'em in.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.l:
There's for your courteſie.
Ex. Jaq. and Gent.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Good pay ſtill, good round pay, this happy fellow
Will ſet me up again; he brings in gold
Faſter than I have leiſure to receive it.
O that his body were not fleſh and fading;
But I'le ſo pap him up— nothing too dear for him;
What a ſweet ſcent he has?— Now what news Jaques?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: He cannot laſt, I pity the poor man,
I ſuffer for him; two Coaches of young City dames,
And they drive as the Devil were in the wheels,
Are ready now to enter: and behind theſe
An old dead-palſied Lady in a Litter,
And ſhe makes all the haſte ſhe can: the man's loſt,
You may gather up his dry bones to make Nine-pins,
But for his fleſh.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Theſe are but eaſie labours
Yet, for I know he muſt have reſt.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: He muſt— you'll beat him off his legs elſe preſently.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: Go in, and bid him pleaſe himſelf, I am pleas'd too:
To morrow's a new day; but if he can
I would have him take pity o' the old Lady.
Alas 'tis charity.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I'le tell him all this,
And if he be not too fool hardy.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: How now?
What news with you?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: You muſt preſently
Shew all the art you have, and for my Lady.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: She may command.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: You muſt not dream nor triſte.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Which way?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: A ſpell you muſt prepare, a powerful one,
Peruſe but theſe directions, you ſhall find all;
There is the picture too, be quick, and faithful,
And do it with that ſtrength—when 'tis perform'd,
Pitch your reward at what you pleaſe, you have it.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: I'le do my beſt, and ſuddenly: but hark ye,
Will you never lye at home again?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Excuſe me,
I have too much buſineſs yet.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: I am right glad on't.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Think on your buſineſs, ſo farewel.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: I'le do it.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Within this hour I'le viſit you again
And give you greater lights.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: I ſhall obſerve ye;
This brings a brave reward, bravely I'le do it,
And all the hidden art I have, expreſs in't.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Now do I look as if I were Crow-trodden,
Eye, how my hams ſhrink under me! O me,
I am broken winded too; is this a life?
Is this the recreation I have aim'd at?
I had a body once, a handſome body,
And wholeſome too. Now I appear like a raſcal,
That had been hung a year or two in Gibbets.
Place me before a Cannon, 'tis a pleaſure;
Stretch me upon a Rack, a recreation;
But women? women? O the Devil! women?

Curt ••
Gul • was never half ſo dangerous.
Is there no way to find the Trap-door again,
And fall into the Cella • , and be taken?
No lucky fortune to direct me that way?
No Gallies to be got, nor yet no Gallows?
For I fear nothing now, no earthly thing
But theſe unſatisfied Men l •• ches, women.
How deviliſhly my bones ake! O the old Lady!
I have a kind of waiting woman lyes croſs my back too,
O how ſhe ſtings! no treaſon to deliver me?
Now what are you? do you mock me?
No Sir, no;
We were your Predeceſſors in this place.
And come to ſee you bear up.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Good Gentlemen;
You ſeem to have a ſnuffing in your head Sir,
A parlous ſnuffing, but this ſame dampiſh air—
A dampiſh air indeed.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Blow your face tenderly,
Your noſe will ne're endure it: mercy o' me,
What are men chang'd to here? is my noſe faſt yet?
Me thinks it ſhakes i'th' hilts: pray tell me gentlemen,
How long is't ſince you flouriſht here?
Not long ſince.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Move your ſelf eaſily, I ſee you are tender,
No • long endured.
The labour was ſo much Sir,
And ſo few to perform it

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Muſt I come to this?
And draw my legs after me like a lame Dog?
I cannot run away, I am too feeble:
Will you ſue for this place again Gentlemen?
No truly Sir, the place has been too warm for our complexions.
We have enough on't, reſt you merry Sir,
We came but to congratulate your fortune,
You have abundance.
Bear your fortune ſoberly,

And ſo we leave you to the next fair Lady.
Ex. the 3

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Stay but a little, and I'le meet you Gentlemen,
At the next Hoſpital: there's no living thus,
Nor am I able to endure it longer,
With all the helps and heats that can be given me,
I am at my trot already: they are fair and young
Moſt of the women that repair unto me,
But they ſtick on like Burs, ſhake me like Feathers.
More Women yet?
Would I were honeſtly married
To any thing that had but half a face,
And not a groat to keep her, nor a ſmock,
That I might be civilly merry when I pleaſed,
Rather than labouring in theſe Fulling mills.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: By this the ſpell begins to work: you are luſty,
I ſee you bear up bravely yet.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Do you hear Lady,
Do not make a game-bear of me, to play me hourly,
And fling on all your whelps; it would not hold;
Play me with ſome diſcretion; to day one courſe,
And two dayes hence another.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: If you be ſo angry
Pay back the mony I redeem'd you at
And take your courſe, I can have men enough:
You have coſt me a hundred crowns ſince you came hither,
In Broths and ſtrengthing Candles; till you do pay me,
If you will eat and live, you ſhall endeavour,
I'le chain you to't elſe.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Make me a Dog kennel,
I'le keep your houſe and bark, and feed on bare bones,
And be whipt out o'doors,
Do you mark me Lady? whipt,
I'le cat old ſhoes.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: In this houſe I am told
There is a ſtranger, of a goodly perſon,
And ſuch a one there was; if I could ſee him,
I yet remember him.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Your buſineſs Sir,
If it be for a woman, ye are couzen'd,
I keep none here. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Certain this is the Gentleman;
The very ſame.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Death, if I had but mony,
Or any friend to bring me from this bondage,
I would Threſh, ſet up a Coblers ſhop, keep Hogs,
And feed with 'em, ſell Tinder-boxes,
And Knights of Ginger-bread, Thatch for three
Half pence a day, and think it Lordly,
From this baſe Stallion trade: why does he eye me,
Eye me ſo narrowly?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: It ſeems you are troubled Sir,
I heard you ſpeak of want.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: 'Tis better hearing
Far, than relieving Sir.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I do not think ſo, you know me not.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Not yet that I remember.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: You ſhall, and for your friend: I am beholding to ye,
Greatly beholding Sir; if you remember,
You fought with ſuch a man, they call'd Duarte,
A proud diſtemper'd man: he was my enemy,
My mortal foe, you ſlew him fairly, nobly.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Speak ſoftly Sir, you do not mean to betray me,
I wiſht the Gallows, now th'are coming fairly.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Be confident, for as I live, I love you,
And now you ſhall perceive it: for that ſervice,
Me, and my purſe command: there, take it to ye,
'Tis gold, and no ſmall ſum, a thouſand Duckets,
Supply your want.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: But do you do this faithfully?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: If I mean ill, ſpit in my face and kick me:
In what elſe I may ſerve you, Sir—

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I thank you,
This is as ſtrange to me as Knights adventures.
I have a project, 'tis an honeſt one,
And now I'le tempt my fortune.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Truſt me with it.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: You are ſo good and honeſt I muſt truſt ye,
'Tis but to carry a letter to a Lady
That ſav'd my life once.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: That will be moſt thankful,
I will do't with all care.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Where are you, white-broth?
Now luſty blood,
Come in, and tell your mony:
'Tis ready here, no threats, nor no orations,
Nor prayers now.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: You do not mean to leave me.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I'le live in Hell ſooner than here, and cooler.
Come quickly come, diſpatch, this air's unwhoſom:
Quickly good Lady, quickly to't.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Well, ſince it muſt be,
The next I'le fetter faſter ſure, and cloſer.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: And pick his bones, as y'have done mine, pox take ye.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: At my lodging for a while, you ſhall be quartered,
And there take Phyſick for your health.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I thank ye,
I have found my Angel now too, if I can keep him.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: YOU like the Letter?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Yes, but I muſt tell you
You tempt a deſperate hazard, to ſollicite
The mother, (and the grieved one too, 'tis rumor'd)
Of him you ſlew ſo lately.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I have told you
Some proofs of her affection, and I know not
A nearer way to make her ſatisfaction
For a loſt Son, than ſpeedily to help her
To a good Husband; one that will beget
Both Sons and Daughters, if ſhe be not barren.
I have had a breathing now, and have recovered
What I loſt in my late ſervice, 'twas a hot one:
It fired and fired me; but all thanks to you Sir,
You have both freed and cool'd me.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: What is done Sir,
I thought well done, and was in that rewarded,
And therefore ſpare your thanks.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I'le no more Whoring:
This fencing 'twixt a pair of ſheets, more wears one
Than all the exerciſe in the world beſides.
To be drunk with good Canary, a meer Julip
Or like gourd-water to't; twenty Surfeits
Come ſhort of one nights work there. If I get this Lady
As ten to one I ſhall, I was ne're denied yet,
I will live wondrous honeſtly; walk before her
Gravely and demurely
And then inſtruct my family; you are ſad,
What do you muſe on Sir?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Truth I was thinking
What courſe to take for the delivery of your letter,
And now I have it: but ſaith did this Lady
(For do not gull your ſelf) for certain know,
You kill'd her Son?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Give me a Book I'le ſwear 't;
Denyed me to the Officers, that purſued me,
Brought me her ſelf to th' door, then gave me gold
To bear my charges, and ſhall I make doubt then
But that ſhe lov'd me? I am confident
Time having ta'ne her grief off, that I ſhall be
Moſt welcome to her: for then to have woo • d her
Had been unſeaſonable.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Well Sir, there's more mony,
To may you handſome; I'le about your buſineſs:
You know where you muſt ſtay?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: There you ſhall find me:
Would I could meet my Brother now, to know,
Whether the Jew, his Genius, or my Chriſtian,
Has prov'd the better friend. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: O who would truſt
Deceiving woman! or believe that one
