The beſt, and moſt Canoniz'd ever was
More than a ſeeming goodneſs? I could rail now
Againſt the ſex, and curſe it; but the theam
And way's too common: yet that Guiomar
My Mother; (nor let that forbid her to be
The wonder of our nation) ſhe that was
Mark'd out the great example, for all Matrons
Both Wife and Widow; ſhe that in my breeding
Expreſt the utmoſt of a Mothers care,
And tenderneſs to a Son; ſhe that yet feigns
Such ſorrow for me; good God, that this mother,
After all this, ſhould give up to a ſtranger,
The wreak ſhe ow'd her Son; I fear her honour.
That he was ſav'd, much joyes me, and grieve only
That ſhe was his preſerver. I'le try further,
And by this Engine, find whether the tears,
Of which ſhe is ſo prodigal, are for me,
Or us'd to cloak her baſe hypocriſie. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Are you aſſur'd the charm prevails?

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Do I live?
Or do you ſpeak to me? Now this very inſtant
Health takes its laſt leave of her; meager paleneſs
Like winter, nips the Roſes and the Lilies,
The Spring that youth, and love adorn'd her face with.
To force affection, is beyond our art,
For I have prov'd all means that hell has taught me,
Or the malice of a woman, which exceeds it,
To change Arnoldo's love, but to no purpoſe:
But for your bond-woman—

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Let her pine and dye;
She remov'd, which like a brighter Sun,
Obſcures my beams, I may ſhine out again,
And as I have been, be admir'd and ſought to:
How long has ſhe to live?

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Lady, before
The Sun twice riſe and ſet, be confident,
She is but dead; I know my Charm hath found her
Nor can the Governours Guard; her lovers tears;
Her Fathers ſorrow, or his power that freed her,
Defend her from it.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: All things have ſucceeded,
As you could wiſh; I ſaw her brought ſick home;
The image of pale death, ſtampt on her fore-head.
Let me adore this ſecond Hecate,
This great Commandreſs, of the fatal Siſters,
That as ſhe pleaſes, can cut ſhort, or lengthen
The thread of life.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Where was ſhe when the inchantment
Firſt ſeis'd upon her?

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Taking the freſh air,
In the company of the Governour, and Count Clodio,
Arnoldo too, was preſent with her Father,
When, in a moment (ſo the ſervants told me)
As ſhe was giving thanks to the Governour,
And Clodio, for her unexpected freedom,
As if ſhe had been blaſted, ſhe ſunk down,
To then amazement.

sp.speaker: Hip
sp.l: 'Tis thy maſter piece
Which I will ſo reward, that thou ſhalt fix here,
And with the hazard of thy life, no more
Make tryal of thy powerful Art; which known
Our Laws call death: off with this Magical Robe,
And be thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Stand cloſe, you ſhall hear more.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: You muſt have patience; all rage is vain now,
And piety forbids, that we ſhould queſtion
What is decreed above, or ask a reaſon
Why heaven determines this or that way of us.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Heaven has no hand in't; 'tis a work of hell.
Her life hath been ſo innocent, all her actions
So free from the ſuſpicion of crime,
As rather ſhe deſerves a Saints place here,
Than to endure, what now her ſweetneſs ſuffers.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Not for her fault, but mine Sir, Zenocia ſuffers:
The ſin I made, when I ſought to raſe down
Arnoldo's love, built on a Rock of truth,
Now to the height is puniſh'd. I profeſs,
Had he no birth, nor parts, the preſent ſorrow
He now expreſſes for her, does deſerve her
Above all Kings, though ſuch had been his rivals.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: All ancient ſtories, of the love of Husbands
To vertuous Wives, be now no more remembred.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: The tales of Turtles, ever be forgotten,
Or, for his ſake believ'd.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: I have heard, there has been
Between ſome married paits, ſuch ſympathy,
That th' Husband has felt really the throws
His Wife then teeming ſuffers, this true grief
Confirms, 'tis not impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: We ſhall find
Fit time for this hereafter; let's uſe now
All poſſible means to help her.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Care, nor coſt,
Nor what Phyſicians can do, ſhall be wanting;
Make uſe of any means or men.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l:
You are noble.
Exeunt Man. Clod. and Char.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Ten Colledges of Doctors ſhall not ſave her.
Her fate is in your hand.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Can I reſtore her?

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: If you command my Art.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: I'le dye my ſelf firſt.
And yet I'le go viſit her, and ſee
This miracle of ſorrow in Arnoldo:
And 'twere for me, I ſhould change places with her,
And dye moſt happy, ſuch a lovers tears
Were a rich monument, but too good for her,
Whoſe miſery I glory in: come Sulpitia,
You ſhall along with me, good Zabulon
Be not ſat off.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: I will attend you Madam. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I have ſerv'd you from my youth, and ever
You have found me faithful: that you live's a treaſure
I'le look up here; not ſhall it be let forth,
But when you give me warrant.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I rely
Upon thy ſaith; nay, no more proteſtations,
Too many of them will call that in queſtion,
Which now I doubt not: ſhe is there?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Alone too,
But take it on my life, your entertainment,
Appearing as you are, will be but courſe,
For the diſpleaſure I ſhall undergo
I am prepar'd.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l:
Leave me, I'le ſtand the hazard.
Exit Servant.
The ſilence that's obſerv'd, her cloſe retirements,
No viſitants admitted, not the day;
Theſe ſable colours, all ſigns of true ſorrow,
Or hers is deeply counterfeit. I'le look nearer,
Manners give leave— ſhe ſits upon the ground;
By heaven ſhe weeps; my picture in her hand too;
She kiſſes it and weeps again.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: There is no ſtarting back now Madam.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: Ha, another murderer! I'le not protect thee,
Though I have no more Sons.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Your pardon Lady,
There's no ſuch foul fact taints me.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: What makes thou here then?
Where are my ſervants, do none but my ſorrows
Attend upon me? ſpeak, what brought thee hither?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: A will to give you comfort.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: Thou art but a man.
And 'tis beyond a humane reach to do it,
If thou could raiſe the dead out of their graves,
Bid time run back, make me now what I was,
A happy Mother; gladly I would hear thee,
But that's impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Pleaſe you but read this;
You ſhall know better there, why I am ſent,
Than if I ſhould deliver it.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: From whom comes it?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: That will inſtruct you. I ſuſpect this ſtranger,
Yet ſhe ſpake ſomething that holds ſuch alliance
With his reports; I know not what to think on't;
What a frown was there? ſhe looks me through, & through,
Now reads again, now pauſes, and now ſmiles;
And yet there's more of anger in't than mirth,
Theſe are ſtrange changes; oh I underſtand it,
She's full of ſerious thoughts.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: You are juſt, you Heavens,
And never do forget to hear their prayers,
That truly pay their vows, the defer'd vengeance,
For you, and my words ſake ſo long defer'd,
Under which as a mountain my heart groans yet
When 'twas deſpair'd of, now is offer'd to me;
And if I loſe it, I am both wayes guilty.
The womans mask, diſſimulation help me.
Come hither friend, I am ſure you know the Gentleman,
That ſent theſe charms.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Charms Lady?

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: Theſe charms;
I well may call them ſo, they've won upon me,
More than ere letter did; thou art his friend,
(The confidence he has in thee, confirms it)
And therefore I'le be open breaſted to thee;
To hear of him, though yet I never ſaw him,
Was moſt deſir'd of all men; let me bluſh,
And then I'le ſay I love him.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: All men ſee,
In this a womans vertue.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: I expected
For the courteſie I did, long ſince to have ſeen him,
And though I then forbad it, you men know,
Between our hearts and tongues there's a large diſtance;
But I'le excuſe him, may be hitherto
He has forborn it, in reſpect my Son
Fell by his hand.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: And reaſon Lady.

sp.speaker: Gui.
sp.l: No, he did me a pleaſure in't, a riotous fellow,
And with that inſolent, not worth the owning;
I have indeed kept a long ſolemn ſorrow,
For my friends ſake partly; but eſpecially
For his long abſence.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: O the Devil.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Therefore
Bid him be ſpeedy; a Prieſt ſhall be ready
To tye the holy knot; this kiſs I ſend him,
Deliver that and bring him.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I am dumb:
A good cauſe I have now, and a good ſword,
And ſomething I ſhall do, I wait upon you. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Manuel, Charino, Arnoldo, Zenocia, born in a chair. 2 Doctors, Clodio.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Give her more air, ſhe dyes elſe.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: O thou dread power,
That mad'ſt this all, and of thy workmanſhip
This virgin wife, the Maſter piece, look down on her;
Let her minds virtues, cloth'd in this fair garment,
That worthily deſerves a better name
Than fleſh and bloud, now ſue, and prevail for her.
Or if thoſe are denyed, let innocence,
To which all paſſages in Heaven ſtand open,
Appear in her white robe, before thy throne;
And mediate for her: or if this age of ſin
Be worthy of a miracle, the Sun
In his diurnal progreſs never ſaw
So ſweet a ſubject to imploy it on.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Wonders are ceas'd Sir, we muſt work by means.

sp.speaker: Arno.
sp.l: 'Tis true, and ſuch reverend Phyſicians are;
To you thus low I fall then; ſo may you ever
Be ſtil'd the hands of Heaven, natures reſtorers;
Get wealth and honours; and by your ſucceſs,
In all your undertakings, propagate
Your great opinion in the world, as now
You uſe your ſaving art; for know good Gentlemen,
Beſides the fame, and all that I poſſeſs,
For a reward, poſterity ſhall ſtand
Indebted to you, for (as Heaven forbid it)
Should my Zenocia dye, robbing this age
Of all that's good or gracefull, times ſucceeding,
The ſtory of her pure life not yet perfect,
Will ſuffer in the want of her example.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Were all the world to periſh with her, we
Can do no more, than what art and experience
Give us aſſurance of, we have us'd all means
To find the cauſe of her diſeaſe, yet cannot;
How ſhould we then, promiſe the cure?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Away,
I did bely you, when I charg'd you with
The power of doing, ye are meer names only,
And even your beſt perfection, accidental;
What ever malady thou art, or Spirit,
As ſome hold all diſeaſes that afflict us,
As love already makes me ſenſible
Of half her ſufferings, eaſe her of her part,
And let me ſtand the butt of thy fell malice,
And I will ſwear th'art mercifull.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Your hand Lady;
What a ſtrange heat is here? bring ſome warm water.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: She ſhall uſe nothing that is yours; my ſorrow
Provides her of a better bath, my tears
Shall do that office.

sp.speaker: Zeno.
sp.l: O my beſt Arnoldo!
The trueſt of all lovers! I would live
Were heaven ſo pleas'd, but to reward your ſorrow
With my true ſervice; but ſince that's denied me,
May you live long and happy: do not ſuffer
(By your affection to me I conjure you)
My ſickneſs to infect you; though much love
Makes you too ſubject to it.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: In this only
Zenocia wrongs her ſervant; can the body
Subſiſt, the Soul departed? 'tis as eaſie
As I to live without you; I am your husband,
And long have been ſo, though our adverſe fortune,
•• ndying us from one hazard to another,
Would never grant me ſo much happineſs,
As to pay a husbands debt; deſpite of fortune,
In death I'le follow you, and guard mine own;
And there enjoy what here my fate forbids me.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: So true a ſorrow, and ſo feelingly
Expreſt, I never read of.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: I am ſtruck
With wonder to behold it, as with pity

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: If you that are a ſtranger, ſuffer for them,
Being tied no further than humanity
Leads you to ſoft compaſſion; think great Sir,
What of neceſſity I muſt endure,
That am a Father?

div.stage: Hippolyta, Zabulon, and Sulpitia at the door.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Wait me there, I hold it
Unfit to have you ſeen; as I find cauſe,
You ſhall proceed.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: You are welcom Lady.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Sir, I come to do a charitable office,
How does the patient?

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: You may enquire
Of more than one; for two are ſick, and deadly,
He languiſhes in her, her health's deſpair'd of,
And in hers, his.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſtrange ſpectacle,
With what a patience they ſit unmov'd?
Are they not dead already?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: By her pulſe,
She cannot laſt a day.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Oh by that ſummons,
I know my time too!

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Look to the man.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Apply
Your Art, to ſave the Lady, preſerve her,
A town is your reward.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: I'le treble it,
In ready gold, if you reſtore Arnoldo;
For in his death I dye too.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Without her
I am no more.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Are you there Madam? now
You may feaſt on my miſeries; my coldneſs
In anſwering your affections, or hardneſs,
Give it what name you pleaſe, you are reveng'd of;
For now you may perceive, our thred of life
Was ſpun together, and the poor Arnoldo
Made only to enjoy the beſt Zenocia,
And not to ſerve the uſe of any other;
And in that ſhe may equal; my Lord Clodio
Had long ſince elſe enjoyed her, nor could I
Have been ſo blind, as not to ſee your great
And many excellencies far, far beyond
Or my deſervings, or my hopes; we are now
Going our lateſt journey, and together,
Our only comfort we deſire, pray give it,
Your charity to our aſhes, ſuch we muſt be,
And not to curſe our memories.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: I am much mov'd.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: I am wholly overcome, all love to women
Farewell for ever; ere you dye, your pardon;
And yours Sir; had ſhe many years to live,
Perhaps I might look on her, as a Brother,
But as a lover never; and ſince all
Your ſad misfortunes had original
From the barbarous Cuſtom practis'd in my Country,
Heaven witneſs, for your ſake I here releaſe it;
So to your memory, chaſte Wives and Virgins
Shall ever pay their vowes. I give her to you;
And wiſh, ſhe were ſo now, as when my luſt
Forc'd you to quit the Country.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: It is in vain
To ſtrive with deſtiny, here my dotage ends,
Look up Zenocia, health in me ſpeaks to you;
She gives him to you, that by divers ways,
So long has kept him from you: and repent not,
That you were once my ſervant, for which health
In recompence of what I made you ſuffer,
The hundred thouſand Crowns, the City owes me,
Shall be your dower.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: 'Tis a magnificent gift,
Had it been timely given.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: It is believe it, Sulpitia.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Quick, undoe the charm;
Ask not a reaſon why; let it ſuffice,
It is my will.

sp.speaker: Sulp.
sp.l: Which I obey and gladly.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Is to be married, ſayeſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: So ſhe ſayes Sir,
And does deſire your preſence. They are born off in chairs.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: And tell her I'le come.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Pray carry them to their reſt; for though already,
They do appear as dead, let my life pay for't,
If they recover not.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: What you have warranted,
Aſſure your ſelf, will be expected from you;
Look to them carefully; and till the tryal,—

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Which ſhall not be above four hours.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Let me
Intreat your companies: there is ſomething
Of weight invites me hence.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We'll wait upon you. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: You underſtand what my directions are,
And what they guide you to; the faithfull promiſe
You have made me all.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We do and will perform it.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: The Governour will not fail to be here preſently;
Retire a while, till you ſhall find occaſion,
And bring me word, when they arrive.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Wee ſhall Madam.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Only ſtay you to entertain.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: I am ready.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: I wonder at the bold, and practis'd malice,
Men ever have o' foot againſt our honours,
That nothing we can do, never ſo vertuous,
No ſhape put on ſo pious, no not think
What a good is, be that good ne're ſo noble,
Never ſo laden with admir'd example,
But ſtill we end in luſt; our aims, our actions,
Nay, even our charities, with luſt are branded;
Why ſhould this ſtranger elſe, this wretched ſtranger,
Whoſe life I ſav'd at what dear price ſticks here yet,
Why ſhould he hope? he was not here an hour,
And certainly in that time, I may ſwear it
I gave him no looſe look, I had no reaſon;
Unleſs my tears were flames, my curſes courtſhips;
The killing of my Son, a kindneſs to me.
Why ſhould he ſend to me, or with what ſafety
(Examining the ruine he had wrought me)
Though at that time, my pious pity found him,
And my word fixt; I am troubled, ſtrongly troubled.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The Gentlemen are come.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Then bid 'em welcom—I muſt retire. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You are welcom Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I thank you friend, I would ſpeak with your Lady.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I'le let her underſtand.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: It ſhall beſit you.

How do I look Sir, in this handſome trim?
Exit Servant.
Me thinks I am wondrous brave.

sp.speaker: Duar.
sp.l: You are very decent.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Theſe by themſelves, without more helps of nature,
Would ſet a woman hard; I know 'em all,
And where their firſt aims light; I'le lay my head on't,
I'le take her eye, as ſoon as ſhe looks on me,
And if I come to ſpeak once, woe be to her,
I have her in a nooze, ſhe cannot ſcape me;
I have their ſeveral laſts.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: You are throughly ſtudied,
But tell me Sir, being unacquainted with her,
As you confeſs you are—

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: That's not an hours work,
I'le make a Nun forget her beads in two hours.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: She being ſet in years, next none of thoſe luſters
Appearing in her eye, that warm the fancy;
Nor nothing in her face, but handſom ruines.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I love old ſtories: thoſe live believ'd, Authentique,
When 20. of your modern faces are call'd in,
For new opinion, paintings, and corruptions;
Give me an old confirm'd face; beſides ſhe ſav'd me,
She ſav'd my life, have I not cauſe to love her?
She's rich and of a conſtant ſtate, a fair one,
Have I not cauſe to wooe her? I have tryed ſufficient
All your young Phillies, I think this back has try'd 'em,
And ſmarted for it too: they run away with me,
Take bitt between the teeth, and play the Devils;
A ſtaied pace now becomes my years; a ſure one,
Where I may ſit and crack no girths.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: How miſerable,
If my Mother ſhould confirm, what I ſuſpect now,
Beyond all humane cure were my condition!
Then I ſhall wiſh, this body had been ſo too.
Here comes the Lady Sir.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Excellent Lady,
To ſhew I am a creature, bound to your ſervice,
And only yours —

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Keep at that diſtance Sir;
For if you ſtir —

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I am obedient.
She has found already, I am for her turn;
With what a greedy hawks eye ſhe beholds me?
Mark how ſhe muſters all my parts.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: A goodly Gentleman,
Of a more manly ſet, I never look'd on.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Mark, mark her eyes ſtill; mark but the carriage of 'em.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: How happy am I now, ſince my Son fell,
He fell not by a baſe unnoble hand?
As that ſtill troubled me; how far more happy
Shall my revenge be, ſince the Sacrifice,
I offer to his grave, ſhall be both worthy
A Sons untimely loſs, and a Mothers ſorrow?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Sir, I am made believe it; ſhe is mine own,
I told you what a ſpell I carried with me,
All this time does ſhe ſpend in contemplation
Of that unmatch'd delight: I ſhall be thankfull to ye;
And if you pleaſe to know my houſe, to uſe it;
To take it for your own.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Who waits without there?

div.stage: Enter Guard, and Servants, they ſeize upon Rut. and bind him.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: How now? what means this, Lady?

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Bind him faſt.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Are theſe the bride-laces you prepare for me?
The colours that you give?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: Fye Gentle Lady,
This is not noble dealing.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Be you ſatisfied,
If ſeems you are a ſtranger to this meaning,
You ſhall not be ſo long.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Do you call this wooing—Is there no end of womens perſecutions?
Muſt I needs fool into mine own deſtruction?
Have I not had fair warnings, and enough too?
Still pick the Devils teeth? you are not mad Lady;
Do I come fairly, and like a Gentleman,
To offer you that honour?

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: You are deceiv'd Sir,

Yo •
• ome beſotted, to your own deſtruction!
I ſent not for you; what honour can ye add to me,
That brake that ſtaff of honour, my age lean'd on?
That rob'd me of that right, made me a Mother?
Hear me thou wretched man, hear me with terrour,
And let thine own bold folly ſhake thy Soul,
Hear me pronounce thy death, that now hangs o're thee,
Thou deſperate fool; who bad thee ſeek this ruine?
What mad unmanly fate, made thee diſcover
Thy curſed face to me again? was't not enough
To have the fair protection of my houſe,
When miſery and juſtice cloſe purſued thee?
When thine own bloudy ſword, cryed out againſt thee,
Hatcht in the life of him? yet I forgave thee.
My hoſpitable word, even when I ſaw
The goodlieſt branch of all my blood lopt from me,
Did I not ſeal ſtill to thee?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I am gone.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: And when thou went'ſt, to Imp thy miſerie,
Did I not give thee means? but hark ungratefull,
Was it not thus? to hide thy face and fly me?
To keep thy name for ever from my memory?
Thy curſed blood and kindred? did I not ſwear then,
If ever, (in this wretched life thou haſt left me,
Short and unfortunate,) I ſaw thee again,
Or came but to the knowledge, where thou wandredſt,
To call my vow back, and purſue with vengeance
With all the miſeries a Mother ſuffers?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I was born to be hang'd, there's no avoiding it.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: And dar'ſt thou with this impudence appear here?
VValk like the winding ſheet my Son was put in,
Stand with thoſe wounds?

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: I am happy now again;
Happy the hour I fell, to find a Mother,
So pious, good, and excellent in ſorrows.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The Governour's come in.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: O let him enter.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I have fool'd my ſelf a fair thred of all my fortunes,
This ſtrikes me moſt; not that I fear to periſh,
But that this unmannerly boldneſs has brought me to it.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Are theſe fit preparations for a wedding Lady?
I came prepar'd a gueſt.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: O give me juſtice;
As ever you will leave a vertuous name,
Do juſtice, juſtice, Sir.

sp.speaker: Gove.
sp.l: You need not ask it,
I am bound to it.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Juſtice upon this man
That kill'd my Son.

sp.speaker: Gove.
sp.l: Do you confeſs the act?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

l.hi: Rutilio?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: 'Tis the ſame.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: How fell he thus?
Here will be ſorrow for the good Arnoldo.

sp.speaker: Gove.
sp.l: Take heed Sir what you ſay.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I have weigh'd it well,
I am the man, nor is it life I ſtart at;
Only I am unhappy I am poor,
Poor in expence of lives, there I am wretched,
That I have not two lives lent me for his ſacrifice;
One for her Son, another for her ſorrows.
Excellent Lady, now rejoyce again,
For though I cannot think, y'are pleas'd in blood,
Nor with that greedy thirſt purſue your vengeance;
The tenderneſs, even in thoſe tears denies that;
Yet let the world believe, you lov'd Duarte;
The unmatcht courteſies you have done my miſeries,
Without this forfeit to the law, would charge me
To tender you this life, and proud 'twould pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Shall I have juſtice?

sp.speaker: Gover.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: I'le ask it for ye,
I'le follow it my ſelf, againſt my ſelf.
Sir, 'Tis moſt ſit I dye; diſpatch it quickly,
The monſtrous burthen of that grief ſhe labours with
Had I a thouſand lives, I' • give 'em all,
Before I would draw one tear more from that vertue.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Be not too cruel Sir, and yet his bold ſword—
But his life cannot reſtore that, he's a man too—
Of a fair promiſe, but alas my Son's dead;
If I have juſtice, muſt it kill hi •

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: If I have not, it kills me, ſtrong and goodly!
Why ſhould he periſh too?

sp.speaker: Gover.
sp.l: It lies in your power,
You only may accuſe him, or may quit him.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: Be there no other witneſſes?

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Not any.
And if I ſave him, will not the world proclaim,
I have forgot a Son, to ſave a murderer?
And yet he looks not like one, he looks manly.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Pity ſo brave a Gentleman ſhould periſh.
She cannot be ſo hard, ſo cruel hearted.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Will you pronounce? yet ſtay a little Sir.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Rid your ſelf, Lady, of this miſery;
And let me go, I do but breed more tempeſts,
With which you are already too much ſhaken.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: Do now, pronounce; I will not hear,

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: You ſhall not,
Yet turn and ſee good Madam.

sp.speaker: Gove.
sp.l: Do not wonder.
'Tis he, reſtor'd again, thank the good Doctor,
Pray do not ſtand amaz'd, it is Duarte;
Is well, is ſafe again.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: O my ſweet Son,
I will not preſs my wonder now with queſtions—
Sir, I am ſorry for that cruelty,
I urg'd againſt you.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Madam, it was but juſtice.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: 'Tis true, the Doctor heal'd this body again,
But this man heal'd my ſoul, made my minde perfect,
The good ſharp leſſons his ſword read to me, ſav'd me;
For which, if you lov'd me, dear Mother,
Honour and love this man.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: You ſent this letter?

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: My boldneſs makes me bluſh now.

sp.speaker: Guio.
sp.l: I'le wipe off that,
And with this kiſs, I take you for my husband,
Your wooing's done Sir; I believe you love me,
And that's the wealth I look for now.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: You have it.

sp.speaker: Dua.
sp.l: You have ended my deſire to all my wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Now 'tis a wedding again. And if Hippolyta
Make good, what with the hazard of her life,
She undertook, the evening will ſet clear
sp.stage: Enter Hippolyta, leading Leopold, Arnoldo, Zenocia, in either hand, Zabulon, Sulpitia.
sp.l: After a ſtormy day.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Here comes the Lady.

sp.speaker: Clod.
sp.l: With fair Zenocia,
Health with life again
Reſtor'd unto her.

sp.speaker: Zen.
sp.l: The gift of her goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Let us embrace, I am of your order too,
And though I once deſpair'd of women, now
I find they reliſh much of Scorpions,
For both have ſtings, and both can hurt, and cure too;
But what have been your fortunes?

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Wee'l defer
Our ſtory, and at time more ſit, relate it.
Now all that reverence vertue, and in that
Zenocias conſtancy, and perfect love,
Or for her ſake Arnoldo, join with us
In th' honour of this Lady.
She deſerves it.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Hippolytas life ſhall make that good hereafter,
Not will I alone better my ſelf but others:
For theſe whoſe wants perhaps have made their actions
Not altogether innocent, ſhall from me
Be ſo ſupplied, that need ſhall not compel them,
To any courſe of life, but what the law
Shall give allowance to.

sp.speaker: Zab.
sp.l: Sulpitia, Your Ladiſhips creatures.

sp.speaker: R t.
sp.l: Be ſo, and no more you man-huckſter.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: And worthy Leopold, you that with ſuch fervour,
So long have ſought me, and in that deſerv'd me,
Shall now find full reward for all your travels,
Which you have made more dear by patient ſufferance.
And though my violent dotage did tranſport me,
Beyond thoſe bounds, my modeſty ſhould have kept in,
Though my deſires were looſe, from unchaſt art
Heaven knows I am free.

sp.speaker: Leop.
sp.l: The thought of that's dead to me;
I gladly take your offer.

sp.speaker: Rut.
sp.l: Do ſo Sir,
A piece of crackt gold ever will weigh down
Silver that's whole.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You ſhall be all my gueſts,
I muſt not be denyed.

sp.speaker: Arn.
sp.l: Come my Zenocia.
Our bark at length has found a quiet harbour;
And the unſpotted progreſs of our loves
Ends not alone in ſafety, but reward,
To inſtruct others, by our fair example;
That though good purpoſes are long withſtood,

The hand of Heaven ſtill guides ſuch as are good.
Ex • o •••

div.head: The Prologue.
div.l: SO free this workes, Gentlemen, from offence,
That we are confident, it needs no defence
From us, or from the Poets—we dare look
On any man, that brings his Table-book
To write down, what again he may repeat
At ſome great Table, to deſerve his meat.
Let ſuch come ſwell'd with malice, to apply
What is mirth here, there for an injurie.
Nor Lord, nor Lady we have tax'd; nor State,
Nor any private perſon, their poor hate
Will be ſtare'd here, for envy ſhall not finde
One touch that may be wreſted to her minde.
And yet deſpair not, Gentlemen, The play
Is quick and witty; ſo the Poets ſay,
And we believe them; the plot neat, and new,
• aſ •• on'd like thoſe, that are approv'd by you.
Only 'twill crave attention, in the moſt;
Becauſe one point unmark'd, the whole is loſt.
Hear firſt then, and judge after, and be free,
And as our cauſe is, let our cenſure be.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: WHY there ſhould be an Epilogue to a play,
I know no cauſe: the old and uſuall way,
For which they were made, was to entreat the grace
Of ſuch as were ſpectators in this place,
And time, 'tis to no purpoſe; for I know
What you reſolve already to beſtow,
Will not be alter'd, what ſo e're I ſay,
In the behalf of us, and of the Play;
Only to quit our doubts, if you think fit,
You may, or cry it up, or ſilence it.

div.head: Another Prologue for the Cuſtom of the Country.
div.l: WE wiſh, if it were poſſible, you knew
What we would give for this nights look, if new.
It being our ambition to delight
Our kind ſpectators with what's good, and right.
Yet ſo far know, and credit me, 'twas made
By ſuch, as were held work men in their Trade,
At a time too, when they as I divine,
Were truly merrie, and drank luſty wine,
The nectar of the Muſes; Some are here
I dare preſume, to whom it did appear
A well-drawn piece, which gave a lawfull birth
To paſſionate Scenes mixt with no vulgar mirth.
But unto ſuch to whom 'tis known by fame
From others, perhaps only by the name,
I am a ſuitor, that they would prepare
Sound palats, and then judge their bill of fare.
It were injuſtice to decry this now
For being like'd before, you may allow
(Your candor ſafe) what's taught in the old ſchools,
All ſuch as liv'd before you, were not fools.

div.head: The Epilogue.
div.l: I Spake much in the Prologue for the Play,
To its deſert I hope, yet you might ſay
Should I change now from that, which then was meant,
Or in a ſyllable grow leſs confident,
I were weak-hearted. I am ſtill the ſame
In my opinion, and forbear to frame
Qualification, or excuſe: If you
Concur with me, and hold my judgement true,
Shew it with any ſign, and from this place,
Or ſend me off exploded, or with grace.

list.item: Briſac, a Juſtice, Brother to Miramont.

q.l: Would'ſt thou all Wit, all Comick Art ſurvey?
Read here and wonder; Fletcher writ the Play.

sp.speaker: Lewis.
sp.p: NAY, I muſt walk you farther.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I am tir'd, Sir, and ne'er ſhall foot it home.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: 'Tis for your health; the want of exerciſe takes from your Beauties, and ſloth dries up your ſweetneſs: That you are my only Daughter and my Heir, is granted; and you in thankfulneſs muſt needs acknowledge, you ever find me an indulgent Father, and open handed.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Nor can you tax me, Sir, I hope, for want of duty to deſerve theſe favours from you.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: No, my Angellina, I love and cheriſh thy obedience to me, which my care to advance thee ſhall confirm: all that I aim at, is, to win thee from the practice of an idle fooliſh ſtate, us'd by great Women, who think any labour (though in the ſervice of themſelves) a blemiſh to their fair fortunes.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Make me underſtand, Sir, what 'tis you point at.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: At the cuſtom, how Virgins of wealthy Families waſte their youth; after a long ſleep, when you wake, your Woman preſents your Breakfaſt, then you ſleep again, then riſe, and being trimm'd up by other hands, y'are led to Dinner, and that ended, either to Cards or to your Couch, (as if you were born without motion) after this to Supper, and then to Bed: and ſo your life runs round without variety or action, Daughter.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: Here's a learned Lecture!

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Frow this idleneſs, Diſeaſes, both in body and in mind, grow ſtrong upon you; where a ſtirring nature, with wholeſome exerciſe, guards both from danger: I'd have thee riſe with the Sun, walk, dance, or hunt, viſit the Groves and Springs, and learn the vertue of Plants and Simples: Do this moderately, and thou ſhalt not, with eating Chalk, or Coles, Leather and Oatmeal, and ſuch other traſh, fall into the Green-ſickneſs.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: With your pardon (were you but pleas'd to miniſter it) I could preſcribe a Remedy for my Lady's health, and her delight too, far tranſcending thoſe your Lordſhip but now mention'd.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: What is it, Sylvia?

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: What is't! a noble Husband; in that word, a noble Husband, all content of Woman is wholly comprehended; He will rouſe her, as you ſay, with the Sun; and ſo pipe to her, as ſhe will dance, ne'er doubt it; and hunt with her, upon occaſion, until both be weary; and then the knowledge of your Plants and Simples, as I take it, were ſuperfluous. A loving, and, but add to it, a gameſome Bedfellow, being the ſure Phyſician.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Well ſaid, Wench.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p:
And who gave you Commiſſion to deliver your
Verdict, Minion?

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: I deſerve a Fee, and not a frown, dear Madam: I but ſpeak her thoughts, my Lord, and what her modeſty refuſes to give voice to. Shew no mercy to a Maidenhead of fourteen, but off with't: let her loſe no time, Sir; Fathers that deny their Daughters lawful pleaſures, when 〈◊〉 for them, in ſome kinds edge their appetites to taſte of the fruit that is forbidden.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: 'Tis well urg'd, and I approve it: No more bluſhing, Girl, thy Woman hath ſpoke truth, and ſo prevented what I meant to move to thee. There dwells near us a Gentleman of bloud, Monſieur Briſac, of a fair Eſtate, ſix thouſand Crowns per annum, the happy Father of two hopeful Sons, of different breeding; the Elder, a meer Scholar; the younger, a quaint Courtier.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Sir, I know them by publick fame, though yet I never ſaw them; and that oppos'd antipathy between their various diſpoſitions, renders them the general diſcourſe and argument; one part inclining to the Scholar Charles, the other ſide preferring Euſtace, as a man compleat in Courtſhip.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: And which way (if of theſe two you were to chuſe a Husband) doth your affection ſway you?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: To be plain Sir, (ſince you will teach me boldneſs) as they are ſimply themſelves, to neither: let a Courtier be never ſo exact, let him be bleſs'd with all parts that yield him to a Virgin gracious; if he depend on others, and ſtand not on his own bottoms, though he have the means to bring his Miſtris to a Maſque, or by conveyance from ſome great ones lips, to taſte ſuch favour from the King: or grant he purchaſe precedency in the Court, to be ſworn a ſervant Extraordinary to the Queen; nay, though he live in expectation of ſome huge preferment in reverſion; if he want a preſent fortune, at the beſt thoſe are but glorious dreams, and only yield him a happineſs in poſſe, not in eſſe; nor can they fetch him Silks from the Mercer, nor diſcharge a Tailors Bill, not in full plenty (which ſtill preſerves a quiet Bed at home) maintain a Family.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Aptly conſider'd, and to my wiſh: But what's thy cenſure of the Scholar?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Troth (if he be nothing elſe) as of the Courtier, all his Songs and Sonnets, his Anagrams, Acroſticks, Epigrams, his deep and Philoſophical Diſcourſe of Nature's hidden Secrets, makes not up a perfect Husband; he can hardly borrow the Stars of the Celeſtial Crown to make me a Tire for my Head, nor Charles's Wain for a Coach, nor Ganymede for a Page, nor a rich Gown from Juno's Wardrobe, nor would I lie in (for I deſpair not once to be a Mother) under Heaven's ſpangled Canopy, or Banquet my Gueſts and Goſſips with imagin'd Nectar; pure Orleans would do better: No, no, Father, though I could be well pleas'd to have my Husband a Courtier, and a Scholar, young, and valiant; theſe are but gawdy nothings, if there be not ſomething to make a ſubſtance.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: And what is that?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: A full Eſtate, and that ſaid, I've ſaid all; and get me ſuch a one with theſe Additions, farewel Virginity, and welcome Wedlock.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: But where is ſuch a one to be met with, Daughter? A black Swan is more common; you may wear grey Treſſes e're we find him.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I am not ſo punctual in all Ceremonies, I will 'bate two or three of theſe good parts, before I'le dwell too long upon the choice.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: Only, my Lord, remember, that he be rich and active, for without theſe, the others yield no reliſh, but theſe perfect. You muſt bear with ſmall ſaults, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Merry Wench, and it becomes you well; I'le to Briſac, and try what may be done; i'th' mean time home, and feaſt thy thoughts with th'pleaſures of a Bride.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: Thoughts are but airy food, Sir, let her taſte them.

div.head: ACTUS I. SCENA II.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Unload part of the Library, and make room for th'other dozen of Carts; I'le ſtraight be with you

sp.speaker: Cook.
sp.p: Why, hath he more Books?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: More than ten Marts ſend over.

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: And can he tell their names?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Their names! he has 'em as perfect as his P ••• Noſter; but that's nothing, h'as read them over leaf by leaf three thouſand times; but here's the wonder, thoug • their weight would ſink a Spaniſh Carrock, without other Ballaſt, he carrieth them all in his head, and yet he wa •• upright.

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: Surely he has a ſtrong brain.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: If all thy pipes of Wine were fill'd with Books, made of the Barks of Trees, or Myſteries writ in old moth eaten Vellam, he would ſip thy Cellar quite dry, and ſtill be thirſty: Then for's Diet, he eats and digeſts more Volumes at a meal, than there would be Larks (though the Sky ſhould fall) devoured in a month in Paris. Yet fear not Sons o'the Buttery and Kitchin, though his learn'd ſtomach cannot be appeas'd; he'll ſeldom trouble you, his knowing ſtomach contemns your Black-Jacks, Butler, and you Flagons; and Cook, thy Boil'd, thy Roſt, thy Bak'd.

sp.speaker: Cook.
sp.p: How liveth he?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Not as other men do, few Princes fare like him; he breaks his faſt with Ariſtotle, dines with Tully, takes his watering with the Muſes, ſups with Livy, then walks a turn or two in Via Lactea, and (after ſix hours conference with the Stars) ſleeps with old Erra Pater.

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: This is admirable.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I'le tell you more hereafter. Here's my old Maſter, and another old ignorant Elder; I'le upon 'em.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: What, Andrew? welcome; where's my Charles? ſpeak, Andrew, where did'ſt thou leave thy Maſter?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Contemplating the number of the Sands in the High way, and from that, purpoſes to make a Judgment of the remainder in the Sea: he is, Sir, in ſerious ſtudy, and will loſe no minute, nor out of's pace to knowledge.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: This is ſtrange.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Yet he hath ſent his duty, Sir, before him in this fair Manuſcript.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: What have we here? Pot-hooks and Andirons!

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I much pity you, it is the Syrian Character, or the Arabick. Would you have it ſaid, ſo great and deep a Scholar as Mr Charles is, ſhould ask bleſſing in any Chriſtian Language? Were it Greek I could interpret for you, but indeed I'm gone no farther.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: And in Greek you can lie with your ſmug Wife Lilly.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: If I keep her from your French Dialect, as I hope I ſhall, Sir; however ſhe is your Land • eſs, ſhe ſhall put you to the charge of no more Soap than uſual for th'waſhing of your Sheets.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Take in the Knave, and let him eat.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And drink too, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: And drink too Sir, and ſee your Maſters Chamber ready for him.

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: Come, Dr Andrew, without Diſputation thou ſhalt Commence i'the Cellar.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I had rather Commence on a cold Bak'd meat.

sp.speaker: Cook.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt ha't, Boy.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
Good Monſieur Lewis, I eſteem my ſelf much honour'd in your clear intent, to joyn our ancient Families, and make them one; and 'twill take from my age and cares, to live and ſee what you have purpos'd but in act, of which your viſit at this preſent is a hopeful Omen; I each minute expecting the arrival of my Sons; I have not wrong d their Birth for want of Means and Education, to ſhape them to that courſe each was addicted; and therefore that we may proceed diſcreetly, ſince what's concluded raſhly ſeldom
• roſpers, you firſt ſhall take a ſtrict peruſal of them, and • en from your allowance, your fair Daughter my faſhion • er affection.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p:
Monſieur Briſac, you offer fair and nobly, and I'le • ot you in the ſame line of Honour; and I hope, being • eſt but with one Daughter, I ſhall not appear imperti
• ently curious, though with my utmoſt vigilance and ſtudy, labour to beſtow her to her worth: Let others ſpeak her • orm, and future Fortune from me deſcending to her; • in that ſit down with ſilence.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
You may, my Lord, ſecurely, ſince Fame aloud • roclaimeth her perfections, commanding all mens tongues 〈◊〉 ſing her praiſes; ſhould I ſay more, you well might cen
•• re me (what yet I never was) a Flatterer. What trampling's • hat without of Horſes?

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: Sir, my young Maſters are newly alighted.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Sir, now obſerve their ſeveral diſpoſitions.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Bid my Supſiſer carry my Hackney to the Butt'ry, • nd give him his Bever; it is a civil and ſober Beaſt, and • ill drink moderately; and that done, turn him into the Quadrangle.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: He cannot out of his Univerſity tone.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Lackey, take care our Courſers be well rubb'd, and •• oath'd; they have out-ſtripp'd the Wind in ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: I marry, Sir, there's metal in this young Fellow!
What a Sheep's look his elder Brother has!

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Your bleſſing, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Riſe, Charles, thou haſt it.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Sir, though it be unuſual in the Court, (ſince 'tis • he Courtiers garb) I bend my knee, and do expect what • ollows.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Courtly begg'd. My bleſſing, take it.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: (to Lew.) Your Lordſhip's vow'd adorer. What thing this Brother is! yet I'le vouchſafe him the new • alian ſhrug —
How clowniſhly the Book-worm does return it?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I'm glad ye are well. Reads.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Pray you be happy in the knowledge of this pair of • ccompliſh'd Monſieurs; they are Gallants that have ſeen • oth Tropicks.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I embrace their love.

sp.speaker: Egr.
sp.p: Which we'll repay with ſervulating.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: And will report your bounty in the Court.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
I pray you make deſerving uſe on't firſt, Euſtace,
• ive entertainment to your Friends; what's in my houſe is • heirs.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Which we'll make uſe of; let's warm our brains with half a dozen Healths, and then hang cold diſcourſe, for • e'll ſpeak Fire-works. Ex.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: What, at his Book already?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Fie, fle, Charles, no hour of interruption?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Plato differs from Socrates in this.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Come, lay them by; let them agree at leiſure.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Man's life, Sir, being ſo ſhort, and then the way • hat leads unto the knowledge of our ſelves, ſo long and • edious, each minute ſhould be precious.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: In our care to manage worldly buſineſs, you muſt • art with this Bookiſh contemplation, and prepare your • elf for action; to thrive in this Age is held the blame of • earning: You muſt ſtudy to know what part of my Land's • ood for the Plough, and what for Paſture; how to buy • nd ſell to the beſt advantage; how to cure my Oxen when • hey're o'er-grown with labour.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
I may do this from what I've read, Sir; for, what • oncerns Tillage, who better can deliver it than Virgil in • is Georgicks? and to cure your Herds, his Bucolicks is a Maſter-piece; but when he does deſcribe the Common
• ealth of Bees, their induſtry, and knowledge of the herbs from which they gather Honey, with their care to place it with decorum in the Hive; then Government among themſelves, their order in going forth, and coming loaden home; their obedience to their King, and his rewards to ſuch as labour, with his puniſhments only inflicted on the ſlothful Drone; I'm raviſh'd with it, and there reap my Harveſt, and there receive the gain my Cattle bring me, and there find Wax and Honey.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: And grow rich in your imagination; heyday, heyday! Georgicks, Bucolicks, and Bees! art mad?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: No, Sir, the knowledge of theſe guards me from it.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: But can you find among your bundle of Books (and put in all your Dictionaries that ſpeak all Tongues) what pleaſure they enjoy, that do embrace a well-ſhap'd wealthy Bride? Anſwer me that.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: 'Tis frequent, Sir, in Story, there I read of all kind of virtuous and vitious women; the antient Spartan Dames, and Roman Ladies, their Beauties and Deformities; and when I light upon a Portia or Cornelia, crown'd with ſtill flouriſhing leaves of truth and goodneſs; with ſuch a feeling I peruſe their Fortunes, as if I then had liv'd, and freely taſted their raviſhing ſweetneſs; at the preſent loving the whole Sex for their goodneſs and example. But on the contrary, when I look on a Clytemneſtra, or a Tullia; the firſt bath'd in her Husband bloud; the latter, without a touch of piety, driving on her Chariot o'er her Father's breathleſs Trunk, horrour invades my faculties; and comparing the multitudes o'th' guilty, with the few that did die Innocents, I deteſt and loath 'em as Ignorance or Atheiſm.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: You reſolve then ne'er to make payment of the debt you owe me.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: What debt, good Sir?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: A debt I paid my Father when I begat thee, and made him a Grandſire, which I expect from you.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: The Children, Sir, which I will leave to all poſterity, begot and brought up by my painful Studies, ſhall be my living Iſſue.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Very well; and I ſhall have a general Collection of all the quiddits from Adam to this time, to be my Granchild.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: And ſuch a one, I hope, Sir, as ſhall not ſhame the Family.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Nor will you take care of my Eſtate?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
But in my wiſhes; for know, Sir, that the wings on which my Soul is mounted, have long ſince born her 〈◊〉 high, to ſtoop to any Prey that ſoars not upwards 〈◊〉 and dunghil minds, compos'd of earth, in that 〈◊〉
•
lement fix all their happineſs; but purer Spirits 〈◊〉 and refin'd, ſhake off that clog of humane frailty; give 〈◊〉 leave t'enjoy my ſelf; that place that does contain my Books (the beſt Compaions) is to me a glorious Court, where hourly I converſe with the old Sages and Philoſophers, and ſometimes for variety, I confer with Kings and Emperors, and weigh their Counſels, calling their Victories (if unjuſtly got) unto a ſtrict accompt, and in my phancy, deface their ill-plac'd Statues; can I then part with ſuch conſtant pleaſures, to embrace uncertain vanities? No, be it your care t'augment your heap of wealth; it ſhall be mine t' increaſe in knowledge—Lights there for my Study—

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Was ever man that had reaſon thus tranſported from all ſenſe and feeling of his proper good? It vexes me, and if I found not comfort in my young Euſtace, I might well conclude my name were at a period!

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: He is indeed, Sir, the ſurer baſe to build on.

div.stage: Enter Euſtace, I gremont, Gowſy, and Andrew.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Sir.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Your ear in private.

sp.speaker: And
sp.p:
I ſuſpect my M ter has ſound harſh welcome, he's gone Supperleſs into his Study; could I find out the cauſe, it
may be borrowing of his Books, or ſo, I ſhall be ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: My duty ſhall, Sir, take any form you pleaſe; and in your motion to have me married, you cut off all dangers the v • olent heats of youth might bear me to.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: It is well anſwer'd.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Nor ſhall you, my Lord, for your fair Daughter ever find juſt cauſe to mourn your choice of me; the name of Husband, not the authority it carries in it, ſhall ever teach me to forget to be, as I am now, her Servant, and your Lordſhip's; and but that modeſty forbids, that I ſhould ſound the Trumpet of my own deſerts, I could ſay, my choice manners have been ſuch, as render me lov'd and remarkable to the Princes of the Blood.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: Nay, to the King.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: Nay to the King and Council.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Theſe are Court admirers, and ever echo him that bears the Bag. Though I be dull-ey'd, I ſee through this jugling.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Then for my hopes.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: Nay certainties.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: They ſtand as fair as any mans. What can there fall in compaſs of her wiſhes, which ſhe ſhall not be ſuddenly poſſeſs'd of? Loves ſhe Titles? by the grace and favour of my Princely Friends, I am what ſhe would have me.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: He ſpeaks well, and I believe him.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: I could wiſh I did ſo. Pray you a word, Sir. He's a proper Gentleman, and promiſes nothing, but what is poſſible. So far I will go with you; nay, I add, he hath won much upon me; and were he but one thing that his Brother is, the bargain were ſoon ſtruck up.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: What's that, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: The Heir.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Which he is not, and I truſt never ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Come, that ſhall breed no difference; you ſee Charles has given o'er the world; I'le undertake, and with much eaſe, to buy his Birth right of him for a Dry-fat of new Books; nor ſhall my ſtate alone make way for him, but my elder Brothers, who being iſſueleſs, to advance our name, I doubt not will add his. Your reſolution?

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: I'le firſt acquaint my Daughter with the proceedings; on theſe terms I am yours, as ſhe ſhall be, make you no ſcruple. Get the Writings ready, ſhe ſhall be tractable; to morrow we will hold a ſecond conference. Farewell noble Euſtace; and you brave Gallants.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Full increaſe of honour wait ever on your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: The Gout rather, and a perpetual Meagrim.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: You ſee, Euſtace, how I travel to poſſeſs you of a Fortune you were not born to; be you worthy of it: I'le furniſh you for a Suitor: viſit her, and proſper in't.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: She's mine, Sir, fear it not: in all my travels, I ne'er met a Virgin that could reſiſt my Courtſhip.
If it take now, we're made for ever, and will revel it.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: In tough Welſh Parſly, which, in our vulgar Tongue, is ſtrong Hempen Halters; my poor Maſter cozen'd, and I a looker on! If we have ſtudi'd our Majors and our Minors, Antecedents and Conſequents, to be concluded Coxcombs, w'have made a fair hand on't. I am glad I have found out all their plots, and their Conſpiracies; this ſhall t'old Monſieur Miramont, one, that though he cannot read a Proclamation, yet dotes on Learning, and loves my Maſter Charles for being a Scholar; I hear he's coming hither, I ſhall meet him; and if he be that old, rough, teſty blade he always us'd to be, I'le ring him ſuch a peal, as ſhall go near to ſhake their Belroom, peradventure beat'm, for he is fire and flax; and ſo have at him. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: NAY, Brother, Brother.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Pray, Sir, be not moved, I meddle with no buſineſs but mine own, and in mine own 'tis reaſon I ſhould govern.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: But how to govern then, and underſtand, Sir, and be as wiſe as y'are haſty, though you be my Brother, and from one bloud ſprung, I muſt tell ye heartily and home too.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: What, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: What I grieve to find, you are a fool, and an ol • fool, and that's two.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: We'll part'em, if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: No, they're entail'd to 'em. Seek to deprive an honeſt noble Spirit, your eldeſt Son, Sir, and your very Image, (but he's ſo like you, that he fares the worſe for't) becauſe, he loves his Book, and dotes on that, and only ſtudies how to know things excellent, above the reach of ſuch courſe Brains as yours, ſuch muddy Fancies, that never will know farther than when to cut your Vines, and cozen Merchants, and choak your hide-bound Tenants with mu • ty Harveſts.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: You go too faſt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: I'am not come to my pace yet. Becauſe h'has made his ſtudy all his pleaſure, and is retir'd into his Contemplation, not medling with the dirt and chaff of Nature, that makes the ſpirit of the mind mud too; therefore muſt he be flung from his inheritance? muſt he be diſpoſſeſs'd, and Monſieur Gingle-boy his younger Brother—

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: You forget your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Becauſe h'has been at Court, and learn'd new Tongues, and how to ſpeak a tedious piece of nothing; to vary his face as Sea-men do their compaſs, to worſhip Images of gold and ſilver, and fall before the She calves of the ſeaſon; therefore muſt he jump into his Brother's Land?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Have you done yet, and have you ſpoke enough it praiſe of Learning, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Never enough.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: But, Brother, do you know what Learning is?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: It is not to be a Juſtice of Peace as you are, and palter out your time i'th' penal Statutes. To hear the curious Tenets controverted between a Proteſtant Conſtable, and Jeſuite Cobler; to pick Natural Philoſophy o •• of Bawdry, when your Worſhip's pleas'd to correctifie a Lady; nor 'tis not the main Moral of blind Juſtice, (which is deep Learning) when your Worſhips Tenants bring a light cauſe, and heavy Hens before ye, both fat and feeble, a Gooſe or Pig; and then you'll ſit like equity with both hands weighing indifferently the ſtate o'th' queſtion. Theſe are your Quodlibets, but no Learning, Brother.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: You are ſo parlouſly in love with Learning, that I'd be glad to know what you underſtand, Brother; I'm ſure you have read all Ariſtotle.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Faith no; but I believe I have a learned faith, S •• , and that's it makes a Gentleman of my ſort; though I ca • ſpeak no Greek, I love the ſound of't, it goes ſo thund'ring as it conjur'd Devils: Charles ſpeaks it loftily, and if thee wert a man, or had'ſt but ever heard of Homers Iliads, Heſ •• d and the Greek Poets, thou wouldſt run mad, and hang th • ſelf for joy th'hadſt ſuch a Gentleman to be thy Son: O he has read ſuch things to me!

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: And you do underſtand 'em, Brother?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p:
I tell thee, No, that's not material; the ſoun • s ſufficient to confirm an honeſt man: Good Brother Briſ •• , does your young Courtier, that wears the fine Cloaths, an • is the excellent Gentleman, (the Traveller, the Soldier, as you think too) underſtand any other power than his Tailor? or knows what motion is more than an Horſe-race? Wh •• the Moon means, but to light him home from Taverns? o • the comfort of the Sun is, but to wear ſlaſh'd clothes in?
• nd muſt this piece of ignorance be popt up, becauſe 't can •• ſs the hand, and cry, ſweet Lady? Say it had been at
• ome, and ſeen the Reliques, drunk your Verdea Wine, • nd rid at Naples, brought home a Box of Venice Treacle • ith it, to cure young Wenches that have eaten Aſhes: Muſt this thing therefore?—

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Yes Sir, this thing muſt; I will not truſt my Land 〈◊〉 one ſo ſotted, ſo grown like a Diſeaſe unto his Study; • e that will fling off all occaſions and cares, to make him • nderſtand what ſtate is, and how to govern it, muſt, by • hat reaſon, be ſlung himſelf aſide from managing. My • ounger Boy is a fine Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: He is an Aſs, a piece of Ginger-bread, gilt over to • leaſe fooliſh Girls puppets.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: You are my elder Brother.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: So I had need, and have an elder Wit, thou'dſt • hame us all elſe. Go to, I ſay, Charles ſhall inherit.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
I ſay, no, unleſs Charles had a Soul to underſtand it; can he manage ſix thouſand Crowns a year out of the Me
• aphyſics? or can all his learn'd Aſtronomy look to my Vineyards? Can the drunken old Poets make up my Vines? (I know they can drink 'em) or your excellent Humaniſts • ell 'em the Merchants for my beſt advantage? Can Hiſto
• y cut my Hay, or get my Corn in? And can Geometry • end it in the Market? Shall I have my ſheep kept with a
• acobs-ſtaff now? I wonder you will magnifie this madman, you that are old, and ſhould underſtand.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p:
Should, ſay'ſt thou? thou monſtrous piece of ignorance in Office! thou that haſt no more knowledge than • hy Clerk infuſes, thy dapper Clerk, larded with ends of Latin, and he no more than cuſtom of offences. Thou un
• eprieveable Dunce! that thy formal Bandſtrings, thy Ring, nor pomander cannot expiate for, doſt thou tell me I ſhould? I'le poſe thy Worſhip in thine own Library and Almanack, which thou art daily poring on, to pick out days of iniquity to cozen fools in, and Full Moons to cut Cattle: doſt thou taint me, that have run over Story, Poetry, Humanity?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: As a cold nipping ſhadow does o'er cars of Corn, and leave 'em blaſted, put up your anger, what I'll do, • 'll do.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt not do.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I will.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Thou art an Aſs then, a dull old tedious Aſs; th' • art ten times worſe, and of leſs credit than Dunce Hollingſhead the Engliſhman, that writes of Shows and Sheriffs.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Well, take your pleaſure, here's one I muſt talk with.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Good-day, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Fair to you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: May I ſpeak w'ye?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: With all my heart, I was waiting on your goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Good morrow, Monſieur Miramont.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: O ſweet Sir, keep your good morrow to cool your Worſhips pottage; a couple of the worlds fools met together to raiſe up dirt and dunghils.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Are they drawn?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: They ſhall be ready, Sir, within theſe two hours; and Charles ſet his hand.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: 'Tis neceſſary; for he being a joint purchaſer, though your Eſtate was got by your own induſtry, unleſs he ſeal to the Conveyance, it can be of no validity.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: He ſhall be ready and do it willingly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: He ſhall be hang'd firſt.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I hope your Daughter likes.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: She loves him well, Sir; young Euſtace is a bait to catch a Woman, a budding ſpritely Fellow; y'are reſolv'd then, that all ſhall paſs from Charles?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: All, all, he's nothing; a bunch of Books ſhall be his Patrimony, and more than he can manage too.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p:
Will your Brother paſs over his Land to your ſon
• uſtace? you know he has no Heir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: He will be flead firſt, and Horſe-collars made of 's skin.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Let him alone, a wilful man; my Eſtate ſhall ſerve the turn, Sir. And how doe • your Da ••• ce • ?

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Ready for the hou • , and like a bluſhing Roſe that ſtays the pulling.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: To morrow then's the day.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Why then to morrow I'll bring the Girl; get you the Writings ready.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: But hark you, Mo ••••• , have you the virtuous conſcience to help to • ob an Heir, an Elder Brother, of that which Nature and the Law flings on him? You were your Father's eldeſt Son, I take it, and had his Land; would you had had his wit too, or his diſcretion, to conſider nobly, what 'tis to deal unworthily in theſe things; you'll ſay he's none of yours, he's his Son; and he will ſay, he is no Son to inherit above a ſhelf of Books: Why did he get him? why was he brought up to write and read, and know theſe things? why was he not like his Father, a dumb Juſtice? a flat dull piece of phlegm, ſhap'd like a man, a reverend Idol in a piece of Arras? Can you lay diſobedience, want of manners, or any capital crime to his charge?

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: I do not, nor do weigh your words, they bite not me, Sir; this man muſt anſwer.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I have don't already, and given ſufficient reaſon to ſecure me: and ſo good morrow, Brother, to your patience.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Good morrow, Monſieur Miramont.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p:
Good Night caps keep brains warm, or Maggots will breed in 'em. Well, Charles, thou ſhalt not want to buy thee Books yet, the faireſt in thy Study are my gift, and the Univerſity of Lovain, for thy ſake, hath taſted of my bounty; and to vex the old doting Fool thy Father, and thy Brother, they ſhall not ſhare a Sol •
of mine between them; nay more, I'll give thee eight thouſand Crowns a year, in ſome high ſtrain to write my Epitaph.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: How do I look now, my Elder Brother? Nay, 'tis a handſome Suit.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: All Courtly, Courtly.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I'll aſſure ye, Gentlemen, my Tailor has travel'd, and ſpeaks as lofty Language in his Bills too; the cover of an old Book would not ſhew thus. Fie, fie; what things theſe Academicks are! theſe Book-worms, how they look!

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: They're meer Images, no gentle motion or behaviour in 'em; they'll prattle ye of Primum Mobile, and tell a ſtory of the ſtate of Heaven, what Lords and Ladies govern in ſuch Houſes, and what wonders they do wh • n they meet together, and how they ſpit Snow, Fire, and Ha •• , like a Jugler, and make a noiſe when they are drunk, which we call Thunder.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: They are the ſneaking'ſt things, and the contemptibleſt; ſuch Small-beer brains, but ask 'em any thing out of the Element of their underſtanding, and they ſtand gaping like a roaſted Pig: do they know what a Court is, of a Council, or how the affairs of Chriſtendom are manag'd? Do they know any thing but a tired Hackney? and they cry abſurd as the Horſe underſtood 'em. They have made a fair Youth of your Elder Brother, a pretty piece of fleſh!

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I thank 'em for't, long may he ſtudy to give me his Eſtate. Saw you my Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: Yes, ſhe's a ſweet young Woman; but be ſure you keep her from Learning.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p:
Songs ſhe may have, and read a little unbak'd Poetry, ſuch as the Dablers of our time contrive, that has no weight nor wheel to move the mind, nor indeed nothing but an empty ſound; ſhe ſhall have cloaths, but not made by Geometry; Horſes and Coach, but of no immortal Race: I will not have a Scholar in my houſe above a gentle Reader; they corrupt the fooliſh Women with their ſubtle
Problems; I'le have my houſe call'd ignorance, to fright prating Ph • loſophers from Entertainment.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: It will do well, love thoſe that love good faſhions, good cloaths, and rich; they invite men to admire 'em, that ſpeak the liſp of Court. Oh 'tis great Learning! to Ride well, Dance well, Sing well, or Whiſtle Courtly, they're rare endowments; that they have ſeen far Countreys, and can ſpeak ſtrange things, though they ſpeak no truths, for then they make things common. When are you marri'd?

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: To morrow,! think; we muſt have a Maſque, Boys, and of our own making.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: 'Tis not half an hours work, a Cupid, and a Fiddle, and the thing's done: but let's be handſome, ſhall's be Gods or Nymphs?

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: What, Nymphs with Beards?

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: That's true, we'll be Knights then; ſome wandring Knights, that light here on a ſudden.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Let's go, let's go, I muſt go viſit, Gentlemen, and mark what ſweet lips I muſt kiſs to morrow.

sp.speaker: Cook
sp.p: And how do's my Maſter?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: He's at's Book; peace, Coxcomb, that ſuch an unlearned tongue as thine ſhould ask for him!

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.p: Do's he not ſtudy conjuring too?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Have you loſt any Plate, Butler?

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: No, but I know I ſhall to morrow at dinner.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Then to morrow you ſhall be turn'd out of your place for't; we meddle with no ſpirit o'th' Buttery, they taſte too ſmall for us; keep me a Pie in Folio, I beſeech thee, and thou ſhalt ſee how learnedly I'le tranſlate him. Shall's have good cheer to morrow?

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.p: Excellent good cheer, Andrew.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: The ſpight on't is, that much about that time, I ſhall be arguing, or deciding rather, which are the Males or Females of Red Herrings, and whether they be taken in the Red Sea only; a queſtion found out by Copernicus, the learned Motion maker.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.p: I marry, Butler, here are rare things; a man that look'd upon him, would ſwear he underſtood no more than we do.

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: Certain, a learned Andrew.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I've ſo much on't, and am ſo loaden with ſtrong underſtanding, I fear, they'll run me mad. Here's a new Inſtrument, a Mathematical Gliſter to purge the Moon with when ſhe is laden with cold phlegmatick humours; and here's another to remove the Stars, when they grow too thick in the Firmament.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.p: O Heavens! why do I labour out my life in a Beefpot? and only ſearch the ſecrets of a Sallad, and know no farther?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: They are not reveal'd to all heads; theſe are far above your Element of Fire, Cook. I could tell you of Archimedes Glaſs, to fire your Coals with; and of the Philoſophers Turf, that ne'er goes out: and, Gilbert Butler, I could taviſh thee with two tare inventions.

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: What are they, Andrew?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: The one to blanch your Bread from chippings baſe, and in a moment, as thou wouldſt an Almond; the Sect of the Epicureans invented that: The other for thy Trenchers, that's a ſtrong, one, to cleanſe you twenty dozen in a minute, and no noiſe heard, which is the wonder, Gilbert; and this was out of Plato's new Idea's.

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: Why, what a learned Maſter do'ſt thou ſerve, Andrew?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Theſe are but the ſcrapings of his underſtanding, Gilbert; with gods and goddeſſes, and ſuch ſtrange people he deals, and treats with in ſo plain a faſhion, as thou do'ſt with thy Boy that draws thy drink, or Ralph there, with his Kitchin Boys and Scalders.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.p: But why ſhould he not be familiar, and talk ſometimes, as other Chriſtians do, of hearty matters, and com • into the Kitchin, and there cut his Breakfaſt?

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p:
And then retire to the Buttery, and there eat it, 〈◊〉 drink a luſty Bowl to my young Maſter, that muſt be not the Heir, he'll do all theſe, I and be drunk too; theſe •
mortal things.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: My Maſter ſtudies immortality.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.p:
Now thou talk'ſt of immortality, how do's thy W ••
Andrew? my old Maſter did you no ſmall Pleaſure when he procur'd her, and ſtock'd you in a Farm. It he ſhould l ••• her now, as he hath a Colts tooth yet, what ſays your lea •
ing and your ſtrange Inſtruments to that, my Andrew? C •• any of your learned Clerks avoid it? can ye put by his Mathematical Engine?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Yes, or I'le break it: thou awaken'ſt me, and I'le peep i'th' Moon this month but I'le watch for him. 〈◊〉 Maſter rings, I muſt go make him a fire, and conjure 〈◊〉 his Books.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.p:
Adieu, good Andrew, and ſend thee manly pati •• with thy learning.
Exe •••

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.p:
I have forgot to eat and ſleep with reading, and al • my faculties turn into ſtudy; 'tis meat and ſleep; what 〈◊〉 I outward garments, when I can cloath my ſelf with unde •
ſtanding? The Stars and glorious Planets have no Tailo • yet ever new they are, and ſhine like Courtiers. The Seaſo • s of the year find no fond Parents, yet ſome are arm'd in ſ •
ver Ice that gliſters, and ſome in gawdy Green come 〈◊〉 like Maſquers. The Silk-worm ſpins her own ſuit and lodging, and has no aid nor partner in her labours. W •• ſhould we care for any thing but knowledge, or look upon the World but to contemn it?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Would you have any thing?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Andrew, I find there is a flie grown o'er the E •• o'th' Bull, which will go near to blind the Conſtellation.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Put a Gold-ring in's noſe, and that will cute him.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Ariadne's Crown's away too; two main Stats the held it faſt are ſlip out.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Send it preſently to Galateo, the Italian St •• wright, he'll ſet it right again with little labour.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Thou art a pretty Scholar.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I hope I ſhall be; have I ſwept Books ſo often to know nothing?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I hear thou art married.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: It hath pleas'd your Father to match me to a Ma •• of his own chuſing; I doubt her Conſtellation's looſe too and wants nailing; and a ſweet Farm he has given us a m ••• off, Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Marry thy ſelf to underſtanding, Andrew; the •• Women are Errata in all Authors, they're fair to ſee to, and bound up in Vellam, ſmooth, white and clear, but th •• contents are monſtrous; they treat of nothing but dull a •• and diſeaſes. Thou haſt not ſo much wit in thy head, as th •• is on thoſe ſhelves, Andrew.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I think I have not, Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: No, if thou had'ſt, thou'ld'ſt ne'er married 〈◊〉 Woman in thy boſom, they're Cataplaſms made o'th' dea ••• ſins: I ne'er ſaw any yet but mine own Mother; or if I did, I did regard them but as ſhadows that paſs by of unde • creatures.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Shall I bring you one? I'le truſt you with my own Wiſe; I would not have your Brother go beyond ye; they' •• the prettieſt Natural Philoſophers to play with.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: No, no, they're Opticks to delude mens eyes with Does my younger Brother ſpeak any Greek yet, Andr ••

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: No, but he ſpeaks High Dutch, and that go •• daintily.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
Reach me the Books down I read yeſterday, a ••
••• e a little fire, and get a manchet; make clean thoſe In
•• uments of Braſs I ſhew'd you, and ſet the great Sphere by; •• en take the Fox tail, and purge the Books from duſt; laſt, • ke your L • lly, and get your part ready.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p:
Shall I go home, Sir? my Wife's name is Lilly,
• ere my beſt part lies, Sir.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I mean your Grammar, O thou Dunderhead • ould'ſt thou be ever in thy Wife's Syntaxis? Let me have 〈◊〉 noiſe, nor nothing to diſturb me; I am to find a ſecret.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: So am I too; which if I find, I ſhall make ſome • art for't— Exeunt.

THis is the day, my Daughter Angellina, the happy, that muſt make you a Fortune, a large and • ll one, my care has wrought it, and yours muſt be as great 〈◊〉 entertain it. Young Euſtace is a Gentleman at all points, • nd his behaviour affable and courtly, his perſon excellent, 〈◊〉 know you find that, I read it in your eyes, you like his •• uth; young handſome people ſhould be match'd together, •• en follows handſome Children, handſome fortunes; the • oſt part of his Father's Eſtate, my Wench, is ti'd in a • inture, that makes up the harmony; and when ye are • arried, he's of that ſoft temper, and ſo far will be chain'd 〈◊〉 your obſervance, that you may rule and turn him as •• u pleaſe. What, are the Writings drawn on your ſide, 〈◊〉 ?

sp.speaker: Not.
sp.p: They are, and here I have ſo fetter'd him, that if •• e Elder Brother ſet his hand to, not all the power of Law all e'er releaſe him.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Theſe Notaries are notable confident Knaves, and •• ble to do more miſchief than an Army. Are all your Clauſes •• re?

sp.speaker: Not.
sp.p: Sure as proportion; they may turn Rivers ſooner • an theſe Writings.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Why did you not put all the Lands in, Sir?

sp.speaker: Not.
sp.p: 'Twas not condition'd; if it had been found, it •• d been but a fault made in the Writing; if not found, all •• e Land.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p:
Theſe are ſmall Devils, that care not who has miſ
•• ief, ſo they make it; they live upon the meer ſcent of •• ſention. 'Tis well, 'tis well; are you contented, Girl? • r your will muſt be known.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p:
A Husband's welcome, and as an humble Wife I'le • ntertain him; no Sovereignty I aim at, 'tis the man's, Sir; •• r ſhe that ſeeks it, kills her husbands honour: The Gen
•• eman I have ſeen, and well obſerv'd him, yet find not that •• ac'd excellence you promiſe; a pretty Gentleman, and • e may pleaſe too, and ſome few flaſhes I have heard come • om him, but not to admiration as to others: He's young, • nd may be good, yet he muſt make it, and I may help, and • elp to thank him alſo. It is your pleaſure I ſhould make him •• ine, and 't has been ſtill my duty to obſerve you.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Why then let's go, and I ſhall love your modeſty. • o Horſe, and bring the Coach out, Angellina; to morrow • ou will look more womanly.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: So I look honeſtly, I fear no eyes, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Briſ.
sp.p: Wait on your Maſter, he ſhall have that befits •• m.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: No Inheritance, Sir?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
You ſpeak like a fool, a coxcomb; he ſhall have an
•• l means to buy him Books, and find him cloathes and • eat, what would he more? Trouble him with Land? 'tis • at againſt his nature. I love him too, and honour thoſe 〈◊〉 in him.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Shall Maſter Euſtace have all?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: All, all; he knows how to uſe it, he's a than bred in the world, th'other i'th' Heavens. My Maſters, pray be wary, and ſ ••• ceable; and Cock, ſee all your Sawe • s be ſharp and poynant in the palate, that they may commend you; look to your Roaſt and •• ak'd meats handſomely, and what new Kickſhaws and delicate made things—Is th' Muſick come?

sp.speaker: But.
sp.p: Yes, Sir, they're here at Breakfaſt.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
There will be a M ••• e too; 〈◊〉 muſt ſee this Room clean, and, Butler, your door open to all good fellows; but have an eye to your Plate, for there be Furies; my Lilly, welcome you are for the L •• e 〈◊〉
• rt it, and ſee it ready for the Table, and ſee the Bride 〈◊〉 made, and look the cords be not cut aſunder by the Gallants too, there be ſuch knacks abroad. Hark hither, Lilly, to morrow night at twelve a clook I'le ſup w'ye: your husband ſhall be ſafe, I'le ſend ye meat too; before I cannot well ſlip from my company.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Will you ſo, will you ſo, Sir? I'le make one to eat it, I may chance make you ſtagger too.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: No anſwer, Lilly?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: One word about the Linen; I'le be ready, and reſt your Worſhips ſtill.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And I'le reſt w'ye, you ſhall ſee what reſt 't will be. Are ye ſo nimble? a man had need have ten pair of ears to watch you.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Wait on your Maſter, for I know he wants ye, and keep him in his Study, that the noiſe do not moleſt him. I will not fail my Lilly—Come in, ſweet-hearts, all to their ſeveral duties. Exeunt

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Are you kiſſing ripe, Sir? Double but my Farm, and kiſs her till thy heart ake. Theſe Smock-vermine, how eagerly they leap at old mens kiſſes, they lick their lips at profit, not at pleaſure; and if 't were not for the ſcurvy name of Cuckold, he ſhould lie with her. I know ſhe'll labour at length with a good Lordſhip. If he had a Wife now, but that's all one, I'le fit him. I muſt up unto my Maſter, he'll be mad with Study— Exit.

div.head: ACTUS III. SCENA III.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: What a noiſe is in this houſe? my head is broken, within a Parentheſis, in every corner, as if the Earth were ſhaken with ſome ſtrange Collect, there are ſtits and motions. What Planet rules this houſe?
Who's there?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: 'Tis I, Sir, faithful Andrew.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Come near, and lay thine ear down; hea • 'ſt no noiſe?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: The Cooks are chopping herbs and mince meat to make Pies, and breaking Marrow-bones—

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Can they ſet them again?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Yes, yes, in Broths and Puddings, and they grow ſtronger for the uſe of any man.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: What ſpeaking's that? ſure there's a Maſſacre.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Of Pigs and Geeſe, Sir, and Turkeys, for the ſpit. The Cooks are angry Sirs, and that makes up the medley.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Do they thus at every Dinner? I ne're mark'd them yet, nor know who is a Cook.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: They're ſometimes ſober, and then they beat as gently as a Tabor.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: What loads are theſe?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Meat, meat, Sir, for the Kitchen, and ſtinking Fowls the Tenants have ſent in; they'll ne'r be ſound out at a general eating; and there's fat Veniſon, Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Why Deer, thoſe that men fatten for their private pleaſures, and let their Tenants ſtarve upon the Commons.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I've read of Deer, but yet I ne'er eat any.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p:
There's a Fiſhmongers Boy with Caviar, Sir,
Anchoves, and Potargo, to make ye drink.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Sure theſe are modern, very modern meats, for I underſtand 'em not.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: No more does any man from Caca merda, or a ſubſtance worſe, till they be greas'd with Oyl, and rubb'd with Onions, and then flung out of doors, they are rare Sallads.

sp.speaker: Char.
