sp.p: And why is all this, prethee tell me, Andrew? are there any Princes to dine here to day? by this abundance ſure there ſhould be Princes; I've read of entertainment for the gods at half this charge; will not ſix Diſhes ſerve 'em? I never had but one, and that a ſmall one.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Your Brother's marri'd this day; he's marri'd your younger Brother Euſtace.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: What of that?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And all the Friends about are bidden hither; there's not a Dog that knows the houſe, but comes too.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Marri'd! to whom?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Why to a dainty Gentlewoman, young, ſweet, and modeſt.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Are there modeſt women? how do they look?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: O you'll bleſs your ſelf to ſee them. He parts with's Books, he ne'er did ſo before yet.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: What does my Father for 'em?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Gives all his Land, and makes your Brother heir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Muſt I have nothing?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Yes, you muſt ſtudy ſtill, and he'll maintain you.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I am his eldeſt Brother.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: True, you were ſo; but he has leap'd o'er your ſhoulders, Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: 'Tis well; he'll not inherit my underſtanding too?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I think not; he'll ſcarce find Tenants to let it out to.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Hark! hark!

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: The Coach that brings the fair Lady.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Now you may ſee her.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Sure this ſhould be modeſt, but I do not truly know what women make of it, Andrew; ſhe has a face looks like a ſtory, the ſtory of the Heavens looks very like her.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: She has a wide face then.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: She has a Cherubin's, cover'd and vail'd with modell bluſhes Euſtace, be happy, whiles poor Charles is patient. Get me my Books again, and come in with me—

div.stage: Enter Briſac, Euſtace, Egremont, Cowſy, Miramont.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Welcome, ſweet Daughter; welcome, noble Brother; and you are welcome, Sir, with all your Writings; Ladys, moſt welcome: What, my angry Brother! you muſt be welcome too, the Feaſt is flat elſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: I am not come for your welcome, I expect none; I bring no joys to bleſs the bed withall; nor Songs, nor Maſques to glorifie the Nuptials; I bring an angry mind to ſee your folly, a ſharp one too, to reprehend you for it.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: You'll ſtay and dine though.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: All your meat ſmells muſty, your Table will ſhew nothing to content me.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I'le anſwer you here's good meat.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: But your ſauce is ſcurvie, it is not ſeaſon'd with the ſharpneſs of diſcretion.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: It ſeems your anger is at me, dear Uncle.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Thou art not worth my anger, th'art a Boy, a lump o'thy Father's lightneſs, made of nothing but antick cloathes and • ringes; look in thy head, and 'twill appear a foot-ball full of fumes and rotten ſmoke. Lady, I pity you; you are a handſome and a ſweet young Lady, and ought to have a handſom man yok'd t'ye, an underſtanding too; this is a Gimcrack, that can get nothing but new faſhions on you; for ſay he have a thing ſhap'd like a child, 'twill either prove a Tumbler or a Tailor.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Theſe are but harſh words, Uncle.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: So I mean 'em. Sir, you play harſher play w'your elder Brother.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I would be loth to give you.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Do not venture, I'le make your wedding cloaths 〈◊〉 cloſer t'ye then; I but diſturb you, I'le go ſee my Nephew

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Pray take a piece of Roſemary.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: I'le wear it, but for the Ladys ſake, and none 〈◊〉 yours; may be I'le ſee your Table too.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Pray do, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: A mad old Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
Yes faith, ſweet Daughter, he has been thus 〈◊〉 whole age, to my knowledge; he has made Charles his He •• I know that certainly; then why ſhould he grudge Euſta ••
any thing?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I would not have a light head, nor one laden w ••• too much learning, as, they ſay, this Charles is, that makes his Book his Miſtris; Sure there's ſomething hid in this 〈◊〉 man's anger, that declares him not a meer ſot.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Come, ſhall we go and ſeal, Brother? all things are ready, and the Prieſt is here. When Charles has ſet his ha •• unto the Writings, as he ſhall inſtantly, then to the Wedding, and ſo to dinner.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Come, let's ſeal the Book firſt for my Daughter Jointure.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
Let's be private in't, Sir.
Ex •••

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Nay, y'are undone.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Hum.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Ha'ye no greater feeling?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: You were ſenſible of the great Book, Sir, when i • fell on your head, and now the houſe is ready to fall, do you fear nothing?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Will he have my Books too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: No, he has a Book, a fair one too, to read on, and read wonders; I would thou hadſt her in thy Study, Nephew, and 'twere but to new ſtring her.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Yes, I ſaw her, and me thought 'twas a curi ••• piece of Learning, handſomely bound, and of a dai •• Letter.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: He flung away his Book.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: I like that in him; would he had flung away his dulneſs too, and ſpoke to her.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: And muſt my Brother have all?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: All that your Father has.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: And that fair woman too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: That woman alſo.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: He has enough then. May I not ſee her ſometimes and call her Siſter? I will do him no wrong.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p:
This makes me mad, I could now cry for anger theſe old Fools are the moſt ſtubborn and the wilfulleſt Coxcombs; Farewell, and fall to your Book, forget your Brother: you are my Heir, and I'le provide y'a Wife: I'le look upon this marriage, though I hate it.
Ex •

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Where is my Son?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: There, Sir, caſting a Figure what chopping children his Brother ſhall have.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: He does well. How do'ſt, Charles? ſtill at thy Book?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: He's ſtudying now, Sir, who ſhall be his Father.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Peace, you rude Knave — Come hither, Charles be merry.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I thank you, I am buſie at my Book, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: You muſt put your hand, my Charles, as I wo •• have you, unto a little piece of Parchment here: only you name; you write a reaſonable hand.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: But I may do unreaſonably to write it. What i • it, Sir?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: To paſs the Land I have, Sir, unto your youngs Brother.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Is't no more?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
No, no, 'tis nothing you ſhall be provided for, and n •• Books you ſhall have ſtill, and new Studies, and have you
means brought in without thy care, Boy, and one ſtill to •• tend you.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: This ſhews your love, Father.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I'm tender to you.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Like a ſtone, I take it.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Why Father, I'll go down, an't pleaſe you let • ne, becauſe I'd ſee the thing they call the Gentlewoman; 〈◊〉 ſee no Woman but through contemplation, and there I'll • o't before the company, and wiſh my Brother fortune.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Do, I prethee.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I muſt not ſtay, for I have things above require my •• udy.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: No, thou ſhalt not ſtay; thou ſhalt have a brave • inner too.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Now has he o'erthrown himſelf for ever; I will • own into the Cellar, and be ſtark drunk for anger. Exeunt.

div.head: ACTUS III. SCENA V.
div.stage: Enter Lewis, Angellina, Euſtace, Prieſt, Ladies, Cowſy, Notary, and Miramont.

sp.speaker: Not.
sp.p: Come, let him bring his Sons hand, and all's done. • s your's ready?

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.p: Yes, I'll diſpatch ye preſently, immediately, for • n truth I am a hungry.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Do, ſpeak apace, for we believe exactly: do not • e ſtay long, Miſtreſs?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I find no fault, better things well done, than want • me to do them. Uncle, why are you ſad?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Sweet ſmelling bloſſom, would I were thine Uncle • o thine own content, I'd make thy Husband's ſtate a • houſand better, a yearly thouſand. Thou haſt miſt a man, 〈◊〉 but that he is addicted to his ſtudy, and knows no other Miſtreſs than his mind) would weigh down bundles of theſe • mpty kexes.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Can he ſpeak, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Faith yes, but not to Women; his language is • o Heaven, and heavenly wonder; to Nature, and her dark • nd ſecret cauſes.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: And does he ſpeak well there?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: O admirably! but he's too baſhful to behold a Woman, there's none that ſees him, and he troubles none.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: He is a man.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Faith yes, and a clear ſweet ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Then converſation me thinks—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: So think I; but it is his rugged Fate, and ſo I • eave you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I like thy nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: See my mad Uncle is courting my fair Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p:
Let him alone; there's nothing that allays an an
• ry mind ſo ſoon as a ſweet Beauty: he'll come to us.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p:
My Father's here, my Brother too! that's a won
• er, broke like a Spirit from his Cell.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Come hither, come nearer, Charles; 'twas your • eſire to ſee my noble Daughter, and the company, and • ive your Brother joy, and then to Seal, Boy; you do, like 〈◊〉 good Brother.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Marry does he, and he ſhall have my love for ever • or't. Put to your hand now.

sp.speaker: Not.
sp.p: Here's the Deed, Sir, ready.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: No, you muſt pardon me a while, I tell ye, I am • n contemplation, do not trouble me.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Come, leave thy Study, Charles.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I'll leave my life firſt; I ſtudy now to be a man, • 've found it. Before what Man was, was but my Argument.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: I like this beſt of all, he has taken fire, his dull • iſt flies away.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Will you write, Brother?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: No, Brother, no; I have no time for poor things, • 'm taking the height of that bright Conſtellation.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I ſay you trifle time, Son.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I will not ſeal, Sir; I am your Eldeſt, and I'll keep my Birth-right, for Heaven forbid I ſhould become example: Had y'only ſhew'd me Land, I had deliver'd it, and been a proud man to have pa • ted with it; 'tis dirt, and labour. Do I ſpeak right, Uncle?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Bravely, my Boy, and bleſs thy tongue.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I'll forward: but you have open'd to me ſuch a treaſure, I find my mind free; Heaven direct my fortune.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Can he ſpeak now? Is this a ſon to ſacrifice?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Such an inimitable piece of Beauty, that I have ſtudied long, and now ſound only, that I'll part ſooner with my ſoul of Reaſon, and be a Plant, a Beaſt, a Fiſh, a Flie, and only make the number of things up, than yield to one foot of Land, if ſhe be ti'd to't.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: He ſpeaks unhappily.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: And methinks bravely. This the meer Scholar?

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: You but vex your ſelf, Brother, and vex your ſtudy too.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Go you and ſtudy, for 'tis time, young Euſtace; you want both man and manners; I've ſtudy'd both, although I made no ſhew on't. Go turn the Volumes over I have read, eat and digeſt them, that they may grow in thee; wear out the tedious night with thy dim Lamp, and ſooner loſe the day, than leave a doubt. Diſtil the ſweetneſs from the Poets Spring, and learn to love; thou know'ſt not what fair is: Traverſe the ſtories of the great Heroes, the wiſe and civil lives of good men walk through; thou haſt ſeen nothing but the face of Countrys, and brought home nothing but their empty words: why ſhouldſt thou wear a Jewel of this worth, that haſt no worth within thee to preſerve her?

lg.l: Beauty clear and fair,
Where the Air
Rather like a perfume dwells,
Where the Violet and the Roſe
The blew Veins in bluſh diſcloſe,
And come to honour nothing elſe.
Where to live near,
And planted there,
Is to live, and ſtill live new;
Where to gain a favour is
More than light, perpetual bliſs.
Make me live by ſerving you.
Dear again back recall
To this light,
A ſtranger to himſelf and all;
Both the wonder and the ſtory
Shall be yours, and eke the glory;
I am your ſervant and your thrall.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Speak ſuch another Ode, and take all yet. What ſay ye to the Scholar now?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I wonder; is he your Brother, Sir?

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Yes, would he were buried; I fear he'll make an Aſs of me a younger.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Speak not ſo ſoftly, Sir, 'tis very likely.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Come, leave your ſinical talk, and let's diſpatch, Charles.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Diſpatch, what?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Why the Land.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: You are deceiv'd, Sir. Now I perceive what 'tis that wooes a woman, and what maintains her when ſhe's woo'd: I'll ſtop here. A wilful poverty ne'er made a Beauty, nor want of means maintain'd it vertuouſly: though land and moneys be no happineſs, yet they are counted good additions. That uſe I'll make; he that neglects a bleſſing, though he want a preſent knowledge how to uſe it, neglects himſelf. May be I have done you wrong, Lady, whoſe love and hope went hand in hand together; may be my Brother, that has long expected the happy hour, and bleſs'd my ignorance; pray give me leave, Sir, I ſhall clear all doubts; why did they ſhew me you? pray tell me that?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: (He'll talk thee into a penſion for thy knavery.)

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: You, happy you, why did you break unto me? The Roſie ſu • ed morn ne'er broke ſo ſweetly: I am a man, and have de •• tes within me, affections too, though they were drown'd a while, and lay dead, till the Spring of beauty rais'd them; till I ſaw thoſe eyes, I was but a lump, a chaos of confuſedneſs dwelt in me; then from thoſe eyes ſhot Love, and he diſtinguiſh'd, and into form he drew my faculties, and now I know my Land, and now I love too.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: We had beſt remove the Maid.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: It is too late, Sir. I have her figure here. Nay ſ • own not, 〈◊〉 there are leſs worthy Souls for younger Brothers; this is no form of Silk, but Sanctity, which wild laſcivious hearts can never dignifie. Remove her where you will, I walk along ſtill, for, like the light, we make no ſeparation; you may ſooner part the Billows of the Sea, and put a barr betwixt their fellowſhips, than blot out my remembrance; ſooner ſhut old Time into a Den, and ſtay his motion, waſh off the ſwift hours from his downy wings, or ſteal Eternity to ſtop his glaſs, than ſhut the ſweet Idea I have in me. Room for an Elder Brother, pray give place, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: H'as ſtudied duel too; take heed, he'll beat thee. H'as frighted the old Juſtice into a Feaver; I hope he'll diſinherit him too for an Aſs; for though he be grave with years, he's a great Baby.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Do not you think me mad?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: No certain, Sir, I have heard nothing from you but things excellent.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: You look upon my cloaths, and laugh at me, my ſcurvy cloaths!

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: They have rich linings, Sir. I would your Brother.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: His are gold and gawdie.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: But touch 'em inwardly, they ſmell of Copper.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Can ye love me? I am an Heir, ſweet Lady, however I appear a poor dependent; love you with honour, I ſhall love ſo ever. Is your eye ambitious? I may be a great man; is't wealth or lands you covet? my Father muſt die.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: That was well put in, I hope he'll take it deeply.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Old men are not immortal, as I take it; is it you look for, youth and handſomneſs? I do confeſs my Brother's a handſome Gentleman, but he ſhall give me leave to lead the way, Lady. Can you love for love, and make that the reward? The old man ſhall not love his heaps of Gold with a more doting ſuperſtition, than I'le love you. The young man his delights, the Merchant, when he ploughs the angry Sea up, and ſees the mountain billows falling on him, as if all the Elements, and all their angers, were turn'd into one vow'd deſtruction; ſhall not with greater joy embrace his ſafety. We'll live together like two wanton Vines, ••• cling our ſouls and loves in one another, we'll ſpring together, and we'll bear one fruit; one joy ſhall make us ſmile, and one grief mourn; one age go with us, and one • ou • of death ſhall ſhut our eyes, and one grave make us happy.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: And one hand ſeal the Match, I'm yours for ever.

sp.speaker: Law.
sp.p: Nay, ſtay, ſtay, ſtay

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Nay certainly, 'tis done, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Theſe was a contract.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p:
Only conditional, that if he had the Land, he had my love too; this Gentleman's the Heir, and he'll maintain it. Pray be not angry, Sir, at what I ſay; or if you be, 'tis at your own adventure. You have the out-ſide of a pretty Gentleman, but by my troth your inſide is but bar
• en; 'tis not a face I only am in love with, nor will I ſay your face is excellent, a reaſonable hunting face to court the wind with; not they're not words, unleſs they be well plac'd too, not your ſweet Dam-mes, not your hired. Verſes, not telling me of Clothes, nor Coach and Horſes, no not your viſits each day in new Suits, nor your black Patches you wear variouſly, ſome cut like Stars, ſome in Half-moons, ſome Lozenges, (all which but ſhew you 〈◊〉 a younger Brother.)

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Gramercy, Wench, thou haſt a noble Soul too.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Nor your long travels, nor your little knowledg • can make me doat upon you. Faith go ſtudy, and g ••• ſome goodneſs, that you may ſhew manly; your Bro •••• at my ſuit I'm ſure will teach you; or only ſtudy ho •• get a Wife, Sir. Y'are caſt far behind, 'tis good you 〈◊〉 be melancholy, it ſhews like a Gameſter that had loſt 〈◊〉 mony, and 'tis the faſhion to wear your arm in a skarf, 〈◊〉 for your have had a ſhrewd cut o'er the fingers.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: But are y'in earneſt?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Yes, believe me, Father, you ſhall ne'er chooſe i • me; y'are old and dim, Sir, and th' ſhadow of the 〈◊〉 Eclips'd your judgment. Y'have had your time without control, dear Father, and you muſt give me leave to ta •• mine now, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: This is the laſt time of asking, will you ſet y •• hand to?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: This is the laſt time of anſwering, I will never.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Out of my doors.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Moſt willingly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: He ſhall, Jew, thou of the Tribe of Many a • a Coxcomb, and never trouble thee more till thy chops be cold, fool.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Muſt I be gone too?

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: I will never know thee.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Then this man will; what Fortune he ſhall 〈◊〉 Father, be't good or bad, I muſt partake it with him.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: When ſhall the Maſque begin?

sp.speaker: Luſt.
sp.p: 'Tis done already; all, all is broken off, I am 〈◊〉 done, Friend, my Brother's wiſe again, and has ſpoil'd 〈◊〉 will not releaſe the Land, has won the Wench too.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: Could he not ſtay till the Maſque was paſt? w • ready. What a ſcurvy trick's this?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p:
O you may vaniſh, perform 〈◊〉 at ſome Hall, whe • the Citizens Wives may ſee't for Six pence a piece, and cold Supper. Come, let's go, Charles. And now, 〈◊〉 noble Daughter, I'le ſell the Tiles of my Houſe, e're th •• ſhalt want, Wench. Rate up your Dinner, Sir, and 〈◊〉 it cheap: ſome younger Brother will take't up in Comm •
dities. Send you joy, Nephew Euſtace; if you ſtudy 〈◊〉 Law, keep your great Pippin-pies, they'll go far with ye

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I'd have your bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: No, no, meet me no more. Farewel, thou 〈◊〉 blaſt mine eyes elſe.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I will not.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Nor ſend not you for Gowns.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I'll wear courſe Flannel firſt.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Come, let's go take ſome counſel.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: 'Tis too late.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Then ſtay and dine; it may be we ſhall vex'em.

sp.speaker: Briſac.
sp.p: NE'er talk to me, you are no men but Maſque • ſhapes, ſhadows, and the ſigns of men, Co • bubbles, that every breath or breaks or blows away. Y •• have no ſouls, no metal in your bloods, no heat to ſtir •• when ye have occaſion: frozen dull things, that muſt be turn'd with Leavers. Are you the Courtiers, and 〈◊〉 travell'd Gallants? the ſpritely Fellows that the people 〈◊〉 of? Ye have no more ſpirit than three ſleepy ſopes.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: What would ye have me do, Sir?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
Follow your Brother, and get ye out of doors, 〈◊〉 ſeek your Fortune. Stand ſtill becalm'd, and let an 〈◊〉 Dotard, a hair-brain'd Puppy, and a Bookiſh Boy, 〈◊〉
• ever knew a Blade above a Pen-knife, and how to cut • is meat in Characters, croſs my deſign, and take thine own • ench from thee, in mine own houſe too? Thou deſpis'd • oor fellow!

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: The reverence that I ever bare to you, Sir, then • o my Uncle, with whom 't had been but ſawcineſs t' have • een ſo rough—

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: And we not ſeeing him ſtrive in his own cauſe, • hat was principal, and ſhould have led us on, thought it ill • anners to begin a quarrel here.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: You dare do nothing. Do you make your care the • xcuſe of your Cowardiſe? Three Boys on Hobby-horſes, • ith three penny Halberds, would beat you all.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: You muſt not ſay ſo.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Yes, and ſing it too.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: You are a man of peace, therefore we muſt give way.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p:
I'll make my way, and therefore quickly leave me, or I'll force you; and having firſt torn off your ſlanting • eathers, I'll trample on 'em; and if that cannot teach you • o quit my houſe I'll, kick ye out of my gates; you gawdy Glow-worms, carrying ſeeming fire, yet have no heat with
• n ye.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: O bleſt travel! how much we owe thee for our power to ſuffer?

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: Some ſplenetive Youths now, that had never ſeen more than thy Country ſmoak, will grow in choler; it would ſhew fine in us.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Ies marry would it, that are prime Courtiers, and muſt know no angers, but give thanks for our injuries, if we purpoſe to hold our places.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Will you find the door? and find it ſuddenly? you ſhall lead the way, Sir, with your perfum'd retinue, and • ecover the now loſt Angellina, or build on it, I will adopt ſome beggar's doubtful iſſue, before thou ſhalt inherit.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: We'll to counſel, and what may be done by man's wit or valour, we'll put in Execution.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Do, or never hope I ſhall know thee. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: O Sir, have I found you?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I never hid my ſelf; whence flows this fury, with which, as it appears, you come to fright me?

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: I ſmell a plot, meer conſpiracy amongſt ye all to defeat me of my Daughter; and if ſhe be not ſuddenly deliver'd, untainted in her reputation too, the beſt of France ſhall know how I am jugled with. She is my Heir, and if ſhe may be raviſh'd thus from my care, farewel Nobility; Honour and Blood are meer neglected nothings.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Nay then, my Lord, you go too far, and tax him, whoſe innocency underſtands not what fear is. If your unconſtant Daughter will not dwell on certainties, muſt you thenceforth conclude that I am fickle? what have I omitted, to make good my integrity and truth? nor can her lightneſs, nor your ſuppoſition, caſt an aſperſion on me.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: I am wounded in fact, nor can words cure it: do not trifle, but ſpeedily, once more I do repeat it, reſtore my Daughter as I brought her hither, or you ſhall hear from me in ſuch a kind, as you will bluſh to anſwer.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: All the world, I think, conſpires to vex me, yet I will not torment my ſelf: ſome ſprightful mirth muſt baniſh the rage and melancholy which hath almoſt choak'd me; t' a knowing man 'tis Phyſick, and 'tis thought on; one merry hour I'll have in ſpight of Fortune, to chear my heart, and this is that appointed; this night I'll hug my Lilly in mine arms, provocatives are ſent before to chear me, we old men need 'em, and though we pay dear for our ſtoln pleaſures, ſo it be done ſecurely, the charge much like a ſharp ſauce, gives 'em reliſh. Well, honeſt Andrew, I gave you a Farm, and it ſhall have a Beacon, to give warning to my other Tenants when the Foe approaches; and preſently, you being beſtowed elſe-where, I'le graff it with dexterity on your forehead; indeed I will, Lilly, I come, poor Andrew. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Do they chaſer roundly?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: As they were rubb'd with Soap, Sir, and now they ſwear aloud, now calm again; like a Ring of Bells, whoſe ſound the wind ſtill alters, and then they ſit in counſel what to do, and then they jar again what ſhall be done; they talk of Warrants from the Parliament, Complaints to the King, and Forces from the Province; they have a thouſand heads in a thouſand minutes, yet ne'er a one head worth a head of Garlick.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Long may they chafe, and long may we laugh at 'em; a couple of pure Puppies yok'd together. But what ſayes the young Courtier Maſter Euſtace, and his two warlike Friends?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: They ſay but little, how much they think I know not; they look ruefully, as if they had newly come from a vaulting houſe, and had been quite ſhot through 'tween wind and water by a ſhe Dunkirk, and had ſprung a Leak, Sir. Certain my Maſter was to blame.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Why, Andrew?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: To take away the Wench o'th' ſudden from him, and give him no lawful warning; he is tender, and of a young Girls conſtitution, Sir, ready to get the Green ſickneſs with conceit. Had he but ta'ne his leave in availing Language, or bought an Elegy of his condolement, that the world might have ta'ne notice, he had been an Aſs, 't had been ſome favour.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Thou ſay'ſt true, wiſe Andrew; but theſe Scholars are ſuch things, when they can prattle.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And very parlous things, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: And when gain the liberty to diſtinguiſh the difference 'twixt a Father and a Fool, to look below, and ſpie a younger Brother pruning up, and dreſſing up his expectations in a rare glaſs of beauty, too good for him; thoſe dreaming Scholars then turn Tyrants, Andrew, and ſhew no mercy.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: The more's the pity, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Thou told'ſt me of a trick to catch my Brother, and anger him a little farther, Andrew. It ſhall be only anger, I aſſure thee, and little ſhame.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And I can fit you, Sir. Hark in your ear.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Thy Wife?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: So I aſſure ye; this night at twelve a clock.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: 'Tis neat and handſome; there are twenty Crowns due to thy project, Andrew; I've time to viſit Charles, and ſee what Lecture he reads to his Miſtris. That done, I'le not fail to be with you.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Nor I to watch my maſter — Exeunt

div.head: ACTUS IV. SCENA III.
div.stage: Enter Angellia, Sylvia, with a Taper.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I'm worſe than e'er I was; for now I fear, that that I love, that that I only dote on; he follows me through every room I paſs, and with a ſtrong ſet eye he gazes on me, as if his ſpark of innocence were blown into a flame of luſt. Virtue defend me. His Uncle too is abſent, and 'tis night; and what theſe opportunities may teach him — What fear and endleſs care 'tis to be honeſt! to be a Maid what miſery, what miſchief! Would I were rid of it, ſo it were fairly.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: You need not fear that, will you be a child ſtill? He follows you, but ſtill to look upon you; or if he did deſire to lie with ye, 'tis but your own deſire, you love for that end; I'le lay my life, if he were now a bed w'ye, he is ſo modeſt; he would fall aſleep ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Dare you venture that?

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: Let him conſent, and have at ye; I fear him not, he knows not what a woman is, nor how to find the myſtery men aim at. Are you afraid of your own ſhadow, Madam?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: He follows ſtill, yet with a ſober face; would I might know the worſt, and then I were ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: Ye may both, and let him but go with ye.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Why do you flie me? what have I ſo ill about me, or within me, to deſerve it?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I am going to bed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: And I am come to light ye; I am a Maid, and 'tis a Maidens office.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: You may have me to bed, Sir, without a ſcruple, and yet I am cha • y too who comes about me. Two Innocents ſhould not ſeat one another.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: The Gentleman ſays true. Pluck up your heart, Madam.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: The glorious Sun both riſing and declining we boldly look upon; even then, ſweet Lady, when, like a modeſt Bride, he draws nights curtains, even then he bluſhes, that men ſhould behold him.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I fear he will perſwade me to miſtake him.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: 'Tis eaſily done, if you will give your mind to't.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Pray ye to your bed.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Why not to yours, dear Miſtris? one heart and one bed

sp.speaker: Ang
sp.p: •• ue, Sir, when 'tis lawful: but yet you know—

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I would not know, forget it; thoſe are but ſickly loves that hang on Ceremonies, nurs'd up with doubts and fears, ours high and healthful, full of belief, and fit to teach the Prieſt: Love ſhall ſeal firſt, then hands confirm the bargain.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I ſhall be a Heretick if this continue. What would you do a bed? you make me bluſh, Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I'd ſee you ſleep, for ſure your ſleeps are excellent, you that are waking ſuch a noted wonder, muſt in your ſlumber prove an admiration. I would behold your dreams too, if 't were poſſible; thoſe were rich ſhowes.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I am becoming Traitor.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Then like blew Neptune courting of an Iſland, where all the perfumes and the precious things that wait upon great Nature are laid up, I'd clip it in my arms, and chaſtly kiſs it, dwell in your boſome like your deareſt thoughts, and ſigh and weep.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I've too much woman in me.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: And thoſe true tears falling on your pure Cryſtals, ſhould turn to armelets for great Queens t'adore.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I muſt be gone.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Do not, I will not hurt ye; this is to let you know, my worthieſt Lady, y'have clear'd my mind, and I can ſpeak of love too: I can not my manners, though I never knew, before theſe few hours, what a Beauty was, and ſuch a one that • i • es all hearts that feel it; yet I have read of vertuous Temperance, and ſtudy'd it among my other Secrets; and 〈◊〉 would I force a ſeparation betwixt this ſpirit and the caſe of fleſh, than but conceive one rudeneſs againſt Chaſt ty.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Then we may walk.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
And talk of any thing, any fit for your ears, and my language; though I was bred up dull, I was ever civil; 'tis true, I have ſound it hard to look on you, and not deſire, 'twill prove a wiſe mans task; yet thoſe deſires I have ſo mingled ſtill, and tempered with the quality of honour, that if you ſhould yield, I ſhould • ate you for't. I am no Courtier of a light co • ition, apt to take fire at every beauteous face; that only ſerves his will and wantonneſs, and lets the ſerious part run by as thin neglected ſand. Whiteneſs of name, you muſt be mine, why ſhould I rob my ſelf of that that lawfully muſt make me happy? why ſhould I ſeek to cuckold my delights, and widow all thoſe ſweets I aim at in you? We 〈◊〉
• oſe our ſelves in Venus Groves of Myrtle, where every little wind ſhall be a Cupid, and ſing of love and ••• th, each •• nd that blows, and curls the velvet leaves, ſhall breed delights, the wanton Springs ſhall call us to 〈◊〉 banks, and on the perfum'd flowers we'll leaſt our ſen ••• , yet we'll walk by untainted of their pleaſures, and as they ••• e pure Temples we'll talk in them.

To bee, and pray then, we may have a fair end of 〈…〉 loves, would I were worth of you, or of ſuch pa
•• nts 〈…〉 you thanks: but I am poor in all but in your love. Once more, good night.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: A good night t'ye, and may the dew of ſleep f • ll gently on you, ſweet one, and lock up thoſe fair lights in pleaſing ſlumbers; no dreams but chaſte and clear attempt your fancy, and break betimes ſweet morn, I've loſt my light elſe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Let it be ever night when I loſe you.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: This Scholar never went to a Free-School, he's ſo ſimple.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Your Brother, with two Gallants, is at door, Sir, and they're ſo violent, they'll take no denial.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: This is no fit time of night.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Let 'em in, Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: They ſtay no leave; ſhall I raiſe the houſe on 'em?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Not a man, nor make no murmur of 't I charge ye.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: They're here, my Uncle abſent, ſtand cloſe to me. How do you, Brother, with your curious ſtory? have you not read her yet ſufficiently?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: No, Brother, no; I ſtay yet in the Preface: the ſtyle's too hard for you.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I muſt entreat her; ſhe's parcel of my goods.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: She's all when you have her.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Hold off your hands, unmannerly, rude Sir; nor I, nor what I have depend on you.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Do, let her alone, ſhe gives good counſel; do not trouble your ſelf with Ladies, they are too light: Let out your Land, and get a provident Steward.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I cannot love ye, let that ſatisfie you; ſuch vanities as you, are to be laugh'd at.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Nay, then you muſt go; I muſt claim mine own.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Away, away with her.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
Let her alone, pray let her alone, and take your Coxcomb up: Let me talk
She ſtrikes off Euſtace's h • t. civilly a while with you, Brother. It may be on ſome terms I may part with her.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: O, is your heart come down? what are your terms, Sir? Put up, put up. Snatches away his ſword.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: This is the firſt and chiefeſt, let's walk a turn. Now ſtand off, fools, I adviſe ye, ſtand as far off as you would hope for mercy: this is the firſt ſword yet I ever handled, and a ſword's a beauteous thing to look upon; and if it hold, I ſhall ſo hunt your inſolence: 'tis ſharp, I'm ſure, and if I put it home, 'tis ten to one I ſhall new pink your Sattins; I find I have ſpirit enough to diſpoſe of it, and will enough to make ye all examples; let me toſs it round, I have the full command on't. Fetch me a native Fencer, I defie him; I feel the fire of ten ſtrong ſpirits in me. Do you watch me when my Uncle is abſent? this is my grief, I ſhall be fleſh'd on Cowards; teach me to fight, I willing am to learn. Are ye all gilded flies, nothing but ſhew in ye? why ſtand ye gaping? who now touches her? who calls her his, or who dares name her to me? but name her as his own; who dares look on her? that ſhall be mortal too; but think, 'tis dangerous. Art thou a fit man to inherit Land, and haſt no wit nor ſpirit to maintain it? Stand ſtill, thou ſign of a man, and pray for thy friends, pray heartily, good prayers may reſtore ye.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: But do not kill 'em, Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: You ſpeak too late, Dear; it is my firſt fight, and I muſt do bravely, I muſt not look with partial eyes on any; I cannot ſpare a button of theſe Gentlemen; did life lie in their heel, Achilles like, I'd ſhoot my anger at thoſe parts, and kill 'em. Who waits within?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: View all theſe, view 'em well, go round about 'em, and ſtill view their faces; round about yet, ſee how death waits upon 'em, for thou ſhalt never view 'em more.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Pray hold, Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
I cannot hold, you ſtand ſo fair before me; I muſt
not • old; 'twill darken all my glories. Go to my Uncle, b • d him poſt to the King, and get my pardon inſtantly, I have need on't.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Are you ſo unnatural?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: You ſhall die laſt, Sir, I'll take thee dead, thou • art no man to fight with. Come, will ye come? Me-thinks I've fought whole Battels.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: We have no quarrel to you that we know on, Sir.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: We'll quit the houſe, and ask ye mercy too. Good Lady, let no murther be done here; we came but to parly.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: How my ſword thirſts after them? Stand away, Sweet.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Pray, Sir, take my ſubmiſſion, and I diſclaim for ever.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Away, ye poor things, ye deſpicable creatures! do you come poſte to fetch a Lady from me? from a poor School-boy that ye ſcorn'd of late, and grow lame in your hearts when you ſhould execute? Pray take her, take her, I am weary of her: What did you bring to carry her?

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: A Coach and four Horſes.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: But are they good?

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: As good as France can ſhew Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Are you willing to leave thoſe, and take your ſafeties? Speak quickly.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Yes with all our hearts.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: 'Tis done then. Many have got one Horſe, I've got four by th' bargain.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: How now, who's here?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Nay, now y'are gone without bail.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: What, drawn, my Friends? Fetch me my two-hand Sword; I will not leave a head on your ſhoulders, Wretches.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: In troth, Sir, I came but to do my duty.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: And we to renew our loves.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Bring me a Blanket. What came they for?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: To borrow me a while, Sir; but one that never fought yet, has ſo curri'd, ſo baſtinado'd them with manly carriage, they ſtand like things Gorgon had turn'd to ſtone: they watch'd your being abſent, and then thought they might do wonders here, and they have done ſo; for by my troth I wonder at their coldneſs, the nipping North or Froſt never came near them; St George upon a ſign would grow more ſenſible. If the name of Honour were for ever to be loſt, theſe were the moſt ſufficient men to do it in all the world; and yet they are but young, what will they riſe to? They're as full of fire as a frozen Glow-worms rattle, and ſhine as goodly: Nobility and patience are match'd rarely in theſe three Gentlemen, they have right uſe on't; they'll ſtand ſtill for an hour and be beaten. Theſe are the Anagrams of three great Worthies.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: They will infect my houſe with cowardize, if they breath longer in it; my roof covers no baffl'd Monſieurs, walk and air your ſelves; as I live they ſtay not here. White-liver'd wretches, without one word to ask a reaſon why. Vaniſh, 'tis the laſt warning, and with ſpeed; for if I take ye in hand, I ſhall diſſect you, and read upon your flegmatick dull Carcaſes. My Horſe again there: I have other buſineſs, which you ſhall hear hereafter, and laugh at it. Good-night Charles, fair goodneſs to your dear Lady; 'tis late, 'tis late.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Pray, Sir, be careful of us.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: It is enough, my beſt care ſhall attend ye.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Are you come, old Maſter? Very good, your Horſe is well ſet up; but ere you part, I'll ride you, and ſpur your Reverend Juſticeſhip ſuch a queſtion, as I ſhall make the ſides of your Reputation bleed, truly I will. Now muſt I play at • o peep— A Banquet— well, Potatoes and Eringoes, and, as I take it, Cantharides—Excellent, a Priapiſm follows, and as I'll handle it, it ſhall, old Lecherous Goat in Authority. Now they begin to Bill; how he ſlavers her! Gramercy Lilly, ſhe ſpits his kiſſes out, and now he offers to fumble, ſhe falls off, (that's a good Wench) and cries fair play above board. Who are they in the corner? As I live, a 〈◊〉 of Fidlers; I ſhall have ſome Muſick yet at my making free o th' Company of Horners; there's the comfort, and a Song too! He beckons for one— Sure 'tis no Anthem, nor no borrow'd Rhymes out of the School of vertue; I will liſten— A Song. This was never pe •• 'd at Geneva, the Note's too ſprightly. So, ſo, the Muſick's paid for, and now what follows? O that Monſieur Miramont would but keep his word; here were a Feaſt to make him fat with laughter; at the moſt 'tis not ſix minutes riding from his houſe, nor will he break, I hope— O are you come, Sir? the prey is in the N • t, and will break in upon occaſion.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt rule me, Andrew. O th'infinite fright that will aſſail this Gentleman! the Quartans, Tertians, and Quotidians that will hang like Serjeants on his Worſhips ſhoulders! the humiliation of the fleſh of this man, this grave, auſtere man will be wondred at. How will thoſe ſolemn looks appear to me; and that ſevere face, that ſpeaks chains and ſhackles? Now I take him in the nick, e' •• I have done with him, he had better have ſtood between two panes of Wainſcot, and made his recantation in the Market, than hear me conjure him.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: He muſt paſs this way to th' only Bed I have; he comes, ſtand cloſe.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Well done, well done, give me my night-cap. So. Quick, quick, untruſs me; I will truſs and • rounce thee. Come, Wench, a kiſs between each point; kiſs cloſe, it is a ſweet Parentheſis.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: Y'are merry, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Merry I will be anon, and thou ſhalt feel it, thou ſhalt, my Lilly.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: Shall I air your Bed, Sir?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: No, no; I'll uſe no Warming pan but thine, Girl, that's all. Come kiſs me again.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: Ha'ye done yet?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: No; but I will do, and do wonders, Lilly. Shew me the way.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: You cannot miſs it, Sir; you ſhall have a Cawdle in the morning for your Worſhip's breakfaſt.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: How, i'th' morning, Lilly? th'art ſuch a witty thing to draw me on. Leave fooling, Lilly, I am hungry now, and th'haſt another Kickſhaw, I muſt taſte it.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: 'Twill make you ſurfeit, I am tender of you: y'have all y'are like to have.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And can this be earneſt?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: It ſeems ſo, and ſhe honeſt.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Have I not thy promiſe, Lilly?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: Yes, and I have performed enough to a man of your years, this is truth; and you ſhall find, Sir, you have kiſs'd and tous'd me, hand I'd my leg and foot; what would you more, Sir? As for the reſt, it requires youth and ſtrength, and the labour in an old man would breed Agues, Sciatica's, and Cramps: You ſhall not curſe me for taking from you what you cannot ſpare, Sir. Be good unto your ſelf, y'have ta'ne already all you can take with eaſe; you are paſt threſhing, it is a work too boiſterous for you, leave ſuch drudgery to Andrew.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: How ſhe jeers him?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: Let Andrew alone with his own tillage, he's tough, and can manure it.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Y'are a quean, a ſcoffing, jeering quean.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: It may be ſo, but I'm ſure I'll ne' • be yours.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Do not provoke me, if thou do'ſt I'll have my Farm again, and turn thee out a begging.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p:
Though you have the will, and want of honeſty to deny your deed, Sir; yet I hope Andrew has got ſo much learning from my young Maſter, as to keep his own; at the worſt I'll tell a ſhort tale to the Judges, for what grave
ends you ſign'd your Leaſe, and on what terms you would revoke it.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Whore, thou dar'ſt not. Yield, or I'll have thee whipt: how my Bloud boils, as if 't were o're a Furnace!

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: I ſhall cool it.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Yet, gentle Lilly, pity and forgive me, I'll be a friend t'ye, ſuch a loving bountiful friend —

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: To avoid Suits in Law, I would grant a little; but ſhould fierce Andrew know it, what would become of me?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: A Whore, a Whore!

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Nothing but well Wench, I ſhall put ſuch a ſtrong bit in his mouth, as thou ſhalt ride him how thou wilt, my Lilly; nay, he ſhall hold the door, as I will work him, and thank thee for the Office.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Take heed, Andrew, theſe are ſhrewd temptations.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Pray you know your Cue, and ſecond me, Sir. By your Worſhip's ſavour.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I come in time to take poſſeſſion of th'Office you aſſign me; hold the door! alas, 'tis nothing for a ſimple man to ſtay without, when a deep underſtanding holds conference within, ſay with his Wife: a trifle, Sir. I know I hold my Farm by Cuckolds Tenure; you are Lord o'th' Soil, Sir. Lilly is a Weſt, a ſtray, ſhe's yours to uſe, Sir, I claim no intereſt in her.

sp.speaker: Bri
sp.p: Art thou ſerious? ſpeak, honeſt Andrew, ſince thou haſt o'er heard us, and wink at ſmall faults, man; I'm but a pidla • , a little will ſerve my turn; thou'lt find enough when I've my belly full: Wilt thou be private and ſilent?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: By all means, I'll only have a Ballad made of't, ſung to ſome lewd Tune, and the name of it ſhall be Juſtice Trap; it will fell rarely with your Worſhips name, and Lilly's on the top.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Seek not the ruine o' my reputation, Andrew.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: 'Tis for your credit, Monſieur Briſac, printed in Capital Letters, then paſted upon all the poſts in Paris.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: No mercy, Andrew?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: O, it will proclaim you from the City to the Court, and prove Sport Royal.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt keep thy Farm.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: He does affect him • nely.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: You trouble me. Then his intent arriving, the vizard of his hypocriſie pull'd of to the Judge criminal.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: O I am undone.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: He's put out of Commiſſion with diſgrace, and hold uncapable of bearing Office ever hereafter. This is my revenge, and this I'll put in practice.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Do but hear me.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: To bring me back from my Grammar to my Hornbook, it is unpardonable.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Do not play the Tyrant; accept of compoſition.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: Hear him, Andrew.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: What compoſition?

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I'll confirm thy Farm, and add unto it a hundred Acres more, adjoyning to it.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Umb, this mollifies; but y'are ſo fickle, and will again deny this, there being no witneſs by.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Call any witneſs, I'll preſently aſſure it.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Say you ſo? troth there's a friend of mine, Sir, within hearing, that's familiar with all that's paſt, his teſtimony will be authentical.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Will he be ſ cret?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: You may tie his tongue up, as you would do your purſe ſtrings.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Ha ha ha!

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: This is my witneſs. Lord how you are troubled! ſi • e you have an Agn • , you ſhake ſo with choler: Here's your loving Brother, Sir, and will tell no body but all he meets, that you have eat a Snake, and are grown young, gameſome, and rampant.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Caught thus?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: If he were o •• that would make jeſts of you, or playne ye, with making your Religious gravity ridiculous to your Neighbours, then you had ſome cauſe to be perplex'd.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I ſhall become diſcourſe for Clowns and Tapſters.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Quick, Lilly, quick, he's now paſt kiſſing, between point and point. He ſwounds, fetch him ſome Cordial— Now put in, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p:
Who may this be? ſure this is ſome miſtake: let me ſee his face, wears he not a falſe beard? it cannot be Br •
ſac that worthy Gentleman, the Pillar and the Patron of his Country; he is too prudent, and too cautelous, experience hath taught him t'avoid theſe fooleries, he is the puniſher, and not the doer; beſides he's old and cold, unfit for Woman: This is ſome counterfeit, he ſhall be whipt for't, ſome baſe abuſer of my worthy Brother.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Open the doors; will ye impriſon me? are ye my Judges?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: The man raves! this is not judicious Briſac: yet now I think on't, h'has a kind of Dog look like my Brother, a guilty hanging face.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I'll ſuffer bravely, do your worſt, do, do.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Why, it's manly in you.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: Nor will I • ail nor curſe, you ſlave, you whore, I will not meddle with you; but all the torments that e're fell on men, that ſed on miſchief, fall heavily on you all.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.p: You have given him a heat, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: He will ride you the better, Lilly.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: We'll teach him to meddle with Scholars.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: He ſhall make good his promiſe t'increaſe thy Farm, Andrew, or I'll jeer him to death. Fear nothing. Lilly, I am thy Champion. This jeaſt goes to Charles, and then I'll hunt him out, and Monſieur Euſtace the gallant Courtier, and laugh heartily to ſee 'em mourn together.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: 'Twill be rare, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: TUrn'd out of doors and baffled!

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: We ſhare with you in the affront.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: Yet bear it not like you with ſuch dejection.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: My Coach and Horſes made the ranſom of ou • Cowardize!

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: Piſh, that's nothing, 'tis damnum reparabile, and ſoon recover'd.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: It is but feeding a Suitor with falſe hopes, and after ſqueeze him with a dozen of Oaths, You are new rigg'd, and this no more remembred.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: And does the Court, that ſhould be the Example and Oracle of the Kingdom, read to us no other Doctrine?

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: None that thrives ſo well as that, within my knowledge.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: Flattery rubs out; but ſince great men learn to admire themſelves, 'tis ſomething creſt-faln.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: To be of no Religion, argues a ſubtle, moral underſtanding, and it is often cheriſh'd.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Piety then, and valour, nor to do and ſuffer wrong, are they no virtues?

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: Rather vices, Euſtace; Fighting! what's fighting? it may be in faſhion among p • ovant ſwords, and Buff-jerkin men: But w'us that ſwim in choice of Silks and Tiſſues; though in defence of that word Reputation, which is indeed a kind of glorious nothing, to loſe a dram of blood muſt needs appear as coarſe as to be honeſt.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: And all this you ſeriouſly believe?

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: It is a faith that we will die in, ſince from the bla •• Guard to the grim Sir in Office, there are few hold oth •• Tenets.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Now my eyes are open, and I behold a ſtrong neceſſity that keeps me knave and coward.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: Y'are the wiſer.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Nor can I change my copy, if I purpoſe to be of your • ociety.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: By no means.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Honour is nothing with you?

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: A meer bubble; for what's grown common, is no • o • e regarded.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: My ſword forc'd from me too, and ſtill detain'd, • ou think 'tis no blemiſh.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p:
Get me a Batton, 'tis twenty times more Court
•• ke, and leſs trouble.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: And yet you wear a ſword.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p:
Yes, and a good one, a Milan hilt, and a Damaſco
• lade for ornament, not uſe, the Court allows it.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Will't not fight of it ſelf?

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: I ne'er tri'd this, yet I have worn as fair as any man; • 'm ſure I've made my Cutler rich, and paid for ſeveral weapons, Turkiſh and Toledo's, two thouſand Crowns, and • et could never light upon a fighting one.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I'le borrow this, I like it well.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: 'Tis at your ſervice, Sir, a Lath in a Velvet Scabbard will ſerve my turn.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p:
And now I have it, leave me; y'are infectious, the plague and leproſie of your baſeneſs ſpreading on all that do • ome near you; ſuch as you render the Throne of Majeſty, • he Court, ſuſpected and contemptible; you are Scarabee's that batten in her dung, and have no palats to taſte her • urious Viands; and like Owles, can only ſee her night de
• ormities, but with the glorious ſplendor of her beauties, you are ſtruck blind as Moles, that undermine the ſum
• tuous Building that allow'd you ſhelter: you ſtick like • unning ulcers on her face, and taint the pureneſs of her na
• ive candor, and being bad Servants, cauſe your Maſters goodneſs to be diſputed of; you make the Court, that is the abſtract of all Academies, to teach and practiſe noble un
• ertakings, (where courage ſits triumphant crown'd with • awrel, and wiſdom loaded with the weight of honour) a • chool of Vices.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: What ſudden rapture's this?

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: A heavenly one, that raiſing me from ſloth and • gnorance, (in which your converſation long hath charm'd • ne) carries me up into the air of action, and knowledge of my ſelf; even now I feel, but pleading only in the Court's defence (though far ſhort of her merits and bright luſtre) a • appy alteration, and full ſtrength to ſtand her Champion againſt all the world, that throw aſperſions on her.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: Sure he'll beat us, I ſee it in his eyes.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: A ſecond Charles; pray look not, Sir, ſo furiouſly.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Recant what you have ſaid, ye Mungrils, and lick • p the vomit ye have caſt upon the Court, where you unworthily have had warmth and breeding, and ſwear that you, like Spiders, have made poiſon of that which was a ſaving Antidote.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: We will ſwear any thing.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: We honour the Court as a moſt ſacred place.

sp.speaker: Egre.
sp.p: And will make oath, if you enjoyn us to'r, nor knave, nor fool, nor coward living in it.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Except you two, you Raſcals.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: Yes, we are all theſe, and more, if you will have • it ſo.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: And that until you are again reform'd and grown new men, you ne'ere preſume to name the Court, or preſs into the Porter's Lodge but for a penance, to be diſciplin'd for your roguery, and this done with true contrition.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: You again may eat ſcraps, and be thankful.

sp.speaker: Cow.
sp.p: Here's a cold breakfaſt after a ſharp nights walking.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Keep your oaths, and without grumbling vaniſh.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: We are gone, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: May all the poorneſs of my ſpirit go with you: the fetters of my thraldom are fil'd off, and I at liberty to right my ſelf; and though my hope in Angellina's little, my honour (unto which compar'd ſhe's nothing) ſhall, like the Sun, diſperſe thoſe lowring Clouds that yet obſcure and dim it; not the name of Brother ſhall divert me, but from him, that in the world's opinion ruin'd me, I will ſeek reparation, and call him unto a ſtrict accompt. Ha! 'tis near day, and if the Muſes friend, Roſe-check'd Aurora, invite him to this ſolitary Grove, as I much hope ſhe will, he ſeldome miſſing to pay his vows here to her, I ſhall hazard to hinder his devotions— The door opens, 'tis he moſt certain, and by's ſide my Sword. Bleſt opportunity.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I have o'er ſlept my ſelf, and loſt part of the morn, but I'le recover it: Before I went to bed, I wrote ſome Notes within my Table-book, which I will now conſider. Ha! what means this? What do I with a Sword? Learn'd Mercury needs not th'aid of Mars, and innocence is to it ſelf a guard, yet ſince Arms ever protect Arts, I may juſtly wear and uſe it; for ſince 'twas made my prize, I know not how I'm grown in love with't, and cannot cat nor ſtudy, and much leſs walk without it. But I trifle, matters of more weight ask my judgment.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Now, Sir, treat of no other Theme, I'le keep you to it, and ſee y'expound it well.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: The ſame, Sir, your younger Brother, who, as duty binds him, hath all this night (turn'd out of door) attended, to bid Good-morrow t'ye.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: This not in ſcorn, commands me to return it. Would you ought elſe?

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: O much, Sir, here I end not, but begin; I muſt ſpeak to you in another ſtrain than yet I ever us'd; and if the language appear in the delivery rough and harſh, you (being my Tutor) muſt condemn your ſelf, from whom I learn'd it.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: When I underſtand (be't in what ſtyle you pleaſe) what's your demand, I ſhall endeavour, in the ſelf-ſame phraſe, to make an anſwer to the point.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I come not to lay claim to your birth-right, 'tis your own, and 'tis fit you enjoy it; nor ask I from you your learning and deep knowledge; (though I am not a Scholar as you are) I know them Diamonds by your ſole induſtry, patience and labour, forc'd from ſteep Rocks, and with much toil attended, and but to few that prize their value granted, and therefore without Rival freely wear them.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Theſe not repin'd at (as you ſeem t'inform me) the motion muſt be of a ſtrange condition, if I refuſe to yield to't; therefore, Euſtace, without this tempeſt in your looks, propound it, and fear not a denial.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I require then (as from an Enemy, and not a Brother) the reputation of a man, the honour, not by a fair War won when I was waking, but in my ſleep of folly raviſh'd from me; with theſe, the reſtitution of my Sword, with large acknowledgment of ſatisfaction, my Coach, my Horſes; I will part with life, ere loſe one hair of them; and, what concludes all, my Miſtris Angellina, as ſhe was before the muſical Magick of thy tongue inchanted and ſeduc'd her. Theſe perform'd, and with ſubmiſſion, and done publickly, at my Father's and my Uncle's interceſſion, (that I put in too) I perhaps may liſten to terms of reconcilement; but if theſe, in every circumſtance, are not ſubſcrib'd to, to the laſt gaſp I defie thee.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Theſe are ſtrict conditions to a Brother.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: My reſt is up, nor will I give leſs.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I'm no Gameſter, Euſtace, yet I can gheſs your reſolution ſtands to win or loſe all; I rejoyce to find ye thus tender of your honour, and that at length you underſtand what a wretched thing you were, how deeply wounded by your ſelf, and made almoſt incurable in your own hopes, the dead fleſh of pale cowardiſe growing over your feſtred • eputation, which no Balm or gentle Unguent could ever make way to; and I am happy that I was the Surgeon that 〈◊〉 apply thoſe burning co • roſives, that render you already •• ſible o'th'danger you were plung'd in, in teaching you, and 〈◊〉 a fair gradation, how far, and with what curious reſpect and care the peace and credit of a man within, (which you 〈◊〉 thought till now) ſhould be preſe • r'd before a gawdy on • e; pray you fix here, for ſo far I go with you.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: This diſcourſe is from the ſubject.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I'le come to it, Brother; but if you think to build upon my ruines, you'll find a falſe foundation: your high offers, taught by the Maſters of dependencies, that by compounding differences 'tween others, ſupply their own neceſſities, with me will never carry 't: as you are my Brother, I will diſpenſe a little, but no more than honour can give way to; nor muſt I deſtroy that in my ſelf I love in you; and therefore let not hopes or threats perſuade you I will deſcend to any compoſition for which I may be cenſur'd.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: You ſhall fight then.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: With much unwillingneſs with you; but if there's no evaſion —

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: None.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Hear yet a word; as for the Sword and other fripperies, in a fair way ſend for them, you ſhall have 'em. But rather than ſurrender Angellina, or hear it again mention'd, I oppoſe my breaſt unto loud thunder, caſt behind me all tyes of Nature.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: She detain'd, I'm deaf to all perſuaſion.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Guard thy ſelf then, Euſtace; I uſe no other Rhetorick.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Claſhing of ſwords ſo near my houſe! Brother oppos'd to Brother! here's no fencing at half ſword, hold, hold, Charles, Euſtace.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Second him, or call in more help. Come not between us, I'le not know nor ſpare you; D'ye fight by th'book?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: 'Tis you that wrong me, off Sir, and ſuddenly, I'le conjure down the Spirit that I have rais'd in him.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Never, Charles, 'tis thine, and in thy death, be doubled in me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p:
I'm out of breath, yet truſt not too muc •
〈◊〉 , Boys; for if you pauſe not ſuddenly, and hear reaſon, 〈◊〉 kill your Uncle, do; but that I'm patient, and not 〈◊〉 lerick old teaſty fool, like your Father, I'd dance a m •
〈◊〉 with you, ſhould make you ſweat your beſt blou ••
〈…〉 would, and it may be I will Charles, I command 〈◊〉 , and Euſtace, I entreat thee, th'art a brave Spark, a tr ••
• ough metall'd blade, and I begin to love thee heartily; give me a fighting Courtier, I'le cheriſh him for example; in our Age they're not born every day.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: You of late, Sir, in me lov'd learning.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: True, but take me w'ye, Charles; 'twas when young Euſtace wore his heart in 's breeches, and ſought his Battels in Complements and Cringes, when's underſtanding wav'd in a flanting Feather, and his beſt contemplation look'd no further than a new faſhion'd doublet; I confeſs then, the lofty noiſe your Greek made, only pleas'd me; but now he's turn'd an Ol ••• r and a Rowland, nay, the whole dozen of Peers are bound up in him: L • t me remember, when I was of his years ••• d look very li • e him; and did you ſee my Picture as I was then, you would ſwear that gallant Euſtace (I mean, now he da • es light) was the true ſubſtance, and the perfect figure. Nay, nay, no anger, you ſhall have enough, Charles.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Sure, Sir, I ſhall not need addition from him.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Nor I from an • , this ſhall decide my intereſt; though I am loſt to all deſerving men, to all that men call good, for ſuffering • ainely inſufferable wrongs, and juſtly ſlighted by yielding to a minute of delay in my revenge, and from that made a ſtranger unto my Father's houſe and favour, o'erwhelm'd with all diſgraces; yet I will mount up ward, and force my ſelf a fortune, though my birth and breeding do deny it

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p:
Such not, Euſtace, by violence, what will be offer'd to you on eaſier compoſition; though I was not alli'd unto your weakneſs, you ſhall find me a Brother to your bravery of ſpirit, and one that, not compell'd to't by your ſword, (which I muſt never fear) will ſhare with you in all but
••• elli • a.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Nobly ſaid, Charles, and learn from my experience, you may hear reaſon, and never maint your fighting; for your credit, which you think you have loſt, ſpare, Charles, and ſwinge me and ſoundly three or four walking vehe • Cloaks, that wear no ſwords to guard 'em yet deſerve 〈◊〉 thou art made up again.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: All this is Lip-ſalve.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: It ſhall be Hearts-eaſe, Euſtace, ere I have done; as for thy Father's anger, now thou dar'ſt fight, ne'er fear it, for I've the dowcets of his gravity faſt in a ſtring, I will ſo pin •• and wring him, that, ſpight of his authority, thou ſha •• make thine own conditions with him.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I'le take leave a little to conſider.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Here comes Andrew.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: But without his comical and learned face; what ſad diſaſter, Andrew?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: You my read, Sir, a Tragedy in my face.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Art thou in earneſt?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Yes, by my life, Sir; and if now you help not, and ſpeedily, by force, or by perſuaſion, my good old Maſter (for now I pity him) is ruin'd for ever.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Ha, my Father!

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: He, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: By what means? ſpeak.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: At the ſuit of Monſieur Lewis; his houſe is ſeiz'd upon, and he in perſon is under guard, (I ſaw it with theſe eyes, Sir) to be convey'd to Paris, and there Sentenc'd.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Nay, then there is no jeſting.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Do I live, and know my Father injur'd?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And what's worſe, Sir, my Ladie Angellina—

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: What of her?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: She's carri'd away too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p:
While you were abſent, a crew of Monſieur Lewis friends and kinſmen, by force, brake in at th' back part of the houſe, and took her away by violence; faithful Andre •
(as this can witneſs for him) did his beſt in her defence, 〈◊〉 'twould not do.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Away, and ſee our Horſes ſadled, 'tis no time to talk, but do. Euſtace, you now are offer'd a ſpatious field, and in a pious War to exerciſe your valour; here's a cauſe, and ſuch a one, in which to fall is honourable, your dutie and reverence due to a fathers name commanding it; but theſe unnatural jars ariſing between Brothers (ſhould you proſper) would ſhame your victory.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I would do much, Sir, but ſtill my reptation!

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Charles ſhall give you all decent ſatisfaction; nay, joyn hands, and heartily, why, this is done like Brothers; and as old as I am, in this cauſe that concerns the honour of our Family, Monſieur Lewis (if reaſon cannot work) ſhall find and feel there's hot blood in this arm, I'le lea • you bravely.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: And if I follow not, a cowards name be branded on my forehead.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: This ſpirit makes you a ſharer in my fortunes.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: And in mine, of which (Briſac once freed, and Angellina again in our poſſeſſion) you ſhall know, my heart ſpeaks in my tongue.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: I dare not doubt it, Sir. Exeunt.

div.head: ACTUS V. SCENA II.
div.stage: Enter Lewis, Briſac, Angellia, Sylvia, Officers.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: I'm deaf to all perſwaſions.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: I uſe none, nor doubt I, though a while my innocence ſuffers, but when the King ſhall underſtand how falſe your malice hath inform'd him, he in juſtice muſt ſet me right again.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p:
Sir, let not paſſion ſo far tranſport you, as to think it reaſon, this violent courſe repairs, but ruins it; that honour you would build up, you deſtroy; what you would ſeem to nouriſh, if reſpect of my preferment or my pattern may challenge your paternal love and care, why do you, now good fortune has provided a better Husband for me that your hopes could ever fancy, ſtrive to rob me of him? In what is my Lord Charles defective, Sir? unleſs deep Learning
be a blemiſh in him, or well proportion'd limbs be • ulcts in nature, or, what you only aim'd at, large Reve
• ues, are, on the ſudden, grown diſtaſteful to you. Of what • an you accuſe him?

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Of a Rape done to Honour, which thy ravenous luſt • ade thee conſent to.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: Her luſt! you are her Father.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: And you her Bawd.

sp.speaker: Syl.
sp.p: Were you ten Lords, 'tis falſe; the pureneſs of her • haſte thoughts entertains not ſuch ſpotted inſtruments.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: As I have a Soul, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: I am not to be alter'd; to ſit down with this diſgrace, would argue me a Peaſant, and not born Noble: all • igour that the Law, and that increaſe of power by favour • ields, ſhall be with all ſeverity inflicted; you have the King's hand for't, no Bail will ſerve, and therefore at your perils, Officers, away with 'em.

sp.speaker: Bri.
sp.p: This is madneſs.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Tell me ſo in open Court, and there I'le anſwer you.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Well overtaken.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Ill if they dare reſiſt.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: He that advances but one ſtep forward dies.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Shew the King's Writ.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Shew your diſcretion, 'twill become you better.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Y'are once more in my power, and if again I part with you, let me for ever loſe thee.

sp.speaker: Euſt.
sp.p: Force will not do't, nor threats; accept this ſervice from your deſpair'd of Euſtace.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And beware your Reverend Worſhip never more attempt to ſearch my Lilly pot, you ſee what follows.

sp.speaker: Lew.
sp.p: Is the King's power contemn'd?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: No, but the torrent o' your wilful folly ſtopp'd. And for you, good Sir, if you would but be ſenſible, what can you wiſh, but the ſatisfaction of an obſtinate will, that is not endear'd to you? rather than be croſs'd in what you purpos'd, you'll undo your Daughter's ſame, the credit of your judgment, and your old fooliſh Neighbour; make your Eſtates, and in a Suit not worth a Cardecue, a prey to Advocates, and their buckram Scribes, and after they have plum'd ye, return home like a couple of naked Fowles without a feather.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: This is a moſt ſtrong truth, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: No, no, Monſieur, let us be right Frenchmen, violent to charge; but when our follies are repell'd by reaſon, 'tis fit that we retreat, and ne'er come on more: Obſerve my learned Charles, he'll get thee a Nephew on Angellina ſhall diſpute in her belly, and ſuck the Nurſ • by Logick: and here's Euſtace, he was an Aſs, but now is grown an Amadis; nor ſhall he want a Wife, if all my Land, for a Joynture, can effect: Y'are a good Lord, and of a gentle nature, in your looks I ſee a kind conſent, and it ſhews lovely: and do you hear, old Fool? but I'le not chide, hereafter, like me, ever doat on Learning, the meer belief is excellent, 'twill ſave you; and next love Valour, though you dare not fight your ſelf, or fright a fooliſh Officer, young Euſtace can do it to a hair. And, to conclude, let Andrew's Farm b' encreas'd, that is your penance, you know for what, and ſee you rut no more; you underſtand me. So embrace on all ſides.

q.l: I'le pay thoſe Bilmen, and make large amends,
Provided we preſerve you ſtill our Friends—

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: BƲT that it would take from our modeſty
To praiſe the Writer, or the Comedy,
Till your fair ſuffrage crown it, I ſhould ſay,
Y'are all moſt welcome to no vulgar Play;
And ſo far w' are confident: And if he
That made it, ſtill lives in your memorie,
You will expect what we preſent to night,
Should be judg'd worthy of your ears and ſight.
You ſhall hear Fletcher in it, his true ſtrain,
And neat expreſſions; living he did gain
Your good opinions; but now dead commends
This Orphan to the care of Noble Friends;
And may it raiſe in you content and mirth,
And be receiv'd for a legit'mate birth.
Your grace erects new Trophies to his fame,
And ſhall, to after-times, preſerve his name.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: 'TIs not the hands, or ſmiles, or common way
Of approbation to a well lik'd Play,
We only hope; but that you freely would
To th' Author's memory ſo far unfold,
And ſhew your loves and liking to his Wit,
Not in your praiſe, but often ſeeing it;
That being the grand aſſurance that can give
The Poet and the Player means to live.

list.item: Don Henrique, an uxorious Lord, cruel to his Brother.
Don Jamie, younger Brother to Don Henrique.
Bartolus, a covetous Lawyer Husband to Amaranta.
Leandro, a Gentleman who wantonly loves the Lawyers Wife.
Aſſiſtant, which we call a Judge.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Violante, ſuppoſed Wife to Don Henrique.
Jacintha, formerly contracted to Don Henrique.
A Woman Moor, Servant to Amaranta.

sp.speaker: Arſenio.
sp.l: LEandro paid all.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: 'Tis his uſual cuſtom,
And requiſite he ſhould: he has now put off
The Funeral black, (your rich heir wears with joy,
When he pretends to weep for his dead Father)
Your gathering Sires, ſo long heap muck together,
That their kind Sons, to rid them of their care,
Wiſh them in Heaven, or if they take a taſte
Of Purgatory by the way, it matters not,
Provided they remove hence; what is befaln
To his Father, in the other world, I ask not;
I am ſure his prayer is heard: would I could uſe one
For mine, in the ſame method.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Fie upon thee.
This is prophane.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Good Doctor, do not ſchool me
For a fault you are not free from: On my life
Were all Heirs in Corduba, put to their Oaths,
They would confeſs with me, 'tis a ſound Tenet:
I am ſure Leandro do's.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: He is th'owner
Of a fair Eſtate.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: And fairly he deſerves it,
He's a Royal Fellow: yet obſerves a mean
In all his courſes, careful too on whom
He ſhowers his bounties: he that's liberal
To all alike, may do a good by chance,
But never out of Judgment: This invites
The prime men of the City to frequent
All places he reſorts to, and are happy
In his ſweet Converſe.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Don Jamie the Brother
To the Grandee Don Henrique, appears much taken
With his behaviour.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: There is ſomething more in't:
He needs his Purſe, and knows how to make uſe on't.
Tis now in faſhion for your Don, that's poor,
To vow all Leagues of friendſhip with a Merchant
That can ſupply his wants, and howſoe're
Don Jamie's noble born, his elder Brother
Don Henrique rich, and his Revenues long ſince
Encreas'd by marrying with a wealthy Heir
Call'd, Madam Vialante, he yet holds
A hard hand o're Jamie, allowing him
A bare annuity only.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Yet 'tis ſaid
He hath no child, and by the Laws of Spain
If he die without iſſue, Don Jamie
• nherits his Eſtate.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Why that's the reaſon
Of their ſo many jarrs: though the young Lord
• e ſick of the elder Brother, and in reaſon
Should flatter, and obſerve him, he's of a nature
Too bold and fierce, to ſtoop ſo, but bears up,
Preſuming on his hopes.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: What's the young Lad
That all of'em make ſo much of?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſweet one,
And the beſt condition'd youth, I ever ſaw yet,
So humble, and ſo affable, that he wins
The love of all that know him, and ſo modeſt,
That (in deſpight of poverty) he would ſtarve
Rather than ask a courteſie: He's the Son
Of a poor caſt Captain, one Octavio;
And She, that once was call'd th'fair Jacinta,
Is happy in being his Mother: for his ſake,
(Though in their Fortunes faln) they are eſteem'd of,
And cheriſh'd by the beſt. O here they come.
I now may ſpare his Character, but obſerve him,
He'l juſtifie my report.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: My good Aſcanio,
Repair more often to me: above Women
Thou ever ſhalt be welcome.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: My Lord your favours
May quickly teach a raw untutour'd Youth
To be both rude and ſawcy.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: You cannot be
Too frequent where you are ſo much deſir'd:
And give me leave (dear friend) to be your Rival
In part of his affection; I will buy it
At any rate.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Stood I but now poſſeſs'd
Of what my future hope preſages to me,
I then would make it clear thou hadſt a Patron
That would not ſay but do: yet as I am,
Be mine, I'le not receive thee as a ſervant,
But as my Son, (and though I want my ſelf)
No Page attending in the Court of Spain
Shall find a kinder maſter.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I beſeech you
That my refuſal of ſo great an offer
May make no ill conſtruction, 'tis not pride
(That common vice is far from my condition)
That makes you a denyal to receive
A favour I ſhould ſue for: nor the faſhion
Which the Country follows, in which to be a ſervant
In thoſe that groan beneath the heavy weight
Of poverty, is held an argument
Of a baſe abject mind, I wiſh my years
Were ſit to do you ſervice in a nature
That might become a Gentleman (give me leave
To think my ſelf one) My Father ſerv'd the King
As a Captain in the field; and though his fortune
Return'd him home a poor man, he was rich
In Reputation, and wounds fairly taken.
Nor am I by his ill ſucceſs deterr'd,
I rather feel a ſtrong deſire that ſways me
To follow his profeſſion, and if Heaven
Hath mark'd me out to be a man, how proud,
In the ſervice of my Country, ſhould I be,
To trail a Pike under your brave command!
There, I would follow you as a guide to honour,
Though all the horrours of the War made up
To ſtop my paſſage.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Thou art a hopeful Boy,
And it was bravely ſpoken: For this anſwer,
I love thee more than ever.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Pity ſuch ſeeds
Of promiſing courage ſhould not grow and proſper.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: What ever his reputed Parents be,
He hath a mind that ſpeaks him right and noble.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: You make him bluſh: it needs not ſweet Aſcanio,
We may hear praiſes when they are deſerv'd,
Our modeſty unwounded. By my life
I would add ſomething to the building up
So fair a mind, and if till you are fit
To bear Arms in the Field, you'l ſpend ſome years
In Salamanca, I'le ſupply your ſtudies
With all conveniences.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Your goodneſs (Signiors)
And charitable favours overwhelm me.
If I were of your blood, you could not be
More tender of me: what then can I pay
(A poor Boy and a ſtranger) but a heart
Bound to your ſervice? with what willingneſs
I would receive (good Sir) your noble offer,
Heaven can bear witneſs for me: but alas,
Should I embrace the means to raiſe my fortunes,
I muſt deſtroy the lives of my poor Parents
(To whow I ow my being) they in me
Place all their comforts, and (as if I were
The light of their dim eyes) are ſo indulgent
They cannot brook one ſhort dayes abſence from me;
And (what will hardly win belief) though young,
I am their Steward and their Nurſe: the bounties
Which others beſtow on me ſerves to ſuſtain 'em,
And to forſake them in their age, in me
Were more than Murther.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: This is a kind of begging
Would make a Broker charitable.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Here, (ſweet heart)
I wiſh it were more.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: When this is ſpent,
Seek for ſupply from me.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Thy piety
For ever be remembred: nay take all,
Though 'twere my exhibition to a Royal
For one whole year.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: High Heavens reward your goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: So Sir, is this a ſlip of your own grafting,
You are ſo prodigal?

sp.speaker: Jam.
