sp.l: A ſlip Sir?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Yes,
A ſlip; or call it by the proper name,
Your Baſtard.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: You are foul-mouth'd; do not provoke me,
I ſhall forget your Birth if you proceed,
And uſe you, (as your manners do deſerve) uncivilly.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: So brave! pray you give me hearing,
Who am I Sir?

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: My elder Brother: One
That might have been born a fool, and ſo reputed,
But that you had the luck to creep into
The world a year before me.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Be more temperate.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: I neither can nor will, unleſs I learn it
By his example: let him uſe his harſh
Unſavoury reprehenſions upon thoſe
That are his Hinds, and not on me. The Land
Our Father left to him alone rewards him,
For being twelve months elder, let that be
Forgotten, and let his Paraſites remember
One quality of worth or vertue in him
That may authorize him, to be a cenſurer
Of me, or my manners, and I will
Acknowledge him for a Tutor, till then, never.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: From whom have you your means Sir?

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: From the will
Of my dead Father; I am ſure I ſpend not
Nor give't upon your purſe.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: But will it hold out
Without my help?

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: I am ſure it ſhall, I'le ſink elſe,
For ſooner I will ſeek aid from a Whore,
Than a courteſie from you.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 'Tis well; you are proud of
Your new Exchequer, when you have cheated him
And worn him to the quick, I may be found
In the Liſt of your acquaintance.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Pray you hold
And give me leave (my Lord) to ſay thus much
(And in mine own defence) I am no Gull
To be wrought on by perſwaſion: nor no Coward
To be beaten out of my means, but know to whom
And why I give or lend, and will do nothing
But what my reaſon warrants; you may be
As ſparing as you pleaſe, I muſt be bold
To make uſe of my own, without your licence.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: 'Pray thee let him alone, he is not worth thy anger.
All that he do's (Leandro) is for my good,
I think there's not a Gentleman of Spain,
That has a better Steward, than I have of him.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Your Steward Sir?

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Yes, and a provident one:
Why, he knows I am given to large expence,
And therefore lays up for me: could you believe elſe
That he, that ſixteen years hath worn the yoke
Of barren wedlock, without hope of iſſue
(His Coffers full, his Lands and Vineyards fruitful)
Could be ſo ſold to baſe and fordid thrift,
As almoſt to deny himſelf, the means
And neceſſaries of life? Alas, he knows
The Laws of Spain appoint me for his Heir,
That all muſt come to me, if I out-live him,
Which ſure I muſt do, by the courſe of Nature,
And the aſſiſtance of good Mirth, and Sack,
How ever you prove Melancholy.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: If I live,
Thou dearly ſhalt repent this.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: When thou art dead,
I am ſure I ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Now they begin to burn
Like oppos'd Meteors.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Give them line, and way,
My life for Don Jamie.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Continue ſtill
The excellent Husband, and joyn Farm to Farm,
Suffer no Lordſhip, that in a clear day
Falls in the proſpect of your covetous eye
To be anothers; forget you are a Grandee;
Take uſe upon uſe, and cut the throats of Heirs
With cozening Mortgages: rack your poor Tenants,
Till they look like ſo many Skeletons
For want of Food; and when that Widows curſes,
The ruines of ancient Families, tears of Orphans
Have hurried you to the Devil, ever remember
All was tak'd up for me (your thankful Brother)
That will dance merrily upon your Grave,
And perhaps give a double Piſtolet
To ſome poor needy Frier, to ſay a Maſs
To keep your Ghoſt from walking.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: That the Law
Should force me to endure this!

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Verily,
When this ſhall come to paſs (as ſure it will)
If you can find a loop-hole, though in Hell,
To look on my behaviour, you ſhall ſee me
Ranſack your Iron Cheſts, and once again
Pluto's flame-colour'd Daughter ſhall be free
To domineer in Taverns, Maſques, and Revels
As ſhe was us'd before ſhe was your Captive.
Me thinks the meer conceipt of it, ſhould make you
Go home ſick, and diſtemper'd; if it do's,
I'le ſend you a Doctor of mine own, and after
Take order for your Funeral.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: You have ſaid, Sir,
I will not fight with words, but deeds to tame you,
Reſt confident I will, and thou ſhalt wiſh

This day thou hadſt been dumb.—
Ex • .

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: You have given him a heat,
But with your own diſtemper.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Not a whit,
Now he is from mine eye, I can be merry,
Forget the cauſe and him: all plagues go with him,
Let's talk of ſomething elſe: what news is ſtirring?
Nothing to paſs the time?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Faith it is ſaid
That the next Summer will determine much
Of that we long have talk'd of, touching the Wars.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: What have we to do with them? Let us diſcourſe
Of what concerns our ſelves. 'Tis now in faſhion
To have your Gallants ſet down in a Tavern,
What the Arch-Dukes purpoſe is the next ſpring, and what
Defence my Lords (the States) prepare: what courſe
The Emperour takes againſt the encroaching Turk,
And whether his Moony-ſtandards are deſign'd
For Perſia or Polonia: and all this
The wiſer ſort of State-Worms ſeem to know
Better than their own affairs: this is diſcourſe
Fit for the Council it concerns; we are young,
And if that I might give the Theme, 'twere better
To talk of handſome Women.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: And that's one,
Almoſt as general.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Yet none agree
Who are the faireſt.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Some prefer the French,
For their conceited Dreſſings: ſome the plump
Italian Bona-Robas, ſome the State
That ours obſerve; and I have heard one ſwear,
(A merry friend of mine) that once in London,
He did enjoy the company of a Gameſter,
(A common Gameſter too) that in one night
Met him th' Italian, French, and Spaniſh wayes,
And ended in the Dutch; for to cool her ſelf,
She kiſs'd him drunk in the morning.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: We may ſpare
The travel of our tongues in forraign Nations,
When in Corduba, if you dare give credit
To my report (for I have ſeen her, Gallants)
There lives a Woman (of a mean birth too,
And meanly match'd) whoſe all-excelling Form
Diſdains compariſon with any She
That puts in for a fair one, and though you borrow
From every Country of the Earth the beſt
Of thoſe perfections, which the Climat yields
To help to make her up, if put in Ballance,
This will weigh down the Scale.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: You talk of wonders.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: She is indeed a wonder, and ſo kept,
And, as the world deſerv'd not to behold
What curious Nature made without a pattern,
Whoſe Copy ſhe hath loſt too, ſhe's ſhut up,
Sequeſtred from the world.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Who is the owner
Of ſuch a Jem? I am fire'd.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: One Bartolus,
〈◊〉 wrangling Advocate.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: A knave on Record.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: I am ſure he cheated me of the beſt part
Of my Eſtate.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Some Buſineſs calls me hence,
And of importance) which denies me leiſure
To give you his full character: In few words
Though rich) he's covetous beyond expreſſion,
And to encreaſe his heap, will dare the Devil,
And all the plagues of darkneſs: and to theſe
• o • alous, as if you would parallel

Old Argu •
to him, you muſt multiply
His Eyes an hundred times: of theſe none ſleep.
He that would charm the heavieſt lid, muſt hire
A better Mercurie, than Jove made uſe of:
Bleſs your ſelves from the thought of him and her,
For 'twill be labour loſt: So farewel Signiors.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Leandro? in a dream? wake man for ſhame.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Trained into a fools paradiſe with a tale
Of an imagin'd Form.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Jamie is noble,
And with a forg'd Tale would not wrong his Friend,
Nor am I ſo much fir'd with luſt as Envie,
That ſuch a churl as Bartolus ſhould reap
So ſweet a harveſt, half my State to any
To help me to a ſhare.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Tuſh do not hope for
• mpoſſibilities.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I muſt enjoy her,
And my prophetique love tells me I ſhall,
Lend me but your aſſiſtance.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Give it o're.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: I would not have thee fool'd.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I have ſtrange Engines
Faſhioning here: and Bartolus on the Anvil,
Diſſwade me not, but help me.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Take your fortune,
If you come off well, praiſe your wit; if not,
Expect to be the ſubject of our Laughter. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You met Don Henrique?

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: What comfort bring you?
Speak cheerfully: how did my letter work
On his hard temper? I am ſure I wrote it
So feelingly, and with the pen of ſorrow,
That it muſt force Compunction.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: You are cozen'd;
Can you with one hand prop a falling Tower?
Or with the other ſtop the raging main,
When it breaks in on the uſurped ſhore?
Or any thing that is impoſſible?
And then conclude that there is ſome way left,
To move him to compaſſion.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Is there a Juſtice
Or thunder (my Octavio) and he
Not ſunk unto the center?

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Good Jacinta,
With your long practiſed patience bear afflictions,
And by provoking call not on Heavens anger,
He did not only ſcorn to read your letter,
But (moſt inhumane as he is) he curſed you,
Curſed you moſt bitterly.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: The bad mans charity.
Oh that I could forget there were a Tye,
In me, upon him! or the relief I ſeek,
(If given) were bounty in him, and not debt,
Debt of a dear accompt!

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Touch not that ſtring,
'Twill but encreaſe your ſorrow: and tame ſilence,
(The Balm of the oppreſſed) which hither to
Hath eas'd your griev'd ſoul, and preſerv'd your fame,
Muſt be your Surgeon ſtill.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: If the contagion
Of my misfortunes had not ſpread it ſelf
Upon my Son Aſcanio, though my wants
Were centupli'd upon my ſelf, I could be patient:
But he is ſo good, I ſo miſerable,
His pious care, his duty, and obedience,
And all that can be wiſh'd for from a Son,
Diſcharg'd to me, and I, barr'd of all means
To return any ſcruple of the debt
I owe him as a Mother, is a Torment,
Too painfull to be born.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: I ſuffer with you,
In that; yet find in this aſſurance comfort,
High Heaven ordains (whoſe purpoſes cannot alter)
Children that pay obedience to their Parents,
Shall never beg their Bread.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Here comes our joy,
Where has my deareſt been?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I have made, Mother,
A fortunate voyage and brought home rich prize,
In a few hours: the owners too contented,
From whom I took it. See here's Gold, good ſtore too,
Nay, pray you take it.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Mens Charities are ſo cold,
That if I knew not, thou wert made of Goodneſs,
'Twould breed a jealouſie in me by what means,
Thou cam'ſt by ſuch a ſum.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Were it ill got,
I am ſure it could not be employed ſo well,
As to relieve your wants. Some noble friends,
(Rais'd by heavens mercy to me, not my merits)
Beſtow'd it on me.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: It were a ſacriledge
To rob thee of their bounty, ſince they gave it
To thy uſe only.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Buy thee brave Cloathes with it.
And ſit thee for a fortune, and leave us
To our neceſſities; why do'ſt thou weep?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Out of my fear I have offended you;
For had I not, I am ſure you are too kind,
Not to accept the offer of my ſervice,
In which I am a gainer; I have heard
My tutor ſay, of all aereal fowl
The Stork's the Embleme of true pietie,
Becauſe when age hath ſeiz'd upon her dam,
And made unfit for flight, the gratefull young one
Takes her upon his back, provides her food,
Repaying ſo her tender care of him,
E're he was ſit to ſly, by bearing her:
Shall I then that have reaſon and diſcourſe
That tell me all I can doe is too little,
Be more unnatural than a ſilly bird?
Or ſeed or cloath my ſelf ſuperfluouſly,
And know, nay ſee you want? holy Saints keep me.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Can I be wretched,
And know my ſelf the Mother to ſuch Goodneſs?

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: Come let us drie our eyes, we'll have a feaſt,
Thanks to our little Steward.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: And in him,
Believe that we are rich.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I am ſure I am,
While I have power to comfort you, and ſerve you.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Is it my fault, Don Henrique, or my fate?
What's my offence? I came young to your bed,
I had a fruitfull Mother, and you met me
With equall ardour in your May of blood,
And why then and I barren?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 'Tis not in Man
To • ell a reaſon for the will of Heaven,
Which is inſ •• utable.
To what uſe ſerve
• ull •• tunes, and the m •• ner ſort of bleſſings,
Wh n that, which is the Crown of all our wiſhes,
Th • period of humane happineſs,
One only Child that may poſſeſs what's ours,

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 'Tis the curſe
Of great Eſtates to want thoſe Pledges, which
The poor are happy in: They in a Cottage,
With 〈◊〉 , behold the Models of their youth,
And as their Root decaies, thoſe budding Branches
Sprout forth and flouriſh, to renew their age;
But this is the beginning, not the end
Of miſery to me, that 'gainſt my will
Since Heaven denies Iſſue of our own)
Muſt leave the •• uit of all my care and travel
To an unthankfull Brother that inſults
On my Calamity.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I will rather chooſe
A Baſtard from the Hoſpital and adopt him,
And nouriſh him as mine own.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Such an evaſion
(My Violante) is forbid to us;
Happy the Romane State, where it was lawfull,
(If our own Sons were vicious) to chooſe one
Out of a vertuous Stock, though of poor Parents,
And make him noble. But the laws of Spain,
(Intending to preſerve all ancient Houſes)
Prevent ſuch free elections; with this my Brother's
Too well acquainted, and this makes him bold to
Reign o're me, as a Maſter.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I will ſire
The Portion I brought with me, e're he ſpend
A Royal of it: no Quirck left? no Quiddit.
That may defeat him?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Were I but confirmed,
That you would take the means I uſe with patience,
As I muſt practiſe it with my diſhonour,
I could lay level with the earth his hopes
That ſoar above the clouds with expectation
To ſee me in my grave.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Effect but this,
And our revenge ſhall be to us a Son
That ſhall inherit for us.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Do not repent
When 'tis too late.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I fear not what may fall
He diſpoſſeſs'd that does uſurp on all. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Leandro, (with a letter writ out) Milanes, and Arſenio.

sp.speaker: M l.
sp.l: CAn any thing but wonder?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Wonder on,
I am as ye ſ • e, and, what will follow, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Why doſt thou put on this form? what can this do?
From lookeſt moſt • illily.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Take a young Clerk,
A halt pin'd puppy that would write for a Royal.
Is this a commanding ſhap • to win a beauty?
To what uſe, what occaſion?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Peace, ye are • ools,
T •• y that pretend to wonders muſt weave cunningly.

sp.speaker: A ſ
sp.l: What manner of acceſs can this get? or if gotten
What credit in her eyes?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Will ye but leave me?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Me thinks a young man and a handſom Gentleman
(But ſure thou art lunatick) me thinks a brave man
That would catch cunningly the beams of beauty,
And ſo diſtribute 'em unto his comfort,
Should like himſelf appear, young, high, and buxom,
And in the brighteſt form.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Ye are cozen'd (Gentlemen)
Neither do I believe this, nor will follow it,
Thus as I am, I will begin my voyage.
When you love, lanch it out in ſilks and velvets,
I'le love in Serge, and will out go your Sattins.
To get upon my great horſe and appear
The ſign of ſuch a man, and trot my meaſures,
Or fiddle out whole froſty nights (my friends)
Under the window, while my teeth keep tune,
I hold no handſomneſs. Let me get in,
There trot and fiddle where I may have fair play.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: But how get in?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Leave that to me, your patience,
I have ſome toyes here that I dare well truſt to:
I have ſmelt a Vicar out, they call him Lopez.
You are ne're the nearer now.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: We do confeſs it.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Weak ſimple men, this Vicar to this Lawyer
Is the moſt inward Damon.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: What can this do?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: We know the fellow, and he dwells there.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: A poor, thin thief: he help? he? hang the Vicar,
Can reading of an— prefer thee?
Thou art dead ſick in love, and hee'l pray for thee.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Have patience (Gentlemen) I ſay this Vicar,
This thing I ſay is all one with the Cloſe Bartolus
(For ſo they call the Lawyer) on his nature
Which I have ſtudied by relation:
And make no doubt I ſhall hit handſomly,
Will I work cunningly, and home: underſtand me.
Next I pray leave me, leave me to my fortune
Difficilia pulchra, that's my Motto (Gentlemen)
I'le win this Diamond from the rock and wear her,
Or—

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Peace, the Vicar: ſend ye a full fail, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: There's your Confeſſor, but what ſhall be your penance?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: A fools head if I fail, and ſo forſake me.
You ſhall hear from me daily.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l:
We will be ready.
Exeunt Mil. Arſ

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Thin world indeed!

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'le let him breath and mark him:
No man would think a ſtranger as I am
Should reap any great commodity from his pigbelly.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Poor ſtirring for poor Vicars.

sp.speaker: Diego.
sp.l: And poor Sextons.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We pray and pray, but to no purpoſe,
Thoſe that enjoy our lands, choak our Devotions.
Our poor thin ſtipends make us arrant dunces,

sp.speaker: Diego.
sp.l: If you live miſerably, how ſhall we do (Maſter)
That are fed only with the ſound of prayers?
We riſe and ring the Bells to get good ſtomachs,
And muſt be fain to eat the ropes with reverence.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: VVhen was there a Chriſtning, Diego?

sp.speaker: Diego.
sp.l: Not this ten weeks:
Alas, they have forgot to get children (Maſter)
The VVars, the Seas, and uſurie undoe us,
Takes off our minds, our edges, blunts our plough-ſhares.
They eat nothing here, but herbs, and get nothing but green ſarc •
There are ſome poor Labourers, that perhaps
Once in ſeven year, with helping one another,
Produce ſome few pin'd-Butter-prints, that ſcarce ho'd
The chriſtning neither.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Your Gallants, they get Honour,
A ſtrange fantaſtical Birth, to defraud the Vicar,
And the Camp Chriſtens their Iſſues, or the Curtizans,
Tis a lewd time.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: They are ſo hard-hearted here too,
They will not dye, there's nothing got by Burials.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Diego, the Air's too pure, they cannot periſh.
To have a thin Stipend, and an everlaſting Pariſh,
Lord what a torment 'tis!

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Good ſenſible Maſter,
You are allow'd to pray againſt all weathers.
(Both foul, and fair, as you ſhall find occaſion)
Ah, not againſt all airs?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: That's not i'th' Canons.
• would it had, 'tis out of our way forty pence.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange, they are ſtarv'd too yet they will not die here,
They will not earth: a good ſtout plague amongſt 'em,
Or half a dozen new fantaſtical Fevers
That would turn up their heels by whole-ſale (Maſter)
And take the Doctors too, in their grave Counſels,
That there might be no natural help for mony:
How merrily would my Bells goe then?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Peace Diego,
The Doctors are our friends, let's pleaſe them well.
For though they kill but ſlow, they are certain, Diego,
We muſt remove into a muddy Air,
A moſt contagious Climate.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: VVe muſt certain,
An air that is the nurſery of agues,
Such agues (Maſter) that will ſhake mens ſouls out,
Ne're ſtay for Poſſets, nor good old wives plaſters.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Gowts and dead Palſies.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: The dead do's well at all times,
Yet Cowts will hang an arſe a long time (Maſter)
Thoſe are rich marle, they make a Church-yard fat,
And make the Sexton ſing, they never miſs, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Then Wills and Funeral Sermons come in ſeaſon,
And Feaſts that make us frolick.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: VVould I could ſee 'em.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And though I weep i'th' Pulpit for my Brother,
Yet (Diego) here I laugh.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: The cauſe requires it.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Since people left to die I am dunce, Diego.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſtrange thing, I have forgot to dig too.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: A pretious pair of youths! I muſt make toward 'em.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Who's that? look it ſeems he would ſpeak to us.
I hope a Marriage, or ſome Will to make, Diego.

sp.speaker: Dic.
sp.l: My friend your buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: 'Tis to that grave Gentleman;
Bleſs your good learning, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And bleſs you alſo,
He bears a promiſing face, there's ſome hope toward.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I have a Letter to your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: VVell Sir,
From whence I pray you?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: From Nova Hiſpania, Sir,
And from an ancient friend of yours.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis well, Sir,
'Tis very well: the devil a one I know there.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Take heed of a Snap, Sir, h'as a cozening countenance,
I do not like his way.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let him goe forward.
Cantabit vacuus, They that have nothing fear nothing,
All I have to loſe, Diego, is my learning,
And when he has gotten that, he may put it in a Nut ſhell.

body.head: LETTER READ.
body.p: SIgnior Lopez, Since my arrival from Cordova to theſe parts, I have written divers Letters unto you, but as yet received no Anſwer of any (Good and very good) And although ſo great a forgetfulneſs might cauſe a want in my due correſpondence, yet the deſire I have ſtill to ſerve you muſt more prevail with me (Better and better: the devil a man know I yet) and therefore with the preſent occaſion offered I am willing to crave a continuance of the favours, which I have heretofore received from you, and do recommend my Son Leandro the Bearer to you with requeſt that he may be admitted in that Ʋniverſitie till ſuch time as I ſhall arrive at home; his ſtudies he will make you acquainted withall: This kindneſs ſhall ſupply the want of your ſlackneſs: And ſo heaven keep you. Yours

sp.l: Alonzo Tiveria, very well,
A very ancient friend of mine, I take it,
For till this hour I never heard his name yet.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: You look, Sir, as if ye had forgot my Father.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: No, no, I look, as I would remember him,
For that I never remembred, I cannot forget, Sir,

l.hi: Alonzo Tiveria?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: The ſame, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And now i'th' Indies?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He may be any where,
For ought that I conſider.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Think again, Sir,
You were Students both at one time in Salamanca,
And, as I take it, Chamber-fellows.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Nay, ſure you muſt remember.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Would I could.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I have heard him ſay, you were Goſſips too.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Very likely,
You did not hear him ſay, to whom? for we Students
May oft-times over-reach our memories.
Do'ſt thou remember, Diego, this ſame Signiour?
Thou haſt been mine theſe twenty years.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Remember?
Why this Fellow would make ye mad: Nova Hiſpania?
And Signiour Tiveria? what are theſe?
He may as well name ye Friends out of Cataya.
Take heed I beſeech your worſhip: do you hear, (my friend')
You have no Letters for me?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Not any letter,
But I was charged to doe my Fathers love
To the old honeſt Sexton Diego: are you he, Sir?

sp.speaker: Dig.
sp.l: Ha? have I friends, and know 'em not? my name is Diego,
But if either I remember you or your Father,
Or Nova Hiſpania (I was never there Sir)
Or any kindred that you have—for heaven ſake, Maſter,
Let's caſt about a little, and conſider,
We may dream out our time.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: It ſeems I am deceiv'd, Sir,
Yet, that you are Don Lopez all men tell me,
The Curate here, and have been ſome time, Sir,
And you the Sexton Diego, ſuch I am ſent to,
The letter tells as much: may be they are dead,
And you of the like names ſucceed: I thank ye Gentlemen,
Ye have done honeſtly, in telling truth,
I might have been forward elſe. For to that Lopez,
That was my Fathers friend, I had a charge,
(A charge of mony) to deliver (Gentlemen)
Five hundred Duckets, a poor ſmall gratuity,
But ſince you are not he—

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Good Sir, let me think,
I pray ye be patient,
Pray ye ſtay a little,
Nay, let me remember, I beſeech ye ſtay, Sir.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: An honeſt noble friend, that ſends ſo lovingly;
An old friend too; I ſhall remember ſure, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Thou ſayſt true Diego.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: 'Pray ye conſider quickly,
Doe, doe, by any means, me thinks already
A grave ſtaid gentleman comes to my memory.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: He's old indeed, ſir.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: With a goodly white Beard,
(For now he muſt be ſo: I know he muſt be)
Signior Alonzo, Maſter.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I begin to have him.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: H'as been from hence, about ſome twenty years, ſir.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Some five and twenty, ſir.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: You ſay moſt true, Sir,
Juſt to an hour; 'tis now juſt five and twenty,
A fine ſtraight timber'd man, and a brave ſoldier,
He married: let me ſee, —

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: De Caſtro is Daughter.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: The very ſame.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Thou art a very Raſcal.
De Caſtro is the Turk to thee, or any thing:
The Mony • abbs 'em into ſtrange remembrances,
For as many Duchets more they would remember Adam.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Give me your hand, you are welcome to your country,
Now I remember plainly, manifeſtly,
As freſhly, as if yeſterdy I had ſeen him,
Moſt heartily welcome: ſinfull that I am,
Moſt ſinfull man! why ſhould I loſe this Gentleman?
This loving old Companion? we had all one ſoul, ſir,
He dwelt here hard by, at a handſome —

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Farm ſir,
You ſay moſt true.

sp.speaker: Lop.

l.hi: Alonzo Tiveria!

sp.l: Lord, Lord that time ſhould play the treacherous knave thus?
Why, he was the only friend I had in Spain, ſir,
I knew your Mother too, a handſome Gentlewoman,
She was married very young: I married 'em:
I do remember now the Maskes and Sports then,
The Fire works, and the fine delights; good faith, ſir,
Now I look in your face, whoſe eyes are thoſe, Diego?
Nay, if he be not juſt Alonzo's picture —

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Lord, how I bluſh for theſe two impudents!

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Well Gentleman, I think your name's Leandro.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: It is indeed, ſir,
Gra'-mercy letter, thou hadſt never known elſe.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I have dandled ye, and kiſt ye and plaid with ye
A hundred, and a hundred times, and danc'd ye,
And ſwong ye in my Bell-ropes, ye lov'd ſwinging.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A ſweet Boy.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Sweet lying knaves.
What would theſe doe for thouſands?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A wondrous ſweet Boy then it was, ſee now
Time that conſumes us, ſhoots him up ſtill ſweeter.
How do's the noble Gentleman? how fares he?
When ſhall we ſee him? when will he bleſs his Country?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: O, very ſhortly, Sir, till his return
He has ſent me over to your charge.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And welcome,
Nay, you ſhall know you are welcome to your friend, ſir.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: And to my Study, Sir, which muſt be the Law.
To further which, he would entreat your care
To plant me in the favour of ſome man
That's expert in that knowledge: for his pains
I have three hundred Duckets more: For my Diet,
Enough, Sir, to defray me: which I am charged
To take ſtill, as I uſe it, from your cuſtodie,
I have the mony ready, and I am weary.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Sit down, ſit down, and once more ye are moſt welcome,
The Law you have hit upon moſt happily,
Here is a Maſter in that art, Bartolus,
A neighbour by, to him I will prefer ye,
A learned man, and my moſt loving neighbour,
I'le doe ye faithfull ſervice, Sir.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: He's an Aſs,
And ſo wee'll uſe him; he ſhall be a Lawyer.
But if ever he recover this mony again —before, Diego,
And get ſome pretty pittance: my Pupill's hungry.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Pray ye Sir, unlade me.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I'le refreſh ye Sir;
When ye want, you know your Exchequer.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: If all this get me but acceſs, I am happy.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Come, I am tender of ye.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I'le go with ye.
To have thus ſort betray'd theſe fools muſt ſlecce me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: My Amaranta, a retir'd ſweet life,
Private and cloſe, and ſtill, and houſwiſely,
Becomes a Wife, ſets off the grace of woman.
At home to be believ'd both young, and handſome,
As Lilies that are cas'd in cryſtall Glaſſes,
Makes up the wonder: ſhew it abroad 'tis ſtale,
And ſtill the more eyes cheapen it 'tis more ſlubber'd,
And what need windowes open to inviting?
Or evening Tarraſſes, to take opinions?
When the moſt wholſome air (my wife) blows inward,
When good thoughts are the nobleſt Companions,
And old chaſt ſtories, wife, the beſt diſcourſes;
But why do I talk thus, that know thy nature?

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: You know your own diſeaſe: diſtruſt, and jealouſ • e,
And thoſe two, give theſe Leſſons, not good meaning,
What trial is there of my honeſtie,
When I am mew'd at home? to what end Husband,
Serves all the vertuous thoughts, and chaſt behaviours
Without their uſes? Then they are known moſt excellent,
When by their contraries they are ſet off, and burniſh'd.
If ye both hold me fair, and chaſt, and vertuous,
Let me goe fearleſs out, and win that greatneſs:
Theſe ſeeds grow not in ſhades, and conceal'd places:
Set 'em i'th heat of all, then they riſe glorious.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Peace, ye are too loud.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: You are too covetous.
If that be rank'd a vertue, you have a rich one.
Set me (like other Lawyers wives) off handſomely,
Attended as I ought, and as they have it,
My Coach, my people, and my handſome women,
My will in honeſt things.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Peace Amaranta.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: They have content, rich clothes, and that ſecures 'em
Binds, to their carefull husbands, their obſervance,
They are merry, ride abroad, meet, laugh.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt too.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: And freely may converſe with proper Gentlem • n.
Suffer temptations daily to their honour.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You are now too far again: thou ſhalt have any thing
Let me but lay up for a handſome Office,
And then my Amaranta —

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: Here's a thing now,
Ye place as pleaſure to me: all my retinue,
My Chamber-maid, my Kitchin-maid, my friend,
And what ſhe ſails in, I muſt doe my ſelf.
A foyle to ſet my Beauty off, I thank ye,
You will place the Devil next for a Companion.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No more ſuch words, good wife,
What would you have, Maid?

sp.speaker: Moor.
sp.l: Maſter Curate, and the Sexton, and a ſtranger, ſir,
Attend to ſpeak with your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: A ſtranger?

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: You had beſt to be jealous of the man you know not

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Pray thee no more of that.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: 'Pray ye goe out to 'em,
That will be ſafeſt for ye, I am well here,
I only love your peace, and ſerve like a ſlave for it.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No, no, thou ſhalt not; 'tis ſome honeſt Client,
Rich, and litigious, the Curate has brought to me,
Pre'thee goe in (my Duck) I'le but ſpeak to 'em,
And return inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: I am commanded,
One day you will know my ſufferance. — Exe.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And reward it.
So, ſo, faſt bind, faſt find; Come in my neighbours,
My loving neighbours pray ye come in, ye are welcome.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Bleſs your good reverence.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Good-day, good Maſter Curate,
And neighbour Diego, welcom: what's your buſineſs?
And 'pray ye be ſhort (good friends) the time is pretious,
Welcom, good Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: To be ſhort then with your Maſterſhip,
(For I know your ſeveral hours are full of buſineſs)
We have brought ye this young-man, of honeſt parents,
And of an honeſt face.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo, Neighbours,
But to what end?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: To be your Pupil, Sir,
Your Servant, if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I have travell'd far, Sir,
To ſeek a worthy man.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Alas, good Gentleman,
• am a poor man, and a private too,
Unfit to keep a Servant of your Reckoning;
My houſe a little Cottage, and ſcarce able
To hold my ſelf, and thoſe poor few live under it;
Beſides, you muſt not blame me Gentlemen,
If I were able to receive a Servant,
To be a little ſcrupulous of his dealing,
For in theſe times —

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Pray let me anſwer that, ſir,
Here is five hundred Duckets, to ſecure him,
He cannot want, Sir, to make good his credit,
Good gold, and coin.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And that's an honeſt pledge;
Yet ſure, that needs not, for his face, and carriage,
Seem to declare an in-bred honeſty.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: And (for I have a ripe mind to the Law, ſir,
In which I underſtand you live a Maſter)
The leaſt poor corner in your houſe, poor Bed, ſir,
(Let me not ſeem intruding to your worſhip)
With ſome Books to inſtruct me, and your counſel,
Shall I reſt moſt content with: other Acquaintance
Than your grave preſence, and the grounds of Law
I dare not covet, nor I will not ſeek, ſir,
For ſurely mine own nature deſires privacy.
Next, for your monthly pains (to ſhew my thanks,)
• do proportion out ſome twenty Duckets;
As I grow riper, more: three hundred now, ſir,
To ſhew my love to learning, and my Maſter,
My diet I'le defray too, without trouble.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Note but his mind to learning.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I do ſtrangely, yes, and I like it too, thanks to his mony.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Would he would live with me, and learn to dig too.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A wondrous modeſt man, ſir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: So it ſeems,
His dear love to his Studie muſt be nouriſh'd,
Neighbour, he's like to prove.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: With your good counſel,
And with your diligence, as you will ply him;
His Parents, when they know your care —

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Come hither.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: An honeſter young man, your worſhip ne're kept,
But he is ſo baſhfull —

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: O I like him better.
Say I ſhould undertake ye, which indeed, ſir,
Will be no little ſtraitneſs to my living,
Conſidering my Affairs, and my ſmall houſe, ſir,
For I ſee ſome promiſes that pull me to ye;
Could you content your ſelf, at firſt thus meanly,
To lie hard, in an out-part of my houſe, ſir?
For I have not many Lodgings to allow ye;
And ſtudie ſhould be ſtill remote from company;
A little fire ſometimes too, to refreſh ye;
A Student muſt be frugal: ſometimes Lights too,
According to your labour.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Any thing, Sir,
That's dry, and wholſome: I am no bred-wanton.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Then I receive you: but I muſt deſire ye
To keep within your conſines.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Ever Sir,
There's the Gold, and ever be your ſervant,
Take it and give me Books: may I but prove, ſir,
According to my wiſh, and theſe ſhall multiply.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Do, ſtudy hard, pray ye take him in, and ſettle him,
He's only fit for you; Shew him his Cell, ſir.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Take a good heart; and when ye are a cunning Lawyer,
I'le ſell my Bells, and you ſhall prove it lawfull.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Come, ſir, with me: neighbours I thank your diligence.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I'le come ſometimes, and crack a caſe with ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Welcom — Exit.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Here's mony got with eaſe: here, ſpend that jovially,
And pray for the fool, the Founder.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Many more fools
I heartily pray may follow his example,
Lawyers, or Lubbers, or of what condition,
And many ſuch ſweet friends in Nova Hiſpania.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: It will do well; let 'em but ſend their monys,
Come from what quarter of the world, I care not,
I'le know 'em inſtantly; nay I'le be kin to 'em;
I cannot miſs a man, that ſends me mony:
Let him law there, long as his Duckets laſt, Boy,
I'le grace him, and prefer him.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I'le turn Trade, Maſter, and now live by the living,
Let the dead ſtink, 'tis a poor ſtinking Trade.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: If the young fool now
Should chance to chop upon his fair Wife, Diego?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: And handle her Caſe, Maſter, that's a law point,
A point would make him ſtart, and put on his Spectacles,
A hidden point, were worth the canvaſſing.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Now ſurely, ſurely, I ſhould love him, Diego,
And love him heartily: nay, I ſhould love my ſelf,
Or any thing that had but that good fortune,
For to ſay truth, the Lawyer is a dog-bolt,
An arrant worm: and though I call him worſhipfull,
I wiſh him a canoniz'd Cuckold, Diego,
Now, if my youth do dub him —

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: He is too demure, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: If he do ſting her home.

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: There's no ſuch matter,
The woman was not born to ſo much bleſſedneſs,
He has no heat: ſtudy conſumes his oyl, Maſter.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let's leave it to the will of Fate, and preſently
Over a cup of luſtie Sack, let's propheſie.
I am like a man that dreamt he was an Emperour,
Come Diego, hope, and whilſt he laſts, we'll lay it on. Ex.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Angelo, Milanes, did you ſee this wonder?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: And you Arſenio?

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Yes he's gone, Sir,
Strangely diſguis'd, he's ſet upon his voyage.
Love guide his thoughts: he's a brave honeſt fellow.
Sit cloſe Don Lawyer, O that arrant knave now,
How he will ſtink, will ſmoak again, will burſt!
He's the moſt arrant Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: He may be more beaſt.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Let him bear ſix, and ſix, that all may blaze him,
The villany he has ſowed into my Brother,
And from his State, the Revenue he has reach'd at:
Pay him, my good Leandro, take my prayers.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: And all our wiſhes plough with his fine white heifer.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Mark him (my dear friend) for a famous Cuckold,
Let it out-live his Books, his pains, and hear me,
The more he ſeeks to ſmother it with Juſtice,
Let it blaze out the more: what news Andrea?

sp.speaker: Andr.
sp.l: News I am loth to tell ye: but I am charg'd, ſir,
Your Brother layes a ſtrict command upon ye,
No more to know his houſe, upon your danger,
I am ſorry, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Faith never be; I am glad on't,
He keeps the houſe of pride, and foolery:
I mean to ſhun it: ſo return my Anſwer,
'Twill ſhortly ſpew him out; Come, let's be merry,
And lay our heads together, carefully
How we may help our friend; and let's lodge near him,
Be ſtill at hand: I would not for my patrimony,
But he ſhould crown his Lawyer, a learned Monſter;
Come, l • t's away, I am ſtark mad till I ſee him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: Why will ye bring men in, and yet be jealous?
Why will ye lodge a young man, a man able,
And yet repine?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He ſhall not trouble thee, ſweet,
A modeſt poor ſlight thing, did I not tell thee
He was only given to the Book, and for that
How Royally he paies? finds his own meat too.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: I will not have him here: I know your courſes,
And what fits you will fall into of madneſs.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Faith, I will not, Wiſe.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: I will not try ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He comes not near thee: ſhall not dare to tread
Within thy Lodgings: in an old out Room
Where Logs, and Coles were laid.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: Now ye lay fire; fire to conſume your quiet.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Didſt thou know him,
Thou wouldſt think as I do: he diſquiet thee?
Thou mayſt wear him next thy heart, and yet not warm him.
His mind (poor man) 's o'th' Law, how to live after,
And not on lewdneſs: on my Conſcience
He knows not how to look upon a Woman
More than by reading what Sex ſhe is.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: I do not like it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou not ſee (Fool)
What preſents he ſends hourly in his gratefulneſs?
What delicate meats?

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: You had beſt truſt him at your Table,
Do, and repent it, do.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: If thou be'ſt willing,
By my troth, I think he might come, he's ſo modeſt,
He never ſpeaks: there's part of that he gave me,
He'll eat but half a dozen bits, and riſe immediately,
Even as he cats, he ſtudies: he'll not diſquiet thee,
Do as thou pleaſeſt, Wife.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: What means this Wood cock? Knock within.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Retire, Sweet, there's one knocks: come in, your buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Ser
sp.l: My Lord, Don Henrique, would entreat ye, Sir,
To come immediately, and ſpeak with him,
He has buſineſs of ſome moment.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'le attend him,
I muſt be gone: I pr • thee think the beſt, Wife,
At my return, I'le tell thee more, good morrow;
Sir, keep ye cloſe, and ſtudy hard: an hour hence
I'le read a new Caſe to ye. Exit. Leandro within.
I'le be ready.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: So many hundred Duckets, to ly ſ • m vily?
And learn the pelting Law? this ſounds but ſlenderly,
But very poorly: I would ſee this fellow,
Very I am ſee him, how he looks: I will find
To what end, and what ſtudy: there's the place:
I'le go oth' other ſ •• e, and take my Fortune.
I think there is a window. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: He's gone out
Now, if I could but ſ •• her: ſhe is not this way:
How naſtily be keeps his houſe? my Chamber,
If I continue long, will choak me up,
If is ſo damp: I ſhall be mortified
For any woman, if I ſtay a month here:
I'le in, and ſtrike my Lute, that ſound may call her. Ex:

lg.l: Deareſt do not you delay me,
Since thou knoweſt I muſt be gone;
Wind and Tide 'tis thought oth •• ay ••
But 'tis wind that muſt be b ••• .

From that breath, whoſe 〈◊〉
•• ll
Indian Odours far excel.
Oh then ſpeak thou faireſt fair,
Kill not him that vows to ſerve thee,
But perfume this neighbouring Air;
Elſe dull ſilence ſure will ſtarve me:
'Tis a word that's quickly ſpoken,
Which being reſtrain'd a heart is broken.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: He keeps very cloſe: Lord, how I long to ſee him.
A Lute ſtrook handſomely, a voice too; I'le hear that:
Theſe Verſes are no Law, they ſound too ſweetly,
Now I am more deſirous. Leandro peeping.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe certain.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: What's that that peeps?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: O admirable face!

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: Sure 'tis the man.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I will go our a little.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: He looks not like a fool, his face is noble:
How ſtill he ſtands!

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I am ſtrucken dumb with wonder,
Sure all the Excellence of Earth dwells here.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: How pale he looks! yet, how his eyes like torc •• s,
Fling their beams round: how manly his face ſhews!
He comes on: ſurely he will ſpeak: he is made moſt handſom •
This is no Clerk behaviour; now I have ſeen ye,
I'le take my time: Husband, ye have brought home tinder

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Sure ſhe has transform'd me,
I had forgot my tongue clean,
I never ſaw a face yet, but this rare one,
But I was able boldly to encounter it,
And ſpeak my mind, my lips were lockt up here.
This is divine, and only ſerv'd with reverence;
O moſt fair cover of a hand far fairer,
Thou bleſſed Innocence, that guards that whiteneſs,

Live next my heart. I am glad I have got a relick,
A 〈…〉
A relick when I pray to it, may work wonders.
Hark, there's ſome noiſe: I muſt retire again.
This bleſſed Apparition makes me happy;
I'le ſuffer, and I'le ſacrifice my ſubſtance,
But I'le enjoy: now ſoftly to my Kennel. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: YOU know my cauſe ſufficiently?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I do Sir.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: And though it will impair my honeſty,
And ſtrike deep at my Credit, yet, my Bartolus,
There being no other evaſion left to free me
From the vexation of my ſpightful Brother,
That moſt inſultingly raigns over me,
I muſt and will go forward.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do, my Lord,
And look not after credit, we ſhall cure that,
Your bended honeſly we ſhall ſet right, Sir,
We Surgeons of the Law do deſperate Cures, Sir,
And you ſhall ſee how heartily I'le handle it:
Mark how I'le knock it home: be of good chear, Sir,
• ou give good Fees, and thoſe beget good Cauſes,
• he Prerogative of your Crowns will carry the matter,
Carry it ſheer) the Aſſiſtant ſits to morrow,
And he's your friend, your monyed men love naturally,
• nd he's your loves are clear, ſo are your Cauſes.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: He ſhall not want for that.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No, no, he muſt not,
• e your Cauſe warmly, Sir, the times are Aguiſh,
• hat holds a Plea in heart; hang the penurious,
• heir Cauſes (like their purſes) have poor Iſſues.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: That way, I was ever bountiful.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Tis true, Sir,
• hat makes ye fear'd, forces the Snakes to kneel to ye,
• ive full of mony, and ſupply the Lawyer,
And take your choice of what mans lands you pleaſe, Sir,
What pleaſures, or what profits; what revenges,
They are all your own: I muſt have witneſſes
• hough, and ready.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: You ſhall not want, my Bartolus.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Subſtantial fearleſs ſouls, that will ſwear ſuddenly,
That will ſwear any thing.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: They ſhall ſwear truth too.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That's no great matter: for variety
They may ſwear truth, elſe 'tis not much look'd after:
• will ſerve Proceſs, preſently, and ſtrongly,
Upon your Brother, and Octavio,
• acintha, and the Boy; provide your proofs, Sir,
And ſet 'em fairly off, be ſure of Witneſſes,
Though they coſt mony, want no ſtore of witneſſes,
• have ſeen a handſome Cauſe ſo foully loſt, Sir,
• o beaſtly caſt away for want of Witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: There ſhall want nothing.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Then be gone, be provident,
• end to the Judge a ſecret way: you have me,
And let him underſtand the heart.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I ſhall, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And feel the pulſes ſtrongly beat, I'le ſtudy,
And at my hour, but mark me, go, be happy,
Go and believe i'th' Law.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I hope 'twill help me. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA II.
div.stage: Enter Lopez, Diego, and four Pariſhioners and Singers.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Ne're talk to me, I will not ſtay amongſt ye,
O • bauſh'd and ignorant lazie knaves I found ye,
And fools I leave ye. I have taught theſe twenty years,
Preacht ſpoon-meat to ye, that a Child might ſwallow,
Yet ye are Block heads ſtill: what ſhould I ſay to ye?
Ye have neither faith, nor mony left to ſave ye,
Am I a fit companion for ſuch Beggers?
If the Shepheard will ſuffer the ſheep to be ſcab'd, Sir—

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: No, no ye are rotten.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Would they were, for my ſake.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I have Nointed ye, and Tarr'd ye with my Doctrine,
And yet the Murren ſticks to ye, yet ye are Mangy,
〈◊〉 will avoid ye.
Pray ye, Sir, be not angry,
• n the pride of your new Caſſock, do not part with us,
We do acknowledge ye are a careful Curate,
And one that ſeldom troubles us with Sermons,
A ſhort ſlice of a Reading ſerves us, Sir,
We do acknowledge ye a quiet Teacher,
Before you'll vex your Audience, you'll ſleep with 'em,
And that's a loving thing.
We grant ye, Sir,
The only benefactor to our Bowling,
To all our merry Sports the firſt provoker,
And at our Feaſts, we know there is no reaſon,
But you that edifie us moſt, ſhould eat moſt.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I will not ſtay for all this, ye ſhall know me
A man born to amore beſeeming fortune
Than ringing all in, to a ront of Dunces.
We will increaſe your Tithes, you ſhall have Eggs too,
Though they may prove moſt dangerous to our Iſſues
I am a Smith; yet thus • a • out of my love,
You ſhall have the tenth Horſe I prick, to pray for,
I am ſure I prick five hundred in a year, Sir.
I am a Cook, a man of a dri'd Conſcience,
Yet thus far I relent: you ſhall have tith Pottage.
Your ſtipend ſhall be rais'd too, good Neighbour Diego.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Would ye have me ſpeak for ye? I am more angry,
Ten times more vex'd, not to be pacified:
No, there be other places for poor Sextons,
Places of profit, Friends, fine ſtirring places,
And people that know how to uſe our Offices,
Know what they were made for: I ſpeak for ſuch Capons?
Ye ſhall find the Key o'th' Church
Under the door, Neighbours,
You may go in, and drive away the Dawes.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: My Surpleſs, with one ſleeve, you ſhall find there,
For to that death of Linnen you have driven me;
And the old Cut work Cope, that hangs by Geometry:
'Pray ye turn 'em carefully, they are very tender;
The remnant of the Books, lie where they did, Neighbours,
Half puft away with the Church wardens pipings,
Such ſmoaky zeals they have againſt hard places.
The Poor mans Box is there too: if ye find any thing
Beſi • e the Poſie, and that half rub'd out too,
For fear it ſhould awake too much charity,
Give it to pious uſes, that is, ſpend it.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: The Bell-ropes, they are ſtrong enough to hang ye,
So we bequeath ye to your deſtiny.
'Pray ye be not ſo haſty.

sp.speaker: Pie.
sp.l: I'le ſpeak a proud word to ye
Would ye have us ſtay?
We do moſt heartily pray ye.
I'le draw as mighty drink, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A ſtrong motive,
The ſtronger ſtill, the more ye come unto me.
And I'le ſend for my Daughter.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This may ſtir too:
The Maiden is of age, and muſt be edified.
You ſhall have any thing: loſe our learned Vicar
And our moſt conſtant friend; honeſt dear Diego?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Yet all this will not do: I'le tell ye, Neighbours,
And tell ye true: if ye will have us ſtay,
If you will have the comforts of our companies,
You ſhall be bound to do us right in theſe points,
You ſhall be bound, and this the obligation,
Dye when 'tis fit, that we may have fit duties,
And do not ſeek to draw— out our undoings,
Marry try'd Women, that are free, and fruitful,
Get Children in abundance, for your Chriſtnings,
Or ſuffer to be got, 'tis equal juſtice,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let Weddings, Chriſtnings, Churchings, Funerals,
And merry Goſſippings go round, go round ſtill,
Round as a Pig, that we may find the profit.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: And let your old men fall ſick handſomely,
And dye immediately, their Sons may ſhoot up:
Let Women dye o'th' Sullens too, tis natural,
But be ſure their Daughters be of age firſt,
That they may ſtock us ſtill: your queazie young Wives
That periſh undeliver'd, I am vext with,
And vext abundantly, it much concerns me,
There's a Childs Burial loſt, look that be mended.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let'em be brought to Bed, then dye when they pleaſe.
Theſe things conſidered, Country-men, and ſworn to.
All theſe, and all our Sports again, and Gambos.
We muſt dye, and we muſt live, and we'll be merry,
Every man ſhall be rich by one another.
We are here to morrow and gone to day, for my part
If getting Children can be friend my Neighbours.
I'le labour hard but I'le fill your Font, Sir.
I have a Mother now, and an old Father,
They are as ſure your own, within theſe two months
My Siſter muſt be pray'd for too, ſhe is deſperate,
Deſperate in love.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Keep deſperate men far from her,
Then 'twill go hard: do you ſee how melancholy?
Do you mark the man? do you profeſs ye love him?
And would do any thing to ſtay his fury?
And are ye unprovided to refreſh him,
To make him know your loves? ſie Neighbours.
We'll do any thing.
We have brought Muſick to appeaſe his ſpirit,
And the beſt Song we'll give him.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: 'Pray ye ſit down, Sir,
They know their duties now, and they ſtand ready
To tender their beſt mirth.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis well, proceed Neighbours,
I am glad I have brought ye to underſtand good manners,
Ye had Puritan hearts a-while, ſpurn'd at all paſtimes,
But I ſee ſome hope now.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: We are ſet, proceed Neighbours.

lg.l: Let the Bells ring, and let the Boys ſing,
The young Laſſes skip and play,
Let the Cups go round, till round goes the ground,
Our Learned old Vicar will ſtay.
Let the Pig turn merrily, merrily ah,
And let the fat Gooſe ſwim,
For verily, verily, verily ah,
Our Vicar this day ſhall be trim.
The ſtew'd Cock ſhall Crow, Cock a-loodle-loo,
A loud Cock-a-loodle ſhall he Crow;
The Duck and the Drake, ſhall ſwim in a lake
Of Omons and Claret below.
Our Wives ſhall be neat, to bring in our meat;
To thee our moſt noble adviſer,
Our pains ſhall be great, and Bottles ſhall ſweat,
And we our ſelves will be wiſer.
We'll labour and ſwinck, we'll kiſs and we'll drink,
And Tithes ſhall come thicker and thicker;
We'll fall to our Plow, and get Children enough,
And thou ſhalt be learned old Vicar.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: What ails this Prieſt? how highly the thing takes it?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Lord how it looks? has he not bought ſome Prebend?
Leandro's mony makes the Raſcal merry,
Merry at heart; he ſpies us.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Be gone Neighbours,
Here are ſome Gentlemen: be gone good Neighbours,
Be gone, and labour to redeem my favour,
No more words, but be gone: theſe two are Gentlemen,
No company for cruſty-handed fellows.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: We will ſtay for a year or two, and try ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Fill all your hearts with joy, we will ſtay with ye,
Be gone, no more; I take your paſtimes graciouſly. Exeunt
Would ye with me, my friends? Pariſhioners.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: We would look upon ye,
For me thinks ye look lovely.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Ye have no Letters?
Nor any kind Remembrances?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Remembrances?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.l: From Nova Hiſpania, or ſome part remote, Sir,
You look like Travel'd men: may be ſome old friends
That happily I have forgot, ſome Signiours
In China or Cataya; ſome Companions—

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: In the Moguls Court, or elſe-where.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: They are mad ſure.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Ye came not from Peru? do they look, Diego,
As if they had ſome myſtery about 'em?
Another Don Alonzo now?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I marry,
And ſo much mony, Sir, from one you know not,
Let it be who it will.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: They have gracious favours.
Would ye be private?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: There's no need on't, Sir,
We come to bring ye a Remembrance from a Merchant.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis very well, 'tis like I know him.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: No, Sir,
I do not think ye do.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A new miſtake, Diego,
Let's carry it decently.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: We come to tell ye,
You have received great ſums from a young Factor
They call Leandro, that has rob'd his Maſter,
Rob'd him, and run away.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Let's keep cloſe, Maſter;
This news comes from a cold Country.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: By my faith it freezes,

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Is not this true? do you ſhrink now good-man Cura •
Do I not touch ye?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We have a hundred Duckets
Yet left, we do beſeech ye, Sir—.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: You'll hang both.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: One may ſuffice.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I will not hang alone, Maſter,
I had the leaſt part, you ſhall hang the higheſt.
Plague o' this Tiveria, and the Letter,
The Devil ſent it poſt, to pepper us,
From Nova Hiſpania, we ſhall hang at home now.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: I ſee ye are penitent, and I have compaſſion:
Ye are ſecure both; do but what we charge ye,
Ye ſhall have more gold too, and he ſhall give it,
Yet ne're indanger ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Command us, Maſter,
Command us preſently, and ſee how nimbly—

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: And if we do not handſomely endeavour—

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Go home, and till ye hear more, keep private,
Till we appear again, no words, Vicar,
There's ſomething added.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: For you too.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We are ready.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Go and expect us hourly, if ye falter,
Though ye had twenty lives—

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: We are fit to loſe 'em.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt expedient that we ſhould hang both.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: If we be hang'd, we cannot blame our fortune.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Farewel, and be your own friends.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We expect ye.— Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA III.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l:
We cited to the Court!
A Bar, Table-book, 2 〈◊〉 and Paper, ſtandiſh ſet 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: It is my wonder.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: But not our fear, Jacintha; wealthy men,
That have Eſtates to loſe; whoſe conſcious thoughts
Are full of inward guilt, may ſhake with horrour
To have their Actions ſifted, or appear
Before the Judge. But we that know our ſelves
As innocent, as poor, that have no Fleece
On which the Talons of the griping Law
Can take ſure hold, may ſmile with ſcorn on all
That can be urg'd againſt us.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I am confident
There is no man ſo covetous, that deſires
To raviſh our wants from us, and leſs hope
There can be ſo much Juſtice left on earth,
• ough ſeed, and call'd upon) to caſe us of
〈◊〉 burthen of our wrongs.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: What thinks Aſcanio?
• hould we be call'd in queſtion, or accus'd
• njuſtly, what would you do to redeem us
• rom tyrannous oppreſſion?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I could pray
• o him that ever has an open ear,
• o hear the innocent, and right their wrongs;
• ay, by my troth, I think I could out-plead
• n Advocate, and ſweat as much as he
Do's for a double Fee, ere you ſhould ſuffer
• n an honeſt cauſe.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: Happy ſimplicitie!

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: My deareſt and my beſt one, Don Jamie.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: And the Advocate, that caus'd us to be ſummon'd.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: My Lord is mov'd, I ſee it in his looks,
And that man, in the Gown, in my opinion
• ooks like a proguing Knave.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Peace, give them leave.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Serve me with Proceſs?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: My Lord, you are not lawleſs.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Nor thou honeſt;
One, that not long ſince was the buckram Scribe,
That would run on mens errands for an Aſper,
And from ſuch baſeneſs, having rais'd a Stock
To bribe the covetous Judge, call'd to the Bar.
• o poor in practice too, that you would plead
A needy Clyents Cauſe, for a ſtarv'd Hen,
Or half a little Loin of Veal, though fly-blown,
And theſe, the greateſt Fees you could arrive at
For juſt proceedings; but ſince you turn'd Raſcal—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Good words, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: And grew my Brothers Bawd,
• n all his vitious courſes, ſoothing him
• n his diſhoneſt practiſes, you are grown
The rich, and eminent Knave, in the Devils name,
What am I cited for?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You ſhall know anon,
And then too late repent this bitter language,
Or I'll miſs of my ends.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Were't not in Court,
〈◊〉 would beat that fat of thine, rais'd by the food
Snatch'd from poor Clyents mouths, into a jelly:
〈◊〉 would (my man of Law) but I am patient,
And would obey the Judge.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Tis your beſt courſe:
Would every enemy I have would beat me,
I would wiſh no better Action.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: 'Save your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: My humble ſervice.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: My good Boy, how doſt thou?
Why art thou call'd into the Court?

div.stage: Enter Aſſiſtant, Henrique, Officer, and Witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I know not,
But 'tis my Lord the Aſſiſtants pleaſure
I ſhould attend here.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: He will ſoon reſolve us.

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.l: Make way there for the Judge.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: How? my kind Brother?
Nay then 'tis rank: there is ſome villany towards.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: This Seſſions purchas'd at your ſuit, Don Henrique,
Hath brought us hither, to hear and determine
Of what you can prefer.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I do beſeech
The honourable Court, I may be heard
In my Advocate.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: 'Tis granted.
Humh, humh.
That Preface,
If left out in a Lawyer, ſpoils the Cauſe,
Though ne're ſo good, and honeſt

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: If I ſtood here,
To plead in the defence of an ill man,
(Moſt equal judge) or to ••• uſe the innocent
(To both which, I profeſs my ſelf a ſtranger)
It would be requiſite I ſhould d ct my Language
With Tropes and Figures, and all flouriſhes
That grace a Rhetorician 'tis confeſs'd
A iulterate Metals need the Gold-ſmiths Art,
To ſet 'em off; what in it ſelf is perfect
Contemns a borrowed gloſs: this Lord (my Client)
Whoſe honeſt cauſe, when 'tis related truly,
Will challenge juſtice, finding in his Conſcience
A tender ſcruple of a fault long ſince
By him committed, thinks it not ſufficient
To be abſolv'd of't by his Confeſſor,
If that in open Court he publiſh not
What was ſo long conceal'd.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: To what tends this?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: In his young years (it is no miracle
That youth, and heat of blood, ſhould mix together)
He look'd upon this woman, on whoſe face
The ruines yet remain, of excellent form,
He look'd on her, and lov'd her.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You good Angels,
What an impudence is this?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And us'd all means
Of Service, Courtſhip, Preſents, that might win her
To be at his devotion: but in vain;
Her Maiden Fort, impregnable held out,
Until he promis'd Marriage; and before
Theſe Witneſſes a ſolemn Contract paſs'd
To take her as his Wife.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Give them their Oath.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: They are incompetent Witneſſes, his own Creature,
And will ſwear any thing for half a Royal.

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.l: Silence.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Proceed.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Upon this ſtrong aſſurance
He did enjoy his wiſhes to the full,
Which ſatisfied, and then with eyes of Judgement
(Hood wink'd with Luſt before) conſidering duly
The inequality of the Match, he being
Nobly deſcended, and allyed, but ſhe
Without a name, or Family, ſecretly
He purchas'd a Divorce, to diſanul
His former Contract, Marrying openly
The Lady Violante.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: As you ſit here
The Deputy of the great King, who is
The Subſtitute of that impartial Judge,
With whom, or wealth, or titles prevail nothing,
Grant to a much wrong'd Widow, or a Wife
Your patience, with liberty to ſpeak
In her own Cauſe, and let me face to face
To this bad man, deliver what he is:
And if my wrongs, with his ingratitude ballanc'd,
Move not compaſſion, let me die unpitied;
His Tears, his Oaths, his Perjuries, I paſs o're;
To think of them is a diſeaſe; but death
Should I repeat them. I dare not deny,
(For Innocence cannot juſtifie what's falſe)
But all the Advocate hath alledged concerning
His falſhood, and my ſhame, in my conſent,
To be moſt true: But now I turn to thee,
To thee Don Henrique, and if impious Acts
Have left thee blood enough to make a bluſh,
I'le paint it on thy cheeks. Was not the wrong
Sufficient to defeat me of mine honour,
To leave me full of ſorrow, as of want,
The witneſs of thy luſt left in my womb,
To teſtifie thy falſhood, and my ſhame?
But now ſo many years I had conceal'd
Thy moſt inhumane wickedneſs, and won
This Gentleman, to hide it from the world,
To Father what was thine (for yet by Heaven,
• hough in the City he paſs'd for my husband,
He never knew me as his wife.)

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange:
Give him an Oath.
I gladly ſwear, and truly.
After all this (I ſay) when I had born
Theſe wrongs, with Saint-like patience, ſaw another
Freely enjoy, what was (in Juſtice) mine,
Yet ſtill ſo tender of thy reſt and quiet,
I never would divulge it, to diſturb
Thy peace at home; yet thou moſt barbarous,
To be ſo careleſs of me, and my fame,
• or all reſpect of thine in the firſt ſtep
To thy baſe luſt, was loſt) in open Court
To publiſh my diſgrace? and on record,
To write me up an eaſie-yielding wanton?
I think can find no precedent: In my extreams,
One comfort yet is left, that though the Law
Divorce me from thy bed, and made free way
To the unjuſt embraces of another,
It cannot yet deny that this thy Son
(Look up Aſcanio ſince it is come out)
Is thy legitimate heir.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Conſederacie!
A trick (my Lord) to cheat me; e're you give
Your Sentence, grant me hearing.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: New Chimera's?

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: I am (my Lord) ſince he is without Iſſue,
Or hope of any, his undoubted heir,
And this forg'd by the Advocate, to defeat me
Of what the laws of Spain confer upon me,
A mee • Impoſture, and conſpiracie
Againſt my future fortunes.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: You are too bold.
Sp • ak to the cauſe Don Henrique.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I confeſs,
(Though the acknowledgment muſt wound mine honour,)
That all the Court hath heard touching this Cauſe,
(Or with me, or againſt me) is moſt true:
The later part my Brother urg'd, excepted:
For what I now doe, is not out of Spleen
(As he pretends) but from remorſe of conſcience
And to repair the wrong that I have done
To this poor woman: And I beſeech your Lordſhip
To think I have not ſo • ar loſt my reaſon,
To bring into my familie, to ſucceed me,
The ſtranger—Iſſue of anothers Bed,
By proof, this is my Son, I challenge him,
Accept him, and acknowledge him, and deſire
By a definitive Sentence of the Court,
He may be ſo recorded, and full power
To me, to take him home.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: A ſecond rape
To the poor remnant of content that's left me,
If this be granted: and all my former wrongs
Were but beginnings to my miſeries,
But this the height of all: • ather than part
With my Aſcan • o, I'le deny my oath,
Profeſs my ſelf a Strumpet, and endure
What puniſhment ſoe're the Court decrees
Againſt a wretch that hath for ſworn her ſelf,
Or pla • 'd the impu • ent whore.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: This taſtes of paſſion,
And that muſt not divert the courſe of Juſtice;
Don He ••••• e, take your Son, with this condition
You give him maintenance, as becomes his birth,
And 'twill ſtand with your honour to doe ſomething
• or this wrong • d woman: I will compel nothing,
But leave it to your will. Break up the Court:
It is in va •• to m ••• me; my doom's paſs'd,
And cannot be revok'd Exit.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 〈◊〉 your reward.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: More cauſes, and ſuch Fees. Now to my Wi • e,
I have too long been abſent: Health to your Lordſhip

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: You all look ſtrangely, and I fear believe
This unexpected fortune makes me proud,
Indeed it do's not: I ſhall ever pay you
The duty of a ſon, and honour you
Next to my Father: good my Lord, for yet
I dare not call you, uncle, be not ſad,
I never ſhall forget thoſe noble favours
You did me being a ſtranger, and if ever
I live to be the maſter of a fortune,
You ſhall command it.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Since it was determin'd
I ſhould be cozen'd, I am glad the profit
Shall fall on thee, I am too tough to melt,
But ſomething I will do.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 'Pray you take leave
Of your ſteward (gentle Brother) the good husband
That takes up all for you.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Very well, mock on,

It is your turn: I may have mine—
Ex •

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: But do not
Forget us, dear Aſcanio.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Do not fear it,
I every day will ſee you: every hour
Remember you in my prayers.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: My grief's too great

To be expreſſed in words—
Ex •

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l:
Take that and leave us,
gives mony to ſa •••
Leave us without reply, nay come back ſirrah
And ſtudy to forget ſuch things as theſe
As are not worth the knowledge. Aſca. offers to fe •••

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: O good Sir,
Theſe are bad principles—

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Such as you muſt learn
Now you are mine, for wealth and poverty
Can hold no friendſhip: and what is my will

You muſt obſerve and do, though good or ill.
Exe •••

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Where is my wife? 'fore heaven, I have done w •• der •
Done mighty things to day, my Amaranta,
My heart rejoyces at my wealthy Gleanings,
A rich litigious Lord I love to follow,
A Lord that builds his happineſs on brawlings,
O 'tis a bleſſed thing to have rich Clyents,
Why, wife I ſay, how fares my ſtudious Pupil?
Hard at it ſtill? ye are too violent,
All things muſt have their reſts, they will not laſt elſe,
Come out and breathe. Leandro wit •••

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I do beſeech you pardon me,
I am deeply in a ſweet point Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'le inſtruct ye:
I ſay take breath, ſeek health firſt, then your ſtudy.
O my ſweet ſoul, I have brought thee golden birds home,
Birds in abundance: I have done ſtrange wonders:
There's more a hatching too.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Have ye done, good husband?
Then 'tis a good day ſpent.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Good enough chicken,
I have ſpread the nets o'th' law, to catch rich booties,
And they come ſluttering in: how do's my Pupil?
My modeſt thing, haſt thou yet ſpoken to him?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: As I paſt by his chamber I might ſee him,
But he is ſo bookiſh.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And ſo baſhfull too,
I' ſaith he is, before he will ſpeak, he will ſtarve th • re.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I pitie him a little.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: So do I too.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: And if he pleaſe to take the air o'th' gardens,
Or walk i'th' inward rooms, ſo he moleſt not —

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He ſhall not trouble thee, he dare not ſpeak to thee.
Bring out the Cheſſe-board,—come let's have a game wiſe,
I'le try your maſterie, you ſay you are cunning

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: As learned as ye are, Sir, I ſhall beat ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Here he ſteals out, put him not out of countenance,
Prethee look another way, he will be gone elſe
Walk and refreſh your ſelf, I'll be with you preſently.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'le take the air a little. Play at cheſs.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Twill be healthfull.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Will ye be there? then here? I'le ſpare ye that man.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Would I were ſo near too, and a mate fitting.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What think ye, Sir, to this? have at your Knight now.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Twas ſubtilly play'd: your Queen lies at my ſervice.
Prethee look off, he is ready to pop in again,
Look off I ſay, do'ſt thou not ſee how he bluſhes?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I do not blaſt him.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: But ye do, and burn too,
What killing looks ſhe ſteals?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I have you now cloſe,
Now for a Mate.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: You are a bleſſed man that may ſo have her.
Oh that I might play with her— knock within.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Who's there? I come, you cannot ſcape me now wife.
I come, I come. knock.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Moſt bleſſed hand that calls him.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Play quickly wife.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: 'Pray ye give leave to think, Sir.

sp.speaker: Moor.
sp.l: An honeſt neighbour that dwells hard by, Sir,
Would fain ſpeak with your worſhip about buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: The devil blow him off.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Play.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I will ſtudy:
For if you beat me thus, you will ſtill laugh at me— knock

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He knocks again; I cannot ſtay. Leandro,
'Pray thee come near.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I am well, Sir, here.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Come hither:
Be not afraid, but come.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Here's none will bite, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: God forbid Lady.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: 'Pray come nearer.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Yes forſooth.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Prethee obſerve theſe men: juſt as they ſtand here,
And ſee this Lady do not alter 'em,
And be not partial, Pupil.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: No indeed Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Let her not move a pawn, I'le come back preſently,
Nay you ſhall know I am a Conquerour.
Have an eye Pupil — Exit.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Can ye play at Cheſs Sir?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: A little, Lady.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: But you cannot tell me
How to avoid this Mate, and win the Game too;
H'as noble eyes: ye dare not friend me ſo far.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I dare do any thing that's in mans power Lady,
To be a friend to ſuch a noble beauty.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: This is no Lawyers language: I pray ye tell me,
Whither may I remove, Ye ſee I am ſet round,
To avoid my husband?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I ſhall tell ye happily,
But happily you will not be inſtructed.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Yes, and thank ye too, ſhall I move this man?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Thoſe are unſeemly: move one can ſerve ye,
Can honour ye, can love ye.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: 'Pray ye tell quickly,
He will return, and then.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'le tell ye inſtantly,
Move me, and I will move any way to ſerve ye,
Move your heart this way, Lady.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: 'Pray ye hear me.
Behold the ſport of love, when he is imperious,
Behold the ſlave of love.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Move my Queen this way?
Sure, he's ſome worthy man: then if he hedge m • ,
Or here to open him.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Do but behold me,
If there be pity in you, do but view me,
But view the miſery I have undertaken
For you, the povertie.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: He will come preſently.
Now play your beſt Sir, though I loſe this Rook here,
Yet I get libertie.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'le ſelfe your fair hand,
And warm it with a hundred, hundred kiſſes.
The God of love warm your deſires but equal,
That ſhall play my game now.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What do you mean Sir?
Why do you ſtop me?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: That ye may intend me.
The time has bleſt us both: love bids us uſe it.
I am a Gentleman nobly deſcended,
Young to invite your love, rich to maintain it.
I bring a whole heart to ye, thus I give it,
And to thoſe burning altars thus I offer,
And thus, divine lips, where perpetual Spring grows—

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Take that, ye are too ſaucy.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: How, proud Lady?
Strike my deſerts?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I was to blame.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What wiſe, there?
Heaven keep my houſe from thieves.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I am wretched:
Opened, diſcovered, loſt to my wiſhes.
I ſhall be whooted at.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What noiſe was this, wiſe?
Why doſt thou ſmile?

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: This proud thing will betray me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Why theſe lie here? what angry, dear?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: No, Sir,
Only a chance, your pupil ſaid he plaid well,
And ſo indeed he do's: he undertook for ye,
Becauſe I would not ſit ſo long time idle,
I made my liberty, avoided your mate,
And he again as cunningly endangered me,
Indeed he put me ſtrangely to it. When preſently
Hearing you come, & having broke his ambuſh too,
Having the ſecond time brought off my Queen fair,
I roſe o'th' ſudden ſmilingly to ſhew ye,
My apron caught the Cheſſe-board, and the men,
And there the noiſe was.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou art grown a Maſter,
For all this I ſhall beat ye.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Or I, Lawyer,
For now I love her more, 'twas a neat anſwer,
And by it hangs a mighty hope, I thank her,
She gave my pate a ſound knock that it rings yet,
But you ſhall have a ſounder if I live lawyer,
My heart akes yet, I would not be in that fear—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I am glad ye are a gameſter, Sir, ſometimes
For recreation we two ſhall fight hard at it.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: He will prove too hard for me.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I hope he ſhall do,
But your Cheſs board is too hard for my head, line that, good Lady.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I have been attoning two moſt wrangling neighbours,
They had no mony, therefore I made even.
Come, let's go in and eat, truly I am hungry.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I have eaten already, I muſt intreat your pardon.
Do as ye pleaſe, we ſhall expect ye at ſupper.
He has got a little heart, now it ſeems handſomly.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You'l get no little head, if I do not look to ye.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: If ever I do catch thee again thou vanity—

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I was to blame to be ſo raſh, I am ſorry—

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: HEar but my reaſons.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: O my patience, hear 'em!
Can cunning falſhood colour an excuſe
With an, ſeeming ſhape of borrowed truth?
Exte • nuate this wofull wrong, not error?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: You gave conſent that, to defeat my brother
I ſhould take any courſe.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: But not to make
The 〈◊〉 more loathſom than the ſoul diſeaſe:
Was't not enough you took me to your bed,
T •• 'd with looſe dalliance, and with emptie veins,
All thoſe abilities ſpent before and waſted,
That could con •• the name of mother on me?
But that to perfect my account of ſorrow
For my long ba •• neneſs) you muſt heighten it
By ſhewing to my face, that you were fruitfull
Hug'd in the baſe embraces of another?
If Solitude that dwelt beneath my roof,
And want of children was a torment to me,
What end of my vextion to behold
A baſtard to upbraid me with my wants?
And hear the name of father paid to ye,
Yet know my ſelf no mother,
What can I ſay?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Shall I confeſs my fault and ask your pardon?
Will that content ye?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: If it could make void,
What is confirm'd in Court: no, no, Don Henrique,
You ſhall know that I find my ſelf abus'd,
And adde to that, I have a womans anger,
And while I look upon this Balilisk,
Whoſe envious eyes have blaſted all my comforts
Reſt confident I'le ſtudy my dark ends,
And not your pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Noble Lady, hear me,
Not as my Fathers ſon, but as your ſervant,
Vouchſafe to hear me, for ſuch in my duty,
I ever will appear: and far be it from
My poor ambition, ever to look on you,
But with that reverence, which a ſlave ſtands bound
To pay a worthy Miſtris: I have heard
That Dames of higheſt place, nay Queens themſelves
Diſdain not to be ſerv'd by ſuch as are
Of meaneſt Birth: and I ſhall be moſt happie,
To be emplo • 'd when you pleaſe to command me
Even in the counſell office, as your Page,
I can wait on your trencher, fill your wine,
Carry your pantoſles, and be ſometimes bleſs'd
In all humilitie to touch your feet:
Or if that you eſteem that too much grace,
I can run by your Coach: obſerve your looks,
And hope to gain a fortune by my ſervice,
With your good ſavour, which now, as a Son,
I date not challenge.
As a Son?
Forgive me,
I will forget the name, let it be death
For me to call you Mother.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Still upbraided?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: No way left to appeaſe you?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: None: now hear me:
Hear what I vow before the face of Heaven,
And if I break it, all plagues in this life,
And thoſe that after death are fear'd fall, on me,
While that this Baſtard ſtaies under my roof,
Look for no peace at home, for I renounce
All Offices of a wife.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: What am I faln to?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I will not eat, nor ſleep with you, and thoſe 〈◊〉
Which I ſhould ſpend in prayers for your health,
Shall be emploi'd in Curſes.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Terrible.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: All the day long, I'le be as tedious to you
As lingring fevers, and I'le watch the nights,
