To ring aloud your ſhame, and break your ſleeps.
Of if you do but ſlumber, I'le appear
In the ſhape of all my wrongs, and like a fury
Fright you to madneſs, and if all this fail
To work out my revenge, I have friends and kinſmen,
That will not ſit down tame with the diſgrace
That's offer'd to our noble familie
In what I ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: How am I divided
Between the duties I owe as a Husband,
And pietie of a Parent?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I am taught Sir
By the inſtinct of nature that obedience
Which bids me to prefer your peace of mind,
Before thoſe pleaſures that are deareſt to me,
Be wholly hers (my Lord) I quit all parts,
That I may challenge: may you grow old together,
And no diſtaſte e're find you, and before
The Characters of age are printed on you
May you ſee many Images of your ſelves,
Though I, like ſome falſe glaſs, that's neverlook'd in,
Am caſt aſide, and broken; from this hour
(Unleſs invited, which I dare not hope for)
I never will ſet my forbidden feet
Over your threſhold: only give me leave
Though caſt off to the world to mention you
In my devotions, 'tis all I ſue for
And ſo I take my laſt leave.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Though I am
Devoted to a wife, nay almoſt ſold
A ſlave to ſerve her pleaſures, yet I cannot
So part with all humanity, but I muſt
Shew ſomething of a Father: thou ſhalt not goe
Unfurniſh'd and unfriended too: take that
To guard thee from neceſſities; may thy goodneſs
Meet many favours, and thine innocence
Deſerve to be the heir of greater fortunes,
Than thou wer't born to. Scorn me not Violante,
This baniſhment is a kind of civil death,
And now, as it were at his funeral
To ſhed a tear or two, is not unmanly,
And ſo farewel for ever: one word more,
Though I muſt never ſee thee (my Aſcanio)
When this is ſpent (for ſo the Judge decreed)
Send to me for ſupply: are you pleas'd now?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Yes: I have cauſe: to ſee you howl and blubber
At the parting of my torment, and your ſhame.
'Tis well: proceed: ſupply his wants: doe doe:
Let the great dower I brought ſerve to maintain
Your Baſtards riots: ſend my Clothes and Iewels,
To your old acquaintaince, your dear dame his Mother.
Now you begin to melt, I know 'twill follow.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Is all I doe miſconſtru'd?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I will take
A courſe to right my ſelf, a ſpeeding one:
By the bleſs'd Saints, I will; if I prove cruel,
The ſhame to ſee thy fooliſh pity, taught me
To loſe my natural ſoftneſs, keep off from me,
Thy flatteries are infectious, and I'le flee thee
As I would doe a Leper.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Let not fury
Tranſport you ſo: you know I am your Creature,
All love, but to your ſelf, with him, hath left me.
• le joyn with you in any thing.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: In vain,
• 'le take mine own waies, and will have no partners.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I will not croſs you.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Do not, they ſhall find
That to a Woman of her hopes beguil'd
A Viper trod on, or an Aſpick's mild. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Sits the game there? I have you by mine order,
〈◊〉 love Leandro for't.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: But you muſt ſhew it
• n lending him your help, to gain him means
And opportunity.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He ſhall want nothing,
〈◊〉 know my Advocate to a hair, and what
Will fetch him from his Prayers, if he uſe any,
I am honyed with the project: I would have him horn'd
For a moſt precious Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: But you loſe time.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I am gone, inſtruct you Diego, you will find him
A ſharp and ſubtle Knave, give him but hints
And he will amplifie. See all things ready,
• 'le fetch him with a vengeance— Exit.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: If he fail now,
We'll give him over too.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Tuſh, he is fleſh'd,
And knows what vein to ſtrike for his own credit.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: All things are ready.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Then we ſhall have a merry Scene, ne're fear it.

div.head: SCENA III.
div.stage: Enter Amaranta, with a note, and Moor.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: Is thy Maſter gone out?

sp.speaker: Moor.
sp.l: Even now, the Curate fetch'd him,
About a ſerious buſineſs as it ſeem'd,
For he ſnatch'd up his Cloak, and bruſh'd his Hat ſtraight,
Set his Band handſomely, and out he gallop'd.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: 'Tis well, 'tis very well, he went out, Egla,
As luckily, as one would ſay, go Husband,
He was call'd by providence: ſling this ſhort Paper
Into Leandro's Cell, and waken him,
He is monſtrous vexed, and muſty, at my Cheſs-play;
But this ſhall ſupple him, when he has read it:
Take your own Recreation for two hours,
And hinder nothing.

sp.speaker: Moor.
sp.l: If I do, I'll hang for't. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: If that you lov'd Aſcanio for himſelf,
And not your private ends, you rather ſhould
Bleſs the fair opportunity, that reſtores him
To his Birth-right, and the Honours he was born to,
Than grieve at his good Fortune.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Grieve, Octavio?
I would reſign my Eſſence, that he were
As happy as my love could faſhion him,
Though every bleſſing that ſhould fall on him,
Might prove a curſe to me: my ſorrow ſprings
Out of my fear and doubt he is not ſafe.
I am acquainted with Don Henrique's nature,
And I have heard too much the fiery temper
Of Madam Violante: can you think
That ſhe, that almoſt is at war with Heaven
For being barren, will with equal eyes
Behold a Son of mine?

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: His Father's care,
That for the want of Iſſue, took him home,
(Though with the forfeiture of his own ſame)
Will look unto his ſafety.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Step-mothers
Have many eyes, to find a way to miſchief,
Though blind to goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: Here comes Don Jamie,
And with him our Aſcanio.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Good youth leave me,
I know thou art forbid my company,
And only to be ſeen with me, will call on
Thy Fathers anger.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Sir, if that to ſerve you
Could loſe me any thing (as indeed it cannot)
I ſtill would follow you. Alas I was born
To do you hurt, but not to help my ſelf,
I was, for ſome particular end, took home,
But am caſt off again.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: The Lady, whom my Father calls his Wife,
Abhors my ſight, is ſick of me, and forc'd him
To turn me out of doors.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: By my beſt hopes
I thank her cruelty, for it comes near
A ſaving Charity.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I am only happy
That yet I can relieve you, 'pray you ſhare
My Father's wondrous kind, and promiſes
That I ſhould be ſupplied: but ſure the Lady
Is a malicious Woman, and I fear
Means me no good.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: I am turn'd a ſtone with wonder,
And know not what to think.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: From my Lady,
Your private ear, and this—

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: New Miracles?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: She ſays, if you dare make your ſelf a Fortune,
She will propoſe the means; my Lord Don Henrique
Is now from home, and ſhe alone expects you,
If you dare truſt her, ſo, if not deſpair of
A ſecond offer. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Though there were an Ambaſh
Laid for my life, I'le on and found this ſecret.
Retire thee, my Aſcanio, with thy Mother:
But ſtir not forth, ſome great deſign's on foot,
Fall what can fall, if e're the Sun be ſet
I ſee you not, give me for dead

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: We will expect you,
And thoſe bleſs'd Angels, that love goodneſs, guard you.

div.head: SCENA V.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Is't poſſible he ſhould be rich?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Moſt poſſible,
He hath been long, though he had but little gettings,
Drawing together, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Accounted a poor Sexton,
Honeſt poor Diego.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I aſſure ye, a cloſe Fellow,
Both cloſe, and ſcraping, and that fills the Bags, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: A notable good fellow too?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Sometimes, Sir,
When he hop'd to drink a man into a Surfeit,
That he might gain by his Grave.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: So many thouſands?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Heaven knows what.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange,
'Tis very ſtrange; but we ſee by endeavour,
And honeſt labour—

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Milo, by continuance
Gr • w from a ſilly Calf (with your worſhips reverence)
To carry a Bull, from a penny, to a pound, Sir,
And from a pound, to many: 'tis the progreſs.
Ye ſay true, but he lov'd to feed well alſo,
And that me thinks—
From another mans Trencher, Sir,
And there he found it ſeaſon'd with ſmall charge:
There he would play the Tyrant, and would devour ye
More than the Graves he made; at home he liv'd
Like a Camelion, ſuckt th'Air of miſery,
And g • ew fat by the Brewis of an Egg-ſhell, Table out, Standiſh, Paper, Stools.
Would ſmell a Cooks-ſhop, and go home and ſurfeit.
And be a month in faſting out that Fever.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Theſe are good Symptoms: do's he lye ſo ſick ſay ye?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Oh, very ſick.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And choſen me Executor?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Only your Worſhip.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No hope of his amendment?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: None, that we find.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He hath no Kinſmen neither?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Truth, very few,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: His mind will be the quieter.
What Doctors has he?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: There's none, Sir, he believes in.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: They are but needleſs things, in ſuch extremities.
Who draws the good mans Will?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Marry that do I, Sir,
And to my grief.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Grief will do little now, Sir,
Draw it to your comfort, Friend, and as I counſel ye,
An honeſt man, but ſuch men live not always:
Who are about him?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Many, now he is paſſing,
That would pretend to his love, yes, and ſome Gentlemen
That would fain counſel him, and be of his Kindred;
Rich men can want no Heirs, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: They do ill,
Indeed they do, to trouble him; very ill, Sir.
But we ſhall take a care.

div.stage: Enter Diego, in a Bed, Milanes, Arſenio, and Pariſhioners.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Will ye come near, Sir?
Pray ye bring him out; now ye may ſee in what ſtate:
Give him freſh Air.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I am ſorry, Neighbour Diego,
To find ye in ſo weak a ſtate.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Ye are welcome,
But I am fleeting, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Me thinks he looks well,
His colour freſh, and ſtrong, his eyes are chearful.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A glimmering before death, 'tis nothing elſe, Sir,
Do you ſee how he ſumbles with the Sheet? do ye note that?

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: My learned Sir, 'pray ye ſit: I am bold to ſend for ye,
To take a care of what I leave.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Do ye hear that?

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Play the Knave finely.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: So I will, I warrant ye,
And carefully.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Pray ye do not trouble him,
You ſee he's weak and has a wandring fancy.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: My honeſt Neighbours, weep not, I muſt leave ye,
I cannot always beat ye company,
We muſt drop ſtill, there is no remedy:
'Pray ye Maſter Cu • ate, will ye write my Teſtament,
And write it largely it may be remembred,
And be witneſs to my Legacies, good Gentlemen;
Your Worſhip I do make my full Executor,
You are a man of wit and underſtanding:
Give me a cup of Wine to raiſe my Spirits,
For I ſpeak low: I would before theſe Neighbours
Have ye to ſwear, Sir, that you will ſee it executed,
And what I g • ve let equally be rendred
For my ſouls health.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I vow it truly, Neighbours,
Let not that trouble ye, before all theſe,
Once more I give my Oath.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Then ſet me higher,
And pray ye come near me all.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We are ready for ye.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Now ſpur the Aſs, and get our friend time.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Firſt then,
After I have given my body to the worms,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Remember your Pariſh, Neighbour.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: You ſpeak truly,
I do remember it, a lewd vile Pariſh,
And pray it may be mended: To the poor of it,
(Which is to all the Pariſh) I give nothing,
For nothing, unto nothing, is moſt natural,
Yet leave as much ſpace, as will build an Hoſpital,
Their Children may pray for me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What do you give to it?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Set down two thouſand Duckets.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Tis a good gift,
And will be long remembred.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: To your worſhip,
(Becauſe you muſt take pains to ſee all finiſh'd)
I give two thouſand more, it may be three, Sir,
A poor gratuity for your pains-taking.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Theſe are large ſums.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Nothing to him that has 'em.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: To my old Maſter Vicar, I give five hundred,
(Five hundred and five hundred are too few, Sir)
But there be more to ſerve.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: This fellow coins ſure.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Give me ſome more drink. Pray ye buy Books, b • Books
You have a learned head, ſtuff it with Libraries,
And underſtand 'em, when ye have done, 'tis Juſtice.
Run not the Pariſh mad with Controverſies,
Nor preach Abſtinence to longing Women,
'Twill burge the bottoms of their Conſciences:
I would give the Church new Organs, but I propheſie
The Church-wardens would quickly pipe'em out o'th' Pariſh
Two hundred Duckets more to mend the Chancel,
And to paint true Orthographie, as many,
They write Sunt with a C, which is abominable,
'Pray you ſet that down; to poor Maidens Marriages.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I that's well thought of, what's your will in that po ••
A meritorious thing.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No end of this Will?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I give per annum two hundred Ells of Lockram,
That there be no ſtrait dealings in their Linnens,
But the Sails cut according to their Burthens.
To all Bell-ringers, I bequeath new Ropes,
And let them uſe 'em at their own diſcretions.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: You may remember us.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I do good Gentlemen,
And I bequeath you both good careful Surgions,
A Legacy, you have need of, more than mony,
I know you want good Diets, and good Lotions,
And in your pleaſures, good take heed.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He raves now,
But 'twill be quickly off.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I do bequeath ye
Commodities of Pins, Brown-papers, Pack-threads,
Roſt Pork, and Puddings, Ginger-bread, and Jews tru •••
Of penny Pipes, and mouldy Pepper, take 'em,
Take 'em even where you pleaſe and be cozen'd with 'em,
I ſhould bequeath ye Executions alſo,
But thoſe I'le leave to th' Law.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Now he grows temperate.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You will give no more?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I am loth to give more from ye,
Becauſe I know you will have a care to execute.
Only, to pious uſes, Sir, a little.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: If he be worth all theſe, I am made for ever.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I give to fatal Dames, that ſpin mens threads out,
• nd poor diſtre • ſed Damſeis, that are militant
• s members of our own Afflictions,

〈◊〉
•••• red Crowns to buy warm Tubs to work in,
〈◊〉 give five hundred pounds to buy a Church-yard,
〈◊〉 ſpacious Church-yard, to lay Thieves and Knaves in,
• ich men and honeſt men take all the room up.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Are ye not weary?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Never of well doing.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Theſe are mad Legacies.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: They were got as madly;
My S • eep, and Oxen, and my moveables,
My Plate, and Jewels, and five hundred Acres;
• have no heirs.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: This cannot be, 'tis monſtrous.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Three Ships at Sea too.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You have made me full Executor?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Full, full, and total, would I had more to give ye,
• ut theſe may ſerve an honeſt mind.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Ye ſay true,
• very honeſt mind, and make it rich too;
• ich, wondrous rich, but where ſhall I raiſe theſe moneys,
• bout your houſe? I ſee no ſuch great promiſes;
Where ſhall I find theſe ſums?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Even where you pleaſe, Sir,
• ou are wiſe and provident, and know buſineſs,
• v'n raiſe 'em where you ſhall think good, I am reaſonable.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Think good? will that raiſe thouſands?
What do you make me?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: You have ſworn to ſee it done, that's all my comfort.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Where I pleaſe? this is pack'd ſure to diſgrace me.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Ye are juſt, and honeſt, and I know you will do it,
•• 'n where you pleaſe, for you know where the wealth is.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I am abuſed, betrayed, I am laugh'd at, ſcorn'd,
• affl'd, and boared, it ſeems.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: No, no, ye are fooled.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Moſt finely fooled, and handſomely, and neatly,
•• ch cunning Maſters muſt be fool'd ſometimes, Sir,
• nd have their Worſhips noſes wiped, 'tis healthful,
We are but quit: you fool us of our moneys
• every Cauſe, in every Quiddit wipe us.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, ha, ſome more drink, for my heart, Gentlemen.
• his merry Lawyer—ha, ha, ha, ha, this Scholar—
• think this fit will cure me: this Executor—
〈◊〉 ſhall laugh out my Lungs.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: This is deriſion above ſufferance, villany
•• otted and ſet againſt me.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Faith 'tis Knavery,
• troth I muſt confeſs, thou art fool'd indeed, Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Did you think, had this man been rich—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: 'Tis well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: He would have choſen ſuch a Wolf, a Canker,
〈◊〉 Maggot-pate, to be his whole Executor?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A Lawyer, that entangles all mens honeſties,
• nd lives like a Spider in a Cobweb lurking,
• nd catching at all Flies, that paſs his pit-falls?
• uts powder to all States, to make 'em caper?
Would he truſt you? Do you deſerve?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I find, Gentlemen,
• his Cataplaſm of a well cozen'd Lawyer
• aid to my ſtomach, leniſies my Feaver,
Methinks I could eat now, and walk a little.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I am aſham'd to feel how ſtat I am cheated,
• ow groſsly, and maliciouſly made a May-game,
〈◊〉 damned trick; my Wife, my Wife, ſome Raſcal:
My Credit, and my Wife, ſome luſtful Villain,
• ome Bawd, ſome Rogue.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Some crafty Fool has found ye:
This 'tis, Sir, to teach ye to be too buſie,
• o covet all the gains, and all the rumours,
• o have a ſtirring Oare in all mens actions.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We did this, but to vex your fine officiouſneſs.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Good yield ye, and good thank ye: I am fooled, Gentlemen;
The Lawyer is an Aſs, I do confeſs it,
A weak dull ſhallow Aſs: good even to your Worſhips:
Vicar, remember: Vicar, Raſcal, remember,
Thou notable rich Raſcal.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I do remember, Sir,
'Pray ye ſtay a little, I have ev'n two Legacies
To make your mouth up, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Remember Varlets,
Quake and remember, Rogues;
I have brine for your Buttocks. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Oh how he frets, and ſumes now like a Dunghil!

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: His gall contains fine ſtuff now to make poyſons,
Rare damned ſtuff.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Let's after him, and ſtill vex him,
And take my Friend off: by this time be has proſper'd,
He cannot loſe this dear time: 'tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Well Diego, thou haſt done.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Haſt done it daintily.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: And ſhalt be as well paid, Boy—

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Go, let's crucifie him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I have told ye all my ſtory, and how deſperately.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: I do believe: let's walk on, time is pretious,
Not to be ſpent in words, here no more wooing,
The open Air's an enemy to Lovers,
Do as I tell ye.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I'le do any thing,
I am ſo over-joy • 'd, I'le fly to ſerve ye

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Take your joy moderately, as it is miniſtred,
And as the cauſe invites: that man's a fool
That at the ſight o'th' Bond, dances and leaps,
Then is the true joy, when the mony comes.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: You cannot now deny me.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: Nay, you know not,
Women have crotchets, and ſtrange fits.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: You ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: Hold ye to that and ſwear it confidently,
Then I ſhall make a ſcruple to deny ye:
'Pray ye let's ſtep in, and ſee a friend of mine,
The weather's ſharp: we'll ſlay but half an hour,
We may be miſs'd elſe: a private fine houſe 'tis, Sir,
And we may find many good welcomes.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: Do Lady,
Do happy Lady.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: All your mind's of doing,
You muſt be modeſter.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I will be any thing. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Open the doors, and give me room to chaſe in
Mine own room, and my liberty: why Maid there,
Open I ſay, and do not anger me,
I am ſubject to much fury: when, ye Diſh clout?
When do ye come? aſleep ye lazie Hell-hound?
Nothing intended, but your caſe, and eating?
No body here? why Wife, why Wife? why Jewel?
No tongue to anſwer me? pre'thee, good Pupil,
Diſpenſe a little with thy careful ſtudy,
And ſtep to th' door, and let me in; nor he neither?
Ha! not at's ſtudy? nor aſleep? nor no body?
I'le make ye hear: the houſe of ignorance,
No ſound inhabits here: I have a Key yet
That commands all: I fear I am Metamorphiz'd.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He keeps his fury ſtill, and may do miſchief.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: He ſhall be hang'd firſt, we'll be ſticklers there, boys.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: The hundred thouſand Dreams now, that poſſeſs him
Of jealouſie, and of revenge, and frailtie,
Of drawing Bills againſt us, and Petitions.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And caſting what his credit ſhall recover.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.l: Let him caſt till his Maw come up, we care not.
You ſhall b ſtill ſe • nt •• . A great noiſe within.
We'll pay him home then;
H ••• w •• t a noiſe he keeps within!

W •
〈…〉 , or the Devil roars there.
〈…〉 Law are broke looſe, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: A ſ
sp.l: H •• ghting ſure.
I' •• t • ll ye that immediately— Exit.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.l: O • doing ſome ſtrange out rage on himſelf.

sp.speaker: A ſ.
sp.l: Ha • g him, 〈◊〉 da •• s not be ſo valiant.
There's no body at home, and he chaſes like a Lyon,
And 〈◊〉 withal. Noiſe ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: No body?
Not a Creature,
Nothing within, but he and his Law tempeſt,
The Ladl • s, D • ſhes, Kettles, how they ſhe all!
And how the Glaſſes through the Rooms!

sp.speaker: Arſ
sp.l: My friend ſure
Has got her out, and now he has made an end on't.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: See where the Sea comes? how it ſoums, and bruſtles?
Th • great L • v • athan o'th' Law, how it tumbles?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Made every way an Aſs? abus'd on all ſides?
And f • om all quarters, people come to laugh at me?
Riſe like a Comet, to be wonder'd at?
A ho ••• d Com t, for Boys tongues, and Ballads?
I will run from my wits.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Do, do, good Lawyer,
And from thy mony too, then thou wilt be quiet.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Here ſhe comes home: now mark the ſalutations;
How like an Aſs my friend goes?
She has pull'd his cars down.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Now, what ſweet voyage? to what Garden, Lady?
Or to what Coulins houſ • ?

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: Is this my welcome?
I cannot go to Church, but thus I am ſcandal'd,
U • no devotion for my ſoul, but Gentlemen

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: • o Church?
Yes, and ye keep ſweet youths to wait upon me,
Sweet bred up youths, to be a credit to me.
T ••• e's your delight again, pray take him to ye,
He never comes nea • me more to debaſe me.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.l: How's this how's this good wiſe, how, has he wrong'd ye?

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.l: I was •• m to drive him like a ſheep before me,
I blu • h to think how people ſteer'd, and ſcorn'd me.
Others have handſome men, that know behaviour,
Place, and obſervance: this ſilly thing knows nothing,
Cannot tell ten; let every Raſcal juſt • e me,
And ſtill I puſh'd him on as he had been coming.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Ha • did ye puſh him on? is he ſo ſtupid?

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.l: When others were attentive to the Prieſt,
G • od devout Gentleman, then fell he faſt,
• aſt, ſound aſleep: then hiſt began the Bag pipes,
〈◊〉 ſeveral ſtops on's no • e made a rate muſick,
A ••• e and l • ud, and thoſe plaid many an Anthem.
• u • out of that, he • ell ſtraight into dreaming.

sp.speaker: Arſ
sp.l: As cunning, as ſhe is ſweet, I like this carriage.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.l: What • id he then?

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.l: Why then be talked in his Sleep too,
Nay, I'le divulge your moral vertues (ſheeps face)
And talk • d a loud, t • at every • a • was fixt to him:
D •• not I ſuffer (do you think) in this time?
〈◊〉 of your baw •• ng Law, of app • lations
O • Declarations, and Excommunications:
Wa •• ants, and • x •• utions: and ſuch Devils
〈◊〉 a • l the Gentlem • n out o'th' Church, by hurryes,

W ••••
〈…〉 , they would never come there again.
Thus am I ſerved and man'd.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I pray ye forgive me,
I muſt confeſs I am not fit to wait upon ye:
Alas, I was brought up—

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: To be an Aſſe,
A Lawyers Aſſe, to carry Books, and Buckrams.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: But what did you at Church?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: At Church, did you ask her?
Do you hear Gentlemen, do you mark that queſtion?
Becauſe you are half an Heretick your ſelf, Sir,
Would ye breed her too? this ſhall to the Inquiſition,
A pious Gentlewoman reproved for praying?
I'le ſee this filed, and you ſhall hear further, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arſ
sp.l: Ye have an ill heart.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: It ſhall be found out, Gentlemen,
There be thoſe youths will ſearch it.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: You are warm Signiour,
But a Faggot will warm ye better: we are witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Enough to hang him, do not doubt.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Nay certain,
I do believe h'as rather no Religion.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: That muſt be known too, becauſe ſhe goes to Church S ••

l.hi: O monſtrum informe ingens!

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Let him go on, Sir,
His wealth will build a Nunnery, a fair one,
And this good Lady, when he is hang'd and rotten,
May there be Abbeſs.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You are cozen'd, honeſt Gentlemen,
I do not forbid the uſe but the form, mark me.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Form? what do you make of form?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: They will undo me,
Swear, as I oft have done, and ſo betray me;
I muſt make fair way, and hereafter, Wife,
You are welcome home, and henceforth take your pleaſure,
Go when ye ſhall think fit, I will not hinder ye,
My eyes are open now, and I ſee my errour,
My ſhame, as great as that, but I muſt hide it.
The whole conveyance now I ſmell, but Baſta,
Another time muſt ſerve: you ſee us friends, now
Heartily friends, and no more chiding, Gentlemen,
I have been too fooliſh, I confeſs, no more words,
No more, ſweet Wife.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: You know my eaſie nature.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Go get ye in: you ſee ſhe has been angry:
Forbear her fight a while and time will pacify;
And learn to be more bold.

sp.speaker: Lean.
sp.l: I would I could,

I will do all I am able.
Ex • t.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do Leandro,
We will not part, but friends of all hands.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Well ſaid,
Now ye are reaſonable, we can look on ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Ye have jerkt me: but for all that I forgive ye,
Forgive ye heartily, and do invite ye
To morrow to a Breakfaſt, I make but ſeldom,
But now we will be merry.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Now ye are friendly,
Your doggedneſs and niggardize ſlung from ye.
And now we will come to ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Give me your hands, all;
You ſhall be welcome heartily.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We will be,
For we'll eat hard.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: The harder, the more welcome,
And till the morning farewell; I have buſineſs. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Farewel good bountiful Bartolus, 'tis a brave wen •• ,
A ſuddain witty thief, and worth all ſervice:
Go we'll all go, and crucifie the Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I'le clap four tire of teeth into my mouth more
But I will grind his ſubſtance.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Well Leandro,
Thou haſt had a ſtrange Voyage, but I hope
Thou rid'ſt now in ſafe harbour.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Let's go drink, Friends,
And laugh aloud at all our merry may-games.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A match, a match, 'twill whet our ſtomachs better.
MAdam, he's come. Chair and ſtools out.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: 'Tis well, how did he look,
•• en he knew from whom you were ſent? was he not ſtartled?
Or confident? or fearful?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: As appear'd
• ike one that knew his fortune at the worſt,
And car'd not what could follow.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: 'Tis the better,
• each me a Chair: ſo, bring him in, be careful
That none diſturb us: I will try his temper,
And if I find him apt for my employments,
• le work him to my ends; if not, I ſhall
• ind other Engines.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: There's my Lady.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Leave us.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: You ſent for me?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I did, and do's the favour,
Your preſent ſtate conſidered and my power,
Deſerve no greater Ceremony?

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Ceremonie?
• ſe to pay that where I owe a duty,
• o • to my Brothers wife: I cannot fawn,
〈◊〉 you expect it from me, you are cozen'd,
And ſo farewel.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: He bears up ſtill; I like it.
• ray you a word.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Yes, I will give you hearing
• a equal terms, and ſit by you as a friend,
• et not ſtand as a Sutor: Now your pleaſure?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: You are very bold.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: 'Tis fit: ſince you are proud,
〈◊〉 was not made to feed that fooliſh humour,
• ith flattery and obſervance.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Yet, with your favour,
A little form joyn'd with reſpect to her,
That can add to your wants, or free you from 'em
Nay raiſe you to a fate, beyond your hopes)
• ight well become your wiſdom.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: It would rather
• rite me a Fool, ſhould I but only think
That any good to me could flow from you,
• hom for ſo many years I have found and prov'd
My greateſt Enemy: I am ſtill the ſame,
My wants have not transform'd me: I dare tell you,
• o your new cerus'd face, what I have ſpoken
•• tely behind your back, what I think of you,
• ou are the proudeſt thing, and have the leaſt
• eaſon to be ſo that I ever read of.
• n ſtature you are a Gianteſs: and your Tailor
Takes meaſure of you with a Jacobs Staff,
〈◊〉 he can never reach you, this by the way
• or your large ſize: now, in a word or two,
• o treat of your Complexion were decorum:
• ou are ſo far from fair, I doubt your Mother
• as too familiar with the Moor that ſerv'd her,
• our Limbs and Features I paſs briefly over,
• s things not worth deſcription; and come roundly
To your Soul, if you have any; for 'tis doubtful.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I laugh at this, proceed.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: This Soul I ſpeak of,
Or rather Salt to keep this heap of fleſh
• rom being a walking ſtench, like a large Inn,
Stands open for the entertainment of
All impious practices: but there's no Corner
An honeſt thought can take up: and as it were not
Sufficient in your ſelf to comprehend
All wicked plots, you have taught the Fool, my Brother,
By your contagion, almoſt to put off
The nature of the man, and turn'd him Devil,
Becauſe he ſhould be like you, and I hope
Will march to Hell together: I have ſpoken,
And if the Limning you in your true Colours
Can make the Painter gracious, I ſtand ready
For my reward, or if my words diſtaſte you,
I weigh it not, for though your Grooms were ready
To cut my Throat for't, be aſſur'd I cannot
Uſe other Language.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: You think you have ſaid now,
Like a brave fellow: in this Womans War
You ever have been train'd: ſpoke big, but ſuffer'd
Like a tame Aſs; and when moſt ſpur'd and gall'd
Were never Maſter of the Spleen or Spirit,
That could raiſe up the anger of a man,
And force it into action.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Yes, vile Creature,
Wer't thou a ſubject worthy of my Sword,
Or that thy death, this moment, could call home
My baniſh'd hopes, thou now wer't dead; dead, woman;
But being as thou art, it is ſufficient
I ſcorn thee, and contemn thee.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: This ſhews nobly,
I muſt confeſs it: I am taken with it,
For had you kneel'd and whin'd and ſhew'd a baſe
And low dejected mind, I had deſpis'd you.
This bravery (in your adverſe fortune) conquers
And do's command me, and upon the ſuddain
I feel a kind of pity, growing in me,
For your misfortunes, pity ſome ſay's the Parent,
Of future love, and I repent my part
So far in what you have ſuffered, that I could
(But you are cold) do ſomething to repair
What your baſe Brother (ſuch Jamie I think him)
Hath brought to ruine.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Be not amaz'd,
Our injuries are equal in his Baſtard,
You are familiar with what I groan for,
And though the name of Husband holds a tye
Beyond a Brother, I, a poor weak Woman,
Am ſenſible, and tender of a wrong,
And to revenge it would break through all lets,
That durſt oppoſe me.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Is it poſſible?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: By this kiſs: ſtart not: thus much, as a ſtranger
You may take from me; but, if you were pleas'd,
I ſhould ſelect you as a boſom friend,
I would print 'em thus, and thus.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Keep off.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Come near,
Near into the Cabinet of my Counſels:
Simplicity and patience dwell with Fools,
And let them bear thoſe burthens, which wiſe men
Boldly ſhake off; be mine and joyn with me,
And when that I have rais'd you to a fortune,
(Do not deny your ſelf the happy means)
You'll look on me with more judicious eyes
And ſwear I am moſt fair.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: What would this Woman?
The purpoſe of theſe words? ſpeak not in riddles,
And when I underſtand, what you would counſel,
My anſwer ſhall be ſuddain.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Thus then Jamie,
The objects of our fury are the ſame,
For young Aſcanio, whom you Snake like hug'd
(Frozen with wants to death) in your warm boſom,
Lives to ſupplant you in your certain hopes,
A •• falls in me all comfort.
Now 'tis plain,
I apprehend you: and were he remov'd
Y •• , once a • ain, were the undoubted heir.
• is not to be deny'd; I was ſee before,
〈…〉 have fir'd me.

〈…〉
• ld ſu •• to it,
〈…〉 out, do you but ſtee •
As I 〈◊〉 you, wee'l bring out Bark into
I •• Port of happineſs.
How?
〈◊〉 death:

〈…〉
•• other; in great fortunes
〈…〉 of States and Kingdom,)
〈…〉 no Rivals.
〈…〉 I think out of a ſ ••• pulous fea • ,

〈…〉
•• pectation, when I may

D ••
•• ing out a little with my conſcience)
Co •• alſo • nd poſſ • ſſion, would not argue
On • that d •• 'd to thrive.
Now you ſp ak like
A man that knows the World.
I needs muſt learn
That have ſo good a Tu ••• ſs: and what think you,
sp.stage: (Don Henrique and Aſ • a • io out off)
sp.l: That none may •• e, that ſhall deſire to trace us
• o ou • black paths, if that Octavio
His ſoft •• Father, and the ſad Ja ••• ta,
( • aith p •• her, and free her from her Sorrows)
S ••• ld fall companions with 'em? When we are red
W ••• murther, let us often bath in blood,
In colour will be ſ • arlet.
And that's glorious,
And will protect the fact.
Suppoſe this done:
(I • undiſcovered) we may get for mony.
(As that • ou know buyes any thing in Rome)
A diſp ••• ſation.
And be married?
O • that be known, t •• ſs up out Gold and Jewels,
And 〈◊〉 to ſome 〈◊〉 State, • n there with ſcorn
Laugh at the laws of Spain.
I were a ••• able.
〈◊〉 ſhall beg • t rare children. I am rapt with

T ••
〈◊〉 imagination.
S • all it be done?
S • all? 'tis too tedious: furniſh me with means
To 〈◊〉 the inſtruments, and to your ſelf
Say it is 〈◊〉 already: I will ſhew you,
〈◊〉 the Sun ſet, how much you have wrought upon me,
〈◊〉 p ovince is only to uſe ſome means,
To find my Brother to the Grove that's neighbour
To the well Port of th' City; leave the reſt
• o •• , own practice, I have talk'd too long,
Put now will doe: this kiſs, with my Confeſſion,
To work a fell revenge: a man's a fool,
It not inſtructed in a Womans School. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA II.
div.stage:
Enter Bartolus, Algazeirs, and a Paratour. 〈◊〉
Table ſet out and ſtools.

sp.l: You are well enough diſguiz'd, furniſh the Table,
Ma •• no ſhew what ye are, till I diſcover:
Not a ſo •• knows ye here: be quick and diligent,
Theſe youths I have invited to a Breakfaſt,
• ut what the Sawes will 〈◊〉 , I am of opinion
I ſhall take of the 〈◊〉 of their Appetites,

〈◊〉 caſe 〈◊〉
•• ns for eating heartily
〈…〉 have plaid their prizes with me,
And 〈…〉 have lighted dangerouſly,
〈…〉 qui •• I hea • 'em coming.
Go off and wait the bringing in your ſervice,
And do it handſomely: you know where to have it.
Welcom i' Faith.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: That's well ſaid, honeſt Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Said like a neighbour.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Welcom all: all over,
And let's be merry.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: To that end we came Sir,
An hour of freedome's worth an age of juglings.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I am come too Sir, to ſpecifie my Stomach
A poor reteiner to your worſhips bountie.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And thou ſhalt have it fill'd my merry Diego,
My liberal, and my bonny bounteous Diego,
Even fill'd till it groan again.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Let it have fair play,
And if it founder then.—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'le tell ye neighbours,
Though I were angry yeſterday with ye all,
And very angry, for methought ye bob'd me.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: No, no, by no means.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No, when I conſidered
It was a jeſt, and carried off ſo quaintly,
It made me merry: very merry, Gentlemen,
I do confeſs I could not ſleep to think on't,
The mirth ſo tickled me, I could not ſlumber.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Good mirth do's work ſo: honeſt mirth,
Now, ſhould we have meant in earneſt—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You ſay true neighbour.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: It might have bred ſuch a diſtaſt and ſowrneſs,
Such fond imaginations in your Brains, Sir,
For things thruſt home in earneſt. —

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Very certain,
But I know ye all for merry waggs, and ere long
You ſhall know me too in another faſhion,
Though y'are pamper'd, ye ſhall bear part o'th'burther
Come wife; Come bid 'em welcom; Come my Jew.
And Pupil, you ſhall come too; ne're hang backward,
Come, come the woman's pleas'd, her anger's over,
Come, be not baſhfull.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What do's he prepare here?
Sure there's no meat i'th' houſe, at leaſt not dreſt,
Do's he mean to mock 'em? or ſome new bred crotcher
Come o're his brains; I do not like his kindneſs:
But ſilence beſt becomes me: if he mean foul play,
Sure they are enough to right themſelves, and let 'em,
I'le ſit by, ſo they beat him not to powder,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Bring in the meat there, ha? Sit down dear up h ••
A little meat needs little Complement,
Sit down I ſay.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What do you mean by this Sir?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Convey away their weapons handſomely.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You know there's none i'th' houſe to anſwer ye,
But the poor Girle; you know there's no meat neither.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Peace and be quiet; I ſhall make you ſmoak e •• e,
There's men and meat enough, ſet it down formally.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I fear ſome lewd trick, yet I dare not ſpeak on't.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I have no dainties for ye Gentlemen,
Not loads of meat, to make the room ſmell of 'em.
Only a diſh to every man I have dedicated,
And if I have pleas'd his appetite.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: O, a Capon,
A Bird of grace, and be thy will, I honour it.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: For me ſome fortie pound of lovely Be •• ,
Plac'd in a mediterranean ſea of Brewis.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Fall to, fall to, that we may drink and laugh 〈◊〉
Wait diligently knaves.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: What rare bit's this?
An execution! bleſs me!

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Nay take it to ye,
• e • 's no avoiding it, 'tis ſomewhat tough Sir,
• t a good ſtomach will endure it eaſily,
• he • um is but a thouſand duckets Sir.

sp.speaker: A ſ.
sp.l: A Capias from my Surgeon, and my Silk-man!
Your carefull makers, but they have mar'd your diet.
•• not, your Swords are gone: there's no avoiding me,
• re theſe are Algazeirs, do you hear that paſſing bell?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A ſtrong Citation, bleſs me!
Out with your Beads, Curate,
•• D • vil's in your diſh: bell, book, and Candle.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.l: A warrant to appear before the Judges!
• mul • needs riſe, and turn to th' wall.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Ye need not,
• our fear I hope will make ye find your Breeches.
We are betrai'd.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Invited do not wrong me,
••• to, good Gueſts, you have diligent men about ye,
• e ſhall want nothing that may perſecute ye,
••• ſe will not ſee ye ſtart; Have I now found ye?
Have I requited ye? You fool'd the Lawyer,
• nd thought it meritorious to abuſe him,
• thick ram-headed knave: you rid, you ſpur'd him,
• nd glorified your wits, the more ye wronged him;
Within this hour ye ſhall have all your Creditours,
• ſecond diſh of new debts, come upon ye,
• nd new invitements to the whip, Don Diego,
• nd Excommunications for the learned Curate,
• Maſque of all your furies ſhall dance to ye.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: You dare not uſe us thus?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You ſhall be bob'd, Gentlemen,
• ir and as I have a life, ye goe to priſon,
• o priſon, without pitie inſtantly,
• efore ye ſpeak another word to priſon.
•• ave a better Guard without, that waits;
• o you ſee this man, Don Curate? 'tis a Paratour
• at comes to tell ye a delightfull ſtory
Of an old whore ye have, and then to teach ye
What is the penaltie; Laugh at me now Sir,
What Legacie would ye bequeath me now,
And pay it on the nail?) to fly my fury?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: O gentle Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou hope I will be gentle,
• hou fooliſh unconſiderate Curate?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let me goe Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'le ſee thee hang firſt.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And as I am a true Vicar,
Hark in your ear, hark ſoftly —

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No, no bribery.
• 'le have my ſwindge upon thee; Sirra? Raſcal?
You Lenten Chaps, you that lay ſick, and mockt me,
Mockt me abominably, abuſed me lewdly,
• 'le make thee ſick at heart, before I leave thee,
And groan, and dye indeed, and be worth nothing,
Not worth a bleſſing, nor a Bell to knell for thee,
A ſheet to cover thee, but that thou ſtealeſt,
• tealeſt from the Merchant, and the Ring he was buried with
• tealeſt from his Grave, do you ſmell me now?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Have mercy on me!

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: No Pſalm of mercy ſhall hold me from hanging thee.
How do ye like your Breakfaſt? 'tis but ſhort, Gentlemen,
But ſweet and healthfull; Your puniſhment, and yours, Sir,
For ſome near reaſons that concern my Credit,
I will take to my ſelf

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Doe Sir, and ſpare not:
I have been too good a wife, and too obedient,
But ſince ye dare provoke me to be fooliſh —

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: She has, yes, and too worthie of your uſage,
Before the world I juſtifie her goodneſs,
And turn that man, that dares but taint her vertues,
To my Swords point; that lying man, that baſe man,
Turn him, but face to face, that I may know him.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What have I here?

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: A Gentleman, a free man,
One that made trial of this Ladies conſtancie,
And found it ſtrong as la • e; leave off your fooling,
For if you follow this courſe, you will be Chronicled
For a devil, whilſt a Saint ſhe is mentioned,
You know my name indeed; I am now no Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Som comfort now I hope, or elſe would I were hanged up.
And yet 〈◊〉 Ju • g • , he ma • es me ſweat.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What news now?

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.l: I will juſtifie upon my life and credit
What you have heard, for truth, and will make proof of.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: I will be ready at the appointed hour there,
And ſo I leave ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Stay I beſeech your worſhip,
And do but hear me.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Good Sir, intend this buſineſs,
And let this bawling fool, no more words lawyer,
And no more angers, for I gueſs your reaſons,
This Gentleman, I'le juſtifie in all places,
And that fair Ladies worth; let who dare croſs it.
The Plot was caſt by me, to make thee jealous,
But not to wrong your wife, ſhe is fair and vertuous.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Take us to mercy too, we beſeech your honour,
We ſhall be juſtified the way of all fleſh elſe.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: No more talk, nor no more diſſention lawyer,
I know your anger, 'tis a vain and flight one,
For if you doe, I'le lay your whole life open,
A life that all the world ſhall — I'le bring witneſs,
And tip before a Judge the ulcerous villanies,
You know I know ye, and I can bring witneſs

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Nay good Sir, noble Sir.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Be at peace then preſently,
Immediatley take honeſt and fair truce
With your good wiſe, and ſhake hands with that Gentleman;
H'as honour'd ye too much, and doe it cheerfully.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Take us along, for Heaven ſake too.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I am friends,
There is no remedie, I muſt put up all,
And like my neighbours rub it out byth' ſhoulders,
And perfect friends; Leandro now I thank ye,
And there's my hand, I have no more grudge to ye,
But I am too mean hence forward for your Companie.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: I ſhall not trouble ye.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: We will be friends too.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.l: Nay Lawyer, you ſhall not fright us farther,
For all your devils we will bolt.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I grant ye,
The Gentleman's your Bail, and thank his coming,
Goe all in peace, but when ye fool next, Gentlemen,
Come not to me to Breakfaſt.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I'le be bak'd firſt.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And pray ye remember, when ye are bold and merry,
The Lawyers Banquet, and the Sawce he gave ye.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Come: goe along; I have employm • nt to ye,
Employment for your lewd brains too, to cool ye,
For all, for every one.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We are all your Servants.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: All, all for any thing, from this day forward
I'le hate all Breakfaſts, and depend on dinners.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: I am glad you come off fair.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: The fair has bleſt me. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA III.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: This is the place, but why we are appointed
By Don Jamie to ſtay here, is a depth
I cannot ſound.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Believ't he is too noble
To purpoſe any thing but for our good.
Had I aſſurance of a thouſand lives,
And with them perpetuitie of pleaſure,
And ſhould loſe all, if he prov'd only falſe,
Yet I durſt run the hazard.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Tis our comfort.
We cannot be more wretched than we are,
And death concludes all miſery.
Undiſcovered
We muſt attend him.
Out ſtay is not long.
With him Don Henrique?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Now I fear;
Be •• lent.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Why doſt thou follow me?

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: To ſave your life,
A p • ot is laid for't, all my wrongs forgot,
I have a Brothers Love.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: But thy falſe ſelf
I fear no enemy.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: You have no friend,
But what breathes in me: If you move a ſtep
Beyond this ground you tread on, you are loſt.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 'Tis by thy practice then: I am ſent hither
To meet her, that prefers my life and ſafetie
Before her own.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: That you ſhould be abus'd thus
With weak credulitie! She for whoſe ſake
You have forgot we had one noble Father,
Or that one Mother bare us, for whoſe love
You brake a contract to which heaven was witneſs,
To ſatisfie whoſe pride and wilfull humour
You have expos'd a ſweet and hopefull Son
To all the miſeries that want can bring him,
And ſuch a Son, though you are moſt obdurate,
To give whom entertainment Savages
Would quit their Caves themſelves, to keep him from
Bleak cold and hunger: This diſſembling woman,
This Idol, whom you worſhip, all your love
And ſervice trod under her feet, deſigns you
To fill a grave, or dead to lye a prey
For Wolves and Vul • ms.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: 'Tis falſe; I defie thee,
And ſtand upon my Guard.

div.stage: Enter Leandro, Milanes, Arſenio, Bart. Lopez, Diego, Octavio, Jacinta, Aſcanio, and Servants.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Alas, 'tis weak:
Come on, ſince you will teach me to be cruel,
By having no faith in me, take your fortune,
Bring the reſt forth, and bind them faſt.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: In what have we offended?

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: I am deaf,
And following my will, I do not ſtand
Accomptable to reaſon: See her Ring
(The firſt pledge of your love, and ſervice to her)
Deliver'd as a Warrant for your death:
Theſe • ags of gold you gave up to her truſt,
(The uſe of which you did deny your ſelf)
Beſtow'd on me, and with a prodigal hand,
Whom • he pick'd forth to be the Architect
Of her moſt bloudy building; and to ſee
Theſe Inſtruments, to bring Materials
To raiſe it up, ſhe bad me ſpare no coſt,
And (as a ſurpluſage) offer'd her ſelf
To be at my devotion.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: O accurs'd!

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: But be incredulous ſtill, think this my plot;
• a •• en excuſes to your ſelf, and ſwear
That ſhe is innocent, that ſhe doats on ye;
To have this, as a fearfull Dream, and that
〈◊〉 he not at my mercy, which in this
I w •• l • h • only. She he • ſelf ſhall give

〈…〉
• ull Sent • n • e, to remove all ſcruple
Who 'tis that ſends you to the other world.
Appears my Violante? ſpeak (my deareſt)
Do's not the object pleaſe you?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: More than if
All treaſure that's above the earth, with that,
That lyes conceal'd in both the Indian Mines,
Were laid down at my feet: O bold Jamy,
Thou only canſt deſerve me.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: I am forward,
And (as you eaſily may perceive,) I ſleep not
On your commands.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: But yet they live: I look'd
To find them dead.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: That was deferr'd, that you
Might triumph in their miſery, and have the power
To ſay they are not.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: 'Twas well thought upon:
This kiſs, and all the pleaſures of my Bed
This night, ſhall thank thee.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Monſter!

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: You Sir, that
Would have me Mother Baſtards, being unable
To honour me with one Child of mine own,
That underneath my roof, kept your caſt-Strumpet,
And out of my Revenues would maintain
Her riotous iſſue: now you find what 'tis
To tempt a woman: with as little feeling
As I turn off a ſlave, that is unfit
To doe me ſervice; or a horſe, or dog
That have out-liv'd their uſe, I ſhake thee off,
To make thy peace with heaven.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I do deſerve this,
And never truly felt before, what ſorrow
Attends on wilfull dotage.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: For you, Miſtris,
That had the pleaſure of his youth before me,
And triumph'd in the fruit that you had by him,
But that I think, to have the Baſtard ſtrangled
Before thy face, and thou with ſpeed to follow
The way he leads thee, is ſufficient torture,
I would cut off thy noſe, put out thine eyes,
And ſet my foot on theſe bewitching lips,
That had the ſtart of mine: but as thou art,
Goe to the grave unpitied.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Who would believe
Such rage could be in woman?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: For this fellow,
He is not worth my knowledge.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Let him live then,
Since you eſteem him innocent.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: No Jamy,
He ſhall make up the meſs: now ſtrike together,
And let them fall ſo.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Unheard of crueltie!
I can endure no longer: ſeiſe on her.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Am I betrai'd?
Is this thy faith, Jamy?

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Could your deſires
Challenge performance of a deed ſo horrid?
Or, though that you had ſold your ſelf to hell,
I ſhould make up the bargain? Live (dear Brother)
Live long, and happy: I forgive you freely;
To have done you this ſervice, is to me
A fair Inheritance: and how e're harſh language
(Call'd on by your rough uſage) paſs'd my lips,
In my heart I ever lov'd you: all my labours
Were but to ſhew, how much your love was cozen'd,
When it beheld it ſelf in this falſe Glaſs,
That did abuſe you; and I am ſo far
From envying young Aſcanio his good fortune,
That if your State were mine, I would adopt him,
Theſe are the Murtherers my noble friends,
Which (to make trial of her bloudy purpoſe)
• won, to come diſguis'd thus.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I am too full
Of grief, and ſhame to ſpeak: but what I'le doe,
•• all to the world proclaim my penitence;
•• d howſoever I have liv'd, I'le die
• much chang'd man.

sp.speaker: Jam.
sp.l: Were it but poſſible
You could make ſatisfaction to this woman,
•• r joyes were perfect.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: That's my only comfort,
That it is in my power: I ne're was married
To this bad woman, though I doted on her,
But daily did defer it, ſtill expecting
When grief would kill Jacintha.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: All is come out,
And finds a fair ſucceſs: take her Don Henrique,
And once again embrace your Son.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Moſt gladly.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Your Brother hath deſerv'd all.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: And ſhall ſhare
The moitie of my State.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: I have heard, advocate,
What an ill Inſtrument you have been to him,
From this time ſtrengthen him with honeſ • counſels,
As you'le deſerve my pardon.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'le change my Copy:
But I am puniſh'd, for I fear I have had
A ſmart blow, though unſeen.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Curate, and Sexton,
I have heard of you too, let me hear no more,
And what's paſt, is forgotten; For this woman,
Though her intent were bloody, yet our Law
Calls it not death: yet that her puniſhment
May deter others from ſuch bad attempts,
The dowry ſhe brought with her, ſhall be emploi'd
To build a Nunnery, where ſhe ſhall ſpend
The remnant of her life.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Since I have miſs'd my ends,
I ſcorn what can fall on me.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: The ſtrict diſcipline
Of the Church, will teach you better thoughts. And Signiors,
You that are Batchelours, if you ever marry,
In Bartolus you may behold the iſſue
Of Covetouſneſs and Jealouſie; and of dotage,
And falſhood in Don Henrique: keep a mean then;

l.hi: For be aſſur'd, that weak man meets all ill,
That gives himſelf up to a womans will.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: TO tell ye (Gentlemen,) we have a Play,
A new one too, and that 'tis launch'd to day,
The Name ye know, that's nothing to my Story;
To tell ye, 'tis familiar, void of Glory,
Of State, of Bitterneſs: of wit you'll ſay,
For that is now held wit, that tends that way,
Which we avoid: To tell ye too 'tis merry,
And meant to make ye pleaſant, and not weary:
The Stream that guides ye, eaſie to attend:
To tell ye that 'tis good, is to no end,
If you believe not. Nay, to goe thus far,
To ſwear it, if you ſwear againſt, is war.
To aſſure you any thing, unleſs you ſee,
And ſo conceive, is vanity in me;
Therefore I leave it to it ſelf, and pray
Like a good Bark, it may work out to day,
And ſtem all doubts; 't was built for ſuch a proof,
And we hope highly: if ſhe lye aloof
For her own vantage, to give wind at will,
Why let her work, only be you but ſtill,
And ſweet opinion'd, and we are bound to ſay,
You are worthy Judges, and you crown the Play.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: THE Play is done, yet our Suit never ends,
Still when you part, you would ſtill part our friends,
Our nobleſt friends; if ought have faln amiſs,
O let it be ſufficient, that it is,
And you have pardon'd it. In Buildings great
All the whole Body cannot be ſo neat,
But ſomething may be mended; Thoſe are fair,
And worthy love, that may deſtroy, but ſpare.

list.item: Valentine, a Gallant that will not be perſwaded to keep his Eſtate.
A Merchant, Friend to Maſter Lovegood.

list.head: companions of Valentine, and Sutors to the Widow.

list.item: Lance, a Falkner, and an ancient ſervant to Valentines Father.
Shorthoſe, the Clown, and ſervant to the Widow.
Roger, Ralph, and Humphrey, three ſervants to the Widow.
Luce, a waiting Gentlewoman to the Widow.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.p: WHen ſaw you Valentine?

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: Not ſince the Horſe-race, he's taken up with thoſe that woo the Widow.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: How can he live by ſnatches from ſuch people? he bore a worthy mind,

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: Alas, he's ſunk, his means are gone, he wants, and which is worſe,
Takes a delight in doing ſo.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: That's ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Runs Lamatick, if you but talk of ſtates, he cannot be brought (now he has ſpent his own) to think there's inheritance, or means, but all a common riches, all men bound to be his Bailiffs.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: This is ſomething dangerous.

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: No Gentleman that has eſtate to uſe it in keeping houſe, or followers, for thoſe wayes he cries againſt, for Eating ſins, dull Surfeits, cramming of Serving men, muſtering of Beggars, maintaining Hoſpitals for Kites, and Cu • s, grounding their fat faiths upon old Country proverbs, God bleſs the Founders; theſe he would have ventured into to more manly uſes, Wit, and carriage, and never thinks of ſtate, or means, the ground-works: holding it monſtrous, men ſhould feed their bodies, and ſtarve their underſtandings

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: That's moſt certain.

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: Yes, if he could ſtay there.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Why let him marry, and that way riſe again.

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: It's moſt impoſſible, he will not look with any handſomeneſs upon a Woman.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Is he ſo ſtrange to Women?

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: I know not what it is, a fooliſh glory he has goe, I know not where, to balk thoſe benefits, and yet he wil converſe and flatter 'em, make 'em, or fair, or ſoul, •• gged, or ſmooth, as his impreſſion ſerves, for he affirms they are only lumps, and undigeſted pieces, lickt over to a form by our affections, and then they ſhow. The Lovers let 'em paſs.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: He might be one, he carries as much promiſe; they are wondrous merry.

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: O their hopes are high, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: Is Valentine come to Town?

sp.speaker: Bella.
sp.p: Laſt night, I heard.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: We miſs him monſtrouſly in our directions, for this Widow is as ſtately, and as crafty, and ſtands I warrant you—

sp.speaker: Hair.
sp.p: Let her ſtand ſure, ſhe falls before us elſe, co •• let's go ſeek Valentine.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: This Widow ſeems a Gallant.

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: A goodly Woman, and to her handſomneſs 〈◊〉 bears her ſtate, reſerved, and great Fortune has made 〈◊〉 Miſtreſs of a full means, and well ſhe knows to uſe it.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I would Valentine had her.

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: There's no hope of that, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: O' that condition, he had his Mortgage in again.

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: I would he had.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p:
Seek means, and ſee what I'le do, however let • e Money be paid in, I never ſought a Gentlemans undo
• g, nor eat the bread of other mens vexations, you told • e of another Brother.

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.p: Yes Sir, more miſerable than he, for he has eat • m, and drunk him up, a handſome Gentleman, and fine • holar.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: What are theſe?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: The Tenants, they'll do what they can.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: It is well prepared, be earneſt, honeſt friends, and •• d upon him, he is deaf to his own good.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: We mean to tell him part of our minds an't pleaſe • ou.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Do, and do it home, and in what my care may • elp, or my perſwaſions when we meet next.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Do but perſwade him fairly; and for your money, • ine, and theſe mens thanks too, and what we can be able.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p:
Y'are moſt honeſt, you ſhall find me no leſs, and 〈◊〉 I leave you, proſper your buſineſs my friends.
Ex. Mer.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Pray Heaven it may, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p:
Nay if he will be mad, I'le be mad with him, and • ell him that I'le not ſpare him, his Father kept good Meat, • ood Drink, good Fellows, good Hawks, good Hounds, • nd bid his Neighbours welcome; kept him too, and ſup
• lied his prodigality, yet kept his ſtate ſtill; muſt we turn Tenants now, after we have lived under the race of Gentry, • nd maintained good Yeomantry, to ſome of the City, to 〈◊〉 great ſhoulder of Mutton and a Cuſtard, and have our • ate turned into Cabbidge Gardens, muſt it be ſo?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: You muſt be milder to him.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: That's as he makes his game.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Intreat him lovingly, and make him feel.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: I'le pinch him to the bones elſe.

sp.speaker: Valen.
sp.p: And tell the Gentleman, I'le be with • im preſently, ſay I want money too, I muſt not fail boy.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: You'l want Cloaths, I hope.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Bid the young Courtier repair to me anon, I'le read • o him.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: He comes, de diligent, but not too rugged, ſtart • im, but affright him not.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Phew, are you there?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: We come to ſee you Nephew, be not angry.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
Why do you dog me thus, with theſe ſtrange peo
• le? why, all the world ſhall never make me rich more, • or maſter of theſe troubles.

sp.speaker: Tenants.
sp.p: We beſeech you for our poor Childrens ſake.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Who bid you get 'em? have you not threſhing work • nough, but Children muſt be bang'd out o'th' ſheaf too? other men with all their delicates, and healthful diets, can • et but wind eggs: you with a clove of Garlick, a piece of Cheeſe would break a Saw, and ſowre Milk, can mount • ike Stallions, and I muſt maintain theſe tumblers.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: You ought to maintain us, we have maintained you, and when you ſlept provided for you; who bought the Silk you wear? I think our labours; reckon, you'll find it ſo: who found your Horſes perpetual pots of Ale, maintain'd your Taverns, and who extol'd you in the Half-crown-boxes, where you might ſit and muſter all the Beauties? we had no hand in theſe; no, we are all puppies?
Your Tenants baſe vexations.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Very well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Had you Land, Sir, and honeſt men to ſerve your purpoſes, honeſt and faithful, and will you run away from 'em, betray your ſelf, and your poor Tribe to miſery; mortgage all us, like old Cloaks; where will you hunt next? you had a thouſand Acres, fair and open: The Kings-Bench is encloſed, there's no good • iding, the Counter is full of tho • as and brakes, take heed Si • , and boggs, you'l quickly find what broth they're made of.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Y'are ſhort and pithy.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: They ſay y'are a fine Gentleman, and of excellent judgement, they report you have a wit; keep your ſelf out o'th' Rain, and take your Cloak with you, which by interpretation is your State, Sir, or I ſhall think your ſame belied you, you have money, and may have means.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I pret • ee leave p • ating, does my good lye within thy brain to further, or my undoing in thy pity? go, go, get you home, there whiſtle to your Ho • ſes, and let them edifie; away, fow Hemp to hang your ſelves withal: what am I to you, or you to me; am I your Landlord, puppies?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: This is un •• vil.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: More unmerciful you, to vex me with theſe Bacon Broth and Puddings, they are the walking ſhapes of all my ſorrows.

sp.speaker: 3 Tenants.
sp.p: Your Fathers Worſhip would have uſed us better.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: My Fathers Worſhip was a Fool.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Hey, hey boys, old Valentine i'ſaith, the old boy ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Fie Couſin.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I mean beſotted to his ſtate, he had never left me the miſery of ſo much means elſe, which till I fold, was a meer meagrim to me: If you will talk, turn out theſe Tenants, they are as killing to my nature Uncle, as water to a Feaver.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: We will go, but it is like Rams, to come again the ſtronger, and you ſhall keep your ſtate.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Thou lyeſt, I will not.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p:
Sweet Sir, thou lyeſt, thou ſhalt, and ſo good morrow.
Exeunt Tenants.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: This was my man, and of a noble breeding: now to your buſineſs Uncle.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: To your ſtate then.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: 'Tis gone, and I am glad on't, name it no more, 'tis that I pray againſt, and Heaven has heard me, I tell you, Sir, I am more fearful of it, I mean, of thinking of more lands, or livings, than ſickly men are travelling of Sundays, for being quell'd with Carriers; out upon't, cav • at emptor, let the fool out-ſweat it, that thinks he has got a catch on't.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: This is madneſs to be a wilful begger.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I am mad then, and ſo I mean to be, will that content you? How bravely now I live, how jo •• nd, how near the firſt inheritance, without fears, how free from t •• e troubles!

sp.speaker: Ʋne.
sp.p: And from means too.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Means? why all good men's my means; my wit's my Plow, the Town's my ſtock, Tavern's my ſtanding houſe, and all the world knows there's no want; all Gentlemen that love Society, love me; all Purſes that wit and pleaſure opens, are my Tenants; every mans Cloaths fit me, the next fair lodging is but my next remove, and when I pleaſe to be more eminent, and take the Air, a piece is lev • ed, and a Coach prepared, and I go I care not whither, what need ſtate here?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: But ſay theſe means were honeſt, will they laſt, Sir?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Far longer than your jerkin, and wear fairer, ſhould I take ought of you, 'tis true, I beg'd now, or which is worſe than that, I ſtole a kindneſs, and which is worſt of all, I loſt my way in't; your mind's encloſed, nothing lies open nobly, your very thoughts are Hinds that work on nothing but daily ſweat and trouble: were my way ſo full of dirt as this, 'tis true I'd ſhift it; are my acquaintance Graſiers? but Sir, know, no man that I am allied to, in my living, but makes it equal, whether his own uſe, o • my neceſſity pull firſt, nor is this forc'd, but the mee • quality and poiſure of goodneſs, and do you think I venture nothing equal?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: You poſe me Couſin.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
What's my knowledge Uncle, is't not worth mony? what's my underſtanding, travel, reading, wit, all theſe
digeſted, my daily making men, ſome to ſpeak, that too much • legm had frozen up, ſome that ſpoke too much, to hold their peace, and put their tongues to penſions, ſome to wear then cloaths, and ſome to keep 'em, theſe are nothing Uncle; beſides theſe wayes, to teach the way of nature, a manly love, community to all that are deſervers, not examining how much, or what's done for them, 'tis wicked, and ſuch a one like you, chews his thoughts doule, making 'em only food for his repentance.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: This cloak and hat Sir, and my Maſters love.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Commend's to thy Maſter, and take that, and leave ' • m at my lodging.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: I ſhall do it Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I do not think of theſe things.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: Pleaſe you Sir, I have gold here for you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Give it me, drink that and commend me to thy Maſter; look you Uncle, do I beg theſe?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: No ſure, 'tis your worth, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: 'Tis like enough, but pray ſatisfie me, are not theſe ways as honeſt as perſecuting the ſtarved inheritance, with muſty Corn, the very rats were fain to run away from, or ſelling rotten wood by the pound, like ſpices, which Gentlemen do after burn by th'ounces? do not I know your way of feeding beaſts with grains, and windy ſtuff, to blow up Butchers? your racking Paſtures, that have eaten up as many •• nging Shepherds, and their iſſues, as Andeluzia breeds? theſe are authentique, I tell you Sir, I would not change ways with you, unleſs it were to ſell your ſtate that hour, and if it were poſſible to ſpend it then too, for all your Beans in Rumnillo, now you know me.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I would you knew your ſelf, but ſince you are grown ſuch a ſtrange enemy to all that ſits you, give me leave to make your Brothers fortune.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: From your mortgage, which yet you may recover, I'le find the means.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Pray ſave your labour Sir, my Brother and my ſelf will run one fortune, and I think what I hold a meer vexation, cannot be ſafe for him, I love him better, he has wit at will, the world has means, he ſhall live without this trick of ſtate, we are heirs both, and all the world before us.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: My laſt offer, and then I am gone.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: What is't, and then I'le anſwer.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: What think you of a wiſe yet to reſtore you, and tell me ſeriouſly without theſe trifles.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And you can find one, that can pleaſe my fancy, you ſhall not find me ſtubborn.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Speak your Woman.

sp.speaker: Val
sp.p: One without eyes, that is, ſelf commendations, for when they find they are handſom, they are unwholſome, one without ears, not giving time to flatterers, for ſhe that hears her ſelf commended, wavers, and points men out a way to make 'em wicked; one without ſubſtance of her ſelf; that woman without the pleaſure of her life, that's wanton; though ſhe be young, forgetting it, though fair, making her glaſs the eyes of honeſt men, not her own admiration, all her ends obedience, all her hours new bleſſings, if there may be ſuch a woman.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Yes there may be.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And without ſtate too

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: You are diſpoſed to trifle, well, fare you well Sir, when you want me next, you'l ſeek me out a better ſence.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Farewell Uncle, and as you love your eſtate, let not me hear on't. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: It ſhall not trouble you, I'le watch him ſtill,
And when his friends fall off then bend his will. Exit.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: I know the cauſe of all this ſadneſs now, your ſiſter • a • ng • oſt all the brave Lovers.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: She has where withall, much good may't do her, prethee ſpeak ſoftly, we are open to mens ears.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Fear not, we are ſafe, we may ſee all that paſs, her all, and make our ſelves merry with their language, a • yet ſtand undiſcovered, be not melancholy, you are as far as ſhe.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Who I? I thank you, I am as haſte ordain'd me, 〈◊〉 thing ſlubber'd, my ſiſter is a goodly portly Lady, a wo • of a preſence, ſhe ſpreads ſattens, as the Kings ſhips 〈◊〉 canvas every where, ſhe may ſpare me her miſen, and 〈◊〉 bonnets, ſtrike her main Petticoat, and yet outſail me, 〈…〉 am a Carvel to her.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: But a tight one.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: She is excellent, well built too.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: And yet ſhe's old.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: She never ſaw above one voyage Luce, and cr • me after another, her Hull will ſerve again, a right go • Merchant: ſhe plaies, and ſings too, dances and diſcourſes comes very near Eſſays, a pretty Poet, begins to piddle w • Philoſophie, a ſubtil Chymick Wench, and can ex •• the Spirit of mens Eſtates, ſhe has the light before her, and cannot miſs her choice for me, 'tis reaſon I wait my • e •• fortune.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: You are ſo baſhfull.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: It is not at firſt word up and ride, thou art cozen, that would ſhew mad i' faith: beſides, we loſe the main pe •• of our politick government: if we become provokers, the • we are fair, and fit for mens imbraces, when like tow • they lie before us ages, yet not carried, hold out th • ſtrongeſt batteries, then compound too without the l •• of honour, and march off with our fair wedding, Colo • ſlying. Who are theſe?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: I know not, nor I care not.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Prethee peace then, a well built Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: But poorly thatcht.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Has he devour'd you too?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: H'as gulp'd me down Lance.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Left you no means to ſtudy?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Not a farthing: diſpatcht my poor annuity I tha • him, here's all the hope I have left, one bare ten ſhillings.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: You are ſit for great mens ſervices.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I am ſit, but who'le take me thus? mens miſeries are now accounted ſtains in their natures. I have travelled, and I have ſtudied long, obſerved all Kingdoms, know all the promiſes of Art and manners, yet that I am not bold, t • cannot flatter, I ſhall not thrive, all theſe are but vain Studies art thou ſo rich as to get me a lodging Lance?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I'le ſell the titles of my houſe elſe, my Horſe, my Hawk, nay's death I'le pawn my wife: Oh Mr. Francis, that I ſhould ſee your Fathers houſe fall thus!

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: An honeſt fellow.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Your Fathers houſe, that fed me, that bred up al my name!

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: A gratefull fellow.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: And fall by—

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Peace, I know you are angry Lance, but I m •• not hear with whom, he is my Brother, and though you hold him ſlight, my moſt dear Brother: A Gentleman, excepting ſome few rubs, he were too excellent to live here elſe, fraughted as deep with noble and brave parts, the iſſues of a noble and manly Spirit, as any he alive. I muſt not hear you; though I am miſerable, and he made me ſo, yet ſtill he is my brother, ſtill I love him, and to that tye of blood link my affections.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: A noble nature! doſt thou know him Luce?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: No, Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Thou ſhouldeſt ever know ſuch good men, what a fair body and mind are married! did he not ſay be wanted?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: What's that to you?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: 'Tis true, but 'tis great pity.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: How ſhe changes! ten thouſand more than he, as handſom men too.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
'Tis like enough, but as I live, this Gentleman • ong ten thouſand thouſand! is there no knowing him? •• y ſhould he want? fellows of no merit, ſlight and puſ •
•• ls, that walk like ſhadows, by leaving no print of what • ey are, or poiſe, let them complain.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Her colour changes ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: This man was made, to mark his wants to waken 〈◊〉 ; alas poor Gentleman, but will that keep him from cold • d hunger, believe me he is well bred, and cannot be but of noble linage, mark him, mark him well.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: 'Is a handſom man.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
The ſweetneſs of his ſufferance ſets him off, O Luce,
•• t whither go I?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: You cannot hide it.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I would he had what I can ſpare.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: 'Tis charitable.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Come Sir, I'le ſee you lodg'd, you have tied my • ngue faſt, I'le ſteal before you want, 'tis but a hanging.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
That's a good fellow too, an honeſt fellow, why, this • ould move a ſtone, I muſt needs know; but that ſome • ther time.
Exit Lance, and Franc.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Is the wind there? that makes for me.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Come, I forgot a buſineſs.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: MY ſiſter, and a woman of ſo baſe a pity! what was the fellow?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Why, an ordinary man, Madam.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Poor?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Poor enough, and no man knows from whence either.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: What could ſhe ſee?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Only his miſery, for elſe ſhe might behold a hundred and ſomer.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Did ſhe change much?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Extreamly, when he ſpoke, and then her pity, like 〈◊〉 Orator, I fear her love framed ſuch a commendation, and • llowed it ſo far, as made me wonder.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
Is ſhe ſo hot, or ſuch a want of lovers, that ſhe muſt • oat upon afflictions? why does ſhe not go romage all the • riſons, and there beſtow her youth, bewray her wanton
• eſs, and flie her honour, common both to beggery: did ſhe • eak to him?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: No, he ſaw us not, but ever ſince, ſhe hath been • ainly troubled.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Was he young?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Yes, young enough.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: And looked he like a Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Like ſuch a Gentleman, that would pawn ten oaths or twelve pence.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: My ſiſter, and ſink baſely! this muſt not be, does • e uſe means to know him?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Yes Madam, and has employed a Squire called ſhorthoſe.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: O that's a precious Knave: keep all this private, but • ill be near her lodging: Luce, what you can gather by any • eans, let me underſtand: I'le ſtop her heat, and turn her • harity another way, to bleſs her ſelf firſt; be ſtill cloſe to • er counſels; a begger and a ſtranger! there's a bleſs'dneſs! • 'le none of that; I have a toy yet, ſiſter, ſhall tell you this • ſoul, and make you find it, and for your pains take you the • aſt gown I wore; this makes me mad, but I ſhall force a • emedy.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: Sirra, we have ſo lookt for thee, and long'd for • hee; this widow is the ſtrangeſt thing, the ſtatelieſt, and • ands ſo much upon her excellencies.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: She hath put us off, this month now, for an anſwer.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: No man muſt viſit her, nor look upon her, no, not ſay, good morrow, not good even, till that's paſt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: She has found want dough you are made of, and ſo kneads you: are you good at nothing, but theſe after games? I have told you often enough what things they are, w • at precious things, theſe widows—

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: If we • ad • m.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Why the Devil has not craft enough to wooe 'em, there be three kinds of fools, mark this noſe Gentlemen, mark it, and underſta •• it.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: Well, go forward.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: An Innocent, a knave fool, a fool politick: the laſt of which are lovers, widow lovers.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.p: Will you allow no fortune?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No ſuch blind one.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: We gave you reaſons, why 'twas needful for us.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: As you are thoſe fools, I did allow thoſe reaſons, but is my Scholars and companions damn'd 'em: do you know what it is to wooe a widow? anſwer me coolely now, and underſtandingly.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: Why to lie with her, and to enjoy her wealth.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Why the • e you are fools ſtill, crafty to catch your ſelves, pure politick fools, I lookt for ſuch an anſwer; once more hear me, it is, to wed a widow, to be doubted mainly, whether the ſtate you have be yours or no, or thoſe old boots you ride in. Mark me, widows are long extents in Law upon news, livings upon their bodies winding-ſheets, they that enjoy 'em, lie but with dead mens monuments, and beget only their own ill Epitaphs: Is not this plain now?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.p: Plain ſpoken.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And plain truth; but if you'le needs do things of danger, do but loſe your ſelves, not any part concerns your underſtandings, for th • u you are Meacocks, fools, and miſerable, march off amain, within an inch of a F •••• g, turn me o'th' toe like a Weather-cock, kill every day a Sergeant for a twelve month, rob the Exchequer, and burn all the Rolls, and theſe will make a ſhew.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: And theſe are trifles.
