sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Conſidered to a Widow, empty nothings, for here you venture but your perſons, there the varniſh of your perſons, your diſcretions; why 'tis a monſtrous thing to marry at all, eſpecially as now 'tis made; me thinks a man, an underſtanding man, is more wiſe to me, and of a nobler • ie, than all theſe trinkets; what do we get by wom • n, but ou • ſenſes, which is the rankeſt part about us, ſatisfied, and when that's done, what are we? Creſt-fallen Cowards. Wh •• benefit can children be, but charges and diſobedience? What's the love they render at one and twenty years? I pray die Father: when they are young, they are like bells rung backwards, nothing but noiſe and giddineſs; and come to years once, there drops a ſon byth' ſwords in his Miſtreſſes quarel, a great joy to his parents: A Daughter ripe too, grows high and luſty in her blood, muſt have a heating, runs away with a ſupple ham'd Servingman: his twenty Nobles ſpent, takes to a trade, and learns to ſpin mens hair off; there's another, and moſt are of this nature, will you marry?

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: For my part yes, for any doubt I feel yet.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And this ſame widow?

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: If I may, and me thinks, however you are pleaſed to diſpute theſe dangers, ſuch a warm match, and for you, Sir, were not hurtfull.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Not half ſo killing as for you, for m • ſhe cannot with all the Art ſhe has, make me more miſerable, or much more fortunate, I have no ſtate left, a benefit that none of you can brag of, and there's the Antidote againſt a Widow, nothing to loſe, but that my ſoul inherits, which ſhe can neither law nor claw away; to that, but little fleſh, it were too much elſe; and that unwholſom too, it were too rich elſe; and to all this contempt of what ſhe do's I can laugh at her tears, neglect her angers, hear her without a faith, ſo pity her as if ſhe were a Traytour, moan her p •• ſon, but deadly hate her pride; if you could do theſe, and had but this diſcretion, and like fortune, it were but an equal venture.
This is malice.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: When ſhe lies with your land, and not with you, grows great with joyntures, and is brought to bed with all the ſtate you have, you'le find this certain; but is it come to paſs you muſt marry, is there no buff will hold you?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: Grant it be ſo.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Then chuſe the tamer evil, take a maid, a maid not worth a penny; make her yours, knead her, and mould her yours, a maid worth nothing, there's a vertuous ſpell in that word nothing; a maid makes conſcience of half a Crown a week for pins and puppits, a maid will be content with one Coach and two Horſes, not falling out becauſe they are not matches; with one man ſatisfied, with one rein guided, with one ſaith, one content, one bed, aged ſhe makes the wiſe, preſerves the fame and iſſue; a widow is a Chriſtmas box that ſweeps all.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: Yet all this cannot ſink us.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: You are my friends, and all my loving friends, I ſpend your mony, yet I deſerve it too, you are my friends ſtill, I • ide your horſes, when I want I ſell 'em; I eat your meat, help to wear her linnen, ſometimes I make you drunk, and then you ſeal, for which I'le do you this commodity, be ruled, and let me try her, I will diſcover her, the truth is, I will never leave to trouble her, till I ſee through her, then if I find her worthy.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: This was our meaning Valentine.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: 'Tis done then, I muſt want nothing.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: Nothing but the woman.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No jealouſie; for when I marry, the Devil muſt be wiſer than I take him; and the fleſh fooliſher: come let's to dinner, and when I am well whetted with wine, have at her. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: But art thou ſure?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: No ſurer than I heard.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: That it was that ſlouting fellows Brother?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Yes, Shorthoſe told me ſo.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: He did ſcarce out the truth?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: It ſeems he did.

sp.speaker: Har.
sp.p: Prethee Luce call him hither, if he be no worſe, I never repent my pity, now ſirra, what was he we ſent you after, the Gentleman i'th' black?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I'th' torn black?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Yes, the ſame Sir.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: What would your Worſhip with him?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Why, my Worſhip would know his name, and what he is.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: 'Is nothing, he is a man, and yet he is no man.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: You muſt needs play the fool.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: 'Tis my profeſſion.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: How is he a man, and no man?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: He's a begger, only the ſign of a man, the buſh pull'd down, which ſhows the houſe ſtands emptie.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: What's his calling?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: They call him begger.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: What's his kindred?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Beggers.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: His worth?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: A learned begger, a poor Scholar.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: How does he live?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Like worms, he eats old Books.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Is Valentine his Brother.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: His begging Brother.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: What may his name be?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Leave your fooling.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: You had as good ſay, leave your living.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Once more tell me his name directly.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I'le be hang'd firſt, unleſs I heard him Chriſtned, but I can tell what fooliſh people call him.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Where lies this learning, Sir?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: In Pauls Church yard forſooth.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I mean the Gentleman, fool.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: O that fool, he lies in looſe ſheets every whe • that's no where.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p:
You have glean'd ſince you came to Londo •
it 〈◊〉 Country, Shorthoſe, you were an arrant fool, a cu •
〈◊〉 coxcombe, here every Tavern teaches you, the pint pot 〈◊〉 ſo belaboured you with wit, your brave acquaintance 〈◊〉 gives you Ale, ſo fortified your mazard, that now there's a • talking to you.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: 'Is much improved, a fellow, a fine diſcourſer.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I hope ſo, I have not waited at the tail of wit 〈◊〉 long to be an Aſs.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: But ſay now, Shorthoſe, my Lady ſhould re ••• into the Country.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I had as lieve ſhe ſhould remove to Heaven, and 〈◊〉 ſoon I would undertake to follow her.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Where no old Charnico is, nor no Anchoves, to Maſter ſuch-a-one, to meet at the Roſe, and bring my La • ſuch-a-ones chief Chamber-maid.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
No bouncing healths to this brave Lad, dear S ••
hoſe, nor down o'th'knees to that illuſtrious Lady.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: No ſiddles, nor no luſty noiſe of drawer, carry 〈◊〉 pottle to my Father Shorthoſe.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: No plays, nor gally foiſts, no ſtrange Embaſſ •• to run and wonder at, till thou beeſt oyl, and then come home again, and lye byth'Legend.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Say ſhe ſhould go.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: If I ſay, I'le be hang'd, or if I thought f ••• would go.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I would go with her.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: But Shorthoſe, where thy heart is?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Do not fright him.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: By this hand Miſtris 'tis a noiſe, a loud one 〈◊〉 and from her own mouth, preſently to be gone too, 〈◊〉 why, or to what end?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: May not a man die firſt? ſhe'l give him ſo 〈◊〉 time.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
Gone o'th' ſudden? thou doſt but jeſt, ſhe muſ •
〈◊〉 mock the Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: She has put them off a month, thy dare not i • her, believe me Miſtris, what I hear I tell you.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Is this true, wench? gone on ſo ſhort a warn •• what trick is this? ſhe never told me of it, it muſt not be ſirra, attend me preſently, you know I have been a caref •• friend unto you, attend me in the Hall, and next be faithf •• cry not, we ſhall not go.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Her Coach may crack.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Which way to live! how dareſt thou come to to •• to ask ſuch an idle queſtion?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Me thinks 'tis neceſſary, unleſs you could reſtor • that Annuitie you have tipled up in Taverns.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
Where haſt thou been, and how brought up Fran ••••
that thou talkeſt thus out of France? thou wert a pretty f • llow, and of a handſom knowledge; who has ſpoiled thee?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: He that has ſpoil'd himſelf, to make him ſport, and by Copie, will ſpoil all comes near him: buy but a Glaſs, 〈◊〉 you be yet ſo wealthy, and look there who?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Well ſaid, old Copihold.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: My heart's good Freehold Sir, and ſo you'l find 〈◊〉 this Gentleman's your Brother, your hopeful Brother, f •• there is no hope of you, uſe him thereafter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: E'ne as well as I uſe my ſelf, what wouldſt thou ha • e Frank?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Can you procure me a hundred pound?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p:
Hark what he ſaies to you, O try your wits, 〈◊〉 ſay you are excellent at it, for your Land has lain long •••
rid, and unſenſible.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p:
And I'le forget all wrongs, you ſee my ſtate, and 〈◊〉
what wretchedneſs your will has brought me; but what it may be, by this benefit, if timely done, and like a noble Brother, both you and I may feel, and to our comforts.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: (A hundred pound!) doſt thou know what thou haſt ſaid Boy?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I ſaid a hundred pound.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
Thou haſt ſaid more than any man can juſtifie, be
•• eve it: procure a hundred pounds! I ſay to thee there's no • uch ſum in nature, forty ſhillings there may be now i'th' Mint and that's a Treaſure, I have ſeen five pound, but let me • ell it, and 'tis as wonderful as Calves with five Legs; here's •• ve • illings, Frank, the harveſt of five weeks, and a good • rop too, take it, and pay thy firſt fruits, I'le come down • nd eat it out.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: 'Tis patience muſt meet with you Sir, not love.

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.p: Deal roundly, and leave theſe fiddle faddles.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Leave thy prating, thou thinkeſt thou art a notable wiſe fellow, thou and thy rotten Sparrow Hawk; two of the reverent.

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.p: I think you are mad, or if you be not, will be, with the next moon, what would you have him do?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.p: To get money firſt, that's to live, you have ſhewed him how to want.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: 'Slife how do I live? why, what dull fool would ask that queſtion? three hundred three pilds more, I and live bravely: the better half o'th' Town live moſt gloriouſly, • nd ask them what ſtates they have, or what Annuities, • r when they pray for ſeaſonable Harveſts: thou haſt a handſome Wit, ſtir into the world, Frank, ſtir, ſtir for ſhame, thou art a pretty Scholar: ask how to live? write, write, write any thing, the World's a fine believing World, write News.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Dragons in Suſſex, Sir, or fiery Battels ſeen in the Air at Aſpurge.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
There's the way Frank, and in the tail of theſe, • right me the Kingdom with a ſharp Prognoſtication, that ſhall ſcowt them, Dearth upon Dearth, like leven Taffaties, predictions of Sea-breaches, Wars, and want of Her
• ings on our Coaſt, with bloudy Noſes.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p:
Whirl-winds, that ſhall take off the top of Gran
• ham Steeple, and clap it on Pauls, and after theſe, a Len
• oy to the City for their ſins.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Probatum eſt, thou canſt not want a penſion, go ſwitch me up a Covey of young Scholars, there's twenty nobles, and two loads of Coals, are not theſe ready wayes? Coſmography thou art deeply read in, draw me a Map from the Mermaid, I mean a midnight Map to ſcape the Watches, and ſuch long ſenſleſs examinations, and Gentlemen ſhall feed thee, right good Gentlemen, I cannot ſtay • ong.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: You have read learnedly, and would you have him follow theſe Megera's, did you begin with Ballads?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Well, I will leave you, I ſee my wants are grown ridiculous, yours may be ſo, I will not curſe you neither; you may think, when theſe wanton fits are over, who bred me, and who ruined me, look to your ſelf, Sir, a providence I wait on.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Thou art paſſionate, haſt thou been brought up with Girls?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Reſt you merry, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Not ſo merry as you ſuppoſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Pray ſtay a while, and let me take a view of you, I may put my Spoon into the wrong Pottage-pot elſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Why, wilt thou muſter us?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: No, you are not he, you are a thought too handſome.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Who wouldſt thou ſpeak withal, why doſt thou peep ſo?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I am looking birds neſts, I can find none in your buſh beard, I would ſpeak with you, black Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: With me, my friend?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Yes ſure, and the beſt friend, Sir, it ſeems you ſpake withal this twelve month, Gentleman, there's money for you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: There's none for you, Sir, be not ſo brief, not a penny; law how he itches at it, ſtand off, you ſtir my colour.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Take it, 'tis money.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: You are too quick too, firſt be ſure you have it, you ſeem to be a Faulkoner, but a fooliſh one.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Take it, and ſay nothing.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: You are cozen'd too, 'tis take it, and ſpend it.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: From whom came it, Sir?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Such another word, and you ſhall have none on't.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I thank you, Sir, I doubly thank you.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Well, Sir, then buy you better Cloaths, and get your Hat dreſt, and your Laundreſs to waſh your Boots white.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Pray ſtay Sir, may you not be miſtaken.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I think I am, give me the money again, come quick, quick, quick.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I would be loth to render, till I am ſure it be ſo.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Hark in your ear, is not your name Franciſco?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Be quiet then, it may Thunder a hundred times, before ſuch ſtones fall: do you not need it?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: And 'tis thought you have it.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I think I have.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Then hold it faſt, 'tis not fly-blown, you may pay for the poundage, you forget your ſelf, I have not ſeen a Gentleman ſo backward, a wanting Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Your mercy, Sir.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Friend, you have mercy, a whole bag full of mercy, be merry with it, and be wiſe.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I would fain, if it pleaſe you, but know—

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: It does not pleaſe me, tell over your money, and be not mad, Boy.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: You have no more ſuch bags?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: More ſuch there are, Sir, but few I fear for you, I have caſt your water, you have wit, you need no money.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Be not amazed, Sir, 'tis good gold, good old gold, this is reſtorative, and in good time, it comes to do you good, keep it and uſe it, let honeſt fingers feel it, yours be too quick Sir.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: He named me, and he gave it me, but from whom.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Let 'em ſend more, and then examine it, this can be but a Preface.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Being a ſtranger, of whom can I deſerve this?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Sir, of any man that has but eyes, and manly underſtanding to find mens wants, good men are bound to do ſo.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Now you ſee, Frank, there are more wayes than certainties, now you believe: What Plow brought you this Harveſt, what ſale of Timber, Coals, or what Annuities? Theſe feed no Hinds, nor wait the expectation of Quarterdaies, you ſee it ſhowers in to you, you are an Aſs, lie plodding, and lie fooling, about this Blazing Star, and that bopeep, whining, and faſting, to find the natural reaſon why a Dog turns twice about before he lie down, what uſe of theſe, or what joy in Annuities, where every man's thy ſtudy, and thy Tenant, I am aſhamed on thee.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Yes, I have ſeen this fellow, there's a wealthy Widow hard by.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Yes marry is there.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I think he's her ſervant, or I am couzen'd elſe, I am ſure on't.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I am glad on't.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: She's a good Woman.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I am gladder.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: And young enough believe.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I am gladder of all, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Frank, you ſhall lye with me ſoon.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I thank my money.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: His money ſhall lie with me, three in a Bed, Sir, will be too much this weather.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Meet me at the Mermaid, and thou ſhalt ſee what things—

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Truſt to your ſelf Sir.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: O Valentine!

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How now, why do you look ſo?

sp.speaker: Bella.
sp.p: The Widow's going, man.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Why let her go, man.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: She's going out o'th' Town.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: The Town's the happier, I would they were all gone.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: We cannot come to ſpeak with her.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Not to ſpeak to her?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: She will be gone within this hour, either now Val.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: Hare. Now, now, now, good Val.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I had rather march i'th' mouth o'th' Cannon, but adiew, if ſhe be above ground, go, away to your prayers, away I ſay, away, ſhe ſhall be ſpoken withall. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Shorthoſe with one boot on, Roger, and Humphrey.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: She will go, Shorthoſe.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Who can help it Roger?

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.p: [within.] Help down with the hangings.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: By and by

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.p: I am making up o'th' trunks here.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Well.

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.p: Who looks to my Ladys wardrobe? Humphrey.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: Here.

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.p: Down with the boxes in the gallery, and bring away he Coach cuſhions.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Will it not rain, no conjuring abroad, nor no devices to ſtop this journey?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Why go now, why now, why o'th' ſudden now? what preparation, what horſes have we ready, what proviſion laid in i'th'Country?

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: Not an egge I hope.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: No nor one drop of good drink boyes, there's the devil.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I heartily pray the malt be muſty, and then we muſt come up again.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: What ſayes the Steward?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: He's at's wits end, for ſome four hours ſince, out of his haſte and providence, he miſtook the Millars mangie mare, for his own nagge.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: And ſhe may break his neck, and ſave the journy. Oh London how I love thee!

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: I have no boots nor none I'le buy: or if I had, refuſe me if I would venture my ability, before a Cloak-Bag, men are men.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: For my part, if I be brought, as I know it will be aimed at, to carry any du • ty dairy Cream-pot, or any gentle Lady of the Laundry, Chambring, or wantonneſs behind my Gelding, with all her Streamers, Knapſacks, Glaſſes, Gugawes, as if I were a running ſlippery, I'le give 'em leave to out my girts, and ſlay me. I'le not be troubled with their Diſtibations, at every half miles end, I underſtand my ſelf, and am reſolved.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: To morrow night at Olivers! who ſhall be there boys, who ſhall meet the wenches?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: The well brew'd ſtand of Ale, we ſhould have met at!

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Theſe griefs like to another Tale of Troy, would mollifie the hearts of barbarous people, and Tom Butcher weep, Aeneas enters, and now the town's loſt.

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.p: Well whither run you, my Lady is mad.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I would ſhe were in Bedlam.

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.p: The carts are come, no hands to help to load 'em? the ſtuff lies in the hall, the plate.
[Within Widow.] Why knaves there, where be theſe idle fellows?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Shall I ride with one Boot?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Why where I ſay?

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.p: Away, away, it muſt be ſo.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: O for a tickling ſtorm, to laſt but ten days. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: BY my troth Miſtris I did it for the beſt.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
It may be ſo, but Luce, you have a tongue, a diſh of meat in your mouth, which if it were minced L •••
would do a great deal better.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: I proteſt Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: It will be your own one time or other: Walter.

sp.speaker: Walter
sp.p: [within.] Anon forſooth.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Lay my hat ready, my fan and cloak, you are ſo 〈◊〉 of providence; and Walter, tuck up my little bow beh ••• the Coach, and bid my maid make ready, my ſweet ſe ••• to your good Lady Miſtreſs; and my dog, good let 〈◊〉 Coachman carry him.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: But hear me.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I am in love ſweet Luce, and you are ſo skilfull, t • I muſt needs undo my ſelf; and hear me, let Oliver pac •• my Glaſs diſcreetly, and ſee my Curles well carried. 〈◊〉 ſweet Luce, you have a tongue, and open tongues have • p •• you know what, Luce.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Pray you be ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Yes and contented too, before I leave you: there's a Roger, which ſome call a Butcher, I ſpeak of certainties, I do not ſiſh Luce, nay do not ſtare, I have a tongue can take too: and a Green Chamber Luce, a back door opens to a long Gallerie; there was a night Luce, do you perceive, 〈◊〉 you perecive me yet? O do you bluſh Luce? a Friday night I ſaw your Saint, Luce: for t'other box of Marmalade, 〈◊〉 thine ſweet Roger, this I heard and kept too.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: E'ne as you are a woman Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: This I allow as good and Phyſical ſometime, t •••• meetings, and for the cheering of the heart, but Luce, to have your own turn ſerved, and to your friend to be a dogbolt.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: I confeſs it Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: As you have made my ſiſter jealous of me, are fooliſhly, and childiſhly purſued it, I have found out y •• haunt, and traced your purpoſes; for which mine ho ••• ſuffers; your beſt waies muſt be applied to bring her 〈◊〉 again, and ſeriouſly and ſuddenly, that ſo I may hare a means to clear my ſelf, and ſhe a fair opinion of me, 〈◊〉 you peeviſh—

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: My power and prayers Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I have been with the Gentleman, he has it, m ••• good may do him with it.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Come, are you ready? you love ſo to delay time, the day grows on.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I have ſent for a few trifles, when thoſe are co •• . And now I know your reaſon.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Know your own honour then, about your buſinſs, 〈◊〉 the Coach ready preſently, I'le tell you more then.

And underſtand it well, you muſt not think your ſiſter 〈◊〉 tender eyed as not to ſee your follies, alas I know your heart and muſt imagine, and truly too; 'tis not your charitie 〈◊〉 coin ſuch ſums to give away as you have done, in that y •• have no wiſdom Iſabel, no nor modeſty, where nobler 〈◊〉 are at home; I tell you, I am aſhamed to find this in yo • years, far more in your diſcretion, none to chuſe but th •• for pity, none to ſeal your thoughts on, but one of no •
ding, of no name; nothing to bring you to but this, 〈◊〉 and hunger: A jolly Joynture ſiſter, you are happy, a mony, no not ten ſhillings.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: You ſearch nearly.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
I know it as I know your folly, one that knows 〈◊〉 where he ſhall eat his next meal, take his reſt, unleſs it 〈◊〉 i'th' ſtocks; what kindred has he, but a more want 〈◊〉
Brother, or what vertues.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: You have had rare intelligence, I ſee, ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Or ſay the man had vertue, is vertue in this age a • ll inheritance? what Joynture can he make you, Plutarchs •• rals, or ſo much penny rent in the ſmall Poets? this is not • ell, 'tis weak, and I grieve to know it.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: And this you quit the town for?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Is't not time?

sp.speaker: Iſab
sp.p: You are better read in my affairs than I am, that's • ll I have to anſwer, I'le go with you, and willingly, and • hat you think moſt dangerous, I'le ſit laugh at.
• or ſiſter 'tis not folly but good diſcretion governs our main •• rtunes.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I am glad to hear you ſay ſo.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: I am for you.

div.stage: Enter Shorthoſe, and Humphrey, with riding rods.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: The Devil cannot ſtay her, ſhe'l on't, eat an egg • ow, and then we muſt away.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p:
I am gaul'd already, yet I will pray, may London
• ayes from henceforth be full of holes, and Coaches crack • heir wheels, may zealous Smiths ſo houſel all our Hack
• eys, that they may feel compunction in their feet, and tire • t High-gate, may it rain above all Almanacks till Carriers •• il, and the Kings Fiſh monger ride like Bike Arion upon 〈◊〉 Trout to London.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: At S. Albanes, let all the Inns be drunk, not an Hoſt • ober to bid her worſhip welcom.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p:
Not a Fiddle, but all preach't down with Puri
• ans; no meat but Legs of Beef.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: No beds but Wool-Packs.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p:
And thoſe ſo crammed with Warrens of ſtarved • leas that bite like Bandogs; let Mims be angry at their S.
• el Swagger, and we paſs in the heat on't and be beaten, beaten • bominably, beaten horſe and man, and all my Ladies linnen • prinkled with ſuds and diſh-water.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Not a wheel but out of joynt.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: Why doſt thou laugh?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: There's a Gentleman, and the rareſt Gentleman, • nd makes the rareſt ſport.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Where, where?

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p:
Within here, h'as made the gayeſt ſport with Tom
• he Coachman, ſo tewed him up with Sack that he lies • aſhing a But of Malmſie for his Mares.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: 'Tis very good.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p:
And talks and laughs, and ſings the rareſt ſongs, and
• horthoſe, he has ſo maul'd the Red Deer pies, made ſuch an • lms i'th' butterie.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Better ſtill.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: My Lady in a rage with the Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: May he anger her into a feather. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I pray tell me, who ſent you hither? for I imagine • t is not your condition, you look ſo temperately, and like a Gentleman, to ask me theſe milde queſtions.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Do you think I uſe to walk of errands, gentle Lady, • r deal with women out of dreams from others?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You have not know me ſure?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Not much.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: What reaſon have you then to be ſo tender of my • redit, you are no kinſman?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: If you take it ſo, the honeſt office that I came to do you, is not ſo heavy but I can return it: now I perceive you • re too proud, not worth my viſit.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Pray ſtay, a little proud.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Monſtrous proud, I griev'd to hear a woman of your value, and your abundant parts ſtung by the people, but • ow I ſee 'tis true, you look upon me as if I were a rude and • aucie fellow that borrowed all my breeding from a dunghil, or ſuch a one, as ſhould now fall and worſhip you in hope of pardon: you are cozen'd Lady, I came to prove opinion a loud liar, to ſee a woman only great in goodneſs, and Miſtreſs of a greater fame than fortune, but—

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You are a ſtrange Gentleman, if I were proud now. I ſhould be monſtrous angry, which I am not, and ſhew the effects of pride; I ſhould deſpiſe you, but you are welcom Sir: To think well of our ſelves, if we deſerve it, it is a luſtre in us, and every good we have, ſtrives to ſhew gracious, what uſe is it elſe? old age like Seer trees, is ſeldom ſeen affected, ſtirs ſometimes at rehearſal of ſuch acts as his daring youth endeavour'd.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: This is well, and now you ſpeak to the purpoſe, you pleaſe me, but to be place proud?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: If it be our own, why are we ſet here with diſtinction elſe, degrees, and orders given us? In you men, 'tis held a coolneſs, if you loſe your right, affronts and loſs of honour: ſtreets, and walls, and upper ends of tables, had they tongues could tell what blood has followed, and what feud about your ranks; are we ſo much below you, that till you have us, are the tops of nature, to be accounted drones without a difference? you will make us beaſts indeed.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Nay worſe than this too, proud of your cloaths, they ſwear a Merce • s Lucifer, a tumour tackt together by a Taylour, nay yet worſe, proud of red and white, a varniſh that butter-milk can better.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Lord, how little will vex theſe poor blind people! if my cloaths be ſometimes gay and glorious, does it follow, my mind muſt be my Mercers too? or ſay my beauty pleaſe ſome weak eyes, muſt it pleaſe them to think, that blows me up, that every hour blows off? this is an Infants anger.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Thus they ſay too, what though you have a Coach lined through with velvet, and four fair Flanders mares, why ſhould the ſtreets be troubled continually with you, till Carmen curſe you? can there be ought in this but pride of ſhew Lady, and pride of bum-beating, till the learned lawyers with their fat bags, are thruſt againſt the bulks till all their cauſes crack? why ſhould this Lady, and t'other Lady, and the third ſweet Lady, and Madam at Mile-end, be daily viſited, and your poorer neighbours, with courſe napſes neglected, faſhions conferr'd about, pouncings, and paintings, and young mens bodies read on like Anatomies.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You are very credulous, and ſomewhat deſperate, to deliver this Sir, to her you know not, but you ſhall confeſs me, and find I will not ſtart; in us all meetings lie open to theſe lewd reports, and our thoughts at Church, our very meditations ſome will ſwear, which all ſhould fear to judge, at leaſt uncharitably, are mingled with your memories, cannot ſleep, but this ſweet Gentleman ſwims in our fancies, that ſcarlet man of war, and that ſmooth Senior; not dreſs our heads without new ambuſhes, how to ſurprize that greatneſs, or that glorie; our very ſmiles are ſubject to conſtructions; nay Sir, it's come to this we cannot piſh, but 'tis a favour for ſome fool or other: ſhould we examine you thus, wer't not poſſible to take you without Perſpectives?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: It may be, but theſe excuſe not.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Nor yours force no truth Sir, what deadly tongues you have, and to thoſe tongues what hearts, and what inventions? O' my conſcience, and 'twere not for ſharp juſtice, you would venture to aim at your own mothers, and account it glorie to ſay you had done ſo: all you think are counſels, and cannot erre, 'tis we ſtill that ſhew double, giddy, or gorg'd with paſſion; we that build Babels for mens conc • uſions, we that ſcatter, as day does his warm light; our killing curſes over Gods creatures, next to the devils malice: lets intreat your good words.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Well, this woman has a brave ſoul.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Are not we gaily bleſt then, and much beholding to you for your ſubſtance? you may do what you liſt, we what beſeems us, and narrowly do that too, and preciſely, our names are ſerved in elſe at Ordinaries, and be •• t abroad in Taverns.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: O moſt brave Wench, and able to redeem an age of women.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
You are no Whoremaſters? Alas, no, Gentlemen, • t w •• e an impudence to think you vicious: you are ſo holy, handſome Ladies fright you, you are the cool things of the time, the temp • tance, mee • Emblems of the Law, and veils of Vertue, you are not daily mending like Dutch Watches, and plaſtering like old Walls; they are not Gentlemen, that with their ſecret ſins increaſe our Surgeons, and • e in Foraign Countries, for new ſores; Women are all theſe V • ces; you are not envious, falſe, covetous, va ••
••••• s, i •
•• ligious, drunken, revengeful, giddieeyed like Pa •• ots, • aters of others honours.
You are angry.

sp.speaker: Wid
sp.p: No by my •• oth, and yet I could ſay more too, for when men make me angry, I am miſerable.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Sure 'tis a man, ſ • e could not bea • it thus bravely elſe, it may he I am tedious.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Not at all, Sir, I am content at this time you ſhould trouble me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: You are diſtruſtful.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Where I find no truth, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Come, come, you are full of paſſion.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Some I have, I were too near the nature o' God • lſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: You are monſtrous peeviſh.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Becauſe they are monſtrous fooliſh, and know not how to uſe that ſhould try me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I was never anſwered thus; were you never drunk Lady?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: No ſure, not drunk, Sir; yet I love good Wine, as I love health and joy of heart, but temperately, why do you ask that queſtion?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: For that ſin that they moſt charge you with, is this ſin's ſe • vant, they ſay you are monſtrous—

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: What, Sir, what?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Moſt ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: It has a nam • ſure?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Infinitely luſtful, without all bounds, they ſwear you kill'd your Husband.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Let us have it all for Heavens ſake, 'tis good mirth, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: They ſay you will have four now, and thoſe ſom ſtuck in four quarters, like four winds to cool you: will ſhe not cry nor cu • ſ • ?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: On with your ſtory.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And that you are forcing out of diſpenſations with ſums of money to that purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Four Husbands! ſhould not I be bleſt, Sir, for example? Lord, what ſhould I do with them? turn a Maltmill, or Tithe them out like Town bulls to my Tenants, you come to make me angry, but you cannot.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I'le make you merry then, you are a brave Woman, and in deſpite of envy a right one, go thy wayes, truth thou art as good a Woman, as any Lord of them all can lay his Leg over, I do not often commend your Sex.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: It ſeems ſo, your commendations are ſo ſtudied for.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I came to ſee you and ſift you into Flowr to know your pureneſs, and I have found you excellent, I thank you; continue ſo, and ſhew men how to tread, and women how to follow: get an Husband, an honeſt man, you are a good woman, and live hedg'd in from ſcandal, let him be too an underſtanding man, and to that ſtedfaſt; 'tis pity your fair Figure ſhould miſcarry, and then your are ſixt: farewel.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Pray ſtay a little, I love your company now you are ſo pleaſant, and to my diſpoſition ſet ſo even.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I can no longer. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: As I live a l ••• fellow, this manly handſome bluntneſs ſhews him honeſt; what is he, or from whence? bleſs me, four Husbands! how prettily he fooled me into Vices, to ſt •• my jealouſie, and find my nature; a proper Gentleman: I am not well o'th' ſudden, ſuch a companion I could live and dye with, his angers are meer mirth.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Come, come, I am ready.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Are you ſo?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p:
What ails ſhe? the Coach ſtaies, and the p •••••
〈◊〉 day goes on, I am as ready now as you deſire, Siſter 〈◊〉 , 〈◊〉 ſtays now, why do you ſit and pout thus?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Prethee be quiet, I am not well.

sp.speaker: Iſa
sp.p: For Heav'ns ſake let's not ride ſtaggering in 〈◊〉 night, come, pray you take ſome Sweet-meats in 〈◊〉 pocket, if your ſtomach —

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I have a little buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: To abuſe me, you ſhall not find new dreams, 〈◊〉 new ſuſpicions, to horſe withal.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Lord who made you a Commander! hey • o, 〈◊〉 heart.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
Is the wind come thither, and Coward like, do y •• loſe your Colours to 'em? are you ſick o'th' Vale • t •••
〈◊〉 Siſter, come let's away, the Country will ſo quicken you and we ſhall live ſo ſweetly: Luce, my Ladies Cloak, 〈◊〉 you have put me into ſuch a gog of going, I would not 〈◊〉 for all the world; if I live here, you have ſo knock'd 〈◊〉 love into my head, that I ſhall love any body, and I 〈◊〉 my body, I know not how, ſo apt — pray let's be g •• Siſter, I ſtand on thorns.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
I prethee Iſabella, i'ſaith I have ſ ••••
• ſineſs t •• concerns me, I will ſuſpect no more, 〈…〉 me, and I'le pay the hundred pound you 〈…〉

div.stage: Enter Shorthoſe, Roger, Humphre • , R • lp • .

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I had rather go, but—

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
Come walk in with me, we'll go to Ca •• , •••
dle the Horſes.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: A Jubile, a Jubile, we ſtay, Boys.

div.stage: Enter Uncle, Lan. Foun. Bella. Hareb • ain following.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Are they behind us?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Cloſe, cloſe, ſpeak aloud, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I am glad my Nephew has ſo much diſc • etio • , 〈◊〉 l • ngth to find his wants: did ſhe entertain him?

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Moſt bravely, nobly, and gave him ſuch a 〈◊〉 come!

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: For his own ſake do you think?

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p:
Moſt certain, Sir, and in his own cauſe beſ •
〈◊〉 himſelf too, and wan ſuch liking from her, ſhe d • t • s • him, h'as the command of all the houſe already.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: He deals not well with his friends.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Let him deal on, and be his own friend, he 〈◊〉 moſt need of her.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I wonder they would put him—

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: You are in the right on't, a man that muſt r ••• himſelf, I knew he would couzen 'em, and glad I am he ha • he watched occaſion, and found it i'th' nick.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: He has deceived me.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I told you howſoever he wheel'd about, he work charge home at length: how I could laugh now, to think of theſe tame fools!

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: 'Twas not well done, becauſe they truſted him, 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: Hark you Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: We are upon a buſineſs, pray excuſe us, they h ••• it home.

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.p: Come let it work good on Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Font.
sp.p: 'Tis true, he is a knave, I ever thought it.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: And we are fools, tame fools.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.p:
Come let's go ſeek him, he ſhall be hang'd before he colt us baſely.
Exe ••

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Art ſure ſhe loves him?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Am I ſure I live? and I have clapt on ſuch accomendation on your revenge.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Faith, he is a pretty Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Handſome enough, and that her eye has ſound 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: He talks the beſt they ſay, and yet the maddeſt.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: H'as the right way.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: How is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Bears it well, as if ſhe cared not, but a man may 〈◊〉 with half an eye through all her forced behaviour, and • d who is her Valentine.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Come let's go ſee her, I long to proſecute.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: By no means Miſtreſs, let her take better hold • ſt.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I could burſt now. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Upbraid me with your benefits, you Pilchers, you • tten, ſold, ſlight fellows? was't not I that undertook • u firſt from empty barrels, and brought thoſe barking • ouths that gaped like bung-holes to utter ſence? where • t you underſtanding? who taught you manners and apt •• riage to rank your ſelves? who filled you in fit Tave • ns? • re thoſe born with your worſhips when you came hither? • at brought you from the Univerſities of moment matter • allow you, beſides your ſmall baſe ſentences?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.p: 'Tis well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
Long Cloaks with two-hand-rapiers, boot-hoſ • s • th penny poſes, and twenty fools opinions, who looked 〈◊〉 you but piping rites that knew you would be prizing, • d Prentices in Paul's Church-yard, that ſcented your want 〈◊〉
Britains Books.

sp.speaker: Font.
sp.p: This cannot ſave you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Taunt my integrity you Whelps?

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.p: You may talk the ſtock we gave you out, but ſee no • ther.

sp.speaker: Hair.
sp.p: You tempt our patience, we have found you out, • d what your truſt comes to, ye're well feathered, thank 〈◊〉 and think now of an honeſt courſe, 'tis time; men now • gin to look, and narrowly into your tumbling tricks, • ey are ſtale.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Is not that he?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: 'Tis he.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Be ſtill and mark him.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How miſerable will theſe poor wretches be when I • ſake 'em! but things have their neceſſities, I am ſo •• y, what a vomit muſt they turn again, now to their own • t Dunghil breeding; never hope after I caſt you off, you • n of Motley, you moſt undone things below pity, any • t has a ſoul and ſix pence dares relieve you, my name • ll bar that bleſſing, there's your Cloak, Sir, keep it • ſe to you, it may yet preſerve you a ſortnight longer • m the fool; your Hat, pray be covered, and there's • Sattin that your Worſhip ſent me, will ſerve you at a • es yet.
Nay, faith Sir, you may e'ne rub theſe out now.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No ſuch relique, nor the leaſt rag of ſuch a ſordid • akneſs ſhall keep me warm, theſe Breeches are mine • n, purchaſed, and paid for, without your compaſſion, Chriſtian Breeches founded in Black-Friers, and ſo I'le • intain 'em.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: So they ſeem, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Only the thirteen ſhillings in theſe Breeches, and • e odd groat, I take it, ſhall be yours, Sir, a mark to • ow a Knave by, pray preſerve it, do not diſpleaſe more, • take it preſently, now help me off with my Boots.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: We are no Grooms, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: For once you ſhall be, do it willingly, or by this • nd I'le make you.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.p: To our own, Sir, we may apply our hands.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: There's your Hangers, you may deſerve a ſtrong • r, and a girdle will hold you without buckles; now I am • rfect, and now the proudeſt of your worſhips tell me I beholding to you.
No ſuch matter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
And take heed how you pity me, 'tis dangerous, • eeding dangerous, to prate of pity; which are the poorer? • u are now puppies; I without you, or you without my • owledge? be Rogues, and ſo be gone, be Rogues and re
• not, for if you do—

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.p: Only thus much, and then we'll leave you the Air is far ſharper than our an ••• , Su, and th • ſe you may reſerve to rail in wa • me • .

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p:
Pray have a care, Sir, of your health.
Ex 〈◊〉 .

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
Yes Hog hounds, more than you can have or your wits; 'tis cold, and I am very ſenſible, extreamly 〈◊〉 too, yet I will not off, till I have ſhamed theſe Raſcals; I have in ſu • ed as ill heats as another, and every way •• o • could periſh my body, you'll b at th •
〈…〉 I a • colder here, not a poor penny •• ft.
'Thas ta • en ra • el • , and now 〈…〉 he 〈◊〉 ruled.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: To him, to whim, abuſ • him, and 〈◊〉 him 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Why how now, 〈…〉 weather?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: As you ſee, Sir, in a • ot ht, I 〈…〉

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: But Cou •• , where 〈◊〉 you ( 〈…〉 are no inheritance, 〈◊〉 ſcruple may compound with 〈◊〉 I take it, this is no faſhion, Couſin.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Not much followed, I muſt confeſs; yet Uncle I determine to try what may be done next Term.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: How came you thus, Sir, for you are ſtrangely moved.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Rags, toys and trifles, fit only for thoſe fools that firſt poſſeſſed 'em, and to thoſe Knaves they are rendred. Freemen, Uncle, ought to appear like innocents, old Adam, a fair Fig-leaſ ſufficient.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Take me with you, were theſe your friends, that clear'd you thus?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Hang friends, and even reckonings that make friends.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I thought till now, there • a • been no ſuch living, no ſuch purchaſe, for all the reſt is la • our as a 〈◊〉 o • honourable friends; do ſuch men as you, Sir, in him of all your underſtandings, travels, and thoſe great g • tt • of nature, aim at no more than caſting off your Coat • ? I am ſtrangely cozen'd.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p:
Should not the Town ſhake at the cold you fee • now, and all the Gently ſuffer interdiction, no more ſenſ • ſpoken, all things
• oth and Vandal, t • ll you be ſummed again, Velvets and Sca • lets, anointed with gold ••• e, and Cloth of ſilver turned into Spaniſh Cottens for a penance, wits blaſted with your Bulls, and Taverns withered, as though the Term lay at St Albans?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Gentlemen, you have ſpoken long and lev •• , I beſeech you take breath a while and hear me, you imagine now, by the twirling of your ſtrings, that I am at the laſt, as alſo that my friends are flown like Swallows after Summer.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And that I have no more in this poor Pannie • , to raiſe me up again above your rents, Uncle.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: All this I do believe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: You have no mind to better me

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Yes, Couſin, and to that • nd I come, and once more offer you all that my power is matter of.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: A match then, lay me down ••• y pounds there.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: There it is, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And on it write, that you are pleaſed to give this, as due unto my merit, without caution of 〈…〉 tedious thanks, or thriſt hereafter to be • op •• for.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: How? Luce l • y • a S •• t and 〈…〉

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Without da • ing, when you are d ••• k, to 〈◊〉 of revilings, to which you are prone in Sack, Uncle.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I thank you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Come, come away, let the young wanton play a while, away I ſay, Sir, let him go forward with his naked faſhion, he will ſeek you too morrow; goodly weather, ſultry hot, ſultry, how I ſweat!

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p:
Farewel, Sir.
Exeunt Uncle and Lance.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
Would I ſweat too, I am monſtrous • ext, and cold too; and theſe are but th •• pumps to walk the
ſtreets in; clothes I muſt get, this faſhion will not fadge with me; beſides, 'tis an ill winter wear, — What art thou? yes, they are clothes, and rich ones, ſome fool has left 'em: and if I ſhould utter — what's this paper here? Let theſe be only worn by the moſt noble and deſerving Gentleman Valentine, — dropt out o'th' clouds! I think they are full of gold too; well, I'le leave my wonder, and be warm again, in the next houſe I'le ſhift.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: WHY do you deal thus with him? 'tis unnobly.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Peace Couſin peace, you are too tender of him, he muſt be dealt thus with, he muſt be cured thus, the violence of his diſeaſe Franciſco, muſt not be jelted with, 'tis grown infectious, and now ſtrong Corroſives muſt cure him.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: H'as had a ſtinger, has eaten off his clothes, the next his skin comes.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: And let it ſearch him to the bones, 'tis better, 'twill make him feel it.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Where be his noble friends now? will his fantaſtical opinions cloath him, or the learned Art of having nothing feed him?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: It muſt needs greedily, for all his friends have ſlung him off, he is naked, and where to skin himſelf again, if I know, or can deviſe how he ſhould get himſelf lodging, his Spirit muſt be bowed, and now we have him, have him at that we hoped for.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Next time we meet him cracking of nuts, with half a cloak about him, for all means are cut off, or borrowing ſix-pence, to ſhew his bounty in the pottage Ordinary?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Which way went he?

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Pox, why ſhould you ask after him, you have been trimm'd already, let him take his fortune, ſom ſpun it out himſelf, Sir, there's no pitie.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Beſides ſome good to you now, from this miſerie.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I riſe upon his ruines! fie, fie, Uncle, fie honeſt Lance. Thoſe Gentlemen were baſe people, that could ſo ſoon take fire to his deſtruction.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: You are a fool, you are fool, a young man.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Morrow Uncle, morrow Frank, ſweet Frank, and how, and how d'ee, think now, how ſhew matters? morrow Bandog.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Is this man naked, forſaken of his friends?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Th'art handſom, Frank, a pretty Gentleman, i'faith thou lookeſt well, and yet here may be thoſe that look as handſom.

sp.speaker: Lance.
sp.p: Sure he can conjure, and has the Devil for his Tailor.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: New and rich! 'tis moſt impoſſible he ſhould recover.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Give him this luck, and fling him into the Sea.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: 'Tis not he, imagination cannot work this miracle.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Yes, yes, 'tis he, I will aſſure you Uncle, the very he, the he your wiſdom plaid withall, I thank you for't, neighed at his nakedneſſe, and made his cold and poverty your paſtime; you ſee I live, and the beſt can do no more Uncle, and though I have no ſtate, I keep the ſtreets ſtill, and take my pleaſure in the Town, like a poor Gentleman, wear clothes to keep me warm, poor things they ſerve me, can make a ſhew too if I liſt, yes uncle, and ring a peal in my pockets, ding dong, uncle, theſe are mad fooliſh wayes, but who can help 'em?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I am amazed.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p:
I'le ſell my Copyhold, for ſince there are ſuch ex ••
lent new nothings, why ſhould I labour? is there no 〈◊〉 haunts him, no Rat, nor no old woman?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: You are Valentine.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I think ſo, I cannot tell, I have been call'd ſo, a •• ſome ſay Chriſtened, why do you wonder at me, and ſw ••• if you had met a Sergeant faſting, did you ever know 〈◊〉 want? y'are fools, a little ſtoop there may be to allay 〈◊〉 he would grow too rank elſe, a ſmall eclipſe to ſhadow 〈◊〉 but out he muſt break, glowingly again, and with a gre • luſtre, look you uncle, motion and majeſty.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I am confounded.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I am of his faith.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Walk by his careleſs kinſman, and turn again a •• walk, and look thus Uncle, taking ſome one by the ha •• he loves beſt, leave them to the mercy of the hog-mar •• come Frank, Fortune is now my friend, let me inſtead thee.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Good morrow Uncle, I muſt needs go with him.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
Flay me, and turn me out where none inhabits, with a two hours I ſhall be thus again, now wonder on, and la •• at your own ignorance.
Ex. Val. and Fran •

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I do believe him.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p:
So do I, and heartily upon my conſcience, b ••••• ſtark naked, he would riſe again, within two hours •
broidered: ſow muſtard-ſeeds, and they cannot come 〈◊〉 thick as his new ſattens do, and clothes of ſilver, there's 〈◊〉 ſtriving.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Let him play a while then, and let's ſearch out wh • hand: —

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I, there the game lies. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Foun.
sp.p: Come, let's ſpeak for our ſelves, we have lodg'd hi • ſure enough, his nakedneſs dare nor peep out to croſs us.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: We can have no admittance.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: Let's in boldly, and uſe our beſt arts, who ſhe dei • to favour, we are all content.

sp.speaker: Foun.
sp.p: Much good may do her with him, no civil wars.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: By no means, now do I wonder in what old tod 〈◊〉 he lies whiſtling for means, nor clothes he hath none, 〈◊〉 none will truſt him, we have made that ſide ſure, teach h •• a new wooing.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: Say it is his Uncles ſpite.

sp.speaker: Foun.
sp.p:
It is all one Gentlemen, 'thas rid us of a fair in ••
brance, and makes us look about to our own fortunes. Wa • are theſe?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
Not ſee this man yet! well, I ſhall be wiſer: but L ••
didſt ever know a woman melt ſo? ſhe is finely hurt to h ••

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Peace, the three Suitors.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I could ſo titter now and laugh, I was loſt Luce, a •• muſt love, I know not what; O Cupid, what pretty gins th •• haſt to halter Woodcocks! and we muſt into the Country 〈◊〉 all haſte, Luce.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: For Heavens ſake, Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Nay, I have done, I muſt laugh though; but Scho •• I ſhall teach you.

sp.speaker: Foun.
sp.p: 'Tis her ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: Save you Ladies.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Fair met Gentlemen, you are viſiting my ſiſter, 〈◊〉 aſſure my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: We would ſain bleſs our eyes.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Behold and welcom, you would ſee her?

sp.speaker: Foun.
sp.p: 'Tis our buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: You ſhall ſee her, and you ſhall talk with her.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: She will not ſee 'em, nor ſpend a word.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I'le make her frat a thouſand, nay now I have foc •• the ſab, I will ſo ſcratch her.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: She cannot endure 'em.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: She loves 'em but too dearly, come follow me, I'le b ••• you toth' party Gentlemen, then make your own condit •••

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: She is ſick you know.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
I'le make her well, or kill her, and take no idle an
• er, you are fools then, nor ſtand off for her ſtate, ſhe'l ſcorn • u all then, but urge her ſtill, and though ſhe fret, ſtill fol
•• w her, a widow muſt be won ſo.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: She ſpeaks bravely.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I would fain have a Brother in law, I love mens • mpany, and if ſhe call for dinner to avoid you, be ſure you • y; follow her into her chamber, if ſhe retire to Pray, pray • th her, and boldly, like honeſt lovers.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: This will kill her.

sp.speaker: Foun.
sp.p: You have ſhewed us one way, do but lead the tother.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I know you ſtand o'thorns, come I'le diſpatch you.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: If you live after this.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I have loſt my aim.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Did you not ſee 'em ſince.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No hang 'em, hang 'em.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Nor will you not be ſeen by 'em?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Let 'em alone Frank, I'le make 'em their own • ſtice, and a jerker.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Such baſe diſcourteous Dog-whelps.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I ſhall dog 'em, and double dog 'em, ere I have done.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p:
Will you go with me, for I would fain find out • is piece of bountie, it was the Widows man, that I am cer
• in of.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: To what end would you go?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: To give thanks.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Hang giving thanks, haſt not thou parts deſerve it? it • cludes a further will to be beholding, beggers can do no • ore at door, if you will go, there lies your way.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I hope you will go.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No not in ceremony, and to a woman, with mine • wn Father, were he living Frank; I would toth' Court • ith Bears firſt, if it be that wench, I think it is, for t'other's • iſer, I would not be ſo lookt upon, and laught at, ſo made ladder for her wit, to climb upon, for 'tis the tarteſt tit in Chriſtendom, I know her well Frank, and have buckled • ith her, ſo lickt, and ſtroaked, ſlear'd upon, and ſtouted, • d ſhown to Chambermaids, like a ſtrange beaſt, ſhe had •• rchaſed with her penny.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: You are a ſtrange man, but do you think it was a • oman?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: There's no doubt on't, who can be there to do it elſe? • eſides the manner of the circumſtances.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p:
Then ſuch courteſies, who ever does 'em ſir, ſaving our own wiſdom, muſt be more lookt into, and better an
• ered, than with deſerving ſlights, or what we ought to have •• nferred upon us, men may ſtarve elſe, means are not got
• en now with crying out I am a gallant fellow, a good Soul
•• er, a man of learning, or fit to be employed, immediate • eſſings ceaſe like miracles, and we muſt grow by ſecond • eans, I pray go with me, even as you love me Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I will come to thee, but Frank, I will not ſtay to hear our ſopperies, diſpatch thoſe e're I come.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: You will not fail me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Some two hours hence expect me.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I thank you, and will look for you. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Who let in theſe puppies? you blind raſcals, you • runken Knaves ſeveral.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Yes for ſooth, I'le let 'em in preſently, — Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Sprecious, you blown Pudding, bawling Rogue.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I bawl as loud as I can, would you have me fetch • m upon my back.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Get 'em out raſcal, out with 'em, out, I ſweat to • ave 'em near me.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I ſhould ſweat more to carry 'em out.

sp.speaker: Roger.
sp.p: They are Gentlemen Madam.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Shall we get 'em into th'butterie, and make'em • runk?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Do any thing, ſo I be eaſed.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Now to her Sir, fear nothing.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Slip aſide boy, I know ſhe loves 'em, howſoever ſ •• carries it, and has invited 'em, my young Miſtreſs told m • ſo.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p:
Away to tables then.
Ex ••• t.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I ſhall burſt with the ſport on't.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: You are too curious Madam, too full of preparation, we expect it not.

sp.speaker: Bella.
sp.p: Me thinks the houſe is handſom, every place decent, what need you be vext?

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: We are no ſtrangers.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: What though we come e're you expected us, do not we know your entertainments Madam are • ee, and fall at all times?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You are merry, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: We come to be merry Madam, and very merry, m • n love to laugh heartily, and now and then Lady a little of our old plea.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I am buſie, and very buſie too, will none deliver me.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: There is a time for all, you may be buſie, but when your friends come, you have as much power Madam.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: This is a tedious torment.

sp.speaker: Foun.
sp.p: How hanſomly this little piece of anger ſhews upon her! well Madam well, you know not how to grace your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: Nay every thing ſhe does breeds a new ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I muſt go up, I muſt go up, I have a buſineſs waits upon me, ſome wine for the Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: Nay, we'l go with you, we never ſaw your chambers yet.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Hold there boyes.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Say I go to my prayers?

sp.speaker: Foun.
sp.p: We'l pray with you, and help your meditations.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: This is boyſterous, or ſay I go to ſleep, will you go to ſleep with me?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: So ſuddenly before meat will be dangerous, we know your dinner's ready Lady, you will not ſleep.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Give me my Coach, I will take the air.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: We'l wait on you, and then your meat after a quickned ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
Let it alone, and call my Steward to me, and bid him bring his reckonings into the Orchard, theſe unmannerly rude puppies —
Exit Widow.

sp.speaker: Foun.
sp.p: We'l walk after you and view the pleaſure of the place.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Let her not reſt, for if you give her breath, ſh •• ſcorn and ſlout you, ſeem how ſhe will, this is the way to win her, be bold and proſper.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: Nay if we do not tire her.— Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I'le teach you to worm me, good Lady ſiſter, and peep into my privacies to ſuſpect me, I'le torture you, with, that you hate, moſt daintily, and when I have done that, laugh at that you love moſt.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: What have you done, ſhe chaſes and ſumes outragiouſly, and ſtill they perſecute her.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Long may they do ſo, I'le teach her to declaim againſt my pities, why is ſhe not gone out o'th' town, but gives occaſion for men to run mad after her?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I ſhall be hanged.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: This in me had been high treaſon, three at a time, and private in her Orchard! I hope ſhe'l caſt her reckonings right now.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Well, I ſhall find who brought 'em.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Why do you laugh ſiſter? I fear me 'tis your trick, 'twas neatly done of you, and well becomes your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: What have you done with 'em?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Lockt 'em i'th' Orchard, there I'le make 'em dance and caper too, before they get their liberty, unmannerly rude puppies.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: They are ſomewhat ſaucy, but yet I'le let 'em out, and once more ſound 'em, why were they not beaten out?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I was about it, but becauſe they came as ſuiters.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Why did you not anſwer 'em?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: They are ſo impudent they will receive none: More yet! how came theſe in?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: At the door, Madam.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: It is that face.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: This is the Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: She ſent the money to?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: The ſame.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I'le leave you, they have ſome buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Nay, you ſhall ſtay, Siſter, they are ſtrangers both to me; how her face alters!

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I am ſorry he comes now.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I am glad he is here now though. Who would you ſpeak with, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: You Lady, or your fair Siſter there, here's a Gentleman that has received a benefit.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: From whom, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: From one of you, as he ſuppoſes, Madam, your man delivered it.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I pray go forward.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: And of ſo great a goodneſs, that he dares not, without the tender of his thanks and ſervice, paſs by the houſe.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Which is the Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: This, Madam.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: What's your name, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: They that know me call me Franciſco, Lady, one not ſo proud to ſcorn ſo timely a benefit, nor ſo wretched to hide a gratitude.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: It is well beſtowed then.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Your fair ſelf, or your Siſter as it ſeems, for what deſert I dare not know, unleſs a handſome ſubject for your charities, or aptneſs in your noble will to do it, have ſhowred upon my wants a timely bounty, which makes me rich in thanks, my beſt inheritance.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I am ſorry 'twas not mine, this is the Gentlewoman, ſie, do not bluſh, go roundly to the matter, the man is a pretty man.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: You have three fine ones.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Then to you, dear Lady?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I pray no more, Sir, if I may perſwade you, your only aptneſs to do this is recompence, and more than I expected.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: But good Lady.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: And for me further to be acquainted with it beſides the imputation of vain glory, were greedy thankings of my ſelf, I did it not to be more affected to; I did it, and if it happened where I thought it ſitted, I have my end; more to enquite is cutious in either of us, more than that ſuſpicious.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: But gentle Lady, 't will be neceſſary.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: About the right way nothing, do not fright it, being to pious uſe and tender ſighted, with the blown face of Complements, it blaſts it; had you not come at all, but thought thanks, it had been too much, 'twas not to ſee your perſon.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: A brave diſſembling Rogue, and how ſhe carries it!

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Though I believe few handſomer; or hear you, though I affect a good tongue well; or try you, though my years deſire a friend, that I relieved you.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: A plagnie cunning quean.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: For ſo I carried it, my end's too glorious in mine eyes, and bettered the goodneſs I propounded with opinion.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Fear her not, Sir.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: You cannot catch me, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Will you both teach, and tie my tongue up Lady?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Let it ſuffice you have it, it was never mine, whileſt good men wanted it.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: This is a Saint ſure.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: And if you be not ſuch a one, reſtore it.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: To commend my ſelf, were more officious 〈◊〉 you think my thanks are, to doubt I may be worth your 〈◊〉 a treaſon, both to mine own good and underſtanding, 〈◊〉 know my mind clear, and though modeſty tells me, 〈◊〉 intreats intrudes; yet I muſt think ſomething, and of fr •• ſeaſon, met with your better taſte, this had not been elſe.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: What ward for that, wench?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Alas, it never touched me.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Well, gentle Lady, yours is the firſt money I 〈◊〉 took upon a forced ill manners.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: The laſt of me, if ever you uſe other.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: How may I do, and your way to be thought: grateful taker?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Spend it, and ſay nothing, your modeſty may deſerve more.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: O Siſter will you bar thankfulneſs?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p:
Dogs dance for meat, would ye have men do work for they can ſpeak, cry out like Wood-mongers, good deeds by the hundreds, I did it that my beſt friend 〈◊〉 not know it, wine and vain glory does as much as I elſe, t •• you will force my merit, againſt my meaning, uſe it in 〈◊〉 beſtowing it, in ſhewing it came to be a benefit, and was ſo; and not examining a Woman did it, or to what 〈◊〉 in not believing ſometimes your ſelf, when drink and ſ ••
ring converſation may ripen ſtrange perſwaſions.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p:
Gentle Lady, I were a baſe receiver of a courteſ • and you a worſe diſpoſer, were my nature unfurniſhed 〈◊〉 theſe fore-ſights. Ladies honours were ever in my th •••
〈◊〉 unſpotted Crimes, their good deeds holy Temples, w ••• the incenſe burns not; to common eyes your fears are ••
tuous, and ſo I ſhall preſerve 'em.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p:
Keep but this way, and from this place to tell me i • you have paid me; and ſo I wiſh you ſee all fortune.
Ex •

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
Fear not, the Woman will be thanked, I do not doubt it. Are you ſo crafty, carry it ſo preciſely? this is • wake my fears, or to abuſe me, I ſhall look narrowly: 〈◊〉 ſpair not Gentlemen, there is an hour to catch a Wo ••• in, if you be wiſe, ſo, I muſt leave you too; Now will 〈◊〉 laugh at my Suitors.
Ex ••

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Sir, what courage?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: This Woman is a founder, and cites Statutes t • all her benefits.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I never knew yet, ſo few years and ſo cunning, ye believe me ſhe has an itch, but how to make her confeſs 〈◊〉 for it is a crafty Tit, and plays about you, will not be home, ſhe would fain, but ſhe dares not; carry your 〈◊〉 but ſo diſcreetly, Sir, that want or wantonneſs ſeem not t • ſearch you, and you ſhall ſee her open.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I do love her, and were I rich, would give us thouſand pound to wed her wit but one hour, oh 'tis a Dragon, and ſuch a ſpritely way of pleaſure, ha Lance.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Your ha Lance broken once, you would cry, ho, ho, Lance.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Some leaden landed Rogue will have this wend now, when all's done, ſome ſuch youth will carry her, and wear her, greaſie out like ſtuff, ſome Dunce that knows 〈◊〉 more but Markets, and admires nothing but a long cha ••• at Sizes: O the fortunes!

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Comfort your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: They are here yet, and alone too, boldly upon 〈◊〉 nay, Miſtreſs, I ſtill told you, how 'twould find your 〈◊〉 this 'tis to venture your charity upon a boy.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Now, what's the matter? ſtand faſt, and like your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Pret hee no more Wench.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: What was his want to you?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: 'Tis true.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Or miſery, or ſay he had been i'th' Cage, was th •• no mercy to look abroad but yours?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: I am paid for fooling.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Muſt every ſlight companion that can purchaſe a 〈◊〉 of poverty and beggerly planet fall under your compaſſ •••

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.p: Here's a new matter.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Nay, you are ſerved but too well, here he ſtaies • et, yet as I live.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: How her face alters on me!

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Out of a conſcience I hope.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I am grad on't.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: How do you gentle Lady?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p:
Much aſhamed Sir, (but firſt ſtand further off me, 〈◊〉 are infectious) to find ſuch vanitie, nay almoſt impudence, where I believ'd a worth: is this your thanks, the grati
• ude you were ſo mad to make me, your trim counſel Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.p: What, Lady?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Take your device again, it will not ſerve Sir, the woman will not bite, you are finely cozened drop it no • ore for ſhame.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p:
Do you think you are here Sir am 〈◊〉
• ur waſt • oateers, your baſe wenches that ſcratch at ſuch 〈◊〉
••• s? you are deluded: This is a Gentlewoman of a noble houſ •
• orn to a better fame than you can build ne • , and eyes above your pitch.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I do acknowledge—

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Then I beſeech you Sir what could'ſee, (ſpeak boldly, • nd ſpeak truly, ſhame the Devil,) in my behaviour of ſuch eaſineſs that you durſt venture to do this?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: You amaze me, this Ring is none of mine, nor did 〈◊〉 drop it.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: I ſaw you drop it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Iſab
sp.p: I took it up too, ſtill looking when your modeſty ſhould miſs it, why, what a childiſh part was this?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I vow.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Vow me no vowes, he that dares do this, has bred himſelf to boldneſs, to forſwear too; there take your gewgaw, you are too much pampered, and I repent my part, • s you grow older grow wiſer if you can, and ſo farewel Sir.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Grow wiſer if you can? ſhe has put it to you, 'tis a • ich Ring, did you drop it?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Never, ne're ſaw it afore, Lance.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Thereby hangs a tail then: what ſlight ſhe makes • o catch her ſelf! look up Sir, you cannot loſe her if you would, how daintily ſhe flies upon the Lure, and cunningly • he makes her ſtops! whiſtle and ſhe'l come to you.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I would I were ſo happy.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Maids are Clocks, the greateſt Wheel they ſhow, goes ſloweſt to us, and make's hang on tedious hopes; the • eſſer, which are concealed, being often oyl'd with wiſhes, • ee like deſires, and never leave that motion, till the • ongue ſtrikes; ſhe is fleſh, blood and marrow, young as her purpoſe, and ſoft as pity; no Monument to worſhip, but a mould to make men in, a neat one, and I know how e're ſhe appears now, which is near enough, you are ſtark blind if you hit not ſoon at night; ſhe would venture forty pounds more but to feel a Flea in your ſhape bite her: drop to more Rings forſooth, this was the prettieſt thing to know her heart by.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Thou putſt me in much comfort.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Put your ſelf in good comfort, if ſhe do not point • ou out the way, drop no more Rings, ſhe'l drop her ſelf • nto you.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I wonder my Brother comes not.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Let him alone, and feed your ſelf on your own fortunes; come be frolick, and let's be monſtrous wiſe and full of counſel, drop no more Rings. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: If you will needs be fooliſh you muſt be uſed ſo: who ſent for you? who entertained you Gentlemen? who bid you welcom hither? you came crowding, and impudently bold; preſs on my patience, as if I kept a houſe for 〈◊〉 Companions, and of all ſorts: will 'have your wills, will vex me and force my liking from you I ne're ow'd • ou?

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: For all this we will dine with you.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: And for all this will have a better anſwer from you.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You ſhall never, neither have an anſwer nor • inner, unleſs you uſe me with a more ſtaid reſpect, and ſtay your time too.

div.stage: Enter Iſabella, Shorthoſe, Roger, Humphrey, Ralph, with diſhes of meat.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Forward with the meat now.

sp.speaker: Rog.
sp.p: Come Gentlemen, march fairly.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Roger, you are a weak Serving man, your white broath runs from you; ſie, how I ſweat un •• r this Pile of Beef; an Elephant can do more! Oh for ſuch a back now, and in theſe times, what might a man arrive at! Gooſe, graſe you up, and Woodcock march behinde thee, I am almoſt ſound • ed.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Who bid you bring the meat yet? away you knaves, I will not dine theſe two hours: how am I vext and chaſed! go carry it back and tell the Cook, he's an arrant Raſ • al, to ſend before I called.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Face about Gentlemen, beat a mou • nfull march then, and give ſome ſupporters, or elſe I periſh—

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: It does me much good to ſee her chafe thus.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: We can ſtay Madam, and will ſtay and dwell here, 'tis good Air.

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: I know you have beds enough, and meat you never want.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You want a little.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: We dare to pretend no. Since you are churliſ • , we'l give you Phyſick, you muſt purge this anger, it burns you and decays you.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: If I had you out once, I would be at the charge of a portcullis for you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Good morrow noble Lady.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Good morrow Sir. How ſweetly now he looks, and how full manly! what ſlaves were theſe to uſe him ſo!

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I come to look a young man I call Brother.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Such a one was here Sir, as I remember your own Brother, but gone almoſt an hour agoe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Good ee'n then.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You muſt not ſo ſoon Sir, here be ſome Gentlemen, it may be you are acquainted with 'em.

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: Will nothing make him miſerable?

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: How glorious!

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: It is the very he, does it rain fortunes, or has he a familiar?

sp.speaker: Hare.
sp.p: How doggedly he looks too?

sp.speaker: Fount.
sp.p: I am beyond my faith, pray let's be going.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Where are theſe Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Here.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Yes I know 'em, and will be more familiar.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: Morrow Madam.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Nay ſtay and dine.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
You ſhall ſtay till I talk with you, and not dine neither, but faſtingly my fury, you think you have undone me, think ſo ſtill, and ſwallow that belief, till you be company for Court-hand Clarks, and ſtarved Atturnies, till you break in at playes like Prentices for three a groat, and crack Nuts with the Scholars in peny Rooms again, and fight for Apples, till you return to what I found you, people be • rai'd into the hands of Fencers, Challengers, Tooth draw is Bills, and tedious Proclamations in Meal-markets, with throngings to ſee Cutpurſes: ſtir not, but hear, and mark, I'le cut your throats elſe, till Water works, and rumours of New Rivers rid you again and run you into queſtions who built Thames, till you run mad for Lotteries, and ſtand there with your Tables to glean the golden Sentences, and cite 'em ſecrely to Servingmen for ſound Eſſayes, till Taverns allow you but a Towel room to Tipple Wine in, that the Bell hath gone for twice, and Glaſſes that look li • e broken promiſes, tied up with wicker proteſlations, •••• ſh Tobacco with half Pipes, nor in half a year once burn •
and Bisket that Bawds have rubb'd their gums upon like Corals to bring the mark again, tell theſe hour Raſcals ſo, this moſt fatal hour will come again, think I ſit down the looſer.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Will you ſtay Gentlemen, a piece of Beef and a cold Capon, that's all, you know you are welcom.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: That was caſt to abuſe us.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.p: Steal off, the Devil is in his anger.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Nay I am ſure you will not leave me ſo diſcourteouſly, now I have provided for you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: What do you here? why do ye vex a woman of her goodneſs, her ſtate and worth? can you bring a fair certificate that you deſerve to be her footmen? husbands, you puppies? husbands for Whores and Bawds, away you wind ſucke • s; do not look big, nor prate, nor ſtay, nor grumble, and when you are gone, ſeem to laugh at my fury, and ſlight this Lady, I ſhall hear, and know this: and though I am not bound to fight for women, as far they are good I dare preſerve 'em: be not too bold, for if you be, I'le ſwinge you monſtrouſly without all pity, your honours now goe, avoid me mainly. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Well Sir, you have delivered me, I thank you, and with your nobleneſs prevented danger, their tongues might utter, we'll all go and eat Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No, no, I dare not truſt my ſelf with women, go to your meat, eat little, take leſs eaſe, and tie your body to a daily labour, you may live honeſtly, and ſo I thank you.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Well go thy ways, thou art a noble fellow, and ſome means I muſt work to have thee know it. Exit.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: MOſt certain 'tis her hands that hold him up, and her ſiſter relieves Frank.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I am glad to hear it: but wherefore do they not purſue this fortune to ſome fair end?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: The women are too craftie, Valentine too coy, and Frank too baſhfull, had any wiſe man hold of ſuch a bleſſing, they would ſtrike it out o'th' ſlint but they would form it.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: The Widow ſure, why does ſhe ſtir ſo early?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: 'Tis ſtrange, I cannot force him to underſtand me, and make a benefit of what I would bring him: tell my ſiſter I'le uſe my devotions at home this morning, ſhe may if ſhe pleaſe go to Church.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Hey ho.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: And do you wait upon her with a torch Sir.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Hey ho.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You lazie Knave.

sp.speaker: Short.
