sp.p: Here is ſuch a tinkle tanklings that we can ne're lie quiet, and ſleep our prayers out. Ralph, pray emptie my right ſhooe that you made your Chamber pot, and burn a little Roſemarie in't, I muſt wait upon my Lady. This morning Prayer has brought me into a conſumption, I have nothing left but fleſh and bones about me.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You drouſie ſlave, nothing but ſleep and ſwilling?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Had you been bitten with Bandog ſleas, as I have been, and haunted with the night Mare.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: With an Ale-pot.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: You would have little liſt to morning Prayers, pray take my fellow Ralph, he has a Pſalm Book, I am an ingrum man.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Get you ready quickly, and when ſhe is ready wait upon her handſomely; no more, be gone.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p:
If I do ſnore my part out —
Exit Short.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Now to our purpoſes.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Good morrow, Madam.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Good morrow, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Good joy and fortune.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Theſe are good things, and worth my thanks, thank you Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Much joy I hope you'l find, we came to grat ••• your new knit marriage-band.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: He's a Gentleman, although he be my kinſm •• my fair Niece.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Niece, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Yes Lady, now I may ſay ſo, 'tis no ſhame to yo • ſay a Gentleman, and winking at ſome light fancies, w •••• you moſt happily may affect him for, as bravely carried, a nobly bred and managed.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: What's all this? I underſtand you not, what Nie •• what marriage-knot?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I'le tell plainly, you are my Niece, and Valentine the Gentleman has made you ſo by marriage.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Marriage?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Yes Lady, and 'twas a noble and vertuous part, t • take a falling man to your protection, and buoy him up again to all his glories.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: The men are mad.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: What though he wanted theſe outward thing • that flie away like ſhadows, was not his mind a full or and a brave one? You have wealth enough to give h •• gloſs and outſide, and he wit enough to give way to love a Lady.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I ever thought he would do well.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Nay, I knew how ever he wheel'd about 〈◊〉 a looſe Cabine, he would charge home at length, like a brave Gentleman; Heavens bleſſing o' your heart Lady, we are ſo bound to honour you, in all your ſervice 〈◊〉 devoted to you.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Do not look ſo ſtrange Widow, it muſt be know • better a general joy; no ſtirring here yet, come, come, 〈◊〉 cannot hide 'em.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Pray be not impudent, theſe are the fineſt toyes, be like I am married then?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: You are in a miſerable eſtate in the worlds account elſe, I would not for your wealth it come to doubting.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: And I am great with child?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p:
No, great they ſay not, but 'tis a full opinion you • with child, and great joy among the Gentlemen, your hu •
band hath beſtirred himſelf fairly.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Alas, we know his private hours of entrance, h •• long, and when he ſtayed, could name the bed too, where i • paid down his firſt-fruits.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I ſhall believe anon.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: And we conſider for ſome private reaſons, you work have it private, yet take your own pleaſure; and ſo good morrow, my beſt Niece, my ſweeteſt.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: No, no, pray ſtay.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I know you would be with him, love him, and love him well.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: You'l find him noble, this may beget —

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: It muſt needs work upon her.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Theſe are fine bobs i'faith, married, and with ch • too! how long has this been, I trow? they ſeem grave fellows, they ſhould not come to ſlout; married, and bedded the world takes notice too! where lies this May game? I could be vext extreamly now, and rail too, but 'tis to 〈◊〉 end, though I itch a little, muſt I be ſcratcht I know not bo • who waits there?

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: Madam.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Make ready my Coach quickly, and wait you only and hark you Sir, be ſecret and ſpeedy, inquire out w ••• he lies.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.p: I ſhall do it, Madam.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Married, and got with child in a dream 〈◊〉 fine i'ſaith, ſure he that did this, would do better wa ••••

div.stage: Enter Valentine, Fran. Lance, and a Boy with a Torch.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Hold thy Torch handſomely: how doſt thou Frank? • ter Baſſel, bear up.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: You have fried me ſoundly, Sack do you call this • ink?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: A ſhrewd dog, Frank, will bite abundantly.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Now could I fight, and fight with thee.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: With me, thou man of Memphis?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p:
But that thou art mine own natural maſter, yet • y ſack ſays thou art no man, thou art a Pagan, and pawn
• thy land, which a noble cauſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
No arms, nor arms, good Lancelot, dear Lance,
• fighting here, we will have Lands boy, Livings, and • tles, thou ſhalt be a Vice-Roy, hang fighting, hang't 'tis • ut of faſhion.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I would fain labour you into your lands again, go • , it is behoveful.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Fie Lance, fie.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I muſt beat ſome body, and why not my Maſter, • efore a ſtranger? charity and beating begins at home.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Come, thou ſhalt beat me.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I will not be compel'd, and you were two Maſters, ſcorn the motion.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Wilt thou ſleep?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I ſcorn ſleep.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Wilt thou go eat?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I ſcorn meat, I come for rompering, I come to • ait upon my charge diſcreetly; for look you, if you will • ot take your Mortgage again, here do I lie St George, and • forth.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And here do I St George, beſtride the Dragon, thus • ith my Lance.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I ſting, I ſting with my tail.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Do you ſo, do you ſo, Sir? I ſhall tail you preſently.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: By no means, do not hurt him.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Take this Nelſon, and now riſe, thou Maiden Knight • f Mallig • , lace on thy Helmet of inchanted Sack, and • harge again.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I'le play no more, you abuſe me, will you go?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I'le bid you good morrow, Brother, for ſleep I • annot, I have a thouſand fancies.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Now thou art arrived, go bravely to the matter, • nd do ſomething of worth, Frank.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p:
You ſhall hear from us.
Exeunt Lance and Frank.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: This Rogue, if he had been ſober, ſure had beaten • ne, is the moſt tettiſh Knave.

div.stage: Enter Uncle and Merchant, Boy with a Torch.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: 'Tis he.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Good morrow.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Why, Sir, good morrow to you too, and you be • o luſty.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: You have made your Brother a fine man, we met • im.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I made him a fine Gentleman, he was a fool before, • rought up amongſt the midſt of Small-Beer-Brew-houſes, what would you have with me?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I come to tell you, your lateſt hour is come.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Are you my ſentence?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: The ſentence of your ſtate.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Let it be hang'd then, and let it be hang'd high enough, I may not ſee it.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: A gracious reſolution.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: What would you have elſe with me, will you go drink, and let the world ſlide, Uncle? Ha, ha, ha, boyes, • rink Sack like Whey, boyes.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Have you no feeling, Sir?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Come hither Merchant: make me a ſupper, thou moſt reverent Land catcher, a ſupper of forty pounds.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: What then, Sir?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Then bring thy Wife along, and thy fair Siſters, • hy Neighbours and their Wives, and all their trinkets, • et me have forty Trumpets, and ſuch Wine, we'll laugh at all the miſeries of Mortgage, and then in ſtate I'le rende • thee an anſwer.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: What ſay you to this?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: I dare not ſay, nor think neither.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Will you redeem your ſtate, ſpeak to the point, Sir?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Not, not if it were mine heir in the Turks Gallies.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Then I muſt take an order?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Take a thouſand, I will not keep it, nor thou ſhalt not have it, becauſe thou cameſt i'th' nick, thou ſhalt not have it, go take poſſeſſion, and be ſure you hold it, hold faſt with both hands, for there be thoſe hounds uncoupled, will ring you ſuch a knell, go down in glory, and march up on my land, and cry, All's mine; cry as the Devil did, and be the Devil, mark what an Echo follows, build fine March-panes, to entertain Sir Silk-worm and his Lady, and pull the Chappel down, and raiſe a Chamber for Miſtreſs Silver-pin, to lay her belly in, mark what an Earthquake comes. Then fooliſh Merchant my Tenants are no Subjects, they obey nothing, and they are people too never Chriſtened, they know no Law nor Conſcience, they'll devour thee; and thou mortal, the ſtopple, they'll confound thee within three days; no bit nor memory of what thou wert, no not the Wart upon thy Noſe there, ſhall be e're heard of more; go take poſſeſſion, and bring thy Children down, to roſt like Rabbets, they love young Toaſts and Butter, Bow-bell Suckers; as they love miſchief, and hate Law, they are Cannibals; bring down thy kindred too, that be not fruitful, there be thoſe Mandrakes that will mollifie 'em, go take poſſeſſion. I'le go to my Chamber, afore Boy go.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: He's mad ſure.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: He's half drunk ſure: and yet I like this unwillingneſs to loſe it, this looking back.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Yes, if he did it handſomely, but he's ſo harſh and ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Believe it 'tis his drink, Sir, and I am glad his drink has thruſt it out.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Cannibals? if ever I come to view his Regiment, if fair terms may be had.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: He tells you true, Sir, they are a bunch of the moſt boiſterous Raſcals diſorder ever made, let 'em be mad once, the power of the whole Country cannot cool 'em, be patient but a while.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: As long as you will, Sir, before I buy a bargain of ſuch Runts, I'le buy a Colledge for Bears, and live among 'em.

div.stage: Enter Franciſco, Lance, Boy with a Torch.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: How doſt thou now?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Better than I was, and ſtraighter, but my head's a Hogſhead ſtill, it rowls and tumbles.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Thou wert cruelly paid.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: I may live to requite it, put a Snaffle of Sack in my mouth and then ride me very well.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: 'Twas all but ſport, I'le tell thee what I mean now, I mean to ſee this Wench.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Where a Devil is ſhe? and there were two, 'twere better.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Doſt thou hear the Bell ring?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Then ſhe comes to prayers, early each morning thither: Now if I could but meet her, for I am of another mettle now.

div.stage: Enter Iſabel, and Shorthoſe with a Torch.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: What light's yon?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Ha, 'tis a light, take her by the hand and court her.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Take her below the girdle, you'l never ſpeed elſe, it comes on this way ſtill, oh that I had but ſuch an opportunity in a Saw-pit, how it comes on, comes on! 'tis here.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: 'Tis ſhe: fortune I kiſs thy hand— Good morrow Lady.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p:
What voice is that, Sirra, do you ſteep as you go,
'tis he, I am glad • a't. Why, Shorthoſe?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Yes forſooth, I was dreamt, I was going to Church.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: She ſees you as plain as I do.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Hold the torch up.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: H • r • 's nothing but a ſtall, and a Butchers Dog aſleep in 't, where did you ſee the voice?
She looks ſtill angry.
To her and meet Sir.
Here, here.
Yes Lady, never bleſs your ſelf, I am but a man, and like an honeſt man, now I will thank you—

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: What do you mean, who ſent for you, who deſired you?

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: Shall I put out the Torch forſooth?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Can I not go about my private meditations, Ha, but ſuch companions as you muſt ruffle me? you had beſt go with me Sir?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: 'T was my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Why, what an impudence is this! you had beſt, being ſo near the Church, provide a Prieſt, and perſwade me to marry you.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: It was my meaning, and ſuch a husband, ſo loving, and ſo carefull, my youth, and all my fortunes ſhall arrive at— Hark you?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: 'Tis ſtrange you ſhould be thus unmannerly, turn home again ſi •• a, you had beſt now force my man to lead your way.
Yes marry ſhall he Lady, forward my friend.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: This is a pretty Riot, it may grow to a rape.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Do you like that better? I can raviſh you an hundred times, and never hurt you.

sp.speaker: Short.
sp.p: I ſee nothing, I am aſleep ſtill, when you have done tell me, and then I'le wake Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Are you in earneſt Sir, do you long to be hang'd?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Yes by my troth Lady in theſe fair Treſſes.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Shall I call out for help?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: No by no means, that were a weak trick Lady, I'le kiſs, and ſtop your mouth.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: You'l anſwer all theſe?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: A thouſand kiſſes more.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I was never abuſed thus, you had beſt give out too, that you ſound me willing, and ſay I doted on you?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: That's known already, and no man living ſhall now carry you from me.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: This is fine i'faith.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: It ſhall be ten times finer.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Well, ſeeing you are ſo valiant, keep your way, I will to Church.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: And I will wait upon you.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: And it is moſt likely there's a Lrieſt, if you dare venture as you profeſs, I would wiſh you look about you, to do theſe rude tricks, for you know the recompences, and truſt not to my mercy.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: But I will Lady.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: For I'le ſo handle you.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: That's it I look for.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: Afore thou dream.

sp.speaker: Shor.
sp.p: Have you done?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Go on Sir, and follow if you dare.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: If I do not, hang me.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.p: 'Tis all thine own boy, an 'twere a million, god a mercy Sack, when would ſmall Beer have done this?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Whoſe that that knocks and bounces, what a Devil ails you, is hell broke looſe, or do you keep an Iron mill?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: 'Tis a Gentlewoman Sir that muſt needs ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: A Gentlewoman? what Gentlewoman, what have I to do with Gentlewomen?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: She will not be anſwered Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
Fling up the bed and let her in, I'le try how gentle ſhe is—
Exit Serve •

This Sack has fill'd my head ſo full of bables, I am a •• mad; what Gentlewoman ſhould this be? I hope ſhe 〈◊〉 brought me no butter print along with her to lay to • charge, if ſhe have 'tis all one, I'le forſwear it.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
O you're a noble Gallant, ſend off your Serve • pray.
Exit Serve • .

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: She will not raviſh me? by this light ſhe loo ••• ſharp ſet as a Sparrow hawk, what wouldſt thou wom •• ?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: O you have uſed me kindly, and like a Gentle ••• this is to truſt to you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Truſt to me, for what?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Becauſe I ſaid in jeſt once, you were a handſom 〈◊〉 one I could like well, and fooling, made you believe I love you, and might be brought to marrie.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: The widow is drunk too.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
You out of this, which is a fine diſcretion, give 〈◊〉 the matter's done, you have won and wed me, and t • you have put, fairly put for an heir too, theſe are fire ••
mours to advance my credit: i'th' name of miſchief who did you mean?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: That you loved me, and that you might be broug •• to marrie me? why, what a Devil do you mean widow?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: 'Twas a fine trick too, to tell the world though you had enjoyed your firſt wiſh you wiſhed, the wealth you aimed at, that I was poor, which is moſt true, I am, ha •• ſold my lands, becauſe I love not thoſe vexations, yet i • mine honours ſake, if you muſt be prating, and for my credits ſake in the Town.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I tell thee widow, I like thee ten times better, 〈◊〉 thou haſt no Lands, for now thy hopes and cares lye on thy husband, if e're thou marryeſt more.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Have not you married me, and for this main cauſe now as you report it, to be your Nurſe?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: My Nurſe? why, what am I grown to, give me the Glaſs, my Nurſe.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p:
You n'er ſaid truer, I muſt confeſs I did a little favour you, and with ſome labour might have been perſ ••
ded, but when I found I muſt be hourly troubled, with ma •
ing broths, and dawbing your decayes with ſwadling, • with ſtitching up your ruines, for the world ſo reports.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Do not provoke me.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: And half an eye may ſee.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Do not provoke me, the world's a lying world, are thou ſnalt find it, have a good heart, and take a ſtrong f ••• to thee, and mark what follows, my Nurſe, yes, you 〈◊〉 rock me: Widow I'le keep you waking.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: You are diſpoſed Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Yes marry am I Widow, and you ſhall feel it, 〈◊〉 and they touch my freehold, I am a Tiger.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Come.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Whither?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
Any whither.
S •••
The ſit's upon me now, the ſit's upon me now,
Come quickly gentle Ladie, the ſit's upon me now,
The world ſhall know they're fools,
And ſo ſhalt thou do too,
Let the Cobler meddle with his tools,
The ſit's upon me now.
Take me quickly, while I am in this vein, away with me for if I have but two hours to conſider, all the widows in the world cannot recover me.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: If you will, go with me Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Yes marrie will I, but 'tis in anger yet, and I will marrie thee, do not croſs me; yes, and I will lie with thee and get a whole bundle of babies, and I will kiſs thee, ſt •• ſtill and kiſs me handſomely, but do not provoke me, 〈◊〉 neither hand nor foot, for I am dangerous, I drunk ſ •• yeſternight, do not allure me: Thou art no widow of t •• s world, come in pitie, and in ſpite I'le marrie thee, not a w ••• more, and I may be brought to love thee. Exeunt

div.stage: Enter Merchant, and Uncle, at ſeveral doors.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Well met again, and what good news yet?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Faith nothing.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: No fruits of what we fowed?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Nothing I hear of.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: No turning in this tide yet?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: 'Tis all flood, and till that fall away, there's no expecting.

div.stage: Enter Fran. Iſab, Lance, Shorthoſe, a torch.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Is not this his younger Brother?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: With a Gentlewoman the widow's ſiſter, as I live • e ſmiles, he has got good hold, why well ſaid Frank i'faith, • et's ſtay and mark.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Well, you are the prettieſt youth, and ſo you have • andled me, think you ha' me ſure.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: As ſure as wedlock.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: You had beſt lie with me too.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Yes indeed will I, and get ſuch black ey'd boyes.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: God a Mercy, Frank.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: This is a merrie world, poor ſimple Gentlewomen that think no harm, cannot walk about their buſineſs, but they muſt be catcht up I know not how.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: I'le tell you, and I'le inſtruct ye too, have I caught • ou, Miſtreſs?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Well, and it were not for pure pity, I would give • ou the ſlip yet, but being as it is.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: It ſhall be better.

div.stage: Enter Valentine, Widow, and Ralph, with a torch.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: My ſiſter, as I live, your Brother with her! ſure, I • hink you are the Kings takers.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Now it works.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Nay, you ſhall know I am a man.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And ſuch proof you ſhall have.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I pray ſpeak ſoftly.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I'le ſpeak it out Widow, yes and you ſhall confeſs too, I am no Nurſe-child, I went for a man, a good one, if you can beat me out o'th' pit.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I did but jeſt with you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I'le handle you in earneſt, and ſo handle you: Nay, when my credit calls.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Are you mad?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I am mad, I am mad.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Good morrow, Sir, I like your preparation.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Thou haſt been at it, Frank.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Yes faith, 'tis done Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Along with me then, never hang an arf • , widow

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: 'Tis to no purpoſe, ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Well ſaid Black-brows, advance your torches Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Yes, yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And keep your ranks.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Lance, carrie this before him.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Carrie it in ſtate.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: What are you, Muſicians? I know your coming, and what are thoſe behind you?

sp.speaker: Muſi.
sp.p: Gentlemen that ſent us to give the Lady a good morrow.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: O I know them, come boy ſing the ſong I taught you,
And ſing it luſtily, come forward Gentlemen, you're welcom,
Welcom, now we are all friends, go get the Prieſt ready,
And let him not be long, we have much buſineſs:
Come Frank, rejoyce with me, thou haſt got the ſtart boy,
But I'le ſo tumble after, come my friends lead,
Lead cheerfully, and let your Fiddles ring boyes,
My follies and my fancies have an end here,
Diſplay the morgage Lance, Merchant I'le pay you,
And every thing ſhall be in joynt again.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.p: Afore, afore.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And now confeſs, and know,

p.hi: Wit without Money, ſometimes gives the blow.

list.item: Wolfort, an uſurper of the Earldom of Flanders.
Gerrard, falſely called Clauſe, King of the Beggars, Father in Law to Florez.
Hubert, an honeſt Lord, a friend to Gerrard.
Florez, falſely called Goſwin, a rich Merchant of Bruges.
Vandunke, a drunken Merchant friend to Gerrard, falſely called Father to Bertha.

list.head: Two Gentlemen diſguiſed under tho's names of Gerrard's party.
WOMEN.
list.item: Jaculin, Daughter to Gerrard, beloved of Hubert.
Bertha called Gertrude, Daughter to the Duke of Brabant, Miſtreſs to Florez.
Mrs Frances, a frow Daughter to Vanlock.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: IS he then taken?

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: And brought back even now, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: He was not in diſgrace?

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: No man more lov'd,
Nor more deſerv'd it, being the only man
That durſt be honeſt in this Court.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Indeed
We have heard abroad, Sir, that the State hath ſuffered
A great change, ſince the Counteſſes death.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: It hath, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: My five years abſence hath kept me a ſtranger
So much to all the occurents of my Country,
As you ſhall bind me for ſome ſhort relation
To make me underſtand the preſent times.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: I muſt begin then with a War was made
And ſeven years with all cruelty continued
Upon our Flanders by the Duke of Brabant,
The cauſe grew thus: during our Earls minority,
Wolfort, (who now uſurps) was employed thither
To treat about a match between our Fail
And the Daughter and Heir of Brabant: during which treaty
The Brabander pretends, this Daughter was
Stoln from his Court, by practice of our State,
Though we are all confirm'd, 'twas a ſought quarrel
To lay an unjuſt g • ipe upon this Earldom,
It being here believ'd the Duke of Brabant
Had no ſuch loſs. This War upon't proclaim'd,
Our Earl, being then a Child, although his Father
Good Gerrard liv'd, yet in reſpect he was
Choſen by the Counteſſes favour, for her Husband,
And but a Gentleman, and Florez holding
His right unto this Country from his Mother,
The State thought fit in this defenſive War,
Wolfort being then the only man of mark,
To make him General.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Which place we have heard
He did diſcharge with houour.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: I, ſo long,
And with ſo bleſt ſucceſſes, that the Brabander
Was forc't (his treaſures waſted, and the choice
Of his beſt men of Armes tyr'd, or cut off)
To leave the field, and ſound a baſe retreat
Back to his Country: but ſo broken both
In mind and means, er'e to make head again,
That hitherto he ſits down by his loſs,
Not daring, or for honour, or revenge
Again to tempt his fortune. But this Victory
More broke our State, and made a deeper hurt
In Flanders, than the greateſt overthrow
She ever receiv'd: For Wolfort, now beholding
Himſelf, and actions, in the flattering glaſs
Of ſelf-deſervings, and that cheriſh't by
• e ſtrong aſſurance of his power, for then
〈◊〉 Captains of the Army were his creatures,
• e common Souldier too at his devotion,
• de ſo by full indulgence to their rapines
• d ſecret bounties, this ſtrength too well known
• d what it could effect, ſoon put in practice,
〈◊〉 further'd by the Child-hood of the Earl:
• d their improvidence, that might have pierc't
• e heart of his deſigns, gave him occaſion
• ſeize the whole, and in that plight you find it.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Sir, I receive the knowledge of thus much,
• a choice favour from you.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: Only I muſt add,
•• es holds out.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Whither, Sir, I am going,
• t there laſt night I had a ſhip put in,
• d my Horſe waits me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: I wiſh you a good journey.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: What? Hubert ſtealing from me? who diſarm'd him?
〈◊〉 was more than I commanded; take your ſword,
• m beſt guarded with it in your hand,
• ave ſeen you uſe it nobly.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: And will turn it
〈◊〉 my own boſom, ere it ſhall be drawn
〈◊〉 worthily or rudely.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: Would you leave me
Without a farewel, Hubert? ſlie a friend
• nwearied in his ſtudy to advance you?
• hat have I e're poſſeſs'd which was not yours?
〈◊〉 either did not court you to command it?
• ho ever yet arriv'd to any grace,
• eward or truſt from me, but his approaches
• ere by your fair reports of him prefer'd?
• d what is more I made my ſelf your Servant,
〈◊〉 making you the Maſter of thoſe ſecrets
Which not the rack of Conſcience could draw from me,
• or I, when I askt mercy, truſt my prayers with;
• et after theſe aſſurances of love,
• heſe tyes and bonds of friendſhip, to forſake me?
• orſake me as an enemy? come you muſt
• ve me a reaſon.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Sir, and ſo I will,
I may do't in private: and you hear it.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: All leave the room: you have your will, ſit down
• nd uſe the liberty of our firſt friendſhip.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Friendſhip? when you prov'd Traitor firſt, that vaniſh'd,
• or do I owe you any thought, but hate,
• now my flight hath forfeited my head;
• nd ſo I may make you firſt underſtand
• hat a ſtrange monſter you have made your ſelf,
welcome it.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: To me this is ſtrange language.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: To you? why what are you?

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: Your Prince and Maſter,
• he Earl of Flanders.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: By a proper title!
• ais'd to it by cunning, circumvention, force,
• ood, and proſcriptions.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: And in all this wiſdom,
• ad I not reaſon? when by Gerrards plots
• hould have firſt been call'd to a ſtrict accompt
• ow, and which way I had conſum'd that maſs
• f money, as they term it, in the War,
Who underhand had by his Miniſters
• etracted my great action, made my faith
• nd loyalty ſuſpected, in which failing
• e ſought my life by practice.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: With what fore-head
• o you ſpeak this to me? who (as I know't)
• uſt, and will ſay 'tis falſe.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: My Guard there.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Sir, you bad me ſit, and promis'd you would hear,
Which I now ſay you ſhall; not a ſound more,
For I that am contemner of mine own,
Am Maſter of your life; then here's a Sword
Between you, and all aids, Sir, though you blind
The credulous beaſt, the multitude, you paſs not
Theſe groſs untruths on me.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: How? groſs untruths?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I, and it is favourable language,
They had been in a mean man lyes, and foul ones.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: You take ſtrange Licence.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Yes, were not thoſe rumours
Of being called unto your anſwer, ſpread
By your own followers? and weak Gerrard wrought
(But by your cunning practice) to believe
That you were dangerous; yet not to be
Puniſh'd by any formal courſe of Law,
But firſt to be made ſure, and have your crimes
Laid open after, which your quaint train taking
You fled unto the Camp, and their crav'd humbly
Protection for your innocent life, and that,
Since you had ſcap'd the fury of the War,
You might not fall by treaſon: and for proof,
You did not for your own ends make this danger;
Some that had been before by you ſuborn'd,
Came forth and took their Oaths they had been hir'd
By Gerrard to your Murther. This once heard,
And eaſily believ'd, th' inraged Souldier
Seeing no further than the outward-man,
Snatch'd haſtily his Arms, ran to the Court,
Kill'd all that made reſiſtance, cut in pieces
Such as were Servants, or thought friends to Gerrard,
Vowing the like to him.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: Will you yet end?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Which he foreſeeing, with his Son, the Earl;
Forſook the City; and by ſecret wayes
As you give out, and we would gladly have it,
Eſcap'd their fury: though 'tis more than fear'd
They fell amongſt the reſt; Nor ſtand you there
To let us only mourn the impious means
By which you got it, but your cruelties ſince
So far tranſcend your former bloody ills,
As if compar'd, they only would appear
Eſſays of miſchief; do not ſtop your ears,
More are behind yet.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: O repeat them not,
'Tis Hell to hear them nam'd.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: You ſhould have thought,
That Hell would be your puniſhment when you did them,
A Prince in nothing but your princely luſts,
And boundleſs rapines.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: No more I beſeech you.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Who was the Lord of houſe or land, that ſtood
Within the proſpect of your covetous eye?

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: You are in this to me a greater Tyrant,
Than e're I was to any.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I end thus
The general grief: now to my private wrong;
The loſs of Gerrards Daughter Jaqueline:
The hop'd for partner of my lawful Bed,
Your cruelty hath frighted from mine arms;
And her I now was wandring to recover.
Think you that I had reaſon now to leave you,
When you are grown ſo juſtly odious,
That ev'n my ſtay here with your grace and favour,
Makes my life irkſome? here, ſurely take it,
And do me but this fruit of all your friendſhip,
That I may dye by you, and not your Hang-man.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: Oh Hubert, theſe your words and reaſons have
As well drawn drops of blood from my griev'd heart,
As theſe tears from mine eyes;
Deſpiſe them not.
By all that's ſacred, I am ſerious, Hubert,
You now have made me ſenſible, what furies,
Whips, Hangmen, and Tormentors a bad man
Do's ever bear about him: let the good
That you this day have done, be ever number'd
The firſt of your beſt actions;
Can you think,
Where Goſwin is or Gerrard, or your love,
Or any elſe, or all that are proſcrib'd?
I will reſign, what I uſurp, or have
Unjuſtly forc'd; the dayes I have to live
Are too too few to make them ſatisfaction
With any penitence: yet I vow to practiſe
All of a man.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: O that your heart and tongue
Did not now differ!

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: By my griefs they do not.
Take the good pains to ſearch them out; 'tis worth it,
You have made clean a Leper: truſt me you have,
And made me once more fit for the ſociety,
I hope of good men.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Sir, do not abuſe
My aptneſs to believe.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: Suſpect not you
A faith that's built upon ſo true a ſorrow,
Make your own ſafetys: ask them all the ties
Humanity can give, Hemskirk too ſhall
Along with you to this ſo wiſh'd diſcovery,
And in my name profeſs all that you promiſe;
And I will give you this help to't: I have
Of late receiv'd certain intelligence,
That ſome of them are in or about Bruges
To be found out: which I did then interpret,
The cauſe of that Towns ſtanding out againſt me;
But now am glad, it may direct your purpoſe
Of giving them their ſafety, and me peace.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Be conſtant to your goodneſs, and you have it.

div.head: SCENA II.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: 'Tis much that you deliver of this Goſwin.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: But ſhort of what I could, yet have the Country
Confirm'd it true, and by a general oath,
And not a man hazard his credit in it:
He beats himſelf with ſuch a confidence
As if he were the Maſter of the Sea,
And not a wind upon the Sailers compaſs,
But from one part or other was his factor,
To bring him in the beſt commodities,
Merchant e're ventur'd for.
'Tis ſtrange.
And yet
This do's in him deſerve the leaſt of wonder,
Compared with other his peculiar faſhions,
Which all admire: he's young, and rich, at leaſt
Thus far reputed ſo, that ſince he liv'd
In Bruges, there was never brought to harbour
So rich a Bottom, but his bill would paſs
Unqueſtion'd for her lading.

sp.speaker: 3 Mer.
sp.l: Yet he ſtill
Continues a good man.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: So good, that but
To doubt him, would be held an injury
Or rather malice, with the beſt that traſſique;
But this is nothing, a great ſtock, and fortune,
Crowning his judgement in his undertakings
May keep him upright that way: But that wealth
Should want the power to make him dote on it,
Or youth teach him to wrong it, beſt commends
His conſtant temper; for his outward habit
'Tis ſuitable to his preſent courſe of life:
His table furniſh'd well, but not with dainties
That pleaſe the appetite only for their rareneſs,
Or their dear price: nor given to wine or women,
Beyond his health, or warrant of a man,
I mean a good one: and ſo loves his ſtate
He will not hazard it at play; nor lend
Upon the aſſurance of a well pen'd Letter,
Although a challenge ſecond the denial
From ſuch as make th' opinion of their valour
Their means of feeding.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: Theſe are wayes to thrive,
And the means not curs'd.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: What follows, this
Makes many venturers with him, in their wiſhes,
For his proſperity: for when deſert
Or reaſon leads him to be liberal,
His noble mind and ready hand contend
Which can add moſt to his free courteſies,
Or in their worth, or ſpeed to make them ſo.
Is there a Virgin of good fame wants dower?
He is a Father to her; or a Souldier
That in his Countreys ſervice, from the war
Hath brought home only ſcars, and want? his houſe
Receives him, and relieves him, with that care
As if what he poſſeſs'd had been laid up
For ſuch good uſes, and he ſteward of it.
But I ſhould loſe my ſelf to ſpeak him further
And ſtale in my relation, the much good
You may be witneſs of, if your remove
From Bruges be not ſpeedy.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: This report
I do aſſure you will not haſten it,
Nor would I wiſh a better man to deal with
For what I am to part with.

sp.speaker: 3 Mer.
sp.l: Never doubt it,
He is your man and ours, only I wiſh
His too much forwardneſs to embrace all bargains
Sink him not in the end.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: Have better hopes,
For my part I am confident; here he comes.

div.stage: Enter Goſwin, and the fourth Merchant.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I take it at your own rates, your wine of Cyprus,
But for your Candy ſugars, they have met
With ſuch foul weather, and are priz'd ſo high
I cannot ſave in them.

sp.speaker: 4. Mer.
sp.l: I am unwilling
To ſeek another Chapman: make me offer
Of ſomething near price, that may aſſure me
You can deal for them.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I both can, and will,
But not with too much loſs; your bill of lading
Speaks of two hundred cheſts, valued by you
At thirty thouſand gilders, I will have them
At twenty eight; ſo, in the payment of
Three thouſand ſterling, you fall only in
Two hundred pound.

sp.speaker: 4 Mer.
sp.l: You know, they are ſo cheap. —

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Why look you; I'le deal farily, there's in priſor,
And at your ſuit, a Pirat, but unable
To make you ſatisfaction, and paſt hope
To live a week, if you ſhould proſecute
What you can prove againſt him: ſet him free,
And you ſhall have your mony to a Stiver,
And preſent payment.

sp.speaker: 4 Mer.
sp.l: This is above wonder,
A Merchant of your rank, that have at Sea
So many Bottoms in the danger of
Theſe water-Thieves, ſhould be a means to ſave 'em,
It more importing you for your own ſafety
To be at charge to ſcour the Sea of them
Than ſtay the ſword of juſtice, that is ready
To fall on one ſo conſcious of his guilt
That he dares not deny it.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: You miſtake me,
If you think I would cheriſh in this Captain
The wrong he did to you, or any man;
I was lately with him, (having firſt, from others
•• e teſtimony been aſſured a man
• more deſert never put from the ſhore)
• ead his letters of Mart from this State granted
〈◊〉 the recovery of ſuch loſſes, as
〈◊〉 had receiv'd in Spain, 'twas that he aim'd at,
• t at three tuns of wine, bisket, or beef,
• hi • n his neceſſity made him take from you.
• he had pillag'd you near, or ſunk your ſhip,
〈◊〉 thrown your men o'r board, then he deſerv'd
•• e Laws extreameſt rigour. But ſince want
〈◊〉 what he could not live without, compel'd him
〈◊〉 that he did (which yet our State calls death)
• ity his misfortune; and to work you
〈◊〉 ſome compaſſion of them, I come up
〈◊〉 your own price: ſave him, the goods are mine;
• not, ſeek elſe-where, I'le not deal for them.

sp.speaker: 4 Mer.
sp.l: Well Sir, for your love, I will once be led
〈◊〉 change my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: For your profit rather.

sp.speaker: 4 Mer.
sp.l: I'le preſently make means for his diſcharge,
•• l when, I leave you.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: What do you think of this?

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: As of a deed of noble pity: guided
〈◊〉 a ſtrong judgement.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: Save you Maſter Goſwin.

sp.speaker: Goſwin.
sp.l: Good day to all.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: We bring you the refuſall
〈◊〉 more Commodities.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Are you the owners
〈◊〉 the ſhip that laſt night put into the Harbour?

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: Both of the ſhip, and lading.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: What's the fraught?

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: Indico, Cochineel, choiſe Chyna ſtuffs.

sp.speaker: 3 Mer.
sp.l: And cloath of Gold brought from Cambal.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Rich lading,
〈◊〉 which I were your Chapman, but I am
•• ready out of caſh.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: I'le give you day
〈◊〉 the moiety of all.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: How long?

sp.speaker: 3 Mer.
sp.l: Six months.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: 'Tis a fair offer: which (if we agree
• bout the prices) I, with thanks accept of,
• nd will make preſent payment of the reſt;
• me two hours hence I'le come aboard.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: The Gunner ſhall ſpeak you welcom.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I'le not fail.

sp.speaker: 3 Mer.
sp.l:
Good morrow.
Ex. Merch.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Heaven grant my Ships a ſafe return, before
• he day of this great payment: as they are
•• pected three months ſooner: and my credit
• ands good with all the world.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Bleſs my good Maſter,
• he prayers of your poor Beadſ-man ever ſhall
〈◊〉 ſent up for you.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: God o'mercy Clauſe,
• here's ſomething to put thee in mind hereafter
• o think of me.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: May he that gave it you
• eward you for it, with encreaſe, good Maſter.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I thrive the better for thy prayers.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I hope ſo.
• his three years have I fed upon your bounties,
• nd by the fire of your bleſt charity warm'd me,
• nd yet, good Maſter, pardon me, that muſt,
• hough I have now receiv'd your alms, preſume
• o make one ſute more to you.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: What is't Clauſe?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Yet do not think me impudent I beſeech you,
• nce hitherto your charity hath prevented
• y begging your relief, 'tis not for mony
• o • cloaths (good Maſter) but your good word for me.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: That thou ſhalt have, Clauſe, for I think thee honeſt.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: To morrow then (dear Mr.) take the trouble
Of walking early unto Beggars Buſh,
And as you ſee me, among others (Brethren
In my affliction) when you are demanded
Which you like beſt among us, point out me,
And then paſs by, as if you knew me not.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: But what will that advantage thee?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: O much Sir,
'Twill give me the preheminence of the reſt,
Make me a King among 'em, and protect me
From all abuſe, ſuch as are ſtronger, might
Offer my age; Sir, at your better leiſure
I will inform you further of the good
It may do to me.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: 'Troth thou mak'ſt me wonder;
Have you a King and common wealth among you?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: We have, and there are States are govern'd worſe.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Ambition among Beggars?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Many great ones
Would part with half their ſtates, to have the place,
And credit to beg in the firſt file, Maſter:
But ſhall I be ſo much bound to your furtherance
In my Petition?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: That thou ſhalt not miſs of,
Nor any worldly care make me forget it,
I will be early there.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs my Maſter. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Higgen, Ferret, Prig, Clauſe, Jaculine, Snap, Ginks, and other beggars.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: COme Princes of the ragged regiment,
You o' the blood, Prig my moſt upright Lord,
And theſe (what name or title, e're they bear)
Jarkman, or Patrico, Cranke, or Clapperdudgeon,
Frater, or Abram man; I ſpeak to all
That ſtand in fair Election for the title
Of King of Beggars, with the command adjoyning,
Higgen, your Orator, in this Inter-regnum,
That whilom was your Dommerer, doth beſeech you
All to ſtand fair, and put your ſelves in rank,
That the firſt Comer, may at his firſt view
Make a free choice, to ſay up the queſtion.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Pr. 'Tis done Lord Higgen.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Thanks to Prince Prig, Prince Ferret.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Well, pray my Maſters all, Ferret be choſen,
Y'are like to have a mercifull mild Prince of me.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: A very tyrant, I, an arrant tyrant,
If e're I come to reign; therefore look to't,
Except you do provide me hum enough
And Lour to bouze with: I muſt have my Capons
And Turkeys brought me in, with my green Geeſe,
And Ducklings i'th' ſeaſon: fine fat chickens,
Or if you chance where an eye of tame Pheſants
Or Partridges are kept, ſee they be mine,
Or ſtraight I ſeize on all your priviledge,
Places, revenues, offices, as forfeit,
Call in your crutches, wooden legs, falſe bellyes,
Fore'd eyes and teeth, with your dead arms; not leave you
A durty clout to beg with o' your heads,
Or an old rag with Butter, Frankincenſe,
Brimſton and Rozen, birdlime, blood, and cream,
To make you an old ſore; not ſo much ſoap
As you may ſome with i'th' Falling ſickneſs;
The very bag you bear, and the brown diſh
Shall be eſcheated. All your daintieſt Dells too
I will deflower, and take your deareſt Doxyes
From your warm ſides; and then ſome one cold night
I'le watch you what old barn you go to rooſt in,
And there I'le ſmother you all i'th' muſty hay.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: This is tyrant-like indeed: But what would Ginks
Or Clauſe be here, if either of them ſhould raign?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: B • ſ •• ask an Aſs, if he were made a Camel,
What he would be; or a dog, and he were a Lyon.

sp.speaker: Ginks.
sp.l: I care not what you are, Sirs, I ſhall be
A Begger ſtill I am ſure, I find my ſelf there.

sp.speaker: Snap.
sp.l: O here a Judge comes.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: 〈◊〉 , a Judge, a Judge.
What all you Sirs? what means this outcry?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Maſter,
A ſort of poor tou's met: Gods fools, good Maſter,
Have had ſome little variance amongſt our ſelves
Who ſhould be honeſteſt of us, and which lives
Uprighteſt in his calling: Now, 'cauſe we thought
We ne're ſhould 'gree on't our ſelves, becauſe
Indeed 'tis hard to ſay: we all diſſolv'd, to put it
To him that ſhould come next, and that's your Maſter-ſhip,
Who, I hope, will 'termine it as your mind ſerves you,
Right, and no otherwiſe we ask it: which?
Which does your worſhip think is he? ſweet Maſter
Look over us all, and tell us; we are ſeven of us,
Like to the ſeven wiſe Maſters, or the Planets.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I ſhould judge this the man with the grave beard,
And if he be not —

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Bleſs you, good Maſter, bleſs you.

sp.speaker: Goſ
sp.l: I would he were: there's ſomething too amongſt you
To keep you all honeſt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Snap.
sp.l: King of Heaven go with you.

sp.speaker: Omn.
sp.l: Now good reward him,
May he never want it, to comfort ſtill the poor, in a good hour.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: What is't? ſee: Snap has got it.

sp.speaker: Snap.
sp.l: A good crown, marry.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: A crown of gold.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: For our new King: good luck.

sp.speaker: Ginks.
sp.l: To the common treaſury with it; if't be gold,
Thither it muſt.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Spoke like a Patriot, Ferret—
King Clauſe, I bid God ſave thee firſt, firſt, Clauſe,
After this golden token of a crown;
Where's oratour Higgen with his gratuling ſpeech now
In all our names?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Here he is pumping for it.

sp.speaker: Gin.
sp.l: H'has cough'd the ſecond time, 'tis but once more
And then it comes.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: So, out with all: expect now

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: That thou art choſen, venerable Clauſe,
Our King and Soveraign; Monarch o'th'Maunders,
Thus we throw up our Nab-cheats, firſt for joy,
And then our ſilches; laſt, we clap our fambles,
Three ſubject ſigns, we do it without envy:
For who is he here did not with thee choſen,
Now thou art choſen? ask 'em: all will ſay ſo,
Nay ſwear't: 'tis for the King, but let that paſs.
When laſt in conference at the bouzing ken
This other day we ſat about our dead Prince
Of famous memory: (reſt go with his rags:)
And that I ſaw thee at the tables end,
Riſe mov'd, and gravely leaning on one Crutch,
Lift the other like a Scepter at my head,
I then preſag'd thou ſhortly wouldſt be King,
And now thou art ſo: but what need preſage
To us, that might have read it in thy beard
As well, as he that choſe thee? by that beard
Thou were found out, and mark'd for Soveraignty,
O happy beard! but happier Prince, whoſe beard
Was ſo remark'd, as marked out our Prince,
Not bating us a hair. Long may it grow,
And thick, and fair, that who lives under it,
May live as ſafe, as under Beggars Buſh,
Of which this is the thing, that but the type.

sp.speaker: Om.
sp.l: Excellent, excellent orator, forward good Higgen,
Give him leave to ſpit: the fine, well-ſpoken Higgen.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: This is the beard, the buſh, or buſhy-beard,
Under whoſe gold and ſilver raign 'twas ſaid
So many ages ſince, we all ſhould ſmile
On impoſitions, taxes, grievances,
Knots in a State, and whips unto a Subject,
Lye lurking in this beard, but all kemb'd out:
If now, the Beard be ſuch, what is the Prince
That owes the Beard? a Father; no, a Grand-father;
Nay the great Grand-father of you his people.
He will not force away your hens, your bacon,
When you have ventur'd hard for't, nor take from you
The fatteſt of your puddings: under him
Each man ſhall eat his own ſtolen eggs, and butter,
In his own ſhade, or ſun-ſhine, and enjoy
His own dear Dell, Doxy, or Mort, at night
In his own ſtraw, with his own ſhirt, or ſheet,
That he hath filch'd that day, I, and poſſeſs
What he can purchaſe, back, or belly-cheats
To his own prop: he will have no purveyers
For Pigs, and poultry.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: That we muſt have, my learned oratour,
It is our will, and every man to keep
In his own path and circuit.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Do you hear?
You muſt hereafter maund on your own pads he ſaies.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: And what they get there, is their own, beſides
To give good words.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Do you mark? to cut been whids,
That is the ſecond Law.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: And keep a foot
The humble, and the common phraſe of begging,
Leſt men diſcover us.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Yes, and cry ſometimes,
To move compaſſion: Sir, there is a table,
That doth command all theſe things, and enjoyns 'em,
Be perfect in their crutches, their feign'd plaiſters,
And their torn paſſ-ports, with the ways to ſtammer,
And to be dumb, and deaf, and blind, and lame,
There, all the halting paces are ſet down,
I'th' learned language.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Thither I refer them,
Thoſe, you at leiſure ſhall interpret to them.
We love no heaps of laws, where few will ſerve.

sp.speaker: Om.
sp.l: O gracious Prince, 'ſave, 'ſave the good King Cla ••

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: A Song to crown him.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Set a Centinel out firſt.

sp.speaker: Snap.
sp.l: The word?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l:
A Cove comes, and fumbumbis to it —
Sna •

body.head: The SONG.
body.l: CAſt our Caps and cares away: this is Beggars Holy-day,
At the Crowning of our King, thus we ever dance and 〈◊〉
In the world look out and ſee: where's ſo happy a Prince as he?
Where the Nation live ſo free, and ſo merry as do we?
Be it peace, or be it war, here at liberty we are,
And enjoy our eaſe and reſt; To the field we are not preſt;
Nor are call'd into the Town, to be troubled with the Gown.
Hang all Officers we cry, and the Magiſtrate too, by;
When the Subſidie's encreaſt, we are not a penny Seſt.
Nor will any go to Law, with the Beggar for a ſtraw.
All which happineſs he brags, he doth owe unto his rags.

sp.speaker: Snap.
sp.l: A Cove comes: Fumbumbis.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: To your poſtures; arm.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Yonder's the Town: I ſee it.

sp.speaker: Hemsk.
sp.l: There's our danger
Indeed afore us, if our ſhadows ſave not.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Bleſs your good Worſhips.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: One ſmall piece of mony.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Amongſt us all poor wretches.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Blind, and lame.

sp.speaker: Ginks.
sp.l: For his ſake that gives all.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Pitifull Worſhips.

sp.speaker: Snap.
sp.l: One little doyt.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: King, by your leave, where are you?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: To buy a little bread.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: To feed ſo many.
Mouths, as will ever pray for you.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Here be ſeven of us.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Seven, good Maſter, O remember ſeven,
Seven bleſſings.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Remember, gentle Worſhip.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: 'Gainſt ſeven deadly ſins.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: And ſeven ſleepers.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: If they be hard of heart, and will give nothing—
Alas, we had not a charity this three dayes.

sp.speaker: Hab.
sp.l: There's amongſt you all.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Heaven reward you.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Lord reward you.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: The Prince of pity bleſs thee.

sp.speaker: Hab.
sp.l: Do I ſee? or is't my fancy that would have it ſo?
Ha? 'tis her face: come hither maid.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: What ha' you,
Bells for my ſquirrel? I ha' giv'n bun meat,
You do not love me, do you? catch me a butterfly,
And I'le love you again; when? can you tell?
Peace, we go a birding: I ſhall have a fine thing. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Her voyce too ſayes the ſame; but for my head
I would not that her manners were ſo chang'd.
Hear me thou honeſt fellow; what's this maiden,
That lives amongſt you here?

sp.speaker: Gin.
sp.l: Ao, ao, ao, ao.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: How? nothing but ſigns?

sp.speaker: Gin.
sp.l: Ao, ao, ao, ao.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: This is ſtrange,
I would fain have it her, but not her thus.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: He is de-de-de-de-de-de-deaf, and du-du-dude— dumb Sir.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Slid they did all ſpeak plain ev'n now me thought.
Do'ſt thou know this ſame maid?

sp.speaker: Snap.
sp.l: Why, why, why, why, which, gu, gu, gu, gu, Gods fool
See was bo-bo-bo-bo born at the barn yonder,
By-be be-be-be-Beggars Buſh-bo-bo-Buſh
Her name is, My-my-my-my-my-match: ſo was her Mo-mo-mo-Mothers too too

sp.speaker: Hab.
sp.l: I underſtand no word he ſays; how long
Has ſhe been here?

sp.speaker: Snap.
sp.l: Lo-lo-long enough to be ni-ni-nigled, and ſne ha' go-go go good luck,

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I muſt be better inform'd, than by this way.
Here was another face too, that I mark'd
Of the old mans: but they are vaniſh'd all
Moſt ſuddenly: I will come here again,
O, that I were ſo happy, as to find it,
What I yet hope: it is put on.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: What mean you Sir,
To ſtay there with that ſtammerer?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Farewell friend,—
It will be worth return, to ſearch: Come,
Protect us our diſguiſe now, pre'thee Hemskirk
If we be taken, how do'ſt thou imagine
This town will uſe us, that hath ſtood ſo long
Out againſt Wolfort?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Ev'n to hang us forth
Upon their walls a ſunning, to make Crows meat,
If I were not aſſur'd o' the Burgomaſter,
And had a pretty excuſe to ſee a niece there,
I ſhould ſcarce venture.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Come 'tis now too late
To look back at the ports: good luck, and enter. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Still blow'ſt thou there? and from all other parts,
Do all my agents ſleep, that nothing comes?
There's a conſpiracy of windes, and ſervants,
If not of Elements, to ha' me break;
What ſhould I think unleſs the Seas, and Sands
Had ſwallow'd up my ſhips? or fire had ſpoil'd
My ware-houſes? or death devour'd my Factors?
I muſt ha' had ſome returns.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: 'Save you Sir.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: 'Save you.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: No news yet o' your Ships?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Not any yet Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange. Exit.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: 'Tis true Sir: what a voyce was here now?
This was one paſſing bell, a thouſand ravens
Sung in that man now, to preſage my ruins.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: Goſwin, good day, theſe winds are very conſtant

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: They are ſo Sir; to hurt —

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: Ha' you had no letters
Lately from England, nor from Denmark?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Neither.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: This wind brings them; not no news over land,
Through Spain, from the Straights?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Not any.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: I am ſorry Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: They talk me down: and as 'tis ſaid of Vulturs
They ſcent a field fought, and do ſmell the carkaſſes
By many hundred miles: So do theſe, my wracks
At greater diſtances. Why, thy will Heaven
Come on, and be: yet if thou pleaſe, preſerve me;
But in my own adventure, here at home,
Of my chaſt love, to keep me worthy of her,
It ſhall be put in ſcale 'gainſt all ill fortunes:
I am not broken yet: nor ſhould I fall,
Me thinks with leſs than that, that ruins all. Exit.

div.head: SCENA III.
div.stage: Enter Van-dunck, Hubert, Hemskirk, and Margaret, Boors.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Captain, you are welcom; ſo is this your friend
Moſt ſafely welcom, though our Town ſtand out
Againſt your Maſter, you ſhall find good quarter:
The troth is, we not love him: Margaret ſome wine,
Let's talk a little treaſon, if we can
Talk treaſon, 'gainſt the traitors; by your leave, Gentlemen,
We, here in Bruges, think he do's uſurp,
And therefore I am bold with him.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Sir, your boldneſs
Happily becomes your mouth, but not our ears,
While we are his ſervants; And as we come nere,
Not to ask queſtions, walk forth on your walls,
Viſit your courts of guard, view your munition,
Ask of your corn-proviſions, nor enquire
Into the leaſt, as ſpies upon your ſtrengths,
So let's entreat, we may receive from you
Nothing in paſſage or diſcourſe, but what
We may with gladneſs, and our honeſties here,
And that ſhall feal our welcom.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Good: let's drink then,
Fill out, I keep mine old pearl ſtill Captain.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I hang faſt man.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Old Jewels commend their keeper, Sir.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Here's to you with a heart, my Captains friend,
With a good heart, and if this make us ſpeak
Bold words, anon, 'tis all under the Roſe
Forgotten: drown all memory, when we drink.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: 'Tis freely ſpoken noble Burgomaſter,
I'le do you right.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Nay Sir mine heer Van-dunck
Is a true Stateſman.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Fill my Captains cup there, O that your Maſter Wolfert
Had been an honeſt man.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Under the Roſe.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Here's to you Marget.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Welcome, welcome Captain.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Well ſaid my pearl ſtill.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: And how does my Niece?
Almoſt a Woman, I think? This friend of mine,
I drew along with me, through ſo much hazard,
Only to ſee her: ſhe was my errand.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: I, a kind Uncle you are (fill him his glaſs)
That in ſeven years, could not find leiſure—

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: No,
〈…〉 ſo much

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: I'le ba • e you ne'r an hour on't,
It was before the Brabander 'gan his War,
For t •• on • l • ine, i'the water there, his Daughter
That never was loſt: yet you could not find time
To ſee a Kinſwoman: but ſhe is worth the ſeeing, Sir,
Now you are come, you ask if ſhe were a Woman?

She is a Woman, Sir, fetch her forth Marget.
Exit Marg.
And a • ine Woman, and has Suitors.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: How?
What Suitors are they?

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Bachellors; young Burgers:
And one, a Gallant, the young Prince of Merchant;
We call him here in Bruges.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: How? a Merchant?
I thought, Vandunke, you had underſtood me better,
And my Niece too, ſo truſted to you by me,
Than t' admit of ſuch in name of Suitors.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Such? he is ſuch a ſuch, as were ſhe mine
I'd give him thirty thouſand crowns with her.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: But the ſame things, Sir, ſit not you and me. Ex.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Why, give's ſome wine, then; this will ſit us all:
Here's to you ſtill, my Captains friend: All out:
And ſtill, would Welfort were an honeſt man,
Under the Roſe, I ſpeak it: but this Merchant
Is a brave boy: he lives ſo, i'the Town here,
We know not what to think on him at ſome times
We •• ar he will be Bankrupt; he do's ſtretch
I enter his credit ſo; embraces all,
And to't, the winds have been contrary long.
• ut then, if he ſhould have all his returns,
We think he would be a King, and are half ſure on't.
Your Maſter is a Traitor, for all this,
Under the Roſe: Here's to you; and uſurps
The Earldom from a better man.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I marry, Sir,
Where is that man?

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Nay ſo • t: and I could tell you
'Tis ten to one I would not: here's my hand,
I love not Welfort: ſit you ſtill, with that:
Here comes my Captain again, and his fine Niece,
And there's my Merchant; view him well: fill wine here.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: You muſt not only know me for your Uncle
Now, but obey me: you, go caſt your ſelf
Away, upon a Dunghil here? a Merchant?
A petty follow? one that makes his Trade
With Oaths and perjuries?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: What is that you ſay, Sir?
If it be me you ſpeak of, as your eye
Seems to direct, I wiſh you would ſpeak to me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Sir, I do ſay, ſhe is no Merchandize,
Will that ſuffice you?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Merchandize good Sir:
Though • e be Kinſman to her, take no leave thence
To uſe me with contempt: I ever thought
Your Niece above all price

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: And do ſo ſtill, Sir,
I aſſ • re you, her • at • s are more than you are worth.
Y •• do not know, what a Gentleman's worth, Sir,
Not can you value him
Well • a •• Merchant.
Nay,
Let him alone, and ply your matter.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: A Gentleman?
What o'the Wool pack? or the Sugar cheſt?
Or liſts of Velvet? which is't pound, or yard,
You vent your Gentry by?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: O Hemskirk, ſye.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Come, do not mind 'em, drink, he is no W • ſ • ,
Captain, I adviſe you.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Alas, my pretty man,
I think't be angry, by its look: Come hither,
Turn this way, a little: if it were the blood
Of Charlemaine, as't may (for ought I know)
Be ſome good Botchers iſſue, here in Bruges

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Nay: I'me not certain of that; of this I am,
If it once buy, and ſell, its Gentry is gone.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: You are angry, though ye laugh.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: No, now 'tis pity
Of your poor argument. Do not you, the Lords
Of Land (if you be any) ſell the graſs,
The Corn, the Straw, the Milk, the Cheeſe?

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: And Butter:
Remember Butter; do not leave out Butter.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l:
The Beefs and Muttons that your grounds are ſto ••
〈◊〉
Swine, with the very maſt, beſide the Woods?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: No, for thoſe fordid uſes we have Tenants,
Or elſe our Bailiffs.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Have not we, Sir, Chap-men,
And Factors, then to anſwer theſe? your honour
Fetch'd from the Heralds ABC, and ſaid over
With your Court faces, once an hour, ſhall never
Make me miſtake my ſelf. Do not your Lawyers
Sell all their practice, as your Prieſts their prayers?
What is not bought, and ſold? The company
That you had laſt, what had you for't, i'faith?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: You now grow ſawcy.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Sure I have been bred
Still, with my honeſt liberty, and muſt uſe it.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Upon your equals then.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Sir, he that will
Provoke me firſt, doth make himſelf my equal.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Do ye hear? no more.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, this little, I pray you,
And't ſhall be aſide, then after, as you pleaſe.
You appear the Uncle, Sir, to her I love
More than mine eyes; and I have heard your ſcorns
With ſo much ſcoffing, and ſo much ſhame,
As each ſtrive which is greater: But, believe me,
I ſuck'd not in this patience with my milk.
Do not preſume, becauſe you ſee me young,
Or caſt deſpights on my profeſſion
For the civility and tameneſs of it.
A good man bears a contumely worſe
Than he would do an injury. Proceed not
To my offence: wrong is not ſtill ſucceſsful,
Indeed it is not: I would approach your Kinſ-woman
With all reſpect, done to your ſelf and her.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Away Companion: handling her? take that.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Nay, I do love no blows, Sir, there's exchange
Hold, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
O murther. He gets Hemskirks a ••
and cats
〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Help my Goſwin.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Man.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Let 'em alone; my life for one.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Nay come,
If you have will.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: None to offend you, I, Sir.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: He that had, thank himſelf: not hand he • ? 〈◊〉
And claſp her, and embrace her; and (would ſhe
Now go with me) bear her through all her Ra • e,
Her Father, Brethren, and her Uncles, arm'd,
And all their Nephews, though they ſtood a wo • d
Off • es, and wall of Canon: kiſs me Gertrude,
• ake not, but kiſs me.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Kiſs him, Girl, I bid you;
My Merchant Royal; fear no Uncles: hang 'em,
Hang up all Uncles: Are not we in Bruges?
Under the Roſe here?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: In this circle, Love,
Thou art as ſafe, as in a Tower of Braſs;
Let ſuch as do wrong, fear.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: I, that's good,
Let Welfort look to that.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Sir, here ſhe ſtands,
Your Niece, and my beloved. One of theſe titles
She muſt apply to; if unto the laſt,
Not all the anger can be ſent unto her,
I • frown, or voyce, or other art, ſhall force her,
Had Hercules a hand in't: Come, my Joy,
Say thou art mine, aloud Love, and profeſs it.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Doe: and I drink to it.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Prethee ſay ſo, Love.

sp.speaker: Cer.
sp.l: 'Twould take away the honour from my bluſhes:
Do not you play the tyrant, ſweet: they ſpeak it.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: I thank you niece.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Sir, thank her for your life,
And fetch your ſword within.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: You inſult too much

With your good fortune, Sir.
Exeunt Goſ. and Ger.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: A brave clear Spirit;
Hemkirk, you were to blame: a civil habit
Oſt covers a good man: and you may meet
In perſon of a Merchant, with a ſoul
As reſolute, and free, and all wayes worthy,
As elſe in any file of man-kind: pray you,
What meant you ſo to ſlight him?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: 'Tis done now,

As • no more of it; I muſt ſuffer.
Exit Hemskirk.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: This
Is •• ll the puniſhment of raſhneſs, ſorrow.
Well; I muſt to the woods, for nothing here
Will be got out. There, I may chance to learn
Somewhat to help my enquiries further.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Ha?
A Looking glaſs?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: How now, brave Burgomaſter?

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: I love no Wolforts, and my name's Vandunk,

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Van drunk it's rather: come, go ſleep within.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Earl Florez is right heir, and this ſame Wolfort
Under the Roſe I ſpeak it—

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Very hardly.

sp.speaker: Vand.
sp.l: Uſurps: and a rank Traitor, as ever breath'd,
And all that do uphold him. Let me goe,
No man ſhall hold me, that upholds him;
Do you uphold him?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Then hold me up. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Sir, I preſume, you have a ſword of your own,
That can ſo handle anothers.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Faith you may Sir.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: And ye have made me have ſo much better thoughts of you
As I am bound to call you forth.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: For what Sir?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: To the repairing of mine honour, and hurt here.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Expreſs your way.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: By ſight, and ſpeedily.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: You have your will: Require you any more?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: That you be ſecret: and come ſingle.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: As you are the Gentleman you would be thought.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Without the Conjuration: and I'le bring
Only my ſword, which I will fit to yours,
He take his length within.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Your place now Sir?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: By the Sand hills.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Sir, nearer to the woods,
If you thought ſo, were ſitter.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: There, then.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Good.
Your time?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: 'Twixt ſeven and eight.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: You'l give me Sir
Cauſe to report you worthy of my Niece,
If you come, like your promiſe.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: If I do not,
Let no man think to call me unworthy firſt,
I'le do't my ſelf, and juſtly with to want her.— Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: COme, Engliſh beer Hoſteſs, Engliſh beer by 'th' belly.

sp.speaker: 2 B.
sp.l: Stark beer boy, ſtout and ſtrong beer: ſo, ſit down Lads,
And drink me upſey Dutch.
Frolick, and fear not.

div.stage: Enter Higgen like a Sow gelder, ſinging.

lg.l: Have ye any work for the Sow-gelder, hoa,
My horn goes too high too low, too high too low.
Have ye any Piggs, Calves, or Colts,
Have ye any Lambs in your holts
To cut for the Stone,
Here comes a cunning one.
Have ye any braches to ſpade,
Or e're a fair maid
That would be a Nun,
Come kiſs me, 'tis done.
Hark how my merry horn doth blow,
Too high too low, too high too low.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: O excellent! two pence a piece boyes, two pence a piece.
Give the boys ſome drink there. Piper, wet your whiſtle,
Canſt tell me a way now, how to cut off my wifes Concupiſcence?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: I'le ſing ye a Song for't.

body.head: The SONG.
body.l: TAke her, and hug her,
And turn her and tug her,
And turn her again boy, again,
Then if ſhe mumble,
Or if her tail tumble,
Kiſs her amain boy, amain.
Do thy endeavour,
To take off her feaver,
Then her diſeaſe no longer will raign.
If nothing will ſerve her,
Then thus to preſerve her,
Swinge her amain boy amain.
Give her cold jelly
To take up her belly,
And once a day ſwinge her again,
If ſhe ſtand all theſe pains,
Then knock out her brains,
Her diſeaſe no longer will reign.

sp.speaker: 1 Bo.
sp.l: More excellent, more excellent, ſweet Sow-gelder.

sp.speaker: 2 Bo.
sp.l: Three-pence a piece, three-pence a piece.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Will you hear a Song how the Devil was g • lded?

sp.speaker: 3 Bo.
sp.l: I, I, let's hear the Devil roar, Sow-gelder.

lg.l: He • an at me firſt in the ſhape of a Ram,
And over and over the Sow Gelder came;
〈◊〉 and I halter'd him faſt by the born,

I pl •••
• ut his Stones as you'd pick out a Corn.
〈◊〉 , quoth the Devil, and forth he ſtunk,
And left us a Carcaſe of Mutton that ſtunk,
The next time I • ode a good mile and a half,

Where 〈◊〉
• e did live in diſguiſe of a Calf,
I 〈◊〉 and I g •• him, ere he did any evil;
He was here at his beſt, but a ſucking Devil.
Man, yet he cry'd, and forth he did ſteal,
And this was ſeld after, for excellent Veal.
Some half a year after in the form of a Pig,
I met with the Rogue, and he look'd very big;
I catch'd at his leg, laid him down on a log,
Ere a man could fa • t twice, I had made him a Hog.
Owgh, quoth the Devil, and forth gave a Jer • ,
That a few was converted, and eat of the Perk.

sp.speaker: 1 Bo.
sp.l: Groats apiece, Groats apiece, Groats apiece,
There ſweet Sow-Gelder.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Will ye ſee any feats of activity,
Some Sleight of hand, Legerdemain? hey paſs,
Preſto, be gone there?

sp.speaker: 2 Bo.
sp.l: Sit down Jugler.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: S • rah, play you your art well; draw near Piper:
Look you, my honeſt friends, you ſee my hands;
Plain dealing is no Devil: lend me ſome Money,
Twelve pence a piece will ſerve.

sp.speaker: 1. 2. B.
sp.l: There, there.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: I thank you,
Thank ye heartily: when ſhall I pay ye?

sp.speaker: All B.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, by th' Maſs this was a fine trick.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: A merry ſleight toy: but now I'll ſhow your Worſhips
A trick indeed.
Mark him well now my Maſters.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Here are three balls,
Theſe balls ſhall be three bullets,
One, two, and three: aſcentibus, malentibus.
Preſto, be gone: they are vaniſh'd: fair play, Gentlemen.
Now theſe three, like three Bullets, from your three Noſes
Will I pluck preſently: fear not, no harm Boys,

l.hi:
T • t •••
• n patul • .

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: Oh, oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: R •• bans ſub jermine ſa •

sp.speaker: 2 B.
sp.l: Ye pull too hard; ye pull too hard.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Stand fai • then:

l.hi: Silver • ramtr • m tram.

sp.speaker: 3 B.
sp.l: Hold, hold, hold.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Come aloſt, bullets three, with a whim-wham.
Have ye their Moneys?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: Oh ta • e Jugler!

sp.speaker: 2 B.
sp.l: Oh admirable Jugler!

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: One trick more yet;
Hey, come aloſt; ſa, ſa, ſlum, ſlum, taradumbis?
Eaſt, Weſt, North, South, now fly like Jack with a bumbis.
Now all your money's gone; pray ſearch your pockets.

sp.speaker: 1 B
sp.l: Humh.

sp.speaker: 2 B.
sp.l: He.

sp.speaker: 3 B.
sp.l: The Devil a penny's here!

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: This was a rare trick.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: But 'twould be a fat rarer to reſtore it.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: I'll do ye that too; look upon me earneſtly,
And move not any ways your eyes from this place,
This Button here? pow, whir, whiſs, ſhake your po ••

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: By th' Maſs 'tis here again, boys.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Reſt ye merry;
My firſt trick has paid me.

sp.speaker: All B.
sp.l: I, take it, take it,
And take ſome drink too.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Not a drop now I thank you,
Away, we are diſcover'd elſe. Ex:

div.stage: Enter Gerrard like a blind Aqua vitae man, and a Boy, ſinging the Song.

lg.l: Bring out your Cony-skins, fair maids to me,
And hold 'em fair that I may ſee;
Grey, black, and blue: for your ſmaller skins,
I'll give ye looking glaſſes, pins:
And for your whole Coney, here's ready, ready Money
Come Gentle Jone, do thou begin
With thy black, black, black, Coney-skin.
And Mary then, and Jane will follow,
With their ſilver hair'd skins, and their yellow
The white Cony-skin, I will not lay by,
For though it be faint, 'tis fair to the eye;
The grey, it is warm, but yet for my Money,
Give me the bonny, bonny black Cony.
Come away fair Maids, your skins will decay:
Come, and take money, maids, put your ware away.
Cony-skins, Cony-skins, have ye any Cony-skins,
I have fine bracelets, and fine ſilver pins.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Buy any Brand Wine, buy any Brand Wine?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Have ye any Cony-skins?

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: My fine Canary bird, there's a Cake for the Worſhip

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: Come fill, fill, fill, fill ſuddenly: let's ſee Sir,
What's this?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: A penny, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: Fill till't be ſix pence,
And there's my Pig.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: This is a Counter, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: A Counter! ſtay ye, what are theſe then?
O execrable Jugler! O damn'd Jugler!
Look in your hoſe, hoa, this comes of looking forward.

sp.speaker: 3 B.
sp.l: Devil a Dunkirk! what a Rogue's this Jugler!
This hey paſs, repaſs, h'as repaſt us ſweetly.

sp.speaker: 2 B.
sp.l: Do ye call theſe tricks.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Have ye any Ends of Gold, or Silver?

sp.speaker: 2 B.
sp.l: This Fellow comes to mock us; Gold or Silver 〈◊〉 Copp ••

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: Yes, my good Friend,
We have e'n an end of all we have.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: 'Tis well Sir,

You have the leſs to care for: Gold and Silver.
Ex •• .

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l:
Have ye any old Cloaks to ſell, have ye any old Clo •• s to ſell?
Ex ••

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: Cloaks! Look about ye Boys: mine's gone!

sp.speaker: 2 B.
sp.l: A— juggle 'em?
—O they're Preſtoes: mine's gone too!

sp.speaker: 3 B.
sp.l: Here's mine yet.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: Come, come let's drink then more Brand Wine.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Here Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: If e'r I catch your Sow-gelder, by this hand I'll ſtrip ha •
Were ever Fools ſo ferkt? We have two Cloaks yet;
And all our Caps; the Devil take the Flincher.

sp.speaker: All B.
sp.l: Yaw, yaw, yaw, yaw.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Good do'n my honeſt Fellows,
You are merry here I ſee.

sp.speaker: 3 B.
sp.l: 'Tis all we have left, Sir.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: What haſt thou? Aqua vitae?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Fill out then;
And give theſe honeſt Fellows round.

sp.speaker: All B.
sp.l: We thank ye.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: May I ſpeak a word in private to ye?

sp.speaker: All B.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: I have a buſineſs for you, honeſt Friends,
If you dare lend your help, ſhall get you crowns.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Ha!
Lead me a little nearer, Boy.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: What is't Sir?
If it be any thing to purchaſe money,
Which is our want, commands us.
All, all, all, Sir.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: You know the young ſpruce Merchant in Bruges?

sp.speaker: 2 B
sp.l: Who? Maſter Goſwin?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: That he owes me money,
And here in town there is no ſtirring of him.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Say ye ſo?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: This day, upon a ſure app ••• ment,

He meets me a mile hence, by th •
〈…〉 ſide,

Under the row of Oaks; do yo •
〈…〉
• t?

sp.speaker: All B.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Give 'em more drink: ſacre if you dare but venture
When I ſhall give the word to ſeize upon him
Here's twenty pound,

sp.speaker: 3 B.
sp.l: Beware the Jugler.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: If he reſiſt, down with him, have no mercy.

sp.speaker: 1 B.
sp.l: I warrant you, we'll hamper him,

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: To diſcharge you,
I have a Warrant here about me.

sp.speaker: 3 B.
sp.l: Here's our Warrant,
This carries fire i'th' Tail.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Away with me then,
The time draws on,
I muſt remove ſo inſolent a Suitor,
And if he be ſo rich, make him pay ranſome
E • e he ſee Bruges Towers again. Thus, wiſe men
Repair the hurts they take by a diſgrace,
And piece the Lions skin with the Foxes caſe.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I am glad I have heard this ſport yet.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: There's for thy drink, come pay the houſe within Boys,
And loſe no time.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Away with all our haſte too. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: No wind blow fair yet? no return of moneys?
Letters? nor any thing to hold my hopes up?
Why then 'tis deſtin'd, that I fall, fall miſerably!
My credit I was built on, ſinking with me.
Thou boyſtrous North-wind, blowing my misfortunes,
And froſting all my hopes to cakes of coldneſs;
Yet ſtay thy fury; give the gentle South
Yet leave to court thoſe ſails that bring me ſafety,
And you auſpicious fires, bright twins in heaven
Daunce on the ſhrowds; he blows ſtill ſtubbornly,
And on his boyſtrous Rack rides my ſad ruin;
There is no help, there can be now no comfort,
To morrow with the Sun-ſet, ſets my credit.
Oh miſery! thou curſe of man, thou plague,
In the midſt of all our ſtrength thou ſtrik'ſt us;
My vertuous Love is loſt too: all, what I have been,
No more hereafter to be ſeen than ſhadow;
To priſon now? well, yet there's this hope left me;
I may ſink fairly under this days venture,
And ſo to morrow's croſs'd, and all thoſe curſes:
Yet manly I'll invite my Fate, baſe fortune
Shall never ſay, ſhe has cut my throat in fear.
This is the place his challenge call'd me to,
And was a happy one at this time for me,
For let me fall before my • oe i'th' field,
And not at Bar, before my Creditors;
Has kept his word: now Sir, your ſwords tongue only
Loud as you dare, all other language—

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Well Sir,
You ſhall not be long troubled: draw.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: 'Tis done Sir,
And now have at ye.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Now.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Betray'd to Villains!
Slaves ye ſhall buy me bravely,
And thou baſe coward.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Now upon 'em bravely,
Conjure 'em ſoundly Boys.

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: Hold, hold.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Lay on ſtill,
Down with that Gentleman to gi • e, ſwinge him to ſ • rrup.
Retire Sir, and take Breath: follow, and take him,
Take all, 'tis lawful prize.

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: We yield.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Down with 'em
Into the Wood, and riſle 'em, tew 'em, ſwinge 'em,
Knock me their brains into their Breeches. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: Hold, hold.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: What theſe men are I know not, nor for what cauſe
They ſhou'd thus thruſt themſelves into my danger,
Can I imagine. But ſure Heavens hand was in't!
