Nor why this coward Knave ſhould deal ſo baſely
To eat me up with Slaves: but Heaven I thank thee,
I hope thou haſt reſerv'd me to an end
Fit for thy creature, and worthy of thine honour:
Would all my other dangers here had ſuffered,
With what a joyful heart ſhould I go home then?
Where now, Heaven knows, like him that waits his ſentence,
Or hears his paſſing Bell; but there's my hope ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Bleſſing upon you Maſter.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Thank ye; leave me,
For by my troth I have nothing now to give thee.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Indeed I do not ask Sir, only it grieves me
To ſee ye look ſo ſad; now goodneſs keep ye
From troubles in your mind.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: If I were troubled,
What could thy comfort do? prithee Clauſe, leave me.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Good Maſter be not angry; for what I ſay
Is out of true love to ye.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I know thou lov'ſt me.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Good Mr. blame that love then, if I prove ſo ſawcy
To ask ye why ye are ſad.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Moſt true, I am ſo,
And ſuch a ſadneſs I have got will ſink me.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Heaven ſhield it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Faith, thou muſt loſe thy Maſter.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I had rather loſe my neck, Sir: would I knew—

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: What would the knowledg do thee good ſo miſerable,
Thou canſt not help thy ſelf? when all my ways
Nor all the friends I have—

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: You do not know Sir,
What I can do: cures ſometimes, for mens cares
Flow, where they leaſt expect 'em.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I know thou wouldſt do,
But farewell Clauſe, and pray for thy poor Maſter.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I will not leave ye.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I dare not leave ye, Sir, I muſt not leave ye,
And till ye beat me dead, I will not leave ye.
By what ye hold moſt precious, by Heavens goodneſs,
As your fair youth may proſper, good Sir tell me:
My mind believes yet ſomethings in my power
May caſe you of this trouble.

sp.speaker: Goſ
sp.l: I will tell thee,
For a hundred thouſand crowns upon my credit,
Taken up of Merchants to ſupply my traffiques,
The winds and weather envying of my fortune,
And no return to help me off, yet ſhewing
To morrow, Clauſe, to morrow, which muſt come,
In priſon thou ſhalt find me poor and broken.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I cannot blame your grief Sir.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Now, what ſay'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I ſay you ſhould not ſhrink, for he that gave ye,
Can give you more, his power can bring ye off Sir,
When friends and all forſake ye, yet he ſees you.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: There's all my hope.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Hope ſtill S •• , are you ty'd
Within the compaſs of a day, good Maſter,
To pay this maſs of mony?
Ev'n to morrow:
But why do I ſtand mocking of my miſery?
Is't not enough the floods, and friends forget me?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Will no leſs ſerve?
What if it would?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Your patience,
I do not ask to mock ye: 'tis a great ſum,
But not for honeſt: have ye no friends left ye,
None that have felt your bounty? worth this duty?

sp.speaker: Goſ
sp.l: Duty? thou know'ſt it not.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: It is a duty,
And as a duty, from thoſe men have felt ye,
Should be return'd again: I have gain'd by ye,
A daily alms theſe ſeven years you have ſhowr'd on me,
Will half ſupply your want?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Why do'ſt thou fool me?
Can'ſt thou work miracles?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: To ſave my Maſter,
I can work this.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Thou wilt make me angry with thee.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: For doing good?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: What power haſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Enquire not:
So I can do it, to preſerve my Maſter;
Nay if it be three parts.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: O that I had it,
But good Clauſe, talk no more, I feel thy charity,
As thou has felt mine: but alas!

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Diſtruſt not,
'Tis that that quenches ye: pull up your Spirit,
Your good, your honeſt, and your noble Spirit;
For if the fortunes often thouſand people
Can ſave ye, reſt aſſur'd; you have forgot Sir,
The good ye did, which was the power you gave me;
Ye ſhall now know the King of Beggars treaſure:
And let the winds blow as they liſt, the Seas roar,
Yet, here to morrow, you ſhall find your harbour.
Here ſail me not, for if I live I'le fit ye.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: How ſain I would believe thee!

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: If I ly Maſter,
Believe no man hereafter.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I will try thee,
But he knows, that knows all.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Know me to morrow,
And if I know not how to cure ye, kill me;
So paſs in peace, my beſt, my worthieſt Maſter. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA III.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Thus have I ſtoln away diſguiz'd from Hemskirk
To try theſe people, for my heart yet tells me
Some of theſe Beggars, are the men I look for:
Appearing like my ſelf, they have no reaſon
(Though my intent is fair, my main end honeſt)
But to avoid me narrowly, that face too,
That womans face, how near it is! O may it
But prove the ſame, and fortune how I'le bleſs thee!
Thus, ſure they cannot know me, or ſuſpect me,
If to my habit I but change my nature;
As I muſt do; this is the wood they live in,
A place fit for concealment: where, till fortune

Crown me with that I ſeek, I'le live amongſt 'em.
Ex •

div.stage: Enter Higgen, Prigg, Ferret, Ginks, and the reſt of the Boors.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Come bring 'em out, for here we ſit in juſtice:
Give to each one a cudgel, a good cudgel:
And now attend your ſentence. That you are rogues,
And miſchievous baſe raſcalls, (there's the point now)
I take it, is confeſs'd.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Deny it if you dare knaves.

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: We are Rogues Sir.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: To amplify the matter then, rogues as ye are,
And lamb'd ye ſhall be e're we leave ye.

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: And to the open handling of our juſtice,
Why did ye this upon the proper perſon
Of our good Maſter? were you drank when you did it?

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: Yes indeed were we.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: You ſhall be beaten ſober.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Was it for want you undertook it?

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: You ſhall be ſwing'd abundantly.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: And yet for all that,
You ſhall be poor rogues ſtill.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Has not the Gentleman,
Pray mark this point Brother Prig, that noble Gentleman
Reliev'd ye often, found ye means to live by,
By imploying ſome at Sea, ſome here, ſome there;
According to your callings?

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt true Sir.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Is not the man, an honeſt man?

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: Yes truly.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: A liberal Gentleman? and as ye are true raſcals
Tell me but this, have ye not been drunk, and often,
At his charge?

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: Often, often.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: There's the point then,
They have caſt themſelves, Brother Prig.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: A ſhrewd point, Brother.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Brother, proceed you now; the cauſe is open,
I am ſome what weary.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Can you do theſe things?
You moſt abhominable ſtinking Raſcals,
You turnip eating Rogues.

sp.speaker: Boors.
sp.l: We are truly ſorry.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Knock at your hard hearts Rogues, and preſently
Give us a ſign you feel compunction,
Every man up with's cudgel, and on his neighbour
Beſtow ſuch alms, 'till we ſhall ſay ſufficient,
For there your ſentence lyes without partiality;
Either of head, or hide Rogues, without ſparing,
Or we ſhall take the pains to beat you dead elſe:
You ſhall know your doom.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: One, two, and three about it.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: That fellow in the blue, has true Compunction,
He beats his fellows bravely, oh, well ſtruck boyes.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Up with that blue breech, now playes he the Derd
So get ye home, drink ſmall beer, and be honeſt;
Call in the Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Do, bring him preſently,
His cauſe I'le hear my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Prig. With all due reverence,
We do reſign Sir.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Now huſſing Sir, what's your name?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: What's that to you Sir?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: It ſhall be ere we part.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: My name is Hemskirk,
I follow the Earl, which you ſhall feel.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: No threatning,
For we ſhall cool you Sir; why did'ſt thou baſely
Attempt the murder of the Merchant Goſwin?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: What power haſt thou to ask me?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I will know it,

O •
• ey thee till thy pain diſcover it.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: He did me wrong, baſe wrong.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: That cannot ſave ye,
Who ſent ye hither? and what further villanies
Have you in hand?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Why would'ſt thou know? what profit,
If I had any private way, could riſe
Out of my knowledge, to do thee commodity?
Be ſorry for what thou haſt done, and make amends fool,
I'le talk no further to thee, nor theſe Raſcals.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Tye him to that tree.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: I have told you whom I follow.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: The Devil you ſhould do, by your villanies,
Now he that has the beſt way, wring it from him.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: I undertake it: turn him to the Sun boyes;
Give me a fine ſharp ruſh, will ye confeſs yet?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Ye have rob'd me already, now you'le murder me.
Murder your noſe a little: does your head purge Sir?
To it again, 'twill do ye good.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Oh,
I cannot tell you any thing.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Proceed then.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: There's maggots in your noſe, I'le fetch 'em out Sir.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: O my head breaks.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: The beſt thing for the rheum Sir,
That falls into your worſhips eyes.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Hold, hold.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Speak then.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: I know not what.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: It lyes in's brain yet,
In lumps it lyes, I'le fetch it out the fineſt;
What pretty faces the fool makes? heigh!

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Hold,
Hold, and I'le tell ye all, look in my doublet;
And there within the lining in a paper,
You ſhall find all.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Go fetch that paper hither,
And let him looſe for this time.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Good ev'n my honeſt friends.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Good ev'n good fellow.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: May a poor huntſman, with a merry heart,
A voice ſhall make the foreſt ring about him,
Get leave to live amongſt ye? true as ſteel, boyes?
That knows all chaſes, and can watch all hours,
And with my quarter ſtaff, though the Devil bid ſtand,
D •• l ſuch an alms, ſhall make him roar again?
Prick ye the fearfull hare through croſs wayes, ſheep-walks,
And force the crafty Reynard climb the quickſetts;
Rouſe ye the lofty Stag, and with my bell-horn,
Ring him a knel, that all the woods ſhall mourn him,
'Till in his funeral tears, he fall before me?
The Polcat, Marterne, and the rich skin'd Lucerne
I know to chaſe, the Roe, the wind out ſtripping
• ſgrin himſelf, in all his bloody anger
I can be at from the bay, and the wild Sounder
Single, and with my arm'd ſtaff, turn the Boar,
Spight of his foamy tuſhes, and thus ſtrike him;
Till he fall down my feaſt.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: A goodly fellow.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: What mak'ſt thee here, ha? aſide

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: We accept thy fellowſhip.

sp.speaker: Hab.
sp.l: Hemskirk, thou art not right I fear, I fear thee.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Here is the paper: and as he ſaid we found it.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Give me it, I ſhall make a ſhift yet, old as I am,
To find your knavery you are ſent here, Sir • a,
To diſcover certain Gentlemen, a ſpy-knave,
And if ye find 'em, if not by perſwaſion
To bring 'em back, by poyſon to diſpatch 'em.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: By poyſon, ha?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Here is another, Hubert;
What is that Hubert Sir?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: You may perceive there.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I may perceive a villany and a tank 〈◊〉 ,
Was he joyn'd partner of thy knavery?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: No.
He had an honeſt end, would I had had ſo,
Which makes him ſcape ſuch cut-throats.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: So it ſeems.
For here thou art commanded, when that Hubert
Has done his beſt and worthieſt ſervice, this way
To cut his throat, for here he's ſet down dangerou • .

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: This is moſt impious.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I am glad we have found ye,
Is not this true?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Yes; what are you the better?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: You ſhall perceive Sir, ere you get your freed ••
Take him aſide, and friend, we take thee to us,
Into our company, thou dar'ſt be true unto us?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: I, and obedient too?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: As you had bred me.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Then take our hand: thou art now a ſervant to
Welcom him all.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Stand off, ſtand off: I'le do it,
We bid ye welcom three wayes; firſt for your perſon,
Which is a promiſing perſon, next for your quality,
Which is a decent, and a gentle quality,
Laſt for the frequent means you have to feed us,
You can ſteal 'tis to be preſum'd.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Yes, veniſon, and if you want —

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: 'Tis well you underſtand right,
And ſhall practiſe daily: you can drink too?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Soundly.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: And ye dare know a woman from a weathercock?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: If I handle her.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Now ſwear him.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: I crown thy nab, with a gag of benbo • ſe,
And ſhall thee by the Salmon into the c • ows,
To mand on the pad, and ſtrike all the cheats;
To Mill from the Ruffmans, commiſion and ſtates,
Twang d • ll's, i' the ſtirom • ll, and let the Q •• re Cuffin:
And Herman Beck ſtrine, and trine to the Ruffin.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Now interpret this unto him.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: I pour on thy pate a pot of good ale,
And by the Rogues o'th' a Rogue thee inſtal:
To beg on the way, to rob all thou meets;
To ſteal from the hedge, both the ſhirt and the ſheets:
And lye with thy wench in the ſtraw till ſhe twang,
Let the Conſtable, Juſtice, and D • vil go hang.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: You are welcom Brother

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Welcom, welcom, welcom, but who ſhall have the keeping
Of this fellow?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Sir, if you dare but truſt me;
For if I have kept wild dogs and beaſts for wonder,
And made 'em tame too: give into my cuſtody
This roaring Raſcal, I ſhall hamper him,
With all his knacks and knaveries, and I fear me
Diſcover yet a further villany in him;
O he ſmells ranck o'th' Raſcal.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Take him to thee,
But if he ſcape —

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Let me be ev'n hang'd for him,
Come Sir, I'le tye ye to my leath.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Away Raſcal.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Be not ſo ſtubborn: I ſhall ſwindge ye ſoundly,
〈…〉 with me.

〈◊〉
• ow come in,
〈…〉 Sir, to your Priſoner.
H • muſt bl •• d both mine eyes, if he get from me.
〈◊〉 ſome victuals, and ſome drink, ſome good drink,
〈…〉 holy to good fortune,
〈…〉 with us.
〈…〉 , Brother, I pray lead,
〈…〉 Brother. Exeunt.
〈…〉 welcome: I have heard your ſcape,
A 〈…〉 , that only lov • s you;
〈…〉 loves you) give her joy leave
〈…〉 what is't makes you ſad man?
Why do you look ſo wild? I • 't • offend you?
〈…〉 my heart, not willingly.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Is't the delay of that y • long have look'd for,
A happy marriage? now I come to urge it.
Now when you pleaſe to finiſh it?
No News yet?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Do you hear Sir?
Yes.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Do you love me?
Have I liv'd
•• all th • happineſs • ortune could ſeat me,
〈…〉 fair opinions?
I have provided
A 〈◊〉 that's ready for u • .
And 〈◊〉 the Devil,
〈…〉 that Devil Chance devour me?
We'll • y to what place you pleaſe.
No St •• p • oſperous!
〈…〉 ſwoop?

You •
• or • love me G • ſwin?
You wi • l not look upon me?
〈…〉 Prayers
〈◊〉 up to Heav • n, with ſuch a zeal as mine are,
〈◊〉 like lazy m • ſts, and never proſper?
〈◊〉 I muſt w ••• , and cold muſt be my comfort;
•••• n • ſs, and want of m • at; alas ſhe w •• ps too,
Which is the t • p of all my ſorrows, Gertrude.
No, no, you will not know me; my poor beauty,
Which • as been worth your eyes.
• he time grows on ſtill;
And 〈…〉 tumbl • ng wave, I ſee my ruine

〈◊〉
• ow • ing over me.
Yet wi • l ye know me?
〈…〉 hundred thouſand Crowns.
Yet will ye love me?
Tell m • but how I have deſerv'd your ſlighting?
〈◊〉 hundred thouſand Crowns?

sp.speaker: Ger
sp.l: 〈◊〉 D • ſſembler.

sp.speaker: Geſ.
sp.l: Of which I have ſcarce ten: O how it ſtarts me!
And may the next you love, hea • ing my ruine.
〈…〉 forget my 〈◊〉 , O my beſt Gertrude,
Crown • d my ••• s and comforts.
〈◊〉 what a •• s ye?
I thought 〈◊〉 a • l been • ext with me.
My mind, Wench,
〈…〉 with ſorrow, 〈◊〉 my memory.
〈…〉 of the knowledg of it?
〈…〉 you • ſorrows,
〈…〉 you love no other Woman?
No, I 〈◊〉
You •• ve no f •• ps loſt lately?
〈…〉 I know o •
〈…〉 no blood, whoſe innocence
〈…〉 this your conſcience.
〈◊〉 by Heaven.
Why ſhould you • e thus then?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Good Gertrude ask not,
Ev'n by the love you bear me.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I am obedient.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Go in, my fair, I will not be long from ye,
Nor long I fear me with thee. At my return
Diſpoſe me as you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: The good gods guide ye.
Now for my ſelf, which is the leaſt I hope 〈◊〉
And when that fails, for mans worſt fortune, pity.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: WHy gentle men, 'tis but a week more, I 〈…〉

But 7. ſhort days, I am not running fr ••
〈◊〉
Nor, i • you give me patience, is it poſſible
All my adventures fail; you have ſhips abroad
• n • ure the beating both of Wind and Weather
I am ſure 't would vex your hearts, to be proteſted;
Ye are all fair Merchants.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: Yes, and muſt have fair play:
There is no living here elſe; one hour's failing
Fails us of all our friends, of all our credits:
For my part, I would ſtay, but my wants tell me,
I muſt wrong others in't.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: No mercy in ye!

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: 'Tis fooliſh to depend on others mercy:
Keep your ſelf right, and even cut your cloth, Sir,
According to your calling, you have liv'd here,
In Lord-like Prodigality, high, and open,
And now ye find what 'tis: the liberal ſpending
The Summer of your Youth, which you ſhould gl • an i • ,
And like the labouring Ant, make uſe and gain of,
Has brought this bitter, ſtormy Winter on ye,
And now you cry.

sp.speaker: 3 Mer.
sp.l: Alas, before your Poverty,
We were no men, of no mark, no endeavour;
You ſtood alone, took up all trade, all buſineſs
Running through your hands, ſcarce a Sail at Sea,
But loaden with your Goods: we poor weak Pedlers:
When by your leave, and much intreaty to it,
We could have ſtowage for a little Cloath,
Or a few Wines, put off, and thank your Worſhip.
Lord, how the World's chang'd with ye? now I hope, 〈◊〉
We ſhall have Sea-room.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Is my miſery
Become my ſcorn too! have ye no humanity?
No part of men left? are all the Bounties in me
To you, and to the Town, turn'd my reproaches?

sp.speaker: 4 Mer.
sp.l: Well, get your moneys ready: 'tis but 2 hours.
We ſhall proteſt ye elſe, and ſuddenly.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: But two days.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l:
Not an hour, ye know the hazard.
Ex ••• .

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: How ſoon my light's put out I hard hearted Br •••
Within thy Walls may never honeſt Merchant
Venture his fortunes more: O my poor Wench too.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Good fortune, Maſter.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Thou miſtak'ſt me, Clauſe,
I am not worth thy Bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Still a ſad man!
sp.stage: Enter Higgen and Prigg, like Port •• s.
sp.l: No belief gentle Maſter? come bring it in then,
And now believe your Beadſman.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Is this certain?
Or doſt thou work upon my troubled ſenſe?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: 'Tis gold, Sir,
Take it and try it.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Certainly 'tis treaſure;
〈◊〉 there be yet this Bleſſing?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Ceaſe your wonder,
You ſhall not ſink, for ne'r a ſowſt Flap-dragon,
〈…〉 a pickl'd Pilcher of 'em all, Sir,
Is there, your full ſum, a hundred thouſand crowns:
〈◊〉 good ſweet Maſter, now be merry; pay 'em,
〈…〉 poor pelting Knaves, that know no goodneſs:
〈…〉 hear your heart up handſomely.
Good Clauſe,
〈◊〉 cam'ſt thou by this mighty Sum? if naughtily,
〈◊〉 muſt not it take it of thee, 'twill undo me.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Fear not, you have it by as honeſt means
• s though your father gave it: Sir, you know not
To what a maſs, the little we get daily,
Mounts in ſeven years; we beg it for Heavens charity,
And to the ſame good we are bound to render it.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: What great ſecurity?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Away with that, Sir,
• ere not ye more than all the men in Bruges;
And all the money in my thoughts—

sp.speaker: Geſ.
sp.l: But good Clauſe,
〈◊〉 may dye preſently.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Then this dies with ye:
Pay when you can good Maſter, I'll no Parchments,
Only this charity I ſhall entreat you;
Leave me this Ring.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Alas, it is too poor, Clauſe.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: 'Tis all I ask, and this withal, that when
〈◊〉 ſhall deliver this back, you ſhall grant me
Freely one poor petition.

sp.speaker: Geſ.
sp.l: There, I confirm it, Gives the Ring.
And may my faith forſake me when I ſhun it.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Away, your time draws on. Take up the money,
And follow this young Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Farewell Clauſe,
And may thy honeſt memory live for ever.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs you, and ſtill keep you, farewel Maſter.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I have lockt my Youth up cloſe enough for gadding,
In • n old Tree, and ſet watch over him.
Now for my Love, for ſure this Wench muſt be ſhe,
She follows me; Come hither, pretty Minche.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: No, no, you'll kiſs.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: So I will.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Y'ded law?
How will ye kiſs me, pray you?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Thus, ſoft as my loves lips.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: What's your Father's name?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: He's gone to Heaven.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Is it not Gerrard, Sweet?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I'll ſtay no longer;
My Mother's an old Woman, and my Brother
Was drown'd at Sea, with catching Cockles. O Love!
O how my heart melts in me: how thou fir'ſt me!

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: 'Tis certain ſhe; pray let me ſee your hand, Sweet?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: No, no, you'l bite it.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Sure I ſhould know that Gymmal!

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Tis certain he: I had forgot my Ring too.
O Hubert! Hubert!

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Ha! methought ſhe nam'd me—
Do you know me, Chick?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: No indeed, I never ſaw ye;
But methinks you kiſs finely.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Kiſs again then;
By Heaven 'tis ſhe.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: O what a joy he brings me!

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: You are not Minche?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes, pretty Gentleman,
And I muſt be marry'd to morrow to a Capper.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Muſt ye my Sweet, and does the Capper love ye?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes, yes, he'l give me pie, and look in mine eyes thus.
'Tis he: 'tis my dear Love: O bleſt Fortune.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: How fain ſhe would conceal her ſelf, yet ſhew it!
Will you love me, and leave that man? I'll ſerve.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: O I ſhall loſe my ſelf!

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I'll wa •• upon you,
And make you dainty Noſe gays.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: And where will you ſtick'em?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Here in my boſom, Sweet, and make a crown of Lilies
For your fair head.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: And will you love me deed law?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: With all my Heart.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Call me to morrow then,
And we'll have brave chear, and go to Church together:
Give you good ev'n Sir.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: But one word fair Minche.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I muſt be gone a milking.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Ye ſhall preſently.
Did you never hear of a young maid called Jacu • n?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I am diſcover'd; hark in your ear, I'll tell ye:
You muſt not know me, kiſs and be conſtant ever.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Heaven curſe me elſe 'tis ſhe, and now I am certain
They are all here: now for my other project— Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Enter Goſwin, 4. Merchants, Higgen, and Prigg.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: Nay, if 'twould do you courteſie.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: None at all, Sir:
Take it, 'tis yours, there's your ten thouſand for ye,
Give in my Bills. Your ſixteen.

sp.speaker: 3 Mer.
sp.l: Pray be pleas'd Sir
To make a further uſe.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: 3 Mer.
sp.l: What I have, Sir,
You may command; pray let me be your Servant.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Put your Hats on: I care not for your courteſies,
They are moſt untimely done, and no truth in 'em.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: I have a frought of Pepper.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Rot your Pepper,
Shall I truſt you again? there's your ſeven thouſand.

sp.speaker: 4 Mer.
sp.l: Or if you want fine Sugar, 'tis but ſending.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: No, I can ſend to Barbary, thoſe people
That never yet knew faith, have nobler freedoms.
Theſe carry to Vanlock, and take my Bills in,
To Peter Zuten theſe: bring back my Jewels,
Why are theſe pieces?

sp.speaker: Sayler.
sp.l: Health to the noble Merchant,
The Suſan is return'd.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Well?

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Well, and rich Sir,
And now put in.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Heaven thou haſt heard my prayers.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: The brave Rebeccah too, bound from the Straits,
With the next Tide is ready to put after.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: What news o'th' fly-boat?

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: If this Wind hold till midnight,
She will be here, and wealthy, 'ſcap'd fairly.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: How, prithee, Sayler?

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Thus Sir, ſhe had fight
Seven hours together, with ſix Turkiſh Gallies,
And ſhe ſought bravely; but at length was boarded
And overlaid with ſtrength: when preſently
Comes boring up the wind Captain Vannoke,
That valiant Gentleman, you redeem'd from priſon;
He knew the Boat, ſet in, and ſought it bravely:
Beat all the Gallies off, ſunk three, redeem'd her,
And as a ſervice to ye ſent her home Sir.

T ••
〈…〉 n • ws •• o drink the Merchants health, Saylor.
〈…〉 and your bounty, and I'le do it to a doyt, S • ,

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: What miracles are pour'd upon this fellow!

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: This he • e I hope, my friends, I ſhall ſcape priſon,
For all your • a • es to catch in.
You may pleaſe Sir
• o 〈◊〉 of your poor ſervants in diſpleaſure,
Who •• all th •• have, goods, moneys, are at your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Goſ
sp.l: I thank you,
W ••• I have 〈◊〉 of you I ſhall forget you:
You are 〈◊〉 I hope.

sp.speaker: Ad.
sp.l: We •• , in your good fortunes.

sp.speaker: Van d.
sp.l: Come Sir, come take your eaſe, you muſt go home
With me, yo •• ier is one weeps and howls.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: A •• how does ſhe?

sp.speaker: Van d.
sp.l: She will be better ſoon I hope.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Why ſoon Sir?

sp.speaker: Van d.
sp.l: Why when you have her in your arms, this night
M • boy ſhe is thy wife.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: With all my heart I take her.

sp.speaker: Van d.
sp.l: We have prepar'd, all thy friends will be there,
And all my Rooms ſhall ſmoak to ſee the revel;
Thou haſt been wrong'd, and no more ſhall my ſervice
What on the knave her Uncle, I have heard all,
All •• s b • ts for my Boy, but thou ſhalt have her;
H •• t •• diſpatch't thy buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Moſt.

sp.speaker: Van d
sp.l: By the maſs Boy,
Thou 〈◊〉 doſt new in wealth, and I joy in it,
〈◊〉 the b • ſt Boy, that Bruges ever nouriſh'd.
Thou haſt been ſad, I'le cheer thee up with Sack,
And when thou a •• luſtly I'le ſling thee to thy Miſtris.
She'l • eg t ••• , 〈◊〉 .
I • o • g to ſee it,
I ha • forgot you: there's for you my friends:
You had but heavy burthens; commend my love
To my beſt love, all the love I have
To honeſt C • auſ, ſhortly I will thank him better. Exit.
By the m •• s a loyal Merchant,
• old by the han • full, here will be ſport ſoon, Prig.
It partly ſeems ſo, and here will I be in a trice.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: And I boy,
Away ap • ce, we are look'd for.
Oh theſe bak'd meats,
M • th • nks I ſmell them hither.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Thy mouth waters. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA IV.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I Muſt not.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l:
〈◊〉
•• in thy power to do it, and in mine
To •• wa •• th to thy w • h • s.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I dare not, no • I will not.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Gentle Hun •• man,
•• ough thou haſt kept me hard, though in thy duty,
W ••• at requir'd to ••• t, th'haſt uſed me ſtubbornly;

I can for •• ve th ••
〈◊〉
You the • a • ls ſervant?
I ſwear I am near as his own thoughts to him;

A ••
〈◊〉 thee
Come, come, leave you p • ating.
I • thou da • 'ſt but try.
I thank you heartily, you will be
〈◊〉 man that will hang m •• ſweet recompence,
〈◊〉 do, but I do not ſay I will,

To 〈◊〉
•• ſt f • llow that would think out,
And 〈…〉 .

sp.speaker: Hem
sp.l: If it be not recompenc'd, and to thy own deſires,
• f within theſe ten days I do not make thee —

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: What, a falſe knave!

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Prethee, prethee conceive me righty, any thing
Of profit or of place that may advance thee.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Why what a Gooſe cap would'ſt thou make me,
Do not I know that men in miſery will promiſe
Any thing, more than their lives can reach at?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Believe me Huntſman,
There ſhall not one ſhort ſyllable
That comes from me, paſs
Without its full performance.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Say you ſo Sir?
Have ye e're a good place for my quality?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: A thouſand Chaſes, Foreſts, Parks: I'le make 〈◊〉
Chief • anger over all the games.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: When?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Preſently.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: This may provoke me: and yet to prove a 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: 'Tis to prove honeſt: 'tis to do good ſervice,
Service for him thou art ſworn to, for thy Prince,
Then for thy ſelf that good; what fool would live here,
Poor, and in miſery, ſubject to all dangers,
Law, and lewd people can inflict, when bravely
And to himſelf he may be law and credit?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Shall I believe thee?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: As that thou holdſt moſt holy.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Ye may play tricks.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Then let me never live more.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Then you ſhall ſee Sir, I will do a ſervice
That ſhall deſerve indeed.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: 'Tis well ſaid, Huntſman,
And thou ſhalt be well thought of.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I will do it: 'tis not your ſetting free, for that meer nothing
But ſuch a ſervice, if the Earl be noble,
He ſhall for ever love me.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: What is't Huntſman?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Do you know any of theſe people live here?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: You are a fool then: here be thoſe, to have 'em,
I know the Earl ſo well, would make him caper.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Any of the old Lords that rebel'd?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Peace, all,
I know'em every one, and can betray 'em.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: But wilt thou doe this ſervice?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: If you'l keep
Your faith, and free word to me.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Wilt thou ſwear me?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: No, no, I will believe ye: more than that too,
Here's the right heir.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: O honeſt, honeſt huntſman!

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Now, how to get theſe Gallants, there's the ma •••
You will be conſtant, 'tis no work for me elſe.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Will the Sun ſhine again?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: The way to get 'em.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Propound it, and it ſhall be done.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: No ſleight;
(For they are Deviliſh crafty, it concerns'em,)
Nor reconcilement, (for they dare not truſt neither)
Muſt doe this trick.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: By force?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I, that muſt doe it.
And with the perſon of the Earl himſelf,
Authority (and mighty) muſt come on 'em:
Or elſe in vain: and thus I would have ye do it.
To morrow-night be here: a hundred men will bear 'em,
(So he be there, for he's both wiſe and valiant,
And with his terrour will ſtrike dead their forces)
The hour be twelve a Clock, now for a guide
To draw ye without danger on theſe perſons,
The woods being thick, and hard to hit, my ſelf
With ſome few with me, made unto our purpoſe,
Beyond the wood, upon the plain, will wait ye
By the great Oak.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: I know it: keep thy faith huntſman,
And ſuch a ſhower of wealth —

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I warrant ye:
M • ſs nothing that I tell ye.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Farewel;
You have your liberty, now uſe it wiſely;
And keep your hour, goe cloſer about the wood there,
For fear they ſpy you.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: And bring no noiſe with ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: All ſhall be done toth' purpoſe: farewel huntſman.

div.stage: Enter Gerrard, Higgen, Prig, Ginks, Snap, Ferret.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Now, what's the news in town?

sp.speaker: Ginks.
sp.l: No news, but joy Sir;
Every man wooing of the noble Merchant,
Who has his hearty commendations to ye.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Yes this is news, this night he's to be married.

sp.speaker: Ginks.
sp.l: Byth' maſs that's true, he marrys Vandunks Daughter,
The dainty black-ey'd bell.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: I would my clapper
Hung in his baldrick, a what a peal could I Ring?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Married?

sp.speaker: Ginks.
sp.l: 'Tis very true Sir, O the pyes,
The piping hot mince-pyes!

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: O the Plum-pottage!

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: For one leg of a gooſe now would I venture a limb boys,
• love a fat gooſe, as I love allegiance,
And — upon the Boors, too well they know it,
And therefore ſtarve their poultry.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: To be married
To Vandunks Daughter?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: O this pertious Merchant:
What ſport he will have? but hark you brother Prig,
• hall we do nothing in the foreſaid wedding?
There's mony to be got, and meat I take it,
What think ye of a moriſe?

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: No, by no means,
That goes no further than the ſtreet, there leaves us,
Now we muſt think of ſomething that muſt draw us
• nto the bowels of it, intoth' buttery,
• nto the Kitchin, into the Cellar, ſomething
That that old drunken Burgo-maſter loves,
What think ye of a waſſel?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: I think worthily.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: And very fit it ſhould be, thou, and Ferret,
And Ginks to ſing the Song: I for the ſtructure,
Which is the bowl.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Which muſt be up-ſey Engliſh,
• trong, luſty London beer; let's think more of it.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: He muſt not marry.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: By your leave in private,
One word Sir, with ye; Gerrard: do not ſtart me,
• know ye, and he knows ye, that beſt loves ye:
Hubert ſpeaks to ye, and you muſt be Gerrard.
The time invites you to it.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Make no ſhow then,
• am glad to ſee you Sir; and I am Gerrard.
How ſtand affairs?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Fair, if ye dare now follow,
Hemskirk I have let goe, and theſe my cauſes,
• 'le tell ye privately, and how I have wrought him,
And then to prove me honeſt to my friends,
• ook upon theſe directions, you have ſeen his.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Then will I ſpeak a ſpeech, and a brave ſpeech
• n praiſe of Merchants, where's the Ape?

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: — Take him,
A gowty Bear-ward ſtole him the other day.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: May his Bears worry him, that Ape had paid it,
What dainty tricks? — O that burſen Bear-ward:
• n his French doublet, with his bliſter'd bullions,
• n a long ſtock ty'd up; O how daintily
Would I have made him wait, and ſhift a trencher,
Carry a cup of wine? ten thouſand ſtinks
Wait on thy mangy hide, thou lowzy Bear ward.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: 'Tis paſſing well, I both believe and joy in't,
And will be ready: keep you here the mean while,
And keep in, I muſt a while forſake ye,
Upon mine anger no man ſtir, this two hours.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Not to the wedding Sir?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Not any whither.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: The wedding muſt be ſeen ſir; we want meat too.
We are horrible out of meat.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Shall it be ſpoken,
Fat Capons ſhak't their mils at's in defiance
And turkey tombs ſuch honorable monuments,
Shall piggs, Sir, that the Parſons ſelf would envy,
And dainty Ducks—

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l:
Not a word more, obey me.
Exit Ger.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Why then come dolefull death, this is ſtat tyranny,
And by this hand —

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: I'le goe ſleep upon't. Exit Hig.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Nay, and there be a wedding, and we wanting,
Farewel our happy days: we do obey Sir. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA V.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: Well met Sir, you are for this luſty wedding.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: I am ſo, ſo are you I take it.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: Yes,
And it much glads me, that to doe him ſervice
Who is the honour of our trade, and luſtre,
We meet thus happily.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: He's a noble fellow,
And well becomes a bride of ſuch a beauty.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: She is paſſing fair indeed, long may their loves
Continue like their youths, in ſpring of ſweetneſs,
All the young Merchants will be here
No doubt on't,
For he that comes not to attend this wedding,
The curſe of a moſt blind one fall upon him,
A loud wi • e, and a lazie: here's Vanlock.

sp.speaker: Vanl.
sp.l: Well overtaken Gentlemen: ſave ye.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: The ſame to you ſir; ſave ye fair Miſtris Francis,
I would this happy night might make you bluſh too.

sp.speaker: Vanl.
sp.l: She dreams apace.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: That's but a drowſie fortune.

sp.speaker: 3 Mer.
sp.l: Nay take us with ye too; we come to that end,
I am ſure ye are for the wedding.

sp.speaker: Vanl.
sp.l: Hand and heart man:
And what their feet can doe, I could have tript it
Before this whorſon gout.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Bleſs ye Maſters.

sp.speaker: Vanl.
sp.l: Clauſe? how now Clauſe? thou art come to ſee thy Maſter,
(And a good maſter he is to all poor people)
In all his joy, 'tis honeſtly done of thee.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Long may he live ſir, but my buſineſs now is
If you would pleaſe to doe it, and to him too.

sp.speaker: Vanl.
sp.l: He's here himſelf.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Stand at the door my friends?
I pray walk in: welcom fair Miſtris Francis,
See what the houſe affords, there's a young Lady
Will bid you welcom.

sp.speaker: Vanl.
sp.l: We joy your happineſs. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I hope it will be ſo: Clauſe nobly welcom,
My honeſt, my beſt friend, I have been carefull
To ſee thy monys —

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Sir, that brought not me,
Do you know this Ring again?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Thou hadſt it of me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And do you well remember yet, the boun you gave me
Upon the return of this?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Yes, and I grant it,
Be it what it will: ask what thou canſt, I'le do it;
Within my power.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ye are not married yet?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: ••• th I ſhall ask you that that will diſturb ye,
But I muſt put ye to your promiſe.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Do,
And if I faint and ſlinch in't—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Well ſaid Maſter,
And yet it grieves me too: and yet it muſt be.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Prethee diſtruſt me not.
You muſt not marry,
That's part of the power you gave me: which to make up,
You muſt preſently depart, and follow me.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Not marry, Clauſe?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Not if you keep your promiſe,
And gave me power to ask.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Pre'thee think better,
I will obey, by Heaven.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I have thought the beſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Give me thy reaſon, do ſt thou fear her honeſty?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Chaſte as the ice, for any thing I know, Sir.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Why ſhould'ſt thou light on that then? to what purpoſe?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I muſt not now diſcover.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Muſt not marry?
Shall I break now when my poor heart is pawn'd?
When all the preparation?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Now or never.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Come, 'tis not that thou would'ſt: thou do'ſt but fright me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Upon my ſoul it is, Sir, and I bind ye.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: C • auſe, can'ſt thou be ſo cruel?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You may break, Sir,
But never more in my thoughts appear honeſt.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Did'ſt ever ſee her?

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: She is ſuch a thing,
O Clauſe, ſhe is ſuch a wonder, ſuch a mirror,
For beauty, and fair vertue, Europe has not:
Why haſt thou made me happy, to undo me?
But look upon her; then if thy heart relent not,
I'le quit her preſently. who waits there?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: [within] Sir.

sp.speaker: Goſ
sp.l: Bid my fai • love come hither, and the Company.
Prethee be good unto me; take a mans heart
And look upon her truly: take a friends heart
And feel what miſery muſt follow this.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Take you a noble heart and keep your promiſe;
I forſook all I had, to make you happy.

div.stage: Enter Gertrude, Vandunk, and the reſt Merchants.

sp.l: Can that thing call'd a Woman, ſtop your goodneſs?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Look there ſhe is, deal with me as thou wilt now,
Did'ſt ever ſee a fa •• er?
She is moſt goodly.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Pray ye ſtand ſtill.
What a • ls my love?
Did'ſt thou ever,
By the fait light of Heaven, behold a ſweeter?
O that thou knew'ſt but love, or ever felt him,
Look well, look narrowly upon her beauties.

sp.speaker: 1 Mer.
sp.l: Sure h'as ſome ſtrange deſign in hand, he ſtarts ſo.

sp.speaker: 2 Mer.
sp.l: This Begga • has a ſtrong power over his pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: View all her body.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis exact and excellent.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Is ſhe a thing then to be loſt thus lightly?
Her mind is ten times ſweeter, ten times nobler,
And but to hear her ſpeak, a Paradiſe,
And ſuch a love ſhe • ears to me, a chaſte love,
A vertuous, fair, and fruitful love: 'tis now too
I am rea • y to enjoy it; the Prieſt ready, Cla • ſe,
To ſay the holy words ſhall make us happy,
This is a cruelty beyond mans ſtudy,
All theſe are ready, all our joyes are ready,
And all the expectation of our friends,
'Twill be her death to do it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Let her dye then.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Thou canſt not: 'tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: It muſt be.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: 'Twill kill me too, 'twill murder me: by heaven C ••••
I'le give thee half I have; come thou ſhalt ſave me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Then you muſt go with me: I can ſtay no longer,
If ye be true, and noble.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: Hard heart, I'le follow:
Pray ye all go in again, and pray be merry,
I have a weighty buſineſs, (give my Cloak there,)
Concerns my life, and ſtate, (make no enquiry,)
This preſent hour befaln me: with the ſooneſt
I ſhall be here again: nay pray go in, Sir,
And take them with you, 'tis but a night loſt, Gentlemen

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: Come, come in, we will not loſe our meat yet,
Nor our good mirth, he cannot ſtay long from her,
I am ſure of that.

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l:
I will not ſtay; believe, Sir.
Ex ••
Gertrude, a word with you.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Why is this ſtop, Sir?

sp.speaker: Goſ.
sp.l: I have no more time left me, but to kiſs thee,

And tell thee this, I am ever thine: farewel wench.
Ex ••

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: And is that all your Ceremony? Is this a wed •••
Are all my hopes and prayers turn'd to nothing?
Well, I will ſay no more, nor ſigh, nor ſorrow;

Till to thy face I prove thee falſe. Ah me!
Ex ••

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: LEad, if thou thinkſt we are right: why doſt thou ma ••
Theſe often ſtands? thou ſaidſt thou knewſt the wa •

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Fear nothing, I do know it: would 'twere homewa ••

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Wrought from me by a Beggar? at the time
That moſt ſhould tye him? 'tis ſome other Love
That hath a more command on his affections,
And he that fetcht him, a diſguiſed Agent,
Not what he perſonated; for his faſhion
Was more familiar with him, and more powerful
Than one that ask'd an alms: I muſt find out
One, if not both: kind darkneſs be my ſhrowd,
And cover loves too curious ſearch in me,
For yet, ſuſpicion, I would not name thee.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Miſtris, it grows ſomewhat pretty and dark.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: What then?

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Nay, nothing; do not think I am afraid,
Although perhaps you are.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I am not, forward.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Sure but you are? give me your hand, fear noth ••
There's one leg in the wood, do not pull me backward:
What a ſweat one on's are in, you or I?
Pray God it do not prove the plague; yet ſure
It has infected me; for I ſweat too,
It runs out at my knees, feel, feel, I pray you.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: What ails the fellow?

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Hark, hark I beſeech you,
Do you hear nothing?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Liſt: a wild Hog,
He grunts: now 'tis a Bear: this wood is full of 'em,
And now, a Wolf, Miſtreſs, a Wolf, a Wolf,
It is the howling of a Wolf.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: The braying of an Aſs, is it not?

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Oh, now one has me;
• h my left baunch, farewel.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Look to your Shanks,
• our Breech is ſafe enough, the Wolf's a Fern-brake.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: But ſee, ſee, ſee, there is a Serpent in it;
〈◊〉 has eyes as broad as Platters; it ſpits fire;
• ow it creeps towards us, help me to ſay my Prayers:
〈◊〉 hath ſwallowed me almoſt, my breath is ſtopt;
〈◊〉 cannot ſpeak: do I ſpeak Miſtreſs? tell me.

sp.speaker: Cer.
sp.l: Why, thou ſtrange timerous Sot, canſt thou perceive
〈◊〉 thing i'th' Buſh but a poor Glo-worm?
It may be 'tis but a Glo-worm now, but 'twill
Grow to a fire-drake preſently.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Come thou from it:
〈◊〉 have a precious guide of you, and a courteous,
• hat gives me leave to lead my ſelf the way thus.
It thunders, you hear that now?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I hear one hollow.
'Tis thunder, thunder:
• ee, a Flaſh of Lightning:
Are you not blaſted Miſtreſs? pull your Mask off,
〈◊〉 has plaid the Barber with me here: I have loſt
My Beard, my Beard, pray God you be not ſhaven,
• Twill ſpoil your Marriage Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: What ſtrange Wonders
• ear fancies in a Coward!

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Now the Earth opens.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Prithee hold thy peace.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Will you on then?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Both love and jealouſie have made me bold,
Where my Fate leads me, I muſt go. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: God be with you then.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: It was the Fellow ſure, he that ſhould guide me,
•• e Hunts-man that did hollow us.

sp.speaker: Woolf.
sp.l: Beſt make a ſtand,
• nd liſten to his next: Ha!

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Who goes there?
Miſtreſs, I am taken.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Miſtreſs? Look forth Souldiers.
What are you Sirrah?

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Truly all is left
Of a poor Boor, by day-light, by night no body,
You might have ſpar'd your Drum, and Guns, and Pikes too
• o • I am none that will ſtand out Sir, I.
You may take me in with a walking Stick,
Even when you pleaſe, and hold me with a packthred.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: What woman was't you call'd to?

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Woman! none Sir.

sp.speaker: Woolf.
sp.l: None! did you not name Miſtreſs?

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Yes. but ſhe's
No woman yet: ſhe ſhould have been this night,
But that a Beggar ſtole away her Bridegroom,
Whom we were going to make hue and cry after;
〈◊〉 tell you true Sir, ſhe ſhould ha' been married to day;
A •• was the Bride and all; but in came Clauſe,
• he old lame Beggar, and whips up Mr Goſwin
Under his arm; away with him as a Kite,
Or an old Fox would ſwoop away a Goſling.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe, 'tis ſhe, 'tis ſhe: Niece?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Ha!

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: She Sir,
This was a noble entrance to your fortune,
That being on the point thus to be married,
Upon her venture here, you ſhould ſurpriſe her.

sp.speaker: Woolf.
sp.l: I begin, Hemskirk, to believe my fate,
Works to my ends.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and this adds truſt
Unto the fellow our guide, who aſſur'd me Florez
•• v'd in ſome Merchants ſhape, as Gerrard did
〈◊〉 the old Beggars, and that he would uſe
All which we find is done — That's he again — Holla

sp.speaker: Woolf.
sp.l: Good, we ſent out to meet him.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Here's the Oa • .

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I am miſerably loſt, thus faln
Into my Uncles hands from all my hopes,
Can I not think away my ſelf and dye.

div.stage:
Enter Hubert, Higgen, Prig, Ferret, Snap, Ginks l •••
Boor •

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I like your habits well: they are ſafe, ſtand cloſe.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: But what's the action we are for now? Ha •
Robbing a Ripper of his Fiſh.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Or taking
A Poulterer Priſoner, without ranſome, Bullyes?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Or cutting off a Convoy of Butter?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Or ſurprizing a Boors ken, for granting cheats!

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Or cackling Cheats?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Or Mergery-praters, Rogers,
And Tibs o'th' Buttery?

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: O I could drive a Regiment
Of Geeſe afore me, ſuch a night as this,
Ten Leagues with my Hat and Staff, and not a 〈◊〉
Heard, nor a wing of my Troops diſordered

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Tell us,
If it be milling of a lag of duds,
The fetching of a back of cloaths or ſo;
We are horribly out of linnen.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: No ſuch matter.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Let me alone with the Farmers dog,
If you have a mind to the cheeſe-loſt; 'tis but thus,
And he is a ſilenc'd Maſtiff, during pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Would it would pleaſe you to be ſilent.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Mum.

sp.speaker: Woolf.
sp.l: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: A friend, the Hunts man.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: O 'tis he.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I have kept touch Sir, which is the 〈◊〉 of theſe
Will he know a man now?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: This my Lord's the Friend,
Hath undertook the ſervice.
If't be worth
His Lordſhips thanks anon, when 'tis done
Lording, I'll look for't, a rude Wood-man,
I know how to pitch my toils, drive in my game:
And I have don't, both Florez and his Father
Old Gerrard, with Lord Arnold of Benthurſea,
Cozen, and Jaculin, young Florez's Siſter:
I have 'em all.

sp.speaker: Woolf.
sp.l: Thou ſpeak'ſt too much, too happy,
To carry faith with it.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: I can bring you
VVhere you ſhall ſee, and find 'em.

sp.speaker: Woolf.
sp.l: VVe will double
VVhat ever Hemskirk then hath promis'd thee.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: And I'll deſerve it treble: what horſe ha' you?

sp.speaker: Woolf.
sp.l: A hundred. That's well: ready to ta ••
Upon ſurpriſe of 'em.

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Divide then
Your force into five Squadrons; for there a ••
So many out-lets, ways through the wood
That iſſue from the place where they are lodg'd
Five ſeveral ways, of all which Paſſages,
VVe muſt poſſeſs our ſelves, to round 'em in;
For by one ſtarting hole they'll all eſcape elſe:
I and 4. Boors here to me will be guides,
The Squadron where you are, my ſelf will lead
And that they may be more ſecure, I'll uſe
My wonted whoops, and hollows, as I were
A hunting for 'em; which will make them reſt
Careleſs of any noiſe, and be a direction
To the other guides, how we approach 'em ſtill.

sp.speaker: Woolf.
sp.l: 'Tis order'd well, and reliſheth the Souldier,
Make the diviſion Hemskirk; you are my charge,
Fair One, I'll look to you.

sp.speaker: Boo.
sp.l: Shall no body need
To look to me? I'll look unto my ſelf

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: 'Tis but this, remember.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Say, 'tis done, Boy Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA II.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: By this time Sir I hope you want no reaſons
Why I broke off your marriage, for though I
Should as a Subject ſtudy you my Prince
In things indifferent, it will not therefore
Diſe •• dit you, to acknowldge me your Father,
• ha • kning to my neceſſary counſels.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Acknowledge you my Father? Sir I do,
A •• may impiety, conſpiring with
My other Sins, ſink me, and ſuddenly
When I forget to pay you a Sons duty
In my obedience, and that help'd forth
With all the cheerfulneſs.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I pray you riſe,
And may thoſe powers that ſee and love this in you,
R • ward you for it: Taught by your example
Having receiv'd the rights due to a Father,
I tender you th' allegeance of a Subject:
Which as my Prince accept of.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Kneel to me?
May mountains firſt fall down beneath their valleys,
And fire no more mount upwards, when I ſuffer
An act in nature ſo prepoſterous;
I muſt o'recome in this, in all things elſe
The victory be yours: could you here read me,
You ſhould perceive how all my faculties
Triumph in my bleſt fate, to be ſound yours;
I am your ſon, your ſon Sir, and am prouder
To be ſo, to the Father, to ſuch goodneſs
(Which heaven be pleas'd, I may inherit from you)
Than I ſhall ever of thoſe ſpecious titles
That plead for my ſucceſſion in the Earldom
(Did I poſſeſs it now) left by my Mother.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I do believe it: but—

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: O my lov'd Father,
Before I knew you were ſo, by inſtinct,
Nature had taught me, to look on your wants,
Not as a ſtranger's: and I know not how,
What you call'd charity, I thought the payment
Of ſome religious debt, nature ſtood bound for;
And 〈◊〉 of all, when your magnificent bounty
In in, low ebb of fortune, had brought in
A ſtood of bleſſings, though my threatning wants
And fear of their effects, ſtill kept me ſtupid,
I ſoon found out, it was no common pity
That led you to it.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Think of this hereafter
When we with joy may call it to remembrance,
There will be a time, more opportune, than now
To end our ſtory, with all circumſtances,
I add this only: when we fled from Wolfort
I ſent you into England, and there placed you
With a brave Flanders Merchant, call'd rich Goſwin,
A man ſupplyed by me unto that purpoſe,
As bound by oath never to diſcover you,
Who dying, left his name and wealth unto you
As his reputed Son, and yet receiv'd ſo;
But now, as Florez, and a Prince, remember
The countreys, and the ſubjects general good
Muſt challenge the firſt part in your affection:
The • ai • maid, whom you choſe to be your wife,
Being ſo fa • beneath you, that your love
Muſt grant ſhe's not your equal.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: In deſcent
Or borrowed glories from dead Anceſtors,
But to, her beauty, chaſtity, and all vertues
• v •• remembred in the beſt of women,
A Mona • ch might receive from her, not give,
Though • he were his Crowns purchaſe; in this only
Be an in ſulyent Father: in all elſe,
Uſe your authority.

div.stage: Enter Hubert, Hemskirk, Wolfort, Bertha, and Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Sir, here be two of 'em,
The Father and the Son, the reſt you ſhall have
As faſt as I can rouze them.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Who's this? Wolfort?

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: I Criple, your ſeigned crutches will not help yo • ,
Nor patch'd diſguiſe that hath ſo long conceal'd you,
It's now no halting: I muſt here find Gerrard,
And in this Merchants habit, one call'd Florez
Who would be an Earl.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: And is, wert thou a ſubject.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Is this that Traitor Wolfort?

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: Yes, but you
Are they that are betrai'd: Hemskirk.
My Goſwin
Turn'd Prince? O I am poorer by this greatneſs,
Than all my former jealouſies or misfortunes.

l.hi: Gertrude?

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: Stay Sir, you were to day too near her,
You muſt no more aim at thoſe eaſie acceſſes,
Leſs you can do't in air, without a head,
Which ſhall be ſuddenly tri'd.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: O take my heart, firſt,
And ſince I cannot hope now to enjoy him,
Let me but fall a part of his glad ranſom.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: You know not your own value, that entreat.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: So proud a fiend as Wolfort.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: For ſo loſt
A thing as Florez.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: And that would be ſo
Rather than ſhe ſhould ſtoop again to thee;
There is no death, but's ſweeter than all life,
When Wolfort is to give it: O my Gertrude,
It is not that, nor Princedom that I goe from,
It is from thee, that loſs includeth all.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: I, if my young Prince knew his loſs, he w ••• ſayſe
Which that he yet may chew on, I will tell him
This is no Gertrude, nor no Hemskirks Niece,
Nor Vandunks Daughter: this is Bertha, Bertha,
The heir of Brabant, ſhe that caus'd the war,
Whom I did ſteal, during my treaty there,
In your minority, to raiſe my ſelf;
I then fore-ſeeing 'twould beget a quarel,
That, a neceſſity of my employment,
The ſame employment, make me maſter of ſtrength,
That ſtrength, the Lord of Flanders, ſo of Brabant,
By marrying her: which had not been to doe Sir,
She come of years, but that the expectation
Firſt of her Fathers death, retarded it,
And ſince the ſtanding out of Bruges, where
Hemskirk had hid her, till ſhe was near loſt:
But Sir, we have recover'd her: your Merchantſhip
May break, for this was one of your beſt bottoms
I think.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Inſolent Devil!

div.stage: Enter Hubert, with Jaqueline, Ginks, and Coſtin.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: Who are theſe, Hemskirk?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: More, more, Sir.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: How they triumph in their treachery!

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Lord Arnold of Benthuſin, this Lord Coſtin,
This Jaqueline the ſiſter unto Florez.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: All found? why here's brave game, this was ſp ••• roy ••
And puts me in thought of a new kind of death for 'em.
Huntſ-man, your horn: firſt wind me Florez fall,
Next Gerrards, then his Daughter Jaquelins,
Thoſe raſcals, they ſhall dye without their rights:
Hang 'em Hemskirk on theſe trees; I'le take
The aſſay of theſe my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Hub.
sp.l: Not here my Lord,
Let 'em be broken up upon a ſcaffold,
I will ſhew the better when their arbour's made.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Wretch, art thou not content thou haſt betrai'd us,
〈◊〉 mock us too?
Falſe Hubert, this is monſtrous.

l.hi: Hubert?

sp.speaker: Hem.
sp.l: Who, this?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Yes this is Hubert, Wolfort,
〈◊〉 he has helpt himſelf to a tree.
The firſt,
••• firſt of any, and moſt glad I have you Sir,
〈◊〉 you goe before, but for a train;
〈…〉 have done this ſervice?
As your Huntſ-man,
〈◊〉 now as Hubert; ſave your ſelves, I will,

〈◊〉
Wolfs a foot, let ſlip; kill, kill, kill, kill.

div.stage: Enter with a drum Van-dunk, Merchants, Higgen, Prig, Ferret, Snap.

sp.l: Betray'd?

sp.speaker: Hab.
sp.l: No, but well catch'd: and I the Huntſman.

sp.speaker: Van-d.
sp.l: How do you Wolfort? Raſcal, good knave Wolfort,
〈◊〉 ſpeak it now without the Roſe, and Hemskirk,
• ogue Hemskirk, you that have no nicce, this Lady
Was ſtoln by you, and ta'ne by you, and now
• eſign'd by me, to the right owner here:
• ake her my Prince.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Can this be poſſible,
W • lcom my love, my ſweet, my worthy love.

sp.speaker: Van-d.
sp.l: I ha' giv'n you her twice: now keep her better, and thank
• ord Hubert, that came to me in Gerrards name,
• nd got me out, with my brave Boyes, to march

〈◊〉
Caeſar, when he bred his Commentaries,
• o I, to 〈◊〉 my Chronicle, came forth

l.hi: Caſar Van-dunk, & veni, vidi, vici,

sp.l: Give me my Bottle, and ſet down the drum;
• ou had your tricks Sir, had you? we ha' tricks too,
• ou ſtole the Lady?

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: And we led your Squadrons,
Where they ha' ſcratch'd their leggs a little, with brambles,
〈◊〉 not their faces.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Yes, and run their heads
• gainſt trees.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: 'Tis Captain Prig, Sir.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: And Coronel Higgen.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: We have fill'd a pit with your people, ſome with leggs,
• ome with arms broken, and a neck or two
〈◊〉 think be looſe.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: The reſt too, that eſcap'd,
Are not yet out o'the briars,

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: And your horſes, Sir,
Are well ſet up in Bruges all by this time:
You look as you were not well Sir, and would be
• cortly let blood; do you want a ſcarf?

sp.speaker: Van-d.
sp.l: A halter.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: 'Twas like your ſelf, honeſt, and noble Hubert:
Can'ſt thou behold theſe mirrors all together,
Of thy long, falſe, and bloody uſurpation?
Thy tyrrannous proſcription, and freſh treaſon:
And not ſo ſee thy ſelf, as to fall down
And ſinking, force a grave, with thine own guilt,
As deep as hell, to cover thee and it?

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: No, I can ſtand: and praiſe the toyles that took me
And laughing in them dye, they were brave ſnares.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: 'Twere truer valour, if thou durſt repent
The wrongs th' haſt done, and live.

sp.speaker: Wol.
sp.l: Who, I repent?
And ſay I am ſorry? yes, 'tis the fool's language
And not for Wolfort.

sp.speaker: Van-d.
sp.l: Wolfort, thou art a Devil,
And ſpeakſt his language, oh that I had my longing
Under this row of trees now would I hang him.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: No let him live, until he can repent,
But baniſh'd from our State, that is thy doom.

sp.speaker: Van-d.
sp.l: Then hang his worthy Captain here, this Hemskirk
For profit of th' example.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: No let him
Enjoy his ſhame too: with his conſcious life,
To ſhew how much our innocence contemns
All practice from the guiltieſt, to moleſt us.

sp.speaker: Van-d.
sp.l: A noble Prince.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Sir, you muſt help to join
Apair of hands, as they have done their hearts here,
And to their loves with joy.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: As to mine own,
My gracious Siſter, worthieſt Brother.

sp.speaker: Van.
sp.l: I'le go afore, and have the bon-fire made,
My fire-works, & flap dragons, and good backrack,
With a peek of little fiſhes, to drink down
In healths to this day.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: 'Slight, here be changes,
The Bells ha' not ſo many, nor a dance, Prig.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Our Company's grown horrible thin by it,
What think you Ferret?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Many I do think,
That we might all be Lords now, if we could ſtand for't.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Not I if they ſhould offer it: I'le diſlodge firſt,
Remove the Buſh to another climat.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Sir, you muſt thank this worthy Burgomaſter,
Here be friends ask to be look'd on too,
And thank'd, who though their trade, and courſe of life
Be not ſo perfect, but it may be better'd,
Have yet us'd me with courteſy, and been true
Subjects unto me, while I was their King,
A place I know not well how to reſign,
Nor unto whom: But this I will entreat
Your grace, command them follow you to Bruges;
Where I will take the care on me, to find
Some manly, and more profitable courſe
To fit them, as a part of the Republique

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Do you hear Sirs? do ſo.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Thanks to your good grace.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: To your good Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: May you both live long. all but Beggars.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Attend meat Van-dunks, the Burgomaſters. Ex.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Yes, to beat hemp, and be whipt twice a week,
Or turn the wheel, for Crab the Rope maker:
Or learn to go along with him, his courſe;
That's a fine courſe now, i' the common-wealth, Prig.
What ſay you to it?

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: It is the backwardſt courſe,
I know i'the world.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Then Higgen will ſcarce thrive by it,
You do conclude?

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: 'Faith hardly, very hardly,

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Troth I am partly of your mind, Prince Prig;
And therefore farewel Flanders, Higgen will ſeek
Some ſafer ſhelter, in ſome other Climat,
With this his tatter'd Colony: Let me ſee
Snap, Ferret, Prig, and Higgen, all are left
O' the true blood: what? ſhall we into England?

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Agreed.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Then bear up bravely with your Brute my lads,
Higgen hath prig'd the prancers in his dayes,
And ſold good penny-worths; we will have a courſe,
The Spirit of Bottom, is grown bottomleſs.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: I'le mand no more, nor cant.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: Yes, your ſixpenny worth
In private, Brother, ſixpence is a ſum
I'le ſteal you any mans Dogg for.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: For ſixpence more
You'l tell the owner where he is.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: 'Tis right,
Higgen muſt practiſe, ſo muſt Prig to eat;
And write the Letter: and gi' the word. But now
No more, as either of theſe.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: But as true Beggars,
As e're we were.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: We ſtand here, for an Epilogue;
Ladies, your bounties firſt, the reſt will follow,
For womens ſavours are a leading alms,
If you be pleas'd look cheerly, throw your eyes
Out at your masks.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: And let your beauties ſparkle.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: So may you ne'er want dreſſings, Jewels, gowns
Still I the faſhion.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: Nor the men you love,
Wealth nor diſcourſe to pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: May you Gentlemen,
Never want good freſh ſuits nor liberty.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: May every Merchant here ſee ſafe his ventures.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: And every honeſt Citizen his debts in.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: The Lawyers again good Clyents.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: And the Clyents good Counſel.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: All the Gameſters here good fortune.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: The Drunkards too good wine.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: The eaters meat
Fit for their taſtes and palats.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: The good wives kind Husbands.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: The young maids choyce of Sutors.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: The Midwives merry hearts.

sp.speaker: Prig.
sp.l: And all good cheer.

sp.speaker: Hig.
sp.l: As you are kind unto us and our Buſh,
We are the Beggars and your daily Beadſmen,
And have your mony, but the Alms we ask
And live by, is your Grace, give that, and then
We'l boldly ſay our word is, Come again.

list.item: King Antigonus, an old Man with young deſires.
Demetrius, Son to Antigonus, in love with Celia.

list.head: Three Kings equal ſharers with Antigonus of what Alexander had, with united powers oppoſing Antigonus.

list.item: Leontius, a brave old merry Souldier, aſſiſtant to Demetrius.

list.head: Servants to Antigonus, and his vices.

list.item: Gentlemen, Friends and followers of Demetrius.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Celia alias Evanthe, Daughter to Seleucus, Miſtris to Demetrius.
Leucippe, a Bawd, Agent for the Kings luſt.

div.head: Scena prima.
div.stage: Enter 2 Uſhers, and Grooms with perfumes.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſher.
sp.l: ROund, round, perfume it round, quick, look ye
Diligently the ſtate be right, are theſe the richeſt
Cuſhions? Fie, fie, who waits i'th' wardrobe?

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: But pray tell me, do you think for certain
• heſe Embaſſadours ſhall have this morning audience?

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: They ſhall have it: Lord that you live at Court
• nd underſtand not! I tell you they muſt have it.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Upon what neceſſity?

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Still you are out of the trick of Court, fell your place,
And ſow your grounds, you are not for this tillage.
Madams, the beſt way is the upper lodgings,
There you may ſee at eaſe.

sp.speaker: Ladies.
sp.l:
We thank you, Sir.
Ex. Ladies, Gent.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Would you have all theſe ſlighted? who ſhould report then,
The Embaſſadors were handſome men? his beard
A neat one? the fire of his eyes quicker than lightning,
And when it breaks, as blaſting? his legs, though litle ones,
Yet movers of a maſs of underſtanding?
Who ſhall commend their Cloaths? who ſhall take notice
Of the moſt wiſe behaviour of their Feathers?
Ye live a raw man here.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: I think I do ſo.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Why, whither would ye all preſs?

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.l: Good Maſter Ʋſher.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: My wife, and ſome few of my honeſt neighbours, here.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Prethee begone thou and thy honeſt Neighbours,
Thou lookſt like an Aſs, why, whither would you ſith face?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: If I might have
But the honour to ſee you at my poor houſe, Sir,
A Capon bridled and ſadled, I'le aſſure your worſhip,
A ſhoulder of Mutton and a pottle of Wine, Sir,
I know your Brother, he was as like ye,
And ſhot the beſt at Buts—

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: A — upon thee.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: Some Muſick I'le aſſure you too,
My toy, Sir, can play o'th' Virginals.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Prethee good toy,
Take away thy ſhoulder of Mutton, it is flie-blown,
And ſhoulder take thy flap along, here's no place for ye;
Nay then you had beſt be knock'd. Ex. Cit.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I wou'd fain ſee him,
The glory of this place makes me remember,
But dye thoſe thoughts, dye all but my deſires,
Even thoſe to death are ſick too; he's not here,
Nor how my eyes may guide me —

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: What's your buſineſs?
Who keeps the outward door there? here's fine ſhuffling,
You waſtcoateer you muſt go back.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: There is not,
There cannot be, ſix days and never ſee me?
There muſt not be deſire; Sir, do you think
That if you had a Miſtris—

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Death, ſhe is mad.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And were your ſelf an honeſt man? it cannot—

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: What a Devil haſt thou to do with me or my honeſty?
Will you be jogging, good nimble tongue,
My fellow door-keeper.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Prethee let her alone.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: The King is coming,
And ſhall we have an agent from the Suburbs
Come to crave audience too?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Before I thought ye
To have a little breeding, ſome tang of Gentry;
But now I take ye plainly,
Without the help of any perſpective,
For that ye cannot alter.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: An Aſs, Sir, you bray as like one,
And by my troth, me thinks as ye ſtand now,
Conſidering who to kick next, you appear to me
Juſt with that kind of gravity, and wiſdom;
Your place may bea • the name of Gentleman,
But if ever any of that butter ſtick to your bread —

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: You muſt be modeſter.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Let him uſe me nobler,
And wear good Cloaths to do good Offices;
They hang upon a fellow of his vertue,
As though they hung on Gibbets.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: A perillous wench.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Thruſt her into a corner, I'le no more on her.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: You have enough, go pretty Maid, ſtand cloſe,
And uſe that little tongue, with a little more temper.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I thank ye, Sir.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: When the ſhow's paſt,
I'le have ye into the Cellat, there we'll dine.
A very pretty wench, a witty Rogue,
And there we'll be as merry; can ye be merry?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: O very merry.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Only our ſelves; this churliſh fellow ſhall not know

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: By no means.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: And can you love a little?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Love exceedingly:
I have cauſe to love you, dear Sir.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Then I'le carry ye,
And ſhew you all the pictures, and the hangings,
The Lodgings, Gardens, and the walks: and then, ſweet,
You ſhall tell me where you lye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Yes marry will I.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: And't ſhall go hard but I'le ſend ye a Veniſon Paſty▪
And bring a bottle of wine along.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Make room there.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Room there afore, ſtand cloſe, the train is coming

div.stage: Enter King Antigonus, Timon, Charinthus, Menipp •

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Have I yet left a beauty to catch fools?
Yet, yet, I ſee him not. O what a miſery
Is love, expected long, deluded longer!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Conduct in the Embaſſadors.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Make room there.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l:
They ſhall not wait long anſwer—
〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Yet he comes not.
Why are eyes ſet on theſe, and multitudes
Follow to make theſe wonders? O good gods!
What would theſe look like if my love were here?
But I am fond, forgetful.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Now your grievance,
Speak ſhort, and have as ſhort diſpatch.

sp.speaker: 1 Emb.
sp.l: Then thus, Sir:
In all our Royal Maſters names, We tell you,
Ye have done injuſtice, broke the bonds of concord,
And from their equal ſhares, from Alexander
Parted, and ſo poſſeſs'd, not like a Brother,
But as an open Enemy, Ye have hedged in
Whole Provinces, man'd and maintain'd theſe injuries;
And daily with your ſword (though they ſtill honour ye)
Make bloudy inroads, take Towns, and ruin Caſtles,
And ſtill their ſufferance feels the weight.

sp.speaker: 2 Em.
sp.l: Think of that love great, Sir, that honor'd friendſhip
Your ſelf held with our Maſters, think of that ſtrength
VVhen you were all one body, all one mind;
VVhen all your ſwords ſtruck one way, when your angers,
Like ſo many brother Billows roſe together,
And curling up your foaming Creſts, defied
Even mighty Kings, and in their falls entomb'd 'em;
O think of theſe; and you that have been Conquerours,
That ever led your Fortunes open ey'd,
Chain'd faſt by confidence; you that fame courted,
Now ye want Enemies and men to match ye,
Let not your own Swords ſeek your ends to ſhame ye.

div.stage: Enter Demetrius with a Javelin, and Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 3 Em.
sp.l: Chooſe which you will, or Peace or War,
We come prepar'd for either.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Room for the Prince there.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Was it the Prince they ſaid? how my heart trembled!
'Tis he indeed; what a ſweet noble fierceneſs
Dwells in his eyes! young Meleager like,
When he return'd from ſlaughter of the Boar,
Crown'd with the loves and honours of the people,
With all the gallant youth of Greece, he looks now,
Who could deny him love?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Hail Royal Father.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Ye are welcome from your ſport, Sir, do you ſee th • s Gent.
You that bring Thunders in your mouths, and Earthquakes
To ſhake and totter my deſigns? can you imagine
(You men of poor and common apprehenſions)
VVhile I admit this man, my Son, this nature
That in one look carries more fire, and fierceneſs,
Than all your Maſters in their lives; dare I admit him,
Admit him thus, even to my ſide, my boſom,
When he is fit to rule, when all men cry him,
And all hopes hang about his head; thus place him,
His weapon hatched in bloud, all theſe attending
When he ſhall make their fortunes, all as ſudden
In any expedition he ſhall point 'em,
As arrows from a Tartars bow, and ſpeeding
D •• e I do this, and fear an enemy?
Fear your great Maſter? yours? or yours?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: O Hercules!
Who ſaies you do, Sir? Is there any thing
In theſe mens faces, or their Maſters actions,
Able to work ſuch wonders?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Now he ſpeaks:
O I could dwell upon that tongue for ever.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: You call 'em Kings, they never wore thoſe Royalties,
Nor in the progreſs of their lives arriv'd yet
At any thought of King: Imperial dignities,
And powerful God-like actions, fit for Princes
They can no more put on, and make 'em ſit right,
Than I can with this mortal hand hold Heaven:
Poor petty men, nor have I yet forgot
The chiefeſt honours time, and merit gave 'em:
L • ſimachus your Maſter, at the beſt,
His higheſt, and his hopeful'ſt Dignities
Was but grand-maſter of the Elephants;
Se ••• chus of the Treaſure; and for Ptolomey,
A thing not thought on then, ſcarce heard of yet,
Some Maſter of Ammunition: and muſt theſe men—

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: What a brave confidence flows from his ſpirit!
O ſweet young man!

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Muſt theſe hold pace with us,
And on the ſame file hang their memories?
Moſt theſe examine what the wills of Kings are?
•• eſcribe to their deſigns, and chain their actions
To their reſtraints? be friends, and foes when they pleaſe?
Send out their Thunders, and their menaces,
As if the ſate of mortal things were theirs?
Go home good men, and tell your Maſters from us,
We do 'em too much honour to force from 'em
Their barren Countries, ruin their vaſt Cities,
And tell 'em out of love, we mean to leave 'em
(Since they will needs be Kings) no more to tread on,
Than they have able wits, and powers to manage,
And ſo we ſhall befriend 'em. Ha! what does ſhe there?

sp.speaker: Emb.
sp.l: This is your anſwer King?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis like to prove ſo.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Fie, ſweet, what makes you here?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Pray ye do not chide me.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: You do your ſelf much wrong and me.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Pray you pardon me,
I feel my fault which only was committed
Through my dear love to you: I have not ſeen ye,
And how can I live then? I have not ſpoke to ye—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I know this week ye have not; I will redeem all.
You are ſo tender now; think where you are, ſweet.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: What other light have I left?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Prethee Celia,
Indeed I'le ſee you preſently.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I have done, Sir:
You will not miſs?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: By this, and this, I will not.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: 'Tis in your will and I muſt be obedient.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: No more of theſe aſſemblies.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I am commanded.

sp.speaker: 1 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Room for the Lady there: Madam, my ſervice—

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: My Coach an't pleaſe you Lady.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Room before there.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: The honour, Madam, but to wait upon you—
My ſervants and my ſtate.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Lord, how they ſtock now?
Before I was afraid they would have beat me;
How theſe flies play i'th' Sun-ſhine? pray ye no ſervices,
Or if ye needs muſt play the Hobby-horſes,
Seek out ſome beauty that affects 'em: farewel,
Nay pray ye ſpare: Gentlemen I am old enough
To go alone at theſe years, without crutches. Exit.

sp.speaker: 2 Ʋſh.
sp.l: Well I could curſe now: but that will not help me,
I made as ſure account of this wench now, immediately,
Do but conſider how the Devil has croſt me,
Meat for my Maſter ſhe cries, well—

sp.speaker: 3 Em.
sp.l: Once more, Sir,
We ask your reſolutions: Peace or War yet?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: War, War, my noble Father.

sp.speaker: 1 Em.
sp.l: Thus I fling it:
And fair ey'd peace, farewel.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You have your anſwer;
Conduct out the Embaſſadours, and give 'em Convoyes.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Tell your high hearted Maſters, they ſhall not ſeek us,
Nor cool i'th' field in expectation of us,
We'l eaſe your men thoſe marches: In their ſtrengths,
And full abilities of mind and courage,
We'l find 'em out, and at their beſt trim buckle with 'em.

sp.speaker: 3 Em.
sp.l: You will find ſo hot a Souldier's welcome, Sir,
Your favour, ſhall not freeze.

sp.speaker: 2 Em.
sp.l: A forward Gentleman,
Pity the Wars ſhould bruiſe ſuch hopes—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l:
Conduct 'em—
Ex. Em.
Now, for this preparation: where's Leontius?
Call him in preſently: for I mean in perſon Gentlemen
My ſelf, with my old fortune—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Royal Sir:
Thus low I beg this honour: fame already
Hath every where rais'd Trophies to your glory,
And conqueſt now grown old, and weak with following
The weary marches and the bloody ſhocks
You daily ſet her in: 'tis now ſcarce honour
For you that never knew to fight, but conquer,
To ſparkle ſuch poor people: the Royal Eagle
