When ſhe hath tri'd yet young ones 'gainſt the Sun,
And ſound 'em right; next teacheth 'em to prey,
How to command on wing, and check below her
Even Birds of noble plume; I am your own, Sir,
You have found my ſpirit, try it now, and teach it
To ſtoop whole Kingdoms: leave a little for me:
Let not your glory be ſo greedy, Sir,
To eat up all my hopes; you gave me life,
If to that life you add not what's more laſting
A noble name, for man, you have made a ſhadow:
Bleſs me this day: bid me go on, and lead,
Bid me go on, no leſs fear'd, than Antigonus,
And to my maiden ſword, tye faſt your fortune:
I know 'twill ſight it ſelf then: dear Sir, honour me:
Never fair Virgin long'd ſo.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Riſe, and command then,
And be as fortunate, as I expect ye:
I love that noble will; your young companions
Bred up and foſter'd with ye, I hope Demetrius,
You will make ſouldiers too: they muſt not leave ye.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Never till life leave us, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: O Leontius,
Here's work for you in hand.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I am ev'n right glad, Sir.
For by my troth, I am now grown old with idleneſs;
I hear we ſhall abroad, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes, and preſently,
But who think you commands now?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Who commands, Sir?
Methinks mine eye ſhould guide me: can there be
(If you your ſelf will ſpare him ſo much honour)
Any found out to lead before your Armies,
So full of faith, and fire, as brave Demetrius?
King Philips Son, at his years was an old Souldier,
'Tis time his Fortune be o' wing, high time, Sir,
So many idle hours, as here he loyters,
So many ever-living names he loſes,
I hope 'tis he,

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis he indeed, and nobly
He ſhall ſet forward: draw you all thoſe Garriſons
Upon the frontiers as you paſs: to thoſe
Joyn theſe in pay at home, our ancient ſouldiers,
And as you go preſs all the Provinces.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We ſhall not ned;
Believe, this hopefull Gentleman
Can want no ſwords nor honeſt hearts to follow him,
We ſhall be full, no fear Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You Leontius,
Becauſe you are an old and faithfull ſervant,
And know the wars, with all his vantages,
Be near to his inſtructions, leſt his youth
Loſe valours beſt companion, ſtaid diſcretion,
Shew where to lead, to lodge, to charge with ſafetie;
In execution not to break, nor ſcatter,
But with a provident anger, follow nobly:
Not covetous of blood, and death, but honour,
Be ever near his watches; cheer his labours,
And where his hope ſtands fair, provoke his valour;
Love him, and think it no diſhonour (my Demetrius)
To wear this Jewel near thee; he is a tri'd one,
And one that even in ſpight of time, that ſunk him,
And froſted up his ſtrength, will yet ſtand by thee,
And with the proudeſt of thine Enemies
Exchange for bloud, and bravely: take his Counſel.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Your grace hath made me young again, and wanton.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She muſt be known and ſuddenly:
Do ye know her? to Minippus.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Char. No, believe Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Did you obſerve her, Timon?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: I look'd on her,
But what ſhe is —

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I muſt have that found.
Come in and take your leave.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: And ſome few Prayers along.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l:
I know my duty,
Exit Ant.
You ſhall be half my Father.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: All your Servant:
Come Gentlemen, you are reſolv'd I am ſure
To ſee theſe wars.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: We dare not leave his fortunes,
Though moſt aſſur'd death hung round about us.

sp.speaker: Leo
sp.l: That bargain's yet to make;
Be not too haſty, when ye face the Enemie,
Nor too ambitious to get honour inſtantly,
But charge within your bounds, and keep cloſe bodies,
And you ſhall ſee what ſport we'l make theſe mad-caps;
You ſhall have game enough, I warrant ye,
Every mans Co • k ſhall fight.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I muſt go ſee Sir:
Brave Sir, as ſoon as I have taken leave,
He meet you in the park;
D • aw the men thither,
Wait you upon Leontius.
We'l attend Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: But I beſeech your Grace, with ſpeed; the ſooner
We are i'th' field.—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: You could not pleaſe me better. Exit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You never ſaw the wars yet?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Not yet Colonel.

sp.speaker: Leo
sp.l: Theſe fooliſh Miſtreſſes do ſo hang about ye,
So whimper, and ſo hug, I know it Gentlemen,
And ſo intice ye, now ye are i'th' bud;
And that ſweet tilting war, with eyes and kiſſes,
Th'alarms of ſoft vows, and ſighs, and fiddle faddles,
Spoils all our trade: you muſt forget theſe knick knacks,
A woman at ſome time of year, I grant ye
She is neceſſarie; but make no buſineſs of her.
How now Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Lieu
sp.l: Oh Sir, as ill as ever;
We ſhall have wars they ſay; they are muſtring yonder:
Would we were at it once: fie, how it plagues me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Here's one has ſerved now under Captain Cupid,

And crackt a Pike in's youth: you ſee what's come o •
•• .

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: No, my diſeaſe will never prove ſo honourabl • .

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why ſure, thou haſt the beſt pox.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: If I have 'em,
I am ſure I got 'em in the beſt company;
They are pox of thirty Coats.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Thou haſt mewed 'em finely:
Here's a ſtrange fellow now, and a brave fellow,
If we may ſay ſo of a pocky fellow,
(Which I believe we may) this poor Lieutenant;
Whether he have the ſcratches, or the ſcabs,
Or what a Devil it be, I'le ſay this for him,
Show him an Enemie, his pain's forgot ſtraight;
And where other men by beds and bathes have eaſe,
And eaſie rules of Phyſick; ſet him in a danger,
A danger, that's a fearfull one indeed,
Ye rock him, and he will ſo play about ye,
Let it be ten to one he ne'er comes off again,
Ye have his heart: and then he works it bravely,
And throughly bravely: not a pang remembred:
I have ſeen him do ſuch things, belief would ſhrink at.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange he ſhould do all this, and diſeas'd ſo.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I am ſure 'tis true: Lieutenant, canſt thou drink well?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Would I were drunk, dog-drunk, I might not feel this.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I would take Phyſick.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: But I would know my diſeaſe firſt.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Why? it may be the Colique: canſt thou blow backward?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: There's never a bag-pipe in the Kingdom better.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Is't not a pleureſie?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: 'Tis any thing
That has the Devil, and death in't: will ye march Gentlemen?
The Prince has taken leave.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: How know ye that?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I ſaw him leave the Court, diſpatch his followers,
And met him after in a by ſtreet: I think
He has ſome wench, or ſuch a toy, to lick over
Before he go: would I had ſuch another
To draw this fooliſh pain down.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Let's away Gentlemen,
For ſure the Prince will ſtay on us.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: We'l attend Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Muſt ye needs go?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Or ſtay with all diſhonour.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Are there not men enough to fight?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Fie Celia.
This ill becomes the noble love you bear me;
Would you have your love a coward?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No; believe Sir,
I would have him fight, but not ſo far off from me.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Wouldſt have it thus? or thus?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: If that be fighting —

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Ye wanton fool: when I come home again
I'le fight with thee, at thine own weapon Celia,
And conquer thee too.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: That you have done already,
You need no other Arms to me, but theſe Sir;
But will you fight your ſelf Sir?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thus deep in bloud wench,
And through the thickeſt ranks of Pikes.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Spur bravely
Your firie Courſer, beat the troops before ye,
And cramb the mouth of death with executions.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I would do more than theſe: But prethee tell me,
Tell me my fair, where got'ſt thou this male Spirit?
I wonder at thy mind.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Were I a man then,
You would wonder more.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Sure thou wouldſt prove a Souldier,
And ſome great Leader.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Sure I ſhould do ſomewhat;
And the firſt thing I did, I ſhould grow envious,
Extreamly envious of your youth, and honour.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And fight againſt me?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Ten to one, I ſhould do it.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thou wouldſt not hurt me?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: In this mind I am in
I think I ſhould be hardly brought to ſtrike ye,
Unleſs 'twere thus; but in my mans mind—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I ſhould be friends with you too,
Now I think better.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Ye are a tall Souldier:
Here, take theſe, and theſe;
This gold to furniſh ye, and keep this bracelet;
Why do you weep now?
You a maſculine Spirit?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No, I confeſs, I am a fool, a woman:
And ever when I part with you—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: You ſhall not,
Theſe tears are like prodigious ſigns, my ſweet one,
I ſhall come back, loaden with fame, to honour thee.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I hope you ſhall:
But then my dear Demetrius,
When you ſtand Conquerour, and at your mercy
All people bow, and all things wait your ſentence;
Say then your eye (ſurveying all your conqueſt)
• inds out a beautie, even in ſorrow excellent,
A conſtant face, that in the midſt of ruine
With a forc'd ſmile, both ſcorns at fate, and fortune:
Say you find ſuch a one, ſo nobly fortified,
And in her figure all the ſweets of nature?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Prethee,
No more of this, I cannot find her.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: That ſhews as far beyond my wither'd beauty;
And will run mad to love ye too.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Do you fear me,
And do you think, beſides this face, this beauty,
This heart, where all my hopes are lock'd —

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I dare not:
No ſure, I think ye honeſt; wondrous honeſt.
Pray do not frown, I'le ſwear ye are.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Ye may chooſe.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: But how long will ye be away?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I know not.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I know you are angry now: pray look upon me:
• e ask no more ſuch queſtions.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: The Drums beat,
I can no longer ſtay.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: They do but call yet:
How fain you would leave my Company?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I wou'd not,
Unleſs a greater power than love commanded,
Commands my life, mine honour.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: But a little.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Prethee farewel, and be not doubtfull of me.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I would not have ye hurt: and ye are ſo ventrous—
But good ſweet Prince preſerve your ſelf, fight nobly,
But do not thruſt this body, 'tis not yours now,
'Tis mine, 'tis only mine: do not ſeek wounds, Sir,
For every drop of blood you bleed —

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I will Celia,
I will be carefull.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: My heart, that loves ye dearly.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Prethee no more, we muſt part:
Hark, they march now. Drums a March.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Pox on theſe bawling Drums: I am ſure you'l kiſs me,
But one kiſs? what a parting's this?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Here take me,
And do what thou wilt with me, ſmother me;
But ſtill remember, if your fooling with me,
Make me forget the truſt —

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I have done: farewel Sir,
Never look back, you ſhall not ſtay, not a minute.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I muſt have one farewel more.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No, the Drums beat;
I dare not ſlack your honour; not a hand more,
Only this look; the gods preſerve, and ſave ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: WHat, have ye found her out?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: We have hearkned after her.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What's that to my deſire?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Your grace muſt give us time,
And a little means.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: She is ſure a ſtranger,
If ſhe were bred or known here—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Your dull endeavours
Should never be employ'd. Welcom Menippus.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I have found her Sir,
I mean the place ſhe is lodg'd in; her name is Celia,
And much adoe I had to purchaſe that too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Doſt think Demetrius loves her?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Much I fear it,
But nothing that way yet can win for certain.
I'le tell your grace within this hour.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A ſtranger?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Without all doubt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But how ſhould he come to her?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: There lies the marrow of the matter hid yet.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Haſt thou been with thy wife?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: No Sir, I am going to her.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Go and diſpatch, and meet me in the garden,
And get all out ye can. Exit.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I'le doe my beſt Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Bleſt be thy wife, thou wert an arrant aſs elſe.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: I, ſhe is a ſtirring woman indeed:
There's a brain Brother.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: There's not a handſom wench of any mettle
Within an hundred miles, but her intelligence
Reaches her, and out-reaches her, and brings her
As confidently to Court, as to a ſanctuary:
What had his mouldy brains ever arriv'd at,
Had not ſhe beaten it out o'th' Flint to faſten him?
They ſay ſhe keeps an office of Concealments:
There is no young wench, let her be a Saint,
Unleſs ſhe live i'th' Center, but ſhe finds her,
And every way prepares addreſſes to her:
If my wife would have followed her courſe Charinthus,
Her lucky courſe, I had the day before him:
O what might I have been by this time, Brother?
But ſhe (forſooth) when I put theſe things to her,
Theſe things of honeſt thrift, groans, O my conſcience,
The load upon my conſcience, when to make us cuc •
They have no more burthen than a brood-grooſe,
But let's doe what we can, though this wench fail us,
Another of a new way will be lookt at:
Come, let's abroad, and beat our brains, time may
For all his wiſdom, yet give us a day. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA II.
div.stage: Drum within, Alarm, Enter Demetrius, and Leontius.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I will not ſee 'em fall thus, give me way Sir,
I ſhall forget you love me elſe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Will ye loſe all?
For me to be forgotten, to be hated,
Nay never to have been a man, is nothing,
So you, and thoſe we have preſerv'd from ſlaughter
Come ſafely off.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I have loſt my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You are cozen'd.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And am moſt miſerable.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: There's no man ſo, but he that makes himſelf ſo.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I will goe on.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You muſt not: I ſhall tell you then,
And tell you true, that man's unfit to govern,
That cannot guide himſelf: you lead an Army?
That have not ſo much manly ſuff'rance leſt ye,
To bear a loſs?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Charge but once more Leontius,
My friends and my companions are engag'd all.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Nay give 'em loſt, I ſaw 'em off their horſes,
And the enemy maſter of their Arms; nor could then
The policie, nor ſtrength of man redeem 'em.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And ſhall I know this, and ſtand fooling?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: By my dead Fathers ſoul you ſtir not, Sir,
Or if you doe, you make your way through me firſt.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thou art a Coward.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: To prevent a Madman.
None but your Fathers Son, durſt call me ſo,
Death if he did — Muſt I be ſcandal'd by ye,
That hedg'd in all the helps I had to ſave ye?
That, where there was a valiant weapon ſtirring,
Both ſearch'd it out, and ſingl'd it, unedg'd it,
For fear it ſhould bite you, am I a coward?
Go, get ye up, and tell 'em ye are the Kings Son;
Hang all your Ladys favours on your Creſt,
And let them fight their ſhares; ſpur to deſtruction,
You cannot miſs the way: be bravely deſperate,
And your young friends before ye, that loſt this battel,
Your honourable friends, that knew no order,
Cry out, Antigonus, the old Antigonus,
The wiſe and fortunate Antigonus,
The great, the valiant, and the fear'd Antigonus,
Has ſent a deſperate ſon, without diſcretion
To bury in an hour his age of honour.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I am aſhamed.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: 'Tis ten to one, I die with ye:
The coward will not long be after ye;
I ſcorn to ſay I ſaw you fall, ſigh for ye,
And tell a whining tale, ſome ten years after
To boyes and girles in an old chimney corner,
Of what a Prince we had, how bravely ſpirited;
How young and fair he fell: we'l all go with ye,
And ye ſhall ſee us all, like ſacrifices
In our beſt trim, fill up the mouth of ruine.
Will this faith ſatisfie your folly? can this ſhow ye
'Tis not to die we fear, but to die poorly,
To fall, forgotten, in a multitude?
If you will needs tempt fortune now ſhe has held ye,
Held ye from ſinking up.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Pray do not kill me,
Theſe words pierce deeper than the wounds I ſuffer,
The ſmarting wounds of loſs.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ye are too tender;
Fortune has hours of loſs, and hours of honour,
And the moſt valiant feel them both: take comfort,
The next is ours, I have a ſoul deſcries it:
The angry bull never goes back for breath,
But when he means to arm his fury double.
Let this day ſet, but not the memorie,
And we ſhall find a time: How now Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Lieu
sp.l: I know not: I am mall'd: we are bravely beaten,
All ou • young gallants loſt.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Thou art hurt.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I am pepper'd,
I was i'th' midſt of all: and bang'd of all hands:
They made an anvile of my head, it rings yet;
Never ſo threſh'd: do you call this ſame? I have fam'd it;
I have got immortal ſame, but I'le no more on't;
I'le no ſuch ſcratching Saint to ſerve hereafter;
O' my conſcience I was kill'd above twenty times,
And yet I know not what a Devil's in't,
I crawled away, and lived again ſtill; I am hurt plagui • y,
But now I have nothing near ſo much pain Colonel,
They have ſliced me for that maladie.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: All the young men loſt?

sp.speaker: Lie.
sp.l: I am glad you are here: but they are all i'th' pound ••
They'l never ride o're other mens corn again, I take it,
Such frisking, and ſuch flaunting with their feathers,
And ſuch careering with their Miſtres favours;
And here muſt he be pricking out for honour,
And there got he a knock, and down goes pilgarlick,
Commends his ſoul to his ſhe-ſaint, and Exit.
Another ſpurs in there, cryes make room villains,
I am a Lord, ſcarce ſpoken, but with reverence
A Raſcal takes him o're the face, and fells him;
There lyes the Lord, the Lord be with him.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Now Sir,
Do you find this truth?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I would not.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Pox upon it,
They have ſuch tender bodies too; ſuch Culiſſes,
That one good handſom blow breaks 'em a pieces.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: How ſtands the Enemy?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Even cool enough too:
For to ſay truth he has been ſhrewdly heated,
The Gentleman no doubt will fall to his jewlips.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He marches not i'th' tail on's.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: No, plague take him,
He'l kiſs our tails as ſoon; he looks upon us,
As if he would ſay, if ye will turn again, friends,
We will belabor you a little better,
And beat a little more care into your coxcombs.
Now ſhall we have damnable Ballads out againſt us,
Moſt wicked madrigals: and ten to one, Colonel,
Sung to ſuch lowſie, lamentable tunes.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Thou art merry,
How e're the game goes: good Sir be not troubled,
A better day will draw this back again.
Pray go, and cheer thoſe left, and lead 'em off,
They are hot, and weary.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I'le doe any thing.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Lieutenant, ſend one preſently away
Toth' King, and let him know our ſtate: and hark ye,
Be ſure the meſſenger adviſe his Majeſtie
To comfort up the Prince: he's full of ſadneſs.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: When ſhall I get a Surgeon? this hot weather,
Unleſs I be well pepper'd, I ſhall ſtink, Colonel.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Go, I'le prepare thee one.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: If ye catch me then,

Fighting again, I'le eat hay with a horſe.
E •• .

div.head: SCENA III.
div.stage: Enter Leucippe (reading) and two Maids at a Table writing.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Have ye written to Merione?

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: Yes, Madam.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: And let her underſtand the hopes ſhe has,
If ſhe come ſpeedilie —

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: All theſe are ſpecified.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: And of the chain is ſent her,
And the rich ſtuff to make her ſhew more handſom here?

sp.speaker: 1 Maid.
sp.l: All this is done, Madam.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: What have you diſpatcht there?

sp.speaker: 2 Maid.
sp.l: A letter to the Country maid, and 't pleaſe ye.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: A pretty girle, but peeviſh, plaguy peeviſh:
Have ye bought the embroydered gloves, and that purſe 〈…〉 ,
And the new Curle?

sp.speaker: 2 Maid.
sp.l: They are ready packt up Madam.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Her maiden head will yield me; let me ſee now;
She is not fifteen they ſay: for her complexion —
Cloe, Cloe, Cloe, here, I have her,
Cloe, the Daughter of a Country Gentleman;
Her age upon fifteen: now her complexion,
A lovely brown; here 'tis; eyes black and rolling,
The body neatly built: ſhe ſtrikes a Lute well,
• gs moſt inticingly, theſe helps conſider'd,
• r maiden-head will amount to ſome three hundred,
〈◊〉 three hundred and fifty Crowns, 'twill bear it handſomly.
• r Father's poor, ſome little ſhare deducted,
• o buy him a hunting Nag; I, 'twill be pretty.
•• o takes care of the Merchants Wife?

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: I have wrought her.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: You know for whom ſhe is?

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: Very well, Madam,
• hough very much ado I had to make her
• pprehend that happineſs.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Theſe Kind are ſubtile;
• d ſhe not cry and blubber when you urg'd her?

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: O moſt extreamly, and ſwore ſhe would rather periſh.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Good ſigns, very good ſigns,
• mptoms of eaſie nature.
•• d ſhe the Plate?

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: She lookt upon't, and left it,
•• d turn'd again, and view'd it.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Very well ſtill.

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: At length ſhe was content to let it lye there,
• ll I call'd for't, or ſo.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: She will come?

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: Do you take me
• r ſuch a Fool, I would part without that promiſe?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: The Chamber's next the Park.

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: The Widow, Madam,
• ou bad me look upon.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Hang her, ſhe is muſty:
• e is no mans meat; beſides, ſhe's poor and ſluttiſh:
〈◊〉 here lyes old Thisbe now, you are ſo long now—

sp.speaker: 2 Ma.
sp.l: Thisbe, Thisbe, Thisbe, agent Thisbe, O I have her,
• e lyes now in Nicopolis.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Diſpatch a Packet,
• nd tell her, her Superiour here commands her
•• e next month not to fail, but ſee deliver'd
• ere to our uſe, ſome twenty young and handſom,
• s a • able Maids, for the Court ſervice,
• s ſhe will anſwer it: we are out of beauty,
•• rly out, and rub the time away here
• ith ſuch blown ſtuff, I am aſham'd to ſend it.
• ho's that? look out, to your buſineſs, Maid, Knock within.
• here's nothing got by idleneſs: there is a Lady,
• hich if I can but buckle with, Altea,
• , A, A, A, Altea young, and married,
• nd a great lover of her husband, well,
• ot to be brought to Court! ſay ye ſo? I am ſorry,
• he Court ſhall be brought to you then; how now, who is't?

sp.speaker: 1 Ma.
sp.l: An ancient woman, with a maid attending,
• pretty Girl, but out of Cloaths; for a little money,
〈◊〉 ſeems ſhe would put her to your bringing up, Madam.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Let her come in. Would you ought with us, good woman?
〈◊〉 pray be ſhort, we are full of buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Wo.
sp.l: I have a tender Girl here, an't pleaſe your honour.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Very well.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: That hath a great deſire to ſerve your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: It may be ſo; I am full of Maids.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: She is young forſooth—.
• nd for her truth; and as they ſay her bearing.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Ye ſay well; come ye hither maid, let me feel your pulſe,
• is ſomewhat weak, but Nature will grow ſtronger,
• et me ſee your leg, ſhe treads but low i'th' Paſterns.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: A cork Heel, Madam.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: We know what will do it,
• ithout your aim, good woman; what do you pitch her at?
• he's but a ſlight toy—cannot hold out long.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Even what you think is meet.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Give her ten Crowns, we are full of buſineſs,
• he is a poor Woman, let her take a Cheeſe home.

• nter the wench i' th' Office.
Ex. Wom. and 1 Ma.

sp.speaker: 2 Ma.
sp.l: What's your name, Siſter?

sp.speaker: Phe.
sp.l: Phebe, forſooth.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: A pretty name; 'twill do well:
Go in, and let the other Maid inſtruct you, Phebe, Ex. Phe.
Let my old Velvet skirt be made fit for her.
I'll put her into action for a Waſt-coat;
And when I have rigg'd her up once, this ſmall Pinnace
Shall fail for Gold, and good ſtore too; who's there?
Lord, ſhall we never have any eaſe in this world! Knock within
Still troubled! ſtill moleſted! what would you have?
I cannot furniſh you faſter than I am able,
And ye were my Husband a thouſand times, I cannot do it.
At leaſt a dozen poſts are gone this morning
For ſeveral parts of the Kingdom: I can do no more
But pay 'em, and inſtruct 'em.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Prithee, good ſweet heart,
I come not to diſturb thee, nor diſcourage thee,
I know thou labour'ſt truly: hark in thine ear.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Ha!
What do you make ſo dainty on't? look there
I am an Aſs, I can do nothing.

sp.speaker: Men.

l.hi: Celia?

sp.l: I, this is ſhe; a ſtranger born.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: What would you give for more now?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Prithee, my beſt Leucippe, there's much hangs on't,
Lodg'd at the end of Mars's ſtreet? that's true too;
At the ſack of ſuch a Town, by ſuch a Souldier
Preſerv'd a Priſoner: and by Prince Demetrius
Bought from that man again, maintain'd and favour'd:
How came you by this knowledg?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Poor, weak man,
I have a thouſand eyes, when thou art ſleeping,
Abroad, and full of buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: You never try'd her?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: No, ſhe is beyond my level; ſo hedg'd in
By the Princes infinite Love and Favour to her—

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: She is a handſome Wench.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: A delicate, and knows it;
And out of that proof arms her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Come in then;
I have a great deſign from the King to you,
And you muſt work like wax now.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: On this Lady?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: On this, and all your wits call home.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I have done
Toys in my time of ſome note; old as I am,
I think my brains will work without barm;
Take up the Books.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: As we go in, I'll tell ye. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter Antigonus, Timon, Lords and a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No face of ſorrow for this loſs, 'twill choak him,
Nor no man miſs a friend, I know his nature
So deep impreſt with grief, for what he has ſuffer'd;
That the leaſt adding to it adds to his ruine;
His loſs is not ſo infinite, I hope, Souldier.

sp.speaker: Soul.
sp.l: Faith neither great, nor out of indiſcretion.
The young men out of heat.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I gueſs the manner.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: The Prince and't like your Grace—s.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You are welcome home, Sir:
Come, no more ſorrow, I have heard your fortune,
And I my ſelf have try'd the like: clear up man,
I will not have ye take it thus; if I doubted.
Your fear had loſt, and that you had turn'd your back to 'em,
Baſely beſought their mercies—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: No, no, by this hand, Sir,
We fought like honeſt and tall men.

sp.speaker: Antig.
sp.l: I know't Leontius: or if I thought
N • gl • ct of rule, having his counſel with ye,
Or too vain glorious appetite of Fame,
Your men forgot and ſcatter'd.

sp.speaker: Leo
sp.l: None of theſe, Sir,
He ſh • w'd himſelf a noble Gentleman,
Every way apt to rule.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Theſe being granted;
Why ſhould you think you have done an act ſo hainous,
That • ought but diſcontent dwells round about ye?
I have loſt a battel.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I, and fought it hard too.
With as much means as man—

sp.speaker: Leo
sp.l: Or D • vil could • uge it.
Twenty to one of our ſide now.
Tu • n Tables,
Beaten like Dogs again, like Owls, you take it
To heart for flying out a mile before 'em;
And to ſay the truth, 'twas no flight neither, Sir,
'T was but a walk, a handſome walk,
I have tumbl'd with this old Body, beaten like a Stock-fiſh,
And ſtuck with Arrows, like an arming Quiver,
Blouded and bang'd almoſt a day before 'em,
And glad I have got off then. Here's a mad Shaver,
He fights his ſhare I am ſure, when e'r he comes to't;
Yet I have ſeen him trip it tithly too,
And cry the Devil take the hindmoſt ever.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I learnt it of my Betters.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Boudge at this?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Has Fortune but one Face?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: In her beſt Vizard
Methinks ſhe looks but lowzily.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Chance, though ſhe faint now,
And ſink below our expectations,
Is there no hope left ſtrong enough to buoy her?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: 'Tis not, this day I fled before the Enemy,
And loſt my People, left mine Honour murder'd,
My maiden Honour, never to be ranſom'd,
(Which to a noble Soul is too too ſenſible)
Afflicts me with this ſadneſs; moſt of theſe,
Time may turn ſtraight again, experience perfect,
And new Swords cut new ways to nobler Fortunes.
O I have loſt—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: As you are mine forget it:
I do not think it loſs.

sp.speaker: Dem
sp.l: O Sir, forgive me,
I have loſt my friends, thoſe worthy Souls bred with me,
I have loſt my ſelf, they were the pieces of me:
I have loſt all Arts, my Schools are taken from me,
Honour and Arms, no emulation left me:
I liv'd to ſee theſe men loſt, look'd upon it:
Theſe men that twin'd their loves to mine, their vertues;
O ſhame of ſhames! I ſaw and could not ſave 'em,
This carries Sulphur in't, this burns, and boils me,
And like a fatal Tomb, beſtrides my memory.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This was hard fortune, but if alive, and taken,
They ſhall be ranſom'd: let it be at Millions.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: They are dead, they are dead.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: When wou'd he weep for me thus?
I may be dead and powder'd.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Good Prince, grieve not:
We are not certain of their deaths: the Enemy,
Though he be hot, and keen,
Yet holds good Quarter.
What Noiſe is this?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: He does not follow us?
Give me a Steeple top?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: They live, they live, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Hold up your manly fate.
They live, they are here, Son.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Theſe are the men.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: They are, and live to honour ye.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: How 'ſcap'd ye noble friends? me thought I ſa •••
Even in the Jaws of Death.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Thanks to our folly,
That ſpur'd us on; we were indeed hedg'd round in't;
And ev'n beyond the hand of ſuccour, beaten,
Unhors'd, diſarm'd: and what we lookt for then, Sir,
Let ſuch poor weary Souls that hear the Bell knoll,
And ſee the Grave a digging, tell.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: For Heavens ſake
Delude mine Eyes no longer! how came ye off?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Againſt all expectation, the brave Selen • as,
I think this day enamour'd on your Vertue,
When, through the Troops, he ſaw ye ſhoot like lightning
And at your manly courage all took fire;
And after that, the miſery we fell to
The never certain Fate of War, conſidering,
As we ſtood all before him, Fortunes ruines,
Nothing but Death expecting, a ſhort time
He made a ſtand upon our Youths and Fortunes.
Then with an eye of mercy inform'd his Judgment,
How yet unripe we were, unblown, unharden'd,
Unfitted for ſuch fatal ends; he cryed out to us,
Go Gentlemen, commend me to your Maſter,
To the moſt High, and Hopeful Prince, Demetrius;
Tell him the Valour that he ſhowed againſt me
This day, the Virgin Valour, and true fire,
Deſerves even from an Enemy this courteſie;
Your Lives, and Arms freely I'll give 'em: thank him.
And thus we are return'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Faith, 'twas well done;
'Twas bravely done; was't not a noble part, Sir?

sp.speaker: Laeu.
sp.l: Had I been there, up had I gone, I am ſure on't;
Theſe noble tricks I never durſt truſt 'em yet.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Let me not live, and't were not a famed honeſty;
It takes me ſuch a tickling way: now would I wiſh Heaven
But e'n the happineſs, e'n that poor bleſſing
For all the ſharp afflictions thou haſt ſent me,
But e'n i'th' head o'th' field, to take Seleucus.
I ſhould do ſomething memorable: fie, ſad ſtill?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Do you grieve, we are come off?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Unranſom'd, was it?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: It was, Sir.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And with ſuch a ſame to me?
Said ye not ſo?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ye have heard it.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: O Leontius!
Better I had loſt 'em all: my ſelf had periſhed,
And all my Fathers hopes.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Mercy upon you;
What ails you, Sir? Death, do not make fools on's,
Neither go to Church, nor tarry at home,
That's a fine Horn-pipe?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What's now your grief, Demetrius?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Did he not beat us twice?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He beat, a Pudding;
Beat us but once.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: H'as beat me twice, and beat me to a Coward.
Beat me to nothing.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Is not the Devil in him?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I pray it be no worſe.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Twice conquer'd me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Bear witneſs all the world, I am a Dunce here.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: With valour firſt he ſtruck me, then with honour,
That ſtroak Leontius, that ſtroak, doſt thou not feel it?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Whereabouts was it? for I remember nothing yet.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: All theſe Gentlemen
That were his Priſoners—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Yes, he ſet 'em free, Sir,
With Arms and honour.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: There, there, now thou haſt it;
At mine own weapon, Courteſie has beaten me,
At that I was held a Maſter in, he has cow'd me,
Hotter than all the dint o'th' Fight he has charg'd me:
Am I not now a wretched fellow? think on't;
And when thou haſt examin'd all wayes honorable,
And find'ſt no door left open to requite this,
Conclude I am a wretch, and was twice beaten.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I have obſerv'd your way, and underſtand it,
And equal love it as Demetrius,
My noble child thou ſhalt not fall in vertue,
〈◊〉 and my power will ſink firſt: you Leontius,
Wait for a new Commiſſion, ye ſhall out again,
And inſtantly: you ſhall not lodge this night here,
Not ſee a friend, nor take a bleſſing with ye,
Before ye be i'th' field: the enemy is up ſtill,
And ſtill in full deſign: Charge him again, Son,
And either bring home that again thou haſt loſt there,
Or leave thy body by him.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Ye raiſe me,
And now I dare look up again, Leontius.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I, I, Sir, I am thinking who we ſhall take of 'em,
To make all ſtraight; and who we ſhall give toth' Devil.
What ſaiſt thou now Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I ſay nothing.
Lord what ail I, that I have no mind to fight now?
I find my conſtitution mightily alter'd
Since I came home: I hate all noiſes too,
Eſpecially the noiſe of Drums; I am now as well
As any living man; why not as valiant?
To fight now, is a kind of vomit to me,
• t goes againſt my ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Good Sir, preſently;
You cannot doe your Son ſo fair a favour.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis my intent: I'le ſee ye march away too.
Come, get your men together preſently, Leontius,
And preſs where pleaſe you, as you march.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We goe Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Wait you on me, I'le bring ye to your command,
And then to fortune give you up.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Ye love me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Goe, get the Drums, beat round, Lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Hark ye, Sir,
I have a fooliſh buſineſs they call marriage.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: After the wars are done.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: The partie ſtaies Sir,
I have giv'n the Prieſt his mony too: all my friends Sir,
My Father, and my Mother.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Will you goe forward?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: She brings a pretty matter with her.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Half a dozen Baſtards.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Some fortie Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A goodly competency.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I mean Sir, pounds a year; I'le diſpatch the matter,
'Tis but a night or two; I'le overtake ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: The 2 old legions, yes: where lies the horſe-quarter?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: And if it be a boy, I'le even make bold Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Away with your whore,
A plague o'your whore, you damn'd Rogue,
Now ye are cur'd and well; muſt ye be clicketing?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I have broke my mind to my Ancient, in my abſence,
He's a ſufficient Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Get forward.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Only receive her portion.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Get ye forward;
Elſe I'le bang ye forward.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Strange Sir,
A Gentleman and an officer cannot have the liberty
To doe the office of a man.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Shame light on thee,
How came this whore into thy head?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: This whore Sir?
'Tis ſtrange, a poor whore.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Do not anſwer me,
Troop, Troop away; do not name this whore again,
Or think there is a whore.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: That's very hard Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: For if thou doſt, look to't, I'le have thee guelded,
I'le walk ye out before me: not a word more. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Ye are the Miſtris of the houſe ye ſay,
Where this young Lady lies.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: For want of a better.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: You may be good enough for ſuch a purpoſe:
When was the Prince with her? anſwer me directly.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Not ſince he went a warring.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Very well then:
What carnal copulation are you privie to
Between theſe two? be not afraid, we are women,
And may talk thus amongſt our ſelves, no harm in't.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: No ſure, there's no harm in't, I conceive that;
But truly, that I ever knew the Gentlewoman
Otherwiſe given, than a hopefull Gentlewoman —

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: You'l grant me the Prince loves her?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: There I am with ye.
And the gods bleſs her, promiſes her mightily.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Stay there a while. And gives her gifts?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Extreamly;
And truly makes a very Saint of her.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I ſhould think now,
(Good woman let me have your judgement with me,
I ſee 'tis none of the worſt: Come ſit down by me)
That theſe two cannot love ſo tenderly.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Being ſo young as they are too.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: You ſay well —
But that methinks ſome further promiſes—

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Yes, yes,
I have heard the Prince ſwear he would marry her.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Very well ſtill: they do not uſe to fall out?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: The tendereſt Chickens to one another,
They cannot live an hour aſunder.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I have done then;
And be you gone; you know your charge, and do it.
You know whoſe will it is; if you tranſgreſs it—
That is, if any have acceſs, or ſee her,
Before the Kings will be fulfill'd —

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Not the Prince, Madam?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: You'l be hang'd if you doe it, that I'le aſſure ye.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: But ne'retheleſs, I'le make bold to obey ye.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Away, and to your buſineſs then.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: 'Tis done, Madam. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: THou haſt taken wondrous pains; but yet Menippus,
You underſtand not of what bloud and country.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I labour'd that, but cannot come to know it.
A Greek I am ſure ſhe is, ſhe ſpeaks this language.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Is ſhe ſo excellent handſom?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Moſt inticing.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sold for a priſoner?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Yes Sir,
Some poor creature.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And he loves tenderly?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: They ſay extreamly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis well prevented then: yes, I perceiv'd it:
When he took leave now, he made a hundred ſtops,
Deſir'd an hour, but half an hour, a minute,
Which I with anger croſs'd; I knew his buſineſs,
I knew 't was ſhe he hunted on; this journey, man,
I beat out ſuddenly for her cauſe intended,
And would not give him time to breath. When comes ſhe?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: This morning Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Lodge her to all delight then:
For I would have her try'd toth' teſt: I know,
She muſt be ſome crackt coyn, not fit his traſſique,
Which when we have found, the ſhame will make him leave her,
Or we ſhall work a nearer way: I'le bury him,
And with him all the hopes I have caſt upon him,
E're he ſhall dig his own grave in that woman:
You know which way to bring her: I'le ſtand cloſe there,
To view her as ſhe paſſes: and do you hear Menippus,
Obſerve her with all ſweetneſs: humour her,
'Twill make her lie more careleſs to our purpoſes.
Away, and take what helps you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I am gone Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Governeſs, from whom was this Gown ſent me?
Prethee be ſerious true; I will not wear't elſe:
'Tis a handſom one.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: As though you know not?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No faith:
But I believe, for certain too, yet I wonder,
Becauſe it was his caution, this poor way,
Still to preſerve me from the curious ſearchings
Of greedy eyes.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You have it: does it pleaſe you?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: 'Tis very rich, methinks too, prethee tell me?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: From one that likes you well, never look coy, Lady;
Theſe are no gifts, to be put off with powtings.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Powtings, and gifts? is it from any ſtranger?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You are ſo curious, that there is no talk to ye.
What if it be I pray ye?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: • npin good Governeſs,
Quick, quick.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Quick, good Governeſs:
Fie on't, how beaſtly it becomes me? poorly?
A trick put in upon me? well ſaid Governeſs:
I vow I would not wear it—out, it ſmells muſty.
Are theſe your tricks? now I begin to ſmell it,
Abominable muſty; will you help me?
The Prince will come again—

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You are not mad ſure?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: As I live I'le cut it off: a pox upon it;
For ſure it was made for that uſe; do you bring me Liveries?
Stales to catch Kites? doſt thou laugh too, thou baſe woman?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I cannot chuſe, if I ſhould be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Abuſe me,
And then laugh at me too?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I do not abuſe ye:
Is it abuſe, to give him drink that's thirſty?
You want cloaths; is it ſuch a hainous ſin I beſeech ye,
To ſee you ſtor'd?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: There is no greater wickedneſs
Than this way.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: What way?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I ſhall curſe thee fearfully,
If thou provok'ſt me further: and take heed, woman;
My curſes never miſs.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Curſe him that ſent it.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Tell but his name —

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You dare not curſe him.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Dare not?
By this fai • light

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You are ſo full of paſſion —

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Dare not be good? be honeſt? dare not curſe him?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I think you dare not: I believe ſo.

sp.speaker: Cel
sp.l: Speak him.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Up with your valour then, up with it bravely,
And take your full charge.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: If I do not, hang me;
Tell but his name.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: 'Twas Prince Demetrius ſent it:
Now, now, give ſite, kill him i'th' eye now Lady.
Is he come home?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo; but your curſe now.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You do not lie, I hope.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You dare not curſe him.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Prethee do not abuſe me: is he come home indeed?
For I would now with all my heart believe thee.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Nay, you may chuſe: alas, I deal for ſtrangers,
That ſend ye ſcurvie muſty Gowns, ſtale Liveries:
I have my tricks.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: 'Tis a good gown, a handſome one;
I did but jeſt; where is he?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: He that ſent it—

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: How? he that ſent it? is't come to that again?
Thou canſt not be ſo fooliſh: prethee ſpeak out,
I may miſtake thee.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I ſaid he that ſent it.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Curſe o' my life: why doſt thou vex me thus?
I know thou meaneſt Demetrius, doſt thou not?
I charge thee ſpeak truth: if it be any other,
Thou knowſt the charge he gave thee, and the juſtice
His anger will inflict, if e're he know this,
As know he ſhall, he ſhall, thou ſpightfull woman,
Thou beaſtly woman; and thou ſhalt know too late t • o,
And feel too ſenſible, I am no ward,
No ſale ſtuff for your money Merchants that ſent it?
Who dare ſend me, or how durſt thou, thou —

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: What you pleaſe:
For this is ever the reward of ſervice.
The Prince ſhall bring the next himſelf.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange
That you ſhould deal ſo peeviſhly: beſhrew ye,
You have put me in a heat.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I am ſure ye have kill'd me:
I ne're receiv'd ſuch language: I can but wait upon ye,
And be your drudge; keep a poor life to ſerve ye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You know my nature is too eaſie, Governeſs,
And you know now, I am ſorry too: how does he?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: O God, my head.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Prethee be well, and tell me,
Did he ſpeak of me, ſince he came? nay, ſee now,
If thou wilt leave this tyranny? good ſweet governeſs,
Did he but name his Celia? look upon me,
Upon my ſaith I meant no harm: here, take this,
And buy thy ſelf ſome trifles: did he good wench?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: He loves ye but too dearly.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: That's my good Governeſs.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: There's more cloaths making for ye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: More cloaths?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: More:
Richer and braver; I can tell ye that news;
And twenty glorious things.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: To what uſe Sirrah?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Ye are too good for our houſe now: we poor wretches
Shall loſe the comfort of ye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No, I hope not.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: For ever loſe ye Lady.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Loſe me? wherefore?
I hear of no ſuch thing.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: 'Tis ſure it muſt be ſo:
You muſt ſhine now at Court: ſuch preparation,
Such hurry, and ſuch hanging rooms —

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Toth' Court wench?
Was it toth' Court thou ſaidſt?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You'l find it ſo.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Stay, ſtay, this cannot be.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I ſay it muſt be:
I hope to find ye ſtill the ſame good Lady.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Toth' Court? this ſtumbles me: art ſure for m • we ••
This preparation is?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: She is perilous crafty:
I fear too honeſt for us all too. Am I ſure I live?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Toth' Court? this cannot down: what ſhould I 〈◊〉 th • r •
Why ſhould he on a ſuddain change his mind thus,
And not make me acquainted? ſure he loves me;
His vow was made againſt it, and mine with him:
At leaſt while this King liv'd: he will come hither.
And ſee me e're I goe?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Wou'd ſome wiſe woman
Had her in working. That I think he will not,
Becauſe he means with all joy there to meet ye.
Ye ſhall hear more within this hour.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: A Courtier?
What may that meaning be? ſure he will ſee me
If he be come, he muſt: Hark ye good Governeſs,
What age is the King of?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: He's an old man, and full of buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I fear too full indeed: what Ladys are there?
I would be loth to want good company.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Delicate young Ladys, as you would deſire;
And when you are acquainted, the beſt company.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: 'Tis very well: prethee goe in, let's talk more.
For though I fear a trick, I'le bravely try it.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I ſee he muſt be cunning,
Knocks this Doe down. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA III.
div.stage: Enter Lieutenant, and Leontius, Drums within.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You ſhall not have your will, ſirrah, are ye running?
Have ye gotten a toy in your heels? Is this a ſeaſon,
When honour pricks ye on, to prick your ears up,
After your whore, your Hobby-horſe?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Why look ye now:
What a ſtrange man are you? would you have a man fight
At all hours all alike?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Do but fight ſomething;
But half a blow, and put thy ſtomach to't:
Turn but thy face, and do make mouths at 'em.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: And have my teeth knockt out; I thank ye heartily,
Ye are my dear friend.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What a Devil ails thee?
D •• long to be hang'd?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Faith Sir, I make no ſuit for't:
Be rather than I would live thus out of charity,
Continually in brawling —

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Art thou not he?
I may be cozen'd —

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I ſhall be diſcover'd.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: That in the midſt of thy moſt helliſh pains,
When thou wert crawling ſick, didſt aim at wonders,
When thou wert mad with pain?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Ye have found the cauſe out;
I had ne're been mad to fight elſe: I confeſs Sir,
The daily torture of my ſide that vext me,
Made me as daily careleſs what became of me,
Till a kind ſword there wounded me, and eas'd me;
'Twas nothing in my valour fought; I am well now,
And take ſome pleaſure in my life, methinks now,
It ſhews as mad a thing to me to ſee you ſcuffle,
And kill one another fooliſhly for honour,
As 'twas to you, ſo ſee me play the coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And wilt thou ne're fight more?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I'th' mind I am in.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Nor never be ſick again?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I hope I ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Prethee be ſick again; prethee, I beſeech thee,
Be juſt ſo ſick again.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I'le juſt be hang'd firſt.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: If all the Arts that are can make a Colique,
Therefore look to't: or if impoſthumes, mark me,
As big as foot-balls—

sp.speaker: Lieu
sp.l: Deliver me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Or ſtones of ten pound weight i'th' kidneys,
Through eaſe and ugly dyets may be gather'd;
I'le feed ye up my ſelf Sir, I'le prepare ye,
You cannot fight, unleſs the Devil tear ye,
You ſhall not want provocations, I'le ſcratch ye,
I'le have thee have the tooth-ach, and the head-ach.

sp.speaker: Lieu
sp.l: Good Colonel, I'le doe any thing.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: No, no, nothing—
Then will I have thee blown with a pair of Smiths bellows,
Becauſe ye ſhall be ſure to have a round gale with ye,
Fill'd full of oyle o'Devil, and Aqua-fortis,
And let theſe work, theſe may provoke.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Good Colonel.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A coward in full bloud; prethee be plain with me,
Will roaſting doe thee any good?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Nor baſting neither, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Marry that goes hard.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Where are you Colonel?
The Prince expects ye Sir; h'as hedg'd the enemy
Within a ſtreight, where all the hopes and valours
Of all men living cannot force a paſſage,
He has 'em now.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I knew all this before Sir,
I chalk'd him out his way: but do you ſee that thing there?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Nay good ſweet Colonel, I'le fight a little.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: That thing?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: What thing? I ſee the brave Lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Rogue, what a name haſt thou loſt?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: You may help it,
Yet you may help't: I'le doe ye any courteſie:
I know you love a wench well.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Look upon him;
Do you look too.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: What ſhould I look on?
I come to tell ye, the Prince ſtayes your direction,
We have 'em now i'th' Coop, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Let 'em reſt there,
And chew upon their miſeries: but look firſt —

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I cannot fight for all this.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Look on this fellow.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: I know him; 'tis the valiant brave Lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Canſt thou hear this, and play the Rogue? ſteal o • f quickly,
Behind me quickly, neatly do it,
And ruſh into the thickeſt of the enemy,
And if thou kill'ſt but two.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: You may excuſe me,
'Tis not my fault: I dare not fight.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Be rul'd yet,
I'le beat thee on; goe wink and fight: a plague upon your ſheeps heart.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: What's all this matter?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Nay I cannot ſhew ye.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Here's twenty pound, goe but ſmell to 'em.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Alas Sir,
I have taken ſuch a cold I can ſmell nothing.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I can ſmell a Raſcal, a rank Raſcal:
Fye, how he ſtinks, ſtinks like a tyred Jade.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: What Sir?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why, that Sir, do not you ſmell him?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Smell him?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I muſt endure.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Stinks like a dead Dog, Carrion —
There's no ſuch damnable ſmell under Heaven,
As the ſaint ſweat of a Coward: will ye fight yet?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Nay, now I defie ye; ye have ſpoke the worſt ye can
Of me, and if every man ſhould take what you ſay
To the heart. —

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: God ha' Mercy,
God ha' Mercy with all my heart; here I forgive thee,
And fight, or fight not, do but goe along with us,
And keep my Dog.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I love a good Dog naturally.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: What's all this ſtir, Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Nothing Sir,
But a ſlight matter of argument.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Pox take thee.
Sure I ſhall love this Rogue, he's ſo pretty a Coward.
Come Gentlemen, let's up now, and if fortune
Dare play the ſlut again, I'le never more Saint her,
Come play-fellow, come, prethee come up; come chicken,
I have a way ſhall fit yet: A tame knave,
Come, look upon us.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I'le tell ye who does beſt boyes. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA IV.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I ſaw her coming out.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Who waits upon her?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Timon, Charinthus, and ſome other Gentlemen,
By me appointed.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Where's your wife?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: She's ready
To entertain her here Sir; and ſome Ladies
Fit for her lodgings.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How ſhews ſhe in her trim now?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Oh moſt divinely ſweet.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Prethee ſpeak ſoftly.
How does ſhe take her coming?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: She bears it bravely,
But what ſhe thinks— For Heaven ſake Sir preſerve me —
If the Prince chance to find this.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Peace ye old fool;
She thinks to meet him here.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: That's all the Project.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Was ſhe hard to bring?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: No ſhe believ'd it quickly,
And quickly made her ſelf fit, the Gown a little,
And thoſe new things ſhe has not been acquainted with,
At leaſt in this place, where ſhe liv'd a priſoner,
Troubled and ſtirr'd her mind. But believe me Sir,
She has worn as good, they ſit ſo apted to her;
And ſhe is ſo great a Miſtris of diſpoſure:
Here they come now: but take a full view of her.

div.stage: Enter Celia, Timon, Charinthus, and Gent.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How cheerfully ſhe looks? how ſhe ſalutes all?
And how ſhe views the place? ſhe is very young ſure:
That was an admirable ſmile, a catching one,
The very twang of Cupids bow ſung in it:
She has two edg'd eyes, they kill o' both ſides.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: She makes a ſtand, as though ſhe would ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Be ſtill then.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Good Gentlemen, trouble your ſelves no further,
I had thought ſure to have met a noble friend here.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Ye may meet many Lady.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Such as you are
I covet few or none, Sir.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Will you walk this way,
And take the ſweets o'th' garden? cool and cloſe, Lady.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Methinks this open air's far better, tend ye that way.
Pray where's the woman came along?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: What woman?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: The woman of the houſe I lay at.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Woman?
Here was none came along ſure.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Sure I am catcht then:
Pray where's the Prince?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: He will not be long from ye,
We are his humble Servants.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I could laugh now,
To ſee how finely I am cozen'd: yet I fear not,
For ſure I know a way to ſcape all dangers.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Madam, your lodgings lye this way.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: My Lodgings?
For Heaven ſake Sit, what office do I bear here?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: The great commander of all hearts.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You have hit it.
I thank your ſweet heart for it. Who are theſe now?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Ladies that come to ſerve ye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Well conſider'd,
Are you my Servants?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Servants to your pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I dare believe ye, but I dare not truſt ye:
Catch'd with a trick? well, I muſt bear it patiently:
Methinks this Court's a neat place: all the people
Of ſo refin'd a ſize —

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: This is no poor Rogue.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Were it a Paradiſe to pleaſe your fancy,
And entertain the ſweetneſs you bring with ye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Take breath;
You are fat, and many words may melt ye,
This is three Bawdes beaten into one; bleſs me Heares,
What ſhall become of me? I am i'th' pitfall:
O' my conſcience, this is the old viper, and all theſe little o •• s
Creep every night into her belly; do you hear plump ſervant
And you my little ſucking Ladies, you muſt teach me,
For I know you are excellent at carriage,
How to behave my ſelf, for I am rude yet:
But you ſay the Prince will come?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Will flie to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: For look you if a great man, ſay the King now
Should come and viſit me?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: She names ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Peace fool.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And offer me a kindneſs, ſuch a kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I, ſuch a kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: True Lady ſuch a kindneſs,
What ſhall that kindneſs be now?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: A witty Lady,
Learn little ones, learn.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Say it be all his favour.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: And a ſweet ſaying 'tis.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And I grow peeviſh?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: You muſt not be neglectfull.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: There's the matter,
There's the main doctrine now, and I may miſs it,
Or a kind handſom Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: You ſay well.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: They'l count us baſely bred.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Not freely nurtur'd.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I'le take thy counſel.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: 'Tis an excellent woman.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I find a notable volum here, a learned one;
Which way? for I would fain be in my chamber;
In truth ſweet Ladies, I grow weary; fie,
How hot the air beats on me?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: This way Madam.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Now by mine honour, I grow wondrous ſaint too.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Your fans ſweet Gentlewomen, your fans.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Since I am fool'd,
I'le make my ſelf ſome ſport, though I pay dear for't. Ex

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: You ſee now what a manner of woman ſhe is Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thou art an aſs.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Is this a fit love for the Prince?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A coxcombe:
Now by my crown a daintie wench, a ſharp wench,
And a matchleſs Spirit: how ſhe jeer'd 'em?
How careleſly ſhe ſcoff'd 'em? uſe her nobly;
I would I had not ſeen her: wait anon,
And then you ſhall have more to trade upon. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We muſt keep a round, and a ſtrong watch to night.
The Prince will not charge the Enemy till the morning:
But for the trick I told ye for this Raſcal,
This rogue, that health and ſtrong heart makes a coward

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I, if it take.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ne're fear it, the Prince has it,
And if he let it fall, I muſt not know it;
He will ſuſpect me preſently: but you two
May help the plough.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: That he is ſick again.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Extreamly ſick: his diſeaſe grown incurable,
Never yet found, nor touch'd at.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Well, we have it,
And here he comes.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: The Prince has been upon him,
What a flatten face he has now? it takes, believe it;
How like an Aſs he looks?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I feel no great pain,
At leaſt, I think I do not; yet I feel ſenſibly
I grow extreamly faint: how cold I ſweat now?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: So, ſo, ſo.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: And now 'tis ev'n too true, I feel a pricking,
A pricking, a ſtrange pricking: how it tingles?
And as it were a ſtitch too: the Prince told me,
And every one cri'd out I was a dead man;
I had thought I had been as well—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Upon him now Boys,
And do it moſt demurely.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: How now Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I thank ye Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Life, how looks this man?
How doſt thou good Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: I ever told ye
This man was never cur'd, I ſee it too plain now;
How do you feel your ſelf? you look not perfect,
How dull his eye hangs?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: That may be diſcontent.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Believe me friend, I would not ſuffer now
The tith of thoſe pains this man feels; mark his forehead
What a cloud of cold dew hangs upon't?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I have it,
Again I have it; how it grows upon me?
A miſerable man I am.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha,
A miſerable man thou ſhalt be,
This is the tameſt Trout I ever tickl'd.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: This way he went.

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: Pray Heaven we find him living,
He's a brave fellow, 'tis pity he ſhould periſh thus.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: A ſtrong hearted man, and of a notable ſufferance.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: How now? how is it man?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Oh Gentlemen,
Never ſo full of pain.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Did I not tell ye?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Never ſo full of pain, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: He is here;
How do you, Sir?

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: Be of good comfort, Souldier,
The Prince has ſent us to you.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Do you think I may live?

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: He alters hourly, ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: Yes, you may live: but—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Finely butted, Doctor.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Do not diſcourage him.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: He muſt be told truth,
Tis now too late to trifle.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Here the Prince comes.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: How now Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Bewailing, Sir, a Souldier,
And one I think, your Grace will grieve to part with,
But every living thing—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: 'Tis true, muſt periſh,
Our lives are but our marches to our graves,
How doſt thou now Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Faith 'tis true, Sir,
We are but ſpans, and Candles ends.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He's finely mortified.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thou art heart whole yet I ſee, he alters ſtrangely,
And that a pace too; I ſaw it this morning in him,
When he poor man, I dare ſwear—

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: No believ't, Sir,
I never felt it.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Here lies the pain now: how he is ſwel'd?

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: The Impoſtume
Fed with a new malignant humour now,
Will grow to ſuch a bigneſs, 'tis incredible,
The compaſs of a Buſhel will not hold it.
And with ſuch a Hell of torture it will riſe too—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Can you endure me touch it?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Oh, I beſeech you, Sir:
I feel you ſenſibly ere you come near me.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: He's finely wrought, he muſt be cut, no Cure elſe,
And ſuddenly, you ſee how faſt he blows out.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Good Maſter Doctors, let me be beholding to you,
I feel I cannot laſt.

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: For what Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: But ev'n for half a dozen Cans of good Wine,
That I may drink my will out: I faint hideouſly.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Fetch him ſome Wine; and ſince he muſt go Gentlemen,
Why let him take his journey merrily.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: That's ev'n the neareſt way.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I could laugh dead now.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Here, off with that.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Theſe two I give your Grace,
A poor remembrance of a dying man, Sir,
And I beſeech you wear 'em out.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I will Souldier,
Theſe are fine Legacies.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Among the Gentlemen,
Even all I have left; I am a poor man, naked,
Yet ſomething for remembrace: four a piece Gentlemen,
And ſo my body where you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: It will work.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I make your Grace my Executor, and I beſeech ye
See my poor Will fulfill'd: ſure I ſhall walk elſe.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: As full as they can be fill'd, here's my hand, Souldier.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: The Wine will tickle him.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I would hear a Drum beat,
But to ſee how I could endure it.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Beat a Drum there. Drum within.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Oh Heavenly Muſick, I would hear one ſing to't;
I am very full of pain.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Sing? 'tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Why, then I would drink a Drum full:
Where lies the Enemy?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Why, here cloſe by.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Now he begins to muſter.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: And dare he fight?
Dare he fight Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: You muſt not cut him:
He's gone then in a moment; all the hope left, is
To work his weakneſs into ſuddain anger,
And make him raiſe his paſſion above his pain,
And ſo diſpoſe him on the Enemy;
His body then, being ſtir'd with violence,
Will purge it ſelf and break the ſore.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: 'Tis true, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: And then my life for his.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I will not dye thus.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: But he is too weak to do—

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Dye like a Dog?

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: I, he's weak, but yet he's heart whole.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Hem.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: An excellent ſign.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Hem.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Stronger ſtill, and better.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Hem, hem; ran, tan, tan, tan, tan. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: Now he's i'th' way on't.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Well go thy waies, thou wilt do ſomething certain.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And ſome brave thing, or let mine ears be cut off.
He's finely wrought.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Let's after him.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I pray, Sir;
But how this Rogue, when this cloud's melted in him,
And all diſcover'd—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: That's for an after mirth, away, away, away. Ex.

div.head: SCENE. VI.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Let no man •• at to dye: we love to ſleep all,
And death is but the ſounder ſleep; all ages,
And all hours call us; 'tis ſo common, eaſie,
That little Children tread thoſe paths before us;
We are not 〈◊〉 , nor our ſouls preſt with ſorrows,
Not go we out like tedious tales, forgotten;
High, high we come, and hearty to our Funerals,
And as the Sun that ſets, in bloud let's fall.

sp.speaker: Lyſi.
sp.l: 'Tis true, they have us faſt, we cannot ſcape 'em,
Not keeps the brow of fortune one ſmile for us,
Diſhonourable ends we can ſcape though,
And (worſe than thoſe Captivities) we can die,
And dying nobly, though we leave behind us
Theſe clods of fleſh, that are too maſſie burthens,
Out living ſouls ſhe crown'd with living conqueſts.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: They have begun, ſight bravely, and fall bravely;
And may that man that ſeeks to ſave his life now
By price, or promiſe, or by fear falls from us,
Never again be bleſt with name of Souldier.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: How now? who charged firſt? I ſeek a brave hand
To ſet me off in death.

sp.speaker: Soul.
sp.l: We are not charg'd, Sir,
The Prince hes ſtill.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: How comes this Larum up then?

sp.speaker: Soul.
sp.l: There is one deſperate fellow, with the Devil in him
(He never durſt do this elſe) has broke into us,
And here he bangs ye two or three before him,
There five or ſix; ventures upon whole Companies.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: And is not ſeconded?

sp.speaker: Soul.
sp.l: Not a man follows.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Not cut i' pieces?

sp.speaker: Soul.
sp.l: Their wonder yet has ſtaid 'em.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Let's in, and ſee this miracle?

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: I admire it. Ex.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Fetch him off, fetch him off; I am ſure he's clouted;
Did I not tell you how 'twould take?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis admirable.

div.stage: Enter Lieutenant with Colours in his hand, purſuing 3 or 4 Souldiers.

sp.l: Follow that blow, my friend, there's at your coxcombs,
I fight to ſave me from the Surgions miſeries.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: How the Knave curries 'em?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: You cannot Rogues,
Till you have my Diſeaſes, flie my fury,
Ye Bread and Butter Rogues, do ye run from me?
And my ſide would give me leave, I would ſo hunt ye,
Ye Potridg gutted Slaves, ye Veal broth Boobies.

div.stage: Enter Demetrius, and Phyſicians, and Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Enough, enough Lieutenant, thou haſt done bravely.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Mir • our of man.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: There's a Flag for ye, Sir,
I took it out o'th' ſhop, and never paid for 't,
I'le to 'em again, I am not come to th' text yet.

sp.speaker: De.
sp.l: No more my Souldier: beſhrew my heart he is hurt ſore.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Hang him, he'l lick all thoſe whole.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: Now will we take him,
And Cure him in a trice.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Be careful of him.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Let me live but two years,
And do what ye will with me;
I never had but two hours yet of happineſs;
Pray ye give me nothing to provoke my valour,
For I am ev'n as weary of this fighting—

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have nothing; come to the Princes Te ••
And there the Surgions preſently ſhall ſearch ye,
Then to your reſt.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: A little handſome Litter
To lay me in, and I ſhall ſleep.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Look to him.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I do believe a Horſe begot this fellow,
He never knew his ſtrength yet; they are our own

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I think ſo, I am cozen'd elſe; I would but ſee now
A way to fetch theſe off, and ſave their honours.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Only their lives.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Pray ye take no way of peace now,
Unleſs it be with infinite advantage.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I ſhall be rul'd;
Let the Battels now move forward,
Our ſelf will give the ſignal:
Now Herald, what's your meſſage?

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: From my Maſters,
This honourable courteſie, a Parley
For half an hour, no more, Sir.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Let 'em come on,
They have my Princely word.

div.stage: Enter Seleticus, Lyſimacus, Ptolomie, Attendants, Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: They are here to attend ye.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Now Princes, your demands?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Peace, if it may be
Without the too much tainture of our honour:
Peace, and we'l buy it too.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: At what price?

sp.speaker: Lyſi.
sp.l: Tribute.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: At all the charge of this War.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: That will not do.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Leontius, you and I have ſerv'd together,
And run through many a Fortune with our ſwords,
Brothers in Wounds and Health; one meat has fed us,
One Tent a thouſand times from cold night cover'd us:
Our loves have been but one; and had we died then,
One Monument had held our names, and actions:
Why do you ſet upon your friends ſuch prices?
And ſacrifice to giddy chance ſuch Trophies?
Have we forgot to dye? or are our vertues
Leſs in afflictions conſtant, than our fortunes?
Ye are deceiv'd old Souldier.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I know your worths,
And thus low bow in reverence to your vertues:
Were theſe my Wars, or led my power in chief here,
I knew then how to meet your memories:
They are my Kings imployments; this man fights now,
To whom I ow all duty, faith, and ſervice;
This man that fled before ye; call back that,
That bloudy day again, call that diſgrace home,
And then an eaſie Peace may ſheath our Swords up.
I am not greedy of your lives and fortunes,
Nor do I gape ungratefully to ſwallow ye.
Honour, the ſpur of all illuſtrious natures,
That made you famous Souldiers, and next Kings,
And not ambitious envy ſtrikes me forward.
Will ye unarm, and yield your ſelves his priſoners?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: We never knew what that ſound meant: no Gy •••
Shall ever bind this body, but embraces;
Nor weight of ſorrow here, till Earth fall on me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Expect our charge then.

sp.speaker: Lyſi.
sp.l: 'Tis the nobler courteſie:
And ſo we leave the hand of Heaven to bleſs us.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Stay, have you any hope?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: We have none left us,
But that one comfort of our deaths together;
Give us but room to fight.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Win it, and wear it.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: Call from the hills thoſe Companies hang o're us,
Like burſting Clouds; and then break in, and take us.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Find ſuch a Souldier will forſake advantage,
And we'll draw off to ſhew I dare be noble,
And hang a light out to ye in this darkneſs,
The light of peace; give up thoſe Cities, Forts,
And all thoſe Frontier Countries to our uſes.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Is this the Peace? Traitors to thoſe that feed us,
Our Gods and people? give our Countries from us?

sp.speaker: Lyſi.
sp.l: Begin the Knell, it ſounds a great deal ſweeter.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: Let looſe your ſervant, death.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Fall fate upon us,
Our memories ſhall never ſtink behind us.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Seleucus, great Seleucus.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.l: The Prince calls, Sir.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thou ſtock of nobleneſs, and courteſie,
Thou Father of the War—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What means the Prince now?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Give me my Standard here.

sp.speaker: Lyſi.
sp.l: His anger's melted.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: You Gentlemen that were his priſoners,
And felt the bounty of that noble nature,
• ay all your hands, and bear theſe Colours to him
The Standard of the Kingdom; take it Souldier.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: What will this mean?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thou haſt won it, bear it off,
And draw thy men home whileſt we wait upon thee.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: You ſhall have all our Countries.

sp.speaker: Lyſi.
sp.l: Ptol. All by Heaven, Sir.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I will not have a ſtone, a buſh, a bramble,
• o, in the way of courteſie, I'le ſtart ye;
Draw off, and make a lane through all the Army,
• hat theſe that have ſubdu'd us, may march through us.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Sir, do not make me ſurfeit with ſuch goodneſs,
• le bear your Standard for ye; follow ye.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I ſwear it ſhall be ſo, march through me fairly,
• nd thine be this days honour, great Seleucus.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: Mirrour of noble minds.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Nay then ye hate me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I cannot ſpeak now: Ex. with Drums, and Shouts.
Well, go thy wayes; at a ſure piece of bravery
• hou art the beſt, theſe men are won by th' necks now:
• le ſend a Poſt away.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.l: NO aptneſs in her?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Not an immodeſt motion,
• nd yet when ſhe is courted,
• akes as wild witty anſwers.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This more fires me,
〈◊〉 muſt not have her thus.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: We cannot alter her.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Have ye put the youths upon her?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: All that know any thing,
• nd have been ſtudied how to catch a beauty,
• ut like ſo many whelps about an Elephant—
The Prince is coming home, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I hear that too,
•• t that's no matter; am I alter'd well?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Not to be known I think, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I muſt ſee her.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I offered all I had, all I could think of,
• ri'd her through all the points o'th' compaſs, I think.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: She ſtudies to undo the Court, to plant here
• he Enemy to our Age, Chaſtity;
She is the firſt, that e're bank'd a cloſe Arbour,
And the ſweet contents within: She hates curl'd heads too,
And ſetting up of b • ards ſhe ſwears is Idolatry.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I never knew ſo fair a face ſo froze;
Yet ſhe would make one think—.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: True by her carriage,
For ſhe's as wanton as a Kid to th' out ſide,
As full of Mocks and Taunts: I kiſs'd her hand too,
Walkt with her half an hour.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: She heard me ſing,
And ſung her ſelf too; ſhe ſings admirably;
But ſtill when any hope was, as 'tis her trick
To miniſter enough of thoſe, then preſently
With ſome new ſlam or other, nothing to the matter,
And ſuch a frown, as would ſink all before her,
She takes her Chamber; come, we ſhall not be the laſt fools.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Not by a hundred I hope; 'tis a ſtrange wench.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This ſcrews me up ſtill higher.

div.stage: Enter Celia, and Ladies behind her.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Here ſhe comes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Then be you gone; and take the Women with ye,
And lay thoſe Jewels in her way.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: If I ſtay longer
I ſhall number as many Lovers as Lais did;
How they ſtock after me? upon my Conſcience,
I have had a dozen Horſes given me this morning,
I'le ev'n ſet up a Troop, and turn She-ſouldier,
A good diſcreet wench now, that were not hidebound
Might raiſe a fine eſtate here, and ſuddenly:
For theſe warm things will give their Souls—I can go no where
Without a world of offerings to my Excellence:
I am a Queen, a Goddeſſe, I know not what—
And no conſtellation in all Heaven, but I out-ſhine it;
And they have found out now I have no eyes
Of mortal lights, but certain influences,
Strange vertuous lightnings, humane nature ſtarts at,
And I can kill my twenty in a morning,
With as much eaſe now—
Ha! what are theſe? new projects?
Where are my honourable Ladies? are you out too?
Nay then I muſt buy the ſtock, ſend me good Carding:
I hope the Princes hands be not in this ſport;
I have not ſeen him yet, cannot hear from him,
And that troubles me: all theſe were recreations
Had I but his ſweet company to laugh with me:
What fellow's that? another Apparition?
This is the lovingſt Age: I ſhould know that face,
Sure I have ſeen't before, not long ſince neither.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She ſees me now: O Heaven, a moſt rare creature!

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Yes, 'tis the ſame: I will take no notice of ye,
But if I do not ſit ye, let me fry for't;
Is all this Cackling for your egg? they are fair ones,
Excellent rich no doubt too; and may ſtumble
