A good ſtaid mind, but I can go thus by 'em;
My honeſt friend; do you ſet off theſe Jewels?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Set 'em off, Lady?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I mean, ſell 'em here, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She's very quick; for ſale they are not meant ſure.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: For ſanctity I think much leſs: good even Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Nay noble Lady, ſtay: 'tis you muſt wear 'em:
Never look ſtrange, they are worthy your beſt beauty.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Did you ſpeak to me?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: To you or to none living:
To you they are ſent, to you they are ſacrificed.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I'le never look a Horſe i'th' mouth that's given:
I thank ye, Sir: I'le ſend one to reward ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Do you never ask who ſent 'em?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Never I:
Nor never care, if it be an honeſt end,
That end's the full reward, and thanks but ſlubber it;
If it be ill, I will not urge the acquaintance.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This has a ſoul indeed: pray let me tell ye—

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I care not if ye do, ſo you do it hanſomly,
And not ſtand picking of your words.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The King ſent 'em.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Away, away, thou art ſome fooliſh fellow,
And now I think thou haſt ſtole 'em too; the King ſent 'em?
Alas good man, wouldſt thou make me believe
He has nothing to do with things of theſe worths,
But want only to ſting 'em? he's an old man,
A good old man, they ſay too: I dare ſwear
Full many a year ago he left theſe gambols:
Here, take your trinkets.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sure I do not lye, Lady.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I know thou lyeſt extreamly, damnably:
Thou haſt a lying face.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I was never thus tatled.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: But ſay I ſhould believe: why are theſe ſent me?
And why art thou the Meſſenger? who art thou?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Lady, look on 'em wiſely, and then conſider
Who can ſend ſuch as theſe, but a King only?
And, to what beauty can they be oblations,
But only yours? for me that am the carrier,
'Tis only ſit you know I am his ſervant,
And have fulfil'd his will.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You are ſhort and pithy;
What muſt my beauty do for theſe?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sweet Lady,
You cannot be ſo hard of underſtanding,
When a King's favour ſhines upon ye gloriouſly,
And ſpeaks his love in theſe—

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: O then love's the matter;
Sir reverence love: now I begin to feel ye:
And I ſhould be the Kings Whore, a brave title;
And go as glorious as the Sun, O brave ſtill:
The chief Commandreſs of his Concubines,
Hurried from place to place to meet his pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A deviliſh ſubtil wench, but a rare ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And when the good old ſpunge had ſuckt my youth dry,
And left ſome of his Royal aches in my bones:
When time ſhall tell me I have plough'd my life up,
And caſt long ſurrows in my face to link me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You muſt not think ſo, Lady.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Then can theſe, Sir,
Theſe precious things, the price of youth and beauty;
This ſhop here of ſin-offerings ſet me off again?
Can it reſtore me chaſte, young, innocent?
Purge me to what I was? add to my memory
An honeſt and a noble ſame? The Kings device;
The ſin's as univerſal as the Sun is,
And lights an everlaſting Torch to ſhame me.
Do you hold ſo ſleight account of a great Kings favour,
That all knees bow to purchaſe?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Prethee peace:
If thou knewſt how ill ſavouredly thy tale becomes thee,
And what ill root it takes—
You will be wiſer.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Could the King find no ſhape to ſhift his pander into,
But reverend Age? and one ſo like himſelf too?
She has found me out.

sp.speaker: Cel
sp.l: Cozen the world with gravity?
Prethee reſolve me one thing, do's the King love thee?
I think he do's.
It ſeems ſo by thy Office:
He loves thy uſe, and when that's ended, hates thee:
Thou ſeemeſt to me a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes, I am one.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And haſt ſought for thy Country?
Many a time.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: May be, commanded too?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I have done, Lady.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: O wretched man, below the ſtate of pity!
Canſt thou forget thou we • t begot in honour?
A f •• e Companion for a King? a Souldier?
Whoſe Nobleneſs dare feel no want, but Enemies?
Canſt thou forget this, and decline ſo wretchedly,
To eat the Bread of Bawdry, of baſe Bawdry?
Feed on the ſcum of Sin? ſling thy Sword from thee?
Diſhonour to the noble name that nurſed thee?
Go, beg diſeaſes: let them be thy Armours,
Thy fights, the flames of Luſt, and their ſoul iſſues.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why then I am a King, and mine own Speaker.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And I as free as you, mine own Diſpoſer:
There, take your Jewels; let them give them luſtres
That have dark Lives and Souls; wear 'em your ſelf, Sir,
You'l ſeem a Devil elſe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I command ye ſtay.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Be juſt, I am commanded.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I will not wrong ye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Then thus low falls my duty.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Can ye love me?
Say I, and all I have—

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I cannot love ye;
Without the breach of faith I cannot hear ye;
Ye hang • pon my love, like froſts on Lilies:

I can dye, but I cannot love: you are anſwer'd.
Ex • .

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l:
I • uſt find apter means, I love her truly.
Ex • .

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Demetr. Leon. Lieu. Gent. Sould. and Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Hither do you ſay ſhe is come?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I am ſure on't:
For whileſt I waited upon ye, putting my Wife in truſt,
I know not by what means, but the King found her,
And hither ſhe was brought; how, or to what end —

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: My Father found her?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: So my Wife informs me.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Leontius, pray draw off the Souldiers,
I would a while be private.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Fall off Gentlemen,

The Prince would be alone.
Ex. Leo. and Soul

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Is he ſo cunning?
There is ſome trick in this, and you muſt know it,
And be an agent too: which if it prove ſo —

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Pull me to pieces, Sir.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: My Father ſound her?
My Father brought her hither? went ſhe willingly?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: My Wife ſayes full of doubts.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I cannot blame her,
No more: there's no truſt, no faith in mankind.

div.stage: Enter Antigonus, Menippus, Leontius, and Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Keep her up cloſe, he muſt not come to ſee her.
You are welcome nobly now, welcome home Gentlemen,
You have done a courteous ſervice on the Enemy
Has tyed his Faith for ever; you ſhall find it;
Ye are not now in's debt Son: ſtill your ſad looks?
Leontius, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Truth Sir, I know not.
We have been merry ſince we went.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I feel it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Come, what's the matter now? do you want mony?
Sure he has heard o'th' wench.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Is that a want, Sir?
I would fain ſpeak to your Grace.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You may do freely.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And not deſerve your anger?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: That ye may too.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: There was a Gentlewoman, and ſometimes my priſoner,
Which I thought well of Sir: your Grace conceives me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I do indeed, and with much grief conceive ye;
With full as much grief as your Mother bare you.
There was ſuch a Woman: would I might as well ſay,
There was no ſuch, Demetrius.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: She was vertuous,
And therefore not unfit my youth to love her:
She was as fair —

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Her beauty I'le proclaim too,
To be as rich as ever raign'd in Woman;
But how ſhe made that good, the Devil knows.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: She was— O Heaven!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The Hell to all thy glories,
Swallow'd thy youth, made ſhipwrack of thine honour:
She was a Devil.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Ye are my Father, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And ſince ye take a pride to ſhew your follies,
I'le muſter 'em, and all the world ſhall view 'em.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What heat is this? the Kings eyes ſpeak his anger.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thou haſt abus'd thy youth, drawn to thy fellowſhip
Inſtead of Arts and Arms, a Womans kiſſes,
The ſubtilties, and ſoft heats of a Harlot.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Good Sir, miſtake her not.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A Witch, a Sorcereſs:
I tell thee but the truth; and hear Demetrius,
Which has ſo dealt upon thy bloud with charms,
Deviliſh and dark; ſo lockt up all thy vertues;
So pluckt thee back from what thou ſprungſt from, glorious.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: O Heaven, that any tongue but his durſt ſay this!
That any heart durſt harbour it! Dread Father,
If for the innocent the gods allow us
To bend our knees—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Away, thou art bewitch'd ſtill;
Though ſhe be dead, her power ſtill lives upon thee.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Dead? O ſacred Sir: dead did you ſay?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She is dead, fool.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: It is not poſſible: be not ſo angry,
Say ſhe is faln under your ſad diſpleaſure,
Or any thing but dead, ſay ſhe is baniſhed,
Invent a crime, and I'le believe it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Dead by the Law: we found her Hell, and her,
I mean her Charms and Spells, for which ſhe periſh'd;
And ſhe confeſt ſhe drew thee to thy ruine,
And purpos'd it, purpos'd my Empires overthrow.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: But is ſhe dead? was there no pity Sir?
If her youth err'd, was there no mercy ſhown her?
Did ye look on her face, when ye condemn'd her?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I look'd into her heart, and there ſhe was hideous.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Can ſhe be dead? can vertue fall untimely?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She is dead, deſervingly ſhe died.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I have done then.
O matchleſs ſweetneſs, whither art thou vaniſhed?
O thou fair ſoul of all thy Sex, what Paradiſe
Haſt thou inrich'd and bleſt? I am your ſon, Sir,
And to all you ſhall command ſtand moſt obedient,
Only a little time I muſt intreat you
To ſtudy to forget her; 'twill not be long, Sir,
Not I long after it: art thou dead Celia,
Dead my poor wench? my joy, pluckt green with violence:
O fair ſweet flower, farewel; Come, thou deſtroyer
Sorrow, thou melter of the ſoul, dwell with me;
Dwell with me ſolitary thoughts, tears, cryings,
Nothing that loves the day, love me, or ſeek me,
Nothing that loves his own life haunt about me:
And Love, I charge thee, never charm mine eyes more,
Nor ne're betray a beauty to my curſes:
For I ſhall curſe all how, hate all, forſwear all,
And all the brood of fruitful nature vex at,
For ſhe is gone that was all, and I nothing— Ex. & Gent.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This opinion muſt be maintained.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: It ſhall be, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let him go; I can at mine own pleaſure
Draw him to th' right again: wait your inſtructions,
And ſee the ſouldier paid, Leontius:
Once more ye are welcome home all.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l:
Health to your Majeſty.
Exit Antig. &c.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Thou wenteſt along the journey, how canſt thou tell?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I did, but I am ſure 'tis ſo: had I ſtaid behind,
I think this had not proved.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A Wench the reaſon?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Who's that talks of a Wench there?

sp.speaker: Leo
sp.l: All this diſcontent
About a Wench?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Where is this Wench, good Colonel?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Prithee hold thy Peace: who calls thee to counſel?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Why, if there be a Wench—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: 'Tis ſit thou know her:
That I'le ſay for thee, and as ſit thou art for her,
Let her be mewed or ſtopt: how is it Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: He's wondrous diſcontent, he'l ſpeak to no man.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: H'as taken his Chamber cloſe, admits no entrance;
Tears in his eyes, and cryings out.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo, Sir,
And now I wiſh my ſelf half hang'd ere I went this journey.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What is this Woman?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I cannot tell ye,
But handſome as Heaven.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: She is not ſo high I hope, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I, that would be known.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I cannot ſhow ye neither;
The King has now diſpos'd of her.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: There lyes the matter:
Will he admit none to come to comfort him?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Not any near, nor, let 'em knock their hearts out,
Will never ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: 'Tis the beſt way if he have her;
For look you, a man would be loth to be diſturb'd in's paſtime;
'Tis every good mans caſe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: 'Tis all thy living,
We muſt not ſuffer this, we dare not ſuffer it:
For when theſe tender ſouls meet deep afflictions,
They are not ſtrong enough to ſtruggle with'em,
But drop away as Snow does, from a mountain,
And in the torrent of their own ſighs ſink themſelves:
I will, and muſt ſpeak to him.

sp.speaker: Lieu:
sp.l: So muſt I too:
He promiſed me a charge.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Of what? of Children
Upon my Conſcience, thou haſt a double company,
And all of thine own begetting already.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: That's all one,
I'le raiſe 'em to a Regiment, and then command 'em,
When they turn diſobedient, unbeget 'em:
Knock 'em o'th' head, and put in new.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A rare way;
But for all this, thou art not valiant enough
To dare to ſee the Prince now?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Do ye think he's angry?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Extreamly vext.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: To the endangering of any man comes near him.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Yet, if thou couldſt but win him out,
What e're thy ſuit were,
Believe it granted preſently.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Yet thou muſt think though,
That in the doing he may break upon ye,
And—

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: If he do not kill me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: There's the queſtion.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: For half a dozen hurts.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Art thou ſo valiant?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Not abſolutely ſo neither: no it cannot be,
I want my impoſtumes, and my things about me,
Yet I'le make danger, Colonel.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: 'Twill be rare ſport,
Howe're it take; give me thy hand; if thou doſt this,
I'le raiſe thee up a horſe Troop, take my word for't.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: What may be done by humane man.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Let's go then.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Away before he cool: he will relapſe elſe. Ex.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Will ſhe not yield?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: For all we can urge to her;
I ſwore you would marry her, ſhe laugh'd extreamly,
An • then ſhe rail'd like thunder.
Call in the Magician.
I muſt, and will obtain her, I am aſhes elſe.
Are all the Philt • rs in? Charms, Powder, Roots?

sp.speaker: Mag.
sp.l: They are all in; and now I only ſtay
The invocation of ſome helping Spirits.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: To your work then, and diſpatch.

sp.speaker: Mag.
sp.l: Sit ſtill, and fear not.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I ſhall ne'r endure theſe fights.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Away with the Woman: go wait without.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: When the Devil's gone, pray call me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Be ſure you make it powerful enough.

sp.speaker: Mag.
sp.l: Pray doubt not — He Conjures.

body.head: A SONG.
body.l: Riſe from the Shades below,
All you that prove
The helps of looſer Love;
Riſe and beſtow
Ʋpon this Cup, what ever may compel
By powerful Charm, and unreſiſted Spell.
A Heart unwarm'd to melt in Loves deſires,
Diſtill into this Liquor all your fires:
Heats, longings, tears,
But keep back frozen fears;
That ſhe may know, that has all power defied,
Art is a power that will not be denied.

body.head: The ANSWER.
body.l: I Obey, I Obey,
And am come to view the day,
Brought along, all may compel,
All the Earth has, and our Hell:
Here's a little, little Flower,
This will make her ſweat an hour,
Then unto ſuch flames ariſe,
A thouſand joys will not ſuffice.
Here's the powder of the Moon,
With which ſhe caught Endymion;
The powerful tears that Venus cryed,
When the Boy Adonis dyed.
Here's Medea's Charm, with which
Jaſons heart ſhe did bewitch,
Omphale this Spell put in,
When ſhe made the Libyan ſpin.
This dull root pluckt from Lethe flood,
Pu • ges all pure thoughts, and good.
Theſe I ſtir thus, round, round, round,
Whilſt our light feet beat the ground.

sp.speaker: Mag.
sp.l: Now Sir, 'tis full, and whoſoever drinks this
Shall violently d • at upon your perſon,
And never ſleep nor eat unſatisfied:
So many hours 'twill work, and work with Violence;
And thoſe expired, 'tis done. You have my art, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: See him rewarded liberally — Leucippe.
Here, take this bowl, and when ſhe calls for Wine next,
Be ſure you give her this, and ſee her drink it,
Delay no time when ſhe calls next.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I ſhall, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let none elſe touch it on your life.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I am charg'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Now if ſhe have an antidote art let her 'ſcape me.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent
sp.l: There's the door, Lieutenant, if you dare do any thing.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Here's no man waits.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: H' as given a charge that none ſhall,
Nor none ſhall come within the hearing of him:
Dare ye go forward?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Let me put on my Skull firſt.
My head's almoſt beaten into th' pap of an Apple.
Are there no Guns i'th' door?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: The Rogue will do it.
And yet I know he has no Stomach to't.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: What loop-holes are there when I knock for ſto ••• ,
For thoſe may pepper me? I can perceive none.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: How he views the Fortification.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Farewel Gentlemen,
If I be kill'd—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We'll ſee thee buried bravely.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Away, how ſhould I know that then? I'll knock ſoftly.
Pray heaven he ſpeak in a low voice now to comfort me:
I feel I have no heart to't: — Is't well, Gentlemen?
Colonel, my Troop—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A little louder.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Stay, ſtay;
Here is a window, I will ſee, ſtand wide.
By— he's charging of a Gun.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: There's no ſuch matter.
There's no body in this room.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: O 'twas a fire-ſhovel:
Now I'll knock louder; if he ſay who's there?
As ſure he has ſo much manners, then will I anſwer him
So finely & demurely; my Troop Colonel— knocks louder.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Knock louder, Fool, he hears not.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: You fool, do you.
Do and you dare now.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I do not undertake it.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Then hold your peace, and meddle with your o •• matters.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l:
Now he will knock.
Knocks loud •• .

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Sir, Sir, will't pleaſe you hear Sir?
Your Grace, I'll look again, what's that?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He's there now.
Lord! How he ſtares! I ne'r yet ſaw him thus alter'd:
Stand now, and take the Troop.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Would I were in't,
And a good horſe under me: I muſt knock again,
The Devil's at my fingers ends: he comes now.
Now Colonel, if I live—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: The Troop's thine own Boy.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: What deſperate fool, ambitious of his ruine?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Your Father would deſire ye, Sir, to come to dinner.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thou art no more.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Now, now, now, now.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Poor Coxcomb:
Why do I aim at thee? Exit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: His fear has kill'd him.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: I proteſt he's almoſt ſtiff: bend him and rub him,
Hold his Noſe cloſe, you, if you be a woman,
Help us a little: here's a man near periſh'd.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Alas alas, I have nothing here about me.
Look to my Bowl; I'll run in preſently
And fetch ſome water: bend him, and ſet him upwards.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A goodly man— Exit.
Here's a brave heart: he's warm again: you ſhall not
Leave us i'th' lurch ſo, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Now he breaths too.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: If we had but any drink to raiſe his Spirits.
What's that i' th' Bowl? upon my life, good Liquor,
She would not own it elſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: He ſees.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Look up Boy.
And take this Cup, and drink it off; I'll pledge thee.
Guide it to his mouth, he ſwallows heartily.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Oh! fear and ſorrow's dry; 'tis off—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Stand up man.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Am I not ſhot?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Away with him, and chear him:
Thou haſt won thy Troop.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I think I won it bravely.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Go, I muſt ſee the Prince, he muſt not live thus;
And let me hear an hour hence from ye.

Well, Sir—
Exeunt Gent. and Lieu.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Here, here: where's the ſick Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He's up, and gone, Lady.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Alas, that I came ſo late.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He muſt ſtill thank ye;
Ye left that in a Cup here did him comfort.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: That in the Bowl?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Yes truly, very much comfort,
He drank it off, and after it ſpoke luſtily.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Did he drink it all?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: All off.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: The Devil choak him;
• am undone: h' as twenty Devils in him;
Undone for ever, left he none?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I think not.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: No, not a drop: what ſhall become of me now?
Had he no where elſe to ſwound? a vengeance ſwound him:
Undone, undone, undone: ſtay, I can lye yet
And ſwear too at a pinch, that's all my comfort.
Look to him; I ſay look to him, & but mark what follows. Ex.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What a Devil ails the Woman? here comes the Prince again,
With ſuch a ſadneſs on his face, as ſorrow,
• orrow her ſelf but poorly imitates.
Sorrow of Sorrows on that heart that caus'd it.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Why might ſhe not be falſe and treacherous to me?
And found ſo by my Father? ſhe was a Woman,
And many a one of that Sex, young and fair,
As fall of faith as ſhe, have fallen, and foully.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: It is a Wench! O that I knew the circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Why might not, to preſerve me from this ruine,
She having loſt her honour, and abuſed me,
My father change the forms o'th' coins, and execute
His anger on a fault ſhe ne'r committed,
Only to keep me ſafe? why ſhould I think ſo?
She never was to me, but all obedience,
Sweetneſs, and love.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: How heartily he weeps now?
• have not wept this thirty years, and upward;
But now, if I ſhould be hang'd I cannot hold from't:
• t grieves me to the heart.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Who's that that mocks me?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A plague of him that mocks ye: I grieve truly,
Truly, and heartily to ſee you thus, Sir:
And if it lay in my power, gods are my witneſs,
Who e'r he be that took your ſweet peace from you;
• am not ſo old yet, nor want I ſpirit—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: No more of that, no more Leontius,
Revenges are the gods: our part is ſufferance:
Farewell, I ſhall not ſee thee long.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Good Sir, tell me the cauſe, I know there is a woman in't;
Do you hold me faithful? dare you truſt your Souldier?
Sweet Prince, the cauſe?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I muſt not, dare not tell it,
And as thou art an honeſt man, enquire not.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Will ye be merry then?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I am wondrous merry.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: 'Tis wondrous well: you think now this becomes ye.
Shame on't, it does not, Sir, it ſhews not handſomely;
If I were thus; you would ſwear I were an Aſs ſtraight;
A wooden aſs; whine for a Wench?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Prithee leave me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I will not leave ye for a tit.

l.hi: Leontius?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: For that you may have any where for ſix pence,
And a dear penny-worth too.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Nay, then you are troubleſome.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Not half ſo troubleſom as you are to your ſelf, Sir;
Was that brave Heart made to pant for a placket:
And now i'th' dog-days too, when nothing dare love!
That noble Mind to melt away and moulder
For a hey nonny, nonny! Would I had a Glaſs here,
To ſhew ye what a pretty toy ye are turn'd to.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: My wretched Fortune.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Will ye but let me know her?
I'll once turn Bawd: go to, they are good mens offices,
And not ſo contemptible as we take 'em for:
And if ſhe be above ground, and a Woman;
I ask no more; I'll bring her o' my back, Sir,
By this hand I will, and I had as lieve bring the Devil,
I care not who ſhe be, nor where I have her;
And in your arms, or the next Bed deliver her,
Which you think fitteſt, and when you have danc'd your galliard.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Away, and fool to them are ſo affected:
O thou art gone, and all my comfort with thee!
Wilt thou do one thing for me?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: All things i' th' World, Sir,
Of all dangers.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Swear.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I will,

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Come near me no more then.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Come no more near me:
Thou art a plague-ſore to me Exit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Give you good ev'n Sir;
If you be ſuffer'd thus, we ſhall have fine ſport.
I will be ſorry yet.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: How now, how does he?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Nay, if I tell ye, hang me, or any man elſe
That hath his nineteen wits; he has the bots I think,
He groans, and roars, and kicks.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Will he ſpeak yet?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Not willingly:
Shortly he will not ſee a man; if ever
I look'd upon a Prince ſo metamorphos'd,
So juggl'd into I know not what, ſhame take me;
This 'tis to be in love.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Is that the cauſe on't?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What is it not the cauſe of but bear-baitings?
And yet it ſtinks much like it: out upon't;
What giants, and what dwarffs, what owls and apes,
What dogs, and cats it makes us? men that are poſſeſt with it,
Live as if they had a Legion of Devils in 'em,
And every Devil of a ſeveral nature;
Nothing but Hey-paſs, re-paſs: where's the Lieutenant?
Has he gather'd up the end on's wits again?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: He is alive: but you that talk of wonders,
Shew me but ſuch a wonder as he is now.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why? he was ever at the worſt a wonder.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: He is now moſt wonderful; a Blazer now, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What ails the Fool? and what Star reigns now Gentlemen
We have ſuch Prodigies?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: 'Twill poſe your heaven-hunters;
He talks now of the King, no other language,
And with the King as he imagines, hourly.
Courts the King, drinks to the King, dies for the King,
Buys all the Pictures of the King, wears the Kings colours.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Does he not lye i'th' King ſtreet too?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: He's going thither,
Makes prayers for the King, in ſundry languages,
Turns all his Proclamations into metre;
Is really in love with the King, moſt dotingly,
And ſwears Adonis was a Devil to him:
A ſweet King, a moſt comely King, and ſuch a King—

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Then down on's marrow-bones; O excellent King
Thus he begins, Thou Light, and Life of Creatures,
Angel-ey'd King, vouchſafe at length thy favour;
And ſo proceeds to inciſion: what think ye of this ſorrow?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Will as familiarly kiſs the King horſes
As they paſs by him: ready to raviſh his footmen.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why, this is above Ela?
But how comes this?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Nay that's to underſtand yet,
But thus it is, and this part but the pooreſt,
'Twould make a man leap over the Moon to ſee him act theſe.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: With ſighs as though his heart would break:
Cry like a breech'd boy, not eat a bit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I muſt go ſee him preſently,
For this is ſuch a gig, for certain, Gentlemen,
The Fiend rides on a Fiddle-ſtick.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Can ye guide me to him for half an hour? I am his
To ſee the miracle.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: We ſure ſhall ſtart him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Are you ſure ſhe drank it?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Now muſt I lye moſt confidently.
Yes Sir, ſhe has drunk it off.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How works it with her?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I ſee no alteration yet.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: There will be,
For he is the greateſt Artiſt living made it.
Where is ſhe now?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: She is ready to walk out, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Stark mad, I know ſhe will be.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: So I hope, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She knows not of the Prince?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Of no man living—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How do I look? how do my cloaths become me?
I am not very grey.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: A very youth, Sir,
Upon my maiden-head as ſmug as April:
Heaven bleſs that ſweet face, 'twill undo a thouſand;
Many a ſoft heart muſt ſob yet, e'r that wither,
Your Grace can give content enough.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Here ſhe comes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How ſhall I keep her off me?

Go, & perfume the room: make all things ready.
Ex. Leu.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No hope yet of the Prince! no comfort of him!
They keep me mew'd up here, as they mew mad folks,
No company but my afflictions.
This royal Devil again! ſtrange, how he haunts me!
How like a poyſon'd potion his eyes fright me!
Has made himſelf handſome too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Do you look now, Lady?
You will leap anon.

sp.speaker: Cel
sp.l: Curl'd and perfum'd? I ſmell him;
He looks on's legs too, ſure he will cut a caper;
God-a mercy, dear December.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: O do you ſmile now,
I knew it would work with you; come hither pretty one.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I like thoſe courteſies well; come hither and kiſs me.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I am reading, Sir, of a ſhort Treatiſe here,
That's call'd the Vanity of Luſt: has your Grace ſeen it?
He ſays here, that an Old Mans looſe deſire
Is like the Glow-worms light, the Apes ſo wonder'd at:
Which when they gather'd ſticks, and laid upon't,
And blew, and blew, turn'd tail, and went out preſently:
And in another place he calls their loves,
Faint Smells of dying Flowers, carry no comforts;
They're doting, ſtinking foggs, ſo thick and muddy,
Reaſon with all his beams cannot beat through 'em.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How's this? is this the potion? you but fool ſtill;
I know you love me.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: As you are juſt and honeſt;
I know I love and honour you: admire you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This makes againſt me, fearfully againſt me,

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: But as you bring your power to perſecute me,
Your traps to catch mine innocence to rob me,
As you layout your luſts to overwhelm me,
Hell never hated good, as I hate you, Sir;
And I dare tell it to your face: What glory
Now after all your Conqueſts got, your Titles,
The ever-living memories rais'd to you,
Can my defeat be? my poor wrack, what triumph?
And when you crown your ſwelling Cups to fortune,
What honourable tongue can ſing my ſtory?
Be as your Emblem is, a gorious Lamp
Set on the top of all, to light all perfectly:
Be as your office is, a god-like Juſtice,
Into all ſhedding equally your Vertues.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She has drencht me now; now I admire her goodneſs.
So young, ſo nobly ſtrong, I never taſted:
Can nothing in the power of Kings perſwade ye?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No, nor that power command me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Say I ſhould force ye?
I have it in my will.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Your will's a poor one;
And though it be a King's Will, a deſpiſed one.
Weaker than Infants legs, your will's in ſwadling Clo •••
A thouſand ways my will has found to check ye;
A thouſand doors to 'ſcape ye, I dare dye, Sir;
As ſuddenly I dare dye, as you can offer:
Nay, ſay you had your Will, ſay you had raviſh'd me,
Perform'd your luſt, what had you purchas'd by it?
What Honour won? do you know who dwells above, S •
And what they have prepar'd for men turn'd Devils?
Did you never hear their thunder? ſtart and tremble,
Death ſitting on your bloud, when their fires viſit us.
Will nothing wring you then do you think? ſit hard here,
And like a Snail curl round about your Conſcience,
Biting and ſtinging: will you not roar too late then?
Then when you ſhake in honour of this Villainy,
Then will I riſe a Star in Heaven, and ſcorn ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Luſt, how I hate thee now! and love this ſweetneſs▪
Will you be my Queen? can that price purchaſe ye?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Not all the World, I am a Queen already,
Crown'd by his Love, I muſt not loſe for Fortune;
I can give none away, ſell none away, Sir,
Can lend no love, am not mine own Exchequer;
For in anothers heart my hope and peace lies.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Your fair hands, Lady? for yet I am not pure enough
To touch theſe Lips, in that ſweet Peace ye ſpoke of.
Live now for ever, and I to ſerve your Vertues—

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Why now you ſhow a god! now I kneel to ye;
This Sacrifice of Virgins Joy ſend to ye:
Thus I hold up my hands to Heaven that touch'd ye,
And pray eternal Bleſſings dwell about ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Vertue commands the Stars: riſe more than Vertue.
Your preſent comfort ſhall be now my buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: All my obedient ſervice wait upon ye. Ex. ſeveraly

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Haſt thou clean forgot the Wars?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Prithee hold thy peace.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: His mind's much elevated now.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo.
Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I am ſo troubled with this Fellow.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He will call me Rogue anon.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis ten to one elſe.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: O King that thou knew'ſt I lov'd thee, how I lov'd thee
And where O King, I barrel up thy beauty.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He cannot leave his Sutlers trade, he woos in't.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: O never, King.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: By this hand, when I conſider—

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: My honeſt friend, you are a little ſawcy.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I told you you would have it.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: When mine own worth—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Is flung into the ballance, and found nothing.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: And yet a Soldier.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: And yet a ſawcy one.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: One that has followed thee.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Fair and far off.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Fought for thy grace.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: 'Twas for ſome grief, you lye Sir.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: He's the ſon of a whore denies this: will that ſatisfie ye?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Yes, very well.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Shall then that thing that honours thee?
• ow miſerable a thing ſoever, yet a thing ſtill;
• od though a thing of nothing, thy thing ever.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Here's a new thing.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: He's in a deep dump now.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I'le fetch him out on't. When's the Kings birth-day?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: When e're it be, that day I'le dye with ringing.
•• d there's the reſolution of a Lover. Exit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A goodly reſolution ſure I take it.
• t is be witch'd, or moop'd, or his brains melted,
• ould he find no body to fall in love with; but the King,
• he good old King, to doat upon him too?
•• y, now I remember, what the fat woman warn'd me,
• nd me remember, and look to him too:
• e hang if ſhe have not a hand in this: he's conjured,
• oe after him, I pity the poor Raſcal,
〈◊〉 the meantime I'le wait occaſion
• o work upon the Prince.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Pray doe that ſeriouſly.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: He's very ill.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I am very ſorry for't,
•• d much aſhamed I have wronged her innocence,
Menippus, guide her to the Princes lodgings,
• here leave her to his love again.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I am glad Sir.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: He will ſpeak to none.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: O I ſhall break that ſilence;
• e quick, take fair attendance.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Yes Sir preſently. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: He will find his tongue, I warrant ye; his health too;
〈◊〉 ſend a phyſick will not fail.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: Fair work it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: We hear the Princes mean to viſit us
〈◊〉 way of truce.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: 'Tis thought ſo.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Come: let's in then,
•• d think upon the nobleſt wayes to meet 'em. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: There's no way now to get in: all the light ſtopt too;
• or can I hear a ſound of him, pray Heaven
• e uſe no violence: I think he has more Soul,
• tronger, and I hope nobler: would I could but ſee once
• his beauty he groans under, or come to know
• ut any circumſtance. What noiſe is that there?
〈◊〉 think I heard him groan: here are ſome coming;
〈◊〉 woman too, I'le ſtand aloof, and view 'em.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Well, ſome of ye have been to blame in this point,
• ut I forgive ye: The King might have pickt out too
• ome fitter woman to have tri'd his valour.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: 'Twas all to the beſt meant, Lady.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I muſt think ſo,
• or how to mend it now: he's here you tell me?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: He's Madam, and the joy to ſee you only
Will draw him out.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I know that womans tongue,
〈◊〉 think I have ſeen her face too: I'le goe nearer:
If this be ſhe, he has ſome cauſe of ſorrow:
'Tis the ſame face; the ſame, moſt excellent woman.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: This ſhould be Lord Leontius: I remember him.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Lady, I think ye know me.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Speak ſoft, good Souldier:
I do, and know ye worthy, know ye noble;
Know not me yet openly, as you love me;
But let me ſee ye again, I'le ſatisfie ye:
I am wondrous glad to ſee thoſe eyes.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You have charged me.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You ſhall know where I am.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I will not off yet:
She goes to knock at's door: This muſt be ſhe
The fellow told me of: right glad I am on't,
He will bolt now for certain.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Are ye within Sir?
I'le trouble you no more: I thank your courteſie,
Pray leave me now.

sp.speaker: All. Me.
sp.l:
We reſt your humble ſervants.
Ex. Me. &c.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: So now my jives are off: pray Heaven he be here!
Maſter, my royal Sir: do you hear who calls ye?
Love, my Demetrius.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Theſe are pretty quail-pipes,
The Cock will Crow anon.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Can ye be drowſie,
When I call at your Window?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I hear him ſtirring:
Now he comes wondring out.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: 'Tis Celias ſound ſure:
The ſweetneſs of that tongue draws all hearts to it;
There ſtands the ſhape too.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: How he ſtares upon her?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Ha? do mine eyes abuſe me?
'Tis ſhe, the living Celia: your hand Lady?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: What ſhould this mean?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: The very ſelf ſame Celia.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: How do ye Sir?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Only turn'd brave.
I heard you were dead my dear one, compleat,
She is wondrous brave, a wondrous gallant Courtier.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: How he ſurveyes me round? here has been foul play.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: How came ſhe thus?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: It was a kind of death Sir,
I ſuffered in your abſence, mew'd up here,
And kept conceal'd I know not how.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: 'Tis likely:
How came you hither Celia? wondrous gallant:
Did my Father ſend for ye?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: So they told me Sir,
And on command too.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I hope you were obedient?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I was ſo ever.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And ye were bravely us'd?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I wanted nothing:
My maiden-head to a mote i'th' Sun, he's jealous:
I muſt now play the knave with him, though I dye for't,
'Tis in my nature.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Her very eyes are alter'd:
Jewels, and rich ones too, I never ſaw yet —
And what were thoſe came for ye?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Monſtrous jealous:
Have I liv'd at the rate of theſe ſcorn'd queſtions?
They ſeem'd of good ſort, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Kind men?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: They were wondrous kind:
I was much beholding to 'em;
There was one Menippus Sir.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: One Menippus,
A notable merry Lord, and a good companion.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And one Charinthus too?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Yes, there was ſuch a one.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And Timon?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt true.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And thou moſt treacherous:
My Fathers bawds by—they never miſs courſe;
And were theſe daily with ye?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Every hour Sir.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And was there not a Lady, a fat Lady?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: O yes; a notable good wench.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: The Devil fetch her.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: 'Tis ev'n the merrieſt wench —

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Did ſhe keep with ye too?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: She was all in all, my bed-fellow, eat with me,
Brought me acquainted.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: You are well know here then?
There is no living here a ſtranger I think.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: How came ye by this brave gown?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: This is a poor one:
Alas, I have twenty ficher: do you ſee theſe jewels?
Why, they are the pooreſt things, to thoſe are ſent me,
And ſent me hourly too.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Is there no modeſtie?
No faith in this fair Sex?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What will this prove too?
For yet with all my wits, I underſtand not.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Come hither; thou art dead indeed, loſt, tainted;
All that I left thee fair, and innocent,
Sweet as thy youth, and carrying comfort in't;
All that I hoped for vertuous, is fled from thee,
Turn'd back, and bankrupt.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: By'r Lady, this cuts ſhrewdly.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thou art dead, for ever dead; ſins ſurfeit ſlew thee;
The ambition of thoſe wanton eyes betrai'd thee;
Go from me, grave of honour; go thou foul one,
Thou glory of thy ſin; go thou deſpis'd one,
And where there is no vertue, nor no virgin;
Where Chaſtity was never known, nor heard of;
Where nothing reigns but impious luſt, and looſer faces.
Go thither, child of bloud, and ſing my doating.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You do not ſpeak this ſeriouſly I hope Sir;
I did but jeſt with you.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Look not upon me,
There is more hell in thoſe eyes, than hell harbours;
And when they flame, more torments.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Dare ye truſt me?
You durſt once even with all you had: your love Sir?
By this fair light I am honeſt.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thou ſubtle Circe,
Caſt not upon the maiden light eclipſes:
Curſe not the day.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Come, come, you ſhall not do this:
How fain you would ſeem angry now, to fright me;
You are not in the field among your Enemies;
Come, I muſt cool this courage.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Out thou impudence,
Thou ulcer of thy Sex; when I firſt ſaw thee,
I drew into mine eyes mine own deſtruction,
I pull'd into my heart that ſudden poyſon,
That now conſumes my dear content to cinders:
I am not now Demetrius, thou haſt chang'd me;
Thou, woman, with thy thouſand wiles haſt chang'd me;
Thou Serpent with thy angel-eyes haſt ſlain me;
And where, before I touch'd on this fair ruine,
I was a man, and reaſon made, and mov'd me,
Now one great lump of grief, I grow and wander.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And as you are noble, do you think I did this?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Put all the Devils wings on, and flie from me.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I will go from ye, never more to ſee ye:
I will ſhe from ye, as a plague hangs o're me;
And through the progreſs of my life hereafter;
Where ever I ſhall find a fool, a falſe man,
One that ne're knew the worth of poliſh'd vertue;
A baſe ſuſpecter of a virgins honour,
A child that flings away the wealth he cri'd for,
Him will I call Demetrius: that fool Demetrius,
That mad man a Demetrius; and that falſe man,
The Prince of broken faiths, even Prince Demetrius.
You think now, I ſhould cry, and kneel down to ye,
Petition for my peace; let thoſe that feel here
The weight of evil, wait for ſuch a favour,
I am above your hate, as far above it,
In all the actions of an innocent life,
As the pure Stars are from the muddy meteors,
Cry when you know your folly: howl and curſe then,
Beat that unmanly breaſt, that holds a falſe heart
When ye ſhall come to know, whom ye have ſlung from ye

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Pray ye ſtay a little.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Not your hopes can alter me,
Then let a thouſand black thoughts muſter in ye,
And with thoſe enter in a thouſand doatings;
Thoſe eyes be never ſhut, but drop to nothing:
My innocence for ever haunt and fright ye:
Thoſe arms together grow in folds; that tongue,
That bold bad tongue that barks out theſe diſgraces.
When you ſhall come to know how nobly vertuous
I have preſerv'd my life, rot, rot within ye.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: What ſhall I doe?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Live a loſt man for ever.
Go ask your Fathers conſcience what I ſuffered,
And through what ſeas of hazards I ſayl'd through:
Mine honour ſtill advanced in ſpight of tempeſts,
Then take your leave of love; and confeſs freely,
You were never worthy of this heart that ſerv'd ye,

And ſo farewel ungratefull —
E •• t

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Is ſhe gone?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l:
I'le follow her, and will find out this matter.—
Ex ••

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Are ye pleas'd now? have you got your hearts g ••
Have I reſtor'd ye that?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Sir even for Heaven ſake,
And ſacred truth ſake, tell me how ye ſound her.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I will, and in few words. Before I tri'd her,
'Tis true, I thought her moſt unfit your fellowſhip,
And fear'd her too: which fear begot that ſtory
I told ye firſt: but ſince, like gold I toucht her.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And how dear Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Heavens holy light's not purer:
The conſtancy and goodneſs of all women
That ever liv'd, to win the names of worthy,
This noble Maid has doubled in her: honour,
All promiſes of wealth, all art to win her,
And by all tongues imploy'd, wrought as much on her
As one may doe upon the Sun at noon day
By lighting Candles up: her ſhape is heavenly,
And to that heavenly ſhape her thoughts are angels.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Why did you tell me Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis true, I err'd in't:
But ſince I made a full proof of her vertue,
I find a King too poor a ſervant for her.
Love her, and honour her; in all obſerve her.
She muſt be ſomething more than time yet tells her:
And certain I believe him beſt, enjoyes her:
I would not loſe the hope of ſuch a Daughter,
To adde another Empire to my honour.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: O wretched ſtate! to what end ſhall I turn me?
And where begins my penance? now, what ſervice
Will win her love again? my death muſt doe it:
And if that ſacrifice can purge my follies,
Be pleas'd, O mightie Love, I dye thy ſervant— Exit

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I Know he do's not deſerve ye; h'as us'd you poorly:
And to redeem himſelf —

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Redeem?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I know it—
There's no way left.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: For Heavens ſake do not name him,
• o not think on him Sir, he's ſo far from me
〈◊〉 all my thoughts now, methinks I never knew him.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: But yet I would ſee him again.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No, never, never.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I do not mean to lend him any comfort;
• ut to afflict him, ſo to torture him;
• hat even his very Soul may ſhake within him:
• o make him know, though he be great and powerfull,
• is not within his aim to deal diſhonourably,
• nd carry it off, and with a maid of your ſort.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs, I could moſt ſpightfully afflict him;
• ow, now, I could whet my anger at him;
• ow, arm'd with bitterneſs, I could ſhoot through him;
〈◊〉 long to vex him.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And doe it home, and bravely.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Were I a man?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I'le help that weakneſs in ye:
〈◊〉 honour ye, and ſerve ye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Not only to diſclaim me,
When he had ſeal'd his vowes in Heaven, ſworn to me,
• nd poor believing I became his ſervant:
• ut moſt maliciouſly to brand my credit,
• tain my pure name.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I would not ſuffer it:
•• e him I would again, and to his teeth too:
• d's precious, I would ring him ſuch a leſſon—

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I have done that already.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Nothing, nothing:
〈◊〉 was too poor a purge; beſides, by this time
• e has found his fault, and feels the hells that follow it.
•• at, and your urg'd on anger to the higheſt,
Why, 'twill be ſuch a ſtroak —

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Say he repent then,
And ſeek with tears to ſoften, I am a woman;
• woman that have lov'd him, Sir, have honour'd him:
• am no more.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why, you may deal thereafter.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: If I forgive him, I am loſt.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Hold there then,
The ſport will be to what a poor ſubmiſſion —
• ut keep you ſtrong.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I would not ſee him.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Yes,
• ou ſhall Ring his knell.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: How if I kill him?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Kill him? why, let him dye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I know 'tis fit ſo.
•• t why ſhould I that lov'd him once, deſtroy him?
• had he ſcap't this ſin, what a brave Gentleman—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs, had this not faln, a nobler,
• handſomer, the whole world had not ſhow'd ye:
• nd to his making ſuch a mind—

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: 'Tis certain:
• ut all this I muſt now forget.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You ſhall not
• f I have any art: goe up ſweet Lady,
And truſt my truth.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: But good Sir bring him not.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I would not for the honour ye are born to,
• ut you ſhall ſee him, and neglect him too, and ſcorn him.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You will be near me then.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I will be with ye;
• et there's ſome hope to ſtop this gap, I'le work hard. Ex.

div.head: SCENA II.
div.stage: Enter Antigonus, Menip. two Gent. Lieutenant, and Lords.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But is it poſſible this fellow took it?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo by the violence it wrought with,
Yet now the fits ev'n off.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I beſeech your Grace.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Nay, I forgive thy wiſe with all my heart,
And am right glad ſhe drank it not her ſelf,
And more glad that the vertuous maid eſcap't it,
I would not for the world 'thad hit: but that this Souldier,
Lord how he looks, that he ſhould take this vomit;
Can he make rimes too?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: H'as made a thouſand Sir,
And plaies the burthen to 'em on a Jews-trump

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: He looks as though he were bepiſt: do you love me Sir?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Yes ſurely even with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I thank ye;
I am glad I have ſo good a ſubject: but pray ye tell me,
How much did ye love me, before ye drank this matter?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Even as much as a ſober man might; and a Souldier
That your grace owes juſt half a years pay to.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Well remembred;
And did I ſeem ſo young and amiable to ye?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Methought you were the ſweeteſt youth—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: That's excellent.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I truly Sir: and ever as I thought on ye,
I wiſhed, and wiſhed —

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What didſt thou wiſh prethee?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Ev'n, that I had been a wench of fifteen for ye,
A handſom wench Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why? God a Mercy Souldier:
I ſeem not ſo now to thee.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Not all out:
And yet I have a grudging to your grace ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thou waſt never in love before?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: Not with a King,
And hope I ſhall never be again: Truly Sir,
I have had ſuch plunges, and ſuch bickrings,
And as it were ſuch runnings atilt within me,
For whatſoever it was provok't me toward ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: God a-mercy ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I had it with a vengeance,
It plaid his prize.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I would not have been a wench then,
Though of this age.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: No ſure, I ſhould have ſpoil'd ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Well, goe thy waies, of all the luſty lovers
That e're I ſaw—wilt have another potion?

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: If you will be another thing, have at ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha: give me thy hand, from henceforth thou art my ſouldier,
Do bravely, I'le love thee as much.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I thank ye;
But if you were mine enemy, I would not wiſh it ye:
I beſeech your Grace, pay me my charge.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: That's certain Sir;
H'as bought up all that e're he found was like ye,
Or any thing you have lov'd, that he could purchaſe;
Old horſes, that your Grace has ridden blind, and foundr'd;
Dogs, rotten hawks, and which is more than all this,
Has worn your Graces Gauntlet in his Bonnet.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Bring in your Bills: mine own love ſhall be ſatisfi'd;
And ſirrah, for this potion you have taken,
I'le point ye out a portion ye ſhall live on.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: 'Twas the beſt draught that e're ye drunk.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I hope ſo.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Are the Princes come toth' Court?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: They are all; and lodg'd Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Come then, make ready for their entertainment,
Which preſently we'l give: wait you on me Sir.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: I ſhall love drink the better whilſt I live hoyes.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Let me but ſee her, dear Leontius;
Let me but dye before her.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Would that would doe it:
If I knew where ſhe lay now, with what honeſtie,
You having ſlung ſo main a miſchief on her,
And on ſo innocent and ſweet a Beauty,
Dare I preſent your viſit?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I'le repent all:
And with the greateſt ſacrifice of ſorrow,
That ever Lover made.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: 'Twill be too late Sir:
I know not what will become of you.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: You can help me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: It may be to her ſight: what are you nearer?
She has ſworn ſhe will not ſpeak to ye, look upon ye,
And to love ye again, O ſhe cries out, and thunders,
She had rather love—there is no hope—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Yes Leontius,
There is a hope, which though it draw no love to it,
At leaſt will draw her to lament my fortune,
And that hope ſhall relieve me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Hark ye Sir, hark ye:
Say I ſhould bring ye —

sp.speaker: Dem
sp.l: Do not not trifle with me?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I will not trifle; both together bring ye,
You know the wrongs ye' done.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I do confeſs 'em.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And if you ſhould then jump into your fury,
And have another querk in your head.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I'le dye firſt.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You muſt ſay nothing to her; for 'tis certain,
The nature of your crime will admit to excuſe.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I will not ſpeak, mine eyes ſhall tell my penance.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You muſt look wondrous ſad too.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I need not look ſo,
I am truly ſadneſs ſ • lf.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: That look will do it:
Stay here, I'le bring her to you inſtantly:
But take heed how you bear your ſelf: ſit down there,
The more humble you are, the more ſhe'l take compaſſion.
Women are per'lous thing to deal upon. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: What ſhall become of me? to curſe my fortune,
Were but to curſe my Father; that's too impious;
But under whatſoever fate I ſuffer,
Bleſs I beſeech thee heaven her harmleſs goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Now arm your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You have not brought him?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Yes faith,
And there he is: you ſee in what poor plight too,
Now you may doe your will, kill him, or ſave him.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I will goe back.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I will be hang'd then Lady,
Are ye a coward now?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I cannot ſpeak to him.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: O me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: There was a ſigh to blow a Church down;
So, now their eyes are fixt, the ſmall ſhot playes,
They will come toth' batterie anon.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: He weeps extreamly.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Rail at him now.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I dare not.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I am glad on't.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Not dare believe his tears.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: You may, bleſt beauty,
For thoſe thick ſtreams that troubled my repentance,
Are crept out long agoe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You ſee how he looks.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: What have I to doe how he looks? how lookt he then,
When with a poiſoned tooth he bit mine honour?
It was your counſel too, to ſcorn and ſlight him

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I, if ye ſaw ſit cauſe; and you confeſt too,
Except this ſin, he was the braveſt Gentleman,
The ſweeteſt, nobleſt: I take nothing from ye,
Not from your anger; uſe him as you pleaſe:
For to ſay truth, he has deſerved your juſtice;
But ſtill conſider what he has been to you.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Pray do not blind me thus.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: O Gentle Miſtris,
If there were any way to expiate
A ſin ſo great as mine, by interceſſion,
By prayers, by daily tears, by dying for ye:
O what a joy would cloſe theſe eyes that love ye.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: They ſay women have tender hearts, I know not,
I am ſure mine melts.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Sir, I forgive ye heartily,
And all your wrong to me I caſt behind me,
And wiſh ye a fit beauty to your vertues:
Mine is too poor, in peace I part thus from you;
I muſt look back: gods keep your grace: he's here ſtill. Ex

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: She has forgiven me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: She has directed ye:
Up, up, and follow like a man: away Sir,
She lookt behind her twice: her heart dwells here Sir,
Ye drew tears from her too: ſhe cannot freeze thus;
The door's ſet open too, are ye a man?
Are ye alive? do ye underſtand her meaning?
Have ye bloud and ſpirit in ye?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I dare not trouble her.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Nay, and you will be nipt i'th' head with nothing,
Walk whining up and down; I dare not, I cannot:
Strike now or never: faint heart, you know what Sir—
Be govern'd by your fear, and quench your fire out.
A Devil on't, ſtands this door ope for nothing?
So get ye together, and be naught: now to ſecure all,

Will I go fetch out a more ſoveraign plaiſter.
Exe ••• .

div.head: SCENA IV.
div.stage: Enter Antigonus, Seleucus, Lyſimachus, Ptolomy, Lieutenant, Gentlemen, Lords.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This peace is fairly made.

sp.speaker: Seleu.
sp.l: Would your Grace wiſh us
To put in more: take what you pleaſe, we yield it;
The honour done us by your ſon conſtrains it,
Your noble ſon.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It is ſufficient, Princes;
And now we are one again, one mind, one body,
And one ſword ſhall ſtrike for us.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: Let Prince Demetrius
But lead us on: for we are his vowed ſervants;
Againſt the ſtrength of all the world we'l buckle.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: And even from all that ſtrength we'l catch at • cto •

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: O had I now recover'd but the fortune
I loſt in Antioch, when mine Unckle periſh'd;
But that were but to ſurfeit me with bleſſings.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: You loſt a ſweet child there.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Name it no more Sir;
This is no time to entertain ſuch ſorrows;
Will your Majeſty do us the honour, we may ſee the Prince,
And wait upon him?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I wonder he ſtayes from us:
How now Leontius, where's my ſon?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Brave Captain.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: Old valiant Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Your Graces are welcom:
Your ſon and't pleaſe you Sir, is new caſhiered yonder,
Caſt from his Miſtris favour: and ſuch a coil there is;
Such fending, and ſuch proving; ſhe ſtands off,
And will by no means yield to compoſition:
He offers any price; his body to her.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: She is a hard Lady, denies that caution.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And now they whine, and now they rave: faith Princes,
'Twere a good point of charity to piece 'em;
For leſs than ſuch a power will doe juſt nothing:
And if you mean to ſee him, there it muſt be,
For there will he grow, till he be tranſplanted.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Beſeech your grace, let's wait upon you thith • r,
That I may ſee that beauty dares deny him,
That ſcornfull beauty.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: I ſhould think it worſe now;
I brought up beauty.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She has too much reaſon for't;
Which with too great a grief, I ſhame to think of,
• ut we'll go ſee this game.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: Rather this wonder.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Be you our guide Leontius, here's a new peace. Ex.

div.head: SCENE V.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Thus far you ſhall perſwade me, ſtill to honour ye,
• till to live with ye, Sir, or near about ye;
• or not to lye, you have my firſt and laſt love:
• ut ſince you have conceiv'd an evil againſt me,
• n evil that ſo much concerns your honour,
• hat honour aim'd by all at for a pattern:
• nd though there be a falſe thought, and confeſt too,
• nd much repentance faln in ſhowrs to purge it;
• et, whileſt that great reſpect I ever bore ye,
Dwells in my bloud, and in my heart that duty;
Had it but been a dream, I muſt not touch ye.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: O you will make ſome other happy?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Never,
Upon this hand I'le ſeal that ſaith.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: We may kiſs,
• ut not thoſe out o'th' peace too.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Thoſe I'le give ye,
• o there you will be pleas'd to pitch your ne ultra,
〈◊〉 will be merry with ye; ſing, diſcourſe with ye,
• e your poor Miſtris ſtill: In truth I love ye.

div.stage: Enter Leontius, Antigonus, Seleucus, Lyſimachus, Ptolomie, Lieutenant, and Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Stay, who are theſe?

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: A very handſom Lady.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: As e're you ſaw.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Pity her heart's ſo cruel.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: How does your Grace? he ſtands ſtill, will not hear us.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: We come to ſerve ye, Sir, in all our fortunes.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: He bows a little now; he's ſtrangely alter'd.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Ha? pray ye a word Leontius, pray ye a word with ye,
Lyſmachus? you both knew mine Enanthe,
〈◊〉 loſt in Antioch, when the Town was taken,
Mine Uncle ſlain, Antigonus had the ſack on't?

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: Yes, I remember well the Girl.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Methinks now
That face is wondrous like her: I have her picture,
The ſame, but more years on her; the very ſame.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: A Cherry to a Chery is not liker.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Look on her eyes.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Moſt certain ſhe is like her:
Many a time have I dandled her in theſe arms, Sir,
And I hope who will more.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What's that ye look at, Prnices?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: This Picture, and that Lady, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Ha! they are near:
They only err in time.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: Did you mark that bluſh there?
That came the neareſt.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I muſt ſpeak to her.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You'll quickly be reſolved.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Your name ſweet Lady?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Enanthe, Sir: and this to beg your bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Do you know me?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: If you be the King Seleucus,
I know you are my Father.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Peace a little,
Where did I loſe ye?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: At the Sack of Antioch,
Where my good Unckle di'd, and I was taken,
By a mean Souldier taken: by this Prince,
This noble Prince, redeem'd from him again,
Where ever ſince I have remain'd his Servant.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: My joys are now too full: welcome Enanthe,
Mine own, my deareſt, and my beſt Enanthe.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And mine too deſperate.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: You ſhall not think ſo,
This is a peace indeed.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I hope it ſhall be,
And ask it firſt.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Moſt Royal Sir, ye have it.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I once more beg it thus.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: You muſt not be deny'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: By me, I am ſure he muſt not: ſure he ſhall not;
Kneeling I give it too; kneeling I take it;
And from this hour, no envious ſpight e're part us.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: The gods give happy joyes; all comforts to ye.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: My new Enanthe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Come, beat all the Drums up,
And all the noble inſtruments of War:
Let 'em fill all the Kingdom with their ſounds;
And thoſe the brazen Arch of Heaven break through,
While to the Temple we conduct theſe two.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: May they be ever loving, ever young,
And ever worthy of thoſe lines they ſprung;
May their fair iſſues walk with time along.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.l: And hang a Coward now; and there's my ſong.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: WOuld ſome man would inſtruct me what to ſay:
For this ſame Prologue, uſual to a Play,
Is tied to ſuch an old form of Petition;
Men muſt ſay nothing now beyond commiſſion:
The Cloaks we wear, the Leggs we make, the place
We ſtand in, muſt be one; and one the face.
Nor alter'd nor exceeded; if it be,
A general hiſſe hangs on our levitie:
We have a Play, a new Play to play now,
And thus low in our Playes behalf we bow;
We bow to beg your ſuffrage, and kind ear;
If it were naught, or that it might appear,
A thing buoy'd up by prayer, Gentlemen,
Believe my faith, you ſhould not ſee me then.
Let them ſpeak then have power to ſtop a ſtorm:
I never lov'd to feel a Houſe ſo warm:
But for the Play if you dare credit me,
I think it well: All new things you ſhall ſee,
And theſe diſpos'd to all the mirth that may;
And ſhort enough we hope: and ſuch a Play
You were wont to like: ſit nobly then, and ſee:
If it miſcarry, pray look not for me.

div.head: Epilogue, Spoke by the Lieutenant.
div.l: I Am not cur'd yet throughly; for believe
I feel another paſſion that may grieve,
All over me I feel it too: and now
It takes me cold, cold, cold, I know not how:
As you are good men help me, a Carowſe
May make me love you all, all here i'th' houſe,
And all that come to ſee me doatingly:
Now lend your hands; and for your courteſie,
The next imployment I am ſent upon,
I'le ſwear you are Phyſicians, the War's none.

div.head: Scena prima.
div.stage: Enter Clorin a Shepherdeſs, having buried her Love in an Arbour.
div.l: HAil, holy Earth, whoſe cold Arms do imbrace
The trueſt man that ever fed his flocks
By the fat plains of fruitful Theſſaly,
Thus I ſalute thy Grave, thus do I pay
My early vows, and tribute of mine eyes
• o thy ſtill loved aſhes; thus I free
My ſelf from all inſuing heats and fires
Of love: all ſports, delights and jolly games
• hat Shepherds hold full dear, thus put I off.
Now no more ſhall theſe ſmooth brows be begirt
With youthful Coronals, and lead the Dance;
• o more the company of freſh fair Maids
• nd wanton Shepherds be to me delightful,
• or the ſhrill pleaſing ſound of merry pipes
• nder ſome ſhady dell, when the cool wind
• lays on the leaves: all be far away,
• ince thou art far away; by whoſe dear ſide
How often have I ſat Crown'd with freſh flowers
• or ſummers Queen, whil'ſt every Shepherds Boy
•• s on his luſty green, with gaudy hook,
• nd hanging ſcrip of fineſt Cordevan.
〈◊〉 thou art gone, and theſe are gone with thee,
• nd all are dead but thy dear memorie;
• hat ſhall out-live thee, and ſhall ever ſpring
Whileſt there are pipes, or jolly Shepherds ſing.
• nd here will I in honour of thy love,
Dwell by thy Grave, forgeting all thoſe joys,
• hat former times made precious to mine eyes,
Only remembring what my youth did gain
• n the dark, hidden vertuous uſe of Herbs:
• hat will I practiſe, and as freely give
• ll my endeavours, as I gain'd them free.
Of all green wounds I know the remedies
• n Men or Cattel, be they ſtung with Snakes,
Or charm'd with powerful words of wicked Art,
Or be they Love-ſick, or through too much heat
Grown wild or Lunatick, their eyes or ears
• hickned with miſty filme of dulling Rheum,
Theſe I can Cure, ſuch ſecret vertue lies
• n Herbs applyed by a Virgins hand:
My meat ſhall be what theſe wild woods afford,
• erries, and Cheſnuts, Plantanes, on whoſe Cheeks,
The Sun ſits ſmiling, and the lofty fruit
• ull'd from the fair head of the ſtraight grown Pine;
On theſe I'le feed with free content and reſt; —
When night ſhall blind the world, by thy ſide bleſt.

sp.speaker: Satyr.
sp.l: Through yon ſame bending plain
That flings his arms down to the main,
And through theſe thick woods have I run,
Whoſe bottom never kiſt the Sun
• ince the luſty Spring began,
All to pleaſe my maſter Pan,
Have I trotted without reſt
To get him Fruit; for at a Feaſt
He entertains this coming night
His Paramour, the Syrinx bright:
But behold a fairer ſight! He ſtands amazed.
By that Heavenly form of thine,
Brighteſt fair thou art divine,
Sprung from great immortal race
Of the gods, for in thy face
Shines more awful Majeſty,
Than dull weak mortalitie
Dare with miſty eyes behold,
And live: therefore on this mold
Lowly do I bend my knee,
In worſhip of thy Deitie;
Deign it Goddeſs from my hand,
To receive what e're this land
From her fertil Womb doth ſend
Of her choice Fruits: and but lend
Belief to that the Satyre tells,
Fairer by the famous wells,
To this preſent day ne're grew,
Never better nor more true.
Here be Grapes whoſe luſty bloud
Is the learned Poets good,
Sweeter yet did never crown
The head of Bacchus, Nuts more brown
Than the Squirrels Teeth that crack them;
Deign O faireſt fair to take them.
For theſe black ey'd Driope
Hath oftentimes commanded me,
With my claſped knee to clime;
See how well the luſty time
Hath deckt their riſing cheeks in red,
Such as on your lips is ſpred,
Here be Berries for a Queen,
Some be red, ſome be green,
Theſe are of that luſcious meat,
The great God Pan himſelf doth eat:
All theſe, and what the woods can yield,
The hanging mountain or the field,
I freely offer, and ere long
Will bring you more, more ſweet and ſtrong,
Till when humbly leave I take,
Leſt the great Pan do awake,
That ſleeping lies in a deep glade,
Under a broad Beeches ſhade,
I muſt go, I muſt run
Swifter than the fiery Sun. Exit.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: And all my fears go with thee.
What greatneſs or what private hidden power,
Is there in me to draw ſubmiſſion
From this rude man, and beaſt? ſure I am mortal:
The Daughter of a Shepherd, he was mortal:
And ſhe that bore me mortal: prick my hand
And it will bleed: a Feaver ſhakes me,
And the ſelf ſame wind that makes the young Lambs ſhrink,
Makes me a cold: my fear ſays I am mortal:
Yet I have heard (my Mother told it me)
And now I do believe it, if I keep
My Virgin Flower uncropt, pure, chaſte, and fair,
No Goblin, Wood-god, Fairy, Elfe, or Fiend,
Satyr or other power that haunts the Groves,
Shall hurt my body, or by vain illuſion
Draw me to wander after idle fires;
Or voyces calling me in dead of night,
To make me follow, and ſo tole me on
Through mire and ſtanding pools, to find my ruine:
Elſe why ſhould this rough thing, who never knew
Manners, nor ſmooth humanity, whoſe heats
Are rougher than himſelf, and more miſhapen,
Thus mildly kneel to me? ſure there is a power
In that great name of Virgin, that binds faſt
All rude uncivil bloods, all appetites
That break their confines: then ſtrong Chaſtity,
Be thou my ſtrongeſt guard, for here I'le dwell
In oppoſition againſt Fate and Hell.

div.stage: Enter an old Shepherd, with him four couple of Shepherds and Shepherdeſſes.

sp.speaker: Old Shep.
sp.l: Now we have done this holy Feſtival
In honour of our great God, and his rites
Perform'd, prepare your ſelves for chaſte
And un • orrupted ſires: that as the Prieſt,
With powerful hand ſhall ſprinkle on yours Brows
His pu • e and holy water, ye may be
From all hot flames of luſt, and looſe thoughts free,
Kneel Shepherds, kneel, here comes the Prieſt of Pan.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Shepherds, thus I purge away,
Whatſoever this great day,
Or the paſt hours gave not good,
To corrupt your Maiden blood:
From the high rebellious heat
Of the Grapes, and ſtrength of meat;
From the wanton quick deſires,
They do kindle by their ſires,
I do waſh you with this water,
Be you pure and fair hereafter.
From your Liver and your Veins,
Thus I take away the ſtains.
All your thoughts be ſmooth and fair,
Be ye freſh and free as Air.
Never more let luſtful heat
Through your purged conduits beat,
Or a plighted troth be broken,
Or a wanton verſe be ſpoken
In a Shepherdeſſes ear;
Go your wayes, ye are all clear.

div.stage: They riſe and ſing in praiſe of Pan.

lg.l: Sing his praiſes that doth h • ep
Our Flocks from harm,
Pan the Father of our Sheep,
And arm in arm
Tread we ſoftly in a round,
Whileſt the hollow neighbouring ground
Fills the Muſick with her ſound.
Pan, O great God Pan, to thee
Thus do we ſing:
Thou that keep'ſt us chaſte and free
As the young ſpring,
Ever be thy honour ſpoke,
From that place the morn is broke,
To that place Day doth unyoke.

div.stage: Exeunt omnes but Perigot and Amoret.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: Stay gentle Amoret, thou fair brow'd Maid,
Thy Shepherd prays thee ſtay, that holds thee dear,
Equal with his ſouls good.

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: Speak; I give
•• ee freedom Shepherd, and thy tongue be ſtill
The ſame it ever was; as free from ill,
As he whoſe converſation never knew
The Court or City be thou ever true.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: When I fall off from my affection,
Or mingle my clean thoughts with foul deſires,
Firſt let our great God ceaſe to keep my ſtocks,
That being left alone without a guard,
The Wolf, or Winters rage, Summers great heat,
And want of Water, Rots; or what to us
Of ill is yet unknown, full ſpeedily,
And in their general ruine let me feel.

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: I pray thee gentle Shepherd wiſh not ſo,
I do believe thee: 'tis as hard for me
To think thee falſe, and harder than for thee
To hold me ſoul.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: O you are fairer far
Than the chaſte bluſhing morn, or that fair ſtar
That guides the wandring Sea men through the deep,
Straighter than ſtraighteſt Pine upon the ſteep
Head of an aged mountain, and more white
Than the rew Milk we ſtrip before day-light
From the full fraighted bags of our fair flocks:
Your hair more beauteous than thoſe hanging leeks,
Of young Apollo.

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: Shepherd be not loſt,
Y'are ſail'd too far already from the Coaſt
Of our diſcourſe.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: Did you not tell me once
I ſhould not love alone, I ſhould not loſe
Thoſe many paſſions, vows, and holy Oaths,
I've ſent to Heaven? did you not give your hand,
Even that fair hand in hoſtage? Do not then
Give back again thoſe ſweets to other men,
You your ſelf vow'd were mine.

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: Shepherd, ſo far as Maidens modeſty
May give aſſurance, I am once more thine,
Once more I give my hand; be ever free
From that great foe to faith, foul jealouſie.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: I take it as my beſt good, and deſire
For ſtronger confirmation of our love,
To meet this happy night in that fair Grove,
Where all true Shepherds have rewarded been
For their long ſervice: ſay ſweet, ſhall it hold?

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: Dear friend, you muſt not blame me if I make
A doubt of what the ſilent night may do,
Coupled with this dayes heat to move your bloud:
Maids muſt be fearful; ſure you have not been
Waſh'd-white enough; for yet I ſee a ſtain
Stick in your Liver, go and purge again.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: O do not wrong my honeſt ſimple truth,
My ſelf and my affections are as pure
As thoſe chaſte flames that burn before the ſhrine
Of the great Dian: only my intent
To draw you thither, was to plight our troths,
With enterchange of mutual chaſte embraces,
And ceremonious tying of our ſelves:
For to that holy wood is conſecrate
A vertuous well, about whoſe flowry banks,
The nimble-footed Fairies dance their rounds,
By the pale moon-ſhine, dipping oftentimes
Their ſtolen Children, ſo to make them free
From dying fleſh, and dull mortalitie;
By this fair Fount hath many a Shepherd ſworn,
And given away his freedom, many a troth
Been plight, which neither envy, nor old time
Could ever break, with many a chaſte kiſs given,
In hope of coming happineſs; by this
Freſh Fountain many a bluſhing Maid
Hath crown'd the head of her long loved Shepherd
With gaudy flowers, whileſt he happy ſung
Layes of his love and dear Captivitie;
There grows all Herbs fit to cool looſer flames
Our ſenſual parts provoke, chiding our bloods,
And quenching by their power thoſe hidden ſparks
That elſe would break out, and provoke our ſenſe
To open fires, ſo vertuous is that place:
Then gentle Shepherdeſs, believe and grant,
• n troth it fits not with that face to ſcant
• our faithful Shepherd of thoſe chaſte deſires
• e ever aim'd at, a •• —

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: Thou haſt prevail'd, farewel, this coming night
• hall crown thy chaſt hopes with long wiſh'd delight.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: Our great god Pan reward thee for that good
• hou haſt given thy poor Shepherd: faireſt Bud
Of Maiden Vertues, when I leave to be
The true Admirer of thy Chaſtitie,
• et me deſerve the hot polluted Name
Of the wild Woodman, or affect ſome Dame,
Whoſe often Proſtitution hath begot
More foul Diſeaſes, than ever yet the hot
• un bred through his burnings, whilſt the Dog
• urſues the raging Lion, throwing Fog,
• nd deadly Vapour from his angry Breath,

• illing the lower World with Plague and Death.
Ex. Am.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: Shepherd, may I deſire to be believ'd,
What I ſhall bluſhing tell?

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: Fair Maid, you may.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Then ſoftly thus, I love thee, Perigot,
• nd would be gladder to be lov'd again,
• han the cold Earth is in his frozen arms
• o clip the wanton Spring: nay do not ſtart,
• or wonder that I woo thee, thou that art
• he prime of our young Grooms, even the top
• f all our luſty Shepherds! what dull eye
• hat never was acquainted with deſire,
• ath ſeen thee wraſtle, run, or caſt the Stone
With nimble ſtrength and fair delivery,
And hath not ſparkled fire, and ſpeedily
• ent ſecret heat to all the neighbouring Veins?
Who ever heard thee ſing, that brought again
• hat freedom back, was lent unto thy Voice;
• hen do not blame me (Shepherd) if I be
•• e to be numbred in this Companie,
•• ce none that ever ſaw thee yet, were free.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: Fair Shepherdeſs, much pity I can lend
• o your Complaints: but ſure I ſhall not love:
〈◊〉 that is mine, my ſelf, and my beſt hopes
• re given already; do not love him then
• hat cannot love again: on other men
• eſtow thoſe heats more free, that may return
• ou fire for fire, and in one flame equal burn.

sp.speaker: Ama.
sp.l: Shall I rewarded be ſo ſlenderly
• or my affection, moſt unkind of men!
〈◊〉 I were old, or had agreed with Art
• o give another Nat •• e to my Cheeks,
〈◊〉 were I common Miſtreſs to the love
〈◊〉 every Swain, or could I with ſuch eaſe
•• ll back my Love, as many a Wanton doth;
• hou might'ſt refuſe me, Shepherd; but to thee
〈◊〉 am only fixt and ſet, let it not be
〈◊〉 Sport, thou gentle Shepherd to abuſe
• he love of ſilly Maid.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: Fair Soul, ye uſe
• heſe words to little end: for know, I may
• etter call back that time was Yeſterday,
• r ſtay the coming Night, than bring my Love
