Satyr ſearch if thou canſt find it.

sp.speaker: Stayr.
sp.l: Here away me thinks I wind it,
Stronger yet: Oh here they be,
Here, here, in a hollow tree,
Two fond mortals have I found.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Bring them out, they are unſound.

sp.speaker: Satyr.
sp.l: By the fingers thus I wring ye,
To my Goddeſs thus I bring ye;
Strife is vain, come gently in,
I ſcented them, they're full of ſin.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Hold Satyr, take this Glaſs,
Sprinkle over all the place,
Purge the Air from luſtfull breath,
To ſave this Shepherdeſs from death,
And ſtand you ſtill whilſt I do dreſs
Her wound for fear the pain encreaſe.

sp.speaker: Sat.
sp.l: From this glaſs I throw a drop
Of Cryſtal water on the top
Of every graſs, on flowers a pair:
Send a fume and keep the air
Pure and wholſom, ſweet and bleſt,
Till this Virgins wound be dreſt.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Satyr, help to bring her in.

sp.speaker: Sat.
sp.l: By Pan, I think ſhe hath no ſin,
She is ſo light: lye on theſe leaves.
Sleep that mortal ſenſe deceives,
Crown thine Eyes, and eaſe thy pain,
Maiſt thou ſoon be well again.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Satyr, bring the Shepherd near,
Try him if his mind be clear.

sp.speaker: Sat.
sp.l: Shepherd come.

sp.speaker: Daph.
sp.l: My thoughts are pure.

sp.speaker: Sat.
sp.l: The better trial to endure.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: In this flame his finger thruſt,
Which will burn him if he luſt;
But if not, away will turn,
As loth unſpotted fleſh to burn:
See, it gives back, let him go,
Farewel mortal, keep thee ſo.

sp.speaker: Sat.
sp.l: Stay fair Nymph, flye not ſo faſt,
We muſt try if you be chaſte:
Here's a hand that quakes for fear,
Sure ſhe will not prove ſo clear.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Hold her finger to the flame,
That will yield her praiſe or ſhame.

sp.speaker: Sat.
sp.l: To her doom ſhe dares not ſtand,
But plucks away her tender hand,
And the Taper darting ſends
His hot beams at her fingers ends:
O thou art foul within, and haſt
A •• nd, if nothing elſe, unchaſte.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: Is not that Cloe? 'tis my Love, 'tis ſhe!
C •• , fair Clor.
My Alexis.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: He.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Let me embrace thee.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Take her hence,
Leſt her ſight diſturb his ſence.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: Take not her, take my life firſt.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: See, his wound again is burſt:
Keep her near, here in the Wood,
Till ha'ſtopt theſe Streams of Blood.
Soon again he eaſe ſhall find,
If I can but ſtill his mind:
This Curtain thus I do diſplay,
To keep the piercing air away.

sp.speaker: Priest.
sp.l: Sure they are loſt for ever; 'tis in vain
To find 'em out with trouble and much pain,
That have a ripe deſire, and forward will
To flye the Company of all but ill,
What ſhall be counſel'd now? ſhall we retire?
Or conſtant follow ſtill that firſt deſire
We had to find them?
Stay a little while;
For if the Morning miſt do not beguile
My ſight with ſhadows, ſure I ſee a Swain;
One of this jolly Troop's come back again.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Doſt thou not bluſh young Shepherd to be known,
Thus without care, leaving thy flocks alone,
And following what deſire and preſent blood
Shapes out before thy burning ſenſe, for good,
Having forgot what tongue hereafter may
Tell to the World thy falling off, and ſay
Thou art regardleſs both of good and ſhame,
Sp •• ning at Vertue, and a vertuous Name,
And like a glorious, deſperate man that buys
A poyſon of much price, by which he dies,
Doſt thou lay out for Luſt, whoſe only gain
Is foul diſeaſe, with preſent age and pain,
And then a Grave? Theſe be the fruits that grow
In ſuch hot Veins that only beat to know
Where they may take moſt eaſe, and grow ambitious
Through their own wanton fire, and pride delicious.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Right holy Sir, I have not known this night,
What the ſmooth face of Mirth was, or the ſight
Of any looſeneſs; muſick, joy, and eaſe,
Have been to me as bitter drugs to pleaſe
A Stomach loſt with weakneſs, not a game
That I am skill'd at throughly; nor a Dame,
Went her tongue ſmoother than the feet of Time,
Her beauty ever living like the Rime
Our bleſſed Tityrus did ſing of yore,
No, were ſhe more enticing than the ſtore
Of fruitful Summer, when the loaden Tree
Bids the faint Traveller be bold and free,
'Twere but to me like thunder 'gainſt the bay,
Whoſe lightning may encloſe but never ſtay
Upon his charmed branches; ſuch am I
Againſt the catching flames of Womans eye.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Then wherefore haſt thou wandred?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: 'Twas a Vow
That drew me out laſt night, which I have now
Strictly perform'd, and homewards go to give
Freſh paſture to my Sheep, that they may live.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: 'Tis good to hear ye, Shepherd, if the heart
In this well ſounding Muſick bear his part.
Where have you left the reſt?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I have not ſeen,
Since yeſternight we met upon this green
To fold our Flocks up, any of that train;
Yet have I walkt theſe Woods round, and have lain
All this ſame night under an aged Tree,
Yet neither wandring Shepherd did I ſee,
Or Shepherdeſs, or drew into mine ear
The ſound of living thing, unleſs it were
The Nightingale among the thick leav'd ſpring
That ſits alone in ſorrow, and doth ſing
Whole nights away in mourning, or the Owl,
Or our great enemy that ſtill doth howl
Againſt the Moons cold beams.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Go and beware
Of after falling.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Father 'tis my care.

sp.speaker: Old.
sp.l: Here comes another Stragler, ſure I ſee
A Shame in this young Shepherd. Daphnis!

sp.speaker: Daph.
sp.l: He.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Where haſt thou left the reſt, that ſhould have been
Long before this, grazing upon the green
Their yet impriſon'd flocks?

sp.speaker: Daph.
sp.l: Thou holy man,
Give me a little breathing till I can
Be able to unfold what I have ſeen;
Such horrour that the like hath never been
Known to the ear of Shepherd: Oh my heart
Labours a double motion to impart
So heavy tidings! You all know the Bower
Where the chaſt Clorin lives, by whoſe great power
Sick men and Cattel have been often cur'd,
There lovely Amoret that was aſſur'd
To luſty Perigot, bleeds out her life,
Forc'd by ſome Iron hand and fatal knife;
And by her young Alexis.

div.stage: Enter Amaryllis running from her Sullen Shepherd.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: If there be
Ever a Neighbour Brook, or hollow tree,
Receive my Body, cloſe me up from luſt
That follows at my heels; be ever juſt,
Thou god of Shepherds, Pan, for her dear ſake
That loves the Rivers brinks, and ſtill doth ſhake
In cold remembrance of thy quick purſuit:
Let me be made a reed, and ever mute,
Nod to the waters fall, whilſt every blaſt
Sings through my ſlender leaves that I was chaſt.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: This is a night of wonder, Amaryll
Be comforted, the holy gods are ſtill
Revengers of th • ſe wrongs.

sp.speaker: Amar.
sp.l: Thou bleſſed man,
Honour'd upon theſe plains, and lov'd of Pan,
Hear me, and ſave from endleſs infamie
My yet unblaſted Flower, Virginitie:
By all the Garlands that have crown'd that head,
By the chaſte office, and the Marriage bed
That ſtill is bleſt by thee, by all the rights
Due to our gods; and by thoſe Virgin lights
That burn before his Altar, let me not
Fall from my former ſtate to gain the blot
That never ſhall be purg'd: I am not now
That wanton Amaryllis: here I vow
To Heaven, and thee grave Father, if I may
Scape this unhappy Night, to know the Day,
To live a Virgin, never to endure
The tongues, or Company of men impure.
I hear him come, ſave me.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Retire a while
Behind th s Buſh, till we have known that vile
Abuſer of young Maidens.

sp.speaker: Sul.
sp.l: Stay thy pace,
Moſt loved Amaryllis, let the Chaſe
Grow calm and milder, flye me not ſo faſt,
I fear the pointed Brambles have unlac'd
Thy golden Buskins; turn again and ſee
Thy Shepherd follow, that is ſtrong and free,
Able to give thee all content and eaſe.
I am not baſhful, Virgin, I can pleaſe
At firſt encounter, hug thee in mine arm,
And give thee many Kiſſes, ſoft and warm
As thoſe the Sun prints on the ſmiling Cheek
Of Plums, or mellow Peaches; I am ſleek
And ſmooth as Neptune, when ſtern Eolus
Locks up his ſurly Winds, and nimbly thus
Can ſhew my active Youth; why doſt thou flye?
Remember Amaryll •• , it was I
That kill'd Alexis for thy ſake, and ſet
An everlaſting hate 'twixt Amoret
And her beloved Perigot: 'twas I
That drown'd her in the W • ll, where ſhe muſt lye
Till Time ſhall leave to be; then turn again,
Turn with thy open arms, and clip the Swain
That hath perform'd all this, turn, turn I ſay:
I muſt not be deluded.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Monſter ſtay,
Thou that art like a Canker to the State
Thou liv'ſt and breath'ſt in, eating with debate
Through every honeſt boſome, forcing ſtill
The Veins of any that may ſerve thy Will,
Thou that haſt offer'd with a ſinful hand
To ſeize upon this Virgin that doth ſtand
Yet trembling here.

sp.speaker: Sull.
sp.l: Good holineſs declare,
What had the danger been, if being bare
I had embrac'd her, tell me by your Art,
What coming wonders would that ſight impart?

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Luſt, and a branded Soul.

sp.speaker: Sull.
sp.l: Yet tell me more,
Hath not our Mother Nature for her ſtore
And great encreaſe, ſaid it is good and juſt,
And wills that every living Creature muſt
Beget his like?

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Ye are better read than I,
I muſt confeſs, in blood and Lechery.
Now to the Bower, and bring this Beaſt along,

Where he may ſuffer Penance for his wrong.
Ex ••• .

div.stage: Enter Perigot with his hands bloody.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.l: Here will I waſh it in this mornings dew,
Which ſhe on every little graſs doth ſtrew
In ſilver drops againſt the Sun's appear:
'Tis holy water, and will make me clear.
My hands will not be cleans'd. My wronged Love,
If thy chaſte ſpirit in the air yet move,
Look mildly down on him that yet doth ſtand
All full of guilt, thy blood upon his hand,
And though I ſtruck thee undeſervedly,
Let my revenge on her that injur'd thee
Make leſs a fault which I intended not,
And let theſe dew drops waſh away my ſpot.
It will not cleanſe. O to what ſacred Flood
Shall I reſort to waſh away this blood?
Amid'ſt theſe Trees the holy Clorin dwells
In a low Cabin of cut Boughs, and heals
All Wounds; to her I will my ſelf addreſs,
And my raſh faults repentantly confeſs;
Perhaps ſhe'll find a means by Art or Prayer,
To make my hand with chaſte blood ſtained, fair:
That done, not far hence underneath ſome Tree,
I'll have a little Cabin built, ſince ſhe
Whom I ador'd is dead, there will I give
My ſelf to ſtrictneſs, and like Clorin live. Exit.

div.stage: The Curtain is drawn, Clorin appears ſitting in the Cab •• , Amoret ſitting on the one ſide of her, Alexis and Cloe on the other, the Satyr ſtanding by.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Shepherd, once more your blood is ſtaid,
Take example by this Maid,
Who is heal'd ere you be pure,
So hard it is lewd luſt to cure.
Take heed then how you turn your eye
On each other luſtfully:
And Shepherdeſs take heed leſt you
Move his willing eye thereto;
Let no wring, nor pinch, nor ſmile
Of yours his weaker ſenſe beguile.
Is your Love yet true and chaſte,
And for ever ſo to laſt?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: I have forgot all vain deſires,
All looſer thoughts, ill tempred fires,
True Love I find a pleaſant fume,
Whoſe moderate heat can ne'r conſume.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: And I a new fire feel in me,
Whoſe chaſte flame is not quencht to be.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Join your hands with modeſt touch,
And for ever keep you ſuch.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.l: You is her Cabin, thus far off I'll ſtand,
And call her forth; for my unhallowed hand
I dare not bring ſo near yon ſacred place.
Clorin come forth, and do a timely grace
To a poor Swain.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: What art thou that doſt call?
Clorin is ready to do good to all:
Come near.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: I dare not.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Satyr, ſee
Who it is that calls on me.

sp.speaker: Sat.
sp.l: There at hand, ſome Swain doth ſtand,
Stretching out a bloudy hand.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: Come Clorin, bring thy holy waters clear,
To waſh my hand.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: What wonders have been here
Tonight? ſtretch forth thy hand young Swain,
W ••• and rub it whileſt I rain
Holy water.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: Still you pour,
But my hand will never ſcower.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Satyr, bring him to the Bower,
We will try the Soveraign power
Of other waters.

sp.speaker: Satyr.
sp.l: Mortal, ſure
'Tis the Blood of Maiden pure
That ſtains thee ſo.

div.stage: The Satyr leadeth him to the Bower, where he ſpieth Amoret, and kneeling down, ſhe knoweth him.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: What e're thou be,
Be'ſt thou her ſpright, or ſome divinitie,
That in her ſhape thinks good to walk this grove,
Pardon poor Ferigot.

sp.speaker: Amor.
sp.l: I am thy love,
Thy Amoret, for evermore thy love:
Strike once more on my naked breaſt, I'le prove
As conſtant ſtill. O couldſt thou love me yet;
How ſoon ſhould I my former griefs forget!

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: So over-great with joy, that you live, now
I am, that no deſire of knowing how
Doth ſeize me; haſt thou ſtill power to forgive?

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: Whileſt thou haſt power to love, or I to live;
More welcome now than hadſt thou never gone
Aſtray from me.

sp.speaker: Peri.
sp.l: And when thou lov'ſt alone
And not I, death, or ſome lingring pain
That's worſe, light on me.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Now your ſtain
This perhaps will cleanſe again;
See the blood that erſt did ſtay,
With the water drops away.
A •• the powers again are pleas'd,
A •• with this new knot appeas'd.
〈◊〉 your hands, and riſe together,
〈◊〉 bleſt that brought you hither.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Go back again what ere thou art, unleſs
S •• eth Maiden thoughts poſſeſs thee, do not preſs
•• is hallowed ground. Go Satyr, take his hand,
And give him preſent trial.

sp.speaker: Satyr.
sp.l: Mortal ſtand,
•• l by fire I have made known
Whether thou be ſuch a one,
That mayſt freely tread this place.
Hold thy hand up; never was
More untainted fleſh than this.
•• reſt, he is full of bliſs.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Then boldly ſpeak, why doſt thou ſeek this place?

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Firſt, honour'd Virgin, to behold thy face
Where all good dwells that is: Next for to try
The truth of late report was given to me:
Thoſe Shepherds that have met with foul miſchance,
Through much neglect, and more ill governance,
Whether the wounds they have may yet endure
The open Air, or ſtay a longer cure.
And laſtly, what the doom may be ſhall light
Upon thoſe guilty wretches, through whoſe ſpight
A • this confuſion fell: For to this place,
T • ou holy Maiden, have I brought the race
Of theſe offenders, who have freely told,
Both why, and by what means they gave this bold
Attempt upon their lives.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Fume all the ground,
And ſprinkle holy water, for unſound
And foul infection 'gins to fill the Air:
It gathers yet more ſtrongly; take a pair
Of Cenſors fill'd with Frankincenſe and Mirrh,
Together with cold Camphyre: quickly ſtir
Thee, gentle Satyr, for the place begins
To ſweat and labour with the abhorred ſins
Of thoſe offenders,; let them not come nigh,
For full of itching flame and leproſie
Their very ſouls are, that the ground goes back,
And ſhrinks to feel the ſullen weight of black
And ſo unheard of venome; hie thee faſt
Thou holy man, and baniſh from the chaſt
Theſe manlike monſters, let them never more
Be known upon theſe downs, but long before
The next Suns riſing, put them from the ſight
And memory of every honeſt wight.
Be quick in expedition, leſt the ſores

Of theſe weak Patients break into new gores.
Ex. Prieſt.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.l: My dear, dear Amoret, how happy are
Thoſe bleſſed pairs, in whom a little jar
Hath bred an everlaſting love, too ſtrong
For time, or ſteel, or envy to do wrong?
How do you feel your hurts? Alas poor heart,
How much I was abus'd; give me the ſmart
For it is juſtly mine.

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: I do believe.
It is enough dear friend, leave off to grieve,
And let us once more in deſpight of ill
Give hands and hearts again.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.l: With better will
Than e're I went to find in hotteſt day
Cool Cryſtal of the Fountain, to allay
My eager thirſt: may this band never break.
Hear us O Heaven,

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: Be conſtant.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.l: Elſe Pan wreak,
With bouble vengeance, my diſloyalty;
Let me not dare to know the company
Of men, or any more behold thoſe eyes.

sp.speaker: Amo.
sp.l: Thus Shepherd with a kiſs all envy dyes.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Bright Maid, I have perform'd your will, the Swain
In whom ſuch heat and black rebellions 〈◊〉 gn
Hath undergone your ſentence, and diſgrace.
Only the Maid I have reſerv'd, whoſe face
Shews much amendment, many a tear doth fall
In ſorrow of her fault, great fair recal
Your heavy doom, in hope of better daies,
Which I dare promiſe; once again upraiſe
Her heavy Spirit that near drowned lyes
In ſelf comſuming care that never dyes,

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: I am content to pardon, call her in;
The Air grows cool again, and doth begin
To purge it ſelf, how bright the day doth ſhow
After this ſtormy Cloud? go Satyr, go,
And with this Taper boldly try her hand,
If ſhe be pure and good, and firmly ſtand
To be ſo ſtill, we have perform'd a work

Worthy the Gods themſelves.
Satyr brings Amaryllis in.

sp.speaker: Satyr.
sp.l: Come forward Maiden, do not lurk
Nor hide your face with grief and ſhame,
Now or never get a name
That may raiſe thee, and recure
All thy life that was impure:
Hold your hand unto the flame,
If thou beeſt a perfect dame,
Or haſt truely vow'd to mend,
This pale fire will be thy friend.
See the Taper hurts her not.
Go thy wayes, let never ſpot
Henceforth ſeize upon thy blood.
Thank the Gods and ſtill be good.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Young Shepherdeſs now ye are brought again
To Virgin ſtate, be ſo, and ſo remain
To thy laſt day, unleſs the faithful love
Of ſome good Shepherd force thee to remove;
Than labour to be true to him, and live
As ſuch a one, that ever ſtrives to give
A b ••••• d memory to after time.
〈◊〉 famous for your good, not for your crime.
〈◊〉 holy man, I offer up again
〈◊〉 patients full of health, and free from pain:
••• p t •• m f om after ills, be ever near
〈…〉 actions, teach them how to clear

〈…〉
• ous way they paſs through, from ſuſpect,
〈…〉 from wrong • ng others, or neglect
Of 〈◊〉 in themſelves, correct the bloud
With thirſty b • ts and labour, let the floud,
O • the next neig • bouring ſpring give remedy
To g ••• ly thri •• , and travel not the tree
That • angs with wanton cluſters, let let not wine,
Unleſs in ſacrifice, or • ites divine,
Be ever known of S •• p •• d, have a care
Thou man of holy life. Now do not ſpare
Their faults through much remiſſneſs, nor forget
To cheriſh him, w • oſe many pains and ſwet
Hath giv'n increaſe, and added to the downs.
Sort all your Shepherds from the la • y clowns
That f •• d it H ſe • s in the budded Brooms:
Teach the young Maidens ſtrictneſs, that the grooms
Baniſh all complements, but ſingle truth
From every tongue, and every Shepherds heart,
Let them ſtill uſe perſwading, but no Art:
Thus holy Prieſt, I wiſh to thee and theſe,
All the beſt goods and comforts that may pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: And all thoſe bleſſings Heaven did ever give,
We pray upon this Bower may ever live.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Kneel every Sh • pherd, whileſt with powerful hand
I bleſs your after labours, and the Land
You ſeed your flocks upon. Great Pan defend you
From misfortune, and amend you,
Keep you from thoſe dangers ſtill,
That are followed by your will,
Give ye means to know at length
All your riches, all your ſtrength,
Cannot keep your foot from falling
To lewd luſt, that ſtill is calling
At your Cottage, till his power
Bring again that golden hour
Of peace and reſt to every ſoul.
May his care of you controul
All diſeaſes, ſores or pain
That in after time may raign
Either in your flocks or you,
Give ye all affections new,
New deſires, and tempers new,
That ye may be ever true.
Now riſe and go, and as ye paſs away
Sing to the God of Sheep, that happy lay,
That honeſt Dorus taught ye, Dorus, he
That was the ſoul and god of melodie.

lg.l: All ye woods, and trees and bowers,
All you vertues and ye powers
That inhabit in the lakes,
In the pleaſant ſprings or brakes,
Move your feet
To our ſound,
Whileſt we greet
All this ground,
With his honour and his name
That defends our flocks from blame.
He is great, and he is juſt,
He is ever good, and muſt
Thus be honour'd: Daffadillies,
Roſes, Pinks, and loved Lillies,
Let us ſting,
Whileſt we ſing,
Ever holy,
Ever holy,
Ever honour'd ever young,

Thus great Pan is ever ſung.
Exe ••• .

sp.speaker: Satyr.
sp.l: Thou divineſt, faireſt, brighteſt,
Thou muſt powerful Maid, and whiteſt,
Thou moſt vertuous and moſt bleſſed,
Eyes of ſtars, and golden treſſed
Like Apollo, tell me ſweeteſt
What new ſervice now is meeteſt
For the Satyr? ſhall I ſtray
In the middle Air, and ſtay
The ſayling Rack, or nimbly take
Hold by the Moon, and gently make
Sute to the pale Queen of night
For a beam to give thee light?
Shall I dive into the Sea,
And bring thee Coral, making way
Through the riſing waves that fall
In ſnowie fleeces; deareſt, ſhall
I catch the wanton Fawns, or Flyes,
Whoſe woven wings the Summer dyes
Of many colours? get thee fruit?
Or ſteal from Heaven old Orpheus Lute?
All theſe I'le venture for, and more,
To do her ſervice all theſe woods adore.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: No other ſervice, Satyr, but thy watch
About theſe thickets, leſt harmleſs people catch
Miſchief or ſad miſchance.

sp.speaker: Satyr.
sp.l: Holy Virgin, I will dance
Round about theſe woods as quick
As the breaking light, and prick
Down the Lawns, and down the vails
Faſter than the Wind-mill ſails.
So I take my leave, and pray
All the comforts of the day,
Such as Phoebus heat doth ſend
On the earth, may ſtill be friend
Thee, and this arbour.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: And to thee,
All thy Maſters love be free.

div.head: To my Friend Maſter JOHN FLETCHER upon his Faithfull Shepherdeſs.
div.l: I Know too well, that, no more than the man
That travels through the burning Deſarts, can
When he is beaten with the raging Sun,
Half ſmother'd in the duſt, have power to run
From a cool River, which himſelf doth find,
E're he be ſlack'd; no more can he whoſe mind
Joyes in the Muſes, hold from that delight,
When nature, and his full thoughts bid him write:
Yet wiſh I thoſe whom I for friends have known,
To ſing their thoughts to no ears but their own.
Why ſhould the man, whoſe wit ne'r had a ſtain,
Ʋpon the publick Stage preſent his vain,
And make a thouſand men in judgment ſit,
To call in queſtion his undoubted wit,
Scarce two of which can underſtand the laws
Which they ſhould judge by, nor the parties cauſe?
Among the rout there is not one that hath
In his own cenſure an explicite faith;
One company knowing they judgement lack,
Ground their belief on the next man in black:
Others, on him that makes ſigns, and is mute,
Some like as he does in the faireſt fute,
He as his Miſtreſs doth, and ſhe by chance:
Nor want there thoſe, who as the Boy doth dance
Between the Acts, will cenſure the whole Play;
Some if the Wax-lights be not new that day;
But multitudes there are whoſe judgement goes
Headlong according to the Actors cloathes.
For this, theſe publick things and I, agree
So all, that but to do a right for thee,
I had not been perſwaded to have hurl'd
Theſe few, ill ſpoken lines, into the world,
•• th to be read, and cenſur'd of, by thoſe,
•• oſe very reading makes Verſe ſenſeleſs Proſe:
Such as muſt ſpend above an hour, to ſpell
A Challenge on a Poſt, to know it well:
•• ſince it was thy hap to throw away
Much wit, for which the people did not pay,
Becauſe they ſaw it not, I not diſlike
This ſecond publication, which may ſtrike
Their conſciences, to ſee the thing they ſcorn'd,
To be with ſo much wit and Art adorn'd.
Beſides one vantage more in this I ſee,
Your cenſurers now muſt have the qualitie
Of reading, which I am afraid is more
〈◊〉 half your ſhrewdeſt Judges had before.

div.head: To the worthy Author Mr. Jo. FLETCHER.

lg.l: THe wiſe, and many headed Bench, that ſits
Ʋpon the Life, and Death of Playes, and Wits,
Compos'd of Gameſter, Captain, Knight, Knight's man,
Lady, or Puſill, that wears mask or fan,
Velvet, or Taffata cap, rank'd in the dark
With the ſhops Foreman, or ſome ſuch brave ſpark,
That may judge for his ſix pence) had, before
They ſaw it half, damn'd thy whole Play, and more,
Their motives were, ſince it had not to doe
With vices, which they look'd for, and came to.
I, that am glad, thy Innocence was thy Guilt,
And wiſh that all the Muſes blood were ſpilt
In ſuch a Martyrdome, to vex their eyes,
Do crown thy murdred Poeme: which ſhall riſe
A glorified work to Time, when Fire,
Or mothes ſhall eat, what all theſe Fools admire.

div.head: This Dialogue newly added, was ſpoken by way of Prologue to both their Majeſties, at the firſt acting of this Paſtoral at Somerſethouſe on Twelfth-night, 1633.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: A Broiling Lamb on Pans chief Altar lies,
My Wreath, my Cenſor, Virge, and Incenſe by
But I delay'd the pretious Sacrifice,
To ſhew thee here, a Gentle Deity.

sp.speaker: Nymph.
sp.l: Nor was I to thy ſacred Summons ſlow,
Hither I came as ſwift as th' Eagles wing,
Or threatning ſhaft from vext Dianaes bow,
To ſee this Iſlands God; the worlds beſt King

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Bleſs then that Queen, that doth his eyes invite
And ears, t'obey her Scepter, half this night.

lg.l: Let's ſing ſuch welcomes, as ſhall make Her ſway
Seem eaſie to Him, though it laſt till day.
Welcom as Peace t'unwalled Cities, when
Famine and Sword leave them more graves than men.
As Spring to Birds, or Noon-dayes Sun to th' old
Poor mountain Muſcovite congeal'd with cold.
As Shore toth' Pilot in a ſafe known Coaſt
When's Card is broken and his Rudder loſt.

list.item: Memnon, the General and the Mad Lover.
Polydor, Brother to Memnon, beloved of Calis.
Syphax, a Souldier in love with the Princeſs.
Stremon, a Souldier that can ſing.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Calis, Siſter to the King, and Miſtris to Memnon.
Lucippe, one of the Princeſſes Women.
Prieſt of Venus, an old wanton.

div.head: Scena prima.
div.stage: Flouriſh. Enter Aſtorax King of Paphos, his Siſter Calis, T ••• , and Cleanthe, Lucippe Gentlewomen, at ••• door; at the other Eumenes a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: H • alth to my Soveraign.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Eumenes, welcome:
Welcome to Paph •• , Souldier, to our love,
And that • a • health ye wiſh us, through the Camp
How does the General, the valiant Memnon,
And how his Wars, Eumenes?

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Better n •• e ſ • ught a dang •• , more approv'd
In way of Wa • , more maſter of his fortunes,
I • p it in leading 'em, in doing valiant,
In following all his deeds to Victories,
And holding fortun • certain there.

sp.speaker: King
sp.l: O Souldier,
Thou ſpeak'ſt a man indeed; a Generals General,
A ſoul conceiv'd a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Ten ſet Battels
Againſt the ſtrong uſurper Diocles
(Whom long experience had begot a Leader,
Ambition rais'd too mighty) hath your Memnon
Won, and won gloriouſly, diſtreſt and ſhook him
Even from the head of all his hopes to nothing:
In three, he beat the Thunder-bolt his Brother,
Forc'd him to wall himſelf up: there not ſafe,
Shook him with war like Engins like an Earthquake,
Till like a Snail he left his ſhell and crawl'd
By night and hideous darkneſs to deſtruction:
Diſarm'd for ever riſing more: Twelve Caſtles,
Some thought impregnable; Towns twice as many;
Countries that like the wind knew no command
But ſavage wildneſs, hath this General
With loſs of blood and youth, through Storms and Tempeſts
Call'd to your fair obedience.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: O my Souldier
That thou wert now within my arms; what drums Drums within.
Are thoſe that beat Eumenes?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: His, my Soveraign;
Himſelf i'th' head of conqueſt drawing home,
An old man now to offer up his glories,
And endleſs conqueſt at your ſhrine.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Goe all,
And entertain him with all Ceremonie,
We'l keep him now a Courtier.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Sir, a ſtrange one,
Pray God his language bear it; by my life, Sir
He knows no complement, nor curious caſting
Of words into fit places e're he ſpeak 'em,
He can ſay fight well fellow, and I'le thank thee:
He that muſt eat, muſt fight; bring up the rear there,
Or charge that wing of horſe home. Flouriſh.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Goe too, goe too.
sp.stage: Enter Memnon, and a train of Courtiers, and Souldiers, two Captains, Chilax.
sp.l: Valiant and wiſe are twins Sir: welcom, welcom,
Welcom my fortunate and famous General,
High in thy Princes favour, as in fame,
Welcom to Peace, and Paphos.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Thank your Grace,
And would to God my dull tongue had that ſweetneſs
To thank you as I ſhould; but pardon me,
My ſword and I ſpeak roughly Sir: your battels
I dare well ſay, I have fought well; for I bring ye
That lazie end you wiſh for Peace, ſo fully,
That no more name of war is: who now thinks
Sooner or ſafer theſe might have been ended,
Begin 'em if he dare again; I'le thank him.
Souldier and Souldiers Mate theſe twenty five years,
At length your General, (as one whoſe merit
Durſt look upon no leſs,) I have waded through
Dangers would damp theſe ſoft ſouls, but to hear of.
The maiden heads of thouſand lives hang here Sir,
••• e which time Prince, I know no Court but Marſhal,
• o oylie language, but the ſhock of Arms,
No dalliance but with death; No lofty meaſures
But weary and ſad marches, cold and hunger,
Larums at midnight Valours ſelf would ſhake at,
Yet I ne're ſhrunk: Balls of conſuming Wildfire,
That lickt men up like lightning, have I laught at,
And toſt 'em back again like childrens trifles.
Upon the edges of my Enemies ſwords
I have marcht like whirle-winds, fury at this hand waiting,
Death at my right; Fortune my forlorn hope,
When I have grapled with deſtruction,
And tug'd with pale fac'd Ruine, Night and Miſchief,
Frighted to ſee a new day break in bloud;
And every where I conquer'd; and for you Sir,
Mothers have wanted wombs to make me famous,
And blown ambition, dangers; Thoſe that griev'd ye,
I have taken order for i'th' earth: thoſe fools
That ſhall hereafter —

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
No more wars my Souldier:
K. takes Mem. aſide and talks with him.
We muſt now treat of peace Sir.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: How he talks,
How gloriouſly.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: A goodly timber'd fellow,
Valiant no doubt.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: If valour dwell in vaunting;
In what a phraſe he ſpeaks, as if his actions
Could be ſet off in nothing but a noiſe;
Sure h'as a drum in's mouth.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I wonder wenches
How he would ſpeak to us.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Nothing but Larum,
Tell us whoſe throat he cut, ſhew us his ſword,
And bleſs it for ſure biting.

sp.speaker: Lucippe.
sp.l: And 't like your Grace,
I do not think he knows us what we are,
Or to what end; for I have heard his followers
Affirm he never ſaw a woman that exceeded
A Sutlers wife yet, or in execution
Old bedrid Beldames without teeth or tongues,
That would not flie his furie? how he looks.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: This way devoutly.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Sure his Lordſhip's viewing
Our Fortifications.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: If he mount at me,
I may chance choak his Battery.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Still his eye
Keeps quarter this way: Venus grant his valour
Be not in love.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: If he be, preſently
Expect a Herald and a Trumpet with ye
To bid ye render; we two Perdu's pay for't elſe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I'le leave ye to my ſiſter, and theſe Ladies
To make your welcom fuller: my good ſouldier
We muſt now turn your ſternneſs into Courtſhip;
When ye have done there, to your fair repoſe Sir: Flouriſh.
I know you need it Memnon; welcom Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Now he begins to march: Madam the Van's yours,
Keep your ground ſure; 'tis for your ſpurrs.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: O Venus.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: How he ſtares on me. He kneels amaz'd, and forgets to ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Knight him Madam, knight him,
He will grow toth' ground elſe.

sp.speaker: Eumenes.
sp.l: Speak Sir, 'tis the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: Ye ſhame your ſelf, ſpeak to her.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Riſe and ſpeak Sir.
Ye are welcome to the Court, to me, to all Sir.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Is he not deaf?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: The Gentleman's not well.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: F • e noble General.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Give him freſh air, his colour goes, how do ye?
The Princeſs will be glad Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Peace, and hear me.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Command a ſilence there.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I love thee Lady.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I thank your Lordſhip heartily: proceed Sir.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Lord how it ſtuck in's ſtomach like a ſurfeit.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: It breaks apace now from him, God be thanked,
What a fine ſpoken man he is.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: A choice one, of ſingular variety in carriage.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Yes and I warrant you he knows his diſtance.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: With all my heart I love thee,

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: A hearty Gentleman,
And I were e'en an arrant beaſt, my Lord,
But I lov'd you again.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Good Lady kiſs me.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: I marry, Mars, there thou cam'ſt cloſe up to her.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Kiſs you at firſt my Lord? 't is no fair faſhion,
Our lips are like Roſe buds, blown with mens breaths,
They loſe both ſap and ſavour; there's my hand Sir,

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Fie, fie, my Lord, this is too rude.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Unhand me,
Conſume me if I hurt her; good ſweet Lady
Let me but look upon thee.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Doe.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Yet —

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Well Sir,
Take your full view.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Bleſs your eyes Sir.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Mercy,
Is this the man they talkt of for a Souldier,
So abſolute an Excellent: O the Gods,
If I were given to that vanitie
Of making ſport with men for ignorance,
What a moſt precious ſubject had I purchas'd?
Speak for him Gentlemen: ſome one that knows,
What the man ails; and can ſpeak ſenſe.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Sure Madam,
This fellow has been a rare Hare finder.
See how his eyes are ſet.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Some one goe with me,
I'le ſend him ſomething for his head, poor Gentleman,
He's troubled with the ſtaggers.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Keep him dark,
He will run Ma • ch mad elſe, the ſumes of Battels
Aſcend into his brains.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Clap to his feet
An old D • um head, to draw the thunder downward.

sp.speaker: Cal
sp.l: Look to him Gentlemen: farewel, Lord I am ſorry
We cannot kiſs at this time, but believe it
From being ſuch ſweet Souldiers; Softly wenches,

Leſt we diſturb his dream.
Exeunt Calis and Ladies.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Why this is Monſtrous.

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: A ſtrange forgetfulneſs, yet ſtill he holds it.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: Though he ne're law a woman of great faſhion
Before this day, yet methinks 'tis poſſible
He might imagine what they are, and what
Belongs unto 'em: meer report of others.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Piſh, his head had other whimſies in't: my Lord,
Death I think y'are ſtruck dumb; my good Lord General.

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: That I do love ye Madam; and ſo love ye
An't like your grace.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: He has been ſtudying this ſpeech.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Who do ye ſpeak to Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Why where's the Lady,
The woman, the fair woman?

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: Who?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: The Princeſs,
Give me the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Give ye counſel rather
To uſe her like a Princeſs: Fy my Lord,
How have you born your ſelf, how naked!
Laid your ſoul open, and your ignorance
To be a ſport to all. Report and honour
Drew he • to doe you favours, and you bluntly,
Without conſidering what, or who ſhe was,
Neither collecting reaſon, nor diſtinction.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Why, what did I my Maſters?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: All that ſhews
A man unhandſom, undigeſted dough.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Did not I kneel unto her?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Dumb and ſenſleſs,
As though ye had been cut out for your fathers tomb,
Or ſtuck a land mark; when ſhe ſpoke unto you,
Being the excellence of all our Iſland,
Ye ſtar'd upon her, as ye had ſeen a monſter.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Was I ſo fooliſh? I confeſs Eumenes,
I never ſaw before ſo brave an outſide,
But did I kneel ſo long?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Till they laught at ye,
And when you ſpoke, I am aſham'd to tell ye
What 'twas my Lord; how far from order;
Bleſs me, is't poſſible the wild noiſe of war
And what ſhe only teaches ſhould poſſeſs ye?
Knowledge to treat with her, and full diſcretion
Being at ſtood ſtill in ye: and in peace,
And manly converſation ſmooth and civil,
Where gracefulneſs and glory twyn together,
Thruſt your ſelf out an exile?
Do you know Sir, what ſtate ſhe carries?
What great obedience waits at her beck continually?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: She ne're commanded
A hundred thouſand men, as I have done,
Nor ne're won battel, Say I would have kiſt her.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: There was a dainty offer too, a rare one.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Why, ſhe is a woman, is ſhe not?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: She is ſo.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Why, very well; what was ſhe made for then?
Is ſhe not young, and handſom, bred to breed?
Do not men kiſs fair women? if they doe,
If lips be not unlawfull ware; Why a Princeſs
Is got the ſame way that we get a begger
Or I am cozen'd; and the ſelf-ſame way
She muſt be handled e're ſhe get another,
That's rudeneſs is it not?

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: To her'tis held ſo, & rudeneſs in that high degree—

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: 'Tis reaſon,
But I will be more punctual; pray what thought ſhe?

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Her thoughts were merciful, but ſhe laught at ye,
Pitying the poorneſs of your complement,
And ſo ſhe left ye. Good Sir ſhape your ſelf
To underſtand the place, and noble perſons
You live with now.

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: Let not thoſe great deſerts
The King hath laid up of ye, and the people,
Be blaſted with Ill bearing.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: The whole name of ſouldier then will ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: She's a ſweet one,
And good ſirs leave your exhortations,
They come untimely to me, I have brains
That beat above your reaches: She's a Princeſs,
That's all: I have killed a King, that's greater.
Come let's to dinner, if the Wine be good,
You ſhall perceive ſtrange wiſdom in my blood.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Well, would thou wert i' the wars again
Old Memnon, there thou wouldſt talk toth' purpoſe,
And the proudeſt of all theſe Court Camelions
Would be glad to find it ſenſe too: plauge of this
Dead peace, this Baſtard breeding, lowzie, lazie idleneſs,
Now we muſt learn to pipe, and pick our livings
Out of old rotten ends: theſe twenty five years
I have ſerv'd my Country, loſt my youth and bloud,
Expos'd my life to dangers more than dayes;
Yet let me tell my wants, I know their anſwers;
The King is bound to right me, they good people
Have but from hand to mouth. Look to your wives
Your young trim wives, your high-day wives, your march panes,
For if the ſouldiers find not recompence,
As yet there's none a hatching; I believe
You men of wares, the men of wars will nick ye,
For ſtarve nor beg they muſt not; my ſmall means
Are gone in fumo: here to raiſe a better
Unleſs it be with lying, or Dog flattering,
At which our Nation's excellent; obſerving Dog-days,
When this good Lady broyles and would be baſted
By that good Lord, or ſuch like moral learnings,
Is here impoſſible; Well; I will rub among'em
If any thing for honeſtie be gotten,
Though't be but bread and cheeſe I can be ſatisfied:
If otherwiſe the wind blow, ſtiff as I am
Yet I ſhall learn to ſhuffle: There's an old Laſs
That ſhall be nameleſs yet alive, my laſt hope,
Has often got me my pocket full of crowns.
If all ſail — Jack-Dawes, are you alive ſtill?
Then I ſee the coaſt clear, when fools and boyes can proſper.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Brave Lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Hail to the man of worſhip.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: You are fine ſirs,
Moſt paſſing fine at all points.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: As ye ſee Sir,
Home-bred and handſome, we cut not out our clothes Sir
At half ſword as your Taylors doe, and pink 'em
With Pikes and Partizans, we live retir'd Sir
Gentlemen like, and Jealous of our honours.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Very fine Fool, and fine Boy, Peace playes with you,
As the wind playes with Feathers, dances ye,
You grind with all guſts, gallants.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: We can bounce Sir,
When you Soldados bend i'th' hams, and frisk too.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: When twenty of your trip coats turn their tippets,
And your cold ſallets without ſalt or vineger
Be wambling in your ſtomachs; hemp and hobnails
Will bear no price now, hangings and old harneſs
Are like to over-run us.

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: Whores and hot houſes.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Surgeons and Syringes ring out your ſance-bells.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Your Jubile, your Jubile.

sp.speaker: Fool.

l.hi: Proh Deum.

sp.l: How our St. Georges will beſtride the Dragons,
The red and ramping Dragons.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Advanc't fool—

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: But then the ſting i'th' tail boy.

sp.speaker: Page.

l.hi: Tanto Melior.

sp.l: For ſo much the more danger, the more honour.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: You're very pleaſant with our occupation Gent.
Which very like amongſt theſe fierie Serpents
May light upon a Blind-worm of your blood,
A Mother or a Siſter.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Mine's paſt ſaddle,
You ſhould be ſure of her elſe: but ſay Sir Huon,
Now the Drums dubbs, and the ſticks turn'd bed-ſtaves,
All the old Foxes hunted to their holes,
The Iron age return'd to Erebus,
And Honorificabilitudinit atibus
Thruſt out o'th'Kingdom by the head and ſhoulders,
What trade do you mean to follow?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That's a queſtion.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Yes and a learned queſtion if ye mark it,
Conſider and ſay on.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Fooling as thou doſt, that's the beſt trade I take it.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Take it ſtraight then
For fear your fellows be before ye, hark ye Lieutenant
Fooling's the thing, the thing worth all your fightings,
When all's done ye muſt fool Sir.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Well, I muſt then.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: But do you know what fooling is? true fooling,
The circumſtances that belong unto it?
For every idle knave that ſhowes his teeth,
Wants and would live, can juggle, tumble, fiddle,
Make a dog face, or can abuſe his fellow,
Is not a fool at firſt daſh; you ſhall find Sir
Strange turnings in this trade; to fool is nothing
As fooling has been, but to fool the fair way,
The new way, as the beſt men fool their friends,
For all men get by fooling, meerly fooling,
Deſert does nothing, valiant, wiſe, vertuous,
Are things that walk by without bread or breeches.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I partly credit that.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Fine wits, fine wits Sir,
There's the young Boy, he does well in his way too,
He could not live elſe in his Maſters abſence;
He tyes a Ladyes garters ſo, ſo prettily,
Say his hand ſlip, but ſay ſo.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Why let it ſlip then.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: 'Tis ten to one the body ſhall come after,
And he that works deſerves his wages.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That's true.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: He riddles finely to a waiting Gentlewoman,
Expounds dreams like a Prophet, dreams himſelf too,
And wiſhes all dreams true; they cry Amen,
And there's a Memorandum: he can ſing too
Bawdy enough to pleaſe old Ladies: he lies rarely,
Pawns ye a ſute of clothes at all points, fully,
Can pick a pocket if ye pleaſe, or casket;
Liſps when he liſts to catch a Chambermaid,
And calls his Hoſteſs mother, theſe are things now,
If a man mean to live: to fight and ſwagger,
Beaten about the Ears with bawling ſheepskins,
Cut to the ſoul for Summer: here an arm loſt,
And there a leg; his honourable head
Seal'd up in ſalves and cereclothes, like a packet,
And ſo ſent over to an Hoſpital, ſtand there, charge there,
Swear there, whore there, dead there,
And all this ſport for cheeſe, and chines of dog-fleſh,
And mony when two wedneſdayes meet together,
Where to be lowzie is a Gentleman,
And he that wears a clean ſhirt has his ſhrowd on.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I'le be your ſcholar, come if I like fooling.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: You cannot chooſe but like it, fight you one day
I'le fool another, when your Surgeon's paid,
And all your leaks ſtopt, ſee whoſe ſtops are heavieſt,
I'le have a ſhilling for a can of wine,
When you ſhall have two Sergeants for a Counter.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Come learn of us Lieutenant, hang your Iron up,
We'l find you cooler wars.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Come let's together,
I'le ſee your tricks, and as I like 'em. — Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Why was there not ſuch women in the camp then
Prepar'd to make me know 'em?

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: 'Twas no place Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: Why ſhould they live in Tumults? they are creatures
Soft and of ſober natures.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Cou'd not your wives,
Your Mothers, or your Siſters have been ſent for
To exerciſe upon?

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: We thank your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: But do you mean?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I do mean.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: What Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: To ſee her,
And ſee thee hang'd too an thou anger'ſt me,
And thouſands of your throats cut, get ye from me,
Ye keep a prating of your points of manners,
And fill my head with lowzie circumſtances,
Better have Ballads in't, your courtly worſhips,
How to put off my hat, you, how to turn me,
And you (forſooth) to blow my noſe diſcreetly;
Let me alone, for I will love her, ſee her,
Talk to her, and mine own way.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: She's the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Why let her be the Devil, I have ſpoke
When Thunder durſt not check me, I muſt love,
I know ſhe was a thing kept for me.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: And I know Sir,
Though ſhe were born yours, yet your ſtrange behaviour
And want —

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Thou lieſt.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: I do not.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ha!

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: I do not lye Sir,
I ſay you want fair language, nay 'tis certain
You cannot ſay good morrow.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ye Dog whelps,
The proudeſt of your prating tongues—

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Doe, kill us,
Kill us for telling truth: for my part, General,
I would not live to ſee men make a may-game
Of him I have made a Maſter, kill us quickly,
Then ye may —

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Doe what you liſt, draw your ſword childiſhly
Upon your Servants that are bound to tell ye;
I am weary of my life.

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: And I.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: And all Sir.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Goe to the Princeſs, make her ſport, cry to her
I am the glorious man of war.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Pray ye leave me,
I am ſorry I was angry, I'le think better,
Pray no more words.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Good Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Nay then.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l:
We are gone Sir.
Exeunt Eume. and Capt.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: How came he hither? ſee for Heavens ſake wenches,
What face, and what poſtures he puts on,
I do not think he is perfect. Mem. walks aſide full of ſtrange geſtures.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: If your love
Have not betray'd his little wits, he's well enough,
As well as he will be.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Mark how he muſes.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: H'as a Batalia now in's brains, he draws out, now
Have at ye Harp • s.
See, ſee, there the fire fails.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Look what an Alphabet of faces he runs through.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: O love, love, how amorouſly thou look'ſt
In an old ruſty armo • .

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I'll away, for by my troth I fear him.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Fear the gods, Madam,
And 〈…〉 what man can do, this fellow
〈…〉 about him and his furies,
H • s La • ums, and his Launces, Swords, and Targets,
Na • d him up in armour Cap a pe,
Yet muſt I •• take within two hours,

It 〈◊〉
•• ſt can go, to give him ſuch a ſhake,
Should ſha • e his Valour off, and make his ſhanks to ake.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: For ſhame no more.
He muſes ſtill.
The Devil
Why ſhould this old dryed timber chopt with thunder—

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Old Wood burns quickeſt.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Out, you would ſay Madam,
Give me a green ſtick that may hold me heat,
And ſmoak me ſoundly too; He turns, and ſees ye. Memnon comes to her.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: There's no avoiding now, have at ye.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Lady.
The more I look upon ye. Stays her.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: The more you may, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Let him alone.
I would deſire your patience.
The more I ſay I look, the more — Stays her.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: My Fortune,
'Tis very apt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Women, let my Fortune
And me alone I wiſh ye, pray come this way,
And ſtand you ſtill there Lady.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Leave the words Sir, and leap into the meaning.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Then again:
I tell you I do love ye.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: No queſtions: pray no more queſtions.
I do love you, infinitely: why do you ſmile?
Am I ridiculous?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am monſtrous fearful, no, I joy you love me.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Joy on then, and be proud on't, I do love you,
Stand ſtill, do not trouble me you Women.
He loves you Lady at whoſe feet have kneel'd
Princes to b • g their • reedome, he whoſe valour
Has over • un whole Kingdoms.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: That makes me doubt, Sir,
'Twill ov • run me too.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: He whoſe Sword.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Talk not ſo big, Sir, you will fright the Princeſs,

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ha.

sp.speaker: Lucippe.
sp.l: No forſooth.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I know ye have done wonders.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I have and will do more and greater, braver;
And for your beauty miracles, name that Kingdom
And take your choice.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Sir I am not ambitious.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ye ſhall be, 'tis the Child of Glory: ſhe that I love
Whom my deſire ſhall magnifie, time ſtories,
And all the Empires of the Earth.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I would ſain ask him

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Prithee be quiet, he will beat us both elſe.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: What will ye make me then, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem
sp.l: I will make thee
Stand ſtill and hold thy peace; I have a heart, Lady.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Ye were a monſter elſe.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: A loving heart,
A truly loving heart.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Alas, how came it?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I would you had it in your hand, ſweet Lady,
To ſee the truth it bears you.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Do you give it.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: That was well thought upon.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: 'Twill put him to't Wench.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: And you ſhall ſee I dare accept it, Sir,
Tak't in my hand and view it: if I find it
A loving and a ſweet heart, as you call it,
I am bound, I am.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: No more, I'll ſend it to ye,
As I have honour in me, you ſhall have it.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Handſomly done, Sir, and perfum'd by all means,
The Weather's warm, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: With all circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: A Napkin wrought moſt curiouſly.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Divinely.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Put in a Goblet of pure Gold.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Yes in Jacinth
That ſhe may ſee the Spirit through,

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Ye have greas'd him
For chewing love again in haſte.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: If he ſhould do it.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: If Heaven ſhould fall we ſhould have larks; he do it!

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: See how he thinks upon't.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: He will think theſe three years
Ere he prove ſuch an Aſs, I lik't his offer,
There was no other way to put him off elſe.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I will do it—
Lady expect my heart.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I do, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Love it, for 'tis a heart that— and ſo I leave ye.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Either he is ſtark mad,
Or elſe I thinks he means it.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: He muſt be ſtark mad
Or elſe he will never do it, 'tis vain Glory,
And want of judgment that provokes this in him;
Sleep and Society cures all: his heart?
No, no, good Gentleman there's more belongs to't,
Hearts are at higher prices, let's go in
And there examine him a little better.
Shut all the doors behind for fear he follow,

I hope I have loſt a lover, and am glad on't.
Ex. Lady.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: 'Tis but to dye, Dogs do it, Ducks with dabling,
Birds ſing away their Souls, & Babies ſleep 'em,
Why do I talk of that is treble vantage?
For in the other World ſhe is bound to have me;
Her Princely word is paſt: my great deſert too
Will draw her to come after preſently,
'Tis juſtice, and the gods muſt ſee it done too.
Beſides, no Brother, Father, Kindred there
Can hinder us, all languages are alike too.
There love is everlaſting, ever young,
Free from Diſeaſes, ages, jealouſies,
Bawds, Beldames, Painters, Purgers: dye? 'tis nothing,
Men drown themſelves for joy to draw in juleps
When they are hot with Wine: In dreams we do it.
And many a handſom Wench that loves the ſport well,
Gives up her Soul ſo in her Lovers boſome;
But I muſt be incis'd firſt, cut and open'd,
My heart, and handſomely, ta'n from me; ſtay there,
Dead once, ſtay, let me think again, who do I know there?
For elſe to wander up and down unwaited on
And unregarded in my place and project,
Is for a Sowters Soul, not an old Souldiers.
My brave old Regiments — I there it goes,
That have been kill'd before me, right. —

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: He's here, and I muſt trouble him.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Then thoſe I have conquer'd
To make my train full.
Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My Captains then—
Sir, I beſeech ye.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: For to meet her there
Being a Princeſs and a Kings ſole Siſter
With great accommodation muſt be cared for.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Weigh but the Souldiers poverty.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Mine own Troop firſt
For they ſhall die.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: How, what's this?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Next—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Shall I ſpeak louder, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: A ſquare Battalia—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: You do not think of us.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Their Armours gilded —

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Good noble Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And round about ſuch Engines
Shall make Hell ſhake.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Ye do not mock me.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: For, Sir,
I will be ſtrong, as brave—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Ye may conſider,
You know we have ſerv'd you long enough.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: No Souldier
That ever landed on the bleſt Elyzium
Did or ſhall march, as I will.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Would ye would march, Sir,
Up to the King and get us—

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: King not Keiſer
Shall equal me in that world.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: What a Devil ails he?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Next, the rare beauties of thoſe Towns I fir'd.

sp.speaker: Ces.
sp.l: I ſpeak of money, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ten thouſand Coaches—

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.l: O pounds, Sir, pounds I beſeech your Lordſhip,
Let Coaches run out of your remembrance.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: In which the wanton Cupids, and the Graces
Drawn with the Weſtern winds kindling deſires,
And then our Poets—

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.l: Then our pay.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: For Chilax when the triumph comes; the Princeſs
Then, for I will have a Heaven made—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Bleſs your Lordſhip!
Stand ſtill, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: So I do, and in it—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Death Sir,
You talk you know not what.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Such rare devices:
Make me I ſay a Heaven.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I ſay ſo too, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: For here ſhall run a Conſtellation.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And there a piſſing Conduit.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ha!

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: With wine, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: A Sun there in his height, there ſuch a Planet.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: But where's our money, where runs that?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Money,
Money an't like your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Why all the carriage ſhall come behind, the ſtuff,
Rich hangings, treaſure;
Or ſay we have none.
I may ſay ſo truly,
For hang me if I have a Groat: I have ſerv'd well
And like an honeſt man: I ſee no reaſon—

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Thou muſt needs die good Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Very well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I will have honeſt, valiant ſouls about me,
I cannot miſs thee.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Dye?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Yes die, and Pelius,
Eumenes and Polybius: I ſhall think
Of more within theſe two hours.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Dye Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I, Sir,
And ye ſhall dye.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: When, I beſeech your Lordſhip?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: To morrow ſee ye do dye.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A ſhort warning,
Troth, Sir, I am • ll prepar'd.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I dye my ſelf then,
Beſide there's reaſon—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I pray thee tell me,
For thou art a great Dreamer.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I can dream, Sir,
If I eat well and ſleep well.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Was it never
By Dream or Apparition open'd to thee—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: He's mad.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: What the other world was, or Elyzium?
Didſt never travel in thy ſleep?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: To Taverns,
When I was drunk o're night; or to a Wench,
There's an Elyzium for ye, a young Lady
Wrapt round about ye like a Snake: is that it?
Or if that ſtrange Elyzium that you talk of
Be where the Devil is, I have dream't of him,
And that I have had him by the horns, and rid him,
He trots the Dagger out o'th' ſheath.

sp.speaker: Mem.

l.hi: Elyzium,

sp.l: The bleſſed fields man.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I know no fields bleſſed, but thoſe I have gain'd by.
I have dream't I have been in Heaven too.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: There, handle that place that's Elyzium.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Brave ſinging, and brave dancing,
And rare things.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: All full of flowers.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And Pot-herbs.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Bowers for lovers,
And everlaſting ages of delight.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I ſlept not ſo far.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Meet me on thoſe banks
Some two days hence.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: In Dream, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: No in death, Sir.
And there I Muſter all, and pay the Souldier.
Away, no more, no more.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: God keep your Lordſhip:
This is fine dancing for us.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Where's the General?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: There's the old ſign of Memnon, where the ſoul is
You may go look as I have.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Why queſtion him and ſee; he talks of Devils,
Hells, Heavens, Princes, Powers, and Potentates,
You muſt to th' pot too.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Do you know Elyzium? a tale he talks the Wild-gooſe chaſe of

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Elyzium? I have read of ſuch a place.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Then get ye to him,

Ye are as fine company as can be ſitted.
Exit Chilax.
Your Worſhips fairly met.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Mercy upon us,
What ails this Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Proviſion—

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: How his head works?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Between two Ribbs,
If he cut ſhort or mangle me; I'le take him
And twirle his neck about.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Now Gods defend us.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: In a pure Cup tranſparent, with a writing
To ſignifie—

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I never knew him thus:
Sure he's bewitch'd, or poyſon'd.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Come hither, Siphax.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Yes, how does your Lordſhip?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Well, God a mercy Souldier, very well,
But prithee tell me—

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Any thing I can, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: What durſt thou do to gain the rareſt Beauty
The World has?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: That the World has? 'tis worth doing.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Is it ſo; but what doing bears it?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Why? any thing; all danger it appears to.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Name ſome of thoſe things: do.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I would undertake, Sir,
A Voyage round about the World.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Short, Siphax.
A Merchant does it to ſpice pots of Ale.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I wou'd ſwim in Armour.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Short ſtill; a poor Jade
Loaden will take a ſtream and ſtem it ſtrongly
To leap a Mare.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: The plague, I durſt.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Still ſhorter,
I'll cure it with an Onion.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Surfeits.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Short ſtill:
They are often Phyſicks for our healths, and help us.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I wou'd ſtand a breach.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Thine honour bids thee, Souldier:
'Tis ſhame to find a ſecond cauſe.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I durſt, Sir,
Light with the ſelleſt Monſter.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: That's the pooreſt,
Man was ordain'd their Maſter; durſt ye dye, Sir?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: How? dye my Lord!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Dye Siphax; take thy Sword,
And come by that door to her; there's a price
To buy a luſty love at.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I am content, Sir,
To prove no Purchaſer.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Away thou World-worm,
Thou win a matchleſs Beauty?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: 'Tis to loſe't Sir,
For being dead, where's the reward I reach at?
The love I labour for?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: There it begins Fool,
Thou art meerly cozen'd; for the loves we now know
Are but the heats of half an hour, and hated
Deſires ſtir'd up by nature to encreaſe her;
Licking of one another to a luſt;
Courſe and baſe appetites, earths meer inheritours
And Heirs of Idleneſs and blood; Pure Love,
That, that the ſoul affects, and cannot purchaſe
While ſhe is loaden with our fleſh, that Love, Sir,
Which is the price of honour, dwells not here,
Your Ladies eyes are lampleſs to that Vertue,
That beauty ſmiles not on a cheek waſht over,
Nor ſcents the ſweet of Ambers; below, Siphax
Below us, in the other World Flyzium,
Where's no more dying, no deſpairing, mourning,
Where all deſires are full, defarts down loaden,
There Siphax, there, where loves are ever living.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Why do we love in this World then?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: To preſerve it,
The maker loſt his work elſe; but mark Siphax,
What iſſues that love bears.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Why Children, Sir.
I never heard him talk thus; thus divinely
And ſenſible before.

sp.speaker: Mem
sp.l: It does ſo, Siphax,
Things like our ſelves, as ſenſual, vain, unvented
Bubbles, and breaths of air, got with an itching
As bliſters are, and bred, as much corruption
Flows from their lives, ſorrow conceives and ſhapes 'em,
And oftentimes the death of thoſe we love moſt.
The bleeders bring them to the World to curſe 'em,
Crying they creep amongſt us like young Cats.
Cares and continual Croſſes keeping with 'em,
They make Time old to tend them, and experience
An aſs, they alter ſo; they grow and goodly,
Ere we can turn our thoughts, like drops of water
They fall into the main, are known no more;
This is the love of this World; I muſt tell thee
For thou art underſtanding.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: What you pleaſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And as a faithful man:
Nay I dare truſt thee,
I love the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: There 'tis, that has fired him,
I knew he had ſome inſpiration.
But does ſhe know it, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Yes marry does ſhe,
I have given my heart unto her.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: If ye love her.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Nay, underſtand me, my heart taken from me,
Out of my Body, man, and ſo brought to her.
How lik'ſt thou that brave offer? there's the love
I told thee of; and after death, the living;
She muſt in juſtice come Boy, ha?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Your heart, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I, ſo by all means, Siphax.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: He loves roaſt well
That cats the Spit.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And ſince thou art come thus fitly,
I'll do it preſently and thou ſhalt carry it,
For thou canſt tell a ſtory and deſcribe it.
And I conjure thee, Siphax, by thy gentry,
Next by the glorious Battels we have fought in,
By all the dangers, wounds, heats, colds, diſtreſſes,
Thy love next, and obedience, nay thy life.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: But one thing, firſt, Sir, if ſhe pleas'd to grant it,
Could ye not love her here and live? conſider.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ha? Yes, I think I could.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: 'Twould be far nearer,
Beſides the ſweets here would induce the laſt love
And link it in.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Thou ſayeſt right, but our ranks here
And bloods are bars between us, ſhe muſt ſtand off too
As I perceive ſhe does.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Deſert and Duty
Makes even all, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Then the King, though I
Have merited as much as man can, muſt not let her,
So many Princes covetous of her beauty;
I wou'd with all my heart, but 'tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Why, ſay ſhe many after.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: No, ſhe dares not;
The gods dare not do ill; come.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Do you mean it?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Lend me thy knife, and help me off.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: For heaven ſake,
Be not ſo ſtupid mad, dear General.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Diſpatch, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: As ye love that ye look for,
Heaven and the bleſſed life.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Hell take thee, Coxcomb,
Why doſt thou keep me from it? thy knife I ſay.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Do but this one thing, on my knees I beg it,
Stay but two hours till I return again.
For I will to her, tell her all your merits,
Your moſt unvalu'd love, and laſt your danger;
If ſhe relent, then live ſtill, and live loving,
Happy, and high in ſavour: if ſhe frown—

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Shall I be ſure to know it?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: As I live, Sir,
My quick return ſhall either bring ye fortune,
Or leave you to your own fate.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Two hours?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l:
Let it be kept, away, I will expect it.
Ex. Mem. Si.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: You dainty wits? two of ye to a Cater,
To cheat him of a dinner?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Ten at Court, Sir,
Are few enough, they are as wiſe as we are.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Hang ye, I'le eat at any time, and any where,
I never make that part of want, preach to me
What ye can do, and when ye liſt.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Your patience,
'Tis a hard day at Court, a fiſh day.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: So it ſeems, Sir,
The fins grow out of thy face.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: And to purchaſe
This day the company of one dear Cuſtard,
Or a meſs of Rice ap Thomas, needs a main wit;
Beef we can bear before us lined with Brewes
And tubs of Pork; vociferating Veals,
And Tongues that ne're told lye yet.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Line thy mouth with 'em.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Thou haſt need, and great need,
For theſe ſinny fiſh-dayes,
The Officers underſtandings are ſo flegmatick,
They cannot apprehend us.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That's great pity,
For you deſerve it, and being apprehended
The whip to boot; Boy what do you ſo near me?
I dare not truſt your touch Boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: As I am vertuous,
What, thieves amongſt our ſelves?

l.hi: Stremon.

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: Lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Welcome a ſhore, a ſhore.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: What Mounſieur Muſick?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: My fine Fool.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Fellow Crack, why what a conſort
Are we now bleſt withal?

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Fooling and ſidling,
Nay and we live not now boys; what new ſongs, Sirra?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: A thouſand, man, a thouſand.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Itching Airs
Alluding to the old ſport.

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: Of all ſizes.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: And how does ſmall Tym Treble here; the heart on't?

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: To do you ſervice.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: O Tym the times, the times Tym.

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: How does the General,
And next what money's ſtirring?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: For the General
He's here, but ſuch a General!
The time's chang'd, Stremon,
He was the liberal General, and the loving,
The feeder of a Souldier, and the Father,
But now become the ſtupid'ſt.

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: Why, what ails he?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Nay, if a Horſe knew, and his head's big enough,
I'le hang for't; did'ſt thou ever ſee a Dog
Run mad o'th' tooth-ache, ſuch another toy
Is he now, ſo he glotes and grins, and bites.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Why hang him quickly,
And then he cannot hurt folks.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: One hour raving,
Another ſmiling, not a word the third hour,
I tell thee Stremon h'as a ſtirring ſoul,
What ever it attempts or labours at
Would wear out twenty bodies in another.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: I'le keep it out of me, for mine's but Buckram,
He would bownce that out in two hours.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Then he talks
The ſtrangeſt and the maddeſt ſtuff from reaſon,
Or any thing ye offer; ſtand thou there,
I'le ſhow thee how he is, for I'le play Memnon
The ſtrangeſt General that ere thou heareſt of, Stremon.

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Go preſently and find me
A black Horſe with a blew tail; bid the blank Cornet
Charge through the Sea, and ſink the Navy: ſoftly,
Our ſouls are things not to be waken'd in us
With larums, and loud bawlings, for in Elyzium
Stilneſs and quietneſs, and •••• neſs, Sirra,
I will have, for it much concerns mine honour,
Such a ſtrong reputation for my welcome
As all the world ſhall ſay: for in the forefront
So many on white Unicorns, next them
My Gentlemen, my Cavaliers and Captains,
Ten deep and trapt with Tenter-hooks to take hold
Of all occaſions: for Friday cannot fiſh out
The end I aim at; tell me of Diocles,
And what he dares do? dare he meet me naked?
Thunder in this hand? in his left—Fool—

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Fool, I would have thee fly i'th' Air, fly ſwiftly
To that place where the Sun ſets, there deliver.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Deliver? what, Sir?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: This Sir, this ye ſlave, Sir, All laugh.
Death ye rude Rogues, ye Scarabe's.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Hold for Heav'ns ſake, Lieutenant, ſweet Lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I have done, Sir.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: You have wrung his neck off.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: No Boy, 'tis the nature
Of this ſtrange paſſion when't hits to hale people
Along by th'hair, to kick 'em, break their heads.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Do ye call this Acting, was your part to beat me?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Yes, I muſt act all that he does.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Plague act ye,
I'le act no more.

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: 'Tis but to ſhew man.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Then man
He ſhould have ſhew'd it only, and not done it,
I am ſure he beat me beyond Action,
Gouts o' your heavy fiſt.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I'le have thee to him,
Thou haſt a fine wit, fine fool, and canſt play rarely.
He'l hug thee, Boy, and ſtroke thee.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: I'le to the ſtocks firſt,
E're I be ſtrok't thus.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: But how came he, Chilax?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I know not that.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: I'le to him.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: He loves thee well,
And much delights to hear thee ſing; much taken
He has been with thy battel ſongs.

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: If Muſick
Can find his madneſs; I'le ſo ſiddle him,
That out it ſhall by th' ſhoulders.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: My fine Fidler,
He'l ſirk you and ye take not heed too: 'twill be rare ſport
To ſee his own trade triumph over him;
For mony there's none ſtirring; try good Stremon
Now what your ſilver ſound can do; our voices
Are but vain Echoes.

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: Something ſhall be done.
Shall make him underſtand all; let's toth' Tavern,
I have ſome few Crowns leſt yet: my whiſtle wet once
I'le pipe him ſuch a Paven—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Hold thy head up,
I'le cure it with a quart of wine; come Coxcomb,
Come Boy take heed of Napkins.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Youl'd no more acting?

sp.speaker: Cin.
sp.l: No more Chicken.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Go then. Exeunt omnes.

div.stage: Enter Siphax at one door, and a Gentleman at the other.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: God ſave you Sir; pray how might I ſee the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Why very ſitly, Sir, ſhe's even now ready
To walk out this way intoth' Park; ſtand there,
Ye cannot miſs her ſight, Sir.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I much thank ye. Exit Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Let's have a care, for I'le aſſure ye Wenches
I wou'd not meet him willingly again;
For though I do not fear him, yet his faſhion
I wou'd not be acquainted much with.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Gentle Lady,
Ye need not fear, the walks are view'd and empty,
But me thinks, Madam, this kind heart of his—

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: He's ſlow a coming.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Keep me ye bleſt Angels,
What killing power is this?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why, doſt thou look for't?
Doſt think he ſpoke in earneſt?

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Methinks, Madam,
A Gentleman ſhould keep his word; and to a Lady,
A Lady of your excellencies.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Out Fool!
Send me his heart? what ſhould we do with't? dance it?

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Dry it and drink it for the Worms.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Who's that?
What man ſtands there?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: A Gentleman,
Which I beſeech your grace to honour ſo much,
As know him for your ſervants Brother.

l.hi: Siphax?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: The ſame an't pleaſe your grace; what does he here?
Upon what buſineſs? and I ignorant?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: He's grown a handſome Gentleman: good Siphax
Y'are welcome from the Wars; wou'd ye with us, Sir?
Pray ſpeak your will: he bluſhes, be not fearfull,
I can aſſure ye for your Siſters ſake, Sir,
There's my hand on it.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Do you hear, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Sure theſe Souldiers
Are all grown ſenſeleſs.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Do ye know where ye are, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Tongue-tyed,
He looks not well too, by my life, I think—

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Speak for ſhame ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: A man wou'd ſpeak—

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Theſe Souldiers
Are all dumb Saints: conſider and take time, Sir,
Let's forward Wenches, come, his Palat's down.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Date theſe men charge i'th' face of fire and bullets?
And hang then heads down at a handſome Woman?

Good maſter Mars, that's a foul fault.
Ex. Prin. Lucippe.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Fye beaſt,
No more my Brother.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Siſter, honoured Siſter.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Diſhonoured fool.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I do confeſs.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Fye on thee.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: But ſtay till I deliver.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Let me go,
I am aſham'd to own thee.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Fare ye well then,
Ye muſt ne're ſee me more.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Why ſtay dear Siphax,
My anger's paſt; I will hear ye ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: O Siſter!

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Out with it Man.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: O I have drunk my miſchief.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Ha? what?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: My deſtruction.
In at mine eyes I have drunk it; O the Princeſs,
The rare ſweet Princeſs!

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: How fool? the rare Princeſs?
Was it the Princeſs that thou ſaid'ſt?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: The Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Thou doſt not love her ſure, thou darſt not.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Yes by Heaven.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Yes by Heaven? I know thou darſt not.
The Princeſs? 'tis thy life the knowledge of it,
Preſumption that will draw into it all thy kindred,
And leave 'em ſlaves and ſuccourleſs; the Princeſs?
Why ſhe's a ſacred thing to ſee and worſhip,
Fixt from us as the Sun is, high, and glorious,
To be ador'd not doted on; deſire things poſſible,
Thou fooliſh young man, nouriſh not a hope
Will hale thy heart out.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: 'Tis my deſtinie,
And I know both diſgrace and death will quit it,
If it be known.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Purſue it not then, Siphax,
Get thee good wholeſome thoughts may nouriſh thee,
Go home and pray.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I cannot.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Sleep then, Siphax,
And dream away thy doting.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I muſt have her,
Or you no more your Brother; work Cleanthe,
Work, and work ſpeedily, or I ſhall die Wench.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Dye then, I dare forget; farewel.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Farewel Siſter.
Farewel for ever, ſee me buried.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Stay.
Pray ſtay: he's all my brothers: no way Siphax,
No other Woman?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: None, none, ſhe or ſinking.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Go and hope well, my life I'le venture for thee
And all my art, a Woman may work miracles;
No more, pray heartily againſt my fortunes,
For much I fear a main one.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I ſhall do it. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter a Prieſteſs of Venus and a Boy.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: FInd him by any means; and good child tell him
He has forgot his old friend, give him this,
And ſay this night without excuſe or buſineſs,
As ever he may find a friend, come to me,
He knows the way and how, begon.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I gallop. Exit Boy.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I have been looking you.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: The fair Cleanthe,
What may your buſineſs be?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: O holy Mother
Such buſineſs, of ſuch ſtrange weight, now or never.
As ye have loved me, as ye do or may do,
When I ſhall find a fit time.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: If by my means
Your buſineſs may be ſitted; ye know me,
And how I am tyed unto you; be bold Daughter
To build your beſt hopes.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: O but 'tis a ſtrange one,
Stuck with as many dangers—

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: There's the working,
Small things perform themſelves and give no pleaſures;
Be confident, through death I'le ſerve.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Here.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Fye no corruption.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Take it; 'tis yours,
And goodneſs is no gall to th' Conſcience,
I know ye have ways to vent it: ye may hold it.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: I'll keep it for ye; when?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: To morrow morning
I'll viſit ye again; and when occaſion
Offers it ſelf—

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: Inſtruct me, and have at ye.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Farewel till then; be ſure.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: As your own thoughts, Lady.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: 'Tis a main work, and full of fear. Exit Cle.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Fools only
Make their effects ſeem fearful, farewell daughter.
This gold was well got for my old tuff Souldier,
Now I ſhall be his ſweet again; what buſineſs
Is this ſhe has a foot? ſome luſty lover
Beyond her line, the young Wench would fain piddle,
A little to revive her muſt be thought of,
'Tis even ſo, ſhe muſt have it; but how by my means,
A Devil, can ſhe drive it? I that wait ſtill
Before the Goddeſs, giving Oracle,
How can I profit her? 'tis her own project,

And if ſhe caſt it falſe, her own fault be it.
Exit Prieſt.
