sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Why, this is utter madneſs.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Thus it is, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Only the Princeſs ſight?

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: All we can judge at.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: This muſt be lookt to timely.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Yes, and wiſely.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: He does not offer at his life?

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Not yet, Sir,
That we can hear of.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Noble Gentlemen,
Let me entreat your watches over him,
Ye cannot do a worthier work.

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: We came, Sir,
Provided for that ſervice.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Where is Chilax?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: A little buſie, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Is the Fool and Boy here?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: They are, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Let 'em be ſtill ſo; and as they find his humours.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Now ye may behold him.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Stand cloſe, and make no noiſe;
By his eyes now, Gentlemen,
I gueſs him full of anger.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Be not ſeen there.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: The hour's paſt long ago, he's falſe and fearful,
Coward, go with thy Caitive ſoul, thou Cur Dog.
Thou cold Clod, wild fire warm thee, monſtrous fearful,
I know the Slave ſhakes but to think on't.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: I know not, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: But I ſhall catch ye, Raſcal,
Your mangy Soul is not immortal here, Sir,
Ye muſt dye, and we muſt meet; we muſt, maggot,
Be ſure we muſt, for not a Nook of Hell,
Not the moſt horrid Pit ſhall harbour thee;
The Devils tail ſha'n't hide thee, but I'll have thee,
And how I'll uſe thee? whips and firebrands:
Toſting thy tail againſt a flame of wild fire,
And baſting it with Brimſtone, ſhall be nothing,
Nothing at all; I'll teach ye to be treacherous:
Was never Slave ſo ſwing'd ſince Hell was Hell
As I will ſwinge thy Slaves Soul; and be ſure on't.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Is this imagination, or ſome circumſtance?
For 'tis extream ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: So is all he does, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Till then I'll leave ye; who's there? where's the Surgeon? Demagoras?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Bring the Surgeon:
And wait you too.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: What wou'd he with a Surgeon?

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Things muſtring in his head: pray mark.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Come hither,
Have you brought your Inſtruments?

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: They are within, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Put to the doors a while there; ye can inciſe
To a hairs breadth without defacing.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And take out fairly from the fleſh.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: The leaſt thing.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Well come hither; take off my doublet,
For look ye Surgeon, I muſt have ye cut
My Heart out here, and handſomly: Nay, ſtare not,
Nor do not ſtart; I'll cut your throat elſe, Surgeon,
Come ſwear to do it.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Good Sir—

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Sirrah, hold him,
I'll have but one blow at his head.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: I'll do it,
Why what ſhould we do living after you, Sir?
We'll dye before if ye pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: No, no.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Living? hang living.
Is there ne'r a Cat hole where I may creep through?
Would I were in the Indies. Aſide.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Swear then, and after my death preſently
To kill your ſelves and follow, as ye are honeſt,
As ye have faiths, and loves to me.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: We'll do it.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Pray do not ſtir yet, we are near enough
To run between all dangers.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Here I am, Sir;
Come, look upon me, view the beſt way boldly,
Fear nothing, but cut home; if your hand ſhake, Sirrah,
Or any way deface my heart i'th' cutting,
Make the leaſt ſcratch upon it; but draw it whole,
Excellent fair, ſhewing at all points, Surgeon,
The Honour and the Valour of the Owner,
Mixt with the moſt immaculate love I ſend it,
Look to't, I'll ſlice thee to the Soul.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Ne'r fear, Sir,
I'll do it daintily; would I were out once.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I will not have ye ſmile, Sirrah, when ye do it,
As though ye cut a Ladies Corn; 'tis ſcurvy:
Do me it as thou doſt thy Prayers, ſeriouſly.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: I'll do it in a dump, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: In a Dog, Sir,
I'll have no dumps, nor dumplins; fetch your tools,
And then I'll tell ye more.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: If I return
To hear more, I'll be hang'd for't.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Quick, quick,

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Yes Sir,

With all the heels we have.
Exeunt Surgeon, Demagoras.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Yet ſtand.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: He'l do it.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: He cannot, and we here.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Why when ye Raſcals,
Ye dull Slaves: will ye come, Sir? Surgeon, ſyringe,
Dog-leach, ſhall I come fetch ye?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Now I'll to him.
God ſave ye honour'd Brother.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My dear Polydore,
Welcome from travel, welcome; and how do ye?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Well Sir, would you were ſo.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I am, I thank ye.
You are a better'd man much, I the ſame ſtill,
An old rude Souldier, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pol
sp.l: Pray be plain, Brother,
And tell me but the meaning of this Viſion,
For to me it appears no more: ſo far
From common Courſe and Reaſon.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: •• ank thee, Fortune,
At length I have found the man: the man muſt do it,
The man in honour b • und.
To 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Hark, ſo • I will bleſs ye with the circumſtance
Of that weak ſhadow that appear'd.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l:
Sp •
〈◊〉 S • . Walks with him.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: It is no Story for all ears.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: The Princeſs? Whiſpers.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Peace and hear all.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: How?
Sure 'tis dangerous
He ſtarts ſo at it.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: You heart? do you know, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Yes, Pray thee be ſofte • .

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Me to do it?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Only reſerv'd, and dedicated.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: For ſhame, Brother,
Know what ye are, a man.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: None of you Athens,
Good ſweet Sir, no Philoſophy, thou ſeel'ſt not
The honourable end, fool.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I am fine I feel
The ſhame and ſcorn that follows; have ye ſerv'd thus long
The glory of your Country, in your Conqueſts?
The envy of your Neighbours, in your Vertues?
Rul'd Armi • s of your own, given Laws to Nations,
Belov'd and fear'd as far as Fame has travell'd,
Call'd the moſt fortunate and happy Memnon,
To loſe all here at home, poorly to loſe it?
Poorly, and pett •• hly, ridiculouſly
To ſling away your fortune? where's your Wiſedom?
Where's that you govern'd others by, diſcretion?
Do's your Rule laſtly hold upon your ſelf? ſie Brother,
How ye are faln? Get up into your honour,
The top branch of your bravery, and from thence,
Look and behold how little Memnon ſeems now.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Hum! 'tis well ſpoken; but doſt thou think young Scholar,
The tongues of Angels from my happineſs
Could turn the end I aim at? no, they cannot.
This is no Book-caſe, Brother; will ye do it?
Uſe no more art, I am reſolv'd.
Ye may Sir
Command me to do any thing that's honeſt,
And for your noble end: but this, it carries—

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ye ſhall not be ſo honour'd; live an Aſs ſtill,
And learn to ſpell for profit: go, go ſtudy.
Ye muſt not hold him up ſo, he is loſt then.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Get thee to School again, and talk of turnips,
And find the natural Cauſe out, why a Dog
Turns thrice about e're he lyes down: there's Learning.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Come, I will do it now; 'tis brave, I find it,
And now allow the reaſon.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: O do you ſo, Sir?
Do ye find it currant?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Yes, yes, excellent.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I told ye.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I was fooliſh: I have here too
The • ateſt way to find the truth out; hark ye?
Ye ſhall be rul'd by me.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: It will be: but

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I reach it,
If the worſt fall, have at the worſt; we'll both go.
But two days, and 'tis thus; ha?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: 'Twill do well ſo.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Then is't not excellent, do ye conceive it?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: 'Twill work for certain.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: O 'twill tickle her,
And you ſhall know then by a line.

sp.speaker: Mem
sp.l: I like it,
But let me not be fool'd again.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Doubt nothing,
You do me wrong then, get ye in there private
As I have taught ye, Buſta.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l:
Work.
Exit Memnon

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I will do.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Have ye found the cauſe?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Yes, and the ſtrangeſt, Gentlemen,
That e'r I heard of, anon I'll tell ye: Stremon
Be you ſtill near him to affect his fancy,
And keep his thoughts off: let the Fool and Boy
Stay him, they may do ſome pleaſure too: Eumenes
What if he had a Wench, a handſome Whore brought,
Rarely dreſt up, and taught to ſtate it?

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: His cauſe is meerly heat: and made believe
It were the Princeſs mad for him.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: I think
'Twere not amiſs.

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: And let him kiſs her.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: What elſe?

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: I'll be his Bawd an't pleaſe you, young and wholeſome
I can aſſure ye he ſhall have.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Faith let him.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: He ſhall, I hope 'twill help him, walk a little
I'll tell you how his caſe ſtands, and my project
In which you may be mourners, but by all means
Stir not you from him, Stremon.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: On our lives, Sir. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: O y'are a precious man? two days in town
And never ſee your old Friend?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Prithee pardon me.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: And in my Conſcience if I had not ſent.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: No more, I would ha' come; I muſt.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: I find ye,
God a mercy want, ye never care for me
But when your Slops are empty.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Ne'r fear that, Wench;
Shall find good currant Coin ſtill, Is this the old Houſe?

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Have ye forgot it?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And the door ſtill ſtanding
That goes into the Temple?

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Still.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: The Robes too,
That I was wont to ſhift in here?

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: All here ſtill.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: O ye tuff Rogue, what troubles have I trotted through?
What fears and frights? every poor Mouſe a Monſter
That I heard ſtir, and every ſtick I trod on,
A ſharp ſting to my Conſcience.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: 'Las poor Conſcience.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And all to liquor thy old Boots, Wench.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Out Beaſt:
How you talk?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I am old, Wench,
And talking to an old man is like a ſtomacher,
It keeps his blood warm.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: But pray tell me?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Any thing.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Where did the Boy meet with ye? at a Wench ſure?
At one end of a Wench, a Cup of Wine, ſure?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt I am too honeſt.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: That's your fault,
And that the Surgeon knows.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Then farewel,
I will not fail ye ſoon.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Ye ſhall ſtay Supper;
I have ſworn ye ſhall, by this ye ſhall.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I will, Wench;
But after Supper for an hour, my buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: And but an hour?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: No by this kiſs, that ended
I will return and all night in thine Arms wench.

sp.speaker: Pr.
sp.l: No more, I'le take your meaning; come 'tis Supper time

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Thou art not well.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Your grace ſees more a great deal
Than I feel. (yet I lye) O Brother!

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Mark her,
Is not the quickneſs of her eye conſumed, wench?
The lively red and white?

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Nay ſhe is much alter'd,
That on my underſtanding, all her ſleeps Lady
Which were as found and ſweet —

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Pray do not force me,
Good Madam, where I am not, to be ill,
Conceit's double ſickneſs; on my faith your highneſs
Is meer miſtaken in me. A Dead March within of Drum and Sagbutts

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am glad on't.
Yet this I have ever noted when thou waſt thus,
It ſtill forerun ſome ſtrange event: my Siſter
D • ed when thou waſt thus laſt: hark hark, ho,
What mournfull noiſe is this comes creeping forward?
Still it grows nearer, nearer, do ye hear it?

div.stage: Enter Polydor, and Captains, Eumenes mourning.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: It ſeems ſome Souldiers funeral: ſee it enters.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: What may it mean?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: The Gods keep ye fair Calis.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: This man can ſpeak, and well; he ſtands and views us;
Wou'd I were ne'r worſe look't upon: how humbly
His eyes are caſt now to the Earth! pray mark him
And mark how rarely he has rankt his troubles:
See now he weeps, they all weep; a ſweeter ſorrow
I never look't upon, nor one that braver
Bec • me his grief; your will with us?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Great Lady, Plucks out the Cup.
Excellent beauty.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: He ſpeaks handſomely.
What a rare rhetorician his grief plaies!
That ſtop was admirable.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: See, ſee thou Princeſs,
T •• great commander of all hearts.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I have found it,
On how my ſoul ſhakes!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: See, ſee the noble heart
Of him that was the nobleſt: ſee and glory
(Like the proud God himſelf) in what thou haſt purchas'd,
Behold the heart of Memnon: does it ſtart ye?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Good gods, what has his wildneſs done?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Look boldlie,
You boldlie ſaid you durſt, look wretched woman,
Nay flie not back fair follie, 'tis too late now,
Vertue and blooming honour bleed to death here,
Take it, the Legacie of Love bequeath'd ye,
Of cruel Love a cruel Legacie;
What was the will that wrought it then? can ye weep?
•• balm it in your trueſt tears
If women can weep a truth, or ever ſorrow ſunk yet
Into the ſoul of your ſex, for 'tis a Jewel
The worlds worth cannot weigh down,
Take it Lady; And with it all (I dare not curſe) my ſorrows,
And may they turn to Serpents.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: How ſhe looks
Still upon him! ſee now a tear ſteals from her.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: But ſtill ſhe keeps her eye firm.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Next read this,
But ſince I ſee your ſpirit ſomewhat troubled
I'le doe it for ye.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: Still ſhe eyes him mainlie.

lg.l: Got happy heart for thou ſhalt lye
Intomb'd in her for whom I dye
Example of her cruelty.
Tell her if ſhe chance to chide
Me for ſlowneſs in her pride
That it was for her I died
If a tear eſcape her eye
'Tis not for my memory
But thy rights of obſequy.
The Altar was my loving breaſt,
My heart the ſacrificed beaſt,
And I was my ſelf the Prieſt
Your body was the ſacred ſhrine,
Your cruel mind the power divine
P •• as'd w • th hearts of men, not • in • .

sp.speaker: Fumen.
sp.l: Now it pours down.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I like it rarelie: Ladie.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: How greedily ſhe ſwallows up his language?

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: Her eye inhabits on him.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Cruel Ladie,
Great as your beautie ſcornfull; had your power
But Cupid has more ſhafts than one, more flames too,
And now he muſt be open ey'd, 'tis Juſtice:
Live to injoy your longing; live and laugh at
The loſſes and the miſeries we ſuffer;
Live to be ſpoken when your crueltie
Has cut off all the vertue from this Kingdom,
Turn'd honour into earth, and faithful ſervice.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I ſwear his ange • 's excellent.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Truth, and moſt tried love
Into diſdain and downfall.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Still more pleaſing.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Live then I ſay famous for civil ſlaughters,
Live and lay out your triumphs, gild your glories,
Live and be ſpoken this is ſhe, this Ladie,
This with the two edg'd eyes, the heart for hardneſs
Outdoing rocks; and coldneſs, rocks of Cryſtal.
This with the ſwelling ſoul, more coy of Courtſhip
Than the proud ſea is when th • ſhores •• brace him;
Live till the mothers find ye, read your ſtory,
And ſow their barren curſes on your beauty,
Till thoſe that have enjoy'd their loves deſpiſe ye,
Till Virgins pray againſt ye, old age find ye,
And even as waſted coals glow in their dying,
So may the Gods reward ye in your aſhes:
But y'are the Siſter of my King; more prophecies
Elſe I ſhould utter of ye, true loves and loyal
Bleſs themſelves ever from ye: ſo I leave ye.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Prethee be angry ſtill young man: good fair Sir
Chide me again, what wou'd this man doe pleas'd,
That in his paſſion can bewitch ſouls? ſtay.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Upon my life ſhe loves him.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Pray ſtay.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I do command ye.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: No, ye cannot Ladie,
I have a ſpell againſt ye, Faith and Reaſon,
Ye are too weak to reach me: I have a heart too,
But not for hawks meat Ladie.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Even for Charity
Leave me not thus afflicted: you can teach me.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: How can you Preach that Charity to others
That in your own ſoul are an Atheiſt,
Believing neither power nor fear? I trouble ye,
The Gods be good unto ye.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Amen.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Ladie. She Swounds

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: O royal Madam, Gentlemen for heaven ſake.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Give her freſh air, ſhe comes again: away ſirs They come back.
And here ſtand cloſe till we perceive the working.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Ye have undone all.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: So I fear.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: She loves ye.
And then all hopes loſt this way.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Peace ſhe riſes.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Now for my purpoſe Fortune.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Where's the Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Gone Madam.
Why gone?

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: H'as diſpatch't his buſineſs.
He came to ſpeak with me,
He did.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: He did not.
For I had many queſtions.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: On my Faith Madam, he
Talk't a great while to ye.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Thou conceiv'ſt not,
He talk't not as he ſhould doe; O my heart
Away with that ſad ſight; didſt thou e're love me.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Why do you make that queſtion?
If thou didſt
Run, run wench, run: nay ſee how thou ſtir'ſt.

sp.speaker: Lucip.
sp.l: Whither?
If 'twere for any thing to pleaſe thy ſelf
Thou woud'ſt run toth' devil: but I am grown—

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Fie Lady.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I ask none of your fortunes, nor your loves,
None of your bent deſires I ſlack, ye are not
In love with all men, are ye? one for ſhame
You will leave your honour'd miſtris? why do ye ſtare ſo?
What is that ye ſee about me, tell me?
Lord what am I become? I am not wilde ſure,
Heaven keep that from me: O Cleanthe help me,
Or I am ſunk to death.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Ye have offended and mightily, love is incenſt againſt ye,
And therefore take my Counſel, to the Temple,
For that's the ſpeedieſt phyſick: before the Goddeſs
Give your repentant prayers: ask her will,
And from the Oracle attend your ſentence,
She is milde and mercifull.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: I will: O Venus
Even as thou lov'ſt thy ſelf!

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l:
Now for my fortune.
Exeunt Cal. and women.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: What ſhall I doe?

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: Why make your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I dare not,
No Gentlemen, I dare not be a villain,
Though her bright beauty would entice an Angel.
I will toth' King my laſt hope: get him a woman
As we before concluded: and as ye paſs
Give out the Spartans are in arms; and terrible;
And let ſome letters to that end be feign'd too
And ſent to you, ſome Poſts too, to the General;
And let me work: be ne're him ſtill.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: We will Sir.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Farewel: and pray for all: what e're I will ye
Doe it, and hope a faſt end.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: The Gods ſpeed ye. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Stremon, Fool, Boy, and Servants.

sp.speaker: Servants.
sp.l: He lies quiet.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Let him lye, and as I told ye
Make ready for this ſhew: h'as divers times
Been calling upon Orpheus to appear
And ſhew the joyes: now I will be that Orpheus,
And as I play and ſing, like beaſts and trees
I wou'd have you ſhap't and enter: thou a Dog, fool,
I have ſent about your ſutes: the Boy a buſh,
An Aſs you, you a Lion.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: I a Dog?
I'le ſit you for a Dog. Bow wow.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: 'Tis excellent,
Steal in and make no noiſe.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Bow wow.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Away Rogue. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Good ſweet friend be not long.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Thou think'ſt each hour ten
Till I be ferreting.

sp.speaker: Prie.
sp.l: You know I love ye.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I will not be above an hour; let thy robe be 〈◊〉

And the door be kept.
Knock C •• ant ••
knocks W •••

sp.speaker: Prie.
sp.l: Who knocks there?
Yet more buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Have ye more penſioners? the Princeſs wom •••
Nay then I'le ſtay a little, what game's a foot now.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Now is the time.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A rank bawd by this hand too,
She grinds o'both ſides: hey boyes.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: How, your Brother Siphax?
Loves he the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Deadlie, and you know
He is a Gentleman deſcended noblie.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: But a rank knave as ever piſt.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Hold Mother,
Here's more gold and ſome jewells.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Here's no villany,
I am glad I came toth' hearing.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Alas Daughter,
What would ye have me doe?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Hold off ye old whore;
There's more gold coming; all's mine, all.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Do ye ſhrink now,
Did ye not promiſe faithfully, and told me
Through any danger?

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Any I can wade through.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Ye ſhall and eaſily, the ſin not ſeen neither,
Here's for a better ſtole and a new vail mother:
Come, ye ſhall be my friend.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: If all hit, hang me, —
I'le make ye richer than the Goddeſs.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Say then,
I am yours, what muſt I doe?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I'th' morning
But very early, will the Princeſs viſit
The Temple of the Goddeſs, being troubled
With ſtrange things that diſtract her: from the Oracle
(Being ſtrongly too in love) ſhe will demand
The Goddeſs pleaſure, and a Man to cure her,
That Oracle you give: deſcribe my Brother,
You know him perfectly.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: I have ſeen him often.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: And charge her take the next man ſhe ſhall meet with
When ſhe comes out: you underſtand me.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Which ſhall be he attending; this is all,
And eaſily without ſuſpicion ended,
Nor none dare diſobey, 'tis Heaven that does it,
And who dares croſs it then, or once ſuſpect it?
The venture is moſt eaſie.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: I will doe it.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: As ye ſhall proſper?

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: As I ſhall proſper?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Take this too, and farewel; but firſt hark hither.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: What a young whore's this to betray her Miſtris?
A thouſand Cuckolds ſhall that Husband be,
That marries thee, thou art ſo miſchievous.
I'le put a ſpoak among your wheels.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Be conſtant.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: 'Tis done.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l:
I'le doe no more at drop ſhot then.
Exit Chilax.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l:
Farewel wench.
Exeunt Prieſt and Cleanthe.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter a Servant, and Stremon, at the door.

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.l: HE ſtirs, he ſtirs.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Let him, I am ready for him,
He ſhall not this day periſh, if his paſſions
May be fed with Muſick; are they ready?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: All, all: ſee where he comes.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l:
I'le be ſtraight for him.
Exit Stremon.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: How ſad he looks and ſullen! Stand cloſe.
Here are the Captains: my fear's paſt now.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Put caſe i'th'other world
She do not love me neither? I am old 'tis certain.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: My blood loſt, and limbs ſtiff; my embraces
Like the cold ſtubborn bark, hoar • e, and heatleſs,
My words worſe: my fame only and atchievements
Which are my ſtrength, my blood, my youth, my faſhion,
Muſt wooe her, win her, wed her; that's but wind,
And women are not brought to bed with ſhadows:
I do her wrong, much wrong; ſhe is young and bleſſed,
Sweet as the ſpring, and as his bloſſoms tender,
And I a nipping North-wind, my head hung
With hails, and froſtie I ſicles: are the ſouls ſo too
When they depart hence, lame and old, and loveleſs?
No ſure, 'tis ever youth there; Time and Death
Follow our fleſh no more: and that forc'd opinion
That ſpirits have no ſexes, I believe not.
There muſt be love, there is love: what art thou?

lg.l: Orpheus I am, come from the deeps below,
To thee fond man the plagues of love to ſhow:
To the fair fields where loves eternal dwell
There's none that come, but firſt they paſs through hell:
Hark and beware unleſs thou haſt lov'd ever,
Belov'd again, thou ſhalt ſee thoſe joyes never.
Hark how they groan that dy'd deſpairing,
O take heed then:
Hark how they howl for over-daring,
All theſe were men.
They that be fools, and dye for fame
They loſe their name;
And they that bleed
Hark how they ſpeed.
Now in cold froſts, now ſcorching fires
They ſit, and curſe their loſt deſires:
Nor ſhall theſe ſouls be free from pains and fears,
Till Women waſt them over in their tears.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: How ſhould I know my paſſage is deni'd me?
Or which of all the Devils dare?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: This Song
Was rarely form'd to fit him.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: Charon O Charon,
Thou waſter of the ſouls to bliſs or bane.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Who calls the Ferry-man of Hell?

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: Come near,
And ſay who lives in joy, and who in fear.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Thoſe that dye well, Eternall joy ſhall follow;
Thoſe that dye ill, their own ſoul fate ſhall ſwallow.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: Shall thy black Bark thoſe guilty ſpirits ſtow
That kill themſelves for love?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: O no, no, no.
My cordage cracks when ſuch great ſins are near,
No wind blows fair, nor I myſelf can ſtear.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: What lovers paſs and in Elyzium raign?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Thoſe Gentle loves that are belov'd again.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: This Souldier loves, and fain wou'd dye to win,
Shall he goe on?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: No 'tis too foul a ſin.
He muſt not come aboard: I dare not • ow,
Storms of deſpair, and guilty blood will blow.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: Shall time releaſe him, ſay?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: No, no, no, no.
Nor time nor death can alter us, nor prayer;
My boat is deſtinie, and who then dare
But thoſe appointed come aboard? Live ſtill,
And love by reaſon, Mortal, not by will.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: And when thy Miſtris ſhall cloſe up thine eyes,

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Then come aboard and paſs,

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: Till when be wiſe.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Till when be wiſe.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: How ſtill he ſits: I hope this Song has ſetled him.

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: He bites his lip, and rowles his fiery eyes, yet
I fear for all this—

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: Stremon ſtill apply to him.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Give me more room, ſweetly ſtrike, divinely
Such ſtrains as old earth moves at.

sp.speaker: Orph.
sp.l: The power I have over both beaſt and plaint,
Thou man alone feelſt miſerable want. Muſick
Strike you rare Spirits that attend my will,
And loſe your ſavage wildneſs by my skill.
This Lion was a man of War that died,
As thou wouldſt do, to gild his Ladies pride:
This Dog a fool that hung himſelf for love:
This Ape with daily hugging of a glove,
Forgot to eat and died. This goodly tree,
And uſher that ſtill grew before his Ladie,
Wither'd at root. This, for he could not wooe,
A grumbling Lawyer: this pyed Bir • a page,
That melted out becauſe he wanted age.
Still theſe lye howling on the Stygian ſhore,

O love no more, O love no more.
Exit Memnon.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: He ſteals off ſilently, as though he would ſleep,
No more, but all be near him, feed his fancie
Good Stremon ſtill; this may lock up his follie.
Yet Heaven knows I much fear him; away ſoftly.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Did I not doe moſt doggedly?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Moſt rarelie.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: He's a brave man, when ſhall we dog again?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Unty me firſt for Gods ſake,

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Help the Boy; he's in a wood poor child: good hony Stremon
Let's have a bear-baiting; ye ſhall ſee me play
The rareſt for a ſingle Dog: at head all;
And if I do not win immortal glorie,
Play Dog play Devil.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Peace for this time.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Prethee
Let's ſing him a black Santis, then let's all howl
In our own beaſtly voices; tree keep your time,
Untye there; bow, wow, wow.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Away ye Aſſe, away.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Why let us doe ſomething
To ſatisfie the Gentleman, he's mad;
A Gentleman-like humour, and in faſhion,
And muſt have men as mad about him.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Peace,
And come in quicklie, 'tis ten to one elſe
He'l find a ſtaff to beat a dog; no more words,
I'le get ye all imployment; ſoft, ſoft in in all. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: When cameſt thou over wench?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: But now this evening,
And have been ever ſince looking out Siphax,
I'th' wars he would have lookt me: ſure h'as gotten
Some other Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A thouſand, wench, a thouſand,
They are as common here as Caterpillers
Among the corn, they eat up all the Souldiers,

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Are they ſo hungry? yet by their leave Philax,
I'le have a ſnatch too.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Doſt thou love him ſtill wench?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Why ſhould I not? he had my Maiden-head
And all my youth.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Thou art come the happieſt,
In the moſt bleſſed time, ſweet wench the fitteſt,
If thou darſt make thy fortune: by this light, Cloe,
And ſo I'le kiſs thee: and if thou wilt but let me,
For 'tis well worth a kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: What ſhou'd I let ye?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Enjoy thy miniken.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Thou art ſtill old Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Still ſtill, and ever ſhall be: if, I ſay,
Thou wo't ſtrike the ſtroke: I cannot do much harm wench.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Nor much good.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Siphax ſhall be thy Husband,
Thy very Husband woman, thy fool, thy Cuckold,
Or what thou wilt make him: I am over joy'd,
Raviſht, clean raviſht with this fortune; kiſs me,
Or I ſhall loſe my ſelf,

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: My Husband ſaid ye?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Said I? and will ſay, Cloe: nay and do it
And do it home too; Peg thee as cloſe to him
As birds are with a pin to one another;
I have it, I can do it: thou wantſt clothes too,
And hee'l be hang'd unleſs he marry thee
E' • e he maintain thee: now he has Ladies, Courtiers
More than his back can bend at, multitudes;
We are taken up for threſhers, will ye bite?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And let me —

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes and let ye —

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: What!

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Why that ye wote of.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I cannot ſtay, take your inſtructions
And ſomething toward houſhold, come, what ever
I ſhall adviſe ye, follow it exactlie,
And keep your times I point ye; for I'le tell ye
A ſtrange way you muſt wade through.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Fear not me Sir.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Come then, and let's diſpatch this modicum,
For I have but an hour to ſtay, a ſhort one,
Beſides more water for another mill,
And old weak over-ſhot I muſt provide for,
There's an old Nunnerie at hand.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A bawdie houſe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: A pox conſume it.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: If the ſtones 'tis built on
Were but as brittle as the fleſh lives in it,
Your curſe came handſomlie: fear not, there's ladies,
And other good ſad people: you pinkt Citizens
Think it no ſhame to ſhake a ſheet there: Come wench.

sp.speaker: Clean
sp.l: A Souldier and ſo fearfull?

sp.speaker: Siph
sp.l: Can ye blame me;
When ſuch a weight lies on me?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Eye upon ye,
I tell ye, ye ſhall have her: have her ſafelie,
And for your wife with her own will.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: Good Siſter —

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: What a diſtruſtfull man are you? to morrow,
To morrow morning —

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: Is it poſſible?
Can there be ſuch a happineſs?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Why hang me
If then ye be not married: if to morrow night,
Ye doe not —

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: O dear Siſter —

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: What ye wou'd doe,
What ye deſire to doe; lie with her: Devil,
What a dull man are you?

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: Nay I believe now,
And ſhall ſhe love me?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: As her life, and ſtroke ye.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: O I will be her Servant.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: 'Tis your dutie.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: And ſhe ſhall have her whole will.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Yes 'tis reaſon,
She is a Princeſs, and by that rule boundleſs.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: What woud'you be? for I wou'd have ye Siſter
Chuſe ſome great place about us: as her woman
Is not ſo fit.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: No, no, I ſhall find places.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: And yet to be a Ladie of her bed chamber,
I hold not ſo fit neither,
Some great title, believe it, ſhall be look't out.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Ye may, a Dutcheſs
Or ſuch a toye, a ſmall thing pleaſes me Sir.

sp.speaker: Sip.
sp.l: What you will Siſter: if a neighbour Prince,
When we ſhall come to raign —

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: We ſhall think on't,
Be ready at the time, and in that place too,
And let me work the reſt, within this half hour
The Princeſs will be going, 'tis almoſt morning,
Away and mind your buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l:
Fortune bleſs us.
Exe •• t.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I do beſeech your grace to baniſh me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Why Gentleman, is ſhe not worthy marriage?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Moſt worthy, Sir, where worth again ſhall meet 〈◊〉
But I like thick clouds ſailing ſlow and heavy,
Although by her drawn higher, yet ſhall hide her,
I dare not be a traitor; and 'tis treaſon,
But to imagine: as you love your honour —

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: 'Tis her firſt maiden doting, and if croſt,
I know it kills her.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: How knows your grace ſhe loves him?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Her woman told me all (beſide his ſtory)
Her maid Lucippe, on what reaſon too,
And 'tis beyond all but enjoying.

sp.speaker: Polydor.
sp.l: Sir,
Even by your wiſdom; by that great diſcretion
Ye owe to rule and order —

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: This man's mad ſure,
To plead againſt his fortune —

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: And the King too,
Willing to have it ſo?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: By thoſe dead Princes
From whoſe deſcents ye ſtand a ſtar admir'd at,
Lay not ſo baſe a lay upon your vertues;
Take heed, for honours ſake take heed: the bramble
No wiſe man ever planted by the roſe,
It cankers all her beauty; nor the vine
When her full bluſhes court the ſun, dares any
Choke up with wanton Ivy: good my Lords,
Who builds a monument, the Baſis Jaſper,
And the main body Brick?

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: Ye wrong your worth,
Ye are a Gentleman deſcended nobly.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: In both bloods truly noble.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Say ye were not,
My will can make ye ſo.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: No, never, never;
'Tis not deſcent, nor will of Princes does it,
'Tis Vertue which I want, 'tis Temperance,
Man, honeſt man: is't fit your Majeſty
Should call my drunkenneſs, my raſhneſs, Brother?
Or ſuch a bleſſed Maid my breach of ſaith,
(For I am moſt laſcivious) and fell angers
In which I am alſo miſchievous, her Husband?
O Gods preſerve her! I am wild as Winter,
Ambitious as the Devil: out upon me,
I hate my ſelf, Sir, if ye dare beſtow her
Upon a Subject, ye have one deſerves her.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: But him ſhe does not love: I know your meaning.
This young mans love unto his noble Brother
Appears a mirrour; what muſt now be done Lords?
For I am gravel'd, if ſhe have not him,
She dies for certain, if his Brother miſs her,
Farewel to him, and all our honours.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: He is dead, Sir,
Your Grace has heard of that, and ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No,
I can aſſure you no, there was a trick in't,
Read that, and then know all; what ails the Gentleman?
Hold him; how do ye Sir? Polydor is ſick o'th' ſudden.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Sick o'th' ſudden,
Extreamly ill, wondrous ill.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Where did it take ye?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Here in my head, Sir, and my heart, for Heaven ſake.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Conduct him to his Chamber preſently,
And bid my Doctors—

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: No, I ſhall be well, Sir,
I do beſeech your Grace, even for the Gods ſake
Remember my poor Brother, I ſhall pray then.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Away, he grows more weak ſtill: I will do it,

Or Heaven forget me ever. Now your Counſels,
Ex. Pol.
For I am at my wits end; what with you Sir?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: Letters from warlike Pelius.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Yet more troubles?
The Spartans are in Arms, and like to win all:
Supplies are ſent for, and the General;
This is more croſs than t'other; come let's to him,
For he muſt have her, 'tis neceſſity,
Or we muſt loſe our honours, let's plead all,
For more than all is needful, ſhew all reaſon
If love can hear o'that ſide, if ſhe yield
We have fought beſt, and won the nobleſt field. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: I have brought the wench, a luſty wench,
And ſomewhat like the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: 'Tis the better, let's ſee her,
And go you in and tell him, that her Grace
Is come to viſit him: how ſleeps he Stremon?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: He cannot, only thinks, and calls on Polydor,
Swears he will not be fool'd; ſometimes he rages,

And ſometimes ſits and muſes.
Exit Stremon

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: He's paſt all help ſure?
How do ye like her?

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: By th' maſs a good round Virgin,
And at firſt ſight reſembling, ſhe is well cloath'd too.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: But is ſhe ſound?

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: Of wind and limb, I warrant her.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: You are inſtucted Lady?

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: Yes, and know, Sir,
How to behave my ſelf, ne're fear.

sp.speaker: Eume.

l.hi: Polybius,

sp.l: Where did he get this Vermin?

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: Hang him Badger,
There's not a hole free from him, whores and whores mates
Do all pay him obedience.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Indeed i'th' War,
His quarter was all Whore, Whore upon Whore,
And lin'd with Whore; beſhrew me 'tis a fair Whore.

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: She has ſmockt away her blood; but fair or ſoul,
Or blind or lame, that can but lift her leg up,
Comes not amiſs to him, he rides like a night Mare,
All Ages, all Religions.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Can ye ſtate it?

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: I'le make a ſhift.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: He muſt lie with ye, Lady.

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: Let him, ne's not the firſt man I have lain with,
Nor ſhall not be the laſt.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: He comes, no more words,
She has her leſſon throughly; how he views her?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Go forward now, ſo, bravely, ſtand!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Great Lady,
How humbly I am bound—

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: You ſhall not kneel, Sir,
Come, I have done you wrong; ſtand my Souldier,
And thus I make amends— Kiſſes him.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: A Plague confound ye,
Is this your ſtate?

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: 'Tis well enough.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: O Lady,
Your Royal hand, your hand my deareſt beauty
Is more than I muſt purchaſe: here divine one,
I dare revenge my wrongs: ha?

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: A damn'd ſoul one.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: The Lees of Baudy prewns: mourning Gloves?
All ſpoil'd by Heaven.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ha! who art thou?

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: A ſhame on ye,
Ye clawing ſcabby Whore.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I ſay, who art thou?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Why 'tis the Princeſs, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: The Devil, Sir,
'Tis ſome Roguey thing.

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: If this abuſe be love, Sir,
Or I that laid aſide my modeſty—

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: So far thou't never find it.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Do not weep,
For if ye be the Princeſs, I will love ye,
Indeed I will, and honour ye, fight for ye,
Come, wipe your eyes; by Heaven ſhe ſtinks; who art thou?
Stinks like a poyſon'd Rat behind a hanging?
Woman, who art? like a rotten Cabbage.

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: Y'are much to blame, Sir, 'tis the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: How?
She the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: And the loving Princeſs.

sp.speaker: 1 Capt.
sp.l: Indeed the doating Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Come hither once more,
The Princeſs ſmells like mornings breath, pure Amber,
Beyond the courted Indies in her ſpices.
Still a dead Rat by Heaven; thou a Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: What a dull Whore is this?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I'le tell ye preſently,
For if ſhe be a Princeſs, as ſhe may be
And yet ſtink too, and ſtrongly, I ſhall find her;
Fetch the Numidian Lyon I brought over,
If ſhe be ſprung from the Royal blood, the Lyon,
He'l do you reverence, elſe—

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: I beſeech your Lordſhip—

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: He'l tear her all to pieces.

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: I am no Princeſs, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Who brought thee hither?

sp.speaker: 2 Capt.
sp.l: If ye confeſs, we'll hang ye.

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: Good my Lord —

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Who art thou then?

sp.speaker: Who.
sp.l: A poor retaining Whore, Sir,
To o • of your Lord 〈◊〉 Captains.
A • as poor Wh •• e,

Go, • a Whore ſtill 〈◊〉 ſtink worſe: Ha, ha, ha.
Ex. Cloe.

What fools are theſe, 〈◊〉 Coxcombs?
Exit Menmon.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: I am • ight • lad yet,
He takes it with ſuch • ightneſs.

sp.speaker: 1 Cap.
sp.l: Me thinks his face too
Is not ſo clouded as it was; how he looks?

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: Where's your dead Rat?

sp.speaker: 2 Cap.
sp.l: T •• D •• di • e upon her
Loins; w •• what a Medieme had he gotten
To try a Whor • ?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: Here's one from Polydor ſtays to ſpeak with ye.

sp.speaker: Eume.
sp.l: With whom?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: With all; where has the General been?
He's laughing to himſelf extreamly.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Come,

I'le tell thee how; I am glad yet he's ſo merry.
Exe • unt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Chillax and Prieſteſs, Calis, Lady and Nun.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: WHat lights are thoſe that enter there, ſtill nearer?
• ague o'your rotten itch, do you draw me hither
Into the Temple to betray me? was there no place
To ſatisfie your ſin in? Gods forgive me,
Still they come forward.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Peace ye fool, I have found it,
'Tis the young Princeſs Calis.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: 'Tis the Devil,
To •• aw us for our catterwawling.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Retire ſoftly,
I did not look for you theſe two hours, Lady,

Beſhrew your haſt: that way.
To Chillax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That goes to the Altar?
Ye old blind Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: I know not, any way;
Still they come nearer,
I'le in to th' Oracle.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That's well remembred I'le in with ye.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l:
Do.
Exeunt Prieſt. and Chilax.

div.stage: Enter Calis and her Train with lights, ſinging: Lucippe, Cleanthe.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: O fair ſweet Goddeſs Queen of Loves,
Soft and gentle, as thy D •• es,
Humble • y'd, and ever ruing
Theſe poor hearts, their Loves purſuing:
O thou • ther of delights,
Crow •• of all happy nights,
Star of dear content, and pleaſure,
Of mutual loves the endleſs treaſure,
Accept this ſacrifice we bring,
Thou continual youth and Spring,
Grant this Lady her deſires,
And every hour we'll crown thy fires.

l.hi: You about her all retire,
Whileſt the Princeſs feeds the fire,
When your Devotions ended be
To the Oracle I will attend ye.

div.stage: Exit Nun and draws the Curtain cloſe to Calis.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: He will abroad.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: How does his humour hold him?

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: He is now grown wondrous ſad, weeps often too,
Talks of his Brother to himſelf, ſtarts ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Does he not curſe?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Nor break out in fury,
Offering ſome new attempt?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Neither; to th' Temple
Is all we hear of now: what there he will do.

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: I hope repent his folly, let's be near him.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Where are the reſt?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: About a buſineſs
Concerns him mainly, if Heav'n cure his madneſs,
He's made for ever, Stremon.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Does the King know it?

sp.speaker: Eumen.
sp.l: Yes, and much troubled with it, he's now 〈◊〉
To ſeek his Siſter out.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l:
Come let's away then.
Exeunt Eumen Strem. 〈◊〉

div.stage: Enter Nun, ſhe opens the Curtain to Calis. Calis at the Oracle.

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: Peace to your Prayers Lady, will it pleaſe ye
To paſs on to the Oracle?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Moſt humbly. Chilax and Prieſt. in the Or ••• .

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Do ye hear that?

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Yes, lie cloſe.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: A wildfire take ye,
What ſhall become of me? I ſhall be hang'd now:
Is this a time to ſhake? a halter ſhake ye,
Come up and juggle, come.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: I am monſtrous fearful.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Up ye old gaping Oyſter, up and anſwer;
A mouldy Mange upon your chops, ye told me
I was ſafe here till the Bell rung.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: I was prevented,
And did not look theſe three hours for the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Shall we be taken?

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Speak for loves ſake, Chilax;
I cannot, nor I dare not.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I'le ſpeak Treaſon, for I had as lieve be hang'd for that.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Good Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Muſt it be ſung or ſaid? what ſhall I tell 'em?
They are here; here now preparing.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: O my Conſcience!

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Plague o' your ſpurgall'd Conſciene, does it tire now?
Now when it ſhould be tuffeſt? I could make thee—

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Save us, we are both undone elſe.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Down ye Dog then,
Be quiet, and be ſtanch to no inundations.

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: Here kneel again, and Venus grant your wiſhes.

l.hi: O Divine Star of Heaven,
Thou in power above the ſeven:
Thou ſweet kindler of deſires,
Till they grow to mutual fires:
Thou, O gentle Queen, that art
Curer of each wounded heart:
Thou the fuel, and the flame;
Thou in Heaven, and here the ſame:
Thou the wooer, and the woo'd:
Thou the hunger, and the food:
Thou the prayer, and the pray'd;
Thou what is, or ſhall be ſaid:
Thou ſtill young, and golden treſſed,
Make me by thy Anſwer bleſſed.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: When?

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Now ſpeak handſomly, and ſmall by all means.

I have told ye what.
• hun ••

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: But I'le tell you a new tale,
Now for my Neck verſe; I have heard thy prayers,
And mark me well.

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: The Goddeſs is diſpleaſed much,
The temple ſhakes and totters; ſhe appears,
Bow, Lady, bow.

l.hi: Purge me the Temple round,
And live by this example henceforth ſound.
Virgin, I have ſeen they tears,
Heard thy wiſhes, and thy fears;
Thy holy Incenſe flew above,
Hark therefore to thy doom in Love;
Had thy heart been ſoft at firſt,
Now thou had'ſt allay'd thy thirſt,
Had thy ſtubborn will but bended,
All thy ſorrows here had ended;
Therefore to be juſt in Love,
A ſtrange Fortune thou must prove,
And, for thou haſt been ſtern and coy,
A dead Love thou ſhalt enjoy.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: O gentle goddeſs!

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.l: Riſe, thy doom is ſaid,
And fear not, I will pleaſe thee with the dead. Venus aſcends.

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: Go up into the Temple and there end
Your holy Rites, the Goddeſs ſmiles upon ye.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I'll no more Oracles, nor Miracles,
Nor no more Church work, I'll be drawn and hang'd firſt.
Am not I torn a pieces with the thunder?
Death, I can ſcarce believe I live yet,
It gave me on the buttocks, a cruel, a huge bang,
I had as lieve ha'had'em ſcratcht with Dog-whips:
& quiet henceforth, now ye feel the end on't,
I would adviſe ye my old friends, the good Gentlewoman
Is •• rucken dumb, and there her Grace ſits mumping
Like an old Ape eating a Brawn; ſure the good Goddeſs
Know my intent was honeſt, to ſave the Princeſs,
And how we young men are entic'd to wickedneſs,
By theſe lewd Women, I had paid for't elſe too.
〈◊〉 monſtrous holy now, and cruel fearful,
O'twas a plaguey thump, charg'd with a vengeance.
sp.stage: Enter Siphax, walks ſoftly over the ſtage, and goes in.
sp.l: Would I were well at home; the beſt is, 'tis not day:
Who's that? ha? Siphax! I'll be with you anon, Sir;
Ye ſhall be oracled I warrant ye,
And thunder'd too, as well as I; your Lordſhip
sp.stage: Enter Memnon, Eumenes, Stremon, and two carrying Torches.
sp.l: Muſt needs enjoy the Princeſs, yes: ha'! Torches?
And Memnon coming this way? he's Dog-mad,
And ten to one appearing thus unto him,
He worries me, I muſt go by him.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ask me no further queſtions; what art thou?
How doſt thou ſtare? ſtand off; nay look upon me,
I do not ſhake, nor fear thee— Draws his Sword.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: He will kill me,
This is for Church work.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Why doſt thou appear now?
Thou wort fairly ſlain: I know thee, Diocles,
And know thine envy to mine honour: but—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Stay Memnon,
I am a Spirit, and thou canſt not hurt me.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: This is the voice of Chilax.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: What makes him thus?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: 'Tis true, that I was ſlain in field, but foully,
By multitudes, not manhood: therefore mark me,
I do appear again to quit mine honour,
And on thee ſingle.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: I accept the challenge.
Where?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: On the Stygian Banks.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: When?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Four days hence.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Go noble Ghoſt, I will attend.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I thank ye.

sp.speaker: Stre.
sp.l: Ye have ſav'd your throat, and handſomly:

Farewel, Sir.
Exit Chilax.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Sing me the Battles of Peluſium,
In which this Worthy dyed.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: This will ſpoil all, and make him worſe
Than e'r he was: ſit down, Sir,
And give your ſelf to reſt.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: Arm, arm, arm, arm, the Scouts are all come in,
Keep your Ranks cloſe, and now your honours win.
Behold from yonder Hill, the Fa • appears,
Bows, Bills, Glaves, Arrows, Shields, and Spears,
Lake a dark Wood he comes, or tempeſt pouring;
O view the Wings of Horſe the Meadows ſcowring,
The vant-guard marches bravely, hark, the Drums— dub, dub.
They meet, they meet, and now the Battle comes:
See how the Arrows fly,
That darken all the Skye;
Hark how the Trumpets ſound,
Hark how the Hils rebound—Tara, tara, tara.
Hark how the Horſes charge: in Boys, Boys in— tara, tara.
The Battel totters; now the wounds begin;
O how they cry,
O how they dy!
Room for the valiant Memnon arm'd with thunder,
See how he breaks the Ranks aſunder:
They flye, they flye, Eumenes has the Chace,
And brave Polybius makes good his place.
To the Plains, to the Woods,
To the Rocks, to the Floods,
They flie for ſuccour: Follow, follow, follow, Hey, hey.
Hark how the Souldiers hollow
Brave Diocles is dead,
And all his Souldiers fled,
The Battel's won, and loſt,
That many a life hath coſt.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Now forward to the Temple. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Are ye gone?
How have I 'ſcap'd this morning! by what miracle!
Sure I am ordain'd for ſome brave end.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: How is it?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Come, 'tis as well as can be.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: But is it poſſible
This ſhould be true you tell me?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt certain.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Such a groſs Aſs to love the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Peace,
Pull your Robe cloſe about ye: you are perfect
In all I taught ye?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Sure.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Gods give thee good luck.
'Tis ſtrange my Brains ſhould still be beating Knavery
For all theſe dangers, but they are needful miſchiefs,
And ſuch are Nuts to me; and I muſt do 'em.
You will remember me—

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: By this kiſs, Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: No more of that, I fear another thunder.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: We are not i'th' Temple, man.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Peace, here he comes,

Now to our buſineſs handſomly; away now.
Ex. Chilax, and Cloe.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: 'Twas ſure the Princeſs, for he kneel'd unto her,
And ſhe lookt every way: I hope the Oracle
Has made me happy; me I hope ſhe lookt for,
sp.stage: Enter Chilax, and Cloe at the other door.
sp.l: Fortune, I will ſo honour thee, Love, ſo adore thee.
S • e is here again, looks round about her, again too,
'Tis done, I know 'tis done; 'tis Chilax with her,
And I ſhall know of him; who's that?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Speak ſoftly,
The Princeſs from the Oracle.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: She views me,
By Heaven ſhe beckons me.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Come near, ſhe wou'd have ye.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: O royal Lady. Kiſſes her hand.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: She wills ye read that, for belike ſhe's bound to ſilence
For ſuch a time; ſhe is wondrous gracious to ye.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: H • av'n make me thankful.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: She would have ye read it. He reads.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Siphax, the will of Heaven hath caſt me on thee
To be thy Wife, whoſe Will muſt be obey'd:
Uſe me with honour, I ſhall love thee dearly,
And make thee underſtand thy worths hereafter;
Convey me to a ſecret Ceremony,
That both our hearts and loves may be united,
And uſe no Language, till before my Brother
We both appear, where I will ſhew the Oracle,
For till that time I am bound, I muſt not anſwer.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: O happy I!

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Ye are a made man.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: But Chilax,
Where are her Women?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: None but your Graces Siſter,
Becauſe ſhe would have it private to the World yet,
Knows of this buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I ſhall thank thee, Chilax,
Thou art a careful man.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Your Graces Servant.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: I'll find a fit place for thee.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: If you will not,
There's a good Lady will, ſhe points ye forward,
Away and take your fortune; not a word, Sir:

So, you are greas'd I hope.
Ex. Si. and Cloe, manet Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Stremon, Fool, Pieus,
Where have you left your Lord?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: I' th' Temple, Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Why are ye from him?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Why, the King is with him,
And all the Lords.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Is not the Princeſs there too?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Yes.
And the ſtrangeſt Coil amongſt 'em; She weeps bitterly:
The King •• treats, and frowns, my Lord like Autumn
Drops off his hopes by handfulls, all the Temple
Sweats with this Agony.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Where's young Polydore?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Dead, as they ſaid, o' th' ſudden.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Dead?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: For certain,
But not yet known abroad.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: There's a new trouble,
A brave young man he was; but we muſt all dye.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Did not the General meet you this morning
Like a tall Stallion Nun?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: No more o' that, Boy.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: You had been fe •• etting.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: That's all one, Fool;
My Maſter Fool that taught my wits to traffick,
What has your Wiſedom done? how have you profited?
Out with your Audit: come, you are not empty,
Put out mine eye with twelve pence? do you ſhaker?
What think you of this ſhaking? here's wit, Coxcomb,
H • B •• s • ha my fine Raſcals, here's a Ring, Pulls out a Purſe.
How •• ght they go!

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: O let me ring the ſore Bell.
And here are thumpers, Chiqueens, golden rogues,
Wit, wit, ye Raſcals.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: I have a Stye here, Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I have no Gold to cure it, not a penny,
Not one croſs, Cavalier; we are dull Souldiers,
Groſs heavy-headed fellows; fight for Victuals?

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Why, ye are the Spirits of the time.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: By no means.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: The valiant firie.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Fie, fie, no.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Be-lee me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I wou'd I cou'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: I will ſatisfie ye.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: But I will not content you; alas poor Boy,
Thou ſhew'ſt an honeſt Nature, weepſt for thy Maſter,
There's a red Rogue to buy thee Handkerchiefs.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: He was an honeſt Gentleman, I have loſt too.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: You have indeed your labour, Fool; but Stremon,
Doſt thou want money too? no Vertue living?
No ſinking out at fingers ends?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Will ye all ſerve me?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: Yes, when ye are Lord General,
For leſs I will not go.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: There's Gold for thee then,
Thou haſt a Souldiers mind. Fool—

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Here, your firſt man.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I will give thee for thy Wit, for 'tis a fine wit,
A dainty diving Wit, hold up, juſt nothing,
Go graze i' th' Commons, yet I am merciful—
There's ſix pence: buy a Saucer, ſteal an old Gown,
And beg i'th' Temple for a Prophet, come away Boys,
Let's ſee how things are carried, Fool, up Sirrah,
You may chance get a dinner: Boy, your preferment
I'll undertake, for your brave Maſters ſake,
You ſhall not periſh.

l.hi: Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Pleaſe me well, Fool.
And you ſhall light my pipes: away to the Temple.
But ſtay, the King's here, ſport upon ſport, Boys.

div.stage: Enter King, Lords, Siphax kneeling, Cloe with a Vail.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What would you have, Captain?
Speak ſuddenly, for I am wondrous buſie.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: A pardon, Royal Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: For that
Which was Heaven's Will, ſhould not be mine alone, Sir;
My marrying with this Lady.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: It needs no pardon,
For Marriage is no Sin.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Not in it ſelf, Sir;
But in preſuming too much: yet Heaven knows,
So does the Oracle that caſt it on me,
And— the Princeſs, royal Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: O be not angry my dread King, your Siſter.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: My Siſter; ſhe's i' th' Temple, Man.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: She is here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: The Captain's mad, ſhe's kneeling at the Altar.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I know ſhe is; with all my heart good Captain,
I do forgive ye both: be unvail'd, Lady. Puts off her Vail
Will ye have more forgiveneſs? the man's frantick,
Come let's go bring her out: God give ye joy, Sir.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: How, Cloe? my old Cloe? Ex. King, Lord.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Even the ſame, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Gods give your manhood much content.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: The Princeſs
Looks ſomething muſty ſince her coming over.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: 'Twere good you'd bruſh her over.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.l: Fools and Fidlers
Make ſport at my abuſe too?

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: O 'tis the Nature
Of us Fools to make bold with one another,
But you are wiſe, brave ſirs.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Cheer up your Princeſs,
Believe it Sir, the King will not be angry,
Or ſay he were; why, 'twas the Oracle.
The Oracle, an't like your Grace, the Oracle.

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: And who, moſt mighty Siphax?

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: With mine own whore.

sp.speaker: C oe.
sp.l: With whom elſe ſhould ye marry, ſpeak your conſcience,
Will ye tranſgreſs the law of Arms, that ever
Rewards the Souldier with his own ſins?

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: Devils.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: Ye had my maiden-head, my youth, my ſweetneſs,
Is it not juſtice then? —

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: I ſee it muſt be,
But by this hand, I'le hang a lock upon thee.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: You ſhall not need, my hon ſty ſhall doe it.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: If there be wars in all the world —

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: I'le with ye,
For you know I have been a Souldier,
Come, curſe on: when I need another Oracle.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Send for me Siphax, I'le fit ye with a Princeſs,
And ſo to both your honours.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: And your graces.

sp.speaker: Siph.
sp.l: The Devil grace ye all.

sp.speaker: Cloe.
sp.l: God a mercy Chilax.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Shall we laugh half an hour now?

sp.speaker: Strem.
sp.l: No the King comes,
And all the train.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Away then; our Act's ended. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter King, Calis, Memnon, and Cleanthe, Lords.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: You know he do's deſerve ye, loves ye dearly,
You know what bloody violence had us'd
Upon himſelf, but that his Brother croſt it,
You know the ſame thoughts ſtill inhabit in him The Hearſe ready, Polydor, Eumenes & Captains.
And covet to take birth: Look on him Lady,
The wars have not ſo far conſum'd him yet,
Cold age diſabled him, or ſickneſs ſunk him
To be abhorr'd: look on his Honour Siſter,
That bears no ſtamp of time, no wrinkles on it,
No ſad demoliſhment, nor death can reach it:
Look with the eyes of Heaven that nightly waken,
To view the wonders of the glorious Maker,
And not the weakneſs: look with your vertuous eyes,
And then clad royaltie in all his conqueſts,
His matchleſs love hung with a thouſand merits,
Eternal youth attending, Fame and Fortune,
Time and Oblivion vexing at his vertues,
He ſhall appear a miracle: look on our dangers,
Look on the publick ruin.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: O, dear Brother.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Fie, let us not like proud and greedy waters
Gain to give off again: this is our Sea,
And you his Cynthia, govern him, take heed,
His flouds have been as high, and full as any,
And gloriouſly now is got up to the girdle,
The Kingdomes he hath purchas'd; noble Siſter,
Take not your vertue from him, O take heed
We ebbe not now to nothing, take heed Calis.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: The will of Heaven not mine, which muſt not alter,
And my eternal doom for ought I know
Is fixt upon me; alas, I muſt love nothing,
Nothing that loves again muſt I be bleſt with:
The gentle Vine climbs up the Oke and clips him,
And when the ſtroke comes, yet they fall together;
Death, death muſt I enjoy, and live to love him,
O noble Sir!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Thoſe tears are ſome reward yet,
Pray let me wed your ſorrows.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Take 'em Souldier,
They are fruitfull ones, lay but a ſigh upon 'em,
And ſtraight they will conceive to infinites;
I told ye what ye would find 'em.

div.stage: Enter Funeral, Captains following, and Eumenes.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How now, what's this? more drops to th' Ocean?
Whoſe body's this?

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: The noble Polydor,
〈◊〉 ſpeaks his death.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My Brother dead?

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: O Goddeſs!
O cruel, cruel Venus, here's my fortune.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Read Captain.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Read aloud: farewel my follies.

div.stage: Eumen. reads to the Excellent Princeſs Calis.

sp.speaker: Eum.
sp.l: Be wiſe, as you are beauteous love with judgement,
And look with clear eyes on my noble Brother,
Value deſert and vertue, they are Jewels,
Fit for your worth and wearing: take heed Lady,
The Gods reward ingratitude moſt grievous;
Remember me no more, or if you muſt,
Seek me in noble Memnons love, I dwell there:
I durſt nor live, becauſe I durſt not wrong him,
I can no more, make me eternal happy
With looking down upon your loves. Farewel.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And did'ſt thou die for me?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Excellent vertue!
What will ye now doe?

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Dwell for ever here Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: For me dear Polydor? O worthy young man!
O love, love, love, love above recompence!
Infinite love, infinite honeſty!
Good Lady leave, you muſt have no ſhare here,
Take home your ſorrows: here's enough to ſtore me,
Brave glorious griefs! was ever ſuch a Brother?
Turn all the ſtories over in the world yet,
And ſearch through all the memories of mankind,
And find me ſuch a friend; h'as out-done all,
Outſtript 'em ſheerly, all, all, thou haſt Polydor,
To die for me; why, as I hope for happineſs,
'Twas one of the rareſt thought on things,
The braveſt, and carried beyond compaſs of our actions,
I wonder how he hit it, a young man too,
In all the bloſſomes of his youth and beautie,
In all the fulneſs of his veins and wiſhes
Woo'd by that Paradiſe, that would catch Heaven;
It ſtarts me extreamly, thou bleſt Aſhes,
Thou faithfull monument, where love and friendſhip
Shall while the world is, work new miracles.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: O! let me ſpeak too.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: No not yet; thou man,
For we are but mans ſhadows,) only man,
I have not words to utter him; ſpeak Lady,
I'le think a while.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: The Goddeſs grants me this yet,
I ſhall enjoy the dead: no tomb ſhall hold thee
But theſe two arms, no Trickments but my tears
Over thy Hearſe, my ſorrows like ſad arms
Shall hang for ever: on the tuffeſt Marble
Mine eyes ſhall weep thee out an Epitaph,
Love at thy feet ſhall kneel, his ſmart bow broken;
Faith at thy head, youth and the Graces mourners;
O ſweet young man!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Now I begin to melt too.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Have ye enough yet Lady? room for a gameſter.
To my fond Love, and all thoſe idle fancies
A long farewel, thou diedſt for me dear Polydor,
To give me peace, thou haſt eternal glory,
I ſtay and talk here; I will kiſs thee firſt,
And now I'le follow thee. Polydor riſes.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Hold, for Heavens ſake!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Ha!
Does he live?
Doſt thou deceive me?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Thus far,
Yet for your good, and honour.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Now dear Siſter.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: The Oracle is ended, noble Sir,
Diſpoſe me now as you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: You are mine then?

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: With all the joyes that may be.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Your conſent Sir?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Ye have it freely.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Walk along with me then,
And as you love me, love my will.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: I will ſo.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Here worthy Brother, take this vertuous Princeſs,
Ye have deſerv'd her nobly, ſhe will love ye,
And when my life ſhall bring ye peace, as ſhe does,
Command it, ye ſhall have it.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Sir, I thank ye.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I never found ſuch goodneſs in ſuch years.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not over doe me, though I die for't,
O how I love thy goodneſs, my beſt Brother,
You have given me here a treaſure to enrich me,
Would make the worthieſt King alive a begger,
What may I give you back again?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Your love Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And you ſhall have it, even my deareſt love,
My firſt, my nobleſt love, take her again, Sir,
She is yours, your honeſty has over-run me,
She • oves ye, loſe her not: excellent Princeſs,
Injoy thy wiſh, and now get Generals.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: As ye love heaven, love him, ſhe is only yours, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: As ye love heaven, love him, ſhe is only yours, Sir,
My Lord, the King.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: He will undoe himſelf Sir,
And muſt without her periſh; who ſhall fight then?
Who ſhall protect your Kingdom?

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Give me hearing,
And after that, belief, were ſhe my ſoul
(As I do love her equal) all my victories,
And all the living names I have gain'd by war,
And loving him that good, that vertuous good man,
That only worthy of the name of Brother,
I would reſign all freely, 'tis all love
To me, all marriage rites, the joy of iſſues
To know him fruitfull, that has been ſo faithfull.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: This is the nobleſt difference; take your choice Siſter.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: I ſee they are ſo brave, and noble both,
I know not which to look on.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Chuſe diſcreetly,
And vertue guide ye, there all the world in one man
Stands at the mark.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: There all mans honeſtie,
The ſweetneſs of all youth—

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: O God's!

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My Armour,
By all the God's ſhe's yours; my Arms, I ſay,
And I beſeech your Grace, give me imployment,
That ſhall be now my Miſtreſs, there my Courtſhip.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have any thing.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: Vertuous Lady,
Remember me, your Servant now; Young man,
You cannot over-reach me in your goodneſs;
O love! how ſweet thou look'ſt now? and how gentle?
I ſhould have ſlubber'd thee, and ſtain'd thy beauty,
Your hand, your hand Sir?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Take her, and Heaven bleſs her.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: 'Tis your will Sir, nothing of my merit;
And as your royal gift, I take this bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: And I from heaven this gentleman: thanks Goddeſs.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: So ye are pleas'd now Lady?

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: Now or never.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My cold ſtiffe carkaſs would have frozen ye,
Wars, wars.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have wars.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: My next brave battel
I dedicate to your bright honour, Siſter,
Give me a favour, that the world may know
I am your Souldier.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: This, and all fair Fortunes.

sp.speaker: Mem.
sp.l: And he that bears this from me, muſt ſtrike boldly.

sp.speaker: Calis.
sp.l: I do forgive thee: be honeſt; no more wench.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Come now to Revels, this bleſt day ſhall prove
The happy crown of noble Faith and Love.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: TO pleaſe all's impoſſible, and to deſpair
Ruins our ſelves, and damps the Writers care:
Would we knew what to doe, or ſay, or when
To find the mindes here equal with the men:
But we muſt venture; now to Sea we goe,
Faire fortune with us, give us room, and blow;
Remember ye're all venturers; and in this Play
How many twelve pences ye have 'ſtow'd this day:
Remember for return of your delight,
We launch, and plough through ſtorms of fear, and ſpight:
Give us your fore winds fairly, fill our wings,
And ſteer us right, and as the Saylor ſings,
Loaden with Wealth, on wanton ſeas, ſo we
Shall make our home-bound-voyage chearfully;
And you our noble Merchants, for your treaſure
Share equally the fraught, we run for pleaſure.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: HEre lyes the doubt now, let our Playes be good,
Our own care ſailing equall in this Flood;
Our preparations new, new our Attire,
Yet here we are becalm'd ſtill, ſtill i'th' mire,
Here we ſtick faſt; Is there no way to clear
This paſſage of your judgement, and our fear,
No mitigation of that law? Brave friends,
Conſider we are yours, made for your ends,
And every thing preſerves it ſelf, each will
If not perverſe, and crooked, utter ſtill
The beſt of that it ventures in: have care
Ev'n for your pleaſurers ſake, of what we are,
And do not ruine all, You may frown ſtill,
But 'tis the nobler way, to check the will.

list.item: Archas, the Loyal Subject, General of the Moſcovites.
Theodore, Son to Archas; valorous, but impatient.
Putskie alias Briskie, a Captain, Brother to Archas.
Alinda alias Archas, Son to Archas.
Burris, an honeſt Lord, the Dukes Favourite.
Boroskie, a malicious ſeducing Councellor to the Duke.
Enſign to Archas, a ſtout merry Souldier.

sp.speaker: The
sp.l: CAptain, your friend's prefer'd, the Princeſs has her,
Who, I aſſure my ſelf, will uſe her nobly;
A pretty ſweet one 'tis indeed.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Well bred, Sir,
I do deliver that upon my credit,
And of an honeſt ſtock.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo, Captain,
And no doubt will do well.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Thanks to your care, Sir;
But tell me Noble Colonel, why this habit
Of diſcontent is put on through the Army?
And why your valiant Father, our great General,
The hand that taught to ſtrike, the Love that led all;
Why he, that was the Father of the War,
He that begot, and bred the Souldier,
Why he ſits ſhaking of his Arms, like Autumn,
His Colours folded, and his Drums cas'd up,
The tongue of War for ever ty'd within us?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: It muſt be ſo: Captain you are a ſtranger,
But of a ſmall time here a Souldier,
Yet that 〈◊〉 ſh • ws ye a right good, and great one,
Elſe I could tell ye • ours are ſtrangely alter'd:
The young Duke • as too many eyes upon him,
Too many • ears 'tis thought too, and to nouriſh thoſe,
Maintains too many Inſtruments.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Turn their hearts,
Or turn their heels up, Heaven: 'Tis ſtrange it ſhould be:
The old Duk • lov'd him dearly.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: And were he not my Father, I durſt tell ye,

The memora ••
• aza • ds he has 〈◊〉 through
Had t • ey been leſs they had been ſafe Putskie,
And ſooner •• ach'd • gard.
There you ſtruck ſure, Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: D •• I n • ver tell thee of a vow he made
Som • yea • s before the old Duke dyed?

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: I have h ard ye
Sp • ak often of that vow; but how it was,
O • to what end, I never underſtood yet.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I'le tell thee then: and then thou wilt find the reaſon:
The laſt great Muſter, ('t was before ye ſerv'd here,
Before th • laſt Duk • s death, whoſe honour'd bones
(To Crown his Fathers hopes) of all the Army:
Who (to be ſhort) put all his power to practiſe;
Faſhion'd, and drew 'em up: but alas, ſo poorly,
So ragg • d •• and looſely, ſo unſouldier'd,
The good Duke bluſh'd, and call'd unto my Father,
Who then was General: Go, Archas, ſpeedily,
And chide the Boy, before the Souldiers find him,
Stand thou between his ignorance and them,
Faſhion then bodies new to thy direction;
Then draw thou up, and ſhew the Prince his errours.
My Sire obey'd, and did ſo; with all duty
Inform'd the Prince, and read him all directions:
I his bred diſtaſte, diſtaſte grew up to anger,
And anger into wild words broke out thus:
Well, Archas, if I live but to command here,
To be but Duke once, I ſhall then remember.
I ſhall remember truly, truſt me, I ſhall,
And by my Fathers hand— the reſt his eyes ſpoke.
To which my Father anſwer'd (ſomewhat mov'd too)
And with a vow he ſeal'd it: Royal Sir,
Since for my faith and fights, your ſcorn and anger
Only purſue me; if I live to that day,
That day ſo long expected to reward me,
By his ſo ever noble hand you ſwore by,
And by the hand of Juſtice, never Arms more
Shall • ib this body in, no • ſword hang here, Sir:
The Conflicts I will do you ſervice then in,
Shall be repentant prayers: So they parted.
The time is come; and now ye know the wonder.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: I find a fear too, which begins to tell me,
The Duke will have but poor and ſlight defences,
If his hot humour raign, and not his honour:
How ſtand you with him, Sir?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: A perdue Captain,
Full of my Fathers danger.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: He has rais'd a young man,
They ſay a ſlight young man, I know him not,
For what deſert?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Believe it, a brave Gentleman,
Worth the Dukes reſpect, a clear ſweet Gentleman,
And of a noble ſoul: Come let's retire us,
And wait upon my Father, who within this hour
You will find an alter'd man.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: I am ſor • y for't, Sir. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Is't not a handſome Wench?

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: She is well enough, Madam:
I have ſeen a better face, and a ſtraighter body,
And yet ſhe is a pretty Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: What thinkſt thou Peteſea?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Alas, Madam, I have no skill, ſhe has a black eye,
Which is of the leaſt too, and the dulleſt water:
And when her mouth was made, for certain Madam,
Nature intended her a right good ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: She has a good hand.

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: 'Tis good enough to hold faſt,
And ſtrong enough to ſtrangle the neck of a Lute.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: What think ye of her colour?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: If it be her own
'Tis good black blood: right weather-proof
I warrant it.

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: What a ſtrange pace ſhe has got?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: That's but her breeding.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: And what a manly body? me thinks ſhe locks
As though ſhe would pitch the Bar, or go to Buffets.

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: Yet her behaviour's utterly againſt it,
For me thinks ſhe is too baſhful.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Is that hurtful?

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: Even equal to too bold: either of 'em, Ma ••• ,
May do her injury when time ſhall ſerve her.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l:
You diſcourſe learnedly, call in the wench.
Ex. C •• .
What envious fools are you? Is the rule general,
That Women can ſpeak handſomly of none,
But thoſe they are bred withal?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Scarce well of thoſe, Madam,
If they believe they may out ſhine 'em any way:
Our natures are like Oyl, compound us with any thing,
Yet ſtill we ſtrive to ſwim o' th' top:
Suppoſe there were here now,
Now in this Court of Moſco, a ſtranger Princeſs,
Of bloud and beauty equal to your excellence,
As many eyes and ſervices ſtuck on her;
What would you think?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: I would think ſhe might deſerve it.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Your Grace ſhall give me leave not to believe ye;
I know you are a Woman, and ſo humour'd:
I'le tell ye Madam, I could then get more Gowns on ye,
More Caps and Feathers, more Scarfs, and more Silk ſtockings
With rocking you aſleep with nightly railings
Upon that Woman, than if I had nine lives
I could wear out: by this hand ye'would ſcratch her eyes out

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Thou art deceiv'd fool;
Now let your own eye mock ye.
Come hither Girl: hang me and ſhe be not a handſom one.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I fear it will prove indeed ſo.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Did you ever ſerve yet
In any place of worth?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: No, Royal Lady.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Hold up your head; fie.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Let her alone, ſtand from her.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: It ſhall be now,
Of all the bleſſings my poor youth has pray'd for,
The greateſt and the happieſt to ſerve you;
And might my promiſe carry but that credit
To be believ'd, becauſe I am yet a ſtranger,
Excellent Lady, when I fall from duty,
From all the ſervice that my life can lend me,
May everlaſting miſery then find me.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: What think ye now? I do believe, and thank ye;
And ſure I ſhall not be ſo far forgetful,
To ſee that honeſt faith die unrewarded:
What muſt I call your name?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Alinda, Madam.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Can ye ſing?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: A little, when my grief will give me leave, Lady.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: What grief canſt thou have Wench?
Thou art not in love?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: If I be Madam, 'tis only with your goodneſs;
For yet I never ſaw that man I ſighed for.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Of what years are you?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: My Mother oft has told me,
That very day and hour this land was bleſt
