With your moſt happy birth, I firſt ſaluted
This worlds fair light: Nature was then ſo buſie,
And all the Graces to adorn your goodneſs,
I ſtole into the world poor and neglected.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Something there was, when I firſt look'd upon thee,
Made me both like and love thee: now I know it;
And you ſhall find that knowledge ſhall not hurt you:
I hope ye are a Maid?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I hope ſo too, Madam;
I am ſure for any man: and were I otherwiſe,
Of all the ſervices my hopes could point at,
I durſt not touch at yours.

div.stage: Flouriſh. Enter Duke, Burris, and Gent.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: The great Duke, Madam.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Good morrow, Siſter.

sp.speaker: O ym
sp.l: A good day to your highneſs.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I am come to pray you uſe no more perſwaſions
For this old ſtubborn man: nay to command ye:
His ſail is ſwell'd too full: he is grown too inſolent,
Too ſelf affected, proud: thoſe poor ſlight ſervices
He has done my Father, and my ſelf, has blown him
To ſuch a pitch, he flyes to ſtoop our favours.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: I am ſorry Sir: I ever thought thoſe ſervices
Both great and noble.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: However, may it pleaſe ye
But to conſider 'em a true hearts Servants,
Done out of faith to you, and not ſelf-fame:
Do but conſider royal Sir, the dangers;
When you have ſlept ſecure, the mid-night tempeſts,
That as he marcht ſung through his aged locks;
When you have fed at full, the wants and famins;
The fires of Heaven, when you have found all temperate,
Death with his thouſand doors —

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I have conſider'd;
No more: and that I will have, ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: For the beſt,
I hope all ſtill.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: What handſom wench is that there?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: My Servant, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Prethee obſerve her Burris,
Is ſhe not wondrous handſom? ſpeak thy freedom.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: She appears no leſs to me Sir.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Of whence is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Her Father I am told is a good Gentleman,
But far off dwelling: her deſire to ſerve me
Brought her to th' Court, and here her friends have left her.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: She may find better friends:
Ye are welcom fair one,
I have not ſeen a ſweeter: By your Ladies leave:
Nay ſtand up ſweet, we'll have no ſuperſtition:
You have got a Servant; you may uſe him kindly,

And he may honour ye:
Ex. Duke and Burris.
Good morrow Siſter.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Good morrow to your Grace. How the wench bluſhes?
How like an Angel now ſhe looks?

sp.speaker: 1 Wom.
sp.l: At firſt jump
Jump into the Dukes arms? we muſt look to you,
In •• ed we muſt, the next jump we are journeymen.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I ſee the ruine of our hopes already,
Would ſhe were at home again, milking her Fathers Cows.

sp.speaker: 1 Wom.
sp.l: I fear ſhe'l milk all the great Courtiers firſt.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: This has not made ye proud?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: No certain, Madam.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: It was the Duke that kiſt ye.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: 'Twas your Brother,
And therefore nothing can be meant but honour.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: But ſay he love ye?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: That he may with ſafety:
A Princes love extends to all his ſubjects.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: But ſay in more particular?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Pray fear not:
For vertues ſake deliver me from doubts, Lady:
'Tis not the name of King, nor all his promiſes,
His glories, and his greatneſs ſtuck about me,
Can make me prove a Traitor to your ſervice:
You are my Miſtris, and my noble Maſter,
Your vertues my ambition, and your favour
The end of all my love, and all my fortune:
And when I fail in that faith —

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: I believe thee,
Come wipe your eyes; I do: take you example—

sp.speaker: Puſ.
sp.l: I would her eyes were out.

sp.speaker: 1 Wom.
sp.l: If the wind ſtand in this door,
We ſhall have but cold cuſtome: ſome trick or other,
And ſpeedily.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Let me alone to think on't.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Come, be you near me ſtill.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: With all my duty. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA III.
div.stage: Enter Archas, Theodor, Putskie, Ancient, and Souldiers, carrying his armour pi • ce-meale, his Colours wound up, and his Drums in Caſes.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: This is the heavieſt march we e're trod Captain.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: This was not wont to be: theſe honour'd pieces
The fierie god of war himſelf would ſmile at,
Buckl'd upon that body, were not wont thus,
Like Reliques to be offer'd to long ruſt,
And heavy ey'd oblivion brood upon 'em.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: There ſet 'em down: and glorious war farewel;
Thou child of honour and ambitious thoughts,
Begot in bloud, and nurs'd with Kingdomes ruines;
Thou golden danger, courted by thy followers
Through fires and famins, for one title from thee —
Prodigal man-kind ſpending all his fortunes;
A long farewel I give thee: Noble Arms,
You ribs for mighty minds, you Iron houſes,
Made to defie the thunder-claps of Fortune,
Ruſt and conſuming time muſt now dwell with ye:
And thou good Sword that knewſt the way to conqueſt,
Upon whoſe fatal edge deſpair and death dwelt,
That when I ſhook thee thus, fore-ſhew'd deſtruction,
Sleep now from bloud, and grace my Monument:
Farewel my Eagle; when thou ſlew'ſt, whole Armies
Have ſtoopt below thee: At Paſſage I have ſeen thee,
Ruffle the Tartars, as they fled thy furie;
And bang 'em up together, as a Taſſel,
Upon the ſtreach, a flock of fearfull Pigeons.
I yet remember when the Volga curl'd,
The aged Volga, when he heav'd his head up,
And rais'd his waters high, to ſee the ruins;
The ruines our Swords made, the bloudy ruins,
Then flew this Bird of honour bravely, Gentlemen;
But theſe muſt be forgotten: ſo muſt theſe too,
And all that tend to Arms, by me for ever.
Take 'em you holy men; my Vow take with 'em,
Never to wear 'em more: Trophies I give 'em,
And ſacred Rites of war to adorn the Temple:
There let 'em hang, to tell the world their maſter
Is now Devotions Souldier, fit for prayer.
Why do ye hang your heads? why look you ſad friends?
I am not dying yet.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: Ye are indeed to us Sir.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Dead to our fortunes, General.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: You'l find a better,
A greater, and a ſtronger man to lead ye,
And to a ſtronger fortune: I am old, friends,
Time, and the wars together make me ſtoop, Gentlenem,
Stoop to my grave: my mind unfurniſh'd too,
Emptie and weak as I am: my poor body,
Able for nothing now but contemplation,
And that will be a task too to a Souldier:
Yet had they but encourag'd me, or thought well
Of what I have done, I think I ſhould have ventur'd
For one knock more, I ſhould have made a ſhift yet
To have broke one ſtaff more handſomly, and have died
Like a good fellow, and an honeſt Souldier,
In the head of ye all, with my Sword in my hand,
And ſo have made an end of all with credit.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: Well, there will come an hour, when all theſe injuries,
Theſe ſecure ſlights —

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Ha! no more of that ſirrah,
Not one word more of that I charge ye.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: I muſt ſpeak Sir.
And may that tongue forget to ſound your ſervice,
That's dumb to your abuſes.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Underſtand fool,
That voluntary I ſit down.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: You are forced, Sir,
〈◊〉 for your ſafety: I too well remember
The time and cauſe, and I may live to curſe 'em:
You made this Vow, and whoſe unnobleneſs,
Indeed forgetfulneſs of good—

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: No more,
As thou art mine no more.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Whoſe doubts and envies —
But the Devil will have his due.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Good gentle Colonel.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: And though diſgraces, and contempt of Honour
Reign now, the Wheel muſt turn again.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Peace Sirrah,
Your ton ••• 's too fancy: do you ſtare upon me?
Down with that head, down ſuddenly, down with it,
Down with that diſobedience; tye that tongue up.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: Tongue?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Do not provoke me to forget my Vow, Sirrah.
And draw that fatal Sword again in anger.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: For Heavens ſake, Colonel,

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Do not let me doubt
Whoſe Son thou art, becauſe thou canſt not ſuffer:
Do not play with mine anger; if thou doſt,
By all the Loyalty my heart holds—

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: I have done, Sir,
Pray pardon me.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I pray be worthy of it:
Be ſhrew your heart, you have vext me.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I am ſorry, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Go to, no more of this: be true and honeſt,
I know ye are man enough, mould it to juſt ends,
And let not my diſgraces, then I am miſerable,
When I have nothing left me but thy angers.

div.stage: F • ouriſh, Enter Duke, Pu •• is, Boroskie, Attend. and Gent.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: And't pleaſ • ye, Sir, the Duke.
Now, what's all this?
The meaning of this c • remonious Emblem?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Your Grace ſhould firſt remember—

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: There's his Nature.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I do, and ſhall remember ſtill that injury,
That at the Muſter, where it pleas'd your Greatneſs
To laugh at my poor Souldierſhip, to ſcorn it;
And more to make me ſeem ridiculous,
Took from my hands my charge.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: O think not ſo, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: And in my Fathers ſight.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Heaven be my witneſs,
I did no more, (and that with modeſty,
With Love and Faith to you) than was my warrant,
And from your Father ſeal'd: no • durſt that rudeneſs,
And impudence of ſcorn fall from my 'haviour,
I ever yet knew duty.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: We ſhall teach ye,
I well remember too, upon ſome words I told ye,
Then at that time, ſome angry words ye anſwer'd,
If ever I were Duke, you were no Souldier.
You have kept your word, and ſo it ſhall be to you,
From henceforth I diſmiſs you; take your eaſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I humbly thank your Grace; this waſted Body,
Beaten and bruis'd with A • ms, dry'd up with troubles,
Is good for nothing elſe but quiet, now Sir,
And holy Prayers; in which, when I forget
To thank Heaven for all your bounteous favours,
May that be deaf, and my Petitions periſh.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: What a ſmooth humble Cloak he has cas'd his pride in'?
And how he has pull'd his Claws in? there's no truſting—

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Speak for the beſt.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Believe I ſhall do ever.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: To make • e underſtand, we feel not yet
Such deatth of Valou • , and Experience,
Such a declining Age of doing Spirits,
That all ſhould be confin'd within your excellence,
And you, or none be honour'd, take Boroskie,
The place he has commanded, lead the Souldier;
A little time will bring thee to his honour,
Which has been nothing but the Worlds opinion,
The Souldiers fondneſs, and a little fortune,
Which I believe his Sword had the leaſt ſhare in.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: O that I durſt but anſwer now.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Good Colonel.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: My heart will break elſe: Royal Sir, I know not
What you eſteem mens lives, whoſe hourly labours,
And loſs of Blood, conſumptions in your ſervice,
Whoſe Bodies are acquainted with more miſeries,
And all to keep you ſafe, than Dogs or Slaves are.
His Sword the leaſt ſhare gain'd?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: You will not fight with me?

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: No Sir, I dare not,
You are my Prince, but I dare ſpeak to ye,
And dare ſpeak truth, which none of their ambitions
That be informers to you, dare once think of,
Yet truth will now but anger ye; I am ſorry for't,
And ſo I take my leave. Exit.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Ev'n when you pleaſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Sirrah, ſee me no more.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And ſo may you too:
You have a houſe i'th' Country, keep you there, Sir,
And when you have rul'd your ſelf, teach your Son manners,
For this time I forgive him,

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Heaven forgive all;
And to your Grace a happy and long Rule here.
And you Lord General, may your fights be proſperous.
In all your Courſe may Fame and Fortune court you.
Fight for your Country, and your Princes ſafety;
Boldly, and bravely face your Enemy,
And when you ſtrike, ſtrike with that killing Vertue,
As if a general Plague had ſeiz'd before ye;
Danger, and doubt, and labour caſt behind ye;
And then come home an old and noble Story.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: A little comfort, Sir.

sp.speaker: Du
sp.l: As little as may be:

Farewel, you know your limit.
Ex. Duke, &c.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Alas, brave Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I do, and will obſerve it ſuddenly,
My Grave; I, that's my limit; 'tis no new thing,
Nor that can make me ſtart, or tremble at it,
To buckle with that old grim Souldier now:
I have ſeen him in his ſowreſt ſhapes, and dreadfull'ſt;
I, and I thank my honeſty, have ſtood him:
That audit's caſt; farewel my honeſt Souldiers,
Give me your hands; farewel, farewel good Ancient,
A ſtout man, and a true, thou art come in ſorrow.
Bleſſings upon your Swords, may they ne'r fail ye;
You do but change a man; your fortune's conſtant;
That by your ancient Valours is ty'd faſt ſtill;
Be valiant ſtill, and good: and when ye fight next,
When flame and fury make but one face of horrour,
When the great reſt of all your honour's up,
When you would think a Spell to ſhake the enemy,
Remember me, my Prayers ſhall be with ye:
So once again farewel.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Let's wait upon ye.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: No, no, it muſt not be; I have now left me
A ſingle Fortune to my ſelf, no more,
Which needs no train, nor complement; good Captain,
You are an honeſt and a ſober Gentleman,
And one I think has lov'd me.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: I am ſure on't.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Look to my Boy, he's grown too headſtrong for me.
And if they think him fit to carry Arms ſtill,
His life is theirs; I have a houſe i'th' Country,
And when your better hours will give you liberty,
See me: you ſhall be welcome. Fortune to ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: I'll cry no more, that will do him no good,
And 'twill but make me dry, and I have no money:
I'll fight no more, and that will do them harm;
And if I can do that, I care not for money:
I could have curſt reaſonable well, and I have had the luck too
To have 'em hit ſometimes. Whoſoever thou art,
That like a Devil didſt poſſeſs the Duke
With theſe malicious thoughts; mark what I ſay to thee,
A Plague upon thee, that's but the Preamble.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: O take the Pox too.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: They'll cure one another;
I muſt have none but kills, and thoſe kill ſtinking:
Or look ye, let the ſingle Pox poſſeſs them,
Or Pox upon Pox.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: That's but ill i'th' arms, Sir.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: 'Tis worſe i'th' Legs, I would not wiſh it elſe:
And may thoſe grow to ſcabs as big as Mole-hills,
And twice a day, the Devil with a Curry-Comb
Scratch 'em, and ſcrub 'em: I warrant him he has 'em.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: May he be ever lowzie.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: That's a pleaſure,
The Beggar's Lechery; ſometimes the Souldiers:
May he be ever lazie, ſtink where he ſtands,
And Maggots breed in's Brains.

sp.speaker: 2 Sold
sp.l: I, marry Sir,
May he fall mad in love with his Grand-mother,
And kiſſing her, may her teeth drop into his mouth,
And one fall croſs his throat, then let him gargle.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Now, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Poſt.
sp.l: Where's the Duke, pray, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Keep on your way, you cannot miſs.

sp.speaker: Poſt.
sp.l: I thank ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: If he be married, may he dream he's cuckol'd,
And when he wakes believe, and ſwear he ſaw it,
Sue a Divorce, and after find her honeſt:
Then in a pleaſant Pigſtye, with his own garters,
And a fine running knot, ride to the Devil.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: If theſe would do—

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: I'll never truſt my mind more,
If all theſe fail.

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: What ſhall we do now, Captain?
For by this honeſt hand I'll be torn in pieces,
Unleſs my old General go, or ſome that love him,
And love us equal too, before I fight more:
I can make a Shooe yet, and draw it on too,
If I like the Leg well.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Fight? 'tis likely:
No, there will be the ſport Boys, when there's need on's.
They think the other Crown will do, will carry us,
And the brave golden Coat of Captain Cankro

sp.speaker: Boroskie.
sp.l: What a noiſe his very name carries?
'Tis Gun enough to fright a Nation,
He needs no Souldiers; if he do, for my part,
I promiſe ye he's like to ſeek 'em; ſo I think you think too,
And all the Army; No, honeſt, brave old Archas,
We cannot ſo ſoon leave thy memory,
So ſoon forget thy goodneſs: he that does,
The ſcandal and the ſcumm of Arms be counted.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: You much rejoice me now you have hit my meaning.
I durſt not preſs ye, till I found your ſpirits:
Continue thus.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: I'll go and tell the Duke on't.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: No, no, he'll find it ſoon enough, and fear it,
When once occaſion comes: Another Packet!
From whence, Friend, come you?

sp.speaker: 2 Poſt.
sp.l: From the Borders, Sir.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: What news, Sir, I beſeech you?

sp.speaker: 2 Poſt.
sp.l: Fire and Sword, Gentlemen;
The Tartar's up, and with a mighty force,
Comes forward, like a tempeſt, all before him
Burning and killing.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Brave Boys, brave news, Boys.

sp.speaker: 2 Poſt.
sp.l: Either we muſt have preſent help—

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Still braver.

sp.speaker: 2 Poſt.
sp.l: Where lies the Duke?

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: He's there.

sp.speaker: 2 Poſt.
sp.l: 'Save ye, Gentlemen. Exit.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: We are ſafe enough, I warrant thee:
Now the time's come.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: I, now 'tis come indeed, and now ſtand firm, Boys,
And let 'em burn on merrily.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: This City would make a fine marvellous Bone-fire:
'Tis old dry timber, and ſuch Wood has no fellow.

sp.speaker: 2 Sold.
sp.l: Here will be trim piping anon and whining,
Like ſo many Pigs in a ſtorm,
When they hear the news once.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Here's one has heard it already;
Room for the General.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: Say I am faln exceeding ſick o'th'ſudden,
And am not like to live.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: If ye go on, Sir,
For they will kill ye certainly; they look for ye.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: I ſee your Lordſhip's bound, take a ſuppoſitory,
'Tis I, Sir; a poor caſt Flag of yours. The fooliſh Tartars
They burn and kill, and't like your honour, kill us,
Kill with Guns, with Guns my Lord, with Guns, Sir.
What ſays your Lordſhip to a chick in ſorrel ſops?

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Go, go thy ways old true-penny,
Thou haſt but one fault: thou art ev'n too valiant.
Come, to'th'Army Gentlemen, and let's make them acquainted.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Away, we are for ye. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Why, whither run ye Fools; will ye leave my Lady?

sp.speaker: Peteſ.
sp.l: The Tartar comes, the Tartar comes.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Why, let him,
I thought you had fear'd no men: upon my conſcience
You have try'd their ſtrengths already; ſtay for ſhame.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Shift for thy ſelf, Alinda. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Beauty bleſs ye:
Into what Grooms Feather-Bed will you creep now?
And there miſtake the enemy; ſweet youths ye are,
And of a conſtant courage; are you afraid of foining?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: O my good Wench, what ſhall become of us?
The Poſts come hourly in, and bring new danger;
The enemy is paſt the Volga, and bears hither
With all the blood and cruelty he carries,
My Brother now will find his fault.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I doubt me,
Somewhat too late, Madam. But pray fear not,
All will be well, I hope. Sweet Madam, ſhake not.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: How cam'ſt thou by this Spirit? our Sex trembles.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I am not unacquainted with theſe dangers;
And you ſhall know my truth, for ere you periſh,
A hundred Swords ſhall paſs through me: 'tis but dying,
And Madam we muſt do it: the manner's all:
You have a Princely Birth, take Princely thoughts to you,
And take my counſel too; go preſently,
With all the haſte ye have, (I will attend ye)
With all the poſſible ſpeed, to old Lord Archas,
He honours ye; with all your art perſwade him,
('Twill be a diſmal time elſe) woo him hither,
But hither Madam, make him ſee the danger;
For your new General looks like an Aſs;
There's nothing in his face but loſs.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: I'll do it.
And thank thee, ſweet Alinda: O my Jewel,
How much I'm bound to love thee! by this hand, Wench,
If thou wert a man—

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I would I were to fight for you.
But haſte dear Madam.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: I need no Spurs Alinda.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: The Lord General ſick now? is this a time
For men to creep into their Beds? What's become, Poſt,
Of my Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Poſt.
sp.l: Beaten, and 't pleaſe your Grace,
And all his Forces ſparkled.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: That's but cold news:
How now, what good news? are the Souldiers ready?

sp.speaker: Ge.
sp.l: Yes Sir, but ſight they will not, nor ſtir from that place
They ſtand in now, unleſs they have Lord Archas
To lead 'em out; they rail upon this General,
And ſing Songs of him, ſ • urvy Songs, to worſe tunes:
And much they ſpare not you, Sir: here they ſwear
They'll ſtand and ſee the City burnt, and dance about it,
Unleſs Lord Archas come before they ſight for't:
It muſt be ſo, Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I could wiſh it ſo too;
And to that end I have ſent Lord Burris to him;
But all I fear will fail; we muſt dye, Gentlemen,
And one ſtroke we'll have for't.
What bring'ſt thou, Burris?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: That I am loth to tell; he will not come, Sir;
I found him at his Prayers, there he tells me,
The Enemy ſhall take him, fit for Heaven:
I urg'd to him all our dangers, his own worths,
The Countries ruine; nay I kneel'd and pray'd him;
He ſhook his head, let fall a tear, and pointed
Thus with his finger to the Ground; a Grave
I think he meant; and this was all he anſwer'd.
Your Grace was much to blame:
Where's the new General?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: He is ſick, poor man.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: He's a poor man indeed, Sir:
Your Grace muſt needs go to the Souldier.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: They have ſent me word
They will not ſtir, they rail at me,
And all the ſpight they have— Shout within.
What ſhout is that there?
Is the Enemy come ſo near?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: I have brought him, Sir,
At length I have woo'd him thus far.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Happy Siſter,
O bleſſed Woman!

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Uſe him nobly, Brother,
You never had more need: And Gentlemen,
All the beſt powers ye have, to tongues turn preſently,
To winning and perſwading tongues: all my art,
Only to bring him hither, I have utter'd;
〈◊〉 it be yours to arm him; And good my Lord,
Though I exceed the limit you allow'd me,
Which was the happineſs to bring ye hither,
And not to urge ye farther; yet, ſee your Country,
Out of your own ſweet Spirit now behold it:
Turn • ound, and look upon the miſeries,
On every ſide the fears; O ſee the dangers;
We find 'em ſooneſt, therefore hear me firſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Next hear your Prince:
You have ſaid you lov'd him, Archas,
And thought your life too little for his ſervice;
Think not your vow too great now, now the time is,
And now you are brought to th' teſt, touch right now Souldier,
Now ſhew the manly pureneſs of thy mettle;
Now 〈◊〉 thou b •• ſt that valued man, that vertue,
That great ob • dience teaching all, now ſtand it.
What I have ſaid forget, my youth was haſty,
And what you ſaid your ſelf forgive, you were an ••• .
If men could live without their faults, they were 〈…〉

He weeps, and holds his hands up: to him, B • r •• s
〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: You have ſhew'd the Prince his faults;
And like a good Surgeon you have laid
That to 'em makes 'em ſmart; he feels it,
Let 'em not feſter now, Sir; your own honour,
The bounty of that mind, and your allegiance,
'Gainſt which I take it, Heaven gives no Command, Sir,
Nor ſeals no Vow, can better teach ye now
What ye have to do, than I, or this neceſſity;
Only this little's left; would ye do nobly,
And in the Eye of Honour truly triumph?
Conquer that mind firſt, and then men are nothing.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Laſt, a poor Virgin kneels; for loves ſake General,
If ever you have lov'd; for her ſake, Sir,
For your own honeſty, which is a Virgin,
Look up, and pity us, be bold and fortunate,
You are a Knight, a good and noble Souldier,
And when your Spurs were given ye, your Sword buc ••• ,
Then were you ſworn for Vertues Cauſe, for Beaut •• s,
For Chaſtity to ſtrike; ſtrike now, they ſuffer;
Now draw your Sword, or elſe you are recreant,
Only a Knight i'th' Heels, i'th' Heart a Coward;

Your firſt Vow honour made, your laſt but anger.
〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: How like my vertuous Wife this thing looks, ſp ••• s
So would ſhe chide my dulneſs: fair one, I thank ye.
My gracious Sir, your pardon, next your hand:
Madam, your favour, and your prayers: Gentlem •• ,
Your wiſhes, and your loves: and pretty ſweet one,
A favour for your Souldier.

sp.speaker: Olymp.
sp.l: Give him this, Wench.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Thus do I tye on Victory.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: My Armour,
My Horſe, my Sword, my tough Staff, and my Fortune,
And Olin now I come to ſhake thy glory.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Go, brave and proſperous, our loves go with th ••

sp.speaker: Olymp.
sp.l: Full of thy vertue, and our Prayers attend t ••• .

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: &c. Loaden with Victory, and we to honour thee.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Come home the Son of Honour,
And I'll ſerve ye. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Burris, and two Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: NO news of Archas yet?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: But now, and't pleaſe ye,
A Poſt came in, Letters he brought none with him,
But this deliver'd: He ſaw the Armies join,
The game of Blood begun, and by our General,
Who never was acquainted but with Conqueſt,
So bravely fought, he ſaw the Tartars ſhaken,
And there he ſaid he left 'em.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Where's Boroskie?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: He's up again, and't pleaſe ye.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Sir, methinks
This News ſhould make ye lightſome, bring joy to ye,

It ſtrikes our hearts with general Comfort.
Exit Duk •
Gone? What ſhould this mean, ſo ſuddenly?
He's well?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: We ſee no other.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Would the reſt were well too,
That put theſe ſtarts into him.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: I'll go after him.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: 'Twill not be ſit, Sir: h'as ſome ſecret in him
He would not be diſturb'd in: know you any thing
Has croſt him ſince the General went?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Not any:
If there had been, I am ſure I ſhould have ſound it:
Only I have heard him oft complain for money:
Money he ſays he wants.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: It may be that then.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: To him that has ſo may wayes to raiſe it,
And thoſe ſo honeſt, it cannot be.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: He comes back,
And Lord Boroskie with him.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: There the game goes,
I fear ſome new thing hatching.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come hither Burris.
Go ſee my Siſter, and commend me to her,
And to my little Miſtriſs give this Token;
Tell her I'le ſee her ſhortly.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l:
Yes, I ſhall, Sir.
Ex. Bur. and Gent.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Wait you without: I would yet try him further.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: 'Twill not be much amiſs: has your Grace heard yet
Of what he has done i'th' Field?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: A Poſt but now
Came in, who ſaw 'em joyn, and has delivered,
The Enemy gave ground before he parted.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: 'Tis well.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come, ſpeak thy mind man: 'tis not for fighting,
A noiſe of War, I keep thee in my boſom;
Thy ends are nearer to me; from my Childhood
Thou brought'ſt me up: and like another nature,
Made good all my neceſſities: ſpeak boldly.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Sir, what I utter, will be thought but envy
Though I intend, high heaven knows, but your honour,
When vain and empty people ſhall proclaim me—
Good Sir excuſe me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Do you fear me for your Enemy?
Speak on your duty.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Then I muſt, and dare, Sir:
When he comes home, take heed the Court receive him not,
Take heed he meet not with their loves and praiſes,
That Glaſs will ſhew him ten times greater, Sir,
And make him ſtrive to make good that proportion,)
Than ere his fortune bred him, he is honourable,
At leaſt I ſtrive to underſtand him ſo,
And of a nature, if not this way poyſon'd,
Perfect enough, eaſie, and ſweet, but thoſe are ſoon ſeduc'd, Sir;
He's a great man, and what that Pill may work,
Prepar'd by general voices of the people,
Is the end of all my Counſel, only this, Sir,
Let him retire a while, there's more hangs by it
Than you know yet: there if he ſtand a while well,
But till the Souldier cool, whom, for their ſervice
You muſt pay now moſt liberally, moſt freely,
And ſhowre your ſelf into 'em; 'tis the bounty
They follow with their loves, and not the bravery.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But where's the Money? how now?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Sir, the Colonel,
Son to the Lord Archas, with moſt happy news
Of the Tartars overthrow, without here
Attends your Graces pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Be not ſeen, Sir,
He's a bold fellow, let me ſtand his Thunders,
To th' Court he muſt not come: no bleſſing here, Sir,
No face of favour, if you love your honour.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Do what you think is meeteſt; I'le retire, Sir. Ex.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Conduct him in, Sir— welcome noble Colonel.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: That's much from your Lordſhip: pray where's the Duke?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: We hear you have beat the Tartar.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Is he buſie, Sir?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Have ye taken Olin yet?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I would fain ſpeak with him.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: How many men have ye loſt?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Do's he lye this way?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: I am ſure you fought it bravely.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I muſt ſee him.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: You cannot yet, ye muſt not, what's your Commiſſion?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: No Gentleman o'th' Chamber here?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Why, pray ye, Sir?
Am not I fit to entertain your buſineſs?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I think you are not, Sir; I am ſure ye ſhall not.
I bring no tales, nor flatteries: in my tongue, Sir,
I carry no fork'd ſtings.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: You keep your bluntneſs.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: You are deceiv'd: it keeps me: I had felt elſe
Some of your plagues ere this: but good Sir trifle not,
I have buſineſs to the Duke.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: He's not well, Sir,
And cannot now be ſpoke withal.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Not well, Sir?
How would he ha'been, if we had loſt? not well, Sir?
I bring him news to make him well: his enemy
That, would have burnt his City here, and your Houſe too,
Your brave gilt houſe, my Lord, your honours hangings,
Where all your Anceſtors, and all their Battels,
Their ſilk and golden Battels are decipher'd:
That would not only have abus'd your buildings,
Your goodly buildings, Sir, and have drunk dry your butte • ies,
Purloin'd your Lordſhips Plate, the Duke beſtow'd on you,
For turning handſomly o'th' toe, and trim'd your Virgins,
Trim'd 'em of a new cut, and't like your Lordſhip,
'Tis ten to one, your Wiſe too, and the curſe is
You had had no remedy againſt theſe Raſcals,
No Law, and't like your Honour; would have kill'd you too
And roaſted ye, and eaten ye, ere this time:
Notable Knaves my Lord, unruly Raſcals:
Theſe youths have we ty'd up, put muzzels on 'em,
And pa • 'd their Nails, that honeſt civil Gentlemen,
And ſuch moſt noble perſons as your ſelf is,
May live in peace, and rule the land with a twine thread.
Theſe news I bring.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: And were they thus deliver'd ye?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: My Lord, I am no pen-man, nor no Orator,
My tongue was never Oyl'd with Here and't like ye,
There I beſeech ye, weigh, I am a Souldier,
And truth I covet only, no fine terms, Sir;
I come not to ſtand treating here; my buſineſs
Is with the Duke, and of ſuch general bleſſing—

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: You have overthrown the enemy, we know it,
And we rejoyce in't; ye have done like honeſt Subjects,
You have done handſomely and well.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: But well, Sir?
But handſomely and well? what are we juglers?
I'le do all that in cutting up a Capon.
But handſomely and well? does your Lordſhip take u •
For the Dukes Tumblers? we have done bravely, Sir,
Ventur'd our lives like men.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Then bravely be it.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: And for as brave rewards we look, and graces,
We have ſweat and bled for't, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: And ye may have it,
If you will ſtay the giving. Men that thank themſelves firſt
For any good they do, take off the luſtre,
And blot the benefit.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Are theſe the welcomes,
The Bells that ring out our rewards? pray heartily,
Early and late, there may be no more Enemies:
Do my good Lord, pray ſeriouſly, and ſigh too,
For if there be—

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: They muſt be met, and fought with.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: By whom? by you? they muſt be met and flatter'd.
Why, what a Devil ail'd ye to do theſe things?
With what aſſurance dare ye mock men thus?
You have but ſingle lives, and thoſe I take it
A Sword may find too: why do ye dam the Duke up?
And choak that courſe of love, that like a River
Should fill our empty veins again with comforts?
But if ye uſe theſe knick knacks,
This faſt and looſe, with faithful men and honeſt,
You'l be the firſt will find it.

div.stage: Enter Archas, Souldiers, Putskey, Ancient, and others.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: You are too untemperate.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Better be ſo, and thief too, than unthankful:
Pray uſe this old man ſo, and then we are paid all.
The Duke thanks ye for your ſervice, and the Court thanks ye,
And wonderful deſirous they are to ſee ye;
Pray Heaven we have room enough to march for May-games,
Pageants, and Bone-fires for your welcome home, Sir.
Here your moſt noble friend the Lord Boroskie,
A Gentleman too tender of your credit,
And ever in the Dukes ear, for your good, Sir,
Crazie and ſickly, yet to be your ſervant,
Has leapt into the open air to meet ye.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: The beſt is, your words wound not, you are welcome home, Sir;
Heartily welcome home, and for your ſervice,
The noble overthrow you gave the Enemy,
The Duke ſalutes ye too with all his thanks, Sir.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Sure they will now regard us.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: There's a reaſon:
But by the changing of the Colonels countenance,
The rolling of his eyes like angry Billows;
I fear the wind's not down yet, Ancient.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: Is the Duke well, Sir?

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: Not much unhealthy,
Only a little grudging of an Ague,
Which cannot laſt: he has heard, which makes him fearful,
And loth as yet to give your worth due welcome,
The ſickneſs hath been ſomewhat hot i'th' Army,
Which happily may prove more doubt than danger,
And more his fear than ſate; yet howſoever,
An honeſt care—

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: Ye ſay right, and it ſhall be;
For though upon my life 'tis but a rumor,
A meer opinion, without faith or fear in't;
For Sir, I thank Heaven, we never ſtood more healthy,
Never more high and luſty; yet to ſatisfie,
We cannot be too curious, or too careful
Of what concerns his ſtate, we'll draw away, Sir,
And lodge at further diſtance, and leſs danger.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: It will be well.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: It will be very ſcurvy:
I ſmell it out, it ſtinks abominably,
Stir it no more.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: The Duke, Sir, would have you too,
For a ſhort day or two, retire to your own houſe,
Whither himſelf will come to viſit ye,
And give ye thanks.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: I ſhall attend his pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: A trick, a louſie trick: ſo ho, a trick Boys.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: How now, what's that?

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: I thought I had found a Hare, Sir,
But 'tis a Fox, an old Fox, ſhall we hunt him?

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: No more ſuch words.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: The Souldier's grown too ſaw • y,
You muſt tie him ſtraiter up.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: I do my beſt, Sir;
But men of free-born minds ſometimes will flie out.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: May not we ſee the Duke?

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: Not at this time, Gentlemen,
Your General knows the cauſe.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: We have no Plague, Sir,
Unleſs it be in our pay, nor no Pox neither;
Or if we had, I hope that good old Courtier
Will not deny us place there.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Certain my Lord,
Conſidering what we are, and what we have done;
If not, what need ye may have, 'twould be better,
A great deal nobler, and taſte honeſter
• o uſe us with more ſweetneſs; men that dig
And laſh away their lives at the Carts tail,
Double our comforts; meat, and their Maſters thanks too,
When they work well, they have; Men of our quality,
When they do well, and venture ſor't with valour,
Fight hard, lye hard, feed hard, when they come home, S •• ,
And know theſe are deſerving things, things worthy,
Can you then blame 'em if their minds a little
Be ſtir'd with glory? 'tis a pride becomes 'em,
A little ſeaſon'd with ambition,
To be reſpected, reckon'd well, and honour'd
For what they have done: when to come home thus poorly,
And met with ſuch unjointed joy, ſo looked on,
As if we had done no more but dreſt a Horſe well;
So entertain'd, as if, I thank ye Gentlemen,
Take that to drink, had pow'r to pleaſe a Souldier?
Where be the ſhouts, the Bells rung out, the people?
The Prince himſelf?

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: Peace: I perceive your eye, Sir,
Is ſixt upon this Captain for his freedom,
And happily you find his tongue too forward;
As I am Maſter of the place I carry,
'Tis fit I think ſo too; but were I this man,
No ſtronger tie upon me, than the truth
And tongue to tell it, I ſhould ſpeak as he do's,
And think with modeſty enough, ſuch Saints
That daily thruſt their loves and lives through hazards,
And fearleſs for their Countries peace, march hourly
Through all the doors of death, and know the darkeſt,
Should better be canoniz'd for their ſervice:
What labour would theſe men neglect, what danger
Where honour is, though ſeated in a Billow,
Riſing as high as Heaven, would not theſe Souldiers,
Like to ſo many Sea-gods charge up to it?
Do you ſee theſe ſwords? times Sythe was ne'er ſo ſharp, Sir;
Nor ever at one harveſt mow'd ſuch handfuls:
Thoughts ne'er ſo ſudden, nor belief ſo ſure
When they are drawn, and were it not ſometimes
I ſwim upon their angers to allay 'em,
And like a calm depreſs their fell intentions;
They are ſo deadly ſure, nature would ſuffer—
And whoſe are all theſe glories? why, their Princes,
Their Countries, and their Friends? Alas, of all theſe,
And all the happy ends they bring, the bleſſings,
They only ſhare the labours: A little joy then,
And outſide of a welcome, at an upſhot
Would not have done amiſs, Sir; but howſoever
Between me and my duty, no crack, Sir,
Shall dare appear: I hope by my example
No diſcontent in them: without doubt Gentlemen,
The Duke will both look ſuddenly and truly
On your deſerts: Methinks 'twere good they were paid, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: They ſhall be immediately; I ſtay for money;
And any favour elſe—

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: We are all bound to ye;
And ſo I take my leave, Sir; when the Duke pleaſes
To make me worthy of his eyes—

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Which will be ſuddenly,
I know his good thoughts to ye.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: With all duty,
And all humility, I ſhall attend, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Once more you are welcome home: theſe ſhall be ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Be ſure we be: and handſomly.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: Wait you on me, Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: And honeſtly: no jugling.

sp.speaker: Arch.
sp.l: Will ye come, Sir? Exit.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Pray do not doubt.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: We are no Boys. Exit.

div.stage: Enter a Gent. and 2 or 3 with Mony.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Here's mony from the Duke, and't pleaſe your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: 'Tis well.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: How ſowre the Souldiers look?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Is't told?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Yes, and for every company a double pay,
And the Dukes love to all.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: That's worth a Ducket.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: You that be Officers, ſee it diſcharg'd then,
Why do not you take it up?

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: 'Tis too heavy:
'Body o'me, I have ſtrain'd mine arm.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Do ye ſcorn it?

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Has your Lorſhip any dice about ye? ſit round Gentlemen,
And come on ſeven for my ſhare.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Do you think Sir,
This is the end we fight? can this durt draw us
To ſuch a ſtupid tameneſs, that our ſervice
Neglected, and look'd lamely on, and skew'd at
With a few honourable words, and this, is righted?
Have not we eyes and ears, to hear and ſee Sir,
And minds to underſtand the ſlights we carry?
I come home old, and full of hurts, men look on me
As if I had got 'em from a whore, and ſhun me;
I tell my griefs, and fear my wants, I am anſwer'd,
Alas 'tis pity! pray dine with me on Sunday:
Theſe are the ſores we are ſick of, the minds maladies,
And can this cure 'em? you ſhould have us'd us nobly,
And for our doing well, as well proclaim'd us
To the worlds eye, have ſhew'd and ſainted us,
Then ye had paid us bravely: then we had ſhin'd Sir,
Not in this gilded ſtuff but in our glory:
You may take back your mony.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: This I fear'd ſtill.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Conſider better Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Thank your Lordſhip:
And now I'le put on my conſidering cap:
My Lord, that I am no Courtier, you may gueſs it
By having no ſute to you for this mony:
For though I want, I want not this, nor ſhall not,
Whilſt you want that civility to rank it
With thoſe rights we expected; mony grows Sir,
And men muſt gather it, all is not put in one purſe.
And that I am no Carter, I could never whiſtle yet:
But that I am a Souldier, and a Gentleman,
And a fine Gentleman, and't like your honour,
And a moſt pleaſant companion: all you that are witty,
Come liſt to my ditty: come ſet in boyes,
With your Lordſhips patience. Song.
How do you like my Song, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Even as I like your ſelf, but 'twould be a great deal better,
You would prove a great deal wiſer, and take this mony,
In your own phraſe I ſpeak now Sir, and 'tis very well
You have learn'd to ſing; for ſince you prove ſo liberal,
To refuſe ſuch means as this, maintain your voice ſtill,
'Twill prove your beſt friend.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſinging age Sir,
A merry moon here now: I'le follow it:
Fidling, and fooling now, gains more than fighting.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: What is't you blench at? what would you ask? ſpeak freely.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.l: And ſo we dare: a triumph for the General.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: And then an honour ſpecial to his vertue.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: That we may be prefer'd that have ſerv'd for it,
And cram'd up into favour like the worſhipful,
At leaſt upon the Cities charge made drunk
For one whole year; we have done 'em ten years ſervice;
That we may enjoy our lechery without grudging,
And mine, or thine be nothing, all things equal,
And catch as catch may, be proclaim'd: that when we borrow;
And have no will to pay again, no Law
Lay hold upon us, nor no Court controule us.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Some of theſe may come to paſs; the Duke may do 'em,
And no doubt will: the General will find too,
And ſo will you, if you but ſtay with patience: I have no power.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Nor will: come fellow Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Pray be not ſo diſtruſtfull.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: There are waies yet,
And honeſt waies; we are not brought up Statues.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: If your Lordſhip
Have any ſilk ſtockings, that have holes i'th' heels,
Or ever an honourable Caſſock that wants buttons,
I could have cur'd ſuch maladies: your Lordſhips cuſtome
And my good Ladies, if the bones want ſetting
In her old bodies —

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: This is diſobedience.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Eight pence a day, and hard Eggs.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Troop off Gentlemen,
Some Coin we have, whilſt this laſts, or our credits,
We'l never ſell our Generals worth for ſix-pence.
Ye are beholding to us.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Fare ye well Sir,
And buy a pipe with that: do ye ſee this skarf Sir?
By this hand I'le cry Brooms in't, birchen Brooms Sir,
Before I eat one bit from your benevolence.
Now to our old occupations again.
By your leave Lord. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: You will bite when ye are ſharper; take up the mony.
This love I muſt remove, this fondneſs to him,
This tenderneſs of heart; I have loſt my way elſe,
There is no ſending man, they will not take it,
They are yet too full of pillage,
They'l dance for't ere't be long:
Come, bring it after.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How now, refus'd their mony?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Very bravely,
And ſtand upon ſuch terms 'tis terrible.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Where's Archas?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: He's retir'd Sir, to his houſe,
According to your pleaſure, full of dutie
To outward ſhew: but what within —

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Refuſe it?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Moſt confidently: 'tis not your revenues
Can feed then Sir, and yet they have found a General
That knows no ebbe of bountie: there they eat Sir,
And loath your invitations.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: 'Tis not poſſible,
He's poor as they.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: You'l find it otherwiſe.
Pray make your journey thither preſently,
And as ye goe I'le open ye a wonder.
Good Sir this morning.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Follow me, I'le doe it. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA II.
div.stage: Enter Olympia, Alinda, Burris, and Gentlewomen.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: But do you think my Brother loves her?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Certain Madam,
He ſpeaks much of her, and ſometimes with wonder,
Oft wiſhes ſhe were nobler born.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Do you think him honeſt?

sp.speaker: B r.
sp.l: Your Grace is nearer to his heart, than I am,
Upon my life I hold him ſo.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: 'Tis a poor wench,
I would not have her wrong'd: methinks my Brother—
But I muſt not give rules to his affections;
Yet if he weigh her worth —

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: You need not fear Madam.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: I hope I ſhall not: Lord Burris
I love her well; I know not, there is ſomething
Makes me beſtow more than a care upon her:
I do not like that ring from him to her;
I mean to women of her way, ſuch tokens
Rather appeal as baits, than royal bounties:
I would not have it ſo.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: You will not find it,
Upon my troth I think his moſt ambition
Is but to let the world know h'as a handſom Miſtris:
Will your grace command me any ſervice to him?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Remember all my duty.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Bleſſings crown ye:
What's your will Lady?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Any thing that's honeſt;
And if you think it fit, ſo poor a ſervice,
Clad in a ragged vertue, may reach him,
I do beſeech your Lordſhip ſpeak it humbly.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Fa •• one I will: in the beſt phraſe I have too,
And ſo I kiſs your hand. Exit.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Your Lordſhips Servant.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Come hither wench, what art thou doing with that Ring?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I am looking on the poſie, Madam.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: What is't?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: The Jewel's ſet within.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: But where the joy wench,
When that inviſible Jewel's loſt? why doſt thou ſmile ſo?
What unhappy meaning haſt thou?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Nothing Madam.
But only thinking what ſtrange ſpells theſe Rings have,
And how they work with ſome.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I fear with you too.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: This could not coſt above a Crown.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Twill coſt you
The ſhaving of your crown, if not the waſhing.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: But he that ſent it, makes the vertue greater.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I and the vice too Madam: goodneſs bleſs me:
How ſit 'tis for my ſinger!

sp.speaker: 2 W.
sp.l: No doubt you'l find too
A finger fit for you.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Si •• ah, Peteſ • a,
What wilt thou give me for the good that follows this?
But thou haſt Rings enough, thou art provided:
Heigh ho, what muſt I doe now?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: You'l be taught that,
The eaſieſt part that e're you learn't, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Ay me, ay me.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: You will divide too, ſhortly,
Your voice comes finely forward.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Come hither wanton,
Thou art not ſurely as thou ſaiſt.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I would not:
But ſure there is a witchcraft in this Ring, Lady,
Lord how my heart leaps!

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Twill goe pit a pat ſhortly.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: And now methinks a thouſand of the Dukes ſhapes.

sp.speaker: 2 W.
sp.l: Will no leſs ſerve ye?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: In ten thouſand ſmiles.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs the wench.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: With eyes that will not be deni'd to enter;
And ſuch ſoft ſweet embraces; take it from me,
I am undone elſe Madam: I'm loſt elſe.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: What ailes the girle?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: How ſuddenly I 'm alter'd!
And grown my ſelf again! do not you feel it?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Wear that, and I'le wear this:
I'le try the ſtrength on't.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: How cold my bloud grows now!
Here's ſacred vertue:
When I leave to honour this,
Every hour to pay a kiſs,
When each morning I ariſe,
Or I forget a ſacrifice:
When this figure in my faith,
And the pureneſs that it hath,
I purſue not with my will,
Neater to arrive at ſtill:
When I loſe, or change this Jewel,
Flie me faith, and heaven be cruel.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: You have half confirm'd me,
Keep but that way ſure,
And what this charm can doe, let me endure. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA III.
div.stage: Enter Archas, Theodore, 2 Daughters Honora and Viola.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Carry your ſelf diſcreetly, it concerns me,
The Duke's come in, none of your froward paſſions,
Nor no diſtaſts to any: Prethee Theodor,
By my life, boy, 'twill ruine me.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I have done Sir,
So there be no foul play he brings along with him.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: What's that to you?
Let him bring what pleaſe him,
And whom, and how.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: So they mean well —

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Is't fit you be a Judge ſirrah?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: 'Tis fit I feel Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Get a banquet ready,
And trim your ſelves up handſomly.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: To what end?
Do you mean to make 'em whores?
Hang up a ſign than,
And ſet 'em out to Livery.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Whoſe ſon art thou?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Yours Sir, I hope: but not of your diſgraces.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Full twenty thouſand men I have commanded,
And all their minds, with this calm'd all their angers;
And ſhall a boy of mine own breed too, of mine own blood,
One crooked ſtick —

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Pray take your way, and thrive in't,
I'le quit your houſe; if taint or black diſhonour
Light on ye, 'tis your own, I have no ſhare in't.
Yet if it do fall out ſo, as I fear it,
And partly find it too —

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Haſt thou no reverence?
No dutie in thee?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: This ſhall ſhew I obey ye:
I dare not ſtay: I would have ſhew'd my love too,
And that you ask as duty, with my life Sir,
Had you but thought me worthy of your hazards,
Which heaven preſerve ye from, and keep the Duke too:
And there's an end of my wiſhes, God be with ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Stubborn, yet full of that we all love, honeſty.
Lord Burris, where's the Duke?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: In the great chamber Sir,
And there ſtayes till he ſee you, ye 'have a fine houſe here.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: A poor contented lodge, unfit for his preſence,
Yet all the joy it hath.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: I hope a great one, and for your good, brave Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I thank ye Lord:
And now my ſervice to the Duke.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: I'le wait on ye. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Duke, Boroskey, Gent. and Attendants.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: May this be credited?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Diſgrace me elſe,
And never more with favour look upon me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: It ſeems impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: It cannot chuſe Sir,
Till your own eyes behold it; but that it is ſo,
And that by this means the too haughtie Souldier
Has been ſo cramm'd and fed, he cares not for ye;
Believe, or let me periſh: Let your eyes
As you obſerve the houſe, but where I point it,
Make ſtay, and take a view, and then you have found it.

div.stage: Enter Archas, Burris, 2 Daughters, and Servant.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I'le follow your direction: welcome Archas,
You are welcome home brave Lord, we are come to viſit ye,
And thank ye for your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: 'Twas ſo poor Sir,
In true reſpect of what I owe your Highneſs,
It merits nothing.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Are theſe fair ones yours, Lord?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Their Mother made me think ſo Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Stand up Ladies:
Beſhrew my heart they are fair ones; methinks fitter
The luſtre of the Court, than thus live darken'd:
I would ſee your houſe Lord Archas, it appears to me
A handſom pile.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: 'Tis neat but no great ſtructure;
I'le be your Graces guide, give me the keyes there.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Lead on, we'l follow ye: begin with the Gallery,
I think that's one.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo, and't pleaſe ye, Sir,
The reſt above are lodgings all.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Go on, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: The Duke gone thither, do you ſay?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Yes marry do I,
And all the Ducklings too; but what they'll do there—

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: I hope they'll crown his ſervice.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: With a Cuſtard;
This is no weather for rewards: they crown his ſervice?
Rather they go to ſhave his Crown: I was rated
As if had been a Dog had worried Sheep, out of doors,
For making but a doubt.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: They muſt now grace him.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Mark but the end.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: I am ſure they ſhould reward him, they cannot want him.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: They that want honeſty, want any thing.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: The Duke is ſo noble in his own thoughts.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: That I grant ye,
If thoſe might only ſway him: but 'tis moſt certain,
So many new born Flies his light gave life to,
Buzze in his beams, Fleſh-flies, and Butterflies,
Hornets, and humming Scarabs, that not one honey Bee
That's loaden with true labour, and brings home
Encreaſe and Credit, can 'ſcape rifling,
And what ſhe ſucks for ſweet, they turn to bitterneſs.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Shall we go ſee what they do, and talk our mind to 'em?

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: That we have done too much, and to no purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Shall we be hang'd for him?
I have a great mind to be hang'd now
For doing ſome brave thing for him; a worſe end will take m •
And for an action of no worth; not honour him?
Upon my Conſcience, even the Devil, the very Devil
Not to belie him) thinks him an honeſt man,
I am ſure he has ſent him ſouls any time theſe twenty years,
A •• e to furniſh all his Fiſh-markets.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Leave thy talking,
And come, let's go to dinner and drink to him,
We ſhall hear more ere ſupper time: if he be honour'd,
He has deſerv'd it well, and we ſhall ſight for't:
If he be ruin'd, ſo, we know the worſt then,
And for my ſelf, I'll meet it.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: I ne'r fear it. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Archas, Boroskey, Burris, Gentlemen, and Attendants.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: They are handſome rooms all, well contriv'd and ſitted,
Full of convenience, the proſpect's excellent.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Now will your Grace paſs down, and do me but the honour
To taſte a Countrey Banquet?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What room's that?
I would ſee all now; what conveyance has it?
I ſee you have kept the beſt part yet; pray open it.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Ha! I miſdoubted this: 'tis of no receipt, Sir,
For your eyes moſt unfit—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I long to ſee it,
Becauſe I would judge of the whole piece: ſome excellent painting,
Or ſome rare ſpoils you would keep to entertain me
Another time, I know.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: In troth there is not,
Nor any thing worth your ſight; below I have
Some Fountains, and ſome Ponds.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I would ſee this now.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Boroskie, thou art a Knave; it contains nothing
But rubbiſh from the other rooms and unneceſſaries:
Will't pleaſe you ſee a ſtrange Clock?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: This or nothing: Little Trunk ready.
Why ſhould you bar it up thus with defences
Above the reſt, unleſs it contain'd ſomething
More excellent, and curious of keeping?
Open't, for I will ſee it.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: The Keys are loſt, Sir:
Does your Grace think if it were fit for you,
I could be ſo unmannerly?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I will ſee it, and either ſhew it—

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Good Sir—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Thank ye, Archas,
You ſhew your love abundantly,
Do I uſe to entreat thus? force it open.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: That were inhoſpitable; you are his Gueſt, Sir,
And with his greateſt joy, to entertain ye.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Hold thy peace, Fool; will ye open it?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Sir, I cannot.
I muſt not if I could.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Go, break it open.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I muſt withſtand that force: Be not too raſh, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Unarm him firſt, then if he be not obſtinate
Preſerve his life.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I thank your Grace, I take it;
And now take you the Keys, go in, and ſee, Sir;
There feed your eyes with wonder, and thank that Traytor,
That thing t • at f • lls his faith for favour. Exit Duke.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Sir, what moves ye?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I have kept mine pure: Lo d Burris, there's a Judas,
That for a ſmile will ſell ye all: a G •• tl • man?
A Whores heart more belief in't.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What's all this, Archas?
I cannot blame you to conceal it ſo,
I his moſt ineſtimable Treaſure.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Yours Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Nor do I wonder now the Souldier ſleights me.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Be not deceiv'd; he has had no favour here, Sir,
Not had you known this now, but for that Pick-thank,
The loſt man in his faith, he has reveal'd it,
To ſuck a little honey from ye has betray'd it.
I ſwear he ſmiles upon me, and forſworn too,
Thou crackt, uncurrant Lord: I'll tell ye all, Sir:
You • Sire, before his death, knowing your temper,
To be as bounteous as the air, and open,
As flowing as the Sea to all that follow'd ye,
Your great mind fit for War and Glory, thriftily
Like a great Husband to preſerve your actions,
Coll • cted all this treaſure; to our truſts,
To mine I mean, and to that long-tongu'd Lord's there,
He gave the knowledg and the charge of all this,
Upon his death-Bed too: And on the Sacrament
He ſwore us thus, never to let this Treaſure
Part f ••• ou • ſecret keepings, till no hope
Of Su ••• ct could relieve ye, all your own waſted,
No help of thoſe that lov'd ye could ſupply ye,
And then ſome great exploit a foot; my honeſty
I would have kept till I had made this uſeful;
I ſhew'd it, and I ſtood it to the tempeſt,
And uſeful to the end 'twas left: I am cozen'd,
And ſo are you too, if you ſpend this vainly;
This Worm that crept into ye has abus'd ye,
Abus'd your fathers care, abus'd his Faith too:
Nor can this maſs of money make him man more,
A flea'd Dog has more ſoul, an Ape more honeſty;
All mine ye have amongſt it, farewel that,
I cannot part with't nobler; my heart's clear,
My Conſcience ſmooth as that, no rub upon't:
But O thy Hell!

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: I ſeek no Heaven from you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Thy gnawin • Hell, Boroskey, it will find thee:
Would ye heap Coals upon his head has wrong'd ye,
Has ruin'd your eſ • ate? give him this money,
Melt it into his mouth.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What little Trunk's t •• t?
That there o'th' top, that's 〈◊〉 ?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: You'll find it rich, Si • ,
Richer I think than all.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: You were not covetous,
Not wont to weave your thoughts with ſuch a courſeneſs;
Pray • a • k not Honeſty.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Be ſure you ſee it.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Bring out the Trunk.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: You'll find that treaſure too,
A • l I have left me now.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What's this, a poor Gown?
And this a piece of Seneca?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Yes ſure, Sir,
More worth than all your Gold, yet ye have enough on't,
And of a Mine far purer, and more precious;
This ſells no friends, nor ſearches into counſels,
And yet all counſel, and all friends live here, Sir;
Betrays no Faith, yet handles all that's truſty:
Will't pleaſe you leave me this?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: With all my heart, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: What ſays your Lordſhip to't?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: I dare not rob ye.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Poor miſerable men, you have rob'd your ſelves both;
This Gown, and this unvalu'd Treaſure, your brave Father,
Found me a Child at School with, in his progreſs.
Where ſuch a love he took to ſome few anſwers,
Unhappy Boyiſh toys hit in my head then,
That ſuddenly I made him, thus as I was,
(For here was all the Wealth I brought his Highneſs)
He carried me to Court, there bred me up,
Beſtow'd his favours on me, taught me the Arms firſt,
With thoſe an honeſt mind, I ſerv'd him truly,
And where he gave me truſt, I think I fail'd not;
Let the World ſpeak: I humbly thank your Highneſs,
You have done more, and nobler, eas'd mine age, Sir;
And to this care a fair Quictus given,
Now to my Book again.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: You have your wiſh, Sir,
Let ſome bring off the treaſure.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Some is his, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: None, none, a poor unworthy reaper,
The Harveſt is his Graces.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Thank you, Archas.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: But will not you repent, Lord? when this is gone
Where will your Lordſhip?—

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Pray take you no care, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Does your Grace like my Houſe?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Wondrous well, Archas,
You have made me richly welcome.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I did my beſt, Sir.
Is there any thing elſe may pleaſe your Grace?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Your Daughters
I had forgot, ſend them to Court.

sp.speaker: Arc
sp.l: How's that, Sir?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I ſaid your Daughters; ſee it done: I'll have 'em
Attend my Siſter, Archas.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Thank your Highneſs.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And ſuddenly. Exit.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Through all the ways I dare,
I'll ſerve your temper, though you try me far. Exit.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Theodore, Putskey, Ancient and Servant.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I wonder we hear no news.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Here's your fathers ſervant,
He comes in haſte too, now we ſhall know all, Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: How now?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I am glad I have met you, Sir; your father
Intreats you preſently make haſte unto him.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What news?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: None of the beſt, Sir, I am aſham'd to tell it,
Pray ask no more.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Did not I tell ye, Gentlemen?
Did not I propheſie? he's undone then.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Not ſo, Sir, but as near it—

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: There's no help now;
The Army's ſcatter'd all, through diſcontent,
Not to be rallied up in haſte to help this.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Plague of the Devil; have ye watch'd your ſeaſons?
We ſhall watch you ere long.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Farewel, there's no cure,
We muſt endure all now: I know what I'll do.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Nay, there's no ſtriving, they have a hand upon us,
A heavy and a hard one.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Now I have it,
We have yet ſome Gentlemen, ſome Boys of mettle,
(What, are we bob'd thus ſtill, colted, and carted?)
And one mad trick we'll have to ſhame theſe Vipers,
Shall I bleſs 'em?

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Farewel; I have thought my way too. Exit

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Were never ſuch rare Cries in Chriſtendome,
As Moſco ſhall afford: we'll live by fooling
Now fighting's gone, and they ſhall find and feel it. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: No more, it muſt be ſo; do you think I would ſend ye,
Your father and your friend—

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Pray Sir, be good to us,
Alas, we know no Court, nor ſeek that knowledge;
We are content with harmleſs things at home,
Children of your content, bred up in quiet,
Only to know our ſelves, to ſeek a Wiſedome
From that we underſtand, eaſie and honeſt;
To make our actions worthy of your Honour,
Their ends as innocent as we begot 'em;
What ſhall we look for Sir, what ſhall we learn there,
That this more private ſweetneſs cannot teach us?
Vertue was never built upon ambition,
Nor the Souls Beauties bred out of Bravery:
What a terrible Father would you ſeem to us,
Now you have moulded us, and wrought our tempers
To eaſie and obedient ways, uncrooked,
Where the fair mind can never loſe nor loiter,
Now to divert our Natures, now to ſtem us
Roughly againſt the tide of all this treaſure?
Would ye have us proud? 'tis ſooner bred than buried;
Wickedly proud? for ſuch things dwell at Court, Sir.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Would ye have your Children learn to forget their father,
And when he dies dance on his Monument?
Shall we ſeek Vertue in a Sattin Gown;
Embroider'd Vertue? Faith in a well-curl'd Feather?
And ſet our Credits to the tune of green ſleeves?
This may be done; and if you like, it ſhall be.
You ſhould have ſent us thither when we were younger,
Our maiden-heads at a higher rate; our Innocence
Able to make a Mart indeed: we are now too old, Sir,
Perhaps they'll think too cunning too, and ſlight us;
Beſides, we are altogether unprovided,
Unfurniſht utterly of the rules ſhould guide us:
This Lord comes, licks his hand, and proteſts to me;
Compares my Beauty to a thouſand fine things;
Mountains, and Fountains, Trees, and Stars, and Goblins;
Now have not I the faith for to believe him;
He offers me the honourable courteſie,
To lye with me all night, what a miſery is this?
I am bred up ſo fooliſhly, alas, I dare not,
And how madly theſe things will ſhew there.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I ſend ye not,
Like parts infected, to draw more corruption;
Like Spiders to grow great, with growing evil:
With your own Vertues ſeaſon'd, and my prayers,
The Card of goodneſs in your minds, that ſhows ye
When ye ſail falſe; the needle toucht with honour,
That through the blackeſt ſtorms, ſtill points at happineſs;
Your Bodies the tall barks, rib'd round with goodneſs,
Your Heavenly Souls the Pilots, thus I ſend you;
Thus I prepare your Voyage; found before ye,
And ever as you fail through this Worlds Vanity,
D • ſcover Sholes, Rocks, Quickſands, cry out to ye,
Like a good Maſter tack about for Honour:
The Court is Vertue's School, at leaſt it ſhould be;
Nearer the Sun the Mine lies, the metal's purer:
Be it granted, if the ſpring be once infected,
Thoſe Branches that flow from him muſt run muddy;
Say you find ſome Sins there, and thoſe no ſmall ones,
And they like lazie fits begin to ſhake ye:
Say they affect your ſtrengths, my happy Children,
Great things through greateſt hazards are atchiev'd ſtill,
And then they ſhine, then goodneſs has his glory,
His Crown faſt rivetted, then time moves under,
Where, through the miſt of errors, like the Sun,
Through thick and pitchy Clouds, he breaks out nobly.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: I thank you Sir, you have made me half a Souldier,
I will to Court moſt willingly, moſt fondly.
And if there be ſuch ſtirring things amongſt 'em,
Such Travellers into Virginia
As Fame reports, if they can win me, take me;
I think I have a cloſe Ward, and a ſure one;
An honeſt mind I hope, 'tis petticoat-proof,
Chain proof, and Jewel-proof; I know 'tis Gold-proof,
A Coach and four Horſes cannot draw me from it:
As for your handſome Faces, and filed Tongues,
Curl'd Millers heads, I have another word for them,
And yet I'll flatter too, as faſt as they do,
And lye, but not as lewdly; Come, be valiant, Siſter,
She that dares not ſtand the puſh o'th' Court, dares nothing,
And yet come off ungraced: Sir, like you,
We both affect great dangers now, and the World ſhall ſee
All glory lies not in Mans Victorie.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Mine own Honora.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I am very fearful,
Would I were ſtronger built: you would have me honeſt?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Or not at all my Viola.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I'll think on't,
For 'tis no eaſie promiſe, and live there:
Do you think we ſhall do well?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Why, what ſhould aile us?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Certain they'll tempt us ſtrongly; beſide the glory
Which Women may affect, they are handſom Gentlemen,
Every part ſpeaks: nor is it one denial,
Not two, nor ten; from every look we give 'em,
They'll frame a hope; even from our prayers, promiſes.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Let 'em feed ſo, and be fat; there is no fear, wench,
Is thou beeſt faſt to thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: I hope I ſhall be;
And your example will work more.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not want it.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: How do you, Sir? can you lend a man an Angel?
I hear you let out money.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Very well, Sir,
You are pleaſantly diſpos'd: I am glad to ſee it.
Can you lend me your patience, and be rul'd by me?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Is't come to patience now?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Is't not a Vertue?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I know not: I ne'r found it ſo.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: That's becauſe
Thy anger ever knows, and not thy judgment.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I know you have been riſl'd.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Nothing leſs, Boy;
Lord, what opinions theſe vain People publiſh!
Rifi'd of what?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Study your Vertue, Patience,
It may get Muſtard to your Meat. Why in ſuch haſte, Sir,
Sent ye for me?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: For this end only, Theodore,
To wait upon your Siſters to the Court;
I am commanded they live there.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: To th' Court, Sir?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: To th' Court I ſay.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: And muſt I wait upon 'em?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Yes, 'tis moſt fit you ſhould, you are their Brother.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Is this the buſineſs? I had thought your mind, Sir,
Had been ſet forward on ſome noble action,
Something had truly ſtir'd ye. To th' Court with theſe?
Why, they are your Daughters, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: All this I know, Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: The good old Woman on a Bed he threw
To th' Court?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Thou art mad.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Nor drunk as you are:
Drunk with your duty, Sir: do you call it duty?
A pox of duty, what can theſe do there?
What ••• uld they do? Can ye look Babies, Siſters,
• n the young Gallants eyes, and twirl their Band ſtrings?
Can ye ride out to air your ſelves? Pray Sir,
Be ſerious with me, do you ſpeak this truly?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Why, didſt thou never hear of Women
Yet at Court, Boy?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Yes, and good Women too, very good Women,
Excellent honeſt Women: but are you ſure, Sir,
That theſe will prove ſo?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: There's the danger, Brother.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: God a mercy Wench, thou haſt a grudging of it.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Now be you ſerious, Sir, and obſerve what I ſay,
Do it, and do it handſomly; go with 'em.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: With all my heart, Sir; I am in no fault now;
If they be thought Whores for being in my Company;
Pray write upon their Backs, they are my Siſters,
And where I ſhall deliver 'em.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Ye are wondrous jocund,
But prithee tell me, art thou ſo lewd a Fellow?
I never knew thee fail a truth.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I am a Souldier,
And ſpell you what that means.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: A Souldier?
What doſt thou make of me?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Your Palate's down, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I thank ye, Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Come, ſhall we to this matter?
You will to Court?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: If you will pleaſe to honour us.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I'll honour ye, I warrant; I'll ſet ye off
With ſuch a luſtre, Wenches; alas poor Viola,
Thou art a fool, thou crieſt for eating white bread:
Be a good Huſwife of thy tears, and ſave 'em,
Thou wilt have time enough to ſhed 'em, Siſter.
Do you weep too? nay, then I'll fool no more.
Come worthy Siſters, ſince it muſt be ſo,
And ſince he thinks it fit to try your Vertues,
Be you as ſtrong to truth, as I to guard ye,
And this old Gentleman ſhall have joy of ye. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Burris take you ten thouſand of thoſe Crowns,
And thoſe two Chains of Pearl they hold the richeſt,
I give 'em ye.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: I humbly thank your Grace;
And may your great example work in me
That noble Charity to men more worthy,
And of more wants.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: You bear a good mind, Burris;
Take twenty thouſand now: be not ſo modeſt,
It ſhall be ſo, I give 'em: go, there's my ring for't.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs your Highneſs ever. Exit.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: You are honeſt.

div.stage: Enter Alinda, and Putskey at door.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: They're coming now to Court, as fair as vertue:
Two brighter Stars ne'er roſe here.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Pe • ce, I have it,
And what my Art can do; the Duke—
I am gone,
Re ••••• r • . Exit.

sp.speaker: Alin
sp.l: I am counſell'd to the full, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: My pretty Miſtris, whither lyes your buſineſs?
How kindly I ſhould take this, were it to me now?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs immediately to your Grace,
At this tim • .

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: You have no addreſs, I do believe ye,
I would ye had.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: 'Twere too much boldneſs, Sir,
Upon ſo little knowledge, leſs deſerving.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: You'll make a perfect Courtier.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: A very poor one.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: A very fun one, ſweet, come hither to me.
What killing eyes this Wench has? in his glory
Not the bright Sun, when the Si • tan Star reigns,
Shines half ſo fiery.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Why does your Grace ſo view me?
Nothing but common handſomneſs dwells here, Sir,
Scarce that: your Grace is pleas'd to mock my meanneſs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not go. I do not lie unto thee,
In my eye thou appear'ſt

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Dim not the ſight, Sir,
I am too dull an obj • ct.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Canſt thou love me?
Canſt thou love him will honour thee?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I can love,
And love as you do too: but 'twill not ſhew well:
Or if it do ſhew here where all light luſtres,
• inſel affections make a glorious gliſtering,
'Twill halt i'th' handſom way.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Are ye ſo cunning?
Doſt think I love not truly?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: No, ye cannot,
You never travel'd that way yet: pray pardon me,
I praie ſo boldly to you.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: There's no harm done.
But what's your reaſon, ſweet?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I would tell your Grace,
But happily—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: It ſhall be pleaſing to me.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I ſhould love you again, and then you would hate me.
With all my ſervice I ſhould follow ye,
And through all dangers.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: This would more provoke me,
More make me ſee thy worths,
More make me meet 'em.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: You ſhould do ſo, if ye did well and truly:
But though ye be a Prince, and have power in ye,
Power of example too, ye have ſail'd and ſalter'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Give me example where?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: You had a Miſtris,
Oh Heaven, ſo bright, ſo brave a dame, ſo lovely,
In all her life ſo true!

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: A Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: That ſerv'd you with that conſtancy, that care,
That lov'd your will, and woo'd it too.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: That not s'd your honour up, held faſt your vertue,
And when ſhe kill encreas'd, not ſtole your goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And I neglected her?
Loſt her, forſook her,
Wantonly ſlung her off.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What was her name?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Her name as lovely as her ſelf, as noble,
And in it all that's excellent.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What was it?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Her name was Beau deſert:
Do you know her now, Sir?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Beau-deſert? I do not remember—

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I know you do not;
Yet ſhe has a plainer name; Lord Archas ſervice;
Do you yet remember her? there was a Miſtris
Fairer than Woman, far fonder to you, Sir,
Than Mothers to their firſt-born joyes: Can you love?
Dare you profeſs that truth to me a ſtranger,
A thing of no regard, no name, no luſtre,
When your moſt noble love you have neglected,
A beauty all the world would woo and honour?
Would you have me credit this? think you can love me,
And hold ye conſtant, when I have read this ſtory?
Is't poſſible you ſhould ever favour me,
To a ſlight pleaſure prove a friend, and faſt too,
When, where you were moſt ty'd, moſt bound to benefit,
Bound by the chains of honeſty and honour,
You have broke and boldly too? I am a weak one,
Arm'd only with my fears: I beſeech your Grace
Tempt me no further.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Who taught you this Leſſon?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Woful experience, Sir: if you ſeek a fair one,
Worthy your love, if yet you have that perfect,
Two Daughters of his ruin'd vertue now
Arrive at Court, excellent fair indeed, Sir,
But this will be the Plague on't, they're excellent honeſt

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I love thy face.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Upon my life ye cannot:
I do not love it my ſelf, Sir, 'tis a lewd one,
So truly ill Art cannot mend it; but if 'twere handſome,
At leaſt if I thought ſo, you ſhould hear me talk, Sir,
In a new ſtrain; and though ye are a Prince,
Make ye Petition to me too, and wait my anſwers;
Yet o' my Conſcience I ſhould pity ye,
After ſome ten years ſiege.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Prethee do now.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: What would ye do?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Why I would lye with ye.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I do not think ye would.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: In troth I would Wench.
Here, take this Jewel.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Out upon't, that's ſcurvy.
Nay, if we do, ſure we'll do for good fellowſhip,
For pure love, or nothing: thus you ſhall be ſure, Sir,
You ſhall not pay too dear for't.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Sure I cannot.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: By'r Lady but ye may: when ye have found me able
To do your work well, ye may pay my wages.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Why does your Grace ſtart back?

sp.speaker: Olym
sp.l: I ha' ſeen that ſhakes me:
Chills all my bloud: O where is faith or goodneſs?
Alinda thou art falſe, falſe, falſe thou fair one,
Wickedneſs falſe; and (wo is me) I ſee it.
For ever falſe.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I am glad 't has taken thus right. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I'le go ask my Lady, Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Whether I ſhall lye with ye, or no: If I find her willing—
For look ye Sir, I have ſworn, while I am in her ſervice—
('Twas a raſh Oath I muſt confeſs.)

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Thou mockſt me.

sp.speaker: Alin.
