sp.l: Why, would ye lye with me, if I were willing?
Would you abuſe my weakneſs?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I would piece it,
And make it ſtronger.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I humbly thank your highneſs,
When you piece me, you muſt piece me to my Coffin:
When you have got my Maiden-head, I take it,
'Tis not an inch of an Apes tail will reſtore it,
I love ye, and I honour ye, but this way
I'le neither love nor ſerve ye.
Heaven change your mind, Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And thine too:
For it muſt be chang'd, it ſhall be. Exit.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter Boroskie, Burris, Theodore, Viola and Honora.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: They are goodly Gentlewomen.
They are,
Wondrous ſweet Women both.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Does your Lordſhip like 'em?
They are my Siſters, Sir; good luſty Laſſes,
They'll do their labour well, I warrant ye,
You'll find no Bed-ſtraw here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Thank ye Brother.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: This is not ſo ſtrongly built: but ſhe is good mettle,
Of a good ſtirring ſtrain too: ſhe goes tith, Sir.
Here they be, Gentlemen, muſt make ye merry,
The toyes you wot of: do you like their complexions?
They be no Moors: what think ye of this hand, Gentlemen?
Here's a white Altar for your ſacrifice:
A thouſand kiſſes here. Nay, keep off yet Gentlemen,
Let's ſtart firſt, and have fair play: what would ye give now
To turn the Globe up, and find the rich Moluccas?
To paſs the ſtraights? here (do ye itch) by St Nicholas,
Here's that will make ye ſcratch and claw,
Claw my fine Gentlemen, move ye in divers ſorts:
Pray ye let me requeſt ye, to forget
To ſay your prayers, whileſt theſe are Courtiers;
Or if ye needs will think of Heaven, let it be no higher
Than their eyes.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: How will ye have 'em beſtow'd, Sir?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Even how your Lordſhip pleaſe,
So you do not bake 'em.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Bake 'em?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: They are too high a meat that way, they run to gelly.
But if you'll have 'em for your own diet, take my counſel,
••• w 'em between two Feather-beds.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Pleaſe you Colonel
To let 'em wait upon the Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Yes, Sir,
And thank your honour too: but then happily,
Theſe noble Gentlemen ſhall have no acceſs to 'em,
And to have 'em buy new Cloaths, ſtudy new faces,
And keep a ſtinking ſtir with themſelves for nothing,
'Twill not be well i'faith: they have kept their bodies,
And been at charge for Bathes: do you ſee that ſhirt there?
Weigh but the moral meaning, 'twill be grievous:
Alas, I brought 'em to delight theſe Gentlemen,
I weigh their wants by mine: I brought 'em wholeſome,
Wholeſome, and young my Lord, and two ſuch bleſſings
They will not light upon again in ten years.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: 'Tis fit they wait upon her.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: They are fit for any thing:
They'll wait upon a man, they are not baſhful,
Carry his Cloak, or unty his points, or any thing,
Drink drunk, and take Tobacco; the familiar'ſt fools—
This wench will leap over Stools too, and ſound a Trumpet,
Wraſtle, and pitch the Bar; they are finely brought up.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Ladies, ye are bound to your Brother,
And have much cauſe to thank him:
I'le eaſe ye of this charge, and to the Princeſs,
So pleaſe you, I'le attend 'em.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Thank your Lordſhip:
If there be e're a private corner as ye go, Sir,
A fooliſh lobbie out o'th' way, make danger,
Try what they are, try—

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Ye are a merry Gentleman.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I would fain be your honours kinſman.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Ye are too curſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Farewel wenches, keep cloſe your ports, y'are waſht elſe.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Brother, beſtow your fears where they are needful.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Honor thy name is, and I hope thy Nature.
Go after, Gentlemen, go, get a ſnatch if you can,
Yond' old Erra Pater will never pleaſe 'em.
Alas I brought 'em for you, but ſee the luck on't,
I ſwear I meant as honeſtly toward ye—
Nay do not cry good Gentlemen: a little counſel
Will do no harm: they'll walk abroad i'th' Evenings,
Ye may ſurprize 'em eaſily, they wear no Piſtols.
Set down your minds in Metre, flowing Metre,
And get ſome good old linnen Woman to deliver it,
That has the trick on't: you cannot fail:
Farewel Gentlemen. Exeunt Gent.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: You have frighted off theſe fleſh flies.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Fleſh-flies indeed my Lord.
And it muſt be very ſtinking fleſh they will not ſeize on.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Your Lordſhip bid me bring this Casket.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Yes, Good Colonel
Commend me to your worthy Father, and as a pledge
He ever holds my love, and ſervice to him,
Deliver him this poor, but hearty token,
And where I may be his—

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Ye are too noble;
A wonder here my Lord, that dare be honeſt,
When all men hold it vitious: I ſhall deliver it,

And with it your moſt noble love. Your ſervant.
Ex. Bur.
Were there but two more ſuch at Court, 'twere Sainted,
This will buy Brawn this Chriſtmas yet, and Muſcadine. Ex.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Enter Ancient, crying Brooms, and after him ſeverally, four Souldiers, crying other things. Boroskie and Gent. over the Stage obſerving them.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Broom, Broom, the bonnie Broom,
Come buy my Birchen Broom,
I'th' Wars we have no more room,
Buy all my bonnie Broom,
For a kiſs take two;
If thoſe will not do,
For a little, little pleaſure,
Take all my whole treaſure:
If all theſe will not do't,
Take the Broom-man to boot.
Broom, Broom, the bonnie Broom.

sp.speaker: 1 Soul.
sp.l: The Wars are done and gone,
And Souldiers now neglected, Pedlers are,
Come Maidens, come alone,
For I can ſhow you handſome, handſome ware;
Powders for, for the head,
And drinks for your bed,
To make ye blith and bonney.
As well in the night we Souldiers can fight,
And pleaſe a young wench as any.

sp.speaker: 2 Soul.
sp.l: I have fine Potato's,
Ripe Potato's.

sp.speaker: 3 Soul.
sp.l: Will ye buy any Honeſty, come away,
I ſell it openly by day,
I bring no forced light, nor no Candle
To cozen ye; come buy and handle:
This will ſhew the great man good,
The Tradeſman where he ſwears and lyes,
Each Lady of a noble bloud,
The City dame to rule her eyes:
Ye are rich men now: come buy, and then
I'le make ye richer, honeſt men.

sp.speaker: 4 Sol.
sp.l: Have ye any crackt maiden-heads, to new leach or mend?
Have ye any old maiden heads to ſell or to change?
Bring 'em to me with a little pretty gin,
I'le clout 'em, I'le mend 'em, I'le knock in a pin,
Shall make 'em as good maids agen,
As ever they have been.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: What means all this, why do y'ſell Brooms Ancient?
Is it in wantonneſs, or want?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: The only reaſon is,
To ſweep your Lordſhips conſcience: here's one for the nonce.
Gape Sir, you have ſwallowed many a goodlier matter—
The only caſting for a crazie conſcience.

sp.speaker: 3 Sol.
sp.l: Will your Lordſhip buy any honeſtie? 'twill be worth your mony.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: How is this?

sp.speaker: 3 Sol.
sp.l: Honeſtie my Lord, 'tis here in a quill.
Take heed you open it not, for 'tis ſo ſubtle,
The leaſt puffe of wind will blow it out o'th' Kingdom.

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: Will your Lordſhip pleaſe to taſte a fine Potato?
'Twill advance your wither'd ſtate.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Fill your honour full of moſt noble itches,
And make Jack dance in your Lordſhips breeches.

l.hi: If your Daughters on their beds,
Have bow'd, or crackt their maiden-heads;
If in a Coach with two much tumbling,
They chance to crie, fie, fo, what fumbling;
If her foot ſtip, and down fall ſhe,
And break her leg 'bove the knee,
The one and thirtieth of Februarie let this beta'ne,
And they ſhall be arrant maids again.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Ye are brave Souldiers; keep your wantonneſs,
A winter will come on to ſhake this wilfulneſs.
Diſport your ſelves, and when you want your mony—

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Broom, Broom, &c. Exeunt Singing.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: You muſt not be of a • fu ••• little one,
〈◊〉 Lady on ſo ſad, you will ne're make Courtiers
With theſe dull ſullen thoughts; this place is pleaſure,
Preſerv'd to that uſe, ſo inhabited;
And theſe that live here, live delightfull, joyfull:
Theſ • are the Gardens of Adonis, Ladies,
Where all ſweets to their free and noble uſes,
•• ow ever young and courted.

sp.speaker: Hon
sp.l: Bleſs me Heaven,
Can things of her years arrive at theſe rudiments?
By your leave fair Gentlewoman, how long have you been here?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Faith much about a week.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: You have ſtudi d hard,
And by my faith arriv'd at a great knowledge.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Were not you baſhfull at firſt?
I, I, for an hour or two:
But when I ſaw people laugh'd at me for it,
And thought it a dull breeding —

sp.speaker: Hon
sp.l: You are govern'd here then
Much after the mens opinions.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Ever Lady.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: And what they think is honourable.—

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Moſt preciſely
We follow with all faith.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: A goodly Catechiſme.
But baſhfull for an hour or two?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Faith to ſay true,
I do not think I was ſo long: for look ye,
'Tis to not end here, put on what ſhape ye will,
And ſome your ſelf with ne're ſo much auſteritie,
You ſhall be courted in the ſame, and won too,
'Tis but ſome two hours more; and ſo much time loſt,
Which we hold pretious here: In ſo much time now
As I have told you this, you may loſe a Servant,
Your age, nor all your Art can e're recover.
Catch me occaſion as ſhe comes, hold faſt there,
Till what you do affect is ripn'd to ye.
Has the Duke ſeen ye yet?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: What if he have not?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: You do your beauties too much wrong, appearing
So full of ſweetneſs, newneſs; ſet ſo richly,
As if a Counſel beyond nature fram'd ye.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: If we were thus, ſay heaven had given theſe b • eſſings
Muſt we turn theſe to ſin oblations?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: How fooliſhly this Countrey way ſhews in ye?
How full of ſlegm? do you come here to pray, Ladies?
You had beſt cry, ſtand away, let me alone Gentlemen,
I'le tell my Father elſe.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: This woman's naught ſure,
A very naughtie woman.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Come, ſay on friend,
I'le be inſtructed by ye.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: You'l thank me for't.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Either I or the devil ſhall: The Duke you were ſp • aking of

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: 'Tis well remembred: yes, let him firſt ſee you,
Appear not openly till he has view'd ye.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: He's a very noble Prince they ſay.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: O wondrous gracious;
And as you may deliver your ſelf at the firſt viewing.
For look ye, you muſt bear your ſelf; yet take heed
It be ſo ſeaſon'd with a ſweet humilitie,
And grac'd with ſuch a bountie in your beautie —

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: But I hope he will offer me no ill?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: No, no:
'Tis like he will kiſs ye, and play with ye.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Play with me, how?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Why, good Lord, that you are ſuch a fool now!
No harm aſſure your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Will he play with me too?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Look babies in your eyes, my prettie ſweet one:
There's a fine ſport: do you know your lodgings yet?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: I hear of none.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I do then, they are handſom,
Convenient for acceſs.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Acceſs?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Yes little one,
For viſitation of thoſe friends and Servants,
Your beauties ſhall make choice of: friends and viſits:
Do not you know thoſe uſes? Alas poor novice;
There's a cloſe Cowch or two, handſomely placed too.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: What are thoſe I pray you?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Who would be troubled with ſuch raw things? they are to lie upon.
And your love by ye; and diſcourſe, and toy in.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Alas I have no love.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: You muſt by any means:
You'l have a hundred, fear not.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Honeſtie keep me:
What ſhall I doe with all thoſe?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: You'l find uſes:
Ye are ignorant yet, let time work; you muſt learn too,
To lie handſomly in your bed a mornings, neatly dreſt
In a moſt curious Waſtcoat, to ſet ye off well,
Play with your Bracelets, ſing: you muſt learn to rhime too,
And riddle neatly; ſtudie the hardeſt language,
And 'tis no matter whether it be ſenſe, or no,
So it go ſeemlie off. Be ſure ye profit
In kiſſing, kiſſing ſweetly: there lies a main point,
A key that opens to all practick pleaſure;
I'le help ye to a friend of mine ſhall teach ye,
And ſuddenlie: your Country way is fulſome.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Have ye ſchools for all theſe myſteries?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: O yes,
And ſeveral hours prefix'd to ſtudie in:
Ye may have Kalenders to know the good hour,
And when to take a jewel: for the ill too,
When to refuſe, with obſervations on 'em;
Under what Sign 'tis beſt meeting in an Arbor,
And in what Bower, and hour it works; a thouſand,
When in a Coach, when in a private lodging,
With all their vertues.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Have ye ſtudied theſe?
How beaſtly they become your youth? how bawdily?
A woman of your tenderneſs, a teacher,
Teacher of theſe lewd Arts? of your full beauty?
A man made up in luſt would loath this in ye:
The rankeſt Leacher, hate ſuch impudence.
They ſay the Devil can aſſume heavens brightneſs,
And ſo appear to tempt us: ſure thou art no woman.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I joy to find ye thus.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Thou haſt no tenderneſs,
No reluctation in thy heart: 'tis miſchief.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: All's one for that; read theſe and then be ſatisfi'd,
A few more private rules I have gather'd for ye,
Read 'em, and well obſerve 'em: ſo I leave ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: A wondorus wicked woman: ſhame go with thee.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: What new Pandoras box is this? I'le ſee it,
Though preſently I tear it. Read Thine Viola,
'Tis in our own wills to believe and follow.

lg.l: Worthy Honora, as you have begun
In vertues ſpotleſs ſchool, ſo forward run:
Purſue that nobleneſs, and chaſte deſire
You ever had, burn in that holy fire;
And a white Martyr to fair memorie
Give up your name, unſoil'd of infamy.

sp.l: How's this? Read yours out Siſter: this amazes me.

l.hi: Fear not thou yet unblaſted Violet,
Nor let my wanton words a doubt beget,
Live in that peace and ſweetneſs of thy bud,
Remember whoſe thou art, and grow ſtill good,
Remember what thou art, and ſtand a ſtorie
Fit for thy noble Sex, and thine own glorie.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: I know not what to think.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Sure a good woman,
An excellent woman, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: It confounds me;
Let 'em uſe all their arts, if theſe be their ends,
The Court I ſay breeds the beſt foes and friends.
Come, let's be honeſt wench, and doe our beſt ſervice.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: A moſt excellent woman, I will love her.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Olympia, with a Casket, and Alinda.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: MAdam, the Duke has ſent for the two Ladies.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: I prethee go: I know thy thoughts are with him.
Go, go Alinda, do not mock me more.
I have found thy heart wench, do not wrong thy Miſtris,
Thy too much loving Miſtris: do not abuſe her.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: By your own fair hands I underſtand ye not.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: By thy own fair eyes I underſtand thee too much,
Too far, and built a faith there thou haſt ruin'd.
Goe, and enjoy thy wiſh, thy youth, thy pleaſure,
E •• oy the greatneſs no doubt he has promiſed,
E • joy the ſervice of all eyes that ſee thee,
The glory thou haſt aim'd at, and the triumph:
Only this laſt love I ask, forget thy Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Oh, who has wrong'd me? who has ruin'd me?
Poor wretched Girle, what poyſon is ſlung on thee?
Excellent vertue, from whence flows this anger?

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Go, ask my Brother, ask the faith thou gav'ſt me,
Ask all my favours to thee, ask my love,
Laſt, thy forgetfulneſs of good: then flye me,
For we muſt part Alinda

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: You are weaty of me;
I muſt confeſs, I was never worth your ſervice,
Your bounteous favours leſs, but that my duty,
My ready will, and all I had to ſerve ye —
O Heaven thou know'ſt my honeſtie.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: No more:
Take heed, heaven has a juſtice: take this ring with ye,
This doting ſpell you gave me: too well Alinda,
Thou knew'ſt the vertue in't; too well I feel it:
Nay keep that too, it may ſometimes remember ye,
When you are willing to forget who gave it,
And to what vertuous end.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Muſt I goe from ye?
Of all the ſorrows ſorrow has—muſt I part with ye?
Part with my noble Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Or I with thee wench.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: And part ſtain'd with opinion? Farewel Lady,
Happy and bleſſed Lady, goodneſs keep ye:
Thus your poor Servant full of grief turns from ye,
For ever full of grief, for ever from ye.
I have no being now, no friends, no Country,
I wander heaven knows whither, heaven knows how.
No life, now you are loſt: only mine innocence,
That little left me of my ſelf, goes with me,
That's all my bread and comfort. I confeſs Madam,
Truely confeſs, the Duke has often courted me.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: And pour'd his Soul into thee, won thee

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Do you think ſo?
Well, time that told this tale, will tell my truth too,
And ſay ye had a faithfull, honeſt Servant:
The buſineſs of my life is now 〈◊〉 pray for ye,
Pray for your vertuous loves; Pray for your children,
When Heaven ſhall make ye happy.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: How ſhe wounds me!
Either I am undone, or ſhe muſt go: take theſe with ye,
Some toyes may doe ye ſervice; and this mony;
And when ye want, I love ye not ſo poorly,
Not yet Alinda, that I would ſee ye periſh.
Prethee be good, and let me hear: look on me,
I love thoſe eyes yet dearly; I have kiſs'd thee,
And now I'le doe't again: Farewel Alinda,
I am too full to ſpeak more, and too wretched. Exit.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: You have my faith,
And all the world my fortune. Exit.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I would fain hear
What becomes of theſe two Wenches:
And if I can, I will doe 'em good.
sp.stage: Enter Gentleman, paſſing over the Stage.
sp.l: Do you hear my honeſt friend?
He knows no ſuch name:
What a world of buſineſs,
Which by interpretation are meer nothings,
Theſe things have here? 'Maſs now I think on't better,
I wiſh he be not ſent for one of them
To ſome of theſe by-lodgings: me thought I ſaw
A kind of reference in his face to Bawderie.
sp.stage: Enter Gentleman, with a Gentlewoman, paſſing over the Stage.
sp.l: He has her, but 'tis none of them: hold faſt thief:
An excellent touzing knave. Miſtris
You are to ſuffer your penance ſome half hour hence now.
How far a fine Court Cuſtard with Plums in it
Will prevail with one of theſe waiting Gentlewomen,
They are taken with theſe ſoluble things exceedingly;
This is ſome yeoman o'th' bottles now that has ſent for her,
〈…〉 calls Father: now woe to this Ale incenſe.
By your leave Sir.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Well Sir; what's your pleaſure with me?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: You do not know the way to the maids lodgings?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes indeed do I Sir.

sp.speaker: The
sp.l: But you will not tell me?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: No indeed will not I, becauſe you doubt it. Exit.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Theſe are fine gim-cracks: hey, here comes another,
A Flagon full of wine in's hand, I take it.
Well met my friend, is that wine?

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: Yes indeed is it.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Faith I'le drink on't then.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: Ye may, becauſe ye have ſworn Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: 'Tis very good, I'le drink a great deal now Sir.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: I cannot help it Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I'le drink more yet.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis in your own hands.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: There's your pot, I thank ye.
Pray let me drink again.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: Faith but ye ſhall not.
Now have I ſworn I take it. Fare ye well Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: This is the ſin'ſt place to live in I e're enter'd.
Here comes a Gentlewoman, and alone; I'le to her.
Madam, my Lord my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Who's your Lord Sir?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: The Lord Boroskey, Lady.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Pray excuſe me:
Here's ſomething for your •• ns: within this hour Sir,
One of the choice young Ladies ſhall attend him:
Pray let it be in that Chamber juts out to the water;
'Tis private and convenient: doe my humble ſ • rvice
To my honourable good Lord, I beſeech ye Sir;
If • t pleaſe you to viſit a poor Lady
You ca •• ie the' haviour of a noble Gentleman.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I ſhall be bold.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: 'Tis a good aptneſs in ye.
I lye here in the Wood-yard, the blue lodgings Sir;
They call me merrily the Lady of the — Sir;
A little I know what belongs to a Gentleman,
And if it pleaſe you take the pains. Exit.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: De • Lady, take the pains?
Why a horſe would not take the pains that thou requir'ſt now,
To cleave old crab tree: one of the choice young Ladies?
I would I had let this Bawd goe, ſhe has frighted me;
I am cruelly afraid of one of my Tribe now;
But if they will doe, the Devil cannot ſtop 'em.
Why ſhould he have a young Lady? are women now
O'th' nature of Bottles, to be ſtopt with Corks?
O the thouſand little furies that flye here now?
How now Captain?

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: I come to ſeek you out Sir,
And all the Town I have travell'd.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What's the news man:

sp.speaker: Putſ
sp.l: That that concerns us all, and very nearly:
The Duke this night holds a great ſcaſt at Court,
To which he bids for gueſts all his old Counſellors,
And all his favourites: your Father's ſent for.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Why he is neither in council, nor in favour.
That's it: have an eye now, or never, and a quick one,
An eye that muſt not wink from good intelligence.
I heard a B • d ſing, they mean him no good office.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Art ſu • e he ſups here?

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Su • e as 'tis day.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: 'Tis like then:
How now, where haſt thou been Ancient?

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Meaſuring the City:
I have left my Brooms at gate here;
By this time the Porter has ſtole 'em to ſweep out Raſca's.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: Broms?

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: I have been crying Brooms all the town over,
And ſuch a Mart I have made, there's no tread near it.
O the young handſom wenches, how they twitter'd,
When they but ſaw me ſhake my ware, and ſing too;
Come hither Maſter Broom man I beſeech ye:
Good Maſter Broom-man hither, cries another.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Thou art a mad fellow.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: They are all as mad as I: they all have traeds no • ,
And roar about the ſtreets like Bull-beggers.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What company of Souldiers are they?

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: By this means I have gather'd
Above a thouſand tall and hardy Souldiers,
If need be Colonel.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: That need's come Ancient,
And 'twas diſcreetly done: goe, draw 'em preſently,
But without ſuſpicion: this night we ſhall need 'em;
Let 'em be near the Court, let Putskie guide 'em;
And wait me for occaſion: here I'le ſtay ſtill.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: If it fall out we are ready; if not we are ſcatter'd:
I'le wait ye at an inch.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Doe, Farewel. Excunt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Are the Souldiers ſtill ſo mutinous?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: More than ever,
No Law nor Juſtice frights 'em: all the Town over
They play new pranks and gambols: no mans perſon,
Of what degree ſoever, free from abuſes:
And durſt they doe this, (let your grace conſider)
Theſe monſtrous, moſt offenſive things, theſe villanies,
If not ſet on, and fed? if not by one
They honour more than you? and more aw'd by him?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Happily their own wants.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: I offer to ſupply 'em,
And every hour make tender of their moneys:
They ſcorn it, laugh at me that offer it:
I fear the next device will be my life Sir;
And willingly I'le give it, ſo they ſtay there.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Do you think Lord Archas privie?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: More than thought,
I know it Sir, I know they durſt not doe
Theſe violent rude things, abuſe the State thus,
But that they have a hope by his ambitions —

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No more: he's ſent for?

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: Yes, and will be here ſure.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Let me talk further with you anon.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: I'le wait Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Did you ſpeak to the Ladies?

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: They'l attend your grace preſently.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How do you like 'em?

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: My eyes are too dull Judges.
They wait here Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Be you gone then: Come in Ladies,
Welcom toth' court ſweet beauties, now the court ſhines,
When ſuch true beams of beauty ſtrike amongſt us:
Welcom, welcom, even as your own joyes welcom.
How do you like the Court? how ſeems it to you?
Is't not a place created for all ſweetneſs?
Why were you made ſuch ſtrangers to this happineſs?
Barr'd the delights this holds? the richeſt jewels
Set ne're ſo well, if then not worn to wonder,
By judging eyes not ſet off, loſe their luſtre:
Your Country ſhades are faint; blaſters of beauty;
The manners like the place, obſcure and heavie;
The Roſe buds of the beauties turn to cankers,
Fat •• with inward thoughts': whilſt there ye wander.
Here Ladies, here, you were not made for Cloiſters,
Here is the Sphere you move in: here ſhine nobly,
And by your powerfull influence command all:
What a ſweet modeſtie dwells round about 'em,
And like a nipping morn pulls in their bloſſoms?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Your grace ſpeaks cunningly, you doe not this,
I hope Sir, to betray us; we are poor triumphs;
Not can our loſs of honour adde to you Sir:
Great men, and great thoughts, ſeek things great and worthy,
Subjects to make 'em live, and not to loſe 'em;
Conqueſts ſo nobly won, can never periſh;
We are two ſimple maids, untutor'd here Sir;
Two honeſt maids, is that a ſin at Court Sir?
Out breeding is obedience, but to good things,
To vertuous and to fair: what wou'd you win on us?
Why do I ask that queſtion, when I have found ye?
Your Preamble has pour'd your heart out to us;
You would diſhonour us; which in your tranſlation
Here at the Court reads thus, your grace would love us,
Moſt dearly love us: ſtick us up for miſtreſſes:
Moſt certain, there are thouſands of our ſex Sir
That would be glad of this, and handſom women,
And crowd into this favour, ſai • young women,

Excellent beauties Sir: when ye ha ••
•• joy'd 'em,
And ſuckt thoſe ſweets they have, what Saints are theſe then?
What worſhip have they won? what name you gheſs Sir,
What ſtorie added to their time, a ſweet one?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: A brave ſpirited wench.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: I'le tell your grace,
And tell ye true: ye are deceiv'd in us two,
Extreamly cozen'd Sir: And yet in my eye
You are the handſomſt man I ever ſo •• t on,
The goodlieſt Gentleman; take that hope with ye;
And were I fit to be your wife (ſo much I honour ye)
Truſt me I would ſcratch for ye but I would have ye.
I would wooe you then.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: She amazes me:
〈◊〉 how am I deceiv'd?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: O we are too honeſt,
Believe it Sir, too honeſt, far too honeſt,
The way that you propound too ignorant,
And there is no medling with us; for we are fools too,
O • ſſinate, peeviſh fools: if I would be ill,
And had a wantons itch, to kick my heels up,
I would not leap into th' Sun, and doe't there,
That all the world might ſee me: an obſcure ſhade Sir,
Dark as the deed, there is no truſting light with it,
Not that that's lighter far, vain-glorious greatneſs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: You will love me as your friend?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: I will honour ye,
As your poor humble handmaid ſerve, and pray for ye.
What ſayes my little one; you are not ſo obſtinate?
Lord how ſhe bluſhes: here are truly fair ſouls:
Come you will be my love?

sp.speaker: Vul.
sp.l: Good Sir be good to me,
Indeed I'le doe the beſt I can to pleaſe ye;
I do beſeech your grace: Alas I fear ye.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What ſhouldſt thou fear?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Fie Sir, this is not noble.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why do I ſtand entreating, where my power—

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: You have no power, at leaſt you ought to have none
In bad and beaſtly things: arm'd thus, I'le dye here,
Before ſhe ſuffer wrong.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Another Archas?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: His child Sir, and his ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I'le deal with you then,
For here's the honour to be won: ſit down ſweet,
Prethee Honora ſit.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Now ye intreat I will Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I doe, and will deſerve it.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: That's too much kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Prethee look on me.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Yes: I love to ſee ye,
And could look on an age thus, and admire ye:
Whilſt ye are good and temperate I dare touch ye,
Kiſs your white hand.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why not my lips?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: I dare Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I do not think ye dare.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: I am no coward.
Dou you believe me now? or now? or now Sir?
You make me bluſh: but ſure I mean no ill Sir:
It had been fitter you had kiſs'd me.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: That I'le doe too.
What haſt thou wrought into me?

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: I hope all goodneſs:
Whilſt ye are thus, thus honeſt, I dare do any thing,
Thus hang about your neck, and thus doat on ye;
Bleſs thoſe fair lights: hell take me if I durſt not —
But good Sir pardon me. Siſter come hither,
Come hither, fear not wench: come hither, bluſh not,
Come kiſs the Prince, the vertuous Prince, the good Prince:
Certain he is excellent honeſt.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Thou wilt make me —

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Sit down, and hug him ſoftly.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Fie Honora,
Wanton Honora; is this the modeſty,
The noble chaſtity your on-ſet ſhew'd me,
At firſt charge beaten back? Away.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Thank ye:
Upon my knees I pray, heaven too may thank ye;
Ye have deceiv'd me cunningly, yet nobly
Ye have cozen'd me: In all your hopefull life yet,
A Scene of greater honour you ne're acted:
I knew ſame was a lyar, too long, and loud tongu'd,
And now I have found it: O my vertuous Maſter.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: My vertuous Maſter • oo.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Now you are thus,
What ſhall become of me let fortune caſt ſor't.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I'le be that fortune, if I live Honora,
Thou haſt done a cure upon me, counſel could not.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Here take your ring Sir, and whom ye mean to ruine,
Give it to her next; I have paid for't dearly.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: A Ring to her?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Why frowns my fair Alinda?
I have forgot both theſe again.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Stand ſtill Sir,
Ye have that violent killing fire upon ye,
Conſumes all honour, credit, faith.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: My Royal Miſtris favour towards me,
Woe-worth ye Sir, ye have poyſon'd, blaſted.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I ſweet?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: You have taken that unmanly liberty,
Which in a worſe man, is vain glorious feigning,
And kill'd my truth.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Upon my life 'tis falſe wench.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Ladies,
Take heed, ye have a cunning gameſter,
A handſom, and a high; come ſtor'd with Antidotes,
He has infections elſe will fire your blouds.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Prethee Alinda hear me.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Words ſteept in hony,
That will ſo melt into your minds, buy Chaſtity,
A thouſand wayes, a thouſand knots to tie ye;
And when he has bound ye his, a thouſand ruines.
A poor loſt woman ye have made me.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I'le maintain thee,
And nobly too.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: That Gin's too weak to take me:
Take heed, take heed young Ladies: ſtill take heed,
Take heed of promiſes, take heed of gifts,
Of forced ſeigned ſorrows, ſighs, take heed.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: By all that's mine, Alinda —

sp.speaker: Al
sp.l: Swear
By your miſchiefs:
O whither ſhall I goe?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Go back again,
I'le force her take thee, love thee.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Fate ye well. Sir,
I will not curſe ye; only this dwell with ye,
When ever ye love, a falſe belief light on ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: We'll take our leaves too, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: Part all the world now,
Since ſhe is gone.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: You are crooked yet, dear Maſter,
And ſtill I ſeat Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I am v •• t,
And ſome ſhall ſin •• t. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange
To me to ſee the Court, and welcome:
O Royal place, how have I lov'd and ſerv'd thee?
Who lies on th ſide, know'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The Lord Burris.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Thou l •• ſt nam'd a Gentleman
I ſtand much bound to:
I think he ſent the Casket, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The ſame, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: An honeſt minded man, a noble Courtier:
The Duke made perfect choice when he took him.
Go you home, I ſhall hit the way
Without a guide now.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You may want ſomething, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Only my Horſes,
Which after Supper let the Groom wait with:
I'le have no more attendance here.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Your will, Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: You are well met here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: How now boy,
How doſt thou?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I ſhould ask
You that queſtion: how do you, Sir?
How do you feel your ſelf?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Why well, and luſty.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What do you here then?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Why I am ſent for
To Supper with the Duke

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Have you no meat at home?
Or do you long to ſeed as hunted Deer do,
In doubt and fear?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I have an excellent ſtomach,
And can I uſe it better
Than among my friends, Boy?
How do the Wenches?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: They do well enough, Sir,
They know the worſt by this time: pray be rul'd, Sir,
Go home again, and if ye have a Supper,
Fat it in quiet there: this is no place for ye,
Eſpecially at this time,
Take my word for't.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: May be they'll drink hard;
I could have drunk my ſhare, Boy.
Though I am old, I will not out.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I hope you will.
Hark in your eat: the Court's
Too quick of hearing.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Not mean me well?
Thou art abus'd and cozen'd.
Away, away.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: To that end Sir, I tell ye.
Away, if you love your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Who dare do theſe things,
That ever heard of honeſty?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Old Gentleman,
Take a fools counſel.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: 'Tis a fools indeed;
A very fools: thou haſt more of
Theſe ſlams in thee, theſe muſty doubts:
Is't fit the Duke ſend for me,
And honour me to eat within his preſence,
And I, like a tale fellow, play at bo peep
With his pleaſure?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Take heed
Of bo peep with your pate, your pate, Sir,
I ſpeak plain language now.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: If 'twere not here,
Where reverence bids me hold,
I would ſo ſwinge thee, thou rude,
Unmanner'd Knave; take from his bounty,
His honour that he gives me, to beget
Sawey, and fullen fears?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: You are not mad ſure:
By this fair light, I ſpeak
But what is whiſper'd,
And whiſper'd for a truth.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: A Dog: drunken people,
That in their Pot ſee viſions,
And turn ſtates, mad-men and Children:
Prethee do not follow me;
I tell thee I am angry:
Do not follow me.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I am as angry
As you for your heart,
I and as wilful too: go, like a Wood-cock,
And thruſt your neck i'th' nooſe.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I'le kill thee,
And thou ſpeakſt but three words more.
Do not follow me. Exit.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: A ſtrange old fooliſh fellow: I ſhall hear yet,
And if I do not my part, hiſs at me. Exit.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Enter two Servants preparing a Banquet.

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: Believe me fellow here will be luſty drinking.
Many a waſht pate in Wine I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: I am glad the old General's come: upon my Co • ſcience
That joy will make half the Court drunk. Hark the Trumpets,
They are coming on; away.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: We'll have a rowſe too. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Duke, Archas, Burris, Boroskie, Attend. Gent.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come ſeat your ſelves: Lord Archas ſit you there.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: 'Tis far above my worth.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I'le have it ſo:
Are all things ready?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: All the Guards are ſet,
The Court Gates are ſhut.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Then do as I preſcrib'd ye.
Be ſure no further.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: I ſhall well obſerve ye.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Come bring ſome wine: here's to my Siſter, Gentlemen;
A health, and mirth to all.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Pray fill it full, Sir.
'Tis a high health to vertue: here Lord Burris,
A maiden health: you are moſt ſit to pledge it,
You have a maiden ſoul and much I honour it.
Paſſion o' me, ye are ſad man.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How now, Burris?
Go to, no more of this.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Take the rowſe freely,
'Twill warm your bloud, and make ye fit for jollity.
Your Graces pardon: when we get a cup, Sir,
We old men prate a pace.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Mirth makes a Banquet;
As you love me no more.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: I thank your Grace.
Give me it; Lord Boroskie.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: I have ill brains, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Damnable ill, I know it.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: But I'le pledge, Sir,
This vertuous health.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: The more unfit for thy mouth.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Come, bring out Robes, and let my gueſts look nobly,
Fit for my love and preſence: begin downward.
Off with your Cloaks, take new.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Your grace deals truly,
Like a munificent Prince, with your poor ſubjects,
Who would not fight for you? what cold dull coward
Durſt ſeek to ſave his life when you would ask it?
Begin a new health in your new adornments,
The Dukes, the Royal Dukes: ha! what have I got
Sir? ha! the Robe of death?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: You have deſerv'd it.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: The Livery of the Grave? do you ſtart all from me?
Do I ſmell of earth already? Sir, look on me,
And like a man; is this your entertainment?
Do you bid your worthieſt gueſts to bloudy Banquets?
A Guard upon me too? this is too ſoul play
Boy to thy good, thine honour; thou wretched Ruler,
Thou Son of fools and flatterers, Heir of hypocrites,
Am I ſerv'd in a Hearſe that ſav'd ye all?
Are ye men or Devils? Do ye gape upon me,
Wider, and ſwallow all my ſervices?
Entomb them firſt, my faith next, then my integrity,
And let theſe ſtruggle with your mangy minds,
Your fear'd, and ſeal'd up Conſciences, till they burſt.

sp.speaker: Boroſ.
sp.l: Theſe words are death.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: No thoſe deeds that want rewards, Sirrah,
Thoſe Battels I have ſought, thoſe horrid dangers,
•• aner than death, and wilder than deſtruction,
Leave march'd upon, theſe honour'd wounds, times ſtory,
The bloud I have loſt, the youth, the ſorrows ſuffer'd,
Theſe are my death, theſe that can ne're be recompenced,
Theſe that ye ſit a brooding on like Toads,
Socking from my deſerts the ſweets and favours,
And render me no pay again but poyſons.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: The proud vain Souldier thou haſt ſet—

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt.
Now by my little time of life lyeſt baſely,
Malitiouſly and loudly: how I ſcorn thee!
If I had ſwel'd the Souldier, or intended
Anact in perſon, leaning to diſhonour,
As ye would ſain have forced me, witneſs Heaven,
Where cleareſt underſtanding of all truth is,
(For theſe are ſpightful men, and know no piety)
When Olin came, grim Olin, when his marches,
His laſt Incurſions made the City ſweat,
And drove before him, as a ſtorm drives Hail,
Such ſhowrs of froſted fears, ſhook all your heart-ſtrings;
Then when the Volga trembled at his terrour,
And hid his ſeven curl'd heads, afraid of bruiſing,
By his arm'd Horſes hoofs; had I been falſe then,
Or blown a treacherous fire into the Souldier,
Had but one ſpark of villany liv'd within me,
Ye • ad had ſome ſhadow for this black about me.
Where was your Souldierſhip? why went not you out?
And all your right honourable valour with ye?
Why met ye not the Tartar, and deſi'd him?
Drew your dead doing ſword, and buckl'd with him?
Shot through his Squadrons like a fiery Meteor?
And as we ſee a dreadful clap of Thunder
Rend the ſtiff hearted Oaks, and toſs their roots up:
Why did not you ſo charge him? you were ſick then,
You that dare taint my credit ſlipt to bed then,
Stewing and fainting with the fears ye had,
A whorſon ſhaking fit oppreſt your Lordſhip:
Bluſh Coward, Knave, and all the world hiſs at thee.

sp.speaker: Da.
sp.l: Exceed not my command. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: I ſhall obſerve it.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Are you gone too? Come weep not honeſt Burris,
Good loving Lord, no more fears: 'tis not his malice,
This fellows malice, nor the Dukes diſpleaſure,
By bold bad men crowded into his nature,
Can ſtartle me: fortune ne're raz'd this Fort yet:
I am the ſame, the ſame man, living, dying;
The ſame mind to 'em both, I poize thus equal;
Only the jugling way that toll'd me to it,
The Judas way, to kiſs me, bid me welcome,
And cut my throat, a little ſticks upon me.
Farewel, commend me to his Grace, and tell him,
The world is full of ſervants, he may have many:
And ſome I with him hon ſt: he s undone elſe:
But ſuch another doating Archas never,
So try'd and touch'd a ſaith: farewell for ever.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Be ſtrong my Lord: you muſt not go thus lightly.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Now, what s to do? what ſayes the Law unto me?
Give me my great offence that ſpeaks me guily.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: La ••• aſ •• e a thouſand petty matters,
As ſcorns, and inſolencies both from your ſelf and followers,
Which you put firſt fire to, and theſe are deadly,
I come to one main cauſe, which though it carries
A ſtrangeneſs in the circumſtance, it carries death too,
Not to be pardon'd neither: ye have done a ſacriledge.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: High Heaven deſend me man: how, how Boroskie?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Ye have took from the Temple thoſe vow'd Arms,
The holy Ornament you hung up there,
No abſolution of your vow, no order
From holy Church to give 'em back unto you
After they were purified from War, and reſted
From bloud, made clean by ceremony: from the Altar
You ſnatch'd 'em up again, again ye wore 'em,
Again you ſtain'd 'em, ſtain'd your vow, the Church too,
And rob'd it of that right was none of yours, Sir,
For which the Law requires your head, ye know it.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Thoſe arms I fought in laſt?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: The ſame.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: God a mercy,
Thou haſt hunted out a notable cauſe to kill me:
A ſubtle one: I dye, for ſaving all you;
Good Sir, remember if you can, the neceſſity,
The ſuddenneſs of time, the ſtate all ſtood in;
I was entrea • ed to, kneel'd to, and pray'd to,
The Duke himſelf, the Princes, all the Nobles,
The cries of Infants, Bed-rid Fathers, Virgins;
Prethee find out a better cauſe, a hand ſomer,
This will undo thee too: people will ſpit at thee,
The Devil himſelf would be aſham'd of this cauſe;
Becauſe my haſte made me forget the ceremony,
The preſent danger every where, muſt my life ſatisfie?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: It muſt, and ſhall.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: O baſe ungrateful people,
Have ye no other Swords to cut my throat with
But mine own nobleneſs? I confeſs, I took 'em,
The vow not yet abſolv'd I hung 'em up with:
Wore 'em, ſought in 'em, gilded 'em again
In the ſierce Tartars blouds; for you I took 'em,
For your peculiar ſafety, Lord, for all,
I wore 'em for my Countries health, that groan'd then:
Took from the Temple, to preſerve the Temple;
That holy place, and all the ſacred monuments,
The reverent ſhrines of Saints, ador'd and honour'd,
Had been conſum'd to aſhes, their own ſacrifice;
Had I been ſtack, or ſtaid that abſolution,
No Prieſt had liv'd to give it; my own honour,
Cure of my Country murder me?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: No, no Sir,
I ſhall force that from ye, will make this cauſe light too,
Away with him: I ſhall pluck down that heart, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Break it thou mayeſt; but if it bend, for pity,
Doggs, and Kites eat it; come I am honours Martyr. Ex.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Exceed my Warrant?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: You know he loves him not.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: He daies as well eat death, as do it, eat wild-fire,
Through a few ſeats I mean to try his goodneſs,
That I may find him ſit, to wear here, Burris;
I know Boroskie hates him, to death hates him,
I know he's a Serpent too, a ſwoln one, Noiſe within.
But I have pull'd his ſting out: what noiſe is that?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: within. Down with 'em, down with 'em, down with the gates.
within. Stand, ſtand, ſtand.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: within. Fire the Palace before ye.

sp.speaker: Bur
sp.l: Upon my life the Souldier, Sir, the Souldier,
A miſerable time is come.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Oh ſave him,
Upon my knees, my hearts knees, ſave Lord Archas,
We are undone elſe.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Dates he touch his Body?

sp.speaker: Gent
sp.l: He tacks him fearfully, moſt fearfully.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Away Burris,
Take men, and take him from him; clap him up,
And if I live, I'll find a ſtrange death for him. Ex. Bur.
Are the Souldiers broke in?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: By this time ſure they are, Sir,
They beat the Gates extreamly, beat the people.

sp.speaker: Du
sp.l: Got me a guard about me; make ſure the lodgings,
And ſpeak the Souldiers fair.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Pray Heaven that take, Sir. Exeunt.
sp.stage: Enter Putskie, Ancient, Souldiers, with Torches.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Give us the General, we'll fire the Court elſe,
Render him ſafe and well.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Do not fire the Cellar,
There's excellent Wine in't, Captain, and though it be cold weather,
I do not love it mull'd; bring out the General,
We'll light ye ſuch a Bone fire elſe: where are ye?
Speak, or we'll toſs your Turrets, peep out of your Hives,
We'll ſmoak ye elſe: Is not that a Noſe there?
• ut out that Noſe again, and if thou dar'ſt
But blow it before us: now he creeps out on's Burrough.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Give us the General.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Yes, Gentlemen;
Of any thing ye can deſire.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: You musk cat,
Cordevant-skin we will not take your anſwer.

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Where is the Duke? ſpeak ſuddenly, and ſend him hither.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Of we'll ſo ſ • ye your Buttocks.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Good ſweet Gentlemen—

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: We are neither good nor ſweet, we are Souldiers,
And you miſcreants that abuſe the General.
Give fire my Boys, 'tis a dark Evening,
Let's light 'em to their lodgings.
sp.stage: Enter Olympia, Honora, Viola, Theodore, Women.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Good Brother be not fierce.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I will not hurt her,
Fear not ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Nav, do what you pleaſe, Sir,
I have a ſorrow that exceeds all yours,
And more, contemns all danger.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Where is the Duke?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: He's here, what would ye Souldiers? wherefore troop ye
Like mutinous mad men thus?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Give me my Father.

sp.speaker: Putſ Anc.
sp.l: Give us out General.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Set him here before us,
Ye ſee the pledge we have got; ye ſee the Torches;
All ſhall to aſhes, as I live, immediately,
A thouſand lives for one.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: But hear me?

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: No, we come not to diſpute.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: By Heaven I ſwear he's rackt and whipt.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Oh my poor Father!

sp.speaker: Putſ.
sp.l: Burn, kill and burn.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Hold, hold, I ſay: hold Souldiers,
On your allegiance hold.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: We muſt not.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Hold:
I ſwear by Heaven he is a barbarous Traitor ſtirs firſt,
A Villain, and a ſtranger to Obedience,
Never my Souldier more, nor Friend to Honour:
Why did you uſe your old Man thus? thus cruelly
Torture his poor weak Body? I ever lov'd ye.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Forget me in theſe wrongs, moſt noble Archas.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I have balm enough for all my hurts: weep no more Sir,
A ſatisfaction for a thouſand ſorrows;
I do believe you innocent, a good man,
And Heaven forgive that naughty thing that wrong'd me:
Why look ye wild, my friends? why ſtare ye on me?
I charge ye, as ye are men, my men, my lovers,
As ye are honeſt faithful men, fair Souldiers,
Let down your anger: Is not this our Soveraign?
The head of mercy, and of Law? who dares then,
But Rebels, ſcorning Law, appear thus violent?
Is this a place for Swords? for threatning fires?
The Reverence of this Houſe dares any touch,
But with obedient knees, and pious duties?
Are we not all his Subjects? all ſworn to him?
Has not he power to puniſh our offences?
And do we not daily fall into 'em? aſſure your ſelves
I did offend, and highly, grievouſly,
This good, ſweet Prince I offended, my life forfeited,
Which yet his mercy and his old love met with,
And only let me feel his light rod this way:
Ye are to thank him for your General,
Pray for his life and fortune; ſwear your bloods for him.
Ye are offenders too, daily offenders,
Proud inſolencies dwell in your hearts, and ye do 'em,
Do 'em againſt his Peace, his Law, his Perſon;
Ye ſee he only ſorrows for your ſins,
And where his power might perſecute, forgives ye:
For ſhame put up your Swords, for honeſty,
For orders ſake, and whoſe ye are, my Souldiers,
Be not ſo rude.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: They have drawn blood from you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: That was the blood rebell'd, the naughty blood,
The proud provoking blood; 'tis well 'tis out, Boy;
Give you example firſt; draw out, and orderly.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Good Brother, do.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Honeſt and high example,
As thou wilt have my Bleſſing follow thee,
Inherit all mine honours: thank ye Theodore,
My worthy Son.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: If harm come, thank your ſelf, Sir,
I muſt obey ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Captain, you know the way now:
A good man, and a valiant, you were ever,
Inclin'd to honeſt things; I thank ye, Captain. Ex Soul
Souldiers, I thank ye all: and love me ſtill,
But do not love me ſo you loſe Allegiance,
Love that above your lives: once more I thank ye.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Bring him to reſt, and let our cares wait on him;
Thou excellent old man, thou top of honour,
Where Juſtice, and Obedience only build,
Thou ſtock of Vertue, how am I bound to love thee!
In all thy noble ways to follow thee!

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Remember him that vext him, Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Remember?
When I forget that Villain, and to pay him
For all his miſchiefs, may all good thoughts forget me.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I am very ſore.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Bring him to Bed with eaſe, Gentlemen,
For every ſtripe I'll drop a tear to waſh 'em,
And in my ſad Repentance—

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Tis too much,
I have a life yet left to gain that love, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: HOw does Lord Archas?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: But weak, and't pleaſe ye;
Yet all the helps that art can, are applied to him;
His heart's untoucht, and whole yet; and no doubt, Sir,
His mind being ſound, his body ſoon will follow.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: O that baſe Knave that wrong'd him, without leave too;
But I ſhall find an hour to give him thanks for't;
He's faſt, I hope.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: As faſt as irons can keep him:
But the moſt fearful Wretch—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: He has a Conſcience,
A cruel ſtinging one I warrant him,
A loaden one: But what news of the Souldier?
I did not like their parting, 'twas too ſullen.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: That they keep ſtill, and I fear a worſe clap;
They are drawn out of the Town, and ſtand in counſels,
Hatching unquiet thoughts, and cruel purpoſes:
I went my ſelf unto 'em, talkt with the Captains,
Whom I found fraught with nothing but loud murmurs,
And deſperate curſes, ſounding theſe words often
Like Trumpets to their angers: we are ruin'd,
Our ſervices turn'd to diſgraces, miſchiefs;
Our brave old General, like one had pilfer'd,
•• rtur'd, and whipt: the Colonels eyes, like torches,
B • ze every where and fright fair peace.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Yet worſe, Sir;
The news is currant now, they mean to leave ye,
B •• ve their Allegiance; and under Olins Charge
The bloody Enemy march ſtraight againſt ye.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: I have heard this too, Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: This muſt be prevented,
And ſuddenly, an • warily.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: 'Tis time, Sir,
But what to miniſter, or how?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Go in with me,
And there we'll think upon't: ſuch blows as theſe,
Equal defences ask, elſe they diſpleaſe. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Lord, what a coil has here been with theſe Souldiers!
They are cruel fellows.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: And yet me thought we found 'em
Handſome enough; I'll tell thee true, Peteſca,
Hookt for other manner of dealings from 'em,
And had prepar'd my ſelf: but where's my Lady?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: In her old dumps within: monſtrous melancholy;
Sure ſhe was mad of this Wench.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: And ſhe bad been a man,
She would have been a great deal madder, I am glad ſhe is ſhifted.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'T was a wicked thing for me to betray her,
And yet I muſt confeſs ſhe ſtood in our lights.
What young thing's this?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Good morrow beauteous Gentlewomen:
Pray ye is the Princeſs ſtirring yet?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: He has her face.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Her every tongue, and tone too: her youth upon him.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I gueſs ye to be the Princeſs Women.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Yes, we are, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Pray is there not a Gentlewoman waiting on her Grace,
Ye call Alinda?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: The Devil ſure in her ſhape.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: I have heard her tell my Lady of a Brother,
An only Brother that ſhe had: in travel—

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Maſs, I remember that: this may be he too:
I would this thing would ſerve her.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: So would I Wench,
We ſhould love him better ſure: Sir, here's the Princeſs,
She beſt can ſatisfie ye.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: How I love that preſence!
O bleſſed Eyes, how nobly ſhine your comforts!

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: What Gentleman is that?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: We know not, Madam:
He ask'd us for your Grace: and as we gueſs it,
He is Alinda's Brother.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Ha! let me mark him:
My grief has almoſt blinded me: her Brother?
By Venus, he has all her ſweetneſs upon him:
Two ſilver drops of dew were never liker.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Gracious Lady—

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: That pleaſant pipe he has too.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Being my happineſs to paſs by this way,
And having as I underſtand by Letters,
A Siſter in your vertuous ſervice, Madam—

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: O now my heart, my heart akes.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: All the comfort
My poor youth has, all that my hopes have built me,
I thought it my firſt duty, my beſt ſervice,
Here to arrive firſt, humbly to thank your Grace
For my poor Siſter, humbly to thank your Nobleneſs,
That bounteous Goodneſs in ye.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: 'Tis he certainly.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: That ſpring of favour to her; with my life, Madam,
If any ſuch moſt happy means might meet me,
To ſhew my thankfulneſs.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: What have I done, Fool!

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: She came a ſtranger to your Grace, no Courtier;
Nor of that curious breed befits your ſervice,
Yet one I dare aſſure my Soul, that lov'd ye
Before ſhe ſaw ye; doted on your Vertues;
Before ſhe knew thoſe fair eyes, long'd to read 'em,
You only had her prayers, you her wiſhes;
And that one hope to be yours once, preſerv'd her.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: I have done wickedly.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: A little Beauty,
Such as a Cottage breeds, ſhe brought along with her;
And yet our Country eyes eſteem'd it much too:
But for her beauteous mind, forget great Lady,
I am her Brother, and let me ſpeak a ſtranger,
Since ſhe was able to beget a thought, 'twas honeſt.
The daily ſtudy how to ſit your ſervices,
Truly to tread that vertuous path you walk in,
So ſir'd her honeſt Soul, we thought her Sainted;
I preſume ſhe is ſtill the ſame: I would fain ſee her,
For Madam, 'tis no little love I owe her.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Sir, ſuch a maid there was, I had—

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: There was, Madam?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: O my poor Wench: eyes, I will ever curſe ye
For your Credulity, Alinda.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: That's her name, Madam.

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Give me a little leave, Sir, to lament her.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Is ſhe dead, Lady?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Dead Sir, to my ſervice.
She is gone, pray ye ask no further.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I obey Madam:
Gone? now muſt I lament too: ſaid ye gone Madam?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Gone, gone for ever.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: That's a cruel ſaying:
Her honour too?

sp.speaker: Olym.
sp.l: Prithee look angry on me,
And if thou ever lovedſt her, ſpit upon me;
Do ſomething like a Brother, like a friend,
And do not only ſay thou lov'ſt her—

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Ye amaze me.

sp.speaker: Oly.
sp.l: I ruin'd her, I wrong'd her, I abus'd her;
Poo • innocent ſoul, I flung her; ſweet Al nda,
Thou vertuous maid, my ſoul now calls thee vertuous.
Why do ye not • ail now at me?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: For what Lad • ?

sp.speaker: Oly.
sp.l: Call me baſe treacherous woman.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Heaven defend me.

sp.speaker: Oly.
sp.l: Raſhly I thought her falſe, and put her from me,
Raſtify, and madly I betrai'd her modeſty,
Put her to wander, heaven knows where: • ay, more Sir,
Stuck a black brand upon her.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: 'Twas not well Lady,

sp.speaker: Oly.
sp.l: 'Twas damnable: ſhe loving me ſo dearly,
Never poo • wench lov'd ſo: Sir believe me,
'Twas the moſt dutrous wench, the beſt companion,
When I was pleas'd, the happieſt, and the gladdeſt,
The modeſteſt ſweet nature dwelt within her:
I ſaw all this, I know all this, I lov'd it,
I doated on it too, and yet I kill'd it:
O what have I forſaken? what have I loſt?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Madam, I'le take my leave, ſince ſhe is wandring,
'Tis ſit I know no reſt.

sp.speaker: Oly.
sp.l: Will you go too Sir?
I have not wrong'd you yet, if you dare truſt me,
For yet I love Alinda there, I honour her,
I love to look upon thoſe eyes that ſpeak her,
To read that face again, (modeſty keep me,)
Alinda, in that ſhape. • ut why ſhould you truſt me,
'Twas I betray'd your Siſter, I undid her;
And believe me, gentle youth, 'tis I weep for her:
Appoint what penance you pleaſe: but ſtay then,
And ſee me perform it: ask what honour this place
Is able to heap on ye, or what wealth:
If following me will like ye, my care of ye,
Which for your ſiſters ſake, for your own goodneſs—

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Not all the honour earth has, now ſhe's gone Lady,
Not all the favour; yet if I ſought preferment,
Under your bounteous Grace I would only take it.
Peace reſt upon ye: one ſad tear every day
For poor Alindas ſake, 'tis ſit ye pay. Exit.

sp.speaker: Oly.
sp.l: A thouſand noble youth, and when I ſleep,
Even in my ſilver ſlumbers ſtill I'le weep. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Have ye been with 'em?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Yes, and't pleaſe • oo • Grace,
But no perſwaſion ſerves 'em, nor no promiſe,
They are fearfull angry, and by this time Sir,
Upon their march to the Enemy.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: They muſt be ſtopt.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I, but what force is able? and what leader—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: How now, have you been with Archas?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Yes, and't pleaſe ye,
And told him all: he frets like a chaſ'd Lyon,
And calls for his Arms: and all thoſe honeſt Courtiers
That dare draw Swords.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Is he able to do any thing?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: His mind is well enough; and where his charge is,
Let him be ne're ſo fore, 'tis a full Army.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Who commands the Rebels?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: The young Colonel,
That makes the old man almoſt mad: he ſwears Sir,
He will not ſpare his Sons head for the Dukedom.

sp.speaker: Du
sp.l: Is the Court in Arms?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: As faſt as they can buſtle,
Every man mad to goe now: inſpir'd ſtrangely,
As if they were to force the Enemy,
I beſeech your grace to give me leave.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Pray go Sir,
And look to the old man well; take up all fairly,
And let no bloud be ſpilt; take general pardons,
And quench this fury with fair peace.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: I ſhall Sir,
Or ſeal it with my ſervice; they are villains:
The Court is up: good Sir, go ſtrengthen 'em,
Your Royal ſight will make 'em ſcorn all dangers;
The General needs no proof.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come let's go view 'em. Ex ••

div.head: SCENA IV.
div.stage: Enter Theodore, Putskie, Ancient, Souldiers, Drums, and Colours.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: 'Tis known we are up, and marching: no ſubmiſſion,
No promiſe of baſe peace can cure our maladies,
We have ſuffer'd beyond all repair of honour:
Your valiant old man's whipt; whipt Gentlemen,
Whipt like a ſlave: that fleſh that never trembled,
Nor ſhrunk one ſinew at a thouſand charges,
That noble body rib'd in arms, the Enemy
So often ſhook at, and then ſhun'd like thunder,
That body's torn with laſhes.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Let's turn head.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Turn nothing Gentlemen, let's march on fairly,
Unleſs they charge us.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Think ſtill of his abuſes,
And keep your angers.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: He was whipt like a top,
I never ſaw a whore ſo lac'd: Court ſchool-butter?
Is this their diet? I'le dreſs 'em one running banquet:
What Oracle can alter us? did not we ſee him?
See him we lov'd?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: And though we did obey him,
Forc'd by his reverence for that time; is't fit Gentlemen?
My noble friends, is't fit we men, and Souldiers,
Live to endure this, and look on too?

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Forward
They ma •• ca •• back the Sun as ſoon, ſtay time,
Preſcribe a Law •• death, as we endure this.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: They will make ye all fair promiſes.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: We • are not.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Uſe all their arts upon ye.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Hang all their arts.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: And happily they'l bring him with 'em.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: March apace then,
He is old and cannot overtake us.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Say he doe.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: We'l run away with him: they ſhall never ſee him more:
The truth is, we'l hear nothing, ſtop at nothing,
Conſider nothing but our way; believe nothing,
Not though they ſay their prayers: be content with nothing,
But the knocking out their brains: and laſt, do nothing
But ban 'em and curſe 'em, till we come to kill 'em.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Remove then forwards bravely; keep your minds whole,
And the next time we face 'em, ſhall be fatal.

div.head: SCENA V.
div.stage: Enter Archas, Duke, Burris, Gent. and Sould.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Peace to your Grace; take reſt Sir, they are before us Duke.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: They are Sir, and upon the march. Exit Duke

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Lord Burris,
Take you thoſe horſe and coaſt 'em: upon the firſt advantage.
If they will not ſlake their march, charge 'em up roundly,
By that time I'le come in.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: I'le do it truly. Ex •

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: How do you feel your ſelf Sir?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Well, I thank ye;
A little weak, but anger ſhall ſupply that;
You will all ſtand bravely to it?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Whilſt we have lives Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Ye ſpeak like Gentlemen; I'le make the knaves know,
The proudeſt, and the ſtrongeſt hearted Rebel,
They have a law to live in, and they ſhall have;
Beat up a pace, by this time he is upon 'em, Drum within.
And ſword, but hold me now, thou ſhalt play ever. Exeunt.
sp.stage: Enter Drums beating, Theodore, Putskie, Ancient, and their Souldiers.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Stand, ſtand, ſtand cloſe, and ſure;
The horſe will charge us.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Let 'em come on, we have provender fit for 'em.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Here comes Lord Burris Sir, I think to parly.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: You are welcom noble Sir, I hope to our part.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: No, valiant Colonel, I am come to chide ye,
To pity ye; to kill ye, if theſe fail me;
Fie, what diſhonour ſeek ye! what black infamy!
Why do ye draw out thus? draw all ſhame with ye?
Are theſe fit cares in ſubjects? I command ye
Lay down your arms again, move in that peace,
That fair obedience you were bred in.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Charge us:
We come not here to argue.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Charge up bravely,
And hotly too, we have hot ſpleens to meet ye,
Hot as the ſhames are offer'd us.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Look behind ye.
Do you ſee that old man? do you know him Souldiers?

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Your Father Sir, believe me—

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: You know his marches,
You have ſeen his executions: is it yet peace?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: We'l dye here firſt.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Farewel: you'l hear on's preſently.
Stay Burris: this is too. poor, too beggerly a body
•• ear the honour of a charge from me,
• ixt of tatter'd Rebels; go provide Gallowſes;
• e are troubled with hot heads, I'le cool ye preſently:
Theſe look like men that were my Souldiers
• ow I behold 'em nearly, and more narrowly,
My honeſt friends: where got they theſe fair figures?
Where did they ſteal theſe ſhapes?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: They are ſtruck already.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Do you ſee that fellow there, that goodly Rebel?
• e looks as like a Captain I lov'd tenderly:
A fellow of a faith indeed.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: He has ſham'd him.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: And that that bears the Colours there, moſt certain
So like an Ancient of mine own, a brave fellow,
A loving and obedient, that believe me Burris,
I a • amaz'd and troubled: and were it not
I know the general goodneſs of my people,
The duty, and the truth, the ſtedfaſt honeſtie,
Adam aſſur'd they would as ſoon turn Devils
As rebels to allegeance, for mine honour.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Here needs no wars.

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: I pray forgive us Sir.

sp.speaker: Anc.
sp.l: Good General forgive us, or uſe your ſword,
• out words are double death.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Good noble General.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Pray Sir be mercifull.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Weep out your ſhames firſt,
• t make me fool for companie: fie Souldiers,
My Souldiers too, and play theſe tricks? what's he there?
•• t I have ſeen his face too; yes, moſt certain
• are a ſon, but I hope he is not here now,
Would much reſemble this man, wondrous near him,
〈◊〉 of his height and making too, you ſeem a Leader.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Good Sir, do not ſhame me more: I know your anger,
A • d leſs than death I look not for.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: You ſhall be my charge Sir, it ſeems you want foes,
When you would make your friends your Enemies.
A running bloud ye have, but I ſhall cure ye.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Good Sir—

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: No more good Lord: beat forward Souldiers:
And you, march in the rear, you have loſt your places.

div.head: SCENA VI.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: You ſhall not be thus fullen ſtill with me Siſter,
You do the moſt unnobly to be angry,
For as I have a ſoul, I never touch'd her,
I never yet knew one unchaſt thought in her:
I muſt confeſs, I lov'd her: as who would not?
I muſt confeſs I doated on her ſtrangely,
I offer'd all, yet ſo ſtrong was her honour,
So fortifi'd as fair, no hope could reach her,
And whilſt the world beheld this, and confirm'd it,
Why would you be ſo jealous?

sp.speaker: Oly.
sp.l: Good Sir pardon me,
I feel ſufficiently my follies penance,
And am aſham'd, that ſhame a thouſand ſorrows
Feed on continually, would I had never ſeen her,
Or with a clearer judgement look'd upon her,
She was too good for me, ſo heavenly good Sir,
Nothing but Heaven can love that ſoul ſufficiently,
Where I ſhall ſee her once again.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No more tears,
If ſhe be within the Dukedom, we'l recover her:
Welcom Lord Burris, fair news I hope.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Moſt fair Sir,
Without one drop of bloud theſe wars are ended,
The Souldier cool'd again, indeed aſham'd Sir,
And all his anger ended.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Where's Lord Archas?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Not far off Sir: with him his valiant ſon,
Head of this fire, but now a priſoner,
And if by your ſweet mercy not prevented,
I fear ſome fatal ſtroke. Drums.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I hear the Drums beat,
Welcom, my worthy friend.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Stand where ye are Sir,
Even as you love your country, move not forward,
Nor plead for peace till I have done a juſtice,
A juſtice on this villain; none of mine now,
A juſtice on this Rebel.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: O my Brother.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: This fatal firebrand—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Forget not old man,
He is thy ſon, of thine own bloud.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: In theſe veins
No treacherie e're harbour'd yet, no mutinie,
I ne're gave life to lewd and headſtrong Rebels.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: 'Tis his firſt fault.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Not of a thouſand Sir,
Or were it ſo, it is a fault ſo mightie,
So ſtrong againſt the nature of all mercy,
His Mother were ſhe living, would not weep for him,
He dare not ſay he would live.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I muſt not Sir,
Whilſt you ſay 'tis not fit: your Graces mercy
Not to my life appli'd, but to my fault Sir,
The worlds forgiveneſs next, laſt, on my knees Sir,
I humbly beg,
Do not take from me yet the name of Father,
Strike me a thouſand blows, but let me dye yours.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: He moves my heart: I muſt be ſuddain with him,
I ſhall grow faint elſe in my execution;
Come, come Sir, you have ſeen death; now meet him bravely.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Hold, hold I ſay, a little hold, conſider
Thou haſt no more ſons Archas to inherit thee.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I have another, and a nobler:
No treaſon ſhall inherit me: young Archas
A h • m as ſweet as young, my Brother breeds him,
My • oole Brother Br • kie breeds him nobly,
Him let your favour find: give him your honour.

div.stage: Enter Putskie (alias Briskie) and Alinda, (alias Archas)

sp.speaker: Pu.
sp.l: Thou haſt no child left Archas, none to inherit thee
Behold thy Brother here, thou bloudy Brother,
As bloo • y to this ſacrifice as thou art:
Heave up thy ſwo •• and mine's heav'd up: ſtrike Archas,
And I'le ſtrike too as ſ ••• tly, as deadly:
Have mercy, and I'le have mercy: the Duke gives it.
Look upon all theſe, how they weep it from thee,
Chooſe quickly, and begin.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: On your obedience,
On your allegeance ſave him.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Take him to ye, Soul. ſhout.
And ſ •• ah, be an honeſt man, ye have reaſon:
I thank ye worthy Brother: welcom child,
Mine own ſweet child.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Why was this boy conceal'd thus?

sp.speaker: Put.
sp.l: Your graces pardon:
Pea • ing the vow you made againſt my Brother,
And that your anger would not only light
On him, but find out all his familie,
This young boy, to preſerve from after danger,
Like a young wench, hither I brought; my ſelf
In the habit of an ordinarie Captain
Diſguis'd, got entertainment, and ſerv'd here
That I might ſtill be ready to all fortunes:
That boy your grace took, nobly entertain'd him,
But thought a Gitle, Alinda, Madam.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Stand away,
And let me look upon him.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: My young Miſtris?
This is a ſtrange metamorphoſis, Alinda?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Your graces humble ſervant.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Come hither Siſter:
I dare yet ſcarce believe mine eyes: how they view one another?
Doſt thou not love this boy well?

sp.speaker: Oly.
sp.l: I ſhould lye elſe,
Truſt me, extreamly lye Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Didſt thou never wiſh Olympia,
It might be thus?

sp.speaker: Oly.
sp.l: A thouſand times.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Here take him:
Nay, do not bluſh: I do not jeſt; kiſs ſweetly:
Boy, ye kiſs faintly boy; Heaven give ye comfort;
Teach him, he'l quickly learn: there's two hearts eas'd not

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: You do me too much honour Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No Archas,
But all I can, I will; can you love me? ſpeak truly.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: Yes Sir, dearly.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Come hither Viola, can you love this man?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I'le do the beſt I can Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Seal it Burris,
We'l all to Church together inſtantly:
And then a vie for boyes; ſtay, bring Boroskie.
I had almoſt forgot that lump of miſchief.
There Archas, take the enemie to honour,
The knave to worth: do with him what thou wilt.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Waſh off your villanies, you feel the burthen.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Forgive me e're I die, moſt honeſt Archas;
'Tis too much honour that I periſh thus;
O ſtrike my faults to kill them, that no memorie,
No black and blaſted infamy hereafter—

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Come, are ye ready?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: And truly penitent, to make your way ſtraight?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Thus I waſh off my ſins.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Stand up, and live then,
And live an honeſt man; I ſcorn mens ruines:
Take him again, Sir, trie him: and believe
This thing will be a perfect man.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I take him.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: And when I fail thoſe hopes, heavens hopes fail me.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: You are old: no more wars Father:
Theodore take you the charge, be General.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: All good bleſs ye.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And my good Father, you dwell in my boſom,
From you riſe all my good thoughts: when I would think
And examine time for one that's fairly noble,
And the ſame man through all the ſtreights of vertue,
Upon this Silver book I'le look, and read him.
Now forward merrily to Hymens rites,
To joyes, and revels, ſports, and he that can
Moſt honour Archas, is the nobleſt man. Exe • t.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: WE need not noble Gentlemen to invite
Attention, preinſtruct you who did write
This worthy Story, being confident
The mirth join'd with prave matter, and Intent
To yield the hearers profit, with delight,
Will ſpeak the maker: and to do him right,
Would ask a Genius like to his; the age
Mourning his loſs, and our now widdowed ſtage
In vain lamenting. I could adde, ſo far
Behind him the moſt modern writers are,
That when they would commend him, their beſt praiſe
R •• , the buildings which they ſtrive to raiſe
•• o • s beſt memory, ſo much a friend
Preſumes to write, ſecure 'twill not offend
The living that are modeſt, with the reſt
That may repine he cares not to conteſt.
This debt to Fletcher paid; it is profeſt
By us the Actors, we will do our beſt
To ſend ſuch favouring friends, as hither come
To grace the Scene, pleas'd, and contented home.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: THough ſomething well aſſur'd, few here repent
Three hours of pretious time, or money ſpent
On our endeavours, Yet not to relye
Too much upon our care, and induſtrie,
'Tis fit we ſhould ask, but a modeſt way
How you approve our action in the play.
If you vouchſafe to crown it with applauſe,
It is your bountie, and you give us cauſe
Hereafter with a general conſent
To ſtudy, as becomes us, your content.

div.head: Rule a Wife, and have a Wife.
Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Juan de Caſtro, and Michael Perez.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: ARE your Companies full, Colonel?

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: No, not yet, Sir:
Nor will not be this month yet, as I reckon;
How riſes your Command?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: We pick up ſtill, and as our monies hold out,
We have men come, about that time I think
We ſhall be full too, many young Gallants go.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: And unexperienced,
The Wars are dainty dreams to young hot ſpirits,
Time and Experience will allay thoſe Viſions,
We have ſtrange things to fill our numbers,
There's one Don Leon, a ſtrange goodly fellow,
Recommended to me from ſome noble Friends,
For my Alferes, had you but ſeen his Perſon,
And what a Giants promiſe it proteſteth.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I have heard of him, and that he hath ſerv'd before too.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: But no harm done, nor never meant, Don Michael,
That came to my ears yet, ask him a queſtion,
• e bluſhes like a Girl, and anſwers little,
In the point leſs, he wears a Sword, a good one,
〈◊〉 good Cloaths too, he is whole skin'd, has no hurt yet,
Good promiſing hopes, I never yet heard certainly
〈◊〉 any Gentleman that ſaw him angry.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Preſerve him, he'll conclude a peace if need be,
• a • y as ſtrong as he will go along with us,
•• at ſwear as valiantly as heart can wiſh,
Their mouths charg'd with ſix oaths at once, and whole ones,
•• at make the drunken Dutch creep into Mole-hills.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: 'Tis true, ſuch we muſt look for: but Mich. Perez,
•• en heard you of Donna Margarita, the great Heireſs?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I hear every hour of her, though I never ſaw her,
• e is the main diſcourſe: noble Don Juan de Caſtro,
• ow happy were that man could catch this Wench up,
•• d live at eaſe! ſhe is fair, and young, and wealthy,
•• nite wealthy, and as gracious too
〈◊〉 all her entertainments, as men report.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: But ſhe is proud, Sir, that I know for certain,
• nd that comes ſeldome without wantonneſs,
• e that ſhall marry her, muſt have a rare hand.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Would I were married, I would find that Wiſdom,
With a light rein to rule my Wife: if ever Woman
〈◊〉 the moſt ſubtile mould went beyond me,
• ould give the Boys leave to whoot me out o'th' Pariſh.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sir, there be two Gentlewomen attend to ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Wait on 'em in.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Are they two handſome Women?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: They ſeem ſo, very handſom, but they are vail'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Thou put'ſt ſugar in my mouth, how it melts with me!
•• ve a ſweet young Wench.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Wait on them in I ſay. Exit Servant.

l.hi: Don Juan.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: How you itch, Michael! how you burniſh!
Will not this Souldiers heat out of your bones yet,
Do your Eyes glow now?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: There be two.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Say honeſt, what ſhame have you then?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I would fain ſee that,
I have been in the Indies twice, and have ſeen ſtrange things,
But two honeſt Women; — one I read of once.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Prithee be modeſt.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I'll be any thing.

div.stage: Enter Servant, Donna Clara, and Eſtiſania vad'd.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: You are welcome Ladies.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Both hooded, I like 'em well though,
They come not for advice in Law ſure hither;
May be they would learn to raiſe th • Pike,
I am for 'em: they are very modeſt, 'tis a fine Preluctium,

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: With me, or with this Gentleman,
Would you ſpeak, Lady?

sp.speaker: Clara.
sp.l: With you, Sir, as I gueſs, Juan de Caſt,

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Her Curtain opens, ſhe is a pretty Gentlewoman

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: I am the Man, and ſhall be bound to Fortune,
I may do any ſervice to your Beauties.

sp.speaker: Clara.
sp.l: Captain, I hear you are marching down to Flanders,
To ſerve the Catholick King.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: I am ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Clara.
