What ſhall I loſe the King for a few kiſſes?
We'l have enough.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I'le to the Duke my couſin, he ſhall to th' King.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: He did me this great office,
I thank his grace for't, ſhould I pray him now,
To undoe't again? fye 'twere a baſe diſcredit.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Would I were able Sir to bear you company,
How willing ſhould I be then, and how merry!
I will not live alone.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Be in peace, you ſhall not. knock within.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What knocking's this? oh Heaven my head, why raſcals
I thinks the war's begun i'th' houſe already.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: The preparation is, they are taking down,
And packing up the hangings, plate and Jewels,
And all thoſe furnitures that ſhall beſit me
When I lye in garriſon.

sp.speaker: Coachm.
sp.l: Muſt the Coach goe too Sir?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: How will your Lady paſs toth' ſea elſe eaſily?
We ſhall find ſhipping for't there to tranſport it.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I goe? alas!

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I'le have a main care of ye,
I know ye are ſickly, he ſhall drive the eaſier,
And all accommodation ſhall attend ye.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Would I were able,

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Come I warrant ye,
Am not I with ye ſweet? are her cloaths packt up,
And all her linnen? give your maids direction,
You know my time's but ſhort, and I am commanded.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Let me have a nurſe,
And all ſuch neceſſary people with me,
And an eaſie bark.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: It ſhall not trot I warrant ye,
Curvet it may ſometimes.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I am with child Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: At four days warning? this is ſomething ſpeedy,
Do you conceive as our jennets do with a weſt winde?
My heir will be an arrant fleet one Lady,
I'le ſwear you were a maid when I firſt lay with ye.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Pray do not ſwear, I thought I was a maid too,
But we may both be cozen'd in that point Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: In ſuch a ſtrait point ſure I could not err Madam.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: This is another tenderneſs to try him,
Fetch her up now.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You muſt provide a cradle, and what a troubles that?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: The ſea ſhall rock it,
'Tis the beſt nurſe; 'twill roar and rock together,
A ſwinging ſtorm will ſing you ſuch a lullaby.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Faith let me ſtay, I ſhall but ſhame ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: And you were a thouſand ſhames you ſhall along with me,
At home I am ſure you'l prove a million,
Every man carries the bundle of his ſins
Upon his own back, you are mine, I'le ſweat for ye.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What Sir, preparing for your noble journey?
'Tis well, and full of care.
I ſaw your mind was wedded to the war,
And knew you would prove ſome good man for your country,
Therefore fair Couſin with your gentle pardon,
I got this place: what, mourn at his advancement?
You are to blame, he will come again ſweet couſin,
Mean time like ſad Penelope and ſage,
Amongſt your maids at home, and huſwifely.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: No Sir, I dare not leave her to that ſolitarineſs,
She is young, and grief or ill news from thoſe quarters
May daily croſs her, ſhe ſhall goe along Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: By no means Captain.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: By all means an't pleaſe ye.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What take a young and tender bodied Lady,
And expoſe her to thoſe dangers, and thoſe tumults,
A ſickly Lady too?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: 'Twill make her well Sir,
There's no ſuch friend to health as wholſom travel.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Away it muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: It ought not Sir,
Go hurry her? it is not humane, Captain.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I cannot blame her tears, fright her with tempeſts,
With thunder of the war.
I dare ſwear if ſhe were able.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: She is moſt able.
And pray ye ſwear not, ſhe muſt goe, there's no remedy,
Nor greatneſs, nor the trick you had to part us,
Which I ſmell too rank, too open, too evident
(And I muſt tell you Sir, 'tis moſt unnoble)
Shall hinder me: had ſhe but ten hours life,
Nay leſs, but two hours, I would have her with me,
I would not leave her ſame to ſo much ruine,
To ſuch a deſolation and diſcredit
As her weakneſs and your hot will wou'd work her to.
What Maſque is this now?
More tropes and figures, to abuſe my ſufferance,
What couſin's this?

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Michael van owle, how doſt thou?
In what dark bath or tod of aged Ivy
Haſt thou lyen hid?

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Things muſt both ebbe and ſlow, Coronel,
And people muſt conceal, and ſhine again.
You are welcom hither as your friend may ſay, Gentleman,
A pretty houſe ye ſee handſomely ſeated,
Sweet and convenient walks, the waters cryſtal.

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: He's certain mad.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: As mad as a French Tayler,
That has nothing in's head but ends of ſuſtians.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: I ſee you are packing now my gentle couſin,
And my wife told me I ſhould find it ſo,
'Tis true I do, you were merry when I was laſt here,
But 'twas your will to try my patience Madam.
I am ſorry that my ſwift occaſions
Can let you take your pleaſure here no longer,
Yet I would have you think my honour'd couſin,
This houſe and all I have are all your ſervants.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: What houſe, what pleaſure Sir, what do you mean?

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: You hold the jeſt ſo ſtill, 'twill prove diſcourteous,
This houſe I mean, the pleaſures of this place.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: And what of them?

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: They are mine Sir, and you know it,
My wiſes I mean, and ſo confer'd upon me,
The hangings Sir I muſt entreat, your ſervants,
That are ſo buſie in their offices,
Again to miniſter to their right uſes,
I ſhall take view o'th' plate anon, and furnitures
That are of under place; you are merry ſtill couſin,
And of a pleaſant conſtitution,
Men of great fortunes make their mirths at placitum.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Prethee good ſtubborn wife, tell me directly,
Good evll wife leave fooling and tell me honeſtly,
Is this my kinſman?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I can tell ye nothing.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I have many kinſmen, but ſo mad a one,
And ſo phantaſtick—all the houſe?

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: All mine,
And all within it. I will not bate ye an ace on't.
Can you not receive a noble courteſie,
And quietly and handſomely as ye ought Couz,
But you muſt ride o'th' top on't?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Canſt thou fight?

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.l: I'le tell ye preſently, I could have done Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: For ye muſt law and claw before ye get it.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Away, no quarrels.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Now I am more temperate,
I'le have it prov'd if you were never yet in Bedlam,
Never in love, for that's a lunacy,
No great ſtate left ye that you never lookt for,
Nor cannot manage, that's a rank diſtemper;
That you were chriſten'd, and who anſwer'd for ye,
And then I yield.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: H'as half perſwaded me I was bred i'th'moon,
I have ne'r a buſh at my breech, are not we both mad,
And is not this a phantaſtick houſe we are in,
And all a dream we do? will ye walk out Sir,
And if I do not beat thee preſently
Into a ſound belief, as ſenſe can give thee,
Brick me into that wall there for a chimny piece,
And ſay I was one o'th' Caeſars, done by a ſeal-cutter.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I'le talk no more, come we'l away immediatly.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Why then the houſe is his, and all that's in it,
I'le give away my skin but I'le undoe ye,
I gave it to his wife, you muſt reſtore Sir,
And make a new proviſion.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Am I mad now or am I chriſten'd, you my page couſ • ,
My mighty Mahound kinſman, what quirk now?
You ſhall be welcom all, I hope to ſee Sir
Your Grace here, and my couz, we are all Souldiers,
And muſt do naturally for one another.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Are ye blank at this? then I muſt tell ye Sir,
Ye have no command, now ye may goe at pleaſure
And ride your aſſe troop, 'twas a trick I us'd
To try your jealouſie upon entreatie,
And ſaving of your wife.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: All this not moves me,
Nor ſtirs my gall, nor alters my affections,
You have more furniture, more houſes Lady,
And rich ones too, I will make bold with thoſe,
And you have Land i'th' Indies as I take it,
Thither we'l goe, and view a while thoſe climats,
Viſit your Factors there, that may betray ye,
'Tis done, we muſt goe.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Now thou art a brave Gentleman,
And by this ſacred light I love thee dearly.
The houſe is none of yours, I did but jeſt Sir,
Nor you are no couz of mine, I beſeech ye vaniſh,
I tell you plain, you have no more right than he
Has, that ſenſeleſs thing, your wife has once more fool'd ye:
Goe ye and conſider.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Good morrow my ſweet couſin, I ſhould be glad Sir.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: By this hand ſhe dies for't,
Or any man that ſpeaks for her. Exit Perez.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Theſe are fine toyes.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Let me requeſt you ſtay but one poor month,
You ſhall have a Commiſſion and I'le goe too,
Give me but will ſo far.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Well I will try ye,
Good morrow to your Grace, we have private buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: If I miſs thee again, I am an arrant bungler.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have my command, and I'le march under thee,
Nay be thy boy before thou ſhalt be baffled,
Thou art ſo brave a fellow.

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: I have ſeen viſions. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Leon, with a letter, and Margarita.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: COme hither wife, do you know this hand?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I do Sir,
'Tis Eſtifania, that was once my woman.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: She writes to me here, that one Cacaſogo
An uſuring Jewellers ſon (I know the Raſcal)
Is mortally faln in love with ye.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Is a monſter, deliver me from mountains.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Do you goe a birding for all ſorts of people?
And this evening will come to ye and ſhew ye Jewels,
And offers any thing to get acceſs to ye,
If I can make or ſport or profit on him,
(For he is fit for both) ſhe bids me uſe him,
And ſo I will, be you conformable, and follow but my will.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I ſhall not fail, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Will the Duke come again do you think?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: No ſure Sir,
H'as now no policie to bring him hither.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Nor bring you to him, if my wit hold fair wife:
Let's in to dinner. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Had I but lungs enough to bawl ſufficiently,
That all the queans in Chriſtendom might hear me,
That men might run away from contagion,
I had my wiſh; would it were moſt high treaſon,
Moſt infinite high, for any man to marry,
I mean for any man that would live hand ſomely,
And like a Gentleman, in his wits and credit.
What torments ſhall I put her to, Phalaris bull now?
Pox they love bulling too well, though they ſmoak for't.
Cut her a pieces? every piece will live ſtill,
And every morſel of her will do miſchief;
They have ſo many lives, there's no hanging of 'em,
They are too light to drown, they are cork and feathers;
To burn too cold, they live like Salamanders;
Under huge heaps of ſtones to bury her,
And ſo depreſs her as they did the Giants;
She will move under more than built old Babel,
I muſt deſtroy her.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: Be cozen'd by a thing of clouts, a ſhe moth,
That every ſilkmans ſhop breeds; to be cheated,
And of a thouſand duckets by a whim wham?

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Who's that is cheated, ſpeak again thou viſion,
But art thou cheated? miniſter ſome comfort:
Tell me directly art thou cheated bravely?
Come, prethee come, art thou ſo pure a coxcomb
To be undone? do not diſſemble with me,
Tell me I conjure thee.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: Then keep thy circle,
For I am a ſpirit wild that flies about thee,
And who e're thou art, if thou be'ſt humane,
I'le let thee plainly know, I am cheated damnably.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: Doſt thou laugh? damnably, I ſay moſt damnably.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: By whom, good ſpirit ſpeak, ſpeak ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: I will utter, laugh till thy lungs crack, by a raſcal woman,
A lewd, abominable, and plain woman.
Doſt thou laugh ſtill?

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: I muſt laugh, prethee pardon me,
I ſhall laugh terribly.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: I ſhall be angry, terrible angry, I have cauſe.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: That's it, and 'tis no reaſon but thou ſhouldſt be angry,
Angry at heart, yet I muſt laugh ſtill at thee.
By a woman cheated? art' ſure it was a woman?

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: I ſhall break thy head, my valour itches at thee.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: It is no matter, by a woman cozen'd,
A real woman?

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: A real Devil,
Plague of her Jewels and her copper chains,
How rank they ſmell.

sp.speaker: Perox.
sp.l: Sweet cozen'd Sir let me ſee them,
I have been cheated too, I would have you note that,
And lewdly cheated, by a woman alſo,
A ſcurvie woman, I am undone ſweet Sir,
Therefore I muſt have leave to haugh.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: Pray ye take it,
You are the merrieſt undone man in Europe.
What need we fiddles, bawdy ſongs and ſack,
When our own miſeries can make us merry?

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.
I have ſeen theſe Jewels, what a notable penniworth
Have you had next our heart? you will not take Sir
Some twenty Duck • ts?

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: Thou art deceiv'd, I will take.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: To clean your bargain now.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: I'le take ſ • me ten, ſome any thing, ſome half ten,
Half a Ducket

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: An excellent lapidary ſet theſe ſtones ſure,
Do you mark their waters?

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: Quick ſand choak their waters,
And hers that bought 'em too, but I ſhall find her.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: And ſo ſhall I, I hope, but do not hurt her,
You cannot find in all this Kingdom,
(If you had need of cozening, as you may have,
For ſuch groſs natures will deſire it often,
'Tis at ſome time too a fine variety,)
A woman that can cozen ye ſo neatly,
She has taken half mine anger off with this trick. Exit.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: If I were valiant now, I would kill this fellow,
I have mony enough lies by me at a pinch
To pay for twenty Raſcals lives that vex me,
I'le to this Lady, there I ſhall be ſatisfied. Exit.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Come, we'l away unto your country houſe,
And there we'l learn to live contently,
This place is full of charge, and full of hurry,
No part of ſweetneſs dwells about theſe cities.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Whither you will, I wait upon your pleaſure;
Live in a hollow tree Sir, I'le live with ye.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I, now you ſtrike a harmony, a true one,
When your obedience waits upon your Husband,
And your ſick will aims at the care of honour,
Why now I dote upon ye, love ye dearly,
And my rough nature falls like roaring ſtreams,
Clearly and ſweetly into your embraces.
O what a Jewel is a woman excellent,
A wiſe, a vertuous and a noble woman!
When we meet ſuch, we bear our ſtamps on both ſides,
And through the world we hold our currant virtues,
Alone we are ſingle medals, only faces,
And wear our fortunes out in uſeleſs ſhadows,
Command you now, and eaſe me of that trouble,
I'le be as humble to you as a ſervant,
Bid whom you pleaſe, invite your noble friends,
They ſhall be welcome all, viſit acquaintance,
God at your pleaſure, now experience
Has link't you faſt unto the chain of goodneſs: Claſhing ſwords. A cry within, down with their ſwords.
What noiſe is this, what diſmal cry?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: 'Tis loud too.
Sure there's ſome miſchief done i'th' ſtreet, look out there.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Look out and help.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Oh Sir the Duke Medina.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: What of the Duke Medina?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Oh ſweet Gentleman, is almoſt ſlain.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Away away and help him, all the houſe help.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: How ſlain? why Margarita,
Why wife, ſure ſome new device they have a foot again,
Some trick upon my credit, I ſhall meet it,
I had rather guide a ſhip Imperial
Alone, and in a ſtorm, than rule one woman.

div.stage: Enter Duke, Margarita, Sanchio, Alonzo, Servant.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: How came ye hurt Sir?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I felt out with my friend the noble Coronel,
My cauſe was naught, for 'twas about your honour:
And he that wrongs the Innocent ne'r proſpers,
And he has left me thus for charity,
Lend me a bed to eaſe my tortur'd body,
That e're I periſh I may ſhow my penitence,
I fear I am ſlain.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Help Gentlemen to carry him,
There ſhall be nothing in this houſe my Lord,
But as your own.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I thank ye noble Sir,

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: To bed with him, and wife give your attendance.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Doctors and Surgions:

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Do not diſquiet me,
But let me take my leave in peace.

div.stage: Ex. Duke, Sanchio, Alon. Marg. Servant.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Afore me
'Tis • arely counterfeited.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: True, it is ſo Sir,
And take you heed, this laſt blow do not ſpoil ye,
He is not hurt, only we made a ſcuffle,
As though we purpos'd anger; that ſame ſcratch
On's hand he took, to colour all and draw compaſſion,
That he might get into your houſe more cunningly:
I muſt not ſtay, ſtand now, and y'are a brave fel • ow.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I thank ye noble Coronel, and I honour ye. Exit Juan.

div.l: Never be quiet?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: He's moſt deſperate ill Sir,
I do not think theſe ten months will recover him.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Does he hire my houſe to play the fool in,
Or do ••• ſtand on Fairy ground, we are haunted,
Are all men and their wives troubled with dreams thus?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: What all you Sir?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Nay what all you ſweet wife,
To put theſe daily paſtimes on my patience?
What doſt thou ſee in me, that I ſhould ſuffer thus,
Have not I done my part like a true Husband,
And paid ſome deſperate debts you never look'd for?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: You have done handſomely I muſt confeſs Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Have I not kept thee waking like a hawk?
And watcht thee with delights to ſatisfy thee?
The very tithes of which had won a Widow.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Alas I pity ye.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Thou wilt make me angry,
Thou never ſaw'ſt me mad yet.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: You are alwaies,
You carry a kind of bedlam ſtill about ye.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: If thou purſueſt me further I run ſtark mad,
If you have more hurt Dukes or Gentlemen,
To lye here on your cure, I ſhall be deſperate,
I know the trick, and you ſhall feel I know it,
Are ye ſo hot that no hedge can contain ye?
I'le have thee let blood in all the veins about thee,
I'le have thy thoughts ſound too, and have them open'd,
Thy ſpirits purg'd, for thoſe are they that fire ye,
Thy maid ſhall be thy Miſtris, thou the maid,
And all thoſe ſerviſe labours that ſhe reach at,
And goe through cheerfully, or elſe ſleep empty,
That maid ſhall lye by me to teach you duty,
You in a pallet by to humble ye,
And grieve for what you loſe.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I have loſt my ſelf Sir,
And all that was my baſe ſelf, diſobedience, kneels
My wantonneſs, my ſtubborneſs I have loſt too,
And now by that pure faith good wives are crown'd with,
By your own nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I take ye up, and wear ye next my heart,
See you be worth it. Now what with you?

sp.speaker: Altea.
sp.l: I come to tell my Lady,
There is a fulſome fellow would fain ſpeak with her.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: 'Tis Cacafogo, goe and entertain him,
And draw him on with hopes.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I ſhall obſerve ye.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I have a rare deſign upon that Gentleman,
And you muſt work too.

sp.speaker: Altea.
sp.l: I ſhall Sir moſt willingly.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Away then both, and keep him cloſe in ſome place
From the Dukes ſight, and keep the Duke in too,
Make 'em believe both, I'le find time to cure 'em. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Perez, and Eſtifania, with a Piſtol, and a Dagge.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Why how darſt thou meet me again thou rebel,
And knowſt how thou haſt uſed me thrice, thou raſcal?
Were there not waies enough to fly my vengeance,
No holes nor vaults to hide thee from my fury,
But thou muſt meet me face to face to kill thee?
I would not ſeek thee to deſtroy thee willingly,
But now thou comeſt to invite me,
And comeſt upon me,
How like a ſheep-biting Rogue taken i'th' manner,
And ready for the halter doſt thou look now?
Thou haſt a hanging look thou ſcurvy thing, haſt ne'r a knife
Nor ever a ſtring to lead thee to Elyſium?
Be there no pitifull 'Pothecaries in this town,
That have compaſſion upon wretched women,
And dare adminiſter a dram of rats-bane,
But thou muſt fall to me?

sp.speaker: Eſtif.
sp.l: I know you have mercy.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.l: If I had tuns of mercy thou deſerv'ſt none,
What new trick is now a foot, and what new houſes
Have you i'th' air, what orchards in apparition,
What canſt thou ſay for thy life?

sp.speaker: Eſtif.
sp.l: Little or nothing,
I know you'l kill me, and I know 'tis uſeleſs
To beg for mercy, pray let me draw my book out,
And pray a little.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Do, a very little,
For I have farther buſineſs than thy killing,
I have mony yet to borrow, ſpeak when you are ready.

sp.speaker: Eſtif.
sp.l: Now now Sir, now, ſhews a Piſtol.
Come on, do you ſtart off from me,
Do you ſwear great Captain, have you ſeen a ſpirit?

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Do you wear guns?

sp.speaker: Eſtif.
sp.l: I am a Souldiers wife Sir,
And by that priviledge I may be arm'd,
Now what's the news, and let's diſcourſe more friendly,
And talk of our affairs in peace.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Let me ſee,
Prethee let me ſee thy gun, 'tis a very pretty one.

sp.speaker: Eſtif.
sp.l: No no Sir, you ſhall feel.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: Hold ye villain, what thine own Husband?

sp.speaker: Eſtif.
sp.l: Let mine own Husband then
Be in's own wits, there, there's a thouſand duckets,
Who mu • provide for you, and yet you'l kill me.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.l: I was not hurt thee for ten thouſand millions.

sp.speaker: Eſtif.
sp.l: When will you redeem your Jewels, I have pawn'd 'em,
You ſee for what, we muſt keep touch.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: I'le kiſs thee,
And get as many more, I'le make thee famous,
Had we the houſe now!

sp.speaker: Eſtif.
sp.l: Come along with me,
If that be vaniſh't there be more to hire Sir.

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: I ſee I am an aſſe when thou art near me.

div.stage: Enter Leon, Margarita, and Altea, with a Taper.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Is the fool come?

sp.speaker: Altea.
sp.l: Yes and i'th' celler faſt,
And there he ſtaies his good hour till I call him,
He will make dainty muſick among the fack-butts,
I have put him juſt, Sir, under the Dukes chamber.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: It is the better.

sp.speaker: Altea.
sp.l: Has given me royally,
And to my Lady a whole load of portigues.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Better and better ſtill, go Margarita,
Now play your prize, you ſay you dare be honeſt,
I'le put ye to your beſt.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Secure your ſelf Sir, give me the candle,
Paſs away in ſilence. Ex. Leon and Altea. She knocks.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Who's there, oh oh.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke within.
sp.l: Have ye brought me comfort?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I have my Lord,
Come forth 'tis I, come gently out I'le help ye,
Come ſoftly too, how do you?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Are there none here?
Let me look round; we cannot be too wary, noiſe below.
Oh let me bleſs this hour, are you alone ſweet friend?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Alone to comfort you. Cacafogo makes a noiſe below.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What's that you tumble?
I have heard a noiſe this half hour under me,
A fearfull noiſe.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: The fat thing's mad i'th' celler,
And ſtumbles from one hogs-head to another,
Two cups more, and he ne'r ſhall find the way out.
What do you fear? come, ſit down by me chearfully,
My Husband's ſafe, how do your wounds?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I have none Lady,
My wounds I counterfeited cunningly, noiſe below.
And feign'd the quarrel too, to injoy you ſweet,
Let's loſe no time, heark the ſame noiſe again.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: What noiſe, why look ye pale? I hear no ſtirring,
This goblin in the vault will be ſo tipled.
You are not well I know by your flying fancy,
Your body's ill at eaſe, your wounds.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I have none, I am as luſty and as full of health,
High in my blood.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Weak in your blood you would ſay,
How wretched is my caſe, willing to pleaſe ye,
And find you ſo diſable?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Believe me Lady.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I know you will venture all you have to ſatisfy me,
Your life I know, but is it fit I ſpoil ye,
Is it my love do you think?

sp.speaker: Cacaf. below.
sp.l: Here's to the Duke.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: It nam'd me certainly,
I heard it plainly ſound.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: You are hurt mortally,
And fitter for your prayers Sir than pleaſure,
What ſtarts you make? I would not kiſs you wantonly,
For the worlds wealth; have I ſecur'd my Husband,
And put all doubts aſide to be deluded?

sp.speaker: Cacaf. below.
sp.l: I come, I come.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs me.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: And bleſs us both, for ſure this is the Devil,
I plainly heard it now, he will come to fetch ye,
A very ſpirit, for he ſpoke under ground,
And ſpoke to you juſt as you would have ſnatcht me,
You are a wicked man, and ſure this haunts ye,
Would you were out o'th' houſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I would I were,
O' that condition I had leapt a window,

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: And that's the leaſt leap if you mean to ſcape Sir,
Why what a frantick man were you to come here,
What a weak man to counterfeit deep wounds,
To wound another deeper?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Are you honeſt then?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Yes then and now, and ever, and excellent honeſt,
And exerciſe this paſtime but to ſhew ye,
Great men are fools ſometimes as well as wretches.
Would you were well hurt, with any hope of life,
Cut to the brains, or run clean through the body,
To get out quietly as you got in Sir,
I wiſh it like a friend that loves ye dearly,
For if my Husband take ye, and take ye thus a counterfeit,
One that would clip his credit out of his honour,
He muſt kill ye preſently,
There is no mercy nor an hour of pity,
And for me to intreat in ſuch an agony,
Would ſhew me little better than one guilty,
Have you any mind to a Lady now?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Would I were off fair,
If ever Lady caught me in a trap more.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: If you be well and luſty, ſy fy ſhake not,
You ſay you love me, come, come bravely now,
Deſpiſe all danger, I am ready for ye.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: She mocks my miſery, thou cruel Lady.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Thou cruel Lord, wouldſt thou betray my honeſty,
Betray it in mine own houſe, wrong my Husband,
Like a night thief, thou darſt not name by day-light?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I am moſt miſerable.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: You are indeed,
And like a fooliſh thing you have made your ſelf ſo,
Could not your own diſcretion tell ye Sir,
When I was married I was none of yours?
Your eyes were then commanded to look off me,
And I now ſtand in a circle and ſecure,
Your ſpells nor power can never reach my body,
Mark me but this, and then Sir be moſt miſerable,
'Tis ſacriledge to violate a wedlock,
You rob two Temples, make your ſelf twice guilty,
You ruine hers, and ſpot her noble Husbands.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Let me be gone, I'le never more attempt ye.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You cannot goe, 'tis not in me to ſave ye,
Dare ye do ill, and poorly then ſhrink under it?
Were I the Duke Medina, I would fight now,
For you muſt fight and bravely, it concerns you,
You do me double wrong if you ſneak off Sir,
And all the world would ſay I lov'd a coward,
And you muſt dye too, for you will be kill'd,
And leave your youth, your honour and your ſtate,
And all thoſe dear delights you worſhip't here. Noiſe below.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: The noiſe again!

sp.speaker: Cacaf. below.
sp.l: Some ſmall beer if you love me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: The Devil haunts you ſure, your ſins are mighty.
A drunken Devil too, to plague your villany.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Preſerve me but this once.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: There's a deep well
In the next yard, if you dare venture drowning,
It is but deah.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I would not dye ſo wretchedly.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Out of a garret window I'le let you down then,
But ſay the rope be rotten, 'tis huge high too.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Have you no mercy?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Now you are frighted throughly,
And find what 'tis to play the fool in folly,
And ſee with clear eyes your deteſted folly,
I'le be your guard.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And I'le be your true ſervant,
Ever from this hour vertuouſly to love ye,
Chaſtly and modeſtly to look upon ye,
And here I ſeal it.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: I may kiſs a ſtranger, for you muſt now be ſo.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: How do you my Lord,
Me thinks you look but poorly on this matter.
Has my wife wounded ye, you were well before,
Pray Sir be comforted, I have forgot all,
Truly forgiven too, wife you are a right one,
And now with unknown nations I dare truſt ye.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: No more ſeign'd fights my Lord, they never proſper.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Who's this? the Devil in the vault?

sp.speaker: Alt.
sp.l: 'Tis he Sir, and as lovingly drunk, as though he had ſtudied it.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: Give me a cup of Sack, and kiſs me Lady,
Kiſs my ſweet face, and make thy Husband cuckold,
An Ocean of ſweet Sack, ſhall we ſpeak treaſon?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: He is Deviliſh drunk.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I had thought he had been a Devil.
He made as many noiſes and as horrible.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Oh a true lover Sir will lament loudly,
Which of the butts is your Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: Butt in thy belly.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: There's two in thine I am ſure, 'tis grown ſo monſtrous.

sp.speaker: Caca.
sp.l: Butt in thy face.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Go carry him to ſleep,
A fools love ſhould be drunk, he has paid well for't too.
When he is ſober let him out to rail,
Or hang himſelf, there will be no loſs of him.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Who's this? my Mauhound couſin?

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.l: Good Sir, 'tis very good, would I had a houſe too,
For there is no talking in the open air,
My Tarmogant Couz, I would be bold to tell ye,
I durſt be merry too, I tell you plainly,
You have a pretty ſeat, you have the luck on't,
A pretty Lady too, I have miſt both,
My Carpenter built in a miſt I thank him,
Do me the courteſie to let me ſee it,
See it but once more. But I ſhall cry for anger.
I'le hire a Chandlers ſhop cloſe under ye,
And for my foolerie, ſell ſope and whip-cord,
Nay if you do not laugh now and laugh heartily,
You are a fool couz.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I muſt laugh a little,
And now I have done, couz thou ſhalt live with me,
My merry couz, the world ſhall not divorce us,
Thou art a valiant man, and thou ſhalt never want,
Will this content thee?

sp.speaker: Perez.
sp.l: I'le cry, and then I'le be thankfull,
Indeed I will, and I'le be honeſt to ye.
I would live a ſwallow here I muſt confeſs.
Wife I forgive thee all if thou be honeſt,
At thy peril, I believe thee excellent.

sp.speaker: Eſtif.
sp.l: If I prove otherwaies, let me beg firſt,
Hold, this is yours, ſome recompence for ſervice,
Uſe it to nobler ends than he that gave it.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And this is yours, your true commiſſion, Sir,
Now you are a Captain.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: You are a noble Prince Sir,
And now a ſouldier, Gentleman, we all rejoyce in't.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Sir, I ſhall wait upon you through all fortunes.

sp.speaker: Alon.
sp.l: And I.

sp.speaker: Altea.
sp.l: And I muſt needs attend my Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Will you goe Siſter?

sp.speaker: Altea.
sp.l: Yes indeed good Brother,
I have two ties, mine own bloud,
And my Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Is ſhe your Siſter?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Yes indeed good wife,
And my beſt Siſter,
For ſhe prov'd ſo, wench,
When ſhe deceiv'd you with a loving Husband.

sp.speaker: Alt.
sp.l: I would not deal ſo truly for a ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.l: Well I could chide ye,
But it muſt be lovingly and like a Siſter,
I'le bring you on your way, and feaſt ye nobly,
For now I have an honeſt heart to love ye,
And then deliver you to the blue Neptune.

sp.speaker: Juan.
sp.l: Your colours you muſt wear, and wear 'em proudly,
Wear 'em before the bullet, and in bloud too,
And all the world ſhall know
We are Vertues ſervants.

l.hi: And all the world ſhall know, a noble mind Makes women beautifull, and envie blind.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: PLeaſure attend ye, and about ye ſit
The ſprings of mirth, fancy, delight and wit
To ſtir you up, do not your looks let fall,
Nor to remembrance our late errors call,
Becauſe this day w' are Spaniards all again,
The ſtory of our Play, and our Scene Spain:
The errors too, do not for this cauſe hate,
Now we preſent their wit and not their ſtate.
Nor Ladies be not angry if you ſee,
A young freſh beauty, wanton and too free,
Seek to abuſe her Husband, ſtill 'tis Spain,
No ſuch groſs errors in your Kingdom raign,
W' are Veſtals all, and though we blow the fire,
We ſeldom make it flame up to deſire,
Take no example neither to begin,
For ſome by precedent delight to ſin:
Nor blame the Poet if he ſlip aſide
Sometimes laſciviouſly if not too wide.
But hold your Fanns cloſe, and then ſmile at eaſe,
A cruel Scene did never Lady pleaſe.
Nor Gentlemen, pray be not you diſpleas'd,
Though we preſent ſome men fool'd, ſome diſeas'd,
Some drunk, ſome mad: we mean not you, you're free,
We taxe no farther than our Comedie,
You are our friends, ſit noble then and ſee.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: GOod night our worthy friends, and may you part
Each with as merry and as free a heart
As you came hither; to thoſe noble eyes
That deign to ſmile on our poor faculties,
And give a bleſſing to our labouring ends,
As we hope many, to ſuch fortune ſends
Their own deſires, wives fair as light as chaſt;
To thoſe that live by ſpight Wives made in haſt.

div.head: The Laws of Candy. A TRAGI-COMEDY.

list.item: Antinous, Son to Caſſilanes, and his Competitor.
Fernando, a Venetian Captain, Servant to Annophel.
Philander, Prince of Cyprus, paſſionately in love with Erota.
Gonzalo, An ambitious Politick Lord of Venice.
Arcanes, a noble Souldier, Friend to Caſſilanes.
Mochingo, an ignorant Servant to Erota.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Erota, a Princeſs, imperious, and of an overweaning Beauty.
Hyparcha, Attendant on the Princeſs Erota.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: SIR, you're the very friend I wiſh'd to meet with,
I have a large diſcourſe invites your ear
To be an Auditor.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: And what concerns it?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: The ſadly thriving progreſs of the loves
Between my Lord, the Prince, and that great Lady,
Whoſe inſolence, and never-yet-match'd Pride,
Can by no Character be well expreſt,
Bet in her only name, the proud Erota.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Alas, Melitus, I ſhould gueſs the beſt
Succeſs your Prince could find from her, to be
As harſh as the event doth prove: but now
'Tis not a time to pity paſſionate grieſs,
When a whole Kingdom in a manner lyes
Upon its Death-Bed bleeding.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Who can tell
Whether or no theſe plagues at once
Hang over this unhappy Land for her ſake
That is a Monſter in it?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Here's the miſery
Of having a Child our Prince; elſe I preſume
The bold Venetians had not dar'd to attempt
So bloody an invaſion.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Yet I wonder
Why (Maſter Secretary) ſtill the Senate
So almoſt ſuperſtitiouſly adores
Gonzalo, the Venetian Lord, conſidering
The outrage of his Countrymen—

sp.speaker: Gaſ
sp.l: The Senate
Is wiſe, and therein juſt, for this Gonzalo,
Upon a Maſſacre performed at Sea
By the Admiral of Venice, on a Merchant
Of Candy, when the cauſe was to be heard
Before the Senate there, in open Court
Profeſſed, that the cruelty the Admiral
Had ſhewed, deſerved not only fine, but death;
For Candy then, and Venice were at peace:
Since when upon a motion in the Senate,
For Conqueſt of our Land, 'tis known for certain,
That only this Gonzalo dar'd to oppoſe it,
His reaſon was, becauſe it too much ſavour'd
Of lawleſs and unjuſt ambition.
The Wars were ſcarce begun, but he (in fear
Of quarrels 'gainſt his life) fled from his Country,
And hither came, where (to confirm his truth)
I know, (Melitus,) he out of his own ſtore,
Hath monied Caſſilanes the General.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: What, without other pledges than Caſſilanes
Bare promiſe of payment?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: No, it may be
He has ſome pretty Lordſhip to retire to;
But thus he hath done; now 'tis fit, Melitus,
The Senate ſhould be thankful, otherwiſe
They ſhould annihilate one of thoſe Laws
For which this Kingdome is throughout the World
Unfollowed and admired.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: What Laws are thoſe, Sir?
Let me ſo much importune you.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: You ſhall,
And they be worth your knowledge: briefly thus:
Who e'r he be that can detect apparently
Another of ingratitude, for any
Received Benefit, the Plaintiff may
Require the Offenders life; unleſs he pleaſe
Freely and willingly to grant remiſſion.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: By which ſtrict Law, the Senate is in danger,
Should they neglect Gonzalo?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Right, the Law
Permits a like equality to Aliens,
As to a home-bred Patriot.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Pray Sir, the other?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Know, Melitus,
The elder Cretans flouriſhed many years,
In War, in Peace unparallel'd, and they
(To ſpur heroick Spirits on to Vertue)
Enacted that what man ſo ere he were,
Did nobleſt in the field againſt his enemy,
So by the general voice approv'd, and known,
Might at his home return, make his demand
For ſatisfaction, and reward.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: They are
Both famous Laws indeed.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Maſter Secretary,
The Senate is about to ſit, and crave
Your preſence.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: What, ſo ſuddenly?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Theſe Letters
Will ſhew the cauſes why.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Heaven, thou n • t great,
And worthy to be thanked!

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Your countenance, Sir,
Doth promiſe ſome good tidings.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: O the beſt
And happieſt for this land that e'r was told!
All the Venetian Forces are defeated.

sp.speaker: Mel
sp.l: How, Sir?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: And what doth add ſome delight more,
There is amongſt the Souldiers a contention
Who ſhall be the triumpher, and it ſtands
Doubtful between a Father and his Son,
Old Caſſilanes, and young Antinous.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: VVhy may not both demand it?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: The Law denies it,
But where the Souldiers do not all conſent,
The Parties in contention, are refer'd
To plead before the Senate; and from them
Upon an open audience to be judg'd
The Chief, and then to make demands.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: You raviſh me
VVith wonder and delight.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Come; as we walk,
I ſhall more fully inform you. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Caſſilanes, Arcanes, Antinous, and Decius.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Admit no Souldier near us till the Senate
Have took their places.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: You are obey'd, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Decius, fall off.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Give leave Arcanes:
Young man, come nearer to me: who am I?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It were a ſin againſt the piety
Of ſilial duty, if I ſhould forget
The debt I owe my Father on my knee:
Your pleaſure?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: VVhat, ſo low? canſt thou find joints,
Yet be an Elephant? Antinous, riſe;
Thou wilt belye opinion, and rebate
The ambition of thy gallantry, that they
Whoſe confidence thou haſt bewitch'd, ſhould ſee
Their little God of War, kneel to his Father,
Though in my hand I did graſp Thunder.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sir,
For proof that I acknowledge you the Author
Of giving me my Birth, I have diſcharg'd
A part of my Obedience. But if now
You ſhould (as cruel fathers do) proclaim
Your right, and Tyrant-like uſurp the glory
Of my peculiar honours, not deriv'd
From ſucceſſary, but purchas'd with my bloud,
Then I muſt ſtand firſt Champion for my ſelf
Againſt all interpoſers.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Boldly urg'd,
And proudly, I could love thee, did not anger
Conſult with juſt diſdain, in open language
To call thee moſt ungrateful. Say freely,
Wilt thou reſign the flatteries whereon
The reeling pillars of a popular breath
Have rais'd thy Giant-like conceit, to add
A ſuffrage to thy Fathers merit? ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sir, hear me: were there not a Chronicle
Well pen'd by all their tongues, who can report
What they have ſeen you do; or had you not
Beſt in your own performance writ your ſelf,
And been your own text, I would undertake
Alone, without the help of Art, or Character,
But only to recount your deeds in Arms,
And you ſhould ever then be fam'd a Preſident
Of living victory: But as you are
Great, and well worthy to be ſtiled Great,
It would betray a poverty of Spirit
In me to obſtruct my fortunes, or deſcent,
If I ſhould coward-like ſurrender up
The intereſt which the inheritance of your vertue
And mine own thrifty fate can claim in honour:
My Lord, of all the maſs of Fame, which any
That wears a Sword, and hath but ſeen me fight,
Gives me, I will not ſhare, nor yield one jot,
One tittle.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Not to me?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You are my Father,
Yet not to you.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Ambitious Boy, how dar'ſt thou
To tell me, that thou wilt contend?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Had I
Been ſlothful, and not follow'd you in all
The ſtreights of death, you might have juſtly then
Reputed me a Baſtard: 'tis a cruelty
More than to murther Innocents, to take
The life of my yet infant-honour from me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Antinous, look upon this badge of age,
Thy Father's grey-hair'd beard: full fifty years,
(And more than half of this, ere thou wert born)
I have been known a Souldier, in which time
I ſound no difference 'twixt War and Peace,
For War was Peace to me, and Peace was War.
Antinous, mark me well; there hath not liv'd
Theſe fifty years a man whom Crete prefer'd
Before thy Father; let me boldly boaſt,
Thy Father, both for Diſcipline and Action
Hath ſo long been the firſt of all his Nation;
Now, canſt thou think it honeſt, charitable,
Nay humane, being ſo young, my Son, my Child,
Be got, bred, taught by me, by me thy Father,
For one days ſervice, and that on thy firſt,
To rob me of a glory which I fought for
A half of hundred years?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: My caſe obſerves
Both equity and preſidents; for Sir,
That very day whereon you got your Fame,
You took it from ſome other, who was then
Chief in repute, as you are now, and has been
Perhaps as many years deſerving that
Which you gain'd in a day, as I have mine.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: But he was not my Father then, Antinous;
Thou leav'ſt out that.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sir, had he been your Father,
He had been then immortal; for a Father
•• eightens his reputation where his Son
•• erits it, as when you give us life,
〈◊〉 life is not diminiſh'd but renew'd
•• s when you are dead, and we are ſtill
Your living Images,

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: So be thou curs'd
I • to • poſterity, as I in thee,
Diſhonourable Boy; O ſhall that Sun,
Which not a year yet ſince beheld me mounted
Upon a fiery Steed, waving my Sword,
And teaching this young Man to manage Arms,
That was a raw, freſh Novice in the feats
Of Chivalrie, ſhall that ſame Sun be witneſs
Againſt this Brat of his Ingratitude?
Who, to eclipſe the light of my renown,
Can no way hope to get a noble Name,
••• t by the treading on his Father's Greatneſs;
Thou wilt not yield?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: My life, but not the prize
My Sword hath purchas'd.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: The Senate,
My Lord, are here at hand, and all the Souldiers
Begin to throng about them.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Now, Arcanes, the—

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: What, Sir?

sp.speaker: Caſ
sp.l: Trifles will affront us; that
Fine fighting Stripling.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Let him have the ſhame on't;
Pleaſe you withdraw on this ſide.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: My great heart
Was never quail'd before.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: My Lord, be confident,
Let not your Father daunt you.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Decius, whither
Muſt I withdraw?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: On this ſide.— See, the Souldiers
Attend your pleaſure—courage, Sir; the Senate.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Way for the Senate.
sp.stage: Enter Porphycio, Poſſenne, (three Senators) Gonzalo, Gaſpero, Souldiers.
sp.l: My good Lords I know not
What tax of arrogance I may incurr,
Should I preſume, though courted by your Favours,
To take a place amongſt you; I had rather
Give proof of my unfeign'd humility
By force, though mean, yet more becoming place,
Than run the hazard of a doubtful cenſure.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: My Lord, your wiſdom is both known and try'd;
We cannot rank you in a nobler Friendſhip
Than your great ſervice to the State deſerves.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: Will't pleaſe you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: What's here, my Lord Porphycio?
It muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: My Lord, you are too modeſt.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: It is no ſeaſon to be troubleſome,
Elſe—but I have done: your Lordſhips are obſerv'd.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Is the demandant ready?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: He is ready.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Produce him then.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Before this ſacred preſence,
I, by a general conſent, am made
The Souldiers voice, and to your gracious Wiſedoms,
Preſent as chief in Arms, his Countries Champion,

l.hi: Caſſilanes.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Moſt reverend Lords, you hear the leſſer number
Of tho • who have been Guardians to this Country,
Approve this Champion; I, in all their names,
Who fought for Candy, here preſent before you
The mightieſt man in Arms, Antinous.
Speak fellow Souldiers.

l.hi: Antinous, Antinous.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Stand by all, ſave the two Competitors.

sp.speaker: Poſſ.
sp.l: My Lords, how much your Countrey owes you both,
The due reward of your deſertful glories
Muſt to Poſterity remain: but yet
Since, by our Law, one only can make claim
To the propoſed honours which you both
(It ſeems) have truly merited, take leave
Freely to plead your rights; we ſhall attend ye.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: Wherein priority of voice is granted,
Lord Caſſilanes to you; for that your rare
And long experience in the Courſe of War,
As well doth challenge it as the beſt priviledge
Of Order and Civility, for that
You are your brave Opponents worthy Father.
Say, Country-men, are you content?

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: I, I.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.l: Right grave, right gracious Fathers; how unfit
It is for me, that all my life time have
Been practis'd in the School of Bloud, and Slaughter
To bandy words now in my lifes laſt farewel,
Your Wiſedomes will conſider; were there pitcht
Another, and another field, like that
Which, not yet three days ſince, this Arm hath ſcatter'd,
Defeated, and made nothing, then the man
That had a heart to think he could but follow
(For equal me he ſhould not) through the lanes
Of danger and amazement, might in that
That only of but following me, be happy,
Reputed worthy to be made my Rival;
For 'tis not, Lords, unknown to thoſe about me,
(My fellow Souldiers) firſt, with what a confidence
I led them on to ſight, went on ſtill, and
As if I could have been a ſecond Nature,
As well in heartening them by my example,
As by my exhortation, I gave life
To quicken courage, to inflame revenge,
To heighten reſolution; in a word,
To out-doe action: It boots not to diſcover,
How that young man, who was not fledg'd nor skill'd
In Martial play, was even as ignorant
As childiſh: But I liſt not to diſparage
His non ability: The ſignal given
Of Battel, when our enemies came on,
(Directed more by ſury, than by warrant
Of Policy and Stratagem) I met them,
I in the ſore front of the Armies met them;
And as if this old weather-beaten body
Had been compos'd of cannon proof, I ſtood
The volleys of their ſhot. I, I my ſelf
Was he that firſt diſ-rankt their woods of Pikes:
But when we came to handy-ſtroaks, as often
As I lent blows, ſo often I gave wounds,
And every wound a death. I may be bold
To juſtifie a truth, this very ſword
Of mine ſlew more than any twain beſides:
And, which is not the leaſt of all my glorie,
When he, this young man, hand to hand in fight,
Was by the General of the Venetians,
And ſuch as were his retinue, unhors'd,
I ſtept between, and reſcu'd him my ſelf,
And whilſt he was re-mounting, I maintain'd
The combate with the gallant General,
Till having taken breath, he throng'd before me,
Renew'd the ſight, and with a fatal blow,
Stole both that honour from me, and his life
From him, whom I before my ſelf alone,
Had more than full three quarters kill'd: a man
Well worthy only by this hand to have dy'd,
Not by a Boys weak puſh: I talk too much,
But 'tis a fault of age: If to bring home
Long peace, long victorie even to your Capitol;
If to ſecure your Kingdom, wives, and children,
Your lives and liberties; if to renown
Your honours through the world, to ſix your names,
Like Blazing ſtars admir'd, and fear'd by all
That have but heard of Candy, or a Cretan,
Be to deſerve the approvement of my man hood,
Then thus much have I done: what more, examine
The annals of my life; and then conſider
What I have been, and am. Lords I have ſaid.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: With reverence to the Senate, is it lawfull,
Without your Cuſtomes breach, to ſay a word?

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Say on my Lord Gonzalo.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: I have heard,
And with no little wonder, ſuch high deeds
Of Chival • ie diſcours'd, that I confeſs,
I do not think the Worthies while they liv'd
All nine, deſerv'd as much applauſe, or memorie,
As this one: But who can do ought to gain
The crown of honour from him, muſt be ſomewhat
More than a man; you tread a dangerous path,
Yet I ſhall hear you gladly: for believe me,
Thus much let me profeſs, in honours cauſe,
I would not to my Father, nor my King,
(My Countries Father) yield: if you tranſcend
What we have heard, I can but only ſay,
That Miracles are yet in uſe. I fear
I have offended.

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: You have ſpoken nobly.
Antinous uſe your priviledge.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Princely Fathers,
E're I begin, one ſuit I have to make,
'Tis juſt, and honourable.

sp.speaker: Porp. Poſſ.
sp.l: Speak, and have it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: That you would pleaſe the ſouldiers might all ſtand
Together by their General.

sp.speaker: Poſſ.
sp.l: 'Tis granted.
All fall to yonder ſide: Go on, Antinous.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſhall be brief and plain: all what my Father
(This Countries Patron) hath diſcours'd, is true.
Fellows in Arms: ſpeak you, is't true?

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.l: True, true.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It follows, that the blaze of my performance
Took light from what I ſaw him do: and thus
A City (though the flame be much more dreadfull)
May from a little ſpark be ſet on fire;
Of all what I have done, I ſhall give inſtance
Only in three main proofs of my deſert.
Firſt I ſought out (but through how many dangers
My Lords judge ye) the chief, the great Commander,
The head of that huge body, whoſe proud weight
Our Land ſhrunk under, him I found and fought with,
Fought with, and ſlew. Fellows in Arms, ſpeak you,
Is't true or not?

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: True, true.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: When he was faln,
The hearts of all our adverſaries
Began to quail, till young Fernando, ſon
To the laſt Duke of Venice gather'd head,
And ſoon renew'd the field, by whoſe example
The bold Venetians doubling ſtrength and courage
Had got the better of the day; our men
Suppoſing that their adverſaries grew
Like Hydra's head, recoyle, and 'gan to flye:
I follow'd them; and what I ſaid, they know;
The ſumme on't is; I call'd them back, new rankt them;
Led on, they follow'd, ſhrunk not tell the end:
Fellows in Arms is't true, or no?

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: True, true.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Laſtly, to finiſh all, there was but one,
The only great exploit; which was to take
Fernando priſoner, and that hand to hand
In ſingle ſight I did: my ſelf without
The help of any arm, ſave the arm of Heaven.
Speak Souldiers, is it true, or no?

l.hi: Antinous, Antinous.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Behold my priſoner, Fathers.

sp.speaker: Fern.
sp.l: This one man
Ruin'd our Army, and hath glorifi'd
Crete in her robes of mightineſs and conqueſt.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: We need not uſe long circumſtance of words,
Antinous thou art conquerer: the Senate,
The ſouldiers, and thy valour have pronounc'd it.

l.hi: Antinous, Antinous.

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: Make thy demand.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Pleaſe ye (my Lords) give leave
That I may part.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: No Caſſilane, the Court
Should therein be diſhonour'd, do not imagin
We prize your preſence at ſo ſlight a rate.
Demand, Antinous.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thus (my Lords) to witneſs
How far I am from arrogance, or thinking
I am more valiant, though more favour'd
Than my moſt matchleſs father, my demand is,
That for a laſting memorie of his name,
His deeds, his real, nay his royal worth,
You ſet up in your Capitol in Braſs
My Fathers Statue, there to ſtand for ever
A Monument and Trophy of his victories,
With this Inſcription to ſucceeding ages,
Great Caſſilanes, Patron of Candy's Peace,

l.hi: Perpetual Triumpher.

sp.speaker: Por. Poſ.
sp.l: It is granted. What more?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No more.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: How Boy?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Thou art immortal,
Both for thy Son-like pietie, and beauties
Of an unconquer'd minde.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: My Priſoner, Lords,
To your more ſacred wiſedoms I ſurrender:
Fit you his ranſom; half whereof I give
For largeſs to the Souldiers: the other half
To the erection of this monument.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.l: Ambitious villain.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Thou art all un-imitable.
My Lords, to work a certain peace for Candy
With Venice, uſe Fernando like a Prince;
His ranſom I'le disburſe what e're it be:
Yet you may ſtay him with you, till conditions
Of amitie ſhall be concluded on:
Are ye content?

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: We are, and ever reſt
Both friends and debters to your nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Souldiers attend me in the Market-place,
I'le thither ſend your largeſs.

l.hi: Antinous, Antinous.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I have a ſute too, Lords.

sp.speaker: Porp. Poſ.
sp.l: Propoſe it, 'tis yours, if fit and juſt.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Let not my ſervices,
My being forty years a drudge, a pack-horſe
To you, and to the State, be branded now
With Ignominy ne're to be forgotten:
Rear me no Monument, unleſs you mean
To have me fam'd a Coward, and be ſtamp'd ſo.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: We underſtand you not.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Proud boy, thou doſt,
And Tyrant like inſult'ſt upon my ſhame.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sir, Heaven can tell, and my integrity,
What I did, was but only to inforce
The Senates gratitude. I now acknowledge it.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Obſerve it Fathers, how this haughty boy
Grows cunning in his envy of mine honours:
He knows no mention can of me be made,
But that it ever likewiſe muſt be told,
How I by him was maſter'd; and for ſurety
That all ſucceeding times may ſo report it,
He would have my diſhonour, and his Triumphs
Ingrav'd in Braſs: hence, hence proceeds the falſhood
O • his inſinuating piety.
Thou art no child of mine: thee and thy bloud.
Here in the Capitol, before the Senate,
I utterly renounce: So thrift and fate
Confirm me; henceforth never ſee my face,
Be, as thou art, a villain to thy Father.
Lords I muſt crave your leaves: come, come Arcanes. Ex.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Here's a ſtrange high-born ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: 'Tis but heat
Of ſuddain preſent rage; I dare aſſure
Antinous of his favour.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I not doubt it,
He is both a good man, and a good Father.
I ſhall attend your Lordſhips.

sp.speaker: Poſſ.
sp.l: Do Antinous.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Yes: feaſt thy Triumphs
With applauſe and pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Por. Poſſ.
sp.l: Lead on. Exeunt. Flor. Cornets.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I utterly renounce—'Twas ſo?
Was't not, my Decius?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Piſh, you know, my Lord,
Old men are cholerick.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And laſtly parted
With, never henceforth ſee my face: O me,
How have I loſt a Father? Such a Father?
Such a one Decius! I am miſerable,
Beyond expreſſion.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Fie, how unbecoming
This ſhews upon your day of ſame?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: O miſchief!
I muſt no more come near him; that I know,
And am aſſur'd on't.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Say you do not?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: True:
Put caſe I do not: what is Candy then
To loſt Antinous? Malta, I reſolve
To end my dayes in thee.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: How's that?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'le trie
All humble means of being reconcil'd,
Which if deny'd, then I may juſtly ſay,
This day has prov'd my worſt: Decius, my worſt,

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Gaſp.
sp.l: NOw to what you have heard; as no man can
Better than I, give you her Character;
For I have been both nurs'd, and train'd up to
Her petulant humours, and been glad to bear them,
Her Brother, my late Maſter, did no leſs:
Strong apprehenſions of her beauty hath
Made her believe that ſhe is more than woman:
And as there did not want thoſe flatterers
'Bout the worlds Conquerour, to make him think,
And did perſwade him that he was a god;
So there be thoſe baſe flies, that will not ſtick
To buzze into her ears ſhe is an Angel,
And that the food ſhe feeds on is Ambroſia.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: She ſhould not touch it then, 'tis Poets fare.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: I may take leave to ſay, ſhe may as well
Determine of her ſelf to be a goddeſs,
With leſſer flatterie than he a god:
For ſhe does conquer more, although not farther.
Every one looks on her, dyes in deſpair,
And would be glad to do it actually,
To have the next age tell how worthily,
And what good cauſe he had to periſh ſo:
Here beauty is ſuperlative, ſhe knows it,
And knowing it, thinks no man can deſerve,
But ought to periſh, and to dye for her:
Many great Princes for her love have languiſh'd,
And given themſelves a willing ſacrifice,
Proud to have ended ſo: And now there is
A Prince ſo madded in his own paſſions,
That he forgets the Royaltie he was born to,
And deems it happineſs to be her ſlave.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: You talk as if you meant to winde me in,
And make me of the number.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Sir, miſtake me not, the ſervice that I owe ye
Shall plead for me: I tell you what ſhe is,
What ſhe expects, and what ſhe will effect,
Unleſs you be the miracle of men,
That come with a purpoſe to behold,
And goe away your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: I thank you, I will do it: But pray reſolve me,
How is ſhe ſtor'd with wit?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: As with beauty,
Infinite, and more to be admired at,
Than medled with.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: And walks her tongue the ſame gate with her feet?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Much beyond: what e're her heart thinks, ſhe utters:
And ſo boldly, ſo readily, as you would judge
It penn'd and ſtudied.

div.stage: Enter Erota, Philander, Annophil, Hyparcha, Mochingo, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: She comes.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: I muſt leave you then,
But my beſt wiſhes ſhall remain with you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Still I muſt thank you.
This is the moſt paſſionate,
Moſt pitifull Prince,
Who in the Caldron of affections,
Looks as he had been par-boy'ld.

sp.speaker: Ph l
sp.l: If I offend with too much loving you,
It is a fault that I muſt ſtill commit,
To make your mercy ſhine the more on me.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: You are the ſelf-ſame creature you condemn,
Or elſe you durſt not follow me with hope
That I can pity you, who am ſo far
From granting any comfort in this kind,
That you and all men elſe ſhall periſh firſt:
I will live free and ſingle, till I find
Something above a man to equal me;
Put all your brave Heroes into one,
Your Kings and Emperours, and let him come
In perſon of a man, and I ſhould ſcorn him:
Muſt, and will ſcorn him.
The god of love himſelf hath loſt his eyes,
His Bow and Torch extinguiſh'd, and the Poets
That made him firſt a god, have loſt their fire
Since I appear'd, and from my eyes muſt ſteal it.
This I dare ſpeak; and let me ſee the man,
Now I have ſpoke it, that doth, dare deny;
Nay, not believe it.

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.l: He is mad that does not.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Have not all the nations of the Earth heard of me?
Moſt come to ſee me, and ſeeing me, return'd
Full of my praiſes? teaching their Chroniclers
To make their Stories perfect? for where the name,
Merely the word of fair Erota ſtands,
It is a laſting Hiſtory to time,
Begetting admiration in the men,
And in my own Sex envie: which glorie's loſt,
When I ſhall ſtick my beautie in a cloud,
And clearly ſhine through it.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: This woman's in the altitudes, and he muſt be
A good Aſtrologer ſhall know her Zodiack.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: For any man to think
Himſelf an able purchaſer of you,
But in the bargain there muſt be declar'd
Infinite bounty: otherwiſe I vow,
By all that's excellent and gracious in you,
I would untenant every hope lodg'd in me,
And yield my ſelf up loves, or your own Martyr.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: So you ſhall pleaſe us.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: O you cannot be
So heavenly, and ſo abſolute in all things,
And yet retain ſuch cruel tyranny.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: I can, I do, I will.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: She is in her
Moods, and her Tenſes: I'le Grammer with you,
And make a trial how I can decline you:
By your leave (great Lady.)

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: What are you?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: A man, a good man, that's a wealthy;
A Proper man, and a proud man too; one
That underſtands himſelf, and knows, unleſs
It be your ſelf, no woman on the Univerſe deſerves him.
Nay, Lady, I muſt tell you too withal,
I may make doubt of that, unleſs you paint
With better judgement next day than on this;
For (plain I muſt be with you) 'tis a dull Fucus.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Knows any one here what this fellow is?

sp.speaker: Atten.
sp.l: He is of Venice (Madam) a great Magnifico,
And gracious with the Senate.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Let him keep then among them; what makes he here?
Here's ſtate enough where I am: here's a do—
You, tell him, if he have ought with us, let him
Look lower, and give it in Petition.

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.l: Mighty Magnifico, my Miſtris bid me tell you,
If you have ought with her, you muſt look lower,
And yield it in Petition.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Here is for thee a Ducket.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: You ſay well Sir, take your own courſe.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: I will not grace you
(Lady) ſo much as take you by the hand;
But when I ſhall vouchſafe to touch your lip,
It ſhall be through your Court a holy-day
Proclaimed for ſo high favour.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: This is ſome
Great mans Jeſter: Sirrah, begon, here is
No place to fool in.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Where are the fools you talk of?
I do keep two.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: No queſtion of it: for
In your ſelf you do maintain an hundred.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: And beſides them I keep a noble train,
Statiſts, and men of action: my purſe is large and deep,
Beyond the reach of riot to draw drie:
Fortune did vie with Nature, to beſtow
(When I was born) her bountie equally:
'Tis not amiſs you turn your eyes from me;
For ſhould you ſtand and gaze me in the face,
You periſh would, like Semele by Jove:
In Venice at this inſtant there do lye
No leſs than threeſcore Ladies in their graves,
And in their Beds five hundred for my love.

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.l: You lie more than they; yet it becomes him bravel;
Would I could walk and talk ſo? I'le endeavour it.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Sir, do you know me?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Yes, you were ſiſter to the late Prince of Candy,
Aunt to this young one: and I in Venice,
Am born a Lord; equall to you in fortunes,
In ſhape; I'le ſay no more, but view.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: There needs no more be ſaid, were I a woman—
O he does rarely: in ſhape; I'le ſay no more,
But view: who could ſay more, who better?
Man is no man, nor woman woman is,
Unleſs they have a pride like one of theſe.
How poor the Prince of Cyprus ſhews to him!
How poor another Lady unto her!
Carriage and State makes us ſeem demi gods,
Humility, like beaſts, worms of the Earth.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Royal Lady, I kiſs your hand.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Sir, I know you not.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: O my noble Brother, welcom from the wars.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Dear Siſter.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: Where is my Father, that you come without him?
We have news of your ſucceſs: he has his health I hope?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes Siſter, he has his health, but is not well.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: How not well? what Riddles do your utter?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'le tell you more in private.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Noble Sir,
I cannot be unmindfull of your merit,
Since I laſt heard it: you are a hopefull youth,
And (indeed) the Soul of Candy.
I muſt ſpeak my thoughts.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: The Prince of Cyprus Brother, good Decius.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I am his Servant.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: You are the Patron of your Countrie, Sir,
So your unimitable deeds proclaim you,
It is no language of my own, but all mens.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Your Enemies muſt needs acknowledge it:
Then do not think it flatterie in your friends,
For if they had a heart, they could not want a tongue.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Is this your Brother Annophil?

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: Yes Madam.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Your name's Antinous?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I am (Lady) that moſt unfortunate man.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: How unfortunate? are you not the Souldier,
The Captain of thoſe Captains, that did bring
Conqueſt and Victory home along with you?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I had ſome ſhare in't; but was the leaſt
Of the leaſt worthy.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: O Sir, in your modeſty you'ld make
A double Conqueſt: I was an ear-witneſs
When this young man ſpoke leſſer than he acted,
And had the Souldiers voice to help him out:
But that the Law compell'd him for his honour,
To inforce him make a claim for his reward,
I well perceive he would have ſtood the man
That he does now, buried his worth in ſilence.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Sir, I hearken not to him, but look on you,
And find more in you than he can relate:
You ſhall attend on me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Madam, your pardon.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Deny it not Sir, for it is more honour
Than you have gotten i'th' field: for know you ſhall,
Upon Erota's asking, ſerve Erota.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I may want anſwers, Lady,
But never want a will to do you ſervice.
I came here to my Siſter, to take leave,
Having enjoyn'd my ſelf to baniſhment,
For ſome cauſe that hereafter you may hear;
And wiſh with me I had not the occaſion.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: There ſhall be no occaſion to divide us:
Dear Madam for my ſake uſe your power,
Even for the ſervice that he ought to owe,
Muſt, and does owe to you, his friends, and country.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Upon your Loyalty to the ſtate and me,
I do command you Sir, not depart Candy:
Am I not your Princeſs?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You are a great Lady.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Then ſhew your ſelf a Servant and a Subject.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I am your vaſſal.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: You are a Coward; I that dare not fight,
Scorn to be vaſſail to any Prince in Europe:
Great is my heart with pride, which I'le encreaſe
When they are gone, with practiſe on my Vaſſals.

sp.speaker: Atten.
sp.l: The noble Caſſilane is come to ſee you Madam.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: There's comfort in thoſe words, Antinous:
For here's the place, and perſons that have power,
To reconcile you to his love again.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: That were a fortunate meeting.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Greatneſs ſtill wait you Lady.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Good Caſſilane, we do maintain our greatneſs,
Through your valour.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: My prayers pull daily bleſſings on thy head,
My un-offending child, my Annophel.
Good Prince, worthy Gonzalo! ha? art thou here
Before me? in every action art thou ambitious?
My duty (Lady) firſt offered here,
And love to thee (my child) though he out-ſtrip me;
Thus in the wars he got the ſtart on me,
By being forward, but performing leſs;
All the endeavours of my life are loſt,
And thrown upon that evil of mine own
Curſed begetting, whom I ſhame to father.
O that the heat thou rob'dſt me of, had burnt
Within my Entrails, and begot a feaver,
Or ſome worſe ſickneſs, for thou art a diſeaſe
Sharper than any Phyſick gives a name to.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: Why do you ſay ſo?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: O Annophil; there is good cauſe my girle:
He has plaid the thief with me, and filch'd away
The richeſt jewel of my life, my honour,
Wearing it publickly with that applauſe,
As if he juſtly did inherit it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Would I had in my Infancy been laid
Within my grave, covered with your bleſſings rather
Than grown up to a man, to meet your curſes.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: O that thou hadſt.
Then I had been the Father of a child,
Dearer than thou wert ever unto me,
When hope perſwaded me I had begot
Another ſelf in thee: Out of mine eyes,
As far as I have thrown thee from my heart,
That I may live and dye forgetting thee.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: How has he deſerv'd this untam'd anger,
That when he might have ask't for his reward
Some honour for himſelf, or maſs of pelf,
He only did requeſt to have erected
Your Statue in the Capitol, with Titles
Ingrav'd upon't, The Patron of his Countrey?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: That, that's the poiſon in the gilded cup,
The Serpent in the flowers, that ſtings my honour,
And leaves me dead in fame: Gods do a juſtice,
And rip his boſom up, that men may ſee,
Seeing, believe the ſubtle practiſes
Written within his heart: But I am heated,
And do forget this preſence, and my ſelf.
Your pardon, Lady.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: You ſhould not ask, 'leſs you knew how to give,
For my ſake Caſſilane, caſt out of your thoughts
All ill conceptions of your worthy ſon,
That (queſtionleſs) has ignorantly offended,
Declared in his penitence.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Bid me dye, Lady, for your ſake I'le do it;
But that you'l ſay is nothing, for a man
That has out-liv'd his honour: But command me
In any thing ſave that, and Caſſilane
Shall ever be your ſervant. Come Annophel,
(My joy in this world) thou ſhalt live with me,
(Retired in ſome ſolitarie nook,)
The comfort of my age; my dayes are ſhort,
And ought to be well ſpent: and I deſire
No other witneſs of them but thy ſelf,
And good Arcanes.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: I ſhall obey you Sir.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Noble Sir:
If you taſte any want of worldly means,
Let not that diſcontent you: know me your friend,
That hath, and can ſupply you.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Sir, I am too much bound to you already,
And 'tis not of my cares the leaſt, to give you
Fair ſatisfaction.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: You may imagine I do ſpeak to that end,
But truſt me, 'tis to make you bolder with me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Sir, I thank you, and may make trial of you,
Mean time my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: Brother be comforted; ſo long as I continue
Within my Fathers love, you cannot long
Stand out an Exile: I muſt goe live with him,
And I will prove ſo good an Orator
In your behalf, that you again ſhall gain him,
Or I will ſtir in him another anger,
And be loſt with you.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.l: Better I wore neglected: for he is haſty,
And through the Choler that abounds in him,

(Wh ••
〈◊〉 the time divides from him his judgement)

For grief will 〈◊〉
• t ſurprize him, and that way
Muſt be his death. the ſword has try'd too often,
And all the deadly Inſtruments of war
Have aim'd at his great heart, but ne're could touch it:
Yet not a limb about him wants a ſcar.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Madam my duty —

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Will you be gone?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I muſt, Lady, but I ſhall be ready,
When you are pleas'd command me, for your ſervice.
Excellent Prince — To all my heartie love,
And a good Farewel.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Thanks honeſt Caſſilane.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Come Annophel.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Shall I not wait upon you Sir?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: From hence you ſhall not ſtir a foot:
Loving Gonzalo, it muſt be all my ſtudy
To requite you.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: If I may be ſo fortunate to deſerve
The name of friend from you, I have enough.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: You are ſo, and you have made your ſelf ſo.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: I will then preſerve it.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Antinous you are my ſervant, are you not?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It hath pleaſed you ſo to grace me.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Why are you then dejected? you will ſay,
You have loſt a father; but you have found a Miſtris
Doubles that loſs: be maſter of your ſpirit;
You have a cauſe for it, which is my favour.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: And mine.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Will no man caſe me of this fool?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Your fellow.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Antinous wait upon us.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſhall Madam.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Nay but Ladie, Ladie.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Sir, you are rude: and if you be the Maſter
Of ſuch means as you do talk of, you ſhould
Learn good manners.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: O Lady, you can find a fault in me,
But not perceive it in your ſelf: you muſt, ſhall hear me:
I love you for your pride, 'tis the beſt vertue
In you.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: I could hang this fellow now: by whom
Are you ſupported, that you dare do this?
Have you not example here in a Prince
Tranſcending you in all things, yet bears himſelf
As doth become a man had ſeen my beautie?
Back to your Country, and your Curtizans,
Where you may be admired for your wealth,
Which being conſum'd, may be a means to gain you
The opinion of ſome wit. Here's nothing
To be got but ſcorn, and loſs of time.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Which are things I delight in.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Antinous follow me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: She is vext to the ſoul.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Let her be vext, 'tis fit ſhe ſhould be ſo:
Give me thy hand Gonzalo, thou art in our favour,
For we do love to cheriſh lofty ſpirits,
Such as percuſſe the Earth, and bound
With an erected countenance to the clouds.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: 'S foot, what thing is this?

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: I do love fire-works, becauſe they mount:
An Exhalation I profeſs to adore,
Beyond a fixed ſtar, 'tis more illuſtrious,
As every thing rais'd out of ſmoak is ſo:
Their vertue is in action: what do you think of me?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Troth Sir,
You are beyond my gheſs, I know you not.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Do you know your ſelf?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Why you and I are one: I am proud, and
Very proud too, that I muſt tell you; I ſaw
It did become you, couſin Gonzalo, prethee
Let it be ſo.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Let it be ſo good couſin.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: I am no great ones fool.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: I hope ſo, for alliance ſake.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Yet I do ſerve the Mighty, Monſtrous, and Magnanimous
Invincible Erota.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: O good couſin, now I have you: I'le meet you in your Coat.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Coat? I have my horſe mans coat I muſt confeſs
Lin'd through with Velvet, and a Scarlet out-ſide;
If you'll meet me in't, I'le ſend for't;
And couſin you ſhall ſee me with much comfort,
For it is both a new one, and a right one,
It did not come collateral.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Adieu good couſin; at this preſent I have ſome buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Farewel, excellent couſin.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: CAndy, I ſay, is loſt already.

sp.speaker: Fern.
sp.l: Yes,
If to be conqueror be to be loſt.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: You have it; one days conqueſt hath undone them.
And ſold them to their vaſſalage; for what
Have I elſe toyl'd my brains, profuſely emptied
My moneys, but to make them ſlaves to Venice,
That ſo in caſe the ſword did loſe his edge,
Then art might ſharpen hers?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Gonzalo how?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Fernando thus: you ſee how through this Land,
Both of the beſt and baſeſt I am honour'd;
I only gave the State of Venice notice,
When, where, and how to land, or you had found
A better entertainment: I was he
Encourag'd young Antinous to affront
The Devil his Father: for the Devil I think
Dares not do more in battel.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: But why did ye?
I find no ſuch great policie in that.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Indeed Fernando, thou canſt fight, not plot:
Had they continu'd one, they two alone
Were of ſufficient courage and performance
To beat an Armie.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Now by all my hopes,
I rather ſhall admire, than envy vertue.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Why then by all your hopes you'l rather have
Your Brains knockt out, than learn how to be wiſe;
You States man? Well Sir, I did more than this,
When Caſſilane crav'd from the common treaſure
Pay for his Souldiers, I ſtrook home, and lent him
An hundred thouſand Duckets.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Marry Sir,
The policy was little, the love loſs,
And honeſty leaſt of all.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: How ſay ye by that?
Go fight, I ſay goe fight, I'le talk no more with you,
You are inſenſible.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Well, I ſhall obſerve ye.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Why look you Sir, by this means have I got
The greateſt part of Caſſilanes eſtate
Into my hands, which he can ne're redeem,
But muſt of force ſink: do you conceive me now?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: So:
But why have you importuned the Senate,
For me to ſojourn with them?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: There's the quinteſſence,
The ſoul, and grand elixir of my wit:
For he (according to his noble nature)
Will not be known to want, though he do want,
And will be bankrupted ſo much the ſooner,
And made the ſubject of our ſcorn and laughter.

sp.speaker: Fern.
sp.l: Here's a perfect plotted ſtratagem.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Why? could you
Imagine, that I did not hate in heart
My Countryes enemies? yes, yes, Fernando,
And I will be the man that ſhall undoe them.

sp.speaker: Fern.
sp.l: Ye are in a ready way.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: I was never out on't.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Peace,
Here comes a wiſe Coxcombe, a tame Coward.
Now worthy Gaſpero, what,
You come (I know) to be my Lord Fernando's
Conducter to old Caſſilane?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: To wait upon him.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: And my Lords the Senators ſent you?

sp.speaker: Gaſp.
sp.l: My noble Lord they did.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: My Lord Fernando,
This Gentleman, (as humble as you ſee him)
Is even this Kingdoms treaſure; In a word,
'Tis his chief glory that he is not wiſer
Than honeſt, nor more honeſt than approv'd
In truth and faith.

sp.speaker: Gaſp.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: You may be bold
To truſt him with your boſom, he'l not deceive
If you relie upon him once.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Your name is Gaſpero?

sp.speaker: Gaſp.
sp.l: Your ſervant.
