sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Go commend me
(Right honeſt Gaſpero) commend me heartily
To noble Caſſilane, tell him my love
Is vow'd to him.

sp.speaker: Gaſp.
sp.l: I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: I know you will.
My Lord I cannot long be abſent from you.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Sir, you are now my guide. Exit.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Thus my deſigns
Run uncontroul'd; yet Venice though I be
Intelligencer to thee, in my brain
Are other large Projects: for if proud Erota
Bend to my lure, I will be Candy's King,
And Duke of Venice too. Ha? Venice too?
O 'twas prettily ſhov'd in: why not? Erota
May in her love ſeal all ſure: if ſhe ſwallow
The bait, I am Lord of both; if not, yet Candy
Deſpight of all her power ſhall be ruin'd.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Urge me no farther Annophel.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Thy fathers poverty has made thee happy;
For though 'tis true, this ſolitary life
Sutes not with youth and beautie, O my child,
Yet 'tis the ſweeteſt Guardian to protect
Chaſt names from Court aſperſions; there a Lady
Tender and delicate in years and graces,
That doats upon the charms of eaſe and pleaſure,
Is ſhip-wrackt on the ſhore; for 'tis much ſafer
To truſt the Ocean in a leaking ſhip,
Than follow greatneſs in the wanton rites
Of luxurie and ſloth.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: My wiſhes Sir,
Have never ſoar'd a higher flight, than truly
To find occaſion wherein I might witneſs
My duty and obedience.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: 'Tis well ſaid,
Canſt thou forbear to laugh Arcanes?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: To look upon my beggerie, to look upon
My patience in my beggerie: Tell me,
Does it ſhew handſom? bravely?
Handſom? thou wilt flatter me,
And ſwear that I am miſerable.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Nothing
More glorifies the noble, and the valiant,
Than to deſpiſe contempt: if you continue
But to enjoy your ſelf, you in your ſelf
Enjoy all ſtore beſides.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: An excellent change:
I that ſome ſeven Apprentice-ſhips commanded
A hundred Miniſters, that waited on
My nod, and ſometimes twenty thouſand ſouldiers,
Am now retir'd, attended in my age
By one poor maid, follow'd by one old man.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Sir, you are lower in your own repute
Than you have reaſon for.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: The Roman Captains,
I mean the beſt, ſuch as with their blouds
Purchas'd their Countreys peace, the Empires glorie,
Were glad at laſt to get them to ſome Farmes,
Off from the clamours of the ingratefull great ones,
And the unſteady multitude, to live
As I do now, and 'twas their bleſſing too,
Let it be ours Arcanes.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I cannot but
Applaud your ſcorn of injuries.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Of injuries?
Arcanes, Annophel, lend both your hands.
So, what ſay ye now?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Why now my Lord —

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I ſwear
By all my paſt proſperities; thus ſtanding
Between you two, I think my ſelf as great,
As mighty, as if in the Capitol
I ſtood amidſt the Senators, with all
The Cretan ſubjects proſtrate at my feet.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: Sir, you are here more ſafe.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: And more beloved:
Why look ye Sirs, I can forget the weakneſs
Of the traduced Souldiers, the neglect
Of the fair-ſpoken Senate, the impietie
Of him, the villain, whom (to my diſhonour)
The World miſcalls my ſon.
But by the —

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Sir, remember that you promis'd no occaſion
Should move your patience.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Thou do'ſt chide me friendly,
He ſhall not have the honour to be thought upon
Amongſt us.
Now? the news?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: The Secretarie,
With the Venetian priſoner, deſire
Admittance to your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: How? to me?
What myſterie is this? Arcanes can they,
Thinkſt thou, mean any good?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: My Lord, they dare not
Intend ought elſe but good.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: 'Tis true, they dare not;
Arcanes welcom them: Come hither Annophel,
Stand cloſe to me, we'l change our affability
Into a form of State: and they ſhall know
Our heart is ſtill our own.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: My Lord —

sp.speaker: Caſp.

l.hi: Arcanes,

sp.l: I know them both: Fernando, as you are
A man of greatneſs, I ſhould under-value
The right my ſword hath fought for, to obſerve
Low-fawning complements, but as you are
A Captive and a ſtranger, I can love you,
And muſt be kind. You are welcom.

sp.speaker: Fern.
sp.l: 'Tis the all
Of my ambition.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: And for proof how much
He truly honours your heroick vertues,
The Senate on his importunity,
Commend him to your Lordſhips guard.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: During the time of his abode in Candy,
To be your houſhold gueſt.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Wherein my Lord,
You ſhall more make me debtor to your nobleneſs,
Than if you had return'd me without ranſom.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.l: Are you in earneſt Sir?

sp.speaker: Fern.
sp.l: My ſute to the Senate
Shall beſt reſolve you that.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.l: Come hither Secretarie,
Look that this be no trick now put upon me:
For if it be—Sirrah—

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: As I have troth
(My Lord) it only is a favour granted
Upon Fernando's motion, from himſelf:
Your Lordſhip muſt conceive, I'de not partake
Ought, but what ſhould concern your honour; Who
Has been the prop, our Countries ſhield, and ſafety,
But the renowned Caſſilane?

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.l: Applauſe?
Is Gaſpero—puff—nothing—why, young Lord,
Would you ſo much be ſequeſter'd from thoſe
That are the blazing Comets of the time,
To live a ſolitary life with me?
A man forſaken? all my hoſpitality
Is now contracted to a few; theſe two,
The tempeſt wearied Souldier, and this Virgin;
We cannot ſeaſt your eyes with Maſques and Revels,
Or Courtly Anticks; the ſad Sports we riot in,
Are tales of ſoughten fields, of Martial ſcars,
And things done long ago, when men of courage
Were held the beſt, not thoſe well-ſpoken Youths,
Who only carry Conqueſt in their tongues:
Now ſtories of this nature are unſeaſonable
To entertain a great Duke's Son with.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Herein
Shall my Captivity be made my happineſs,
Since what I loſe in freedom, I regain
(With int'reſt) by converſing with a Souldier,
So matchleſs for experience, as great Caſſilane:
'Pray Sir, admit me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: If you come to mock me,
I ſhall be angry.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: By the love I bear
To goodneſs, my intents are honourable.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Then in a word, my Lord, your viſitations
Shall find all due reſpect: but I am now
Grown old, and have forgot to be an Hoſt;
Come when you pleaſe, you are welcome.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Sir, I thank you.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: Good Sir, be not too urgent; for my Father
Will ſoon be mov'd: yet, in a noble way
Of courteſie, he is as eaſily conquer'd.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Lady, your words are like your beauty, powerful;
I ſhall not ſtrive more how to do him ſervice,
Than how to be your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: She's my Daughter,
And does command this Houſe.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: So I conceive her.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Do you hear?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: My honour'd Lord.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Commend me to them:
Tell 'em I thank them.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Whom, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: The Senate;
Why, how come you ſo dull? O they are gracious,
And infinitely grateful— Thou art eloquent,
Speak modeſtly in mentioning my ſervices;
And if ought fall out in the By, that muſt
Of meer neceſſity touch any act
Of my deſerving praiſes, bluſh when you talk on't,
'Twill make them bluſh to hear on't.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Why, my Lord—

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Nay, nay, you are too wiſe now; good, obſerve me.
I do not rail againſt the hopeful Springall,
That builds up Monuments in Braſs; rears Trophies
With Mottoes and Inſcriptions, quaint devices
Of Poetry and Fiction; let's be quiet.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: You muſt not croſs him.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Not for Candy's Wealth.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: You ſhall for ever make me yours.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: 'Twere pity to double your Captivity.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Who's here, Decius?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Ha! Decius? who nam'd Decius?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: My duty to your Lordſhip, I am bold,
Preſuming on your noble, and known goodneſs
To—

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Preſent you with this—

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Letter?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Yes, my honour'd Lord.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: From whom?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: 'Pleaſe you peruſe
The inſide, and you ſhall find a name ſubſcrib'd,
In ſuch humility, in ſuch obedience,
That you your ſelf will judge it tyranny
Not to receive it favourably.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Hey-day!
Good words my Maſters: this is Court-infection,
And none but Cowards ply them: tell me, Decius,
Without more circumſtance, who is the Sender?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Your moſt griev'd Son, Antinous.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: On my life
A Challenge; ſpeak, as thou art worthy, ſpeak;
I'll anſwer't.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Honour'd Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: No honour'd Sirs—
Fool your young Idol with ſuch pompous Attributes.
Say briefly, what contains it?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: 'Tis a lowly
Petition for your favour.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Raſh young man,
But that thou art under my own roof, and know'ſt
I dare not any way infringe the Laws
Of Hoſpitality, thou ſhould'ſt repent
Thy bold and rude intruſion. But preſume not
Again to ſhew thy Letter, for thy life;
Decius, not for thy life.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Nay then, (my Lord)
I can with-hold no longer; you are too rough,
And wreſtle againſt nature with a violence
More than becomes a Father; wherein would ye
Come nearer to the likeneſs of God,
Than in your being entreated? Let not thirſt
Of Honour, make you quite forget you are
A Man, and what makes perfect manhoods, comforts
A Father.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: If a memory remain
Of my departed Mother; if the purity
Of her unblemiſh'd faith deſerve to live
In your remembrance, let me yet by theſe
Awake your love to my uncomforted Brother.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I am a Stranger, but ſo much I tender
Your Sons deſertful Vertues, that I vow
His Sword ne'r conquer'd me ſo abſolutely,
As ſhall your courteſie, if you vouchſafe
At all our inſtances, to new receive him
Into your wonted favour.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Sir, you cannot
Require more low ſubmiſſion.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: Am I not
Grown vile yet in your eyes? then by the name
Of Father, let me once more ſue for him,
Who is the only now remaining Branch
With me, of that moſt ancient root, whoſe Body
You are, dear Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: 'Tis well, an hoſt of furies
Could not have baited me more torturingly,
More rudely, or more moſt unnaturally.
Decius, I ſay, let me no more hear from him;
For this time go thou hence, and know from me
Thou art beholding to me that I have not
Kill'd thee already, look to't next, look to't.
Arcanes fie, fie Annophel. Exit.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: He's gone;
Chaf'd beyond ſufferance; we muſt follow him.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Lady, this Letter is to you.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: Come with me,
For we muſt ſpeak in private; 'pleaſe you, Sir,
To ſee what entertainment our ſad houſe
Can yield? Exit.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I ſhall attend you, Lady.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: How do you like
To ſojourn here, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: More than to feaſt
With all the Princes of the Earth beſides:
Gonzalo told me that thou wert honeſt.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Yes Sir,
And you ſhall find it.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Shall I?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: All my follies
Be •• ſe recorded to my ſhame.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Enough,
My heart is here for ever lodg'd.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: The Lady

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: The place admits no time to utter all,
But Gaſpero if thou wilt prove my friend,
I'll ſay thou art—

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Your Servant; I conceive ye,
We'll chuſe ſome fitter leiſure.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Never man
Was (in a moment) or more bleſs'd or wretched. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Hyparcha (placing two Chairs) Antinous, and Erota.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Leave us,

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: I ſhall. Exit.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Antinous, ſit down.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: I ſay ſit down, I do command you ſit;
For look what honour thou doſt gain by me,
I cannot loſe it: happy Antinous,
The graces and the higher Deities
Smil'd at thy Birth, and ſtill continue it:
Then think that I (who ſcorn leſſer examples)
Muſt do the like: ſuch as do taſte my power,
And talk of it with fear and reverence,
Shall do the ſame unto the man I favour.
I tell thee Youth, thou haſt a conqueſt won,
Since thou cam'ſt home, greater than that laſt,
Which dignified thy Fame, greater than if
Thou ſhould'ſt go out again, and conquer farther;
For I am not aſhamed to acknowledge
My ſelf ſubdued by thee.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Great Lady—

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Sit ſtill, I will not hear thee elſe; now ſpeak,
And ſpeak like my Antinous, like my Souldier,
Whom Cupid, and not Mars hath ſent to Battel.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I muſt (I ſee) be ſilent.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: So thou maiſt;
There's greater action in it than in clamour,
A look (if it be gracious) will begin the War,
A word conclude it; then prove no Coward,
S nce thou haſt ſuch a friendly enemy,
That teaches thee to conquer.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You do amaze me, Madam,
I have no skill, no practice in this War,
And whether you be ſerious, or pleaſe
To make your ſport on a dejected man,
I cannot rightly gueſs; but be it as it will,
It is a like unhappineſs to me:
My diſcontents bear thoſe conditions in them,
And lay me out ſo wretched, no deſigns
(However truly promiſing a good)
Can make me reliſh ought but a ſweet bitter
Voluntary Exile.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Why an Exile?
What comfort can there be in thoſe Companions
Which ſad thoughts bring along with?

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: Madam. Muſick.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Whence comes this well tun'd ſound?

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: I know not, Madam.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Liſten Wench;
Whatever friendly hands they are that ſend it, Song.
Let 'em play on; they are Maſters of their faculty:
Doth it pleaſe you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: According to the time.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Go to 'em, Wench,
And tell 'em, we ſhall thank 'em; for they have kept
As good time to our diſpoſition, as to their inſtruments;
Unleſs Antinous ſhall ſay he loves,
There never can be ſweeter accents utter'd.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Let then the heart that did employ thoſe hands,
Receive ſome ſmall ſhare of your thanks with them,
'Tis happineſs enough that you did like it;
A fortune unto me, that I ſhould ſend it
In ſuch a lucky minute; but to obtain
So gracious welcome did exceed my hopes.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Good Prince, I thank you for't.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: O Madam, pour not (too faſt) joys on me,
But ſprinkle 'em ſo gently I may ſtand 'em;
It is enough at firſt, you have laid aſide
Thoſe cruel angry looks out of your eyes,
With which (as with your lovely) you did ſtrike
All your Beholders in an Ecſtaſie.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Philander, you have long profeſt to love me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Have I but profeſt it, Madam?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Nay, but hear me?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: More attentively than to an Oracle.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: And I will ſpeak more truly, if more can be;
Nor ſhall my language be wrapt up in Riddles,
But plain as truth it ſelf; I love this Gentleman,
Whoſe grief has made him ſo uncapable
Of Love, he will not hear, at leaſt not underſtand it.
I, that have lookt with ſcornful eyes on thee,
And other Princes, mighty in their ſtates,
And in their friends as fortunate, have now pray'd,
In a petitionary kind almoſt,
This man, this well-deſerving man, (that I muſt ſay
To look upon this beauty, yet you ſee
He caſts his eyes rather upon the ground,
Than he will turn 'em this way; Philander,
You look pale; I'll talk no more.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Pray go forward; I would be your Martyr,
To dye thus, were immortally to live.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Will you go to him then, and ſpeak for me?
You have loved longer, but not ferventer,
Know how to ſpeak, for you have done it like
An Orator, even for your ſelf; then how will you for me
Whom you profeſs to love above your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: The Curſes of Diſſemblers follow me
Unto my Grave, and if I do not ſo.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: You may (as all men do) ſpeak boldlier, better
In their friends cauſe ſtill, than in your own;
But ſpeak your utmoſt, yet you cannot feign,
I will ſtand by, and bluſh to witneſs it.
Tell him, ſince I beheld him, I have loſt
The happineſs of this life, food, and reſt;
A quiet boſome, and the ſtate I went with.
Tell him how he has humbled the proud,
And made the living but a dead Erota.
Tell him withal, that ſhe is better pleas'd
With thinking on him, than enjoying theſe.
Tell him—Philander, Prince; I talk in vain
To you, you do not mark me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Indeed I do.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: But thou doſt look ſo pale,
As thou wilt ſpoil the ſtory in relating.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Not, if I can but live to tell it.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: It may be you have not the heart.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I have a will I am ſure how e'r my heart
May play the Coward, but if you pleaſe, I'll try.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: If a kiſs will ſtrengthen thee, I give you leave
To challenge it, nay, I will give it you.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: O that a man ſhould taſte ſuch heavenly bliſs,
And be enjoyn'd to beg it for another!

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Alas, it is a miſery I grieve
To put you to, and I will ſuffer rather
In his tyranny, than thou in mine,

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Nay Madam, ſ nce I cannot have your love,
For I had rather have within the grave
Your love, than you ſhould want it upon earth.
But how can I hope, with a feeble tongue
To inſtruct him in the rudiments of love,
When your moſt powerful Beauty cannot work it?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Do what thou wilt (Philander) the requeſt
Is ſo unreaſonable, that I quit thee of it.
I deſire now no more but the true patience,
And fortitude of Lovers, with thoſe helps
Of ſighs and tears, which I think is all the Phyſick—

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: O if he did but hear you 'twere enough;
And I will 'wake him from his Apoplexie.

l.hi: Antinous.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: My Lord?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Nay, 'pray,
No courteſie to me, you are my Lord,
(Indeed you are) for you command her heart
That commands mine; nor can you want to know it.
For look you, ſhe that told it you in words,
Explains it now more paſſionately in tears;
Either thou haſt no heart, or a marble one,
If thoſe drops cannot melt it; prithee look up
And ſee how ſorrow ſits within her eyes,
And love the grief ſhe goes with (if not her)
Of which thou art the Parent; and never yet
Was there (by Nature) that thing made ſo ſtony
But it would love what ever it begot.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: He that begot me did beget theſe cares
Which are good iſſues, though happily by him
Eſteemed Monſters: Nay, the ill-judging World
Is likely enough to give them thoſe Characters.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What's this to love, and to the Lady? he's old,
Wrathful, perverſe, ſelf-will'd, and full of anger,
Which are his faults; but let them not be thine;
He thruſts you from his love, ſhe pulls thee on;
He doubts your Vertues, ſhe doth double them;
O either uſe thine own eyes, or take mine,
And with them my heart, then thou wilt love her,
Nay, dote upon her more than on thy duty,
And men will praiſe thee equally for it;
Neglecting her, condemn thee as a man
Unworthy ſuch a fortune: O Antinous,
'Tis not the friendſhip that I bear to thee,
But her command, that makes me utter this;
And when I have prevail'd, let her but ſay,
Philander, you muſt dye or this is nothing,
It ſhall be done together with a breath,
With the ſame willingneſs I live to ſerve her.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: No more, Philander.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: All I have done, is little yet to purpoſe,
But ere I leave him I will perceive him bluſh;
And make him feel the paſſions that I do,
And every true Lover will aſſiſt me in't,
And lend me their ſad ſighs to blow it home,
For Cupid wants a Dart to wound this boſome.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: No more, no more, Philander, I can endure no more,
Pray let him go; go good Antinous, make peace
With your own mind, no matter though I periſh. Ex.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: I Cannot help it.

sp.speaker: Moch.
sp.l: Nor do I require it,
The malady needs no Phyſician,
Help hoſpital people.

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: I am glad to hear
You are ſo valiant.

sp.speaker: Moch.
sp.l: Valiant?
Can any man be proud that is not valiant?
Fooliſh Woman, what would'ſt thou ſay? thou—
I know not what to call thee.

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: I can you,
For I can call you Coxcomb, Aſs, and Puppy.

sp.speaker: Moch.
sp.l: You do doe it, I thank you.

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: That you'll loſe a Fortune,
Which a Cobler better deſerves than thou doſt.

sp.speaker: Moch.
sp.l: Do not provoke my magnanimity,
For when I am incens'd I am inſenſible,
Go tell thy Lady, that hath ſent me word
She will diſcard me, that I diſcard her,
And throw a ſcorn upon her, which I would not,
But that ſhe does me wrong.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Do you not glory in your Conqueſt more,
To take ſome great man Priſoner, than to kill him?
And ſhall a Lady find leſs mercy from you,
That yields her ſelf your Captive, and for her Ranſome,
Will give the Jewel of her life, her heart,
Which ſhe hath lockt from all men but thy ſelf?
For ſhame (Antinous) throw this dulneſs off;
Art thou a man no where but in the field?

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: He muſt hear Drums, and Trumpets ere he ſleeps,
And at this inſtant dreams he's in his Armour;
Theſe iron-hearted Souldiers are ſo cold,
Till they be beaten to a Womans Arms,
And then they love 'em better than their own;
No Fort can hold them out.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What pity it is (Madam) that your ſelf,
Who are all Excellence, ſhould become ſo wretched,
To think on ſuch a Wretch as Grief hath made me!
Seldome deſpairing men look up to Heaven,
Although it ſtill ſpeak to 'em in its Glories;
For when ſad thoughts perplex the mind of man,
There is a Plummet in the heart that weighs,
And pulls us (living) to the duſt we came from;
Did you but ſee the miſeries you purſue,
(As I the happineſs that I avoid
That doubles my afflictions) you would flye
Unto ſome Wilderneſs, or to your Grave,
And there find better Comforts than in me,
For Love and Cares can never dwell together.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: They ſhould,
If thou hadſt but my Love and I thy Cares.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What wild Beaſt in the Deſart but would be
Taught by this Tongue to leave his Cruelty,
Though all the beauties of the face were vail'd!
But I am ſavager than any Beaſt,
And ſhall be ſo till Decius does arrive,
Whom with ſo much ſubmiſſion I have ſent
Under my hand, that if he do not bring
His Benediction back, he muſt to me
Be much more cruel than I to you.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Is't but your Fathers pardon you deſire?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: With his love, and then nothing next that, like yours.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Decius is come.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: O welcome Friend; if I apprehend not
Too much of joy, there's comfort in thy looks.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: There is indeed; I prithee Decius ſpeak it.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: How! prithee Decius! this Woman's ſtrangely alter'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why doſt not ſpeak (good friend) and tell me how
The reverend Bleſſing of my life receiv'd
My humble lines; wept he for joy?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: No, there's a Letter will inform you more;
Yet I can tell you what I think will grieve you,
The Old Man is in want and angry ſtill,
And poverty is the Bellows to the Coal
More than diſtaſte from you as I imagine.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What's here? how's this? It cannot be! now ſure
My griefs delude my ſenſes.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: In his looks
I read a world of Changes; Decius, mark
With what a ſad amazement he ſurveys
The News; canſt thou gueſs what 'tis?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: None good, I fear.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: I fear ſo too; and then—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It is her hand.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Are you not well?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Too well: if I were ought
But Rock, this Letter would conclude my miſeries,
Peruſe it (Lady) and reſolve me then,
In what a caſe I ſtand.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Sir, the worſt is,
Your Fathers lowneſs and diſtaſte.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No, Decius,
My Siſter writes Fernando has made ſuit
For love to her; and to expreſs ſincerely
His conſtant truth, hath like a noble Gentleman,
Diſcovered plots of treachery; contriv'd
By falſe Gonzalo, not intending more
The utter ruine of our houſe, than generally
Candies Confuſion.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: 'Tis a generous part
Of young Fernando.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis, and I could wiſh
All thrift to his affections, Decius.
You find the ſum on't, Madam.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Yes, I do.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And can you now yet think a heart oppreſt
With ſuch a throng of cares, can entertain
An amorous thought? Love frees all toils but one,
Calamity and it can ill agree.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Wil't pleaſe you ſpeak my doom?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Alas, great Lady,
Why will you flatter thus a deſperate Man
That is quite caſt away? O had you not
Procur'd the Senates Warrant to enforce
My ſtay, I had not heard of theſe ſad News.
What would ye have me do?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Love me, or kill me,
One word ſhall ſentence either; for as Truth
• s juſt, if you refuſe me, I am reſolute
Not to out-live my thraldome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Gentle Lady.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Say, muſt I live, or dye?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: My Lord, how can you
Be ſo inexorable? here's Occaſion
Of ſuccouring your Father in his wants
Securely profer'd, pray Sir, entertain it.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: What is my ſentence?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What you pleaſe to have it.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: As thou art gentle ſpeak thoſe words again.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Madam, you have prevail'd; yet give me leave
Without offence, ere I reſign the intereſt
Your heart hath in my heart, to prove your ſecreſie.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Antinous, 'tis the greateſt argument
Of thy affections to me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Madam, thus then,
My Father ſtands for certain ſums engag'd
To treacherous Gonzalo; and has morgag'd
The greateſt part of his eſtate to him;
If you receive this Morgage, and procure
Acquittance from Gonzalo to my Father,
I am what you would have me be.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: You'll love me then?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Provided (Madam) that my Father know not
I am an Agent for him.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: If I fail
In this, I am unworthy to be lov'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Then (with your favour) thus I ſeal my truth,
Today, and Decius witneſs how unchangingly
I ſhall ſtill love Erota.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Thou haſt quickned
A dying heart, Antinous.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: This is well;
Much happineſs to both.

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: The Lord Gonzalo
Attends you, Madam.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Comes as we could wiſh,
Withdraw Antinous, here's a Cloſet, where
You may partake his errand; let him enter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Madam you muſt be wary. Exit.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Fear it not,
I will be ready for him; to entertain him
With ſmiling Welcome. Noble Sir, you take
Advantage of the time; it had been fit
Some notice of your preſence might have faſhion'd
A more prepared ſtate.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Do you mock me, Madam?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Truſt me, you wrong your judgment, to repute
My Gratitude a fault; I have examin'd
Your portly carriage, and will now confeſs
It hath not ſlightly won me.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: The Wind's turn'd;
I thought 'twould come to this; it pleas'd us, Madam,
At our laſt interview, to mention Love;
Have you conſider'd on't?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: With more than common
Content: but Sir, if what you ſpoke you meant,
(As I have cauſe to doubt) then—

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: What, (ſweet Lady?)

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Methinks we ſhould lay by this form of ſtatelineſs;
Loves Courtſhip is familiar, and for inſtance,
See what a change it hath begot in me,
I could talk humbly now, as Lovers uſe.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: And I, and I, we meet in one ſelf-centre
Of bleſt Conſent.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: I hope my weakneſs, Sir,
Shall not deſerve neglect; but if it prove ſo
I am not the firſt Lady has been ruin'd
By being too credulous; you will ſmart for't one day.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Angel-like Lady, let me be held a Villain,
If I love not ſincerely.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Would I knew it.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Make proof by any fit Command.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: What, do you mean to marry me?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: How! mean? nay more, I mean
To make you Empreſs of my Earthly Fortunes,
Regent of my deſires, for did you covet
To be a real Queen, I could advance you.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Now I perceive you ſlight me, and would make me
More ſimple than my Sexes frailty warrants.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: But ſay your mind, and you ſhall be a Queen.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: On thoſe Conditions, call me yours.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Enough.
But are we ſafe?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Aſſuredly.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: In ſhort,
Yet, Lady, firſt be plain; would you not chuſe
Much rather to prefer your own Sun-riſing,
Than any's elſe though ne'r ſo near entituled
By Blood, or right of Birth?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: 'Tis a queſtion
Needs not a reſolution.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Good; what if
I ſet the Crown of Candy on your head?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: I were a Queen indeed then.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Madam, know
There's but a Boy 'twixt you and it; ſuppoſe him
Tranſhap'd into an Angel.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Wiſe Gonzalo,
I cannot but admire thee.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: 'Tis worth thinking on;
Beſides, your Husband ſhall be Duke of Venice.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Gonzalo, Duke of Venice?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: You are mine you ſay?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Piſh: you but dally with me; and would lull me
In a rich golden dream.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: You are too much diſtruſtfull of my truth.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Then you muſt give me leave to apprehend
The means, and manner how.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Why thus—

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: You ſhall not,
We may be over-heard; Affairs and counſels
Of ſuch high nature, are not to be truſted
Not to the Air it ſelf, you ſhall in writing,
Draw out the full deſign; which if effected,
I am as I profeſs.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: O I applaud
Your ready care, and ſecreſie.

sp.speaker: Er.

l.hi: Gonzalo,

sp.l: There is a bar yet, 'twixt our hopes and us,
And that muſt be remov'd.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: What is't?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Old Caſſilane.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Ha? fear not him: I build upon his ruines
Already.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: I would find a ſmoother courſe
To ſhift him off.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: As how?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: We'l talk in private,
I have a ready plot.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: I ſhall adore you. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Madam, although I • ate unnoble practices,

And the 〈◊〉
• ave perform d no more than what
I on ••• , for honours ſafety: yet Annophel,
T • love hath been the ſpur, to urge me forward
For ſpeedier diligence.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: Sir your own fame
And memory will beſt •• ward themſelves.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: All gain is loſs (ſweet beauty) if I miſs
My comforts here: The Brother and the Siſter
Have double conquer'd me, but thou maiſt triumph.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: Good Sir, I have a Father.

sp.speaker: Fern.
sp.l: Yes, a brave one;
Could'ſt thou obſcure thy beauty, yet the happineſs
Of being but his Daughter, were a dower
Fit for a Prince: what ſay ye?

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: You have deſerv'd
As much as I ſhould grant.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: By this fair hand
I take poſſeſſion.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: What in words I dare not,
Imagine in my ſilence.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Thou art all vertue.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I'le tell thee how: Baldwin the Emperour,
Pretending title, more through tyranny,
Than right of conqueſt, or deſcent, uſurp'd
The ſtile of Lord o're all the Grecian Iſlands,
And under colour of an amity
With Creet, prefer'd the Marqueſs Mountferato
To be our Governor; the Cretians vex'd
By the ambitious Turks, in hope of aid
From the Emperour, receiv'd for General,
This Mountferato; he (the wars appeaſed)
Plots with the ſtate of Venice, and takes money
Of them for Candy: they paid well, he ſteals
Away in ſecret; ſince which time, that right
The ſtate of Venice claims o're Candy, is
By purchaſe, not inheritance or Conqueſt:
And hence grows all our quarrel.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: So an Uſurer
Or Lumbard-Jew, might with ſome bags of traſh,
Buy half the Weſtern world.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Mony, Arcanes,
Is now a God on Earth: it cracks virginities,
And turns a Chriſtian, Turk;
Bribes juſtice, cut-throats honour, does what not?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Not captives Candy.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Nor makes thee diſhoneſt,
Nor me a Coward—Now Sir, here is homely,
But friendly entertainment.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Sir, I find it.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: And like it, do ye not?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: My repair ſpeaks for me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Fernando we were ſpeaking off—how this?

div.stage: Enter Gonzalo, and Gaſpero, with a Casket.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Your friend, and ſervant.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Creditors, my Lord,
Are Maſters and no Servants: as the world goes,
Debters are very ſlaves to thoſe to whom
They have been beholding to; in which reſpect,
I ſhould fear you Gonzalo.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Me, my Lord?
You owe me nothing.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: What, nor love, nor mony?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Yes, love, I hope, not mony.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: All this braverie
Will ſcarcely make that good.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: 'Tis done already:
See Sir, your Mortgage which I only took,
In caſe you and your ſon had in the wars
Miſcarried: I yield it up again: 'tis yours.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Are ye ſo conſcionable?

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: 'Tis your own.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Piſh, piſh, I'le not receive what is not mine,
That were a dangerous buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Sir, I am paid for't,
The ſummes you borrowed, are return'd; The b •• ds
Cancell'd, and your acquittance formerly ſeal'd:
Look here Sir, Gaſpero is witneſs to it.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: My honoured Lord, I am.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: My Lord Fernando,
Arcanes and the reſt, you all ſhall teſtifie,
That I acquit Lord Caſſilane for ever,
Of any debts to me.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: 'Tis plain and ample:
Fortune will once again ſmile on us fairly.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: But hark ye, hark ye, if you be in earneſt,
Whence comes this bounty? or whoſe is't?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: In ſhort,
The great Erota by this Secretary,
Return'd me my full due.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Erota? why
Should ſhe do this?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: You muſt ask her the cauſe,
She knows it beſt.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: So ho, Arcanes, none
But women pity us? ſoft-hearted women?
I am become a brave fellow now, Arcanes,
Am I not?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Why Sir, if the gracious Princeſs
Have took more ſpecial notice of your ſervices,
And means to be more thankfull than ſome others,
It were an injury to gratitude,
To diſeſteem her favours.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: Sir ſhe ever
For your ſake moſt reſpectively lov'd me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: The Senate, and the body of this Kingdom
Are herein (let me ſpeak it without arrogance)
Beholding to her: I will thank her for it;
And if ſhe have reſerv'd a means whereby
I may repay this bounty with ſome ſervice,
She ſhall be then my Patroneſs: come Sirs,
We'l taſte a cup of wine together now.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Fernando, I muſt ſpeak with you in ſecret.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: You ſhall—Now Gaſpero, all's well.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: There's news
You muſt be acquainted with.
Come, there is no maſter-piece in Art, like Policie.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Fer
sp.l: THE Senate is inform'd at full.

sp.speaker: Mic.

l.hi: Gonzalo

sp.l: Dreams not of my arrival yet.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Nor thinks
'Tis poſſible his plots can be diſcover'd:
He ſats himſelf with hopes of Crowns, and Kingdoms,
And laughs ſecurely, to imagine how
He means to gull all but himſelf: when truly,
None is ſo groſly gull'd as he.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: There was never
A more arch villain.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Peace, the Senate comes.

div.stage: Enter Porphicio, Poſ. Senators, and Gaſpero, Attend.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: How cloſely Treaſon cloaks it ſelf in forms
Of Civil honeſty?

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: And yet how palpably
Does heaven reveal it?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Gracious Lords.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: The Embaſſadour,
Lord Paulo Michael, Advocate
To the great Duke of Venice.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: You are moſt welcome,
Your Maſter is a juſt and noble Prince.

sp.speaker: Mic.
sp.l: My Lords, he bad me ſay, that you may know
How much he ſcorns, and (as good Princes ought)
Defies baſe indirect, and godleſs treacheries;
To your more Sacred wiſdomes he refers
The puniſhment due to the falſe Gonzalo,
Or elſe to ſend him home to Venice.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Herein
• he Duke is royal: Gaſpero, the Prince

〈◊〉
Cyprus anſwer'd he would come.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: My Lords,
He will not long be abſent.

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: You Fernando,
Have made the State your debter: worthy Prince,
We ſhall be ſutors to you for your preſence,
〈◊〉 hearing, and determining of matters
Greatly concerning Candy.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Fathers, I am
A ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Why, the cauſe, my Lord, concerns
A ſtranger: pleaſe you ſeat your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: How e're
Infit, ſince you will have it ſo, my Lords,
You ſhall command me.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: You my Lord Fernando,
With the Ambaſſador, withdraw a while.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: My Lords, we ſhall. Ex.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Melitus, and the Secretary,
Give notice to Gonzalo, that the Senate
Requires his preſence. Ex. Gaſ. and Mel.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What concerns the buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: Thus noble Prince —

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Let me alone, thou troubleſt me,
will be heard.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: You know not what you do.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Forbear: who's he that is ſo rude? what's he that dares
• o interrupt our counſels?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: One that has guarded,
Thoſe Purple robes from Cankers worſe than Moths,
One that hath kept your fleeces on your backs,
That would have been ſnatch'd from you: but I ſee
'Tis better now to be a Dog, a Spaniel
In times of Peace, then boaſt the bruiſed ſcars,
Purchas'd with loſs of bloud in noble wars,
My Lords, I ſpeak to you.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: Lord Caſſilane,
We know not what you mean.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Yes, you are ſet
Upon a bench of juſtice; and a day
Will come (hear this, and quake ye potent great ones)
When you your ſelves ſhall 〈◊〉 before a judge,
Who in a pair of ſcales will w • igh your actions,
Without abatement of one grain: as then
You would be ſound full weight, I charge ye fathers
Let me have juſtice now.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Lord Caſſilane,
What ſtrange diſtemperature provokes diſtruſt
Of our impartiality? be ſure
We'l flatter no mans injuries.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: 'Tis well;
You have a Law, Lords, that without remorſe
Dooms ſuch as are belepred with the curſe
Of ſoul ingratitude unto death.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: We have.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Then do me juſtice.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Mad-man, whither run'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Peace Decius, I am deaf.

sp.speaker: Hyp.
sp.l: Will you forget
Your greatneſs, and your modeſty?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Hyparcha leave, I will not hear.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Lady; great, gentle, Lady.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Prethee young man forbear to interrupt me,
Triumph not in thy fortunes; I will ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: More uproars yet! who are they that diſturb us?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: The viper's come; his fears have drawn him hither,
And now, my Lords, be Chornicled for ever,
And give me juſtice againſt this vile Monſter,
This baſtard of my bloud.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: 'Tis juſtice, Fathers,
I ſue for too: and though I might command it,
(If you remember Lords, whoſe child I was)
Yet I will humbly beg it; this old wretch
Has forfeited his life to me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Tricks, tricks;
Complots, devices, 'twixt theſe pair of young ones,
To blunt the edge of your well temper'd Swords,
Wherewith you ſtrike offenders, Lords, but I
Am not a baby to be fear'd with bug bears,
'Tis juſtice I require.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: And I.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You ſpeak too tenderly; and too much like your ſelf
To mean a cruelty; which would make monſtrous
Your Sex: yet for the loves ſake, which you once
Pleas'd to pretend, give my griev'd Father leave
To urge his own revenge; you have no cauſe
For yours: keep peace about ye.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Will you hear me?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Here's ſome ſtrange novelty.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Sure we are mock'd,
Speak one at once: ſay wherein hath your Son
Tranſgreſs'd the Law?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: O the groſs miſts of dulneſs!
Are you this Kingdomes Oracles, yet can be
So ignorant? firſt hear, and then conſider.
That I begot him, gave him birth and life,
And education, were, I muſt confeſs,
But duties of a Father: I did more;
I taught him how to manage Arms, to dare
An Enemy; to court both death and dangers;
Yet theſe were but additions to compleat
A well accompliſh'd Souldier: I did more yet.
I made him chief Commander in the field
Next to my ſelf, and gave him the full proſpect
Of honour, and preferment; train'd him up
In all perfections of a Martialliſt:
•• at he unmindful of his gratitude,
You know with what contempt of my deſerts,
Firſt kick'd againſt mine honour, ſcorned all
My ſervices; then got the palm of glory
Unto himſelf: yet not content with this,
He (laſtly) hath conſpir'd my death, and ſought
Means to engage me to this Lady's debt,
Whoſe bounty all my whole eſtate could never
Give ſatisfaction to: now honoured Fathers,
For this cauſe only, if your Law be law,
And you the Miniſters of juſtice; then
Think of this ſtrange ingratitude in him.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Can this be ſo Antinous?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis all true,
Nor hath my much wrong'd father limn'd my faults
In colours half ſo black, as in themſelves,
My guilt hath dy'd them: were there mercy left,
Yet mine own ſhame would be my Executioner:
Lords, I am guilty.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Thou belieſt, Antinous,
Thine innocence: alas, my Lords, he's deſperate,
And talks he knows not what: you muſt not credit
His lunacy; I can my ſelf diſprove
This accuſation: Caſſilane, be yet
More mercifull; I beg it.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Time, nor ſate,
The world, or what is in it, ſhall not alter
My reſolution: he ſhall dye.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: The Senats
Prayers, or weeping Lovers, ſhall not alter
My reſolution: thou ſhalt dye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why Madam,
Are ye all Marble?

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Leave your ſhifts Antinous,
What plead you to your Fathers accuſation?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Moſt fully guilty.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: You have doom'd your ſelf,
We cannot quit you now.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: A burthen'd conſcience
Will never need a hang-man: hadſt thou dar'd
To have deni'd it, then this Sword of mine
Should on thy head have prov'd thy tongue a lyar.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Thy ſword? wretched old man, thou haſt liv'd too long
To carry peace or comfort to thy grave;
Thou art a man condemn'd: my Lords, this tyrant
Had periſh'd but for me, I ſtill ſuppli'd
His miſerable wants; I ſent his Daughter
Mony to buy him food; the bread he eat,
Was from my purſe: when he (vain-gloriouſly)
To dive into the peoples hearts, had pawn'd
His birth-right, I redeem'd it, ſent it to him,
And for requitall, only made my ſuite,
That he would pleaſe to new receive his ſon
Into his favour, for whoſe love I told him
I had been ſtill ſo friendly: but then he
As void of gratitude, as all good nature,
Diſtracted like a mad man, poaſted hither
To pull this vengeance on himſelf, and us;
For why, my Lords, ſince by the Law, all means
Is blotted out of your commiſſion,
As this hard hearted Father hath accus'd
Noble Antinous, his unblemiſhed Son,
So I accuſe this Father, and crave judgement.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: All this is but deceit, meer trifles forg'd
By combination to defeat the proceſs
Of Juſtice, I will have Antinous life.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Sir, what do ye mean?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: I will have Caſſilane's.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Cunning and cruel Lady, runs the ſtream
Of your affections this way? have you not
Conqueſt enough by treading on my grave?
Unleſs you ſend me thither in a ſhrowd
Steept in my fathers bloud? as you are woman,
As the proteſts of love you vow'd were honeſt;
Be gentler to my Father.

sp.speaker: Er.

l.hi: Caſſilane,

sp.l: Thou haſt a heart of flint: let my intreaties,
My tears, the Sacrifice of griefs unfeigned,
Melt it: yet be a Father to thy ſon,
Unmask thy long beſotted judgement, ſee
A low obedience kneeling at the feet
Of nature, I beſeech you.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Piſh, you cozen
Your hopes: your plots are idle: I am reſolute.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Antinous, urge no further.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Hence thou Sorcery
Of a beguiling ſoftneſs, I will ſtand,
Like the earths center, unmov'd; Lords your breath
Muſt finiſh theſe diviſions: I confeſs
Civility doth teach I ſhould not ſpeak
Againſt a Lady of her birth, ſo high
As great Erota, but her injuries
And thankleſs wrongs to me, urge me to cry
Aloud for juſtice, Fathers.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Whither run you?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: For (honoured fathers) that you all may know
That I alone am not unmatchable
In crimes of this condition, leſt perhaps
You might conceive, as yet the caſe appears,
That this foul ſtain, and guilt runs in a bloud;
Before this preſence, I accuſe this Lady
Of as much vile ingratitude to me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Impudent Traitor!

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Her? O ſpare Antinous;
The world reputes thee valiant, do not ſoyle
All thy paſt nobleneſs with ſuch a cowardize.
As murthering innocent Ladies will ſtamp on thee.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Brave Prince, with what unwillingneſs I force
Her follies, and in thoſe her ſin, be witneſs,
All theſe about me: ſhe is bloudy minded,
And turns the juſtice of the Law to rigor:
It is her cruelites, not I accuſe her:
Shall I have Audience?

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Let him ſpeak my Lords.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Your memory will rot.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Caſt all your eyes
On this, what ſhall I call her? truthleſs woman,
When often in my diſcontents, the ſway
Of her unruly bloud, her untam'd paſſion,
(Or name it as you liſt) had hour by hour
Solicited my love, ſhe vow'd at laſt
She could not, would not live unleſs I granted
What ſhelong ſued for: I in tender pity,
To ſave a Lady of her birth from ruine,
Gave her her life, and promis'd to be hers:
Nor urg'd I ought from her, but ſecreſie,
And then enjoyn'd her to ſupply ſuch wants
As I perceiv'd my Fathers late engagements
Had made him ſubject to; what ſhall I heap up
Long repetitions? ſhe to quit my pity,
Not only hath diſcover'd to my Father
What ſhe had promis'd to conceal, but alſo
Hath drawn my life into this fatal forfeit;
For which ſince I muſt dye, I crave a like
Equality of juſtice againſt her;
Not that I covet bloud, but that ſhe may not
Practiſe this art of falſehood on ſome other,
Perhaps more worthy of her love hereafter.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: If this be true —

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: My Lords, be as the Law is,
Indifferent, upright, I do plead guilty:
Now Sir, what glory have you got by this?
'Las man, I meant not to outlive thy doom,
Shall we be friends in death?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Hear me, the villain
Scandals her, honour'd Lords.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Leave off to doat,
And dye a wiſe man.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I am over-reach'd,
And maſter'd in my own reſolution.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Will ye be wilfull Madam? here's the curſe
Of loves diſdain.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Why ſit you like dumb Statues?
Demur no longer.

sp.speaker: Poſ.

l.hi: Caſſilane, Erota,

sp.l: Antinous, death ye ask; and 'tis your dooms,
You in your follies liv'd, dye in your follies.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I am reveng'd, and thank you for it.

sp.speaker: Er.
sp.l: Yes, and I: Antinous hath been gracious.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sir, may I preſume to crave a bleſſing from you
Before we part?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Yes, ſuch a one as Parents
Beſtow on curſed ſons, now now I laugh
To ſee how thoſe poor younglings are both cheated
Of life and comfort: look ye, look ye, Lords,
I go but ſome ten minutes (more or leſs)
Before my time, but they have finely cozen'd
Themſelves of many, many hopefull years
Amidſt their prime of youth and glory; now
My vengeance is made full. Welcom my joy,
Thou com'ſt to take a ſeaſonable bleſſing
From thy half buried Fathers hand; I am dead
Already girle, a d ſo is ſhe and he,
We all are worms-meat now.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: I have heard all;
Nor ſhall you dye alone: Lords on my knees
I beg for juſtice too.

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: 'Gainſt whom, for what?

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: Firſt let me be reſolv'd; does the Law favour
None, be they ne're ſo mighty?

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: Not the greateſt.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: Then juſtly I accuſe of foul ingratitude
My Lords, you of the Senate all, not one
Excepted.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Porp. Us?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Annophel—

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: You are the Authors
Of this unthrifty bloud-ſhed; when your enemies
Came marching to your gates, your children ſuck'd not
Safe at their Mothers breaſts, your very Cloyſters
Were not ſecure, your ſtarting-holes of refuge
Not free from danger, nor your lives your own:
In this moſt deſperate Ecſtaſie, my Father,
This aged man, not only undertook
To guard your lives, but did ſo; and beat off
The daring foe; for you he pawn'd his lands,
To pay your Souldiers, who without their pay
Refus'd to ſtrike a blow: but, Lords, when peace
Was purchas'd for you, and victorie brought home,
Where was your gratitude, who in your Coffers
Hoarded the ruſtie treaſure which was due
To my unminded Father? he was glad
To live retir'd in want, in penurie,
Whilſt you made feaſts of ſurfeit, and forgot
Your debts to him: The ſum of all is this,
You have been unthankfull to him; and I crave
The rigor of the Law againſt you all.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: My Royal ſpirited daughter!

sp.speaker: Ero.

l.hi: Annophel

sp.l: Thou art a worthy wench; let me embrace thee.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: Lords, why do ye keep your ſeats? they are no places
For ſuch as are offenders.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Though our ignorance
Of Caſſilanes engagements might aſſwage
Severity of juſtice, yet to ſhew
How no excuſe ſhould ſmooth a breach of Law,
I yield me to the trial of it.

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: So muſt I:
Great Prince of Cyprus, you are left
The only Moderator in this difference;
And as you are a Prince be a Protector
To wofull Candy.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What a Scene of miſerie
Hath thine obdurate frowardneſs (old man)
Drawn on thy Countries boſom? and for that
Thy proud ambition could not mount ſo high
As to be ſtil'd thy Countries only Patron,
Thy malice hath deſcended to the depth
Of Hell, to be renowned in the Title
Of the deſtroyer? doſt thou yet perceive
What curſes all poſterity will brand
Thy grave with? that at once haſt rob'd this Kingdom
Of honour and of ſafety.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Children yet unborn
Will ſtop their ears when thou art nam'd.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: The world will be too little to contain
The memorie of this deteſted deed;
The Furies will abhorr it.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: What the ſword
Could not enforce, your peeviſh thirſt of honour
(A brave, cold, weak, imaginarie fame)
Hath brought on Candy: Candy groans, not theſe
That are to die.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: 'Tis happineſs enough
For them, that they ſhall not ſurvive to ſee
The wounds wherewith thou ſtab'ſt the land that gave
Thee life and name.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: 'Tis Candy's wrack ſhall feel—

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: The miſchief of your folly.

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: Poſ. Annophel—

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: I will not be entreated.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Prethee Annophel.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: Why would ye urge me to a mercy which
You in your ſelf allow not?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: 'Tis the Law,
That if the party who complains, remit
The offender, he is freed: is't not ſo Lords?

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: Poſ. 'Tis ſo.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Antinous, By my ſhame obſerve
What a cloſe witch-craft popular applauſe is:
I am awak'd, and with clear eyes behold
The Lethargie wherein my reaſon long
Hath been be-charm'd: live, live, my matchleſs ſon,
Bleſt in thy Fathers bleſſing; much more bleſt
In thine own vertues: let me dew thy cheeks
With my unmanly tears: Riſe, I forgive thee:
And good Antinous, if I ſhall be thy Father
Forgive me: I can ſpeak no more.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Dear Sir,
You new beget me now — Madam your pardon,
I heartily remit you.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: I as freely
Diſcharge thee Caſſilane.

sp.speaker: Anno.
sp.l: My gracious Lords,
Repute me not a blemiſh to my Sex,
In that I ſtrove to cure a deſperate evil
With a more violent remedy: your lives,
Your honours are your own.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Then with conſent
Be reconcil'd on all ſides: Pleaſe you Fathers
To take your places.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Let us again aſcend,
With joy and thankfulneſs to Heaven: and now
To other buſineſs Lords.

div.stage: Enter Gaſpero, and Melitus, with Gonzalo.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Two hours and more Sir,
The Senate hath been ſet.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: And I not know it?
Who ſits with them?

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: My Lord, the Prince of Cyprus.

sp.speaker: Gonz.

l.hi: Gaſpero,

sp.l: Why how comes that to paſs?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Some weighty cauſe
I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Now Lords the buſineſs? ha?
Who's here, Erota?

sp.speaker: Porp.
sp.l: Secretarie do your charge
Upon that Traitor.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Traitor?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Yes, Gonzalo, Traitor,
Of treaſon to the peace and ſtate of Candy,
I do atteſt thee.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Me? thou Dog?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: With Licence
From this grave Senate, I arreſt thee likewiſe
Of treaſon to the State of Venice.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Ha?
Is Michael here? nay then I ſee
I am undone.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: I ſhall not be your Queen,
Your Dutcheſs, or your Empreſs.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Dull, dull brain.
O I am fool'd?

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Look Sir, do you know this hand?

sp.speaker: Mic.
sp.l: Do you know this Seal? Firſt, Lords, he writes to Venice,
To make a perfect league, during which time
He would in private keep ſome Troops in pay,
Bribe all the Centinels throughout this Kingdom,
Corrupt the Captains; at a Banquet poyſon
The Prince, and greateſt Peers, and in concluſion
Yield Candy ſlave to Venice.

sp.speaker: Gaſ.
sp.l: Next, he contracted
With the Illuſtrious Princeſs, the Lady Erota,
In hope of marriage with her, to deliver
All the Venetian gallantry, and ſtrength,
Upon their firſt arrival, to the mercy
Of her and Candy.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: This is true, Gonzalo.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Let it be true: what then?

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: My Lord Ambaſſadour,
What's your demand?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: As likes the State of Candy,
Either to ſentence him as he deſerves
Here, or to ſend him like a ſlave to Venice.

sp.speaker: Porph.
sp.l: We ſhall adviſe upon it.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: O the Devils,
That had not thruſt this trick into my pate—
A Politician fool? deſtruction plague
Candy and Venice both.

sp.speaker: Poſ.
sp.l: Porp. Away with him.

sp.speaker: Mel.
sp.l: Come Sir, I'le ſee you ſafe. Exeunt Gonz. Mel.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Lords, e're you part
Be witneſs to another change of wonder;
Antinous, now be bold, before this preſence,
Freely to ſpeak, whether or no I us'd
The humbleſt means affection could contrive,
To gain thy love.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Madam, I muſt confeſs it,
And ever am your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Yes Antinous,
My ſervant, for my Lord thou ſhalt be never:
I here diſclaim the intereſt thou hadſt once
In my too paſſionate thoughts. Moſt noble Prince,
If yet a relique of thy wonted flames
Live warm within thy boſom, then I bluſh not
To offer up the aſſurance of my faith,
To thee that haſt deſerv'd it beſt.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: O Madam,
You play with my calamity.

sp.speaker: Erot.
sp.l: Let heaven
Record my truth for ever.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: With more joy
Than I have words to utter, I accept it.
I alſo pawn you mine.

sp.speaker: Ero.
sp.l: The man that in requital
Of noble and un-ſought affection
Grows cruel, never lov'd, nor did Antinous.
Yet herein (Prince) ye are beholding to him;
For his neglect of me humbled a pride,
Which to a vertuous wife had been a Monſter.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: For which I'le rank him my deſerving friend.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Much comfort dwell with you, as I could wiſh
To him I honour moſt.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: O my Antinous,
My own, my own good ſon.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: One ſuit I have to make.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: To whom Fernando?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Lord Caſſilane to you.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: To me?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: This Lady
Hath promiſed to be mine.

sp.speaker: Ann.
sp.l: Your bleſſing Sir;
Brother your love.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You cannot Sir beſtow her
On a more noble Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Saiſt thou ſo?
Antinous I confirm it. Here Fernando,
Live both as one; ſhe is thine.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And herein Siſter,
I honour you for your wife ſetled love.
This is a day of Triumph, all Contentions
Are happily accorded: Candy's peace
Secur'd, and Venice vow'd a worthy friend. Exeu • .

list.item: Achoreus, an honeſt Counſellor, Prieſt of Iſis.
Photinus, a Politician, minion to Ptolomy.
Achillas, Captain of the Guard to Ptolomy.
Labienus, a Roman Souldier, and Nuncio.
Seeva, a free Speaker, alſo Captain to Caeſar.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Cleopatra, Queen of Aegypt. Caeſar's Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: I Love the King, nor do diſpute his power,
(For that is not confin'd, nor to be cenſur'd
By me, that am his Subject) yet allow me
The liberty of a Man, that ſtill would be
A friend to Juſtice, to demand the motives
That did induce young Ptolomy, or Photinus,
(To whoſe directions he gives up himſelf,
And I hope wiſely) to commit his Siſter,
The Princeſs Cleopatra (if I ſaid
The Queen (Achillas) 'twere (I hope) no treaſon,
She being by her Fathers Teſtament
(Whoſe memory I bow to) left Co-heir
In all he ſtood poſſeſt of.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: 'Tis confeſt
(My good Achoreus) that in theſe Eaſtern Kingdoms
Women are not exempted from the Sceptre,
But claim a priviledge, equal to the Male;
But how much ſuch diviſions have ta'en from
The Majeſty of Egypt, and what factions
Have ſprung from thoſe partitions, to the ruine
Of the poor Subject, (doubtful which to follow,)
We have too many, and too ſad examples,
Therefore the wiſe Photinus, to prevent
The Murthers, and the Maſſacres, that attend
On diſunited Government, and to ſhew
The King without a Partner, in full ſplendour,
Thought it convenient the fair Cleopatra,
(An attribute not frequent to the Climate)
Should be committed in ſafe Cuſtody,
In which ſhe is attended like her Birth,
Until her Beauty, or her royal Dowre,
Hath found her out a Husband.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: How this may
Stand with the rules of policy, I know not;
Moſt ſure I am, it holds no correſpondence
With the Rites of Aegypt, or the Laws of Nature;
But grant that Cleopatra can ſit down
With this diſgrace (though inſupportable)
Can you imagine, that Romes glorious Senate
(To whoſe charge, by the will of the dead King
This government was deliver'd) or great Pompey,
(That is appointed Cleopatra's Guardian
As well as Ptolomies) will e're approve
Of this raſh counſel, their conſent not ſought for,
That ſhould authorize it?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: The Civil war
In which the Roman Empire is embarqu'd
On a rough Sea of danger, does exact
Their whole care to preſerve themſelves, and gives them
No vacant time to think of what we do,
Which hardly can concern them.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: What's your opinion
Of the ſucceſs? I have heard, in multitudes
Of Souldiers, and all glorious pomp of war,
Pompey is much ſuperiour.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: I could give you
A Catalogue of all the ſeveral Nations
From whence he drew his powers: but that were tedious.
They have rich arms, are ten to one in number,
Which makes them think the • ay alrea • y won;
And Pompey being maſter of the S • a,
Such plenty of all delicates are brought in,
As if the place on which they are ent ••• c • 'd,
Were not a Camp of Souldiers, but Rom • ,
In which Lucullus and Apicius joyn'd,
To make a publique Feaſt: they at Dirachium
Fought with ſucceſs; but knew not to make uſe of
Fortunes fair offer: ſo much I have heard
Caeſar himſelf confeſs.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: Where are they now?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: In Theſſalie, near the Pharſalian plains
Where Caeſar with a handfull of his Men
Hems in the greater number: his whole troops
Exceed not twenty thouſand, but old Souldiers
Fleſh'd in the ſpoils of Germany and France,
Inur'd to his Command, and only know
To fight and overcome; And though that Famine
Raigns in his Camp, compelling them to taſt
Bread made of roots, forbid the uſe of man,
(Which they with ſcorn threw into Pompeys Camp
As in deriſion of his Delicates)
Or corn not yet half ripe, and that a Banquet:
They ſtill beſiege him, being ambitious only
To come to blows, and let their ſwords determine
Who hath the better Cauſe.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: May Victory
Attend on't, where it is.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: We every hour
Expect to hear the iſſue.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Save my good Lords;
By Iſis and Oſiris, whom you worſhip;
And the four hundred gods and goddeſſes
Ador'd in Rome, I am your honours ſervant.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: Truth needs, Septinius, no oaths.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: You are cruel,
If you deny him ſwearing, you take from him
Three full parts of his language.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Your Honour's bitter,
Confound me, where I love I cannot ſay it,
But I muſt ſwear't: yet ſuch is my ill fortune,
Nor vows, nor proteſtations win belief,
I think, and (I can find no other reaſon)
Becauſe I am a Roman.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: No Septinius,
To be a Roman were an honour to you,
Did not your manners, and your life take from it,
And cry aloud, that from Rome you bring nothing
But Roman Vices, which you would plant here,
But no ſeed of her vertues.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: With your reverence
I am too old to learn.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: Any thing honeſt,
That I believe, without an oath.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: I fear
Your Lordſhip has ſlept ill to night, and that
Invites this ſad diſcourſe: 'twill make you old
Before your time: — O theſe vertuous Morals,
And old religious principles, that fool us!
I have brought you a new Song, will make you laugh,
Though you were at your prayers.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: What is the ſubject?
Be free Septinius.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: 'Tis a Catalogue
Of all the Gameſters of the Court and City,
Which Lord lyes with that Lady, and what Gallant
Sports with that Merchants wife; and does relate
Who ſells her honour for a Diamond,
Who, for a tiſſew robe: whoſe husband's jealous,
And who ſo kind, that, to ſhare with his wife,
Will make the match himſelf:
Harml • s conceits,
Though fools ſay they are dangerous: I ſang it
The laſt night at my Lord Photinus table.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: How? as a Fidler?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: No Sir, as a Gueſt,
A welcom gueſt too: and it was approv'd of
By a dozen of his friends, though they were touch'd in't:
For look you, 'tis a kind of merriment,
When we have laid by fooliſh modeſty
(As not a man of faſhion will wear it)
To talk what we have done; at leaſt to hear it;
If meerily ſet down, it fires the blood,
And heightens Creſt-faln appetite.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: New doctrine!

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Was't of your own compoſing?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: No, I bought it
Of a skulking Scribler for two Ptolomies:
But the hints were mine own; the wretch was fearfull:
But I have damn'd my ſelf, ſhould it be queſtion'd,
That I will own it.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: And be puniſhed for it:
Take heed: for you may ſo long exerciſe
Your ſcurrilous wit againſt authority,
The Kingdoms Counſels; and make profane Jeſts,
(Which to you (being an atheiſt) is nothing)
Againſt Religion, that your great maintainers
(Unleſs they would be thought Co-partners with you)
Will leave you to the Law: and then, Septinius,
Remember there are whips.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: For whore's I grant you,
When they are out of date, till then are ſafe too,
Or all the Gallants of the Court are Eunuchs,
And for mine own defence I'le only add this,
I'le be admitted for a wanton tale
To ſome moſt private Cabinets, when your Prieſt hood
(Though laden with the myſteries of your goddeſs)
Shall wait without unnoted: ſo I leave you
To your pious thoughts. Exit.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſtrange impudence,
This fellow does put on.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: The wonder great,
He is accepted of.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Vices, for him,
Make as free way as vertues doe for others.
'Tis the times fault: yet Great ones ſtill have grace'd
To make them ſport, or rub them o're with flattery,
Obſervers of all kinds.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: No more of him,
He is not worth our thoughts: a Fugitive
From Pompeys army: and now in a danger
When he ſhould uſe his ſervice.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: See how he hangs
On great Photinus Ear.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Hell, and the furies,
And all the plagues of darkneſs light upon me:
You are my god on earth: and let me have
Your favour here, fall what can fall hereafter.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Thou art believ'd: doſt thou want mony?

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Or haſt thou any ſuite? theſe ever follow
Thy vehement proteſtations.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: You much wrong me;
How can I want, when your beams ſhine upon me,
Unleſs employment to expreſs my zeal
To do your greatneſs ſervice? do but think
A deed ſo dark, the Sun would bluſh to look on,
For which Man-kind would curſe me, and arm all
The powers above, and thoſe below againſt me:
Command me, I will on.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: When I have uſe,
I'le put you to the teſt.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: May it be ſpeedy,
And ſomething worth my danger: you are cold,
And know not your own powers: this brow was faſhion'd
To wear a Kingly wreath, and your grave judgment,
Given to diſpoſe of monarchies, not to govern
A childs affairs, the peoples eye's upon you,
The Souldier courts you: will you wear a garment
Of ſordid loyalty when 'tis out of faſhion?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: When Pompey was thy General, Septinius,
Thou ſaidſt as much to him.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: All my love to him,
To Caeſar, Rome, and the whole world is loſt
In the Ocean of your Bounties: I have no friend,
Project, deſign, or Countrey, but your favour,
Which I'le preſerve at any rate.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: No more;
When I call on you, fall not off: perhaps
Sooner than you expect, I may employ you,
So leave me for a while.

sp.speaker: Sep.
sp.l: Ever your Creature. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Good day Achoreus; my beſt friend Achillas,
Hath fame deliver'd yet no certain rumour
Of the great Roman Action?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: That we are
To enquire, and learn of you Sir: whoſe grave care
For Egypts happineſs, and great Ptolomies good,
Hath eyes and ears in all parts.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: I'le not boaſt,
What my Intelligence coſts me: but 'ere long
You ſhall know more. The King, with him a Roman.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: The ſcarlet livery of unfortunate war
Dy'd deeply on his face.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: 'Tis Labienus
Caeſars Lieutenant in the wars of Gaul,
And fortunate in all his undertakings:
But ſince theſe Civil jars he turn'd to Pompey,
And though he followed the better Cauſe
Not with the like ſucceſs.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Such as are wiſe
Leave falling buildings, flye to thoſe that riſe;
But more of that hereafter.

sp.speaker: Lab.
sp.l: In a word, Sir,
Theſe gaping wounds, not taken as a ſlave,
Speak Pompey's loſs: to tell you of the Battail,
How many thouſand ſeveral bloody ſhapes
Death wore that day in triumph: how we bore
The ſhock of Caeſars charge: or with what fury
His Souldiers came on as if they had been
So many Caeſars, and like him ambitious
To tread upon the liberty of Rome:
How Fathers kill'd their Sons, or Sons their Fathers,
Or how the Roman Piles on either ſide
Drew Roman blood, which ſpent, the Prince of weapons,
(The ſword) ſucceeded, which in Civil wars
Appoints the Tent on which wing'd victory
Shall make a certain Stand; then, how the Plains
Flow'd o're with blood, and what a cloud of vulturs
And other birds of prey, hung o're both armies,
Attending when their ready Servitors,
(The Souldiers, from whom the angry gods
Had took all ſenſe of reaſon, and of pity)
Would ſerve in their own carkaſſes for a feaſt,
How Caeſar with his Javelin force'd them on
That made the leaſt ſtop, when their angry hands
Were lifted up againſt ſome known friends face;
Then coming to the body of the army
He ſhews the ſacred Senate, and forbids them
To waſt their force upon the Common Souldier,
Whom willingly, if e're he did know pity,
He would have ſpar'd.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: The reaſon Labienus?

sp.speaker: Lab.
sp.l: Full well he knows, that in their blood he was
To paſs to Empire, and that through their bowels
He muſt invade the Laws of Rome, and give
A period to the liberty of the world.
Then ſell the Lepidi, and the bold Corvini,
The fam'd Torquati, Scipio's, and Marcelli,
(Names next to Pompeys, moſt renown'd on Earth)
The Nobles, and the Commons lay together,
And Pontique, Punique, and Aſſyrian blood
Made up one crimſon Lake: which Pompey ſeeing,
And that his, and the fate of Rome had left him
Standing upon the Rampier of his Camp,
Though ſcorning all that could fall on himſelf,
He pities them whoſe fortunes are embarqu'd
In his unlucky quarrel; cryes aloud too
That they ſhould ſound retreat, and ſave themſelves:
That he deſir'd not, ſo much noble blood
Should be loſt in his ſervice, or attend
On his misfortunes: and then, taking horſe
With ſome few of his friends, he came to Lesbos,
And with Cornelia, his Wife, and Sons,
He's touch'd upon your ſhore: the King of Parthia,
(Famous in his defeature of the Craſſi)
Offer'd him his protection, but Pompey
Relying on his Benefits, and your Faith,
Hath choſen Aegypt for his Sanctuary,
Till he may recollect his ſcattered powers,
And try a ſecond day: now Ptolomy,
Though he appear not like that glorious thing
That three times rode in triumph, and gave laws
To conquer'd Nations, and made Crowns his gift
(As this of yours, your noble Father took
From his victorious hand, and you ſtill wear it
At his devotion) to do you more honour
In his declin'd eſtate, as the ſtraightſt Pine
In a full grove of his yet flouriſhing friends,
He flyes to you for ſuccour, and expects
The entertainment of your Fathers friend,
And Guardian to your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: To ſay I grieve his fortune
As much as if the Crown I wear (his gift)
Were raviſh'd from me, is a holy truth,
Our Gods can witneſs for me: yet, being young,
And not a free diſpoſer of my ſelf;
Let not a few hours, borrowed for advice,
Beget ſuſpicion of unthankfulneſs,
(Which next to Hell I hate) pray you retire,
And take a little reſt, and let his wounds
Be with that care attended, as they were
Cary'd on my fleſh: good Labienus, think
The little reſpite, I deſire ſhall be
Wholly emploi'd to find the readieſt way
To doe great Pompey ſervice.

sp.speaker: Lab.
sp.l: May the gods
(As you intend) protect you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: Sit: ſit all,
It is my pleaſure: your advice, and freely.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: A ſhort deliberation in this,
May ſerve to give you counſel: to be honeſt,
Religious and thankfull, in themſelves
Are forcible motives, and can need no flouriſh
Or gloſs in the perſwader; your kept faith,
(Though Pompey never riſe to th' height he's fallen from)
Caeſar himſelf will love; and my opinion
Is (ſtill committing it to graver cenſure)
You pay the debt you owe him, with the hazard
Of all you can call yours,

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: What's yours, Photinus?)

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Achoreus (great Ptolomy) hath counſell'd
Like a Religious, and honeſt man,
Worthy the honour that he juſtly holds
In being Prieſt to Iſis: But alas,
What in a man, ſequeſter'd from the world,
Or in a private perſon, is prefer'd,
No policy allows of in a King,
To be or juſt, or thankfull, makes Kings guilty,
And faith (though prais'd) is puniſh'd that ſupports
Such as good Fate forſakes: joyn with the gods,
Obſerve the man they favour, leave the wretched,
The Stars are not more diſtant from the Earth
Than profit is from honeſty; all the power,
Prerogative, and greatneſs of a Prince
Is loſt, if he deſcend once but to ſteer
His courſe, as what's right, guides him: let him leave
The Scepter, that ſtrives only to be good,
Since Kingdomes are maintain'd by force and blood.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: Oh wicked!

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: Peace: goe on.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Proud Pompey ſhews how much he ſcorns your youth,
In thinking that you cannot keep your own
From ſuch as are or'e come. If you are tired
With being a King, let not a ſtranger take
What nearer pledges challenge: reſign rather
The government of Aegypt and of Nile
To Cleopatra, that has title to them,
At leaſt defend them from the Roman gripe,
What was not Pompeys, while the wars endured,
The Conquerour will not challenge; by all the world
Forſaken and deſpis'd, your gentle Guardian
His hopes and fortunes deſperate, makes choice of
What Nation he ſhall fall with: and purſu'd
By their pale ghoſts, ſlain in this Civil war,
He flyes not Caeſar only, but the Senate,
Of which, the greater part have clo • 'd the hunger
Of ſharp Pharſalian fowl, he flies the Nations
That he drew to his Quarrel, whoſe Eſtates
Are ſunk in his: and in no place receiv'd,
Hath found out Aigypt, by him yet not ruin'd:
And Potolmy, things conſider'd, juſtly may
Complain of Pompey: wherefore ſhould he ſtain
Our Aegypt, with the ſpots of civil war?
Or make the peaceable, or quiet Nile
Doubted of Caeſar? wherefore ſhould he draw
His loſs, and overthrow upon our heads?
Or chooſe this place to ſuffer in? already
We have offended Caeſar, in our wiſhes,
And no way left us to redeem his favour
But by the head of Pompey.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: Great Oſiris,
Defend thy Aegypt from ſuch cruelty,
And barbarous ingratitude!

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Holy trifles,
And not to have place in deſigns of State;
This ſword, which Fate commands me to unſheath,
I would not draw on Pompey, if not vanquiſh'd.
I grant it rather ſhould have paſs'd through Caeſar,
But we muſt follow where his fortune leads us;
All provident Princes meaſure their intents
According to their power, and ſo diſpoſe them:
And thinkſt thou (Ptolomy) that thou canſt prop
His Ruines, under whom ſad Rome now ſuffers?
Or 'tempt the Conquerours force when 'tis confirm'd?
Shall we, that in the Battail ſate as Neuters
Serve him that's overcome? No, no, he's loſt.
And though 'tis noble to a ſinking friend
To lend a helping hand, while there is hope
He may recover, thy part not engag'd
Though one moſt dear, when all his hopes are dead,
To drown him, ſet thy foot upon his head.

sp.speaker: Ach.
sp.l: Moſt execrable Counſel.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: To be follow'd,
'Tis for the Kingdoms ſafety.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: We give up
Our abſolute power to thee: diſpoſe of it
As reaſon ſhall direct thee.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Good Achillas,
Seek out Septinius: do you but ſooth him,
He is already wrought: leave the diſpatch
To me of Labienus: 'tis determin'd
Already how you ſhall proceed: nor Fate
Shall alter it, ſince now the dye is caſt,
But that this hour to Pompey is his laſt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Apol.
sp.l: Is the Queen ſtirring, Eros?

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: Yes, for in truth
She touch'd no bed to night.

sp.speaker: Apol.
sp.l: I am ſorry for it,
And wiſh it were in me, with my hazard,
To give her eaſe.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Sir, ſhe accepts your will,
And does acknowledge ſhe hath found you noble,
So far, as if reſtraint of liberty
Could give admiſſion to a thought of mirth,
She is your debtor for it.

sp.speaker: Apol.
sp.l: Did you tell her
Of the ſports I have prepar'd to entertain her?
She was us'd to take delight, with her fair hand,
To angle in the Nile, where the glad fiſh
(As if they knew who 'twas ſought to deceive 'em)
Contended to be taken: other times
To ſtrike the Stag, who wounded by her arrows,
Forgot his tears in death, and kneeling thanks her
To his laſt gaſp, then prouder of his Fate,
Than if with Garlands Crown'd, he had been choſen
To fall a Sacrifice before the altar
Of the Virgin Huntreſs: the King, nor great Photinus
Forbid her any pleaſure; and the Circuit
In which ſhe is confin'd, gladly affords
Variety of paſtimes, which I would
Encreaſe with my beſt ſervice.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: O, but the thought
That ſhe that was born free, and to diſpenſe
Reſtraint, or liberty to others, ſhould be
At the devotion of her Brother, whom
She only knows her equal, makes this place
In which ſhe lives (though ſtor'd with all delights)
A loathſome dungeon to her.

sp.speaker: Apol.
sp.l: Yet, (howe're
She ſhall interpret it) I'le not be wanting
To do my beſt to ſerve her: I have prepar'd
Choiſe Muſick near her Cabinet, and compos'd
Some few lines, (ſet unto a ſolemn time)
In the praiſe of impriſonment. Begin Boy.

body.head: The SONG.
body.l: LOok out bright eyes, and bleſs the air:
Even in ſhadows you are fair.
Shut-up beauty is like fire,
That breaks out clearer ſtill and higher.
Though your body be confin'd,
And ſoft Love a priſoner bound,
Yet the beauty of your mind
Neither cheek, nor chain hath found.
Look out nobly then, and dare
Even the Fetters that you wear.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: But that we are aſſur'd this taſtes of duty,
And love in you, my Guardian, and deſire
In you, my Siſter, and the reſt, to pleaſe us,
We ſhould receive this, as a ſawcy rudeneſs
Offer'd our private thoughts. But your intents
Are to delight us: alas, you waſh an Ethiop:
Can Cleopatra, while ſhe does remember
Whoſe Daughter ſhe is, and whoſe Siſter? (O
I ſuffer in the name) and that (in Juſtice)
There is no place in Aegypt, where I ſtand,
But that the tributary Earth is proud
To kiſs the foot of her, that is her Queen,
Can ſhe, I ſay, that is all this, e're reliſh
Of comfort, or delight, while baſe Photinus,
Bond-man Achillas, and all other monſters
That raign o're Ptolomy, make that a Court,
Where they reſide, and this, where I, a Priſon?
But there's a Rome, a Senate, and a Caeſar,
(Though the great Pompey lean to Ptolomy)
May think of Cleopatra.

sp.speaker: Ap.
sp.l: Pompey, Madam?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: What of him? ſpeak: if ill, Apollodorus,
It is my happineſs: and for thy news
Receive a favour (Kings have kneel'd in vain for)
And kiſs my hand.

sp.speaker: Ap.
sp.l: He's loſt.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Speak it again?

sp.speaker: Ap.
sp.l: His army routed: he fled and purſu'd
By the all-conquering Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Whither bends he?
