And as in Pompey I began a name
I'le perfect it in Caeſar.

div.stage: Enter (above) Caeſar, Ptolomy, Achoreus, Apollodorus, Antony, Dolabella.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: 'Tis reſolv'd then,
We'll force our paſſage.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: See, they do appear
As they deſir'd a Parley.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: I am proud yet
I have brought 'em to capitulate.

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: Now, Photinus?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Now, Ptolomy?

sp.speaker: Ptol.
sp.l: No addition?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: We are equal,
Though Caeſars name were put into the ſcale,
In which our worth is weigh'd.
Preſumptuous Villain,
Upon what grounds haſt thou preſum'd to raiſe
Thy ſervile hand againſt the King, or me,
That have a greater name?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: On thoſe, by which
Thou didſt preſume to paſs the Rubicon
Againſt the Laws of Rome; and at the name
Of Traitor ſmile; as thou didſt when Marcellus,
The Conſul, with the Senates full conſent
Pronounc'd thee for an Enemy to thy Country,
Yet thou wentſt on, and thy rebellious Cauſe
Was crown'd with fair ſucceſs: Why ſhould we fear then?
Think on that, Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: O the gods! be brav'd thus,
And be compell'd to bear this from a Slave
That would not brook Great Pompey his Superiour?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Thy glories now have toucht the higheſt point,
And muſt deſcend.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Deſpair, and think we ſtand
The Champions of Rome, to wreak her wrongs,
Upon whoſe liberty thou haſt ſet thy foot.

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: And that the Ghoſts of all thoſe noble Romans
That by thy Sword fell in this Civil War
Expect revenge.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Dar'ſt thou ſpeak, and remember
There was a Pompey?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: There is no hope to 'ſcape us:
If that againſt the odds we have upon you
You dare come forth, and fight, receive the honour
To dye like Romans, if ye faint, reſolve
To ſtarve like Wretches; I diſdain to change
Another ſyllable with you. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let us dye nobly;
And rather fall upon each others Sword
Than come into theſe Villains hands.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: That Fortune,
Which to this hour hath been a Friend to Caeſar,
Though for a while ſhe cloath her Brow with frowns,
Will ſmile again upon me: who will pay her,
Or ſacrifice, or Vows, if ſhe forſake
Her beſt of works in me? or ſuffer him,
Whom with a ſtrong hand ſhe hath led triumphant
Through the whole weſtern world, and Rome acknowledg'd
Her Soveraign Lord, to end in gloriouſly
A life admir'd by all? The threatned danger
Muſt by a way more horrid be avoided,
And I will run the hazard; Fire the Palace,
And the rich Magazines that neighbour it,
In which the Wealth of Egypt is contain'd:
Start not, it ſhall be ſo; that while the people
Labour in quenching the enſuing flames,
Like Caeſar, with this handful of my friends
Through Fire, and Swords I force a paſſage to
My conquering Legions. King, if thou dar'd follow
VVhere Caeſar leads, or live or dye a Free man;
If not, ſtay here a Bond man to thy Slave,
And dead, he thought unworthy of a Grave. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III.

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: I feel my reſolution melts again
And that I am not Knave alone, but fool,
In all my purpoſes. The Devil, Photinus,
Employs me as a Property, and grown uſeleſs
Will ſhake me off again; he told me ſo
When I kill'd Pompey; nor can I hope better,
When Caeſar is diſpatch'd; Services done
For ſuch as only ſtudy their own ends,
Too great to be rewarded, are return'd
With deadly hate; I learn'd this Principle
In his own School, yet ſtill he fools me, well;
And yet he truſts me: Since I in my nature
Was faſhion'd to be falſe, wherefore ſhould I
That kill'd my General, and a Roman, one
To whom I ow'd all nouriſhments of life,
Be true to an Egyptian? To ſave Caeſar,
And turn Photinus's plots on his own head,
As it is in my power, redeem my credit,
And live to lye and ſwear again in faſhion,
Oh, 'twere a maſter-piece? ha! — me Caeſar,
How's he got off!

div.stage: Enter Caeſar, Ptolomy, Antony, Dolabella, Achoreus, Apollodorus, Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: The fire has took,
And ſhews the City like a ſecond Troy,
The Navy too is ſcorch'd, the people greedy
To ſave their Wealth and Houſes, whilſt their Souldiers
Make ſpoil of all; only Achillas's Troops
Make good their Guard, break through them, we are ſafe;
I'll lead you like a Thunder-bolt.

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: Stay, Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: Who's this? the Dog, Septimius?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Cut his throat.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: You bark'd but now, fawn you ſo ſoon?

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: O hear me,
What I'll deliver is for Caeſars ſafety,
For all your good.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Good from a mouth like thine,
That never belch'd but blaſphemy, and treaſon on Feſ ••• days

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: I am an altered man, altered indeed,
And will give you cauſe to ſay I am a Roman.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: Rogue, I grant thee.

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: Truſt me, I'll make the paſſage ſmooth, and eaſie
For your eſcape.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'll truſt the Devil ſooner,
And make a ſafer Bargain.

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: I am truſted
With all Photinus's ſecrets.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: There's no doubt then
Thou wilt be falſe.

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: Still to be true to you.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: And very likely.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: Be brief, the means?

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: Thus, Caeſar,
To me alone, but bound by terrible oaths
Not to diſcover it, he hath reveal'd
A diſmal Vault, whoſe dreadful mouth does open
A mile beyond the City: in this Cave
Lye but two hours conceal'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: If you believe him,
He'll bury us alive.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: I'll flye in the Air firſt,

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: Then in the dead of night I'll bring you back
Into a private room, where you ſhall find
Photinus, and Achillas, and the reſt
Of their Commanders cloſe at Council.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: Good, what follows?

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: Fall me fairly on their throats,
Their heads cut off and ſhorn, the multitude
Will eaſily diſperſe.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: O Devil! away with him;
Not true to Friend nor Enemy? Caeſar ſcorns
To find his ſafety, or revenge his wrongs
So baſe a way; or owe the means of life
To ſuch a leprous Traytor. I have towr'd
For Victory like a Faulcon in the Clouds,
Nor dig'd for't like a Mole; our Swords and Cauſe
Make way for us, and that it may appear
We took a noble Courſe, and hate baſe Treaſon,
Some Souldiers that would merit Caeſar's favour,
Hang him on yonder Turret, and then follow
The lane this Sword makes for you. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: Here's a Belt,
Though I dye for it I'll uſe it.

sp.speaker: 2 Sold.
sp.l: 'Tis too good
To truſs a Cur in.

sp.speaker: Sept.
sp.l: Save me, here's Gold.

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: If Rome
Were offered for thy ranſom, it could not help thee.

sp.speaker: 2 Sold.
sp.l: Hang not an arſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: Goad him on with thy Sword;
Thou doſt deſerve a worſer end, and may
All ſuch conclude ſo, that their friends betray. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IV.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: We are loſt.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: Undone.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Confuſion, Fire, and Swords,
And fury in the Souldiers face more horrid
Circle us round.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: The Kings Command they laugh at,
And jeer at Caeſars threats.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: My Brother ſeiz'd on
By the Roman, as thought guilty of the tumult,
And forc'd to bear him company, as mark'd out
For his protection or revenge.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: They have broke
Into my Cabinet; my Trunks are ranſack'd.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: I have loſt my jewels too: but that's the leaſt:
The barbarous Raſcals, againſt all humanity,
Or ſenſe of pity, have kill'd my little Dog,
And broke my Monkeys Chain.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: They rifled me:
But that I could endure, would they proceed no further.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: O my Siſter!

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: My Queen, my Miſtreſs!

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Can you ſtand unmov'd
VVhen the Earth-quake of Rebellion ſhakes the City,
And the Court trembles?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Yes, Arſino,
And with a Maſculine Conſtancy deride
Fortunes worſt malice, as a Servant to
My Vertues, not a Miſtreſs; then we forſake
The ſtrong Fort of our ſelves, when we once yield,
Or ſhrink at her aſſaults; I am ſtill my ſelf,
And though diſrob'd of Soveraignty, and raviſh'd
Of ceremonious duty, that attends it,
Nay, grant they had ſlav'd my Body, my free mind
Like to the Palm-tree walling fruitful Nile,
Shall grow up ſtraighter and enlarge it ſelf
'Spight of the envious weight that loads it with:
Think of thy Birth (Arſino) common burdens
Fit common Shoulders; teach the multitude
By ſuffering nobly what they fear to touch at;
The greatneſs of thy mind does ſoar a pitch,
Their dim eyes (darkened by their narrow ſouls)
Cannot arrive at.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: I am new created,
And owe this ſecond being to you (beſt Siſter)
For now I feel you have infus'd into me
Part of your fortitude.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: I ſtill am fearful;
I dare not tell a lie; you that were born
Daughters and Siſters unto Kings, may nouriſh
Great thoughts, which I, that am your humble handmaid
Muſt not preſume to rival.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Yet (my Eros)
Though thou haſt profited nothing by obſerving
The whole cou ſe of my life, learn in my death,
Though not to equal, yet to imitate
Thy fearleſs Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: O, a man in Arms!
His Weapon drawn too?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Though upon the point
Death ſate, I'll meet it, and outdare the danger.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Keep the Watch ſtrong, and guard the paſſage ſure
That leads unto the Sea.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: What Sea of rudeneſs
Breaks in upon us? or what Subjects Breath
Dare raiſe a ſtorm, when we command a calm?

Are Duty and Obedience ſled 〈◊〉
• aven?
And in their room ambition an • p • i • e
Sent into Egypt? That Face ſpeaks thee, Photinus,
A thing thy Mother brought into the World;
My Brother's and my Slave: but thy behaviour,
Oppos'd to that, an inſolent intruder
Upon that Soveraignty thou ſhouldſt bow to.
If in the Gulph of baſe ingratitude,
All loyalty to Ptolomy the King
Be ſwallowed up, remember who I am,
Whoſe Daughter and whoſe Siſter; or ſuppoſe
That is forgot too; let the name of Caeſar
Which Nations quake at, ſtop the deſperate madneſs
From running headlong on to thy Confuſion.
Throw from thee quickly thoſe rebellious Arms,
And let me read ſubmiſſion in thine Eyes;
Thy wrongs to us we will not only pardon,
But be a ready advocate to plead fo • thee
To Caeſar, and my Brother.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Plead my Pardon?
To you I bow, but ſcorn as much to ſtoop thus
To Ptolomy or Caeſar, Nay, the gods,
As to put off the figure of a man,
All my deſigns, my counſels, and dark ends
Were aim'd to purchaſe you.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: How durſt thou, being
The ſcorn of baſeneſs, nouriſh ſuch a thought?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: They that have power are royal; and thoſe baſe
That live at the devotion of another.
VVhat birth gave Ptolomy, or fortune Caeſar,
By Engines faſhion'd in this Protean Anvil
I have made mine; and only ſtoop at you,
Whom I would ſtill preſerve free to command me;
For Ceſar's frowns, they are below my thoughts,
And but in theſe fair Eyes I ſtill have read
The ſtory of a ſupream Monarchy,
To which all hearts with mine gladly pay tribute,
Photinus's Name had long ſince been as great
As Ptolomies e'r was, or Caeſars is,
This made me as a weaker tye to unlooſe
The knot of Loyalty, that chain'd my freedom,
And ſlight the fear that Caeſars threats might cauſe,
That I and they might ſee no Sun appear
But Cleopatra in the Egyptian Sphear.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: O Giant-like Ambition! marryed to
Cymmerian darkneſs! inconſiderate Fool,
(Though flatter'd with ſelf-love) could'ſt thou believe,
Were all Crowns on the Earth made into one,
And that (by Kings) ſet on thy head; all Scepters,
Within thy graſp, and laid down at my feet,
I would vouchſafe a kiſs to a no man?
A guelded Eunuch?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Faireſt, that makes for me,
And ſhews it is no ſenſual appetite,
But true love to the greatneſs of thy Spirit,
That when that you are mine ſhall yield me pleaſures,
Hymen, though bleſſing a new married Pair
Shall bluſh to think on, and our certain iſſue,
The glorious ſplendor of dread Majeſty,
Whoſe beams ſhall dazel Rome, and aw the world,
My wants in that kind others ſhall ſupply,
And I give way to it.

sp.speaker: C eo.
sp.l:
Baſ •• tha •
•• y Birth;

Can there be ge •••
• nd hear this, and no thunder
Rain thee into the Earth?

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: They are aſleep,
And cannot hear thee;
Or with open Eyes,
Did Jove look on us, I would laugh and ſwear
That his artillery is cloy'd by me:
Or if that they have power to hurt, his Bolts
Are in my hand.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Moſt impious!

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: They are dreams,
Religious Fools ſhake at: yet to aſſure thee,
If Nemeſis, that ſcourges pride and ſcorn,
Be any thing but a name, ſhe lives in me;
For by my ſelf (an oath to me more dreadful
Than Stix is to your gods) weak Ptolomy dead,
And Caeſar (both being in my toil) remov'd,
The pooreſt Raſcals that are in my Camp
Shall in my preſence qu • nc • their luſtful heat
In thee, and young Arſino, while I laugh
To hear you howl in vain:
I deride thoſe gods,
That you think can protect you.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: To prevent thee,
In that I am the Miſtreſs of my Fate;
So hope I of my ſiſter to confirm it.
I ſpit at thee, and ſcorn thee.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: I will tame
That haughty courage, and make thee ſtoop too.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Never,
I was born to command, and will dye ſo.

div.stage: Enter Achillas, and Souldiers, with the Body of Ptolomy.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: The King dead? this is a fair entrance to
Our future happineſs.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: Oh my dear Brother!

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Weep not, Arſino, common women do ſo,
Nor loſe a tear for him, it cannot help him;
But ſtudy to dye nobly.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: Caeſar fled!
'Tis deadly aconite to my cold heart,
It choaks my vital Spirits: where was your care?
Did the Guards ſleep?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: He rowz'd them with his Sword;
We talk of Mars, but I am ſure his Courage
Admits of no compariſon but it ſelf,
And (as inſpir'd by him) his following friends
With ſuch a confidence as young Eagles prey
Under the large wing of their fiercer Dam,
Brake through our Troops and ſcatter'd them, he went on
But ſtill purſu'd by us, when on the ſudden,
He turn'd his head, and from his Eyes ſlew terrour;
Which ſtrook in us no leſs fear and amazement,
Than if we had encounter'd with the lightning
Hurl'd from Jove's cloudy Brow.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: 'Twas like my Caeſar

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: We faln back, he made on, and as out fear
Had parted from us with his dreadful looks,
Again we follow'd, but got near the Sea;
On which his Navy anchor'd; in one hand
Holding a Scroll he had above the waves,
And in the other graſping faſt his Sword,
As it had been a Trident forg'd by Vulcan
To calm the raging Ocean, he made away
As if he had been Neptune, his friends like
So many Tritons follow'd, their bold ſhouts
Yielding a chearful muſick; we ſhowr'd darts
Upon them, but in vain, they reach'd their ſhips
And in their ſafety we are ſunk; for Caeſar
Prepares for War.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: How fell the King?

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Unable
To follow Caeſar, he was trod to death
By the Purſuers, and with him the Prieſt
Of Iſis, good Achoreus.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: May the Earth
Lye gently on their aſhes.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: I feel now,
That there are powers above us; and that 'tis not
Within the ſearching policies of man
To alter their decrees.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: I laugh at thee;
Where are thy threats now, Fool, thy ſcoffs and ſcorns
Againſt the gods? I ſee calamity
Is the beſt Miſtreſs of Religion,
And can convert an Atheiſt. Shout within.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: O they come,
Mountains fall on me! O for him to dye
That plac'd his Heaven on Earth, is an aſſurance
Of his deſcent to Hell; where ſhall I hide me?
The greateſt daring to a man diſhoneſt,
Is but a Baſtard Courage, ever fainting. Exit.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: Look on your Caeſar; baniſh fear, my faireſt,
You now are ſafe.

sp.speaker: Sce.
sp.l: By Venus, not a kiſs
Till our work be done; the Traitors once diſpatch'd
To it, and we'll cry aim.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: I will be ſpeedy. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Farewel again, Arſino; how now, Eros?
Ever faint-hearted?

sp.speaker: Eros.
sp.l: But that I am aſſur'd,
Your Excellency can command the General,
I fear the Souldiers, for they look as if
They would be nibling too.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: He is all honour,
Nor do I now repent me of my favours,
Nor can I think that Nature e'r made a Woman
That in her prime deſerv'd him.

div.stage: Enter Caeſar, Sceva, Antonie, Dolabella, Souldiers, with the Heads.

sp.speaker: Arſ.
sp.l: He's come back,
Purſue no further; curb the Souldiers fury.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: See (beauteous Miſtris) their accurſed heads
That did conſpire againſt us.

sp.speaker: Sce.
sp.l: Furies plague 'em,
They had too fair an end to dye like Souldiers,
Pompey fell by the Sword, the Croſs or Halter
Should have diſpatch'd them.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: All is but death, good Sceva,
Be therefore ſatisfied: and now my deareſt,
Look upon Caeſar, as he ſtill appear'd
A Conquerour, and this unfortunate King
Entomb'd with honour, we'll to Rome, where Caeſar
Will ſhew he can give Kingdoms; for the Senate,
(Thy Brother dead) ſhall willingly decree
The Crown of Egypt (that was his) to thee.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: NEW Titles warrant not a Play for new,
The Subject being old; and 'tis as true,
Freſh and neat matter may with eaſe be fram'd
Out of their Stories, that have oft been nam'd
With glory on the Stage; what borrows he
From him that wrote old Priam's Tragedy,
That writes his love to Hecuba? Sure to tell
Of Caeſars amorous heats, and how he fell
In the Capitol, can never be the ſame
To the Judicious; Nor will ſuch blame
Thoſe who pen'd this, for Barr'enneſs when they find
Young Cleopatra here, and her great Mind
Expreſs'd to the height, with us a Maid, and free,
And how he rated her Virginitie.
We treat not of what boldneſs ſhe did dye,
Nor of her fatal Love to Antony.
What we preſent and offer to your view,
Upon their faiths the Stage yet never knew.
Let Reaſon then firſt to your Wills give laws,
And after judge of them and of their cauſe.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: I Now ſhould wiſh another had my place,
But that I hope to come off, and with Grace;
And but expreſs ſome ſign that you are pleas'd,
We of our doubts, they of their fears are eas'd.
I would beg further (Gentlemen) and much ſay
In favour of our ſelves, them, and the Play;
Did I not reſt aſſur'd, the moſt I ſee
Hate Impudence, and cheriſh Modeſtie.

div.head: THE Little French Lawyer. A COMEDY.

list.item: Dinant, a Gentleman that formerly loved, and ſtill pretended to love Lamira.
Cleremont, a merry Gentleman, his Friend.
Champernell, a lame old Gentleman, Husband to Lamira.
Vertaign, a Noble-man, and a Judge.
Monſieur La Writt, a wrangling Advocate, or the Little Lawyer.
Sampſon, a fooliſh Advocate, Kinſman to Vertaign.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Lamira, Wife to Champernell, and Daughter to Vertaign.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: DIſſwade me not.

sp.speaker: Clere.
sp.l: It will breed a brawl.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I care not, I wear a Sword.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: And wear diſcretion with it,
Or caſt it off, let that direct your arm,
'Tis madneſs elſe, not valour, and more baſe
Than to receive a wrong.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Why would you have me
Sit down with a diſgrace, and thank the doer?
We are not Stoicks, and that paſſive courage
Is only now commendable in Lackies,
Peaſants, and Tradeſmen, not in men of rank
And qualitie, as I am.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Do not cheriſh
That daring vice, for which the whole age ſuffers.
The blood of our bold youth, that heretofore
Was ſpent in honourable action,
Or to defend, or to enlarge the Kingdom,
For the honour of our Country, and our Prince,
Pours it ſelf out with prodigal expence
Upon our Mothers lap, the Earth that bred us
For every trifle; and theſe private Duells,
Which had their firſt original from the Frcenh
(And for which, to this day, we are juſtly cenſured)
Are baniſht from all civil Governments:
Scarce three in Venice, in as many years;
In Forence, they are rarer, and in all
The fair Dominions of the Spaniſh King,
They are never heard of: Nay, thoſe neighbour Countries,
Which gladly imitate our other follies,
And come at a dear rate to buy them of us,
Begin now to deteſt them.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Will you end yet —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: And I have heard that ſome of our late Kings,
For the lie, wearing of a Miſtris favour,
A cheat at Cards or Dice, and ſuch like cauſes,
Have loſt as many gallant Gentlemen,
As might have met the great Turk in the field
With confidence of a glorious Victorie,
And ſhall we then —

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: No more, for ſhame no more,
Are you become a Patron too? 'tis a new one,
No more on't, burn't, give it to ſome Orator,
To help him to enlarge his exerciſe,
With ſuch a one it might do well, and profit
The Curat of the Pariſh, but for Cleremont,
The bold, and undertaking Cleremont,
To talk thus to his friend, his friend that knows him,
Dinant that knows his Cleremont, is abſurd,
And meer Apocrypha.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Why, what know you of me?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Why if thou haſt forgot thy ſelf, I'le tell thee,
And not look back, to ſpeak of what thou wert
At fifteen, for at thoſe years I have heard
Thou waſt fleſh'd, and enter'd bravely.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Well Sir, well.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: But yeſterday, thou waſt the common ſecond,
Of all that only knew thee, thou hadſt bills
Set up on every poſt, to give thee notice
Where any difference was, and who were parties;
And as to ſave the charges of the Law
Poor men ſeek arbitrators, thou wert choſen
By ſuch as knew thee not, to compound quarrels:
But thou wert ſo delighted with the ſport,
That if there were no juſt cauſe, thou wouldſt make one,
Or be engag'd thy ſelf: This goodly calling
Thou haſt followed five and twenty years, and ſtudied
The Criticiſmes of contentions, and art thou
In ſo few hours transform'd? certain this night
Thou haſt had ſtrange dreams, or rather viſions.

sp.speaker: Clere.
sp.l: Yes, Sir,
I have ſeen fools, and fighters, chain'd together,
And the Fighters had the upper hand, and whipt firſt,
The poor Sots laughing at 'em: What I have been
It skils not, what I will be is reſolv'd on.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Why then you'l fight no more?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Such is my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: On no occaſion?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: There you ſtagger me.
Some kind of wrongs there are which fleſh and blood
Cannot endure.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Thou wouldſt not willingly
Live a proteſted coward, or be call'd one?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Words are but words.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Nor wouldſt thou take a blow?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Not from my friend, though drunk, and from an enemy
I think much leſs.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: There's ſome hope of thee left then,
Wouldſt thou hear me behind my back diſgrac'd?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Do you think I am a rogue? they that ſhould do it
Had better been born dumb.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Or in thy preſence
See me o'recharg'd with odds?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I'd fall my ſelf firſt.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Would'ſt thou endure thy Miſtris be taken from thee,
And thou ſit quiet?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: There you touch my honour,
No French-man can endure that.

sp.speaker: Dic.
sp.l: Pl — upon thee,

Why doſt thou talk of Peace then? that da •• ſ •
•• llet
Nothing, or in thy ſelf, or in thy friend
That is unmanly?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: That I grant, I cannot:
But I'le not quarrel with this Gentleman
For wearing ſlammel Breeches, or this Gameſter
For playing a thouſand pounds, that owes me nothing;
For this mans taking up a common Wench
In raggs, and lowſie, then maintaining her
Caroach'd in cloth of Tiſſue, nor five hundred
Of ſuch like toyes, that at no part concern me;
Marry, where my honour, o • my friend is queſtioned,
I have a Sword, and I think I may uſe it
To the cutting of a Raſcals throat, or ſo,
Like a good Chriſtian.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Thou art of a fine Religion,
And rather than we'l make a Schiſm in friendſhip
I will be of it: But to be ſerious,
Thou art acquainted with my tedious love ſuit
To fair Lamira?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Too well Sir, and remember
Your preſents, courtſhip, that's too good a name,
Your ſlave-like ſervices, your morning muſique;
Your walking three hours in the rain at midnight,
To ſee her at her window, ſometimes laugh'd at,
Sometimes admitted, and vouchſaf'd to kiſs
Her glove, her skirt, nay, I have heard, her ſlippers,
How then you triumph'd?
Here was love forſooth.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Theſe follies I deny not,
Such a contemptible thing my dotage made me,
But my reward for this —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: As you deſerv'd,
For he that makes a goddeſs of a Puppet,
Merits no other recompence.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: This day friend,
For thou art ſo —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I am no flatterer.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: This proud, ingratefull ſhe, is married to
Lame Champernel.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I know him, he has been
As tall a Sea-man, and has thriv'd as well by't,
The loſs of a legg and an arm deducted, as any
That ever put from Marſeilles: you are tame,
Pl—on't, it mads me; if it were my caſe,
I ſhould kill all the family.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Yet but now
You did preach patience.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I then came from confeſſion,
And 'twas enjoyn'd me three hours for a penance,
To be a peaceable man, and to talk like one,
But now, all elſe being pardon'd, I begin
On a new Tally, Foot do any thing,
I'le ſecond you.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I would not willingly
Make red, my yet white conſcience, yet I purpoſe
In the open ſtreet, as they come from the Temple,
(For this way they muſt paſs,) to ſpeak my wrongs,
And do it boldly. Muſick playes.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Were thy tongue a Cannon,
I would ſtand by thee, boy, they come, upon 'em.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Obſerve a little firſt.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: This is fine fidling.

div.stage: Enter Vertaign, Champernel, Lamira, Nurſe, Beaupre, Verdore. An Epithalamium.

lg.l: COme away, bring on the Bride
And place her by her Lovers ſide:
Yo • fair troop of Maids attend her,
Pure and holy thoughts befriend her.
Bluſh, and wiſh, you Virgins all,
Many ſuch fair nights may fall.

lg.head: Chorus.
lg.l: Hymen, fill the houſe with joy,
All thy ſacred fires employ:
Bleſs the Bed with holy love,
Now fair orb of Beauty move.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Stand by, for I'le be heard.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: This is ſtrange rudeneſs.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: 'Tis courtſhip, ballanced with injuries,
You all look pale with guilt, but I will dy
Your cheeks with bluſhes, if in your ſcar'd veins
There yet remain ſo much of honeſt blood
To make the colour; firſt to ye my Lord,
The Father of this Bride, whom you have ſent
Alive into her grave.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: How? to her grave?

sp.speaker: Dina.
sp.l: Be patient Sir, I'le ſpeak of you anon
You that allow'd me liberal acceſs,
To make my way with ſervice, and approv'd of
My birth, my perſon, years, and no baſe fortune:
You that are rich, and but in this held wiſe too,
That as a Father ſhould have look'd upon
Your Daughter in a husband, and aim'd more
At what her youth, and heat of blood requir'd
In lawfull pleaſures, than the parting from
Your Crowns to pay her dowr: you that already
Have one foot in the grave, yet ſtudy profit,
As if you were aſſur'd to live here ever;
What poor end had you, in this choice? in what
Deſerve I your contempt? my houſe, and honours
At all parts equal yours, my lame as fair,
And not to praiſe my ſelf, the City ranks me
In the firſt file of her moſt hopefull Gentry:
But Champernel is rich, and needs a nurſe,
And not your gold: and add to that, • e's old too,
His whole eſtate in likelihood to deſcend
Upon your Family; Here was providence,
I grant, but in a Nobleman baſe thrift:
No Merchants nay, no Pirats, ſell for Bondmen
Their Country-men, but you, a Gentleman,
To ſave a little gold, have ſold your Daughter
To worſe than ſlaverie.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: This was ſpoke home indeed.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: Sir, I ſhall take ſome other time to tell you,
That this harſh language was delivered to
An old man, but my Father.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: At your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Proceed in your deſign, let me alone,
To anſwer him, or any man.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: You preſume
Too much upon your name, but may be couzen'd.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: But for you, moſt unmindfull of my ſervice,
For now I may upbraid you, and with honour,
Since all is loſt, and yet I am a gainer,
In being deliver'd from a torment in you,
For ſuch you muſt have been, you to whom nature
Gave with a liberal hand moſt excellent form,
Your education, language, and diſcourſe,
And judgement to diſtinguiſh, when you ſhall
With feeling ſorrow underſtand how wretched
And miſerable you have made your ſelf,
And but your ſelf have nothing to accuſe,
Can you with hope from any beg compaſſion?
But you will ſay, you ſerv'd your Fathers pleaſure,
Forgetting that unjuſt commands of Parents
Are not to be obey'd, or that you are rich,
And that to wealth all pleaſure elſe are ſervants,
Yet but conſider, how this wealth was purchas'd,
'Twill trouble the poſſeſſion.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: You Sir know
I got it, and with honour.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: But from whom?
Remember that, and how: you'l come indeed
To houſes bravely furniſh'd, but demanding
Where it was bought, this Souldier will not lie,
But anſwer truly, this rich cloth of Arras
I made my prize in ſuch a Ship, this Plate
Was my ſhare in another; theſe fair Jewels,
Coming a ſhore, I got in ſuch a Village,
The Maid, or Matron kill'd, from whom they were raviſh'd,
The Wines you drink are guilty too, for this,
This Candie Wine, three Merchants were undone,
Theſe Suckets break as many more: in brief,
All you ſhall wear, or touch, or ſee, is purchas'd
By lawleſs force, and you but revel in
The tears, and grones of ſuch as were the owners.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: 'Tis falſe, moſt baſely falſe.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Let loſers talk.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Laſtly, thoſe joyes, thoſe beſt of joyes, which Hymen
Freely beſtows on ſuch, that come to tye
The ſacred knot he bleſſes, won unto it
By equal love, and mutual affection,
Not blindly led with the deſire of riches,
Moſt miſerable you ſhall never taſte of.
• his Marriage night you'l meet a Widows bed,
Or failing of thoſe pleaſures all Brides look for,
Sin in your wiſh it were ſo.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: Thou art a Villain,
A baſe, malitious ſlanderer.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Strike him.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: No, he is not worth a blow.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: O that I had thee
In ſome cloſe vault, that only would yield room
To me to uſe my Sword, to thee no hope
To run away, I would make thee on thy knees,
Bite out the tongue that wrong'd me.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Pray you have patience.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: This day I am to be your Soveraign,
Let me command you.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: I am loſt with rage,
And know not what I am my ſelf, nor you:
Away, dare ſuch as you, that love the ſmoke
Of peace more than the fire of glorious War,
And like unprofitable drones, feed on
Your grand • ires labours, that, as I am now,
Were gathering Bees, and fill'd their Hive, this Country
With brave triumphant ſpoils, cenſure our actions?
You object my prizes to me, had you ſeen
The horrour of a Sea-ſight, with what danger
I made them mine; the fire I fearleſs fought in,
And quench'd it in mine enemies blood, which ſtraight
Like oyle pour'd out on't, made it burn anew;
My Deck blown up, with noiſe enough to mock
The lowdeſt thunder, and the deſperate fools
That Boorded me, ſent, to deſie the tempeſts
That were againſt me, to the angrie Sea,
Frighted with men thrown o're; no victory,
But in deſpight of the four Elements,
The Fire, the Air, the Sea, and ſands hid in it
To be atchiev'd, you would confeſs poor men,
(Though hopeleſs, ſuch an honourable way
To get or wealth, or honour) in your ſelves
He that through all theſe dreadfull paſſages
Purſued and overtook them, unaffrighted,
Deſerves reward, and not to have it ſtil'd
By the baſe name of theft.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: This is the Courtſhip,
That you muſt look for, Madam.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Twill do well,
When nothing can be done, to ſpend the night with:
Your tongue is ſound good Lord, and I could wiſh
For this young Ladyes ſake this leg, this arm,
And there is ſomething elſe, I will not name,
(Though 'tis the only thing that muſt content her)
Had the ſame vigour.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: You ſhall buy theſe ſcoffs
With your beſt blood: help me once noble anger,
(Nay ſtir not, I alone muſt right my ſelf)
And with one leg tranſport me, to correct
Theſe ſcandalous praters: O that noble wounds Falls.
Should hinder juſt revenge? D'ye jear me too?
I got theſe, not as you do, your diſeaſes
In Brothels, or with riotous abuſe
Of wine in Taverns; I have one leg ſhot,
One arm diſabled, and am honour'd more,
By loſing them, as I did, in the face
Of a brave enemy, than if they were
As when I put to Sea; you are French-men only,
In that you have been laied, and cur'd, goe to:
You mock my leg, but every bone about you,
Makes you good Almanack-makers, to foretell
What weather we ſhall have.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Put up your Sword,

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Or turn it to a Crutch, there't may by uſefull,
And live on the relation to your Wife
Of what a brave man you were once.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: And tell her,
What a fine vertue 'tis in a young Lady
To give an old man pap.

sp.speaker: Cer.
sp.l: Or hire a Surgeon
To teach her to roul up your broken limbs.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: To make a Pulteſs, and endure the ſcent
Of oils, and naſty Plaſters.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Fie Sir, fie,
You that have ſtood all dangers of all kinds, to
Yield to a Rivalls ſcoffe?

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Shed tears upon
Your Wedding day? this is unmanly Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: They are tears of anger: O that I ſhould live
To play the woman thus! All powerfull heaven,
Reſtore me, but one hour, that ſtrength again,
That I had once, to chaſtiſe in theſe men
Their folies, and ill manners, and that done,
When you pleaſe, I'le yield up the fort of life,
And do it gladly.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: We ha' the better of him,
We ha' made him cry.

sp.speaker: Verdo.
sp.l: You ſhall have ſatisfaction.
And I will do it nobly, or diſclaim me.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: I ſay no more, you have a Brother, Siſter,
This is your wedding day, we are in the ſtreet,
And howſoever they forget their honour,
'Tis fit I loſe not mine, by their example.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: If there be Laws in Paris, look to anſwer
This inſolent affront.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: You that live by them,
Study 'em for heavens ſake; for my part I know not
Nor care not what they are. Is their ought elſe
That you would ſay?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Nothing, I have my ends.
Lamira weeps, I have ſaid too much I fear;
So dearly once I lov'd her, that I cannot
Endure to ſee her tears. Exeunt Dinant, and Cleremont.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: See you perform it,
And do it like my Nephew.

sp.speaker: Verdo.
sp.l: If I fail in't
Ne'r know me more, Couſin Beaupre.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: Repent not
What thou haſt done, my life, thou ſhalt not find
I am decrepit; in my love and ſervice,
I will be young, and conſtant, and believe me,
For thou ſhalt find it true, in ſ • orn of all
The ſcandals th • ſe rude men have thrown upon me
I'le meet thy pleaſures with a young mans ardour,
And in all circumſtances of a Husband,
Perform my part.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Good Sir, I am your ſ • rv • nt,
And 'tis too late now, i • I did repent,
(Which as I am a virgin yet, I do not)
To undoe the • not, that by the Church is tyed.
Only I would beſeech ye, as you have
A good opinion of me, and my vertues,
For ſo you have pleas'd to ſtile my innocent weakneſs,
That what hath paſs'd be w • en Dinant and me,
Or what now in your hearing he hath ſpoken,
Beget not doubts, or fears.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: I apprehend you,
You think I will be jealous; as I live
Thou art miſtaken ſweet; and to confirm it
Diſcourſe with whom thou wilt, ride where thou wilt,
Feaſt whom thou wilt, as often as thou wilt,
For I will have no other guards upon thee
Than thine own thoughts.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: I'le uſe this liberty
With moderation Sir.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: I am reſolv'd.
Steal off, I'le follow you.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: Come Sir, you droop;
Till you find cauſe, which I ſhall never give,
Diſlike not of your Son in Law.

sp.speaker: Verta
sp.l: Sir, you teach me
The language I ſhould uſe; I am moſt happy
In being ſo near you. Exeunt Verdone, and Beaupre.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: O my fears! good nurſe
Follow my Brother unobſerv'd, and learn
Which way he takes.

sp.speaker: Nurſ.
sp.l: I will be carefull Madam. Exit Nurſe.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: Between us complements are ſuperfluous,
On Gentlemen, th' affront we have met here
We'l think upon hereafter, 'twere unfit
To cheriſh any thought to breed unreſt,
Or to our ſelves, or to our Nuptial feaſt. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: We ſhall have ſport, ne'r fear't.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: What ſport I prethee?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Why we muſt fight, I know it, and I long • or't,
It was apparent in the fiery eye
Of young Verdo • e, Beaupre look'd pale and ſhook too,
Familiar ſigns of anger. They are both brave fellows
Tri'd and approv'd, and I am proud to encounter
With men, from whom no honour can be loſt;
They will play up to a man, and ſet him off.
When e're I go to the field, heaven keep me from
The meeting of an unfleſh'd youth or, Coward,
The firſt, to get a name, comes on too hot,
The Coward is ſo ſwift in giving ground,
There is no overtaking him without
A hunting Nag, well breath'd too.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: All this while,
You ne'r think on the danger.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Why 'tis no more
Than meeting of a dozen friends at Supper,
And drinking hard; miſchief comes there unlook'd for,
I am ſure as ſuddain, and ſtrikes home as often,
For this we are prepar'd.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Lamira Loves
Her Brother Beaupre dearly.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: What of that?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: And ſhould he call me to account for what
But now I ſpake, nor can I with mine honour
Recant my words, that little hope is left me,
E're to enjoy what (next to Heaven) I long for,
Is taken from me.
Why what can you hope for,
She being now married?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Oh my Cleremont,
To you all ſecrets of my heart lye open,
And I reſt moſt ſecure that whatſoe're
I lo • k up there, is as a private thought,
And will no farther wrong me. I am a French-man,
And for the greater part we are born Courtiers,
She is a woman, and however yet
No heat of ſervice had the power to melt
Her frozen Chaſtity, time and opportunitie
May work her to my ends, I confeſs ill ones,
And yet I muſt purſue 'em: now her marriage,
In probabilitie, will no way hurt,
But rather help me.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Sits the wind there? pray you tell me
How far off dwells your love from luſt?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Too near,
But prethee chide me not.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Not I, goe on boy,
I have faults my ſelf, and will not reprehend
A crime I am not free from: for her Marriage,
I do eſteem it (and moſt batchellors are
Of my opinion) as a fair protection,
To play the wanton without loſs of honour.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Would ſhe make uſe of't ſo, I were moſt happy.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: No more of this, Judge now,
Whether I have the gift of prophecie.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Monſieur Dinant,
I am glad to find you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I am at your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: Good Monſieur Cleremont, I have long wiſh'd
To be known better to you.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: My deſires
Embrace your wiſhes Sir.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Sir, I have ever
Eſteem'd you truly noble, and profeſs
I ſhould have been moſt proud, to have had the honour
To call you Brother, but my Fathers pleaſure
Denied that happineſs. I know no man lives,
That can command his paſſions, and therefore
Dare not condemn the late intemperate language
You were pleas'd to uſe to my Father and my Siſter,
He's old and ſhe a woman, I moſt ſorrie
My honour does compel me to entreat you,
To do me the favour, with your ſword to meet me
A mile without the Citie.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: You much honour me
In the demand, I'le gladly wait upon you.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: O Sir you teach me what to ſay: the time?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: With the next Sun, if you think fit.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: The place?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Near to the vineyard eaſtward from the Citie.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: I like it well, this Gentleman if you pleaſe
Will keep me company.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: That is agreed on;
And in my friends behalf I will attend him.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: You ſhall not miſs my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Good day Gentlemen. Ex. Beaup. and Verd.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: At your Commandment.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Proud to be your ſervants.
I think there is no Nation under Heaven
That cut their enemies throats with complement,
And ſuch fine tricks as we do: If you have
Any few Prayers to ſay, this night you may
Call 'em to mind and uſe 'em, for my ſelf,
As I have little to loſe, my care is leſs,
So till to morrow morning I bequeath you
To your devotions; and thoſe paid, but uſe
That noble courage I have ſeen, and wo
Shall ſight, as in a Caſtle.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Thou art all honour,
Thy reſolution would ſteel a Coward,
And I moſt fortunate in ſuch a Friend;
All tenderneſs and nice reſpect of woman
Be now far from me, reputation take
A full poſſeſſion of my heart, and prove
Honour the firſt place holds, the ſecond Love. Ex • u ••

sp.speaker: Lami.
sp.l: Sleeps my Lord ſtill, Charlote?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Not to be wak'd.
By your Ladiſhips cheerfull looks I well perceive
That this night the good Lord hath been
At an unuſual ſervice, and no wonder
If he reſt after it.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: You are very bold.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Your Creature Madam, and when you are pleas'd
Sadneſs to me's a ſtranger, your good pardon
If I ſpeak like a fool, I could have wiſht
To have ta'ne your place to night, had bold Dinant
Your firſt and moſt obſequious ſervant taſted
Thoſe delicates, which by his lethargie
As it appears, have cloy'd my Lord.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: No more.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: I am ſilenc'd, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Saw you my nurſe this morning?

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: No, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: I am full of fears. Knock within.
Who's that?

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: She you enquir'd for.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Bring her in, and leave me. Exit Charlote.
Now nurſe what news?

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: O Ladie dreadfull ones.
They are to fight this morning, there's no remedie.
I ſaw my Lord your Brother, and Verdone
Take horſe as I came by.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Where's Cleremont?

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: I met him too, and mounted.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Where's Dinant?

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: There's all the hope, I have ſtaid him with a trick,
If I have done well ſo.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: What trick?

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: I told him,
Your Ladiſhip laid your command upon him,
To attend you preſently, and to confirm it,
Gave him the ring he oft hath ſeen you wear,
That you beſtowed on me: he waits without
Diſguis'd, and if you have that power in him,
As I preſume you have, it is in you
To ſtay or alter him.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Have you learnt the place,
Where they are to encounter?

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: Yes 'tis where
The Duke of Burgundie met Lewis th' eleventh.

sp.speaker: Lamir.
sp.l: Enough, I will reward thee liberally, Exit Nurſe.
Goe bring him in: full dear I loved Dinant,
While it was lawfull, but thoſe fires are quench'd,
I being now anothers, truth forgive me
And let diſſimulation be no crime,
Though moſt unwillingly I put it on
To guard a Brothers ſafetie.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Now your pleaſure,
Though ill you have deſerv'd it, you perceive
I am ſtill your fool, and cannot but obey
What ever you command.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: You ſpeak, as if
You did repent it, and 'tis not worth my thanks then,
But there has been a time, in which you would
Receive this as a favour.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Hope was left then
Of recompence.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Why I am ſtill Lamira,
And you Dinant, and 'tis yet in my power,
I dare not ſay I'le put it into act,
To reward your love and ſervice.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: There's ſome comfort.

sp.speaker: Lami.
sp.l: But think not that ſo low I prize my fame,
To give it up to any man that refuſes
To buy it, or with danger of performance
Of what I ſhall enjoin him.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Name that danger
Be it of what horrid ſhape ſoever Ladie
Which I will ſhrink at; only at this inſtant
Be ſpeedie in't.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: I'le put you to the trial:
You ſhall not light to day, do you ſtart at that?
Not with my Brother, I have heard your difference,
Mine is no Helens beauty to be purchas'd
With blood, and ſo defended, if you look for
Favours from me, deſerve them with obedience,
There's no way elſe to gain 'em.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: You command
What with mine honour I cannot obey
Which lies at pawn againſt it, and a friend
Equally dear as that, or life, engag'd,
Not for himſelf, but me.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Why, fooliſh man,
Dare you ſolicite me to ſerve your luſt,
In which not only I abuſe my Lord,
My Father, and my family, but write whore,
Though not upon my forehead, in my conſcience,
To be read hourly, and yet name your honour?
Yours ſuffers but in circumſtance; mine in ſubſtance.
If you obey me, you part with ſome credit,
From whom? the giddy multitude; but mankind
Will cenſure me, and juſtly.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I will loſe,
What moſt I do deſire, rather than hazard
So dear a friend, or write my ſelf a coward,
'Tis better be no man.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: This will not do;
Why, I deſire not, you ſhould be a coward,
Nor do I weigh my Brothers life with yours,
Meet him, fight with him, do, and kill him fairly,
Let me not ſuffer for you, I am careleſs.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Suffer for me?

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: For you, my kindneſs to you
Already brands me with a ſtrumpets name.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: O that I knew the wretch!

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: I will not name him,
Nor give you any Character to know him;
But if you dare, and inſtantly ride forth
At the weſt port of the City, and defend there
My reputation, againſt all you meet,
For two hours only, I'le not ſwear Dinant,
To ſatisfie, (though ſure I think I ſhall)
What ever you deſire, if you denie this,
Be deſperate, for willingly, by this light,
I'le never ſee thee more.

sp.speaker: Din
sp.l: Two hours, do you ſay?

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: Only two hours.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I were no Gentleman,
Should I make ſcruple of it; this favour arms me,
And boldly I'll perform it. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lamira.
sp.l: I am glad on't.
This will prevent their meeting yet, and keep
My Brother ſafe, which was the mark I ſhot at. Exit.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Cleremont, as in the field.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I Am firſt i'th' field, that honour's gain'd of our ſide,
Pray Heaven I may get off as honourablie,
The hour is paſt, I wonder Dinant comes not,
This is the place, I cannot ſee him yet;
It is his quarel too that brought me hither,
And I ne'r knew him yet, but to his honour
A firm and worthy Friend, yet I ſee nothing,
Nor Horſe nor man, 'twould vex me to be left here,
To th' mercy of two ſwords, and two approv'd ones.
I never knew him laſt.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: You are well met Cleremont.

sp.speaker: Verdo.
sp.l: You are a fair Gentleman, and love your friend Sir.
What are you ready? the time has overta'ne us.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: And this you know the place.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: No Dinant yet?

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: We come not now to argue, but to do;
We wait you Sir.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: There's no time paſt yet Gentlemen,
We have day enough: is't poſſible he comes not?
You ſee I am • ea •• here, and do but ſtay
Till my Friend come, walk but a turn or two,
'Twill not be long.

sp.speaker: Verd
sp.l: We came to fight.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Ye ſhall 〈◊〉 Gentlemen,
And fight enough, but a ſhort turn or two,
I think I ſee him, ſet up your watch, we'l fight by it.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: That is not he; we will not be deluded.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Am I bob'd thus? pray tak • a pipe of tobacco,
Or ſing but ſome new air; by that time, Gentlemen—

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: Come d • aw your Sword, you know the cuſtome here Sir,
Firſt come, firſt ſerv'd.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Though it be held a cuſtom,
And practiſed ſo, I do not hold it honeſt;
What honour can you both win on me ſingle?

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Yield up your Sword then.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Yield my Sword? that's Hebrew;
I'le be firſt cut a pecies; hold but a while,
I'le take the next that comes.
You are an old Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Yes indeed am I, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: And wear no Sword?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I need none, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I would you did, and had one;
I want now ſuch a fooliſh courteſie.
You ſee theſe Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: You want a ſecond.
In good Faith Sir, I was never handſom at it,
I would you had my Son, but he's in Italy,
A proper Gentleman; you may do well gallants
If your quarrel be not capital, to have more mercy,
The Gentleman may do his Country—

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Now I beſeech you, Sir,
If you dare not fight, do not ſtay to beg my pardon.
There lies your way.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Good morrow Gentlemen. Exit.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: You ſee your fortune,
You had better yield your Sword.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Pray ye ſtay a little.
Upon mine honeſtie, you ſhall be fought with;
Well, Dinant, well, theſe wear ſwords and ſeem brave fellows.
As you are Gentlemen, one of you ſupply me.
I want a S • cond now to meet theſe gallants,
You know what honour is.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Sir you muſt pardon us,
We goe about the ſame work, you are ready for;
And muſt fight preſently, elſe we were your ſervants.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: God ſpeed you, and good day. Exit Gent.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Am I thus Colted?

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Come either yield —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: As you are honeſt Gentlemen,
Stay but the next, and then I'le take my fortune,
And if I fight not like a man — Fy Dinant,
Cold now and treacherous.

sp.speaker: La Writ.
sp.l: I underſtand your cauſes.
Yours about corn, yours about pins and glaſſes,
Will you make me mad, have I not all the parcells?
And his Petition too, about Bell-ſounding?
Send in your witneſſes, what will you have me do?
Will you have me break my heart? my brains are melted;
And tell your Maſter, as I am a Gentleman,
His Cauſe ſhall be the firſt, commend me to your Miſtris,
And tell her, if there be an extraordinary feather,
And tall enough for her—I ſhall diſpatch you too,
I know your cauſe, for tranſporting of Farthingales
Trouble me no more, I ſay again to you,
No more vexation: bid my wife ſend me ſome puddings;
I have a Cauſe to run through, requires puddings,
Puddings enough. Farewel.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: God ſpeed you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Would he would take this fellow.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: A rare Youth.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: If you be not haſtie, Sir.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Yes, I am haſtie,
Exceeding haſtie, Sir, I am going to the Parliament,
You underſtand this bag, if you have any buſineſs
Depending there, be ſhort, and let me hear it,
And pay your Fees.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Faith, Sir, I have a buſineſs,
But it depends upon no Parliament.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: I have no skill in't then.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I muſt deſire you,
'Tis a Sword matter, Sir.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: I am no Cutler,
I am an Advocate, Sir.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: How the thing looks?

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: When he brings him to ſight.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Be not ſo haſtie,
You wear a good Sword.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: I know not that,
I never drew it yet, or whether it be a Sword —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I muſt entreat you try, Sir, and bear a part
Againſt theſe Gentlemen, I want a ſecond;
Ye ſeem a man, and 'tis a noble office.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: I am a Lawyer, Sir, I am no fighter.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: You that breed quarels, Sir, know beſt to ſatisfie.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: This is ſome ſport yet.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: If this fellow ſhould fight.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: And for any thing I know, I am an arrant coward,
Do not truſt me, I think I am a coward.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Try, try, you are miſtaken: walk on Gentlemen,
The man ſhall follow preſently.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Are ye mad Gentleman?
My buſineſs is within this half hour.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: That's all one,
We'll diſpatch within this quarter, there in that bottom,
'Tis moſt convenient Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Well, we'll wait, Sir.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: Why this will be a comick fight, you'l follow.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: As I am a true-man, I cannot fight.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Away, away,
I know you can: I like your modeſty,
I know you will fight and ſo fight, with ſuch metal,
And with ſuch judgement meet your enemies fury;
I ſee it in your eye, Sir.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I'le be hang'd then;

And I charge you in the Kings name, name more f • g •
〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I charge you in the Kings name, play the man,
Which if you do not quickly, I begin with you,
I'le make you dance, do you ſee your fiddleſtick?
Sweet Avocate thou ſhalt fight.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Stand farther Gentleman,
Or I'le give you ſuch a duſt o'th' chapps —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Spoke bravely,
And like thy ſelf, a noble Advocate:
Come to thy tools.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I do not ſay I'le fight;

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I ſay thou ſhalt, and bravely.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: If I do fight;
I ſay, if I do, but do not depend upon't,
And yet I have a fooliſh itch upon me,
What ſhall become of my Writings?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Let 'em ly by,
They will not run away, man.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I may be kill'd too,
And where are all my cauſes then? my buſineſs?
I will not fight, I cannot fight, my Cauſes—

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt fight, if thou hadſt a thouſand cauſes,
Thou art a man to fight for any cauſe,
And carry it with honour.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Hum, ſay you ſo? if I ſhould
Be ſuch a coxcombe to prove valiant now —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I know thou art moſt valiant.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Do you think ſo?
I am undone for ever, if it prove ſo,
I tell you that, my honeſt friend, forever;
For I ſhall ne're leave quarrelling.
How long muſt we fight? for I cannot ſtay,
Nor will not ſtay, I have buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: We'l do't in a minute, in a moment.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Here will I hang my bag then, it may ſave my belly,
I never lov'd cold Iron there.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: You do wiſely.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Help me to pluck my Sword out then, quickly, quickly,
'Thas not ſeen Sun theſe ten years.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: How it grumbles?
This Sword is vengeance angry.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Now I'le put my hat up,
And ſay my prayers as I goe; away boy,
If I be kill'd, remember the little Lawyer. Exe • t.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: They are both come on, that may be a ſtubborn raſcal,
Take you that ground,
I'le ſtay here, fight bravely.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: To't chearfully my boyes, you'l let's have far play,
None of your foyning tricks.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Come forward Monſieur; fig • t
What haſt thou there? a pudding in thy belly?
I ſhall ſee what it holds.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Put your ſpoon home then:
Nay, ſince I muſt fight, have at you without wit, Sir:
God a mercy bagg.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Nothing but bumbaſt in ye?
The Rogue winks and fights.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l:
Now your fine fencing, Sir: Beau. loſes his ſword La-writ tread
〈◊〉 .
Stand off, thou dieſt on point elſe,
I have it, I have it: yet further off:
I have his Sword.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Then keep it, be ſure you keep it

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I'le put it in my mouth elſe.
Stand further off yet, and ſtand quietly,
And look another way, or I'le be with you,
Is this all? I'le undertake within theſe two daies
To furniſh any Cutler in this Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: Pox, what fortune's this? diſarm'd by a pupp • e?
A ſnail? a Dog?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: No more o' theſe words Gentleman,
Sweet Gentleman, no more, do not provoke me,
Go walk i'th' horſe-fair; whiſtle Gentleman,
What muſt I do now?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Help me, I am almoſt breathleſs.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: With all my heart, there's a cold pye for you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Thou ſtrik'ſt me, fool.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Thou fool, ſtand further off then,
Deliver, deliver.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Hold faſt. He ſtrikes up the others heels, and takes his Sword too.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I never fail in't,
There's twelve pence, go buy you two leaden Daggers,
Have I done well?
Moſt like a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: And we two baſely loſt.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: 'Tis but a fortune,
We ſhall yet find an hour. Ex. Beau. Verd. ſad.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I ſhall be glad on't.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Where's my cloak, and my trinkets?
Or will you fight any longer, for a craſh or two?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I am your noble friend, Sir.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: It may be ſo.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: What honour ſhall I do you,
For this great courteſie?

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: All I deſire of ye,
Is to take the quarrel to your ſelf, and let me hear no more on't,
I have no liking to't, 'tis a fooliſh matter,
And help me to put up my Sword.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Moſt willingly.
But I am bound to gratifie you, and I muſt not leave you.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I tell you, I will not be gratified,
Nor I will hear no more on't: take the Swords too,
And do not anger me but leave me quietly.
For the matter of honour, 'tis at your own diſpoſure,
And ſo, and ſo. Exit La-writ.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: This is a moſt rare Lawyer:
I am ſure moſt valiant. Well Dinant, as you ſatisfie me,
I ſay no more: I am loaden like an Armorer. Exit Cler.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: To be diſpatcht upon a ſleeveleſs errand?
To leave my friend engag'd, mine honour tainted?
Theſe are trim things. I am ſet here like a Perdue,
To watch a fellow, that has wrong'd my Miſtris,
A ſcurvy fellow that muſt paſs this way,
But what this ſcurvy fellow is, or whence,
Or whether his name be William or John,
Or Anthony or Dick, or any thing, I know not;
A ſcurvy raſcally fellow I muſt aim at,
And there's the office of an Aſſe flung on me.
S • re Cleremont has fought, but how come off,
And what the world ſhall think of me hereafter:
Well, woman, woman, I muſt look your raſcals,
And loſe my reputation: ye have a fine power over us.
Theſe two long hours I have trotted here, and curiouſly
Survey'd all goers by, yet find no raſcal,
Nor any face to quarel with: La-writ ſings within, then Enters.
What's that?
This is a raſcally voice, ſure it comes this way.

sp.speaker: La-writ.

l.hi: He ſtrook ſo hard, the Baſon broke,

sp.l: And Tarquin heard the ſound.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: What Miſter thing is this? let me ſurvey it.

l.hi: And then he ſtrook his neck in two.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: This may be a raſcal, but 'tis a mad raſcal,
What an Alphabet of faces he puts on?
Hey how it fences? if this ſhould be the rogue,
At 'tis the likelieſt rogue I ſee this day —

l.hi: Was euer man for Ladies ſake? down, down.

sp.l: And what are you good Sir? down, down, down, down.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: What's that to you good Sir? down, down.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: A pox on you good Sir, down, down, down,
You with your Buckram bag, what make you here?
And from whence come you? I could fight with my ſhadow now.

sp.speaker: La-wr.
sp.l: Thou fierce man that like Sir Lancelot doſt appear,
I need not tell thee what I am, nor eke what I make here.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: This is a precious knave, ſtay, ſtay, good Triſtram,
And let me ask thy mightineſs a queſtion,
Did ye never abuſe a Lady?

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Not; to abuſe a Lady, is very hard, Sir.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Say you ſo, Sir?
Didſt thou never abuſe her honour?

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Not; to abuſe her honour, is impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Certain this is the raſcal: What's thy name?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: My name is Cock o' two, uſe me reſpectively,
I will be Cock of three elſe.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: What's all this?
You ſay, you did abuſe a Lady.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: You ly.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: And that you wrong'd her honour.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: That's two lyes,
Speak ſuddenly, for I am full of buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: What art thou, or what canſt thou be, thou pea-gooſe,
That dar'ſt give me the ly thus? thou mak'ſt me wonder.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: And wonder on, till time make all things plain.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: You muſt not part ſo, Sir, art thou a Gentleman?

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Ask thoſe upon whoſe ruins I am mounted.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: This is ſome Cavellero Knight o'th' Sun.

sp.speaker: La-wr.
sp.l: I tell thee I am as good a Gentleman as the Duke:
I have atchieved — goe follow thy buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: But for this Lady, Sir —

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Why, hang this Lady, Sir,
And the Lady Mother too, Sir, what have I to do with Ladies?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Tis the little Lawyers voice: has he got my way?
It ſhould be hereabouts.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Ye dry bisket rogue,
I will ſo ſwinge you for this blaſphemie—
Have I found you out?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: That ſhould be Dinants tongue too.

sp.speaker: La-wr.
sp.l: And I defy thee do thy worſt: O ho quoth Lancelot tho.
And that thou ſhalt know, I am a true Gentleman,
And ſpeak according to the phraſe triumphant;
Thy Lady is a ſcurvy Lady, and a ſhitten Lady,
And though I never heard of her, a debo • ed Lady,
And thou, a ſquire of low degree; will that content thee?
Doſt thow way-lay me with Ladies? A pretty ſword, Sir,
A very pretty ſword, I have a great mind to't.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: You ſhall not loſe your longing, rogue.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Hold, hold.
Hold Dinant, as thou art a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: As much as you will, my hand is in now.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I am your friend, Sir: Dinant you draw your ſword
Upon the Gentleman preſerv'd your honour:
This was my ſecond, and did back me nobly,
For ſhame forbear.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I ask your mercy, Sir, and am your ſervant now.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: May we not fight then?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I am ſure you ſhall not now.

sp.speaker: La-wr.
sp.l: I am ſorry for't, I am ſure I'le ſtay no longer then,
Not a jot longer: are there any more on ye afore?
I will ſing ſtill, Sir. Exit La-writ, ſinging.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I look now you ſhould chide me, and 'tis fit,
And with much bitterneſs expreſs your anger,
I have deſerv'd: yet when you know —.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I thank ye,
Do you think that the wrong you have off'red me,
The moſt unmanly wrong, unfriendly wrong—

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I do confeſs —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: That boyiſh ſleight —

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Not ſo, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: That poor and baſe renouncing of your honour,
Can be allaied with words?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I give you way ſtill.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Coloured with ſmooth excuſes? Was it a friends part,
A Gentlemans, a mans that wears a Sword,
And ſtands upon the point of reputation,
To hide his head then, when his honour call'd him?
Call'd him aloud, and led him to his fortune?
To halt and ſlip the coller? by my life,
I would have given my life I had never known thee,
Thou haſt eaten Canker-like into my judgement
With this diſgrace, thy whole life cannot heal again.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: This I can ſuffer too, I find it honeſt.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Can you pretend an excuſe now may abſolve you,
Or any thing like honeſt, to bring you off?
• ngage me like an Aſſe?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Will you but hear me?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Expoſe me like a Jade to tug, and hale through,
• augh'd at, and almoſt hooted? your diſgraces
Invite mans Swords and angers to diſpatch me.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: If you will be patient.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: And be abus'd ſtill: But that I have call'd thee friend,
And to that name allow a Sanctuary,
You ſhould hear further from me, I would not talk thus:
But hence forth ſtand upon your own bottom, Sir,
And b • a • your own abuſes, I ſcorn my ſword
Should travel in ſo poor and empty quarrels.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Ha'you done yet? take your whole ſwing of anger,
I'le beat all with content.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Why were you abſent?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: You know I am no Coward, you have ſeen that,
And therefore, out of • ea • forſook you not:
You know I am not falſe, of a treacherous nature,
Apt to betray my friend, I have fought for you too;
You know no buſineſs, that concern'd my ſtate,
My kindred, or my life.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Where was the fault then?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: The honour of that Lady I adore,
Her credit, and her name: ye know ſhe ſent for me,
And with what haſte.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: What was he that traduc'd?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: The man i'th' Moon, I think, hither I was ſent,
But to what end —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: This is a pretty ſlim ſlam.

sp.speaker: O. La.
sp.l: I am glad I have met you Sir, I have been ſeeking,
And ſeeking every where.
And now you have found him,
• clare what buſineſs, our Embaſſadour.

sp.speaker: O Lady.
sp.l: What's that to ye good man ſ • outer? O Sir, my Lady.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: 〈◊〉 thee no more of thy Lady, I have too much on't.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Let me have a little, ſpeak to me.
To you Sir?
'Tis more than time: All occaſions ſet aſide Sir,
Or whatſoever may be thought a buſineſs —

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: What then?
Repair to me within this hour.
Where?

sp.speaker: O. Lady.
sp.l: What's that to you? come you, Sir, when y'are ſent for.
God a m • y Mumpſinnes,
You may goe Dina • t, and follow this old Fairie,
Till you have loſt your ſelf, your friends, your credit,
And Hunt away your youth in rare adventures,
I can but gri • v • I have known you.

sp.speaker: Old Lady.
sp.l: Will ye goe Sir?
I come not often to you with theſe bleſſings,
You my believe that thing there, and repent it,
That do • ged thing.
Peace tou • hwood.
I will not goe:
〈…〉 your Lady ſeek ſome fool to • awn on her,
〈…〉 vp • 'd pupp • , to make ſport with,

I • av •
〈◊〉 her mi • th too long, thus I ſhake from me

Th •
〈…〉 put on; thus her enchantments
〈…〉 like wind, no more her beauty—

sp.speaker: Old Lady.
sp.l: Take heed Sir what you ſay.
• oe forward, Dinant.
The charms ſhot from her eyes —

sp.speaker: Old Lady.
sp.l: Be wiſe.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Be Valiant.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: That tongue that tells fair tales to 〈…〉
Shall never rack me more.

sp.speaker: Old Lady.
sp.l: Stay there.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Goe forward.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I will now hear her, ſee her as a woman,
Survey her, and the power man has allow'd, Sir,
As I would do the courſe of common things,
Unmov'd, unſtruck.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Hold there, and I forgive thee.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: She is not fair, and that that makes her proud,
Is not her own, our eyes beſtow it on her,
To touch and kiſs her is no bleſſedneſs,
A Sun-burnt Ethiops lip's as ſoft as her's.
Goe bid her ſtick ſome other triumph up,
And take into her favour ſome dull fool,
That has no pretious time to loſe, no friends,
No honour, nor no life, like a bold Merchant,
A bold and banquerupt man, I have ventur'd all theſe,
And ſplit my bottom: return this anſwer to her,
I am awake again and ſee her miſchiefs,
And am not now, on every idle errand,
And new coyn'd anger, to be hurried,
And then deſpis'd again, I have forgot her.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: If this be true —

sp.speaker: O. Lady.
sp.l: I am ſorry, I have troubled you,
More ſorrie, that my Lady has adventur'd
So great a favour in ſo weak a mind:
This hour you have refus'd that when you come to know it,
Will run you mad, and make you curſe that fellow,
She is not fair, nor handſom, ſo I leave you.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Stay Lady, ſtay, but is there ſuch a buſineſs?

sp.speaker: O. Lady.
sp.l: You would break your neck 'twere yours.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: My back, you would ſay.

sp.speaker: O. La.
sp.l: But play the friends part ſtill, Sir, and undoe him,
'Tis a fair office.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I have ſpoke too liberally.

sp.speaker: O. Lady.
sp.l: I ſhall deliver what you ſay.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: You ſhall be hang'd firſt,
You would fain be prating now; take the man with ye • .

sp.speaker: O. Lady.
sp.l: Not I, I have no power.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: You may goe Dinant.

sp.speaker: O. Lady.
sp.l: 'Tis in's own will, I had no further charge, S • ,
Than to tell him what I did, which if I had thought
It ſhould have been receiv'd ſo —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Faith you may,
You do not know how far it may concern you.
If I perceiv'd any trick in't.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: 'Twill end there.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Tis my fault then, there is an hour in fortune,
That muſt be ſtill obſerv'd: you think I'le chide you,
When things muſt be, nay ſee, an he will hold his head up?
Would ſuch a Lady ſend, with ſuch a charge too?
Say ſhe has plaid the fool, play the fool with her again,
The great fool, the greater ſtill the better.
He ſhall goe with you woman.

sp.speaker: Old Lady.
sp.l: As it pleaſe him,
I know the way alone elſe.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Where is your Lady?

sp.speaker: O. Lady.
sp.l: I ſhall direct you quickly.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Well, I'le goe,
But what her wrongs will give me leave to ſay.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: We'll leave that to your ſelves: I ſhall hear from you.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: As ſoon as I come off —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Come on then bravely;
Farewel till then, and play the man.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: You are merry;
All I expect is ſcorn: I'le lead you Lady.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Champernel, Lamira, Beaupre, Verdone, Charlotte.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: WE'l venture on him.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Out of my doors I charge thee, ſee me no more.

sp.speaker: Lami.
sp.l: Your Nephew?

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: I diſclaim him,
He has no part in me, nor in my blood,
My Brother that kept fortune bound, and leſt
Conqueſt hereditary to his Iſſue
Could not beget a coward.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: I fought, Sir,
Like a good fellow, and a Souldier too,
But men are men, and cannot make their fates:
Aſcribe you to my Father what you pleaſe,
I am born to ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: All diſgraces wretch.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Good Sir be patient.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Was there no tree,
(For to fall by a noble enemies ſword,
A Coward is unworthy) nor no River,
To force thy life out backward or to drown it,
But that thou muſt ſurvive thy imfamie?
And kill me with the ſight of one I hate,
And gladly would forget?

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Sir, his misfortune
Deſerves not this reproof.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: In your opinion,
'Tis fit you two ſhould be of one belief,
You are indeed fine gallants, and fight bravely
I'th' City with your tongues, but in the field
Have neither ſpirit to dare nor power to do,
Your ſwords are all lead there.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: I know no duty,
(How ever you may wreak your ſpleen on him,)
That bindes me to endure tnis.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: From Dinant
You'l ſuffer more; that ever curſed I,
Should give my honour up, to the defence
Of ſuch a thing as he is, or my Lady
That is all Innocent, for whom a dove would
Aſſume the courage of a daring Eagle,
Repoſe her confidence in one that can
No better guard her. In contempt of you
I love Dinant, mine enemy, nay admire him,
His valour claims it from me, and with juſtice,
He that could fight thus, in a cauſe not honeſt,
His ſword edg'd with defence of right and honour,
Would pierce as deep as lightning, with that ſpeed too,
And kill as deadly.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: You are as far from juſtice
In him you praiſe, as equitie in the cenſure
You load me with.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Dinant? he durſt not meet us.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How? durſt not, Brother?

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Durſt not, I repeat it.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: Nor was it Cleremont's valour that diſarm'd us,
I had the better of him; for Dinant,
If that might make my peace with you, I dare
Write him a Coward upon every poſt,
And with the hazard or my life defend it.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: If 'twere laid at the ſtake you'd loſe it, Nephew.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Came he not, ſay you?

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: No, but in his room,
There was a Devil, hir'd from ſome Magician
I'th' ſhape of an Atturney.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: 'Twas he did it.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: And his the honour.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: I could wiſh Dinant —
But what talk I of one that ſtept aſide,
And durſt not come?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I am ſuch a friend to truth,
I cannot hear this: why do you detract
Thus poorly (I ſhould ſay to others baſely)
From one of ſuch approv'd worth?

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Ha! how's this?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: From one ſo excellent in all that's noble,
Whoſe only weakneſs is exceſs of courage?
That knows no enemies, that he cannot maſter,
But his affections, and in them, the worſt
His love to me.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: To you?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, to me,
I dare (for what is that which Innocence dares not)
To you profeſs it; and he ſhun'd not the Combat
For fear or doubt of theſe: bluſh and repent,
That you in thought e're did that wrong to valour.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: Why, this is rare.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: 'Fore heaven, exceeding rare;
Why modeſt Lady, you that ſing ſuch Encomiums
Of your firſt Suiter —

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: How can ye convince us
In your reports?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: With what you cannot anſwer,
'Twas my command that ſtaid him.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Your command?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Mine, Sir, and had my will rank'd with my power,
And his obedience, I could have ſent him
With more eaſe, weaponleſs to you, and bound,
Than have kept him back, ſo well he loves his honour
Beyond his life.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Better, and better ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I wrought with him in private to divert him
From your aſſur'd deſtruction, had he met you.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: In private?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Yes, and us'd all Arts, all Charms
Of one that knew her ſelf the abſolute Miſtris
Of all his faculties.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Gave all rewards too
His ſervice could deſerve; did not he take
The meaſure of my ſheets?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Do not look yellow,
I have cauſe to ſpeak; frowns cannot fright me,
By all my hopes, as I am ſpotleſs to you,
If I reſt once aſſur'd you do but doubt me,
Or curb me of that freedom you once gave me —

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: What then?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I'le not alone abuſe your bed, that's nothing,
But to your more vexation, 'tis reſolv'd on,
I'le run away, and then try if Dinant
Have courage to defend me.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: Impudent!

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: And on the ſudden —

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: How are ye transform'd
From what you were?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I was an innocent Virgin,
And I can truly ſwear, a Wiſe as pure
As ever lay by Husband, and will dy ſo,
Let me live unſuſpected, I am no ſervant,
Nor will be us'd like one: If you deſire
To keep me conſtant as I would be, let
Truſt and belief in you beget and nurſe it;
Unneceſſary jealouſies make more whores
Than all baits elſe laid to entrap our frailties.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: There's no conteſting with her, from a child
Once mov'd, ſhe hardly was to be appeas'd,
Yet I dare ſwear her honeſt.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: So I think too,
On better judgement: I am no Italian
To lock her up: nor would I be a Dutchman,
To have my Wife, my ſoveraign, to command me:
I'le try the gentler way, but if that fail,
Believe it, Sir, there's nothing but extreams
Which ſhe muſt feel from me.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: That, as you pleaſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: You have won the breeches, Madam, look up ſweetly,
My Lord limps toward you.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: You will learn more manners

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: This is a fee, for counſel that's unask'd for.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Come, I miſtook thee ſweet, prethee forgive me,
I never will be jealous: e're I cheriſh
Such a mechanick humour, I'le be nothing;
I'le ſay, Dinant is all that thou wouldſt have him,
Will that ſuffice?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Tis well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Uſe thy freedom
Uncheck'd, and unobſerv'd, if thou wilt have it,
Theſe ſhall forget their honour, I my wrongs.
We'll all dote on him, hell be my reward
If I diſſemble.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: And that hell take me
If I affect him, he's a luſtfull villain,
(But yet no coward) and ſollicites me
To my diſhonour, that's indeed a quarrel,
And truly mine, which I will ſo revenge,
As it ſhall fright ſuch as dare only think
To be adulterers.

sp.speaker: Cham
sp.l: Uſe thine own waies,
I give up all to thee.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: O women, women!
When you are pleas'd you are the leaſt of evils.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: I'le time to't, but provokt, the worſt of Devils.

div.stage: Enter Monſieur Sampſon, and three Clients.

sp.speaker: Samp.
sp.l: I know Monſieur La writ.

sp.speaker: 1 Cly.
sp.l: Would he knew himſelf, Sir.

sp.speaker: Samp.
sp.l: He was a pretty Lawyer, a kind of pretty Lawyer,
Of a kind of unable thing.

sp.speaker: 2 Cly.
sp.l: A fine Lawyer, Sir,
And would have ſ • k'd you up a buſineſs,
And out of this Court into that.

sp.speaker: Samp.
sp.l: Ye are too forward
Not ſo fine my friends, ſomething he could have done,
But ſhort ſhort.

sp.speaker: 1 Cy.
sp.l: I know your worſhips favour,
You are Nephew to the Judge, Sir.

sp.speaker: Samp.
sp.l: It may be ſo,
And ſomething may be done, without trotting i'th' dirt, friends;
It may be I can take him in his Chamber,
And have an hours talk, it may be ſo,
And tell him that in's ear; there are ſuch courteſies;
I will not ſay, I can.

sp.speaker: 3 Cly.
sp.l: We know you can, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Peradventure I, peradventure no: but where's La-writ?
Where's your ſufficient Lawyer?

sp.speaker: 1 Cly.
sp.l: He's blown up, Sir.

sp.speaker: 2 Cly.
sp.l: Run mad and quarrels with the Dog he meets;
He is no Lawyer of this world now.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Your reaſon?
Is he defunct? is he dead?

sp.speaker: 2 Cly.
sp.l: No he's not dead yet, Sir;
But I would be loth to take a leaſe on's life for two hours:
Alas, he is poſſeſt Sir, with the ſpirit of fighting
