And quarrels with all people: but how he came to it—

sp.speaker: Samp.
sp.l: If he fight well and like a Gentleman,
The man may fight, for 'tis a lawfull calling.
Look you my friends, I am a civil Gentleman,
And my Lord my Uncle loves me.

sp.speaker: 3 Cly.
sp.l: We all know it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I think he does, Sir, I have buſineſs too, much buſineſs,
Turn you ſome forty or fifty Cauſes in a week;
Yet when I get an hour of vacancie,
I can fight too my friends, a little does well,
I would be loth to learn to fight.

sp.speaker: 1 Cly.
sp.l: But and't pleaſe you Sir,
His fighting has neglected all our buſineſs,
We are undone, our cauſes caſt away, Sir,
His not appearance.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: There he fought too long,
But ne'r the leſs things muſt be as they may,
And there be wayes —

sp.speaker: 1 Cly.
sp.l: We know, Sir, if you pleaſe —

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Something I'le do: goe rally up your Cauſes.

div.stage: Enter La-writ, and a Gentleman, at the door.

sp.speaker: 2 Cly.
sp.l: Now you may behold Sir,
And be a witneſs, whether we lie or no.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I'le meet you at the Ordinary, ſweet Gent • emen,
And if there be a wench or two —

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: We'll have 'em.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: No handling any Duells before I come,
We'll have no going elſe, I hate a coward.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: There ſhall be nothing done.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Make all the quarrels
You can deviſe before I come, and let's all fight,
There is no ſport elſe.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: We'll ſee what may be done, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Cly.
sp.l: Ha? Monſieur La writ.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Baffled in way of buſineſs,
My cauſes caſt away, Judgement againſt us?
Why there it goes.

sp.speaker: 2 Cly.
sp.l: What ſhall we do the whilſt Sir?

sp.speaker: La-wr.
sp.l: Breed new diſſentions, goe hang your ſelves
'Tis all one to me; I have a new trade of living.

sp.speaker: 1 Cli.
sp.l: Do you hear what he ſaies Sir?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: The Gentleman ſpeaks finely.

sp.speaker: La-wr.
sp.l: Will any of you fight? Fighting's my occupation
If you find your ſelves aggriev'd.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: A compleat Gentleman.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Avant thou buckram budget of petitions,
Thou ſpittle of lame cauſes; I lament for thee,
And till revenge be taken —

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt excellent.

sp.speaker: La-wr.
sp.l: There, every man chuſe his paper, and his place.
I'le anſwer ye all, I will neglect no mans buſineſs
But he ſhall have ſatisfaction like a Gentleman,
The Judge may do and not do, he's but a Monſieur.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: You have nothing of mine in your bag, Sir.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I know not Sir,
But you may put any thing in, any fighting thing.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: It is ſufficient, you may hear hereafter.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I reſt your ſervant Sir.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: No more words Gentlemen
But follow me, no more words as you love me,
The Gentleman's a noble Gentleman.
I ſhall do what I can, and then —

sp.speaker: Cli.
sp.l: We thank you Sir. Ex. Sam. and Clients.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Not a word to diſturb him, he's a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Not cauſe go o' my ſide? the judge caſt all?
And becauſe I was honourably employed in action,
And not appear'd, pronounce? 'tis very well,
'Tis well faith, 'tis well, Judge.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Who have we here?
My little furious Lawyer?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I ſay 'tis well,
But mark the end.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: How he is metamorphos'd?
Nothing of Lawyer left, not a bit of buckram,
No ſolliciting face now,
This is no ſimple converſion.
Your ſervant Sir, and Friend.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: You come in time, Sir,

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: The happier man, to be at your command then.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: You may wonder to ſee me thus; but that's all one,
Time ſhall declare; 'tis true I was a Lawyer,
But I have mew'd that coat, I hate a Lawyer,
I talk'd much in the Court, now I hate talking,
I did you the office of a man.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs it.

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: And budg'd not, no I budg'd not.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: No, you did not.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: There's it then, one good turn requires another.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Moſt willing Sir, I am ready at your ſervice.

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: There, read, and underſtand, and then deliver it.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: This is a Challenge, Sir,

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: 'Tis very like, Sir,
I ſeldom now write Sonnets.

sp.speaker: Cler.

l.hi: O admirantis,

sp.l: To Monſieur Vertaign, the Preſident.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: I chuſe no Fool, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Why, he's no Sword-man, Sir.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: Let him learn, let him learn,
Time, that trains Chickens up, will teach him quickly.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: VVhy, he's a Judge, an Old Man.

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: Never too Old
To be a Gentleman; and he that is a Judge
Can judge beſt what belongs to wounded honour.
There are my griefs, he has caſt away my cauſes,
In which he has bowed my reputation.
And therefore Judge, or no Judge.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Pray be rul'd Sir,
This is the maddeſt thing—

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: You will not carry it.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I do not tell you ſo, but if you may be perſwaded.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: You know how you us'd me when I would not fight,
Do you remember, Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: The Devil's in him.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: I ſee it in your Eyes, that you dare do it,
You have a carrying face, and you ſhall carry it.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: The leaſt is Baniſhment.

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: Be baniſh'd then;
'Tis a friends part, we'll meet in Africa,
Or any part of the Earth.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Say he will not fight.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: I know then what to ſay, take you no care, Sir,

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Well, I will carry it, and deliver it,
And to morrow morning meet you in the Louver,
Ti • l when, my ſervice.

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: A Judge, or no Judge, no Judge. Exit La-writ.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: This is the prettieſt Rogue that e'r I read of,
None to provoke to th'field, but the old Preſident;
What face ſhall I put on? if I come in earneſt,
I am ſure to wear a pair of Bracelets;
This may make ſome ſport yet, I will deliver it,
Here comes the Preſident.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: I ſhall find time, Gentlemen,
To do your cauſes good, is not that Cleremont?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis he my Lord.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: Why does he ſmile upon me?
Am I become ridiculous? has your fortune, Sir,
Upon my Son, made you contemn his Father?
The glory of a Gentleman is fair bearing.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Miſtake me not my Lord, you ſhall not find that,
I come with no blown Spirit to abuſe you,
I know your place and honour due unto it,
The reverence to your ſilver Age and Vertue.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: Your face is merry ſtill.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: So is my buſineſs,
And I beſeech your honour miſtake me not,
I have brought you from a wild or rather Mad-man
As mad a piece of— you were wont to love mirth
In your young days, I have known your Honour woo it,
This may be made no little one, 'tis a Challenge, Sir,
Nay, ſtart not, I beſeech you, it means you no harm,
Nor any Man of Honour, or Underſtanding,
'Tis to ſteal from your ſerious hours a little laughter;
I am bold to bring it to your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: 'Tis to me indeed;
Do they take me for a Sword-man at theſe years?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Tis only worth your Honours Mirth, that's all Sir
'T had been in me elſe a ſawcy rudneſs.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: From one La writ, a very punctual Challenge.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: But if your Lordſhip mark it, no great matter.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: I have known ſuch a wrangling Advocate,
Such a little figent thing; Oh I remember him,
A notable talking Knave, now out upon him,
Has challeng'd me downright, defied me mortally
I do remember too, I caſt his Cauſes.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Why, there's the quarrel, Sir, the mortal quarrel.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: Why, what a Knave is this? as y'are a Gentleman,
Is there no further purpoſe but meer mirth?
What a bold Man of War! he invites me roundly.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: If there ſhould be, I were no Gentleman,
Nor worthy of the honour of my Kindred.
And though I am ſure your Lordſhip hates my Perſon,
Which Time may bring again into your favour,
Yet for the manners—

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: I am ſatisfied,
You ſee, Sir, I have out-liv'd thoſe days of fighting,
And therefore cannot do him the honour to beat him my ſelf;
But I have a Kinſman much of his ability,
His Wit and Courage, for this call him Fool,
One that will ſpit as ſenſeleſs fire as this Fellow.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: And ſuch a man to undertake, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: Nay he's too forward; theſe two pitch Barrels together.
Upon my ſoul, no harm.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: It makes me ſmile,
Why, what a ſtinking ſmother will they utter?
Yes, he ſhall undertake, Sir, as my Champion,
Since you propound it mirth, I'll venture on it,
And ſhall defend my cauſe, but as y'are honeſt
Sport not with bloud.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Think not ſo baſely, good Sir.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: A Squire ſhall wait upon you f • om my Kinſman,
To morrow morning make you ſport at full,
You want no Subject; but no wounds.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: That's my care.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: And ſo good day. Ex. Vertaign, and Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Many unto your honour.
This is a noble Fellow, of a ſweet Spirit,
Now muſt I think how to contrive this matter,
For together they ſhall go.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: O Cleremont,
I am glad I have found thee.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I can tell thee rare things.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: O, I can tell thee rarer,
Doſt thou love me?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Love thee?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Doſt thou love me dearly?
Dar'ſt thou for my ſake?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Any thing that's honeſt.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Though it be dangerous?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Pox o' dangerous.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Nay wondrous dangerous.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Wilt thou break my heart?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Along with me then.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I muſt part to morrow.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: You ſhall, you ſhall, be faithful for this night,
And thou haſt made thy friend.
Away, and talk not. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: O Nurſe, welcome, where's Dinant?

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: He's at my back.
'Tis the moſt liberal Gentleman, this Gold
He gave me for my pains, nor can I blame you,
If you yield up the fort.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How? yield it up?

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: I know not, he that loves, and gives ſo largely,
And a young Lord to boot, or I am cozen'd,

May ente •
• very where.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Thou'lt make me angry.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Why, if you are, I hope here's one will pleaſe you,
Look on him with my Eyes, good luck go with you:
Were I young for your ſake —

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I thank thee, Nurſe.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: I would be tractable, and as I am—

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Leave the room,
So old, and ſo immodeſt I and be careful,
Since whiſpers will 'wake ſleeping jealouſies,
That none diſturb my Lord. Exit Nurſe.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Will you diſpatch?
Till you come to the matter be not rapt thus,
Walk in, walk in, I am your ſcout for once,
You owe me the like ſervice.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: And will pay it.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: As you reſpect our lives, ſpeak not ſo loud.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Why, do it in dumb ſhew then, I am ſilenc'd.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Be not ſo haſty, Sir, the golden Apples
Had a fell Dragon for their Guard, your pleaſures
Are to be attempted with Herculean danger,
Or never to be gotten.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Speak the means.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Thus briefly, my Lord ſleeps now, and alas,
Each Night, he only ſleeps.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Go, keep her ſtirring.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Now if he 'wake, as ſometimes he does,
He only ſtretches out his hand and feels,
Whether I am a bed, which being aſſur'd of,
He ſleeps again; but ſhould he miſs me, Valour
Could not defend our lives.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: What's to be done then?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Servants have ſervile faiths, nor have I any
That I dare truſt; on noble Cleremont
We ſafely may rely.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: What man can do,
Command and boldly.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Thus then in my place,
You muſt lye with my Lord.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: With an old man?
Two Beards together, that's prepoſterous.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: There is no other way, and though 'tis dangerous,
He having ſervants within call, and arm'd too,
Slaves fed to act all that his jealouſie
And rage commands them, yet a true friend ſhould not
Check at the hazard of a life.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I thank you,
I love my friend, but know no reaſon why
To hate my ſelf; to be a kind of pander,
You ſee I am willing,
But to betray mine own throat you muſt pardon.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Then I am loſt, and all my hopes defeated,
Were I to hazard ten times more for you,
You ſhould find, Cleremont—

sp.speaker: Cler
sp.l: You ſhall not outdo me,
Fall what may fall, I'll do't.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: But for his Beard—

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: To cover that you ſhall have my night Linnen,
And you diſpos'd of, my Dinant and I
Will have ſome private conference.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Private doing,
Or I'll not venture.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: That's as we agree. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Nurſe, and Charlotte, paſs over the Stage with Pillows, Night cloaths, and ſuch things.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: What can this Woman do, preſerving her honour?
I have given her all the liberty that may be,
I will not be far off though, nor I will not be jealous,
Nor truſt too much, I think ſhe is vertuous,
Yet when I hold her beſt, ſhe's but a Woman,
As full of frailty as of faith, a poor ſleight Woman,
And her beſt thoughts, but weak fornifications,
There may be a Mine wrought: Well, let 'em work that,
I ſhall meet with it, till the ſigns be monſtrous,

And ſtick upon my head, I will not believe it, Standi •
〈◊〉
She may be, and ſhe may not, now to my obſervation.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Why do you make me ſtay ſo? if you love me—

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: You are too hot and violent.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Why do you ſhift thus
From one Chamber to another?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: A little delay, Sir,
Like fire, a little ſprinkled o'r with water
Makes the deſires burn clear, and ten times hotter.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Why do you ſpeak ſo loud? I pray'e go in,
Sweet Miſtriſs, I am mad, time ſteals away,
And when we would enjoy—

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Now fie, fie, Servant,
Like ſenſual Beaſts ſhall we enjoy our pleaſures?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: 'Pray do not kiſs me then.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Why, that I will, and you ſhall find anon, ſervant.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Softly, for heavens ſake, you know my friend's engag'd,
A little now, now; will ye go in again?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Why do you laugh ſo loud, Precious?
Will you betray me; ha' my friends throat cut!

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Come, come, I'll kiſs thee again.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Will you ſo? you are liberal,
If you do cozen me—

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: What's this?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Wine, Wine, a draught or two.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: What does this Woman here?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: She ſhall not hinder you.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: This might have been ſpar'd,
'Tis but delay and time loſt; pray ſend her ſoftly off.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Sit down, and mix your ſpirits with Wine,
I will make you another Hercules.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I dare not drink;
Fie, what delays you make? I dare not,
I ſhall be drunk preſently, and do ſtrange things then.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Not drink a cup with your Miſtriſs! O the pleaſure

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Lady, why this? Muſick

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: We muſt have mirth to our Wine, Man.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Pl— o' the Muſick.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: God-a-mercy Wench,
If thou doſt cuckold me I ſhall forgive thee.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: The houſe will all riſe now, this will diſturb all.
Did you do this?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Peace, and ſit quiet, fool,
You love me, come, ſit down and drink.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: What a Devil ail you?
How cold I ſweat! a hogs pox ſtop your pipes, Muſick.
The thing will 'wake; now, now, methinks I find
His Sword juſt gliding through my throat. What's that?
A vengeance choak your pipes. Are you there, Lady?
Stop, ſtop thoſe Raſcals; do you bring me hither
To be cut into minced meat? why Dinant?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I cannot do withal;
I have ſpoke, and ſpoke; I am betray'd and loſt too.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Do you hear me? do you underſtand me?
'Plague dam your Whiſtles. Muſick • .

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Twas but an over-ſight, they have done, lye down.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Would you had done too,
You know not
In what a miſery and fear I lye.
You have a Lady in your arms.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I would have — The Recorde • aga • .

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: I'll watch you Goodman Wou'd have.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Remove for Heavens ſake,
And fall to that you come for.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Lie you down,
'Tis but an hours endurance now.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I dare not, ſoftly ſweet Lady— heart?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Tis nothing but your fear, he ſleeps ſtill ſoundly,
Lie gently down.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Pray make an end.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Come, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Theſe Chambers are too near. Ex. Din. Lam.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: I ſhall be nearer;
Well, go thy wayes, I'le truſt thee through the world,
Deal how thou wilt: that that I never feel,
I'le never fear. Yet by the honour of a Souldier,
I hold thee truly noble: How theſe things will look,
And how their blood will curdle! Play on Children,
You ſhall have pap anon. O thou grand Fool,
That thou knew'ſt but thy fortune— Muſick done.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Peace, good Madam,
Stop her mouth, Dinant, it ſleeps yet, 'pray be wary,
Diſpatch, I cannot endure this miſery,
I can hear nothing more; I'll ſay my prayers,
And down again— Whiſtle within.
A thouſand Alarms fall upon my quarters,
Heaven ſend me off; when I lye keeping Conrſes.
Pl— o' your fumbling, Dinant; how I ſhake!

'Tis ſtill again: would I were in the Indies.
Exit Cler.

div.stage: Enter Dinant, and Lamira: a light within.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Why do you uſe me thus? thus poorly? baſely?
Work me into a hope, and then deſtroy me?
Why did you ſend for me? this new way train me?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Mad-man, and fool, and falſe man, now I'll ſhew thee.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: 'Pray put your light out.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Nay I'll hold it thus,
That all chaſte Eyes may ſee thy luſt, and ſcorn it.
Tell me but this when you firſt doted on me,
And made ſuit to enjoy me as your Wife,
Did you not hold me honeſt?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Yes, moſt vertuous.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: And did not that appear the only luſtre
That made me worth your love and admiration?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs—

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Why would you deal ſo baſely?
So like a thief, a Villain?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Peace, good Madam.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I'll ſpeak aloud too; thus maliciouſly,
Thus breaking all the Rules of honeſty,
Of honour and of truth, for which I lov'd you,
For which call'd you ſervant, and admir'd you;
To ſteal that Jewel purchas'd by another,
•• ouſly ſet in Wedlock, even that Jewel,
Becauſe it had no flaw, you held unvaluable:
Can he that has lov'd good, dote on the Devil?
For he that ſeeks a Whore, ſeeks but his Agent;
Or am I of ſo wild and low a blood?
• o nurs'd in infamies?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I do not think ſo,
And I repent.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: That will not ſerve your turn, Sir.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: It was your treaty drew me on.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: But it was your villany
• e you purſue it; I drew you but to try
• ow much a man, and nobly thou durſt ſtand,
• ow well you had deſerv'd the name of vertuous;
• et you like a wild torrent, mix'd with all
• aſely and baſe affections came floating on,
• lling your poyſon'd billows—

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Will you betray me?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: To all the miſeries a vext Woman may.

sp.speaker: Dan.
sp.l: Let me but out,
• ve me but room to • oſs my Sword about me,
• d I will tell you y'are a treacherous woman,
〈◊〉 that I had but words!

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: They will not ſerve you.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: But two-edg'd words to cut thee; a Lady traytor?
Periſh by a proud Puppet? I did you too much honour,
To tender you my love, too much reſpected you
To think you worthy of my worſt embraces
Go take your Groom, and let him dally with you,
Your greaſie Groom; I ſcorn to imp your lame ſtock,
You are not fair, no • handſome, I lyed lou • ly,
This tongue abus'd you when it ſpoke you beauteous.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Tis very well, 'tis brave.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Put out your light.
Your laſcivious eyes are f •• mes enough
For Fools to find you out; a Lady Plotte • !
Muſt I begin your ſacrifice of miſchief?
I and my friend, the firſt-fruits of that bloud,
You and your honou able Husband aim at?
Crooked and wretched you are both.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: To you, Sir,
Yet to the Eye of Juſtice ſtraight as Truth.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Is this a womans love? a womans in • y?
Do you profeſs this ſeriouſly? do you laugh at me?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Din
sp.l: Pl— light upon your ſcorns upon your flatteries,
A b • d 〈…〉 upon your cheeks,
And • laſ • , • a • l, 〈◊〉 thoſe • s of Pride that paint you;
•• th • n you • s to fright m • n from theſe dangers:
Raiſe up you • t • op • , Clerem •• .

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: VVhat a vengeance 〈◊〉 you?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: VVhat diſmal noiſ • is there no honour in you?
Cleremont, we are betrayed, betrayed, ſold by a woman;

D ••
〈…〉 forth 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Are we made ſtales to one another?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Yes, we are undone, loſt.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: You ſhall pay for't grey beard.
Up, up, you ſleep your laſt elſe. Lights above, two Servants and Anabel.

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: No, not yet, Sir,
La • y, look up, would you have wrong'd this Beauty?
VVake ſo 〈◊〉 a Virgin with rough t • rms?
You wear a Sword, we muſt entreat you leave it.

sp.speaker: 2 Serv.
sp.l: Fye Sir, ſo ſweet a lady?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Was this my bed fellow, pray give me leave to look,
I am not m • yet, I may be by and by.
Did this lye • e?
Did I fear this? is this a Cauſe to ſhake at?
Away with m ••• r ſhame, I am a Raſcal.

div.stage: Enter Champernel, Beaupre, Verdone, Lamira, Anabel, Cleremont, and two Servants.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I am • az'd too.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: VVe'll recover you.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: You walk like Robin good-fellow all the houſe over,
And every man afraid of you.
'Tis well, Lady;
Th • honour of this deed will be your own,
The world ſhall know your bounty.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: VVhat ſhall we do with 'em?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: G • ld me,
For 'tis not fit I ſhould be a man again,
I am an Aſs, a Dog.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Take your revenges,
You know my Husbands wrongs and your own loſſes.

sp.speaker: Anab.
sp.l: A brave man, an admirable brave man;
VVell, well, I would not be ſo tryed again;
A very handſome proper Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: VVill you let me lye by her but one hour more,
And then hang me?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: We wait your malice, put your ſwords home bravely,
You have reaſon to ſeek bloud.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Not as you are noble.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Hands off, and give them liberty, only diſarm 'em.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: We have done that already.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: You are welcome, Gentl • men,
I am glad my houſe has any pleaſure for you,
I keep a couple of Ladies here, they ſay fair,
And you are young and handſome, Gentlemen;
Have you any more mind to Wenches?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: To be abus'd too? Lady, you might have help'd this.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Sit now 'tis paſt, but 't may be I may ſtand
Your friend hereafter, in a greater matter.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Never whilſt you live.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: You cannot tell— now, Sir, a parting hand.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Down and Roſes:
Well I may live to ſee you again. A dull Rogue,
No revelation in thee.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Were you well frighted?
Were your fitts from the heart, of all colds and colours?
That's all your puniſhment.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: It might have been all yours,
Had not a block-head undertaken it.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Your ſwords you mnſt leave to theſe Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: And now, when you dare fight,
We are on even lee again.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: 'Tis well:
To be a Miſtris, is to be a monſter,
And ſo I leave your houſe, and you for ever.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Leave your wild luſts, and then you are a maſter.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: You may depart too.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I had rather ſtay here.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Faith we ſhall fright you worſe.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Not in that manner,
There's five hundred Crowns, fright me but ſo again.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Come Cleremont, this is the hour of fool.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Wiſer the next ſhall be or we'll to School. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: How coolly theſe hot gallants are departed?
Faith Couſin, 'twas unconſcionably done,
To lye ſo ſtill, and ſo long.

sp.speaker: Anab.
sp.l: 'Twas your pleaſure,
If 'twere a fault, I may hereafter mend.

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: O my beſt Wife,
Take now what courſe thou wilt, and lead what life.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: The more truſt you commit, the more care ſtill,
Goodneſs and vertue ſhall attend my will.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Let's laugh this night out now, and count our gains.
We have our honours home, and they their pains.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: IT holds, they will go thither.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: To their Summer-houſe?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Thither i'th' evening, and which is the moſt infliction,
Only to inſult upon our miſeries.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Are you provided?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Throughly?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Throughly.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Baſ • a, enough, I have your mind, I will not fail you.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: At ſuch an hour.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Have I a memory?
A Cauſe, and Will to do? thou art ſo ſullen—

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: And ſhall be, till I have a fair reparation.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I have more reaſon, for I ſcaped a fortune,
Which if I come ſo near again: I ſay nothing,
But if I ſweat not in another faſhion—
O, a delicate Wench.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: 'Tis certain a moſt handſome one.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: And me thought the thing was angry with it ſelf too
It lay ſo long conceal'd, but I muſt part with you,
I have a ſcene of mirth, to drive this from my heart,
And my hour is come.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Miſs not your time.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I dare not. Exeunt ſeverally.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I preſume, Sir, you now need no inſtruction,
But fairly know, what belongs to a Gentleman;
You bear your Uncles cauſe.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Do not diſturb me,
I underſtand my cauſe, and the right carriage.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Be not too bloody.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: As I find my enemy; if his ſword bite,
If it bite, Sir, you muſt pardon me.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: No doubt he is valiant,
He durſt not undertake elſe,

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: He's moſt welcome,
As he is moſt valiant, he were no man for me elſe.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: But ſay he ſhould relent.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: He dies relenting,
I cannot help it, he muſt dies relenting,
If he pray, praying, ipſo facto, praying,
Your honourable way admits no prayer,
And if he fight, he falls, there's his quietus.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Y'are nobly punctual, let's retire and meet 'em,
But ſtill, I ſay, have mercy

sp.speaker: Samp.
sp.l: I ſay, honour. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Champernel, Lamira, Anabel, Beaupre, Verdone, Charlote and a Servant.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Will not you go ſweet-heart?

sp.speaker: Champ.
sp.l: Go? I'le fly with thee.
I ſtay behind?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: My Father will be there too,
And all our beſt friends.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: And if we be not merry,
We have hard luck, Lady.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: Faith let's have a kind of play.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: What ſhall it be?

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: The ſtory of Dinant.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: With the merry conceits of Cleremont,
His Fits and Feavers.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: But I'le lie ſtill no more.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: That, as you make the Play, 'twill be rare ſport,
And how 'twill vex my gallants, when they hear it?
Have you given order for the Coach?

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Yes, Madam.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: My eaſie Nag, and padd.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: 'Tis making ready.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Where are your Horſes?

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: Ready at an hour, Sir: we'll not be laſt.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Fie, what a night ſhall we have!
A roaring, merry night.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: We'll flie at all, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: I'le flie at thee too, finely, and ſo ruffle thee,
I'le try your Art upon a Country pallet.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Brag not too much, for fear I ſhould expect it,
Then if you fail—

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Thou ſaieſt too true, we all talk.
But let's in, and prepare, and after dinner
Begin our mirthful pilgrimage.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: He that's ſad,
A crab-face'd Miſtris cleave to him for this year. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Since it cannot be the Judge—

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Tis a great deal better.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: You are ſure, he is his kinſman? a Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: As arrant a Gentleman, and a brave fellow,
And ſo near to his blood—

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: It ſhall ſuffice,
I'le ſet him further off, I'le give a remove
Shall quit his kindred, I'le lopp him.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Will ye kill him?

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: And there were no more Couſins in the world I ki • him,
I do mean, Sir, to kill all my Lords kindred.
For every cauſe a Couſin.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: How if he have no more Couſins?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: The next a kin then to his Lordſhips favour;
The man he ſmiles upon.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Why this is vengeance, horrid, and dire.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: I love a dire revenge:
Give me the man that will all others kill,
And laſt himſelf,

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: You ſtole that reſolution.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I had it in a Play, but that's all one,
I wou'd ſee it done.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Come, you muſt be more merciful.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: To no Lords Couſins in the world, I hate 'em;
A Lords Couſin to me is a kind of Cockatrice,
If I ſee him firſt, he dies.
A ſtrange Antipathy.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: What think you of their Nieces?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: If I like 'em,
They may live, and multiply, 'tis a cold morning.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Tis ſharp indeed; you have broke your faſt?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: No verily.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Your valour would have ask'd a good foundation.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Hang him, I'le kill him faſting.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Here they come,
Bear your ſelf in your language, ſmooth and gently,
When your ſwords argue.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: 'Pray Sir, ſpare your precepts.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I have brought you, Sir—

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: 'Tis very well, no words,
You are welcome, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I thank you, Sir, few words.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: I'le kill you for your Uncles ſake.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I love you,
I'le cut your throat for your own ſake.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I eſteem of you.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Let's render 'em honeſt, and fair, Gentlemen,
Search my friend, I'le ſearch yours.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: That's quickly done.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: You come with no Spells, nor Witchcrafts?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I come fairly to kill him honeſtly.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Hang Spells, and Witchcrafts,
I come to kill my Lords Nephew like a Gentleman,
• d ſo I kiſs his hand.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: This Doublet is too ſtiff.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Off with't, I hate it,
And all ſuch fortifications, feel my skin,
〈◊〉 that be ſtiff, flea that off too.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis no ſoft one.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Off with't, I ſay:
The fight with him like a flea'd Cat.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: You are well, you are well.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: You muſt uncaſe too.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Yes, Sir.
〈◊〉 tell me this, why ſhould I mix mine honour
With a fellow, that has ne're a lace in's ſhirt?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: That's a main point, my friend has two.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: That's true, Sir.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: Baſe and degenerate Couſin, doſt not thou know
〈◊〉 old, and tatter'd colours, to the enemy,
〈◊〉 of more honour, and ſhews more ominous?
• his ſhirt, five times, victorious I have fought under,
• ad cut through ſquadrons of your curious cut-works,
〈◊〉 I will do through thine, ſhake, and be ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: This is unanſwerable.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: But may I fight with a foul ſhirt?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Moſt certain, ſo it be a fighting ſhirt,
• et it be ne're ſo foul, or lowſie, Caeſar wore ſuch a one.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Saint Denis then: I accept your ſhirt.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Not ſo forward, firſt you muſt talk,
• is a main point, of the French method,
Talk civilly, and make your cauſe Authentick.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: No weapon muſt be near you, nor no anger.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: When you have done, then ſtir your reſolutions,
〈◊〉 to your Weapons bravely.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: 'Tis too cold;
This for a Summer fight.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Not for a world you ſhould tranſgreſs the rules.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: 'Tis pieviſh weather,
I had rather fight without.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: An 'twere in a River.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Where both ſtood up to th' chins.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Then let's talk quickly,
Pl— o' this circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Are the Horſes come yet?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Yes certain: give your ſwords to us, now civilly.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: We'll ſtand a while off; take 〈◊〉 things, and leave'em,
You know when, and let the children play:
This is a dainty time of year for puppies,
Would the old Lord were here.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: He would dye with laughter.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I am ſorry I have no time to ſee this game out,
Away, away.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Here's like to be a hot fight,
Call when y'are fit. Ex. Cler. and Gent.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Why look you Sir, you ſeem to be a Gentleman,
And you come in honour of your Uncle, boh, boh, 'tis very cold;
Your Uncle has offer'd me ſome few affronts,
Paſt fleſh and blood to bear: boh, boh, wondrous cold.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: My Lord, mine Uncle, is an honourable man,
And what he offers, boh, boh, cold indeed,
Having made choice of me, an unworthy kinſman,
Yet take me with you: boh, boh, peſtilence cold,
Not altogether.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Boh, boh, I ſay altogether.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: You ſay you know not what then? boh, boh, Sir.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Sir me with your ſword in your hand;
You have a ſcurvy Uncle, you have a moſt ſcurvy cauſe,
And you are— boh, boh.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Boh, boh, what?

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: A ſhitten ſcurvy Couſin.

sp.speaker: Samp.
sp.l: Our Swords; our Swords;
Thou art a Dog, and like a Dog, our Swords.

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: Our weapons Gentlemen ha? where's your ſecond?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Where's yours?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: So ho; our weapons.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Wa, ha, ho, our weapons;
Our Doublets and our weapons, I am dead.

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: Firſt, ſecond, third, a pl— be wi'you Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Are theſe the rules of honour? I am ſtarv'd.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: They are gone, and we are here; what ſhall we do?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: O for a couple of Faggots.

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: Hang a couple of Faggots.
Dar'ſt thou take a killing cold with me?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I have it already.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: Rogues, Thieves, boh, boh, run away with our Doublets?
To fight at Bu • l • ts now, 'twere ſuch a May-game.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: There were no honour in't, pl— on't, 'tis ſcurvy.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: Or to revenge my wrongs at fifty-cuffes.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: My Lord, mine Uncles cauſe, depend on Boxes?

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: Let's go in queſt, if we ever recover 'em.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I, come, our Colds together, and our Doublets.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: Give me thy hand; thou art a valiant Gentleman,
I ſay if ever we recover 'em—

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Let's get into a houſe and warm our hearts.

sp.speaker: La w.
sp.l: There's ne're a houſe within this mile, beat me,
Kick me and beat me as I go, and I'le beat thee too,
To keep us warm; if ever we recover 'em—
Kick hard, I am frozen: ſo, ſo, now I feel it.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I am dull yet.

sp.speaker: La-w.
sp.l: I'le warm thee, I'le warm thee— Gentlemen?
Rogues, Thieves, Thieves: run now I'le follow thee. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Vertaign, Champernel, Beaupre, Verdone, Lamira, Annabel, Charlote, Nurſe.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Uſe legs, and have legs.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: You that have legs ſay ſo,
I put my one to too much ſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Verdo.
sp.l: Your Horſe, Sir,
Will meet you within half a mile.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I like
The walk ſo well, I ſhould not miſs my Coach,
Though it were further. Annabel thou art ſad:
What ails my Niece?

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: She's ſtill muſing, Siſter,
How quietly her late bed-fellow lay by her.

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: Old as I am, he would have ſtartled me,
Nor can you blame her.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Had I ta'ne her place,
I know not, but I fear, I ſhould ha'ſhreek'd,
Though he had never offer'd—

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Out upon thee,
Thou wouldſt have taught him.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: I think, with your pardon,
That you wiſh now you had.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: I am glad I yield you Cornet.
Such ample ſcope of mirth. Muſick within.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Nay, be not angry,
There's no ill meant: ha? Muſick, and choice Muſick?

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: 'Tis near us in the Grove; what courteous bounty
Beſtows it on us? my dancing days are done;
Yet I would thank the giver, did I know him.

sp.speaker: Verdo.
sp.l: 'Tis queſtionleſs, ſome one of your own Village,
That hearing of your purpos'd journey thither,
Prepares it for your entertainment, and
The honour of my Lady.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I think rather,
Some of your Lordſhips Clients.

sp.speaker: Beaup.
sp.l: What ſay you Couſin,
If they ſhould prove your Suitors?

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: That's moſt likely.

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: I ſay if you are noble, be't who will,
Go preſently and thank 'em: I can jump yet,
Or tread a meaſure.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Like a Millers Mare.

sp.speaker: Nurſ.
sp.l: I warrant you well enough to ſerve the Country,
I'le make one, and lead the way. Exit.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Do you note,
How zealous the old Crone is?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: And you titter
As eagerly as ſhe: come ſweet, we'll follow,
No ill can be intended. Muſick ends.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: I ne're fear'd yet. Exeunt.

body.head: SONG in the Wood.
body.l: THis way, this way come and hear,
You that hold theſe p eaſures dear,
Fill your ears with our ſweet ſound,
Whilſt we melt the frozen ground:
This way come, make haſte oh fair,
Let your clear eyes gild the Air;
Come and bleſs us with your fight,
This way, this way, ſeek delight.

div.stage: Enter a company of Gentlemen, like Ruffians.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: They are ours, but draw them on a little further
From the foot path into the neighbouring thicket,
And we may do't, as ſafe as in a Caſtle.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: They follow ſtill; the Preſident Vertaigne
Comes on a pace, and Champernel limps after;
The Women, as if they had wings, and walk't
Upon the Air, fly to us.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: They are welcome,
We'll make 'em ſport; make a ſtand here, all know
How we are to proceed.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: We are inſtructed. Still Muſick within.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: One ſtrain or two more. Gent. off.
sp.stage: Enter Vertaigne, Champernel, Beaupre, Verdone, Lamira, Anabel, Nurſe, Charlote.
sp.l: Excellent, they are come.

sp.speaker: Nurſe.
sp.l: We cannot miſs, in ſuch a buſineſs, yet
Mine ear ne'r fail'd me. Muſick for the Dance.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Would we were at it once,
I do not walk, but Dance.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You ſhall have dancing.
Begin, and when I give the word—

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: No more:
We are inſtructed. Dance.

sp.speaker: Beaupre.
sp.l: But win us fairly—

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: O Sir, we do not come to try your valour,
But to poſſeſs you, yet we uſe you kindly
In that, like Engliſh Thieves, we kill you not,
But are contented with the ſpoil.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Oh Heaven!
How hath mine age deſerv'd this?

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Hell confound it,
This comes of walking; had I kept my legs,
Or my good Horſe, my Armour on,
My Staff in my reſt, and this good Sword too, fr • nd,
How I would break and ſcatter theſe.

sp.speaker: All Gent.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Do you ſcorn me Rogues?

sp.speaker: Nurſ.
sp.l: Nay, Gentlemen, kind Gentlemen,
Or honeſt keepers of theſe woods, but hear me,
Be not ſo rough; if you are taken with
My beauty, as it hath been worth the ſeeking,
Some one or two of you try me in private,
You ſhall not find me ſqueamiſh.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Do not kill me,
And do your worſt, I'le ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Peace vile creatures,

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: Do you know me, or my place, that you preſume not
To touch my perſon?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: If you are well, reſt ſo,
Provoke not angry Waſps.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: You are Waſps indeed,
Never created to yield Wax or Honey,
But for your Countries torment; yet if you are men,
(As you ſeem ſuch in ſhape) if true born French-men,
However want compels you to theſe courſes,
Reſt ſatisfied with what you can take from us,
(Theſe Ladies honours, and our liberties ſafe)
We freely give it.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You give but our own.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Look on theſe grey hairs, as you would be old,
Their tears, as you would have yours to find mercy
When Juſtice ſhall o'retake you.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Look on me,
Look on me Raſcals, and learn of me too,
That have been in ſome part of your profeſſion,
Before that moſt of you ere ſuck'd, I know it,
I have rode hard, and late too.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Take heed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Then uſe me like a Brother of the Trade,
For I have been at Sea, as you on land are,
Reſtore my Matrimony undefil'd,
Wrong not my Neece, and for our gold or ſilver,
If I purſue you, hang me.

sp.speaker: Nurſ.
sp.l: 'Tis well offer'd,
And as I ſaid, ſweet Gentlemen, with ſowre faces,
If you are high, and want ſome ſport, or ſo,
(As living without action here, you may do)
Forbear their tender griſſels, they are meat
Will waſh away, there is no ſubſtance in it,
We that are expert in the game, and tough too,
Will hold you play.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: This Hen longs to be troden.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Lackey, my Horſe.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: This way, I heard the cries
Of diſtreſs'd Women.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Stand upon your guard.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Who's here? my witty, ſcornful Lady-plot
In the hands of Ruffians?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: And my fine cold virgin,
That was inſenſible of man, and woman?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Juſtice too,
Without a ſword to guard it ſelf?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: And valour with its hands bound?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: And the great Souldier dull?
Why this is ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Dinant as thou art noble —

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: As thou art valiant Cleremont —

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: As ever I appear'd lovely —

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: As you ever hope
For what I would give gladly —
Pretty conjurations.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: All injuries a little laid behind you.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Shew your ſelves men, and help us.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Though your many
And groſs abuſes of me ſhould more move me
To triumph in your miſeries than relieve you,—
Yet that hereafter you may know that I
The ſcorn'd and deſpis'd Dinant, know what does
Belong to honour, thus —

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I will ſay little, Fight.
Speak thou for me.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: 'Tis bravely fought.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Brave tempers,
To do thus for their enemies.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: They are loſt yet.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You that would reſcue others, ſhall now feel
What they were born to.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Hurry them away. Ex. Manent Vert. and Champernel.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: That I could follow them.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: I only can lament my fortune, and deſire of heaven
A little life for my revenge.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: The Provoſt
Shall fire the woods, but I will find 'em out,
No cave, no rock, nor hell ſhall keep them from
My ſearching vengeance.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: O cold! O fearfull cold! plague of all ſeconds.

sp.speaker: Samp.
sp.l: O for a pint of burnt wine, or a ſip
Of aqua-fortis.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: The rogues have met with theſe two
Upon my life and rob'd 'em.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: As you are honourable Gentlemen,
Impart unto a couple of cold combatants.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: My Lord, mine uncle as I live.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Pox take him.
How that word has warm'd my mouth?

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Why how now Couſin?
Why, why? and where man, have you been? at a Poulters
That you are cas'd thus like a rabbet? I could laugh now,
And I ſhall laugh, for all I have loſt my Children,
Laugh monſtrouſly.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: What are they?

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Give me leave Sir,
Laugh more and more, never leave laughing.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Why 'tis ſuch a thing I ſmell it Sir, I ſmell it,
Such a ridiculous thing, —

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Do you laugh at me my Lord?
I am very cold, but that ſhould not be laught at.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: What art thou?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: What art thou?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: If he had his doublet. —
And his ſword by his ſide, as a Gentleman ought to have.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Peace Monſieur Sampſon.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Come hither little Gentleman.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Baſe is the • ave commanded: come to me.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: This is the little advocate.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: What advocate?

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: The little advocate that ſent me a challenge,
I told you that my Nephew undertook it,
And what 'twas like to prove: now you ſee the iſſue.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Is this the little Lawyer?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: You have a ſword Sir,
And I have none, you have a doublet too
That keeps you warm, and makes you merry.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: If your Lordſhip knew
The nature, and the nobleneſs of the Gentleman,
Though he ſhew ſlight here, and at what guſts of danger
His manhood has arrived,
But that
Mens fates are fooliſh,
And often headlong overrun their fortunes.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: That little Lawyer would ſo prick his ears up,
And bite your honour by the noſe.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Say you ſo Sir?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: So niggle about your grave ſhins Lord Vertagine too

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: No more ſweet Gentleman, no more of 〈◊〉 .

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I will have more, I muſt have more.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Out with it.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Nay he is as brave a fellow —

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l:
Have I caught you? Strikes hi •
• en.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Do not kill him, do not kill him.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: No, no, no, I will not. Do you peep ag •
Down down proud heart.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: O valour,
Look up brave friend, I have no means to reſcue thee,
My Kingdom for a ſword.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: I'le ſword you preſently,
I'le claw your skin coat too.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Away good Sampſon,
You goe to graſs elſe inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: But do not murder my brave friend.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Not one word.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: If you do ſirra—

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Muſt I goe off diſhonour'd?

Adverſity tries valour, ſo I leave thee.
〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Are you a Lawyer Sir?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I was, I was Sir.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Nay never look, your Lawyers pate is broken,
And your litigious blood about your ears ſirra,
Why do you fight and ſnarle?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I was poſſeſt.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: I'le diſpoſſeſs you.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

l.hi: Et tu Brute?

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Beat him no more.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Alas Sir I muſt beat him,
Beat him into his buſineſs again, he will be loſt elſe.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: Then take your way.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Ly ſtill, and doe not ſtruggle.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I am patient,
I never ſaw my blood before, it jades me,
I have no more heart now than a gooſe.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Why ſirra, why do you leave your trade, your trade of living,
And ſend your challenges like thunderbolts,
To men of honour'd place?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I underſtand Sir,
I never underſtood before your beating.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Does this work on you?

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Do you thank me for't?

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: As well as a beaten man can.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: And do you promiſe me,
To fall cloſe to your trade again? leave brawling?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: If you will give me leave and life.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: And ask this noble man forgiveneſs?

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Heartily.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Riſe then, and get you gon • , and let me hear of you
As of an advocate new vampt; no more words,
Get you off quickly, and make no murmurs,
I ſhall purſue you elſe.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: I have done ſweet Gentlemen. Exit.

sp.speaker: Verta.
sp.l: But we forget our ſelves, our friends and Children.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: We'l raiſe the country firſt, then take our fortunes.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Shall I entreat for what I may command?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Think on my birth.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Here I am only Noble,
A King, and thou in my dominions, fool,
A ſubject and a ſlave.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Be not a Tyrant,
A raviſher of honour, gentle Sir,
And I will think ye ſuch, and on my knees,
As to my Soveraign, pay a Subjects duty,
With prayers and tears.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I like this humble carriage,
I will walk by, but kneel you ſtill and weep too,
It ſhews well, while I meditate on the prey,
Before I ſeize it.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Is there no mercie, Heaven?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Not kiſs you?
I will kiſs and kiſs again.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Savage villain!
My Innocence be my ſtrength, I do defie thee,
Thus ſcorn and ſpit at thee; will you come on Sir?
You are hot, there is a cooler.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: A virago?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: No, loathſome Goat, more, more, I am that Goddeſs,
That here with whips of ſteel in hell hereafter
Scourge rape and theft.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: I'le try your deity.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: My chaſtity, and this knife held by a Virgin,
Againſt thy luſt, thy ſword and thee a Beaſt,
Call on for the encounter.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Now what think you? Throws her and taks her Knife.
Are you a Goddeſs?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: In me their power ſuffers,
That ſhould protect the Innocent.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I am all ſ • e,
And thou ſhalt quench it, and ſerve my pleaſures.
Come partner in the ſpoil and the reward,
Let us enjoy our purchaſe.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: O Dinant!
O Heaven! O Husband!

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: O my Cleremont!

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Two are our ſlaves they call on, bring 'em forth
As they are chain'd together, let them ſee
And ſuffer in the object.
sp.stage: Enter Dinant, and Cleremont, bound by the reſt of the Gent.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: While we ſit
And without pity hear 'em.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: By my life,
I ſuffer more for thee than for my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Be a man Cleremont, and look upon 'em
As ſuch that not alone abus'd our ſervice,
Feel us with hopes moſt bitter in digeſtion,
But when love fa • 'd, to draw on further miſchief,
The baits they laid for us, were our own honours,
Which thus hath made us ſlaves too, worſe than ſlaves.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: He dies.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Pray hold, give him a little reſpite.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I ſee you now beyond expreſſion wretched,
The wit you brag'd of fool'd, that boaſted honour,
As you believ'd compaſs'd with walls of braſs,
To guard it ſure, ſubject to be o'r • thrown
With the leaſt blaſt of luſt.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: A moſt ſad truth.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: That confidence which was not to be ſhaken
In a perpetual ſ • v • , and thoſe favours,
Which with ſo ſtrong and Ceremonious duty
Your love • and a Gentleman long ſought for,
Sought, ſued, and kneel'd in vain for, muſt you yield up
To a licentious villain, that will hardly
Allow you thanks for't.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Something I muſt ſay too,
And to you pretty one, though crying one;
To be hang'd now, when theſe worſhipful benchers pleaſe,
Though I know not their faces that condemn me,
A little ſtartles me, but a man is nothing,
A Maidenhead is the thing, the thing all aim at;
Do not you wiſh now, and wiſh from your heart too,
When ſcarce ſweet with my fears, I long lay by you
Thoſe fears you and your good Aunt put upon me,
To make you ſport, you had given a little hint,
A touch or ſo, to tell me I was mortal,
And by a mortal woman?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Pray you no more.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: If I had loos'd that virgin Zone, obſerve me,
I would have hired the beſt of all our Poets
To have ſung ſo much, and ſo well in the honour
Of that nights joy, that Ovids afternoon,
Nor his Corinna ſhould again be mention'd.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: I do repent, and wiſh I had.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: That's comfort,
But now —

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Another that will have it offer'd,
Compel it to be offer'd, ſhall enjoy it.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: A rogue, a ruffian.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: As you love your throat,—

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Away with them.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: O Cleremont!

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: O Dinant!

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I can but add your ſorrows to my ſorrows,
Your fears to my fears.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: To your wiſhes mine,
This ſlave may prove unable to perform,
Till I perform the task that I was born for.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Amen, amen.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Drag the ſlaves hence, for you
A while I'le lock you up here, ſtudy all ways
You can to pleaſe me, or the deed being done,
You are but dead.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: This ſtrong Vault ſhall contain you,
There think how many for your maidenhead
Have pin'd away, and be prepar'd to loſe it
With penitence.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: No humane help can ſave you.

sp.speaker: Ladyes.
sp.l: Help, help?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: You cry in vain, rocks cannot hear you.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: A Horrid noiſe of Muſique within, Enter one and opens the door, in which Lamira and Anabel were ſhut, they in all fear.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: O Couſin how I ſhake all this long night!
What frights and noiſes we have heard, ſtill they encreaſe,
The villains put on ſhapes to torture us,
And to their Devils form ſuch preparations
As if they were a hatching new diſhonours,
And fatal ruine, part dull mans invention.
Goe not too far, and pray good Couſin Anabel,
Hark a new noiſe. A ſtrange Muſick. Sackbut & Trup Muſick.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: They are exquiſite in miſchief,
I will goe on, this room gives no protection,
More than the next, what's that? how ſad and hollow,
The ſound comes to us. Thieves peepi • g. Louder.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Groaning? or ſinging is it?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: The wind I think, murmuring amongſt old rooms.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Now it grows lowder, ſure ſome ſad preſage
Of our foul loſs — look now they peep.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Pox peep 'em.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: O give them gentle language.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Give 'em rats-bane. Peep ab • a.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Now they are above.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: I would they were i'th' Center.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Thou art ſo fooliſh deſperate.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Since we muſt loſe.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Call 'em brave fellows, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Call 'em rogues,
Rogue as they are, rude rogues, uncivil villains.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Look an thou woo't beware, doſt thou feel the danger?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Till the danger feel me, thus will I talk ſtill,
And worſe when that comes too; they cannot eat me.
This is a puniſhment, upon our own prides
Moſt juſtly laid; we muſt abuſe brave Gentlemen,
Make 'em tame fools, and hobby-horſes, laugh and jear at
Such men too, and ſo handſom and ſo Noble,
That howſoe're we ſeem'd to carry it —
Wou'd 'twere to do again.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I do confeſs couſin,
I was too harſh, too fooliſh.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Do you feel it?
Do you find it now? take heed o'th' puniſhment,
We might have had two gallant Gentlemen,
Proper, young, O how it tortures me!
Two Devils now, two raſcals, two and twenty—

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: O think not ſo.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Nay an we 'ſcape ſo modeſtly —

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: May we be worthy any eyes, or knowledge,
When we are uſed thus?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Why not? why do you cry?
Are we not women ſtill? what were we made for?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: But thus, thus baſely —

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: 'Tis againſt our vills,
And if there come a thouſand ſo,—

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Out on thee.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: You are a fool, what we cannot reſiſt,
Why ſhould we grieve and bluſh for? there be women,
And they that bear the name of excellent women
Would give their whole eſtates to meet this fortune.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Hark, a new noiſe. New ſound within.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Let 'em goe on, I fear not,
If wrangling, fighting and ſcratching cannot preſerve me,
Why ſo be it Couſin; if I be ordain'd
To breed a race of rogues.—

div.stage: Enter four over the ſtage with Beaupre, and Verdone, bound and halters about their necks.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: They come.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Be firm,
They are welcom.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: What mask of death is this? O my dear Brother.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: My Couz too; why now y'are glorious villains.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: O ſhall we loſe our honours?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Let 'em goe,
When death prepares the way, they are but Pageants.
Why muſt theſe dye?

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: Lament your own misfortunes,
We periſh happily before your ruins.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Has miſchief ne'r a tongue?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Yes fooliſh woman,
Our Captains will is death.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: You dare not do it.
Tell thy baſe boiſterous Captain what I ſay,
Thy lawleſs Captain that he dares not;
Do you laugh you rogue? you pamper'd rogue?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Good Sir,
Good Couſin gently, as y'are a Gentleman,—

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: A Gentleman? a ſlave, a dog, the devils harbinger.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Sir as you had a Mother.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: He a Mother?
• me not the name of Mother, a ſhe Bear
A bloody old wolf bitch, a woman Mother?
Looks that rude lump, as if he had a Mother?
• at him? hang him, do thy worſt, thou dar'ſt not,
T • ou dar'ſt not wrong their lives, thy Captain dares not,
They are perſons of more price.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: What e're we ſuffer
Let not your angers wrong you.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: You cannot ſuffer,
The men that do this deed, muſt live i'th' moon
Free from the gripe of Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Is it not better?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Is it not better? let 'em goe on like raſcals
And put falſe faces on; they dare not do it;
Flatter ſuch ſcabbs of nature?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Woman, woman
The next work is with you.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Unbind thoſe Gentlemen,
And put their fatal fortunes on our necks

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: As you have mercy do.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: As you are monſters.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Fright us no more with ſhipwrack of our honours
Nor if there be a guilt by us committed
Let it endanger thoſe.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: I ſay they dare not,
There be a thouſand gallouſes, ye rogues,
Tortures, ye bloody rogues, wheels.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Away.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Stay.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Stay.
Stay and I'le flatter too: good ſweet fac'd Gentlemen,
You excellent in honeſty; O Kinſmen!
O Noble kinſmen!

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Away with 'em. Ex. Ver. Beaup. and Gent

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Stay yet.
The Devil and his lovely dam walk with you,
Come fortify your ſelf, if they do dy,
Which all their ruggedneſs cannot rack into me,
They cannot find an hour more Innocent,
Nor more friends to revenge 'em.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Now ſtand conſtant,
For now our tryal's come.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: This beautie's mine,
Your minute moves not yet.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: She ſinks if Chriſtian,
If any ſpark of noble heat.—

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Riſe Lady
And fearleſs riſe, there's no diſhonour meant you,
Do you know my tongue?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: I have heard it.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Mark it better,
I am one that loves you, fairly, nobly loves you,
Look on my face?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: O Sir?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: No more words, ſoftly
Hark, but hark wiſely how, underſtand well,
Suſpect not, fear not.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: You have brought me comfort.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: If you think me worthy of your husband,
I am no rogue nor Begger, if you dare do thus —

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: You are Monſieur Cleremont.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I am the ſame,
If you dare venture, ſpeak, if not I leave you,
And leave you to the mercy of theſe villains
That will not wooe ye much.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Save my reputation,
And free me from theſe ſlaves.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: By this kiſs I'le do it,
And from the leaſt diſhonour they dare aim at you,
I have a Prieſt too, ſhall be ready.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: You are forward.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Is this my conſtant couſin? how ſhe whiſpers,
Kiſſes and huggs the thief!

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: You'l offer nothing.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Till all be tyed,
Not as I am a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Can you relieve my Aunt too?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Not yet Miſtris,
But fear nothing, all ſhall be well, away quickly
It muſt be done i'th' moment or —

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: I am with ye.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I'le know now who ſleeps by me, keep your ſtanding.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Well, go thy way, and thine own ſhame dwell with thee.
Is this the conſtancy ſhe ſhew'd, the bravery?
The dear love and the life ſhe ow'd her kinſmen?
O brave tongue, valiant glorious woman?
Is this the noble anger you arriv'd at?
Are theſe the thieves you ſcorn'd, the rogues you rail'd at?
The ſcal • and ſcums of nature? O fair modeſty,
Excellent vertue, whither art thou fled?
What hand O Heaven is over us, when ſtrong virgins
Yield to their f • ars, and to their fears their fortunes?
Never belief come • ear me more, farewel wench,
A long farewel from all that ever knew thee:
My turn is n • xt,
I am reſolv'd, it comes
But in a nobler ſhape, ha?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Bleſſe ye Lady.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Indeed Sir, I had need of many bleſſings,
For all the hours I have had ſince I came here,
Have been ſo many curſes. How got you liberty?
For I preſume you come to comfort me.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: To comfort you, and love you, 'tis moſt true,
My bondage was as yours, as full of bitterneſs
And every hour my death.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Heaven was your comfort.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Till the laſt evening, ſitting full of ſadneſs,
Wa • l • ng, ſweet Miſtris, your unhappy fortunes,
(Mine own I had the leaſt care of) round about me
The Captain and the company ſtood gaping,
When I began the ſtory of my love
To you fai • Saint, and with ſo full a ſorrow,
Follow'd each point, that even from thoſe rude eyes,
T • a • n • ver knew w • at 〈…〉 or mercy,
〈…〉 Miſtris,
And let no 〈◊〉 unholy hearts ou • to you
The ſoft plum'd god will ſee again, thus taken,
As men transform'd with the ſtrange tale I told,
They ſtood a • z'd, then bid me riſe and live,
Take liberty and means to ſee your p • on,
And wiſht me proſperous in your love, wi • h you ſo,
Be wiſe and loving Lady, ſhew but you ſo.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: O Sir, are theſe fit hours to talk of love in?
Shall we make fools of our afflictions?
Can any thing ſound ſweetly in mine ears,
Where all the noiſe of bloody horrour i • ?
My Brother, and my Couſin, they are dead Sir,
Dead, baſely dead, is this an age to fool in?
And I my ſ •• f, I know not what I ſhall be,
Yet I muſt thank you, and if happily
You had ask'd me yeſterday, when theſe were living,
And my fears leſs, I might have hearkned to you.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Peace to your grief, I bind you to your word.

div.stage: Enter Cleremont, Anabel, Beaupre, Verdone, Charlote, Nurſe, the two Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How? do you conjure?
Not to raiſe dreadfull apparitions, Madam,
But ſuch as you would gladly ſee.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: My Brother, and nephew living?

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: And both owe their lives
To the favour of theſe Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: Who deſerve
Our ſervice, and for us, your gracious thanks.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Which I give freely, and become a ſuitor,
To be hereafter more familiar Kiſſe.
With ſuch g • eat worth and vertue.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Ever think us
Your ſervants, Madam.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Why if thou wilt needs know
How we are f ••• d, I will diſcover it,
And with laconick brevity: theſe Gentlemen
This night incountring with thoſe outlaws that
Yeſterday made us priſoners, and as we were
Attempted by 'em they with greater courage,
(I am ſure with better fortune) not alone,
Guarded themſelves, but forc'd the bloody thieves,
Being got between them, and this helliſh Cave,
For ſafety of their lives, to fly up higher
Into the woods, all left to their poſſeſſion,
This ſav'd your Brother, and your nephew from
The gibbet, this redeem'd me from my Chains,
And gave my friend his liberty, this preſerv'd
Your honour ready to be loſt.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: But that
I know this for a ly, and that the thieves
And gentlemen, are the ſame men, by my practice
Suborn'd to this, he does deliver it
With ſuch a conſtant brow, that I am doubtfull,
I ſhould believe him too.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: If we did well,
We are rewarded.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Thanks but takes away
From what was freely purpos'd.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Now by this hand,
You have ſo cunningly diſcharg'd your parts,
That while we live, reſt confident you ſhall
Command Dinant and Cleremont; nor Beaupre,
Nor Verdone ſcents it: for the Ladies, they
Were eaſie to be gull'd.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Twas but a jeſt,
And yet the jeſt may chance to break our necks
Should it be known.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Fear nothing.

sp.speaker: Din.

l.hi: Cleremont,

sp.l: Say, what ſucceſs?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: As thou wouldſt wiſh, 'tis done Lad,
The grove will witneſs with me, that this night
I lay not like a block: but how ſpeed you?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I yet am in ſuſpence, deviſe ſome means
To get theſe off, and ſpeedily.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: I have it,
Come, we are dull, I think that the good fellows,
Our predeceſſors in this place, were not
So fooliſh, and improvident husbands, but
'Twill yield us meat and wine.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Let's ranſack it,
'Tis ours now by the Law.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: How ſay you ſweet one,
Have you an appetit?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: To walk again
I'th' Woods, if you think fit, rather than eat.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: A little reſpite prethee; nay bluſh not,
You ask but what's your own, and warrantable:

l.hi: Monſieur, Beaupre, Verdone,

sp.l: What think you of the motion?

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: Lead the way.

sp.speaker: Beau.
sp.l: We follow willingly. Ex. Man. Din. and Lam.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: When you ſhall think fit,
We will expect you.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Now be miſtris of
Your promiſe Lady.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Twas to give you hearing.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: But that word hearing, did include a grant,
And you muſt make it good.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Muſt?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Muſt and ſhall,
I will be fool'd no more, you had your tricks;
Made properties of me, and of my friend;
Preſum'd upon your power, and whip'd me with
The rod of mine own dotage: do not flatter
Your ſelf with hope, that any humane help
Can free you, and for aid by miracle
A baſe unthankfull woman is unworthy.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: You will not force me?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Rather than enjoy you
With your conſent, becauſe I will torment you;
I'le make you feel the effects of abus'd love,
And glory in your torture.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Brother, Nephew,
Help, help, for Heavens ſake.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Tear your throat, cry louder,
Though every leaf, theſe trees bear, were an Echo,
And ſummon'd in your beſt friends to redeem you,
It ſhould be fruitleſs: 'tis not that I love you,
Or value thoſe delights you prize ſo high,
That I'le enjoy you, a French crown will buy
More ſport, and a companion, to whom,
You in your beſt trim are an Ethiop.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Forbear me then.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Not ſo, I'le do't in ſpite,
And break that ſtubborn diſobedient will,
That hath ſo long held out, that boaſted honour
I will make equal with a common Whores;
The ſpring of Chaſtity, that fed your pride,
And grew into a River of vain glory,
I will defile with mudd, the mudd of luſt,
And make it loathſome even to goats.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: O Heaven!
No pity Sir?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: You taught me to be cruel,
And dare you think of mercy? I'le tell thee fool,
Thoſe that ſurpriz'd thee, were my inſtruments,
I can plot too, good Madam, you ſhall find it:
And in the ſtead of licking of my fingers,
Kneeling and whining like a boy new breech'd,
To get a toy forſooth, not worth an apple,
Thus make my way, and with Authority
Command what I would have.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I am loſt for ever:
Good Sir, I do confeſs my fault, my groſs fault,
And yield my ſelf up, miſerable guilty;
Thus kneeling I confeſs, you cannot ſtudy
Sufficient puniſhments to load me with;
I am in your power, and I confeſs again,
You cannot be too cruel: if there be,
Beſides the loſs of my long guarded honour,
Any thing elſe to make the ballance even,
Pray put it in, all hopes, all helpes have left me;
I am girt round with ſorrow; hell's about me,
And raviſhment the leaſt that I can look for,
Do what you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Indeed I will do nothing,
Nor touch nor hurt you Lady, nor had ever
Such a lewd purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Can there be ſuch goodneſs,
And in a man ſo injur'd?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Be confirm'd in't.
I ſeal it thus: I muſt confeſs you vex'd me,
In fooling me ſo often, and thoſe fears
You threw upon me call'd for a requital,
Which now I have return'd, all unchaſt love
Dinant thus throws away; live to man-kind,
As you have done to me, and I will honour
Your vertue, and no more think of your beauty.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: All I poſſeſs, comes ſhort of ſatisfaction.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: No complements: the terrours of this night
Imagine but a fearfull dream, and ſo
With eaſe forget it: for Dinant, that labour'd
To blaſt your honour, is a Champion for it,
And will protect and guard it.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Tis as ſafe then,
As if a compleat Army undertook it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Do not perſwade me gentle Monſieur Sampſon,
I am a mortal man again, a Lawyer,
My martiall part I have put off.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Sweet Monſieur,
Let •• t our honours teach us.

sp.speaker: La writ.
sp.l: Monſieur Sampſon,
My honourable friend, my valiant friend,
Be but ſo beaten, forward my brave Clients,
I am yours, and you are mine again, be but ſo thraſht,
Receive that Caſtigation with a cudgel.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Which calls upon us for a Reparation.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I have, it coſt me half a crown, I bear it
All over me, I bear it Monſieur Sampſon;
The oyls, and the old woman that repairs to me,
To 'noint my beaten body.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: It concerns you,
You have been ſwing'd.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Let it concern thee too;
Goe and be beaten, ſpeak ſcurvy words, as I did,
Speak to that Lion Lord, waken his anger,
And have a hundred Baſtinado's, doe;
Three broken pates, thy teeth knockt out, do Sampſon,
Thy valiant arms and leggs beaten to Poulteſſes,
Do ſilly Sampſon, do.

sp.speaker: 1 Cly.
sp.l: You wrong the Gentleman,
To put him out of his right mind thus:
You wrong us, and our Cauſes.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Down with him Gentlemen,
Turn him, and beat him, if he break our peace,
Then when thou haſt been Lam'd, thy ſmall guts periſht,
Then talk to me, before I ſcorn thy counſel,
Feel what I feel, and let my Lord repair thee.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: And can the brave La-writ—

sp.speaker: 2 Cly.
sp.l: Tempt him no further,
Be warn'd and ſay no more.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: If thou doeſt, Sampſon,
Thou ſeeſt my Mirmidons, I'le let 'em looſe,
That in a moment —

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I ſay nothing, Sir, but I could wiſh—

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: They ſhall deſtroy thee wiſhing;
There's ne'r a man of theſe, but have loſt ten cauſes,
Dearer then ten mens lives; tempt, and thou dieſt:
Goe home, and ſmile upon my Lord, thine Uncle,
Take Mony of the men thou mean'ſt to Couſin,
Drink Wine, and eat good meat, and live diſcreetly,
Keep thy hand from thy ſword, and from thy Laundreſs placket,
And thou wilt live long.

sp.speaker: 1 Cly.
sp.l: Give ear, and be inſtructed.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: I find I am wiſer than a Juſtice of Peace now,
Give me the wiſdom that's beaten into a man
That ſticks ſtill by him: art thou a new man?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Yes, yes,
Thy learned precepts have inchanted me.

sp.speaker: La-writ.
sp.l: Goe my ſon Sampſon, I have now begot thee,
I'le ſend thee cauſes; ſpeak to thy Lord, and live,
And lay my ſhare by, goe and live in peace,
Put on new ſuits, and ſhew ſit for thy place;
That man neglects his living, is an Aſſe: Exit Samp.
Farewel; come chearily boyes, about our buſineſs,
Now welcom tongue again, hang Swords.

sp.speaker: 1 Cly.
sp.l: Sweet Advocate. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: I know not wench, they may call 'em what they will,
Outlawes, or thieves, but I am ſure, to me
One was an honeſt man, he us'd me well,
What I did, 'tis no matter, he complain'd not.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs, there was one bold with me too,
Some coy thing would ſay rude, but 'tis no matter,
I was to pay a Waiting womans ranſom,
And I have don't, and I would pay't again,
Were I ta'n to morrow.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Alas, there was no hurt,
If't be a ſin for ſuch as live at hard meat,
And keep a long Lent, in the woods as they do,
To taſte a little fleſh.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: God help the Courtiers,
That lye at rack and manger.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: I ſhall love
A thief the better for this while I live,
They are men of a charitable vocation,
And give where there is need, and with diſcretion,
And put a good ſpeed penny in my purſe,
That has been empty twenty years.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Peace Nurſe,
Farewel, and cry not roſt meat, me thinks Cleremont
And my Lady Anabel are in one night,
Familiarly acquainted.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: I obſerve it,
If ſhe have got a penny too.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: No more,
My Lord Monſieur Vertaigne, the provoſt too,
Haſte and acquaint my Lady. Ex. Nur. and Char.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Wonderous ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: 'Tis true Sir, on my credit.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: O mine honour.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I have been provoſt-Marſhal twenty years,
And have truſſed up a thouſand of theſe raſcals,
But ſo near Paris yet I never met with
One of that Brotherhood.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: We to our coſt have,
But will you ſearch the wood?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: It is beſet,
They cannot ſcape us, nothing makes me wonder,
So much as having you within their power
They let you goe, it was a Courteſy,
That French thieves uſe not often, I much pity
The Gentle Ladies, yet I know not how,
I rather hope than fear.
sp.stage: Enter Dinant, Cleremont, Verdone, Beaupre, Lamira, Anabel, Charlote, Nurſe.
sp.l: Are theſe the priſoners?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: We were ſuch.

sp.speaker: Verd.
sp.l: Kill me not, exceſs of joy.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: I ſee thou liveſt, but haſt thou had no ſoul play?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: No on my ſoul, my uſage hath been noble,
Far from all violence,

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: How were you freed?
But kiſs me firſt, we'l talk of that at leaſure,
I am glad I have thee; Niece how you keep off,
As you knew me not?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Sir, I am where
I owe moſt duty.

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: 'Tis indeed moſt true Sir,
The man that ſhould have been your bedfellow
Your Lordſhips bedfellow, that could not ſmell out
A Virgin of ſixteen, that was your fool,
To make you merry, this poor ſimple fellow
Has met the maid again, and now ſhe knows
He is a man.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: How! is ſhe diſhonoured?

sp.speaker: Cler.
sp.l: Not unleſs marriage be diſhonourable,
Heaven is a witneſs of our happy contract,
And the next Prieſt we meet ſhall warrant it
To all the world: I lay with her in jeaſt,
'Tis turn'd to earneſt now.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Is this true, Niece?

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: Her bluſhing ſilence grants it; nay Sir ſtorm not,
He is my friend, and I can make this good,
His birth and fortunes equal hers, your Lordſhip
Might have ſought out a worſe, we are all friends too,
All differences end thus. Now Sir, unleſs
You would raiſe new diſſentions, make perfect
What is ſo well begun.

sp.speaker: Vert.
sp.l: That were not manly.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Let me perſwade you.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Well God give you joy,
She ſhall not come a Begger to you Sir.
For you Monſieur Dinant 'ere long I'le ſhew you
Another Niece, to this not much inferiour,
As you ſhall like proceed.

sp.speaker: Din.
sp.l: I thank you Sir.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Back then to Paris: well that travel ends
That makes of deadly enemies perfect friends.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: TO promiſe much, before a play begin,
And when 'tis done, ask pardon, were a ſin
We'l not be guilty of: and to excuſe
Before we know a fault, were to abuſe
The writers and our ſelves, for I dare ſay
We all are fool'd if this be not a Play,
And ſuch a play as ſhall (ſo ſhould plays do)
Imp times dull wings, and make you merry too.
'Twas to that purpoſe writ, ſo we intend it
And we have our wiſht ends, if you commend it.

div.head: Epilogue.
