l.hi: Gentlemen,

div.l: I Am ſent forth to enquire what you decree
Of us and of our Poets, they will be
This night exceeding merry, ſo will we
If you approve their labours. They profeſs
You are their Patrons, and we ſay no leſs,
Reſolve us then, for you can only tell
Whether we have done id'ly or done well.

list.head: 4 Noble Panders, and flatterers to the Emperour.

list.item: Maximus, a great Souldier, Husband to Lucina.

list.head: two bold and faithful Eunuchs, Servants to Aecius.
WOMEN.
list.item: Lucina, the chaſt abuſed Wife of Maximus.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: I Never ſaw the like, ſhe's no more ſtirr'd,
No more another Woman, no more alter'd
With any hopes or promiſes laid to her
(Let 'em be ne're ſo weighty, ne're ſo winning)
Than I am with the motion of mine own legs.

sp.speaker: Pro.

l.hi: Chilax,

sp.l: You are a ſtranger yet in theſe deſigns,
At leaſt in Rome; tell me, and tell me truth,
Did you ere know in all your courſe of practice,
In all the wayes of Women you have run through
(For I preſume you have been brought up Chilax,
As we to fetch and carry.)

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: True I have ſo.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Did you I ſay again in all this progreſs,
Ever diſcover ſuch a piece of beauty,
Ever ſo rare a Creature, and no doubt
One that muſt know her worth too, and affect it,
I and be flatter'd, elſe 'tis none: and honeſt?
Honeſt againſt the tide of all temptations,
Honeſt to one man, to her Husband only,
And yet not eighteen, not of age to know
Why ſhe is honeſt?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I confeſs it freely,
I never ſaw her fellow, nor e're ſhall,
For all our Grecian Dames, all I have tri'd,
(And ſure I have tri'd a hundred, if I ſay two
I ſpeak within my compaſs) all theſe beauties,
And all the conſtancy of all theſe faces,
Maids, Widows, Wives, of what degree or calling,
So they be Greeks, and fat, for there's my cunning,
I would undertake and not ſweat for't, Proculus,
Were they to try again, ſay twice as many,
Under a thouſand pound, to lay 'em bedrid;
But this Wench ſtaggers me.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: Do you ſee theſe Jewels?
You would think theſe pretty baits; now I'le aſſure ye
Here's half the wealth of Aſia.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: Theſe are nothing
To the full honours I propounded to her;
I bid her think, and be, and preſently
What ever her ambition, what the Counſel
Of others would add to her, what her dreams
Could more enlarge, what any Preſident
Of any Woman riſing up to glory,
And ſtanding certain there, and in the higheſt,
Could give her more, nay to be Empreſs.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: And cold at all theſe offers?

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: Cold as Cryſtal,
Never to be thaw'd again.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I tri'd her further,
And ſo far, that I think ſhe is no Woman,
At leaſt as Women go now.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: Why what did you?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I offered that, that had ſhe been but Miſtris
Of as much ſpleen as Doves have, I had reach'd her;
A ſafe revenge of all that ever hates her,
The crying down for ever of all beauties
That may be thought come near her.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: That was pretty.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I never knew that way fail, yet I'le tell ye
I offer'd her a gift beyond all yours,
That, that had made a Saint ſtart, well conſider'd,
The Law to be her creature, ſhe to make it,
Her mouth to give it, every creature living
From her aſpect, to draw their good or evil
Fix'd in 'em ſpight of Fortune; a new Nature
She ſhould be called, and Mother of all ages,
Time ſhould be hers, and what ſhe did, lame vertue
Should bleſs to all poſterities: her Air
Should give us life, her earth and water feed us.
And laſt, to none but to the Emperour,
(And then but when ſhe pleas'd to have it ſo)
She ſhould be held for mortal.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: And ſhe heard you?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Yes, as a Sick man hears a noiſe, or he
That ſtands condemn'd his judgment, let me periſh,
But if there can be vertue, if that name
Be any thing but name and empty title,
If it be ſo as fools have been pleas'd to feign it,
A power that can preſerve us after aſhes,
And make the names of men out-reckon ages,
This Woman has a God of vertue in her.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: I would the Emperor were that God.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: She has in her
All the contempt of glory and vain ſeeming
Of all the Stoicks, all the truth of Chriſtians,
And all their Conſtancy: Modeſty was made
When ſhe was firſt intended: when ſhe bluſhes
It is the holieſt thing to look upon;
The pureſt temple of her ſect, that ever
Made Nature a bleſt Founder.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Is there no way
To take this Phenix?

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: None but in her aſhes.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: If ſhe were fat, or any way inclining
To eaſe or pleaſure, or affected glory,
Proud to be ſeen and worſhip'd, 'twere a venture;
But on my ſoul ſhe is chaſter than cold Camphire.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: I think ſo too; for all the waies of Woman,
Like a full ſail ſhe bears againſt: I askt her
After my many offers walking with her,
And her as many down-denyals, how
If the Emperour grown mad with love ſhould force her:
She pointed to a Lucrece, that hung by,
And with an angry look, that from her eyes
Shot Veſtal fire againſt me, ſhe departed.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: This is the firſt wench I was ever pos'd in,
Yet I have brought young loving things together
This two and thirty years.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: I find by this wench
The calling of a Bawd to be a ſtrange,
A wiſe, and ſubtile calling; and for none
But ſtaid, diſcreet, and underſtanding people:
And as the Tutor to great Alexander,
Would ſay, a young man ſhould not dare to read
His moral books, till after five and twenty;
So muſt that he or ſhe, that will be bawdy,
(I mean diſcreetly bawdy, and be truſted)
If they will riſe, and gain experience,
Well ſteept in years, and diſcipline, begin it,
I take it 'tis no Boys play.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: Well, what's thought of?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: The Emperour muſt know it.

sp.speaker: Lyc.
sp.l: If the woman ſhould chance to fail too.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: As 'tis ten to one.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Why what remains, but new nets for the purchaſe?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Let's go conſider then: and if all fail,
This is the firſt quick Eele, that ſav'd her tail. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ardel.
sp.l: You ſtill inſiſt upon that Idol, Honour,
Can it renew your y • uth, can it add wealth,
That takes off wrinkles: can it draw mens eyes,
To gaze upon you in your age? can honour,
That truly is a Saint to none but Souldiers,
And look'd into, bears no reward but danger,
Leave you the moſt reſpected perſon living?
Or can the common kiſſes of a Husband,
(Which to a ſprightly Lady is a labour)
Make ye almoſt Immortal? ye are cozen'd,
The honour of a woman is her praiſes;
The way to get theſe, to be ſeen, and ſought too,
And not to bury ſuch a happy ſweetneſs
Under a ſmoaky roof.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I'le hear no more.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: That white, and red, and all that bleſſed beauty,
Kept from the eyes, that make it ſo, is nothing;
Then you are rarely fair, when men proclaim it;
The Phenix, were ſhe never ſeen, were doubted;
That moſt unvalued Horn the Unicorn
Bears to oppoſe the Huntſman, were it nothing
But tale, and meer tradition, would help no man;
But when the vertue's known, the honour's doubled:
Vertue is either lame, or not at all,
And love a Sacriledge, and not a Saint,
When it bars up the way to mens Petitions.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Nay ye ſhall love your Husband too; we come not
To make a Monſter of ye.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Are ye women?

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: You'll find us ſo, and women you ſhall thank too,
If you have grace to make your uſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Fye on ye.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Alas poor baſhful Lady, by my ſoul,
Had ye no other vertue, but your bluſhes,
And I a man, I ſhould run mad for thoſe:
How daintily they ſet her off, how ſweetly!

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Come Goddeſs, come, you move too near the earth,
It muſt not be, a better Orb ſtayes for you:
Here: be a Maid, and take 'em.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray leave me.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: That were a ſin ſweet Lady, and a way
To make us guilty of your melancholy:
You muſt not be alone; in converſation
Doubts are reſolv'd, and what ſticks near the conſcience
Made eaſie, and allowable.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Ye are Devils,

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: That you may one day bleſs for your damnation.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I charge ye in the name of Chaſtity,
Tempt me no more; how ugly ye ſeem to me?
There is no wonder men defame our Sex,
And lay the vices of all ages on us,
When ſuch as you ſhall bear the names of women;
If ye had eyes to ſee your ſelves, or ſence
Above the baſe rewards ye play the bawds for:
If ever in your lives ye heard of goodneſs,
(Though many Regions off, as men hear Thunder)
• f ever ye had Mothers, and they ſouls:
If ever Fathers, and not ſuch as you are;
If ever any thing were conſtant in you,
Beſides your ſins, or coming, but your courſes;
If ever any of your Anceſtors
Dyed worth a noble deed, that would be cheriſh'd;
Soul-frighted with this black infection,
You would run from one another, to repentance,
And from your guilty eyes drop out thoſe ſins,
That made ye blind, and beaſts.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Ye ſpeak well, Lady;
A ſign of fruitful education,
If your religious zeal had wiſdom with it.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: This Lady was ordain'd to bleſs the Empire,
And we may all give thanks for't.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: I believe ye.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: If any thing redeem the Emperour
From his wild flying courſes, this is ſhe;
She can inſtruct him if ye mark; ſhe is wiſe too.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Exceeding wiſe, which is a wonder in her,
And ſo religious, that I well believe,
Though ſhe would ſin ſhe cannot.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: And beſides,
She has the Empires cauſe in hand, not loves;
There lies the main conſideration,
For which ſhe is chiefly born.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: She finds that point
Stronger than we can tell her, and believe it
I look by her means for a reformation,
And ſuch a one, and ſuch a rare way carried
That all the world ſhall wonder at.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: 'Tis true;
I never thought the Emperor had wiſdom,
Pity, or fair affection to his Country,
Till he profeſt this love: gods give 'em Children,
Such as her vertues merit, and his zeal.
I look to ſee a Numa from this Lady,
Or greater than Octavius.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Do you mark too,
Which is a Noble vertue, how ſhe bluſhes,
And what a flowing modeſty runs through her,
When we but name the Emperour?

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: But mark it,
Yes, and admire it too, for ſhe conſiders,
Though ſhe be fair as Heaven, and vertuous
As holy truth, yet to the Emperour
She is a kind of nothing but her ſervice,
Which ſhe is bound to offer, and ſhe'll do it,
And when her Countries cauſe commands affection,
She knows obedience is the key of vertues,
Then flye the bluſhes out like Cupid's arrows,
And though the tye of Marriage to her Lord
Would fain cry, ſtay Lucina, yet the cauſe
And general wiſdom of the Princes love,
Makes here find ſurer ends and happier,
And if the firſt were chaſte, this is twice doubled.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Her tartneſs unto us too.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: That's a wiſe one.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: I rarely like, it ſhews a riſing wiſdom,
That chides all common fools as dare enquire
What Princes would have private

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: What a Lady
Shall we be bleſt to ſerve?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Go get ye from me:
Ye are your purſes Agents, not the Princes
Is this the vertuous Lo • e ye train'd me out to?
Am I a woman fit to imp your v • ces?
But that I had a Mother, and a woman
Whoſoever living fame turns all it touches,
Into the good it ſelf is, I ſhould now
Even doubt my ſelf, I have been ſ • arch't ſo near
The very ſoul of honour: why ſhould you two.
That happily have been as chaſte as I am,
Fairer, I think, by much, for yet your faces,
Like ancient well built piles, ſhew worthy ruins,
After that Angel age, turn mortal Devils?
For ſhame, for woman-hood, for what ye have been,
For rotten Cedars have born goodly branches,
If ye have hope of any Heaven, but Court,
Which like a Dream, you'l find hereafter vani • h,
Or at the beſt but ſubject to repentance,
Study no more to be ill ſpoken of;
Let women live themſelves, if they muſt fall,
Their own deſtruction find 'em, not your F • vours.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Madam, ye are ſo excellent in all,
And I muſt tell it you with admiration,
So true a joy ye have, ſo ſweet a fear,
And when ye come to anger, tis ſo noble,
That for mine own part, I could ſtill offend,
To hear you angry; women that want t •
Are either Fools, or Cowards

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l:
She were a Miſtris for no p •
〈…〉
Could ſhe not frown a raviſh'd kiſs 〈…〉

And ſuch an anger as this Lady lea •
〈◊〉
Stuck with ſuch pleaſing • angers. 〈…〉
Which of ye all could hold from?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I perceive ye,
Your own dark ſins dwell with ye, and t' at pr •
You ſell the chaſtity of modeſt wives at
Runs to diſeaſes with your bones: I ſcor • ,
And all the nets ye've pitcht to catch my v •
Like Spiders Webs, I ſweep away before me
Go tell the Emperour, ye have met a woman,
That neither his own perſon, which is God like,
The world he rules, nor what that world can purchaſe,
Nor all the glories ſubject to a Caeſar,
The honours that he offers for my body,
The hopes, gifts, everlaſting flatteries,
Nor any thing that's his, and apt to tempt me,
No not to be the Mother of the Empire,
And Queen of all the holy fires he worſhips,
Can make a Whore of.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: You miſtake us Lady.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Yet tell him this has thus much weaken'd me,
That I have heard his Knaves, and you his Matrons,
Fit Nurſes for his ſins, which gods forgive me;
But ever to be leaning to his folly,
Or to be brought to love his luſt, aſſure him,
And from her mouth, whoſe life ſhall make it certain,
I never can: I have a noble Husband,
Pray tell him that too, yet a noble name,
A Noble Family, and laſt a Conſcience:
Thus much for your anſwer: For your ſelves,
Ye have liv'd the ſhame of women, dye the better. Exit Luc.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: What's now to do?

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Ev'n as ſhe ſaid, to dye,
For there's no living here, and women thus,
I am ſure for us two.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Nothing ſtick upon her?

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: We have loſt a maſs of mony; well Dame Vertue,
Yet ye may halt if good luck ſerve.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Worms take her,
She has almoſt ſpoil'd our trade.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: So godly;
This is ill breeding, Phorba.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: If the women
Should have a longing now to ſee this Monſter,
And ſhe convert 'em all.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: That may be, Phorba,
But if it be, I'll have the young men gelded;
Come, let's go think, ſhe muſt not ſcape us thus;
Th • re is a certain ſeaſon, if we hit,
That women may be rid without a Bit. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I cannot blame the Nations, noble friend,
That they fall off ſo faſt from this wild man,
When (under our Allegiance be it ſpoken,
And the moſt happy tye of our affections)
The worlds weight groans beneath him; Where lives vertue,
Honour, diſcretion, wiſdom? who are call'd
And choſen to the ſteering of the Empire
But Bawds, and ſinging Girls? O my Aecius
The glory of a Souldier, and the truth
Of men made up for goodneſs ſake, like ſhells
Grow to the ragged walls for want of action;
Only your happy ſelf, and I that love you,
Which is a larger means to me than favour.
No more, my worthy friend, though theſe be truths,
And though theſe truths would ask a Reformation,
At leaſt a little ſquating: yet remember,
We are but Subj cts, Maximus; obedience
To what is done, and grief for what is ill done,
Is all we can call ours: The hearts of Princes
Are like the Templ • s of the gods; pure incenſe,
Until unhallowed hands defile thoſe offerings,
Burns ever there; we mu • t not put 'em out,
Becauſe the Prieſts that touch thoſe ſweets, are wicked;
We dare not, deareſt Friend, nay mo • we cannot,
While we conſider who we are, and how,
To what laws bound, much more to what Law-giver;
Whileſt Majeſty is made to be obeyed,
And not to b inquired into, whilſt gods and angels
Make but a rule as we do, though a ſtricter;
Like deſperate and unſeaſon'd Fools let flye
Our killing angers, and forſake our honours.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: My noble Friend, from whoſe inſtructions
I never yet took ſurfeit, weigh but thus much,
Nor think I ſpeak it with ambition,
For by the gods, I do not; why Aecius,
Why are we thus, or how become thus wretched?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: You'll fall again into your fit.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I will not;
Or are we now no more the Sons of Romans,
No more the followers of their happy fortunes,
But conquer'd Gauls, or Quivers for the Parthians?
Why, is this Emperour, this man we honour,
This God that ought to be?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: You are too curious.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Good, give me leave, why is this Author of us?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: I dare not hear ye ſpeak thus.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I'll be modeſt,
Thus led away, thus vainly led away,
And we Beholders? miſconceive me not,
I ſow no danger in my words; But wherefore,
And to what end, are we the Sons of Fathers
Famous and faſt to Rome? why are their Vertues
Stampt in the dangers of a thouſand Battels?
For goodneſs ſake, their honours, time outdaring?
I think for our example.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Ye ſpeak nobly.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Why are we ſeeds of theſe then, to ſhake hands
With Bawds and baſe informers, kiſs diſcredit,
And court her like a Miſtriſs? 'pray, your leave yet;
You'll ſay the Emperour is young, and apt
To take impreſſion rather from his pleaſures
Than any conſtant worthineſs, it may be,
But why do theſe, the people call his pleaſures,
Exceed the moderation of a man?
Nay to ſay juſtly, friend, why are they vices,
And ſuch as ſhake our worths with forreign Nations?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: You ſearch the ſore too deep, and I muſt tell ye.
In any other man this had been boldneſs,
And forewarded; 'pray depreſs your ſpirit,
For though I conſtantly believe you honeſt,
Ye were no friend for me elſe, and what now
Ye freely ſpake, but good you owe to th'Empire,
Yet take heed, worthy Maximus, all ears
Hear not with that diſtinction mine do, few
You'll find admoniſhers, but urgers of your actions,
And to the heavieſt (friend;) and pray conſider
We are but ſhadows, motions others give us,
And thougn our pities may become the times,
Juſtly our powers cannot; make me worthy
To be your friend ever in fair Allegiance,
But not in force; For durſt mine own ſoul urge me,
(And by that Soul I ſpeak my juſt affections)
To turn my hand from Truth, which is obedience,
And give the helm my Vertue holds, to Anger;
Though I had both the Bleſſings of the Bruti,
And both their inſtigations, though my Cauſe
Carried a face of Juſtice beyond theirs,
And as I am a ſervant to my fortunes,
That daring ſoul, that firſt taught diſobedience,
Should feel the firſt example: ſay the Prince,
As I may well believe, ſeems vicious,
Who juſtly knows 'tis not to try our honours?
Or ſay he be an ill Prince, are we therefore
Fit ſires to purge him? No, my deareſt friend,
The Elephant is never won with anger,
Nor muſt that man that would reclaim a Lion,
Take him by th' teeth.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I pray miſtake me not.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Our honeſt actions, and the light that breaks
Like morning from our ſervice, chaſte and bluſhing,
Is that that pulls a Prince back; then he ſees,
And not till then truly repents his errours,
When Subjects Cryſtal Souls are glaſſes to him.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: My ever honour'd friend, I'll take your counſel.
The Emperour appears, I'll leave ye to him.
And as we both affect him, may he flouriſh. Exit Max.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Is that the beſt news?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Yet the beſt we know, Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Bid Maximus come to me, and be gone then;
Mine own head be my helper, theſe are fools:
How now Aecius, are the Souldiers quiet?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Better I hope, Sir, than they were.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: They are pleas'd, I hear,
To cenſure me extreamly for my pleaſures,
Shortly they'll fight againſt me.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Gods defend, Sir.
And for their cenſures they are ſuch ſhrew'd Judgers;
A donative of ten Seſtertias
I'll undertake ſhall make 'em ring your praiſes
More than they ſang your pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I believe thee;
Art thou in love, Aecius, yet?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: O no Sir;
I am too courſe for Ladies; my embraces,
That only am acquainted with Alarms,
Would break their tender Bodies.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Never fear it,
They are ſtronger than ye think, they'll hold the Hammer.
My Empreſs ſwears thou art a luſty Souldier,
A good one I believe thee.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: All that goodneſs
Is but your Graces Creature.

sp.speaker: Emp
sp.l: Tell me truly,

Fo •
• ou dar'ſt tell me.
Any thing concerns ye,
Tha • 's fit for me to ſpeak and you to pardon.

sp.speaker: Emp
sp.l: What ſay the Souldiers of me, and the ſame words,

Min ••
• m not, good Aecius, but deliver
The very forms and tongues they talk withal.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: I'll tell your Grace, but with this caution
You be not ſtir'd, for ſhould the gods live with us,
Even thoſe we certainly believe are righteous,
Give 'em but drink, they would cenſure them too.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Forward.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Then to begin, they ſay you ſleep too much,
By which they judge your Majeſty too ſenſual,
Apt to decline your ſtrength to eaſe and pleaſures,
And when you do not ſleep, you drink too much,
From which they fear ſuſpicions firſt, then ruines;
And when ye neither drink nor ſleep, ye wench much,
Which they affirm firſt breaks your underſtanding,
Then takes the edge of Honour, makes us ſeem,
That are the ribs, and rampires of the Empire,
Fencers, and beaten Fools, and ſo regarded;
But I believe 'em not; for were theſe truths,
Your vertue can correct them.

sp.speaker: Emp
sp.l: They ſpeak plainly.
They ſay moreover (ſince your Grace will have it,
For they will talk their freedoms, though the Sword
Were in their throat) that of late time, like Nero,
And with the ſame forgetfulneſs of glory,
You have got a vein of fidling, ſo they term it.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Some drunken dreams, Aecius.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: So I hope, Sir:
And that you rather ſtudy cruelty,
And to be fear'd for blood, than lov'd for bounty,
Which makes the Nations, as they ſay, deſpiſe ye,
Telling your years and actions by their deaths,
Whoſe truth and ſtrength of duty made you Caeſar:
They ſay beſides you nouriſh ſtrange devourers,
• ed with the fat o'th' Empire, they call Bawds,
Lazie and luſtful Creatures that abuſe ye,
A • eople as they term 'em, made of paper,
In which the ſecret ſins of each man's monies
Are ſeal'd and ſent a working.
What ſin's next?
For I perceive they have no mind to ſpare me.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Nor hurt you o' my ſoul, Sir; but ſuch People
(Nor can the power of man reſtrain it)
When they are full of meat and eaſe, muſt prattle.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Forward.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: I have ſpoken too much, Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I'll have all.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: It fits not
Your ears ſhould hear their Vanities; no profit
Can juſtly riſe to you from their behaviour,
Unleſs ye were guilty of thoſe crimes.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: It may be
I am ſo, therefore forward.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: I have ever
Learn'd to obey, nor ſhall my life reſiſt it.

sp.speaker: Emp
sp.l: No more Apologies.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: They grieve beſides, Sir,
To ſee the Nations, whom our ancient Vertue
With many a weary march and hunger conquer'd,
With loſs of many a daring life ſubdu'd,
Fall from their fair obedience, and even murmur
To ſee the warlike Eagles mew their honours
In obſcure Towns, that wont to prey on Princes,
They cry for Enemies, and tell the Captains
The fruits of Italy are luſcious, give us Egypt,
Or ſandy Africk to diſplay our valours,
There where our Swords may make us meat, and danger
Digeſt our well got Vyands; here our weapons
And bodies that were made for ſhining braſs,
Are both unedg'd and old with eaſe and women.
And then they cry again, where are the Germans,

Lin'd with hot Spain, o •
Gallia, bring 'em on,
And let the Son of War, ſteel'd Mithridates,
Lead up his winged Parthians like a ſtorm,
Hiding the face of Heaven with ſhowrs of Arrows?
Yet we dare fight like Romans; then as Souldiers
Tir'd with a weary march, they tell their wounds
Even weeping ripe they were no more nor deeper,
And glory in thoſe ſcars that make them lovely,
And ſitting where a Camp was, like ſad Pilgrims
They reckon up the times, and living labours
Of Julius or Germanicus, and wonder
That Rome, whoſe Turrets once were topt with Honours,
Can now forget the Cuſtom of her Conqueſts;
And then they blame your Grace, and ſay Who leads us,
Shall we ſtand here like Statues? were our Fathers
The Sons of lazie Moors, our Princes Perſians,
Nothing but ſilks and ſoftneſs? Curſes on 'em
That firſt taught Nero wantonneſs and blood,
Tiberius doubts, Caligula all vices;
For from the ſpring of theſe, ſucceeding Princes—
Thus they talk, Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Well,
W • y do you hear theſe things?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Why do you do 'em?
I take the gods to witneſs, with more ſorrow,
And more vexation do I hear theſe tainters
Than were my life dropt from me through an hour glaſs.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Belike then you believe 'em, or at leaſt
Are glad they ſhould be ſo; take heed, you were better
Build your own Tomb, and run into it living,
Than dare a Princes anger.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: I am old, Sir,
And ten years more addition, is but nothing;
Now if my life be pleaſing to ye, take it,
Upon my knees, if ever any ſervice,

(As let 〈◊〉
• ag ſome have been worthy notice)
If ev • an • wo • th, o • truſt ye gave me
Deſerv d a word • pect, if all my actions,
The ha • of my youth, colds, burnings, wants,
By that ſtil • ye hav • ſtampt upon me, Souldier,
Let me not fa • l into the hands of Wretches.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I underſtand you not.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Let not this body
That has look'd bravely in his blood for Caeſar,
And cov • tous of wounds, and for your ſafety,

After th •
•• eape of Swords, Spears, Slings, and Arrows,
'Gainſt which my beaten body was mine armour,
The Seas and thirſty Deſarts now be purchaſe
For Slav • s, and baſe Informers; I ſee anger,
And death look through your Eyes; I am markt for ſlaughter,
And know the telling of this truth has made me
Only my laſt P • tition, ſacred Caeſar,
Is, I may dye a Roman.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Riſe, my friend ſtill,
And worthy of my love, reclaim the Souldier,
I'll ſtudy to do ſo upon my ſelf too,
Go, keep your Command, and proſper.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Lif • to Caeſar— Exit Aecius

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Lord Maximus attends your Grace.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Go tell him
I'll meet him in the Gallery:
The honeſty of this Aecius,
Who is indeed the Bull-wark of the Empire,
Has div'd ſo deep into me, that of all
The ſins I covet, but this Womans beauty,
With much repentance now I could be quit of;
But ſhe is ſuc • a pleaſure, being good,
That though I were a god, ſhe'd fire my blood.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter the Emperour, Maximus, Licinius, Proculus, Chilax, as at Dice.

sp.speaker: Emp
sp.l: NAy ye ſhall ſet my hand out, 'tis not juſt
I ſhould neglect my fortune now 'tis proſperous.
If I have any thing to ſet your Grace,
But Cloaths or good conditions, let me periſh.
You have all my money, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: And mine.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: And mine too.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Unleſs your Grace will credit us.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: No bare board.
Then at my Garden-Houſe.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: The Orchard too.

sp.speaker: Lic.
sp.l: And't pleaſe your Grace.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Have at 'em.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: They are loſt.

sp.speaker: Lic.
sp.l: Why, farewel Fig-trees.

sp.speaker: Emp
sp.l: Who ſets more?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: At my horſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: The dapl'd Spaniard?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: He.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: He's mine.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: He is ſo.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Your ſhort horſe is ſoon curried.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: So it ſeems, Sir,
So may your Mare be too, if luck ſerve.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Nothing my Lord, but grieving at my fortune.

sp.speaker: Emp
sp.l: Come Maximus, you were not wont to flinch thus.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I have loſt all.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: There's a Ring yet.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: This was not made to loſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Some love token;
Set it I ſay.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I do beſeech your Grace,
Rather name any houſe I have.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: How ſtrange
And curious you are grown of toys! redeem't
If ſo I win it, when you pleaſe, to morrow,
Or next day, as you will, I care not,
But only for my lucks ſake, 'tis not Rings
Can make m • richer.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Will you throw, Sir? there 'tis.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Why, then have at it fairly, mine.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Your Grace
Is only ever fortunate; to morrow,
And't be your pleaſure, Sir, I'll pay the price on't.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: To morrow you ſhall have it without price, Sir,
But this day 'tis my Victory; good Maximus,
Now I bethink my ſelf, go to Aecius,
And bid him muſter all the Cohorts preſently;
They mutiny for pay I hear, and be you
Aſſiſtant to him; when you know their numbers,
Ye ſhall have monies for 'em, and above,
Something to ſtop their tongues withal.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I will Sir,
And gods preſerve you in this mind ſtill.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Shortly I'll ſee 'em march my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Gods ever keep ye — Exit Maximus.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: To what end do you think this Ring ſhall ſerve now?
For ye are Fellows only know by rote,
As Birds record their leſſons.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: For the Lady.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: But how for her?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: That I confeſs I know not.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Then pray for him that does: fetch me an Eunuch
That never ſaw her yet, and you two ſee
The C • t made like a Paradiſe. Exit Chilax.

sp.speaker: Lic.
sp.l: We will, Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Full of fair ſhews and Muſicks; all your arts
(As I ſhall give inſtructions) ſcrew to th' higheſt,
For my main piece is now a doing; and for fear
You ſhould not take, I'll have another Engine,
Such as if vertue be not only in her,
She ſhall not chuſe but lean to, let the Women
Put on a graver ſhew of welcome.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: They are a thought too eager.

div.stage: Enter Chilax, and Lycias the Eunuch.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Here's the Eunuch.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: Long life to Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I muſt uſe you, Lycias:
Come, let's walk in, and then I'll ſhew ye all,
If women may be frail, this wench ſhall fall. Exeunt

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Sirrah, what ails my Lady that of late
She never cares for Company?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I know not,
Unleſs it be that Company cauſes Cuckolds.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: That were a childiſh fear.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What were thoſe Ladies,
Came to her lately
From the Court?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: The ſame wench,
Some grave inſtructors on my life, they look
For all the world like old hatcht hilts.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis true, Wench,
For here and there, and yet they painted well too,
One might diſcover where the Gold was worn,
Their iron ages.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: If my judgement fail not,
They have been ſheathed like rotten Ships.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It may be.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: For if you mark their rudders, they hang wealth.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: They have paſt the line belike; wouldſt live Clau • s
Till thou wert ſuch as they are?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Chimney pieces:
Now heaven have mercy upon me, and young men,
I had rather make a drollery till thirty,
While I am able to endure a tempeſt,
And hear my fights out bravely, till my tackle
Whilſtl'd i'th' Wind, and held againſt all weathers,
While I were able to bear with my tyres,
And ſo diſcharge 'em, I would willingly
Live, Marcellina, not till barnacles
Bred in my ſides.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thou art i'th' right, Wench;
For who would live whom pleaſures had forſaken,
To ſtand at mark, and cry a Bow ſhort, Seigneur?
Were there not men came hither too?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Brave fellows:
I fear me Bawds of five i'th' Pound.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: How know you?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: They gave me great lights to it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Take heed, Claudia.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Let them take heed, the ſpring comes on.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To me now
They ſeem'd as noble Viſitants.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: To me now
Nothing leſs, Marcellina, for I markt 'em,
And by this honeſt light, for yet 'tis morning,
Saving the reverence of their gilded doublets,
And Millan skins.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thou art a ſtrange Wench, Claudia.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Ye are deceiv'd, they ſhew'd to me directly
Court Crabs that creep a ſide-way for their living,
I know 'em by the Breeches that they beg'd laſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Peace, my Lady comes; what may that be?

div.stage: Enter Lucina, and Lycias, the Eunuch.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: A Sumner
That cites her to appear.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No more of that wench.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: Madam, what anſwer to your Lord?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Pray tell him, I am ſubject to his will.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: Why weep you Madam?
Excellent Lady, there are none will hurt you.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I do beſeech you tell me Sir.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: What, Lady?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Serve ye the Emperor?

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: I do.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: In what place?

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: In's chamber Madam.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Do ye ſerve his will too?

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: In fair and juſt commands.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Are ye a Roman?

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: Yes noble Lady, and a Mantuan.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: What office bore your parents?

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: One was Pretor.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Take heed then how you ſtain his reputation.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: Why worthy Lady?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: If ye know, I charge ye,
Ought in this Meſſage, but what honeſty,
The truſt and fair obedience of a ſervant
May well deliver, yet take heed, and help me.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: Madam, I am no Broker.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: I'le be hang'd then.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: Nor baſe procurer of mens luſts; Your husband,
Pray'd me to do this office, I have done it,
It reſts in you to come, or no.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I will Sir.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: If ye miſtruſt me, do not.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Ye appear ſo worthy,
And to all my ſenſe ſo honeſt,
And this is ſuch a certain ſign ye have brought me,
That I believe.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: Why ſhould I cozen you?
Or were I brib'd to do this villany,
Can mony proſper, or the fool that takes it,
When ſuch a vertue falls?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Ye ſpeak well Sir;
Would all the reſt that ſerve the Emperour,
Had but your way.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: And ſo they have ad unguem.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Pray tell my Lord, I have receiv'd his Token,
And will not fail to meet him; yet good Sir, thus much
Before you goe, I do beſeech ye too,
As little notice as ye can, deliver
Of my appearance there.

sp.speaker: Eun.
sp.l: It ſhall be Madam,
And ſo I wiſh you happineſs.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I thank you — Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA II. Tumult & noiſe within.
div.stage: Enter Aecius, purſuing Pontius, the Captain, and Maximus, following.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Temper your ſelf Aecius.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: Hold my Lord,
I am a Roman, and a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Pray Sir.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Thou art a lying Villain, and a Traytor;
Give me my ſelf, or by the Gods my friend
You'l make me dangerous; how dar'ſt thou pluck
The Souldiers to ſedition, and I living,
And ſow Rebellion in 'em, and even then
When I am drawing out to action?

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: Hear me.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Are ye a man?

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: I am a true hearted, Maximus,
And if the Villain live, we are diſhonour'd.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: But hear him what he can ſay.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: That's the way,
To pardon him; I am ſo eaſie natur'd,
That if he ſpeak but humbly I forgive him.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: I do beſeech ye noble General.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Has found the way already give me room,
One ſtroak, and if he ſcape me then h'as mercy.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: I do not call ye noble, that I fear ye,
I never car'd for death; if ye will kill me,
Conſider firſt for what, not what you can do.
'Tis true, I know ye for my General,
And by that great Prerogative may kill.
But do it juſtly then.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: He argues with me,
A made up Rebel.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Pray conſider,
What certain grounds ye have for th • .

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: What grounds?
Did I not take him preaching to the Souldier
How lazily they liv'd, and what diſhonours
It was to ſerve a Prince ſo full of woman?
Thoſe were his very words, friend.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Theſe, Aecius,
Though they were raſhly ſpoke, which was an errour
(A great one Pontius) yet from him that hungers
Fo • wars, and brave imployment, might be pardon'd.
The heart, and harbou 'd thoughts of ill, make Traytors,
Not ſpleeny ſpeeches.
Why ſhould you protect him?
Goe to, it ſhews not honeſt.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Taint me not,
For that ſhews worſe A • cius: All your friendſhip
And that p entended love ye lay upon me,
Hold back my honeſty, is like a favour
You do you ſlave to day, to morrow hang him,
Was I your boſome piece for this?

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Forgive me,
The nature of my zeal, and for my Country,
Makes me ſometimes forget my ſelf; for know,
Though I moſt ſtrive to be without my paſſions,
I am no God: For you Sir, whoſe infection
Has ſpread it ſelf like poyſon through the army,
And caſt a killing fog on fair allegiance,
Firſt thank this noble Gentleman, ye had dy'd elſe;
Next from your place, and honour of a Souldier,
I here ſeclude you.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: May I ſpeak yet?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Hear him.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: And while Aecius holds a reputation,
At leaſt command, ye bear no arms for Rome Sir.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: Againſt her I ſhall never: the condemn'd man
Has yet that priviledge to ſpeak, my Lord;
Law were not equall elſe.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Pray hear Aecius,
For happily the fault he has committed,
Though I believe it mighty, yet conſidered,
If mercy may be thought upon, will prove
Rather a haſtie ſin, than heynous.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Speak.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: 'Tis true my Lord, ye took me tir'd with peace,
My words almoſt as ragged as my fortunes.
'Tis true I told the Souldier, whom we ſerv'd,
And then bewail'd, we had an Emperour
Led from us by the flouriſhes of Fencers;
I blam'd him too for women.

sp.speaker: Aec.
sp.l: To the reſt Sir.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: And like enough I bleſt him then as Souldiers
Will do ſometimes: 'Tis true I told 'em too,
We lay at home, to ſhow our Country
We durſt goe naked, durſt want meat, and mony,
And when the ſlave drinks wine, we durſt be thirſtie:
I told 'em this too, that the Trees and Roots
Were our beſt pay-maſters; the Charity
Of longing women, that had bought our bodies,
Our beds, fires, Taylers, Nurſes. Nay I told 'em,
(For you ſhall hear the greateſt ſin, I ſaid Sir)
By that time there be wars again, our bodies
Laden with ſca • s, and aches, and ill lodgings,
H • ats, and perpetual wants, were fitter prayers
And certain graves, than cope the foe on crutches:
'Tis likely too, I counſell'd 'em to turn
Their warlike pikes to plough-ſhares, their ſure Targets
And Swords hatcht with the bloud of many Nations,
To Spades, and prunning Knives, for thoſe get mony,
Th • i • warlike Eagles, into Daws, or Starlings,
To • ve an Ave Caeſar as he paſſes,
And be rewarded with a thouſand drachma's,

For th •
〈◊〉 but years and be • ts.
W • at thin • you,
Were theſe words to be ſpoken by a Captain,
One that ſhould g • ve example?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: 'Twas too much.

sp.speaker: Pon
sp.l: My Lord, I did not wooe 'em from the Empire,

No •
〈◊〉 'em turn their daring ſteel 'gainſt Caeſar,
The Gods for ever hate me, if that motion
Were part of me: Give me but imployment, Sir;
And way to live, and where you hold me vicious,
Bred up in mutiny, my Sword ſhall tell ye,
And if you pleaſe, that place I held, maintain it,
'Gainſt the moſt daring foes of Rome. I am honeſt,
A lover of my Country, one that holds
His life no longer his, than kept for Caeſar.
Weigh not (I thus low on my knee beſeech you)
What my rude tongue diſcovered, 'twas my want,
No other pair of Pontius: you have ſeen me,
And you my Lord, do ſomething for my Country,
And both beheld the wounds I gave and took,
Not like a backward Traytor.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: All this language
Makes but againſt you Pontius, you are caſt,
And by mine honour, and my love to Caeſar,
By me ſhall never be reſtor'd; In my Camp
I will not have a tongue, though to himſelf
Dare talk but near ſedition; as I govern,
All ſhall obey, and when they want, their duty
And ready ſervice ſhall redreſs their needs,
Not prating what they would be.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: Thus! leave ye,
Yet ſhall my prayers ſtill, although my fortunes
Muſt follow you no more, be ſtill about ye,
Gods give ye where ye fight the Victory,
Ye cannot caſt my wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Come my Lord,
Now to the Field again.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Alas poor Pontius. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENA IV.
div.stage: Enter Chilax, at one door, Licinius, and Balbus, at another.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: How how?

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: She's come.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: Then I'le to'th Emperour. Exit Balbus.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Do; Is the Muſick placed well?

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Licinius, you and Proclus receive her
In the great Chamber, at her entrance,
Let me alone; and do you hear Licinius,
Pray let the Ladies ply her further off,
And with much more diſcretion: one word more.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: Are the Jewels, and thoſe ropes of Pearl,
Laid in the way ſhe paſſes?

sp.speaker: Lici
sp.l: Take no care man — Exit Licinius.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: What is ſhe come?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: She is Sir; but 'twere beſt,
Your Grace were ſeen laſt to her.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: So I mean;
Keep the Court emptie Proculus.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: 'Tis done Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Be not too ſudden to her.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Good your Grace,
Retire, and man your ſelf; let us alone,
We are no children this way: do you hear Sir?
'Tis neceſſary that her waiting women
Be cut off in the Lobby, by ſome Ladies,
They'd break the buſineſs elſe.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: 'Tis true, they ſhall.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Remember your place Proculus.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I warrant ye.— Exeunt Emp. Bal. and Pro.

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: She enters: who are waiters there? the Emperour
Calls for his Horſe to air himſelf.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I am glad,
I come ſo happily to take him abſent,
This takes away a little fear; I know him,
Now I begin to fear again: O honour,
If ever thou hadſt temple in weak woman,
And ſacrifice of modeſty burnt to thee,
Hold me faſt now, and help me.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Noble Madam,
Ye are welcom to the Court, moſt nobly welcom,
Ye are a ſtranger Lady.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I deſire ſo.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: A wondrous ſtranger here,
Nothing ſo ſtrange:
And therefore need a guide I think.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I do Sir,
And that a good one too.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: My ſervice Lady,
Shall be your guide in this place; But pray ye tell me,
Are ye reſolv'd a Courtier?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: No I hope Sir.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: You are, Sir?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Yes, my fair one.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: So it ſeems,
You are ſo ready to beſtow your ſelf,
Pray what might coſt thoſe Breeches?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Would you wear 'em?
Madam ye have a witty woman.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Two Sir,
Or elſe ye underbuy us.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Leave your talking:
But is my Lord here, I beſeech ye, Sir?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: He is ſweet Lady, and muſt take this kindly,
Exceeding kindly of ye, wondrous kindly
Ye come ſo far to viſit him: I'le guide ye.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Whither?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Why to your Lord.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Is it ſo hard Sir,
To find him in this place without a Guide?
For I would willingly not trouble you.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: It will be ſo for you that are a ſtranger;
Nor can it be a trouble to do ſervice
To ſuch a worthy beauty, and beſides—

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I ſee he will goe with us.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Let him amble.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: It fits not that a Lady of your reckoning
Should paſs without attendants.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I have two Sir.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: I mean without a man; You'l ſee the Emperour?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Alas I am not fit Sir.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: You are well enough,
He'l take it wondrous kindly: Hark.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Ye flatter,
Good Sir, no more of that.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Well, I but tell ye.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Will ye goe forward, ſince I muſt be man'd,
Pray take your place.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Cannot ye man us too Sir?

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Give me but time.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And you'l try all things.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: No:
I'le make no ſuch promiſe.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: If ye do Sir,
Take heed ye ſtand to't.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Wondrous merry Ladies. Ex.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: The wenches are diſpos'd, pray keep your way Sir.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: She is coming up the ſtairs; Now the Muſick;
And as that ſtirs her, let's ſet on: perfumes there.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Diſcover all the Jewels.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: Peace. Muſick.

lg.l: NOw the luſty Spring is ſeen,
Golden yellow, gaudy Blew,
Daintily invite the view.
Every where, on every Green,
Roſes bluſhing as they blow,
And inticing men to pull,
Lillies whiter than the ſnow,
Woodbines of ſweet hony full.
All Loves Emblems and all cry,
Ladys, if not pluckt we dye.
Yet the luſty Spring hath ſtaid,
Bluſhing red and pureſt white,
Daintily to love invite,
Every Woman, every Maid,
Cherries kiſſing as they grow;
And inviting men to taſte,
Apples even ripe below,
Winding gently to the waſte:
All loves emblems and all cry,
Ladies, if not pluckt we dye.
HEar ye Ladies that deſpiſe
What the mighty Love has done,
Fear examples, and be wiſe,
Fair Caliſto was a Nun,
Laeda ſailing on the ſtream,
To deceive the hopes of man,
Love accounting but a dream,
Doted on a ſilver Swan,
Danae in a Brazen Tower,
Where no love was, lov'd a Showr.
Hear ye Ladys that are coy,
What the mighty Love can do,
Fear the fierceneſs of the Boy,
The chaſte Moon he makes to wooe:
Veſta kindling holy fires,
Circled round about with ſpies,
Never dreaming looſe deſires,
Doting at the Altar dies.
Ilion in a ſhort hour higher
He can build, and once more fire.

div.stage: Enter Chilax, Lucina, Claudia, and Marcellina.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Pray Heaven my Lord be here, for now I fear it.
Well Ring, if thou bee'ſt counterfeit, or ſtoln,
As by this preparation I ſuſpect it,
Thou haſt betrai'd thy Miſtris: pray Sir forward,
I would fain ſee my Lord.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: But tell me Madam,
How do ye like the Song?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I like the air well,
But for the words, they are laſcivious,
And over light for Ladies,

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: All ours love 'em.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: 'Tis like enough, for yours are loving Ladies.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: Madam, ye are welcom to the Court. Who waits?
Attendants for this Lady.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Ye miſtake Sir;
I bring no triumph with me.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: But much honour.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Why this was nobly done; and like a neighbour,
So freely of your ſelf to be a viſitant,
The Emperour ſhall give ye thanks for this.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: O no Sir;
There's nothing to deſerve 'em.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Yes, your preſence.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Good Gentlemen be patient, and believe
I come to ſee my husband, on command too,
I were no Courtier elſe.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: That's all one Lady,
Now ye are here, y'are welcom, and the Emperour
Who loves ye, but too well.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: No more of that Sir.
I came not to be Catechiz'd.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Ah Sirrah;
And have we got you here? ſaith Noble Lady,
We'l keep you one month Courtier.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Gods defend Sir,
I never lik'd a trade worſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Hark ye.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Ye are grown the ſtrangeſt Lady.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: By Heaven,
'Tis true I tell ye, and you'l find it.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I?
I'le rather find my grave, and ſo inform him.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Is it not pity Gentlemen, this Lady,
(Nay I'le deal roughly with ye, yet not hurt ye)
Shold live alone, and give ſuch heavenly beauty
Only to walls, and hangings?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Good Sir, patience:
I am no wonder, neither come to that end,
Ye do my Lord an injury to ſtay me,
Who though ye are the Princes, yet dare tell ye
He keeps no wife for your wayes.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: Well, well Lady;
However you are pleas'd to think of us,
Ye are welcom, and ye ſhall be welcome.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Shew it
In that I come for then, in leading me
Where my lov'd Lord is, not in flattery:— Jewels ſhew'd.
Nay ye may draw the Curtain, I have ſeen 'em,
But none worth half my honeſty.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Are theſe Sir,
Laid here to take?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Yes, for your Lady, Gentlewomen.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: We had been doing elſe.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: Meaner Jewels
Would fit your worths.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: And meaner clothes your bodies.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: The Gods ſhall kill me firſt.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: There's better dying;
I'th' Emperours arms goe to, but be not angry—
Theſe are but talks ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Where is this ſtranger? ruſhes, Ladys, ruſhes,
Ruſhes as green as Summer for this ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Here's Ladies come to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: You are gone then?
I take it 'tis your Q •

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Or rather manners,
You are better fitted Madam, we but tire ye,
Therefore we'l leave you for an hour, and bring
Your much lov'd Lord unto you — Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Then I'le thank ye,
I am betrai'd for certain; well Lucina,
If thou do'ſt fall from vertue, may the Earth
That after death ſhould ſhoot up gardens of thee,
Spreading thy living goodneſs into branches,
Fry from thee, and the hot Sun find thy vices.

sp.speaker: Pho.
sp.l: You are a welcom woman.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: Bleſs me Heaven,
How did you find the way to Court?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I know not,
Would I had never trod it.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Prethee tell me,
Good noble Lady, and good ſweet heart love us,
For we love thee extreamly; is not this place
A Paradiſe to live in?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: To thoſe people
That know no other Paradiſe but pleaſure,
That little I enjoy contents me better.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: What, heard ye any Muſick yet?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Too much.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: You muſt not be thus froward; what, this gown
Is one o'th' prettieſt by my troth Ardelia,
I ever ſaw yet; 'twas not to frown in Lady,
Ye put this gown on when ye came.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: How do ye?
Alas poor wretch how cold it is!

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Content ye;
I am as well as may be, and as temperate,
If ye will let me be ſo: where's my Lord?
For there's the buſineſs that I came for, Ladies.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: We'l lead ye to him, he's i'th' Gallery.

sp.speaker: Ard.
sp.l: We'l ſhew ye all the Court too.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Shew me him,
And ye have ſhew'd me all I come to look on.

sp.speaker: Phor.
sp.l: Come on, we'l be your guides, and as ye goe,
We have ſome pretty tales to tell ye Lady,
Shall make ye merry too; ye come not here,
To be a ſad Lucina.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Would I might not.— Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: Now the ſoft Muſick; Balbus run—

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: I flye Boy— Exit Balbus.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: The women by this time are worming of her, —
If ſhe can hold out them, the Emperour Muſick.
Takes her to task: he has her; hark the Muſick.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Good your Grace,
Where are my women Sir?

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: They are wiſe, beholding
What you think ſcorn to look on, the Courts bravery:
Would you have run away ſo ſlily Lady,
And not have ſeen me?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I beſeech your Majeſtie,
Conſider what I am, and whoſe.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I do ſo.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Believe me, I ſhall never make a whore Sir.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: A friend ye may, and to that man that loves ye,
More than you love your vertue.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Sacred Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: You ſhall not kneel to me ſweet.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Look upon me,
And if ye be ſo cruel to abuſe me,
Think how the Gods will take it; does this beauty
Afflict your ſoul? I'le hide it from you ever,
Nay more, I will become ſo leprous,
That ye ſhall curſe me from ye: My dear Lord
Has ſerv'd ye ever truly, fought your Battels,
As if he daily long'd to dy for Caeſar,
Was never Traytor Sir, no • n • ver tainted
In all the actions of his life.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I know it.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Hi • ſame and family have grown together,
And ſpred together like to ſailing Cedars,
Over the Roman Diadem; O let not,
As ye have any fleſh that's humane in you,
The having of a modeſt wife decline him,
Let not my vertue be the wedge to break him.
I do not think ye are laſcivious,
Theſe wanton men belye ye, you are Caeſar,
Which is the Father of the Empires honour,
Ye are too near the nature of the Gods,
To wrong the weakeſt of all creatures, women.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I dare not do it here, riſe fair Lucina,
I did but try your temper, ye are honeſt,
And with the commendations wait on that
I'le lead ye to your Lord, and give you to him:
Wipe your fair eyes: he that endeavours ill,
May well delay, but never quench his hell.— Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Chilax, Licinius, Proculus, and Balbus.

sp.speaker: Chil.
sp.l: 'TIS done Licinius.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Chil
sp.l: I ſhame to tell it,
If there be any juſtice, we are Villains,
And muſt be ſo rewarded.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.l: If it be done,
I take it 'tis no time now to repent it,
Let's make the beſt o'th' trade.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Now vengeance take it,
Why ſhould not he have ſetled on a beauty,
Whoſe honeſty ſtuck in a piece of tiſſue,
Or one a Ring might rule, or ſuch a one
That had an itching husband to be honourable,
And ground to get it: if he muſt have women,
And no allay without 'em, why not thoſe
That know the miſery, and are beſt able
To play a game with judgement? ſuch as ſhe is,
Grant they be won with long ſiege, endleſs travel,
And brought to opportunity with millions,
Yet when they come to motion, their cold vertue
Keeps 'em like cakes of Ice; I'le melt a Cryſtal,
And make a dead flint fire himſelf, e're they
Give greater heat, than new departing embers
Give to old men that watch 'em.

sp.speaker: Lici.
sp.l: A good Whore
Had ſav'd all this, and happily as wholſom,
I, and the thing once done too, as well thought of,
But this ſame chaſtity forſooth.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: A Pox on't,
Why ſhould not women be as free as we are?
They are, but not in open, and far freer,
And the more bold ye bear your ſelf, more welcom,
And there is nothing you dare ſay, but truth,
But they dare hear.—

sp.speaker: Chi.
sp.l: The Emperour! away,
And if we can repent, let's home and pray. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Your only vertue now is patience,
Take heed, and ſave your honour; if you talk.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: As long as there is motion in my body,
And life to give me words, I'le cry for juſtice.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: Juſtice ſhall never hear ye, I am juſtice.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Wilt thou not kill me, Monſter, Raviſher,
Thou bitter bane o'th' Empire, look upon me,
And if thy guilty eyes dare ſee theſe ruines,
Thy wild luſt hath laid level with diſhonour,
The ſacrilegious razing of this Temple,
The mother of thy black ſins would have bluſh'd at,
Behold and curſe thy ſelf; the Gods will find thee,
That's all my refuge now, for they are righteous,
Vengeance and horror circle thee; the Empire,
In which thou liv'ſt a ſtrong continued ſurfeit,
Like poyſon will diſgorge thee, good men raze thee
For ever being read again, — but vicious.
Women, and fearfull Maids, make vows againſt thee:
Thy own Slaves, if they hear of this, ſhall hate thee;
And thoſe thou haſt corrupted firſt fall from thee;
And if thou let'ſt me live, the Souldier,
Tir'd with thy Tyrannies, break through obedience,
And ſhake his ſtrong Steel at thee.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: This prevails not;
Nor any Agony ye utter Lady,
If I have done a ſin, curſe her that drew me,
Curſe the firſt cauſe, the witchcraft that abus'd me,
Curſe thoſe fair eyes, and curſe that heavenly beauty,
And curſe your being good too.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Glorious thief,
What reſtitution canſt thou make to ſave me?

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I'le ever love, and honour you.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Thou canſt not,
For that which was mine honour, thou haſt murdred,
And can there be a love in violence?

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: You ſhall be only mine.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Yet I like better
Thy villany, than flattery, that's thine own,
The other baſely counterfeit; flye from me,
Or for thy ſafety ſake and wiſdom kill me,
For I am worſe than thou art; thou maiſt pray,
And ſo recover grace; I am loſt for ever,
And if thou let'ſt me live, th'art loſt thy ſelf too.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: I fear no loſs but love, I ſtand above it.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Call in your Lady Bawds, and guilded Pander's
And let them triumph too, and ſing to Caeſar,
Lucina's faln, the chaſt Lucina's conquer'd;
Gods! what a wretched thing has this man made me?
For I am now no wife for Maximus,
No company for women that are vertuous,
No familie I now can claim, nor Country,
Nor name, but Caeſar's whore; O ſacred Caeſar,
(For that ſhould be your title) was your Empire,
Your Rods, and Axes, that are types of Juſtice,
Thoſe fires that ever burn, to beg you bleſſings,
The peoples adoration, fear of Nations,
What victory can bring ye home, what elſe
The uſefull Elements can make your ſervants,
Even light it ſelf, and ſuns of light, truth, Juſtice,
Mercy, and ſtarlike pietie ſent to you,
And from the gods themſelves, to raviſh women?
The curſes that I owe to Enemies,
Even thoſe the Sabines ſent, when Romulus,
(As thou haſt me) raviſh'd their noble Maids,
Made more, and heavier, light on thee.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: This helps not.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: The ſins of Tarquin be remember'd in thee,
And where there has a chaſt wife been abus'd,
Let it be thine, the ſhame thine, thine the ſlaughter,
And laſt for ever thine, the fear'd example.
Where ſhall poor vertue live, now I am faln?
What can your honours now, and Empire make me,
But a more glorious Whore?

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: A better woman,
But if ye will be blind, and ſcorn it, who can help it?
Come leave theſe lamentations, they do nothing,
But make a noyſe, I am the ſame man ſtill,
Were it to do again; therefore be wiſer,
By all this holy light, I ſhould attempt it,
Ye are ſo excellent, and made to raviſh,
There were no pleaſure in ye elſe.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Oh villain.

sp.speaker: Emp.
sp.l: So bred for mans amazement, that my reaſon
And every help to hold me right has loſt me;
The God of love himſelf had been before me
Had he but power to ſee ye; tell me juſtly,
How can I chooſe but err then? if ye dare
Be mine, and only mine, for ye are ſo pretious,
I envie any other ſhould enjoy ye,
Almoſt look on ye; and your daring husband
Shall know h'as kept an offring from the Empire,
Too holy for his Altars; be the mightieſt,
More than my ſelf I'le make it: if ye will not
Sit down with this, and ſilence, for which wiſdom
Ye ſhall have uſe of me, and much honour ever,
And be the ſame you were; if ye divulge it,
Know I am far above the faults I do,
And thoſe I do I am able to forgive too;
And where your credit in the knowledge of it,
May be with gloſs enough ſuſpected, mine
Is as mine own command ſhall make it:
Princes though they be ſometime ſubject to looſe whiſpers,
Yet wear they two edged ſwords for open cenſures:
Your husband cannot help ye, nor the Souldier;
• our husband is my creature, they my weapons,
And only where I bid 'em ſtrike; I feed 'em,
Nor can the Gods be angry at this action,
For as they make me mo • , they mean me happieſt,
Which I had never been without this pleaſure:
Conſider, and farewell: you'l find your women
At home before ye, •• ey have had ſome ſport too,
But are more thankful for it— Exit Emperour.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Deſtruction find thee.
Now which way muſt I go? my honeſt houſe
Will ſhake to ſhelter me, my husband flee me,
My Family, becauſe they are honeſt, and deſire to be ſo,
Muſt not endure me, not a neighbour know me:
What woman now dare ſee me without bluſhes,
And pointing as I paſs, there, there, behold her,
Look on her little Children, that is ſhe,
That handſome Lady, mark; O my ſad fortunes,
Is this the end of goodneſs, this the price
O • all my early prayers to protect me,
Why then I ſee there is no God but power,
Nor vertue now alive that cares for us,
But what is either lame or ſenſual,
How had I been thus wretched elſe?

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Let Titius
Command the company that Pontius loſt,
And ſee the Foſſes deeper.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: How now ſweet heart,
What make you here, and thus?

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Lucina weeping!
This muſt be much offence.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Look up and tell me,
Why are you thus? My Ring? O friend, I have found it,
Ye are at Court, ſweet.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Yes, this brought me hither.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Riſe, and goe home: I have my fears Aecius:
Oh my beſt friend, I am ruin'd, go Lucina,
Already in thy tears I have read thy wrongs,
Already found a Caeſar; go thou Li • ly,
Thou ſweetly drooping flower: go ſilver Swan,
And ſing thine own ſad requiem: goe Lucina,
And if thou dar'ſt, outlive this wrong.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: I dare not.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Is that the Ring ye loſt?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: That, that, Aecius,
That curſed Ring, my ſelf, and all my fortunes:
'Thas pleas'd the Emperour, my noble maſter,
For all my ſervices, and dangers for him,
To make me mine own Pander, was this juſtice?
Oh my Aecius, have I liv'd to bear this?

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Farewel for ever Sir.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: That's a ſad ſaying,
But ſuch a one becomes ye well Lucina:
And yet me thinks we ſhould not part ſo lightly,
Our loves have been of longer growth, more rooted
Than the ſharp word of one farewel can ſcatter,
Kiſs me: I find no Caeſar here; theſe lips
Taſte not of Raviſher in my opinion.
Was it not ſo?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: O yes.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I dare believe thee,
For thou wert ever truth it ſelf, and ſweetneſs;
Indeed ſhe was, Aecius.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: So ſhe is ſtill.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Once more, O my Lucina, O my Comfort,
The bleſſing of my Youth, the life of my life.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: I have ſeen enough to ſtagger my obedience;
Hold me ye equal Gods, this is too ſinful.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Why wert thou choſen out to make a Whore of?
To me thou wert too chaſte; fall Cryſtal Fountains,
And ever feed your ſtreams you riſing ſorrows,
Till you have dropt your Miſtris into Marble:
Now go for ever from me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Long farewel, Sir.
And as I have been loyal, gods think on me.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Stay, let me once more bid farewel, Lucina,
Farewel thou excellent example of us,
Thou ſta • y Vertue, fare thee well, ſeek Heaven,
And there by Caſſiopea ſhine in Glory,
We are too baſe and dirty to preſerve thee.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Nay, I muſt kiſs too; ſuch a kiſs again,
And from a Woman of ſo • e a Vertue,
Aecius muſt not take; Farewel thou Phoenix,
If thou wilt dye, Lucina; which well weigh'd,
If you can ceaſe a while from theſe ſtrange thoughts,
I wiſh were rather alter'd.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Miſtake not;
I would not ſtain your honour for the Empire,
Nor any way decline you to diſcredit,
'Tis not my fair profeſſion, but a Villains;
I find and feel your loſs as deep as you do,
And am the ſame, Aecius, ſtill as honeſt,
The ſame life I have ſtill for Maximus,
The ſame Sword wear for you, where Juſtice wills me,
And 'tis no dull one; therefore miſconceive me not;
Only I would have you live a little longer,
But a ſhort year.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: She muſt not.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why ſo long, Sir,
Am I not grey enough with grief already?

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: To draw from that wild man a ſweet repentance,
And goodneſs in his days to come.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: They are ſo,
And will be ever coming, my Aecius.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: For who knows but the ſight of you, preſenting
His ſwoln ſins at the full, and your fair vertues,
May like a fearful Viſion fright his follies,
And once more bend him • ight again? which bleſſing
(If your dark wrongs would give you leave to read)
Is more than death, and the reward more glorious;
Death, only • aſ • you, this, the whole Empire;
Beſides, compell'd and forc'd with violence,
To what ye have done, the deed is none of yours,
No, no • the juſtice neither; ye may live,
And ſtill a worthier Woman, ſtill more honoured;
For are thoſe trees the worſe we tear the fruits from?
Or ſhould the eternal gods deſire to periſh
Becauſe we daily violate their truths,
Which is the Chaſtity of Heaven? No, Lady,
If ye dare live, ye may; and as our ſins
Make them more full of equity and juſtice,
So this compulſive wrong makes you more perfect;
The Empire too will bleſs you

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Noble Sir,
If ſhe were any thing to me but honour,
And that that's wedded 〈◊〉 too, laid in,
Not to be worn away without my being;
Or could the wrongs be hers alone, or mine,
Or both our wrongs, not ty'd to after iſſues,
Not bo •• anew in all our names and kindreds,
I would deſire her live, nay more, compel her:
But ſince it was not Youth, but Malice did it,
And not her own, nor mine, but both our loſſes,
Nor ſtays it there, but that our names muſt find it,
Even thoſe to come; and when they read, ſhe liv'd,
Muſt they not ask how often ſhe was raviſh'd,
And make a doubt ſhe lov'd that more than Wedlock?
Therefore ſhe muſt not live.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Therefore ſhe muſt live,
To teach the world, ſuch deaths are ſuperſtitious.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: The tongues of Angels cannot alter me,
For could the World again reſtore my Credit,
As fair and abſolute as firſt I bred it,
That world I ſhould not truſt again: The Empire
By my life, can get nothing but my ſtory,
Which whilſt I breath muſt be but his abuſes;
And where ye counſel me to live, that Caeſar
May ſee his errours and repent, I'll tell ye,
His penitence is but encreaſe of pleaſures,
His prayers never ſaid but to deceive us,
And when he weeps (as you think) for his Vices,
'Tis but as killing drops from baleful Yew-Trees,
That rot their honeſt Neighbour; If he can grieve
As one that yet deſires his free Converſion,
And almoſt glories in his penitence,
I'll leave him Robes to mourn in, my ſad aſhes.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: The farewels then of happy ſouls be with thee,
And to thy memory be ever ſung
The praiſes of a juſt and conſtant Lady,
This ſad day whilſt I live, a Souldiers tears
I'll offer on thy Monument, and bring
Full of thy noble ſelf with tears untold yet,
Many a worthy Wife, to weep thy ruine.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: All that is chaſte upon thy Tomb ſhall flouriſh,
All living Epitaphs be thine, Time, Story;
And what is left behind to piece our lives
Shall be no more abus'd with tales and trifles,
But full of thee, ſtand to eternity.

sp.speaker: Aeci.
sp.l: Once more farewel, go find Elyzium,
There where the happy Souls are crown'd with Bleſſings,
There where 'tis ever Spring and ever Summer.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: There where no bedrid juſtice comes; truth, honour,
Are keepers of that bleſſed Place; go thither,
For here thou liv'ſt chaſte Fire in rotten Timber.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: And ſo our laſt farewels.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Gods give thee Juſtice— Exit Lucina.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: His thoughts begin to work, I fear him, yet
He ever was a noble Roman, but
I know not what to think on't, he hath ſuffered
Beyond a man if he ſtand this.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Aecius,
Am I alive, or has a dead ſleep ſeiz'd me?
It was my Wife the Emperour abus'd thus,
And I muſt ſay I am glad I had her for him;
Muſt I not, my Aecius?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: I am ſtricken
With ſuch a ſtiff amazement, that no anſwer
Can readily come from me, nor no comfort,
Will ye go home, or go to my houſe?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Neither;
I have no home, and you are mad, Aecius,
To keep me company, I am a fellow
My own Sword would forſake, not tyed unto me;
A Pander is a Prince, to what I am faln;
I dare do nothing.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Ye do better.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I am made a branded Slave, Aecius,
And yet I bleſs the Maker;
Death o' my Soul, muſt I endure this tamely?
Muſt Maximus be mention'd for his tales?
I am a Child too; what ſhould I do railing?
I cannot mend my ſelf, 'tis Caeſar did it,
And what am I to him?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: 'Tis well conſider'd;
However you are tainted, be no Traitor
Time may outwear the firſt, the laſt lives ever.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: O that thou wert not living, and my friend.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: I'll bear a wary Eye upon your actions,
I fear ye, Maximus, nor can I blame thee
If thou break'ſt out, for by the gods thy wrong
Deſerves a general ruine: do ye love me?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: That's all I have to live on.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Then go with me,
Ye ſhall not to your own houſe.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Nor to any.
My griefs are greater far than Walls can compaſs,
And yet I wonder how it happens with me,
I am not dangerous, and o' my Conſcience,
Should I now ſee the Emperour i'th heat on't,
I ſhould not chide him for't, an awe runs through me,
I feel it ſenſibly that binds me to it,
'Tis at my heart now, there it ſits and rules,
And methinks 'tis a pleaſure to obey it.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: 'This is a mask to cozen me; I know ye,
And how far ye dare do; no Roman farther,
Nor with more fearleſs Valour; and I'll watch ye,
Keep that obedience ſtill.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Is a Wifes loſs
(For her abuſe much good may do his Grace,
I'll make as bold with his Wife, if I can)
More than the fading of a few freſh colours,
More than a luſty ſpring loſt?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: No more, Maximus,
To one that truly lives.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Why, then I care not, I can live well enough, Aecius:
For look you friend, for vertue, and thoſe trifles,
They may be bought they ſay.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: He's craz'd a little,
His grief has made him talk things from his Nature.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: But Chaſtity is not a thing I take it
To get in Rome, unleſs it be beſpoken
A hundred years before; Is it Aecius?
By't Lady, and well handled too i'th' breeding.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Will ye go any way?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I'll tell thee, friend;
If my Wife for all this ſhould be a Whore now,
A kind of Kicker out of ſheets, 'twould vex me,
For I am not angry yet; the Emperour
Is young and handſome, and the Woman Fleſh,
And may not theſe two couple without ſcratching?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Alas, my noble friend.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Alas not me,
I am not wretched, for there's no man miſerable
But he that makes himſelf ſo.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Will ye walk yet?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Come, come, ſhe dare not dye, friend, that's the truth on't,
She knows the inticing ſweets and delicacies
Of a young Princes pleaſures, and I thank her,
She has made a way for Maximus to riſe by.
Will't not become me bravely? why do you think
She wept, and ſaid ſhe was raviſh'd? keep it here
And I'll diſcover to you.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: She knows
I love no bitten fleſh, and out of that hope
She might be from me, ſhe contriv'd this knavery;
Was it not monſtrous, friend?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Does he but ſeem ſo,
Or is he mad indeed?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Oh gods, my heart!

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Would it would fairly break.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Methinks I am ſomewhat wilder than I was,
And yet I thank the gods I know my duty.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Nay, you may ſpare your tears; ſhe's dead.
She is ſo.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Why, ſo it ſhould be: how?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: When firſt ſhe enter'd
Into her houſe, after a world of weeping,
And bluſhing like the Sun-ſet, as we ſee her;
Dare I, ſaid ſhe, defile this houſe with Whore,
In which his noble family has flouriſh'd?
At which ſhe fell, and ſtir'd no more; we rub'd her. Exit Clau.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: No more of that; be gone; now my Aecius,
If thou wilt do me pleaſure, weep a little,
I am ſo parch'd I cannot: Your example
Has brought the rain down now: now lead me friend,
And as we walk together, let's pray together truly,
I may not fall from faith.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: That's nobly ſpoken.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Was I not wild, Aecius?

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Somewhat troubled.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I felt no ſorrow then; Now I'll go with ye,
But do not name the Woman; fye, what fool
Am I to weep thus? Gods, Lucina, take thee,
For thou wert even the beſt and worthieſt Lady.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Good Sir, no more, I ſhall be melted with it.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I have done, and good Sir comfort me;
Would there were wars now.

sp.speaker: Aecius.
sp.l: Settle your thoughts, come.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: So I have now, friend,
Of my deep lamentations here's an end. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Phid.
sp.l: By my faith, Captain Pontius, beſides pity
Of your faln fortunes, what to ſay I know not,
For 'tis too true the Emperour deſires not,
But my beſt maſter, any ſouldier near him.

sp.speaker: Aret.
sp.l: And when he underſtands, he caſt your fortunes
For diſobedience, how can we incline him,
(That are but under perſons to his favours)
To any fair opinion? Can ye ſing?

sp.speaker: Pont.
sp.l: Not to pleaſe him, Aretus, for my Songs
Go not to th'Lute, or Viol, but to th' Trumpet,
My tune kept on a Target, and my ſubject
The well ſtruck wounds of men, not love, or women.

sp.speaker: Phid.
sp.l: And thoſe he underſtands not.

sp.speaker: Pont.
sp.l: He ſhould, Phidias.

sp.speaker: Aret.
sp.l: Could you not leave this killing way a little?
You muſt, if here you would plant your ſelf, and rather
Learn as we do, to like what thoſe affect
That are above us; wear their actions,
And think they keep us warm too; what they ſay,
Though oftentimes they ſpeak a little fooliſhly,
Not ſtay to conſtrue, but prepare to execute,
And think however the end falls, the buſineſs
Cannot run empty handed.

sp.speaker: Phid.
sp.l: Can ye flatter,
And if it were put to you, lye a little?

sp.speaker: Pont.
sp.l: Yes, if it be a living

sp.speaker: Aret.
sp.l: That's well ſaid then.

sp.speaker: Pont.
sp.l: But muſt theſe lies and flatteries be believ'd then?

sp.speaker: Phid.
sp.l: Oh yes, by any means.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: By any means then
I cannot lie nor flatter.

sp.speaker: Aret.
sp.l: Ye muſt ſwear too,
If ye be there.

sp.speaker: Pont.
sp.l: I can ſwear if they move me

sp.speaker: Phid.
sp.l: Cannot ye forſwear too?

sp.speaker: Pont.
sp.l: The Court for ever,
If it be grown ſo wicked.

sp.speaker: Aret.
sp.l: You ſhould procure a little too.

sp.speaker: Pont.
sp.l: VVhat's that?
Mens honeſt ſayings for my truth?

sp.speaker: Aret.
sp.l: Oh no, Sir;
But womens honeſt actions for your trial.

sp.speaker: Pont.
sp.l: Do you do all theſe things?

sp.speaker: Phid.
sp.l: Do you not like 'em?

sp.speaker: Pont.
sp.l: Do you ask me ſeriouſly, or trifle with me?
I am not ſo low yet to be your mirth.

sp.speaker: Are.
sp.l: You do miſtake us, Captain, for ſincerely,
VVe ask you how you like 'em?

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: Then ſincerely,
• ell ye I abhor 'em; they are ill ways,
And I will ſtarve before I fall into 'em,
The doers of 'em Wretches, their baſe hungers
C • r • not whoſe Bread they eat, nor how they get it.

sp.speaker: Aret.
sp.l: What then, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.l: If you profeſs this wickedneſs,
Becauſe ye have been Souldiers, and born Arms,
The Servants of the brave A cius,
And by him put to th'Emperour, give me leave,
Or I muſt take it elſe, to ſay ye are Villains,
For all your Golden Coats, deboſh'd, baſe Villains,
Yet I do wear a Sword to tell you ſo,
Is this the way you mark out for a Souldier,
A Man that has commanded for the Empire,
And both the Reputation of a Man?
Are there not lazie things enough call'd fools and cowards,
And poor enough to be prefer'd for Panders,
But wanting Souldiers muſt be Knaves too? ha!
This the trim courſe of life; were not ye born Bawds,
And ſo inherit but your Rights? I am poor,
And may expect a worſe; yet digging, pruning,
Men • ing of broken ways, carrying of water,
Hanting of Worts and Onions, any thing
That's honeſt, and a Mans, I'll rather chuſe,
I, and live better on it, which is juſter,
Drink my well gotten water with more pleaſure,
When my endeavours done, and wages paid me,
Than you do wine, eat my courſe Bread, not curſſt,
And mend upon't, your diets are diſeaſes,
And ſleep as ſoundly, when my labour bids me,
As any forward Pander of ye all,
And riſe a great deal honeſter; my Garments,
Though not as yours, the ſoft ſins of the Empire,
Yet may be warm, and keep the biting wind out,
When every ſingle breath of poor opinion
Finds you through all your Velvets.

sp.speaker: Aret.
sp.l: You have hit it,
Nor are we thoſe we ſeem, the Lord Aecius
Put us good men to th' Emperour, ſo we have ſerv'd him,
Though much neglected for it; So dare be ſtill;
Your Curſes are not ours; we have ſeen your fortune,
But yet know no way to redeem it: Means,
Such as we have, ye ſhall not want, brave Pontius,
But pray be temperate, if we can wipe out
The way of your offences, we are yours, Sir;
And you ſhall live at Court an honeſt •• lan too.

sp.speaker: Phid.
sp.l: That little meat and means we have, we'll ſhare it,
Fear not to be as we are; what we told ye,
Were but meer tryals of your truth: y'are worthy,
And ſo we'll ever hold ye; ſuffer better,
And then you are a right Man, Pontius,
If my good Maſter be not ever angry,
Ye ſhall command again.
I have found two good men: uſe my life,
For it is yours, and all I have to thank ye— Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: There's no way elſe to do it, he muſt dye,
This friend muſt dye, this ſoul of Maximus,
Without whom I am nothing but my ſhame,
This perfectneſs that keeps me from opinion,
Muſt dye, or I muſt live thus branded ever:
A hard choice, and a fatal; Gods ye have given me
