sp.l: We bar all prayers. Exeunt all but Hylas

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: This laſt Wench! I, this laſt wench was a fair one,
A dainty Wench, a right one; a Devil take it,
What do I ail? to have fifteen now in liking,
Enough a Man would think to ſtay my ſtomach?
But what's fifteen, or fifteen ſcore to my thoughts?
And wherefore are mine Eyes made, and have lights,
But to encreaſe my Objects? This laſt Wench
Sticks plaguey cloſe to me, a hundred pound
I were as cloſe to her; If I lov'd now,
As many fooliſh men do, I ſhould run mad.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Sirrah, no more of your French ſhrugs I adviſe you.
If you be lowzie ſhift your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: May it pleaſe your Worſhip.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Only to ſee my Son, my Son, good Launcelot;
Your Maſter and my Son; Body O me Sir,
No money, no more money, Monſieur Launcelot,
Not a Denier, ſweet Signior; bring the Perſon,
The perſon of my Boy, my Boy Tom, Monſieur Thomas,
Or get you gone again, du gata whee, Sir;
Baſſa micu, good Launcelot, valetote.
My Boy or nothing.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Then to anſwer punctually.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: I ſay to th' purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Then I ſay to th' purpoſe,
Becauſe your Worſhips vulgar Underſtanding
May meet me at the neareſt; your Son, my Maſter,
Or Monſieur Thomas, (for ſo his Travel ſtiles him)
Through many foreign plots that Vertue meets with,
And dangers (I beſeech ye give attention)
Is at the laſt arriv'd
To ask your (as the French man calls it ſweetly)
Benediction de jour en jour.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Sirrah, do not conjure me with your French furies.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Che ditt'a vou, Monſieur.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Che doga vou, Raſcal;
Leave me your rotten language, and tell me plainly,
And quickly, Sirrah, leſt I crack your French Crown,
What your good Maſter means; I have maintain'd
You and your Monſieur, as I take it, Launcelot,
Theſe two years at your ditty vous, your jours.
Jour me no more, for not another penny
Shall paſs my purſe.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Your Worſhip is erroneous,
For as I told you, your Son Tom, or Thomas,
My maſter and your Son is now arriv'd
To ask you, as our Language bears it neareſt,
Your quotidian Bleſſing, and here he is in Perſon.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: What, Tom! Boy, welcome with all my heart, Boy
Welcome, 'ſaith thou haſt gladded me at ſoul, Boy,
Infinite glad I am, I have pray'd too, Thomas,
For you wild Thomas, Tom, I thank thee heartily
For coming home.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Sir, I do find your Prayers
Have much prevail'd above my ſins.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Elſe certain I had periſh'd with my rudeneſs,
Ere I had won my ſelf to that diſcretion,
I hope you ſhall hereafter find.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Humh, humh,
Diſcretion? is it come to that? the Boy's ſpoil'd.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Sirrah, you Rogue, look for't, for I will make thee
Ten times more miſerable than thou thought'ſt thy ſelf
Before thou travell'dſt; thou haſt told my Father,
I know it, and I find it, all my Rogueries
By meer way of prevention to undo me.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Sir, as I ſpeak eight languages, I only
Told him you came to ask his benediction,

l.hi: De jour en jour.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: But that I muſt be civil,
I would beat thee like a Dog. Sir, however
The Time I have miſpent may make you doubtful,
Nay harden your belief 'gainſt my Converſion.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: A pox o' travel, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Yet dear Father
Your own experience in my after courſes.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Prithee no more, 'tis ſcurvy; there's thy Siſter.—
Undone without Redemption; he eats with picks,
Utterly ſpoil'd, his ſpirit baffled in him:
How have I ſin'd that this affliction
Should light ſo heavy on me? I have no more Sons;
And this no more mine own, no ſpark of Nature
Allows him mine now, he's grown tame; my grand curſe
Hang o'r his head that thus transform'd thee: travel?
I'll ſend my horſe to travel next; we Monſieur.
Now will my moſt canonical dear Neighbours
Say I have found my Son, and rejoyce with me,
Becauſe he has mew'd his mad tricks off: I know not,
But I am ſure this Monſieur, this fine Gentleman
Will never be in my Books like mad Thomas,
I muſt go ſeek an Heir, for my inheritance
Muſt not turn Secretary; my name and quality
Has kept my Land three hundred years in madneſs,
And it ſlip now, may it ſink. Exit.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Excellent Siſter,
I am glad to ſee thee well; but where's thy father?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Gone diſcontent, it ſeems.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: He did ill in it
As he does all; for I was utterring
A handſome Speech or two, I have been ſtudying
E'r ſince I came from Paris: how glad to ſee thee!

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I am gladder to ſee you, with more love too
I dare maintain it, than my Father's ſorry
To ſee (as he ſuppoſes) your Converſion;
And I am ſure he is vext, nay more, I know it,
He has pray'd againſt it mainly; but it appears, Sir,
You had rather blind him with that poor opinion
Than in your ſelf correct it: deareſt Brother,
Since there is in our uniform reſemblance,
No more to make us two but our bare Sexes;
And ſince one happy Birth produc'd us hither,
Let one more happy mind.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: It ſhall be, Siſter,
For I can do it when I liſt; and yet, Wench,
Be mad too when I pleaſe; I have the trick on't:
Beware a Traveller.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Leave that trick too.

sp.speaker: Thom:
sp.l: Not for the world: but where's my Miſtreſs,
And prithee ſay how does ſhe? I melt to ſee her,
And preſently: I muſt away.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Then do ſo,
For o' my faith, ſhe will not ſee you Brother.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Not ſee me? I'll—

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Now you play your true ſelf;
How would my father love this! I'll aſſure you
She will not ſee you; ſhe has heard (and loudly)
The gambols that you plaid ſince your departure,
In every Town ye came, your ſeveral miſchiefs,
Your rowſes and your wenches; all your quarrels,
And the no cauſes of 'em; theſe I take it
Although ſhe love ye well, to modeſt ears,
To one that waited for your reformation,
To which end travel was propounded by her Uncle,
Muſt needs, and reaſon for it, be examined,
And by her modeſty, and fear'd too light too,
To fyle with her affections; ye have loſt her
For any thing I ſee, exil'd your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: No more of that, ſweet Doll, I will be civil.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: But how long?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Would'ſt thou have me loſe my Birth-right?
For yond old thing will diſinherit me
If I grow too demure; good ſweet Doll, prithee,
Prithee, dear Siſter, let me ſee her.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Nay, I beſeech thee, by this light.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I, ſwagger.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Kiſs me, and be my friend, we two were twins,
And ſhall we now grow ſtrangers?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: 'Tis not my fault.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Well, there be other women, and remember
You, you were the cauſe of this; there be more lands too,
And better People in 'em, fare ye well,
And other loves; what ſhall become of me
And of my vanities, becauſe they grieve ye?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Come hither, come, do you ſee that Cloud that flies there?
So light are you, and blown with every fancy:
Will ye but make me hope ye may be civil?
I know your Nature's ſweet enough, and tender,
Not grated on, nor curb'd: do you love your Miſtreſs?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: He lies that ſays I do not.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Would ye ſee her?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: If you pleaſe, for it muſt be ſo.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: And appear to her
A thing to be belov'd?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Change then
A little of your wildneſs into wiſdom,
And put on a more ſmoothneſs;
I'll do the beſt I can to help ye, yet
I do proteſt ſhe ſwore, and ſwore it deeply,
She would never ſee you more; where's your mans heart now?
What, do you faint at this?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: She is a woman;
But him ſhe entertains next for a ſervant,
I ſhall be bold to quarter.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: No thought of fighting;
Go in, and there we'll talk more, be but rul'd,
And what lies in my power, ye ſhall be ſure of. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: He cannot be ſo wild ſtill.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt certain,
I have now heard all, and all the truth.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Grant all that;
Is he the firſt that has been giv'n a loſt man,
And yet come fairly home? he is young and tender,
And fit for that impreſſion your affections
Shall ſtamp upon him, age brings on diſcretion,
A year hence, theſe mad toys that now poſſeſs him
Will ſhew like Bugbears to him, ſhapes to fright him;
Marriage diſſolves all theſe like miſts.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: They are grounded
Hereditary in him, from his father,
And to his grave they will haunt him.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: 'Tis your fear
Which is a wiſe part in you; yet your love
However you may ſeem to leſſen it
With theſe diſlikes, and choak it with theſe errors,
Do what you can, will break out to excuſe him,
Ye have him in your heart, and planted, Couſin,
From whence the power of reaſon, nor diſcretion
Can ever root him.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Planted in my heart, Aunt?
Believe it no, I never was ſo liberal;
What though he ſhew a ſo ſo comely fellow
Which we call pretty? or ſay it may be handſom?
What though his promiſes may ſtumble at
The power of goodneſs in him, ſometimes uſe too?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: How willingly thy heart betrays thee, Couſin?
Cozen thy ſelf no more; thou haſt no more power
To leave off loving him than he that's thirſty
Has to abſtain from drink ſtanding before him;
His mind is not ſo monſtrous for his ſhape,
If I have Eyes, I have not ſeen his better.
A handſome brown Complexion.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Reaſonable,
Inclining to a tawncy.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Had I ſaid ſo
You would have wiſh'd my tongue out; then his making.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Which may be mended; I have ſeen legs ſtraighter,
And cleaner made.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: A body too.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Far neater,
And better ſet together.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: God forgive thee.
For againſt thy Conſcience thou lyeſt ſtubbornly.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: I grant 'tis neat enough.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: 'Tis excellent,
And where the outward parts are fair and lovely,
(Which are but moulds o'th' mind) what muſt the ſoul be?
Put caſe youth has his ſwinge, and fiery Nature
Flames to mad uſes many times.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: All this
You only uſe to make me ſay I love him;
I do confeſs I do, but that my fondneſs
Should ſling it ſelf upon his deſperate follies.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: I do not counſel that, ſee him reclaim'd firſt,
Which will not prove a miracle, yet Mary,
I am afraid 'twill vex thee horribly
To ſtay ſo long.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: No, no Aunt, no, believe me.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: What was your dream to night? for I obſerv'd ye
Hugging of me, with good dear ſweet Tom.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Fye, Aunt,
Upon my Conſcience.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: On my word 'tis true, Wench;
And then ye kiſs'd me, Mary, more than once too,
And ſigh'd, and O ſweet Tom again; nay, do not bluſh,
Ye have it at the heart, Wench.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: I'll be hang'd firſt,
But you muſt have your way.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: And ſo will you too,
Or break down hedges for it. Dorothea,
The welcom'ſt woman living; how does thy Brother?
I hear he's turn'd a wondrous civil Gentleman
Since his ſhort travel.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: 'Pray Heaven he make it good, Alice.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: How do ye friend? I have a quarrel to ye,
Ye ſtole away and left my company.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: O pardon me, dear friend, it was to welcome
A Brother that I have ſome Cauſe to love well.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Prithee how is he? thou ſpeak'ſt truth.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Not perfect,
I hope he will be.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Never: h'as forgot me,
I hear Wench, and his hot love too.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Thou would'ſt howl then.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: And I am glad it ſhould be ſo; his travels
Have yielded him variety of Miſtreſſes,
Fairer in his eye far.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: O cogging Raſcal!

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: I was a fool, but better thoughts I thank heaven.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: 'Pray do not think ſo, for he loves you dearly,
Upon my troth moſt firmly, would fain ſee you.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: See me friend! do you think it fit?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: It may be,
Without the loſs of credit too; he's not
Such a prodigious thing, ſo monſtrous,
To fling from all ſociety.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: He's ſo much contrary
To my deſires, ſuch an antipathy
That I muſt ſooner ſee my grave.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Dear friend,
He was not ſo before he went.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: I grant it,
For then I daily hop'd his fair Converſion.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Come, do not mask your ſelf, but ſee him freely,
Ye have a mind.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: That mind I'll maſter then.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: And is your hate ſo mortal?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Not to his perſon,
But to his qualities, his mad-cap follies,
Which ſtill like Hydras heads grow thicker on him.
I have a credit, friend, and Maids of my ſort,
Love where their modeſties may live untainted.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I give up that hope then; 'pray for your friends ſake,
If I have any intereſt within ye,
Do but this courteſie, accept this Letter.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: From him?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: The ſame; 'tis but a minutes reading,
And as we look on ſhapes of painted Devils,
Which for the preſent may diſturb our fancy,
But with the next new object loſe 'em, ſo
If this be foul, ye may forget it, 'pray.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Have ye ſeen it, friend?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I will not lie; I have not,
But I preſume, ſo much he honours you,
The worſt part of himſelf was caſt away
When to his beſt part he writ this.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: For your ſake,
Not that I any way ſhall like his ſcribling.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: A ſhrewd diſſembling Quean.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I thank ye, dear friend,
I know ſhe loves him.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Yes, and will not loſe him,
Unleſs he leap into the Moon, believe that,
And then ſhe'l ſcramble too; young wenches loves
Are like the courſe of quartans, they may ſhift
And ſeem to ceaſe ſometimes, and yet we ſee
The leaſt diſtemper pulls 'em back again,
And ſeats 'em in their old courſe; fear her not,
Unleſs he be a Devil.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Now Heaven bleſs me.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: What has he writ?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Out, out upon him.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Ha, what has the mad man done?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Worſe, worſe, and worſe ſtill.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Some Northern Toy, a little broad.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Still fouler?
Hey, hey Boys, goodneſs keep me; Oh.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: What ail ye?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Here, take your Spell again, it burns my fingers.
Was ever Lover writ ſo ſweet a Letter?
So elegant a ſtyle? pray look upon't;
The rareſt inventory of rank Oaths
That ever Cut-purſe caſt.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: What a mad Boy is this?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Only i'th' bottom
A little Julip gently ſprinkled over
To cool his mouth, leſt it break out in bliſters,
Indeed law. Yours for ever.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I am ſorry.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You ſhall be welcome to me, come when you pleaſe,
And ever may command me vertuouſly,
But for your Brother, you muſt pardon me,
Till I am of his nature, no acceſs friend,
No word of viſitation, as ye love me,
And ſo for 'now I'le leave ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: What a letter
Has this thing written, how it roars like thunder?
With what a ſtate he enters into ſtile?
Dear Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Out upon him bedlam.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Well, there be waies to reach her yet: ſuch likeneſs
As you two carry me thinks.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I am mad too,
And yet can apprehend ye: fare ye well,
The fool ſhall now fiſh for himſelf.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Be ſure then
His tewgh be tith and ſtrong: and next no ſwearing,
He'l catch no fiſh elſe, Farewel Dol.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Farewel Alice. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: INdeed he's much chang'd, extreamly alter'd,
His colour faded ſtrangely too.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: The air,
The ſharp and nipping air of our new climate
I hope is all, which will as well reſtore
To health again th' affected body by it,
And make it ſtronger far, as leave it dangerous;
How do's my ſweet, our bleſſed hour comes on now
Apace my Cellide, (it knocks at door)
In which our loves, and long deſires like rivers
Riſing aſunder far, ſhall fall together,
Within theſe too daies dear.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: When heaven, and you Sir
Shall think it fit: for by your wills I am govern'd.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: 'Twere good ſome preparation.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: All that may be:
It ſhall be no blind wedding: and all the joy
Of all our friends I hope: he looks worſe hourly,
How does my friend, my ſelf? he ſweats too coldly,
His pulſe, like the ſlow dropping of a ſpowt,
Scarce gives his function: how is't man, alas Sir,
You look extreme ill: is it any old grief,
The weight of which?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: None, gentle Sir, that I feel,
Your love is too too tender,
Nay believe Sir.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You cannot be the maſter of your health,
Either ſome feaver lyes in wait to catch ye,
Whoſe harbinger's already in your face
We ſee preparing: or ſome diſcontent,
Which if it lye in this houſe, I dare ſay
Both for this noble Gentleman, and all
That live within it, ſhall as readily
Be purg'd away, and with as much care ſoften'd,
And where the cauſe is.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: 'Tis a joy to be ill,
Where ſuch a vertuous fair Phyſitian
Is ready to relieve: your noble cares
I muſt, and ever ſhall be thankfull for,
And would my ſervice (I dare not look upon her).—
But be not fearfull, I feel nothing dangerous,
A grudging caus'd by th' alteration
Of air, may hang upon me: my heart's whole,
(I would it were.)

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I knew the cauſe to be ſo.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: No, you ſhall never know it.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Some warm broths
To purge the bloud, and keep your bed a day Sir,
And ſweat it out.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: I have ſuch cordials,
That if you will but promiſe me to take 'em,
Indeed you ſhall be well, and very quickly,
I'le be your Doctor, you ſhall ſee how finely
I'le fetch ye up again.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: He ſweats extreamly:
Hot, very hot: his pulſe beats like a drum now,
Feel S • ſter, feel, feel ſweet.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: How that touch ſtung me?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: My gown there.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And thoſe julips in the window.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Some ſ • e his b • d made.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: This is moſt unhappy,
Take courage man, 'tis nothing but an ague.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And this ſhall be the laſt fit.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Not by thouſands:
Now what 'tis to be truly miſerable,
I feel at full experience.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: He grows fainter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Come, lead him in, he ſhall to bed: a vomit,
I'le have a vomit for him.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: A purge firſt,
And if he breath'd a vein.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: No, no, no bleeding,
A Clyſter will cool all.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Be of good cheer Sir.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: He's loth to ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: How hard he holds my hand aunt?

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: I do not like that ſign.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Away to's chamber,
Softly, he's full of pain, be diligent
With all the care ye have: would I had ſcus'd him.

div.head: SCENA II.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Why do you rail at me? do I dwell in her
To force her to do this or that? your letter,
A wilde-fire on your letter; your ſweet Letter;
You are ſo learned in your writs: ye ſtand now
As if ye had worried ſheep: you muſt turn tippet,
And ſuddenly, and truely, and diſcreetly
Put on the ſhape of order and humanity,
Or you muſt marry Maikyn the May Lady:
You muſt, dear Brother: do you make me carrier
Of your confound-mee's, and your culverings?
Am I a ſeemly agent for your oaths?
Who would have writ ſuch a deboſh'd?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Your patience,
May not a man profeſs his love?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: In blaſphemies?
Rack a maids tender ears, with dam's and Devils?

sp.speaker: Thom
sp.l: Out, out upon thee,
How would you have me write?
Begin with my love premiſed? ſurely,
And by my truly Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Take your own courſe,
For I ſee all perſwaſion's loſt upon ye:
Humanitie, all drown'd: from this hour fairly
I'le waſh my han • s of all ye do: farewel Sir.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Thou art not mad?

sp.speaker: Dor
sp.l: No, if I were, dear Brother
I would keep you company: get a new Miſtreſs
Some ſuburb Saint, that ſix pence, and ſome others
Will draw to parley: carowſe her health in Cans
And candles ends, and quarrel for her beauty,
Such a ſweet heart muſt ſerve your turn: your old love
Releaſes ye of all your tyes; diſclaims ye
And utterly abjures your memory
Till time has better manag'd ye, will ye command me—

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: What, bob'd of all ſides?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Any worthy ſervice
Unto my Father Sir, that I may tell him
Even to his peace of heart, and much rejoycing
Ye are his true Son Tom ſtill? will it pleaſe ye
To beat ſome half a dozen of his ſervants preſently,
That I may teſtifie you have brought the ſame faith
Unblemiſh'd home, ye carried out? or if it like you
There be two chamber maids within, young wenches,
Handſom and apt for exerciſe: you have been good, Sir,
And charitable though I ſay it Signiour
To ſuch poor orphans: and now, by th' way I think on't
Your young rear Admiral, I mean your laſt baſtard
Don John, ye had by Lady Blanch the Dairy Maid,
Is by an Academy of learned Gypſies,
Foreſeeing ſome ſtrange wonder in the infant
Stoln from the Nurſe, and wanders with thoſe Prophets.
There is plate in the parlour, and good ſtore Sir,
When your wants ſhall ſupply it. So moſt humbly
(Firſt rendring my due ſervice) I take leave Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Why Doll, why Doll I ſay: my letter ſub'd too,
And no acceſs without I mend my manners?
All my deſignes in Limbo? I will have her,
Yes, I will have her, though the Devil roar,
I am reſolv'd that, if ſhe live above ground,
I'le not be bob'd i'th' noſe with every bobtail:
I will be civil too, now I think better,
Exceeding civil, wondrous finely carried:
And yet be mad upon occaſion,
And ſtark mad too, and ſave my land: my Father,
I'le have my will of him, how e're my wench goes. Exit.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Sirrah, I ſay ſtill you have ſpoil'd your Maſter: leave your ſtiches:
I ſay thou haſt ſpoil'd thy Maſter.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.l: I ſay how Sir?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Marry thou haſt taught him like an arrant raſcal,
Firſt to read perfectly: which on my bleſſing
I warn'd him from: for I knew if he read once,
He was a loſt man. Secondly, Sir Launcelot,
Sir lowſie Launcelot, ye have ſuffer'd him
Againſt my power firſt, then againſt my precept,
To keep that ſimpring ſort of people company,
That ſober men call civil: mark ye that Sir?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.l: And't pleaſe your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: It does not pleaſe my worſhip,
Nor ſhall not pleaſe my worſhip: thirdly and laſtly,
Which if the law were here, I would hang thee for,
(However I will lame thee) like a villain,
Thou haſt wrought him
Clean to forget what 'tis to do a miſchief,
A handſom miſchief, ſuch as thou knew'ſt I lov'd well.
My ſervants all are ſound now, my drink ſowr'd,
Not a horſe pawn'd, nor plaid away: no warrants
Come for the breach of peace.
Men travel with their mony, and nothing meets 'em:
I was accurs'd to ſend thee, thou wert ever
Leaning to lazineſs, and loſs of ſpirit,
Thou ſlept'ſt ſtill like a cork upon the water.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.l: Your worſhip knows, I ever was accounted
The moſt deboſh'd, and pleaſe you to remember,
Every day drunk too, for your worſhips credit,
I broke the Butlers head too.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: No, baſe Palliard,
I do remember yet that anſlaight, thou waſt beaten,
And ſtedſt before the Butler; a black jack
Playing upon thee furiouſly, I ſaw it:
I ſaw thee ſcatter'd rogue, behold thy Maſter.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: What ſweet content dwells here!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.l: Put up your Book Sir,
We are all undone elſe.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Tom, when is the horſe-race?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: I know not Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: You will be there?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Not I Sir,
I have forgot thoſe journeys.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Spoil'd for ever.
The Cocking holds at Derby, and there will be
Jack Wild-oats, and Will Purſer.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: I am ſorry, Sir,
They ſhould employ their time ſo ſlenderly,
Their underſtandings will bear better courſes.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Yes, I will marry again: but Monſieur Thomas,
What ſay ye to the Gentleman that challeng'd ye
Before he went, and the fellow ye fell out with?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: O good Sir,
Remember not thoſe follies; where I have wrong'd, Sir,
(So much I have now learn'd to diſcern my ſelf)
My means, and my repentance ſhall make even,
Nor do I think it any imputation
To let the Law perſwade me.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Any Woman:
I care not of what colour, or complexion,
Any that can bear Children: reſt ye merry. Exit.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Ye have utterly undone; clean diſcharg'd me,
I am for the ragged Regiment.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Eight languages,
And wither at an old mans words?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: O pardon me.
I know him but too well: eightſcore I take it
Will not keep me from beating, if not killing:
I'le give him leave to break a leg, and thank him:
You might have ſav'd all this, and ſworn a little:
What had an oath or two been? or a head broke,
Though 'thad been mine, to have ſatisfied the old man?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: I'le break it yet.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Now 'tis too late, I take it:
Will ye be drunk to night, (a leſs intreaty
Has ſerv'd your turn) and ſave all yet? not mad drunk,
For then ye are the Devil, yet the drunker,
The better for your Father ſtill: your ſtate is deſperate,
And with a deſperate cure ye muſt recover it:
Do ſomething, do Sir: do ſome drunken thing,
Some mad thing, or ſome any thing to help us.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Go for a Fidler then: the poor old Fidler
That ſayes his Songs: but firſt where lyes my Miſtris,
Did ye enquire out that?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I'th' Lodge, alone Sir,
None but her own Attendants.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: 'Tis the happier:
Away then, find this Fidler, and do not miſs me
By nine a Clock.

l.hi: Via.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: My Father's mad now,
And ten to one will diſinherit me:
I'le put him to his plunge, and yet be merry.
What Ribabald?

l.hi: Don Thomaſio.
De bene venew.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: I do embrace your body:
How do'ſt thou Sam?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: The ſame Sam ſtill: your friend Sir.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: And how is't bouncing boyes?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Thou art not alter'd,
They ſaid thou wert all Monſieur.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: O believe it,
I am much alter'd, much another way:
The civil'ſt Gentleman in all your Country:
Do not ye ſee me alter'd? yea, and nay Gentlemen,
A much converted man: where's the beſt wine boys?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: A ſound Convertite.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: What, haſt thou made up twenty yet?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: By'r Lady,
I have giv'n a ſhrewd puſh at it, for as I take it,
The laſt I fell in love with, ſcor'd ſixteen.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Look to your skin, Rambaldo the ſleeping Gyant
Will rowze and rent thee piece-meal.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: He ne'r perceives 'em
Longer than looking on.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Thou never meaneſt then
To marry any that thou lov'ſt?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: No ſurely,
Nor any wiſe man I think; marriage?
Would you have me now begin to be prentice,
And learn to cobble other mens old Boots?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Why, you may take a Maid.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Where? can you tell me?
Or if 'twere poſſible I might get a Maid,
To what uſe ſhould I put her? look upon her,
Dandle her upon my knee, and give her ſugar-ſops?
All the new Gowns i'th' Pariſh will not pleaſe her,
If ſhe be high bred, for there's the ſport ſhe aims at,
Nor all the feathers in the Fryars.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Then take a Widow,
A good ſtanch wench, that's tith.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: And begin a new order,
Live in a dead mans monument, not I, Sir,
I'll keep mine own road, a true mendicant;
What pleaſure this day yields me, I never covet
To lay up for the morrow; and methinks ever
Anothers mans Cook dreſſes my diet neateſt.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Thou waſt wont to love old women, fat and flat noſed,
And thou would'ſt ſay they kiſs'd like Flounders, flat
All the face over.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I have had ſuch damſels
I muſt confeſs.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Thou haſt been a precious Rogue.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Only his eyes; and o' my Conſcience
They lye with half the Kingdom.

div.stage: Enter over the Stage, Phyſicians and others.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: What's the matter?
Whither go all theſe men-menders, theſe Phyſicians?
Whoſe Dog lies ſick o'th' mulligrubs?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: O the Gentleman,
The young ſmug Seigniour, Maſter Valentine
Brought out of travel with him, as I hear,
Is faln ſick o'th' ſudden, deſperate ſick,
And likely they go thither.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Who? young Frank?
The only temper'd ſpirit, Scholar, Souldier,
Courtier; and all in one piece? 'tis not poſſible.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: There's one can better ſatisfie you.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Miſtreſs Alice,
I joy to ſee you, Lady.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Good Monſieur Thomas,
You're welcome from your travel; I am haſty,
A G • ntleman lyes ſick, Sir.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: And how doſt thou?
I muſt know, and I will know.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Excellent well,
As well as may be, thank ye.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: I am glad on't,
And prithee hark.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: I cannot ſtay.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: A while, Alice.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Never look ſo narrowly, the mark's in her mouth ſtill.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I am looking at her legs, prithee be quiet.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: I cannot ſtay.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: O ſweet Alice.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: A clean inſtep,
And that I love a life, I did not mark
This woman half ſo well before, how quick
And nimble like a ſhadow, there her leg ſhew'd;
By th'maſs a neat one, the colour of her Stocking,
A much inviting colour.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: My good Monſieur,
I have no time to talk now.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Pretty Breeches,
Finely becoming too.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: By Heaven.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: She will not,
I can aſſure you that, and ſo

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: But this word.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: I cannot, nor I will not, good Lord Exit.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Well, you ſhall 〈◊〉 more from me

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: We'll go 〈◊〉
'Tis Charity; b ••• ies, I know ſhe is there.
And under viſitation I ſhall ſee her,
Will ye along?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: By any mean •

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Be ſure then
I be a civil man: I have ſport • n hand, Bo •• ,
Shall make mirth for a M •• riage d • y.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Away then. Exeunt.

stage.hi:
Enter three Phyſicians with an Ʋ
••• al.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: A Pleuriſie, I ſee it.

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: I rather hold it
For tremor Cordis.

sp.speaker: 3 Phy.
sp.l: Do you mark the Faece • ?
'Tis a moſt peſtilent contagious • ea ••• ,
A ſu ••• it, a plaguey ſurfeit; he muſt bl • e •

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: By no means.

sp.speaker: 3 Phy.
sp.l: I ſay bleed.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: I ſay 'tis dangerous,
The Perſon being ſpent ſo much b • fore hand,
And Nature drawn ſo low, Clyſters, Cool Clyſters.

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: Now with you favours I ſhould think a Vomit:
For take away the Cauſe, the Effect muſt follow,
The Stomach's ſoul and fur'd, the pot's unflam'd yet.

sp.speaker: 3 Phy.
sp.l: No, no, we'll rectifie that part by mild means,
Nature ſo ſunk muſt find no violence.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Will't pleaſe ye draw near? the weak Gentleman
Grows worſe and worſe ſtill.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: Come, we will attend him.

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: He ſhall do well, my friend.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: My Maſters love, Sir.
Excellent well I warrant thee, right and ſtraight, friend.

sp.speaker: 3 Phy.
sp.l: There's no doubt in him, none at all, ne'r fear him

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: That he is deſperate ſick I do believe well,
And that without a ſpeedy cure it kills him,
But that it lyes within the help of Phyſick
Now to reſtore his health, or art to cure him;
Believe it you are cozen'd; clean beſide it.
I would tell ye the true cauſe too, but 'twould vex ye,
Nay, run ye mad.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: May all I have reſtore him?
So dearly and ſo tenderly I love him,
I do not know the cauſe why, yea my life too.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Now I perceive ye ſo well ſet, I'll tell you,

l.hi: Hei mihi quod nullis Amor est medicabilis herbis.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: 'Twas that I only fear'd: good friend go from me,
I find my heart too full for further conference;
You are aſſur'd of this?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: 'Twill prove too certain,
But bear it nobly, Sir, Youth hath his errours.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I ſhall do, and I thank ye; 'pray ye no words on't.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I do not uſe to talk, Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Ye are welcome;
Is there no Conſtancy in earthly things,
No happineſs in us, but what muſt alter?
No life without the heavy load of Fortune?
What miſeries we are, and to our ſelves,
Even 〈◊〉 wh n full content ſeems to ſit by us,
What • aily ſores and ſorrows?

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: O dear Brother,
The Gentleman if ever you will ſee him
Alive as I think.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: O he faints, for Heavens ſake,
For Heavens ſake, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Go comfort him, dear Siſter. Exit Alice.
And ou • word, ſweet, with you: then we'll go to him.
What think you i • this Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: M • p ty thinks, Sir,
'Tis gre •• mi • fortun • that 〈◊〉 ſhould thus periſh.

sp.speaker: Val
sp.l: I • is in • eed, 〈◊〉 , he muſt dye.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: That were a cruelty, when car • may cure him,
Why do you weep ſo, Sir? he may recover.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: He may, but with much danger; my ſweet Cellide,
You have a powerful tongue.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: To do you ſervice.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I will betray his grief; he loves a Gentlewoman,
A friend of yours, whoſe heart another holds,
He knows it too; yet ſuch a ſway blind fancy,
And his not daring to deliver it,
Have won upon him, that they muſt undo him:
Never ſo hopeful and ſo ſweet a Spirit,
Misfortune fell ſo foul on.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Sure ſhe's hard hearted,
That can look on, and not relent, and deeply
At ſuch a miſery; ſhe is not married?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Not yet.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Nor near it?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: When ſhe pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And pray Sir,
Does he deſerve her truly, that ſhe loves ſo?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: His love may m ••• t much, his Perſon little,
For there the match lyes mangled.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Is he your friend?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: He ſhould be, for he is near me.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Will not he dye then,
When th'other ſhall recover?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Ye have pos'd me.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Methinks he ſhould go near it, if he love her;
If ſhe love him.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: She does, and would do equal.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: 'Tis a hard task you put me; yet for your ſake
I will ſpeak to her, all the art I have;
My beſt endeavours; all his Youth and Perſon,
His mind more full of beauty; all his hopes
The memory of ſuch a ſad example,
Ill ſpoken of, and never old; the curſes
Of loving maids, and what may be alledg'd
I'll lay before her: what's her Name? I am ready.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: But will you deal effectually?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Moſt truly;
Nay, were it my ſelf, at your entreaty.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And could ye be ſo pitiful?

sp.speaker: Cel
sp.l: So dutiful;
Becauſe you urge it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: It may be then
It is your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: It is indeed, I know it,
And now know how ye love me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: O my deareſt,
Let but your goodneſs judge; your own part's pity;
Set but your eyes on his afflictions;
He is mine, and ſo becomes your charge: but think
What ruine Nature ſuffers in this young man,
What loſs humanity, and noble manhood;
Take to your better judgment my declining,
My Age hung full of impotence, and ills,
My Body budding now no more: ſeer Winter
Hath ſeal'd that ſap up, at the beſt and happieſt
I can but be your infant, you my Nurſe,
And how unequal deareſt; where his years,
His ſweetneſs, and his ever ſpring of goodneſs,
My fortunes growing in him, and my ſelf too,
Which makes him all your old love; miſconceive not,
I ſay not this as weary of my bondage,
Or ready to infringe my faith; bear witneſs,
Thoſe eyes that I adore ſtill, thoſe lamps that light me
To all the joy I have.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: You have ſaid enough, Sir,
And more than e'r I thought that tongue could utter,
But you are a man, a falſe man too.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Dear Cellide.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: And now, to ſhew you that I am a woman
Rob'd of her reſt, and fool'd out of her fondneſs,
The Gentleman ſhall live, and if he love me,
Ye ſhall be both my triumphs; I will to him,
And as you careleſly fling off your fortune,
And now grow weary of my eaſie winning,
So will I loſe the name of Valentine,
From henceforth all his flatteries, and believe it,
Since ye have ſo ſlightly parted with affection,
And that affection you have pawn'd your faith for;
From this hour no repentance, vows, nor prayers
Shall pluck me back again; what I ſhall do,
Yet I will undertake his cure, expect it,
Shall miniſter no comfort, no content
To either of ye, but hourly more vexations.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Why, let him dye then.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No, ſo much I have loved
To be commanded by you, that even now,
Even in my hate, I will obey your wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: What ſhall I do?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Dye like a fool unſorrow'd,
A bankrupt fool, that flings away his Treaſure;
I muſt begin my cure.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And I my Croſſes. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Frank ſick, Phyſicians, and an Apothecary

sp.speaker: 1 Phy
sp.l: CLap on the Cataplaſm.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.l: Good Gentlemen,
Good learned Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: And ſee theſe broths there,
Ready within this hour, pray keep your arms in,
The air is raw, and miniſters much evil.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: 'Pray leave me; I beſeech ye leave me, Gentlemen,
I have no other ſickneſs but your preſence,
Convey your Cataplaſms to thoſe that need 'em,
Your Vomits, and your Clyſters.

sp.speaker: 3 Phy.
sp.l: Pray be rul'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: Bring in the Lettice Cap; you muſt be ſhaved, Sir,
And then how ſuddenly we'll make you ſleep!

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.l: Till dooms-day: what unneceſſary nothings
Are theſe about a wounded mind?

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: How do ye?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: What queſtions they propound too! how do you, Sir?
I am glad to ſee you well.

sp.speaker: 3 Phy.
sp.l: A great diſtemper, it grows hotter ſtill.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: Open your mouth, I pray, Sir.

sp.speaker: Frank.
sp.l: And can you tell me
How old I am then? there's my hand, pray ſhew me
How many broken ſhins within this two year.
Who would be thus in fetters, good maſter Doctor,
And you dear Doctor, and the third ſweet Doctor,
And precious maſter Apothecary, I do pray ye
To give me leave to live a little loonger,
Ye ſtand before me like my Blacks.

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: 'Tis dangerous,
For now his fancy turns too.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: By your leave Gentlemen:
And pray ye your leave a while too, I have ſomething
Of ſecret to impart unto the Patient.
With all our hearts.
I mary ſuch a Phyſick
May chance to find the humour: be not long Lady,
For we muſt miniſter within this half hour. Ex. Phyſ.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: You ſhall not ſtay for me.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Would you were all rotten
That ye might only intend one anothers itches:
Or would the Gentlemen with one conſent
Would drink ſmall Beer but ſeven years, and aboliſh
That wild fire of the blood, unſatiate wenching,
That your two Indies, ſprings and falls might fail ye,
What torments theſe intruders into bodies.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: How do you worthy Sir?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Bleſs me, what beams
Flew from theſe Angel eyes! O what a miſery
What a moſt ſtudied torment 'tis to me now
To be an honeſt man! dare ye ſit by me?

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Yes, and do more than that too: comfort ye,
I ſee ye have need.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: You are a fair Phyſician:
You bring no bitterneſs gilt o're, to gull us,
No danger in your looks, yet there my death lyes.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: I would be ſorry, Sir, my charity
And my good wiſhes for your health ſhould merit
So ſtubborn a conſtruction: will it pleaſe ye
To taſte a little of this Cordial
For this I think muſt cure ye.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Of which Lady?
Sure ſhe has found my grief: why do you bluſh ſo?

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Do you not underſtand? of this, this Cordial.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: O my afflicted heart: ſhe is gone for ever.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: What heaven have ye brought me Lady?

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Do not wonder:
For 'tis no impudence, nor want of honour
Makes me do this: but love to ſave your life, Sir,
Your life too excellent to loſe in wiſhes,
Love, vertuous love.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: A vertuous bleſſing crown ye,
O goodly ſweet, can there be ſo much charity
So noble a compaſſion in that heart
That's fill'd up with anothers fair affections?
Can mercy drop from thoſe eyes?
Can miracles be wrought upon a dead man,
When all the power ye have, and perfect object
Lyes in anothers light, and his deſerves it?

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Do not deſpair: nor do not think too boldly,
I dare abuſe my promiſe, 'twas your friends
And ſo faſt tyed, I thought no time could ruin:
But ſo much has your danger, and that ſpell
The powerfull name of friend, prevail'd above him
To whom I ever owe obedience,
That here I am, by his command to cure ye,
Nay more for ever, by his full reſignment,
And willingly I ratifie it.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Hold for Heaven ſake,
Muſt my friends miſery make me a triumph?
Bear I that noble name, to be a Traitor?
O vertuous goodneſs, keep thy ſelf untainted:
You have no power to yield, nor he to render,
Nor I to take: I am reſolv'd to die firſt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Ha! ſaiſt thou ſo? nay then thou ſhalt not periſh.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: And though I love ye above the light ſhines on me,
Beyond the wealth of Kingdoms, free content,
Sooner would ſnatch at ſuch a bleſſing offer'd
Than at my pardon'd life by the law forfeited,
Yet, yet O noble Beauty, yet O Paradiſe
For you are all the wonder reveal'd of it,
Yet is a gratitude to be preſerv'd,
A worthy gratitude to one moſt worthy
The name, and nobleneſs of friends.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Pray tell me
If I had never known that Gentleman,
Would not you willingly embrace my offer?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Do you make a doubt?

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: And can ye be unwilling
He being old and impotent? his aim too
Levell'd at you, for your good? not conſtrain'd,
But out of cure, and counſel? Alas conſider,
Play but the Woman with me, and conſider
As he himſelf does, and I now dare ſee it,
Truly conſider, Sir, what miſery.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: For vertues ſake take heed.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: What loſs of youth,
What everlaſting baniſhment from that
Our years do only covet to arrive at,
Equal affections 〈…〉 and ſhot together:
What living name can dead age leave behind him,
What art of memory but fruitleſs doating?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: This cannot be.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: To you unleſs ye apply it
With more and firmer faith, and ſo digeſt it,
I ſpeak but of things poſſible, not done
Nor like to be, a Poſſet cures your ſickneſs,
And yet I know ye grieve this; and howſoever
The worthineſs of friend may make ye ſtagger,
Which is a fair thing in ye, yet my Patient,
My gentle Patient, I would fain ſay more
If you would underſtand.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: O cruel Woman.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Yet ſure your ſickneſs is not ſo forgetful,
Nor you ſo willing to be loſt.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Pray ſtay there:
Me thinks you are not fair now; me thinks more,
That modeſt vertue, men delivered of you,
Shews but like ſhadow to me, thin, and fading.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Excellent friend.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Ye have no ſhare in goodneſs:
Ye are belyed; you are not Cellide,
The modeſt, immaculate: who are ye?
For I will know: what Devil, to do miſchief
Unto my vertuous friend, hath ſhifted ſhapes
With that unblemiſhed beauty?

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Do not rave, Sir,
Nor let the violence of thoughts diſtract ye,
You ſhall enjoy me: I am yours: I pity,
By thoſe fair eyes I do.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: O double hearted!
O Woman, perfect Woman! what diſtraction
Was meant to mankind when thou was't made a Devil?
What an inviting Hell invented? tell me,
And if you yet remember what is goodneſs,
Tell me by that, and truth, can one ſo cheriſh'd
So ſainted in the ſoul of him, whoſe ſervice
Is almoſt turn'd to ſuperſtition,
Whoſe every day endeavours and deſires
Offer themſelves like Incenſe on your Altar,
Whoſe heart holds no intelligence, but holy
And moſt Religious with his love; whoſe life
(And let it ever be remembred Lady)
Is drawn out only for your ends.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: O miracle!

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Whoſe all, and every part of man: pray make me
Like ready Pages wait upon your pleaſures;
Whoſe breath is but your bubble. Can ye, dare ye,
Muſt ye caſt off this man, though he were willing,
Though in a nobleneſs, • o croſs my danger
His friendſhip durſt confirm it, without baſeneſs,
Without the ſtain of honour? ſhall not people
Say liberally hereafter, there's the Lady
That loſt her Father, friend, herſelf, her faith too,
To fawn upon a ſtranger, for ought you know
As ••• thleſs as your ſ • lf, in love as fruitleſs.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: • ake her with all my heart, thou art ſo honeſt
〈…〉 moſt neceſſa • y I be undone.

sp.speaker: Cell
sp.l: With all my ſoul poſſeſs 〈◊〉 . Exit Val.
I'll 〈◊〉 m nute,
I ſco • n • d and hated ye, and came to cozen ye:
I 〈…〉 thoſe things might draw a wonder on me,
To make ye mad.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Good Heaven, what is this Woman?

sp.speaker: Cell
sp.l: Not did your danger, but in charity,
Move me a whit: nor you appear unto me
More than a common object; yet now truly,
Truly, and nobly I do love ye dearly,
And from this hour ye are the man I honour,
You are the man, the excellence, the honeſty,
The only friend, and I am glad your ſickneſs
Fell ſo moſt happily at this time on ye,
To make this truth the worlds.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Whither do you drive me?

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Back to your honeſty, make that good ever,
'Tis like a ſtrong built Caſtle, ſeated high,
That draws on all ambitions, ſtill repair it,
Still fortifie it: there are thouſand foes
Beſides the Tyrant Beauty, will aſſail it:
Look to your Centinels that watch it hourly,
Your eyes, let them not wander.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Is this ſerious?
Or dos ſhe play ſtill with me?

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Keep your ears,
The two main Po • ts that may betray ye, ſtrongly
From light belief firſt, then from flattery,
Eſpecially where Woman b • ats the parley:
The body of your ſtrength, your noble heart

From every yielding to diſ • one ••
• nds,
Rig'd • ound about with vertue, that no breaches,
No ſubtil minds may meet ye.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: How like the Sun
Labouring in his Eclipſe, dark, and prodigious,
She ſhew'd till now? when having won her way,
How full of wonder he breaks out again,
And ſheds his vertuous beams: excellent Angel,
For no leſs can that heavenly mind proclaim thee,
Honour of all thy ſex, let it be lawful,
And like a Pilgrim thus I kneel to beg it,
Not with prophane lips now, nor burnt affections,
But, reconcil'd to faith, with holy wiſhes,
To kiſs that virgin hand.

sp.speaker: C l.
sp.l: Take your deſire, Sir,
And in a nobler way, for I dare truſt ye,
No other fruit my love muſt every yield ye,
I fear no more: yet your moſt conſtant memory
(So much I am wedded to that worthineſs)
Shall ever be my Friend, Companion, Husband.
Farewel, and fairly govern your affections,
Stand, and deceive me not: O noble young man,
I love thee with my ſoul, but dare not ſay it:
Once more farewel, and proſper. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Goodneſs guide thee:
My wonder like to fearful ſhapes in dreams,
Has wakened me out of my ſit of folly,
But not to ſhake it off: a ſpell dwells in me,
A hidden charm ſhot from this beauteous Woman,
That late can ne'r avoid, nor Phyſick find,
And by her counſel ſtrengthen'd: only this
Is all the help I have, I love fair vertue.
Well, ſomething I muſt do, to be a friend,
Yet I am poor, and tardy: ſomething for her too
Though I can never reach her excellence,
Yet but to give an offer at a greatneſs.

div.stage: Enter Valentine, Thomas, Hylas, and Sam.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Be not uncivil Tom, and take your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Do you think I am mad? you'l give me leave
To try her fairly?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Do your beſt.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Why there Boy,
But where's the ſick man?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Where are the Gentlewom • n
That ſhould attend him? there's the Patient.
Me thinks theſe Women—

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Thou think'ſt nothing elſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Go to him friend, and comfort him: I'le lead ye.
O my beſt joy, my worthieſt friend, pray pardon me,
I am ſo over-joy'd I want expreſſion:
I may live to be thankful: bid your friends welcome.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: How do'ſt thou Frank? how do'ſt thou Boy? beat up man:
What, ſhrink i'th' ſinews for a little ſickneſs?

l.hi: Deavolo morte.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I am o'th' mending hand.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: How like a Flute thou ſpeak'ſt: o'th' mending hand man?
Gogs bores, I am well, ſpeak like a man of worſhip.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Thou art a mad companion: never ſtaid Tom.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Let Rogues be ſtaid that have no habitation,
A Gentleman may wander: ſit thee down Frank,
And ſee what I have brought thee: come diſcover,
Open the Scene, and let the work appear.
A friend a • need you Rogue is worth a million.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: What haſt thou there, a julip?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: He muſt not touch it,
'Tis preſent death.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Ye are an Aſs, a twirepipe,
A Jeffery John bo peepe, thou mimiſter,
Thou men • a left-handed pack-ſaddle, out puppey,
My fri • nd Frank, but a very fooliſh fellow:
Do ſt thou ſee that Bottle? view it well.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: I do Tom.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: There be as many lives in't, as a Cat carries,
'Tis everlaſting liquor.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Old Sack, Boy,
Old reverend Sack, which for ought that I can read yet,
Was that Philoſophers Stone the wiſe King Ptolomeus
Did all his wonders by.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: I ſee no harm Tom,
Drink with a moderation.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Drink with ſuger,
Which I have ready here, and here a glaſs boy,
Take me without my tools.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Pray Sir be temperate,
You know your own ſtate beſt.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Sir, I much thank ye,
And ſhall be careful: yet a glaſs or two
So ſit I find my body, and that ſo needful.

sp.speaker: Tho
sp.l: Fill it, and leave your fooling: thou ſay'ſt true Frank.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: W •• re are theſe Women I ſay?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt neceſſary,
Hang up your Julips and your Portugal Poſſets,
Your barley Broths, and ſorrel Sops, they are mangy,
And breed the Scratches only: give me Sack:
I wonder where this Wench is though: have at thee.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: So long, and yet no bolting?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Do, I'le pledge thee.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Take it off thrice, and then cry heigh like a Huntſ-man
With a clear heart, and no more ſits I warrant thee.

The only Cordial, Frank.
Phyſ. and Serv. wit • in.

sp.speaker: 1 Phyſ.
sp.l: Are the things ready?
And is the Barber come?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: An hour ago, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Phyſ.
sp.l: Bring out the Oyls then.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Now or never Gentlemen,
Do me a kindneſs and deliver me.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: From whom boy?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: From theſe things, that talk within there,
Phyſicians, Tom, Phyſicians, ſcowring-ſticks,
They mean to read upon me.

stage.hi: Enter three Phyſ. Apoth. and Barber.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Let 'em enter.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: And be thou confident, we will deliver thee:
For look ye Doctor, ſay the Devil were ſick now,
His horns ſaw'd off, and his head bound with a Biggin,
Sick of a Calenture, taken by a Sur •• it
Of ſtinking ſouls at his Nephews, and St Dunſtans,
What would you miniſter upon the ſudden?
Your judgment ſhort and ſound.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: A fools head.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: No Sir,
It muſt be a Phyſicians for three cauſes,
The firſt becauſe it is a bald-head likely,
Which will down eaſily without Applepap.

sp.speaker: 3 Phy.
sp.l: A main cauſe.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: So it is, and well conſider'd.
The ſecond, for 'tis fill'd with broken Greek, Sir,
Which will ſo tumble in his ſtomach, Doctor,
And work upon the crudities, conceive me,
The fears, and the fiddle-ſtrings within it,
That thoſe damn'd ſouls muſt diſ • inbogue again •

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Or meeting with the ſtygian humour.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Right, Sir.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Forc'd with a Cataplaſm of Crackers.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Ever.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Scowre all before him, like a Scavenger,

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Satisfeciſti domine, my laſt cauſe,
My laſt is, and not leaſt, moſt learned Doctors,
Becauſe in moſt Phyſicians heads (I mean thoſe
That are moſt excellent, and old withal,
And angry, though a Patient ſay his prayers,
And Paracelſians that do trade with poiſons,
We have it by tradition of great writers)
There is a kind of Toad-ſtone bred, whoſe vertue
The Doctor being dri'd.

sp.speaker: 1 Phy.
sp.l: We are abus'd ſirs.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I take it ſo, or ſhall be, for ſay the Belly-ake
Caus'd by an inundation of Peaſe-porridge,
Are we therefore to open the port Vein,
Or the port Eſquiline?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: A learned queſtion:
Or grant the Diaphragma by a Rupture,
The ſign being then in the head of Capricorn.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Meet with the paſſion Huperchondriaea,
And ſo cauſe a Carnoſity in the Kidneyes.
Muſt not the brains, being butter'd with this humour—
Anſwer me that.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Moſt excellently argued.

sp.speaker: 2 Phy.
sp.l: The next fit you will have, my moſt fine Scholar,
Bedlam ſhall find a Salve for: fare ye well Sir,
We came to do you good, but theſe young Doctors
It ſeems have bor'd our Noſes.

sp.speaker: 3 Phy.
sp.l: Drink hard Gentlemen,
And get unwholeſome drabs: 'tis ten to one then
We ſhall hear further from ye, your note alter'd. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: And wilt thou be gone, ſaies one?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: And wilt thou be gone, ſaies t'other?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Then take the odd crown
To mend thy old Gown.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: And we'l be gone all together.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: My learned Tom.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sir, the young Gentlewomen
Sent me to ſee what company ye had with ye,
They much deſire to viſit ye.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Pray ye thank 'em,
And tell 'em my moſt ſickneſs is their abſence:
Ye ſee my company.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Come hither Crab,
What Gentlewomen are theſe? my Miſtris?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: And who elſe?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Miſtreſs Alice.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Hark ye ſirrah,
No word of my being here, unleſs ſhe know it.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I do not think ſhe does.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Take that, and mum then.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You have ty'd my tongue up. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Sit you down good Francis,
And not a word of me till ye hear from me,
And as you find my humour, follow it:
You two come hither, and ſtand cloſe, unſeen Boys,
And do as I ſhall tutor ye.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: What, new work?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Prethee no more but help me now.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I would fain talk
With the Gentlewomen

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Talk with the Gentlewomen?
Of what forſooth? whoſe Maiden head the laſt Mask
Suffer'd impreſſion? o • whoſe Clyſter wrought beſt?
Take me as I ſhall tell thee.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: To what end?
What other end came we along?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Be rul'd though.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Your weaſel face muſt needs be fe • retting
About the Farthing ale;
Do as I bid ye,
Or by this light—

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Come then.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Stand cloſe and mark me.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: All this forc'd foolery will never do it.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: I hope we bring ye health, Sir: how is't with ye?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: You look far better truſt me, the freſh colour
Creeps now again into his cheeks.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: Your enemy
I ſee has done his worſt. Come, we muſt have ye
Luſty again, and frolick man; leave thinking.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Indeed it does ye harm, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: My beſt viſitants,
I ſhall be govern'd by ye.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: You ſhall be well then,
And ſuddenly, and ſoundly well.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: This Air, Sir,
Having now ſeaſon'd ye, will keep ye ever.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: No, no, I have no hope, nor is it fit friends,
My life has been ſo lewd, my looſe condition,
Which I repent too late, ſo lamentable,
That any thing but curſes light upon me,
Exorbitant in all my wayes.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: Who's that, Sir,
Another ſick man?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Sure I know that voice well.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: In all my courſes, careleſs diſobedience.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: What a ſtrange fellow's this?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: No counſel friends,
No look before I leapt.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: Do you know the voyce, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Yes, 'tis a Gentlemans that's much afflicted
In's mind: great pity Ladies.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: Now heaven help him.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: He came to me, to ask free pardon of me,
For ſome things done long ſince, which his diſtemper
Made to appear like wrong, but 'twas not ſo.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: O that this could be truth.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Perſwade your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: To what end Gentlemen, when all is periſh'd
Upon a wrack, is there a hope remaining?
The Sea, that ne'r knew ſorrow, may be pitiful,
My credit's ſplit, and ſunk, nor is it poſſible,
Were my life lengthened out as long as —

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I like this well.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Your mind is too miſtruſtful.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: I have a vertuous Siſter, but I ſcorn'd her,
A Miſtris too, a noble Gentlewoman,
For goodneſs all out going.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Now I know him.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: With theſe eyes friends, my eyes muſt never ſee more.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: This is for your ſake Mary: take heed Couſin,
A man is not ſo ſoon made.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: O my fortune!
But it is juſt, I be deſpis'd and hated.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Deſpair not, 'tis not manly: one hours goodneſs
Strikes off an infinite of ills.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Weep truly
And with compaſſion, Couſin.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: How exactly
This cunning young Thief playes his part!

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Well Tom,
My Tom again, if this be truth.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: She weeps Boy.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: O I ſhall die.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Now Heaven defend.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Thou haſt her.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Come lead me to my Friend to take his farewel,
And then what fortune ſhall befal me, welcome,
How does it ſhow?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: O rarely well.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Say you ſo, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: O ye grand Aſs.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: And are ye there my Juggler?
Away we are abus'd, Alice.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Fool be with thee. Ex. Mary and Alice.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Gone; ſhe found you out, and finely,
In your own nooſe ſhe halter'd ye: you muſt be whiſpering
To know how things ſhew'd: not content to fare well
But you muſt roar out roaſt-meat; till that ſuſpicion
You carried it moſt neatly, ſhe believed too
And wept moſt tenderly; had you continu'd,
Without doubt you had brought her off.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: This was thy Roguing,
For thou wert ever whiſpering: fye upon thee
Now could I break thy head.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: You ſpoke to me firſt.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Do not anger me,
For by this hand I'le beat the buzard blind then.
She ſhall not ſcape me thus: farewel for this time.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Good night, 'tis almoſt bed time: yet no ſleep
Muſt enter theſe, till I work a wonder. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt along too, for I mean to plague thee
For this nights ſins, I will never leave walking of thee
Till I have worn thee out.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Your will be done, Sir.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: You will not leave me, Sam.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Not I.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Away then: I'le be your guide now, if my man be truſty,
My ſpightful Dame, I'le pipe ye ſuch a hunſup
Shall make ye dance a tipvaes: keep cloſe to me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Never perſwade me, I will marry again,
What ſhould I leave my ſtate to, Pins and Poaking ſticks,
To Farthingals, and •• ownces? to ſore-horſes
And an old Leather Bawdy houſe behind 'em,
To thee?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: You have a Son, Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Where, what is he?
Who is he like?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt, thou haſt marr'd him,
Thou, and thy prayer books: I do diſclaim him:
Did not I take him ſinging yeſternight
A godly Ballad, to a godly tune too,
And had a Catechiſm in's pocket, Damſel,
One of your dear diſciples, I perceive it?
When did he ride abroad ſince he came over?
What Tavern has he us'd to? what things done
That ſhews a man, and mettle? when was my houſe
At ſuch a ſhame before, to creep to bed
At ten a clock, and twelve, for want of company?
No ſinging, nor no dancing, nor no drinking?
Thou think'ſt not of theſe ſcandals; when, and where
Has he but ſhew'd his ſword of late?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Deſpair not
I do beſeech you, Sir, nor tempt your weakneſs,
For if you like it ſo, I can aſſure you
He is the ſame man ſtill.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Would thou wert aſhes
On that condition; but believe it Goſſip
You ſhall know you have wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: You never, Sir,
So well I know my duty: and for Heaven ſake,
Take but this counſel with ye ere you marry,
You were wont to hear me: take him, and confeſs him,
Search him to the quick, and if you find him falſe,
Do as you pleaſe; a Mothers name I honour.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: He is loſt, and ſpoil'd, I am reſolv'd my roof
Shall never harbour him: and for you Minion
I'le keep you cloſe enough, leſt you break looſe,
And do more miſchief; get ye in: who waits? Exit Dor.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Do you call, Sir?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Seek the Boy: and bid him wait
My pleaſure in the morning: mark what houſe
He is in, and what he does: and truly tell me.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I will not fail, Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: If ye do, I'le hang ye. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Keep you the back door there, and be ſure
None of her ſervants enter, or go out,
If any Woman paſs, ſhe is lawful prize, Boys,
Cut off all convoyes.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Who ſhall anſwer this?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Why, I ſhall anſwer it, you fearful widgeon,
I ſhall appear to th' action.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: May we diſcourſe too,
On honourable terms?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: With any Gentlewoman
That ſhall appear at window: ye may rehearſe too
By your commiſſion ſafely, ſome ſweet parcels
Of Poetry to a Chamber-maid.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: May we ſing too?
For there's my maſter-piece.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: By no means, no Boys,
I am the man reſerv'd for Air, 'tis my part,
And if ſhe be not rock, my voyce ſhall reach her:
Ye may record a little, or ye may whiſtle,
As time ſhall miniſter, but for main ſinging,
Pray ye ſatisfie your ſelves: away, be careful.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: But hark ye, one word Tom, we may be beaten,

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: That's as ye think good your ſelves: if you deſerve it,
Why 'tis the eaſieſt thing to compaſs: beaten?
What Bugbears dwell in thy brains? who ſhould beat thee?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: She has men enough.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Art not thou man enough too?
Thou haſt fleſh enough about thee: if all that maſs
Will not maintain a little ſpirit, hang it,
And dry it too for dogs-meat: get you gone;
I have things of moment in my mind: that door,
Keep it as thou would'ſt keep thy Wife from a Servingman.
No more I ſay: away, Sam.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: At your will, Sir. Exeunt Hylas and Sam.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I have him here, a rare Rogue, good ſweet Maſter,
Do ſomething of ſome ſavour ſuddenly,
That we may eat, and live: I am almoſt ſtarv'd,

l.hi: No point manieur, no point devein, no Signieur,

sp.l: Not by the vertue of my languages,
Nothing at my old maſters to be hoped for,
O Signieur du, nothing to line my life with,
But cold Pyes with a cudgel, till you help us.
Nothing but famine frights thee: come hither Fidler,
What Ballads are you ſeen in beſt? be ſhort Sir.

sp.speaker: Fidler.
sp.l: Under your maſterſhips correction, I can ſing
The Duke of Norfolk, or the merry Ballad
Of Diverus and Lazarus, the Roſe of England,
In Creet when Dedimus firſt began,
Jonas his crying out againſt Coventry.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Excellent,
Rare matters all.

sp.speaker: Fid.
sp.l: Mawdlin the Merchants Daughter,
The Devil, and ye dainty Dames.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Rare ſtill.

sp.speaker: Fid.
sp.l: The landing of the Spaniards at Bow,
With the bloudy battel at Mile-end.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: All excellent:
No tuning as ye love me; let thy Fidle
Speak Welch, or any thing that's o •• of all tune,
The vilder ſtill the better, like thy ſelf,
For I preſume thy voice will make no trees dance.

sp.speaker: Fid.
sp.l: Nay truly, ye ſhall have it ev'n as homely.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Keep ye to that key, are they all a bed trow?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I hear no ſtirring any where, no light
In any window, 'tis a night for the nonce Sir.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Come ſtrike up then: and ſay the Merchants daughter,
We'l bear the burthen: proceed to inciſion Fidler. Song.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Who's there? what noiſe is this? what rogue
At theſe hours?

sp.speaker: Thom.

l.hi: O what is that to you my fool?
O what is that to you,
Pluck in your face you bawling Aſs,
Or I will break your brow.

sp.l: A new Ballad, a new, a new.

sp.speaker: Fid.
sp.l: The twelfth of April, on May day,
My houſe and goods were burnt away, &c. Maid above.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Why who is this?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: O damſel dear,
Open the door, and it ſhall appear,
Open the door,
O • entle ſquire.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: I'le ſee thee hang'd firſt: farewel my dear,
'Tis maſter Thomas, there he ſtands.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange
That nothing can redeem him: rail him hence,
Or ſing him out in's own way, any thing
To be deliver'd of him.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Then have at him:
My man Thomas did me promiſe.

l.hi: He would viſit me this night.
I am here Love, tell me dear Love,
How I may obtain thy ſight.
Come up to my window love, come, come, come,
Come to my window my dear,
The wind, nor the rain ſhall trouble thee again,
But thou ſhalt be lodged here.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: And art thou ſtrong enough?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Up, up, I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: What do'ſt thou mean to do?

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Good Miſtreſs peace,
I'le warrant ye we'l cool him: Madge. Madge above.

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.l: I am ready.

sp.speaker: Tho.

l.hi: The love of Greece, and it tickled him ſo,
That he deviſed a way to goe.

sp.l: Now ſing the Duke of Northumberland.

l.hi: And climbing to promotion,
He fell down ſuddenly

stage.hi: vi • ard • roaring, offers to kiſs him, 〈…〉 f • ll down.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Farewel Sir.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: What •• all thou don • ? thou h • ſt bro •• his neck

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Not hurt him.
He pitcht upon his legs like a Cat.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: O woman:
O miſerable woman, I am ſpoil'd,
My leg, my leg, my leg, oh both my legs!

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: I told thee what t • ou ha •• done, miſchief go with thee.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: O I am lam'd for ever: O my leg,
Broken in twenty places: O take h • ed,
Take heed of women, ••• ler: oh a Surgeon,
A Surgeon, or I dye: oh my good p • ople,
No charitable people, all deſpightfull,
Oh what a miſery am I in! oh my leg.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Be patient Sir, be patient: let me bind it.

div.stage: Enter Samuel, and Hylas, with his he • d br • ken.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Oh do not touch it rogue

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: My head, my head,
Oh my head's kill'd.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: You muſt be courting wenche •
Through key-holes, Captain Hylas, come and be comforted,
The skin is ſcarce broke.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: O my leg.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: How do ye Sir?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Oh maim'd for ever with a fall, he's ſpoil'd too,
I ſee his brains.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Away with me for Gods ſake,
A Surgeon.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Here's a night indeed.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: A Surgeon. Ex. all but Fi • ler.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Go run for help.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Run all, and all too little,
O curſed beaſt that hurt him, run, run, flye,
He will be dead elſe.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Good friend go you too.

sp.speaker: Fid.
sp.l: Who pays me for my Muſick?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Pox o' your Muſick,
There's twelve pence for ye.

sp.speaker: Fid.
sp.l: There's two groats again forſooth,
I never take above, and reſt ye m •• ry. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: A greaſe pot guild your fidle ſtrings: how do you,
How is my dear?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Why well I thank ye ſweet heart,
Shall we walk in, for now there's none to trouble us?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Are ye ſo crafty, Sir? I ſhall meet with ye,
I knew your trick, and I was willing: my Tom,
Mine own Tom, now to ſatisfie thee, welcom, welcom,
Welcom my beſt friend to me, all my deareſt.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Now ye are my noble Miſtreſs: we loſe time ſweet.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I think they are all gone.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: All, ye did wiſely.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: And you as craftily.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: We are well met Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Come, let's goe in then lovingly: O my Skarf Tom.
I loſt it thereabout, find it, and wear it
As your poor Miſtreſs favour. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: I am made now,
I ſee no venture is in no hand: I have it,
How now? the door lock't, and ſhe in before?
Am I ſo trim'd?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: One parting word ſweet Thomas,
Though to ſave your credit, I diſcharg'd your Fidler,
I muſt not ſatisfie your folly too Sir,
Ye'are ſubtle, but believe it Fox, I'le find ye,
The Surgeons will be here ſtraight, roar again boy,
And break thy legs for ſhame, thou wilt be ſport elſe,
Good night.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: S • e ſa •• s moſt true, I muſt not ſtay: ſhe has bob'd me,
Which if I live, I'le recompence, and ſhortly,
Now for a Ballad to bring me off again.

l.hi: All young me • be warn'd by me, how you do goe a wooing.
Seek not to cl • mb, for fear ye fall, thereby comes your undoing, &c.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: HE cannot goe and take no farewel of me,
Can he be ſo unkind? he's but retir'd
Into the Garden or the Orchard: ſee Sirs.
He would not ride there certain, thoſe were planted
Only for walks I take it.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Ride? nay then,
Had he a horſe out?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: So the Groom delivers
Somewhat before the break of day.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: He's gone,
My beſt friend's gone Alice; I have loſt the nobleſt,
The trueſt, and the moſt man I e're found yet.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Indeed Sir, he deſerves all praiſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: All Siſter,
All, all, and all too little: O that honeſty,
That e • mine honeſty, unſpotted ever,
That perfect goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Sure he will return Sir,
He cannot be ſo harſh.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: O never, never,
Never return, thou know'ſt not where the cauſe lyes.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: He was the worthieſt welcom.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: He deſerv'd it.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Nor wanted, to our knowledge.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I will tell thee,
Within this hour, things that ſhall ſtartle thee,
He never muſt return.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Good morrow Signieur.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Good morrow Maſter Michael.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: My good neighbour,
Me thinks you are ſtirring early ſince your travel,
You have learn'd the rule of health ſir, where's your miſtreſs?
She keeps her warm I warrant ye, i' bed yet?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I think ſhe does.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: 'Tis not her hour of waking.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Did you lye with her, Lady?

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Not to night Sir,
Nor any night this week elſe.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: When laſt ſaw ye her?

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Late yeſte • night.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Was ſhe' bed then?

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: No Sir,
I felt her at her prayers: why do ye ask me?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I have been ſtrangely haunted with a dream
All this long night, and after many wakings,
The ſame dream ſtill; me thought I met young Cellide
Juſt at S. Katherines gate the Nunnery.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Mic.
sp.l: Her face ſlubber'd o' • e with tears, and troubles,
Me thought ſhe cry'd unto the Lady Abbeſs,
For charity receive me holy woman,
A Maid that has forgot the worlds affections,
Into thy virgin order: me thought ſhe took her,
Put on a Stole, and ſacred robe upon her,
And there I left her.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Dream?

sp.speaker: Mich
sp.l: Good Miſtreſs Alice
Do me the favour (yet to ſatisfie me)
To ſtep but up, and ſee.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: I know ſhe's there Sir,
And all this but a dream.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: You know not my dreams,
They are unhappy ones, and often truths,
But this I hope, yet.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: I will ſatisfie ye. Exit

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Neighbours, how does the Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I know not,
Dream of a Nunnery?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: How found ye my words
About the nature of his ſickneſs Valentine?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Did ſhe not cry out, 'twas my folly too
That forc'd her to this nunnery? did ſhe not curſe me?
For God ſake ſpeak: did you not dream of me too,
How baſely, poorly, tamely, like a fool,
Tir'd with his joyes?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Alas poor Gentleman,
Ye promis'd me Sir to bear all theſe croſſes.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I bear 'em till I break again.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: But nobly,
Truly to weigh.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Good neighbours, no more of it,
Ye do but fling flax on my fire: where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: Not yonder Sir, nor has not this night certain
Been in her bed.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: It muſt be truth ſhe tells ye,
And now I'le ſhew ye why I came: this morning
A man of mine being employed about buſineſs,
Came early home, who at S. Katherines Nunnery,
About day peep, told me he met your Miſtreſs,
And as I ſpoke it in a dream, ſo troubled
And ſo received by the Abbeſs, did he ſee her,
The wonder made me riſe, and haſt unto ye
To know the cauſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Farewel, I cannot ſpeak it. Exit Val.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: For Heaven ſake leave him not.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I will not Lady.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Alas, he's much afflicted,

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: We ſhall know ſhortly more, apply y ••
At home good Alice, and truſt him to my 〈◊〉 ,

Nay, do not weep, all ſhall be well, deſpair not.
〈◊〉 .

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: At Valentines houſe ſo merry?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: As a pie Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: So gameſom doſt thou ſay?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I am ſure I heard it.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Ballads, and Fidles too?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: No, but one Fidle;
But twenty noyſes.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Did he do deviſes?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The beſt deviſes Sir: here's my fellow Launcelot
He can inform ye all: he was among 'em,
A mad thing too: I ſtood but in a corner.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Come Sir, what can you ſay? is there any hope yet
Your Maſter may return?

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: He went far elſe,
I will aſſure your worſhip on my credit
By the faith of a Travellor, and a Gentleman,
Your ſon is found again, the ſon, the Tom.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Is he the old Tom?

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: The old Tom.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Go forward.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Next, to conſider how he is the old Tom.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Handle me that.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: I would ye had ſeen it handled
Laſt night Sir, as we handled it: cap à pe,
Footra for leers, and learings; O the noiſe,
The noiſe we made.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Good, good.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: The windows clattering
And all the Chambermaids in ſuch a whobub,
One with her ſmock half off, another in haſt
With a ſerving mans hoſe upon her head.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Good ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: A fellow railing out of a loop-hole there,
And his mouth ſtopt with durt.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: I' faith a fine Boy.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Here one of our heads broke.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Excellent good ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: The Gentleman himſelf, young M. Thomas,
Inviron'd with his furious Myrmidons
The fiery Fidler, and my ſelf; now ſinging,
Now beating at the door, there parlying,
Courting at that window, at the other ſcalling
And all theſe ſeveral noiſes to two Trenchers,
Strong with a bottom of brown thred, which ſhow'd admirable.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: There eat, and grow again, I am pleas'd.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Nor here Sir,
Gave we the frolick over: though at length
We quit the Ladies Skonce on compoſition;
But to the ſilent ſtreets we turn'd our furies:
A ſleeping watchman here we ſtole the ſhooes from,
There made a noiſe, at which he wakes, and follows:
The ſtreets are durty, takes a queen-hith cold,
Hard cheeſe, and that choaks him o' Munday next:
Windows, and ſigns we ſent to Erebus;
Acrue of bawling curs we entertain'd laſt,
When having let the pigs looſe in out pariſhes,
O the brave cry we made as high as Algate!
Down comes a Conſtable, and the Sow his Siſter
Moſt traiterouſly tramples upon Authority,
There a whole ſtand of rug gowns rowted manly
And the Kings peace put to ſlight: a purblind pig here
Runs me his head into the Admirable Lanthorn,
Out goes the light, and all turns to confuſion:
A potter riſes, to enquire this paſſion,
A Boar imboſt takes ſanctuary in his ſhop,
When twenty dogs ruſh after, we ſtill cheering,
Down goe the pots, and pipkins, down the pudding pans,
The cream-bolls cry revenge here, there the candleſticks.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: If this be true, thou little tyney page,
