This tale that thou tell'ſt me,
Then on thy back will I preſently hang
A handſom new Livery:
But if this be falſe, thou little tyney page
As falſe it well may be,
Then with a cudgel of four foot long
I'le beat thee from head to toe.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Will the boy come?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: He will Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Time tries all then.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Here he comes now himſelf Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: To be ſhort Thomas,
Becauſe I feel a ſcruple in my conſcience
Concerning thy demeanour, and a main one,
And therefore like a Father would be ſatisfi'd,
Get up to that window there, and preſently
Like a moſt compleat Gentleman, come from Tripoly.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Good Lord Sir, how are you miſled: what fancies
(Fitter for idle boys, and drunkards, let me ſpeak't,
And with a little wonder I beſeech ou)
Choak up your noble judgement?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: You Rogue Launcelot,
You lying Raſcal.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Will ye ſpoil all again Sir.
Why, what a Devil do you mean?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Away knave,
Ye keep a company of ſawcy fellows,
Deboſh'd, and daily drunkards, to devour ye,
Things, whoſe dull ſouls, tend to the Celler only,
Ye are ill advis'd Sir, to commit your credit.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Sirrah, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Let me never eat again Sir,
Nor feel the bleſſing of another blew-coat,
If this young Gentleman, ſweet Maſter Thomas,
Be not as mad as heart can wiſh: your heart Sir,
If yeſternights diſcourſe: ſpeak fellow Robin,
And if thou ſpeakeſt leſs than truth.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange theſe varlets.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: By theſe ten bones Sir, if theſe eyes, and ears
Can hear and ſee.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Extream ſtrange, ſhould thus boldly
Bud in your ſight, unto your ſon.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: O deu guin
Can ye deny, ye beat a Conſtable
Laſt night?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: I touch Authoritie, ye Raſcal?
I violate the Law?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Good Maſter Thomas.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Did you not take two wenches from the watch too
And put 'em into pudding lane?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: We mean not
Thoſe civil things you did at M. Valentines,
The Fiddle, and the fa'las.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: O ſtrange impudence!
I do beſeech you Sir give no ſuch licence
To knaves and drunkards, to abuſe your ſon thus:
Be wiſe in time, and turn 'em off: we live Sir
In a State govern'd civilly, and ſoberly,
Where each mans actions ſhould confirm the Law,
Not crack, and cancel it.

sp.speaker: Seb.

l.hi: Lancelot du Lake,

sp.l: Get you upon adventures: caſt your coat
And make your exit.

l.hi: Pur lamour de dieu.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Pur me no purs: but pur at that door, out Sirrah,
I'le beat ye purblind elſe, out ye eight languages.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: My bloud upon your head. Exit Lan.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Purge me 'em all Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: And you too preſently.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Even as you pleaſe Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Bid my maid ſervant come, and bring my Daughter,
I will have one ſhall pleaſe me. Exit ſervant.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt fit Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Bring me the mony there: here M. Thomas.
sp.stage: Enter two Servants with two bags.
sp.l: I pray ſit down, ye are no more my ſon now,
Good Gentleman be cover'd.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: At your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: This mony I do give ye, becauſe of whilom
You have been thought my ſon, and by my ſelf too,
And ſome things done like me: ye are now another:
There is two hundred pound, a civil ſumme
For a young civil man: much land and Lordſhip
Will as I take it now, but prove temptation
To dread ye from your ſetled, and ſweet carriage.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: You ſay right Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Nay I beſeech ye cover.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: At your diſpoſe: and I beſeech ye too Sir,
For the word civil, and more ſetled courſe
It may but put to uſe, that on the intereſt
Like a poor Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: It ſhall, to my uſe,
To mine again: do you ſee Sir: good fine Gentleman,
I give no brooding mony for a Scrivener,
Mine is for preſent traffick, and ſo I'le uſe it.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: So much for that then.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: For the main cauſe Monſieur,
I ſent to treat with you about, behold it;
Behold that piece of ſtory work, and view it.
I want a right heir to inherit me,
Not my eſtate alone, but my conditions,
From which you are revolted, therefore dead,
And I will break my back, but I will get one.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Will you chooſe there Sir?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: There, among thoſe Damſels,
In mine own tribe: I know their qualities
Which cannot fail to pleaſe me: for their beauties
A matter of a three farthings, makes all perfect,
A little beer, and beef broth: they are ſound too.
Stand all a breaſt: now gentle M. Thomas
Before I chooſe, you having liv'd long with me,
And happily ſometimes with ſome of theſe too,
Which fault I never frown'd upon; pray ſhew me
(For fear we confound out Genealogies)
Which have you laid aboord? ſpeak your mind freely,
Have you had copulation with that Damſel?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: I have.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Stand you aſide then: how with her Sir?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: How, is not ſeemly here to ſay.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Here's fine ſport.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Retire you too: ſpeak forward M. Thomas.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: I will: and to the purpoſe; even with all Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: With all? that's ſomewhat large.

sp.speaker: Dor
sp.l: And yet you like it.
Was ever ſin ſo glorious?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: With all Thomas?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: All ſurely Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: A ſign thou art mine own yet,
In again all: and to your ſeveral functions. Ex. Maids.
What ſay you to young Luce, my neighbours Daughter,
She was too young I take it, when you travel'd;
Some twelve years old?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Her will was fifteen Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: A pretty anſwer, to cut off long diſcourſe,
For I have many yet to ask ye of,
Where I can chooſe, and nobly, hold up your finger
When ye are right: what ſay ye to Valeria
Whoſe husband lies a dying now? why two,
And in that form?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Her husband is recover'd.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: A witty moral: have at ye once more Thomas,
The Siſters of St. Albons, all five; dat boy,
Dat's mine own boy.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Now out upon thee Monſter.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Still hoping of your pardon.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: There needs none man:
A ſtraw on pardon: prethee need no pardon:
I'le aske no more, nor think no more of marriage,
For o' my conſcience I ſhall be thy Cuckold:
There's ſome good yet left in him: bear your ſelf well,
You may recover me, there's twenty pound Sir,
I ſee ſome ſparkles which may flame again,
You may eat with me when you pleaſe, you know me.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Why do you lye ſo damnably, ſo fooliſhly?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou long to have thy head broke? hold thy peace
And do as I would have thee, or by this hand
I'le kill thy Parrat, hang up thy ſmall hand,
And drink away thy dowry to a penny.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Was ever ſuch a wilde Aſſe?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Prethee be quiet.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: And do'ſt thou think men will not beat thee monſtrouſly
For abuſing their wives and children?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: And do'ſt thou think
Mens wives and children can be abus'd too much?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I wonder at thee.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Nay, thou ſhalt adjure me
Before I have done.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: How ſtand ye with your miſtreſs?

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: I ſhall ſtand nearer
E're I be twelve hours older: there's my buſineſs,
She is monſtrous ſubtile Dol.

sp.speaker: Dol.
sp.l: The Devil I think
Cannot out-ſubtile thee.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: If he play fair play,
Come, you muſt help me preſently.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I diſcard ye.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not ſleep nor eat.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I'le no hand with ye,
No bawd to your abuſes.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: By this light Dol,
Nothing but in the way of honeſty.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Thou never knew'ſt that road: I hear your vigils.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Sweet honey Dol, if I do not marry her,
Honeſtly marry her, if I mean not honourably,
Come, thou ſhalt help me, take heed how you vex me,
I'le help thee to a husband too, a fine Gentleman,
I know thou art mad, a tall young man, a brown man,
I ſwear he has his maidenhead, a rich man.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: You may come in to dinner, and I'le anſwer ye.

sp.speaker: Tom.
sp.l: Nay I'le go with thee Dol: four hundred a year wench.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Good Sir go back again, and take my counſel,
Sores are not cur'd by ſorrows, nor time broke from us,
Pull'd back again by ſighs.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: What ſhould I do friend?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Do that that may redeem ye, go back quickly,
Sebaſtians Daughter can prevail much with her,
The Abbeſs is her Aunt too.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: But my friend then
Whoſe love and loſs is equal ty'd.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Content ye,
That ſhall be my task if he be alive,
Or where my travel and my care may reach him,
I'le bring him back again.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Say he come back
To piece his poor friends life out? and my Miſtreſs
Be vow'd for ever a recluſe?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: So ſuddenly
She cannot, haſt ye therefore inſtantly away Sir,
To put that Daughter by; firſt as to a Father,
Then as a friend ſhe was committed to ye,
And all the care ſhe now has: by which priviledge
She cannot do her this violence,
But you may break it, and the law allows ye.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: O but I forc'd her to it.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Leave diſputing
Againſt your ſelf, if you will needs be miſerable
Spight of her goodneſs, and your friends per • waſions.
Think on, and thrive thereafter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I will home then.
And follow your advice, and good, good Michael.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: No more, I know your ſoul's divided, Valentine,
Cure but that part at home with ſpeedy marriage
E're my return, for then thoſe thoughts that vext her,
While there ran any ſtream for looſe affections,
Will be ſtopt up, and chaſte ey'd honour guide her.
Away, and hope the beſt ſtill: I'le work for ye,
And pray too heartily, away, no more words. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I care not for my broken head,
But that it ſhould be his plot, and a wench too,
A lowzie, lazie wench prepar'd to do it.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Thou hadſt as good be quiet, for o' my conſcience
He'l put another on thee elſe.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I am reſolv'd
To call him to account, was it not manifeſt
He meant a miſchief to me, and laughed at me,
When he lay roaring out, his leg was broken,
And no ſuch matter? had he broke his neck,
Indeed 'twould ne'r have griev'd me; gallows gall him.
Why ſhould he chuſe out me?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Thou art ever ready
To thruſt thy ſelf into theſe ſhe occaſions,
And he as full of knavery to accept it.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Well, if I live I'll have a new trick for him.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: That will not be amiſs, but to fight with him
Is to no purpoſe; beſides, he's truly valiant,
And a moſt deadly hand; thou never fought'ſt yet,
Nor o' my Conſcience haſt no faith in fighting.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: No, no, I will not fight.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Beſides the quarrel,
Which has a woman in't to make it ſcurvy,
Who would lye ſtinking in a Surgeons hands,
A month or two this weather? for believe it,
He never hurts under a quarters healing.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: No, upon better thought, I will not fight, Sam,
But watch my time.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: To pay him with a project;
Watch him too, I would wiſh ye; prithee tell me,
Doſt thou affect theſe women ſtill?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Yes, 'ſaith, Sam,
I love 'em ev'n as well as e'r I did,
Nay, if my brains were beaten out, I muſt to 'em.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Doſt thou love any woman?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Any woman
Of what degree or calling.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Of any age too?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Of any age, from fourſcore to fourteen, Boy,
Of any faſhion.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: And defect too?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Right,
For thoſe I love to lead me to repentance;
A woman with no Noſe, after my ſurquedry,
Shews like King Philip's Moral, Memento mori;
And ſhe that has a wooden leg, demonſtrates
Like Hypocrites, we halt before the gallows;
An old one with one tooth, ſeems to ſay to us,
Sweets meat have ſowr ſauce; ſhe that's full of aches,
Crum not your Bread before you taſte your Porridge,
And many morals we may find.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: 'Tis well, Sir,
Ye make ſo worthy uſes; but quid igitur,
What ſhall we now determine?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Let's conſider
An hour or two how I may fit this fellow.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Let's find him firſt, he'll quickly give occaſion,
But take heed to your ſelf, and ſay I warn'd ye;
He has a plaguey pate.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: That at my danger. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Enter Saylers ſinging to them, Michael, and Francis.

sp.speaker: Sayl.
sp.l: Aboard, aboard, the wind ſtands fair.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Theſe call for Paſſengers, I'll ſtay and ſee
What men they take aboard.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: A Boat, a Boat, a Boat.

sp.speaker: Sayl.
sp.l: Away then.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Whither are ye bound, Friends?

sp.speaker: Sayl.
sp.l: Down to the Straits.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Ha! 'tis not much unlike him.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: May I have paſſage for my money?

sp.speaker: Sayl.
sp.l: And welcome too.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: 'Tis he, I know 'tis he now.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Then merrily aboard, and noble friend,
Heavens goodneſs keep thee ever, and all vertue
Dwell in thy boſome, Cellide, my laſt tears
I leave behind me thus, a ſacrifice,
For I dare ſtay no longer to betray ye.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Be not ſo quick, Sir; Saylers I here charge ye
By virtue of this Warrant, as you will anſwer it,
For both your Ship and Merchant I know perfectly,
Lay hold upon this fellow.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Fellow?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sayl.
sp.l: No hand to Sword, Sir, we ſhall maſter ye,
Fetch out the manacles.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: I do obey ye;
But I beſeech you, Sir, inform me truly
How I am guilty.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: You have rob'd a Gentleman,
One that you are bound to for your life and being;
Money and horſe unjuſtly ye took from him,
And ſomething of more note, but— for y'are a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: It ſhall be ſo, and here I'll end all miſeries,
Since friendſhip is ſo cruel, I confeſs it,
And which is more, a hundred of theſe robberies:
This Ring I ſtole too from him, and this Jewel,
The firſt and laſt of all my wealth; forgive me
My innocence and truth, for ſaying I ſtole 'em,
And may they prove of value but to recompence
The thouſandth part of his love, and bread I have eaten;
'Pray ſee 'em render'd noble Sir, and ſo
I yield me to your power.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Guard him to th' water,
I charge you, Saylers, there I will receive him,
And back convey him to a Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Sayl.
sp.l: Come, Sir,
Look to your neck, you are like to ſail i'th air now.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Come quickly, quickly, paint me handſomely,
Take heed my noſe be not in grain too;
Come Doll, Doll, diſen me.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: If you ſhould play now
Your Devils parts again.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Yea and nay, Dorothy:

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: If ye do any thing, but that ye have ſworn to,
Which only is acceſs.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: As I am a Gentleman;
Out with this hair, Doll, handſomely.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: You have your Breeches?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: I prithee away, thou know'ſt I am monſtrous tickliſh,
What, doſt thou think I love to blaſt my Buttocks?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I'll plague ye for this Roguery; for I know well
What ye intend, Sir.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: On with my muffler.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Ye are a ſweet Lady; come, let's ſee you courteſie;
What, broke i'th bum? hold up your head.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Plague on't,
I ſhall bepiſs my Breeches if I cowr thus,
Come, I am ready.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: At all points as like, Sir,
As if you were my Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Who goes with ye?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: None but my fortune, and my ſelf. Exit Tho.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: 'Bleſs ye:
Now run for thy life, and get before him,
Take the by-way, and tell my Couſin Mary
In what ſhape he intends to come to cozen her;
I'll follow at thy heels my ſelf, fly Wench.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: I'll do it. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: My Father has met him; this goes excellent,
And I'll away in time; look to your Skin, Thomas. Exit.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: What, are you grown ſo corn fed, Goody Gillian,
You will not know your Father? what vagaries
Have you in hand? what out-leaps, durty heels,
That at theſe hours of night ye muſt be gadding,
And through the Orchard take your private paſſage?
What, is the breeze in your Breech? or has your Brother
Appointed you an hour of meditation
How to demean himſelf; get ye to bed, drab,
Or I'll ſo crab your Shoulders; ye demure Slut,
Ye civil diſh of ſliced Beef, get ye in.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: I wi' not, that I wi' not.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Is't ev'n ſo, Dame?
Have at ye with a night Spell then.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: 'Pray hold, Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: St. George, St. George, our Ladies Knight,
He walks by day, ſo does he by night,
And when he had her found,
He her beat, and her bound,
Until to him her troth ſhe plight,
She would not ſtir from him that night.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Then have at ye with a Counter Spell,
From Elves, Hobs, and Fayries, that trouble our Dayries,
From Fire-Drakes and Fiends, and ſuch as the Devil ſends,
Defend us good Heaven. Exit.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Bleſs me maſter; look up, Sir, I beſeech ye'
Up with your eyes to heaven.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Up with your noſe, Sir,
I do not bleed, 'twas a ſound knock ſhe gave me,
A plaguey mankind Girl, how my brains totters?
Well, go thy ways, thou haſt got one thouſand pound more
With this dog trick,
Mine own true ſpirit in her too.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: In her? alas Sir,
Alas poor Gentlewomen, ſhe a hand ſo heavy,
To knock ye like a Calf down, or ſo brave a courage
To beat her father? if you could believe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Who would'ſt thou make me believe it was, the Devil?

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: One that ſpits fire as faſt as he ſometimes, Sir,
And changes ſhapes as often; your Son Thomas;
Never wonder, if it be not he, ſtraight hang me.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: He? if it be ſo,
I'll put thee in my Will, and there's an end on't.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: I ſaw his legs, h'as Boots on like a Player,
Under his wenches cloaths, 'tis he, 'tis Thomas
In his own Siſters Cloaths, Sir, and I can waſt him.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: No more words then, we'll watch him, thou'ſt not believe Launce,
How heartily glad I am.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: May ye be gladder,
But not this way, Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: No more words, but watch him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: When comes he?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Preſently.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Then get you up, Doll,
Away, I'll ſtraight come to you: is all ready?

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: All.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Let the light ſtand far enough.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: 'Tis placed ſo.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Stay you to entertain him to his chamber,
But keep cloſe, Wench, he flyes at all.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: You need no more inſtruction?

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: I am perfect. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: More ſtops yet? ſure the fiend's my ghoſtly father,
Old Valentine; what wind's in his poop?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Lady,
You are met moſt happily; O gentle Doll,
You muſt now do me an eſpecial favour.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: What is it, maſter Valentine? I am ſorely troubled
With a ſalt rheum faln i' my gums.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I'll tell ye,
And let it move you equally; my bleſt Miſtreſs,
Upon a ſlight occaſion taking anger,
Took alſo (to undo me) your Aunts Nunnery,
From whence by my perſwaſion to redeem her,
Will be impoſſible: nor have I liberty
To come and viſit her; my good, good Dorothy,
You are moſt powerful with her, and your Aunt too,
And have acceſs at all hours liberally,
Speak now or never for me.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: In a Nunnery?
That courſe muſt not be ſuffered, Maſter Valentine,
Her Mother never knew it; rare ſport for me;
Sport upon ſport, by th' break of day I'll meet ye,
And fear not, Man, we'll have her out I warrant ye,
I cannot ſtay now.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: You will not break?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: By no means.
Good night.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Good night kind Miſtreſs Doll. Exit.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: This thrives well,
Every one takes me for my Siſter, excellent;
This Nunnery's faln ſo pat too, to my figure,
Where there be handſome wenches, and they ſhall know it,
If once I creep in, ere they get me out again;
Stay, here's the houſe, and one of her Maids.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Who's there?
O Miſtreſs Dorothy! you are a ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Still Miſtreſs Dorothy? this geer will cotton.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Will you walk in, Forſooth?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Where is your Miſtreſs?

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Not very well; ſhe's gone to bed, I am glad
You are come ſo fit to comfort her.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Yes, I'll comfort her.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: 'Pray make not much noiſe, for ſhe is ſure aſleep,
You know your ſide, creep ſoftly in, your company
Will warm her well.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: I warrant thee I'll warm her.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Your Brother has been here, the ſtrangeſt fellow.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: A very Rogue, a rank Rogue.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: I'll conduct ye
Even to her Chamber-door, and there commit ye. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Come Sir, for this night I ſhall entertain ye,
And like a Gentleman, how e'r your fortune
Hath caſt ye on the worſt part.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: How you pleaſe, Sir,
I am reſolv'd, nor can a joy or miſery
Much move me now.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I am angry with my ſelf now
For putting this forc'd way upon his patience,
Yet any other courſe had been too ſlender:
Yet what to think I know not, for moſt liberally
He hath confeſs'd ſtrange wrongs, which if they prove ſo,
How e'r the others long love may forget all,
Yet 'twas moſt fit he ſhould come back, and this way.
Drink that; and now to my care leave your Priſoner,
I'll be his guard for this night.

sp.speaker: Officers.
sp.l: Good night to your Worſhip.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Good night, my honeſt friends; come, Sir, I hope
There ſhall be no ſuch cauſe of ſuch a ſadneſs
As you put on.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: 'Faith, Sir, my reſt is up,
And what I now pull ſhall no more afflict me
Than if I plaid at ſpan-Counter, nor is my face
The map of any thing I ſeem to ſuffer,
Lighter affections ſeldom dwell in me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: A conſtant Gentleman; would I had taken
A Feaver when I took this harſh way to diſturb him.
Come, walk with me, Sir, ere to morrow night
I doubt not but to ſee all this blown over. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I Have dog'd his Siſter, ſure 'twas ſhe,
And I hope ſhe will come back again this night too;
Sam I have loſt of purpoſe; now if I can
With all the art I have, as ſhe comes back,
But win a parley for my broken Pate,
Off goes her maiden-head, and there's vindicta.
They ſtir about the houſe, I'll ſtand at diſtance. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Mary and Dorothy, and then Thomas and Maid.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Is he come in?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Speak ſoftly,
He is, and there he goes.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Good night, good night, Wench.

div.stage: A Bed diſcovered with a Black-moore in it.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: As ſoftly as you can. Exit.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: I'll play the mouſe, Nan,
How cloſe the little thief lies!

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: How he itches?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: What would you give now to be there, and I
At home, Mall?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: Peace for ſhame.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: In what a figure
The little fool has pull'd it ſelf together!
Anon you will lye ſtraighter;
Ha! there's rare circumſtance
Belongs to ſuch a treatiſe; do ye tumble?
I'll tumble with ye ſtraight, wench: ſhe ſleeps ſoundly,
Full little think'ſt thou of thy joy that's coming,
The ſweet, ſweet joy, full little of the kiſſes,
But thoſe unthought of things come ever happieſt.
How ſoft the Rogue feels! O ye little Villain,
Ye delicate coy Thief, how I ſhall thrum ye?
Your fy away, good ſervant, as you are a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Mary:
sp.l: Prithee leave laughing.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Out upon ye, Thomas,
What do you mean to do? I'll call the houſe up.
O God, I am ſure ye will not, ſhall not ſerve ye,
For up ye go now and ye were my father.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Your courage will be cool'd anon.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: If it do I'll hang for't,
Yet I'le be quartered here firſt.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: O fierce Villain.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: What would he do indeed, Doll?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: You had beſt try him.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: I'll kiſs thee ere I come to bed, ſweet Mary.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Prithee leave laughing.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: O for gentle Nicholas.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: And view that ſtormy face that has ſo thundred me,
A coldneſs crept over't now? by your leave, candle,
And next door by yours too, ſo, a pretty, pretty,
Shall I now look upon ye? by this light it moves me.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Much good may it do you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Holy Saints defend me,
The Devil, Devil, Devil, O the Devil.

sp.speaker: Ma. Dor.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, ha, the Devil, O the Devil.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: I am abus'd moſt damnedly, moſt beaſtly,
Yet if it be a ſhe-Devil; but the houſe is up,
And here's no ſtaying longer in this Caſſock.
Woman, I here diſclaim thee; and in vengeance
I'll marry with that Devil, but I'll vex thee.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: By'r Lady, but you ſhall not, Sir, I'll watch ye.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Plague o'your Spaniſh leather hide: I'll waken ye;
Devil good night: good night, good Devil.

sp.speaker: Moor.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Roar again, Devil, roar again. Exit Tho.

sp.speaker: Moor.
sp.l: O, O, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Open the doors before him; let him vaniſh:
Now, let him come again, I'll uſe him kinder.
How now Wench?

sp.speaker: Moor.
sp.l: 'Pray lye here your ſelf next, Miſtreſs,
And entertain your ſweet-heart.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: What ſaid he to thee?

sp.speaker: Moor.
sp.l: I had a ſoft Bed, and I ſlept out all
But his kind farewel: ye may bake me now,
For o' my conſcience, he has made me Veniſon.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Alas poor Kate: I'll give thee a new Petticoat.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: And I a Waſtecoat, wench.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Draw in the Bed, Maids,
And ſee it made again; put freſh ſheets on too,
For Doll and I; come Wench, let's laugh an hour now.
To morrow, early, will we ſee young Cellide,
They ſay ſhe has taken a Sanctuary; Love and they
Are thick ſown, but come up ſo full of thiſtles.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: They muſt needs, Mall, for 'tis a pricking age grown,
Prithee to bed, for I am monſtrous ſleepy.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.l: A match, but art not thou thy Brother?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I would I were, Wench,
You ſhould hear further.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Come, no more of that, Doll. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I heard the doors clap; now, and't be thy will, wench.
By th' Maſs ſhe comes; you are ſurely met fair Gentlewoman,
I take it, Miſtreſs Doll Sebaſtians Daughter.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: I take right, Sir; Hylas, are you ferretting?
I'll fit you with a penny-worth preſently.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: How dare you walk ſo late, ſweet, ſo weak guarded?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: 'Faith Sir, I do no harm, nor none I look for,
Yet I am glad I have met ſo good a Gentleman,
Againſt all chances; for though I never knew ye,
Yet I have heard much good ſpoke of ye.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Hark ye,
What if a man ſhould kiſs ye?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: That's no harm, Sir;
'Pray God he 'ſcapes my Beard, there lies the miſchief.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Her lips are monſtrous rugged, but that ſurely
Is but the ſharpneſs of the weather; hark ye once once more,
And in your ear, ſweet Miſtreſs, for ye are ſo,
And ever ſhall be from this hour: I have vow'd it.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Why, that's my daughter, Rogue, doſt thou not ſee her
Kiſſing that fellow there, there in that corner?

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Kiſſing?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Now, now, now they agree o'th' match too.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Nay then you love me not.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: By this white hand, Doll.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs I have long deſir'd your ſight, Sir.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Why, there's the Boots ſtill, Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Hang Boots, Sir,
Why, they'll wear Breeches too.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Diſhoneſt me?
Not for the World.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Why, now they kiſs again, there
I knew 'twas ſhe, and that her crafty ſtealing
Out the back way muſt needs have ſuch a meaning.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: I am at my ſmall wits ends.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: If ye mean honourably.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: Did ſhe ne'r beat ye before, Sir?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Why doſt thou follow me?
Thou Raſcal, Slave, haſt thou not twice abus'd me?
Haſt thou not ſpoil'd the Boy? by thine own Covenant,
Wouldſt thou not now be hang'd?

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: I think I would, Sir,
But you are ſo impatient; does not this ſhew, Sir,
(I do beſeech ye ſpeak, and ſpeak with judgment,
And let the caſe be equally conſider'd)
Far braver in your Daughter? in a Son now,
'Tis nothing, of no mark; every man does it,
But to beget a Daughter, a man maiden,
That reaches at theſe high exploits, is admirable;
Nay, ſhe goes far beyond him; for when durſt he,
But when he was drunk, do any thing to ſpeak of?
This is Sebaſtian truly.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Thou ſayeſt right, Launce,
And there's my hand once more.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Not without Marriage.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Didſt thou hear that?

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: I think ſhe ſpoke of Marriage.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: And he ſhall marry her, for it ſeems ſhe likes him,
And their firſt Boy ſhall be my heir.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.l: I, marry,
Now ye go right to work.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Fye, fie, Sir,
Now I have promis'd ye this night to marry,
Would ye be ſo intemperate? are ye a Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I have no maw to marriage, yet this Raſcal
Tempts me extreamly: will ye marry preſently?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Get you afore, and ſtay me at the Chapel,
Cloſe by the Nunnery, there you ſhall find a night Prieſt,
Little Sir Hugh, and he can ſay the Matrimony
Over without Book, for we muſt have no company,
Nor light, for fear my Father know, which muſt not yet be;
And then to morrow night.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Nothing to night, Sweet?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: No, not a bit, I am ſent of buſineſs,
About my dowry, Sweet, do not ſpoil all now,
'Tis of much haſte: I can ſcarce ſtay the marriage,
Now if you love me, get you gone.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: You'll follow?

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Within this hour, my ſweet Chick.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Kiſs.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: A Rope kiſs ye,
Come, come, I ſtand o' thorns.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Methinks her mouth ſtill
Is monſtrous rough, but they have ways to mend it,
Farewel.

sp.speaker: Thom.
sp.l: Farewel, I'll fit ye with a wife, Sir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Come, follow cloſe, I'll ſee the end ſhe aims at,
And if he be a handſome fellow, Launcelot,
Fiat, 'tis done, and all my ſtate is ſetled. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Come to your Mattins Maids; theſe early hours
My gentle Daughter, will diſturb a while
Your fair eyes, nurtur'd in eaſe.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: No, vertuous Mother,
'Tis for my holy health, to purchaſe which,
They ſhall forget the Child of eaſe, ſoft ſlumbers.
O my afflicted heart, how thou art tortur'd!
And Love, how like a Tyrant thou reign'ſt in me,
Commanding and forbidding at one inſtant;
Why came I hither, that deſire to have
Only all liberty to make me happy?
Why did'ſt thou bring that young man home, O Valentine,
That vertuous Youth? why didſt thou ſpeak his goodneſs
In ſuch a phraſe, as if all tongues, all praiſes
Were made for him? O fond and ignorant!
Why didſt thou foſter my affection
Till it grew up to know no other Father,
And then betray it?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Can ye ſing?

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Yes, Mother,
My ſorrows only.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Be gone, and to the Quire then. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter Michael and Servant, and Francis.

sp.speaker: M ch.
sp.l: Haſt thou enquir'd him out?

sp.speaker: Serv
sp.l: He's not at home, Sir,
His Siſt • r thinks he's gone to th' Nunnery.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Moſt likely; I'll away, an hour hence, Sirrah,
Come you along with this young Gentleman,
Do him all ſervice, and fair office.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Yes Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Where haſt thou been, man?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Is there ne'r a ſhop open?
I'll give thee a pair of Gloves, Sam.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: What doſt thou think?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Thou art not married?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: By th' maſs but I am, all to be married,
I am i'th' order now, Sam.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: To whom prithee?
I thought there was ſome ſuch trick in't, you ſtole from me,
But who, for Heavens ſake?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Ev'n the ſweeteſt woman,
The rareſt Woman, Samuel, and the luſtieſt,
But wondrous honeſt, honeſt as the ice, Boy,
Not a bit before hand, for my life, Sirrah,
And of a luſty kindred.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: But who, Hylas?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: The young Gentleman and I are like to be friends again,
The fates will have it ſo.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Who, Monſieur Thomas?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: All wrongs forgot.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: O now I ſmell ye, Hylas;
Does he know of it?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: No, there's the trick I owe him;
'Tis done, Boy, we are faſt 'faith, my Youth now
Shall know I am aforehand, for his qualities.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Is there no trick in't?

sp.speaker: Hyl
sp.l: None, but up and ride, Boy:
I have made no Joynture neither, there I have paid him.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: She's a brave wench.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: She ſhall be as I'll uſe her,
And if ſhe anger me, all his abuſes
I'll clap upon her Caſſock.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Take heed, Hylas.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: 'Tis paſt that, Sam, come, I muſt meet her preſently,
And now ſhalt ſee me a moſt glorious Husband.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: In troth, Sir, you never ſpoke to me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Can ye forget me?
Did not you promiſe all your help and cunning
In my behalf, but for one hour to ſee her,
Did you not ſwear it? by this hand, no ſtrictneſs
Nor rule this houſe holds, ſhall by me be broken.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I ſaw ye not theſe two days.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Do not wrong me,
I met ye, by my life, juſt as you entred
This gentle Ladies Lodge, laſt night, thus ſuited
About eleven a clock.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: 'Tis true, I was there,
But that I ſaw or ſpoke to you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I have found it,
Your Brother Thomas, Doll.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Pray Sir, be ſatisfi'd,
And wherein I can do you good, command me.
What a mad fool is this? ſtay here a while, Sir,
Whilſt we walk in, and make your peace. Exit.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I thank ye. Squeak with •• .

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter there among theſe maids?
Now benedicite, have ye got the breeze there?
Give me my holy ſprinkle.

sp.speaker: 1 Nun.
sp.l: O Madam, there's a ſtrange thing like a Gentlewoman,
Like Miſtreſs Dorothy, I think the fiend
Crept into th' Nunnery we know not which way,
Plays revel rout among us.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Give me my holy water-pot.

sp.speaker: 1 Nun.
sp.l: Here, Madam.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Spirit of earth or air, I do conjure thee, Squeak within.
Of water or of fire.

sp.speaker: 1 Nun.
sp.l: Hark Madam, hark.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Be thou Ghoſt that cannot reſt,
Or a ſhadow of the bleſt,
Be thou black, or white, or green,
Be thou heard, or to be ſeen.

sp.speaker: 2 Nun.
sp.l: It comes, it comes.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: What are ye? ſpeak, ſpeak gently,
And next, what would ye with me?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Any thing you'l let me.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: You are no Woman certain.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Nor you no Nun, nor ſhall not be.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: What make ye here?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: I am a holy Fryer.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Is this the Spirit?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Nothing but ſpirit Aunt.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Now out upon thee.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Peace, or I'le conjure too, Aunt.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Why come you thus?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: That's all one, here's my purpoſe:
Out with this Nun, ſhe is too handſome for ye,
I'le tell thee, Aunt, and I ſpeak it with tears to thee,
If thou keepſt her here, as yet I hope thou art wiſer,
Mark but the miſchief follows.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: She is a Votreſs.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Let her be what ſhe will, ſhe will undo thee,
Let her but one hour out, as I direct ye,
Or have among your Nuns again.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: You have no project
But fair and honeſt?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: As thine eyes, ſweet Abbeſs.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I will be rul'd then.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Thus then and perſwade her,
But do not juggle with me, if ye do Aunt.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I muſt be there my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Away and fit her.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Come Daughter, you muſt now be rul'd, or never.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: I muſt obey your will.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: That's my good Daughter. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: What a coyle has this fellow kept i'th' Nunnery,
Sure he has run the Abbeſs out of her wits.

sp.speaker: Do.
sp.l: Out of the Nunnery I think, for we can neither ſee her,
Nor the young Cellide.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Pray Heavens he be not teaſing.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Nay you may thank your ſelf, 'twas your own ſtructures.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Why there's the Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Maſs 'tis ſhe indeed;
How ſmart the pretty Thief looks? 'morrow Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Good morrow to you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: How ſtrange ſhe bears it?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Maids muſt do ſo, at firſt.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Would ye ought with us, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Yes marry would I,
A little with your Ladyſhip.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Your will, Sir.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Doll, I would have ye preſently prepare your ſelf
And thoſe things you would have with you,
For my houſe is ready.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: How, Sir?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: And this night not to fail, you muſt come to me,
My friends will all be there too: for Trunks, and thoſe things,
And houſhold-ſtuff, and cloaths you would have carried,
To morrow, or the next day, I'le take order:
Only what mony you have, bring away with ye,
And Jewels.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Jewels, Sir?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I, for adornment,
There's a bed up, to play the game in, Dorothy:
And now come kiſs me heartily.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Who are you?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: This Lady ſhall be welcome too.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: To what, Sir?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Your neighbour can reſolve ye.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: The man's fooliſh,
Sir, you look ſoberly: who is this fellow,
And where's his buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: By Heaven, thou art abus'd ſtill.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: It may be ſo: Come, ye may ſpeak now boldly,
There's none but friends, Wench.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Came ye out of Bedlam?
Alas, 'tis ill, Sir, that ye ſuffer him
To walk in th' open Air thus: 'twill undo him.
A pretty handſome Gentleman: great pity.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Let me not live more if thou be'ſt not cozen'd.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Are not you my Wife? did not I marry you laſt night
At St Michaels Chapel?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Did not I ſay he was mad?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Are not you Miſtreſs Dorothy, Thomas's Siſter?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There he ſpeaks ſence, but I'le aſſure ye, Gentleman,
I think no Wife of yours: at what hour was it?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: 'S pretious; you'l make me mad; did not the Prieſt,
Sir Hugh, that you appointed, about twelve a Clock
Tye our hands faſt? did not you ſwear you lov'd me?
Did not I court ye, coming from this Gentlewomans?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Good Sir, go ſleep: for if I credit have,
She was in my arms then, abed.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I told ye.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Be not ſo confident.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: By th' maſs, ſhe muſt, Sir;
For I'le no Husband here, before I know him:
And ſo good morrow to ye: Come, let's go ſeek 'em.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I told ye what ye had done.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Is the Devil ſtirring?
Well, go with me; for now I will be married. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE VIII.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I have brought him back again.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: You have done a friendſhip,
Worthy the love you bear me.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Would he had ſo too.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: O he's a worthy young man.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: When all's try'd,
I fear you'll change your faith: bring in the Gentleman.

div.stage: Enter Francis, Servant, Abbeſs, and Cellide, ſeverally

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: My happy Miſtreſs too! now Fortune help me,
And all you Stars that govern chaſt deſires
Shine fair, and lovely.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: But one hour, dear Daughter,
To hear your Guardian, what he can deliver
In Loves defence, and his: and then your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Though much unwilling, you have made me yield,
More for his ſake I ſee: how full of ſorrow
Sweet catching ſorrow, he appears? O love,
That thou but knew'ſt to heal, as well as hurt us.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Be rul'd by me: I ſee her eye faſt on him:
And what ye heard, believe, for 'tis ſo certain
He neither dar'd, nor muſt oppoſe my evidence;
And be you wiſe, young Lady, and believe too,
This man you love, Sir?

sp.speaker: Val
sp.l: As I love my ſoul, Sir.
This man you put into a free poſſeſſion
Of what his wants could ask: or your ſelf render?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And ſhall do ſtill.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Nothing was barr'd his liberty
But this fair Maid; that friendſhip firſt was broken,
And you, and ſhe abus'd; next, (to my ſorrow
So fair a form ſhould hide ſo dark intentions)
He hath himſelf confeſs'd (my purpoſe being
Only to ſtop his journey, by that policy
Of laying Felony to his charge, to fright the Sailers)
Divers abuſes done, Thefts often practis'd,
Monyes, and Jewels too, and thoſe no trifles.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: O where have I beſtrew'd my faith! in neither!
Let's in for ever now, there is vertue.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Nay do not wonder at it, he ſhall ſay it:
Are ye not guilty thus?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Yes: O my Fortune!

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: To give a proof I ſpeak not enviouſly,
Look here; do you know theſe Jewels?

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: In, good Mother.

div.stage: Enter Thomas, Dorothy, and Mary: then Sebaſtian, and Launcelot.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Theſe Jewels I have known.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: You have made brave ſport.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: I'le make more, if I live Wench,
Nay do not look on me; I care not for ye.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Do you ſee now plain? that's Miſtris Dorothy,
And that's his Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Peace, let my joy work eaſily,
Ha, boy! art there my boy? mine own boy, Tom, boy,
Home Lance, and ſtrike a freſh piece of Wine, the Town's ours.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Sure, I have know theſe Jewels.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: They are they, certain.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Good Heaven, that they were.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: I'le pawn my life on't,
And this is he; come hither Miſtris Dorothy,
And Miſtris Mary: who does that face look like;
And view my Brother well?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: In truth like him.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Upon my troth exceeding like.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: Beſhrew me,
But much, and main reſemblance, both of face
And lineaments of body: now Heaven grant it.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: My Brother's full of paſſion, I'le ſpeak to him.
Now, as you are a Gentleman, reſolve me,
Where did you get theſe Jewels?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Now I'le tell ye,
Becauſe blind fortune yet may make me happy,
Of whom I had 'em I have never heard yet,
But from my infancy, upon this arm
I ever wore 'em.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: 'Tis Franciſco, Brother,
By Heaven I ty'd 'em on: a little more, Sir,
A little, little more, what parents have ye?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: None,
That I know yet: the more my ſtubborn fortune,
But as I heard a Merchant ſay that bred me,
Who, to my more affliction, dyed a poor man,
When I teach'd eighteen years.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: What ſaid that Merchant?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: He ſaid, an infant, in the Genoway Galleys,
But from what place he never could direct me,
I was taken in a Sea-fight, and from a Mariner,
Out of his manly pity he redeem'd me.
He told me of a Nurſe that waited on me,
But ſhe, poor ſoul, he ſaid was killed.
A Letter too I had enclos'd within me,
To one Caſtruccio a Venetian Merchant,
To bring me up: the man, when years allow'd me,
And want of friends compell'd, I ſought, but found him
Long dead before, and all my hopes gone with him.
The Wars was my retreat then, • nd my travel
In which I found this Gentlemans free bounty,
For which Heaven recompenc'd him: now ye have all

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And all the worldly bliſs that Heaven can ſend me,
And all my prayers and thanks.

sp.speaker: Alice.
sp.l: Down o' your knees, Sir,
For now you have found a Father, and that Father
That will not venture ye again in Galleys.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: 'Tis true, believe her, Sir, and we all joy with ye.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: My beſt friend ſtill: my deareſt: now Heaven bleſs thee.
And make me worthy of this benefit.
Now my beſt Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Cel.
sp.l: Now Sir, I come to ye.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: No, no, let's in Wench.

sp.speaker: Cell.
sp.l: Not for the world, now, Mother,
And thus, Sir, all my ſervice I pay to you,
And all my love to him.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And may it proſper,
Take her Franciſco: now no more young Callidon,
And love her dearly, for thy Father does ſo.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: May all hate ſeek me elſe, and thus I ſeal it.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Nothing but mirth now, friends.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Nay, I will find him.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: What do all theſe here?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: You are a truſty Husband,
And a hot lover too.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Nay then, good morrow,
Now I perceive the Knavery.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: I ſtill told ye.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Stay, or I'le make ye ſtay: come hither, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Why how now Miſtris Thomas?

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Peace a little,
Thou would'ſt fain have a Wife?

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Not I, by no means.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have a wife, and a fruitful wife, for I find, Hylas,
That I ſhall never be able to bring thee Children.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: A notable brave boy.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: I am very well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt be better, Hylas, thou haſt 7 hundred pound a year,
And thou ſhalt make her 3 hundred j • ynture.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt boy, and ſhalt beſtow
Two hundred pound in Cloaths, look on her,
A delicate luſty wench, ſhe has fifteen hundred,
And feaſible: ſtrike hands, or I'le ſtrike firſt.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: You'l let me like?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: He's a good handſome fellow,
Play not the fool.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Strike, Brother Hylas, quickly.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: If you can love me, well.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: If you can pleaſe me.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Try that out ſoon, I ſay, my Brother Hylas.

sp.speaker: Sam.
sp.l: Take her, and uſe her well, ſhe's a brave Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: You muſt allow me another Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Then you muſt allow me another Servant.

sp.speaker: Hyl.
sp.l: Well, let's together then, a luſty kindred.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: I'le give thee five hundred pound more for that word.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Now Sir, for you and I to make the feaſt full.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: No, not a bit, you are a vertuous Lady,
And love to live in contemplation.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Come fool, I am friends now.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: The fool ſhall not ride ye,
There lye my Woman, now my man again,
And now for travel once more.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: I'le barr that firſt.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: And I next.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Hold your ſelf contented: for I ſay I will travel,
And ſo long I will travel, till I find a Father
That I never knew, and a Wife that I never look'd for,
And a ſtate without expectation,
So reſt you merry Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: You ſhall not,
Upon my faith, I love you now extreamly,
And now I'le kiſs ye.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: This will not do it, Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Why when we are married, we'l do more.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: There's all Boy,
The keyes of all I have, come, let's be merry,
For now I ſee thou art right.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Shall we to Church ſtraight?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Now preſently, and there with nuptial
The holy Prieſt ſhall make ye happy all.

sp.speaker: Tho.
sp.l: Away then, fair afore.

div.head: TO THE NOBLE HONOURER OF THE Dead Author's Works and Memory, Maſter CHARLES COTTON.
div.p: MY directing of this piece unto you, renders me obvious to many cenſures, which I would willingly prevent by declaring mine own and your right thereto. Mine was the fortune to be made the unworthy preſerver of it; yours is the worthy opinion you have of the Author and his Poems; neither can it eaſily be determined, whether your affection to them hath made you (by obſerving) more able to judge of them, than your ability to judge of them hath made you to affect them, deſervedly, not partially. In this preſumptuous act of mine, I expreſs my twofold zeal; to him and your noble ſelf, who have built him a more honourable monument in that fair opinion you have of him, than any inſcription ſubject to the wearing of time can be. You will find him in this Poem as active as in others, to many of which, the dull apprehenſions of former times gave but ſlender allowance, from malitious cuſtom more than reaſon: yet they have ſince by your candid ſelf and others, been clearly vindicated. You ſhall oblige by your acceptance of this acknowledgment (which is the beſt I can render you, mine own weak labours being too unworthy your judicious peruſal) him that is ambitious to be known

closer.signed: Your moſt humble Servant, RICHARD BROME.

list.item: Antonio, an old ſtout Gentleman, Kinſman to Petruccio.
Three Gentlemen, friends to the Duke.
Peter Vecchio, a Teacher of Latine and Muſick, a reputed Wizard.

list.head: two Servants to Don John and Frederick.
WOMEN.
list.item: Conſtancia, Siſter to Petruccio, and Miſtriſs to the Duke.
Old Gentlewoman, Landlady to Don John and Frederick.
Conſtancia, a Whore to old Antonio.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter 2. Serving men, Peter and Anthony.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: I WOULD we were remov'd from this town, Anthony,
That we might taſte ſome quiet; for mine own part,
I'm almoſt melted with continual trotting
After enquiries, dreams, and revelations,
Of who knows whom, or where? ſerve wenching ſoldiers,
That knows no other Paradiſe but Plackets:
I'll ſerve a Prieſt in Lent firſt, and eat Bell ropes.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thou art the froward'ſt fool—

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: VVhy, good tame Anthonie?
Tell me but this; to what end came we hither?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: To wait upon our Maſters.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: But how, Anthony?
Anſwer me that; reſolve me there, good Anthony?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: To ſerve their uſes.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Shew your uſes, Anthony.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: To be imploy'd in any thing.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: No Anthony,
Not any thing I take it; nor that thing
VVe travel to diſcover, like new iſlands;
A ſ • lt itch ſerve ſuch uſes; in things of moment
Concerning things, I grant ye, not things errant,
Sweet Ladies things, and things to thank the Surgeon;
In no ſuch things, ſweet Anthony, put caſe—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Come, come, all will be mended; this inviſible woman
Of infinite report for ſhape and vertue,
That bred us all this trouble to no purpoſe,
They are determin'd now no more to think on,
But fall cloſe to their ſtudies.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: VVas there ever
Men known to run mad with report before?
Or wonder after they know not where
To find? or if found, how to enjoy? are mens brains
Made now adays of malt, that their affections
Are never ſober? but like drunken People
Founder at every new Fame? I do believe too
That men in love are ever drunk, as drunken men
Are ever loving.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Prithee be thou ſober,
And know, that they are none of thoſe, not guilty
Of the leaſt vanity of love, only a doubt
Fame might too far report, or rather flatter
The Graces of this Woman, made them curious
To find the truth, which ſince they find ſo blocked
And lockt up from their ſearches, they are now ſetled
To give the wonder over.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Would they were ſetled
To give me ſome new ſhoos too: for I'll be ſworn
Theſe are e'en worn out to the reaſonable ſouls
In their good worſhips buſineſs; and ſome ſleep
Would not do much amiſs, unleſs they mean
To make Bell man on me; and what now
Mean they to ſtudy, Anthony, moral Philoſophy
After their mar-all women?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Mar a fools head.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Twill mar two fools heads and they take not heed,
Beſides the Giblets to 'em.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Will you walk, Sir,
And talk more out of hearing? your fools head
May chance to find a wooden night-cap elſe.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I never layin any.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Then leave your lying,
And your blind propheſying: here they come,
You had beſt tell them as much.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I am no tell-tale. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I would we could have ſeen her though; for ſure
She muſt be ſome rare Creature, or Report lies.
All mens Reports too.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I could well wiſh I had ſeen her;
But ſince ſhe is ſo conceal'd, ſo beyond venture
Kept and preſerv'd from view, ſo like a Paradiſe,
Plac'd where no knowledge can come near her; ſo guarded,
As 'twere impoſſible, though known, to reach her,
I have made up my belief.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Hang me from this hour
If I more think upon her, or believe her,
But as ſhe came a ſtrong Report unto me,
So the next Fame ſhall loſe her.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis the next way;
But whither are you walking?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: My old Round
After my meat, and then to Bed.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis healthful.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Will not you ſtir?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I have a little buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Upon my life this Lady ſtill—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Then you will loſe it.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: 'Pray let's walk together.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Now I cannot.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I have ſomething to impart.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: An hour hence
I will not miſs to meet you.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I'th' high ſtreet;
For not to lie, I have a few Devotions
To do firſt, then I am yours.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Remember. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Antonio, and two Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Cut his wind-pipe I ſay.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Fye, Antonio.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Or knock his brains out firſt, and then forgive him,
If you do thruſt, be ſure it be to th'hilts,
A Surgeon may ſee through him.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You are too violent.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Too open undiſcreet.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Am I not ruin'd?
The honour of my houſe crack'd? my bloud poyſon'd?
My Credit and my Name?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Be ſure it be ſo,
Before ye uſe this violence: Let not doubt,
And a ſuſpecting anger ſo much ſway ye,
Your wiſedom may be queſtion'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſay kill him,
And then diſpute the cauſe; cut off what may be,
And what is ſhall be ſafe.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Hang up a true man,
Becauſe 'tis poſſible he may be thieviſh!
Alas, is this good Juſtice?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I know as certain
As day muſt come again, as clear as truth,
And open as belief can lay it to me,
That I am baſely wrong'd, wrong'd above recompence;
Maliciouſly abus'd, blaſted for ever
In name and honour, loſt to all remembrance,
But what is ſmear'd, and ſhameful; I muſt kill him,
Neceſſity compells me.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: But think better.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: There is no other cure left; yet witneſs with me,
All that is fair in man, all that is noble,
I am not greedy of this life I ſeek for,
Nor thirſt to ſhed mans blood, and would 'twere poſſible,
I wiſh it with my ſoul, ſo much I tremble
To offend the ſacred Image of my Maker,
My ſword could only kill his Crimes; no, 'tis Honour,
Honour, my noble friends, that Idol, Honour,
That all the world now worſhips, not Petruchio
Muſt do this Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let it once be done,
And 'tis no matter, whether you, or honour,
Or both, be acceſſary.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Do you weigh, Petruchio,
The value of the perſon, power, and greatneſs,
And what this ſpark may kindle?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: To perform it,
So much I am ty'd to Reputation,
And Credit of my houſe, let it raiſe wild-fires,
That all this Dukedom ſmoak, and ſtorms that toſs me
Into the waves of everlaſting ruine,
Yet I muſt through; if ye dare ſide me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Dare?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Y'are friends indeed, if not.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Here's none flyes from you,
Do it in what deſign ye pleaſe, we'll back ye.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: But then be ſure ye kill him.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Is the cauſe
So mortal, nothing but his life?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Believe me,
A leſs offence has been the deſolation
Of a whole name.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: No other way to purge it?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: There is, but never to be hoped for.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Think an hour more,
And if then ye find no ſafer Road to guide ye,
We'll ſet up our Reſts Too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Mine's up already,
And hang him for my part
Goes leſs than life.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: If we ſee noble cauſe, 'tis like our Swords
May be as free and forward as your words. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: The civil order of this Town, Bologna,
Makes it belov'd and honour'd of all Travellers,
As a moſt ſafe retirement in all troubles;
Beſide the wholſome ſeat, and noble temper
Of thoſe minds that inhabit it, ſafely wiſe,
And to all ſtrangers vertuous; But I ſee
My admiration has drawn night upon me,
And longer to expect my friend may pull me
Into ſuſpicion of too late a ſtirrer,
Which all good Governments are jealous of.
I'll home, and think at liberty: yet certain,
'Tis not ſo far night as I thought; for ſee,
A fair houſe yet ſtands open, yet all about it
Are cloſe, and no lights ſtirring, there may be foul play;
I'le venture to look in: if there be knaves,
I may do a good office. woman within.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Signieur?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: What? how is this?

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Signieur Fabritio?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I'le go nearer.

l.hi: Fabritio?

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: This is a womans tongue, here may be good done.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Who's there?

l.hi: Fabritio?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Where are ye?

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Here.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: O come, for Heavens ſake!

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: I muſt ſee what this means.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: I have ſtay'd this long hour for you, make no noiſe,
For things are in ſtrange trouble: here, be ſecret,
'Tis worth your care; begon now; more eyes watch us,
Than may be for our ſafeties.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: Hark ye?

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Peace: good night.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: She is gone, and I am loaden; fortune for me;
It weighs well, and it feels well; it may chance
To be ſome pack of worth: byth' maſs 'tis heavie;
If it be Coyn or Jewels, 'tis w •• th w • lcom:
I'le ne're refuſe a fortune: I am co ••••
'Tis of no common price: now to my lodg •• g.
If it hit right, I'le bl • ſs this night. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange,
I cannot meet him; ſure he has encountred
Some light o' love or other, and there means
To play at in and in for this night. Well Don John,
If you do ſpring a leak, or get an itch,
Till ye claw off your curl'd pate, thank your night-walks:
You muſt be ſtill a bootchalling: one round more,
Though it be late, I'le venture to diſcover ye,
I do not like your out-leaps. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Welcom to Town, are ye all fit?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: To point Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Where are the horſes?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Where they were appointed.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Be private, and whatſoever fortune
Offer it ſelf, let's ſtand ſure.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: Fear not us,
E're ye ſhall be endangered, or deluded,
We'll make a black night on't.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No more, I know it;
You know your Quarters?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Will you go alone Sir?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Ye ſhall not be far from me, the leaſt noiſe
Shall bring ye to my reſcue.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: We are counſell'd. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Was ever man ſo paid for being curious?
Ever ſo bob'd for ſearching out adventures,
As I am? did the Devil lead me? muſt I needs be peeping
Into mens houſes where I had no buſineſs,
And make my ſelf a miſchief? 'Tis well carried;
I muſt take other mens occaſions on me,
And be I know not whom: moſt finely handled:
What have I got by this now? what's the purchaſe?
A piece of evening Arras work, a child,
Indeed an Infidel: this comes of peeping:
A lump got out of lazineſs; good white bread
Let's have no bawling with ye: 'ſdeath, have I
Known wenches thus long, all the ways of wenches,
Their ſnares and ſubtilties? have I read over
All their School learnings, div'd into their quiddits,
And am I now bum-fidled with a Baſtard?
Fetch'd over with a Card of five, and in mine old days,
After the dire maſſacre of a million
Of Maiden heads? caught the common way, i'th' night too
Under anothers name, to make the matter
Carry more weight about it? well Don John,
You will be wiſer one day, when ye have purchas'd
A beavy of theſe Butter-prints together,
With ſearching out conceal'd iniquities,
Without commiſſion: why, it would never grieve me,
If I had got this Ginger-bread: never ſtirr'd me,
So I had had a ſtroak for't: 't had been Juſtice
Then to have kept it; but to raiſe a dayrie
For other mens adulteries, conſume my ſelf in candles,
And ſcowring works, in Nurſes Bells and Babies,
Only for charity, for meer I thank you,
A little troubles me: the leaſt touch for it,
Had but my breeches got it, had contented me.
Whoſe e're it is, ſure 't had a wealthy Mother,
For 'tis well cloathed, and if I be not cozen'd,
Well lin'd within: to leave it here were barbarous,
And ten to one would kill it: a more ſin
Then his that got it: well, I will diſpoſe on't,
And keep it, as they keep deaths heads in rings,
To cry memento to me; no more peeping.
Now all the danger is to qualifie
The good old gentlewoman, at whoſe houſe we live,
For ſhe will fall upon me with a Catechiſm
Of four hours long: I muſt endure all;
For I will know this Mother: Come good wonder,
Let you and I be jogging: your ſtarv'd trebble
Will waken the rude watch elſe: all that be
Curious night-walkers, may they find my fee. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Sure he's gone home:
I have beaten all the purlews,
But cannot bolt him: if he be a bobbing,
'Tis not my care can cure him: To morrow morning
I ſhall have further knowledge from a Surgeon's—
Where he lyes moor'd, to mend his leaks.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I'm ready,
And through a world of dangers am flown to ye.
Be full of haſte and care, we are undone elſe:
Where are your people? which way muſt we travel?
For Heaven ſake ſtay not here Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What may this prove?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Alas I am miſtaken, loſt, undone,
For ever periſh'd. Sir, for Heaven ſake tell me,
Are ye a Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I am.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Of this place?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No, born in Spain.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: As ever you lov'd honour,
As ever your deſires may gain their ends,
Do a poor wretched woman but this benefit,
For I am forc'd to truſt ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Y'ave charm'd me,
Humanity and honour bids me help ye;
And if I fail your truſt.—

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: The time's too dangerous
To ſtay your proteſtations: I believe ye,
Alas, I muſt believe ye: From this place,
Good noble Sir, remove me inſtantly,
And for a time, where nothing but your ſelf,
And honeſt converſation may come near me,
In ſome ſecure place ſertle me: what I am
And why thus boldly I commit my credit
Into a ſtrangers hand, the fears and dangers,
That force me to this wild courſe, at more leiſure
I ſhall reveal unto you.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come, be hearty,
He muſt ſtrike through my life that takes ye from me.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: He will ſure come. Are ye well arm'd?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Never fear us.
Here's that will make 'em dance without a Fiddle.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: We are to look for no weak foes, my friends,
Nor unadviſed ones.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Beſt gameſters make the beſt game,
We ſhall fight cloſe and handſom then.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.

l.hi: Antonio,

sp.l: You are a thought too bloudy.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why? all Phyſicians
And penny Almanacks allow the opening
Of veins this moneth: why do ye talk of bloudy?
What come we for, to fall to cuffes for apples?
What, would ye make the cauſe a Cudgel quarrel?
On what terms ſtands this man? is not his honour
Open'd to his hand, and pickt out like an Oyſter?
His credit like a qua • t pot knockt together,
Able to hold no liquor? clear but this point.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Speak ſoftly, gentle couſin.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'le ſpeak truly;
What ſhould men do ally'd to theſe diſgraces,
Lick o're his enemie, ſit down, and dance him?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: You are as far o'th', bow hand now.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And crie;
That's my fine boy, thou wilt do ſo no more child.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Here are no ſuch cold pities.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: By Saint Jaques
They ſhall not find me one: here's old tough Andrew,
A ſpecial friend of mine, and he but hold,
I'le ſtrike 'em ſuch a hornpipe: knocks I come for,
And the beſt bloud I light on; I profeſs it,
Not to ſcare Coſter-mongers; If I loſe mine own,
Mine audits caſt, and farewel five and fifty.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Let's talk no longer, place your ſelves with ſilence,
As I directed ye, and when time calls us,
As ye are friends, ſo ſhew your ſelves.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: So be it. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IX.
div.stage: Enter Don John, and his Land-lady.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Nay Son, if this be your regard.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Good Mother.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Good me no goods; your couſin, and your ſelf
Are welcom to me, whilſt you bear your ſelves
Like honeſt and true Gentlemen: Bring hither
To my houſe, that have ever been reputed
A Gentlewoman of a decent, and fair carriage,
And ſo behav'd my ſelf —

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I know ye have.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Bring hither, as I ſay, to make my name
Stink in my neighbours noſtrils? your Deviſes,
Your Brats, got out of Alligant, and broken oaths?
Your Linſey Woolſy work, your haſty puddings?
I, foſter up your filch'd iniquities?
Y'are deceiv'd in me, Sir, I am none
Of thoſe receivers.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Have I not ſworn unto you,
'Tis none of mine, and ſhew'd you how I found it?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Ye found an eaſie fool that let you get it,
She had better have worn paſterns.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Will ye hear me?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Oaths? what do you care for oaths to gain your en • s.
When ye are high and pamper'd? What Saint know y • ?
Or what Religion, but your purpos'd lewdneſs,
Is to be look'd for of ye? nay, I will tell ye,
You will then ſwear like accus'd Cut-purſes,
As far off truth too; and lye beyond all Faulconers:
I'me ſick to ſee this dealing.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Heaven forbid Mother.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Nay, I am very ſick.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Who waits there?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sir. within.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Bring down the bottle of Canary wine

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Exceeding ſick, Heav'n help me.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Haſte ye Sirrah,
I muſt ev'n make her drunk; nay gentle mother.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Now fie upon ye, was it for this purpoſe
You fetch'd your evening walks for your digeſtions,
For this pretended holineſs? no weather,
Not before day could hold ye from the Matins.
Were theſe your bo-peep prayers? ye' have pray'd well,
And with a learned zeal: watcht well too. your Saint
It ſeems was pleas'd as well: ſtill ſicker, ſicker.

div.stage: Enter Anthony, with a bottle of wine.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: There is no talking to her till I have drencht her.
Give me: here mother take a good round draught,
'Twill purge ſpleen from your ſpirits: deeper mother.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I, I, ſon, you imagine this will mend all.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: All i' faith Mother.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I confeſs the Wine
Will do his part.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I'le pledge ye.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: But ſon John.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: I know your meaning mother; touch it once more,
Alas you look not well; take a round draught,
It warms the bloud well, and reſtores the colour,
And then we'll talk at large.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: A civil Gentleman?
A ſtranger? one the Town holds a good regard of?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Nay I will ſilence thee.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: One that ſhould weigh his fair name? oh, a ſtitch!

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: There's nothing better for a ſtitch, good Mother,
Make no ſpare of it, as you love your health,
Mince not the matter.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: As I ſaid, a Gentleman,
Lodge in my houſe? now heav'ns my comfort, Signior!

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I look'd for this.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I did not think you would have us'd me thus;
A woman of my credit: one, heaven knows,
That lov'd you but too tenderly.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Dear Mother,
I ever found your kindneſs, and knowledge it.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: No, no, I am a fool to counſel ye. Where's the infant?
Come, let's ſee your Workmanſhip.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: None of mine, Mother,
But there 'tis, and a luſty one.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs thee,
Thou hadſt a haſty making; but the beſt is,
'Tis many a good mans fortune: as I live
Your own eyes Signior, and the nether lip
As like ye, as ye had ſpit it.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I am glad on't.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Bleſs me, what things are theſe?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I thought my labour
Was not all loſt, 'tis gold, and theſe are jewels,
Both rich, and right I hope.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Well, well ſon John,
I ſee ye are a wood man, and can chuſe
Your dear, though it be i'th' dark, all your diſcretion
Is not yet loſt; this was well clapt aboard:
Here I am with you now; when as they ſay
Your pleaſure comes with profit; when ye muſt needs do,
Do where ye may be done to, 'tis a wiſedom
Becomes a young man well: be ſure of one thing,
Loſe not your labour and your time together,
It ſeaſons of a fool, ſon, time is pretious,
Work wary whilſt ye have it: ſince ye muſt traffick
Sometimes this ſlippery way, take ſure hold Signior,
Trade with no broken Merchants, make your lading,
As you would make your reſt, adventurouſly,
But with advantage ever.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: All this time Mother,
The child wants lookng to, wants meat and Nurſes.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Now bleſſing o' thy care; it ſhall have all,
And inſtantly; I'le ſeek a Nurſe my ſelf, ſon;
'Tis a ſweet child: ah my young Spaniard,
Take you no further care Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Yes of theſe Jewels,
I muſt by your leave Mother: theſe are yours,
To make your care the ſtronger: for the reſt
I'le find a Maſter; the gold for bringing up on't,
I freely render to your charge.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: No more words,
Nor no more children, (good ſon) as you love me,
This may do well.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I ſhall obſerve your Morals.
But where's Don Frederick, Mother?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Ten to one
About the like adventure: he told me,
He was to find you out. Exit.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Why ſhould he ſtay thus?
There may be ſome ill chance in't: ſleep I will not,
Before I have found him: now this woman's pleas'd,
I'le ſeek my friend out, and my care is eas'd. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Believe Sir, 'tis as poſſible to do it,
As to remove the City; the main faction
Swarm though the ſtreets like hornets, arm'd with angers
Able to ruine States: no ſafety left us,
Nor means to dye like men, if inſtantly
You draw not back again.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: May he be drawn
And quarter'd too, that turns now; were I ſurer
Of death than thou art of thy fears, and with death
More than thoſe fears are too.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Sir, I fear not.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I would not crack my vow, ſtart from my honour,
Becauſe I may find danger; wound my ſoul,
To keep my body ſafe.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I ſpeak not Sir,
Out of a baſeneſs to you.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No, nor do not
Out of a baſeneſs leave me: what is danger,
More than the weakneſs of our apprehenſions?
A poor cold part o'th' bloud? who takes it hold of
Cowards, and wicked livers: valiant minds,
Were made the Maſters of it: and as hearty Sea-men
In deſperate ſtorms, ſtem with a little Rudder
The tumbling ruines of the Ocean:
So with their cauſe and ſwords do they do dangers.
Say we were ſure to dye all in this venture,
As I am confident againſt it: is there any
Amongſt us of ſo fat a ſenſe, ſo pamper'd,
Would chuſe luxuriouſly to lye a bed,
And purge away his ſpirit, ſend his ſoul out
In Sugar-ſops, and Syrups? Give me dying
As dying ought to be, upon mine enemy,
Parting with man-kind, by a man that's manly:
Let 'em be all the world, and bring along
Cain's envy with 'em, I will on.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: You may Sir,
But with what ſafety?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Since 'tis come to dying,
You ſhall perceive Sir, here be thoſe amongſt us
Can dye as decently as other men,
And with as little cermony: on brave Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: That's ſpoken heartily.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: And he that flinches,
May he dye lowzie in a ditch.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No more dying,
There's no ſuch danger in it:
What's a clock?

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: Somewhat above your hour.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Away then quickly,
Make no noiſe, and no truble will attend us. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE XI.
div.stage: Enter Frederick, and Peter, (with a candle.)

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Give me the candle: ſo, go you out that way.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: What have we now to do?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And o' your life Sirrah,
Let none come near the door without my knowledge,
No not my Landlady, nor my friend.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: 'Tis done Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Nor any ſerious buſineſs that concerns me.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: Is the wind there again?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Be gone.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: I am Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Now enter without fear. — And noble Lady
That ſafety and civility ye wiſh'd for
Shall truly here attend you: no rude tongue
Nor rough behaviour knows this place, no wiſhes
Beyond the moderation of a man,
Dare enter here; your own deſires and Innocence,
Joyn'd to my vow'd obedience, ſhall protect you,
Were dangers more than doubts.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Ye are truly noble,
And worth a womans truſt: let it become me,
(I do beſeech you, Sir) for all your kindneſs,
To render with my thanks, this worthleſs trifle;
I may be longer troubleſome.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Fair offices
Are ſtill their own rewards: Heav'n bleſs me Lady
From ſelling civil courteſies: may it pleaſe ye,
If ye will force a favour to oblige me,
Draw but that cloud aſide, to ſatisfie me
For what good Angel I am engag'd.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: It ſhall be,
For I am truly confident ye are honeſt:
The Piece is ſcarce worth looking on.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Truſt me
The abſtract of all beauty, ſoul of ſweetneſs,
Defend me honeſt thoughts, I ſhall grow wild elſe:
What eyes are there, rather what little heavens,
To ſtir mens contemplations? what a Paradiſe
Runs through each part ſhe has? good bloud be temperate:
I muſt look off: too excellent an object
Confounds the ſenſe that ſees it. Noble Lady,
If there be any further ſervice to caſt on me,
Let it be worth my life, ſo much I honour ye,
Or the engagement of whole Families.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Your ſervice is too liberal, worthy Sir,
Thus far I ſhall entreat.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Command me Lady,
You make your power too poor.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: That preſently
With all convenient haſte, you would retire
Unto the ſtreet you found me in.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis done.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: There, if you find a Gentleman oppreſt
With force and violence, do a mans office,
And draw your ſword to reſcue him.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: He's ſafe,
Be what he will, and let his foes be Devils,
Arm'd with your pity, I ſhall conjure 'em.
Retire, this key will guide ye: all things neceſſary
Are there before ye.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: All my prayers go with ye. Ex ••

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye clap on proof upon me: men ſay gold
Does all, engages all, works through all dangers:
Now I ſay beauty can do more: The Kings Exchequer,
Not all his wealthy Indies, could not draw me
Through half thoſe miſeries this piece of pleaſure
Might make me leap into: we are all like ſea-Cards,
All our endeavours and our motions,
(As they do to the North) ſtill point at beauty,
Still at the faireſt: for a handſom woman,
(Setting my ſoul aſide) it ſhould go hard,
But I would ſtrain my body: yet to her,
Unleſs it be her own free gratitude,
Hopes ye ſhall dye, and thou tongue rot within me,
E're I infringe my faith: now to my reſcue. Exit.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke, purſued by Petruccio, Antonio, and that Faction.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: YOu will not all oppreſs me?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Kill him i'th' wanton eye: let me come to him.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Then ye ſhall buy me dearly.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Say you ſo Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſay cut his Wezand, ſpoil his piping;
Have at your love-ſick heart Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Sure 'tis fighting.
My friend may be engag'd: fie Gentlemen,
This is unmanly odds.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'le ſtop your mouth Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Nay, then have at thee freely: Du. fals down, Don John beſtrides him.
There's a plumb Sir to ſatisfie your longing.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Away: I hope I have ſped him: here comes reſcue,
We ſhall be endangered: where's Antonio?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I muſt have one thruſt more Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Come up to me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
