sp.l: A miſchief confound your fingers.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: How is't?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Well:
Ha's given me my quietus eſt, I felt him
In my ſmall guts, I'me ſure, has feez'd me:
This comes of ſiding with ye.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Can you go Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſhould go man, and my head were off,
Never talk of going.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Come, all ſhall be well then,
I hear more reſcue coming.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let's turn back then;
My skull's uncloven yet, let me but kill.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Away for Heaven ſake with him.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: How is't?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Well Sir,
Only a little ſtagger'd.

sp.speaker: Faction Duke.
sp.l: Let's purſue 'em.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No not a man, I charge ye: thanks good coat,
Thou haſt ſav'd me a ſhrewd welcom: 'twas put home too,
With a good mind I'me ſure on't.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Are ye ſafe then?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: My thanks to you brave Sir, whoſe timely valour,
And manly courteſie came to my reſcue.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Ye' had foul play offer'd ye, and ſhame befal him
That can paſs by oppreſſion.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: May I crave Sir,
But thus much honour more, to know your name?
And him I am ſo bound to?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: For the Bond Sir,
'Tis every good mans tye: to know me further
Will little profit ye; I am a ſtranger,
My Country Spain; my name Don John, a Gentleman
That lye here for my ſtudy.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I have heard Sir,
Much worthy mention of ye, yet I find
Fame ſhort of what ye are.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: You are pleas'd Sir,
To expreſs your courteſie: may I demand
As freely what you are, and what miſchance
Caſt you into this danger?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: For this preſent
I muſt deſire your pardon: you ſhall know me
E're it be long Sir, and a nobler thanks
Than now my will can render.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Your will's your own Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What is't you look for ſir, have you loſt any thing?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Only my hat i'th' ſcuffle; ſure theſe fellows
Were night-ſnaps.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No, believe Sir: pray ye uſe mine,
For 'twill be hard to find your own now.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Indeed ye ſhall, I can command another:
I do beſeech ye honour me.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I will Sir,
And ſo I'le take my leave.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Within theſe few days
I hope I ſhall be happy in your knowledge,
Till when I love your memory. Exit Duke, &c.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I yours.
This is ſome noble fellow.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis is tongue ſure.

l.hi: Don John?
Don Frederick?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye' re fairly met Sir:
I thought ye had been a Bat-fowling: prethee tell me,
What Revelations haſt thou had to night,
That home was never thought of?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Revelations?
I'le tell thee Frederick, but before I tell thee,
Settle thy underſtanding.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis prepar'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Why then mark what ſhall follow. This night Frederick,
This bawdy night.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I thought no leſs.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: This blind night,
What doſt think I have got?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: The Pox it may be.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Would 'twere no worſe: ye talk of Revelations,
I have got a Revelation will reveal me
An arrant Coxcomb while I live.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What is't?
Thou haſt loſt nothing?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: No, I have got I tell thee.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What haſt thou got?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: One of the Infantry, a child.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: A chopping child, man.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Give ye joy, Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: A lump of lewdneſs Frederick, that's the truth on't:
This Town's abominable.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I ſtill told ye John
Your whoring muſt come home; I counſell'd ye:
But where no grace is—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: 'Tis none 'o mine, man.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Anſwer the Pariſh ſo.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Cheated introth:
Peeping into a houſe, by whom I know not,
Nor where to find the place again: no Frederick,
Had I but kiſſ the ring for't; 'tis no poor one,
That's my beſt comfort, for't has brought about it
Enough to make it man.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Where is't?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: At home.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: A ſaving voyage: But what will you ſay Signior,
To him that ſearching out your ſerious worſhip,
Has met a ſtranger fortune?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: How, good Frederick?
A militant gi • le now to this boy would hit it?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No, mine's a nobler venture: What do you think Sir
Of a diſtreſſed Lady, one whoſe beauty
Would overſell all Italy?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Where is ſhe—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: A woman of that rare behaviour,
So qualified, as admiration
Dwells round about her: of that perfect ſpirit—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I marry Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: That admirable carriage,
That ſweetneſs in diſcourſe; young as the morning,
Her bluſhes ſtaining his.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: But where's this creature?
Shew me but that.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: That's all one, ſhe's forth-coming,
I have her ſure Boy.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Hark ye Frederick,
What truck betwixt my Infant?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis too light Sir,
Stick to your charges good Don John, I am well.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: But is there ſuch a wench?

sp.speaker: Fred
sp.l: Firſt tell me this,
Did ye not lately as ye walk'd along,
Diſcov •• people that were arm'd, and likely
To do offence?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Yes marry, and they urg'd it
As far as they had ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Pray go forward.

sp.speaker: Joh.
sp.l: A Gentleman I found ingag'd amongſt 'em,
It ſeems of noble breeding, I'm ſure brave metal,
As I return'd to look you, I ſet in to him,
And without hurt (I thank heaven) reſcued him,
And came my ſelf off ſafe too.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: My work's done then:
And now to ſatisfie you, there is a woman,
Oh John, there is a woman—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Oh, where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And one of no leſs worth than I aſſure ye;
And which is more, faln under my protection.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I'am glad of that: forward ſweet Frederick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And which is more than that, by this nights wandring,
And which is moſt of all, ſhe is at home too Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Come, let's be gone then.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes, but 'tis moſt certain,
You cannot ſee her, John.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She has ſworn me
That none elſe ſhall come near her: not my Mother,
Till ſome f • w doubts are clear'd.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Not look upon her? What chamber is ſhe in?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: In ours.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Let's go I ſay:
A womans oaths are wafers, break with making,
They muſt for modeſtie a little: we all know it.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No, I'le aſſure you Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Not ſee her?
I ſmell an old dog trick of yours, well Frederick,
Ye talkt to me of whoring, let's have fair play,
Square dealing I would wiſh ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: When 'tis come,
(Which I know never will be) to that iſſue,
Your ſpoon ſhall be as deep as mine Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Tell me,
And tell me true, is the cauſe honourable,
Or for your caſe?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: By all our friendſhip, John,
'Tis honeſt, and of great end.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I am anſwer'd:
But let me ſee her though: leave the door open
As ye go in.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I dare not.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Not wide open,
But juſt ſo, as a jealous husband
Would level at his wanton wife through.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: That courteſie,
If ye deſire no more, and keep it ſtrictly,
I dare afford ye: come, 'tis now near morning. Exit.

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nay the old woman's gone too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She's a Catterwauling
Among the gutters: But conceive me, Peter,
Where our good Maſters ſhould be?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Where they ſhould be
I do conceive, but where they are, good Anthony—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I, there it goes: my Maſters bo-peep with me,
With his ſlye popping in and out again,
Argued a cauſe, a frippery cauſe.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Believe me,
They bear up with ſome carvel.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I do believe thee,
For thou haſt ſuch a Maſter for that chaſe,
That till he ſpend his main Maſt—

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Pray remember
Your courteſie good Anthony, and withal,
How long 'tis ſince your Maſter ſprung a leak,
He had a ſound one ſince he came.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Hark.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: What? Lute ſounds within.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Doſt not hear a Lute?
Again?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Where is't?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Above in my Maſters chamber.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: There's no creature: he hath the key himſelf man.

body.l: MErcileſs Love, whom nature hath deny'd
The uſe of eyes, leſt thou ſhould'ſt take a pride
And glorie in thy murthers: Why am I
That never yet tranſgreſs'd thy deity,
Never broke vow, from whoſe eyes never
Flew diſdainfull dart
Whoſe hard heart never,
Slew thoſe rewarders?
Thou art young and fair,
Thy Mother ſoft and gentle as the air,
Thy holy fire ſtill burning, blown with praier.
Then everlaſting Love reſtrain thy will
'Tis God-like to have power but not to kill.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This is his Lute: let him have it.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I grant you; but who ſtrikes it?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: An admirable voice too, hark ye.

sp.speaker: Pet.

l.hi: Anthony,

sp.l: Art ſure we are at home?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Without all doubt, Peter.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Then this muſt be the Devil.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let it be, Sing again.
Good Devil ſing again: O dainty Devil!
Peter, believe it, a moſt delicate Devil,
The ſweeteſt Devil —

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: If ye could leave peeping.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I cannot by no means.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Then come in ſoftly,
And as ye love your faith, preſume no further
Than ye have promiſed.

l.hi: Baſta.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What make you up ſo early Sir?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: You Sir in your contemplations.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: O pray ye peace Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why peace Sir?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Do you hear?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: 'Tis your Lute.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Pray ye ſpeak ſoftly,
She's playing on't.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The houſe is haunted Sir,
For this we have heard this half year.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye ſaw nothing?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Not I.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nor I Sit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Get us our breakfaſt then,
And make no words on't; we'll undertake this ſpirit,
If it be one.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This is no Devil Peter. Sing.
Mum, there be Bats abroad. Exeunt Servants.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Stay, now ſhe ſings.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: An Angels voice I'le ſwear.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why did'ſt thou ſhrug ſo?
Either allay this heat; or as I live
I will not truſt ye.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Paſs: I warrant ye. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: To curſe thoſe ſtars, that men ſay govern us,
To rail at fortune, fall out with my Fate,
And tax the general world, will help me nothing:
Alas, I am the ſame ſtill, neither are they
Subject to helps, or hurts: Our own deſires
Are our own fates, our own ſtars, all our fortunes,
Which as we ſway 'em, ſo abuſe, or bleſs us.

div.stage: Enter Frederick, and Don John, peeping.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace to your meditations.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Pox upon ye,
Stand out o'th' light.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: I crave your mercy Sir,
My minde o're-charg'd with care made me unmannerly.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Pray ye ſet that mind at reſt, all ſhall be perfect.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I like the body rare, a handſom body,
A wondrous handſom body: would ſhe would turn:
See, and that ſpightful puppy be not got
Between me and my light again.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis done,
As all that you command ſhall be: the Gentleman
Is ſafely off all danger.

l.hi: O de dios.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: How ſhall I thank ye Sir? how ſatisfie?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Speak ſoftly, gentle Lady, all's rewarded,
Now does he melt like Marmalad.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis certain,
Thou art the ſweeteſt woman I e're look'd on:
I hope thou art not honeſt.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: None diſturb'd ye?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Not any Sir, nor any ſound came near me,
I thank your care.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis well.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I would fain pray now,
But the Devil and that fleſh there, o' the world,
What are we made to ſuffer?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: He'll enter;
Pull in your head and be hang'd.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Hark ye Frederick,
I have brought ye home your Pack-ſaddle.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Pox upon ye.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Nay let him enter: fie my Lord the Duke,
Stand peeping at your friends.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye are cozen'd Lady,
Here is no Duke.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: I know him full well Signior.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Hold thee there wench.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: This mad-brain'd fool will ſpoil all.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: I do beſeech your grace come in.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: My Grace,
There was a word of comfort.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Shall he enter?
Who e're he be?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Well follow'd Frederick.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come in then.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: 'Bleſs ye Lady.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Nay ſtart not, though he be a ſtranger to ye,
He's of a noble ſtrain, my kinſman, Lady,
My Country-man, and fellow Traveller,
One bed contains us ever, one purſe feeds us,
And one faith free between us; do not fear him,
He's truly honeſt.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: That's a lye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And truſty:
Beyond your wiſhes: valiant to defend,
And modeſt to converſe with, as your bluſhes.

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: Now may I hang my ſelf; this commendation
Has broke the neck of all my hopes: for now
Muſt I cry, no forſooth, and I forſooth, and ſurely,
And truly as I live, and as I am honeſt.
Has done theſe things for 'nonce too; for he knows
Like a moſt envious Raſcal as he is,
I am not honeſt, nor deſire to be,
Eſpecially this way: h'as watch'd his time,
But I ſhall quit him.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Sir, I credit ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Go kils her John.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Plague o' your commendations.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Sir, I ſhall now deſire to be a trouble.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Never to me, ſweet Lady: Thus I ſeal
My faith, and all my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: One word Signior.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Now 'tis impoſſible I ſhould be honeſt,
She kiſſes with a conjuration
Would make the Devil dance: what points ſhe at?
My leg I warrant, or my well knit body,
Sit faſt Don Frederick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Twas given him by that Gentleman
You took ſuch care of; his own being loſt i'th' ſcuffle.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: With much joy may he wear it: 'tis a right one,
I can aſſure ye Gentleman, and right happy
May you be in all fights for that fair ſervice.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why do ye bluſh?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: 'T had almoſt cozen'd me,
For not to lye, when I ſaw that, I look'd for
Another Maſter of it: but 'tis well. Knock within.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Who's there?
Stand ye a little cloſe: Come in Sir, Exit Conſt.
Now what's the news with you?

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: There is a Gentleman without,
Would ſpeak with Don John.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Who Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I do not know Sir, but he ſhews a man
Of no mean reckoning.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let him ſhew his name,
And then return a little wiſer.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Well Sir. Exit Anthony.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How do you like her John?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: As well as you Frederick,
For all I am honeſt: you ſhall find it ſo too.

sp.speaker: Fred
sp.l: Art thou not honeſt?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Art thou an Aſs?
And modeſt as her bluſhes? What block-head
Would e're have popt out ſuch a dry Apologie,
For his dear friend? and to a Gentlewoman,
A woman of her youth, and delicacy.
They are arguments to draw them to abhor us.
An honeſt moral man? 'tis for a Conſtable:
A handſome man, a wholſome man, a tough man,
A liberal man, a likely man, a man
Made up like Hercules, unſlak'd with ſervice:
The ſame to night, to morrow night, the next night,
And ſo to perpetuitie of pleaſures,
Theſe had been things to hearken to, things catching:
But you have ſuch a ſpic'd conſideration,
Such qualms upon your worſhips conſcience,
Such-chil blains in your bloud, that all things pinch ye,
Which nature, and the liberal world makes cuſtom,
And nothing but fair honour, O ſweet honor,
Hang up your Eunuch honour: That I was truſty,
And valiant, were things well put in; but modeſt!
A modeſt Gentleman! O wit where waſt thou?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I am ſorrie John.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: My Ladies Gentlwoman
Would laugh me to a Shool-boy, make me bluſh
With playing with my Codpiece point: fie on thee,
A man of thy diſcretion?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: It ſhall be mended:
And henceforth ye ſhall have your due.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I look for't: How now, who is't?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A Gentleman of this Town
And calls himſelf Petrucchio.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I'le attend him.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: How did he call himſelf?

sp.speaker: Fre.

l.hi: Petrucchio,

sp.l: Does it concern you ought?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: O Gentlemen,
The hour of my deſtruction is come on me,
I am diſcover'd, loſt, left to my ruine:
As ever ye had pity —

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Do not fear,
Let the great devil come, he ſhall come through me:
Loſt here, and we about ye?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Fall before us?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: O my unfortunate eſtate, all angers
Compar'd to his, to his —

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let his, and all mens,
Whilſt we have power and life—ſtand up for heaven ſake.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I have offended heaven too; yet heaven knows—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: We are all evil:
Yet Heaven forbid we ſhould have our deſerts.
What is he?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Too too near to my offence Sir;
O he will cut me piece-meal.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis no Treaſon?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Let it be what it will, if he cut here,
I'le find him cut-work.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: He muſt buy you dear,
With more than common lives.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Fear not, nor weep not:
By heaven I'le fire the Town before ye periſh,
And then, the more the merrier, we'l jog with ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come in, and dry your eyes.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Pray no more weeping:
Spoil a ſweet face for nothing? my return
Shall end all this I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Heaven grant it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: This man ſhould be of ſpecial rank:
For theſe commends carry no common way,
No ſlight worth with 'em:
He ſhall be he.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: 'Save ye Sir: I am ſorrie
My buſineſs was ſo unmannerly, to make ye
Wait thus long here.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Occaſions muſt be ſerv'd Sir:
But is your name Don John?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: It is Sir.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Then,
Firſt, for your own brave ſake I muſt embrace ye:
Next, from the credit of your noble friend
Hernando de Alvara, make ye mine:
Who lays his charge upon me in this Letter
To look ye out, and for the goodneſs in ye,
Whilſt your occaſions make ye reſident
In this place, to ſupply ye, love and honour ye;
Which had I know ſooner —

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Noble Sir,
You'l make my thanks too poor: I wear a ſword, Sir,
And have a ſervide to be ſtill diſpos'd of,
As you ſhall pleaſe command it.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Gentle Sir,
That manly courteſie is half my buſineſs:
And to be ſhort, to make ye know I honour ye,
And in all points believe your worth like Oracle,
And how above my friends, which are not few,
And thoſe not ſlack, I eſtimate your vertues,
Make your ſelf underſtand, This day Petrucchio,
A man that may command the ſtrength of this place,
Hazard the boldeſt ſpirits, hath made choice
Only of you, and in a noble office.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Forward, I am free to entertain it.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Thus then:
I do beſeech ye mark me.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I ſhall do it.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Ferrara's Duke, would I might call him worthie,
But that, he has raz'd out from his family,
As he has mine with Infamie, This man,
Rather this powerfull Monſter, we being left
But two of all our houſe, to ſtock our memories,
My Siſter, and my ſelf; with arts, and witchcrafts,
Vows, and ſuch oaths heaven has no mercy for,
Drew to diſhonour this weak maid, by ſtealths,
And ſecret paſſages I knew not of,
Oft he obtain'd his wiſhes, oft abus'd her:
I am aſham'd to ſay the reſt: This purchas'd,
And his hot bloud allay'd, as friends forſake us
At a miles end upon our way, he left her,
And all our name to ruine.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: This was foul Play,
And ought to be rewarded ſo.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: I hope ſo;
He ſcap'd me yeſter-night: which if he dare
Again adventure for, Heaven pardon him,
I ſhall with all my heart.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: For me, brave Signior,
What do ye intend?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Only, fair Sir, this truſt,
Which from the commendations of this Letter,
I dare preſume well plac'd, nobly to bear him
By word of mouth a ſingle challenge from me,
That man to man, if he have honour in him,
We may decide all difference.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Fair, and noble,
And I will do it home: When ſhall I viſite ye?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Pleaſe you this after-noon, I will ride with you:
For at a Caſtle ſix miles hence, we are ſure
To find him.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I'le be ready.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: To attend ye,
My man ſhall wait: with all my love. Ex. Petr.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: My ſervice ſhall not fail ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How now?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: All's well: who doſt thou think this wench is?
Gheſs, and thou canſt?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I cannot.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Be it known then,
To all men by theſe preſents, this is ſhe,
She, ſhe, and only ſhe, our curious coxcombs
Were errant two moneths after.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Who, Conſtantia?
Thou talk'ſt of Cocks and Bulls.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I talk of wenches,
Of cocks and Hens Don Frederick; this is the Pullet
We two went proud after.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: It cannot be.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: It ſhall be;
Siſter to Don Petrucchio: I know all man.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Now I believe.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Go to, there has been ſtirring,
Fumbling with Linnen Frederick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis impoſſible,
You know her fame was pure as fire.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: That pure fire
Has melted out her maiden-head: ſhe is crackt:
We have all that hope of our ſide, boy.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thou tell'ſt me,
To my imagination, things incredible:
I ſee no looſe thought in her.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: That's all one,
She is looſe i'th' hilts by heaven: but the world muſt know
A fair way, upon vow of marriage.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: There may be ſuch a ſlip.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: And will be, Frederick,
Whil'ſt the old game's a foot: I fear the boy
Will prove hers too I took up.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Good circumſtance
May cure all this yet.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: There thou hitſt it, Frederick:
Come, let's walk in and comfort her: her being here
Is nothing yet ſuſpected: anon I'le tell thee
Wherefore her Brother came, who by this light
Is a brave noble fellow, and what honour
H'as done to me a ſtranger: there be Irons
Heating for ſome, will hiſs into their heart blouds,
E're all be ended; ſo much for this time.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Well Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: COme, ye do know.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I do not by this hand Miſtris.
But I ſuſpect.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: That if egges continue
At this price, women will ne're be ſav'd
By their good works.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I will know.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: Ye ſhall, any thing
Lyes in my power: The Duke of Loraine now
Is ſeven thouſand ſtrong: I heard it of a fiſh-wife,
A woman of fine knowledge.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Sirrah, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: The Popes Bulls are broke looſe too, and 'tis ſuſpected
They ſhall be baited in England.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Very well Sir.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: No, 'tis not ſo well neither.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: But I ſay to ye,
Who is it keeps your Maſter company?

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: I ſay to you, Don John.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I ſay what woman?

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: I ſay ſo too.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I ſay again, I will know?

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: I ſay 'tis fit ye ſhould.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: And I tell thee
He has a woman here.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: And I tell thee
'Tis then the better for him.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: You are no Bawd now?

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: Would I were able to be call'd unto it:
A worſhipfull vocation for my elders;
For as I underſtand it is a place
Fitting my betters far.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Was ever Gentlewoman
So frumpt off with a fool? well ſawcy Sirrah,
I will know who it is, and for what purpoſe;
I pay the rent, and I will know how my houſe
Comes by theſe Inflammations: if this geer hold,
Beſt hang a ſign-poſt up, to tell the Signiors,
Here ye may have lewdneſs at Liverie.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: 'T would be a great eaſe to your age.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How now?
Why what's the matter Land-lady?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: What's the matter?
Ye uſe me decently among ye Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Who has abus'd her, you Sir?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: 'Ods my witneſs
I will not be thus treated, that I will not.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: I gave her no ill language.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt lewdly,
Thou tookſt me up at every word I ſpoke,
As I had been a Mawkin, a flurt Gillian;
And thou thinkſt, becauſe thou canſt write and read,
Our noſes muſt be • nder thee.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Dare you Sirrah?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Let but the truth be known Sir, I beſeech ye,
She raves of wenches, and I know not what Sir.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Go to, thou know'ſt too well, thou wicked varlet,
Thou inſtrument of evil.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: As I live Sir,
She is ever thus till dinner.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Get ye in,
I'le anſwer you anon Sir.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: By this hand
I'le break your Poſlet pan. Exit.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Then by this hood
I'le lock the meat up.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Now your grief, what is't?
For I can gheſſe —

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Ye may with ſhame enough,
If there were ſhame amongſt ye; nothing thought on,
But how ye may abuſe my houſe? not ſatisfi'd
With bringing home your Baſtards to undoe me,
But you muſt drill your whores here too? my patience
(Becauſe I bear, and bear, and carry all,
And as they ſay am willing to groan under)
Muſt be your make-ſport now.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No more of theſe words,
Nor no more murmurings Lady: for you know
That I know ſomething. I did ſuſpect your anger,
But turn it preſently and handſomely,
And bear your ſelf diſcreetly to this woman,
For ſuch an one there is indeed.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: 'Tis well ſon.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Leaving your devils Matins, and your melancholies,
Or we ſhall leave our lodgings.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: You have much need
To uſe theſe vagrant ways, and to much profit:
Ye had that might content
(At home within your ſelves too) right good Gentlemen,
Wholſome, and ye ſaid handſom: But you gallants,
Beaſt that I was to believe ye —

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Leave your ſuſpicion:
For as I live there's no ſuch thing.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Mine honour;
And 'twere not for mine honour.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come, your honour,
Your houſe, and you too, if you dare believe me,
Are well enough: ſleek up your ſelf, leave crying,
For I muſt have ye entertain this Lady
With all civility, ſhe well deſerves it,
Together with all ſecreſie: I dare truſt ye,
For I have found ye faithfull: when you know her,
You will find your own fault: no more words, but do it.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: You know you may command me.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Worſhipful Lady,
How does thy velvet Scabbard? by this hand
Thou lookſt moſt amiably, now could I willingly,
And 'twere not fo • abuſing thy Geneva print there,
Venture my Body with thee.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: You'll leave this Roguery
When you come to my years.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: By this light
Thou art not above fifteen yet, a meer Girl,
Thou haſt not half thy teeth: come—

sp.speaker: Fred
sp.l: Prithee John
Let her alone, ſhe has been vex'd already;
She'll grow ſtark mad, man.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I would ſee her mad,
An old mad woman—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Prithee be patient.

sp.speaker: John
sp.l: Is like a Millers Maro, troubled with tooth-ach.
She'll make the rareſt faces.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Go, and do it,
And do not mind this fellow.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Well, Don John,
There will be times again; when O good Mother,
What's good for a Carnoſity in the Bladder?
O the green water, Mother.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Doting take ye;
Do ye remember that?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She has paid ye now, Sir.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Clary, ſweet mother, clary.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Are ye ſatisfied?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I'll never whore again, never give petticoats
And Waſtcoats at five pound apiece: good mother,
Quickly mother; now mock on Son.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: A Devil grind your old Chaps. Exit Landlady.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: By this hand, wench,
I'll give thee a new hood for this.
Has ſhe met with your Lordſhip?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Touch-wood take her.
She's a rare ghoſtly Mother.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Below attends ye
The Gentlemans man, Sir, that was with you.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Well, Sir;
My time is come then; yet if my project hold,
You ſhall not ſtay behind; I'll rather truſt
A Cat with ſweet milk, Frederick; by her face,
I feel her fears are working.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Is there no way,
I do beſeech ye think yet, to divert
This certain danger?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis impoſſible;
Their Honours are engag'd.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Then there muſt be murther,
Which, Gentlemen, I ſhall no ſooner hear of,
Than make one in't: you may if you pleaſe, Sir,
Make all go leſs yet.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Lady, were't mine own Cauſe,
I could diſpenſe; but loaden with my friends truſt,
I muſt go on; though general maſſacres
As much I fear

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Do ye hear, Sir; for Heavens pity
Let me requeſt one love of you.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes, any thing.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: This Gentleman I find too reſolute,
Too hot and fiery for the Cauſe; as ever
You did a vertuous deed, for honours ſake
Go with him, and allay him; your fair temper
And noble diſpoſition, like wiſh'd ſhowrs,
May quench thoſe eating fires, that would ſpoil all elſe.
I ſee in him deſtruction.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I will do it;
And 'tis a wiſe conſideration,
To me a bounteous favour, hark ye, John;
I will go with ye.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Indeed I will,
Ye go upon a hazard; no denial,
For as I live, I'll go.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Then make ye ready,
For I am ſtraight o' horſe-back.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: My Sword on,
I am as ready as you; what my beſt labour,
With all the art I have can work upon 'em,
Be ſure of, and expect fair end; the old Gentlewoman
Shall wait upon you; ſhe is both grave and private,
And ye may truſt her in all points.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: You are noble;
And ſo I kiſs your hand.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: That ſeal for me too,
And I hope happy iſſue, Lady.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: All Heavens Care upon ye, and my Prayers.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: So,
Now my mind's at reſt.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Away, 'tis late, John. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Antonio, a Surgeon, and 2 Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Come, Sir, be hearty, all the worſt is paſt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Give me ſome Wine.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: 'Tis death, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis a Horſe, Sir.
To be dreſt to the tune of Ale only!
Nothing but ſawces to my ſores!

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Fie, Antonio,
You muſt be govern'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: H'as given me a damn'd Clyſter,
Only of ſand and ſnow water, Gentlemen,
Has almoſt ſcour'd my guts out.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: I have giv'n you that, Sir,
Is fitteſt for your ſtate.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And here he feeds me
With rotten ends of Rooks, and drown'd Chickens,
And when I go to bed (by Heaven 'tis true Gentlemen)
He rolls me up in Lints, with Labels at 'em,
That I am juſt the man i'th' Almanack,
In Head and Face, is Aries place.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Will't pleaſe ye
To let your friends ſee you open'd?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Will't pleaſe you, Sir,
To let me have a wench? I feel my Body
Open enough for that yet.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: How, a Wench?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why look ye, Gentlemen; thus I am us'd ſtill,
I can get nothing that I want.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Leave theſe things,
And let him open ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: D' ye hear, Surgeon?
Send for the Muſick, let me have ſome pleaſure
To entertain my friends, beſides your Sallads,
Your green ſalves, and your ſearches, and ſome Wine too,
That I may only ſmell to it; or by this light
I'll dye upon thy hand, and ſpoil thy cuſtome.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Let him have Muſick.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: 'Tis in the houſe, and ready,
If he will ask no more but Wine— Muſick.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: He ſhall not drink it.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Will theſe things pleaſe ye?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes, and let 'em ſing

l.hi: John Dorrie.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis too long.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'll have John Dorrie,
For to that warlike tune I will be open'd:
Give me ſome drink, have ye ſtopt the leaks well, Surgeon,
All will run out elſe?

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Fear not.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sit down, Gentlemen:
And now advance your Plaiſters. Song of John Dorrie.
Give 'em ten ſhillings, friends; how do ye find me?
What ſymptoms do you ſee now?

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: None, Sir, dangerous;
But if you will be rul'd—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What time?

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: I can cure you
In forty days, if you will not tranſgreſs me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I have a Dog ſhall lick me whole in twenty;
In how long canſt thou kill me?

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Preſently.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Do it, there's more delight in't.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You muſt have patience.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Man, I muſt have buſineſs; this fooliſh fellow
Hinders himſelf; I have a dozen Raſcals
To hurt within theſe five days; good man-mender,
Stop me with ſome Parſley, like ſtuft Beef,
And let me walk abroad.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Ye ſhall walk ſhortly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: For I muſt find Petrucchio.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Time enough.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Come, lead him in, and let him ſleep: within theſe three days
We'll beg ye leave to play.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: And then how things fall,
We'll certainly inform ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But Surgeon, promiſe me
I ſhall drink Wine then too.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: A little temper'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Nay, I'll no tempering, Surgeon.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Well, as't pleaſe ye,
So ye exceed not.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Farewell: and if ye find
The mad Slave that thus ſlaſh'd me, commend me to him,
And bid him keep his Skin cloſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Take your reſt, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: I have told ye all I can, and more than yet
Thoſe Gentlemen know of me; ever truſting
Your Counſel and Concealment; for to me
You ſeem a worthy Woman; one of thoſe
Are ſeldome found in our Sex, wiſe and vertuous,
Direct me I beſeech ye.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Ye ſay well, Lady,
And hold ye to that point, for in theſe buſineſſes
A Womans Counſel that conceives the matter,
(Do ye mark me? that conceives the matter, Lady)
Is worth ten mens engagements: She knows ſomething,
And out of that can work like Wax; when men
Are giddy-headed, either out of Wine,
Or a more Drunkenneſs, vain Oſtentation,
Diſcovering all; there is no more keep in 'em
Than hold upon an Eeles tail; Nay, 'tis held faſhion
To defame now all they can.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: I, but theſe Gentlemen—

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Do not you truſt to that; theſe Gentlemen
Are as all Gentlemen of the ſame Barrel;
I, and the ſelf ſame pickle too. Be it granted,
They have us'd ye with reſpect and fair behaviour,
Ere ſince ye came, do you know what muſt follow?
They are Spaniards, Lady, Gennets of high mettle,
Things that will thraſh the Devil, or his Dam,
Let 'em appear but cloven.

sp.speaker: Canſt.
sp.l: Now Heaven bleſs me.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Mad Colts will court the wind; I know 'em, Lady,
To the leaſt hair they have; and I tell you,
Old as I am, let but the pint pot bleſs 'em,
They'll offer to my years—

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Such rude gambol • —

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: To you?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I, and ſo handle me, that oft I am forc'd
To fight of all four for my ſafety; there's the younger,
Don John, the arranteſt Jack in all this City;
The other, Time has blaſted, yet he will ſtoop,
If not o'rflown, and freely on the quarry;
Has been a Dragon in his days. But Tarmont,
Don Jenkin is the Devil himſelf, the dog-days,
The moſt incomprehenſible Whore-maſter,
Twenty a night is nothing; Beggars, Broom-women,
And thoſe ſo miſerable, they look like famine,
Are all ſweet Ladies in his drink.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: He's a handſome Gentleman;
Pity he ſhould be maſter of ſuch follies.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: He's ne'r without a noiſe of Sirynges
In's Pocket, thoſe proclaim him; birding Pills,
Waters to cool his Conſcience, in ſmall Viols:
With thouſand ſuch ſufficient emblems; the truth is,
Whoſe Chaſtity he chops upon he cares not,
He flies at all; Baſtards upon my conſcience,
He has now in making, multitudes; the laſt night
He brought home one; I pity her that bore it,
But we are all weak Veſſels, ſome rich Woman
(For wiſe I dare not call her) was the mother,
For it was hung with Jewels; the bearing Cloath
No leſs than Crimſon Velvet.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: 'Tis true, Lady.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: Was it a Boy too?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: A brave Boy; deliberation
And judgment ſhew'd in's getting, as I'll ſay for him,
He's as well paced for that ſport—

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: May I ſee it?
For there is a neighbour of mine, a Gentlewoman,
Has had a late miſchance, which willingly
I would know further of; now if you pleaſe
To be ſo courteous to me.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Ye ſhall ſee it:
But what do ye think of theſe men now ye know 'em,
And of the cauſe I told ye of Be wiſe,
Ye may repent too late elſe; I but tell you
For your own good, and as you will find it, Lady.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: I am advis'd.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: No more words then; do that,
And inſtantly, I told ye of, be ready;
Don John, I'll fit you for your frumps.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: I ſhall be:
But ſhall I ſee this Child?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Within this half hour,
Let's in, and there think better; ſhe that's wiſe,
Leaps at occaſion firſt; the reſt pay for it. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter Petrucchio, Don John, and Frederick.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Sir, he is worth your knowledg, and a Gentleman
If I that ſo much love him, may commend him.
Of free and vertuous parts; and one, if foul play
Should fall upon us, for which fear I brought him,
Will not flye back for phillips.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Ye much honour me,
And once more I pronounce ye both mine.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Stay, what Troop
Is that below i' th' Valley there?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Hawking I take it.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: They are ſo; 'tis the Duke, 'tis even he, Gentlemen,
Sirrah, draw back the Horſes till we call ye,
I know him by his Company.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I think too
He bends up this way.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: So he does.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Stand you ſtill
Within that Covert till I call: you, Frederick,
By no means be not ſeen, unleſs they offer
To bring on odds upon us, he comes forward,
Here will I wait him fairly: to your Cabins.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I need no more inſtruct ye?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Fear me not,
I'le give it him, and boldly. Ex. Pet. and Fred.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Feed the Hawks up,
We'll flie no more to day, O my bleſt fortune!
Have I ſo fairly met the man?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Ye have, Sir,
And him you know by this.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Sir all the honour,
And love—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I do beſeech your Grace ſtay there,
(for I know you too now) that love and honour
I come not to receive; nor can you give it,
Till ye appear fair to the world; I muſt beſeech ye
Diſmiſs your train a little.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Walk aſide,
And out of hearing I command ye: Now, Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Laſt time we met, I was a friend.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And Nobly,
You did a friends office: let your buſineſs
Be what it may, you muſt be ſtill—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Your pardon,
Never a friend to him, cannot be friend
To his own honour.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: In what have I tranſgreſs'd it?
Ye make a bold breach at the firſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Bolder,
You made that breach that let in infamy,
And ruine, to ſurpriſe a noble ſtock.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Be plain, Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I will, and ſhort;
Ye have wrong'd a Gentleman,
Little behind your ſelf, beyond all juſtice,
Beyond mediation of all friends.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: The man, and manner of wrong?

sp.speaker: John.

l.hi: Petrucchio,

sp.l: The wrong, ye have Whor'd his Siſter.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What's his will in't?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: His will is to oppoſe you like a Gentleman,
And ſingle, to decide all.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Now ſtay you, Sir,
And hear me with the like belief: this Gentleman,
His Siſter that you nam'd, 'tis true I have long lov'd,
Nor was that love laſcivious, as he makes it;
As true, I have enjoy'd her: no leſs truth,
I have a Child by her: but that ſhe, or he,
Or any of that family are tainted,
Suffer diſgrace, or ruin, by my pleaſures,
I wear a Sword to ſatisfie the world no,
And him in this cauſe when he pleaſe; for know, Sir,
She is my Wife, contracted before Heaven,
(Witneſs I owe more tye to, than her Brother)
Nor will I flye from that name, which long ſince
Had had the Churches approbation,
But for his jealous danger.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Sir, your pardon,
And all that was my anger, now my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Fair Sir, I knew I ſhould convert ye; had we
But that rough man here now too—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: And ye ſhall, Sir,
Whoa, hoa, hoo.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I hope ye have laid no Ambuſh?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Only friends.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: My noble Brother welcome:
Come put your anger off, we'll no fighting,
Unleſs you will maintain I am unworthy
To bear that name.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Do you ſpeak this heartily?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Upon my ſoul, and truly; the firſt Prieſt
Shall put you out of theſe doubts.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Now I love ye;
And I beſeech you pardon my ſuſpicions,
You are now more than a Brother, a brave friend too.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: The good man's over-joy'd.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How, how, how goes it?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Why, the man has his Mare again, and all's well, Frederick,
The Duke profeſſes freely he's her Husband.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis a good hearing.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Yes, for modeſt Gentlemen.
I muſt preſent ye: may it pleaſe your Grace,
To number this brave Gentleman, my friend,
And noble kinſman, amongſt thoſe your ſervants.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: O my brave friend! you ſhower your bounties on me
Amongſt my beſt thoughts, Signior, in which number
You being worthily diſpos'd already,
May place your friend to honour me.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: My love, Sir,
And where your Grace dares truſt me, all my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Why? this is wondrous happy: But now Brother,
Now comes the bitter to our ſweet: Conſtantia.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why, what of her?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nor what, nor where, do I know?
Wing'd with her fears laſt night, beyond my knowledge,
She quit my houſe, but whither—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let not that—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No more good Sir, I have heard too much.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nay ſink not,
She cannot be ſo loſt.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Nor ſhall not, Gentlemen;
Be free again, the Lady's found; that ſmile, Sir,
Shews ye diſtruſt your Servant.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I do beſeech ye.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Ye ſhall believe me: by my ſoul ſhe is ſafe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Heaven knows, I would believe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye may ſafely.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: And under noble uſage: this fair Gentleman
Met her in all her doubts laſt night, and to his Guard,
(Her fears being ſtrong upon her) ſhe gave her perſon,
Who waited on her to our lodging; where all reſpect,
Civil and honeſt ſervice now attend her.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Ye may believe now.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes, I do, and ſtrongly:
Well my good friends, or rather my good Angels,
For ye have both preſerv'd me; when theſe vertues
Dye in your friends remembrance—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Good your Grace,
Loſe no more time in complement, 'tis too precious,
I know it by my ſelf there can be no Hell
To his that hangs upon his hopes; eſpecially
In way of luſtly pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: He has hit it.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: To horſe again then, for this night I'le crown
With all the joyes ye wiſh for.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Happy Gentlemen. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: This is the maddeſt miſchief: never fool
Was ſo ſob'd off, as I am; made ridiculous,
And to my ſelf mine own Aſs: truſt a Woman?
I'le truſt the Devil firſt; for he dare be
Better than's word ſometime: what faith have I br • ke?
In what obſervance fail'd? Let me conſider,
For this is monſtrous uſage.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let them talk,
We'll ride on fair and ſoftly.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Well, Conſtantia.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Conſtantia, what's this fellow? ſtay by all means.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Ye have ſpun your ſelf a fair thread now.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Stand ſtill, John.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: What cauſe had you to fly? what fear poſſeſt ye?
Were you not ſafely lodg'd from all ſuſpicion?
Us'd with all gentle means? did any know
How ye came thither, or what your ſin was.

sp.speaker: Fred.

l.hi: John,

sp.l: I ſmell ſome juggling, John.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Yes, Frederick, I fear it will be found ſo.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: So ſtrangely,
Without the counſel of your friends; ſo deſperately
To put all dangers on ye?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: So deceitfully,
After a ſtrangers lure!

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Did ye mark that, Frederick?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: To make ye appear more monſter; and the Law
More cruel to reward ye? to leave all,
All that ſhould be your ſafegard, to ſeek evils?
Was this your wiſdom? this your promiſe? well,
He that incited ye—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Mark that too.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: 'Had better have plough'd farther off; now Lady,
What will your laſt friend, he that ſhould preſerve ye,
And hold your credit up, the brave Antonio,
Think of this ſlip? he'll to Petrucchio,
And call for open juſtice.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe, Frederick

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: But what that he is, John?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I do not doubt yet
To bolt ye out, for I know certainly
Ye are about the Town ſtill: ha, no more words. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Very well.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Diſcreetly.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Finely carried.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You have no more of these tricks?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Ten to one, Sir,
I ſhall meet with 'em if ye have.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Is this honeſt?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Was it in you a friends part to deal double?
I am no Aſs Don Frederick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And Don John,
It ſhall appear I am no fool;
Diſgrace me to make your ſelf a lecher?
'Tis boyiſh, 'tis baſe.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: 'Tis falſe, and moſt unmanly to upbraid me,
Nor will I be your bolſter, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Thou wanton boy, thou hadſt better have been Eunuch,
Thou common womans courteſie, than thus
Laſcivious, baſely to have bent mine honour.
A friend? I'e make a horſe my friend firſt.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Holla, holla,
Ye kick too faſt, Sir: what ſtrange brains have you got,
That dare crow out thus bravely? I better been an Eunuch?
I privy to this dog trick? clear your ſelf,
For I know where the wind ſits, and moſt nobly,
Or as I have a life—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No more: they're horſes. A noiſe within like horſes.
Nor ſhew no diſcontent: to morrow comes;
Let's quietly away: if ſhe be at home,
Our jealouſies are put off.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: The fellow,
We have loſt him in our ſpleens, like fools.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come, Gentlemen,
Now ſet on roundly: ſuppoſe ye have all Miſtreſſes,
And mend your pace according.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Then have at ye. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Petrucchio, Frederick, and John.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: NOW to Bologna, my moſt honoured Brother,
I dare pronounce ye a hearty, and ſafe welcome,
Our loves ſhall now way-lay ye; welcome, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: The ſame to you brave Sir; Don Frederick,
Will ye ſtep in and give the Lady notice
Who comes to honour her?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Bid her be ſudden,
We come to ſee no curious wench: a night-gown
VVill ſerve the turn: here's one that knows her nearer.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I'le tell her what ye ſay, Sir. Exit Fred.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: My dear brother,
Ye are a merry Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Now will the ſport be,
To obſerve her alterations; how like a wildfire
She'll leap into your boſom; then ſeeing me,
Her conſcience, and her fears creeping upon her,
Dead as a fowl at ſouſe, ſhe'll ſink.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Fair Brother,
I muſt intreat you—

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: I conceive your mind, Sir,
I will not chide her: yet ten Duckets, Duke,
She falls upon her knees, ten more ſhe dare not—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I muſt not have her frighted.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: VVell you ſhall not:
But like a Summers evening againſt heat,
Mark how I'le guild her cheeks?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: How now?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye may, Sir:
Not to abuſe your patience, noble friends,
Nor hold ye oft with tedious circumſtance,
For you muſt know—

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: VVhat?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: VVhere is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Gone, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: VVhat did you ſay, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Gone, by Heaven removed,
The woman of the houſe too.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Well Don Frederick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Don John, it is not well, but—

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Gone?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: This fellow
Can teſtifie I lye not.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: Some four hours after
My Maſter was departed, with this Gentleman,
My fellow and my ſelf being ſent of buſineſs,
(As we muſt think) of purpoſe—

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Hang theſe circumſtances,
They appear like Owls, to ill ends.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Now could I eat
The Devil in his own broth, I am ſo tortur'd.
Gone?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Gone?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Directly gone, fled, ſhifted: what would you have me ſay?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Well, Gentlemen,
Wrong not my good opinion.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: For your Dukedom
I will not be a Knave, Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: He that is,
A rot run in his bloud.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: But hark ye Gentlemen,
Are ye ſure ye had her here, did ye not dream this?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Have you your noſe, Sir?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Then we had her.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Since you are ſo ſhort, believe your having her
Shall ſuffer more conſtruction.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Let it ſuffer,
But if I be not clear of all diſhonour,
Or practice that may taint my reputation,
And ignorant of where this Woman is,
Make me your Cities monſter.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I believe ye.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I could lye with a Witch now, to be reveng'd,
Upon that Raſcal did this.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Only thus much
I would deſire your Grace, for my mind gives me
Before night yet ſhe is yours: ſtop all opinion,
And let no anger out, till full cauſe call it,
Then every mans own work's to juſtifie him,
And this day let us give to ſearch: my man here
Tells me, by chance he ſaw out of a window
(Which place he has taken notice of) ſuch a face
As our old Landladies, he believes the ſame too,
And by her hood aſſures it: Let's firſt thither,
For ſhe being found, all's ended.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come, for Heavens ſake,
And Fortune, and thou be'ſt not ever turning,
If there be one firm ſtep in all thy reelings,
Now ſettle it, and ſave my hopes: away friends. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: With all my Jewels?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: All, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And that mony
I left i'th' trunk?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The Trunk broke, and that gone too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Franciſco of the plot?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Gone with the wench too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The mighty pox go with 'em: belike they thought
I was no man of this world, and thoſe trifles
Would but diſturb my conſcience.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sure they thought, Sir,
You would not live to perſecute 'em.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Whore and Fidler,
Why, what a confort have they made? Hen and Bacon?
Well my ſweet Miſtris, well good Madam mar-tail?
You that have hung about my neck, and lick't me,
I'le try how handſomely your Ladyſhip
Can hang upon a Gallows, there's your Maſter-piece;
But hark ye Sirrah, no imagination
Of where they ſhould be?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: None, Sir, yet we have ſearch'd
All places we ſuſpected; I believe, Sir,
They have taken towards the Ports.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Get me a conjurer,
One that can raiſe a water Devil, I'le port 'em;
Play at duck and drake with my mony; take heed Fidler;
I'le dance ye by this hand, your Fidle ſtick
I'le greaſe of a new faſhion, for preſuming
To meddle with my degamboys: get me a Conjurer,
Enquire me out a man that lets out Devils:
None but my C. Cliffe ſerve your turn?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I know not—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: In every ſtreet, Tom fool, any blear-ey'd people
With red heads, and flat noſes can perform it;
Thou ſhalt know 'em by their half Gowns and no Breeches:
Mount my Mare Fidler? ha boy! up at firſt daſh?
Sit ſure, I'le clap a nettle, and a ſmart one,
Shall make your Filly firk: I will fine Fidler,
I'le put you to your plunge, Boy: Sirrah meet me
Some two hours hence at home; in the mean time
Find out a conjurer and know his price,
How he will let his Devils by the day out,
I'le have 'em, and they be above ground. Ex. Ant.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Now bleſs me,
What a mad man is this? I muſt do ſomething
To pleaſe his humour: ſuch a man I'le ask for,
And tell him where he is: but to come near him,
Or have any thing to do with his don Devils,
I thank my fear, I dare not, nor I will not. Exit.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Petrucchio, Frederick, John, Peter, and Servant with Bottles.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Whither wilt thou lead us?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: 'Tis hard by, Sir.
And ten to one this wine goes thither.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Forward.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Are they grown ſo merry?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt moſt likely,
She has heard of this good fortune, and determines
To waſh her ſorrows off.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo; that houſe, Sir,
Is it: out of that window certainly
I ſaw my old Miſtreſſes face.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: They are merry indeed, Muſick.
Hark I hear Muſick too.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Excellent Muſick.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Would I were ev'n among 'em, and alone now;
A pallat for the purpoſe in a corner,
And good rich Wine within me; what gay ſport
Could I make in an hour now?

body.head: SONG.
body.l: Welcome ſweet liberty, and care farewel,
I am mine own,
She is twice damn'd, that lives in Hell,
When Heaven is ſhown.
Budding beauty, blooming years
Were made for pleaſure, farewel fears,
For now I am my ſelf, mine own command,
My fortune alwayes in my hand.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Hark a voice too;
Let's not ſtir yet by any means.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Was this her own voice?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes, ſure.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis a rare one.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: The Song confirms her here too: for if ye mark it,
It ſpake of liberty, and free enjoying
The happy end of pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Look ye there, Sir,
Do ye know that head?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis my good Landlady,
I find fear has done all this.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: She I ſwear,
And now do I know by the hanging of her Hood,
She is parcel drunk: ſhall we go in?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Not yet, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: No, let 'em take their pleaſure

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: When it is higheſt, Muſick.
We'll ſtep in, and amaze 'em: peace, more Muſick.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: This Muſick murders me: what bloud have I now?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I ſhould know that face. Enter Fran. and Exit.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: By this light 'tis he, Frederick.
That bred our firſt ſuſpicions, the ſame fellow.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: He that we overtook, and overheard too,
Diſcourſing of Conſtantia.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Still the ſame;
Now he ſlips in.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She muſt be here Sir:
This is the very fellow, I told your Grace
We found upon the way; and what his talk was.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Why, ſure I know this fellow; yes, 'tis he,
Franciſco, Antonio's Boy, a rare Muſician,
He taught my Siſter on the Lute, and is ever
(She loves his voice ſo well) about her: certain,
Without all doubt ſhe is here: it muſt be ſo.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Here? that's no queſtion: what ſhould our hen o'th' game elſe
Do here without her? if ſhe be not here
(I am ſo confident) let your grace believe,
We two are arrant Raſcals, and have abus'd ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I ſay ſo too.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Why there's the hood again now,
The guard that guides us; I know the fabrick of it,
And know the old tree of that ſaddle yet, 'twas made of,
A hunting hood, obſerve it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Who ſhall enter?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: I'le make one.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I, another.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But ſo carry it,
That all her joyes flow not together.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: If we told her,
Your grace would none of her?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: By no means Signior,
'Twould turn her wild, ſtark frantick.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Or aſſur'd her —

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Nothing of that ſtern nature: this ye may Sir,
That the conditions of our fear yet ſtand
On nice and dangerous knittings: or that a little
I ſeem to doubt the child.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Would I could draw her
To hate your grace with theſe things.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Come let's enter. Ex. Petr. and John.
And now he ſees me not, I'le ſearch her ſoundly.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Now luck of all ſides. Muſick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Doubt it not: more Muſick:
Sure ſhe has heard ſome comfort.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes, ſtand ſtill Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: This is the maddeſt ſong.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Applyed for certain
To ſome ſtrange melancholy ſhe is loaden with.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Now all the ſport begins—hark?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: They are amongſt 'em,
The fears now, and the ſhakings? Trampling above.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Our old Lady
(Hark how they run) is even now at this inſtant
Ready to loſe her head-piece by Don John,
Or creeping through a Cat hole. Petr. and John within.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Bring 'em down,
And you Sir, follow me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: He's angry with 'em,
I muſt not ſuffer this.

sp.speaker: John, within.
sp.l: Bowl down the Bawd there
Old Erra mater: you Lady leachery,
For the good will I bear to th' game, moſt tenderly
Shall be lead out, and laſh'd.

div.stage: Enter Petrucchio, John, Whore, and Bawd, with Franciſco.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is this Conſtantia?
Why Gentlemen? what do you mean? is this ſhe?

sp.speaker: Whore.
sp.l: I am Conſtantia Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: A whore ye are Sir.

sp.speaker: Whore.
sp.l: 'Tis very true: I am a whore indeed Sir.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: She will not lye yet, though ſhe ſteal.

sp.speaker: Whore.
sp.l: A plain whore,
If you pleaſe to imploy me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And an impudent —

sp.speaker: Whore.
sp.l: Plain dealing now is impudence.
One, if you will Sir, can ſhew ye as much ſport
In one half hour, and with as much variety,
As a far wiſer woman can in half a year:
For there my way lies.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is ſhe not drunk too?

sp.speaker: Whore.
sp.l: A little guilded o're Sir,
Old ſack, old ſack boys.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: This is ſaliant.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: A brave bold quean.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is this your certainty?
Do ye know the man ye wrong thus, Gentlemen?
Is this the woman meant?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: That your Land lady?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I know not what to ſay.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Am I a perſon
To be your ſport, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I do believe now certain
I am a knave; but how, or when —

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What are you?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Bawd to this piece of pye meat.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.l: A poor Gentlewoman
That lyes in Town, about Law buſineſs,
And't like your worſhips.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: You ſhall have Law, believe it.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.l: I'le ſhew your Maſterſhip my caſe.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: By no means,
I had rather ſee a Cuſtard.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.l: My dead Husband
Left it even thus Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Bleſs mine eyes from blaſting,
I was never ſo frighted with a caſe.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.l: And ſo Sir —

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Enough, put up good velvet head.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What are you two now,
By your own free confeſſions?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What you ſhall think us,
Though to my ſelf I am certain, and my life
Shall make that good and perfect, or fall with it.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: We are ſure of nothing, Fred. that's the truth on't:
I do not think my name's Don John, nor dare not
Believe any thing that concerns me, but my debts,
Nor thoſe in way of payment: things are ſo carried,
What to entreat your grace, or how to tell ye
We are, or we are not, is paſt my cunning,
But I would fain imagine we are honeſt,
And o' my conſcience, I ſhould fight in't —

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Thus then,
For we may be all abus'd.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: 'Tis poſſible,
For how ſhould this concern them?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Here let's part —
Until to morrow this time: we to our way,
To make this doubt out, and you to your way;
Pawning our honours then to meet again,
When if ſhe be not found.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: We ſtand engaged
To anſwer any worthy way we are call'd to.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We ask no more.

sp.speaker: Whore.
sp.l: Ye have done with us then?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: No, Dame.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But is her name Conſtantia?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Yes a moveable
Belonging to a friend of mine: come out Fidler,
What ſay you to this Lady? be not fearfull.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Saving the reverence of my Maſters pleaſure,
I ſay ſhe is a whore, and that ſhe has robb'd him,
Hoping his hurts would kill him.

sp.speaker: Whore.
sp.l: Who provok't me?
Nay Sirrah ſqueak, I'le ſee your treble ſtrings
Ty'd up too; if I hang, I'le ſpoil your piping,
Your ſweet face ſhall not ſave ye.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Thou damn'd impudence,
And thou dry'd Devil; where's the officer?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: He's here Sir.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Lodge theſe ſafe, till I ſend for 'em;
Let none come to 'em, nor no noiſe be heard
Of where they are, or why: away.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: By this hand
A handſom whore: Now will I be arreſted,
And brought home to this officers: a ſtout whore,
I love ſuch ſtirring ware: pox o' this buſineſs,
A man muſt hunt out morſels for another,
And ſtarve himſelf: a quick-ey'd whore, that's wild-fire,
And makes the bloud dance through the veins like billows.
I will reprieve this whore.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Well, good luck with ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: As much attend your grace.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: To morrow certain —

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: If we out live this night Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Come Don John,
We have ſomething now to do.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I am ſure I would have.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: If ſhe be not found, we muſt fight.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I am glad on't,
I have not fought a great while.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: If we dye —

sp.speaker: Jo.
sp.l: There's ſo much mony ſav'd in lecherie. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Petrucchio, below, and Vecchio, above.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: IT ſhould be hereabouts.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Your grace is right,
This is the houſe, I know it.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Grace?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: 'Tis further
By the deſcription we received.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Good my Lord the Duke,
Believe me, for I know it certainly,
This is the very houſe.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: My Lord the Duke?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Pray Heaven this man prove right now.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Believe it, he's a moſt ſufficient Scholar,
And can do rare tricks this way; for a figure,
Or raiſing an appearance, whole Chriſtendom
Has not a better; I have heard ſtrange wonders of him.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But can he ſhew us where ſhe is?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Moſt certain,
And for what cauſe too ſhe departed.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Knock then,
For I am great with expectation,
Till this man ſatisfie me: I fear the Spaniards,
Yet they appear brave fellows: can he tell us?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: With a wet finger, whether they be falſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Away then.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Who's within here?

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Your grace may enter.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How can he know me?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: He knows all.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: And you Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: What do you call his name?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why, Peter Vecchio.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: They ſay he can raiſe Devils,
Can he make 'em
Tell truth too, when he has rais'd 'em? for believe it,
Theſe Devils are the lyingſt Raſcals.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: He can compel 'em.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: With what? can he
I'ye ſquibs in their tails, and fire the truth out?
Or make 'em eat a bawling Puritan,
VVhoſe ſanctified zeal ſhall rumble like an Earth-quake?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: VVith Spells man.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I with ſpoons as ſoon, doſt thou think
The Devil ſuch an Aſſe as people make him?
Such a poor coxcomb? ſuch a penny foot-poſt?
Compel'd with croſs and pile to run of errands?
VVith Aſteroth, and Behemoth, and Belfagor?
VVhy ſhould he ſhake at ſounds, at lives in a ſmiths forge?
Or if he do —

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: VVithout all doubt he do's John.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: VVhy ſhould not Bilbo raiſe him, or a pair of bullyons,
They go as big as any? or an unſhod Car,
VVhen he goes tumble, tumble o're the ſtones,
Like Anacreons drunken verſes,
Theſe make as fell a noiſe; me thinks the colick
VVell handled, and fed with ſmall beer —

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis the vertue —

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: The vertue? nay, and goodneſs fetch him up once,
H'as loſt a friend of me; the wiſe old Gentleman
Knows when, and how; I'le lay this hand to two pence,
Let all the Conjurers in Chriſtendom,
VVith all their ſpells, and vertues call upon him,
And I but think upon a wench, and follow it,
He ſhall be ſooner mine than theirs; where's vertue?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thou art the moſt ſufficient, (I'le ſay for thee)
Not to believe a thing —

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: O Sir, ſlow credit
Is the beſt child of knowldge; I'le go with ye,
And if he can do any thing, I'le think
As you would have me.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let's enquire along,
For certain we are not far off.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Nor much nearer. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: You loſt her yeſter-night.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: How think you Sir?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is your name Vecchio?

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And you can ſhew me
Theſe things you promiſe.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Your graces word bound to me,
No hand of Law ſhall ſeize me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: As I live Sir —

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: And as I live, that can do ſomething too Sir.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: I take your promiſes: ſtay here a little,
Till I prepare ſome Ceremonies, and I'le ſatisfie ye.
The Ladies name's Conſtantia?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: I come ſtraight. Exit Vec.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Sure he's a learned man.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: The moſt now living;
Did your grace mark when we told all theſe circumſtances,
How ever and anon he bolted from us
To uſe his ſtudies help?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Now I think rather
To talk with ſome familiar.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Not unlikely,
For ſure he has 'em ſubject.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How could he elſe
Tell when ſhe went, and who went with her?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: True.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Or hit upon mine honour: or aſſure me
The Lady lov'd me dearly?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: 'Twas ſo.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Now,
I do beſeech your grace ſit down, and you Sir;
Nay pray ſit cloſe like Brothers.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: A rare fellow.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: And what ye ſee, ſtir not at, nor uſe a word,
Until I ask ye; for what ſhall appear
Is but weak apparition and thin air,
Not to be held, nor ſpoken to. Knocking within. John, Frederick, and a Servant within.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We are counſell'd—

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: What noiſe is that without there?

sp.speaker: Fred. within.
sp.l: We muſt ſpeak with him.

sp.speaker: Serv. within.
sp.l: He's buſie, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: John within.
sp.l: That's all one friend,
We muſt and will ſpeak with him.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Let 'em in, Sir,
We know their tongues and buſineſs, 'tis our own,
And in this very cauſe that we now come for,
They alſo come to be inſtructed.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Let 'em in then:
Sit down, I know your meaning.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: The Duke before us?
Now we ſhall ſure know ſomething.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Not a queſtion,
But make your Eyes your Tongues—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: This is a ſtrange Jugler,
Neither indent before-hand for his payment,
Nor know the Breadth of the buſineſs; ſure his Devil
Comes out of Lapland, where they ſell men Winds
For dead drink, and old Doublets.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace, he conjures.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Let him, he cannot raiſe my Devil.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Prithee Peace.

l.hi: Appear, appear,
And you ſoft Winds ſo clear,
That dance upon the leaves, and make them ſing
Gentle Love-lay to the Spring,
Gilding all the Vaies below,
With your Verdure as ye blow,
Raiſe theſe forms from under ground
With a ſoft and happy ſound.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: This is an honeſt Conjurer, and a pretty Poet;
I like his words well, there's no bumbaſt in 'em,
But do you think now he can cudgel up the Devil
With this ſhort Staff of Verſes?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace, the Spirits— 2 ſhapes of women paſſing by.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Nay, and they be no worſe—

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Do ye know theſe faces?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Sit ſtill upon your lives then, and mark what follows;
Away, away.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Theſe Devils do not paint ſure?
Have they no ſweeter ſhapes in Hell?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Hark now, John. Conſtantia paſſes by.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I, marry, this moves ſomething like, this Devil
Carries ſome metal in her gate.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: I find ye,
You would ſee her face unvail'd?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Be uncovered.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: O Heaven!

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Peace.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: See how ſhe bluſhes.

sp.speaker: John.

l.hi: Frederick,

sp.l: This Devil for my mony; this is ſhe, Boy,
Why doſt thou ſhake? I burn.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Sit ſtill, and ſilent.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: She looks back at me, now ſhe ſmiles, Sir.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Silence.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I muſt riſe, or I burſt. Exit Conſtantia.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Ye ſee what follows—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: O gentle Sir, this ſhape agen.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: I cannot.
'Tis all diſſolv'd again; this was the Figure?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: The very ſame, Sir.
No hope once more to ſee it?

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: You might have kept it longer, had ye 〈◊〉
Now 'tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: No means to find it?

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l:
Yes, that there is, ſit ſtill a while, ther •
〈◊〉
To thaw the wonder from your hearts; 〈◊〉 wel • , Exit V •• .

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: This Conjurer is a right good fellow too,
A Lad of mettle; two ſuch Devils more
Would make me a Conjurer; what wine is it?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Hollock.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: The Devil's in it then; look how it dances
Well, if I be—

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: We are all before ye,
That's your beſt comfort, Sir.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: By th' Maſs, brave Wine;
Nay, and the Devils live in this Hell, I dare venture
Within theſe two months yet to be delivered
Of a large Legion of 'em.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Here he comes,
Silence of all ſides, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Good your Grace,
Obſerve a ſtricter temper, and you too, Gallants,
You'll be deluded all elſe. This merry D v l
That next appears, for ſuch a one you'll find it,
Muſt be call'd up by a ſtrange incantation,
A Song, and I muſt ſing it: 'pray bear with me,
And pardon my rude Pipe; for yet, ere pa • ting
Twenty to one I pleaſe ye.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: We are arm'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Nor ſhall you ſee us more trangreſs.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What think'ſt thou
Now, John?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Why, now do I think, Frederick,
(And if I think amiſs Heaven pardon me)
This honeſt Conjurer, with ſome four or five
Of his good fellow Devils and my ſelf,
Shall be yet drunk ere midnight.

body.head: SONG.

lg.l: COme away, thou Lady gay,
Hoist: how ſhe ſtumbles?
Hark how ſhe mumbles
Dame Gillian.
By old Claret I enlarge thee,
By Canary thus I char • e thee,
By Britain, Mat •• wghn, and • e • ter
Appear and anſwer me in meeter.

body.l: Anſwer. You'll tarry 〈…〉

lg.l: Once again I conjure thee,
By the Poſe in thy Noſe,
And the Gout in thy Toes;
By thine old dryed Skin,
And the Mummie within;
By thy little, little Ruff,
And thy Hood that's made of Stuff;
By thy Bottle at thy Breech,
And thine old ſalt Itch;
By the Stakes, and the Stones,
That have worn out thy Bones.
Appear.
Appear
Appear.

body.l: Anſwer. Oh I am here.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace, he conjures.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Why, this is the Song, Frederick; twenty pound now,
To ſee but our Don Gillian.

stage.hi: Enter Land lady and the Child.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace, it appears.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I cannot peace; Devils in French hoods, Frederick?
Satans old Syringes?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What's this?

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Peace.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: She, Boy.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What doſt thou mean?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: She, Boy, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: She Boy,
The very Child too, Frederick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She laughs on us
Aloud, John, has the Devil theſe affections?
I do believe 'tis ſhe, indeed.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Stand ſtill.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I will not;
Who calls Jeronimo from his naked Bed?
Sweet Lady, was it you? if thou beeſt the Devil,
Firſt, having croſt my ſelf, to keep out wildfire,
Then ſaid ſome ſpecial Prayers to defend me
Againſt thy moſt unhallowed Hood, have at thee.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Hold, Sir, I am no Devil.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: That's all one.

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I am your very Landlady.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I defie thee;
Thus as St. Dunſtan blew the Devil's Noſe
With a pair of tongs, even ſo, Right Worſhipful—

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Sweet Son, I am old Gillian.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: This is no Spirit.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Art thou old Gillian, fleſh and bone?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I am, Son.

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Sit ſtill, Sir, now I'll ſhew you all. Ex. Vec.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Where's thy Bottle?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: Here, I beſeech ye, Son—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: For I know the Devil
Cannot aſſume that ſhape.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe, John, certain—

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: A hogs pox o' your mouldy chaps, what makes you
Tumbling and juggling here?

sp.speaker: Land.
sp.l: I am quit now, Seignior,
For all the pranks you plaid, and railings at me,
For to tell true, out of a trick I put
Upon your high behaviours, which was a lie,
But then it ſerv'd my turn, I drew the Lady
Unto my Kinſman's here, only to torture
Your Don-ſhips for a day or two; and ſecure her
Out of all thoughts of danger; here ſhe comes now.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: May I yet ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: Yes, and embrace her too,
For one that loves you dearer—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: O my Sweeteſt.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Bluſh not, I will not chide ye.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: To add more
Unto the joy I know, I bring ye, ſee Sir,
The happy fruit of all our Vows!

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Heavens Bleſſing
Be round about thee ever.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: Pray bleſs me too,
For if your Grace be well inſtructed this way,
You'll find the keeping half the getting.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How, Sir?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.l: I'll tell you that anon.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: 'Tis true, this Gentleman
Has done a charity worthy your favour,
And let him have it, dear Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: My beſt Lady
He has, and ever ſhall have: ſo muſt you, Sir,
To whom I am equal bound as to my being.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Your Graces humble ſervant—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Why kneel you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Vec.
sp.l: For pardon for my boldneſs: yet 'twas harmleſs,
And all the art I have, Sir; thoſe your Grace ſaw,
Which you thought ſpirits, were my Neighbours Children
Whom I inſtruct in Grammar here, and Muſick;
Their ſhapes, the Peoples fond opinions,
Believing I can conjure, and oft repairing
To know of things ſtoln from 'em, I keep about me,
And always have in readineſs, by conjecture
Out of their own confeſſions, I oft tell 'em
Things that by chance have fallen out ſo; which way
(Having the perſons here, I knew you ſought for)
I wrought upon your Grace; my end is mirth,
And pleaſing, if I can, all parties.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I believe it,
For you have pleas'd me truly: ſo well pleas'd me,
That when I ſhall forget it—

sp.speaker: Pet.
