As thy Prince do s't before thee? that doſt never
Wear thy own face, but put'ſt on his, and gather'ſt
Baits for his Ears: liv'ſt wholly at his beck,
And e're thou dar'ſt utter a thought's thine own,
Muſt expect his; creep'ſt forth and wad'ſt into him
As if thou wert to paſs a Ford, there proving
Yet if thy tongue may ſtop on ſafely or no;
Then bring'ſt his vertue aſleep, and ſtay'ſt the wheel
Both of his reaſon and judgment, that they move not,
Whit'ſt over all his vices; and at laſt
Doſt draw a Cloud of words before his eyes,
Till he can n ither ſee thee nor himſelf?
Wretch, I dare give him honeſt counſels, I,
And love him while I tell him truth; old Aubrey
Dares goe the ſtraighteſt way, which ſtill's the ſhorteſt,
W •• k on the thorns thou ſcatter'ſt, Paraſite,
And tread 'em into nothing: and if thou
Thou let'ſt a look fall, of the leaſt diſlike,
I'll rip thy Crown up with my Sword at height,
And pluck thy skin over thy face, in ſight
Of him thou flatter'ſt; unto thee I ſpeak it,
Slave, againſt whom all Laws ſhould now conſpire,
And every Creature that hath ſenſe, be arm'd,
As 'gainſt the common Enemy of Mankind;
That ſleep'ſt within thy Maſters Ear, and whiſper'ſt
'Tis better for him to be fear'd than lov'd;
Bid'ſt him truſt no mans friendſhip, ſpare no blood
That may ſecure him: 'tis no cruelty
That hath a ſpecious end; for Soveraignty
Break all the Laws of kind; if it ſucceed,
An honeſt, noble, and praiſe-worthy deed;
While he that takes thy poyſons in, ſhall feel
Their virulent workings in a point of time,
When no Repentance can bring aid, but all
His ſpirits ſhall melt, with what his Conſcience burn'd,
And dying in flatterers arms, ſhall fall unmourn'd.
There's matter for you now.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: My Lord, this makes not for loving of my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Loving? no;
They hate ill Princes moſt that make them ſo.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: I'll hear no more.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Alas, 'tis for my Brother: I beſeech your Highneſs.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: How, a Brother? had not Lone my ſelf? did title
Move me when it was fit that he ſhould dye? away.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Brother, loſe no word more, leave my good Cauſe
T' upbraid the Tyrant, I'm glad I'm faln
Now in thoſe times that will'd ſome great example
T' aſſure men we can dye for honeſty.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Sir, you are brave, 'pray that you hold your neck
As bravely forth anon unto your Headſman.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Would he would ſtrike as bravely, and thou by,
Rollo, 'twould make thee quake to ſee me dye.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: What's his offence?

sp.speaker: Ham
sp.l: For giving Gisbert burial, who was ſometimes his Maſter.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Yes, Lord Aubrey,
My gratitude and humanity are my crimes.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Why bear you him not hence?

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: My Lord, (ſtay Souldiers)
I do beſeech your Highneſs, do not loſe
Such men for ſuch ſlight cauſes. This is one
Has ſtill been faithful to you, a try'd ſoul
In all your fathers Battles; I have ſeen him
Beſtride a friend againſt a ſcore of Foes,
And look, he looks as he would kill his hundred
For you, Sir, were you in ſome danger.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Till he kill'd his Brother, his Chancellour, then his
Maſter, to which he can add nought to equal Nero,
But killing of his Mother.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Peace, brave Fool,
Thou valiant Aſs: here is his Brother too, Sir,
A Captain of your Guard, hath ſerv'd you long,
With the moſt noble witneſs of his truth
Mark'd in his face, and every part about him,
That turns not from an enemy. But view him,
Oh do not grieve him, Sir, if you do mean
That he ſhall hold his place: it is not ſafe
To tempt ſuch ſpirits, and let them wear their Swords,
You'll make your Guards your terrours by theſe Acts,
And throw more hearts off from you than you hold;
And I muſt tell you, Sir, (with my old freedom,
And my old faith to boot) you have not liv'd ſo
But that your ſtate will need ſuch men, ſuch hands
Of which here's one, ſhall in an hour of tryal,
Do you more certain ſervice with a ſtroke,
Than the whole bundle of your flatterers
With all the unſavory unction of their tongues.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Peace, talker.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: One that loves you yet, my Lord,
And would not ſee you pull on your own ruines.
Mercy becomes a Prince, and guards him beſt,
Awe and affrights are never tyes of Love;
And when men begin to fear the Prince, they hate him.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Am I the Prince, or you?

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: My Lord, I hope I have not utter'd ought ſhould urge that queſtion.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Then practiſe your obedience, ſee him dead.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: My Lord?

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: I'll hear no more.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I'm ſorry then; there's no ſmall deſpair, Sir, of their
Safety, whoſe ears are blockt up againſt truth; come, captain.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I thank you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: For what? for ſeeing thy brother die a man, and honeſt?
Live thou ſo, Captain, I will aſſure thee,
Although I die for't too; come— Ex. all but Rol. & Lat.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Now Latorch, what do you think?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: That Aubrey's ſpeech and manners ſound ſomewhat of the boldeſt.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: 'Tis his cuſtome.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: It may be ſo, and yet be worth a fear.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: If we thought ſo, it ſhould be worth his life, and quickly too.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: I dare not, Sir, be authour
Of what I would be, 'tis ſo dangerous:
But with your Highneſs favour and your licence.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: He talks, 'tis true; he is licens'd: leave him,
We now are Duke alone, Latorch, ſecur'd;
Nothing left ſtanding to obſcure our proſpect,
We look right forth, beſide, and round about us,
And ſee it ours with pleaſure: only one
Wiſh'd joy there wants to make us to poſſeſs it,
And that is Edith, Edith, ſhe that got me
In blood and tears, in ſuch an oppoſite minute,
As had I not at once felt all the flames
And ſhafts of Love ſhot in me (his whole armory)
I ſhould have thought him as far off as Death.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: My Lord, expect a while, your happineſs
Is nearer than you think it, yet her griefs
Are green and freſh, your vigilant Latorch
Hath not been idle; I have leave already
To viſit her, and ſend to her.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: My life.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: And if I find not out as ſpeedy ways,
And proper inſtruments to work and bring her
To your fruition; that ſhe be not watch'd
Fame to your Highneſs wiſh, ſay you have no ſervant
Is capable of ſuch a truſt about you,
Or worthy to be Secretary of your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Oh my Latorch, what ſhall I render thee
For all thy travels, care, and love?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Sir, one ſuit, which I will ever importune, till you grant me.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: About your Mathematicians?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Yes, to have
The Scheme of your Nativity judg'd by them,
I have't already erected; O my Lord,
You do not know the labour of my fears,
My doubts for you are ſuch as cannot hope
Any ſecurity, but from the Stars;
Who, being rightly ask'd, can tell man more
Than all power elſe, there being no power beyond them.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: All thy petitions ſtill are care of us,
Ask for thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: What more can concern me; than this?

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Well, riſe true honeſt man, and go then,
We'l ſtudy our ſelves a means how to reward thee.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Your grace is now inſpir'd; now, now your highneſs
Begins to live, from this hour count your joyes:
But, Sir, I muſt have warrants, with blanks figur'd,
To put in names, ſuch as I like.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: You ſhall.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: They dare not elſe offer, Sir, at your figure?
Oh I ſhall bring you wonders; there's a Frier
Ruſee, an admirable man, another
A Gentleman, and then Lafiske,
The mirrour of his time; 'twas he that ſet it.
But there's one Norbret, (him I never ſaw)
Has made a mirrour, a meer Looking-glaſs,
In ſhew you'ld think't no other; the form oval,
As I am given to underſtand by letter,
Which renders you ſuch ſhapes, and thoſe ſo differing,
And ſome that will be queſtion'd and give anſwers;
Then has he ſet it in a frame, that wrought
Unto the revolutions of the Stars,
And ſo compact by due proportions
Unto their harmony, doth move alone
A true automaton; thus Daedalus Statues,
Or Vulcans Tools —

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Doſt thou believe this?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Sir? why, what ſhould ſtay my faith, or turn my ſenſe?
He has been about it above twenty years,
Three ſevens, the powerfull, and the perfect numbers;
And Art and time, Sir, can produce ſuch things.
What do I read there of H • arbas banquet?
The great Gymnoſophiſt, that had his Butlers
And carvers of pure gold waiting at table?
The images of Mercury, too, that ſpoke?
The wooden door that ſlew? a ſnake of braſs
That hiſt? and birds of Silver that did ſing?
All thoſe new done by the Mathematicks,
Without which there's no ſcience, nor no truth.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: You are in your ſphear, Latorch: and rather
Than I'le contend w'ye for it, I'le believe it,
Y'have won upon me that I wiſh to ſee
My fate before me now, what e're it be.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: And I'le endeavour, you ſhall know with ſpeed,
For which I ſhould have one of truſt go with me,
If you pleaſe, Hamond, that I may by him
Send you my firſt diſpatches; after I
Shall bring you more, and as they come ſtill more.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Take your way,
Chooſe your own means, and be it proſperous to us. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Ruſee, de Bube, la Fiske, Norbret, Pippeau.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Come, bear up Sirs, we ſhall have better days,
My Almanack tells me.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: What is that? your rump?

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: It never itch'd in vain yet, ſlide la Fiske,
Throw off thy ſluggiſh face, I cannot abide
To ſee thee look like a poor Jade i'th' pound,
That ſaw no meat theſe three days.

sp.speaker: Fiske.
sp.l: 'Slight, to me
It ſeems thirteen dayes ſince I ſaw any.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: I can't remember that I ever ſaw
Or meat or mony, you may talk of both
To open a mans ſtomach or his purſe,
But feed 'em ſtill with air.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: Friar, I fear
You do not ſay your Office well a dayes.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Pox, he feeds
With leachery, and lives upon th'exchange
Of his two Eggs and Puddings with the market women.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: And what do you Sir, with the Advocates wife,
Whom you perſwade, upon your Doctoral bed,
To take the Mathematical trance ſo often?

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Come, we are ſtark naught all, bad's the beſt of us,
Four of the ſeven deadly ſpots we are;
Beſides our Leachery, we are envious,
And moſt, moſt gluttonous when we have it thus,
Moſt covetous now we want it; then our Boy
He is a fifth ſpot, ſloth and he undoes us.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: 'Tis true, the child was wont to be induſtrious,
And now and then ſent to a Merchants wife
Sick of the Husband, or a ſwearing Butler
That miſt of his Bowls, a crying Maid
Had loſt a Silver ſpoon; the Curry comb
Sometimes was wanting; there was ſomething gotten;
But now —

sp.speaker: Pip.
sp.l: What now? Did not I yeſter-morning
Bring you in a Cardecu there from the Peaſant,
Whoſe aſs I had driven aſide, and hid, that you
Might conjure for him? and then laſt night,
Six Soulz from the Cooks wife, you ſhar'd among you
To ſet a figure for the Peſtle I ſtole,
It is not at home yet; theſe things, my Maſters,
In a hard time, they would be thought on: you
Talk of your lands and Caſtles in the air,
Of your twelve houſes there: but it is I
That bring you in your rents for 'em, 'tis Pippeau
That is your bird-call.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Faith he does well,
And cuts through the Elements for us, I muſt needs ſay
In a fine dextrous line.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: But not as he did
At firſt, then he would ſail with any wind
Int' every Creek and Corner.

sp.speaker: Pip.
sp.l: I was light then,
New built and rigg'd when I came to you, Gentlemen,
But now with often and far venturing for you
Here be leaks ſprung, and whole Planks wanting ſee you;
If you'l new ſheath me again, yet I am for you
To any bog or ſleights, where e're you'l ſend me,
For as I am, where can this ragged Bark
Put in for any ſervice; 'leſs it be
O'th' Iſle of Rogues, and there turn Pirate for you.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Faith he ſays reaſon, Fryer, you muſt leave
Your neat criſp Claret, and fall to your Cyder
A while; and you la Fiske, your larded Capons
And Turkys for a time, and take a good
Clean Tripe in your way; de Bube too muſt content him with wholſom two ſouz'd petitoes, no more Crown Ordinaries, till we have cloath'd our Infant.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: So you'l keep
Your own good motions, Doctor, your dear ſelf.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Yes, for we all do know the Latitude
Of your Concupiſcence.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Here about your belly.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: You'l pick a bottle open or a whimſey,
As ſoon as the beſt of us.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: And dip your wriſt-bands,
(For Cuff's y'have none) as comely in the ſauce the Bell rings.
As any Courtier—hark, the Bell, who is there?

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Good luck I do conjure thee, Boy look out.

sp.speaker: Pip.
sp.l: They are Gallants, courtiers, one of 'em is Exit and enter again.
Of the Dukes bed-chamber.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Latorch, down,
On with your gown, there's a new ſuite arriv'd, To Norbret.
Did I not tell you, Sons of hunger? Crowns,
Crowns are coming toward you, wine and wenches
You ſhall have once again, and Fidlers:
Into your ſtudyes cloſe; each lay his ear
To his door, and as you hear me to prepare you
So come, and put me on that viſard only.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: You'l not be far hence Captain, when the
Buſineſs is done you ſhall receive preſent diſpatch.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I'le walk Sir, in the Cloyſter. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Monſieur Latorch; my Son,
The Stars are happy ſtill that guide you hither.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: I'me glad to hear their Secretary ſay ſo,
My learned Father Ruſſe, where's la Fiske,
Monſieur de Bube, how do they?

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: At their ſtudyes,
They are the Secretaries of the Stars, Sir,
Still at their books, they will not be pull'd off,
They ſtick like cupping glaſſes; if ever men
Spoke with the tongue of deſtiny, 'tis they.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: For loves ſake let's ſalute 'em.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Boy, go ſee,
Tell them who's here, ſay, that their friends do challenge
Some portion of their time, this is our minute,
Pray'em they'l ſpare it: they are the Sun and Moon
Of knowledge; pity two ſuch noble lights
Should live obſcur'd here in an Univerſity,
Whoſe beams were fit to'illumine any court
Of Chriſtendom.

div.stage: Enter la Fisk, de Bube, and Pippeau.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: The Duke will ſhortly know 'em.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Well, look upon the Aſtrolabe; you'l find it
Four Almucanturies at leaſt.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: It is ſo.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Still of their learned ſtuff, they care for nothing,
But how to know, as neglient of their bodies
In dyet, or elſe, eſpecially in their cloaths,
As if they had no change.

sp.speaker: Pip.
sp.l: They have ſo little
As well may free them from the name of ſhifters.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Monſieur Latorch?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: How is it, learned Gentlemen, with both your vertues?

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: A moſt happy hour, when we ſee you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: When you hear me then
It will be happier; the Duke greets you both
Thus, and though you may touch no mony, Father,
Yet you may take it.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: 'Tis his highneſs bounty,
But yet to me, and theſe that have put off
The world, ſuperfluous.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: We have heard of late of his highneſs good ſucceſs.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: And gratulate it.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Indeed he hath ſcap'd a ſtrange Conſpiracy,
Thanks to his Stars; which Stars he prayes by me,
You would again conſult, and make a Judgement
On what you lately erected for my love.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Oh, Sir, we dare not.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: For our lives.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: It is the Princes Scheam.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: T'incounter with that fear,
Here's to aſſure you, his Signet, write your names,
And be ſecured all three.

sp.speaker: Bud.
sp.l: We muſt intreat ſome time, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lat
sp.l: I muſt then intreat, it be as preſent as you can.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Have you the Scheam here?

sp.speaker: Lat
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: I would you had Sir another warrant.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: What would that do?

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Marty we have a Doctor Sir, that in this buſineſs
Would not perform the ſecond part.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Not him that you writ to me of?

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: The very ſame.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: I ſhould have made it, Sir, my ſuit to ſee him,
Here is a warrant Father, I conceiv'd
That he had ſolely applyed himſelf to Magick.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: And to their ſtudies too Sir, in this field
He was initiated, but we ſhall hardly
Draw him from his chair.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Tell him he ſhall have gold.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Oh, ſuch a ſyllable would make him to forſwear
Ever to breath in your ſight.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: How then?

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Sir, he if you do pleaſe to give him any thing,
Muſt have't convey'd under a paper.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Or left behind ſome book in his ſtudy.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: Or in ſome old wall.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Where his familiars may tell him of it, and that pleaſes him, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: Or elſe I'le go and aſſay him.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Take gold with you.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: That will not be amiſs; give it the Boy, Sir,
He knows his holes, and how to bait his Spirits.

sp.speaker: Pip.
sp.l: We muſt lay in ſeveral places, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: That's true, that if one come not, the other may hit.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Well, go then, is he ſo learned, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: The very top of our profeſſion; mouth of the fates,
Pray Heaven his Spirits be in a good humor to take,
They'l fling the gold about the houſe elſe.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: I, and beat the Fryer if he go not well
Furniſht with holy-water,

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Sir, you muſt obſerve him.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: Not croſs him in a word, for then he's gone.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: If he do come, which is a hazard, yet—
Maſs he's here, this is ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Where is our Scheme,
Let's ſee, diſpatch, nay fumbling now, who's this?

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Chief Gentleman of the Dukes Chamber, Doctor.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Oh, let him be, good even to him, he's a courtier,
I'le ſpare his complement, tell him: what's here?
The geniture Nocturnal, Longitude
At forty nine and ten minutes? How are the cardins?

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Libra in twenty four, forty four minutes,
And Capricorn.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I ſee it, ſee the Planets,
Where, how are they diſpos'd? the Sun and Mercury,
Mars with the Dragons tail in the third houſe,
And pars Fortunae in the Imo Coeli,
Then Jupiter in the twelfth, the Cacodemon.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: And Venus in the ſecond Inferna Porta.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I ſee it, peace, then Saturn in the Fifth,
Luna i'th' Seventh, and much of Scorpio,
Then Mars his Gaudium, riſing in th'aſcendent,
And joyn'd with Libra too, the houſe of Venus,
And Juniu Coeli, Mars his exaltation
In the ſeventh houſe, Aries being his natural houſe
And where he is now ſeated, and all theſe ſhew him
To be the Almuten.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Yes, he's Lord of the Geniture,
Whether you examine it by Ptolomeys way,
Or Meſſethales, Lael, or Alkindus.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: No other Planet hath ſo many dignities
Either by himſelf, or in regard of the Cuſps.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Why hold your tongue then if you know it; Venus
The Lady of the Horoſcope, being Libra,
The other part, Mars rules: So that the geniture,
Being Nocturnal, Luna is the higheſt,
None elſe being in ſufficient dignity,
She being in Aries in the Seventh houſe,
Where Sol exalted, is the Alchoroden.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: Yes, for you ſee he hath his Termin
In the degrees where ſhe is, and enjoyes
By that, ſix dignities.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: Which are clearly more
Than any elſe that view her in the Scheam.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Why I ſaw this, and could have told you too,
That he beholds her with a Trine aſpect
Here out of Sagittary, almoſt partile,
And how that Mars out of the ſelf ſame houſe,
(But another Sign) here by a Platique aſpect
Looks at the Hilege, with a Quartile ruling
The houſe where the Sun is; all this could I
Have told you, but that you'll outrun me; and more,
That this ſame Quartile aſpect to the Lady of life,
Here in the ſeventh, promiſes ſome danger,
Canda Draconis being ſo near Mars,
And Caput Algol in the houſe of Death.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: How, Sir? I pray you clear that.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: What is the queſtion firſt?

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Of the Dukes life, what dangers threaten him?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Apparent, and thoſe ſuddain, when the Hyley
Or Alchorodon by direction come
To a Quartile oppoſition of the place
Where Mars is in the Geniture (which is now
At hand) or elſe oppoſe to Mars himſelf; expect it.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: But they may be prevented.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Wiſdom only
That rules the Stars, may do it; for Mars being
Lord of the Geniture in Capricorn,
Is, if you mark it, now a Sextile here,
With Venus Lady of the Horoſcope.
So ſhe being in her Exilium, which is Scorpio,
And Mars his Gaudium, is o'rerul'd by him,
And clear debilitated five degrees
Beneath her ordinary power, ſo
That, at the moſt ſhe can but mitigate.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: You cannot name the perſons bring this danger?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: No, that the Stars tell us not, they name no man,
That is a work, Sir, of another place.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Tell him whom you ſuſpect, and he'll gueſs ſhrewdly.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Sir, we do fear one Aubrey; if 'twere he
I ſhould be glad; for we ſhould ſoon prevent him.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: I know him, the Dukes Kinſman, a tall man?
Lay hold of't Norbret.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Let me pauſe a little,
Is he not near of kin unto the Duke?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Yes, reverend Sir.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: 'Fart for your reverence, keep it till then; and ſomewhat high of ſtature?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: He is ſo.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: How old is he?

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: About ſeven and fifty.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: His head and beard inclining to be grey.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Right, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: And fat?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: He is ſomewhat corpulent, is he not?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: You ſpeak the man, Sir.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Well, look to him, farewel. Exit Norb.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Oh, it is Aubrey; Gentlemen, I pray you,
Let me receive this under all your hands.

sp.speaker: Ruſ.
sp.l: Why, he will ſhew you him in his Magick glaſs
If you intreat him, and but gratifie A ſpirit or two more.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: He ſhall eat gold
If he will have it, ſo ſhall you all; there's that
Amongſt you firſt, let me have this to ſend
The Duke in the mean time; and then what ſights
You pleaſe to ſhew; I'le have you ſo rewarded
As never Artiſts were, you ſhall to Court
Along with me, and there wait you fortunes.

sp.speaker: Bub.
sp.l: We have a pretty part of't in our pockets;
Boy we will all be new, you ſhall along too. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: Good Madam, hear the ſuit that Edith urges,
With ſuch ſubmiſs beſeeches; nor remain
So ſtrictly bound to ſorrow for your ſon,
That nothing elſe, though never ſo befitting,
Obtains your ears, or obſervation.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: What would ſhe ſay? I hear.

sp.speaker: Edith.
sp.l: My ſuit is, Madam,
That you would pleaſe to think as well of juſtice
Due to your ſons revenge, as of more wrong added
To both your ſelves for it, in only grieving.
Th' undaunted power of Princes ſhould not be
Confin'd in deedleſs cold calamity;
Anger, the Twin of ſorrow, in your wrongs
Should not be ſmother'd, when his right of birth
Claims th'Air as well, and force of coming forth.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Sorrow is due already, anger never
Should be conceived but where it may born
In ſome fact fit t'employ his active flame,
That elſe conſumes who bears it, and abides
Like a falſe ſtar that quenches as it glides.

sp.speaker: Ed.
sp.l: I have ſuch means t'employ it as your wiſh
Can think no better, eaſier, or ſecurer;
And ſuch as but th' honours I intend
To your partakings, I alone could end:
But your parts in all dues to crying blood
For vengeance in the ſhedder, are much greater:
And therefore ſhould work your hands to his ſlaughter
For your conſent to which, 'twere infinite wrong
To your ſevere and moſt impartial juſtice,
To move you to forget ſo falſe a ſon
As with a Mothers duty made you curſe him.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: Edith, he is forgot, for any ſon
Born of my Mother, or to me a Brother.
For ſhould we ſtill perform our rights to him
We ſhould partake his wrongs, and as foul be
In blood and damned parricide as he.
And therefore tell the happy means that Heaven
Puts in thy hand, for all our long'd for freedom
From ſo abhorr'd and impious a monſter.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Tell what ſhe will, I'le lend nor hand nor ear
To whatſoever Heaven puts in her power. Exit Sophia.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: How ſtrange ſhe is to what ſhe chiefly wiſhes?
Sweet Edith be not any thought the more
Diſcourag'd in thy purpoſe, but aſſured,
Her heart and prayers are thine; and that we two
Shall be enough to all we wiſh to do.

sp.speaker: Edith.
sp.l: Madam, my ſelf alone, I make no doubt
Shall be afforded power enough from Heaven
To end the murtherer: all I wiſh of you,
Is but ſome richer Ornaments and Jewels
Than I am able to provide my ſelf,
To help out the defects of my poor Beauty,
That yet hath been enough, as now it is,
To make his fancy mad with my deſire?
But you know, Madam, Women never can
Be too fair to torment an amorous man;
And this mans torments I would heighten ſtill,
Till at their higheſt he be fit to kill.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have all my Jewels and my Mothers,
And thou ſhalt paint too, that his bloods deſire
May make him periſh in a painted fire;
Haſt thou been with him yet?

sp.speaker: Edith.
sp.l: Been with him? no;
I ſet that hour back to haſte more his longing;
But I have promis'd to his inſtruments,
The admittance of a viſit at our houſe,
Where yet I would receive him with all luſtre
My ſorrow would give leave to, to remove
Suſpicion of my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have
All I can add, ſweet wench, in Jewels, tyres,
I'le be my ſelf thy dreſſer; nor may I
Serve my own love with a contracted Husband
More ſweetly, nor more amply than maiſt thou
Thy forward will with his bewitch'd affections:
Affect'ſt thou any perſonal aid of mine
My nobleſt Edith?

sp.speaker: Edith.
sp.l: Nought but your kind prayers
For full effect and ſpeed of my affair.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: They are thine, my Edith, as for me, my own;
For thou well know'ſt, if blood ſhed of the beſt
Should cool and be forgotten, who would fear
To ſhed blood ſtill? or where, alas, were then
The endleſs love we owe to worthy men?

sp.speaker: Ed.
sp.l: Love of the worthieſt ever bleſs your highneſs. Exe.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Rollo with a glaſs, Aubrey, and Servants.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: I Never ſtudied my glaſs till now,
It is exceeding well; now leave me; Couſin,
How takes your eye the object?

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I have learn'd
So much Sir of the Courtier, as to ſay
Your perſon does become your habit;
But being called unto it by a noble War,
Would grace an armour better.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: You are ſtill
For that great Art of which you are the Maſter;
Yet I muſt tell you, that to the encounters
We oft attempt, arm'd only thus, we bring
As troubled blood, fears mixt with flatt'ring hopes,
The danger in the ſervice too as great,
As when we are to charge quite through and through
The body of an Army.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I'le not argue
How you may rank the dangers, but will die in't,
The ends which they arrive at, are as diſtant
In every circumſtance, as far as honour
Is from ſhame and repentance.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: You are ſowr?

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I would ſpeak my free thoughts, yet not appear ſo;
Nor am I ſo ambitious of the title
Of one that dares talk any thing that was
Againſt the torrent of his own opinion,
That I affect to ſpeak ought may offend you:
And therefore gracious Sir, be pleas'd to think
My manners or diſcretion have inform'd me
That I was born, in all good ends, to ſerve you:
And not to check at what concerns me not:
I look not with ſore eyes on your rich out-ſide,
Nor rack my thoughts to find out to what purpoſe
'Tis now employ'd; I wiſh it may be good,
And that, I hope, offends not for a ſubject
Towards his Prince in things indifferent;
To uſe the auſtereneſs of a cenſuring Cato
Is arrogance, not freedom.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: I commend
This temper in you, and will cheriſh it.
They come from Rome, Latorch imployed you?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: True Sir.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: I muſt not now be troubled with a thought
Of any new deſign; good Aubrey read 'em,
And as they ſhall direct you, uſe my power,
Or to reply or execute.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I will, Sir.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: And Captain bring a ſquadron of our Guard
To th' houſe that late was Baldwins, and there wait me.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Some two hours hence.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: With my beſt care.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Inſpire me Love, and be thy deity,
Or ſcorn'd or fear'd, as now thou favour'ſt me. Exit Rollo.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: My ſtay to do my duty, may be wrongs
Your Lordſhips privacy.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Captain, your love
Is ever welcome; I intreat your patience
While I peruſe theſe.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I attend your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: How's this, a plot on me?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: What is contain'd
In th' letters that I brought, that thus tranſports him?

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: To be wrought on by Rogues, and have my head
Brought to the Axe by Knaves that cheat for bread?
The Creatures of a Paraſite, a ſlave;
I find you here Latorch, not wonder at it;
But that this honeſt Captain ſhould be made
His inſtrument, afflicts me; I'le make trial
Whether his will or weakneſs made him do it.
Captain you ſaw the Duke when he commanded
I ſhould do what theſe letters did direct me,
And I preſume you think I'le not neglect
For fear or favour, to remove all dangers
How near ſoever that man can be to me
From whom they ſhould have birth.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: It is confirm'd.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Nor would you Captain, I believe, refuſe,
Or for reſpect of thankfulneſs, or hopes,
To uſe your ſword with fulleſt confidence
Where he ſhall bid you ſtrike.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I never have done.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Nor will I think—

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I hope it is not queſtion'd.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: The means to have it ſo, is now propos'd you.
Draw, ſo, 'tis well, and next cut off my head.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: What means your Lordſhip?

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: 'Tis, Sir, the Dukes pleaſure:
My innocence hath made me dangerous,
And I muſt be remov'd, and you the man
Muſt act his will.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I'le be a Traytor firſt, before I ſerve it thus.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: It muſt be done,
And that you may not doubt it, there's your warrant,
But as you read, remember Hamond, that
I never wrong'd one of your brave profeſſion;
And, though it be not manly, I muſt grieve
That man of whoſe love I was moſt ambitious
Could find no object of his hate but me.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: It is no time to talk now, honour'd Sir,
Be pleas'd to hear thy ſervant, I am wrong'd,
And cannot, being now to ſerve the Duke,
Stay to expreſs the manner how; but if
I do not ſuddenly give you ſtrong proofs,
Your life is dearer to me than my own,
May I live baſe, and dye ſo: Sir, your pardon. Exit Ham.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I am both waies ruin'd, both waies mark't for ſlaughter
On every ſide, about, behind, before me,
My certain fate is fix't: were I a Knave now,
I could avoid this: had my actions
But meer relations to their own ends, I could 'ſcape now:
Oh honeſty! thou elder child of vertue,
Thou ſeed of Heaven, why to acquire thy goodneſs
Should malice and diſtruſt ſtick thorns before us,
And make us ſwim unto thee, hung with hazards?
But Heaven is got by ſuffering, not diſputing;
Say he knew this before-hand, where am I then?
Or ſay he does know it, where's my Loyalty?
I know his nature, troubled as the Sea,
And as the Sea devouring when he's vex'd,
And I know Princes are their own expounders.
Am I afraid of death? of dying nobly?
Of dying in mine innocence uprightly?
Have I met death in all his forms, and fears,
Now on the points of Swords, now pitch'd on Lances?
In fires, and ſtorms of Arrows, Battels, breaches,
And ſhall I now ſhrink from him, when he courts me
Smiling and full of ſanctity? I'le meet him;
My Loyal hand and heart ſhall give this to him,
And though it bear beyond what Poets feign
A puniſhment, duty ſhall meet that pain;
And my moſt conſtant heart to do him good,
Shall check at neither pale affright nor bloud.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: The Dutcheſs preſently would crave your preſence.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I come; and Aubrey now reſolve to keep
Thy honour living, though thy body ſleep. Exit.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Edith, a Boy, and a Banquet ſet out.

sp.speaker: Edith.
sp.l: Now for a Fathers murther, and thy ruine,
All chaſtity ſhall ſuffer if he raign;
Thou bleſſed ſoul, look down, and ſteel thy Daughter,
Look on the ſacrifice ſhe comes to ſend thee,
And through the bloudy clouds behold my piety,
Take from my cold heart fear, from my ſex pity,
And as I wipe theſe tears off, ſhed for thee,
So all remembrance may I loſe of mercy;
Give me a womans anger bent to bloud,
The wildneſs of the winds to drown his prayers,
Storm-like may my deſtruction fall upon him,
My rage like roving billows as they riſe,
Pour'd on his ſoul to ſink it, give me flattery,
(For yet my conſtant ſoul ne'r knew diſſembling)
Flattery the food of Fools, that I may rock him
And lull him in the Down of his deſires;
That in the height of all his hopes and wiſhes,
His Heaven forgot, and all his luſts upon him,
My hand, like thunder from a cloud, may ſeize him.
I hear him come, go boy, and entertain him.

lg.l: TAke, Oh take thoſe lips away
That ſo ſweetly were forſworn,
And thoſe eyes, like break of day,
Lights that do miſlead the Morn,
But my kiſſes bring again,
Seals of love, though ſeal'd in vain.
Hide, Oh hide thoſe hills of Snow,
Which thy frozen bloſſome bears,
On whoſe tops the Pinks that grow
Are of thoſe that April wears,
But firſt ſet my poor heart free,
Bound in thoſe Ivy chains by thee.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: What bright ſtar, taking beauties form upon her,
In all the happy luſtre of Heavens glory,
Has drop'd down from the Skye to comfort me?
Wonder of nature, let it not prophane thee
My rude hand touch thy beauty, nor this kiſs,
The gentle ſacrifice of love and ſervice,
Be offer'd to the honour of thy ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: My gracious Lord, no deity dwells here,
Nor nothing of that vertue, but obedience,
The ſervant to your will affects no flattery.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Can it be flattery to ſwear thoſe eyes
Are loves eternal lamps he fires all hearts with?
That tongue the ſmart ſtring to his bow? thoſe ſighs
The deadly ſhafts he ſends into our ſouls?
Oh, look upon me with thy ſpring of beauty.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Your grace is full of game.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: By Heaven, my Edith,
Thy Mother fed on Roſes when ſhe bred thee.

sp.speaker: Ed.
sp.l: And thine on brambles that have prick'd her heart out.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: The ſweetneſs of the Arabian wind ſtill blowing
Upon the treaſures of perfumes and ſpices,
In all their pride and pleaſures call thee Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Wil't pleaſe you ſit Sir?

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: So you pleaſe ſit by me.
Fair gentle maid, there is no ſpeaking to thee,
The excellency that appears upon thee
Tyes up my tongue: pray ſpeak to me.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Of what Sir?

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Of any thing, any thing is excellent.
Will you take my directions? ſpeak of love then;
Speak of thy fair ſelf Edith; and while thou ſpeak'ſt,
Let me, thus languiſhing, give up my ſelf wench.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: H'as a ſtrange cunning tongue, why do you ſigh Sir?
How maſterly he turns himſelf to catch me?

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: The way to Paradiſe, my gentle maid,
Is hard and crooked, ſcarce Repentance finding,
With all her holy helps, the door to enter,
Give me thy hand, what doſt thou feel?

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Your tears Sir.
You weep extreamly; ſtrengthen me now juſtice.
Why are theſe ſorrows Sir?

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Thou't never love me
If I ſhould tell thee, yet there's no way left
Ever to purchaſe this bleſt Paradiſe,
But ſwimming thither in theſe tears.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: I ſtagger.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Are they not drops of blood?

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: They're for blood then,
For guiltleſs blood, and they muſt drop, my Edith,
They muſt thus drop, till I have drown'd my miſchiefs.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: If this be true, I have no ſtrength to touch him.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: I prethee look upon me, turn not from me;
Alas I do confeſs I'me made of miſchiefs,
Begot with all mans miſeries upon me;
But ſee my ſorrows, maid, and do not thou,
Whoſe only ſweeteſt ſacrifice is ſoftneſs,
Whoſe true condition, tenderneſs of nature.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: My anger melts, Oh, I ſhall loſe my juſtice.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Do not thou learn to kill with cruelty,
As I have done, to murther with thy eyes,
(Thoſe bleſſed eyes) as I have done with malice.
When thou haſt wounded me to death with ſcorn,
(As I deſerve it Lady) for my true love,
When thou haſt loaden me with earth for ever,
Take heed my ſorrows, and the ſtings I ſuffer;
Take heed my nightly dreams of death and horrour
Purſue thee not: no time ſhall tell thy griefs then,
Nor ſhall an hour of joy adde to thy beauties.
Look not upon me as I kill'd thy Father,
As I was ſmear'd in blood, do not thou hate me,
But thus in whiteneſs of my waſh't repentance,
In my hearts tears and truth of love to Edith,
In my fair life hereafter.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: He will fool me.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Oh with thine Angel eyes behold and cloſe me,
Of Heaven we call for mercy and obtain it;
To Juſtice for our right on Earth and have it;
Of thee I beg for love, ſave me, and give it.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Now heaven thy help, or I am gone for ever,
His tongue has turn'd me into melting pity.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Keep the doors ſafe, and upon pain of death
Let no man enter till I give the word.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: We ſhall Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Here he is in all his pleaſure; I have my wiſh.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: How now? why doſt thou ſtare ſo?

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: A help, I hope.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: What doſt thou here? who ſent thee?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: My Brother, and the baſe malicious Office
Thou mad'ſt me do to Aubrey; pray.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Pray?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Pray, pray if thou canſt pray, I ſhall kill thy ſoul elſe,
Pray ſuddenly.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Thou can'ſt not be ſo trayterous.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: It is a Juſtice; ſtay Lady;
For I perceive your end; a womans hand
Muſt not rob me of vengeance.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: 'Tis my glory.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: 'Tis mine, ſtay, and ſhare with me; by the gods, Rollo,
There is no way to ſave thy life.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: No?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: No, it is ſo monſtrous, no repentance cures it.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Why then thou ſhalt kill her firſt, and what this blood
Will caſt upon thy curſed head.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Poor Guard Sir.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Spare not brave Captain.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Fear, or the Devil has thee.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Such fear Sir as you gave your honor'd Mother,
When your moſt vertuous Brother, ſhield-like, held her;
Such I'le give you, put her away.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: I will not, I will not die ſo tamely.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Murtherous villain, wilt thou draw ſeas of blood upon thee?

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Fear not, kill him good Captain, any way diſpatch
Him, my body's honor'd with that ſword that through me,
Sends his black ſoul to Hell: Oh, but for one hand.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Shake him off bravely.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: He's too ſtrong, ſtrike him.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Oh, am I with you Sir? now keep you from him,
What, has he got a knife?

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Look to him Captain, for now he will be miſchievous.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Do you ſmile Sir?
Do's it ſo tickle you? have at you once more.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Oh bravely thruſt; take heed he come not in Sir;
To him again, you give him too much reſpite.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Yet will you ſave my life, and I'le forgive thee,
And give thee all, all honours, all advancements,
Call thee my friend.

sp.speaker: Ed.
sp.l: Strike, ſtrike, and hear him not,
His tongue will tempt a Saint.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Oh for my ſoul ſake.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Save nothing of him.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Now for your farewel,
Are you ſo wary? take you that.

sp.speaker: Rol.
sp.l: Thou, that too;
Oh thou haſt kill'd me baſely, baſely, baſely. Dyes.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: The juſt reward of murther falls upon thee.
How do you Sir? has he not hurt you?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: No, I feel not any thing.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I charge you let us paſſe. within.

sp.speaker: Gua.
sp.l: You cannot yet Sir.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I'le make way then.

sp.speaker: Gua.
sp.l: We are ſworn to our Captain, and till he give the word.

div.stage: Enter Sophia, Matilda, Aubrey, Lords and attendants.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Now let them in there.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Oh, here he lies,
Sorrow on ſorrow ſeeks me, Oh, in his blood he lyes.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Had you ſpoke ſooner
This might have been prevented;
Take the Dutcheſs,
And lead her off, this is no ſight for her eyes.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: Oh, bravely done wench.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: There ſtands the noble doer.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: My honour ever ſeek thee for thy juſtice,
Oh 'twas a deed of high and brave adventure,
A juſtice even for heaven to envy at,
Farewel my ſorrows, and my tears take truce,
My wiſhes are come round: Oh bloody Brother,
Till this hour never beauteous; till thy life,
Like a full ſacrifie for all thy miſchiefs,
Flow'd from thee in theſe rivers, never righteous:
Oh how my eyes are quarri'd with their joys now?
My longing heart even leaping out for lightneſs?
But dye thy black ſins with thee, I forgive thee.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Who did this deed?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I, and I'le anſwer it. Dies.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: He faints, oh that ſame curſed knife has kill'd him.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: He ſnatch'd it from my hand, for whom I bore it,
And as they grappl'd.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Juſtice is ever equal,
Had it not been on him, th'adſt dy'd too honeſt.
Did you know of his death?

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Yes, and rejoyce in't.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I'me ſorry for your youth then; though the ſtrictneſs
Of Law ſhall not fall on you, that of life
Muſt preſently, go to a Cloyſter, carry her,
And there for ever lead your life in penitence.

sp.speaker: Edi.
sp.l: Beſt Father to my ſoul, I give you thanks, Sir,
And now my fair revenges have their ends,
My vows ſhall be my kin, my prayers my friends. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Stay there, I'le ſtep in and prepare the Duke.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: We ſhall have brave rewards?

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: That is without queſtion.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: By this time where's my huſſing friend Lord Aubrey?
Where's that good Gentleman? oh, I could laugh now,
And burſt my ſelf with meer imagination;
A wiſe man, and a valiant man, a juſt man;
To ſuffer himſelf be juggl'd out of the world,
By a number of poor Gipſeys? farewel Swaſh buckler,
For I know thy mouth is cold enough by this time;
A hundred of ye I can ſhave as neatly,
And ne'r draw bloud in ſhew: now ſhall my honour,
My power and vertue walk alone: my pleaſure
Obſerv'd by all, all knees bend to my worſhip,
All ſutes to me as Saint of all their fortunes,
Prefer'd and crowded to, what full place of credit,
And what place now? your Lordſhip? no, 'tis common,
But that I'le think to morrow on; now for my buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Dead, my Maſter dead? Aubrey alive too?

sp.speaker: Gua.
sp.l: Latorch, Sir.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Seize his body.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: My Maſter dead?

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: And you within this half hour,
Prepare your ſelf good Devil, you muſt to it,
Millions of gold ſhall not redeem thy miſchief,
Behold the Juſtice of thy practice, villain;
The maſs of murthers thou haſt drawn upon us:
Behold thy doctrine; you look now for reward, Sir,
To be advanc'd, I'm ſure, for all your labours?
And you ſhall have it, make his gallows higher
By ten foot at the leaſt, and then advance him.

sp.speaker: Lat.
sp.l: Mercy, mercy.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: 'Tis too late fool,
Such as you meant for me, away with him. He is led out.
What gaping knaves are theſe, bring 'em in fellows,
Now, what are you?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Mathematicians, if it pleaſe your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: And you drew a figure?

sp.speaker: Fiſ.
sp.l: We have drawn many.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: For the Duke, I mean; Sir Latorchs knaves you are.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: We know the Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: What did he promiſe you?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: We are paid already.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: But I will ſee you better paid, go whip them.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: We do beſeech your Lordſhip, we were hir'd.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I know you were, and you ſhall have your hire;
Whip 'em extremely, whip that Doctor there,
Till he record himſelf a Rogue.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I am one, Sir.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Whip him for being one, and when th'are whip't,
Lead 'em to the gallows to ſee their patron hang'd;
Away with them. They are led out.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Ah, good my Lord.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Now to mine own right, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: You have the next indeed, we all confeſs it,
And here ſtand ready to inveſt you with it.

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: Which to make ſtronger to you, and the ſurer
Than bloud or miſchiefs dare infringe again,
Behold this Lady, Sir, this noble Lady,
Full of the bloud as you are, of that nearneſs,
How bleſſed would it be?

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: I apprehend you, and ſo the fair Matilda dare accept
Me her ever conſtant ſervant.

sp.speaker: Mat.
sp.l: In all pureneſs,
In all humility of heart and ſervices,
To the moſt noble Aubrey, I ſubmit me.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Then this is our firſt tye, now to our buſineſs.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: We are ready all to put the honour on you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Aub.
sp.l: Theſe ſad rites muſt be done firſt, take up the bodys,
This, as he was a Prince, ſo Princely funeral
Shall wait upon him: on this honeſt Captain,
The decency of arms; a tear for him too.

l.hi: So, ſadly on, and as we view his blood,
May his Example in our Rule raiſe good.

list.head: Perſons Repreſented in the Play.
list.item: De-Gard, A Noble ſtay'd Gentleman that being newly lighted from his Travels, aſſiſts his Siſter Oriana in her chaſe of Mirabel the Wild-Gooſe.
La-Caſtre, the Indulgent Father to Mirabell.
Mirabell, the Wild-Gooſe, a Travell'd Monſieur, and great defyer of all Ladies in the way of Marriage, otherwiſe their much looſe ſervant, at laſt caught by the deſpis'd Oriana.
Pinac, his fellow Traveller, of a lively ſpirit, and Servant to the no leſs ſprightly Lillia-Bianca.
Belleur, Companion to both, of a ſtout blunt humour, in love with Roſalura.
Nantolet, Father to Roſalura and Lillia-Bianca.
Lugier, the rough and confident Tutor to the Ladies, and chief Engine to entrap the Wild-Gooſe.
Oriana, the fair betroth'd of Mirabell, and witty follower of the Chaſe.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Monſieur De Gard, and a Foot-Boy.
div.l: SIrrah, you know I have rid hard; ſtir my Horſe well
And let him want no Litter.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I am ſure I have run hard,
Would ſome body would walk me, & ſee me Litter'd;
For I think my fellow horſe, cannot in reaſon
Deſire more reſt, nor take up his Chamber before me,
But we are the Beaſts now, and the Beaſts are our Maſters.

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: When you have done, ſtep to the Ten Crown Ordinary.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: With all my heart, Sir,
For I have a Twenty Crown ſtomach.

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: And there beſpeak a dinner.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Yes Sir, preſently.

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: For whom, I beſeech you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: For my ſelf, I take it, Sir.

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: In truth ye ſhall not take it, 'tis not meant for you,
There's for your Provender: Beſpeak a Dinner
For Monſieur Mirabell, and his Companions,
They'll be in Town within this hour.
When you have done, Sirrah,
Make ready all things at my Lodging, for me,
And wait me there.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: The Ten Crown Ordinary?

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: Yes Sir, if you have not forgot it.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I'le forget my feet firſt;
'Tis the beſt part of a Foot-mans faith. Exit Boy.

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: Theſe youths
For all they have been in Italy, to learn thrift,
And ſeem to wonder at mens laviſh waies,
Yet they cannot rub off old friends, their French itches;
They muſt meet ſometimes to diſport their Bodies
With good Wine, and good Women; and good ſtore too.
Let 'em be what they will, they are Arm'd at all points
And then hang ſaving. Let the Sea grow high,
This Ordinary can • it 'em of all ſizes,
They muſt ſalute their Country with old cuſtomes.

sp.speaker: Ori
sp.l: Brother.

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: My deareſt Siſter.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Welcome, welcome:
Indeed ye are welcome home, moſt welcome.

sp.speaker: De Ga
sp.l: Thank ye,
You are grown a handſome woman, Oriana,
( ••• ſh at your faults) I am wondrous glad to ſee ye.
Monſieur La Caſtre: Let not my Affection
To my fair Siſter, make me be held unmannerly:
I am glad to ſee ye well, to ſee ye luſty,
Good health about ye, and in fair company,
Believe me, I am proud—

sp.speaker: La Caſt.
sp.l: Fair Sir, I thank ye:
Monſieur de Gard, you are welcome from your journey,
Good men, have ſtill good welcome: give me your hand, Sir.
Once more, you are welcome home: you look ſtill younger.

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: Time has no leaſure to look after us.
We wander every where: Age cannot find us.

sp.speaker: La Caſt.
sp.l: And how does all?

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: All well, Sir; and all luſty.

sp.speaker: La Caſt.
sp.l: I hope my Son be ſo, I doubt not, Sir,
But you have often ſeen him in your journeys,
And bring me ſome fair News.

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: Your Son is well, Sir,
And grown a proper Gentleman: he is well, and luſty,
Within this e ght hours, I took leave of him,
And over-ey'd him, having ſome ſlight buſineſs
That forc'd me out o' th' way: I can aſſure you
He will be here to night.

sp.speaker: La Caſt.
sp.l: Ye make me glad, Sir,
For o' my faith, I almoſt long to ſee him,
Me thinks he has been away—

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: Tis but your tenderneſs;
What are three years? a love-ſick wench will allow it:
His friends that went out with him are come back too;
Belleur, and young Pinac: he bid me ſay little,
Becauſe he means to be his own glad Meſſenger.

sp.speaker: La Ca.
sp.l: I thank ye for this news, Sir, he ſhall be welcome,
And his friends too: indeed I thank you heartily:
And how (for I dare ſay, you will not flatter him)
Has Italy wrought on him? has he mew'd yet
His wild fantaſtick Toyes? they ſay that Climate
Is a great purger of thoſe humorous Fluxes.
How is he improved, I pray ye?

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: No doubt, Sir, well.
H'as born himſelf a full, and noble Gentleman,
To ſpeak him farther is beyond my Charter.

sp.speaker: La Caſt.
sp.l: I am glad to hear ſo much good; Come, I ſee
You long to enjoy your Siſter: yet I muſt intreat ye
Before I go, to ſup with me to night
And muſt not be deni'd.

sp.speaker: De Ga.
sp.l: I am your ſervant

sp.speaker: La-C
sp.l: Where you ſhall meet fair, merry, and noble Company.
My neighbour Natolet, and his two fair Daughters.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: Your ſupper's ſeaſon'd well, Sir. I ſhall wait upon ye.

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: Till then I'le leave ye: and y'are once more welcome.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: I thank ye, noble Sir. Now, Oriana, Exit.
How have ye done ſince I went? have ye had your health well?
And your mind free?

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: You ſee I am not bated;
Merry, and eat my meat.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: A good preſervative.
And how have you been us'd? You know, Oriana,
Upon my going out, at your requeſt,
I left your Portion in La Caſtre's hands,
(The main Means you muſt ſtick to) for that reaſon
(And 'tis no little one) I ask ye, Siſter,
With what humanity he entertains ye,
And how ye find his courteſie?

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Moſt ready.
I can aſſure you, Sir, I am us'd moſt nobly.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: I am glad to hear it: But I prethee tell me,
(And tell me true) what end had you, Oriana,
In truſting your mony here? He is no Kinſman,
Nor any tie upon him of a Guardian;
Nor dare I think ye doubt my prodigality.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: No, certain, Sir, none of all this provoked me;
Another private reaſon.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: 'Tis not private,
Nor carryed ſo: 'tis common (my fair Siſter)
Your love to Mirabel; your bluſhes tell it:
'Tis too much known, and ſpoken of too largely;
And with no little ſhame I wonder at it.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Is it a ſhame to love?

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: To love undiſcreetly:
A Virgin ſhould be tender of her honour,
Cloſe, and ſecure.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I am as cloſe as can be,
And ſtand upon as ſtrong and honeſt guards too;
Unleſs this Warlike Age need a Port-cullis:
Yet I confeſs, I love him.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: Hear the people.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Now I ſay hang the people: He that dares
Believe what they ſay, dares be mad, and give
His Mother, nay his own Wife up to Rumor;
All grounds of truth they build on, is a Tavern,
And their beſt cenſure's Sack, Sack in abundance:
For as they drink, they think: they ne're ſpeak modeſtly
Unleſs the wine be poor, or they want mony.
Believe them? believe Amadis de Gaul,
The Knight o'th' Sun, or Palmerin of England;
For theſe, to them, are modeſt, and true ſtories.
Pray underſtand me; if their tongues be truth,
And if in Vino veritas be an Oracle,
What Woman is, or has been ever honeſt?
Give 'em but ten round cups, they'll ſwear Lucretia
Dy'd not for want of power to reſiſt Tarquin,
But want of Pleaſure, that he ſtay'd no longer:
And Portia, that was famous for her Piety
To her lov'd Lord, they'll face ye out, dy'd o'th'Pox.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: Well, there is ſomething, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: If there be, Brother,
'Tis none of their things, 'tis not yet ſo monſtrous;
My thing is Marriage: And at his return
I hope to put their ſquint-eyes right again.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: Marriage? 'tis true; his Father is a rich man;
Rich both in land and money: he his heir,
A young and handſome man, I muſt confeſs too;
But of ſuch qualities, and ſuch wild flings,
Such admirable imperfections, Siſter,
(For all his Travel, and bought experience)
I ſhould be loth to own him for my Brother:
Methinks a rich mind in a ſtate indifferent
Would prove the better fortune.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: If he be wild,
The reclaiming him to good, and honeſt, (Brother)
Will make much for my honour; which, if I proſper,
Shall be the ſtudy of my love, and life too.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: Ye ſay well; would he thought as well, and loved too.
He Marry? he'll be hanged firſt: he knows no more
What the conditions and the ties of Love are,
The honeſt purpoſes and grounds of Marriage,
Nor will know, nor be ever brought t' endeavour,
Than I do how to build a Church; he was ever
A looſe and ſtrong defier of all order,
His Loves are wanderers, they knock at each door,
And taſte each diſh, but are no reſidents:
Or ſay he may be brought to think of Marriage,
(As 'twill be no ſmall labour) thy hopes are ſtrangers.
I know there is a labour'd match, now follow'd,
(Now at this time, for which he was ſent for home too)
Be not abus'd, Natolet has two fair Daughters,
And he muſt take his choice.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Let him take freely;
For all this I deſpair not; my mind tells me
That I, and only I, muſt make him perfect;
And in that hope I reſt.

sp.speaker: De-Gar.
sp.l: Since y'are ſo confident,
Proſper your hope; I'll be no adverſary;
Keep your ſelf fair and right, he ſhall not wrong ye.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: When I forget my vertue, no man know me. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Mirabel, Pinac, Bellure, and Servants.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Welcome to Paris once more, Gentlemen;
We have had a merry and a luſty Ordinary,
And Wine, and good meat, and a bounſing Reckoning;
And let it go for once; 'Tis a good Phyſick,
Only the Wenches are not for my diet,
They are too lean and thin; their embraces brawn-faln.
Give me the plump Venetian, fat, and luſty,
That meets me ſoft and ſupple; ſmiles upon me,
As if a Cup of full Wine leapt to kiſs me;
Theſe ſlight things I affect not.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: They are ill built;
Pin buttockt, like your dainty Barbaries,
And weak i'th' paſterns; they'll endure no hardneſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: There's nothing good, or handſom bred amongſt us:
Till we are travel'd, and live abroad, we are Coxcombs:
Ye talk of France, a ſlight unſeaſon'd Country,
Abundance of groſs food, which makes us Block-heads:
We are fair ſet out indeed, and ſo are fore-horſes:
Men ſay we are great Courtiers, men abuſe us:
We are wiſe, and valiant too, non credo, Seignior:
Our Women the beſt Linguiſts? they are Parrats;
O' this ſide the Alpes they are nothing but meer Drolleries:
Ha, Roma la Santa, Italy for my money,
Their policies, their cuſtoms, their frugalities,
Their courteſies ſo open, yet ſo reſerved too,
As when ye think y'are known beſt, ye are a ſtranger;
The very pick-teeth ſpeak more man than we do,
And ſeaſon of more ſalt.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: 'Tis a brave Country:
Not peſter'd with your ſtubborn preciſe Puppies,
That turn all uſeful and allow'd contentments
To ſcabs and ſcruples; hang 'em Capon-worſhippers.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I like that freedom well, and like their Women too,
And would fain do as others do; but I am ſo baſhful,
So naturally an Aſs: Look ye, I can look upon 'em,
And very willingly I go to ſee 'em,
(There's no man willinger) and I can kiſs 'em,
And make a ſhift—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: But if they chance to flout ye,
Or ſay ye are too bold; fie, Sir, remember;
I pray • it farther off;—

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis true, I am humbled,
I am gone, I confeſs ingenuouſly I am ſilenced,
The ſpirit of Amber cannot force me anſwer.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Then would I ſing and dance.

sp.speaker: Bel,
sp.l: You have wherewithal, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: And charge her up again.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I can be hang'd firſt;
Yet where I faſten well I am a tyrant.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why, thou darſt fight?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes, certainly, I dare fight;
And fight with any man at any weapon,
Would the other were no more; but a pox on't,
When I was ſometimes in my height of hope,
And reaſonable valiant that way, my heart harden'd,
Some ſcornful jeſt or other chops between me
And my deſire: what would ye have me to do then, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Belvere, you muſt be bolder: Travel three years,
And bring home ſuch a Baby to betray ye
As baſhfulneſs? a great fellow, and a Souldier?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You have the gift of impudence, be thankful;
Every man has not the like talent: I will ſtudy
And if it may be reveal'd to me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Learn of me,
And of Pinac: no doubt you'll find employment;
Ladies will look for Courtſhip.

sp.speaker: Pic.
sp.l: 'Tis but fleſhing,
But ſtanding one good brunt or two: haſt thou any mine to marriage?
We'l provide theeſome ſoft natur'd wench, that's dumb too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Or an old woman that cannot refuſe thee in charity.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: A dumb woman, or an old woman, that were eager
And car'd not for Diſcourſe, I were excellent at.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: You muſt now put on boldneſs, there's no avoiding it;
And ſtand all hazards; flye at all games bravely;
They'll ſay you went out like an Oxe, and return'd like an Aſs elſe.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I ſhall make danger ſure.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am ſent for home now,
I know it is to marry, but my Father ſhall pardon me,
Although it be a witty Ceremony,
And may concern me hereafter in my Gravity;
I will not loſe the freedom of a Traveller;
A new ſtrong luſty Bark cannot ride at one Anchor;
Shall I make divers ſuits to ſhew to the ſame eyes?
'Tis dull and home-ſpun; Study ſeveral pleaſures,
And want employments for 'em? I'll be hang'd firſt;
Tye me to one ſmock? make my travels fruitleſs?
I'll none of that; for every freſh behaviour,
By your leave, Father, I muſt have a freſh Miſtriſs,
And a freſh favour too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I like that paſſingly;
As many as you, will ſo they be willing,
Willing, and gentle, gentle.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: There's no reaſon
A Gentleman, and a Traveller ſhould be clapt up,
For 'tis a kind of Baeboes to be married
Before he manifeſt to the World his good parts:
Tug ever like a Raſcal at one Oar?
Give me the Italian liberty.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That I ſtudy;
And that I will enjoy; Come, go in Gentlemen,
There mark how I behave my ſelf, and follow. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Enter La-Caſtre, Natolet, Lugien, Roſa Lieura, Lylia-Biancha.

sp.speaker: La-Caſ.
sp.l: You and your beauteous daughters are moſt welcome,
Beſhrew my blood they are fair ones; welcom Beauties,
Welcome, ſweet Birds.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: They are bound much to your courteſies.

sp.speaker: La-Caſ.
sp.l: I hope we ſhall be nearer acquainted.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: That's my hope too.
For certain, Sir, I much deſire your Alliance:
You ſee 'em, they are no Gypſies, for their breeding,
It has not been ſo coarſe, but they are able
To rank themſelves with women of fair faſhion;
Indeed they have been trained well.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Thank me.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: Fit for the Heirs of that State I ſhall leave 'em;
To ſay more, is to ſell 'em. They ſay your Son
Now he has travell'd muſt be wondrous curious,
And choice in what he takes: theſe are no coarſe ones;
Sir, here's a merry wench, let him look to himſelf,
(All heart, i'faith) may chance to ſtartle him;
For all his care, and travell'd caution,
May creep into his Eye; if he love Gravity,
Affect a ſolemn face, there's one will fit him.

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: So young, and ſo demure?

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: She is my Daughter,
Elſe I would tell you, Sir, ſhe is a Miſtriſs
Both of thoſe manners and that modeſty
You would wonder at: She is no often Speaker,
But when ſhe does, ſhe ſpeaks well; Nor no Reveller,
Yet ſhe can dance, and has ſtudied the Court Elements,
And ſings, as ſome ſay, handſomely; if a woman,
With the decency of her Sex, may be a Scholar,
I can aſſure ye, Sir, ſhe underſtands too.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Theſe are fit Garments, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Thank them that cut 'em;
Yes, they are handſome women; they have handſome parts too;
Pretty becoming parts.

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: 'Tis like they have, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Yes, yes, and handſome Education they have had too,
Had it abundantly: they need not bluſh at it;
I taught it, I'll avouch it.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: You ſay well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: I know what I ſay, Sir, and I ſay but right, Sir;
I am no Trumpet of their Commendations
Before their Father; elſe I ſhould ſay farther.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: 'Pray ye, what's this Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: One that lives with me, Sir;
A man well bred and learn'd, but blunt and bitter,
Yet it offends no wiſe man; I take pleaſure in't:
Many fair gifts he has, in ſome of which
That lye moſt eaſie to their underſtandings,
H'as handſomely bred up my Girls, I thank him.
I have put it to 'em, that's my part, I have urg'd it,
It ſeems they are of years now to take hold on't.
He's wondrous blunt.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: By my faith I was afraid of him:
Does he not fall out with the Gentlewomen ſometimes?

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: No, no, he's that way moderate, and diſcreet, Sir.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: If he did, we ſhould be too hard for him.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Well ſaid Sulphur:
Too hard for thy Husbands head if he wear not armour.

div.stage: Enter Mirabel, Pinac, De-Gard, and Oriana.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: Many of theſe bickrings, Sir.

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: I am glad they are no Oracles;
Sure, as I live, he beats them, he's ſo puiſant.

sp.speaker: Or
sp.l: Well, if ye do forget—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Prithee hold thy peace;
I know thou art a pretty wench; I know thou lov'ſt me,
Preſerve it till we have a fit time to diſcourſe on't,
And a fit place: I'll eaſe thy heart I warrant thee:
Thou ſeeſt I have much to do now.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I am anſwer'd, Sir:
With me ye ſhall have nothing on theſe conditions.

sp.speaker: De Gard.
sp.l: Your Father and your friends.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: You are welcome home, Sir;
'Bleſs ye, ye are very welcome:
'Pray know this Gentleman,
And theſe fair Ladies.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: Monſieur Mirabell,
I am much affected with your fair return, Sir;
You bring a general joy.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I bring you ſervice,
And theſe bright Beauties, Sir.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: Welcome home, Gentlemen,
Welcome, with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Bel. Pin.
sp.l: We thank ye, Sir.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Your friends will have their ſhare too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Sir, we hope
They'll look upon us, though we ſhew like ſtrangers.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.l: Monſieur De Gard, I muſt ſalute you alſo,
And this fair Gentlewoman: you are welcome from your Travel too.
All welcome, all.

sp.speaker: De Gard.
sp.l: We render ye our loves, Sir:
The beſt Wealth we bring home: By your Favours, Beauties,
One of theſe two: you know my meaning.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: Well, Sir:
They are fair and handſom, I muſt needs confeſs it;
And let it prove the worſt, I ſhall live after it,
Whilſt I have meat and drink Love cannot ſtarve me;
For if I dye o' th' firſt fit I am unhappy,
And worthy to be buried with my heels upward.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To marry, Sir?

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: You know I am an old man,
And every hour declining to my Grave,
One foot already in, more Sons I have not,
Nor more I dare not ſeek whilſt you are worthy,
In you lies all my hope, and all my name,
The making good or wretched of my memory,
The ſafety of my ſtate.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And you have provided
Out of this tenderneſs theſe handſom Gentlewomen,
Daughters to this rich man, to take my choice of?

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: I have, dear Son.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis true, ye are old, and feebled;
Would ye were young again, and in full vigor;
I love a bounteous Fathers life, a long one,
I am none of thoſe that when they ſhoot to ripeneſs,
Do what they can to break the boughs they grew on;
I wiſh ye many years and many Riches,
And pleaſures to enjoy 'em: But for Marriage,
I neither yet believe in't, nor affect it,
Nor think it fit.

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: You will render me your reaſons?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, both ſhort and pithy, and theſe they are:
You would have me marry a Maid?

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: A Maid? what elſe?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, there be things called Widows, dead mens Wills,
I never lov'd to prove thoſe; nor never long'd yet
To be buried alive in another mans cold monument.
And there be maids appearing, and maids being:
The appearing are fantaſtick things, meer ſhadows;
And if you mark 'em well, they want their heads too;
Only the World to cozen miſty eyes,
Has clapt 'em on new faces. The maids being,

If he have neither fear bef •••
〈◊〉 eyes, nor fortune;
And let him take heed how he gathers theſe too,
For look ye, father they are juſt like melons,
Musk melons are the emblems of theſe maids;
Now they are ripe, now cut 'em, they taſte pleaſantly,
And are a dainty fruit digeſted eaſily:
Neglect this preſent time, and come to morrow,
They are ſo ripe they are rotten gone, their ſweetneſs
Run into humour, and their taſte to ſurfeit.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Why, theſe are now ripe, Son.

sp.speaker: Mir
sp.l: I'll try them preſently,
And if I like their taſte—

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: 'Pray ye pleaſe your ſelf, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That liberty is my due, and I'll maintain it:
Lady, what think you of a handſom man now?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: A wholſom too, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That's as you make your Bargain.
A handſom, wholſom man then, and a kind man,
To cheer your heart up, to rejoyce you, Lady?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I love rejoycing.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To lye cloſe to you?
Cloſe as a Cockle? keep the cold nights from you?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: That will be lookt for too, our bodies ask it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And get two Boys at every Birth?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: That's nothing,
I have known a Cobler do it, a poor thin Cobler;
A Cobler out of mouldy Cheeſe perform it,
Cabbage, and coarſe black Bread; methinks a Gentleman
Should take foul ſcorn to have an awl outname him.
Two at a Birth? why, every houſe-Dove has it:
That man that feeds well, promiſes as well too,
I ſhould expect indeed ſomething of worth from.
Ye talk of two?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She would have me get two dozen,
Like Buttons, at a Birth.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: You love to brag, Sir.
If you proclaim theſe offers at your Marriage,
You are a pretty timber'd man, take heed.
They may be taken hold of, and expected,
Yes, if not hoped for at a higher rate too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I will take heed, and thank ye for your counſel:
Father, what think you?

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: 'Tis a merry Gentlewoman;
Will make, no doubt, a good wife.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Not for me:
I marry her, and happily get nothing;
In what a ſtate am I then? Father, I ſhall ſuffer
For any thing I hear to the contrary, more majorum,
I were as ſure to be a Cuckold, Father,
A Gentleman of Antler.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Away, away, fool.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: As I am ſure to fail her expectation,
I had rather get the Pox than get her Babies.

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: Ye are much to blame; if this do not affect ye,
'Pray try the other; ſhe's of a more demure way.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: That I had but the audacity to talk thus!
I love that plain-ſpoken Gentlewoman admirably,
And certain I could go as near to pleaſe her,
If down-right doing— ſhe has a per'lous Countenance,
If I could meet one that would believe me,
And take my honeſt meaning without circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You ſhall have your will, Sir, I will try the other,
But 'twill be to ſmall uſe. I hope, fair Lady
(For methinks in your eyes I ſee more mercy)
You will enjoin your Lover a leſs penance;
And though I'll promiſe much, as men are liberal,
And vow an ample ſacrifice of ſervice,
Yet your diſcretion, and your tenderneſs,
And thriftineſs in Love, good huſwives carefulneſs
To keep the ſtock entire—

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Good Sir, ſpeak louder,
That theſe may witneſs too ye talk of nothing,
I ſhould be loth alone to bear the burthen
Of ſo much indiſcretion.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Hark ye, hark ye;
Ods bobs, you are angry, Lady.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Angry? no, Sir;
I never own'd an anger to loſe poorly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: But you can love for all this, and delight too,
For all your ſet-auſterity, to hear
Of a good husband, Lady?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: You ſay true, Sir:
For by my troth, I have heard of none theſe ten years,
They are ſo rare, and there are ſo many, Sir,
So many longing women on their knees too,
That pray the dropping down of theſe good husbands,
The droping down from heaven; for they are not bred there.
That you may gueſs at all my hope, but hearing—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why may not I be one?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: You were near 'em once, Sir,
When ye came over the Alpes; thoſe are near Heaven;
But ſince ye miſs'd that happineſs, there is no hope of ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Can ye love a man?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Yes, if the man be lovely;
That is, be honeſt, modeſt; I would have him valiant,
His anger ſlow, but certain for his honour;
Travell'd he ſhould be, but through himſelf exactly;
For 'tis fairer to know manners well than Countries;
He muſt be no vain Talker, nor no Lover
To hear himſelf talk, they are brags of a wanderer,
Of one finds no retreict for fair behaviour;
Would ye learn more?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Learn to hold your peace then,
Fond Girls are got with tongues, women with tempers.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Women, with I know what; but let this vaniſh:
Go thy way good Wife Bias; ſure thy Husband
Muſt have a ſtrong Philoſophers ſtone, he will ne'r pleaſe thee elſe.
Here's a ſtarcht piece of auſterity; do you hear, Father?
Do you hear this moral Lecture?

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Yes, and like it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why, there's your judgment now; there's an old bolt ſhot:
This thing muſt have the ſtrangeſt obſervation,
Do you mark me (father?) when ſhe is married once,
The ſtrangeſt cuſtom too of admiration
On all ſhe does and ſpeaks, 'twill be paſt ſufferance;
I muſt not lie with her in common language,
Nor cry have at thee, Kate, I ſhall be hiſs'd then;
Nor eat my meat without the ſawce of ſentences,
Your powder'd Beef, and Problems, a rare diet;
My firſt Son, Monſieur Ariſtotle, I know it,
Great Maſter of the Metaphyſicks, or ſo;
The ſecond Solon, and the beſt Law-ſetter;
And I muſt look Egyptian God fathers,
Which will be no ſmall trouble: my eldeſt daughter
Sapho, or ſuch a ſi •• ling kind of Poeteſs,
And brought up, invita Minerva, at her needle.
My dogs muſt look their names too, and all Spartan,
Lelaps, Melampus; no more Fox and Baudiface.
I married to a ſullen ſet of ſentences?
To one that weighs her words and her behaviours
In the gold-weights of diſcretion? I'll be hang'd firſt.

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: Prithee reclaim thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Pray ye give me time then;
If they can ſet me any thing to play at,
That ſeems fit for a Gameſter, have at the faireſt
Till I ſee more, and try more.

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: Take your time then,
I'll bar ye no fair liberty: come Gentlemen,
And Ladies come: to all once more welcome,
And now let's in to ſupper.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How doſt' like 'em?

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: They are fair enough, but of ſo ſtrange behaviours.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Too ſtrange for me; I muſt have thoſe have mettle,
And mettle to my mind; Come, let's be merry.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Bleſs me from this woman: I would ſtand the Cannon
Before ten words of hers.

sp.speaker: De-Gar.
sp.l: Do you find him now?
Do you think he will be ever firm?

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I fear not. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: NE'r tell me of this happineſs, 'tis nothing;
The ſtate they bring with being ſought to ſcurvey,
I had rather make mine own play, and I will do.
My happineſs is in mine own content,
〈…〉 of ſuch glorious trifles,
〈…〉 t ouſand more. For my humour,
〈…〉 , that ſticks to me,
〈…〉 Companion; there's a Beauty:
Good women too, as the Age reckons 'em,
More than I have employment for.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: You are happy.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: My only fear is, that I muſt be forced
Againſt m • nature, to conceal my ſelf.
Health, and an able Body are two jewels.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: If either of theſe two women were offered to me now,
I would think otherwiſe, and do accordingly:
Yes, and recant my hereſies, I would fain, Sir;
And be more tender of opinion,
And put a little off my travel'd liberty
Out of the way, and look upon 'em ſeriouſly.
Methinks this grave carried wench.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Methinks the other,
The home-ſpoken Gentlewoman, that deſires to be fruitful,
That treats of the full manage of the matter,
For there lies all my aim; that wench, methinks
If I were but well ſet on; for ſhe is a fable,
If I were but hounded right, and one to teach me:
She ſpeaks to th' matter, and comes home to th' point:
Now do I know I have ſuch a body to pleaſe her,
As all the Kingdom cannot fit her with, I am ſure on't,
If I could but talk my ſelf into her favour.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That's eaſily done.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: That's eaſily ſaid, would 'twere done;
You ſhould ſee then how I would lay about me;
If I were vertuous, it would never grieve me,
Or any thing that might juſtifie my modeſty,
But when my nature is prone to do a charitie,
And my calfs tongue will not help me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Will ye go to 'em?
They cannot but take it courteouſly.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I le do my part,
Though I am ſure 'twill be the hardeſt I e're plaid yet,
A way I never try'd too, which will ſtagger me,
And if it do not ſhame me, I am happy.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Win 'em, and wear 'em, I give up my intereſt.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: What ſay ye, Monſieur Bellure?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Would I could ſay,
Or ſing, or any thing that were but handſom,
I would be with her preſently.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Yours is no venture;
A merry ready wench.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: A vengeance ſquibber;
She'l ſteer me out of faith too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'le be near thee;
Pluck up thy heart, I'le ſecond thee at all brunts;
Be angry if ſhe abuſe thee, and beat her a little,
Some women are won that way.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Pray be quiet,
And let me think: I am reſolv'd to go on;
But how I ſhall get off again —

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am perſwaded
Thou wilt ſo pleaſe her, ſhe will go near to raviſh thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I would 'twere come to that once: let me pray a little.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Now for thine honour Pinac; board me this modeſty,
Warm but this frozen ſnow-ball, 'twill be a conqueſt
(Although I know thou art a fortunate Wencher,
And haſt done rarely in thy daies) above all thy ventures.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You will be ever near?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: At all neceſſities,
And take thee off, and ſet thee on again, Boy;
And cheriſh thee, and ſtroak thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Help me out too?
For I know I ſhall ſtick i'th' mire: if ye ſee us cloſe once,
Be gone, and leave me to my fortune, ſuddenly,
For I am then determin'd to do wonders.
Farewel, and ſling an old ſhooe: how my heart throbs!
Would I were drunk: Farewel Pinac; Heaven ſend us
A joyfull and a merry meeting, man.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Farewel,
And chear thy heart up; and remember Bellure
They are but women.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I had rather they were Lyons.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: About it; I'le be with you inſtantly. Exeunt.
Shall I ne'r be at reſt? no peace of conſcience?
No quiet for theſe creatures? Am I ordain'd
To be devour'd quick by theſe ſhe-Canibals?
Here's another they call handſom, I care not for her,
I ne'r look after her: when I am half tipled
