It may be I ſhould turn her, and peruſe her,
Or in my want of women, I might call for her;
But to be haunted when I have no fancie,
No maw to th' matter—Now, why do you follow me?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I hope, Sir, 'tis no blemiſh to my vertue,
Nor need you (out of ſcruple) ask that queſtion,
If you remember ye, before your Travel
The contract you ty'd to me: 'tis my love, Sir,
That makes me ſeek ye, to confirm your memory,
And that being fair and good, I cannot ſuffer:
I come to give ye thanks too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: For what 'prethee?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: For that fair piece of honeſty ye ſhew'd, Sir,
That conſtant nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How? for I am ſhort headed.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I'le tell ye then; for refuſing that free offer
Of Monſieur Natolets; thoſe handſom Beauties,
Thoſe two prime Ladies, that might well have preſt ye,
If not to have broken, yet to have bow'd your promiſe,
I know it was for my ſake, for your faith ſake,
You ſlipt 'em off: your honeſty compell'd ye.
And let me tell ye, Sir, it ſhew'd moſt handſomly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And let me tell thee, there was no ſuch matter:
Nothing intended that way of that nature;
I have more to do with my honeſty than to fool it,
Or venture it in ſuch leak barks as women;
I put 'em off, becauſe I lov'd 'em not,
Becauſe they are too queazie for my temper,
And not for thy ſake, nor the Contract ſake,
Nor vows, nor oaths; I have made a thouſand of 'em,
They are things indifferent, whether kept or broken;
Meer venial ſlips, that grow not near the conſcience;
Nothing concerns thoſe tender parts; they are trifles;
For, as I think, there was never man yet hop'd for
Either conſtancie, or ſecrecie, from a woman,
Unleſs it were an Aſs ordain'd for ſufferance;
Nor to contract with ſuch can be a Tial;
So let them know again; for 'tis a Juſtice,
And a main point of civil policie,
What e're we ſay or ſwear, they being Reprobates,
Out of the ſtate of faith, we are clear of all ſides,
And 'tis a curious blindneſs to believe us.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: You do not mean this ſure?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes ſure, and certain,
And hold it poſitively, as a Principle,
As ye are ſtrange things, and made of ſtrange fires and fluxes,
So we are allow'd as ſtrange wayes to obtain ye,
But not to hold; we are all created Errant.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: You told me other tales.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I not deny it;
I have tales of all ſorts for all ſorts of women,
And proteſtations likewiſe of all ſizes,
As they have vanities to make us coxcombs;
If I obtain a good turn, ſo it is,
I am thankfull for it: if I be made an Aſs,
The mends are in mine own hands, or the Surgeons,
And there's an end on't.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Do not you love me then?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: As I love others, heartily I love thee,
When I am high and luſty, I love thee cruelly:
After I have made a plenteous meal, and ſatisfi'd
My ſenſes with all delicates, come to me,
And thou ſhalt ſee how I love thee.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Will not you marry me?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, certain, no, for any thing I know yet;
I muſt not loſe my liberty, dear Lady,
And like a wanton ſlave cry for more ſhackles.
What ſhould I marry for? Do I want any thing?
Am I an inch the farther from my pleaſure?
Why ſhould I be at charge to keep a wife of mine own,
When other honeſt married men will eaſe me?
And thank me too, and be beholding to me:
Thou thinkſt I am mad for a Maiden-head, thou art cozen'd;
Or if I were addicted to that diet
Can you tell me where I ſhould have one? thou art eighteen now,
And if thou haſt thy Maiden-head yet extant,
Sure 'tis as big as Cods-head: and thoſe grave diſhes
I never love to deal withal: Do'ſt thou ſee this book here?
Look over all theſe ranks; all theſe are women,
Maids, and pretenders to Maiden-heads; theſe are my conqueſts,
All theſe I ſwore to marry, as I ſwore to thee,
With the ſame reſervation, and moſt righteouſly,
Which I need not have done neither; for alas they made no ſcruple,
And I enjoy'd 'em at my will, and left 'em:
Some of 'em are married ſince, and were as pure maids again,
Nay o' my conſcience better than they were bred for;
The reſt fine ſober women.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Are ye not aſham'd, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No by my troth, Sir; there's no ſhame belongs to it;
I hold it as commendable to be wealthy in pleaſure,
As others do in rotten ſheep, and paſture.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Are all my hopes come to this? is there no faith?
No troth? nor modeſty in men?

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: How now Siſter,
Why weeping thus? did I not propheſie?
Come tell me why —

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I am not well; 'pray ye pardon me. Exit.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: Now Monſieur Mirabel, what ails my Siſter?
You have been playing the wag with her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: As I take it,
She is crying for a cod-piece; is ſhe gone?
Lord, what an Age is this! I was calling for ye,
For as I live I thought ſhe would have raviſh'd me.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: Ye are merry Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt this book, de Gard, this Inventory.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: The debt-book of your Miſtreſſes, I remember it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why this was it that anger'd her; ſhe was ſtark mad
She found not her name here, and cry'd down-right,
Becauſe I would not pity her immediately,
And put her in my liſt.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: Sure ſhe had more modeſty.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Their modeſty is anger to be over done;
They'l quarrel ſooner for precedence here,
And take it in more dudgeon to be ſlighted,
Than they will in publique meetings; 'tis their natures:
And alas I have ſo many to diſpatch yet,
And to provide my ſelf for my affairs too,
That in good faith —

sp.speaker: de Gard.
sp.l: Be not too glorious fooliſh;
Summe not your Travels up with vanities,
It ill becomes your expectation:
Temper your ſpeech, Sir; whether your looſe ſtory
Be true, or falſe (for you are ſo free, I fear it)
Name not my Siſter in't; I muſt not hear it;
Upon your danger name her not: I hold her
A Gentlewoman of thoſe happy parts and carriage,
A good mans tongue may be right proud to ſpeak her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Your Siſter, Sir? d'ye blench at that? d'ye cavil?
Do you hold her ſuch a piece, ſhe may not be play'd withal?
I have had an hundred handſomer and nobler,
Have ſu'd to me too for ſuch a courteſie:
Your Siſter comes i'th' rear: ſince ye are ſo angry,
And hold your Siſter ſuch a ſtrong Recuſant,
I tell ye I may do it, and it may be will too,
It may be have too, there's my free confeſſion;
Work upon that now.

sp.speaker: de Gard.
sp.l: If I thought ye had, I would work,
And work ſuch ſtubborn work, ſhould make your heart ake;
But I believe ye, as I ever knew ye,
A glorious talker, and a Legend maker
Of idle tales, and trifles; a depraver
Of your own truth; their honours fly about ye;
And ſo I take my leave, but with this caution,
Your ſword be ſurer than your tongue, you'l ſmart elſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I laugh at thee, ſo little I reſpect thee;
And I'le talk louder, and deſpiſe thy Siſter;
Set up a Chamber-maid that ſhall out-ſhine her,
And carry her in my Coach too, and that will kill her.
Go get thy Rents up, go.

sp.speaker: de Gard.
sp.l: Ye are a fine Gentleman. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Now have at my two youths, I'le ſee how they do,
How they behave themſelves, and then I'le ſtudy
What wench ſhall love me next, and when I'le loſe her. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pinac.
sp.l: Art thou her ſervant, ſaiſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Her poor creature,
But ſervant to her horſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pinac.
sp.l: Canſt thou ſhew me
The way to her chamber? or where I may conveniently
See her, or come to talk to her?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: That I can, Sir;
But the queſtion is whether I will or no.

sp.speaker: Pinac.
sp.l: Why I'le content thee.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why I'le content thee then; now ye come to me.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: There's for your diligence.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: There's her chamber, Sir;
And this way ſhe comes out; ſtand ye but here, Sir,
You have her at your proſpect, or your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Is ſhe not very angry?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You'l find that quickly:
May be ſhe'll call ye ſawcy ſcurvey fellow,
Or ſome ſuch familiar name: 'may be ſhe knows ye,
And will ſling a Piſs-pot at ye, or a Pantofle,
According as ye are in acquaintance: if ſhe like ye,
'May be ſhe'll look upon ye, 'may be no,
And two moneths hence call for ye.

sp.speaker: Pinac.
sp.l: This is fine.
She is monſtrous proud then?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: She is a little haughtie;
Of a ſmall body, ſhe has a mind well mounted.
Can ye ſpeak Greek?

sp.speaker: Pinac.
sp.l: No, certain.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Get ye gone then;
And talk of ſtars, and firmaments, and fire-drakes.
Do you remember who was Adams School-maſter,
And who taught Eve to ſpin? ſhe knows all theſe,
And will run ye over the beginning o'th' world
As familiar as a Fidler.
Can ye ſit ſeven hours together, and ſay nothing?
Which ſhe will do, and when ſhe ſpeaks, ſpeak Oracles;
Speak things that no man underſtands, nor her ſelf neither.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Thou mak'ſt me wonder.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Can ye ſmile?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Yes willingly:
For naturally I bear a mirth about me.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: She'l ne'r endure ye then; ſhe is never merry;
If ſhe ſee one laugh, ſhe'll ſwound paſt Aqua vitae:
Never come near her, Sir; if ye chance to venture,
And talk not like a Doctor, you are damn'd too;
I have told enough for your crown, and ſo good ſpeed ye. Ex.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I have a pretty task, if ſhe be thus curious,
As ſure it ſeems ſhe is; if I fall off now,
I ſhall be laugh'd at fearfully; if I go forward,
I can but be abus'd, and that I look for,
And yet I may hit right, but 'tis unlikely.
Stay, in what mood and figure ſhall I attempt her?
A careleſs way? no, no, that will not waken her;
Beſides, her gravity will give me line ſtill,
And let me loſe my ſelf; yet this way often
Has hit, and handſomly. A wanton method?
I, if ſhe give it leave to ſink into her conſideration;
But there's the doubt: if it but ſtir her blood once,
And creep into the crannies of her phanſie,
Set her a gog: but if ſhe chance to ſlight it,
And by the pow'r of her modeſty fling it back,
I ſhall appear the arrantſt Raſcal to her,
The moſt licentious knave, for I ſhall talk lewdly.
To bear my ſelf auſterely? rate my words,
And fling a general gravitie about me,
As if I meant to give Laws? but this I cannot do,
This is a way above my underſtanding;
Or if I could, 'tis odds ſhe'll think I mock her;
For ſerious and ſad things are ever ſtill ſuſpicious.
Well, I'le ſay ſomething.
But learning I have none, and leſs good manners,
Eſpecially for Ladies; well, I'le ſet my beſt face;
I hear ſome coming; this is the firſt woman
I ever fear'd yet, the firſt face that ſhakes me,

sp.speaker: Li.
sp.l: Give me my hat Petella, take this veil off,
This ſullen cloud, it darkens my delights;
Come wench be free, and let the Muſick warble,
Play me ſome luſty meaſure.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: This is ſhe ſure,
The very ſame I ſaw, the very woman,
The Gravitie I wonder'd at: Stay, ſtay,
Let me be ſure; ne'r truſt me, but ſhe danceth,
Summer is in her face now, and ſhe skippeth:
I'le go a little nearer.

sp.speaker: Li.
sp.l: Quicker time fellows,
I cannot find my legs yet, now Petella.

sp.speaker: Pe.
sp.l: I am amaz'd, I am ſounder'd in my fancies.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Hah, ſay ye ſo; is this your gravitie?
This the auſteritie ye put upon ye?
I'le ſee more o' this ſport.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: A Song now;
Call in for a merry, and a light Song,
And ſing it with a liberal ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Yes, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: And be not amaz'd Sirrah, but take us for your own company.
Let's walk our ſelves: come wench, would we had a man or two.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Sure ſhe has ſpi'd me, and will abuſe me dreadfully,
She has put on this for the purpoſe; yet I will try her.
Madam, I would be loth my rude intruſion,
Which I muſt crave a pardon for —

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: O ye are welcom,
Ye are very welcom, Sir, we want ſuch a one;
Strike up again: I dare preſume ye dance well:
Quick, quick, Sir, quick, the time ſteals on.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I would talk with ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Talk as ye dance.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She'l beat him off his legs firſt,
This is the fineſt Maſque.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Now how do ye, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: You have given me a ſhrewd heat.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: I'le give ye a hundred.
Come ſing now, ſing; for I know ye ſing well,
I ſee ye have a ſinging face.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: A fine Modeſty!
If I could, ſhe'd never give me breath,
Madam would I might ſit and recover.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Sit here, and ſing now,
Let's do things quickly, Sir, and handſomly,
Sit cloſe wench, cloſe, begin, begin. Song.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I am leſſon'd.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: 'Tis very pretty i'faith, give me ſome wine now.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I would fain ſpeak to ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: You ſhall drink firſt, believe me:
Here's to ye a luſty health.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I thank ye Lady,
Would I were off again; I ſmell my miſery;
I was never put to this rack; I ſhall be drunk too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: If thou be'ſt not a right one, I have loſt mine aim much:
I thank Heaven that I have ſcap'd thee; To her Pinac;
For thou art as ſure to have her, and to groan for her—
I'le ſee how my other youth does; this ſpeeds trimly:
A fine grave Gentle woman and worth much honour. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Now? how do ye like me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I like ye rarely.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Ye ſee, Sir, though ſometimes we are grave and ſilent,
And put on ſadder diſpoſitions,
Yet we are compounded of free parts, and ſometimes too
Our lighter, airie, and our fierie mettles
Break out, and ſhew themſelves; and what think you of that Sir?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Good Lady ſit, for I am very weary;
And then I'le tell ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Fie, a young man idle?
Up, and walk; be ſtill in action.
The motions of the body are fair beauties,
Beſides 'tis cold; ods-me Sir, let's walk faſter,
What think ye now of the Lady Felicia?
And Bella fronte the Dukes fair Daughter? ha?
Are they not handſom things? there is Duaria,
And brown Olivia.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I know none of 'em.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: But brown muſt not be caſt away, Sir; if young Lelia
Had kept her ſelf till this day from a Husband,
Why what a Beauty, Sir? you know Iſmena
The fair Iem of Saint Germans?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: By my troth I do not.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: And then I know you muſt hear of Briſac,
How unlike a Gentleman —

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: As I live I have heard nothing.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Strike me another Galliard.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: By this light I cannot;
In troth I have ſprain'd my leg, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Now ſit ye down, Sir,
And tell me why ye came hither, why ye choſe me out?
What is your buſineſs? your errant? diſpatch, diſpatch?
'May be ye are ſome Gentlemans man, and I miſtook ye,
That have brought me a Letter, or a haunch of Veniſon,
Sent me from ſome friend of mine.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Do I look like a Carrier?
You might allow me what I am, a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Cry 'ye mercie, Sir, I ſaw ye yeſterday,
You are new come out of Travel, I miſtook ye;
And how do all our impudent friends in Italie?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Madam, I came with duty, and fair courteſie,
Service, and honour to ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Ye came to jear me:
Ye ſee I am merry, Sir, I have chang'd my copy:
None of the Sages now, and 'pray ye proclaim it,
Fling on me what aſperſion you ſhall pleaſe, Sir,
Of wantonneſs, or wildneſs, I look for it;
And tell the world I am an hypocrite,
Mask in a forc'd and borrow'd ſhape, I expect it;
But not to have you believ'd; for mark ye, Sir,
I have won a nobler eſtimation,
A ſtronger tie by my diſcretion
Upon opinion (how e're you think I forced it)
Than either tongue or art of yours can ſlubber,
And when I pleaſe I will be what I pleaſe, Sir,
So I exceed not Mean; and none ſhall brand it
Either with ſcorn or ſhame, but ſhall be ſlighted.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Lady, I come to love ye.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Love your ſelf, Sir,
And when I want obſervers, I'll ſend for ye:
Heigh, ho; my ſit's almoſt off, for we do all by ſits, Sir:
If ye be weary, ſit till I come again to ye. Exit

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: This is a wench of a dainty ſpirit; but hang me if I know yet
Either what to think, or make of her, ſhe had her will of me,
And baited me abundantly, I thank her,
And I confeſs I never was ſo blurred,
Nor ever ſo abus'd; I muſt bear mine own ſins;
Ye talk of Travels, here's a curious Country,
Yet I will find her out, or forſwear my facultie. Exit.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ne'r vex your ſelf, nor grieve; ye are a fool then.

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: I am ſure I am made ſo: yet before I ſuffer
Thus like a girl, and give him leave to triumph—

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: You ſay right; for as long as he perceives ye
Sink under his proud ſcornings, he'll laugh at ye:
For me ſecure your ſelf; and for my Siſter,
I partly know her mind too: howſoever
To obey my Father we have made a tender
Of our poor beauties to the travel'd Monſieur;
Yet two words to a bargain; he flights us
As skittiſh things, and we ſhun him as curious.
May be my free behaviour turns his ſtomach,
And makes him ſeem to doubt a looſe opinion.
I muſt be ſo ſometimes, though all the world ſaw it.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Why ſhould not ye? Are our minds only meaſur'd?
As long as here ye ſtand ſecure.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye ſay true;
As long as mine own Conſcience makes no queſtion,
What care I for Report? That Woman's miſerable
That's good or bad for their tongues ſake: Come let's retire.
And get my veil Wench: By my troth your ſorrow,
And the conſideration of mens humorous maddings,
Have put me into a ſerious contemplation.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Come 'ſaith, let's ſit, and think.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: That's all my buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why ſtandſt thou peeping here? thou great ſlug, forward.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She is there, peace.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why ſtandſt thou here then,
Sneaking, and peaking, as thou would'd ſteal linnen?
Haſt thou not place and time?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I had a rare ſpeech
Studied, and almoſt ready, and your violence
Has beat it out of my brains.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Hang your rare ſpeeches,
Go me on like a man.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Let me ſet my Beard up.
How has Pinac performed?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: He has won already:
He ſtands not thrumming of caps thus.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Lord, what ſhould I ail?
What a cold I have over my ſtomach; would I had ſome Hum.
Certain I have a great mind to be at her:
A mighty mind.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: On fool.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Good words, I beſeech ye;
For I will not be abuſed by both.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Adieu, then,
I will not trouble you, I ſee you are valiant,
And work your own way.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Hiſt, hiſt, I will be rul'd,
I will 'ſaith, I will go preſently:
Will ye forſake me now and leave me i'th'ſuds?
You know I am falſe-hearted this way; I beſeech ye,
Good ſweet Mirabel; I'le cut your throat if ye leave me,
Indeed I will ſweet heart.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I will be ready,
Still at thine elbow; take a mans heart to thee,
And ſpeak thy mind: the plainer ſtill the better.
She is a woman of that free behaviour,
Indeed that common courteſie, ſhe cannot deny thee;
Go bravely on.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Madam— keep cloſe about me,
Still at my back. Madam, ſweet Madam—

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ha;
What noiſe is that, what ſaucy ſound to trouble me?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What ſaid ſhe?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am ſaucy.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis the better.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She comes; muſt I be ſaucy ſtill?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: More ſaucy.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Still troubled with theſe vanities? Heaven bleſs us;
What are we born to? would ye ſpeak with any of my people?
Go in, Sir, I am buſie.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: This is not ſhe ſure:
Is this two Children at a Birth? I'le be hang'd then:
Mine was a merry Gentlewoman, talkt daintily,
Talkt of thoſe matters that befitted women;
This is a parcel-pray'r-book; I'm ſerv'd ſweetly;
And now I am to look too; I was prepar'd for th' other way.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Do you know that man?

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Sure I have ſeen him, Lady.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Methinks 'tis pity ſuch a luſty fellow
Should wander up and down and want employment.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She takes me for a Rogue: you may do well, Madam,
To ſtay this wanderer, and ſet him a work, forſooth,
He can do ſomething that may pleaſe your Ladiſhip.
I have heard of Women that deſire good breedings,
Two at a birth, or ſo.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: The fellow's impudent.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Sure he is crazed.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I have heard of men too, that have had good manners;
Sure this is want of grace; indeed 'tis great pity
The young man has been bred ſo ill; but this lewd Age
Is full of ſuch examples.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am ſounder'd,
And ſome ſhall rue the ſetting of me on.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ha? ſo bookiſh, Lady, is it poſſible?
Turn'd holy at the heart too? I'le be hang'd then.
Why this is ſuch a feat, ſuch an activity,
Such faſt and looſe: a yeyl too for your Knavery?

l.hi: O dio, dio!

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: What do you take me for, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: An hypocrite, a wanton, a diſſembler,
How e're ye ſeem, and thus ye are to be handled.
Mark me Belleur, and this you love, I know it.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Stand off, bold Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You wear good Cloaths to this end,
Jewels, love Feaſts, and Maſques.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye are monſtrous ſaucy.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: All this to draw on fools? and thus, thus Lady,
Ye are to be lull'd.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Let her alone, I'le ſwinge ye elſe,
I will 'faith; for though I cannot skill o'this matter
My ſelf, I will not ſee another do it before me,
And do it worſe.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Away, ye are a vain thing;
You have travell'd far, Sir, to return again
A windy and poor Bladder: you talk of Women,
That are not worth the favour of a common one;
The grace of her grew in an Hoſpital:
Againſt a thouſand ſuch blown fooleries
I am able to maintain good Womens honours,
Their freedoms, and their fames, and I will do it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She has almoſt ſtruck me dumb too.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And declaim
Againſt your baſe malicious tongues; your noiſes;
For they are nothing elſe: You teach behaviours?
Or touch us for our freedom? teach your ſelves manners,
Truth and ſobriety, and live ſo clearly
That our lives may ſhine in ye; and then task us:
It ſeems ye are hot, the ſuburbs will ſupply ye.
Good Women ſcorn ſuch Gameſters; ſo I'le leave ye,
I am ſorry to ſee this: 'faith Sir, live fairly. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This woman, if ſhe hold on, may be vertuous,
'Tis almoſt poſſible: we'll have a new day.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Ye brought me on, ye forced me to this foolery;
I am aſham'd, I am ſcorn'd, I am flurted; yes, I am ſo:
Though I cannot talk to a woman like your worſhip,
And uſe my phraſes, and my learned figures,
Yet I can fight with any man.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Fie.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I can, Sir,
And I will fight.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: With whom?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: With you, with any man;
For all men now will laugh at me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Prethee be moderate.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: And I'le beat all men. Come.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I love thee dearly.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I beat all that love, Love has undone me;
Never tell me, I will not be a Hiſtory.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou art not.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Sfoot I will not; give me room,
And let me ſee the proudeſt of ye jeer me,
And I'le begin with you firſt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Prethee Belleur;
If I do not ſatisfie thee—

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Well, look ye do:
But now I think on't better, 'tis impoſſible;
I muſt beat ſome body, I am maul'd my ſelf,
And I ought in juſtice—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, no, no, ye are couzen'd;
But walk, and let me talk to thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Talk wiſely,
And ſee that no man laugh upon no occaſion;
For I ſhall think then 'tis at me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Nor no more talk of this.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Do'ſt think I am maddiſh?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I muſt needs fight yet; for I find it concerns me,
A pox on't, I muſt fight.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Faith thou ſhalt not. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter De Gard, and Leverdure, alias Lugier.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: I Know ye are a Scholar, and can do wonders.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: There's no great Scholarſhip belongs to this, Sir;
What I am, I am; I pity your poor Siſter,
And heartily I hate theſe Travellers,
Theſe Gim-cracks, made of Mops, and Motions:
There's nothing in their houſes here but hummings;
A Bee has more brains. I grieve, and vex too
The inſolent licentious carriage
Of this out-facing fellow, Mirabell,
And I am mad to ſee him prick his plumes up.

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: His wrongs you partly know.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Do not you ſtir, Sir,
Since he has begun with wit, let wit revenge it;
Keep your ſword cloſe, we'll cut his throat a new way.
I am aſham'd the Gentlewoman ſhould ſuffer
Such baſe lewd wrongs.

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: I will be rul'd, he ſhall live,
And left to your revenge.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: I, I, I'le fit him:
He makes a common ſcorn of handſome Women;
Modeſty, and good manners are his May-games:
He takes up Maidenheads with a new Commiſſion;
The Church warrant's out of date: follow my Counſel,
For I am zealous in the Cauſe.

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: I will, Sir;
And will be ſtill directed: for the truth is
My Sword will make my Siſter ſeem more monſtrous:
Beſides there is no honour won on Reprobates.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: You are i'th' right: The ſlight he has ſhew'd my Pupils,
Sets me a fire too: go I'le prepare your Siſter,
And as I told ye.

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: Yes all ſhall be fit, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: And ſeriouſly, and handſomely.

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: A little counſel more.

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: 'Tis well.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Moſt ſtately.
See that obſerv'd; and then.

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: I have ye every way.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Away then and be ready.

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: With all ſpeed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: We'll learn to travel too, may be beyond him.
Good day, Fair beauties.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: You have beautified us.
We thank ye, Sir, ye have ſet us off moſt gallantly
With your grave precepts.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We expected Husbands
Out of your Documents, and taught behaviours;
Excellent Husbands, thought men would run ſtark mad on us,
Men of all Ages, and all ſtates: we expected
An Inundation of deſires, and offers,
A Torrent of trim Suitors: all we did,
Or ſaid, or purpos'd to be Spells about us,
Spells to provoke—

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Ye have provoke'd us finely,
We follow'd your directions, we did rarely,
We were Stately, Coy, Demure, Careleſs, Light, Giddy,
And play'd at all points: This you ſwore would carry.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We made Love, and contemn'd Love. Now ſeem'd holy
With ſuch a reverent put-on Reſervation
Which could not miſs according to your Principles,
Now gave more hope again. Now cloſe, now publick,
Still up and down, we beat it like a Billow;
And ever thoſe behaviours you read to us,
Subtil, and new. But all this will not help us.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: They help to hinder us of all Acquaintance,
They have frighted off all Friends: what am I better
For all my Learning, if I love a Dunce,
A handſome dunce? to what uſe ſerves my Reading?
You ſhould have taught me what belongs to Horſes,
Doggs, Dice, Hawks, Banquets, Masks, free and fair Meetings,
To have ſtudied Gowns and Dreſſings.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Ye are not mad ſure.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We ſhall be if we follow your encouragements;
I'le take mine own way now.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: And I my fortune:
We may live Maids elſe till the Moon drop Mil-ſtones;
I ſee your modeſt Women are taken for monſters,
A Dowry of good breeding is worth nothing.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Since ye take it ſo to th' heart, pray'ye give me leave yet,
And ye ſhall ſee how I'le convert this Heretick;
Mark how this Mirabell—

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Name him no more:
For, though I long for a Husband, I hate him,
And would be marryed ſooner to a Monkey,
Or to a Jack of Straw, than ſuch a Juggler.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am of that mind too; he is too nimble,
And plays at faſt and looſe too learnedly
For a plain-meaning Woman; that's the truth on't.
Here's one too, that we love well, would be angry;
And reaſon why: No, no, we will not trouble ye
Nor him, at this time: may he make you happy.
We'll turn our ſelves looſe now, to our fair fortunes,
And the down-right way.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: The winning-way we'll follow,
We'll bait, that men may bite fair, and not be frighted;
Yet we'll not be carryed ſo cheap neither: we'll have ſome ſport,
Some mad-Morris or other for our mony, Tutor.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: 'Tis like enough: proſper your own Devices;
Ye are old enough to chooſe: But for this Gentlewoman,
So pleaſe her, give me leave.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I ſhall be glad, Sir,
To find a friend, whoſe pity may direct me.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: I'le do my beſt, and faithfully deal for ye;
But then ye muſt be ruled.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: In all, I vow to ye.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Do, do: he has a lucky hand ſometimes, I'le aſſure ye:
And hunts the recovery of a loſt Lover deadly.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: You muſt away ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: And I'le inſtruct ye:
Here ye can know no more.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: By your leave, ſweet Ladies,
And all our Fortunes, arrive at our own wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Amen, Amen.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: I muſt borrow your man.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: 'Pray take him;
He is within: to do her good, take any thing,
Take us, and all.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: No doubt ye may find Takers;
And ſo we'll leave ye to your own diſpoſes. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Now which way, Wench.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We'll go a brave way; fear not:
A ſafe, and ſure way too: and yet a by-way,
I muſt confeſs I have a great mind to be married.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: So have I too, a grudging of good-will that way;
And would as fain be diſpatch'd. But this Monſieur Quickſilver.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: No, no: we'll bar him, by, and Main: Let him trample;
There is no ſafety in his Surquedrie:
An Army-Royal of women, are too few for him,
He keeps a Journal of his Gentleneſs,
And will go near to print his fair diſpatches,
And call it his triumph over time and women:
Let him paſs out of memory: what think ye
Of his two Companions?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Pinac methinks is reaſonable;
A little modeſtie he has brought home with him,
And might be taught in time ſome handſom duty.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: They ſay he is a wencher too.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I like him better:
A free light touch or two becomes a Gentleman,
And ſets him ſeemly off: ſo he exceed not,
But keep his compaſs, clear he may be lookt at;
I would not marry a man that muſt be taught,
And conjur'd up with kiſſes; the beſt game
Is plaid ſtill by the beſt Gameſters.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Fie upon thee!
What talk haſt thou?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Are not we alone, and merry?
Why ſhould we be aſham'd to ſpeak what we think? thy Gentleman
The tall fat fellow; he that came to ſee thee.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Is't not a goodly man?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: A wondrous goodly!
H'as weight enough I warrant thee: Mercy upon me;
What a Serpent wilt thou ſeem under ſuch a S. George.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Thou art a fool; give me a man brings Mettle,
Brings ſubſtance with him; needs no Broths to Lare him:
Theſe little fellows ſhew like Fleas in boxes,
Hop up and down, and keep a ſtir to vex us;
Give me the puiſſant Pike, take you the ſmall ſhot.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Of a great thing I have not ſeen a duller,
Therefore methinks, ſweet Siſter —

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Peace: he's modeſt:
A baſhfulneſs, which is a point of grace, wench:
But when theſe fellows come to moulding, Siſter,
To heat, and handling: as I live, I like him;
And methinks I could form him.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Peace: the Fire-drake.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Bleſs ye ſweet beauties: ſweet incomparable Ladies:
Sweet wits: ſweet humours: 'Bleſs you, learned Lady,
And you, moſt holy Nun; 'Bleſs your Devotions.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: And 'bleſs your brains, Sir, your moſt pregnant brains, Sir,
They are in Travel, may they be delivered
Of a moſt hopeful Wild-Gooſe.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: 'Bleſs your manhood:
They ſay ye are a Gentleman of action,
A fair accompliſh'd man; and a rare Engineer,
You have a trick to blow up Maidenheads,
A ſubtle trick, they ſay abroad.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I have Lady.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And often glory in their Ruines.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes forſooth;
I have a ſpeedy trick: pleaſe you to try it:
My Engine will diſpatch ye inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I would I were a woman, Sir, fit for ye,
As there be ſuch, no doubt, may Engine you too;
May with a Counter-mine blow up your valour:
But in good faith, Sir, we are both too honeſt:
And the plague is, we can not be perſwaded:
For, look ye: if we thought it were a glory
To be the laſt of all your lovely Ladies.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come, come; leave prating: this has ſpoil'd your Market;
This pride, and pufft-up heart, will make ye faſt, Ladies,
Faſt, when ye are hungry too.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: The more our pain, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: The more our health, I hope too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Your behaviours
Have made men ſtand amaz'd; thoſe men that lov'd ye;
Men of fair States and parts; your ſtrange conventions
Into I know not what, nor how, nor wherefore;
Your ſcorns of thoſe that came to viſit ye;
Your ſtudied Whim-whams; and your fine ſet faces:
What have theſe got ye? proud, and harſh opinions;
A Travel'd-Monſieur, was the ſtrangeſt Creature,
The wildeſt Monſter to be wondred at:
His Perſon made a publique Scoff, his knowledge,
(As if he had been bred 'mongſt Bears or Bandoggs)
Shunn'd and avoided: his converſation ſnuft at.
What Harveſt brings all this?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I pray ye proceed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Now ye ſhall ſee in what eſteem a Traveller,
An underſtanding Gentleman, and a Monſieur
Is to be held, and to your griefs confeſs it,
Both to your griefs, and galls.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: In what I pray ye, Sir?
We would be glad to underſtand your excellence.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Goe on, (ſweet Ladies) it becomes ye rarely.
For me, I have bleſt me from ye, ſcoff on ſeriouſly,
And note the Man ye mock'd: you, (Lady Learning)
Note the poor Traveller, that came to viſit ye,
That flat unfurniſh'd fellow: note him throughly,
You may chance to ſee him anon.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Tis very likely.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And ſee him Courted by a Travell'd Lady,
Held dear, and honour'd by a vertuous virgin,
May be a Beautie, not far ſhort of yours, neither
It may be, clearer.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Not unlikely.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Younger:
As killing eyes as yours: a wit as poynant
May be, a State to that may top your Fortune;
Enquire how ſhe thinks of him, how ſhe holds him;
His good parts; in what precious price already;
Being a ſtranger to him, how ſhe courts him;
A ſtranger to his Nation too, how ſhe dotes on him:
Enquire of this; be ſick to know: Curſe, Lady,
And keep your chamber: cry, and curſe: a ſweet one,
A thouſand in yearly land; well bred; well friended:
Travell'd, and highly followed for her faſhions.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Bleſs his good fortune, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This ſcurvy fellow;
I think they call his name Pinac; this ſerving-man
That brought ye Veniſon, as I take it, Madam;
Note but this Scab; 'tis ſtrange that this courſe creature,
That has no more ſet off, but his jugglings,
His travell'd tricks.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Good, Sir, I grieve not at him,
Nor envy not his fortune: yet I wonder,
He's handſom; yet I ſee no ſuch perfection.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Would I had his fortune: for 'tis a woman
Of that ſweet temper'd nature, and that judgment,
Beſides her ſtate, that care, clear underſtanding,
And ſuch a wife to bleſs him.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Pray ye whence is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Of England, and a moſt accompliſh'd Lady,
So modeſt that mens eyes are frighted at her,
And ſuch a noble carriage. How now Sirrah?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Sir, the great Engliſh Lady.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What of her, Sir?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Has newly left her coach, and coming this way,
Where you may ſee her plain: Monſieur Pinac,
The only man that leads her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: He is much honored;
Would I had ſuch a favour: now vex Ladies,
Envy, and vex, and rail.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye are ſhort of us, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Bleſs your fair fortune, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I nobly thank ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is ſhe married, friend?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: No, no.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A goodly Lady;
A ſweet and delicate aſpect: mark, mark, and wonder!
Haſt thou any hope of her?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: A little.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Follow cloſe then:
Loſe not that hope.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: To you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Gentle Lady.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: She is fair indeed.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I have ſeen a fairer, yet
She is well.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Her clothes fit handſom too.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: She dreſſes prettily.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And by my faith ſhe is rich, ſhe looks ſtill ſweeter.
A well bred woman, I warrant her.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Do you hear, Sir;
May I crave this Gentlewomans name?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Mariana, Lady.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I will not ſay I ow ye a quarel Monſieur
For making me your Stale: a noble Gentleman
Would have had more courteſie; at leaſt, more faith,
Than to turn off his Miſtris at firſt trial:
You know not what reſpect I might have ſhew'd ye;
I find ye have worth.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I cannot ſtay to anſwer ye;
Ye ſee my charge: I am beholding to ye
For all your merry tricks ye put upon me,
Your bobs, and baſe accounts: I came to love ye,
To wooe ye, and to ſerve ye; I am much indebted to ye
For dancing me off my legs; and then for walking me;
For telling me ſtrange tales I never heard of,
More to abuſe me; for miſtaking me,
When ye both knew I was a Gentleman,
And one deſerv'd as rich a match as you are.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Be not ſo bitter, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: You ſee this Lady:
She is young enough, and fair enough to pleaſe me,
A woman of a loving mind, a quiet,
And one that weighs the worth of him that loves her,
I am content with this, and bleſs my fortune,
Your curious Wits, and Beauties.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Faith ſee me once more.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I dare not trouble ye.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: May I ſpeak to your Lady?

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: I pray ye content your ſelf: I know ye are bitter,
And in your bitterneſs, ye may abuſe her;
Which if ſhe comes to know, (for ſhe underſtands ye not)
It may breed ſuch a quarrel to your kindred,
And ſuch an indiſcretion fling on you too;
For ſhe is nobly friended.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I could eat her.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Reſt as ye are, a modeſt noble Gentlewoman,
And afford your honeſt neighbours ſome of your prayers. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What think you now?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Faith ſhe's a pretty Whiting;
She has got a pretty catch too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You are angry;
Monſtrous angry now; grievouſly angry;
And the pretty heart does ſwell now.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No in troth, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And it will cry anon; a pox upon it:
And it will curſe it ſelf: and eat no meat, Lady;
And it will fight.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Indeed you are miſtaken;
It will be very merry.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Why, Sir, do you think
There are no more men living, nor no handſomer
Than he, or you, By this light there be ten thouſand?
Ten thouſand thouſand: comfort your ſelf, dear Monſieur,
Faces, and bodies, Wits, and all Abiliments
There are ſo many we regard 'em not.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That ſuch a noble Lady, I could burſt now,
So far above ſuch trifles?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You did laugh at me,
And I know why ye laughed.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I pray ye be ſatisfied;
If we did laugh, we had ſome private reaſon,
And not at you.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Alas, we know you not, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'le make you know me; ſet your faces ſoberly;
Stand this way, and look ſad; I'le be no May-game;
Sadder; demurer yet.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: What's the matter?
What ails this Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Bel
sp.l: Go off now backward, that I may behold ye;
And not a ſimper on your lives.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: He's mad ſure.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Do you obſerve me too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I may look on ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Why do you grin? I know your minde.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You do not,
You are ſtrangely humorous: is there no mirth, nor pleaſure,
But you muſt be the object?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Mark, and obſerve me;
Where ever I am nam'd;
The very word ſhall raiſe a general ſadneſs,
For the diſgrace this ſcurvy woman did me;
This proud pert thing; take heed ye laugh not at me;
Provoke me not, take heed.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I would fain pleaſe ye;
Do any thing to keep ye quiet.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Hear me,
Till I receive a ſatisfaction
Equal to the diſgrace, and ſcorn ye gave me:
Ye are a wretched woman; till thou woo'ſt me,
And I ſcorn thee aſmuch, as ſeriouſly
Jear, and abuſe thee; ask what Gill thou art;
Or any baſer name; I will proclaim thee;
I will ſo ſing thy vertue; ſo be-paint thee.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Nay, good Sir, be more modeſt.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Do you laugh again?
Becauſe ye are a woman ye are lawleſs,
And out of compaſs of an honeſt anger.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Good Sir, have a better belief of me.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Away dear Siſter. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is not this better now, this ſeeming madneſs,
Than falling out with your friends?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Have I not frighted her?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Into her right wits, I warrant thee: follow this humor,
And thou ſhalt ſee how proſperouſly 'twill guide thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am glad I have found a way to woo yet, I was afraid once
I never ſhould have made a civil Suiter.
Well, I'le about it ſtill. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Do, do, and proſper.
What ſport do I make with theſe fools? What pleaſure
Feeds me, and fats my ſides at their poor innocence?
sp.stage: Enter Leverduce, alias Lugier, Mr. Illiard.
sp.l: Wooing and wiving, hang it: give me mirth,
Witty and dainty mirth: I ſhall grow in love ſure
With mine own happy head. Who's this? To me, Sir?
What youth is this?

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, I would ſpeak with you,
If your name be Monſieur Mirabel.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ye have hit it,
Your buſineſs, I beſeech ye?

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.l: This it is, Sir,
There is a Gentlewoman hath long time affected ye,
And lov'd ye dearly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Turn over, and end that ſtory,
'Tis long enough: I have no faith in women, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo, Sir: I do not come to woo for her,
Or ſing her praiſes, though ſhe well deſerve 'em,
I come to tell ye, ye have been cruel to her,
Unkind and cruel, falſer of faith, and careleſs,
Taking more pleaſure in abuſing her,
Wreſting her honour to your wild diſpoſes,
Than noble in requiting her affection:
Which, as ye are a man, I muſt deſire ye
(A Gentleman of rank) not to perſiſt in,
No more to load her fair name with your injuries.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why, I beſeech ye, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.l: Good Sir, I'le tell ye,
And I'le be ſhort: I'le tell ye, becauſe I love ye,
Becauſe I would have you ſhun the ſhame may follow:
There is a noble man, new come to Town, Sir,
A noble and a great man that affects her,
A Coutrey-man of mine, a brave Savoyan,
Nephew to th'Duke, and ſo much honours her,
That 'twill be dangerous to purſue your old way,
To touch at any thing concerns her honour,
Believe, moſt dangerous: her name is Oriana,
And this great man will marry her: take heed, Sir;
For howſoe'r her Brother, a ſtaid Gentleman,
Lets things paſs upon better hopes, this Lord, Sir,
Is of that fiery, and that poynant metal,
(Eſpecially provok'd on by affection)
That 'twill be hard: but you are wiſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A Lord, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.l: Yes, and a noble Lord.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Send her good fortune,
This will not ſtir her Lord; a Barronneſs,
Say ye ſo; ſay ye ſo? by'r Lady, a brave title;
Top, and top gallant now; 'ſave her great Ladiſhip.
I was a poor ſervant of hers, I muſt confeſs, Sir,
And in thoſe daies, I thought I might be jovy,
And make a little bold to call into her:
But Baſto, now; I know my rules and diſtance;
Yet, if ſhe want an Uſher: ſuch an implement;
One that is throughly pac'd; a clean made Gentleman;
Can hold a hanging up; with approbation
Plant his hat formally, and wait with patience
I do beſeech you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.l: Sir, leave your ſcoffing;
And as ye are a Gentleman, deal fairly:
I have given ye a friends counſel, ſo I'le leave ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: But hark ye, hark ye, Sir; is't poſſible
I may believe what you ſay?

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.l: You may chuſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No Baits? No Fiſh-hooks, Sir? No Gins? No Nooſes?
No Pitfals to catch Puppies?

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.l: I tell ye certain;
You may believe; if not, ſtand to the danger. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A Lord of Savoy ſaies he? The Dukes Nephew?
A man ſo mighty? By 'Lady a fair marriage;
By my faith, a handſom fortune: I muſt leave prating;
For to confeſs the truth, I have abuſed her,
For which I ſhould be ſorry, but that will ſeem ſcurvy;
I muſt confeſs, ſhe was ever ſince I knew her
As modeſt, as ſhe was fair: I am ſure ſhe lov'd me;
Her means good; and her breeding excellent;
And for my ſake ſhe has refus'd fair matches:
I may play the fool finely. Stay who are theſe?
'Tis ſhe, I am ſure; and that the Lord it ſhould ſeem,
He carries a fair Port; is a handſom man too:
I do begin to feel, I am a Coxcomb.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Good my Lord, chuſe a nobler: for I know
I am ſo far below your rank and honour,
That what ye can ſay this way, I muſt credit
But ſpoken to beget your ſelf ſport: Alas, Sir,
I am ſo far off from deſerving you,
My beauty ſo unfit for your Affection,
That I am grown the ſcorn of common Railers,
Of ſuch injurious things, that when they cannot
Reach at my perſon, he with my reputation:
I am poor beſides.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: Ye are all wealth and goodneſs;
And none but ſuch as are the ſcum of men,
The Ulcers of an honeſt ſtate; Spight-weavers,
That live on poyſon only, like ſwoln ſpiders,
Dare once profane ſuch excellence, ſuch ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This man ſpeaks loud indeed.

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: Name but the men, Lady;
Let me but know theſe poor, and baſe depravers;
Lay but to my revenge their perſons open,
And you ſhall ſee how ſuddenly, how fully
For your moſt beauteous ſake, how direfully
I'le handle their deſpights. Is this thing one?
Be what he will.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: Dare your malicious tongue, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I know you not; nor what you mean.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Good my Lord.

sp.speaker: de Ga.
sp.l: If he, or any he.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I beſeech your honour.
This Gentleman's a ſtranger to my knowledge,
And no doubt, Sir, a worthy man.

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: Your mercy;
But had he been a tainter of your honour;
A blaſter of thoſe beauties raign within ye;
But we ſhall find a fitter time: dear Lady,
As ſoon as I have freed ye from your Guardian,
And done ſome honour'd offices unto ye,
I'le take ye with thoſe faults the world flings on ye;
And dearer than the whole world I'le eſteem ye. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This is a thundring Lord; I am glad I ſcap'd him:
How lovingly the wench diſclaim'd my villany?
I am vext now heartily that he ſhall have her;
Not that I care to marry, or to loſe her;
But that this Bilbo-Lord ſhall reap that Maiden-head
That was my due; that he ſhall rig and top her;
I'de give a thouſand Crowns now, he might miſs her.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Nay, if I bear your blows, and keep your counſel, you have good luck, Sir; I'le teach ye to ſtrike lighter.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come hither, honeſt fellow; canſt thou tell me
Where this great Lord lies? This Savoy Lord? Thou met'ſt him;
He now went by thee certain.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes, he did, Sir;
I know him; and I know you are fool'd.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come hither,
Here's all this, give me truth.

sp.speaker: Sir.
sp.l: Not for your mony;
(And yet that may do much) but I have been beaten:
And by the worſhipfull Contrivers beaten, and I'le tell ye;
This is no Lord, no Savoy Lord.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Go forward.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: This is a Trick, and put upon ye groſly
By one Lugier; the Lord is Monſieur de-Gard, Sir;
An honeſt Gentleman, and a neighbour here;
Their ends you underſtand better than I, ſure.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Now I know him.
Know him now plain.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I have diſcharg'd my colours; ſo God b'y ye, ſir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What a purblinde Puppy was I; now I remember him.
All the whole caſt on's face, though 'twere umber'd,
And mask'd with patches: what a dunder-whelp
To let him domineer thus: how he ſtrutted,
And what a load of Lord he clapt upon him?
Would I had him here again, I would ſo bounce him,
I would ſo thank his Lordſhip for his lewd plot:
Do they think to carry it away, with a great band made of bird-pots.
And a pair of pin-buttockt breeches? Ha! 'Tis he again
He comes, he comes, he comes; have at him.

sp.speaker: Sings.
sp.l: My Savoy Lord, why doſt thou frown on me?
And will that ſavour never ſweeter be?
Wilt thou I ſay, for ever play the fool?
de Gard be wiſe, and Savoy go to School.
My Lord de Gard, I thank ye for your Antick;
My Lady bright, that will be ſometimes Frantick;
You worthy Train, that wait upon this Pair,
'Send you more wit, and they a bouncing Baire
And ſo I take my humble leave of your honours. Exit.

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: We are diſcover'd, there's no remedy
Lelia Biancha's man upon my life,
In ſtubbornneſs, becauſe Lugier corrected him.
(A ſhameleſs ſlaves plague on him for a Raſcal.)

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I was in a perfect hope; the bane on't is now,
He will make mirth on mirth, to perſecute us.

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: We muſt be patient; I am vext to the proof too,
I'le try once more; then if I ſail: Here's one ſpeaks.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Let me be loſt, and ſcorn'd firſt.

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: Well, we'll conſider,
Away, and let me ſhift; I ſhall be hooted elſe.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: FAint not; but do as I direct ye, truſt me;
Believe me too, for what I have told ye, Lady,
As true as you are Lelia, is Authentick;
I know it, I have found it; 'tis a poor courage
Flies off for one repulſe; theſe Travellers
Shall find before we have done, a home-ſpun wit,
A plain French underſtanding may cope with 'em;
They have had the better yet, thank your ſweet Squire, here;
And let 'em brag: you would be reveng'd?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Yes ſurely.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: And married too?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Then be Counſel'd,
You know how to proceed: I have other Irons
Heating as well as yours: and I will ſtrike
Three blows with one Stone home, be rul'd, and happie;
And ſo I leave ye. Now is the time.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I am ready,
If he do come to do me.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Will ye ſtand here,
And let the people think, ye are God knows what Miſtris?
Let Boys, and Prentices preſume upon ye?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Pre'thee hold thy peace.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Stand at his dore, that hates ye?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Pre'thee leave prating,

sp.speaker: Sir.
sp.l: 'Pray ye go to th' Tavern. I'le give ye a Pint of wine there,
If any of the Mad-cap Gentlemen ſhould come by
That take up women upon ſpeciall warrant,
You were in a wiſe caſe now.

div.stage: Enter Mirabel, Pinac, Mariana, Prieſt, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Give me the Garland,
And wait you here.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She is here to ſeek thee, Sirrah.
I told thee what would follow, ſhe is mad for thee;
Shew, and advance. So early ſtirring Lady?
It ſhews a buſie mind, a fancie troubled:
A willow Garland too? Is't poſſible?
'Tis pity ſo much beautie ſhould lie muſtie,
But 'tis not to be help'd now.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: The more's my Miſerie.
Good fortune to ye, Ladie, you deſerve it:
To me, too late Repentance; I have ſought it:
I do not envy, though I grieve a little,
You are Miſtris of that happineſs, thoſe Joyes
That might have been, had I been wiſe • but fortune.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: She underſtands ye not, 'pray ye do not trouble her;
And do not croſs me like a Hare thus, 'tis as ominous.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I come not to upbraid your Levitie
Though ye made ſhew of Love, and though I lik'd ye
To claim an intereſt; we are yet both Strangers,
But what we might have been, had you perſever'd, Sir,
To be an eye-ſore to your loving Lady;
This garland ſhews, I give my ſelf forſaken;
(Yet ſhe muſt pardon me, 'tis moſt unwillingly:)
And all the power and intereſt I had in ye;
As I perſwade my ſelf, ſomewhat ye lov'd me;
Thus patiently I render up, I offer
To her that muſt enjoy ye: and ſo bleſs ye;
Only, I heartily deſire this Courteſie,
And would not be deni'd: to wait upon ye
This day, to ſee ye ty'd, then no more trouble ye.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: It needs not, Ladie.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Good Sir, grant me ſo much.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: 'Tis private, and we make no invitation.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: My preſence, Sir, ſhall not proclaim it publick.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: May be 'tis not in Town.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I have a Coach, Sir,
And a moſt ready will to do you ſervice.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Strike now or never; make it ſure: I tell thee,
She will hang her ſelf, if ſhe have thee not.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: 'Pray ye, Sir,
Entertain my noble Miſtris: only a word or two
With this importunate woman, and I'le relieve ye.
Now ye ſee what your ſlings are, and your fancies,
Your ſtates, and your wild ſtubborneſs, now ye mind
What 'tis to gird and kick at mens fair ſervices,
To raiſe your pride to ſuch a pitch, and glory
That goodneſs ſhews like gnats, ſcorn'd under ye,
'Tis ugly, naught, a ſelf will in a woman,
Chain'd to an over-weening thought, is peſtilent,
Murthers fair fortune firſt; then fair opinion:
There ſtands a Pattern, a true patient Pattern,
Humble, and ſweet.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I can but grieve my ignorance,
Repentance ſome ſay too, is the beſt ſacrifice;
For ſure, Sir, if my chance had been ſo happy,
(As I confeſs I was mine own deſtroyer)
As to have arrived at you; I will not propheſie,
But certain, as I think, I ſhould have pleas'd ye;
Have made ye as much wonder at my courteſie,
My love, and duty, as I have diſhearten'd ye,
Some hours we have of youth, and ſome of folly;
And being free-born Maids, we take a liberty,
And to maintain that, ſometimes we ſtrain highly.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Now ye talk reaſon.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: But being yoak'd, and govern'd,
Married, and thoſe light vanities purg'd from us;
How fair we grow, how gentle, and how tender,
We twine about thoſe loves that ſhoot-up with us?
A ſullen woman fear, that talks not to ye;
She has a ſad and darkn'd ſoul, loves dully:
A merry and a free wench, give her liberty;
Believe her in the lighteſt form ſhe appears to ye,
Believe her excellent, though ſhe deſpiſe ye,
Let but theſe fits and flaſhes paſs, ſhe will ſhew to ye;
As Jewels rub'd from duſt, or Gold new burniſh'd:
Such had I been, had you believ'd.

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: And to your happineſs, I dare aſſure ye
If True love be accounted ſo; your pleaſure,
Your will, and your command had tyed my Motions:
But that hope's gone; I know you are young, and giddy,
And till you have a Wife can govern with ye,
You ſail upon this wold-Sea, light and empty;
Your Bark in danger daily; 'tis not the name neither
Of Wife can ſteer ye; but the noble nature,
The diligence, the care, the love, the patience,
She makes the Pilot, and preſerves the Husband,
That knows, and reckons every Rib he is built on;
But this I tell ye, to my ſhame.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: I admire ye,
And now am ſorry, that I aim beyond ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: So, ſo, ſo, fair and ſoftly. She is thine own, Boy,
She comes now, without Lure.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: But that it muſt needs
Be reckon'd to me as a wantonneſs,
Or worſe, a madneſs, to forſake a Bleſſing,
A Bleſſing of that hope.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I dare not urge ye,
And yet, dear Sir.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt certain, I had rather,
If 'twere in my own choice, for you are my country-woman,
A Neighbour, here born by me, ſhe a Stranger;
And who knows how her friends?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Do as you pleaſe, Sir,
If ye be faſt; not all the World; I love ye,
'Tis moſt true, and clear, I would perſwade ye;
And I ſhall love you ſtill.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Go, get before me;
So much you have won upon me; do it preſently:
Here's a Prieſt ready; I'll have you.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Not now, Sir,
No, you ſhall pardon me; advance your Lady,
I dare not hinder your moſt high Preferment,
'Tis honour enough for me I have unmask'd ye.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: How's that?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I have caught ye, Sir, alas, I am no States-woman,
Nor no great Traveller, yet I have found ye,
I have found your Lady too, your beauteous Lady;
I have found her birth and breeding too, her diſcipline;
Who brought her over, and who kept your Lady;
And when he laid her by, what vertuous Nunnery
Receiv'd her in; I have found all theſe: are ye blank now?
Methinks ſuch travel'd wiſdoms ſhould not fool thus;
Such excellent indiſcretions.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How could ſhe know this?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Tis true, ſhe's Engliſh born, but moſt part French now,
And ſo I hope you'll find her, to your comfort,
Alas, I am ignorant of what ſhe coſt ye;
The price of theſe hired cloaths I do not know Gentlemen;
Thoſe Jewels are the Brokers, how ye ſtand bound for 'em.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Will you make this good?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Yes, yes, and to her face, Sir,
That ſhe is an Engllſh Whore, a kind of fling duſt,
One of your London Light o' Loves; a right one,
Came over in thin Pumps, and half a Petticoat,
One Faith, and one Smock, with a broken Haberdaſher;
I know all this without a Conjurer;
Her name is jumping Joan, an ancient Sin-Weaver;
She was firſt a Ladies Chamber-maid, there ſlip'd
And broke her leg above the knee; departed
And ſet up ſhop her ſelf. Stood the fierce Conflicts
Of many a furious Term; there loſt her colours,
And laſt ſhip'd over hither.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: We are betray'd.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Do you come to fright me with this myſtery?
To ſtir me with a ſtink none can endure, Sir?
I pray ye proceed, the Wedding will become ye;
Who gives the Lady? you? an excellent Father;
A careful man, and one that knows a Beauty,
'Send ye fair Shipping, Sir, and ſo I'll leave ye,
Be wiſe and manly, then I may chance to love ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: As I live I am aſham'd, this wench has reach'd me,
Monſtrous aſham'd, but there's no remedy,
This skew'd eye'd Carrion.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: This I ſuſpected ever,
Come, come, uncaſe, we have no more uſe of ye;
Your Cloaths muſt back again.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir, ye ſhall pardon me;
'Tis not our Engliſh uſe to be degraded;
If you will viſit me, and take your venture,
You ſhall have pleaſure for your properties;
And ſo ſweet heart.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Let her go, and the Devil go with her;
We have never better luck with theſe preludiums;
Come, be not daunted; think ſhe is but a woman,
And let her have the Devils wit, we'll reach her.

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye have now redeem'd my good opinion, Tutor,
And ye ſtand fair again.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: I can but labour,
And ſweat in your affairs; I am ſure Belleur
Will be here inſtantly, and uſe his anger,
His wonted harſhneſs.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I hope he will not beat me.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: No ſure, he has more manners; be you ready.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes, yes, I am, and am reſolv'd to ſit him,
With patience to outdo all he can offer;
But how does Oriana?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Worſe, and worſe ſtill;
There is a ſad houſe for her: ſhe is now,
Poor Lady, utterly diſtracted.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Pity!
Infinite pity! 'tis a handſome Lady,
That Mirabel's a Beaſt, worſe than a Monſter,
If this affliction work not.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Are ye ready?
Belleur is coming on, here, hard behind me,
I have no leiſure to relate my Fortune.
Only I wiſh you may come off as handſomely,
Upon the ſign you know what. Exit.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Well, well, leave me.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How now?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye are welcome, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis well ye have manners:
That Court'ſie again, and hold your Countenance ſtai'dly;
That look's too light; take heed: ſo, ſit ye down now,
And to confirm me that your Gall is gone,
Your bitterneſs diſpers'd, for ſo I'll have it:
Look on me ſtedfaſtly, and whatſoe'r I ſay unto ye,
Move not, nor alter in your face, ye are gone then:
For if you do expreſs the leaſt diſtaſte,
Or ſhew an angry wrinkle, mark me, woman,
We are now alone, I will ſo conjure thee;
The third part of my Execution
Cannot be ſpoke.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am at your diſpoſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Now riſe, and woo me a little, let me hear that faculty:
But touch me not, nor do not lie I charge ye.
Begin now.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: If ſo mean and poor a Beauty
May ever hope the Grace.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Ye cog, ye flatter,
Like a lewd thing ye lie: may hope that grace?
Why, what grace canſt thou hope for? Anſwer not,
For if thou doſt, and lieſt again I'll ſwindge thee:
Do not I know thee for a peſtilent Woman?
A proud at both ends? Be not angry,
Nor ſtir not o' your life.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am counſell'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Art thou not now (confeſs, for I'll have the truth out)
As much unworthy of a man of merit,
Or any of ye all? Nay, of meer man?
Though he were crooked, cold, all wants upon him:
Nay, of any diſhoneſt thing that bears that figure:
As Devils are of mercy?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We are unworthy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Stick to that truth, and it may chance to ſave thee.
And is it not our bounty that we take ye?
That we are troubled, vex'd, or tortur'd with ye?
Our meer and ſpecial bounty?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Our pity,
That for your wickedneſs we ſwindge ye ſoundly;
Your ſtubbornneſs, and your ſtout hearts, we be-labour ye,
Anſwer to that.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I do confeſs your pity.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: And doſt not thou deſerve in thine own perſon?
(Thou Impudent, thou Pert; do not change countenance.)

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I dare not, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: For if ye do.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am ſetled.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Thou Wag-tail, Peacock, Puppy, look on me:
I am a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: It ſeems no leſs, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: And dareſt thou in thy Surquedry?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I beſeech ye;
It was my weakneſs, Sir, I did not view ye,
I took no notice of your noble parts,
Nor call'd your perſon, nor your proper faſhion.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: This is ſome amends yet.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I ſhall mend, Sir, daily,
And ſtudy to deſerve.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Come a little nearer;
Canſt thou repent thy villainy?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Moſt ſeriouſly.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: And be aſham'd?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I am aſham'd.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Cry.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: It will be hard to do, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Cry inſtantly;
Cry monſtrouſly, that all the Town may hear thee;
Cry ſeriouſly, as if thou hadſt loſt thy Monkey;
And as I like thy tears.

div.stage: Enter Lelia, and four Women laughing.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Now.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How? how? do ye jear me?
Have ye broke your bounds again, Dame?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes, and laugh at ye,
And laugh moſt heartily.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: What are theſe, Whirl-winds?
• s Hell broke looſe, and all the Furies flutter'd?
Am I greas'd once again?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes indeed are ye;
And once again ye ſhall be, if ye quarrel,
Do you come to vent your ſury on a Virgin?
• s this your Manhood, Sir?

sp.speaker: 1 Wom.
sp.l: Let him do his beſt,
Let's ſee the utmoſt of his indignation,
I long to ſee him angry; Come, proceed, Sir.
Hang him, he dares not ſtir, a man of Timber.

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: Come hither to fright maids with thy Bul ſaces?
To threaten Gentlewomen? Thou a man? A May pole,
A great dry Pudding.

sp.speaker: 2 Wom.
sp.l: Come, come, do your worſt, Sir;
Be angry if thou darſt.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: The Lord deliver me!

sp.speaker: 4 Wom.
sp.l: Do but look ſcurvily upon this Lady,
Or give us one foul word. We are all miſtaken,
This is ſome mighty Dairy-maid in Mans Cloaths.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: I am of that mind too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: What will they do to me!

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: And hired to come and abuſe us; a man has manners;
A Gentleman, Civility, and Breeding:
Some Tinkers Trull, with a Beard glew'd on.

sp.speaker: 1 Wom.
sp.l: Let's ſearch him;
And as we find him.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Let me but depart from ye,
Sweet Chriſtian-women.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: Hear the Thing ſpeak, Neighbours.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis but a ſmall requeſt; if e'r I trouble ye,
If e'r I talk again of beating Women,
Or beating any thing that can but turn to me;
Of ever thinking of a handſome Lady
But vertuouſly and well; of ever ſpeaking
But to her honour; This I'll promiſe ye,
I will take Rhubarb, and purge Choler mainly,
Abundantly I'll purge.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.l: I'll ſend ye Broths, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I will be laugh'd at, and endure it patiently,
I will do any thing.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I'll be your Bayl then;
When ye come next to woo, 'pray come not boiſterouſly,
And furniſh'd like a Bear-ward.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No in truth, forſooth.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I ſcented ye long ſince.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I was to blame ſure,
I will appear a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: 'Tis the beſt for ye,
For a true noble Gentleman's a brave thing;
Upon that hope we quit ye. You fear ſeriouſly?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes truly do I; I confeſs I fear ye,
And honour ye, and any thing.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Farewel then.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: And when ye come to woo next bring more mercy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: A Dairy-maid! a Tinkers-Trull! Heaven bleſs me!
Sure if I had provok'd 'em, they had quarter'd me.
I am a moſt ridiculous Aſs, now I perceive it:
A Coward, and a Knave too.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis the mad Gentleman:
Let's ſet our Faces right.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No, no, laugh at me;
And laugh aloud.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: We are better manner'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I do deſerve it; call me Patch, and Puppy,
And beat me if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: No indeed, we know ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Death, do as I would have ye.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: You are an Aſs then;
A Coxcomb, and a Calf.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am a great Calf;
Kick me a little now: Why, when? Sufficient:
Now laugh aloud, and ſcorn me; ſo good b'ye;
And ever when ye meet me laugh.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: We will, Sir. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Enter Nantolet, La-Caſtre, De-Gard, Lugier, Mirabel.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Your patience, Gentlemen: why do ye bait me?

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.l: Is't not a ſhame you are ſo ſtubborn hearted,
So ſtony and ſo dull to ſuch a Lady,
Of her Perfections, and her Miſery?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Does ſhe not love ye? does not her diſtraction
For your ſake only, her moſt pitied lunacie
Of all but you, ſhew ye? does it not compel ye?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Soft and fair, Gentlemen, pray ye proceed temperately.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: If ye have any feeling, any ſenſe in ye,
The leaſt touch of a noble heart.

sp.speaker: La Caſ.
sp.l: Let him alone;
It is his glory that he can kill Beauty,
Ye bear my Stamp, but not my Tenderneſs;
Your wild unſavoury Courſes ſet that in ye!
For ſhame, be ſorry, though ye cannot cure her,
Shew ſomething of a Man, of a fair Nature.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ye make me mad.

sp.speaker: De-Gard.
sp.l: Let me pronounce this to ye,
You take a ſtrange felicity in ſlighting
And wronging Women, which my poor Siſter feels now,
Heavens hand be gentle on her: Mark me, Sir,
That very hour ſhe dies, there's ſmall hope otherwiſe,
That minute you and I muſt grapple for it,
Either your life or mine.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Be not ſo hot, Sir,
I am not to be wrought on by theſe policies,
In truth I am not; Nor do I fear the tricks,
Or the high ſounding threats of a Savoyan;
I glory not in Cruelty, ye wrong me;
Not grow up water'd with the tears of Women;
This let me tell ye, howſoe'r I ſhew to ye,
Wild, as ye pleaſe to call it, or ſelf-will'd;
When I ſee cauſe I can both do and ſuffer,
Freely, and feelingly, as a true Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: O pity, pity, thouſand, thouſand pities!

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Alas poor Soul! ſhe will dye; ſhe is grown ſenſleſs;
She will not know, nor ſpeak now.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Dye for love!
And love of ſuch a Youth! I would dye for a Dog firſt,
He that kills me I'll give him leave to eat me;
I'll know men better ere I ſigh for any of 'em.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Ye have done a worthy act, Sir; a moſt famous;
Ye have kill'd a Maid the wrong way, ye are a conqueror.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: A Conquerour? a Cobler; hang him Sowter;
Go hide thy ſelf for ſhame, go loſe thy memory;
Live not 'mongſt Men; thou art a Beaſt, a Monſter;
A Blatant Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: If ye have yet any honeſty,
Or ever heard of any; take my Counſel;
Off with your Garters: and ſeek out a Bough,
A handſom Bough; (for I would have ye hang like a Gentleman;)
And write ſome doleful matter to the World,
A Warning to hard hearted men.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Out Kitlings:
What Catterwauling's here? what Gibbing?
Do you think my heart is ſoftned with a black Santis?
Shew me ſome reaſon.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Here then, here is a reaſon.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: Now, if ye be a man, let this ſight ſhake ye.

sp.speaker: La. C.
sp.l: Alas poor Gentlewoman! do you know me, Lady?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: How ſhe looks up, and ſtares!

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I know ye very well;
You are my Godfather; and that's the Monſieur.

sp.speaker: De-Gar.
sp.l: And who am I?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: You are Amadis de Gaul, Sir.
Oh oh, my heart! were ye never in love, ſweet Lady?
And do you never dream of Flowers and Gardens?
I dream of walking Fires; take heed, it comes now;
Who's that? pray ſtand away; I have ſeen that face ſure;
How light my head is!

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Take ſome reſt.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I cannot,
For I muſt be up to morrow to go to Church,
And I muſt dreſs me, put my new Gown on,
And be as fine to meet my Love: Heigh ho!
Will not you tell me where my Love lies buried?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: He is not dead: beſhrew my heart, ſhe ſtirs me.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: He is dead to me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is't poſſible my Nature
Should be ſo damnable, to let her ſuffer?
Give me your hand.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: How ſoft you feel, how gentle!
I'll tell you your fortune, Friend.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How ſhe ſtares on me!

sp.speaker: Or.
sp.l: You have a flattering face, but 'tis a fine one;
I warrant you may have a hundred Sweet-hearts;
Will ye pray for me? I ſhall dye to morrow,
And will ye ring the Bells?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am moſt unworthy,
I do confeſs, unhappy; do you know me?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I would I did.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Oh fair tears, how ye take me!

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Do you weep too? you have not loſt your Lover;
You mock me; I'l go home, and pray.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Pray ye pardon me:
Or if it pleaſe ye to conſider juſtly,
Scorn me, for I deſerve it: Scorn, and ſhame me:
Sweet Oriana.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Let her alone, ſhe trembles;
Her ſits will grow more ſtrong if ye provoke her.

sp.speaker: La Caſ.
sp.l: Certain ſhe knows ye not, yet loves to ſee ye:
How ſhe ſmiles now!

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Where are ye? Oh, why do you laugh? come, laugh at me;
What a Devil? art thou ſad, and ſuch a ſubject,
Such a ridiculous ſubject as I am
Before thy face?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Prithee put off this lightneſs;
This is no time for mirth, nor place; I have us'd too much on't:
I have undone my ſelf, and a ſweet Lady,
By being too in dulgent to my foolery,
Which truly I repent; look here.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: What a •• s ſhe?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Alas, ſhe's mad.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Mad?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, too ſure for me too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Doſt thou wonder at that? by this light they are all ſo;
They are coz'ning mad, they are brawling mad, they are proud mad:
They are all, all mad; I came from a World of mad Women.
Mad as March-Hares; get 'em in Chains, then deal with 'em.
There's one that's mad; ſhe ſeems well, but ſhe is dog mad.
Is ſhe dead doſt think?

sp.speaker: Min.
sp.l: Dead! Heaven forbid.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Heaven further it;
For till they be key cold dead, there's no truſting of 'em,
Whate'r they ſeem, or howſoe'r they carry it,
Till they be chap faln, and their Tongues at peace,
Nail'd in their Coffins ſure, I'll ne'r believe 'em,
Shall I talk with her?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, dear friend, be quiet,
And be at peace a while.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'll walk aſide,
And come again anon: but take heed to her,
You ſay ſhe is a Woman?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Take great heed:
For if ſhe do not cozen thee, then hang me.
Let her be mad, or what ſhe will, ſhe'll cheat thee. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Away, wild Fool: how vile this ſhews in him now!
Now take my faith, before ye all I ſpeak it,
And with it, my repentant love.

sp.speaker: La-C.
sp.l: This ſeems well.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Were but this Lady clear again, whoſe ſorrows
My very heart melts for; were ſhe but perfect
(For thus to marry her would be two miſeries,)
Before the richeſt and the nobleſt Beauty,
France, or the World could ſhew me; I would take her.
As ſhe is now, my Tears and Prayers ſhall wed her.

sp.speaker: De-Gar.
sp.l: This makes ſome ſmall amends.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: She beckons to ye,
To us too, to go off.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: Let's draw aſide all.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh my beſt friend; I would fain.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What? ſhe ſpeaks well,
And with another voice.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: But I am fearful,
And ſhame a little ſtops my tongue.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Speak boldly.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Tell ye, I am well, I am perfect well: 'pray ye mock not;
And that I did this to provoke your Nature,
Out of my infinite and reſtleſs love,
To win your pity; pardon me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Go forward;
Who ſet ye on?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: None, as I live, no Creature;
Not any knew, or ever dream'd what I meant;
Will ye be mine?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis true, I pity ye:
But when I marry ye, ye muſt be wiſer:
Nothing but Tricks? Devices?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Will ye ſhame me?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: The Woman's well; ſhe was only mad for Marriage,
Stark mad to be ſton'd to death; give her good counſel,
Will this world never mend? are ye caught, Damſel?

div.stage: Enter Belleur, La Caſtre, Lugier, Nantolet, De Gard, Roſalure, and Bianca.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How goes it now?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou art a kind of Prophet,
The Woman's well again, and would have gull'd me;
Well, excellent well: and not a taint upon her.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Did not I tell ye? Let 'em be what can be;
Saints, Devils, any thing, they will abuſe us;
Thou wert an Aſs to believe her ſo long, a Coxcomb;
Give 'em a minute they'll abuſe whole millions.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And am not I a rare ſhyſician, Gentlemen,
That can cure deſperate mad minds?

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: Be not inſolent.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Well, go thy waies: from this hour, I diſclaim thee,
Unleſs thou haſt a trick above this: then I'le love thee.
Ye owe me for your Cure; pray have a care of her,
For ſear ſhe fall into Relapſe: come Belleur.
We'll ſet up Bills, to Cure Diſeaſed Virgins.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Shall we be merry?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: But I'le no more projects;
If we could make 'em mad, it were ſome maſtery. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lal.
sp.l: I am glad ſhe is well again.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: So am I, certain,
Be not aſhamed.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I ſhall never ſee a man more.

sp.speaker: De Gar.
sp.l: Come ye are a fool: had ye but told me this trick,
He ſhould not have gloried thus.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: He ſhall not long neither.

sp.speaker: La C.
sp.l: Be r • l'd, and be at peace: ye have my conſent,
And what power I can work with.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: Come, leave bluſhing;
We are your friends; an honeſt way compell'd ye;
Heaven will not ſee ſo true a love unrecompenc'd;
Come in, and ſlight him too.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: The next ſhall hit him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: 'TWill be diſcover'd.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: That's the worſt can happen:
If there be any way to reach, and work upon him;
Upon his nature ſuddenly, and catch him: that he loves,
Though he diſſemble it, and would ſhew contrary,
And will at length relent, I'le lay my Fortune,
Nay more, my life.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: Is ſhe won?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Yes, and ready,
And my deſignments ſet.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: They are now for Travel,
All for that Game again: they have forgot wooing.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Let 'em; we'll travel with 'em.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: Where's his Father /

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Within; he knows my mind too and allows it;
Pities your Siſters Fortune moſt ſincerely;
And has appointed, for our more aſſiſtance,
Some of his ſecret Friends.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: 'Speed the Plough.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Well ſaid;
And be you ſerious too.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: I ſhall be diligent.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Let's break the Ice for one, the reſt will drink too
(Believe me, Sir) of the ſame Cup; my young Gentlewomen
Wait but who ſets the game a foot; though they ſeem ſtubborn,
Reſerv'd, and proud now, yet I know their hearts,
Their Pulſes how they beat, and for what cauſe, Sir;
And how they long to venture their Abilities
In a true Quarrel; Husbands they muſt, and will have,
Or Nunneries, and thin Collations
To cool their bloods; let's all about our buſineſs,
And if this fail, let Nature work.

sp.speaker: De G.
sp.l: Ye have arm'd me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: La-Caſt.
sp.l: Will ye be wilful then?

sp.speaker: Mir.
