sp.l: 'Pray, Sir, your pardon,
For I muſt Travel: lie lazy here,
Bound to a Wife? Chain'd to her ſubtleties,
Her humours, and her wills, which are meer Fetters;
To have her to day pleas'd, to morrow peeviſh,
The third day mad, the fourth rebellious?
You ſee, before they are married, what Moriſcoes,
What Maſques, and Mummeries they put upon us,
To be ty'd here, and ſuffer their Lavalto's?

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.l: 'Tis your own ſeeking.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, to get my freedom;
Were they as I could wiſh 'em.

sp.speaker: La Caſt.
sp.l: Fools, and Meacocks,
To endure what you think fit to put upon 'em:
Come, change your mind.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Not before I • ave chang'd Air, Father.
When I know Women worthy of my company,
I will return again and wait upon 'em;
Till then (dear Sir) I'le amble all the world over,
And run all hazards, miſery, and poverty,
So I eſcape the dangerous Bay of Matrimony.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Are ye reſolv'd?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes certain; I will out again.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: We are for ye, Sir; we are your ſervants once more;
Once more we'll ſeek our fortune in ſtrange Countries;
Ours is too ſcornful for us.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Is there ne're a Land
That ye have read, or heard of, (for I care not how far it be,
Nor under what peſtiferous Star it lies)
A happy Kingdom where there are no Women?
Nor have been ever? Nor no mention
Of any ſuch lewd things, with lewder qualities?
For thither would I Travel; where 'tis Felony
To confeſs he had a Mother: a Miſtris, Treaſon.

sp.speaker: La-Caſt.
sp.l: Are you for Travel too?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: For any thing;
For living in the Moon, and ſtopping hedges,
E're I ſtay here to be abus'd, and baffl'd.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.l: Why did ye not break your minds to me? they are my Daughters;
And ſure I think I ſhould have that command over 'em,
To ſee 'em well beſtow'd: I know ye are Gentlemen,
Men of fair Parts and States; I know your Parents;
And had ye told me of your fair Affections—
Make but one tryal more; and let me ſecond ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No I'le make Hob-nails firſt, and mend old Kettles:
Can ye lend me an Armour of high proof, to appear in,
And two or three Field-pieces to defend me?
The Kings Guard are meer Pigmeys.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: They will not eat ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes, and you too, and twenty ſatter Monſieurs,
If their high ſtomachs hold: they came with Chopping-knives,
To cut me into Rands, and Sirloins, and ſo powder me.
Come, ſhall we go?

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: You cannot be ſo diſcourteous
(If ye intend to go) as not to viſit 'em,
And take your leaves.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That we dare do, and civilly,
And thank 'em too.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Yos, Sir, we know that honeſty.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'le come i'th' Rear, forty foot off, I'le aſſure ye,
With a good Gun in my hand; I'le no more Amazons,
I mean, no more of their frights; I'le make my three legs
Kiſs my hand twice; and if I ſmell no danger;
If the enterview be clear, may be I'le ſpeak to her;
I'le wear a privy coat too; and behind me,
To make thoſe parts ſecure, a Bandog.

sp.speaker: La Caſt.
sp.l: You are a merry Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: A wary Gentleman; I do aſſure ye,
I have been warn'd, and muſt be arm'd.

sp.speaker: La-Caſt.
sp.l: Well, Son,
Theſe are your haſty thoughts, when I ſee you are bent to it,
Then I'le believe, and joyn with ye; So we'll leave ye:
There's a Trick will make ye ſtay.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: I hope ſo. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: We have won immortal Fame now, if we leave 'em.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: You have, but we have loſt.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pinac, thou art cozen'd;
I know they love ye; and to gain ye handſomly,
Not to be thought to yield, they would give millions;
Their Fathers willingneſs, that muſt needs ſhew ye.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: If I thought ſo.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ye ſhall be hang'd, ye Recreant,
Would ye turn Renegado now?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No let's away, Boys,
Out of the Air, and tumult of their Villanies;
Though I were married to that Graſhopper,
And had her faſt by th' legs I ſhould think ſhe would cozen me.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Monſieur Mirabel, I take it?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Y'are i'th' right, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: I am come to ſeek ye, Sir; I have been at your Fathers,
And underſtanding you were here.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ye are welcom:
May I crave your name?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Foſs, Sir, and your ſervant;
That you may know me better; I am Factor
To your old Merchant, Leverdure.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How do's he?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Well, Sir, I hope: he is now at Orleance,
About ſome buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You are once more welcom,
Your Maſter's a right honeſt man; and one
I am much beholding to, and muſt very ſhortly
Trouble his love again.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: You may be bold, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Your buſineſs if you pleaſe now?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: This it is, Sir,
I know ye well remember in your travel
A Genoa Merchant.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I remember many.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: But this man, Sir, particulary; your own benefit
Muſt needs imprint him in ye; one Alberto;
A Gentleman you ſav'd from being Murther'd
A little from Bollonia,
I was then my ſelf in Italie, and ſuppli'd ye,
Though haply, you have forgot md now.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, I remember ye,
And that Alberto too: a noble Gentleman:
More to remember, were to thank my ſelf, Sir.
What of that Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: He is dead.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am ſorry.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: But on his death-bed, leaving to his Siſter
All that he had, beſide ſome certain Jewels,
Which with a Ceremony, he bequeath'd to you,
In gratefull memory: he commanded ſtrictly
His Siſter, as ſhe lov'd him and his peace,
To ſee thoſe Jewels ſafe, and true deliver'd;
And with them, his laſt love. She, as tender
To obſerve his will, not truſting friend, nor ſervant,
With ſuch a weight, is come her ſelf to Paris,
And at my Maſters houſe.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You tell me a wonder.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: I tell ye a truth, Sir: She is young, and handſom,
And well attended: of much State, and Riches;
So loving, and obedient to her Brother;
That on my conſcience, if he had given her alſo,
She would moſt willingly have made her tender.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: May not I ſee her?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: She deſires it heartily.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And preſently?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: She is now about ſome buſineſs,
Paſſing accompts of ſome few debts here owing,
And buying Jewels of a Merchant.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is ſhe wealthie.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: I would ye had her, Sir, at all adventure,
Her Brother had a main State.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And fair too?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: The prime of all thoſe parts of Italie,
For beautie, and for Courteſie.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I muſt needs ſee her.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: 'Tis all her buſineſs, Sir. Ye may now ſee her,
But to morrow will be fitter for your viſitation;
For ſhe is not yet prepared.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Only, her ſight, Sir;
And when you ſhall think ſit for further viſit.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Sir, ye may ſee her; and I'le wait your coming.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And I'le be with ye inſtantly. I know the houſe,
Mean time, my love, and thanks, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Your poor Servant.— Exit Alberto.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Thou haſt the ſtrangeſt Luck: what was that?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: An honeſt noble Merchant, 'twas my chance
To reſcue from ſome rogues had almoſt ſlain him;
And he in kindneſs to remember this.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Now we ſhall have you,
For all your proteſtations, and your forwardneſs,
Find out ſtrange fortunes in this Ladies eyes,
And new enticements to put off your journey;
And who ſhall have honour then?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, no, never fear it:
I muſt needs ſee her, to receive my Legacy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: If it be ty'd up in her ſmock, heaven help thee:
May not we ſee too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, afore we go:
I muſt be known my ſelf e're I be able
To make thee welcom: wouldſt thou ſee more women?
I thought you had been out of love with all.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I may be,
I find that, with the leaſt encouragement:
Yet I deſire to ſee whether all Countries
Are naturally poſſeſs'd with the ſame ſpirits;
For if they be, I'le take a Monaſtery,
And never trav •• ; for I had rather be a Frier,
And live mew'd up, than be a fool, and flouted.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Well, well, I'le meet ye anon; then tell you more, boys;
For certain, we ſhall go, I think, when I have ſeen her,
And view'd her well.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Go, go, and we'll wait for ye;
Your fortune directs ours.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You ſhall find us i'th' Tavern,
Lamenting in Sack and Sugar for our loſſes;
If ſhe be right Italian, and want ſervants,
You may prefer the propereſt man.
How I could worry a woman now?

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Come, come, leave prating;
Ye may have enough to do, without this boaſting.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Enter Lugier, de-Gard, Roſalu. and Lelia.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: This is the laſt adventure.

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: And the happieſt,
As we hope too.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We ſhould be glad to find it.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Who ſhall conduct us thither?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Your man is ready,
For I muſt not be ſeen; no, nor this Gentleman;
That may beget ſuſpicion: all the reſt
Are people of no doubt; I would have ye, Ladies,
Keep your old liberties, and as we inſtruct ye:
Come, look not pale; you ſhall not loſe your wiſhes;
Nor beg 'em neither: but be your ſelves, and happy.

sp.speaker: Roſ
sp.l: I tell ye true, I cannot hold off longer,
Nor give no more hard language.

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: You ſhall not need.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I love the Gentleman, and muſt now ſnow it;
Shall I beat a proper man out of heart?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: There's none adviſes ye.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: 'Faith I repent me too.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Repent, and ſpoil all,
Tell what ye know, ye had beſt.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I'le tell what I think;
For if he ask me now, if I can love him,
I'le tell him yes, I can: The man's a kind man;
And out of his true honeſty affects me;
Although he plaid the fool, which I requited;
Muſt I ſtill hold him at the ſtaves end?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: You are two ſtrange women.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We may be, if we fool ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Dare ye believe me?
Follow but this advice I have ſet you in now,
And if ye loſe: would ye yield now ſo baſely?
Give up without your honours ſaved /

sp.speaker: de-Gard.
sp.l: Fie, Ladies.
Perſerve your freedom ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Well, well, for this time.

sp.speaker: Lug
sp.l: And carry that full ſtate.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: That's as the wind ſtands:
If it begin to chop about, and ſcant us;
Hang me, but I know what I'le do: come direct us,
I make no doubt, we ſhall do handſomly.

sp.speaker: de-Ga.
sp.l: Some part o'th' way we'll wait upon ye, Ladies;
The reſt your man ſupplies.

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: Do well, I'le honour ye. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter Factor, and Mirabel, Oriana, and two Merchants.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Look ye, Sir, there ſhe is, you ſee how buſie;
Methinks you are infinitely bound to her, for her journey.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How gloriouſly ſhe ſhews: She is a tall woman.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Of a fair Size, Sir. My Maſter not being at home,
I have been ſo out of my wits, to get her company:
I mean, Sir, of her own fair ſex, and faſhion.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Aſa • off, ſhe is moſt fair too.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Near, moſt Excellent.
At length, I have entreated two fair Ladies,
And happily you know 'em: the young Daughters
Of Monſieur Nantolet.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I know 'em well, Sir.
What are thoſe? Jewels?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: All.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: They make a rich ſhew?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: There is a matter of ten thouſand pounds too
Was owing here: you ſee thoſe Merchants with her;
They have brought it in now.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How handſomly her ſhape ſhews?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Thoſe are ſtill neat: your Italians are moſt curious:
Now ſhe looks this way.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She has a goodly preſence,
How full of courteſie? Well, Sir, I'le leave ye,
And if I may be bold to bring a friend or two;
Good noble Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: No doubt, ye may, Sir.
For you have moſt command.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I have ſeen a wonder. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Is he gone?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Taken to the utmoſt,
A wonder dwells about him.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: He did not gueſs at me?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: No, be ſecure; ye ſhew another woman,
He is gone to fetch his friends.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Where are the Gentlewomen?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Here, here, now they are come,
Sit ſtill, and let them ſee ye.
Enter Roſalure, Lelia, Servant.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Pray ye, where's my friend, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: She is within, Ladies, but here's another Gentlewoman,
A ſtranger to this Town: ſo pleaſe you viſit her,
'Twill be well taken.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Where is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: There, above, Ladies.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Bleſs me: what thing is this? two Pinacles
Upon her pate! Is't not a glode to catch Wood-cocks?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Peace, ye rude knave.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: What a bouncing Bum ſhe has too?
There's Sail enough for a Carrack.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: What is this Lady?
For as I live, ſhe's a goodly woman.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Gheſs, gheſs.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I have not ſeen a nobler Preſence.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis a luſtie wench: now could I ſpend my forty-pence,
With all my heart, to have but one fling at her;
To give her but a waſhing blow.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Ye Raſcal.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I that's all a man has, for's good will: 'twill be long enough,
Before ye cry come Anthonie, and kiſs me.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I'le have ye whipt.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Has my friend ſeen this Lady?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Yes, yes, and is well known to her.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I much admire her Preſence.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: So do I too:
For I proteſt, ſhe is the handſomeſt,
The rareſt, and the neweſt to mine eye
That ever I ſaw yet.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I long to know her;
My friend ſhall do that kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: So ſhe ſhall Ladies,
Come, pray ye come up.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: O me.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Hang me if I knew her:
Were I a man my ſelf, I ſhould now love ye;
Nay, I ſhould doat.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I dare not truſt mine eyes;
For as I live ye are the ſtrangeſt alter'd,
I muſt come up to know the truth.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: So muſt I, Lady,
For I am a kind of unbeliever too.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Get ye gone, Sirrah;
And what ye have ſeen, be ſecret in: you are paid elſe,
No more of your long tongue.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Will ye go in Ladies,
And talk with her? Theſe venturers will come ſtraight:
Away with this fellow.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: There, Sirrah, go, diſport ye.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I would the trunk-hos'd-woman would go with me.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Is ſhe ſo glorious handſom?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You would wonder:
Our Women look like Gipſies, like Gills to her:
Their Clothes and faſhions beggerly, and Bankrupt:
Baſe, old, and ſcurvy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How looks her face?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Moſt heavenly:
And the becoming-motion of her bodie
So ſets her off.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Why then we ſhall ſtay.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pardon me:
That's more than I know: if ſhe be that woman,
She appears to be.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: As 'tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I ſhall then tell ye more.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Did ye ſpeak to her?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No, no, I only ſaw her: She was buſie:
Now I go for that end: and mark her, Gentlemen,
If ſhe appear not to ye one of the ſweeteſt,
The handſomeſt, the faireſt in behaviour:
We ſhall meet the two wenches there too, they come to viſit her,
To wonder, as we do.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Then we ſhall meet 'em.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I had rather meet two Bears.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: There you may take your leaves, diſpatch that buſineſs,
And as ye find their humours.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Is your love there too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: No certain, ſhe has no great heart to ſet out again.
This is the houſe, I'le uſher ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'le bleſs me,
And take a good heart if I can.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come, nobly. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: They are come in: Sit you two off, as ſtrangers,
There Ladie: where's the boy? be readie, Sirrah,
And clear your Pipes, the Muſick now: they enter. Muſick

sp.speaker: Pi.
sp.l: What a ſtate ſhe keeps! how far off they ſit from her!
How rich ſhe is! I marry, this ſhews bravely.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She is a luſty wench: and may allure a good man,
But if ſhe have a tongue, I'le not give two pence for her:
There ſits my Fury: how I ſhake to ſee her!

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: Madam, this is the Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How ſweet ſhe kiſſes!
She has a Spring dwells on her lips: a paradiſe:
This is the Legacie.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: From the honor'd dead I bring
Thus his love and laſt offring.
Take it nobly, 'tis your due,
From a friendſhip ever true.
From a faith &c.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Moſt noble Sir,
This from my now dead Brother, as his love,
And gratefull memory of your great benefit:
From me my thanks, my wiſhes, and my ſervice.
Till I am more acquainted I am ſilent,
Only I dare ſay this, you are truly noble.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What ſhould I think?

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Think ye have a handſom fortune,
Would I had ſuch another.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ye are well met Gentlemen,
We hear ye are for travel?

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Ye hear true, Ladie,
And come to take our leaves.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: We'll along with ye,
We ſee you are grown ſo witty by your Journey,
We cannot chooſe but ſtep out too: This Lady
We mean to wait upon as far as Italy

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'll travel into Wales, amongſt the mountains;
I hope they cannot find me.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: If you go further;
So good, and free ſociety we hold ye,
We'll jog along too.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Are ye ſo valiant Lady?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: And we'll be merry, Sir, and laugh.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: It may be
We'll go by Sea.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Why 'tis the only voyage;
I love a Sea-voyage, and a bluſtring tempeſt;
And let all ſplit.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: This is a dainty Damoſel:
I think 'twill tame ye: can ye ride poſt?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: O excellently: I am never weary that way:
A hundred mile a day is nothing with me.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'le travel under ground: do you hear (ſweet Lady?)
I find it will be dangerous for a woman.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: No danger, Sir, I warrant; I love to be under.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I ſee ſhe will abuſe me all the world over:
But ſay we paſs through Germany, and drink hard?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: We'll learn to drink and ſwagger too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: She'l beat me.
Lady, I'le live at home.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And I'le live with thee;
And we'll keep houſe together.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'le keep hounds firſt;
And thoſe I hate right heartily.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: I go for Turky,
And ſo it may be up into Perſia.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: We cannot know too much, I'le travel with ye.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: And you'l abuſe me?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Like enough.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: 'Tis dainty.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I will live in a bawdy-houſe.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I dare come to ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Say, I am diſpos'd to hang my ſelf?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: There I'le leave ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am glad I know how to avoid ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: May I ſpeak yet?

sp.speaker: Fac.
sp.l: She beckons to ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Lady, I could wiſh, I knew to recompence,
Even with the ſervice of my life, thoſe pains,
And thoſe high favours you have thrown upon me;
Till I be more deſertful in your eye;
And till my duty ſhall make known I honour ye:
Nobleſt of women, do me but this favour,
To accept this back again, as a poor teſtimony.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I muſt have you too with 'em; elſe the will,
That ſays they muſt reſt with ye, is infring'd, Sir;
Which pardon me, I dare not do.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Take me then;
And take me with the trueſt love.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: 'Tis certain,
My Brother lov'd ye dearly, and I ought
As dearly to preſerve that love. But, Sir,
Though I were willing, theſe are but your Ceremonies.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: As I have life, I ſpeak my ſoul.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I like ye.
But how you can like me, without I have Teſtimony,
A Stranger to ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'le marry ye immediately,
A fair State I dare promiſe ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yet ſhe'll couzen thee.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Would ſome fair Gentleman durſt promiſe for ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: By all that's good.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: And we'll make up the reſt, Lady.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Then Oriana takes ye; nay, ſhe has caught ye;
If ye ſtart now let all the world cry ſhame on ye:
I have out travell'd ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Did not I ſay ſhe would cheat thee?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I thank ye, I am pleas'd, ye have deceiv'd me;
And willingly I ſwallow it, and joy in't;
And yet perhaps I know ye: whoſe plot was this?

sp.speaker: Lug.
sp.l: He is not aſham'd that caſt it: he that executed,
Followed your Fathers will.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What a world's this, nothing but craft, and cozenage?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Who begun, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Well; I do take thee upon meer Compaſſion;
And I do think, I ſhall love thee. As a Teſtimony,
I'le burn my book, and turn a new leaf over,
But theſe fine clothes you ſhall wear ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I obey you, Sir, in all.

sp.speaker: Nant.
sp.l: And how! how, daughters! what ſay you to theſe Gentlemen?
What ſay ye, Gentlemen, to the Girles?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: By my troth—if ſhe can love me.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: —How long?

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Nay, if once ye love.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Then take me,
And take your chance.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Moſt willingly, ye are mine, Lady:
And if I uſe ye not, that ye may love me.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: A Match i' faith.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Why now ye travel with me.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: How that thing ſtands!

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: It will if ye urge it.
'Bleſs your five wits.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Nay, 'prethee ſtay, I'le have thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You muſt ask me leave firſt.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Wilt thou uſe me kindly;
And beat me but once a week?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: If ye deſerve no more.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And wilt thou get me with child?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Doſt thou ask me ſeriouſly?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes indeed do I.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes, I will get thee with child: come preſently,
And 't be but in revenge, I'le do thee that courteſie.
Well, if thou wilt fear God, and me; have at thee.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I'le love ye, and I'le honour ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I am pleas'd then.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This Wild-Gooſe Chaſe is done, we have won o' both ſides.
Brother, your love: and now to Church of all hands;
Let's loſe no time.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: Our travelling, lay by.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No more for Italy; for the Low-Countries. Exeunt.

div.head: A Wife for a Month; A TRAGI-COMEDY.

list.item: Alphonſo, King of Naples, elder Brother to Frederick.
Frederick, unnatural and libidinous Brother to Alphonſo, and uſurper of his Kingdom.
Sorano, a Lord, Brother to Evanthe, Frederick's wicked inſtrument.
Valerio, a noble young Lord, ſervant to Evanthe.
Rugio, an honeſt Lord, friend to Alphonſo.
Podramo, a neceſſary creature to Sorano.
Caſtruccio, Captain of the Cittadel, an honeſt man.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Queen, Wife to Frederick, a vertuous Lady.
Evanthe, Siſter to Sorano, the chaſte Wife of Valerio, or a Wife for a Month.
Caſſandra, an old Bawd, Waiting-woman to Evanthe.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter King Frederick, Sorano, Valerio, Camillo, Cleanthes, Menallo, and Attendants.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: WILL your Grace ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Let me alone, Sorano,
Although my thoughts ſeem ſad, they are welcome to me.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: You know I am private as your ſecret wiſhes,
Ready to fling my ſoul upon your ſervice,
E're your command be on't.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Bid thoſe depart.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: You muſt retire my Lords.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: What new deſign is hammering in his head now?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Let's pray heartily
None of our heads meet with it, my Wife's old,
That's all my comfort.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Mine's ugly, that I am ſure on,
And I think honeſt too, 'twould make me ſtart elſe.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Mine's troubled in the Country with a Feaver,
And ſome few infirmities elſe; he looks again,
Come let's retire, certain 'tis ſome ſhe-buſineſs,
This new Lord is imployed.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I'le not be far off, becauſe I doubt the cauſe. Ex.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Are they all gone?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: All but your faithful Servant.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: I would tell thee,
But 'tis a thing thou canſt not like.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Pray ye ſpeak it, is it my head? I have it ready for ye, Sir:
Is't any action in my power? my wit?
I care not of what nature, nor what follows.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: I am in love.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: That's the leaſt thing of a thouſand,
The eaſieſt to atchieve.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: But with whom, Sorano?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: With whom you pleaſe, you muſt not be deny'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Say it be with one of thy Kinſwomen.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Say withal,
I ſhall more love your Grace, I ſhall more honour ye,
And would I had enough to ſerve your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Why 'tis thy Siſter then, the fair Evanthe,
I'le be plain with thee.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: I'le be as plain with you, Sir,
She brought not her perfections to the world,
To lock them in a caſe, or hang 'em by her,
The uſe is all ſhe breeds 'em for, ſhe is yours, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Doſt thou mean ſeriouſly?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: I mean my Siſter,
And if I had a dozen more, they were all yours:
Some Aunts I have, they have been handſome Women,
My Mother's dead indeed, and ſome few Couſins
That are now ſhooting up, we ſhall ſee ſhortly.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: No, 'tis Evanthe.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: I have ſent my man unto her,
Upon ſome buſineſs to come preſently
Hither, ſhe ſhall come; your Grace dare ſpeak unto her?
Large golden promiſes, and ſweet language, Sir,
You know what they work, ſhe is a compleat Courtier,
Beſides I'le ſet in.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She waits upon my Queen,
What jealouſie and anger may ariſe,
Incenſing her?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: You have a good ſweet Lady,
A Woman of ſo even and ſtill a temper,
She knows not anger; ſay ſhe were a fury,
I had thought you had been abſolute, the great King,
The fountain of all honours, plays and pleaſures,
Your will and your commands unbounded alſo;
Go get a pair of Beads and learn to pray, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: My Lord, your ſervant ſtayes.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Bid him come hither, and bring the Lady with him.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I will woo her,
And either loſe my ſelf, or win her favour.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: She is coming in.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thy eyes ſhoot through the door,
They are ſo piercing, that the beams they dart
Give new light to the room.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Whither doſt thou go?
This is the Kings ſide, and his private lodgings,
What buſineſs have I here?

sp.speaker: Pod.
sp.l: My Lord ſent for ye.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: His lodgings are below, you are miſtaken,
We left them at the ſtair-foot.

sp.speaker: Pod.
sp.l: Good ſweet Madam,

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: I am no Counſellor, nor important Sutor,
No have no private buſineſs through theſe Chambers,
To feel him this way, o' my life thou art drunk,
Or worſe than drunk, hir'd to convey me hither
To ſome baſe end; now I look on thee better,
Thou haſt a bawdy face, and I abhor thee,
A beaſtly bawdy face, I'le go no further.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Nay ſhrink not back, indeed you ſhall good Siſter,
Why do you bluſh? the good King will not hurt ye,
He honours ye, and loves ye.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Is this the buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Yes, and the beſt you ever will arrive at if you be wiſe.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: My Father was no bawd, Sir,
Nor of that worſhipful ſtock as I remember.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Your are a Fool.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: You are that I ſhame to tell ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Gentle Evanthe.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: The gracious Queen, Sir,
Is well and merry, Heaven be thanked for it,
And as I think ſhe waits you in the Garden.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Let her wait there, I talk not of her Garden,
I talk of thee ſweet Flower.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Your Grace is pleaſant,
To miſtake a Nettle for a Roſe.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: No Roſe, nor Lilly, nor noglorious Hyacinth
Are of that ſweetneſs, whiteneſs, tenderneſs,
Softneſs, and ſatisfying bleſſedneſs
As my Evanthe.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Your Grace ſpeaks very feelingly,
I would not be a handſome wench in your way, Sir,
For a new Gown.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thou art all handſomneſs,
Nature will be aſham'd to frame another
Now thou art made, thou haſt rob'd her of her cunning:
Each ſeveral part about thee is a beauty.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Do you hear this Siſter?

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Yes, unworthy Brother, but all this will not do.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: But love Evanthe.
Thou ſhalt have more than words, wealth, eaſe, and honours,
My tender Wench.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Be tender of my credit,
And I ſhall love you, Sir, and I ſhall honour ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I love thee to enjoy thee, my Evanthe,
To give thee the content of love.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Hold, hold, Sir, ye are too fleet,
I have ſome buſineſs this way, your Grace can ne'r content.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: You ſtubborn toy.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Good my Lord Bawd I thank ye.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not go believe me, ſweet Evanthe,
So high I will advance thee for this favour,
So rich and potent I will raiſe thy fortune,
And thy friends mighty.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Good your Grace be patient,
I ſhall make the worſt honourable wench that ever was,
Shame your diſcretion, and your choice.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Shall I be rich do you ſay, and glorious,
And ſhine above the reſt, and ſcorn all beauties,
And mighty in command?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt be any thing.

sp.speaker: Eva.
sp.l: Let me be honeſt too, and then I'le thank ye.
Have you not ſuch a title to beſtow too?
If I prove otherwiſe, I would know but this, Sir;
Can all the power you have or all the riches,
But tye mens tongues up from diſcourſing of me,
Their eyes from gazing at my glorious folly,
Time that ſhall come, from wondering at my impudence,
And they that read my wanton life from curſes?
Can you do this? have ye this Magick in ye?
This is not in your power, though you be a Prince, Sir,
No more than evil is in holy Angels,
Nor I, I hope: get wantonneſs confirm'd
By Act of Parliament an honeſty,
And ſo receiv'd by all, I'le hearken to ye.
Heaven guide your Grace.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Evanthe, ſtay a little,
I'le no more wantonneſs, I'le marry thee.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: What ſhall the Queen do?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I'le be divorced from her.

sp.speaker: Eva.
sp.l: Can you tell why? what has ſhe done againſt ye?
Has ſhe contrived a Treaſon 'gainſt your Perſon?
Abus'd your bed? does diſobedience urge ye?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: That's all one, 'tis my will.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: 'Tis a moſt wicked one,
A moſt abſurd one, and will ſhow a Monſter;
I had rather be a Whore, and with leſs ſin,
To your preſent luſt, than Queen to your injuſtice.
Yours is no love, Faith and Religion ſly it,
Nor has no taſte of fair affection in it,
Some Helliſh flame abuſes your fair body,
And Helliſh furies blow it; look behind ye,
Divorce ye from a Woman of her beauty,
Of her integrity, her piety?
Her love to you, to all that honours ye,
Her chaſte and vertuous love, are theſe fit cauſes?
What will you do to me, when I have cloy'd ye?
You may find time out in eternity,
Deceit and violence in heavenly Juſtice,
Life in the grave, and death among the bleſſed,
Ere ſtain or brack in her ſweet reputation.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: You have fool'd enough, be wiſe now, and a woman,
You have ſhew'd a modeſty ſufficient,
If not too much for Court.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: You have ſhew'd an impudence,
A more experienc'd bawd would bluſh and ſhake at;
You will make my kindred mighty.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Prethee hear me.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: I do Sir, and I count it a great offer.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Any of thine.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: 'Tis like enough you may clap honour on them,
But how 'twill ſit, and how men will adore it,
Is ſtill the queſtion. I'le tell you what they'l ſay, Sir,
What the report will be, and 'twill be true too,
And it muſt needs be comfort to your Maſter,
Theſe are the iſſues of her impudence:
I'le tell your Grace, ſo dear I hold the Queen,
So dear that honour that ſhe hurs'd me up in,
I would firſt take to me, for my luſt, a Moor,
One of your Gally-ſlaves, that cold and hunger,
Decrepit miſery, had made a mock-man,
Than be your Queen.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You are bravely reſolute.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: I had rather be a Lep • r, and be ſhun'd,
And dye by pieces, rot into my grave,
Leaving no memory behind to know me,
Than be a high Whore to eternity.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: You have another Gameſter I perceive by ye,
You durſt not ſlight me elſe.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: I'le find him out,
Though he lye next thy heart hid, I'le diſcover him,
And ye proud peat, I'le make you curſe your inſolence.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Tongue of an Angel, and the truth of Heaven,
How am I bleſt! Exit Val.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Podramo go in haſt
To my Siſters Gentlewoman, you know her well,
And bid her ſend her Miſtris preſently
The leſſer Cabinet ſhe keeps her Letters in,
And ſuch like toyes, and bring it to me inſtantly. Away.

sp.speaker: Pod.
sp.l: I am gone. Exit.

div.stage: Enter the Queen with two Ladies.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: The Queen.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Let's quit the place, ſhe may grow jealous.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: So ſuddenly departed! what's the reaſon?
Does my approach diſpleaſe his Grace? are my eyes
So hateful to him? or my converſation
Infected, that he flies me? Fair Evanthe,
Are you there? then I ſee his ſhame.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: 'Tis true, Madam,
'Thas pleas'd his goodneſs to be pleaſant with me.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange to find thy modeſty in this place,
Does the King offer fair? does thy face take him?
Ne'r bluſh Evanthe, 'tis a very ſweet one,
Does he rain gold, and precious promiſes
Into thy lap? will he advance thy fortunes?
Shalt thou be mighty, Wench?

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Never mock, Madam;
'Tis rather on your part to be lamented,
At leaſt reveng'd, I can be mighty Lady,
And glorious too, glorious and great, as your are.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: He will Marry thee?

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Who would not be a Queen, Madam?

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: 'Tis true Evanthe, 'tis a brave ambition,
A golden dream, that may delude a good mind,
What ſhall become of me?

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: You muſt learn to pray,
Your age and honour will become a Nunnery.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Wilt thou remember me? Weeps.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: She weeps. Sweet Lady
Upon my knees I ask your ſacred pardon,
For my rude boldneſs: and know, my ſweet Miſtris,
If e're there were ambition in Evanthe,
It was and is to do you faithful duties;
'Tis true I have been tempted by the King,
And with no few and potent charms, to wrong ye,
To violate the chaſte joyes of your bed;
And thoſe not taking hold, to uſurp your ſtate;
But ſhe that has been bred up under ye,
And daily fed upon your vertuous precepts,
Still growing ſtrong by example of your goodneſs,
Having no errant motion from obedience,
Flyes from theſe vanities, as meer illuſions;
And arm'd with honeſty, defies all promiſes.
In token of this truth, I lay my life down
Under your ſacred foot, to do you ſervice.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Riſe my true friend, thou vertuous bud of beauty,
Thou Virgins honour, ſweetly blow and flouriſh,
And that rude nipping wind, that ſeeks to blaſt thee,
Or taint thy root, be curſt to all poſterity;
To my protection from this hour I take ye,
Yes, and the King ſhall know—

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Give his heat way, Madam,
And 'twill go out again, he may forget all. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: What have we to do with the times? we cannot cure 'em
Let 'em go on, when they are ſwoln with Surfeits
They'l burſt and ſtink, then all the world ſhall ſmell 'em.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: A man may live a bawd, and be an honeſt man.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Yes, and a wiſe man too, 'tis a vertuous calling.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: To his own Wife eſpecially, or to his Siſter,
The nearer to his own bloud, ſtill the honeſter;
There want ſuch honeſt men, would we had more of 'em.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: To be a villain is no ſuch rude matter.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: No, if he be a neat one, and a perfect,
Art makes all excellent: what is it, Gentlemen,
In a good cauſe to kill a dozen Coxcombs,
That blunt rude fellows call good Patriots?
Nothing, nor ne'r look'd after.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: 'Tis e'en as much, as eaſie too, as honeſt, and as clear,
To raviſh Matrons, and deflower coy Wenches,
But here they are ſo willing, 'tis a complement.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: To pull down Churches with pretenſion
To build 'em fairer, may be done with honour,
And all this time believe no gods.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: I think ſo, 'tis faith enough if they name 'em in their angers,
Or on their rotten Tombs ingrave an Angel;
Well, brave Alphonſo, how happy had we been,
If thou had'ſt raign'd!

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Would I had his Diſeaſe,
Tyed, like a Leproſie to my poſterity,
So he were right again.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: What is his Malady?

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Nothing but ſad and ſilent melancholy,
Laden with griefs and thoughts, no man knows why neither;
The good Brandino Father to the Princeſs,
Uſed all the art and induſtry that might be,
To free Alphonſo from this dull calamity,
And ſeat him in his rule, he was his eldeſt
And nobleſt too, had not fair nature ſtopt in him,
For which cauſe this was choſen to inherit,
Frederick the younger.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Does he uſe his Brother
With that reſpect and honour that befits him?

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: He is kept privately, as they pretend,
To give more eaſe and comfort to his ſickneſs;
But he has honeſt ſervants, the grave Rugio,
And Fryar Marco, that wait upon his Perſon.
And in a Monaſtery he lives.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: 'Tis full of ſadneſs,
To ſee him when he comes to his Fathers Tomb,
As once a day that is his Pilgrimage,
Whilſt in D • votion, the Quire ſings an Anthem:
How piouſly he kneels, and like a Virgin
That ſome croſs Fate had cozen'd of her Love,
Weeps till the ſtubborn Marble ſweats with pity,
And to his groans the whole Quire bears a Chorus.

div.stage: Enter Frederick, Sorano, with the Cabinet, and Podramo.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: So do I too. The King with his Contrivers,
This is no place for us. Exeunt Lords.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: This is a jewel,
Lay it aſide, what paper's that?

sp.speaker: Pod.
sp.l: A Letter,
But 'tis a womans, Sir, I know by the hand,
And the falſe Orthography, they write old Saxon.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: May be her ghoſtly Mother's that inſtructs her.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: No, 'tis a Couſins, and came up with a great Cake.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: A pair of Gloves the Dutcheſs gave her,
For ſo the outſide ſays

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: That other paper?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: A Charm for the tooth-ach, here's nothing but Saints and Croſſes.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Look in that Box, methinks that ſhould hold ſecrets.

sp.speaker: Pod.
sp.l: 'Tis Paint, and curls of Hair, ſhe begins to exerciſe.
A glaſs of Water too, I would fain taſte it,
But I am wickedly afraid 'twill ſilence me,
Never a Conduit-Pipe to convey this wat • r.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Theſe are all Rings Deaths heads, and ſuch Memento's
Her Grandmother, and worm-eaten Aunts left to her,
To tell her what her Beauty muſt arrive at.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: That, that.

sp.speaker: Pod.
sp.l: They are written ſongs, Sir, to provoke young Ladies;
Lord, here's a Prayer Book, how theſe-agree!
Here's a ſtrange union.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Ever by a ſurfeit you have a julep ſet to cool the Patient.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thoſe, thoſe.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: They are Verſes to the bleſt Evanthe.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thoſe may diſcover,
Read them out, Sorano,

body.head: To the bleſt Evanthe.
body.l: Let thoſe complain that feel Loves cruelty,
And in ſad legends write their woes,
With Roſes gently has corected me,
My War is without rage or blows:
My Miſtriſs eyes ſhine fair on my deſires,
And hope ſprings up enflam'd with her new fires.
No more an Exile will I dwell,
With folded arms, and ſighs all day,
Reckoning the torments of my Hell,
And ſtinging my ſweet joys away:
I am cal'd home again to quiet peace,
My Miſtriſs ſmiles, and all my ſorrows ceaſe.
Yet what is living in her Eye?
Or being bleſt with her ſweet tongue,
If theſe no other joys imply?
A golden Give, a pleaſing wrong:
To be your own but one poor Month, I'd give
My Youth, my Fortune, and then leave to live.

sp.l: This is my Rival, that I knew the hand now.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: I know it, I have ſeen it, 'tis Valerio's
That hopeful Gentlemans, that was brought up with ye,
And by your charge, nouriſh'd and fed
At the ſame Table, with the ſame allowance.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: And all this courteſie to ruine me?
Croſs my deſires? 'had better have fed humblier,
And ſtood at greater diſtance from my fury:
Go for him quickly, find him inſtantly,
Whilſt my impatient heart ſwells high with choler;
Better have lov'd deſpair, and ſafer kiſs'd her. Ex. Lords.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Thou old weak fool, doſt thou know to what end,
To what betraying end he got this Casket?
Durſt thou deliver him without my Ring,
Or a Command from mine own mouth, that Cabinet
That holds my heart? you unconſiderate Aſs,
You brainleſs Ideot.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I ſaw you go with him,
At the firſt word commit your Perſon to him,
And make no ſcruple, he is your Brothers Gentleman,
And for any thing I know, an honeſt man;
And might not I upon the ſame ſecurity deliver him a Box?

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: A Bottle-head.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You ſhall have cauſe to chafe, as I will handle it.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: I had rather thou hadſt delivered me to Pirats,
Betray'd me to uncurable diſeaſes,
Hung up my Picture in a Market-place,
And ſold me to wild Bawds.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: As I take it, Madam,
Your maiden-head lies not in that Cabinet,
You have a Cloſer, and you keep the Key too,
Why are you vex'd thus?

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: I could curſe thee wickedly,
And wiſh thee more deformed than Age can make thee,
Perpetual hunger, and no teeth to ſatisfie it,
Wait on thee ſtill, nor ſleep be found to eaſe it;
Thoſe hands that gave the Casket, may the Palſie
For ever make unuſeful, even to feed thee:
Long winters, that thy Bones may turn to Iſicles,
No Hell can thaw again, inhabit by thee.
Is thy Care like thy Body, all one crookedneſs?
How ſcurvily thou cryeſt now? like a Drunkard,
I'll have as pure tears from a dirty ſpout;
Do, ſwear thou didſt this ignorantly, ſwear it,
Swear and be damn'd, thou half Witch.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Theſe are fine words, well Madam, Madam.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: 'Tis not well, thou mummy,
'Tis impudently, baſely done, thou durty—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Has your young ſanctity done railing, Madam,
Againſt your innocent 'Squire? do you ſee this Sonnet,
This loving Script? do you know from whence it came too?

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: I do, and dare avouch it pure, and honeſt.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You have private Viſitants, my noble Lady,
That in ſweet numbers court your goodly Vertues,
And to the height of adoration.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Well, Sir,
There's neither Hereſie nor Treaſon in it.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: A Prince may beg at the door, whilſt theſe feaſt with ye;
A favour or a grace, from ſuch as I am,
Courſe common things. You are welcome; Pray come neat Sir,
Do you know this paper?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I am betray'd; I do, Sir,
'Tis mine, my hand and heart, if I dye for her,
I am thy Martyr, Love, and time ſhall honour me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: You ſawcy Sir, that came in my Ladies name,
For her gilt Cabinet, you cheating Sir too,
You ſcurvy Uſher, with as ſcurvy legs,
And a worſe face, thou poor baſe hanging holder,
How durſt thou come to me with a lye in thy mouth?
An impudent lye?

sp.speaker: Pod.
sp.l: Hollow, good Gill, you hobble.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: A ſtinking lye, more ſtinking than the teller,
To play the pilfering Knave? there have been Raſcals
Brought up to fetch and carry, like your Worſhip,
That have been hang'd for leſs, whipt they are daily,
And if the Law will do me right—

sp.speaker: Pod.
sp.l: What then old Maggot?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Thy Mother was carted younger; I'll have thy hide,
Thy mangy hide, embroider'd with a dog-whip,
As it is now with potent Pox, and thicker.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Peace good Antiquity, I'll have your Bones elſe
Ground into Gunpowder to ſhoot at Cats with;
One word more, and I'll blanch thee like an almond,
There's no ſuch cure for the ſhe-falling ſickneſs
As the powder of a dryed Bawds Skin, be ſilent.
You are very prodigal of your ſervice here, Sir,
Of your life more it ſeems.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I repent neither,
Becauſe your Grace ſhall underſtand it comes
From the beſt part of Love, my pure affection,
And kindled with chaſte flame, I will not flye from it,
If it be errour to deſire to marry,
And marry her that ſanctity would dote on,
I have done amiſs, if it be a Treaſon
To graft my ſoul to Vertue, and to grow there,
To love the tree that bears ſuch happineſs;
Conceive me, Sir, this fruit was ne'r forbidden;
Nay, to deſire to taſte too, I am Traytor;
Had you but plants enough of this bleſt Tree, Sir,
Set round about your Court, to beautifie it,
Deaths twice ſo many, to diſmay the approachers,
The ground would ſcarce yield Graves to noble Lovers.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: 'Tis well maintain'd, you wiſh and pray to fortune,
Here in your Sonnet, and ſhe has heard your prayers,
So much you dote upon your own undoing,
But one Month to enjoy her as your Wife,
Though at the expiring of that time you dye for't.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I could wiſh many, many Ages, Sir,
To grow as old as Time in her embraces,
If Heaven would grant it, and you ſmile upon it;
But if my choice were two hours, and then periſh,
I would not pull my heart back.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You have your wiſh,
Tomorrow I will ſee you nobly married,
Your Month take out in all content and pleaſure;
The firſt day of the following Month you dye for't;
Kneel not, not all your Prayers can divert me;
Now mark your ſentence, mark it, ſcornful Lady,
If when Valerio's dead, within twelve hours,
For that's your lateſt time, you find not out
Another Husband on the ſame condition
To marry you again, you dye your ſelf too.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Now you are merciful, I thank your Grace.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: If when you are married, you but ſeek to 'ſcape
Out of the Kingdom, you, or ſhe, or both,
Or to infect mens minds with hot commotions,
You dye both inſtantly; will you love me now, Lady?
My tale will now be heard, but now I ſcorn ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Is our fair love, our honeſt, our entire,
Come to this hazard?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: 'Tis a noble one, and I am much in love with malice for it,
Envy could not have ſtudied me a way,
Nor fortune pointed out a path to Honour,
Straighter and nobler, if ſhe had her eyes;
When I have once enjoy'd my ſweet Evanthe,
And bleſt my Youth with her moſt dear embraces,
I have done my journey here, my day is out,
All that the World has elſe is foolery,
Labour, and loſs of time; what ſhould I live for?
Think but mans life a Month, and we are happy.
I would not have my joys grow old for any thing;
A Paradiſe, as thou art, my Evanthe,
Is only made to wonder at a little;
Enough for human eyes, and then to wander from.
Come, do not weep, ſweet, you diſhonour me,
Your tears and griefs but queſtion my ability,
Whether I dare dye; Do you love Entirely?

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: You know I do.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Then grudge not my felicity.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: I'll to the Queen.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Do any thing that's honeſt,
But if you ſue to him, in Death I hate you. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: WAS there ever heard of ſuch a Marriage?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Marriage and Hanging go by deſtiny,
'Tis the o • d Proverb, now they come toget • er.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: But a Month married, then to loſe his life ſor't?
I would have a long Month ſure, that pays the Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Or get all the Almanacks burnt, that were a rare trick,
And have no Month remembred. How now Tony?
Whoſe water are you caſting?

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: A ſick Gentlemans,
Is very ſick, much troubled with the Stone,
He ſhould not live above a Month, by his Urine,
About St. David's Day it will go hard with him,
He will then be troubled with a pain in his Neck too.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: A peſtilent fool; when wilt thou marry, Tony?

sp.speaker: Ton.
sp.l: When I mean to be hang'd, & 'tis the ſurer contract.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: What think you of this Marriage of Valerio's?

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: They have given him a hot Cuſtard, and mean to burn his mouth with it; had I known he had been given to dye honourably, I would have helpt him to a Wench, a rare one, ſhould have kill'd him in three weeks, and ſav'd the ſentence.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: There be them would have ſpared ten days of that too.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: It may be ſo, you have Women of all Vertues:
There be ſome Guns that I could bring him too,
Some mortar-pieces that are plac'd i'th' Suburbs,
Would tear him into quarters in two hours,
There be alſo of the race of the old Cockatrices,
That would diſpatch him with once looking on him.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: What Month wouldſt thou chuſe, Tony, if thou hadſt the like Fortune?

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: I would chuſe a mull'd ſack month, to comfort my Belly, for ſure my Back would ake for't, and at the months end I would be moſt diſmally drunk, & ſcorn the gallows.

sp.speaker: Me.
sp.l: I would chuſe March, for I would come in like a Lion.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: But you'd go out like a Lamb when you went to hanging.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.l: I would take April, take the ſweet o'th' year,
And kiſs my Wench upon the tender flowrets,
Tumble on every Green, and as the Birds ſung,
Embrace, and melt away my Soul in pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: You would go a Maying gayly to the Gallows.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Prithee tell us ſome news.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: I'll tell ye all I know,
You may be honeſt, and poor fools, as I am,
And blow your fingers ends.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: That's no news, Fool.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: You may be knaves then when you pleaſe, ſtark knaves,
And build fair houſes, but your heirs ſhall have none of 'em.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Theſe are undoubted.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Truth is not worth the hearing,
I'll tell you news then; There was a drunken Saylor,
That got a Mermaid with child as ſh • went a milking,
And now ſhe ſues him in the Bawdy Court for it,
The infant-Monſter is brought up in Fiſh-Street.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: I, this is ſomething.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: I'll tell you more, there was a Fiſh taken,
A monſtrous Fiſh, with a ſword by his ſide, a long ſword,
A Pike in's Neck, and a Gun in's Noſe, a huge Gun,
And letters of Mart in's mouth, from the Duke of Florence.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: This is a monſtrous lye.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: I do confeſs it:
Do you think I would tell you truths, that dare not hear 'em?
You are honeſt things, we Courtiers ſcorn to converſe with.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: A plaguey fool: but • et's conſider, Gentlemen,
Why the Queen ſtrives not to oppoſe this ſentence,
The Kingdoms honour ſuffers in this cruelty.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: No doubt the Queen, though ſhe be vertuous,
Winks at the Marriage, for by that only means
The Kings flame leſſens to the youthful Lady,
If not goes out; within this Month, I doubt not,
She hopes to rock aſleep his anger alſo;
Shall we go ſee the preparation?
'Tis time, for ſtrangers come to view the wonder.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Come, let's away, ſend my friends happier weddings.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: You ſhall be merry, come, I'll have it ſo,
Can there be any nature ſo unnoble?
Or anger ſo inhumane to purſue this?

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: I fear there is.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: Your fears are poor and fooliſh,
Though he be haſty, and his anger death,
His will like torrents, not to be reſiſted,
Yet Law and Juſtice go along to guide him;
And what Law, or what Juſtice can he find
To juſtifie his Will? what Act or Statute,
By Humane, or Divine eſtabliſhment,
Left to direct us, that makes Marriage death?
Honeſt fair Wedlock? 'twas given for encreaſe,
For preſervation of Mankind I take it;
He muſt be more than man then that dare break it.
Come, dreſs ye handſomely, you ſhall have my jewels,
And put a ſace on that contemns baſe fortune,
'Twill make him more inſult to ſee you fearful,
Outlook his anger.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: O my Valerio!
Be witneſs my pure mind, 'tis thee I grieve for.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: But ſhew it not, I would ſo crucifie him
With an innocent neglect of what he can do,
A brave ſtrong pious ſcorn, that I would ſhake him;
Put all the wanton Cupids in thine eyes,
And all the graces on that nature gave thee,
Make up thy beauty to that height of excellence,
I'll help thee, and forgive thee, as if Venus
Were now again to catch the god of War,
In his moſt rugged anger, when thou haſt him,
(As 'tis impoſſible he ſhould reſiſt thee)
And kneeling at thy conquering feet for mercy,
Then ſhew thy Vertue, then again deſpiſe him,
And all his power, then with a look of honour
Mingled with noble chaſtity, ſtrike him dead.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Good Madam dreſs me,
You arm me bravely.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: Make him know his cruelty
Begins with him firſt, he muſt ſuffer for it,
And that thy ſentence is ſo welcome to thee,
And to thy noble Lord, you long to meet it.
Stamp ſuch a deep impreſſion of thy Beauty
Into his ſoul, and of thy worthineſs,
That when Valerio and Evanthe ſleep
In one rich earth, hung round about with bleſſings,
He may run mad, and curſe his act; be luſty,
I'll teach thee how to dye too, if thou fear'ſt it.

sp.speaker: Ev.
sp.l: I thank your Grace, you have prepar'd me ſtrongly,
And my weak mind.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: Death is unwelcome never,
Unleſs is it be to tortur'd minds and ſick ſouls,
That make their own Hells; 'tis ſuch a benefit
When it comes crown'd with honour, ſhews ſo ſweet too!
Though they paint it ugly, that's but to reſtrain us,
For every living thing would love it elſe,
Fly boldly to their peace ere Nature call'd 'em;
The Reſt we have from labour, and from trouble
Is ſome Incitement, every thing alike,
The poor Slave that lies private has his liberty,
As amply as his Maſter, in that Tomb
The Earth as light upon him, and the flowers
That grow about him, ſmell as ſweet, and flouriſh.
But when we love with honour to our ends,
When Memory and Vertue are our Mourners;
What pleaſure's there! they are infinite, Evanthe;
Only, my vertuous Wench, we want our ſenſes,
That benefit we are barr'd, 'twould make us proud elſe,
And lazy to look up to happier life,
The Bleſſings of the people would ſo ſwell us.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: Good Madam, dreſs me, you have dreſt my ſoul,
The merrieſt Bride I'll be for all this miſery,
The proudeſt to ſome Eyes too.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: 'Twill do better, come, ſhrink no more.

sp.speaker: Evan.
sp.l: I am too confident. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: You are too remiſs and wanton in your angers,
You mold things handſomely, and then neglect 'em;
A powerful Prince ſhould be conſtant to his power ſtill,
And hold up what he builds, then People fear him;
When he lets looſe his hand it ſhews a weakneſs,
And men examine or contemn his greatneſs:
A ſcorn of this high kind ſhould have call'd up
A revenge equal, not a pity in you.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She is thy Siſter.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: And ſhe were my Mother,
Whilſt I conceive 'tis you ſhe has wrong'd, I hate her,
And ſhake her nearneſs off; I ſtudy, Sir,
To ſatisfie your angers that are juſt,
Before your pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I have done that already,
I fear has pull'd too many curſes on me.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Curſes or envies, on Valerio's head,
Would you take my counſel, Sir, they ſhould all light,
And with the weight not only crack his ſcull,
But his fair credit; the exquiſite vexation
I have devis'd, ſo pleaſe you give way in't,
And let it work, ſhall more afflict his ſoul,
And trench upon that honour that he brags of,
Than fear of Death in all the frights he carries;
If you ſit down here they will both abuſe ye,
Laugh at your poor relenting power, and ſcorn ye.
What ſatisfaction can their deaths bring to you,
That are prepar'd, and proud to dye, and willingly,
And at their ends will thank you for that honour?
How are you nearer the deſire you aim at?
Or if it be revenge your anger covets,
How can their ſingle deaths give you content, Sir?
Petty revenges end in blood, ſleight angers,
A Princes rage ſhould find out new diſeaſes,
Death were a pleaſure too, to pay proud fools with.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What ſhould I do?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Add but your power unto me,
Make me but ſtrong by your protection,
And you ſhall ſee what joy, and what delight,
What infinite pleaſure this poor Month ſhall yield him.
I'll make him wiſh he were dead on his Marriage-day,
Or bed-rid with old age, I'll make him curſe,
And cry and curſe, give me but power.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You have it,
Here, take my Ring, I am content he pay for't.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: It ſhall be now revenge, as I will handle it,
He ſhall live after this to beg his life too,
Twenty to one by this thread, as I'll weave it,
Evanthe ſhall be yours.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Take all authority, and be moſt happy.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Good Sir, no more pity. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Tony, three Citizens, and three Wives.

sp.speaker: 1 Wife.
sp.l: Good Maſter Tony, put me in.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Where do you dwell?

sp.speaker: 1 Wife.
sp.l: Forſooth, at the ſign of the great Shoulder of Mutton.

sp.speaker: Ton.
sp.l: A hungry man would hunt your houſe out inſtantly,
Keep the Dogs from your door; Is this Lettice Ruff your
Husband? a fine ſharp ſallet to your ſign.

sp.speaker: 2 Wife.
sp.l: Will you put me in too?

sp.speaker: 3 Wife.
sp.l: And me, good Maſter Tony.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Put ye all in? you had beſt come twenty more; you
Think 'tis eaſie, a trick of legerdemain, to put ye all in,
'Twould poſe a fellow that had twice my body,
Though it were all matle into chines and fillets.

sp.speaker: 2 Wi.
sp.l: Put's into th' wedding, Sir, we would fain ſee that.

sp.speaker: 1 Wife.
sp.l: And the brave Maſque too.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: You two are pretty women, are you their husbands?

sp.speaker: 2 Citiz.
sp.l: Yes, for want of better.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: I think ſo too, you would not be ſo mad elſe
To turn 'em looſe to a company of young Courtiers,
That ſwarm like Bees in May, when they ſee young wenches;
You muſt not ſqueak.

sp.speaker: 3 Wife.
sp.l: No Sir, we are better tutor'd.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Nor if a young Lord offer you the courteſie—

sp.speaker: 2 Wife.
sp.l: We know what 'tis, Sir.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Nor you muſt not grumble,
If you be thruſt up hard, we thruſt moſt furiouſly.

sp.speaker: 1 Wife.
sp.l: We know the worſt.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Get you two in then quietly,
And ſhift for your ſelves; we muſt have no old women,
They are out of uſe, unleſs they have petitions,
Beſides they cough ſo loud they drown the Muſick.
You would go in too, but there is no place for ye?
I am ſorry for't, go and forget your wives,
Or pray they may be able to ſuffer patiently.
You may have Heirs may prove wiſe Aldermen,
Go, or I'le call the Guard.

sp.speaker: 3 Citi.
sp.l: We will get in, we'l venture broken pates elſe.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: 'Tis impoſſible,
You are too ſecurely arm'd; how they flock hither,
And with what joy the women run by heaps
To ſee this Marriage! they tickle to think of it,
They hope for every month a husband too;
Still how they run, and how the wittals follow 'em,
The weak things that are worn between the leggs,
That bruſhing, dreſſing, nor new naps can mend,
How they poſt to ſee their own confuſion?
This is a merry world.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Look to the door Sirrah,
Thou art a fool, and may'ſt do miſchief lawfully.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Give me your hand, you are my Brother fool,
You may both make the Law, and marr it preſently.
Do you love a wench?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Who does not, fool?

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Not I, unleſs you will give me a longer leaſe to marry her.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: what are all theſe that come, what buſineſs have they?

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Some come to gape, thoſe are my fellow fools;
Some to get home their wives, thoſe be their own fools;
Some to rejoyce with thee, thoſe be the times fools;
And ſome I fear to curſe thee, thoſe are poor fools,
sp.stage: Enter Caſſander, an old Lady paſſing over.
sp.l: A •• t people call them honeſt. Look, look King, look,
A weather-beaten Lady new caresn'd.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: An old one.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: The glaſſes of her eyes are new rub'd over,
And the worm-eaten records in her face are daub'd up neatly?
She layes her breaſts out too, like to poch'd eggs
That had the yelks ſuckt out; they get new heads alſo,
New teeth, new tongues, for the old are all worn out,
And as 'tis hop'd, new tayls.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: For old Courtiers,
The young ones are too ſtirring for their travels.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Go leave your knavery, and help to keep the door well,
I will have no ſuch preſs.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: Lay thy hand o'thy heart King.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I'le have ye whipt.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: The fool and thou art parted. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Sorano work, and free me from this ſpell,
'Twixt love and ſcorn there's nothing felt but hell. Exit,

div.stage: Enter Valerio, Camillo, Cleanthes, Menallo, and Servants.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Tye on my Scarf, you are ſo long about me,
Good my Lords help, give me my other Cloak,
That Hat and Feather, Lord what a Taylor's this,
To make me up thus ſtraight! one ſigh would burſt me,
I have not room to breath, come button, button,
Button, apace.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: I am glad to ſee you merry Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: 'Twould make you merry had you ſuch a wife,
And ſuch an age to injoy her in.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: An ago Sir?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: A moneth's an age to him that is contented,
What ſhould I ſeek for more? give me my ſword.
Ha my good Lords, that every one of you now
Had but a Lady of that youth and beauty
To bleſs your ſelves this night with, would ye not?
Pray ye ſpeak uprightly.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: We confeſs ye happy,
And we could well wiſh ſuch another Banquet,
But on that price my Lord—

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: 'Twere nothing elſe,
No man can ever come to aim at Heaven,
But by the knowledge of a Hell. Theſe ſhooes are heavy,
And if I ſhould be call'd to dance they'l clog me,
Get me ſome pumps; I'le tell ye brave Cami lo,
And you dear friends, the King has honour'd me,
Out of his gracious favour has much honour'd me,
To limit me my time, for who would live long?
Who would be old? 'tis ſuch a wearineſs,
Such a diſeaſe, that hangs like lead upon us.
As it increaſes, ſo vexations,
Griefs of the minde, pains of the feeble body,
Rheums, coughs, catarrhs, we are but our living coffins;
Beſides, the fair ſoul's old too, it grows covetous,
Which ſhews all honour is departed from us,
And we are Earth again.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: You make fair uſe Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I would not live to learn to lye Cleanthes
For all the world, old men are prone to that too;
Thou that haſt been a Souldier, Menallo,
A noble Souldier, and defied all danger,
Adopted thy brave arm the heir to victory,
Would'ſt thou live ſo long till thy ſtrength forſook thee?
Till thou grew'ſt only a long tedious ſtory
Of what thou hadſt been? till thy ſword hang by,
And lazie Spiders fill'd the hilt with cobwebs?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: No ſure, I would not.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: 'Tis not ſit ye ſhould,
To dye a young man is to be an Angel,
Our great good parts put wings unto our ſouls:
We'l have a rouſe before we go to bed friends,
Pray ye tell me, is't a hanſome Mask we have?

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: We underſtand ſo.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And the young gent. dance?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: They do Sir, and ſome dance well.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: They muſt before the Ladies,
We'l have a rouſe before we go to bed friends,
A luſty one, 'twill make my blood dance too. Muſick

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Ten if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And we'l be wondrous merry,
They ſtay ſure, come, I hear the Muſick forward,
You ſhall have all Gloves preſently. Exit.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: We attend Sir, but firſt we muſt look to th'
Doors. Knocking within.
The King has charged us. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: What a noiſe do you keep there? call my fellows O' the Guard; you muſt ceaſe now untill the King be Enter'd, he is gone to th' Temple now.

sp.speaker: 2 Serv.
sp.l: Look to that back door, and keep it faſt,
They ſwa • m like Bees about it.

div.stage: Enter Camillo, Cleanthes, Menallo, Tony, following.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Keep back thoſe Citizens, and let their wives in,
Their handſome wives.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: They have crowded me to Veriuyce,
I ſweat like a Butter-box.

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: Stand further off there.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Take the women aſide, and talk with 'em in private,
Give 'em that they came for.

sp.speaker: Tony.
sp.l: The whole Court cannot do it;
Beſides, the next Mask if we uſe 'em ſo,
They'l come by millions to expect our largeſs;
We have broke a hundred heads.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Are they ſo tender?

sp.speaker: Ton.
sp.l: But 'twas behind, before they have all murrions.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Let in thoſe Ladies, make 'em room for ſhame there.

sp.speaker: Ton.
sp.l: They are no Ladies, there's one bald before 'em,
A gent bald, they are curtail'd queans in hired clothes,
They come out of Spain I think, they are very ſultry.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Keep 'em in breath for an Embaſſadour.
Me thinks my noſe ſhakes at their memories,
What bounſing's that?

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: I am one of the Muſick Sir.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: I have ſweat-meats for the banquet.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Let 'em in.

sp.speaker: Ton.
sp.l: They lye my Lord, they come to ſeek their wives,
Two broken Citizens.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Break 'em more, they are but bruſled yet.
Bold Raſcals, offer to diſturb your wives?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Lock the doors faſt, the Muſick, hark, the King comes.

body.l: The King, Queen, Valerio, Evanthe, Ladies, Attendants, Camillo, Cleanthes, Sorano, Menallo.

l.stage: Cupid deſcends, the Graces ſitting by him, Cupid being bound the Graces unbind him, he ſpeaks.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: Unbind me, my delight, this night is mine,
Now let me look upon what Stars here ſhine,
Let me behold the beauties, then clap high
My cullor'd wings, proud of my Deity;
I am ſatisfied, bind me again, and faſt.
My angry Bow will make too great a waſt
Of beauty elſe, now call my Maskers in,
Call with a Song, and let the ſports begin;
Call all my ſervants the effects of love,
And to a meaſure let them nobly move.
Come you ſervants of proud love,
Come away:
Fairly, nobly, gently move.
Too long, too long you make us ſtay;
Fancy, Deſire, Delight, Hope, Fear,
Diſtruſt and Jealouſie, be you too here;
Conſuming Care, and raging Ire,
And Poverty in poor attire,
March fairly in, and laſt Deſpair;
Now full Muſick ſtrike the Air.

body.stage: Enter the Maskers, Fancy, Deſire, Delight, Hope, Fear, Diſtruſt, Jealouſie, Care, Ire, Deſpair, they dance, after which Cupid ſpeaks.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: Away, I have done, the day begins to light,
Lovers, you know your ſate, good night, good night.

body.stage: Cupid and the Graces aſcend in the Chariot.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Come to the Banquet, when that's ended Sir,
I'le ſee you i' bed, and ſo good night; be merry,
You have a ſweet bed fellow.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I thank your Grace,
And ever ſhall be bound unto your nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I pray I may deſerve your thanks, ſet forward.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter divers Monks, Alphonſo going to the Tomb, Rugio, and Frier Marco, diſcover the Tomb and a Chair.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: THe night grows on, lead ſoftly to the Tomb,
And ſing not till I bid ye; let the Muſick
Play gently as he paſſes.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.l: O fair picture,
That wert the living hope of all our honours;
How are we baniſht from the joy we dreamt of?
Will he ne're ſpeak more?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis full three moneths Lord Rugio,
Since any articulate ſound came from his tongue,
Set him down gently. Sits in a Chair.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.l: What ſhould the reaſon be Sir?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: As 'tis in nature with thoſe loving Husbands,
That ſympathize their wives pains, and their throes
When they are breeding, and 'tis uſuall too,
We have it by experience; ſo in him Sir,
In this moſt noble ſpirit that now ſuffers;
For when his honour'd Father good Brandino
Fell ſick, he felt the griefs, and labour'd with them,
His fits and his diſeaſe he ſtill inherited,
Grew the ſame thing, and had not nature check'd him,
Strength, and ability, he had dyed that hour too.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.l: Embleme or noble love!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That very minute
His Fathers breath forſook him, that ſame inſtant,
A rare example of his piety,
And love paternal, the Organ of his tongue.
Was never heard to ſound again; ſo near death
He ſeeks to wait upon his worthy Father,
But that we force his meat, he were one body.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.l: He points to'th' Tomb.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That is the place he honours,
A houſe I fear he will not be long out of.
He will toth' Tomb, good my Lord lend your hand;
How ſing the Funeral Song, and let him kneel,
For then he is pleas'd. A Song.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.l: Heaven lend thy powerfull hand,
And eaſe this Prince.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: He will paſs back again. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: They drink abundantly, I am hot with wine too,
Luſtily warm, I'le ſteal now to my happineſs,
'Tis midnight, and the ſilent hour invites me,
But ſhe is up ſtill, and attends the Queen;
Thou dew of wine and ſleep hang on their eye-lids,
Steep their dull ſenſes in the healths they drink,
That I may quickly find my lov'd Evanthe.
The King is merry too, and drank unto me,
Sign of fair peace, O this nights bleſſedneſs!
If I had forty heads I would give all for't.
Is not the end of our ambitions,
Of all our humane ſtudies, and our travels,
Of our deſires, the obtaining of our wiſhes?
Certain it is, and there man makes his Center.
I have obtain'd Evanthe, I have married her,
Can any fortune keep me from injoying her?
I have my wiſh, what's left me to accuſe now?
I am friends with all the world, but thy baſe malice;
Go glory in thy miſchiefs thou proud man,
And cry it to the world thou haſt ruin'd vertue;
Flow I contemn thee and thy petty malice!
And with what ſcorn, I look down on thy practice!

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: You'l ſing me a new Song anon Valerio,
And wiſh theſe hot words—

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I deſpiſe thee fellow,
Thy threats, or flatteries, all I fling behind me;
I have my end, I have thy noble Siſter,
A name too worthy of thy blood; I have married her,
And will injoy her too.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: 'Tis very likely.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And that ſhort moneth I have to bleſs me with her
I'le make an age, I'le reckon each embrace
A year of pleaſure, and each night a Jubile,
Every quick kiſs a Spring; and when I mean
To loſe my ſelf in all delightfulneſs,
Twenty ſweet Summers I will tye together
In ſpight of thee, and thy malignant Maſter:
I will dye old in love, though young in pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: But that I late thee deadly, I could pity thee,
Thou art the pooreſt miſerable thing
This day on earth; I'le tell thee why Valerio,
All thou eſteemeſt, and build'ſt upon for happineſs,
For joy, for pleaſure, for delight is paſt thee,
And like a wanton dream already vaniſht.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Is my love falſe?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: No, ſhe is conſtant to thee,
Conſtant to all thy miſery ſhe ſhall be,
And curſe thee too.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Is my ſtrong body weakn'd,
Charm'd, or abus'd with ſubtle drink? ſpeak villain.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Neither, I dare ſpeak, thou art ſtill as luſty
As when thou lov'dſt her firſt, as ſtrong and hopefull,
The month thou haſt given thee is a month of miſery,
And where thou think'ſt each hour ſhall yield a pleaſure,
Look for a killing pain, for thou ſhalt find it
Before thou dyeſt, each minute ſhall prepare it,
And ring ſo many knels to ſad afflictions;
The King has given thee a long month to dye in,
And miſerably dye.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Undo thy Riddle,
I am prepar'd what ever • ate ſhall follow.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Doſt thou ſee this Ring?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I know it too.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Then mark me,
By vertue of this Ring this I pronounce to thee,
'Tis the Kings will.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Let me know it ſuddenly.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: If thou doſt offer to touch Evanthes body
Beyond a kiſs, though thou art married to her,
And lawfully as thou think'ſt may'ſt injoy her,
That minute ſhe ſhall dye.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: O Devil —

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: If thou diſcover this command unto her,
Or to a friend that ſhall importune thee,
And why thou abſtaineſt, and from whoſe will, ye all periſh,
Upon the ſelf-ſame forfeit: are ye fitted Sir?
Now if ye love her, ye may preſerve her life ſtill,
If not, you know the worſt, how falls your month out?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: This tyranny could never be invented
But in the ſchool of Hell, Earth is too innocent;
Not to injoy her when ſhe is my wife?
When ſhe is willing too?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: She is moſt willing,
And will run mad to miſs; but if you hit her,
Be ſure you hit her home, and kill her with it;
There are ſuch women that will dye with pleaſure:
The Are will follow elſe, that will not fail
To fetch her Maiden head, and diſpatch her quickly;
Then ſhall the world know you are the cauſe of Murther,
And as 'tis requiſite your life ſhall pay for't

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Thou doſt but jeſt, thou canſt not be ſo monſtrous
As thou proclaim'ſt thy ſelf; thou art her Brother,
And there muſt be a feeling heart within thee
Of her afflictions; wert thou a ſtranger to us,
And bred amongſt wild rocks, thy nature wild too,
Affection in thee as thy breeding, cold,
And unrelenting as the rocks that nouriſht thee,
Yet thou muſt ſhake to tell me this; they tremble
When the rude ſea threatens divorce amongſt 'em,
They that are ſenceleſs things ſhake at a tempeſt;
Thou art a man —

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Be thou too then, 'twill try thee,
And patience now will beſt become thy nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Invent ſome other torment to afflict me,
All, if thou pleaſe, put all afflictions on me,
Study thy brains out for 'em, ſo this be none
I care not of what nature, nor what cruelty,
Nor of what length.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: This is enough to vex ye.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: The tale of Tantalus is now prov'd true,
And from me ſhall be regiſtred Authentick;
To have my joyes within my arms, and lawfull,
Mine own delights, yet dare not touch.
Even as thou hateſt me Brother, let no young man know this,
As thou ſhalt hope for peace when thou moſt needeſt it,
Peace in thy ſoul, deſire the King to kill me,
Make me a traitor, any thing, I'le yield to it,
And give thee cauſe ſo I may dye immediately;
Lock me in Priſon where no Sun may ſee me,
In wails ſo thick no hope may e're come at me;
Keep me from meat, and drink, and ſleep, I'le bleſs thee;
Give me ſome damned potion to deliver me,
That I may never know my ſelf again, forget
My Country, kindred, name and fortune; laſt,
That my chaſte love may never appear before me,
This were ſome comfort.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: All I have I have brought ye,
And much good may it do ye my dear Brother,
See ye obſerve it well; you will find about ye
Many eyes ſet, that ſhall o're-look your actions,
If you tranſgreſs ye know, and ſo I leave ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Heaven be not angry, and I have ſome hope yet.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Haſt thou been with him?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Yes, and given him that Sir
Will make him curſe his Birth; I told ye which way.
Did you but ſee him Sir, but look upon him,
With what a troubled and dejected nature
He walks now in a miſt, with what a ſilence,
As if he were the ſhrowd he wrapt himſelf in,
And no more of Valerio but his ſhadow,
He ſeeks obſcurity to hide his thoughts in,
You would wonder and admire for all you know it,
His jollity is down, valed to the ground Sir,
And his high hopes of full delights and pleaſures
Are turn'd tormenters to him, ſtrong diſeaſes.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: But is there hope of her?

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: It muſt fall neceſſary,
She muſt diſlike him, quarrel with his perſon,
For women once deluded are next Devils,
And in the height of that opinion Sir,
You ſhall put on again, and ſhe muſt meet ye.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I am glad of this.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: I'le tell ye all the circumſtance
Within this hour, but ſure I heard your grace
To day as I attended, make ſome ſtops,
Some broken ſpeechs, and ſome ſighs between,
And then your Brothers name I heard diſtinctly,
And ſome ſad wiſhes after.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ye are i'th' right Sir,
I would he were as ſad as I could wiſh him,
Sad as the Earth.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Would ye have it ſo?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Thou heareſt me,
Though he be ſick with ſmall hope of recovery,
That hope ſtill lives, and mens eyes live upon it,
And in their eye their wiſhes; my Sorano,
Were he but cold once in the tomb he dotes on,
As 'tis the fitteſt place for melancholy,
My Comt ſhould be another Paradiſe,
And flow with all delights.

sp.speaker: Sor.
sp.l: Go to your pleaſures, let me alone with this,
Hope ſhall not trouble ye, nor he three dayes.

sp.speaker: Fred.
