sp.l: A loving fool I know it,
By your bloudleſs froſty lips; then having related
How much you ſuffer for her, and how well
You do deſerve it—

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: How? to ſuffer?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: No, Sir, to have your love return'd.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: That's good, I thank you.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I will deliver her an Inventory
Of your good parts: as this, your precious noſe
Dropping affection; your high forehead reaching
Almoſt to the Crown of your head; your ſlender waſte,
And a back not like a threſhers, but a bending,
And Court-like back, and ſo forth, for your Body.
But when I touch your mind, for that muſt take her,
(Since your out-ſide promiſes little) I'll enlarge it,
(Though ne'r ſo narrow) as your arts to thrive,
Your compoſition with the Cook and Butler
For Cony-Skins and Chippings, and half a ſhare
With all the under Officers of the houſe,
In ſtrangers bounties, that ſhe ſhall have all,
And you as 'twere her Bailiff.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: As I will be.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: As you ſhall, ſo I'll promiſe. Then your qualities,
As playing on a Gyttern, or a Jews-Trump.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: A little too on the Viol.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Fear you nothing.
Then ſinging her aſleep with curious Catches
Of your own making; for as I have heard,
You are Poetical.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Something given that way;
Yet my works ſeldom thrive: and the main reaſon
The Poets urge for't, is, becauſe I am not
As poor as they are.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Very likely; fetch her
While I am in the vein.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: 'Tis an apt time, my Lady being at her Prayers

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Let her pray on.
Nay go, and if upon my interceſſion
She do you not ſome favour, I'll diſclaim her;
I'll ruminate on't the while.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: A hundred Crowns is your reward.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Without 'em — nay no trifling. Ex. Mal.
That this dull clod of ignorance ſhould know
How to get money, yet want eyes to ſee
How groſly he's abus'd, and wrought upon!
When he ſhould make his will, the Rogue's turn'd rampant,
As he had renew'd his youth; a handſome wench,
Love one a ſpittle-whore would run away from?
Well, Maſter Steward, I will plead for you
In ſuch a method, as it ſhall appear
You are ſit to be a property.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Yonder he walks
That knows my worth and value, though you ſcorn it.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: If my Lady know not this—

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I'll anſwer it:
If you were a Nun I hope your Couſin German
Might talk with you through a grate, but you are none,
And therefore may come cloſer; ne'r hang off,
As I live you ſhall bill; ye may ſalute as ſtrangers,
Cuſtom allows it. Now, now, come upon her
With all your Oratory,
As a young Advocate ſhould, and leave no Vertue
Of mine unmentioned, I'll ſtand centinel;
Nay keep the door my ſelf. Exit.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: How have you work'd
This piece of motley to your ends?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Of that at leaſure, Miſtriſs. Kiſſing.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Lower, you are too loud,
Though the fool be deaf, ſome of the houſe may hear you.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Suppoſe they ſhould, I am a Gentleman,
And held your Kinſman, under that I hope
I may be free.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I grant it, but with caution;
But be not ſeen to talk with me familiarly,
But at fit diſtance, or not ſeen at all,
It were the better; you know my Ladies humour,
She is all honour, and compos'd of goodneſs,
(As ſhe pretends) and you having no buſineſs,
How jealous may ſhe grow?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I will be rul'd.
But you have promis'd, and I muſt enjoy you.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: We ſhall find time for that; you are too haſty,
Make your ſelf fit and I ſhall make occaſion,
Deliberation makes beſt in that buſineſs,
And contents every way.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: But you muſt feed
This fooliſh Steward with ſome ſhadow of
A future favour, that we may preſerve him
To be our inſtrument.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Hang him.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: For my ſake, Sweet,
I undertook to ſpeak for him, any Bauble,
Or ſlight employment in the way of ſervice,
Will feed him fat.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Leave him to me.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: She comes, my Lady.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I will ſatisfie her.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: How far have you prevail'd?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Obſerve.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Monſi • ur Malfort,
I muſt be brief, my couſin hath ſpoke much
In your behalf, and to give you ſome proof,
I entertain you as my ſervant,
You ſhall have the grace.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Upon your knee receive it.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: And take it as a ſpecial favour from me,
To tye my ſhooe.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: I am o're-joy'd.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Good reaſon.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: You may come higher in time.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: No more, the Lady.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: She frowns.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I thank you for this viſit couſin,
But without leave hereafter from my Lady,
I dare not change diſcourſe with you.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Pray you take your mornings draught.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I thank you: Exeunt Leon, Malf.
Happineſs attend your honour.

sp.speaker: Caliſt.
sp.l: Who gave warrant to this private parle?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: My innocence; I hope
My conference with a kinſman cannot call
Your anger on me.

sp.speaker: Caliſt.
sp.l: Kinſman? Let me have
No more of this, as you deſire you may continue mine.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Why madam (under pardon)
Suppoſe him otherwiſe: yet coming in
A lawfull way, it is excuſable.

sp.speaker: Caliſt.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I grant you are made of pureneſs,
And that your tenderneſs of honour holds
The ſoveraigntie o're your paſſions. Yet you have
A noble Husband, with allow'd embraces,
To quench laſcivious fires, ſhould ſuch flame in you,
As I muſt ne're believe. Were I the wife
Of one that could but zanie brave Cleander,
Even in his leaſt perf • ctions, (excuſe
My o're-bold inference) I ſhould deſire
To meet no other object.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: You grow fancie. Do I look further?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: No, dear Madam: and
It is my wonder or aſtoniſhment rather,
You could deny the ſervice of Liſander;
A man without a rival: one the King
And Kingdom gazes on with admiration,
For all the excellencies a Mother could
Wiſh in her only Son.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Did not mine honour
And obligation to Cleander, force me
To be deaf to his complaints?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Tis true; but yet
Your rigor to command him from your preſence,
Argu'd but ſmall compaſſion; the Groves
Witneſs his grievous ſufferings, your fair name
Upon the rinde of every gentle Poplar,
And amorous My • tle, (trees to Venus ſacred)
With adoration carv'd, and knee'ld unto,
This you (unſ •• n of him) both ſaw and heard
Without compaſſion, and what receiv'd he
For his true ſorrows? but the heavy knowledge,
That 'twas your peremptory will and pleaſure,
(How e're my Lord liv'd in him) he ſhould quit
Your ſight and houſe for ever.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I confeſs I gave him a ſtrong potion to work
Upon his hot bloud, and I hope 'twill cure him.
Yet I could wiſh the cauſe had concern'd others,
I might have met his ſorrows with more pity;
At leaſt have lent ſome counſel to his miſeries,
Though now for honours ſake, I muſt forget him,
And never know the name more of Liſander:
Yet in my juſtice I am bound to grant him,
(Laying his love aſide) moſt truely noble.
But mention him no more, this inſtant hour
My Brother Lidian, new return'd from travel,
And his brave friend Clarange, long ſince rivals
For fair and rich Olinda, are to hear
Her abſolute determination, whom
She pleaſes to elect: ſee all things ready
To entertain 'em: and on my diſpleaſure
No more words of Liſander.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: She endures to hear him nam'd by no tongue but her own.
How e're ſhe carries it, I know ſhe loves him. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Hard nature: hard condition of poor women!
That where we are moſt ſu'd to, we muſt flye moſt.
The trees grow up, and mix together freely,
The Oak's not envious of the ſailing Cedar,
The luſtie Vine not jealous of the Ivie
Becauſe ſhe clips the Elm; the flowers ſhoot up,
And wantonly kiſs one another hourly,
This bloſſome glorying in the others beauty,
And yet they ſmell as ſweet, and look as lovely:
But we are ty'd to grow alone. O honour,
Thou hard Law to our lives, chain to our freedoms
He that invented thee had many curſes;
How is my ſoul divided? O Cleander,
My beſt deſerving husband! O Liſander,
The trueſt lover that e're ſacrific'd
To Cupid againſt Hymen! O mine honour;
A Tyrant, yet to be obey'd! and 'tis
But juſtice we ſhould thy ſtrict Laws endure,
Since our obedience to thee keeps us pure. Exit.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: How inſupportable the difference
Of dear friends is, the ſorrow that I feel
For my Liſanders abſence, one that ſtamps
A reverend print on friendſhip, does aſſure me.
You are rivals for a Lady, a fair Lady,
And in the acquiſition of her favours,
Hazard the cutting of that Gordian knot
From your firſt childhood to this preſent hour,
By all the tyes of love and amity faſten'd.
I am bleſt in a wife (Heaven make me thankfull)
Inferiour to none (ſans pride I ſpeak it)
Yet if I were a free-man, and could purchaſe
At any rate the certainty to enjoy
Liſanders converſation while I liv'd,
Forgive me my Caliſta, and the Sex,
I never would ſeek change.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: My Lord and Brother,
I dare not blame your choice, Liſanders worth
Being a Miſtris to be ever courted;
Nor ſhall our equal ſuit to fair Olinda
Weaken, but adde ſtrength to our true affection,
With zeal ſo long continued.

sp.speaker: Claran.
sp.l: When we know
Whom ſhe prefers, as ſhe can chooſe but one,
By our ſo long tri'd friendſhip we have vow'd
The other ſhall deſiſt.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: 'Tis yet your purpoſe,
But how this reſolution will hold
In him that is refus'd, is not alone
Doubtfull, but dangerous.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: The rich heir is come Sir.

sp.speaker: Cleand.
sp.l: Madam Olinda?

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and makes choice,
After ſome little conference with my Lady,
Of this room to give anſwer to her ſuitors.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Already both look pale, between your hopes
To win the prize, and your deſpair to loſe
What you contended for.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: No Sir, I am arm'd.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I confident of my intereſt.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I'le believe ye when you have endur'd the teſt.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Is not your garter
Unty'd? you promis'd that I ſhould grow higher
In doing you ſervice.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Fall off or you loſe me. Exit Malfort.
Nay take your place, no Paris now ſits judge
On the contending goddeſſes. You are
The Deitie that muſt make curſt or happy
One of your languiſhng ſervants.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: I thus look with equal eyes on both; either deſerves
A fairer fortune than they can in reaſon
Hope for from m • ; f • om Lidian I expect,
When I have made him mine, all pleaſures that
The ſweetneſs of his manners, youth, and vertues
Can give aſſurance of: but turning this way

To •• av •
Claran • e, in his face appears
A •• nd of Maj • ſty which ſhould command,
Not ſue for favour. If the faireſt Lady
Of France, ſet forth with natures beſt endowments
N •• ſhould I adde a Princeſs of the bloud,
D •• now lay claim to either for a husband,
So vehement my affection is to both,
My envie at her happineſs would kill me.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: The ſtrangeſt love I ever heard.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: You can enjoy but one.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: The more I ſay the merrier.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: Witneſs theſe tears I love both, as I know
You burn with equal flames, and ſo affect me;
Abundance makes me poor; ſuch is the hard
Condition of my fortune; be your own judges;
If I ſhould favour both, 'twill • aint my honour,
And that before my life I muſt prefer;
• f one I lean to, the other is diſvalued;
You are fierie both, and love will make you warmer.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: The warmer ſtill the fitter. You are a fool Lady.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: To what may love, and the Devil jealouſie ſpur you
Is too apparent: my name's call'd in queſtion:
Your ſwords flie out, your angers range at large:
Then what a murther of my modeſty follows?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Take heed of that by any means: O innocent,
That will deny a bleſſing when 'tis offer'd,
Would I were murther'd ſo, I would thank my modeſty.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: What pauſe you on?

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: It is at length reſolv'd.

sp.speaker: Clara.
sp.l: We are on the Rack, uncertain expectation
T • e greateſt torture.
Command what you pleaſe,
And you ſhall ſee how willingly we will execute.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: Then hear what for your ſatisfaction,
And to preſerve your friendſhip I reſolve
Againſt my ſelf, and 'tis not to be alter'd:
You are both brave gentlemen, I'le ſtill profeſs it,
Both noble ſervants, for whoſe gentle offers,
T • e undeſerving, and the poor Olinda
Is ever bound; you love both, fair, and vertuouſly;
Would I could be ſo happy to content both:
Which ſince I cannot, take this reſolute anſwer;
Go f • om me both contentedly, and he
That laſt makes his return, and comes to viſit,
Comes to my bed. You know my will: farewel;
M • heart's too big to utter more: come friend.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I'le wait on you to your Coach.
You both look blank, I cannot blame you.

sp.speaker: lad.
sp.l: We have our diſpatches.

sp.speaker: Clarar.
sp.l: I'le home.

sp.speaker: lad
sp.l: And I'le abroad again, Farewel.

sp.speaker: Clarar.
sp.l: Farewel to ye.
Their blunted departure troubles me: I fear
A ſuddain and a dangerous diviſion
Of their long love will follow: have you took
Your leave of fair Olinda?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: She is gone Sir.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Had you brought news Liſander were return'd too,
I were moſt happy.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Still upon Liſander?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I know he loves me, as he loves his health
And Heaven knows I love him.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I find it ſo:
For me you have forgot, and what I am to you.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: O think not ſo. If you had loſt a Siſter
You lock'd all your delights in, it would grieve you:
A little you would wander from the fondneſs
You ow'd your husband: I have loſt a friend,
A noble friend, all that was excellent
In man, or man-kind, was contain'd within him,
That loſs my wife—

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Madam, your noble Father —
A fee for my good news.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why? what of him Sir?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Is lighted at the door, and longs to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Caliſt.
sp.l: Attend him hither.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: O my dear Laſander.
But I'le be merry: let's meet him my Caliſta.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I hope Liſanders love will now be buried:
My Father will bring joy enough for one moneth,
To put him out of memorie.

div.stage: Enter Dorilaus, hi • arm in a ſcarff.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: How do you Son?
Bleſs my fair child, I am come to viſit yee,
To ſee what houſe you keep, they ſay you are bountifull,
I like the noiſe well, and I come to trie it.
Ne're a great belly yet? how have you trifl'd?
If I had done ſo (Son) I ſhould have heard on't
On both ſides by Saint Denis.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: You are nobly welcom Sir:
We have time enough for that.

sp.speaker: Dorilaus.
sp.l: See how ſhe bluſhes!
'Tis a good ſign you'l mend your fault, how doſt thou,
My good Caliſta?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Well, now I ſee you Sir;
I hope you bring a fruitfulneſs along with ye.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Good luck, I never miſs, I was ever good at it:
Your mother groan'd for't wench, ſo did ſome other,
But I durſt never tell.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: How does your arm Sir?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Have you been let bloud of late?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Againſt my will Sir.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: A fall dear Father?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: No, a Gun, dear Daughter;
Two or three Guns; I have one here in my buttock,
'Twould trouble a Surgeons teeth to pull it out.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: O me! O me!

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Nay, if you fall to fainting,
'Tis time for me to trudge: art ſuch a coward,
At the meer name of hurt to change thy colour?
I have been ſhot that men might ſee clean through me,
And yet I fainted not: beſides my ſelf,
Here a • e an hoſpital of hurt men for ye.

div.stage: Enter Servants, wounded in ſeveral places.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: What ſhould this wonder be?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am amaz'd at it.

sp.speaker: Doril.
sp.l: What think ye of theſe? they are every one hurt ſoundly,
Hurt to the proof, they are through, and through I aſſure ye;
And that's good game, they ſcorn your puling ſcratches.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Who did this Sir?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Leave crying, and I'le tell you,
And get your plaiſters, and your warm ſtupes ready:
Have you ne're a Shepheard that can tarr us over?
'Twill prove a buſineſs elſe, we are ſo many.
Coming to ſee you, I was ſet upon,
I and my men, as we were ſinging frolickly,
Not dreaming of an ambuſh of baſe Rogues,
Set on i'th' foreſt, I have forgot the name —

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: 'Twixt this, and Fountaine-Bleau,
In the wild Foreſt?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: The ſame, the ſame, in that accurſed Foreſt,
Set on by villains, that make boot of all men,
The Peers of France are pillage there, they ſhot at us,
Hurt us, un-hors'd us, came to the ſword, there pli'd us,
Oppreſt us with freſh multitudes, freſh ſhot ſtill,
Rogues that would hang themſelves for a freſh doublet,
And for a Scarlet Caſſock kill their Fathers.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Lighted you among theſe?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Among theſe murtherers,
Our poor blouds were ingag'd: yet we ſtrook bravely,
And more than once or twice we made them ſhun us,
And ſhrink their rugged heads: but we were hurt all.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: How came you off? for I even long to hear that.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: After our prayers made to Heaven to help us,
Or to be mercifull unto our ſouls;
So near we were. Alas poor wench, wipe, wipe.
See Heaven ſends remedy.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am glad 'tis come Sir,
My heart was even a bleeding in my body.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: A curl'd hair Gentleman ſtept in, a ſtranger,
As he rod by, belike he heard our bickering,
Saw our diſtreſſes, drew his ſword, and prov'd
He came to execute, and not to argue.
Lord what a lightning methought flew about him,
When he once toſs'd his blade! in face Adonis,
While peace inhabited between his eye-brows:
But when his noble anger ſtirr'd his metal,
And blew his fierie parts into a flame,
Like Pallas, when ſhe ſits between two armies,
Viewing with horrid brows their ſad events,
Such then he look'd: and as her ſhield had arm'd him.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: This man Sir were a friend to give an age for.
This Gentleman I muſt love naturally:
Nothing can keep me off; I pray you go on Sir.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I will, for now you pleaſe me: this brave youth,
This bud of Mars, for yet he is no riper,
When once he had drawn bloud, and fleſh'd his ſword,
Fitted his manly metal to his ſpirit,
How he beſtirr'd him! what a lane he made!
And through their fierie Bullets thruſt ſecurely:
The hardned villains wondring at his confidence,
Lame as I was I follow'd, and admir'd too,
And ſtirr'd, and laid about me with new ſpirit,
My men too with new hearts thruſt into action,
And down the Rogues went.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I am ſtruck with wonder.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Remember but the ſtorie of ſtrong Hector,
When like to lightning he broke through his vanguard,
How the Greeks frighted ran away by Troops,
And trod down Troops to ſave their lives: ſo this man
Diſpers'd theſe ſlaves: had they been more and mightier,
He had come off the greater, and more wonder.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Where is the man, good Sir, that we may honour him?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: That we may fall in ſuperſtition to him.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I know not that, from me he late departed,
But not without that pious care to ſee ſafe
Me, and my weak men lodg'd, and dreſs'd; I urg'd him
Firſt hither, that I might more freely thank him:
He told me he had buſineſs, crav'd my pardon,
Buſineſs of much import.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Know you his name?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: That he deny'd me too: a vow had bar'd him.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: In that he was not noble to be nameleſs.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Daughter you muſt remember him when I am dead,
And in a noble ſort requite his piety,
'Twas his deſire to dedicate this ſervice
To your fair thoughts.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: He knows me then?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I nam'd you,
And nam'd you mine: I think that's all his knowledge.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: No name, no being?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Now I am mad to know him:
Saving mine honour, any thing I had now
But to enjoy his ſight, but his bare picture;
Make me his Saint, I muſt needs honour him.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: I know his name.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: There's thy reward for't; ſpeak it.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: His man told me, but he deſir'd my ſilence.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: O Jaſper ſpeak, 'tis thy good Maſters cauſe too:
We all are bound in gratitude to compel thee.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Liſander? Yes, I am ſure it was Liſander.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Liſander? 'twas Liſander.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: 'Tis Liſander. O my baſe thoughts! my wicked!
To make queſtion this act could be another mans:
'Tis Liſander, a handſome timber'd man?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: My Liſander! Was this friends abſence to be mourn'd?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I grant it:
I'le mourn his going now, and mourn it ſeriouſly:
When you weep for him, Sir, I'le bear you company.
That ſo much honour, ſo much honeſty
Should be in one man, to do things thus bravely,
Make me his Saint, to me give this brave ſervice:
What may I do to recompence his goodneſs?
I cannot tell.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Come Sir, I know you are ſickly, ſo are your men.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs I am weak,
And fitter for a bed than long diſcourſes.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: You ſhall hear to morrow, to morrow provide Surgeons.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Liſander —

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: What new fire is this? Liſander— Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Liſ
sp.l: PR • thee good Lancelot remember that
Thy Maſter's life is in thy truſt, and therefore
Be very carefull.

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.l: I will loſe mine own, rather than hazard yours.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Take what diſguiſe
You in your own diſcretion ſhall think fitteſt,
To keep your ſelf unknown.

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.l: I warrant ye;
'Tis not the firſt time I have gone inviſible:
I am as fine a Fairie in a buſineſs
Concerning night-work —

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Leave your vanities:
With this purſe (which deliver'd,
You may ſpare your Oratory) convey this Letter to
Caliſta's woman.

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.l: 'Tis a handſom girle, Miſtris Clarinda.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I have made her mine. You know your work.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: And if I ſweat not in it,
At my return diſcard me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: O Caliſta! the faireſt! cruelleſt!

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: So early ſtirring? a good day to you.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I was viewing Sir,
The ſite of your houſe, and the handſomneſs about it:
Believe me it ſtands healthfully and ſweetly.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: The houſe and Maſter of it really
Are ever at your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I return it:
Now if you pleaſe go forward in your ſtorie
Of your dear friend and Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I will tell it,
And tell it ſhort, becauſe 'tis breakfaſt time,
(And love is a tedious thing to a quick ſtomach)
You eat not yeſter-night.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I ſhall endure Sir.

sp.speaker: Clara.
sp.l: My ſelf (and as I then deliver'd to you)
A Gentleman of noble hope, one Lidian,
Both brought up from our infancy together,
One company, one friendſhip, and one exerciſe
Ever affecting, one bed holding us,
One grief, and one joy parted ſtill between us,
More than companions, twins in all our actions,
We grew up till we were men, held one heart ſtill:
Time call'd us on to Arms, we were one Souldier,
Alike we ſought our dangers and our honours,
Gloried alike one in anothers nobleneſs:
When Arms had made us fit, we were one lover,
We lov'd one woman, lov'd without diviſion,
And woo'd a long time with one fair affection;
And ſhe, as it appears, loves us alike too.
At length conſidering what our love muſt grow to,
And covet in the end, this one was parted,
Rivals and honours make men ſtand at diſtance.
We then woo'd with advantage, but were friends ſtill,
Saluted fairly, kept the peace of love,
We could not both enjoy the Ladies favour,
Without ſome ſcandal to her reputation,
We put it to her choice, this was her ſentence,
To part both from her, and the laſt returning
Should be her Lord; we obey'd, and now you know it;
And for my part, (ſo truely I am touch'd with't)
I will go far enough, and be the laſt too,
Or ne're return.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: A ſentence of much cruelty;
But mild, compar'd with what's pronounc'd on me.
Our loving youth is born to many miſeries.
What is that Lidian pray ye?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Caliſta's Brother, if ever you have heard of that fair Lady.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I have ſeen her Sir.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Then you have ſeen a wonder.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I do confeſs: of what years is this Lidian?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: About my years: there is not much between us.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I long to know him.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Tis a vertuous longing,
As many hopes hang on his noble head,
As bloſſoms on a bough in May, and ſweet ones.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Ye are a fair ſtorie of your friend.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Of truth Sir: now, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: There is a Gentleman
At door, would ſpeak with you on private buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: With me?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: He ſaies ſo, and brings haſte about him.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Wait on him in. Exit Servant.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I will retire the while, to the next room.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: We ſhall not long diſturb you.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: Save ye, Sir.

sp.speaker: Clara.
sp.l: The like to you, fair Sir: pray you come near.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: Pray you inſtruct me for I know you not.
With Monſieur Clarange I would ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I am he, Sir:
Ye are nobly welcome; I wait your buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: This will inform you.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Will you pleaſe to ſit down? Reads.
He ſhall command me Sir, I'le wait upon him
Within this hour.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: Y'are a noble Gentleman,
Wil't pleaſe you bring a friend? we are two of us,
And pity either, Sir, ſhould be unfurniſh'd.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I have none now, and the time is ſet ſo ſhort,
'Twill not be poſſible.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: Do me the honour:
I know you are ſo full of brave acquaintance,
And worthy friends, you cannot want a partner:
I would be loth to ſtand ſtill, Sir; beſides,
You know the cuſtom, and the vantage of it,
If you come in alone.

sp.speaker: C ar.
sp.l: And I muſt meet it.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: Send, we'l defer an hour, let us be equal:
Games won and loſt on equal terms ſhew faireſt.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Tis to no purpoſe to ſend any whither,
Unleſs men be at home by Revelation:
So pleaſe you breath a while; when I have done with him,
You may be exercis'd too: I'le trouble no man.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: They are very loud. Now what's the news?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I muſt leave you,
Leave you a while, two hours hence I'le return friend.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: A little buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: And't be but a little, you may take me with ye.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Twill be a trouble to you.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: No indeed, to do you ſervice, I account a pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I muſt alone.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Tis neceſſity —
Before you paſs the walks, and back again,
I will be with ye.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: If it be not unmannerly
To preſs you, I would go.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I'le tell you true, Sir,
This Gentleman and I upon appointment,
Are going to viſit a Lady.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I am no Capuchin, why ſhould not I go?

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: Take the Gentleman,
Come he may ſee the Gentlewoman too,
And be moſt welcom, I do beſeech you take him.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: By any means, I love to ſee a Gentlewoman,
A prettie wench too.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Well, Sir, we'll meet you,
And at the place: My ſervice to the Lady.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: I kiſs your hand. Exit.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Prethee read o're her Letter.

sp.speaker: Liſander

body.p: I Know you have conſider'd the dark ſentence Olinda gave us, and that (however ſhe diſguis'd it) it pointed more at our ſwords edges than our bodies baniſhments; the laſt muſt injoy her: if we retire, our youths are loſt in wandring; in emulation we ſhall grow old men, and feeble, which is the ſcorn of love, and ruſt of honour, and ſo return more fit to wed our Sepulchers, than the Saint we aim at; let us therefore make our journey ſhort, and our hearts ready, and with our ſwords in our hands put it to fortune, which ſhall be worthy to receive that bleſſing, I'le ſtay you on the mountain, our old hunting place, this Gentleman alone runs the hazard with me, and ſo I kiſs your hand.

sp.l: Is this your wench? you'l find her a ſharp Miſtris.
What have I thruſt my ſelf into? is this that Lidian
You told me of?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: The ſame.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: My Ladies Brother?
No cauſe to heave my ſword againſt but his?
To ſave the Father yeſterday, and this morning,
To help to kill the Son? this is moſt courteous?
The only way to make the Daughter doat on me.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Why do you muſe? would ye go off?

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: No, no, I muſt on now; this will be kindly taken;
No life to ſacrifice, but part of hers?
Do you fight ſtraight?

sp.speaker: Clara.
sp.l: Yes, preſently.

sp.speaker: Liſan.
sp.l: To morrow then,
The balefull tidings of this day will break out,
And this nights Sun will ſet in bloud; I am troubl'd:
If I am kill'd, I am happy.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Will you go friend?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I am ready Sir, fortune thou haſt made me monſtrous.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Your couſin, and my true friend, luſty Leon,
Shall know how you uſe me.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Be more temperate,
Or I will never uſe, nor know you more
I'th' way of a ſervant: all the houſe takes notice
Of your ridiculous fopperie; I have no ſooner
Perform'd my duties in my Ladies chamber,
And ſhe ſcarce down the ſtairs, but you appear
Like my evil ſpirit to me.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Can the fiſh live out of the water, or the Salamander
Out of the fire? or I live warm, but in
The f • ying pan of your favour?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Pray you forget
Your curious compariſons, borrowed from
The pond, and kitchin, and remember what
My Ladies pleaſure is for th' entertainment
Of her noble Father.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I would learn the art of memory in your table book.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Very good ſir, no more but up and ride, I apprehend
Your meaning, ſoft fire makes ſweet mault Sir:
I'le anſwer you in a Proverb.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: But one kiſs from thy hony lip.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You fight too high, my hand is
A fair aſcent from my foot, his ſlavering kiſſes
Spoil me more gloves, —enough for once, you'l ſurfeit
With too much grace.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Have you no imployment for me?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Yes, yes, go ſend for Leon, and convey him
• nto the private Arbour, from his mouth
• hear your praiſes with more faith.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I am gone; yet one thing e're I go, there's at the door
The rareſt Fortune-teller, he hath told me
The ſtrangeſt things; he knows ye are my Miſtris,
And under ſeal deliver'd how many Children
• ſhall beg • t on you, pray you give him hearing,
He'l make it good to you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: A cunning man
Of your own making, howſoe'r I'le hear him
At your intreaty.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Now I perceive ye love me,
At my entreaty, come in friend—remember
To ſpeak as I directed, he knows his leſſon,
And the right way to pleaſe her; this it is
To have a head-piece. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Lancelot, like a Fortune-teller, with a Purſe, and two Letters in it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis ſaid you can tell fortunes to come.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Yes Miſtris and what's paſt;
Unglove your hand, by this ſtraight line I ſee
You have lain crooked.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: How? lain crooked?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Yes; and in that poſture plaid at the old game,
(No body hears me, and I'le be no blab)
And at it loſt your maiden-head.
A ſhrewd fellow;
'Tis truth, but not to be confeſs'd; in this
Your palmiſtry deceives you, ſomething elſe Sir.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Ye are a great woman with your Lady, and
Acquainted with her counſels.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Still more ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: There is a noble Knight Liſander loves her,
Whom ſhe regards not, and the deſtinies
With whom I am familiar, have deliver'd
That by your means alone, he muſt enjoy her.
Your hand again, yes, yes; you have already
Promis'd him your aſſiſtance, and what's more,
Taſted his bounty, for which, from the skye
There are 200. crowns dropp'd in a Purſe,
Look back, you'l find it true; nay, open it,
'Tis good Gold I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: How, two Letters? the firſt indors'd to me? this to my Lady?
Subſcrib'd Liſander?

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: And the fortune-teller, his ſervant Lancelot.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: How had I loſt my eyes,
That I could not know thee? not a word of the loſs
Of my virginity.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Nor who I am.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I'le uſe all ſpeedy means for your diſpatch
With a welcom anſwer, but till you receive it,
Continue thus diſguis'd, Monſieur Malfort
(You know the way to humour him) ſhall provide
A lodging for you, and good entertainment;
Nay, ſince we trade both one way, thou ſhalt have
Some feeling with me, take that.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Bountifull wench may'ſt thou ne're want imployment.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nor ſuch pay boy. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Lidian, Alcidon, (at one door) Liſander, Clarange, (at another.)

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: You're welcom.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: Let us do our office firſt,
And then make choice of a new piece of ground
To try our fortunes.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: All's fair here.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: And here, their ſwords are equal.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: If there be any odds in mine, we will exchange.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: We'l talk of that
When we are farther off, farewel.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Farewel friend. Ex. Liſander, and Alcidon.

sp.speaker: Lidi.
sp.l: Come let us not be idle.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I will find you imployment, fear not.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: You know Sir, the cauſe that brings as hither.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: There needs no more diſcourſing,
No time, nor place for repetition now.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: Let our ſwords argue, and I wiſh Clarange,
The proud Olinda ſaw us.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Would ſhe did;
What ever eſtimation ſhe holds of me,
She ſhould behold me like a man fight for her.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: 'Tis nobly ſaid; ſet on love; and my fortune—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: The ſame for me, come home brave Lidian,
'Twas manly thruſt, this token to the Lady,
Ye have it Sir, deliver it, take breath,
I ſee ye bleed apace, ye ſhall have fair play.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: You muſt lye there a while, I cannot help you.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: Nay, then my fortune's gone, I know I muſt dye:
Yet dearly will I ſell my love, come on both,
And uſe your fortunes, I expect no favour;
Weak as I am, my confidence ſhall meet ye.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Yield up your cauſe and live.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: What doſt thou hold me?
A recreant, that prefers life before credit?
Though I bleed hard, my honour finds no Iſſue,
That's conſtant to my heart.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Have at your life then.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Hold, or I'le turn, and bend my ſword againſt ye;
My cauſe Clarange too, view this brave Gentleman,
That yet may live to kill you, he ſtands nobly,
And has as great a promiſe of the day
As you can tye unto your ſelf, he's ready,
His ſword as ſharp, view him with that remembrance,
That you deliver'd him to me Clarange:
And with thoſe eyes, that clearneſs will become ye:
View him, as you reported him; ſurvey him,
Fix on your friendſhip Sir, I know you are noble,
And ſtep but inward to your old affection;
Examine but t • at ſoul grew to your boſom,
And try then if your ſword will bite, it cannot,
The edge will turn again, aſham'd, and blunted;
Lidian, you are the pattern of fair friendſhip,
Exampled for your love, and imitated,
The Temple of true hearts, ſtor'd with affections,
For ſweetneſs of your ſpirit made a Saint,
Can you decline this nobleneſs to anger?
To mortal anger? 'gainſt the man ye love moſt?
Have ye the name of vertuous, not the nature?

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: I will ſit down.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: And I'le ſit by you, Lidian.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: And I'le go on, can Heaven be pleas'd with theſe things?
To ſee two hearts that have been twin'd together,
Married in friendſhip • o • the world, to wonder,
Of one growth, of one nouriſhment, one health,
Thus mortally divorc'd for one weak woman?
Can love be pleas'd? love is a gentle ſpirit,
The wind that blows the April flowers, not ſofter;
She is drawn with doves to ſhew her peacefulneſs,
Lions and bloody Pards are Mars's ſervants;
Would ye ſerve love? do it with humbleneſs,
Without a noiſe, with ſtill prayers, and ſoft murmurs;
Upon her Altars offer your obedience,
And not your brawls; ſhe's won with tears, not terrors:
That fire ye kindle to her deity
Is only gratefull when it's blown with ſighs,
And holy Incenſe flung with white hand-innocence;
Ye wound her now; ye are too ſuperſtitious,
No ſacrifice of bloud, or death ſhe longs for.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: Came he from Heaven?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: He tells us truth good Lidian.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: That part of noble love which is moſt ſweet,
And gives eternal being to fair beauty,
Honour, you hack i' pieces with your ſwords,
And that ye fight to crown, ye kill, fair credit.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Thus we embrace, no more fight, but all friendſhip,
And where love pleaſes to beſtow his benefits,
Let us not argue.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: Nay, brave Sir, come in too;
You may love alſo, and may hope, if ye do,
And not rewarded for't, there is no juſtice;
Farewel friend, here let's part upon our pilgrimage,
It muſt be ſo, Cupid draws on our ſorrows.
And where the lot lights —

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I ſhall count it happineſs,
Farewel, dear friend.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Firſt, let's relieve the Gentleman
That lyes hurt in your cauſe, and bring him off,
And take ſome care for your hurts, then I will part too,
A third unfortunate, and willing wanderer. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: My fears foreſaw 'twould come to this.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I would your ſentence had been milder.

sp.speaker: Olin.
sp.l: 'Tis paſt help now.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I ſhare in your deſpair, and yet my hopes
Have not quite left me, ſince all poſſible means
Are practiſed to prevent the miſchief following
Their mortal meeting, my Lord is coaſted one way,
My Father, though his hurts forbad his travel,
Hath took another, my Brother in Law Beronte
A third, and every minute we muſt look for
The certain knowledge, which we muſt endure
With that calm patience heav'n ſhall pleaſe to lend us.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Dead both?

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Such is the rumour, and 'tis general.

sp.speaker: Olin.
sp.l: I hear my paſſing bell.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am in a fevour.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: They ſay their ſeconds too; but what they are,
Is not known yet, ſome worthy fellows certain.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Where had you knowledge?

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Of the Country people, 'tis ſpoken every where.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I heard it ſo too;
And 'tis ſo common, I do half believe it,
You have loſt a Brother, wench, he lov'd you well,
And might have liv'd to have done his country ſervice,
But he is gone, thou fell'ſt untimely, Lidian,
But by a valiant hand, that's ſome ſmall comfort,
And took him with thee too, thou lov'ſt brave company,
Weeping will do no good, you loſt a ſervant,
He might have liv'd to have been your Maſter, Lady,
But you fear'd that.

sp.speaker: Olin.
sp.l: Good Sir, be tender to me,
The news is bad enough, you need not preſs it,
I lov'd him well, I lov'd 'em both.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo.
How many more have you to love ſo Lady?
They were both fools to fight for ſuch a Fiddle;
Certain there was a dearth of noble anger,
When a ſlight woman was thought worth a quarrel.

sp.speaker: Olin.
sp.l: Pray you think nobler.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I'le tell thee what I think, the plag •• , war, famine,
Nay put in dice and drunkenneſs (and thoſe
You'l grant are pretty helps) kill not ſo many
(I mean ſo many noble) as your loves do,
Rather your lewdneſs, I crave your mercy, women,
Be not offended if I anger ye.
I am ſure ye have touch'd me deep, I came to be merry,
And with my children, but to ſee one ruin'd
By this fell accident— are they all dead?
If they be, ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: What news?

div.stage: Enter Beronte, Alcidon, Clarinda, following with a Letter.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: What, dead? ye poſe me;
I underſtand you not.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: My Brother Lidian, Clarange, and their ſeconds.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Here is one of 'em, and ſure this Gentleman's alive.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: I hope ſo, ſo is your Son, Sir, ſo is brave Clarange:
We were all hurt, that bred the general rumour,
But friends again all, and like friends we parted.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Heard ye of Liſander?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Yes, and miſs'd him narrowly:
He was one of the combatants, fought with this Gentl • man.
Second againſt your Brother, by his wiſdom
(For certainly good fortune follows him)
All was made peace, I'le tell you the reſt at dinner,
For we are hungry.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: I before I eat
Muſt pay a vow I am ſworn to; my life, Madam,
Was at Liſander's mercy, I live by it;
And for the noble favour, he deſir'd me
To kiſs your fair hand for him, offering
This ſecond ſervice as a Sacrifice
At the Altar of your vertues.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Come joy on all ſides;
Heaven will not ſuffer honeſt men to periſh.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Be proud of ſuch a friend.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Forgive me, Madam,
It was a grief might have concern'd you n • a • too.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: No work of excellence but ſtill Liſander,
Go thy waies, Worthy.

sp.speaker: Olin.
sp.l: We'l be merry too,
Were I to ſpeak again, I would be wiſer.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Too much of this rare cordial makes me ſick,
However I obey you.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: Now or never is an apt time to move her, Madam.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: Your ſervant, I would ſpeak with your Ladyſhip.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why doſt thou look about?

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: I have private buſineſs

•• at no •• muſt hear but you •
Liſander—

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Nay, is not here, but would entreat this favour,
Some of your Balſam from your own hand given,
For he is much hurt, and that he thinks would cure him.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: He ſhall have all, my Prayers too.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: But conceive me,
It muſt be from your ſelf immediately,
Pity ſo brave a Gentleman ſhould periſh,
He is ſuperſtitious, and he holds your hand
Of infinite power; I would not urge this, Madam,
But only in a mans extreams to help him.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Let him come (good wench) 'tis that I wiſh, I am happy in't,
My husband his true friend, my noble father,
The fair Olinda, all deſire to ſee him;
He ſhall have many hands.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: That he deſires not,
Nor eyes but yours, to look upon his miſeries,
For then he thinks 'twould be no perfect cure, Madam,
He would come private.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: How can that be here?
I ſhall do wrong unto all thoſe that honour him,
Beſides my credit.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Dare ye not truſt a hurt man?
Not ſtrain a courteſie to ſave a Gentleman?
To ſave his life that has ſav'd all your family?
A man that comes like a poor mortifi'd Pilgrim,
Only to beg a Bleſſing and depart again?
He would but ſee you, that he thinks would cure him.
But ſince you find fit reaſons to the contrary,
And that it cannot ſtand with your clear honour,
Though you beſt know how well he has deſerv'd of ye:
I'll ſend him word back though I grieve to do it,
Grieve at my ſoul, for certainly 'twill kill him,
What your will is.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Stay, I will think upon't; where is he, Wench?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: If you deſire to ſee him,
Let not that trouble you, he ſhall be with you,
And in that time that no man ſhall ſuſpect ye;
Your honour, Madam, is in your own free keeping;
Your care in me; in him all honeſty;
If ye deſire him not, let him paſs by ye,
And all this buſineſs reckon but a dream.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Go in, and counſel me, I would fain ſee him,
And willingly comfort him.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Tis in your power;
And if you dare truſt me, you ſhall do it ſafely,
Read that, and let that tell you, how he honours you.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Clarinda with a Key, and Leon.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: THis happy Night. Kiſſes her.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Preſerve this eagerneſs
Till we meet nearer, there is ſomething done
Will give us opportunity.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Witty Girl, the plot?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: You ſhall hear that at leiſure,
The whole houſe reels with joy at the report
Of Lidians ſafety, and that joy encreas'd
From their affection to the brave Liſander,
In being made the happy inſtrument to compound
The bloudy difference.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: They will hear ſhortly that
Will turn their mirth to mourning, he was then
The principal means to ſave two lives, but ſince
There are two faln, and by his ſingle hand,
For which his life muſt anſwer, if the King,
Whoſe arm is long, can reach him.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: We have now no ſpare time to hear ſtories, take this Key,
'Twill make your paſſage to the banquetting houſe
I'th' Garden free.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: You will not fail to come?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: For mine own ſake ne'r doubt it; now for Liſander.

div.stage: Enter Dorilaus, Cleander, Servants with lights.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: To bed, to bed, 'tis very late.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: To bed all, I have drunk a health too much.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: You'll ſleep the better,
My uſual phyſick that way.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Where's your Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: She is above, but very ill, and aguiſh;
The late fright of her Brother has much troubl'd her:
She would entreat to lye alone.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Her pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Commend my love to her, and my Prayers for her health,
I'll ſee her ere I go. Exeunt; manet Clarinda.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: All good reſt to ye;
Now to my watch for Liſander, when he is furniſh'd,
For mine own friend, ſince I ſtand Centinel,
I love to laugh i'th' evenings too, and may,
The priviledg of my place will warrant it. Exit.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: You have done well hitherto; where are we now?

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.l: Not far from the houſe, I hear by th' Owls,
There are many of your Welch falkoners about it;
Here were a night to chuſe to run away with
Another mans Wife, and do the feat.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Peace Knave,
The houſe is here before us, and ſome may hear us;
The Candles are all out.

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.l: But one i'th' Parlour,
I ſee it ſimper hither, pray come this way.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Step to the Garden-door, and feel and 't be open.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: I am going, luck deliver me from the ſaw pits,
Or I am buried quick; I hear a Dog,
No, 'tis a Cricket, ha? here's a Cuckold buried,
Take heed of his horns, Sir, here's the door, 'tis open.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Friend.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Sir, Liſander?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Ye are welcome, follow me, and make no noiſe.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Go to your horſe, and keep your watch with care,
And be ſure ye ſleep not.

sp.speaker: Lan.
sp.l: Send me out the Dairy-maid
To play at trump with me, and keep me waking,
My fellow horſe and I muſt now diſcourſe
Like two learned Almanack-Makers, of the Stars,
And tell what a plentiful year 'twill prove of Drunkards.
If I had but a pottle of Sack, like a ſharp prickle,
To knock my Noſe againſt when I am nodding,
I ſhould ſing like a Nightingale, but I muſt
Keep watch without it, I am apt to dance,
Good fortune guide me from the Faries Circles. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Clarinda with a Taper, and Liſander with a Piſtol, two Chairs ſet out.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Come near, Caliſta ſitting behind a Curtain.
I'll leave ye now, draw but that Curtain,
And have your wiſh; now, Leon, I am for thee,
We that are ſervants muſt make uſe of ſtoln hours,
And be glad of ſnatch'd occaſions. Exit.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: She is aſleep,
Fierce Love hath clos'd his lights, I may look on her,
Within her eyes 'has lo • kt the graces up,
I may behold and live; how ſweet ſhe breaths!
The orient morning breaking out in odours
Is not ſo full of perfumes, as her breath is;
She is the abſtract of all Excellence, and ſcorns a Parallel.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Your ſervant, your moſt obedient ſlave (adored Lady)
That comes but to behold thoſe eyes again,
And pay ſome Vows I have to ſacred Beauty,
And ſo paſs by; I am blind as ignorance,
And know not where I wander, how I live,
Till I receive from their bright influence
Light to direct me, for Devotions ſake,
You are the Saint I tread theſe holy ſteps to,
And holy Saints are all relenting ſweetneſs,
Be not enrag'd, nor be not angry with me;
The greateſt attribute of Heaven is mercy;
And 'tis the Crown of Juſtice, and the glory
Where it may kill with right, to ſave with pity.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why do you kneel? I know you come to mock me,
T'upbraid me with the benefits you have giv'n me,
Which are too many, and too mighty, Sir,
For my return; and I confeſs 'tis juſtice,
That for my cruelty you ſhould deſpiſe me,
And I expect however you are calm now,
A foyl you ſtrive to ſet your cauſe upon,
It will break out; Caliſta is unworthy,
Coy, proud, diſdainful, I acknowledge all,
Colder of Comfort than the frozen North is,
And more a ſtranger to Liſanders worth,
His youth and faith, than it becomes her gratitude,
I bluſh to grant it, yet take this along,
A ſoveraign medicine to allay diſpleaſure,
May be an argument to bring me off too;
She is married, and ſhe is chaſte, how ſweet that ſounds?
How it perfumes all air 'tis ſpoken in?
O dear Liſander! would you break this union?

sp.speaker: Liſ
sp.l: No, I adore it; let me kiſs your hand,
And ſeal the fair faith of a Gentleman on it.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: You are truly valiant, would it not afflict ye
To have the horrid name of Coward touch you?
S • ch is the Whore to me.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I nobly thank ye;
And may I be the ſame when I diſhonour ye;
This I may do again. Kiſſing her hand.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Ye may, and worthily;
Such comforts Maids may grant with modeſty,
And neither make her poor nor wrong her bounty;
Noble Liſander, how fond now am I of ye?
I heard you were hurt.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: You dare not heal me, Lady?
I am hurt here; how ſweetly now ſhe bluſhes?
Excellent Objects kill our ſight, ſhe blinds me;
The Roſes in the pride of May ſhew pale to her;
O Tyrant, Cuſtom! and O Coward, Honour!
How ye compel me to put on mine own Chains?
May I not kiſs ye now in ſuperſtition?
For you appear a thing that I would kneel to;
Let me err that way. Kiſſes her.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Ye ſhall err for once, I have a kind of noble pity on you,
Among your manly ſufferings, make this moſt,
To err no farther in deſire, for then, Sir,
You add unto the gratitudes I owe you;
And after death, your dear friends ſoul ſhall bleſs you.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I am wondrous honeſt.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I dare try. Kiſſes.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I have taſted a bleſſedneſs too great for dull mortality,
Once more, and let me dye.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I dare not murther,
How will maids curſe me if I kill with kiſſes?
And young men flye th' embraces of fair Virgins?
Come, pray ſit down, but let's talk temperately.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Is my dear friend abed?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Yes, and aſleep;
Secure aſleep, 'tis midnight too, Liſander,
Speak not ſo loud.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: You ſee I am a Statue,
I could not ſtand elſe as I had eaten Ice,
Or took into my bloud a drowzie Poyſon,
And Natures nobleſt, brighteſt flame burns in me;
Midnight? and I ſtand quietly to behold it ſo?
The Alarm rung, and I ſleep like a Coward?
I am worn away, my faith, my dull obedience
Like Crutches, carry my decayed Body
Down to the Grave, I have no youth within me,
Yet happily you love too.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Love with honour.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Honour? what's that? 'tis but a ſpecious title
We ſhould not prize too high.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Dearer than life.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: The value of it is as time hath made it,
And time and cuſtome have too far inſulted,
We are no gods, to be always tyed to ſtrictneſs,
'Tis a preſumption to ſhew too like 'em;
March but an hour or two under Loves Enſigns,
We have Examples of great memories—

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: But ſoul ones too, that greatneſs cannot cover,
That Wiſe that by Example ſins, ſins double,
And pulls the Curtain open to her ſhame too;
Methinks to enjoy you thus—

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: 'Tis no joy, Lady,
A longing Bride if ſhe ſtop here, would cry,
The Bridegroom too, and with juſt cauſe curſe Hymen;
But yield a little, be one hour a Woman,
(I do not ſpeak this to compel you, Lady)
And give your Will but motion, let it ſtir
But in the taſte of that weak fears call evil,
Try it to underſtand it, we'll do nothing,
You'll ne'r come to know pure good elſe.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Fie, Sir.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I have found a way, let's ſlip into this errour
As Innocents, that know not what we did;
As we were dreaming both, let us embrace;
The ſin is none of ours then, but our fancies;
What have I ſaid? what blaſphemy to honour?
O my baſe thoughts! pray ye take this and ſhoot me.
My Villain thoughts! Noiſe within.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I weep your miſeries, and would to heaven— what noiſe?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: It comes on louder.
Kill me, and ſave your ſelf; ſave your fair honour,
And lay the fault on me, let my life periſh,
My baſe laſcivious life, ſhoot quickly, Lady.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Not for the World, retire behind the hangings,
And there ſtand cloſe— my husband, cloſe, Liſander,

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Deareſt, are you well?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: O my ſad heart, my head, my head.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Alas, poor ſoul! what do you do out of your bed?
You take cold, my Caliſta; how do ye?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Not ſo well, Sir, to lie by ye, my Brothers fright—

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: I had a frightful dream too,
A very frightful dream, my beſt Caliſta;
Methought there came a Dragon to your Chamber,
A furious Dragon (Wife) I yet ſhake at it;
Are all things well?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Shall I ſhoot him?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: No, all well, Sir,
'Twas but your care of me, your loving care,
Which always watches.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: And methought he came
As if he had riſen thus out of his Den,
As I do from theſe Hangings.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Dead.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Hold, good Sir.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: And forc'd ye in his arms thus.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: 'Twas but fancy
That troubled ye, here's nothing to diſturb me,
Good Sir, to reſt again, and I am now drowzie,
And will to bed; make no noiſe, dear Husband,
But let me ſleep; before you can call any body, I am abed.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: This, and ſweet reſt dwell with ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Come out again, and as you love, Liſander,
Make haſte away, you ſee his mind is troubled;
Do you know the door ye came in at?
Well, ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: And can ye hit it readily?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I warrant ye;
And muſt I go? Muſt here end all my happineſs?
Here in a dream, as if it had no ſubſtance?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: For this time, friend, or here begin our ruins;
We are both miſerable.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: This is ſome comfort
In my afflictions; they are ſo full already,
They can find no encreaſe.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Dear, ſpeak no more.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: You muſt be ſilent then.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Farewel, Liſander, thou joy of man, farewel.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Farewel, bright Lady,
Honour of woman-kind, a heavenly bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Be ever honeſt.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I will be a dog elſe;
The vertues of your mind I'll make my Library,
In which I'll ſtudy the celeſtial beauty;
Your Conſtancy, my Armour that I'll fight in;
And on my Sword your Chaſtity ſhall ſit,
Terrour to rebel bloud.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Once more, farewel; Noiſe within.
O that my modeſty cou'd hold you ſtill, Sir— he comes again.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Heaven keep my hand from murther,
Murther of him I love.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Away, dear friend,
Down to the Garden ſtairs, that way, Liſander,
We are betray'd elſe.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Honour guard the innocent. Exit Liſander.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Still up? I fear'd your health.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: 'Has miſs'd him happily;
I am going now, I have done my meditations,
My heart's almoſt at peace.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: To my warm Bed then.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I will, pray ye lead. A Piſtol ſhot within.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: A Piſtol ſhot i'th' houſe?
At theſe hours? ſure ſome thief, ſome murtherer;
Riſe, ho! riſe all, I am betray'd.

sp.speaker: Cal
sp.l: O Fortune!
O giddy thing! he has met ſome oppoſition,
And kill'd; I am confounded, loſt for ever.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Now, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Thieves, my noble Father, Villains and Rogues.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Indeed! I heard a Piſtol, let's ſearch about.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: To bed again, they are gone, Sir,
I will not bid you thank my valour ſor't;
Gone at the Garden door; there were a dozen,
And bravely arm'd, I ſaw 'em.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I am glad, glad at the heart.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: One ſhot at me, and miſs'd me.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: No, 'twas at me, the Bullet ſlew cloſe by me,
Cloſe by my ear; another had a huge Sword,
Flouriſh'd it thus; but at the point I met him,
But the Rogue taking me to be your Lordſhip,
(As ſure your Name is terrible, and we
Not much unlike in the dark) roar'd out aloud,
'Tis the kill Crow, Dorilaus, and away
They ran as they had flown; now you muſt love me,
Or fear me for my Courage, Wench.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: O Rogue!
O lying Rogue, Liſander ſtumbled, Madam,
At the Stairs head, and in the fall the ſhot went off;
Was gone before they roſe.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I thank Heaven for't.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I was frighted too, it ſpoil'd my game with Leon.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: You muſt ſit up; and they had come to your Chamber
What pranks would they have plaid? how came the door open?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I heard 'em when they forc'd it; up I roſe,
Took Durindana in my hand; and like
Orlando, iſſu'd forth.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I know you are valiant.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: To bed again,
And be you henceforth provident, at ſun-riſing
We muſt part for a while.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: When you are a bed,
Take leave of her, there 'twill be worth the taking;
Here 'tis but a cold Ceremony, ere long
We'll find Liſander, or we have ill-fortune.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Lock all the doors faſt.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Though they all ſtood open,
My name writ on the door, they dare not enter. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Clarange, Fryar with a letter.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Turn'd Hermit?

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: Yes, and a devout one too; I heard him preach.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: That leſſens my belief,
For though I grant my Lidian a Scholar,
As far as fits a Gentleman, he hath ſtudied
Humanity, and in that he is a Maſter;
Civility of manners, Courtſhip, Arms;
But never aim'd at (as I could perceive)
The deep points of Divinity.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: That confirms his
Devotion to be real, no way tainted
With oſtentation, or hyprociſie,
The cankers of Religion; his Sermon
So full of gravity, and with ſuch ſweetneſs
Deliver'd, that it drew the admiration
Of all the hearers on him; his own Letters
To you, which witneſs he will leave the World,
And theſe to fair Olinda, his late Miſtriſs,
In which he hath with all the moving language
That ever expreſs'd Rhetorick, ſolicited
The Lady to forget him, and make you
Bleſſed in her embraces, may remove
All ſcrupulous doubts.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: It ſtrikes a ſadneſs in me.
I know not what to think of 't.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: Ere he entred
His ſolitary Cell, he pen'd a Ditty,
His long, and laſt farewel to Love and Women,
So feelingly, that I confeſs however
It ſtands not with my order to be taken
With ſuch poetical Raptures; I was mov'd,
And ſtrangely with it.

sp.speaker: C ar.
sp.l: Have you the Copy?

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: Yes, Sir;
My Novice too can ſing it, if you pleaſe
To give him hearing.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: And it will come timely,
For I am full of melancholy thoughts,
Againſt which I have heard with reaſon Muſick
To be the ſpeedieſt cure, 'pray you apply it.

body.head: A Song by the Novice.
body.l: A Dieu ſond love, farewel you wanton powers,
I am free again;
Thou dull Diſeaſe of bloud, and idle hours;
Bewitching pain,
Flye to the Fools that ſigh away their time,
My nobler love to Heaven doth climb,
And there behold Beauty still young,
That Time can ne'r corrupt, nor Death deſtroy;
Immortal ſweetneſs by fair Angels ſung,
And honour'd by Eternity and Joy:
There lives my love, thither my hopes aſpire,
Fond love declines, this heavenly loves grows higher.

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.l: How do ye approve it?

sp.speaker: Claran.
sp.l: To its due deſert,
It is a Heavenly Hymn, no ditty Father,
It paſſes through my ears unto my ſoul,
And works divinely on it; give me leave
A little to conſider; ſhall I be
Outdone in all things? nor good of my ſelf,
No • by example? ſhall my looſe hope ſtill,
The viands of a fond affection, feed me
As I were a ſenſual beaſt? ſpiritual food
Refus'd by my ſick palat? 'tis reſolv'd.
How far off Father, doth this new made Hermit
Make his abode?

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.l: Some two dayes journey Son.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Having reveal'd my fair intentions to ye,
I hope your piety will not deny me
Your aids to further 'em?

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.l: That were againſt a good mans charity.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: My firſt requeſt is,
You would ſome time, for reaſons I will ſhew you,
Defer delivery of Lidians Letters
To fair Olinda.

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: For what follows,
You ſhall direct me; ſomething I will do,
A new born zeal, and friendſhip prompts me to. Ex.

div.stage: Enter Dorilaus, Cleander, Chamberlain, Table, Tapers, and three ſtools.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: We have ſupp'd well friend; let our beds be ready,
We muſt be ſtirring early.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: They are made Sir.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I cannot ſleep yet, where's the jovial hoſt
You told me of? 'thas been my cuſtom ever
To parley with mine hoſt.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: He's a good fellow,
And ſuch a one I know you love to laugh with;
Go call your Maſter up.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: He cannot come Sir.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Is he a bed with his wife?

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: No certainly.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Or with ſome other gueſts?

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Neither and 't like ye.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Why then he ſhall come by your leave my friend,
I'le fetch him up my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: Indeed you'l fail Sir.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Is he i'th' houſe?

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: No, but he is hard by Sir;
He is faſt in's grave, he has been dead theſe three weeks.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Then o' my conſcience he will come but lamely,
And diſcourſe worſe.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Farewel mine honeſt Hoſt then,
Mine honeſt merry Hoſt; will you to bed yet?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: No, not this hour, I prethee ſit and chat by me.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Give us a quart of wine then, we'l be merry.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: A match my Son; pray let your wine be living,
Or lay it by your Maſter.

sp.speaker: Cham.
sp.l: It ſhall be quick Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Has not mine Hoſt a wife?
A good old woman.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Another coffin, that is not ſo handſom;
Your Hoſteſſes in Innes ſhould be blith things,
Pretty, and young to draw in paſſengers;
She'l never fill her beds well, if ſhe be not beauteous.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: And courteous too.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I, I, and a good fellow,
That will miſtake ſometimes a Gentleman
For her good man; well done; here's to Liſander.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: My full love meets it; make fire in our lodgings,
We'l trouble thee no farther; to your Son. Ex. Cham.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Put in Clarange too; off with't, I thank ye;
This wine drinks merrier ſtill, O for mine Hoſt now,
Were he alive again, and well diſpos'd,
I would ſo claw his pate.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Y'are a hard drinker.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I love to make mine Hoſt drunk, he will lye then
The rareſt, and the roundeſt, of his friends,
His quarrels, and his gueſts, and they are the beſt bands too,
Take 'em in that tune.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: You know all.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I did Son, but time, and arms have worn me out.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: 'Tis late Sir, I hear none ſtirring. A lute is ſtruck

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Hark, what's that, a Lute?
'Tis at the door I think.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: The doors are ſhut faſt.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: 'Tis morning ſure, the Fiddlers are got up
To fright mens ſleeps, have we ne're a piſpot ready?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Now I remember, I have heard mine Hoſt that's dead,
Touch a lute rarely, and as rarely ſing too,
A brave ſtill mean.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I would give a brace of French Crowns
To ſee him riſe and Fiddle— Hark, a Song.

body.head: A SONG.
body.l: 'TIS late and cold, ſtir up the fire;
Sit cloſe, and draw the Table nigher;
Be merry, and drink wine that's old,
A hearty medicine 'gainſt a cold.
Your bed of wanton down's the beſt,
Where you ſhall tumble to your reſt;
I could wiſh you wenches too,
But I am dead and cannot do;
Call for the beſt the houſe may ring,
Sack, White, and Claret let them bring,
And drink apace while breath you have,
You'l find but cold drink in the grave;
Plover, Partridge for your dinner,
And a Capon for the ſinner,
You ſhall find ready when you are up,
And your horſe ſhall have his ſup:
Welcom welcom ſhall flye round,
And I ſhall ſmile though under ground.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Now as I live, it is his voice.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: He ſings well, the Devil has a pleaſant pipe.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: The fellow lyed ſure.
He is not dead, he's here: how pale he looks!

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Is this he?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: You are welcom noble Gentlemen,
My brave old gueſt moſt welcom.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Lying knaves,
To tell us you were dead, come ſit down by us,
We thank ye for your Song.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Would 't had been better.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Speak, are ye dead?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Yes indeed am I Gentlemen,
I have been dead theſe three weeks.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Then here's to ye, to comfort your cold body.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: What do ye mean? ſtand further off.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I will ſtand nearer to him,
Shall he come out on's coffin to bear us company,
And we not bid him welcom? come mine Hoſt,
Mine honeſt Hoſt, here's to ye.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Spirits Sir, drink not.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Why do ye appear?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: To wait upon ye Gentlemen,
'Thas been my duty living, now my farewel;
I fear ye are not us'd accordingly.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I could wiſh you warmer company mine Hoſt,
How ever we are us'd.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Next to entreat a courteſie,
And then I go to peace.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Is't in our power?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Yes and 'tis this, to ſee my body buried
In holy ground, for now I lye unhallowed,
By the clacks fault; let my new grave be made
Amongſt good fellows, that have died before me,
And merry Hoſtes of my kind.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: It ſhall be done.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: And forty ſtoops of wine drank at thy funeral.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Do you know our travel?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Yes, to ſeek your friends,
That in afflictions wander now.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Alas!

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Seek 'em no farther, but be confident
They ſhall return in peace.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: There's comfort yet.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: Pray ye one word more, is't in your power mine Hoſt,
Anſwer me ſoftly, ſome hours before my death,
To give me warning?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I cannot tell ye truly,
But if I can, ſo much alive I lov'd ye,
I will appear again, adieu. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Adieu, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I am troubl'd; theſe ſtrange apparitions are
For the moſt part fatal.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: This if told, will not
Find credit, the light breaks a pace, let's lie down
And take ſome little reſt, an hour or two,
Then do mine hoſt's deſire, and ſo return,
I do believe him.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: So do I, to reſt, Sir. Exeunt.

l.hi: Clarinda?

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Is the houſe well ordered?
The doors look'd to now in your Maſters abſence?
Your care, and diligence amongſt the Servants?

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: I am ſtirring, Madam.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: So thou art, Clarinda,
More than thou ought'ſt I am ſure, why doſt thou bluſh?

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: I do not bluſh.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why doſt thou hang thy head wench?

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: Madam, ye are deceiv'd, I look upright,
I underſtand ye not: ſhe has ſpied Leon, Aſide.
Shame of his want of caution.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Look on me; what, bluſh again?

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: 'Tis more than I know, Madam;
I have no cauſe that I find yet.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Examine then.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: Your Ladyſhip is ſet I think to ſhame me.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Do not deſerv't, who lay with you laſt night?
What bed-fellow had ye? none of the maids came near ye.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: Madam, they did.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: 'Twas one in your Couſins cloaths then,
And wore a ſword; and ſure I keep no Amazons;
Wench do not lye, 'twill but proclaim thee guilty;
Lyes hide our ſins like nets; like perſpectives,
They draw offences nearer ſtill, and greater:
Come, tell the truth.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: You are the ſtrangeſt Lady
To have theſe doubts of me; how have I liv'd, Madam?
And which of all my careful ſervices deſerves theſe ſhames?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Leave facing, 'twill not ſerve ye,
This impudence becomes thee worſe than lying.
I thought ye had liv'd well, and I was proud of 't;
But you are pleas'd to abuſe my thoughts; who was't?
Honeſt repentance yet will make the fault leſs.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: Do ye compel me? do you ſtand ſo ſtrict too?
Nay, then have at ye; I ſhall rub that ſore, Madam,
(Since ye provoke me) will but vex your Ladyſhip;
Let me alone.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I will know.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: For your own peace,
The peace of your own conſcience ask no farther;
Walk in, and let me alone.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: No, I will know all.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Why, then I'le tell ye, 'twas a man I lay with,
Never admire, 'tis eaſie to be done, Madam,
And uſual too, a proper man I lay with;
Why ſhould you vex at that? young as Liſander,
And able too; I grudge not at your pleaſure,
Why ſhould you ſtir at mine? I ſteal none from ye.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: And doſt thou glory in this ſin?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I am glad on't, to glory in't is for a mighty Lady
That may command.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Why didſt thou name Liſander?

sp.speaker: Clari.
sp.l: Does it anger ye? does it a little gall ye?
I know it does, why would ye urge me Lady?
Why would ye be ſo curious to compel me?
I nam'd Liſander as my preſident,
The rule I err'd by, you love him, I know it,
I grudg'd not at it, but am pleas'd it is ſo;
And by my care and diligence you enjoy'd him,
Shall I for keeping counſel, have no comfort?
Will you have all your ſelf? ingroſs all pleaſure
Are ye ſo hard hearted? why do ye bluſh now, Madam?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: My anger bluſhes, not my ſhame, baſe woman.

sp.speaker: Clari.
sp.l: I'le make your ſhame bluſh, ſince you put me to't.
Who lay with you t'other night?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: With me? ye monſter.

sp.speaker: Clari.
sp.l: Whoſe ſweet embraces circled ye? not your husbands;
I wonder ye dare touch me in this point, Madam?
Stir her againſt ye in whoſe hand your life lies?
More than your life, your honour? what ſmug Amazon
Was that I brought you? that maid had ne're a petticoat?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: She'l half perſwade me anon, I am a beaſt too,
And I miſtruſt my ſelf, though I am honeſt
For giving her the Helm, thou knoweſt, Clarinda,
(Ev'n in thy conſcience) I was ever vertuous;
As far from luſt in meeting with Liſander,
As the pure wind in welcoming the morning;
In all the coverſation I had with him,
As free, and innocent, as you fair Heaven;
Didſt not thou perſwade me too?

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: Yes, I had reaſon for't,
And now you are perſwaded I'le make uſe on't.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: If I had ſin'd thus, and my youth entic'd me,
The nobleneſs and beauty of his perſon,
Beſide the mighty benefits I am bound to,
Is this ſufficient warrant for thy weakneſs?
If I had been a whore, and crav'd thy counſel
In the conveyance of my fault and faithfulneſs,
Thy ſecrecie, and truth in hiding of it;
Is it thy juſtice to repay me thus?
To be the Maſter ſinner to compel me?
And build thy luſts ſecurity on mine honour?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: They that love this ſin, love their ſecurity;
Prevention, Madam, is the nail I knock'd at,
And I have hit it home, and ſo I'le hold it,
And you muſt pardon me, and be ſilent too,
And ſuffer what ye ſee, and ſuffer patiently;
I ſhall do worſe elſe.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Thou canſt not touch my credit:
Truth will not ſuffer me to be abus'd thus.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: Do not you ſtick to truth, ſhe is ſeldom heard, Madam,
A poor weak tongue ſhe has, and that is hoarſe too
With pleading at the bars, none underſtand her,
Or if you had her, what can ſhe ſay for ye?
Muſt ſhe not ſwear he came at midnight to ye,
The door left open, and your husband cozen'd
With a feign'd ſickneſs?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: But by my ſoul I was honeſt, thou know'ſt I was honeſt.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: That's all one what I know,
What I will teſtifie is that ſhall vex ye;
Truſt not a guilty rage with likelihoods,
And on apparent proof, take heed of that, Madam;
If you were innocent (as it may be ye are)
I do not know, I leave it to your conſcience,
It were the weakeſt and the pooreſt part of ye,
Men being ſo willing to believe the worſt,
So open eyed in this age to all infamie,
To put your fame in this weak bark to the venture.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: What do I ſuffer! O my precious honour,
Into what box of evils have I lock'd thee!
Yet rather than be thus outbrav'd, and by
My drudg, my footſtool, one that ſued to be ſo;
Periſh both life, and honour. Devil thus
I dare thy worſt, defie thee, ſpit at thee,
And in my vertuous rage, thus trample on thee;
Awe me thy Miſtris, whore, to be thy baud?
Out of my houſe, proclaim all that thou knoweſt,
Or malice can invent, fetch jealouſie
From Hell, and like a furie breath it in
The boſom of my Lord; and to thy utmoſt
Blaſt my fair fame, yet thou ſhalt feel with horror
To thy ſear'd conſcience, my truth is built
On ſuch a firm baſe, that if e're it can
Be forc'd, or undermin'd by thy baſe ſcandals, Exit.
Heaven keeps no guard on innocence.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: I am loſt,
In my own hopes forſaken, and muſt fall
The greateſt torment to a guilty woman
Without revenge, till I can faſhion it
I muſt ſubmit, at leaſt appear as if
I did repent, and would offend no farther.
Monſieur Beronte my Lords Brother is
Oblig'd unto me for a private favour;
'Tis he muſt mediate for me; but when time
And opportunity bids me ſtrike, my wreak
Shall pour it ſelf on her nice chaſtitie
Like to a torrent, deeds, not words ſhall ſpeak me. Exit.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: YE are opportunely net.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Your countenance expreſſes haſt mixt with ſome fear.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: You'l ſhare with me in both, as ſoon as you are made
Acquainted with the cauſe, if you love vertue,
In danger not ſecure; I have no time
For circumſtance, inſtruct me if Liſander
Be in your Brothers houſe?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Upon my knowledge he is not there.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: I am glad on't.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Why good Sir?
(Without offence I ſpeak it) there's no place
In which he is more honour'd, or more ſafe,
Than with his friend Cleander.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: In your votes
I grant it true, but as it now ſtands with him,
I can give reaſon to make ſatisfaction
For what I ſpeak; you cannot but remember
The ancient difference between Liſander
And Cloridon, a man in grace at Court?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: I do; and the ſoul plot of Cloridons kinſman
Upon Liſanders life, for a fall given to Cloridon
'Fore the King, as they encountred at a ſolemn tilting.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: It is now reveng'd:
In brief, a challenge was brought to Liſander
By one Chryſantes; and as far as valour
Would give him leave, declin'd by bold Liſander:
But peace refus'd, and braves on braves heap'd on him,
Alone he met the oppoſites, ending the quarrel
With both their lives.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: I am truly ſorry for't.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: The King incenſed for his favorites death,
Hath ſet a price upon Liſanders head,
As a reward to any man that brings it
Alive, or dead; to gain this every where
He is purſu'd, and laid for; and the friendſhip
Between him and your noble Brother known,
His houſe in reaſon cannot paſs unſearcht,
And that's the principal cauſe that drew me hither,
To haſten his remove, if he had choſen
This Caſtle for his ſanctuary.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: 'Twas done nobly,
And you moſt welcom; this night pray you take
A lodging with us; and at my intreaty
Conceal this from my Brother, he is grown
Exceeding ſad of late; and the hard fortune
Of one he values at ſo high a rate,
Will much encreaſe his melancholy.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: I am tutor'd: pray you lead the way.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: To ſerve you I will ſhew it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Nothing more certain than to dye, but when
Is moſt uncertain: if ſo, every hour
We ſhould prepare us for the journey, which
