Is not to be put off, I muſt ſubmit
To the divine decree, not argue it,
And chearfully I welcom it: I have
Diſpos'd of my eſtate, confeſs'd my ſins,
And have remiſſion from my Ghoſty Father,
Being at peace too here: the apparition
Proceeded not from fancy, Dorilaus
Sav • it, and heard it with me, it made anſwer
To our demands, and promis'd, if 'twere not
Deny'd to him by fate, he would forewarn me
Of my approaching end, I feel no ſymptome
Of ſickneſs, yet I know not how a dulneſs
Invades me all over. Ha?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I come Sir,
To keep my promiſe; and as far as ſpirits
Are ſenſible of ſorrow for the living,
I grieve to be the meſſenger to tell you,
E're many hours paſs, you muſt reſolve
To fill a grave.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: And feaſt the worms?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Even ſo Sir.

sp.speaker: Clea.
sp.l: I hear it like a man.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: It well becomes you, there's no evading it.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: Can you diſcover by whoſe means I muſt dye?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: That is deny'd me:
But my prediction is too ſure; prepare
To make your peace with heaven. So farewel Sir. Ex.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I ſee no enemy near; and yet I tremble
Like a pale coward: my ſad doom pronounc'd
By this aerial voice, as in a glaſs
Shews me my death in its moſt dreadfull ſhape.
What rampire can my humane frailty raiſe
Againſt the aſſault of fate? I do begin
To fear my ſelf, my inward ſtrengths forſake me,
I muſt call out for help. Within there? haſte,
And break in to my reſcue.

div.stage: Enter Dorilaus, Caliſta, Olinda, Beronte, Alcidon, Servants, and Clarinda, at ſeveral doors.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Reſcue? where? ſhew me your danger.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I will interpoſe
My loyall breaſt between you and all hazard.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Your Brothers Sword ſecures you.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: A true friend will dye in your defence.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: I thank ye,
To all my thanks, Encompaſs'd thus with friends
How can I fear? and yet I do, I am wounded,
Mortally wounded: nay it is within,
I am hurt in my minde: One word—

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: A thouſand:

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: I ſhall not live to ſpeak ſo many to you.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Why? what for bids you?

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: But even now the ſpirit
Of my dead Hoſt appear'd, and told me, that
This night I ſhould be with him: did you not meet it?
It went out at that door.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: A vain Chimera
Of your imagination: can you think
Mine Hoſt would not as well have ſpoke to me now,
As he did in the Inn? theſe waking dreams
Not alone trouble you, but ſtrike a ſtrange
Diſtraction in your Family: ſee the tears

Of my poor Daughter, fai •
Olinda's ſadneſs,
Your Brothers, and your friends grief, ſervants ſorrow.
Good Son bear up, you have many years to live
A comfort to us all: let's in to ſupper;
Ghoſts never walk till after mid-night, if
I may believe my Grannam. We will waſh
Theſe thoughts away with Wine, ſpight of Hobgoblins.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: You reprehend me juſtly: gentle Madam,
And all the reſt, forgive me, I'le endeavour
To be merry with you.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: That's well ſaid.

sp.speaker: Beron.
sp.l: I have procur'd your pardon.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Once more I receive you
Into my ſervice: but take eſpecial care
You fall no further.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Never Madam: Sir,
When you ſhall find fit time to call me to it,
I will make good what I have ſaid.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Till when, upon your life be ſilent.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: We will have a health unto Liſander.

sp.speaker: Cle.
sp.l: His name, Sir,
Somewhat revives me; but his ſight would cure me.
How ever let's to ſupper.

sp.speaker: Olin.
sp.l: Would Clarange
And Lidian were here too, as they ſhould be,
If wiſhes cou'd prevail.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: They are fruitleſs, Madam. Ex.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: If that report ſpeak truth, Clarinda is
Diſcharg'd her Ladies ſervice, and what burthen
I then have drawn upon me is apparent,
The crop ſhe reapt from her attendance was
Her beſt Revenue, and my principal means
Clarinda's bounty, though I labour'd hard for't,
A younger Brother's fortune: muſt I now
Have ſoure ſawce after ſweet meats? and be driv'n
To leavie half a Crown a week, beſides
Clouts, Sope, and Candles, for my heir Apparent,
If ſhe prove, as ſhe ſwears ſhe is with child;
Such as live this way, find like me, though wenching
Hath a fair face, there's a Dragon in the tail of't
That ſtings toth' quick. I muſt skulk here, until
I am reſolv'd: how my heart pants between
My hopes and fears! ſhe's come; are we in the Port?
If not, let's ſink together.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Things go better
Than you deſerve; you carry things ſo openly,
I muſt bear every way, I am once more
In my Ladies grace.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: And I m yours.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: It may be; but I have ſworn unto my Lady never
To ſin again.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: To be ſurpriz'd —the ſin
Is in it ſelf excuſable; to be taken
Is a crime, as the Poet writes.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: You know my weakneſs,
And that makes you ſo confident. You have got
A fair ſword, was it not Liſanders?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Yes Wench,
And I grown valiant by the wearing of it:
It hath been the death of two. With this Liſander
Slew Clorindon, and Chryſanthes. I took it up,
Broken in the handle, but that is reform'd,
And now in my poſſeſſion; the late Maſter
Dares never come to challenge it: this ſword,
And all the weapons that I have, are ever
Devoted to thy ſervice: Shall we bill?
I am very gameſome.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I muſt firſt diſpoſe of
The fool Malfort; he hath ſmoak'd you, and is not,
But by ſome new device to be kept from me:
I have it here ſhall fit him: you know where
You muſt expect me, with all poſſible ſilence
Get thither.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: You will follow?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Will I live?
She that is forfeited to luſt muſt dye,
That humour being unfed; begone, here comes Exit Le.
My champion in Armour.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: What adventure
I am bound upon I know not, but it is
My Miſtreſſes pleaſure that I ſhould appear thus.
I may perhaps be terrible to others,
But as I am, I am ſure my ſhadow frights me,
The claſhing of my Armour in my ears,
Sounds like a paſſing-bell; and my Buckler, puts me
In mind of a Bier; this my broad Sword a pick-axe
To dig my grave: O love, abominable love,
What Monſters iſſue from thy diſmal den,
Clarinda's placket, which I muſt encounter,
Or never hope to enter?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Here's a Knight errant, Monſieur Malfort.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Stand, ſtand, or I'le fall for ye.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Know ye not my voice?

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Yes, 'twas at that I trembl'd.
But were my falſe friend Leon here—

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Tis he.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Where? where?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: He is not come yet.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: 'Tis well for him,
I am ſo full of wrath.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Or fear—This Leon,
How e're my Kinſman, hath abus'd you groſly,
And this night vowes to take me hence perforce,
And marry me to another: 'twas for this,
(Preſuming on your love) I did entreat you
To put your armour on, that with more ſafety
You might defend me.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: And I'le do it bravely.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: You muſt ſtand here to beat him off, and ſuffer
No humane thing to paſs you, though it appear
In my Lords ſhape, or Ladies: be not cozen'd
With a diſguiſe.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I have been fool'd already, but now I am wife.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: You muſt ſwear not to ſtir hence.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Upon theſe lips.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Nor move untill I call you?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I'le grow here rather.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: This nights task well ended,
I am yours to morrow. Keep ſure guard. Exit Clar.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: Adieu;
My honey-comb how ſweet thou art, did not
A neſt of Hornets keep it? what impoſſibilities
Love makes me undertake? I know my ſelf
A natural Coward, and ſhould Leon come,
Though this were Cannon proof, I ſhould deliver
The wench before he ask'd her. I hear ſome ſooting:
'Tis he; where ſhall I hide my ſelf? that is
My beſt defence.

sp.speaker: Ce.
sp.l: I cannot ſleep, ſtrange viſions
Make this poor life, I fear'd of late to loſe,
A toy that I grow weary of.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: 'Tis Leon.

sp.speaker: Ce.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: If you are come, Sir, for Clarinda;
I am glad I have her for you; I reſign
My intereſt; you'll find her in her Chamber,
〈◊〉 ſtay up to tell you ſo.
Clarinda, and Leon!
There is ſomething more in this
Than I can ſtay to ask. Exit.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: What a cold pickle
(And that none of the ſweeteſt) do I find
My poor ſelf in?

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: [Speaks within.] Yield villain.

div.stage: Enter Clarinda and Leon, running. Cleander following.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Tis my Lord,
Shift for your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: His life
Shall firſt make anſwer Kills Cleander.
For this intruſion.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: I am going away,
I am gone already. Falls in a ſwoon.

sp.speaker: Clean.
sp.l: Heaven take mercy on
My ſoul; too true preſaging Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: He's dead,
And this wretch little better:
Do you ſtare upon your
Handy work?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I am amaz'd.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Get o're the Garden wall, flye for your life,
But leave your ſword behind; enquire not why:
I'le faſhion ſomething out of it, though I periſh,
Sha • l make way for revenge.

sp.speaker: Leon
sp.l: Theſe are the fruits
Of luſt, Clarinda.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Hence, repenting Milk-ſop. Exit Leon.
Now 'tis too late. Liſanders ſword, I that, Puts the ſword in Malfort's hand.
That is the Baſe I'le build on. So, I'le raiſe
The houſe. Help, murther, a moſt horrid
Murther. Monſieur Beronte, noble Dorilaus,
All buried in ſleep? Aye me a murther,
A moſt unheard of murther.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: More lights Knaves;
B • ronte, Alcidon; more lights.

div.stage: Enter Beronte, Alcidon, and Servants with lights.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: By this I ſee too much.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: My Son Cleander bathing
In his own gore The Devil, to tell truth, i'th' ſhape of
An Hoſt!

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: My Brother?

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: I have been
I'th' other world, in Hell I think, theſe Devils
With fire-brands in their paws ſent to torment me,
Though I never did the deed, for my lewd purpoſe
To be a Whore maſter.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: 'Tis one in Armour. A bloudy ſword in his hand.
Sans queſtion the murtherer.
Who I? you do me wrong,
I never had the heart to kill a Chicken;
Nor do I know this ſword.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: I do, too well.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: I have ſeen Liſander wear it.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: This confirms
W •• t yeſter-night I whiſper'd: let it work,
The circumſtance may make it good.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: My Lord? and I his murtherer?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Drag the villain hence,
The Rack ſhall forc • a free confeſſion from him.

sp.speaker: Malf.
sp.l: I am ſtruck dumb;
You need not ſtop my mouth.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Away with him. Exit with Malfort.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Where is my Lord?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: All that
Remains of him lies there: look on this object,
And then turn marble.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I am ſo already,
Made fit to be his Monument: but wherefore
Do you, that have both life and motion leſt you,
Stand ſad ſpectators of his death.
And not bring forth his murtherer?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: That lies in you: you muſt, and ſhall produce him.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: She, Beronte?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: None elſe.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Thou ly'ſt, I'le prove it on thy head,
Or write it on thy heart.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: Forbear, there is
Too much blood ſhed already.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Let not choler
Stifle your judgment; many an honeſt Father
Hath got a wicked Daughter. If I prove not
With evident proofs her han • was in the bloud
Of my dear Brother, (too good a Husband for her)
Give your revenge the • eins, and ſpur it forward.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: In any circumſtance but ſhew her guilty,
I'le ſtrike the firſt ſtroak at her.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Let me ask
A queſtion calmly: do you know this Sword?
Have you not ſeen Liſander often wear it?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: The ſame with which he reſcued me.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I do, what inference from this to make me guilty?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Was he not with you in the houſe to night?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: No on my ſoul.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Nor ever heretofore
In private with you, when you feign'd a ſickneſs,
To keep your Husband abſent?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Never, Sir, to a diſhoneſt end.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Was not this Woman
Your inſtrument? her ſilence does confeſs it.
Here lyes Cleander dead, and here the ſword
Of falſe Liſander, too long cover'd with
A maſque of ſeeming truth.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: And is this all
The proof you can alledge? Liſander guilty,
Or my poor Daughter an Adultereſs?
Suppoſe that ſhe had chang'd diſcourſe with one
To whom ſhe ow'd much more?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Thou haſt thy ends, wicked Clarinda. She falls.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: Help, the Lady ſinks, malice hath kill'd her.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I would have her live,
Since I dare ſwear ſhe's innocent: 'tis no time
Or place to argue now: this cauſe muſt be
Decided by the Judge; and though a Father,
I will deliver her into the hands
Of Juſtice. If ſhe prove true gold when try'd,
She's mine: if not, with curſes I'le diſclaim her:
Take up your part of ſorrow, mine ſhall be
Ready to anſwer with her life the fact
That ſhe is charg'd with.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Sir, I look upon you as on a Father.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: With the eyes of ſorrow
I ſee you as a Brother: let your witneſſes
Be ready.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: 'Tis my care.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: I am for Lidian.
This accident no doubt will draw him from
His Hermits life.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Things yet go right, perſiſt, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: L ſan.
sp.l: Are the horſes dead?

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.l: Out-right. If you ride at this rate,
You muſt reſolve to kill your two a day,
And that's a large proportion.

sp.speaker: Liſan.
sp.l: Will you pleaſe
At any price, and ſpeedily, to get freſh ones.
You know my danger, and the penalty
That follows it, ſhould I be apprehended.
Your duty in obeying my commands,
Will in a better language ſpeak your ſervice,
Than your unneceſſary, and untimely care of my expence.

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.l: I am gone, Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Liſan.
sp.l: In this thicket
I will expect you: Here yet I have leiſure
To call my ſelf unto a ſtrict account
For my paſs'd life, how vainly ſpent: I would
I ſtood no farther guilty: but I have
A heavier reckoning to make: This hand
Of late as white as innocence, and unſpotted,
Now wears a purple colour, dy'd in gore,
My ſoul of the ſame tincture; pur-blind paſſion,
With flattering hop • s, would keep me from deſpair,
Pleading I was provok'd to it; but my reaſon
Breaking ſuch thin and weak defences, tells me
I have done a double murther; and for what?
Was it in ſervice of the King? his Edicts
Command the contrary: or for my Country?
Her Genius, like a mourning mother, anſwers
In Cloridon, and Chryſ • nthes ſhe hath loſt
Two hopeful ſons, that might have done their parts,
To guard her from Invaſion: for what cauſe then?
To keep th' opinion of my valour upright,
I'th' popular breath, a ſandy ground to build on;
Bought with the Kings diſpleaſure, as the breach
Of Heavens decrees, the loſs of my true comforts,
In Parents, Kinſmen, Friends, as the fruition
Of all that I was born to, and that ſits
Like to a hill of Lead here, in my exile,
(Never to be repeal'd, if I eſcape ſo)
I have cut off all hopes ever to look on
Divine Caliſta, from her ſight, and converſe,
For ever baniſh'd.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: I ſhould know this voice,
His naming too my Siſter, whom Liſander
Honour'd, but in a noble way, aſſures me
That it can be no other: I ſtand bound
To comfort any man I find diſtreſs'd:
But to aid him that ſav'd my life, Religion
And Thankfulneſs commands, and it may be
High providence for this good end hath brought him
Into my ſolitary walk. Liſander, noble Liſander.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Whatſoe'er thou a • t,
That honorable attribute thou giv'ſt me,
I can pretend no right to: come not near me,
I am infectious, the ſanctity
Of thy profeſſion (for thou appeareſt
A reverend Hermite) if thou flye not from me,
As from the Plague or Leproſie, cannot keep thee
From being polluted.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: With good counſel, Sir,
And holy prayers to boot I may cure you,
Though both wayes ſo infected. You look wildly,
Peace to your conſcience, Sir, and ſtare upon me,
As if you never ſaw me: hath my habit
Alter'd my face ſo much, that yet you know not
Your ſervant Lidian?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I am amaz'd!
So young, and ſo religious?

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: I pu poſe (Heaven make me thankful for't) to leave the world:
I have made ſome trial of my ſtrengths in this
My ſolitary life; and yet I find not
A faintneſs to go on.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Above belief: do you inhabit here?

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: Mine own free choice, Sir:
I live here poorly, but contentedly,
Becauſe I find enough to feed my fortunes;
Indeed too much: theſe wild fields are my gardens,
The Cryſtal Rivers they afford their waters,
And grudge not their ſweet ſtreams to quench afflictions;
The hollow rocks their beds, which though they are hard,
(The Emblems of a doting lovers fortune)
Yet they are quiet; and the weary ſlumbers
The eyes catch there, ſofter than beds of Down, Friend;
The Birds my Bell to call me to devotions;
My Book the ſtory of my wandring life,
In which I find more hours due to repentance
Than time hath told me yet.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Anſwer me truly.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: I will do that without a conjuration.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I'th' depth of meditation do you not
Sometimes think of Olinda?

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: I endeavour
To raze her from my memory, as I wiſh
You would do the whole Sex, for know, Liſander,
The greateſt curſe brave man can labour under,
Is the ſtrong Witch-craft of a Womans eyes;
Where I find men I preach this doctrine to 'em:
As you are a Scholar, knowledge make your Miſtris,
The hidden beauties of the Heavens your ſtudy;
There ſhall you find fit wonder for your faith,
And for your eye in-imitable objects:
As you are a profeſs'd ſouldier, court your honour,
Though ſhe be ſtern, ſhe is honeſt, a brave Miſtris;
The greater danger you oppoſe to win her,
She ſhews the ſweeter, and rewards the nobler;
Womans beſt loves to hers meer ſhadows be,
For after death ſhe weds your memory.
Theſe are my contemplations.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Heavenly ones;
And in a young man more remarkable.
But wherefore do I envy, and not tread in
This bleſſed tract? here's in the heart no falſhood
To a vow'd friend, no quarrels ſeconded
With Challenges, which anſwer'd in defence
Of the word Reputation, murther follows.
A man may here repent his ſins, and though
His hand like mine be ſtain'd in bloud, it may be
With penitence and true contrition waſh'd off;
You have prov'd it, Lidian.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: And you'll find it true, if you perſevere.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Here then ends my flight,
And here the fury of the King ſhall find me
Prepar'd for Heaven, if I am mark'd to dye;
For that I truly grieve for.

div.stage: Enter Fryar, and Clarange in Fryars habit.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: Keep your ſelf conceal'd, I am inſtructed.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: How the ſight
Of my dear friend confirms me.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: What are theſe?

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: Two reverend Fryers, one I know.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: To you
This journey is devoted.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: Welcome, Father.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: I know your reſolution ſo well grounded,
And your adieu unto the world ſo conſtant,
That though I am th' unwilling meſſenger
Of a ſtrange accident to try your temper,
It cannot ſhake you. You had once a friend,
A noble friend, Clarange.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: And have ſtill, I hope, good Father.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: Your falſe hopes deceive you,
He's dead.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Clarange dead?

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: I buried him;
Some ſaid he dy'd of melancholy, ſome of love,
And of that fondneſs periſh'd.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: O Clarange!

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Haſt thou ſo much brave nature, noble Lidian,
So tenderly to love thy Rivals memory?
The bold Liſander weeps too.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: I expected that you would bear this better

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: I am a man, Sir, and my great loſs weigh'd duly—

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: His laſt words were
After confeſſion, live long, dear Lidian,
Poſſeſs'd of all thy wiſhes; and of me
He did deſire, bathing my hand with tears,
That with my beſt care, I ſhould ſeek, and find you,
And from his dying mouth prevail ſo with you,
That you a while ſhould leave your Hermits ſtrictneſs,
And on his Monument pay a tear or two,
To witneſs how you lov'd him.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: O my heart! to witneſs how I lov'd him? would he had not
Led me into his Grave, but ſacrific'd
His ſorrows upon mine, he was my friend,
My noble friend, I will bewail his aſhes;
His fortunes, and poor mine were born together,
And I will weep 'em both; I will kneel by him,
And on his hallow'd Earth do my laſt duties.
I'll gather all the pride of Spring to deck him,
Wood bines ſhall grow upon his honour'd Grave;
And as they proſper, claſp to ſhew our friendſhip,
And when they wither, I'll dye too.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Who would not
Deſire to dye, to be bewail'd thus nobly?

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: There is a Legacy he hath bequeath'd you;
But of what value I muſt not diſcover,
Until thoſe Rites and pious Ceremonies
Are duly tender'd.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: I am too full of ſorrow to be inquiſitive.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: To think of his,
I do forget mine own woes.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: Graze thy fill, now
Thou haſt done thy buſineſs; ha! who have we here?
Liſander, Lidian, and two Reverend Fryars?
What a ſtrange ſcene of ſorrow is expreſs'd
In different poſtures, in their looks and ſtation?
A common Painter eying theſe to help
His dull invention, might draw to the life
The living Sons of Priam, as they ſtood
On the pale Walls of Troy, when Hector fell
Under Achilles's Spear; I come too late,
My Horſe, though good and ſtrong, mov'd like a Tortoiſe;
Ill News had wings, and hath got here before me.
All Pythagoreans? not a word?

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: O Alcidon—
Deep Rivers with ſoft murmurs glide along.
The ſhallow roar; Clarange!

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Cloridon, Chryſanthes, ſpare my grief, and apprehend
What I ſhould ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: Their fates I have long ſince
For your ſakes mourn'd; Clarange's death, for ſo
Your ſilence doth confirm, till now I heard not;
Are theſe the bounds that are preſcrib'd unto
T •• ſwelling ſeas of ſorrow?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: The bounds, Alcidon?
Can all the winds of miſchief, from all Quarters,

l.hi: Euphrates, Ganges, Tigris, Volga, Po,

sp.l: Paying at once their tribute to this Ocean,
Make it ſwell higher? I am a Murtherer,
Baniſh'd, proſcrib'd, is there ought elſe that can
Be added to it?

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: I have loſt a friend,
Priz'd dearer than my being, and he dead,
My miſeries at the height contemn the worſt
Of Fortunes malice.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: How our humane weakneſs,
Grown deſperate from ſmall diſaſters, makes us
Imagine them a period to our ſorrows!
When the firſt ſyllable of greater woes
Is not yet written.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Speak it at large,
Since grief muſt break my heart, I am ambitious
It ſhould be exquiſite.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: It muſt be told,
Yet ere you hear it, with all care put on
The ſureſt armour anvil'd in the Shop
Of paſſive fortitude; the good Cleander,
Your friend, is murther'd.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: 'Tis a terrible pang,
And yet it will not do, I live yet, act not
The Torturers part; if that there be a blow
Beyond this, give it, and at once diſpatch me.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: Your Sword died in his heart-bloud was found near him,
Your private Conference at mid-night urg'd
With fair Caliſta; which by her whoſe pure truth,
Would never learn to tell a lie, being granted,
She by enrag'd Beronte is accus'd
Of Murther and Adultery, and you
(However I dare ſwear it falſe) concluded
Her principal Agent,

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: Wave upon wave rowls o'r me.
My Siſter? my dear Siſter?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Hold, great heart.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: Tear open his Doublet.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Is this wound too narrow
For my life to get out at? Bring me to
A Cannon loaded, and ſome pitying friend
Give fire unto it, while I nail my breaſt
Unto his thundring mouth, that in the inſtant,
I may be piece-meal torn, and blown ſo far,
As not one joint of my diſmember'd limbs
May ever be by ſearch of man found out.
Cleander! Yet, why name I him? however
His fall deſerv'd an Earth-quake, if compar'd
With what true honour in Caliſta ſuffers,
Is of no moment; my good Angel keep me
From Blaſphemy, and ſtrike me dumb before,
In th' agony of my ſpirit, I do accuſe
The Powers above, for their unjuſt permiſſion
Of Vertue, innocent Vertue, to be branded
With the leaſt vicious mark.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I never ſaw a man ſo far tranſported.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: Give it way, 'tis now no time to ſtop it.

sp.speaker: Lanc.
sp.l: Sir, I have bought
Freſh horſes; and as you reſpect your life,
Speedily back 'em; the Archers of the Kings guard
Are every where in queſt of you.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: My life?
Periſh all ſuch with thee that wiſh it longer,
Let it but clear Calista's innocence, Strikes Lancelot.
And Neſtor's Age, to mine was Youth, I'll flye
To meet the rage of my incenſed King,
And wiſh his favourites Ghoſt appear'd in Flames,
To urge him to revenge; let all the tortures
That Tyranny e're found out circle me,
Provided Juſtice ſet Calista free.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: I'll follow him

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: I am rooted here.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: Remember your dear friends laſt requeſt, your ſiſters dangers,
With the aids that you may lend her

sp.speaker: Lid
sp.l: 'Pray you ſupport me,
My Legs deny their Office.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I grow ſtill
Farther engag'd unto his matchleſs vertues,
And I am dead indeed, until I pay
The debt I owe him in a noble way. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: THou haſt him ſafe?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: As faſt as locks can make him;
He muſt break through three doors, and cut the throats
Of ten tall fellows, if that he 'ſcape us;
Beſides, as far as I can apprehend,
He hath no ſuch invention, for his looks
Are full of penitence.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Truſt not a Knaves look,
They are like a Whores Oaths;
How does my poor Daughter
Brook her reſtraint?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: With ſuch a reſolution
As well becomes your Lordſhips Child. Knock within.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Monſieur Lemure.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: This is a ſpecial favour,
And may ſtand an example in the Court
For courteſie; it is the Clients duty
To wait upon his Patron; you prevent me,
That am your humble Suitor.

sp.speaker: Lem.
sp.l: My near place
About the King, though it ſwell others, cannot
Make me forget your worth and Age, which may
Challenge much more reſpect; and I am ſorry
That my endeavours for you have not met with
The good ſucceſs I wiſh'd; I mov'd the King
With my beſt advantage both of time and place,
I'th' favour of your Daughter.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: How do you find his Majeſty affected?

sp.speaker: Lem.
sp.l: Not to be
Sway'd from the rigour of the Law; yet ſo far
The rarity of the Cauſe hath won upon him,
That he reſolves to have in his own perſon
The hearing of it; her tryal will be noble,
And to my utmoſt ſtrength, where I may ſerve her
My aids ſhall not be wanting.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I am your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Lem.
sp.l: One word more; if you love Liſanders life,
Adviſe him, as he tenders it, to keep
Out of the way; if he be apprehended,
This City cannot ranſom him; ſo good morrow. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: All happineſs attend you; go thy ways,
Thou haſt a clear and noble ſoul; for thy ſake
I'll hold that man mine enemy, who dares mutter,
The Court is not the ſphere where vertue moves,
Humanity, and Nobleneſs waiting on her.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Two Gentlemen (but what they are I know not,
Their faces are ſo muſtl'd) preſs to ſee you,
And will not be deny'd.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: What e'r they are, I am too old to fear.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: They need no Uſher, they make their own way.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Take you yours, Liſander; Exit Servant.
My joy to ſee you, and my ſorrow for
The danger you are in, contend ſo here,
Though different paſſions, nay oppos'd in Nature,
I know not which to entertain.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Your hate ſhould win the victory from both, with juſtice,
You may look on me as a Homicide,
A man whoſe life is forfeited to the Law,
But if (howe'r I ſtand accus'd) in thought
I ſin'd againſt Cleanders life, or live
Guilty of the diſhonour of your Daughter,
May all the miſeries that can fall on man
Here, or hereafter, circle me.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: To me this proteſtation's uſeleſs, I embrace you,
As the preſerver of my life, the man
To whom my ſon ows his, with life, his honour,
And howſoever your affection
To my unhappy Daughter, though it were
(For I have ſifted her) in a noble way,
Hath printed ſome taint on her fame, and brought
Her life in queſtion, yet I would not purchaſe
The wiſh'd recovery of her reputation,
With ſtrong aſſurance of her innocence
Before the King her Judge, with certain loſs
Of my Liſander, for whoſe life, if found,
There's no redemption; my exceſs of love,
(Though to enjoy you one ſhort day would lengthen
My life a dozen years) boldly commands me,
Upon my knees, which yet were never bent,
But to the King and Heaven, to entreat you
To flye hence with all poſſible ſpeed, and leave
Calista to her fortune.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: O bleſſed Saints, forſake her in affliction? can you
Be ſo unnatural to your own bloud,
To one ſo well deſerving, as to value
My ſafety before hers? ſhall innocence
In her be branded, and my guilt eſcape
Unpuniſh'd? does ſhe ſuffer ſo much for me,
For me unworthy, and ſhall I decline
(Fating the bitter bread of baniſhment)
The courſe of Juſtice to draw out a life?
(A life? I ſtyle it falſe, a living death)
Which being uncompell'd, laid down will clear her,
And write her name a new in the fair legend
Of the beſt women? ſeek not to diſſwade me,
I will not, like a careleſs Poet, ſpoil
The laſt Act of my Play, till now applauded,
My giving the World juſt cauſe to ſay, I fear'd
Death more than loſs of Honour.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: But ſuppoſe Heaven hath deſign'd ſome
Other ſaving means for her deliverance?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Other means? that is
A miſchief above all I have groan'd under;
Shall any other pay my debt, while I
Write my ſelf Bankrupt? or Caliſta owe
The leaſt beholdingneſs for that which ſhe
On all the bonds of gratitude I have ſeal'd to,
May challenge from me to be freely tender'd?
Avert it mercy! I will go to my Grave,
Without the curſes of my Creditors;
I'll vindicate her fair name, and ſo cancel
My obligation to her, to the King,
To whom I ſtand accountable for the loſs
Of two of his lov'd ſubjects lives, I'll offer
Mine own in ſatisfaction, to Heaven
I'll pay my time Repentance, to the tim • s,
Preſent, and future, I'll be regiſter'd
A memorable Preſident to admoniſh
Others, however valiant, not to truſt
To their abilities to dare, and do,
And much leſs for the airy words of Honour,
And falſe ſtamp'd reputation to ſhake off
The Chains of their Religion and Allegiance,
The principal means appointed to prefer
Societies and Kingdoms. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Let's not leave him; his mind's much troubles.

sp.speaker: Alc.
sp.l: Were your Daughter free,
Since from her dangers his diſtraction riſes,
His cauſe is not ſo deſperate for the ſlaughter
Of Cloridon, and Chryſanthes, but it may
Find paſſage to the mercy of the King,
The motives urg'd in his defence, that forc'd him
To act that bloudy Scene.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Heaven can ſend ayds,
When they are leaſt expected, let us walk,
The hour of tryal draws near.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: May it end well. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: That for my love you ſhould turn Hermit Lidian,
As much amazes me, as your report Clarange's dead.

sp.speaker: Lidi.
sp.l: He is ſo, and all comforts
My youth can hope for, Madam, with him buried;
Nor had I ever left my cell, but that
He did injoin me at his death to ſhed
Some tears of friendſhip on his Monument,
And thoſe laſt Rites perform'd, he did dequeath you
As the beſt legacie a friend could give,
Or I indeed could wiſh to my embraces.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtill more ſtrange, is there no foul play in it?
I muſt confeſs I am not ſorry Sir
For your fair fortune; yet 'tis fit I grieve
The moſt untimely death of ſuch a Gentleman,
He was my worthy Servant.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: And for this acknowledgment, if I could prize you at
A higher rate I ſhould, he was my friend:
My deareſt friend.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: But how ſhould I be aſſur'd Sir
(For ſlow belief is the beſt friend of truth)
Of this Gentlemans death? if I ſhould credit it,
And afterward it fall out contrary,
How am I ſham'd? how is your vertue tainted?

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: There is a Frier that came along with me,
His buſineſs to deliver you a Letter
From dead Clarange: You ſhall hear his Teſtimonie.
Father, my reverend Father, look upon him,
Such holy men are Authors of no Fables.

div.stage: Enter Clarange, (with a Letter writ out) and Frier.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: They ſhould not be, their lives and their opinions,
Like brighteſt pureſt flames ſhould ſtill burn upwards,
To me Sir? delivers the Letter.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: If you are the fair Olinda—

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.l: I do not like theſe croſs points.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Give me leave, I am neareſt to my ſelf. What I have plotted
Shall be purſu'd: you muſt not over-rule me.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: Do you put the firſt hand to your own undoing?
Play to betray your game? Mark but this letter.
Lady I am come to claim your noble promiſe, Reads.
If you be Miſtris of your word, ye are mine,
I am laſt return'd: your riddle is diſſolv'd,
And I attend your faith, Your humble ſervant Clarange.
Is this the Frier that ſaw him dead?
'Tis he.
Clarange on my life: I am defeated:
Such reverend habits juggle? my true ſorrow
For a falſe friend not worth a tear derided?

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.l: You have abus'd my truſt.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: It is not well, nor like a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: All ſtratagems
In love, and that the ſharpeſt war, are lawfull,
By your example I did change my habit,
Caught you in your own toyle, and triumph in it,
And what by policy's got, I will maintain
With valour, no Liſander ſhall come in again to fetch you off.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: His honour'd name
Pronounc'd by ſuch a treacherous tongue is tainted,
Maintain thy treaſon with thy ſword? With what
Contempt I hear it! in a Wilderneſs
I durſt encounter it, and would, but that
In my retired hours, not counterfeited
As thy religious ſhape was, I have learn'd
When Juſtice may determine ſuch a cauſe,
And o • ſuch weight as this fair Lady is,
Muſt not be put to fortune, I appeal
Unto the King, and he whoſe wiſedom knows
To do his ſubjects right in their eſtates,
As graciouſly with judgement will determine
In points of honour.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: I'le ſteer the ſame courſe with you.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I'le ſtand the tryal.

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.l: What have you done? or what intend you?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ask not, I'le come off with honour. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Beronte, Clarinda, Malſort, a Bar ſet forth, Officers.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Be conſtant in your proofs: ſhould you ſhrink back now,
Your life muſt anſwer it, nor am I ſafe.
My honour being engag'd to make that good
Which you affirm.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I am confident, ſo dearly
I honour'd my dead Lord, that no reſpect,
Or of my Ladies bounties (which were great ones
I muſt confeſs) nor of her former life,
For whil • that ſhe was chaſt, indeed I lov'd her,
Shall hinder me from lending my aſſiſtance
Unto your juſt revenge—mine own I mean, Aſide.
If Leon keep far off enough, all's ſecure:
Liſander dares not come in, modeſt bluſhes
Parted with me long ſince, and impudence
Arm'd with my hate, unto her innocence ſhall be
The weapon I will ſight with now.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: The rack
Being preſented to you, you'l roar out
What you conceal yet,

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Conceal? I know nothing
But that I ſhall be hang'd, and that I look for,
It is my deſtiny, I ever had
A hanging look; and a wiſe woman told me,
Though I had not the heart to do a deed
Worthy the halter, in my youth or age,
I ſhould take a turn with a wry mouth, and now
'Tis come about: I have pen'd mine own ballad
Before my condemnation, in fear
Some t • mer ſhould prevent me: here's my Lady?
Would I were in heaven, or a thouſand miles hence,
That I might not bluſh to look on her.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: You behold this preparation, and the enemies
Who are to fight againſt your life, yet if
You bring no witneſs here, that may convince ye
Of breach of ſaith to your Lords bed, and hold up
Unſpotted hands before the King, this tryal
You are to undergo, will but refine,
And not conſume your honour.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: How confirm'd
I am here, whatſoever Fate falls on me,
You ſhall have ample teſtimony; till the death
Of my dear Lord, to whoſe ſad memory
I pay a mourning widows tears, I liv'd
Too happy in my holy day trim of glorie,
And courted with felicitie, that drew on me,
With other helps of nature, as of fortune,
The envie, not the love of moſt that knew me,
This made me to preſume too much, perhaps
Too proud; but I am humbled; and if now
I do make it apparent, I can bear
Adverſity with ſuch a conſtant patience
As will ſet off my innocence, I hope Sir,
In your declining age, when I ſhould live
A comfort to you, you ſhall have no cauſe,
How e're I ſtand accus'd, to hold your honour
Ship-wrack'd in ſuch a Daughter.

sp.speaker: Oli.
sp.l: O beſt friend, my honour's at the ſtake too, for—

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Be ſilent; the King.

sp.speaker: Lem.
sp.l: Sir, if you pleaſe to look upon
The Priſoner, and the many ſervices
Her Father hath done for you—

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: We muſt look on
The cauſe, and not the perſons. Yet beholding
With an impartial eye, th' excelling beauties
Of this fair Lady, which we did believe
Upon report, but till now never ſaw'em,
It moves a ſtrange kind of compaſſion in me;
Let us ſurvey you nearer, ſhe's a book
To be with care perus'd; and 'tis my wonder,
I • ſuch miſhapen gueſts, as luſt and murther,
At any price ſhould ever find a lodging
In ſuch a beauteous Inne! Miſtake us not,
Though we admire the outward ſtructure, if
The rooms be ſoul within, expect no favour.
I were no man, if I could look on beautie
Diſtreſs'd, without ſome pity; but no King,
If any ſuperficial gloſs of feature
Could work me to decline the courſe of Juſtice.
But to the cauſe, Cleander's death, what proofs
Can you produre againſt her?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Royal Sir, touching that point my Brothers death,
We build on ſuppoſitions.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Suppoſitions? how? Is ſuch a Lady Sir to be condemn'd
On ſuppoſitions?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: They are well grounded Sir:
And if we make it evident ſhe is guilty
Of the firſt crime we charge her with, Adulterie,
That being the parent, it may find belief,
That murther was the iſſue.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: We allow
It may be ſo; but that it may be, muſt not
Infer a neceſſary conſequence
To caſt away a Ladies life. What witneſſes
To make this good?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: The principal, this woman,
For many years her ſervant; ſhe hath taken
Her oath in Court. Come forward.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: By my Crown a lying face.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: I ſwore Sir for the King:
And if you are the partie, as I do
Believe you are, for you have a good face,
How ever mine appears, ſwearing for you Sir,
I ought to have my oath paſs.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Impudent too? well, what have you ſworn?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: That this Lady was
A goodly tempting Lady, as ſhe is:
How thinks your Majeſtie? and I her ſervant,
Her officer as one would ſay, and truſted
With her cloſeſt Chamber-ſervice; that Liſander
Was a fine timber'd Gentleman, and active,
That he cou'd do ſine gambolls
To make a Lady merrie; that this pair,
A very loving couple, mutually
Affected one another: ſo much for them Sir.
That I, a ſimple waiting-woman, having taken
My bodily oath, the firſt night of admittance
Into her Ladiſhips ſervice, on her ſlippers,
(That was the book) to ſerve her will in all things,
And to know no Religion but her pleaſure,
'Tis not yet out of faſhion with ſome Ladies;
Thar I, as the premiſſes ſhew, being commanded
To do my function, in conveyance of
Liſander to her chamber, (my Lord abſent,
On a pretended ſickneſs) did the feat,
(It cannot be deny'd) and at dead mid night
Leſt 'em together: what they did, ſome here
Can eaſily imagine? I have ſaid, Sir.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: The Devils Oratrix.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Then you confeſs you were her Bawd?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: That's courſe, her Agent Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: So, goodie Agent? and you think there is
No puniſhment due for you agentſhip?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Let her ſuffer firſt,
Being my better, for adulterie,
And I'le endure the Mulct impos'd on Bawds,
Cull it by the worſt name.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Live I to hear this?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Take her aſide. Your anſwer to this Lady?
Cal. Heav'n grant me patience: to be thus confronted,
(O pardon Royal Sir a womans paſſion)
By one, and this the worſt of my miſ-fortunes,
That was my ſlave, but never to ſuch ends Sir,
Would give a ſtatue motion into furie:
Let my paſs'd life, my actions, nay intentions,
Be by my grand accuſer juſtly cenſur'd,
(For her I ſcorn to anſwer) and if they
Yield any probability of truth
In that ſhe urges, then I will confeſs
A guilty cauſe; the peoples voyce, which is
The voyce of truth, my husbands tenderneſs
In his affection to me, that no dotage
But a reward, of humbleneſs, the friendſhip
Echo'd through France between him and Liſander,
All make againſt her; for him, in his abſence,
(What ever imputation it draw on me)
I muſt take leave to ſpeak: 'tis true, he lov'd me,
But not in ſuch a wanton way, his reaſon
Maſter'd his paſſions: I grant I had
At mid-night conference with him; but if he
Ever receiv'd a farther favour from me,
Than what a Siſter might give to a Brother,
May I ſink quick: and thus much, did he know
The ſhame I ſuffer for him, with the loſs
Of his life for appearing, on my ſoul
He would maintain.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: And will, thou clear example of womens pureneſs.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Though we hold her ſuch,
Thou haſt expreſs'd thy ſelf a deſperate fool,
To thruſt thy head into the Lions jawes,
The juſtice of thy King.

sp.speaker: Liſan.
sp.l: I came prepar'd fort,
And offer up a guilty life to clear
Her innocence; the oath ſhe took, I ſwear to;
And for Cleanders death, to purge my ſelf
From any colour malice can paint on me,
Or that ſhe had a hand in't, I can prove
That fatal night when he in his own houſe fell,
And many daies before, I was diſtant from it
A long daies journey.

sp.speaker: Clarin.
sp.l: I am caught.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: If ſo,
How came your ſword into this ſtewards hands? ſtand forth.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I have heard nothing that you ſpake:
I know I muſt dye, and what kind of death
Pray you reſolve me, I ſhall go away elſe
In a qualm; I am very faint.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Carry him off, his ſear will kill him. Ex. with Mal.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Sir, 'twas my ambition,
My Daughters reputation being wounded
I'th' general opinion, to have it
Cur'd by a publick trial; I had elſe
Forborn your Majeſties trouble: I'le bring forth
Cleanders murtherer, in a wood I heard him
As I rode ſadly by, unto himſelf
With ſome compunction, though this devil had none,
Lament what he had done, curſing her luſt,
That drew him to that blody fact.

sp.speaker: Le.
sp.l: To leſſen
The foulneſs of it, for which I know juſtly
I am to ſuffer, and with my laſt breath
To free theſe innocents, I do confeſs all;
This wicked woman only guilty with me.

sp.speaker: Clari.
sp.l: Is't come to this? thou puling Rogue, dye thou
With prayers in thy mouth; I'le curſe the laws
By which I ſuffer, all I grieve for is,
That I dye unreveng'd.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: But one word more Sir,
And I have done; I was by accident where
Liſander met with Cloridon, and Cryſanthes,
Was an ear witneſs when he ſought for peace,
Nay, begg'd it upon colder terms than can
Almoſt find credit, his paſt deeds conſidered,
But they deaf to his reaſons, ſeverally
Aſſaulted him, but ſuch was his good fortune,
That both fell under it; upon my death
I take it uncompel'd, that they were guilty
Of their own violent ends; and he againſt
His will, the inſtrument.
This I will ſwear too, for I was not far off.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: They have alledg'd
As much to wake your ſleeping mercy, Sir,
As all the Advocates of France can plead
In his defence.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: The criminal judge ſhall ſentence
Theſe to their merits—with mine own hand, Lady,
I take you from the bar and do my ſelf
Pronounce you innocent. Ex. with Leon, and Clari.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Long live the King.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: And to confirm you ſtand high in our favour,
And as ſome recompence for what you have
With too much rigour in your trial ſuffered;
Ask what you pleaſe, becoming me to grant,
And be poſſeſt of't.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Sir, I dare not doubt
Your royal promiſe, in a King it is
A ſtrong aſſurance, that emboldens me
Upon my humble knees to make my boon,
Liſander's pardon.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: My good Genius did prompt her to it.
At your feet thus proſtrate, I ſecond her petition.

sp.speaker: Alci.
sp.l: Never King
Pour'd forth his mercie on a worthier ſubject.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: To witneſs my repentance for the wrong
In my unjuſt ſuſpicion I did both;
I join in the ſame ſuit.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: The life you give,
Still ready to lay down for your ſervice,
Shall be againſt your enemies imploy'd,
Nor hazarded in brawles.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Mercie, dread Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: So many preſſing me, and with ſuch reaſons
Moving compaſſion, I hope it will not
Be cenſur'd levity in me, though I borrow
In this from juſtice to relieve my mercy;
I grant his pardon at your interceſſion,
But ſtill on this condition; you Liſander,
In expiation of your guilt, ſhall build
A monument for my Cloridon, and Cryſanthes:
And never henceforth draw a Sword, but when
By us you are commanded, in defence of
The flower de Luce, and after one years ſorrow
For your dear friend, Cleanders wretched fate,
Marry Caliſta.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: On your ſacred hand, I vow to do it ſeriouſly.

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: Great Sir, ſtay,
Leave not your ſeat of juſtice, till you have
Given ſentence in a cauſe as much important
As this you have determined.

l.hi: Lidian?

sp.speaker: Lid.
sp.l: He Sir, your humbleſt ſubject, Jaccuſe Clarange
Of falſhood in true friendſhip at the height;
We both were ſuiters to this Lady, both
Injoyn'd one pennance.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Trouble not the King
With an unneceſſarie repetition
Of what the court's familiar with already.

l.hi: Clarange?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: With a ſhaven crown?

sp.speaker: Olin.
sp.l: Moſt ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Look on thy rival, your late ſervant, Madam,
But now devoted to a b • tter Miſtris,
The Church, whoſe orders I have took upon me:
There deliver up my intereſt to her;
And what was got with cunning as you thought,
I ſimply thus ſurrender: heretofore,
You did outſtrip me in the race of fri • ndſhip,
I am your equal now.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l:
A ſuit ſoo •
〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: And joyning thus your hands, I know 〈…〉
I may do in the Church my Friers O ••
In marrying you.

sp.speaker: Lid
sp.l: 〈◊〉 victory is 〈◊〉 Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: It is a glorious one, and well ſets o •
Our Scene of m • rcy; to the dead we tender
Our ſorrow, to the living ample wiſhes
Of future happineſs: 'tis a Kings duty
To prove himſelf a Father to his ſubjects:
And I ſhall hold it if this w • ll ſucceed,
A meritorious, and praiſe worthy deed. Exeunt.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: A Story, and a known one, long ſince writ,
Truth muſt take place, and by an able wit,
Foul mouth'd detraction daring not deny
To give ſo much to Fletchers memory;
If ſo, ſome may object, why then do you
Preſent an old piece to us for a new?
Or wherefore will your profeſt Writer be
(Not tax'd of theft before) a Plagiary?
To this he anſwers in his juſt defence,
And to maintain to all our Innocence,
Thus much, though he hath travell'd the ſame way,
Demanding, and receiving too the pay
For new Poem, you may find it due,
He having neither cheated us, nor you;
He vowes, and deeply, that he did nor ſpare
The utmoſt of his ſtrengths, and his beſt care
In the reviving it, and though his powers
Could not as he deſired, in three ſhort hours
Contract the Subject, and much leſs expreſs
The changes, and the various paſſages
That will be look'd for, you may hear this day
Some Scenes that will confirm it is a play,
He being ambitious that it ſhould be known
What's good was Fletchers, and what ill his own.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: STill doubtfull, and perplex'd too, whether he
Hath done Fletcher right in this Hiſtorie,
The Poet ſits within, ſince he muſt know it,
He with reſpect deſires that you would ſhew it
By ſome accuſtomed ſign, if from our action,
Or his indeavours you meet ſatisfaction,
With ours he hath his ends, we hope the beſt,
To make that certainty in you doth reſt.

list.item: Pedro, the Pilgrim, a noble Gentleman, Servant to Alinda.
Roderigo, rival to Pedro, Captain of the Out-laws.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Alinda, Daughter to Alphonſo, Pedro's Lady.
Juletta, Alinda's Maid, a witty Laſs.

sp.speaker: Curio
sp.l: SIgnior Alphonſo, ye are too rugged to her,
Believe too full of harſhneſs.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Yes, it ſeems ſo.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: A Father of ſo ſweet a child, ſo happy,
Fye, Sir, ſo excellent in all endowments,
In bleſſedneſs of beauty, ſuch a mirror.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: She is a fool, away.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Can ye be angry?
Can any wind blow rough, upon a bloſſom
So fair, and tender? Can a Fathers nature,
A noble Fathers too?

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: All this is but prating:
Let her be rul'd; let her obſerve my humour,
With my eyes let her ſee; with my ears liſten;
I am her Father: I begot her, bred her,
And I will make her—

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: No doubt ye may compel her,
But what a miſchievous, unhappy fortune
May wait upon this will of yours, as commonly
Such forcings ever end in hates and ruines.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Is't not a man I wiſh her to? a ſtrong man?
What can ſhe have? what could ſhe have? a Gentleman?
A young man? and an able man? a rich man?
A handſome man? a valiant man? do you mark me?
None of your pieced-companions, your pin'd-Gallants,
That flie to fitters, with every flaw of weather:
None of your impt bravadoes: what can ſhe ask more?
Is not a metal'd man fit for a woman?
A ſtrong chin'd man? I'le not be fool'd, nor flurted.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: I grant ye Roderigo is all theſe,
And a brave Gentleman: muſt it therefore follow
Upon neceſſity ſhe muſt doat upon him?
Will ye allow no liberty in chooſing?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Alas ſhe is tender yet.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Enough, enough, enough, Sir:
She is malleable: ſhe'll endure the hammer,
And why not that ſtrong workman that ſtrikes deepeſt?
Let me know that? ſhe is fifteen, with the vantage,
And if ſhe be not ready now for mannage—

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: You know he is a baniſh'd man: an Out-law;
And how he lives: his nature rough, and bloody
By cuſtomary Rapines: now, her ſweet humour
That is as eaſie as a calm, and peaceful,
All her affections, like the dews on Roſes,
Fair as the flowers themſelves: as ſweet and gentle:
How would you have theſe meet?

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: A bed, a bed, Sir:
Let her be the faireſt Roſe, and the ſweeteſt,
Yet I know this fair Roſe muſt have her prickles:
I grant ye Roderigo is an out Law.
An eaſie compoſition calls him in again,
He is a valiant man, and he is a rich man,
And loves the fool: a little rough by cuſtom:
She'l like him ten times better. She'l doat upon him,
If ere they come to grapling, run mad for him;
But there is another in the wind, ſome Caſtrel
That hovers over her, and dares her daily,
Some flickring ſlave.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: I dare not think ſo poorly.

sp.speaker: A p.
sp.l: Something there is, and muſt be: but I ſhall ſeent it
And hunt it narrowly.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: I never ſaw her yet
Make offer at the leaſt glance of affection,
But ſtill ſo modeſt, wiſe—

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: They are wiſe to gull us.
There was a fellow, old Ferando's ſon,
I muſt confeſs handſome, but my enemy,
And the whole family I hate: young Pearo,
That fellow I have ſeen her gaze upon,
And turn, and gaze again, and make ſuch offers,
As if ſhe would ſhoot her eyes like Meteors at him:
But that cauſe ſtands removed.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: You need not doubt him,
For long ſince as 'twas thought on a griev'd Conſcience,
He left his Father, and his Friends: more pity:
For truth reports he was a noble Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Let him be what he will: he was a beggar,
And there I'le leave him.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: The more the Court muſt anſwer;
But certainly I think, though ſhe might favour him,
And love his goodneſs, as he was an honeſt man:
She never with looſe eyes ſtuck on his perſon.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: She is ſo full of Conſcience too, and charity,
And outward holineſs, ſhe will undo me:
Relieves more Beggars, than an Hoſpital;
And all poor Rogues, that can but ſay their prayers,
And tune their pipes to Lamentations,
She thinks ſhe is bound to dance to: good morrow to you,
And that's as ye deſerve too: you know my mind,
And ſtudy to obſerve it: do it cheerfully,
And readily, and home.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I ſhall obey ye.
But, noble Sir.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Come, come, away with your flatteries,
And your fine phraſes.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Pray ye be gentle to her.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: I know 'em; and know your feats: if you will find me
Noble and loving, ſeek me in your duty,
You know I am too indulgent.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Alas, poor Lady.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: To your devotions: I take no good thing from you.
Come Gentlemen; leave pitying, and moaning of her
And praiſing of her vertues: and her whim-whams,
It makes her proud, and ſturdy.

sp.speaker: Seb. Cur.
sp.l: Good hours wait on ye. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I thank ye, Gentlemen: I want ſuch comforts:
I would thank you too Father: but your cruelty
Hath almoſt made me ſenſeleſs of my duty,
Yet ſtill I muſt know: would I had known nothing.
What Poor attend my charity to day, wench?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Of all ſorts, Madam; your open handed bounty
Make's 'em flock every hour: ſome worth your pity,
But others that have made a trade of begging.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Wench, if they ask it truly, I muſt give it:
It takes away the holy uſe of charity
To examine wants.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I would you would be merry:
A cheerful giving hand, as I think, Madam,
Requires a heart as chearful.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Alas Juletta,
What is there to be merry at? what joy now,
Unleſs we fool our own afflictions,
And make them ſhew ridiculous?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Sure, Madam,
You could not ſeem thus ſerious, if you were married,
Thus ſad, and full of thoughts.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Married? to whom, wench?
Thou thinkſt if there be a young handſome fellow,
As thoſe are plentiful, our cares are quenched then.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Madam, I think a luſty handſome fellow
If he be kind, and loving, and a right one,
Is even as good a Pill, to purge this melancholy,
As ever Galen gave, I am ſure more natural:
And merrier for the heart, than Wine and Saffron:
Madam, wanton youth is ſuch a Cataplaſme.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Who has been thy Tutor, Wench?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Even my own thoughts, Lady:
For though I be bar'd the liberty of talking,
Yet I can think unhappily, and as near the mark, Madam
'Faith, marry, and be merry.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Who will have me?
Who will be troubled with a pettiſh Girl?
It may be proud, and to that vice expenceful?
Who can aſſure himſelf, I ſhall live honeſt?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Let every man take his fortune.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: And o' my Conſcience
If once I grow to breeding, a whole Kingdom
Will not contain my ſtock.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: The more the merrier:
'Tis brave to be a mother of new Nations.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Why, I ſhould bury a hundred Husbands.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis no matter!
As long as ye leave ſufficient men to flock ye.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Is this thy mirth? are theſe the joyes of marriage?
Away light headed fool; are theſe contentments?
If I could find a man—

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: You may a thouſand.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Meer men I know I may: and there a Woman
Has liberty, (at leaſt ſhe'l venture for it)
To be a monſter and become the time too;
But to enjoy a man, from whoſe example
(As from a compaſs) we may ſteer our fortunes,
Our actions, and our age; and ſafe arrive at
A memory that ſhall become our aſhes,
Such things are few, and far to ſeek; to find one
That can but rightly mannage the wild beaſt, Woman,
And ſweetly govern with her. But no more of this, Wench,
'Tis not for thy diſcourſe: Let's in, and ſee
What poor afflicted wait our charity. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter a Porter, 4 Beggers, Pedro, and a Pilgrim.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: Stand off, and keep your ranks: twenty foot further:
There louſe your ſelves with reaſon and diſcretion.
The Sun ſhines warm: the farther ſtill the better,
Your beaſts will bolt anon, and then 'tis dangerous.

sp.speaker: 1 Beg.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs our Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: Does the crack go that way?
'Twill be o'th' other ſide anon.

sp.speaker: 2 Beg.
sp.l: Pray ye friend.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: Your friend? and why your friend? why goodman turncoat
What doſt thou ſee within me, or without me,
Or what itch doſt thou know upon me, tell me,
That I ſhould be thy friend? what do I look like
Any of thy acquaintance hung in Gibbets?
Haſt thou any Friends, Kindred, or Alliance,
Or any higher ambition, than an Alms-basket?

sp.speaker: 2 Beg.
sp.l: I would be your worſhips friend.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: So ye ſhall, Sirrah,
When I quarter the ſame louſe with ye.

sp.speaker: 3 Beg.
sp.l: 'Tis twelve o'clock.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: 'Tis ever ſo with thee, when thou haſt done ſcratching,
For that provokes thy ſtomach to ring noon;
O the infinite Seas of Porridge thou haſt ſwallow'd!
And yet thou lookſt as if they had been but Glyſters;
Thou feedſt abundance, thou hadſt need of ſuſtenance;
Alms do you call it to relieve theſe Raſcals?
Nothing but a general rot of ſheep can ſatisfie 'em.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Did not I tell you, how ſhe would undo me?
What Marts of Rogues, and Beggers?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: 'Tis charity
Methinks, you are bound to love her for—

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Yes, I warrant ye,
If men could ſale to Heaven in Porridge-pots,
With maſts of Beef, and Mutton, what a Voyage ſhould I make?
What are all theſe?

sp.speaker: 1 Beg.
sp.l: Poor people, and 't like your worſhip.

sp.speaker: 1 Beg.
sp.l: Wretched poor people.

sp.speaker: 3 Beg.
sp.l: Very hungry people.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: And very Louſy.

sp.speaker: 4 Beg.
sp.l: Yes forſooth, ſo, ſo.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: I'le undertake five hundred head about 'em,
And that's no needy Graſier.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: What are you?

sp.speaker: Pil.
sp.l: Strangers that come to wonder at your charity,
Yet people poor enough to beg a bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Uſe them with ſavour, Sir, their ſhews are reverent,
It ſeems ye are holy Pilgrims?

sp.speaker: Pil.
sp.l: Ye gueſs right, Sir,
And bound far off, to offer our devotions.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: What make ye this way? we keep no Reliques here,
Nor holy Shrines.

sp.speaker: Pil.
sp.l: The holieſt we ere heard of;
Ye keep a living monument of goodneſs,
A Daughter of that pious excellence,
The very Shrines of Saints ſink at her vertues,
And ſwear they cannot hold pace with her pieties,
We come to ſee this Lady: not with prophane eyes,
Nor wanton bloods, to doat upon her beauties,
But through our tedious wayes to beg her bleſſings.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: This is a new way of begging, and a neat one,
And this cries mony for reward, good ſtore too;
Theſe commendations beg not with bag, and bottle;
Well, well, the Sainting of this Woman, Gentlemen,
I know what it muſt come to: theſe Women Saints
Are plaguy heavy Saints: they out weigh a he-ſaint
Three thouſand thick; I know: I feel.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Ye are more afraid than hurt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Have you your commendations ready too?
He bows, and nods.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: A handſome well built perſon.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: What Country-craver are you? nothing but motion?
A puppet-Pilgrim?

sp.speaker: Pil.
sp.l: He's a ſtranger, Sir;
This four days I have Travel'd in his Company,
But little of his buſineſs, or his Language
As yet I have underſtood.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Both young and handſome,
Only the Sun has been too ſaucy with him.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Would ye have mony, Sir, or meat? what kind of bleſſing
Does your devotion look for? Still more ducking?
Be there any Saints, that underſtand by ſigns only?
More motion yet? this is the prettieſt Pilgrim,
The pink of Pilgrims: I'le be for ye, Sir;
Do ye diſcourſe with ſigns? ye are heartily welcome:
A poor viaticum; very good gold, Sir:
But holy men affect a better treaſure.
I kept it for your goodneſs, but ne'rtheleſs
Since it can prove but burthenſome to your holineſs,
And that you affect light prayer, fit for carriage,
I'le put this up again

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Ye are too unreverent.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Ye talk too broad! muſt I give way, and wealth too
To every toy, that carries a grave ſeeming?
Muſt my good Angels wait on him? if the proud hilding
Would yield but to my will, and know her duty
I know what I would ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Good Sir, be patient,
The wrongs ye do theſe men, may light on you,
Too heavy too: and then you will wiſh you had ſaid leſs;
A comely and ſweet uſage becomes ſtrangers.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: We ſhall have half the Kingdom ſtrangers ſhortly,
And this fond prodigality be ſuffer'd;
But I muſt be an Aſs, ſee 'em relieved, ſirrah;
If I were young again, I would ſooner get Bear-whelps,
And ſafer too, than any of theſe ſhe-ſaints,
But I will break her.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Such a face for certain.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Me thinks I have ſeen it too: but we are cozen'd;
But fair befal thee Pilgrim, thou lookſt lovely. Exit.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: Will ye troop up, ye Porridge Regiment?
Captain Poors quarter will ye move?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Ye dull Knave,
Are not theſe wretches ſerved yet?

sp.speaker: Beg.
sp.l: 'Bleſs my Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Do you make ſport, Sir, with their miſeries?
Ye drouſie Rogue.

sp.speaker: Por.
sp.l: They are too high fed, Madam,
Their ſtomachs are a ſleep yet.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Serve 'em plentifully,
Or I'le ſerve you out next: even out o' doors, ſirrah;
And ſerve 'em quickly too.

sp.speaker: Beg.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs the Lady.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Bleſs the good end I mean it for.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I would I knew it:
If it be for any mans ſake, I'le cry Amen too.
Well, Madam, ye have even as pretty a port of Penſioners.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Vain-glory would ſeek more, and handſomer.
But I appeal to vertue what my end is; Ex. Beggers.
What men are theſe?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: It ſeems they are holy Pilgrims:
That handſome youth ſhould ſuffer ſuch a penance,
Would I were even the Saint they make their vowes to,
How eaſily I would grant!

sp.speaker: Pil.
sp.l: Heavens grace in-wheel ye:
And all good thoughts, and prayers dwell about ye,
Abundance be your friend; and holy charity
Be ever at your hand to crown ye glorious.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I thank ye, Sir; peace guide your travels too,
And what you wiſh for moſt, end all your troubles;
Remember me by this: and in your prayers
When your ſtrong heart melts, meditate my poor fortunes
All my Devotions wait upon your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Are you of this Country, Sir?
Yes, worthieſt Lady,
But far off bred; my Fortunes farther from me.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Gentle, I dare believe.
I have liv'd freer.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I am no inquiſitor, that were too curious;
Whatever Vow, or Penance pulls you on, Sir;
Conſcience, or Love, or ſtubborn Diſobedience,
The Saint ye kneel to, hear, and eaſe your travels.
Yours ne'r begin; and thus I ſeal my Prayers.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: How conſtantly this man looks? how he ſighs?
Some great affliction hatches his Devotions,
Right holy Sir, how young, and ſweet he ſuffers?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Would I might ſuffer with him.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: He turns from us;
Alas, he weeps too; ſomething preſſes him
He would reveal, but dare not; Sir, be comforted,
Ye come for that; and take it; if it be want, Sir,
To me ye appear ſo worthy of relieving,
I am your Steward; Speak, and take; he's dumb ſtill;
Now as I have a faith, this man ſo ſtirs me,
His modeſty makes me afraid I have treſpaſſed.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Would he wou'd ſtir me too, I like his ſhape well.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: May be he would ſpeak alone; go off; Juletta,
Afflicted hearts fear their own motions.
Be not far off.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Would I were nearer to him,
A young ſmug handſom holineſs has no fellow. Exit.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Why do you grieve? do you find your penance ſharp?
Or are the vows ye've made too mighty for ye?
Does not the World allure ye to look back,
And ſorrow for the ſweet time ye have loſt?
Ye are young, and fair; be not deluded, Sir,
A manly made-up heart contemns theſe ſhadows,
And yours appear no leſs, griefs for your fears,
For hours ill-ſpent, for wrongs done raſh, and rudely,
For foul contempts, for faiths ill violated,
Become fears well; I dare not task your goodneſs;
And then a ſorrow ſhews in his true glory,
When the whole heart is excellently ſorry,
I pray ye be comforted.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I am, dear Lady,
And ſuch a comfort ye have caſt upon me,
That though I ſtruggle with mine own calimities
Too mighty, and too many for my mannage,
And though, like angry waves, they curl'd upon me,
Contending proudly who ſhould firſt devour me,
Yet I would ſtem their danger.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: He ſpeaks nobly;
What do you want?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: All that can make me happy;
I want my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Your ſelf? who rob'd ye, Pilgrim?
Why does he look ſo conſtantly upon me?
I want my ſelf; indeed, ye holy Wanderers
Are ſaid to ſeek much, but to ſeek your ſelves—

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I ſeek my ſelf, and am but my ſelfs ſhadow,
'Have loſt my ſelf; and now am not ſo noble.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I ſeek my ſelf; ſomething I yet remember
That bears that Motto; 'tis not he, he's younger,
And far more tender; for that ſelf-ſake (Pilgrim)
Be who it will, take this.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Your hand I dare take,
That be far from me, Lady, thus I kiſs it,
And thus I bleſs it too; Be conſtant fair ſtill,
Be good, and live to be a great example. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: One word more (Pilgrim) has amaz'd me ſtrangly,
Be conſtant fair ſtill; 'tis the Poſie here;
And here without, Be good; he wept to ſee me. Juletta.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Take this Key, and fetch me
The marygold-Jewel that lies in my little Cabinet;
I think 'tis that; what eyes had I to miſs him? Ex. Jul.
O me, what thoughts? he had no beard then, and
As I remember well, he was more ruddy.
If this be he, he has a manly face yet,
A goodly ſhape.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Here Madam.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Let me ſee it;
'Tis ſo true, it muſt be he, or nothing,
He ſpake the words juſt as they ſtand engraven here:
I ſeek my ſelf, and am but my ſelfs ſhadow;
Alas, poor man! didſt thou not meet him, Juletta?
The Pilgrim, Wench?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: He went by long ago, Madam.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I forgot to give him ſomething.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Twas ill done, Lady;
For o' my troth, he is the handſomeſt man
I ſaw this many a day; would he had all my wealth,
And me to boot; what ails ſhe to grow ſo ſullen?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Come, I forgot, but I will recompence it.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Alphonſo, Curio, Seberto, Juletta, Porter, and Servants.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: CAN ſhe ſlip through a Cat-hole? tell me that; reſolve me;
Can ſhe flye in the air? is ſhe a thing inviſible?
Gone, and none know it!

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: You amaze your ſervants.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Some pelting Rogue has watcht her hour of itching,
And claw'd her, claw'd her, do you mark me? claw'd her;
Some that I foſter up.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: They are all here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Let 'em be where they will, they are arrant Raſcals,
And by this hand, I'll hang all.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Deal calmly;
You will not give 'em time to anſwer ye.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I'll choak 'em, famiſh 'em, what ſay you, Wagtail?
You knew her mind; you were of counſel with her,
Tell me, and tell me true.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Ask with diſcretion.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Diſcretion? hang diſcretion, hang ye all:
Let me know where ſhe is.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Would you know o' me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: O' thee, Sir? I, o' thee, Sir; what art thou Sir?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Her woman, Sir, and't like your Worſhip, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Her Bawd, her Fiddle-ſtick;
Her Lady-fairy, to oyl the doors o' nights,
That they may open with diſcretion,
Her Gin, her Nut-Crack.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis very well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt; 'tis damnable ill, 'tis moſt abominable;
Will ye confeſs (Thing')

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Say I were guilty, Sir;
I would be hang'd before I would confeſs;
Is this a World to confeſs in?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Deal directly.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Yes, if my matter lye direct before me;
But when I am forc'd, and ferretted.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Tell me the truth,
And as I live, I'll give thee a new Petticoat.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And you would give me ten, I would not tell ye,
Truths bear a greater price than you are aware of.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Deal modeſtly.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I do not pluck my Cloaths up,

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: What ſay you, Sirrah? you? or you? are ye dumb all?

sp.speaker: Port.
sp.l: I ſaw her laſt night, and't ſhall like your Worſhip,
When I ſerv'd in her Livery.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: What's that, Sirrah?

sp.speaker: Port.
sp.l: Her Chamber-pot, and't pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: A new Livery.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Where lay ſhe? who lay with her?

sp.speaker: Port.
sp.l: In truth, not I, Sir;
I lay with my fellow Frederick in the flea-Chamber,
And't like your Worſhip, we are almoſt worried.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I left her by her ſelf, in her own Cloſet,
And there I thought ſhe had ſlept.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Why lay you from her?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: It was her will I ſhould; ſhe is my Miſtriſs,
And my part is obedience.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Were all the doors lock'd?

sp.speaker: Port.
sp.l: All mine.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: And mine; ſhe could not get out thoſe ways
Unleſs ſhe leapt the walls; and thoſe are higher
Than any Womans courage dare aſpire at.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Come, you muſt know.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Conceal it not, but deal plain.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: If I did know, and her truſt lay upon me,
Not all your angers nor your flatteries
Should make me ſpeak, but having no more intereſt
Than I may well deliver to the air,
I'll tell ye what I know, and tell it liberally,
I think ſhe is gone, becauſe we cannot find her;
I think ſhe is weary of your tyranny,
And therefore gone; may be ſhe is in love;
May be in love, where you ſhow no great liking,
And therefore gone; May be ſome point of Conſcience,
Or vow'd Devotion.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Theſe are nothing, minion;
You that can aim at theſe, muſt know the truth too.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Any more truth than this if I know, hang me,
Or where to ſearch for it, if I make a lye
To gain your love, and envy my beſt Miſtriſs,
Pin me againſt a wall with my heels upward,

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Out of my doors.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: That's all my poor petition;
For if your houſe were Gold, and ſhe not in it,
Sir, I ſhould count it but a Cage to whiſtle in.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Whore, if ſhe be above ground, I will have her.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I would live in a Coal-pit then, were I your daughter.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Certain ſhe does not know, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Hang her, hang her;
She knows too much; ſearch all the houſe, all corners,
And where 'tis poſſible ſhe may go out, Ex. Servants.
If I do find your tricks.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Reward me for 'em.
Or if I had ſuch tricks, you could diſcover
So weak, and ſleightly woven, you might look through,
All the young Girls ſhould hoot me out o' th' Pariſh;
You are my Maſter, but you own an anger
Becomes a School Boy that hath loſt his Apples;
Will ye force things into our knowledges?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Come hither, Juletta, thou didſt love me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And do ſtill,
You are my Ladies Father, and I reverence ye.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Thou would'ſt have pleas'd my humour.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Any good way,
That carried not ſuſpicion in't, or flattery,
Or fail of truſt.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Come, come, thou wouldſt have—

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Stay, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: And thou haſt felt my bounty for't, and ſhalt do.
Doſt thou want Cloaths or Money?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Both.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: 'Shalt have both.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: But not this way, I had rather be an Adamite,
And bring Fig-tree leaves into faſhion again.
If you were young, Sir,
Handſome, and fitted to a Womans appetite;
And a giddy-headed Girl, that car'd for nothing,
Much might be done; then you might ſumble with me,
And think to grope out matters of ſome moment,
Which now you will put too ſhort for;
For what you have ſeen hitherto,
And know by me, has been but honeſt ſervice,
Which I dare pin i'th' market-place to anſwer;
And let the World, the Fleſh, and Devil examine it,
And come you in too, I dare ſtand your ſtricteſt.
And ſo much good may do you, with your dreams of courteſie

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: This is moſt monſtrous.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Sure ſhe does not know, Sir;
She durſt not be ſo confident, and guilty.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: How now, what news? what hopes and ſteps diſcovered?
Speak any thing that's good, that tends to th' matter;
Do you ſtand ſtaring ſtill?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: We are no gods, Sir,
To ſay ſhe is here or there, or what ſhe is doing;
But we have ſearch'd.

sp.speaker: Port.
sp.l: I am ſure ſhe is not i'th' Cellar;
For look you, Sir, if ſhe had been i'th' Cellar—

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I am ſure thou haſt been there.

sp.speaker: Port.
sp.l: As I carried the matter,
For I ſearch'd every piece of Wine; yes ſure, Sir,
And every little Terſe, that could but teſtifie;
And I drew hard to bolt her out.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Away with him;
Fling him i'th' Hay-mow, let him lye a mellowing;
He ſtinks of Muskadel like an Engliſh Chriſtmas;
Are theſe your cares? your ſervices?

sp.speaker: 2 Serv.
sp.l: Pray ye hear, Sir,
We have found where ſhe went out, her very footing.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Where, where? go on.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Obſerve then with more ſtayedneſs.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: Searching the Garden at the little Poſtern
That opens to the Park, we firſt diſcovered it.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: A little foot?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: It muſt be hers, or none, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: How far beyond that?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: To the Park it leads us,
But there the ground being hard, we could not mark it.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: She always kept that Key; I was a Coxcomb,
A Fool, an Aſs, to give a Girl that liberty;
Saddle my Horſes, Rogues, ye drunken Varlets,
Your precious diligence lies in Pint-pots,
Your Brains in Butts, my Horſes, ye pin-Buttocks.
You'll bear me Company?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: We dare not leave ye,
Unleſs we found a quieter ſoul within ye.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: If we may do the Lady any ſervice,
Sweet, gentle Soul.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I ſay again, my horſes,
Are ye ſo hot? have ye your private Pilgrimages?
Muſt ye be jumping, Joan? I'll wander with ye;
I'll jump ye, and I'll juggle ye, my horſes;
And keep me this young Lirry-poop within doors,
I will diſcover, Dame.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis fit you ſhould, Sir,
If ye knew what; well Love, if thou beeſt with her,
Or what power elſe that arms her reſolution,
Conduct her fair, and keep her from this mad-man,
Direct her to her wiſhes; dwell about her,
That no diſhonourable end o'r take her,
Danger, or want; and let me try my fortune.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: You know the place we meet in?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: We ſhall hit it.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: And as ye are honeſt Gentlemen, endeavour.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: We'l ſearch the beſt we can; if ſhe light in our hands.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I'll tye her to the horſe-tail.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: We know how to uſe her,
But not your way, for all your ſtate.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Make haſte there;
And get you in, and look to th' houſe. If you ſtir out, Damſel,
Or ſet a foot any new motion this way,
When I come home (which will be ſuddenly)
You know my mind; if you do play the Raſcal,
I have my eyes and ears in ſundry places,
If ye do praunce.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I ſhall do that that's ſit, Sir;
And fit to croſs your fooleries; I'll fail elſe:
And ſo I'll to my Chamber. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: To your Prayers,
And leave your ſtubborn tricks; ſhe is not far yet,
She cannot be, and we dividing ſuddenly.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Keep her from thy hands, I beſeech.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Our horſes;
Come chearfully. I'll teach her to run gadding. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Out-law.
sp.l: Captain, y'are not merry.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: We get nothing,
We have no ſport; whoring and drinking ſpoils us,
We keep no Guards.

sp.speaker: 2 Out-law.
sp.l: There come no Paſſengers,
Merchants, nor Gentlemen, nor whoſoever,
But we have tribute.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: And whilſt we ſpend that idlely,
We let thoſe paſs that carry the beſt purchaſe.
I'll have all ſearch'd, and brought in: Rogues, and Beggars,
Have got the trick now to become Bank-maſters.
I'll have none ſcape; only my friends and neighbours,
That may deliver to the King my innocence;
Thoſe I would have regarded; 'tis policy.
But otherwiſe nor gravities, nor ſhadows,
Appear they how they will, they may have purſes,
