For they ſhall pay.

sp.speaker: 3 Out-law.
sp.l: You ſpeak now like a Captain.
And if we ſpare, fley us, and coin our Caſſocks,
Will ye look blith?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You hear no preparation
The King intends againſt us yet?

sp.speaker: 4 Out-law.
sp.l: Not a word, Sir,
Good man, he's troubled with matter of more moment,
Hummings of higher nature vex his brains, Sir,
Do not we ſee his Garriſons?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Who are out now?

sp.speaker: 4 Out-law.
sp.l: Good fellows, Sir, that if there be any purchaſe ſtirring
Will ſtrike it dead; Jaques, and Lopez, Lads,
That know their Quarters, as they know their Knapſacks;
And will not off.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Where is the Boy ye brought me?
A pretty Lad, and of a quick capacity,
And bred up neatly.

sp.speaker: 1 Out-law.
sp.l: He's within at meat, Sir,
The Knave is hungry, yet he ſeaſons all
He eats or drinks with many tears and ſighings,
The ſaddeſt appetite I ever lookt on
The Boy is young, 'tis fear, and want of company,
He knows, and loves; uſe him not rough, and harſhly,
He will be quickly bold; I'll entertain him;
I want a pretty Boy to wait upon me,
And when I am ſad or ſleepy, to prate to me;
Beſides there's ſomething in his face I like well.
And ſtill the more I look, more like; let him want nothing,
And uſe him gently, all.

sp.speaker: 2 Out-law.
sp.l: Here's a ſmall Box, Sir,
We took about him, which he griev'd to part with,
May be ſome Wealth.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Alas, ſome little money
The poor Knave carried to defray his lodgings,
I'll give it him again, and add unto it.
'Twere ſin to open ſuch a petty purchaſe.
sp.stage: Enter Lopez, and Jaques with Pedro.
sp.l: How now, who is this? what have you brought me, Souldiers?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We know not well, what a ſtrange ſlaving fellow,
Sullen enough I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Where took ye him?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Upon the Skirt o' th' wood, viewing, and gaping,
And ſometime ſtanding ſtill, as if he had meant
To view the beſt acceſſes to our quarters;
Money he has enough; and when we threatned him,
He ſmil'd, and yielded; but not one word utter'd.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: His habit ſays he's holy, if his heart
Keep that proportion too, 'tis beſt ye free him,
We keep his wallet here, I am ſure 'tis heavy.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Pilgrim, come hither, Sir, are you a Pilgrim?
A piece of pretty holineſs; do you ſhrink, Sir?
A ſmug young Saint. What Country were you born in?
Ye have a Spaniſh face; In a dumb Province?
And had your Mother too this excellent Vertue?
No tongue do you ſay? ſure ſhe was a matchleſs woman;
What a fine family is this man ſprung from!
Certain he was begotten in a Calm,
When all was huſh'd; the Midwife was dumb Midnight;
Are ye ſeal'd up? or do you ſcorn to anſwer?
Ye are in my hands, and I have Medicines for ye
Can make ye ſpeak: pull off his Bonnet, Souldiers;
Ye have a ſpeaking face.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I am ſure a handſome;
This Pilgrim cannot want She Saints to pray to.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Stand nearer, ha?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Come, do your worſt, I am ready.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Is your tongue found? go off, and let me talk with him;
And keep your watches round.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We are ready, Captain.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: So, now what are ye?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Am I?
My habit ſhews me what I am

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Thy heart
A deſperate fool, and ſo thy fate ſhall tell thee.
What Devil brought thee hither? for I know thee.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I know thou doſt, and ſince it is my fortune
To light into thy fingers, I muſt think too
The moſt malicious of all Devils brought me,
Yet ſome men ſay thou art noble.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Not to thee,
That were a benefit to mock the Giver,
Thy father hates my friends, and family,
And thou haſt been the heir of all this malice.
Can two ſuch ſtorms meet then, and part with kiſſing?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: You have the mightier hand.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: And ſo I'll uſe it.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I cannot hinder ye; leſs can I beg
Submiſſive at his knees that knows not honour,
That bears the Stamp of Man, and not his Nature;
Ye may do what ye pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I will do all.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And when you have done all, which is my poor •• ine,
(For farther your baſe malice cannot venture)
Diſhonours ſelf will cry you out a Coward.
Hadſt thou been brave, and noble, and an Enemy,
Thou wouldſt have ſought me whilſt I carried Arms,
Whilſt my good Sword was my profeſſion,
And then have cryed out, Pedro, I defie thee;
Then ſtuck Alphonſo's quarrel on the point,
The mercenary anger thou ſerv'ſt under,
To get his Daughter. Then thou ſhouldſt have brav'd me,
And arm'd with all thy Families hate upon thee,
Done ſomething worthy fear; Now poor and baſely
Thou fetſt Toyls to betray me; and like the Pe • ant,
That dares not meet the Lion in the face,
Dig'ſt crafty pit-falls: thou ſham'ſt the Spaniſh Honour;
Thou haſt neither point of Man, nor Conſcience in thee.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Sir, Sir, y'are brave, ye plead now in a Sanctuary,
You think your Pilgr • ims Bulwa • k can defend ye;
You will not find it ſo,

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I look not for't.
The more unhallowed ſoul haſt thou to offer it.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: VVhen you were braveſt, Sir, and your ſword ſharpeſt,
I durſt affront ye; when the Court Sun gilded ye,
And every cry was the young hopeful Pedro,
Alonſo's ſprightly Son; then durſt I meet ye,
When you were Maſter of this fame, and faſhion,
And all your glories in the full Meridian,
The Kings proof-favour buckled on your body;
Had we then come to competition,
Which I have often ſought.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.l: And I de •• 'd too.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You ſhould have ſeen this Sword, how e're you ſlight it,
And felt it too; ſharper than ſorrow felt it,
In execution quicker than thy ſcorns;
Thou ſhould'ſt have ſeen all this, and ſhrunk to ſee it.
Then like a Gentleman I would have us'd thee,
And given thee the fair fortune of thy being,
Then with a Souldiers arm I had honour'd thee;
But ſince thou ſtealſt upon me like a Spie,
And thief-like thinkſt that holy caſe ſhall carry thee
Through all my purpoſes, and ſo betray me,
Baſe as the act, thy end be, and I forget thee.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: What poor evaſions thou buildſt on, to abuſe me?
The goodneſs of a man ne'r taught theſe principles.
I come a Spie? durſt any noble ſpirit
But on this habit, to become a Traitor?
Even in an Enemy ſhew me this antipathy
Where there is Chriſtian faith, and this not reverenced:
I come a Spie? no Roderigo, no,
A • ater of thy perſon, a maligner?
So far from that, I brought no malice with me,
But rather when I meet thee, tears to ſoften thee;
When I put on this habit, I put off
All fires, all angers, all thoſe ſtarts of youth
• hat clapt too rank a bias to my being,
And drew me from the right mark all ſhould aim at;
In ſtead of ſtubborn ſteel, I put on prayers;
For raſh and haſly heats, a ſweet repentance:
Long weary ſteps, and vows, for my vain glories.
O Roderigo.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: If thy tongue could ſave thee,
Pra • ing be thy bail, thou haſt a rare benefit.
Souldiers, come out, and bring a halter with ye;
I'le forgive your holy habit, Sir, but I'le hang you.

sp.speaker: 1 Out l.
sp.l: Wherefore this halter Captain?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: For this traytor.
So, put it on him, and then tie him up.
Do you want a Band Sir? this is a courſe wearing,
Twill • it but ſcu • vily upon this collar;
But patience is as good as a French Pickadel.
What's his fault, Captain?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: 'Tis my will he periſh,
And that's his fault.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: A Captain of good government.
Come Souldiers, come, ye are roughly bred, and bloody,
• h • w your obedience, and the joy ye take
In executing impious commands,
Ye have a Captain ſeals your liberal pardons,
Be no more Chriſtians, put religion by,
'Twill make ye cowards: feel no tenderneſs,
Nor let a thing call'd conſcience trouble ye;
Alas, 'twill b • eed delay. Bear no reſpect
To what I ſeem; were I a Saint indeed,
Why ſhould that ſtagger ye? you know not holineſs:
To be excellent in evil, is your goodneſs;
And be ſo, 'twill become ye: have no hearts,
For fea • you ſhould repent: that will be dangerous:
For if there be a knocking there, a pricking,
And that pulſe beat back to your conſiderations,
How ye have laid a ſti •• hand on Religion—

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Truſs him I ſay.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And violated faith.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Hea • him not prate.

sp.speaker: Ped
sp.l: Why, what a thing will this be?
What ſtrange confuſion then will breed among ye?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Will none of ye obey?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: What Devils vex ye?
The fears ye live in and the hourly dangers
Will be delights to theſe: thoſe have their ends,
But theſe outlive all time, and all repentance:
And if it creep into your conſcience once,
Be ſure ye lock that cloſe.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Why ſtand ye gazing?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Farewel ſleep, peace, all that are humane comforts,
Better ye had been Trees, or Stones, and happier;
For thoſe die here, and ſeek no further being,
Nor hopes, nor puniſhments.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Rots take ye, Raſcals.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: What would you have us do?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Diſpatch the prater.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And have religious blood hang on our conſciences?
We are bad enough already: ſins enough
To make our graves even loath us.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: No man love me?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Although I be a thief, I am no hangman;
They are two mens trades, and let another execute.
Lay violent hands on holy things?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Baſe Cowards,
Put to your powers, ye raſcals, I command ye.
Holy, or unholy, if I ſay it,
I'le have it done.

sp.speaker: 1 Out-l.
sp.l: If I do't, let me ſtarve for't.
Or I.
Or I: we will obey things handſom,
And bad enough, and overdo obedience:
But to be made ſuch inſtruments of miſchief.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I have done as many villanies as another,
And with as little reluctation,
Let me come clear of theſe, and wipe that ſcore off.
Put me upon a felt and known perdition?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Have ye conſpir'd, ye ſlaves?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: How vilely this ſhows,
In one that would command anothers temper,
And bear no bound in's own?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Am I thus jaded?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Is it my life thou long'ſt for Roderigo?
And can no ſacrifice appeaſe thy malice,
But my blood ſpilt? do it thy ſelf, diſpatch it;
And as thou takſt the whole revenge unto thee,
Take the whole ſin upon thee; and be mighty,
Mighty in evil, as thou art in anger:
And let not theſe poor wretches houl for thy ſake.
Thoſe things that in thine own glaſs ſeem moſt monſtrous,
Wouldſt thou abuſe their weak ſights with, for amiable?
Is it, thou thinkſt to fear me with thy terrors,
And into weak condition draw my vertue?
If I were now to learn to die I would ſue thee:
Or did I fear death, then I would make thee glorious.
But knowing what, and how far I can ſuffer;
And all my whole life being but deaths preface,
My ſleep but at next door.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Are ye ſo valiant?
I'le make ye feel: I'le make ye know, and feel too;
And Raſcals, you ſhall tremble. Keep him here,
And keep him ſafe too: if he ſcape your guards—

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Fear not, I will not.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: As I live, ye die for't;
I will not be thus baſſled. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: What a Devil have ye done, Pilgrim? or what miſchief
Have you conſpir'd, that he ſhould rage and rave thus?
Have you kill'd his Father, or his Mother? or ſtrangled any of his kindred?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Has he no Siſters? have you not been bouncing
About their belly-pieces?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Why ſhould that be dangerous,
Or any way deſerve death? is it not natural?
Bar us the Chriſtian liberty of women,
And build us up with brick, take away our free-ſtone.

sp.speaker: 1 Out-l.
sp.l: Becauſe thou art holier than he, upon my conſcience
He does not envy thee: that's not his quarrel;
For look you, that might be compounded without prayers.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Nor that thou ſeemſt an honeſter man: for here
We have no trading with ſuch Tinſel-ſtuff;
To be an excellent thief, is all we aim at.
Wilt thou take a ſpit and ſtride, and ſee if thou canſt outrun us?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I ſcorn to ſhift his fury, keep your obedience;
For though your government admit no preſident,
Keep your ſelves carefull in't.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Thou wilt be hang'd then.
I cannot die with ſewer faults upon me.

sp.speaker: 2 Out-l.
sp.l: Tis ten to one he will ſhoot him: for the Devil's in him
If he hang him himſelf.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He has too proud a nature:
He will compel ſome one.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I am confident.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And ſo are all I think.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Be not moleſted,
If I muſt die, let it not trouble you;
It ſtirs not me: it is the end I was born for.
Only this honeſt office I deſire ye,
(If there be courteſie in men of your breed)
To ſee me buried; not to let his fury
Expoſe my body to the open violence
Of beaſts, and fowls: ſo far I urge humanity.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: He ſhall not deny us that: we'l ſee ye under ground,
And give ye a volly of as good cups of Sack,
For that's our Diſcipline.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He comes again,
As high in rage as ever; the boy with him.

sp.speaker: 1 Out-l.
sp.l: Will he compel the child?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He is bent to do it,
And muſt have ſome body.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: If thou lov'ſt me do it:
Love me, or love me not, I ſay thou ſhalt do it:
Stare not, nor ſtagger, Sirrah; if ye deny me,
Do you ſee this Rogue?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: What would ye have me do Sir?
Heavens goodneſs bleſs me.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Do? why hang a Raſcal,
That would hang me.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I am a boy, and weak, Sir.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Thou art ſtrong enough to tie him to a Bough,
And turn him off: come, thou ſhalt be my Jewel,
And I'le allow thee horſe, and all thy pleaſures,
And twenty gallant things: I'le teach thee arms too;
Make thee mine heir.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Let me inherit death firſt.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Make me not angry, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Which is the man, Sir?
I'le pluck up the beſt heart I can yet.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Fear not,
It is my will: That in the Pilgrims coat there,
That Devil in the Saints skin.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Guard me goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Diſpatch him preſently.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I wait your worſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Will the boy do it? is the rogue ſo confident?
So young, ſo deep in blood?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He ſhakes, and trembles.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Doſt thou ſeek more coals ſtill to fear thy conſcience.
Work ſacred innocence, to be a Devil?
Do't thy ſelf for ſhame, thou beſt becom'ſt it.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Sirrah, I ſcorn my finger ſhould be 'ſil'd with thee;
And yet I'le have it done: this child ſhall ſtrangle thee,
A crying Gi • le, if ſhe were here, ſhould maſter thee.

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: How ſhould I ſave him? how my ſelf from violence?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Leave your tongue-valour, and diſpatch your hate, Sir;
The patience of my death, ſhall more torment thee,
(Thou painted honour, thou baſe man made backward)
Than all my life has fear'd thee.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Gag him, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: The Boy looks cheerfully now: ſure he will do it

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: He will mall him elſe.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Are ye prepar'd to die, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Yes boy, and rea • y; prethee to thy buſineſs

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Why are ye then ſo angry? ſo perplext, Sir?
Patience wins Heaven, and not the heat of paſſion.
Why do you • ayle?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: The boy's a pretty Prieſt.

sp.speaker: Ped
sp.l: I thank ye gentle child, you teach me truely

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: You ſeem to fear too.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Thou feeſt more, than I feel, boy.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: You tremble ſure.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: No ſure boy, 'tis thy tenderneſs:
Prethee make haſte, and let that g • lph be ſatisfied

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: Are ye ſo willing to go to it?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Moſt willing:
I would not borrow from his courteſie
One hour of life, to gain an age of glory.

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: And is you r • ckoning ſtraight Sir?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: As ſtraight as truth, boy:
I cannot go more joyfully to a wedding.

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: Then to your prayers: I'le diſpatch ye preſently.
Now guide my tongue, thou bleſſedneſs.

sp.speaker: Rod
sp.l: A good boy.

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: But hark ye Sir, one word; and pray ye reſolve me
Let me ſpeak privately.

sp.speaker: Rod
sp.l: What wouldſt thou have child?

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: Shall this man die?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Why doſt thou make that queſtion?

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: Pray ye he not angry: if he muſt, I'le do it.
But muſt he now?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: What elſe? who date r • prieve him?

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: Pray ye think again; and as your injuries
Are great, and full, you ſuffer from this fellow,
Do not ye purpoſe ſo to ſuit your vengeance?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I do, and muſt.

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: You cannot if he die now.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Cannot?

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: No, cannot: be not vext, you'l find it.
I have 〈◊〉 , and I know it certain,
Ye 〈◊〉 below him: loſe all you angers

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Why, my beſt boy?

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: I love, and tender ye,
I would 〈◊〉 ye elſe. Is that revenge,
To flight your cauſe, and Saint your enemy,
Clap the Doves wings of downy peace unto him,
And let him ſoa • to Heaven, whilſt you are ſighing?
Is this revenge?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I would have him die.

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: Prepar'd thus?
The bleſſing of a Father never teach'd it:
His contemplation now ſcorns ye, contemns ye,
And all the tortures ye can uſe. Let him die thus;
And theſe that know and love revenge will laugh at ye:
Here lies the honour of a well-bred anger,
To make his enemy ſhake and tremble under him;
Doubt, nay, almoſt deſpair, and then confound him:
This man ye rock a ſleep, and all your rages
Are Requiems to his parting ſoul, meer Anthems.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Indeed he is ſtrongly built.

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: You cannot ſhake him;
And the more weight ye put on his foundation,
Now as he ſtands, ye ſix him ſtill the ſtronger;
If ye love him, honour him, would heap upon him
Friendſhips and benefits beyond example,
Hope him a Star in Heaven, and there would ſtick him,
Now take his life.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I had rather take mine own, Boy.

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: I'le caſe him preſently.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Stay, be not haſty.

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: Bleſs my tongue ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: What has the boy done to him?
How dull, and ſtill he looks?

sp.speaker: Alm.
sp.l: You are a wiſe man,
And long have buckled with the worlds extremities,
A valiant man, and no doubt know both fortunes,
And would ye work your Maſter-piece thus madly,
Take the bare name of honour, that will pity ye
When the world knows ye have prey'd on a poor Pilgrim?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: The boy has ſtagger'd me: what would'ſt thou have me?

sp.speaker: Ali.
sp.l: Have ye? do you not feel Sir? do's it not ſtir ye?
Do you ask a child? I would have ye do moſt bravely,
Becauſe I moſt affect ye: like your ſelf Sir,
Scorn him, and let him go; ſeem to contemn him,
And now ye have made him ſhake, ſeal him his pardon,
When he appears a ſubject ſit for anger,
And fit for you, his pious Armour off,
His hopes no higher than your ſword may reach at,
Then ſtrike, and then ye know revenge; then take it.
I hope I have turn'd his mind.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Let the fool go there,
I ſcorn to let looſe ſo baſe an anger
May light on thee: See me no more, but quit me;
And when we meet again.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I'le thank ye Captain. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Why this was like your ſelf: but which way goes he?
Shall we ne're happy meet?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I am drowſie: Boy,
Go with me, and diſcourſe: I like thy company
O Child! I love thy tongue.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I ſhall wait on ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: The Boy has don't: a Plaguey witty Raſcal.
And I ſhall love him terribly.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: 'Twas he moſt certain,
For if ye mark, how earneſt he was with him,
And how he labour'd him.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A cunning villain,
But a good rogue; 'This boy will make's all honeſt.

sp.speaker: 1 Out l.
sp.l: I ſcarce believe that: but I like the boy well.
Come let's to Supper; then upon our watches.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This Pilgrim ſ • ap'd a joyfull one.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Let's drink round
To the boys health, and then about our buſineſs.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Roderigo, Jaques, Lopez, and three Out-Laws.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: NOne of you know her?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Alas Sir, we never ſaw her:
Nor ever heard of her, but from your report.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: No happy eye?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I do not think 'tis ſhe, Sir,
Me thinks a woman dares not.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Thou ſpeak'ſt poorly,
What dares not woman, when ſhe is provok'd?
Or what ſeems dangerous to Love, or fury?
That it is ſhe, this has confirm'd me certain,
Theſe Jewels here, a part of which I ſent her,
And though unwilling, yet her Father wrought her
To take, and wear.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A wench, and we not know it?
And among us? where were our underſtandings?
I could have gheſs'd unhappily: have had ſome feeling
In ſuch a matter: Here are as pretty fellows,
At the diſcovery of ſuch a • igambob:
A handſome wench too? ſure we have loſt our faculties,
We have no motions: what ſhould ſhe do here, Sir?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: That's it that troubles me: O that baſe raſcal!
There lies the miſery: how cunningly ſhe quit him,
And how ſhe urg'd? had ye been conſtant to me,
I ne're had ſuffer'd this.

sp.speaker: 1 Out l.
sp.l: Ye might have hang'd him:
And would he had been hang'd, that's all we care ſor't:
So our hands had not don't.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: She is gone again too,
And what care have ye for that? gone, and conte • n 〈◊〉 .
Maſter'd my will, and power, and now laughs at m • .

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: The Devil that brought her hither, Sir I think
Has carryed her back again inviſible,
For we ne're knew, not heard of her departure.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: No living thing came this night through out watch.
She went with you.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Was by me till I ſlept,
But when I wak'd, and call'd: O my dull pate here,
If I had open'd this when it was given me,
This Roguy Box.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: We could but give it ye.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Pilgrim? a Pox o' Pilgrims, there the game go • s,
There's all my fortune fled; I know it, I feel it.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Bring me unto thy Captain: where's thy Captain?
I am founder'd, melted, ſome fairy thing or other
Has led me dancing; the Devil has haunted me
I'th' likeneſs of a voyce: give me thy Captain

sp.speaker: 2 Out-l.
sp.l: He's here Sir, there he ſtands.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: How do'ſt thou Captain?
I have been fool'd and jaded, made a dog bolt.
My Daughter's run away: I have been haunted too,
I have loſt my horſe; I am hungry, and out of my wits alſo.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l:
Come in: I'le tell you what I know: ſtrang •
〈◊〉
And take your eaſe; I'le follow her recover • ,
Theſe ſhall be yours the whil'ſt, and do ye ſervice.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Let me have drink enough: I am almoſt choak'd •• e.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You ſhall have any thing; what think you now, S • u •••• ?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I think a woman, is a woman, that's any thing.
The next we take, we'l ſ • arch a little nearer,
We'l not be boyed again with a pair of bre • c • es. Ex •••

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: He's gone in here: This is Rod • ri • o's quarter,
And I'le be with him ſoon: I'le 〈…〉 ,
A little better than I have done: all this long night
I have let him out o'th' wa • , • o try his patience,
And made him ſwear, and curſe; and pray, and ſwear again.
And cry for anger; I made him leave his horſe too,
Where he can never find him more; whiſtled to him,
And then he would run through thick and thin, to reach me,
And down in this ditch; up again, and ſhake him,
And ſwear ſome certain bleſſings; then into that buſh
Pop goes his pate, and all his face is comb'd over,
And I ſit laughing: a hundred tricks, I have ſerv'd him:
And I will double 'em, before I leave him;
I'le teach his anger to diſpute with women.
But all this time, I cannot meet my Miſtreſs,
I cannot come to comfort her; that grieves me,
For ſure ſhe is much afflicted: till I do,
I'le haunt thy Ghoſt Alphonſo; I'le keep thee waking,
Yes, I muſt get a Drum: I am villanous weary,
And yet I'le trot about theſe villages
Till I have got my will, and then have at ye.
I'le make your anger drop out at your elbows e're I leave ye.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange, in all the circuit we have ridden,
We cannot croſs her: no way light upon her.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: I do not think ſhe is gone thus far, or this way,
For certain if ſhe had, we ſhould have reach'd her,
Made ſome diſcovery, heard ſome news; we have ſeen nothing

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Nor paſs by any body that could promiſe any thing.
She is certainly diſguis'd, her modeſty
••• ſt never venture elſe.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Let her take any ſ • ape.
And let me ſee it once, I can diſtinguiſh it.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: So ſhould I think too: has not her Father found her:

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: No, I'le be hang'd then; he has no patience
Unleſs ſhe light in's teeth, to look about him.
He gueſſes now, and chaſes and frets like Tinſel.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Let him go on, he cannot live without it.
But keep her from him, heaven: where are we Curio?
In a wood I think, hang me if I know elſe.
And yet I have ridden all theſe coaſts, at all hours,
And had an aim.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: I would we had a guide.
And if I be not much awry Seberto,
Not far off ſhould be Roderigo's quarter,
For in this faſtneſs if I be not cozen'd,
He and his out-laws live.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: This is the place then
We appointed him to meet in.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Yes, I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Would we could meet ſome living thing: what's that there?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: A boy, I think, ſtay; why may not he direct us?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I am hungry, and I am weary, and I cannot find him.
Keep my wits Heaven, I feel 'em wavering,
O God my head.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Boy, doſt thou hear, thou ſtripling?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Now they will tear me, torture me, now Roderigo
Will hang me without mercy; ha?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Come hither.
A very pretty boy: what place is this, child?
And whither doſt thou travel? how he ſtares!
Some ſtubborn Maſter has abus'd the boy,
And beaten him: how he complains! whither goeſt thou?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I go to Segovia Sir, to my ſick Mother,
I have been taken here by drunken thieves,
And (O my bones!) I have been beaten Sir.
Miſ-us'd, and rob'd: extreamly beaten Gentlemen,
O God, my ſide!

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: What beaſts would uſe a boy thus?
Look up, and be of good cheer.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: O, I cannot.
My back, my back, my back.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: What thieves?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I know not.
But they call the Captain Roderigo.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Look ye,
I knew we were thereabouts.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou want any thing?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Nothing but eaſe, but eaſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: There's ſome mony,
And get thee to thy Mother.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I thank ye Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: This was extreamly foul, to vex a child thus.
Come, let's along, we cannot loſe our way now. Ex.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Though ye are honeſt men, I fear your fingers,
And glad I am got off; O how I tremble!
Send me but once within his arms dear fortune,
And then come all the world: what ſhall I do now?
'Tis almoſt night again, and where to lodge me,
Or get me meat, or any thing, I now not.
Theſe wild woods, and the fancies I have in me,
Will run me mad.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Boy, Boy.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: More ſet to take me?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou hear boy? thou pointer.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: 'Tis a boy too,
A Lacky Boy: I need not fear his fierceneſs.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Canſt thou beat a Drum?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: A Drum?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: This thing, a Drum here.
Didſt thou never ſee a Drum? Canſt thou make this grumble?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Julettas face, and tongue; is ſhe run mad too?
Here may be double craſt: I have no skill in't.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I'le give thee a royal but to go along with me.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I care not for thy royal, I have other buſineſs,
Drum to thy ſelf, and daunce to it.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Sirrah, Sirrah.
Thou ſcurvy Sirrah; thou ſnotty nos'd ſcab, do'ſt thou hear me?
If I lay down my Drum.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Here comes more Company,
I fear a plot, Heaven ſend me fairly from it. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Baſto; who's here?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Captain, do you need me farther?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: No not a foot: give me the gown: the ſword now.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: This is the Devil thief, and if he take me,
Woe be to my Gally gaskins.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Certain Sir,
She will take her patches off, and change her habit.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Let her do what ſhe pleaſe: No, no, Al •• d • ,
You cannot cozen me again in a Boys figure,
Nor hide the beauty of that face in patches,
But I ſhall know it.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: A boy his face in patches?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Nor ſhall your tongue again bewitch mine anger,
If ſhe be found i'th' woods, ſend me word preſently,
And I'le return; ſhe cannot be far gone yet:
If ſhe be not, expect me; when ye ſee me,
Uſe all your ſervice to my friend A phonſo,
And have a care to your buſineſs: farewel,
No more, farewel. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I am heartily glad thou art gone yet.
This boy in patches, was the boy came by me,
The very ſame, how haſtily it ſhifted?
What a mop eyed aſs was I, I could not know her,
This muſt be ſhe, this is ſhe, now I remember her,
How loth ſhe was to talk too, how ſhe ſcar'd me:
I could now piſs mine eyes out for meer anger:
I'le follow her, but who ſhall vex her Father then?
One flurt at him, and then I am for the voyage,
If I can croſs the Captain too: Come Tabor. Exit.

div.head: SCENE IV.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Are they all ſet?

sp.speaker: 1 Out l.
sp.l: All, and each quarter quiet.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Is the old man aſleep?

sp.speaker: 1 Out-l.
sp.l: An hour agoe Sir.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: We muſt be very carefull in his abſence,
And very watchfull.

sp.speaker: 1 Out-l.
sp.l: It concerns us nearly,
He will not be long from us.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: No, he cannot

sp.speaker: 1 Out l.
sp.l: A little heat of love, which he muſt wander out.
And then again: hark.

sp.speaker: Jap.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: 1 Out l
sp.l: 'Tis not the wind ſure:
That's ſtill and calm, no noiſe, nor flux of waters.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I hear a Drum, I think.

sp.speaker: 1 Out l.
sp.l: That, that;
It beats again now.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Now it comes nearer: ſure we are ſurprized, Sir;
Some from the Kings command: we are loſt, we are dead all.

sp.speaker: 1 Out l.
sp.l: Hark, hark, a charge now: my Captain has betray'd us,
And left us to this ruine, run away from us.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Another beats o' that ſide.

sp.speaker: 2 Out-l.
sp.l: Fly, flie, Jaques,
We are taken in a toyle: ſnapt in a pitſal;
Methinks I feel a Sword already ſhave m • .

sp.speaker: 3 Out-l.
sp.l: A thouſand horſe and foot, a thouſand pioneers,
If we get under-ground, to fetch us out again;
And every one an Axe to cut the woods down.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This is the diſmalſt night— Exit.
Where's my Nag now?
And what make I here to be hang'd? What Devil
Brought me into this danger? Is there ne'er a hole,
That I may creep in deep enough, and die quickly?
Ne'r an old ditch to choke in? I ſhall be taken
For their Commander now, their General,
And have a commanding Gallows ſet up for me
As high as a May pole, and naſty Songs made on me,
Be printed with a Pint-pot and a Dagger.
They are all kill'd by this time: Can I pray?
Let me ſee that firſt: I have too much fear to be faithful.
Where's all my State now? I muſt go hunt for Daughters;
Daughters, and Damſels of the Lake, damned Daughters.
A hundred Crowns for a good tod of Hay,
I hear 'em coming: I feel the nooze about me.

div.stage: Enter Seberto, Curio, Outlaws, and Jaques.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Why do you fear, and fly? here are no Souldiers;
None from the King to vex ye.

sp.speaker: 1 Out l.
sp.l: The Drum, the Drum, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: I never ſaw ſuch Pigeon hearted people:
What Drum? what danger? who's that that ſhakes behind there?
Mercy upon me, Sir, why are ye fear'd thus?

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Are we all kill'd, no mercy to be hoped for?
Am I not ſhot do you think?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: You are ſtrangely frighted,
Shot with a fiddle-ſtick: who's here to ſhoot ye?
A drum we ſaw indeed, a boy was beating it,
And hunting Squirrels by Moon-light.
Nothing elſe, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Not any thing: no other perſon ſtirring.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: O that I had that boy: this is that Devil,
That fairy Rogue, that haunted me laſt night;
H'as ſleeves li •• Dragons wings.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: A little Foot-boy.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Come, let's go in, and let me get my cloaths on;
If ere I ſtay here more to be thus martyr'd—
Did ye not meet the wench?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: No ſure, we met her not.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: She has been here in Boys apparel, Gentlemen,
A gallant thing, and famous for a Gentlewoman.
And all her face patcht over for diſcovery:
A Pilgrim too, and thereby hangs a circumſtance,
That ſhe hath plaid her maſter-prize, a rare one.
I came too ſhort.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Such a young Boy we met, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: In a gray Hat.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: The ſame: his face all patcht too.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: 'Twas ſhe, a rot run with her; ſhe, that rank ſhe;
Walk in, I'le tell ye all, and then we'll part again,
But get ſome ſtore of Wine: this fright ſits here yet. Ex.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: What a fright I have put 'em in; what a brave hurry.
If this do bolt him, I'le be with him again
With a new part, was never play'd; I'le ſerk him.
As he hunts her, ſo I'le hunt him: I'le claw him.
Now will I ſee if I can croſs her footing:
Yet ſtill I'le watch his water, he ſhall pay for't;
And when he thinks moſt malice, and means worſe,
I'le make him know the Mare's the better Horſe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Ye are a ſtranger, Sir, and for humanity,
Being come within our walls, I would ſhew you ſomething.
Ye have ſeen the Caſtle?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Yes Sir, 'tis a ſtrong one,
And well maintain'd.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Why are you ſtill thus ſad, Sir?
How do ye like the walks?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: They are very pleaſant;
Your Town ſtands cool and ſweet.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: But that I would not
Affect you with more ſadneſs, I could ſhew ye
A place worth view.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Shows ſeldom alter me, Sir;
Pray ye ſpeak it, and then ſhew it.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis a houſe here
Where people of all ſorts, that have been viſited
With Lunacies, and Follies wait their cures,
There's fancies of a thouſand ſtamps and faſhions,
Like flies in ſeveral ſhapes buz round about ye,
And twice as many geſtures; ſome of pity,
That it would make ye melt to ſee their paſſions:
And ſome as light again, that would content ye.
But I ſee, Sir, your temper is too modeſt,
Too much inclin'd to contemplation,
To meet with theſe?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: You could not pleaſe me better;
And I beſeech you, Sir, do me the honour
To let me wait upon ye.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Since ye are willing,
To me it ſhall be a pleaſure to conduct ye.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I never had ſuch a mind yet to ſee miſery. Exe.

div.head: SCENE VI.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: Carry mad Beſs ſome meat, ſhe roars like Thunder;
And tie the Parſon ſhort, the Moon's i'th' full,
H'as a thouſand Pigs in's brains: Who looks to the Prentice?
Keep him from Women, he thinks h'as loſt his Miſtris;
And talk of no ſilk ſtuffs, 'twill run him horn mad.

sp.speaker: 2 Keep.
sp.l: The Juſtice keeps ſuch a ſtir yonder with his Charges,
And ſuch a coil with warrants.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: Take away his Statutes;
The Devil has poſſeſt him in the likeneſs
Of penal Laws: keep him from Aqua vitae,
For if that ſpirit creep into his Quorum,
He will commit us all: how is it with the Scholar?

sp.speaker: 2 Keep.
sp.l: For any thing I ſee, he's in his right wits.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: Thou art an aſs; in's right wits, goodman coxcomb?
As though any man durſt be in's right wits, and be here.
It is as much as we dare be that keep 'em.

sp.speaker: Engl.
sp.l: Give me ſome drink.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: O, there's the Engliſh man.

sp.speaker: Engl.
sp.l: Fill me a thouſand pots, and froth 'em, froth 'em.
Down o' your knees, ye Rogues, and pledge me roundly;
One, two, three, and four; we ſhall all be merry within this hour.
To the great Turk.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: Peace, peace thou Heathen drunkard;
Theſe Engliſh are ſo Malt-mad, there's no medling with 'em:
When they have a fruitful year of Barly there,
All the whole Iſland's thus.

sp.speaker: Engl.
sp.l: A ſnuff, a ſnuff, a ſnuff.
A lewd notorious ſnuff: give't him again, boy.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: God-ye-good even, Gaffer.

sp.speaker: 2 Keep.
sp.l: Who let the Fool looſe?

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: If any of the mad-men take her, ſhe is pepper'd,
They'll bounce her loins.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Will ye walk into the coal houſe?

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: She is as leacherous too as a ſhe Ferret.

sp.speaker: 2 Keep.
sp.l: Who a vengeance looks to her? go in Kate,
I'le give thee a fine Apple.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Will ye buſs me?
And tickle me, and make me laugh?

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: I'le whip ye.

sp.speaker: Engl.
sp.l: Fool, fool, come up to me fool.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Are ye peeping?

sp.speaker: Engl.
sp.l: I'le get thee with five fools.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: O fine, O dainty.

sp.speaker: Engl.
sp.l: And thou ſhalt lie in a horſe-cloth, like a Lady.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: And ſhall I have a Coach?

sp.speaker: Engl.
sp.l: Drawn with four Turkeys,
And they ſhall tread thee too.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: We ſhall have eggs then;
And ſhall I ſit upon 'em?

sp.speaker: Engl.
sp.l: I, I, and they ſhall be all addle,
And make an admirable Tanzey for the Devil.
Come, come away, I am taken with thy love fool,
And will mightily belabour thee.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: How the fool bridles? how ſhe twitters at him?
Theſe Engliſh men would ſtagger a wiſe woman.
If we ſhould ſuffer her to have her will now,
We ſhould have all the women in Spain as mad as ſhe here.

sp.speaker: 2 Keep.
sp.l: They would ſtrive who ſhould be moſt fool:
Away with her.

div.stage: Enter Maſter, three Gentlemen, a mad Scholar, and Pedro.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: Pray ye ſtay a little: let's hear him ſing, h'as a fine breaſt.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: Here comes my Maſter; to the ſpit ye whore,
And ſtir no more abroad, but tend your buſineſs;
You ſhall have no more ſops i'th' pan elſe, nor no Porridge:
Beſides, I'le whip your breech.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: I'le go in preſently.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I'le aſſure ye, Sir, the Cardinal's angry with ye
For keeping this young man.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: I am heartily ſorry.
If ye allow him ſound, pray ye take him with ye.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: This is the place, and now obſerve their humours.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: We can find nothing in him light, nor tainted;
No ſtartings, nor no rubs, in all his anſwers,
In all his Letters nothing but diſcretion,
Learning, and handſome ſtile.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Be not deceived, Sir,
Mark but his look.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: His grief, and his impriſonment
May ſtamp that there.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Pray talk with him again then.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: That will be needleſs, we have tried him long enough,
And if he had a taint we ſhould have met with't.
Yet to diſcharge your care—

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: A ſober youth:
Pity ſo heavy a croſs ſhould light upon him.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: You find no ſickneſs?

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: None Sir, I thank Heaven,
Nor nothing that diverts my underſtanding.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Do you ſleep a nights?

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: As ſound, and ſweet, as any man.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Have ye no fearful dreams?

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: Sometimes, as all have
That go to bed with raw and windy ſtomachs;
Elſe I am all one piece.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Is there no unkindneſs
You have conceiv'd from any friend or parent?
Or ſcorn from what ye lov'd?

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: No, truely Sir:
I never yet was maſter of a faith
So poor, and weak, to doubt my friend or kindred,
And what love is, unleſs it lie in learning
I think I am ignorant.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: This man is perfect,
A civiller diſcourſer I ne'r talk'd with.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: You'l find it otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: I muſt tell ye true, Sir,
I think ye keep him here to teach him madneſs.
Here's his diſcharge from my Lord Cardinal;
And come Sir, go with us.

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: I am bound unto ye,
And farewel Maſter.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Farewel Stephano,
Alas poor man.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: What flaws, and whi • l • s of weather,
How dark, and hot, and fu •• of mutiny!
And ſtill grows loud • r.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: It has been ſtubborn w • ather

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Strange work at Sea, I fear m • there's old tumbling

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Bleſs my old Unkles Bark, I have a •• nture.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: And I more than I would wiſh to loſe
Do you fear?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Ha! how he looks?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Nay, mark 〈◊〉 b • tter Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Mercy upon m • : how his • y • s are altered

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Now tell me how ye like him: wheth •• now
He be that p • f • ct man ye credited?

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: Do's the Sea ſtagger ye?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Now ye have hit the nick

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: Do ye fear the billows?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: What ails him? who has ſtir'd him?

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: Be not ſhaken,
Nor let the ſinging of the ſtorm ſhoot through ye,
Let it blow on, blow on: let the clouds wraſtle,
And let the vapours of the earth turn mutinous.
The Sea in hideous mountains riſe and tumble
Upon a Dolphins back, I'le make all tr • mbl • ,
For I am Neptune.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Now what think ye of him?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Alas poor man.

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: Your Bark ſhall plough through all,
And not a Singe ſo fancy to diſturb her.
I'le ſee h • r ſafe, my power ſhall ſail b • fore her

lg.l: Down ye an • ry waters all,
Ye loud whiſtling whi • l • winds fall;
Down ye proud Waves, ye ſtorms ceaſe;
I command ye, be at peace.
Fright not with your churl • ſh Notes,
Nor bruiſe the Keel of • ark that ſlotes:
No devouring Fiſh come nigh,
Nor Monſter in my Empery,
Once ſhew his head, or terror bring;
But let the weary Saylor ſing:
Amphitrite with white arms
Strike my Lute, I le ſing Charms.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: He muſt have Muſick now: I muſt obſerve him,
His ſit will grow too full elſe. Muſick, Song.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: I muſt pity him

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Now he will in himſelf moſt quietly,
And clean forget all, as he had done nothing.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: We are ſorry, Sir: and we have ſeen a wonder;
From this hour we'll believe, and ſo we'll leave ye. Ex.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: This was a ſtrange fit.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Did ye mark him, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: He might have cozen'd me with his behaviour.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Many have ſworn him right, and I have thought ſo:
Yet on a ſudden, from ſome word, or other,
When no man could expect a ſit, he has flown out:
I dare not give him will.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Pray Heaven recover him.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Muſt I come in too?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: No, my pretty Lad;
Keep in thy Chamber Boy; 'ſhalt have thy ſupper.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I pray ye what is he, Sir?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: A ſtrange • oy, that laſt night
Was found i'th' Town, a little craz'd, diſtracted,
And ſo ſ • nt hither.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: How the pretty Knave looks,
And plays, and peeps upon me! ſure ſuch eyes
I have ſeen, and lov'd: what fair han • s? certainly—

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Good Sir, you'l make him worſe.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I pray believe not.
Alas, why ſhold I hurt him? how he ſmiles!
The very ſhape, and ſweetneſs of Alinda:
Let me look once again: were it in ſuch clothes
As when I ſaw her laſt; this muſt be ſhe.
How tenderly it ſtroaks me?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Pray ye be mild Sir;
I muſt attend elſewhere. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Pray ye be ſecure Sir,
What would ye ſay? how my heart beats and trembles!
He holds me hard by th' hand; O my life, her fleſh too!
I know not what to think: her tears, her true ones;
Pure orient tears: Hark, do you know me little one?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: O Pedro Pedro!

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: O my ſoul!

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: What fit's this?
The Pilgrim's off the hooks too.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Let me hold thee,
And now come all the world, and all that hate me.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Be wiſe, and not diſcovered: O how I love ye!
How do ye now?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I have been miſerable;
But your moſt vertuous eyes have cur'd me, Pedro:
Pray ye think it no immodeſty, I kiſs ye,
My head's wild ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Be not ſo full of paſſion,
Nor do not hang ſo greedily upon me;
'Twill be ill taken.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Are ye weary of me?
I will hang here eternally, kiſs ever,
And weep away for joy.

sp.speaker: Maſter.
sp.l: I told ye Sir,
What ye would do: for ſhame do not afflict him;
You have drawn his fit upon him fearfully:
Either depart, and preſently; I'le force ye elſe.
Who waits within?

div.stage: Enter two Keepers to fetch 'em off.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Alas good Sir.
This is the way never to hope recovery.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Stay but one minute more, I'le complain to the Governour,
Bring in the boy: do you ſee how he ſwells, and tears himſelf?
Is this your cure? Be gone; if the boy miſcarry
Let me ne'r find you more, for I'le ſo hamper ye—

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: You were to blame: too raſh.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Farewel for ever. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: YOU are now within a mile o'th' Town Sir: if my buſineſs
Would give me leave, I would turn and wait upon ye;
But for ſuch Gentlemen as you enquire of,
Certain, I ſaw none ſuch: But for the boy ye ſpoke of,
I will not ſay 'tis he, but ſuch a one;
Juſt of that height.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: In ſuch clothes?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I much miſtake elſe,
Was ſent in th' other night, a little maddiſh,
And where ſuch people wait their cures —

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I underſtand ye.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: There you may quickly know.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I thank ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: So do I too: and if there be ſuch a place,
I ask no more: but you ſhall hear more of me,
She may be there, and you may play the tyrant;
I'le ſee what I can do: I am almoſt found • ed
In following him; and yet I'le never leave him,
• le crawl of all four firſt; my cauſe is meritorious,
And come what can come.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: All you have told me is certain;
Complexion, and all elſe.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: It may be ſhe then;
And I'le ſo fumble her: is ſhe grown mad now?
Is her blood ſet ſo high? I'le have her madded,
I'le have her worm'd.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Mark but the end, old Maſter,
If thou beeſt not ſick o'th' Bots within theſe five hours,
And kickſt and roar'ſt; I'le make ye fart fire, Signior.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Here's one o'th' houſe, a fool, an idiot Sir;
May be ſhe is going home; ſhe'l be a guide to ye:
And ſo I kiſs your hand. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I am your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: O now I am loſt, loſt, loſt, Lord, how I tremble!
My Father, arm'd in all his hates and angers;
This is more miſery than I have ſcap'd yet.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Fool, fool.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: He knows me not; will ye give me two pence?
And gaffer, here's a Crow-flower, and a Dazie;
I have ſome pie in my pocket too.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: This is an arrant fool,
An ignorant thing.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Believe ſo, and I am happy.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Doſt thou dwell in Sigovia, fool?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: No no, I dwell in Heaven.
And I have a fine little houſe, made of Marmalad.
And I am a lone woman, and I ſpin for Saint Peter;
I have a hundred little children, and they ſing Pſalms with me.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: 'Tis pity this pretty thing ſhould want underſtanding.
But why do I ſtand talking with a coxcombe?
If I do find her, if I light upon her,
I'le ſay no more. Is this the way to th' Town, fool?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: You muſt go over the top of that high ſteeple, G • ffer.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: A plague o' your fools face.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: No, take her counſel.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: And then you ſhall come to a River twenty mile ov • r,
And twenty mile and ten: and then you muſt pray, Gaffer;
And ſtill you muſt pray, and pray.
Pray Heaven deliver me
From ſuch an aſs, as thou art.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Amen, ſweet Gaffer.
And fling a ſop of Suger-cake into it;
And then you muſt leap in naked.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Would he would believe her.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: And ſink ſeven daies together; can ye ſink gaffer?

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Yes coxcomb, yes; prethee farewel: a pox on thee.
A plague o' that fool too, that ſet me upon thee.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: And then I'le bring you a ſup of Milk ſhall ſerve ye:
I am going to get Apples.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: Go to th' Devil:
Was ever man tormented with a puppy thus?
Thou tell me news? thou be a guide?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: And then Nunkle —

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Prethee keep on thy way (good Naunt) I could rail now
Theſe ten hours at mine own improvidence:
Get Apples, and be choak'd: farewel. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Farewel Nunkle.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I rejoyce in any thing that vexes him;
And I ſhall love this fool extreamly for't:
Could I but ſee my Miſtris now, to tell her
How I have truly, honeſtly wrought for her,
How I have worn my ſelf away, to ſerve her.
Fool, there's a Royal for the ſport thou mad'ſt me,
In croſſing that old fool, that parted from thee.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Thou art honeſt ſure; but yet thou muſt not ſee me:
I thank ye little Gentleman: Heaven bleſs ye
And I'le pray for ye too: pray ye keep this Nutmeg.
'Twas ſent me from the Lady of the Mountain,
A golden Lady.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: How prettily it prattles!

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: 'Tis very good to rub your underſtanding:
And ſo good night, the Moon's up.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Pretty innocent.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Now fortune, if thou darſt do good, protect me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I'll follow him to yond'Town; he ſhall not 'ſcape me.
Stay, I muſt counterfeit a Letter by the way firſt,
And one that muſt carry ſome credit with it; I am wide elſe,
And all this to no purpoſe that I aim at.
A Letter muſt be had, and neatly handled;
And then, if Goodwife Fortune do not fail me,
Have at his Skirts; I ſhall worſe anger him
Than ever I have done, and worſe torment him.
It does me good to think how I ſhall conjure him,
And crucifie his crabbedneſs; he's my Maſter,
Put that's all one; I'll lay that on the left hand,
He would now perſecute my harmleſs Miſtriſs,
A fault without forgiveneſs, as I take it;
And under that bold Banner flies my vengeance,
A meritorious War, and ſo I'll make it.
I'th' name of innocence, what's this the fool gave me?
She ſaid 'twas good to rub my underſtanding.
What ſtrange Concealment? Bread or Cheeſe, or a Cheſnut,
Ha! 'tis a Ring, a pretty Ring, a right one;
A Ring I know too! the very ſame Ring;
O admirable Blockhead! O baſe Eyes!
A Ring my Miſtriſs took from me, and wore it;
I know it by the Poſie:
None could deliver this, but ſhe her ſelf too;
Am I twice ſand-blind? twice ſo near the Bleſſing
I wou • d arrive at? and block-like never know it?
I am veng'ance angry, but that ſhall light on thee,
And heavily, and quickly, I pronounce it;
There are ſo many croſs ways, there's no following her;
And yet I muſt not now; I hope ſhe is right ſtill,
For all her outward ſhew, for ſure ſhe knew me;
And in that hope, ſome few hours I'll forget her. Exit.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: She is not to be recovered, which I vex at;
And he beyond my veng'ance, which torments me;
O! I am fool'd and ſleighted, made a Raſcal;
My hopes are flatter'd, as my preſent fortunes;
Why ſhould I wander thus, and play the Coxcomb?
Tire out my peace and pleaſure for a Girl?
A Girl that ſcorns me too? a thing that hates me?
And conſidered at the beſt, is but a ſhort Breakfaſt
For a hot appetite: why ſhould I walk and walk thus?
And fret my ſelf, and travel like a Carrier,
And peep, and watch? want Meat, and Wine, to cheriſh me,
When thouſand women may be had, ten thouſand,
And thank me too, and I ſit ſtill: well, trim Beauty
And Chaſtity, and all that ſeem to ruine me,
Let me not take ye, let me not come near ye,
For I'll ſo trim ye, I'll ſo buſtle with ye;
'Tis not the name of Virgin ſhall redeem ye,
I bear a hate about me ſcorns thoſe follies.
To find this Villain too, for there's my main prize:
And if he ſnap me then.

sp.speaker: Alind.
sp.l: Is not that Pedro?
Tis he, 'tis he: O!

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: What art thou?

sp.speaker: Alind.
sp.l: Ha? now, now, now,
O now moſt miſerable.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: What a Devil art thou?
No end of my misfortunes, Heaven?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: What antick?
Speak Puppet, ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Alind.
sp.l: That habit to betray me?
Ye holy Saints, can ye ſee this?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: It danceth;
The Devil in a Fools Coat, is he turn'd Innocent?
What mops and mows it makes! heigh! how it frisketh?
Is't not a Fairy, or ſome ſmall Hobgoblin?
It has a mortal face, and I have a great mind to it,
But if it ſhould prove the Devil then.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Come hither.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I think 'twill raviſh me,
It is a handſome thing, but horribly Sun-burnt,
What's that it points at?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Doſt thou ſee that ſtar there,
That juſt above the Sun?
Prithee go thither, and light me this Tobacco,
And ſtop it with the horns o'th' Moon.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: The thing's mad,
Abominably mad, her brains are butter'd,
Go ſleep, fool, ſleep.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Thou canſt not ſleep ſo ſweetly;
For ſo I can ſay my Prayers, and then ſlumb ••

lg.l: I am not proud, nor full of Wi • e,
This little Flower will make me fine;
Cruel in He • rt, for I will cry,
If I ſe • a Sp •• row dye;
I am not watchful to do ill,
Such as are, bid them go ſleep.

sp.l: Do, do, do, and ſee if they can.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: It ſaid true.
I fe • l it ſi • k into me forcibly:
Sure tis a kind of Sibyl, ſome mad Prophet;
I feel my wildneſs bound, and f • tter'd in me.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Give me your hand, and I'll tell you what's your fortune.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Here, prithee ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: Fye, fye, fye, fye, fye.
Waſh your hands, and pare your nails, and look finely,
You ſhall never kiſs the Kings Daughter elſe.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I waſh 'em daily.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: But ſtill you foul 'em faſter.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: This goes nearer.
You'll have two Wives.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Two Wives?

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I, two fine Gentlewomen,
Make much of 'em; for they'll ſtick cloſe to you, Sir:
And theſe two, in two days.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: That's a fine Riddle.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: To day you ſhall wed ſorrow,
And repentance will come to morrow.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Sure ſhe's inſpired.
I'll ſing ye a fine Song, Sir.

lg.l: He called down his merry men a • l,
By one, by two, by three,
William would fain have been the firſt,
But now the laſt is he.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: This the meer Chronicle of my miſhaps.

sp.speaker: Alin.
sp.l: I'll bid you good ev'n, for my Boat ſtays for me yonder,
And I muſt ſup with the Moon to Night in the Mediterraneum. Exit.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: When fools and mad folks will be Tutors to me,
And feel my ſores, yet I unſenſible;
Sure it was ſet by Providence upon me
To ſteer my heart right, I am wondrous weary,

My thoughts too, which add mo ••
〈…〉 to me;
I have been ill, and (which is worſe) purſu' • it,
And ſtill run on; I muſt think b • tter, nobler,
And be another thing, or not at all.
I'll lye down, and take reſt; and goodneſs guard me.

sp.speaker: 1 Peſ.
sp.l: We have 'ſcap'd to day well; certa n if the Out-laws
Had known we had b • en ſtirring, we ha • pa • d for't.

sp.speaker: 2 Peſ.
sp.l: 'Plague on 'em, they have rob'd me thrice.

sp.speaker: 3 Peſ.
sp.l: And me five times:
Beſide they made my Daughter one of us too
An arrant Drum: O, they are the lewdeſt Raſcals,
The Captain ſuch a damn'd piece of iniquitie:
But we are far enough off on 'em, that's the beſt on't,
They cannot hear.
They'le come to me familiarly
And eat up all I have: drink up my wine too,
And if there be a Servant that contents 'em,
Let her keel hold, they'l give her Stowage enough:
We have no Children now, but Thieves, and Outlaws.
The very Beats in their Mothers bellies have their qualities.
They'l ſt • al into the world.
Would we had ſome of 'em here.
I, o' that condition we could Maſter 'em,
They are ſtu • dy knaves.
A D • vil take their ſturdineſs,
We can neither keep our wives from 'em nor our States,
We pay the Rent, and they poſſeſs the benefit.
What's this lies here? is it drunk, or ſober?
It ſleeps, and ſoundly too.
'Tis an old woman
That keeps ſheep hereabouts: it turns, and ſtretches.
Do's ſhe keep ſheep with a ſword?
It has a Beard too.
Peace, peace: it is the Devil Roderigo,
Peace of all hands, and look.
'Tis he.
Sp • ak ſoftly.
Now we may fit him.
Stay, ſtay: let's be provid • nt.
Kill him, and wake him then.
Let me come to him,
Ev'n one blow at his pate, if e're he wake more.
So, ſo, ſo, lay that by.
I muſt needs kill him,
It ſtands with my reputation.
Stand off, I ſay:
And let us ſome way make him ſure; then torture him.
To kill him preſently, has no pleaſure in't.
H'as been tormenting of us, at leaſt this twelve moneth.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Oh me!

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: He comes: he comes.
Has he no Guns about him?
Softly again: no, no: take that hand eaſily,
And tye it faſt there: that to th' other bough there.
Faſt, faſt, and eaſie leſt he wake.
Have we got ye?
This was a benefit we never aim'd at.
Out with your knives, and let's carve this Cockthief,
Daintily carve him.
I would he had been uſed thus
Ten year agoe; we might have thought we had children.
O, that Sir Nicholas now our Prieſt were here,
What a ſweet Homily would he ſay over him,
• o ſinging all in, with his wife in the Bell-frey?
He would ſtand up ſtiffe girt, now pounce him lightly
And as he roars, and rages, let's go deeper:
Come near: you are dim-ey'd: on with your ſpectacles.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: O, what torments me thus? what ſlaves, what villains?
O ſpare me, do not murther me.
We'l but tickle ye,
You have tickled us at all points.
Where are his Emblemes?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: As ye are men, and Chriſtians.
Yes we hear ye,
And you ſhall hear of us too.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Oh no mercy.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: What noiſe is this? what roar? I cannot find her,
She is got free again: but where, or which way?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: O villains, beaſts.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Murdering a man, ye Raſcals?
Ye inhumane ſlaves, off, off, and leave this cruelty,
Or as I am a Gentleman: do ye brave me?
Then have among ye all, ye ſlaves, ye cowards,
Take up that ſword, and ſtand: ſtay ye baſe raſcals,
Ye cut-throat rogues.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Away, away. Exeunt Peſ.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Ye dog-whelps.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: O, I am now more wretched far, than ever.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: A violence to that habit? ha? Roderigo.
What makes he here, thus clad? is it repentance,
Or only a fair ſhew to guile his miſchiefs?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: This benefit has made me ſhame to ſee him,
To know him, bluſh.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: You are not much hurt?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: No Sir;
All I can call a hurt, ſticks in my conſcience,
That pricks and tortures me.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Have ye conſider'd
The nature of theſe men, and how they us'd ye?
Was it fair play? did it appear to you handſom?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I dare not ſpeak: or if I do 'tis nothing
Can bring me off, or juſtifie me.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Was it noble
To be o're-laid with odds, and violence?
Manly, or brave in theſe thus to oppreſs ye?
Do you bluſh at this, in ſuch as are meer rudeneſs,
That have ſtopt ſouls, that never knew things gentle?
And dare you glorifie worſe in your ſelf Sir?
Ye us'd me with much honour, and I thank ye,
In this I have requited ſome: ye know me:
Come turn not back, ye muſt, and ye ſhall know me;
Had I been over ſeaſon'd with baſe anger,
And ſuited all occaſions to my miſchiefs,
Bore no reſpect to honeſty, Religion,
No ſaith, no common tye of man, humanity,
Had I had in me, but given reins, and licence
To a tempeſtuous will, as wild as winter,
This day, know Roderigo, I had ſet
As ſmall a price upon thy life and fortunes,
As thou didſt lately on mine innocence;
But I reſerve thee to a nobler ſervice.

sp.speaker: Rod
sp.l: I thank ye, and I'le ſtudy more to honour ye:

You have the 〈◊〉
•• r ſoul, I muſt confeſs it,
And 〈…〉 la • ter of your goodneſs.

Thoug •
〈…〉 I would now recover,
And my 〈…〉 grow handſom in an inſtant,
Yet touching but the pureneſs of your metal,
Something ſhall ſhew like gold, at leaſt ſha • l gliſter,
That men may hope, although the mind be rugged,
Stony, and hard to work, yet time, and honour
Shall find and bring forth that, that's rich and worthy.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I'le trie that: and toth' purpoſe: ye told me Sir
In noble emulation, ſo I take it;
I'le put your hatred far off, and forget it,
You had a fair deſire to try my valour:
You ſeem'd to court me to it; you have found a time,
A weapon in your hand, an equal enemy,
That, as he puts this off, puts off all injuries,
And only now for honours ſake defies ye:
Now, as you are a man, I know you are valiant,
As you are gentle bred, a Souldier faſhioned.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: His vertue ſtartles me. I dare fight Pedro.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And as you have a Miſtris that you honour,
Mark me, a Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: A handſome Miſtris,
As you dare hold your ſelf deſerving of her.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Deſerving? what a word was that to fire me?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I could compel ye now without this circumſtance,
But I'le deal free, and fairly, like a Gentleman:
As ye are worthy of the name ye carry,
A daring man.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: O that I durſt not ſuffer:
For all I dare do now, implies but penance.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Now do me noble right.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I'll ſatisfie ye;
But not by th' ſword, pray you hear me, and allow me;
I have been rude; but ſhall I be a Monſter,
And teach my Sword to hurt that that preſerv'd me?
Though I be rough by nature, ſhall my name
Inherit that eternal ſtain of barbarous?
Give me an enemy, a thing that hates ye,
That never heard of yet, nor felt your goodneſs,
That is one main antipathy to ſweetneſs;
And ſet me on, you cannot hold me Coward;
If I have ever err'd, 'thas been in hazard;
The temper of my Sword ſtarts at your Vertue,
And will flye off, nay it will weep to light ye;
Things excellently mingled, and of pure nature,
Hold ſacred Love, and peace with one another,
See how it turns.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: This is a ſtrange Converſion:
And can ye fail your Miſtriſs? can ye grow cold
In ſuch a caſe?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Thoſe heats that they add to us,
(O noble Pedro) let us feel 'em rightly,
And rightly but conſider how they move us.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Is not their honour ours?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: If they be vertuous,
And then the Sword adds nothing to their luſtre,
But rather calls in queſtion what's not doubted;
If they be not, the beſt Swords, and beſt valours
Can never fight 'em up to fame again;
No, not a Chriſtian War, and that's held pious.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: How bravely now he is tempered! I muſt fight,
And rather make it honourable, than angry,
I would not task thoſe ſins to me committed.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You cannot, Sir, you have caſt thoſe by: diſcarded 'em,
And in a noble mind, ſo low, and looſely
To look back, and collect ſuch lumps, and lick 'em
Into new horrid forms again—

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Still braver.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: To fight, becauſe I dare, were worſe and weaker
Than if I had a woman in my cauſe, Sir,
And more proclaim'd me fool: yet I muſt confeſs
I have been covetous of all occaſions,
And this I have taken upon truſt, for noble,
The more ſhame mine: deviſe a way to fight thus,
That like the wounded air, no bloud may iſſue,
Nor where the Sword ſhall enter, no loſt ſpirit,
And ſet me on: I would not ſcare that body,
That vertuous, valiant body, nor deface it
To make the Kingdom mine: if one muſt bleed,
Let me be both the Sacrifice and Altar,
And you the Prieſt; I have deſerv'd to ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: The noble Roderigo, now I call ye,
And thus my love ſhall ever count, and hold ye,

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I am your ſervant, Sir, and now this habit,
Devotion, not diſtruſt ſhall put upon me,
I'll wait upon your fortunes, that's my way now,
And where you grieve, or joy, I'll be a Partner.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I thank ye, Sir, I ſhall be too proud of ye,
O I could tell ye ſtrange things.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I gueſs at 'em,
And I could curſe my ſelf, I made 'em ſtranger;
Yet my mind ſays you are not far from happineſs.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: It ſhall be welcome; come, let's keep up thus ſtill,
And be as we appear; Heavens hand may bleſs us.

div.head: SCENE III.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, here be ſuch people; but how pleaſing
They will appear to you.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: 'Pray let me ſee 'em,
I come to that end; 'pray let me ſee 'em all.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: They will confound ye, Sir, like Bells rung backward,
They are nothing but Confuſion, and meer Noiſes.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: May be I love a noiſe; but hark ye, Sir,
Have ye no Boys? handſome young Boys?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Yes, one, Sir,
A very handſome Boy.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Long here?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: But two days;
A little crazed; but much hope of recovery.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: I, that Boy, let me ſee, may be I know him,
That Boy I ſay; this is the Boy he told me of,
And it muſt need be ſhe; that Boy, I beſeech ye, Sir,
That Boy I come to ſee.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: And ye ſhall ſee him;
Or any elſe: but pray be not too violent.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I know what to do, I warrant ye; I am for all fancies;
I can talk to 'em, and diſpute.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: As madly;
For they are very mad, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Let 'em be horn mad.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: We have few Citizens: they have Bedlams of their own, Sir,
And are mad at their own charges.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Who lyes here?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: 'Pray ye do not diſturb 'em, Sir, here lie ſuch youths
Will make you ſtart if they but dance their trenchmores,
Fetch out the Boy, Sirrah; hark!

div.stage: Shake Irons within. Engliſh mad-men, Scholar, Parſon, Jenkin.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Heigh Boys.

sp.speaker: Eng.
sp.l: Bounce,
Clap her o'th' ſtar-board; bounce, top the Can.

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: Dead ye dog, dead, do ye quarrel in my Kingdom?
Give me my trident.

sp.speaker: Eng.
sp.l: Bounce, 'twixt wind and water,
Loaden with Mackrel; O brave meat.

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: My Sea horſes;
I'll charge the Northern Wind, and break his Bladder,

sp.speaker: Parſ.
sp.l: I'll ſell my Bells before I be out-brav'd thus.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: What's he? what's he?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: A Parſon, Sir, a Parſon
That run mad for tyth Goſlings.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Green ſuwce cure him.

sp.speaker: Parſ.
sp.l: I'll curſe ye all, I'll excommunicate ye;
Thou Engliſh Heretick, give me the tenth Pot.

sp.speaker: Eng.
sp.l: Sue me, I'll drink up all, bounce I ſay once more,
O have I ſplit your Mizen? blow, blow thou Weſt-wind,
Blow till thou rive, and make the Sea run roaring.
I'll hiſs it down again with a Bottle of Ale.

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: Triton, why Triton.

sp.speaker: Eng.
sp.l: Triton's drunk with Metheglin.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Strike, ſtrike the ſurges, ſtrike.

sp.speaker: Eng.
sp.l: Drink, drink, 'tis day light;
Drink, didle, didle, didle, drink, Parſon, proud Parſon;
A Pigs tail in thy teeth, and I defie thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Give me ſome porridg, or I'll damn thee, Engliſh.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: How comes this Engliſh mad man here?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Alas, that's no queſtion;
They are mad every where, Sir;
Their fits are cool now, let 'em reſt.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Mad Gallants;
Moſt admirable mad; I love their faces.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: Ye ſtinking Whore, who knew of this? who lookt to him?
'Pox take him, he was ſleepy when I left him.

sp.speaker: 2 Keep.
sp.l: Certain he made the fool drunk.

sp.speaker: Mast.
sp.l: How now, who's this here?
Where is the Boy?

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: The Boy, Sir?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: I, the Boy, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Keep.
sp.l: Here's all the Boys we found.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Theſe are his Cloaths.
But where's the Boy?

sp.speaker: She-fool.
sp.l: The Boy is gone a Maying,
He'll bring me home a Cuckows Neſt; do you hear, Maſter?
I put my Cloaths off, and I dizen'd him,
And pin'd a Plum in's forehead, and a feather,
And buſs'd him twice, and bid him go ſeek his fortune;
He gave me this fine money, and fine Wine too,
And bid me ſop; and gave me theſe trim Cloaths too,
And put 'em on.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Is this the Boy you would ſhew?

sp.speaker: She fool.
sp.l: I'll give you two pence, Maſter.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Am I fool'd of all ſides?
I met a fool i'th' Woods, they ſaid ſhe dwelt here,
In a long pied Coat.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: That was the very Boy, Sir.
I, I, I, I gave him leave to play, forſooth,
He'll come again to morrow, and bring peaſcods.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: I'll bring your bones.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: 'Pox o' your fools, and Bedlams,
'Plague o' your Owls and Apes.
'Pray ye, Sir, be tamer,
We cannot help this preſently, but we ſhall know;
I'll recompence your Care too.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Know me, a pudding,
You juggle, and ye fiddle; fart upon ye;
I am abuſed.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: 'Pray ye, Sir. Welſh mad-man.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: And I will be abuſed, Sir,
And you ſhall know I am abuſed.

sp.speaker: Welſh.
sp.l: Whaw, Mr. Keeper.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: 'Pox o' thy whaws, and thy whyms,
Pox o' thy urſhip.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Give me ſome Ceeze, and Onions; give me ſome waſh brew,
I have— in my bellies, give me abundance,
Pendragon was a Shentleman, marg you, Sir,
And the Organs at Rexum were made by Revelations,
There is a ſpirit blows, and blows the Bellows,
And then they ſing.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: What Moon-calf's this? what dream?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: 'Pray ye, Sir, obſerve him,
He is a Mountain • er, a man of Goteland.

sp.speaker: Welſh.
sp.l: I will beat thy face as black as a blue Clout,
I will leave no more ſheet in thine eyes.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: He will not hurt ye.

sp.speaker: Welſh.
sp.l: Give me a great deal of Guns; thou art the Devils,
I know thee by thy tails; poor Owen's hungry,
I will peg thy bums full of Bullets.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: This is the rareſt Raſcal,
He ſpeaks as if he had butter-milk in's mouth,
Is this any thing akin to th' Engliſh?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: The elder Brother, Sir,
He run mad becauſe a Rat eat up's Cheeſe.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: H'ad a great deal of reaſon, Sir.

sp.speaker: Welſh.
sp.l: Baſilus manus, is for an old Codpiſs, mark ye,
I will borrow thy U • ſhips Whore to ſeal a Letter.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Now he grows villainous.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Methinks he's beſt now.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Away with him.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: He ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Sir, he muſt.

sp.speaker: Welſh.
sp.l: I will ſing and dance,
Do any thing.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Wilt thou declaim in Greek?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Away with the fool,
And whip her foundly, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: She fool.
sp.l: I'll tell no more tales. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Or wilt thou flye i'th' air?

sp.speaker: Eng
sp.l: Do, and I'll catch thee,
And like a wiſp of Hay, I'll whirl, and whirl thee,
And puff thee up, and puff thee up.

sp.speaker: Schol.
sp.l: I'll ſave thee,
And thou ſhalt fall into the Sea, ſoft, ſoftly.

sp.speaker: Welſh.
sp.l: I'll get upon a mountain, and call my Country-men.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: They all grow wild, away with him for Heavens ſake,
Sir, ye are much to blame.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: No, no, 'tis brave, Sir,
Ye have cozen'd me; I'll make you mad.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: In with him,
And look him faſt.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I'll ſee him in his lodging. Exit.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: What means this Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: He's in; have at him,
Are you the Maſter, Sir?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: What would you with him?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I have a buſineſs from the Duke of Medina,
Is there not an old Gentleman come lately in?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Yes, and a wild one too, but not a Priſoner.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Did you obſerve him well? 'tis like it may be he.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: I have ſeen younger men of better temper.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: You have hit the cauſe I come for; there's a Letter,
Pray ye peruſe it well; I ſhall be wi' ye;
And ſuddenly, I fear not, finely, daintily,
I ſhall ſo feed your fierce vexation,
And raiſe your Worſhips ſtorms; I ſhall ſo niggle ye,
And juggle ye, and fiddle ye, and firk ye:
I'll make ye curſe the hour ye vext a Woman;
I'll make ye ſhake when our Sex are but ſounded;
For the Lords ſake we ſhall have him at; I long to ſee it
As much as for my wedding night; I gape after it.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: This Letter ſays the Gentleman is lunatick,
I half ſuſpected it.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis very true, Sir,
And ſuch pranks he has plaid.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: He's ſome great man,
The Duke commands me with ſuch care to look to him,
And if he grow too violent, to correct him,
To uſe the ſpeedieſt means for his recovery,
And thoſe he muſt find ſharp.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: The better for him.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: How got ye him hither?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: With a train, I told him;
He's in love with a Boy, there lyes his melancholy.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Hither he came to ſeek one.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Yes, I ſent him,
Now had we dealt by force, we had never brought him!

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Here was a Boy.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: He ſaw him not?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: He was gone firſt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: It is the better; look you to your charge well;
I'll ſee him lodged, for ſo the Duke commanded me,
He will be very rough.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We are us'd to that, Sir,
And we as rough as he, if he give occaſion.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: You will find him gainful, but be ſure ye curb him,
And get him, if ye can fairly, to his lodging,
I am afraid ye will not.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We muſt ſweat then.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: What doſt thou talk to me of noiſes? I'l have more noiſe,
I'll have all looſe, and all ſhall play their prizes;
Thy Maſter has let looſe the Boy I lookt for,
Baſely convey'd him hence.

sp.speaker: Keep.
sp.l: Will ye go out, Sir?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I will not out; I will have all out with me,
I'll have thy Maſter in; he's only mad here:
And Rogues, I'll have ye all whipt; heigh, mad Boys, mad Boys.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Do you perceive him now?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: 'Tis too apparent.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I am glad ſhe is gone; he raves thus.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Do you hear, Sir?
'Pray will ye make leſs ſtir, and ſee your Chamber,
Call in more help, and make the Cloſet ready.

sp.speaker: Keep.
sp.l: I thought he was mad; I'll have one long laſh at ye.
My Chamber? where my Chamber? why my Chamber?
Where's the young Boy?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Nay, Pray ye, Sir, be more modeſt
For your own Credit ſake; the people ſee ye,
And I would uſe ye with the beſt.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Beſt, hang ye,
What doſt thou think me mad?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Pray, and be civil,
Heaven may deliver ye.
Into a rogues hands.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: You do but draw more miſery upon ye,
And add to your diſeaſe.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Get from me.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: No Sir,
You muſt not be left ſo: bear your ſelf civilly,
And 'twill be better for ye: ſwell not, nor chafe not.

sp.speaker: Alp.
sp.l: I am a Gentleman, and a neighbour, raſcal.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: A great deal the more pity: I have heard of ye.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Excellent Maſter.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: The Duke is very tender too.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Am I lunatique? am I run mad?
What doſt thou talk to me of Dukes, and Devils,
Why do the people gape ſo?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Do not anger 'em,
But go in quietly, and ſlip in ſoftly
They will ſo tew ye, elſe, I am commanded Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Why, prethee why?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Ye are dog-mad: you perceive it not,
Very far mad: and whips will ſcant recover ye.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Ha! whips?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: I whips, and ſore whips, and ye were a Lord Sir,
If ye be ſtubborn here.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Whips? what am I grown?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: O I could burſt: hold, hold, hold, hold o' both ends,
How he looks, pray heaven, he be not mad indeed.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I do not perceive I am ſo; but if you think it,
Nor I'le be hangd if 't be ſo.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Do you ſee this Sir? Irons brought in.
Down with that Devil in ye.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Indeed I am angry,
But I'le contain my ſelf: O I could burſt now,
And tear my ſelf, but theſe rogues will torment me,
Mad in mine old days? make mine own afflictions?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: What do you mutter Sir?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Nothing, Sir, nothing;
I will go in, and quietly, moſt civilly:
And good Sir, let none of your tormentors come about me,
You have a gentle face; they look like Dragons.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Be civil and be ſafe: come, for theſe two daies
Ye muſt eat nothing neither: 'twill eaſe your ſits Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: 'Twill ſtarve me Sir; but I muſt bear it joyfully.
I may ſleep?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Yes, a little: go in with theſe men.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: O miſerable me! Exit.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: I'le follow preſently,
You ſee 'tis done Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Ye have done it handſomely,
And I'le inform the Duke ſo: pray ye attend him,
Let him want nothing, but his will.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: He ſhall not,
And if he be rebellious —

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Never ſpare him:
