To take your leave of folly, and now melt
Even in repeating her?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I had forgot me.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: As you will ſtill do.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: No, the ſtrongeſt man
May have the grudging of an ague on him,
This is no more; let's go, I would fain be fit
To be thy friend again, for now I am no mans.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Go you, I dare not go, I tell you truly
Nor were it wiſe I ſhould.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I am well,
And if I can, will keep my ſelf ſo.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Ha? thou mak'ſt me ſmile, though I have little cauſe,
To ſee how prettily thy fear becomes thee;
Art thou not ſtrong enough to ſee a woman?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Yes, twenty thouſand: but not ſuch a one
As you have made her: I'le not lye for th' matter:
I know I am frail, and may be cozen'd too
By ſuch a Syren.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Faith thou ſhalt go, Angelo.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Faith but I will not; no I know how far Sir
I am able to hold out, and will not venture
Above my depth: I do not long to have
My ſleep ta'ne from me, and go pulingly
Like a poor wench had loſt her market-mony;
And when I ſee good meat, ſit ſtill and ſigh,
And call for ſmall beer; and conſume my wit
In making Anagrams, and faithful poſies;
I do not like that Itch, I am ſure I had rather
Have the main pox, and ſafer.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt go,
I muſt needs have thee as a witneſs with me
Of my repentance; as thou lov'ſt me go.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Well I will go, ſince you will have it ſo,
But if I prove a fool too, look to have me
Curſe you continually, and fearfully,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And if thou ſeeſt me fall again, good Angelo
Give me thy counſel quickly leſt I periſh.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Pray Heaven I have enough to ſave my ſelf,
For as I have a ſoul, I had rather v • nture
Upon a ſavage Iſland, than this woman. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: From whom Sir, comes this bounty? for I think
You are miſtaken.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: No Sir, 'tis to you
I am ſure my Miſtris ſent it.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Who's your Miſtris,
That I may give her thanks?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: The vertuous Widow.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: The vertuous widow Sir? I know none ſuch:
Pray what's her name?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Laelia.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I knew you err'd,
'Tis not to me I warrant ye; there Sir,
Carry it to thoſe ſhe feeds fat with ſuch favours,
I am a ſtranger to her.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Good Sir take it,
And if you will, I'le ſwear ſhe ſent it to you,
For I am ſure mine eye never went off ye
Since you forſook the Gentlemen you talk'd with
Juſt at her door.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Indeed I talkt with two
Within this half hour in the ſtreet.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: 'Tis you Sir,
And none but you I am ſent to: wiſer men
Would have been thankful ſooner, and receiv'd it,
'Tis not a fortune every man can brag of,
And from a woman of her excellence.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Well Sir, I am Catechiz'd; what more belongs to't?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: This only Sir; ſhe would intreat you come
This evening to her without fail.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: You gheſs where.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Sir I have a tongue elſe. Exit Ser.
She is down right Devil; or elſe my wants
And her diſobedience have provok't her
To look into her foul ſelf, and be ſorry.
I wonder how ſhe knew me? I had thought
I had been the ſame to all, I am to them
That chang'd me thus Heaven pardon me for lying,
For I have paid it home: many a good man
That had but found the profit of my way
Would forſwear telling true again in haſt.
Here are my praters; now if I did well
I ſhould belabour 'em, but I have ſound
Away to quiet 'em, worth a thouſand on't.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: If we could get a fellow that would do it.

sp.speaker: Fat.
sp.l: What villany is now in hand?

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: 'Twill be hard to be done in my opinion
Unleſs we light upon an Engliſh-man
With ſeven-ſcore ſurfeits in him.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Are the Engliſh-men ſuch ſtubborn drinkers?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Not a leak at Sea
Can ſuck more liquor; you ſhall have their children
Chriſtened in mull'd ſack, and at five years old, able
To knock a Dane down: Take an Engliſh-man
And cry St. George, and give him but a raſher,
And you ſhall have him upon even terms
Defy a hog • head; ſuch a one would do it
Home boy, and like a work-man: at what weapon?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Sherry ſack: I would have him drink ſtark dead
If it were poſſible: at worſt paſt portage.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: What is the end then?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Doſt thou not perceive it?
If he be drunk dead, there's a fair end of him.
If not, this is my end, or by enticing,
Or by deceiving, to conduct him where
The fool is, that admires him; and if ſober,
His nature be ſo rugged, what will't be
When he is hot with wine? come let's about it,
If this be done but handſomely, I'le pawn
My head ſhe hath done with Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: This may do well.

sp.speaker: Fat.
sp.l: Here's a new way to murther men alive,
I'le choak this train: God ſave ye Gentlemen.
It is to you, ſtay: yes it is to you.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: VVhat's to me?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: You are fortunate,
I cannot ſtand to tell you more now, meet me
Here ſoon, and you'l be made a man. Exit Father.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: What Viſion's this?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: I know not.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Well, I'le meet it,
Think you o'th' other, and let me a while
Dream of this fellow.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: For the Drunkard, Lodovick,
Let me alone.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Come, let's about it then. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, pray let me laugh extreamly.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why? prethee why? haſt thou ſuch cauſe?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Yes faith, my Brother will be here ſtraightway, and—

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: VVhat?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: The other party: ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: VVhat party?
VVench thou art not drunk?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: No faith.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Faith thou haſt been among the bottles Clora.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Faith but I have not Frank: Prethee be handſom,
The Captain comes along too, wench.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: O is that it
That tickles ye?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Yes, and ſhall tickle you too,
You underſtand me?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: By my troth thou art grown
A ſtrange lewd wench: I muſt e'ne leave thy company,
Thou wilt ſpoil me elſe.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Nay, thou art ſpoil'd to my hand;
Hadſt thou been free, as a good wench ought to be,
When I went firſt a birding for thy Love,
And roundly ſaid, that is the man muſt do it,
I had done laughing many an hour agoe.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: And what doſt thou ſee in him, now thou knowſt him
To be thus laught at?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Prethee be not angry
And I'le ſpeak freely to thee.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Do, I will not.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Then as I hope to have a handſom husband,
This fellow in mine eye, (and Frank I am held
To have a ſhrewd gheſs at a pretty fellow)
Appears a ſtrange thing.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why, how ſtrange for Gods ſake?
He is a man, and one that may content
(For any thing I ſee) a right good woman:
And ſure I am not blind.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: There lyes the queſtion?
For, (but you ſay he is a man, and I
Will credit you,) I ſhould as ſoon have thought him
Another of Gods creatures; out upon him,
His body, that can promiſe nothing
But lazineſs and long ſtrides.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Theſe are your eyes;
Where were they Clora, when you fell in love
With the old foot-man, for ſinging of Queen Dido?
And ſwore he look'd in his old velvet trunks
And his ſlic't Spaniſh Jerkin, like Don John?
You had a parlous judgment then, my Clora.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Who told you that?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: I heard it.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Come, be friends,
The Souldier is a Mars, no more, we are all
Subject to ſlide away.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Nay, laugh on ſtill.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: No ſaith, thou art a good wench, and 'tis pity
Thou ſhouldſt not be well quarried at thy entring,
Thou art ſo high flown for him: Look, who's there?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Prethee go ſingle, what ſhould I do there?
Thou knowſt I hate theſe viſitations,
As I hate peace or perry.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Wilt thou never
Make a right man?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You make a right fool of me
To lead me up and down to viſit women,
And be abus'd and laugh'd at; let me ſtavre
If I know what to ſay, unleſs I ask 'em
What their ſhooes coſt?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Fye upon thee, coward,
Canſt thou not ſing?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Thou knoweſt I can ſing nothing
But Plumpton park.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Thou't be bold enough,
When thou art enter'd once.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I had rather enter
A breach: if I miſcarry, by this hand
I will have you by th' ears for't.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Save ye Ladies.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Sweet Brother I dare ſwear, you're welcom hither,
So is your Friend;

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Come, bluſh not, but ſalute 'em.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Good Sir believe your Siſter; you are moſt welcom,
So is this worthy Gentleman whoſe vertues
I ſhall be proud to be acquainted with.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: She has found me out already, and has paid me;
Shall we be going?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Peace;
Your goodneſs Lady
Will ever be afore us, for my ſelf
I will not thank you ſingle, leſt I leave
My friend, this Gentleman, out of acquaintance.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: More of me yet?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Would I were able, Sir,
From either of your worths to merit thanks.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: But Brother, is your friend thus ſad ſtill? methinks
'Tis an unſeemly nature in a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: What hath ſhe to do with me, or my behaviour?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: He do's but ſhew ſo, prethee to him Siſter.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: If I do not break thy head, I am no Chriſtian,
If I get off once.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Sir, we muſt intreat you
To think your ſelf more welcom, and be merry,
'Tis pity a fair man of your proportion
Should have a ſoul of ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Very well;
Pray Gentlewoman what would you have me ſay?

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Do not you know, Sir?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Not ſo well as you
That talk continually.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: You have hit her, Sir.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: I thank him, ſo he has,
Fair fall his ſweet face for't.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Let my face
Alone, I would wiſh you, leſt I take occaſion
To bring a worſe in queſtion.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Meaning mine?
Brother, where was your friend brought up? h'as ſure
Been a great lover in his youth of pottage,
They lye ſo dull upon his underſtanding.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: No more of that, thou'lt anger him at heart.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Then let him be more manly, for he looks
Like a great School-boy that had been blown up
Laſt night at duſt-point.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: You will never leave
Till you be told how rude you are, fye Clora.
Sir will it pleaſe you ſit?

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: And I'le ſit by you.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Woman be quiet, and be rul'd I would wiſh you.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: I have done, Sir Captain.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Art thou not aſham'd?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You are an aſſe, I'le tell you more anon,
You had better have been hang'd than brought me hither.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: You are grown a ſullen fool; either be handſom,
Or by this light I'le have wenches bait thee;
Go to the Gentlewoman, and give her thanks,
And hold your head up; what?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: By this light I'le brain thee.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Now o' my faith this Gentleman do's nothing
But it becomes him rarely; Clora, look
How well this little anger, if it be one,
Shews in his face.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes, it ſhews very ſweetly.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Nay do not bluſh Sir, o' my troth it does,
I would be ever angry to be thus.
Fabritio, o' my conſcience if I ever
Do fall in love, as I will not forſwear it
• ill I am ſomething wiſer, it muſt be,
I will not ſay directly with that face,
But certainly, ſuch another as that is,
And thus diſpoſe my chance to hamper me.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Doſt thou hear this, and ſtand ſtill?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You will prate ſtill;
I would you were not women, I would take
A new courſe with ye.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Why couragious?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: For making me a ſtone to whet your tongues on.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Prethee ſweet Captain.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Go, go ſpin, go hang.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Now could I kiſs him.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: If you long for kicking,
You'r beſt come kiſs me, do not though, I'de wiſh ye,
I'le ſend my Foot-man to thee, he ſhall leap thee,
And thou wantſt horſing: I'le leave ye Ladies.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Beſhrew my heart you are unmannerly
To offer this unto a Gentleman
Of his deſerts, that comes ſo worthily
To viſit me, I cannot take it well.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I come to viſit you, you fooliſh woman?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I thought you did Sir, and for that I thank you,
I would be loth to loſe thoſe thanks; I know
This is but ſome odd way you have, and faith
It do's become you well to make us merry;
I have heard often of your pleaſant vein.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: What wouldſt thou ask more?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Pray thou ſcurvy fellow
Thou haſt not long to live; adieu dear Damſels,
You filthy women farewel, and be ſober,
And keep your chambers.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Farewel old Don Diego.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Away, away, you muſt not ſo be angry,
To part thus roughly from us; yet to me
This do's not ſhew, as if it were yours, the wars
May breed men ſomething plain I know,
But not thus rude; give me your hand good Sir
I know 'tis white, and—

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: If I were not patient,
What would become of you two prating houſwives?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: For any thing I know, we would in to ſupper,
And there begin a health of luſty Claret
To keep care from our hearts, and it ſhould be—

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Faith to whom? Mark but this Jacomo.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Even to the handſomeſt fellow now alive.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Do you know ſuch a one?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: He may be gheſt at,
Without much travel.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: There's another item.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: And he ſhould be a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: 'Twould be better.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: And yet not you ſweet Captain.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why not he?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Well; I ſhall live to ſee your husbands beat you,
And hiſs 'em on like ban-dogs.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Green ſickneſſes and ſerving-men light on ye
With greaſy Codpieces, and woollen ſtockings,
The Devil (if he dare deal with two women)
Be of your counſels: farewel Plaiſterers— Exit Jac.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: This fellow will be mad at Mid-ſummer
Without all doubt.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I think ſo too.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I am ſorry,
He's gone in ſuch a rage; but ſure this holds him
Not every day.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: 'Faith every other day
If he come near a woman.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: I wonder how his mother could endure
To have him in her Belly, he's ſo boyſterous.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: He's to be made more tractable I doubt not.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes, if they taw him as they do whit-leather
Upon an iron, or beat him ſoft like Stock-fiſh.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter Lelia and her waiting-woman with a Vail.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Art t' ſure 'tis he?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Yes, and another with him.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: The more the merrier; did you give that money
And charg'd it to be delivered where I ſhew'd you?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Yes, and what elſe you bad me.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: That brave fellow,
Though he be old, whate'r he be, ſhews toughneſs,
And ſuch a one I long for, and muſt have
At any price; theſe young ſoft melting griſtles
Are only for my ſafer ends.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: They are here.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Give me my Vail, and bid the Boy go ſing
That ſong above, I gave him; the ſad ſong;
Now if I miſs him, I am curſt, go, wench,
And tell 'em I have utterly forſworn
All company of men, yet make a venture
At laſt to let 'em in; thou knowſt theſe things,
Do 'em to th' life.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: I warrant you I am perfect.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Some ill woman for her uſe would give
A million for this Wench, ſhe is ſo ſubtle.

div.stage: Enter to the door Julio, and Angelo.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Good Sir, deſire it not, I dare not do it,
For ſince your laſt being here, Sir, believe me,
She has griev'd her ſelf out of all Company,
And (ſweet Soul) almoſt out of life too.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Prithee,
Let me but ſpeak one word.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: You will offend, Sir,
And yet your name is more familiar with her
Than any thing but ſorrow, good Sir, go.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: This little Varlet hath her Leſſon perfect,
Theſe are the baits they bob with.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Faith I will not.

sp.speaker: Wom
sp.l: I ſhall be chidden cruelly for this;
But you are ſuch a Gentleman—

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: No more.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: There's a new Tyre, wench; peace, thou art well enough.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: What, has ſhe muſick?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Yes, for Heavens ſake ſtay,
'Tis all ſhe feeds upon.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Alas, poor ſoul.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Now will I pray devoutly, for there's need on't.

body.head: The SONG.
body.l: A Way delights, go ſeek ſome other dwelling,
For I muſt dye:
Farewel falſe Love, thy tongue is ever telling
Lye after Lye.
For ever let me reſt now from thy ſmarts,
Alas, for pity go,
And fire their hearts
That have been hard to thee, mine was not ſo.
Never again deluding Love ſhall know me,
For I will dye;
And all thoſe griefs that think to over-grow me,
Shall be as I:
For ever will I ſleep, while poor Maids cry,
Alas, for pity stay,
And let us dye
With thee, men cannot mock us in the day.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Miſtriſs? not one word, Miſtriſs if I grieve ye
I can depart again.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Let's go then quickly,
For if ſhe get from under this dark Cloud,
We ſhall both ſweat I fear, for't.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Do but ſpeak
Though you turn from me, and ſpeak bitterly,
And I am gone, for that I think will pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Oh, that all women were thus ſilent ever,
What fine things they were!

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: You have look'd on me,
When (if there be belief in Womens words
Spoken in tears) you ſwore you lov'd to do ſo.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: O me, my heart!

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Now, Julio, play the man,
Or ſuch another O me will undo thee:
Would I had any thing to keep me buſie,
I might not hear her; think but what ſhe is,
Or I doubt mainly, I ſhall be i'th' maſh too.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Pray ſpeak again.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Where is my Woman?

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: Here.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Mercy upon me! what a face ſhe has?
Would it were vail'd again.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Why did you let
This flattering man in to me? did not I
Charge thee to keep me from his eyes again,
As carefully as thou wouldſt keep thine own?
Thou haſt brought me poyſon in a ſhape of Heaven,
Whoſe violence will break the hearts of all,
Of all weak Women, as it hath done mine,
That are ſuch fools to love, and look upon him.
Good Sir, be gone, you know not what an eaſe
Your abſence is.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: By Heaven ſhe is a wonder,
I cannot tell what 'tis, but I am quamiſh.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Though I deſire to be here more than Heaven,
As I am now, yet if my ſight offend you,
So much I love to be commanded by you,
That I will go; farewel—

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I ſhould ſay ſomething
E're you depart, and I would have you hear me;
But why ſhould I ſpeak to a man that hates me,
And will but laugh at any thing I ſuffer?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: If this be hate—

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Away, away, deceiver.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Now help me, Angelo!

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I am worſe than thou art.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Such tears as thoſe might make another Woman
Believe thee honeſt, Julio, almoſt me,
That know their ends, for I confeſs they ſtir me.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: What will become of me? I cannot go now
If you would hang me, from her; O brave Eye!
Steal me away, Julio.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Alas, poor man! I am loſt again too, ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No, I will ſooner truſt a Crocodile
When he ſheds tears, for he kills ſuddenly,
And ends our cares at once; or any thing
That's evil to our Natures, than a man;
I find there is no end of his deceivings,
Nor no avoiding 'em, if we give way;
I was requeſting you to come no more
And mock me with your ſervice, 'tis not well,
Nor honeſt, to abuſe us ſo far; you may love too;
For though, I muſt confeſs, I am unworthy
Of your love every way; yet I would have you
Think I am ſomewhat too good to make ſport of.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Will you believe me?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: For your Vows and Oaths,
And ſuch deceiving tears as you ſhed now,
I will, as you do, ſtudy to forget 'em.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Let me be moſt deſpis'd of men—

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No more;
There is no new way left, by which your cunning
Shall once more hope to catch me; no, thou falſe man,
I will avoid thee, and for thy ſake all
That bear thy ſtamp, as counterfeit in love,
For I am open ey'd again, and know thee;
Go, make ſome other weep, as I have done,
That dare believe thee; go, and ſwear to her
That is a ſtranger to thy cruelty,
And knows not yet what man is, and his lyings,
How thou di'ſt daily for her; pour it out
In thy beſt lamentations; put on ſorrow,
As thou canſt, to deceive an Angel, Julio,
And vow thy ſelf into her heart, that when
I ſhall leave off to curſe thee for thy falſhood,
Still a forſaken Woman may be found,
To call to Heaven for vengeance.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: From this hour,
I heartily deſpiſe all honeſt Women;
I care not if the World took knowledg on't,
I ſee there's nothing in them, but that folly
Of loving one man only; give me henceforth,
(Before the greateſt Bleſſing can be thought of)
If this be one, a Whore; that's all I aim at.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Miſtriſs, the moſt offending man is heard
Before his ſentence, why will you condemn me
E're I produce the truth to witneſs with me,
How innocent I am of all your angers?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: There is no truſting of that tongue, I know't,
And how far if it be believ'd, it kills; no more, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: It never lied to you; if it did,
'Twas only when it call'd you mild and gentle.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Good Sir, no more; make not my underſtanding,
After I have ſuffer'd thus much evil by you,
So poor to think I have not reach'd the end
Of all your forc'd affections; yet becauſe
I once lov'd ſuch a ſorrow too too dearly,
As that would ſtrive to be; I do forgive ye
Even heartily, as I would be forgiven,
For all your wrongs to me; my charity
Yet loves you ſo far, (though again I may not)
And wiſh when that time comes, you will love truly,
(If you can ever do ſo) you may find
The worthy fruit of your affections,
True love again, not my unhappy Harveſt,
Which, like a fool, I ſow'd in ſuch a heart,
So dry and ſtony, that a thouſand ſhowers
From theſe two eyes, continually raining,
Could never ripen.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Y' have conquer'd me;
I did not think to yield, but make me now,
Even what you will, my Lelia, ſo I may
Be but ſo truly happy to enjoy you.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No, no, thoſe fond imaginations,
Are dead and buried in me, let 'em reſt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I'll marry you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: The Devil thou wilt, Julio,
How that word waken'd me! come hither, friend,
Thou art a fool, look ſtedfaſtly upon her,
Though ſhe be all that I know excellent,
As ſhe appears, though I could fight for her,
And run through fire; though I am ſtark mad too
Never to be recover'd, though I would
Give all I had i'th' World to lye with her
Even to my naked ſoul, I am ſo far gone,
Yet, methinks ſtill, we ſhould not dote away
That that is ſomething more than ours, our honours.
I would not have thee marry her by no means,
Yet I ſhould do ſo; is ſhe not a Whore?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: She is; but ſuch a one—

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: 'Tis true, ſhe's excellent,
And when I well conſider, Julio,
I ſee no reaſon we ſhould be confin'd
In our affections; when all Creatures elſe
Enjoy ſtill where they like.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And ſo will I then.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: He's faſt enough I hope now, if I hold him.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: You muſt not do ſo though, now I conſider
Better what 'tis.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Do not conſider, Angelo,
For I muſt do it.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: No, I'll kill thee firſt,
I love thee ſo well, that the worms ſhall have thee
Before this Woman, friend.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: It was your counſel.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: As I was a Knave,
Not as I lov'd thee.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: All this is loſt upon me, Angelo,
For I muſt have her; I will marry ye
When ye pleaſe: pray look better on me.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Nay then no more, friend; farewel, Julio,
I have ſo much diſcretion left me yet
To know, and tell thee, thou art miſerable.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Stay, thou art more than ſhe, and now I find it.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Is he ſo?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: No, I'll ſee thee ſtarv'd firſt. Exit Lelia.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Friend.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Fly her as I do, Julio, ſhe's a Witch.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Beat me away then, I ſhall grow here ſtill elſe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: That were the way to have me grow there with thee,
Farewel for ev • r. Exit Angelo

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Stay, I am uncharm'd,
Farewel thou curſed houſe, from this hour be
More hated of me than a Leproſie. Exit Julio.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Both gone? a plague upon 'em both,
Am I deceiv'd again? Oh, I would rail
And follow 'em, but I fear the ſpight of people,
Till I have emptied all my gall; the next
I ſeize upon ſhall pay their follies
To the laſt penny; This will work me worſe,
He that comes next, by Heav'n ſhall feel their curſe. Exit.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Enter Jacomo at one door, Fabricio at another.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: O, ye are a ſweet youth, ſo uncivilly
To rail, and run away?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: O! are you there, Sir?
I am glad I have found ye, you have not now your Ladi •
To ſhew your wit before.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Thou wou'lt not, wou'lt 'ou?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: What a ſweet youth I am, as you have made me,
You ſhall know preſently.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Put up your Sword,
I have ſeen it often, 'tis a Fox.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: It is ſo,
And you ſhall feel it too; will you diſpatch, Sir?
And leave your mirth out? or I ſhall take occaſion
To beat ye, and diſgrace ye too.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Well, ſince there is no other way to deal with you,
Let's ſee your Sword, I am ſure you ſcorn all odds,
I will fight with you—

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: How now? They meaſure, and Fab. gets his Sword.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Nay, ſtand out,
Or by this light, I'll make ye.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: This is ſcurvy,
And out of fear done.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: No, Sir, out of judgment,
For he that deals with thee, thou'rt grown ſo boyſterous,
Muſt have more wits, or more lives than another,
Or always be in Armour, or inchanted,
Or he is miſerable.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Your end of this, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: My end is only mirth to laugh at thee,
Which now I'll do in ſafety; ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'S heart? then I am grown ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Thou art,
And wilt be ſhortly ſport for little Children,
If thou continueſt this rude ſtubborneſs.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: O God, for any thing that had an edge?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Fye, what a ſhame it is,
To have a Lubber ſhew his teeth?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Why doſt thou laugh at me, thou wretched fellow?
Speak with a Pox; and look ye render me
Juſt ſuch a reaſon—

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I ſhall dye with laughing.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: As no man can find fault with; I ſhall have
Another Sword, I ſhall, ye ſtearing Puppy.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Does not this teſtineſs ſhew finely in thee?
Once more take heed of Children, if they find thee,
They'll break up School to bear thee Company,
Thou wilt be ſuch a paſtime, and whoot at thee,
And call thee Bloody-Bones, and Spade, and Spit-fire,
And Gaffer Mad-man; and go by Jeronimo,
And will with a wiſp, and come aloft, and crack rope,
And old Saint Dennis with the dudgeon Codpiſs?
And twenty ſuch names.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: No, I think they will not.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Yes, but they will; and Nurſes ſtill their Children
Only with thee, and here take him, Jacomo.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: God's precious, that I were but over thee
One Steeple height, I would fall and break thy Neck.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: This is the reaſon I laugh at thee,
And while thou art thus, will do; tell me one thing.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I wonder how thou durſt thus queſtion me;
Prithee reſtore my Sword.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Tell me but one thing,
And it may be I will; Nay Sir, keep out.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Well, I will be your fool now, ſpeak your mind, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Art thou not breeding teeth?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: How? Teeth?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Yes, teeth, thou wouldſt not be ſo froward elſe.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Teeth?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Come, 'Twill make thee
A little rheumatick, but that's all one,
We'll have a Bib, for ſpoiling of thy Doublet;
And a fring'd Muckender hang at thy Girdle,
I'll be thy Nurſe, and get a Coral for thee,
And a fine Ring of Bells.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Faith, this is ſomewhat
Too much, Fabricio, to your friend that loves you;
•• thinks your goodneſs rather ſhould invent
A way to make my follies leſs, than breed 'em;
I ſho • ld have been more moderate to you,
But I ſee ye deſpiſe me.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Now I love ye,
There take your Sword: continue ſo; I dare not
Stay now to try your patience, ſoon I'll meet ye,
And as you love your honours, and your ſtate,
Redeem your ſelf well to the Gentlewoman,
Farewel till ſoon. Exit Fabricio.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Well, I ſhall think of this. Exit Jacomo.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter Hoſt, Piſo, and Boy with a Glaſs of Wine.

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: Nothing i'th' World, but a dry'd Tongue or two—

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Taſte him, and tell me.

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: Is a valiant wine,
This muſt be mine, Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: This ſhall be ipſe,
Oh, he's a deviliſh biting wine, a Tyrant
Where he lays hold, Sir, this is he that ſcorns
Small Beer ſhould quench him; or a fooliſh Candle
Bring him to Bed; no, if he flinch I'll ſhame him,
And draw him out to mull amongſt old Midwives.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: There is a Souldier, I would have thee better
Above the reſt, becauſe he thinks there's no man
Can give him drink enough.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: What kind of man?

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: That thou mayſt know him perfectly, he's one
Of a left-handed making, a lank thing;
As if his Belly were ta'n up with ſtraw
To hunt a match.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Has he no Beard to ſhew him?

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: 'Faith, but a little, yet enough to note him,
Which grows in parcels, here and there a remnant;
And that thou mayſt not miſs him, he is one
That wears his forehead in a velvet ſcabbard.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: That note's enough, he's mine, I'll fuddle him,
Or lye i'th' ſuds; you will be here too?

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: Yes, 'Till ſoon, farewel, and bear up.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: If I do not,
Say I am recreant, I'll get things ready.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'TIS ſtrange thou ſhould'ſt be thus, with thy diſcretion.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I am ſure I am ſo.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I am well you ſee.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Keep your ſelf warm then, and go home, & ſleep,
And pray thou mayſt continue ſo;
Would I had gone to th' Devil of an arrant,
When I was made a fool to ſee her; Leave me,
I am not fit for converſation.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Why, thou art worſe than I was.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Therefore leave me,
The nature of my ſickneſs is not eas'd
By company or counſel, I am mad,
And if you follow me with queſtions,
Shall ſhew my ſelf ſo.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: This is more than errour.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: 'Pray be content, that you have made me thus,
And do not wonder at me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Let me know, but what you mean to do, and I am gone.
I would be loth to leave you thus elſe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Nothing
That needs your fear, that is ſufficient;
Farewel, and pray for me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I would not leave you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: You muſt, and ſhall.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I will then, would yond' Woman
Had been ten fathom under ground, when firſt
I ſaw her eyes.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Yet ſhe had been dangerous,
For to ſome wealthy Rock of precious ſtone,
Or mine of Gold, as tempting, her fair Body
Might have been turn'd, which once found out by labour,
And brought to uſe, having her Spells within it,
Might have corrupted States, and ruin'd Kingdoms,
Which had been fearful, (Friend) go, when I ſee thee
Next, I will be as thou art, or no more.
'Pray do not follow me, you'll make me angry.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Heav'n grant you may be right again.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Amen. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Score a gallon of Sack, and a pint of Olives to the Unicorn.

sp.speaker: Above, within.
sp.l: Why drawer?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Anon, anon.

sp.speaker: Another Boy.
sp.l: Look into the Nags head there.

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: Score a quart of Claret to the Bar,
And a pound of Sauſages into the Flower-pot.

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: The Devil's in their throats; anon, anon.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: Mull a pint of Sack there for the women in the
Flower-deluce, and put in ginger enough, they belch like potguns,
And Robin fetch Tobacco for the Peacock, they will not be
Drunk till mid-night elſe: how now, how does my Maſter?

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: Faith he lyes drawing on a pace.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: That's an ill ſign.

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: And fumbles with the pots too.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Then there's no way but one with him.

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: All the reſt,
Except the Captain, are in Limbo patrum,
Where they lye ſod in ſack.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Does he bear up ſtill?

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: Afore the wind ſtill, with his lights up bravely,
All he takes in I think he turns to Juleps,
Or h'as a world of Stowage in his belly,
The reſt look all like fire-drakes, and lye ſcatter'd
Like ruſhes round about the room. My Maſter
Is now the loving'ſt man, I think, above ground.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Would he were always drunk then.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: Drawer.

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: Anon, anon Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: And ſwears I ſhall be free to morrow, and ſo weeps
And calls upon my Miſtris.

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: Then he's right.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: And ſwears the Captain muſt lye this night with her
And bad me break it to her with diſcretion,
That he may leave an iſſue after him,
Able to entertain a Dutch Ambaſſador,
And tells him feelingly how ſweet ſhe is,
And how he ſtole her from her friends i'th' Country;
And brought her up diſguiz'd with the Carriers,
And was nine nights bereaving her her maidenhead,
And the tenth got a drawer, here they come.
Within cry drawer. Anon, anon, ſpeak to the Tyger, Peter.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: There's my Bells boys, my ſilver Bell.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Would he were hang'd
As high as I could ring him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Captain.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Hoe Boy.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Robin, ſufficient ſingle Beer, as cold as cryſtal,
Quench Robin, quench.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: I am gone Sir.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Shall we bear up ſtill? Captain how I love thee!
Sweet Captain let me kiſs thee, by this hand
I love thee next to Malmſey in a morning,
Of all things tranſitory.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I love thee too, as far as I can love a fat man.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou Captain?
Sweetly? and heartily?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: With all my heart Boy.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Then welcom death, come cloſe mine eyes ſweet Captain
Thou ſhalt have all.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: What ſhall your wife have then?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Why ſhe ſhall have beſides my bleſſing, and a ſilver ſpoon,
Enough to keep her ſtirring in the world,
Three little Children, one of them was mine
Upon my conſcience, th' other two are Pagans.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Twere good ſhe had a little fooliſh mony,
To rub the time away with.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Not a rag,
Not a Deniere, no, let her ſpin a Gods name:
And raiſe her houſe again.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not dye though:
Boy ſee your Maſter ſafe delivered,
He's ready to lye in.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Good night.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Good morrow,
Drink till the Cow come home, 'tis all pay'd boyes.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: A pox of Sack.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Marry bleſs my Buts, Sack is a jewel,
'Tis comfortable, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: More Beer boy,
Very ſufficient ſingle Beer.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Here Sir.
How is it Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: But ev'n ſo, ſo.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Go before finely Robin, and prepare
My wife, bid her be right and ſtreight, I come boy.
And Sirrah, if they quarrel, let 'em uſe
Their own diſcretions, by all means, and ſtir not,
And he that's kill'd ſhall be as ſweetly buried;
Captain, adieu, adieu ſweet bully Captain,
One kiſs before I dye, one kiſs.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Farewel Boy.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: All my ſweet boys farewel. Exit Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Go ſleep, you are drunk.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Come gentlemen, I'le ſee you at your lodging,
You look not luſtily, a quart more.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: No Boy.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Get us a Torch.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: 'Tis day Sir.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: That's all one.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Are not thoſe the ſtars, thou ſcurvy Boy?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Is not Charles-wain there, tell me that, there?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes;
I have paid 'em truly: do not vex him Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Confeſs it Boy, or as I live I'le beat
Mid-night into thy brains.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I do confeſs it.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Then live, and draw more ſmall Beer preſently.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Come Boyes, let's hug together, and be loving,
And ſing, and do brave things cheerly my hearts,
A pox o' being ſad; now could I fly
And turn the world about upon my finger,
Come ye ſhall love me, I am an honeſt fellow:
Hang care and fortune, we are friends.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: No Captain.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Do not you love me? I love you two dearly.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: No by no means; you are a fighting Captain,
And kill up ſuch poor people as we are, by th' dozens.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: As they kill flyes with Fox-tails, Captain.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Me thinks now as I ſtand, the Captain ſhews
To be a very mercifull young man.
(And pre'thee Piſo, let me have thy opinion)

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Then he ſhall have mercy, that merciful is,
Or all the Painters are Apocrypha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I am glad you have your wits yet, will ye go?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: You had beſt ſay we are drunk.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Ye are.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Ye lye.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Y'are raſcals, drunken raſcals.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: 'Tis ſufficient.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: And now I'le tell you why, before I beat ye,
You have been tampring any time theſe three days,
Thus to diſgrace me.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: That's a lye too.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Well Sir,
Yet I thank fate I have turn'd your points on you,
For which I'le ſpare ye ſomewhat, half a beating.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: I'le make you fart fire Captain, by this hand,
And ye provoke, do not provoke I'de wiſh you.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: How do you like this?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Sure I am inchanted.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Stay till I draw.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Diſpatch then, I am angry.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: And thou ſhalt ſee how ſuddenly I'll kill thee.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Thou darſt not draw, ye cold, tame, mangy Cowards,
Ye drunken Rogues, can nothing make you valiant?
Not wine, nor beating?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: If this may be ſuffer'd,
'Tis very well.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Go there's your way, go and ſleep:
I have pity on you, you ſhall have the reſt
To morrow when we meet.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Come Lodowick,
He's monſtrous drunk now, there's no talking with him.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I am ſo; when I am ſober, I'le do more.
Boy where's mine Hoſt?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: He's on his bed aſleep Sir. Ex. Boy.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Let him alone then: now am I high proof
For any action, now could I fight bravely,
And charge into a wild fire; or I could love
Any man living now, or any woman,
Or indeed any creature that loves Sack
Extreamly, monſtrouſly; I am ſo loving,
Juſt at this inſtant, that I might be brought
I feel it, with a little labour, now to talk
With a Juſtice of peace, that to my nature
I hate next an ill Sword: I will do
Some ſtrange brave thing now, and I have it here:
Pray Heaven the air keep out; I feel it buzzing. Exit.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: She loves him too much, that's the plain truth Frederick,
For which if I might be believ'd, I think her
A ſtrange forgetter of her ſelf; there's Julio,
Or twenty more —

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: In your eye I believe you,
But credit me the Captain is a man,
Lay but his rough affections by, as worthy.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: So is a reſty Jade a horſe of ſervice,
If he would leave his nature; give me one
By your leave Sir to make a husband of
Not to be wean'd, when I ſhould marry him;
Me thinks a man is miſery enough.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You are too bitter,
I would not have him worſe.
Yet I ſhall ſee you hamper'd one day Lady,
I do not doubt it, for this hereſie.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: I'le burn before; come pre'thee leave this ſadneſs;
This walking by thy ſelf to ſee the Devil,
This mumps, this Lachrymae, this love in ſippets;
It ſits thee like a French-hood.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Does it ſo?
I am ſure it fits thee to be ever talking,
And nothing to the purpoſe, take up quickly;
Thy wit will founder of all four elſe wench,
If thou hold'ſt this pace; take up when I bid thee.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Before your Brother, fy?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I can endure it.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Here's Raw-head come again; Lord how he looks!
Pray we 'ſcape with broken pates.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Were I he,
Thou ſhould'ſt not want thy wiſh, he has been drinking,
Has he not Frederick?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes, but do not find it.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Peace and let's hear his wiſdom.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You will mad him.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I am ſomewhat bold, but that's all one.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: A ſhort and pithy ſaying of a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: A I live
Thou art a ſtrange mad wench.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: To make a Parſon.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Ladyes I mean to kiſs ye.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: How he wipes his mouth like a young Preacher;
We ſhall have it.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: In order as you lye before me; firſt
I'le begin with you.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: With me Sir?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: If you will promiſe me to kiſs in eaſe,
I care not if I venture.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I will kiſs according to mine own inventions
As I ſhall ſee cauſe; ſweetly I would wiſh you,
I love ye.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Do you Sir?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes indeed do I,
Would I could tell you how.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I would you would Sir.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I would to Heaven I could, but 'tis ſufficient,
I love you with my heart.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Alas poor heart.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: And I am ſorry; but we'l talk of that
Hereafter, if it pleaſe Heaven.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Ev'n when you will Sir.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: He's diſmal drunk, would he were muzled.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You
I take it are the next.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Go to him fool.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Not I, he will bite me.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: When wit? when?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Good Captain.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Nay, and you play bo peep; I'le ha' no mercy
But catch as catch may.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Nay, I'le not defend ye.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Good Captain do not hurt me, I am ſorry
That e're I anger'd ye.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I'le tew you for't
By this hand wit, unleſs you kiſs diſcreetly.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: No more Sir.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes a little more ſweet wit,
One taſt more o' your office: go thy wayes
With thy ſmall kettle Drums; upon my conſcience
Thou art the beſt, that e're man laid his leg o'er.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: He ſmells juſt like a Cellar,
Fye upon him.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Sweet Lady now to you.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: For loves ſake kiſs him.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I ſhall not keep my countenance.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Trye pre'thee.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Pray be not coy ſweet woman, for I'le kiſs ye,
I am blunt
But you muſt pardon me.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: O God, my ſides.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Why ha, ha, ha? why laugh?
Why all this noiſe ſweet Ladyes?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Luſty Laurence,
See what a Gentlewoman you have ſaluted;
Pray God ſhe prove not quick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Where were thine eyes
To take me for a woman? ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Who art'a, art'a mortal?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I am Frederick

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Then Frederick is an Aſſe,
A ſcurvy Frederick to laugh at me.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Sweet Captain.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Away woman;
Go ſtitch and ſerve, I deſpiſe thee woman,
And Frederick ſhall be beaten; 'Sfut ye Rogue
Have you none elſe to make your puppies of, but me?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I pre'thee be more patient
There's no hurt done.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Sfut but there ſhall be, Scab.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Help, help for loves ſake.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Who's within there?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: So now you have made a fair hand.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: You have kill'd me— Fall as kill'd.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Call in ſome Officers, and ſtay the Captain.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You ſhall not need.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: This is your drunkenneſs.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: O me, unhappy Brother, Frederick,
Look but upon me, do not part ſo from me,
Set him a little higher, he is dead.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: O villain, villain.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: How now what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: O Sir my Brother! O my deareſt Brother!

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: This drunken trowgh has kill'd him.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Kill'd him?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Yes.
For Heavens ſake hang him quickly, he will do
Ev'ry day ſuch a murder elſe, there is nothing
But a ſtrong Gallows that can make him quiet,
I finde it in his nature too late.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Pray be quiet,
Let me come to him.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Some go for a Surgeon.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: O what a wretched woman has he made me!
Let me alone good Sir.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: To what a fortune,
Haſt thou reſerv'd thy life!

l.hi: Fabritio.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Never entreat me, for I will not know thee,
Nor utter one word for thee, unleſs it be
To have thee hang'd; for Heaven ſake be more temperate.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I have a ſword ſtill, and I am a villain.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: &c. Hold, hold, hold.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Away with him for Heavens ſake
He's too deſperate for our enduring.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Come, you ſhall ſleep, come ſtrive not
I'le have it ſo, here take him to his lodging, and
See him laid before you part. Exeunt Jac. with Ser.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: We will Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Ne're wonder, I am living yet, and well,
I thank you Siſter for your grief, pray keep it
Till I am fitter for it.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Do you live Sir?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes, but 'twas time to counterfeit, he was grown
To ſuch a madneſs in his wine.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: 'Twas well Sir,
You had that good reſpect unto his temper,
That no worſe follow'd.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: If I had ſtood him, certain one of us muſt have periſh'd.
How now Frank?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Beſhrew my heart I tremble like an aſpin.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Let him come here no more for Heavens ſake
Unleſs he be in chains.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I would fain ſee him
After he has ſlept, Fabritio, but to try
How he will be; chide him, and bring him back.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: You'l never leave till you be worried with him.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Come Brother, we'l walk in, and laugh a little
To get this Fever off me.

sp.speaker: C or.
sp.l: Hang him ſquib,
Now could I grind him into priming powder.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Pray will you leave your fooling?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Come, all friends.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Thou art enough to make an age of men ſo,
Thou art ſo croſs and peeviſh.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I will chide him,
And if he be not graceleſs, make him cry for't.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: I would go a mile (to ſee him cry) in ſlippers
He would look ſo like a whey cheeſe.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Would we might ſee him once more.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: If you dare
Venture a ſecond tryal of his temper
I make no doubt to bring him.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: No, good Frank,
Let him alone, I ſee his vein lyes only
For falling out at Wakes and Bear-baitings,
That may expreſs him ſturdy.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Now indeed
You are too ſharp ſweet Siſter, for unleſs
It be this ſin, which is enough to drown him,
I mean this ſowrneſs, he's as brave a fellow,
As forward, and as underſtanding elſe
As any he that lives.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I do believe you,
And good Sir when you ſee him, if we have
Diſtaſted his opinion any way,
Make peace again.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I will: I'le leave ye Ladies.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Take heed you had beſt, h'as ſworn to pay you elſe.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I warrant you, I have been often threatned.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: When he comes next, I'le have the cough or toothach,
Or ſomething that ſhall make me keep my chamber,
I love him ſo well.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Would you would keep your tongue. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE IV.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I cannot keep from this ungodly woman,
This Lelia, whom I know too, yet am caught,
Her looks are nothing like her; would her faults
Were all in Paris print upon her face,
Cum Privilegio, to uſe 'em ſtill,
I would write an Epiſtle before it, on the inſide of her maſque
And dedicate it to the whore of Babylon, with a preface upon
Her noſe to the gentle Reader; and they ſhould be to be ſold
At the ſign of the whores head i'th' pottage pot, in what
Street you pleaſe. But all this helps not me; — I
Am made to be thus catch'd, paſt any redreſs, with a thing
I contemn too.
I have read Epict • tus twice over againſt the
Deſire of theſe outward things, and ſtill her face runs in
My mind, I went to ſay my prayers, and they were
So laid out o'th' way, that if I could find any prayers I
Had, I'm no Chriſtian,
This is the door, and the ſhort
Is, I muſt ſee her again.— He knocks.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: 'Tis I, I would ſpeak with your Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Did ſhe ſend for you?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: No, what then? I would ſee her, prethee by thy leave.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Not by my leave; for ſhe will not ſee you, but
doth hate you, and
Your friend, and doth wiſh you both hang'd, which being ſo proper
Men, is great pity, that you are not.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: For your ſweet ſelf in particular, who ſhe reſolves perſwaded your
Friend to neglect her, ſhe deemeth whip-cord the moſt
Convenient unction for your back and ſhoulders.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Let me in, I'le ſatisfie her.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: And if it ſhall happen that you are in doubt of theſe my ſpeeches,
Inſomuch 〈◊〉 you ſhall ſpend more time in arguing at the
Door, I am fully perſwaded that my Miſtris in perſon from
Above, will utter her mind more at large by way of
Urine upon your head, that it may ſink the more ſoundly
Into your underſtanding faculties.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: This is the ſtrangeſt thing, good pretty ſoul, 〈◊〉
doſt thou uſe me ſo?
I pray thee let me in ſweet-heart.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Indeed I cannot ſweet-heart.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Thou art a handſom one, and this croſſeneſs do's not become thee.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Alas I cannot help it.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Eſpecially to me; thou knowſt when I was here, I ſaid I lik'd thee of
All thy Miſtriſs Servants.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: So did I you, though it be not my fortune to expreſs
It at this preſent: for truly if you would cry, I cannot
Let you in.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Pox on her, I muſt go the down-right way: look you
Here is ten pound for you, let me ſpeak with her.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: I like your gold well, but it is a thing by heaven
I cannot do, ſhe
Will not ſpeak with you, eſpecially at this time, ſhe has affairs.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: This makes her leave her jeſting yet, but take it
And let me ſee her, bring me to a place
Where undiſcerned of her ſelf I may
Feed my deſiring eyes but half an hour.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Why faith I think I can, and I will ſtretch my wits
And body too for gold: if you will ſwear as you
Are gentle, not to ſtir, or ſpeak, where you ſhall
See or hear, now, or hereafter: give me your gold, I'le plant you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Why, as I am a Gentleman, I will not.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Enough, quick, follow me.

sp.speaker: S.
sp.l: Why where's this maid, ſhe has much care of her buſineſs, Nell?
I think ſhe be ſunk; — why Nell—whiew—

sp.speaker: Maid within.
sp.l: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I pray you heartily come away, oh, come, come, the Gentleman
My Miſtris invited, is coming down the ſtreet, and the banquet
Not yet brought out?— They bring in the Banquet.

sp.speaker: Lel. within.
sp.l: Nell, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: I come forſooth.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Now muſt I walk: when there's any fleſhly matters in hand, my
Miſtris ſends me of a four hours errand: but if I go not
About mine own bodily buſineſs as well as ſhe, I am a Turk.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: What, all wide open? 'Tis the way to ſin
Doubtleſs; but I muſt on; the gates of Hell
Are not more paſſable than theſe; how they
Will be to get out, God knows, I muſt try.
'Tis very ſtrange, if there be any life
Within this houſe, would it would ſhew it ſelf.
What's here? a Banquet? and no mouth to eat,
Or bid me do it? this is ſomething like
The entertainment of adventurous Knights
Entring enchanted Caſtles: For the manner
Though there be nothing diſmal to be ſeen
Amazes me a little; what is meant
By this ſtrange invitation? I will ſound
My Daughters meaning e're I ſpeak to her,
If it be poſſible, for by my voyce — Muſique.
She will diſcover me! hark, whence is this.

lg.l: COme hither you that love, and hear me ſing
of joyes ſtill growing
Green, freſh, and luſty, as the pride of Spring,
and over blowing.
Come hither youths that bluſh, and dare not know
what is deſire,
And old men worſe than you, that cannot blow
one ſpark of fire.
And with the power of my enchanting Song,
Boyes ſhall be able men, and old men young.
Come hither you that hope, and you that cry,
leave off complaining,
Youth, ſtrength, and beauty, that ſhall never dye,
are here remaining.
Come hither fools, and bluſh, you ſtay ſo long
from being bleſt,
And mad men worſe than you, that ſuffer wrong,
Yet ſeek no reſt.
And in an hour, with my enchanting Song,
You ſhall be ever pleas'd, and young maids long.

div.stage: Enter Lelia, and her Maid with a Night-gown and Slippers.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Sir you are welcom hither, as this kiſs
Given with a larger freedom than the uſe
Of ſtrangers will admit, ſhall witneſs to you.
Put the gown on him, in this chair ſit down;
Give him his ſlippers: be not ſo amaz'd,
Here's to your health, and you ſhall feel this wine
Stir lively in me, in the dead of night,
Give him ſome wine; fall to your banquet Sir,
And let us grow in mirth; though I am ſet
Now thus far off you, yet four glaſſes hence
I will ſit here,
And try, till both our bloods
Shoot up and down to find a paſſage out,
Then mouth to mouth will we walk up to bed,
And undreſs one another as we go;
Where both my treaſure, body, and my ſoul
Are your's to be diſpos'd of.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Umh, umh. — Makes ſigns of his white head & heard.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: You are old,
Is that your meaning? why, you are to me
The greater novelty, all our freſh youth
Are daily offer'd me, though you perform
As you think little, yet you ſatisfie
My appetite: from your experience
I may learn ſomething in the way of luſt
I may be better for. But I can teach
Theſe young ones;
But this day I did refuſe
A paire of 'em, Julio, and Angelo,
And told them they were as they were
Raw fools and whelps. Ang. makes diſcontented ſigns.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Pray God he ſpeak not.Maid laies her finger croſs her mouth to him.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Why ſpeak you not ſweet ſir?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Umh.— Stops his ears, ſhews he is troubled with the Muſick

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Peace there, that muſique, now Sir ſpeak
To me.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Umh. — Points at the Maid.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Why? would you have her gone? you need not keep
Your freedom in for her; ſhe knows my life
That ſhe might write it;
Think ſhe is a ſtone.
She is a kind of bawdy Confeſſor,
And will not utter ſecrets.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Umh. — Points at her again.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Be gone then, ſince he needs will have it ſo,
'Tis all one. Exit Maid.— Fath. locks the door.
Is all now as you would? come meet me then,
And bring a thouſand kiſſes on thy lips,
And I will rob thee of 'em, and yet leave
Thy lips as wealthy as they were before.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Yes, all is as I would but thou.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: By Heaven 'tis my Father.— Starts.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: And I do beſeech thee
Leave theſe unheard of luſts which worſe become thee,
Than mocking of thy Father; let thine eyes
Reflect upon thy ſoul, and there behold
How loathed black it is; and whereas now
Thy face is heavenly fair, but thy mind foul,
Go but into thy Cloſet, and there cry
Till thou haſt ſpoil'd that face, and thou ſhalt find
How excellent a change thou wilt have made
For inward beauty.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Though I know him now
To be my Father, never let me live
If my luſt do abate,
I'le take upon me
To have known him all this while.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Look, doſt thou know me?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I knew ye Sir before.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: VVhat didſt thou do?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Knew you, and ſo unmov'dly have you born
All the ſad croſſes that I laid upon you,
VVith ſuch a noble temper, which indeed
I purpoſely caſt on you, to diſcern
Your carriage in calamity, and you
Have undergone 'em with that brave contempt,
That I have turn'd the reverence of a child
Into the hot affection of a Lover.
Nor can there on the earth be found but yours
A ſpirit fit to meet with mine.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: A woman? thou art not ſure.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Look and believe.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Thou art
Something created to ſucceed the Devil
When he grows weary of his envious courſe,
And compaſſing the World; but I believe thee
Thou didſt but mean to try my patience,
And doſt ſo ſtill; but better be advis'd,
And make thy tryal with ſome other things,
That ſafelier will admit a dalliance;
And if it ſhould be earneſt, underſtand
How curſt thou art, ſo far from Heaven,
That thou believ'ſt it not enough to damn alone,
Or with a ſtranger, but wouldſt heap all ſins
Unnatural upon this aged head,
And draw thy Father to thy Bed, and Hell.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: You are deceiv'd, Sir, 'tis not againſt nature
For us to lye together; if you have
An Arrow of the ſame Tree with your Bow,
Is't more unnatural to ſhoot it there
Than in another? 'Tis our general nature
To procreate, as fire is to conſume,
And it will trouble you to find a ſtick
The fire will turn from; If't be Natures will
We ſhould not mix, ſhe will diſcover to us
Some moſt apparent croſsneſs, as our organs
Will not be fit; which, if we do perceive,
We'll leave, and think it is her pleaſure
That we ſhould deal with others.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: The doors are faſt, thou ſhalt not ſay a Prayer,
'Tis not Heavens will thou ſhouldſt, when this is done
I'll kill my ſelf, that never man may tell me
I got thee.

div.stage: Father draws his Sword, Angelo diſcovers himſelf.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I pray you, Sir, help her, for Heavens ſake, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Hold, Reverend Sir, for honour of your Age.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: For ſafety of your Soul, and of the Soul
Of that too-wicked woman yet to dye.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: What art thou? and how cam'ſt thou to that place?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I am a man ſo ſtrangely hither come,
That I have broke an Oath in ſpeaking this,
But I believe 'twas better broke than kept,
And I deſire your patience; let me in,
And I proteſt I will not hinder you
In any act you wiſh, more than by word,
If ſo I can perſwade you, that I will not
Uſe violence, I'll throw my Sword down to you;
This houſe holds none but I, only a maid
Whom I will lock faſt in as I come down.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I do not know thee, but thy tongue doth ſeem
To be acquainted with the truth ſo well,
That I will let thee in; throw down thy Sword.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: There 'tis.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: How came he there? I am betray'd to ſhame,
The fear of ſudden death ſtruck me all over
So violently, that I ſcarce have breath
sp.stage: He lets in Angelo, and locks the Door.
sp.l: To ſpeak yet; but I have it in my head,
And out it ſhall, that (Father) may perhaps
O'r-reach you yet.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Come, Sir, what is't you ſay?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: My Angelo, by all the joys of love,
Thou art as welcome as theſe pliant arms
Twin'd round, and faſt about thee, can perſwade thee.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Away.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I was in ſuch a fright before thou cam'ſt,
Yond' old mad fellow (it will make thee laugh,
Though it feared me) has talkt ſo wildly here—
Sirrah, he ruſh'd in at my doors, and ſwore
He was my Father, and I think believ'd it;
But that he had a Sword, and threatned me—
I' faith he was good ſport, good, thruſt him out,
That thou and I may kiſs together; wilt thou?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Are you her Champion? and with theſe fair words
Got in to reſcue her from me? Offers to run at him.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Hold, Sir,
I ſwear I do not harbour ſuch a thought,
I ſpeak it not, for that you have two Swords,
But for 'tis truth.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Two Swords, my Angelo?
Think this, that thou haſt two young brawny arms
And ne'r a Sword, and he has two good Swords,
And ne'r an arm to uſe 'em; ruſh upon him,
I could have beaten him with this weak Body,
If I had had the ſpirit of a man.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Stand from me, and leave talking, or, by Heaven,
I'll trample thy laſt damning word out of thee.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Why do you hinder me then? ſtand away,
And I will rid her quickly.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Would I were
Clear of this buſineſs, yet I cannot pray.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Oh, be advis'd, why you were better kill her
If ſhe were good; convey her from this place,
Where none but you, and ſuch as you appoint,
May viſit her; where, let her hear of nought
But death and damning, which ſhe hath deſerv'd,
Till ſhe be truly, juſtly ſorrowful,
And then lay mercy to her, who does know
But ſhe may mend?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: But whither ſhould I bear her?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: To my houſe,
'Tis large, and private, I will lend it you.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I thank you, Sir, and happily it fits
With ſome deſign I have: but how ſhall we
Convey her?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Will they carry me away?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: For ſhe will ſcratch and kick, and ſcream ſo loud
That people will be drawn to reſcue her.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Why? none can hear her here but her own maid,
Who is as faſt as ſhe.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: But in the ſtreet?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Why, we will take 'em both into the Kitchen,
There bind 'em, and then gag 'em, and then throw 'em
Into a Coach I'll bring to the back-door,
And hurry 'em away.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: It ſhall be ſo,
I owe you much for this, and I may pay you,
There is your Sword, lay hold upon her quickly,
This way with me, thou diſobedient Child,
Why does thy ſtubborn heart beat at thy breaſt?
Let it be ſtill, for I will have it ſearch'd
Till I have found a Well of living tears
Within it, that ſhall ſpring out of thine eyes,
And flow all o'r thy Body foul'd with ſin,
Till it have waſh'd it quite without a ſtain. They drag her.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Help, help, ah! ah!
Murther, I ſhall be murthered, I ſhall be murthered.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: This helps thee not.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Baſely murthered, baſely.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I warrant you. Exeunt.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: THis roguey Captain has made fine work with us.

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: I would the Devil in a ſtorm would carry him
Home to his Garriſon again; I ake all over,
That I am ſure of; certainly my Body
s of a wild-fire, for my head rings backward,
Or elſe I have a moriſe in my brains.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I'll deal no more with Souldiers; well remembred,
Did not the Viſion promiſe to appear
About this time again?

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: Yes, here he comes;
He's juſt on's word.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: O, they be here together,
She's penitent, and by my troth I ſtagger
Whether (as now ſhe is) either of theſe
Two fools be worthy of her; yet becauſe
Her youth is prone to fall again, ungovern'd,
And marriage now may ſtay her, one of 'em;
And Piſo, ſince I underſtand him abler,
Shall be the man; the other bear the charges,
And willingly, as I will handle it.
I have a Ring here, which he ſhall believe
Is ſent him from a woman I have thought of;
But e're I leave it, I'll have one of his
In pawn worth two on't; for I will not loſe
By ſuch a meſs of ſugar-ſops as this is:
I am too old.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: It moves again, let's meet it.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Now if I be not out, we ſhall have fine ſport,
I am glad I have met you, Sir, ſo happily,
You do remember me I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I do, Sir.

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: This is a ſhort praeludium to a challenge.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: I have a meſſage, Sir, that much concerns you,
And for your ſpecial good; nay, you may hear too.

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: What ſhould this fellow mean?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: There is a Lady,
(How the poor thing begins to warm already)
Come to this town, (as yet a ſtranger here, Sir)
Fair, young, and rich, both in poſſeſſions,
And all the graces that make up a Woman,
A Widow, and a vertuous one; it works,
He needs no broth upon't.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: What of her, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: No more but this; ſhe loves you.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Loves me?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Yes,
And with a ſtrong affection, but a fair one,
If ye be wiſe and thankful ye are made; there's the whole matter.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I am ſure I hear this.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Here is a Ring, Sir, of no little value;
Which after ſhe had ſeen you at a window,
She bad me haſte, and give it, when ſhe bluſh'd
Like a blown Roſe.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: But pray, Sir, by your leave—
Methinks your years ſhould promiſe no ill meaning.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I am no Bawd, nor Cheater, nor a Courſer
Of broken winded women; if you fear me,
I'll take my leave, and let my Lady uſe
A fellow of more form; an honeſter
I am ſure ſhe cannot.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Stay, you have confirm'd me,
Yet let me feel; you are in health?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I hope ſo,
My water's well enough, and my pulſe.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Then
All may be excellent; pray pardon me,
For I am like a Boy that had found money,
Afraid I dream ſtill.

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: Sir, what kind of woman?
Of what proportion is your Lady?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: I'll tell you preſently her very Picture,
Do you know a woman in this town they call
(Stay, yes, it is ſo) Lelia?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Not by ſight.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Nor you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Neither.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Theſe are precious Rogues
To rail upon a woman they never ſaw;
So they would uſe their Kindred.

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: We have heard though
She is very fair and goodly.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Such another,
Juſt of the ſame Complexion, making, ſpeech,
But a thought ſweeter is my Lady.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Then
She muſt be excellent indeed.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Indeed ſhe is,
And you will find it ſo; you do believe me?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Yes marry do I, and I am ſo alter'd—

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Your happineſs will alter any man:
Do not delay the time, Sir; at a houſe
Where Don Valaſco lay, the Spaniſh Seignior
(Which now is Seignior Angelo's) ſhe is.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I know it.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: But before you ſhew your ſelf,
Let it be night by all means, willingly
By day ſhe would not have ſuch Gallants ſeen
Repair unto her, 'tis her modeſty.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I'll go and fit my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Do, and be ſure
You ſend proviſion in, in full abundance,
Fit for the Marriage; for this night I know
She will be yours, Sir, have you never a token
Of worth to ſend her back again? you muſt,
She will expect it.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Yes, pray give her this.
And with it all I have; I am made for ever. Exit Lod.

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: Well, thou haſt fools luck; ſhould I live as long
As an old Oak, and ſay my prayers hourly,
I ſhould not be the better of a penny;
I think the Devil be my ghoſtly father;
Upon my conſcience I am full as handſome,
I am ſure I have more wit, and more performance,
Which is a pretty matter.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Do you think, Sir,
That your friend, Seignior Piſo, will be conſtant
Unto my Lady? you ſhould know him well.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Who? Seignior Piſo?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Yes, the Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Why, you are wide, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Is not his name Piſo?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: No, mine is Piſo.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: 'Tis indeed, Sir,
And his is Lodowick.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Then I am undone, Sir,
For I was ſent at firſt to Piſo; what a Raſcal
Was I, ſo ignorantly to miſtake you?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Peace,
There is no harm done yet.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Now 'tis too late,
I know my errour;
At turning of a Street,
For you were then upon the right hand of him,
You chang'd your places ſuddenly; where I
(Like a croſs block-head) loſt my memory;
What ſhall I do? my Lady utterly
Will put me from her favour.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Never fear it,
I'll be thy guard I warrant thee; O, O,
Am I at length reputed? for the Ring,
I'll fetch it back with a light vengeance from him;
H'ad better keep tame Devils than that Ring;
Art thou not Steward?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Piſ.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt be ſhortly.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Lord, how he takes it!

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: I'll go ſhift me ſtreight;
Art t' ſure was to Piſo?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: O, too ſure, Sir.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: I'll mount thee if I live for't,
Give me patience, heav'n, to bear this bleſſing I beſeech thee;
I am but man, I prithee break my head
To make me underſtand I am ſenſible.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Lend me your Dagger, and I will, Sir.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: No.
I believe now like a good Chriſtian.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Good Sir, make haſt; I dare not go without ye
Since I have ſo miſtaken.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: 'Tis no matter,
Meet me within this half hour at St. Marg'rets.
Well, go thy ways, old Lad, thou haſt the trick on't.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: How now? the news?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Well, paſſing well, I have 'em,
Both in a leaſh, and made right for my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I am glad on't, I muſt leave you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: VVhither man?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: If all go right I may be faſt enough too.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I cry you mercy, Sir, I know your meaning,
Clora's the woman, ſhe's Frank's Bedfellow,
Commend me to 'em, go, Julio,
Bring 'em to ſupper all, to grace this matter;
They will ſerve for witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I will, farewel.

div.stage: Exit Julio at one door, and Ang. and Fath. at another.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Clora, Frank, and Frederick, and Maid.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Siſter, I brought you Jacomo to the door,
He has forgot all that he ſaid laſt night;
And ſhame of that makes him loth to come,
I left Fabricio perſwading him, but 'tis in vain.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Alas, my fortune, Clora.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Now Frank, ſee what a kind of man you love,
That loves you when he's drunk.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: If ſo,
'Faith, I would marry him; my friends I hope
Would make him drink.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: 'Tis well conſider'd, Frank, he has ſuch pretty humours then,
Beſides, being a Souldier, 'tis better he ſhould love
You when he's drunk, than when he's ſober, for then he
Will be ſure to love you the greateſt part on's life.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: And were not I a happy woman then?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: That ever was born, Frank, i' faith—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: How now, what ſays he?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: 'Faith, you may as well 'tice a Dog up with a Whip and Bell
As him, by telling him of Love and Women, he ſwears
They mock him.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Look how my Siſter weeps.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Why, who can help it?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Yes, you may ſafely ſwear ſhe loves him.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Why, ſo I did; and may do all the oaths,
Arithmetick can make, e're he believe me;
And ſince he was laſt drunk, he is more jealous
They would abuſe him; if we could perſwade him
She lov'd, he would embrace it.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: She her ſelf
Shall bate ſo much of her own modeſty
To ſwear it to him, with ſuch tears as now
You ſee rain from her.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I believe 'twould work,
But would you have her do't i'th' open ſtreet?
Or if you would, he'll run away from her,
How ſhall we get him hither?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: By entreaty.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt impoſſible, no, if we could
Anger him hither, as there is no way
But that to bring him, and then hold him faſt,
Women, and men, whilſt ſhe delivers to him the truth
Seal'd with her tears, he would be plain
As a pleas'd Child; he walks below for me
Under the window.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: We'll anger him I warrant ye,
Let one of the maids take a good Bowl of water,
Or ſay it be a piſs-pot, and pour't on's head.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Content, hang me if I like not the caſt of it rarely, for no queſtion
It is an approv'd Receipt to fetch ſuch a fellow;
Take all the women-kind in this houſe, betwixt the Age of one,
And one hundred, and let them take unto them a pot or a
Bowl containing ſeven quarts or upwards, and let them
Never leave, till the above named
Pot or Bowl become full, then let one of them ſtretch out
Her Arm, and pour it on his head, and probatum est, it
Will fetch him, for in his anger he will run up, and then let
Us alone.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Go you and do it. Exit Maid.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Good Clora, no.

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Away I ſay, & do it, never fear, we have enough of that
Water ready diſtill'd.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Why, this will make him mad, Fabricio,
He'll neither love me drunk nor ſober now.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I warrant you; what, is the wench come up?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Art thou there, wench?

sp.speaker: Wench.
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Look out then if thou canſt ſee him.

sp.speaker: Wench.
sp.l: Yes, I ſee him, and by my troth he ſtands ſo fair I could not
Hold were he my Father, his hat's off too, and he's ſcratching
His head.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: O, waſh that hand I prithee.

sp.speaker: Wench.
sp.l: 'Send thee good luck, this the ſecond time I have thrown thee
Out to day, ha, ha, ha, juſt on's head.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Alas!

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: What does he now?

sp.speaker: Wench.
sp.l: He gathers ſtones, God's light, he breaks all the Street windows.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: VVhores, Bawds, your windows, your windows.

sp.speaker: Wench.
sp.l: Now he is breaking all the low windows with
His Sword,
Excellent ſport, now he's beating a fellow that laugh'd at him,
Truly the man takes it patiently; now he goes down the ſtreet
Gravely, looking on each ſide, there's not one more dare laugh.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Does he go on?

sp.speaker: Wench.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Fabricio, you have undone a Maid
By treachery; know you ſome other better,
You would prefer your friend to? if you do not
Bring him again, I have no other hope,
But you that made me loſe hope, if you fail me,
I ne'r ſhall ſee him, but ſhall languiſh out
A diſcontented life, and dye contemn'd.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: This vexes me, I pray you be more patient,
If I have any truth, let what will happen,
I'll bring him preſently, do ye all ſtand
At the Street door, the maids, and all, to watch
VVhen I come back, and have ſome private place
To ſhuffle me into; for he ſhall follow
In fury, but I know I can out-run him
As he comes in, clap all faſt hold on him;
And uſe your own diſcretions.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: VVe will do it.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: But ſuddenly, for I will bring him hither
VVith that unſtopt ſpeed, that he ſhall run over
All that's in's way; and though my life be ventur'd
'Tis no great matter, I will do't.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: I thank you,
VVorthy Fabricio. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I ever knew no woman could abide me,
But am I grown ſo contemptible, by being once drunk
Amongſt 'em, that they begin to throw piſs on my head?
For ſurely it was piſs, huh, huh. ſeem to ſmell.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Jacomo, how do'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Well, ſomething troubled with wateriſh humours.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Foh, how thou ſtink'ſt! pre'thee ſtand further off me,
Me thinks theſe humours become thee better than thy dry
Cholerick humours, or thy wine-wet humours; ha?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You're pleaſant, but Fabritio know I am not in the mood of
Suffering jeſts.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: If you be not i'th' mood I hope you will not be moody,
But truly I cannot blame the Gentlewomen, you ſtood eveſdropping
Under their window, and would not come up.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Sir, I ſuſpect now, by your idle talk
Your hand was in't, which if I once believe,
Be ſure you ſhall account to me.

sp.speaker: Fab.
