sp.l: The Gentlewomen and the Maids have counted to you already,
The next turn I ſee is mine.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Let me dye but this is very ſtrange; good Fabritio
Do not provoke me ſo.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Provoke you? you're grown the ſtrangeſt fellow; there's no
Keeping company with you, phiſh; take you that.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: O all the Devils! ſtand Slave. Fab. gives him a box o'th' ear ſuddenly, and throws him from him, and goes his way, whilſt Jaco. draws his Sword.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Follow me if thou dar'ſt.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Stay coward, ſtay.— Jac. runs after Fabricio.

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter Fred. Fra. Clora, and Servant, and Maid.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: Be ready for I ſee Fabritio running,
And Jacomo behind him.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Where's the place?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l:
That way Fabritio.
Exit Fabritio.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Where art thou treacher, Fred. Clor. and Maid, lay hold on Jacomo.
What is the matter Sirs?
Why do you hold me? I am baſely wrong'd,
Torture, and hell be with you; let me go.they drag him to a chair and hold him down in't.

sp.speaker: Fre.
sp.l: Good Jac. be patient, and but hear
What I can ſay, you know I am your friend,
If you yet doubt it, by my ſoul I am.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: S'death ſtand away;
I would my breath were poyſon.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: As I have life, that which was thrown on you,
And this now done, were but to draw you hither
For cauſes weighty, that concern your ſelf,
Void of all malice, which this Maid my Siſter
Shall tell you.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Puh, a pox upon you all; you will not hold me
For ever here, and till you let me go,
I'le talk no more.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: As you're a Gentleman
Let not this boldneſs make me be believ'd
To be immodeſt; if there were a way
More ſilently to be acquainted with you,
God knows, that I would chooſe, but as it is
Take it in plainneſs: I do love you more
Than you do your content, if you refuſe
To pity me, I'le never ceaſe to weep,
And when mine eyes be out I will be told
How faſt the tears I ſhed for you do fall,
And if they do not ſlow abundantly,
I'le fetch a ſigh ſhall make 'em ſtart, and leap,
As if the fire were under.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Fine mocking, fine mocking.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Mocking? look how ſhe weeps.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Do's ſhe counterfeit crying too?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Behold how the tears flow, or pity her
Or never more be call'd a man.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: How's this? ſoft you, ſoft you my Maſters: is't poſſible think you,
She ſhould be in earneſt?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Earneſt? I in earneſt: ſhe's a fool to break ſo many ſleeps,
That would have been ſound ones, & venture ſuch a fane, and
So much life, for e're an humorous aſſe i'th' world.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why Clora? I have known you cry as much
For Julio, that has not half his worth,
All night you write and weep too much I fear,
I do but what I ſhould.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: If I do write,
I am anſwer'd Frank.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: I would I might be ſo.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Good Frederick let me go, I would fain try
If that thing do not counterfeit.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Give me your Sword then.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: No, but take my word,
As I am man, I will not hurt a creature
Under this roof, before I have deliver'd
My ſelf, as I am now, into your hands,
Or have your full conſent.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: It is enough.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Gentlewoman, I pray you let me feel your face; I am an
Infidel, if ſhe do not weep: Stay, where's my handkerchief?
I'le wipe the old wet off, freſh tears come, pox on't
I am a handſom, gracious fellow amongſt women, and
Knew't not Gentlewoman; how ſhould I know theſe tears are
For me? is not your Mother dead?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: By heaven they are for you.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Slight I'le have my head curl'd, and powder'd to morrow
By break of day; if you love me, I pray you kiſs me,
For if I love you, it ſhall be ſuch love, as I will not be
Aſham'd of, if this be a mock — kiſſes.
It is the heartieſt, and the ſweeteſt mock
That e're I taſted, mock me ſo again — kiſs again

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Fy Jacomo? why do you let her kneel
So long?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: It's true I had forgot it— lifts her up.
And ſhould have done this twelve-moneth; pray you riſe.
Frederick, if I could all this while have been perſwaded ſhe could
Have lov'd me, doſt thou think I had not rather kiſs her
Than another ſhould? and yet you may gull me for ought
I know, but if you do, hell take me if I do not cut
All your throats ſleeping.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Oh do not think of ſuch a thing.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Otherwiſe, ſhe be in earneſt, the ſhort is I am.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Alas, I am.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: And I did not think it poſſible any woman
Could have lik'd this face, it's good for nothing, is't?

sp.speaker: Clor.
sp.l: Yes it's worth forty ſhillings to pawn, being lin'd almoſt quite
Through with velvet.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: 'Tis better than your Julio's.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Thou thinkeſt ſo,
But otherwiſe, in faith it is not Frank—whilſt Jacomo is kiſſing Frank.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Hiſt Jacomo; How do'ſt thou Boy? ha?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Why very well, I thank you Sir.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou perceive the reaſon of matters, and paſſages
Yet Sirrah, or no?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Tis wondrous good Sir.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I have done ſimply for you, but now you are beaten to ſome
Underſtanding, I pray you dally not with the Gentlewoman
But diſpatch your Matrimony, with all convenient ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: He gives good counſel.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: And I will follow it.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: And I you, prethee do not take it unkindly,
For truſt me I boxt thee for thy advancement,
A fooliſh deſire I had to joggle thee into preferment.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: I apprehend you Sir, and if I can ſtudy out a courſe
How a baſtinadoing may any wayes raiſe your fortunes
In the State, you ſhall be ſure on't.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Oh Sir keep your way, God ſend you much joy.

sp.speaker: Clora.
sp.l: And me my Julio.

sp.speaker: O God I hear his voyce, now he is true,
sp.l: Have at a marriage Frank, as ſoon as you— Exeunt all but Fred.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: Sir I would ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: What is your haſtly buſineſs friend?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: The Duke commands your preſent attendance at Court.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: The cauſe?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: I know not in particular; but this
Many are ſent for more, about affairs
Forraign I take it Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I will be there
Within this hour, return my humble ſervice.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: I will Sir. Exit Meſſenger.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Farewel friend, what new's with you?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: My Miſtris would deſire you Sir to follow
With all the haſt you can, ſhe is gone to Church,
To marry Captain Jacomo, and Julio
To do as much for the young merry Gentlewoman,
Fair Miſtris Clora?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Julio marry Clora?
Thou art deceiv'd I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: No ſure Sir,
I ſaw their lips as cloſe upon the bargain
As Cockles.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Give 'em joy, I cannot now go,
The Duke hath ſent for me in haſt.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: This note Sir, when you are free, will bring you where they are. Ex.

sp.speaker: Fred. reads.
sp.l: You ſhall find us all at Signeur Angelo's,
Where Piſo, and the worthy Lelia
Of famous memory are to be married,
And we not far behind.
Would I had time
To wonder at this laſt couple in hell.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: You are ſtai'd for Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: I come, pray God the buſineſs
Hold me not from this ſport, I would not loſe it. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Enter Father, Piſo, Angelo, and Lelia.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: God give you joy, and make you live together
A happy pair.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: I do not doubt we ſhall.
There was never poor gentleman had ſuch a ſudden fortune,
I could thruſt my head betwixt two pales, and ſtrip me out of
My old skin like a Snake: will the gueſts come thou ſaidſt
Thou ſenteſt for to ſolemnize the Nuptials?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: They will, I lookt for 'em e're this.

div.stage: Enter Julio, Jacomo, Fabritio, Frank, Clora.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: By your leave all.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: They're here Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Eſpecially fair Lady
I ask your pardon, to whoſe marriage-bed
I wiſh all good ſucceſs, I have here brought you
Such gueſts as can diſcern your happineſs,
And beſt do know how to rejoyce at it;
•• e • u • h a fortune they themſelves have run,
The worthy Jacomo, and his fair Bride,
Noble Fabritio, whom this age of peace
Has not yet taught to love ought but the warrs,
And his true friends, this Lady who is but
A piece of me. Exit Father.

sp.speaker: Leli.
sp.l: Sir, you are welcom all,
Are they not Sir?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Bring in ſome wine, ſome of the wine Lodowick the fool
Sent hither: who ever thou bid'ſt welcom ſhall find it.

sp.speaker: Leli.
sp.l: An unepected honour you have done
To our too haſty wedding.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Faith Madam, our weddings were as haſty as yours,
We are glad to run up and down any whither, to ſee where
We can get meat to our wedding.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: That Lodowick hath provided too, good Aſſe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I thought you Julio would not thus have ſtollen a marriage
Without acquainting your friends.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Why I did give thee inklings.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: If a marriage ſhould be thus ſtubber'd up in a play, e're almoſt
Any body had taken notice you were in love, the Spectators
Would take it to be but ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: This was the firſt, and I will never hide
Another ſecret from you.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Sir, yonder's your friend Lodowick, hide your ſelf
And 'twill be the beſt ſport —

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Gentlemen, I pray you take no notice, I'm here.
The coxcomb Lodowick is coming in.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Is that the Lady?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: That is my Lady.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: As I live ſhe's a fair one; what make all theſe here?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: O Lord Sir ſhe is ſo peſter'd—

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Now will the ſport be, it runs right as Julio told us.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Fair Lady health to you; ſome words I have, that
Require an utterance more private,
Than this place can afford.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: I'le call my husband,
All buſineſs I hear with his ears now.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Good Madam no, but I perceive your jeſt,
You have no husband, I am the very man
That walk'd the ſtreets ſo comely.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Are you ſo?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Yes faith, when Cupid firſt did prick your heart.
I am not cruel, but the love begun
I'th' ſtreet I'le ſatisfie i'th' chamber fully.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: To ask a Madman whether he be mad
Were but an idle queſtion, if you be,
I do not ſpeak to you, but if you be not
Walk in the ſtreets again, and there perhaps
I may dote on you, here I not endure you.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Good Madam ſtay, do not you know this Ring?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: Yes it was mine, I ſent it by my Man,
To change and ſo he did, it has a blemiſh,
And this he brought me for it; did you change it?
Are you a Goldſmith?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Sure the world is mad,
Sirrah, did you not bring me this ring from your Lady?

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Yes ſurely Sir, did I, but your worſhip muſt ev'n bear with me;
For there was a miſtaking in it, and ſo, as I was
Saying to your worſhip, my Lady is now married.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Married? to whom?

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: To your worſhips friend Piſo.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: S'death to Piſo?

sp.speaker: Piſo within.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Yes Sir I can aſſure you ſhe's married to him, I ſaw't
With theſe gray eyes.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Why what a Rogue art thou then? thou haſt made in's mouth.
Me ſend in proviſion too.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: O a Gentleman ſhould not have ſuch foul words
But your Worſhips proviſion could not have come in at a fitter time;
Will it pleaſe you to taſt any of your own wine?
It may be the Vintner has cozen'd you.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Pox I am mad.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: You have always plots Sir, and ſee how they fall out.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: You had a plot upon me, how do you like this?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: I do not ſpeak to you.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Becauſe you dare not.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: But I will have one of that old Rogues teeth ſet in this Ring.

sp.speaker: Fat.
sp.l: Do'ſt not thou know that I can beat thee?
Doſt thou know it now? (diſcovers himſelf.)

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: He beat me once indeed.

sp.speaker: Fat.
sp.l: And if you have for got it, I can call a witneſs,
Come forth Piſo—remember you it?

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Faith I do call to minde ſuch a matter.

sp.speaker: Fat.
sp.l: And if I cannot ſtill do't, you are young
And will aſſiſt your Father in law.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: My Father in law?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Your Father in law, as ſure as this is widow Lelia.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: How widow Lelia?

sp.speaker: Fat.
sp.l: I' faith 'tis ſhe, Son.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, let my proviſion go, I am glad I
Have miſt the woman.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: Have you put a whore upon me?

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: By heaven you do me wrong, I have a heart
As pure as any womans, and I mean
To keep it ſo for ever.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: There is no ſtarting now, Son, if you offer't
I can compel you, her eſtate is great,
But all made o're to me, before this match,
Yet if you uſe her kindly, as I ſwear
I think ſhe will deſerve, you ſhall enjoy it
During your life, all ſave ſome ſlender piece
I will reſerve for my own maintenance,
And if God bleſs you with a child by her,
It ſhall have all.

sp.speaker: Piſo.
sp.l: So I may have the means,
I do not much care what the woman is:
Come my ſweet heart, as long as I ſhall find
Thy kiſſes ſweet, and thy means plentifull,
Let people talk their tongues out.

sp.speaker: Lel.
sp.l: They may talk
Of what is paſt, but all that is to come
Shall be without occaſions.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Shall we not make Piſo, and Lodowick friends?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Hang 'em they dare not be Enemies, or if they be,
The danger is not great, welcom Frederick

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Firſt joy unto you all; and next I think
We ſhall have wars.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Give me ſome wine, I'le drink to that.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: I'le pledge.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: But I ſhall loſe you then.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Not a whit wench; I'le teach thee preſently to be a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.l: Fabritio's command, and yours are both reſtor'd.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Bring me four glaſſes then.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Where are they?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: You ſhall not drink 'em here, 'tis ſupper time,
And from my houſe no creature here ſhall ſtir
Theſe three dayes, mirth ſhall flow as well as wine.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Content, within I'le tell you more at large
How much I am bound to all, but moſt to you,
Whoſe undeſerved liberality
Muſt not eſcape thus unrequited.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: 'Tis happineſs to me, I did ſo well:
Of every noble action, the intent
Is to give worth reward, vice, puniſhment.

div.head: Prologue.
div.l: TO pleaſe you with this Play, we fear will be
(So does the Author too) a myſtery
Somewhat above our Art; For all mens eyes,
Ears, faiths, and judgements, are not of one ſize.
For to ſay truth, and not to flatter ye,
This is nor Comedy, nor Tragedy,
Nor Hiſtory, nor any thing that may
(Yet in a week) be made a perfect Play:
Yet thoſe that love to laugh, and thoſe that think
Twelve pence goes farther this way than in drink,
Or Damſels, if they mark the matter through,
May ſtumble on a fooliſh toy, or two
Will make 'em ſhew their teeth: pray, for my ſake
(That likely am your firſt man) do not take
A diſtaſte before you feel it: for ye may
When this is hiſt to aſhes, have a Play.
And here, to out-hiſs this; be patient then,
(My honour done) y'are welcom Gentlemen.

div.head: Epilogue.
div.l: IF you miſlike (as you ſhall ever be
Your own free Judges) this Play utterly,
For your own Nobleneſs yet do not hiſs,
But as you go by, ſay it was amiſs;
And we will mend: Chide us, but let it be
Never in cold blood: O' my honeſty
(If I have any) this I'le ſay for all,
Our meaning was to pleaſe you ſtill, and ſhall.

list.item: Diocles, of a private Souldier elected Co-Emperour.
Maximinian, Nephew to Diocles, and Emperour by his donation.
Volutius Aper, Murtherer of Numerianus, the late Emperour.
Niger, a noble Souldier, Servant to the Emperour.
Camurius, a Captain, and Creature of Aper's,
Geta, a Jeſter, Servant to Diocles, a merry Knave.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Caſſana, Siſter to Coſroe, a Captive, waiting on Aurelia.
Druſilla, Niece to Delphia, in love with Diocles.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: YOU buz into my head ſtrange likelihoods,
And fill me full of doubts; but what proofs, Niger,
What certainties, that my moſt noble Brother
Came to his end by murther? Tell me that,
Aſſure me by ſome circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Niger.
sp.l: I will, Sir,
And as I tell you truth, ſo the gods proſper me,
I have often nam'd this Aper.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: True, ye have done;
And in myſterious ſenſes I have heard ye
Break out o'th' ſudden, and abruptly.

sp.speaker: Niger.
sp.l: True, Sir;
Fear of your unbelief, and the times giddineſs
Made me I durſt not then go farther. So your Grace pleaſe,
Out of your wonted goodneſs, to give credit,
I ſhall unfold the wonder.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: Do it boldly;
You ſhall have both our hearty loves, and hearings.

sp.speaker: Niger.
sp.l: This Aper then, this too much honour'd Villain,
(For he deſerves no mention of a good man)
Great Sir, give ear; this moſt ungrateful, ſpightful,
Above the memory of mankind, miſchievous,
VVith his own bloody hands.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Take heed.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: I am in, Sir;
And if I make not good my ſtory.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: Forward;
I ſee a truth would break out; be not fearful.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: I ſay this Aper, and his damn'd Ambition,
Cut off your Brothers hopes, his life, and fortunes;
The honour'd Numerianus fell by him,
Fell baſely, moſt untimely, and moſt treacherouſly:
For in his Litter, as he bore him company,
Moſt privately and cunningly he kill'd him;
Yet ſtill he fills the faithful Souldiers ears
With ſtories of his weakneſs, of his life,
That he dare not venture to appear in open,
And ſhew his warlike face among the Souldiers;
The tenderneſs and weakneſs of his eyes
Being not able to endure the Sun yet.
Slave that he is, he gives out this infirmity
(Becauſe he would diſpatch his honour too)
To ariſe from wantonneſs, and love of women,
And thus he juggles ſtill.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: O moſt pernicious,
Moſt bloody, and moſt baſe! Alas, dear Brother,
Art thou accus'd, and after death thy memory
Loaden with ſhames and lies? Thoſe pious tears
Thou daily ſhowe •• ſt upon my Fathers monument,
(When in the Perſian Expedition
He fell unfortunately by a ſtroke of Thunder)
Made thy defame and ſins? thoſe wept out eyes,
The fair examples of a noble nature,
Thoſe holy drops of Love, turn'd by depravers
(Malicious poyſon'd tongues) to thy abuſes?
We muſt not ſuffer this.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: It ſhows a truth now;
And ſure this Aper is not right nor honeſt,
He will not come near me.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: No, he dare not;
He has an inmate here, that's call'd a conſcience,
Bids him keep off.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: My Brother honour'd him,
Made him firſt Captain of his Guard, his next friend;
Then to my Mother (to aſſure him nearer)
He made him Husband.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: And withal ambitious;
For when he trod ſo nigh, his falſe feet itch'd, Sir,
To ſtep into the State.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: If ye believe, Brother,
Aper a bloody Knave (as 'tis apparent)
Let's leave diſputing, and do ſomething noble.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Siſter, be rul'd, I am not yet ſo powerful
To meet him in the field; he has under him
The Flower of all the Empire, and the ſtrength,
The Britain, and the German Cohorts; pray ye be patient,
Niger, how ſtands the Souldier to him?

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: In fear more, Sir,
Than love or honour; he has loſt their fair affections,
By his moſt covetous and greedy griping:
Are ye deſirous to do ſomething on him,
That all the World may know ye lov'd your Brother?
And do it ſafely too without an Army?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Moſt willingly.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: Then ſend out a Proſcription,
Send ſuddenly; And to that man that executes it
(I mean, that brings his head) add a fair payment,
No common Summ; then ye ſhall ſee I fear not,
Even from his own Camp, from thoſe men that follow him,
Follow, and flatter him, we ſhall find one,
And if he miſs, one hundred that will venture it.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: For his reward, it ſhall be ſo, dear Brother,
So far I'll honour him that kills the Villain;
For ſo far runs my love to my dead Brother,
Let him be what he will, baſe, old, or crooked,
He ſhall have me; nay, which is more, I'll love him
I will not be deny'd.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: You ſhall not, Siſter;
But ye ſhall know, my love ſhall go along too;
See a Proſcription drawn; and for his recompence,
My Siſter, and half Partner in the Empire;
And I will keep my word.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: Now ye do bravely.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: And though it coſt my life, I'll ſee it publiſh'd.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Away then for the buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: I am gone, Sir;
You ſhall have all diſpatch'd to night.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Be proſperous.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: And let the Villain fall.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: Fear nothing, Madam.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: 'Tis true, that Diocles is courteous,
And of a pleaſant nature, ſweet and temperate;
His Couſin Maximinian proud and bloudy.

sp.speaker: Delph.
sp.l: Yes, and miſtruſtful too, my Girl, take heed,
Although he ſeem to love thee, and affect
Like the more Courtier, curious complement;
Yet have a care.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: You know all my affection,
And all my heart-deſires are ſet on Diocles;
But, Aunt, how coldly he requites this courteſie!
How dull and heavily he looks upon me!
Although I woo him ſometimes beyond modeſty,
Beyond a Virgins care; how ſtill he ſlights me,
And puts me ſtill off with your Prophecy,
And the performance of your late prediction,
That when he is Emperour, then he will marry me;
Alas, what hope of that?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Peace, and be patient,
For though he be now a man moſt miſerable,
Of no rank, nor no badge of honour on him,
Bred low and poor, no eye of favour ſhining;
And though my ſure Prediction of his Riſing
(Which can no more fail than the day or night does,
Nay, let him be aſleep, will overtake him)
Hath found ſome rubs and ſtops, yet hear me, Neece,
And hear me with a faith, it ſhall come to him;
I'll tell thee the occaſion.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Do, good Aunt;
For yet I am ignorant.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Chiding him one day
For being too near, and ſparing for a Souldier,
Too griping, and too greedy; he made anſwer,
When I am Caeſar, then I will be liberal.
I, preſently inſpir'd with holy fire,
And my prophetick Spirit burning in me,
Gave anſwer from the gods, and this it was,

l.hi: Imperator eris Romae, cum Aprum grandem interſeceris:

sp.l: Thou ſhalt be Emperour, O Diocles,
When thou haſt kill'd a mighty Boar. From that time
(As giving credit to my words) he has employ'd
Much of his life in hunting; many Boars
Hideous and fierce, with his own hands he has kill'd too,
But yet not lighted on the fatal one,
Should raiſe him to the Empire; Be not ſad, Neece,
E're long he ſhall; Come, let's go entertain him,
For by this time I gueſs he comes from hunting;
And by my Art I find this very inſtant
Some great deſign's o' foot.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: The gods give good, Aunt. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Enter Diocles, Maximinian, Geta, with a Boar.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Lay down the Boar.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: With all my heart; I am weary on't;
I ſhall turn Jew if I carry many ſuch burthens:
Do you think, Maſter, to be Emperour
With killing Swine? you may be an honeſt Butcher,
Or allied to a ſeemly family of fowſe-wives.
Can you be ſuch an Aſs, my Reverend Maſter,
To think theſe ſprings of Pork will ſhoot up Caeſars?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: The fool ſays true.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Come, leave your fooling, Sirrah,
And think of what thou ſhalt be when I am Emperour.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Would it would come with thinking, for then o' my conſcience,
I ſhould be at leaſt a Senator.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: A Sowter;
For that's a place more fitted to thy nature,
If there could be ſuch an expectation;
Or ſay, the Devil could perform this wonder;
Can ſuch a Raſcal as thou art, hope for honour?
Such a log-carrying Lowt?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Yes, and bear it too,
And bear it ſwimmingly. I am not the firſt Aſs, Sir,
Has born good office, and perform'd it reverendly.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Thou being the Son of a Tiler, canſt thou hope to be a Senator?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Thou being the Son of a Tanner, canſt thou hope to be an Emperor?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Thou ſayſt true, Geta, there's a ſtop indeed;
But yet the bold and vertuous—

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Ye are right, Maſter,
Right as a Gun; For we the vertuous,
Though we be Kennel-rakers, Scabs, and Scoundrels,
We the diſcreet and bold; and yet, now I remember it,
We Tilers may deſerve to be Senators;
And there we ſtep before you thick-skin'd Tanners,
For we are born three ſtories high; no baſe ones,
None of your groundlings, maſter.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I like thee well,
Thou haſt a good mind, as I have, to this Honour.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: As good a mind, Sir, of a ſimple plaiſterer—
And when I come to execute my office,
Then you ſhall ſee.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: An Officer in fury;
An Officer as he ought to be; do you laugh at it?
Is a Senator (in hope) worth no more reverence?
By theſe hands I'll clap you by th' heels the firſt hour of it.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: O' my Conſcience, the fellow believes.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I, do, do, Geta,
For if I once be Emperour—

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Then will I
(For wiſe men muſt be had to prop the Republick)
Not bate ye a ſingle ace of a ſound Senator.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: But what ſhall we do the whilſt?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Kill Swine, and ſowſe 'em,
And eat 'em when we have bread.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Why didſt thou run away
When the Boar made toward thee? art thou not valiant?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: No indeed am I not; and 'tis for mine honour too;
I took a Tree, 'tis true, gave way to the Monſter;
Hark what diſcretion ſays, let fury paſs;
From the tooth of a mad Beaſt, and the tongue of a Slanderer
Preſerve thine honour.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: He talks like a full Senator:
Go, take it up, and carry it in, 'tis a huge one,
We never kill'd ſo large a Swine, ſo fierce too,
I never met with yet.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Take heed, it ſtirs again;
How nimbly the Rogue runs up! he climbs like a Squirrel.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Come down, ye Dunce, is it not dead?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: I know not.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: His throat is cut, and his bowels out.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: That's all one,
I am ſure his teeth are in; and for any thing I know,
He may have Pigs of his own nature in's Belly.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Come, take him up I ſay, and ſee him dreſt,
He is fat, and will be luſty m • at: away with him,
And get ſome of him ready for our Dinner.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Shall he be roaſted whole,
And ſerv'd up in a ſouce-tub? a portly ſervice,
I'll run i'th' wheel my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Sirrah, leave your prating,
And get ſome piece of him ready preſently,
We are weary both, and hungry.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: I'll about it.
What an inundation of Brewiſs ſhall I ſwim in? Exit.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Thou art ever dull and melancholy, Couſin,
Diſtruſtful of my hopes.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Why, can you blame me?
Do men give credit to a Jugler?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Thou knowſt ſhe is a Propheteſs.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: A ſmall one,
And as ſmall profit to be hop'd for by her.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Thou art the ſtrangeſt man; how does thy hurt?
The Boar came near you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: A ſcratch, a ſcratch.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: It akes and troubles thee, and that makes thee angry.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Not at the pain, but at the practice, Uncle,
The butcherly, baſe cuſtom of our lives now;
Had a brave enemies Sword drawn ſo much from me,
Or danger met me in the head o'th' Army,
To have bluſh'd thus in my blood, had been mine honour.
But to live baſe, like Swine-herds, and believe too,
To be fool'd out with tales, and old wives dreams,
Dreams, when they are drunk.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Certain you much miſtake her.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Miſtake her? hang her; to be made her Purveyors,
To feed her old Chaps; to provide her daily,
And bring in Feaſts while ſhe ſits farting at us,
And blowing out her Prophecies at both ends.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Prithee be wiſe; Doſt thou think, Maximinian,
So great a reverence, and ſo ſtai'd a knowledge—

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Sur-reverence, you would ſay; what truth? what knowledg?
What any thing but eating is good in her?
'Twould make a fool propheſie to be fed continually;
What do you get? your labour and your danger;
Whilſt ſhe ſits bathing in her larded fury,
Inſpir'd with full deep Cups, who cannot propheſie?
A Tinker, out of Ale, will give Predictions;
But who believes?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: She is a holy Druid,
A woman noted for that faith, that piety,
Belov'd of Heaven.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Heaven knows, I do not believe it:
Indeed I muſt confeſs they are excellent Juglers;
Their age upon ſome fools too flings a confidence:
But what grounds have they? what elements to work on:
Show me but that; the Sieve, and Sheers? a learned one,
I have no patience to diſpute this Queſtion,
'Tis ſo ridiculous; I think the Devil does help 'em,
Or (rather mark me well) abuſe 'em, Uncle;
For they are as fit to deal with him; theſe old women,
They are as jump, and ſquar'd out to his nature—

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Thou haſt a perfect malice.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: So I would have
Againſt theſe purblind Prophets; for look ye, Sir,
Old women will lie monſtrouſly; ſo will the Devil,
Or elſe he has had much wrong; upon my knowledge,
Old women are malicious; ſo is he;
They are proud and covetous, revengeful, lecherous;
All which are excellent attributes of the Devil;
They would at leaſt ſeem holy; ſo would he;
And to vail over theſe villainies, they wou'd propheſie;
He gives them leave now and then to uſe their cunnings,
Which is, to kill a Cow, or blaſt a Harveſt,
Make young Pigs pipe themſelves to death, choak poultry,
And chafe a dairy-wench into a feaver
With pumping for her butter.
But when he makes theſe Agents to raiſe Emperours,
When he diſpoſes Fortune as his Servant,
And tyes her to old wives tails—

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Go thy ways,
Thou art a learned Scholar, againſt credit,
You hear the Prophecie?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Yes, and I laugh at it;
And ſo will any man can tell but twenty,
That is not blind, as you are blind and ignorant:
Do you think ſhe knows your fortune?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I do think it.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I know ſhe has the name of a rare Sooth-ſayer;
But do you in your Conſcience believe her holy?
Inſpir'd with ſuch prophetick Fire?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Yes, in my conſcience.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: And that you muſt upon neceſſity,
From her words, be a Caeſar?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: If I live_

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: There's one ſtop yet.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: And follow her directions.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: But do not juggle with me.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: In faith, Couſin,
So full a truth hangs ever on her Prophecies,
That how I ſhould think otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Very well, Sir;
You then believe (for methinks 'tis moſt neceſſary)
She knows her own Fate?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I believe it certain.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Dare you but be ſo wiſe to let me try it,
For I ſtand doubtful.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Come nearer to me,
Becauſe her cunning Devil ſhall not prevent me;
Cloſe, cloſe, and hear; If ſhe can turn this deſtiny,
I'll be of your faith too.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Forward, I fear not;
For if ſhe knows not this, ſure ſhe knows nothing;
I am ſo confident—

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: 'Faith, ſo am I too,
That I ſhall make her Devils ſides hum.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: She comes here;
Go take your ſtand.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Now holly, or you howl for't.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: 'Tis pity this young man ſhould be ſo ſtubborn.
Valiant he is, and to his valour temperate,
Only diſtruſtful of delays in Fortune;
I love him dearly well.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Now, my Son Diocles,
Are ye not weary of your game to day?
And are ye well?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Yes, Mother, well and luſty,
Only ye make me hunt for empty ſhadows.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: You muſt have patience, Rome was not built in one day:
And he that hopes, muſt give his hopes their Currents.
You have kill'd a mighty Boar.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: But I am no Emperour:
Why do you fool me thus, and make me follow
Your flattering expectation hour by hour?
Riſe early, and ſleep late? to feed your appetites,
Forget my Trade, my Arms? forſake mine honour,
Labour and ſweat to arrive at a baſe memory?
Oppoſe my ſelf to hazards of all ſorts,
Only to win the barbarous name of Butcher?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Son, you are wiſe.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: But you are cunning, Mother;
And with that Cunning, and the faith I give you,
Ye lead me blindly to no end, no honour:
You find ye are daily fed, you take no labour;
Your family at eaſe, they know no market,
And therefore to maintain this, you ſpeak darkly,
As darkly ſtill ye nouriſh it, whilſt I,
Being a credulous and obſequious Coxcomb,
Hunt daily, and ſweat hourly, to find out
To clear your myſtery; kill Boar on Boar,
And make your Spits and Pots bow with my Bounties;
Yet I ſtill poorer, further ſtill—

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Be provident,
And tempt not the gods dooms; ſtop not the glory
They are ready to fix on ye. Ye are a fool then;
Chearful and grateful takers, the gods love,
And ſuch as wait their pleaſures with full hopes;
The doubtful and diſtruſtful man Heaven frowns at.
What I have told you by my inſpiration,
I tell ye once again, muſt, and ſhall find ye.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: But when? or how?

l.hi: Cùm Aprum interfeceris.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I have kill'd many.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Not the Boar they point ye;
Nor muſt I reveal further, till you clear it.
The lots of glorious men are wrapt in myſteries,
And ſo deliver'd; common and ſlight Creatures,
That have their ends as open as their actions,
Eaſie and open fortunes follow.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I ſhall try
How deep your inſpiration lies hid in ye,
And whether your brave ſpirit have a buckler
To keep this arrow off, I'll make you ſmoke elſe.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Knowing my fortune ſo preciſely, punctually,
And that it muſt fall without contradiction,
Being a ſtranger, of no tye unto ye,
Methinks you ſhould be ſtudied in your own,
In your own deſtiny, methinks, moſt perfect,
And every hour, and every minute, Mother,
So great a care ſhould Heaven have of her Miniſters;
Methinks your fortunes both ways ſhould appear to ye,
Both to avoid and take. Can the Stars now,
And all thoſe influences you receive into you,
Or ſecret inſpirations ye make ſhew of,
If an hard fortune hung, and were now ready
To pour it ſelf upon your life, deliver ye?
Can they now ſay, take heed?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Ha? pray ye come hither.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I would know that; I fear your Devil will cozen ye,
And ſtand as cloſe as ye can, I ſhall be with ye.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: I find a preſent ill.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: But I ſcorn it.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Do ye ſo? do ye ſo?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Yes, and laugh at it, Diocles.
Is it not ſtrange theſe wild and fooliſh men
Should dare to oppoſe the power of Deſtiny?
That power the gods ſhake at? Look yonder, Son.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Have ye ſpy'd me? then have at ye.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Do, ſhoot boldly,
Hit me, and ſpare not, if thou canſt.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Shoot, Couſin.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I cannot; mine arm's dead, I have no feeling;
Or if I could ſhoot, ſo ſtrong is her arm'd Vertue,
She would catch the arrow flying.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Poor doubtful people,
I pity your weak faiths.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Your mercy, Mother,
And from this hour a Deity I crown ye.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: No more of that.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: O let my Prayers prevail too,
Here like a tree, I dwell elſe; free me, Mother,
And greater than great Fortune, I'll adore thee.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Be free again, and have more pure thoughts in ye.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Now I believe your words moſt conſtantly,
And when I have that power ye have promis'd to me.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Remember then your Vow, my Niece Druſilla,
I mean to marry her, and then ye proſper.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I ſhall forget my life elſe.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: I am a poor weak woman, to me no worſhip.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: And ſhall he have as you ſay, that kills this Aper?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Now mark and underſtand.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: The Proſcription's up
I'th' Market place, 'tis up, there ye may read it,
He ſhall have half the Empire.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: A pretty farm i' faith.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: And the Emperours Siſter, bright Aurelia,
Her to his wife.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Ye ſay well, Friend, but hark ye,
Who ſhall do this?

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: You, if you dare.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: I think ſo;
Yet I could poyſon him in a Pot of Perry,
He loves that veng'ancely; But when I have done this,
May I lye with the Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: Lye with her? what elſe, man?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Yes, man,
I have known a man married that never lay with his Wife:
Thoſe dancing days are done.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: Theſe are old Souldiers,
And poor it ſeems, I'll try their appetites.
'Save ye, brave Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Sir, ye talkt of Proſcriptions?

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: 'Tis true, there is one ſet up from the Emperour
Againſt Volutius Aper.

l.hi: Aper?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Now;
Now have you found the Boar?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I have the meaning;
And bleſſed Mother—

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: He has ſcorn'd his Maſter,
And bloodily cut off by treachery
The noble Brother to him.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: He lives here, Sir,
Sickly and weak.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: Did you ſee him?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: He is murthered;
So ye ſhall find it mentioned from the Emperour;
And honeſt faithful Souldiers, but believe it;
For, by the gods, ye will find it ſo, he is murthered,
The manner how, read in the large Proſcription.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: It is moſt true, Son, and he cozens ye,
Aper's a Villain falſe.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I thank ye, Mother,
And dare believe ye; hark ye, Sir, the recompence?
As ye related.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: Is as firm as faith, Sir;
Bring him alive or dead.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: You took a fit time,
The General being out o'th' Town; for though we love him not,
Yet had he known this firſt, you had paid for't dearly.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: 'Tis Niger, now I know him; honeſt Niger,
A true ſound man, and I believe him conſtantly;
Your buſineſs may be done, make no great hurry
For your own ſafety.

sp.speaker: Nig.
sp.l: No, I am gone; I thank ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Pray, Maximinian, pray.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I'll pray, and work too.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I'll to the Market-place, and read the offer,
And now I have found the Boar.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Find your own faith too,
And rememher what ye have vow'd.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: O Mother.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Proſper.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: If my maſter and I do this, there's two Emperours,
And what a ſhow will that make? how we ſhall bounce it?

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: LEave us, and not vouchſafe a parting kiſs
To her that in his hopes of greatneſs lives,
And goes along with him in all his dangers?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: I grant 'twas moſt inhumane.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: O, you give it
Too mild a name; 'twas more than barbarous,
And you a Partner in't.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: I, Druſilla?

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Yes,
You have blown his ſwoln Pride to that vaſtneſs,
As he believes the Earth is in his fathom,
This makes him quite forget his humble Being;
And can I hope that he, that only fed
With the imagin'd food of future Empire,
Diſdains even thoſe that gave him means and life
To nouriſh ſuch deſires, when he's poſſeſs'd
Of his ambitious ends (which muſt fall on him,
Or your Predictions are falſe) will ever
Deſcend to look on me!

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Were his intents
Perfidious as the Seas or Winds, his heart
Compos'd of falſhood; yet the benefit,
The greatneſs of the good he has from you,
(For what I have confer'd, is thine, Druſilla)
Muſt make him firm, and thankful; But if all
Remembrance of the debts he ſtands engag'd for,
Find a quick Grave in his Ingratitude,
My powerful Art, that guides him to this height
Shall make him curſe the hour he e'r was rais'd,
Or ſink him to the Centre.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: I had rather
Your Art could force him to return that ardour
To me, I bear to him; or give me power
To moderate my paſſions; yet I know not,
I ſhould repent your grant, though you had ſign'd it,
(So well I find he's worthy of all ſervice)
But to believe that any check to him
In his main hopes, could yield content to me,
Were treaſon to true love, that knows no pleaſure,
The object that it dotes on ill affected.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Pretty ſimplicity; I love thee for't,
And will not ſit an idle looker on,
And ſee it cozen'd; dry thy innocent eyes,
And caſt off jealous fears, (yet promiſes
Are but lip comfort) and but fancy ought
That's poſſible in Nature, or in Art,
That may advance thy comfort, and be bold
To tell thy Soul 'tis thine; therefore ſpeak freely.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: You new create me. To conceal from you
My virgin-fondneſs, were to hide my ſickneſs
From my Phyſician. O dear Aunt, I languiſh
For want of Diocles's ſight; he is the Sun
That keeps my blood in a perpetual Spring;
But in his abſence, cold benumming Winter
Seizes on all my faculties. Would you bind me
(That am your Slave already) in more fetters,
And (in the place of ſervice) to adore you?
O bear me then (but 'tis impoſſible,
I fear to be effected) where I may
See how my Diocles breaks thorow his dangers,
And in what heaps his honours flow upon him,
That I may meet him, in the height and pride
Of all his glories, and there (as your gift)
Challenge him as mine own.

sp.speaker: Del
sp.l: Enjoy thy wiſhes;
This is an eaſie Boon, which at thy years,
I could have given to any; but now grown
Perfect in all the hidden myſteries
Of that inimitable Art, which makes us
Equal even to the gods, and Natures wonders,
It ſhall be done, as fits my skill and glory:
To break thorow bolts, and locks, a Scholars prize
For Thieves, and Pick-locks: to paſs thorow an Army
Cover'd with night, or ſome diſguiſe, the practice
Of poor and needy Spies: No, my Druſilla,
From Ceres I will force her winged Dragons,
And in the air hung over the Tribunal;
(The Muſick of the Spheres attending on us.)
There, as his good Star, thou ſhalt ſhine upon him,
If he prove true, and as his Angel guard him.
But if he dare be falſe, I, in a moment
Will put that glorious light out, with ſuch horrour,
As if the eternal Night had ſeiz'd the Sun,
Or all things were return'd to the firſt Chaos,
And then appear like Furies.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: I will do
What e're you ſhall command.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Reſt then aſſur'd,
I am the Miſtris of my Art, and fear not. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Aper, Camurius, Guard, a Litter covered.

sp.speaker: Aper.
sp.l: Your care of your ſick Emperour, fellow-ſouldiers,
In colours to the life, doth ſhew your love,
And zealous duty: O continue in it.
And though I know you long to ſee and hear him,
Impute it not to pride, or Melancholy,
That keeps you from your wiſhes: ſuch State-vices
(Too too familiar with great Princes) are
Strangers to all the actions of the life
Of good Numerianus: Let your patience
Be the Phyſitian to his wounded eyes,
(Wounded with pious ſorrow for his Father)
Which time and your ſtrong Patience will recover,
Provided it prove conſtant.

sp.speaker: 1 Guard.
sp.l: If he counterfeit,
I will hereafter truſt a prodigal heir,
When he weeps at his Fathers Funeral.

sp.speaker: 2 Guard.
sp.l: Or a young widow following a bed-rid husband,
(After a three years groaning) to the Fire.

sp.speaker: 3 Guard.
sp.l: Note his humility, and with what ſoft murmurs
He does enquire his pleaſures.

sp.speaker: 1 Guard.
sp.l: And how ſoon
He is inſtructed.

sp.speaker: 2 Guard.
sp.l: How he bows again too.

sp.speaker: Aper.
sp.l: All your commands (dread Caeſar) I'll impart
To your moſt ready Souldier, to obey them;
So take your reſt in peace. It is the pleaſure
Of mighty Caeſar (his thanks ſtill remembred
For your long patience, which a donative,
Fitting his State to give, ſhall quickly follow)
That you continue a ſtrict Guard upon
His ſacred perſon, and admit no ſtranger
Of any other Legion, to come near him;
You being moſt truſted by him. I receive
Your anſwer in your ſilence. Now, Camurius,
Speak without flattery; Hath thy Aper acted
This paſſion to the life?

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: I would applaud him,
Were he ſaluted Caeſar: but I fear
Theſe long protracted counſels will undo us;
And 'tis beyond my reaſon, he being dead,
You ſhould conceal your ſelf, or hope it can
Continue undiſcover'd.

sp.speaker: Aper.
sp.l: That I have kill'd him,
Yet feed theſe ignorant fools with hopes he lives,
Has a main end in't. The Pannonian Cohorts
(That are my own, and ſure) are not come up,
The German Legions waver, and Charinus
(Brother to this dead dog) (hells plagues on Niger)
Is jealous of the murther; and, I hear,
Is marching up againſt me. 'Tis not ſafe,
Till I have power, to juſtifie the Act,
To ſhew my ſelf the authour: be therefore careful
For an hour or two (till I have fully ſounded
How the Tribunes and Centurious ſtand affected)
That none come near the Litter. If I find them
Firm on my part, I dare profeſs my ſelf,
And then live Aper's equal.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Does not the body
Begin to putrifie?

sp.speaker: Aper.
sp.l: That exacts my haſte:
When, but even now, I feign'd obedience to it,
As I had ſome great buſineſs to impart,
The ſcent had almoſt choak'd me: be therefore curious:
All keep at diſtance. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: I am taught my part;
Haſte you to perfect yours.

sp.speaker: 1 Guard.
sp.l: I had rather meet
An enemy in the field, than ſtand thus nodding
Like to a rug-gown'd Watch-man.

sp.speaker: Geta.
sp.l: The Watch at noon?
This is a new device.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Stand.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I am arm'd
Againſt all danger.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: If I fear to follow,
A Cowards name purſue me.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Now my Fate
Guide and direct me.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: You are rude and ſawcy,
With your forbidden feet to touch this ground,
Sacred to Caeſar only, and to theſe
That do attend his perſon; Speak, what are you?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: What thou, nor any of thy faction are,
Nor ever were: Souldiers, and honeſt men.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: So blunt?

sp.speaker: Geta.
sp.l: Nay, you ſhall find he's good at the ſharp too.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: No inſtruments of craft: engines of murther,
That ſerve the Emperour only with oil'd tongues,
Sooth and applaud his vices, play the Bauds
To all his appetites; and when you have wrought
So far upon his weakneſs, that he's grown
Odious to the ſubject and himſelf,
And can no further help your wicked ends,
You rid him out of the way.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Treaſon?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: 'Tis truth,
And I will make it good.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Lay hands upon 'em,
Or kill them ſuddenly.

sp.speaker: Geta.
sp.l: I am out at that;
I do not like the ſport.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: What's he that is
Owner of any vertue worth a Roman,
Or does retain the memory of the Oath
He made to Caeſar, that dares lift his Sword
Againſt the man that (careleſs of his life)
Comes to diſcover ſuch a horrid Treaſon,
As when you hear't, and underſtand how long
Y'ave been abus'd, will run you mad with fury?
I am no ſtranger, but (like you) a Souldier,
Train'd up one from my youth: and there are ſome
With whom I have ſerv'd, and (not to praiſe my ſelf)
Muſt needs confeſs they have ſeen Diocles
In the late Britain wars, both dare and do
Beyond a common man.

l.hi: Diocles?

sp.speaker: 2 Guard.
sp.l: I know him,
The braveſt Souldier of the Empire.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Stand:
If thou advance an inch, thou art dead. Dio. kills Camu.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Die thou,
That durſt oppoſe thy ſelf againſt a truth
That will break out, though mountains cover it.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: I fear this is a ſucking Pig; no Boar,
He falls ſo eaſie.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Hear me, fellow Souldiers;
And if I make it not apparent to you
This is an act of Juſtice, and no Murther,
Cut me in pieces; I'le diſperſe the cloud
That hath ſo long obſcur'd a bloody act
Ne'r equall'd yet: you all knew with what favours
The good Numerianus ever grac't
The Provoſt Aper?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: True.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: And that thoſe bounties
Should have contain'd him (if he e're had learn'd
The Elements of honeſty and truth)
In loyal duty: But ambition never
Looks backward on deſert, but with blind haſte
Boldly runs on. But I loſe time. You are here
Commanded by this Aper to attend
The Emperours perſon; to admit no ſtranger
To have acceſs to him, or come near his Litter,
Under pretence (forſooth) his eyes are ſore,
And his minde troubled: no, my friends, you are cozen'd;
The good Numerianus now is paſt
The ſenſe of wrong or injury.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: How, dead?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Let your own eyes inform you.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: An Emperours Cabinet?
Fough, I have known a Charnel-houſe ſmell ſweeter.
If Emperours fleſh have this ſavour, what will mine do,
When I am rotten?

sp.speaker: 1 Guard.
sp.l: Moſt unheard of villany.

sp.speaker: 2 Guard.
sp.l: And with all cruelty to be reveng'd.

sp.speaker: 3 Guard.
sp.l: Who is the murtherer? name him, that we may
Puniſh it in his family.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Who but Aper?
The barbarous and moſt ingrateful Aper,
His deſperate Poniard printed on his breaſt
This deadly wound: hate to vow'd enemies
Finds a full ſatisfaction in death;
And Tyrants ſeek no farther. He (a Subject,
And bound by all the Ties of love and duty)
Ended not ſo; but does deny his Prince
(Whoſe ghoſt forbad paſſage to his reſt,
Mourns by the Stygian ſhore) his Funeral-Rites.
Nay, weep not; let your loves ſpeak in your anger;
And, to confirm you gave no ſuffrage to
The damned Plot, lend me your helping hands
To wreak the Parricide: and if you find
That there is worth in Diocles to deſerve it,
Make him your leader.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: A Diocles, a Diocles.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: We'll force him from his Guards. And now, my Stars,
If you have any good for me in ſtore,
Shew it, when I have ſlain this fatal Boar. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Enter Delphia and Druſilla, in a Throne drawn by Dragons.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Fix here, and reſt a while your Sail-ſtretch'd wings
That have out-ſtript the winds: the eye of Heaven
Durſt not behold your ſpeed, but hid it ſelf
Behind the groſſeſt clouds; and the pale Moon
Pluckt in her ſilver horns, trembling for fear
That my ſtrong Spells ſhould force her from her Sphere;
Such is the power of Art.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Good Aunt, where are we?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Look down, Druſilla, on theſe lofty Towers,
Theſe ſpacious ſtreets, where every private houſe
Appears a Palace to receive a King:
The ſite, the wealth, the beauty of the place,
Will ſoon inform thee 'tis imperious Rome,
Rome, the great Miſtris of the conquer'd world.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: But without Diocles, it is to me
Like any wilderneſs we have paſs'd o're:
Shall I not ſee him?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Yes, and in full glory,
And glut thy greedy eyes with looking on
His proſperous ſucceſs: Contain thy ſelf;
For though all things beneath us are tranſparent,
The ſharpeſt ſighted, were he Eagle-ey'd,
Cannot diſcover us: nor will we hang
Idle Spectators to behold his triumph:
sp.stage: Enter Diocles, Maximinian, Guard, Aper, Senators, Geta, Officers, with Litter.
sp.l: But when occaſion ſhall preſent it ſelf,
Do ſomething to add to it. See, he comes.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: How god-like he appears! with ſuch a grace
The Giants that attempted to ſcale Heaven,
When they lay dead on the Phlegrean plain,
Mars did appear to Jove.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Forbear.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Look on this,
And when with horrour thou haſt view'd thy deed,
(Thy moſt accurſed deed) be thine own judge,
And ſee (thy guilt conſider'd) if thou canſt
Perſwade thy ſelf (whom thou ſtand'ſt bound to hate)
To hope or plead for mercy.

sp.speaker: Aper.
sp.l: I confeſs
My life's a burden to me.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Thou art like thy name,
A cruel Boar, whoſe ſhout hath rooted up
The fruitfull Vineyard of the common-wealth:
I long have hunted for thee, and ſince now
Thou art in the Toyl, it is in vain to hope
Thou ever ſhalt break out: thou doſt deſerve
The Hangmans hook, or to be puniſhed
More majorum, whipt with rods to death,
Or any way, that were more terrible.
Yet, ſince my future fate depends upon thee,
Thus, to fulfull great Delphia's Prophecie,
Aper (thou fatal Boar) receive the honour Kills Aper.
To fall by Diocles hand. Shine clear, my Stars,
That uſher'd me to taſte this common air
In my entrance to the world, and give applauſe
To this great work. Muſick.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Strike Muſick from the Spheres.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: O now you honour me.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Ha! in the Air!

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Miraculous.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: This ſhews the gods approve
The Perſon, and the Act: then if the Senate
(For in their eyes I read the Souldiers love)
Think Diocles worthy to ſupply the place
Of dead Numerianus, as he ſtands
His Heir, in his revenge, with one conſent
Salute him Emperour.

sp.speaker: Senat.
sp.l: Long live Diocles:
Auguſtus, Pater Patriae, and all Titles,
That are peculiar only to the Caeſars,
We gladly throw upon him.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: We confirm it,
And will defend his honour with our Swords
Againſt the world: raiſe him to the Tribunal.

sp.speaker: 1 Sen.
sp.l: Fetch the Imperial Robes: and as a ſign
We give him abſolute power of life and death,
Bind this Sword to his ſide.

sp.speaker: 2 Sen.
sp.l: Omit no Ceremony
That may be for his honour.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Still the gods
Expreſs that they are pleas'd with this election.

sp.speaker: Geta.
sp.l: My Maſter is an Emperour, and I feel
A Senators Itch upon me: would I could hire
Theſe fine inviſible Fidlers to play to me
At my inſtalment.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I embrace your loves,
And hope the honours that you heap upon me,
Shall be with ſtrength ſupported. It ſhall be
My ſtudie to appear another Atlas,
To ſtand firm underneath this heaven of Empire,
And bear it boldly. I deſire no Titles,
But as I ſhall deſerve 'em. I will keep
The name I had, being a private man,
Only with ſome ſmall difference; I will add
To Diocles but two ſhort ſyllables,
And be called Diocleſianus.

sp.speaker: Geta.
sp.l: That is fine:
I'le follow the faſhion; and when I am a Senator,
I will be no more plain Geta, but be call'd
Lord Getianus.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: He ne'er thinks of me,
Nor of your favour.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: If he dares prove falſe,
Theſe glories ſhall be to him as a dream,
Or an inchanted banquet.

sp.speaker: Niger.
sp.l: From Charinus,
From great Charinus, who with joy hath heard
Of your proceedings, and confirms your honours:
He, with his beauteous Siſter, fair Aurelia,
Are come in perſon, like themſelves attended
To gratulate your fortune. Loud Muſick.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: For thy news,
Be thou in France Pro-conſul: let us meet
The Emperour with all honour, and embrace him.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: O Aunt, I fear this Princeſs doth eclipſe
Th' opinion of my beauty, though I were
My ſelf to be the judge.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Rely on me.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: 'Tis vertue, and not birth that makes us noble:
Great actions ſpeak great minds, and ſuch ſhould govern;
And you are grac't with both. Thus, as a Brother,
A fellow, and Co-partner in the Empire,
I do embrace you: may we live ſo far
From difference, or emulous Competition,
That all the world may ſay, Although two Bodies,
We have one Mind.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: When I look on the Trunk
Of dear Numerianus, I ſhould waſh
His wounds with tears, and pay a Siſters ſorrow
To his ſad fate: but ſince he lives again
In your moſt brave Revenge, I bow to you,
As to a power that gave him ſecond life,
And will make good my promiſe. If you find
That there is worth in me that may deſerve you,
And that in being your wife, I ſhall not bring
Diſquiet and diſhonour to your Bed,
Although my youth and fortune ſhould require
Both to be ſu'd and ſought to, here I yield
My ſelf at your devotion.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: O you gods,
Teach me how to be thankful: you have pour'd
All bleſſings on me, that ambitious man
Could ever fancie: till this happy minute,
I ne're ſaw beauty, or believ'd there could be
Perfection in a woman. I ſhall live
To ſerve and honour you: upon my knees
I thus receive you; and, ſo you vouchſafe it,
This day I am doubly married; to the Empire,
And your beſt-ſelf.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Falſe and perfidious villain.—

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Let me fall headlong on him: O my ſtars!
This I foreſaw and fear'd.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Call forth a Flamen,
This knot ſhall now be ti'd.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: But I will looſe it,
If Art or Hell have any ſtrength.

div.stage: Enter a Flamen, Thunder, and Lightning.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Prodigious!

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: How ſoon the day's orecaſt!

sp.speaker: Fla.
sp.l: The Signs are fatal:
Juno ſmiles not upon this Match, and ſhews too
She has her thunder.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Can there be a ſtop
In my full fortune?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: We are too violent,
And I repent the haſte: we firſt ſhould pay
Our lateſt duty to the dead, and then
Proceed diſcreetly. Let's take up the body,
And when we have plac'd his aſhes in his Urn,
We'll try the gods again for wiſe men ſay,
Marriage and Obſequies do not ſuit one day.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: So, 'tis deferr'd yet, in deſpite of falſhood:
Comfort Druſilla, for he ſhall be thine,
Or wiſh, in vain, he were not. I will puniſh Aſcend.
His perjury to the height. Mount up, my birds;
Some Rites I am to perform to Hecate,
To perfect my deſigns; which once perform'd,
He ſhall be made obedient to thy Call,
Or in his ruine I will bury all. Aſcends throne.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: What powerful Star ſhin'd at this mans Nativity?
And bleſs'd his homely Cradle with full glory?
What throngs of people preſs and buz about him,
And with their humming flatteries ſing him Caeſar?
Sing him aloud, and grow hoarſe with ſaluting him?
How the fierce-minded Souldier ſteals in to him,
Adores and courts his honour? at his devotion
Their lives, their vertues, and their fortunes laying?
Charinus ſues, the Emperour intreats him,
And as a brighter flame, takes his beams from him.
The bleſs'd and bright Aurelia, ſhe doats on him,
And, as the god of Love, burns incenſe to him.
All eyes live on him. Yet I am ſtill Maximinian,
Still the ſame poor and wretched thing, his ſervant.
What have I got by this? where lies my glory?
How am I rais'd and honour'd? I have gone as far
To woo this purblind honour, and have paſs'd
As many dangerous Expeditions,
As noble, and as high; nay, in his deſtinie
(Whilſt 'twas unknown) have run as many hazards,
And done as much; ſweat thorow as many perils;
Only the Hang-man of Volutius Aper
(Which I miſtook) has made him Emperour,
And me his ſlave.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Stand ſtill; he cannot ſee us,
Till I pleaſe: mark him well, this diſcontentment
I have forc'd into him, for thy cauſe, Druſilla.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Can the gods ſee this;
See it with juſtice, and confer their bleſſings
On him, that never flung one grain of incenſe
Upon their Altars? never bow'd his knee yet;
And I that have march'd foot by foot, ſtruck equally,
And whilſt he was a gleaning, have been praying,
Contemning his baſe covetous —

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Now we'll be open.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Bleſs me, and with all reverence.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Stand up, Son,
And wonder not at thy ungratefull Uncle:
I know thy thoughts, and I appear to eaſe 'em.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: O Mother, did I ſtand the tenth part to ye
Engag'd and fetter'd, as mine Uncle does,
How would I ſerve, how would I fall before ye?
The poorer powers we worſhip.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Peace, and flatter not;
Neceſſitie and anger draws this from ye;
Of both which I will quit ye: For your Uncle
I ſpoke this honour, and it fell upon him;
Fell, to his full content: he has forgot me,
For all my care; forgot me, and his vow too:
As if a dream had vaniſh'd, ſo h'as loſt me,
And I him: let him now ſtand faſt. Come hither;
My care is now on you.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: O bleſſed Mother!

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Stand ſtill, and let me work. So now, Maximinian,
Go, and appear in Court, and eye Aurelia:
Believe, what I have done, concerns ye highly.
Stand in her view, make your addreſſes to her:
She is the Stair of honour. I'le ſay no more,
But Fortune is your ſervant: go.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: With reverence;—
All this as holy truths. Exit.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Believe, and proſper.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Yet all this cures not me; but as much credit,
As much belief from Diocleſian.

div.stage: Enter Geta, Lictors, and Suitors, (with Petitions.)

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Be not dejected; I have warn'd ye often:
The proudeſt thoughts he has, I'le humble. Who's this?
O 'tis the fool and knave grown a grave Officer:
Here's hot and high preferment.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: What's your Bill?
For Gravel for the Appian way, and Pills?
Is the way rheumatick?

sp.speaker: 1 Suitor.
sp.l: 'Tis Piles, and't pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Remove me thoſe Piles to Port Eſquiline,
Fitter the place, my friend: you ſhall be paid.

sp.speaker: 1 Suit.
sp.l: I thank your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Thank me when ye have it;
Thank me another way, ye are an Aſſe elſe.
I know my office: you are for the ſtreets, Sir.
Lord, how ye throng! that knave has eaten Garlick;
Whip him, and bring him back.

sp.speaker: 3 Suitor.
sp.l: I beſeech your Worſhip;
Here's an old reckoning for the dung and dirt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: It ſtinks like thee: away. Yet let him tarry,
His Bill ſhall quit his Breath. Give your Petitions
In ſeemly ſort, and keep your hat off, decently.
For ſcowring the water-courſes thorow the Cities?
A fine periphraſis of a kennel-raker.
Did ye ſcour all, my friend? ye had ſome buſineſs:
Who ſhall ſcour you? you are to be paid, I take it,
When Surgeons ſwear you have perform'd your office.

sp.speaker: 4 Suit.
sp.l: Your Worſhip's merry.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: We muſt be ſometimes wittie,
To nick a knave; 'tis as uſeful as our gravitie.
I'le take no more Petitions; I am peſter'd;
Give me ſome reſt.

sp.speaker: 4 Suit.
sp.l: I have brought the gold (and't pleaſe ye)
About the Place ye promiſed.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: See him enter'd.
How does your Daughter?

sp.speaker: 4 Suit.
sp.l: Better your worſhip thinks of her.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: This is with the leaſt. But let me ſee your Daughter.
'Tis a good forward maid; I'le joyn her with ye.
I do beſeech ye, leave me.

sp.speaker: Lictor.
sp.l: Ye ſee the Edile's buſie.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: And look to your places, or I'le make ye ſmoke elſe.
Sirrah, I drank a cup of wine at your houſe yeſterday;
A good ſmart wine.

sp.speaker: Lictor.
sp.l: Send him the piece, he likes it.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: And ate the beſt wild Boar at that ſame Farmers.

sp.speaker: 2 Su.
sp.l: I have half left yet: your worſhip ſhall command it.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: A bit will ſerve: give me ſome reſt: gods help me.
How ſhall I labour when I am a Senator?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: 'Tis a fit place indeed. 'Save your Maſterſhip;
Do you know us, Sir?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Theſe women are ſtill troubleſom.
There be houſes providing for ſuch wretched women,
And ſome ſmall Rents, to ſet ye a ſpinning.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Sir,
We are no Spinſters; nor, if you look upon us,
So wretched as you take us.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Does your Mightineſs
That is a great deſtroyer of your Memorie,
Yet underſtand our faces?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: 'Prethee keep off, woman;
It is not fit I ſhould know every creature.
Although I have been familiar with thee heretofore,
I muſt not know thee now: my place neglects thee.
Yet, becauſe I daign a glimpſe of your remembrances,
Give me your Suits, and wait me a month hence.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Our Suits are, Sir, to ſee the Emperour,
The Emperour Diocleſian, to ſpeak to him,
And not to wait on you. We have told you all, Sir.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: I laugh at your ſimplicitie, poor women:
See the Emperour? why you are deceiv'd: now
The Emperour appears but once in ſeven years,
And then he ſhines not on ſuch weeds as you are.
Forward, and keep your State, and keep beggers from me.

sp.speaker: Druſ.
sp.l: Here is a prettie youth. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: He ſhall be prettie,
Or I will want my will, ſince ye are ſo high, Sir.
I'le raiſe ye higher, or my art ſhall fail me.
Stand cloſe, he comes.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: How am I croſs'd and tortur'd?
My moſt wiſh'd happineſs, my lovely Miſtris,
That muſt make good my hopes, and link my greatneſs,
Yet ſever'd from mine arms? Tell me, high heaven,
How have I ſinn'd, that you ſhould ſpeak in thunder,
In horrid thunder, when my heart was ready
To leap into her breaſt? the Prieſt was ready?
The joyful virgins and the young men ready?
When Hymen ſtood with all his flames about him
Bleſſing the bed? the houſe with full joy ſweating?
And expectation, like the Roman Eagle,
Took ſtand, and call'd all eyes? It was your honour;
And e're you give it full, do you deſtroy it?
Or was there ſome dire Star? ſome Devil that did it?
Some ſad malignant Angel to mine honour?
With you I dare not rage.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: With me thou canſt not,
Though it was I. Nay, look not pale and frighted;
I'le fright thee more. With me thou canſt not quarrel;
I rais'd the thunder, to rebuke thy falſhood:
Look here, to her thy falſhood. Now be angry,
And be as great in evil as in Empire.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Bleſs me, ye Powers.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Thou haſt full need of bleſſing.
'Twas I, that at thy great Inauguration,
Hung in the air unſeen: 'twas I that honour'd thee
With various Muſicks, and ſweet ſounding airs:
'Twas I inſpir'd the Souldiers heart with wonder,
And made him throw himſelf, with love and duty,
Low at thy feet: 'twas I that fix'd him to thee,
But why did I all this? To keep thy honeſtie,
Thy vow and faith; that once forgot and ſlighted —
Aurelia in regard, the Marriage ready,
The Prieſt and all the Ceremonies preſent,
'Twas I that thundred loud; 'twas I that threatned;
'Twas I that caſt a dark face over heaven,
And ſmote ye all with terrour.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Yet conſider,
As ye are noble, as I have deſerv'd ye;
For yet ye are free: if neither faith nor promiſe,
The deeds of elder times may be remembred,
Let theſe new-dropping tears; for I ſtill love ye,
Theſe hands held up to heaven.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: I muſt not pity ye;
'Tis not wiſe in me.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: How? not wiſe?

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Nor honourable.
A Princeſs is my Love, and doats upon me:
A fair and lovely Princeſs is my Miſtris.
I am an Emperour: conſider, Propheteſs,
Now my embraces are for Queens and Princeſſes,
For Ladies of high mark, for divine beauties
To look ſo low as this cheap common ſweetneſs,
Would ſpeak me baſe, my names and glories nothing.
I grant I made a vow; what was I then?
As ſhe is now, of no ſort, (hope made me promiſe)
But now I am; to keep this vow, were monſtrous,
A madneſs, and a low inglorious fondneſs.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Take heed, proud man.

sp.speaker: Druſ.
sp.l: Princes may love with Titles,
But I with Truth.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Take heed; here ſtands thy deſtinie;
Thy Fate here follows.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Thou doating Sorcereſs,
Wouldſt have me love this thing, that is not worthy
To kneel unto my Saint? to kiſs her ſhadow?
Great Princes are her ſlaves; ſelected beauties
Bow at her beck: the mighty Perſian's Daughter
(Bright as the breaking Faſt, as mid-day glorious)
Waits her commands, and grows proud in her pleaſures.
I'le ſee her honour'd: ſome Match I ſhall think of,
That ſhall advance ye both; mean time I'll favour ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Mean time I'le haunt thee. Cry not (wench) be confident,
E're long, thou ſhalt more pity him (obſerve me)
And pity him in truth, than now thou ſeek'ſt him:
My art and I are yet companions Come, Girl. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: I am too merciful, I find it, friends,
Of too ſoft a nature to be an Officer;
I bear too much remorſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Lict.
sp.l: 'Tis your own fault, Sir;
For look you, one ſo newly warm in Office
Should lay about him blindfold, like true Juſtice,
Hit where it will: the more ye whip and hang, Sir,
(Though without cauſe; let that declare it ſelf afterward)
The more ye are admired.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: I think I ſhall be. —

sp.speaker: 2 Lict.
sp.l: Your worſhip is a man of a ſpare body,
And prone to anger.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Nay, I will be angry,
And, the beſt is, I need not ſhew my reaſon.

sp.speaker: 2 Lict.
sp.l: You need not, Sir, your place is without reaſon;
And what you want in growth and full proportion,
Make up in rule and rigour.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: A rare Counſellor;
Inſtruct me further. Is it fit, my friends,
The Emperour my Maſter Diocleſian
Should now remember or the times or manners
That call'd him plain down Diocles?

sp.speaker: 1 Lict.
sp.l: He muſt not,
It ſtands not with his Royaltie.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: I grant ye,
I being then the Edile Getianus,
A man of place, and Judge, is it held requiſite
I ſhould commit to my conſideration
Thoſe Raſcals of removed and ragged hours,
That with unreverend mouths call'd me Slave Geta?

sp.speaker: 2 Lict.
sp.l: You muſt forget their names; your honour bids ye.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: I do forget; but I'le hang their natures:
I will aſcend my place, which is of Juſtice;
And mercy, I forget thee.

sp.speaker: Suitor.
sp.l: A rare Magiſtrate!
Another Solon ſure.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Bring out the offenders.

sp.speaker: 1 Lict.
sp.l: There are none yet, Sir, but no doubt there will be.
But if you pleaſe touch ſome things of thoſe natures.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: And am I ready, and mine anger too?
The melancholy of a Magiſtrate upon me,
And no offenders to execute my fury?
Ha? no offenders, knaves?

sp.speaker: 1 Lict.
sp.l: There are knaves indeed, Sir,
But we hope ſhortly to have 'em for your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: No men to hang or whip? are you good officers,
That provide no fuel for a Judges fury?
In this place ſomething muſt be done; this Chair, I tell ye,
When I ſit down, muſt ſavour of Severitie:
Therefore I warn ye all, bring me lewd people,
Or likely to be lewd; twigs muſt be cropt too:
Let me have evil perſons in abundance,
Or make 'em evil; 'tis all one, do but ſay ſo,
That I may have fit matter for a Magiſtrate;
And let me work. If I ſit empty once more,
And loſe my longing, as I am true Edile,
And as I hope to rectifie my Countrie,
You are thoſe ſcabs I will ſcratch off from the Commonwealth;
You are theſe Raſcals of the State I treat of,
And you ſhall find and feel.—

sp.speaker: 2 Lict.
sp.l: You ſhall have many,
Many notorious people.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Let 'em be people,
And take ye notorious to your ſelves. Mark me, my Lictors,
And you, the reſt of my Officials;
If I be angry, as my place will ask it,
And want fit matter to diſpoſe my Authoritie,
I'le hang a hundred of ye: I'le not ſtay longer,
Nor enquire no further into your offences:
It is ſufficient that I find no Criminals,
And therefore I muſt make ſome: if I cannot,
Suffer my ſelf; for ſo runs my Commiſſion.

sp.speaker: Suitor.
sp.l: An admirable, zealous and true Juſtice.

sp.speaker: 1 Lict.
sp.l: I cannot hold: if there be any people,
Of what degree ſoever, or what qualitie,
That would behold the wonderful works of Juſtice
In a new Officer, a man conceal'd yet,
Let him repair, and ſee, and hear, and wonder
At the moſt wiſe and gracious Getianus.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: This qualifies a little. What are theſe?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: You ſhall not mourn ſtill: times of recreation,
To allay this ſadneſs, muſt be ſought. What's here?
A ſuperſtitious flock of ſenſleſs people
Worſhipping a ſign in Office?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Lay hold on her,
And hold her faſt,
She'll ſlip thorow your fingers like an Eel elſe;
I know her tricks: hold her, I ſay, and bind her,
Or hang her firſt, and then I'le tell her wherefore.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: What have I done?

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Thou haſt done enough to undo thee;
Thou haſt preſſed to the Emperours preſence without my warrant,
I being his key and image.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: You are an image indeed,
And of the courſeſt ſtuff, and the worſt making
That e're I look'd on yet: I'le make as good an image of an Aſſe.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Beſides, thou art a woman of a lewd life.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: I am no whore, Sir, nor no common fame
Has yet proclaim'd me to the people, vitious.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Thou art to me a damnable lewd woman,
Which is as much as all the people ſwore it;
I know thou art a keeper of tame Devils:
And whereas great and grave men of my place
Can by the Laws be allow'd but one apiece,
For their own ſervices and recreations;
Thou, like a traiterous quean, keepſt twenty devils;
Twenty in ordinary.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Pray ye, Sir, be pacified,
If that be all: and if ye want a ſervant,
You ſhall have one of mine ſhall ſerve for nothing,
Faithful, and diligent, and a wiſe Devil too;
Think for what end.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Let her alone, 'tis uſeful;
We men of buſineſs muſt uſe ſpeedie ſervants:
Let me ſee your family.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Think but one, he is ready.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: A Devil for intelligence? No, no,
He will lye beyond all travellers. A State Devil?
Neither; he will undo me at mine own weapon.
For execution? he will hang me too.
I would have a handſom, pleaſant and a fine ſhe-devil,
To entertain the Ladies that come to me;
A travell'd Devil too, that ſpeaks the tongues,
And a neat carving Devil. Muſick.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Be not fearful.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: A prettie brown devil i'faith; may I not kiſs her?

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Yes, and embrace her too; ſhe is your ſervant.
Fear not; her lips are cool enough.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: She is marvellous well mounted; what's her name?

l.hi: Lucifera.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Come hither, Lucifera, and kiſs me.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: Let her ſit on your knee.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: The Chair turns: hey-boys:
Pleaſant i'faith, and a fine facetious Devil. Dance.

sp.speaker: Del.
sp.l: She would whiſper in your ear, and tell ye wonders.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Come; what's her name?

l.hi: Lucifera.

sp.speaker: Get.
sp.l: Come, Lucie, come, ſpeak thy mind. I am certain burnt to aſhes.
I have a kind of Glaſſe-houſe in my cod-piece.
Are theſe the flames of State? I am roſted over,
Over, and over-roſted. Is this Office?
The pleaſure of authoritie? I'le no more on't,
Till I can puniſh Devils too; I'le quit it.
Some other Trade now, and ſome courſe leſs dangerous,
Or certainly I'le tyle again for two pence. Exit.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Enter Charinus, Aurelia, Caſſana, Ambaſſadours, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: Never diſpute with me; you cannot have her:
Nor name the greatneſs of your King; I ſcorn him:
Your knees to me are nothing; ſhould he bow too,
It were his dutie, and my power to ſlight him.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: She is her woman; never ſue to me;
And in her power to render her, or keep her;
And ſhe, my Siſter, not to be compell'd,
Nor have her own ſnatch'd from her.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: We deſire not,
But for what ranſom ſhe ſhall pleaſe to think of;
Jewels, or Towns, or Provinces.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: No ranſom,
No, not your Kings own head, his crown upon it,
And all the low ſubjections of his people.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Fair Princes ſhould have tender thoughts.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: Is ſhe too good
To wait upon the mighty Emperours Siſter?
What Princeſs of that ſweetneſs, or that excellence,
Sprung from the proudeſt, and the mightieſt Monarchs,
But may be highly bleſt to be my ſervant?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt true, mighty Lady.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: Has my fair uſage
Made you ſo much deſpiſe me and your fortune,
That ye grow weary of my entertainments?
Henceforward, as ye are, I will command ye,
And as you were ordain'd my priſoner,
My ſlave, and one I may diſpoſe of any way,
No more my fair Companion: tell your King ſo:
And if he had more Siſters, I would have 'em,
And uſe 'em as I pleaſe. You have your anſwer.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: We muſt take ſome other way: force muſt compel it. Ex.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: Now if thou beeſt a Propheteſs, and canſt do
Things of that wonder that thy tongue delivers,
Canſt raiſe me too: I ſhall be bound to ſpeak thee:
I half believe, confirm the other to me,
And Monuments to all ſucceeding Ages,
Of thee, and of thy piety. — Now ſhe eyes me.
Now work great power of art: ſhe moves unto me:
How ſweet, how fair, and lovely her aſpects are!
Her eyes like bright Eoan flames ſhoot thorow me.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: O my fair friend, where have you been?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: What am I?
What does ſhe take me for? work ſtill, work ſtrongly.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: Where have you fled, my loves and my embraces?

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I am beyond my wits.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: Can one poor Thunder,
Whoſe cauſes are as common as his noiſes,
Make ye defer your lawful and free pleaſures?
Strike terrour to a Souldiers heart, a Monarchs?
Thorow all the fires of angry heaven, thorow tempeſts
That ſing of nothing but deſtruction,
Even underneath the bolt of Jove, then ready,
And aiming dreadfully, I would ſeek you,
And flie into your arms.

sp.speaker: Max.
sp.l: I ſhall be mighty,
And (which I never knew yet) I am goodly;
For certain, a moſt handſom man.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Fie, Siſter,
What a forgetful weakneſs is this in ye?
What a light preſence? theſe are words and offers
Due only to your husband Diocleſian;
This free behaviour only his.

sp.speaker: Aur.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange
That only empty names compel affections:
This man, ye ſee, give him what name or title,
Let it be ne're ſo poor, ne're ſo deſpis'd, Brother,
This lovely man. —

sp.speaker: Max.
