And of a ſweeter flame than all the earths odours?
Why have I ſung your praiſes, ſ • rew'd your Temples,
And crown'd your Holy Prieſts with Virgin Roſes?
Is it we hold ye powerful, to deſtroy us?
Believe, and honor ye, to ſee us ruin'd?
Theſe tears of anger thus I ſprinkle toward ye,
You that dare ſleep ſecure whilſt Virgins ſuffer,
Theſe ſtick like Comets, blaze eternally,
Till, with the wonder, they have wak'd your juſtice,
And forc't ye fear our curſes, as we yours.
My ſhame ſtill follows me, and ſtill proclaims me;
He turns away in ſcorn, I am contemned too,
A more unmanly violence than the other;
Bitten, and ſlung away? What e'r you are
Sir, you that have abus'd me, and now moſt baſely
And ſacrilegiouſly robb'd this fair Temple,
I ſling all theſe behind me, but look upon me,
But one kind loving look, be what ye will,
So from this hour you will be mine, my Husband;
And you his hand in miſchief, I ſpeak to you too,
Counſel him nobly now; you know the miſchief,
The moſt unrighteous act he has done, perſwade him,
Perſwade him like a friend, knock at his Conſcience
Till fair Repentance follow: yet be worthy of me,
And ſhew your ſelf, if ever good thought guided ye;
You have had your ſoul will, make it yet fair with marriage;
Open your ſelf and take me, wed me now: Draws his Dagger.
More fruits of villany? your Dagger? come
Ye are merciful, I thank you for your medicine:
Is that too worthy too?
Devil, thou with him,
Thou penny Bawd to his Luſt, will not that ſtir thee?
Do you work by tokens now? Be ſure I live not,
For your own ſafeties knaves. I will ſit patiently:
But as ye are true villains, the Devils own ſervants,
And thoſe he loves and truſts, make it as bloody
An Act, of ſuch true horror, Heaven would ſhake at,
'Twill ſhew the braver: goodneſs hold my hope faſt,
And in thy mercies look upon my ruines,
And then I am right: my eyes grow dead and heavy:
sp.stage: Enter ſix diſguis'd, ſinging and dancing to a horrid Muſick, and ſprinkling water on her face.
sp.l: Wrong me no more as ye are men.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: She is faſt.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Away with her. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: Now Gentlemen, the time's come now t'enjoy
That fruitful happineſs my heart has long'd for:
This day be happy call'd, and when old Time
Brings it about each year, crown'd with that ſweetneſs
It gives me now, ſee every man obſerve it,
And laying all aſide bears ſhew of buſineſs,
Give this to joy and triumph: How fits my cloaths?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent,
sp.l: Handſome, and wondrous well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Do they ſhew richly?
For to thoſe curious eyes even beauty envies,
I muſt not now appear poor, or low faſhion'd;
Methinks I am younger than I was, far younger;
And ſuch a promiſe in my bloud I feel now,
That if there may be a perpetual youth
Beſtowed on man, I am that ſoul ſhall win it:
Does my hair ſtand well, Lord how ill-favourdly
You have dreſt me to day? how baldly? why this Cloak?

sp.speaker: 2 Gen,
sp.l: Why 'tis the richeſt, Sir,

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: And here ye have put me on
A pair of Breeches look like a pair of Bagpipes.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Believe Sir, they ſhew bravely.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Why theſe Stockins?

sp.speaker: 2 Gen.
sp.l: Your Leg appears—

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Pe • h, I would have had 'em Peach-colour,
All young, and new about me: and this Scarf here
A goodly thing: you have trickt me like a Puppet.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: I'll undertake to rig forth a whole Navy,
And with leſs labor than one man in love.
They are never pleas'd.

sp.speaker: 2 Gen.
sp.l: Methinks he looks well.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Well:
As man can look, as handſome: now do I wonder
He found not fault his Noſe was put on ugly,
Or his Eyes lookt too gray, and rail at us,
They are the way wards things, theſe Lovers.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: All will be right
When once it comes to th' puſh.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I would they were at it
For our own quiet ſake.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Come, wait upon me,
And bear your ſelves like mine, my friends, and nobly. Ex.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Theanor, Crates, and Erates, bringing Merione.

sp.speaker: Erat.
sp.l: This is her Brothers door.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: There lay her down then.
Lay her along: ſhe is faſt ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: As forgetfulneſs.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Be not you ſtirr'd now, but away to your Mother,
Give all attendance, let no ſtain appear
Of fear, or doubt in your face: carry your ſelf confidently.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: But whither runs your drift now?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: When ſhe wakes,
Either what's done will ſhew a meer dream to her,
And carry no more credit: or ſay ſhe find it,
Say ſhe remember all the circumſtances,
Twenty to one the ſhapes in which they were acted,
The horrors, and the ſtill affrights we ſhew'd her,
Riſing in wilder figures to her memory
Will run her mad, and no man gueſs the reaſon:
If all theſe fail, and that ſhe riſe up perfect,
And ſo collect her ſelf, believe this, Sir,
Not knowing who it was that did this to her,
Nor having any power to gheſs; the thing done too
Being the utter undoing of her honor
If it be known, and to the worlds eye publiſh'd,
Eſpecially at this time when Fortune courts her,
She muſt and will conceal it; nay, forget it,
The woman is no Lucrece; get you gone Sir,
And as you would have more of this ſport, fear not.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I am confirm'd, farewel.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Farewel, away Sir:
Diſperſe your ſelves, and as you love his favour,
And that that crowns it, Gold, no tongues amongſt ye.
You know your charge, this way goes no ſuſpicion. Ex.

div.stage: Enter Agenor, and Leonides, with two Gent.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: You are ſtirring early, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: It was my duty
To wait upon your Grace.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: How fares your Siſter,
My beauteous Miſtriſs, what is ſhe ready yet?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: No doubt ſhe'll loſe no time Sir, young Maids in her way
Tread upon thorns, and think an hour an age
Till the Prieſt has done his part, that theirs may follow:
I ſaw her not ſince yeſterday i' th' evening:
But Sir, I am ſure ſhe is not ſlack; believe me,
Your grace will find a loving ſoul.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: A ſweet one,
And ſo much joy I carry in the thought of it,
So great a happineſs to know ſhe is mine;
Believe me noble Brother, that to expreſs it
Methinks a Tongue's a poor thing: can do nothing,
Imagination leſs: who's that that lies there?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Where Sir?

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Before the door, it looks like a woman:

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: This way I came abroad, but then there was nothing,
One of the Maids o'rwatch'd belike:

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: It may be.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: But methinks this is no fit place to ſleep in.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis ſure a woman Sir, ſhe has jewels on too:
She fears no foul play ſure.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Bring a Torch hither,
Yet t'is not perfect day: I ſhould know thoſe Garments.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: How ſound ſhe ſleeps?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I am ſorry to ſee this.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Do you know her?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And you now I am ſure Sir.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: My Miſtriſs, how comes this?

div.stage: Enter Queen, Theanor, Beliza, Euphanes, Neanthes, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: The Queen and her train?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: You know my pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: And will be moſt careful.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Be not long abſent, the ſuit you preferr'd
Is granted.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: This fellow mounts apace, and will
Towre o'r us like a Falcon.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Good morrow to ye all, why ſtand ye wondring?
Enter the houſe Sir, and bring out your Miſtriſs,
You muſt obſerve our Ceremonies: what's the matter?
What's that ye ſtand at? How Merione?
Aſleep i'th' ſtreet? belike ſome ſudden Palſie
As ſhe ſtept out laſt night upon devotion,
To take her farewel of her Virgin ſtate,
The air being ſharp and piercing, ſtruck her ſuddenly:
See if ſhe breath.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: A little.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Wake her then,
'Tis ſure a fit.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: She wakes her ſelf,
Give room to her.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: See how the ſpirits ſtruggle to recover,
And ſtrongly reinforce their ſtrength; for certain
This was no natural ſleep.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I am of your mind, Madam.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: No Son, it cannot be.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Pray Heaven no trick in't;
Good Soul ſhe little merits ſuch a miſchief.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: She is broad awake now, and her ſence cleers up,
'Twas ſure a fit; ſtand off.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: The Queen, my Love here,
And all my noble friends? Why where am I?
How am I tranc'd, and moap'd? i'th'ſtreet? Heaven bleſs.
Shame to my Sex; oth' ground too? O I remember —

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: How wild ſhe looks?

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Oh my cold heart, how ſhe trembles?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Oh I remember, I remember.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: My ſhame, my ſhame, my ſhame: Oh I remember
My never-dying ſhame.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Here has been villanie.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I fear ſo too.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: You are no Furies are ye?
No horrid ſhapes ſent to affright me?

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: No ſweet,
We are your friends: look up, I am Agenor,
O my Merione, that loves you dearly:
And come to marry ye.

sp.speaker: Leo
sp.l: Siſter, what ail ye?
Speak out your griefs, and boldly —

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Something ſticks here
Will choak ye elſe.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I hope it will.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Be free Lady,
You have your loving friends about ye.

sp.speaker: Ah.
sp.l: Dear Merione,
By the unſpotted love I ever bore ye,
By thine own goodneſs—

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Oh 'tis gone, 'tis gone Sir,
I am now I know not what: pray ye look not on me,
No name is left me, nothing to inherit
But that deteſted, baſe, and branded —

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Speak it,
And how; diſeaſes of moſt danger
Their cauſes once diſcover'd are eaſily cur'd:
My fair Merione.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I thank your love Sir;
When I was fair Merione, unſpotted,
Pure, and unblaſted in the bud you honour'd,
White as the heart of truth, then Prince Agenor,
Even then I was not worthy of your favour;
Wretch that I am, leſs worthy now of pitty:
Let no good thing come near me, virtue flie me;
You that have honeſt noble names deſpiſe me,
For I am nothing now but a main peſtilence
Able to poiſon all. Send thoſe unto me
That have forgot their names, ruin'd their fortunes,
Deſpis'd their honours; thoſe that have been Virgins
Raviſh'd and wrong'd,, and yet dare live to tell it.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Now it appears too plain.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Send thoſe ſad people
That hate the light, and curſe ſociety;
Whoſe thoughts are Graves, and from whoſe eyes continually
Their melting ſouls drop out, ſend thoſe to me;
And when their ſorrows are moſt excellent,
So full that one grief more cannot be added,
My Story like a torrent ſhall devour 'em.
Hark, it muſt out; but pray ſtand cloſe together,
And let not all the world hear.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Speak it boldly.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: And Royal Lady, think but charitably,
Your Grace has known my breeding.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Prethee ſpeak it.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Is there no ſtranger here? ſend off your ſervants,
And yet it muſt be known: I ſhake.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Sweet Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I am abus'd, baſely abus'd; do you gheſs yet?
Come cloſe, I'll tell ye plainer; I am whor'd,
Raviſh'd, and robb'd of Honour.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Oh the Devil.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: What helliſh Slave was this?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: A wretch, a wretch,
A damned wretch: do you know the Villain, Lady?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Not by gheſs?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Oh no.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: It muſt be known,

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Where was the place?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I know not neither.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: O Heaven,
Is this the happy time? my hope to this come?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Neither the man nor circumſtances?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: His tongue,
Did you not hear his tongue, no voice?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: None, none Sir:
All I know of him was his violence.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: How came ye hither, Sweet?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I know not neither.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: A cunning piece of villany.
All I remember
Is only this: Going to Veſtas Temple
To give the goddeſs my laſt Virgin prayers,
Near to that place I was ſuddainly ſurpriz'd,
By five or ſix diſguis'd, and from thence violently
To my diſhonour hal'd: that Act perform'd,
Brought back, but how, or whether, till I wak'd here.—

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: This is ſo monſtrous, the gods cannot ſuffer it;
I have not read in all the villanies
Committed by the moſt obdurate Raſcals,
An act ſo tru y impious.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Would I knew him.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: He muſt be known, the Devil cannot hide him.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: If all the Art I have, or power can do it,
He ſhall be found, and ſuch a way of juſtice
Inflicted on him: A Lady wrong'd in my Court,
And this way rob'd, and ruin'd?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Be contented Madam,
If he be above ground I will have him.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Fair virtuous Maid, take comfort yet and flouriſh,
In my love flouriſh: the ſtain was forc'd upon ye
None of your wills, nor yours; riſe, and riſe mine ſtill,
And riſe the ſame white, ſweet, fair ſoul, I lov'd ye,
Take me the ſame.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I kneel and thank ye, Sir,
And I muſt ſay ye are truly honourable:
And dare confeſs my Will, yet ſtill a Virgin;
But ſo unfit and weak a Cabinet
To keep your love and virtue in am I now,
That have been forc'd and broken, loſt my luſtre,
I mean this body, ſo corrupt a Volume
For you to ſtudy goodneſs in, and honor,
I ſhall intreat your Grace, confer that happineſs
Upon a beauty ſorrow never ſaw yet:
And when this grief ſhall kill me, as it muſt do,
Only remember yet ye had ſuch a Miſtriſs;
And if ye then dare ſhed a tear, yet honour me:
Good Gentlemen, expreſs your pities to me,
In ſeeking out this villany; and my laſt ſuit
Is to your Grace, that I may have your favour
To live a poor recluſe Nun with this Lady,
From Court and company, till Heaven ſhall hear me,
And ſend me comfort, or death end my miſery.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Take your own Will, my very heart bleeds for thee.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Farwell Merione, ſince I have not thee.
I'll wed thy goodneſs, and thy memory.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And I her fair revenge.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Away: let's follow it,
For he is ſo rank i' th' wind we cannot miſs him. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Conon, you are welcome home, ye are wondrous welcome,
Is this your firſt arrival?

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Sir, but now
I reacht the Town.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Y'are once more welcome then.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: I thank ye, noble Sir.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Pray ye do me the honor
To make my poor houſe firſt—

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Pray Sir excuſe me,
I have not ſeen mine own yet; nor made happy
Theſe longing eyes with thoſe I love there: what's this a Tavern?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo by the outſide.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Step in here then,
And ſince it offers it ſelf ſo freely to us,
A place made only for liberal entertainment,
Let's ſeek no further, but make uſe of this,
And after the Greek faſhion, to our friends
Crown a round cup or two.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Your pleaſure, Sir.
Drawers, who waits within?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: Anon, anon Sir.

sp.speaker: Vint.
sp.l: Look into the Lilly-pot: why Mark there;
You are welcome Gentlemen; heartily welcome
My noble friend.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Let's have good Wine mine Hoſt,
And a fine private room.

sp.speaker: Vint.
sp.l: Will ye be there Sir?
What is't you'll drink? I'll draw your Wine my ſelf:
Quiſſions ye knaves: why when?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: Anon, anon Sir.

sp.speaker: Vint.
sp.l: Chios, or Lebos, Greek?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Your beſt and neateſt.

sp.speaker: Vint.
sp.l: I'll draw ye that ſhall dance.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Away, be quick then. Exit. Vintner

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: How does your Brother, Sir, my noble friend
The good Euphanes? in all my courſe of travel
I met not with a Gentleman ſo furniſh'd
In gentleneſs and courteſie; believe Sir,
So many friendly Offices I receiv'd from him,
So great, and timely, and enjoy'd his company
In ſuch an open and a liberal ſweetneſs,
That when I dare forget him—

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: He's in good health, Sir,
But you will find him a much alter'd man,
Grown a great Courtier, Sir.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: He's worthy of it.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: A man drawn up, that leaves no print behind him
Of what he was: thoſe goodneſſes you ſpeak of
That have been in him, thoſe that you call freedoms,
Societies, and ſweetneſs, look for now, Sir,
You'll find no ſhadows of them left, no ſound,
The very Air he has liv'd in alter'd: now behold him,
And you ſhall ſee a thing walk by, look big upon ye,
And cry for place; I am the Queens, give room there:
If you bow low, may be he'll touch the Bonnet,
Or ſling a forced ſmile at ye for a favour.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: He is your brother, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Theſe forms put off,
Which travel, and Court Holy-water ſprinkle on him,
I dare accept, and know him: you'll think it ſtrange, Sir,
That even to me, to me his natural Brother,
And one by birth he owes a little honor too—
(But that's all one) come, give me ſome Wine, mine Hoſt,
Here's to your fair return.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I wonder at it,
But ſure he has found a nature not worth owning
In this way; elſe I know he is tender carried.
I thank ye, Sir: and now durſt I preſume
For all you tell me of theſe alterations,
And ſtops in his ſweet nature, which till I find ſo,
I have known him now ſo long, and look'd ſo through him,
You muſt give me leave to be a little faithleſs:
I ſay for all theſe, if you pleaſe to venture
I'll lay the Wine we drink, let me ſend for him
(Even I that am the pooreſt of his fellowſhip)
But by a Boy oth' houſe too, let him have buſineſs,
Let him attend the Queen, nay let his Miſtriſs
Hold him betwixt her arms, he ſhall come to me,
And ſhall drink with me too, love me, and heartily,
Like a true honeſt man bid me welcome home.
I am confident.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: You will looſe.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: You'l ſtand to th'wager?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Go Boy, and tell Euphanes.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: He's now gone up the ſtreet Sir,
With a great train of Gallants.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: What think you now Sir?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Go, and overtake him,
Commend my love unto him: my name is Conon,
Tell him I am new arriv'd, and where I am,
And would requeſt to ſee him preſently:
Ye ſee I uſe old dudgen phraſe to draw him.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I'll hang and quarter when you draw him hither.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Away Boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I am gone Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Here's to you now,
And you ſhall find his travel has not ſtopt him
As you ſuppoſe, nor alter'd any freedome,
But made him far more clear and excellent;
It draws the groſneſs off the underſtanding,
And renders active and induſtrious ſpirits:
He that knows moſt mens manners, muſt of neceſſity
Beſt know his own, and mend thoſe by example:
'Tis a dull thing to travell like a Mill-horſe,
Still in the place he was born in, lam'd and blinded;
Living at home is like it: pure and ſtrong ſpirits
That like the fire ſtill covet to fly upward,
And to give fire as well as take it; cas'd up, and mewd here
I mean at home, like luſty metled Horſes,
Only ty'd up in Stables, to pleaſe their Maſters,
Beat out their fiery lives in their own Litters,
Why do not you travel Sir?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I have no belief in't
I ſee ſo many ſtrange things, half unhatcht, to
Return, thoſe that went out men, and good men,
They look like potch'd Eggs with the ſouls ſuckt out
Empty and full of wind: all their affections
Are bak'd in Rye cruſt, to hold carriage
From this good Town to th'other: and when they are open'd,
They are ſo ill cooked and mouldy—

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Ye are pleaſant.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I'll ſhew ye a pack of theſe: I have 'em for ye,
That have been long in travel too.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Pleaſe you Sir.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: You know the Merchants walk, Boy?

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: Very well.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: And you remember thoſe Gentlemen were here
The other day with me?

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Then go thither,
For there I am ſure they are, pray 'em come hither,
(And uſe my name) I would be glad to ſee 'em.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Your Brother's coming in Sir.

sp.speaker: Vint.
sp.l: Odds my paſſion,
Out with the Plate ye knaves: bring the new Quiſhions,
And waſh thoſe Glaſſes I ſet by for high days,
Perfume the rooms along, why Sirrah.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Here Sir.

sp.speaker: Vint.
sp.l: Bid my Wife make her ſelf ready handſomly,
And put on her beſt Apron: it may be
The noble Gentleman will look upon her.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Where is he Boy?

sp.speaker: Vint.
sp.l: Your worſhip's heartily welcome,
It joyes my very heart to ſee ye here Sir.
The Gentleman that ſent for your honor—

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: O good mine Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Vint.
sp.l: To my poor homely houſe, and't like your honor.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: I thank thine honor good mine Hoſt, where is he?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: What think ye now? my beſt Euphanes.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Conon, welcome my friend, my noble friend how is it?
Are you in ſafety come, in health?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: All health, all ſafety,
Riches, and all that makes content and happineſs
Now I am here I have: how have you far'd Sir?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Well, I thank Heaven, and never nearer friend
To catch at great occaſion.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Indeed I joy in't.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Nor am I for my ſelf born in theſe fortunes.
In truth I love my friends.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: You were noble ever.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I thought you had not known me. Euph. ſalutes Cra.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Yes, ye are my Brother,
My elder Brother too, would your affections
Were able but to ask that love I owe to ye,
And as I give, preſerve it: here friend Conon,
To your fair welcome home.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Dear Sir, I thank ye,
Fill it toth'brim, Boy: Crates.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I'll pledge you,
But for that glorious Comet lately fired.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Fie, fie Sir, fie.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Nay, let him take his freedomes,
He ſtirs not me I vow to ye; much leſs ſtains me.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Sir, I cannot talk with that neat travelling tongue.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: As I live, he has the worſt belief in men abroad.
I am glad I am come home.

sp.speaker: 2 Boy.
sp.l: Here are the Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: O let 'em enter: now you that truſt in travel,
And make ſharp Beards, and little Breeches Deities,
You that inhaunce the daily price of Tooth-picks,
And hold there is no homebred happineſs,
Behold a model of your minds and actions.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Though this be envious, yet done ith' way of mirth,
I am content to thank ye for't.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: 'Tis well yet.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Let the Maske enter.

div.stage: Enter Onos, his Unkle and Tutor.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: A pretty Taverne 'faith, of a fine ſtructure.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Bear your ſelf like a Gentleman, here's ſix pence,
And be ſure you break no Glaſſes.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Hark ye Pupill,
Go as I taught you, hang more upon your hams,
And put your knees out bent: there, yet a little:
Now I beſeech ye, be not ſo improvident
To forget your travelling pace, 'tis a main poſture,
And to all unayr'd Gentlemen will betray you:
Play with your Piſa Beard: why, where's your bruſh Pupill?
He muſt have a Bruſh Sir.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: More charge yet?

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Here, take mine,
Theſe elements of travel he muſt not want Sir.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Ma'foy, he has had ſome nineteen pence in elements,
What would you more?

l.hi: Durus mehercle pater.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: What Monſieur Onos, the very pump of travell?
Sir, as I live you have done me the greateſt kindnes,
O my fair Sir, Lampree, the careful Unkle
To this young hopeful iſſue; Monſieur Tutor too,
The father to his mind; Gome, come, let's hug Boyes,
Why what a bunch of travel do I embrace now,
Methinks I put a Girdle about Europe;
How has the boy profited?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: He has enough Sir,
If his too fiery mettle do not mar it.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Is he not thrifty yet?

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: That's all his fault,
Too bounteous minded being under age too,
A great conſumer of his ſtock in Pippins,
Had ever a hot ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Come hither Onos,
Will you love me for this fine Apple?

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: We.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: And will ye be rul'd by me ſometimes?

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: 'Faith I will.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: That's a good boy.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Pray give not the child ſo much fruit,
He's of a raw Complexion

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: You Monſieur hard ege,
Do you remember me? Do you remember
When you and your Conſort travell'd through Hungary?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: He's in that circuit ſtill.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Do you remember
The cantell of immortal Cheeſe ye carried with ye,
The half cold Gabbedge in a leather Sachell,
And thoſe invincible Eggs that would lye in your bowells
A fortnight together, and then turn to bedſtaves;
Your ſowre milk that would choak an Iriſh man,
And bread was bak'd in Caeſars time for the Army?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Providence, providence.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: The ſoul of travel.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Can the boy ſpeak yet?

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Yes, and as fine a Gentleman,
I thank my able knowledge, he has arriv'd at,
Only a little ſparing of his Language,
Which every man of obſervation —

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: And of as many tongues.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Pray be content Sir,
You know you are for the bodily part, the Purſe,
I for the magazin, the mind.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Come hither ſpringall.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: That in the Almain Tongue ſignifies a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: What think you of the forms of Italy or Spain?

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: I love mine own Countrey Pippin.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Nobly anſwer'd,
Born for his Countrey firſt.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: A great Philoſopher:
What Horſes do you prefer?

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: The white horſe Sir,
There where I lye; honeſt and a juſt beaſt,

sp.speaker: Tut
sp.l: O caput lepidum: a Child to ſay this,
Are theſe figures for the mouths of Infants?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Onos, what wenches?
Come, tell me true.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: I cannot ſpeak without book.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: When ſhall we have one, ha?

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Steal me from mine Unckle,
For look you, I am broke out horribly
For want of fleſhly Phyſick: they ſay I am too young,
And that 'twill ſpoyle my growth but could you help me?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Meet me to morrow man, no more.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: You think now
Ye have open'd ſuch a ſhame to me of travell,
By ſhewing theſe thin Cubs: ye have honour'd us
Againſt your will, proclaim'd us excellent:
Three Frails of Sprats carried from Mart; to Mart,
Are as much Meat as theſe, to more uſe travell'd;
A bunch of bloted fools: me thinks your judgment
Should look abroad ſometimes without your envy.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Such are moſt of you: ſo I take my leave,
And when you find your Womens favor fail,
'Tis ten to one you'l know your ſelf, and ſeek me
Upon a better Muſter of your manners.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: This is not handſome Sir.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Pray take your pleaſure,
You wound the wind as much —

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Come you with me,
I have buſineſs for you preſently: there's for your Wine,
I muſt confeſs I loſt it.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Shall I ſteal to ye
And ſhall we ſee the Wench?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: A dainty one.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: And have a diſh of Pippins?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: What a peck man.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Will you wait Sir.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Pray let's meet oftner Gentlemen,
I would not loſe ye.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: O ſweet Sir.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Do you think I would,
Such noted men as you?

sp.speaker: Onos, Ʋnc. Tut.
sp.l: We are your Servants. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: That thing they would keep in everlaſting nonage,
My brother for his own ends has thruſt on
Upon my Miſtriſs, 'tis true, he ſhall be rich
If ever he can get that Rogue his Unkle
To let him be of years to come to inherit it,
Now what the main drift is —

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Say ye ſo? no more words,
I'll keep him company till he be of years,
Though it be a hundred years, but I'll diſcover it;
And ten to one I'll croſs it too.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: You are honeſt,
And I ſhall ſtudy ſtill your love: farewell Sir,
For theſe few hours I muſt deſire your pardon,
I have buſineſs of importance: once a day
At leaſt I hope you'll ſee me: I muſt ſee you elſe:
So, once more ye are welcome.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: All my thanks Sir,
And when I leave to love you, life go from me. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: WHy Sir, the Kingdomes his, and no man now
Can come to Corinth, or from Corinth go
Without his Licence; he puts up the tithes
Of every office through Achaia;
From Courtier to the Carter hold of him:
Our Lands, our Liberties, nay very Lives
Are ſhut up in his Cloſet, and let looſe
But at his pleaſure; Books, and all diſcourſe
Have now no Patron, nor direction,
But glorified Euphanes: our Cups are guilty
That quench our thirſts, if not unto his health;
Oh, I could eat my heart, and fling away
My very Soul for anguiſh: gods, nor men
Should tollerate ſuch diſproportion.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: And yet is he belov'd: whether't be virtue,
Or ſeeming virtue which he makes the cloak
To his ambition.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Be it which it will:
Your Highneſs is too tame, your eyes too film'd
To ſee this, and ſit ſtill: the Lion ſhould not
Tremble to hear the bellowing of the Bull;
Nature excuſe me, though he be my Brother,
You are my Countries Father, therefore mine:
One parallel line of Love I bend on him,
All lines of love and duty meet in you
As in their Center: therefore hear, and weigh
What I ſhall ſpeak: You know the Queen your Mother
Did, from a private ſtate your Father raiſe,
So all your Royalty you hold from her;
She is older than ſhe was, therefore more doating,
And what know we but blindneſs of her love
(That hath from underneath the foot of fortune
Set even Euphanes foot, on fortunes head)
Will take him by the hand, and cry, Leap now
Into my bed; 'tis but a trick of age;
Nothing impoſſible.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What do you infer on this?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Your pardon Sir:
With reverence to the Queen; yet why ſhould I
Fear to ſpeak plain what pointeth to your good?
A good old Widow is a hungry thing,
(I ſpeak of other Widows, not of Queens.)

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Speak to thy purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I approach it: Sir,
Should young Euphanes claſpe the Kingdome thus,
And pleaſe the good old Lady ſome one night;
What might not ſhe be wrought to put on you,
Quite to ſupplant your birth? neither is ſhe
Paſt children as I take it.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Crates, Thou ſhak'ſt me;
Thou, that doſt hate thy Brother for my love,
In my love find one; henceforth be my brother:
This Gyant I will fell beneath the earth;
I will ſhine out, and melt his artful wings:
Euphanes, from my mothers ſea of favors
Spreads like a River, and runs calmly on,
Secure yet from my ſtormes; like a young pine
He grows up planted under a fair Oake,
Whoſe ſtrong large branches yet do's ſhelter him,
And every Traveller admires his beauty;
But like a wind, I'l work into his crancks,
Trouble his ſtream, and drown all Veſſels that
Ride on his Greatneſs: under my Mothers arms,
Like to a ſtealing tempeſt will I ſearch,
And rend his root from her protection.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I, now Theanor ſpeaks like Prince Theanor.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: But how ſhall we provoke him to our ſnares?
He has a temper malice cannot move
To exceed the bounds of judgement; he is ſo wiſe,
That we can pick no cauſe to affront him.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: No?
What better than his croſſing your intent?
The ſuit I had to ye? Conons forfeit ſtate
(Before he travel'd) for a Riot he
Hath from your Mother got reſtored to him:

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Durſt he? what is this Conon?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: One that hath,
As people ſay, in foreign Countries pleaſur'd him.
sp.stage: Enter Onos, Ʋncle, Tutor, Neanthes, Soſicles, Eraton.
sp.l: But now no more;
They have brought the Travellors I told you of,
That's the ſweet youth, that is my Brothers Rivall,
That curles his head, for he has little hair,
And paints his vizor, for it is no face,
That ſo deſires to follow you, my Lord:
Shew 'em ſome countenance, and it will beget
Our ſport at leaſt.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What villanous Crab-tree legs he makes?
His ſhins are full of true-love knots.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: His legs were ever villanous, ſince I knew him.

sp.speaker: Era.
sp.l: Faith his Uncles ſhanks are ſomewhat the better.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: But is't poſſible he ſhould believe he is not of age?
He is 50. man, in's Jubile I warrant: s'light, he
Looks older then a groat, the very ſtamp on's face is why
Worne out with handling.

sp.speaker: Soſ.
sp.l: Why I tell you all men believe it when they hear him ſpeak,
He utters ſuch ſingle matter in ſo infantly a voice.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: He looks as like a fellow that I have ſeen accommodate Gentlemen with Tobacco in our Theaters.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Moſt illuſtrious Prince.

sp.speaker: Era.
sp.l: A pox on him, he is guelt, how he trebles?

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: I am a Gentleman a both ſides.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: He means (ſot'pleaſe your highneſs) both by Father and Mother.

sp.speaker: Soſ.
sp.l: Thou a Gentleman? thou an Aſs.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: He is nere the farther from being a Gent. I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: May it pleaſe your Grace, I am another,

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: He is another Aſs he ſays, I believe him.

sp.speaker: Ʋncle.
sp.l: We be three, Heroicall Prince.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: Nay then we muſt have the Picture of 'em, and the Word Nos ſumus.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: That have travell'd all parts of the Globe together.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: For my part, I have ſeen the viciſſitude of fortune before.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Peace Ʋncle, for though you ſpeak a little better than I

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: 'Tis a very little, in truth.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Yet we muſt both give place, as they ſay to the beſt Speaker
The Tutor.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Yet ſince it hath pleaſed your radience to decline ſo low, as on us,
Poor and unworthy dunghils—

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: What a ſtinking knaves this?

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Our Peregrination was nere ſo facilitated, as ſince we enter'd the line of your gracious favor, under whoſe beamy aſpect, and by which infallible Mathematical compaſs, may we but hereafter preſume to ſail, our induſtries have reach't their deſir'd termination and period; and we ſhall voluntarily ſacrifice our lives to your reſplendent eyes, both the Altars and fires of our devoted offerings.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Oh divine Tutor!

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Can you hold Sir?

sp.speaker: Era
sp.l: He has ſpoken this very ſpeech to ſome Whore in Corinth.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: A plague on him for a fuſtian Dictionary; on my conſcience this is the Ʋliſſ • an Traveller that ſent home his Image riding upon Elephants to the great Mogoll.

sp.speaker: Soſ.
sp.l: The ſame: his wit is ſo huge, nought but an Elephant could carry him.

sp.speaker: Era.
sp.l: So heavy you mean.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: Theſe three, are ev'n the fin'ſt one fool tripartite, that was ere diſcovered.

sp.speaker: Soſ.
sp.l: Or a treatiſe of famine divided into three branches.

sp.speaker: Era.
sp.l: The Prince ſpeaks.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I thank ye for your loves; but as I told you,
I have ſo little means, to do for thoſe
Few followers I have already, that
I would have none ſhiprack themſelves, and fortune,
Upon my barren ſhelf: Sue to Euphanes.
For he is Prince, and Queen, I would have no man
Curſe me in his old age.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Alaſs Sir, they deſire to follow you
But a far off, the farther off the better.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: I Sir, and't be ſeven mile off, ſo we may but follow you, only to countenance us in the confronts and affronts, which (according to your Highneſs will) we mean on all occaſions to put upon the Lord Euphanes.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: He ſhall not want gibing nor jeering, I warrant him, if he do, I'l forſwear wit.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: It has forſworn thee, I'l ſwear, it is the ancient enemy to thy houſe.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Well, be it ſo; I here receive ye; for my followers a great way off.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: Seven miles, my Lord, no further.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: By what time, Sir, (by this meaſure) may I come to follow him in his Chamber?

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: Why when his Chamber, Sir, is ſeven miles long.

div.stage: Enter Euphanes, Conon, Page, Gent. Attendants.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Make way there for my Lord Euphanes.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Look Sir, Jove appears,
The Peacock of our State, that ſpreads a train
Brighter than Iris bluſhes after rain.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: You need not thank me Conon, in your love
You Antidated what I can do for you,
And I, in gratitude, was bound to this,
And am to much more: and what ere he be
Can with unthankfulneſs aſſoile me, let him
Dig out mine eyes, and ſing my name in verſe,
In Ballad verſe, at every drinking houſe,
And no man be ſo charitable to lend me
A Dogg to guide my ſteps.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: Haile to Euphanes.

sp.speaker: Soſ.
sp.l: Mighty Euphanes.

sp.speaker: Era.
sp.l: The great Prince Euphanes.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Key of the Court, and Jewell of the Queen.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Sol in our Firmament.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Pearl in the States eye.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: Being a black man.

sp.speaker: Era.
sp.l: Miſtreſs of the Land.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: Our humble, humble poor Petitions are,
That we may hold our places.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: May we?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Yes; be you malicious knaves ſtill; and you fools.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: This is the Princes, and your brothers ſpight.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: I know't, but will not know it.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Yonder they are.
Who's fine child's this?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Unckle, le'be,
Let him alone, he is a mighty Prince.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: I ask your Highneſs pardon: I proteſt
By Jupiter I ſaw you not.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Humh, it may be ſo,
You have rais'd ſuch mountaines 'twixt your eyes and me,
That I am hidden quite: what do ye mean Sir?
You much forget your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: I ſhould much more,
Not to remember my due duty to your Grace;
I know not wherein I have ſo tranſgreſs'd
My ſervice to your Highneſs, to deſerve
This rigour and contempt, not from you only
But from your followers, with the beſt of whom
I was an equal in my loweſt ebbe:
Beſeech you Sir, reſpect me as a Gentleman,
I will be never more in heart to you:
Five fair Deſcents I can derive my ſelf,
From Fathers worthy both in Arts and Armes.
I know your goodneſs companies your greatneſs
But that you are perverted: Royal Sir,
I am your humbleſt ſubject, uſe your pleaſure,
But do not give protection to the wrongs
Of theſe ſubordinate Slaves, whom I could cruſh
By that great deſtined favor, which my Miſtris
And your majeſtick Mother deignes to me,
But in reſpect of you: I know lean envy
Waites ever on the ſteps of virtue advanc'd:
But why your Mothers grace gets me diſgrace,
Or renders me a ſlave to bear theſe wrongs
I do not know.
Oh Mediocrity,
Thou prizeleſs jewel, only mean men have
But cannot value; like the precious Jem,
Found in the Mukhill by the ignorant Cock.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Your creamy words, but cozen: how durſt you
Intercept me ſo lately to my Mother?
And what I meant your Brother, you obtain'd
Unto the forfeitoe again.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Your anſwer to that my Lord, my Brother.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: May I periſh
• ere I heard you intended ſuch a ſuit,
Though 'twould have ſtuck an ignominious brand
Upon your Highneſs, to have given your ſervant
A Gentlemans whole ſtate of worth and quality,
Confiſcate only for a youthful brawle.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Your rudiments are too ſawcy: teach your Page.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I, ſo are all things but your flatterers.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Hold you your prating.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: You know where you are, you fleeten face.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Yet Sir, to appeaſe and ſatiſfie your anger.
Take what you pleaſe from me, and give it him
In lieu of this: you ſhall not take it neither,
I freely will impart it, half my ſtate,
Which Brother if you pleaſe—

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Ile ſtarve in Chains firſt,
Eat my own armes.

sp.speaker: Euph
sp.l: Oh that you ſaw your ſelf:
You ne'r made me ſuch offer in my poorneſs,
And 'cauſe (to do you eaſe) I ſought not to you.
You thus maligne me; yet your nature muſt not
Corrupt mine, nor your rude examples lead me:
If mine can mend you, I ſhall joy; you know
I fear you not: you have ſeen me proved a man
In every way of fortune, 'tis my comfort
I know no more ſuch Brothers in the World
As Crates is.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Nor I ſuch as Euphanes:
The temper of an Angel reigns in thee.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Your Royal Mother Sir, (I had forgot)
Entreats your preſence.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: You have done her errand,
I may do yours. Exit.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Let it be truth my Lord.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Crates, Ile queſtion you for this.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Piſh, your worſt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Away you hounds after your ſcent.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Come, we'll ſcorn to walk to'm: now they are gone,
We'l away too. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Why bear you this my Lord?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: To ſhew the paſſive fortitude the beſt;
Vertue's a ſolid Rock, whereat being aym'd
The keeneſt darts of envy, yet unhurt
Her Marble Heroes ſtand, built of ſuch Baſes,
Whilſt they recoyle, and wound the Shooters faces.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: My Lord, the Queen.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Gentle Euphanes, how,
How do'ſt thou honeſt Lord? oh how I joy
To ſee what I have made, like a choyce Workman,
That having fram'd a Maſter-piece, doth reap
An univerſal commendation.
Princes are Gods in this. I'll build thee yet
(The good foundation ſo pleaſes me)
A ſtory or two higher; let dogs bark,
They are fools that hold them dignified by blood,
They ſhould be only made great that are good.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Oraculous Madam.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Sirrah, I was thinking
If I ſhould marry thee, what merry tales
Our neighbour Iſlands would make of us;
But let that paſs, you have a Miſtriſs
That would forbid our Banes: troth I have wiſh'd
A thouſand times that I had been a man,
Than I might ſit a day with thee alone,
And talk,
But as I am I muſt not; there's no skill
In being good, but in not being thought ill.
Sirrah, who's that?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: So't pleaſe your Majeſty
Conon, the friend I ſu'd for.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: 'Tis diſpatch'd.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Gracious Madam.
I owe the gods and you my life.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: I thank you,
I thank you heartily; and I do think you
A very honeſt man, he ſays you are:
But now I'll chide thee; what's the cauſe my Son,
For my eye's every where, and I have heard,
So inſolently do's thee Contumelies
Paſt ſufferance (I am told) yet you complain not,
As if my juſtice were ſo partial
As not to right the meaneſt: credit me,
I'll call him to a ſtrict account, and fright,
By his example, all that dare curb me
In any thing that's juſt: I ſent you for him.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Humbly he did return, he would wait on you:
But let me implore your Majeſty, not to give
His Highneſs any check, for worthleſs me;
They are Court canckers, and not Counſellors
That thus inform you: they do but hate the Prince,
And would ſubvert me: I ſhould curſe my fortune
Even at the higheſt, to be made the ginne
To unſcrew a Mothers love unto her Son:
Better had my pale flame in humble ſhades
Been ſpent unſeen, than to be raiſed thus high,
Now to be thought a meteor to the State,
Portending ruine and contagion:
Beſeech you then reſt ſatisfi'd, the Prince
Is a moſt noble natur'd Gentleman,
And never did to me but what I took
As favors from him, my blown billowes muſt not
Strive 'gainſt my ſhore, that ſhould confine me, nor
Juſtle with Rocks to break themſelves to pieces.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Well, thou'rt the compoſition of a god:
My Lion, Lamb, my Eaglet, and my Dove,
Whoſe ſoul runs clearer then Dianas Fount,
Nature pick'd ſeveral flowers from her choyce banks
And bound them up in thee, ſending thee forth
A Poſie for the boſome of a Queen.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: The Prince attends you.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Farewell my good Lord.
My honeſt man; ſtay, haſt no other ſuit?
I prethee tell me; Sirrah, thine eye ſpeaks
As if thou hadſt: out with it modeſt fool.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: With favor Madam, I would crave your leave
To Marry, where I am bound in gratitude,
The immediate means ſhe was to all my Being:
Nor do I think your wiſdom ſacred Queen
Fetters in favors, taking from me ſo
The liberty that meaneſt men enjoy.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: To marry? you are a fool: thou'ſt anger'd me:
Leave me, I'll think on't: Exit Euph. and Conon.
Only to try thee this, for though I love thee,
I can ſubdue my ſelf: but ſhe that can
Enjoy thee, doth enjoy more than a man.
Nay riſe without a bleſſing, or kneel ſtill:
What's Sir the reaſon you oppoſe me thus,
And ſeek to darken what I would have ſhine?
Eclipſe a fire much brighter than thy ſelf,
Making your Mother not a competent Judge
Of her own actions?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Gracious Madam, I
I have done no more than what in royalty
(And to preſerve your fame) was fit to do:
Heard you the peoples talk of you, and him
You favor ſo, his greatneſs, and your love,
The pitty given to me, you would excuſe me,
They prate as if he did diſhonor you:
And what know I, but his own laviſh tongue
Has uttered ſome ſuch ſpeeches; he is call'd
The King of Corinth.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: They are traitors all:
I wear a Chriſtal caſement 'fore my heart,
Through which each honeſt eye may look in to't:
Let it be proſpect unto all the world,
I care not this.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: This muſt not be my way;
Your pardon gracious Madam: theſe incitements
Made me not ſhew ſo clear a countenance
Upon the Lord Euphanes as I would:
Which ſince your Majeſty affects ſo grievouſly
I'll clear the black cloud of it, and henceforth
Vow on this knee all love and grace to him.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Riſe with my bleſſing, and to prove this true,
Bear him from me this Cabinet of Jewels
In your own perſon, tell him, for his marrying
He may diſpoſe him how, and when he pleaſe. Exit Quee.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I ſhall diſcharge my duty and your will. Crates?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I have heard all my Lord, how luckely
Fate pops her very ſpindle in our hands:
This Marriage with Beliza you ſhall croſs,
Then have I one attempt for Lamprias more
Upon this Phaeton: where's Merione's Ring,
That in the Rape you took from her?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: 'Tis here.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: In and affect our purpoſe: you my Lord
Shall diſobey your Mothers charge, and ſend
This Cabinet by ſome ſervant of her own,
That what ſucceeds may have no reference
Unto your Highneſs.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: On, my engine on.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Now, if we be not ſtruck by Heavens own hand,
We'l ruine him, and on his ruines ſtand. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Agenor, Leonidas, Merione, Beliza. A ſad Song.

body.l: WEep no more, nor ſigh nor groan
Sorrow calls no time that's gone
Ʋiolets pluck'd, the ſweeteſt raine
Makes not freſh nor grow again;
Trim thy locks, look cheerefully
Fates hidd', ends, eyes cannot ſee.
Joyes as winged dreams fly faſt
Why ſhould ſadneſs longer laſt.
Grief is but a wound to woe
Gent'leſt fair, mourne, mourne no moe.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Theſe heavy Ayres feed ſorrow in her Lady,
And nouriſh it too ſtrongly; like a Mother
That ſpoiles her Child with giving on't the will.

body.l: COurt Ladies laugh, and wonder. Here is one
That weeps becauſe her Maiden head is gone
Whilſt you do never frett, nor chafe, nor cry
But when too long it keeps you company,
Too well you know, Maids are like Towns on fire
Waſting themſelves, if no man quench deſire.
Weep then no more fool: a new Maidenhead
Thou ſuffer'ſt loſs of, in each chaſt tear ſhed.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Some lighter note.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: How like a hill of Snow ſhe ſits, and melts
Before the unchaſt fire of others luſt?
What heart can ſee her paſſion and not break?

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Take comfort gentle Madam; you know well
Even actual ſins committed without will,
Are neither ſins nor ſhame, much more compell'd;
Your honor's no whit leſs, your Chaſtity
No whit impair'd, for fair Merione
Is more a Virgin yet then all her Sex:
Alaſs, 'tis done; why burne theſe Tapers now?
Wicked and frantick Creatures joy in night.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Imagine faire Merione had dream'd
She had been raviſh'd, would ſhe ſit thus then
Excruciate?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Fye, fye, how fond is this?
What reaſon for this ſurfeit of remorſe?
How many that have done ill and proceed,
Women that take degrees in wantonneſs,
Commence, and riſe in rudiments of Luſt,
That feel no ſcruple of this tenderneſs?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Piſh.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Nor are you matchleſs in miſhap, even I
Do bear an equal part of miſery;
That love, belov'd, a man the Crown of men,
Whom I have friended, and how raiſed 'tis better
That all do know and ſpeak it than my ſelf:
When he ſail'd low I might have made him mine,
Now at his full gale, it is queſtionable
If ever I o're-take him.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Wherefore ſits
My Phebe ſhawdowed in a ſable cloud?
Thoſe pearly drops which thou let's fall like beades,
Numbring on them thy veſtal Oriſons
Alas are ſpent in vain: I love thee ſtill,
In mid'ſt of all theſe ſhowres thou ſweetlier ſent'ſt,
Like a green Meadow on an April day,
In which the Sun and weſt-wind play together,
Striving to catch and drink the balmy drops.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The Lord Euphanes Madam. Exit Mer.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Poor Merione,
She loathes the light, and men. Exit.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: The virtuous gods preſerve my Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: O my moſt honor'd Lord, thoſe times are chang'd,

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Let times and men change, could Heaven change,
Should never change, to be devoted ever Euphanes
To fair Beliza, ſhould my load of honors,
Or any Grace which you were Author of
Detract mine honor, and diminiſh Grace?
The gods forbid: you here behold your ſervant,
Your Creature, gentle Lady, whoſe ſound ſleeps
You purchas'd for him: whoſe food you paid for,
Whoſe garments were your charge, whoſe firſt preferment
You founded: then, what ſince the gracious Queen
Hath, or can rear, is upon your free Land,
And you are Miſtris of.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Mock me not gentle Lord,
You ſhine now in too high a ſphear for me,
We are Plannets now disjoyn'd for ever: yet
Poor ſuperſtitious innocent that I am,
Give leave that I may lift my hands, and love
Not in Idolatry, but perfect zeal:
For credit me, I repent nothing I have done,
But were it to begin would do the ſame.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: There are two Seas in Corinth, and two Queens,
And but there, not two ſuch in the ſpacious Univerſe;
I came to tender you the man you have made,
And like a thankful ſtream to retribute
All you my Ocean have enrich'd me with.
You told me once you'ld marry me.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Another mock? you were wont to play fair play,
You ſcorn poor helps; he that is ſure to win,
May ſlight mean hearts, whoſe hand commands the Queen.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Let me be held the Knave through all the Stock
When I do ſlight my Miſtris; you know well
The gracious inclination of the Queen,
Who ſent me leave this morning to proceed
To marry as I ſaw convenience,
And a great gift of Jewels: Three days hence
The general ſacrifice is done to Veſta,
And can you by then be accommodated
Your ſervant ſhall wait on you to the Temple.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Till now
I never felt a real joy indeed.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Here then I ſeal my duty, here my love,
Till which vouchſafe to wear this Ring, dear Miſtris;
'Twas the Queens Token, and ſhall celebrate
Our Nuptialls.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Honour ſtill raiſe, and preſerve
My honor'd Lord, as he preſerves all honor. Exit Euph.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Why ſhift you places thus Merione,
And will not lend a word? Could'ſt thou ſo ſoon
Leave ſorrow as the place, how bleſt were I,
But 'twill not be; grief is an impudent gueſt,
A follower every where, a hanger on,
That words nor blows can drive away.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Dear Siſter.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Who can be ſad? out with theſe Tragick Lights,
And let day repoſſeſs her natural howres:
Tear down theſe blacks, caſt ope' the Caſements wide,
That we may jocondly behold the Sun.
I did partake with ſad Merione
In all her mourning: let her now rejoyce
With glad Beliza, for Euphanes is
As full of love, full of humility
As when he wanted.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Oh — that.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Help, ſhe faints:
Her grief has broke her heart.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: No — that — that.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Miſtris, what point you at?
Her lamps are out, yet ſtill ſhe extends her hand
As if ſhe ſaw ſomething antipathous
Unto her virtuous life.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Still, ſtill ſhe points,
And her lips move, but no articulate ſound
Breathes from 'em: Siſter, ſpeak, what moves you thus?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Her ſpirits return.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Oh, hide that fatal Ring,
Where had it you Beliza?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: What hid fate
Depends on it? Euphanes gave it me
As holy pledge of future Mariage.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Then is Euphanes the foul Raviſher?
Let me ſpeak this and dye. That diſmal night
Which ſeal'd my ſhame upon me, was that Ring,
The partner of my rob'd virginity.

l.hi: Euphanes?

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Strange.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Impoſſible to have redreſs on him,
Chief ſervant to the Queen —ha! I have read
Somewhere I am ſure, of ſuch an injury
Done to a Lady: and how ſhe durſt dye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Oh follow her Beliza.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: To aſſure her,
The unlikelihood of this.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Love hides all ſins.
What's to be done Leonidas? Exit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why this:
Amazement takes up all my faculties;
The plagues of gods and men will muſter all
To avenge this tyranny. Oh frontleſs man,
To dare do ill, and hope to bear it thus:
Firſt let's implore, then cure.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Who, who can truſt
The gentle looks and words of two-fac'd man?
Like Corinths double torrent, you and I
Will ruſh upon the Land; nor ſhall the Queen
Defend this Villain in his villany:
Luſts violent flames can never be withſtood
Nor quench'd, but with as violent ſtreams of blood.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Crates, Ʋncle, Tutor, and Onos

sp.speaker: Ono.
sp.l: THinks he to carry her and live.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo,
And ſhe will carry him the ſtory ſays.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Well, hum—
Have I for this thou fair but falſeſt fair
Stretch'd this ſame ſimple leg over the Sea?
What though my baſhfulneſs, and tender years,
Durſt ne're reveal my affection to thy teeth?
Deep love ne're tatles, and (ſay they) loves bit
The deeper dip'd, the ſweeter ſtill is it.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: Oh, ſee the power of Love: he ſpeaks in ryme.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Oh, love would make a dog howle in ryme:
Of all the Lovers yet I have heard or read
This is the ſtrangeſt: but his Guardian,
And you his Tutor ſhould inform him better,
Thinks he, that love is anſwer'd by inſtinct?

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: He ſhould make means,
For certain Sir, his baſhfulneſs undo's him,
For from his Cradle h'had a ſhameful face.
Thus walks he night and day, eats not a bit,
Nor ſleeps one jot, but's grown ſo humerous;
Drinks Ale, and takes Tobacco as you ſee;
Wear's a Steeletto at his Codpeece cloſe,
Stabs on the leaſt occaſion: ſtroaks his beard,
Which now he puts i'th poſture of a T.
The Roman T. your T. beard is the faſhion,
And twifold doth expreſs the enamour'd Courtier,
As full as your fork-carving Travellor.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Oh, black clouds of diſcontent invellop me,
Garters fly off: go Hatband, bind the browes
Of ſome dull Citizen that fears to ake:
And Leg appear now in ſimplicity
Without the trapings of a Courtier:
Burſt Bottons, burſt, your Bachelor is worm'd.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: A worm-eaten Batchelor th'rt indeed.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: And Devil melancholly poſſeſſes me now.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Croſs him not in this fit I adviſe you Sir.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Dye crimſon Roſe, that didſt adorn theſe cheeks,
For ytch of love is now broke forth on me.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Poor Boy, 'tis true: his wriſts and hands are ſcabby.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Burn eyes out in your ſockets, ſink and ſtink:
Teeth I will pick ye to the very bones,
Hang hair like Hemp, or like the Iſling Curs,
For never Powder, nor the Criſping-iron
Shall touch theſe dangling locks — oh — Ruby lips,
Love hath to you been like Wine-vinegar,
Now you look wan and pale, lips, ghoſts ye are,
And my diſgrace ſharper than Muſtard-ſeed.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: How like a Chaundler he do's vent his paſſions,

l.hi: Riſum teneatis?

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Well ſung the Poet,
Love is a golden hubo, full of Dreams:
That ripen'd breaks, and fills us with extreams.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: A gold buble, pupill, Oh groſs ſo • aeciſme
To chaſter eares that underſtand the Latine.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: I will not be corrected now:
I am in love, revenge is now the Cud
That I do chaw: I'll challenge him.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I marry Sir.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Your honor bids you Nephew, on, and proſper.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: But none will bear it from me, times are dangerous.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Carry it your ſelf man.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Tutor, your counſel: Il'l do nothing Sir
Without him.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: This may rid thee, (valiant Cuz.)
Whom I have kept this forty year my Ward:
Fain would I have his ſtate, and now of late
He did inquire at Epheſus for his age,
But the Church Book being burnt with Dian's Temple
He loſt his ayme: I have try'd to famiſh him,
Marry he'll live o'th ſtones: and then for Poyſons,
He is an Antidote 'gainſt all of 'em;
He ſprung from Mithridates; he is ſo dry and hot,
He will eat Spiders faſter than a Monkey:
His Maw (unhurt) keeps Quickſilver like a bladder,
The largeſt dole of Camphire, Opium,
Harmes not his Brain; I think his Skul's as empty
He wil eat toſts of: H • nbane I am ſure
And Hemlock I have made his Pot-herbs often.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: If he refuſe you, yours is then the honor:
If he accept, he being ſo great, you may
Crave both to chooſe the Weapon, time, and place,
Which may be ten years hence, and Calicut,
Or underneath the line to avoid advantage.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: I am reſolved.

sp.speaker: Tut
sp.l: By your favor Pupill,
Whence ſhall this challe • ge • iſe? for you muſt ground it
On ſome ſuch fundamental baſe, or matter
As now the Gentry ſet their lives upon.
Did you ere cheat him at ſome Ordinary,
And durſt he ſay ſo, and be angry? if thus,
Then you muſt challenge him: hath he call'd your whore,
Whore; though ſhe be (beſide yours) twenty mens?
Your honor, reputation is touched then,
And you muſt challenge him: Has he deny'd
On thirty damme's to accommodate money,
Though he have broke threeſcore before to you?
Here you muſt challenge him: Durſt he ever ſhun
To drink two pots of Ale wi'ye? or to wench
Though weighty buſineſs otherwiſe importun'd?
He is a proud Lord,
And you may challenge him: Has he familiarly
Diſlik'd your yellow Starch, or ſaid your Dublet
Was not exactly frenchiſi'd? or that, that report
In fair terms was untrue? or drawn your Sword,
Cry'd 'twas ill mounted? Has he given the lye
In circle, or oblique, or ſemi-circle,
Or direct parrallel? you muſt challenge him.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: He never gave my direct apparrel the lye in's life.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: But for the crown of all, Has he refus'd
To pledge your Miſtris health though he were ſick?
And crav'd your pardon? you muſt challenge him,
There's no avoiding: one or both muſt drop.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Exquiſite Tutor.

sp.speaker: Nean.
sp.l: Crates, I have ſought you long, what make you here
Fooling with theſe three farthings, while the Town
Is all in uproar, and the Prince our Maſter
Seis'd by Leonidas, and Agenor) carried
And Pri • oner kept i'th • Caſtle, flanckes
The weſt part of the City, where they vow
To hold him, till your Brother, Lord Euphanes
Be rendr'd to 'em, with his life to ſatisfie
The Rape, by him ſuſpected to Merione?
The Queen refuſes to d • him,
Pawning her knowledge for his innocency,
And dares 'em do their worſt on Prince Theanor,
The whole State's in combuſtion.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Fatall Ring.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: What will become of us?

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: And ſhe hath given Commiſſion to Euphanes
And Conon (who have • avied men already)
With violence to ſurprize the Tow • e, and take 'em.
What will you do?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Along wi'ye, and prevent
A farther miſchief: Gentlemen, our intents
We muſt defer: you are the Princes followers.

sp.speaker: Nea.
sp.l: Will ye walk with us?

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: You ſhall pardon us.

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: We are his followers afar off you know.
And are contented to continue ſo.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: Sir Boy.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Sir Fool? a Challenge to my Lord?
How dar'ſt thou, or thy ambs—ace here think of him,
Ye Crow-pick'd heads, which your thin ſhoulders bear
As does the Poles on Corinth Bridge the Traitors:
Why you three Nine-pins you talk of my Lord,
And challenges? you ſhall not need: come draw,
His Page is able to ſwindge three ſuch whelpes:
Uncle, why ſtand ye off: long-man advance.

sp.speaker: Onos.
sp.l: S'light, what have we done Tutor?

sp.speaker: Tut.
sp.l: He is a Boy,
And we may run away with honour.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: That ye ſhall not,
And b • ing a Boy I am fitter to encounter
A Child in Law as you are, under twenty:
Thou ſot, thou three-ſcore Sot, and that's a Child
Again I grant you.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Nephew, here's an age:
Boyes are turn'd men, and men are Children.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Away you Pezants with your bought Gentry;
Are not you he, when your fellow Paſſengers,
Your laſt tranſportment being aſſayl'd by a Galley
Hid your ſelf i'the Cabbin: and the Fight done
Peep'd above Hatches, and cry'd, Have we taken,
Or are we tane? Come, I do want a ſlipper,
But this ſhall ſerve: Swear all as I would have you,
Or I will call ſome dozen brother Pages,
(They are not far off I am ſure) and we will blancket
You untill you piſs again.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Nay, we will ſwear Sir.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.l: T'is your beſt courſe:
Firſt, you ſhall ſwear never to name my Lord,
Or hear him nam'd hereafter, but bare-headed.
Next, to begin his health in every place,
And never to refuſe to pledge it, though
You ſurfeit to the death. Laſtly, to hold
The pooreſt, litleſt Page in reverence;
To think him valianter, and a better Gentleman
Than you three ſtamp'd together: and to give him
Wine and Tobacco whereſoe're you meet,
And the beſt meat if he can ſtay.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We ſwear it loyally.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Then I diſmiſs you
True Leigemen to the Panto ••• e:
I had more Articles, but I have buſineſs
And cannot ſtay now: ſo adieu dear Monſieur,

l.hi: Tres noble & tres puiſſant.

sp.speaker: Ʋnc.
sp.l: Adieu Monſieur.

l.hi: A voſtre ſervice & commandement.

sp.speaker: Tut
sp.l: I told you Pupill, you'ld repent this foolery.

sp.speaker: On.
sp.l: Who, I repent? you are miſtaken Tutor,
I ne're repented any thing yet in my life,
And ſcorne to begin now: Come, let's be melancholly.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: 'Twere better treat with 'em.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: I will no Treaties
With a League-breaker and a Rebell; ſhall I
Article with a Traitor? be compell'd
To yield an innocent unto their fury
Whom I have prov'd ſo to you?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Gracious Queen,
Though your own god-like diſpoſition
Would ſuccor Virtue, and protect the right,
Yet for the publick good, for the dear ſafety
Of your moſt Royal only Son, conſent
To give me up the ſacrifice to their malice,
My life is aym'd at, and 'twere better far
The blood of twenty thouſand ſuch as I
Purpled our Seas, than than that your Princely Son
Should be endanger'd.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Still well ſaid honeſt Fool,
Were their demand but one hair from thy head,
By all the gods Il'd ſcorn 'em: were they here,
The Majeſty that dwels upon this brow
Should ſtrike 'em on their knees: As for my Son,
Let 'em no more dare than they'l anſwer, I
An equal Mother to my Countrey, am,
And every virtuous Son of it is Son
Unto my boſome, tender as mine own.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Oh, you are heavenly Madam, and the gods
Can ſuffer nothing paſs to injure you:
The life that Conon promis'd, he ſtands now
Ready to pay with joy.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Farewell both,
Succeſs attend you: you have Souldiers been,
Tam Marti quam Mercurio: if you bring not peace
Bring me their heads.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I will put fair for one. Exeunt Quee. Lords.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Double the Guard upon her Highneſs Perſon,

sp.speaker: Conon.
sp.l: You muſt perform a friendly part,
Which I ſhall counſel you.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I am your ſervant. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Make good that Fortification, and the Watch
Keep ſtill upon the Battlements; Royall Sir,
Weigh but our injuries, we have told you fully
The manner and the matter hales us thus;
Nor ſhall this upſtart Muſhrum bred i'th night,
Sit brooding underneath your Mothers wings
His damn'd impieties.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: For your ſelf brave Prince,
Fear nothing that this face of arms preſents:
We ask the Raviſher, and have no means
To win him from your moſt indulgent Mother
But by this practice.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Stout Leonidas,
Princely Agenor, your wrongs cry ſo loud,
That who ſo would condemn you is not heard:
I blame you not, who but Euphanes durſt
Make Stories like to this? My wrong's as ſtrong
Aske my revengeful arm to ſtrengthen yours:
As for my fear, know you, and Greece throughout.
Our Mother was a Spartan Princeſs born,
That never taught me to ſpell ſuch a word.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Sir, you do tempt your life.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Conon, no more.
Do thus as thou wouldſt ſave it. Sound Trumpet within.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: What Trumpet's this?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Beneath I do perceive
Two armed men, ſingle, that gives us ſummons
As they would treat.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Let us deſcend.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: My Lord,
I would you would excuſe me, and proceed
According to the Queens directions.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Friend,
As thou wouldſt wear that title after death.

div.stage: Enter below Theanor, Agenor, Leonidas, and Soldiers. Perform my charge: no Soldier on his life Approach us nearer.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Safety to both the Princes, Loyalty
To you Lord General, the Queen, your Miſtriſs
As well as ours, though not to fear, to cut
Civil diſſention from her Land, and ſave
Much guiltleſs blood, that uprore ever thirſts,
And for the ſafeguard of her Son, by me
(As you demand) hath ſent the Lord Euphanes
To plead his own cauſe, or to ſuffer death
As you ſhall find him worthy; ſo delivering
The Prince back, I ſhall leave him to your Guard.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: The Queen is good and gracious: kiſs her hand.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: And ſeal our duties: Sir, depart in peace.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Oh Sir, you now perceive, when in the ſcales
Nature, and fond affection weigh together,
One poizes like a feather, and you know my Lords
What's to be done.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Your Highneſs is unarm'd,
Pleaſe you to uſe mine, and to lead the Army
Back to your Mother: Conon, march you with 'em.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: I will my Lord: But not ſo far as not
To bring you help if danger look upon you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Why do you look ſo ſtrangely, fearfully,
Or ſtay your deathful hand, be not ſo wiſe
To ſtop your rage: look how unmov'dly, here
I give my ſelf my Countreys ſacrifice,
An innocent ſacrifice: Truth laughs at death,
And terrifies the killer more than kill'd;
Integrity thus armleſs ſeeks her foes,
And never needs the Target nor the Sword,
Bow, nor invenom'd ſhafts.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We are amaz'd,
Not at your eloquence, but impudence,
That dare thus front us.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Kill him, who knows not
The iron forehead that bold miſchief wears.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Forbear a while Agenor, I do tremble,
And ſomething ſits like virtue in his face,
Which the gods keep.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Agenor, ſtrike Leonidas
You that have purchas'd Fame on certain grounds,
Loſe it on ſuppoſition? ſmear your hands
In guiltleſs blood, laugh at my Martyrdom:
But yet remember, when Poſterity
Shall read your Volumes fill'd with virtuous acts,
And ſhall arrive at this black bloody leaf,
Noting your fooliſh barbariſms, and my wrong,
(As time ſhall make it plain) what follows this
Diſciphering any noble deed of yours
Shall be quite loſt, for men will read no more.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why? dare you ſay you are innocent?

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: By all the gods, as they
Of this foul crime, why Gent. pry clean through my life,
Then weigh theſe circumſtances: think you that he
Which made day night, and men to furies turn'd,
Durſt not truſt ſilence, vizors, nor her ſence
That ſuffer'd; but with Charms and Potions
Caſt her aſleep, (for all this I have enquir'd
Acted the Fable of Proſerpines Rape,
The place (by all deſcription) like to Hell:
And all to perpetrate unknown his Luſt,
Would fondly in his perſon bring a Ring,
And give it a betrothed Wife, ith' ſame houſe
Where the poor injur'd Lady liv'd and groan'd.

sp.speaker: Ag,
sp.l: Hell gives us Art to reach the depth of ſin,
B • t leaves us wretched fools, when we are in.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Had it given me that Art, and left me ſo,
I would not thus into the Lions jaws
Have thruſt my ſelf (defenceleſs for your good,
The Princes ſafety, or the Common-weals:
You know the Queen deny'd me, and ſent us
Commanders to ſurprize you, and to raze
This Tower down, we had power enough to do it,
Or ſtarve you, as you ſaw, and not to tender
My Perſon to your wrath, which I have done,
Knowing my heart as pure as infants ſleep.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What think you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: No harm I am ſure: I weep.

sp.speaker: Euph
sp.l: The gods are juſt, and mighty: but to give you
Further aſſurance, and to make your ſelves
Judges and witneſſes of my innocence
Let me demand this queſtion, On what night
Was this ſoul deed committed?

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: On the F • e before our Marriage meant.

sp.speaker: Euph.

l.hi: Leonidas,

sp.l: (Your rage being off, that ſtill drowns memory)
Where was your ſelf and I that very night,
And what our conference?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: By the gods 'tis true:
• oth in her Highneſs Chamber conferring
Even of this Match until an hour of day,
And then came I to call you: we are ſham'd.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Utterly loſt, and ſham'd.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Neither be chear'd,
He that could find this out, can pardon it,
And know this Ring was ſent me from the Queen,
How ſhe came by it, yet is not enquir'd,
Deeper occurrents hang on't: and pray Heaven
That my ſuſpitions prove as falſe as yours,
Which (for the World) till I have greater proof
I dare not utter what, nor whom they touch;
Only this build upon, with all my nerves
I'll labour with ye, till time waken truth.
There are our ſwords Sir, turn the points on us,
Puniſh rebellion, and revenge your wrong,

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Sir, my revenge ſhall be to make your peace,
Neither was this rebellion, but raſh love.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: How's this? unarm'd left, now found doubly arm'd?
And thoſe that would have ſlain him at his feet?
Oh Truth, thou art a mighty Conquereſs:
The Queen (my Lord) perplex'd in care of you,
That, croſs to her command, hazard your ſelf
In perſon, here is come into the Field,
And like a Leader, marches in the head
Of all her Troops, vows that ſhe will demoliſh
Each ſtone of this proud Tower be you not ſafe:
She chaſes like ſtorms in Groves, now ſighs, now weeps,
And both ſometimes, like Rain and Wind commixt,
Abjures her Son for ever, leſs himſelf
Do fetch you off in perſon, that did give
Your ſelf to ſave him of your own free will,
And ſwears he muſt not, nor is it to live.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Oh ſhe's a Miſtriſs for the gods.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: And thou a godlike ſervant fit for her.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Wide Greece
May boaſt, becauſe ſhe cannot boaſt thy like.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Thus Conon tell her Highneſs.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: My joy flies.

sp.speaker: Eup.
sp.l: Let's toward her march: ſtern Drum ſpeak gentle peace.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We are priſoners, lead us, ne'r was known
A preſident like this: one unarm'd man
(Suſpe • ted) to captive with golden words
(Truth being his ſhield) ſo many arm'd with ſwords. Ex.

div.stage: Enter (at one door) Queen, Theanor, Crates, Conon, Lords, Soldiers, (at another) Euphanes (with two ſwords) Agenor, Leonidas, Soldiers: Euphanes preſents Leonidas on his knees to the Queen: Agenor bare-headed, makes ſhew of ſorrow to the Queen, ſhe ſtamps, and ſ • ems to be angry at the firſt. Euphanes perſwades her, lay a • their ſwords at her feet, ſhe gives them their ſwords again, they kiſs her hand and embrace, the Soldiers lift up Euphanes, and ſhout: Theanor and Crates diſcovered, Conon whiſpers with Crates, Euphanes with Agenor, and Leonidas obſerves it, who ſeem to promiſe ſomething, Euphanes directs his Page ſomewhat.
Exeunt all but Theanor and Crates.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: We are not lucky Crates, this great torrent
Bears all before him.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Such an age as this
Shall ne'r be ſeen again: virtue grows fat,
And villany pines; the Furies are aſleep,
Miſchief 'gainſt goodneſs aim'd, is like a ſtone,
Unnaturally forc'd up an eminent hill
Whoſe weight falls on our heads and buries us,
We ſpringe our ſelves, we ſink in our own bogs.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What's to be done?

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Repent and grow good.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Piſh,
'Tis not the faſhion (fool) till we grow old:
The peoples love to him now ſcares me more
Than my fond Mothers: both which, like two floods
Bearing Euphanes up; will o'rflow me,
And he is worthy, would he were in Heaven,
But that hereafter: Crates help me now,
And henceforth be at eaſe.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Your Will my Lord?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Beliza is to marry him forthwith,
I long to have the firſt touch of her too,
That will a little quiet me.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Fie Sir,
You'll be the Tyrant to Virginity;
To fall but once is manly, to perſevere
Beaſtly, and deſperate.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Croſs me not, but do't:
Are not the means, the place, the inſtruments
The very ſame? I muſt expect you ſuddenly. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: I muſt obey you.
Who is in evil once a companion
Can hardly ſhake him off, but muſt run on.
Here I appointed Conon to attend
Him, and his ſword: he promis'd to come ſingle.
To avoid prevention: he is a man on's word.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: You are well met Crates.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: If we part ſo Conon.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Come, we muſt do theſe mutual offices,
We muſt be our own Seconds, our own Surgeons,
And fairly fight, like men, not on advantage.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: You have an honeſt boſom.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Yours ſeems ſo.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Let's pair our ſwords: you are a juſt Gentleman,

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: You might be ſo: now ſhake hands if you pleaſe,
Though't be the cudgel faſhion, 'tis a friendly one.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: So, ſtand off.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: That's my cue to beckon 'em. Exit.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Crates, to expoſtulate your wrongs to me
Were to doubt of 'em, or wiſh your excuſe
In words, and ſo return like maiden Knights:
Yet freely thus much I profeſs, your ſpleen
And rugged carriage toward your honour'd Brother
Hath much more ſtirr'd me up, than min own cauſe,
For I did ne'r affect theſe bloody men,
But hold 'em fitter be made publick Hangmen:
Or Butchers call'd, than valiant Gentlemen:
'Tis true ſtamp'd valour does upon juſt grounds,
Yet for whom juſtlier ſhould I expoſe my life
Than him, unto whoſe virtue I owe all

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Conon, you think by this great deed of yours
To inſinuate your ſelf a lodging nearer
Unto my Brothers heart: ſuch men as you
Live on their undertakings for their Lords,
And more diſable them by anſwering for 'em
Than if they ſate ſtill, make 'em but their whores,
For which end Gallants now adays do fight:
But here we come not to upbraid; what men
Seem, the raſh world will judge; but what they are
Heaven knows: and this—Horſes, we are deſcry'd,
One ſtroke for fear of laughter.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Half a ſcore.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Hold, hold: on your allegiance hold.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: He that ſtrikes next—

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Falls like a Traitor on our ſwords.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Oh Heaven, my Brother bleeds: Conon, thou art
A villain, an unthankful man, and ſhalt
Pay me thy bloud for his, for his is mine:
Thou wert my friend, but he is ſtill my Brother;
And though a friend ſometimes be nearer ſaid
In ſome gradation it can never be
Where that ſame Brother can be made a friend,
Which deareſt Crates thus low I implore;
What in my poverty I would not ſeek,
Becauſe I would not burthen you, now here
In all my height of bliſs I beg of you,
Your friendſhip; my advancement, Sir, is yours;
I never held it ſtrange, pray uſe it ſo:
We are but two, which Number Nature fram'd
In the moſt uſeful faculties of man,
To ſtrengthen mutually and relieve each other:
Two eyes, two ears, two arms, two legs and feet,
That where one faild, the other might ſupply;
And I, your other eye, ear, your arm and leg,
Tender my ſervice, help and ſuccor to ye.

sp.speaker: Ag.
sp.l: Leo. A moſt divine example.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: For dear Brother,
You have been blind, and lame, and deaf to me,
Now be no more ſo: in humility
I give ye the duty of a younger Brother,
Which take you as a Brother, not a Father,
And then you'll pay a duty back to me.

sp.speaker: Cra.
sp.l: Till now I have not wept theſe thirty years.

sp.speaker: Euph.
sp.l: Diſcording Brothers, are like mutual legs
Supplanting one another: he that ſeeks
Aid from a ſtranger and forſakes his Brother,
Does but like him that madly lops his arm,
And to his body joyns a wooden one:
Cuts off his natural leg, and truſts a Crutch,
Plucks out his eye to ſee with Spectacles.

sp.speaker: Cra.
