Dwell in 'em to deſtruction; thorow their Phalanx
Strike, as thou ſttrik'ſt a proud tree; ſhake their Bodies,
Make their ſtrengths totter, and their topleſs fortunes
Unroot and reel to ruine.

sp.speaker: 1 Daugh.
sp.l: O thou god,
Thou feared god, if ever to thy juſtice
Inſulting wrongs, and raviſhments of Women,
Women deriv'd from thee, their ſhames, the ſufferings
Of thoſe that daily fill'd thy Sacrifice
With Virgin incenſe, have acceſs, now hear me,
Now ſnatch thy thunder up, now on theſe Romans,
Deſpiſers of thy power, of us defacers,
Revenge thy ſelf, take to thy killing anger,
To make thy great work full, thy juſtice ſpoken,
An utter rooting from this bleſſed Iſle
Of what Rome is or has been.

sp.speaker: Bon.
sp.l: Give more incenſe,
The gods are deaf and drowſie; no happy flame
Riſes to raiſe our thoughts: Pour on.

sp.speaker: 2 Daugh.
sp.l: See heaven.
And all you pow'rs that guide us, ſee, and ſhame
We kneel ſo long for pity over your Altars;
Since 'tis no light oblation that you look for,
No incenſe offering, will I hang mine eyes;
And as I wear theſe ſtones with hourly weeping,
So will I melt your pow'rs into compaſſion.
This tear for Proſutagus my brave Father,
Ye gods, now think on Rome; this for my Mother,
And all her miſeries; yet ſee, and ſave us;
But now ye muſt be open-ey'd. See; heaven,
Oh ſee thy ſhow'rs ſtoln from thee; our diſhonours,
Oh Siſter, our diſhonors: can ye be gods,
And theſe ſins ſmother'd?

sp.speaker: Bon.
sp.l: The ſire takes.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: It does ſo,
But no flame riſes. Ceaſe your fearful prayers,
Your whinings, and your tame petitions;
The gods love courage arm'd with confidence,
And prayers fit to pull them down: weak tears
And troubled hearts, the dull twins of cold ſpirits,
They ſit and ſmile at. Hear how I ſalute 'em:
Divine Andate, thou who hold'ſt the reins
Of furious Battels, and diſordred War,
And proudly roll'ſt thy ſwarty chariot wheels
Over the heaps of wounds and carcaſſes,
Sailing through ſeas of blood; thou ſure-ſteel'd ſternneſs,
Give us this day good hearts, good enemies,
Good blowes o'both ſides, wounds that fear or flight
Can claim no ſhare in; ſteel us both with angers,
And warlike executions fit thy viewing;
Let Rome put on her beſt ſtrength, and thy Britain,
Thy little Britain, but as great in fortune,
Meet her as ſtrong as ſhe, as proud, as daring;
And then look on, thou red ey'd god: who does beſt,
Reward with honor; who deſpair makes flie,
Unarm for ever, and brand with infamy:
Grant this, divine Andate, 'tis but juſtice;
And my firſt blow thus on thy holy Altar A flame ariſes.
I ſacrifice unto thee.

sp.speaker: Bon.
sp.l: It flames out Muſick.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Now ſing ye Druides. Song.

sp.speaker: Bon.
sp.l: 'Tis out again.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: H'as given us leave to fight yet; we ask no more,
The reſt hangs in our reſolutions:
Tempt her no more.

sp.speaker: Bon.
sp.l: I would know farther Coſen.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Her hidden meaning dwels in our endeavors;
Our valors are our beſt gods. Cheer the Soldier,
And let him eat.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: He's at it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Away then;
When he has done, let's march. Come, fear not Lady,
This day the Roman gains no more ground here,
But what his body lies in.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Now I am confident. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: We dare not hazard it: beſide our lives,
It forfeits all our underſtandings.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Gentlemen,
Can ye forſake me in ſo juſt a ſervice,
A ſervice for the Common-wealth, for honor?
Read but the Letter; you may love too.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Read it:
If there be any ſafety in the circumſtance,
Or likelihood 'tis love, we will not fail ye.
Read it good Curius.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Willingly.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Now mark it.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: reads. Health to thy heart, my honoured Junius,
And all thy love requited: I am thine,
Thine everlaſtingly, thy love has won me,
And let it breed no doubt; our new acquaintance
Compels this, 'tis the gods decree to bleſs us.
The times are dangerous to meet; yet fail not,
By all the love thou bear'ſt me I conjure thee,
Without diſtruſt of danger, to come to me,
For I have purpos'd a delivery
Both of my ſelf and fortune this bleſt day
Into thy hands, if thou thinkſt good: to ſhew thee
How infinite my Love is, even my Mother
Shall be thy priſoner, the day yours without hazard;
For I beheld your danger like a Lover,
A juſt affecter of thy faith: Thy goodneſs,
I know, will uſe us nobly, and our Marriage
If not redeem, yet leſſen Romes Ambition.
I 'm weary of theſe miſeries: Uſe my Mother,
(if you intend to take her) with all honour,
And let this diſobedience to my parents
Be laid on love, not me. Bring with thee, Junius,
Spirits reſolv'd to fetch me off, the nobleſt,
Forty will ſerve the turn; juſt at the joyning
Of both the battels, we will be weakly guarded;
And for a guide, within this hour ſhall reach thee
A faithful friend of mine: the gods, my Junius,
Keep thee, and me to ſerve thee: young Bon • ica.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: This letter carries much belief, and moſt objections
Anſwer'd, we muſt have doubted.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Is that fellow
Come to ye for a guide yet?

sp.speaker: Jun
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: And examin'd?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Far more then that; he has felt tortures, yet
He vows he knows no more than this truth.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Strange.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: If ſhe mean what ſhe writes, as't may be probable,
'Twill be the happieſt vantage we can lean to.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: I'll pawn my ſoul ſhe means truth.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Think an hour more,
Then if your confidence grow ſtronger on ye,
We'll ſet in with ye.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Nobly done; I thank ye;
Ye know the time.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: We will be either ready
To give ye preſent counſell, or joyn with ye.

div.stage: Enter Swetonius, Petillius, and Demetrius, Macer.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: No more as ye are Gentlemen. The general.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Draw out apace, the enemy waits for us;
Are ye all ready?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: All our Troops attend, Sir.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: I am glad to hear you ſay ſo, Junius.
I hope ye are diſpoſſeſt.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: I hope ſo too, Sir,

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Continue ſo. And Gentlemen, to you now;
To bid you fight is needleſs, ye are Romans,
The name will fight it ſelf; To tell ye who
You go to fight againſt, his power, and nature,
But loſs of time: yet know it, know it poor,
And oft have made it ſo. To tell ye farther,
His Body ſhows more dreadful than it has done,
To him that fears, leſs poſſible to deal with,
Is but to ſtick more honor on your actions,
Load ye with virtuous names, and to your memories
Tye never dying time, and fortune conſtant.
Go on in full aſſurance, draw your ſwords
As daring and as confident as juſtice;
The gods of Rome fight for ye; loud Fame calls ye,
Pitch'd on the topleſs Apenine, and blows
To all the under world: all Nations,
The ſeas, and unfrequented deſerts, where the ſnow dwels,
Wakens the ruin'd monuments, and there
Where nothing but eternal death and ſleep is,
Informs again the dead bones With your virtues.
Go on, I ſay, valiant and wiſe, rule heaven,
And all the great aſpects attend 'em. Do but blow
Upon this enemy, who, but that we want foes,
Cannot deſerve that name; and like a myſt,
A lazie fog, before your burning valors
You'll find him fly to nothing, This is all,
We have ſwords, and are the ſons of antient Romans,
Heirs to their endleſs valors, fight and conquer.

sp.speaker: De.
sp.l: Dem. 'Tis done.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: That man that loves not this day,
And hugs not in his arms the noble danger,
May he dye fameleſs and forgot.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Sufficient,
Up to your Troops, and let your drums beat thunder,
March cloſe, and ſudden like a tempeſt: all executions
Done without ſparkling of the Body: keep your phalanx
Sure lin'd, and piec'd together; your pikes forward,
And ſo march like a moving Fort: ere this day run,
We ſhall have ground to add to Rome, well won. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Nen.
sp.l: The Roman is advanc'd from yound' hills brow,
We may behold him, Caratach. A March.

div.stage: Drums within at one place afar off.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Let's thither,
I ſee the duſt flie. Now I ſee the body,
Obſerve 'em, Nennuis, by—a handſome Body,
And of a few, ſtrongly and wiſely joynted:
Swetonius is a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Nen.
sp.l: As I take it,
That's he that gallops by the Regiments,
Viewing their preparations.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Very likely,
He ſhews no leſs than General: ſee how bravely
The Body moves, and in the head how proudly
The Captains ſtick like plumes: he comes apace on;
Good Nennius go, and bid my ſtout Lieutenant
Bring on the firſt ſquare Body to oppoſe 'em,
And as he charges, open to incloſe 'em:
The Queen move next with hers, and wheel about,
To gain their backs, in which I'll lead the Vantguard.
We ſhall have bloody crowns this day, I ſee by't;
Haſt thee good Nennius, I'll follow inſtantly.
How cloſe they march, as if they grew together? March.
No place but lin'd alike: ſure from oppreſſion;
They will not change this figure: we muſt charge 'em,
And charge 'em home at both ends, Van and Rere,
sp.stage: Drums in another place afar off.
sp.l: They never totter elſe. I hear our Muſick,
And muſt attend it: Hold good ſword, but this day,
And bite hard where I hound thee, and hereafter
I'll make a relique of thee, for young Souldiers
To come like Pilgrimes to, and kiſs for Conqueſts.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Now is the time, the fellow ſtays.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: What think ye?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: I think 'tis true.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Alaſs, if 'twere a queſtion,
If any doubt or hazzard fell into't,
Do ye think mine own diſcretion ſo ſelf-blind,
My care of you ſo naked, to run headlong?

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Let's take Petillius with us.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: By no means:
He's never wiſe but to himſelf, nor courteous,
But where the end' his own: we are ſtrong enough,
If not to many. Behind yonder hill
The follow tells me ſhe attends, weak guarded,
Her Mother and her Siſter.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I would venture.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: We ſhall not ſtrike five blows for't, weigh the good,
The general good may come.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Away, I'll with ye,
But with what doubt?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Fear not, my ſoul for all. Exeunt.
sp.stage: Alarms, Drums and Trumpets in ſeveral places afar off, as at a main Battell.

div.head: Scaena Quinta.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Here ye may ſee 'em all, Sir: from this hill
The Country ſhews off levell.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Gods defend me,
What multitudes they are, what infinites?
The Roman power ſhews like a little Star
Hedg'd with a double hollo. Now the knell rings,
Heark how they ſhout to th'battel; how the air
Totters and reels, and rends apieces, Druſus,
With the huge vollied clamours.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Now they charge.
Oh gods, of all ſides, fearfully.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Little Rome,
Stand but this growing Hydra one ſhort hour,
And thou haſt out-done Hercules.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: The duſt hides 'em,
We cannot ſee what follows.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: They are gone,
Gone, ſwallow'd Druſus, this eternal Sun
Shall never ſee 'em march more.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: O turn this way,
And ſee a modell of the field, ſome forty,
Againſt four hundred.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Well fought, bravely follow'd;
O nobly charg'd again, charg'd home too: Druſus,
They ſeem to carry it: now they charge all, Loud.
Cloſe, cloſe, I ſay; they follow it: ye gods,
Can there be more in men? more daring ſpirits?
Still they make good their fortunes. Now they are gone too,
For ever gone: ſee Druſus at their backs
A fearful Ambuſh riſes. Farewell valours,
Excellent valours: O Rome, where's thy wiſdome?

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: They are gone indeed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Look out toward the Army,
I am heavy with theſe ſlaughters.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: 'Tis the ſame ſtill,
Covered with duſt and fury.

div.stage: Enter the two Daughters, with Junius, Curius, Decius, and Souldiers.

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: Bring 'em in,
Tie 'em, and then unarm 'em.

sp.speaker: 1. Daugh.
sp.l: Valiant Romans,
Ye are welcome to your Loves.

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: Your death, fools.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: We deſerve 'em,
And women do your worſt.

sp.speaker: 1. Daugh.
sp.l: Ye need not beg it.

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: Which is kind Junius?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: This.

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: Are you my ſweet heart?
It looks ill on't: how long is't, pretty ſoul,
Since you and I firſt lov'd? Had we not reaſon
To doat extreamly upon one another?
How does my Love? this is not he: my chicken
Could prate finely, ſing a love-ſong.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Monſter.

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: Oh, now it courts.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Arm'd with more malice
Then he that got thee has the divell.

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: Good.
Proceed, ſweet chick.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: I hate thee, that's my laſt.

sp.speaker: 2. Daug.
sp.l: Nay, and ye love me, forward: No? Come ſiſter,
Let's prick our anſwers on our arrows points,
And make 'em laugh a little. Ye damn'd Leachers,
Ye proud improvident fools, have we now caught ye?
Are ye i'th nooſe? Since ye are ſuch loving creatures,
We'ell be your Cupids: Do ye ſee theſe arrows?
We'll ſend them to your wanton livers, goats.

sp.speaker: 1. Dau.
sp.l: O how I'll trample on your hearts, ye villains,
Ambitious ſalt-itch ſlaves: Romes maſter ſins,
The mountain Rams topt your hot mothers.

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: Dogs,
To whoſe brave founders a ſalt whore gave ſuck;
Theeves, honors hangmen, do ye grin? perdition
Take me for ever, if in my ſelf anger, Enter Caratach.
I do not out-do all example.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Where,
Where are theſe Ladies? ye keep noble quarter,
Your Mother thinks ye dead or taken; upon which,
She will not move her Battel. Sure theſe faces
I have beheld and known, they are Roman Leaders,
How came they here?

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: A trick Sir, that we us'd,
A certain policy conducted 'em
Unto our ſnare: we have done ye no ſmall ſervice;
Theſe us'd as we intend, we are for th'battel,

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: As you intend? taken by treachery?

sp.speaker: 1. Daugh.
sp.l: Is't not allow'd?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thoſe that ſhould gild our Conqueſt,
Make up a Battel worthy of our winning,
Catch'd up by craft?

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: By any means that's lawful.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: A womans wiſdom in our triumphs? out,
Out ye ſluts, ye follies; from our ſwords
Filth our revenges baſely? arm again, Gentlemen:
Soldiers, I charge ye help 'em.

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: By—Uncle,
We will have vengeance for our rapes.

sp.speaker: Car
sp.l: By —
You ſhould have kept your legs cloſe then: diſpatch there.

sp.speaker: 1. Daug.
sp.l: I will not off thus.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: He that ſtirs to execute,
Or ſhe, though it be your ſelves, by him that got me,
Shall quickly feel mine anger: one great day given us,
Not to be ſnatch'd out of our hands but baſely;
And we muſt ſhame the gods from whence we have it,
With ſetting ſnares for Soldiers? I'll run away firſt,
Be hooted at, and children call me coward,
Before I ſet up ſcales for Victories:
Give 'em their ſwords.

sp.speaker: 2. Daugh.
sp.l: O gods.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Bear off the women
Unto their Mother.

sp.speaker: 2. Dau.
sp.l: One ſhot, gentle Uncle.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: One cut her fiddle-ſtring: Bear 'em off I ſay.

sp.speaker: 1. Dau.
sp.l: The— take this fortune.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Learn to ſpin,
And curſe your knotted hemp: go Gentlemen,
Safely go off, up to your Troops: be wiſer,
There thank me like tall Soldiers: I ſhall ſeek ye.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: A noble worth.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Well Junius.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Pray ye no more.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: He bluſhes, do not load him.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Where's your love now? Drums loud again.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Puffe, there it flies: Come, let's redeem our follies.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Awake, Sir; yet the Roman Bodie's whole,
I ſee 'em clear again.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Whole? 'tis not poſſible:
Druſus they muſt be loſt.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: By—they are whole, Sir,
And in brave doing; ſee, they wheel about
To gain more ground.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: But ſee there, Druſus, ſee,
See that huge Battel moving from the mountains,
Their gilt coats ſhine like Dragons ſcales, their march
Like a rough tumbling ſtorm; ſee them, and view 'em,
And then ſee Rome no more: ſay they fail; look,
Look where the armed carts ſtand; a new Army:
Look how they hang like falling rocks, as murdring
Death rides in triumph Druſus: fell deſtruction
Laſhes his fiery horſe, and round about him
His many thouſand ways to let out ſouls.
Move me again when they charge, when the mountain
Melts under their hot wheels, and from their Ax'trees
Huge claps of thunder plough the ground before 'em,
Till then I'll dream what Rome was.

sp.speaker: Swet
sp.l: O bravely fought; honor till now nere ſhow'd
Her golden fate i'th' field. Like Lions, Gentlemen,
Y'have held your heads up this day: Where's young Junius,
Curius and Decius?

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Gone to heaven, I think, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sw.
sp.l: Their worths go with 'em: breathe a while: How do ye?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Well; ſome few ſcurvy wounds, my heart's whole yet.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Would they would give us more ground.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Give? we'll have it.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Have it? and hold it too, deſpight the devill.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Lead up to th'head, and line: ſure the Qs. Battell
Begins to charge like wild-fire: where's the General?

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Oh, they are living yet. Come my brave ſoldiers,
Come, let me powr Romes bleſſing on ye; Live,
Live, and lead Armies all: ye bleed hard.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Beſt:
We ſhall appear the ſterner to the foe.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: More wounds, more honor.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Loſe no time.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Away then,
And ſtand this ſhock, ye have ſtood the world.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Wee'll grow to't.
Is not this better than lowſie loving?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: I am my ſelf, Petillius.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: 'Tis I love thee. Exeunt Romans.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Charge 'em i'th'flanks: O ye have plaid the fool,
The fool extreamly, the mad fool.

sp.speaker: Bon.
sp.l: Why Coſin?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: The woman fool. Why did you give the word
Unto the carts to charge down, and our people
In groſs before the Enemy? we pay for't,
Our own ſwords cut our throats: why? —on't;
Why do you offer to command? the divell,
The divell, and his dam too, who bid you
Meddle in mens affairs? Exeunt Queen, &c.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: I'll help all.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Home,
Home and ſpin woman, ſpin, go ſpin, ye trifle.
Open before there, or all's ruine, How, Showts within.
Now comes the Tempeſt; on our ſelves, by—
O woman, ſcurvie woman, beaſtly woman. Exeunt.

l.hi: Victoria, Victoria.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: How's that, Druſus?

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: They win, they win, they win; oh look, look, look, Sir,
For heavens ſake look, the Britains fly, the Britains fly. Victoria.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Soft, ſoft, purſue it ſoft; excellent Soldiers,
Cloſe, my brave fellows, honorable Romans:
Oh cool thy mettle Junius, they are ours,
The world cannot redeem 'em: ſtern Petillius,
Govern the conqueſt nobly: ſoft, good Soldiers. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Shame, whither flie ye, ye unlucky Britains?
Will ye creep into your mothers wombs again? Back cowards.
Hares, fearful Hares, Doves in your angers; leave me?
Leave your Queen deſolate? her hapleſs children.
To Roman rape again and fury?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Flye, ye buzzards,
Ye have wings enough, ye fear: get thee gone, woman,
Shame tread upon thy heels: all's loſt, all's loſt, heark,
Heark how the Romans ring our knels. Ext. Bond, &c.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Good Uncle,
Let me go too.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: No boy, the fortune's mine,
I muſt not leave thee; get behind me; ſhake not,
I'll breech ye, if ye do boy: Come, brave Romans,
All is not loſt yet.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Now I'll thank thee, Caratach. Fight. Drums.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thou art a Soldier: ſtrike home, home, have at ye.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: His blows fall like huge ſledges on an anvil.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: I am weary.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: So am I.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Send more ſwords to me.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Let's ſit and reſt. Sit down.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: What think ye now?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: O Druſus,
I have loſt mine honor, loſt my name,
Loſt all that was my light: theſe are true Romans,
And I a Britain coward, a baſe Coward;
Guide me where nothing is but deſolation,
That I may never more behold the face
Of Man, or Mankind know me: O blind Fortune,
Haſt thou abus'd me thus?

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Good Sir, be comforted;
It was your wiſdom rul'd ye; pray ye go home,
Your day is yet to come, when this great fortune
Shall be but ſoil unto it. Retreat.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Fool, fool, Coward. Exit Penyus and Druſus.

div.stage: Enter Swetonius, Demetrius, Soldiers, Drum and Colours.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Draw in, draw in: well have you ſought, and worthy
Romes noble recompence; look to your wounds,
The ground is cold and hurtful: the proud Queen
Has got a Fort, and there ſhe and her Daughters
Defie us once again. To morrow morning
Wee'll ſeek her out, and make her know, our Fortunes
Stop at no ſtubborn walls: Come, ſons of honor,
True virtues heirs; thus hatch'd with Britain blood,
Let's march to reſt, and ſet in gules like Suns.
Beat a ſoft march, and each one eaſe his neighbours. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Petillius, Junius, Decius, Demetrius ſinging.

l.hi: Smooth was his cheek,
And his chin it was ſleek,
With whoop, he has done wooing.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Junius was this Captains name,

l.hi: A lad for a laſſes viewing,
Full black his eye, and plump his thigh,
Made up for loves purſuing:
Smooth was his cheeck.
And his chin it was ſleek.
With whoop, he has done wooing.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: O my vex'd thief, art thou come home again?
Are thy brains perfect?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Sound as bels.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Thy back-worm
Quiet, and caſt his ſting, boy?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Dead, Petillius,
Dead to all folly, and now my anger only.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Why, that's well ſaid: hang Cupid and his qu • ve • .
A drunken brawling Boy; thy honour'd ſaint
Be thy ten ſhillings, Junius, there's the money,
And there's the ware; ſquare dealing: this but ſweats thee
Like a Meſh nag, and makes thee look pin buttock'd.
The other runs thee whining up and down
Like a pig in a ſtorm, fills thy brains full of madneſs,
And ſhews thee like a long Lent, thy brave body
Turn'd to a tail of green-fiſh without butter.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: When thou lov'ſt next, love a good cup of W • .
A Miſtreſs for a King, ſhe leaps to kiſs thee,
Her red and white's her own; ſhe makes good blood,
Takes none away; what ſhe heats ſleep can help,
Without a groping Surgeon.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: I am counſell'd,
And henceforth, when I doat again,—

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Take heed,
Ye had almoſt paid for't.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Love no more great Ladies,
Thou canſt not ſtep amiſs then; there's no delight in 'em.
All's in the whiſtling of their ſnacht up ſilks;
They're only made for handſome view, not handling;
Their bodies of ſo weak and waſh a temper,
A rough pac'd bed will ſhake 'em all to pieces;
A tough hen pulls their teeth out, tyres their ſouls;
Plenae rimarum ſunt, they are full of rynnet,
And take the skin off where they are taſted; ſhun 'em,
They live in culliſſes like rotten cocks
Stew'd to a tenderneſs, that holds no tack:
Give me a thing I may cruſh.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Thou ſpeak'ſt truly:
The War • ſhall be my Miſtriſs now.

sp.speaker: Petil.
sp.l: Well choſen,
For ſhe's a bownſing laſs, ſhe'll kiſs thee at night, boy,
And break thy pate i'th' morning.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Yeſterday
I found thoſe favors infinite.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Wench good enough,
But that ſhe talks too loud.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: She talks to th'purpoſe,
Which never Woman did yet: ſhe'll hold grapling,
And he that layes on beſt, is her beſt ſervant:
All other loves are meer catching of dotrels,
Stretching of legs out only, and trim lazineſs. Enter
Here comes the General. Swet. Curius, & Macer.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: I am glad ye have found ye:
Are thoſe come in yet that purſu'd bold Caratach?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Not yet Sir, for I think they mean to lodge him.
Take him I know they dare not, 'twill be dangerous.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Then haſte Petillius, haſte to Penyus,
I fear the ſtrong conceit of what diſgrace
Has pull'd upon himſelf, will be his ruine:
I fear his ſoldiers fury too; haſte preſently,
I would not loſe him for all Britain. Give him, Petillius,

sp.speaker: Petil.
sp.l: That that ſhall, choak him.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: All the noble counſell,
His fault forgiven too, his place, his honor,

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: For me, I think, as handſome.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: All the comfort.
And tell the Souldier, 'twas on our command
He drew not to the Battell.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I conceive Sir,
And will do that ſhall cure all.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Bring him with ye
Before the Queens Fort, and his Forces with him,
There you ſhall find us following of our Conqueſt:
Make haſte.

sp.speaker: Petil.
sp.l: The beſt I may. Exit.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: And noble Gentlemen,
Up to your Companies: we'll preſently
Upon the Queens purſuit: there's nothing done
Till ſhe be ſeiz'd; without her nothing won. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: How does my Boy?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I would do well, my heart's well;
I do not fear.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: My good Boy.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I know, Uncle,
We muſt all dye; my little brother dy'd,
I ſaw him dye, and he dy'd ſmiling: ſure,
There's no great pain in't Uncle. But pray tell me,
Wither muſt we go when we are dead?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Strange queſtions!
Why, to the bleſſed'ſt place Boy: ever ſweetneſs
And happineſs dwells there.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Will you come to me?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Yes, my ſweet boy.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Mine Aunt too, and my Coſins?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: All, my good child.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: No Romans, Uncle?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: No Boy.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: I ſhould be loath to meet them there.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: No ill men,
That live by violence, and ſtrong oppreſſion,
Come thither: 'tis for thoſe the gods love, good men.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Why, then I care not when I go; for ſurely
I am perſwaded they love me: I never
blaſphem'd 'em, Uncle, nor tranſgreſt my parents;
I always ſaid my Prayers.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt go then,
Indeed thou ſhalt.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: When they pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: That's my good boy.
Art thou not weary, Hengo?

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Weary, Uncle?
I have heard you ſay you have march'd all day in Armour.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I have, boy.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Am not I your Kinſman?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: And am not I as fully allyed unto you
In thoſe brave things, as blood?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thou art too tender.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: To go upon my legs? they were made to bear me.
I can play twenty mile a day, I ſee no reaſon
But to preſerve my Countrey and my ſelf,
I ſhould march forty.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: What, wouldſt thou be
Living to wear a mans ſtrength?

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Why a Caratach,
A Roman-hater, a ſcourge ſent from Heaven Drum
To whip theſe proud theeves from our Kingdom. Heark,
Heark, Uncle, heark, I hear a Drum.

div.stage: Enter Judas and his people to the door.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Beat ſoftly,
Softly, I ſay; they are here: who dare charge?

sp.speaker: 1. gold.
sp.l: He.
That dares be knockt o'th' head: I'll not come near him.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Retire again, and watch then. How he ſtares!
H'as eyes would kill a dragon: mark the boy well;
If we could take or kill him. A —on ye,
How fierce ye look? ſee how he broods the boy;
The devil dwels in's ſcabbard. Back, I ſay,
Apace, apace, h'as found us. They retire.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Do ye hunt us?

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Uncle, good Uncle ſee, the thin ſtarv'd Raſcal,
The eating Roman, ſee where he thrids the thickets:
Kill him, dear Uncle, kill him; one good blow
To knock his brains into his breech; ſtrike's head off,
That I may piſs in's face.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Do ye make us Foxes?
Here, hold my charging ſtaff, and keep the place boy.
I'am at bay, and like a bull I'll bear me.
Stand, ſtand, ye Rogues, ye Squirrels. Exit.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Now he pays 'em:
O that I had a mans ſtrength.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Here's the boy;
Mine own, I thank my Fortune.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Uncle, uncle;
Famine is faln upon me, uncle.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Come, Sir,
Yield willingly, your Uncle's out of hearing,
I'll ti • le your young ta • l elſe.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: I defie thee,
Thou mock-made man of mat: charge home, ſi • ha:
Hang thee, baſe ſlave, thou ſhak'ſt.

sp.speaker: Jud,
sp.l: Upon my conſcience
The boy will beat me: how it looks, how bravely,
How confident the worm is: a ſcabb'd boy
To handle me thus? yield or I cut thy head off.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Thou dar'ſt not cut my finger: here't is, touch it.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: The boy ſpeaks ſword and buckler, Prethee yield, boy:
Come, here's an apple, yield.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: By—he fears me.
I'll give you ſharper language: When, ye coward,
When come ye up?

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: If he ſhould beat me—

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: When, Sir?
I long to kill thee; come, thou can'ſt not ſcape me.
I have twenty ways to charge thee; twenty deaths
Attend my bloody ſtaff.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Sure't is the devil,
A dwarf, devil in a doublet.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: I have kill'd a Captain, ſirha, a brave Captain,
And when I have done, I have kickt him thus. Look here,
See how I charge this ſtaff.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Moſt certain
This boy will cut my throat yet.

sp.speaker: 1. Sold.
sp.l: Flee, flee, he kills us.

sp.speaker: 2. Sould.
sp.l: He comes, be comes.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: The devil take the hindmoſt.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Run, run, ye Rogues, ye precious Rogues, ye rank Rogues.
A comes, a comes, a comes, a comes: that's he, boys.
What a brave cry they make?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: How does my chicken?

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: 'Faith, uncle, grown a Soldier, a great Soldier;
For by the virtue of your charging-ſtaff,
And a ſtrange fighting face I put upon't,
I have outbrav'd hunger.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: That's my boy, my ſweet boy.
Here, here's a Roman's head for thee.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Good proviſion.
Before I ſtarve, my ſweet-fac'd Gentleman,
I'll trie your favour.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: A right compleat Soldier.
Come, chicken, let's go ſeek ſome place of ſtrength
(The Countrey's full of Scouts) to reſt a while in,
Thou wilt not elſe be able to endure
The journey to my Countrey, fruits, and water,
Muſt be your food a while, boy.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Any thing:
I can eat moſs, I can live on anger,
To vex theſe Romans. Let's be wary, Uncle.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I warrant thee; come chearfully.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: And boldly

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: The ſoldier ſhall not grieve ye.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Pray ye forſake me;
Look not upon me, as ye love your Honors;
I am ſo cold a coward, my infection
Will choke your virtues like a damp elſe.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Dear Captain.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Moſt honour'd Sir.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Moſt hated, moſt abhor'd;
Say ſo, and then ye know me, nay, ye pleaſe me.
O my dear credit, my dear credit.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Sure
His mind is dangerous.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: The good gods cure it.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: My honour got thorow fire, thorow ſtubborn breaches
Thorow Battels that have been as hard to win as heaven,
Thorow death himſelf, in all his horrid trims,
Is gone for ever, ever, ever, Gentlemen,
And now I am left to ſcornful tales and laughters,
To hootings at, pointing with fingers, That's he,
That's the brave Gentleman forſook the battel,
The moſt wiſe Penyus, the diſputing coward.
O my good ſword, break from my ſide, and kill me;
Cut out the coward from my heart.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Ye are none.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: He lyes that ſays ſo: by — he lyes, lyes baſely,
Baſer than I have done. Come, ſoldiers, ſeek me,
I have robb'd ye of your virtues: Juſtice, ſeek me,
I have broke my fair obedience, loſt ſhame take me,
Take me, and ſwallow me, make ballads of me;
Shame, endleſs ſhame: and pray do you forſake me.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: What ſhall we do?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Good Gentlemen forſake me:
You were not wont to be commanded. Friends, pray do it,
And do not fear; for as I am a coward
I will not hurt my ſelf: when that mind takes me,
I'll call to you, and ask your help. I dare not.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Good morrow, Gentlemen; where's the Tribune?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Whence come ye, good Petillius?

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: From the General.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: With what, for heavens ſake?

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: With good counſel, Druſus,
And love, to comfort him.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Good Regulus
Step to the Soldier, and allay his anger;
For he is wild as winter.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: O, are ye there? have at ye. Sure he's dead,
It cannot be he dare out-live this fortune:
He muſt die, 'tis moſt neceſſary; men expect it;
And thought of life in him, goes beyond coward.
Forſake the field ſo baſely? fie upon't!
So poorly to betray his worth; ſo coldly
To cut all credit from the ſoldier? ſure
If this man mean to live, as I ſhould think it
Beyond belief, he muſt retire where never
The name of Rome, the voice of Arms, or Honour
Was known or heard of yet: he's certain dead,
Or ſtrongly means it; he's no Soldier elſe,
No Roman in him; all he has done, but outſide,
Fought either drunk or deſperate. Now he riſes.
How does Lord Penyus?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: As ye ſee.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I am glad on't;
Continue ſo ſtill. The Lord General,
The valiant General, great Swetonius—

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: No more of me is ſpoken; my name's periſh'd.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: He that commanded fortune and the day
By his own valour and diſcretion,
When, as ſome ſay, Penyus refuſed to come,
But I believe 'em not, ſent me to ſee ye.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Ye are welcome; and pray ſee me; ſee me well,
Ye ſhall not ſee me long.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I hope ſo, Penyus;
The gods defend, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: See me, and underſtand me: This is he
Left to fill up your triumph; he that baſely
Whiſtled his honour off to th'wind; that coldly
Shrunk in his politick head, when Rome like reapers
Sweat blood, and ſpirit, for a glorious harveſt,
And bound it up, and brought it off: that fool,
That having gold and copper offer'd him,
Refus'd the wealth, and took the waſt: that ſoldier
That being courted by loud fame and fortune,
Labour in one hand, that propounds us gods,
And in the other, glory that creates us,
Yet durſt doubt, and be damned.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: It was an errour.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A foul one, and a black one.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Yet the blackeſt
May be waſht white again.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Never.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Your leave, Sir,
And I beſeech ye note me; for I love ye,
And bring all comfort: Are we gods,
Allied to no infirmities? are our natures
More than mens natures? when we ſlip a little
Out of the way of virtue, are we loſt?
Is there no medicine called Sweet mercy?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: None, Petillius;
There is no mercy in mankind can reach me,
Nor is it fit it ſhould; I have ſinn'd beyond it.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Forgiveneſs meets with all faults.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Tis all faults,
All ſins I can commit, to be forgiven:
'Tis loſs of whole man in me, my diſcretion
To be ſo ſtupid, to arrive at pardon.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: O but the General —

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: He's a brave Gentleman,
A valiant, and a loving; and I dare ſay
He would, as far as honor durſt direct him,
Make even with my fault, but 'tis not honeſt,
Nor in his power: examples that may nouriſh
Neglect and diſobedience in whole bodies.
And totter the eſtates and faiths of armies,
Muſt not be plaid withall; nor out of pitty
Make a General forget his duty:
Nor dare I hope more from him than is worthy.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: What would ye do?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Dye.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: So would ſullen children,
Women that want their wills, ſlaves, diſobedient,
That fear the law, die. Fie, great Captain; you
A man to rule men, to have thouſand lives
Under your Regiment, and let your paſſion
Betray your reaſon? I bring you all forgiveneſs,
The nobleſt kind commends, your place, your honour.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Prethee no more; 'tis fooliſh: didſt not thou?
By—thou didſt, I over-heard thee, there,
There where thou ſtandſt now, deliver me for raſcal,
Poor, dead, cold coward, miſerable, wretched,
If I out-liv'd this ruine?

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: And thou diſt it nobly,
Like a true man, a ſouldier: and I thank thee,
I thank thee, good Petillius; thus I thank thee,

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Since ye are ſo juſtly made up, let me tell ye,
'Tis fit ye dye indeed.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: O how thou lov'ſt me!

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: For ſay he had forgiven ye; ſay the peoples whiſpers
Were tame again, the time run out for wonder,
What muſt your own Command think, from whoſe Swords
Ye have taken off the edges, from whoſe valours
The due and recompence of Arms; nay, made it doubtful
Whither they knew obedience? muſt not theſe kill ye?
Say they are won to pardon ye, by meer miracle
Brought to forgive ye; what old valiant Souldier,
What man that loves to fight, and fight for Rome,
Will ever follow you more? dare ye know theſe ventures?
If ſo, I bring ye comfort; dare ye take it?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: No, no, Petillius, no.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: If your mind ſerve ye.
Ye may live ſtill; but how? yet pardon me,
You may outwear all too, but when? and certain
There is a mercy for each fault, if tamely
A man will take't upon conditions.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: No, by no means: I am only thinking now, Sir,
(For I am reſolved to go) of a moſt baſe death,
Fitting the baſeneſs of my fault. I'll hang.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Ye ſhall not; y'are a Gentleman I honor,
I would elſe flatter ye, and force ye live,
Which is far baſer. Hanging? 'tis a dogs death,
An end for ſlaves.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The fitter for my baſeneſs.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Beſides, the man that's hang'd, preaches his end,
And fits a ſign for all the world to gape at.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: That's true: I'll take a fitter poiſon.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: No,
'Tis equal ill; the death of rats and women,
Lovers, and lazie boys, that fear correction,
Die like a man.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Why my ſword then.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I, If your Sword be ſharp, Sir,
There's nothing under heaven that's like your Sword;
Your Sword's a death indeed.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: It ſhall be ſharp, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Why Mithridates was an arrant aſſe
To dye by poiſon, if all Boſphorus
Could lend him Swords: your Sword muſt do the deed:
'Tis ſhame to dye choak'd, fame to dye and bleed.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Thou haſt confirmed me: and, my good Petillius,
Tell me no more I may live.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: 'Twas my Commiſſion;
But now I ſee ye in a nobler way,
A way to make all even.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Fare-well, Captain:
Be a good man, and fight well: be obedient:
Command thy ſelf, and then thy men. Why ſhakeſt thou?

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I do not Sir.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I would thou hadſt, Petillius:
I would find ſomething to forſake the world with
Worthy the man that dies: a kind of earth-quake
Through all ſtern valors but mine own.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I feel now
A kind of trembling in me.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Keep it ſtill,
As thou lov'ſt virtue, keep it.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: And brave Captain,
The graet and honoured Penyus.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: That again:
O how it heightens me! again, Petillius.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Moſt excellent Commander.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Thoſe were mine,
Mine, only mine.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: They are ſtill.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Then to keep 'em
For ever falling more, have at ye, heavens,
Ye everlaſting powers, I am yours: The work's done,
That neither fire nor age, nor melting envy
Shall ever conquer. Carry my laſt words
To the great General: kiſs his hands and ſay,
My ſoul I give to heaven, my fault to juſtice
Which I have done upon my ſelf: my virtue,
If ever there was any in Poor Penyus,
Made more, and happier, light on him. I faint.
And where there is a foe, I wiſh him fortune.
I dye: lye lightly on my aſhes, gentle earth.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: And on my ſin. Farewell, great Penyus,
The ſouldier is in fury. Now I am glad
'Tis done before he comes. This way, for me,
The way of toile; for thee, the way of honor. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Druſus and Regulus with Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Sould.
sp.l: Kill him, kill him, kill him.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: What will ye do?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Good ſoldiers, honeſt ſoldiers.

sp.speaker: Sould.
sp.l: Kill him, kill him, kill him.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Kill us firſt; we command too.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Valiant Soldiers,
Conſider but whoſe life ye ſeek. O Druſus,
Bid him be gone, he dies elſe. Shall Rome ſay
(Ye moſt approved Souldiers) her dear children
Devoured the fathers of the fights? ſhall rage
And ſtubborn fury guide thoſe ſwords to ſlaughter,
To ſlaughter of their own, to civil ruine?

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: O let 'em in: all's done, all's ended, Regulus,
Penyus has found his laſt eclipſe. Come, Souldiers,
Come, and behold your miſeries: come bravely,
Full of your mutinous and bloody angers,
And here beſtow your darts. O only Romane,
O father of the Wars.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Why ſtand ye ſtupid?
Where be your killing furies? whoſe ſword now
Shall firſt be ſheath'd in Penyus? do ye weep?
Howl out, ye wretches, ye have cauſe: howl ever.
Who ſhall now lead ye fortunate? whoſe valor
Preſerve ye to the glory of your Countrey?
Who ſhall march out before ye, coy'd and courted
By all the Miſtriſſes of War, care, counſel,
Quick-ey'd experience, and victory twin'd to him?
Who ſhall beget ye deeds beyond inheritance
To ſpeak your names, and keep your honors living,
When children faill, and time that takes all with him,
Build houſes for ye to oblivion?

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: O ye poor deſperate fools: no more now, ſouldiers?
Go home, and hang your arms up; let ruſt rot 'em;
And humble your ſtern valors to ſoft prayers;
For ye have ſunk the frame of all your virtues;
The ſun that warm'd your bloods is ſet for ever:
I'll kiſs thy honor'd cheek. Farewell, great Penyus,
Thou thunder-bolt, farewell. Take up the body;
To morrow morning to the Camp convey it.
There to receive due Ceremonies. That eye
That blinds himſelf with weeping, gets moſt glory.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Swetonius, Junius, Decius, Demetrius, Curius, and Souldiers: Bonduca, two Daughters, and Nennius, above. Drum and Colours.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Bring up the Catapults and ſhake the wall,
We will not be out out-brav'd thus.

sp.speaker: Nen.
sp.l: Shake the earth,
Ye cannot ſhake our ſouls. Bring up your Rams,
And with their armed heads, make the Fort totter;
Ye do but rock us into death. Exit Nennius.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: See, Sir,
See the Icenian Queen in all her glory
From the ſtrong battlements proudly appearing,
As if ſhe meant to give us laſhes.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Yeild, Queen.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: I am unacquainted with that language, Roman.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Yield honour'd Lady, and expect our mercy,
We love thy nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: I thank ye, ye ſay well;
But mercy and love are ſins in Rome and hell.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Ye cannot ſcape our ſtrength; ye muſt yield, Lady,
Ye muſt adore and fear the power of Rome.
If Rome be earthly, why ſhould any knee
With bending adoration worſhip her?
She's vitious; and your partial ſelves confeſs,
Aſpires the height of all impiety:
Therefore 'tis fitter I ſhould reverence
The thatched houſes where the Britains dwell
In careleſs mirth, where the bleſt houſhold gods
See nought but chaſt and ſimple purity.
'Tis not high power that makes a place divine,
Nor that the men from gods derive their line
But ſacred thoughts in holy boſoms ſtor'd,
Make people noble, and the place ador'd.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Beat the wall deeper.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Beat it to the center,
We will not ſink one thought.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: I'll make ye.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: 2. Dau.
sp.l: O mother, theſe are fearful hours: ſpeak gently.
To theſe fierce men, they will afford ye pitty.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Pitty? thou fearful girl; 'tis for thoſe wretches
That miſery makes tame. Wouldſt thou live leſs?
Waſt not thou born a Princeſs? Can my blood,
And thy brave fathers ſpirit, ſuffer in thee
So baſe a ſeparation from thy ſelf,
As mercy from theſe Tyrants? Thou lov'ſt luſt ſure,
And long'ſt to proſtitute thy youth and beauty
To common ſlaves for bread. Say they had mercy;
The divel a relenting conſcience:
The lives of Kings reſt in their Diadems,
Which to their bodies lively ſouls do give,
And ceaſing to be Kings, they ceaſe to live.
Show ſuch another fear, and —
I'll fling thee to their fury.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: He is dead then?

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I think ſo certainly; yet all my means, Sir,
Even to the hazzard of my life—

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: No more:
We muſt not ſeem to mourn here.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: There's a breach made,
Is it your will we charge, Sir?

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Once more mercy,
Mercy to all that yield

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: I ſcorn to anſwer:
Speak to him girl; and hear thy Siſter.

sp.speaker: 1. Dau.
sp.l: General,
Hear me, and mark me well, and look upon me
Directly in my face, my womans face.
Whoſe only beauty is the hate it bears ye;
See with thy narroweſt eyes, thy ſharpeſt wiſhes,
Into my ſoul, and ſee what there inhabits;
See if one fear, one ſhadow of a terror,
One paleneſs dare appear but from my anger,
To lay hold on your mercies. No, ye fools,
Poor fortunes fools, we were not born for triumphs,
To follow your gay ſports, and fill your ſlaves
With hoots and acclamations.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Brave behaviour.

sp.speaker: 1. Dau.
sp.l: The children of as great as Rome, as noble,
Our names before her, and our deeds her envy;
Muſt we guild ore your Conqueſt, make your State,
That is not fairly ſtrong, but fortune?
No, no, ye Romans, we have ways to ſcape ye,
To make ye poor again, indeed our priſoners,
And ſtick our triumphs full.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: 's death, I ſhall love her.

sp.speaker: 1. Dau.
sp.l: To torture ye with ſuffering, like our ſlaves;
To make ye curſe our patience, wiſh the world
Were loſt again, to win us only, and eſteem
The end of all ambitions.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Do ye wonder?
We'll make our monuments in ſpite of fortune,
In ſpight of all your Eagles wings: we'll work
A pitch above ye; and from our height we'll ſtoop
As fearleſs of your bloody ſoars; and fortunate,
As if we prey'd on heartleſs doves.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Strange ſtiffneſs.
Decius, go charge the breach. Exit Decius.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Charge it home, Roman,
We ſhall deceive thee elſe. Where's Nennius?

sp.speaker: Nen.
sp.l: They have made a mighty breach.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Stick in thy body,
And make it good but half an hour.

sp.speaker: Nen.
sp.l: I'll do it.

sp.speaker: 1. Dau.
sp.l: And then be ſure to dye.

sp.speaker: Nen.
sp.l: It ſhall go hard elſe.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Fare well with all my heart; we ſhall meet yonder,
Where few of theſe muſt come.

sp.speaker: Nen.
sp.l: Gods take thee, Lady.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Bring up the ſwords, and poiſon.

div.stage: Enter one with Swords, and a great Cup.

sp.speaker: 2. Dau.
sp.l: O my fortune!

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: How, how, ye whore?

sp.speaker: 2. Dau.
sp.l: Good mother, nothing to offend ye.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Here, wench:
Behold us, Romans.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Mercy yet.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: No talking:
Puff, there goes all your pitty. Come, ſhort prayers,
And let's diſpach the buſineſs: you begin,
Shrink not; I'll ſee ye do't.

sp.speaker: 2. Dau.
sp.l: O gentle mother,
O Romans, O my heart; I dare not.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Woman, woman,
Unnatural woman.

sp.speaker: 2. Dau.
sp.l: O perſwade her, Romans:
Alaſs, I am young, and would live. Noble mother,
Can ye kill that ye gave life? are my years
Fit for deſtruction?

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Yield, and be a Queen ſtill,
A mother and a friend.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Ye talk: come, hold it,
And put it home.

sp.speaker: 1. Dau.
sp.l: Fie, ſiſter, fie,
What would you live to be?

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: A whore ſtill.

sp.speaker: 2 Dau.
sp.l: Mercy.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Hear her, thou wretched woman.

sp.speaker: 2 Dau.
sp.l: Mercy, mother:
O whither will you ſend me? I was once
Your darling, your delight.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: O gods,
Fear in my family? do it, and nobly.

sp.speaker: 2 Dau.
sp.l: O do not frown then.

sp.speaker: 1 Daugh.
sp.l: Do it, worthy Siſter:
'Tis nothing, 'tis a pleaſure; we'll go with ye,

sp.speaker: 2 Daugh.
sp.l: Oh if I knew but whither.

sp.speaker: 1 Daugh.
sp.l: To the bleſſed,
Where we ſhall meet our Father.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Woman.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Talk not.

sp.speaker: 1 Daugh.
sp.l: Where nothing but true joy is.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: That's a good wench, mine own ſweet girl; put it cloſe to thee.

sp.speaker: 2 Daugh.
sp.l: Oh comfort me ſtill for heavens ſake.

sp.speaker: 1 Daugh.
sp.l: Where eternal
Our youths are, and our beauties; where no Wars come,
Nor luſtful ſlaves to raviſh us.

sp.speaker: 2 Daugh.
sp.l: That ſteels me:
Along farewel to this world.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Good: I'll help thee.

sp.speaker: 1 Daugh.
sp.l: The next is mine.
Shew me a Roman Lady in all our ſtories,
Dare do this for her honor: they are cowards,
Eat coals like compell'd Cats: your great Saint Lucrece
Dy'd not for honor; Tarquin topt her well,
And mad ſhe could not hold him, bled.

sp.speaker: Petil.
sp.l: By—
am in love: I would give an hundred pound now
But to lie with this womans behaviour. Oh the devil.

sp.speaker: 1 Daugh.
sp.l: Ye ſhall ſee me example. All your Rome,
If I were proud and lov'd ambition;
If I were luſtful, all your ways of pleaſure;
If I were greedy, all the wealth ye conquer—

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: Make haſte.

sp.speaker: 1 Daugh.
sp.l: I will_Could not intice to live
But two ſhort hours this frailty: would ye learn
How to die bravely Romans, to fling off
This caſe of fleſh, loſe all your cares for ever?
Live as we have done, well, and fear the gods,
Hunt Honor, and not Nations with your ſwords,
Keep your minds humble, your devotions high;
So ſhall ye learn the nobleſt part, to die. Dies.

sp.speaker: Bend.
sp.l: I come, wench; to ye all Fates hangmen; you
That eaſe the aged deſtinies, and cut
The threds of Kingdoms, as they draw 'em: here,
Here's the draught would ask no leſs than Caeſar
To pledge it for the glories ſake.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Great Lady.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Make up your own conditions.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: So we will.

sp.speaker: Swet,
sp.l: Stay.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Stay,

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Be any thing.

sp.speaker: Bond.
sp.l: A Saint, Swetonius,
When thou ſhalt fear, and die like a ſlave. Ye fools,
Ye ſhould have ti'd up death firſt, when ye conquer'd,
Ye ſweat for us in vain elſe: ſee him here,
He's ours ſtill, and our friend; laughs at your pities;
And we command him with as eaſie reins
As do our enemies. I feel the poiſon.
Poor vanquiſh'd Romans, with what matchleſs tortures
Could I now rack ye? But I pittie ye,
Deſiring to die quiet: nay, ſo much
I hate to proſecute my victory,
That I will give ye counſel e'r I die.
If you will keep your Laws and Empire whole,
Place in your Romans fleſh, a Britain ſoul. Dies.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Deſperate and ſtrange,

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: 'Tis won, Sir, and the Britains
All put to th' ſword.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Give her fair Funeral;
She was truly noble, and a Queen.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: —Take it,
A Love-mange grown upon me? what, a ſpirit?

sp.speaker: Jun,
sp.l: I am glad of this, I have found ye.

sp.speaker: Petil.
sp.l: In my belly,
Oh how it tumbles?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Ye good gods, I thank ye. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Caratach upon a rock, and Hengo by him, ſleeping.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thus we afflicted Britains climb for ſafeties,
And to avoid our dangers, ſeek deſtructions;
Thus we awake to ſorrows. O thou Woman,
Thou agent for adverſities, what curſes
This day belong to thy improvidence?
To Britanie by thy means, what ſad millions
Of Widows weeping eyes? The ſtrong mans valour
Thou haſt betraid to fury; the childs fortune
To fear and want of friends, whoſe pieties
Might wipe his mournings off, and build his ſorrows
A houſe of reſt by his bleſt Anceſtors:
The Virgins thou haſt rob'd of all their wiſhes,
Blaſted their blowing hopes, turned their ſongs,
Their mirthful marriage-ſon • to funerals,
The Land thou haſt left a wilderneſs of wretches.
The boy begins to ſtir: thy ſafety made,
Would my ſoul were in Heaven.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: O noble Uncle,
Look out: I dream'd we were betrai'd.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: No harm, boy;
'Tis but thy emptineſs that breeds theſe fancies:
Thou ſhalt have meat anon,

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: A little, Uncle,
And I ſhall hold out bravely. What are thoſe?
Look, Uncle, look, thoſe multitudes that march there?
They come upon us ſtealing by.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I ſee 'em;
And prethee be not fearful.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Now ye hate me,
Would I were dead.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt I love thee dearly.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Did I e'r ſhrink yet, Uncle? were I a man now;
I ſhould be angry with ye.

div.stage: Enter Druſus, Regulus, and Soldiers, with Penyus's Herſe, Drums and Colours.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: My ſweet chicken,
See, they have reach'd us, and as it ſeems they bear
Some ſoldiers body, by their ſolemn geſtures,
And ſad ſolemnities; it well appears too
To be of eminence. Moſt worthy Soldiers,
Let me intreat your knowledge to inform me
What noble Body that is which you bear
With ſuch a ſad and ceremonious grief,
As if ye meant to wooe the World and Nature
To be in love with death? Moſt honorable
Excellent Romans, by your antient valours,
As ye love Fame, reſolve me.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: 'Tis the Body
Of the great Captain Penyus, by himſelf
Made cold and ſpiritleſs.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: O ſtay, ye Romans,
By the Religion which you owe thoſe gods
That lead ye on to Victories, by thoſe glories
Which made even pride a virtue in ye—

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Stay:
What's thy Will, Caratach

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Set down the body,
The body of the nobleſt of all Romans,
As ye expect an offering at your Graves
From your friends ſorrows, ſet it down awhile.
That with your griefs an enemy may mingle;
A noble enemy that loves a Soldier;
And lend a tear to virtue; even your foes,
Your wild foes, as you call'd us, are yet ſtor'd
With fair affections, our hearts freſh, our ſpirits,
Though ſometime ſtubborn, yet when virtue dies,
Soft and relenting as a Virgins prayers,
Oh ſet it down.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Set down the body, ſoidiers.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thou hallowed relique, thou rich Diamond
Cut with thine own duſt; thou for whoſe wide fame
The world appears too narrow, mans all thoughts,
Had they all tongues, too ſilent; thus I bow
To thy moſt honour'd aſhes: though an enemy,
Yet friend to all thy worths: ſleep peaceably;
Happineſs crown thy ſoul, and in thy earth
Some Lawrel fix his ſeat, there grow, and flouriſh,
And make thy grave an everlaſting triumph.
Farewell all glorious Wars, now thou art gone,
And honeſt Arms adieu: all noble battels
Maintain'd in thirſt of honour, not of bloud,
Farewell for ever.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Was this Roman, Uncle,
So good a man?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thou never knew'ſt thy Father.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: He dy'd before I was born.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: This worthy Roman
Was ſuch another piece of endleſs honor,
Such a brave ſoul dwelt in him: their proportions
And faces were not much unlik, boy; excellent nature,
See how it works into his eyes; mine own boy.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: The multitudes of theſe men, and their fortunes,
Could never make me fear yet: one mans goodneſs—

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: O now thou pleaſeſt me: weep ſtill, my child,
As if thou ſaw'ſt me dead; with ſuch a flux
Or flood of ſorrow: ſtill thou pleaſeſt me.
And worthy ſoldiers, pray receive theſe pledges,
Theſe hatchments of our griefs, and grace us ſo much
To place 'em on his Hearſe. Now if ye pleaſe,
Bear off the noble burden; raiſe his pile
High as Olympus, make heaven to wonder
To ſee a ſtar upon earth out-ſhining theirs.
And ever loved, ever living be
Thy honoured and moſt ſacred memory.

sp.speaker: Dru.
sp.l: Thou haſt done honeſtly, good Caratach,
And when thou dieſt, a thouſand virtuous Romans
Shall ſing thy ſoul to heaven. Now march on, ſoldiers.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Now dry thine eyes, my boy.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Are they all gone?
I could have wept this hour yet.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Come, take cheer,
And raiſe thy ſpirit, child: if but this day
Thou canſt bear out thy faintneſs, the night coming
I'll faſhion our eſcape.

sp.speaker: Heng.
sp.l: Pray fear not me;
Indeed I am very hearty.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Be ſo ſtill;
His miſchiefs leſſen, that controuls his ill. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: What do I ail, i'th' name of heaven I did but ſee her,
And ſee her die: ſhe ſtinks by this time ſtrongly,
Abominably ſtinks: ſhe was a woman,
A thing I never car'd for: but to die ſo,
So confidently, bravely, ſtrongly; Oh the devil,
I have the bots, by—ſhe ſcorn'd us ſtrangely,
All we could do, or durſt do; threatned us
With ſuch a noble anger, and ſo governed
With ſuch a fiery ſpirit—; the plain bots;
A—upon the bots, the love-bots: hang me,
Hang me even out o'th' way, directly hang me.
Oh penny pipers, and moſt painful penners
Of bountiful new Ballads, what a ſubject,
What a ſweet ſubject for your ſilver founds,
Is crept upon ye?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Here he is; have at him. Sings.
She ſet the ſword unto her Breaſt.
great pity it was to ſee,
That three drops of her Life-warm bloud,
run trickling down her knee.
Art thou there, bonny boy? and i'faith how doſt thou?

sp.speaker: Petil.
sp.l: Well, gramercie, how doſt thou? h'as found me,
Sented me out: the ſhame the devil ow'd me.
H'as kept his day with. And what news, Junius?

l.hi: It was an old tale ten thouſand times told,
Of a young Lady was turn'd into mold,
Her life it was lovely, her death it was bold.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: A cruel rogue, now h'as drawn, purſue it on me,
He hunts me like a devil. No more ſinging;
Thou haſt got a cold: come, let's go drink ſome Sack, boy.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha,

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Why doſt thou laugh?
What Mares neſt haſt thou found?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.
I cannot laugh alone: Decius, Demetrius,
Curius, oh my ſides, Ha, ha, ha,
The ſtrangeſt jeſt.

sp.speaker: Petil.
sp.l: Prethee no more.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: The admirableſt fooling.

sp.speaker: Pet,
sp.l: Thou art the prettieſt fellow.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Sirs.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Why Junius;
Prethee away, ſweet Junius.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Let me ſing then.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Whoa, here's a ſtir now: ſing a ſong o' ſix pence,
By—(if) prethee;—on't: Junius.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: I muſt either ſing; or laugh.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: And what's your reaſon?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: What's that to you?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: And I muſt whiſtle.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Do ſo.
Oh, I hear 'em coming.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I have a little buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not go, believe it: what a Gentleman
Of thy ſweet converſation?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Captain Junius,
Sweet Captain, let me go with all celerity;
Things are not always one: and do not queſtion,
Nor jeer, nor gybe: none of your doleful Ditties,
Nor your ſweet converſation, you will find then
I may be anger'd.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: By no means, Petillius;
Anger a man that never knew paſſion?
'Tis moſt impoſſible: a noble Captain,
A wiſe and and generous Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Pet.

l.hi: Tom Puppie.

sp.l: Leave this way to abuſe me: I have found ye,
But for your mothers ſake I will fo • give ye.
Your ſubtil underſtanding may diſcover
(As you think) ſome trim toy to make you merry;
Some ſtraw to tickle ye; but do not truſt to't;
Y' are a young man, and may do well: be ſober:
Carry your ſelf diſcreetly.

sp.speaker: Jun,
sp.l: Yes forſooth.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: How does the brave Petillius?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Monſtrous merry:
We two were talking what a kind of thing
I was when I was in love; what a ſtrange monſter
For little Boys and Girls to wonder at;
How like a fool I lookt.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: So they do all,
Like great dull ſlavering fools.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Petillius ſaw too.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: No more of this, 'tis ſcurvie, peace.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: How naſtily,
Indeed, how beaſtly all I did became me?
How I forgot to blow my noſe? there he ſtands,
An honeſt and a wiſe man; if himſelf
(I dare avouch it boldly, for I know it)
Should find himſelf in love—

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I am angry.

sp.speaker: Jun,
sp.l: Surely his wiſe ſelf would hang his beaſtly ſelf,
His underſtanding-ſelf ſo mawl his aſs-ſelf—

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: He's bound to do it; for he knows the follies,
The poverties, and baſeneſs that belongs to't,
Ha's read upon the reformations long.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: He has ſo.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: 'Tis true, and he muſt do't:
Nor is it fit indeed any ſuch coward—

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: You'll leave prating.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Should dare come near the Regiments, eſpecially
Thoſe curious puppies (for believe there are ſuch)
That only love behaviours: thoſe are dog-whelps,
Dwindle away, becauſe a Woman dies well;
Commit with paſſions only: fornicate
With the free ſpirit merely: you, Petillius,
For you have long obſerv'd the World.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Doſt thou hear?
I'll beat thee damnably within theſe three hours:
Go pray; may be I'll kill thee. Farewel Jack-daws. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: What a ſtrange thing he's grown?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: I am glad he is ſo;
And ſtranger he ſhall be before I leave him.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Is 't poſſible her mere death—

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: I obſerv'd him,
And found him taken, infinitely taken
With her bravery, I have follow'd him,
And ſeen him kiſs his ſword ſince, court his ſcabbard,
Call dying, dainty deer; her brave mind, Miſtriſs;
Caſting a thouſand ways, to give thoſe forms,
That he might lie with 'em, and get old Armors:
He had got me o' th' hip once: it ſhall go hard, friends,
But he ſhall find his own coin.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: How now Macer?
Is Judas yet come in? Enter Judas.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Yes, and has loſt
Moſt of his men too. Here he is.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: What news?

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: I have lodg'd him; rouze him he that dares.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Where, Judas?

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: On a ſteep rock i' th' woods, the boy too with him,
And there he ſwears he will keep his Chriſtmas Gentlemen,
But he will come away with full conditions,
Bravely, and like a Britain: he paid part of us.
Yet I think we fought bravely: for mine own part,
I was four ſeveral times at half ſword with him,
Twice ſtood his partizan: but the plain truth is,
He's a meer devil, and no man; i' th' end he ſwing'd us,
And ſwing'd us ſoundly too, he fights by Witchcraft:
Yet for all that I ſee him lodg'd.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Take more men,
And ſcout him round. Macer, march you along.
What victuals has he?

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Not a piece of Bisket,
Not ſo much as will ſtop a tooth; nor Water,
More than they make themſelves: they lie
Juſt like a brace of Bear-whelps, cloſe, and crafty,
Sucking their fingers for their food.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Cut off then
All hope of that way: take ſufficient forces.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: But uſe no foul play, on your lives: that man
That does him miſchief by deceit, I'll kill him.

sp.speaker: Macer.
sp.l: He ſhall have fair play, he deſerves it.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Hark ye.
What ſhould I do there then? you are brave Captains,
Moſt valiant men; go up your ſelves; uſe virtue,
See what will come on't: pray the Gentleman
To come down, and be taken. Ye all know him,
I think ye have felt him too: there ye ſhall find him,
His ſword by his ſide, plums of a pound weight by him
Will make your chops ake: you'll find it a more labour
To win him living, than climbing of a Crows-neſt.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Away, and compaſs him; we ſhall come up
I am ſure within theſe two hours. Watch him cloſe.

sp.speaker: Macer.
sp.l: He ſhall flee thorow the air, if he eſcape us.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: What's this loud lamentation?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: The dead body
Of the great Penyus is new come to the Camp, Sir.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Dead!

sp.speaker: Macer.
sp.l: By himſelf, they ſay.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: I fear'd that fortune.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Peace guide him up to heaven.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l:
Away good Macer.
Exeunt Macer and Judas.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: If thou be'ſt guilty,
Some ſullen plague thou hat'ſt moſt light upon thee.
The Regiment return on Junius,
He well deſerves it.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Draw out three Companies,
Yours Decius, Junius, and thou Petillius,
And make up inſtantly to Caratach,
He's in the Wood before ye; we ſhall follow
After due ceremony done to the dead,
The noble dead: Come: let's go burn the Body.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: The Regiment given from me; diſgrac'd openly;
In love too with a trifle to abuſe me?
A merry world, a fine world: ſerv'd ſeven years
To be an aſs o'both ſides, ſweet Petillius,
You have brought your hogs to a fine market: you are wiſe, Sir,
Your honourable brain-pan full of crotchets,
And underſtanding Gentleman; your projects
Caſt with aſſurance ever: wouldſt not thou now
Be bang'd about the pate, Petillius
Anſwer to that ſweet ſoldier; ſurely, ſurely,
I think ye would; pull'd by the noſe, kick'd; hang thee,
Thou art the arrant'ſt Raſcal: truſt thy wiſdom
With any thing of weight; the wind with feathers.
Out ye blind puppie; you command? you govern?
Dig for a groat a day, or ſerve a Swine-herd;
Too noble for thy nature too. I muſt up;
But what I ſhall do there, let time diſcover. Exit

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Macer and Judas, with meat and a bottle,

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Hang it o' th' ſide o' th' rock, as though the Britains
Stole hither to relieve him; who firſt ventures
To fetch it off, is ours. I cannot ſee him.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: He lies cloſe in a hole above, I know it,
Gnawing upon his anger: ha? no, 'tis not he,

sp.speaker: Macer.
sp.l: 'Tis but the ſhaking of the boughs,

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: —Shake 'em,
I am ſure they ſhake me ſoundly. There.

sp.speaker: Macer.
sp.l: 'Tis nothing.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Make no noiſe if he ſtir, a deadly tempeſt
Of huge ſtones fall upon us: 'tis done: away cloſe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Sleep ſtill, ſleep ſweetly child, 'tis all thou feedſt on.

No gentle Britain
• ear; no valiant charity
To bring thee food? poor knave, thou art ſick extreme ſick,
Almoſt grown wild for meat; and yet thy goodneſs
Will not confeſs, nor ſhew it. All the woods
Are double lin'd with ſoldiers; no way left us
To make a noble ſcape: I'll ſit down by thee,
And when thou wak'ſt, either get meat to ſave thee,
O • loſe my life i'th' purchaſe, Good gods comfort thee.

sp.speaker: Guide.
sp.l: Ye are not far off now, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Draw the Companies
The cloſeſt way thorow the woods; we'll keep on this way.

sp.speaker: Guide.
sp.l: I will Sir: half a furlong more you'll come
Within the ſight o' th' Rock; keep on the left ſide,
You'll be diſcover'd elſe: I'll lodge your Companies
In the wild Vines beyond ye.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: Do ye mark him?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Yes, and am ſorry for him.

sp.speaker: Petill.

l.hi: Junius,

sp.l: Pray let me ſpeak two words with you.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Walk afore,
I'll overtake ye ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Dec.
sp.l: I will. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Now, Captain.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: You have oft told me, you have lov'd me, Junius.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Moſt ſure I told you truth then.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: And that love
Should not deny me any honeſt thing.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: It ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Dare ye ſwear it?
I have forgot all paſſages between us
That have been ill, forgiven too, forgot you.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: What would this man have? By — I do, Sir,
So it be fit to grant ye.

sp.speaker: Petell.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt honeſt.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Why, then I'll do it.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Kill me.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Pray kill me.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Kill ye?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I, kill me quickly, ſuddenly,
Now kill me.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: On what reaſon? ye amaze me.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: If ye do love me, kill me, ask me not why:
I would be killed, and by you.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Mercy on me,
What ails this man? Petillius.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Pray ye diſpatch me,
Ye are not ſafe whilſt I live: I am dangerous,
Troubled extreamly, even to miſchief, Junius,
An enemy to all good men: fear not, 'tis juſtice;
I ſhall kill you elſe.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Tell me but the cauſe,
And I will do it.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I am diſgrac'd, my ſervice
Slighted, and unrewarded by the General,
My hopes left wild and naked; beſides theſe,
I am grown ridiculous, an aſs, a folly
I dare not truſt my ſelf with: prethee kill me.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: All theſe may be redeem'd as eaſily
As you would heal your finger.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Nay—

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Stay, I'll do it,
You ſhall not need your anger: But firſt, Petillius,
You ſhall unarm your ſelf; I dare not truſt
A man ſo bent to miſchief.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: There's my ſword;
And do it handſomely.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Yes, I will kill ye,
Believe that certain: but firſt I'll lay before ye
The moſt extreme fool ye have plaid in this,
The honor purpos'd for ye, the great honor
The General intended ye,

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: And then I'll kill ye,
Becauſe ye ſhall die miſerable. Know Sir,
The Regiment was given me, but till time
Call'd ye to do ſome worthy deed, might ſtop
The peoples ill thoughts of ye, for Lord Penyus,
I mean his death. How ſoon this time's come to ye,
And haſted by Swetonius? Go, ſays he,
Junius and Decius, and go thou Petillius;
Diſtinctly, thou Petillius, and draw up,
To take ſtout Caratach; there's the deed purpos'd,
A deed to take off all faults, of all natures:
And thou Petillius; Mark it, there's the honor,
And that done, all made even.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Stay.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: No, I'll kill ye.
He knew thee abſolute, and full in ſoldier,
Daring beyond all dangers, found thee out
According to the boldneſs of thy ſpirit,
A Subject, ſuch a Subject.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Harke ye Junius,
I will live now.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: By no means. Wooed thy worth,
Held thee by the chin up, as thou ſunk'ſt, and ſhew'd thee
How Honor held her arms out: Come, make ready,
Since ye will die an aſs.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Thou wilt not kill me?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: By—but I will, Sir: I'll have no man dangerous
Live to deſtroy me afterward. Beſides, you have gotten
Honor enough, let young men riſe now. Nay,
I do perceive too by the General, (which is
One main cauſe ye ſhall die) how e'r he carry it,
Such a ſtrong doting on ye, that I fear,
You ſhall command in chief: how are we paid then?
Come, if you will pray, diſpatch it.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Is there no way?

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Not any way to live.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: I will do any thing,
Redeem my ſelf at any price: good Junius,
Let me but die upon the Rock, but offer
My life up like a Soldier.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: You will ſeek then
To out-doe every man.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Believe it Junius,
You ſhall goe ſtroke by ſtroke with me.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: You'l leave off too,
As you are noble, and a ſoldier,
For ever theſe mad fancies.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Dare ye truſt me?
By all that's good and honeſt.

sp.speaker: Jun,
sp.l: There's your ſword then,
And now come on a new man: Virtue guide thee. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Caratach, and Hengo on the Rock.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Courage my Boy, I have found meat: look Hengo,
Look where ſome bleſſed Britain, to preſerve thee,
Has hung a little food and drink: cheer up Boy,
Do not forſake me now.

sp.speaker: Hengo.
sp.l: Oh Uncle. Uncle,
I feel I cannot ſtay long: yet I'll fetch it,
To keep your noble life: Uncle, I am heart-whole,
And would live.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt, long I hope.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: But my head, Uncle:
Methinks the Rock goes round.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Mark 'em well, Judas.

sp.speaker: Jud.
sp.l: Peace, as you love your life.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Do not you hear
The noiſe of Bels?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Of Bels Boy? 'tis thy fancie,
Alas, thy bodies full of wind.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Methinks, Sir,
They ring a ſtrange ſad knell, a preparation
To ſome near funeral of State: nay, weep not,
Mine own ſweet Uncle, you will kill me ſooner.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Oh my poor chicken.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Fie, faint-hearted Uncle:
Come, tie me in your Belt, and let me down.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I'll go my ſelf Boy.

sp.speaker: Hengo.
sp.l: No, as ye love me, Uncle;
I will not eat it, if I do not fetch it;
The danger only I deſire: pray tie me.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I will, and all my care hang o'r thee: come child,
My valiant child,

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Let me down apace, Uncle,
And ye ſhall ſee how like a Daw I'll whip it
From all their policies: for 'tis moſt certain
A Roman train: and ye muſt hold me ſure too,
You'll ſpoil all elſe. When I have brought it Uncle,
We'll be as merry—

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Go i' th' name of heaven, Boy.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Quick, quick, Uncle, I have it. Oh.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: What ail'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: O my beſt Uncle, I am ſlain.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I ſee ye, and heaven direct my hand: deſtruction
Caratach kills Judas with a ſtone from the rock.
Go with thy coward ſoul. How doſt thou Boy?
Oh villain, pocky villain.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Oh Uncle, Uncle,
Oh how it pricks me: am I preſerv'd for this?
Extremely pricks me.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Coward, raſcal Coward,
Dogs eat thy fleſh.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Oh I bleed hard: I faint too, out upon't,
How ſick I am? the lean Rogue, Uncle.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Look Boy,
I have laid him ſure enough.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Have ye knockt his brains out?

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I warrant thee for ſtirring more: cheer up, child.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Hold my ſides hard, ſtop, ſtop, oh wretched fortune,
Muſt we part thus? Still I grow ſicker, Uncle.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Heaven look upon this noble child.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I once hop'd
I ſhould have liv'd to have met theſe bloody Romans
At my ſwords point, to have reveng'd my Father,
To have beaten 'em: oh hold me hard. But Uncle—

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt live ſtill I hope Boy. Shall I draw it?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Ye draw away my ſoul then, I would live
A little longer; ſpare me heavens, but only
To thank you for your tender love. Good Uncle,
Good noble Uncle weep not.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Oh my chicken,
My dear Boy, what ſhall I loſe?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Why, a child,
That muſt have died however: had this ſcap'd me,
Feaver or famine—I was born to die. Sir.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: But thus unblown, my boy?

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I go the ſtraighter
My journey to the gods: Sure I ſhall know ye
When ye come, Uncle.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Yes, Boy

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: And I hope
We ſhall enjoy together that great bleſſedneſs
You told me of.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Moſt certain, child.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: I grow cold,
Mine eyes are going.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Lift 'em up.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Pray for me;
And noble Uncle, when my bones are aſhes,
Think of your little Nephew. Mercy.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Mercy.
You bleſſed Angels take him.

sp.speaker: Hen.
sp.l: Kiſs me: ſo.
Farewel, farewel. Dies.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Farewel the hopes of Britain,
Thou Royal graft, Farewel for ever. Time and Death,
Ye have done your worſt. Fortune now ſee, now proudly
Pluck off thy vail, and view thy triumph: Look
Look what thou haſt brought this Land to. Oh fair flower,
How lovely yet thy ruines ſhow, how ſweetly
Even death embraces thee! The peace of heaven,
The fellowſhip of all great ſouls be with thee.
sp.stage: Enter Petillius and Junius on the rock.
sp.l: Hah? dare ye Romans? ye ſhall win me bravely.
Thou art mine. Fight

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Not yet, Sir,

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Breath ye, ye poor Romans,
And come up all, with all your antient valors,
Like a rough wind I'll ſhake your ſouls, and ſend 'em—

div.stage: Enter Swetonius, and all the Roman Captains.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Yield thee bold Caratach; by all—
As I am Soldier, as I envie thee,
I'll uſe thee like thy ſelf, the valiant Britain.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Brave ſoldier yield; thou ſtock of Arms and Honor,
Thou filler of the World with Fame and Glory.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: Moſt worthy man, we'll wooe thee, be thy priſoners.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Excellent Britain, do me but that Honor,
That more to me than Conqueſts, that true happineſs,
To be my friend.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Oh Romans, ſee what here is:
Had this Boy liv'd—

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: For Fames ſake, for thy Swords ſake,
As thou deſireſt to build thy virtues greater:
By all that's excellent in man, and honeſt—

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I do believe: Ye have had me a brave foe;
Make me a noble friend, and from your Goodneſs,
Give this Boy honourable earth to lie in.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: He ſhall have fitting Funeral.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: I yield then.
Not to your blows, but your brave courteſies.

sp.speaker: Petill.
sp.l: Thus we conduct then to the arms of Peace
The wonder of the World.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Thus I embrace thee, Flouriſh.
And let it be no flattery that I tell thee,
Thou art the only Soldier.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: How to thank ye,
I muſt hereafter find upon your uſage.
I am for Rome.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Ye muſt.

sp.speaker: Car.
sp.l: Then Rome ſhall know
