The man that makes her ſpring of glory grow.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Petillius, you have ſhown much worth this day,
redeem'd much error,
Ye have my love again; preſerve it, Junius,
With you I make him equal in the Regiment.

sp.speaker: Jun.
sp.l: The elder and the nobler: I'll give place, Sir.

sp.speaker: Swet.
sp.l: Ye ſhew a friends ſoul.
March on, and through the Camp in every tongue.
The Virtues of great Caratach be ſung.

div.head: The Knight of the Burning Peſtle.
To the Readers of this COMEDY.
div.p: GEntlemen, the World is ſo nice in theſe our times, that for Apparel, there is no faſhion, For Muſick, which is a rare Art, (though now ſlighted) No Inſtrument; For Diet, none but the French Kickſhoes that are delicate; and for Plaies, no invention but that which now runneth an invective way, touching ſome particular perſons, or elſe it is contemned before it is throughly underſtood. This is all that I have to ſay, That the Author had no intent to wrong any one in this Comedy, but as a merry paſſage, here and there interlaced t with delight, which he hopes will pleaſe all, and be hurtful to none.

div.head: The PROLOGUE.
div.p: WHere the Bee can ſuck no Honey, ſhe leaves her ſting behind; and where the Bear cannot find Origanum to heal his grief, he blaſteth all other leaves with his breath. We fear it is like to fare ſo with us; that ſeeing you cannot draw from our labours ſweet content, you leave behind you a ſower miſ-like, and with open reproach blame our good meaning, becauſe you cannot reap the wonted mirth. Our intent was at this time to move inward delight, not outward lightneſs; and to b breed (if it might be) ſoft ſmiling, not loud laughing: knowing it (to the wiſe) to be a great pleaſure, to hear Counſel mixed with Wit, as to the fooliſh to have ſport mingled with rudeneſs. They were baniſhed the Theater of Athens, and from Rome hiſſed, that brought Paraſites on the Stage with apiſh actions, or Fools with uncivil habits, or Courtezans with immodeſt words. We have endeavoured to be as far from unſeemly ſpeeches, to make your ears glow, as we hope you will be free from unkind reports, or miſtaking the Authors intention (who never aimed at any one particular in this Play,) to make our cheeks bluſh. And thus I leave it, and thee to thine own cenſure, to like, or diſlike. Vale.

list.head: The Actors Names.
list.item: The Citizens wife, and Ralph her man, ſitting below amidſt the Spectators.
Maſter Humphrey, a friend to the Merchant.
Michael, a ſecond Son of Miſtriſs Merry-thought.
A Boy that Danceth and Singeth.

div.l: FRrom all that's near the Court, from all that's great
Within the compaſs of the City-walls
We now have brought our Scene.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Hold your peace good-man boy.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: What do you mean Sir?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: That you have no good meaning: Theſe ſeven years there hath been Plays at this Houſe, I have obſerved it, you have ſtill girds at Citizens; and now you call your Play The London Merchant. Down with your Title, Boy, down with your Title.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Are you a member of the noble City?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: I am.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: And a Free-man?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Yea, and a Grocer.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: So Grocer, then by your ſweat favour, we intend no abuſe to the City.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: No ſir,
Yes ſir,
If you were not reſolv'd to play the Jacks,
What need you ſtudy for new ſubjects,
Purpoſely to abuſe your betters?
Why could not you be contented,
As well as others,
With the Legend of Whittington,
Or the life and death of Sir Thomas Greſham?
With the building of the Royal Exchange?
Or the ſtorie of Queen Elenor,
With the rearing of London bridge upon Woollſacks?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: You ſeem to be an underſtanding man:
What would you have us do ſir?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Why?
Preſent ſomething notably
In honor of the Commons of the City.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Why,
What do you ſay, to the life and death of fat Drake,
Or the repairing of Fleet Privies?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: I do not like that,
But I will have a Citizen,
And he ſhall be of my own Trade.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Oh,
You ſhould have told us your mind
A month ſince,
Our Play is ready to begin now.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: 'Tis all one for that,
I will have a Grocer,
And he ſhall do admirable things.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: What will you have him do?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Marry I will have him—

sp.speaker: Wife,
sp.l: Husband, Husband.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Peace, Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Hold thy peace Ralph,
I know what I do,
I warrant ye.
Husband, Husband.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: What ſay'ſt thou Conie?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Let him kill a Lion with a Peſtle Husband,
Let him kill a Lion with a Peſtle.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: So he ſhall,
I'll have him kill a Lion with a peſtle.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Husband,
Shall I come up Husband?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: I Cony.
Ralph, help your Miſtriſs this way:
Pray Gentlemen make her a little room,
I pray you ſir
Lend me your hand to help up my Wife:
I thank you ſir.
So.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: By your leave Gentlemen all,
I'm ſomething troubleſome,
I'm a ſtranger here,
I was ne'r at one of theſe Play, as they ſay, before;
But I ſhould have ſeen Jane Shore once,
And my Husband
Hath promiſed me any time this Twelvemonth,
To carrie me to the Bold Beauchams,
But in truth he did not;
I pray you bear with me.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Boy,
Let my Wife and I have a couple of ſtools,
And then begin,
And let the Grocer do rare things.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: But ſir,
We have never a Boy to play him,
Every one hath a part already.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Husband, Husband,
For gods ſake let Ralph play him,
Beſhrew me if I do not think
He will go beyond them all.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Well remembred wife,
Come up Ralph,
I'll tell you Gentlemen,
Let them but lend him a ſuit of reparrel, and neceſſaries,
And by gad,
If any of them all blow wind in the tail on him,
I'll be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I pray you youth,
Let him have a ſuit of reparrel,
I'll be ſworn Gentlemen,
My Husband tells you true,
He will act you ſometimes at our houſe,
That all the neighbors cry out on him:
He will fetch you up a couraging part ſo in the Garret,
That we are all as fear'd I warrant you,
That we quake again:
We'll fear our children with him,
If they be never ſo unruly,
Do but cry,
Ralph comes, Ralph comes to them,
And they'll be as quiet as Lambs.
Hold up thy head Ralph,
Shew the Gentlemen what thou canſt do,
Speak a huffing part,
I warrant you the Gentlemen will accept of it.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Do Ralph, do.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: By heaven
(Methinks) it were an eaſie leap
To pluck bright honor from the pale-fac'd Moon,
Or dive into the bottom of the Sea,
Where never fathome line toucht any ground,
And pluck up drowned honor
From the lake of Hell.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: How ſay you Gentlemen,
Is it not as I told you?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Nay Gentlemen,
He hath plaid before, my husband ſays, Muſidorus
Before the Wardens of our company.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: I, and he ſhould have plaid Jeronimo
With a ſhoo-maker for a wager.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: He ſhall have a ſuit of apparel,
If he will go in.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: In Ralph, in Ralph,
And ſet out the Grocers in their kind,
If thou lov'ſt me.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I warrant our Ralph will look finely,
When he's dreſt,

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: But what will you have it call'd?

l.hi: The Grocers Honor.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Methinks,

Me 〈◊〉
The Knight of the bunrning Peſtle were better.
I'll be ſworn Husband.
•• at's as good a name as can be.

sp.speaker: Cit,
sp.l: Let it be ſo, begin, begin;
My Wife and I will ſit down.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I pray you do.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: What ſtately Muſick have you?
You have Shawnes.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Shawns? no.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: No?
I'm a thief if my mind did not give me ſo.
Ralph plaies a ſtately part,
And he muſt needs have Shawns:
I'll be at the charge of them my ſelf,
Rather than we'll be without them.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: So you are like to be.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Why and ſo I will be,
There's two ſhillings,
Let's have the Waits of Southwark,
They are as rare fellows as any are in England;
And that will fetch them all o'r the water, with a vengeance,
As if they were mad.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: You ſhall have them:
Will you ſit down then?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: I, come Wife.

sp.speaker: Wifc.
sp.l: Sit you merry all Gentlemen,
I'm bold to ſit amongſt you for my eaſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: From all that's near the Court,
From all that's great
Within the compaſs of the City walls,
We now have brought our Scaene:
Flie far from hence
All private taxes, immodeſt phraſes,
What e'r may but ſhew like vicious:
For wicked mirth never true pleaſure brings,
But honeſt minds are pleas'd with honeſt things.
Thus much for that we do:
But for Ralphs part
You muſt anſwer for your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Take you no care for Ralph,
He'll diſcharge himſelf I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I'faith Gentlemen,
I'll give my my word for Ralph.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Merchant and Jaſper his Man.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Sirrah, I'll make you know you are my Prentice,
And whom my charitable love redeem'd
Even from the fall of fortune; gave thee heat
And growth, to be what now thou art, new caſt thee,
Adding the truſt of all I have at home,
In forreign Staples, or upon the Sea
To thy direction, ti'de the good opinions
Both of ſelf and friends to thy endeavors,
So fair were thy beginnings: but with theſe
As I remember you had never charge,
To love your Maſters Daughter, and even then,
When I had found a wealthy Husband for her,
I take it, Sir, you had not: but however,
I'll break the neck of that Commiſſion,
And make you know you are but a Merchants Factor.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Sir,
I do liberally confeſs I am yours,
Bound both by love and duty to your ſervice;
In which my labor hath been all my profit;
I have not loſt in bargain, nor delighted
To wear your honeſt gains upon my back,
Nor have I given a penſion to my bloud,
Or laviſhly in play conſum'd your ſtock.
Theſe, and the miſeries that do attend them,
I dare with innocence, proclaim are ſtrangers
To all my temperate actions: for your Daughter,
If there be any love to my deſervings,
Born by her virtuous ſelf, I cannot ſtop it:
Nor am I able to refrain her wiſhes.
She's private to her ſelf, and beſt of knowledge,
Whom ſhe'll make ſo happy as to ſigh for·
Beſides, I cannot think you mean to match her,
Unto a fellow of ſo lame a preſence,
One that hath little left of Nature in him.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: 'Tis very well, Sir, I can tell your wiſdom
How all this ſhall be cur'd.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Your care becomes you.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.l: And thus it ſhall be, Sir, I here diſcharge you,
My houſe, and ſervice, take your liberty,
And when I want a Son I'll ſend for you.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Theſe be the fair rewards of them that love,
Oh you that live in freedom never prove
The travel of a mind led by deſire.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Why how now friend, ſtruck with my Fathers thunder?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Struck, and ſtruck dead, unleſs the remedy
Be full of ſpeed and virtue; I am now,
What I expected long, no more your father's.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: But mine.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: But yours, and only yours I am,
That's all I have to keep me from the ſtatute:
You dare be conſtant ſtill?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: O fear me not.
In this I dare be better than a woman.
Nor ſhall his anger, nor his offers move me,
Were they both equal to a Princes power.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: You know my Rival?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Yes, and love him dearly,
Even as I love an ague, or foul weather,
I prethee Jaſper fear him not.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Oh no,
I do not mean to do him ſo much kindneſs,
But to our own deſires you know the plot
We both agreed on.
Yes, and will perform
My part exactly.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: I deſire no more,
Farewel, and keep my heart, 'tis yours.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: I take it,
He muſt do miracles,
Makes me forſake it.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Fie upon 'em little infidels,
What a matter's here now?
Well, I'll be hang'd for a half-penny,
If there be not ſome abomination knavery in this Play,
Well, let 'em look to't,
Ralph muſt come,
And if there be any tricks a brewing —

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Let 'em brew and bake too Husband, a gods name,
Ralph will find all out I warrant you,
And they were older than they are.
I pray my pretty youth, is Ralph ready?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: He will be preſently.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Now I pray you make my commendations unto him,
And withal, carry him this ſtick of Licoras,
Tell him his Miſtriſs ſent it him,
And bid him Miſtriſs ſent it him,
'Twill open his pipes the better, ſay.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Come, Sir, ſhe's yours, upon my faith ſhe's yours,
You have my hand, for other idle letts
Between your hopes and her, thus, with a wind,
They are ſcattered, and no more: my wanton Prentice,
That like a bladder blew himſelf with love,
I have lett out, and ſent him to diſcover
New maſters yet unknown.

sp.speaker: Humph.
sp.l: I thank you Sir,
Indeed I thank you, Sir, and e'r I ſtir,
It ſhall be known however you do deem,
I am of gentle blood and gentle ſeem.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Oh Sir, I know it certain.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Sir, my friend,
Although as Writers ſay, all things have end,
And that we call a Pudding, hath his two,
Oh let it not ſeem ſtrange I pray to you,
If in this bloudy ſimile, I put
My love, more endleſs, than frail things or gut.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Husband,
I prethee ſweet lamb tell me one thing,
But tell me truly:
Stay youths I beſeech you,
Till I queſtion my Husband.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: What is it Mouſe?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Sirrah,
Didſt thou ever ſee a prettier child?
How it behaves it ſelf, I warrant ye:
And ſpeaks and looks, and pearts up the head?
I pray you brother with your favour,
Were you never none of Mr. Moncaſters Scholars?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Chickin,
I prethee heartily contain thy ſelf,
The childer are pretty childer,
But when Ralph comes, Lamb.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I when Ralph comes, Conie,
Well my youth you may proceed

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Well Sir, you know my love, and reſt, I hope
Aſſur'd of my conſent; get but my daughters,
And wed her when you pleaſe: you muſt be bold,
And clap in cloſe unto her, come, I know
You have language good enough to win a wench.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: A whoreſone tyrant,
Hath been an old ſtringer in his days,
I warrant him.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: I take your gentle offer, and withal
Yield love again for love reciprocal.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What Luce, within there?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Call'd you Sir?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I did
Give entertainment to this Gentleman,
And ſee you be not froward to her, Sir:
My preſence will but be an eye-ſoar to you.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Fair Miſtriſs Luce, how do you, are you well?
Give me your hand, and then I pray you tell,
How doth your little Siſter, and your Brother?
And whether you love me or any other.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Sir, theſe are quickly anſwer'd.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: So they are,
Where Women are not cruel: but how far
Is it now diſtant from the place we are in,
Unto that bleſſed place your Fathers Warren.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: What makes you think of that, Sir?

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Even that face,
For ſtealing Rabbets whilome in that place,
God Cupid, or the Keeper, I know not whether,
Unto my coſt and charges brought you thither,
And there began.

sp.speaker: Luec.
sp.l: Your game, Sir.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Let no game,
Or any thing that tendeth to the ſame,
Be evermore remembred, thou fair killer
For whom I ſate me down and brake my Tiller.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: There's a kind Gentleman, I warrant you, when will you do as much for me George?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Beſhrew me Sir, I am ſorry for your loſſes,
But as the proverb ſays, I cannot cry,
I would you had not ſeen me.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: So would I.
Unleſs you had more maw to do me good.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Why, cannot this ſtrange paſſion be withſtood,
Send for a Conſtable and raiſe the Town.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Oh no, my valiant love will batter down
Millions of Conſtables, and put to flight,
Even that great Watch of Midſummer day at night.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Beſhrew me, Sir, 'twere good I yielded then,
Weak Women cannot hope, where valiant men
Have no reſiſtance.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Yield then, I am full
Of pity, though I ſay it, and can pull
Out of my pocket thus a pair of Gloves.
Look Lucy, look, the dogs tooth, nor the Doves
Are not ſo white as theſe; and ſweet they be,
And whipt about with ſilk, as you may ſee:
If you deſire the price, ſute from your eye,
I beam to this place, and you ſhall eſpie
F. S. which is to ſay my ſweeteſt Honey,
They coſt me three and two pence, or no money.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Well Sir, I take them kindly, and I thank you;
What would you more?

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Why then farewel.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Nor ſo, nor ſo, for Lady I muſt tell,
Before we part, for what we met together,
God grant me time, and patience, and fair weather.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Speak and declare your mind in terms ſo brief.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: I ſhall; then firſt and foremoſt for relief
I call to you, if that you can afford it,
I care not at what price, for on my word, it
Shall be repaid again, although it coſt me
More than I'll ſpeak of now, for love hath toſt me
In furious blanket like a Tennis-ball,
And now I riſe aloft, and now I fall.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Alas good Gentleman, alas the day.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: I thank you heartily, and as I ſay,
Thus do I ſtill continue without reſt,
I' th' morning like a man, at night a beaſt,
Roaring and bellowing mine own diſquiet,
That much I fear, forſaking of my diet,
Will bring me preſently to that quandary,
I ſhall bid all adieu.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Now by S. Mary
That were great pity.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: So it were beſhrew me,
Then eaſe me luſty Luce, and pity ſhew me.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Why Sir, you know my will is nothing worth
Without my Fathers grant, get his conſent,
And then you may with aſſurance try me.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: The Worſhipful your Sire will not deny me,
For I have ask'd him, and he hath reply'd,
Sweet Maſter Humphrey, Luce ſhall be thy Bride.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Sweet Maſter Humphrey then I am content.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: And ſo am I in truth.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Yet take me with you,
There is another clauſe muſt be annext,
And this it is I ſwore, and will perform it,
No man ſhall ever joy me as his wife,
But he that ſtole me hence: if you dare venture,
I am yours; you need not fear, my father loves you:
If not, farewel for ever.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Stay Nymph, ſtay,
I have a double Gelding coloured bay,
Sprung by his Father from Barbarian kind,
Another for my ſelf, though ſomewhat blind,
Yet true as truſty tree.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: I am ſatisfied,
And ſo I give my hand, our courſe muſt lie
Through Waltham Forreſt, where I have a friend

Will entertain us, ſo farewell Sir Humphrey.
Exit Luce.
And think upon your buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Though I die,
I am reſolv'd to venture liſe and lim,
For one ſo young, ſo fair, ſo kind, ſo trim, Exit Hum.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: By my faith and troth George, and as I am virtuous, It is e'n the kindeſt young man that ever trode on ſhooe-leather: well, go thy waies, if thou haſt her not, 'tis not thy fault 'iſaith.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: I prethee Mouſe be patient, a ſhall have her, or I'll make ſome of 'em ſmoak for't.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Thats my good lamb George, fie, this ſtinking Tobacco kills men, would there were none in England: now I pray Gentlemen, what good does this ſtinking Tobacco? do you nothing; I warrant you make chimneys a your faces: Oh Husband, Husband, now, now there's Ralph, there's Ralph.

div.stage: Enter Ralph, like a Grocer in's ſhop, with two Prentices, reading Palmerin of England.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Peace fool, let Ralph alone, hark you Ralph; do not ſtrain your ſelf too much at the firſt, peace, begin Ralph.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: Then Palmerin and Trineus ſnatching their Lances from their Dwarfs, and claſping their Helmets, gallopt amain after the Giant, and Palmerin having gotten a ſight of him, came poſting amain, ſaying, Stay traiterous thief, for thou maiſt not ſo carry away her, that is worth the greateſt Lord in the World, and with theſe words gave him a blow on the Shoulder, that he ſtruck him beſides his Elephant; and Trineus coming to the Knight that had Agricola behind him, ſet him ſoon beſides his horſe, with his neck broken in the fall, ſo that the Princeſs getting out of the throng, between joy and grief ſaid; All happy Knight, the mirror of all ſuch as follow Arms, now may I be well aſſured of the love thou beareſt me, I wonder why the Kings do not raiſe an Army of fourteen or fifteen hundred thouſand men, as big as the Army that the Prince of Portigo brought againſt Ro • icler, and deſtroy theſe Giants, they do much hurt to wandring Damſels, that go in queſt of their Knights.

sp.speaker: Wife,
sp.p: Faith Husband, and Ralph ſays true, for they ſay the King of Portugal cannot ſit at his meat, but the Giants and the Ettins will come and ſnatch it from him.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Hold thy tongue; on Ralph.

sp.speaker: Ralph,
sp.p: And certainly thoſe Knights are much to be commended, who neglecting their poſſeſſions, wander with a Squire and a Dwarfe through the Deſarts, to relieve poor Ladies.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I by my faith are they Ralph, let 'em ſay what they will, they are indeed: our Knights neglect their poſſeſſions well enough, but they do not the reſt.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: There are no ſuch courteous, and fair well-ſpoken Knights in this age, they will call one the Son of a whore, that Palmerin of England, would have called fair Sir; and one that Roſicler would have called Right beautiful Damſel, they will call Damn'd bitch.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I'll be ſworn will they Ralph, they have called me ſo an hundred times about a ſcurvy pipe of Tobacco.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: But what brave ſpirit could be content to ſit in his ſhop with a ſlapet of Wood, and a blew Apron before him ſelling Methridatam and Dragons water to viſited houſes, that might purſue ſeats of Arms, and through his noble atchievements, procure ſuch a famous Hiſtory to be written of, in his Heroick proweſſe.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Well ſaid Ralph, ſome more of thoſe words Ralph.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: They go finely by my troth.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: Why ſhould I not then purſue this courſe, both for the credit of my ſelf and our company, for amongſt all the worthy Books of Atchievements, I do not call to mind, that I yet read of a Grocer Errant, I will be the ſaid Knight: Have you heard of any that hath wandred unfurniſhed of his Squire and Dwarfe? my elder Prentice Tom ſhall be my truſty Squire, and little George my Dwarfe, hence my blew Apron, yet in remembrance of my former Trade, upon my ſhield ſhall be pourtraid a Burning Peſtle, and I will be call'd the Knight of the burning Peſtle.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Nay, I dare ſwear thou wilt not forget thy old Trade, thou wert ever meek. Ralph, Tim, Tim. Anon.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: My beloved Squire, and George my Dwarfe, I charge you that from henceforth you never call me by any other name, but the Right courteous and valiant Knight of the Burning Peſtle, and that you never call any Female by the name of a Woman or Wench, but fair Lady, if ſhe have her deſires; if not, diſtreſſed Damſel; that you call all Forreſts and Heaths, Deſarts, and all Horſes Palfries.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: This is very fine: faith do the Gentlemen like Ralph, think you Husband?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: I, I warrant thee, the Players would give all the ſhooes in their ſhop for him.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: My beloved Squire Tim, ſtand out, admit this were a Deſart, and over it a Knight Errant pricking, and I ſhould bid you enquire of his intents, what would you ſay?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: Sir, my Maſter ſent me to know whither you are riding?

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: No, thus; fair Sir, the Right courteous, and valiant Knight of the Burning Peſtle, commanded me to enquire upon what adventure you are bound, whether to relieve ſome diſtreſſed Damſel, or otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Whorſon blockhead cannot remember.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I'faith, and Ralph told him on't before: all the Gentlemen heard him, did he not Gentlemen, did not Ralph tell him on't?

sp.speaker: George.
sp.p: Right courteous and valiant Knight of the Burning Peſtle, here is a diſtreſſed Damſel, to have a halfepenny worth of Pepper.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: That's a good boy, ſee, the little boy can hit it, by my troth it's a fine child.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: Relieve her with all courteous language, now ſhut up ſhop, no more my Prentice, but my truſty Squire and Dwarfe, I muſt beſpeak my Shield, and arming Peſtle.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Go thy ways Ralph, as I am a true man, thou art the beſt on 'em all.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: What ſay you Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I prethee come again quickly, ſweet Ralph.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: By and by. Exit Ralph.

div.stage: Enter Jaſper and his Mother Miſtriſs Merry-thought.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Give thee my bleſſing? no, I'll never give thee my bleſſing, I'll ſee thee hang'd firſt; it ſhall ne'r be ſaid I gave thee my bleſſing: thou art thy Fathers own Son, of the bloud of the Merry-thoughts; I may curſe the time that e'r I knew thy Father, he hath ſpent all his own, and mine too, and when I tell him of it, he laughs and dances, and ſings and cries; A merry heart lives long-a. And thou art a waſt-thrift, and art run away from thy Maſter, that lov'd thee well, and art come to me, and I have laid up a little for my younger Son Michael, and thou thinkſt to bezle that, but thou ſhalt never be able to do it, Come hither Michael, come Michael, down on thy knees, thou ſhalt have my bleſſing. Enter Michael.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: I pray you Mother pray to God to bleſs me.

sp.speaker: Miſt Mer.
sp.p: God bleſs thee: but Jaſper ſhall never have my bleſſing, he ſhall be hang'd firſt, ſhall he not Michael? how ſaiſt thou?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: Yes forſooth Mother and grace of God.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: That's a good boy.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I'faith it's a fine ſpoken child:

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.p: Mother, though you forget a Parents love,
I muſt preſerve the duty of a child:
I ran not from my Maſter, nor return
To have your ſtock maintain my idleneſs.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Ungracious child I warrant him, harke how he chops Logick with his Mother: thou hadſt beſt tell her ſhe lies, do, tell her ſhe lies.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: If he were my ſon, I would hang him up by the heels, and flea him, and ſalt him, whorſon halter-ſack.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.p: My coming only is to beg your love,
Which I ever though I never gain it,
And howſoever you eſteem of me,
There is no drop of bloud hid in theſe veins,
But I remember well belongs to you,
That brought me forth; and would be glad for you
To rip them all again, and let it out.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: I'faith I had ſorrow enough for thee: (God knows) but I'll hamper thee well enough: get thee in thou vagabond, get thee in, and learn of thy brother Michael.

p.hi: Noſe, Noſe, jolly red Noſe, and who gave thee this jolly red Noſe?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Hark my Husband he's ſinging and hoiting,
And I'm fain to car • and care, and all little enough.
Husband, Charles, Charles Merry-thought.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Nutmegs and Gingers, Cinamon and Cloves,
And they gave me this jolly red Noſe.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: If you would conſider your eſtate, you would have little liſt to ſing, I-wiſſe.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: It ſhould never be conſider'd, while it were an eſtate, if I thought it would ſpoil my ſinging.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: But how wilt thou do Charles, thou art an old man, and thou canſt not work, and thou haſt not forty ſhillings left, and thou eateſt good meat, and drinkeſt good drink, and laugheſt?

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: And will doe.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: But how wilt thou come by it Charles?

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: How? why how have I done hitherto theſe forty years? I never came into my Dining-room, but at eleven and ſix a clock, I found excellent meat and drink a' th' Table: my Cloaths were never worn out, but next morning a Tailor brought me a new ſuit; and without queſtion it will be ſo ever! uſe makes perfectneſs, If all ſhould fail, it is but a little ſtraining my ſelf extraordinary, and laugh my ſelf to death.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: It's a fooliſh old man this: is not he George?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Yes Cunny.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Give me a penny i' th' purſe while I live George.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: I by Lady Cunnie, hold thee there.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Well Charles, you promis'd to provide for Jaſper, and I have laid up for Michael: I pray you pay Jaſper his portion, he's come home, and he ſhall not conſume Michaels ſtock: he ſaies his Maſter turn'd him away, but I promiſe you truly, I think he ran away.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: No indeed Miſtriſs Merry-thought, though he be a notable gallows, yet I'll aſſure you his Maſter did turn him away, even in this place, 'twas i'faith within this half hour, about his Daughter, my Husband was by.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Hang him rogue, he ſerv'd him well enough: love his Maſters Daughter! by my troth Cunnie, if there were a thouſand boys, thou wouldſt ſpoil them all, with taking their parts; let his Mother alone with him.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I George, but yet truth is truth.

sp.speaker: Old. Mer.
sp.p: Where is Jaſper? he's welcome however, call him in, he ſhall have his portion, is he merry?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: I foul chive him, he is too merry. Jaſper. Michael.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Welcome Jaſper, though thou run'ſt away, welcome, God bleſs thee, 'tis thy mothers mind thou ſhouldſt receive thy portion: thou haſt been abroad, and I hope haſt learnt experience enough to govern it: thou art of ſufficient years, hold thy hand: one, two, three, four, five, ſix, ſeven, eight, nine, there is ten ſhillings for thee, thruſt thy ſelf into the world with that, and take ſome ſetled courſe, if fortune croſs thee, thou haſt a retiring place; come home to me, I have twenty ſhillings left, be a good Huſband, that is, wear ordinary Cloaths, eat the beſt meat, and drink the beſt drink; be merry, and give to the poor, and and believe me, thou haſt no end of thy goods.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.p: Long may you live free from all thought of ill,
And long have cauſe to be thus merry ſtill.
But Father?

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: No more words Jaſper, get thee gone, thou haſt my bleſſing, thy Fathers ſpirit upon thee. Farewel Jaſper; but yet, or e'r you part (oh cruel) kiſs me, kiſs me ſweeting, mine own dear jewel: So, now begone; no words.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: So Michael, now get thee gone too.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: Yes forſooth Mother, but I'll have my Father's bleſſing firſt.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: No Michael, 'tis no matter for his bleſſing; thou haſt my bleſſing, begone; I'll fetch my money and jewels, and follow thee: I'll ſtay no longer with him I warrant thee; truly Charles I'll begon too.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: What you will not?

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: What you will not?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Yes indeed will I.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Hay ho, farewel Nan, I'll never truſt wench more again, if I can.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: You ſhall not think (when all your own is gone) to ſpend that I have been ſcraping up for Michael.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Farewel good wife, I expect it not; all I have to do in this world, is to be merry: which I ſhall, if the ground be not taken from me: and if it be,
When Earth and Seas from me are reſt,
The Skies aloft for me are left.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I'll be ſworn he's a merry old Gentleman for all that: Hark, hark Husband, hark, Fiddles, Fiddles; now ſurely they go finely. They ſay 'tis preſent death for theſe Fidlers to tune their Rebecks before the great Turks grace, is 't not George? But look, look, here's a youth dances: now good youth do a turn o' th' toe; Sweet: heart, I'faith I'll have Ralph come, and do ſome of his Gambols; he'll ride the Wild Mare Gentlemen, 'twould do your hearts good to ſee him: I thank you kind youth, pray bid Ralph come.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Peace Connie. Sirrah, you ſcurvy boy, bid the Players ſend Ralph, or by gods—and they do not, I'll tear ſome of their Periwigs beſide their heads: this is all Riff-Raff.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: And how faith? how goes it now Son Humphrey?

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Right worſhipful and my beloved friend
And Father dear, this matter's at an end.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: 'Tis well, it ſhould be ſo, I'm glad the Girl
Is found ſo tractable.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Nay, ſhe muſt whirl
From hence, and you muſt wink: for ſo I ſay,
The ſtory tells to morrow before day.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: George, doſt thou think in thy conſcience now 'twill be a match? tell me but what thou think'ſt ſweet Rogue, thou ſeeſt the poor Gentleman (dear heart) how it labours and throbs I warrant you, to be at reſt: I'll go move the Father for't.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: No, no, I prethee ſit ſtill Honey-ſuckle, thou'lt ſpoil all; if he deny him, I'll bring half a dozen good fellows my ſelf, and in the ſhutting of an evening knock't up, and there's an end.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I'll buſs thee for that I'faith boy; well George, well you have been a wag in your days I warrant you: but God forgive you, and I do with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: How was it Son? you told me that to morrow
Before day break, you muſt convey her hence.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: I muſt, I muſt, and thus it is agreed,
Your Daughter rides upon a brown-bay Steed,
I on a Sorrel, which I bought of Brian,
The honeſt Hoſt of the red roaring Lion
In Waltham ſituate: then if you may,
Conſent in ſeemly ſort, leſt by delay,
The fatal Siſters come, and do the office,
And then you'll ſing another Song.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Alas.
Why ſhould you be thus full of grief to me,
That do as willing as your ſelf agree
To any thing ſo it be good and fair?
Then ſteal her when you will, if ſuch a pleaſure
Content you both, I'll ſleep and never ſee it,
To make your joys more full: but tell me why
You may not here perform your marriage?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Gods bleſſing o'thy ſoul, old man, i' faith thou art loth to part true hearts: I ſee a has her, George, and I'm as glad on't; well, go thy ways Humphrey for fair a ſpoken man, I believe thou haſt not thy fellow within the walls of London, and I ſhould ſay the Suburbs too, I ſhould not lie: why doſt not thou rejoyce with me George?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: If I could but ſee Ralph again, I were as merry as mine Hoſt i' faith.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: The cauſe you ſeem to ask, I thus declare;
Help me oh Muſes nine, your Daughter ſware
A fooliſh oath, the more it was the pity:
Yet none but my ſelf within this City
Shall dare to ſay ſo, but a bold defiance
Shall meet him, were he of the noble Science.
And yet ſhe ſware, and yet why did ſhe ſwear?
Truly I cannot tell, unleſs it were
For her own eaſe: for ſure ſometimes an oath,
Being ſworn thereafter, is like cordial broth.
And this it was, ſhe ſwore never to marry,
But ſuch a one whoſe mighty arm could carry
(As meaning me, for I am ſuch a one)
Her bodily away through ſtick and ſtone,
Till both of us arrive at her requeſt,
Some ten miles off in the wide Waltham Forreſt.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: If this be all, you ſhall not need to fear
Any denial in your love, proceed,
I'll neither follow, nor repent the deed.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Good night, twenty good nights, and twenty more,
And twenty more good nights, that makes threeſcore.

div.stage: Enter Miſtriſs Merry-thought, and her Son Michael.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Come Michael, art thou not weary Boy?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: No forſooth Mother not I.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Where be we now child?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: Indeed forſooth Mother I cannot tell, unleſs we be at Mile-end, is not all the world Mile-end, Mother?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: No Michael, not all the world boy; but I can aſſure thee Michael, Mile-end is a goodly matter, there has been a pitcht field my child, between the naughty Spaniels, and the Engliſhmen, and the Spaniels ran away Michael, and the Engliſhmen followed: my neighbor Coxſtone was there boy, and kill'd them all with a birding-piece.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: Mother forſooth.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: What ſays my white boy?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: Shall not my Father go with us too?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: No Michael, let thy Father go ſnick up, he ſhall never come between a pair of ſheets with me again, while he lives: let him ſtay at home and ſing for his ſupper boy; come child ſit down, and I'll ſhew my boy-fine knacks indeed, look here Michael, here's a Ring, and here's a Bruch, and here's a Bracelet, and here's two Rings more, and here's Money, and Gold by th' eye my boy.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: Shall I have all this Mother?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: I Michael thou ſhalt have all Michael.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: How lik'ſt thou this wench?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I cannot tell, I would have Ralph, George; I'll ſee no more elſe indeed: law, and I pray you let the youths underſtand ſo much by word of mouth, for I will tell you truly, I'm afraid o'my boy: come, come George, let's be merry and wiſe, the child's a fatherleſs child, and ſay they ſhould put him into a ſtrait pair of Gaskins, 'twere worſe than knot-graſs, he would never grow after it.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Here's Ralph, here's Ralph

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: How do you Ralph? you are welcome Ralph, as I may ſay, it' a good boy, hold up thy head, and be not afraid, we are thy friends. Ralph, the Gentlemen will praiſe thee Ralph, if thou plai'ſt thy part with audacity, begin Ralph a Gods name.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: My truſty Squire unlace my Helme, give me my hat, where are we, or what deſart might this be?

sp.speaker: Dw.
sp.p: Mirror of Knigthood, this is, as I take it, the perilous Waltham Down; in whoſe bottom ſtands the inchanted Valley.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Oh Michael, we are betraid, we are betraid, here be Giants, flie boy, flie boy flie.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Lace on my Helme again: what noiſe is this?
A gentle Lady flying the embrace
Of ſome uncourteous Knight, I will relieve her.
Go Squire, and ſay, the Knight that wears this Peſtle
In honor of all Ladies ſwears revenge
Upon that recreant Coward that purſues her,
Goe comfort her, and that ſame gentle Squire
That bears her company.

sp.speaker: Squ.
sp.l: I go brave Knight.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: My truſty Dwarf and friend, reach me my ſhield,
And hold it while I ſwear, firſt by my Knighthood,
Then by the ſoul of Amadis de Gaule,
My famous Anceſtor, then by my Sword,
The beauteous Brionella girt about me,
By this bright burning Peſtle of mine honor,
The living Trophie, and by all reſpect
Due to diſtreſſed Damſels, here I vow
Never to end the queſt of this fair Lady,
And that forſaken Squire, till by my valour
I gain their liberty.

sp.speaker: Dw.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs the Knight
That thus relieves poor errant Gentlewomen. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I marry Ralph, this has ſome favour in't, I would ſee the proudeſt of them all offer to carry his Books after him. But George, I will not have him go away ſo ſoon, I ſhall be ſick if he go away, that I ſhall; call Ralph again George, call Ralph again, I prethee ſweetheart let him come fight before me, and let's ha ſome Drums, and Trumpets, and let him kill all that comes near him, and thou lov'ſt me George.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Peace a little bird, he ſhall kill them all, and they were twenty more on 'em then there are,

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Now fortune, if thou be'ſt not only ill,
Shew me thy better face, and bring about
Thy deſperate wheel, that I may climb at length
And ſtand, this is our place of meeting,
If love have any conſtancy. Oh age!
Where only wealthy men are counted happy:
How ſhall I pleaſe thee? how deſerve thy ſmiles?
When I am only rich in miſery?
My fathers bleſſing, and this little coin
Is my inheritance, a ſtrong revenue,
From earth thou art, and to earth I give thee,
There grow and multiply, whilſt freſher air Spies the Casket.
Breeds me a freſher fortune: how, illuſion!
What hath the Devil coyn'd himſelf before me?
'Tis mettle good, it rings well, I am waking,
And taking too I hope, now Gods dear bleſſing
Upon his heart that left it here, 'tis mine,
Theſe pearls, I take it, were not left for Swine. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I do not like that this unthrifty youth ſhould embeſil away the money, the poor Gentlewoman his mother will have a heavy heart for it, God knows.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: And reaſon good, ſweet heart.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: But let him go, I'll tell Ralph a tale in's ear, ſhall fetch him again with a wanion, I warrant him, if he be above ground; and beſides George, here be a number of ſufficient Gentlemen can witneſs, and my ſelf, and your ſelf, and the Muſicians, if we be call'd in queſtion, but here comes Ralph, George, thou ſhalt hear him ſpeak, as he were an Emperal.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Comes not Sir Squire again?

sp.speaker: Dwarf.
sp.l: Right courteous Knight,
Your Squire doth come, and with him comes the Lady.
sp.stage: Enter Miſtriſs Mer. and Michael, and Squire.
sp.l: For and the Squire of Damſels as I take it.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Madam, if any ſervice or devoir
Of a poor errant Knight may right your wrongs,
Command it, I am preſt to give you ſuccor,
For to that holy end I bear my Armour.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.l: Alas, Sir, I am a poor Gentlewoman, and I
have loſt my money in this Forreſt.
Deſart, you would ſay, Lady, and not loſt
Whilſt I have Sword and Launce, dry up your tears
Which ill befits the beauty of that face:
And tell the ſtory, if I may requeſt it,
Of your diſaſtrous fortune.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Out alas, I left a thouſand pound a thouſand pound, e'n all the money I had laid up for this youth, upon the ſight of your Maſterſhip, you lookt ſo grim, and as I may ſay it, ſaving your preſence, more like a Giant than a mortal man.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: I am as you are, Lady, ſo are they
All mortal, but why weeps this gentle Squire?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Has he not cauſe to weep do you think, when he has loſt his inheritance?

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Young hope of valour, weep not, I am here
That will confound thy foe, and pay it dear
Upon his coward head, that dare denie,
Diſtreſſed Squires, and Ladies equity.
I have but one horſe, on which ſhall ride
This Lady fair behind me, and before
This courteous Squire, fortune will give us more
Upon our next adventure; fairly ſpeed
Beſide us Squire aed Dwarfe to do us need. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cit,
sp.p: Did not I tell you Nell what your man would do? by the faith of my body wench, for clean action and good delivery, they may all caſt their caps at him.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: And ſo they may i'faith, for I dare ſpeak it boldly, the twelve Companies of London cannot match him, timber for timber: well George, and he be not inveigled by ſome of theſe paltery Players, I ha much marvel: but George we ha done our parts, if the Boy have any grace to be thankful.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Yes, I warrant you duckling.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Good Miſtriſs Luce, how ever I in fault am,
For your lame horſe; you're welcome unto Waltham.
But which way now to go, or what to ſay
I know not truly till it be broad day.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: O fear not maſter Humphrey, I am guide
For this place good enough.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Then up and ride,
Or if it pleaſe you, walk for your repoſe,
Or ſit, or if you will, go pluck a Roſe:
Either of which ſhall be indifferent,
To your good friend and Humphrey, whoſe conſent
Is ſo intangled ever to your will,
As the poor harmleſs horſe is to the ill.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Faith and you ſay the word, we'll e'n ſit down,
And take a nap.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: 'Tis better in the Town,
Where we may nap together: for believe me,
To ſleep without a ſnatch would mickle grieve me.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: You're merry maſter Humphrey.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: So I am,
And have been every merry from my Dam.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Your Nurſe had the leſs labour.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Faith it may be,
Unleſs it were by chance I did beray me.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Luce, dear friend Luce,

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Here Jaſper.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: You are mine.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: If it be ſo, my friend, you uſe me fine:
What do you think I am?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: An arrant Noddy.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: A word of obloquie: now by gods body,
i'll tell thy Maſter, for I know thee well.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Nay, and you be ſo forward for to tell,
Take that, and that, and tell him, Sir, I gave it:
And ſay I paid you well.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: O Sir I have it,
And do confeſs the payment, pray be quiet.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Go, get you to your night-cap and the diet,
To cure your beaten bones.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Alas, poor Humphrey,
Get thee ſome wholſome broth with Sage and Cumfrie:
A little oil of Roſes and a Feather
To noint thy back withal.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: When I came hither,
Would I had gone to Paris with John Dorry.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Farewel my pretty Nump, I am very ſorry
I cannot bear thee company.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Farewel,
The Devils Dam was ne'r ſo bang'd in Hell. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: This young Jaſper will prove me another Things, a my conſcience and he may be ſuffered; George, doſt not ſee George how a ſwaggers, and flies at the very heads a fokes as he were a Dragon; well if I do not do his leſſon for wronging the poor Gentleman, I am no true Woman, his friends that brought him up might have been better occupied, I wis, then have taught him theſe fegaries: he's e'n in the high-way to the Gallows, God bleſs him.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: You're too bitter, Connie, the young man may do well enough for all this.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Come hither maſter Humphrey, has he hurt you? now beſhrew his fingers for't, here Sweet-heart, here's ſome Green Ginger for thee, now beſhrew my heart, but a has Pepper-nel in's head, as big as a Pullets egg: alas, ſweet Lamb, how thy Temples beat; take the peace on him ſweet heart, take the peace on him.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: No, no, you talk like a fooliſh woman, I'll ha Ralph fight with him, and ſwinge him up well-favour'dly: ſirrah boy come hither, let Ralph come in and fight with Jaſper,

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I and beat him well,, he's an unhappy boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir, you muſt pardon us, the plot of our Play lies contrary, and 'twill hazard the ſpoiling of our Play.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Plot me no plots, I'll ha Ralph come out, I'll make your houſe too hot for you elſe.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Why Sir, he ſhall, but if any thing fall out of order, the Gentlemen muſt pardon us.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Go your ways good-man boy, I'll hold him a penny he ſhall have his belly full of fighting now, ho here comes Ralph, no more.

div.stage: Enter Ralph, 〈◊〉 Michael, Squire. and Dwarf.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: What Knight is that, Squire, ask him if he keep
The paſſage bound by love of Lady fair,
Or elſe but prickant.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Sir, I am no Knight,
But a poor Gentleman, that this ſame night,
Had ſtoln from me on yonder Green,
My lovely Wife, and ſuffered to be ſeen
Yet extant on my ſhoulderr ſuch a greeting,
That whilſt I live, I ſhall think of that meeting.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I Ralph, he beat him unmercifully, Ralph, and thou ſpar'ſt him Ralph, I would thou wert hang'd,

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: No more, wife, no more.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Where is the Caitiff wretch hath done this deed,
Lady, your pardon, that I may proceed
Upon the queſt of this injurious Knight.
And thou fair Squire repute me not the worſe,
In leaving the great venture of the purſe,
And the rich Casket till ſome better leiſure.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Here comes the Broker hath purloin'd my treaſure.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Go, Squire, and tell him I am here,
And Errant Knight at Arms, to crave delivery
Of that fair Lady to her own Knights arms.
If he deny, bid him take choice of ground,
And ſo defie him.

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.l: From the Knight that bears
The Golden Peſtle; I defie thee Knight.
Unleſs thou make fair reſtitution
Of that bright Lady.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Tell the Knight that ſent thee
He is an aſs, and I will keep the wench,
And knock his Head-piece.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Thou art but dead,
If thou recall not thy uncourteous terms:

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Break's pate Ralph, break's pate Ralph, ſoundly.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Come Knight, I am ready for you, now your Peſtle.
Shall try what temper, Sir, your Mortar's of:
With that he ſtood upright in his ſtirrops,
And gave the Knight of the Calve-skin ſuch a knock,
That he forſook his horſe, and down he fell,
And then he leaped upon him, and plucking off his Helmet.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Nay, and my noble Knight be down ſo ſoon,
Though I can ſcarcely go, I needs muſt run-

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Run Ralph, run Ralph, run for thy life boy, Jaſper comes, Jaſper comes.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.p: Come Luce, we muſt have other Arms for you, Humphrey and Golden Peſtle both adieu. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Sure the Devil, God bleſs us, is in this Springald, why George, didſt ever ſee ſuch a fire-drake, I am afraid my boy's miſcarried; if he be, though he were Maſter Merry-thoughts Son a thouſand times, if there be any Law in England, I'll make ſome of them ſmart for't.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: No, no, I have found out the matter ſweet-heart, Jaſper is enchanted as ſure as we are here, he is enchanted, he could no more have ſtood in Ralph's hands, than I can ſtand in my Lord Mayor's: I'll have a Ring to diſcover all enchantments, and Ralph ſhall beat him yet: be no more vext, for it ſhall be ſo.

div.stage: Enter Ralph, Squire, Dwarfe, Miſtriſs Merry-thought, and Michael.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Oh Husband, here's Ralph again, ſtay Ralph, let me ſpeak with thee, how doſt thou Ralph? art thou not ſhrewdly hurt? the foul great Lungies laid unmercifully on thee, there's ſome Sugar-candy for thee, proceed, thou ſhalt have another bout with him.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: If Ralph had him at the Fencing-School, if he did not make a puppy of him, and drive him up and down the School, he ſhould ne'r come in my ſhop more.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Truly maſter Knight of the Burning Peſtle, I am weary.

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: Indeed-law Mother, and I am very hungry.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Take comfort gentle Dame, and your fair Squire.
For in this Deſart there muſt needs be plac'd
Many ſtrong Caſtles, held by courteous Knights,
And till I bring you ſafe to one of thoſe
I ſwear by this my Order ne'r to leave you.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Well ſaid Ralph, George, Ralph was ever comfortable, was he not?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Yes Duck.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I ſhall ne'r forget him: when we had loſt our child, you know it was ſtraid almoſt alone, to Puddle-wharfe, and the Cryers were abroad for it, and there it had drown'd it ſelf but for a Sculler, Ralph was the moſt comfortableſt to me: peace Miſtriſs, ſaies he, let it go, I'll get you another as good, did he not George? did he not ſay ſo?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Yes indeed did he Mouſe.

sp.speaker: Dwarfe.
sp.p: I would we had a meſs of Pottage, and a pot of Drink, Squire, and were going to bed.

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.p: Why we are at Waltham Towns end, and that's the Bell Inne.

sp.speaker: Dwarfe.
sp.l: Take courage valiant Knight, Damſel, and Squire,
I have diſcovered, not a ſtones caſt off,
An antient Caſtle held by the old Knight
Of the moſt holy Order of the Bell,
Who gives to all Knights Errant entertain:
There plenty is of food, and all prepar'd,
By the white hands of his own Lady dear.
He hath three Squires that welcome all his Gueſts:
The firſt, High Chamberlain, who will ſee
Our beds prepar'd, and bring us ſnowy ſheets,
Where never footman ſtretch'd his butter'd Hams.
The ſecond height Tapſtro, who will ſee
Our pots full filled, and no froth therein;
The third, a gentle Squire Oſtlero height,
Who will our Palfries ſlick with wiſps of ſtraw,
And in the Maunger put them Oats enough,
And never greaſe their teeth with Candle-ſnuffe.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: That ſame Dwarfe's a pretty boy, but the Squire's a grout-nold.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: Knock at the Gates my Squire, with ſtately Lance.

sp.speaker: Tap.
sp.p: Who's there, you're welcome Gentlemen, will you ſee a room?

sp.speaker: Dwarfe.
sp.p: Right courteous and valiant Knight of the Burning Peſtle, This is the Squire Tapſtro.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Fair Squire Tapſtro, I a wandring Knight,
Height of the Burning Peſtle in the queſt
Of this fair Ladies Casket, and wrought purſe,
Loſing my ſelf in this vaſt wilderneſs,
And to this Caſtle well by fortune brought,
Where hearing of the goodly entertain
Your Knight of holy Order of the Bell,
Gives to all Damſels, and all Errant Knights,
I thought to knock, and now am bold to enter.

sp.speaker: Tapſt.
sp.p: An't pleaſe you ſee a chamber, you are very welcome. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: George, I would have ſomething done, and I cannot tell what it is.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: What is it Nell?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Why George, ſhall Ralph beat no body again? prethee ſweet-heart let him.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: So he ſhall Nell, and if I joyn with him, we'll knock them all.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: O George, here's maſter Humphrey again now, that loſt Miſtriſs Luce, and Miſtriſs Luce's Father, maſter Humphrey will do ſome bodies arrant I warrant him.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Father, it's true in arms I ne'r ſhall claſp her,
For ſhe is ſtoln away by your man Jaſper.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I thought he would tell him.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Unhappy that I am to loſe my child:
Now I begin to think on Jaſper's words,
Who oft hath urg'd to me thy fooliſhneſs,
Why didſt thou let her go, thou lov'ſt her not,
That wouldſt bring home thy life, and not bring her.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Father forgive me, I ſhall tell you true,
Look on my ſhoulders they are black and blue,
Whilſt too and fro fair Luce and I were winding,
He came and baſted me with a hedge binding.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Get men and horſes ſtraight, we will be there
Within this hour; you know the place again?

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: I know the place where he my loins did ſwaddle,
I'll get ſix horſes, and to each a ſaddle.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Mean time I'll go talk with Jaſpers Father.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: George, What wilt thou lay with me now, that Maſter Humphrey has not Miſtriſs Luce yet, ſpeak George what wilt thou lay with me?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: No Nell, I warrant thee, Jaſper is at Puckeridge with her by this.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Nay George, you muſt conſider Miſtriſs Lucies feet are tender, and beſides, 'tis dark, and I promiſe you truly, I do not ſee how he ſhould get out of Waltham Forreſt with her yet.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Nay Cunny, what wilt thou lay with me that Ralph has her not yet.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I will not lay againſt Ralph, Honny, becauſe I have not ſpoken with him: but look George, peace, here comes the merry old Gentleman again.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: When it was grown to dark midnight,
And all were faſt aſleep,
In came Margarets grimly Ghoſt,
And ſtood at William's feet.

I have money, and meat, and drink before hand, till to morrow at noon, why ſhould I be ſad? methinks I have halfe a dozen jovial ſpirits within me, I am three merry men, and three merry men: To what end ſhould any man be ſad in this world? give me a man that when he goes to hanging cries troul the black boul to me: and a Woman that will ſing a catch in her Travel. I have ſeen a man come by my door, with a ſerious face, in a black cloak, without a Hatband, carrying his head as if he lookt for pins in the ſtreet. I have lookt out of my window halfe a year after, and have ſpied that mans head upon London Bridge: 'tis vile, never truſt a Tailor that does not ſing at his work, his mind is of nothing but filching.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Mark this George, 'tis worth noting: Godfrey my Tailor, you know never ſings, and he had fourteen yards to make this Gown; and I'll be ſworn, Miſtriſs Peniſtone the Drapers Wife had one made with twelve.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: 'Tis mirth that fills the veins with blood,
More than Wine, or Sleep, or Food,
Let each man keep his heart at eaſe
No man dies of that diſeaſe,
He that would his body keep
From diſeaſes, muſt not weep,
But whoever laughs and ſings,
Never his body brings
Into Feavers, Gouts, or Rhumes,
Or lingringly his Lungs conſumes:
Or meets with aches in the bone,
Or Catarrhs, or griping Stone:
But contented lives for aye,
The more he laughs, the more he may.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Look George, how ſayſt thou by this George? is't not a fine old man? Now Gods bleſſing a thy ſweet lips. When wilt thou be ſo merry George? Faith thou art the frowningſt little thing, when thou art angry, in a Countrey.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Peace Conny, Thou ſhalt ſee him took down too I warrant thee: here's Luce's Father come now.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: As you came from Walſingam, from the Holy Land, there met you not with my true love by the way as you came.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Oh Maſter Merry-thought! my Daughters gone,
This mirth becomes you not, my Daughter's gone.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Why an if ſhe be, what care I?
Or let her come, or go, or tarry.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Mock not my miſery, it is your Son,
Whom I have made my own, when all forſook him,
Has ſtoln my only joy, my child away.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: He ſet her on a milk white Steed, and himſelf upon a gray,
He never turn'd his face again, but he bore her quite away.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Unworthy of the kindneſs I have ſhewn
To thee, and thine: too late, I well perceive
Thou art conſenting to my Daughters loſs.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Your Daughter, what a-ſtirs here wi' y'r daughter? Let her go, think no more on her, but ſing loud. If both my ſons were on the gallows, I would ſing down, down, down: they fall down, and ariſe they never ſhall.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Oh might I behold her once again.
And ſhe once more embrace her aged ſire.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Fie, how ſcurvily this goes: and ſhe once more embrace her aged ſire? you'll make a dog on her, will ye; ſhe cares much for her aged ſire, warrant you.
sp.l: She cares not for her Daddy, nor ſhe cares not for her Mammy.
For ſhe is, ſhe is, ſhe is my Lord of Low-gaves Laſſie.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: For this thy ſcorn I will purſue
That ſon of thine to death.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Do, and when you ha kill'd him,
Give him flowers i'now Palmer, give him flowers i'now,
Give him red and white, and blue, green, and yellow.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: I'll fetch my Daughter.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: I'll hear no more o' your Daughter, it ſpoils my mirth.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: I ſay I'll fetch my Daughter.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Was never man for Ladies ſake, down, down,
Tormented as I Sir Guy? de derry down,
For Lucies ſake, that Lady bright, down, down,
As over men beheld with eye? de derry down.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: I'll be reveng'd by heaven.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: How doſt thou like this George?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Why this is well Cunnie: but if Ralph were hot once: thou ſhouldſt ſee more.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: The Fidlers go again Husband.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: I Nell, but this is ſcurvy Muſick: I gave the whoreſon gallows money, and I think he has not got me the Waits of Southwark, if I hear him not anan, I'll twinge him by the ears.
Your Muſicians play Baloo.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: No good George, let's ha Lachrymae.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Why this is it Cunny.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: It's all the better George: now ſweet Lamb, what ſtory is that painted upon the cloth? the confutation of Saint Paul?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: No Lamb, that's Ralph and Lucrece.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Ralph and Lucrece? which Ralph? our Ralph?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: No Mouſe, that was a Tartarian.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: A Tartarian? well, I wo'd the Fidlers had done, that we might ſee our Ralph again.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Come my dear, though we have loſt our way,
We have not loſt our ſelves: are you not weary
With this nights wandring, broken from your reſt?
And frighted with the terror that attends
The darkneſs of this wild unpeopled place?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: No my beſt friend, I cannot either fear,
Or entertain a weary thought, whilſt you
(The end of all my full deſires) ſtand by me:
Let them that loſe their hopes, and live to languiſh
Amongſt the number of forſaken Lovers,
Tell the long weary ſteps, and number time,
Start at a ſhadow, and ſhrink up their bloud,
Whilſt I (poſſeſt with all content and quiet)
Thus take my pretty love, and thus embrace him.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: You have caught me Luce, ſo faſt, that whilſt I live
I ſhall become your faithful priſoner:
And wear theſe chains for ever. Come, ſit down,
And reſt your body, too too delicate
For theſe diſturbances; ſo, will you ſleep?
Come, do not be more able than you are,
I know you are not skilful in theſe Watches,
For Women are no ſoldiers; be not nice,
But take it, ſleep I ſay.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: I cannot ſleep.
Indeed I cannot friend.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Why then we'll ſing,
And try how that will work upon our ſences.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: I'll ſing, or ſay, or any thing but ſleep.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Come little Mermaid, rob me of my heart
With that inchanting voice.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: You mock me Jaſper

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Tell me (deareſt) what is Love?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: 'Tis a lightning from above,
'Tis an Arrow, 'tis a Fire,
'Tis a Boy they call deſire.
'Tis a ſmile
Doth beguile

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: The poor hearts of men that prove,
Tell me more, are Women true?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Some Love change, and ſo do you.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Are they fair, and never kind?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Yes, when men turn with the wind.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Are they froward?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Ever toward
Thoſe that love, to love anew.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Diſſemble it no more, I ſee the God
Of heavy ſleep, lay on his heavy Mace,
Upon your eye-lids.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: I am very heavy.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Sleep, ſleep, and quiet reſt crown thy ſweet thoughts:
Keep from her fair blood diſtempers, ſtartings,
Horrors and fearful ſhapes: let all her dreams
Be joys, and chaſte delights, embraces, wiſhes,
And ſuch new pleaſures as the raviſh'd ſoul
Gives to the ſences. So my charms have took.
Keep her you powers divine, whilſt I contemplate
Upon the wealth and beauty of her mind.
She is only fair, and conſtant: only kind,
And only to thee Jaſper. Oh my joyes!
Whither will you tranſport me? let not fulneſs
Of my poor buried hopes come up together,
And over-charge my ſpirits; I am weak,
Some ſay (how ever ill) the Sea and Women
Are govern'd by the Moon, both ebb and flow,
Both full of changes: yet to them that know,
And truly judge, theſe but opinions are,
And hereſies to bring on pleaſing War
Between our tempers, that without theſe were
Both void of after-love, and preſent fear.
Which are the beſt of Cupid. O thou child!
Bred from deſpair, I dare not entertain thee,
Having a love without the faults of Women,
And greater in her perfect goods th • n men:
Which to make good, and pleaſe my ſelf the ſtronger,
Though certainly I am certain of her love,
I'll try her, that the world and memory
May ſing to after-times her conſtancy.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Luce awake. Luce why do you fright me friend,
With thoſe diſtempered looks? what makes your ſword
Drawn in your hand? who hath offended you?
I prethee Jaſper ſleep, thou art wild with watching,

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Come make your way to Heaven, and bid the world
(With all the villanies that ſtick upon it)
Farewell; you're for another life.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Oh Jaſper.
How have my tender years committed evil,
(Eſpecially againſt the man I love)
Thus to be cropt untimely?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Fooliſh girl,
Canſt thou imagine I could love his daughter
That flung me from my fortune into nothing?
Diſcharged me his ſervice, ſhut the doors
Upon my poverty, and ſcorn'd my prayers,
Sending me, like a boat without a malt,
To ſink or ſwim? Come, by this hand you dye,
I muſt have life and blood to ſatisfie
Your fathers wrongs.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Away George, away, raiſe the Watch at Ludgate, and bring a Mitrimus from the Juſtice for this deſperate Villain. Now I charge you Gentlemen, ſee the Kings peace kept. O my heart what a varlet's this, to offer Man-ſlaughter upon the harmleſs Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: I warrant thee (ſweet heart) we'll have him hampered.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Oh Jaſper! be not cruel,
If thou wilt kill me, ſmile, and do it quickly.
And let not many deaths appear before me.
I am a woman made of fear and love
A weak, weak woman, kill not with thy eyes,
They ſhoot me through and through. Strike I am ready.
And dying ſtill I love thee.

div.stage: Enter Merchant, Humphrey, and his Men.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Where abouts?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: No more of this, now to my ſelf again.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: There, there he ſtands with Sword like martial Knight.
Drawn in his hand, therefore beware the fight
You that are wiſe: for were I good Sir Bevis,
I would not ſtay his coming, by your leaves.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.l: Sirrah, reſtore my daughter.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Sirrah, no.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Upon him then.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: So, down with him, down with him, down with him: cut him i'the leg boyes, cut him i'th'leg.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.p: Come your ways Minion, I'll provide a Cage for you, you're grown ſo tame. Horſe her away.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Truly I'm glad your forces have the day. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: They are gone, and I am hurt, my Love is loſt, manet Jaſper.
Never to get again. Oh me unhappy!
Bleed, bleed, and dye, I cannot: Oh my folly!
Thou haſt betray'd me, Hope where art thou ſled?
Tell me if thou be'ſt any where remaining.
Shall I but ſee my love again? Oh no!
She will not dain to look upon her Butcher,
Nor is fit ſhe ſhould; yet I muſt venter.
Oh chance, or fortune, or what ere thou art
That men adore for powerful, hear my cry,
And let me loving live; or looſing dye.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Is a gone George?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: I conny.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Marry and let him go (ſweet heart) by the faith a my body a has put me into ſuch a fright, that I tremble (as they ſay) as 'twere an Aſpine leaf: look a my little finger George, how it ſhakes: now in truth every member of my body is the worſe for't.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Come, hug in mine arms ſweet Mouſe, he ſhall not fright thee any more: alaſs mine own dear heart how it quirers.

div.stage:
Ent ••
Miſtris Merry-thought, Rafe, Michael, Squire, Dwarfe, Hoſt, and a Tapſter.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: O Rafe, how doſt thou Rafe? how haſt thou ſlept to night? has the Knight us'd thee well?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Peace Nell, let Rafe alone.

sp.speaker: Tapſt.
sp.l: Maſter, the reckoning is not paid.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Right courteous Knight, who for the orders ſake
Which thou haſt tane, hang'ſt out the holy Bell,
As I this flaming Peſtle bear about,
We render thanks to your puiſſant ſelf,
Your beauteous Lady, and your gentle Squires,
For thus refreſhing of our wearied limbs,
Stifned with hard atchievements in wild Deſart.

sp.speaker: Tapſt.
sp.l: Sir, there is twelve ſhillings to pay.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Thou merry Squire Tapſtero, thanks to thee,
For comforting our ſouls with double Jug,
And if adventurous Fortune prick thee forth,
Thou jovial Squire, to follow ſeats of Arms,
Take heed thou tender every Ladies cauſe,
Every true Knight, and every Damſel fair
But ſpill the blood of treacherous Sarazens,
And falſe inchanters, that with Magick ſpels,
Have done to death full many a noble Knight.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Thou valiant Knight of the burning Peſtle, give ear to me, there is twelve ſhillings to pay, and as I am a true Knight, I will not bate a penny.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: George, I prethee tell me, muſt Rafe pay twelve ſhillings now?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: No, Nel, no, nothing but the old Knight is merry with Rafe.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: O is't nothing elſe? Rafe will be as merry as he.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Sir Knight, this mirth of yours becomes you well,
But to requite this liberal courteſie,
If any of your Squires will follow Arms,
He ſhall receive from my Heroick hand
A Knighthood, by the virtue of this Peſtle.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Fair Knight, I thank you for your noble offer,
Therefore gentle Knight,
Twelve ſhillings you muſt pay, or I muſt cap you.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Look George, did not I tell thee as much, the Knight of the Bell is in earneſt, Rafe ſhall not be beholding to him, give him his money George, and let him go ſnick up.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Cap Rafe? no, hold your hand ſir Knight of the Bell, there's your Money, have you any thing to ſay to Rafe now? cap Rafe?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I would you ſhould know it, Rafe has friends that will not ſuffer him to be capt for ten times ſo much, and ten times to the end of that, now take thy courſe Rafe.

sp.speaker: M. mer.
sp.p: Come Michael, thou and I will go home to thy father, he hath enough left to keep us a day or two, and we'll ſet fellows abroad to cry our Purſe and Casket: Shall we Michael?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: I, I pray mother, in truth my feot are full of chilblains with travelling.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Faith and thoſe chilblaines are a foul trouble, Miſtris Merry-thought when your youth comes home, let him rub all the ſoles of his feet, and his heels, and his ankles, with a Mouſeskin; or if none of your can catch a Mouſe, when he goes to bed, let him rowl his feet in the warm embers, and I warrant you he ſhall be well, and you may make him put his fingers between his toes, and ſmell to them, it's very ſoveraign for his head, if he be coſ • ive.

sp.speaker: Miſt. mer.
sp.p: Maſter Knight of the burning Peſtle, my ſon Michael, and I bid you farewell, I thank your Worſhip hartily for your kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Fare-well fair Lady, and your tender Squire.
If pricking through theſe Deſarts, I do hear
Of any traiterous Knight who through his guile,
Hath light upon your Casket and your Purſe,
I will deſpoil him of them and reſtore them.

sp.speaker: Miſt. mer.
sp.l: I thank your Worſhip. Exit with Michael

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Dwarf bear my ſhield, Squire elevate my lance,
And now farewell you Knight of holy Bell,

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: I, I Rafe, all is paid.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: But yet before I go, ſpeak worthy Knight,
If oft you do of ſad adventures know,
Where errant Knights may through his proweſs win
Eternal fame, and free ſome gentle ſouls,
From endleſs bounds of ſteel and lingring pain.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Sirrah go to Nick the Barber, and bid him prepare himſelf, as I told you before quickly.

sp.speaker: Tap.
sp.l: I am gone Sir. Exit Tapſter.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Sir Knight, this wilderneſs affordeth none
But the great venture, where full many a Knight
Hath tried his proweſs, and come off with ſhame,
And where I would not have you looſe your life,
Againſt no man, but furious fiend of Hell.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Speak on Sir Knight, tell what he is, and where:
For here I vow upon my blazing badge,
Never to blaze a day in quietneſs;
But bread and water will I only eat,
And the green herb and rock ſhall be my couch
Till I have queld that man, or beaſt, or fiend,
That works ſuch damage to all Errant Knights.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Not far from hence, near a craggy cliff
At the North end of this diſtreſſed Town,
There doth ſtand a lowly houſe
Ruggedly builded, and in it a Cave
In which an ugly Giant now doth won,
Ycleped Barbaroſo: in his hand
He ſhakes a naked Lance of pureſt ſteel,
With ſleeves turn'd up, and him before he wears,
A motly garment to preſerve his clothes
From blood of thoſe Knights which he maſſacres,
And Ladies Gentle: without his door doth hang
A copper baſon, on a prickant Spear;
At which, no ſooner gentle Knights can knock,
But the ſhrill ſound, fierce Barbaroſo hears,
And ruſhing forth, brings in the Errant Knight,
And ſets him down in an inchanted chair:
Then with an Engine, which he hath prepar'd
With forty teeth, he claws his courtly crown,
Next makes him wink, and underneath his chin,
He plants a brazen piece of mighty board,
And knocks his bullets round about his cheeks,
Whilſt with his fingers, and an inſtrument
With which he ſnaps his hair off, he doth fill
The wretches ears with a moſt hideous noyſe.
Thus every Knight Adventurer he doth trim,
And now no creature dares encounter him.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: In Gods name, I will fight with him, kind ſir,
Go but before me to this diſmal Cave
Where this huge Giant Barbaroſo dwells,
And by that virtue that brave Roſicleere,
That damn'd brood of ugly Giants ſlew,
And Palmerin Frannarco overthrew:
I doubt not but to curb this Traytor foul,
And to the Devil ſend his guilty Soul.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Brave ſprighted Knight, thus far I will perform
This your requeſt, I'll bring you within ſight
Of this moſt loathſome place, inhabited
By a more lothſome man: but dare not ſtay,
For his main force ſwoops all he ſees away.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Saint George ſet on before, march Squire and Page. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: George, doſt think Rafe will confound the Giant?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: I hold my cap to a farthing he does: why Nell, I ſaw him wreſtle with the great Dutchman, and hurle him.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Faith and that Dutchman was a goodly man, if all things were anſwerable to his bigneſs: and yet they ſay there was a Scottiſhman higher than he, and that they two and a Knight met, and ſaw one another for nothing: but of all the ſights that ever were in London, ſince I was married, methinks the little child that was ſo fair grown about the members, was the prettieſt, that and the Hermaphrodite.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Nay, by your leave Nil, Ninivie was better.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Ninivie, O that was the ſtory of Jone and the wall, was it not George?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Yes lamb. Enter Miſtris Merry-totgght.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Look George, here comes Miſtris Merry-thoughauh ain, and I would have Rafe come and fight with the Gyant, I tell you true I long to ſee't.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Good Miſtriſs Merri-thought be aone, I pray you for my ſake, I pray you forbear a little, you ſhall have audience preſently, I have a little buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Miſtris Merri-thought,, if it pleaſe you to refrain your paſſion a little, till Rafe have diſpatcht the Giant out of the way, we ſhall think our ſelves much bound to thank you: I thank you good Miſtris Merri-thought.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Boy, come hither, ſend away Rafe and this whoreſon Giant quickly.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: In good faith ſir we cannot, you'l utterly ſpoil our Play, and make it to be hiſt, and it coſt money, you will not ſuffer us to go on with our plots, I pray Gentlemen rule him.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Let him come now and diſpatch this, and I'll trouble you no more.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Will you give me your hand of that?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Give him thy hand George, do, and I'll kiſs him, I warrant thee the youth means plainly.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I'll ſend him to you preſently. Exit Boy.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I thank you little youth, feth the child hath a ſweet breath George, but I think it be troubled with the Worms, Carduus Benedictus and Mares milk were the only thing in the world for't. O Rafe's here George; God ſend thee good luck Rafe.

div.stage: Enter Rafe, Hoſt, Squire, and Dwarf.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Puiſſant Knight yonder his Manſion is,
Lo, where the Spear and Copper Baſon are,
Behold the ſtring on which hangs many a tooth,
Drawn from the gentle jaw of wandring Knights,
I dare not ſtay to ſound, he will appear. Exit Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: O faint not heart, Suſan my Lady dear:
The Coblers Maid in Milkſtreet, for whoſe ſake,
I take theſe Arms, O let the thought of thee,
Carry thy Knight through all adventurous deeds,
And in the honor of thy beauteous ſelf,
May I deſtroy this monſter Barbaroſo,
Knock Squire upon the Baſon till it break Enter. Barba.
With the ſhrill ſtrokes, or till the Giant ſpake.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: O George, the Giant, the Giant, now Rafe for thy life.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What fond unknowing wight is this, that dares,
So rudely knock at Barbaroſſa's Cell,
Where no man comes, but leaves his fleece behind?

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: I, traiterous Caitiffe, who am ſent by fate
To puniſh all the ſad enormities
Thou haſt committed againſt Ladies gentle,
And Errant Knights, Traytor to God and men:
Prepare thy ſelf, this is the diſmal hour
Appointed for thee to give ſtrict account
Of all thy beaſtly treacherous villanies.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Fool-hardy Knight, full ſoon thou ſhalt aby
This fond reproach, thy body will I bang, He takes down his pole.
And loe upon that ſtring thy teeth ſhall hang:
Prepare thy ſelf, for dead ſoon ſhalt thou be.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Saint George for me They fight.

sp.speaker: Barba.
sp.l: Gargantua for me.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: To him Rafe, to him, hold up the Giant, ſet out thy leg before Rafe.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Falſifie a blow Rafe, falſifie a blow, the Giant lies open on the left ſide.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Bear't off, bear't off ſtill; there boy, O Rafe's almoſt down, Rafe's almoſt down.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Suſan inſpire me, now have up again.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Up, up, up, up, up, ſo Rafe, down with him, down with him Rafe.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Fetch him over the hip boy.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: There boy, kill, kill, kill, kill, kill, Rafe.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: No Rafe, get all out of him firſt.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Preſumptuous man, ſee to what deſperate end
Thy treachery hath brought thee, the juſt Gods,
Who never proſper thoſe that do deſpiſe them,
For all the villanies which thou haſt done
To Knights and Ladies, now have paid thee home,
By my ſtiff arm, a Knight adventurous.
But ſay, vile wretch, before I ſend thy ſoul
To ſad Avernus, whither it muſt go,
What captives holdſt thou in thy ſable cave?

sp.speaker: Barba.
sp.l: Go in and free them all, thou haſt the day.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Go Squire and Dwarf, ſearch in this dreadful cave,
And free the wretched priſoners from their bonds.

sp.speaker: Barb.
