sp.l: I crave for mercy as thou art a Knight,
And ſcornſt to ſpill the blood of thoſe that beg.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Thou ſheweſt no mercy, nor ſhalt thou have any,
Prepare thy ſelf, for thou ſhalt ſurely dye.

div.stage: Enter Squire leading one winking, with a Baſon under his chin.

sp.speaker: Squire.
sp.l: Behold brave Knight here is one priſoner,
Whom this wild man hath uſed as you ſee.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: This is the wiſe word I hear the Squire ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Speak what thou art, and how thou haſt been us'd,
That I may give him condign puniſhment

sp.speaker: 1. Kni.
sp.l: I am a Knight that took my journey poſt
Northward from London, and in courteous wiſe,
This Gyant train'd me to his den,
Under pretence of killing of the itch,
And all my body with a powder ſtrew'd,
That ſmarts and ſtings, and cut away my beard,
And my curl'd locks wherein were Ribands ty'de,
And with a water waſht my tender eyes,
Whilſt up and down about me ſtill he skipt,
Whoſe virtue is, that till my eyes be wip't
With a dry cloth, for this my ſoul diſgrace,
I ſhall not dare to look a dog i'th'face.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Alaſs poor Knight, relieve him Rafe, relieve poor Knights whilſt you live.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: My truſty Squire convey him to the Town,
Where he may find relief, adieu fair Knight. Exit Knight.

div.stage: Enter Dwarf leading one with a patch o'er his Noſe,

sp.speaker: Dwar.
sp.l: Puiſſant Knight of the burning Peſtle height,
See here another wretch, whom this ſoul beaſt
Hath ſcorcht and ſcor'd in this inhumane wiſe.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Speak me thy name, and eke thy place of birth,
And what hath been thy uſage in this Cave.

sp.speaker: 2. Knight.
sp.l: I am a Knight, Sir Pock-hole is my name,
And by my birth I am a Londoner,
Free by my Copy, but my Anceſtors
Were Frenchmen all, and riding hard this way.
Upon a trotting horſe my bones did ake,
And I faint Knight to eaſe my weary limbes,
Light at this Cave, when ſtraight this furious fiend,
With ſharpeſt inſtrument of pureſt ſteel,
Did cut the griſtle of my Noſe away,
And in the place this velvet plaſter ſtands,
Relieve me gentle Knight out of his hands.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Good Rafe relieve Sir Pockhole, and ſend him away, for in truth his breath ſtinks.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Convey him ſtraight after the other Knight:
Sir Pockhole fare you well.

sp.speaker: 3. Knight.
sp.l: Kind Sir goodnight Exit.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Deliver us.

sp.speaker: Woman.
sp.l: Deliver us.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Harke George, what a woful cry there is, I think ſome woman lyes in there.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: Deliver us

sp.speaker: Woman.
sp.l: Deliver us.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: What gaſtly noiſe is this? ſpeak Barbaroſo
Or by this blazing ſteel thy head goes off.

sp.speaker: Barb.
sp.l: Priſoners of mine, whom I in diet keep,
Send lower down into the Cave,
And in a Tub that's heated ſmoaking hot,
There may they find them and deliver them.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Run Squire and Dwarf, deliver them with ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: But will not Rafe kill this Giant, ſurely I am afraid if he let him go he will do as much hurt, as ever he did.

sp.speaker: Citizen.
sp.l: Not ſo Mouſe neither, if he could convert him.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I George, if he could convert him; but a Gyant is not ſo ſoon converted as one of us ordinary people. There's a pretty tale of a Witch, that had the Divels mark about lier, God bleſs us, that had a Gyant to her ſon, that was call'd Lob-lie-by-the-fire, didſt never hear it George.

div.stage: Enter Squire leading a man with a glaſs of Lotion in his hand, and the Dwarf leading a woman, with Dyet-bread and Drink.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Peace Nell, here comes the priſoners.

sp.speaker: Dwar.
sp.l: Here be theſe pined wretches, manfull Knight,
That for this ſix weeks have not ſeen a wight.

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.l: Deliver what you are, and how you came
To this ſad Cave, and what your uſage was?

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: I am an errant Knight that followed Arms,
With ſpear and ſhield, and in my tnder years
I ſtrucken was with Cupids fiery ſhaft,
And fell in love with this my Lady dear,
And ſtole her from her friends in Turne-ball ſtreet,
And bore her up and down from Town to Town,
Where we did eat and drink and Muſick here;
Till at the length at this unhappy Town
We did arrive, and coming to this Cave,
This beaſt us caught, and put us in a Tub,
Where we this two months ſweat, and ſhould have done.
Another Month if you had not relieved us.

sp.speaker: Wom.
sp.l: This bread and water hath our dyet been,
Together with a rib cut from a neck
Of burned Mutton, hard hath been our fare,
Releaſe us from this ugly Gyants ſnare.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.l: This hath been half the food we have receiv'd,
But only twice a day for novelty,
He gave a ſpoonful of his hearty broth Pulls out a ſiringe.
To each of us, through this ſame tender quill.

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.l: From this infernall Monſter you ſhall go,
That uſeth Knights and gentle Ladies ſo.
Convey them hence. Exeunt man and woman.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Cunny, I can tell thee the Gentleman like Rafe.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I George, I ſee it well enough. Gentlemen I thank you all heartily for gracing my man Ralph, and I promiſe you, you ſhall ſee him oftner.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Mercy great Knight, I do recant my ill,
And henceforth never gentle blood will ſpill.

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.l: I give thee mercy, but yet thou ſhalt ſwear
Upon my burning Peſtle to perform
Thy promiſe utter'd.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I ſwear and kiſs.

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.l: Depart then and amend.
Come Squire and Dwarf, the Sun grows towards his ſet,
And we have many more adventures yet. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Now Raph is in this humor, I know he would ha beaten all the boys in the houſe, if they had been ſet on him.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I George, but it is well as it is: I warrant you the gentlemen do conſider what it is to overthrow a Gyant: but look George, here comes Miſtriſs Merri-thought, and her ſon Michael, now you are welcome Miſtriſs Merri-thought, now Raph has done you may go on.

sp.speaker: Miſt. mer·
sp.l: Micke My Boy?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.l: I forſooth Mother.

sp.speaker: Miſt. mer.
sp.p:
Be merry Micke, we are at home now: where I warrant you, you ſhall find the houſe flung out of the
windows: Hark: hey dogs, hey, this is the old world y'faith with my Husband: I'll get in among them, I'll play them ſuch leſſon, that they ſhall have little liſt to come ſcraping hither again. Why Maſter Merry-thought, Huſband, Charles Merry-thought.

sp.speaker: Old Mer. within.
sp.p: If you will ſing, and dance, and laugh, and hollow, and laugh again: and then cry there boys there: why then,
sp.l: One, two, three, and four,
We ſhall be merry within this hour.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Why Charles do you not know your own natural wife? I ſay open the door, and turn me out thoſe mangy companions; 'tis more than time that they were fellow like with you: you are a Gentleman Charles, and an old man, and father of two children; and I my ſelf, (though I ſay it) by my mothers ſide, Niece to a Worſhipful Gentleman, and a Conductor, he has been three times in his Majeſties ſervice at Cheſter, and is now the fourth time, God bleſs him, and his charge upon his journey.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.

l.hi: Go from my window, love go:
Go from my window my dear,
The wind and the rain will drive you back again,
You cannot be lodged here.

sp.p: Hark you Miſtriſs Merri-thought, you that walk upon Adventures, and forſake your Husband, becauſe he ſings with never a penny in his purſe; what ſhall I think my ſelf the worſe? Faith no, I'll be merry.
You come not here, here's none but Lads of mettle, lives of a hundred years, and upwards, care never drunk their bloods, nor want made them warble.
sp.l: Hey-ho, my heart is heavy.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Why M. Merrithought, what am I that you ſhould laugh me to ſcorn thus abruptly? am I not your fellow-feeler, (as we may ſay) in all our miſeries? your comforter in health and ſickneſs? have I not brought you Children? are they not like you Charles? look upon thine own Image, hard-hearted man; and yet for all this—

sp.speaker: Old Mer. within.
sp.p: Begon, begon my juggy, my puggy, begon my love my dear.
The weather is warm, 'twill do thee no harm, thou canſt not be lodged here.
Be merry boys, ſome light muſick, and more wine.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: He's not in earneſt, I hope George, is he?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: What if he be, ſweet heart?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Marry if he be George, I'll make bold to tell him he's an ingrant old man, to uſe his bed-fellow ſo ſcurvily.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: What how does he uſe her Honey?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Marry come up ſir ſauce-box, I think you'll take his part, will you not? Lord how hot are you grown: you are a fine man an you had a fine Dog, it becomes you ſweetly.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Nay, prethee Nell chide not: for as I am an honeſt man, and a true Chriſtian Grocer, I do not like his doings.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I cry you mercy then George, you know we are all frail, and full of infirmities. Dee hear Maſter Merri-thought, may I crave a word with you?

sp.speaker: Old Mer within.
sp.l: Strike up lively lads.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I had not thought in truth, Maſter Merri-thought, that a man of your age and diſcretion (as I may ſay) being a Gentleman, and therefore known by your gentle conditions, could have uſed ſo little reſpect to the weakneſs of his wife: for your wife is your own fleſh, the ſtaff of your age, your yoke-fellow, with whoſe help you draw through the myre of this tranſitory world: Nay, ſhe's your own rib. And again—

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: I come not hither for thee to teach,
I have no pulpit for thee to preach,
I would thou hadſt kiſt me under the breech,
As thou art a Lady gay.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Marry with a vengeance,
sp.p: I am heartily ſorry for the poor Gentlewoman: but if I
were thy wife, i'faith gray-beard, i'faith—

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: I prethee ſweet Hony-ſuckle, be content.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Give me ſuch words that am a Gentlewoman born, hang him hoary Raſcal. Get me ſome drink George, I am almoſt molten with fretting: now beſhrew his Knaves heart for it.

sp.speaker: Old mer.
sp.p: Play me a light Lavalto: come, be frollick, fill the good fellows wine.

sp.speaker: Miſt. mer.
sp.p: Why Maſter Merri-thought, are you diſpoſed to make me wait here: you'll open I hope, i'll fetch them that ſhall open elſe.

sp.speaker: Old mer.
sp.p: Good woman, if you will ſing, I'll give you ſomething, if not —

body.head: SONG.
body.l: You are no love for me Marget, I am no love for you.
Come aloft Boys, aloft.

sp.speaker: Miſt. mer.
sp.p: Now a Churles fart in your teeth Sir: Come Mick, we'll not trouble him, a ſhall not ding us i'th'teeth with his bread and his broth, that he ſhall not: come boy, I'll provide for thee, I warrant thee: wee'll go to Maſter Venterwels the Merchant, I'll get his letter to mine Hoſt of the Bell in Waltham, there I'll place thee with the Tapſter, will not that do well for thee Mick? and let me alone for that old Cuckoldly Knave your father, I'll uſe him in his kind, I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Come George, where's the beer?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Here Love.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: This old fornicating fellow will not out of my mind yet; Gentlemen, I'll begin to you all, I deſire more of your acquaintance, with all my heart. Fill the Gentlemen ſome beer George.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Look George, the little boy's come again, methinks he looks ſomething like the Prince of Orange in his long ſtocking, if he had a little harneſs about his neck. George, I will have him dance Fading; Fading, is a fine Jig I'll aſſure you Gentlemen: begin brother, now a capers ſweet heart, now a turn a th'toe, and then tumble: cannot you tumble youth?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: No indeed forſooth.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Nor eat fire?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Neither.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Why then I thank you heartily, there's two pence to buy you points withall.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.p: There boy, deliver this: but do it well. Haſt thou
provided me four luſty fellows?
sp.l: Able to carry me? and art thou perfect
In all thy buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Sir you need not fear,
I have my leſſon here, and cannot miſs it:
The men are ready for you, and what elſe
Pertains to this imployment.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: There my boy,
Take it, but buy no land.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Faith ſir 'twere rare
To ſee ſo young a purchaſer: I flie,
And on my wings carry your deſtiny. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Go, and be happy: Now my lateſt hope
Forſake me not, but fling thy Anchor out,
And let it hold: ſtand, fix thou rolling ſtone,
Till I enjoy my deareſt: hear me all
You powers that rule in men celeſtial. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wife,
sp.p: Go thy ways, thou art as crooked a ſprig as ever grew, in London, I warrant him he'll come to ſome naughty end or other: for his looks ſay no leſs: Beſides, his father (you know George) is none of the beſt, you heard him take me up like a Gill flirt: and ſing bawdy Songs upon me: but i'faith if I live George—

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Let me alone ſweet-heart, I have a trick in my head ſhall lodge him in the Arches for one year, and make him ſing Peccavi, 'ere I leave him, and yet he ſhall never know who hurt him neither.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Do my good Geerge, do.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: What ſhall we have Rafe do now boy?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: You ſhall have what you will ſir.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Why ſo ſir, go and fetch me him then, and let the Sophy of Perſia come and chriſten him a child.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Believe me Sir, that will not do ſo well, 'tis ſtale, it has been had before at the Red Bull.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: George, let Rafe travell over great hills, and let him be weary, and come to the King of Cracovia's houſe, covered with velvet, and there let the Kings daughter ſtand in her window all in beaten gold, combing her golden locks with a comb of Ivory, and let her ſpye Rafe, and fall in love with him, and come down to him, and carry him into her fathers houſe, and then let Rafe talk with her.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Well ſaid Nel, it ſhall be ſo: boy let's ha't done quickly.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir, if you will imagine all this to be done already, you ſhall hear them talk together: but we cannot preſent a houſe covered with black Velvet, and a Lady in beaten gold.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Sir Boy, lets ha't as you can then.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Beſides, it will ſhew ill-favoredly to have a Grocers Prentice to court a Kings daughter.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Will it ſo Sir? you are well read in Hiſtories: I pray you what was Sir Dagonet? was not he Prentice to a Grocer in London? read the Play of the Four Prentices of London, where they toſs their Pikes ſo: I pray you fetch him in Sir, fetch him in.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: It ſhall be done, it is not our fault Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Now we ſhall ſee fine doings I warrant thee George.
O here they come; how prettily the King of Cracovia's daughter is dreſt.

div.stage: Enter Rafe and the Lady, Squire and Dwarf.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: I Nell, it is the faſhion of that Countrey, I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Welcome ſir Knight unto my fathers Court.
King of Moldavia, unto me Pompiona
His daughter dear: but ſure you do not like
Your entertainment, that will ſtay with us
No longer but a night.

sp.speaker: Raph.
sp.l: Damſell right fair,
I'm on many ſad adventures bound,
That call me forth into the Wilderneſs:
Beſides, my horſes back in ſomething gal'd,
Which will enforce me ride a ſober pace.
But many thanks (fair Lady) be to you,
For uſing errant Knight with courteſie.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: But ſay (brave Knight) what is your name and birth?

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: My name is Rafe, I am an Engliſhman,
As true as ſteel, a hearty Engliſhman,
And Prentice to a Grocer in the Strand,
By deed indent, of which I have one part:
But fortune calling me to follow Arms,
On me this holy Order I did take,
Of burning Peſtle, which in all mens eyes,
I bear, confounding Ladies enemies.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Oft have I heard of your brave Countrymen,
And fertile ſoil, and ſtore of wholoſome food;
My father oft will tell me of a drink
In England found, and Nipitato call'd.
Which driveth all the ſorrow from your hearts.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Lady 'tis true, you need not lay your lips
To better Nipitato than there is.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: And of a wild-fowl he will often ſpeak,
Which poudred beef and muſtard called is:
For there have been great Wars 'twixt us and you,
But truely Rafe, it was not long of me.
Tell me then Rafe could you contented be,
To wear a Ladies favor in your ſhield?

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: I am a Knight of Religious Order,
And will not wear a favor of a Ladies
That truſts in Antichriſt, and falſe traditions.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Well ſaid Rafe, convert her if thou canſt.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Beſides, I have a Lady of my own
In merry England; for whoſe virtuous ſake
I took theſe Arms, and Suſan is her name,
A Coblers maid in Milkſtreet, whom I vow
Nere to forſake, whilſt life and Peſtle laſt.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Happy that Cobling Dame, who ere ſhe be
That for her own (dear Rafe) hath gotten thee.
Unhappy I, that nere ſhall ſee the day
To ſee thee more, that bear'ſt my heart away.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Lady farewell, I muſt needs take my leave.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Hard-hearted Rafe, that Ladies doſt deceive.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Hark thee Rafe, there's money for thee; give ſomething in the King of Cracovia's houſe, be not beholding to him.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Lady before I go, I muſt remember
Your fathers Officers, who truth to tell,
Have been about me very diligent:
Hold up thy ſnowy hand thou princely maid,
There's twelvepence for your fathers Chamberlain.
And another ſhilling for his Cook,
For by my troth the Gooſe was roſted well.
And twelve pence for your fathers Horſe-keeper,
For nointing my horſe back, and for his butter
There is another ſhilling to the maid
That waſht my boot-hoſe, there's an Engliſh groat,
And twopence to the boy that wip't my boots.
And laſt, fair Lady, there is for your ſelf
Three pence to buy you pins at Bumbo Fair.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Full many thanks, and I will keep them ſafe
Till all the heads be off, for thy ſake Rafe.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Advance my Squire and Dwarf, I cannot ſtay.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Thou kil'ſt my heart in parting thus away.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I commend Rafe, yet that he will not ſtoop to a Cracovian, there's properer women in London than any are there I-wis. But here comes Maſter Humphrey, and his love again, now George.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: I Cunny, peace.

div.stage: Enter Merchant, Humphrey, Luce, and Boy.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.l: Go get you up, I will not be intreated.
And Goſſip mine I'll keep you ſure hereafter
From gadding out again, with boys and unthrifts,
Come they are womens tears, I know your faſhion.
Go ſirrah, lock her in, and keep the key. Exit Luce and Boy.
Safe as your life. Now my ſon Humphrey,
You may both reſt aſſured of my love
In this, and reap your own deſire.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: I ſee this love you ſpeak of, through your daughter.
Although the hole be little, and hereafter
Will yield the like in all I may or can,
Fitting a Chriſtian, and a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Merc·
sp.l: I Do believe you (my good ſon) and thank you.
For 'twere an impudence to think you flattered.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: It were indeed, but ſhall I tell you why,
I have been beaten twice about the lye.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.l: Well ſon, no more of complement, my daughter
Is yours again; appoint the time and take her.
Wee'll have no ſtealing for it, I my ſelf
And ſome few of our friends will ſee you married.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: I would you would i'faith, for be it known
I ever was afraid to lye alone.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Some three days hence then.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Three days, let me ſee,
'Tis ſomewhat of the moſt, yet I agree,
Becauſe I mean againſt the pointed day,
To viſit all my friends in new array. Enter ſervant.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Sir, there's a Gentlewoman without would ſpeak with your Worſhip.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: What is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sir I askt her not.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Bid her come in.

sp.speaker: Miſt. mer.
sp.l: Peace be to your Worſhip, I come as a poor
Suitor to you Sir, in the behalf of this child.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Are you not wiſe to Merri-thought?

sp.speaker: Miſt. mer.
sp.p: Yes truly, would I had nere ſeen his eyes, he has undone me and himſelf, and his children, and there he lives at home and ſings, and hoyts, and revels among his drunken companions, but I warrant you, where to get a penny to put bread in his mouth, he knows not: And therefore if it like your Worſhip, I would intreat your Letter, to the honeſt Hoſt of the Bell in Waltham, that I may place my child under the protection of his Tapſter, in ſome ſetled courſe of life.

sp.speaker: Mer
sp.l: I'm glad the heavens have heard my prayers: thy Husband
When I was ripe in ſorrows laught at me,
Thy ſon, like an unthankful wretch, I having
Redeem'd him from his fall, and made him mine,
To ſhew his love again, firſt ſtole my daughter:
Then wrong'd this Gentleman, and laſt of all,
Gave me that grief, had almoſt brought me down
Unto my grave, had not a ſtronger hand
Reliev'd my ſorrows, go, and weep as I did,
And be unpittied, for here I profeſs
An everlaſting hate to all thy name.

sp.speaker: Miſt. mer.
sp.p: Will you ſo Sir, how ſay you by that? come Micke, let him keep his wind to cool his Pottage, we'll go to thy Nurſes, Micke, ſhe knits ſilk ſtockings boy, and we'll knit too boy, and be beholding to none of them all. Exeunt Michael and Mother.

div.stage: Enter a Boy with a Letter.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Sir, I take it you are the Maſter of this houſe.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: How then boy?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Then to your ſelf Sir, comes this Letter.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: From whom my pretty boy?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: From him that was your ſervant, but no more
Shall that name ever be, for he is dead,
Grief of your purchas'd anger broke his heart,
〈◊〉 ſaw him dye, and from his hand receiv'd
This paper with a charge to bring it hither,
Read it, and ſatisfie your ſelf in all.

sp.speaker: Merch.

body.head: LETTER.
body.p: SIR that I have wronged your love, I muſt confeſs, in which I have purchaſt to my ſelf, beſides mine own undoing, the ill opinion of my friends, let not your anger, good Sir, outlive me, but ſuffer me to reſt in peace with your forgiveneſs; let my body (if a dying man may ſo much prevail with you) be brought to your daughter, that ſhe may know my hot flames are now buried, and withall, receive a teſtimony of the zeal I bore her vertue: farewell for ever, and be ever happy.

sp.l: Gods hand is great in this, I do forgive him,
Yet am I glad he's quiet, where I hope
He will not bite again: boy bring the body,
And let him have his will, if that be all.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: 'Tis here without Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: So Sir, if you pleaſe
You may conduct it in, I do not fear it.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: I'll be your Uſher boy, for though I ſay it,
He ow'd me ſomething once, and well did pay it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: If there be any puniſhment inflicted
Upon the miſerable, more than yet I feell,
Let it together ſeize me, and at once
Preſs down my ſoul, I cannot bear the pain
Of theſe delaying tortures: thou that art
The end of all, and the ſweet reſt of all;
Come, come oh death bring me to thy peace,
And blot out all the memory I nouriſh
Both of father and my cruel friend.
O wretch'd maid ſtill living to be wretched,
To be a ſay to fortune in her changes.
And grow to number times and woes together,
How happy had I been, if being born
My grave had been my cradle? Enter ſervant.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: By your leave
Young Miſtris, here's a boy hath brought a Coffin,
What a would ſay I know not: but your father
Charg'd me to give you notice, here they come.

div.stage: Enter two bearing a Coffin, Jaſper in it.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: For me I hope 'tis come, and 'tis moſt welcome

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Fair Miſtriſs, let me not add greater grief
To that great ſtore you have already; Jaſper
That whilſt he liv'd was yours, now dead,
And here inclos'd, commanded me to bring
His body hither, and to crave a tear
From thoſe fair eyes, though he deſerve not pitty,
To deck his Funeral; for ſo he bid me
Tell her for whom he di'd.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: He ſhall have many: Exeunt Coffin-carrier and Boy.
Good friends depart a little, whilſt I take
My leave of this dead man, that once I lov'd:
Hold, yet a little, life, and then I give thee
To thy firſt heavenly being; O my friend!
Haſt thou deceiv'd me thus, and got before me?
I ſhall not long be after, but believe me,
Thou wert too cruel Jaſper 'gainſt thy ſelf,
In puniſhing the fault I could have pardoned,
With ſo untimely death; thou didſt not wrong me,
But ever wer't moſt kind, moſt true, moſt loving
And I the moſt unkind, moſt falſe, moſt cruell.
Didſt thou but ask a tear? I'll give thee all,
Even all my eyes can pour down, all my ſigh's
And all my ſelf, before thou goeſt from me
There are but ſparing Rites: But if thy ſoul
Be yet about this place, and can behold
And ſee what I prepare to deck thee with,
It ſhall go up, born on the wings of peace,
And ſatisfied: firſt will I ſing thy Dirge,
Then kiſs thy pale lips, and then dye my ſelf,
And fill one Coffin and one grave together.

lg.l: Come you whoſe loves are dead,
And whilſt I ſing
Weep and wring
Every hand and every head,
Bind with Cipreſs and ſad Ewe,
Ribbands black, and Candles blue,
For him that was of men moſt true.
Come with heavy mourning,
And on his grave
Let him have
Sacrifice of ſighs and groaning,
Let him have fair flowers enow,
White and purple, green and yellow,
For him that was of men moſt true.

sp.l: Thou fable cloth, ſad cover of my joys,
I lift thee up, and thus I meet with death.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: And thus you meet the living.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: Save me Heaven.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Nay, do not flye me fair, I am no ſpirit,
Look better on me, do you know me yet?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: O thou dear ſhadow of my friend.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Dear ſubſtance,
I ſwear I am no ſhadow feel my hand,
It is the ſame it was, I am your Jaſper,
Your Jaſper that's yet living, and yet loving,
Pardon my raſh attempt, my fooliſh proof
I put in practice of your conſtancy:
For ſooner ſhould my ſword have drunk my blood,
And ſet my ſoul at liberty, than drawn
The leaſt drop from that body, for which boldneſs
Doom me to any thing: if death, I take it
And willingly.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: This death I'll give you for it,
So, now I am ſatisfied: you are no ſpirit,
But my own trueſt, trueſt, trueſt friend,
Why do you come thus to me?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Firſt, to ſee you,
Then to convey you hence.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.l: It cannot be,
For I am lockt up here, and watcht at all hours,
That 'tis impoſſible for me to ſcape.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Nothing more poſſible, within this Coffin
Do you convey your ſelf, let me alone,
I have the wits of twenty men about me,
Only I crave the ſhelter of your Cloſet
A little and then fear me not; creep in
That they may preſently convey you hence:
Fear nothing deareſt love, I'll be your ſecond,
Lye cloſe, ſo, all goes well yet; boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: At hand Sir.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Convey away the Coffin, and be wary.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: 'Tis done already.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Now muſt I go conjure. Exit.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Boy, boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Your ſervant Sir.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.p: Do me this kindneſs boy, hold here's a crown: before thou bury the body of this fellow, carry it to his old merry father, and ſalute him from me, and bid him ſing, he hath cauſe.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I will Sir.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.p: And then bring me word what tune he is in, and have another crown: but do it truly.
sp.l: I have fitted him a bargain, now, will vex him.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: God bleſs your Worſhips health Sir.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Farewell boy. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Ah old Merry-thought, art thou there again? let's hear ſome of thy Songs.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Who can ſing a merrier note
Th •• be that cannot change a great?
sp.p: Not a Dinner left, and yet my heart leaps; I do wonder yet, as old as I am, that any man will follow a Trade, or ſerve, that may ſing and laugh, and walk the ſtreets: my wife and both my ſons are I know not where, I have nothing left, nor know I how to come by meat to ſupper, yet am I merry ſtill; for I know I ſhall find it upon the Table at ſix a Clock; therefore hang Thought
sp.l: I would not be a Servingman to carry the cloke-bag ſtill.
Nor would I be a Fawlconer the greedy Hawkes to fill.
But I would be in a good houſe, and have a good Maſter • o:
But I would eat and drink of the beſt, and no work would I do.
sp.p: This is that keeps life and ſoul together, mirth: this is the Philoſophers ſtone that they write ſo much on, that keeps a man ever young.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir, they ſay they know all your Money is gone, and they will truſt you for no more drink.

sp.speaker: Old mer.
sp.p: Will they not? let 'em chuſe: the beſt is I have mirth at home, and need not ſend abroad for that; let them keep their drink to themſelves.
sp.l: For Jillian of Berry, ſhe dwells on a hill,
And ſhe hath good Beer and Ale to ſell,
And of good fellows ſhe thinks no ill,
And thither will we go now, now, now, and thither
Will we go now.
And when you have made a little ſtay,
You need not know what is to pay,
But kiſs your Hoſteſs and go your way. And thither, &c.

sp.speaker: 2. Boy.
sp.l: Sir, I can get no bread for ſupper.

sp.speaker: Old mer.
sp.p: Hang bread and ſupper, let's preferve our mirth, and we ſhall never feel hunger, I'll warrant you, let's have a Catch, boy follow me, come ſing this Catch.
sp.l: Ho, ho, no body at home, meat, nor drink, nor money ha we none, fill the pot Eedy, never more need I.

sp.speaker: Old mer.
sp.p: So boyes enough, follow me, let's change our place and we ſhall laugh afreſh. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Let him go George, a ſhall not have any countenance from us, not a good word from any i'th' Company, if I may ſtrike ſtroke in't.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: No more, a ſhannot love; but Nell, I will have Rafe, do a very notable matter now, to the eternal honour and glory of all Grocers: ſirrah, you there, boy, can none of you hear?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir, your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Let Rafe come out on May day in the morning, and ſpeak upon a Conduit with all his Scarfs about him, and his Feathers, and his Rings, and his Knacks.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Why ſir, you do not think of our plot, what will become of that then?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Why ſir, I care not what become on't, I'll have him come out, or I'll fetch him out my ſelf, I'll have ſomething done in honor of the City: beſides he hath been long enough upon Adventures, bring him out quickly, for I come amongſt you—

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Well ſir, he ſhall come out, but if our Play miſcarry, Sir you are like to pay for't. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Bring him away then.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: This will be brave i'faith: George ſhall not he dance the Morrice too for the credit of the Strand.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: No ſweet-heart it will be too much for the boy. O there he is Nell, he's reaſonable well in reparel, but he has not Rings enough.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: London, to thee I do preſent the merry Month of May,

l.hi: Let each true Subject be content to hear me what I ſay:
For from the top of Conduit head, as plainly may appear,
I will both tell my name to you, and wherefore I came here.

sp.l: My name is Rafe, by due deſcent, though not ignoble I,

l.hi: Yet far inferiour to the flock of gracious Grocery.
And by the Common-counſel of my fellows in the Strand,
With gilded Staff, and croſſed Skarfe, the May-lord here I ſtand.
Rejoyce O Engliſh hearts, rejoyce, rejoyce O Lovers dear;
Rejoyce O City, Town, and Countrey, rejoyce eke every Shire;
For now the flagrant flowers do ſpring and ſprout in ſeemly ſort,
The little Birds do ſit and ſing, the Lambs do make fine ſport,
And now the Burchin Tree doth bud that makes the Schoolboy cry,
The Morrice rings while Hobby horſe doth foot it featuouſly:
The Lords and Ladies now abroad for their diſport and play,
Do kiſs ſometimes upon the Graſs, and ſometimes in the Hay.
Now butter with a leaf of Sage is good to purge the blood,

sp.l: Fly Venus and Phlebotomy for they are neither good.

l.hi: Now little fiſh on tender ſtone, begin to caſt their bellies,
And ſluggiſh ſnails, that erſt were mute, do creep out of their ſhellies,
The rumbling Rivers now do warm for little boys to paddle,
The Sturdy Steed, now goes to graſs, and up they hang his ſaddle.
The heavy Hart, the blowing Buck, the Raſcall and the Pricket,
Are now among the Yeomans Peaſe, and leave the fearful thicket.
And be like them, O you, I ſay, of this ſame noble Town,
And lift aloft your velvet heads, and ſlipping of your gown:
With bels on legs, and napkins clean unto your ſhoulders ti'de,
With Scarfs and Garters as you pleaſe, and Hey for our Town cry'd:
March out and ſhew your willing minds, by twenty, and by twenty,

sp.l: To Hogſdon or to Newington, where Ale and Cakes are plenty.
And let it nere be ſaid for ſhame, that we the youths of London,

l.hi: Lay thruming of our caps at home, and left our cuſtom undone.
Ʋp then I ſay, both young and old, both man and maid a Maying
With Drums and Guns that bounce aloud, and merry Taber playing.
Which to prolong, God ſave our King, and ſend his Countrey peace,
And root out Treaſon from the Land, and ſo my friends I ceaſe.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.p: I will have no great ſtore of company at the wedding, a couple of neighbors and their wives, and we will have a Capon in ſtewed broth, with marrow, and a good piece of beef, ſtuck with Roſe-mary.

div.stage: Enter Jaſper and his face mealed.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Forbear thy pains fond man, It is too late.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs me: Jaſper?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: I, I am his Ghoſt
Whom thou haſt injur'd for his conſtant love:
Fond worldly wretch, who doſt not underſtand
In death that true hearts cannot parted be.
Firſt know thy daughter is quite born away,
On wings on Angels: through the liquid Ayre
Too far out of thy reach, and never more
Shalt thou behold her face: But ſhe and I
Will in another world enjoy our loves,
Where neither fathers anger, poverty,
Nor any croſs that troubles earthly men
Shall make us ſever our united hearts,
And never ſhalt thou ſit, or be alone
In any place, but I will viſit thee
With gaſtly looks, and put into thy mind
The great offences which thou didſt to me.
When thou art at thy Table with thy friends,
Merry in heart, and ſild with ſwelling wine,
I'll come in midſt of all thy pride and mirth,
Inviſible to all men but thy ſelf,
And whiſper ſuch a ſad tale in thine ear,
Shall make thee let the Cup fall from thy hand,
And ſtand as mute and pale as Death it ſelf.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Forgive me Jaſper; Oh! what might I do?
Tell me to ſatisfie thy troubled Ghoſt?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: There is no means, too late thou thinkſt on this.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: But tell me what were beſt for me to do?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Repent thy deed, and ſatisfie my father,
And beat fond Humphrey out of thy doors. Exit Jaſp

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Look George, his very Ghoſt would have folks beaten.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Father, my bride is gone, fair Miſtris Luce,
My ſoul's the font of vengeance, miſchiefs ſluce.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Hence fool out of my ſight, with thy fond paſſion,
Thou haſt undone me.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: Hold my father dear,
For Luce thy daughters ſake, that had no peer.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Thy father fool? there's ſome blows more, begon.
sp.l: Jaſper, I hope thy Ghoſt be well appeaſed,
To ſee thy will perform'd, now I'll go
To ſatisfie thy father for thy wrongs. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hum.
sp.l: What ſhall I do? I have been beaten twice.
And Miſtris Luce is gone? help me device:
Since my true-love is gone, I never more,
Whilſt I do live, upon the Skie will pore;
But in the dark will wear out my ſhoo-ſoles
In paſſion, in Saint Faiths Church under Pauls. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: George call Rafe hither, if you love me call Rafe hither, I have the braveſt thing for him to do George,; prethee. call him quickly

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Rafe, why Rafe boy.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.l: Here Sir.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Come hither Rafe, come to thy Miſtris Boy.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Rafe I would have thee call all the youths together in battle-ray, with Drums, and Guns, and flags, and march to Mile-end in pompous faſhion, and there exhort your Souldiers to be merry and wiſe, and to keep their beards from burning Rafe, and then skirmiſh, and let your flags fly, and cry, kill, kill, kill: my husband ſhall lend you his Jerkin Rafe, and there's a Scarfe for the reſt, the houſe ſhall furniſh you, and we'll pay for't: do it bravely Rafe, and think before whom you perform, and what perſon you repreſent.

sp.speaker: Rafe.
sp.p: I warrant you Miſtreſs, if I do it not, for the honor of the City, and the credit of my Maſter, let me never hope for freedome.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: 'Tis well ſpoken i'faith; go thy waies, thou art a ſpark indeed.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Ralph, double your files bravely Ralph.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: I warrant you Sir, Exit Ralph.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Let him look narrowly to his ſervice, I ſhall take him elſe; I was there my ſelf a Pike-man once, in the hotteſt of the day, wench, had my feather ſhot ſhaer away, the fringe of my pike burnt off with powder, my pate broken with a ſcouring-ſtick, and yet I thank God I am here. Drum within.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Hark George, the Drums.

sp.speaker: Cit,
sp.p: Ran, tan; tan, tan, ran tan: Oh wench an thou hadſt but ſeen little Ned of Aldgate, drum Ned, how he made it roar again, and laid on like a tyrant: and then ſtruck ſoftly till the Ward came up, and then thundred again, and together we go: ſa, ſa, ſa, bounce quoth the Guns: courage my hearts, quoth the Captains: Saint George, quoth the pike-men; and withal here they lay, and there they lay: And yet for all this I am here wench.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Be thankful for it George, for indeed 'tis wonderful.

div.stage: Enter Ralph and his company with Drums and Colours.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: March fair my hearts; Lieutenant beat the rear up: Ancient let your Colours flie; but have a great care of the Butchers hooks at White-Chappel, they have been the death of many a fair Ancient. Open your files, that I may take a view both of your perſons and munition: Serjeant call a Muſter.

sp.speaker: Serg.
sp.p: A ſtand, William Hamerton Pewterer.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Here Captain.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: A Corſlet and a Spaniſh Pike; 'tis well, can you ſhake it with a terror?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: I hope ſo Captain.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: Charge upon me, 'tis with the weakeſt: put more ſtrength William Hamerton, more ſtrength: as you were again; proceed Serjeant.

sp.speaker: Serj.
sp.p: George Green-gooſe, Poulterer.

sp.speaker: Green.
sp.p: Here.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: Let me ſee your Peece neighbor Green-gooſe, when was ſhe ſhot in?

sp.speaker: Green.
sp.p: And like you maſter Captain, I made a ſhot even now, partly to ſcour her, and partly for audacity.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: It ſhould ſeem ſo certainly, for her breath is yet inflamed: beſides, there is a main fault in the touch-hole, it runs and ſtinketh; and I tell you moreover, and believe it. Ten ſuch touch-holes would breed the Pox in the Army; Get you a Feather, neighbor, get you a Feather, ſweet Oil, and Paper, and your Peece may do well enough yet. Where's your Powder?

sp.speaker: Green.
sp.p: Here.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: What in a Paper? As I am a Soldier and a Gentleman, it craves a Martial Court: you ought to die for't. Where's your horn? anſwer me to that.

sp.speaker: Green.
sp.p: An't like you Sir, I was oblivious.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: It likes me not it ſhould be ſo; 'tis a ſhame for you, and a ſcandal to all our Neighbors, being a man of worth and eſtimation, to leave your horn behind you: I am afraid 'twill breed example. But let me tell you no more on't; ſtand, till I view you all. What's become o'th' noſe of your flaske?

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.p: Indeed law Captain, 'twas blown away with powder.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: Put on a new one at the Cities Charge. Where's the ſtone of this Peece?

sp.speaker: 2 Sold.
sp.p: The Drummer took it out to light Tobacco.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.p: 'Tis a fault my friend, put it in again: you want a Noſe, and you a Stone; Serjeant, take a note on't, for I mean to ſtop it in the pay. Remove and march, ſoft and fair Gentlemen; ſoft and fair: double and files, as you were, faces about. Now you with the ſodden face, keep in there: look to your Match ſirrah, it will be in your fellows flask anon. So make a Creſcent now, advance your Pikes, ſtand and give ear, Gentlemen, Countrey-men, Friends, and my fellow-Soldiers, I have brought you this day from the Shop of Security, and the Counters of Content, to meaſure out in theſe furious fields, Honor by the ell, and Proweſs by the pound: Let it not, O let it not, I ſay, be told hereafter, the noble iſſue of this City fainted: but bear your ſelves in this fair action, like men, valiant men, and free men: Fear not the face of the enemy: nor the noiſe of the Guns: for believe me brethren, the rude rumbling of a Brewers Carr is more terrible, of which you have a daily experience: Neither let the ſtink of Powder offend you, ſince a more valiant ſtink is nightly with you. To a reſolved mind, his home is every where: I ſpeak not this to take away the hope of your return; for you ſhall ſee (I do not doubt it) and that very ſhortly, your loving wives again, and your ſweet children, whoſe care doth bear you company in baskets. Remember then whoſe cauſe you have in hand, and like a ſort of true-born Scavengers, ſcour me this famous Realm of enemies. I have no more to ſay but this: Stand to your tacklings lads, and ſhew to the world, you can as well brandiſh a ſword, as ſhake an Apron. Saint George, and on my hearts. Omnes. Saint George, Saint George. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: 'Twas well done Ralph, I'll ſend thee a cold Capon a field, and a bottle of March-beer; and, it may be, come my ſelf to ſee thee.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Nel, the boy hath deceiv'd me much, I did not think it had been in him: he has perform'd ſuch a matter wench, that if I live, next year I'll have him Captain of the Galliſoiſt, or I'll want my Will.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Yet I thank God, I break not a rinkle more than I had, not a ſtoop boys? Care live with Cats, I defie thee, my heart is as ſound as an Oak; and though I want drink to wet my whiſtle, I can ſing.
sp.l: Come no more there boys, come no more there:
For we ſhall never whilſt we live, come any more there.

div.stage: Enter a Boy with a Coffin.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: God ſave you Sir.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: It's a brave Boy: can'ſt thou ſing?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I can ſing, but 'tis not ſo neceſſary at this time.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Sing we, and chaunt it, whilſt love doth grant it.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir, Sir, if you knew what I have brought you, you would have little lift to ſing.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Oh the Mimon round, full long I have thee ſought.
And now I have thee found, and what haſt thou here brought?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A Coffin, Sir, and your dead Son Jaſper in it.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Dead? why farewell he:
Thou waſt a bonny boy, and I did love thee.

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Then I pray you Sir, do ſo ſtill.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Jaſper's Ghoſt? thou art welcome from Stygian lake ſo ſoon,
Declare to me what wondrous things in Pluto's court are done

sp.speaker: Jaſ.
sp.l: By my troth ſir, I ne'r came there, 'tis too hot for me Sir.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: A merry Ghoſt, a very merry Ghoſt.
And where is your true love? Oh where is yours?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.l: Marry look you Sir. Heaves up the Coffin.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Ah ha! Art thou good at that i' faith?
With hey trixie terlerie-whiskin, the world it runs on wheels.
When the young mans — up goes the Maidens heels.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: What Mr. Merri-thought, will you not let's in? what do you think ſhall become of us?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.l: What voice is that that calleth at our door?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: You know me well enough, I am ſure I have not been ſuch a ſtranger to you.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: And ſome they whiſtled, and ſome they ſung, Hey down, down: and ſome did loudly ſay, ever as the Lord Barnets horn blew, Away Muſgrave away.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: You will not have us ſtarve here, will you Maſter Merry-thought?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.p: Nay, good Sir be perſwaded, ſhe is my Mother: if her offences have been great againſt you, let your own love remember ſhe is yours, and ſo forgive her.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Good maſter Merry-thought, let me intreat you, I will not be denied.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Why Maſter Merry-thought, will you be a vext thing ſtill?

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Woman I take you to my love again, but you ſhall ſing before you enter: therefore diſpatch your ſong, and ſo come in.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Mer.
sp.p: Well, you muſt have your Will when all's done, Mich. what ſong canſt thou ſing Boy?

sp.speaker: Mich.
sp.p: I can ſing none forſooth, but a Ladies Daughter of Paris properly.
Mich. Mer. Song. It was a Ladies Daughter, &c.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Come, you're welcome home again.
If ſuch danger be in playing, and jeſt muſt to earneſt turn,
You ſhall go no more a Maying.

sp.speaker: Merch. within.
sp.p: Are you within Sir, Maſter Merry-thought?

sp.speaker: Jaſp.
sp.p: It is my Maſters voice, good Sir, go hold him talk whilſt we convey our ſelves into ſome inward room.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: What are you? are you merry? you muſt be very merry if you enter.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I am Sir.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Sing then.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Nay, good Sir open to me.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Sing, I ſay, or by the merry heart, you come not in.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Well Sir, I'll ſing.
sp.l: Fortune my foe, &c.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: You are welcome Sir, you are welcome: you ſee your entertainment, pray you be merry.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Oh Maſter Merry-thought, I am come to aske you
Forgiveneſs for the wrongs I offered you,
And your moſt virtuous Son, they're infinite,
Yet my contrition ſhall be more than they.
I do confeſs my hardneſs broke his heart.
For which juſt heaven hath given me puniſhment
More than my age can carry, his wandring ſpirit
Not yet at reſt, purſues me every where,
Crying, I'll haunt thee for thy cruelty.
My Daughter ſhe is gone, I know not how,
Taken inviſible, and whether living,
Or in grave, 'tis yet uncertain to me.
Oh Maſter Merry-thought, theſe are the Weights,
Will ſink me to my grave, forgive me Sir.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Why Sir, I do forgive you, and be merry.
And if the wag in's life time, plaid the knave.
Can you forgive him too?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: With all my heart Sir.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Speak it again, and heartily.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I do Sir.
Now by my ſoul I do.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: With that came out his Paramour,
She was as white as the Lilly Flower,
Hey troul, trolie lolie.
With that came out her own dear Knight,
He was as true as ever did ſight, &c.
sp.p: Sir, if you will forgive 'em, clap their hands together, there's no more to be ſaid i'th' matter.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: i do, I do.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: I do not like this, peace boys, hear me one of you, every bodies part is come to an end but Ralph's, and he's left out,

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: 'Tis long of your ſelf Sir, we have nothing to do with his part.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Ralph. Come away, make on him as you have done of the reſt-boys come.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Now good Husband, let him come out and die.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: He ſhall Nell, Ralph, come away quickly and die boy.

sp.speaker: Boy
sp.p: 'Twill be very unfit he ſhould die ſir, upon no occaſion, and in a Comedy too.

sp.speaker: Cit,
sp.p: Take you no care for that Sir boy, is not his part at an end, think you, when he's dead? come away Ralph.

div.stage: Enter Ralph, with a forked arrow through his head.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: When I was mortal, this my coſtive corps
Did lap up Figs and Raiſons in the Strand,
Where ſitting I eſpi'd a lovely Dame,
Whoſe Maſter wrought with Lingell and with All,
And underground he vampied many a Boot,
Straight did her love prick forth me, tender ſprig:
To follow feats of Arms in warlike wiſe,
Through Waltham Deſart; where I did perform
Many atchievements, and did lay on ground
Huge Barbaroſo, that inſulting Giant,
And all his Captives ſoon ſet at liberty.
Then honor prickt me from my native ſoil,
Into Moldavia, where I gain'd the love
Of Pompiana his beloved Daughter:
But yet prov'd conſtant to the black thumm'd Maid
Suſan, and ſcorn'd Pompianaes love:
Yet liberal I was, and gave her pins,
And money for her Fathers Officers,
I then returned home, and thruſt my ſelf
In action, and by all means choſen was
The Lord of May,, where I did flouriſh it,
With Scarfs and Rings, and Poeſie in my hand:
Afrer this action I preferred was,
And choſen City-Captain at Mile-end,
With Hat and Feather, and with leading ſtaff,
And train'd my men, and brought them all off clear
Save one man that beraid him with the noiſe.
But all theſe things I Ralph did undertake,
Only for my beloved Suſans ſake.
Then coming home, and ſitting in my ſhop
With Apron blew, Death came unto my ſtall
To cheapen Aquavitae; but e'r I
Could take the bottle down, and fill a taſte,
Death come and caught a pound of Pepper in his hand,
And ſprinkled all my Face and Body o'r,
And in an inſtant vaniſhed away.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: 'Tis a pretty fiction i'faith.

sp.speaker: Ralph.
sp.l: Then took I up my Bow and Shaft in hand,
And walkt in Moor-fields, to cool my ſelf,
But there grim cruel death met me again,
And ſhot this forked Arrow through my head,
And now I faint, therefore be warn'd by me,
My fellows every one, of forked heads.
Farewel all you good boys in merry London,
Ne'r ſhall we more upon Shrove-Tueſday meet,
And pluck down houſes of iniquity.
My pain increaſeth: I ſhall never more
Hold open, whilſt another pumps both legs,
Nor daub a Sattin Gown with rotten Eggs:
Set up a ſtake, Oh never more I ſhall,
I die, flie, flie my ſoul to Grocers Hall. oh, oh, oh, &c.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p:
Well ſaid Ralph, do your obeyſance to the Gentlemen, and go your ways well ſaid Ralph.
Exit Ralph.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.p: Methinks all we, thus kindly and unexpectedly reconciled, ſhould not part without a Song.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: A good motion.

sp.speaker: Old Mer.
sp.l: Strike up then.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: Better Muſick ne'r was known,
Than a Quire of hearts in one.
Let each other that hath been,
Troubled with the gall or ſpleen:
Learn of us to keep his brow,
Smooth and plain as ours are now.
Sing though before the hour of dying
He ſhall riſe, and then be crying,
Hey ho, 'Tis nought but mirth,
That keeps the bodie from the earth.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Come Nell. ſhall we go, the Play's done?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Nay, by my ſaith George, I have more manners than ſo, I'll ſpeak to theſe Gentlemen firſt: I thank you all Gentlemen, for your patience and countenance to Ralph, a poor fatherleſs child, and if I may ſee you at my houſe, it ſhould go hard, but I would have a pottle of Wine, and a Pipe of Tobacco for you; for truly I hope you like the youth, but I would be glad to know the truth: I refer it to your own diſcretions, whether you will applaud him or no, for I will wink, and whilſt you ſhall do what you will, I thank you with all my heart, God give you good night, come George.

div.head: The Perſons Repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Leonardo, a noble Genoeſe, Father to Mark Antonio.
Don Zanchio, an old lame angry Soldier, Father to Leocadia.
Alphonſo, a cholerick Don, Father to Theodoſia.
Philippo, Son to Alphonſo, Lover of Leocadia.
Pedro, a Gentleman and friend to Leonardo.
Rodorigo, General of the Spaniſh Gallies.

list.head: WOMEN.
Love-ſick Ladies in purſuit of M. Anton.

list.item: Eugenia, Wife to the Governor of Barcellona.
Hoſteſs, Wife to the Hoſt of Barcellona.

div.p: The Scene Barcellona and the Road.

div.head: Scaena Prima
div.stage: Enter Incubo the Bailiff, Diego the Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: SIgnior Don Diego, and mine Hoſt, ſave thee.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I thank you Mr. Baily.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: O the block!

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Why, how ſhould I have anſwer'd?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Not with that
Negligent rudeneſs: But I kiſs your hands
Signior Don Incubo de Hambre, and then
My Titles: Maſter Baily of Caſtle-blanco:
Thou ne'r wilt have the elegancy of an Hoſt;
I ſorrow for thee, as my friend and Goſſip:
No ſmoak, nor ſteam out-breathing from the kitchen?
There's little life i'th Hearth then.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I, there, there,
That is his friendſhip, harkening for the ſpit,
And ſorrow that he cannot ſmell the pot boil.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Strange
An Inn ſhould be ſo curſt, and not the ſign
Blaſted, nor withered; very ſtrange, three days now,
And not an Egg eat in it, nor an Onion.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I think they ha' ſtrew'd the high-ways with caltraps, I,
No horſe dares paſs 'em; I did never know
A week of ſo ſad doings, ſince I firſt
Stood to my Sign-poſt,

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Goſſip, I have found
The root of all: kneel, it is thy ſelf
Art cauſe thereof: each perſon is the Founder
Of his own fortune, good or bad; but mend it,
Call for thy Cloak, and Rapier.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Do, call,
And put 'em on in haſte: Alter thy fortune,
By appearing worthy of her: Doſt thou think
Her good face e'r will know a man in cuerpo?
In ſingle body, thus? in Hoſe, and Doublet
The horſe-boys garb? baſe blank, and halfe blank cuerpo?
Did I, or Mr Dean of Sivil our neighbor
E'r reach our dignities in cuerpo, think'ſt thou,
In ſquirting Hoſe and Doublet? Signior, no,
There went more to't: there were Cloaks, Gowns, Caſſocks,
And other paramentos; Call, I ſay,
His Cloak, and Rapier here.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: What means your Worſhip?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Bring forth thy Husbands Sword: ſo hang it on,
And now his cloak, here caſt it up; I mean
Goſſip, to change your luck, and brink you gueſts.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Why? is there charm in this?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Expect; now walk,
But not the pace of one that runs on errands;
For, want of gravity in an Hoſt, is odious:
You may remember Goſſip, if you pleaſe,
(Your Wife being then th' Infanta of the Gipſies,
And your ſelf governing a great mans Mules then)
Me a poor Squire at Madrid attending
A Maſter of Ceremonies; But a man, believe it,
That knew his place to the gold weight, and ſuch
Have I heard him ought ſay, ought every Hoſt
Within the Catholique Kings Dominions
Be in his own houſe.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: A Maſter of Ceremonies;
At leaſt Vice-Maſter, and to do nought in cuerpo,
That was his Maxim, I will tell thee of him:
He would not ſpeak with an Ambaſſadors Cook,
See a cold bake-meat from a forreign part
In cuerpo: had a dog but ſtaid without,
Or beaſt of quality, as an Engliſh Cow,
But to preſent it ſelf, he would put on
His Savoy chain about his neck, the ruff
And cuffs of Holland, then the Naples Hat
With the Rome Hat-band, and the Florentine Agat,
The Millan Sword, the Cloak of Genoa, ſet
With Flemiſh buttons; all his given pieces
To entertain 'em in, and complement Knock within.
With a tame Conie, as with the Prince that ſent it.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Liſt. who is there?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: A gueſt and 't be thy will.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Look Spowſe, cry luck, and we be encounter'd: ha?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Luck then, and good, for 'tis a fine brave gueſt,
With a brave horſe.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Why now, believe of cuerpo.
As you ſhall ſee occaſion: go, and meet him.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Look to my horſe, I pray you, well.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: He ſhall, Sir.
Inc. Oh how beneath his rank and call was that now?
Your horſe ſhall be entreated as becomes
A horſe of faſhion, and his inches.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Look to the Cavalier: what ails he? ſtay
If it concern his horſe, let it not trouble him,
He ſhall have all reſpect the place can yield him
Either of barley, or freſh ſtraw.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Good Sir
Look up.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: He ſinks, ſomewhat to caſt upon him,
He'll go away in cuerpo elſe.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: What, Wife!
Oh your hot waters quickly, and ſome cold
To caſt in his ſweet face.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Alas, fair flower?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Does any body entertain his Horſe?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Yes, Lazaro has him.

div.stage: Enter Hoſteſs with a glaſs of water.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Go you ſee him in perſon.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Sir, taſte a little of this, of mine own water,
I did diſtill't my ſelf; ſweat Lilly look upon me,
You are but newly blown, my pretty Tulip.
Faint not upon your ſtalk, 'tis firm and freſh
Stand up ſo bolt upright, you are yet in growing

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Pray you let me have a chamber.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: That you ſhall, Sir.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: And where I may be private, I intreat you.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: For that in troth Sir, we ha no choice: our houſe
Is but a vent of need, that now and then
Receives a gueſt, between the greater Towns
As they come late; only one room,

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: She means, Sir, it is none
Of thoſe wild, ſcatter'd heaps, call'd Inns, where ſcarce
The Hoſt is heard, though he wind his horn t'his people,
Here is a competent pile, wherein the man,
Wife, Servants, all do live within the whiſtle

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Only one room.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: A pretty modeſt quadrangle
She will deſcribe to you.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Wherein ſtands two Beds Sir.
We have, and where, if any gueſt do come,
He muſt of force be lodg'd, that is the truth, Sir.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: But if I pay you for both your beds, methinks
That ſhould alike content you.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: That it ſhall, Sir.
If I be paid, I am paid.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Why, there's a Ducket
Will that make your content?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Oh the ſweet face on you:
A Ducket? yes, and there were three beds Sir,
And twice ſo many rooms, which is one more,
You ſhould be private in 'em all, in all Sir,
No one ſhould have a piece of a bed with you
Not maſter Dean of Sivil himſelf, I ſwear.
Though he came naked hither, as once he did
When h' had like t'have been tane a bed with the Moor
And gueſt by her Maſter: you ſhall be as private,
As if you lay in's own great houſe that's haunted,
Where no body comes, they ſay:

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I thank you Hoſteſs.
Pray you, will you ſhew me in.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Yes marry will I Sir,
And pray that not a flea, or a chink vex you. Exit Hoſt and Theo.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: You forget ſupper: Goſſip: move for ſupper

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange what love to a beaſt may do, his Horſe
Threw him into this ſit.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: You ſhall excuſe me
It was his being in cuerpo, meerly caus'd it.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Do you think ſo Sir?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Moſt unlucky cuerpo.
Naught elſe, he looks as he would eat Partridge,
This gueſt; ha' you 'em ready in the houſe?
And a fine piece of Kid now? and freſh garlick
With Sardinia and Zant Oil? how now?
Has he beſpoke, what will he have a brace,
Or but one Partridge, or a ſhort leg'd Hen,
Daintyly carbonado'd?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: 'Laſs the dead
May be as ready for a ſupper as he.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: He has no mind to eat, more than his ſhadow:

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Say you.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: How does your worſhip

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I put on
My left ſhooe firſt to day, now I perceive it,
And skipt a bead in ſaying 'em 'ore; elſe
I could not be thus croſs'd: He cannot be
Above ſeventeen; one of his years, and have
No better a ſtomach?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: And in ſuch good cloaths too.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Nay, theſe do often make the ſtomach worſe, wiſe,
That is no reaſon.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I could, at his years, Goſſips
(As temperate as you ſee me now) have eaten
My brace of Ducks, with my half Gooſe, my Conie,
And drink my whole twelve Marvedis in Wine
As eaſie as I now get down three Olives

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: And, with your temperance-favour, yet I think
Your worſhip would put to't at ſix and thirty
For a good wager; and the meal in too.

sp.speaker: Inc,
sp.l: I do not know what mine old mouth can do.
I ha not prov'd it lately.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: That's the grief, Sir.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: But is he without hope then gone to bed?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I fear ſo, Sir, h'as lock'd the door cloſe to him
Sure he is very ill.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: That is with faſting,
You ſhould ha told him Goſſip, what you had had,
Given him the Inventory of your kitchen,
It is the picklock in an Inn, and often
Opens a cloſe barr'd ſtomach: what may he be troh?
Has he ſo good a Horſe?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Oh a brave Jennet,
As e'r your worſhip ſaw.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: And he eats?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Strongly,

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: A mighty Soleciſme, heaven give me patience,
What creatures has he?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: None.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: And ſo well cloath'd,
And ſo well mounted?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: That's all my wonder, Sir,
Who he ſhould be; he is attir'd and hors'd
For the Conſtables Son of Spain.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: My wonders more
He ſhould want appetite: well a good night
To both my Goſſips: I will for this time
Put off the thought of ſupping: In the morning
Remember him of breakfaſt pray you.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I ſhall Sir.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: A hungry time Sir.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: We that live like mice Exit Incubo.
On others meat, muſt watch when we can get it.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Yes, but I would not tell him: Our fair gueſt
Says, though he eats no ſupper he will pay for one.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Good news: we'll eat it ſpouſe, t' his health,
'Twas politickly done t'admit no ſharers.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Look to the Mules there, where's mine Hoſt?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Here Sir.
Another Fayerie.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Bleſs me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: From what ſweet Hoſteſs?
Are you afraid o' your gueſts?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: From Angels, Sir,
I think there's none but ſuch come here to night,
My houſe had never ſo good luck afore
For brave, fine gueſts; and yet the ill luck on't is
I cannot bid you welcome.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: No?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Not lodge you Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Not, Hoſteſs?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: No in troth Sir, I do tell you
Becauſe you may provide in time: my beds
Are both tane up by a young Cavalier
That will and muſt be private.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: He has paid Sir
For all our Chambers.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Which is one: and Beds
Which I already ha told you are two: But Sir,
So ſweet a creature, I am very ſorry
I cannot lodge you by him; you look ſo like him
Yo' are both the lovelieſt pieces.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What train has he?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: None but himſelf

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And will no leſs than both beds
Serve him?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: H'as given me a Ducket for 'em.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Oh.
You give me reaſon Hoſteſs: Is he handſome,
And young do you ſay?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Oh Sir, the delicat'ſt fleſh
And fineſt cloths withal, and ſuch a horſe,
With ſuch a Saddle.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: She's in love with all.
The horſe, and him, and Saddle, and cloths, good woman,
Thou juſtifieſt thy Sex; lov'ſt all that's brave:
Sure though I lye o' th' ground, I'll ſtay here now
And have a ſight of him: you'll give me houſe-room,
Fire, and freſh meat, for money, gentle Hoſteſs;
And make me a pallat?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Sir, ſhe ſhall do reaſon....
I underſtood you had another Gueſt, Goſſips,
Pray you let his Mule be lookt to, have good ſtraw,
And ſtore of bran: And Goſſip, do you hear,
Let him not ſtay for ſupper: What good Fowl ha' you?
This Gentleman would eat a Pheaſant.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: 'Laſs Sir;
We ha' no ſuch.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I kiſs your hands fair Sir.
What ha you then? ſpeak what you have? I'm one Sir
Here for the Catholique King, an Officer
T' enquire what gueſts come to theſe places; you Sir
Appear a perſon of quality, and 'tis fit
You be accommodated: why ſpeak you not,
What ha' you Woman? are you afraid to vent
That which you have?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: This is a moſt ſtrange man;
T' appoint my meat.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: The half of a cold hen, Sir,
And a boil'd quarter of Kid, is all i' th' houſe.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Why all's but cold; let him ſee it forth,
Cover, and give the eye ſome ſatisfaction,
A Travellers ſtomach muſt ſee bread and ſalt,
His belly is nearer to him, than his kindred;
Cold hen's a pretty meat Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What you pleaſe;
I am reſolv'd t' obey.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: So is your Kid,
With Pepper, Garlick, and the juyce of an Orange:
She ſhall with Sallads help it, and clean linnen;
Diſpatch; what news at Court Sir?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Faith, new tires
Moſt of the Ladies have, the men old Suits:
Only the Kings Fool has a new Coat
To ſerve you.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I did gueſs you came from thence, Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: But I do know I did not.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I miſtook Sir.
What hear you of the Archdukes?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Troth your queſtion.

stage.hi: Enter Hoſteſs and Servants with Table.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Of the French buſineſs, What?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: As much.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: No more?
They ſay the French: Oh that'ts well: come, I'll help you:
Have you no Jiblets now? or a broil'd raſher.
Or ſome ſuch preſent diſh t' aſſiſt?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Not any Sir.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: The more your fault: you nev'r ſhould be without
Such aids: what cottage would ha' lack'd a Pheaſant
At ſuch a time as this? well, bring your Hen,
And Kid forth quickly.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: That ſhould be my prayer
To ſcape his Inquiſition.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Sir, the French,
They ſay are divided 'bout their match with us,
What think you of it.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: As of naught to me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Nay, it's as little to me too: but I love
To ask after theſe things, to know the affections
Of States and Princes, now and then for bettring.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Of your own ignorance.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Yes Sir:

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Many do ſo.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I cannot live without it: what do you hear
Of our Indian Fleet; they ſay they are well return'd.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I had no venture with 'em Sir; had you?

div.stage: Enter Hoſteſs and Servants with meat.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Why do you ask Sir?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: 'Cauſe it might concern you,
It does not me.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Oh here's your meat come.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Thanks,
I welcome it at any price.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Some ſtools here,
And bid mine Hoſt bring Wine, I'll try your Kid,
If he be ſweet: he looks well, yes, he is good;
I'll carve you Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: You uſe me too too Princely:
Taſt, and carve too.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I love to do theſe Offices.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I think you do: for whoſe ſake?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: For themſelves Sir,
The very doing of them is reward

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: 'Had little faith would not believe you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Goſſip, ſome Wine.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Here 'tis: and right St. Martyn.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Meaſure me out a glaſs.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I love the humanity
Us'd in this place:

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Sir, I ſalute you here.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I kiſs your hands Sir.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Good wine, it will beget an appetite:
Fill him, and ſit down, Goſſip, entertain
Your noble gueſt here,, as becomes your title.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Pleaſe you to like this Wine Sir?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I diſlike
Nothing mine Hoſt, but that I may not ſee
Your conceal'd gueſt: here's to you.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: In good faith Sir;
I wiſh you as well as him: would you might ſee him

sp.speaker: Inc,
sp.l: And wherefore may he not:

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: 'Has lock'd himſelf Sir
Up, and has hir'd both the beds o' my wife
At extraordinary rate.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I'll give as much
If that will do't, for one, as he for both;
What ſay you mine Hoſt, the door once open
I'll fling my ſelf upon the next bed to him
And there's an end of me till morning; noiſe
I will make none

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I wiſh your worſhip well—but

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: His honor is engag'd: And my ſhe-Goſſip
Hath paſt her promiſe, hath ſhe not?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Yes truly:

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: That toucheth to the credit of the houſe:
Well, I will eat a little, and think: how ſay you Sir
Unto this brawn o' th' Hen?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I ha' more mind
To get this bed Sir.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Say you ſo: Why then
Giv't me agen, and drink to me: mine Hoſt
Fill him his Wine: thou'rt dull, and doſt not praiſe it,
I eat but to teach you the way Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Sir:
Find but the way to lodge me in this chamber
I'll give mine Hoſt two Duckets for his bed,
And you Sir two Reals: here's to you

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Excuſe me,
I am not mercenary: Goſſip pledge him for me,
I'll think a little more; but ev'n one bit
And then talk on: you cannot interrupt me.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: This piece of wine Sir, coſt me

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Stay: I have found:
This little morſel, and then: here's excellent garlick:
Have you not a bunch of grapes now: or ſome Bacon
To give the mouth a reliſh?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Wife, do you hear?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: It is no matter: Sir give mine Hoſt your Duckets.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: How Sir?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Do you receive 'em: I will ſave
The honeſty of your houſe: and yours too Goſſip,
And I will lodge the Gentleman: ſhew the chamber.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Good Sir do you hear.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Shew me the chamber.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Pray you Sir,
Do not diſturb my gueſts.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Diſturb? I hope
The Catholick King Sir, may command a lodging
Without diſturbing in his Vaſſals houſe,
For any Miniſter of his, emploid
In buſineſs of the State. Where is the door?
Open the door, who are you there? within?
In the Kings name. Theodoſia within.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: What would you have?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Your key Sir,
And your door open: I have here command
To lodge a Gentleman, from the Juſtice, ſent
Upon the Kings affairs.

sp.speaker: Theod.
sp.l: Kings and neceſſities
Muſt be obey'd: the key is under the door.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: How now Sir, are you fitted? you ſecur'd?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Your two Reals are grown a piece of Eight.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Excuſe me Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: 'Twill buy a Hen; and Wine
Sir, for to morrow. Exit Phil.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I do kiſs your hands Sir
Well this will bear my charge yet to the Gallies
Where I am owing a Ducket: whither this night
By the Moons leave I'll march: for in the morning

Early, they put from Port St. Maries.
Ex. all but Diego.

sp.speaker: Die.

l.hi: Lazaro.

sp.l: How do the horſes?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Would you would go and ſee Sir,
A — of all Jades, what a clap h'as given me:
As ſure as you live Maſter he knew perfectly
I couzen'd him on's Oats: he lookt upon me
And then he ſheer'd, as who ſhould ſay, take heed ſirrah:
And when he ſaw our half Peck, which you know
Was but an old Court diſh, lord how he ſtampt:
I thought 't had been for joy, when ſuddenly
He cuts me a back caper with his heels
And takes me juſt o'th' crupper, down came I,
And all my ounce of Oats: Then he neigh'd out
As though he had had a Mare by th' tail.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Faith Lazaro
We are too blame to uſe the poor dumb ſerviters
So cruelly.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Yonder's this other Gentleman's horſe
Keeping our Lady Eve: the devil a bit
H'as got ſince he came in yet: there he ſtands
And looks, and looks, but 'tis your pleaſure, Sir,
He ſhall look lean enough: h'as Hay before him
But 'tis as big as Hemp, and will as ſoon choak him,
Unleſs he eat it butter'd: he had four ſhooes
And good ones when he came: 'tis a ſtrange wonder
With ſtanding ſtill he ſhould caſt three.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: O Lazaro.
The Devil's in this Trade: truth never knew it
And to the devil we ſhall travel, Lazaro
Unleſs we mend our manners: once every week
I meet with ſuch a knock to mollifie me
Sometimes a dozen to awake my conſcience
Yet ſtill I ſleep ſecurely.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Certain Maſter
We muſt uſe better dealing.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: 'Faith for mine own part
Not to give ill example to our iſſues,
I could be well content to ſteal but two girths,
And now and then a ſaddle-cloth: change a bridle
Only for exerciſe.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: If we could ſtay there
There were ſome hope on's Maſter: but the devil is
We are drunk ſo early we miſtake whole Saddles
Sometimes a horſe; and then it ſeems to us too
Every poor jade has his whole peck, and tumbles
Up to his ears in clean ſtraw, and every bottle
Shews at the leaſt a dozen; when the truth is, Sir,
There's no ſuch matter, not a ſmell of Provinder,
Not ſo much ſtraw as would tie up a horſe tail,
Nor any thing i' th' rack, but two old Cobwebs
And ſo much rotten Hay as had been a hens neſt.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Well, theſe miſtakings muſt be mended, Lazaro,
Theſe apparitions, that abuſe our ſences,
And make us ever apt to ſweep the manger.
But put in nothing; theſe fancies muſt be forgot
And we muſt pray it may be reveal'd to us
Whoſe horſe we ought, in conſcience, to couzen,
And how, and when; A Parſons Horſe may ſuffer
A little greazing in his teeth, 'tis wholſome;
And keeps him in a ſober ſhuffle: and his Saddle
May want a ſtirrop. and it may be ſworn
His Learning lay on one ſide, and ſo broke it:
H'as ever Oats in's Cloak-bag to prevent us
And therefore 'tis a meritorious office
To tythe him ſoundly.

sp.speaker: Laz,
sp.l: And a Grazier may
(For thoſe are pinching puckfoyſts, and ſuſpitious)
Suffer a myſt before his eyes ſometimes too,
And think he ſees his horſe eat halfe a buſhel:
When the truth is, rubbing his gums with ſalt,
Till all the skin come off: he ſhall but mumble
Like an old Woman that were chewing Brawn,
And drop 'em out again.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: That may do well too,
And no doubt 'tis but venial, But good Lazaro
Have you a care of underſtanding horſes,
Horſes that know the world: let them have meat
Till their teeth ake; and rubbing till their ribs
Shine like a wenches forehead; they are devils

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: And look into our dealings: as ſure as we live
Theſe Courtiers horſes are a kind of Welſh Prophets,
Nothing can be hid from 'em: For mine own part
The next I cozen of that kind ſhall be founder'd,
And of all four too: I'll no more ſuch complements
Upon my crupper.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Steal but a little longer
Till I am lam'd too, and we'll repent together,
It will not be above two daies.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: By that time
I ſhall be well again, and all forgot Sir.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Why then I'll ſtay for thee. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Theodoſio and Phillipo on ſeveral Beds.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Oh,—ho? oh—ho?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Oh—oh? heart — heart—heart—heart?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: When wilt thou break?—break, break, break?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Ha?
I would the voice were ſtrong, or I nearer,

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Shame, ſhame, eternal ſhame? what have I done?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Done?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: And to no end, what a wild journey
Have I more wildly undertaken?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Journey?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: How, without counſel? care? reaſon, or fear?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Whither will this fit carry?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Oh my folly,

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: This is no common ſickneſs.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: How have I left
All I ſhould love, or keep? oh heaven.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Sir,

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: How do you gentle Sir?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Alas my fortune

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: It ſeems your ſorrow oppreſſes: pleaſe your goodneſs,
Let me bear half, Sir: a divided burthen
Is ſo made lighter.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Oh,

sp.speaker: Phil,
sp.l: That ſigh betraies
The fulneſs of your grief

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I, if that grief
Had not bereft me of my underſtanding,
I ſhould have well remembred where I was,
And in what company; and clapt a lock
Upon this tongue for talking.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Worthy Sir
Let it not add to your grief, that I have heard
A ſigh or groan come from you: That is all Sir:

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Good Sir no more: you have heard too much I fear,
Would I had taken Poppy when I ſpake it.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: It ſeems you have an ill belief of me
And would have fear'd much more, had you ſpoke ought
I could interpret. But believe it Sir
Had I had means to look into your breaſt,
And tane you ſleeping here, that ſo ſecurely
I might have read all that your woe would hide
I would not have betraid you.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Sir, that ſpeech
Is very noble, and almoſt would tempt
My need to truſt you.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: At your own election,
I dare not make my faith ſo much ſuſpected
As to proteſt again: nor am I curious
To know more than is fit.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Sir, I will truſt you
But you ſhall promiſe Sir to keep your bed,
And whatſoe'r you hear, not to importune
More I beſeech you from me

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Sir I will not.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Than I am prone to utter.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: My faith for it.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: If I were wiſe, I yet ſhould hold my peace
You will be noble?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: You ſhall make me ſo
If you'll but think me ſuch.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I do: then know
You are deceiv'd with whom you have talk'd ſo long.
I am a moſt unfortunate loſt woman.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Do not ſtir Sir: I have here a Sword.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Not I ſweet Lady: of what blood, or name.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: You'll keep your faith.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I'll periſh elſe.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Believe then
Of birth too noble for me, ſo deſcended—
I am aſham'd, no leſs than I am affrighted.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Fear not: by all good things, I will not wrong you.

sp.speaker: Theo.
