sp.l: I am the Daughter of a noble Gentleman
Born in this part of Spain: my fathers name Sir:
But why ſhould I abuſe that reverence
When a childs duty has forſaken me.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: All may be mended, in fit time too: ſpeak it

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Alphonſo, ſir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Alphonſo? What's your own name?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Any baſe thing you can invent.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Deal truly.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: They call me Theodoſia.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Ha? and love
Is that that hath chang'd you thus?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Ye have obſerv'd me
Too nearly Sir, 'tis that indeed: 'tis love Sir:
And love of him (oh heavens) why ſhould men deal thus?
Why ſhould they uſe their arts to cozen us?
That have no cunning, but our fears about us?
And ever that too late too; no diſſembling
Or double way but doating: too much loving?
Why ſhould they find new oaths, to make more wretches?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What may his name be?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Sir, a name that promiſes
Methinks no ſuch ill uſage: Mark—Antonio
A noble neighbors ſon: Now I muſt deſire ye
To ſtay a while: elſe my weak eyes muſt anſwer

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I will:—Are ye yet ready? what is his quality?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: His beſt a thief Sir: that he would be known by
Is heir to Leonardo, a rich Gentleman:
Next of a handſome body, had heaven made him
A mind fit to it. To this man my fortune,
(My more than purblind fortune) gave my faith,
Drawn to it by as many ſhews of ſervice
And ſigns of truth, as ever falſe tongue utter'd:
Heaven pardon all.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: 'Tis well ſaid: forward Lady.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Contracted Sir, and by exchange of rings
Our ſouls deliver'd: nothing left unfiniſh'd
But the laſt work, enjoying me, and Ceremony.
For that I muſt confeſs was the firſt wiſe doubt
I ever made: yet after all this love Sir,
All this profeſſion of his faith; when daily
And hourly I expected the bleſt Prieſt
He left me like a dream, as all this ſtory
Had never been, nor thought of, why, I know not;
Yet I have called my conſcience to confeſſion,
And every ſyllable that might offend
I have had in ſhrift: yet neither loves Law Signior,
Nor tye of Maidens duty, but deſiring
Have I tranſgreſt in: left his father too,
Nor whither he is gone, or why departed
Can any tongue reſolve me: All my hope
(Which keeps me yet alive, and would perſwade me
I may be once more happy, and thus ſhapes me
A ſhame to all my modeſt Sex) is this Sir,
I have a Brother and his old Companion,
Student in Salamanca, there my laſt hope
If he be yet alive, and can be loving
It left me to recover him: For which travel
In this Sute left at home of that dear Brothers
Thus as you find me, without fear, or wiſdom,
I have wander'd from my Father, fled my friends,
And now am only child of hope and danger:
You are now ſilent Sir: this tedious ſtory
(That ever keeps me waking) makes you heavy:
'Tis fit it ſhould do ſo: for that, and I
Can be but troubles.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: No, I ſleep not Lady:
I would I could: oh heaven is this my comfort?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: What ail you gentle Sir?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Why do you groan ſo?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I muſt, I muſt; oh miſery;

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: But now Sir,
You were my comfort: if any thing afflict ye
Am not I fit to bear a part on't? and by your own rule?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: No; if you could heal, as you have wounded me,
But 'tis not in your power.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I fear intemperance.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Nay, do not ſeek to ſhun me: I muſt ſee you:
By heaven I muſt: hoa, there mine Hoſt: a Candle:
Strive not, I will not ſtir ye.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Noble Sir
This is a breach of promiſe.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Tender Lady
It ſhall be none but neceſſary: hoa, there,
Some light, ſome light for heavens ſake.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Will ye betray me?
Are ye a Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Good woman:

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: If I be prejudicial to you, curſe me.

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: Ye are early ſtirring Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Give me your Candle
And ſo good morrow for a while.

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: Good morrow Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: My Brother Don Philippo: nay Sir, kill me
I ask no mercy Sir, for none dare know me,
I can deſerve none: As ye look upon me
Behold in infinite theſe foul diſhonors,
My noble Father, then your ſelf, laſt all
That bear the name of kindred, ſuffer in me:
I have forgot whoſe child I am; whoſe Siſter:
Do you forget the pity tied to that:
Let not compaſſion ſway you: you will be then
As foul as I, and bear the ſame brand with me,
A favourer of my fault: ye have a ſword Sir,
And ſuch a cauſe to kill me in.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Riſe Siſter,
I wear no ſword for Women: nor no anger
While your fair chaſtity is yet untouch'd.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: By thoſe bright Stars, it is Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: For my Siſter
I do believe ye: and ſo neer blood has made us
With the dear love I ever bore your virtues
That I will be a Brother to your griefs too:
Be comforted, 'tis no diſhonor Siſter
To love, nor to love him you do: he is a Gentleman
Of as ſweet hopes, as years, as many promiſes,
As there be growing Truths, and great ones.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: O Sir I

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Do not deſpair.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Can ye forgive?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Yes Siſter,
Though this be no ſmall error, a far greater.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: And think me ſtill your Siſter?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: My dear Siſter.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: And will you counſel me?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: To your own peace too:
Ye ſhall love ſtill.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: How good ye are?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: My buſineſs,
And duty to my Father: which now drew me
From Salamanca I will lay aſide
And only be your Agent to perſwade ye
To leave both love, and him, and well retire ye.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Oh gentle Brother.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I perceive 'tis folly:
Delaies in love, more dangerous.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Noble Brother.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Fear not, I'll run your own way: and to help you,
Love having rackt your paſſions beyond counſel:
I'll hazard mine own fame: whither ſhall we venture?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Alas, I know not Sir

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Come, 'tis bright morning
Let's walk out, and conſider: you'll keep this habit.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I would Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Then it ſhall be: what muſt I call ye?
Come, do not bluſh: pray ſpeak, I may ſpoil all elſe.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Pray call me Theodoro.

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: Are ye ready?
The day draws on apace: once more good morrow.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Good morrow gentle Hoſt: now I muſt thank ye:

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Who doſt thou think this is?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Were you a wench Sir,
I think you would know before me.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Mine own Brother.

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: By th' Maſſe your noſes are akin: ſhould I then
Have been ſo barbarous to have parted Brothers?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: You knew it then.

sp.speaker: Dieg.
sp.l: I knew 'twas neceſſary
You ſhould be both together: Inſtinct Signior,
Is a great matter in an Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I am ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Is not mine Hoſt up yet?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I'll ſee.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Siſter, withdraw your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Signior Philippo.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Noble Don Pedro, where have you been this way?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I came from Port St. Maries, whence the Gallies
Put this laſt tide, and bound for Barcelona,
I brought Mark-antonie upon his way

l.hi: Marc-antonie?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Who is turn'd Soldier,
And entertain'd in the new Regiment,
For Naples?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Is it poſſible?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And put they in at Barcelona?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: So
One of the Maſters told me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Which way go you Sir?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Home.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And I for Sivil: pray you Sir; ſay not
That you ſaw me, if you ſhall meet the queſtion,
I have ſome little buſineſs

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Were it leſs Sir.
It ſhall not become me, to loſe the caution:
Shall we breakfaſt together?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I'll come to you Sir:
Siſter you hear this: I believe your fortune
Begins to be propitious to you: we will hire
Mules of mine Hoſt here: if we can, himſelf
To be our guide, and ſtraight to Barcelona,
This was as happy news, as unexpected
Stay you till I rid him away.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I will. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: KNock at the door.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis open Sir,

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: That's all one,
Knock when I bid you.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Will not your Worſhip enter?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Will not you learn more manners Sir, and do that
Your Maſter bids ye; knock ye knave, or I'll knock
Such a round peal about your pate: I enter
Under his roof, or come to ſay god ſave ye
To him, the Son of whoſe baſe dealings has undone me?
Knock louder, louder yet: I'll ſtarve, and rot firſt,
This open air is every mans.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser. within.
sp.l: Come in Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: No, no Sir, I am none of theſe Come in Sirs,
None of thoſe viſitants: bid your wiſe Maſter
Come out, I have to talk unto him: go Sir

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: Your worſhip may be welcome.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Sir, I will not,
I come not to be welcome: good my three Duckets,
My pickell'd ſprat a day, and no oil to't,
And once a year a cotten coat, leave prating
And tell your Maſter I am here.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: I will Sir.
This is a ſtrange old man. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I welcome to him?
I'll be firſt welcome to a Peſthouſe: Sirrah
Let's have your valour now cas'd up, and quiet
When an occaſion calls, 'tis wiſdom in ye,
A Servingman's diſcretion: if you do draw,
sp.stage: Enter Leonardo, and Don Zanchio (carried by two Servants in a chair.)
sp.l: Draw but according to your entertainment;
Five Nobles worth of fury.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Signior Alphonſo,
I hope no diſcontent from my Will given,
Has made ye ſhun my houſe:
An credit me amongſt my fears 'tis greateſt
To miniſter offences.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: O good Signior
I know ye for Italian breed, fair tongu'd,
Spare your Apologies, I care not for 'em,
As little for your love Sir; I can live
Without your knowledge, eat mine own, and ſleep
Without dependences, or hopes upon ye.
I come to ask my Daughter.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Gentle Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I am not gentle Sir, nor gentle will be
Till I have juſtice, my poor child reſtor'd
Your caper-cutting boy has run away with?
Young Signior ſmooth-face, he that takes up wenches
With ſmiles, and ſweet behaviors, Songs, and Sonnets,
Your high fed Jennet, that no hedge can hold
They ſay you bred him for a Stallion.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Fie Signior, there be times, and terms of honor
To argue theſe things in, deſcidements able
To ſpeak ye noble Gentlemen, ways punctual
And to the life of credit, ye are too rugged.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I am too tame Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Will ye hear but reaſon?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: No, I will hear no reaſon: I come not hither
To be popt off with reaſon; reaſon then.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Why Signior, in all things there muſt be method,
Ye choak the child of honor elſe, diſcretion,
Do you conceive an injury?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: What then Sir?

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Then follow it in fair terms, let your ſword bite
When time calls, not your tongue.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I know Sir
Both when and what to do without directions,
And where, and how, I come not to be tutor'd,
My cauſe is no mans but mine own: you Signior,
Will ye reſtore my Daughter?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Who detains her?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: No more of theſe ſlight ſhifts

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ye urge me Signior
With ſtrange injuſtice: becauſe my Son has err'd

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Mark him.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Out of the heat of youth: dos't follow
I muſt be father of his crimes,

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I ſay ſtill.
Leave off your Rhetorick, and reſtore my Daughter.
And ſuddainly: bring in your rebel too,
Mountdragon, he that mounts without commiſſion
That I may ſee him puniſhed, and ſeverely,
Or by that holy Heaven, I'll fire your houſe,
And there's my way of honor.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Pray give me leave
Was not man made the nobleſt creature?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Should not his mind then anſwer to his making,
And to his mind his actions, if this ought to be,
Why do we run a blind way from our worths,
And cancel our diſcretions, doing thoſe things
To cure offences, are the moſt offences?
We have rules of juſtice in us; to thoſe rules
Let us apply our angers: you can conſider
The want in others of theſe terminations
And how unfurniſh'd they appear.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Hang others,
And where the wrongs are open, hang reſpects,
I come not to conſider.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Noble Sir,
Let us argue cooly, and conſider like men.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Like men!

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ye are too ſudain ſtill.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Like men Sir?

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: It is fair language, and ally'd to honor.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Why, what ſtrange beaſt would your grave reverence
Make me appear? like men!

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Taſte but that point Sir,
And ye recover all.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I tell thy wiſdom
I am as much a man, and as good a man.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: All this is granted Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: As wiſe a man.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Ye are not tainted that way.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: And a man
Dares make thee no man; or at beſt, a baſe man.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Fie, fie, here wants much carriage.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Hang much carriage.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Give me good language.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Sirrah Signior, Give me my Daughter.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I am as gentle as your ſelf, as free born.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Obſerve his way.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: As much reſpect ow'd to me.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: This hangs together nobly.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And for Civil,
A great deal more it ſeems: go look your Daughter.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: There ye went well off Signior.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: That rough tongue
You underſtand at firſt: you never think Sir
Out of your mightineſs, of my loſs: here I ſtand
A patient Anvil, to your burning angers
Made ſubject to your dangers; yet my loſs equal:
Who ſhall bring home my Son?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: A whipping Beadle.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why, is your Daughter whoriſh?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Ha, thou dar'ſt not,
By heaven I know thou dar'ſt not.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I dare more Sir
If you dare be uncivil.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Laugh too, Pidgeon.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: A fitter time for fames ſake: two weak Nurſes
Would laugh at this; are there no more days coming,
No ground but this to argue on? no ſwords left
Nor friends to carry this, but your own furies?
Alas! it ſhows too weakly.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Let it ſhow,
I come not here for ſhews: laugh at me ſirrah?
I'll give ye cauſe to laugh.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ye are as like ſir
As any man in Spain.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: By heaven I will,
I will brave Leonardo.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Brave Alphonſo.
I will expect it then.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Hold ye there both,
Theſe terms are noble.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Ye ſhall hear ſhortly from me.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Now diſcreetly.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Aſſure your ſelf ye ſhall: do ye ſee this ſword ſir?
He has not caſt his teeth yet.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Rarely carried.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: He bites deep: moſt times mortal: Signior
I'll hound him at the fair and home.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Still nobly.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: And at all thoſe that dare maintain ye.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: How you ſhall pleaſe ſir, ſo it be fair, though certain,
I had rather give you reaſon.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Fairly urg'd too.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: This is no age for reaſon; prick your reaſon
Upon your ſwords point.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: Admirably follow'd.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: And there I'll hear it: ſo till I pleaſe, live Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And ſo farewel, you're welcome.

sp.speaker: Zanch.
sp.l: The end crowns all things
Signior, ſome little buſineſs paſt, this cauſe I'll argue
And be a peace between ye, if't ſo pleaſe ye,
And by the ſquare of honor to the utmoſt:
I feel the old man's maſter'd by much paſſion,
And too high rackt, which makes him overſhoot all
His valour ſhould direct at, and hurt thoſe
That ſtand but by as blenchers: this he muſt know too,
As neceſſary to his judgement, doting women
Are neither ſafe nor wiſe adventurers: conceive me,
If once their will have wander'd; nor is't then
A time to uſe our rages: for why ſhould I
Bite at the ſtone, when he that throws it wrongs me?
Do not we know that Women are moſt wooers
Though cloſeſt in their carriage? Do not all men know,
Scarce all the compaſs of the Globe can hold 'em
If their affections be afoot? ſhall I then covet
The follies of a ſhe-fool, that by nature
Muſt ſeek her like, by reaſon, be a woman,
Sink a tall ſhip, becauſe the ſails defie me?
No, I diſdain that folly; he that ventures
Whilſt they are fit to put him on, has found out
The everlaſting motion in his ſcabbard.
I doubt not to make peace: and ſo for this time
My beſt love, and remembrance.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Your poor Servant. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Where will our Horſes meet us?

sp.speaker: Diego.
sp.l: Fear not you Sir,
Some half mile hence my worſhips man will ſtay us,
How is it with my young bloods? come, be jovial,
Let's travel like a merry flock of wild Geeſe,
Every tongue talking.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: We are very merry;
But do you know this way, Sir?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Is't not dangerous?
Methinks theſe woody thickets ſhould harbor knaves.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I fear none but fair wenches; thoſe are thieves,
May quickly rob me of my good conditions,
If they cry Stand once: but the beſt is Signiors
They cannot bind my hands: for any elſe,
They meet an equal knave, and there's my Paſsport:
I have ſeen fine ſport in this place: had theſe three tongues,
They would tell ye pretty matters: do not you fear, though
They are not every daies delights.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What ſport Sir?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Why to ſay true, the ſport of all ſports.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What was't?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Such turning up of Taffataes; and you know
To what rare whiſtling tunes they go, far beyond
A ſoft wind in the ſhrowds: ſuch ſtand there,
And down i'th' other place; ſuch ſupplications
And ſubdiviſions for thoſe toys their honors,
One, as ye are a Getleman in this buſh,
And oh ſweet Sir, what mean ye? there's a bracelet,
And uſe me I beſeech ye like a woman;
And her petition's heard: another ſcratches,
And cries ſhe will die firſt, and then ſwounds: but certain
She is brought to life again, and does well after.
Another, ſave mine honor, oh mine honor,
My Husband ſerves the Duke, Sir, in his kitchen;
I have a cold pie for ye; fie, fie, fie Gentlemen,
Will nothing ſatisfie, where's my Husband?
Another cries, do ye ſee Sir how they uſe me,
Is there no Law for theſe things?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: And good mine Hoſt,
Do you call theſe fine ſports?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: What ſhould I call 'em,
They have been ſo call'd theſe thouſand years and upwards.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: But what becomes o' th' men?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: They're ſtript and bound,
Like ſo many Adams, with fig-leaves afore 'em,
And there's their innocence.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Would we had known this?
Before we reacht this place.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Come, there's no danger,
Theſe are but ſometimes chances.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Now we muſt through.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Stand to it Signiors.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: No it needs not,
I know the face; 'tis honeſt.

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: What mine Hoſt:
Mine everlaſting honeſt Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Maſs Baily:
Now in the name of an ill reckoning
What make you walking this round?

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: A— of this round,
And of all buſineſs too, through woods, and raſcals,
They have rounded me away a dozen Duckets,
Beſides a fair round Cloak: Some of 'em knew me,
Elſe they had caſed me like a Cunnie too,
As they have done the reſt, and I think roaſted me,
For they began to baſte me ſoundly: my young Signiors,
You may thank heaven, and heartily, and hourly,
You ſet not out ſo early; ye had been ſmoak'd elſe
By this true hand he had Sirs, finely ſmoak'd,
Had ye been Women, ſmockt too.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Heaven defend us.

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Nay, that had been no prayer, there were thoſe
That run that prayer out of breath, yet fail'd too.
There was a Fryer, now ye talk of prayer,
With a huge bunch of Beads, like a rope of Onions:
I am ſure as big, that out of fear and prayer,
In halfe an hour, wore 'em as ſmall as Bugles,
Yet he was flead too.

sp.speaker: Phil,
sp.l: At what hour was this?

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Some two hours ſince.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Do you think the paſſage ſure now.

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Yes, a rope take 'em, as it will, and bleſs 'em,
They have done for this day ſure.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Are many rifled?

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: At the leaſt a dozen,
And there left bound.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: How came you free?

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: A curteſie
They uſe out of their rogueſhips, to bequeath
To one, that when they give a ſign from far
Which is from out of danger; he may preſently
Releaſe the reſt, as I met you, I was going,
Having the ſign from yonder hill to do it.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Alas poor men.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Mine Hoſt, pray go untie 'em.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Let me alone for cancelling: where are they?

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: In every buſh, like black birds, you cannot miſs 'em.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I need not ſtalk unto 'em, Exit.

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: No, they'l ſtand ye,
My buſie life for yours Sir: you would wonder
To ſee the ſeveral tricks and ſtrange behaviours
Of the poor raſcals in their miſeries,
One weeps, another laughs at him for weeping,
A third is monſtrous angry, he can laugh
And cries, go too, this is no time; he laughs ſtill,
A fourth exhorts to patience: him a fifth man
Curſes for tameneſs; him a Fryer ſchools,
All hoot the Fryer, here one ſings a Ballad,
And there a little Curate confutes him,
And in this linſey-woolſey way, that would make a dog
Forget his dinner, or an old man fire,
They rub out for their ranſoms: Amongſt the reſt,
There is a little boy rob'd, a fine child,
It ſeems a Page: I muſt confeſs my pitty
(As tis a hard thing in a man of my place)
To ſhew compaſſion, ſtirr'd at him, ſo finely
And without noiſe he carries his afflictions,
And looks as if he had but dreamt of loſing.
sp.stage: Enter Hoſt and Leocadia, and others as rob'd.
sp.l: This boy's the glory of this robbery,
The reſt but ſhame the action: now ye may hear 'em,

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Come lads, 'tis Holy-day: hang cloaths, 'tis hot,
And ſweating Agues are abroad.
It ſeems ſo;
For we have met with rare Phyſitians
To cure us of that malady.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Fine footing,
Light and deliver: now my boys: Maſter Fryer,
How does your Holineſs, bear up man; what
A cup of neat Sack now and a toaſt: ha, Fryer,
A warm plaiſter to your belly Father,
There were a bleſſing now.

sp.speaker: Fryer.
sp.l: Ye ſay your mind Sir.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Where my fine Boy: my poynter.

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: There's the wonder.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: A rank whore ſcratch their ſides till the pox follow
For robbing thee, thou haſt a thouſand ways
To rob thy ſelf boy, Dice, and a Chamber-Devil.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ye are deceiv'd Sir.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: And thy Maſter too boy.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: A ſweet-fac'd boy indeed: what rogues were theſe?
What barbarous, brutiſh ſlaves to ſtrip this beauty?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Come hither my boy: alas! he's cold, mine Hoſt,
We muſt intreat your Cloak.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Can ye intreat it.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: We do preſume ſo much, you have other garments.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Will you intreat thoſe too?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Your Mule muſt too,
To the next Town, you ſay 'tis near: in pitty
You cannot ſee this poor Boy periſh.
I know ye have a better ſoul, we'll ſatisfie ye.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſtrange fooliſh trick I have, but I cannot help it,
I am ever cozen'd with mine own commendations;
It is determin'd then I ſhall be robb'd too.
To make up vantage to this dozen: here Sir,
Heaven has provided ye a ſimple garment
To ſet ye off: pray keep it handſomer
Than you kept your own; and let me have it render'd,
Bruſh'd and diſcreetly folded.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I thank ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Who wants a Doublet?
I.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Where will you have it?
From you Sir, if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Oh, there's the point, Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: My honeſt friends, I am ſorry for your fortunes,
But that's but poor relief: here are ten Duckets,
And to your diſtribution, holy Sir,
I render 'em: and let it be your care
To ſee 'em, as your wants are, well divided.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Plain dealing now my friends: and Father Fryer,
Set me the Sadle right; no wringing Fryer,
Nor tithing to the Church, theſe are no duties;
Scour me your conſcience, if the Devil tempt ye
Off with our cord, and ſwinge him.

sp.speaker: Fry.
sp.l: Ye ſay well Sir.

sp.speaker: All,
sp.l: Heaven keep your goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Peace keep you, farewel friends.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Farewel light-Horſe-men. Ex. the rob'd.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Which way travel you Sir.

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: To the next Town.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Do you want any thing.

sp.speaker: Bail.
sp.l: Only diſcretion to travel at good hours,
And ſome warm meat to moderate this matter,
For I am moſt outragious cruel hungry.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I have a ſtomach too ſuch as it is.
Would poſe a right good paſty, I thank heaven for't.

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Cheeſe, that would break the teeth of a new handſaw,
I could endure now like an Oaſtrich, or ſalt beef,
That Ceſar left in pickel.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Take no care,
We'll have meat for you, and enough: I th' mean time
Keep you the horſe way, leſt the fellow miſs us,
We'll meet ye at the end o' th' wood.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Make haſte then. Ex. Hoſt and Bayl.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: My pretty Sir till your neceſſities
Be full ſupplied, ſo pleaſe you truſt our friendſhips,
We muſt not part.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ye have pull'd a charge upon ye,
Yet ſuch a one as ever ſhall be thankful.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Ye have ſaid enough, may I be bold to ask ye,
What Province you were bred in? and of what Parents?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Ye may Sir: I was born in Andaluzia,
My name Franciſco, ſon to Don Henriques

l.hi: De Cardinas.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Our noble neighbor.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Son to Don Henriques?
I know the Gentleman: and by your leave Sir,
I know he has no ſon.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: None of his own Sir,
Which makes him put that right upon his Brother
Don Zanchio's childrne: one of which I am,
And therefore do not much err.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Still ye do Sir,
For neither has Don Zanchio any ſon;
A Daughter, and a rare one is his heir,
Which though I never was ſo bleſt to ſee,
Yet I have heard great good of.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Urge no further,
He is aſhamed, and bluſhes.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Sir,
If it might import you to conceal your ſelf,
I ask your mercy, I have been ſo curious:

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Alas! I muſt ask yours Sir: for theſe lies,
Yet they were uſeful ones; for by the claiming
Such noble parents, I believ'd your bounties
Would ſhew more gracious: The plain truth is Gentlemen,
I am Don Zanchio's Stewards ſon, a wild boy,
That for the fruits of his unhappineſs,
Is faign to ſeek the wars.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: This is a lie too.
If I have any ears.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Theo;
sp.l: Mark his language,
And ye ſhall find it of too ſweet a reliſh
For one of ſuch a breed: I'll pawn my hand,
This is no boy.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: No boy? what would you have him?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I know no boy: I watcht how fearfully,
And yet how ſuddainly he cur'd his lies,
The right wit of a Woman: Now I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What are ye ſure?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: That 'tis no boy: I'll burn in't.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Now I conſider better, and take council,
Methinks he ſhows more ſweetneſs in that face,
Than his fears dare deliver.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: No more talk on't,
There hangs ſome great weight by it: ſoon at night
I'll tell ye more.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Come Sir, what e'r you are
With us, embrace your liberty, and our helps
In any need you have.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: All my poor ſervice
Shall be at your command Sir, and my prayers.

sp.speaker: Phil,
sp.l: Let's walk apace; hunger will cut their throats elſe. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Rodorigo, Markantonio, and a Ship-maſter, two Chairs ſet out.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Call up the Maſter.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Here Sir.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Honeſt Maſter,
Give order all the Gallies with this tyde
Fall round, and near upon us; that the next wind
We may weigh off together, and recover
The Port of Bareelona, without parting.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Your pleaſure's done Sir. Ex.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Signior Markantonio,
Till meat be ready, let's ſit here and prepare
Our ſtomachs with diſcourſes.

sp.speaker: Mar-.
sp.l: What you pleaſe Sir.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Pray ye anſwer me to this doubt.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: If I can Sir.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Why ſhould ſuch plants as you are; pleaſure children,
That owe their bluſhing years to gentle objects,
Tenderly bred, and brought up in all fulneſs,
Deſire the ſtubborn wars?

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: In thoſe 'tis wonder,
That make their eaſe their god, and not their honor:
But noble General my end is other,
Deſire of knowledge Sir, and hope of tying
Diſcretion to my time, which only ſhews me,
And not my years, a man, and makes that more.
Which we call handſome, the reſt is but Boys beauty,
And with the Boy conſum'd.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Ye argue well Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Nor do I wear my youth, as they wear breeches,
For object, but for uſe: my ſtrength for danger,
Which is the liberal part of man, not dalliance,
The wars muſt be my Miſtreſs Sir,

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Oh Signior,
You'll find her a rough wench.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: When ſhe is won once,
She'll ſhow the ſweeter Sir.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You can be pleas'd, though
Sometimes to take a tamer?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis a truth Sir,
So ſhe be handſome, and not ill condition'd.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: A Soldier ſhould not be ſo curious.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: I can make ſhift with any for a heat Sir.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Nay, there you wrong your youth too: and however
You are pleas'd to appear to me, which ſhews well Signior,
A tougher ſoul than your few years can teſtifie:
Yet, my young Sir, out of mine own experience
When my ſpring was, I am able to confute ye,
And ſay, y' had rather come to th' ſhock of eies,
And boldly march up to your Miſtriſs mouth,
Then to the Cannons.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That's as their lading is Sir.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: There be Trenches
Fitter and warmer for your years, and ſafer
Than where the bullet plaies.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Ther's it I doubt Sir.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You'll eaſily find that faith: But come, be liberal,
What kind of Woman, could you make beſt wars with

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: They are all but heavy marches.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Fie Marckantonio,
Beauty in no more reverence?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: In the Sex Sir,
I honor it, and next to honor, love it,
For there is only beauty; and that ſweetneſs
That was firſt meant for modeſty: ſever it
And put it in one woman, it appears not,
'Tis of too rare a nature, ſhe too groſs
To mingle with it.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: This is a meer hereſie.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Which makes 'em ever mending; for that gloſs
That cozens us for beauty, is but bravery,
An outward ſhew of things well ſet, no more:
For heavenly beauty, is as heaven it ſelf Sir,
Too excellent for object, and what is ſeen
Is but the vail then, airy clouds; grant this
It may be ſeen, 'tis but like ſtars in twinklings.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: 'Twas no ſmall ſtudy in their Libraries
Brought you to this experience: But what think ye
Of that fair red and white, which we call Beauty?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why? 'tis our creature Sir, we give it 'em,
Becauſe we like thoſe colours, elſe 'tis certain
A blew face with a motley noſe would do it;
And be as great a beauty, ſo we lov'd it;
That we cannot give, which is only beauty,
Is a fair Mind.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: By this rule, all our choices
Are to no ends.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Except the dull end, Doing.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Then all to you ſeem equal?

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Very true Sir,
And that makes equal dealing: I love any
That's worth love.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: How long love ye Signior?

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Till I have other buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Do you never
Love ſtedfaſtly one woman?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis a toil Sir
Like riding in one rode perpetually,
It offers no variety.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Right youth,
He muſt needs make a Soldier; nor do you think
One Woman, can love one man?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, that may be.
Though it appear not often; they are things ignorant,
And therefore apted to that ſuperſtition
Of doting fondneſs; yet of late years Signior,
That worlds well mended with 'em, fewer are found now
That love at lenghth, and to the right mark, all
Stir now as as the time ſtirs; fame and faſhion
Are ends they aim at now, and to make that love
That wiſer ages held ambition;
They that cannot reach this may love by Index;
By every days ſurveying who beſt promiſes,
Who has done beſt, who may do, and who mended
May come to do again: who appear neareſt
Either in new ſtampt clothes; or courteſies,
Done but from hand to mouth neither; nor love they theſe things
Longer than new are making, nor that ſucceſſion
Beyond the next fair feather: Take the City,
There they go to't by gold weight, no gain from 'em
All they can work by fire and water to 'em,
Profit is all they point at, if there be love
'Tis ſhew'd ye by ſo dark a light, to bear out
The bracks and old ſtains in it, that ye may purchaſe
French Velvet better cheap, all loves are endleſs.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Faith, if you have a Miſtriſs, would ſhe heard you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Twere but the vent'ring of my place, or ſwearing
I meant it but for argument, as Schoolmen
Diſpute high queſtions.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: What a world is this
When young men dare determine what thoſe are
Age and the beſt experience ne'r could aim at.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: They were thick ey'd then Sir; now the print is bigger
And they may read their fortunes without ſpectacles,

sp.speaker: Rod
sp.l: Did you ne'r love?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Faith yes, once after ſupper,
And the ſit held till midnight.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Hot, or ſhaking.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To ſay true, both.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: How did ye rid it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thus Sir,
I laid my hand upon my heart, and bleſt me
And then ſaid over certain charms I had learn'd
Againſt mad dogs, for love and they are all one;
Laſt thought upon a windmil, and ſo ſlept,
And was well ever after.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: A rare Phyſitian,
What would your practiſe gain ye?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: The wars ended,
I mean to uſe my Art, and have theſe fools
Cut in the head like Cats, to ſave the kingdom,
Another Inquiſition.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: So old a Soldier
Out of the wars, I never knew yet practiſed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I ſhall mend every day; but noble General,
Believe this, but as this you nam'd. diſcourſes,

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Oh ye are a cunning Gameſter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Mirths and toys
To coſin time withal, for o'my troth Sir,
I can love; I think, well too; well enough
And think as well of women as they are,
Pretty fantaſtick things, ſome more regardful,
And ſome few worth a ſervice: I am ſo honeſt,
I wiſh 'em all in heaven, and you know how hard Sir
'Twill be to get in there with their great farthingals.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Well Marcantonio, I would not looſe thy company
For the beſt Galley I command.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Faith General,
If theſe diſcourſes pleaſe ye, I ſhall fit ye
Once every day. Knock within.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Thou canſt not pleaſe me better: hark, they call
Below to dinner: ye are my Cabbin gueſt,
My boſom's, ſo you pleaſe Sir.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Your poor Servant. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter ſecond Hoſt, and his Wife.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Let 'em have meat enough Woman, half a Hen;
There be old rotten Pilchards, put 'em off too,
'Tis but a little new anointing of 'em.
And a ſtrong onion, that confounds the ſtink.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: They call for more Sir.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Knock a dozen eggs down,
But then beware your wenches.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: More than this too?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Worts, worts, and make 'em porridge: pop 'em up wench
But they ſhall pay for Cullyſes.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: All this is nothing;
They call for Kid and Partridge.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Well remembred,
Where's the Faulconers half dog he left?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: It ſtinks Sir,
Paſt all hope that way.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Run it o'r with Garlick,
And make a Roman diſh on't.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Pray ye be patient,
And get proviſion in; theſe are fine gentlemen,
And liberal gentlemen; they have unde quare
No mangey Muleters, nor pinching Poſts.
That ſeed upon the parings of Musk-millions
And Radiſhes, as big and tough as Rafters:
Will ye be ſtirring in this buſineſs? here's your brother,
Mine old Hoſt of Oſſuna, as wiſe as you are,
That is, as knaviſh; if ye put a trick,
Take heed he do not find it.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I'll be wagging.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: 'Tis for your own commodity: why wenches:
Anon forſooth. within.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Who makes a fire there? and who gets in water?
Let Oliver goe to the Juſtice, and beſeech his Worſhip
We may have two ſpits going; and do you hear Druce,
Let him invite his Worſhip, and his Wives Worſhip,
To the left-Meat to morrow,

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Where's this Kitchen?

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Even at the next door Signior: what old Don?
We meet but ſeldom.

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Prethee be patient Hoſteſs,
And tell me where the meat is.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Faith Maſter Baylie,
How have ye done? and how man?

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Good ſweet Hoſteſs,
What ſhall we have to dinner?

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: How does your woman,
And a fine Woman ſhe is, and a good Woman;
Lord, how you bear your years?

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Is't Veal or Mutton,
Beef, Bacon, Pork, Kid, Pheaſant, or all theſe,
And are they ready all?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: The hours that have been
Between us two, the merry hours: Lord!

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Hoſteſs,
Dear Hoſteſs do but hear; I am hungry.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Ye are merrily diſpos'd Sir,

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Monſtrous hungry,
And hungry after much meat, I have brought hither
Right worſhipful to pay the reckoning,
Money enough too with 'em, deſire enough
To have the beſt meat, and of that enough too:
Come to the point ſweet wench, and ſo I kiſs thee.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have any thing, and inſtantly
E'r you can lick your ears, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: Portly meat,
Bearing ſubſtantial ſtuff, and fit for hunger
I do beſeech ye Hoſteſs firſt, then ſome light garniſh,
Two Pheaſants in a diſh, if ye have Leverits,
Rather for way of ornament, than appetite
They may be look'd upon, or Larks: for Fiſh,
As there is no great need, ſo I would not wiſh ye
To ſerve above four diſhes, but thoſe full ones;
Ye have no Cheeſe of Parma?

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Very old Sir.

sp.speaker: Bayl,
sp.l: The leſs will ſerve us, ſome ten pound,

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Alas Sir,
We have not halfe theſe dainties.

sp.speaker: Bayl,
sp.l: Peace good Hoſteſs,
And make us hope ye have.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have all Sir,

sp.speaker: Bay.
sp.l: That may be got for money.

div.stage: Enter Diego, the Hoſt, and a Boy.

sp.speaker: Hoſt. Diego,
sp.l: Where's your Maſter?
Bring me your Maſter, Boy: I muſt have liquor
Fit for the Mermydons; no daſhing now child
No conjurings by candle light, I know all;
Strike me the oldeſt Sack, a piece that carries
Point blank to this place boy, and batters; Hoſteſs,
I kiſs thy hands through which many a round reckoning
And things of moment have had motion.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Still mine old Brother.

sp.speaker: Hoſt. Die.
sp.l: Set thy Seller open,
For I muſt enter, and advance my Colours,
I have brought three Dons indeed wench, Dons with Duckets
And thoſe Dons muſt have dainty Wine, pure Bacchus
That bleeds the life blood: what is your cure ended?

sp.speaker: Bayl.
sp.l: We ſhall have Meat man,

sp.speaker: Hoſt. Die,
sp.l: Then we will have Wine man,
And Wine upon Wine, cut and drawn with Wine.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have all, and more than all.

sp.speaker: Bay.
sp.l: All, well then.

sp.speaker: Hoſt. Die.
sp.l: Away, about your buſineſs, you with her
For old acquaintance ſake, to ſtay your ſtomach. Exit Hoſteſs and Bayliff.
And Boy, be you my guide, ad inferos,
For I will make a full deſcent in equipage.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I'll ſhew you rare Wine.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Die. Stinging geer.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Divine Sir.

sp.speaker: Hoſt. Die.
sp.l: O divine boy, march, march my child, rare Wine boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: As any is in Spain Sir.

sp.speaker: Hoſt. Die.
sp.l: Old; and ſtrong too,
Oh my fine boy, clear too?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: As Chriſtal Sir, and ſtrong as truth.

sp.speaker: Hoſt. Die.
sp.l: Away boy,
I am enamor'd, and I long for Dalliance,
Stay no where child, not for thy fathers bleſſing,
I charge thee not to ſave thy Siſters honor,
Nor to cloſe thy Dames eies, were ſhe a dying
Till we arrive, and for thy recompence
I will remember thee in my Will.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Ye have ſaid Sir, Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: MIne Hoſt, is that Apparel got ye ſpoke of?
Ye ſhall have ready money.

sp.speaker: 2 Hoſt.
sp.l: 'Tis come in, Sir, he has it on Sir
And I think 'twill be fit, and o' my credit
'Twas never worn but once Sir, and for neceſſity
Pawn'd to the man I told ye of.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Pray bargain for it,
And I will be the pay-maſter.

sp.speaker: 2 Hoſt.
sp.l: I will Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And let our meat be ready when you pleaſe,
I mean as ſoon.

sp.speaker: 2 Hoſt.
sp.l: It ſhall be preſently.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: How far ſtands Barcelona?

sp.speaker: 2 Hoſt.
sp.l: But two Leagues off Sir,
You may be there by three a clock.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I am glad on't. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Signior Franciſco, why I draw you hither
To this remote place, marvel not, for truſt me
My innocence yet never knew ill dealing,
And as ye have a noble temper, ſtart not
Into offence, at any thing my knowledge,
And for your ſpecial good, would be inform'd of,
Nor think me vainly curious.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Worthy Sir,
The courteſies you and your noble Brother,
Even then when few men find the way to do 'em,
I mean in want, ſo freely ſhowr'd upon me,
So truly, and ſo timely miniſter'd,
Muſt, if I ſhould, ſuſpect thoſe minds that made 'em,
Either proclaim me an unworthy taker,
Or worſe, a baſe beleever; Speak your mind Sir
Freely, and what you pleaſe, I am your Servant

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Then my young Sir know, ſince our firſt acquaintance
Induc'd by circumſtances that deceive not
To clear ſome doubts I have; nay bluſh not Signior,
I have beheld ye narrowly: more bluſhes.
Sir, ye give me ſo much light, I find ye
A thing confeſt already: yet more bluſhes?
You would ill cover an offence might ſink ye
That cannot hide your ſelf; why do ye ſhake ſo?
I mean no trouble to ye; this fair hand
Was never made for hardneſs, nor thoſe eies
(Come do not hide 'em,) for rough objects, harke ye,
Ye have betraid your ſelf, that ſigh confirms me;
Another? and a third too? then I ſee
Theſe boys cloths do but pinch ye, come, be liberal,
Ye have found a friend that has found you, diſguiſe not
That loaden ſoul that labors to be open:
Now you muſt weep, I know it, for I ſee
Your eies down laden to the lids, another
Manifeſt token that my doubts are perfect;
Yet I have found a greater; tell me this
Why were theſe holes left open, there was an error,
A foul one my Franciſco, have I caught ye?
Oh pretty Sir, the cuſtom of our Countrey
Allows men none in this place: Now the ſhow'r comes.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Oh Signior Theodoro.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: This ſorrow ſhows ſo ſweetly
I cannot chooſe but keep it company:
Take truce and ſpeak Sir: and I charge your goodneſs,
By all thoſe perfect hopes that point at virtue,
By that remembrance theſe fair tears are ſhed for,
If any ſad misfortune have thus form'd ye,
That either care or counſel may redeem,
Pain, purſe, or any thing within the power
And honor of free gentlemen, reveal it,
And have our labors.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I have found ye noble
And ye ſhall find me true; your doubts are certain,
Nor dare I more diſſemble; I am a woman,
The great example of a wretched woman.
Here you muſt give me leave to ſhew my ſex;
And now to make ye know how much your credit
Has won upon my ſoul, ſo it pleaſe your patience,
I'll tell you my unfortunate ſad ſtory.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Sit down and ſay on Lady:

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I am born Sir
Of good and honeſt parents, rich, and noble,
And not to lie, the Daughter of Don Zanchio,
If my unhappy fortune have not loſt me:
My name call'd Leocadia, even the ſame
Your worthy brother did the ſpecial honor
To name for beautiful; and without pride
I have been often made believe ſo Signior;
But that's impertinent: Now to my ſorrows;
Not far from us a Gentleman of worth,
A neighbor and a noble viſitor,
Had his abode; who often met my Father
In gentle ſports of Chaſe, and River-Hawking
In Courſe and Riding; and with him often brought
A Son of his, a young and hopeful Gentleman,
Nobly train'd up, in years fit for affection,
A ſprightly man, of underſtanding excellent,
Of ſpeech and civil 'haviour, no leſs powerful;
And of all parts, elſe my eies lied, abundant:
We grew acquainted, and from that acquaintance
Nearer into affection; from affection
Into belief.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Then we durſt kiſs.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Go forward.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: But oh, man, unconſtant, careleſs man,
Oh ſubtle man, how many are thy miſchiefs;
Oh Mark-antonio, I may curſe thoſe kiſſes.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: What did you call him Lady?

sp.speaker: Leo.

l.hi: Mark-antonio

sp.l: The name to me of miſery.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Pray foreward.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: From theſe we bred deſires ſir; but loſe me heaven
If mine were luſtful.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I believe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: This nearneſs
Made him importunate; When to ſave mine honor
Love having full poſſeſſion of my powers,
I got a Contract from him.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Sealed?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And ſworn too;
Which ſince, for ſome offence heaven laid upon me,
I loſt among my monies in the robbery,
The loſs that makes me pooreſt: this won from him
Fool that I was; and too too credulous,
I pointed him a by-way to my chamber
The next night at an hour.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Pray ſtay there Lady;
And when the night came, came he, kept he touch with ye?
Be not ſo ſhamefac'd; had ye both your wiſhes?
Tell me, and tell me true, did he enjoy ye,
Were ye in one anothers arms abed? the Contract
Confirm'd in full joys there? did he lie with ye?
Anſwer to that; ha? did your father know this,
The good old man, or kindred privy to't?
And had ye their conſents? did that nights promiſe
Make ye a Mother?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Why do you ask ſo nearly?
Good Sir, do's it concern you any thing?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: No Lady.
Only the pitty why you ſhould be uſed ſo
A little ſtirs me, but did he keep his promiſe?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: No, no Signior,
Alas he never came, nor never meant it,
My Love was fool'd, time numbred to no end,
My expectation flouted, and gheſſe you Sir,
What dor unto a doating Maid this was,
What, a baſe breaking off?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: All's well then Lady;
Go forward in your Story.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Not only fail'd Sir
Which is a curſe in Love, and may he find it
When his affections are full-wing'd, and ready
To ſtoop upon the quarry, then when all
His full hopes are in's arms: not only thus Sir
But more injurious, faithleſs, treacherous,
Within two daies fame gave him far remov'd
With a new love, which much againſt my conſcience
But more againſt my cauſe, which is my hell
I muſt confeſs a fair one, a right fair one,
Indeed of admirable ſweetneſs, Daughter
Unto another of our noble neighbors
The thief call'd Theodoſia; whoſe perfections
I am bound to ban for ever, curſe to wrinckles,
As heaven I hope will make 'em ſoon; and aches;
For they have rob'd me poor unhappy wench
Of all, of all Sir, all that was my glory
And left me nothing but theſe tears, and travel:
Upon this certain news, I quit my Father
And if you be not milder in conſtruction
I fear mine honour too: and like a Page
Stole to Oſſuna, from that place to Sivil,
From thence to Barcelona I was travelling
When you o'er-took my miſery, in hope to hear of
Gallies bound up for Italy; for never
Will I leave off the ſearch of this bad man
This filcher of affections, this love-Pedler,
Nor ſhall my curſes ceaſe to blaſt her beauties
And make her name as w • andring as her nature
Till ſtanding face to face before their luſts
I call heavens juſtice down.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: This ſhows too angry
Nor can it be her fault ſhe is belov'd,
If I give meat, muſt they that eat it ſurfeit?

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: She loves again Sir, there's the miſchief of it
And in deſpight of me to drown my bleſſings
Which ſhe ſhall dearly know.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Ye are too violent.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: She has Devils in her eyes, to whoſe devotion
He offers all his ſervice.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Who can ſay
But ſhe may be forſaken too? he that once wanders
From ſuch a perfect ſweetneſs, as you promiſe
Has he not ſtill the ſame rule to deceive?

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: No, no they are together, love together
Paſt all deceipt of that ſide; ſleep together,
Live, and delight together, and ſuch deceipt
Give me in a wild deſert.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: By your leave Lady
I ſee no honour in this cunning.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Honour?
True, none of her part, honour, ſhe deſerves none,
'Tis ceas'd with wandring Ladies ſuch as ſhe is,
So bold and impudent.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I could be angry
Extreamly angry now beyond my nature
And 'twere not for my pitty: what a man
Is this to do theſe wrongs: believe me Lady
I know the maid, and know ſhe is not with him.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: I would you knew ſhe were in heaven.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: And ſo well know her
That I think you are cozen'd.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: So I ſay Sir.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I mean in her behaviour
For truſt my faith ſo much I dare adventure for her credit
She never yet delighted to do wrong.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: How can ſhe then delight in him? dare ſhe think?
Be what ſhe will, as excellent as Angels
My love ſo fond, my wiſhes ſo indulgent
That I muſt take her prewnings; ſtop at that
She has tyr'd upon; No Sir, I hold my beauty
Waſh but theſe ſorrows from it, of a ſparkle
As right and rich as hers, my means as equal,
My youth as much unblown; and for our worths
And weight of virtue

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Do not task her ſo far.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: By heaven ſhe is cork, and clouds, light, light Sir, vapor
But I ſhall find her out, with all her witchcrafts,
Her paintings, and her powncings: for 'tis art
And only art preſerves her, and meer ſpels
That work upon his powers; let her but ſhew me
A ruin'd cheek like mine, that holds his colour
And writes but ſixteen years in ſpight of ſorrows;
An unbathed body; ſmiles, that give but ſhaddows,
And wrinkle not the face; beſides ſhe is little,
A demy dame, that makes no object.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Nay.
Then I muſt ſay you err; for credit me
I think ſhe is taller than your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Why let her
It is not that ſhall mate me; I but ask
My hands may reach unto her.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Gentle Lady
'Tis now ill time of farther argument,
For I perceive your anger voyd of counſel,
Which I could wiſh more temperate.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Pray forgive me
If I have ſpoken uncivilly: they that look on
See more than we that play: and I beſeech ye
Impute it loves offence, not mine; whoſe torments,
If you have ever lov'd, and found my croſſes,
You muſt confeſs are ſeldom ty'd to patience,
Yet I could wiſh I had ſaid leſs.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: No harm then;
Ye have made a full amends; our company
You may command, ſo pleaſe you in your travels
With all our faith and furtherance; let it be ſo.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Ye make too great an offer.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Then it ſhall be.
Go in and reſt your ſelf, our wholſome dyet
Will be made ready ſtraight: But heark ye Lady
One thing I muſt entreat, your leave, and ſufferance
That theſe things may be open to my Brother
For more reſpect and honor.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Do your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: And do not change this habit by no means
Unleſs ye change your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Which muſt not yet be.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: It carries ye concealed and ſafe.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: I am counſell'd. Exit.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What's done?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Why all we doubted; 'tis a woman,
And of a noble ſtrain too, gheſs.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I cannot.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: You have heard often of her.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Stay I think not.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Indeed ye have; 'tis the fair Leocadia
Daughter unto Don Zanchio, our noble neighbor.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Nay?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe Sir, o'my credit.

sp.speaker: Phil.

l.hi: Leocadia,

sp.l: Piſh Leocadia, it muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: It muſt be, or be nothing.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Pray give me leave to wonder, Leocadia?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: The very ſame.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: The Damſel Leocadia
I gheſt it was a woman, and a fair one
I ſee it through her ſhape, tranſparent plain
But that it ſhould be ſhe; tell me directly.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: By heavens 'tis ſhe.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: By heaven then 'tis a ſweet one.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: That's granted too.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: But heark ye, heark ye Siſter,
How came ſhe thus diſguis'd?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I'll tell you that too
As I came on the ſelf-ſame ground, ſo us'd too.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: By the ſame man?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: The ſame too.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: As I live
You lovers have fine fancies,
Wonderous fine ones.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Pray heaven you never make one.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Faith I know not,
But in that mind I am, I had rather cobble,
'Tis a more Chriſtian Trade; pray tell me one thing
Are not you two now monſtrous jealous
Of one another?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: She is much of me
And has rayl'd at me moſt unmercifully
And to my face, and o'my conſcience
Had ſhe but known me, either ſhe or I
Or both, had parted with ſtrange faces
She was in ſuch a fury.

sp.speaker: Phil.

l.hi: Leocadia?

sp.l: Do's ſhe ſpeak handſomly?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Wondrous well Sir
And all ſhe do's becomes her, even her anger.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: How ſeemed ſhe when you found her?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Had you ſeen
How ſweetly fearful her pretty ſelf
Betray'd her ſelf, how neat her ſorrow ſhow'd,
And in what hanſome phraſe ſhe put her ſtory,
And as occaſion ſtirr'd her how ſhe ſtarted
Though roughly, yet moſt aptly, into anger,
You would have wonder'd.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Do's ſhe know ye?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: No,
Nor muſt not by no means.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: How ſtands your difference?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I'll tell ye that ſome fitter time, but truſt me
My Marc-antonio has too much to anſwer.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: May I take knowledge of her?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Yes ſhe is willing.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Pray uſe her as ſhe is, with all reſpects then,
For ſhe is a woman of a noble breeding.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Ye ſhall not find me wanting.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Which way bears ſhe?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Our way, and to our end.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I am glad on't; hark ye,
She keeps her ſhape? Enter Leocadia.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Yes, and I think by this time
Has mew'd her old.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: She is here: by heaven a rare one,
An admirable ſweet one, what an eye
Of what a full command ſhe bears, how gracious
All her aſpect ſhows; bleſs me from a feaver
I am not well o'th ſuddain.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Noble friends
Your meat and all my ſervice waits upon ye.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Ye teach us manners Lady; all which ſervice
Muſt now be mine to you, and all too poor too;
Bluſh not, we know ye, for by all our faiths
With us your honor is in ſanctuary
And ever ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: I do well believe it,
Will ye walk nearer Sir. Exit.
She ſhows ſtill fairer,
Yonger in every change, and clearer, neater;
I know not, I may fool my ſelf, and finely
Nouriſh a wolfe to eat my heart out; Certain
As ſhe appears now, ſhe appears a wonder,
A thing amazes me; what would ſhe do then
In womans helps, in ornaments apt for her
And deckings to her delicacy? without all doubt
She would be held a miracle; nor can I think
He has forſaken her: Say what ſhe pleaſe,
I know his curious eye, or ſay he had,
Put caſe he could be ſo boy-blind and fooliſh,
Yet ſtil I fear ſhe keeps the Contract with her
Not ſtoln as ſhe affirms, nor loſt by negligence,
She would looſe her ſelf firſt, 'tis her life, and there
All my hopes are diſpatch'd; O noble love
That thou couldſt be without this jealouſie,
Without this paſſion of the heart, how heavenly
Wouldſt thou appear unto us? Come what may come
I'll ſee the end on't: and ſince chance has caſt her
Naked into my refuge, all I can
She freely ſhall command, except the man. Exit.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Don Pedro do you think aſſuredly
The Galleys will come round to Barcelona
Within theſe two days?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Without doubt.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And think ye
He will be with 'em certainly?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: He is ſir
I ſaw him at their ſetting off,

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Muſt they needs
Touch there for water as you ſay?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: They muſt ſir
And for freſh meat too. few or none go by it
Beſide ſo great a Fleet muſt needs want trimming
If they have met with fowl ſeas, and no harbor
On this ſide Spain, is able without danger
To moore 'em, but that haven.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Are the wars
His only end?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: So he profeſſes.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Bears he
Any command amongſt 'em?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Good regard
With all; which quickly will prefer him.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Pray Sir tell me,
And as you are a Gentleman be liberal.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I will Sir, and moſt true.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Who ſaw ye with him;

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: None but things like himſelf; young Souldiers
And Gentlemen deſirous to ſeek honor.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Was there no woman there, nor none diſguis'd
That might be thought a woman in his language?
Did he not let ſlip ſomething of ſuſpition
Touching that wanton way.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Believe me Sir
I neither ſaw, nor could ſuſpect that face
That might be doubted womans, yet I am ſure
Aboard him I ſee all that paſt, and 'tis impoſſible
Among ſo many high ſet bloods there ſhould be
A woman, let her cloſe her ſelf within a cockle,
But they would open her, he muſt not love
Within that place alone, and therefore ſurely
He would not be ſo fooliſh had he any,
To truſt her there; for his diſcourſe, 'twas ever.
About his buſineſs, war, or mirth to make us
Reliſh a Can of Wine well; when he ſpoke private
'Twas only the remembrance of his ſervice,
And hope of your good prayers for his health Sir,
And ſo I gave him to the ſeas.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I thank ye,
And now am ſatisfied, and to prevent
Suſpitions that may nouriſh dangers Signior,
For I have told you how the mad Alphonſo
Chafes like a Stag i'th toyl, and bends his fury
'Gainſt all, but his own ignorance; I am determin'd
For peace ſake and the preſervation
Of my yet untoucht honor, and his cure
My ſelf to ſeek him there, and bring him back
As teſtimony of an unſought injury
By either of our actions; That the world,
And he if he have reaſon, may ſee plainly
Opinion is no perfect guide; nor all fames
Founders of truths: In the mean time this courteſie
I muſt intreat of you Sir, Be my ſelf here
And as my ſelf command my family.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Ye lay too much truſt on me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: 'Tis my love Sir,
I will not be long from ye; if this queſtion
Chance to be call'd upon ere my return
I leave your care to anſwer; ſo Farewell Sir.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Ye take a wiſe way; All my beſt endeavors
Shall labor in your abſence; peace go with ye. Exit Lec.
A noble honeſt Gentleman, free hearted
And of an open faith, much loving, and much loved,
And father of that goodneſs only malice
Can truly ſtir againſt, what dare befall
Till his return I'll anſwer. Exit Ped.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Walk off Sirrah,
But keep your ſelf within my call?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: I will Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: And ſtir my horſe for taking cold: within there,
Hoa people; you that dwell there my brave Signior
What are ye all a ſleep? is't that time with ye?
I'll ring a little lowder.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Sir who ſeek ye?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Not you Sir; Where's your Maſter?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I ſerve no man
In way of pay Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Where's the man o'th houſe then?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: What would you have with him Sir?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Do you ſtand here Sir
To ask men queſtions when they come?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I would ſir
Being his friend, and hearing ſuch alarmes
Know how men come to viſit him.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Ye ſhall Sir,
Pray tell his mightineſs here is a Gentleman
By name Alphonſo, would intreat his conference
About affairs of State Sir, are ye anſwer'd?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I muſt be Sir,

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Stay, ſet me down, ſtay Signior,
You muſt ſtay, and ye ſhall ſtay.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Meaning me Sir?

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Yes you Sir, you I mean, I mean you.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Well Sir.
Why ſhould I ſtay?

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: There's reaſon.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Reaſon Sir?

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I reaſon Sir
My wrong is greateſt, and I will be ſerved firſt,
Call out the man of fame?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: How ſerv'd Sir,

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Thus ſir,

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: But not before me.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Before all the world ſir
As my caſe ſtands.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I have loſt a daughter ſir.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I have loſt another worth five ſcore of her ſir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Ye muſt not tell me ſo.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I have, and heark ye?
Make it up five ſcore more: Call out the fellow,
And ſtand you by ſir.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: This is the mad morriſs.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: And I ſtand by?

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I ſay ſtand by, and do it.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Stand by among thy lungs.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Tu • n preſently
And ſay thy prayers, thou art dead.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I ſcorn thee
And ſcorn to ſay my prayers more than thou do'ſt,
〈◊〉 is the moſt wrong, and my daughter deareſt
And mine ſhall firſt be righted.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Shall be righted.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: A third may live I ſee, pray hear me Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Shall be.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I ſhall be righted.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Now?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Now.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Before I ſtir.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Before me.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Before any.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Doſt thou conſider what thou ſay'ſt? haſt thou friends here
Able to quench my anger, or perſwade me
After I have beaten thee into one main bruiſt
And made thee ſpend thy ſtate in rotten apples,
Thou canſt at length be quiet, ſhall I kill thee
Divide thee like a rotten Pumpion,
And leave thee ſtincking to poſterity,
There's not the leaſt blow I ſhall give; but do's this
Urge me no farther: I am firſt.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I'll hang firſt.
No goodman glory, 'tis not your bravado's,
Your punctual honor, nor ſoldadoſhip.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Set me a little nearer.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Let him ſally.
Lin'd with your qui • cks of carriage and diſcretion
Can blow me off my purpoſe. Where's your credit
With all your ſchool points now? your decent arguing
And apt time for performing: where are theſe toys,
Theſe wiſe ways, and moſt honorable courſes,
To take revenge? how dar'ſt thou talk of killing,
Or think of drawing any thing but ſquirts
When letchery has dry foundrerd thee?

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Neerer yet,
That I may ſpit him down: thou look'ſt like a man.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I would be thought ſo Sir.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Prethee do but take me,
And fling me upon that Puppy.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Do for heavens ſake,
And ſee but how I'll hug him,

sp.speaker: Saneh.
sp.l: Yet take warning.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Faith Gentlemen, this is a needleſs quarrel.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: And do you deſire to make one?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: As a friend Sir,
To tell you all this anger is but loſt Sir,
For Leonardo is from home.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: No, no Sir.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Indeed he is.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Where dare he be, but here Sir,
When men are wrong'd, and come for ſatisfactions.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: It ſeems he has done none Sir; for his buſineſs
Clear of thoſe cares, hath carried him for ſometime
To Barcelona: if he had been guilty,
I know he would have ſtayd, and clear'd all difference
Either by free confeſſion, or his ſword.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: This muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Sure as I live, it is Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Sure, as we all live,
He's run away for ever: Barcelona.!
Why? 'tis the key for Italy, from whence
He ſtole firſt hither.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: And having found his knaveries
Too groſs to be forgiven, and too open,
He has found the ſame way back again: I believe too
The good graſs Gentleman, for his own eaſe,
Has taken one o'th'Fillyes: Is not his ſtuff ſold.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I fear his worſhips ſhoos too; to eſcape us,
I do not think he has a diſh within doors,
A louſe left of his linnage.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Ye are too wide Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Or one poor wooden ſpoon,

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Come in and ſee Sir

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I'll ſee his houſe on fire firſt.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Then be pleaſed Sir
To give better cenſure.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I will after him,
And ſearch him like conceal'd land, but I'll have him,
And though I find him in his ſhrift, I'll kill him.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I'll bear ye company.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Pray have a care then,
A moſt ſpecial care, indeed a fear,
Ye do not anger me.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I will obſerve ye,
And if I light upon him handſomly.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Kill but a piece of him, leave ſome Alphonſo
For your poor Friends.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I fear him not for all this.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Shall we firſt go home,
For it may prove a voyage, and diſpoſe
Of things there; heaven knows what may follow.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: No,
I'll kill him in this ſhirt I have on: let things
Govern themſelves, I am maſter of my honor
At this time, and no more; let wife, and land,
Lie lay till I return.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I ſay amen to't:
But what care for our monies?

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I will not ſpend
Above three ſhillings, till his head be here,
Four is too great a ſum for all his Fortunes.
Come take me up inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Farewell to you Sir,
And if your friend be in a featherbed,
Sow'd up to ſhrowd his fears, tell him 'tis folly,
For no courſe but his voluntary hanging
Can get our pardons. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Theſe I think would be
Offence enough, if their own indiſcretions
Would ſuffer 'em: two of the old ſeditious,
When they want enemies, they are their own foes:
Were they a little wiſer, I ſhould doubt 'em:
Till when I'll ne'r break ſleep, nor ſuffer hunger
For any harm he ſhall receive: for 'tis as eaſie
If he be guilty, to turn theſe two old men
Upon their own throats, and look on, and live ſtill,
As 'tis to tell five pound: a great deal ſooner,
And ſo I'll to my meat, and then to hawking. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Sir, this is complement; I pray you leave me.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Sir, it is not.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Why? I would only ſee the Town.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: And only that I come to ſhew you.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Which I can ſee without you.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: So you may
Plainly, not ſafely: For ſuch difference
As you have ſeen betwixt the ſea and earth
When waves riſe high, and land would beat 'em back
As fearful of Invaſion; ſuch we find
When we land here at Barcelona.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Beſides our General of the Galleys, fearing
Your haſty nature, charg'd me not return
Without you ſafe.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: O Sir, that Roderigo
Is noble, and do's miſtake my temper.
There is not in the world, a mind leſs apt
To conceive wrongs, or do 'em; has he ſeen me
In all this voyage, in the which he pleaſes.
To call me friend, let ſlip a haſty word?
S'light Sir: yonder is a Lady valid,
For properneſs beyond compariſon,
And ſure her face is like the reſt: we'll ſee't.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Why? you are haſty Sir already: know you
What 'tis you go about.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Yes, I would ſee
The womans face.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: By heaven you ſhall not do't:
You do not know the cuſtom of the place:
To draw that curtain here, though ſhe were mean,
Is mortall.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Is it? earth muſt come to earth
At laſt, and by my troth, I'll try it Sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Then I muſt hold you faſt. By all the faith
That can be plac'd in man, 'tis an attempt
More dangerous than death, 'tis death and ſhame:
I know the Lady well.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Is ſhe a Lady?
I ſhall the more deſire to ſee her Sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: She is Alanſo's wife, the Governor,
A noble Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Then let me go,
If I can win her, you and I will govern
This Town Sir, fear it not, and we will alter
Theſe barbarous cuſtoms then; for every Lady
Shall be ſeen daily, and ſeen over too.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Come, do not jeſt, nor let your paſſions bear you
To ſuch wild enterpriſes: hold you ſtill,
For as I have a ſoul, you ſhall not do't.
She is a Lady of unblemiſh'd fame,
And here to offer that affront, were baſe:
Hold on your way, and we will ſee the Town,
And overlook the Ladies.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: I am ſchool'd,
And promiſe you I will: but good Sir, ſee,
She will paſs by us now; I hope I may
Salute her thus far off.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: 'S foot, are you mad?
'Twill be as ill as th'other.

sp.speaker: 1. Attend.
sp.l: What's the matter?
What would that fellow have?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Good Sir forbear.

sp.speaker: 1. Atten.
sp.l: It ſeems you are new landed: would you beg
Any thing here?

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Yes Sir, all happineſs
To that fair Lady, as I hope.

l.hi: Markantonio.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Her face, which needs no hiding: I would beg
A ſight of.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Now go on, for 'tis too late
To keep this from a tumult.

sp.speaker: 1 Attend.
sp.l: Sirrah, you
Shall ſee a fitter object for your eyes,
Then a fair Ladies face.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: For heavens ſake, raiſe not
A quarrel in the ſtreets for me.

sp.speaker: 1. Attend.
sp.l: Slip in then;
This is your door.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Will you needs quarrel then?

sp.speaker: 1. Attend.
sp.l: We muſt, or ſuffer
This outrage: is't not all your minds Sirs, ſpeak?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Then I do beſeech ye, let my Lord.
Not think the quarrel about me; for 'tis not. Exit.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: See happily ſome of our Galley ſouldiers
Are come aſhoar.

sp.speaker: 1. Attend.
sp.l: Come on Sir, you ſhall ſee
Faces enough.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Some one of you call to.
Our General, the whole rore of the Town
Comes in upon us.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: I have ſeen Sir better
Perhaps, than that was cover'd; and will yet.
See that, or ſpoil yours.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: On, why ſtart you back?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Alaſs Sir, they are fighting.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Let's begon,
See, ſee, a handſome man ſtrook down.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Ho General,
Look out, Antonio is in diſtreſs.

l.hi: Antonio.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Antonio! 'tis he.

sp.speaker: Rod. within.
sp.l: Ho, Gunner make a ſhot into the Town,
I'll part you: bring away Antonio a ſhot.
Into my Cabben. Exit Attendants and Townſmen.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I will do that office.
I fear it is the laſt, that I ſhall do him.

div.stage: Exit Souldiers and Gentlemen with Marckantonio.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: The laſt, why will he dye?

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Since I have found him; happineſs leave me,
When I leave him.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Why Theodoſia?
My ſiſter; wake: alaſs, I griev'd but now
To ſee the ſtreets ſo full; and now I grieve
To ſee them left ſo empty: I could wiſh,
Tumult himſelf were here, that yet at leaſt
Amongſt the band, I might eſpie ſome face
So pale and fearful, that would willingly
Embrace an arrand for a Cordial,
Or Aquavitae, or a cup of ſack,
Or a Phyſitian: but to talk of theſe
She breaths: ſtand up, O Theodoſia,
Speak but as thou wert wont, give but a ſigh,
Which is but the moſt unhappy piece of life,
And I will ever after worſhip ſadneſs,
Apply my ſelf to grief; prepare and build
Altars to ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: O Philippo, help me.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I do; theſe are my arms, Philippo's arms,
Thy Brothers arms that hold thee up.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: You help me
To life: but I would ſee Antonio
That's dead.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt ſee any thing; how doſt thou?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Better, I thank you.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Why that's well: call up
Thy ſenſes, and uncloud thy cover'd ſpirits.
How now?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Recover'd: but Antonio,
Where is he?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: We will find him: art thou well?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Perfectly well, ſaving the miſs of him;
And I do charge you here, by our allyance,
And by the love which would have been betwixt us,
Knew we no kindred; by that killing fear,
Mingled with twenty thouſand hopes and doubts,
Which you may think, plac'd in a Lovers heart,
And in a Virgins too, when ſhe wants help,
To grant me your aſſiſtance, to find out
This man alive, or dead; and I will pay you
In ſervice, tears, or prayers, a world of wealth:
But other treaſure, I have none: alas!
You men have ſtrong hearts; but we feeble maids
Have tender eyes, which only given be
To blind themſelves, crying for what they ſee.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Why do'ſt thou charge me thus? have I been found
Slow to perform, what I could but imagine
Thy wiſhes were; have I at any time
Tender'd a buſineſs of mine own, beyond
A vanity of thine? have I not been
As if I were a ſenſleſs creature, made
To ſerve thee without pow'r of queſtioning,
If ſo, why fear'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I am ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Come; then let's go: where's Leocadia?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I know not Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Where's Leocadia?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I do not know,

sp.speaker: Phil.

l.hi: Leocadia,

sp.l: This Tumult made the ſtreets as dead as night,
A man may talk as freely: what's become
Of Leocadia?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: She's run away.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Begone, and let us never more behold
Each others face, till we may, both together,
Faſten our eyes on her: accurſed be
Thoſe tender cozening names of charity,
And natural affection, they have loſt
Me only by obſerving them, what coſt
Travel, and fruitleſs wiſhes may in vain
Search through the world, but never find again.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Good Sir be patient, I have done no fault
Worthy this baniſhment.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Yes Leocadia,
The Lady ſo diſtreſs'd, who was content
To lay her ſtory, and to lay her heart
As open as her ſtory to your ſelf,
Who was content, that I ſhould know her Sex,
Before diſſembl'd and to put her ſelf
Into my conduct, whom I undertook
Safely to guard, is in this Tumult loſt.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: And can I help it Sir?

sp.speaker: Phil
sp.l: No, would thou couldſt,
You might have done, but for that zeald religion
You women bear to ſwownings, you do pick
Your times to faint when ſome body is by:
Bound or by nature, or by love, or ſervice
To raiſe you from that well diſſembled death:
Inform me but of one that has been found
Dead in her private chamber by her ſelf,
Where ſickneſs would no more forbear, than here,
And I will quit the reſt for her.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I know not
What they may do, and how they may diſſemble;
But by my troth, I did not.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: By my troth,
Would I had try'd; would I had let thee layn,
And followed her.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I would you had done ſo
Rather, than been ſo angry: where's Antonio?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Why do'ſt thou vex me with theſe queſtions?
I'll tell thee where, he's carried to the Galleys,
There to be chain'd, and row, and beat, and row
With knotted ropes, and pizzels; if he ſwound,
He has a doſe of bisket.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: I am glad
He is alive.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Was ever man thus troubled,
Tell me where Leocadia is?

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Good brother be not ſo haſty, and I think I can:
You found no error in me, when I firſt
Told you ſhe was a woman, and believe me
Something I have found out, which makes me think.
Nay, almoſt know ſo well, that I durſt ſwear
She follow'd hurt Antonio.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What do we

stage.hi: Enter the Governor, two Attendants, and the Townſmen.

sp.l: Then lingring here; we will aboard the Galleys
And find her.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Made he a ſhot into the Town?

sp.speaker: 1. Attend.
sp.l: He did Sir.

sp.speaker: Gov.
