sp.l: Call back thoſe Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1. Attend.
sp.l: The Governor, commands you back.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: We will obey him Sir.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You gave him cauſe to ſhoot; I know, he is
So far from raſh offence, and holds with me
Such curious friendſhip: could not one of you
Have call'd me while 'twas doing, ſuch an uproar,
Before my dore too?

sp.speaker: 1. Townſ.
sp.l: By my troth Sir, we were ſo buſy in the publick cauſe, of our own
Private falling out: that we forgot it: at home we ſee now
You were not, but as ſoon as the ſhot made us fly, we ran
Away as faſt as we could to ſeek your honor.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: 'Twas gravely done; but no man tells the cauſe
Or chance, or what it was that made you differ.

sp.speaker: 1. Townſ.
sp.l: For my part Sir, if there were any that I knew
Of, the ſhot drove it out of my head, do you know any neighbours.

sp.speaker: all.
sp.l: Not we, not we.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Not we! nor can you tell.

sp.speaker: 1. Attend.
sp.l: No other cauſe,
But the old quarrel betwixt the Town and the Galleys.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Come nearer Gentlemen: what are your names?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: My name Philippo.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: And mine Theodoro.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Strangers you are it ſeems.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Newly arriv'd.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Then you are they begun this Tumult.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Cov.
sp.l: Speak one of you.

sp.speaker: 1. Attend.
sp.l: They are not, I can quit 'em.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Yet we ſaw part, and an unhappy part
Of this debate, a long ſought friend of ours
Strook down for dead, and born unto the Galleys,
His name is Markantonio.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: And another
Of our company, a Gentleman
Of noble birth, beſides accompanyed
With all the gifts of nature, raviſh'd hence
We know not how, in this diſſention.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Get you home all, and work; and when I hear
You meddle with a weapon any more
But thoſe belonging to your Trades, i'll lay you
Where your beſt Cuſtomers ſhall hardly find you. Exit. Townſmen.
I am ſorry gentlemen, I troubled you,
Being both ſtrangers, by your tongues, and looks,
Of worth: To make ye ſome part of amends
If there be any thing in this poor Town
Of Barcelona that you would command,
Command me.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Sir, this wounded Gentleman,
If it might pleaſe you, if your pow'r and love
Extend ſo far, I would be glad to wiſh
Might be remov'd into the Town for cure:
The Galleys ſtay not, and his wound I know
Cannot endure a voyage.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Sir, he ſhall,
I warrant you: Go call me hither Sirrah,
One of my other Servants. Exit 1. attendane.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: And beſides.
The Gentleman we loſt, Signior Franciſco,
Shall be render'd too.

sp.speaker: Gover.
sp.l: And he Sir too: Go ſirrah, bear this ring
To Roderigo, my moſt noble friend,
The General of the Galleys: Tell him this. Exit ſervant.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Now we ſhall have 'em both.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Bleſt be thy thoughts
For apprehending this: bleſt be thy breath
For uttering it.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen, you ſhall
Enter my roof: and I will ſend for Surgeons,
And you ſhall ſee your friends here preſently.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: His name was Markantonio.

sp.speaker: Gover.
sp.l: I know it,
And have ſent word ſo.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Did you not forget
Franciſco's name?

sp.speaker: Gover.
sp.l: Nor his: y'are truly welcome,
To talk about it more, were but to ſay
The ſame word often over: you are welcome. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Markantonio, carried, Leocadia following; and the Servant. 2 Soldiers carrying him.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: This is the houſe Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Enter it, I pray you,
For I am faint, although I think my wound
Be nothing. Soldiers, leave us now: I thank you.

sp.speaker: 1. Sold.
sp.l: Heaven ſend you health Sir.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Let me lead you in.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.l: My wound's not in my feet; I ſhall entreat 'em
I hope to bear me ſo far. Exit.

sp.speaker: 2. Sold.
sp.l: How ſeriouſly theſe land men fled, when our General made a
Shot, as if he had been a warning to call 'em to their Hall.

sp.speaker: 1. Sold.
sp.l: I cannot blame 'em, What man have they now in the
Town, able to maintain a Tumult, or uphold a matter out
Of ſquare if need be? O the quiet hurley burleys that I
Have ſeen in this Town, when we have fought four hours
Together, and not a man amongſt us ſo impertinent or
Modeſt to ask why? but now the pillars that bare
Up this bleſſed Town in that regular debate, and
Scambling, are dead, the more's the pitty.

sp.speaker: 2. Sold.
sp.l: Old Ignatio lives ſtill.

sp.speaker: 1. Sold.
sp.l: Yes, I know him: he will do prettily well at a mans liver:
But where is there any man now living in the Town
That hath a ſteady hand, and underſtands Anatomy
Well? if it come to a particular matter of the lungs,
Or the ſpleen, why? alas Ignatio is to ſeek; are
There any ſuch men left as I have known, that
Would ſay they would hit you in this place? is there
Ever a good heartiſt, or a member-percer, or a
Small-gut man left in the Town, anſwer
Me that?

sp.speaker: 2. Sold.
sp.l: Maſs, I think there be not.

sp.speaker: 1. Sold.
sp.l: No, I warrant thee. Come, come, 'tis time
We were at the Galleys. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Governor, Eugenia, Markantonio, Philippo, Theodoſia, Leocadia, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Gover.
sp.l: Sir, you may know by what I ſaid already,
You may command my houſe; but I muſt beg
Pardon to leave you, if the publick buſineſs
Forc'd me not from you, I my ſelf ſhould call it
Unmannerly: but good Sir, do you give it
A milder name: it ſhall not be an hour
Ere I return.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Sir, I was nere ſo poor.
In my own thoughts, as that I want a means
To requite this with.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Sir, within this hour. Exit.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: This the Lady that I quarrell'd for?
O luſt if wounds cannot reſtrain thy power,
Let ſhame: nor do I feel my hurt at all,
Nor is it ought, only I was well beaten:
If I purſue it, all the civil world
That ever did imagine the content
Found in the band of man and wife unbroke,
The reverence due to houſholds, or the blemiſh
That may be ſtuck upon poſterity
Will catch me, bind me, burn upon my forehead,
This is the wounded ſtranger, that receiv'd
For charity into a houſe, attempted—
I will not do it.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Sir, how do you do now?
That you walk off.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Worſe Madam, than I was;
But it will over.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Sit, and reſt a while.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Where are the Surgeons?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Sir, it is their manner,
When they have ſeen the wound eſpecially,
The patient being of worth, to go conſult,
Which they are now at in another room,
About the dreſſing.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Madam, I do feel my ſelf not well

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Alaſs!

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: How do you Sir.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Will you drink waters?

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: No good Madam, 'tis not
So violent upon me; nor I think
Any thing dangerous: but yet there are
Some things that ſit ſo heavy on my conſcience,
That will perplex my mind, and ſtop my cure,
So that unleſs I utter 'em. A ſcratch
Here on my thumb will kill me: Gentlemen,
I pray you leave the room, and come not in
Your ſelves, or any other till I have
Open'd my ſelf to this moſt honour'd Lady.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: We will not

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: O bleſt! he will diſcover now
His love to me.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Now he will tell the Lady
Our Contract. Exit.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: I do believe he will confeſs to me
The wrong he did a Lady in the ſtreets;
But I forgive him.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Madam, I perceive
My ſelf grow worſe and worſe.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Shall I call back your friends?

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: O no, but e'r I do impart
What burthens me ſo ſore, let me intreat you,
(For there is no truſt in theſe Surgeons)
To look upon my wound; it is perhaps
My laſt requeſt: But tell me truely too,
That muſt be in how far do you imagine
It will have pow'r upon me.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Sir, I will.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: For heavens ſake, ſoftly: oh, I muſt needs lay
My head down eaſily, whilſt you do it.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Do Sir,
'Tis but an ordinary blow; a child
Of mine has had a greater, and been well;
Are you faint hearted?

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Why do you ſigh?
There is no danger in the world in this;
I wonder it ſhould make a man ſit down;
What do you mean, why do you kiſs my breaſts?
Lift up your head, your wound, may well endure it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: O Madam, may I not expreſs affection,
Dying-affection too I fear, to thoſe
That do me favors, ſuch as this of yours.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: If you mean ſo, 'tis well; but what's the buſineſs
Lies on your conſcience?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I will tell you Madam.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Tell me and laugh?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: But I will tell you true
Though I do laugh, I know as well as you
My wound is nothing, nor the power of earth
Could lay a wound upon me in your preſence,
That I could feel; but I do laugh to think
How covertly, how far beyond the reach
Of men, and wiſe men too, we ſhall deceive 'em,
Whilſt they imagine I am talking here
With that ſhort breath I have, ready to ſwound
At every full point; you my ghoſtly Mother
To hear my ſad confeſſion, you and I
Will on that bed within, prepar'd for me,
Debate the matter privately.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Forbear,
Thou wert but now as welcome to this houſe
As certain cures to ſick men, and juſt now
This ſudain alteration makes thee look
Like plagues come to infect it; if thou knewſt
How loathſome thou wilt be, thou wouldſt intreat
Theſe wals, or poſts to help thee to a hurt,
Paſt thy diſſimulation.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Gentle Madam
Call 'em not in?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: I will not yet, this place
I know to be within the reach of tongue,
And ears, thou canſt not force me; therefore hear me
What I will tell thee quickly, thou art born
To end ſome way more diſeſteem'd than this,
Or which is worſe, to dye of this hurt yet,
Come Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Good Madam.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Madam how is't? is Mark-antonio well?
Methinks your looks are alter'd, and I ſee
A ſtrange diſtemper in you.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: I am wrought
By that diſſembling man, that fellow worth
Nothing but kicking.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Gentle Madam ſpeak
To me alone let not them underſtand
His fault, he will repent I dare ſwear.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: I'll tell it you in private.

sp.speaker: Phil.

l.hi: Mark-antonio,

sp.l: How do you?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stand farther off I pray you
Give me ſome ayre.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Good Brother, will he ſcape,
The Surgeons ſay there is no danger.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Scape?
No doubt he will.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Alas will he not leave
This trying all, Madam, I do beſeech you
Let me but ſpeak to him, you and theſe by,
And I dare almoſt promiſe you to make him
Shew himſelf truly ſorrowful to you, beſides a ſtory I ſhall open to you,
Not put in ſo good words but in it ſelf
So full of chance, that you will eaſily
Forgive my tediouſneſs, and be well pleas'd
With that ſo much afflicts me.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Good Sir do.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And I deſire no interruption
Of ſpeech may trouble me till I have ſaid
What I will quickly do.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: What will ſhe ſay.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen, I pray you lend your ears,
And keep your voyces.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Signior Mark-antonio
How do you do?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh the Surgeons.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Let me tell you
Who know as well as you, you do diſſemble,
It is no time to do ſo; leave the thoughts
Of this vain world, forget your fleſh and blood,
And make your ſpirit an untroubled way
To paſs to what it ought.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Y're not in earneſt?
Why I can walk Sir, and am well.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: 'Tis true
That you can walk, and do believe y're well:
It is the nature, as your Surgeons ſay
Of theſe wounds, for a man to go, and talk,
Nay merrily, till his laſt hour, his minute:
For heaven ſake Sir, ſit down again.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Alaſs
Where are the Surgeons?

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Sir, they will not come,
If they ſhould dreſs you, you would dye they ſay
Ere one would tell twenty; trouble not your mind,
Keep your head warm, and do not ſtir your body,
And you may live an hour.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh heavens, an hour?
Alaſs, it is to little too remember
But half the wrongs that I have done; how ſhort
Then for contrition, and how leaſt of all
For ſatisfaction?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: But you deſire
To ſatisfie?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Heaven knows I do.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Then know
That I am he, or ſhe, or what you will
Moſt wrong'd by you; your Leocadia,
I know you muſt remember me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh heaven!

sp.speaker: Lec.
sp.l: That loſt her friends, that loſt her fathers houſe,
That loſt her fame in looſing of her Sex,
With theſe ſtrange garments, there is no excuſe
To hinder me, it is within your power
To give me ſatisfaction; you have time
Left in this little piece of life to do it:
Therefore I charge you for your conſcience ſake,
And for our fame, which I would fain have live
When both of us are dead, to celebrate
That Contract; which you have both ſeal'd and ſworn
Yet ere you dye, which muſt be haſtily
Heaven knows.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Alaſs, the ſting of conſcience
To death-ward for our faults; draw nearer all
And hear what I unhappy man ſhall ſay;
Firſt Madam I deſire your pardon; next
(I feel my ſpirits fail me) Gentlemen
Let me ſhake hands with you, and let's be friends,
For I have done wrong upon wrong ſo thick
I know not where, that every man methinks
Should be mine enemy; Forgive me both.
Laſtly 'tis true (oh I do feel the power
Of death ſeize on me) that I was contracted
By ſeal and oath to Leocadia;
(I muſt ſpeak faſt, becauſe I fear my life
Will elſe be ſhorter than my ſpeech would be)
But 'tis impoſſible to ſatisfie
You Leocadia, but by repentance,
Though I can dyingly, and boldly ſay
I know not your diſhonor, yet that was
Your virtue, and not mine, you know it well;
But herein lies th'impoſſibility,
O Theodoſia, Theodoſia,
I was betroth'd to Theodoſia
Before I ever ſaw thee; heaven forgive me
She is my wife this half hour whilſt I live.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: That's I, that's I, I'm Theodoſia,
Hear me a little now, who have not ſuffer'd
Diſgrace at all methinks, ſince you confeſs
What I ſo long have ſought for, here is with me
Philippo too my Brother.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am glad;
All happineſs to him; come let me kiſs thee
Beg pardon of that Maid for my offence,
And let me farther, with a dying breath
Tell in thine ear the reſt of my deſires.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: I am afraid they will all four turn women
If we hold longer talk.

sp.speaker: Leoc.
sp.l: Alaſs there is
No hope for me; that's Theodoſia
And that her Brother, I am only ſorry
I was beholding to 'em; I will ſearch
Over the world, as careleſs of my fortunes,
As they of me, till I can meet a curſe
To make theſe almoſt killing-ſorrows worſe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Sir, as I live ſhe ly'd, only to draw
A juſt confeſſion from you, which ſhe hath
A happy one for me, ask of this Lady,
Ask of my Brother.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Sir, ſhe did diſſemble,
Your wound is nothing.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Leocadia's gone. Exit.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: Riſe up, and ſtir your ſelf, 'tis but amazement
And your imagination that afflicts you,
Look you Sir now.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I think 'tis ſo indeed.

sp.speaker: Theo.
sp.l: The Surgeons do not come, becauſe they ſwear
It needs no dreſſing.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: You ſhall talk with 'em
Within, for your own fancy.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Where's your Brother, and Leocadia?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Within belike.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I feel my ſelf methinks as well as ever.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Keep then your mind ſo too; I do forgive
The fault you did to me; But here is one
Muſt not be wrong'd hereafter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Neither ſhall ſhe
When I make jeſts of oaths again, or make
My luſt play with religion, when I leave
To keep true joys for her, and yet within
My ſelf true ſorrow for my paſſed deeds,
May I want grace, when I would fain repent,
And find a great and ſodain puniſhment. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: WHere is mine Hoſt, did not he ſee him neither?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Not I, i'faith Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Nor the muleter?

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Nay he is paſt ſeeing, unleſs it be in's ſleep,
By this time; all his viſions were the pots,
Three hours ſince Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Which way ſhould ſhe take?
Nay, look you now; do you all ſtand ſtill? good Heaven
You might have lighted on him, now this inſtant?
For loves ſake ſee him out, who ever find him
I will reward his fortune as his diligence;
Get all the Town to help, that will be hir'd,
Their pains I'll turn to annual holiday,
If it ſhall chance, but one bring word of her,
Pray you about it.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Her Sir? who do you mean?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: (I had forgot my ſelf) the Page I meant
That came along with us.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: He you gave the clothes too?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I ga' the clothes to; Raſcal?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: Nay good Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why doſt thou mention or upbraid my courteſies
Slave?

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: For your honor Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Wretch; I was honor'd,
That ſhe would wear 'em (he, I would ſay) 's death?
Go, get, and find 'em out, or never ſee me,
I ſhall betray my love e'r I poſſeſs it,
Some Star direct me, or ill Planet ſtrike me. Exit Phil.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Beſt to divide.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I'll this way.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: And I this.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: I, as you, find him for a Real.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: 'Tis done.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: My courſe is now directly to ſome Ple-houſe
I know the Pages compaſs.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I think rather
The ſmock-ſide o'th' Town, the ſurer harbor
At his years to put in.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: If I do find
The hungry haunt, I take him by the teeth now.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: I by the tail, yet I as you.

sp.speaker: Die.
sp.l: No more. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Dear Leocadia, where canſt thou be fled
Thus like a ſpirit hence? and in a moment?
What cloud can hide thee from my following ſearch
If yet thou art a body? ſure ſhe hath not
Tane any houſe? ſhe did too late leave one
Where all humanity of a place receiv'd her,
And would, (if ſhe had ſtaid) have help'd to right
The wrong her fortune did her; yet ſhe muſt
Be enter'd ſomewhere, or be found, no ſtreet,
Lane, paſſage, corner, turn, hath ſcap'd enquiry:
If her deſpair had raviſh'd her to air
She could not yet be rarified ſo
But ſome of us ſhould meet her? though their eyes
Perhaps be leaden, and might turn; mine would
Strike out a lightning for her, and divide
A miſt as thick as ever darkneſs was,
Nay ſee her through a quarry; they do lye,
Lye groſly that ſay love is blind; by him,
And heaven they lye; he has a ſight can pierce
Through Ivory, as cleer as it were horn,
And reach his object.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: Sir, he's found, he's found.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Ha? where? But reach that happy Note again
And let it reliſh truth, thou art an Angel.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: He's here; faſt by Sir, calling for a Boat
To go aboard the Gallies.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Where, where; hold thee. Exit.

sp.speaker: Inc.
sp.l: He might ha' kept this now; I had nought to ſhew for't,
If he had had the wit t' have gone from's word,
Theſe direct men, they are no men of faſhion,
Talk what you will, this is a very ſmelt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Upon your Art Sir, and your faith to aſſiſt it
Shall I believe you then his wound's not mortal?

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Sir, 'tis not worth your queſtion; leſs your fear.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You doe reſtore me Sir, I pray you accept
This ſmall remembrance of a fathers thanks
For ſo aſſur'd a benefit.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Excuſe me.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Sir, I can ſpare it, and muſt not believe
But that your fortune may receiv't, except
You'ld ha' methink you live not by your practice.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: I crave your pardon Sir; you teach me manners.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I crave your love and friendſhip, and require
As I have made now, both my ſelf and buſineſs
A portion of your care, you will but bring me
Under the perſon of a call'd aſſiſtant
To his next opening, where I may but ſee him,
And utter afew words to him in private,
And you will merit me; for I am loth
Since here I have not to appear my ſelf,
Or to be known unto the Governor,
Or make a tumult of my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: Neither
I hope will be your need Sir; I ſhall bring you
Both there, and off again without the hazard. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.

sp.speaker: Ph.
sp.l: Will you not hear me!

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I have heard ſo much
Will keep me deaf for ever; No, Mark-antonio,
After thy ſentence, I may hear no more,
Thou haſt pronounc'd me dead.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Appeal to reaſon,
She will reprieve you from the power of grief,
Which rules but in her abſence; Hear me ſay
A ſoveraign meſſage from her, which in duty,
And love to your own ſafety, you ought hear:
Why do you ſtrive ſo? whither would you flie?
You cannot wreſt your ſelf away from care,
You may from counſel; you may ſhift your place
But not your perſon; and another Clyme
Makes you no other.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: For paſſions ſake,
(Which I do ſerve, honor, and love in you)
If you will ſigh, ſigh here; If you would vary
A ſigh to tears, or out-cry, do it here.
No ſhade, no deſart, darkneſs, nor the grave
Shall be more equal to your thoughts than I,
Only but hear me ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What would you ſay?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: That which ſhall raiſe your heart, or pull down mine,
Quiet your paſſion, or provoke mine own;
We muſt have both one balſome, or one wound,
For know (lov'd fair) ſince the firſt providence
Made me your reſcue, I have read you through,
And with a wondring pity look'd on you,
I have obſerv'd the method of your blood,
And waited on it even with ſympathy
Of alike Red, and Paleneſs in mine own;
I knew which bluſh was angers, which was loves,
Which was the eye of ſorrow, which of truth:
And could diſtinguiſh honor from diſdain
In every change: and you are worth my ſtudy;
I ſaw your voluntary miſery
Suſtain'd in travel: A diſguis'd Maid
Wearied with ſeeking: and with finding loſt,
Neglected, where you hop'd moſt, or put by;
I ſaw it, and have laid it to my heart,
And though it were my Siſter which was righted,
Yet being by your wrong, I put off nature,
Could not be glad, where I muſt bound to triumph;
My care for you, ſo drown'd reſpect of her;
Nor did I only apprehend your bonds,
But ſtudied your releaſe: and for that day
Have I made up a ranſom, brought you a health
Preſervative 'gainſt chance, or injury,
Pleaſe you apply it to the grief; my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Humph.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Nay, do not think me leſs than ſuch a cure,
Antonio was not; And 'tis poſſible
Philippo may ſucceed: My bloud and houſe
Are as deep rooted: and as fairly ſpread,
As Mark-antonio, and in that, all ſeek,
Fortune hath given him no precedency:
As for our thanks to Nature I may burn
Incenſe as much as he; I ever durſt
Walk with Antonio by the ſelf-ſame light
At any feaſt, or triumph, and ne'r car'd
Which ſide my Lady or her woman took
In their ſurvey; I durſt have told my tale too
Though his diſcourſe new ended.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: My repulſe.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Let not that torture you, wbich makes me happy
Nor think that conſcience (fair) which is no ſhame;
'Twas no repulſe, I was your Dowry rather:
For then methought a thouſand graces met
To make you lovely, and ten thouſand ſtories
Of conſtant virtue, which you then out-reach'd,
In one example did proclaim you rich:
Nor do I think you wretched, or diſgrac'd,
After this ſuffering, and do therefore take
Advantage of your need; but rather know
You are the charge and buſineſs of thoſe powers,
Who, like beſt Tutors, do inflict hard tasks
Upon great Natures, and of nobleſt hopes;
Read trivial Leſſons, and halfe lines to ſluggs;
They that live long, and never feel miſchance,
Spend more than halfe their age in ignorance.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: 'Tis well you think ſo.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: You ſhall think ſo too,
You ſhall ſweet Leocadia, and do ſo.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Good Sir no more; you have too fair a ſhape
To play ſo ſoul a part in, as the Tempter:
Say that I could not make peace with fortune, who,
Who ſhould abſolve me of my vow yet; ha?
My Contract made?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Your Contract?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Yes, my Contract,
Am I not his? his wife?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Sweet, nothing leſs.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I have no name then?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Truly then you have not;
How can you be his wife, who was before
Anothers Husband?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Oh, though he diſpence
With his faith given, I cannot with mine.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: You do miſtake (cleer ſoul) his precontract
Doth annul yours, and you have giv'n no faith
That ties you in Religion, or humanity,
You rather ſin againſt that greater precept,
To covet what's anothers; Sweet, you do,
Believe me, who dare not urge diſhoneſt things,
Remove that ſcruple therefore, and but take
Your dangers now, into your judgements skale
And weigh them with your ſafeties: Think but whither
Now you can goe: what you can do to live?
How near you ha' barr'd all Ports to to your own ſuccor,
Except this one that I here open Love.
Should you be left alone, you were a prey
To the wild luſt of any, who would look
Upon this ſhape like a temptation,
And think you want the man you perſonate;
Would not regard this ſhift, which love put on,
As virtue forc'd, but covet it like vice;
So ſhould you live the ſlander of each Sex,
And be the child of error and of ſhame;
And which is worſe, even Mark-antoni •
Would be call'd juſt, to turn a wanderer off,
And Fame report you worthy his contempt;
Where if you make new choice, and ſettle here,
There is no further tumult in this ſtood,
Each current keeps his courſe, and all ſuſpitions
Shall return honors: Came you forth a Maid?
Go home a Wiſe • alone? and in diſguiſe?
Go home a waited Leocadia:
Go home, and by the viruue of that charm
Transform all miſchiefs, as you are transform'd;
Turn your offended Fathers wrath to wonder,
Add all his loud grief to a ſilent welcome:
Unfold the Riddles you have made, what ſay you?
sp.stage: Enter Sanchio carried, Alphonſo, and Servants.
sp.l: Now is the time; delay is but deſpair,
If you be chang'd, let a kiſs tell me ſo.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I am: but how, I rather feel than know.

sp.speaker: Sanc.
sp.l: Come Sir; you are welcome now to Barcelona,
Take off my hood.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Who be theſe? ſtay, let's view 'em?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: 'Twas a long journey: are you not weary Sir?

sp.speaker: Sanc.
sp.l: Weary? I could have rid it in mine Armour.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Alas!

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What ail you dear?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: It is my Father,

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Your Father: which?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He that is carried: oh
Let us make hence.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: For loves ſake: good my heart.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Into ſome houſe before he ſee me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Dear,
Be not thus frighted,

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Oh his wrath is tempeſt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Sweet, take your ſpirit to you, and ſtay, be't he,
He cannot know you in this habit, and me
I'm ſure he leſs knows, for he never ſaw me.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Ha? who is that? my Son Philippo?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Sir,

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Why, what make you here? Is this Salamanca?
And that your ſtudy? ha? nay ſtay him too,
We'll ſee him by his leave.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: You muſt not ſtrive Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: No, no, come near.

sp.speaker: Sanc.
sp.l: My Daughter: Leocadia?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: How Sir, your Daughter?

sp.speaker: Sanc.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and as ſure
As that's your Son: Come hither: what now? run
Out o' your ſex? breech'd? was't not enough
At once to leave thy Father, and thine honor,
Unleſs th' hadſt quit thy ſelf too.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Sir, what fault
She can be urg'd of, I muſt take on me
The guilt and puniſhment.

sp.speaker: Sanc.
sp.l: You muſt Sir: how
If you ſhall not, though you muſt? I deal not
With boys Sir; I, you have a Father here
Shall do me right.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Thou art not mad, Philippo?
Art thou Mark-antonie? Son to Leonardo?
Our buſineſs is to them.

sp.speaker: Sanc.
sp.l: No, no, no, no.
I'll ha' the buſineſs now: with you, none elſe,
Pray you let's ſpeak, in private: (carry me to him)
Your Son's the raviſher Sir, and here I find him:
I hope you'll give me cauſe to think you noble,
And do me right, with your ſword Sir, as becomes
One gentleman of honor to another;
All this is fair Sir: here's the Sea faſt by,
Upon the ſands, we will determine
'Tis that I call you to; let's make no daies on't,
I'll lead your way; to the ſea-ſide Raſcals.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Sir
I would beſeech your ſtay; he may not follow you.

sp.speaker: San.
sp.l: No, turn, I'll kill him here then: Slaves, Rogues, Bloks.
Why do you not bear me to him? ha' you been
Acquainted with my motions, loggs, ſo long
And yet not know to time 'em.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Were you Sir
Not impotent.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Hold you your peace Boy.

sp.speaker: Sanc.
sp.l: Impotent,
'Death, I'll cut his throat firſt, and then his Fathers.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: You muſt provide you then a ſharper Razor
Than is your tongue, for I not fear your ſword.

sp.speaker: Sanc.
sp.l: 'Heart bear me to either of 'em.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Pray Sir your patience.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: My curſe light on thee if thou ſtay him.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Hold.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter, Gentlemen, what tumult
Is this you raiſe i'th' ſtreet? before my door?
Know you what 'tis to draw a weapon here?

sp.speaker: Sanc.
sp.l: Yes, and to uſe it (bear me up to him, Rogues)
Thus, at a Traitors heart.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Truer than thine.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Strike, ſtrike; Some of the people diſarm 'em,
Kill 'em if they reſiſt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Nay generous Sir
Let not your courteſie turn fury now.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Lay hold upon 'em, take away their weapons,
I will be worth an anſwer, e'r we part.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: 'Tis the Governor Sir.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I yield my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: My Sword? what thinkſt thou of me? pray thee tell me.

sp.speaker: 1 Attend.
sp.l: As of a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: No more?

sp.speaker: 1 Attend.
sp.l: Of worth,
And quality.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: And I ſhould quit my ſword
There were ſmall worth or quality in that friend;
Pray thee learn thou more worth and quality
Than to demand it.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Force it I ſay.

sp.speaker: 1 Attend.
sp.l: The Governor
You hear, commands.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: The Governr ſhall pardon me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: How, Leocadia gone again? Exit Phi.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: He ſhall friend
I'th' point of honor; by his leave, ſo tell him,
His perſon and authority I acknowledge,
And do ſubmit me to it; but my Sword,
He ſhall excuſe me, were he fifteen Governors;
That and I dwell together, and muſt yet
Till my hands part, aſſure him.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I ſay force it.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Stay, hear me. Haſt thou ever read Caranza?
Underſtandſt thou honor, Noble Governor?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: For that we'll have more fit diſpute.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Your name Sir?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You ſhall know that too: but on colder terms,
Your blood and brain are now too hot to take it.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Force my Sword from me? this is an affront.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Bring 'em away.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: You'll do me reparation. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I have for ever loſt her, and am loſt,
And worthily my tameneſs hath undone me;
She's gone hence, aſham'd of me: yet I ſeek her.
Will ſhe be ever found to me again,
Whom ſhe ſaw ſtand ſo poorly, and dare nothing
In her defence, here? when I ſhould have drawn
This Sword out like a Meteor, and have ſhot it
In both our Parents eies, and left 'em blind
Unto their impotent angers? Oh I am worthy
On whom this loſs and ſcorn ſhould light to death,
Without the pity that ſhould wiſh me better,
Either alive, or in my Epitaph,

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Well Son, your Father is too near himſelf
And hath too much of nature to put off
Any affection that belongs to you,
I could have only wiſh'd you had acquainted
Her Father, whom it equally concerns,
Though y'had preſum'd on me: it might have open'd
An eaſier gate, and path to both our joyes:
For though I am none of thoſe flinty Fathers
That when their children do but natural things,
Turn rock and offence ſtraight: yet Mark-antonio,
All are not of my quarry.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis my fear Sir;
And if hereafter I ſhould e'r abuſe
So great a piety, it were my malice.

sp.speaker: Atten.
sp.l: We muſt intreat you Gentlemen to take
Another room, the Governor is coming
Here, on ſome buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: We will give him way.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I will have right Sir on you; that believe,
If there be any Marſhals Court in Spain.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: For that Sir we ſhall talk.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: —Do not ſlight me,
Though I am without a Sword.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Keep to your Chair Sir.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: —Let me fall, and hurle my chair! (ſlaves) at him.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You are the more temper'd man Sir: let me intreat
Of you the manner how this brawl fell out,

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Fell out? I know not how: nor do I care much:
But here we came Sir to this Town together,
Both in one buſineſs, and one wrong, engag'd,
To ſeek one Leonardo, an old Genocſe,
I ha' ſaid enough there; would you more? falſe father
Of a falſe ſon, call'd Mark-antonio,
Who had ſtole both our Daughters; and which Father
Conſpiring with his Son in treachery,
It ſeem'd, to flie our ſatisfaction,
Was, as we heard, come private to this Town
Here to take ſhip for Italy,

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You heard
More than was true then: by the fear, or falſhood,
And though I thought not to reveal my ſelf
(Pardon my manners in't to you) for ſome
Important reaſons; yet being thus character'd
And challeng'd, know I dare appear, and doe
To who dares threaten.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I ſay he is not worthy
The name of man, or any honeſt preface,
That dares report or credit ſuch a ſlander.
Do you Sir ſay it?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I doe ſay it.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Hold.
Is this your father Signior Mark-antonio?
You have ill requited me thus to conceal him
From him would honor him, and do him ſervice.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: 'Twas not his fault Sir.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Where's my Lord?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Sweet-heart.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Know you theſe Gentlemen? they are all the fathers
Unto our friends.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: So it appears my Dove.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Sir, I ſay nothing: I do want a Sword.
And till I have a Sword I will ſay nothing.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Good Sir, command theſe Gentlemen their Arms;
Entreat 'em as your friends, not as your priſoners.
Where be their Swords?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Reſtore each man his weapon.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: It ſeems thou haſt not read Caranza, fellow
I muſt have reparation of honor,
As well as this: I find that wounded.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Sir,
I did not know your quality, if I had
'Tis like I ſhould have done you more reſpects.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: It is ſufficient, by Caranza's rule.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: I know it is Sir.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Have you read Caranza Lady?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: If you mean him that writ upon the Duel,
He was my kinſman.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Lady, then you know
By the right noble writings of your kinſman,
My honor is as dear to me, as the Kings.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: 'Tis very true Sir.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Therefore I muſt crave
Leave to go on now with my firſt dependance.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: What ha' you more?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: None here good Signior.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I will, refer me to Caranza ſtill.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Nay love, I prethee let me manage this.
With whom is't Sir?

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: With that falſe man Alphonſo.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Why he has th' advantage Sir, in legs.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: But I
In truth, in hand and heart, and a good Sword.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: But how if he will not ſtand you Sir?

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: For that,
Make it no queſtion Lady, I will ſtick
My feet in earth down by him, where he dare.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: O would thou wouldſt.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: I'll do't.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Let me kiſs him.
I fear thou wilt not yet.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Why Gentlemen,
If you'll proceed according to Caranza,
Methinks an eaſier way, were too good chairs,
So you would be content Sir, to be bound,
'Cauſe he is lame? I'll fit you with like weapons,
Piſtols and Ponyards, and ev'n end it. If
The difference between you be ſo mortal.
It cannot be tane up.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Tane up? take off
This head firſt.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Come bind me in a chair.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Yes, do.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: What mean you, Dove.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Let me alone,
And ſet 'em at their diſtance: when you ha' done
Lend me two Ponyards; I'll have Piſtols ready
Quickly.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: She is not here Mark-antonio,
Saw you not Leocadia?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Not I brother.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Brother let's ſpeak with you; you were falſe unto her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I was, but have ask'd pardon: why do you urge it?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: You were not worthy of her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: May be I was not;
But 'tis not well, you tell me ſo.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: My Siſter
Is not ſo fair.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It skils not.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Nor ſo virtuous.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, ſhe muſt be as virtuous.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I would fain—

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What brother?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Strike you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I ſhall not bear ſtrokes,
Though I do theſe ſtrange words.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Will you not kill me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For what good brother?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why, for ſpeaking well
Of Leocadia,

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No indeed.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Nor ill
Of Theodoſia?

div.stage: Enter Eugenia, Leocadia, Theodoſia, and one with two Piſtols.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Neither.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Fare you well then.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Nay, you ſhall have as noble ſeconds too
As ever Dueliſts had; give 'em their weapons:
Now St. Jago.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: Are they charg'd?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Charg'd Sir?
I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Would they were well diſcharg'd.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I like a Sword much better I confeſs.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Nay, wherefore ſtay you? ſhall I mend your mark?
Strike one another, thorough theſe?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: My love.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: My Theodoſia.

sp.speaker: Sanch.
sp.l: I ha' not the heart.

sp.speaker: Alph.
sp.l: Nor I.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Why here is a dependence ended.
Unbind that Gentleman; come take here to you
Your Sons and Daughters, and be friends. A feaſt
Waits you within, is better than your fray:
Lovers, take you your own, and all forbear
Under my roof, either to bluſh or fear.
My love, what ſay you? could Caranza himſelf
Carry a buſineſs better?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: It is well:
All are content I hope, and we well eas'd.
If they for whom we have done all this be pleas'd. Exeunt.

div.head: PROLOGUE.
div.l: TO this place Gentlemen, full many a day
We have bid ye welcome; and to many a Play:
And thoſe whoſe angry ſouls were not diſeas'd
With Law, or lending Money, we have pleas'd;
And make no doubt to do again. This night
No mighty matter, nor no light,
We muſt intreat you look for: A good tale,
Told in two hours, we will not fail
If we be perfect, to rehearſe ye: New
I am ſure it is, and handſome; but how true
Let them diſpute that writ it. Ten to one
We pleaſe the Women, and I would know that man
Follows not their example? If ye mean
To know the Play well, travel with the Scene.
For it lies upon the Road; if we chance tire,
As ye are good men, leave us not i' th' mire,
Another bait may mend us: If you grow
A little gall'd or weary; cry but hoa,
And we'll ſtay for ye. When our journey ends
Every mans Pot I hope, and all part friends.

div.head: The Perſons Repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Ferrand, The libidinous Tyrant of Naples.
Virolet, A noble Gent. ſtudious of his Countries freedom.

list.head: Two honeſt Gentlemen, confederates with Virolet.

list.item: Ronvere, A villain, Captain of the Guard.
Pandulpho, A noble Gentleman of Naples, Father to Virolet.
The Duke of Seſſe, An enemy to Ferrand, proſcribed and turn'd Pirate.
Aſcanio, Nephew and ſucceſſor to Ferrand.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Juliana, The matchleſeſs Wife of Virolet,
Martia, Daughter to the Duke of Seſſe.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: BOy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: If my wife ſeek me, tell her that
Deſigns of weight, too heavy for her knowledge,
Exact my privacy

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I ſhall, Sir.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Do then,
And leave me to my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: 'Tis a raw morning
And would you pleaſe to interpret that for duty
Which you may conſtrue boldneſs, I could wiſh
To arm your ſelf againſt it, you would uſe
More of my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I have heat within here,
A noble heat (good boy) to keep it off,
I ſhall not freeze; deliver my excuſe, Enter Juliana.
And you have done your part,

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: That is prevented,
My Lady follows you.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Since I muſt be croſt then,
Let her perform that office.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I obey you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Prethee to bed; to be thus fond's more tedious
Than if I were neglected.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis the fault then
Of Love and Duty, which I would fall under,
Rather than want that care which you may challenge
As due to my obedience.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I confeſs
This tenderneſs argues a loving Wife,
And more deſerves my hearts beſt thanks, than anger.
Yet I muſt tell ye Sweet, you do exceed
In your affection, if you would ingroſs me
To your delights alone.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I am not jealous,
If my embraces have diſtaſted you,
As I muſt grant you every way ſo worthy
That 'tis not in weak woman to deſerve you,
Much leſs in miſerable me, that want
Thoſe graces, ſome more fortunate are ſtor'd with.
Seek any whom you pleaſe, and I will ſtudy
With my beſt ſervice to deſerve thoſe favors,
That ſhall yield you contentment.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: You are miſtaken.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: No, I am patient Sir, and ſo good morrow;
I will not be offenſive.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Hear my reaſons.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Though in your life a widdows bed receives me,
For your ſake I muſt love it. May ſhe proſper
That ſhall ſucceed me in it, and your ardor
Laſt longer to her.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: By the love I bear,
Firſt to my Countreys peace; next to thy ſelf
To whom compar'd, my life I rate at nothing;
Stood here a Lady that were the choice abſtract
Of all the beauties nature ever faſhion'd,
Or Art gave ornament to, compar'd to thee,
Thus as thou art obedient and loving,
I ſhould contemn and loath her.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I doe believe.
How I am bleſt
In my aſſur'd belief? this is unfeign'd;
And why this ſadneſs then?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Why Juliana,
Believe me, theſe my ſad and dull retirements,
My often, nay almoſt continued Faſts,
Sleep baniſht from my eyes, all pleaſures, ſtrangers,
Have neither root nor growth from any cauſe
That may arrive at Woman. Shouldſt thou be,
As chaſtity forbid, falſe to my bed,
I ſhould lament my fortune, perhaps puniſh
Thy falſhood, and then ſtudy to forget thee:
But that which like a never-emptied ſpring,
Feeds high the torrent of my ſwelling grief,
Is what my Countrey ſuffers; there's a ground
Where ſorrow may be planted, and ſpring up,
Through yielding rage, and womaniſh deſpair,
And yet not ſhame the owner.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I do believe it true,
Yet I ſhould think my ſelf a happy woman,
If, in this general and timely mourning,
I might or give to you, or elſe receive
A little lawful comfort.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Thy diſcretion
In this may anſwer for me; look on Naples
The Countrey where we both were born and bred,
Naples the Paradiſe of Italy,
As that is of the earth; Naples, that was
The ſweet retreat of all the worthieſt Romans,
When they had ſhar'd the ſpoils of the whole world;
This flouriſhing Kingdom, whoſe inhabitants
For wealth and bravery, liv'd like petty Kings,
Made ſubject now to ſuch a tyrannie.
As that fair City that receiv'd her name
From Conſtantine the great, now in the power
Of barbarous Infidels, may forget her own;
To look with pity on our miſeries;
So far in our calamities we tranſcend her.
For ſince this Arragonian tyrant, Ferrand,
Seiz'd on the goverment, there's nothing left us
That we can call our own, but our afflictions.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And hardly thoſe; the Kings ſtrange cruelty,
Equals all preſidents of tyranny.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Equal ſay you?
He has out-gone, the worſt compar'd to him;
Nor Phalaris, nor Dionyſius,
Caligula, nor Nero can be mention'd;
They yet as Kings, abus'd their Regal power;
This as a Merchant, all the Countreys fat.
He wholly does ingroſs unto himſelf;
Our Oils he buys at his own price, then ſells them
To us, at dearer rates; our Plate and Jewels,
Under a fain'd pretence of publique uſe,
He borrows; which deny'd his inſtruments force,
The Races of our horſes he takes from us;
Yet keeps them in our paſtures; rapes of Matrons,
And Virgins, are too frequent; never man
Yet thank'd him for a pardon; for Religion,
It is a thing he dreams not of.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I have heard,
How true it is, I know not; that he ſold
The Biſhoprick of Tarent to a Jew,
For thirteen thouſand Duckets.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I was preſent,
And ſaw the money paid; the day would leave me,
E'r I could number out his impious actions;
Or what the miſerable Subject ſuffers;
And can you entertain in ſuch a time,
A thought of dalliance? tears, and ſighs, and groans,
Would better now become you.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: They indeed are,
The only weapons, our poor Sex can uſe,
When we are injur'd; and they may become us;
But for men that were born free men, of Ranck;
That would be Regiſtred Fathers of their Countrey;
And to have on their Tombs in Golden Letters,
The noble ſtile of Tyrant-killers, written;
To weep like fools and Women, and not like wiſe men.
To practiſe a redreſs, deſerves a name,
Which ſits not me to give.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Thy grave reproof:
If what thou doſt deſire, were poſſible
To be effected, might well argue it,
As wiſe as loving; but if you conſider,
With what ſtrong guards this Tyrant is defended:
Ruffins, and male-contents drawn from all quarters;
That only know, to ſerve his impious Will;
The Cittadels built by him in the neck
Of this poor City; the invincible ſtrength,
Nature by Art aſſiſted, gave this Caſtle;
And above all his fear; admitting no man
To ſee him, but unarm'd; it being death
For any to approach him with a weapon.
You muſt confeſs, unleſs our hands were Cannons,
To batter down theſe walls; our weak breath Mines,
To blow his Forts up; or our curſes lightning,
To force a paſſage to him; and then blaſt him;
Our power is like to yours, and we, like you,
Weep our misfortunes.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Walls of Braſs reſiſt not
A noble undertaking; nor can vice,
Raiſe any Bulwark, to make good the place,
Where virtue ſeeks to enter; then to fall
In ſuch a brave attempt, were ſuch an honor
That Brutus, did he live again, would envy,
Were my dead Father in you, and my Brothers;
Nay, all the Anceſtors I am deriv'd from;
As you, in being what you are, are all theſe.
I had rather wear a mourning Garment for you,
And ſhould be more proud of my widdowhood;
You dying for the freedom of this Countrey;
Than if I were aſſur'd, I ſhould enjoy
A perpetuity of life and pleaſure
With you, the Tyrant living.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Till this minute;
I never heard thee ſpeak; O more than woman!
And more to be belov'd; can I find out
A Cabinet, to lock a ſecret in,
Of equal truſt to thee? all doubts, and fears,
That ſcandalize your Sex, be far from me;
Thou ſhalt partake my near and deareſt councils,
And further them with thine.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I will be faithful,

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Know then this day, ſtand heaven propitious to us,
Our liberty begins.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: In Ferrands death?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: 'Tis plotted love, and ſtrongly, and believe it,
For nothing elſe could do it, 'twas the thought,
How to proceed in this deſign and end it.
That made ſtrange my embraces,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Curs'd be ſhe,
That's ſo indulgent to her own delights,
That for their ſatisfaction, would give
A ſtop to ſuch a glorious enterprize:
For me, I would not for the world, I had been
Guilty of ſuch a crime; go on and proſper.
Go on my deareſt Lord, I love your Honor
Above my life; nay, yours; my prayers go with you;
Which I will ſtrengthen with my tears: the wrongs
Of this poor Countrey, edge your ſword; Oh may it
Pierce deep into this Tyrants heart, and then
When you return bath'd in his guilty blood;
I'll waſh you clean with fountains of true joy.
But who are your aſſiſtants? though I am
So covetous of your glory, that I could wiſh
You had no ſharer in it. Knock.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Be not curious.
They come, however you command my boſom,
To them I would not have you ſeen.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I am gone Sir,
Be confident, and may my reſolution
Be preſent with you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Such a Maſculine ſpirit.
With more than Womans virtues, were a Dower
To weigh down a Kings fortune.

sp.speaker: Briſſ.
sp.l: Good day to you.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: You are an early ſtirrer.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: What new face,
Bring you along?

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: If I ſtand doubted Sir?
As by your looks I gueſs it: you much injure
A man that loves, and truly loves this Countrey,
With as much zeal as you doe; one that hates
The Prince by whom it ſuffers, and as deadly;
One that dares ſtep as far to gain my freedom,
As any he that breaths; that wears a ſword
As ſharp as any 's.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Nay, no more compariſons.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: What you but whiſper, I dare ſpeak aloud,
Stood the King by; have means to put in act too
What you but coldly plot; if this deſerve then
Suſpition in the beſt, the boldeſt, wiſeſt?
Purſue your own intents, I'll follow mine;
And if I not out-ſtrip you—

sp.speaker: Briſſ.
sp.l: Be aſſur'd Sir,
A conſcience like this can never be ally'd
To treachery.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Who durſt ſpeak ſo much,
But one that is like us, a ſufferer,
And ſtands as we affected?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: You are cozen'd
And all undone; every Intelligencer
Speaks Treaſon with like licence; is not this
Ronvere, that hath for many years been train'd
In Ferrand's School, a man in truſt and favour,
Rewarded too, and highly?

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Grant all this,
The thought of what he was, being as he is now
A man diſgrac'd, and with contempt thrown off;
Will ſpurr him to revenge, as ſwift as they,
That never were in favour.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Poor and childiſh.

sp.speaker: Briſſ.
sp.l: His regiment is caſt, that is moſt certain;
And his command in the Caſtle given away.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: That on my knowledge.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Groſſer ſtill, what Shepheard
Would yield the poor remainder of his Flock,
To a known Wolf; though he put on the habit,
Of a moſt faithful dog, and bark like one?
As this but only talks.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Yes, he has means too.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I know it to my grief, weak men I know it;
To make his peace, if there were any war
Between him and his Maſter, betraying
Our innocent lives.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: You are too ſuſpitious
And I have born too much, beyond my temper,
Take your own waies, I'll leave you.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: You may ſtay now;
You have enough. and all indeed you fiſh'd for;
But one word Gentlemen: have you diſcover'd
To him alone our plot?

sp.speaker: Briſſ.
sp.l: To him and others, that are at his devotion.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Worſe and worſe:
For were he only conſcious of our purpoſe,
Though with the breach of Hoſpitable laws,
In my own houſe, I'de ſilence him for ever:
But what is paſt my help, is paſt my care.
I have a life to loſe.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Have better hopes.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: And when you know, with what charge I have further'd
Your noble undertaking, you will ſwear me
Another man; the guards I have corrupted:
And of the choice of all our nobleſt youths,
Attir'd like Virgins; ſuch as Hermits would
Welcome to their ſad cells, prepar'd a Maske;
As done for the Kings pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: For his ſafety
I rather fear; and as a pageant to
Uſher our ruine.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: We as Torch-bearers
Will wait on theſe, but with ſuch art and cunning;
I have conveigh'd ſharp poniards in the Wax,
That we may paſs, though ſearch't through all his guards
Without ſuſpition, and in all his glory,
Oppreſs him, and with ſafety.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: To be effected.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: You are doubtful ſtill.

sp.speaker: Briſſ.
sp.l: But we reſolv'd to follow him, and if you
Deſiſt now Virolet, we will ſay 'tis fear,
Rather than providence. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: And ſo we leave you,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: To your wiſe doubts, and to my better counſels;
Oh! pardon me my Lord, and truſt me too;
Let me not like Caſſandra propheſie truths,
And never be believ'd, before the miſchief:
I have heard all; know this Ronvere a villain,
A villain that hath tempted me, and plotted
This for your ruine, only to make way
To his hopes in my embraces; at more leiſure
I will acquaint you, wherefore I conceal'd it
To this laſt minute; if you ſtay, you are loſt,
And all prevention too late. I know,
And 'tis to me known only, a dark cave
Within this houſe, a part of my poor Dower,
Where you may lie conceal'd, as in the center,
Till this rough blaſt be o'r, where there is air,
More then to keep in life; Ferrand will find you,
So curious his fears are.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: 'Tis better fall
Than hide my head, now 'twas thine own advice,
My friends engag'd too.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: You ſtand further bound,
Than to weak men that have betrai'd themſelves,
Or to my counſel, though then juſt and loyal:
Your phanſie hath been good, but not your judgement,
In choice of ſuch to ſide you; will you leap
From a ſteep Tower, becauſe a deſperate fool
Does it, and truſts the wind to ſave his hazard?
There's more expected from you; all mens eies are fixt
On Virolet, to help, not hurt them;
Make good their hopes and ours, you have ſworn often,
That you dare credit me; and allow'd me wiſe
Although a woman; even Kings in great actions,
Wait opportunity, and ſo muſt you, Sir,
Or looſe your underſtanding.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Thou art conſtant;
I am uncertain fool, a moſt blind fool;
Be thou my guide.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: If I fail to direct you,
For torment or reward, when I am wretched,
May conſtancy forſake me.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I've my ſafety.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Why are you rapt thus?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Peace, thou art a fool.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: But if I were a flatterer like your worſhip,
I ſhould be wiſe and rich too;
There are few elſe that proſper, Bawds excepted,
They hold an equal place there.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: A ſhrewd knave;
But oh the King, the happy King

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Why happy?
In bearing a great burthen.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: What bears he,
That's born on Princes ſhoulders?

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: A Crowns weight,
Which ſets more heavy on his head, than the Oar
Slaves dig out of the Mines, of which 'tis made.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Thou worthily art his fool, to think that heavy
That carries him in the air; the reverence due
To that moſt ſacred Gold, makes him ador'd,
His Footſteps kiſt, his ſmiles to raiſe a begger
To a Lords fortune; and when he but frowns,
The City quakes.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Or the poor Cuckolds in it,
Coxcombs I ſhould ſay, I am of a fool,
Grown a Philoſopher, to hear this paraſite.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: The delicates he is ſerv'd with ſee and envy.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: I had rather have an Onion with a ſtomack,
Than theſe without one.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: The Celeſtial Muſick,
Such as the motion of the eternal ſphears Still muſick.
Yields Jove, when he drinks Nectar.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Here's a fine knave, yet hath too many fellows.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Then the beauties,
That with variety of chice embraces, Theſe paſs o'r.
Renew his age.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Help him to crouch rather,
And the French Cringe, they are excellent Surgeons that way.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Oh Majeſty! let others think of heaven,
While I contemplate thee.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: This is not Atheiſme, but Court obſervance.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Now the God appears, uſher'd with earth-quakes.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Baſe Idolatry. Flouriſh.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Theſe meats are poiſoned, hang
The Cooks; no note more on
Forfeit of your fingers; do you
Envie me a minutes ſlumber, what are theſe?

sp.speaker: 1 Gu.
sp.l: The Ladies appointed by your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: To the purpoſe, for what appointed?

sp.speaker: 1 Gu.
sp.l: For your graces pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: To ſuck away the little blood is left me,
By my continual cares; I am not apt now,
Injoy them firſt, taſte of my Diet once;
And your turns ſerv'd, for fifty Crowns apiece
Their Husbands may redeem them.

sp.speaker: Wo.
sp.l: Great Sir, mercy.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I am deaf, why ſtare you? is what we command
To be diſputed, who's this? bring you the dead
T' upbraid me to my face?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Hold Emperor;
Hold mightieſt of Kings, I am thy vaſſal,
Thy footſtool that durſt not preſume to look
On thy offended face.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Caſtruchio riſe.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Let not the lightning of thy eie conſume me,
Nor hear that muſical tongue, in dreadful thunder,
That ſpeaks all mercy.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Here's no flattering rogue.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Ferrand, that is the Father of his people,
The glory of mankind.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: No more, no word more;
And while I tell my troubles to my ſelf,
Be Statues without motion of voice,
Though to be flatter'd is an itch to greatneſs,
It now offends me.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Here's the happy man;
But ſpeak who dares.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: When I was innocent;
I yet remember I could eat and ſleep,
Walk unaffrighted, but now terrible to others:
My guards cannot keep fear from me
It ſtill purſues me; Oh! my wounded conſcience,
The Bed I would reſt in, is ſtuft with thorns;
The grounds ſtrew'd o'r with adders, and with aſpicks
Where e'r I ſet my foot, but I am in,
And what was got with cruelty, with blood,
Muſt be defended, though this life's a hell,
I fear a worſe hereafter. Ha!

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Welcome Ronvere, welcome my golden plummer
With which I ſound mine enemies depths and angers,
Haſt thou diſcover'd.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: All as you could wiſh Sir,
The Plot, and the contrivers; was made one
Of the conſpiracie.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Is Virolet in?

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: The head of all, he only ſcented me:
And from his fear, that I plaid falſe is fled;
The reſt I have in fetters

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Death and Hell.
Next to my mortal foe the pirate Seſſe,
I aim'd at him; he's virtuous, and wiſe,
A lover of his freedom and his Countries
Dangerous to ſuch as govern by the ſword,
And ſo to me: no tract which way he went,
No means to overtake him?

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: There's ſome hope left;
But with a rough hand, to be ſeiz'd upon.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: What is't?

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: If any know, or where he is,
Or which way he is fled, it is his wife;
Her with his Father I have apprehended,
And brought among the reſt.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: 'Twas wiſely order'd,
Go fetch them in, and let my executioners Exit Ronvere.
Appear in horror with the rack.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: I take it Signior, this is no time for you to flatter,
Or me to fool in.

sp.speaker: Caſt:
sp.l: Thou art wiſe in this, let's off, it is unſafe to be near Jove.
When he begins to thunder.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Good morality. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I that have pierc'd into the hearts of men;
Forc'd them to lay open with my looks,
Secrets, whoſe leaſt diſcovery was death,
Will rend for what concerns my life, the fortreſs,
Of a weak womans faith.

div.stage: Enter Ronvere, Guard, Executioners, with a Rack, Camillo, Briſſonet, Pandulfo, Juliana.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.l: What e're we ſuffer,
The weight that loads a Traitors
Heart ſits ever, heavy on thine.

sp.speaker: Briſſ.
sp.l: As we are caught by thee,
Fall thou by others.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Piſh poor fools, your curſes will
Never reach me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Now by my Virolets life;
Father, this is a glorious ſtage of murther.
Here are fine properties too, and ſuch ſpectators.
As will expect good action, to the life;
Let us perform our parts, and we ſhall live,
When theſe are rotten, would we might begin once;
Are you the Maſter of the company?
Troth you are tedious now.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: She does deride me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Thee and thy power, if one poor ſyllable
Could win me an aſſurance of thy favor,
I would not ſpeak it, I deſire to be
The great example of thy cruelty,
To whet which on, know Ferrand, I alone
Can make diſcovery, where my Virolet is,
Whoſe life, I know thou aim'ſt at, but if tortures
Compel me to't, may hope of heaven forſake me;
I dare thy worſt.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Are we contemn'd?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Thou art,
Thou and thy Miniſters, my life is thine;
But in the death of victory ſhall be mine.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: We have ſuch a Miſtriſs here to teach us courage,
That cowards might learn from her.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: You are ſlow; Put on the rack.
Begin the Scene thou miſerable fool,
For ſo I'll make thee.

sp.speaker: Jul,
sp.l: 'Tis not in thy reach;
I am happy in my ſufferings, thou moſt wretched.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: So brave! I'll tame you yet, pluck hard villains;
Is ſhe inſenſible? no ſigh nor groan? or is ſhe dead?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: No tyrant, though I ſuffer
More than a woman, beyond fleſh and blood;
'Tis in a cauſe ſo honourable, that I ſcorn
With any ſign that may expreſs a ſorrow
To ſhew I do repent.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Confeſs yet,
And thou ſhalt be ſafe.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis wrapt up in my ſoul,
From whence thou canſt not force it.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I will be
Ten daies a killing thee.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Be twenty thouſand,
My glory lives the longer.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: 'Tis a miracle,
She tires th' executioners,
And me.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Unlooſe her, I am conquer'd, I muſt take
Some other way; reach her my chair, in honor
Of her invincible fortitude.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Will you not
Diſpatch the reſt?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: When I ſeem merciful,
Aſſure thy ſelf Ronvere, I am moſt cruel.
Thou wonder of thy Sex, and of this Nation,
That haſt chang'd my ſeverity to mercy,
Not to thy ſelf alone, but to thy people,
In which I do include theſe men, my enemies:
Unbind them.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: This is ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: For your intent
Againſt my life, which you dare not denie,
I only ask one ſervice.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: Above hope.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: There rides a Pyrate neer, the Duke of Seſſe,
My enemy and this Countreys, that in bonds
Holds my dear friend Aſcanio: free this friend:
Or bring the Pyrats head; beſides your pardon,
And honor of the action, your reward
Is forty thouſand Ducates. And becauſe
I know that Virolet is as bold as wiſe,
Be he your General, as pledge of your faith,
That you will undertake it, let this old man,
And this moſt conſtant Matron ſtay with me:
Of whom, as of my ſelf, I will be careful;
She ſhall direct you where her Husband is.
Make choice of any ſhip you think moſt uſeful.
They are rig'd for you.

div.stage: Exeunt Guard, with Juliana and Pand.

sp.speaker: Briſ.
sp.l: We with joy accept it.

sp.speaker: Cam.
sp.l: And will proclaim King Ferrant merciful.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: The myſterie of this, my Lord? or are you
Chang'd in your nature?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I'll make thee private to it.
The lives of theſe weak men, and deſperate woman,
Would no way have ſecur'd me, had I took them;
'Tis Virolet I aim at; he has power,
And knows to hurt. If they encounter Seſſe,
And he prove conqueror, I am aſſur'd
They'll find no mercy: if that they prove victors,
I ſhall recover, with my friend his head
I moſt deſire of all men.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Now I have it.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I'll make thee underſtand the drift of all.
So we ſtand ſure, thus much for thoſe that fall. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Lay here before the wind; up with your Canvaſe,
And let her work, the wind begins to whiſtle;
Clap all her ſtreamers on, and let her dance,
As if ſhe were the Minion of the Ocean.
Let her beſtride the billows till they roar,
And curle their wanton heads. Ho, below there:
Ho, ho, within.
Lay her North-eaſt, and thruſt her miſſen out,
The day grows fair and clear, and the wind courts us.
Oh for a luſty ſail now, to give chaſe to.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: A ſtubborn Bark, that wou'd but bear up to us,
And change a broadſide bravely.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Where's the Duke?

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: I have not ſeen him ſtir to day.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Oh Gunner,
What bravery dwells in his age, and what valour?
And to his friends, what gentleneſs and bounty?
How long have we been inhabitants at Sea here?

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Some fourteen years.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: By fourteen lives I ſwear then,
This Element never nouriſht ſuch a Pirate;
So great, ſo fearleſs, and ſo fortunate,
So patient in his want, in Act ſo valiant.
How many ſail of well mann'd ſhips before us,
As the Bonuto does the flying Fiſh,
Have we purſued and ſcour'd, that to outſtrip us,
They have been fain to hang their very ſhirts on?
What Gallies have we bang'd, and ſunk, and taken;
Whoſe only fraughts were fire, and ſtern defiance?
And nothing ſpoke but Bullet in all theſe.
How like old Neptune have I ſeen our General
Standing i' th' Poop, and toſſing his Steel Trident,
Commanding both the Sea and Winds to ſerve him?

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: His Daughter too, which is the honor Boatſwain,
Of all her ſex; that Martial Maid.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: A brave wench.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: How oftentimes, a fight being new begun,
Has ſhe leap'd down, and took my Linſtock from me,
And crying, now fly righ, and fir'd all my chaſers?
Then like the Image of the warlike Goddeſs,
Her Target brac'd upon her arm, her ſword drawn,
And anger in her eies leapt up again,
And bravely hall'd the Bark. I have wondred Boatſwain,
That in a body made ſo delicate,
So ſoft for ſweet embraces, ſo much fire,
And manly ſoul, not ſtarting at a danger.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Her noble Father got her in his fury,
And ſo ſhe proves a Soldier.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: This too I wonder at
Taking ſo many ſtrangers as he does,
He uſes them with that reſpect and coolneſs,
Not making prize, but only borrowing
What may ſupply his want: nor that for nothing;
But renders back what they may ſtand in need of,
And then parts lovingly: Where, if he take
His Countreyman, that ſhould be neareſt to him,
And ſtand moſt free from danger, he ſure pays for't:
He drowns or hangs the men, ranſacks the Bark,
Then gives her up a Bonfire to his fortune.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: The wrongs he has receiv'd from that dull Countrey
That's all I know has purchas'd all his cruelty.
We fare the better; cheerly, cheerly boys,
The ſhip runs merrily, my Captain's melancholly,
And nothing cures that in him but a Sea-ſight:
I hope to meet a ſail-boy, and a right one.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: That's my hope too, I am ready for the paſtime.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: I' th' mean time let's beſtow a Song upon him,
To ſhake him from his dumps, and bid good day to him.
Ho, in the hold.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Here, here.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: To th' Main top, Boy.
And thou kenſt a ſhip that dares defie us,
Here's Gold,

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I am gone. Exit Boy.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l:
Come ſirs, a quaint Levet.
Trump. a Levet.
To waken our brave General. Then to our labor.

div.stage: Enter Duke of Seſſe above, and his daughter Martia like an Amazon.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: I thank you loving mates; I thank you all,
There's to prolong your mirth, and good morrow to you.

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: Take this from me, you're honeſt, valiant friends;
And ſuch we muſt make much of. Not a ſail ſtirring?

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Not any within ken yet.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Without doubt Lady
The wind ſtanding ſo fair and full upon us,
We ſhall have ſport anon. But noble General,
Why are you ſtill ſo ſad? you take our edge off;
You make us dull, and ſpiritleſs.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: I'll tell ye,
Becauſe I will provoke you to be fortunate;
For when you know my cauſe, 'twill double arm you.
This woman never knew it yet; my daughter,
Some diſcontents ſhe has.

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: Pray ſir go forward.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Theſe fourteen years, I have ſtored it here at Sea,
Where the moſt curious thought could never find it.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Call up the Maſter, and all the Mates.

div.stage: Enter below the Maſter and Sailers.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Good morrow.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Good morrow to our General, a good one,
And to that Noble Lady all good wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: I thank you Maſter.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Mark me, thus it is then;
Which I did never think to have diſcovered,
Till full revenge had wooed me; but to ſatisfie
My faithful friends, thus I caſt off my burden.
In that ſhort time I was a Courtier,
And followed that moſt hated of all Princes,
Ferrant, the full example of all miſchiefs,
Compell'd to follow to my ſoul a ſtranger,
It was my chance one day to play at Cheſſe
For ſome few Crowns, with a mynion of this Kings,
A mean poor man, that only ſerv'd his pleaſures;
Removing of a Rook, we grew to words;
From this to hotter anger: to be ſhort,
I got a blow.

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: How, how my Noble Father:

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: A blow my girl, which I had ſoon repaid,
And ſunk the ſlave for ever, had not odds
Thruſt in betwixt us. I went away diſgrac'd—

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: For honors ſake not ſo Sir.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: For that time, wench;
But call'd upon him, like a Gentleman,
By many private friends; knockt at his valour,
Courted his honor hourly to repair me;
And though he were a thing my thoughts made ſlight on,
And only worth the fury of my footman,
Still I purſu'd him Nobly.

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: Did he eſcape you?
My old brave father, could you ſit down ſo coldly?

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Have patience, and know all. Purſu'd him fairly,
Till I was laugh'd at, ſcorn'd, my wrongs made Maygames.
By him unjuſtly wrong'd, ſhould be all juſtice,
The ſlave protected; yet at length I found him,
Found him, when he ſuppos'd all had been buried;
And what I had received, durſt not be queſtioned;
And then he fell, under my Sword he fell,
For ever ſunk; his poor life, like the air,
Blown in an empty bubble, burſt, and left him,
No noble wind of memory to raiſe him.
But then began my miſery, I fled;
The Kings frowns following, and my friends deſpair;
No hand that durſt relieve: my Countrey fearful,
Baſely and weakly fearful of a tyrant;
Which made his bad Will worſe, ſtood ſtill and wondred,
Their virtues bedrid in 'em; then my girl,
A little one, I ſnatch'd thee from thy Nurſe,
The modell of thy fathers miſeries:
And ſome ſmall wealth was fit for preſent carriage,
And got to Sea; where I profeſt my anger,
And will do, whilſt that baſe ungrateful Countrey,
And that bad King, have blood or means to quench me.
Now ye know all.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We know all, and admire all;
Go on, and do all ſtill, and ſtill be fortunate.

sp.speaker: Daught.
sp.l: Had you done leſs, or loſt this Noble anger,
You had been worthy then mens empty pities,
And not their wonders. Go on, and uſe your juſtice.
And uſe it ſtill with that fell violence,
It firſt appeared to you; if you go leſs,
Or take a dyating mercy to protection,
The honor of a Father I diſclaim in you,
Call back all duty; and will be prouder of
Th' infamous and baſe name of a whore,
Than daughter to a great Duke and a coward.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Mine own ſweet Martia, no: thou knowſt my nature,
It cannot, muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: I hope it ſhall not.
But why Sir do you keep alive ſtill young Aſcanio,
Prince of Roſſana, King Ferrants moſt belov'd one,
You took two months agoe?
Why is not he flung 'overboard, or hang'd?

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: I'll tell thee girl:
It were a mercy in my nature now,
So ſoon to break the bed of his afflictions;
I am not ſo far reconcil'd yet to him,
To let him die that were a benefit.
Beſides, I keep him as a bait and diet,
To draw on more, and nearer to the King,
I look each hour to hear of his Armados,
And a hot welcome they ſhall have.

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: But hark you?
If you were overſway'd with odds—

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: I find you:
I would not yield; no girl, no hope of yielding,
Nor fling my ſelf one hour into their mercies,
And give the tyrant hope to gain his kingdom.
No, I can ſink wench, and make ſhift to die;
A thouſand doors are open, I ſhall hit one.
I am no niggard of my life ſo it go nobly:
All waies are equal, and all hours; I care not.

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: Now you ſpeak like my father.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Noble General,
If by our means they inherit ought but bangs,
The mercy of the main yard light upon us.
No, we can ſink too, Sir, and ſink low enough,
To poſe their cruelties, to follow us:
And he that thinks of life, if the world go that way,
A thouſand cowards ſuck his bones.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Let the worſt come,
I can unbreech a Cannon, and without much help
Turn her into the Keel; and when ſhe has ſplit it,
Every man knows his way, his own prayers,
And ſo good night I think.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We have liv'd all with you, Boy a top.
And will die with you General.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: I thank you Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Boy above.
sp.l: A Sail, a Sail.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: A cheerful ſound.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A Sail.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Of whence? of whence boy?

sp.speaker: Boy
sp.l: A luſty Sail.

sp.speaker: Daugh.
sp.l: Look right, and look again.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: She plows the Sea before her,
And fomes i'th' mouth.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Of whence?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I ken not yet ſir.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Oh may ſhe prove of Naples.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Prove the Devil,
We'll ſpit out fire as thick as ſhe.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Hoy.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Brave boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Of Naples, Naples, I think of Naples Maſter,
Methinks I ſee the Arms.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Up, up another,
And give more certain ſigns. Exit Sailor.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: All to your buſineſs,
And ſtand but right and true.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Hang him that halts now.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Sh'as us in chaſe.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We'll ſpare her our main top-ſail,
He ſhall not look us long, we are no-ſtarters.
Down with the foreſail too, we'll ſpoom before her.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Gunner, good noble Gunner, for my honor
Load me but theſe two Minions in the chape there;
And load 'em right, that they may bid fair welcome,
And be thine eye, and level as thy heart is.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Madam, I'll ſcratch 'em out, I'll piſs 'em out elſe.

sp.speaker: Sayl, above.
sp.l: Ho.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Of whence now?

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: Of Naples, Naples, Naples.
I ſee her top-Flag, how ſhe quarters Naples.
I hear her Trumpets.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Down, ſhe's welcome to us.
Every man to his charge, mann her i'th' bow well.
And place your Rakers right, Daughter be ſparing.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I ſwear I'll be above Sir, in the thickeſt,
And where moſt danger is, I'll ſeek for honor.
They have begun, hark how their Trumpets call us.
Hark how the wide-mouth'd Cannons ſing amongſt us.
Hark how they ſail; out of our ſhels for ſhame Sir.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Now fortune and my cauſe.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Be bold and conquer. Exit.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: They'll board us once again, they're tuff and valiant.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Twice we have blown 'em into th' air like feathers.
And made 'em dance.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Good boys, fight bravely, manly.
They come on yet, clap in her ſtern, and yoke 'em.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: You ſhould not need, I have proviſion for 'em;
Let 'em board once again, the next is ours.
Stand bravely to your Pikes, away, be valiant.
I have a ſecond courſe of ſervice for 'em,
Shall make the bowels of their Bark ake, boy,
The Duke fights like a Dragon. Who dares be idle? Exit.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Down with 'em, ſtow 'em in

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Cut their throats, 'tis brotherhood to fling 'em into the Sea.
The Duke is hurt, ſo is his lovely Daughter Martia.
We have the day yet.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Pox fire 'em, they have ſmoak'd us, never ſuch plums yet ſlew.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: They have rent the ſhip, and bor'd a hundred holes
She ſwims ſtill luſtily.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: She made a brave fight, and ſhe ſhall be cur'd
And make a braver yet.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Bring us ſome Canns up, I am as hot as fire.

sp.speaker: Boat.
sp.l: I am ſure I am none o'th' cooleſt.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: My Cannons rung like Bels. Here's to my Miſtriſs.
The dainty ſweet braſs Minion: ſplit their Fore-Maſt,
She never fail'd.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Ye did all well, and truly, like faithful honeſt men,

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: But is ſhe rich Maſter? Trumpets flouriſh.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Rich for my Captains purpoſe howſoever,
And we are his. How bravely now he ſhows,
Heated in blood and anger? how do you Sir?
Not wounded mortally I hope?

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: No Maſter, but only wear the livery of fury.
I am hurt, and deep.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: My Miſtriſs too?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: A ſcratch man,
My needle would ha done as much good Sir?
Be provident and careful.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Prethee peace girl,
This wound is not the firſt blood I have bluſht in,
Ye ſought all like tall men, my thanks among ye,
That ſpeaks not what my purſe means, but my tongue, ſoldiers.
