Now Sir, to you that ſought me out, that found me,
That found me what I am, the Tyrant's Tyrant;
You that were imp'd, the weak arm to his folly,
You are welcome to your death.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I do expect it,
And therefore need no compliment, but wait it.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Thou bor'ſt the face once of a Noble Gentleman,
Rankt in the firſt f • le of the virtuous,
By every hopeful ſpirit, ſhewed and pointed,
Thy Countries love; one that advanc'd her honor,
Not tainted with the baſe and ſervile uſes
The Tyrant ties mens ſouls to. Tell me Virolet,
If ſhame have not forſook thee, with thy credit?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: No more of theſe Racks; what I am, I am.
I hope not to go free with poor confeſſions;
Nor if I ſhew ill, will I ſeem a monſter,
By making my mind priſoner; do your worſt.
When I came out to deal with you, I caſt it,
Only thoſe baſe inflictions fit for ſlaves,
Becauſe I am a Gentleman.—

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Thou art none.
Thou waſt while thou ſtoodſt good, th'art now a villain.
And agent for the devil.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: That tongue lies.
Give me my ſword again, and ſtand all arm'd;
I'll prove it on ye all, I am a Gentleman,
A man as fair in honor, rate your priſoners,
How poor and like a Pedagogue it ſhews?
How far from Nobleneſs? 'tis fair, you may kill's;
But to defame your victory with foul language.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Go fling him over-board; I'll teach you ſirrah.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: You cannot teach me to die. I could kill you now
With patience, in deſpiſing all your cruelties.
And make you choke with anger.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Away I ſay.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay Sir, h'as given you ſuch bold language,
I am not reconcil'd to him yet, and therefore
He ſhall not have his wiſh obſerv'd ſo nearly,
To die when he pleaſe; I beſeech you ſtay Sir.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Do with him what thou wilt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Carry him to th' Bilboes,
And clap him faſt there, with the Prince.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Do Lady,
For any death you give, I am bound to bleſs you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now to your Cabin, Sir; pray lean upon me,
And take your reſt, the Surgeons wait all for you.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Thou mak'ſt me bluſh to ſee thee bear thy fortunes;
Why, ſure I have no hurt, I have not fought ſure?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: You bleed apace, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Ye grow cold too.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: I muſt be rul'd, no leaning,
My deepeſt wounds ſcorn Crutches.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: A brave General. Flour. Trumpets, Cornets.

sp.speaker: 1 Sail.
sp.l: Will they not moore her?

sp.speaker: 2 Sail.
sp.l: Not till we come to the Fort,
This is too weak a place for our defences,
The Carpenters are hard at work; ſhe ſwims well,
And may hold out another fight. The ſhip we took
Burns there to give us light.

sp.speaker: 1 Sayl.
sp.l: She made a brave fight.

sp.speaker: 2 Sayl.
sp.l: She put us all in fear.

sp.speaker: 1 Sail.
sp.l: Beſhrew my heart did ſhe.
Her men are gone to Candia, they are pePper'd,
All but this priſoner.

sp.speaker: 2 Sayl.
sp.l: Sure he's a brave fellow.

sp.speaker: 1 Sayl.
sp.l: A ſtubborn knave, but we have pul'd his bravery.
sp.stage: He diſcovers Virolet and Aſcanio in the Bilb • es.
sp.l: Look how he looks now: come let's go ſerve his dyet,
Which is but bread and water.

sp.speaker: 2 Sayl.
sp.l: He'll grow fat on't. Exeunt Sailors.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs I have endur'd much miſery,
Even almoſt to the ruine of my ſpirit,
But ten times more grows my affliction,
To find my friend here.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Had we ſerv'd our Countrey,
Or honeſties, as we have ſerv'd our follies,
We had not been here now?

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: 'Tis too true Virolet.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: And yet my end in vent'ring for your ſafety,
Pointed at more than Ferrant's Will, a baſe one;
Some ſervice for mine own, ſome for my Nation,
Some for my friend; but I am rightly paid,
That durſt adventure ſuch a noble office,
From the moſt treacherous command of miſchief;
You know him now?

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: And when I nearer knew him,
Then when I waited, Heaven be witneſs with me,
(And if I lie my miſeries ſtill load me)
With what tears I have wooed him, with what prayers.
What weight of reaſons I have laid, what dangers;
Then, when the peoples curſes flew like ſtorms;
And every tongue was whetted to defame him,
To leave his doubts, his tyrannies, his ſlaughters,
His fell oppreſſions: I know I was hated too.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: And all mankind that knew him: theſe confeſſions
Do no good to the world, to heaven they may.
Let's ſtudy to die well, we have liv'd like coxcombs.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: That my misfortune, ſhould loſe you too.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Yes;
And not only me, but many more, and better:
For my life, 'tis not this; or might I ſave yours,
And ſome brave friends I have engag'd, let me go;
It were the meritorious death I wiſh for,
But we muſt hang or drown like whelps.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: No remedy.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: On my part I expect none. I know the man,
And know he has been netled to the quick too,
I know his nature.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: A moſt cruel nature.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: His wrongs have bred him up. I cannot blame him.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: He has a daughter too, the greateſt ſcorner,
And moſt inſulter upon miſery.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: For thoſe, they are toys to laugh at, not to lead men:
A womans mirth or anger, like a meteor
Glides and is gone, and leaves no crack behind it;
Our miſeries would ſeem like maſters to us,
And ſhake our manly ſpirits into feavers,
If we reſpected thoſe; the more they glory.
And raiſe inſulting Trophies on our ruines;
The more our virtues ſhine in patience.
Sweet Prince, the name of death was never terrible
To him that knew to live; nor the loud torrent
Of all afflictions, ſinging as they ſwim,
A gall of heart, but to a guilty conſcience:
Whilſt we ſtand fair, though by a two-edg'd ſtorm,
We find untimely falls, like early Roſes;
Bent to the earth, we bear our native ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: Good Sir go on.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: When we are little children,
And cry and fret for every toy comes croſs us;
How ſweetly do we ſhew, when ſleep ſteals on us?
When we grow great, but our affections greater,
And ſtruggle with this ſtubborn twin, born with us;
And tug and pull, yet ſtill we find a Giant:
Had we not then the priviledge to ſleep,
Our everlaſting ſleep? he would make us Idiots;
The memory and monuments of good men
Are more than lives, and though their tombs want tongues,
Yet have they eies that daily ſweat their loſſes;
And ſuch a tear from ſtone, no time can value.
To die both young and good, are natures curſes
As the world ſaies; ask truth, they are bounteous bleſſings:
For then we reach at Heaven, in our full virtues,
And fix our ſelves new Stars, crown'd with our goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: You have double arm'd me. Strange Muſick within, Plohoys.
Hark what noiſe is this?
What horrid noiſe is the Sea pleas'd to ſing.
A hideous Dirge to our deliverance?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Stand faſt now.

div.stage: Within ſtrange cries, horrid noiſe, Trumpets.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I am fixt.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: We fear ye not. Enter Martia.
Let death appear in all ſhapes, we ſmile on him.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: The Lady now.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: The face o' th' Mask is alter'd.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: What will ſhe do?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Do what ſhe can, I care not.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: She looks on you Sir.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Rather ſhe looks through me,
But yet ſhe ſtirs me not.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Poor wretched ſlaves,
Why do you live? or if ye hope for mercy,
Why do not you houl out, and fill the hold
With lamentations, cries, and baſe ſubmiſſions,
Worthy our ſcorn?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Madam, you are miſtaken;
We are no ſlaves to you, but to blind fortune;
And if ſhe had her eyes; and durſt be certain,
Certain our friend, I would not bow unto her;
I would not cry, nor ask ſo baſe a mercy:
If you ſee any thing in our appearance,
Worthy your ſexes ſoftneſs and your own glory:
Do it for that, and let that good reward it:
We cannot beg.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I'll make you beg, and bow too.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Madam for what?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: For life; and when you hope it,
Then will I laugh and triumph on your baſeneſs.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Madam, 'tis true, there may be ſuch a favour
And we may ask it too; ask it with honor;
And thank you for that favour, nobly thank you,
Though it be death; but when we beg a baſe life,
And beg it of your ſcorn—

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Y'are couzen'd woman,
Your handſomneſs may do much, but not this way;
But for your glorious hate—

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Are ye ſo ſtubborn?
Death, I will make you bow.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: It muſt be in your bed then;
There you may work me to humility.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Why, I can kill thee.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: If you do it handſomely;
• t may be I can thank you, elſe—

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: So glorious?

sp.speaker: Aſſca.
sp.l: Her cruelty now works.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Yet woot thou?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Wilt thou for life ſake?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: No, I know your ſubtilty.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: For honor ſake?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I will not be a Pageant,
My mind was ever firm, and ſo I'll loſe it.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I'll ſtarve thee to it.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I'll ſtarve my ſelf, and croſs it.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I'll lay thee on ſuch miſeries —

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I'll wear 'em,
And with that wantonneſs, you do your Bracelets.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I'll be a month a killing thee.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Poor Lady,
I'll be a month a dying then: what's that?
There's many a Calenture out-does your cruelty.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: How might I do in killing of his body,
To ſave his Noble mind? Who waits there?

div.stage: Enter a Sailor, with a rich Cap and Mantle.

sp.speaker: Sayl.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Unbolt this man, and leave thoſe things behind you:
And ſo away, now put 'em on. Exit Sailer

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: To what end?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: To my End, to my Will.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I thank you.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Nay, now you thank me, I'll do more. I'll tell ye,
I am a ſervant to your courteſie.
And ſo far will be woo'd: but if this triumph
Be only aim'd to make your miſchief glorious;
Lady, y'ave put a richer ſhroud upon me,
Which my ſtrong mind ſhall ſuffer in.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Come hither,
And all thy bravery put into thy carriage,
For I will admire thee.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Whither will this woman?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Take heed my friend.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Look as thou ſcorn'dſt my cruelty:
I know thou doſt.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I never fear'd nor flatter'd.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: No if thou hadſt, thou hadſt died, and I had gloried.
I ſuffer now, and thou which art my priſoner,
Haſt nobly won the free power to deſpiſe me.
I love thee, and admire thee for thy Nobleneſs;
And, for thy manly ſufferance, am thy ſervant.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Good Lady, mock me not.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: By heaven I love thee;
And by the ſoul of love, am one piece with thee.
Thy mind, thy mind; thy brave, thy manly mind:
That like a Rock, ſtands all the ſtorms of fortune,
And beats 'em roaring back they cannot reach thee:
That lovely mind I dote on, not the body;
That mind has rob'd me of my liberty:
That mind has darken'd all my bravery,
And into poor deſpis'd things, turn'd my angers.
Receive me to your love Sir, and inſtruct me;
Receive me to your bed, and marry me;
I'll wait upon you, bleſs the hour I knew you.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Is this a new way?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: If you doubt my faith.
Firſt take your liberty; I'll make it perfect,
Or any thing within my power.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I love you;
But how to recompence your love with marriage?
Alas, I have a wife.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Dearer than I am?
That will adventure ſo much for your ſafety?
Forget her father's wrongs, quit her own honor,
Pull on her, for a ſtrangers ſake, all curſes?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Shall this Prince have his freedom too?
Elſe all I love is gone, all my friends periſh.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: He ſhall.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: What ſhall I do?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: If thou deſpiſe my courteſie,
When I am dead, for grief I am forſaken,
And no ſoft hand left to aſſwage your ſorrows;
Too late, but too true, curſe your own cruelties.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: Be wiſe; if ſhe be true, no thred is left elſe,
To guide us from this labyrinth of miſchief;
Nor no way for our friends.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Thus then I take you:
I bind ye to my life, my love.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I take you,
And with the like bond tye my heart your ſervant;
W' are now almoſt at Harbor, within this hour,
In the dead watch, I'll have the Long-boat ready;
And when I give the word, be ſure you enter,
I'll ſee ye furniſht both immediately,
And like your ſelf ſome truſty man ſhall wait you,
The watch I'll make mine own; only my love
Requires a ſtronger vow, which I'll adminiſter
Before we go.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I'll take it to confirm you.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Goe, in there are the keys, unlock his fetters,
And arm ye Nobly both; I'll be with you preſently;
And ſo this loving kiſs.

sp.speaker: Aſcan.
sp.l: Be conſtant Lady. Exeunt omnes.

div.stage: Enter the Duke of Seſſe by Torch-light, Maſter and Surgeon with him.

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: You grow ſo angry Sir, your wound goes backward.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: I am angry at the time, at none of you,
That ſends but one poor ſubject for revenge;
I would have all the Court, and all the villanie,
Was ever practis'd under that foul Ferrant
Tyrant, and all to quench my wrath.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Be patient,
Your grace may find occaſion every hour,
For certain they will ſeek you to ſatisfie,
And to the full, your anger.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: 'Death, they dare not:
They know that I command death, feed his hunger,
And when I let him looſe—

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: You'll never heal Sir,
If theſe extreams dwell in you, you are old,
And burn your ſpirits out with this wild anger.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Thou lieſt, I am not old, I am as luſty
And full of manly heat as them, or thou art.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: No more of that.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: And dare ſeek out a danger;
And hold him at the ſwords point, when thou trembleſt
And creepeſt into thy box of ſalves to ſave thee.
Oh Maſter, I have had a dreadful dream to night!
Me-thought the ſhip was all on fire, and my lov'd Daughter
To ſave her life, leapt into the Sea; where ſuddainly
A ſtranger ſnatcht her up, and ſwam away with her.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: 'Twas but the heat o' th' ſight Sir.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Look out, what's that?

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: The Long-boat as I live.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Ho, there i'th' Long-Boat.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: What noiſe is that? Hoy.
I hear Sir,— Exit Maſter.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: The devil or his dam; hail her agen boys.

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: The Long-boat, ho, the Long-boat.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Why, the Long-boat.
Where is the Long-boat?

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: She is ſtolen off.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Who ſtole her?
Oh my prophetique ſoul!

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Your Daughters gone Sir?
The priſoners and ſix Sailors, Rogues.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Miſchief, ſix thouſand plagues ſail with 'em;
They'r in her yet, make out.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We have ne'r a Boat.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Who knew of this trick?

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Weigh Anchors and away.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: We ha no wind Sir,
They'll beat us with their Oars.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Then ſink 'em Gunner,
Oh ſink 'em, ſink 'em, ſink 'em, claw 'em Gunner;
As ever thou haſt lov'd me.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: I'll do reaſon,
But I'll be hang'd before I'll hurt the Lady. Exit Gun.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Who knew of this? Trump. a piece or two go off.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We ſtand all clear.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: What Devil
Put this baſe trick into her tail? my Daughter,
And run away with rogues! I hope ſhe's ſunk, A piece or two.
Or torn to pieces with the ſhot, rots find her,
The leproſie of whore ſtick ever to her,
Oh ſhe has ruin'd my revenge.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: She is gone, Sir.
I cannot reach her with my ſhot.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Riſe winds,
Blow till ye burſt the Air, and ſwell the Seas,
That they may ſink the Stars, Oh dance her, dance her;
Shee's impudently wanton, dance her, dance her,
Mount her upon your ſurges, cool her, cool her;
She runs hot like a whore, cool her, cool her
Oh now a ſhot to ſink her, cut Cables,
I will away, and where ſhe ſets her foot
Although it be in Ferrants Court, I'll follow her,
And ſuch a Fathers vengeance ſhall ſhe ſuffer—
Dare any man ſtand by me?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: All, all.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: All Sir.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: And the ſame cup you taſte.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Cut Cables then;
For I ſhall never ſleep nor know what peace is,
Till I have pluckt her heart out;

sp.speaker: All within.
sp.l: Oh main there. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Ferrant. Ronvere, Caſtruccio, Villio, and Guard.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: You are too gentle, Sir. Flouriſh Cornets

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: You are too careleſs:
The creatures I have made, no way regard me:
Why ſhould I give you names, titles of honor,
Rob families to fill your private houſes.
For your advancement, draw all curſes on me,
Wake tedious winter nights, to make them happy
That for me break no ſlumber?

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: What we can,
We dare do.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Why is your Soverigns life then
(In which you live, and in whoſe fall your honors,
Your wealth, your pomp, your pride, and all muſt ſuffer)
No better guarded? Oh my cruel Stars,
That mark me out a King, raiſing me on
This pinnacle of greatneſs, only to be
The nearer blaſting!

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: What think you now Caſtruccio?
Is not this a merry life?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Still thou art couzen'd;
It is a glorious royal diſcontentment;
How bravely it becomes him!

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: To be made
The common Butt, for every ſlave to ſhoot at;
No peace, no reſt I take, but their alarms
Beat at my heart: why do I live, or ſeek then,
To add a day more to theſe glorious troubles?
Or to what end when all I can arrive at,
Is but the ſumming up of fears and ſorrows;
What power has my command, when from my boſom
Aſcanio, my moſt dear, and lov'd Aſcanio,
Was ſnatch'd, ſpite of my Will, ſpite of my Succor,
And by mine own proud ſlave, retein'd moſt miſerable?
And ſtill that villain lives to nip my pleaſures,
It being not within my power to reach him.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.l: Time may reſtore all this; and would you hear
Whoſe counſel never fail'd you.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Tell me no more,
I faint beneath the burthen of my cares;
And yield my ſelf moſt wretched.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: On my knees
I beg it, mighty Sir, vouchſafe me hearing.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Speak, ſpeak, and I thus low, ſuch is my fortune,
Will hear what thou canſt ſay.

sp.speaker: Vil,
sp.l: Look but on this,
Has not a man that has but means to keep
A Hawk, a Greyhound, and a Hunting Nag,
More pleaſure than this King?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: A dull fool ſtill,
Make me a King, and let me ſcratch with care,
And ſee who'll have the better; give me rule
Command, obedience, pleaſure of a King,
And let the Devil roar? The greateſt corroſive
A King can have, is of more precious tickling,
And handled to the height, more dear delight,
Than other mens whole lives, let 'em be ſafe too.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Think of the mutinous people.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Hang the people,
Give me the pleaſure, let me do all, awe all,
Enjoy their Wives and States at my diſcretion,
And peg 'em when I pleaſe, let the ſlaves mumble. E •• t.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: But ſay they ſhould be vex'd, and riſe againſt thee?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Let 'em riſe, let 'em riſe: give me the bridle here,
And ſee if they can crack my girtlis: ah Villio,
Under the Sun there's nothing ſo voluptuous
As riding of this Monſter, till he founder.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Who's that ſo loud?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: I am dumb: is not this rare?
Kings looks make Pythagoreans; is not this
A happineſs Villio?

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Yes, to put to ſilence
A fawning ſycophant.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Thou ſpeak'ſt truth in all,
And mercy is a vice, when there needs rigor,
Which I, with all ſeverity, will practice;
And ſince, as ſubjects they pay not obedience,
They ſhall be forc'd as ſlaves: I will remove
Their means to hurt, and with the means, my fears;
Goe you the fatal executioners
Of my commands, and in our name proclaim,
That from this hour I do forbid all meetings,
All private conferences in the City:
To feaſt a neighbor ſhall be death: to talk,
As they meet in the ſtreets, to hold diſcourſe,
By writing, nay by ſigns; ſee this perform'd,
And I will call your cruelty, to thoſe
That dare repine at this, to me true ſervice.

sp.speaker: 1 Gard.
sp.l: This makes for us.

sp.speaker: 2 Gard.
sp.l: I, now we have employments,
If we grow not rich, 'twere fit we ſhould be beggars.

l.hi: Ronvere.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Thou enemy to Majeſty?
What think'ſt thou of a kingdom?

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: As of a man
That hath power to do ill.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Or a thing rather
That does divide an Empire with the gods;
Obſerve but with how little breath he ſhakes
A populous City, which would ſtand unmov'd
Againſt a whirlwind.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Then you make him more
Than him that rules the winds.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: For me I do profeſs it,
Were I offer'd to be any thing on earth
I would be mighty Ferrant.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: who names me?
Deliver thy thoughts ſlave, thy thoughts, and truly
Or be no more.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: They rather will deſerve.
Your favour than your fury; I admire,
(As who does not, that is a loyal ſubject?)
Your wiſdom, power, your perfect happineſs,
The moſt bleſt of mankind.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Didſt thou but feel.
The weighty ſorrows that fit on a Crown,
Though thou ſhouldſt find one in the ſtreets Caſtruccio.
Thou wouldſt not think it worth the taking up;
But ſince thou art enamour'd of my fortune,
Thou ſhalt e'r long taſte of it.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: But one day,
And then let me expire.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Goe to my Wardrobe,
And of the richeſt things I wear, cull out,
What thou thinkſt fit: do you attend him ſirrah;

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: I warrant you I ſhall be at his elbow,
The fool will never leave him. Exit Caſt. Villio.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Made for ever. A ſhout within.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: What ſhout is that, draw up our Guards.

div.stage: Enter Virolet, Aſcanio, and a Servant.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Thoſe rather
Speak joy than danger.
Bring her to my houſe,
I would not have her ſeen here.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: My Aſcanio!
The moſt deſir'd of all men, let me die
In theſe embraces; how wert thou redeem'd?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: Sir, this is my preſerver.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: At more leiſure,
I will enquire the manner, and the means,
I cannot ſpare ſo much time now from my
More ſtrickt embraces: Virolet, welcome too,
This ſervice weighs down your intended Treaſon;
You long have been mine enemy, learn now
To be my friend and loyal, I ask no more,
And live as free as Ferrant; let him have
The forty thouſand crowns I gladly promis'd,
For my Aſcanio's freedom, and deliver
His Father, and his wife to him in ſafety,
Something hath paſſed which I am ſorry for,
But 'twill not now be help'd; come my Aſcanio,
And reap the harveſt of my winter travels. Flouriſh Cornets.
My beſt Aſcanio, my lov'd Aſcanio.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: My Lord, all former paſſages forgot, Exit Fer. Aſcanio.
I am become a ſuitor.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: To me Virolet?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: To you. yet will not beg the courteſie,
But largely pay you for it.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: To the purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: The forty thouſand crowns the King hath given me,
I will beſtow on you, if by your means
I may have liberty for a divorce
Between me and my wife.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Your Juliano?
That for you hath indur'd ſo much, ſo nobly?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: The more my ſorrow; but it muſt be ſo.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: I will not hinder it: without a bribe,
For mine own ends, I would have further'd this.
I will uſe all my power.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: 'Tis all I aske:
Oh my curs'd fate, that ever man ſhould hate
Himſelf for being belov'd, or be compell'd
To caſt away a Jewel, Kings would buy,
Though with the loſs of Crown and Monarchy! Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Seſſe.
sp.l: How do I look?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: You are ſo ſtrangely alter'd.
We ſcarce can know you, ſo young again, and utterly
From that you were, figure, or any favour;
Your friends cannot diſcern you.

sp.speaker: Seſſe.
sp.l: I have none,
None but my fair revenge, and let that know me!
You are finely alter'd too.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: To pleaſe your humour,
But we may paſs without diſguiſe. our living
Was never in their element.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: This Jew ſure,
That alter'd you; is a mad knave:

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Oh! a moſt excellent fellow.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: How he has mew'd your head, has rub'd the ſnow off.
And run your beard into a peak of twenty.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Stopt all the crannies in your face,

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Moſt rarely.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: And now you look as plump, your eies as ſparkling,
As if you were to leap into a Ladies ſaddle.
Has he not ſet your noſe awry?

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: The better.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: I think it be the better, but 'tis awry ſure;
North and by Eaſt, I, there's the point it ſtands in;
Now halfe a point to the Southward.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: I could laugh;
But that my buſineſs requires no mirth now;
Thou art a merry fellow,

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: I would the Jew Sir,
Could ſteer my head right, for I have ſuch a ſwimming in't,
Ever ſince I went to Sea firſt.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Take Wine and purge it.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: I have had a thouſand pils of Sack, a thouſand;
A thouſand pottle Pills.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Take more.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Good Doctor,
Your patient is eaſily perſwaded.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: The next fair open weather
Methinks this Jew
If he were truly known to founder'd Courtiers,
And decay'd Ladies that have loſt their fleeces
On every buſh, he might pick a pretty living.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: The beſt of all our gallants, ſhould be glad of him;
For if you mark their marches, they are tender,
Soft, ſoft and tender, then but obſerve their bodies,
And you ſhall find 'em cemented by a Surgeon,
Or ſome Phyſitian for a year or two,
And then to th' tub again, for a new pickle.
This Jew might live a Gentile here. Ent. 2 Cittizens at both doors, ſaluting afar off.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: What are theſe?
Stand c • oſe and mark?

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Theſe are no men, th'are motions.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: What ſad and ruthful faces!

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: How they duck!
This ſenceleſs, ſilent courteſie methinks,
Shews like two Turks, ſaluting one another,
Upon two French Porters backs.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: They are my Countrey-men,
And this, ſome forc'd infliction from the tyrant;
What are you, why is this? why move thus ſilent
As if you were wandring ſhadows? why ſo ſad?
Your tongues ſeal'd up; are ye of ſeveral Countries?
You underſtand not one another?

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: That's an Engliſhman,
He looks as though he had loſt his dog.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Your habits
Shew ye all Neopolitanes; and your faces
Deliver you oppreſſed things; ſpeak boldly:
Do you groan and labor under this ſtiff yoak?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: They ſhake their heads and weep.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Oh miſery!
Give plenteous ſorrow, and no tongues to ſhew 'em!
This is a ſtudied cruelty.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.l: Begone Sir,
t ſeems you are a ſtranger, and ſave your ſelf;

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: You wonder here at us; as much we wonder
To hear you ſpeak ſo openly, and boldly,
The Kings command being publiſht to the contrary;
'Tis death here, above two, to talk together;
And that muſt be but common ſalutation neither,
Short, and ſo part.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: How ſhould a man buy muſtard,
If he be forc'd to ſtay the making of it?

sp.speaker: Within 1.
sp.l: Clear all the ſtreets before the King:

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.l: Get off Sir,
And ſhift as we muſt do. Exeunt Citizens.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: I'll ſee his glory.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Stand faſt now and like men. Flouriſh Colours.

div.stage: Enter Caſtruccio like the King, in the midſt of a Guard. Villio.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Begin the game, Sir,
And pluck me down the Row
Of houſes there.
They hide the view o' th' hill; and ſink thoſe Merchants,
Their ſhips are foul and ſtink.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: This is a ſweet youth.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: All that are taken in aſſemblies,
Their houſes and their wives, their wealths are forfeit,
Their lives at your devotion. Villains, Knaves,
I'll make you bow and ſhake, I'll make you kneel Rogues.
How brave 'tis to b a King?

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Here's fine tumbling,

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: No man ſhall ſit i' th' temple near another

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Nor lie with his own wife.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: All upon pain
Of preſent death, forget to write.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: That's excellent,
Carriers and Footpoſts, will be arrant rebels.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: No character, or ſtamp; that may deliver
This mans intention, to that man i' th' Countrey.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Nay, an you cut off, after my hearty commendatinos.
Your friend and Oliver. No more.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: No man ſmile,
And wear face of mirth; that fellows cunning,
And hides a double heart, he's your prize, ſmoke him.

div.stage: Enter Virolet, Ronvero, Aſcanio, and Martia paſſing over.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: What baſe abuſe is this? Ha? 'tis her face ſure,
My priſoners with her too? by heaven wild whore
Now is my time.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Do what you will.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Stay hold yet,
My Countrey ſhall be ſerv'd firſt, let her go,
We'll have an hour for her to make her tremble.
Now ſhew our ſelves, and bleſs you with your valours.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Here's a whole plump of Rogues. Virolet and they off again.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Now for your Countrey.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Away with 'em and hang 'em; ſhew no mercy,
I ſay no mercy.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Be it ſo upon 'em.

sp.speaker: Guard,
sp.l: Treaſon, treaſon, treaſon.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Cut the ſlaevs to giggets.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Down with the Bul-beefs.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Hold, hold, I command you,—look here.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: A miſerable thing, I am no King Sir.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Sirrah your fools-face has preſerv'd your life.
Wear no more Kings coats, you have ſcap'd a ſcouring.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: I'ſt not the King.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: No, 'tis a prating Raſcal,
The puppy makes him mirth.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Yes Sir I am a puppy.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: I beſeech you let me hang him,
I'll do't in my Belt ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: As you are honourable,
It is enough you may hang me.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: I'll hang a ſquib at's tail
That ſhall blow both his buttocks; like a petard

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Do any thing.
But do not kill me Gentlemen. Enter Citizen.

sp.speaker: Boateſ.
sp.l: Let's flea him, and have him flye blown.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Away, and ſave your lives.
The King himſelf is coming on; if you ſtay,
You are loſt for ever; let not ſo much nobleneſs
Wilfully periſh.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: How near?

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.l: He's here behind you. Ex. Seſſ. Boatſw. Saylers, Citizens.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: We thank you. vaniſh.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Double the Guards and take in men that dare,
Theſe ſlaves are frighted; where are the proud Rebels?
To what protection fled? what villain leads 'em?
Under our noſe diſtur'd our reſt?

sp.speaker: Ronver.
sp.l: We ſhall hear,
For ſuch a ſearch I have ſent, to hunt the Traytors.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Yet better men I ſay, we ſtand too open:
How now Caſtruchio? how do you like our glory?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs, 'twas ſomewhat more than my match Sir;
This open glory agrees not with my body,
But if it were ith' Caſtle, or ſome ſtrength,
Where I might have my ſwinge.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: You have been ſwing'd brother;
How theſe delights have tickled you? you itch yet?
Will you walk out again in pomp?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Good Fool.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Theſe rogues muſt be rebuked, they are too ſawcy,
Theſe peremptory Knaves Will you walk out Sir,
And take the remnant of your Coronation?
The people ſtay to ſee it.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Do not vex him,
H'as grief enough in's bones; you ſhall to the Citadel,
And like my ſelf command, there uſe your pleaſure,
But take heed to your perſon.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: The more danger,
Still the more honor Brother.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: If I reign not then,
And like a King, and thou ſhalt know it fool,
And thou ſhalt feel it fool.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Fools ſtill are freemen,
I'll ſue for a protection, till thy reign's out.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: The people have abus'd the liberty
I late allow'd, I now proclaim it ſtraighter,
No men ſhall walk together nor ſalute;
For they that do ſhall dye.

sp.speaker: Ronver.
sp.l: You hit the right Sir;
That liberty cut off, you are free from practiſe.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Renew my guards.

sp.speaker: Ronver.
sp.l: I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: And keep ſtrict watches;
One hour of joy I ask.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: You ſhall have many. Exeunt Flor. Cor. Pandulfo and Juliana, led by two of the guard, as not yet fully recovered.

sp.speaker: 1. Guard.
sp.l: You are now at liberty, in your own houſe Lady,
And here our charge takes end.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: 'Tis now a Cuſtom.
We muſt even wooe thoſe men deſerve worſt of us,
And ſo we thank your labors; there's to drink,
For that, and miſchief are your occupations;
And to mean well to no man, your chief'ſt harveſts.

sp.speaker: 2. Gard.
sp.l: You give liberally; we hope Sir, er't be long,
To be oftner acquainted with your bounty,
And ſo we leave you.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Do, for I dote not on ye;

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: But where's my Husband? what ſhould I do here?
Or what ſhare have I in this joy, call'd liberty,
Without his company? Why did you flatter me,
And tell me he was return'd, his ſervice honor'd?

sp.speaker: 1 Gard.
sp.l: He is ſo, and ſtands high in the Kings favor,
His friends redeemed, and his own liberty,
From which yours is deriv'd, confirm'd; his ſervice,
To his own wiſh, rewarded: ſo fare-well Lady. Ex. Guard.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Go perſecute the good, and hunt ye hell-hounds,
Ye Leeches of the time, ſuck till ye burſt ſlaves;
How does my girl?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Weak yet, but full of comfort;

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Sit down, and take ſome reſt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: My heart's whole Father;
That joys, and leaps, to hear my Virolet,
My Dear, my life, has conquer'd his afflictions.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Thoſe rude hands, and that bloody will that did this,
That durſt upon thy tender body print
Theſe Characters of cruelty; hear me heaven.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: O Sir be ſparing.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: I'll ſpeak it, tho I burſt;
And tho the ayr had ears, and ſerv'd the Tyrant,
Out it ſhould go: O here me thou great Juſtice;
The miſeries that wait upon their miſchiefs,
Let them be numberleſs, and no eye pitty
Them when their ſouls are loaden, and in labour,
And wounded through, and through, with guilt and horror;
As mine is now with grief; let men laugh at 'em
Then, when their monſtrous ſins, like earth-quakes, ſhake 'em,
And thoſe eyes, that forgot heaven would look upward,
The bloody 'larms, of the conſcience beating,
Let mercy flye, and day ſtrook into darkneſs,
Leave their blind ſouls, to hunt out their own horrors.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Enough, enough, we muſt forget dear Father;
For then we are glorious formes of heaven; and live,
When we can ſuffer, and as ſoon forgive.
But where's my Lord? methinks I have ſeen this houſe,
And have been in't before.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Thine own houſe jewel.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Mine, without him? or his, without my company?
I think it cannot be: it was not wont Father.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Some buſineſs with the King, (let it be good, heaven)
Reteins him ſure. Enter Boy.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: It muſt be good and noble,
For all men that he treats with taſt of virtue;
His words and actions are his own; and Honour's
Not brought, nor compell'd from him.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Here's the Boy.
He can confirm us more, how ſad the child looks?
Come hither Lucio; how, and where's thy Maſter?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Speak gentle Boy.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Is he return'd in ſafety?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: If not, and that thou knowſt is miſerable,
Our hopes and happineſs declin'd for ever;
Study a ſorrow excellent as thy Maſter,
Then if thou canſt live leave us.

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.l: Noble Madam,
My Lord is ſafe return'd, ſafe to his friends, and fortune,
Safe to his Countrey, entertain'd with honour,
Is here within the houſe.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Do not mock me.

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.l: But ſuch a melancholly hangs on his mind,
And in his eyes inhabit ſuch ſad ſhadowes;
But what the cauſe is—

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Go tell him we are here Boy,
There muſt be no cauſe now.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Haſt thou forgot me?

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.l: No nobleſt Lady.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Tell him I am here,
Tell him his wife is here, ſound my name to him,
And thou ſhalt ſee him ſtart; ſpeak Juliana,
And like the Sun that labors through a tempeſt,
How ſuddainly he will diſperſe his ſadneſs?

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Go I command thee inſtantly,
And charge him on his duty.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: On his love Boy:
I would fain go to him.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Away, away, you are fooliſh.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Bear all my ſervice ſweet Boy.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Art thou here ſtill?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And tell him what thou wilt that ſhall become thee.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Ith' houſe, and know we are here. Ex. Boy.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: No, no, he did not;
I warrant you he did not: could you think
His love had leſs than wings, had he but ſeen me;
His ſtrong affection any thing but ſire
Conſuming all weak lets and rubs before it,
Till he had met my flame, and made one body?
If ever heavens high bleſſings met in one man,
And there erected to their holy uſes
A ſacred mind fit for their ſervices,
Built all of poliſht honor, 'twas in this man:
Miſdoubt him not.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: I know he's truely noble;
But why this ſadneſs, when the general cauſe
Requires a Jubile of joy?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I know not. Enter Virolet and Boy.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Pray heaven you find it not.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I hope I ſhall not:
O here he comes, and with him all my happineſs;
He ſtays and thinks, we may be too unmannerly;
Pray give him leave. they ſtand off.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: I do not like this ſadneſs.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: O hard condition of my miſery!
Unheard of plagues! when to behold that woman,
That chaſt and virtuous woman, that preſerv'd me,
That pious wife, wedded to my afflictions,
Muſt be more terrible than all my dangers.
O fortune, thou haſt rob'd me of my making,
The noble building of a man, demoliſht,
And flung me headlong, on a ſin ſo baſe
Man and mankind contemn; even beaſts abhor it,
A ſin more dull than drink, a ſhame beyond it;
So foul, and far from faith; I dare not name it,
But it will cry it ſelf out, loud ingratitude.
Your bleſſing Sir.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: You have it in abundance;
So is our joy, to ſee you ſafe.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: My Dear one;

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: H'as not forgot me yet: O take me to you Sir.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Muſt this be added to increaſe my miſery,
That ſhe muſt weep for joy, and looſe that goodneſs?
My Juliana, even the beſt of women,
Of wives the perfecteſt, let me ſpeak this,
And with a modeſty declare thy vertues,
Chaſter than Chryſtal, on the Scythian Clifts
The more the proud winds Court, the more the purer.
Sweeter in thy obedience than a Sacrifice;
And in thy mind a Saint, that even yet living,
Produceſt miracles, and women daily,
With crooked and lame ſouls creep to thy goodneſs,
Which having toucht at, they become examples.
The fortitude of all their ſex, is Fable
Compar'd to thine, and they that fill'd up glory,
And admiration, in the age behind us,
Out of their celebrated urns, are ſtarted,
To ſtare upon the greatneſs of thy ſpirit;
Wondring what new Martyr heaven has begot,
To fill the times with truth, and eaſe their ſtories:
Being all theſe, and excellent in beauty,
(For noble things dwell in the nobleſt buildings)
Thou haſt undone thy husband, made him wretched,
A miſerable man, my Juliana,
Thou haſt made thy Virolet.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Now goodneſs keep me;
Oh! my dear Lord.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: She wrong you? what's the meaning?
Weep not, but ſpeak, I charge you on obedience;
Your Father charges you, ſhe make you miſerable?
That you your ſelf confeſs.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I do, that kils me;
And far leſs I have ſpoke her than her merit.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: It is ſome ſin of weakneſs, or of Ignorance?
For ſure my Will—

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: No, 'tis a ſin of excellence:
Forgive me heaven, that I prophane thy bleſſings:
Sit ſtill; I'll ſhew you all. Exit Virolet.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: What means this madneſs?
For ſure there is no taſt of right man in it;
Grieves he our liberty, our preſervation?
Or has the greatneſs of the deed he has done,
Made him forget, for whom, and how he did it,
And looking down upon us, ſcorn the benefit?
Well Virolet, if thou beeſt proud, or treacherous.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: He cannot Sir, he cannot; he will ſhew us,
And with that reaſon ground his words.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: He comes.
What Maſque is this? what admirable beauty?
Pray heaven his heart be true.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: A goodly woman.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Tell me my dear; and tell me without flattery,
As you are nobly honeſt, ſpeak the truth;
What think you of this Lady?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: She is moſt excellent.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Might not this beauty tell me it's a ſweet one,
Without more ſetting off, as now it is,
Thanking no greater Miſtreſs than meer nature,
Stagger a conſtant heart?

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: She is full of wonder I
But yet; yet Virolet.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Pray by your leave Sir!

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: She would amaze:

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: O! would ſhe ſo? I thank you;
Say to this beauty, ſhe have all additions,
Wealth, noble birth.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: O hold there.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: All virtues,
A mind as full of candor as the truth is,
I, and a loving Lady.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: She muſt needs
(I am bound in conſcience to confeſs) deſerve much.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Nay, ſay beyond all theſe, ſhe be ſo pious,
That even on ſlaves condemn'd ſhe ſhowre her benefits,
And melt their ſtubborn Bolts with her ſoft pitty,
What think you then?

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: For ſuch a noble office,
At theſe years, I ſhould dote my ſelf; take heed boy,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: If you be he, that have receiv'd theſe bleſſings,
And this the Lady: love her, honor her;
You cannot do too much, to ſhew your gratitude,
Your greateſt ſervice will ſhew off too ſlender.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: This is the Lady; Lady of that bounty,
That wealth, that noble name, that all I ſpoke of:
The Prince Aſcanio and my ſelf, the ſlaves
Redeem'd, brought home, ſtill guarded by her goodneſs,
And of our liberties you taſt the ſweetneſs;
Even you ſhe has preſerv'd too, lengthen'd your lives.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And what reward do you purpoſe? it muſt be a main one,
If love will do it we'll all, ſo love her, ſerve her.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: It muſt be my love.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Ha!

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Mine, my only love,
My everlaſting love:

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Pray have patience.
The recompence ſhe ask'd, and I have render'd,
Was to become her husband: then I vowed it,
And ſince I have made it good.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Thou durſt not.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Done Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Be what you pleaſe, his happineſs yet ſtays with me,
You have been mine; oh my unhappy fortune.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Nay, break and dye;

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: It cannot yet: I muſt live,
Till I ſee this man, bleſt in his new love,
And then:

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: What haſt thou done? thou baſe one tell me,
Thou barren thing of honeſty, and honor;
What haſt thou wrought? Is not this ſhe, look on her,
Look on her, with the eyes of gratitude,
And wipe thy falſe tears off; Is not this ſhe,
That three times on the Rack, to guard thy ſafety,
When thou ſtood'ſt loſt, and naked to the Tyrant;
Thy aged Father here, that ſhames to know thee,
Ingag'd ith' jaws of danger; was not this ſhe,
That then gave up her body to the torture?
That tender body, that the wind ſings through;
And three times, when her ſinews, crack'd and tortur'd,
The beauties of her body turn'd to ruines;
Even then, within her patient heart, ſhe lock'd thee;
Then hid thee from the Tyrant, then preſerv'd thee,
And canſt thou be that ſlave?

sp.speaker: Martia.
sp.l: This was but duty,
She did it for her Husband, and ſhe ought it;
She has had the pleaſure of him, many an hour,
And if one minutes pain cannot be ſuffer'd;
Mine was above all theſe, a nobler venter,
I ſpeak it boldly, for I loſt a Father.
He has one ſtill, I left my friends, he has many;
Expos'd my life, and honor to a cruelty,
That if it had ſeiz'd on me, racks and tortures,
Alas, they are Triumphs to it: and had it hit,
For this mans love, it ſhould have ſhewed a triumph,
Twiſe loſt, I freed him; Roſſana loſt before him,
His fortunes with him; and his friends behind him:
Twiſe was I rack'd my ſelf for his deliverance,
In honor firſt and name, which was a torture
The hang-man never heard of; next at Sea,
In our eſcape, where the proud waves took pleaſure
To toſs my little Boat up like a bubble,
Then like a meteor in the ayr he hung,
Then catch'd and flung him in the depth of darkneſs;
The Cannon from my incenſed Fathers Ship,
Ringing our Knell, and ſtill as we peep'd upward,
Beating the raging ſurge, with fire and Bullet,
And I ſtood fixt for this mans ſake, and ſcorn'd it;
Compare but this:

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: 'Tis too true; O my fortune!
That I muſt equally be bound to either:

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: You have the better and the nobler Lady,
And now I am forc'd, a lover of her goodneſs.
And ſo far have you wrought for his deliverance,
That is my Lord, ſo lovingly and nobly,
That now methinks I ſtagger in my Title.
But how with honeſty? for I am a poor Lady,
In all my dutious ſervice but your ſhadow,
Yet would be juſt; how with fair fame and credit,
I may go off; I would not be a ſtrumpet:
O my dear Sir, you know:

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: O truth, thou knoweſt too.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Nor have the world ſuſpect, I fell to miſchief.

sp.speaker: Law.
sp.l: Take you no care for that, here's that has done it,
A fair divorce, 'tis honeſt too.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: The devil,
Honeſt? to put her off?

sp.speaker: Law.
sp.l: Moſt honeſt Sir,
And in this point moſt ſtrong.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: The cauſe, the cauſe Sir?

sp.speaker: Law.
sp.l: A juſt cauſe too.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: As any is in hell, Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Law.
sp.l: For barrenneſs, ſhe never brought him children.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Why art thou not divorc'd? thou canſt not get 'em,
Thy neighbors, thy rank neighbors: O baſe jugling,
Is ſhe not young?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Women at more years Sir,
Have met that bleſſing; 'tis in heavens high power.

sp.speaker: Law.
sp.l: You never can have any:

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Why quick Lawyer?
My Philoſophical Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Law.
sp.l: The Rack has ſpoil'd her
The diſtentions of thoſe parts, hath ſtopt all fruitfulneſs.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: O I could curſe.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And am I grown ſo miſerable,
That mine own pitty muſt make me wretched?
No cauſe againſt me, but my love and duty?
Farewell Sir, like obedience, thus I leave you,
My long farewell: I do not grudge, I grive Sir,
And if that be offenſive, I can dye,
And then you are fairly free: good Lady love him;
You have a noble, and an honeſt Gentleman,
I ever found him ſo, the world has ſpoke him,
And let it be your part ſtill to deſerve him:
Love him no leſs than I have done, and ſerve him,
And heaven ſhall bleſs you; you ſhall bleſs my aſhes
I give you up the houſe, the name of wife,
Honor, and all reſpect I borrowed from him,
And to my grave I turn: one farewell more,
Nothing divide your Loves, not want of Children,
Which I ſhall pray againſt, and make you fruitful;
Grow like two equal flames, riſe high and glorious,
And in your honor'd age burn out together:
To all I know, farewell:

sp.speaker: Ronver.
sp.l: Be not ſo griev'd Lady,
A nobler fortune.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Away thou paraſite.
Diſturb not my ſad thoughts, I hate thy greatneſs.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: I hate not you, I am glad ſhe's off theſe hinges,
Come, let's purſue. Ex. Ronvere and Law.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: If I had breath to curſe thee,
Or could my great heart utter, farewell villain,
Thy houſe, nor face agen, Exit Pand.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let 'em all go.
And now let us rejoyce, now freely take me,
And now embrace me Virolet, give the rites
Of a brave Husband to his love.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I'll take my leave too.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: How take your leave too?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: The houſe is furniſh'd for you,
You are Miſtreſs, may command.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Will you to bed Sir?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: As ſoon to hell, to any thing I hate moſt;
You muſt excuſe me, I have kept my word.
You are my Wife, you now enjoy my fortune.
Which I have done to recompence your bounty:
But to yield up thoſe chaſt delights and pleaſures,
Which are not mine, but my firſt vowes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You jeaſt.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: You will not find it ſo, to give you thoſe
I have divorc'd, and loſt with Juliana,
And all fires of that nature —

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Are you a Husband?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: To queſtion hers, and ſatisfie your flames,
That held an equal beauty, equal bounty—
Good heaven forgive; no, no, the ſtrict forbearance,
Of all thoſe joys, like a full ſacrifice,
I offer to the ſufferings of my firſt love,
Honor, and wealth, attendance, ſtate, all duty,
Shall wait upon your will, to make you happy,
But my afflicted mind, you muſt give leave Lady,
My weary Trunk muſt wander.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Not enjoy me?
Go from me too?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: For ever thus I leave you;
And how ſo e're I fare, live you ſtill happy. Exit Virol.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Since I am ſcorn'd, I'll hate thee, ſcorn thy gifts too,
Thou miſerable fool, thou fool to pitty,
And ſuch a rude, demoliſht thing, I'll leave thee,
In my revenge: for fooliſh love, farewell now,
And anger, and the ſpite of woman enter,
That all the world ſhall ſay, that read this ſtory,
My hate, and not my love, begot my glory.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: He that fears death, or tortures, let him leave me.
The ſtops that we have met with, Crown our Conqueſt.
Common attempts are fit for common men;
The rare, the rareſt ſpirits. Can we be daunted?
We that have ſmil'd at Sea at certain ruines,
Which men on ſhore but hazarded would ſhake at:
We that have liv'd free, in deſpite of fortune,
Laught at the out-ſtretch'd Arm of Tyranny,
As ſtill too ſhort to reach us, ſhall we faint now?
No my brave mates, I know your fiery temper,
And that you can, and dare, as much as men:
Calamity, that ſevers worldly friendſhips,
Could ne'r divide us, you are ſtill the ſame;
The conſtant followers of my baniſht fortunes;
The Inſtruments of my revenge; the hands
By which I work, and faſhion all my projects.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: And ſuch we will be ever.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: 'Slight Sir, Cramme me
Into a Cannons mouth, and ſhoot me at
Proud Ferrand's head: may only he fall with me,
My life I rate at nothing.

sp.speaker: Boatſw.
sp.l: Could I but get,
Within my ſwords length of him; and if then
He ſcape me, may th'account of all his ſins
Be added unto mine.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: 'Tis not to dye Sir,
But to dye unreveng'd, that ſtaggers me:
For were your ends ſerv'd, and our Countrey free,
We would fall willing ſacrifices.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: To riſe up.
Moſt glorious Martyrs.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: But the reaſon why
We wear theſe ſhapes?

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Only to get acceſs:
Like honeſt men, we never ſhall approach him,
Such are his fears, but thus attir'd like Switzers,
And faſhioning our language to our habits;
Bold, bloody, deſperate, we may be admitted
Among his guard. But if this fail I'll try
A thouſand others, out-do Proteus
In various ſhapes, but I will reach his heart.
And ſeal my anger on't.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: The Lord Ronvere.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Shall we begin with him?

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: He is not ripe yet,
Nor fit to fall: as you ſee me begin,
With all care Imitate.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: We are inſtructed.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Would we were at it once.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Keep a ſtrict watch,
And let the guards be doubled, this laſt night
The King had fearful dreams.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: 'Tis a good Omen
To our attempts.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: What men are theſe? what ſeek you?

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Imployment.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Of what nature?

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: We are Soldiers;
We have ſeen Towns and Churches ſet on fire;
The Kennels runing blood, Coy virgins raviſh'd;
The Altars ranſack'd, and the holy reliques,
Yea, and the Saints themſelves, made lawful ſpoyls,
Unto the Conquerors: but theſe good days are paſt,
And we made Beggars, by this idle peace,
For want of action. I am Sir no ſtranger
To the Goverment of this ſtate, I know the King
Needs men, that only do what he commands,
And ſearch no farther: 'tis the profeſſion
Of all our Nation, to ſerve faithfully,
Where th'are beſt payed: and if you entertain us,
I do not know the thing you can command,
Which we'll not put in act.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: A goodly Perſonage.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: And if you have an Enemy, or ſo
That you would have diſpatch'd.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: They are here, can fit you.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Or if there be an Itch, though to a man.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: You ſhall tye
Our conſciences in your purſe ſtrings.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Gentlemen,
I like your freedome: I am now in haſt,
But wait for my return. I like the Raſcals,
They may be uſeful.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: We'll attend you Sir:

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Do, and be confident of entertainment;
I hope you will deſerve it. Exit Ron. and Guard.

sp.speaker: Seſs.
sp.l: O, no doubt Sir:
Thus far we are proſperous; we'll be his guard;
Till Tyranny and pride find full reward: Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: My bleſſing? no; a Fathers heavy curſe,
Purſue, and overtake him,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Gentle Sir.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: My name, and Family, end in my ſelf
Rather then live in him.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Dear Sir forbear,
A fathers curſes, hit far off, and kill too.
And like a murthering piece ayms not at one,
But all that ſtand within the dangerous level.
Some bullet may return upon your ſelf too,
Though againſt nature, if you ſtill go on
In this unnatural courſe.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Thou art not made
Of that ſame ſtuff as other women are:
Thy injuries would teach patience to blaſpheme,
Yet ſtill thou art a Dove.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I know not malice, but like an innocent, ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: More miraculous!
I'll have a woman Chronicled, and for goodneſs,
Which is the greateſt wonder. Let me ſee,
I have no Son to inherit after me;
Him I diſclaim.
What then? I'll make thy vertues my ſole heir;
Thy ſtory I'll have written, and in Gold too;
In proſe and verſe, and by the ableſt doers:
A word or two of a kind ſtep-father
I'll have put in, good Kings and Queens ſhall buy it.
And if the actions of ill great women,
And of the modern times too, are remembred,
That have undone their husbands and their families,
What will our ſtory do? It ſhall be ſo,
And I will ſtreight about it. Exit Pand.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Such as love
Goodneſs for glory, have it for reward;
I love mine for it ſelf: let innocence
Be written on my Tomb, though ne're ſo humble,
'Tis all I am ambitious of. But I
Forget my vows.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: 'Fore me you are not modeſt,
Nor is this Courtlike. Would you take it well,
If ſhe ſhould rudely preſs into your Cloſet,
When from your ſeveral Boxes you chooſe paint,
To make a this days face with?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: What's the matter:

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Pray know her pleaſure firſt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: To whom ſpeak you Boy?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Your Ladiſhips pardon. That proud Lady thief,
That ſtole away my Lord from your embraces,
(Wrinckles at two and twenty on her cheeks for't,
Or Mercury unallayed, make bliſters on it)
Would force a viſit.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And dare you deny her,
Or any elſe that I call mine? No more,
Attend her with all reverence and reſpect;
The want in you of manners, my Lord may
Conſtrue in me for malice. I will teach you
How to eſteem and love the beauty he dotes on;
Prepare a Banquet.
Madam, thus my duty
Stoops to the favor you vouchſafe your ſervant,
In honouring her houſe.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Is this in ſcorn?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: No by the life of Virolet: give me leave
To ſwear by him, as by a Saint I worſhip,
But am to know no farther, my heart ſpeaks that
My ſervants have been rude, and this boy (doting
Upon my ſorrows) hath forgot his duty:
In which, that you may think I have no ſnare,
Sirra, upon your knees, deſire her pardon.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I dare not diſobey you.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Prethee riſe,
My anger never looks ſo low: I thank you.
And will deſerve it, if we may be private,
I came to ſee and ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Be gone. Exit Boy.
Good Madam ſit.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I rob you of your place then.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: You have deſerv'd a better, in my bed;
Make uſe of this too: Now your pleaſure Lady.
If in your breaſt there be a worthy pitty,
That brings you for my comfort, you do nobly:
But if you come to triumph in your conqueſt,
Or tread on my calamities, 'twill wrong
Your other excellencies. Let it ſuffice,
That you alone enjoy the beſt of men,
And that I am forſaken.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: He the beſt?
The ſcum and ſhame of mankind.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Virolet, Lady?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Bleſt in him? I would my youth had choſen
Conſuming feavers, bed-rid age
For my companions, rather then a thing
To lay whoſe baſeneſs open, would even poyſon
The tongue that ſpeaks it.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Certainly from you
At no part he deſerves this; and I tell you,
Durſt I pretend but the leaſt title to him,
I ſhould not hear this.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: He's an impudent villain,
Or a malicious wretch: to you ungrateful;
To me beyond expreſſion barbarous.
I more then hate him; from you he deſerves
A death moſt horrid: from me, to dye for ever,
And know no end of torments. Would you have comfort?
Would you waſh off the ſtain that ſticks upon you,
In being refus'd? Would you redeem your fame,
Shipwrack'd in his baſe wrongs? if you deſire this,
It is not to be done with ſlaviſh ſuffering,
But by a Noble anger, making way
To a moſt brave revenge, we may call juſtice;
Our injuries are equal; joyn with me then,
And ſhare the honor,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I ſcarce underſtand you,
And know I ſhall be moſt unapt to learn
To hate the man I ſtill muſt love and honor.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: This fooliſh dotage in ſoft-hearted women,
Makes proud men inſolent: but take your way,
I'll run another courſe.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: As you are noble,
Deliver his offence.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: He has denied
The rites due to a wife.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: O me moſt happy,
How largely am I payd for all my ſufferings?
Moſt honeſt Virolet, thou juſt performer
Of all thy promiſes: I call to mind now,
When I was happy in thoſe joys you ſpeak of,
In a chaſt bed, and warranted by Law too,
He oft would ſwear, that if he ſhould ſurvive me,
(Which then I knew he wiſht not) never woman
Should taſt of his embraces; this one act
Makes me again his debtor.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: And was this
The cauſe my youth and beauty were contemn'd?
If I ſit down here! wel—

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I dare thy worſt,
Plot what thou canſt, my piety ſhall guard him
Againſt thy malice. Leave my houſe and quickly,
Thou wilt infect theſe innocent walls. By virtue
I will inform him of thy bloody purpoſe,
And turn it on thine own accurſed head;
Believ't I will. Exit Juliana.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: But 'tis not in thy power
To hinder what I have decreed againſt him.
I'll ſet my ſelf to ſale, and live a ſtrumpet;
Forget my birth, my father, and his honor,
Rather then want an inſtrument to help me
In my revenge. The Captain of the guard; —
(Bleſt opportunity) courts me.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Sad and troubled?
How brave her anger ſhews? how it ſets off
Her natural beauty? under what happy ſtar
Was Virolet born, to be belov'd and ſought to,
By two incomparable women? nobleſt Lady,
I have heard your wrongs and pitty them: and if
The ſervice of my life could give me hope
To gain your favor, I ſhould be moſt proud
To be commanded.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: 'Tis in you, my Lord,
To make me your glad ſervant.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Name the means.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis not preferment, Jewels, Gold, or Courtſhip.
He that deſires to reap the harveſt of
My youth and beauty, muſt begin in blood,
And right my wrongs.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: I apprehend you Madam,
And reſt aſſured 'tis done; I am provided
Of inſtruments to fit you: To the King,
I'll inſtantly preſent you; if I fail,
He ſhall make good your ayms: he's leſs then man,
That to atchieve your favor, would not do
Deeds, fiends would fear to put their agents to. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Quod invitus facis, non eſt ſcelus. 'Tis an axiome,
Now whether willingly I have departed
With that I lov'd: with that, above her life
Lov'd me again, crownd me a happy husband,
Was full of children her afflictions,
That I begot, that when our age muſt periſh,
And all our painted frailties turn'd to aſhes,
Then ſhall they ſtand and propogate our honors.
Whether this done, and taking to protection
A new ſtrange beauty, it was a uſeful one:
How to my luſt? if it be ſo, I am ſinful;
And guilty of that crime I would fling from me.
Was there not in it this fair courſe of virtue?
This pious courſe, to ſave my friends, my Countrey,
That even then had put on a mourning garment,
And wept the deſolation of her children?
Her nobleſt children? Did not ſhe thruſt me on,
And to my duty clapt the ſpur of honor?
Was there a way, without this woman, left me
To bring 'em off? the marrying of this woman?
If not, why am I ſtung thus? why tormented?
Or had there been a wild deſire joyn'd with it,
How eaſily, both theſe, and all their beauties
Might I have made mine own? why am I toucht thus,
Having perform'd the great redemption,
Both of my friends and family? fairly done it?
Without baſe and laſcivious ends; O Heaven,
Why am I ſtill at War thus? why this a miſchief,
That honeſty and honor had propounded,
I, and abſolv'd my tender will, and chid me,
Nay then unwillingly flung me on?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: He's here Madam;
This is the melancholly walk he lives in,
And chooſes ever to increaſe his ſadneſs.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Stand by.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe: how I ſhake now and tremble?
The virtues of that mind are torments to me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Sir, if my hated face ſhall ſtir your anger,
Or this forbidden path I tread in vex you;
My love, and fair obedience left behind me,
Your pardon asked, I ſhall return and bleſs you.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Pray ſtay a little, I delight to ſee you;
May not we yet, though fortune have divided us,
And ſet an envious ſtop between our pleaſures,
Look thus one at another? ſigh and weep thus?
And read in one anothers eyes, the Legends,
And wonders of our old loves? be not fearful,
Though you be now a Saint, I may adore you:
May I not take this hand, and on it ſacrifice
The ſorrows of my heart? white ſeal of virtue.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: My Lord, you wrong your wedlock.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Were ſhe here,
And with her all ſevere eyes to behold us,
We might do this; I might name Juliana,
And to the reverence of that name, bow thus:
I might ſigh Juliana ſhe was mine once;
But I too weak a guard for that great treaſure—
And whilſt ſhe has a name, believe me Lady,
This broken heart ſhall never want a ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Forget her ſir, your honor now commands you
You are anothers, keep thoſe griefs for her,
She richly can reward 'em. I would have ſpoken with you.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: What is your will? for nothing you can ask,
So full of goodneſs are your words and meanings,
Muſt be denied: ſpeak boldly.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I thank you ſir. I come not
To beg, or flatter, only to be believ'd,
That I deſire: for I ſhall tell a ſtory,
So far from ſeeming truth, yet a moſt true one;
So horrible in nature, and ſo horrid;
So beyond wickedneſs, that when you hear it,
It muſt appear the practice of another,
The caſt and malice of ſome one you have wrong'd much,
And me, you may imagine me accuſe too,
Unleſs you call to mind my daily ſufferings;
The infinite obedience I have born you,
That hates all name and nature of revenge.
My love, that nothing but my death can ſever,
Rather than hers I ſpeak of.

sp.speaker: Vir.

l.hi: Juliana,

sp.l: To make a doubt of what you ſhall deliver,
After my full experience of your virtues,
Were to diſtruſt a providence; to think you can lie,
Or being wrong'd, ſeek after foul repairings,
To forge a Creed againſt my faith.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I muſt do ſo, for it concerns your life Sir;
And if that word may ſtir you, hear and proſper:
I ſhould be dumb elſe, were not you at ſtake here.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: What new friend have I found, that dares deliver
This loaden trunk from his afflictions?
What pittying hand, of all that feels my miſeries,
Brings ſuch a benefit?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Be wiſe and manly,
And with your honor fall, when Heaven ſhall call you,
Not by a helliſh miſchief.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Speak my bleſt one,
How weak and poor I am, now ſhe is from me?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Your wife.

sp.speaker: Viro.
sp.l: How's that?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Your wife.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Be tender of her, I ſhall believe elſe—

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I muſt be true; your ear, ſir;
For 'tis ſo horrible, if the ayr catch it,
Into a thouſand plagues, a thouſand monſters,
It will diſperſe it ſelf, and fright reſiſtance. Whiſpers.

sp.speaker: Viro.
sp.l: She ſeek my life with you? make you her agent?
Another love? O ſpeak but truth.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Be patient,
Dear as I love you, elſe I leave you wretched.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Forward, 'tis well, it ſhall be welcome to me;
I have liv'd too long, numbred too many days,
Yet never found the benefit of living;
Now when I come to reap it with my ſervice,
And hunt for that my youth and honor aims at,
The Sun ſets on my fortune red and bloody,
And everlaſting night begins to cloſe me,
'Tis time to dye.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: She comes her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Believe Lady,
And on this Angel hand, your ſervant ſeals it,
You ſhall be Miſtriſs of your whole deſires,
And what ye ſhall command.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Ha mynion,
My precious Dame, are you there? nay go forward,
Make your complaints, and pour out your fain'd pitties,
Slave, like to him you ſerve: I am the ſame ſtill,
And what I purpoſe, let the world take witneſs,
Shall be ſo finiſht, and to ſuch example,
Spite of your poor preventions, my dear Gentleman,
My honorable man, are you there too?
You and your hot deſire? your mercy Sir,
I had forgot your greatneſs,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis not well Lady.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Lord, how I hate this fellow now; how deſperately
My ſtomach ſtands againſt him; this baſe fellow,
This gelded fool!

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Did you never hea • of modeſty?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Yes, when I heard of you and ſo believ'd it,
Thou bloodleſs, brainleſs fool.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Thou deſpiſed fool,
Thou only ſign of man, how I contemn thee!
Thou woven worthy in a piece of Arras,
Fit only to enjoy a wall; thou beaſt
Beaten to uſe; Have I preſerv'd a beauty,
A youth, a love, to have my wiſhes blaſted?
My dotings, and the joys I came to offer,
Muſt they be loſt, and ſleighted by a dormouſe?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Uſe more reſpect; and woman, 'twill become you;
At leaſt, leſs tongue.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I'll uſe all violence,
Let him look for't.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Dare you ſtain thoſe beauties,
Thoſe heavenly ſtamps, that raiſe men up to wonder,
With harſh and crooked motions? are you ſhe
That overdid all ages, with your honor;
And in a little hour dare looſe this triumph?
Is not this man your husband?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: He's my halter;
Which (having ſued my pardon) I fling off thus,
And with him all I brought him, but my anger;
Which I will nouriſh to the deſolation,
Not only of his folly, but his friends,
And his whole name.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: 'Tis well, I have deſerved it.
And if I were a woman, I would rail too.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Nature nere promiſed thee a thing ſo noble.
Take back your love, your vow, I give it freely;
I poorly ſcorn it; graze now where you pleaſe:
That that the dulneſs of thy ſoul neglected,
Kings ſue for now. And mark me, Virolet,
Thou image of a man, obſerve my words well.
At ſuch a bloody rate I'll ſell this beauty,
This handſomneſs thou ſcornſt and flingſt away,
Thy proud ungrateful life ſhall ſhake at: take your houſe,
The petty things you left me give another;
And laſt, take home your trinket: fare you well, Sir,

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: You have ſpoke like your ſelf;
Y'are a brave Lady. Exeunt Ronvere and Martia.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Why do you ſmile, Sir?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: O my Juliana,
The happineſs this womans ſcorn has given me,
Makes me a man again; proclaims it ſelf,
In ſuch a general joy, through all my miſeries,
That now methinks—

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Look to your ſelf dear Sir,
And trifle not with danger that attends you;
Be joyful when y'are free.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Did you not hear her?
She gave me back my vow, my love, my freedom;
I am free, free as air; and though to morrow
Her bloody will meet with my life, and ſink it,
And in her execution tear me piecemeal:
Yet have I time once more to meet my wiſhes,
Once more to embrace my beſt, my nobleſt, trueſt;
And time that's warranted.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Good Sir, forbear it:
Though I confeſs, equal with your deſires
My wiſhes riſe, as covetous of your love,
And to as warm alarums ſpur my will to:
Yet pardon me, the Seal oth'Church dividing us,
And hanging like a threatning flame between us,
We muſt not meet, I dare not.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: That poor disjoynting
That only ſtrong neceſſity thruſt on you,
Not crime, nor ſtudied cauſe of mine: how ſweetly,
And nobly I will bind again and cheriſh;
How I will recompence one dear imbrace now,
One free affection! how I burn to meet it!
Look now upon me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I behold you willingly,
And willingly would yield, but for my credit.
The love you firſt had was preſerv'd with honor,
The laſt ſhall not cry whore; you ſhall not purchaſe
From me a pleaſure, that have equally
Lov'd your fair fame as you, at ſuch a rate:
Your honeſty and virtue muſt be bankrupt,
If I had lov'd your luſt, and not your luſtre;
The glorious luſtre of your matchleſs goodneſs,
I would compel you now to be! —forgive me,
Forgive me Sir, how fondly ſtill I love you!
Yet nobly too; make the way ſtraight before me,
And let but holy Hymen once more guide me,
Under the Ax upon the Rack again,
Even in the bed of all afflictions,
Where nothing ſings our Nuptials but dire ſorrows,
With all my youth and pleaſure I'll imbrace you,
Make Tyranny and death ſtand ſtill affrighted,
And at our meeting ſouls amaze our miſchiefs;
Till when, high heaven defend you, and peace guide you.
Be wiſe and manly, make your fate your own,
By being maſter of a providence,
That may controle it.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Stay a little with me,
My thoughts have chid themſelves: may I not kiſs you?
Upon my truth I am honeſt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I believe ye;
But yet what that may raiſe in both our fancies,
What iſſues ſuch warm parents breed.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I obey you,
And take my leave as from the Saint that keeps me.
I will be right again, and once more happy
In thy unimitable love.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I'll pray for ye,
And when you fall I have not long to follow. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Seſſe, Maſter, Boteſwain, and Gunner, at one door, Martia and Ronvere, at another.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Now we have got free credit with the Captain.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Soft, ſoft, he's here again: Is not that Lady—
Or have I loſt mine eyes? a ſalt rhume ſeizes 'em;
But I ſhould know that face.

sp.speaker: Botſ.
sp.l: Make him not madder,
Let him forget the woman; ſteer a lar-board.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: He will not kill her.

sp.speaker: Botſ.
sp.l: Any thing he meets;
He's like a Hornet now, he hums, and buzzes;
Nothing but blood and horror.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: I would ſave the Lady,
For ſuch another Lady.

sp.speaker: Botſ.
sp.l: There's the point;
And you know there want women of her mettle.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: 'Tis true, they bring ſuch children now,
Such demilancies,
Their fathers ſocks will make them Chriſtning clothes.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: No more, they view us.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: You ſhall play a while,
And ſun your ſelf in this felicity,
You ſhall you glorious whore, I know you ſtill.
But I ſhall pick an hour when moſt ſecurely —
I ſay no more.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Do you ſee thoſe? thoſe are they
Shall act your will; come hither my good fellows:
You are now the Kings. Are they not goodly fellows?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: They have bone enough, if they have ſtout heart to it.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Still the old wench.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Pray Captain, let me ask you
What Noble Lady's that? 'tis a rude queſtion,
But I deſire to know.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: She is for the King, Sir;
Let that ſuffice for anſwer.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Is ſhe ſo Sir?
In good time may ſhe curſe it.
Muſt I breed hackneys for his grace?

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: What wouldſt thou do
To merit ſuch a Ladies favor?

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Any thing.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: That can ſupply thy wants, and raiſe thy fortunes?

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Let her command, and ſee what I dare execute.
I keep my conſcience here; if any man
Oppoſe her will, and ſhe would have him humbled,
Whole families between her and her wiſhes—

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We have ſeen bleeding throats ſir, Cities ſackt;
And infants ſtuck upon their pikes.

sp.speaker: Boteſ.
sp.l: Houſes a fire, and handſome mothers weeping.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Which we have heaped upon the pile like ſacrifices.
Churches and Altars, Prieſts and all devotions,
Tumbled together into one rude Chaos.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: We know no fear Sir, but want of imployment.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Nor other faith but what our purſes preach.
To gain our ends we can do any thing,
And turn our ſouls into a thouſand figures;
But when we come to do—

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I like theſe fellows.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Be ready and wait here within this hour
I'll ſhew you to the King, and he ſhall like ye:
And if you can deviſe ſome entertainment
To fill his mirth, ſuch as your Countrey uſes,
Preſent it, and I'll ſee it grac'd.
After this Comicke Scene we ſhall imploy you,
For one muſt dye.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: What is he ſir? ſpeak boldly,
For we dare boldly do.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: This Ladies husband;
His name is Virolet.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: We ſhall diſpatch it. Exit Martia, Ronvere.
O damned, damned thing: a baſe whore firſt:
And then a murtherer, I'll look to you.

sp.speaker: Botſ.
sp.l: Can ſhe be grown ſo ſtrange?

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: She has an itch;
I'll ſcratch you my dear daughter, I'll ſo claw you;
I'll curry your hot hide; married and honour'd?
And turn thoſe holy bleſſings into brothels?
Your beauty into blood? I'll hunt your hotneſs.
I'll hunt you like a train.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We did all pitty her.

sp.speaker: Seſ,
sp.l: Hang her, ſhe is not worth mans memory;
She's falſe and baſe, and let her fright all ſtories.
Well, though thou beeſt mine enemy, I'll right thee,
And right thee Nobly.

sp.speaker: Botſ
sp.l: Faith ſir, ſince ſhe muſt go,
Let's ſpare as few as may be.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: We'll take all,
And like a torrent ſweep the ſlaves before us.
You dare endure the worſt?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: You know our hearts ſir,
And they ſhall bleed the laſt, ere we ſtart from ye.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: We can but dye, and ere we come to that,
We ſhall pick out ſome few examples for us.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Then wait the firſt occaſion, and like Curtius,
I'll leap the gulph before you, fearleſs leap it:
Then follow me like men, and if our virtues
May buoy our Countrey up, and ſet her ſhining
In her firſt ſtate; our fair revenges taken,
We have our noble ends or elſe our aſhes. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: As you are noble, keep me from diſcovery,
And let me only run a ſtrangers fortune;
For when the King ſhall find I am his daughter
He ever holds moſt ominous, and hates moſt:
With what eyes can he look, how entertain me,
But with his fears and cruelties?

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: I have found you,
Suſpect not, I am bound to what you like beſt,
What you intend, I dare not be ſo curious
To queſtion now, and what you are, lies hid here.
The King comes, make your fortune, I ſhall joy in't.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: All things are ready ſir to make you merry,
And ſuch a King, you ſhall behold him now.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I long for't,
For I have need of mirth.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: The Lady ſir.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Now as I am a King, a ſprightly beauty,
A goodly ſweet aſpect! my thanks Ronvere,
My beſt thanks; on your lips I ſeal your wiſhes,
Be what you can; imagine mine, and happy.
And now ſit down and ſmile; come my Aſcanio;
And let this Monarch enter.

div.stage: Enter Seſſ. and Mr. Bortſw. Gunner, and Saylors.

sp.speaker: Ronv.
sp.l: Theſe are the Switzers:
I told your grace of.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Goodly promiſing fellows,
With faces to keep fools in awe, I like 'em;
Go guard the preſence well, and do your duties,
To morrow I ſhall take a farther view:

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: You ſhall Sir,
Or I ſhall looſe my will; how the whore's mounted?
