How ſhe ſits thron'd? thou blaſing muddy meteor,
That frighteſt the under world with luſtful flaſhes,
How I ſhall daſh thy flames? away, no word more:
sp.stage: Ex. Seſſ. and his company. Floriſh Cor.

div.stage: Enter Villio, Caſtruchio, Doctor, and a Guard.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Now, here he comes in glory; be merry Maſters,
A Banquet too? meat conveyed away.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: O, he muſt ſit in State Sir!

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: How rarely he is uſher'd? can he think now
He is a King indeed?

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: Mark but his countenance.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Let me have pleaſures infinite, and to the height,
And women in abundance, many women,
I will diſport my grace,
Stand there and long for me.
What have ye brought me here? is this a Feaſt
Fit for a Prince? a mighty Prince? are theſe things,
Theſe preparations, ha?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: May it pleaſe your grace?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: It does not pleaſe my grace: where are the Marchpanes,
The Cuſtards double royal, and the ſubtilties?
Why, what weak things are you to ſerve a Prince thus?
Where be the delicates oth' earth and ayr?
The hidden ſecrets of the Sea? am I a plow-man,
You pop me up with porridge? hang the Cooks.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: O moſt Kingly:
What a Majeſtick anger?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Give me ſome wine.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: He cools agen now.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Fool where are my Players?
Let me have all in pomp; let 'em play ſome love matter,
To make the Ladies itch, I'll be with you anon Ladies;
You black eyes, I'll be with you.
Give me ſome wine I ſay,
And let me have a Maſque of Cuckolds enter:
Of mine own Cuckolds,
And let them come in, peeping and rejoycing.
Juſt as I kiſs their wives, and ſomewhat glorying.
Some wine I ſay, then for an excellent night-piece,
To ſhew my glory to my loves, and minions,
I will have ſome great Caſtle burnt.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Hark you brother:
If that be to pleaſe theſe Ladies, ten to one
The fire firſt takes upon your own, look to that;
Then you may ſhew a night piece.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Where's this wine?
Why ſhall I choak? do ye long all to be tortur'd?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Here Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Why, what is this? why Doctor.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Wine and water Sir.
'Tis Soveraign for your heat, you muſt endure it.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Moſt excellent to cool your night-piece Sir.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: You are of a high and cholerick complexion,
And you muſt have allayes.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Shall I have no ſheere wine then?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Not for a world: I tender your dear life Sir;
And he is no faithful ſubject—

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: No, by no means:
Of this you may drink, and never hang, nor quarter,
Nor never whip the fool, this liquors merciful.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: I will ſit down and eat then: Kings when th'are hungry,
May eat I hope?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Yes, but they eat diſcreetly.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Come, taſt this diſh, and cut me liberally;
I like ſauce well.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Fie 'tis too hot Sir:
Too deeply ſeaſon'd with the ſpice, away with't,
You muſt acquaint your ſtomach with thoſe dyets
Are temperately nouriſhing.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: But pray ſtay Doctor,
And let me have my meat again.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: By no means:
I have a charge concerns my life.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: No meat neither;
Do Kings never eat Doctor?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Very little Sir.
And that too very choice.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Your King never ſleeps Brother,
He muſt not ſleep, his cares ſtill keep him waking.
Now he that eats and drinks much is a dormouſe;
The third part of a wafer is a weeks diet.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Appoint me ſomething then.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: This I feel good;
But it melts too ſuddainly; yet, how, that gone too!
Ye are not mad! I charge you: take away.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: For your health Sir,
A little quickens nature, much depreſſes.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Eat nothing for my health? that's a new dyet,
Let me have ſomething, ſomething has ſome ſavor.
Why thou uncourteous Doctor, ſhall I hang thee?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: 'Tis better Sir than I ſhould let you ſurfeit,
My death were nothing.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: To looſe a King, were terrible.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Nay, then I'll carve my ſelf, I'll ſtay no ceremonies.
This is a Patridge Pye, I am ſure that's nouriſhing,
Or Galen is an Aſs: 'tis rarely ſeaſon'd:
Ha Doctor have I hit right? a mark a mark there? take away.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: What ails thy grace?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Retriv thoſe Patridges.
Or as I am a King—

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Pray Sir be patient,
They are flowen too far.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Theſe are breath'd pyes an't pleaſe you,
And your hawkes are ſuch Buzards.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: A King and have nothing,
Nor can have nothing!

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: What think you of pudding?
A pudding Royal?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: To be royally ſtarv'd,
Whip me this fool to death; he is a blockhead.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Let 'em think they whip me, as we think you a King:
'Twill be enough.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: As for your dainty Doctor, the Table taken away,
All gone, all ſnatch'd away, and I unſatisfied,
Without my wits being a King and hungry?
Suffer but this thy treaſon? I tell thee Doctor.
I tell it thee, in earneſt, and in anger,
I am damnably hungry; my very grace is hungry.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: A hungry grace is fitteſt to no meal Sir.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Some two hours hence, you ſhall ſee more: but ſtill Sir
You muſt retain an excellent and ſtrict dyet.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: It ſharpens you, and makes your wit ſo poynant, Sir
Your very words will kill.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: A bit of Marmalade
No bigger than a Peaſe.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: And that well butter'd,
The ayr thrice purified, and three times ſpirited;
Becomes a King: your rare conſerve of nothing
Breeds no offence.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Am I turn'd King Camelion,
And keep my Court ith'ayr?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: They vex him cruelly.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: In two days more they'll ſtarve him.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Now the women, there's no food left but they.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: They'll prove ſmall nouriſhment.
Yet h'as another ſtomach and a great one,
I ſee by his eye.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: I'll have mine own power here;
Mine own Authority; I need no tutor.
Doctor this is no dyet.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: It may be Sir

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: Birlady, it may turn to a dry dyet;
And how thy grace, will ward that—

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Stand off Doctor;
And talk to thoſe that want ſaith.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Hot and mighty.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: He will cool apace, no doubt.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Fair, plump, and red,
A forehead high, an eye revives the dead;
A lip like ripeſt fruit, inviting ſtill.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: But O, the ruſhy well. below the hill,
Take heed of that, for though it never fail
Take heed I ſay, for thereby hangs a tail.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: I'll get ye all with Child.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: With one Child Brother,
So many men in a Blew Coat.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Had I fed well.
And drunk good ſtore of wine, ye had been bleſt all,
Bleſt all with double Births; come kiſs me greedily,
And think no more upon your fooliſh Husbands,
They are tranſitory things: a Kings fame meets you.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Vaniſh away. Ex. Women.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: How, they gone too? my guard there:
Take me this devil Doctor, and that fool there,
And ſow 'em in a ſack; bring back the women,
The lovely women, drown theſe rogues or hang 'em.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: He is in earneſt Sir.
I muſt needs take him off.

div.stage: Enter Seſſ. Maſter, Boatſw. Gunner and Saylors.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: In ſerious earneſt,

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Now, now be free.
Now liberty, now Countrey-men ſhake from ye
The Tyrants yoke.
All liberty, liberty, liberty.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Treaſon, treaſon, treaſon.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: We are betray'd, fly to the Town, cry treaſon,
And raiſe our faithful friends; O my Aſcanio.

sp.speaker: Aſca.
sp.l: Make haſt, we have way enough.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Treaſon, treaſon. Ex. Fer. Aſca. and guard.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Spare none, put all to th'ſword: a vengeance ſhake thee;
Art thou turn'd King again?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: I am a Raſcal:
Spare me but this time, if ever I ſee King more,
Or once believe in King.

sp.speaker: Seſs.
sp.l: The ports are ours.
The treaſure and the port, fight bravely Gentlemen;
Cry to the Town, cry liberty and honor;
Waken their perſecuted ſouls, cry loudly,
We'll ſhare the wealth among ye.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Do you hear Captain?
If ever you hear me, name a King.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: You ſhall not

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Or though I live under one, obey him.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: This Rogue again.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Away with him good Gunner.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Why look ye Sir? I'll put you to no charge;
I'll never eat.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: I'll take a courſe, you ſhall not,
Come, no more words.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: Say nothing when you kill me.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: He's taken to the Towers ſtrength;
Now ſtand ſure Gentlemen.
We have him in a pen, he cannot ſcape us,
The reſt oth'Caſtle's ours; liberty, liberty?
What is this City up?

sp.speaker: Boatſw.
sp.l: They are up and glorious,
And rouling like a ſtorm they come; their Tents
Ring nothing but liberty and freedome.
The women are in Arms too.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Let 'em come all.
Honour and liberty.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Honor and liberty. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: This woman threats, her eyes, even red with fury
Which like prodigious meteors, foretold
Aſſur'd deſtruction, are ſtill before me.
Beſides I know ſuch natures unacquainted
With any mean, or in their love, or hatred,
And ſhe that dar'd all dangers to poſſeſs him,
Will check at nothing, to revenge the loſs
Of what ſhe held ſo dear, I firſt diſcover'd
Her bloody purpoſes, which ſhe made good,
And openly profeſs'd 'em; that in me
Was but a cold affection; charity
Commands ſo much to all; for Virolet
Methinks I ſhould forget my Sexes weakneſs,
Riſe up, and dare beyond a womans ſtrength;
Then do not counſel: he is too ſecure,
And in my judgment, 'twere a greater ſervice
To free him from a deadly Enemy,
Then to get him a friend. I undertook too,
To croſs her plots, oppos'd my piety,
Againſt her malice; and ſhall vertue ſuffer?
No Martia, wer't thou here equally armed,
I have cauſe, ſpite of thy maſculine breeding,
That would aſſure the victory: my angel
Direct and help me.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: The State in Combuſtion,
Part of the Cittadel forc'd, the treaſure ſeiz'd on;
The guards corrupted, arm themſelves againſt
Their late protected Maſter; Ferrant fled too,
And with ſmall ſtrength, into the Caſtle's Tower,
The only Aventine, that now is left him?
And yet the undertakers, nay, performers,
Of ſuch a brave and glorious enterprize,
Are yet unknown: they did proceed like men,
I like a child; and had I never truſted
So deep a practice unto ſhallow fools,
Beſides my ſouls peace, in my Juliana,
The honor of this action had been mine,
In which, accurs'd, I now can claim no ſhare.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Ronvere! 'tis he, a thing, next to the devil
I moſt deteſt and like him terrible;
Martia's right hand, the inſtrument I fear too,
That is put to her bloody will, into act.
Have I not will enough, and cauſe too mighty?
Weak womens fear, fly from me.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Sure this habit,
This likeneſs to Ronvere, which I have ſtudied,
Either admits me ſafe to my deſign,
Which I too cowardly have halted after,
And ſuffer'd to be raviſht from my glory;
Or ſinks me and my miſeries together;
Either concludes me happy.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: He ſtands muſing,
Some miſchief is now hatching:
In the full meditation, of his wickedneſs,
I'll ſink his curſed ſoul: guide my hand heaven,
And to my tender arm give ſtrength, and fortune,
That I may do a pious deed, all ages
Shall bleſs my name for; all remembrance crown me.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: It ſhall be ſo.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: It ſhall not, take that token,
And bear it to the luſtful arms of Martia,
Tell her, for Virolets dear ſake, I ſent it.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: O I am happy, let me ſee thee,
That I may bleſs the hand that gave me liberty,
O courteous hand, nay thou haſt done moſt nobly,
And heaven has guided thee, 'twas their great juſtice;
O bleſſed wound that I could come to kiſs thee!
How beautiful, and ſweet thou ſhew'ſt!

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Sigh not,
Nor weep not dear, ſhed not thoſe ſovereign Balſames
Into my blood; which muſt recover me;
Then I ſhall live again, to do a miſchief,
Againſt the mightineſs of love and virtue,
Some baſe unhallowed hand ſhall rob thy right of.
Help me, I faint: ſo.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: O unhappy wench!
How has my zeal abus'd me; you that guard virtue,
Were ye aſleep? or do you laugh at innocence?
You ſuffer'd this miſtake? O my dear Virolet!
An everlaſting curſe follow that forme
I ſtrook thee in, his name be ever blaſted:
For his accurſed ſhadow has betray'd
The ſweetneſs of all youth, the nobleneſs,
The honour, and the valor; wither'd for ever
The beauty and the bravery of all mankind:
O my dull, devils eyes.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: I do forgive you,
By this, and this I do? I know you were cozen'd;
The ſhadow of Ronvere, I know you aym'd at,
And not at me; but 'twas moſt neceſſary,
I ſhould be ſtruck, ſome hand above directed you:
For Juliana could not ſhew her juſtice
Without depriving high heaven of his glory,
Or any ſubject fit for her, but Virolet:
Forgive me too, and take my laſt breath ſweet one,
This the new marriage of our ſouls together;
Think of me Juliana, but not often,
For fear my faults ſhould burthen your affections,
Pray for me, for I faint.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: O ſtay a little,
A little little Sir. Offers to kill her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Fye Juliana.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Shall I outlive the virtue, I have murder'd?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Hold, or thou hat'ſt my peace, give me the dagger,
On your obedience, and your love, deliver it.
If you do thus; we ſhall not meet in heaven ſweet;
No guilty blood comes there; kill your intentions,
And then you conquer: there where I am going,
Would you not meet me Dear?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: And ſtill love me?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: And ſtill behold you.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Live then till heaven calls you.
Then ripe and full of ſweetneſs you riſe ſainted.
Then I that went before you to prepare,
Shall meet and welcome you, and daily court you
With Hymnes of holy Love—I go out,
Give me your hand, farewell, in peace farewell,
Remember me, farewell. dyes.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Sleep you ſweet glaſſes,
An everlaſting ſlumber crown thoſe Chryſtals,
All my delight adue, farewell, Dear Virolet,
Dear, Dear, moſt Dear; O I can weep no more,
My body now is fire, and all conſuming,
Here will I ſit, forget the world and all things,
And only wait what heaven ſhall turn me to,
For now methinks I ſhould not live. She ſits down.

sp.speaker: Pond.
sp.l: O my ſweet daughter,
The work is finiſht now, I promis'd thee:
Here are thy virtues ſhewed, here regiſter'd,
And here ſhall live for ever.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Blot it, burn it,
I have no virtue, hateful I am as hell is.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Is not this Virolet?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Ask no more queſtions,
Miſtaking him I kill'd him.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: O my Son,
Nature turns to my heart again, my dear Son,
Son of my age, would'ſt thou go out ſo quickly?
So poorly take thy leave, and never ſee me?
Was this a kind ſtroak daughter? could you love him?
Honour his Father, and ſo deadly ſtrike him?
O wither'd timeleſs youth, are all thy promiſes,
Thy goodly growth of Honors come to this?
Do I halt ſtill ith'world, and trouble nature,
When her main pieces founder, and fail dayly?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: He does weep certain: what bodie's that lies by him?
How do you do Sir?

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: O look there Lucio,
Thy Maſter, thy beſt Maſter.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Woe is me.
They have kill'd him, ſlain him baſely, O my Maſter!

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Well daughter well; what heart had you to do this?
I know he did you wrong; but 'twas his fortune,
And not his fault, for my ſake that have lov'd you,
But I ſee now you ſcorn me too.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: O Miſtreſs?
Can you fit there, and his cold body breathleſs?
Baſely upon the earth?

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Let her alone Boy,
She glories in his end.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: You ſhall not ſit here,
And ſuffer him you loved-ha! good Sir come hither,
Come hither quickly, heave her up; O heaven Sir,
O God, my heart, ſh's cold; cold and ſtiff too:
Stiff as a ſtake, ſhe's dead.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: She's gone, nere bend her.
I know her heart, ſhe could not want his company:
Bleſſing go with thy ſoul, ſweet Angels ſhadow it
O, that I were the third now, what a happineſs?
But I muſt live, to ſee you layd in earth both,
Then build a Chapel to your memories,
Where all my wealth ſhall faſhion out your ſtories.
Then dig a little grave beſides, and all's done.
How ſweet ſhe looks, her eyes are open ſmiling,
I thought ſhe had been alive, you are my charge Sir,
And amongſt you, I'll ſee his goods diſtributed.
Take up the bodies, mourn in heart my friends,
You have loſt two noble ſuccors; follow me,
And thou ſad Countrey, weep this miſery. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Seſſ. Boatſwaine, Maſter, Gunner, Citizens, and Souldiers, as many as may be.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Keep the Ports ſtrongly mann'd, and let none enter,
But ſuch as are known Patriots.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Liberty, liberty,

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſubſtantial thing, and not a word
You men of Naples, which if once taken from us,
All other bleſſings leave us; 'tis a jewel
Worth purchaſing, at the dear rate of life,
And ſo to be defended. O remember
What you have ſuffer'd, ſince you parted with it;
And if again you wiſh not to be ſlaves,
And properties to Ferrand's pride and luſt,
Take noble courage, and make pefect what
Is happily begun.

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.l: Our great preſerver,
You have infranchis'd us, from wretched bondage.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.l: And might be known, to whom we owe our freedom,
We to the death would follow him.

sp.speaker: 3. Cit.
sp.l: Make him King,
The Tyrant once remov'd.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: That's not my end.
'Twas not ambition that brought me hither,
With theſe my faithful friends, nor hope of ſpoil;
For when we did poſſeſs the Tyrants treaſure,
By force extorted from you, and employed,
To load you with moſt miſerable thraldome,
We did not make it ours, but with it purchas'd
The help of theſe, to get you liberty,
That for the ſame price kept you in ſubjection.
Nor are we Switzers, worthy Countrey-men,
But Neapolitans, now eye me well;
And tho the reverend Emblems of mine age,
My ſilver locks are ſhorne, my beard cut off,
Partaking yet of an adulterate Colour;
Tho 14 years you have not ſeen this face,
You may remember it, and call to mind,
There was a Duke of Seſſ, A much wrong'd Prince,
Wrong'd by this Tyrant Ferrand.

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.l: Now I know him.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.l: 'Tis he, long live the Duke of Seſſ.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: I thank you.
The injuries I receiv'd, I muſt confeſs,
Made me forget the love I owed this Country,
For which I hope, I have given ſatisfaction,
In being the firſt that ſtir'd, to give it freedome;
And with your loves and furtherance, will call back,
Long baniſht peace, and plenty, to this people:

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.l: Lead where you pleaſe, we'll follow.

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.l: Dare all dangers.

div.stage: Enter Pandulf, the Bodies of Virolet, and Juliana upon a Hearſe.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: What ſolemn funeral's this?

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: There reſt a while,
And if't be poſſible there can be added
Wings to your ſwift deſire of juſt revenge,
Hear, (if my tears will give way to my words)
In brief a moſt ſad ſtory.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Speak, what are they?
I know thee well Pandulfe.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: My beſt Lord?
As far as ſorrow will give leave, moſt welcome;
This Virolet was, and but a Son of mine,
I might ſay, the moſt hopeful of our Gentry;
And though unfortunate, never ignoble:
But I'll ſpeak him no farther. Look on this,
This face, that in a ſavage would move pitty,
The wonder of her Sex, and having ſaid
'Tis Juliana, Eloquence will want words
To ſet out her deſervings; this bleſt Lady
That did indure the Rack, to ſave her Husband,
That Husband, who, in being forc'd to leave her,
Indur'd a thouſand tortures; by what practiſe,
I know not, (but 'twas ſure a cunning one)
Are made, the laſt I hope, but ſad examples
Of Ferrands tyranny. Convey the bodies hence.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Expreſs your ſorrow
In your revenge, not teares, my worthy Soldiers:
That fertile earth that teem'd ſo many children,
To feed his cruelty, in her wounded wombe,
Can hardly now receive 'em.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: We are cold,
Cold walls ſhall not keep him from us.

sp.speaker: Gun.
sp.l: Were he cover'd with mountains, and room only for a
Bullet to be ſent level at him, I would ſpeed him.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Let's ſcale this petty Tower; at Sea we are Falcons,
And fly unto the main top in a moment.
What then can ſtop us here?

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.l: We'll tear him piece-meal.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: Or eat a paſſage to him.

sp.speaker: Seſ.
sp.l: Let diſcretion
Direct your anger; that's a victory,
Which is got with leaſt loſs, let us make ours ſuch:
And therefore friends, while we hold parley here,
Raiſe your ſcalado on the other ſide,
But enter'd wreak your ſuffrings.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.l: In our wrongs.
There was no mean.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: Nor in our full revenge
Will we know any.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Be appeas'd good man,
No ſorrow can redeem them from deaths Priſon;
What his inevitable hand hath ſeiz'd on,
The world cannot recover. All the comfort
That I can give to you, is to ſee vengeance
Pour'd dreadfully upon the Authors head,
Of which their aſhes may be ſenſible,
That have faln by him. Sound a parley.

div.stage: Enter Ferrand, Martia, Aſcanio, and Ronvere, above.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: They appear.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: 'Tis not that we eſteem rebellions Traytors
Worthy an anſwer to their proudeſt Summons
That we vouchſafe our preſence; or to exchange
One ſyllable with 'em: but to let ſuch know,
Though circled round with treaſon, all points bent
As to their Center at my heart, 'tis free,
Free from f a • , villains, and in this weak Tower
Ferrand commands as abſolute, as when
He trod upon your necks, and as much ſorns you.
And when the Sun of Majeſty ſhall break through
The clouds of your rebellion, every beam
Inſtead of comfortable heat ſhall ſend
Conſuming plagues among you; and you call
That government which you term'd tyrannous
Hereafter, gentle.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Flatter not thy ſelf
With theſe deluding hopes, thou cruel beaſt,
Thou art ith'toyle, and the glad Huntſman prouder,
By whom thou art taken, of his prey, than if
(Like thee) he ſhould command, and ſpoil his Forreſt.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: What art thou?

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: To thy horror Duke of Seſſe.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: The Divel.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Reſerv'd for thy damnation.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Why ſhakes my love?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: O I am loſt for ever;
Mountains divide me from him; ſome kind hand
Prevent our fearful meeting: Or lead me
To the ſteep rock, whoſe rugged brows are bent
Upon the ſwelling main; there let me hide me:
And as our bodies then ſhall be divided,
May our ſouls never meet.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Whence grows this, Sweeteſt?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There are a thouſand furies in his looks;
And in his deadly ſilence more loud horror,
Than when in hell the tortur'd and tormentors
Contend whoſe ſhreeks are greater. Wretched me!
It is my father.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Yes, and I will own her, Sir,
Till my revenge. It is my daughter, Ferrand;
My daughter thou haſt whor'd.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I triumph in it:
To know ſhe's thine, affords me more true pleaſure,
Than the act gave me, when even at the height,
I crack'd her Virgin zone. Her ſhame dwell on thee,
And all thy family; may they never know
A female iſſue, but a whore; Aſcanio.
Ronvere, look cheerfull; be thou a man too,
And learn of me to dye. That we might fall,
And in our ruines ſwallow up this Kingdom,
Nay the whole world, and make a ſecond Chaos.
And if from thence a new beginning riſe,
Be it recorded this did end with us;
And from our duſt hath embryon.

sp.speaker: Ron.
sp.l: I liv'd with you,
And will dye with you; your example makes me
Equally bold.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: And I reſolv'd to bear
What ere my fate appoints me.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: They are ours,
Now to the ſpoyl.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Pitty the Lady; to all elſe be deaf. Exeunt.
Within, Kill, kill, kill. Alarum Flo. Trumpets. Retreat.

div.stage: Enter Seſſe with Ferrands head, the Citizens, Maſter, Boteſwaine, Gunner, Souldiers bringing in Aſcanio, and Martia.

sp.speaker: Seſs.
sp.l: Cruel beginnings meet with cruel ends;
And the beſt ſacrifice to Heaven for peace,
Is tyrants blood: and thoſe that ſtuck faſt to him,
Fleſh'd inſtruments in his commands to miſchief,
With him diſpatch'd.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: They are cut off.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: 'Tis well.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Thanks to the Duke of Seſſe.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Pay that to Heaven,
And for a general joy, give general thanks:
For bleſſings nere deſcend from Heaven, but when
A grateful Sacrifice aſcends from men.
To your devotion, leave me, there's a Scene,
Which I would act alone; yet you may ſtay,
For wanting juſt ſpectators, 'twill be nothing.
The reſt forbear me.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Liberty, liberty, liberty.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I would I were as far beneath the Centre,
As now I ſtand above it; how I tremble!
Thrice happy they that dyed; I dying live
To ſtand the whirlwind of a fathers fury.
Now it moves toward me.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Thou, I want a name,
By which to ſtile thee: All articulate ſounds
That do expreſs the miſchief of vile woman,
That are, or have been, or ſhall be, are weak
To ſpeak thee to the height. Witch, Parricide,
For thou, in taking leave of modeſty,
Haſt kild thy father, and his honor loſt;
He's but a walking ſhadow to torment thee.
To leave, and rob thy father; then ſet free
His foes, whoſe ſlavery he did prefer
Above all treaſure, was a ſtrong defeazance
To cut off, even the ſureſt bonds of mercy.
After all this, having given up thy ſelf,
Like to a ſenſual beaſt, a ſlave to luſt,
To play the whore, and then (high Heaven it racks me)
To find out none to quench thy appetite,
But the moſt cruel King, whom next to Hell,
Thy father hated; and whoſe black imbraces
Thou ſhouldſt have fled from, as the whips of furies;
What canſt thou look for?

div.stage: Enter Pandulph, and bodies born on the Herſe.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Death; and 'tis not in you
To hurt me farther: my old reſolution,
Take now the place of fear; in this I liv'd,
In this I'll dye, your daughter.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Look but here;
You had I know, a guilty hand in this;
Repent it Lady.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Juliana dead?
And Virolet?

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: By her unwilling hand.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Fates you are equal. What can now fall on me,
That I will ſhrink at? now unmov'd I dare
Look on your anger, and not bend a knee
To ask your pardon; let your rage run higher
Than billows rais'd up by a violent Tempeſt,
And be, as that is, deaf to all intreaties:
They are dead, and I prepar'd; for in their fall
All my deſires are ſumm'd up.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Impudent too?
Die in it wretch.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Stay Sir. Boatſ. kills her.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: How dar'ſt thou villain,
Snatch from my ſword the honor of my juſtice?

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: I never did you better ſervice Sir,
Yet have been ever faithful. I confeſs
That ſhe deſerv'd to dye; but by whoſe hand?
Not by a fathers. Double all her guilt,
It could not make you innocent, had you done it.
In me 'tis murder, in you 'twere a crime
Heaven could not pardon. Witneſs that I love you,
And in that love I did it.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: Thou art Noble,
I thank thee for't; the thought of her dye with her.

sp.speaker: Aſc.
sp.l: My turn is next: ſince ſhe could find no mercy,
What am I to expect?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: With one voyce, Sir,
The Citizens ſalute you with the ſtile
Of King of Naples.

sp.speaker: Seſſ.
sp.l: I muſt be excus'd,
The burden is too heavy for my ſhoulder,
Beſtow it where 'tis due Stand forth Aſcanio,
It does belong to you; live long and wear it,
And warn'd by the example of your Unkle,
Learn that you are to govern men, not beaſts:
And that it is a moſt improvident head,
That ſtrives to hurt the limbs that do ſupport it.
Give burial to the dead; for me, and mine,
We will again to Sea, and never know,
The place, which in my birth firſt gave me woe. Exeunt

div.head: THE Maid in the Mill. A COMEDY.
The Perſons Repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Otrante a Spaniſh Count, in love with Florimel.
Julio, A Noble Man, Ʋncle to Antonio.
Bellides, Father to Iſmenia, Enemy to Julio.
Liſauro, Brother to Iſmenia, Bellides Son.
Terzo, Kinſman to Liſauro, and friend to Bellides.
Antonio, In love with Iſmenia, an enemy to Bellides.
Martino, Friend to Antonio, and his ſecret Rival
Lords, attending the King in progreſs.
Franio, A Miller, ſuppoſed Father to Florimell.
Buſtopha, Franio his Son, a Clown.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Iſmenia, Daughter to Bellides, Miſtriſs of Antonio.
Aminta, Couſen to Iſmenia, and her private competrix in Antonio's love.
Florimell, Suppoſed Daughter to Franio, Daughter to Julio, ſtolen from him a child.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Liſauro, Terzo, Iſmenia, and Aminta.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: LEt the Coach go round, we'll walk along theſe Meadows:
And meet at Port again: Come my fair Siſter,
Theſe cool ſhades will delight ye,

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Pray be merry,
The Birds ſing as they meant to entertain ye,
Every thing ſmiles abroad; methinks the River
(As he ſteals by) curles up his head, to view ye:
Every thing is in love.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: You would have it ſo.
You that are fair, are eaſie of belief, Coſen,
The theam ſlides from your tongue.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I fair? I thank ye:
Mine's but ſhadow when your Sun ſhines by me.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: No more of this, you know your worth (Aminta)
Where are we now?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Hard by the Town (Iſmena)

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: Cloſe by the Gates;

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: 'Tis a fine Ayr.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: A delicate;
The way ſo ſweet and even, that the Coach
Would be a tumbling trouble to our pleaſures:
Methinks I am very merry:

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I am ſad:

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You are ever ſo when we entreat ye (Coſen)

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I have no reaſon: ſuch a trembling here
Over my heart methinks:

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Sure you are faſting;
Or not ſlept well to night; ſome dream (Iſmena?)

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: My dreams are like my thoughts, honeſt and innocent,
Yours are unhappy? who are theſe that coaſt us? Enter Antonio and Martin.
You told me the walk was private.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt commonly:

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Two proper men: It ſeems they have ſome buſineſs,
With me none ſure; I do not like their faces;
They are not of our Company:

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: No Coſen:
Liſauro, we are dog'd.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I find it (Coſen)

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What handſome Lady?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, ſhe's very handſome.
They are handſome both.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Martin, ſtay we are coſen'd.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I will go up; a woman is no wild-fire.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Now by my life ſhe is ſweet: Stay good Martin,
They are of our enemies; the houſe of Belides.
Our mortal enemies:

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let 'em be devils,
They appear ſo handſomly, I will go forward;
If theſe be enemies, I'll ne'r ſeek friends more.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Prethee forbear, the Gentlewomen.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That's it (man)
That moves me like a Gin.
'Pray ye ſtand off Ladies:

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: They are both our enemies: both hate us equally;
By this fair day our mortal foes.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: I know 'em,
And come here to affront: how they gape at us?
They ſhall have gaping work.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Why your ſwords, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: Pray ye ſtand you off, Coſen,
And good now leave your whiſtling: we are abus'd all:
Back, back I ſay:

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Go back.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: We are no dogs Sir,
To run back on command.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: We'll make ye run, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Having a civil charge of handſome Ladies,
We are your ſervants: pray ye no quarrel Gentlemen.
There's way enough for both.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: We'll make it wider.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: If you will fight, arm'd from this Saint; have at ye.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: O me unhappy, are ye Gentlemen?
Diſcreet, and Civil, and in open view thus?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What will men think of us; nay you may kill us;
Mercy o'me; through my petticoat; what bloody Gentlemen!

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Make way through me, ye had beſt, and kill an innocent
Brother, why Coſen: by this light I'll dye too:
This Gentleman is temperate: be you merciful:
Alaſs, the Swords.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You had beſt run me through
'Twill be a valiant thruſt.

sp.speaker: Iſm,
sp.l: I faint amongſt ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Pray ye be not fearful: I have done (ſweet Lady)
My ſwords already aw'd, and ſhall obey ye:
I come not here to violate ſweet beauty,
I bow to that.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Brother, you ſee this Gentleman,
This noble Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Let him avoid then,
And leave our Walk.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The Lady may command Sir,
She bears an eye more dreadful than your weapon.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: What a ſweet nature this man has? dear brother,
Put up your ſword.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: Let them put up and walk then:

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No more loud words: there's time enough before us:
For ſhame put up, do honor to theſe beauties:

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Our way is this,
We will not be denyed it.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: And ours is this, we will not be croſs'd in it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What ere your way is (Lady) 'tis a fair one;
And may it never meet with rude hands more,
Nor rough uncivil Tongues. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I thank ye Sir,
Indeed I thank ye nobly: a brave Enemy,
Here's a ſweet temper now: This is a man (Brother)
This Gentleman's anger is ſo nobly ſeated,
That it becomes him: Yours proclaim ye Monſters.
What if he be our Houſe-Foe? we may brag on't:
We have ne'er a friend in all our Houſe ſo honorable:
I had rather from an Enemy, my Brother,
Learn worthy diſtances and modeſt difference,
Than from a race of empty friends, loud nothings:
I am hurt between ye.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: So am I, I fear too: Dear Coſen
Why look ye pale? where are ye hurt?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I know not,
But here methinks.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Unlace her gentle Couſen.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: My heart, my heart, and yet I bleſs the Hurter.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Is it ſo dangerous?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Nay, nay, I faint not.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Here is no blood that I find, ſure 'tis inward:

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Yes, yes, 'tis inward: 'twas a ſubtle weapon,
The hurt not to be cur'd I fear.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: The Coach there.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: May be a fright.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Aminta, 'twas a ſweet one,
And yet a cruel.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Now I find the wound plain:
A wondrous handſome Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Oh no deeper:
Prethee be ſilent, (wench) it may be thy caſe.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You muſt be ſearched; the wound will rancle, Coſen
And of ſo ſweet a nature.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Dear Aminta:
Make it not ſorer.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: And on my life admires ye.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Call the Coach, Coſen.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: The Coach, the Coach.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: 'Tis ready bring the Coach there.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Well my brave Enemies, we ſhall yet meet ye,
And our old hate ſhall teſtifie.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: It ſhall (Coſen.) Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Their ſwords, alaſs, I weigh 'em not (dear Friend)
The indiſcretion of the Owners blunts 'em;
The fury of the Houſe affrights not me,
It ſpends it ſelf in words: (Oh me Martine)
There was a two edg'd eye, a Lady carried
A weapon that no valor can avoyd,
Nor Art (the hand of Spirit) put aſide.
O Friend, it broke out on me like a bullet
Wrapt in a cloud of fire: that point (Martine)
Dazled my ſence? and was too ſubtle for me,
Shot like a Comet in my face, and wounded
(To my eternal ruine, my hearts valor.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Methinks ſhe was no ſuch piece.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Blaſpheme not Sir,
She is ſo far beyond weak commendation,
That impudence will bluſh to think ill of her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I ſee it not, and yet I have both eyes open:
And I could judge, I know there is no beauty
Till our eyes give it 'em, and make 'em handſome;
What's red and white, unleſs we do allow 'em?
A green face elſe; and me-thinks ſuch an other.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Peace thou leud Heretick; Thou judge of beauties?
Thou haſt an excellent ſenſe for a ſign-poſt (Friend)
Doſt thou not ſee? I'll ſwear thou art ſoon blind elſe,
As blind as ignorance; when ſhe appeared firſt
Aurora breaking in the eaſt, and through her face,
As if the hours and graces had ſtrew'd Roſes,
A bluſh of wonder flying; when ſhe was frighted
At our uncivil ſwords, didſt thou not mark
How far beyond the purity of ſnow
The ſoft wind drives whiteneſs of innocence,
Or any thing that bears Celeſtial paleneſs,
She appear'd o'th' ſodain? Didſt thou not ſee her tears
When ſhe intreated? O thou Reprobate!
Didſt thou not ſee thoſe orient tears flow'd from her,
The little Worlds of Love? A ſet (Martine)
Of ſuch ſanctified Beads, and a holy heart to love
I could live ever a Religious Hermite.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I do believe a little, and yet methinks
She was of the loweſt ſtature.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A rich Diamond
Set neat and deep, Natures chief Art (Martine)
Is to reſerve her Models curious,
Not cumberſome and great; and ſuch an one
For fear ſhe ſhould exceed, upon her matter
Has ſhe fram'd this; Oh 'tis a ſpark of beauty,
And where they appear ſo excellent in little,
They will but flame in great; Extention ſpoils 'em:
Martine learn this, the narrower that our eyes
Keep way unto our object, ſtill the ſweeter
That comes unto us: Great bodies are like Countries,
Diſcovering ſtill, toyl and no pleaſure finds 'em.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A rare Coſmographer for a ſmall Iſland,
Now I believe ſhe is handſome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Believe heartily,
Let thy belief, though long a coming, ſave thee.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: She was (certain) fair.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But heark ye (friend Martine)
Do not believe your ſelf too far before me,
For then you may wrong me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Who bid ye teach me?
Do you ſhow me meat, and ſtitch my lips (Antonio?)
Is that fair play?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Now if thou ſhouldſt abuſe me,
And yet I know thee for an errant wencher,
A moſt immoderate thing, thou canſt not love long.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A little ſerves my turn, I fly at all games,
But I believe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How if we never ſee her more?
She is our enemy.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why are you jealous then?
As far as I conceive ſhe hates our whole Houſe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yet (good Martine)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Come, come, I have mercy on ye:
You ſhall enjoy her in your dream (Antonio)
And I'll not hinder: though now I perſwade my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sit with perſwaſion down, and you deal honeſtly:
I will look better on her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay, who's this, Friend?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Is't not the other Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, a Letter.
She brings to challenge ſure: if ſhe do (Antonio)
I hope ſhe'll be a Second too; I am for her.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: A good hour Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You are welcome Lady;
'Tis like our late rude paſſage has powr'd on us
Some reprehenſion.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: No I bring no anger,
Though ſome deſerv'd it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sure we were all to blame, Lady;
But for my part (in all humility
And with no little ſhame) I ask your pardons,
Indeed I wear no ſword to fright ſweet beauties.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You have it, and this Letter; pray ye Sir view it,
And my Commiſſion's done.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Have ye none for me Lady?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Not at this time.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am ſorry for't; I can read too.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I am glad: but Sir, to keep you in your exerciſe,
You may chance meet with one ill written.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thank ye,
So it be a womans; I can pick the meaning,
For likely they have but one end.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You ſay true Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Martine, my wiſhes are come home and loaden,
Loaden with brave return: moſt happy, happy:
I am a bleſſed man: where's the Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Gone, the ſpirit's gone, what news?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis from the Lady;
From her we ſaw: from that ſame miracle,
I know her name now: read but theſe three lines;
Read with devotion, friend, the lines are holy.

l.hi: I dare not chide ye in my Letter, (Sir)
'Twill be too gentle: If you pleaſe to look me
In the Weſt-ſtreet, and find a fair Stone window,
Carved with white Cupids; there I'll entertain ye:
Night and diſcretion guide ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Give it me again: Come, come, fly, fly, I am all fire.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There may be danger.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: So there is to drink
When men are thirſty, to eat haſtily
When we are hungry: ſo there is in ſleep, Friend,
Obſtructions then may riſe and ſmother us,
We may dye laughing, choak'd even at devotions:
An Apoplexie, or a ſodain Palſey
May ſtrike us down.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: May be a train to catch ye.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Then I am caught: and let Love anſwer for it.
'Tis not my folly, but his infamy,
And if he be ador'd, and dare do vild things.—

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Well, I will go.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She is a Lady, Sir,
A Maid, I think, and where that holy ſpell
Is flung about me, I ne're fear a villany,
'Tis almoſt night: away friend.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am ready,
I think I know the houſe too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Then are we happy. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Did you meet him?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: And did you give my Letter?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: To what end went I?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Are ye ſure it was he?
Was it that Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Do you think I was blind?
I went to ſeek no Carrier, nor no Midwife.

sp.speaker: Iſ.
sp.l: What kind of man was he? thou mayſt be deceiv'd Friend

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: A man with a noſe on's face: I think he had eyes too,
And hands: for ſure he took it.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: What an anſwer?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What queſtions are theſe to one that's hot and troubled?
Do you think me a Babe? am I not able (Coſin)
At my years and diſcretion, to deliver
A Letter handſomely! Is that ſuch a hard thing?
Why every Wafer-woman will undertake it:
A Sempſters girl, or a Tailors wife will not miſs it:
A Puritan Hoſteſs (Coſin) would ſcorn theſe queſtions.
My legs are weary.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I'll make 'em well again.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Are they at ſupper?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Yes, and I am not well,
Nor deſire no company: look out, 'tis darkiſh.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I ſee nothing yet: aſſure your ſelf, Iſmena,
If he be a man, he will not miſs.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: It may be he is modeſt,
And that may pull him back from ſeeing me;
Or has made ſome wild conſtruction of my eaſineſs:
I bluſh to think what I writ.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What ſhould ye bluſh at?
Bluſh when you act your thoughts, not when you write 'em;
Bluſh ſoft between a pair of ſheets, ſweet Coſin,
Though he be a curious carried Gentleman, I cannot think
He's ſo unnatural to leave a woman,
A young, a noble, and a beauteous woman,
Leave her in her deſires: Men of this age
Are rather prone to come before they are ſent for.
Hark, I hear ſomething: up to th'Chamber, Coſin,
You may ſpoil all elſe.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Let me ſee, they are Gentlemen;
It may be they.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: They are they: get ye up,
And like a Land-ſtar draw him.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I am ſhame-fac'd Exit.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This is the ſtreet.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am looking for the houſe:
Cloſe, cloſe, pray ye cloſe here.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No, this is a Merchants;
I know the man well:

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And this a Pothecaries: I have lain here many times.
For a looſeneſs in my hilts.

sp.speaker: Amt.
sp.l: Have ye not paſt it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No ſure:
There is no houſe of mark that we have ſcaped yet.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What place is this?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Speak ſofter: 'may be ſpies;
If any, this, a goodly window too,
Carv'd far above, that I perceive: 'tis dark,
But ſhe has ſuch a luſtre.

div.stage: Enter Iſmena and Aminta above with a Taper.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes Martine,
So radiant ſhe appears.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Elſe we may miſs, Sir:
The night grows vengeance black, pray heaven ſhe ſhine clear:
Hark, hark, a window, and a candle too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Step cloſe, 'tis ſhe: I ſee the cloud diſperſe,
And now the beauteous Planet.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Ha, 'tis indeed,
Now by the ſoul of love a Divine Creature.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Sir, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Moſt bleſſed Lady.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: 'Pray ye ſtand out.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You need not fear, there's no body now ſtirring.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Beyond his commendation I am taken,
Infinite ſtrangely taken.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I love that Gentleman,
Methinks he has a dainty nimble body:
I love him heartily.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: 'Tis the right Gentleman:
•• t what to ſay to him, Sir.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Speak.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I wait ſtill,
And will do till I grow another Pillar,
To prop this houſe, ſo it pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Speak ſoftly,
And 'pray ye ſpeak truly too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I never ly'd, Lady.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: And don't think me impudent to ask ye,
I know ye are an enemy, ſpeak low,
But I would make ye a friend.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I am friend to beauty;
There's no handſomneſs, I dare be foe to.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Are ye married?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Are ye betrothed?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No, neither?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Indeed (fair Sir.)

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Indeed (fair ſweet) I am not.
Moſt beauteous Virgin, I am free as you are.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: That may be, Sir, then ye are miſerable,
For I am bound.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Happy the bonds that hold ye;
Or do you put them on your ſelf for pleaſure?
Sure they be ſweeter far than liberty:
There is no bleſſedneſs but in ſuch bondage:
Give me that freedom (Madam) I beſeech ye,
(Since you have queſtion'd me ſo cunningly)
To ask you whom you are bound to, he muſt be certain
More than humane, that bounds in ſuch a beauty:
Happy that happy chain, ſuch links are heavenly.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Pray ye do not mock me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Pray ye (Lady) tell me.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Will ye believe, and will ye keep it to ye?
And not ſcorn what I ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I dare not, Madam,
As Oracle what you ſay, I dare ſwear to.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I'll ſet the candle by: for I ſhall bluſh now;
Fie, how it doubles in my mouth? it muſt out,
'Tis you I am bound to.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Speak that word again.
I underſtand ye not.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: 'Tis you I am bound to.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Here is another Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: 'Tis you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: He may be lov'd too.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Not by thee, firſt curſe me.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: And if I knew your name.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Antonio (Madam)

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Antonio, take this kiſs, 'tis you I am bound to.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And when I ſet ye free, may heaven forſake me,

l.hi: Iſmena.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Yes, now I perceive ye love me,
You have learn'd my name.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Hear but ſome vows I make to ye:
Hear but the proteſtations of a true love.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: No, no, not now: vows ſhould be cheerful things,
Done in the cleereſt light, and nobleſt teſtimony:
No vow, dear Sir, tie not my fair belief
To ſuch ſtrict terms: thoſe men have broken credits,
Looſe and diſmembred faiths (my dear Antonio)
That ſplinter 'em with vows: am I not too bold?
Correct me when you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I had rather hear ye,
For ſo ſweet Muſick never ſtruk mine ears yet:
Will you believe now?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I am yours.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Speak louder,
If ye anſwer the Prieſt ſo low, you will loſe your wedding.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Would I might ſpeak, I would holloa.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Take my heart,
And if it be not firm and honeſt to you,
Heaven—

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Peace, no more: I'll keep your heart, and credit it.
Keep you your word: when when will you come again (Friend?)
For this time we have woo'd indifferently.
I would fain ſee ye, when I dare be bolder.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why any night: only (dear noble Miſtriſs)
Pardon three daies: my Uncle Julio
Has bound me to attend him upon promiſe,
Upon expectation too: we have rare ſports there,
Rare Countrey ſports, I would you could but ſee 'em.
Dare ye ſo honor me?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I dare not be there,
You know I dare not, no, I muſt not (Friend)
Where I may come with honourable freedom:
Alas, I am ill too; we in love.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You flout me.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Truſt me I do not: I ſpeak truth, I am ſickly,
And am in love: but you muſt be Phyſician.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'll make a plaiſter of my beſt affection.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Be gone, we have ſupp'd, I hear the people ſtir,
Take my beſt wiſhes: give me no cauſe (Antonio)
To curſe this happy night.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'll loſe my life firſt,
A thouſand kiſſes.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Take ten thouſand back again.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am dumb with admiration: ſhall we goe, Sir?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Doſt thou know his Uncle?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: No, but I can ask, Coſin.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I'll tell thee more of that, come, let's to bed both,
And give me handſome dreams, Love, I beſeech thee.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: 'Has given ye a handſome ſubject.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Pluck to the windows. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: THe thundring Seas, whoſe watry fire waſhes
The whiting mops:
The gentle Whale whoſe feet ſo ſell
Flies o'r the Mountains tops. within Franio.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Boy.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: The thundring.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why boy Buſtofa.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Here I am, the gentle Whale.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Oh, are you here, Sir? where's your Siſter?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: The gentle Whale flies o'r the Mountain tops.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Where's your Siſter (man)

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Waſhes the whiting-Mops.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Thou ly'ſt, ſhe has none to waſh Mops?
The boy is half way out of his wits, ſure:
Sirrah, who am I?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: The thundring Seas.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Mad, ſtark mad.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Will you not give a man leave to con?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Yes, and fe • ſe too, e'r I have done with you Sirrah,
Am I your father?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: The queſtion is too hard for a child, ask me any thing
That I have learn'd, and I'll anſwer you.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Is that a hard queſtion? Sirrah, am not I your Father

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: If I had my Mother-wit I could tell you.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Are you a thief?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: So far forth as the Son of a Miller.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Will you be hang'd?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Let it go by elderſhip. The gentle Whale. —

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Sirrah, lay by your fooliſh ſtudy there,
And beat your brains about your own affairs: or —

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I thank you; you'ld have me goe under the ſails
And beat my brains about your Mill? a natural
Father you are.—

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I charge you goe not to the ſports to day:
Laſt night I gave you leave, now I recant.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Is the wind turn'd ſince laſt night?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Marry is it, Sir, go no farther than my Mill;
There's my command upon you.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I may go round about then as your Mill does?
I will ſee your Mill gelded, and his Stones fry'd in ſteaks,
E'r I deceive the Countrey ſo: have I not my part to ſtudy?
How ſhall the ſports go forward, if I be not there?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: They'll want their fool indeed, if thou be'ſt not there.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Conſider that, and go your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I have fears, (Sir,) that I cannot utter,
You goe not, nor your Siſter: there's my charge.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: The price of your golden thumb cannot hold me.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I, this was ſport that I have tightly lov'd,
I could have kept company with the Hounds.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: You are fit for no other company yet.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Run with the Hare; and bin in the whore's tail y'faith:

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: That was before I was born,
I did ever miſtruſt I was a Baſtard,
Becauſe Lapis is in the ſingular number with me.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Leave thou that game (Geraſto) and chaſe here,
Do thou but follow it with my deſires,
Thou'lt not return home empty.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I am prepar'd
(My Lord) with advantages: and ſee
Yonder's the ſubject I muſt work upon:

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Her brother 'tis: methinks it ſhould be eaſie:
That groſs compound cannot but diffuſe
The ſoul in ſuch a latitude of eaſe,
As to make dull her faculties, and lazie:
What wit above the leaſt can be in him,
That Reaſon ties together?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: I have prov'd it, Sir,
And know the depth of it: I have the way
To make him follow me a hackney-pace,
With all that fleſh about him; yes, and dragg
His Siſter after him: This baits the old one,
Rid you him, and leave me to the other. Exit.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: 'Tis well: Oh Franio, the good day to you;
You were not wont to hear this Muſick ſtanding:
The Beagle and the Bugle ye have lov'd,
In the firſt rank of Huntſmen.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: The dogs cry out of him now.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Sirrah, leave your barking, I'll bite you elſe:

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Curr, Curr.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Slave, do'ſt call me dog?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Oh ſie Sir, he ſpeaks Latine to you,
He would know why you'll bite him.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Reſponde cur; You ſee his underſtanding (my Lord.)

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I ſhall have a time to curry you for this:
But (my Lord) to anſwer you, the daies have been
I muſt have footed it before this Horn-pipe,
Though I had hazarded my Mill a fire,
And let the ſtones grind empty: but thoſe dancings
Are done with me: I have good will to it ſtill,
And that's the beſt I can do,

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Come, come, you ſhall be hors'd:
Your company deſerves him, though you kill him,
Run him blind, I care not.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: He'll do't o'th' purpoſe (my Lord) to bring him up to the Mill.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Do not tempt me too far (my Lord.)

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: There's a foot i'th' ſtirrop: I'll not leave you now:
You ſhall ſee the Game fall once again:

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Well (my Lord) I'll make ready my legs for you,
And try 'em once a horſeback: ſirrah, my charge, keep it.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Yes, when you pare down your diſh for conſcience ſake.
When your thumb's coyn'd into bone & legalis,
When you are a true Man-Miller.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: What's the matter Buſtofa?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: My Lord; if you have e'r a drunken Jade that has the ſtaggers,
That will fall twice the height of our Mill with him: ſet him out o' the
O'th' back on him: a galled Jennet that will winch him there
Saddle, and break one on's necks, or a ſhank of him was
A fool going that way, but the Aſſe had better luck;)
Or one of your brave Barharies, that would paſs the Straits, and run
Into his own Countrey with him; the firſt Moor he met, would
Cut his throat for Complexions ſake: there's as deadly feud between
A Moor and a Miller, as between black and white.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Fie, fie, this is unnatural Buſtofa,
Unleſs on ſome ſtrong cauſe.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Be Judge (my Lord)
I am ſtudied in my part: the Julian Feaſt is to day: the Countrey
Expects me; I ſpeak all the dumb ſhews: my Siſter choſen for
A Nimph. The gentle Whale whoſe feet ſo fell: Cry mercy,
That was ſome of my part: But his charge is to keep the Mill,
And diſappoint the Revels.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Indeed, there it ſpeaks ſhrewdly for thee; the Countrey expecting.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I, and for mine own grace too.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Yes, and being ſtudied too: and the main Speaker too.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: The main? why all my Speech lies in the main,
And the dry ground together: The thundering ſeas whoſe, &c.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Nay, then thou muſt go, thou'lt be much condemn'd elſe.
But then o'th' other ſide, obedience.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Obedience?
But ſpeak your conſcience now (my Lord)
Am not I paſt asking bleſſing at theſe years?
Speak as you're a Lord, if you had a Miller to your father.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I muſt yield to you (Buſtofa,) your reaſons
Are ſo ſtrong, I cannot contradict: This I think,
If you goe; your Siſter ought to go along with you.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: There I ſtumble now: ſhe is not at age.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Why, ſhe's fifteen, and upwards.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Thereabouts.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: That's womans ripe age; as full as thou art
At one and twenty: ſhe's manable, is ſhe not?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I think not: poor heart, ſhe was never try'd in my conſcience.
'Tis a coything; ſhe will not kiſs you a clown, not if he
Would kiſs her.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: What man?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Not if he would kiſs her, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Oh, 'twas cleanlier than I expected: well Sir,
I'll leave you to your own; but my opinion is,
You may take her along: this is half way:
The reſt (Geraſto) and I hunt my prey,— Exit.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Away with the old Miller (my Lord) and the Mill
Strikes ſail preſently.

div.stage: Enter Pedro, with Geraſto blind, ſinging.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Come follow me (you Countrey-Laſſes)
And you ſhall ſee ſuch ſport as paſſes:
You ſhall Dance, and I will Sing;
Pedro he ſhall rub the ſtring:
Each ſhall have a looſe bodied Gown
Of green; and laugh till you lie down.
Come follow me, come follow, &c.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: O ſweet Diego, the ſweeteſt Diego, ſtay: Siſter Florimel.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: What's that, Brother?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Didſt not hear Diego? Hear him, and thou'lt be raviſh'd.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I have heard him ſing, yet unraviſh'd, Brother.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: You had the better luck (Siſter.) I was raviſh'd
By my own conſent: Come away: for the Sports.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I have the fear of a Father on me (Brother.)

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Out: the thief is as ſafe as in his Mill: he's hunting with our
Great Land-lord, the Don Otrante. Strike up Diego.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: But ſay he return before us, where's our excuſe?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Strike up Diego. Haſt no ſtrings to thy apron?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Well, the fault lie upon your head (Brother.)

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: My faults never mount ſo high (girl) they riſe but to
My middle at moſt. Strike up Diego.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Follow me by the ear, I'll lead thee on (Buſtofa) and
Pretty Florimel thy Siſter: oh that I could ſee her.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Oh Diego, there's two pities upon thee; great pitie thou art blind;
And as great a pity, thou canſt not ſee.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: You ſhall have Crowns of Roſes, Dayſies,
Buds, where the honey-maker gazes;
You ſhall taſte the golden thighs,
Such as in Wax-Chamber lies.
What fruit pleaſe you, taſte, freely pull,
Till you have all your bellies full.
Come follow me. &c.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Oh, Diego, the Don was not ſo ſweet when he perfum'd the Steeple. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why, how now (Friend) thou art not loſt agen?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Not loſt? why, all the world's a wilderneſs:
Some places peopled more by braver beaſts
Than others are: But faces, faces (man)
May a man be caught with faces?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Without wonder,
'Tis odds againſt him: May not a good face
Lead a man about by th' noſe? 'las,
The noſe is but a part againſt the whole.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But is it poſſible that two faces
Should be ſo twin'd in form, complexion,
Figure, aſpect? that neither wen, nor mole,
The Table of the brow, the eyes luſtre,
The lips cherry; neither the bluſh nor ſmile
Should give the one diſtinction from the other?
Does Nature work in molds?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Altogether.
We are all one mold, one duſt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thy reaſon's moldie.
I ſpeak from the Form, thou the Matter.
Why? was't not ever one of Natures Glories,
Nay, her great piece of wonder, that amongſt
So many millions millions of her works
She left the eye diſtinction, to cull out
The one from th'other; yet all one name, the face?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You muſt compare 'em by ſome other part
Of the body, if the face cannot do't.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Didſt ask her name?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, and who gave it her?
And what they promis'd more, beſides a ſpoon,
And what Apoſtles picture: ſhe is chriſtned too,
In token wherefore ſhe is call'd Iſabella,
The daughter of a Countrey plow-ſwain by:
If this be not true, ſhe lies.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She cannot;
It would be ſeen a bliſter on her lip,
Should falſhood touch it, it is ſo tender:
Had her name held, 't had been Iſmenia,
And not another of her name.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Shall I ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes, if thou'lt ſpeak truth: Is ſhe not wondrous like?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: As two garments of the ſame faſhion,
Cut from the ſame piece, yet if any excell,
This has the firſt; and in my judgement 'tis ſo.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis my opinion.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Were it the face
Where mine eye ſhould dwell, I would pleaſe both
With this, as ſoon as one with the other.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And yet the other is the caſe of this.
Had I not look'd upon Iſmenia,
I ne'r had ſtaid beyond good-morrows time
In view of this.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Would I could leave him here,
'Twere a free paſſage to Iſmenia:
I muſt now blow, as to put out the fire
Yet kindle't more. You not conſider Sir,
The great diſparitie is in their bloods,
Eſtates and fortunes: there's the rich beauty
Which this poor homelineſs is not endow'd with;
There's difference enough.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The leaſt of all.
Equality is no rule in Loves Grammar:
That ſole unhappineſs is left to Princes
To marry bloud: we are free diſpoſers,
And have the power to equalize their blouds
Up to our own; we cannot keep it back,
'Tis a due debt from us.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I Sir, had you
No Father nor Uncle, nor ſuch hinderers,
You might do with your ſelf at your pleaſure;
But as it is.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: As it is; 'tis nothing:
Their powers will come too late, to give me back
The yeſterday I loſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Indeed, to ſay ſooth,
Your oppoſition from the other part
Is of more force; there you run the hazard
Of every hour a life, had you ſupply;
You meet your deareſt enemy in love
With all his hate about him: 'Twill be more hard
For your Iſmenia to come home to you,
Than yuu to goe to Countrey Iſabell.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Tuſh: 'tis not fear removes me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No more: your Uncle.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Oh, the good hour upon you Gentlemen:
Welcome Nephew; Speak it to your friend Sir,
It may be happier receiv'd from you,
In his acceptance.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I made bold, Uncle,
To do it before; and I think he believes it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Twas never doubted, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Here are ſports (Dons)
That you muſt look on with a loving eye,
And without Cenſure, 'leſs it be giving
My countrey neighbors loves their yearly offerings
That muſt not be refus'd; though't be more pain
To the Spectator, than the painful Actor,
'Twill abide no more teſt than the tinſel
We clad our Masks in for an hours wearing,
Or the Livery Lace ſometimes on the cloaks
Of a great Don's Followers: I ſpeak no further
Than our own Countrey, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For my part, Sir,
The more abſurd, 't ſhall be the better welcome.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: You'll find the gueſt you look for: I heard Confin,
You were at Toledo th' other day.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Not late, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Oh ſie! muſt I be plainer? You chang'd the point
With Tirſo and Liſauro, two of the Stock
Of our Antagoniſts, the Belides.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A meer proffer, Sir; the prevention
Was quick with us: we had done ſomewhat elſe:
This Gentleman was engag'd in't.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I am
The enemy to his foe for it: that wild-fire
Will crave more than fair water, to quench it
I ſuſpect. Whence it will come I know not.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I was about a gentle reconcilement,
But I do fear I ſhall goe back agen.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Come, come; The Sports are coming on us:
Nay, I have more gueſts to grace it: Welcome
Don Goſtanco, Giraldo, Philippo: Seat, ſeat all. Muſick.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: Love is little, and therefore I preſent him;
Love is a fire, therefore you may lament him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Alas poor Love, who are they that can quench him?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: He's not without thoſe members, fear him not.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: Love ſhoots, therefore I bear his bow about.
And Love is blind, therefore my eyes are out.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I never heard Love give reaſon for what he did before.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: Let ſuch as can ſee, ſee ſuch as cannot: behold,
Our goddeſſes all three ſtrive for the ball of Gold:
And here fair Paris comes, the hopeful youth of Troy,
Queen Hecub's darling-ſon, King Priams only joy.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Is this Paris? I ſhould have taken him for Hector rather.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Paris at this time: Pray you hold your prating.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Paris can be angry.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Oh at this time
You muſt pardon him; he comes as a Judge.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: —Mercy on all that looks upon him, ſay I.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: The thundring ſeas whoſe watry fire waſhes the Whiting Mops.
The gentle Whale, whoſe feet ſo fell, flies o'r the mountain tops.
No roars ſo fierce, no throats ſo deep, no howls can bring ſuch fears.
As Paris can, if Garden from he call his Dogs and Bears.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I, thoſe they were, that I fear'd all this while.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Yes Jack-an-Apes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I thank you good Paris.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: You may hold your peace, and ſtand further out o'th way then:
The lines will fall where they light,
Yes Jack-an-Apes, he hath to ſports, and faces make like mirth,
Whilſt bellowing buls, the horned beaſts; do toſs from ground to earth:
Blind Bear there is, as Cupid blind.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: That Bear would be whip'd for loſing of his eies.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Be whipped man may ſee,
But we preſent no ſuch content, but Nymphs ſuch as they be.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Theſe are long lines.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Can you blame him, leading Buls and Bears in 'em

div.stage: Enter Shepherd ſinging, with Iſmena, Aminta, Florimel, (as Juno, Pallas, Venus,) and three Nymphs attending.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Go Cupid blind, conduct the dumb, for Ladies muſt not ſpeak here:
Let ſhepherds ſing with dancing feet, and cords of muſick break here.
Now Ladies fight, with heels ſo light, by lot your luck muſt fall,
Where Paris pleaſe, to do you eaſe, and give the golden Ball. Dance.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If you plaid Paris now Antonio, where would you beſtow it?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I prethee, Friend,
Take the full freedom of thought, but no words.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Proteſt there's a third, which by her habit,
Should perſonate Venus, and by conſequence
Of the Story, receive the honors prize:
And were I a Paris, there it ſhould be.
Do you note her?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No; mine eye is ſo fixed,
I cannot move it.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: The dance is ended; Now to judgement Paris.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Here Juno, here: but ſtay, I do eſpy
A pretty gleek coming from Pallas eye:
Here Pallas, here: yet ſtay agen: methinks
I ſee the eye of lovely Venus winks:
Oh cloſe them both: ſhut in thoſe golden eyn,
And I will kiſs thoſe ſweet blind cheeks of thine.
Juno is angry: yes, and Pallas frowns,
Would Paris now were gone from Ida's downs.
They both are fair, but Venus has the Mole,
The faireſt hair, and ſweeteſt dimple hole:
To her, or her, or her, or neither;
Can one man pleaſe three Ladies altogether?
No, take it Venus, toſs it at thy pleaſure,
Thou art the Lovers friend beyond his meaſure,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Paris has done what man can do, pleas'd one,
Who can do more?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay, here's another perſon.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Come lovely Venus, leave this lower Orb,
And mount with Mars, up to his glorious Sphere.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: How now, what's he:

sp.speaker: Flor.
sp.l: I'm ignorant what to do, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Thy ſilver-yoke of Doves are in the Team,
And thou ſhalt fly through Apollo's Beam:
I'll ſee thee ſeated in thy golden Throne,
And hold with Mars a ſweet conjunction. Exit.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Ha? what follow's this? has carried away my Siſter Venus:
He never rehears'd his part with me before.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: What follows now Prince Paris?

l.hi: within.—Help, help, help.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Hue and cry, I think Sir, this is Venus voice,
Mine own Siſter Florinels.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What is there ſome Tragick-Act behind?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: No, no, altogether Comical; Mars and Venus
Are in the old conjunction it ſeems.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis very improper then, for Venus
Never cries out when ſhe conjoyns with Mars.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: That's true indeed: they are out of their parts ſure,
It may be 'Tis the Book-holders fault: I'll go ſee.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: How like you our Countrey Revels, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: All Gent.
sp.l: Oh, they commend themſelves, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Methinks now
Juno and Minerva ſhould take revenge on Paris.
It cannot end without it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I did expect
Inſtead of Mars, the Storm-Goaler Eolus,
And Juno proff'ring her Deiopeia
As ſatisfaction to the bluſtring god,
To ſend his Toſſers forth.

sp.speaker: Jul,
sp.l: It may ſo follow,
Lets not prejudicate the Hiſtory.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Oh, oh, oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: So, here's a Paſſion towards.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Help, help, if you be Gentlemen; my Siſter,
My Venus, ſhe's ſtolen away.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: The ſtory changes from our expectation,

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Help my father the Miller will hang me elſe: god Mars.
Is a bawdy Villain: he ſaid ſhe ſhould ride upon Doves:
She's hors'd, ſhe's hors'd, whether ſhe will or no.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sure I think he's ſerious.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: She's hors'd upon a double Gelding, and a Stone-horſe in the breech
Of her: the poor wench cries help, and I cry help, and none
Of you will help.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Speak, is it the ſhow, or doſt thou bawl?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: A pox on the Ball: my Siſter bawls, and I bawl:
Either bridle horſe and follow, or give me a halter
To hang my ſelf: I cannot run ſo faſt as a hog.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Follow me, I'll fill the Countrey with purſuit
But I will find the thief: my houſe thus abus'd?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: 'Tis my houſe that's abus'd, the Siſter of my fleſh and bloud: oh, oh, Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Wench.
sp.l: 'Tis time we all ſhift for cur ſelves, if this be ſerious.
However I'll be gone.
And I. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You need not fright your beauties pretty ſouls,
With the leaſt pale complexion of a fear.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Juno has better courage: and Minerva's more diſcreet

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Alas my courage was ſo counterfeit
It might have been ſtruck from me with a Feather.
Juno ne'r had ſo weak a preſenter.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Sure I was ne'r the wiſer for Minerva,
That I find yet about me.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: My dwelling, Sir?
'Tis a poor yeomans roof, ſcarce a league off,
That never ſham'd me yet.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Your gentle pardon:
I vow my erring eies had almoſt caſt you
For one of the moſt mortal enemies
That our Family has.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I'm ſorry, Sir,
I am ſo like your foe: 'Twere fit I haſted
From your offended ſight.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Oh, miſtake not,
It was my error, and I do confeſs it:
You'll not believe you'r welcome; nor can I ſpeak it;
But there's my friend can tell you, pray hear him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Shall I tell her Sir? I'm glad of the employment.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A kinſwoman to that beauty:

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: A kin to her, Sir,
But nothing to her beauty.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Do not wrong it, 'tis not far behind her.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Her hinder parts are not far off, indeed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let me but kiſs you with his ardor now,
You ſhall feel how he loves you.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Oh forbear:
'Tis not the faſhion with us, but would you.
Perſwade me that he loves me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I'll warrant you
He dies in't: and that were witneſs enough on't.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Love me Sir? can you tell me for what reaſon?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Fie, will you ask me that which you have about you?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I know nothing Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let him find it then;
He conſtantly believes you have the thing
That he muſt love you for: much is apparent,
A ſweet and lovely beauty.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: So Sir; Pray you
Show me one thing: Did he ne'r love before?
(I know you are his boſom-Counſellor)
Nay then I ſee your anſwer is not ready:
I'll not believe you if you ſtudy farther.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Shall I ſpeak truth to you?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Or ſpeak no more.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There was a ſmile thrown at him, from a Lady
Whoſe deſerts might buy him trebble, and lately
He receiv'd it, and I know where he loſt it,
In this face of yours: I know his heart's within you.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: May I know her name?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: In your ear you may
With vow of ſilence.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: He'll not give over Sir:
If he ſpeak for you, he'll ſure ſpeed for you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But that's not the anſwer to my queſtion.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You are the firſt in my Virgin-conſcience
That e'r ſpoke Love to her: oh, my heart!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How do you?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Nothing Sir: but would I had a better face.
How well your pulſe beats.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Healthfully, does it not?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: It thumps prettily, methinks.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Alack, I hear it
With much pity: how great is your fault too,
In wrong to the good Lady?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You forget
The difficult paſſage he has to her,
A hell of feud's between the Families.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: And that has often Love wrought by advantage
To peaceful reconcilement.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: This way 'tis worſer; 't may ſeed again in her
Unto another generation:
For where (poor Lady) is her ſatisfaction?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It comes in me; to be truth, I love her
(I'll go no farther for compariſon)
As dear as he loves you.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: How if ſhe love not?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Tuſh: be that my pains: You know not what Art
I have thoſe ways.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Beſhrow you, you have practis'd upon me,
Well, ſpeed me here, and you with your Iſmenia.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Go, the condition's drawn, ready dated,
There wants but your hand to't.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Truely you have taken great pains, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A friendly part, no more (ſweet Beauty.)

sp.speaker: Am
sp.l: They are happy, Sir, have ſuch friends as you are.
But do you know you have done well in this?
How will his Allies receive it? ſhe (though I ſay't)
Is of no better bloud than I am.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There I leave it, I'm at fartheſt that way.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: You ſhall extend your vows no larger now.
My heart calls you mine own: and that's enough.
Reaſon, I know, would have all yet conceal'd.
I ſhall not leave you unſaluted long
Either by Pen or Perſon.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You may diſcourſe
With me, when you think y'are alone, I ſhall
Be preſent with you.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Come Coſin, will you walk?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Alas, I was ready long ſince: in conſcience
You would with better will yet ſtay behind.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Oh Love, I never thought thou'dſt been ſo blind.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You'll anſwer this Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: If er't be ſpoke on:
I purpoſe not to propound the queſtion.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis true, the poor knave ſaid: ſome Raviſher,
Some of Luſts Bloud-hounds have ſeiz'd upon her:
The Girl is hurried, as the devil were with 'em
And help'd their ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It may be not ſo ill, Sir.
A well-prepared Lover may do as much
In hot bloud as this, and perform't honſtly.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: What? ſteal away a Virgin 'gainſt her will?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It may be any mans caſe; deſpiſe nothing:
And that's a thief of a good quality,
Moſt commonly he brings his theft home again,
Though with a little ſhame.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: There's a charge by't
Fall'n upon me: Paris (the Millers ſon)
Her brother, dares not venture home again
Till better tidings follow of his Siſter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Y'are the more beholding to the miſchance, Sir:
Had I gone a Boot-haling, I ſhould as ſoon
Have ſtoll'n him as his Siſter: Marry then,
To render him back in the ſame plight he is
May be coſtly: his fleſh is not maintain'd with little.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I think the poor knave will pine away,
He cries all to be pittied yonder,

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Pray you Sir, let's go ſee him: I ſhould laugh
To ſee him cry, ſure.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Well, you are merry, Sir.
Antonio, keep this charge; I have fears
Move me to lay it on you: Pray forbear
The ways of your enemies, the Bellides.
I have reaſon for my Injunction, Sir. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Aminta (as a Page with a Letter.)

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: To me, Sir? from whom?

sp.speaker: Am.
