sp.l: A friend, I dare vow, Sir.
Though on the enemies part: the Lady Iſmenia.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Take heed, bluſh not too deep; let me adviſe you
In your anſwer, 't muſt be done heedfully.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſhould not ſee a Maſculine in peace
Out of that houſe.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Alas, I'm a child, Sir,
Your hates cannot laſt till I wear a ſword.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Await me for your anſwer.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: He muſt ſee her,
To manifeſt his ſhame: 'tis my advantage;
While our bloud's under us, we keep above:
But then we fall, when we do fall in love. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: MY Lord, my Lord, your houſe hath injur'd me,
Rob'd of all the joys I had on earth.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Where wert thou brought up (fellow?)

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: In a Mill.
You may perceive it by my loud exclaims,
Which muſt riſe higher yet.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Obſtreperous Carle,
If thy throats tempeſt; could oe'rturn my houſe,
What ſatisfaction were it for thy child:
Turn thee the right way to thy journeys end.
Wilt have her where ſhe is not?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Here was ſhe loſt,
And here muſt I begin my footing after;
From whence, until I meet a pow'r to puniſh,
I will not reſt: You are not quick to grief.
Your hearing's a dead ſenſe. Were yours the loſs,
Had you a Daughter, perhaps be-whor'd,
(For to what other end ſhould come the thief?
You'ld play the Miller then, be loud and high.
But being not a ſorrow of your own,
You have no help nor pity for another,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Oh, thou haſt op'd a Sluce was long ſhut up,
And let a floud of grief in; a buried grief
Thy voice hath wak'd again: a grief as old
As likely 'tis thy child is; friend, I tell thee,
I did once loſe a Daughter.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Did you, Sir?
Beſeech you then, how did you bear her loſs?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: With thy grief trebled.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: But was ſhe ſtolen from you?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Yes, by devouring thieves, from whom cannot
Ever return a ſatisfaction:
The wild beaſts had her in her ſwathing clothes.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Oh much good do 'em with her.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Away tough churle.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Why, ſhe was better eaten than my child,
Better by beaſts, than beaſtly men devoured,
They took away a life, no honor from her:
Thoſe beaſts might make a Saint of her, but theſe
Will make my child a devil but was ſhe, Sir,
Your only Daughter?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I ne'r had other (Friend.)

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.l: Where are you (man?) your buſineſs lies not here,
Your Daughters in the Pound, I have found where;
'Twill coſt you dou dear, her freedom.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I'll break it down,
And free her without pay:
Horſe-locks nor chains ſhall hold her from me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I'll take this relief.
I now have time to ſpeak alone with grief. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: How? my Landlord? he's Lord of my Lands
But not my Cattle: I'll have her again (Gil.)

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.l: You are not mad upon the ſudden now.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: No Gill. I have been mad theſe five hours:
I'll ſell my Mill, and buy a Roring.
I'll batter down his houſe, and make a Stewes on't,

sp.speaker: Gill.
sp.l: Will you gather up your wits a little
And hear me? the King's near by in progreſs,
Here I have got our ſupplication drawn,
And there's the way to help us.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Give it me (Gill.)
I will not fear to give it to the King:
To his own hands (God bleſs him) will I give it,
And he ſhall ſet the Law upon their ſhoulders,
And hang 'em all that had a hand in it.

sp.speaker: Gill.
sp.l: Where's your Son?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: He ſhall be hang'd in flitches:
The Dogs ſhall eat him in Lent, there's Cats-meat
And Dogs-meat enough about him.

sp.speaker: Gi l.
sp.l: Sure the poor Girl is the Counts whore by this time.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: If ſhe be the Counts whore, the whores Count
Shall pay for it: He ſhall pay for a new Maiden-head.

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.l: You are ſo violous: this I'm reſolv'd,
If ſhe be a whore once, I'll renounce her,
You know, if every man had his right,
She's none of our child, but a meer foundling,
(And I can gueſs the owner for a need too)
We have but foſter'd her.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Gill. no more of that,
I'll cut your tongue out, if you tell thoſe tales.
Hark, hark, theſe Toaters tell us the King's coming:
Get you gone; I'll ſee if I can find him. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Liſauro, Terſa, Pedro, and Moncado.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Does the King remove to day?

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: So ſaies the Harbengers,
And keeps his way on to Valentia,
There ends the progreſs.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: He hunts this morning Gentlemen,
And dines i'th' fields: the Court is all in readineſs.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Pedro, did you ſend for this Tailor? or you Moncado?
This light French Demi-launce that follows us.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: No, I aſſure ye on my word, I am guiltleſs,
I owe him too much to be inward with him.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: I am not quit I am ſure: there is a reckoning
Of ſome four ſcarlet cloaks, and two lac'd ſuits
Hangs on the ſile ſtill, like a fearful Comet
Makes me keep off.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I am in too Gentlemen,
I thank his faith, for a matter of three hundred.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: And I for two, what a devil makes he this way?
I do not love to ſee my ſins before me.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: 'Tis the vacation, and theſe things break out
To ſee the Court, and glory in their debtors.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: What do you call him for? I never love
To remember their names that I owe money to,
'Tis not gentile; I ſhun 'em like the plague ever.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: His name's Vertigo: hold your heads, and wonder,
A French-man, and a founder of new Faſhions:
The revolutions of all ſhapes and habits
Run madding through his brains; Enter Vertigo.

sp.speaker: Monc.
sp.l: He is very brave.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: The ſhreds of what he ſteals from us. believe it,
Makes him a mighty man: he comes, have at ye.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Save ye together, my ſweet Gentlemen,
I have been looking—

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: Not for Money, Sir?
You know the hard time.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Pardon me ſweet (Signior)
Good faith the leaſt thought in my heart, your love Gentlemen,
Your love's enough for me: Money, hang money:
Let me preſerve your love.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Yes marry ſhall ye,
And we our credit, you would ſee the Court?

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: He ſhall ſee every place.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Shall I i'faith Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: The Cellar, and the Buttry, and the Kitchin,
The Paſtry, and the Pantry.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: I, and taſte too
Of every Office: and be free of all too:
That he may ſay when he comes home in glory.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: And I will ſay, i'faith, and ſay it openly,
And ſay it home too: Shall I ſee the King alſo?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Shalt ſee him every day: ſhalt ſee the Ladies
In their French clothes: ſhalt ride a hunting with him,
Shalt have a Miſtriſs too: we muſt fool handſomely
To keep him in belief, we honor him,
He may call on us elſe,

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: A pox upon him.
Let him call at home in's own houſe for ſalt butter.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: And when the King puts on a new ſuit.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt ſee it firſt,
And defect his doublets: that thou maiſt be perfect.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: The Wardrobe I would fain view, Gentlemen,
Fain come to ſee the Wardrobe.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt ſee it,
And ſee the ſecret of it, dive into it:
Sleep in the Wardrobe, and have Revelations
Of faſhions five years hence.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Ye honor me.
Ye infinitely honor me.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: Any thing i'th' Court, Sir,
Or within the compaſs of a Courtier.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: My wife ſhall give ye thanks.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: You ſhall ſee any thing.
The privateſt place, the ſtool, and where 'tis emptied.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Ye make me bluſh, ye pour your bounties, Gentlemen,
In ſuch abundance.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I will ſhew thee preſently
The order that the King keeps when he comes
To open view, that thou may'ſt tell thy neighbors
Over a ſhoulder of mutton, thou haſt ſeen ſomething,
Nay, thou ſhalt preſent the King for this time.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Nay, I pray Sir.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: That thou maiſt know what State there does belong to it;
Stand there I ſay, and put on a ſad countenance,
Mingled with height: be cover'd, and reſerved;
Move like the Sun, by ſoft degrees, and glorious,
Into your order (Gentlemen) uncover'd,
The King appears; We'll ſport with you a while, Sir,
I am ſure you are merry with us all the year long (Tailor)
Move ſofter ſtill, keep in that fencing leg; Monſieur,
Turn to no ſide.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: What's this that appears to him?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: 'Has a petition, and he looks moſt lamentably,
Miſtake him, and we are made.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: This is the King ſure,
The glorious King, I know him by his gay clothes.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Now bear your ſelf that you may ſay hereafter.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I have recover'd breath, I'll ſpeak unto him preſently,
May it pleaſe your gracious Majeſty to conſider
A poor mans caſe?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: What's your Will, Sir?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: You muſt accept, and read it.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: The Tailor will run mad upon my life for't.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: How he mumps and bridles: he will ne'r cut clothes again.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: And what's your grief?

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: He ſpeaks i'th' noſe like his gooſe.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I pray you read there; I am abus'd and frumpt, Sir,
By a great man that may do ill by authority;
Poor honeſt men are hang'd for doing leſs, Sir,
My child is ſtolen, the Count Otrante ſtole her;
A pretty child ſhe is, although I ſay it,
A handſome Mother, he means to make a whore of her,
A ſilken whore, his knaves have filch'd her from me;
He keeps lewd knaves, that do him beaſtly offices:
I kneel for Juſtice. Shall I have it Sir?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What Pageant's this?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: The King:
Tailor, ſtand off, here ends your aparition:
Miller, turn round, and there addreſs your paper,
There, there's the King indeed.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: May it pleaſe your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Why didſt thou kneel to that fellow?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: In good faith, Sir,
I thought he had been a King, he was ſo gallant:
There's none here wears ſuch gold.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: So fooliſhly,
You have golden buſineſs ſure; becauſe I am homely
Clad, in no glitt'ring ſuit, I am not look'd on:
Ye fools that wear gay cloaths, love to gap'd at,
What are you better when your end calls on you?
Will gold preſerve ye from the grave? or jewels?
Get golden Minds, and fling away your Trappings
Unto your bodies, miniſter warm raiments,
Wholſome and good; glitter within and ſpare not:
Let my Gourt have rich ſouls, their ſuits I weigh not:
And what are you that took ſuch State upon ye?
Are ye a Prince?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: The Prince of Tailors, Sir,
We owe ſome money to him, and't like your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: If it like him, would ye ow'd more, be modeſter,
And you leſs ſaucy, Sir: and leave this place:
Your Preſſing-iron will make no perfect Courtier:
Goe ſtitch at home, and cozen your poor neighbors,
Show ſuch another pride, I'll have ye whipt for't,
And get worſe clothes, theſe but proclaim your fellony.
And what's your Paper?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I beſeech you read it.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What's here? the Count Otrante task'd for a baſe villany,
For ſtealing of a maid?

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: The Count Otrante?
Is not the fellow mad, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fra,
sp.l: No, no, my Lord,
I am in my wits, I am a labouring man,
And we have ſeldome leiſure to run mad,
We have other buſineſs to employ our heads in,
We have little Wit to loſe too: if we complain,
And if a heavie load lie on your ſhoulders,
Worſe than a ſack of Meal, and oppreſs our poverties,
We are mad ſtreight, and whop'd, and ty'd in fetters,
Able to make a horſe mad, as you uſe us,
You are mad for nothing, and no man dare proclaim it,
In you a wildneſs is a noble trick,
And cheriſh'd in ye, and all men muſt love it:
Oppreſſions of all ſorts, ſit like new clothes,
Neatly and handſomely upon your Lordſhips:
And if we kick when your honors ſpur us,
We are Knaves and Jades, and ready for the Juſtice.
I am a true Miller.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Then thou art a wonder.

sp.speaker: 2 Lor.
sp.l: I know the the man reputed for a good man
An honeſt and ſubſtantial fellow.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: He ſpeaks ſence,
And to the point: Greatneſs begets much rudeneſs,
How dare you (Sirrah) 'gainſt ſo main a perſon,
A man of ſo much Noble note and honor,
Put up this baſe complaint? Muſt every Peaſant
Upon a ſaucy Will affront great Lords!
All fellows (Miller?)

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I have my reward, Sir,
I was told one greatneſs would protect another,
As beams ſupport their fellows; now I find it:
If't pleaſe your Grace to have me hang'd, I am ready,
'Tis but a Miller, and a Thief diſpach'd:
Though I ſteal bread, I ſteal no fleſh to tempt me.
I have a wife, and 't pleaſe him to have her too,
With all my heart; 'twill make my charge the leſs, Sir,
She'll hold him play awhile: I have a boy too,
He's able to inſtruct his Honors hogs,
Or rub his horſe-heels: when it pleaſe his Lordſhip
He may him his ſlave too, or his bawd:
The boy is well bred, can exhort his Siſter:
For me, the Priſon, or the Pillory,
To loſe my gods, and have mine ears cropt off;
Whipt like a Top, and have a paper ſtuck before me,
For abominable honeſty to his own Daughter,
I can endure, Sir: the Miller has a ſtout heart,
Though as his Toal-pin.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I ſuſpect this ſhrewdly,
Is it his Daughter that the people call
The Millers fair Maid?

sp.speaker: 2 Lor.
sp.l: It ſhould ſeem ſo, Sir.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Be ſure you be i'th' right, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: If I be i'th' wrong, Sir,
Be ſure you hang me, I will ask no courteſie:
Your Grace may have a Daughter, think of that, Sir,
She may be fair, and ſhe may be abuſed too:
A King is not exempted from theſe caſes:
Stolen from your loving care.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I do much pity him.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: But heaven forbid ſhe ſhould be in that venture
That mine is in at this hour: I'll aſſure your Grace
The Lord wants a water-Mill, and means to grind with her
Would I had his ſtones to ſet, I would fit him for it.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Follow me, Miller, and let me talk with ye farther,
And keep this private all upon your Loyalties:
To morrow morning, though I am now beyond him,
And the leſs lookt for, I'll break my Faſt with the good Count.
No more, away, all to our ſports, be ſilent. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: What Grace ſhall I have now?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Chooſe thine own Grace,
And go to dinner when thou wilt, Vertigo,
We muſt needs follow the King.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: You heard the ſentence.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: If you ſtay here
I'll ſend thee a ſhoulder of Veniſon:
Go home, go home, or if thou wilt diſguiſe,
I'll help thee to a place to feed the dogs.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Or thou ſhalt be ſpecial Tailor to the Kings Monkey,
'Tis a fine place, we cannot ſtay.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: No Money,
Nor no Grace, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: 'Tis too early Tailor.
The King has not broke his Faſt yet.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: I ſhall look for ye
The next Term, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not miſs us:
Prethee provide ſome clothes, and doſt thou hear Vertigo
Commend me to thy Wife: I want ſome ſhirts too.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: I have Chambers for ye all.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: They are too muſty,
When they are clear we'll come.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: I muſt be patient
And provident, I ſhall never get home elſe. Exe •• t.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Prethee be wiſer wench, thou canſt not ſcape me,
Let me with love and gentleneſs injoy that
That may be ſtill preſerv'd with love, and long'd for:
If violence lay rough hold, I ſhall hate thee,
And after I have enjoy'd thy Maiden-head,
Thou wilt appear ſo ſtale and ugly to me
I ſhall deſpiſe thee, caſt thee off.

sp.speaker: Flor.
sp.l: I pray ye Sir,
Begin it now, and open your doors to me,
I do confeſs I am ugly; let me go, Sir:
A Gipſey-girl: Why would your Lordſhip touch me?
Fye, 'tis not noble: I am homely bred,
Courſe, and unſit for you: why do you flatter me?
There be young Ladies, many that will love ye,
That will dote on ye: you a handſome Gentleman,
What will they ſay when once they know your quality?
A Lord, a Miller? take your Toal diſh with ye:
You that can deal with Gudgins, and courſe flower,
'Tis pitty you ſhould taſt what manchet means:
Is this fit Sir, for your repute and honor?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I'll love thee ſtill.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: You cannot, there's no ſympathy
Between our births, or breeding, arts, conditions,
And where theſe are at difference, ther's no liking:
This hour it may be I ſeem handſome to you,
And you are taken with variety
More than with beauty: to morrow when you have enjoy'd me,
Your heat and luſt aſſwag'd, and come to examine
Out of a cold and penitent condition
What you have done, whom you have ſhar'd your love with,
Made partner of your bed, how it will vex ye,
How you will curſe the devil that betrayd ye,
And what ſhall become of me then?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Wilt thou hear me?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: As haſty as you were then to enjoy me,
As precious as this beauty ſhew'd unto ye,
You'll kick me out of dores, you will whore and ban me:
And if I prove with child with your fair iſſue,
Give me a penſion of five pound a year
To breed your Heir withall, and ſo good ſpeed me.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I'll keep thee like a woman.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I'll keep my ſelf Sir,
Keep my ſelf honeſt Sir; there's the brave keeping:
If you will marry me.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Alaſs poor Florimell.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I do confeſs I am too courſe and baſe Sir
To be your wife, and it is ſit you ſcorn me,
Yet ſuch as I have crown'd the lives of great ones:
To be your whore I am ſure I am too worthy,
(For by my troth Sir, I am truly honeſt)
And that's an honor equal to your greatneſs.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I'll give thee what thou wilt.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Tempt me no more then:
Give me that peace, and then you give abundance,
I know ye do but try me, ye are noble,
All theſe are but to try my modeſty,
If you ſhould find me eaſie, and once coming,
I ſee your eyes already how they would fright me;
I ſee your honeſt heart how it would ſwell
And burſt it ſelf into a grief againſt me:
Your tongue in noble anger, now, even now Sir,
Ready to rip my looſe thoughts to the bottom,
And lay my ſhame unto my ſelf, wide open:
You are a noble Lord, you pitty poor maids,
The people are miſtaken in your courſes:
You, like a father, try 'em to the uttermoſt.
As they do Gold: you purge the droſs from them,
And make them ſhine.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: This cunning cannot help ye:
I love ye to enjoy: I have ſtol'n ye
To enjoy ye now, not to be fool'd with circumſtance,
Yield willingly, or elſe.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I will force ye.
I will not be delay'd, a poor baſe wench
That I, in curteſie, make offer to,
Argue with me?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Do not, you will looſe your labor,
Do not my Lord, it will become ye poorly:
Your courteſie may do much on my nature,
For I am kind as you are, and as tender:
If you compel, I have my ſtrengths to flye to,
My honeſt thoughts, and thoſe are guards about me:
I can cry too, and noiſe enough I dare make,
And I have curſes, that will call down thunder,
For all I am a poor wench, heaven will hear me:
My body you may force, but my will never;
And be ſure I do not live if you do force me,
Or have no tongue to tell your beaſtly Story,
For if I have, and if there be a juſtice.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Pray ye go in here: I'll calm my ſelf for this time.
And be your friend again.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I am commanded. Exit.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: You cannot ſcape me, yet I muſt enjoy ye,
I'll lie with thy wit, though I miſs thy honeſty:
Is this a wench for a Boors hungry boſom?
A morſel for a Peaſants baſe embraces?
And muſt I ſtarve, and the meat in my mouth?
I'll none of that.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: How now my Lord, how ſpeed ye?
Have ye done the deed?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: No, pox upon't, ſhe is honeſt.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Honeſt, what's that? you take her bare denial,
Was there ever wench brought up in a mill, and honeſt?
That were a wonder worth a Chronicle,
Is your belief ſo large? what did ſhe ſay to ye?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: She ſaid her honeſty was all her dowry,
And preach'd unto me, how unſit, and homely,
Nay how diſhonourable it would ſeem in me
To act my will; popt me i'th mouth with modeſty.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: What an impudent Quean was that? that's their trick ever.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: And then diſcours'd to me very learnedly
What fame and loud opinion would tell of me:
A wife ſhe touch'd at

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Out upon her Varlet.
Was ſhe ſo bold? theſe home-ſpun things are evils,
They'll tell ye a thouſand lies, if you'll believe 'em;
And ſtand upon their honors like great Ladies,
They'll ſpeak unhappily too: good words to cozen ye,
And outwardly ſeem Saints: they'll cry down-right alſo,
But 'tis for anger that you do not cruſh 'em.
Did ſhe not talk of being with child?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: She toucht at it,

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: The trick of an arrant whore to milk your Lordſhip;
And then a penſion nam'd?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: No, no, ſhe ſcorn'd it:
I offer'd any thing, but ſhe refus'd all,
Refus'd it with a confident hate.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: You thought ſo,
You ſhould have taken her then, turn'd her, and tew'd her
I'th' ſtrength of all her reſolution, flatter'd her,
And ſhak't her ſtubborn will: ſhe would have thank'd ye,
She would have lov'd ye infinitely, they muſt ſeem modeſt,
It is their parts: if you had plaid your part Sir.
And handl'd her as men do unman'd Hawks,
Caſt her, and malde her up in good clean linnen,
And there have coyed her, you had caught her heart-ſtrings
Theſe tough Virginities they blow like white thornes
In ſtorms and tempeſts.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: She is beyond all this,
As cold, and harden'd, as the Virgin Cryſtal.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Oh force her, force her, Sir, ſhe longs to be raviſh'd
Some have no pleaſure but in violence;
To be torn in pieces is their paradiſe:
'Tis ordinary in our Countrey, Sir, to raviſh all
They will not give a penny for their ſport
Unleſs they be put to it, and terribly,
And then they ſwear they'll hang the man comes near 'em,
And ſwear it on his lips too.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: No, no forcing,
I have an other courſe, and I will follow it,
I command you, and do you command your fellows,
That when you ſee her next, diſgrace, and ſcorn her,
I'll ſeem to put her out o'th' dores o'th' ſodain
And leave her to conjecture, then ſeize on her
Away, he ready ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: We ſhall not fail, Sir. Exit.

l.hi: Florimell.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I am ſure you have now conſider'd
And like a wiſe wench weigh'd a friends diſpleaſure,
Repented your proud thoughts, and caſt your ſcorn off.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: My Lord, I am not proud, I was never beautiful.
Nor ſcorn I any thing that's juſt and honeſt.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Come, to be ſhort, can ye love yet? you told me
Kindneſs would far compell ye: I am kind to ye,
And mean to exceed that way.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I told ye too, Sir,
As far as it agreed with modeſty,
With honour, and with honeſty I would yield to ye:
Good my Lord: take ſome other Theam: for Love,
Alaſs, I never knew yet what it meant,
And on the ſudden Sir, to run through Volumes
Of his moſt myſtick art, 'tis moſt impoſſible;
Nay, to begin with luſt, which is an Hereſie,
A foul one too; to learn that in my childhood:
O good my Lord.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: You will not out of this ſong,
Your modeſty, and honeſty, is that all?
I will not force ye.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Ye are too noble, Sir.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Nor will I woo ye at that infinite price
It may be you expect.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I expect your pardon,
And a diſcharge (my Lord) that's all I look for.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: No, nor fall ſick for love.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: 'Tis a heathful year Sir.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Look ye, I'll turn ye out o'dores, and ſcorn ye.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Thank ye my Lord.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: A proud ſlight Peat I found ye,
A fool (it may be too.)

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: An honeſt woman,
Good my Lord think me.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: And a baſe I leave ye,
So fare-ye-well. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: What doſt thou ſtay for? doſt thou not know the way,
Thou baſe unprovident whore?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Good words, pray ye Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: Has my Lord ſmoak'd ye over, good-wife Miller?
Is your Mill broken that you ſtand ſo uſeleſs?

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: An impudent Quean, upon my life ſhe is unwholſome
Some baſe diſcarded thing my Lord has found her,
He would not have turn'd her off o'th'ſudden elſe.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Now againſt every ſack (my honeſt ſweet heart)
With every Smig and Smug.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I muſt be patient.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: And every greaſie gueſt, and ſweaty Raſcall
For his Royal hire between his fingers, Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: I fear thou haſt given my Lord the—thou damn'd thing.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: I have ſeen her in the Stewes.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: The knave her father
Was Bawd to her there, and kept a Tipling houſe,
You muſt even to it again: a modeſt function.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: If ye had honeſty, ye would not uſe me
Thus baſely, wretchedly, though your Lord bid ye,
But he that knows.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Away thou carted impudence,
You meat for every man: a little meal
Flung in your face, makes ye appear ſo proud.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: This is inhumane. Let theſe tears perſuade you,
If ye be men, to uſe a poor girl better;
I wrong not you, I am ſure I call you Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: What buſineſs is here? away, are not you gone yet?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: My Lord, this is not well: although you hate me,
For what I know not; to let your people wrong me,
Wrong me maliciouſly, and call me.—

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Peace,
And mark me what we ſay adviſedly;
Mark, as you love that that you call your credit;
Yield now, or you are undone: your good name's periſh'd
Not all the world can buy your reputation;
'Tis ſunk for ever elſe, theſe peoples tongues will poiſon ye
Though you be white as innocence they'll taint ye,
They will ſpeak terrible and hideous things,
And people in this age are prone to credit,
They'll let fall nothing that may brand a woman,
Conſider this, and then be wiſe and tremble,
Yield yet, and yet I'll ſave ye.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I'll ſhow ye,
Their mouths I'll ſeal up, they ſhall ſpeak no more
But what is honorable and honeſt of ye,
And Saint like they ſhall worſhip ye: they are mine,
And what I charge them Florimell.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I am ruin'd,
Heaven will regard me yet, they are barbarous wretches:
Let me not fall (my Lord.)

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: You ſhall not Florimell:
Mark how I'll work your peace, and how I honor ye.
Who waits there? come all in.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: Your pleaſure Sir.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Who dare ſay this ſweet beauty is not heavenly?
This virgin, the moſt pure the moſt untainted,
The holieſt thing?

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: We know it (my dear Lord)
We are her ſlaves: and that proud impudence
That dares diſparage her, this ſword (my Lord.)

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: They are raſcals, baſe, the ſons of common women
That wrong this virtue, or dare own a thought
But fair and honorable of her: when we ſlight her,
Hang us, or cut's in pieces: let's tug i'th' Gallies.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: Brand us for villains.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Why ſure I dream: theſe are all Saints.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Go, and live all her ſlaves.

sp.speaker: Ger.
sp.l: We are proud to do it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: What think ye now? am not I able Florimell
Yet to preſerve ye?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I am bound to your Lordſhip,
Ye are all honour, and good my Lord but grant me,
Untill to morrow, leave to weigh my fortunes,
I'll give you a free anſwer, perhaps a pleaſing,
Indeed I'll do the beſt I can to ſatisfie ye.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Take your good time, this kiſs, till then farewell, Sweet. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: By all means diſcharge your follower.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: If we can get him off: Sirrah Buſtofa
Thou muſt needs run back.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: But I muſt not unleſs you ſend
A Bier, or a Lictor at my back, I do not uſe to run
From my friends.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Well, go will ſerve turn: I have forgot.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: What Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: See if I can think on't now.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I know what 'tis now.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A Piſtolet of that.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Done, you have forgot a deviſe to ſend me away,
You are going a ſmocking perhaps.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: His own, due, due i'faith Antonio,
The Piſtolet's his own.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I confeſs it,
There 'tis: now if you could afford out of it
A reaſonable excuſe to mine Uncle.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Yes, I can:
But an excuſe will not ſerve your turn: it muſt be a lye,
A full lye, 'twill do no good elſe: if you'll go to
The price of that?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Is a lye dearer than an excuſe?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Oh, treble; this is the price of an excuſe: but a lye is two more:
Look how many foyles go to a fair fall, ſo many excuſes to
A full lye, and leſs cannot ſerve your turn, let any Tailor
I'th' Town make it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why 'tis reaſonable, give him his price:
Let it be large enough now.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I'll warrant you, cover him all over.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I would have proof of one now.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: What? ſcale my invention before hand? you ſhall pardon
Me for that; well, I'll commend you to your Uncle, and
Tell him you'll be at home at ſupper with him.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: By no means, I cannot come to night (man)

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I know that too, you do not know a lye when you ſee it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Remember it muſt ſtretch for all night.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I ſhall want ſtuffe, I doubt 'twill come to the other Piſtolet.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Well, lay out, you ſhall be no looſer Sir.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: It muſt be faced, you know, there will be a yard of diſſimulation
At leaſt (City-meaſure) and cut upon an untroth or two: Lyned
With Fables, that muſt needs be, cold weather's coming, if it had
A gallon of hypocriſie, 'twould do well: and hooked
Together with a couple of conceits,
That's neceſſity; well, I'll bring in my
Bill: I'll warrant you as fair a lye by that time I have done
With it, as any Gentleman i'th' Town can ſwear to, if he
Would betray his Lord and Maſter. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: So, ſo, this neceſſary trouble's over.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I would you had bought an excuſe of him
Before he went: you'll want one for Iſmenia.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Tuſh, there needs none, there's no ſuſpition yet,
And I'll be arm'd before the next encounter,
In a faſt tye with my fair Iſabel.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, you'll find your errand is before you now.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Oh Gentlemen, look to your ſelves, ye are
Men of another world elſe; your enemies are upon you;
The old houſe of the Bellides will fall upon your heads:
Signior Liſauro.

l.hi: Liſauro?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: And Don what call you him? he's a Gentleman:
Yet he has but a Yeomans name,
Don Tarſo, Tarſo, and a dozen at their heels.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Liſauro, Tarſo, nor a dozen more
Shall fright me from my ground, nor ſhun my path,
Let 'em come on in their ableſt fury.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis worthily reſolved: I'll ſtand by you Sir,
This way, I am thy true friend.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: I'll be gone Sir, that one may live to tell what's become of you.
sp.l: Put up, put up, will you never learn to know a lye
From an Eſop's Fables? there's a taſt for you now. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Look Sir, what time of day is it?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I know not, my eyes go falſe, I dare not truſt 'em now,
I prethee tell me (Martin) if thou canſt,
Is that Iſmenia or Iſabella.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: This is the Lady, forget not Iſabella.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: If this face may be borrowed and lent out,
If it can ſhift ſhoulders, and take other tyres,
So, 'tis mine where ere I find it.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Be ſudden. Exit Aminta.
I cannot hold out long.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Believ't ſhe frowns.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let it come, ſhe cannot frown me off on't;
How prettily it wooes me to come nearer?
How do you do (Lady) ſince yeſterdays pains?
Were you not weary? of my faith.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I think you were.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What Lady?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Weary of your faith; 'tis a burthen
That men faint under, though they bear little of it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: So, this is to the purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You came home
In a fair hour I hope?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: From whence Sir?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.p: Sir, there's a Gentlewoman without deſires to ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: They were pretty homely toyes: but your preſence
Made them illuſtrious.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: My Coſen ſpeaks to you.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: A Gentlewoman Sir, Iſabella
She names her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: So, ſo, it hits finely now.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Name your ſelf how you pleaſe: ſpeak what you pleaſe,
I'll hear you cheerfully.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: You are not well,
Requeſt her in, ſhe may have more acquaintance
With his paſſions, and better cure for'em.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: She's nice in that (Madam) poor ſoul it ſeems
She's fearful of your diſpleaſure.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I'll quit her
From that preſently, and bring her in my ſelf. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: How careleſly do you behave your ſelf,
When you ſhould call all your beſt faculties
To counſel in you? how will you anſwer
The breach you made with fair Iſmenia?
Have you forgot the retrograde vow you took
With her, that now is come in evidence?
You'll dye upon your ſhame, you need no more
Enemies of the houſe, but the Lady now:
You ſhall have your diſpatch.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Give me that face,
And I am ſatisfied upon whoſe ſhoulders
So ere it grows: Juno deliver us
Out of this amazement: Beſeech you Goddeſs
Tell us of our friends, how does Iſmenia?
And how does Iſabella? both in good health
I hope, as you your ſelf are.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I am at fartheſt
In my counterfeit: my Antonio
I have matter againſt you may need pardon,
As I muſt crave of you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Obſerve you Sir,
What evidence is come againſt me? what think you
The Hydra-headed Jury will ſay to't?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis I am fool'd,
My hopes are pour'd into the bottomleſs tubs,
'Tis labour for the houſe of Bellides:
I muſt not ſeem ſo yet: but in ſooth (Lady)
Did you imagine your changeable face
Hid you from me? By this hand I knew you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I went by the face: and by theſe eyes I
Might have been deceived.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: You might indeed (Antonio)
For this Gentleman did vow to Iſabella,
That he it was that lov'd Iſmenia,
And not Antonio?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Good, was not that
A manifeſt confeſſion that I knew you?
I elſe had been unjuſt unto my friend:
'Twas well remembred, there I found you out
And ſpeak your conſcience now.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But did he ſo proteſt?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Yes, I vow to you, had Antonio
Wedded Iſabella, Iſmenia
Had not been loſt, there had been her lover.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why much good do you friend, take her to you:
I crave but one, here have I my wiſh full,
I am glad we ſhall be ſo near neighbors.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Take both Sir, Juno to boot: three parts in one,
S. Hilarie bleſs you, now opportunity
Beware to meet with falſhood, if thou canſt
Shun it, my friends faith's turning from him.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Might I not juſtly accuſe Antonio.
For a love-wanderer? you know no other
But me, for another, and confeſs troth now?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Here was my guide, where ere I find this face,
I am a Lover, marry, I muſt not miſs
This freckle then, I have the number of 'em,
Nor this dimple, nor a ſilk from this brow,
I carry the full Idea ever with me;
If nature can ſo punctually parallel,
I may be cozened.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Well, all this is even:
But now, to perfect all, our love muſt now
Come to our Enemies hands, where neither part
Will ever give conſent to't.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Moſt certain:
For which reaſon it muſt not be put to'em:
Have we not prevention in our own hands.
Shall I walk by the tree? deſire the fruit,
Yet be ſo nice to pull till I ask leave
Of the churliſh Gard'ner, that will deny me?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: O Antonio.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis manners to fall to
When grace is ſaid.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: That holy acts to come.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You may open an oyſter or two before grace.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Are there not double vows, as valuable
And as well ſpoke as any Frier utters?
Heaven has heard all.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Yes: but ſtayes the bleſſing,
Till all dues be done: heaven is not ſerv'd by halfs.
We ſhall have ne'r a fathers bleſſing here,
Let us not loſe the better, from above.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You take up weapons of unequal force,
It ſhows you cowardly: heark in your ear.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Have I loſt all imployment? Would this proffer
Had been to me, though I had paid it
With a reaſonable pennance.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Have I paſt
All thy fore-lock (Time?) I'll ſtretch a long arm
But I'll catch hold again: Do but look back
Over thy ſhoulder, and have a pull at thee.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I hear you (Sir) nor can I hear too much
While you ſpeak well: You know th'accuſtom'd place
Of our night-parley: if you can aſcend,
The window ſhall receive you. You may find there
A corrupted Church-man to bid you welcome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I would meet no other man.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Aminta, you hear this.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: With joy (Madam) 'cauſe it pleaſes you.
It may be mine own caſe another time:
Now you go the right way; ask the Banes out,
Put it paſt father, or friends, to forbid it,
And then you're ſure. Sir, your Hymen Taper
I'll light up for you: the window ſhall ſhow you
The way to Seſtos.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I'll venture drowning.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: The ſimile holds not; 'tis hanging rather.
You muſt aſcend your Caſtle by a Ladder;
To the foot I'll bring you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Leave me to climb it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If I do turn you off?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Till night fare-well:
Then better.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Beſt it ſhould be;
But peeviſh hatred keeps back that degree. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I never look'd ſo ſmooth as now I purpoſe:
And then beware: Knave is at worſt of knave
When he ſmiles beſt, and the moſt ſeems to ſave. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: My mind's unquiet; while Antonio
My Nephew's abroad, my heart is not at home,
Only my fears ſtay with me; bad company:
But I cannot ſhift 'em off. This hatred
Betwixt the houſe of Bellides and us,
Is not fair war: 'tis civil, but uncivil.
We are near neighbors, were of love as near,
Till a croſs miſconſtruction ('twas no more
In conſcience) put us ſo far aſunder:
I would 'twere reconcil'd; it has laſted
Too many Sun-ſets, if grace might moderate:
Man ſhould not loſe ſo many days of peace
To ſatisfie the anger of one minute.
I could repent it heartily. I ſent
The knave to attend my Antonio too,
Yet he returns no comfort to me neither.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: No: I muſt not.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Hah; hee's come.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I muſt not: 'twill break his heart to hear it.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: How? there's bad tidings: I muſt obſcure and hear it;
He will not tell me for breaking of my heart,
'Tis half ſplit already.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: I have ſpi'd him: Now to knock down a Do • with a lye, a ſilly harmleſs lye; 'twill be valiantly done, and nobly perhaps.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: I cannot hear him now.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Oh the bloody days that we live in; the envious, malitious, deadly days that we draw breath in!

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Now I hear too loud.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: The Children that ever ſhall be born may rue it; for men that are ſlain now might have liv'd to have got children, that might have curs'd their fathers.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Oh, my poſterity is ruin'd.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Oh ſweet Antonio.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Oh dear Antonio.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Yet it was nobly done of both parts: When he and Liſauro met.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Oh, death Has parted 'em.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Welcome my mortal foe (ſays one,) Welcome my deadly enemy (ſays th'other:) off go their doublets, they in their ſhirts, and their ſwords ſtark naked; here lies Antonio, here lies Liſauro: he comes upon him with an Embroccado, that he puts by with a puncta reverſa; Liſauro recoils me two paces and ſome ſix inches back, takes his carrere, and then, on.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Runs Antonio quite thorow,

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Oh villain.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Quite thorow between the arm and the body: ſo yet he had no hurt at that bout.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Goodneſs be praiſed.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: But then, at next encounter, he fetches me up Liſauro; Liſauro makes out a long at him, which he thinking to be a Paſſado, Antonio's foot ſlipping: down: oh down.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: O now thou art loſt.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Oh, but the quality of the thing: both Gentlemen, both Spaniſh Chriſtians, yet one man to ſhed

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Say his enemies blood.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: His hair, may come by divers caſualties, though he never go into the field with his foe: but a man to loſe nine ounces and two drams of blood at one wound, thirteen and a ſcruple at another, and to live till he dye in cold blood: yet the Surgeon (that cur'd him) ſaid if Pia-mater had not been periſh'd, he had been a lives man till this day.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: There he concludes he is gone.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: But all this is nothing: now I come to the point.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: I, the point, that's deadly: the antient blow
Over the buckler, ne'r went half ſo deep.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Yet pitty bids me keep in my charity: for me to pull an old mans ears from his head with telling of a Tale: oh fowle Tale! No, be ſilent Tale. Farthermore, there is the charge of Buriall; every one will cry Blacks, Blacks, that had but the leaſt finger dipt in his blood, though ten degrees remov'd when 'twas done. Moreover, the Surgeon (that made an end of him) will be paid: Sugar-plums and ſweet breads; yet I ſay, the man may recover again, and dye in his bed.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: What motley ſtuff is this? Sirrha, ſpeak truth
What hath befallen my dear Antonio?
Reſtrain your pitty in concealing it;
Tell me the danger full; take off your care
Of my receiving it: kill me that way,
I'll forgive my death; what thou keepſt back from truth
Thou ſhalt ſpeak in pain; do not look to find
A limb in his right place, a bone unbroke,
Nor ſo much fleſh unbroil'd of all that mountain,
As a worm might ſup on, diſpatch, or be diſpatch'd.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Alaſs Sir, I know nothing, but that Antonio is a man of Gods making to this hour, 'tis not two ſince I left him ſo.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Where didſt thou leave him?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: In the ſame clothes he had on when he went from you.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Does he live?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: I ſaw him drink.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Is he not wounded?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p:
He may have a cut i'th'leg by this time; for Don
• artin and he were at whole ſlaſhes.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Met he not with Liſauro?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: I do not know her.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Her? Liſauro is a man, as he is.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: I ſaw ne'er a man like him.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Didſt thou not diſcourſe a fight betwixt Ant. and Liſ?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: I to my ſelf; I hope a man may give himſelf the lye if it pleaſe him.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Didſt thou lye then?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: As ſure as you live now.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: I live the happier by it: when will he return?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: That he ſent me to tell you, within theſe ten days at fartheſt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Ten days? he's not wont to be abſent two.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Nor I think he will not, he ſaid he would be at home to morrow, but I love to ſpeak within my compaſs.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: You ſhall ſpeak within mine Sir, now. Within there.
Take this fellow into cuſtody, keep him ſafe
I charge you.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Safe? do you hear? take notice what plight you find me in, if there want but a collop or a ſteak o'me, look to't.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: If my Nephew return not in his health to morrow,
Thou goeſt to th'Rack.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Let me go to th'manger firſt; I had rather eat oats than hay. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: By your leave, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: For ought I know yet, you are welcome Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Read that, and tell me ſo: or if thy ſpectacles be not eaſie,
Keep thy noſe unſadl'd, and ope thine ears;
I can ſpeak thee the contents, I made 'em;
'Tis a challenge, a fair one, I'll maintain't:
I ſcorn to hire my Second to deliver't,
I bring't my ſelf: Doſt know me, Julio?

l.hi: Bellides?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes: is not thy hair on end now?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Somewhat amaz'd at thy raſh hardineſs;
How durſt thou come ſo near thine enemy?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Durſt?
I dare come nearer: thou'rt a fool, Julio.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Take it home to thee with a knave to boot.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Knave to thy teeth again: and all that's quit:
Give me not a fool more than I give thee,
Or if thou doſt, look to hear on't again.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: What an encounter's this?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: A noble one:
My hand is to my words, thou haſt it there,
There I do challenge thee, if thou dar'ſt be
Good friends with me; or I'll proclaim thee coward.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Be friends with thee?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I'll ſhew thee reaſons for't:
A pair of old Coxcombs (now we go together)
Such as ſhould ſtand examples of diſcretion,
The rules of Grammar to unwilling youth
To take out leſſons by; we that ſhould check
And quench the raging fire in others bloods,
We ſtrike the battel to deſtruction?
Read 'em the black art? and make 'em believe
It is divinity? Heathens, are we not?
Speak thy conſcience, how haſt thou ſlept this month,
Since this Fiend haunted us?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Sure ſome Good Angel
Was with us both laſt night: ſpeak thou truth now,
Was it not laſt nights motion?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Doſt not think
I would not lay hold of it at firſt proffer?
Should I n'er ſleep again?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Take not all from me;
I'll tell the doctrine of my viſion.
Say that Liſauro (beſt of thy blood)
Or any one, the leaſt allyed to thee,
Should be the prey unto Liſauro's ſword,
Or any of the houſe of Bellides?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Mine was the juſt inverſion: on, on.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: How would thine eyes have emptied thee in ſorrow,
And left the Conduit of nature drie?
Thy hands have turn'd rebellious to the balls,
And broke the glaſſes, with thine own curſes
Have torn thy ſoul, left thee a Statue
To propagate thy next poſterity.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Yes, and thou cauſer: ſo it ſaid to me,
They fight but your miſchiefs: the young men were friends,
As is the life and blood coagulate
And curded in one body; but this is yours,
An inheritance that you have gather'd for 'em,
A Legacie of blood to kill each other
Throughout your Generations. Was't not ſo?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Word for word.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Nay, I can go farther yet.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis far enough; Let us attone it here.
And in a reconciled circle fold
Our friendſhip new again.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: The ſign's in Gemini,
An auſpicious houſe, 't has join'd both ours again.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: You cannot proclaim me coward now, Don Bellides.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No: thou 'rt a valiant fellow: ſo am I:
I'll fight with thee at this hug, to the laſt leg
I have to ſtand on, or breath or life left.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: This is the ſalt unto humanity,
And keeps it ſweet.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Love! oh life ſtinks without it.
I can tell you news.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Good has long been wanting.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I do ſuſpect, and I have ſome proof on't,
(So far as a Love-Epiſtle comes to)
That Antonio (your Nephew) and my daughter
Iſmenia are very good friends before us.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: That were a double wall about our houſes,
Which I could wiſh were built.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I had it
From Antonio's Intimate, Don Martin:
And yet (me thought) it was no friendly part
To ſhow it me.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Perhaps 't was his conſent:
Lovers have policies as well as Stateſmen:
They look not always at the mark they aim at.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Wee'll take up cudgels, and have one bowt with 'em,
They ſhall know nothing of this union:
And till they find themſelves moſt deſperate,
Succor ſhall never ſee 'em.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I'll take your part Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: It grows late; there's a happy day paſt us.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: The example I hope to all behind it. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Stand fair, light of Love, which epithite and place
Adds to thee honour, to me it would be ſhame,
We muſt be weight in love, no grain too light;
Thou art the Land-mark, but if love be blind,
(As many that can ſee have ſo reported)
What benefit canſt thou be to his darkneſs?
Love is a jewel (ſome ſay) ineſtimable,
But hung at the ear, deprives our own ſight,
And ſo it ſhines to others, not our ſelves.
I ſpeak my skill, I have only heard on't,
But I could wiſh a nearer document,
Alaſs, the ignorant deſire to know:
Some ſay Love's but a toy, and with a but.
Now methinks I ſhould love it ne'er the worſe,
A toy is harmleſs ſure, and may be plaid with,
It ſeldome goes without his adjunct, pretty,
A pretty toy we ſay, 'tis meeter to joy too.
Well, here may be a mad night yet for all this,
Here's a Prieſt ready, and a Lady ready:
A chamber ready, and a bed ready,
'Tis then but making unready, and that's ſoon done:
My Lady is my Coſen; I, my ſelf,
Which is neareſt then? My deſires are mine,
Say they be hers too, is't a hanging matter?
It may be ventur'd in a worſer cauſe,
I muſt go queſtion with my conſcience:
I have the word; Centinel, do thou ſtand,
Thou ſhalt not need to call, I'll be at hand. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Are we not dog'd behind us, thinkſt thou friend?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I heard not one bark, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: There are that bite
And bark not (man:) me-thought I ſpy'd two fellows
That through two ſtreets together walk'd aloof,
And wore their eyes ſuſpiciouſly upon us.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Your Jealouſie, nothing elſe; or ſuch perhaps
As are afraid as much of us, who knows
But about the like buſineſs? but for your fears ſake
I'll adviſe and intreat one curteſie.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What's that friend?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I will not be denyed, Sir,
Change your upper garments with me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It needs not.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I think ſo too, but I will have it ſo,
If you dare truſt me with the better Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Nay then.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If there ſhould be danger towards,
There will be the main mark I'm ſure.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Here thou tak'ſt from me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Tuſh, the General
Muſt be ſafe, how ere the Battle goes:
See you the Beacon yonder?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes, we are near ſhore.

div.stage: Enter 2. Gentlemen with weapons drawn, they ſet upon Martin: Antonio purſues them out in reſcue of Martin.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Come, Land, Land, you muſt clamber by the cliffe,
Here are no ſtairs to riſe by.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I are you there? fight and Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Aminta above, and Martin return'd again aſcends.

l.hi: Antonio?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes Iſmenia.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Thine own.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Quench the light, thine eyes are guides illuſtrious.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: 'Tis neceſſary. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Your legs have ſav'd your lives, who ere you are,
Friend. Martin? where art thou? not hurt I hope:
Sure I was fartheſt in the purſuit of 'em:
My pleaſures are forgotten through my fears:
The lights extinct, it was diſcreetly done:
They could not but have notice of the broil,
And fearing that might call up company,
Have carefully prevented, and cloſed up:
I do commend the heed; oh, but my friend,
I fear his hurt: friend? friend? it cannot be
So mortal, that I ſhould loſe thee quite, friend?
A groan, any thing that may diſcover thee:
Thou art not ſunk ſo far, but I might hear thee:
I'll lay mine ear as low as thou canſt fall:
Friend, Don Martin, I muſt anſwer for thee,
'Twas in my cauſe thou feel'ſt, if thou be'ſt down,
Such dangers ſtand betwixt us and our ioyes,
That ſhould we forethink ere we undertake,
Wee'ld ſit at home, and ſave. What a night's here?
Purpos'd for ſo much joy, and now diſpos'd
To ſo much wretchedneſs? I ſhall not reſt in't:
• f I had all my pleaſures there within,
• ſhould not entertain 'em with a ſmile.
Good night to you: Mine will be black and ſad,
A friend cannot, a woman may be bad. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: O thou falſe,

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Do your daringſt, he's mine own,
Soul and body mine, church and chamber mine,
Totally mine.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Dar'ſt thou face thy falſhood?

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Shall I not give a welcome to my wiſhes
Come home ſo ſweetly: farewell your company
Till you be calmer woman. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Oh what a heap
Of miſery has one night brought with it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Where is he? do you turn your ſhame from me?
You'r a blind Adultereſs, you know you are.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: How's that Antonio?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Till I have vengeance,
Your ſin's not pardonable: I'll have him,
If hell hide him not: y'have had your laſt of him. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: What did he ſpeak? I underſtood him not,
He call'd me a foul name, it was not mine,
He took me for another ſure.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Ha? are you there?
Where's your ſweet heart? I have found you Traytor
To my houſe: wilt league with mine enemy?
You'll ſhed his blood, you'll ſay: hah? will you ſo?
And fight with your heels upwards? No Minion,
• have a husband for you, ſince y'are ſo rank,
And ſuch a husband as thou ſhalt like him,
Whether thou wilt or no: Antonio?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: It thunders with the ſtorm now.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: And to night
I'll have it diſpatch'd: I'll make it ſure, I,
By to morrow this time thy Maiden-head
Shall not be worth a Chicken, if it were
Knockt at an out-cry: go, I'll ha'ye before me:
Shough, ſhough, up to your coop, Pea-Hen.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Then I'll try my wings. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I, are you good at that? ſtop, ſtop thief, ſtop there.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Now having leiſure, and a happy wind,
Thou mayſt at pleaſure cauſe the ſtones to grind,
Sayls ſpread, and griſt here ready to be ground,
Fie, ſtand not idlely, but let the Mill go round.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Why doſt thou ſing and dance thus? why ſo merry?
Why doſt thou look ſo wantonly upon me?
And kiſs my hands?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: If I were high enough,
I would kiſs your lips too.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Do, this is ſome kindneſs,
This taſtes of willingneſs, nay, you may kiſs
Still, but why o'th' ſudden now does the fit take ye,
Unoffer'd, or uncompell'd? why theſe ſweet curteſies?
Even now you would have bluſh'd to death to kiſs thus:
Prethee let me be prepar'd to meet thy kindneſs,
I ſhall be unfurniſh'd elſe to hold thee play, wench:
Stay now a little, and delay your bleſſings;
If this be love, methinks it is too violent:
If you repent you of your ſtrictneſs to me,
It is ſo ſudden, it wants circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Fy, how dull?

body.head: 2. SONG.
body.l: How long ſhall I pine for love?
how long ſhall I ſue in vain?
How long like the Turtle-Dove
ſhall I heavi • ly thus complain?
Shall the ſayls of my love ſtand ſtill?
Shall the griſts of my hopes be unground?
Oh fie, oh fie, oh fie,
Let the Mill, let the Mill go round.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Prethee be calm a little,
Thou mak'ſt me wonder, thou that wert ſo ſtrange,
And read ſuch pious rules to my behavior
But yeſternight, thou that wert made of modeſty,
Shouldſt in a few ſhort minutes turn thus deſperate.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: You are too cold.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I do confeſs I freeze now,
I am another thing all over me:
It is my part to wooe, not to be courted:
Unfold this Riddle, 'tis to me a wonder,
That now 'oth' inſtant ere I can expect,
Ere I can turn my thoughts, and think upon
A ſeparation of your honeſt carriage
From the deſires of youth, thus wantonly,
Thus beyond expectation.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I will tell ye,
And tell ye ſeriouſly, why I appear thus,
To hold ye no more ignorant and blinded,
I have no modeſtie, I am truly wanton:
I am that you look for Sir; now come up roundly:
If my ſtrict face and counterfeited ſtatelyneſs
Could have won on ye, I had caught ye that way,
And you ſhould never have come to have known who hurt ye.
Prethee (ſweet Count) be more familiar with me.
How ever we are open in our natures,
And apt to more deſires than you dare meet with,
Yet we affect to lay the gloſs of good on't:
I ſaw you touch not at the bait of chaſtity,
And that it grew diſtaſteful to your palate
To apppear ſo holy, therefore I take my true ſhape:
Is your bed ready Sir? you ſhall quickly find me.

body.head: 3. SONG
body.l: On the bed Ile throw thee, threw thee down;
Down being laid, ſhall we be afraid
To try the rights that b • long to love?
No, no, there I'll woe thee with a Crown,
Crown our deſires, kindle the fires,
When love requires we ſhould wanton prove,
We'll kiſs, we'll ſport, we'll laugh, we'll play,
If thou com'ſt ſhort, for thee I'll ſtay,
If thou unskilful art on the ground,
I'll kindly teach, we'll have the Mill go round.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Are ye no Maid.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Alas (my Lord) no certain:
I am ſorry you are ſo innocent to think ſo,
Is this an age for ſilly Maids to thrive in?
It is ſo long too ſince I loſt it Sir,
That I have no belief I ever was one:
What ſhould you do with Maiden-heads? you hate 'em,
They are peeviſh, petty things, that hold no game up,
No pleaſure neither, they are ſport for Surgeons:
I'll warrant you I'll fit you beyond Maiden-head:
A fair and eaſie way men travel right in,
And with delight, diſcourſe, and twenty pleaſures,
They enjoy their journey; mad men creep through hedges.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I am metamorphos'd: why do you appear,
I conjure ye, beyond belief thus wanton?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Becauſe I would give ye
Pleaſure beyond belief.

body.head: 4. SONG.
body.l: Think me ſtill in my Fathers Mill,
where I have oft been found-a
Thrown on my back, on a well-fill'd ſack,
while the Mill has ſtill gone round-a:
Prethe ſirrah try thy skill,
and again let the mill go round-a.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Then you have traded?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Traded? how ſhould I know elſe how to live Sir,
And how to ſatisfie ſuch Lords as you are,
Our beſt gueſts, and our richeſt?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: How I ſhake now?
You take no baſe men?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Any that will offer,
All manner of men, and all Religions Sir,
We touch at in our time: all States and Ages,
We exempt none.

body.head: 5. SONG.
body.l: The young one, the old one, the fearful, the bold one,
the lame one, though nere ſo unſound,
The Jew or the Turk, have leave for to work,
the whilſt that the M • ll goes round.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: You are a common thing then.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: No matter ſince you have your private pleaſure,
And have it by an Artiſt excellent,
Whether I am thus, or thus, your men can tell ye.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: My Men? Defend me, how I freeze together,
And am on Ice? do I bite at ſuch an Orange
After my men? I am preferr'd.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Why ſtay ye?
Why do we talk my Lord, and loſe our time?
Pleaſure was made for lips, and ſweet embraces,
Let Lawyers uſe their tongues: pardon my Modeſty,
This deſperate way muſt help; or I am miſerable.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: She turns, and wipes her face, ſhe weeps for certain,
Some new way now, ſhe cannot be thus beaſtly,
She is too excellent fair to be thus impudent:
She knows the elements of common looſeneſs,
The art of lewdneſs: that, that, that, how now, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The King (and't pleaſe your Lordſhip) is alighted
Cloſe at the gate.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: The King?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: And calls for ye Sir.
Means to break-faſt here too.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Then I am happy.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Stol'n ſo ſuddenly? go lock her up.
Lock her up where the Courtiers may not ſee her,
Lock her up cloſely, ſirrah, in my cloſet.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I will (my Lord) what does ſhe yield yet? Exit.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Peace:
She is either a damn'd divel, or an Angel,
No noiſe (upon your life Dame) but all ſilence.

div.stage: Enter King, Lords, Vertigo, Liſauro, Terſo.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Your Majeſty heaps too much honor on me,
With ſuch delight to view each ſeveral corner
Of a rude pile: there's no proportion in't, Sir.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Me-thinks 'tis handſome, and the rooms along
Are neat, and well contriv'd: the Gallery
Stands pleaſantly and ſweet: what rooms are theſe?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: They are ſluttiſh ones.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Nay, I muſt ſee.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Pray ye do Sir,
They are lodging-chambers over a homely garden.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Fit ſtill, and handſome; very well: and thoſe?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Thoſe lead to the other ſide o'th' houſe, and't like ye

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Let me ſee thoſe.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Ye may, the dores are open.
What would this view mean? I am half ſuſpitious.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: This little Room?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: 'Tis mean: a place for traſh Sir,
For rubbiſh of the houſe.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I would ſee this too:
I will ſee all.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I beſeech your Majeſty,
The ſavor of it, and the courſe appearance.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: 'Tis not ſo bad, you would not offend your houſe with it,
Come, let me ſee.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Faith Sir,

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: I'faith I will ſee.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: My Groom has the key Sir, and 'tis ten to one—

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: But I will ſee it: force the lock (my Lords)
There be ſmiths enough to mend it: I perceive
You keep ſome rare things here, you would not ſhow Sir.

sp.speaker: Ter.
sp.l: Here's a fair maid indeed.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: By my faith is ſhe;
A hanſome girl: come forward, do not fear wench.
I marry, here's a treaſure worth concealing:
Call in the Miller.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Then I am diſcover'd.
I confeſs all before the Miller comes Sir,
'Twas but intention, from all act I am clear yet.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Is this your daughter?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Yes, and't pleaſe your Highneſs.
This is the ſhape of her, for her ſubſtance Sir,
Whether ſhe be now honorable or diſhonorable:
Whether ſhe be a white-roſe, or a canker is the queſtion:
I thank my Lord, he made bold with my Philly,
If ſhe be for your pace, you had beſt preſerve her Sir,
She is tender mouth'd, let her be broken handſomly.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Maid, were you ſtoln?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I went not willingly,
And't pleaſe your Grace, I was never bred ſo boldly.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: How has he us'd ye?

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Yet Sir, very nobly.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Be ſure ye tell truth, and be ſure (my Lord)
You have not wrong'd her: if ye have, I tell ye
You have loſt me, and your ſelf too: ſpeak again (wench)

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: He has not wrong'd me, Sir; I am yet a maid:
By all that's white and innocent, I am Sir,
Only I ſuffer'd under ſtrong temptations.
The heat of youth; but heaven deliver'd me.
My Lord, I am no whore, for all I faigned it,
And faign'd it cunningly, and made ye loath me:
'Twas time to out-do you: I had been rob'd elſe,
I had been miſerable, but I forgive ye.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What recompence for this?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: A great one Sir,
Firſt a repentance, and a hearty one.
Forgive me ſweet.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: I do my Lord.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: I thank ye;
The next take this, and theſe: all I have Florimel.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: No good my Lord, theſe often corrupt Maidens:
I dare not touch at theſe; they are lime for Virgins;
But if you'll give me.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Any thing in my power.
Or in my purchaſe.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Take heed (noble Sir)
You'll make me a bold asker.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Ask me freely.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Ask you? I do ask you, and I deſerve ye,
I have kept ye from a crying ſin would damn ye
To Men and Time: I have preſerv'd your credit,
That would have died to all poſterity:
Curſes of maids ſhall never now afflict ye,
Nor Parents bitter tears make your name barren:
If he deſerves well that redeems his Countrey,
And as a Patriot be remembred nobly,
Nay, ſet the higheſt: may not I be worthy
To be your friend, that have preſerv'd your honor?

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: You are, and thus I take ye: thus I ſeal ye
Mine own, and only mine.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Count, ſhe deſerves ye,
And let it be my happineſs to give ye,
I have given a virtuous maid, now I dare ſay it,
'Tis more then blood; I'll pay her portion Sir,
And't ſhall be worthy you.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I'll ſell my Mill,
I'll pay ſome too: I'll pay the Fidlers.
And we'll have all i'th'Country at this wedding,
Pray let me give her too, here my Lord take her,
Take her with all my heart, and kiſs her freely,
Would I could give you all this hand has ſtol'n too,
In portion with her, 'twould make her a little whiter.
The wind blows fair now, get me a young Miller.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: She muſt have new clothes.

sp.speaker: Tir.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Yes marry muſt ſhe.
If't pleaſe ye (Madam) let me ſee the ſtate of your body.
I'll fit you inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Art not thou gone yet?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: And't pleaſe your Grace, a gown, a handſome gown now,
An orient gown.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Nay, take thy pleaſure of her.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Of cloth of Tiſſew I can ſit ye (Madam)
My Lords, ſtand out o'th' light, a curious body,
The neateſt body in Spain this day: with embroidered flow'rs,
A clinquant Petticoat of ſome rich ſtuffe,
To catch the eye: I have a thouſand faſhions.
O ſleeve, O ſleeve: I'll ſtudy all night (Madam)
To magnifie your ſleeve.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Do, ſuperſtitious Tailor,
When ye have more time.

sp.speaker: Flo.
sp.l: Make me no more then woman,
And I am thine.

sp.speaker: Otr.
sp.l: Sir, haply my Wardrobe with your help
May fit her inſtantly: will you try her?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: If I fit her not, your Wardrobe cannot.
But if the faſhion be not there, you marre her.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Is my offence ſo great, ere I be convict,
To be torn with Raſcals? If it be Law,
Let 'em be wild horſes rather than theſe.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What •• that?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: This is a man ſuſpected of murther, if it pleaſe your Grace.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: It pleaſes me not (friend) But who ſuſpects him?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: We that are your Highneſs extraordinary officers, • e that have taken our oaths to maintain you in peace.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: 'Twill be a great charge to you.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: 'Tis a great charge indeed; but then we call our neighbors to help us. This Gentleman and another were fallen out (yet that's more then I am able to ſay, for I heard no words between 'em, but what their weapons ſpoke, Claſh, and Clatter) which we ſeeing, came with our Bills of government, and firſt knock'd down their weapons, and then the men.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: And this you did to keep the peace?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Yes, and't like your Grace, we knock'd 'em down to keep the peace: this we laid hold on, the other we ſet in the ſtocks. That I could do by mine own power, without your Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: How ſo, Sir?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.l: I am a Shoo-maker by my Trade.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Oh my Husband!
Why ſtands my husband as a man endanger'd?
Reſtore him me, as you are merciful,
I'll anſwer for him.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What woman's this? what husband? hold thy bawling,
I know thee for no wife.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You married me laſt night.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thou lyeſt: I neither was in Church nor houſe
Laſt night, nor ſaw I thee: a thing that was my friend,
I ſcorn to name now, was with Iſmenia,
Like a thief, and there he violated
A ſacred truſt. This thou mayſt know (Aminta.)

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Are not you he?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No; nor a friend of his:
Would I had kill'd him: I hope I have.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: That was my Husband (Royal Sir) that man,
That excellent man.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: That villain, that thief.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Have I caught you Sir? well overtaken.
This is mine enemy: pardon, (my Soveraign.)

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Good charity, to crave pardon for your enemy.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Mine own pardon (Sir) for my joyes rudeneſs,
In what place better could I meet my foe,
And both of us ſo well provided too?
He with ſome black blood-thirſty crime upon him,
That (ere the horſe-leech burſt) will ſuck him dry:
I with a ſecond accuſation,
Enough to break his neck, if need ſhould be,
And then to have even Juſtice it ſelf to right us:
How ſhould I make my joyes a little civil,
They might not keep this noyſe?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Here is ſome hope.
Should the ax be dull, the halter's preparing.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: What's your accuſation, Sir? We have heard the former.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Mine (my Lord?) a ſtrong one.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: A falſe one, Sir.
At leaſt malicious: an evidence
Of hatred and deſpight: He would accuſe
My poor kinſman of that he never dream'd of,
Nor waking ſaw; the ſtealing of his daughter,
She whom, I know, he would not look upon.
Speak Antonio, Didſt thou ever ſee her?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I have ſeen her.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Ah ha, friend Julio.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: He might, but how? with an unheedful eye,
An accidental view, as men ſee multitudes
That the next day dare not preciſely ſay
They ſaw that face, or that amongſt 'em all.
Didſt thou ſo look on her?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Guilty, guilty:
His looks hang themſelves.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Your patience (Genleman.)
I pray you tell me if I be in errour,
I may ſpeak often when I ſhould but hear:
This is ſome ſhow you would preſent us with,
And I do interrupt it: Pray you ſpeak,
(It ſeems no more) Is't any thing but a ſhow?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: My Lord, this Gentlewoman can ſhow you all,
So could my daughter too: if ſhe were here;
By this time they are both immodeſt enough:
Shee's fled me, and I accuſe this thief for't.
Don Martin, his own friend's my teſtimony:
A practis'd night-work.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: That Martin's the other
In your cuſtodie; he was forgotten:
Fetch him hither.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Wee'll bring the Stocks and all elſe, and't pleaſe your Grace.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: That man's my husband certain, inſtead of this:
Both would have deceiv'd, and both beguil'd.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Soh hoh, Miller, Miller, look out Miller: is there n'ere a Miller amongſt you here, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Tir.
sp.l: Yes Sir, here is a Miller amongſt Gentlemen,
A Gentleman Miller.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: I ſhould not be far off then; there went but a pair of ſheers and a bodkin between us. Will you to work Miller? Here's a maid has a ſack full of news for you: ſhall your ſtones walk? will you grind Miller?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: This your ſon, Franio?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: My ungratious, my diſobedient,
My unnatural, my rebel ſon (my Lord.)

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Fie, your hopper runs over, Miller.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: This villain (of my own fleſh and blood) was acceſſary
To the ſtealing of my daughter.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Oh Mountain,
Shalt thou call a molehill a ſcab upon the face
Of the earth? though a man be a thief, ſhall a Miller call
Him ſo? Oh egregious!

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Remember Sirrha, who you ſpeak before.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I ſpeak before a Miller,
A thief in grain; for he ſteals corn: He that ſteals
A wench, is a true man to him.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.p: Can you prove that? you may help another cauſe that was in pleading.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I'll prove it ſtrongly.
He that ſteals corn, ſteals the bread of the Common-wealth;
sp.p: He that ſteals a wench, ſteals but the fleſh.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.p: And how is the bread ſtealing more criminal then the fleſh?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: He that ſteals bread, ſteals that which is lawful every day:
sp.l: He that ſteals fleſh, ſteals nothing from the faſting day:
Ergo to ſteal the bread is the arranter theft.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: This is to ſome purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: Again, he that ſteals fleſh ſteals for his own belly full:
He that ſteals bread, robs the guts of others:
Ergo, The arranter thief the bread-ſtealer.
sp.p: Again he that ſteals fleſh, ſteals once, and gives over; yes, and often pays for it: the other ſteals every day, without ſatisfaction. To conclude, Bread-ſtealing is the more capital crime: for what he ſteals he puts it in at the head: he that ſteals fleſh (as the Dutch Author ſays) puts it in at the foot (the lower member.) Will you go as you are now, Miller?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: How has this ſatisfied you, Don Bellides?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Nothing (my Lord) my cauſe is ſerious.
I claim a daughter from that loving thiefe there.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I would I had her for you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Ah ha, Julio.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: How ſaid you, Antonio? Wiſh you, you had his daughter?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: With my ſoul I wiſh her; and my body
Shall periſh, but I'll injoy my ſouls wiſh.
I would have ſlain my friend for his deceit,
But I do find his own deceit hath paid him.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Will you vex my ſoul forth? no other choice
But where my hate is rooted? Come hither Girl,
Whoſe pretty maid art thou?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: The child of a poor man, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: The better for it. With my Soveraigns leave,
I'll wed thee to this man, will he, nill he.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Pardon me, Sir, I'll be no Love enforcer:
I uſe no power of mine unto thoſe ends.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Wilt thou have him?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Not unleſs he love me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I do love thee: Farewell all other Beauties:
I ſettle here: you are Iſmenia.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: The ſame I was: better nor worſe, (Antonio)

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I ſhall have your conſent here, I'm ſure, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: With all my heart, Sir. Nay, if you accept it,
I'll do this kindneſs to mine enemy,
And give her as a Father.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Shee'll thank you as a Daughter.
Will you not, Iſmenia?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How? Iſmenia?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Your daughter, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Is't poſſible? Away you feeble witted things,
You thought you had caught the old ones: you wade, you wade
In ſhallow fords: we can ſwim, we: look here,
We made the match: we are all friends good friends;
Thin, thin: why the fool knew all this, this fool.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Keep that to your ſelf, Sir; What I knew I knew: This ſack is a witneſs. Miller, this is not for your thumming. Here's gold lace: you may ſee her in her holliday clothes if you will; I was her ward-robe-man.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You beguil'd me well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Did you ſpeak to me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It might ſeem to you, Martin, your conſcience
Has quick ears.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: My ſight was a little dim i'th' dark indeed,
So was my feeling cozen'd; yet I'm content:
I am the better underſtander now,
I know my wife wants nothing of a woman;
There y'are my Junior.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You are not hurt?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Not ſhrewdly hurt; I bave good fleſh to heal, you ſee,
Good round fleſh: theſe cherries will be worth chopping,
Crack ſtones and all; I ſhould not give much to boot
To ride in your new, and you in my old ones now.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You miſtake the weapon: are you not hurt?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A little ſcratch: but I ſhall claw it off well enough.

sp.speaker: Gill.
sp.l: I can no longer own what is not mine
With a free conſcience: My Liege, your pardon.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: For what? who knows this woman?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: I beſt, my Lord,
I have been acquainted with her theſe forty Summers,
And as many Winters, were it Spring agen;
She's like the Gout I can get no cure for her.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Oh, your Wife, Franio?

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: 'Tis oh my wife indeed, my Lord,
A painful ſtitch to my ſide; would it were pick'd out.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Well Sir, your ſilence.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Will you be older and older every day than other? the longer you live the older ſtill? Muſt his Majeſty command your ſilence ere you'l hold your tongue?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Your reprehenſion runs into the ſame fault:
'Pray Sir, will you be ſilent.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I have told him of this before now, my Liege, but
Age will have his courſe, and his weakneſſes.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Good Sir, your forbearance.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: And his frailties, and his follies, as I may ſay, that cannot hold his tongue ere he be bidden.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Why Sirha?

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: But I believe your Majeſty will not be long troubled with him: I hope that woman has ſomething to confeſs will hang them both.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Sirha, you'll pull your deſteny upon you
If you ceaſe not the ſooner.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.p: Nay, I have done, my Liege, yet it grieves me that I ſhould call that man Father, that ſhould be ſo ſhameleſs, that being commanded to hold his tongue.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: To th'Porters Lodge with him.

sp.speaker: Buſt.
sp.l: I thank your Grace, I have a friend there.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Speak woman, if any interruption meet thee more,
It ſhall be puniſh'd ſharply.

sp.speaker: Gill.
sp.l: Good my Liege, (I dare not)
Ask you the queſtion why that old man weeps.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: Who? Count Julio? I obſerv'd it not.
You hear the queſtion Sir, will you give the cauſe?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Oh my Lord, it hardly will get paſſage,
It is a ſorrow of that greatneſs grown,
'Leſs it diſſolve in tears, and come by parcels.
