Of ſuch an exquiſite form?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Moſt exquiſite.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: And well deſcended?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: So the habit promis'd,
In which ſhe was taken.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Of what years?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: 'Tis ſaid
A Virgin of fourteen.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I pity her,
And wiſh ſhe were mine, that I might have the means
T'entertain her gently.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: She's now Miranda's,
And as I have heard, made it her ſuit to be ſo.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Miranda's? then her fate deſerves not pity,
But envy rather.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Envy Oriana?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Yes, and their envy that live free.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Why, ſhe's falln into the hands of one,
So full of that, which in men we ſtile goodneſs,
That in her being his ſlave, ſhe is happier far
Than if ſhe were confirm'd the Sultan's Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Miranda is indeed a Gentleman
Of fair deſert, and better hopes, but yet
He hath his equals.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Where? I would go far,
As I am now, though much unfit for travails,
But to ſee one that without injury
Might be put in the ſcale, or paralell'd,
In any thing that's Noble, with Miranda;
His knowledge in all ſervices of war,
And ready courage, to put into act
That knowing judgement, as you are a Soldier
You beſt may ſpeak of. Nor can you deliver,
Nor I hear with delight, a better ſubject.
And heaven did well, in ſuch a lovely feature
To place ſo chaſte a mind; for he is of
So ſweet a carriage, ſuch a winning nature,
And ſuch a bold, yet well-diſpos'd behaviour;
And to all theſe, h'as ſuch a charming tongue,
That if he would ſerve under Loves freſh colours,
What monumental Trophies might he raiſe,
Of his free conqueſts, made in Ladies favors?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Yet you did reſiſt him, when he was
An earneſt ſuitor to you.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Yes I did;
And if I were again ſought to, I ſhould;
But muſt aſcribe it rather to the fate
That did appoint me yours, than any power
Which I can call mine own.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Even ſo?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Thanks fortune,
The plot I had to raiſe, in him, doubts of her,
Thou haſt effected.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I could tell you too,
What cauſe I have to love him, with what reaſon.
In thankfulneſs, he may expect from me,
All due obſervance; but I paſs that, as
A benefit, for which, in my behalf,
You are his debtor.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: I perceive it takes,
By his chang'd looks.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: He is not in the City?
Is he my Lord?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Who Lady?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Why Miranda,
Having you here, can there be any elſe
Worth my enquiry?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: This is ſomewhat more
Than love to virtue,

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Faith when he comes hither
(As ſometimes, without queſtion you ſhall meet him)
Invite him home.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: To what end?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: To dine with us,
Or ſup.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: And then to take a hard bed with you:
Mean you not ſo?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: If you could win him to it,
'Twould be the better; for his entertainment,
Leave that to me, he ſhall find Noble uſage,
And from me a free welcome.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Have you never
Heard of a Roman Lady (Oriana)
Remembred as a preſident for Matrons,
(Chaſte ones, I pray you underſtand) whoſe husband
Tax'd for his ſowre breath by his enemy,
Condemn'd his wife, for not acquainting him
With his infirmity?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: 'Tis a common one;
Her anſwer was, having kiſs'd none but him,
• he thought it was a general diſeaſe
All men were ſubject to; but what infer you
From that my Lord?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Why, that this virtuous Lady
Had all her thoughts ſo fixed upon her Lord,
That ſhe could find no ſpare time to ſing praiſes
Of any other; nor would ſhe imploy
Her husband (though perhaps in debt to years
As far as I am) for an inſtrument
To bring home younger men that might delight her
With their diſcourſe, or—

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: What my Lord?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Their perſons,
Or if I ſhould ſpeak plainer—

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: No it needs not,
You have ſaid enough to make my innocence know
• t is ſuſpected.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: You betray your ſelf
To more than a ſuſpition; could you elſe
To me that live in nothing but love to you
Make ſuch a groſs diſcovery, that your luſt
Had ſold that heart I thought mine, to Miranda?
Or riſe to ſuch a height in impudence,
• s to preſume to work my yielding weakneſs
To play for your bad ends, to my diſgrace,
The Wittal, or the Pander?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Do not ſtudy
To print more wounds, (for that were tyranny)
Upon a heart that is pierced through already.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Thy heart? thou haſt pierc'd through mine honor falſe one,
The honor of my houſe, fool that I was,
To give it up to the deceiving truſt
Of wicked woman: for thy ſake vild creature,
For all I have done well, in my life,
I have dig'd a grave, all buried in a wife;
For thee I have defi'd my conſtant Miſtriſs,
That never fail'd her ſervant, glorious war;
For thee, refus'd the fellowſhip of an Order
Which Princes, through all dangers, have been proud
To fetch as far as from Jeruſalem:
And am I thus rewarded?

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: By all goodneſs,
You wrong my Lady, and deſerve her not,
When you are at your beſt: repent your raſhneſs,
'Twill ſhow well in you.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Do, and ask her pardon.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: No, I have liv'd too long, to have my faith
(My tri'd faith) call'd in queſtion, and by him
That ſhould know true affection is too tender
To ſuffer an unkind touch, without ruine;
Study ingratitude, all, from my example;
For to be thankful now, is to be falſe.
But be it ſo, let me dye, I ſee you wiſh it;
Yet dead for truth, and pities ſake, report
What weapon you made choice of, when you kild me.

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: She faints.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: What have ye done?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: My laſt breath cannot
Be better ſpent, than to ſay I forgive you;
Nor is my death untimely, ſince with me
I take along, what might have been hereafter
In ſcorn delivered for the doubtful iſſue
Of a ſuſpected mother.

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: Oh, ſhe's gone.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: For ever gone. Are you a man?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: I grow here.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Open her mouth, and power this Cordial in it;
If any ſpark of life be unquench'd in her,
This will recover her.

sp.speaker: Vel.
sp.l: 'Tis all in vain,
She's ſtiffe already: live I, and ſhe dead?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: How like a murtherer I ſtand? look up,
And hear me curſe my ſelf, or but behold
The vengeance I will take for't Oriana,
And then in peace forſake me: Jealouſie,
Thou loathſome vomit of the fiends below,
What deſperate hunger made me to receive thee
Into my heart, and ſoul? I'll let thee forth,
And ſo in death find eaſe; and does my fault then
Deſerve no greater puniſhment? no, I'll live
To keep thee for a fury to torment me,
And make me know what hell is on the earth:
All joyes and hopes forſake me; all mens malice,
And all the plagues they can inflict, I wiſh it
Fall thick upon me: let my tears be laught at,
And may mine enemies ſmile to hear me groane;
And dead, may I be pitied of none. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray you Sir why was the Ordnance of the Fort.
Diſcharg'd ſo ſodainly?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: 'Twas the Governors pleaſure,
In honor of the Dane, a cuſtom us'd,
To ſpeak a Soldiers welcome.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Tis a fit one:
But is my Maſter here too?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Three days ſince.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Might I demand without offence, ſo much,
Is't pride in him (however now a ſlave)
That I am not admitted to his preſence?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: His curteſie to you, and to mankind
May eaſily reſolve you, he is free
From that poor vice which only empty men
Eſteem a virtue.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What's the reaſon then,
As you imagine, Sir?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Why I tell you;
You are a woman of a tempting beauty,
And he, however virtuous, as a man
Subject to humane frailties; and how far
They may prevail upon him, ſhould he ſee you,
He is not ignorant: and therefore chooſes,
With care t'avoid the cauſe that may produce
Some ſtrange effect, which will not well keep ranck
With the rate temperature, which is admired
In his life hitherto.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: This much increaſes
My ſtrong deſire to ſee him.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: It ſhould rather
Teach you to thank the Prophet that you worſhip,
That you are ſuch a mans, who though he may
Do any thing which youth and heat of blood
Invites him to, yet dares not give way to them:
Your entertainment's Noble, and not like
Your preſent fortune; and if all thoſe tears
Which made grief lovely in you, in the relation
Of the ſad ſtory, that forc'd me to weep too,
Your husbands hard fate were not counterfeit;
You ſhould rejoyce that you have means to pay
A chaſt life to his memory, and bring to him
Thoſe ſweets, which while he liv'd, he could not taſt of;
By if you wantonly beſtow them on
Another man you offer violence
To him, though dead; and his griev'd ſpirit will ſuffer
For your immodeſt looſeneſs.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why, I hope, Sir,
My willingneſs to look on him, to whom
I owe my life and ſervice, is no proof
Of any unchaſt purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: So I wiſh too,
And in the confidence it is not, Lady,
I dare the better tell you he will ſee you
This night, in which by him I am commanded,
To bring you to his chamber, to what end
I eaſily ſhould gueſs, were I Miranda;
And therefore, though I can yield little reaſon,
(But in a general love to womens goodneſs)
Why I ſhould be ſo tender of your honor,
I willingly would beſtow ſome counſail of you,
And would you follow it?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Let me firſt hear it,
And then I can reſolve you.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: My advice then
Is, that you would not, (as moſt Ladies uſe
When they prepare themſelves for ſuch encounters)
Study to add, by artificial dreſſings
To native excellence; yours (without help)
But ſeen as it is now, would make a Hermit
Leaves his deaths head, and change his after hopes
Of endleſs comforts for a few ſhort minutes
Of preſent pleaſures; to prevent which, Lady,
Practice to take away from your perfections,
And to preſerve your chaſtity unſtain'd,
The moſt deform'd ſhape that you can put on
To cloud your bodies fair gifts, or your minds,
(It being laboured to ſo chaſt an end)
Will prove the faireſt ornament.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: To take from
The workmanſhip of Heaven is an offence
As great, as to endeavor to add to it;
Of which, I'll not be guilty: Chaſtity
That lodges in deformity, appears rather
A mulct impos'd by nature, than a bleſſing;
And 'tis commendable only when it conquers,
Though nere ſo oft aſſaulted, in reſiſtance:
For me, I'll therefore ſo diſpoſe my ſelf,
That if I hold out, it ſhall be with honor;
Or if I yield, Miranda ſhall find ſomething
To make him love his victory. Exit.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: With what cunning
This woman argues for her own damnation?
Nor ſhould I hold it for a miracle,
Since they are all born Sophiſters to maintain
That luſt is lawful, and the end and uſe
Of their creation: would I never had
Hop'd better of her; or could not believe,
Though ſeen the ruin, I muſt ever grieve. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Miranda, Norandine, Servants with Lights.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'll ſee you in your chamber. A Table n •• , two fi •• s.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Pray ye no farther:
It is a ceremony I expect not,
I am no ſtranger here, I know my lodging,
An have ſlept ſoundly there, when the Turks Cannon
Playd thick upon't: O 'twas Royal Muſick,
And to procure a ſound ſleep for a Souldier,
Worth forty of our Fiddles. As you love me
Preſs it no farther.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You will overcome.
Wait on him carefully.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I have took ſince ſupper
A rouſe or two too much, and by—
It warms my blood.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You'll ſleep the better for't.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: —on't, I ſhould, had but I a kind wench
To pull my Boot-hoſe off, and warm my night-cap,
There's no charm like it: I love old Adams way;
Give me a diligent Eve, to wait towards bed-time,
Hang up your ſmooth chin page: and now I think on't,
Where is your Turkiſh Priſoner?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: In the Caſtle,
But yet I never ſaw her.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Fie upon you:
See her for ſhame; or hark ye, if you would
Perform the friends part to me, the friends part,
It being a faſhion of the laſt edition,
Far from panderiſm, now ſend her to me;
You look ſtrange on't, no entertainment's perfect
Without it on my word; no livery like it;
There's no ſuit got without it,
Gold is an aſs to't.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Go to bed, to bed.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Well, if ſhe come, I doubt not to convert her,
If not, the ſin lye on your head.
Good night Exit Nor. and Servants.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: There you ſhall find him Lady: you know what I have ſaid,
And if you pleaſe you may make uſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: No doubt Sir.

sp.speaker: Gol.
sp.l: From hence I ſhall hear all.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Come hither young one.
Beſhrew my heart: a handſome wench: come nearer,
A very handſome one: do not you grieve, Sweet,
You are a priſoner?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: The loſs of liberty
No doubt Sir, is a heavy and a ſharp burden
To them that feel it truely: But your ſervant,
Your humble handmayd, never felt that rigor,
Thanks to that noble will: no want, no hunger,
(Companions ſtill to ſlaves) no violence
Nor any unbeſeeming act, we ſtart at,
Have I yet with; all content and goodneſs,
Civility, and ſweetneſs of behaviour
Dwell round about me; therefore worthy Maſter,
I cannot ſay I grieve my liberty.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Do not you fancy me too cold a Soldier,
Too obſtinate an enemy to youth,
That had ſo fair a jewel in my Cabinet,
And in ſo long a time, would nere look on it?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: What can ſhe ſay now?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sure I deſir'd to ſee ye,
And with a longing wiſh.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: There's all her virtue.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Purſu'd that full deſire to give ye thanks Sir,
The only Sacrifice I have left, and ſervice,
For all the virtuous care you have kept me ſafe with.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: She holds well yet.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: The pretty fool ſpeaks finely:
Come ſit down here.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: O Sir, 'tis moſt unſeemly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'll have it ſo: ſit cloſe, now tell me truly,
Did you ere love yet?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My years will anſwer that Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And did you then love truly?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: So I thought Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Can ye love me ſo?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Now!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: With all my duty;
I were unworthy of thoſe favors elſe,
You daily ſhowre upon me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What thinkſt thou of me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I think ye are a truly worthy Gentleman,
A pattern, and a pride to the age ye live in,
Sweet as the commendations all men give ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A pretty flattering rogue, dare ye kiſs that ſweet man
Ye ſpeak ſo ſweetly of? Come.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Farewell virtue.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What haſt thou got between thy lips? kiſs once more.
Sure thou haſt a ſpell there.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: More than ere I knew Sir.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: All hopes go now.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I muſt tell you a thing in your ear, and you muſt hear me,
And hear me willingly, and grant me ſo too,
'Twill not be worth my asking elſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: It muſt be
A very hard thing Sir, and from my power,
I ſhall deny your goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis a good wench; I muſt lye with ye Lady.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Tis ſomething ſtrange:
For yet in all my life I knew no bedfellow.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You will quickly find that knowledge.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: To what end Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Art thou ſo innocent, thou canſt not gueſs at it?
Did thy dreams never direct thee?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Faith none yet Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'll tell thee then: I would meet thy youth, and pleaſure;
Give thee my youth for that, by heaven ſhew fires me,
And teach thy fair white arms, like wanton Ivies
A thouſand new embraces.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Is that all Sir?
And ſay I ſhould try, may not we lie quietly?
Upon my conſcience I could.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That's as we make it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Grant that, that likes ye beſt, what would ye do then?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What would I do? certainly I am no baby,
Nor brought up for a Nun; hark in thine ear.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Fie, fie, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I would get a brave boy on thee,
A warlike boy.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sure we ſhall get ill Chriſtians.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: We'll mend 'em in the breeding then.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sweet Maſter.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Never belief in woman come near me more.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My beſt and nobleſt Sir, if a poor Virgin,
(For yet by—I am ſo) ſhould chance ſo far
(Seeing your excellence, and able ſweetneſs)
To forget her ſelf, and ſlip into your boſome,
Or to your bed, out of a doting on ye,
Take it the beſt way; have you that cruel heart,
That murd'ring mind too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes by my troth (ſweet) have I,
To lie with her.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: And do you think it well done?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That's as ſhe'll think when 'tis done; come to bed wench,
For thou art ſo pretty, and ſo witty a companion,
We muſt not part to night.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Faith let me go Sir,
And think better on't.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yfaith thou ſhalt not;
I warrant thee I'll think on't.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I have heard 'em ſay here,
You are a Maid too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I am ſure I am, wench,
If that will pleaſe thee.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I have ſeen a wonder,
And would you looſe that for a little wantonneſs,
(Conſider my ſweet Maſter, like a man, now,)
For a few honied kiſſes, ſleight embraces,
That glory of your youth that crown of ſweetneſs?
Can ye deliver that unvalued treaſure?
Would ye forſake, to ſeek your own diſhonor,
What gone, no age recovers, nor repentance,
To a poor ſtranger?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Hold there again, thou art perfect.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I know you do but try me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And I know
I'll try you a great deal farther: prethee to bed;
I love thee, and ſo well: come kiſs me once more;
Is a maiden-head ill beſtow'd o'me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What's this Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why, 'tis the badge (my Sweet) of that holy Order
I ſhortly muſt receive, the Croſs of Malta.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What virtue has it?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: All that we call virtuous.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Who gave it firſt?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: He that gave all, to ſave us.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why then 'tis holy too?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: True ſign of holineſs,
The badge of all his Soldiers that profeſs him.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: The badge of all his Soldiers that profeſs him,
Can't ſave in dangers?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: In troubles comfort?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You ſay true, ſweet.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: In ſicknes, reſtore health?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: All this it can do.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Preſerve from evils that afflict our frailties.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I hope ſhe will be Chriſtian: all theſe truly.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why are you ſick then, ſick to death with luſt?
In danger to be loſt? no holy thought,
In all that heart, nothing but wandring frailties
Wild as the wind, and blind as death or ignorance,
Inhabit there.

sp.speaker: dMir.
sp.l: Forgive me heaven, ſhe ſays true.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Dare ye profeſs that badge, prophane that goodneſs?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Thou haſt redeem'd thy ſelf again, moſt rarely.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: That holineſs and truth ye make me wonder at?
Blaſt all the bounty heaven gives, that remembrance.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: O excellent woman.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Fling it from ye quickly,
If ye be thus reſolv'd; I ſee a virtue
Appear in't like a ſword, both edges flaming
That will conſume ye, and your thoughts, to aſhes,
Let them profeſs it that are pure, and noble,
Gentle, and juſt of thought, that build the croſs,
Not thoſe that break it, by—if ye touch me,
Even in the act, I'll make that croſs, and curſe ye.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You ſhall not (fair) I did diſſemble with ye,
And but to try your faith, I faſhion'd all this:
Yet ſomething you provokt me: this fair croſs:
By me (if he but pleaſe to help, firſt gave it)
Shall nee'r be worn upon a heart corrupted;
Go to your reſt, my modeſt, honeſt ſervant,
My fair, and virtuous maid, and ſleep ſecure there,
For when you ſuffer, I forget this ſign here.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: A man of men too: O moſt perfect Gentleman!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: All ſweet reſt to you ſir; I am half a Chriſtian,
The other half, I'll pray for; then for you, Sir;

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This is the fowleſt play I'll ſhew, good night, ſweet.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: The Sun's not ſet yet?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Would it were,
Never to riſe again to light the world.
And yet, to what vain purpoſe do I wiſh it.
Since though I were inviron'd with thick miſts,
Black as Cymerian darkneſs, or my crimes,
There is that here, upon which as an anvile
Ten thouſand hammers ſtrike, and every ſpark
They force from it, to me's an other Sun
To light me to my ſhame?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Take hope, and comfort.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: They are aides indeed, but yet as far from me,
As I from being innocent: this cave faſhion'd
By provident nature, in this ſolid Rock
To be a den for beaſts, alone, receives me,
And having prov'd an enemy to mankind,
All humane helps forſake me.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: I'll nee'r leave you,
And wiſh you would call back that noble courage
That old invincible fortitude of yours
That us'd to ſhrink at nothing.
Then it did not.
But 'twas when I was honeſt; then in the height
Of all my happineſs, of all my glories,
Of all delights, that made life pretious to me
I durſt dye Rocca; death it ſelf then to me
Was nothing terrible, becauſe I knew,
The ſame of a good Knight would ever live
Freſh on my memory; but ſince I fell
From my integrity, and diſmis'd thoſe guards,
Thoſe ſtrong aſſurances of innocence,
That conſtancy fled from me, and what's worſe,
Now I am loathſome to my ſelf; and life
A burthen to me, rack'd with ſad remembrance
Of what I have done, and my preſent horrors
Unſufferable to me, tortur'd with deſpair
That I ſhall nee'r find mercy: hell about me,
Behind me, and before me, yet I dare not,
Still fearing worſe, put off my wretched Being.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: To ſee this would deter a doubtful man
From miſchievous intents, much more the practice.
Of what is wicked: here's the Moore, look up Sir,
Some eaſe may come from her.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: New trouble rather,
And I expect it.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Who is this? Mountferrat?
Riſe up for ſhame, and like a river dri'd up
With a long drought, from me, your bounteous Sea
Receive thoſe tides of comfort that flow to you;
If ever I look lovely: if deſert.
Could ever challenge welcome; if revenge,
And unexpected wreak, were ever pleaſing
Or could endear the giver of ſuch bleſſings,
All theſe I come adorn'd with, and, as due,
Make challenge of thoſe ſo long wiſh'd embraces
Which you (unkind) have hitherto deny'd me.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Why, what have you done for me?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Made Gomera
As truely miſerable, as you thought him happy,
Could you wiſh more?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: As if his ſickneſs could
Recover me; the injuries I receiv'd
Were Oriana's.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: She has paid dear for 'em,
She's dead.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Dead; my hate could reach no farther:
Taking advantage of her in a ſwoon,
Under pretence to give a Cordial to her
I poyſon'd her: what ſtupid dulneſs is this?
What you ſhould entertain with ſacrifice,
Can you receive ſo coldly?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Bloody deeds
Are grateful offerings, pleaſing to the devill,
And thou, in thy black ſhape, and blaker actions
Being hels perfect character, art delighted
To do what I thought infinitely wicked,
Tremble to hear: thou haſt, in this taen from me
All means to make amends with penitence,
To her wrong'd virtues, and diſpoil'd me of
The poor remainder of that hope was left me,
For all I have already, or muſt ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: I did it for the beſt.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: For thy worſt ends,
And be aſſur'd but that, I think to kill thee
Would but prevent, what thy deſpair muſt force thee
To do unto thy ſelf, and ſo to add to
Thy moſt aſſur'd damnation, thou wert dead now.
But get thee from my ſight: and if luſt of me
Did ever fire thee (love I cannot call it)
Leap down from thoſe ſteep Rocks, or take advantage
Of the next tree to hang thy ſelf, and then
I may laugh at it.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: In the mean time
I muſt be bold, to do ſo much for you, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Why grinſt thou, devil?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: That 'tis in my power,
To puniſh thy ingratitude; I made trial
But how you ſtood affected, and ſince I know
I'm us'd only for a property,
I can, and will revenge it to the full.
For underſtand, in thy contempt of me,
Thoſe hopes of Oriana, which I could
Have chang'd to certainties, are loſt for ever.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Why, lives ſhe?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Yes, but never to Mountferrat,
Although it is in me, with as much eaſe
To give her freely up to thy poſſeſſion,
As to remove this ruſh; which yet deſpair of:
For by much wrong'd love, flattery, nor threats,
Tears, prayers, nor vowes, ſhall ever win me to it:
So with my curſe I leave thee.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Prethee ſtay,
Thou know'ſt I dote on thee, and yet thou art
So peeviſh, and perverſe, ſo apt to take
Triffles unkindly from me.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: To perſwade me
To break my neck, to hang, then damn my ſelf,
With you are trifles.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: 'Twas my melancholy
That made me ſpeak I know not what: forgive,
I will redeem my fault.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Believe him Lady.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: A thouſand times I will demand thy pardon,
And keep the reckoning on thy lips with kiſſes.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: There's ſomething elſe, that would prevail more with me.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have all thy wiſhes do but bleſs me
With means to ſatisfie my mad deſires
For once in Oriana and for ever
I am thine, only thine my beſt Abdella.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Were I aſſur'd of this, and that you would
Having enjoy'd her—

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Any thing: make choice of
Thine own conditions.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Swear then, that perform'd,
To free me from all doubts and fears hereafter)
To give me leave to kill her.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: That our ſafety
Muſt of neceſſity urge us to.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Then know
• t was not poyſon, but a ſleeping potion
Which ſhe receiv'd; yet of ſufficient ſtrength
• o to bind up her ſences, that no ſign
Of life appear'd in her: and thus thought dead,
• n her beſt habit, as the cuſtom is
You know in Malta, with all ceremonies
• he's buried in her families monument,
• n the Temple of St. John; I'll bring you thither,
Thus, as you are diſguis'd; ſome ſix hours hence
The potion will leave working.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Let us haſte then.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Be my good angel, guide me.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: But remember,
You keep your Oath.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: As I deſire to proſper
• n what I undertake.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: I ask no more. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Here ſir, I have got the Key; I borrow'd it
• f him that keeps the Church, the door is open.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Look to the horſes then, and pleaſe the fellow.
• fter a few devotions, I'll retire.
• e not far off, there may be ſome uſe of ye,
Give me the light: come friend, a few good prayers
Were not beſtow'd in vain now, even from you Sir.
Men that are bred in blood, have no way left 'em,
• o bath, no purge, no time to wear it out
• r waſh it off, but penitence, and prayer:
• am to take the order, and my youth
• oaden I muſt confeſs with many follies,
Circled and bound about with ſins as many
• s in the houſe of memory live figures.
My heart I'll open now, my faults confeſs,
• nd raiſe a new man, heaven, I hope, to a new life.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I have no great devotion, at this inſtant,
• ut for a prayer or two, I will not out Sir,
• old up your finger, when you have pray'd enough.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Go you to that end.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I ſhall nee'r pray alone ſure,
• have been ſo us'd to anſwer the Clerk: would I had a
• aſhion, for I ſhall ne'r make a good Hermit, and kneel
• ll my knees are horn, theſe ſtones are plaguy hard;
• here ſhall I begin now? for if I do not obſerve a method,
• hall be out preſently.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: What's that Sir? did ye hear?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Ha; to your prayers.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: 'Twas here abouts, t'has put me clean away now,
• ſhall nee'r get in again, ha, by Land,
• nd water, all children, and all women,
• here it was I left.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Never tell me Sir,
• ere's ſomething got amongſt us.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I heard a groan:
A diſmal one, —

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, Oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Here, 'tis here Sir, 'tis here Sir;
A devil in the wall.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis ſome illuſion
To fright us from devotion—

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Why 'tis here,
The ſpirit of a hunteſman choak'd with butter:
Here's a new tomb, new trickments too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: For certain,
This has not been three days here.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: And a Tablet
With rimes upon't.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I prethee read 'em Norandine.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: An Epi—and Epi—taff. I think 'tis, I 'tis taff, an Epitaff.
Upon the moſt excell, excell—lent—and.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou canſt not read.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I have ſpoyl'd mine eyes with gunpowder,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: An Epitaph upon the moſt virtuous, and excellent Lady
The honor of Chaſtity, Oriana.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: The grand maſters ſiſter: how a devil came ſhe here?
When ſlipt ſhe out o'th' way, the ſtone's but half upon her.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſodain change: certain the miſchief
Mountferrat offer'd to her broak her heart-ſtrings.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Would he were here, I would be the clerk my ſelf,
And by this little light, I would bury him alive here:
Here's no lamenting now.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: There 'tis

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sure from the monument, the very ſtone groanes for her.
Oh, dear Lady: bleſſing of women, virtue of thy ſex;
How art thou ſet for ever, how ſtol'n from us.
Babling, and prating now converſe with women.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Sir, it riſes, it looks up. She riſes up.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs us.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: It is in womans cloathes, it riſes higher.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: It looks about, and wonders, ſure ſhe lives Sir.
'Tis ſhe, 'tis Oriana, 'tis that Lady.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Shall I go to her?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Where am I!

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Stand ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: What place is this?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: She is as live as I am.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: What ſmell of earth, and rotten bones, what dark place?
Lord, whither am I carried?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: How ſhe ſtares,
And ſets her eyes upon him.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How is't dear Lady?
Do you know me, how ſhe ſhakes?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: You are a man.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: A man that honors you.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: A cruel man,
Ye are all cruel: are you in your grave too?
For there's no truſting cruel man, above ground.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Byr'Lady that goes hard.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To do you ſervice
And to reſtore ye to the joys you were in.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I was in joyes indeed, and hope—

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: She ſinks again
Again ſhe's gone; ſhe's gone: gone as a ſhadow,
She ſinks for ever, friend.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: She is cold now,
She is certainly departed, I muſt cry too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: The bleſſed angels guide thee; put the ſtone too,
Beauty thou art gone to duſt, goodneſs to aſhes.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Pray take it well: we muſt all have our hours Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I, thus we are; and all our painted glory,
A buble that a boy blows in toth' ayr,
And there it breaks.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I am glad ye ſav'd her honor yet.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Would I had ſav'd her life now too: oh heaven
For ſuch a bleſſing, ſuch a timely bleſſing
O friend, what dear content 'twould be, what ſtory
To keep my name from worms?

sp.speaker: Oria
sp.l: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: She lives again.
'Twas but a trance.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Pray ye call my man in preſently
Help with the ſtone firſt, oh ſhe ſtirs again.
Oh call my man away.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I fly, I fly Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Upon my knees O heaven, O heaven I thank thee.
The living heat ſteals into every member;
Come help the Coffin out ſoftly, and ſodainly;
Where is the Clerk?

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Drunk above he is ſure Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sirrah, you muſt be ſecret.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: As your ſoul Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Softly good friend, take her into your armes.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Put in the cruſt again.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And bring her out there when I am a horſeback
My man, and I will tenderly conduct her
Unto the Fort; ſtay you, and watch what iſſue,
And what inquirie's for the body.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And when ye have done, come back to me.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Softly, oh ſoftly.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: She grows warmer ſtill Sir.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: What ſhall I do with the Key?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Thou canſt not ſtir now,
Leave it ith'door, go get the horſes ready. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Rocca, Mountferrat, Abdella, with a dark Lanthorn.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: The door's already opne, the Key in it.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: What were thoſe paſt by?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Some ſcout of Soldiers, I think.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: It may well be ſo, for I ſaw their horſes:
They ſaw not us I hope.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: No, no, we were cloſe,
Beſide they were far off.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: What time of night is't?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Much about twelve I think.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Let me go in firſt
For by the leaving open of the door here
There may be ſome body in the Church: give me the Lanthorne.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: You'll love me now I hope.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Make that good to me
Your promiſe is engaged for.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Why ſhe is there
Ready prepar'd, and much about this time
Life will look up again.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Come in all's ſure,
Not a foot ſtirring, nor a tongue.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs me,
I never enter'd with ſuch unholy thoughts
This place before.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Ye are a fearful fool,
If men have appetites allow'd 'em,
And warm deſires, are there not ends too for 'em?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Whether ſhall we carry her?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Why, to the bark, Sir,
I have provided one already waits us;
The wind ſtands wondrous fair too for our paſſage.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: And there when ye have enjoy'd her, for ye have that liberty
Let me alone to ſend her to feed fiſhes:
I'll no more ſighs for her.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Where is the monument?
Thou art ſure ſhe will awake about this time?

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Moſt ſure, if ſhe be not knockt oth'head: give me the Lanthorn,
Here 'tis, how is this, the ſtone off?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: I, and nothing
Within the monument, that's worſe; no body
I am ſure of that, nor ſign of any here,
But an empty Coffin.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: No Lady?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: No, nor Lord Sir,
This Pye has been cut up before.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Either the Devil
Muſt do theſe tricks—

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Or thou, damn'd one, worſe;
Thou black ſwoln pitchy cloud, of all my afflictions:
Thou night hag, gotten when the bright Moon ſuffer'd:
Thou hell it ſelf confin'd in fleſh: what trick now?
Tell me, and tell me quickly what thy miſchief
Has done with her, and to what end, and whether
Thou haſt remov'd her body, or by this holy place
This Sword ſhall cut thee into thouſand pieces,
A thouſand thouſand, ſtrow thee ore the Temple
A ſacrifice to thy black fire, the Devil.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Tell him, you ſee he's angry.

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Let him burſt,
Neither his ſword, nor anger do I ſhake at,
Nor will yield to feed his poor ſuſpitions,
His idle jealouſies, and mad dogs heats
One thought againſt my ſelf: ye have done a brave deed;
A manly, and a valiant piece of Service:
When ye have kill'd me, reckon't amongſt your Battels;
I am ſorry ye are ſo poor, ſo weak a Gentleman,
Able to ſtand no fortune: I diſpoſe of her?
My miſchief make her away? a likely project,
I muſt play booty againſt my ſelf, if any thing croſs ye,
I am the devil, and the devils heir,
All plagues, all miſchiefs.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Will ye leave and do yet?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I have done too much,
Far, far too much, for ſuch a thankleſs fellow,
If I be devil, you created me;
I never knew thoſe arts, nor bloody practiſes
(—o'your cunning heart, that mine of miſchief)
Before your flatteries won 'em into me.
Here did I leave her, leave her with that certainty
About this hour to wake again.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Where is ſhe?
This is the laſt demand.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Did I now know it,
And were I ſure, this were my lateſt minute,
I would not tell thee: ſtrike, and then I'll curſe thee:

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: I ſee a light, ſtand cloſe, and leave your angers
We all miſcarry elſe.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I am now careleſs,

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Peace, prethee peace, ſweet, peace, all friends

sp.speaker: Abd.
sp.l: Stand cloſe then.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Wait there Boy, with the light, till I call to thee
In darkneſs was my ſoul and ſences clouded
When my fair Jewel fell, the night of jealouſie,
In all her blackneſs drawn about my judgment:
No light was let into me, to diſtinguiſh
Betwixt my ſuddain anger and her honor,
A blind ſad Pilgrimage ſhall be my pennance,
No comfort of the day will I look up at:
Far darker than my jealous Ignorance
Each place of my aboad ſhall be my prayers
No ceremonious lights ſhall ſet off more:
Bright Armes, and all that carry luſtre, life,
Society, and ſolace, I forſake ye.
And were it not once more to ſee her beauties,
(For in her bed of death, ſhe muſt be ſweet ſtill,)
And on her cold ſad lips ſeal my repentance;
Thou child of heaven, fair light I could not miſs thee.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I know the tongue, would I were out again.
I have done him too much wrong to look upon him.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: There is no ſhifting now, boldneſs, and confidence
Muſt carry it now away: he is but one neither,
Naked as you are, of a ſtrength far under.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: But he has a cauſe above me.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: That's as you handle it.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Peace: he may go again, and never ſee us.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: I feel I weep apace, but where's the flood,
The torrent of my tears, to drown my fault in?
I would I could now, like a loaden cloud,
Begotten in the moiſt ſouth, drop to nothing.
Give me the Torch, Boy.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Now he muſt diſcover us.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: He has already, never hide your head
Be bold and brave, if we muſt dye together.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Who's there? what friend to ſorrow? The Tomb wide open
The Stone off too? the body gone, by—
Look to the door Boy: keep it faſt, who are ye?
What ſacrilegious villains? falſe Mounteferrat,
The woolf to honor, has thy helliſh hunger,
Brought thee to tear the body out oth'tomb too?
Has thy foul mind ſo far wrought on thee? ha,
Are you there too? nay, then I ſpie a villany
I never dream'd of yet, thou ſinful uſher
Bred from that rottenneſs, that bawd to miſchief,
Do you bluſh through all your blackneſs? will not that hide it?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I cannot ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: You are well met, with your dam, Sir,
Art thou a Knight? did ever on that ſword,
The Chriſtian cauſe ſit nobly? could that hand fight,
Guided by fame, and fortune? that heart inflame thee,
With virtuous fires of valour, to fall off,
Fall off ſo ſuddainly, and with ſuch foulneſs,
As the falſe Angels did, from all their glory?
Thou art no Knight, honor thou never heard'ſt of,
Nor brave deſires could ever build in that breaſt.
Treaſon, and tainted thoughts, are all the Gods
Thou worſhip'ſt, all the ſtrength thou hadſt, and fortune;
Thou didſt things out of fear, and falſe heart, villain
Out of cloſe traps and treacheries, they have raiſed thee.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Thou rav'ſt old man.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Before thou get'ſt off from me,
Halſt thou the glory of thy firſt figthts on thee
Which thou haſt baſely loſt, thy nobleſt fortunes,
And in their greateſt luſtres, I would make thee,
Before we part, confeſs, nay, kneel, and do it,
Nay, crying kneel, coldly, for mercy, crying:
Thou art the recreant'ſt Rogue, time ever nouriſh'd,
Thou art a dog, I will make thee ſwear, a dog
A mangy Cur-dog; do you creep behind the Altar?
Look how it ſweats, to ſhelter ſuch a raſcall;
Firſt, with thy venemous tooth infect her chaſt life,
And then not dare to do; next, rob her reſt,
• teal her dead body out oth'grave.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I have not.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Prethee come out, this is no place to • el in,
Valiant Mountferrat come,

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I will not ſtir.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Thou haſt thy ſword about thee,
That good ſword, that never faill'd thee: prethee come,
We'll have but five ſtroaks for it; on, on Boy,
Here's one would fain be acquainted with thee,
Would wondrous fain cleave that Calves-head of yours Sir,
Come, prethee let's diſpatch, the Moon ſhines finely:
Prethee be kill'd by me, thou wilt be hang'd elſe,
But it may be, thou long'ſt to be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Out with him, Sir,
You ſhall have my ſword too: when he's diſpatch'd once,
We have the world before us.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Wilt thou walk fellow,
I never knew a Rogue, hang arſe-ward ſo,
And ſuch a deſperate knave too.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Pray go with him,
Something I'll promiſe too,

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: You would be kill'd then?
No remedy; I ſee,

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: If thou dar'ſt do it?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Yes, now I dare; lead out, I'll follow preſently
Under the Mount I'll meet ye.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Go before me,
• 'll have ye in a ſtring too.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: As I am a Gentleman,
And by this holy place I will not fail thee,
Fear not, thou ſhalt be kill'd, take my word for it
• will not fail.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: If thou ſcap'ſt thou haſt Cats luck.
The Mount?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: The ſame: make haſt, I am there before elſe.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Go get ye home; now if he ſcape I am a Coward.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Well, now I am reſolv'd, and he ſhall find it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How is it with the Lady?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sir, as well
As it can be with one, who feeling knowes now
What is the curſe the divine juſtice lay'd
On the firſt ſinful woman.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Is ſhe in travel?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Yes ſir; and yet the troubles of her mind
Afflict her more, than what her body ſuffers,
For in the extremity of her pain, me cryes out,
Why am I here? Where is my Lord Gomera,
Then ſometimes names Miranda, and then ſighes,
As if to ſpeak, what queſtionleſs ſhe loves well,
If heard, migth do her injury.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: Heavens ſweet mercy
Look gently on her,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Prethee tell her, my Prayers
Are preſent with her, and good wench provide
That ſhe want nothing: what's thy name?

l.hi: Lucinda.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Lucinda? there's a proſperous omen in it,
Be a Lucina to her, and bring word
That ſhe is ſafe delivered of her burthen,
And thy reward's thy liberty: come Collonna,
We will go ſee how th'Engineer has mounted
The Cannon the great Maſter ſent, be careful
To view the works, and learn the diſcipline
That is us'd here: I am to leave the world
And for your ſervice, which I have found faithful,
The charge that's mine, if I have any power
Hereafter may concern you.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: I ſtill find
A noble Maſter in you,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis but juſtice,
Thou do'ſt deſerve it in thy care, and duty. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Gomera, Mountferrat, Rocca, Abdella, with a Piſtol.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Here's even ground, I'll ſtir no foot beyond it,
Before I have thy head.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Draw Rocca.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Coward,
Hath inward guilt, robb'd thee as well of courage
As honeſty? that without odds thou dar'ſt not
Anſwer a ſingle Enemy?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: All advantage
That I can take, expect.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: We know you are valiant,
Nor do we purpoſe to make farther trial
Of what you can do now: but to diſpatch you.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: And therefore fight, and pray together,

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Villains,
Whoſe baſeneſs, all diſgraceful words made one,
Cannot expreſs; ſo ſtrong is the good cauſe
That ſeconds me, that you ſhall feel, with horror
To your proud hopes, what ſtrength is in that arm,
Though old, that holds a ſword made ſharp by juſtice

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: You come then here, to prate? fight

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Help Rocca, now,
Or I am loſt for ever; how comes this?
Are villany and weakneſs twyns?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: I am gone too.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: You ſhall not ſcape me, wretches,

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I muſt do it,
All will go wrong elſe. ſhoots him.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Treacherous bloody woman,
What haſt thou done?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Done a poor womans part,
And in an inſtant, what theſe men ſo long
Stood fooling for.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: This ayd was unexpected,
I kiſs thee for't,

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: His right arms only ſhot,
And that compell'd him to forſake his ſword,
He's elſe unwounded.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Cut his throat.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Forbear.
Yet do not hope 'tis with intent to ſave thee.
But that thou mayſt live to thy farther torment,
To ſee who triumphs over thee: come Mountferrat,
Here join thy foot to mine, and let our hearts
Meet with our hands, the contract that is made
And cemented with blood, as this of ours is,
Is a more holy ſanction, and much ſurer,
Than all the ſuperſtitious ceremonies
You Chriſtians uſe.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Who's this?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Betray'd again?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: By the report it made, and by the wind
The Piſtol was diſcharg'd here.

sp.speaker: Gom.

l.hi: Norandine.

sp.l: As ever thou lov'ſt valor, or wear'ſt Arms
To puniſh baſeneſs, ſhew it.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: O the devil,
Gomera wounded, and my Brache black beauty
An actor in it?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: If thou ſtrik'ſt, I'll ſhoot thee.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: How? fright me with your Pot-gun? what art thou?
Good heaven, the Rogue, the traytor rogue Mountferrat,
To ſwinge the neſt of you, is a ſport unlook'd for,
Hels—conſume you.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: As thou art a man,
I am wounded, give me time to anſwer thee.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Durſt thou urge this? this hand can hold a ſword yet.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Well done: to ſee this villain, makes my hurts
Bleed freſh again, but had I not a bone whole,
In ſuch a cauſe I ſhould do thus, thus Raſcals.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Diſarm them, and ſhoot any that reſiſts.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Hold Corporal; I am Gomera,

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: 'Tis well yet, that once in an age you can
Remember what you watch for: I had thought
You had again been making out your parties
For ſucking piggs.
'Tis well:

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: As you will anſwer
The contrary with your lives, ſee theſe forth coming.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: That we ſhall do.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: You bleed apace: good Soldiers
Go help him to a Surgeon,

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.l: Dare the worſt,
And ſuffer like your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: From me learn courage.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Now for Miranda, this news will be to him
As welcome as 'tis unexpected: Corporal,
There's ſomething for thy care to night; my horſe there.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: How do's my Boy?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh, wondrous luſty Madam,
A little Knight already: you ſhall live
To ſee him toſs a Turk.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Gentle Lucinda,
Much muſt I thank thee for thy care, and ſervice.
And may I grow but ſtrong to ſee Valetta,
My husband, and my brother, thou ſhalt find
I will not barely thank thee.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Look Captain, we muſt ride away this morning
The Auberge ſits to day, and the great Maſter
Writes plainly, I muſt or deliver in
(The year expir'd) my probation weed,
Or take the Cloak: you likewiſe Norandine
For your full ſervice, and your laſt aſſiſtance
In falſe Mountferrats apprehenſion
Are here commanded to aſſociate me; my twin in this high honor.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.p: I'll none on't: do they think to bind me to live chaſt, ſober, and temperately, all days of my life? they may as ſoon tye an Engliſhman to live ſo; I ſhall be a ſweet Dane, a ſweet Captain, go up and down drinking ſmall beer, and ſwearing 'ods neagues, no, I'll live a Squire at Arms ſtill, and do thou ſo too; and tho • beeſt wiſe: I have found the myſtery now, why the Gentlemen wear but three bars of the croſs, and the Knights the whole one.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why Captain?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.p: Marry Sir, to put us in remembrance, we are 〈◊〉 three quarters croſs'd in our licence, and pleaſures: 〈◊〉 the po •• Knights croſs'd altogether; the brothers a • Arms, a • ay yet meet with their Siſters at Arms, no • and then, in brotherly love; but the poor Knights cannot get a Lady for love, nor money: 'tis not ſo in other Countries I wis, pray haſte you, for I'll along, and ſee what will come on't. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Collonna, provide ſtrait, all neceſſaries
For this remove, the Lytter for the Lady,
And let Lucinda bear her company,
You ſhall attend on me.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: With all my duties Exit.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: How fare you gracious Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: O Miranda.
You pleas'd to honor me with that fair title
When I was free, and could diſpoſe my ſelf;
But now, no ſmile, no word, no look, no touch
Can I impart to any, but as theft
From my Gomera, and who dares accept,
Is an uſurper.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Leave us; I have touch'd thee,
(Thou fairer virtue, than thou'rt beautiful)
Hold but this teſt, ſo rich an ore was never
Tryed by the hand of man, on the vaſt earth:
Sit brighteſt Oriana, is it ſin
Still to profeſs I love you, ſtill to vow
I ſhall do ever? heaven my witneſs be,
'Tis not your eye, your cheek, your tongue, no part
That ſuperficially doth ſnare young men,
Which has caught me; read over in your thoughts
The ſtory that this man hath made of you,
And think upon his merit.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Only thought
Can comprehend it.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: And can you be ſo
Cruel, thankleſs, to deſtroy his youth
That ſav'd your honor, gave you double life?
Your own, and your fair Infants? that when fortune
(The blind foe to all beauty, that is good,)
Pandied you from one hazard to another,
Was even heavens Meſſenger, by providence
Call'd to the Temple, to receive you there,
Into theſe Arms, to give eaſe to your throwes,
As if't had thunder'd; take thy due Miranda,
For ſhe was thine; Gomera's jealouſie
Struck death unto thy heart; to him be dead,
And live to me, that gave thee ſecond life:
Let me but now enjoy thee: Oh regard
The torturing fires of my affections.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh maſter them, Miranda, as I mine;
Who follows his deſires, ſuch tyrants ſerves
As will oppreſs him inſupportably.
My flames, Miranda, riſe as high as thine,
For I did love thee 'fore my marriage,
Yet would I now conſent, or could I think
Thou wert in earneſt, (which by all the ſouls
That have (for chaſtity) been ſanctified
I cannot) in a moment I do know
Thou'ldſt call fair temperance up to rule thy blood,
Thy eye was ever chaſte, thy countenance too honeſt,
And all thy wooings was like Maidens talk;
Who yieldeth unto pleaſures, and to luſt
Is a poor captive, that in Golden Fetters
(And pretious (as he thinks) but holding gyves)
Frets out his life.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Find ſuch another woman,
And take her for his labour, any man:

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: I was not worthy of thee, at my beſt,
Heaven knew I was not, I had had thee elſe;
Much leſs now gentle Sir; Miranda's deeds
Have been as white as Oriana's fame,
From the beginning to this point of time,
And ſhall we now begin to ſtain both thus?
Think on the legend which we two ſhall breed
Continuing as we are, for chaſteſt dames
And boldeſt Soldiers to peruſe and read,
I and read thorough, free from any act
To cauſe the modeſt caſt the book away,
And the moſt honour'd Captain fold it up.

sp.speaker: Mir,
sp.l: Faireſt; let go my hand: my pulſe beats thick,
And my mov'd blood, rides high in every vain,
Lord of thy ſelf now, Soldier, and ever:
I would not for Aleppo, this frail Bark,
This bark of fleſh, no better ſteers-man had
Than has Mountferrat's: may you kiſs me, Lady?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: No; though't be no eſſential injury,
It is a circumſtance due to my Lord,
To none elſe: and my deareſt friend, if hands
Playing together, kindle heat in you,
What may the game at Lips provoke unto?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Oh what a tongue is here? whil'ſt ſhe doth teach
My heart to hate my fond unlawful love,
She talks me more in love, with love to her,
My fires ſhe quencheth with her arguments,
But as ſhe breathes 'em, they blow freſher fires.
• it further: now my flame cools; Husband, Wife,
There is ſome holy myſtery in thoſe names
That ſure the unmarried cannot underſtand.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Now thou art ſtrait, and doſt enamour me,
• o far beyond a carnal earthly love;
My very ſoul doats on thee, and my ſpirits
• o embrace thine, my mind doth thy mind kiſs,
And in this pure conjunction we enjoy
• heavenlier pleaſure than if bodies met:
This, this is perfect love, the other ſhort,
• et languiſhing fruition, every Swain
• nd ſweating Groom may claſp, but ours refin'd
Two in ten ages cannot reach unto;
Nor is our ſpiritual love, a barren joy,
For mark what bleſſed iſſue we'll beget,
Dearer than children to poſterity,
A great example to mens continence,
And womens chaſtity, that is a child
More fair and comfortable, than any heir.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: If all wives were but ſuch, luſt would not find
One corner to inhabit, ſin would be
So ſtrange, remiſſion ſuperfluous:
But one petition, I have done.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: What (Sweet)

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To call me Lord, if the hard hand of death
Seize on Gomera firſt.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Oh, much too worthy;
How much you undervalue your own price,
To give your unbought ſelf, for a poor woman,
That has been once ſold, us'd, and loſt her ſhow?
I am a garment worn, a veſſel crack'd,
A Zone unti'd, a Lilly trode upon,
A fragrant Flower cropt by another hand,
My colour ſully'd, and my odor's chang'd,
If when I was new bloſſom'd, I did fear
My ſelf unworthy of Miranda's ſpring,
Thus over-blown, and ſeeded, I am rather
Fit to adorn his Chimney, than his bed.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Riſe miracle: ſave Malta, with thy virtue,
If words could make me proud, how has ſhe ſpoke,
Yet I will try her to the very block:
Hard-hearted, and uncivil Oriana,
Ingrateful payer of my Induſtries,
That with a ſoft painted hypocriſie
Cozen'ſt, and jeer'ſt my perturbation,
Expect a witty, and a fell revenge:
My comfort is, all men will think thee falſe,
Beſide thy Husband having been thus long
(On this occaſion) in my Fort, and power.
sp.stage: Enter Nor. Collonna, & Lucinda, with a Child.
sp.l: I'll hear no more words: Captain, let's away
With all care ſee to her: and you Lucinda
Attend her diligently: ſhe is a wonder.

sp.speaker: Nor
sp.l: Have you found ſhe was well deliver'd:
What, had ſhe a good Midwife, is all well?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You are merry Norandine.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why weep you, Lady?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Take the poor Babe along.

sp.speaker: Col,
sp.l: Madam, 'tis here.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Diſſembling death, why didſt thou let me live
To ſee this change, my greateſt cauſe to grieve? Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Aſtorius, Caſtriot, Valetta, Gomera, Synnet, Knights, two Biſhops, Mountferrat guarded by Corporal and Soldiers, Abdella, a Gentleman with a Cloak, ſword, and Spur •• : Gomera.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: A tender Husband haſt thou ſhew'd thy ſelf
My deareſt brother, and thy memory
After my life in brazen Characters;
Shall monumentally be regiſter'd
To ages conſequent, till times running hand,
Beats back the world, to undiſtinguiſh'd Chaos,
And on the top of that thy name ſhall ſtand
Freſh, and without decay.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Oh honor'd Sir!
If hope of this, or any bliſs to come,
Could lift my load of grief off from my ſoul,
Or expiate the treſpaſs 'gainſt my wife,
That in one hours ſuſpition I begat,
I might be won to be a man again,
And fare like other Husbands, ſleep and eat,
Laugh, and forget my pleaſing penitence;
But till old nature can make ſuch a wife
Again, I vow ne'r to reſume the order
And habits that to men are neceſſary,
All breath I'll ſpend in ſighs, all ſound in groans,
And know no company but my waſting moans.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: This will be wilful murder on your ſelf,
Nor like a Chriſtian do you bear the chance
Which th' inſcrutable Will of Heaven admits.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: What would you have my weakneſs do, that
Suffer'd it ſelf thus to be practis'd on,
By a damn'd hell-hound, and his agent dam,
The impious Midwife, to abortive births,
And cruel inſtrument to his decrees?
By forgery they firſt aſſail'd her life,
Heaven playing with us yet, in that, he wrought
My deareſt friend, the ſervant to her virtue
To combat me, againſt his Miſtriſs truth.
That yet effectleſs, this enchanting Witch,
Bred baneful jealouſie againſt my Lady,
My moſt immaculate Lady, which ſeiz'd on her
Almoſt to death: Oh yet! not yet content,
She in my hand put (to reſtore her life
As I imagin'd) what did execute
Their deviliſh malice, farther, great with child,
Was this poor innocent, that too was loſt,
They doubled death upon her, not ſtaying there,
They have done violence unto her Tomb,
Not granting reſt unto her in the grave:
I wiſh Miranda had enjoy'd my prize;
For ſure I'm puniſh'd for uſurping her,
Oh what a Tyger is reſiſted Luſt?
How it doth forrage all?

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Part of this tale
I grant you true; but 'twas not poiſon given her?

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: I would it had, we had been far enough,
If we had been ſo wiſe, and had not now
Stood curteſing for your mercies here.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: Beſide,
What is become o' th' body? we know not.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Peace impudence,
And dear Gomera practiſe patience
As I my ſelf muſt, by ſome means at laſt
We ſhall diſſolve this Riddle.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Wherefore comes
This villain in this feſtival array,
As if he triumph'd for his treachery?

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: That is by our appointment: give us leave,
You ſhall know why anon.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: One of the Eſguard.

sp.speaker: Eſg.
sp.l: The Gentlemen are come.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Truce then awhile,
With our ſad thoughts; what are you both reſolv'd?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Not I my Lord, your down-right Captain ſtill
I'll live, and ſerve you, not that altogether
I want compunction of conſcience,
I have enough to ſave me; and that's all,
Bar me from drink, and drabs, ev'n hang me too,
You muſt ev'n make your Captains Capons firſt,
I have too much fleſh for this ſpiritual Knighthood,
And therefore do deſire forbearance, Sir,
Till I am older, or more mortifi'd,
I am too ſound yet,

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: What ſay you Miranda?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: With all pure zeal to Heaven, duty to you,
I come to undergo it.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Proceed to th' ceremony.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Before you match with this bright honor'd title,
Admir'd Miranda, pardon what in thought
I ever did tranſgreſs againſt your virtue;
And may you find more joy with your new Bride
Than poor Gomera e'r enjoy'd with his,
But 'twas mine own crime, and I ſuffer for't:
Long wear your dignity, and worthily,
Whilſt I obſcurely in ſome corner vaniſh.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Have ſtronger thoughts, and better, firſt I crave
According to the order of the Court
I may diſpoſe my Captives, and the Fort,
That with a clean and purified heart
The fitlier I may endue my Robe.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: 'Tis granted.

div.stage: Enter Oriana vail'd, Ladies, Lucinda, Child.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Bring the Captives. To your charge
And ſtaid tuition, my moſt noble friend;
I then commend this Lady; ſtart not off
A fairer, and a chaſter never liv'd;
By her own choice you are her Guardian,
For telling her I was to leave my Fort,
And to abandon quite all worldly cares.
Her own requeſt was, to Gomera's hands
She might be given in cuſtody, for ſh'ad heard
He was a Gentleman wiſe, and temperate,
Full of humanity to Women-kind,
And 'cauſe he had been married, knew the better
How to entreat a Lady.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: What Countrey-woman is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Born a Greek.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Gomera, 'twill be barbarous to denie
A Lady, that unto your refuge flies,
And ſeeks to ſhrowd her under virtues wing.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Excuſe me noble Sir; oh think me not
So dull a devil, to forget the loſs
Of ſuch a matchleſs wife as I poſſeſs'd,
And ever to endure the ſight of woman:
Were ſhe the abſtract of her ſex for form,
The only warehouſe of perfection.
Were there no Roſe nor Lilly but her Cheek,
No Muſick but her tongue, Virtue but hers;
She muſt not reſt near me, my vow is graven,
Here in my heart, irrevocably breath'd
And when I break it.

sp.speaker: Aſt.
sp.l: This is rudeneſs Spaniard,
Unſeaſonably you play the Timoniſt,
Put on a diſpoſition is not yours,
Which neither fits you, nor becomes you.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſt.
sp.l: We cannot force you, but we would perſwade.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Beſeech you Sir, no more, I am reſolv'd
To forſake Malta, tread a pilgrimage
To fair Jeruſalem, for my Ladies ſoul,
And will not be diverted.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You muſt bear
This Child along w'ye then.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: What Child?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Nay then Gomera, thou art injurious,
This Child is thine, and this rejected Lady
Thou haſt as often known, as thine own wife,
And this I'll make good on thee, with my ſword.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Thou durſt as well blaſpheme: if ſuch a ſcandal—
(I crave the rights due to a Gentleman)
Woman unvail.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Will you refuſe me yet?

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: My Wife!

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: My Siſter!

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Some body, thank Heaven
I cannot ſpeak.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: All praiſe be ever given:

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: This ſaves our lives, yet would ſhe had been dead
The very ſight of her afflicts me more
Than fear of puniſhment, or my diſgrace.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: How came you to the Temple?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sir, to do
My poor devotions, and to offer thanks
For ſcaping a temptation near perform'd
With this fair Virgin. I reſtore a wife
Earth cannot parallel: and buſie nature
• f thou wilt ſtill make women, but remember
To work 'em by this ſampler; take heed, Sir,
Henceforth you never doubt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: When I do
Death take me ſuddainly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To increaſe your happineſs
To your beſt wife take this addition.

sp.speaker: Gom.
sp.l: Alack my poor knave.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: The confeſſion
The Moor made 't ſeems was truth.

sp.speaker: Nor.
Ori.
sp.l: What is't Miranda?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: That you would pleaſe Lucinda might attend you.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: That ſuit Sir, I conſent not to.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My husband?
My deareſt Angelo?

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: More Jiggam-bobs; is not this the fellow that ſwom
Like a duck to th' ſhore in our ſea-ſervice?

sp.speaker: Col
sp.l: The very ſame, do not you know me now, Sir,
My name is Angelo, though Colonna vail'd it,
Your Countrey-man and kinſman born in Florence,
Who from the neighbor-Iſland here of Goza
Was captive led, in that unfortunate day
When the Turk bore with him three thouſand ſouls;
Since in Conſtantinople have I liv'd
Where I beheld this Turkiſh Damſel firſt.
A tedious ſuitor was I for her love,
And pittying ſuch a beauteous caſe ſhould hide
A ſoul prophan'd with infidelity,
A labour'd her converſion with my love,
And doubly won her; to fair faith her ſoul
She firſt betroth'd, and then her faith to me,
But fearful there to conſummate this contract
We fled, and in that flight were ta'en again
By thoſe ſame Gallies, 'fore Valetta fought.
Since in your ſervice I attended her,
Where, what I ſaw, and heard, hath joy'd me more
Than all my paſt afflictions griev'd before.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Wonders crown wonders; take thy wife Miranda,
Be henceforth called our Malta's better Angel,
And thou her evil, Mountferrat.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.p: We'll call him Cacodemon, with his black gib there, his Succuba, his devils ſeed, his ſpawn of Phlegeton, that o' my conſcience was bred o' the ſpume of Cocitus; do ye ſnarle you black Jill? ſhe looks like the Picture of America.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Why ſtay we now.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This laſt petition to the Court,
I may bequeath the keeping of my Fort
To this my kinſman, toward the maintenance
Of him, and his fair virtuous wife; diſcreet,
Loyal, and valiant I dare give him you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: You muſt not ask in vain, Sir.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.l: My beſt thanks
To you my noble Coſin, and my ſervice
To the whole Court; may I deſerve this bounty.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Proceed to th' ceremony, one of our Eſguard
Degrade Mountferrat firſt.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: I will not ſue
For mercy, 'twere in vain; fortune thy worſt.

div.stage: An Altar diſcover'd, with Tapers, and a Book on it. The two Biſhops ſtand on each ſide of it; Mountferrat, as the Song is ſinging, aſcends up the Altar.
div.l: See, ſee, the ſtain of honor, virtues foe;
Of Virgins fair fames, the foul overthrow,
That broken hath his oath of chaſtity
Diſhonor'd much this holy dignity,
Off with his Robe, expell him forth this place,
Whilſt we rejoyce, and ſing at his diſgrace.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Since by thy actions thou haſt made thy ſelf
Unworthy of that worthy ſign thou wear'ſt,
And of our ſacred order, into which
For former virtues we receiv'd thee firſt,
According to our Statutes, Ordinances,
For praiſe unto the good, a terror to
The bad, and an example to all men;
We here deprive thee of our habit, and
Declare thee unworthy our ſociety,
From which we do expell thee, as a rotten
Corrupted and contagious member.

sp.speaker: Eſq.
sp.l: Uſing th' authority th' Superior
Hath given unto me, I untie this knot,
And take from thee the pleaſing yoak of heaven:
We take from off thy breaſt this holy croſs
Which thou haſt made thy burthen, not thy prop;
Thy ſpurs we ſpoil thee of, leaving thy heels;
Bare of thy honor, that have kick'd againſt
Our Orders precepts: next we reave thy ſword,
And give foe to goodneſs, and to Heaven,
Laſt, 'bout thy ſtiffneck, we this halter hang,
And leave thee to the mercy of thy Court.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Inveſt Miranda.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: Fair child of virtue, honors bloom
That here with burning zeal doſt come
With joy to ask the white croſs cloak,
And yield unto this pleaſing yoak
That being young, vows chaſtity,
And chooſeſt wilful poverty;
As this flame mounts, ſo mount thy zeal, thy glory
Riſe paſt the Stars, and fix in Heaven thy ſtory.

sp.speaker: 1 Biſh.
sp.l: Whar crave you, gentle Sir?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Humble admittance
To be a brother of the holy Hoſpital
Of great Jeruſalem.

sp.speaker: 2 Biſh.
sp.l: Breathe out your vow.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: To heaven, and all the bench of Saints above
Whoſe ſuccor I implore t' enable me,
I vow henceforth a chaſte life, not to enjoy
Any thing proper to my ſelf; obedience
To my ſuperiors, whom Religion,
And Heaven ſhall give me: ever to defend
The virtuous fame of Ladies, and to oppugne
Even unto death the Chriſtian enemy,
This do I vow to accompliſh.

sp.speaker: Eſq.
sp.l: Who can tell,
Has he made other vow, or promis'd marriage
To any one, or is in ſervitude?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: He's free from all theſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Biſh.
sp.l: Put on his ſpurs, and girt him with the ſword,
The ſcourge of Infidels, and tipes of ſpeed.
Buildſt thy faith on this?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: On him that dy'd
On ſuch a ſacred figure, for our ſins.

sp.speaker: 2 Biſh.
sp.l: Here, then we fix it on thy left ſide, for
Thy increaſe of faith, Chriſtian defence, and ſervice
To th' poor, and thus near to thy heart we plant it
That thou maiſt love it even with all thy heart,
With thy right hand protect, preſerve it whole,
For if thou fighting 'gainſt heavens enemies
Shalt flie away, abandoning the croſs
The Enſign of thy holy General,
With ſhame thou juſtly ſhalt be robb'd of it
Chas'd from our company, and cut away
As an infectious putrified limb,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I ask no favour.

sp.speaker: 1 Biſh.
sp.l: Then receive the yoak
Of him that makes it ſweet, and light, in which,
Thy ſoul find her eternal reſt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Moſt welcome.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Welcome, our noble Brother.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Break up the Court; Mountferrat, though your deeds
Conſpiring 'gainſt the lives of innocents
Hath forfeited your own, we will not ſtain
Our white croſs with your blood: your doom is the •
o marry this coagent of your miſchiefs
Which done, we baniſh you the continent,
If either, after three daies here be found
The hand of Law laies hold upon your lives.

sp.speaker: Nor.
sp.l: Away French ſtallion, now you have a Barbary mare of your own, go leap her, and engender young devilings.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: We will find ſomething, noble Norandine
To quit your merit: ſo to civil feaſts,
According to our cuſtoms; and all pray
The dew of grace, bleſs our new Knight to day.

div.head: Loves Cure, or the Martial Maid A COMEDY.
The Perſons Repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Vitelli, a young Gentleman, enemy to Alvarez,
Lamoral, a fighting Gallant, friend to Vitelli.
Anaſtro, an honeſt Gentleman, friend to Vitelli,
Don Alvarez, a noble Gent. Father to Lucio, and Clara.
Lucio, Son to Alvarez, a brave young Gent. in womans habit.
Bobbadilla, a witty knave, ſervant to Eugenia, and Steward vant to Alvarez.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Eugenia, a virtuous Lady, wife to Don Alvarez.
Clara, Daughter to Eugenia, a martial Maid, valiant and chaſte, enamoured of Vitelli.
Genevora, Siſter to Vitelli, in love with Lucio.
Malroda, a wanton Miſtiriſs of Vitelli.

div.head: A PROLOGUE At the reviving of this PLAY.
div.l: STatues and Pictures challenge price and fame;
If they can juſtly boaſt, and prove they came
From Phidias or Apelles. None denie,
Poets and Painters hold a ſympathy;
Yet their works may decay, and loſe their grace,
Receiving blemiſh in their Limbs or Face.
When the Minds Art has this preheminence,
She ſtill retaineth her firſt excellence.
Then why ſhould not this dear Piece be eſteem'd
Child to the richeſt fancies that e'r teem'd?
When not their meaneſt off-ſpring, that came forth,
But bore the image of their Fathers worth.
Beaumonts, and Fletchers, whoſe deſert out-wayes
The beſt applauſe, and their leaſt ſprig of Boyes
Is worthy Phaebus; and who comes to gather
Their fruits of wit, he ſhall not rob the treaſure.
Nor can you ever ſurfeit of the plenty,
Nor can you call them rare, though they be dainty.
The more you take, the more you do them right,
And we will thank you for your own delight.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: ALvarez pardon'd?

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: And return'd

sp.speaker: Lamo.
sp.l: I ſaw him land
At St. Lucars, and ſuch a general welcome,
Fame as harbinger to his brave actions,
Had with the eaſie people, prepar'd for him,
As if by his command alone, and fortune
Holland, with thoſe low Provinces, that hold out
Againſt the Arch-Duke, were again compell'd
With their obedience to give up their lives
To be at his Devotion.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: You amaze me,
For though I have heard, that when he fled from Sevil
To ſave his life (than forfeited to Law
For murth'ring Don Pedro my dear Uncle)
His extream wants enforc'd him to take pay
I'th' Army, ſate down then before Oſtend,
'Twas never yet reported, by whoſe favour
He durſt preſume to entertain a thought
Of coming home with pardon.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: 'Tis our nature
Or not to hear, or not to give belief
To what we wiſh far from our enemies.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Sir, 'tis moſt certain, the Infanta's Letters
Aſſiſted by the Arch-Dukes, to King Philip,
Have not alone ſecur'd him from the rigor
Of our Caſtilian Juſtice, but return'd him
A free man and in grace.

sp.speaker: Vie.
sp.l: By what curs'd means
Could ſuch a fugitive ariſe unto
The knowledge of their Highneſſes? much more
(Though known) to ſtand but in the leaſt degree
Of favour with them?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: To give ſatisfaction
To your demand, though to praiſe him I hate,
Can yield me ſmall contentment, I will tell you,
And truly, ſince ſhould I detract his worth,
'Twould argue want of merit in my ſelf.
Briefly to paſs his tedious pilgrimage
For ſixteen years, a baniſh'd guilty man,
And to forget the ſtorms, th' affrights, the horrors
His conſtancy, not fortune, overcame,
I bring him, with his little ſon, grown man
(Though 'twas ſaid here, he took a Daughter with him)
To Oſtend's bloody ſiege that ſtage of war,
Wherein the flower of many Nations acted,
And the whole Chriſtian world ſpectators were;
There by his Son, or were he by adoption,
Or nature his, a brave Scene was preſented,
Which I make choice to ſpeak of, ſince from that
The good ſucceſs of Alvarez, had beginning.

sp.speaker: Vil.
sp.l: So I love virtue in an enemy
That I deſire in the relation of
This young mans glorious deed, you'ld keep your ſelf
A friend to truth, and it.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Such was my purpoſe;
The Town being oft aſſaulted, but in vain,
To dare the proud defendents to a ſally,
Weary of eaſe, Don Inigo Peralta,
Son to the General of our Caſtile forces,
All arm'd, advanc'd within ſhot of their Walls,
From whence the Musquetiers plaid thick upon him,
Yet he (brave youth) as careleſs of the danger,
As careful of his honor, drew his ſword,
And waving it about his head, as if
He dar'd one ſpirited like himſelf, to trial
Of ſingle valor, he made his retreat
With ſuch a ſlow, and yet majeſtique pace,
As if he ſtill call'd loud, dare none come on?
When ſodainly, from a poſtern of the Town
Two gallant horſemen iſſued, and o'ertook him,
The Army looking on, yet not a man
That durſt relieve the raſh adventurer,
Which Lucio, ſon to Alvarez then ſeeing,
As in the vant-guard he ſate bravely mounted,
Or were it pity of the youths misfortune,
Care to preſerve the honor of his Countrey,
Or bold deſire to get himſelf a name,
He made his brave Horſe like a whirlwind bear him,
Among the Combatants: and in a moment
Diſcharg'd his Petronel, with ſuch ſure aim
That of the adverſe party from his horſe,
One tumbled dead, then wheeling round, and drawing
A Faulcion, ſwift as lightning he came on
Upon the other, and with one ſtrong blow,
In view of the amazed Town, and Camp,
He ſtruck him dead, and brought Peralta off
With double honor to himſelf.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Twas brave:
But the ſucceſs of this?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: The Camp receiv'd him
With acclamations of joy and welcome,;
And for addition to the fair reward
Being a maſſy chain of Gold given to him
By young Peralta's Father, he was brought
To the Infanta's preſence, kiſs'd her hand,
And from that Lady, (greater in her goodneſs
Than her high birth) had this encouragement:
Go on young man; yet not to feed thy valour
With hope of recompence to come, from me,
For preſent ſatisfaction of what's paſt,
Ask any thing that's fit for me to give,
And thee to take, and be aſſur'd of it.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Excellent Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: And ſtil'd worthily
The heart-bloud, nay the Soul of Soldiers.
But what was his requeſt?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: That the repeal
Of Alvarez makes plain: he humbly begg'd
His Fathers pardon, and ſo movingly
Told the ſad ſtory of your Uncles death
That the Infanta wept, and inſtantly,
Granting his ſuit, working the Arch-Duke to it,
Their Letters were directed to the King,
With whom they ſo prevail'd, that Alvarez
Was freely pardon'd.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Tis not in the King
To make that good.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: Not in the King? what ſubject
Dares contradict his power?

sp.speaker: Vit;
sp.l: In this I dare,
And will: and not call his prerogative
In queſtion, nor preſume to limit it.
I know he is Maſter of his Laws,
And may forgive the forfeits made to them,
But not the injury done to my honor;
And ſince (forgetting my brave Uncles merits
And many ſervices, under Duke D' Alva)
He ſuffers him to fall, wreſting from Juſtice
The powerful ſword, that would revenge his death,
I'll fill with this Aſtrea's empty hand,
And in my juſt wreak, make this arm the Kings,
My deadly hate to Alvarez, and his houſe,
Which as I grew in years, hath ſtill encreas'd,
As if it call'd on time to make me man,
Slept while it had no object for her fury
But a weak woman, and her talk'd of Daughter:
But now, ſince there are quarries, worth her fight
Both in the father, and his hopeful ſon,
I'll boldly caſt her off, and gorge her full
With both their hearts: to further which, your friendship,
And oaths: will your aſſiſtance, let your deeds
Make anſwer to me: uſeleſs are all words
Till you have writ performance with your ſwords.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Go fetch my work: this Ruffe was not well ſtarch'd,
So tell the maid, 't has too much blew init,
And look you that the Partridge and the Pullen
Have clean meat, and freſh water, or my Mother
Is like to hear on't,

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Oh good St. Jaques help me: was there ever ſuch an Hermaphrodite heard of? would any wench living, that ſhould hear and ſee what I do, be wrought to believe, that the beſt of a man lies under this Petticoat, and that a Cod-piece were far fitter here, than a Pinn'd Placket?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: You had beſt talk filthily: do; I have a tongue
To tell my Mother, as well as ears to hear
Your ribaldry.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Nay you have ten womens tongues that way I am ſure: why my young Maſter or Miſtriſs, Madam, Don, or what you will, what the devil have you to do with Pullen, or Partridge? or to ſit pricking on a clout all day? you have a better needle, I know, and might make better work, if you had grace to uſe it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Why, how dare you ſpeak this before me, ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Bob.
