sp.p: Nay rather, why dare not you do what I ſpeak? —though my Lady your mother, for fear of Vitelli and his faction, hath brought you up like her Daughter, and has kept you theſe 20 years, which is ever ſince you were born, a cloſe priſoner within doors, yet ſince you are a man, and are as well provided as other men are, methinks you ſhould have the ſame motions of the fleſh, as other Cavaliers of us are inclin'd unto

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Indeed you have cauſe to love thoſe wanton motions,
They having hope you to an excellent whipping,
For doing ſomething, I but put you in mind of it,
With the Indian Maid, the Governor ſent my mother
From Mexico.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Why, I but taught her a Spaniſh trick in charity, and holpe the King to a ſubject that may live to take Grave Maurice priſoner, and that was more good to the State, than a thouſand ſuch as you are ever like to doe: and I will tell you, (in a fatherly care of the Infant I ſpeak it) if he live (as bleſs the babe, in paſſion I remember him) to your years, ſhall he ſpend his time in pinning, painting, purling, and perfuming as you do? no, he ſhall to the wars, uſe his Spaniſh Pike, though with the danger of the laſh, as his father has done, and when he is provoked, as I am now, draw his Toledo deſperately, as—

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: You will not kill me? oh.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: I knew this would ſilence him: how he hides his eies?
If he were a wench now, as he ſeems, what an advantage
Had I, drawing two Toledo's, when one can do this?
But oh me, my Lady: I muſt put up: young Maſter
I did but jeſt: Oh cuſtom, what haſt thou made of him?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: For bringing this, be ſtill my friend; no more
A ſervant to me.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Here,
Even here, where I am happy to receive
Aſſurance of my Alvarez return,
I will kneel down: and may thoſe holy thoughts
That now poſſeſs me wholly, make this place
A Temple to me, where I may give thanks
For this unhop'd for bleſſing Heavens kind hand
Hath pour'd upon me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Let my duty Madam
Preſume, if you have cauſe of joy, to intreat
I may ſhare in it.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: 'Tis well, he has forgot how I frighted him yet.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt: but firſt kneel with me Lucio,
No more Poſthumia now, thou haſt a Father,
A Father living to take off that name,
Which my too credulous fears, that he was dead,
Beſtow'd upon thee: thou ſhalt ſee him Lucio
And make him young again, by ſeeing thee,
Who only hadſt a being in my Womb
When he went from me, Lucio: Oh my joyes,
So far tranſport me, that I muſt forget
The ornaments of Matrons, modeſty,
And grave behaviour; but let all forgive me
If in th' expreſſion of my ſoul's beſt comfort
Though old, I do a while forget mine age
And play the wanton in the entertainment
Of thoſe delights I have ſo long deſpair'd of.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Shall I then ſee my Father?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: This hour Lucio;
Which reckon the beginning of thy life
I mean that life, in which thou ſhalt appear
To be ſuch as I brought thee forth, a man,
This womaniſh diſguiſe, in which I have
So long conceal'd thee, thou ſhalt now caſt off,
And change thoſe qualities thou didſt learn from me,
For maſculine virtues, for which ſeek no tutor,
But let thy fathers actions be thy precepts;
And for thee Zancho, now expect reward
For thy true ſervice.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Shall I? you hear fellow Stephano, learn to know me more reſpectively; how doſt thou think I ſhall become the Stewards chair, ha? will not theſe ſlender hanches ſhow well with a chain, and a gold night-Cap after ſupper, when I take the accompts?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Haſte, and take down thoſe Blacks with which my chamber
Hath like the widow, her ſad Miſtriſs, mourn'd,
And hang up for it, the rich Perſian Arras,
Us'd on my wedding night, for this to me
Shall be a ſecond marriage: ſend for Muſique,
And will the Cooks to uſe their beſt of cunning
To pleaſe the palat.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Will your Ladyſhip have a Potato-pie, 'tis a good ſtirring diſh for an old Lady, after a long Lent.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Begone I ſay: why Sir, you can goe faſter?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: I could Madam: but I am now to practiſe the Stewards pace, that's the reward I look for: every man muſt faſhion his gate, according to his calling: you fellow Stephano, may walk faſter, to overtake preferment: ſo, uſher me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray Madam, let the waſtcoat I laſt wrought
Be made up for my Father: I will have
A Cap, and Boot-hoſe ſutable to it.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Of that
We'll think hereafter Lucio: our thoughts now
Muſt have no object but thy Fathers welcome,
To which thy help —

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: With humble gladneſs, Madam. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Where loſt we Syavedra?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: He was met
Ent'ring the City by ſome Gentlemen
Kinſmen, as he ſaid of his own, with whom
For compliment ſake (for ſo I think he term'd it)
He was compell'd to ſtay: though I much wonder
A man that knows to do, and has done well
In the head of his troop, when the bold foe charg'd home,
Can learn ſo ſodainly to abuſe his time
In apiſh entertainment: for my part
(By all the glorious rewards of war)
I had rather meet ten enemies in the field
All ſworn to fetch my head, than be brought on
To change an hours diſcourſe with one of theſe
Smooth City-fools, or Tiſſue-Cavaliers,
The only Gallants, as they wiſely think,
To get a Jewel, or a wanton Kiſs
From a Court-lip, though painted.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: My Love Clara,
(For Lucio is a name thou muſt forget
With Lucio's bold behaviour) though thy breeding
I' th' Camp, may plead ſomething in the excuſe
Of thy rough manners, cuſtom having chang'd,
Though not thy Sex, the ſoftneſt of thy nature,
And fortune (then a cruel ſtepdame to thee)
Impos'd upon thy tender ſweetneſs, burthens
Of hunger, cold, wounds, want, ſuch as would crack
The ſinews of a man, not born a Soldier:
Yet now ſhe ſmiles, and like a natural mother
Looks gently on thee, Clara, entertain
Her proffer'd bounties with a willing boſom;
Thou ſhalt no more have need to uſe thy ſword;
Thy beauty (which even Belgia hath not alter'd)
Shall be a ſtronger guard, to keep my Clara,
Than that has been, (though never us'd but nobly)
And know thus much.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Sir, I know only that
It ſtands not with my duty to gain-ſay you,
In any thing: I muſt, and will put on
What faſhion you think beſt: though I could wiſh
I were what I appear.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Endeavour rather Muſick.
To be what you are, Clara entring here,
As you were born, a woman.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Let choice Muſick
In the beſt voice that e'er touch'd humane ear,
For joy hath ti'd my tongue up, ſpeak your welcome.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: My ſoul (for thou giv'ſt new life to my ſpirit)
Myriads of joyes, though ſhort in number of
Thy virtues, fall on thee; Oh my Eugenia,
Th' aſſurance that I do embrace thee, makes
My twenty years of • orrow but a dream,
And by the Nectar, which I take from theſe,
I feel my age reſtor'd, and like old Aeſon
Grow young again.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: My Lord, long wiſh'd for welcome,
'Tis a ſweet briefneſs, yet in that ſhort word
All pleaſures which I may call mine, begin,
And may they long increaſe, before they find
A ſecond period: let mine eies now ſurfeit
On this ſo wiſh'd for object, and my lips
Yet modeſtly pay back the parting kiſs
You truſted with them, when you fled from Sevil,
With little Clara my ſweet daughter: lives ſhe?
Yet I could chide my ſelf, having you here
For being ſo covetous of all joyes at once,
T' enquire for her, you being alone, to me
My Clara, Lucio, my Lord, my ſelf,
Nay more than all the world.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: As you, to me are

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Sit down, and let me feed upon the ſtory
Of your paſt dangers, now you are here in ſafety
It will give relliſh, and freſh appetite
To my delights, if ſuch delights can cloy me.
Yet do not Alvarez, let me firſt yield you
Account of my life in your abſence, and
Make you acquainted how I have preſerv'd
The Jewel left lock'd up in my womb,
When you, in being forc'd to leave your Countrey,
Suffer'd a civil death. Within claſhing ſwords

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Doe my Eugenia,
'Tis that I moſt deſire to hear,

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Then know. Sayavedra within,

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: What noiſe is that?

sp.speaker: Saya.
sp.l: If you are noble enemies, Vitelli within.
Oppreſs me not with odds, but kill me fairly,

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Stand off, I am too many of my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Murther, murther, murther, your friend my Lord,
Don Sayavedra is ſet upon in the ſtreets, by your enemies
Vitelli, and his Faction: I am almoſt kill'd with looking on them.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: I'll free him, or fall with him: draw thy ſword
And follow me.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Fortune, I give thee thanks
For this occaſion once more to uſe it.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Nay, hold not me Madam; if I do any hurt, hang me Exit.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh I am dead with fear! let's flie into
Your Cloſet, Mother.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: No hour of my life
Secure of danger? heav'n be merciful,
Or now at once diſpach me.

div.stage: Enter Vitelli, purſued by Alvarez, and Sayavedra, Clara beating of Anaſtro.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Follow him
Leave me to keep theſe of.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Aſſault my friend
So near my houſe?

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Nor in it will ſpare thee,
Though 'twere a Temple: and I'll make it one,
I being the Prieſt, and thou the ſacrifice,
I'll offer to my Uncle.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Haſte thou to him,
And ſay I ſent thee:

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Twas put bravely by,
And that: and yet comes on, and boldly rare,
In the wars, where emulation and example
Joyn to increaſe the courage, and make leſs
The danger; valour, and true reſolution
Never appear'd ſo lovely, brave again:
The beſt of virtue, fortitude would dye with him:
And can I ſuffer it? forgive me duty,
So I love valour, as I will protect it
Againſt my Father, and redeem it, though
'Tis forfeited by one I hate.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Come on,
All is not loſt yet: You ſhall buy me dearer
Before you have me: keep off.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Fear me not,
Thy worth has took me priſoner, and my ſword
For this time knows thee only for a friend,
And to all elſe I turn the point of it.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Defend your Fathers enemy?

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Art thou mad?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Are you men rather? ſhall that valour, which
Begot you lawful honor in the wars,
Prove now the Parent of an infamous Baſtard
So foul, yet ſo long liv'd, as murther will
Be to your ſhames? have each of you, alone
With your own dangers only, purchas'd glory
From multitudes of enemies, not allowing
Thoſe neareſt to you, to have part in it,
And do you now joyn, and lend mutual help
Againſt a ſingle oppoſite? hath the mercy
Of the great King, but newly waſh'd away
The blood, that with the forfeit of your life
Cleav'd to your name, and family like an ulcer,
In this again to ſet a deeper dye
Upon your infamy: you'll ſay he is your foe,
And by his raſhneſs call'd on his own ruin;
Remember yet, he was firſt wrong'd, and honor
Spurr'd him to what he did, and next the place
Where now he is: your houſe, which by the laws
Of hoſpitable duty ſhould protect him;
Have you been twenty years a ſtranger to it,
To make your entrance now in blood? or think you
Your countrey-man, a true born Spaniard, will be
An offering fit, to pleaſe the genius of it?
No, in this I'll preſume to teach my Father,
And this firſt Act of diſobedience ſhall
Confirm I am moſt dutiful.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: I am pleas'd
With what I dare not give allowance to;
Unnatural wretch, what wilt thou do?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Set free
A noble enemy: come not on, by—
You paſs to him, through me: the way is open:
Farewel: when next I meet you, do not look for
A friend, but a vow'd foe; I ſee you worthy,
And therefore now preſerve you, for the honor
Of my ſword only:

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Were this man a friend,
How would he win me, that being my vow'd foe
Deſerves ſo well? I thank you for my life;
• ut how I ſhall deſerve it, give me leave
Hereafter to conſider. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Quit thy fear,
All danger is blown over: I have Letters
To the Governor, in the Kings name, to ſecure us,
From ſuch attempts hereafter: yet we need not,
That have ſuch ſtrong Guards of our own, dread others;
And to increaſe thy comfort, know, this young man
Whom with ſuch fervent earneſtneſs you eye,
• s not what he appears, but ſuch a one
As thou with joy wilt bleſs, thy Daughter Clara.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: A thouſand bleſſings in that word.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: The reaſon
Why I have bred her up thus, at more leaſure
I will impart unto you, wonder not
At what you have ſeen her do, it being the leaſt
Of many great and valiant undertakings
She hath made good with honor.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: I'll return
The joy I have in her, with one as great
To you my Alvarez: you, in a man,
Have given to me a Daughter: in a Woman,
I give to you a Son, this was the pledge
You left here with me, whom I have brought up
Different from what he was, as you did Clara,
And with the like ſucceſs; as ſhe appears
Alter'd by cuſtom, more than Woman, he
Transform'd by his ſoft life, as leſs than man.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Fortune, in this gives ample ſatisfaction
For all our ſorrows paſt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My deareſt Siſter.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Kind Brother.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Now our mutual care muſt be
Imploy'd to help wrong'd nature, to recover
Her right in either of them, loſt by cuſtom:
To you I give my Clara, and receive
My Lucio to my charge: and we'll contend
With loving induſtry, who ſooneſt can
Turn this man woman, or this woman man. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: BOy: and Cloak, and Rapier; it fits not a Gentleman of my rank, to walk the ſtreets in Querpo.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Nay, you are a very rank Gent. Signior, I am very hungry, they tell me in Sevil here, I look like an Eel, with a mans head: and your neighbor the Smith here hard by, would have borrowed me th' other day, to have fiſh'd with me, becauſe he had loſt his Angle-rod.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Oh happy thou Lazarillo (being the cauſe of other mens wits) as in thine own: live lean, and witty ſtill: oppreſs not thy ſtomach too much: groſs feeders, great ſleepers, fat bodies; fat bodies, lean brains: No Lazarillo, I will make thee immortal, change thy Humanity into Deity, for I will teach thee to live upon nothing.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Faith Signior, I am immortal then already, or very near it, for I do live upon little or nothing: be like that's the reaſon the Poets are ſaid to be immortal, for ſome of them live upon their wits, which is indeed as good as little or nothing: But good Maſter, let me be mortal ſtill, and let's goe to ſupper.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Be abſtinent; ſhew not the corruption of thy generation: he that feeds, ſhall die, therefore, he that feeds not ſhall live.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I; but how long ſhall he live? there's the queſtion.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: As long as he can without feeding: did'ſt thou read of the miraculous Maid in Flanders?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: No, nor of any Maid elſe; for the miracle of Virgieity now-a-days ceaſes, e'r the Virgin can read Virginity?

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: She that liv'd three years without any other ſuſtenance, than the ſmell of a Roſe.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I heard of her Signior, but they ſay her guts ſhrunk all into Lute-ſtrings, and her neather-parts cling'd together like a Serpents Tail, ſo that though ſhe continued a woman ſtill above the girdle, beneath yet ſhe was monſter.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: So are moſt women, believe it.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Nay all women Signior, that can live only upon the ſmell of a Roſe.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: No part of the Hiſtory is fabulous.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I think rather no part of the Fable is Hiſtorical: but for all this, Sir, my rebellious ſtomach will not let me be immortal: I will be as immortal, as mortal hunger will ſuffer: put me to a certain ſtint Sir, allow me but a red herring a day.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: O' de dios: wouldſt thou be gluttonous in thy delicacies?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: He that cats nothing but a red herring a day, ſhall ne'r be broil'd for the devil's raſher: a Pilchard, Signior, a Surdiny, an Olive, that I may be a Philoſopher firſt, and immortal after.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Patience Lazarillo; let contemplation be thy food awhile: I ſay unto thee, one Peaſe was a Soldiers Provant a whole day, At the deſtruction of Jeruſalem.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I; and it were any where but at the deſtruction of a place, I'll be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: Signior Pachieco Alaſto, my moſt ingenious Cobler of Sevil, the bonos noxios to your Signiorie.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Signior Metaldi de Forgio, my moſt famous Smith, and man of Mettle, I return your courteſie ten fold, and do humble my Bonnet beneath the Shooe-ſole of your congie: the like to you Signior Mendoza Pediculo de Vermim, my moſt exquiſite Hoſe-heeler.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Here's a greeting betwixt a Cobler, a Smith, and a Smith, and a Botcher: they all belong to the foot, which makes them ſtand ſo much upon their Gentrie.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Ah Signior ſee: nay, we are all Signiors here in Spain, from the Jakes-farmer to the Grandee, or Adelantado: this Botcher looks as if he were Dough-bak'd, a little Butter now, and I could eat him like an Oaten-cake: his fathers diet was new Cheeſe and Onions when he got him: what a ſcallion-fac'd raſcal 'tis?

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: But why Signior Pachieco, do you ſtand ſo much on the priority, and antiquity of your quality (as you call it) in compariſon of ours?

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.p: I; your reaſon for that.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Why thou Iron-pated Smith: and thou Woollen-witted Hoſe-heeler: hear what I will ſpeak indifferently (and according to antient Writers) of our three profeſſions: and let the upright Lazarillo be both judge and moderator.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Still am I the moſt immortally hungry; that may be.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Suppoſe thou wilt derive thy Pedigree, like ſome of the old Heroes, (as Hercules, Aeneas, Achilles) lineally from the gods, making Saturn thy great Grandfather, and Vulcan thy Father: Vulcan was a god.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: He'll make Vulcan your godfather by and by.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p:
Yet I ſay, Saturn was a crabbed block-head, and Vulcan a limping Horn-head, for Venus his wife was a ſtrumpet, and Mars begot all her Children; therefore however, thy original muſt of neceſſity ſpring from Baſtardie: further, what can be a more deject ſpirit in man, than to lay his hands under every ones horſes feet, to do him ſervice, as thou doſt? For thee, I will be brief, thou doſt botch, and not mend, thou art a hider of enormities, viz, Scabs,
chilblains, and kib'd heels: much prone thou art to Sects, and Hereſies, diſturbing State, and Government; for how canſt thou be a ſound member in the common-wealth, that art ſo ſubject to ſtitehes in the ankles? bluſh, and be ſilent then, oh ye Mechanicks, compare no more with the politick Cobler: For Coblers (in old time) have propheſied, what may they do now then, that have every day waxed better, and better? have we not the length of every mans foot? are we not daily menders? yea, and what menders? not horſe-menders.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Nor manners-menders.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.p: But ſoul-menders: Oh divine Coblers; do we not, like the wiſe man, ſpin out our own threds, (or our wives for us?) do we not by our ſowing the Hide, reap the Beef? are not we of the Gentle-craft, whilſt both you are but Crafts-men; You will ſay, you fear neither Iron nor Steel, and what you get is wrought out of the fire; I muſt anſwer you again, though, all this is but forgery: You may likewiſe ſay, a man's a man, that has but a hoſe on his head: I muſt likewiſe anſwer, that man is a botcher, that has a heel'd hoſe on his head: to conclude, there can be no compariſon with the Cobler, who is all in all in the Common-wealth, has his politique eye and ends on every mans ſteps that walks, and whoſe courſe ſhall be laſting to the worlds end.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: I give place: the wit of man is wonderful: thou haſt his the nail on the head, and I will give thee ſix pots for't, thou I ne'r clinch ſhooe again.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Who's this? oh our Alguazier: as arrant a knave as e'er wore one head under two offices: he is one ſide Alguazier.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: The other ſide Serjeant,

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.p: That's both ſides carrion I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: This is he apprehends whores in the way of juſtice, and lodges 'em in his own houſe, in the way of profit: he with him, is the Grand Don Vitelli, 'twixt whom and Fernando Alvarez, the mortal hatred is; he is indeed my Don's Bawd, and does at this preſent, lodge a famous Curtizan of his, lately come from Madrid.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Let her want nothing Signior, ſhe can aske:
What loſs or injury you may ſuſtain
I will repair, and recompence your love:
Only that fellows coming I miſlike,
And did fore-warn her of him: bear her this
With my beſt love, at night I'll viſit her.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I reſt your Lordſhips Servant.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Good ev'n, Signiors:
Oh Alvarez, thou haſt brought a Son with thee
Both brightens, and obſcures our Nation,
Whoſe pure ſtrong beams on us, ſhoot like the Suns
On baſer fires: I would to heaven my bloud
had never ſtain'd thy bold unfortunate hand,
That with mine honor I might emulate,
Not perſecute ſuch virtue: I will ſee him,
Though with the hazard of my life: no reſt
In my contentious ſpirits, can I find
Till I have gratify'd him in like kind. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: I know you not: what are ye? hence ye baſe Beſegnios.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Mary Catzo Signior Alguazier, d' ye not know us? why, we are your honeſt neighbors, the Cobler, Smith, and Botcher, that have ſo often ſate ſnoaring cheek by joll with your Signiorie, in rug at midnight.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Nay, good Signior, be not angry: you muſt underſtand, a Cat, and ſuch an Officer ſee beſt in the dark.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: By this hand, I could find in my heart to ſhooe his head.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Why then know you, Signior; thou mongril, begot at midnight, at the Goal gate, by a Beadle, on a Catchpoles wife, are not you he that was whipt out of Toledo for perjury.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Next; condemn'd to the Gallies for pilfery, to the Buls pizel.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: And after call'd to the Inquiſition, for Apoſtacie.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Are not you he that rather than you durſt goe an induſtrious voyage being preſs'd to the Iſlands, ſkulk'd till the Fleet was gone, and then earn'd your Royal a day by ſquiring puncks, and puncklings up and down the City?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Are not you a Portuguize born, deſcended o' the Moors, and came hither into Sevil with your Maſter, a • arrant Tailor, in your red Bonnet, and your blue Jacket, louſie, though now your block-head be cover'd with the Spaniſh block, and your laſhed Shoulders with a Velvet Pet.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Are not you he that have been of thirty callings, yet ne'r a one lawful? that being a Chandler firſt, profeſs'd ſincerity, and would ſell no man Muſtard to his Beef on the Sabbath, and yet ſold Hypocriſie all your life time?

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: Are not you he, that were ſince a Surgeon to the Stews, and undertook to cure what the Church it ſe •• could not, Strumpets that riſe to your office by being a great Don's Bawd?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: That commit men nightly, offenceleſs, for the gain of a groat a priſoner, which your Beadle ſeems to put up, when you ſhare three pence?

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.p: Are not you he that is a kiſſer of men, in drunkenneſs, and a berayer in ſobriety?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: Diabolo: they'll rail me into the Gallies again.

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: Yes Signior, thou art even he we ſpeak of all thi • while: thou mayſt by thy place now, lay us by the heels: 'tis true: but take heed, be wiſer, pluck not ruin on thine own head: for never was there ſuch an Anatomie, as we ſhall make thee then: be wiſe therefore, thou child of the night! be friends, and ſhake hands, thou art a proper man, if thy beard were redder: remember thy worſhipful function, a Conſtable; though thou turn'ſt day into night, and night into day, what of that? watch leſs and pray more: Let not thy mittens abate the talons of thy authority, but gripe theft and whoredom, whereſoever th •• meet'ſt 'em: bear 'em away like a tempeſt, and lodge 'em ſafely in thne own houſe:

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Would you have whores and thieves lodgd in ſuch a houſe?

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: They ever do ſo: I have found a thief, or a wh ••• there, when the whole Suburbs could not furniſh me.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: But why do they lodge there?

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: That they may be ſafe and forth-coming: for in the morning uſually, the thief is ſent to the Goal, and the whore proſtrates her ſelf to the Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Admirable Pachiecho.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.p: Thou Cobler of Chriſtendom.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: There is no railing with theſe rogues: I will cloſe with 'em, till I can cry quittance: why Signiors, and my honeſt neighbors, will you impute that as a neglect of my friends, which is an imperfection in me? I have been S •• dblind from my infancy: to make you amends you ſhall ſup with me.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Shall we ſup with ye, Sir? O' my conſcience, they have wrong'd the Gentleman extreamly.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: And after ſupper, I have a project to employ y •• in, ſhall make you drink and eat merrily this month: I am a little knaviſh: why, and doe not I know all you to be knaves?

sp.speaker: Pac.
sp.p: I grant you, we are all knaves, and will be your knaves: But oh, while you live, take heed of being a pro •• knave.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.p: On then paſs: I will bear out my ſtaffe, and my ſtaffe ſhall bear out me.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Oh Lazarillo, thou art going to ſupper.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Pray be not angry.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p:
I am angry, and I will be angry Diabolo: what
ſhould you do in the Kitchin, cannot the Cooks lick their • ingers without your overſeeing? nor the maids make pot
• age, except your dogs-head be in the pot? Don Lucio, Don
•••• -Quean, Don Spinſter, wear a Petticoat ſtill, and put •• on your Smock a' Monday: I will have a baby o' clouts made for it, like a great girl: nay, if you will needs be •• arching of Ruffs, and ſowing of Black-work, I will of a mild, and loving Tutor, become a Tyrant, your Father • as committed you to my charge, and I will make a man • or a mouſe on you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What would you have me do? this ſcurvy ſword
So galls my thigh: I would 't were burnt: piſh, look,
This Cloak will ne'r keep on: theſe Boots too hide-bound,
Make me walk ſtiff, as if my legs were frozen,
And my Spurs gingle like a Morris-dancer:
Lord, how my head akes with this roguiſh Hat;
This maſculine attire is moſt uneaſie,
I am bound up in it: I had rather walk
In folio, again, looſe like a woman.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: In Foolio, had you not?
Thou mock to heav'n, and nature, and thy Parents,
Thou tender Leg of Lamb; oh, how he walks
As if he had bepiſs'd himſelf, and fleers!
• s this a gate for the young Cavalier,
Don Lucio, Son and Heir to Alvarez?
Hasit a corn? or do's it walk on conſcience,
• t treads ſo gingerly? Come on your ways,
Suppoſe me now your Fathers foe, Vitelli,
And ſpying you i' th' ſtreet, thus I advance
I twiſt my Beard, and then I draw my ſword.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Alas.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: And thus accoſt thee: traiterous brat,
How durſt thou thus confront me? impious twig
Of that old •• ock, dew'd with my kinſmans gore,
Draw, for I'll quarter thee in pieces four.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Nay, prethee Bobadilla, leave thy fooling,
Put up thy ſword, I will not meddle with ye;
I, juſtle me, I care not: I'll not draw,
Pray be a quiet man.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: D' ye hear: anſwer me, as you would do Don Vitelli, or I'll be ſo bold as to lay the pomel of my ſword over the hilts of your head: my name's Vitelli, and I'll have the wall.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why then I'll have the kennel: what a coil you keep?
Signior, what happen'd 'twixt my Sire and your
Kinſman, was long before I ſaw the world,
No fault of mine, nor will I juſtifie
My Fathers crimes: forget Sir, and forgive,
'Tis Chriſtianity: I pray put up your ſword,
I'll give you any ſatisfaction
That may become a Gentleman: however
I hope you are bred to more humanity
Than to revenge my Fathers wrong on me
That crave your love, and peace: law-you-now Zancho
Would not this quiet him, were he ten Vitellies.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Oh craven-chicken of a Cock o' th' game: well, what remedy? did thy Father ſee this, O' my conſcience, he would cut off thy Maſculine gender, crop thine ears, beat out thine eyes, and ſet thee in one of the Pear trees for a ſcare-crow: As I am Vitelli, I am ſatisfied; but as I am Bobadilla, Spindola, Zancho, Steward of the houſe, and thy Fathers Servant, I could find in my heart to lop off the hinder part of thy face, or to beat all thy teeth into thy mouth: Oh thou whay-blooded milk-ſop, I'll wait upon thee no longer, thou ſhalt ev'n wait upon me: come your ways Sir, I ſhall take a little pains with ye elſe.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Where art thou brother Lucio? ran tan tan ta ran tan ran tan tan ta, ta ran tan tan tan. Oh, I ſhall no more ſee thoſe golden daies, theſe clothes will never fadge with me: a—O' this filthy vardingale, this hip-hape: brother, why are womens hanches only limited, confin'd, hoop'd in, as it were with theſe ſame ſcurvy vardingales?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Becauſe womens hanches only are moſt ſubject to diſplay and flie out.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Bobadilla, rogue, ten Duckets, I hit the prepuce of thy Codpiece.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Hold, if you love my life, Siſter: I am not Zancho Bobadilla, I am your brother Lucio: what a fright you have put me in?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Brother? and wherefore thus?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Why, Maſter Steward here, Signior Zancho, made me change: he does nothing but miſ-uſe me, and call me Coward, and ſwears I ſhall wait upon him.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p: Well: I do no more than I have authority for: would I were away though: for ſhe's as much too maniſh, as he too womaniſh: I dare not meddle with her, yet I muſt ſet a good face on't (if I had it) I have like charge of Madam, I am as well to mollifie you, as to quallifie him: what have you to do with Armors, and Piſtols, and Javelins, and ſwords, and ſuch tools? remember Miſtriſs; nature hath given you a ſheath only, to ſignifie women are to put up mens weapons, not to draw them: look you now, is this a fit trot for a Gentlewoman? You ſhall ſee the Court-Ladies move like Goddeſſes, as if they trode air; they will ſwim you their meaſures, like Whiting-mops, as if their feet were finns, and the hinges of their knees oil'd: doe they love to ride great horſes, as you do? no, they love to ride great aſſes ſooner: faith, I know not what to ſay t' ye both: Cuſtom hath turn'd nature topſie-turvie in you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay, but Maſter Steward.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: You cannot trot ſo faſt, but he ambles as ſlowly.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Signior Spindle, will you hear me,

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: He that ſhall come to beſtride your Virginity, had better be affot o'er the Dragon.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Ver well.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Did ever Spaniſh Lady pace ſo?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Hold theſe a little.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I'll not touch 'em, I.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Firſt doe I break your Office o're your pate,
You Dog-skin-fac'd rogue, pilcher, you poor John,
Which I will beat to Stock-ſiſh.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Siſter.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You Cittern-head, who have you talk'd to, ha?
You naſty, ſtinking, and ill-countenanc'd Cur.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: By this hand, I'll bang your brother for this, when I get him alone.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: How? kick him Lucio, he ſhall kick you Bob,
Spight o' the noſe, that's flat: kick him, I ſay,
Or I will cut thy head off.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Softly y' had beſt.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Now, thou lean, dry'd, and ominous viſag'd knave,
Thou falſe and peremptory Steward, pray,
For I will hang thee up in thine own chain.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Good Siſter do not choak him.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Murder, murder. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Well: I ſhall meet with ye: Lucio, who bought this?
'Tis a reaſonable good one; but there hangs one
Spain's Champion ne'er us'd truer: with this Staffe
Old Alvarez has led up men ſo cloſe,
They could almoſt ſpit in the Cannons mouth,
Whilſt I with that, and this well mounted, ſcour'd
A Horſe-troop through, and through, like ſwift deſire,
And ſeen poor rogues retire, all gore, and gaſh'd
Like bleeding Shads.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Bleſs us, Siſter Clara.
How deſperately you talk: what d' ye call
This Gun a dag?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I'll give't thee: a French petronel:
You never ſaw my Barbary, and Lufanta
Beſtow'd upon me, as yet Lucio?
Walk down, and ſee it

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What into the Stable?
Not I, the Jades will kick: the poor Groom there
Was almoſt ſpoil'd the other day.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Fie on thee,
Thou wilt ſcarce be a man before thy Mother.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: When will you be a woman?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Would I were none.
But natures privy Seal aſſures me one.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Thou anger'ſt me: can ſtrong habitual cuſtome
Work with ſuch Magick on the mind and manners,
In ſpight of ſex and nature? find out ſirrah,
Some skilful fighter.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: I will rectifie,
And redeem eithers proper inclination,
Or bray 'em in a morter, and new mold 'em. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Believe your eyes, Sir, I tell you, we waſh an Ethiop.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſtrike it for ten Duckets.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: How now Clara,
Your Breeches on ſtill? and your petticoat
Not yet off Lucio? art thou not guelt?
Or did the cold Muſcovite beget thee,
That lay here Lieger in the laſt great froſt?
Art not thou Clara, turn'd a man indeed
Beneath the girdle? and a woman thou?
I'll have you ſearch'd by,—I ſtrongly doubt;
We muſt have theſe things mended: come goe in. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: With Lucio ſay you? there is for you.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: And there is for thee.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: I thank you: you have now bought a little advice
Of me; if you chance to have conference with that
Lady there, be very civil, or look to your head: ſhe has
Ten nails, and you have but two eies: If any fooliſh
Hot motions ſhould chance to riſe in the Horizon
Under your equinoctial there, qualifie it as well as
You can, for I fear the elevation of your pole will
Not agree with the Horoſcope of her conſtitution:
She is Bell the Dragon I aſſure you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Are you the Lucio, Sir, that ſav'd Vitelli?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Not I indeed, Sir, I did never brable;
There walks that Lucio Metamorphoſed. Exit.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Do ye mock me?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: No, he does not: I am that
Suppoſed Lucio that was, but Clara,
That is, and daughter unto Alvarez.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Amazement daunts me; would my life were riddles,
So you were ſtill my fair Expoſitor:
Protected by a Lady from my death.
Oh, I ſhall wear an everlaſting bluſh
Upon my cheek from this diſcovery:
Oh, you the faireſt Soldier, I e'er ſaw;
Each of whoſe eyes, like a bright beamy Shield,
Conquers without blows, the contentious.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Sir, guard your ſelf, you are in your enemies houſe,
And may be injur'd.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Tis impoſſible:
Foe, nor oppreſſing odds dares prove Vitelli,
If Clara ſide him, and will call him friend,
I would the difference of our bloods were ſuch
As might with any ſhift be wip'd away:
Or would to heaven your ſelf were all your name;
That having loſt blood by you, I might hope
To raiſe blood from you. But my black-wing'd fate
Hovers averſely over that fond hope:
And he, whoſe tongue thus gratifies the daughter,
And Siſter of his enemy wears a ſword
To rip the Father and the Brother up.
Thus you that ſav'd this wretched life of mine,
Have ſav'd it to the ruin of your friends.
That my affections ſhould promiſcuouſly
Dart love and hate at once, both worthily?
Pray let me kiſs your hand.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You are treacherous,
And come to do me miſchief.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Speak on ſtill:
Your words are falſer (fair) than my intents,
And each ſweet accent far more treacherous; for
Though you ſpeak ill of me, you ſpeak ſo well,
I doe deſire to hear you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Pray be gone:
Or kill me if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Oh, neither can I,
For to be gone, were to deſtroy my life;
And to kill you, were to deſtroy my ſoul:
I am in love, yet muſt not be in love:
I'll get away apace: yet valiant Lady,
Such gratitude to honor I do owe,
And ſuch obedience to your memory,
That if you will beſtow ſomething, that I
May wear about me, it ſhall bind all wrath,
My moſt inveterate wrath, from all attempts,
Till you and I meet next.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: A favour, Sir?
Why, I will give ye good counſel.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: That already,
You have beſtowed; a Ribbon, or a Glove.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay, thoſe are tokens for a waiting-maid
To trim the Butler with,

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Your feather.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Fie; the wenches give them to their ſerving-men.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: That little Ring.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Twill hold you but by th' finger;
And I would have have you faſter.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Any thing
That I may wear, and but remember you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: This ſmile: my good opinion, or my ſelf.
But that it ſeems you like not

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Yes, ſo well:
When any ſmiles, I will remember yours;
Your good opinion ſhall in weight poize me
Againſt a thouſand ill: Laſtly, your ſelf,
My curious eye now figures in my heart,
Where I will wear you; till the Table break.
So, whiteſt Angels guard you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Stay Sir, I
Have fitly thought to give, what you as fitly
May not diſdain to wear.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Cla,
sp.l: This Sword.
I never heard a man ſpeak till this hour.
His words are golden chains, and now I fear
The Lyoneſſe hath met a tamer here:
Fie, how his tongue chimes: what was I ſaying?
Oh: this favour I bequeath you, which I tie
In a Love-knot, faſt, ne'er to hurt my friends;
Yet be it fortunate 'gainſt all your foes
(For I have neither friend, nor foe, but yours)
As e'er it was to me: I've kept it long,
And value it, next my Virginity:
But good, return it, for I now remember
I vow'd, who purchas'd it, ſhould have me too.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Would that were poſſible: but alas it is not;
Yet this aſſure your ſelf, moſt honour'd Clara,
I'll not infringe a particle of breath
My vow hath offered to ye: nor from this part
Whilſt it hath edge, or point, or I a heart. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Oh, leave me living: what new exerciſe
Is crept into my breaſt, that blauncheth clean
My former nature? I begin to find
I am a woman, and muſt learn to fight
A ſofter ſweeter battel, than with ſwords.
I am ſick methinks, but the diſeaſe I feel
Pleaſeth, and puniſheth: I warrant love
Is very like this, that folks talke of ſo;
I skill not what it is, yet ſure even here,
• ven in my heart, I ſenſibly perceive
• t glows, and riſeth like a glimmering flame,
• ut know not yet the Eſſence on't, nor name. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: HE muſt not? nor he ſhall not, who ſhall lett him?
You politique Diego, with your face of wiſdom;
Don-blirt, the—on your Aphoriſmes,
Your grave, and Sage-Ale Phyſiognomy:
Do not I know thee for the Alguazier,
Whoſe dunghil all the Pariſh Scavengers
Could never rid? thou Comedy to men,
Whoſe ſerious folly is a Butt for all
To ſhoot their wits at; whilſt thou haſt not wit,
Nor heart, to anſwer, or be angry.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Lady.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Peace, peace, you rotten Rogue, ſupported by
A ſtaffe of rottener office: dare you check
Any acceſſes, that I will allow?
Pi • rato is my friend, and viſits me
In lawful ſort to eſpouſe me as his wife;
And who will croſs, or ſhall our enter-views?
You know me ſirrah, for no Chambermaid,
That caſt her belly, and her waſtecoat lately;
Thou think'ſt thy Conſtableſhip is much: not ſo,
I am ten offices to thee: I, thy houſe,
Thy houſe, and office is maintain'd by me.

sp.speaker: Alg
sp.l: My houſe-of-office is maintain'd i' th' garden:
Go too, I know you, and I have contriv'd;
Y'are a delinquent, but I have contriv'd
A poiſon, though not in the third degree:
I can ſay, black's your eye, though it be grey;
I have conniv'd at this, your friend, and you:
But what is got by this connivency?
I like his feather well: a proper man,
Of good diſcourſe, fine converſation,
Valiant, and a great carrier of the buſineſs,
Sweet breaſted, as the Nightingale, or Thruſh:
Yet I muſt tell you; you forget your ſelf,
My Lord Vitellies love, and maintenance
Deſerves no other Jack i' th' box, but he:
What though he gather'd firſt the golden fruit,
And blew your pigs-coat up into a bliſter,
When you did wait at Court upon his mother;
Has he not well provided for the barn?
Beſide, what profit reap I by the other?
• f you will have me ſerve your pleaſure, Lady,
Your pleaſure muſt accommodate my ſervice;
As good be virtuous and poor, as not
Thrive by my knavery, all the world would be
Good, proſper'd goodneſs like to villany.
I am the Kings Vice-gerent by my place;
His right Lieutenant in mine own precinct.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Thou art a right raſcal in all mens precincts;
Yet now my pair of twins, of fool, and knave,
Look we are friends; there's Gold for thee, admit
Whom I will have, and keep it from my Don;
And I will make thee richer than thou 'rt wiſe:
Thou ſhalt be my Bawd, and my Officer:
Thy children ſhall eat ſtill, my good night Owl,
And thy old wife ſell Andirons to the Court,
Be countenanced by the Dons, and wear a hood,
Nay, keep my Garden-houſe; I'll call her Mother,
Thee Father, my good poyſonous Red-hair'd Dill,
And Gold ſhall daily be thy Sacrifice,
Wrought from a fertile Iſland of mine own,
Which I will offer, like an Indian Queen.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: And I will be thy devil, thou my fleſh,
With which I'll catch the world.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Fill ſome Tobacco,
And bring it in: if Piorato come
Before my Don, admit him; if my Don
Before my Love, conduct him, my dear Devil. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I will my dear Fleſh: firſt come, firſt ſerv'd. Well ſaid
Oh equal Heaven, how wiſely thou didſpoſeſt
Thy ſeveral gifts? one's born a great rich fool,
For the ſubordinate knave to work upon:
Anothers poor, with wits addition,
Which well or ill-us'd, builds a living up;
And that too from the Sire oft deſcends:
Only fair virtue, by traduction
Never ſucceeds, and ſeldom meets ſucceſs,
What have I then to do with't? My free will
Left me by heaven, makes me or good, or ill:
Now ſince vice gets more in this vicious world
Than Piety, and my Stars confluence
Enforce my diſpoſition to affect
Gain, and the name of rich, let who will practiſe
War, and grow that way great: religious,
And that way good: my chief felicity
Is wealth the nurſe of ſenſuality:
And he that mainly labours to be rich,
Muſt ſcratch great ſcabs, and claw a Strumpets itch. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Piorato, and Babadilla, with Letters.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: To ſaay, Sir, I will wait upon your Lord,
Were not to underſtand my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: To ſay Sir,
You will do any thing but wait upon him,
Were not to underſtand my Lord.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: I'll meet him
Some half hour hence, and doubt not but to render
His Son a man again: the cure is eaſie,
I have done divers.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Women do ye mean, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Cures I do mean, Sir: be there but one ſpark
Of fire remaining in him unextinct,
With my diſcourſe I'll blow it to a flame;
And with my practice into action:
I have had one ſo full of childiſh fear,
And womaniſh-hearted ſent to my advice,
He durſt not draw a knife to cut his meat.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: And how Sir, did you help him?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Sir, I kept him
Seven daies in a dark room by a Candle-light,
A plenteous Table ſpread with all good meats,
Before his eyes, a Caſe of keen broad Knives,
Upon the board, and he ſo watch'd he might not
Touch the leaſt modicum, unleſs he cut it:
And thus I brought him firſt to draw a knife.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Good.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Then for ten daies did I diet him
Only with burnt Pork, Sir, and gammons of Bacon;
A pill of Caveary now and then,
Which breeds choler aduſt your know,

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: 'Tis true.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: And to purge phlegmatick humor, and cold crudities;
In all that time he drank me Aqua-fortis,
And nothing elſe but—

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Aqua-vitae Signior,
For Aqua-fortis poiſons.

sp.speaker: Pio.

l.hi: Aqua-fortis

sp.l: I ſay again: what's one man's poiſon, Signior,
Is anothers meat or drink.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Your patience, Sir;
By your good patience. h' had a huge cold ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: I fir'd it: and gave him then three ſweats
In the Artillery-yard three drilling daies:
And now he'll ſhoot a Gun, and draw a Sword,
And fight with any man in Chriſtendom.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: A receipt for a coward: I'll be bold, Sir,
To write your good preſcription.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Sir, hereafter
You ſhall, and underneath it put probatum:
Is your chain right?

sp.speaker: Bob,
sp.l: 'Tis both right and juſt Sir;
For though I am a Steward, I did get it
With no mans wrong.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You are witty.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: So, ſo.
Could you not cure one Sir, of being too raſh
And over-daring? there now's my diſeaſe:
Fool-hardy as they ſay, for that in ſooth,
I am.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Moſt eaſily.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: To make you drunk, Sir,
With ſmall Beer once a day, and beat you twice,
Till you be bruis'd all over: if that help not,
Knock out your brains.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: This is ſtrong Phyſick Signior,
And never will agree with my weak body:
I find the medicine worſe than the malady,
And therefore will remain fool-hardy ſtill:
You'll come, Sir?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: As I am a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: A man o' th' Sword ſhould never break his word.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: I'll overtake you: I have only, Sir
A complimental viſitation
To offer to a Miſtriſs lodg'd here by.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: A Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Fair, and comely?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Oh Sir, the Paragon, the Non-paril
Oh Sevil, the moſt wealthy Mine of Spain,
For beauty, and perfection.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Say you ſo?
Might not a man entreat a crurteſie,
To walk along with you Signior, to peruſe
This dainty Mine, though not to dig in't Signior?
Hauh—I hope you'll not denie me, being a ſtranger;
Though I am a Steward, I am fleſh and blood,
And frail as other men,

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Sir, blow your noſe:
I dare not for the world: no, ſhe is kept
By a great Don, Vitelli.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: 'Tis true,

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: See, things will veer about: this Don Vitelli
Am I to ſeek now, to deliver Letters
From my young Miſtriſs Clara: and I tell you,
Under the Roſe, becauſe you are a ſtranger,
And my ſpecial friend, I doubt there is
A little fooliſh love betwixt the parties,
Unknown unto my Lord.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Happy diſcovery:
My fruit begins to ripen: hark you Sir,
I would not wiſh you now, to give thoſe Letters:
But home, and ope this to Madona Clara,
Which when I come I'll juſtifie, and relate
More amply, and particularly.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: I approve
Your counſel, and will practiſe it: bazilos manos:
Here's two chewres chewr'd: when wiſdom is imploy'd
'Tis ever thus: your more acquaintance, Signior:
I ſay not better, leaſt you think, I thought not
Yours good enough. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Your ſervant excellent Steward.
Would all the Dons in Spain had no more brains,
Here comes the Alguazier: dieu vous guard Monſieur.
Is my Cuz ſtirring yet?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Your Cuz (good coſin?)
A whore is like a fool, a kin to all
The gallants in the Town: Your Guz, good Signior,
Is gone abroad; Sir, with her other Coſin,
My Lord Vitelli: ſince when there hath been
Some dozen Coſins here to enquire for her.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: She's greatly ally'd Sir.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Marry is ſhe, Sir,
Come of a luſty kindred: the truth is,
I muſt connive no more: no more admittance
Muſt I conſent to; my good Lord has threatned me,
And you muſt pardon.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Out upon thee man,
Turn honeſt in thine age? one foot i'th' grave?
Thou ſhalt not wrong thy ſelf ſo, for a million:
Look, thou three-headed Cerberus (for wit
I mean) here is one ſop, and two, and three,
For every chop a bit.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I marry Sir:
Well, the poor heart loves you but too well.
We have been talking on you 'faith this hour:
Where, what I ſaid, goe too: ſhe loves your valour;
Oh, and your Muſick moſt abominably:
She is within Sir, and alone: what mean you?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: That is your Sergeants ſide, I take it Sir;
Now I endure your Conſtables much better;
There is leſs danger in't: for one you know
Is a tame harmleſs monſter in the light,
The Sergeant ſalvage both by day, and night

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I'll call her to you for that.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: No, I will charm her.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: She's come.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: My Spirit.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Oh my Sweet,
Leap hearts to lips, and in our kiſſes meet.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Turn, turn thy beauteous face away,
How pale and ſickly looks the day,
In emulation ofthy brighter beams!
Oh envious light, fli, lie, begone,
Come night, and piece two breaſts as one;
When what love does, we will repeat in dreams.
Yet (thy eyes open) who can day hence fright,
Let but their Lids fall, and it will be night.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Well, I will leave you to your fortitude;
And you to temperance: ah, ye pretty pair,
'Twere ſin to ſunder you. Lovers being alone
Make one of two, and day and might all one.
But fall not out, I charge you, keep the peace;
You know my place elſe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: No, you will not marry:
You are a Courtier, and can ſing (my Love)
And want no Miſtriſſes: but yet I care not,
I'll love you ſtill; and when I am dead for you,
Then you'll believe my truth.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You kill me (fair)
It is my leſſon that you ſpeak: have I
Inany circumſtancwe deſerv'd this doubt?
I am not like your falſe and perjur'd Don
That here maintains you, and has vow'd his faith,
And yet attempts in way of marriage
A Lady not far off.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: How's that?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo:
And therefore Miſtiſs, now the time is come
You may demand his promiſe; and I ſwear
〈◊〉 marry you with ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: And with that Gold
• hich Don Vitellia gives, you'll walk ſome voyage
• id leave me to my Trade; and laugh, and brag,
•• w you o'er-reach'd a whore, and gull'd a Lord.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You anger me extreamly: fare you well.
• hat ſhould I ſay to be believ'd? expoſe me
〈◊〉 any hazard; or like jealous Juno
Th' incenſed ſtep-mother of Hercules)
• eſign me labours moſt impoſſible,
〈◊〉 doe 'em, or die in 'em; ſo at laſt
• ou will believe me.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Come, we are friends: I do,
• m thine, walk in: my Lord has ſent me outſides,
• tthou ſhalt have 'em, the colours are too ſad:

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: 'Faith Miſtriſs, I want clothes indeed.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I have
•• me Gold too, for my ſervant.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: And I have
〈◊〉 better mettal for my Miſtriſs. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Vitelli and Alguazier, at ſeveral doors.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Undone—wit now or never help me: my Maſter
• e will cut my throat, I am a dead Conſtable;
• nd he'll not be hang'd neither, there's the grief:
• he party, Sir, is here.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: He was here;
〈◊〉 cry your Lordſhip mercy: but I ratled him;
〈◊〉 told him here was no companions
• or ſuch debauch'd, and poor condition'd fellows;
〈…〉 bid him venture not ſo deſperately
The cropping of his ears, ſlitting his noſe,
Or being gelt.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Twas well done.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Pleaſe your honor,
〈◊〉 told him there were Stews, and then at laſt
•• ore three or four great oaths ſhe was remov'd,
Which I did think I might, in conſcience,
• eing for your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: What became of him?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Faith Sir, he went away with a flea in's ear,
• ike a poor cur, clapping his trundle tail
Betwixt his legs.—A chi ha, a chi ha, a chi ha—now luck.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: 'Tis he, do as I told thee: Bleſs thee Signior.
Oh, my dear Lord.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Malroda, what alone?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: She never is alone, that is accompanied
With noble thoughts, my Lord; and mine are ſuch,
Being only of your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Pretty Laſs.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Oh my good Lord, my Picture's done: but 'faith
It is not like; nay, this way Sir, the light
Strikes beſt upon it here.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Excellent wench. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I am glad the danger's over. Exi.t

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Tis wondrous like,
But that Art cannot counterfeit what Nature
Could make but once,

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: All's clear; another tune
You muſt hear rom me now: Vitelli, thou'rt
A moſt perfidious and a perjur'd man,
As ever did uſurp Nobility.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: What meanſt thou Mal?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Leave your betraying ſmiles,
And change the tunes of your inticing tongues
To penitential prayers; for I am great
In labour, even with anger, big with child
Of womans rage, bigger than when my womb
Was pregnant by thee: go ſeducer, flie
Out of the world, let me the laſt wretch be
Diſhonored by thee: touch me not, I loath
My very heart, becauſe thou lay'ſt there long;
A woman's well help'd up, that's confident
In e'er a glittering outſide on you all:
Would I had honeſtly been match'd to ſome
Poor Countrey-ſwain, e'er known the vanity
Of Court: peace then had been my portion,
Nor had been cozen'd by an hours pomp
To be a whore unto my dying day.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Oh the uncomfortable waies ſuch women have,
Their different ſpeech and meaning, no aſſurance
In what they ſay or do: Diſſemblers
Even in their prayers, as if the weeping Greek
That flatter'd Troy a-fire, had been their Adam;
Lyers, as if their mother had been made
Only of all the falſhood of the man,
Diſpos'd into that rib: Do I know this,
And more: nay, all that can concern this Sex,
With the true end of my creation?
Can I with rational diſcourſe ſometimes
Advance my ſpirit into Heaven, before
'T has ſhook hands with my body, and yet blindly
Suffer my filthy fleſh to maſter it,
With ſight of ſuch fair frail beguiling objects?
When I am abſent, eaſily I reſolve
Ne'er more to entertain thoſe ſtrong deſires
That triumph o'er me, even to actual ſin;
Yet when I meet again thoſe ſorcerers eies,
Their beams my hardeſt reſolutions thaw,
As if that cakes of Ice and July met,
And her ſighs powerful as the violent North,
Like a light feather twirl me round about
And leave me in mine own low ſtate again.
What ayl'ſt thou? prethee weep not: Oh, thoſe tears
If they were true, and rightly ſpent, would raiſe
A flow'ry ſpring i'th' midſt of January:
Celeſtial Miniſters with Chryſtal cups
Would ſtoop to ſave 'em for immortal drink:
But from this paſſion; why all this?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Do ye ask?
You are marrying: having made me unfit
For any man, you leave me fit for all:
Porters muſt be my burthens now, to live,
And fitting me your ſelf for Carts, and Beadles,
You leave me to 'em: And who of allthe world
But the virago, your great Arch-foes daughter?
But on: I care not, this poor ruſh: 'twill breed
An excellent Comedy: ha, ha: 't makes me laugh:
I cannot chooſe: the beſt is, ſome report
It is a match for fear, not love o' your ſide.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Why how the devil knows ſhe, that I ſaw
This Lady? are all whores, piec'd with ſome witch?
I will be merry, 'faith 'tis true, ſweet heart,
I Am to marry?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Are you? you baſe Lord,
By—I'll piſtol thee.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: A roaring whore?
Take heed, there's a Correction-houſe hard by:
You ha' learn'd this o' your ſwordman, that I warn'd you of
Your Fencers, and your drunkards: but whereas
You upbraid me with oaths, why I muſt tell you
I ne'er promis'd you marriage, nor have vow'd,
But ſaid I lov'd you, long as your remain'd
The woman I expected, or you ſwore,
And how you have fail'd of that (ſweet-heart) you know.
You fain would ſhew your power, but fare you well,
I'll keep no more faith with an infidel.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Nor I my boſome for a Turk: d' ye hear?
Goe, and the devil take me, if ever
I ſee you more: I was too true.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Come, piſh:
That devil take the falſeſt of us two.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Amen.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: You are an ill Clark; and curſe your ſelf:
Madneſs tranſports you: I confeſs, I drew you
Unto my Will: but you muſt know that muſt not
Make me doat on the habit of my ſin.
I will, to ſettle you to your content,
Be maſter of my word: and yet he ly'd
That told you I was marrying, but in thought:
But will you ſlave me to your tyranny
So cruelly I ſhall not dare to look
Or ſpeak to other women? make me not
Your ſmock's Monopolie: come, let's be friends:
Look, here's a Jewel for thee: I will come
At night, and —

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: What 'yfaith: you ſhall not, Sir.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Faith, and troth, and verily, but I will

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Half drunk, to make a noiſe, and rail?

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: No, no,
Sober, and dieted for the nonce: I am thine,
I have won the day.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: The night (though) ſhall be mine. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Clara, and Bobadilla with Letters.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What ſaid he, ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Little, or nothing: faith I ſaw him not,
Nor will not: he doth love a ſtrumpet, Miſtriſs,
Nay, keeps her ſpitefully, under the Conſtables noſe,
It ſhall be juſtified by the Gentleman
Your brothers Maſter that is now within
A practiſing: there are your Letters: come
You ſhall not caſt your ſelf away, while I live,
Nor will I venture my Right worſhipful place
In ſuch a buſineſs—here's your Mother, down:
And he that loves you: another 'gates fellow, I wiſh,
If you had any grace.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Well rogue.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: I'll in, to ſee Don Lucio manage, he'll make
A pretty piece of fleſh, I promiſe you,
He does already handle his weapon finely. Exit.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: She knows your love, Sir, and the full allowance
Her Father and my ſelf approve it with,
And I muſt tell you, I much hope it hath
Wrought ſome impreſſion by her alteration;
She ſighs, and ſaies, forſooth, and cries heigh-ho,
She'll take ill words o' th' Steward, and the Servants,
Yet anſwer affably, and modeſtly:
Things Sir, not uſual with her: there ſhe is,
Change ſome few words.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Madam, I am bound t'ye;
How now, fair Miſtriſs, working?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Yes forſooth,
Learning to live another day.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: That needs not.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: No forſooth: by my truly but it does,
We knew not what we may come to.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Come, I ha begg'd leave for you to play.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Forſooth
'Tis ill for a fair Lady to be idle.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: She had better be well-buſied, I know that.
Turtle: me thinks you mourn, ſhall I ſit by you?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If you be weary, Sir, you had beſt be gone
(I work not a true ſtitch) now you're my mate.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: If I be ſo, I muſt do more than ſide you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ev'n what you will, but tread me.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Shall we bill?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Oh no, forſooth.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Being ſo fair, my Clara,
Why d'ye delight in Black-work?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Oh White, Sir,
The faireſt Ladies like the blackeſt men:
I ever lov'd the colour: all black things
Are leaſt ſubject to change,

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Why, I do love
A black thing too: and the moſt beauteous faces
Have oftneſt of them: as the blackeſt eyes,
Jet-arched brows, ſuch hair: I'll kiſs your hand.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Twill hinder me my work Sir: and my Mother
Will chide me, if I do not do my taske.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Your Mother, nor your Father ſhall chide: you
Might have a prettier taske, would you be rul'd,
And look with open eyes.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſtare upon you
And broadly ſee you, a wondrous proper man,
Yet 'twere a greater taske for me to love you
Than I ſhall ever work Sir, in ſeven year,
—O' this ſtitching, I had rather feel
Two, than ſow one:—this rogue h' as given me a ſtitch
Clean croſs my heart:
Now you grow troubleſome: piſh, the man is fooliſh.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Pray wear theſe trifles.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Neither you, nor trifles,
You are a trifle, wear your ſelf, Sir, out,
And here no more trifle the time away.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Come; you're deceiv'd in me, I will not wake,
Nor faſt, nor dye for you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Gooſe, be not you deceiv'd,
I cannot like, nor love, nor live with you,
Nor faſt, nor watch, nor pray for you.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Her old fit.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Sure this is not the way, nay, I will break
Your melancholly.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſhall break your pate then,
Away, you ſanguine ſcabbard.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Out upon thee
Thou'lt break my heart, I am ſure,

div.stage: Enter Alvarez, Piorato, Lucio, and Bobadilla.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: She's not yet tame.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: On Sir; put home: or I ſhall goad you here
With this old Fox of mine, that will bite better:
Oh, the brave age is gone; in my young daies
A Chevalier would ſtock a needleſs point
Three times together: ſtrait i' th' hams?
Or ſhall I give ye new Garters?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Faith old Maſter.
There's little hope: the linnen ſure was danck
He was begot in, he's ſo faint, and cold:
Ev'n ſend him to Toledo, there to ſtudy,
For he will never fadge with theſe Toledos;
Bear ye up your point there; pick his teeth: Oh baſe.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Fie: you are the moſt untoward Scholar: bear
Your body gracefully: what a poſture's there?
You lie too open-breaſted.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You'ld never
Make a good Stateſ-man:

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray no more.
I hope to breathe in peace, and therefore need not
The practiſe of theſe dangerous qualities,
I do not mean to live by't; for I truſt
You'll leave me better able.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Not a Button:
Let's goe get us a new heir.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: I by my troth: your Daughter's as untoward.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: I will break thee bone by bone, and bake thee,
E'r I'll ha' ſuch a wooden Son to inherit:
Take him a good knock; ſee how that will work.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Now, for your life Signior:

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh: alas, I am kill'd
My eye is out: look Father Zancho:
• 'll play the fool no more thus, that I will not.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Heart: ne'r a rogue in Spain ſhall wrong my brother
Whilſt I can hold a ſword.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Hold Madam, Madam.

l.hi: Clara.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Daughter.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Miſtreſs:

sp.speaker: Pio.

l.hi: Bradamante.

sp.l: Hold, hold I pray,

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: The devil's in her, o'the other ſide ſure,
There's Gold for you: they have chang'd what ye calt's:
Will no cure help? well I have one experiment,
And if that fail, I'll hang him, then here's an end on't.
Come you along with me: and you Sir: Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Now are you going to drowning. Alv. Eug. Luc. Bob. Exit
For me, and would prove more then my match.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You'r he ſpoke of Vitelli to the Stewerd:

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Yes, and I thank you, you have beat me for't.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But are you ſure you do not wrong him?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Sure?
So ſure, that if you pleaſe venture your ſelf
I'll ſhew you him, and his Cokatrice together,
And you ſhall hear 'em talk.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Will you? by—Sir
You ſhall endear me ever: and I ask
You mercy

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You were ſomewhat boyſtrous.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: There's Gold to make you amends: and for this pains,
I'll gratifie you farther: I'll but maſque me
And walk along with ye: faith let's make a night on't. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Alguazier, Pachieco, Mendoza, Metaldi, Lazarillo.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l:
Come on my brave water-Spaniels, you that hunt Ducks in the night: and hide more knavery under your gownes than your betters: obſerve my precepts, and edi
• ie by my doctrine: at yond corner will I ſet you; if drun
• ards moleſt the ſtreet, and fall to brabling, knock you • own the malefactors, and take you up their cloaks and • ats, and bring them to me: they are lawful priſoners, • nd muſt be ranſom'd ere they receive liberty: what elſe: • ou are to execute upon occaſion, you ſufficiently know, • nd therefore I abbreviate my Lecture.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: We are wiſe enough, and warm enough.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Vice this night ſhall be apprehended.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: The terror of rug-gownes ſhall be known: and our bilſs
Diſcharge us of after recknings.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: I will do any thing, ſo I may eat.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Lazarillo, We will ſpend no more; now we are grown worſe, we will live better: let us follow our calling • aithfully.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Away, then the common-wealth is our Miſtreſs: and who
Would ſerve a common Miſtreſs, but to gain by her?

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Vitelli, Lamorall, Genevora, Anaſtro, and two Pages with lights.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I pray you ſee the Maſque, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ana.
sp.l: 'Tis early night yet.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: O if it be ſo late, take me along:
I would not give advantage to ill tongues
To tax my being here, without your preſence
To be my warrant.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: You might ſpare this, Siſter,
Knowing with whom I leave you; one that is
By your allowance, and his choice, your Servant,
And may my councel and perſwaſion work it,
Your husband ſpeedily: For your entertainment
My thanks; I will not rob you of the means
To do your Miſtriſs ſome acceptable ſervice
In waiting on her to my houſe.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: My Lord,

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: As you reſpect me, without farther trouble
Retire, and taſt thoſe pleaſures prepar'd for you,
And leave me to my own ways.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: When you pleaſe Sir. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: You'll leave my Chamber?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Let us but bill once,
My Dove, my Sparrow, and I, with my office
Will be thy ſlaves for ever.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Are you ſo hot?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: But taſt the difference of a man in place,
You'l find that when authority pricks him forward,
Your Don, nor yet your Diego comes not near him
To do a Lady right: no men pay dearer
For their ſtoln ſweets, than we: three minutes trading
Affords to any ſinner a protection
For three years after: think on that, I burn;
But one drop of your bounty.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Hence you Rogue,
Am I fit for you? is't not grace ſufficient
To have your ſtaff, a bolt to bar the door
Where a Don enters, but that you'l preſume
To be his taſter?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Is no more reſpect
Due to his rod of juſtice?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Do you diſpute?
Good Doctor of the Dungeon, not a word more,
—If you do, my Lord Vitelli knows it.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Why I am big enough to anſwer him,
Or any man.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: 'Tis well. Vitelli within.

l.hi: Malroda.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: You know the voice, and now crowch like a Cur,
Tane worrying ſheep: I now could have you guelded
For a Bawd rampant: but on this ſubmiſſion
For once I ſpare you

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I will be reveng'd—
My honorable Lord.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: There's for thy care

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I am mad, ſtark mad: proud Pagan ſcorn her hoſt?
I would I were but valiant enough to kick her,
I'll wiſh no manhood elſe.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I am gone. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: You ſee I have kept my word.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But in this object
Hardly deſerv'd my thanks.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Is there ought elſe
You will command me?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Only your ſword
Which I muſt have: nay willingly I yet know
To force it, and to uſe it.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: 'Tis yours Lady.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ask no other guard.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: If ſo I leave you:
And now, if that the Conſtable keep his word,
A poorer man may chance to gull a Lord.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: By this good—you ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: By this—
I muſt, and will, Malroda; What do you make
A ſtranger of me?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I'll be ſo to you,
And you ſhall find it.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Theſe are your old arts
T'endear the game you know I come to hunt for,
Which I have born too coldly.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Do ſo ſtill,
For if I heat you, hang me.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: If you do not
I know who'll ſtarve for't: why, thou ſhame of women,
Whoſe folly, or whoſe impudence is greater
Is doubtful to determine; this to me
That know thee for a whore.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: And made me one,
Remember that.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Why ſhould I but grow wiſe
And tye that bounty up, which nor diſcretion
Nor honor can give way to; thou wouldſt be
A Bawd e're twenty, and within a Month
A barefoot, lowzie, and diſeaſed whore,
And ſhift thy lodgings oftner than a rogue
That's whipt from poſt to poſt.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Piſh: all our Colledge
Know you can rail well in this kind.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: For me
He never ſpake ſo well.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I have maintain'd thee
The envy of great fortunes, made thee ſhine
As if thy name were glorious: ſtuck thee full
Of jewels, as the firmament of Stars,
And in it made thee ſo remarkable
That it grew queſtionable, whether virtue poor,
Or vice ſo ſe forth as it is in thee,
Were even by modeſties ſelf to be preferr'd,
And am I thus repaid?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: You are ſtill my debtor;
Can this (though true) be weigh'd with my loſt honor,
Much leſs my faith? I have liv'd private to you,
And but for you, had ne'r known what luſt was,
Nor what the ſorrow for't.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Tis falſe.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: 'Tis true,
But how return'd by you, thy whole life being
But one continued act of luſt, and Shipwrack
Of womens chaſtities.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: But that I know
That ſhe that dares be damn'd, dares any thing,
I ſhould admire thy tempting me: but preſume not
On the power you htink you hold o'e my affections,
It will deceive you: yield, and preſently
Or by the inflamed blood, which thou muſt quench
I'll make a forcible entry.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Touch me not:
You know I have a throat,—if you do
I will cry out a rape, or ſheath this here,
Ere I'll be kept, and us'd for Julip-water
T'allay the heat which luſhious meats and wine
And not deſire hath rais'd.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: A deſperate devil,
My blood commands my reaſon; I muſt take
Some milder way.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I hope (dear Don) I fit you.
The night is mine, although the day was yours
You are not faſting now: this ſpeeding trick
Which I would as a principle leave to all,
That make their maintenance out of their own Indies,
As I do now; my good old mother taught me,
Daughter, quoth ſhe, conteſt not with your lover
His ſtomach being empty; let wine heat him,
And then you may command him: 'tis a ſure one:
His looks ſhew he is coming.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Come this needs not,
Eſpecially to me: you know how dear
I ever have eſteemed you.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Loſt again.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: That any fight of yours, hath power to change
My ſtrongeſt reſolution, and one tear
Sufficient to command a pardon from me,
For any wrong from you, which all mankind
Should kneel in vain for.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Pray you pardon thoſe
That need your favor, or deſire it.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Prethee.
Be better temper'd: I'll pay as a forfeit
For my raſh anger, this purſe fil'd with Gold.
Thou ſhalt have ſervants, gowns, attires, what not?
Only continue mine.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: 'Twas this I fiſh'd for

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Look on me, and receive it.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Well, you know
My gentle nature, and take pride t'abuſe it:
You ſee a trifle pleaſes me, we are friends;
This kiſs, and this confirms it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: With my ruine.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: I'll have this diamond, and this pearl.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: They are yours.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: But will you not, when you have what you came for,
Take them from me to morrow? 'tis a faſhion
Your Lords of late have us'd.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: But I'll not follow.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: That any man at ſuch a rate as this
Should pay for his repentance.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Shall we to bed now?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Inſtantly, Sweet; yet now I think on't better
There's ſomething firſt that in a word or two
I, muſt acquaint you with.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Can I cry ay me,
To this againſt my ſelf? I'll break this match,
Or make it ſtronger with my blood. Deſcends.

div.stage: Enter Alguazier, Piorato, Pacchieco, Metaldi, Mendoza, Lazarillo, &c.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I am yours.
A Don's not priviledg'd here more than your ſelf,
Win her, and wear her.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Have you a Prieſt ready.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I have him for thee, Lad; and when I have
Married this ſcornful whore to this poor gallant,
She will make ſuit to me; there is a trick
To bring a high-pris'd wench upon her knees:
For you my fine neat Harpyes ſtretch your tallons
And prove your ſelves true night-Birds.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Take my word
For me and all the reſt.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: If there be meat
Or any banquet ſtirring, you ſhall ſee
How I'll beſtow my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: When they are drawn,
Ruſh in upon 'em: all's fair prize you light on:
I muſt away: your officer may give way
To the Knavery of his watch, but muſt not ſee it.
You all know here to find me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: There look for us.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: My Piorato, welcome, welcome:
Faith had you not come when you did my Lord
Had done I know not what to me.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I am gul'd,
Firſt cheated of my Jewels, and then laug'd at:
Sirha, what makes you here?

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: A buſineſs brings me,
More lawful than your own,

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: How's that, you ſlave?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: He's ſuch, that would continue her a whore
Whom he would make a wife of.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I'll tread upon
The face you doat on, ſtrumpet.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Keep the peace there.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: A plot upon my life too?

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: Down with him.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Show your old valor, and learn from a woman;
One Eagle has a world of odds againſt
A flight of Dawes, as theſe are.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Get you off,
I'll follow inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Run for more help there. Exeunt all but Vit. and Clara.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Loſs of my gold, and jewels, and the wench too
Afflicts me not ſo much, as th'having Clara
The witneſs of my weakneſs.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: He turns from me,
And yet I may urge merit, ſince his life
Is made my ſecond gift.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: May I ne'r proſper
If I know how to thank her.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Sir, your pardon
For preſſing thus beyond a Virgins bounds
Upon your privacies: and let my being
Like to a man, as you are, be th' excuſe
Of my ſolliciting that from you, which ſhall not
Be granted on my part, although deſir'd
By any other: Sir, you underſtand me,
and 'twould ſhew nobly in you, to prevent
From me a farther boldneſs, which I muſt
Proceed in, if you prove not merciful,
Though with my loſs of bluſhes and good name.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Madam, I know your will, and would be thankful
Ifit were poſſible I could affect
The daughter of an enemy.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: That fair falſe one
Whom with fond dotage you have long purſu'd
Had ſuch a father: ſhe to whom you pay
Dearer for your diſhonor, than all titles
Ambitious men hunt for, are worth.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Tis truth.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Yet, with her, as a friend you ſtill exchange
Health for diſeaſes, and, to your diſgrace,
Nouriſh the rivals to your preſent pleaſures,
At your own charge, us'd as a property
To give a ſafe protection to her luſt,
Yet ſhare in nothing but the ſhame of it.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Grant all this ſo, to take you for a wife
Were greater hazard; for ſhould I offend you
(As 'tis not eaſy ſtill to pleaſe a woman)
You are of ſo great a ſpirit, that I muſt learn
To wear your petticoat, for you will have
My breeches from me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Rather from this hour
I here abjure all actions of a man,
And will eſteem it happineſs from you
To ſuffer like a woman: love, true love
Hath made a ſearch within me, and expell'd
All but my natural ſoftneſs, and made perfect
That which my parents care could not begin.
I will ſhow ſtrength in nothing, but my duty,
And glad deſire to pleaſe you, and in that
Grow every day more able.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Could this be,
What a brave race might I beget? I find
A kind of yielding; and no reaſon why
• ſhould hold longer out: ſhe's young, and fair,
And chaſt; for ſure, but with her leave, the Devil
Durſt not attempt her: Madam, though you have
A Soldiers arm, your lips appear as if
They were a Ladies,

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: They dare Sir, from you
Endure the tryal.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Ha: once more I pray you:
The beſt I ever taſted; and 'tis ſaid
I have prov'd many, 'tis not ſafe I fear
To ask the reſt now: well, I will leave whoring
And luck herein ſend me with her: worthieſt Lady,
I'll wait upon you home, and by the way
(If ere I marry, as I'll not forſwear it)
Tell you, you are my wife.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Which if you do,
From me all man-kind women, learn to woe. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Alguazier, Pachieco, Metaldi, Mendoza, Lazarillo.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: A cloak? good purchaſe, and rich hangers? well,
We'll ſhare ten Piſtolets a man.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Yet ſtill
I am monſtrous hungry: could you not deduct
So much out of the groſs ſum, as would purchaſe
Eight loynes of Veal, and ſome two dozen of Capons?

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: O ſtrange proportion for five.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: For five? I have
A legion in my ſtomach that have kept
Perpetual faſt theſe ten years: for the Capons,
They are to me but as ſo many black Birds:
May I but eat once, and be ſatisfied,
