Let the fates call me, when my ſhip is fraught,
And I ſhall hang in peace.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Steal well to night,
And thou ſhalt feed to morrow; ſo now you are
Your ſelves again, I'll raiſe another watch
To free you from ſuſpition: ſet on any
You meet with boldly: I'll not be far off,
T'aſſiſt you, and protect you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: O brave officer.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Would every ward had one but ſo well given,
And we would watch, for rug, in gowns of velvet.

sp.speaker: Mend.
sp.l: Stand cloſe, a prize.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: Satten, and gold Lace, Lads.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Why do'ſt thou hang upon me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo dark
I dare not ſee my way: for heaven ſake father
Let us go home.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: No, ev'n here we'll leave you:
Let's run away from him, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh 'las.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Thou haſt made me mad: and I will beat thee dead,
Then bray thee in a morter, and new mold thee,
But I will alter thee.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: 'Twil never be:
He has been three days practiſing to drink,
Yet ſtill he ſips like to a waiting woman,
And looks as he were murdering of a fart
Among wild Iriſh ſwaggerers.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I have ſtill
Your good word, Zancho, father.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Milk-ſop, coward;
No houſe of mine receives thee: I diſclaim thee,
Thy mother on her knees ſhall not entreat me
Hereafter to acknowledge thee.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray you ſpeak for me.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: I would; but now I cannot with mine honor.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: There's only one courſe left, that may redeem thee,
Which is, to ſtrike the next man that you meet,
And if we chance to light upon a woman,
Take her away, and uſe her like a man,
Or I will cut thy hamſtrings.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: This makes for us.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: What do'ſt thou do now?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sir, I am ſaying my prayers;
For being to undertake what you would have me,
I know I cannot live.

div.stage: Enter Lamorall, Genevora, Anaſtro, and Pages with Lights.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Madam, I fear
You'll wiſh you had us'd your coach: your brothers houſe
Is yet far off.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: The better ſir: this walk
Will help digeſtion after your great ſupper,
Of which I have fed largely.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: To your task,
Or elſe you know what follows:

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I am dying:
Now Lord have mercy on me: by your favor,
Sir I muſt ſtrike you.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: For what cauſe?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I know not:
And I muſt likewiſe talk with that young Lady,
An hour in private.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: What you muſt, is doubtful,
But I am certain Sir, I muſt beat you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Help, help.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Not ſtrike again?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How, Alvarez?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: This for my Lord Vitellis love.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Break out,
And like true theeves, make prey on either ſide,
But ſeem, to help the ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Oh my Lord,
They have beat him on his knees.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Though I want courage:
I yet have a ſons duty in me, and
Compaſſion of a fathers danger; that,
That wholly now poſſeſſes me.

sp.speaker: Alv.

l.hi: Lucio.

sp.l: This is beyond my hope.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: So Lazarillo,
Take up all boy: well done.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: And now ſteal off
Cloſely and cunningly.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: How? have I found you?
Why Gentlemen, are you mad, to make your ſelves
A prey to Rogues?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Would we were off.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Theeves, theeves.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Defer our own contention: and down with them.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I'll make you ſure.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Now he plays the Devil.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: This place is not for me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I'll follow her
Half of my pennance is paſt oe'r. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Alguazier, Aſſiſtant, and other Watches.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: What noyſe?
What tumult's there? keep the Kings peace I charge you.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: I am glad he's come yet.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: O, you keep good Guard
Upon the City, when men of our ranck
Are ſet upon in the ſtreets.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: The aſſiſtants
Shall hear on't be aſſur'd.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: And if he be
That careful Governor he is reported,
You will ſmart for it.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Patience, good Signiors:
Let me ſurvey the Raſcals: O, I know them,
And thank you for them: they are pilf'ring rogues
Of Andaluza that have perus'd
All Priſons in Caſtile: I dare not truſt
The dungeon with them: no, I'll have them home
To my own houſe.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: We had rather go to priſon.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Had you ſo dog-bolts? yes, I know you had:
You there would uſe your cunning fingers on
The ſimple locks; you would: but I'll prevent you.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: My Miſtriſs loſt, good night. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Your Son's gone too,
What ſhould become of him?

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Come of him, what will:
Now he dares fight, I care not: I'll to bed,

Look to your priſoners Alguazier.
Exit with Bob • .

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: All's clear'd:
Droop not for one diſaſter: let us hug,
And triumph in our knaveries.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: This confirms
What was reported of him.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: 'Twas done bravely.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I muſt a little glory in the means
We Officers have, to play the Knaves, and ſafely:
How we break through the toyles, pitch'd by the Law,
Yet hang up them that are far leſs delinquents:
A ſimple ſhopkeeper's carted for a bawd
For lodging (though unwittingly) a ſmock-Gamſter:
Where, with rewards, and credit I have kept
Malroda in my houſe, as in a cloyſter,
Without taint, or ſuſpition.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: But ſuppoſe
The Governor ſhould know't?

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: He? good Gentleman,
Let him perplex himſelf with prying into
The meaſures in the market, and th'abuſes
The day ſtands guilty of: the pillage of the night
Is only mine, mine own fee ſimple;
Which you ſhall hold from me, tenants at will,
And pay no rent for't.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Admirable Landlord.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: Now we'll go ſearch the Taverns, commit ſuch
As we find drinking: and be drunk our ſelves
With what we take from them: theſe ſilly wretches
Whom I for form ſake only have brought hither
Shall watch without, and guard us.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: And we will
See you ſafe lodg'd, moſt worthy Alguazier,
With all of you his comrads.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: 'Tis the Governor.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: We are betray'd?

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: My guard there; bind them faſt:
How men in high place and authority
Are in their lives and eſtimations wrong'd
By their ſubordinate Miniſters? yet ſuch
They cannot but imploy: wrong'd juſtice finding
Scarce one true ſervant in ten officers.
'T'expoſtulate with you, were but to delay
Your crimes due puniſhment, which ſhall fall upon you
So ſpeedily, and ſeverely, that it ſhall
Fright others by th'example: and confirm
How ever corrupt Officers may diſgrace
Themſelves, 'tis not in them to wrong their place.
Bring them away.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: We'll ſuffer nobly yet,
And like to Spaniſh Gallants.

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: And we'll hang ſo.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: I have no ſtomach to it: but I'll endeavor.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Nay you are rude; pray you forber, you offer now
More than the breeding of a Gentleman
Can give you warrant for.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Tis but to kiſs you,
And think not I'll receive that for a favour
Which was enjoyn'd me for a pennance, Lady.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: You have met a gentle confeſſor, and for once
So then you will reſt ſatisfied) I vouchſafe it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Reſt ſatisfied with a kiſs? why can a man
Deſire more from a woman? is there any
Pleaſure beyond it? may I never live
• f I know what it is.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Sweet Innocence.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What ſtrange new motions do I feel? my veins
Burn with an unknown fire: in every part
• ſuffer alteration: I am poyſon'd,
Yet languiſh with deſire again to taſt it,
• o ſweetly it works on me.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I ne'r ſaw
A lovely man, till now.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: How can this be?
• he is a woman, as my mother is,
And her I have kiſs'd often, and brought off
My lips unſcortch'd; yours are more lovely, Lady,
And ſo ſhould be leſs hurtful: pray you vouchſafe
Your hand to quench the heat tane from your Lip,
Perhaps that may reſtore me.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Willingly.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: The flame increaſes: if to touch you, burn thus,
What would more ſtrict embraces do? I know not,
And yet methinks to die ſo, were to aſcend
To heaven, through Paradiſe.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I am wounded too,
Though modeſty forbids that I ſhould ſpeak
What ignorance makes him bold in: why do you fix
Your eyes ſo ſtrongly on me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Pray you ſtand ſtill,
There is nothing elſe, that is worth the looking on:
• could adore you, Lady.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Can you love me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: To wait on you, in your chamber, and but touch
What you, by wearing it, have made divine,
Were ſuch a happineſs. I am reſolved,
• 'll ſell my liberty to you for this glove,
And write my ſelf your ſlave.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: On eaſier terms,
Receive it as a friend.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How! giving favor!
I'll have it with his heart.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: What will you do?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: As you are merciful, take my life rather.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Will you depart with't ſo?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Do's that grieve you?

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I know not: but even now you appear valiant.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Twas to preſerve my father: in his cauſe
I could be ſo again.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Not in your own? Kneel to thy Rival and thine enemy?
Away unworthy creature, I begin
To hate my ſelf, for giving entrance to
A good opinion of thee: for thy torment,
• f my poor beauty be of any power,
Mayſt thou doat on it deſperately: but never
Preſume to hope for grace, till thou recover
And wear the favor that was raviſh'd from thee.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: He wears my head too then.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Poor fool, farewell. Exit.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My womaniſh ſoul, which hitherto hath govern'd
This coward fleſh, I feel departing from me;
And in me by her beauty is inſpir'd
A new, and maſculine one: inſtructing me
What's fit to do or ſuffer; powerful love
That haſt with loud, and yet a pleaſing thunder
Rous'd ſleeping manhood in me, thy new creature,
Perfect thy work ſo that I may make known
Nature (though long kept back) will have her own.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Can it be poſſible, that in ſix ſhort hours
The ſubject ſtill the ſame, ſo many habits
Should be remov'd? or this new Lucio, he
That yeſternight was baffeld and diſgrac'd,
And thank'd the man that did it, that then kneeld
And blubber'd like a woman, ſhould now dare
On terms of honor ſeek reparation
For what he then appeard' not capable of?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Such miracles, men that dare do injuries
Live to their ſhames to ſee, and for puniſhment
And ſcourge to their proud follies.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Prethee leave me:
Had I my Page, or foot-man here to fleſh thee,
I durſt the better hear thee.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: This ſcorn needs not:
And offer ſuch no more.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Why ſay I ſhould,
You'll not be angry?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Indeed I think I ſhall,
Would you vouchſafe to ſhew your ſe;lf a Captain,
And lead a little farther, to ſome place
That's leſs frequented.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: He looks pale.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: If not,
Make uſe of this.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: There's anger in his eyes too:
His geſture, voyce, behaviour, all new faſhion'd;
Well, if it does endure in act the triall
Of what in ſhow it promiſes to make good,
Ʋlyſſes Cyclops, Io's transformation,
Eurydice fetch from Hell, with all the reſt
Of Ovids Fables, I'll put in your Creed;
And for proof, all incredible things may be,
Write down that Lucio, the coward Lucio,
The womaniſh Lucio fought.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: And Lamorall,
The ſtill imploy'd great duelliſt Lamorall,
Took his life from him.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Twill not come to that ſure:
Methinks the only drawing of my Sword
Should fright that confidence.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: It confirms it rather.
To make which good, know you ſtand now oppos'd
By one that is your Rival, one that wiſhes
Your name and title greater, to raiſe his;
The wrong you did, leſs pardonable than it is,
But your ſtrength to defend it, more than ever
It was when juſtice friended it. The Lady
For whom we now contend, Genevora
Of more deſert, (if ſuch incomparable beauty
Could ſuffer an addition) your love
To Don Vitelli multipli'd, and your hate
Againſt my father and his houſe increas'd;
And laſtly, that the Glove which you there wear,
To my diſhonour, (which I muſt force from you)
Were dearer to you than your life.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: You'l find
It is, and ſo I'll guard it:

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: All theſe muſt meet then
With the black infamy, to be foyl'd by one
That's not allowd a man: to help your valor,
That falling by your hand, I may, or dye,
Or win in this one ſingle oppoſition
My Miſtriſs, and ſuch honor as I may
Inrich my fathers Arms with.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Tis ſaid Nobly;
My life with them are at the ſtake.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: At all then. Fight.

sp.speaker: Lam,
sp.l: She's yours, this and my life too follow your fortune,
And give not only back that part, the looſer
Scorns to accept of —

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: My poor life,
Which do not leave me as a farther torment,
Having diſpoil'd me of my Sword, mine honor,
Hope of my Ladies grace, fame, and all elſe
That made it worth the keeping.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I take back
No more from you, than what you forc'd from me;
And with a worſer title: yet think not
That I'll diſpute this, as made inſolent
By my ſucceſs, but as one equal with you,
If ſo you will accept me; that new courage,
Or call it fortune if you pleaſe, that is
Conferr'd upon me by the only ſight
Of fair Genevora, was not beſtow'd on me
To bloody purpoſes: nor did her command
Deprive me of the happineſs to ſee her
But till I did redeem her favor from you;
Which only I rejoyce in, and ſhare with you
In all you ſuffer elſe.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: This curteſie
Wounds deeper than your Sword can, or mine own;
Pray you make uſe of either, and diſpatch me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: The barbarous Turk is ſatisfied with ſpoil;
And ſhall I, being poſſeſt of what I came for,
Prove the more Infidel?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: You were better be ſo,
Than publiſh my diſgrace, as 'tis rhe cuſtom,
And which I muſt expect.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Judge better on me:
I have no tongue to trumpet mine own praiſe
To your diſhonor: 'tis a baſtard courage
That ſeeks a name out that way, no true born one;
Pray you be comforted, for by all goodneſs
But to her virtuous ſelf, the beſt part of it,
I never will diſcover on what terms
I came by theſe: which yet I take not from you,
But leave you in exchange of them, mine own,
With the deſire of being a friend; which if
You will not grant me, but on farther trial
Of manhood in me, ſeek me when you pleaſe,
(And though I might refuſe it with mine honor)
Win them again, and wear them: ſo good morrow. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I ne'r knew what true valor was till now;
And have gain'd more by this diſgrace, than all
The honors I have won: they made me proud,
Preſumptuous of my fortune; a mere beaſt,
Faſhiond by them, only to dare and do:
Yielding no reaſons for my wilful actions
But what I ſtuck on my Swords point, preſuming
It was the beſt Revenew. How unequal
Wrongs well maintain'd makes us to others, which
Ending with ſhame teach us to know our ſelves,
I will think more on't.

l.hi: Lamorall.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: My Lord?

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I came to ſeek you.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: And unwillingly;
You ne'r found me tell now: your pleaſure Sir?

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: That which will pleaſe thee friend: thy vowd love to me
Shall now be put in action: means is offer'd
To uſe thy good Sword for me; that which ſtill
Thou wearſt, as if it were a part of thee.
Where is it?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Tis chang'd for one more fortunate:
Pray you enquire not how.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Why, I ne'r thought
That there was muſick in't, but aſcribe
The fortune of it to the arm.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Which is grown weaker too. I am not (in a word)
Worthy your friendſhip: I am one new vanquiſh'd,
Yet ſhame to tell by whom.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: But I'll tell thee
'Gainſt whom thou art to fight, and there redeem
Thy honor loſt, if there be any ſuch:
The King, by my long ſuit, at length is pleas'd
That Alvarez and my ſelf, with eithers Second,
Shall end the difference between our houſes,
Which he accepts of, I make choice of thee;
And where you ſpeak of a diſgrace, the means
To blot it out, by ſuch a publick trial
Of thy approved valor, will revive
Thy antient courage. If you imbrace it do;
If not, I'll ſeek ſome other.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: As I am
You may command me.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Spoke like that true friend
That loves not only for his private end. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Genevora, with a Letter and Bobadilla.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: This from Madona Clara?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: Yes, an't pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Alvarez daughter?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: The ſame, Lady.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: She,
That ſav'd my brothers life?

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: You are ſtill in the right,
She wil'd me wait your walking forth: and knowing
How neceſſary a diſcreet wiſe man
Was in a buſineſs of ſuch weight, ſhe pleas'd
To think on me: it may be in my face
Your Ladyſhip, not acquainted with my wiſdom,
Finds no ſuch matter: what I am, I am;
Thought's free, and think you what you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange,

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.l: That I ſhould be wiſe, Madam?

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: No, thou art ſo;
There's for thy pains: and prethee tell thy Lady
I will not fail to meet her: I'll receive
Thy thanks and duty in thy preſent abſence:
Farewell, farewell, I ſay, now thou art wiſe. Exit Bob.
She writes here, ſhe hath ſomething to impart
That may concern my brothers life, I know not,
But general fame does give her out ſo worthy,
That I dare not ſuſpect her: yet wiſh Lucio,
Were Maſter of her mind: but fie upon't;
Why do I think on him? ſee, I am puniſh'd for it,
In his unlook'd for preſence: Now I muſt
Endure another tedious piece of Courtſhip,
Would make one forſwear curteſie.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Gracious Madam,
The ſorrow paid for your juſt anger towards me
• riſing from my weakneſs, I preſume
To preſs into your preſence, and deſpair not
An eaſie pardon.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: He ſpeaks ſence: oh ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: And yet believe, that no deſire of mine,
Though all are too ſtrong in me, had the power
For their delight, to force me to infringe
What you commanded, it being in your part
To leſſen your great rigor when you pleaſe,
And mine to ſuffer with an humble patience
What you'l impoſe upon it.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Courtly too.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Yet hath the poor, and contemn'd Lucio, Madam,
Made able only by his hope to ſerve you)
Recover'd what with violence, not juſtice,
Was taken from him: and here at your feet
With theſe, he could have laid the conquer'd head
Of Lamorall ('tis all I ſay of him)
For rudely touching that, which as a relique
〈◊〉 ever would have worſhip'd, ſince 'twas yours.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Valiant, and every thing a Lady could
Wiſh in her ſervant.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: All that's good in me,
That havenly love, the oppoſite to baſe luſt,
Which would have all men worthy, hath created;
Which being by your beams of beauty form'd,
Cheriſh as your own creature.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I am gone
Too far now to diſſemble: riſe, or ſure
〈◊〉 muſt kneel with you too: let this one kiſs
Speak the reſt for me: 'tis too much I do,
And yet, if chaſtity would, I could wiſh more.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: In overjoying me, you are grown ſad;
What is it Madam? by—
There's nothing that's within my nerves (and yet
Favour'd by you, I ſhould as much as man)
But when you pleaſe, now or on all occaſions
You can think of hereafter, but you may
Diſpoſe of at your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: If you break.
That oath again, you looſe me. Yet ſo well
〈◊〉 love you, I ſhall never put you to't;
And yet forget it not: reſt ſatisfied
With that you have receiv'd now: there are eyes
May be upon us, till the difference
Between our friends are ended: I would not
Be ſeen ſo private with you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I obey you.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: But let me hear oft from you, and remember
I am Vitellies Siſter.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: What's that Madam?

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Nay nothing, fare you well: who feels loves ſire,
Would ever ask to have means to deſire. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Aſſiſtente, Sayavedra, Anaſtro, Herald, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſ.
sp.l: Are they come in?

sp.speaker: Har.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſ.
sp.l: Read the Proclamation,
That all the people here aſſembled may
Have ſatisfaction, what the Kings dear love,
In care of the Republick, hath ordained;
Attend with ſilence: read aloud.

body.head: Herald Reads.
body.p: FOrasmuch as our high and mighty Maſter, Philip, the potent and moſt Catholick King of Spain, hath not only in his own Royal perſon, been long, and often ſollicited, and grieved, with the deadly and honorable hatred, ſprung up betwixt the two antient and moſt uncurable deſcended Houſes of theſe his two dearly and equally beloved Subjects, Don Ferdinando de Alvarez, and Don Pedro de Vit • lli: (all which in vain his Majeſty hath often endeavored to reconcile and qualifie:) But that alſo through the debates, quarrels, and outrages daily ariſing, falling, and flowing from theſe great heads, his publick civil Government is ſeditiouſly and barbarouſly moleſted and wounded, and many of his chief Gentry (no leſs tender to his Royal Majeſty then the very branches of his own ſacred blood) ſpoyled, loſt, and ſubmerged, in the impious inundation and torrent of their ſtill-growing malice: It hath therefore pleaſed His ſacred Majeſty, out of his infinite affection to preſerve his Common-wealth, and general peace, from farther violation, (as a ſweet and heartily loving father of his people) and on the earneſt petitions of theſe arch-enemies, to Order, and ordain, that they by ready, each with his well-choſen and beloved friend, armed at all points like Gentlemen, in the Caſtle of St. Jago, on this preſent Monday morning betwixt eight and nine of the clock, where (before the combattants be allowed to commence this granted Duel) This to be read aloud for the publick ſatisfaction of his Majeſties well beleved Subjects.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Hark their Drums ſpeak their inſatiate thirſt
Of blood, and ſtop their ears 'gainſt pious peace,
Who gently whiſpering, implores their friendſhip?

sp.speaker: Aſſiſ.
sp.l: Kings nor authority can maſter fate;
Admit 'em then, and blood extinguiſh hate.

div.stage: Enter ſeverally, Alvarez, and Lucio, Vitelli and Lamora.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Stay, yet be pleas'd to think, and let not daring
Wherein men now adaies exceed even beaſts,
And think themſelves not men elſe, ſo tranſport you
Beyond the bounds of Chriſtianity:
Lord Alvarez, Vitelli, Gentlemen,
No Town in Spain, from our Metropolis
Unto the rudeſt hovel, but is great
With your aſſured valors daily proofs:
Oh will you then, for a ſuperfluous fame,
A ſound of honor, which in theſe times, all
Like hereticks profeſs (with obſtinacy)
But moſt erroneouſly venture your ſouls,
'Tis a hard task, through a Sea of blood
To ſail, and land at Heaven?

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I hope not
If juſtice be my Pilot: but my Lord,
You know, if argument, or time, or love,
Could reconcile, long ſince we had ſhook hands;
I dare proteſt, your breath cools not a vein
In any one of us, but blows the fire
Which nought but blood reciprocal can quench.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Vitelli, thou ſayſt bravely, and ſayſt right,
And I will kill thee for't, I love thee ſo.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Ha, ha, old man; upon thy death I'll build
A ſtory (with this arm) for thy old wife
To tell thy daughter Clara ſeven years hence
As ſhe ſits weeping by a winters fire,
How ſuch a time Vitelli ſlew her husband
With the ſame Sword his daughter favor'd him,
And lives, and wears it yet: Come Lamorall,
Redeem thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Lam.

l.hi: Lucio, Genevora

sp.l: Shall on this Sword receive thy bleeding heart,
For my preſented hat, laid at her feet.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Thou talk'ſt well Lamorall, but 'tis thy head
That I will carry to her to thy hat:
Fie Father, I do cool too much.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Oh boy:
Thy fathers true Son:
Beat Drums,—and ſo good morrow to your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Brave reſolutions.

sp.speaker: Anaſt.
sp.l: Brave, and Spaniſh right.

l.hi: Lucio.
Vitelli.
Alvarez.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: How the devil
Got theſe Cats into th'gutter? my puſſe too?

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Hear us.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: We muſt be heard.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: We will be heard
Vitelli, look, ſee Clara on her knees
Imploring thy compaſſion: Heaven, how ſternly
They dart their emulous eyes, as if each ſcorn'd
To be behind the other in a look!
Mother, death needs no Sword here: oh my Siſter
(Fate fain would have it ſo) perſuade, entreat,
A Ladies tears are ſilent Orators
(Or ſhould be ſo at leaſt) to move beyond
The honeſt tongu'd-Rhetorician:
Why will you fight? why do's an uncles death
Twenty year old, exceed your love to me
But twenty days? whoſe forc'd cauſe, and fair manner
You could not underſtand, only have heard.
Cuſtom, that wrought ſo cunningly on nature
In me, that I forgot my ſex, and knew not
Whether my body female were, or male,
You did unweave, and had the power to charm
A new creation in me, made me fear
To think on thoſe deeds I did perpetrate,
How little power though you allow to me
That cannot with my ſighs, my tears, my prayers
Move you from your own loſs, if you ſhould gain.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: I muſt forget you Clara, 'till I have
Redeem'd my unkles blood, that brands my face
Like a peſtiferous Carbuncle: I am blind
To what you do: deaf to your cries: and Marble
To all impulſive exorations.
When in this point, I have perch'd thy fathers ſoul,
I'll tender thee this bloody reeking hand
Drawn forth the bowels of that murtherer:
If thou canſt love me then, I'll marry thee,
And for thy father loſt, get thee a Son;
On no condition elſe.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Moſt barbarous.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Savage.

sp.speaker: Anaſt.
sp.l: Irreligious.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Oh Lucio!
Be thou merciful: thou bear'ſt fewer year • ,
Art lately wean'd from ſoft effiminacy,
A maidens manners, and a maidens heart
Are neighbors ſtill to thee: be then more mild,
Proceed not to this combat; be'ſt thou deſperate
Of thine own life? yet (deareſt) pitty mine
Thy valour's not thine own, I gave it thee,
Theſe eyes begot it, this tongue bred it up,
This breaſt would lodge it: do not uſe my gifts
To mine own ruine: I have made thee rich,
Be not ſo thankleſs, to undo me for't

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Miſtriſs, you know I do not wear a vein.
I would not rip for you, to do you ſervice:
Life's but a word, a ſhadow, a melting dream,
Compar'd to eſſential, and eternal honor.
Why, would you have me value it beyond
Your brother: if I firſt caſt down my ſword
May all my body here, be made one wound,
And yet my ſoul not find heaven thorough it.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: You would be catter-walling too, but peace,
Go, get you home, and provide dinner for
Your Son, and me: wee'll be exceeding merry:
Oh Lucio, I will have thee cock of all
The proud Vitellies that do live in Spain:
Fie, we ſhall take cold: hunch:—I am hoarſe
Already.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How your Siſter whets my ſpleen!
I could eat Lucio now:

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Vitelli, Brother,
Ev'n for your Fathers ſoul, your uncles blood,
As you do love my life: but laſt, and moſt
As you reſpect your own Honor, and Fame,
Throw down your ſword; he is moſt valiant
That herein yields firſt.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Peace, you fool.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why Lucio,
Do thou begin; 'tis no diſparagement:
He's elder, and thy better, and thy valor
Is in his infancy.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Or pay it me,
To whom thou ow'ſt it: Oh, that conſtant time
Would but go back a week, then Lucio
Thou would'ſt not dare to fight.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Lucio, thy Mother,
Thy Mother begs it: throw thy ſword down firſt.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: I'll throw his head down after then.

sp.speaker: Gen.

l.hi: Lamorall.

sp.l: You have often ſwore you'ld be commanded by me.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Never to this: your ſpight, and ſcorn Genevora,
Has loſt all power in me:

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Your hearing for ſix words.

sp.speaker: Aſſ. Say. An.
sp.l: Strange obſtinacy!

sp.speaker: Al. Vit. Lu. Lam.
sp.l: We'll ſtay no longer.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Then by thy oath Vitelli,
Thy dreadful oath, thou wouldſt return that Sword
When I ſhould ask it, give it to me, now,
This inſtant I require it.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: By thy vow,
As dreadful Lucio, to obey my will
In any one thing I would watch to challenge,
I charge thee not to ſtrike a ſtroak: now he
Of our two brothers that loves perjury
Beſt, and dares firſt be damn'd, infringe his vow.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: Excellent Ladies.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Piſh, you tyrannize.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: We did equivocate.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: On.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Then Lucio,
So well I love my husband, for he is ſo,
(Wanting but ceremony) that I pray
His vengeful ſword may fall upon thy head
Succesfully for falſe-hood to his Siſter.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: I likewiſe pray (Vitelli) Lucio's ſword
(Who equally is my husband as thou hers)
May find thy falſe heart, that durſt gage thy faith,
And durſt not keep it.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Are you men, or ſtone.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Men, and we'll prove it with our ſwords:

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Your hearing for ſix words, and we have done,
Zancho come forth—we'll fight our challenge too:
Now ſpeak your reſolutions. Enter Bobidilla with two ſwords and a Piſtol.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Theſe they are,
The firſt blow given betwixt you, ſheathes theſe ſwords
In one anothers boſomes.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: And rogue, look
You at that inſtant do diſcharge that Piſtol
Into my breaſt: if you ſtart back, or quake,
I'll ſtick you like a Pig.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: —Hold? you are mad.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: This we ſaid: and by our hope of bliſs
This we will do: ſpeak your intent.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Gen. Strike.

sp.speaker: Eug.
sp.l: Shoot.

sp.speaker: All. Vit. Lat. La.
sp.l: Hold, hold: all friends.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Come down.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Theſe deviliſh women
Can make men friends and enemies when they liſt.

sp.speaker: Say.
sp.l: A gallant undertaking and a happy;
Why this is noble in you: and will be
A welcomer preſent to our Maſter Philip
Than the return from his Indies.

div.stage: Enter Clara, Genevora, Eugenia, and Bobadilla.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Father, your bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Take her: if ye bring not
Betwixt you, boys that will find out new worlds,
And win 'em too, I'm a falſe Prophet.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Brother.
There is a Siſter, long divided ſtreams
Mix now at length, by fate.

sp.speaker: Bob.
sp.p:
I am not regarded: I was the careful Steward that provided theſe Inſtruments of peace, I put the longeſt weapon in your Siſters hand, (my Lord) becauſe ſhe was the ſhorteſt Lady: For likely the ſhorteſt Ladies love the longeſt—men: And for mine own part, I could have diſcharged •• t: my Piſtol is no ordinary Piſtol, it has two ramming bullets; but thought I, why ſhould I ſhoot my two bullets into my old Lady? if they had gone, I would not have ſtaid • ong after: I would ev'n have died too, bravely y' • aith, like •
Roman Steward: hung my ſelf in mine own chain, and there had been a ſtory of Bobadilla, Spindola, Zancho, for after ages to lament: hum: I perceive, I am not only not regarded, but alſo not rewarded.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Prethee peace: 'ſhalt have a new chain, next Saint Jaques day, or this new gilt:

sp.p: I am ſatisfied: let virtue have her due: And yet I am melancholy upon this atonement: pray heaven the State •• ue it not: I would my Lord Vitellie's Steward, and I could meet: they ſhould find it ſhould coſt 'em a little more to make us friends: well, I will forſwear wine, and women for a year: and then I will be drunk to morrow, and run a whoring like a dog with a broken bottle at's tail; then will I repent next day, and forſwear 'em again more vehemently: be forſworn next day again, and repent my repentance: for thus a melancholy Gentleman doth, and ought to live.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Nay, you ſtall dine with me: and afterward
I'll with ye to the King: But firſt, I will
Diſpatch the Caſtles buſineſs, that this day
May be compleat. Bring forth the malefactors.
sp.stage: Enter Alguazier, Pachieco, Metaldi, Mendoza, Lazaril, Piorato, Malroda, and Guard.
sp.l: You Alguazier, the Ringleader of theſe
Poor fellows, are degraded from your office,
You muſt return all ſtolen goods you receiv'd,
And watch a twelve month without any pay:
This, if you fail of, (all your goods confiſcate)
You are to be whipt, and ſent into the Gallies.

sp.speaker: Alg.
sp.l: I like all, but reſtoring that Catholique Doctrine.
I do diſlike: Learn all ye officers
By this to live uprightly (if you can.) Exit.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: You Cobler, to tanſlate your manners new,
Are doom'd to th' Cloiſters of the Mendicants,
With this your brother, botcher, there for nothing
To cobble, and heel hoſe for the poor Friers,
Till they allow you pennance for ſufficient,
And your amendment; then you ſhall be freed,
And may ſet up again,

sp.speaker: Pach.
sp.l: Mendoza, come,
Our ſouls have trode awry in all mens ſight,
We'll underlay 'em, till they go upright,

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Smith, in thoſe ſhackles you for your hard heart
Muſt lie by th' heels a year.

sp.speaker: Met.
sp.l: I have ſhod your horſe, my Lord. Exit.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Away: for you, my hungry white-loaf'd face,
You muſt to th' Gallies, where you ſhall be ſure
To have no more bits, than you ſhall have blows.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Well, though herrings want, I ſhall have rowes.

sp.speaker: Aſſiſt.
sp.l: Signior, you have prevented us, and puniſh'd
Your ſelfe ſeverelier than we would have done.
You have married a whore: may ſhe prove honeſt.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: 'Tis better, my Lord, than to marry an honeſt woman,
That may prove a whore,

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: 'Tis a hanſome wench: and thou canſt keep her tame
I'll ſend you what I promis'd.

sp.speaker: Pio.
sp.l: Joy to your Lordſhips.

sp.speaker: Alv.
sp.l: Hear may all Ladies learn, to make of foes
The perfect'ſt friends: and not the perfect'ſt foes
Of deareſt friends, as ſome do now a daies.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.l: Behold the power of love, to nature loſt
By cuſtome irrecoverably, paſt the hope
Of friends reſtoring, Love hath here retriv'd
To her own habit, made her bluſh to ſee
Her ſo long monſtrous Metamorphoſes,
May ſtrange affairs never have worſe ſucceſs. Exeunt.

div.head: EPILOGUE.
div.l: OƲr Author fears there are ſome Rebel hearts,
Whoſe dulneſs doth oppoſe loves piercing darts;
Such will be apt to ſay there wanted wit,
The language low, very few Scaenes are writ
With ſpirit and life; ſuch odd things as theſe
He cares not for, nor ever means to pleaſe;
For if your ſelves a Miſtriſs or loves friends,
Are lik'd with this ſmooth Play he hath his ends.

div.head: The Perſons Repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Duke of Siena, Suitor to Belvidere.
Silvio, A Gentleman of quality, ſervant to Belvidere.
Claudio, Silvio's friend, brother to Iſabella.
Bartello, Captain of the Citadel, Ʋncle to Silvio.
Lopez, A ſordid Ʋſurer, the jealous Husband of Iſabella
Penurio, A hungry ſervant to Lopez.
Soto, A merry ſervant to Claudio.
Bomby, An enemy to Watches and May-poles.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Belvidere, A virtuous Princeſs, daughter to the Dutcheſs in love with Silvio.
Iſabella, Wife to Lopez, and Siſter to Claudio.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: TIs true ſhe is a right good Princeſs, and a juſt one,
And Florence when ſhe ſets, has loſt a Planet.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: My Miſtriſs? I tell thee gentle Nephew,
There is not ſuch another friend to goodneſs,
To down-right dealing, to faith and true heart
Within the Chriſtian confines: Before ſhe bleſt us,
Juſtice was a Cheeſe-monger, a meer Cheeſe-monger,
Weigh'd nothing to the world but Mites and Maggots,
And a main ſtink: Law like a Horſe-courſer,
Her rules, and precepts hung with gawdes and ribbonds
And pamper'd up to couſen him that bought her,
When ſhe her ſelf was hackney, lame, and founder'd.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: But the ſweet Lady,
Belvidere the bright one—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I, there's a face indeed: Oh my dear Nephew,
Could a young fellow of thy fiery mettle
Freeze, and that Lady in his Arms?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I think not.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou haſt a parlous judgement; but let that paſs,
She is as truly virtuous, fair, and noble,
As her great Mother's good: and that's not ordinary.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: But why (ſo many Princes, and ſo great ones
Being Suitors) ſhould the Dutcheſs deny to match her?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: She is a Jewel man, hangs in her boſom,
Her only Child: with her eies ſhe ſees all things,
Diſcourſes with her tongue, and pluck her from her
(So dotingly the old one loves her young one)
You pluck her heart out too: Beſides, of late daies,
The Duke of Milan, who could never win her
By Love, nor Treaty, laid a cloſe train for her
• n her own private Walks: ſome forty Horſe-men,
• o to ſurprize her; which we found, and dealt with,
And ſent 'em running home to the Duke their Maſter,
Like Dogs with bottles at their tails.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Since that, I heard Sir,
She has ſent, her to your Cittadel to ſecure her,
My coſin Rodope, your wife attending her.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You hear a truth, and all convenient pleaſures
Are there proportion'd for her.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I would fain, Sir,
Like one that owes a dutious ſervice to her
Sometimes ſo pleaſe you—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Gentle Coſin pardon me,
I muſt not, nor you muſt not dare to offer,
The laſt Edict lies on his life purſues it;
Your friend, Sir, to command, abroad to love you
To lend ye any thing I have, to wait upon ye,
But in the Cittadel where I ſtand charg'd,
Not a bit upon a march: no ſervice, Sir,
No, good Sir by no means: I kiſs your hands, Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: To your keeping only? none elſe to look upon her?
None but Bartello worthy her attendance?
No faith but his to ſerve her? Oh Belvidere,
Thou Saint to whom my youth is ſacrific'd,
Thou point to which my life turns, and my fortune,
Art thou lock'd from me now? from all my comforts,
Art thou ſnatch'd violently? thou hear'ſt me not,
Nor canſt thou ſee (fair ſoul) thy ſervants mournings,
Yet let thy gentle heart feel what his abſence,
The great divorſe of minds ſo truly loving,
So long, and nurs'd in one affection
Even from our infant eyes, ſuck'd in and nouriſh'd:
Oh let it feel but that, and there ſtand conſtant
And I am bleſt. My dear Aunt Rodope,
That is her Governeſs, did love me dearly,
There's one hope yet to ſee her: when he is abſent
• may be ventur'd, and ſhe may work it cloſely:
〈◊〉 know the Ladies will goe equal with me,
And ſo the danger of the Edict avoided;
• et me think more, for I muſt try all hazards.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Will ye go yonder, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Yes marry will I Sir.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: And by this Ladder?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: By that Ladder, coxcombe.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Have ye any more necks at home when this is broken,
• or this will crack with the beſt friend he has Sir?
• r can you pitch of all four, like an Ape now?
• et me ſee you tumble.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You are very pleaſant Sir,

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: No truly Sir, I ſhould be loath to ſee ye
• ome fluttering down like a young Rook, cry ſquab,
And take ye up with your brains beaten into your buttocks.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l:
Hold your peace Aſſe: who's this ſtands muſing here?
• ylvio?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Who calls me?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: One moſt glad to ſee you Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: My deareſt Claudio? what make you thus private,
• nd with a preparation of this nature?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: We have leave to play, and are going to climb Birds neſts.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Prethee what is it friend? why ſtart ye from me?
〈◊〉 your old Miſtriſs grown ſo coy and cruel,
• e muſt be ſcal'd? it ſeems you are loath to tell me,
• ce twenty years continuance of our friendſhip
• ay not be worth the weight of ſuch a ſecret,
Twill be but rude to aske again: ſave ye.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay ſtay, dear Silvio, if you love me take it:
• till you know it, never woman labour'd
• I do now.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I'll doe my beſt to eaſe it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You have heard the Lady Belvidere —

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: What heard Sir?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Heard to the Cittadel, upon ſome fears
She is confin'd.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Why dreams he on this beauty?
'Tis true, I have heard it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And that no acceſs,
No bleſſing from thoſe eyes, but with much hazard,
Even hazard of a life.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: He dares not love her;
I have heard that too: but whither points your purpoſe?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Oh Silvio, let me ſpeak that none may hear me,
None but thy truth: I have lov'd this Lady long,
Long given away my life to her devotion,
Long dwelt upon that beauty to my ruine.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Do's ſhe know this?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: No, there begins my miſery,
Ixion-like, I have only yet clasp'd clouds,
And fed upon poor empty dreams that ſtarve me.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And what do you mean to do now?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Though I dye for't.
Though all the tortures in the world hung on me,
Arm'd with imperious Love, I ſtand prepar'd now,
With this to reach her Chamber: there to ſee her,
And tell her boldly with what truth I love her.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Twill not be eaſily done Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Oh my Silvio,
The hardeſt things are ſweeteſt in poſſeſſion.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Nor will ſhew much diſcretion.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Love is blind man,
And he that looks for reaſon there far blinder.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Have ye conſider'd ripely?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: All that may fall,
And arm'd againſt that all.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Her honor too?
What ſhe may ſuffer in this raſh adventure
The beauty of her name?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I'll doe it cloſely,
And only at her window, with that caution—

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Are there no Guards?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Corruption chokes their ſervice.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Or do you hold her bred ſo light a woman
To hold commerce with ſtrange tongues?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why this ſervice,
This only hazard of my life muſt tell her,
Though ſhe were Veſtas ſelf, I muſt deſerve her.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I would not have ye go: pray let it ſink here,
And think a nobler way to raiſe your ſervice,
A ſafer and a wiſer.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis too late, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Then I muſt ſay, You ſhall not goe.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſhall not?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: You ſhall not go: that part bred with ye, friendſhip
Bids me ſay boldly ſo, and you obſerve me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You ſtretch that tye too far.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I'll ſtretch it farther:
The honor that I bear that ſpotleſs virtue
You ſouly ſeek to taint, unnobly covet,
Bids me command ye ſtay: if not, thus force ye.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: This will be worſe than climbing.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why do ye draw Sir?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: To kill thee, if thy baſe will be thy Maſter,

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ever was your friend.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Whilſt thou wert honeſt,
And not a Night-thief of anothers honor;
I never call'd a fool my friend, a mad man,
That durſt expoſe his ſame to all opinions,
His life to unhoneſt dangers: I never lov'd him,
Durſt know his name, that ſought a Virgins ruine,
Nor ever took I pleaſure in acquaintance
With men, that give as looſe rains to their fancies
As the wild Ocean to his raging fluxes:
A noble ſoul I twin with, and my love
Followes his life, dares maſter his affections.
Will ye give off, or fight?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I will not fight with ye:
The ſacred name of friend ties up that anger,
Rather I'll ſtudy.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Do, to be a friend ſtill.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If this way, I ſhall never hold.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I'll watch ye:
And if I catch ye falſe: by heaven ye dye for't,
All love forgot.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: When I fear that, I am fit for't. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Lopez at a Table with Jewels and Money upon it, an Egg roaſting by a Candle.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Whilſt prodigal young gaudy fools are banqueting,
And launching out their ſtates to catch the giddy,
Thus do I ſtudy to preſerve my fortune,
And hatch with care at home the wealth that Saints me.
Here's Rubies of Bengala, rich, rich, glorious;
Theſe Diamonds of Ormus bought for little,
Here vented at the price of Princes Ranſomes;
How bright they ſhine like conſtellations,
The South Seas treaſure here, Pearl, fair and orient
Able to equal Cleopatra's Banquet:
Here chains of leſſer ſtones for Ladies luſters,
Ingotts of Gold, Rings, Brooches, bars of Silver,
Theſe are my ſtudies to ſet off in ſale well,
And not in ſenſual ſurfeits to conſume 'em;
How roſts mine egg; he heats apace, I'll turn him:
Penurio, where you knave do you wait? Penurio,
You lazie knave.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Did you call Sir?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Where's your Miſtriſs?
What vanity holds her from her attendance?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The very ſight of this egg has made him cockiſh,
What would a dozen butter'd do? She is within Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Within Sir, at what thrif ye knave? what getting?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Getting a good ſtomach Sir, and ſhe knew where to get meat to it,
She is praying heartily upon her knees Sir,
That Heaven would ſend her a good bearing dinner.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Nothing but gluttony and ſurfeit thought on,
Health flung behind: had ſhe not yeſternight ſirrah
Two Sprats to ſupper, and the oil allowable?
Was ſhe not ſick with eating? Hadſt not thou,
(Thou moſt ungrateful knave, that nothing ſatisfies)
The water that I boil'd my other egg in
To make thee hearty broth?

sp.speaker: Pen,
sp.l: 'Tis true, I had Sir;
But I might as ſoon make the Philoſophers Stone on't,
You gave it me in water, and but for manners ſake,
I could give it you again, in wind, it was ſo hearty
I ſhall turn piſſing-Conduit ſhortly: my Miſtriſs comes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Welcome my Dove.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Pray ye keep your welcome to ye,
Unleſs it carries more than words to pleaſe me,
Is this the joy to be a Wife? to bring with me,
Beſides the nobleneſs of blood I ſpring from,
A full and able portion to maintain me?
Is this the happineſs of youth and beauty,
The great content of being made a Miſtriſs,
To live a Slave ſubject to wants and hungers,
To jealouſies for every eye that wanders?
Unmanly jealouſie.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Good Iſabella.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Too good for you: do you think to famiſh me,
Or keep me like an Alms-woman in ſuch rayment,
Such poor unhandſome weeds? am I old, or ugly?
I never was bred thus: and if your miſery
Will ſuffer wilful blindneſs to abuſe me,
My patience ſhall be no Bawd to mine own ruine.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Tickle him Miſtris: to him.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Had ye love in ye,
Or any part of man—

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Follow that Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Or had humanity but ever known ye,
You would ſhame to uſe a woman of my way thus,
So poor, and baſely; you are ſtrangely jealous of me
If I ſhould give ye cauſe.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: How Iſabella?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: As do not venture this way to provoke me.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Excellent well Miſtriſs,

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: How's this Iſabella?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: 'Twill ſtir a Saint, and I am but a woman,
And by that tenure may—

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: By no means chicken,
You know I love ye: fie, take no example
By thoſe young gadding Dames: (you are noted virtuous)
That ſtick their Husbands wealth in trifles on'em
And point 'em but the way to their own miſeries:
I am not jealous, kiſs me, — I am not:
And for your Diet, 'tis to keep you healthful,
Surfeits deſtroy more than the ſword: that I am careful
Your meat ſhould be both neat, and cleanly handled
See, Sweet, I am Cook my ſelf, and mine own Cater.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A—of that Cook cannot lick his fingers.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I'll add another diſh: you ſhall have Milk to it,
'Tis nouriſhing and good.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: With Butter in't Sir?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This knave would breed a famine in a Kingdom:
And cloths that ſhall content ye: you muſt be wiſe then,
And live ſequeſtred to your ſelf and me,
Not wandring after every toy comes croſs ye,
Nor ſtruck with every ſpleen: what's the knave doing? Penuria

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Hunting Sir, for a ſecond courſe of Flies here,
They are rare new Sallads.

sp.speaker: Lop,
sp.l: For certain Iſabella
This ravening fellow has a Wolf in's fellow:
Untemperate knave, will nothing quench thy appetite?
I ſaw him eat two Apples, which is monſtrous.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: If you had given me thoſe 't had been more monſtro •

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis a main miracle to feed this villain,
Come Iſabella, let us in to ſupper,
And think the Roman dainties at our Table,
'Tis all but thought. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Would all my thoughts would do it:
The Devil ſhould think of purchaſing that Egg-ſhell,
To victual out a Witch for the Burmoothes:
'Tis Treaſon to any good ſtomach living now
To hear a tedious Grace ſaid, and no meat to't,
I have a Radiſh yet, but that's but tranſitory. Exit.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Can any living man, unleſs a Raſcal
That neither knows himſelf, nor a faſhion'd Gentleman
Take me for a worſe man than my Maſter now?
I am naturally proud in theſe clothes: but if pride now
Should catch a fall in what I am attempting,
'Tis but a Proverb ſound, and a neck broken,
That's the worſt can come on't, a Gentleman's gone then,
A Gentleman o'th' firſt houſe, there's the end on't:
My Maſter lies moſt pittifully complaining,
Wringing and kicking up to th' ears in love yonder,
And ſuch a lamentable noiſe he keeps, it kills me:
I have got his cloaths, and if I can get to her
By hook or crook here, ſuch a ſong I'll ſing her—
I think I ſhall be hang'd, but that's no matter,
What's a hanging among friends: I am valiant now as an Elephant,
I have conſider'd what to ſay too: let me ſee now,
This is the place, 'tis plaguy high: ſtay at that lower window
Let me aim finely now, like a good Gunner,
〈◊〉 may prove but a whipping.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I ſaw ſome body
Paſs by me now, and though it were dark, me-thought yet
• knew the clothes: ha, let me not be cozen'd,
The Ladder too, ready to fling it? monſtrous,
'Tis he, 'tis Claudio: moſt voluptuous villain,
Scandal to womans credit: Love, I forget thee,

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: What will he do i'th' name of Heaven, what's that there?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And all the friendſhip that I bore thee, bury here.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: What has he in's hand? I hope but a Cudgel.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Thy faul'ts forgive O Heaven: farewel thou traitor.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I am ſlain: I am ſlain.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: He's down, and dead: dead certain,
'Twas too raſh, too full of ſpleen, ſtark dead:
This is no place now to repent in, only
Would I had given this hand that ſhot the Piſtol
I had miſs'd thee, and thou wer't once more Claudio. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why ſhould I love thus fooliſhly? thus deſperately?
And give away my heart where no hope's left me?
Why ſhould not the true counſel of a friend reſtrain me?
The Devils mouth I run into affright me,
The honor of the Lady, charm my wildneſs;
I have no power, no Being of my ſelf,
No reaſon ſtrong enough now left within me
To bind my Will: Oh Love, thou god, or devil,
Or what thou art, that playes the tyrant in me.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Oh.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What's that cry?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: A Surgeon, a Surgeon,
Twenty good Surgeons.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis not far from me,
Some murther o' my life,

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Will you let me dye here?
No drink come, nor no Surgeon?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis my man ſure,
His voice, and here he lies: how is it with thee?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I am ſlain, Sir, I am ſlain.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Slain? Who has ſlain thee?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Kill'd, kill'd, out-right kill'd.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Where's thy hurt?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I know not,
But I am ſure I am kill'd.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Canſt thou ſit up,
That I may find the hurt out?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I can ſit up,
But ne'er the leſs I am ſlain.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis not o'this ſide?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: No Sir, I think it be not.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nor o' this ſide,
Was it done with a ſword?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: A Gun, a Gun, ſweet Maſter.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: The devil a bullet has been here: thou art well man.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: No ſure I am kill'd.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Let me ſee thy thighs, and belly,
As whole as a fiſh for any thing I ſee yet:
Thou bleed'ſt no where.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I think I do not bleed, Sir,
But yet I am afraid I am ſlain.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Stand up fool,
Thou haſt as much hurt as my nail; who ſhot thee,
A Pottle, or a Pint?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Signior Silvio ſhot me
In theſe clothes; taking me for you, and ſeeing
The Ladder in my hand here, which I ſtole from ye,
Thinking to have gone to the Lady my ſelf, and have ſpoke for ye

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If he had hit ye home, he had ſerv'd ye right ſirrah,
You ſaucy rogue, how poor my intent ſhews to me,
How • aked now, and fooliſh?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Are ye ſure he has not hit me,
It gave a monſtrous bounce?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You roſe o' your right ſide,
And ſaid your prayers too, you had been payed elſe:
But what need'ſt thou a Bullet, when thy fear kills thee?
Sirrah, keep your own counſel for all this, you'll be hang'd elſe,
If it be known.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: If it be by my means, let me;
I am glad I am not kill'd, and far more gladder
My Gentleman-like humor's out: I feel 'tis dangerous,
And to be a gentleman, is to be kill'd twice a week.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Keep your ſelf cloſe i'th' Countrey for a while ſirrah.
There's Money, walk to your friends.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: They have no Piſtols,
Nor are no Gentlemen, that's my comfort. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I will retire too, and live private; for this Silvio,
Inflam'd with nobleneſs, will be my death elſe;
And if I can forget this love that loads me,
At leaſt the danger: and now I think on't better,
I have ſome concluſions elſe invites me to it. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Rodope, and Silvio at ſeveral doors.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: NEphew.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: My dear Aunt.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Would you go by thus ſlily,
And never ſee me, not once ſend in to me
Your loving Aunt? ſhe that above all thoſe
I call my kindred, honour'd you, and placed you
Neareſt my heart?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I thank you worthy Aunt
But ſuch at this time are my occaſions—

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You ſhall not goe yet, by my faith you ſhall not,
I will not be deny'd: why look ye ſad Nephew?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I am ſeldom other: Oh, this blood ſits heavy:
As I walk'd this way late laſt night,
In meditation of ſome things concern'd me—

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: What Nephew?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Why methought I heard a Piece, Lady,
A Piece ſhot off, much about this place too,
But could not judge the cauſe, nor what it boaded,
Under the Caſtle-wall.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: We heard it too,
And the Watch purſu'd it preſently, but found nothing,
Not any tract.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I am right glad to hear it:
The Ruffians ſurely that command the night
Have found him, ſtript him: and into the River
Convey'd the body.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You look ſtill ſadder, Nephew,
Is any thing within theſe walls to comfort ye?
Speak, and be Maſter of it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ye are a right Courtier,
A great Profeſſor, but a poor performer.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Do you doubt my faith: you never found me that way.
I dare well ſpeak it boldly, but a true friend.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Continue then.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Try me, and ſee who falters.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I will, and preſently: 'tis in your power
To make me the moſt bound man to your courteſie.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Let me know how, and if I fail —

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Tis thus then,
Get me acceſs to the Lady Belvidere,
But for a minute, but to ſee her: your Husband now
Is ſafe at Court, I left him full employ'd there.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You have ask'd the thing without my power to grant ye,
The Law lies on the danger: if I lov'd ye not
• would bid ye goe, and there be found, and dye for't.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I knew your love, and where there ſhew'd a danger
How far you durſt ſtep for me: give me a true friend;
That where occaſion is to do a benefit
Aims at the end, and not the rubs before it;
I was a fool to ask ye this, a more fool
To think a woman had ſo much noble nature
To entertain a ſecret of this burthen;
Ye had beſt to tell the Dutcheſs I perſwaded ye,
That's a fine courſe, and one will win ye credit;
Forget the name of Coſin, blot my blood out,
And ſo you raiſe your ſelf, let me grow ſhorter.
A woman friend? he that believes that weakneſs
Steers in a ſtormy night without a Compaſs.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: What is't I durſt not do might not impeach ye?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Why this ye dare not do, ye dare not think of.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: 'Tis a main hazard.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: If it were not ſo
I would not come to you to ſeek a favour.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You will loſe your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: The loſs ends with my ſelf then.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: You will but ſee her?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Only look upon her.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Not ſtay:

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Preſcribe your time.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Not traffique with her
In any cloſe diſhonourable action?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Stand you your ſelf by.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I will venture for ye,
Becauſe ye ſhall be ſure I am a touch'd friend,
I'll bring her to ye: come walk, you know the Garden,
And take this key to open the little Poſtern,
There ſtand no guards.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I ſhall ſoon find it Aunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Sol.
sp.l: Is the Captain come home?

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: No, who commands the Guard to night?

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: I think Petruchio.

sp.speaker: 2 Sold.
sp.l: What's the Word?

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: None knows yet,

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: I would this Lady were married out o'th' way once,
Or out of our cuſtodies; I wiſh they would take in more companies,
For I am ſure we feel her in our duties ſhrewdly.

sp.speaker: 1 Sol.
sp.l: 'Tis not her fault I warrant ye, ſhe is ready for't,
And that's the plague, when they grow ripe for marriage
They muſt be ſlipt like Hawkes,

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: Give me a mean wench,
No State doubt lies on her, ſhe is alwayes ready.

sp.speaker: 1 Sol.
sp.l: Come to the Guard, 'tis late, and ſure the Captain
Can not be long away.

sp.speaker: 2 Sol.
sp.l: I have watch'd theſe three nights,
To morrow they may keep me tame for nothing. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Silvio, Belvidere, and Rodope with a Light.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: This is the place I think; what Light is that there?
The Lady and my Coſin?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Is this the Garden?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Yes Madam.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Oh my bleſſed Miſtriſs,
Saint of my ſoul.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Speak ſoftly: take me to ye,
Oh Silvio, I am thine, thine ever Silvio.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Is this your promiſe, Sir? Lady your honor?
I am undone if this be ſeen, diſgrac'd,
Fallen under all diſcredit.

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Do you love ſtill?
Dear, do you keep your old faith?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ever Lady;
And when that fails me, all that's good forſake me.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Do not you ſhame? Madam, I muſt not ſuffer this,
I will not ſuffer it; men call you virtuous,
What do you mean to loſe your ſelf thus; Silvio?
I charge thee get away, I charge you retire ye,
I'll call the Watch elſe,

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Call all the world to ſee us,
We live in one anothers happineſs,
And ſo will die.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Here will I hang for ever.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: As ye reſpect me, as hereafter Madam
You would enjoy his love—nothing prevail with ye?
I'll try my ſtrength then; get thee gone thou villain,
Thou Promiſe-breaker.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I am tide, I cannot.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I'll ring the Bell then.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ring it to death, I am fixt here.

div.stage: Enter Bartello, two Soldiers with lights.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: I ſaw a Light over the Garden walk,
Hard by the Ladies Chamber, here's ſome knavery
As I live, I ſaw it twice.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: The Guard, the Guard there;
I muſt not ſuffer this, it is too miſchievous.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Light up the Torch, I fear'd this, ha? young Silvio?
How got he in?

sp.speaker: 1 Sold.
sp.l: The Devil brought him in ſure
He came not by us.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: My wife between 'em buſling?
Guard, pull him off.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: Now, now, ye feel the miſery.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: You, Madam, at an hour ſo far undecent?
Death, O my ſoul! this is a ſoul fault in ye,
Your mothers care abus'd too, Light's to her Chamber,
I am ſorry to ſee this,

sp.speaker: Bell.
sp.l: Farewel my Silvio,
And let no danger ſink thee.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Nor death Lady. Exeunt Bell. Rod.

sp.speaker: Birt,
sp.l: Are ye ſo hot? I ſhall prepare ye Phyſick
Will purge ye finely, neatly: you are too fiery,
Think of your prayers, Sir, an you have not forgot 'em;
Can ye flie i' th' air, or creep ye in at key-holes?
I have a Gin will catch ye though you conjur'd:
Take him to Guard to night, to ſtrong and ſure Guard;
I'll back to th' Dutcheſs preſently: no leſs ſport ſerve ye,
Than the Heir to a Dukedom? play at puſh-pin there Sir?
It was well aim'd, but plague upon't, you ſhot ſhort,
And that will loſe your game.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I know the loſs then.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Now, in this habit may I ſafely ſee
How my incenſed friend carries my murther,
Who little I imagin'd had been wrought
To ſuch a height of rage, and much I grieve now
Mine own blind paſſion had ſo maſter'd me,
I could not ſee his love, for ſure he loves her,
And on a nobler ground than I pretended,
It muſt be ſo, it is ſo; what Penurio,
My ſhotten friend, what wind blew you?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Faith 'tis true,
Any ſtrong wind will blow me like a Feather,
I am all Air, nothing of earth within me,
Nor have not had this month, but that good Dinner
Your Worſhip gave me yeſterday, that ſtaies by me,
And gives me ballaſt, elſe the Sun would draw me?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But does my Miſtriſs ſpeak ſtill of me?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Yes, Sir,
And in her ſleep, that makes my Maſter mad too,
And turn and fart for anger.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Art ſure ſhe ſaw me?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: She ſaw ye at a window.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt true,
In ſuch a place I ſaw a Gentlewoman,
A young, ſweet, handſome woman.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: That's ſhe, that's ſhe Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And well ſhe view'd me, I view'd her.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Still ſhe Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: At laſt ſhe bluſh'd, and then look'd off.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: That bluſh, Sir,
If you can read it truly —

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But didſt thou tell her,
Or didſt thou fool me, thou knew'ſt ſuch a one?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I told her, and I told her ſuch a ſweet tale —

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But did ſhe hear thee?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: With a thouſand ears, Sir,
And ſwallow'd what I ſaid as greedily,
As great-belly'd women do Cherries, ſtones and all Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Methinks ſhe ſhould not love thy Maſter?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Hang him Pilcher,
There's nothing loves him: his own Cat cannot endure him,
She had better lye with a Bear, for he is ſo hairy,
That a tame Warren of Fleas frisk round about him.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And wilt thou work ſtill?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Like a Miner for ye.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And get acceſs,

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Or conjure you together,
'Tis her deſire to meet: ſhe is poyſon'd with him,
And till ſhe take a ſweet freſh air, that's you Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: There's money for thee: thou art a precious Varlet
Be fat, be fat, and blow thy Maſter backward.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Blow you my Miſtriſs Sir, as flat as a Flounder,
Then blow her up again, as Butchers blow their Veals;
If ſhe dye upon the ſame
•• ry her, bury her in Gods name.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Thou art a merry knave: by this hand I'll feed thee,
Till thou crack'ſt at both ends, if thou dar'ſt do this
Thou ſhalt eat no fantaſtical Porridge,
Nor lick the diſh where oil was yeſterday.
Duſt, and dead Flies to day; Capons, fat Capons—

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Oh hearty ſound.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Cramb'd full of itching Oyſters.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Will ye have the Dutcheſs?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And Lobſters big as Gauntlets,
Thou ſhalt deſpiſe baſe Beef.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I do deſpiſe it,
And now methinks I feel a Tart come ſliding.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Leaping into thy mouth: but firſt deal faithfully.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: When will ye come?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: To morrow.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I'll attend ye,
For then my Maſter will be out in buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What news abroad?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Mas, as I was coming to you,
I heard that Signior Silvio, a good Gentleman,
Many a good meal I have eaten wit him —

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What of him?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Was this day to be arraigned before the Dutcheſs,
•• t why, I could not hear.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Silvio arraign'd?
Go, get ye gone, and think of me.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I flie Sir. Exit Pen.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Arraign'd? for what? for my ſuppoſed death? no,
That cannot be ſure, there's no rumor of it,
• e it what it will, I will be there and ſee it,
•• d if my help will bring him off, he has it. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Dutcheſs, Lords, Silvio priſoner, Belvidere, Bartello, Rodope, Clark, Counſellors, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Read the Edict laſt made,
Keep ſilence there.

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: If any man of what condition ſoever, and a ſubject after the publiſhing of this Edict, ſhall without ſpecial Licence from the great Dutcheſs, attempt or buy, offer, or make an attempt, to ſolicite the love of the Princeſs Belvidere, the perſon ſo offending, ſhall forfeit his life.

sp.speaker: Counſ.
sp.l: The reaſon why my Royal Miſtriſs here
In her laſt Treaty with Sien as Duke,
• romis'd her beauteous daughter there in marriage,
The Duke of Milan, rival in this fortune,
Un-nobly ſought by practice to betray her;
Which found, and croſs'd, the Cittadel receiv'd her
There to ſecure her Mothers word; the laſt cauſe
So many Gentlemen of late enamour'd
On this moſt beauteous Princeſs, and not brooking
One more than other, to deſerve a favour,
Bloud has been ſpilt, many brave ſpirits loſt,
And more, unleſs ſhe had been kept cloſe from their violence,
Had like to have followed: therefore for due prevention
Of all ſuch hazards and unnoble actions,
This laſt Edict was publiſh'd, which thou Silvio
Like a falſe man, a bad man, and a Traitor
Haſt rent a-peeces, and contemn'd, for which cauſe
Thou ſtandeſt a guilty man here now.

sp.speaker: Clark.
sp.l: Speak Silvio,
What canſt thou ſay to avoid the hand of Juſtice?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Nothing, but I confeſs, ſubmit, and lay my head to it.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Have ye no eyes my Lords, no underſtandings?
The Gentleman will caſt himſel away,
Caſt himſelf wilfully: are you, or you guilty?
No more is he, no more taint ſticks upon him:
I drew him thither; 'twas my way betrai'd him,
I got the entrance kept, I entertain'd him,
I hid the danger from him, forced him to me,
Poor gentle ſoul, he's in no part tranſgreſſing,
I wrote unto him.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Do not wrong that honor.
Caſt not upon that pureneſs theſe aſperſions,
It was my love, my violence,
My life muſt anſwer it: I broke in to her,
Tempted the Law, ſolicited unjuſtly.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: As there is truth in Heaven, I was the firſt cauſe:
How could this man have come to me, left naked
Without my counſel and proviſion?
What hour could he find out to paſs the Watches,
But I muſt make it ſure firſt? Reverend Judges,
Be not abus'd, nor let an innocent life lie
Upon your ſhaking Conſcience; I did it,
My love the main wheel that ſet him a going:
His motion but compell'd.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Can ye believe this?
And know with what a modeſty and whiteneſs
Her life was ever ranck'd? Can you believe this
And ſee me here before ye, young and wilful?
Apt to what danger Love dares thruſt me on,
And where Law ſtops my way, apt to contemn it?
If I were baſhful, old, or dull, and ſleepy
In Loves allarms, a woman might awake me,
Direct, and clew me out the way to happineſs:
But I, like fire, kindled with that bright beauty,
Catch hold of all occaſions, and run through 'em.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I charge ye, as your honeſt ſouls will anſwer it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I charge ye, as you are the friends to virtue,
That has no pattern living but this Lady.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Let not his blood—

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Let not her wilfulneſs—
For then you act a Scene Hell will rejoyce at.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: He is clear.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: She is as white in this as Infants.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: The god of Love protect your cauſe, and help ye,
Two nobler pieces of affection
Theſe eyes ne'er look'd on, if ſuch goodneſs periſh,
Let never true hearts meet again, but break. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: A ſtrange exemple of ſtrong love, a rare one.

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: Madam, we know not what to ſay, to think on.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs it ſtrikes me tender too,
Searches my Mothers heart: you found 'em there?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Yes certain Madam.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: And ſo linked together?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: As they had been one piece of Alablaſter.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Nothing diſhonourable?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: So let my ſoul have happineſs,
As that thought yet durſt never ſeek this boſom.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: What ſhall I do? 'has broke my Law, abus'd me,
Fain would I know the truth, either confeſs it,
And let me underſtand the main offender,
Or both ſhall feel the torture.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Are ye a Mother;
The Mother of ſo ſweet a Roſe as this is?
So pure a Flower? and dare ye loſe that nature?
Dare ye take to your ſelf ſo great a wickedneſs,
(Oh holy Heaven) of thinking what may ruine
This goodly building? this Temple where the gods dwell?
Give me a thouſand tortures, I deſerve 'em,
And ſhew me death in all the ſhapes imagin'd.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No death but I will anſwer it, meet it, ſeek it;
No torture but I'll laugh upon't, and kiſs it.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: This is no way.

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: They ſay no more for certain
Than their ſtrong hearts will ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: I have bethought me;
No Lords, although I have a Child offending,
Nature dares not forget ſhe is a Child ſtill;
Till now, I never look'd on love imperious:
I have bethought me of a way to break ye,
To ſeparate, though not your loves, your bodies:
Silvio attend, I'll be your Judge my ſelf now,
The ſentence of your death (becauſe my Daughter
Will bear an equal part in your afflictions)
I take away and pardon: this remains then
An eaſie and a gentle puniſhment,
And this ſhall be fulfill'd: becauſe unnobly
You have ſought the love, and marriage of a Princeſs,
The abſolute and ſole Heir of this Dukedom,
By that means, as we muſt imagine ſtrongly,
To plant your ſelf into this rule hereafter,
We here pronounce ye a man baniſh'd from us

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: For ever baniſh'd Lady?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Yet more mercy,
But for a year: and then again in this place
To make your full appearance: yet more pitty,
If in that time you can abſolve a queſtion,
Writ down within this ſcrowl, abſolve it rightly,
This Lady is your wife, and ſhall live with ye;
If not, you looſe your head.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I take this honor,
And humbly kiſs thoſe Royal hands.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Receive it: Bartello, to your old guard take the Princeſs,
And ſo the Court break up.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Farewel to all,
And to that ſpotleſs heart my endleſs ſervice. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: What will this prove?

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: I'll tell you a year hence, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Are you pleas'd now? have not I wrought this wonder

l.hi: Non eben fatto Signieur.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Rarely Penurio

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Cloſe, cloſe then, and work wax.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I am ſtudying for thee
A dinner, that ſhall victual thee for ten year.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Do you hear Miſtriſs?
You know what a dundir whelp my Maſter is,
I need not preach to ye, how unfit and wanting
To give a woman ſatisfaction:
How he ſtinks, and ſnores, a Bull's a better bed-fellow;
And for his love, never let that deceive ye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Nay ſure he loves me not.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: If he could coyn ye,
Or turn ye into mettal, much might be then;
He loves not any thing but what is traffique:
I have heard him ſwear, he would ſell ye to the Grand Signior.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: The Turk?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The very Turke, and how they would uſe ye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I'll fit him for't: the Turk?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I know the price too:
Now ye have time to pay him, pay him home Miſtriſs;
Pay him o' th' pate, clout him for all his courteſies;
Here's one that dances in your eyes, young delicate
To work this vengeance; if ye let it ſlip now,
There is no pittying of ye, od's precious, Miſtriſs,
Were I his wife, I would ſo mall his Mazard,
'Tis charity, meer charity, pure charity,
Are you the firſt? has it not been from Eves time,
Women would have their ſafe revenges this way?
And good and gracious women, excellent women;
Is't not a handſome Gentleman? a ſweet Gentleman;
View him from head to foot, a compleat Gentleman;
When can ye hope the like again? I leave ye,
And my revenge too, with ye; I know my office,
I'll not be far off, be not long a fumbling,
When danger ſhall appear, I'll give the 'larme. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You are welcome, Sir, and would it were my fortune
To afford a Gentleman of your fair ſeeming,
A freer entertainment than this houſe has,
You partly know, Sir.—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Know, and pity Lady,
Such ſweetneſs in the bud, ſhould be ſo blaſted;
Dare you make me your Servant?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Dare you make Sir,
That ſervice worthy of a womans favour
By conſtancy and goodneſs?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Here I ſwear to ye,
By the unvalued love I bear this beauty,
(And kiſs the Book too) never to be recreant,
To honour ye, to truly love, and ſerve ye,
My youth to wait upon ye, what my wealth has.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Oh make me not ſo poor to ſell affection,
Thoſe bought loves Sir, wear faſter than the moneys;
A handſome Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: A moſt delicate ſweet one,
Let my truth purchaſe then.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I ſhould firſt try it,
But you may happily.—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You ſhall not doubt me,
I hope ſhe loves me; when I prove falſe, ſhame take me;
Will ye believe a little?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I fear, too much, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And will ye love a little?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: That ſhould be your part:

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Thus I begin then, thus and thus.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: A good beginning,
We have a proverb ſaies, makes a good ending.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Say ye ſo? 'tis well inferr'd.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Good Sir, your patience:
• thinks I have ventur'd now, like a weak Bark
〈◊〉 a broken billow, that will ſwallow me,
• pon a rough Sea of ſuſpitions,
• ack round with jealous rocks.

sp.speaker: Pen. within.
sp.l: A hem, a hem there.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: This is my man; my fears too ſoon have found me,
Now what's the news?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A pox of yonder old Rigel,
The Captain, the old Captain.

sp.speaker: Iſab?
sp.l: What old Captain?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Captain courageous yonder of the Caſtle,
Captain, Don Diego, old Bartello.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Where is he?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: He's coming in:
'Twould vex the Devil, that ſuch an old Potgun as this,
That can make no ſport, ſhould hinder them that can do it.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I would not have him ſee the Gentleman,
•• r all the world, my credit were undone then.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Shall I fling a piſs-pot on's head as he comes in,
And take him into th' kitchin, there to drie him.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: That will not do; and he is ſo humorous too
• will come in.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What is he?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: One much troubles me.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: And can do nothing, cannot eat.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Your ſight now,
•• t of a driveling dotage he bears to me,
• ay make him tell my husband, and undo me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What would ye have me do?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: But for a while Sir,
• p here behind this hanging, preſently
O anſwer him, and then —

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I will obey ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Where's my rich Jeweller? I have ſtones to ſett.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: He is abroad, and ſure Sir.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: There's for your ſervice:
• here's the fair Lady? all alone ſweet beauty?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: She's never much alone Sir, that's acquainted
With ſuch companions as good honeſt thoughts are.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'll ſit down by thee, and I'll kiſs thy hand too,
•• d in thine ear ſwear by my life I love thee.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ye are a merry Captain.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And a mad one, Lady;
〈◊〉 th' mas thou haſt goodly eies, excellent eies, wench,
〈◊〉 twinkling rogues, look what thy Captain brings thee,
Thou muſt needs love me, love me heartily,
〈◊〉 me, and love me, hug me cloſe.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Fie Captain.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Nay, I have ſtrength, and I can ſtrain ye ſirrah,
•• d vault into my ſeat as nimbly, little one.
〈◊〉 any of you ſmooth-chinn'd boys in Florence,
〈◊〉 muſt needs commit a little folly with ye,
〈◊〉 not be long, a brideling caſt, and away wench;
• he bob-nail thy husband's as fitly out o' th' way now?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Do you think he keeps a bawdy-houſe?
