sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That's all one.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Or did you ever ſee that lightneſs in my carriage,
〈◊〉 you might promiſe to your ſelf—.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Away fool,
〈◊〉 good turn's a good turn; I am an honeſt fellow:

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You have a handſome wife, a virtuous Gentlewoman,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: They are not for this time o'th' year.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: A Lady,
• at ever bore that great reſpect to you,
• t noble conſtancy.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That's more than I know.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Oh Miſtriſs, ye are undone, my Maſter's coming

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Coming hard by here.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Plague conſume the Raſcal,
Shall I make petty-patties of him?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Now what love Sir?
Fear of your coming made him jealous firſt;
Your finding here, will make him mad and deſperate,
And what in that wild mood he will execute—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I can think of nothing, I have no wit left me,
Certain my head's a Muſtard-pot.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I have thought Sir,
And if you'll pleaſe to put in execution
What I conceive—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'll do it, tell it quickly.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Draw your ſword quickly, and go down in rag'd,
As if you had perſu'd ſome • oe up hither,
And grumble to your ſelf extreamly, terribly,
But not a word to him, and ſo paſs by him.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'll do it perfectly.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Stand you ſtill good Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Raſcal, ſlave, villain, take a houſe ſo poorly,
After thou haſt wrong'd a Gentleman, a Soldier,
Baſe Poultroon boy, you will forſake your neaſt ſirrah.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: The matter, good ſweet Captain?

sp.speaker: Bart
sp.l: Run-away rogue,
And take a houſe to cover thy baſe cowardize,
I'll whip ye, I'll ſo ſcourge ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Mercy upon me,
What's all this matter wife?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Did you meet the mad man?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I never ſaw the Captain ſo provok'd yet.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Oh he's a Devil ſure' a moſt bloody devil,
He follow'd a young Gentleman, his ſword drawn,
With ſuch a fury, how I ſhake to think on't,
And foyn'd, and ſlaſh'd at him, and ſwore he'd kill him,
Drove him up hither, follow'd him ſtill bloodily,
And if I had not hid him, ſure had ſlain him;
A mercileſs old man.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Moſt virtuous Lady,
Even as the giver of my life, I thank ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This fellow muſt not ſtay here, he is too handſome;
He is gone Sir, and you may paſs now with all ſecurity,
I'll be your guide my ſelf, and ſuch a way
I'll lead ye, none ſhall croſs, nor none ſhall know ye.
The door's left open Sirrah, I'll ſtarve you for this trick,
I'll make thee faſt o' Sundaies; and for you Lady,
I'll have your Lodgings farther off, and cloſer,
I'll have no ſtreet-lights to you; will you go Sir?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I thank ye Sir: the devil take this fortune;
And once more all my ſervice to your goodneſs. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Now could I eat my very arms for madneſs,
Croſs'd in the nick o' th' matter? vengeance take it,
And that old Cavalier that ſpoil'd our Cock-fight;
I'll lay the next plot ſurer.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I am glad and ſorry;
Glad, that I got ſo fairly off ſuſpition;
Sorry, I loſt my new lov'd friend.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Not loſt Miſtriſs;
I'll conjure once again to raiſe that ſpirit;
In, and look ſoberly upon the matter,
We'll ring him one peal more, and if that fall,
The devil tak the Clappers, Bells, and all. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: NOw Rodope, How do you find my daughter?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Madam, I find her now what you would have her,
What the State wiſhes her; I urg'd her fault to her,
Open'd her eyes, and made her ſee the miſchief
She was running with a headlong will into,
Made her ſtart at her folly, ſhake and tremble,
At the meer memory of ſuch an ignorance,
She now contemns his love, hates his remembrance,
Cannot endure to hear the name of Silvio;
His perſon ſpits at.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: I am glad to hear this.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: And humbly now to your Will, your care, Madam,
Bends her affections, bows her obedience;
Syenna's Duke, with new eyes now ſhe looks on,
And with a Princely love, fit for his perſon.
Returns that happineſs; and joy he look'd for;
The general good of both the neighbor Dukedoms,
Not any private end, or raſh affection
She aims at now: hearing the Duke arriv'd too,
(To whom ſhe owes all honor, and all ſervice,)
She charg'd me kneel thus at your Graces feet,
And not to riſe without a general pardon.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: She has it, and my love again, my old love,
And with more tenderneſs I meet this penitence,
Than if ſhe ne'er had ſtarted from her honor;
I thank ye Rhodope, am bound to thank ye,
And daily to remember this great ſervice,
This honeſt faithful ſervice; go in peace,
And by this Ring, delivered to Bartello,
Let her enjoy our favour, and her liberty,
And preſently to this place, with all honor,
See her conducted.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Your Grace has made me happy. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: Syenna's noble Duke, craves his admittacne.

div.stage: Enter Duke of Syenna with Attendants.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Go; wait upon his Grace; fair Sir, you are welcome,
Welcome to her ever admir'd your virtues:
And now methinks, my Court looks truly noble;
You have taken too much pains Sir.

sp.speaker: Syen.
sp.l: Royal Lady,
To wait upon your Grace is but my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Keep that Sir, for the Saint ye have vow'd it to.

sp.speaker: Syen.
sp.l: I keep a life for her: ſince your Grace pleaſes
To jump ſo happily into the matter,
I come indeed to claim your Royal promiſe,
The beauteous Belvidere in marriage,
I come to tender her my youth, my fortune,
My everlaſting love.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: You are like to win, Sir:
All is forgot, forgiven too; no ſadneſs
My good Child, you have the ſame heart ſtill here,
The Duke of Syenna, Child, pray uſe him nobly.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: An Angel beauty.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Your Grace is fairly welcome,
And what in modeſty a bluſhing maid may
Wiſh to a Gentleman of your great goodneſs;
But wiſhes are too poor a pay for Princes.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: You have made me richer than all States and Tit •
One kiſs of this white hand's above all honors,
My faith dear Lady, and my fruitful ſervice,
My duteous zeal—

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Your Grace is a great Maſter,
And ſpeaks too powerfully to be reſiſted:
Once more you are welcome, Sir, to me you are welcom •
To her that honors ye; I could ſay more Sir,
But in anothers tongue 'twere better ſpoken,

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: As wiſe as fair, you have made your ſervant happ •
I never ſaw ſo rich a Mine of ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Will your Grace pleaſe, after your painful jour •
To take ſome reſt? Are the Dukes Lodgings ready?

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: All Madam.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Then wait upon his Grace, all, and to morrow,
We'll ſhew ye in what high eſteem we hold ye,
Till then a fair repoſe.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l:
My faireſt ſervice. Exit Duke,
•

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: You have ſo honour'd me, my deareſt daught ••
So truly pleas'd me in this entertainment,
I mean your loving carriage to Syenna,
That both for ever I forget all treſpaſſes,
And to ſecure you next of my full favour,
Ask what you will within my power to grant ye,
Ask freely: and if I forget my promiſe—
Ask confidently.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You are too Royal to me;
To me that have ſo fooliſhly tranſgreſs'd you,
So like a Girl, ſo far forgot my virtue,
Which now appears as baſe and ugly to me,
As did his Dream, that thought he was in Paradiſe,
Awak'd and ſaw the Devil; how was I wander'd?
With what eies could I look upon that poor, that courſ thi •
That wretched thing call'd Sylvio? that (now) deſpis'd thi ••
And loſe an object of that graceful ſweetneſs,
That god-like preſence as Syenna is?
Darkneſs, and cheerful day, had not ſuch difference:
But I muſt ever bleſs your care, your wiſdom,
That led me from this labyrinth of folly,
How had I ſunk elſe? what example given?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Prethee no more, and as thou are my beſt one,
Ask ſomething that may equal ſuch a goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Why did ye let him go ſo ſlightly from ye,
More like a man in triumph, than condemn'd:
Why did ye make his pennance but a queſtion,
A Riddle, every idle wit unlocks.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: 'Tis not ſo,
Nor do not fear it ſo: he will not find it,
I have given that (unleſs my ſelf diſcover it)
Will coſt his head.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis ſubject to conſtruction?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: That it is too.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: It may be then abſolv'd,
And then are we both ſcorn'd and laugh'd at, Madam;
Beſide the promiſe you have ty'd upon it,
Which you muſt never keep.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: I never meant it.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: For heaven ſake let me know it, 'tis my Suit to ye
The Boon you would have me ask; let me but ſee it,
That if there be a way to make't ſo ſtrong,
No wit nor powerful reaſon can run through it,
For my diſgrace, I may beg of heaven to grant it.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Fear not, it has been put to ſharper judgements
Than e'er he ſhall arrive at: my dear Father,
That was as fiery in his underſtanding,
And ready in his wit as any living,
Had it two years, and ſtudied it, yet loſt it:
This night ye are my Bed-fellow, there Daughter
Into your boſom I'll commit this ſecret,
And there we'll both take counſel.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I ſhall find
Some trick I hope too ſtrong yet for his mind. Exeu •

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Methinks I am batten'd well of late, grown luſty,
〈◊〉 high, and kicking, thanks to the bounteous Rugio;
• d now, methinks I ſcorn theſe poor repaſts,
• eeſe-parings, and the ſtinking tongues of Pilchers;
But why ſhould I remember theſe? they are odious,
They are odious in mine eyes; the full fat diſh now,
The bearing diſh is that I reverence,
The diſh an able Serving-man ſweats under,
And bends i'th' hams, as if the houſe hung on him,
That diſh is the diſh: hang your bladder Bankets,
Or halfe a dozen of Turnops and two Muſhrumps,
Theſe when they breed their beſt, hatch but two belches;
The ſtate of a fat Turkey, the decorum
He marches in with, all the train and circumſtance;
'Tis ſuch a matter, ſuch a glorious matter,
And then his ſauce with Oranges and Onions,
And he diſplaid in all parts, for ſuch a diſh now,
And at my need I would betray my Father,
And for a roſted Conger, all my Countrey.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: What my friend Lean-gut, how does thy beauteous Miſtriſs?
And where's your Maſter Sirrah? where's that horn-pipe?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: My Miſtriſs, Sir, does as a poor wrong'd Gentlewoman,
Too much, heaven knows, oppreſt with injuries,
May do and live.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Is the old fool ſtill jealous?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: As old fools are, and will be ſtill the ſame, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He muſt have cauſe: he muſt have cauſe.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Tis true, Sir,
And would he had with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: He ſhall have.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: For then he had Salt to his Saffron porridge,

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Why do not I ſee thee ſometime? why thou ſtarv'd raſcal?
Why do not ye come to me, you precious bow-caſe?
I keep good meat at home, good ſtore.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I will not fail ye all next week.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou art welcome,
I have a ſecret I would fain impart to thee,
But thou art ſo thin, the wind will blow it from thee,
Or men will read it through thee.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Wrap't up in beef Sir,
〈◊〉 good groſs beef, let all the world look on me,
The Engliſh have that trick to keep intelligence.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: A wittty knave, firſt there's to tie your tongue up.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Dumb as a Dog, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Next, hark in your ear, Sirrah.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Well, very well, excellent well: 'tis done, Sir,
Say no more to me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Say and hold.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Tis done, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: As thou lov'ſt butter'd eggs, ſwear.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Let me kiſs the Book firſt,
But here's my hand, brave Captain.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Look ye hold, ſirrah. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Oh the moſt precious vanity of this world;
When ſuch dry'd Neats-tongues muſt be ſoak'd and larded
With young fat ſupple wenches? Oh the Devil.
What can he do, he cannot ſuck an egg off
• t his back's looſe i'th' hilts: go thy wayes Captain,
Well may thy warlike name work Miracles,
But if e'er thy founder'd courſer win much more,
Or ſtand right but one train —
Now Signior Shadow,
• hat art thou thinking of, how to rob thy Maſter?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Of his good deeds? The Thief that undertakes that
Muſt have a hook will poze all Hell to hammer:
Have ye dined Gentlemen, or do you purpoſe?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Dined, two long hours ago.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Pray ye take me with ye.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: To ſupper doſt thou mean?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: To any thing
That has the ſmell of meat in't: tell me true, Gentlemen,
Are not you three going to be ſinful?
To iropard a joynt, or ſo? I have found your faces,
And ſee whore written in your eyes.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: A parlous raſcal,
Thou art much upon the matter.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Have a care Gentlemen,
'Tis a ſore age, very ſore age, lewd age,
And women now are like old Knights adventures,
Full of inchanted flames, and dangerous.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Where the moſt danger is, there's the moſt hon • r.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I grant ye, honor moſt conſiſts in ſufferance,
And by that rule you three ſhould be moſt honorable.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: A ſubtle Rogue: but canſt thou tell Penurio
Where we may light upon—

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A learned Surgeon?

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: Pox take ye fool; I mean good wholſome wenches.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: 'Faith wholſome women will but ſpoil ye too,
For you are ſo us'd to ſnap-haunces: But take my counſel,
Take fat old women, fat, and five and fifty,
The Dog-dayes are come in.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent
sp.l: Take fat old women?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The fatter and the older, ſtill the better,
You do not know the pleaſure of an old Dame,
A fat old Dame, you do not know the knack on't:
They are like our countrey Grotts, as cool as Chriſtmas,
And ſure i' th' keels.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Hang him ſtarv'd fool: he mocks us.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: Penurio, thou know'ſt all the handſome wenches?
What ſhall I give thee for a Merchants wife now?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I take no money Gentlemen, that's baſe,
I trade in meat, a Merchants wife will coſt ye
A glorious Capon; a great ſhoulder of Mutton;
And a Tart as big as a Conjurers Circle

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: That's cheap enough.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: And what a Haberdaſhers?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Worſe meat will ſerve for her, a great Gooſe-Pie,
But you muſt ſend it out o' th' Countrey to me,
It will not do elſe: with a piece of Bacon,
And if you can, a pot of Butter with it.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Now do I aim at horſe-fleſh: what a Parſons?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A Tithe-Pig has no fellow, if I fetch her,
If ſhe be Puritane, Plumb-porridge does it,
And a fat loin of Veal, well ſauc'd and roaſted,

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: We'll meet one night, and thou ſhalt have all theſe;
O' that condition we may have the wenches
A dainty raſcal.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: When your ſtomachs ſerve ye,
(For mine is ever ready) I'll ſupply ye.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Farewel, and there's to fill thy paunch,

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Brave Gentleman.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Hold ſirrah, there.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Any young wench i' th' Town, Sir.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: It ſhall go round. Exit Gent.

sp.speaker: Pen
sp.l: Moſt honorable Gentlemen,
All theſe are Courtiers, but they are meer Coxcombs,
And only for a wench, their purſes open,
Nor have they ſo much judgement left to chuſe her;
If e'r they call upon me, I'll ſo fit 'em,
I have a pack of wry-mouth'd mackrel Ladies,
Stink like a ſtanding ditch, and thoſe dear Damſels;
But I forget my buſineſs, I thank ye Monſieurs,
I have a thouſand whimſeys in my brain now. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter (to a Banquet) Dutcheſs, Syenna, Lords, Attendants.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Your Grace ſhall now perceive how much we honor ye
• nd in what dear regard we hold your friendſhip:
• ill you ſit Sir, and grace this homely Banquet?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Madam, to your poor friend, you are too magnificent.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: To the Dukes health, and all the joyes I wiſh him,
• et no man miſs this cup: have we no Muſick?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Your noble favours ſtill you heap upon me,
• ut where's my virtuous Miſtriſs, ſuch a Feaſt,
• nd not her ſparkling beauty here to bleſs it?
Methinks it ſhould not be, it ſhews not fully.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Young Ladies Sir; are long, and curious
• putting on their trims, forget how day goes,
• nd then 'tis their good morrow when they are ready:
Go ſome and call her, and wait upon her hither,
Tell her the Duke and I deſire her company:
• warrant ye, a hundred dreſſings now
• he has ſurvey'd, this, and that faſhion look'd on,
• or Ruffs and Gowns; caſt this away, theſe Jewels
• uited to theſe and theſe knots: o' my life Sir,
• he fears your curious eye will ſoon diſcover elſe:
Why ſtand ye ſtill, why gape ye on one another?
Did I not bid ye go, and tell my Daughter?
Are ye nailed here? nor ſtir? nor ſpeak? who am I,
And who are you?

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: Pardon me, gracious Lady,
The fear to tell you that you would not hear of
Makes us all dumb, the Princeſs is gone, Madam.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Gone? whither gone? ſome wiſer fellow anſwer me

sp.speaker: 2 Lord.
sp.l: We ſought the Court all over, and believe Lady
No news of where ſhe is, nor how convey'd hence.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: It cannot be, it muſt not be.

sp.speaker: 1 Lord.
sp.l: 'Tis true, Madam,
No room in all the Court, but we ſearch'd through it,
Her women found her want firſt, and they cry'd to us.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Gone? ſtol'n away? I am abus'd, diſhonour'd,

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: 'Tis I that am abus'd, 'tis I diſhonour'd.
Is this your welcome, this your favour to me?
To foiſt a trick upon me, this trick too,
To cheat me of my love? Am I not worthy?
Or ſince I was your gueſt, am I grown odious?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Your Grace miſtakes me, as I have a life, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: And I another, I will never bear this,
Never endure this dor.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: But hear me patiently.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Give me my Love.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: As ſoon as care can find her,
And all care ſhall be uſed.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: And all my care too,
To be reveng'd; I ſmell the trick, 'tis too rank,
Fie, how it ſmells o' th' Mother.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: You wrong me, Duke.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: For this diſgrace ten thouſand Florentines
Shall pay their deareſt bloods, and dying curſe ye,
And ſo I turn away your mortal enemy. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Since ye are ſo high and hot Sir, ye have half arm'd us,
Be careful of the Town, of all the Caſtles,
And ſee ſupplies of Soldiers every where,
And Muſters for the Field when he invites us,
For he ſhall know 'tis not high words can fright us,
My Daughter gone? has ſhe ſo finely cozen'd me?
This is for Silvio's ſake ſure, Oh cunning falſe one;
Publiſh a Proclamation thorough the Dukedom.
That whoſoe'er can bring to th' Court young Silvio,
Alive or dead, beſide our thanks and favour,
Shall have two thouſand Duckets for his labour;
See it diſpatch'd, and ſent in haſte: Oh baſe one. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Iſabella, and Penurio with a Light.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Was't thou with Rugio?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Yes marry was I cloſely.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: And does he ſtill remember his poor Miſtriſs?
Does he deſire to ſee me?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Yes, and preſently:
Puts off all buſineſs elſe, lives in that memory,
And will be here according to directions,

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: But where's thy Maſter?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Where a coxcomb ſhould be,
Waiting at Court with his Jewels,
Safe for this night I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I am bound to thee.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I would ye were, as cloſe as I could tye ye,

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thou art my beſt, my trueſt friend.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I labour
I moil and toil for ye: I am your hackney.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: If ever I be able—

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Steal the great Cheeſe Miſtriſs,
Was ſent him out o'th' Countrey.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Any thing.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: That's meat, 'tis lawful Miſtriſs: where's the Caſtle Cuſtard.
He got at Court?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: He has lock'd it in's ſtudy.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Get a warrant to ſearch for counterfeit Gold.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Give me thy Candle,
I'll find a time to be thy careful Cater.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: And many a time I'll find to be his Cook,
And dreſs his Calves head to the ſweeteſt ſauce Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: To bed Penurio, go, the reſt is my charge,
I'll keep the Watch out.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Now if you ſpare him— Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Peace fool,
I hope my Rugio will not fail, 'twould vex me:
Now to my ſtring; ſo, ſure he cannot miſs now,
And this end to my finger I'll lie down,
For on a ſuddain I am wondrous heavy,
'Tis very late too; if he come and find this,
And pull it, though it be with eaſie motion
I ſhall ſoon waken, and as ſoon be with him.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Thou ſecret friend, how am I bound to love thee
And how to hug thee for thy private ſervice?
Thou art the Star all my ſuſpitions ſail by,
The fixed point my wronged honor turns to,
By thee I ſhall know all, find all the ſubtilties
Of deviliſh women, that torment me daily:
Thou art my Conjurer, my Spell, my Spirit,
All's huſh'd and ſtill, no ſound of any ſtirring,
No tread of living thing: the Light is in ſtill,
And there's my Wife, how prettily the fool lies,
How ſweet, and handſomely, and in her clothes too,
Waiting for me upon my life; her fondneſs
Would not admit her reſt till I came to her:
O careful fool, why am I angry with thee?
Why do I think thou hat'ſt thy loving Husband?
I am an Aſs, an over-doting Coxcomb,
And this ſweet ſoul, the mirror of perfection:
How admirable fair and delicate,
And how it ſtirs me, I'll ſing thy ſweets a Requiem,
But will not waken thee.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: OH fair ſweet face, oh eyes celeſtial bright,
Twin Stars in Heaven, that now adorn the night;
Oh fruitful Lips, where Cherries ever grow,
And Damask cheeks, where all ſweet beauties blow;
Oh thou from head to foot divinely fair,
Cupid's moſt cunning Nets made of that hair,
And as he weaves himſelf for curious eyes;
Oh me, Oh me, I am caught my ſelf, he cries:
Sweet teſt about thee ſweet and golden ſleep,
Soft peaceful thoughts, your hourly watches keep,
Whilſt I in wonder ſing this ſacrifice,
To beauty ſacred, and thoſe Angel-eyes.

sp.l: Now will I ſteal a kiſs, a dear kiſs from her,
And ſuck the Roſie breath of this bright beauty;
What a Devil is this? ty'd to her finger too?
A ſtring, a damned ſtring to give intelligence
Oh my lov'd key, how truly haſt thou ſerv'd me;
I • follow this: ſoft, ſoft, to th' door it goes,
And through to th' other ſide; a damned ſtring 'tis,
I am abus'd, topt, cuckolded, fool'd, jaded,
Ridden to death, to madneſs; ſtay, this helps not:
Stay, ſtay, and now invention help me,
I'll ſit down by her, take this from her eaſily,
And thus upon mine own: Dog, I ſhall catch ye,
With all your cunning, Sir: I ſhall light on ye,
I felt it pull ſure: yes, but wondrous ſoftly,
'Tis there again, and harder now, have at ye,
Now and thou ſcap'ſt, the Devil's thy ghoſtly father. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Sure 'twas my husband's voice, the ſtring is gone too,
He has found the trick on't: I am undone, betray'd,
And if he meet my friend he periſhes,
What fortune follows me, what ſpightful fortune?
Hoa Jaquenet.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Here Miſtriſs, do you call me?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Didſt thou hear no noiſe?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I hear my Maſter mad yonder,
And ſwears, and chafes—

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Dar'ſt thou do one thing for me?
One thing concerns mine honor, all is loſt elſe?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Name what you will.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: It can bring but a beating,
Which I will recompence ſo largely—

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Name it.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Sit here, as if thou wert aſleep.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Is that all?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: When he comes in, whate'er he do unto thee
(The worſt will be but beating) ſpeak not a word,
Not one word as thou loveſt me.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I'll run through it.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I'll carry away the Candle. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And I the blows Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Have you put your light out? I ſhall ſtumble to ye,
You whore, you cunning whore, I ſhall catch your rogue too,
H'as light legs elſe, I had ſo Ferret-claw'd him:
Oh have I found ye? do ye play at dog-ſleep ſtill whore?
Do you think that can protect ye? yes, I will kill thee,
But firſt I'll bring thy friends to view thy villanies,
Thy whoriſh villanies: and firſt I'll beat thee,
Beat thee to pin-duſt, thou falt whore, thou varlet,
Scratch out thine eyes; I'll ſpoil your tempting viſage;
Are ye ſo patient? I'll put my nails in deeper,
Is it good whoring? whoring ye baſe raſcal?
Is it good tempting men with ſtrings to ride ye?
So, I'll fetch your kindred, and your friends, whore,
And ſuch a Juſtice I will act upon thee. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: What is he gone?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: The Devil go with him Miſtriſs,
Has harrowed me, plough'd Land was ne'r ſo harrow'd:
I had the moſt adoe to ſave mine eyes.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Has paid thee,
•• t I'll heal all again with good Gold. Jaquenet;
H'as damned nails.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: They are ten-penny nails I think Miſtriſs:
I'll undertake he ſhall ſtrike 'em through an inch board.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Go up, and waſh thy ſelf: take my Pomatum,
And now let me alone to end the Tragedy.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: You had beſt beware.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I ſhall deal ſtoutly with him,
Reach me my Book, and ſee the door made faſt wench,
And ſo good night: now to the matter politick.

sp.speaker: Lop. Within.
sp.l: You ſhall ſee what ſhe is, what a ſweet jewel.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Who's there, what mad-man knocks? is this an hour
And in mine Husband's abſence?

sp.speaker: Lop. Within.
sp.l: Will ye open?
You know my voice ye whore, I am that Husband:
Do you mark her ſubtilty? but I have paid her,
I have ſo ferk'd her face: here's the blood Gentlemen,
Ecce ſignum: I have ſpoil'd her Goatiſh beauty,
Obſerve her how ſhe looks now, how ſhe is painted,
Oh 'tis the moſt wicked'ſt whore, and the moſt treacherous—

div.stage: Enter Lopez, Bartello, Gent. and two Gentlewomen.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Here walks my coſin full of meditation,
Arm'd with religious thoughts.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Is this the monſter?

sp.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
sp.l: Is this the ſubject of that rage you talk'd of,
That naughty woman you had pull'd a-pieces?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Here's no ſuch thing.

sp.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
sp.l: How have ye wrong'd this beauty?
Are not you mad my friend? what time o' th' moon is't?
Have not you Maggots in your brains?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe ſure.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Where's the ſcratch'd face ye ſpoke of, the torn garments,
And all the hair pluck'd off her head?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Believe me.
'Twere better far you had loſt your pair of pibbles,
Than ſhe the leaſt adornment of that ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Is not this blood?

sp.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
sp.l: This is a monſtrous folly,
A baſe abuſe.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thus he does ever uſe me,
And ſticks me up a wonder, not a woman,
Nothing I doe, but's ſubject to ſuſpition;
Nothing I can do, able to content him.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Lopez, you muſt not use this.

sp.speaker: 2 Gentlew.
sp.l: 'Twere not amiſs, Sir.
To give ye ſauce to your meat, and ſuddainly.

sp.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
sp.l: You that dare wrong a woman of her goodneſs,
Thou have a Wife, thou have a Bear ty'd to thee,
To ſcratch thy jealous itch, were all o' my mind,
I mean all women, we would disburthen ye
Of that that breeds theſe fits, theſe dog-flaws in ye,
A Sow-guelder ſhould trim ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: A rare cure Lady,
And one as fit for him as a Thief for a halter,
You ſee this youth: will you not cry him quittance,
Body 'me, I would pine, but I would pepper him,
I'll come anon, he, hang him, poor pompillion:
How like a wench bepiſt he looks, I'll come Lady;
Lopez, The Law muſt teach ye what a wife is,
A good, a virtuous wife.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I'll ne'r live with him,
I crave your loves all to make known my cauſe,
That ſo a fair Divorce may paſs between us,
I am weary of my life: in danger hourly.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You ſee how rude you are, I will not miſs ye,
Unſufferable rude: I'll pay him ſoundly,
You ſhould be whipt in Bedlam: I'll reward him.

sp.speaker: 2 Gentlew.
sp.l: Whipping's too good.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I think I am alive ſtill,
And in my wits.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'll put a trick upon him,
And get his goods confiſcate: you ſhall have 'em;
I will not fail at nine.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I think I am here too,
And once I would have ſworn I had taken her napping,
I think my name is Lopez.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Fie for ſhame, Sir,
You ſee you have abus'd her, fouly wrong'd her,
Hung ſcandalous and courſe opinions on her,
Which now you find but children of ſuſpition:
Ask her forgiveneſs, ſhew a penitence,
She is my kinſwoman, and what ſhe ſuffers
Under ſo baſe and beaſtly jealouſies,
I will redreſ • elſe, I'll ſeek ſatisfaction.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Why, every boy i'th' Town will piſs upon thee.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I am ſorry for't.

sp.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
sp.l: Down o' your marrow-bones.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Even ſorry from my heart: forgive me ſweet wife,
Here I confeſs moſt freely I have wrong'd ye,
As freely here I beg a pardon of ye,
From this hour no debate, no croſs ſuſpition—

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: To ſhew ye Sir I underſtand a wives part,
Thus I aſſure my love, and ſeal your pardon.

sp.speaker: 2 Gentlew.
sp.l: 'Tis well done, now to bed, and there confirm it.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: And ſo good night.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Aware relapſes,, Lopez. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Now Iſabella tell me truth, and ſuddainly,
And do not juggle with me, nor diſſemble,
For as I have a life ye dye then: I am not mad,
Nor does the Devil work upon my weakneſs,
Tell me the trick of this, and tell me freely.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Will then that ſatisfie ye?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: If ye deal ingeniouſly.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I'll tell ye all, and tell ye true and freely.
Bartello was the end of all this jealouſie,
H • s o • ten viſitations brought by you, firſt
Bred all theſe fits, and theſe ſuſpitions:
I knew your falſe key, and accordingly
I fram'd my plot, to have you take him finely,
Too poor a pennance for the wrong his wife bears,
His worthy virtuous wife: I felt it ſenſibly
When ye took off the ſtring, and was much pleas'd in't,
Becauſe I wiſh'd his importunate dotage paid well,
And had you ſtaid two minutes more, ye had had him.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: This ſounds like truth.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Becauſe this ſhall be certain,
Next time he comes, as long he cannot tarry,
Your ſelf ſhall ſee, and hear, his lewd temptations.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Till then I am ſatisfied, and if this prove true,
Hence-forward Miſtriſs of your ſelf I give ye,
And I to ſerve ye: For my luſty Captain,
I'll make him dance, and make him think the Devil
Claws at his breech, and yet I will not hurt him:
Come now to bed, and prove but conſtant this way,
I'll prove the man you ever wiſhed.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You have bleſt me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Silv.
sp.l: VVHat labour and what travel have I run through
And through what Cities to abſolve this Riddle
Diviners, Dreamers, School-men, deep Magicians,
All have I try'd, and all give ſeveral meaning,
And from all hope of any future happineſs,
To this place am I come at length, the Countrey,
The people ſimple, plain, and harmleſs witty,
Whoſe honeſt labours Heaven rewards with plenty
Of Corn, Wine, Oyl, which they again as thankful,
To their new Crops, new paſtimes celebrate,
And crown their joyful harveſts with new voices;
By a rich Farmer here I am entertain'd,
And rank'd among the number of his ſervants,
Not gueſſing what I am, but what he would have me,
Here may be ſo much wit (though much I fear it)
To undo this knotty queſtion; and would to Heaven.
My fortunes had been hatch'd with theirs, as innocent,
And never known a pitch above their plainneſs.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: That it is, that it is, what's this word now? this
Is a plaguy word, that it is r. e. a. that it is, reaſon,
By your leave, Mr. Soto, by your leave, you are too quick, Sir,
There's a ſtrange parlous T. before the reaſon,
A very tall T. which makes the word High Treaſon.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: What Treaſon's that? does this fellow underſtand Himſelf?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Pitch will infect, I'll meddle no more with this geer;
What a devil ails this fellow? this fooliſh fellow?
Being admitted to be one of us too,
That are the maſters of the ſports proceeding,
Thus to appear before me too, unmorris'd?
Do you know me friend?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: You are my Maſters Son, Sir,

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: And do you know what ſports are now in ſeaſon?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I hear there are ſome a-foot.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Where are your Bells then?
Your Rings, your Ribons, friend? & your clean Napkins?
Your Noſegay in your hat, pinn'd up, am not I here?
My fathers eldeſt Son, and at this time, Sir,
I would have ye know it, though ye be ten times his ſervant
A better man than my father far, Lord of this Harveſt, Sir,
And ſhall a man of my place want attendance?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Twas want of knowledge, Sir, not duty, bred this,
I would have made Suit elſe for your Lordſhips ſervice.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: In ſome ſort I am ſatisfied now, mend your manners,
But thou art a melancholy fellow, vengeance melancholy,
And that may breed an inſurrection amongſt us;
Go too, I'll lay the beſt part of two pots now
Thou art in love, and I can gueſs with whom too,
I ſaw the wench that twir'd and twinkled at thee,
The other day; the wench that's new come hither,
The young ſmug wench.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: You know more than I feel Sir.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Go too, I'll be thy friend, I'll ſpeak a good word for thee,
And thou ſhalt have my Lordſhips countenance to her;
May be I have had a ſnap my ſelf, may be I, may be no,
We Lords are allow'd a little more.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Tis fit, Sir,
I humbly thank ye, you are too too tender of me,
But what Sir, I beſeech ye, was that paper,
Your Lordſhip was ſo ſtudiouſly imployed in,
When ye came out a-doors?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Thou meaneſt this paper.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: That Sir, I think.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Why, 'tis a Proclamation,
A notable piece of villany, as ever thou heard'ſt in thy life,
By mine honor it is.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: How Sir? or what concerns it?

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: It comes ye from the Dutcheſs, a plaguy wiſe woman,
To apprehend the body of one Silvio,
As arrant a Raſcal as ever piſt againſt a poſt,
And this ſame Silvio, or this foreſaid raſcal,
To bring before her, live or dead; for which good ſervice
The man that brings him, has two thouſand Duckets;
Is not this notable matter now?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo indeed,
This Proclamation bears my bane about it;
Can no reſt find me? no private place ſecure me?
But ſtill my miſeries like blood-hounds haunt me?
Unfortunate young man, which way now guides thee,
Guides thee from death? the Countrey's laid round for thee,
Oh Claudi • , now I feel thy blood upon me,
Now it ſpeaks loudly here, I am ſure againſt me,
Time now has found it out, and truth proclaim d it,
And Juſtice now crie • out, I muſt die for it.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Haſt thou read it?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: And doſt thou know that Silvio.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I never ſaw him, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I have, and know him too,
I know him as well as I know thee, and better,
And if I light upon him, for a trick he plaid me once,
A certain kind of dog-trick, I'll ſo fiddle him,
Two thouſand Duckets, I'll ſo pepper him,
And with that money I'll turn Gentleman,
Worth a brown Baker's dozen of ſuch Silvios.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: There is no ſtaying here, this rogue will know me,
And for the money ſake betray me too;
I muſt bethink me ſuddenly and ſafely.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Mine own dear Lady, have-at-thy honey-comb,
Now, for the honor of our Town, Boyes, trace ſweetly,
Who a vengeance ails this whobub: pox refuſe 'em,
Cannot they let us dance in our own defence here?

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.l: Arm, honeſt friends, arm ſuddenly and bravely,
And with your antient reſolutions follow me;
Look how the Beacons ſhow like Comets, your poor neighbors
Run maddingly affrighted through the Villages;
Syenna's Duke is up, burns all before him,
And with his ſword, makes thouſand mothers childleſs.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: What's this to our Morris-dancers?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: This may ſerve my turn.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: There's ne'r a Duke in Chriſtendom but loves a May-game.

sp.speaker: Capt.
sp.l: At a horſe you were always ceaz'd, put your Son on him,
And arm him well i'th' States name, I command ye;
And they that dare go voluntary, ſhall receive reward.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I dare go no way, Sir, this is ſtrange, Maſter Captain,
You cannot be content to ſpoil our ſport here,
Which I do not think your Worſhip's able to anſwer,
But you muſt ſet us together by the ears with I know not who too?
We are for the bodily part o'th' dance.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Arm him ſuddainly,
This is no time to fool, I ſhall return ye elſe,
A rebel to the General, State, and Ducheſs,
And how you'll anſwer then —

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: I have no more Sons, Sir,
This is my only boy; I beſeech ye Maſter Captain.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I am a rank coward too, to ſay the truth, Sir,
I never had good luck at buffets neither.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Here's vorty ſhillings, ſpare the child

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: I cannot.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Are ye a man? will ye caſt away a May-Lord?
Shall all the wenches in the Countrey curſe ye?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: An't pleaſe you Captain, I'll ſupply his perſon,
'Tis pity their old cuſtom ſhould be frighted,
Let me have Horſe, and good Arms, I'll ſerve willingly,
And if I ſhrink a foot of ground, Hell take me.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: A promiſing Aſpect, face full of courage,
I'll take this man, and thank ye too.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: There's for thee,
'Tis in a clout, but good old Gold.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I thank ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Goe ſaddle my fore-horſe, put his feather on too,
He'll praunce it bravely, friend, he fears no Colours,
And take the Armor down, and ſee him dizin'd,

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Farewel, and if thou cary'ſt thy ſelf well in this matter,
I ſay no more, but this, there muſt be more May-Lords,
And I know who are fit.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Dance you, I'll fight, Sir,

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Away, away.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Farewel, I am for the Captain. Exit.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Now to this matter again my honeſt fellows,
For if this goe not forward, I • oreſee friends,
This war will fright our neighbors out o'th' villages;
Cheer up your hearts, we ſha •• hear better news, boys.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: Surely I will dance no more, 'tis moſt ridiculous,
I find my wives inſtructions now mere verities,
My learned wives, ſhe often hath pronounc'd to me
My ſafety Bomby, defie theſe ſports, thou art damn'd elſe,
This Beaſt of Babylon, I will never back again,
His pace is ſure prophane, and his lewd Wi-hees,
The Sons of Hymyn and Gymyn, in the wilderneſs.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Fie neighbor Bomby, in your fits again,
Your zeal ſweats, this is not careful, neighbor,
The Hobby-horſe, is a ſeemly Hobby-horſe.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: And as pretty a beaſt on's inches, though I ſay it.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: The Beaſt is an unſeemly, and a lewd Beaſt,
And got at Rome by the Popes oach-Horſes,
His mother was the Mare of ignorance.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Cobler thou ly'ſt, and thou wert a thouſand Coblers
His mother was an honeſt Mare, and a Mare of good credit,
I know the Mare, and if need be, can bring witneſs;
And in the way of honeſty I tell thee,
Scorn'd any Coach-Horſe the Pope had: thou art fooliſh,
And thy blind zeal makes thee abuſe the Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I do defie thee, and thy foot-cloth too,
And tell thee to thy face, this prophane riding
I feel it in my conſcience, and I dare ſpeak it,
This un-edified ambling, hath brought a ſcourge upon us,
This Hobby-horſe ſincerity we • iv'd in
War, and the ſword of ſlaughter: • renounce it,
And put the beaſt off, thus, the beaſt po • luted,
And now no more ſhall hop on high Bomby,
Follow the painted pipes of high pleaſures.
And with the wicked, dance the devils meaſures;
Away thou pamper'd jade of vanity,
Stand at the Livery of lewd delights now,
And eat the provinder of prick-ear'd • o • ly,
My dance ſhall be to the pipe of perſecution.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: Will you daunce no more neighbor?

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: Surely no,
Carry the Beaſt to his Crib: I have renounc'd him
And all his works.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Shall the Hobby-horſe be forgot then?
The hopeful Hobby-horſe, ſhall he lye founder'd?
If thou do'ſt this, thou art but a caſt-away Cobler:
My anger's up, think wiſely, and think quickly,
And look upon the quondam beaſt of pleaſure,
If thou doſt this (mark me, thou ſerious Sowter)
Thou Bench-whiſtler of the old tribe of toe-pieces,
If thou doſt this, there ſhall be no more ſhooe-mending,
Every man ſhall have a ſpecial care of his own ſoul:
And in his pocket carry his two Confeſſors,
His Yugel, and his Nawl: if thou doſt this —

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: He will dance again for certain.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I cry out on't,
'Twas the fore-running ſin brought in thoſe Tilt-ſtaves,
They brandiſh 'gainſt the Church, the devil calls May-poles,

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Take up your Horſe again, and girth him to ye,
And girth him handſomely, good neighbor Bomby.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I ſpit at him.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Spit in the Horſe face, Cobler?
Thou out of tune, Pſalm-ſinging ſlave; ſpit in his viſnomy?

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I ſpit again, and thus I riſe againſt him:
Againſt this Beaſt: that ſignify'd deſtruction.
Fore-ſhew'd i'th' falls of Monarchies.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: I'th' face of him?
Spit ſuch another ſpit by this hand Cobler
I'll make ye ſet a new piece o' your noſe there,
Tak't up I ſay, and dance without more bidding,
And dance as you were wont: you have been excellent
And art ſtill, but for this new nicity,
And your wives learned Lectures: take up the Hobby-horſe
Come, 'tis a thing thou haſt lov'd with all thy heart Bomby,
And would'ſt do ſtill but for the round-breech'd brothers:
You were not thus in the morning; tak't up I ſay,
Do not delay but do it: you know I am officer;
And I know 'tis unfit all theſe good fellows
Should wait the cooling of your zealous porridge;
Chuſe whether you will dance, or have me execute:
• 'll clap your neck i'th' ſtocks, and thrre I'll make ye
Dance a whole day, and dance with theſe at night too,
You mend old ſhooes well, mend your old manners better,
And ſuddenly ſee you leave off this ſincereneſs.
This new hot Batch, borrowed from ſome brown Baker,
Some learned brother, or I'll ſo bait ye for't,
Take it quickly up.

sp.speaker: Hob.
sp.l: I take my perſecution,
And thus I am forc'd a by-word to my brethren.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Strike up, ſtrike up: ſtrike merrily.

sp.speaker: Far.
sp.l: To it roundly,
Now to the harveſt feaſt: then ſport again boyes. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: What ſhall I do? live thus unknown, and baſe ſtill?
Or thruſt my ſelf into the head o'th' Battel?
And there like that I am, a Gentleman,
And one that never fear'd the face of danger,
(So in her angry eyes ſte carried honor)
Fight nobly, and (to end my cares) die nobly?

body.head: Song within.
body.l: SIlvio go on, and raiſe thy noble mind
To noble ends; fling courſe baſe thoughts behind:
Silvio, thou Son of everliving fame,
Now aim at virtue, and a Noble Name.
Silvio conſider, Honor is not won,
Nor virtue reach'd, till ſome brave thing be done:
Thy Countrey calls thee now; ſhe burns, and bleeds,
Now raiſe thy ſelf, young man, to noble deeds.
Into the battel Silvio, there ſeek forth
Danger, and blood, by them ſtands ſacred worth.

sp.l: What heavenly voice is this that follows me?
This is the ſecond time 't has waited on me,
Since I was arm'd, and ready for the battel;
It names me often, ſteels my heart with courage.
And in a thouſand ſweet notes comforts me;
What Beldam's this? how old ſhe is, and ugly,
Why does ſhe follow me?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Be not diſmaid Son,
I wait upon thee for thy good, and honor,
'Twas I that now ſung to thee, ſtirr'd thy mind up,
And rais'd thy ſpirits to the pitch of nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Though ſhe be old, and of a crooked carkaſs,
Her voice is like the harmony of Angels.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Thou art my darling, all my love dwels on thee
The Son of virtue, therefore I attend thee;
Enquire not what I am, I come to ſerve thee,
For if thou be'ſt inquiſitive, thou haſt loſt me:
A thouſand long miles hence my dwelling is,
Deep in a Cave, where but mine own, no foot treads,
There by mine Art, I found what danger (Silvio)
And deep diſtreſs of heart, thou wert grown into,
A thouſand Leagues I have cut through empty air,
Far ſwifter than the ſayling rack that gallops
Upon the wings of angry winds, to ſeek thee.
Sometimes o'er a ſwelling tide, on a Dolphins back I ride,
Sometimes paſs the earth below, and through the unmoved Center go;
Sometimes in a flame of fire, like a Meteor I aſpire,
Sometimes in mine own ſhape, thus, when I help the virtuous,
Men of honourable minds, command my Art in all his kinds;
Purſue the noble thought of War, from thy Guard I'll not be far,
Get thee worſhip on thy foe, laſting Fame is gotten ſo.
Single Syennas Duke alone, hear thy friends, thy Countrey groan,
And with thy manly arm ſtrike ſure, then thou haſt wrought thine own free cure.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Some Sybel ſure, ſome ſoul heaven loves, and favours.
And lends her their free powers, to work their wonders?
How ſhe incites my courage?

sp.speaker: Bel.

l.hi: Sylvio,

sp.l: I knew thee many daies ago,
Foreſaw thy love to Belvidere, the Dutcheſs daughter, and her Heir;
Knew ſhe lov'd thee, and know what paſt; when you were found i'th' Caſtle faſt
In one anothers arms; forſaw the taking of ye and the Law
And ſo thy innocence I loved, the deepeſt of my skill I proved;
Be rul'd by me, for to this hour, I have dwelt about thee with my power.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I will, and in the courſe of all obſerve thee,
For thou art ſure an Angel ſent to me.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Get thee gone then to the fight, longer ſtay but robs thy right;
When thou grow'ſt weary I'll be near, then think on beauteous Belvidere,
For every precious thought of her, I'll lend thine honor a new ſpurre;
When all is done, meet here at night; Go and be happy in the ſight. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I certainly believe I ſhall do nobly,
And that I'll bravely reach at too, or die. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Is the ſo loving ſtill?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: She is mad with Love,
As mad as ever unworm'd dog was, Signior,
And does ſo weep, and curſe, for your prevention,
Your croſſes in your love; it frets me too,
I am fall'n away to nothing, to a ſpindle,
Grown a meer man of mat, no ſoul within me,
Pox o'my Maſter, Sir, will that content ye?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: This rogue but cozens me, and ſhe neglects me,
Upon my life there are ſome other gameſters,
Nearer the wind than I, and that prevents me,
Is there no other holds acquaintance with her?
Prethee be true, be honeſt, do not mock me,
Thou knoweſt her heart, no former intereſt
She has vow'd a favour too? and cannot handſomely
Go off, but by regaining ſuch a friendſhip?
There are a thouſand handſome men, young, wealthy,
That will not ſtick at any rate, nor danger,
To gain ſo ſweet a prize; nor can I blame her,
If where ſhe finds a comfort, ſhe deal cunningly,
I am a ſtranger yet.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Ye are all ſhe looks for,
And if there be any other, ſhe neglects all,
And all for you: I would you ſaw how grievouſly
And with what hourly lamentations.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I know thou flatter'ſt me; tell me but truth,
Look here, look well, the beſt meat in the Dukedom,
The rareſt, and the choiceſt of all Diets,
The will I give thee, but to ſatisfie me;
That is, not to diſſemble; this rare Lobſter,
This Pheaſant of the Sea, this diſh for Princes,
And all this thou ſhalt enjoy, eat all thy ſelf,
Have good Greek Wine, or any thing belongs to it,
A wench, if it deſire one.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: All this, Signior?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: All, and a greater far than this.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A greater?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If thou deſerve by telling truth.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: A wench too?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Or any thing, but if you play the knave now,
The cozening knave, beſides the loſs of this,
In which thou haſt parted with a paradiſe,
I ne'er will give thee meat more, not a morſel,
No ſmell of meat by my means ſhall come near thee,
Nor name of any thing that's nouriſhing,
But to thy old part Tantalus again,
Thou ſhalt return, and there ſnap at a ſhadow.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Upon this point, had I intended Treaſon,
Or any thing might call my life in queſtion,
Follow'd with all the tortures time could think on,
Give me but time to eat this lovely Lobſter,
This Alderman o'th' Sea, and give me Wine to him,
I would reveal all, and if that all were too little,
More than I knew; Bartello holds in with her,
The Captain of the Cittadel, but you need not fear him,
His tongue's the ſtiffeſt weapon that he carries.
He is old, and out of uſe; there are ſome other,
Men, young enough, handſome, and bold enough,
Could they come but to make their game once; but they want Sir,
They want the unde quare, they are laid by then.
You only are the man ſhall knock the nail in—

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: How now Penurio?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Your worſhip's fairly met, Sir.
You ſhall hear further from me, ſteal aſide, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Remember your Maſter for thoſe Chains.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: They are ready, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: What young thing's this? by his habit he's a Merchant;
• fear he trades my way too, you dryed dog-fiſh,
What bait was that?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Who Sir, the thing went hence now?
A notable young whelp.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: To what end ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Came to buy Chains and Rings, is to be married,
An Aſſe, a Coxcomb, h'as nothing in's houſe Sir;
I warrant you think he came to ſee my Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: I doubt it ſhrewdly.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Away, away 'tis fooliſh;
He has not the face to look upon a Gentlewoman,
A poor skim'd thing, his Mothers maids are fain, Sir
To teach him how to kiſs, and againſt he is married,
To ſhew him on which ſide the ſtirrop ſtands.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: That's a fine youth.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Thou wouldſt hang thy ſelf, that thou hadſt half his power,
Thou empty Potgun.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Am I come fit Penurio?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: As fit as a fiddle,
My Maſter's now abroad about his buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: When thou cam'ſt to me home to day, I half ſuſpected
My wife was jealous, that ſhe whispered to thee.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: You deſerve well the whilſt, there's no ſuch matter,
She talk'd about ſome toyes my Maſter muſt bring to her,
You muſt not know of.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: I'll take no noat Penurio.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: No, nor you ſhall not, till yon have it ſoundly.
This is the braveſt Capitano Pompo.
But I ſhall pump ye anon, Sir.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Oh my Bartello

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Ye pretty Rogue; you little Rogue, you ſweet Rogue,
Away Penurio, go and walk i'th' Horſe-Fair.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You do not love me?

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Thou lieſt, thou little raſcal;
There ſirrah, to your Centry.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: How the Colt itches?
I'll help ye to a Curry-comb ſhall claw ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: And how much doſt thou love me?

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Let's go in quickly,
I'll tell thee preſently, I'll meaſure it to thee.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: No buſſes firſt? ſit o'my knee, my brave boy,
My valiant boy; do not look ſo fiercely on me,
Thou wilt fright me with thy face; come buſs again Chick,
Smile in my face you mad thing.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: I am mad indeed wench,
Precious, I am all o' fire.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I'll warm thee better.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I'll warm thee too, or I'll blow out my bellows;
Ha, ye ſweet rogue, you loving rogue, a boy now,
A Soldier I will get ſhall prove a fellow.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Miſtriſs, look to your ſelf, my Maſter's coming.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: The devil come, and go with him.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The devil's come indeed, he brings your wife, Sir.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: We are undone, undone then.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: My wife with him?
Why this is a diſmal day.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: They are hard by too, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I muſt not, dare not ſee her.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Nor my Husband,
For twenty thouſand pound.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That I were a Cat now,
Or any thing could run into a Bench-hole,
Saint Anthonies Fire upon the rogue has brought her;
Where ſhall I be? juſt i'th' nick o'th' matter?
When I had her at my mercy? think for heaven ſake,
My wife, all the wild furies hell has.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Up the Chimney.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: They'll ſmoke me out there preſently.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: There, there, it muſt be there,
We are all undone elſe: it muſt be up the Chimney.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Give me a Ladder.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You muſt uſe your Art, Sir,
Alas, we have no Ladders.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Pox o'thy Husband,
Does he never mend his houſe?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: No, nor himſelf neither:
Up nimbly, Sir, up nimbly.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt I am fat,
Thou mercileſs lean rogue.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Will ye be kill'd?
For if he take ye —

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Lend me thy ſhoulder.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Soft, Sir,
You'll tread my ſhoulder-bones into my ſides elſe,
Have ye faſt hold o'th' barrs?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: A vengeance barr 'em.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Patience good Captain, Patience: quickly, quickly.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do you think I am made of ſmoke?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Now he talks of ſmoke,
What if my Maſter ſhould call for fire?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Will ye Martyr me?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: He muſt needs have it.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Will ye make me Bacon?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: We'll do the beſt we can, are all things ready?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: All, all, I have 'em all.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Go let 'em in then,
Not a word now on your life.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I hang like a Meteor.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: You are welcome Lady.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: You are too too courteous,
But I ſhall make amends, fair Iſabella.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Welcome my worthy friend, moſt kindly welcome.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: I hear on't, and I'll fit him for his foolery.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Some Sweet meats wife: ſome Sweet meats preſently.

sp.speaker: Bart.
sp.l: Oh my ſowre ſauce.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l:
Away quick Iſabella.
Exit Iſab.
Did you hear him?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Yes, yes, perfectly, proceed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Speak loud enough: Dare ye at length but pity me?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: 'Faith Sir, you have us'd ſo many reaſons to me,
And thoſe ſo powerfully —

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Keep this kiſs for me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And do I ſtand and hear this?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: This for me, Sir,
This is ſome comfort now: Alas my Husband—
But why do I think of ſo poor a fellow,
So wretched, ſo debauch'd?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: That's I, I am bound to hear it.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: I dare not lye with him, he is ſo rank a Whoremaſter.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And that's a dangerous point.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Upon my conſcience, Sir,
He would ſtick a thouſand baſe diſeaſes on me.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And now muſt I ſay nothing.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I am ſound Lady.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: That's it that makes me love ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Let's kiſs again then.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Do, do.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Do, the Devil
And the grand Pox do with ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Do ye hear him? well —
Now, what's the news with you?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The ſound of War, Sir,
Comes ſtill along: The Duke will charge the City,
We have loſt they ſay.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: What ſhall become of me then,
And my poor wealth;

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Even hang'd, I hope.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Remove your Jewels preſently,
And what you have of wealth into the Cittadel,
There all's ſecure.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I humbly thank ye Lady:
Penurio, get me ſome can climb the Chimney,
For there my Jewels are, my beſt, my richeſt,
I hid 'em, fearing ſuch a blow.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Moſt happily:
I have two boys that uſe to ſweep foul Chimneys,
Truly I brought 'em, Sir, to mock your worſhip,
For the great Fires ye keep, and the full Diet.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I forgive thee knave, where are they?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Here Sir, here:
Monſieur Black, will your ſmall worſhip mount:

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Madam è be com to creep up into your
Chimney, and make you Boy ſings.
Cleane, as any Lady in de world: Ma litla, litla frera, and è,
Chanta, frere, chanta.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Come Monſieur, mountè, mountè, mount Monſieur Muſtard-pot. Boy ſings.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: Monſieur è have dis for votra barba, ple ta vou Monſieur.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Mount è Monſieur, mountè dere be ſome fine tings.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: He will creep like de Ferret Monſieur.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Dere in the Chimney. The Boy above ſinging.

sp.speaker: 1 Boy.
sp.l: He be de ſheilde due ſhauſon, Madam.

div.stage: Boy goes in behind the Arras.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: There's a Birds-neſt, I wou'd have ye climb it Monſieur,
Up my fine ſinging Monſieur: that's a fine Monſieur.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Watch him, he do not ſteal.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I warrant ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Theſe Boys are knaviſh. Boy within, Madam here be de Rat, de Rat, Madam.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I'll look to him tightly

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Lord, what comes here,
A walking apparition? Boy ſings upon Bartello's Shoulder.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Saint Chriſtopher.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Mercy o' me, what is it?
How like my Husband it looks?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Get ye down devil,
I'll break your neck elſe: was ever man thus chimnied?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Go pay the boys well; ſee them ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Come Monſieur Devils, come my Black-berries
I'll butter ye o'both ſides.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Nay, ev'n look Sir, are you cooled now, Captain?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: I am cuckolled, and fool'd to boot too:
Fool'd fearfully, fool'd ſhamefully.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: You are welcome Sir,
I am glad I have any thing within theſe doors Sir
To make ye merry: you love my wife, I thank ye.
You have ſhew'd your love.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Wife, am I this? this odd matter,
This monſtrous thing?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: You ought, but yet you are not:
I have been bold with you Sir, but yet not baſely,
As I have faith I have not.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Sir, believe it,
'Twas all meant but to make you feel your treſpaſs;
We knew your hour, and all this faſhion'd for it.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Were you o'th' plot too?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Yes by my troth, ſweet Captain.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: You will forgive me wife?

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: You will deſerve it?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: Put that to th' venture.

sp.speaker: Rho.
sp.l: Thus am I friends again then,
And as you ne'er had gone aſtray, thus kiſs ye.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.l: And I'll kiſs you, and you too ask forgiveneſs,
Kiſs my wife Lopez, 'tis but in jeſt remember;
And now all friends together to my Caſtle,
Where we'll all dine, and there diſcourſe theſe ſtories,
And let him be Chimney-ſwept in's luſt that glories. Ex •

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Hail reverend Dame, heaven wait upon thy ſtudie •

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: You are all well met Son: what is the Battel ended

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Mother, 'tis done.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: How has thy honour proſper'd?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: The Dutcheſs has the day, Syenna's priſoner:
Arm'd with thy powerful Art, this arm diſmounted him,
Receiv'd him then on foot, and in fair valour.
Forc'd him mine own, this Jewel I took from him,
It hung upon his cask, the Victors triumph:
And to the Dutcheſs now a Priſoner
I have render'd him: Come off again unknown, Mother.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: 'Tis well done, let me ſee the Jewel Son;
'Tis a rich one, curious ſet, fit for a Princeſs Burgonet:
This rich Token late was ſent, by the Dutcheſs with inter ••
The Marriage next day to begin: Doſt thou know what' • hid within?
Wipe thine eyes, and then come near, ſee the beaut • ous Belvidere:
Now behold it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Oh my Saint.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Wear it nobly, do not faint.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: How bleſt am I in this rich ſpoil, this Picture,
For ever will I keep it here, here Mother,
For ever honor it: how oft, how chaſtly
Have I embrac'd the life of this, and kiſt it?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: The day draws on that thou muſt home return,
And make thy anſwer to the Dutcheſs queſtion
I know it troubles thee, for if thou fail in't.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Oh, I muſt dye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Fear not, fear not, 'Ill be nigh,
Caſt thy trouble on my back, Art nor cunning ſhall not lack,
To preſerve thee, ſtill to keep, what thy envious foemen ſeek;
Go boldly home, and let thy mind, no diſtruſtful croſſes find:
All ſhall happen for the beſt; ſouls walk through ſorrows that are bleſt.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Then I go confident.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: But firſt my Son, a thankful ſervice muſt be done,
The good old woman for her pain, when every thing ſtands fair again,
Muſt ask a poor Boon, and that granting, there's nothing to thy journey wanting.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Except the trial of my ſoul to miſchief,
And as I am a Knight, and love mine honor,
I grant it whatſoever.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Thy pure ſoul
Shall never ſink for me, nor howl.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Then any thing.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: When I ſhall ask, remember.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: If I forget, heavens goodneſs forget me.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: On thy journey then awhile, to the next croſs way and ſtile,
I'll conduct thee, keep thee true, to thy Miſtriſs and thy vow,
And let all their envies fall, I'll be with thee, and quench all. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: LAdy, the ſtubborn war's more mild than you are,
That allows Ranſom, and the Priſoner taken—

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: We muſt not be too haſty: Remember Sir,
The wrong and violence you have offer'd us,
Burnt up our frontier Towns, made prey before ye
Both of our Beaſts, and Corn; ſlain our dear ſubjects,
Open'd the fountain eyes of thouſand widows,
That daily fling their curſes on your fury;
What ordinary ſatisfaction can ſalve this?
What haſty thought-on Ranſome give a remedy?
You muſt excuſe us yet, we'll take more counſel:
In the mean time, not as a priſoner,
But as a noble Prince we entertain ye.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: I am at your mercy Lady, 'tis my fortune,
My ſtubborn fate; the day is yours, you have me,
The valour of one ſingle man has croſs'd me,
Croſt me and all my hope; for when the Battel's
Were at the hotteſt game of all their furies,
And conqueſt ready then to crown me Victor.
One ſingle man broke in, one ſword, one vertue,
And by his great example thouſands followed,
Oh how I ſhame to think on't, how it ſhakes me!
Nor could our ſtrongeſt head then ſtop his fury,
But like a tempeſt bore the field before him,
Till he arriv'd at me, with me he buck'lled,
A while I held him play; at length his violence
Beat me from my ſaddle, then on foot purſu'd me,
There triumph'd once again, then took me priſoner:
When I was gone, a fear poſſeſt my people.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: One ſingle arm, in a juſt cauſe, heaven proſpers.
Is not this ſtranger Knight as yet diſcover'd,
That we may give his virtue a due honor?

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: Not yet that we hear Madam, but to that purpoſe,
Two daies ago we publiſh'd Proclamations.

div.stage: Enter Soto with a Trumpet, and Silvio.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Oh dainty Dutcheſs, here I bring that Knight
Before thy fragrant face, that warlike wight,
He that Syenna's Duke, and all his Louts
Beat (as the Proverb ſeemly ſaies) to clouts:
He that unhors'd the man o' fame to boot,
And bootleſs taught his Grace to walk afoot:
He that your writings (pack'd to every pillar)
Promis'd promotion to, and ſtore of ſiller,
That very man I ſet before thy Grace,
And once again pronounce, this man it was.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: A pretty fooliſh Squire, what muſt the Knight be?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Some Jugler or ſome Mad man,

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I was not ſo,
When thy faint Troops in flocks I beat before me,
When, through the thickeſt of thy warlike horſe,
I ſhot my ſelf even to thy Standard Duke,
And there found thee, there ſingled thee, there ſhew'd thee
The temper of my Sword. 'Tis true, thou ſtoodſt me,
And like a noble ſoldier bidſt me welcome;
And this I'll ſay, More honor in that arme,
I found and tryed, than all thy Army carried:
What follows thy impriſonment can tell thee.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: His fair relation carries truth and virtue,
And by thoſe Arms I ſee, (for ſuch were his,
So old, ſo ruſty) this may be he that forc'd me.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Do you know this Jewel, from your Cask I rent it,
Even as I clos'd, and forced ye from your ſaddle;
Do you now remember me -

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: This is the valour
Madam, for certain he, it muſt be he,
That day I wore this Jewel, you remember it.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Yes, very well; not long before I ſent it.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: That day I loſt this Jewel, in fight I loſt it,
I felt his ſtrokes, and felt him take it from me,
I wore it in my Cask; take it again Sir,
You won it nobly, 'tis the prize of honor.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: My Father and my ſelf are made for ever.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Kneel down brave Sir thus my Knight firſt I raiſe ye,
Gird on a Sword; next General of my Army, Diſcovers himſelf.
Give him a ſtaff; laſt, one in Counſel near me.
Now, make us happy with your ſight: how? Silvio?
Have I on thee beſtow'd this love, this honor?
The Treaſons thou haſt wrought ſet off with favours?
Unarm him preſently: Oh thou foul Traitor,
Traitor to me, mine honor, and my Countrey,
Thou kindler of theſe Wars.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Miſtake not Madam.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Away with him to priſon,
See him ſafe kept, the Law ſhall ſhortly ſirrah,
Find fitter Titles for ye, than I gave ye.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: This is the youth that kill'd me, I'll be quit with him,
What a blind rogue was I, I could never know him?
And't pleaſe your Grace, I claim the benefit
Of the Proclamation that proclaim'd him Traitor,
I brought him in.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have thy reward for't.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Let him be hang'd, or drown'd then,

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Away with him.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Madam, I crave your promiſe firſt; you are tyed to it,
You have paſt your Princely word.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Prove it, and take it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: This is the day appointed,
Appointed by your Grace for my appearance,
To anſwer to the Queſtion.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: I remember it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I claim it then,

sp.speaker: Dutch,
sp.l: If you perform it not,
The penalty you claim too.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I not repent it;
If I abſolve the words?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Your life is free then,
You have drawn a ſpeedy courſe above my wiſhes,
To my revenge, be ſure ye hit it right,
Or I'll be ſure you ſhall not ſcape the danger.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: My reſt is up now Madam.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Then play it cunningly.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Now, where's the Hag? where now are all her promiſes,
She would be with me, ſtrengthen me, inform me?
My death will now be double death, ridiculous?
She was wont ſtill to be near, to feel my miſeries,
And with her Art, I ſee her no where now;
What have I undertaken? now ſhe fails me,
No comfort now I find, how my ſoul ſtaggers?
Till this hour never fear nor doubt poſſeſt me,
She cannot come, ſhe will not come, ſhe has fool'd me;
Sure, ſhe is the Devil, has drawn me on to ruine,
And now to death bequeaths me in my danger.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: He ſtands diſtracted, and his colour changes.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: I have given him that will make his blood forſake him;
Shortly his life.

sp.speaker: Sy,
sp.l: His hands and contemplation
Have motion ſtill, the reſt is earth already.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Come, will ye ſpeak or pray? your time grows out Sir;
How every where he looks? he's at laſt caſt.

div.stage: Enter Belvidere, and ſecretly gives him a paper, and Exit.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: His colour comes again freſh.

sp.speaker: Duc
sp.l: 'Tis a flaſh, Sir,
Before the flame burns out; can ye yet anſwer?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Yes Madam, now I can.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: I fear you'll ſail in't.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And do not think my ſilence a preſage,
Or Omen to my end, you ſhall not find it;
I am bred a Soldier not an Orator:
Madam, peruſe this ſcrowl, let that ſpeak for me,
And as you are Royal, wrong not the conſtruction.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: By heaven you ſhall have fair play.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I ſhall look for't.

lg.head: Queſtion.
lg.l: TEll me what is that only thing,
For which all women long;
Yet having what they moſt deſire,
To have it do's them wrong.

lg.head: Anſwer.
lg.l: TIs not to be chaſte, nor fair,
Such gifts malice may impair;
Richly trimm'd to walk or ride,
Or to wanton uneſpy'd;
To preſerve an honeſt name,
And ſo to give it up to fame;
Theſe are toys. In good or ill
They deſire to have their Will;
Yet when they have it, they abuſe it,
For they know not how to uſe it.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: You have anſwer'd right, and gain'd your life,
I give it.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Oh happy Hag! But my moſt gracious Madam,
Your promiſe ty'd a nobler favour to me.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: 'Tis true, my Daughter too.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I hope you will keep it.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: 'Tis not in my power now, ſhe is long ſince wander'd,
Stol'n from Court, and me; and what I have not
I cannot give: no man can tell me of her,
Nor no ſearch find her out: and ifot Silvio,
Which ſtrongly I believe—

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Mock me not Lady,
For as I am a ſervant to her virtue,
Since my firſt hour of exile, I ne'er ſaw her.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: That ſhe is gone, 'tis too too true, and lamentable,
Our laſt hope was in you.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: What do I hear then,
And wherefore have I life beſtow'd and honor?
To what end do I walk? for men to wonder at,
And fight, and fool? pray ye take your honors from me,
(My ſorrows are not fit companions for 'em)
And when ye pleaſe my life: Art thou gone Miſtriſs,
And wander'ſt heaven knows where? this vow I make thee,
That till I find thee out, and ſee thoſe fair eyes;
Thoſe eyes that ſhed their lights, and life into me,
Never to know a friend, to ſeek a kindred,
To reſt where pleaſure dwels, and painted glory,
But through the world; the wide world, thus to wander,
The wretched world alone, no comfort with me,
But the meer meditations of thy goodneſs:
Honor and greatneſs, thus adieu.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Stay Silvio,
And Lady ſit again, I come for Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: What would ſhe now?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: To claim thy promiſe Silvio,
The boon thou ſwor'ſt to give me.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: What may this be,
A Woman or a Devil?

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: 'Tis a Witch ſure,
And by her means he came to untwiſt this Riddle.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: That I am bound to her for my life, mine honor;
And many other thouſand ways for comfort
I here confeſs: confeſs a promiſe too,
That what ſhe would aske me to requite theſe favours,
Within the endeavour of my life to grant,
I would; and here I ſtand my words full maſter.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I wiſh no more: great Lady, witneſs with me,
The boon I crave for all my ſervice to thee,
Is now to be thy wife, to grant me marriage.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: How? for to marry thee? ask again woman,
Thou wilful woman, ask again.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: No more Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ask Land, and Life.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I aske thee for a Husband.

sp.speaker: Soto.
sp.l: Marry her, and beat her into Gun-powder,
She would make rare Crackers.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Ask a better fortune,
Thou art too old to marry: I a Soldier,
And always married to my ſword.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Thy word Fool,
Break that, and I'll break all thy fortunes yet.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: He ſhall not,
I am witneſs to his faith? and I'll compel it.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: 'Tis fit ye hold your word, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Oh moſt wretched.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: This was a fortune now beyond my wiſhes,
For now my Daughter's free, if e'er I find her.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: But not from me.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: You are ſharer in this happineſs,
My ſelf will wait upon this marriage,
And do the old woman all the honor poſſible.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: I'll lead the Knight, and what there wants in dalliance,
We'll take it out in drink.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Oh wretched Silvio. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Haſt thou ſent for him,

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: A young man, ſaiſt thou?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Yes, very young, and very amorous.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And handſome?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: As the Town affords.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: And dar'ſt thou
Be ſo far good, and Miſtriſs of thine honor,
To ſlight theſe?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: For my Husband's ſake to curſe 'em,
And ſince you have made me Miſtriſs of my fortune,
Never to point at any joy, but Husband,
I could have cozen'd ye, but ſo much I love ye,
And now ſo much I weigh the eſtimation
Of an unſpotted wife—

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I dare believe thee,
And never more ſhall doubt torment my ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: How now Penurio?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: The thing is comming, Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I'll take my ſtanding.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Do, and I'll take mine. Exit Lopez.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Where didſt thou leave him?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I left him in a Cellar,
Where he has paid me titely, paid me home Miſtriſs,
We had an hundred and fifty healths to you, ſweet Miſtriſs,
Miſtriſs, ſhall I ſpeak a fooliſh word to ye?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: What's that Penurio?
The fellow's drunk.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I would fain know your body.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: How's that? how's that prethee?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: I would know it carnally,
I would conglutinate.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: The reaſon ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Lobſter, ſweet Miſtriſs, Lobſter.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thy Maſter hears.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Lobſter, ſweet Maſter, Lobſter.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thou art the moſt pretious rogue.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Moſt pretious Lobſter.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Do you ſee who's here? go ſleep ye drunken raſcal.

sp.speaker: Pen.
sp.l: Remember you refuſe me arm'd in Lobſter. Exit.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Oh my loſt Rugio, welcome, welcome, welcome,
A thouſand welcomes here I'll ſeal.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Pray ye ſtay, Lady,
Do you love me ever at this rate? or is the fit now,
By reaſon of ſome wrong done by your Husband,
More fervent on ye?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Can I chuſe but love thee?
Thou art my Martyr, thou haſt ſuffered for me,
My ſweet, ſweet Rugio.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Do you do this ſeriouſly?
'Tis true, I would be entertained thus.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Theſe are nothing,
No kiſſes, no embraces, no endearments,
To thoſe—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Do what you will,

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Thoſe that ſhall follow,
Thoſe I will crown our love withal; why ſigh ye?
Why look ye ſad my dear one?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay, faith nothing,
But methinks ſo ſweet a beauty, as yours ſhews to me,
And ſuch an innocence as you may make it,
Should hold a longer Siege.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Ha, you ſpeak truth, Sir,

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I would not have it ſo.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: And now methinks,
Now I conſider truly what becomes me,
I have been cozen'd, fearfully abus'd,
My reaſon blinded.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay, I did but jeſt with ye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I'll take ye at your word, and thank ye for't Sir;
And now I ſee no ſweetneſs in that perſon,
Nothing to ſtir me to abuſe a Husband,
To ruine my fair fame.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Good Iſabella.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: No handſome man, nor any thing to doat on,
No face, no tongue to catch me, poor at all points,
And I an aſs.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why do ye wrong me Lady?
If I were thus, and had no youth upon me,
My ſervice of ſo mean a way to win ye,
(Which you your ſelf are conſcious muſt deſerve ye,
If you had thrice the beauty you poſſeſs, muſt reach ye)
If in my tongue your fame lay wrack'd, and ruin'd
With every cup I drink: if in opinion
I were a loſt, defam'd man: but this is common
Where we love moſt, where moſt we ſtake our fortunes,
There leaſt and baſeſt we are rewarded: fare ye well,
Know now I hate you too as much, contemn ye,
And weigh my credit at as high a value.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: May be I did but jeſt.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ye are a woman,
And now I ſee your wants, and mine own follies,
And task my ſelf with indiſcretion,
For doating on a face ſo poor.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Say ye ſo Sir,
(I muſt not loſe my end) I did but jeſt with you,
Only fool'd thus to try your faith: my Rugio,
Do you think I could forget?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis no matter.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Is't poſſible I ſhould forſake a conſtancy,
So ſtrong, ſo good, ſo ſweet?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: A ſubtle woman.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You ſhall forgive me, 'twas a trick to try ye,
And were I ſure he lov'd me —

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Do you doubt now?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I do not doubt, but he that would profeſs this,
And bear that full affection you make ſhew of,
Should do —

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What ſhould I do?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I cannot ſhew ye.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I'll try thee damnedſt Devil: hark ye Lady,
