No man ſhall dare do more, no ſervice top me,
I'll marry ye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: How Sir?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Your Husband's ſentenc'd,
And he ſhall dye.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Dye?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Dye for ever to ye,
The danger is mine own.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Dye did ye tell me?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: He ſhall dye, I have caſt the way.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Oh foul man,
Malicious bloody man.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: When ſhall he dye, Sir,
By whom, and how?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Haſt thou betraid me, woman?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Baſe man, thou would'ſt eave ruin'd me, my name too
And like a Toad, poiſon'd my virtuous memory:
Further than all this, doſt thou ſee this friend here,
This only friend, ſhame take thy Luſt and thee,
And ſhake thy ſoul, his life, the life I love thus,
My life in him, my only life thou aim'ſt at.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Am I catcht thus?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: The Law ſhall catch ye better.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: You make a trade of betraying Womens honors,
And think it noble in ye to be luſtful,
Report of me hereafter—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Fool'd thus finely?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I muſt intreat ye walk, Sir, to the Juſtice,
Where if he'll bid ye kill me—

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Pray ſtay awhile, Sir,
I muſt uſe a Players ſhift, do you know me now Lady?

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Your brother Claudio ſure.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Oh me, 'tis he Sir,
Oh my beſt brother.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: My beſt ſiſter now too,
I have tryed ye, found ye ſo, and now I love ye,
Love ye ſo truly nobly.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Sir, I thank ye,
You have made me a moſt happy man.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Thank her Sir,
And from this hour preſerve that happineſs,
Be no more fool'd with jealouſie.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: I have loſt it,
And take me now new born again, new natur'd.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I do, and to that promiſe tye this faith,
Never to have a falſe thought tempt my virtue.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Enough, enough, I muſt deſire your preſence,
My Coſin Rhodope has ſent in all haſte for us,
I am ſure you will be welcome.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I'll wait on ye.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: What the Project is —

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: We ſhall know when we are there, Sir, Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Joy to you Silvio, and your young fair Bride,
You have ſtolen a day upon us; you cannot wooe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: The joyes of Hell hang over me, oh miſchief,
To what a fortune has the Devil driven me?
Am I reſerv'd for this?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Beſhrew me, Sir,
But you have gotten you a right fair bedfellow,
Let you alone to chuſe.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I beſeech your Grace,
'Tis miſery enough to have met the Devil,
Not mens reproaches too.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: How old is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: A very Girl, her eye delivers it.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Her teeth are ſcarce come yet.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: What goodly children
Will they two have now? ſhe is rarely made to breed on,
What a ſweet timber'd body?

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Knotty i' th' back,
But will hold out the ſtronger; What a noſe?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: I marry, ſuch a noſe, ſo rarely mounted,
Upon my conſcience, 'twas the part he doted on.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: And that fine little eye to it, like an Elephant's.

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.l: Yes, if her feet were round, and her ears ſachels.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: For any thing we know.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Have ye no mercy?
No pity in your bloods to uſe a wretch thus?
You Princes in whoſe hearts the beſt compaſſions,
Neareſt to thoſe in Heaven, ſhould find fit places,
Why do you mock at miſery? fling ſcorns and baſeneſs
Upon his broken back, that ſinks with ſorrows?
Heaven may reward you too, and an hour come,
When all her great deſignes ſhall ſhew ridiculous,
And your hearts pinch'd like mine.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Fie Sir, ſo angry
Upon your wedding day? go ſmug your ſelf,
The Maid will come anon: what Muſick's this?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: I warrant you ſome noble preparation.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Let's take our places then.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: More of theſe Devils dumps?
Muſt I be ever haunted with theſe witchcrafts?

div.stage: Enter a Masquerado of ſeveral ſhapes, and Dances, after which, enter Belvidere and diſperſes them; before the Maskers enter two Preſenters, among which are Bartello, Lopez, Claudio, Iſabella, Rhodope, Soto, Penurio, Jaquenet.

sp.speaker: 1 Pre.
sp.l: Room, room for merry ſpirits, room,
Hither on command we come,
From the good old Beldam ſent,
Cares and ſorrows to prevent.
Look up Silvio, ſmile, and ſing,
After winter comes a Spring.
Fear not faint fool what may follow,
Eyes that now are ſunk and hollow,
By her Art may quick return
To their flames again, and burn.
Art commands all youth, and blood,
Strength and beauty it makes good.
Fear not then, deſpair not, ſing
Round about as we do ſpring:
Cares and ſorrows caſt away,
This is the old wives Holy-day.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Who is this?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: The ſhape of Belvidere.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Now Silvio,
How doſt thou like me now?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Thus I kneel to thee.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Stand up, and come no nearer, mark me well too,
For if thou troubleſt me, I vaniſh inſtantly:
Now chuſe wiſely, or chuſe never,
One thou muſt enjoy for ever.
Doſt thou love me thus?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Moſt dearly.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: Take heed fool, it concerns thee nearly.
If thou wilt have me young and bright,
Pleaſing to thine eye and ſight,
Courtly, and admir'd of all,
Take heed leſt thy fame do fall,
I ſhall then be full of ſcorn,
Wanton, proud, beware the horn,
Hating what I lov'd before,
Flattery apt to fall before,
All conſuming, nothing getting,
Thus thy fair name comes to ſetting.
But if old, and free from theſe
Thou ſhalt chuſe me, I ſhall pleaſe:
I ſhall then maintain thee ſtill,
With my virtue and my skill
Still increaſe and build thy name,
Chuſe now Silvio, here I am.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I know not what to ſay, which way to turn me,
Into thy Soveraign will I put my anſwer.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: I thank ye Sir, and my Will thus rewards ye,
Take your old Love, your beſt, your deareſt Silvio:
No more Spells now, nor further ſhapes to alter me,
I am thy Belvidere indeed. Dear Mother,
There is no altering this; heavens hand is with it:
And now you ought to give me, he has fairly won me.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: But why that Hag?

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: In that ſhape moſt ſecure ſtill,
I followed all your fortunes, ſerv'd, and counſell'd ye,
I met ye at the Farmers firſt, a Countrey wench,
Where fearing to be known, I took that habit,
And to make ye laughing ſport at this mad marriage,
By ſecret aid of my friend Rhodope
We got this Maske.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And I am ſure I have ye.

sp.speaker: Bel.
sp.l: For ever now, for ever.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: You ſee it muſt be,
The wheel of deſtiny hath turn'd it round ſo.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: It muſt, it is, and curs'd be he that breaks it.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: I'll put a choice to you, Sir: ye are my priſoner.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: I am ſo, and I muſt be ſo, till it pleaſe you—

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: Chuſe one of theſe, either to pay a Ranſom,
At what a rate I ſhall ſet it, which ſhall be high enough,
And ſo return a Free-man, and a Batchelor,
Or give me leave to give you a fit wife,
In honor every way yours Graces equal,
And ſo your Ranſom's paid.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: You ſay moſt nobly,
Silvio's example's mine, pray chuſe you for me.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: I thank ye Sir, I have got the maſtry too,
And here I give your Grace a Husbands freedom:
Give me your hand, my Husband.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: You much honor me,
And I ſhall ever ſerve ye for this favour.
Come Lopoz, let us give our wives the breeches too,
For they will have 'em.

sp.speaker: Lop.
sp.l: Whilſt they rule with virtue
I'll give 'em, skin and all.
We'll ſ • rach it off elſe.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I am glad ye live, more glad ye live to honor,
And from this hour a ſtronger love dwell with us;
Pray you take your man again.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: He knows my houſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Dutch.
sp.l: 'Tis ſin to keep you longer from your loves,
We'll lead the way; and you young men that know not
How to preſerve a wife, and keep her fair,
Give 'em their ſoveraign Wills, and pleas'd they are.

div.head: THE NIGHT-WALKER, OR THE LITTLE THIEF. A Comedy.
Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Tom Lurcher, and Jack Wild-brain.

l.hi: JAck.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: What wind brought thee hither?
In what hollow tree, or rotten wall
Haſt thou been like a Swallow all this winter,
Where haſt thou been man?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Following the Plow.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: What Plow? Thou haſt no Land,
Stealing is thy own purchaſe.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: The beſt inheritance.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Not in my opinion,
Thou hadſt five hundred pound a year.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Tis gone,
Prethee no more on't, have I not told thee,
And oftentimes, nature made all men equal,
Her diſtribution to each child alike;
Till labour came and thruſt a new Will in,
Which I allow not: till men won a priviledge
By that they call endeavour, which indeed
Is nothing but a lawful Coſenage,
An allowed way to cheat, why ſhould my neighhor
That hath no more ſoul than his Horſe-keeper,
Nor bounteous faculties above a Broom-man,
Have forty thouſand pounds, and I four groats;
Why ſhould he keep it?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.l: Thy old opinion ſtill.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Why ſhould that Scrivener,
That ne'er writ reaſon in his life, nor any thing
That time e'ver gloried in, that never knew
How to keep any courteſie conceal'd,
But Noverint Ʋniverſi muſt proclaim it,
Purchaſe perpetually, and I a raſcal:
Conſider this, why ſhould that mouldy Cobler
Marry his Daughter to a wealthy Merchant,
And give five thouſand pounds, is this good juſtice?
Becauſe he has a tougher conſtitution;
Can feed upon old Songs, and ſave his money,
Therefore muſt I go beg?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: What's this to thee?
Thou canſt not mend, if thou beeſt determin'd
To rob all like a Tyrant, yet take heed
A keener juſtice do not overtake thee,
And catch you in a Nooze.
I am no Wood-cock,
He that ſhall ſit down frighted with that foolery
• s not worth pity, let me alone to ſhuffle,
Thou art for wenching.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: For beauty I, a ſafe courſe,
No halter hangs in the way, I defie it.
But a worſe fate, a wilful poverty,
For where thou gain'ſt by one that indeed loves thee,
A thouſand will draw from thee, 'tis thy deſtiny;
One is a kind of weeping croſs Jack,
A gentle Purgatory, do not ſling at all,
You'll pay the Box ſo often, till you periſh.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Take you no care for that ſir, 'tis my pleaſure,
I will imploy my wits a great deal faſter
Than you ſhall do your fingers, and my loves,
If I miſtake not, ſhall prove riper harveſt
And handſomer, and come within leſs danger.
Where's thy young Siſter?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I know not where ſhe is, ſhe is not worth caring for,
She has no wit.
Oh you'd be nibling with her,
She's far enough I hope, I know not where,
She's not worth caring for, a ſullen thing,
She wou'd not take my counſel Jack,
And ſo I parted from her.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Leave her to her wants?

sp.speaker: Lur,
sp.l: I gave her a little money, what I could ſpare,
She had a mind to th'Countrey, ſhe is turn'd,
By this, ſome Farriers dairy maid, I may meet her
Riding from Market one day, 'twixt her Dorſers,
If I do, by this hand I wo'not ſpare
Her butter pence.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Thou wilt not rob thy Siſter.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: She ſhall account me for her Egs and Cheeſes.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: A pretty Girl, did not old Algripe love her?
A very pretty Girl ſhe was.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Some ſuch thing,
•• t he was too wiſe to faſten; let her paſs.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Then where's thy Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Where you ſha'not find her,
Nor know what ſtuff ſhe is made on; no indeed Sir,
I chooſe her not for your uſe.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Sure ſhe is handſome.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Yes indeed is ſhe, ſhe is very handſome, but that's all one.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: You'll come to th' Marriage?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Is it to day.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Now, now, they are come from Church now.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Any great preparation,
Does Juſtice Algripe ſhew his power?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Very glorious, and glorious people there.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I may meet with him yet e're I dye as cunning as he is.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: You may do good Tom, at the carriage,
We have plate and dainty things.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Do you no harm Sir;
For yet methinks the Marriage ſhould be mar'd
If thou maiſt have thy will, farewell, ſay nothing. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: You are welcome noble friends.
I thank you Sir,
Nephew to the old Lady, his name is Wildbrain,
And wild his beſt condition.
I have heard of him,
I pray ye tell me Sir, is young Maria merry
After her Marriage rites? does ſhe look lively?
How does ſhe like her man?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Very ſcurvily,
And as untowardly ſhe prepares her ſelf,
•• t 'tis mine Aunts will, that this dull mettal
•• t be mixt with her to allay her handſomeneſs.
Had Heartlove no faſt friends?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: His means are little,
And where thoſe littles are, as little comforts
Ever keep company: I know ſhe loves him,
His memory beyond the hopes of —
Beyond the Indies in his mouldy Cabinets,
But 'tis her unhandſome fate.
I am ſorry for't,
Here comes poor Frank, nay we are friends, ſtart not Sir,
We ſee you'r willow and are ſorry for't,
And though it be a wedding we are half mourners.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Good Gentlemen remember not my fortunes,
They are not to be help'd by words.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Look up man,
A proper ſenſible fellow and ſhrink for a wench?
Are there no more? or is ſhe all the handſomneſs?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Prethee leave fooling.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Prethee leave thou whining,
Have maids forgot to love?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: You are injurious.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Let 'em alone a while, they'll follow thee.
Come good Frank.
Forget now, ſince there is no remedy,
And ſhew a merry face, as wiſe men would do.
Be a free gueſt, and think not of thoſe paſſages.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Think how to nick him home, thou knowſt ſhe
Graff me a dainty medler on his crabſtocke; (dotes on thee
Pay me the dreaming puppy.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Well, make your mirth, the whilſt I bear my miſery:
Honeſt minds would have better thoughts.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: I am her Kinſman,
And love her well, am tender of her youth,
Yet honeſt Frank, before I would have that ſtinkard,
That walking rotten tombe, enjoy her maidenhead.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Prethee leave mocking.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Prethee Frank believe me,
Go to conſider, hark, they knock to dinner. Knock within.
Come wo't thou go?
I prethee Frank go with us,
And laugh and dance as we do.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: You are light Gentlemen,
Nothing to weigh your hearts, pray give me leave,
I'll come and ſee, and take my leave.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: We'll look for you,
Do not deſpair, I have a trick yet. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: When I am miſchievous I will believe your projects:
She is gone, for ever gone, I cannot help it,
My hopes and all my happineſs gone with her.
Gone like a pleaſing dream: what mirth and joillity
Raigns round about this houſe? how every office
Sweats with new joyes, can ſhe be merry too?
Is all this pleaſure ſet by her appointment?
Sure ſhe hath a falſe heart then; ſtill they grow lowder,
The old mans God, his gold, has won upon her,
(Light hearted Cordial Gold) and all my ſervices
That offered naked truth, are clean forgotten:
Yet if ſhe were compell'd, but it cannot be,
If I could but imagine her will mine,
Although he had her body.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: He ſhall come in.
Walk without doors o'this day, though an enemy,
It muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: You muſt compel him Madam.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: No ſhe ſhall fetch him in, Nephew it ſhall be ſo.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: It will be fitteſt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Can fair Maria look again upon me?
Can there be ſo much impudence in ſweetneſs?
Or has ſhe got a ſtrong heart to defie me?
She comes her ſelf: how rich ſhe is in Jewels!
Methinks they ſhow like frozen Iſicles,
Cold winter had hung on her, how the Roſes
That kept continual ſpring within her cheeks
Are withered with old mans dull embraces?
She would ſpeak to me. I can ſigh too Lady
But from a ſounder heart: yes, and can weep too
But 'tis for you, that ever I believ'd you,
Tears of more pious value than your marriage;
You would encaſe your ſelf, and I muſt credit you,
So much my old obedience compels from me;
Go, and forget me, and my poverty,
I need not bid you, you are too perfect that way:
But ſtill remember that I lov'd Maria,
Lov'd with a loyal love, nay turn not from me,
I will not ask a tear more, you are bountiful,
Go and rejoyce, and I will wait upon you
That little of my life left.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Good Sir hear me,
What has been done, was the act of my obedience
And not my will: forc'd from me by my parents,
Now 'tis done, do as I do, bear it handſomly
And if there can be more ſociety
Without diſhonor to my tye of marriage
Or place for noble love, I ſhall love you ſtill,
You had the firſt, the laſt, had my will proſper'd;
You talk of little time of life: dear Frank,
Certain I am not married for eternity,
The joy my marriage brings tells me I am mortal.
And ſhorter liv'd than you, elſe I were miſerable;
Nor can the gold and eaſe his age hath brought me
Add what I coveted, content go with me,
They ſeek a day of joy, prethee let's ſhow it,
Though it be forc'd, and by this kiſs believe me
However, I muſt live at his command now,
I'll dye at yours.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I have enough, I'll honor ye. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Here are my trinkets, and this luſty marriage
I mean to viſit, I have ſhifts of all ſorts,
And here are a thouſand wheels to ſet 'em working,
I am very merry, for I know this wedding
Will yield me luſty pillage: if mad Wildgooſe
That deboſh'd rogue keep but his antient revels,
And breed a hubbub in the houſe I am happy.
Now what are you?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A poor diſtreſſed Boy, Sir,
Friendleſs and comfortleſs, that would intreat
Some charity and kindneſs from your worſhip,
I would fain ſerve, Sir, and as fain endeavour
With dutious labour to deſerve the love
Of that good Gentleman ſhould entertain me.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A pretty Boy, but of too mild a breeding,
Too tender, and too baſhful a behaviour,
What canſt thou do?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I can learn anything,
That's good and honeſt, and ſhall pleaſe a Maſter.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: He bluſhes as he ſpeaks, and that I like not,
I love a bold and ſecure confidence,
An impudence that one may truſt, this boy now:
Had I inſtructed him, had been a Jewel,
A treaſure for my uſe, thou canſt not lye?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I would not willingly.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Nor thou haſt not wit
To diſſemble neatly?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Do you love ſuch boys, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Oh mainly, mainly, I would have my Boy impudent,
Out-face all truth, yet do it piouſly:
Like Proteus, caſt himſelf into all forms,
As ſuddain and as nimble as his thoughts,
Blanch at no danger, though it be the Gallows,
Nor make no conſcience of a coſenage,
Though it be i'th' Church. Your ſoft, demure, ſtill children—
Are good for nothing, but to get long Graces—
And ſing Songs to dull tunes; I would keep thee
And cheriſh thee, hadſt thou any active quality,
And be a tender Maſter to thy knavery,
But thou art not for my uſe.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: Do you ſpeak this ſeriouſly?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Yes indeed do I.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Would you have your boy Sir
Read in theſe moral miſchiefs?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Now thou mov'ſt me.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: And be a well-train'd youth in all activities?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: By any means.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Or do you this to try me,
Fearing a proneſs.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I ſpeak this to make thee.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Then take me Sir, and cheriſh me, and love me,
You have me what you would: believe me, Sir
I can do any thing for your advantage,
I gueſs at what you mean; I can lie naturally,
As eaſily, as I can ſleep Sir, and ſecurely:
As naturally I can ſteal too.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: That I am glad on,
Right heartily glad on, hold thee there, thou art excellent

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Steal any thing from any body living.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Not from thy Maſter.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: That's mine own body:
And muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: The boy mends mightily.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A rich man, that like ſnow heaps up his moneys,
I have a kind of pious zeal to meet ſtill;
A fool that not deſerves 'em, I take pitty on,
For fear he ſhould run mad, and ſo I eaſe him.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Excellent boy, and able to inſtruct me,
Of mine own nature juſt.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I ſcorn all hazard,
And on the edge of danger I do beſt, Sir,
I have a thouſand faces to deceive,
And to thoſe, twice ſo many tongues to flatter,
An impudence, no braſs was ever tougher,
And for my conſcience.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Peace, I have found a Jewel,
A Jewel all the Indies cannot match,
And thou ſha't feel

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: This title, and I ha' done, Sir;
I never can confeſs, I ha' that ſpell on me;
And ſuch rare modeſties before a Magiſtrate,
Such innocence to catch a Judge, ſuch ignorance.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I'll learn of thee, thou art mine own, come boy,
I'll give thee action preſently,

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Have at you.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: What muſt I call thee?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Snap, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt natural,
A name born to thee, ſure thou art a Fairy,
Shew but thy skill, and I ſhall make thee happy.

div.stage: Enter Lady, Nurſe, Miſtriſs, Newlove, Tobie.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Where be theſe knaves? who ſtrues up all the liveries.
Is the Bride's bed made?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Yes Madam and a Bell
Hung under it artificially.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Out knave, out,
Muſt we have 'larms now?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: A little warning
That we may know to begin our healths Madam;
The Juſtice is a kind of old Jade, Madam,
That will goe merrieſt with a Bell.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: All the houſe drunk.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: This is a houſe of Jubile.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Are the beſt hangings up? and the Plate ſet out?
Who makes the Poſſet, Nurſe?

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: The dayrie mayd,
And ſhee'll put that in, will make him caper:
Well Madam, well, you might ha'choſe another,
A handſomer for your years.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Peace, he is rich Nurſe,
He is rich, and that's beauty.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: I am ſure he is rotten,
Would he had been hang'd when he firſt ſaw her. Termagant!

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: What an angry Quean is this, where
Who looks to him?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: He is very merry Madam,
M. Wildbrain, has him in hand, ith'bottom o'th'Sellar
He ſighs and tipples.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Alaſs good Gentleman,
My heart's ſore for thee.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Sorrow muſt have his courſe, ſirra,
Give him ſome Sack to dry up his remembrance,
How does the Bridegroom, I was afraid of him.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: He is a trim youth to be tender of, hemp take him.
Muſt my ſweet new blown Roſe find ſuch a winter
Before her ſpring be near.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Peace, peace, thou art fooliſh.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: And dances like a Town-top: and reels, and hobbles.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Alaſs, good Gentleman, give him not much wine.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: He ſhall ha'none by my conſent.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Are the women comforting my daughter?

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: Yes, yes, Madam,
And reading to her a pattern of true patience,
They read and pray for her too.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: They had need,
Ye had better marry her to her grave a great deal:
There will be peace and reſt, alaſs poor Gentlewoman,
Muſt ſhe become a Nurſe now in her tenderneſs?
Well Madam, well my heart bleeds.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Thou art a fool ſtill.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Pray heaven I be.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: And an old fool to be vext thus.
'Tis late ſhe muſt to bed, go knave be merry,
Drink for a boy, away to all your charges. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Do as thou wo't, but if thou doſt refuſe it
Thou art the ſtupid'ſt aſs, there's no long arguing,
Time is too precious Franke.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I am hot with wine.
And apt now to believe, but if thou doſt this
Out of a villany, to make me wrong her.
As thou art prone enough.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Does ſhe not love thee?
Did ſhe not cry down-right e'n now to part with thee?
Had ſhe not ſwounded if I had not caught her?
Canſt thou have more?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs all this.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Do not ſtand prating, and miſdoubting, caſting,
If ſhe go from thee now, ſhe's loſt for ever;
Now, now ſhe's going, ſhe that loves thee going,
She whom thou lov'ſt.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Pray let me think a little.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: There is no leiſure; think when thou haſt imbrac'd her.
Can ſhe imagine thou diſt ever honor her?
Ever believe thy oaths, that tamely ſuffer'ſt
An old dry ham of horſe-fleſh to enjoy her?
Enjoy her maiden-head; take but that from her
That we may tell poſterity a man had it,
A handſome man, a Gentleman, a young man,
To ſave the honor of our houſe, the credit,
'Tis no great matter I deſire.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I hear you.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Free us both from the fear of breeding fools
And ophs, got by this ſhadow: we talk too long.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: She is going to bed, among the women,
What opportunity can I have to meet her?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Let me alone, haſt thou a will? ſpeak ſoundly,
Speak diſcreetly, ſpeak home and handſomly,
Is't not pitty, nay miſery, nay infamy to leave
So rare a pie to be cut up by a raskal.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I will go preſently, now, now, I ſtay thee.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Such a dainty Doe, to be taken
By one that knows not neck-beef from a Pheſant,
Nor cannot relliſh Braggat from Ambroſia.
Is it not conſcience?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Yes, yes, now I feel it.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: A meritorious thing.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Good Father Wildgooſe,
I do confeſs it.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.l: Come then follow me.
And pluck a mans heart up, I'll lock thee privately,
Where ſhe alone ſhall preſently paſs by,
None near to interupt thee but be ſure;

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I ſhall be ſure enough, lead on, and crown me.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: No wringings in your mind now as you love me. Ex.

div.stage: Enter Lady, Maria, Juſtice, Gent. Nurſe, Newlove.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: 'Tis time you were a bed.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I prethee ſweet-heart
Conſider my neceſſity, why art ſad?
I muſt tell you a tale in your ear anon.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Of Tom Thumb.
I believe that will prove your ſtiffeſt ſtory.

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: I pitty the young wench.
And ſo do I too.
Come, old ſticks take fire.
But the plague is, he'll burn out inſtantly;
Give him another cup.
Thoſe are but flaſhes,
A tun of ſack wonot ſet him high enough.
Will ye to bed?

sp.speaker: M.
sp.l: I muſt.
Come, have a good heart,
And win him like a bowle to lye cloſe to you,
Make your beſt uſe.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Nay prethee Duck go inſtantly,
I'll dance a Jig or two to warm my body.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: 'Tis almoſt midnight.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Prethee to bed Maria.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Go you aſore, and let the Ladies follow,
And leave her to her thoughts a while, there muſt be
A time of taking leave of theſe ſame fooleries
Bewailling others maiden-heads.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Come then,
We'll wait in the next room.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Do not tarry.
For if thou doſt, by my troth I ſhall fall aſleep Mall. Ex.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Do, do, and dream of Doterels, get you to bed quickly,
And let us ha'no more ſtir, come now, no crying,
'Tis too late now, carry your ſelves diſcreetly.
The old thief loves thee dearly, that's the benefit.
For the reſt you muſt make your own play, Nay not that way,
They'll pull ye all to pieces, for your whim-whams,
Your garters and your gloves, go modeſtly,
And privately ſteal to bed, 'tis very late Mall,
For if you go by them ſuch a new larum.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I know not which way to avoid'em.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: This way,
This through the Cloyſters: and ſo ſteal to bed,
When you are there once, all will ſeparate
And give ye reſt, I came out of my pitty
To ſhew you this.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I thank you.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: Here's the keyes,
Go preſently and lock the doors faſt after ye,
That none ſhall follow.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Good night.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: Good night ſweet Coſen.
A good, and ſweet night, or I'll curſe thee Frank. Exit

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: She ſtay's long, ſure young Wildgooſe has abus'd me,
He has made ſport wi'me, I may yet get out again,
And I may ſee his face once more, I ha'foul intentions,
But they are drawn on by a fouler dealing
Hark, hark, it was the door,
Something comes this way, wondrous ſtill and ſtealing
May be ſome walking ſpirit to affright me.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Oh heaven my fortune.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: 'Tis her voice, ſtay.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Save me,
Bleſs me you better powers.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I am no devil.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Y'are little better to diſturb me now.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: My name is Hartlove.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Fye, fye, worthy friend.
Fye noble Sir.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I muſt talk farther with ye,
You know my fair affection.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: So preſerve it,
You know I am married now, for ſhame be civiller,
Not all the earth ſhall make me.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Pray walk this way,
And if you ever lov'd me.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Take heed Frank
How you divert that love to hate, go home prethee.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Shall he enjoy that ſweet?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Nay pray unhand me.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: He that never felt what love was.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Then I charge you ſtand farther off.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I am tame, but let me walk wi'ye,
Talk but a minute.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: So your talk be honeſt,
And my untainted honor ſuffer not,
I'll walk a turn or two.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Give me your hand then. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Wildbrain, Juſtice, Lady, Nurſe, Gent. Women, Newlove.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: Shee's not in her Chamber

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: She is not here.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: And I'll tell you what I dream'd.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Give me a Torch.

sp.speaker: 1. G.
sp.l: Be not too haſty Sir.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Nay let him go.
For if my dream be true he muſt be ſpeedy,
He will be trickt, and blaz'd elſe.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: As I am a woman
I cannot blame her if ſhe take her liberty,
Would ſhe would make thee Cuckold, thou old bully,
A notorious cuckold for tormenting her.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I'll hang her then.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: I'll bleſs her then, ſhe does juſtice,
Is this old ſtinking dogs-fleſh for her dyet?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Prethee honeſt Nurſe do not fret too much,
For fear I dream you'll hang your ſelf too.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: The Cloiſter?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Such was my fancy, I do not ſay 'tis true,
Nor do I bid you be too confident.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Where are the keyes, the keyes I ſay.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: I dream'd ſhe had 'em to lock her ſelf in.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: What a devil do you mean?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: No harm, good Nurſe be patient.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: They are not in the window, where they uſe to be.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: What fooliſh dreams are theſe?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I am mad.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: I hope ſo,
If you be not mad, I'll do my beſt to meyake.
This is ſome trick.
I ſmell the Wildgooſe.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen, come quickly I beſeech you,
Quick as you can, this may be your caſe Gentlemen.
And bring ſome light, ſome lights. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Mov • faſter, faſter, you'll come too late elſe.
I'll ſtay behind and pray for ye, I had rather ſhe were diſhoneſt
Than thou ſhouldſt have her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Y'are moſt unmanly, yet I have ſome breath left;
And this ſteel to defend me, come near me,
For if you offer but another violence,
As I have life I'll kill you, if I miſs that,
Upon my own heart will I execute,
And let that fair belief out, I had of you.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Moſt vertuous Maid, I have done, forgive my follies:
Pardon, O pardon, I now ſee my wickedneſs,
And what a monſtrous ſhape it puts upon me,
On your fair hand I ſeal.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Down with the door.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: We are betraid, oh Franke, Franke,

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: I'll dye for ye
Rather than you ſhall ſuffer, I'll— Enter all.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Now enter.
Enter ſweet Gentlemen, mine eyes, mine eyes,
Oh how my head askes.
Is it poſſible?
Hold her, ſhe ſinks.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: A plot upon my honor
To poyſon my fair name, a ſtudied villany,
Farewell, as I have hope of peace, I am honeſt,

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: My brains, my brains, my monſtrous brains, they bud ſure.

sp.speaker: Nu.
sp.l: She is gone, ſhe is gone.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: A handſome riddance of her.
Would I could as eaſily loſe her memory.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Is this the ſweet of Marriage, have I bred thee
For this reward?
Hold, hold, he's deſperate too.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Be ſure ye hold him faſt, we'll bind him over
To the next Seſſions, and if I can, I'll hang him.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Nay then I'll live to be a terror to thee,
Sweet Virgin Roſe farewell: heaven has thy beauty,
That's only fit for heaven. I'll live a little
To find the Villain out that wrought this injury,
And then moſt bleſſed ſoul, I'll climb up to thee.
Farewell, I feel my ſelf another creature. Exit.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Oh miſery of miſeries.

sp.speaker: Nu.
sp.l: I told ye Madam.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Carry her in, you will pay back her portion?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: No not a penny, pay me back my credit,
And I'll condition wi'ye.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: A ſad wedding,
Her grave muſt be her Bridal bed: oh Mall,
Would I had wed thee to thy own content,
Then I had had thee ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I am mad, farewell,
Another wanton wife will prove a hell. Exeunt.

div.head: Actus Secundus.
div.stage: Enter Tom. Lurch, and his Boy.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: What haſt thou done?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I have walked through all the lodgings.
A ſilence as if death dwelt there inhabits.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: What haſt thou ſeen?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Nought but a ſad confuſion
Every thing left in ſuch a looſe diſorder
That were there twenty theeves, they would be laden.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: 'Tis very well, I like thy care, but 'tis ſtrange
A wedding night ſhould be ſo ſolitary.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Certainly there is ſome cauſe, ſome death or ſickneſs
Is faln ſuddenly upon ſome friend,
Or ſome ſtrange news is come.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Are they all a bed?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I think ſo, and ſound aſleep, unleſs it be
Some women that keep watch in a low parlor,
And drink, and weep, I know not to what end.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Where's all the plate?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Why lockt up in that room.
I ſaw the old Lady, ere ſhe went to bed
Put up her plate, and ſome of the rich hangings
In a ſmall long cheſt, and chains and rings are there too,
It ſtands cloſe by the Table on a form.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Twas a good notice, didſt thou ſee the men.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I ſaw them ſad too, and all take their leaves,
But what they ſaid I was too far to hear Sir.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Tis daintily diſcover'd, we ſhall certainly
Have a moſt proſperous night, which way?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A cloſe one,
A back door, that the women have left open,
To go in and out to fetch neceſſaries,
Cloſe on the Garden ſide.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I love diligence,
Wert thou not fearful?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Fearful? I'll be hang'd firſt.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Say they had ſpied thee.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I was then determin'd
To have cry'd down right too, and have kept 'em company,
As one that had an intereſt in their ſadneſs,
Or made an errand to I know not whom Sir.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: My dainty Boy, let us diſcharge, that plate
Makes a perpetual motion in my fingers,
Till I have faſt hold of it.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Pray be wiſe Sir, do't handſomly, be not greedy,
Lets handle it with ſuch an excellence
As if we would bring thieving into honor:
We muſt diſguiſe, to fright theſe reverend wathces.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Still my bleſt Boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: And clear the room of drunken jealouſies,
The cheſt is of ſome weight, and we may make
Such noiſe ith'the carriage we may be ſnap'd.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Come open, here's a devils face.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: No, no, Sir, wee'l have no ſhape ſo terrible,
We will not do the devil ſo much pleaſure,
To have him face our plot.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A winding ſheet then.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: That's too cold a ſhift,
I would not wear the reward of my wickedneſs,
I wonder you are an old thief, and no cunninger,
Where's the long Cloak?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Here, here.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Give me the Turbant
And the falſe beard, I hear ſome coming this way,
Stoop, ſtoop, and let me ſit upon your ſhoulders,
And now as I direct, ſtay, let them enter,
And when I touch move forward, make no noiſe.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Oh 'tis a ſad time, all the burnt wine is burnt Nic.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: We may thank your dry chaps for't, the Canarie's gone too
No ſubſtance for a ſorrowful mind to work upon,
I cannot mourn in beer, if ſhe ſhould walk now
As diſcontented ſpirits are wont to do.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: And meet us in the Cellar.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: What fence have we with ſingle beer againſt her?
What heart can we defie the Devil with?

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: The March beer's open.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: A fortification of March beer will do well,
I muſt confeſs 'tis a moſt mighty Armor,
For I preſume I cannot pray.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Why Nicolas?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: We Coachmen have ſuch tumbling faiths, no prayrs
Can go an even pace.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Hold up your candle.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Verily Nurſe, I have cry'd ſo much
For my young Miſtriſs, that is mortified,
That if I have not more • ack to ſupport me,
I ſhall even ſleep: heiho, for another flagon;
Theſe Burials, and Chriſtnings are the mournful matters,
And they ask more drink.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Drink to a ſad heart's needful.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Mine's ever ſad, for I am ever dry Nurſe.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Methinks the light burns blew, I prethee ſnuff it,
There's a thief in't I think.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: There may be one near it.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: What's that that moves there, ith' name of—Nicholas?
That thing that walks.

sp.speaker: Ta.
sp.l: Would I had a Ladder to behold it,
Mercy upon me, the Ghoſt of one oth'Guard ſure,
'Tis the devil by his clawes, he ſmels of Brimſtone,
Sure he farts fire, what an Earth-quake I have in me;
Out with thy Prayer-book Nurſe.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: It fell ith' the frying pan, and the Cat's eat it.
I have no power to pray, it grows ſtill onger,
'Tis Steeple high now, and it ſayls away Nurſe.
Lets call the butler up, for he ſpeaks Latine,
And that will daunt the devil: I am blaſted,
My belly's grown to nothing.

sp.speaker: Nu.
sp.l: Fye, fye, Tobie. Exit.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: So let them go, and whilſt they are aſtoniſh'd
Let us preſently upon the reſt now ſuddenly.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Off, off, and up agen, when we are near the parlor,
Art ſure thou knowſt the Cheſt?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Though it were ith'dark Sir,
I can go to't.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: On then and be happy. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: How my haunches quake, is the thing here ſtill?
Now can I out-do any Button-maker, at his own trade,
I have fifteen fits of an Ague, Nurſe, 'tis gone I hope,
The hard-hearted woman has left me alone. Nurſe—
And ſhe knows too I ha but a lean conſcience to keep me company. Noiſe within.
The devil's among 'em in the Parlour ſure,
The Ghoſt three ſtories high, he has the Nurſe ſure,
He is boyling of her bones now, hark how ſhe whiſtles:
There's Gentlewomen within too, how will they do?
I'll to the Cook, for he was drunk laſt night,
And now he is valiant, he is a kin to th'devil too,
And fears no fire.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: No light?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: None left Sir,
They are gone, and carried all the candles with 'em,
Their fright is infinite, let's make good uſe on't,
We muſt be quick ſir, quick, or the houſe will riſe elſe.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Was this the Cheſt?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: There was two of 'em.
Or I miſtake.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I know the right, no ſtay Sir,
Nor no diſcourſe, but to our labor luſtily,
Put to your ſtrength and make as little noiſe,
Then preſently out at the back door.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Come Boy.
Come happy child and let me hug thy excellence. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: What thouſand noiſes paſs through all the rooms?
What cryes and hurries? ſure the devil's drunk.
And tumbles through the houſe, my villanies
That never made me apprehend before
Danger or fear, a little now moleſt me;
My Coſens death ſits heavy o'my conſcience,
Would I had been half hang'd when I hammer'd it.
I aim'd at a living divorce, not a burial
That Frank might have had ſome hope: hark ſtill
In every room confuſion, they are all mad,
Moſt certain all ſtark mad within the houſe,
A puniſhment inflicted for my lewdneſs,
That I might have the more ſenſe of my miſchief,
And run the more mad too, my Aunt is hang'd ſure,
Sure hang'd her ſelf, or elſe the fiend has fetch'd her.
I heard a hundred cryes, the Devil, the Devil,
Than roaring, and then tumbling, all the chambers
Are a meer Babel, or another Bedlam.
What ſhould I think? I ſhake my ſelf too:
Can the Devil find no time, but when we are merry,
Here's ſomething comes.

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: Oh that I had ſome company,
I care not what they were, to eaſe my miſery,
To comfort me.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Whoſe that?

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: Again? nay then receive—

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Hold, hold I am no fury.
The Merchants wife.

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: Are ye a man? pray heaven you be.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: I am.

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: Alaſs I have met Sir
The ſtrangeſt things to night.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Why do you ſtare.

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: Pray comfort me, and put your candle out,
For if I ſee the ſpirit again I dye for't.
And hold me faſt, for I ſhall ſhake to pieces elſe.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: I'll warrant you, I'll hold ye,
Hold ye as tenderly; I have put the light out,
Retire into my Chamber, there I'll watch wi'ye,
I'll keep you from all frights.

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: And will ye keep me.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Keep you as ſecure Lady.

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: You muſt not wrong me then, the devil will have us.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: No, no, I'll love you, then the devil will fear us.
For he fears all that love, pray come in quickly,
For this is the malicious houſe he walks in,
The hour he blaſts ſweet faces, lames the limbs in,
Depraves the ſenſes, now within this half hour
He will have power to turn all Citizens wives
Into ſtrange Creatures, Owles, and long-tail'd Monkeys,
Jayes, Pies, and Parrots, quickly, I ſmell his brimſtone.

sp.speaker: New.
sp.l: It comes agen I am gone ſhift for your ſelf Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Sure this whole night is nothing but illuſion,
Here's nothing comes, all they are mad, damn'd devil
To drive her back again, 't had been thy policy
To have let us alone, we might have done ſome fine thing
To have made thy hel-hood laugh, 'tis a dainty wench,
If I had her again, not all your fellow goblins,
Nor all their clawes ſhould ſcratch her hence, I'll ſtay ſtill,
May be her fright will bring her back again,
Yet I will hope.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: I can find no bed, no body, nor no chamber,
Sure they are all ith' Cellar, and I cannot find that neither,
I am led up and down like a tame aſs, my light's out
And I grope up and down like blind-man-buffe,
And break my face, and break my pate.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: It comes again ſure
I ſee the ſhadow, I'll have faſter hold now,
Sure ſhe is mad, I long to lye with a mad-woman,
She muſt needs have rare new tricks.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: I hear one whiſper
If it be the devil now to allure me into his clutches,
For devils have a kind of tone like crickets,
I have a glimpſe of her guiſe, 'tis ſhe would ſteal me,
But I'll ſtand ſure.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: I have but a dram of wit left,
And that's even ready to run, oh for my bed now.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: She nam'd a bed, I like that, ſhe repents ſure,
Where is ſhe now?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Are you there, In, In, In preſently.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: I feel his talents through me,
'Tis an old haggard devil, what will he do with me?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Let me kiſs thee firſt, quick, quick.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: A leacherous Devil.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: What a hairy whore 'tis, ſure ſhe has a muffler.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: If I ſhould have a young Satan by him, for I dare not deny him,
In what caſe were I? who durſt deliver me?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: 'Tis but my fancy, ſhe is the ſame, in quickly, gently my Sweet girl.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Sweet devil be good to me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Where's my love, Boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: She's coming with a Candle
To ſee our happy prize.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I am cruel weary.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I cannot blame ye, plate is very heavy
To carry without light or help.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: The fear too
At every ſtumble to be diſcover'd boy,
At every cough to raiſe a Conſtable,
Well, we'll be merry now.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: We have ſome reaſon;
Things compaſs'd without fear or eminent danger,
Are too luxurious ſir to live upon.
Money and wealth got thus are as full venture,
And carry in their nature as much merit
As his, that digs 'em out' oth' mine, they laſt too
Seaſon'd with doubts and dangers moſt delitiouſly,
Riches that fall upon us are too ripe,
And dull our appetites.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Moſt learned child.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Y'are welcome, where have you left it.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: In the next room, hard by.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Is it plate all.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: All, all, and Jewels, I am monſtrous weary,
Prethee let's go to bed.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Prethee let's ſee it firſt.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: To morrow's a new day ſweet.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Yes to melt it,
But let's agree to night, how it ſhall be handled,
I'll have a new gown.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Shat have any thing.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: And ſuch a riding ſuit as Miſtreſs Newloves:
What though I be no Gentlewoman born,
I hope I may atchieve it by my carriage.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Thou ſayſt right.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: You promis'd me a horſe too, and a lackquay.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt have horſes ſix, and a poſtilion.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: That will be ſtately ſweet heart a poſtilion.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Nay, we'll be in faſhion; he ſhall ride before us
In winter, with as much dirt would dampe a musket;
The inſide of our coach ſhall be of ſcarlet.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: That will be dear.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: There is a dye projecting
Will make it cheap, wench, come thou ſhalt have any thing.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Where is this cheſt, I long, ſweet, to behold
Our Indies.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Miſtreſs lets melt it firſt, and then 'tis fit
You ſhould diſpoſe it, then 'tis ſafe from danger.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: I'll be a loving Miſtreſs to my boy too.
Now fetch it in and lets rejoyce upon't.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Hold your light Miſtreſs, we may ſee to enter.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Ha what's here? call you this a cheſt?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: We ha miſt Sir.
Our haſte and want of light made us miſtake.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: A very Coffin.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: How! a Coffin? Boy, 'tis very like one.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: The devil ow'd us a ſhame, and now he has paid us.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Is this your Treaſure?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Bury me alive in't.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: It may be there is no room.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Nay, I will ſearch it:
I'll ſee what wealth's within, — a womans face,
And a fair womans.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I cannot tell ſir,
Belike this was the ſadneſs that poſſeſt 'em;
The plate ſtood next, I'm ſure.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I ſhake, I ſhake Boy, what a cold ſweat?—

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: This may work, what will become on's Sir?

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: She is cold, dead cold: de'e find' your conſcience,
De'e bring your Gillians hither—nay, ſhe's puniſh'd,
• oo • conceal'd love's cas'd up?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Tis Maria, the very ſame, the Bride, new horror!

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Theſe are fine tricks, you hope ſhe's in a ſound
〈◊〉 I'll take order ſhe ſhall ne'r recover
To bore my Noſe, come, take her up and bury her
•• ickly, or I'll cry out; take her up inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Be not ſo haſty fool, that may undo us;
We may be in for murther ſo; be patient,
Thou ſeeſt ſhe's dead, and cannot injure thee.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: I am ſure ſhe ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Be not, Sir, dejected,
Too much a ſtrange miſtake! this had not been elſe,
It makes me almoſt weep to think upon't.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: What an unlucky thief am I?

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: I'll no conſidering, either beſtir your ſelf, or —

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Hold.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Let it not ſtay, to ſmell then, I will not
•• dure the ſtink of a Rival.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Would 'twere there again.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: We muſt bury her.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: But were o'th ſudden, or with what providence,
That no eyes watch us.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Take a Spade and follow me,
The next fair ground we meet, make the Church-yard;
•• I live, I'll ſee her lodg'd. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: It muſt be ſo,
〈◊〉 heavy my heart is, I ha no life left.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I am paſt thinking too, no underſtanding,
•• I ſhould miſs the right Cheſt.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: The happy Cheſt.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: That, which I ſaw and markt too.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Well paſſion wo'not help us,
Had I twenty falls for this?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: 'Twas my fault ſir.
And twenty thouſand fears for this, oth'devil,
Now could I curſe, well, we have her now,
And muſt diſpoſe her.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Hang both for two blind buzzards, here's a Spade
Quickly or I'll call the neighbors.
There's no remedy,
Would the poor hungry priſoners had this paſtie. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Juſtice, and a Servant with a light.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Twas a ſtrange miſchance Sir.

sp.speaker: Ju
sp.l: Miſchance, ſayſt? No 'twas happineſs to me,
There's ſo much charge ſav'd, I have her portion,
I'll marry twenty more on ſuch conditions.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Did it not trouble you Sir,
To ſee her dead?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Not much, I thank my conſcience;
I was tormented till that happen'd, furies
Were in my brain to think my ſelf a Cuckold
At that time of the night:
When I come home, I charge you ſhut my doors,
Locks, bolts, and bars, are little enough to ſecure me.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why, and pleaſe you?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Fool to ask that queſtion;
To keep out women, I expect her Mother
Will viſit me with her clamors, oh I hate
Their noiſe, and do abhor the whole ſex heartily;
They are all walking Devils, Harpyes: I will ſtudy
A week together how to rail ſufficiently,
Upon 'em all, and that I may be furniſh'd,
Thou ſhalt buy all the railing Books and Ballads,
That Malice hath invented againſt women,
I will read nothing elſe, and practiſe 'em,
Till I grow fat with curſes.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: If you'll go
To th'charge, let me alone to find you Books.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: They come neer us

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Whats that?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Where? hold up the Torch Knave.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Did you hear nothing, 'tis a —

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Why doſt make a ſtand?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Whats that?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Where, where, doſt ſee any thing?
We are hard by the Church-yard, and I was never
Valiant at midnight in ſuch irkſome places;
They ſay Ghoſts walk ſometimes, hark, de'e hear nothing?

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: No farther, dig here, and lay her in quickly.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: What light is that Boy, we ſhall be diſcover'd;
Set the Coffin up an end, and get behind me,
There's no avoiding.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Where's that groan? I begin to be afraid.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: What ſhall we do Sir?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: We are almoſt at home now, thou muſt go forward,
Perhaps 'twas my imagination.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Tis he?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I know him too, let me alone.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Oh Sir, a Ghoſt, the very Ghoſt of Miſtreſs Bride,
I have no power to run away.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Curſed Ghoſt, bleſs me, preſerve me,
I do command thee what ſo ore thou art,
I do conjure thee leave me; do not fright me;
If thou beeſt a devil vex me not ſo ſoon,
If thou beeſt.
The ſpirit of my wife.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Thy Wife.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I ſhall be tormented.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Thy abus'd wife, that cannot peaceably
Enjoy her death, thou haſt an evil conſcience.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I know it

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Among thy other ſins which black thy ſoul,
Call to thy mind thy vow made to another,
Whom thou haſt wrong'd, and make her ſatisfaction
Now I am dead, thou perjur'd man: or elſe
A thouſand black tormentors ſhall purſue thee,
Untill thou leap into eternal flames;
Where gold which thou ador'ſt here on earth
Melted, the fiends ſhall powre into thy throat;
For this time paſs, go home and think upon me.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Away.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: There are more ſpirits.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Thank you dear wife,
I'll beſtow twenty nobles of a Tomb for thee,
Thou ſhalt not walk and catch cold after death.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: So, ſo, they'r gone, 'twas my ingenious raſcal:
But how doſt thou know he made vows to another?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I over-heard the woman talk to night on't;
But now let's loſe no time Sir, pray lets bury
This Gentlewoman, where's my Miſtreſs?

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Here I durſt not tarry.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: We ha ſo coſen'd the old forty i'th hundred,
And the devil hinder him not, he'll go a pilgrimage;
But come, about our buſineſs, ſet her down again.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: She groans, ha.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Again, ſhe ſtirs.

sp.speaker: Mi.
sp.l: Lets fly, or elſe we ſhall be torn in pieces.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: And you be good at that, bury your ſelf,
Or let the Sexton take ye for his fee,
Away boy. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am very cold, dead cold;
Where am I? What's this? a Coffin? where have I been?
Mercy defend me: Ha? I do remember
I was betray'd, and ſwounded, my heart akes,
I am wondrous hungry too, dead bodies eat not;
Sure I was meant for burial, I am frozen;
Death, 'like a cake of Ice dwells round about me;
Darkneſs ſpreads o're the world too, where? what path?
Beſt providence direct me.

div.head: Actus Tertius.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Thou art the moſt unfortunate fellow;

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: Why Aunt what have I done?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: The moſt malicious varlet,
Thy wicked head never at reſt, but hammering,
And haching helliſh things, and to no purpoſe,
So thou mayſt have thy baſe will.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: Why do you rail thus?
Cannot a ſcurvy accident fall out,
But I muſt be at one end on't?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Thou art at both ends.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: Cannot young ſullen wenches play the fools
And marry, and dye, but I muſt be the agent?
All that I did (and if that be an injury,
Let the world judge it) was but to perſwade her,
And (as I take it) I was bound to it too,
To make the reverend coxcombe her husband Cuckold:
What elſe could I adviſe her? was there harm i'this?
You are of years, and have run through experience,
Would you be content if you were young again,
To have a continual cough grow to your pillow?
A rottenneſs, that vaults are perfumes to;
Hang in your roof, and like a fog infect you?
Anointed hammes, to keep his hinges turning,
Reek ever in your noſe, and twenty night caps,
With twenty ſeveral ſweats?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Some Jew, ſome Juſtice,
A thouſand heathen ſmels to ſay truth Madam,
And would you mellow my young pretty Miſtriſs
In ſuch a miſ-ken?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Sirra,
Where's the body of my Girl?

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: I know not,
I am no Conjurer, you may look the body,
I was like to be ſtol'n away my ſelf, the Spirit
Had like to ha ſurpris'd me in the ſhape of a woman,
Of a young woman, and you know thoſe are dangerous.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: So had I Madam, ſimply though I ſtand here,
I had been raviſh'd too: I had twenty Spirits,
In every corner of the houſe a Fiend met me.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: You lye like Raskals,
Was Miſtriſs Newlove ſuch a ſpirit Sir?
To fright your worſhip;
Well, I diſcharge you Sir, y'are now at liberty,
Live where you pleaſe, and do what pranks you fancy,
You know your ſubſtance: though you are my Nephew,
I am no way bound Sir to protect your miſchief;
So fare you well.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: Farewell good Aunt, I thank you,
Adiew honeſt Nick, the devil if he have power,
Will perſecute your old bones, for this Marriage,
Farewell Miſtreſs Win.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: And ſhall we part with dry lips?
Shall we that have been fellow devils together
Flinch for an old womans fart?

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: 'Tis a fine time a night too, but we muſt part Nic ••

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Shall we never ring again? ne're toſs the tenor,
And roul the changes into a Cup of Clarret?
You ſhall not want what ere I lay my hands on,
As I am ſure Automedon the Coachman,
Shall be diſtributed; bear up, I ſay, hang ſorrow,
Give me that bird abroad that lives at pleaſure,
Sam the Butler's true, the Cook a reverend Trojan,
The Faulkner ſhall ſell his Hawks, and ſwear they we • rotten,
There be ſome wandring ſpoons, that may be met with
I'll pawn a Coach horſe, peace, utter no ſentences.
The harſhneſs ſhall be us'd in our wars alſo;
Or ſhall I drive her (tell me but your will now,
Say but the word) over ſome rotten bridg,
Or by a Marl-pit ſide, ſhe may ſlip in daintily,
Let me alone for my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: No, no, farewell Toby,
Farewell ſpiny Nicholas, no ſuch thing,
There be ways i'the world, if you ſee me
A day or two hence, may be wee'l crack a quart yet,
And pull a bell, commend to the houſhold;
Nay, cry not Toby, 'twill make thy head giddy.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Sweet Maſter Wildbraine.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: No more Toby, go the times may alter—
But where's the coarſe of my dead coſen,
(If ſhe be dead) I hop'd 'thad but diſſembled
That ſits heavy here: Toby, honeſt Toby,
Lend me thy Lanthorn, I forgot 'twas dark,
I had need look to my ways now.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Take a lodging with me to night in the Stable,
And ride away to morrow with one of the horſes,
Next your heart, pray do.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: No, good night good neighbor Toby, I will wande •
I ſcorn to ſubmit my ſelf, ere I have rambled,
But whither, or with what, that's more material;
No matter, and the worſt come, it is but ſtealing,
And my Aunt wo'not ſee me hang'd for her own credit,
And farewel in a Halter coſts me nothing. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: The night, and all the evil the night covers,
The Goblins, Haggs, and the black ſpawn of darkneſs,
Cannot fright me: no death, I dare thy cruelty.
For I am weary both of life and light too;
Keep my wits heaven, they ſay ſpirits appear
To melancholy minds, and the graves open,
I would fain ſee the fair Maria's ſhadow,
But ſpeak unto her ſpirit e'er I dyed,
But ask upon my knees a mercy from her;
I was a villain, but her wretched kinſman,
That ſet his plot, ſhall with his heart-blood ſatisfie
Her injur'd life and honor, what light's this?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: It is but melancholy walking thus;
The Tavern doors are baracado'd too,
Where I might drink till morn in expectation;
I cannot meet the Watch neither; nothing in
The likeneſs of a Conſtable, whom I might,
In my diſtreſs, abuſe, and ſo be carried,
For want of other lodging, to the Counter.
'Tis his voice, Fate, I thank thee.

sp.speaker: Wild:
sp.l: Ha, who's that, and thou be'ſt a man ſpeak?
Frank Hartlove, then I bear my deſtinies,
Thou art the man of all the world I wiſh'd for;
My Aunt has turn'd me out a doors, ſhe has,
〈◊〉 this unchriſtian hour, and I do walk,
Methinks like Guido Faux with my dark Lanthorn,
• ealing to ſet the Town a fire; i'th' Countrey
〈◊〉 ſhould be tane for William o' the Wiſpe,
〈◊〉 : Robin Good-fellow, and how doſt Frank?
The worſe for you.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Come, tha'rt a fool, art going to thy lodging?
〈◊〉 lie with thee to night, and tell thee ſtories,
〈◊〉 many devils we ha met withal;
Our houſe is haunted Frank, whole legions,
〈◊〉 ſaw fifty for my ſhare.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Didſt not fright 'em?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: How; fright 'em? no, they frighted me ſufficiently.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Thou hadſt wickedneſs enough to make them ſtare,
•• be afraid o'thee, malicious devil;
•• draw thy ſword, for by Maria's ſoul;
•• not let thee ſcape to do more miſchief.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Thou art mad, what doſt mean?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: To kill thee, nothing elſe will eaſe my anger,
〈◊〉 injury is freſh, I bleed withal,
For can that word expreſs it, theres no peace in't,
〈◊〉 muſt it be forgiven, but in death;
Therefore call up thy valour, if thou'ſt any.
• nd ſummon up thy ſpirits to defend thee;
•• heart muſt ſuffer for thy damn'd practiſes,
• gainſt thy noble coſin, and my innocence.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Hold, hear a word; did I do any thing
〈◊〉 for your good, that you might have her,
But in that deſperate time I might redeem her,
•• hough with ſhow of loſs.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Out ugly villain,
〈◊〉 on her the moſt hated name of whore
〈◊〉 the worlds eye, and face it out in courteſie,
〈◊〉 him to ſee't, and make me drunk to attempt it.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I hear ſome voices this way.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: No more, if you can pray, do it as you fight.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: What n •• frights oppoſ •• me? I have heard that tongue

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: 'Tis my fortune.
You could not take me in a better time, Sir,
I ha nothing to loſe but the love I lent thee,
My life my ſword protect.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I know 'em both, but to prevent their ruines,
Muſt not diſcover—ſtay men moſt deſperate;
The miſchief you are forward to commit
Will keep me from my grave, and tie my ſpirit
To endleſs troubles elſe.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Ha, 'tis her Ghoſt.

l.hi: Maria?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Hear me both, each wound you make
Runs through my ſoul, and is a new death to me,
Each threatening danger will affright my reſt;
Look on me Hartlove, and my kinſman view me;
Was I not late in my unhappy marriage,
Sufficient miſerable? full of all misfortunes?
But you muſt add, with your moſt impious angers,
Unto my ſleeping duſt this inſolence?
Would you teach time to ſpeak eternally
Of my diſgraces; make Records to keep 'em,
Keep them in braſs? fight then, and kill my honor;
Fight deadly both, and let your bloody ſwords,
Through my reviv'd, and reeking infamy
(That never ſhall be purg'd) find your own ruines:
Hartlove, I lov'd thee once, and hop'd again
In a more bleſſed love to meet thy ſpirit,
• f thou kill'ſt him, thou art a murtherer,
And murther ſhall never inherit heaven:
My time is come, my concealed grave expects me,
Farewel, and follow not, your feet are bloody,
And will pollute my peace: I hope they are melted,
This is my way ſure Exit.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Stay bleſſed ſoul.

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: Would ſhe had come ſooner, and ha ſav'd ſome blood.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Doſt bleed?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Yes certainly, I can both ſee and feel it.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: Now I well hope it is not dangerous;
Give me thy hand, as honor guides me,
I'll know thee again.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I thank thee heartily;
I know not where to get a Surgeon;
This viſion troubles me, ſure ſhe is living,
And I was fooliſh blind, I could not find it;
I bleed apace ſtill, and my heart grows heavy,
If I go far I faint, I'll knock at this houſe,
They may be charitable, would 'twere perfect day.

sp.speaker: Miſt.
sp.l: 'Tis not he: What would you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I would crave a little reſt Lady,
And for my hurts ſome Surgerie, I am a Gentleman
That fortune of a fight —

sp.speaker: Miſt.
sp.l: A handſome Gentleman,
Alas he bleeds, a very handſome Gentleman,

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: A ſweet young wench, beſhrew my heart a fair one;
Fortune has made me ſome recompence,

sp.speaker: Miſt.
sp.l: Pray come in, the air is hurtful for you,
Pray let me lead you,, I'll have a bed for you preſently,
I'll be your Surgeon too, alas ſweet Gentleman,

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I feel no hurts, the morning comes too faſt now.

sp.speaker: Miſt.
sp.l: Softly, I beſeech you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: He is not up yet Madam, what meant you
To come forth ſo early?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: You blockhead;
Your eyes are ſow'd up ſtill, they cannot ſee
When it is day: oh my poor Maria;
Where be the women?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: They ſaid they would follow us.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: He ſhall not laugh thus at my miſery,
And kill my child, and ſteal away her body,
And keep her portion too.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Let him be hang'd for't,
You have my voice.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Theſe women not come yet?
A Son-in-law, I'll keep a Conjurer,
But I'll find out his knavery.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Do, and I'll help him.
And if he were here, this whip ſhould conjure him,
Here's a Capias, and it catch hold on's breech,
I'de make him ſoon believe the Devil were there.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: An old Uſurer.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: He married the money, that's all he lookt for;
For your daughter, let her ſink or ſwim.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I'll ſwim him;
This is his houſe, I wonder they ſtay thus,
That we might rail him out on's wits.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: They'll come,
Fear not Madam, and bring clappers with 'em,
Or ſome have loſt their old wont, I have heard,
No diſparagement to your Ladyſhip, ſome o' their tongues
Like Tom-a-Lincoln, three miles off.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Oh fie,
How tedious are they?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: What and we loſt no time,
You and I ſhall make a ſhift to begin with him,
And tune our Inſtruments till the Conſort come
To make up the full noiſe, I'll knock.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Who's that rapt ſo ſaucily?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: 'Tis I, Toby, come down, or elſe we'll fetch you down,
Alas, this is but the Saints-bell, here's a Gentlewoman
Will ring you another peal, come down, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Some new fortifications, look to my doors,
Put double barrs, I will not have her enter,
Nor any of her Tribe, they come to terrifie me:
Keep out her tongue too, if you can.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I hear you,
And I will ſend my tongue up to your worſhip,
The eccho of it ſhall flye o'er the ſtreet;
My Daughter that thou killedſt with kindneſs (Jew)
That thou betrayedſt to death, thou double Jew,
And after ſtol'ſt her body.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Jew's too good for him,

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I defie you both;
Thy daughter plaid the villain and betraid me.
Betrai'd my honor.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Honor, Raſcal,
And let that bear an action, I'll try it with thee,
Honor?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Oh Reprobate!

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Thou muſty Juſtice,
Buy an honourable halter and hang thy ſelf.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: A worſhipful ropes end is too good for him.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Get honor that way, thou wot die a dog elſe.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Come and be whipt firſt.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Where is her Portion.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Where I'll keep it ſafely.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Traitor, thou ſhalt not keep it.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: More of the kennel? put more bolts to th'doors there,
And arm your ſelves, hell is broke looſe upon us.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: I am glad y'are come, we'll blow the houſe down.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Oh Nurſe, I have ſuch cauſe—

sp.speaker: Wo.
sp.l: Villain, viper, although you had no cauſe, we are bound
To help.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Yes, and believe, we come not here to examine,
And if you pleaſe we'll fire the houſe

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Call the Conſtable.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: A charitable motion, fire is comfortable.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: No, no, we'll only let him know our minds,
We will commit no outrage, he's a Lawyer,

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Give me my Musket.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Where's my daughters body,
That I may bury it?

sp.speaker: Wo.
sp.l: Speak, or we'll bury thee,

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Alive, we'll bury thee, ſpeak old Iniquity.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Bury him alive by all means for a teſtimony.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Their voices make my houſe reel, oh for Officers,
I am in a dream, thy daughters ſpirit
Wa'ks a nights, and troubles all the neighhors:
Go hire a Conjurer, I'll ſay no more.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: The Law ſhall ſay more,

sp.speaker: Wo. Nur.
sp.l: We are witneſſes,
And if thou be'ſt not hang'd —

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Buy a Book of good manners,
A ſhort Book of good manners.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Buy a ballad, a ballad of the maid was got with child

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: That might ha been my caſe laſt night,
I'll ha't, what e'er it coſt me.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A ballad of the Witches hang'd at Ludlow.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: I will have that too;
There was an Aunt of mine, I think amongſt 'em,
I would be glad to hear her Teſtament.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A new Book of Women,

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: The thunder's laid, how they ſtare at him

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A new Book of Fools, a ſtrange Book,
Very ſtrange fools.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I'll owe thee a good turn, whate'er thou art.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A Book of Walking Spirits.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: That I like not.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Nor I, they walk'd me the Fools Morris.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A Book of Wicked Women.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: That's well thought on.
Of rude, malicious Women, of proud Women,
Of ſcolding Women, we ſhall ne'er get in.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A ballad of wrong'd Maids.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I'll buy that.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A little, very little Book,
Of good and godly Women, a very little one,
So little you may put it in a Nutſhel.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: With a ſmall print that no body can read it.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Peace ſirrah, or I'll tear your Books.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Open the door and let him in, I love him.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A Book of evil Magiſtrates.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I marry d'ye hear that Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: And their eviller wives,
That wear their Places in their Petticoats.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: D'ye hear that Lady.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A Book new printed againſt Playing,
Dancing, Masking, May-poles; a zealous Brothers Book
And full of Fables.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Another Book of Women, of mad women,

Women that were born in March.
E •

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Are you got in?
We would ha pull'd your knaves hide elſe; this fellow
Was ſent to abuſe us, but we ſhall have tim •
To talk more with this Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Farewel Madam, as you like this, come viſit me ag •
You and your treble ſtrings, now ſcold your hearts out—

sp.speaker: Wo.
sp.l: Shall he carry it thus away?

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Go to the Judge, and what you'll have us ſwear •

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I thank ye heartily,
I'll keep that for the laſt, I will go home,
And leave him to his Conſcience for a while,
If it ſleep long, I'll wake it with a vengeance. E •
What book has he given thee?
A dainty book, a book of the great Navy,
Of fifteen hundred ſhips of Cannon-proof,
Built upon Whales to keep their keels from ſinking:
And Dragons in 'em, that ſpit fire ten mile;
And Elephants that carry goodly Caſtles.
Doſt thou believe it?
Shall we not believe Books in print?
I have John Taylors book of Hempſeed too,
Which for two lines I hapned on by chance,
I reverence.
I prethee what are they?
They are ſo pat upon the time, as if
He ſtudied to anſwer the late Hiſtriomaſtix,
Talking of change and transformations,
That wittily, and learnedly he bangs him,
So many a Puritans ruff, though ſtarch'd in print,
And confute Horace with a Water Poet:
A Play in the Puritans ruff? I'll buy his Works for't,
What haſt there a Ballad too?
This is a piece of Poetry indeed;
What noiſe is that?
Some cry i th' ſtreets; prethee ſing on. Sing again.
Agen, doſt not hear? 'tis i'th' houſe certainly?
'Tis a ſtrange noiſe? and has a tang o'th' Juſtice.
Let's ſee? Exit.

div.stage: Enter the Servants bringing in their Maſter bound and gagg'd.

sp.l: Untie his feet, pull out his gagg, he will choak elſe,
What deſperate rogues were theſe.
Give him freſh air.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I will never ſtudy books more:
I am undone, theſe villains have undone me.
Rifled my Desk, they have undone me learnedly:
A fire take all their Books, I'll burn my Study:
Where were you raſcals when the villains bound me,
You could not hear.?
He gave us Books, Sir, dainty Books to buſie us;
And we were reading, in that which was the Brew-houſe;
A great way off, we were ſinging Ballads too;
And could not hear

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: This was a precious thief,
A ſubtle trick to keep my ſervants ſafe.
What ha you loſt Sir?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: They ranſack'd all before my face, and threatned
To kill me if I cough'd, they have a chain,
My rings, my box of caſting gold, my purſe too.
They robb'd me miſerably; but that which moſt grieves me,
They took away ſome Writings; 'twas a rogue
That knew me, and ſet on by the old Lady,
I will indite her for't.
Shall we purſue 'em?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Run, run, curſed raskals,
I am out of my wits, let not a creature in,
No not with neceſſaries.
We ſhall be ſtarv'd.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I'll buy my meat at window as they paſs by;
I wo'nt truſt my Scrivenor, he has books too;
And bread I'll ha flung up; I charge ye all
〈◊〉 all the books i'th' houſe.
Your little Prayer Book?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I'll never pray agen, I'll have my doors
Made up, nothing but walls, and thick ones too;
No ſound ſhall tempt me agen, remember I
Have forſwore books,
If you ſhould be call'd to take your oath?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I will forſwear all oaths, rather than ſee
• thing but in the likeneſs of a book:
And I were condemn'd, I'll rather chuſe to hang,
Than read agen; come in, and ſearch all places,
They may be about the houſe, were the doors lock'd?
But the keys in 'em, and if they be gone,
They could not want wit to lock us in, Sir,

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Never was a man ſo miſerably undone,
• would loſe a limb, to ſee their rogueſhips totter.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Thy brothers daughter, ſaiſt, and born in Wales?

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: I have long time deſired to ſee her, and I hope
Your Ladyſhip will not be offended.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: No, no.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: I ſhould be happy, if ſhe might be ſerviceable
To you Madam.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Beſhrew me, but at firſt, ſhe took me much,
Is ſhe not like Maria? ſetting aſide
Her language very like her, and I love her
The better for't, I prethee call her hither,
She ſpeaks feat Engliſh.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Why Guennith, Guennith, du hummah Guennith.
She is courſe Madam, after her countrey guiſe,
And were ſhe in fine cloths—

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I'll have her handſome:
What part of Wales were you born in?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: In Abehundis Madam.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: She ſpeaks that name in Welſh, which we call Brecknock.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: What can you do?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Her was toe many tings in Walls, know not the faſhion in Londons? her was milk the Cows, make ſeeze and buters, and ſpin very well the Welſh freeze, her was Cooke to te Mountain Cots, and ſing very fine prittiſh tunes, was mage good ales and breds, and her know to dance on Sundays, marge you now Madams.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: A pretty innocence, I do like her infinitely, Nurſe,
And if I live—

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Here is Mr. Hartlove, Madam, come to ſee you.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Alas poor Gentleman, prethee admit him.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Madam, I am come to take my laſt leave.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: How Sir?

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Of all my home affections, and my friends,
For the intereſt you had once in Maria,
I would acquaint you when I leave the kingdom.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Would there were any thing in my poor power
That might divert your Will, and make you happy;
I am ſure I have wrong'd her too, but let your pardon
Aſſure me you are charitable; ſhe's dead
Which makes us both ſad: What do you look on?
The likeſt face—

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Pleſſe us awle, why does that ſentilman make ſuch unders and mazements at her, I know her not.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Be not offended maid.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: How the wench bluſhes, ſhe repreſents Marias loſs to him.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Will the ſentilman hurt her? pray you be her defences, was have mad phiſnomies, is her troubled with Lunaticks in her prain pans, bleſs us awle.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Where had you this face?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Her faces be our none, I warrant her.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: I wonot hurt you, all the lineaments
That built Maria up; all thoſe ſpringing beauties
Dwell on this thing, change but her tongue I know her:
Let me ſee your hand.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Du Guin. was never thieves, and robberies; here is no ſindge in her hands warrant her.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Truſt me, the ſelf-ſame white,
And ſoftneſs, prethee ſpeak our Engliſh Dialect.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Ha leggs? what does her ſpeage hard urds to her to make poor Guennith ridicles, was no mannerly ſentilman to abuſe her.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: By the love,
That everlaſting love I bear Maria—

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p:
Maria, her name was Guenith, and good names, was poor elſe, oman maid, her have no fine kanags to madge her trickſie
in her own cuntries was held a fine enſe her can tels her, and honeſt enſe too, marg you dat now, her can keep her little legs cloſe enough, warrant her.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: How prettily this anger ſhews.
She gabbles innocently.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Madam farewel, and all good fortune dwell we'e,
With me my own affections; farewel Maid,
Fair gentle Maid.
She ſighs.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Du cat a whee.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: I cannot goe, there's ſomewhat calls me back.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Poor Franke,
How gladly would I entertain thy love,
And meet thy worthy flame, but ſhame forbids, me:
sp.p: If pleaſe her Ladyſhip dwell here with Guenneth, and learn to ſpinn and card ull, to mage flannells, and linſeyes ulſeis, ſall tawgco'd urds to her Ladyſhips urſhips for her.
sp.l: The tears of true affection, woe is me,
Oh curſed love that glories in maids miſeries,
And true mens broken hearts.

sp.speaker: La.
