sp.l: Alas I pity him, the wench is rude, and knows you not, forgive her.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Wype your nyes yray you, though was porn in Walls 'mong craggy rocks, and mountains, yet heart is ſoft, look you hur can weep too, when hur ſee men mage prinie tears and lamentations.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: How hard ſhe holds me?
Juſt as Maria did, weeps the ſame drops,
Now as I have a living ſoul, her ſight too;
What ſhall I think, is not your name Maria,
If it be not, delude me with ſo much charity
To ſay it is.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Upon her life, you was mighty deal in love with ſome podies, your pale ſeekes and hollow nyes, and pantings upon her poſom, know very well, becauſe look you, her think her honeſt ſentilman, you ſall call her Maria.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Good Madam, think not ill I am thus ſaucy,

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Oh no Sir, be you not angry with the wench.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: I am moſt pleas'd.
Lets interrupt him, he'll be mad outright elſe.
Obſerve a little more.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Would I could in your language beg a kiſs,

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: If her have neceſſities of a kiſs, look you, dere is one in ſarities.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Let me ſuffer death,
If in my apprehenſion two twinn'd cherries
Be more a kinn, than her lips to Maria's:
And if this harſh illuſion would but leave her,
She were the ſame, good Madam, ſhall I have
Your conſent now?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: To what?

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: To give this Virgin to me.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: She's not mine, this is her kinſwoman,
And has more power to diſpoſe; alas, I pity him.
Pray gentleman prevail with him to goe;
More that I wiſh his comfort than his abſence.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: You have been always kind to me, will you
Deny me your fair Coſin?

sp.speaker: Nu.
sp.l: 'Twere fit you firſt obtain'd her own conſent.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: She is no friend that wiſhes my departure,
I doe not trouble you.
'Tis not Maria.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Her ſhadow is enough, I'll dwell with that,
Purſue your own ways, ſhall we live together?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: If her will come to morrow and tauge to her, her will tell her more of her meanings, and then if her be melancholy, her will ſing her a Welch Song too, to make her merries, but Guenith was very honeſt; her was never love but one ſentleman, and he was bear her great teal of good-ills too, was marry one day S. Davy, her give her five pair of white gloves, if her will dance at her weddings.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: All I am worth,
And all my hopes this ſtrange voice would forſake her,
For then ſhe ſhud be— prethee ſtay a little,
Hark in thine ear, diſſemble not, but tell me,
And ſave my life; I know you are Maria:
Speak but as I doe, ten words to confirm me;
You have an Engliſh ſoul, do not diſguiſe it
From me with theſe ſtrange accents—She pinch'd hard
Again, and ſigh'd.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: What ails the Wench? Exit.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Why, Guenith.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: She's gone too.
Come leave this dream.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: A dream? I think ſo;
But 'twas a pleaſing one, now I'll obey,
And forget all theſe wonders, lead the way. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: HOneſt Toby?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Sweet Mr. Wildbrain,—I am glad I ha met w'ye

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Why, did my Aunt ſend for me?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Your Aunt's a mortal, and thinks not on you
For ought I can perceive.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Is my coſin alive agen?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Neither, and yet we do not hear
That ſhe's buried.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: What ſhould make thee glad then?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: What ſhould make me glad? have I not cauſe,
To ſee your Princely body well, and walk thus,
Look blithe and bonny, and your Wardrobe whole ſtill?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: The caſe is clear, and I ha found a Mine,
A perfect Indie, ſince my Aunt caſhier'd me;
What think'ſt of this?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Oh delicate bells.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Thou putteſt me in mind,
We are to ring anon, I mean to ſend for thee;
Meet me at the old Pariſh Church.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Say no more.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: When thy Lady is a bed, we ha conſpir'd
A midnight peal for joy.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: If I fail, hang me i' th' bell-ropes.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: And how? and how does my Aunt?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: She's up to th' ears in Law;
I do ſo whirl her to the Counſellors chambers,
And back again, and bounce her for more money,
And too again, I know not what they do with her;
But ſhe's the merrieſt thing among theſe Law-drivers;
And in their ſtudies half a day together;
If they do get her with Magna Charta, ſhe ſwears,
By all the ability of her old body,
She will ſo claw the Juſtice, ſhe will ſell
The tiles of the houſe ſhe vows, and Sack out o'th' Cellar,
(That ſhe worſhips to Idolatry) but ſhe'll hang him.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I would ſhe could: but hark thee honeſt Toby.
If a man have a Miſtriſs, may we not,
Without my Aunts leave, borrow now and then
A Coach to tumble in, towards the Exchange,
And ſo forth?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: A Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Wil.
sp.l: She may be thine when we are married.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Command, I'll carry you both in pomp;
And let my Lady go a foot a Law-catching,
And exerciſe her corns: where is ſhe Maſter John?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: 'Shat ſee her.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Shall we ring for her?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: And drink her health?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Drink ſtifly for five hours.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: We'll drink fifteen.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: To night? we will ha twenty Torches then,
And through the ſtreets drive on triumphantly;
Triumphantly we'll drive, by my Ladies door,
As I am a Chriſtian, Coachman, I will rattle you
And Urine in her porch, and ſhe ſhall fear me:
If you ſay more, I ſhall run mad outright,
I will drink Sack, and ſurfeit inſtantly;
I know not where I am now. Exit,

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: Hold for thy buttons ſake, the knave's tranſported.

l.hi: Jack Wildbrain?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Honeſt Tom, how thrives the fellonious world with thee now?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: You look and talk as you were much exalted.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Th'art i'th' right Tom. I'll tell thee firſt,
I ha ſhook off my Aunt, and yet I live ſtill,
And drink, and ſing; her houſe had like to ha ſpoil'd me;
I keep no hours now;
Nor need any falſe key
To the old womans Cabinets, I ha money
Upon my word, and pawn no oaths to th' Butler.
No matrimonial proteſtations
For Sack-poſſets to the Chambermaid,
I praiſe my Fate, there be more ways to th' wood Tom.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Prethee releaſe my wonder.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I'll increaſe it, wipe thine eyes,
Here is a chain worth money, and ſome man had it,
A fooliſt Diamond, and other trifles—

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: The very ſame, Oh Gipſey! Infidel!
All that I ſweat, and ventur'd my neck for,
He has got already; who would truſt a ſtrumpet:

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: This? This is nothing to what I poſſeſs
At home.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: What home?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: A houſe that ſhall be nameleſs;
The Miſtriſs of it mine too, ſuch a piece
For fleſh and blood, added to that ſo loving—

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Is ſhe married?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I know not, nor I care not;
• ut ſuch a prize, ſo mounting, ſo delicious,
Thou wilt run mad, I'll tell thee more hereafter,

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Nay, prethee a word more.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I took no pains to find out all this Paradiſe,
My deſtiny threw me upon't i'th dark, I found it
Wanting a Lodging too.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: No old acquaintance?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Never, never ſaw her;
But theſe things happen not in every age:
I cannot ſtay, if thou wilt meet anon
At my own randevow, thou knoweſt the Tavern,
We'll ſup together, after that a company
Of merry lads have made a match to ring.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: You keep your exerciſe, i'th' old Church?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: No other,
There is no Muſick to the Bells, we wo'd
Have Bonfires if we durſt, and thou wo'd come
It ſhall coſt thee nothing Tom, hang pilfering,
And keep me company, in time I may
Shew thee my wench too.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I cannot promiſe; but you will be there?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: We'll toſs the Bells, and make the Steeple
Roar boy, but come to ſupper then.

sp.speaker: Lur,
sp.l: My hand, and expect me:
Yes, I will come or ſend, and to ſome purpoſe;
Art come boy?
sp.stage: Enter Boy with Gown, Beard, and Conſtables ſtaff.
sp.l: Excellent, Knave, how didſt thou purchaſe theſe?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: The ſtaff I ſtole laſt night from a ſleeping Conſtable;
The reſt I borrowed by my acquaintance with
The Players boyes; you were beſt to loſe no time, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: So, ſo, help boy, 'tis very well, do I not look
Like one that breaks the Kings peace with authority?
You know your charge, prepare things handſomely,
My diligent boy, and leave me to my office,

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: There wants nothing already; but I fly Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Now Fortune prove no ſlut, and I'll adore thee.

sp.speaker: Within. Ser.
sp.l: Whoſe there? Knocks.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A friend wo'd ſpeak with Maſter Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Who are you?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I am the Conſtable.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: My Maſter is not at leaſure to hear buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: How? Not at leaſure to do the King ſervice;
Take heed what you ſay, Sir; I know his worſhip,
If he know my buſineſs, would no excuſe.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You muſt go to another Juſtice, I'll aſſure
My Maſter is not well in health.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I know not,
But if your worſhipful be not at leaſure
To do himſelf a benefit, I am gone Sir,
An infinite benefit, and the State ſhall thank him for't;
Thank him, and think on him too; I am an Officer.
And know my place, but I do love the Juſtice;
I honor any authority above me:
Beſide, he is my neighbor, and I worſhip him.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You have no Books, nor Ballads, Mr Conſtable,
About you?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: What ſhould I doe with Books? does it become
A man of my place to underſtand ſuch matters?
Pray call your Maſter, if he pleaſe to follow me,
I ſhall diſcover to him ſuch a plot,
Shall get him everlaſting fame, I'll be hang'd for't,
And he be not knighted inſtantly, and for reward
Have ſome of the malefactors Lands, I'll bring him too;
But I cannot delay time. Within.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: A Conſtable Sir, would ſpeak about ſome buſineſs,
He ſays will bring you Fame, and mighty profit.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Pleaſe your worſhip come down, I'll make you happy;
The notabl'ſt piece of villany I have in hand Sir,
And you ſhall find it out; I ha made choice
To bring your worſhip to the firſt knowledge, and
Thank me, as you find the good on't afterwards.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: What is it? Treaſon?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Tis little better, I can tell you I have lodg'd
A crew of the moſt rank and deſperate villains:
They talk of robberies and waies they did 'em;
And how they left men bound in their ſtudies.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: With Books and Ballads?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: That Sir, that, and murders,
And thouſand knaveries more, they're very rich Sir,
In Money, Jewels, Chains, and a hundred more
Devices.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Happy, happy Conſtable, I meet ye
At the back door, get ready knaves.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Not a man I beſeech you,
I have privately appointed ſtrength about me,
They cannot ſtart, your men would breed ſuſpition;
All my deſire is, you would come alone;
That you might have the hope of the enterpriſe,
That you might hear 'em firſt, and then proceed, Sir,

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I come, I come.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Tis very well. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Keep all my doors faſt, 'tis ſomething late.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: So, ſo, and pleaſe your worſhip I direct you.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: My Maſter ſtaies, I doubt his lime-twigs catch not,
If they doe, all's provided; but I all
This while forget my own ſtate, fair Maria
Is certainly alive, I met her in
Another habit, with her Nurſe, 'twas ſhe:
There is ſome trick in't, but when this is over,
I'll find it out, this project for the Uſurer
May have good effect; however, 'twill be ſport
To mortifie him a little;
He's come without him:
Have you fail'd, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Proſper'd? my little Ingineer; away,
He is i'th' next room, be not you ſeen, ſirrah. Exit.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: The pitfall's ready, never Juſtice
Was catcht in ſuch a nooze: e'er he get out.
He ſhall run through a ſcouring purgatory,
Shall purge him to the quick, 'tis night already. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Come ſoftly, yet Sir, ſoftly, are you not weary?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Th'aſt brought me into a melancholy place,
I ſee no creature.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: This is, Sir, their Den
Where they ſuppoſe themſelves ſecure, I am faint,
With making haſte; but I muſt be thus troubled,
And therefore never go without a Cordial; Seems to drink.
Without this I ſhould dye;
How it refreſhes me
Already? will't pleaſe your worſhip? I might have had
The manners to ha' let you drink before me;
Now am I luſty.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: 'Twas a good taſte.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Taſte? how d'ye find the virtue, nay Sir, ſpare it not:
My wife has the Receipt, does it not ſtir
Your Worſhips body? when you come to examine,
'Twill make you ſpeak like thunder.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Hoy he.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: It works already.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Is there never a chair, I was wearier than I thought,
But who ſhall we have to take 'em. Mr. Conſtable?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Let me alone, when I but give the watch-word
We will have men enough to ſurprize an Army.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I begin to be ſleepy; what, haſt a chair?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: They do not dream of us, 'tis early riſing;
Care, care, and early riſing, Common-wealths men
Are ever ſubject to the nods; ſit down, Sir,
A ſhort nap is not much amiſs; ſo, ſo, he's faſt;
Faſt as a fiſh i'th' net, he has winking powder
Shall work upon him to our wiſh, remove him,
Nay, we may cut him into collops now
And he ne'r ſeel; have you prepar'd the vault, ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Yes, yes, Sir, every thing in's place.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: When you have plac'd him, you and I boy
Muſt about another project hard by, his potion
Will bind him ſure enough till we return,
This villany weighs mainly, But we'll purge ye. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sex.
sp.l: Now for mine ears, mine ears be conſtant to me;
They ring a wager, and I muſt deal juſtly, ha boys.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Doſt hear 'em, hark, theſe be the Ringers?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Are you ſure the ſame?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Or my directions fail;
The coaſt is clear:
How the bells go? how daintily they tumble?
And methinks they ſeem to ſay; Fine fools I'll fit you.

sp.speaker: Sex.
sp.l: Excellent agen, good boys—oh that was nought.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Be you conceal'd by any means yet, hark,
They ſtop, I hope they'll to't agen, cloſe Sir.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: A palpable knock.

sp.speaker: Ring.
sp.l: 'Twas none.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Be judg'd by the Sexton then,
If I have ears.

sp.speaker: Sex.
sp.l: A knock, a knock, a groſs one.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Carman, your gallon of wine, you ring moſt impiouſly,
Art thou o'th' worſhipful company of the Knights o'th Weſt,
And handle a bell with no more dexterity?
You think you are in Thames-ſtreet
Juſtling the Carts: oh a clean hand's a Jewel.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Good ſpeed to your good exerciſe.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Y' are welcome

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I come, Sir, from a Gentleman, and neighbor hard by,
One that loves your Muſick well.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: He may have more on't,
Handle a bell, as you were haling timber?
Groſs, groſs, and baſe, abſurd.

sp.speaker: Ring.
sp.l: I'll mend it next peal.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: To intreat a knowledge of you, whether it be
By the Ear you ring thus cunningly, or by the Eye;
For to be plain, he has laid ten pounds upon't.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: But which way has he laid?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: That your Ear guides you,
And not your Eye.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Has won, has won, the Ear's our only inſtrument:

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: But how ſhall we be ſure on't.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Put all the lights out, to what end ſerve our eyes then?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: A plain Caſe,

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: You ſay true, 'tis a fine cunning thing to ring by th' Ear ſure
And can you ring i'th' dark ſo?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: All night long, boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: 'Tis wonderful, let this be certain Gentlemen,
And half his wager he allows among ye;
Is't poſſible you ſhould ring ſo?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Poſſible, thou art a child, I'll ring when I am dead drun •
Out with the lights, no twinkling of a candle,
I know my rope too, as I know my noſe,
And can bang it ſoundly i'th' dark, I warrant you..

sp.speaker: Wi.
sp.l: Come, let's confirm him ſtraight, and win the wager. Ex •

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Let me hear to ſtrengthen me;
And when y'ave rung, I'll bring the money to you.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: So, ſo, follow 'em;
They ſhall have a cool reward, one hath gold of mine,
Good ſtore in's pocket, Ring
But this will be reveng'd in a ſhort warning.
They are at it luſtily; hey, how wantonly
They ring away their cloaths, how it delights me;

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Here, here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Haſt Wildbrain's?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: His whole cafe, Sir; I felt it out, and by the guards
This ſhould be the Coachmans, another ſuit too.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Away boy, quickly now to the Uſurer,
His hour to wake approaches.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: That once finiſhed,
You'll give me leave to play, Sir: here they come. Ex •

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I am monſtrous weary.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Fie, how I ſweat? Reach me my cloak to cover me,
I run to oyl like a Porpiſe: 'twas a brave peal.

sp.speaker: Sex.
sp.l: Let me light the candle firſt, then I'll wait on you.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: A very brave peal.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Carman, you came in cloſe now.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Sure 'tis paſt midnight.

sp.speaker: Ring.
sp.l: No ſtirring in the ſtreets I hear.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Walk further, was that a pillar? 'tis harder than • noſ •
Where's the boy promis'd us five pounds?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Room, I ſweat ſtill; come, come, my cloak,
I ſhall take cold.

sp.speaker: Sex.
sp.l: Where lies it?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Here, here, and all our cloaths.

sp.speaker: Sex.
sp.l: Where, where?

sp.speaker: Ring.
sp.l: I'th' corner.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Is thy candle blind too, give me the bottle,
I can drink like a Fiſh now, like an Elephant.

sp.speaker: Sex.
sp.l: Here are the corners, but here are no cloaths;
Yes, here is a cuff.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: A cuff? give me the candle,
Cuffes wonot cover me—I ſmell the knavery.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Is't come to a cuff? my whole ſuit turned to a button?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Now am I as cold again as though 'twere Chriſtmas;
Cold with my fear, I'll never ring by the ear more.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: My new cloaths vaniſh'd?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: All my cloaths Toby.

sp.speaker: Ring.
sp.l: Here's none.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Not one of my dragons wings left to adorn me,
Have I muted all my feathers?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Cheated by the ear; a plot to put out the candle;
I could be mad; my chain, my rings, the gold, the gold.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: The cold, the cold I cry, and I cry truly,
Not one ſleeve, nor a cape of a cloak to warm me.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: What miſerable fools were we?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: We had e'en beſt, gentlemen,
Every man chuſe his rope again, and faſten it,
And take a ſhort turn to a better fortune,
To be bawds to our miſeries, and put our own lights out?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Prethee Sexton lets have a fire at thy houſe.
A good fire, we'll pay thee ſome way for't, I am ſtone cold.

sp.speaker: Sex.
sp.l: Alas I pity you, come quickly Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Sure I ha been in a dream, I had no Miſtriſs,
Nor gold, nor cloaths, but am a ringing raſcal.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: Fellows in affliction, let's take hands all,
Now are we fit for tumblers.

div.stage: Enter Lurcher and others, bringing in Algripe.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: So, ſo, preſently his ſleep will leave him.
And wonder ſeize upon him,
B • d 'em within be ready.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: What ſound's this?
What horrid dinne? what diſmal place is this?
I never ſaw before, and now behold it;
But by the halflight of a Lamp, that burns here:
My ſpirits ſhake, tremble through my body;
Help, help,
sp.stage: Enter two Furies, with black Tapers.
sp.l: Mercy protect me, my ſoul quakes,
What dreadful apparitions! how I ſhudder!

l.hi: Algripe.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: What are you?
We are hellhounds, hellhounds, that have commiſſion
From the Prince of darkneſs,
To fctch thy black ſoul to him.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Am I not alive ſtill?
Thou art, but we have brought thee inſtruments
Will quickly rid thy miſerable life, Stabb,
Poyſon.
Hang thy ſelf, this choice is offer'd,
Thou canſt not hope for heaven; thy baſe ſoul is
Loſt to all hope of mercy.
Quickly, quickly,
The torments, cool.
And all thy friends expect thee.
Come with us to that pit of endleſs horror,
Or we will force thee.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Oh, oh, oh.
Groans are too late, ſooner the raviſher,
Whoſe ſoul is hurl'd into eternal froſt,
Stung with the force of twenty thouſand winters,
To puniſh the diſtempers of his blood,
Shall hope to get from thence, than thou avoid
The certainty of meeting hell • where he is,
Shall murderers be there for ever dying,
Their ſouls ſhot through with Adders, torn on Engines,
Dying as many deaths for killing one,
Could any imagination number them,
As there be moments in eternity:
And ſhall that Juſtice ſpare thee, that haſt ſlain,
Murdered by thy extortion ſo many?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Oh, oh.
Do execution quickly, or we'll carry thee alive to hell

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Gently, gentle devils, do not force me
To kill my ſelf, nor do not you do't for me;
Oh let me live, I'll make amends for all.
Tell us of thy repentance? perjur'd villain,
Pinch off his fleſh, he muſt be whipt, ſalted and whipt.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Oh miſery of miſeries!

sp.speaker: Recorders 1. 2.
sp.l: Tear his accurſed limbs, to hell with him, ha!
A miſchief on that innocent face, away. Creeps in.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Malicious furies hence, choak not the ſeeds
Of holy penitence.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: This muſt be an Angel,
How at his preſence the fiends crawl away?
Here is ſome light of mercy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Be thou wiſe,
And entertain it, wretched, wretched man;
What poor defence hath all thy wealth been to thee?
What ſays thy conſcience now?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Be my good Angel, here I promiſe thee,
To become honeſt, and renounce all villany;
Enjoyn me any pennance, I'll build Churches;
A whole City of Hoſpitals.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Take heed,
There is no dallying, nor are theſe impos'd.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Name any thing within my power, ſweet Angel;
And if I do not faithfully perform it,
Then whip me every day, burn me each minute,
Whole years together let me freeze to Iſicles.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I'th' number of thy foul oppreſſions;
Thou haſt undone a faithful Gentleman,
By taking forfeit of his Land.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Young Lurcher,
I do confeſs.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: He lives moſt miſerable,
And in deſpair may hang or drown himſelf;
Prevent his ruine, or his blood will be
More ſin in thy account: haſt thou forgotten
He had a ſiſter?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I do well remember it.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Couldſt thou for Mammon break thy ſolemn vow,
Made once to that unhappy maid, that weeps
A thouſand tears a day for thy unkindneſs,
Was not thy faith contracted, and thy heart?
And couldſt thou marry another?

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: But ſhe is dead,
And I will make true ſatisfaction.

sp.speaker: Boy
sp.l: What do I inſtance theſe that haſt been falſe
To all the world.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: I know it, and will henceforth
Practice repentance, do not frown ſweet Angel;
I will reſtore all Mortgages, forſwear
Abominable Uſury, live chaſte;
For I have been wanton in my ſhroud, my age;
And if that poor innocent maid, I ſo abus'd,
Be living, I will marry her, and ſpend
My days to come religiouſly.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I was commanded but a Meſſenger
To tell thee this, and reſcue thee from thoſe,
Whoſe malice would have dragg'd thee quick to hell,
If thou abuſe this mercy and repent not,
Double damnation will expect thee for it;
But if thy life be virtuous hereafter,
A bleſſedneſs ſhall reward thy good example,
Thy fright hath much diſtracted thy weak ſences,
Drink of this viol, and renew thy ſpirits
I ha done my office, think on't and be happy.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: So, ſo, he gapes already, now he's faſt;
Thou haſt acted rarely, but this is not all;
Firſt, help to convey him out o' th' vault.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: You will diſpenſe with me now, as you promis'd, Sir,

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: We will make ſhift without thee, th'aſt done well,
By our device this bondage may ſcape hell. Exit.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Didſt think Maria, this poor outſide, and
Diſſembling of thy voice could hide thee from
A mothers ſearching eye, though too much fear,
Leſt thou wert not the ſame, might blind a Lover
That thought thee dead too, oh my dear Maria,
I hardly kept my joyes in from betraying thee:
Welcome again to life, we ſhall find out
The myſtery of thy abſence; conceal
Thy perſon ſtill, for Algripe muſt not know thee:
And exerciſe this pretty Dialect;
If there be any courſe in Law to free thee,
Thou ſhalt not be ſo miſerable; be ſilent
Good Nurſe.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Yo • ſhould not need to fear me, Madam,
I do not love the uſuring Jew ſo well;
Beſide, 'twas my trick to diſguiſe her ſo.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Be not dejected Mall.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Your care may comfort me;
But I deſpair of happineſs:

sp.speaker: Hartlove,
sp.l: I dare not ſee him.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: We'll withdraw.
I ſhall but grieve to ſee his paſſions too,
Since there's no poſſibility to relieve him.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: The world's a Labyrinth, where unguided men
Walk up and down to ſind their wearineſs;
No ſooner have we meaſured with much toil
One crooked path with hope to gain our freedom,
But it betrays us to a new affliction;
What a ſtrange mockery will man become
Shortly to all the creatures?
Oh Maria • !
If thou be'ſt dead, why does thy ſhadow fright me?
Sure 'tis becauſe I live; were I but certain
To meet thee in one grave, and that our duſt
Might have the priviledge to mix in ſilence,
How quickly ſhould my ſoul ſhake off this burthen!
Thus far my wiſhes have ſucceſs, I'll loſe
No time: Sir, are not you call'd Mr. Hartlove?
Pardon my rudeneſs.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: What does that concern
Thee Boy, 'tis a name cannot advantage thee;
And I am weary on't.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Had you conce • l'd,
Or I forgot it, Sir, ſo large were my
Directions, that you could not ſpeak this language,
But I ſhould know you by your ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Thou
Wert well inform'd, it ſeems; well, what's your buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I come to bring you comfort.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Is Maria
Alive agen? that's ſomewhat, and yet not
Enough to make my expectation riſe, to
Paſt half a bleſſing; ſince we cannot meet
To make it up a full one; th'art miſtaken.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: When you have heard me, you'll think otherwiſe:
In vain I ſhould report Maria living:
The comfort that I bring you, muſt depend
Upon her death.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Th'art a diſſembling boy,
Some one has ſent thee to mock me; though my anger
Stoop not to puniſh thy green years unripe
For malice; did I know what perſon ſent thee
To tempt my ſorrow thus, I ſhould reveng it.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Indeed I have no thought ſo uncharitable,
Nor am I ſent to grieve you, let me ſuffer
More puniſhment than ever boy deſerv'd,
If you do find me falſe; I ſerve a Miſtriſs
Would rather dye than play with your misfortunes;
Then good Sir hear me out.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Who is your Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Before I name her, give me ſome encouragement,
That you receive her meſſage: ſhe is one
That is full acquainted with your miſery,
And can bring ſuch a portion of her ſorrow
In every circumſtance ſo like your own,
You'll love and pity her, and wiſh your griefs
Might marry one anothers.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Thou art wild?
Canſt thou bring comfort from ſo ſad a creature?
Her miſerable ſtory can at beſt,
But ſwell my Volume, large enough already.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: She was late belov'd, as you were, promis'd faith,
And marriage; and was worthy of a better
Than he, that ſtole Maria's heart.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: How's that?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Juſt as Maria dealt with your affection,
Did he that married her deal with my Miſtriſs,
When careleſs both of Honor and Religion,
They cruelly gave away their hearts to ſtrangers.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Part of this truth I know, but prethee boy
Proceed to that thou cam'ſt for; thou didſt Promiſe
Something, thy language cannot hitherto
Encourage me to hope for.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: That I come to:
My Miſtriſs thus unkindly dealt withal,
You may imagine, wanted no affliction;
And had e'r this, wept her ſelf dry as Marble,
Had not your fortune come to her relief,
And twinn to her own ſorrow brought her comfort.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Could the condition of my fate ſo equal,
Leſſen her ſufferings?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I know not how
Companions in grief ſometimes diminiſh
And make the preſſure eaſie by degrees:
She threw her troubles off, remembring yours,
And from her pity of your wrongs, there grew
Affection to your perſon thus increas'd,
And with it, confidence, that thoſe whom Nature
Had made ſo even in their weight of ſorrow,
Could not but love as equally one another,
Were things but well prepar'd, this gave her boldneſs
To employ me thus far.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: A ſtrange meſſage, boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: If you incline to meet my Miſtriſs love,
It may beget your comforts; beſides that,
'Tis ſome revenge, that you above their ſcorn
And pride can laugh at them, whoſe perjury
Hath made you happy, and undone themſelves.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Have you done boy?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Only this little more;
When you but ſee, and know my Miſtriſs well,
You will forgive my tediouſneſs, ſhe's fair,
Fair as Maria was.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: I'll hear no more,
• o fooliſh boy, and tell thy fonder Miſtriſs
• e has no ſecond Faith to give away;
•• d mine was given to Maria, though her death
Allow me freedom, ſee the Picture of her.
• would give ten thouſand Empires for the ſubſtance;
Yet for Maria's ſake, whoſe divine Figure
That rude frame carries, I will love this counterfeit
Above all the world, and had thy Miſtriſs had all
The grace and bloſſom of her ſex; now ſhe
• s gone, that was, walking, a Spring of beauty,
I would not look upon her.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Sir, your pardon,

•
• ave but done a meſſage, as becomes
A ſervant, nor did ſhe on whoſe commands
• gladly waited, bid me urge her love
To your diſquiet, ſhe would chide my diligence
• f I ſhould make you angry.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Pretty boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Indeed I fear I have offended you:
Pray if I have, enjoyn me any pennance for it:
• have perform'd one duty, and could as wi • lingly
To purge my faul • , and ſhew I ſuffer with you,
• l • ad your cauſe to another.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: And I'll take thee
At thy word boy, thou haſt a moving language,
That pretty innocent, Copy of Maria
〈◊〉 all I love, I know not how to ſpeak,
Winn her to think well of me, and I wi • l
Reward thee to thy wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I undertake
Nothing for gain, but ſince you have reſolv'd,
To love no other, I'll be faithful to you,
And my prophetick thoughts bid me already
•• y I ſhall proſper.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Thou wert ſent to bleſs me.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Pray give us opportunity.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Be happy. Exit.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: He's gone.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: With your fair leave Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Have you buſineſs with her pray you?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I have a meſſage from a Gentleman,
Pleaſe you vouchſafe your ear more private.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: You ſhall have my abſence Neece. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Was the ſentleman afear'd to declare his matters openly, here was no bodies was not very honeſt, if her like 〈◊〉 her errands the petter, was wiſt to keep her preaths 〈◊〉 cool her porridges, can tell her, that now for aule her •• ivate hearings and tawgings.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: You may, if pleaſe you, find another language.
And with leſs pains be underſtood.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: What is her meaning?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Come, pray ſpeak your own Engliſh.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Have boyes loſt her itts and memories? bleſs us aule.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I muſt be plain then, come, I know you are
•• is, this thin vail cannot obſcure you:
I'll tell the world you live, I have not loſt ye,
S •• ce firſt with grief and ſhame to be ſurpriz'd,
A violent trance, took away ſhew of life;
I could diſcover by what accident
You were convey'd away at midnight, in
Your coffin, could declare the place, and minute,
When you reviv'd, what you have done ſince as perfectly—

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Alas, I am betraid to new misfortunes.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: You are not, for my knowledge, I'll be dumb
For ever, rather than be ſuch a traitor;
•• deed I pity you, and bring no thoughts,
〈◊〉 f • ll of peace, call home your modeſt blood,
•• le hath too long uſurp'd upon your face;
Think upon love agen, and the poſſeſſion
Of full blown joyes, now ready to ſalute you.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Theſe words undo me more than my own griefs.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I ſee how fear would play the tyrant with you,
But I'll remove ſuſpition; have you in
Your heart, an entertainment for his love
To whom your Virgin faith made the firſt promiſe?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: If thou mean'ſt Hartlove, thou doſt wound me ſtill,
I have no life without his memory,
Nor with it any hope to keep it long:
Thou ſeeſt I walk in darkneſs like a thief,
That fears to ſee the world in his own ſhape,
My very ſhadow frights me, 'tis a death
To live thus, and not look day in the face,
Away, I know thee not.

sp.speaker: Boy
sp.l: You ſhall hereafter know, and thank me Lady,
I'll bring you a diſcharge at my next viſit,
Of all your fears, be content, fair Maria,
'Tis worth your wonder.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Be wiſe and ſilent,
Dreſs your ſelf, you ſhall be what you wiſh.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Do this, and be
My better Angel.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: All your care's on me. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prim • .

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I Muſt applaud thy diligence.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: It had been nothing
To have left him in t • e Porch; I call'd his ſervants,
With wonders they acknowledg'd him, I pretended
It was ſome ſpice, ſure of the falling ſickneſs,
And that, 'twas charity to bring him home;
They rubb'd and chaf'd him, ply'd him with Strong water,
Still he was ſenſeleſs, clamors could not wake him;
I wiſh'd 'em then get him to bed, they did ſo,
And almoſt ſmother'd him with ruggs and pillows;
And 'cauſe they ſhould have no cauſe to ſuſpect me,
I watch'd them till he wak'd.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Twas excellent.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: When his time came to yawn, and ſtretch himſelf,
I bid 'em not be haſty to diſcover
How he was brought home; his eyes fully open
With trembling he began to call his ſervants,
And told 'em he had ſeen ſtrange viſions,
That ſhould convert him from his heathen courſes;
They wondred, and were ſilent, there he preach'd
How ſweet the air of a contented conſcience
Smelt in his noſe now, ask'd 'em all forgiveneſs
For their hard paſture ſince they liv'd with him;
Bid 'em believe, and fetch out the cold Sur-loin:
Pierce the ſtrong beer, and let the neighbors joy in't:
The conceal'd Muskadine ſhould now lie open
To every mouth; that he would give to th' poor,
And mend their wages; that his doors ſhould be
Open to every miſerable ſutor.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: What ſaid his ſervants then?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: They durſt not ſpeak,
But bleſt themſelves, and the ſtrange means that had
Made him a Chriſtian in this over-joy,
I took my leave, and bad 'em ſay their prayers,
And humor him, leſt he turn'd Jew agen.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Enough, enough. Who's this?
'Tis one of my ringers; ſtand cloſe, my Ladies Coachman.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Buy a mat for a bed, buy a mat;
Would I were at rack and manger among my horſes;
We have divided the Sextons
Houſhold-ſtuff among us, one has the rugg, and he's
Turn'd Iriſh, and another has a blanket, and he muſt beg in't
The ſheets ſerve another for a frock, and with the bed-cord,
He may paſs for a Porter, nothing but the mat would fall
To my ſhare, which with the help of a tune and a haſſock
Out o'th' Church, may diſguiſe me till I get home;
A pox o' bell-ringing by the ear, if any man take me
At it agen, let him pull mine to the Pillory: I could wiſh
I had loſt mine, ears, ſo I had my cloaths again:
The weather wo'not allow this faſhion,
I do look for an Ague beſides.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: How the raskal ſhakes?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Here are company:
Buy a Mat for a Bed, buy a Mat,
A haſſock for your feet, or a Piſs clean and ſweet;
Buy a Mat for a Bed, buy a Mat:
Ringing I renounce thee, I'll never come to church more.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: You with a Mat.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: I am call'd.
If any one ſhould offer to buy my Mat, what a caſe were I in?
Oh that I were in my Oat-tub with a horſe-loaf,
Something to hearten me:
I dare not hear 'em;
Buy a mat for a bed, buy a mat.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: He's deaf.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: I am glad, I am: buy a mat for a bed.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: How the raskal ſweats? What a pickle he's in?
Every ſtreet he goes through will be a new torment.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.l: If ever I meet at midnight more a jangling:
I am cold, and yet I drop; buy a mat for a bed, buy a mat.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: He has puniſhment enough. Exit.
Who's this, my tother youth? he is turn'd Bear.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I am halfe afraid of my ſelf: this poor ſhift
I got o'th' Sexton to convey me handſomly
To ſome harbor, the wench will hardly know me;
They'll take me for ſome Watchman o'th' pariſh;
I ha ne'r a penny left me, that's one comfort;
And ringing has begot a monſtrous ſtomach,
And that's another miſchief: I were beſt go home,
For every thing will ſcorn me in this habit.
Beſides, I am ſo full of theſe young bell-ringers;
If I get in adoors, not the power o'th' countrey,
Nor all my Aunts curſes ſhall diſembogue me.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Bid her come hither preſently,—hum, 'tis he.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I am betraid to one that will eternally laugh at me,
Three of theſe rogues will jeer a horſe to death.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: 'Tis Mr. Wildbrain ſure, and yet me thinks
His faſhion's ſtrangely alt'red, ſirrah Watchman,
You rugamuffin, turn you louzie Bears skin:
You with the Bed-rid Bill.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: H'as found me out;
There's no avoiding him, I had rather now
Be arraign'd at Newga • e for a robbery,
Than anſwer to his Articles: your Will Sir,
I am in haſte.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Nay, then I will make bold wi'ye;
A Watchman, and aſham'd to ſhew his countenance,
His face of authority? I have ſeen that phyſiognomy;
Were you never in priſon for pilfering?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: How the rogue worries me.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Why may not this
Be the villain robb'd my houſe laſt night,
And walks diſguis'd in this malignant rugg,
Arm'd with a tun of Iron? I will have you
Before a Magiſtrate.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: What will become of me?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: What art thou? ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I am the wandring Jew, and pleaſe your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: By your leave Rabbi, I will ſhew you then
A Synagogue, iclip't Bridewel, where you,
Under correction, may reſt your ſelf:
You have brought a bill to guard you, there be dog-whpis
To firk ſuch rugg'd currs, whips without bells
Indeed.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Bells.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: How he ſweats?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I muſt be known, as good at firſt; now jeer on,
But do not anger me too impudently,
The Rabbi will be mov'd then.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: How? Jack Wildbrain,
What time o'th' Moon man, ha? what ſtrange bells
Haſt in thy brains?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: No more bells,
No more bells, they ring backwards.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Why, where's the wench, the bleſſing that befel thee
The unexpected happineſs? where's that Jack?
Where are thy golden days?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: It was his trick, as ſure as I am louzie,
But how to be reveng'd—

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Fie, fie, Jack,
Marry a Watchmans widow in thy young daies,
With a revenue of old Iron and a Rugg?
Is this the Paragon, the dainty piece,
The delicate divine rogue?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: 'Tis enough, I am undone,
Mark'd for a miſery, and ſo leave prating;
Give me my Bill.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: You need not ask your Taylors,
Unleſs you had better Linings; it may be,
To avoid ſuſpition, you are going thus
Diſguis'd to your fair Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Mock no further,
Or as I live, I'll lay my Bill o' thy pate,
I'll take a Watchmans fury into my fingers,
To ha no judgement to diſtinguiſh perſons,
And knock thee down.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Come, I ha done, and now
Will ſpeak ſome comfort to thee, I will lead thee
Now to my Miſtriſs hitherto conceal'd;
She ſhall take pity on thee too, ſhe loves
A handſome man; thy miſery invites me
To do thee good, I'll not be jealous, Jack;
Her beauty ſhall commend it ſelf; but do not,
When I have brought you into grace, ſupplant me.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Art thou in earneſt? by this cold Iron—

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: No oaths, I am not coſtive; here ſhe comes.
Sweet-heart, I have brought a Gentleman,
A friend of mine to be acquainted with you,
He's other than he ſeems; why d'ye ſtare thus?

sp.speaker: Miſt.
sp.l: Oh Sir, forgive me, I have done ye wrong.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: What's the matter? didſt ever ſee her afore Jack

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Prethee do what thou wot wi'me, if thou haſt
A mind, hang me up quickly.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Never deſpair, I'll give thee my ſhare rather,
Take her, I hope ſhe loves thee at firſt ſight,
She has petticoats will patch thee up a ſuit;
I reſign all, only I'll keep theſe trifles.
I took ſome pains for 'em, I take it Jack;
What think you pink of beauty, come let me
Counſel you both to marry, ſhe has a trade,
If you have audacity to hook in Gameſters:
Let's ha a wedding, you will be wondrous rich;
For ſhe is impudent, and thou art miſerable;
'Twill be a rare match.

sp.speaker: Miſt.
sp.l: As you are a man, forgive me, I'll redeem all.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: You wo'not to this geer of marriage then?

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: No, no, I thank you Tom, I can watch for
A groat a night, and be every gentlemans fellow. Exit M •

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Riſe and be good, keep home and tend your buſine •

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Thou haſt don't to purpoſe, give me thy hand To •
Shall we be friends? thou ſeeſt what ſtate I am in,
I'll undertake this pennance to my Aunt,
Where, if I be received again for currant,
And fortu • e ſmile once more.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Nay, nay, I'm ſatisfied, ſo farew • l honeſt louzie Jack.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: I cannot help it, ſome men meet with ſtrange deſtinies.
• f things go right thou mayſt be hang'd, and I
May live to ſee't, and purchaſe thy apparel:
So farewel Tom. commend me to thy Polcat. Exit.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Now that I have my counſel ready, and my cauſe ripe;
The Judges all inform'd of the abuſes;
Now that he ſhould be gone.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: No man knows whether,
And yet they talk he went forth with a Conſtable
Th • t told him of ſtrange buſineſs that would bring him
Money and Lands, and Heaven knows what; but they
Have ſearch'd, and cannot find out ſuch an Officer:
And as a ſecret, Madam, they told your man
Nicholas, whom you ſent thither as a ſpie,
They had a ſhrewd ſuſpition 'twas the devil
I'th' likeneſs of a Conſtable, that has tempted him:
By this time to ſtrange things; there have been men
As rich as he, have met convenient rivers,
And ſo forth; many trees have born ſtrange fruits:
D'ye think he has not hang'd himſelf?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: If he be hang'd, who has his goods?

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: They are forfeited, they ſay.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: He has hang'd himſelf for certain then,
Only to coſin me of my Girls portion.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Very likely.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Or did not the Conſtable carry him to ſome priſon?

sp.speaker: Nu.
sp.l: They thought on that too, and ſearch'd every where.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: He may be cloſe for treaſon, perhaps executed,

sp.speaker: Nu.
sp.l: Nay, they did look among the quarters too,
And muſt • red all the bridge-houſe for his night-cap.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Madam, here is the gentleman agen.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: What Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: He that lov'd my young Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Alas, 'tis Hartlove, 'twill but feed his melancholy.
To let him ſee Maria, ſince we dare not
Yet tell the world ſhe lives; and certainly,
Did not the violence of his paſſion blind him,
〈◊〉 would ſee paſt her borrowed tongue and habit.

sp.speaker: Nu.
sp.l: Pleaſe you entertain him awhile, Madam,
〈◊〉 caſt about for ſomething with your daughter.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Do what thou wot, pray Mr. Har • love enter.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Madam, I come to ask your gentle pardon.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Pardon, for what? you ne' • offended me.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Y •• , if ye be the mother of Maria.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I was her mother, but that word is cancell'd,
And buried with her in that very minute
Her ſoul fled from her; we loſt both our names
Of mother and of daughter.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Alas, Madam,
If your relation did conſiſt but in
Thoſe naked terms, I had a title nearer,
••• ce love unl • es more than the tie of blood;
No matter for the empty voice of mother;
Your nature ſtill is left, which in her abſence
〈◊〉 love Maria, and not ſee her aſhes
A • d memory polluted.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: You amaze me, by whom?

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: By me, I am the vile profaner.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Why do you ſpeak thus indiſcr • etly, Sir?
You ever honour'd her.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: I did live,
But ſince ſhe died, I ha been a villain to her.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I do beſeech you ſay not ſo; all this
Is but to make me know how much I ſinn'd
In forcing her to marry.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Do not mock me,
I charge you by the Virgin you have wept for;
For I have done an impious act againſt her,
A deed able to fright her from her ſleep,
And through her marble, ought to be reveng'd;
A wickedneſs, that if I ſhould be ſilent,
You as a witneſs muſt accuſe me for't.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Was I a witneſs?

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Yes, you knew I lov'd
Maria once; or grant, you did but think ſo,
By what I ha profeſt, or ſhe has told you,
Was't not a fault unpardonable in me,
When I ſhould drop my tears upon her grave,
Yes, and proof ſufficient.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: To what?

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: That I, forgetful of my fame and vows
To fair Maria, e'r the worm could pierce
Her tender ſhroud, had chang'd her for another;
Did you not bluſh to ſee me turn a rebel?
So ſoon to court a ſhadow, a ſtrange thing,
Without a name? Did you not curſe my levity,
Or think upon her death with the leſs ſorrow
That ſhe had ſcap'd a puniſhment more killing,
Oh how I ſhame to think on't.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Sir, in my
Opinion, 'twas an argument of love
To your Maria, for whoſe ſake you could
Affect one that but carried her ſmall likeneſs.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: No more, you are too charitable, but
I know my guilt, and will from henceforth never
Change words with that ſtrange maid, whoſe innocent face
Like your Maria's won ſo late upon me:
My paſſions are corrected, and I can
Look on her now, and woman-kind, without
Love in a thought; 'tis thus, I came to tell you,
If after this acknowledgement, you'll be
So kind to ſhew me in what ſilent grave
You have diſpos'd your daughter, I will ask
Forgiveneſs of all her duſt, and never leave,
Till with a loud confeſſion of my ſhame,
I wake her ghoſt, and that pronounce my pardon:
Will you deny this favour? then farewel,
I'll never ſee you more: ha!

div.stage: Enter Nurſe, Maria in her own apparel, after ſome ſhew of wonder, he goes towards her.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Be not deluded, Sir, upon my life
This is the ſoul whom you but thought Maria
In my daughters habit; what did you mean Nurſe?
I knew ſhe would but cozen you, is ſhe not like now?
One dew unto another is not nearer.

sp.speaker: Nu.
sp.l: She thinks ſhe is a gentlewoman;
And that imagination has ſo taken her,
See ſcorns to ſpeak, how handſomly ſhe carries it,
As if ſhe were a well bred thing, her body?
And I warrant you, what looks?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Pray be not fooliſh.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: I diſturb no body, ſpeak but half a word
And I am ſatisfied, but what needs that?
I'll ſwear 'tis ſhe.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: But do not, I beſeech you,
For truſt me, Sir, you know not what I know.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Peace then,
And let me pray, ſhe holds up her hands with me.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: This will betray all.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Love ever honor'd,
And ever young, thou Soveraign of all hearts,
Of all our ſorrows, the ſweet eaſe. She weeps now.
Does ſhe ſtill coſin me?

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: You will ſee anon,
'Twas her deſire, expect the iſſue, Madam.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: My ſoul's ſo big, I cannot pray; 'tis ſhe,
I will go nearer.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Here's Mr. Algripe, and other ſtrangers, Madam.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Here good Lady,
Upon my knees I ask thy worſhips pardon;
Here's the whole ſumm I had with thy fair Daughter;
Would ſhe were living, I might have her peace too,
And yield her up again to her old liberty:
I had a wife before, and could not marry;
My pennance ſhall be on that man that honor'd her,
To conferr ſome Land.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: This is incredible.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: 'Tis truth

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Do you know me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Ha. the Gentleman I deceiv'd.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: My name is Lurcher.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: 'Shat have thy Mortgage.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: I ha that already, no matter for the Deed
If you releaſe it.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I'll do't before thy witneſs;
But where's thy Siſter? if ſhe live I am happy, though
I conceal our contract, which was
Stolen from me with the Evidence of this Land.

div.stage: The Boy goes to Maria, and gives her a paper; ſhe wonders, and ſmiles upon Hartlove, he amaz'd, approaches her: afterward ſhe ſhews it her mother, and then gives it to Hartlove.

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: Your daughter ſmiles.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I hope ſhe lives, but where, I cannot tell, Sir.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Even here, and pleaſe you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis ſhe;
To work thy fair way, I preſerved you brother,
That would have loſt me willingly, and ſerv'd ye
Thus like a boy; I ſerved you faithfully,
And caſt your plots to preſerve your credit;
Your ſoul ones I diverted to fair uſes;
So far as you would hearken to my counſel;
That all the world may know how much you owe me.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Welcome entirely, welcome my dear Alathe,
And when I loſe thee agen, bleſſing forſake me:
Nay, let me kiſs thee in theſe cloaths.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: And I too,
And bleſs the time I had ſo wiſe a ſiſter, wer't thou the little thief?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I ſtole the contract, I muſt confeſs,
And kept it to my ſelf, it moſt concern'd me.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Cotracted? this deſtroys his after marriage.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Dare you give this hand
To this young Gentleman? my heart goes with it.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Maria alive! how my heart's exalted, 'tis my duty;
Take her Frank Hartlove, take her; and all joyes
With her; beſides ſome Lands to advance her Joynture:

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: What I have is your own, and bleſſings crown ye.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: Give me room,
And freſh air to conſider, Gentlemen,
My hopes are too high.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Be more temperate,
Or I'll be Welſh again.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: A day of wonder.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: Lady, your love, I ha kept my word; there was
A time, when my much ſuffering made me hate you,
And to that end I did my beſt to croſs you:
And fearing you were dead, I ſtole your Coffin,
That you might never more uſurp my Office:
Many more knacks I did, which at the Weddings
Shall be told of as harmleſs tales.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Hollow your throats a pieces, I am at home;
If you can roar me out again —

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: What thing is this?

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: A continent of Fleas: room for the Pageant;
Make room afore there; your kinſman Madam.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: My kinſman? let me wonder!

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Do, and I'll wonder too to ſee this company
At peace one with another; 'tis not worth
Your admiration, I was never dead yet;
Y're merry Aunt, I ſee, and all your company:
If ye be not, I'll fool up, and provoke ye:
I will do any thing to get your love again:
I'll forſwear Midnight, Taverns and Temptations;
Give good example to your Grooms, the Maids
Shall go to bed, and take their reſt this year;
None ſhall appear with bliſters in their bellies.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: And when you will fool again, you may go ring.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Madam, have mercy.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Your ſubmiſſion, Sir,
I gladly take; we will
Enquire the reaſon of this habit afterwards;
Now you are ſoundly ſham'd, well, we reſtore you
Where's Toby?
Where's the Coachman?

sp.speaker: Nur.
sp.l: He's a bed, Madam.
And has an ague, he ſays.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: I'll be his Phyſitian.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: We muſt a foot then.

sp.speaker: Lur.
sp.l: E'er the Prieſt ha done
Toby ſhall wait upon you with his Coach,
And make your Flanders Mares dance back agen we'ye,
I warrant you Madam you are mortified,
Your ſute ſhall be granted too.

sp.speaker: Wild.
sp.l: Make, make room afore thee.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Home forward with glad hearts, home child.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I wait you.

sp.speaker: Ha.
sp.l: On joyfully, the cure of all our grief,
Is owing to this pretty little Thief. Exeunt omnes

div.head: THE WOMANS PRIZE, OR THE TAMER TAM'D. A Comedy.
The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Moroſo, an old rich doating Citizen, ſuitor to Livia.
Petruchio, An Italian Gent. Husband to Maria.
Rowland, A young Gent. in love with Livia.
Petronius, Father to Maria and Livia.

list.head: Women.
The two maſculine daughters of Petronius.

list.item: • iancha, Their Coſin, and Commander in chief.

list.head: To the relief of the Ladies, of which, two were drunk.

div.head: PROLOGUE.
div.l: LAdies to you, in whoſe defence and right,
Fletchers brave Muſe prepar'd her ſelf to fight
I battel without blood, 'twas well fought, too,
(The victory's yours, though got with much ado.)
We do preſent this Comedy, in which
Arivulet of pure wit flows, ſtrong and rich
I • Fancy, Language, and all parts that may
Add Grace and Ornament to a merry Play.
Which this may prove. Yet not to go too far
In promiſes from this our Female War.
We do intreat the angry men would not
Expect the mazes of a ſubtle plot,
Set Speeches, high Expreſſions, and what's worſe,
In a true Comedy, politick diſcourſe.
The end we aim at, is to make you ſport;
Yet neither gall the City, nor the Court.
Hear, and obſerve his Comique ſtrain, and when
Y are ſick of melancholy, ſee't agen.
'Tis no dear Phyſick ſince 'twill quit the coſt:
Or his intentions with our pains, are loſt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Moroſo, Sophocles, and Tranio, with Roſemary, as from a wedding.

sp.l: GOd give 'em joy.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Amen.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Amen, ſay I too:
The pudding's now i'th' proof, alas poor wench.
Through what a mine of patience muſt thou work,
〈◊〉 thou know'ſt good hour more?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: 'Tis too true: Certain,
Methinks her father has dealt harſhly with her,
Exceeding harſhly, and not like a Father,
To match her to this Dragon; I proteſt
I pity the poor Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Methinks now,
He's not ſo terrible as people think him.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: This old thief flatters, out of meer devotion,
To pleaſe the Father for his ſecond daughter.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: But ſhall he have her?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes, when I have Rome.
And yet the father's for him.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I'll aſſure ye,
I hold • im a good man.
Yes ſure a wealthy,
But whether a good womans man, is doubtful.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Would 'twere no worſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What though his other wife,
Out of her moſt abundant ſoberneſs,
Out of her daily hue and cries upon him,
(For ſure ſhe was a rebel) turn'd his temper,
And forc'd him blow as high as ſhe? dos't follow
He muſt retain that long ſince buried Tempeſt,
To this ſoft Maid?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I fear it.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: So do I too:
And ſo far, that if God had made me woman,
And his wife that muſt be—

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: What would you do, Sir?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I would learn to eat coals with an angry Cat,
And ſpit ſire at him: I would (to prevent him)
Do all the ramping, roaring tricks, a whore
Being drunk, and tumbling ripe, would tremble at:
There is no ſafety elſe, nor moral wiſdom.
To be a wife, and his.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: So I ſhould think too.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: For yet the bare remembrance of his firſt wife
(I tell ye on my knowledge, and a truth too)
Will make him ſtart in's ſleep, and very often
Cry out for Cudgels, Coleſtaves, any thing;
Hiding his breeches out of fear, her Ghoſt
Should walk, and wear 'em yet. Since his firſt marriage,
He is no more the ſtill Petruchio,
Than I am Babylon.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: He's a good fellow,
And on my word I love him: but to think
A fit match for this tender ſoul—.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: His very frown, if ſhe but ſay her prayers
Louder than men talk treaſon, makes him tinder;
The motion of a Dial, when he's teſty,
Is the ſame trouble to him as a Water-work;
She muſt do nothing of her ſelf; not eat,
Drink, ſay Sir, how do ye? make her ready, unready,
Unleſs he bid her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: He will bury her,
Ten pound to twenty ſhillings, within theſe three weeks

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I'll be your half.

div.stage: Enter Jaques with a pot of Wine.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: He loves her moſt extreamly,
And ſo long 'twill be Honey-moon. Now Jaques.
You are a buſie man I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes certain,
This old ſport muſt have eggs,

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Not yet this ten daies.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Sweet Gentlemen with Muskadel.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That's right, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: This fellow broods his Maſter: ſpeed ye Jaques.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: We ſhall be for you preſently.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Your worſhips
Shall have it rich and neat: and o' my conſcience
As welcome as our Lady-day: Oh my old Sir,
When ſhall we ſee your worſhip run at Ring?
That hour, a ſtanding were worth money.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: So Sir.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Upon my little honeſty, your Miſtriſs,
If I have any ſpeculation, muſt think
This ſingle thrumming of a Fiddle,
Without a Bow, but even poor ſport.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Y'are merry.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Would I were wiſe too: ſo God bleſs your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: The fellow tells you true. Exit Jaq.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: When is the day man?
Come, come, you'll ſteal a marriage.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Nay, believe me:
But when her Father pleaſes, I am ready,
And all my friends ſhall know it.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Why no • now?
One charge had ſerv'd for both.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: There's reaſon in't.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Call'd Rowland—

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Will ye walk?
They'll think we are loſt: Come Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You have wip'd him now.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: So will he never the wench, I hope.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I wiſh it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Now Livia, if you'll go away to night,
If your affections be not made of words.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I love you, and vou know how dearly Rowland,
Is there none near us? my affections ever
Have been your ſervants; with what ſuperſtition
I have ever Sainted you—

sp.speaker: Row:
sp.l: Why then take this way.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: 'Twill be a childiſh, and a leſs proſperous courſe;
Than 〈◊〉 that knows not care: why ſhould we do
Our honeſt and our hearty love ſuch wrong,
To over-run our fortunes?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Then you flatter.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Alas, you know I cannot.

sp.speaker: Rom.
sp.l: What hope's left elſe
But flying to enjoy ye?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: None ſo far,
For let it be admitted, we have time,
And all things now in other expectation,
My father's bent againſt us; what but ruine,
Can ſuch a by-way bring us? if your fears
Would let you look with my eyes, I would ſhew you,
And certain, how our ſtaying here would win us
A courſe, though ſomewhat longer, yet far ſurer.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And then Moroſo h'as ye.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: No ſuch matter
For hold this certain, begging, ſtealing, whoring,
Selling, (which is a ſin unpardonable)
Of counterfeit Cods, or muſty Engliſh Croacus;
Switches, or Stones for th' tooth-ache ſooner finds me,
Than that drawn Fox Moroſo.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: But his money,
If wealth may win you—

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: If a Hog may be
High Prieſt among the Jews? his money Rowland?
Oh Love forgive me, what faith haſt thou?
Why, can his money kiſs me?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Behind,
Laid out upon a Petticoat: or graspe me
While I cry, Oh good thank you? o'my troth
Thou mak'ſt me merry with thy fear: or lie with me,
As you may do? alas, what fools you men are?
His mouldy money? half a dozen Riders,
That cannot ſit, but ſtampt faſt to their Saddles?
No Rowland, no man ſhall make uſe of me;
My beauty was born free, and free I'll give it
To him that loves, not buys me. You yet doubt me,

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I cannot ſay I doubt ye.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Goe thy ways,
Thou art the prettieſt puling piece of paſſion:
Y'faith I will not fail thee.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I had rather—

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Prethee believe me, if I do not carry it,
For both our goods—

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: But—

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: What but?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I would tell you.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I know all you can tell me; all's but this,
〈◊〉 would have me, and lie with me; is't not ſo?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Why you ſhall; will that content you? Goe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am very loth to goe.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Now o' my conſcience
Thou art an honeſt fellow: here's my Siſter;
Go, prethee go; this kiſs, and credit me,
E'r I am three nights older, I am for thee:
You ſhall hear what I do.
Farewel.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewel. Exit Rowland.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Alas poor fool, how it looks?
It would ev'n hang it ſelf, ſhould I but croſs it.
For pure love to the matter I muſt hatch it.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Nay, never look for merry hour, Maria,
If now you make it not; let not your bluſhes,
Your modeſty, and tenderneſs of ſpirit,
Make you continual Anvile to his anger:
Believe me, ſince his firſt wife ſet him going,
Nothing can bind his rage: Take your own council,
You ſhall not ſay that I perſwaded you.
But if you ſuffer him—

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay, ſhall I do it?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Have you a ſtomach to't?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I never ſhew'd it.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: 'Twill ſhew the rarer and the ſtronger in you.
〈◊〉 do not ſay I urg'd you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am perfect,
Like Curtius, to redeem my Countrey, I have
L • ap'd into this gulph of marriage, and I'll do it.
Farewel all poorer thoughts, but ſpight and anger,
Till I have wrought a miracle. Now coſin,
• am no more the gentle, tame Maria;
•• ſtake me not; I have a new ſoul in me
• ade of a North wind, nothing but tempeſt;
• ad like a tempeſt ſhall it make all ruin,
Till I have run my Will out.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: This is brave now,
If you continue it; but your own Will lead you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Adieu all tenderneſs, I dare continue;
Maids that are made of fears, and modeſt bluſhes,
V •• w me, and love example.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Here is your Siſter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Here is the brave old mans love.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: That loves the young man.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I and hold thee there wench: what a grief of heart is't?
When Paphos Revels ſhould rowze up old night,
To ſweat againſt a Cork; to lie and tell
The clock o'th lungs, to riſe ſport ſtarv'd?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Dear Siſter,
Where have you been, you talk thus?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why at Church, wench;
Where I am ti'd to talke thus: I am a wife now.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: It ſeems ſo, and a modeſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You are an aſs;
When thou art married once, thy modeſty
Will never buy thee pins.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: 'Bleſs me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: From what?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: From ſuch a tame fool as our coſin Livia?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: You are not mad.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes wench, and ſo muſt you be,
〈◊〉 none of our acquaintance: mark me Livia;
〈◊〉 indeed fit for our ſex: 'Tis bed time.
• ardon me yellow Hymen, that I mean
Thine offerings to protract, or to keep faſting
〈◊〉 valiant Bridegroom.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Whither will this woman?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: You may perceive her end.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Or rather fear it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Dare you be partner in't?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Leave it Maria,
I fear I have mark'd too much, for goodneſs leave it;
Diveſt you with obedient hands, to bed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To bed? no Livia, there are Comets hang
Prodigious over that yet; there's a fellow
Muſt yet before I know that heat (ne'r ſtart wench)
Be made a man, for yet he is a monſter;
Here muſt his head be Livia.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Never hope it.
'Tis as eaſie with a Sive to ſcoop the Ocean, as
To tame Petruchio.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay: Lucina hear me,
Never unlock the treaſure of my womb
For humane fruit, to make it capable;
Nor never with thy ſecret hand make brief
A mothers labor to me; if I do
Give way unto my married Husband's Will,
Or be a Wife in any thing but hopes,
Till I have made him eaſie as a child,
And tame as fear, he ſhall not win a ſmile,
Or a pleas'd look, from this auſterity,
Though it would pull another Joynture from him,
And make him ev'ry day another man;
And when I kiſs him, till I have my Will,
May I be barren of delights, and know
Only what pleaſures are in dreams, and gueſſes.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: A ſtrange Exordium.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: All the ſeveral wrongs
Done by Imperious Husbands to their Wives
Theſe thouſand years and upwards, ſtrengthen thee:
Thou haſt a brave cauſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And I'll do it bravely,
Or may I knit my life out ever after.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: In what part of the world got ſhe this ſpirit?
Yet pray Maria, look before you truly,
Beſides the obedience of a wife;
Which you will find a heavy imputation,
Which yet I cannot think your own, it ſhews
So diſtant from your ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis I ſwear.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Weigh but the perſon, and the hopes you have,
To work this deſperate cure.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A weaker ſubject
Would ſhame the end I aim at, diſobedience.
You talk too tamely: By the faith I have
In mine own noble Will, that childiſh woman
That lives a priſoner to her Husbands pleaſure,
Has loſt her making, and becomes a beaſt,
Created for his uſe, not fellowſhip.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: His firſt wife ſaid as much.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: She was a fool,
And took a ſcurvy courſe; let her be nam'd
'Mongſt thoſe that wiſh for things, but dare not do 'em:
I have a new dance for him.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Are you of this faith?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Yes truly, and will die in't.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Why then let's all wear breeches.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now thou com'ſt near the nature of a woman;
Hang theſe tame hearted Eyaſſes, that no ſooner
See the Lure out, and hear their Husbands hollow,
But cry like Kites upon 'em: The free Haggard
(Which is that woman, that hath wing, and knows it,
Spirit and plume) will make an hundred checks,
To ſhew her freedom, ſail in ev'ry air,
And look out ev'ry pleaſure; not regarding
Lure, nor quarry, till her pitch command
What ſhe deſires, making her foundred keeper
Be glad to fling out trains, and golden ones,
To take her down again.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: You are learned, Siſter;
Yet I ſay ſtill take heed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A witty ſaying;
I'll tell thee Livia, had this fellow tired
As many wives as horſes under him,
With ſpurring of their patience; had he got
A Patent, with an Office to reclaim us,
Confirm'd by Parliament; had he all the malice
And ſubtilty of Devils, or of us,
Or any thing that's worſe than both.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Hey, hey boys, this is excellent.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Or could he
Caſt his wives new again, like Bels, to make 'em
Sound to his Will; or had the fearful name
Of the firſt breaker of wild women: yet,
Yet would I undertake this man, thus ſingle,
And, ſpight of all the freedom he has reach'd to,
Turn him and bend him as I liſt, and mold him
Into a babe again; that aged women,
Wonting both teeth and ſpleen, may Maſter him.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Thou wilt be chronicl'd.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That's all I aim at.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs, I do with all my heart
Hate an imperious Husband, and in time
Might be ſo wrought upon.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: To make him cuckold?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If he deſerve it.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Then I'll leave ye Ladies.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Thou haſt not ſo much noble anger in thee.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Go ſleep, go ſleep, what we intend to do,
Lies not for ſuch ſtarv'd ſouls, as thou haſt Livia.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Good night: the Bridegroom will be with you preſently.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That's more than you know,

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: If ye work upon him,
As you have promiſed, ye may give example,
Which no doubt will be followed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Good night: we'll trouble you no further.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If you intend no good, pray do no harm.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: None, but pray for you. Exit Livia.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Cheer wench.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now Byancha,
Thoſe wits we have, let's wind 'em to the height.
My reſt is up wench, and I pull for that
Will make me ever famous. They that lay
Foundations, are half-builders, all men ſay.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: My Maſter forſooth.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh how does thy Maſter? prethee commend me to him.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: How's this? my Maſter ſtays forſooth.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why let him ſtay, who hinders him forſooth?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: The Revel's ended now,
To viſit you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am not ſick.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I mean to ſee his chamber forſooth.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Am I his Groom? where lay he laſt night forſooth?

sp.speaker: Jap.
sp.l: In the low matted Parlour.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: There lies his way by the long Gallery.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I mean your chamber: y'are very merry Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis a good ſign I am ſound hearted Jaques:
But if you'll know where I lie, follow me;
And what thou ſeeſt, deliver to thy Maſter.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Do gentle Jaques. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Ha, is the wind in that door?
By'r Lady we ſhall have foul weather then:
I do not like the ſhuffling of theſe women,
They are mad beaſts, when they knock their heads together:
I have obſerv'd them all this day; their whispers,
One in anothers ear, their ſigns and pinches,
And breaking often into violent laughters:
As if the end they purpos'd were their own.
Call you this weddings? Sure this is a knavery,
A very trick, and dainty knavery,
Marvellous finely carried, that's the comfort:
What would theſe women do in ways of honor?
That are ſuch Maſters this way? Well, my Sir
Has been as good at finding out theſe toys,
As any living; if he loſe it now,
At his own peril be it. I muſt follow. Exi •

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Servants with Lights, Petruchio, Petronius,, Moroſo, Tranio, and Sophocles.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: You that are married, Gentlemen; have at ye
For a round wager now.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Of this nights Stage?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I am your firſt man, a pair of Gloves of twenty ſhilling •

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Done: who takes me up next? I am for all bet •

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Well luſty Lawrence, were but my night now,
Old as I am, I would make you clap on Spurs,
But I would reach you, and bring you to your trot too:
I would Gallants.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Well ſaid good Will; but where's the ſtaff boy, ha
Old father Time, your hour-glaſs is empty.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A good tough train would break thee all to pieces;
Thou haſt not breath enough to ſay thy prayers.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: See how theſe boys deſpiſe us. Will you to bed ſon
This pride will have a fall.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Upon your daughter;
But I ſhall riſe again, if there be truth
In Eggs, and butter'd Parſnips.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Will you to bed ſon, and leave talking?
To morrow morning we ſhall have you look,
For all your great words, like St. George at Kingſton,
Running a foot-back from the furious Dragon,
That with her angry tail belabours him
For being lazie.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: His courage quench'd, and ſo far quench'd —

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: 'Tis well Sir.
What then?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Fly, fly, quoth then the fearfuldwarfe;
Here is no place for living man.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: Well my maſters, if I do ſink under my buſine • as I find 'tis very poſſible, I am not the firſt that has m • carried; So that's my comfort, what may be done wit • out impeach or waſte, I can and will do.
How now, is my fair Bride a bed?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: No truly, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.p: Not a bed yet? body o' me: we'll up and • her: here's a coil with a Maiden-head, 'tis not intail'd, it?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: If it be, I'll try all the Law i'th' Land, but I'll it off: let's up, let's up, come.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: That you cannot neither.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Unleſs you'll drop through the Chimney like a D • or force a breach i'th' windows: you may untile the ho • 'tis poſſible.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: What doſt thou m • an?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: A moral, Sir, the Ballad will expreſs it:

p.hi: The wind and the rain, has turn'd you back again,

sp.p: And you cannot be lodged there. The truth is, all the d •
Are baracadoed; not a Cathole, but holds a murd'rer i •
She's victuall'd for this month.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: Art not thou drunk?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: He's drunk, he's drunk; come, come, let's up.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Yes, yes, I am drunk: ye may go up, ye may • tlemen, but take heed to your heads: I ſay no more.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: I'll try that.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.p: How doſt thou ſay? the door faſt lock'd fellow

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p:
Yes truly Sir, 'tis lock'd, and guarded too; two as deſperate tongues planted behind it, as e'er yet • ter'd: they ſtand upon their honors, and will not give
without ſtrange compoſition, I'll aſſure you; marching a • ay with their Pieces cockt, and Bullets in their mouths, will not ſatisfie them.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: How's this? how's this? they are—
Is there another with her?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Yes marry is there, and an Enginier.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Who's that for Heavens ſake?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Colonel Byancha, ſhe commands the works: Spi •• la's but a Ditcher to her, there's a half-moon: I am but a poor man, but if you'll give me leave, I'll venture a years wages, draw all your force before it, and mount your ableſt Piece of battery, you ſhall not enter it theſe three nights yet.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: I ſhould laugh at that good Jaques.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: Beat back again, ſhe's fortified for ever.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Am I drunk now, Sir?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: He that dares moſt, go up now, and be cool'd.
I have ſcap'd a pretty ſcowring.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: What are they mad? have we another Bedlam?
They do not talke I hope?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: Oh terribly, extreamly fearful, the noiſe at London-bridge is nothing near her.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: How got ſhe tongue?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: As you got tail, ſhe was born to't.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: Lock'd out a doors, and on my wedding night?
Nay, and I ſuffer this, I may goe graze:
Come Gentlemen, I'll batter; are theſe virtues?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p:
Do, and be beaten off with ſhame, as I was: I went up, came to th'door, knock'd, no body anſwer'd; knock'd lo • der, yet heard nothing: would have broke in by force; when ſuddainly a Water-work flew from the window with ſuch violence, that had I not duck'd quickly like a Fryer,
••• ra quis neſcit? The chamber's nothing but a meer Oſtend, in every window Pewter Cannons mounted, you'll quickly •• d with what they are charg'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: Why then tantara for us.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.p: And all the lower Works lin'd ſure with ſmall ſhot, long tongues with Fire-locks, that at twelve ſcore blank hit to the heart: now and ye dare go up.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: The window opens, beat a parley firſt;
I am ſo much amaz'd, my very hair ſtands.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Why how now Daughter: what intrench'd?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A little guarded for my ſafety, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: For your ſafety Sweet-heart? why who offends you?
I come not to uſe violence.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I think you cannot, Sir, I am better fortified.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I know your end,
You would fain reprieve your Maiden-head
A night, or two.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, or ten, or twenty, or ſay an hundred;
Or indeed, till I liſt lie with you.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: That's a ſhrewd ſaying from this preſent hour,
I never will believe a ſilent woman.
When they break out they are bonfires.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Till you liſt, lie with him? why who are you Madam?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: That trim Gentlemans wife, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Cry you mercy, do you command too?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes marry does ſhe, and in chief.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: I do command, and you ſhall go without:
(I mean your wife, for this night)

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And for the next too wench, and ſo as'tfol wols
Thou wilt not, wilt 'a?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes indeed dear father,
A • d till he ſeal to what I ſhall ſet down,
〈◊〉 any thing I know for ever.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Indeed theſe are Bug-words.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You hear Sir, ſhe can talk, God be thanked.

sp.speaker: Petru.
