sp.l: I would I heard it not, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I find that all the pity beſtow'd upon this woman,
Makes but an Anagram of an ill wife,
For ſhe was never virtuous.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You'll let me in I hope, for all this jeſting.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Hope ſtill, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: You will come down I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am ſure I will not.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I'll fetch you then.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: The power of the whole County cannot, Sir,
Unleſs we pleaſe to yield, which yet I think
We ſhall not; charge when you pleaſe, you ſhall
Hear quickly from us.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Bleſs me from a chicken of thy hatching,
Is this wiving?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Prethee Maria tell me what's the reaſon,
And doe it freely, you deal thus ſtrangely with me?
You were not forc'd to marry, your conſent
Went equally with mine, if not before it:
I hope you do not doubt I want that mettle
A man ſhould have to keep a woman waking;
I would be ſorry to be ſuch a Saint yet:
My perſon, as it is not excellent,
So 'tis not old, nor lame, nor weak with Phyſick,
But well enough to pleaſe an honeſt woman,
That keeps her houſe, and loves her Husband.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: My means and my conditions are no ſhamers
Of him that owes 'em, all the world knows that,
And my friends no reliers on my fortunes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: All this I believe, and none of all theſe parcels
I dare accept againſt; nay more, ſo far
I am from making theſe the ends I aim at,
Theſe idle outward things, theſe womens fears,
That were I yet unmarried, free to chooſe
Through all the Tribes of man, I'll take Petruchio
In's ſhirt, with one ten Groats to pay the Prieſt,
Before the beſt man living, or the ableſt
That e'er leap'd out of Lancaſhire, and they are right ones.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Why do you play the fool then, and ſtand prating
Out of the window like a broken Miller!

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If you will have me credit you Maria,
Come down, and let your love confirm it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay there, Sir, that bargain's yet to make.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Play ſure wench, the Pack s in thine own hand.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Let me die lowſie, if theſe two wenches
Be not brewing knavery to ſtock a Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why this is a Riddle:
I love you, and I love you not.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It is ſo:
And till your own experience do untie it,
This diſtance I muſt keep,

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If you talk more,
I am angry, very angry.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am glad on't, and I will talk.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Prethee peace,
Let me not think thou art mad. I tell thee woman,
If thou goeſt forward, I am ſtill Petruchio.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And I am worſe, a woman that can fear
Neither Petruchio Furius, nor his fame,
Nor any thing that tends to our allegeance;
There's a ſhort method for you, now you know me.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If you can carry't ſo, 'tis very well.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: No, you ſhall carry it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Peace gentle Low-bel.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Uſe no more words, but come down inſtantly,
I charge thee by the duty of a child.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Prethee come Maria, I forgive all.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay there; That duty, that you charge me by
(If you conſider truly what you ſay)
Is now another man's, you gave't away
I' th' Church, if you remember, to my Husband:
So all you can exact now, is no more
But only a due reverence to your perſon,
Which thus I pay: Your bleſſing, and I am gone
To bed for this night.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: This is monſtrous:
That bleſſing that St. Dunſtan gave the Devil,
If I were neer thee, I would give thee —
Pull thee down by th' noſe.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Saints ſhould not rave, Sir;
A little Rubarb now were excellent.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Then by that duty you owe to me Maria,
Open the door, and be obedient: I am quiet yet.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do confeſs that duty, make your beſt on't.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why give me leave, I will.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Sir, there's no learning
An old ſtiff Jade to trot, you know the moral.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yet as I take it, Sir, I owe no more
Than you owe back again.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You will not Article?
All I owe, preſently, let me but up, I'll pay.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Y'are too hot, and ſuch prove Jades at length;
You do confeſs a duty, or reſpect to me from you again:
That's very near, or full the ſame with mine?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Then by that duty, or reſpect, or what
You pleaſe to have it, go to bed and leave me,
And trouble me no longer with your fooling;
For know, I am not for you.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Well, what remedy?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: A ſine ſmart Cudgel. Oh that I were near thee.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: If you had teeth now, what a caſe were we in?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Theſe are the moſt authentique Rebels, next
Tyrone, I ever read of.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A week hence, or a fortnight, as you bear you,
And as I find my Will obſerv'd, I may,
With interceſſion of ſome friends, be brought
May be to kiſs you; and ſo quarterly
To pay a little Rent by compoſition,
You underſtand me?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Thou Boy thou.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Well there are more Maids than Maudlin, that's my comfort.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, and more men than Michael.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I muſt not to bed with this ſtomach, and no moat Lady.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Feed where you will, ſo it be ſound and wholſome,
Elſe live at Livery, for I'll none with you.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: You had beſt back one of the Dairy Maids, they'll carry.
But take heed to your girths, you'll get a bruiſe elſe.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now if thou wouldſt come down and tender me:
All the delights due to a marriage-bed,
Study ſuch kiſſes as would melt a man,
And turn thy ſelf into a thouſand Figures,
To add new flames unto me, I would ſtand
Thus heavy, thus regardleſs, thus deſpiſing
Thee, and thy beſt allurings: all the beauty
That's laid upon your bodies, mark me well,
For without doubt your mind's are miſerable,
You have no Masques for them: all this rare beauty,
Lay but the Painter and the Silk-worm by,
The Doctor with his Dyets, and the Tailor,
And you appear like flea'd Cats, not ſo handſome.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And we appear like her that ſent us hither,
That only excellent and beauteous nature;
Truly our ſelves for men to wonder at,
But too divine to handle; we are Gold,
In our own natures pure; but when we ſuffer
The husbands ſtamp upon us, then allays,
And baſe ones of you men are mingled with us,
And make us bluſh like Copper.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Then, and never
Till then are women to be ſpoken of,
For till that time you have no ſouls I take it:
Good night: come Gentlemen; I'll faſt for this night,
But by this hand, well; I ſhall come up yet?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: There will I watch thee like a wither'd Jury,
Thou ſhalt neither have meat, Fire, nor Candle,
Nor any thing that's eaſie: do you rebel ſo ſoon?
Yet take mercy.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Put up your Pipes: to bed Sir, I'll aſſure you
A months ſiege will not ſhake us.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Well ſaid Colonel.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To bed, to bed Petruchio: good night Gentlemen.
You'll make my Father ſick with ſitting up:
Here you ſhall find us any time theſe ten days,
Unleſs we may march off with our contentment.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I'll hang firſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And I'll quarter if I do not,
I'll make you know, and fear a wife Petruchio,
There my cauſe lies.
You have been famous for a woman-tamer,
And bear the fear'd-name of a brave Wife-breaker:
A woman now ſhall take thoſe honors off,
And tame you; nay, never look ſo bigg, ſhe ſhall believe me,
And I am ſhe: what think ye; good night to all,
Ye ſhall find Centinels.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: If ye dare ſally. Exeunt above.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: The devil's in 'em, ev'n the very devil, the down-right devil.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.p: I'll devil 'em: by theſe ten bones I will: I'll bring it to the old Proverb, no ſport no pie:—taken dow • i'th' top of all my ſpeed? this is fine dancing: Gentlemen ſtick to me. You ſee our Freehold's touch'd, and by thi • light, we will beleagure 'em, and either ſtarve 'em out, or make 'em recreant.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I'll ſee all paſſages ſtopt, but thoſe about 'em:
If the good women of the Town dare ſuccor 'em,
We ſhall have wars indeed.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I'll ſtand perdue upon 'em.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: My Regiment ſhall lie before.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I think ſo. 'tis grown too old to ſtand.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Let's in, and each provide his tackle,
We'll fire 'em out, or make 'em take their pardons:
Hear what I ſay on their bare knees—
Am I Petruchio, fear'd, and ſpoken of,
And on my wedding night am I thus jaded? Exeunt om •

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Rowland and Pedro at ſeveral doors.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Now Pedro?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Very buſie Maſter Rowland.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What haſte man?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I beſeech you pardon me,
I am not mine own man.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thou art not mad?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: No; but believe me, as haſty—

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: The cauſe good Pedro?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: There be a thouſand Sir; you are not married?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Not yet.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Keep your ſelf quiet then.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: You'll find a Fiddle
That never will be tun'd elſe: from all women — Exi •

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What alls the fellow tro? Jaques?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Your friend Sir.
But very full of buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Nothing but buſineſs?
Prethee the reaſon, is there any dying?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I would there were Sir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: But thy buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I'll tell you in a word, I am ſent to lay
An Impoſition upon Souſe and Puddings.
Paſties, and penny Cuſtards, that the women
May not relieve you Rebels: Fare ye well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: How does my Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Like a reſty jade.
She's ſpoil'd for riding. Exit Jaques.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What a devil ail they?
Cuſtards, and penny Paſties, Fools and Fiddles,
What's this to th' purpoſe? Oh well met.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Now Rowland.
I cannot ſtay to talk long.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What's the matter?
Here's ſtirring, but to what end? whither goe you?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: To view the Works.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What Works?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: The womens Trenches.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Trenches? are ſuch to ſee?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I do not jeſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I cannot underſtand you.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Do not you hear
In what ſtate of quarrel the new Bride
Stands with her Husband?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Let him ſtand with her, and there's an end.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: It ſhould be, but by'r Lady
She holds him out at Pikes end, and deſies him,
And now is fortifi'd, ſuch a Regiment of Rutters
Never defied men braver: I am ſent
To view their preparation.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: This is news
Stranger, than Arms in the air: you ſaw not
My gentle Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes, and meditating
Upon ſome ſecret buſineſs, when ſhe had found it
She leap'd for joy, and laugh'd, and ſtraight retir'd
To ſhun Moroſo.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: This may be for me.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Will you along?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Farewel. Exit Sophocles.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewel, Sir.
What ſhould her muſing mean, and what her joy in't,
• f not for my advantage? ſtay ye; may not
sp.stage: Enter Livia at one door, and Moroſo at another, hearkning.
sp.l: That bob-tail jade Moroſo, with his Gold,
His gew-gaudes, and the hope ſhe has to ſend him
Quickly to duſt, excite this? here ſhe comes,
And yonder walks the Stallion to diſcover:
Yet I'll ſalute her: ſave you beauteous Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: The Fox is kennell'd for me: ſave you Sir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why do you look ſo ſtrange?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I uſe to look Sir
Without examination.
Twenty Spur-Royals for that word.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Belike then
The object diſcontents you?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Yes it does.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Is't come to this? you know me, do you not?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Yes, as I may know many by repentance.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why do you break your faith?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I'll tell you that too,
You are under age, and no band holds upon you.
Excellent wench.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Sue out your underſtanding,
And get more hair to cover your bare knuckle;
(For boys were made for nothing, but dry kiſſes)
And if you can, more manners.
Better ſtill.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: And then if I want Spaniſh Gloves, or Stockings,
A ten pound Waſtecoat, or a Nag to hunt on,
〈◊〉 may be I ſhall grace you to accept 'em.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewel, and when I credit women more,
• ay I to Smithfield, and there buy a Jade,
• And know him to be ſo) that breaks my neck.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Becauſe I have known you, I'll be thus kind to you;
•• rewel, and be a man, and I'll provide you,
••• auſe I ſee y'are deſperate, ſome ſtaid Chamber-maid.
That may relieve your youth with wholſome doctrine.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: She's mine from all the world: ha wench?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Ha Chicken? — gives him a box o'th' ear, and Ex.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: How's this? I do not love theſe favors: ſave you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: The devil take thee — wrings him by th' noſe.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: There's a Love-token for you: thank me now.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I'll think on ſome of ye, and if I live,
My noſe alone ſhall not be plaid withal. Exit.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: A Box o' th' ear do you ſay?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Yes ſure, a ſound one,
Beſide my noſe blown to my hand; if Cupid
Shoot Arrows of that weight, I'll ſwear devoutly,
H'as ſued his Livery, and is no more a boy.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: You gave her ſome ill language?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Not a word,

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Or might be you were fumbling?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Would I had Sir.
I had been a forehand then; but to be baffl'd,
And have no feeling of the cauſe

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Be patient,
I have a medicine clapt to her back will cure her.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: No ſure it muſt be afore, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: O' my conſcience,
When I got theſe two wenches (who till now
Ne'r ſhew'd their riding) I was drunk with Baſtard,
Whoſe nature is to form things like it ſelf
Heady, and monſtrous: did ſhe ſ • ight him too?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: That's all my comfort: a meer Hobby-horſe
She made child Rowland: s'foot ſhe would not know him,
Not give him a free look, not reckon him
Among her thoughts, which I held more than wonder,
I having ſeen her within's three days kiſs him.
With ſuch an appetite as though ſhe would eat him.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: There is ſome trick in this: how did he take it;

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Ready to cry; he ran away.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I fear her.
And yet I tell you, ever to my anger,
She is as tame as innocency; it may be
This blow was but a favour.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I'll be ſworn 'twas well tied on then.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Goe too, pray forget it,
I have beſpoke a Prieſt: and within's two hours
I'll have ye married; will that pleaſe you?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I'll ſee it done my ſelf, and give the Lady
Such a ſound exhortation for this knavery
I'll warrant you, ſhall make her ſmell this month on't.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Nay good Sir be not violent.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Neither —

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: It may be
Out of her earneſt love there grew a longing
(As you know women have ſuch toys) in kindneſs,
To give me a box o'th' ear, or ſo.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: It may be.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I reckon for the beſt ſtill: this night then
I ſhall enjoy her.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: You ſhall handſel her.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Old as I am, I'll give her one blow for't
Shall make her groan this twelve-month,

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Where's your Joynture?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I have a Joynture for her.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Have your Council perus'd it yet?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: No Council but the night, and your ſweet daughter,
Shall e'r peruſe that joynture.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Very well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: I'll no demurrers on't, nor no rejoynders.
The other's ready ſeal'd.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Come then let's comfort
My Son Petruchio, he's like little Children
That looſe their baubles, crying ripe.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Pray tell me,
Is this ſtern woman ſtill upon the flaunt
Of bold defiance?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Still, and ſtill ſhe ſhall be,
Till ſhe be ſtarv'd out, you ſhall ſee ſuch juſtice,
That women ſhall be glad after this tempeſt,
To tie their husbands ſhooes, and walk their horſes.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: That were a merry world: do you hear the rumor?
They ſay the women are in inſurrection,
And mean to make a—

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: They'll ſooner
Draw upon walls as we do: Let 'em, let 'em,
We'll ſhip 'em out in Cuck-ſtools, there they'll ſail
As brave Columbus did, till they diſcover
The happy Iſlands of obedience.
We ſtay too long, Come.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Now St. George be with us. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Now if I can but get in handſomely,
Father I ſhall deceive you; and this night
For all your private plotting I'll no wedlock;
I have ſhifted ſail, and ſind my Siſters ſafety
A ſure retirement; pray to heaven that Rowland
Do not believe too far, what I ſaid to him,
For you old Foxcaſe forc'd me, that's my fear.
Stay, let me ſee, this quarter ſierce Petruchio
Keeps with his Myrmidons, I muſt be ſuddain,
If he ſeize on me, I can look for nothing
But Marſhal-Law; to this place have I ſcap'd him;
Above there.

l.hi: Chevai'a.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: A friend.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Who are you?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Look out and know.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Alas poor wench, who ſent thee?
What weak fool made thy tongue his Orator?
I know you come to parly.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Y'are deceiv'd,
Urg'd by the goodneſs of your cauſe, I come
To do as you do.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Y'are too weak, too fooliſh,
To cheat us with your ſmoothneſs: do not we know
Thou haſt been kept up tame?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Believe me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, prethee good Livia
Utter thy Eloquence ſomewhere elſe.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Good Coſin
Put up your Pipes; we are not for your palate
Alas we know who ſent you.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: O' my word —

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Stay there; you muſt not think your word,
Or by your Maidenhead, or ſuch Sunday oaths,
Sworn after Even-Song, can inveigle us
To loſ • our hand-faſt: did their wiſdoms think
That ſent you hither, we would be ſo fooliſh,
To entertain our gentle Siſter Sinon,
And give her credit, while the wooden Jade
Petruchio ſtole upon us: no good Siſter,
Go home, and tell the merry Greeks that ſent you,
Ilium ſhall burn, and I, as did Aeneas,
Will on my back, ſpite of the Myrmidons,
Carry this warlike Lady, and through Seas
Unknown, and unbeliev'd, ſeek out a Land,
Where like a race of noble Amazons
We'll roo • our ſelves, and to our endleſs glory
Live, and deſpiſe baſe men.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I'll ſecond ye.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: How long have you been thus?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: That's all one, Coſin,
I ſtand for freedom now.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Take heed of lying;
For by this light, if we do credit you,
And find you tripping, his infliction
That kill'd the Prince of Orange, will be ſport
To what we purpoſe,

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Let me feel the heavieſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Swear by thy Sweet-heart Rowland (for by your maiden-head,
I fear 'twill be too late to ſwear) you mean
Nothing but fair and ſafe, and honourable
To us, and to your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I ſwear.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Stay yet,
Swear as you hate Moroſo, that's the ſureſt,
And as you have a certain fear to ſind him
Worſe than a poor dry'd Jack, full of more aches
Than Autumn has; more knavery, and uſury,
And foolery, and brokery, than dogs-ditch:
As you do conſtantly believe he's nothing
But an old empty bag with a grey beard,
And that Beard ſuch a bob-tail, that it looks
Worſe than a Mares tail eaten off with Fillies:
As you acknowledge that young handſome wench
That lies by ſuch a Bilboa blade that bends
With ev'ry paſs he makes, to th' hilts, miſerable,
A dry Nurſe to his Coughs. a fewterer
To ſuch a naſty fellow, a robb'd thing
Of all delights youth looks for: and to end,
One caſt away on courſe beef, born to bruſh
That everlaſting Caſſock that has worn
As many Servants out, as the Northeaſt paſſage
Has conſum'd Sailors: if you ſwear this, and truly
Without the reſervation of a gown
Or any meritorious Petticoat,
'Tis like we ſhall believe you.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I do ſwear it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Stay yet a little; came this wholſome motion
(Deal truly Siſter) from your own opinion,
Or ſome ſuggeſtion of the Foe?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Nev'r fear me,
For by that little faith I have in Husbands,
And the great zeal I bear your cauſe, I come
Full of that liberty you ſtand for, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If we believe, and you prove recreant, Livia,
Think what a maim you give the noble Cauſe
We now ſtand up for: Think what women ſhall,
An hundred years hence, ſpeak thee, when examples
Are look'd for, and ſo gr • at ones, whoſe relations,
Spoke as we do 'em wench, ſhall make new cuſtoms,

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: If you be falſe, repent, go home, and pray,
And to the ſerious women of the City
Confeſs your ſelf; bring not a ſin ſo hainous
To load thy ſoul to this place: mark me Livia,
If thou be'ſt double, and betray'ſt our honors,
And we fail in our purpoſe: get thee where
There is no women living, nor no hope
There ever ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: If a Mothers daughter,
That ever heard the name of ſtubborn husband
Find thee, and know thy ſin.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Nay, if old age,
One that has worn away the name of woman,
And no more left to know her by, but railing,
No teeth, nor eyes, nor legs, but wooden ones
Come but i'th' wind-ward of thee, for ſure ſhe'll ſmell the •
Thou'lt be ſo rank, ſhe'll ride thee like a night-Mare,
And ſay her Prayers back-ward to undo thee:
She'll curſe thy meat and drink, and when thou marrieſt,
Clap a ſound ſpell for ever on thy pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Children of five year old, like little Fairies,
Will pinch thee into motley: all that ever
Shall live, and hear of thee, I mean all women,
Will (like ſo many furies) ſhake their keys;
And toſs their flaming diſtaffs o'r their heads,
Crying revenge: take heed, 'tis hideous:
Oh 'tis a fearful office, if thou hadſt
(Though thou be'ſt perfect now) when thou cam'ſt hither,
A falſe imagination, get thee gone,
And as my learned Coſin ſaid, repent,
This place is ſought by ſoundneſs.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: So I ſeek it,
Or let me be a moſt deſpis'd example.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do believe thee, be thou worthy of it.
You come not empty?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: No, here's Cakes, and cold meat,
And Tripe of proof: behold, here's Wine and Beer,
Be ſuddain, I ſhall be ſurpriz'd elſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Meet at the low parlour door, there lies a cloſe way:
What fond obedience you have living in you,
Or duty to a man before you enter,
Fling it away, 'twill but defile our Off'rings.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Be wary as you come,

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I warrant ye. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Mai.
sp.l: How goes your buſineſs Girls?
A foot, and fair.
If fortune favour us: away to your ſtrength,
The Countrey Forces are arriv'd, be gone,
We are diſcover'd elſe.
Arm, and be valiant.
Think of our cauſe.
Our Juſtice.
'Tis ſufficient. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaene Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Rowland and Tranio at ſeveral doors.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Now Rowland?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: How doe you?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: How doſt thou man?
Thou look'ſt ill:

sp.speaker: Bow.
sp.l: Yes, pray can you tell me Tranio,
Who knew the devil firſt?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A woman.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: So. Were they not well acquainted?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: May be ſo,
For they had certain Dialogues together.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: He ſold her fruit, I take it?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes, and Cheeſe
That choak'd all mankind after.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Canſt thou tell me
Whether that woman ever had a faith
After ſhe had eaten?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That's a School-queſtion

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: No,
'Tis no queſtion, for believe me Tranio,
That cold fruit after eating bre • d naught in her
But windy promiſes, and chollick vows
That broke out both ways.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thou haſt heard I am ſure
Of Eſculapius, a far famed Surgeon,
One that could ſet together quarter'd Traitors
And make 'em honeſt men.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: How doſt thou Rowland?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Let him but take, (if be dare do a cure
Shall get him fame indeed) a faithleſs woman,
There will be credit for him, that will ſpeak him,
A broken woman Tranio, a baſe woman,
And if he can cure ſuch a rack of honor
Let him come here, and practice.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Now for honors ſake,
Why what ail'ſt thou Rowland?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am ridden Tranio.
And ſpur-gall'd to the life of patience
(Heaven keep my wits together) by a thing
Our worſt thoughts are too noble for, a woman.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Your Miſtriſs has a little frown'd it may be?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: She was my Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Is ſhe not?

sp.speaker: Rdw.
sp.l: No Tranio.
She has done me ſuch diſgrace, ſo ſpitefully
So like a woman bent to my undoing,
That henceforth a good horſe ſhall be my Miſtriſs,
A good Sword, or a Book: and if you ſee her,
Tell her I beſeech you, even for love ſake.—

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I will Rowland.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: She may ſ • oner
Count the good I have thought her,
Our old love and our friend • hip,
Shed one true tear, mean one hour conſtantly,
Be old and honeſt, married, and a maid,
Than make me ſee her more, or more believe her:
And now I have met a meſſenger, farewel Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Alas poor Rowland, I will do it for thee:
This is that dog Moroſo, but I hope
To ſee him cold i'th' mouth firſt, e'r he enjoy her:
I'll watch this young man, deſperate thoughts may ſeize him,
And if my purſe or council can, I'll eaſe him. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Petronius, Moroſo, and Sophocles.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: For look you Gentlemen, ſay that I grant her,
Out of my free and liberal love, a pardon,
Which you, and all men elſe know, ſhe deſerves not,
(Teneatis amici) can all the world leave laughing?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I think not.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: No by—they cannot;
For pray conſider, have you ever read,
Or heard of, or can any man imagine.
So ſtiff a Tom-boy, of ſo ſet a malice,
And ſuch a brazen reſolution,
As this young Crab-tree? and then anſwer me,
And mark but this too friends, without a cauſe,
Not a foul word come croſs her, not a fear,
She juſtly can take hold on, and do you think
I muſt ſleep out my anger, and endure it,
Sow pillows to her eaſe, and lull her miſchief?
Give me a Spindle firſt: no, no my Maſters,
Were ſhe as fair as Nell-a-Greece, and houſewife,
As good as the wiſe Sailors wife, and young ſtill,
Never above fifteen, and theſe tricks to it,
She ſhould ride the wild Mare once a week, ſhe ſhould,
(Believe me friends ſhe ſhould) I would tabor her,
Till all the Legions that are crept into her,
Flew out with fire i'th' tails.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Methinks you err now,
For to me ſeems, a little ſufferance
Were a far ſurer cure.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, I can ſuffer,
Where I ſee promiſes of peace and amendment.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Give her a few conditions.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I'll be hanged firſt.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Give her a Crab-tree Cudgel.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: So I will;
And after it a flock-bed for her bones.
And hard eggs, till they brace her like a Drum,
She ſhall be pamper'd with —
She ſhall not know a ſtool in ten months, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: This muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Arm, arm, out with your weapons,
For all the women in the Kingdom's on ye;
They ſwarm like waſps, and nothing can deſtroy 'em,
But ſtopping of their hive, and ſmothering of 'em

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Stand to your guard, Sir, all the devils extant
Are broke upon us like a cloud of thunder;
There are more women marching hitherward,
In reſcue of my Miſtriſs, than e'er turn'd tail
At Sturbridge Fair, and I believe, as fiery.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: The forlorn-hope's led by a Tanner's wife,
I know her by her Hide, a deſperate woman:
She flead her Husband in her youth, and made
Raynes of his Hide to ride the pariſh. Take 'em all together,
They are a genealogy of Jennets, gotten
And born thus by the boiſterous breath of Husbands;
They ſerve ſure, and are ſwift to catch occaſion,
(I mean their ſoes or Husbands) by the forelocks,
And there they hang like favours; cry they can
But more for Noble ſpight, than fear: and crying
Like the old Giants that were foes to heaven,
They heave ye ſtool on ſtool, and fling main Pot-lids
Like maſſie Rocks, dart Ladles, toſſing Irons,
And Tongs like Thunderbolts, till over laid,
They ſall beneath the weight; yet ſtill aſpiring
At thoſe Emperious Godheads that would tame 'em.
There's ne'r a one of theſe, the worſt and weakeſt,
(Chuſe where you will,) b • t dare attempt the raiſing,
Againſt the ſoveraign peace of Puritans,
A May-pole and a Morris, maugre mainly
Their zeal, and Dudgeon-daggers: and yet more,
Dares plant a ſtand of batt'ring Ale againſt 'em,
And drink 'em out o'th' pariſh.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Lo you fierce Petruchio, this comes of your impatience.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: There's one brought in the Bears againſt the Canons
Of the Town, made it good, and fought 'em.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Another to her everlaſting fame, erected
Two Ale-houſes of eaſe: the Quarter-Seſſions
Running againſt her roundly; in which buſineſs
Two of the diſanullers loſt their night-caps:
The Conſtable, to her eternal glory,
Drunk hard, and was converted, and ſhe victor.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Then are they victualed with Pies and Puddings,
(The trappings of good Stomachs) noble Ale
The true defender, Sauſages, and ſmoak'd ones,
If need be, ſuch as ſerve for Pikes; and Pork,
(Better the Jews ne'r hated:) here and there
A bottle of Metheglin, a ſtout Britain
That will ſtand to 'em; what elſe they want, they war for.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Come to council.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Now you muſt grant conditions, or the Kingdom
Will have no other talke but this.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Away then, and let's adviſe the beſt.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Why do you tremble?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Have I liv'd thus long to be knockt o'th' head,
With half a Waſhing-beetle: pray be wiſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Come, ſomething I'll do, but what it is, I know not.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: To Council then, and let's avoid their follies.
Guard all the doors, or we ſhall not have a Cloak left.

div.head: Scaena Tertia:
div.stage: Enter Petronius, Petruchio, Moroſo, Sophocles, and Tranio.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I am indifferent, though I muſt confeſs,
I had rather ſee her carted.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No more of that, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Are ye reſolv'd to give her fair conditions?
'Twill be the ſafeſt way.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I am diſtracted,
Would I had run my head into a halter
When I firſt woo'd her: if I offer peace,
She'll urge her own conditions, that's the devil.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Why, ſay ſhe do?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Say, I am made an Aſs, then;
I know her aim: may I, with reputation
(Anſwer me this) with ſafety of mine honor,
(After the mighty manage of my firſt wife,
Which was indeed a fury to this Filly,
After my twelve ſtrong labours to reclaim her,
Which would have made Don Hercules horn mad,
And hid him in his Hide) ſuffer this Cicely?
E're ſhe have warm'd my ſheets, e're grappell'd with me,
This Pinck, this painted Foiſt, this Cockle-boat,
To hang her Fights out, and defie me friends,
A well known man of war? if this be equal,
And I may ſuffer, ſay, and I have done?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I do not think you may.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You'll make it worſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Pray hear me good Petruchio: but ev'n now,
You were contented to give all conditions,
To try how far ſhe would carry: 'Tis a folly,
(And you will find it ſo) to clap the curb on,
E're you be ſure it proves a natural wildneſs,
And not a forc'd. Give her conditions,
For on my life this trick is put into her,

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I ſhould believe ſo too.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: And not her own.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You'll find it ſo.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Then if ſhe flownder with you,
Clap ſpurs on, and in this you'll deal with temperance,
Avoid the hurry of the world.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: And looſe. Muſick above.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: No honor on my life, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I will do it.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: It ſeems they are very merry.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why Heaven hold it.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Now Jaques?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: They are i'th' flaunt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes we hear 'em.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: They have got a ſtick of Fiddles, and they firk it,
In wondrous ways, the two grand Capitano's,
(They brought the Auxiliary Regiments)
Dance with their coats tuckt up to their bare breeches,
And bid the Kingdom kiſs 'em, that's the burden;
They have got Metheglin, and audacious Ale;
And talk like Tyrants.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How knoweſt thou?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I peept in
At a looſe Lansket.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: A Health for all this day
To the woman that bears the ſway
And wears the breeches;
Let it come, let it come.
Let this health be a Seal,
For the good of the Common-weal
the woman ſhall wear the breeches.
Let's drink then and laugh it
And merrily merrily quaff it
And tipple, and tipple a round
here's to thy fool,
and to my fool.
Come, to all fools
though it coſt us wench, many a pound.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Hark.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: A Song, pray ſilence. All the Women above. Citizens and Countrey women.
They look out.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Good ev'n Ladies.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Good you good ev'n Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: How have you ſlept to night?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Exceeding well Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Did you not wiſh me with you?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, believe me,
I never thought upon you.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Is that he?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: She has drank hard, mark her Hood.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You are—

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Learnedly drunk, I'll hang elſe: let her utter.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And I muſt tell you, viva voce friend,
A very fooliſh fellow.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: There's an Ale figure.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I thank you Suſan Brotes.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Forward Siſter.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You have eſpouſed here a hearty woman,
A comly, and courageous.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Well, I have ſo.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And to the comfort of diſtreſſed damſels,
Women out-worn in wedlock; and ſuch veſſels,
This woman has defied you.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: It ſhould ſeem ſo.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And why?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, can you tell?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: For thirteen cauſes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Pray by your patience Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Forward Siſter.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Do you mean to treat of all theſe?

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Who ſhall let her?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Do you hear, Velvet hood, we come not now
To hear your doctrine

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: For the firſt, I take it,
• t doth divide it ſelf into ſeven branches.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Hark you good Maria,
Have you got a Catechiſer here?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Good zeal.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Good three pil'd predication, will you peace,
And hear the cauſe we come for?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Yes bob-tails
We know the cauſe you come for, here's the cauſe,
But never hope to carry her, never dream
Or flatter your opinions with a thought
Of baſe repentance in her.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Give me Sack,
By this, and next ſtrong Ale.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Swear forward Siſter.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: By all that's cordial, in this place we'll bury
Our bones, fames, tongues, our triumphs and all
That ever yet was chronicl'd of woman;
But this brave wench, this excellent deſpiſer,
This bane of dull obedience, ſhall inherit
His liberal Will, and march off with conditions
Noble, and worth her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: She ſhall Tom Tilers,
And brave ones too, my Hood ſhall make a Hearſe-cloth,
And I'll lie under it like Jone o' Gaunt,
E'r I go leſs, my Diſtaff ſtuck up by me,
For the eternal Trophy of my conqueſts;
And loud fame at my head with two main bottles,
Shall fill to all the world the glorious fall
Of old Don Gillian.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Yet a little further,
We have taken Arms in reſcue of this Lady;
Moſt juſt and Noble: if ye beat us off
Without conditions, and we recant,
• ſe us as we deſerve; and firſt degrade us
• f all our antient chambring: next that
The Symbols of our ſecreſie, ſilk Stockings,
Hew of our heels; our petticoats of Arms
Tear off our bodies, and our Bodkins break
Over our coward heads.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And ever after
To make the tainture moſt notorious,
At all our Creſts, videlicet our Plackets.
Let Laces hang, and we return again
Into our former titles, Dary-maids.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: No more wars: puiſſant Ladies, ſhew conditions
And freely I accept 'em.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Call in Livia;
She's in the Treaty too.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: How, Livia?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Hear you that Sir?
There's the conditions for ye, pray peruſe 'em.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Yes, there ſhe is: 't had been no right rebellion,
Had ſhe held off; what think you man?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Nay nothing.
I have enough o'th' proſpect: o' my conſcience,
The worlds end, and the goodneſs of a woman
Will come together.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Are you there ſweet Lady?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Cry you mercy Sir, I ſaw you not: your bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Yes, when I bleſs a jade, that ſtumbles with me.
How are the Articles?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: This is for you Sir;
And I ſhall think upon't.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: You have us'd me finely.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: There's no other uſe of thee now extant,
But to be hung up, Caſſock, Cap, and all,
For ſome ſtrange monſter at Apothecaries.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I hear you whore.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: It muſt be his then Sir,
For need will then compel me.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Bleſſing on thee.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: There's no talking to 'em;
How are they Sir?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: As I expected: Liberty and clothes, Reads.
When, and in what way ſhe will: continual moneys,
Company, and all the houſe at her diſpoſe;
No tongue to ſay, why is this? or whether will it;
New Coaches, and ſome buildings, ſhe appoints here;
Hangings, and Hunting-horſes: and for Plate
And Jewels for her private uſe, I take it,
Two thouſand pound in preſent: then for Muſick,
And women to read French;

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: This muſt not be.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And at the latter end a clauſe put in,
That Livia ſhall by no man be importun'd.
This whole month yet, to marry.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: This is monſtrous.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: This ſhall be done, I'll humor her awhile:
If nothing but repentance and undoing
Can win her love, I'll make a ſhift for one.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: When ye are once a bed, all theſe conditions
Lie under your own ſeal.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Do you like 'em?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes.
And by that faith I gave you 'fore the Prieſt
I'll ratifie 'em.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Stay, what pledges?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, I'll take that oath;
But have a care you keep it.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: 'Tis not now
As when Andrea liv'd.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: If you do juggle,
Or alter but a Letter of theſe Articles
We have ſet down the ſelf-ſame perſecution.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Miſtruſt him not.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: By all my honeſty—

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Enough, I yield.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: What's this Inſerted here?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: That the two valiant women that commanded here
Shall have a Supper made 'em, and a large one,
And liberal entertainment without grudging,
And pay for all their ſoldiers.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: That ſhall be too;
And if a Tun of Wine will ſerve to pay 'em,
They ſhall have juſtice: I ordain ye all
Pay-maſters, Gentlemen,

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Then we ſhall have ſport boys,

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: We'll meet you in the Parlor.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Ne'r look ſad, Sir, for I will do it,

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: There's no danger in't.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: For Livia's Article you ſhall obſerve it,
I have ti'd my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: A long then: now
Either I break, or this ſtiff plant muſt bow. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: COme you ſhall take my counſel.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I ſhall hang firſt.
I'll no more love, that's certain, 'tis a bane,
(Next that they poiſon Rats with) the moſt mortal:
No, I thank Heaven, I have got my ſleep again,
And now begin to write ſence; I can walk ye
A long hour in my chamber like a man,
And think of ſome thing that may better me;
Some ſerious point of Learning, or my ſtate;
No more ay-mees, and Miſtriſſes, Tranio,
Come near my brain. I'll tell thee, had the devil
But any eſſence in him of a man,
And could be brought to love, and love a woman,
'Twould make his head ake worſer than his horns do;
And firk him with a fire he never felt yet,
Would make him dance. I tell thee there is nothing
(It may be thy caſe Tranio, therefore hear me:)
Under the Sun (reckon the maſs of follies
Crept into th' world with man) ſo deſperate,
So mad, ſo ſenceleſs, poor and baſe, ſo wretched,
Roguy, and ſcurvy,

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Whether wilt thou Rowland?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: As 'tis to be in love.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: And why for virtue ſake?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And why for virtue's ſake? doſt thou not conceive me?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No by my troth.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Pray then and heartily,
For fear thou fall into't: I'll tell thee why too,
(For I have hope to ſave thee) when thou loveſt,
And firſt beginſt to worſhip the gilt calf:

sp.speaker: Imprimis,
sp.l: thou haſt loſt thy gentry,
And like a Prentice, flung away thy Freedom,
Forthwith thou art a ſlave.
That's a new Doctrine.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Next thou art no more man.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: What then?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: A Fryppery;
Nothing but braided hair and penny ribbond,
Glove, Garter, Ring, Roſe, or at beſt a Swabber,
If thou canſt love ſo near to keep thy making,
Yet thou wilt loſe thy language.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Oh Tranio,
Thoſe things in love, ne'er talk as we do,

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: No, without doubt, they ſigh, and ſhake the head,
And ſometimes whiſtle dolefully.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No tongue?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes Tranio, but no truth in't, nor no reaſon,
And when they cant (for 'tis a kind of canting)
Ye ſhall hear, if you reach to underſtand 'em
(Which you muſt be a fool firſt, or you cannot)
Such gibb'riſh; ſuch believe me, I proteſt Sweet,
And oh dear Heavens, in which ſuch conſtellations
Reign at the births of Lovers, this is too well,
And daigne me Lady, daigne me I beſeech ye
You poor unworthy lump, and then ſhe licks him.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A—on't, this is nothing.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thou haſt hit it:
Then talks ſhe ten times worſe, and wryes, and wriggles,
As though ſhe had the Itch (and ſo it may be.)

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Why thou art grown a ſtrange diſcoverer.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Of mine own follies Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Wilt thou Rowland,
Certain ne'er love again?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I think ſo, certain,
And if I be not dead drunk I ſhall keep it.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Tell me but this; what doſt thou think of women?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why, as I think of Fiddles, they delight me,
Till their ſtrings break.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: What ſtrings?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Their modeſties,
Faiths, Vows, and Maidenheads, for they are like Kits
They have but four ſtrings to 'em.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: What wilt thou
Give me for ten pound now, when thou next loveſt,
And the ſame woman ſtill?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Give me the money;
A hundred, and my Bond for't.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: But pray hear me,
I'll work all means I can to reconcile ye:

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Do, do, Give me the money;

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Work Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You ſhall go ſometimes where ſhe is.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes ſtraight.
This is the firſt good I e'er got by woman.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You would think it ſtrange now, if another beauty
As good as hers, ſay better.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Conceive me,
This is no point o'th' wager.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: That's all one,

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Love you as much, or more, than now ſhe hates you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: 'tis a good hearing, let 'em love: ten pound more
I never love that woman.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: There it is;
And ſo an hundred, if you loſe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: 'Tis done;
Have you another to put in?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No, no Sir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am very ſorry: now will I erect
A new game, and go hate for th' bell; I am ſure
I am in excellent caſe to win.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I muſt have leave.
To tell you, and tell truth too, what ſhe is,
And how ſhe ſuffers for you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Ten pound more,
I never believe you.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No Sir, I am ſtinted.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Well, take your beſt way then.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Let's walk, I am glad
Your ſullen Feavor's off.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Shalt ſee me Tranio
A monſtrous merry man now: let's to the Wedding,
And as we go, tell me the general hurry
Of theſe mad wenches and their works.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And do thy worſt.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Something I'll do. Exeu •

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Do Tranio.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: A pair of Stocks beſtride 'em; Are they gone?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: Yes they are gone; and a • l the pans i'th Town
Beating before 'em: What ſtrange admonitions
They gave my Maſter, and how fearfully
They threaten'd, if he broke 'em?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: O' my Conſcience
H'as found his full match now.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: That I believe too.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: How did ſhe entertain him?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: She lookt on him.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: But ſcurvely.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: With no great affection
That I ſaw: and I heard ſome ſay he kiſs'd her,
But 'twas upon a treaty, and ſome copies
Say, but her Cheek.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Jaques, What wouldſt thou give
For ſuch a Wife now?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Full as many Payers
As the moſt zealous Puritane conceives
Out of the meditation of fat Veal,
Or Birds of prey, cram'd Capons, againſt Players,
And t • as good a tune too, but againſt her:
That heaven would bleſs me from her: mark it Pedro,
If this houſe be not turn'd within this fortnight
With the foundation upward, I'll be carted.
My comfort is yet, that thoſe Amorites,
That came to back her cauſe, thoſe Heathen Whores,
Had their Hoods hallowed with Sack.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: How Div'liſh drunk they were?

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: And how they tumbled, Pedro, Didſt thou marke
The Countrey Cavaliero?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Out upon her,
How ſhe turn'd down the Bragget?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I that ſunk her.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: That Drink was well put to her; What a Somer ſalt
When the chair fel, ſhe fetch'd, with her heels upward?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And what a piece of Landskip ſhe diſcover'd?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Didſt mark her, when her hood fell in the Poſſet?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes, and there rid, like a Dutch-Hoy; the Tumbrel,
When ſhe had got her ballaſſe.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: That I ſaw too.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: How fain ſhe would have drawn on Sophocles
To come aboard, and how ſhe ſimper'd it—

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I warrant her, ſhe has been a worthy ſtriker.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I'th heat of Summer there had been ſome hope on't.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Hang her.

sp.speaker: Jac.
sp.l: She offer'd him a Harry-groat, and belcht out,
Her ſtomach being blown with Ale, ſuch Courtſhip,
Upon my life has giv'n him twenty ſtools ſince:
Believe my Calculation, theſe old Women,
When they are tippled, and a little heated,
Are like new wheels, they'l roare you all the Town ore
Till they be greas'd.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: The City Cinque-a-pace
Dame Toſt and Butter, had the Bob too?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes,
But ſhe was ſullen drunk, and given to filching,
I ſee her offer at a Spoon; my Maſter —
I do not like his look, I fear h'as faſted
For all this preparation; lets ſteal by him. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Not let you touch her all this night?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Not touch her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Where was your courage?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Where was her obedience?
Never poor Man was ſham'd ſo; never Raſcal
That keeps a ſtud of Whores was us'd ſo baſely.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Pray you tell me one thing truly;
Do you love her?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I would I did not, upon that condition
I paſt thee half my Land.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: It may be then,
Her modeſty requir'd a little violence?
Some Women love to ſtruggle.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: She had it,
And ſo much that I ſweat for't, ſo I did,
But to no end: I waſht an Ethiope
She ſwore my force might weary her, but win her
• never could, nor ſhould, ti • l ſhe conſented;
And I might take her body priſoner,
But for her mind or appetite—

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange;
This woman is the firſt I ever read of,
Re • us'd a warranted occaſion,
And •• anding on ſo fair termes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I ſhall quit her.
Us'd you no more art?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, I ſwore to her,
And by no little ones, if preſently
Wi • hout more diſputation on the matter,
She gr • w not nearer to me, and diſpatcht me
Out of the pains I was, for I was nettl'd,
And willingly, and eagerly, and ſweetly,
I would to her Chamber-maid, and in her hearing
Begin her ſuch a hunte • -up.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Then ſhe ſtarted?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: No more than I do now; marry ſhe anſwered
But there was one call'd Jaques, a poor Butler
One that might well content a ſingle woman.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: And he ſhould tilt her.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: To that ſence, and laſt
She bad me yet theſe ſix nights look for nothing,
Nor ſtrive to purchaſe it, but fair good night,
And ſo good morrow, and a kiſs or two
To cloſe my ſtomach, for her vow had ſeal'd it,
And ſhe would keep it conſtant.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Stay ye, ſtay ye,
Was ſhe thus when you woo'd her?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Nothing Sophocles,
More keenely eager, I was oft afraid
She had been light, and eaſie, ſhe would ſhowre
Her kiſſes ſo upon me.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Then I fear
An other ſpoke's i'th wheele.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now thou haſt found me,
There gnawes my Devil, Sopho • les, O patience
Preſerve me; that I make her not example
By ſome unworthy way; as fleaing her,
Boyling, or making verjuice, drying her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I hear her.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Mark her then, and ſee the heir
Of ſpight and prodigality, ſhe has ſtudied
A way to begger's both, and by this hand
sp.stage: Maria at the dore, and Servant and Woman
sp.l: She ſhall be, if I live, a Doxy.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Fy Sir.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do not like that dreſſing, tis too poor,
Let me have ſix gold laces, broad and maſſy,
And betwixt ev'ry lace a rich Embroydry,
Line the Gown through with Pluſh perfum'd, and purffle
All the ſleeves down with Pearl.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What think you Sophocles.
In what point ſtands my ſtate now?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For thoſe hangings.
Let'em be carried where I gave appointment,
They are too baſe for my uſe, and beſpeak
New Pieces of the Civil Wars of France,
Let 'em be large and lively, and all ſilk work,
The borders Gold.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I marry ſir, this cuts it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That fourteen yards of Satten give my Woman,
I do not like the colour, 'tis too civil:
Ther's too much Silk i'th lace too; tell the Dutchman
Tha • brought the Mares, he muſt with all ſpeed ſend me
An other ſuit of Horſes, and by all means
Ten caſt of Hawkes for th'River, I much care not
What price they bear, ſo they be ſound, and flying,
For the next Winter, I am for the Country;
And mean to take my pleaſure; where's the Horſeman?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: She means to ride a great Horſe.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: With a ſide ſadle?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, and ſhee'l run a tilt within this twelve-month

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To morrow I'll begin to learn, but pray ſir
Have a great care he be an eaſie doer,
'Twill ſpoil a Scholar elſe.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: An eaſie doer,
Did you hear that?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes, I ſhall meet her morals
Ere it be long I fear not.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: O good morrow.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Good morrow Lady, how is't now.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Faith ſickly,
This houſe ſtands in an ill ayr.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yet more charges?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Subject to rots, and rheums; out on't, 'tis nothing
But a tild fog.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What think you of the Lodge then?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I like the ſeat, but 'tis too little, Sophocles
Let me have thy opinion, thou haſt judgment.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: 'Tis very well.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What if I pluck it down,
And build a ſquare upon it, with two courts
Still riſing from the entrance?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And i'th midſt
A Colled • e for young Scolds.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And to the Southward
Ta • e in a Garden of ſome twenty Acres,
And caſt it of the Italian faſhion, hanging.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And you could caſt your ſelf ſo too; pray Lady
Will not this coſt much Money?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Some five thouſand,
Say ſix: I'll have it Battel'd too.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And gilt; Maria,
This is a fearful courſe you take, pray think on't,
You are a Woman now, a Wife, and his
That muſt in honeſty, and juſtice look for
Some due obedience from you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That bare word
Shall coſt you many a pound more, build upon't;
Tell me of due obedience? VVhat's a Husband?
VVhat are we mar i • d for, to carry Sumpters?
Are we not one peece with you, and as worthy
Our own intentions, as you yours?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Pray hear me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Take two ſmall drops of water, equal weigh'd,
Tell me which is the heavieſt, and which ought
Firſt to deſcend in duty?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You miſtake me;
I urge not ſervice from you, nor obedience
In way of duty, but of love, and Credit;
All I expect is but a noble care
Of what I have brought you, and of what I am,
And what our name may be.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: That's in my making.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: 'Tis true it is ſo.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes, it is Petruchio,
For there was never Man without our molding,
VVithout our ſtamp upon him, and our juſtice,
Left any thing three ages after him
Good, and his own.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Good Lady underſtand him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do too much, ſweet Sophocles, he's one
Of a moſt ſpightful ſelf condition,
Never at peace with any thing but Age,
That has no teeth left to return his anger:
A Bravery dwells in his blood yet, of abuſing
His firſt good wife; he's ſooner fire than powder,
And ſooner miſchief.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If I be ſo ſodain
Do not you fear me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No nor yet care for you,
And if it may be lawful, I defie you:

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Do's this become you now?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It ſhall become me.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Thou diſobedient, weak, vain-glorious woman,
Were I but half ſo wilful, as thou ſpightful,
I ſhould now drag thee to thy duty.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Drag me?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: But I am friends again: take all your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now you perceive him Sophocles.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I love thee
Above thy vanity, thou faithleſs creature.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Would I had been ſo happy when I Married,
But to have met an honeſt Man like thee,
For I am ſure thou art good, I know thou art honeſt,
A hanſome hurtleſs man, a loving man,
Though never a penny with him; and thoſe eyes,
That face, and that true heart; weare this for my ſake,
And when thou think'ſt upon me pity me:
I am caſt away, Exit Mar.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: VVhy how now man?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Pray leave me,
And follow your advices.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: The Man's jealous:

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I ſhall find a time ere it be long, to ask you
One or two fooliſh queſtions.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I ſhall anſwer
As well as I am able, when you call me:
If ſhe mean true, tis but a little killing,
And if I do not venture it's—
Farewel ſir. Exit Soph.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Pray farewel. Is there no keeping
A VVife to one mans uſe? no wintering
Theſe cattel without ſtraying? 'Tis hard dealing,
Very hard dealing, Gentlemen, ſtrange dealing:
Now in the name of madneſs, what Star raign'd,
VVhat dog-ſtar, bull, or bear-ſtar, when I married
This ſecond wife, this whirlwind, that takes all
VVithin her compaſs? was I not well warn'd,
(I thought I had, and I believe I know it,)
And beaten to repentance in the dayes
Of my firſt doting? had I not wife enough
To turn my love to? did I want vexation,
Or any ſpecial care to kill my heart?
Had I not ev'ry morning a rare breakfaſt,
Mixt with a learned Lecture of ill language,
Louder than Tom o'Lincoln; and at dinner,
A dyet of the ſame diſh? was there evening
That ere paſt over us, without thou Knave,
Or thou VVhore for digeſtion? had I ever
A pull at this ſame poor ſport men run mad for
But like a Cur I was fain to ſhew my teeth firſt,
And almoſt worry her? and did Heaven forgive me,
And take this Serpent from me? and am I
Keeping tame Devils now again? my heart akcs;
Something I muſt do ſpeedily: I'll die,
• f I can hanſomely, for that's the way
To make a Raſcal of her; I am ſick,
And I'll goe very near it, but I'll periſh. Exit.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Livia, Byancha, Tranio, and Rowland.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Then I muſt be content, Sir, with my fortune.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And I with mine.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I did not think, a look,
Or a poor word or two, could have diſplanted
Such a fix'd conſtancy, and for your end too.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Come come, I know your courſes: there's your gew-gaws,
Four Rings, and Bracelets, and the Purſe you gave me,
The Money's ſpent in entertaining you
At Plays, and Cherry-gardens.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: There's your Chain too.
But if you'll give me leave, I'll wear the hair ſtill;
I would yet remember you.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Give him his love wench;
The young Man has imployment for't:

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Fie Rowland.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: You cannot fie me out a hundred pound
With this poor plot: yet, let me ne'r ſee day more,
If ſomething do not ſtruggle ſtrangely in me.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Young Man, let me talk with you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Well, young Woman.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: This was your Miſtriſs once.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Are ye honeſt?
I ſee you are young, and hanſome.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am honeſt.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Why that's well ſaid: and there's no doubt your judgement
Is good enough, and ſtrong enough to tell you
Who are your foes, and friends: Why did you leave her?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: She made a puppy of me.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Be that granted:
She muſt do ſo ſometimes, and oftentimes;
Love were too ſerious elſe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: A witty Woman.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Had you lov'd me—

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I would I had.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: And dearly;
And I had lov'd you ſo: you may love worſe Sir,
But that is not material.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I ſhall looſe.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Some time or other for variety
I ſhould have call'd you Fool, or Boy, or bid you
• ay with the Pages: but have lov'd you ſtill,
Out of all queſtion, and extreamly too;
You are a Man made to be loved:

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: This Woman.
Either abuſes me, or loves me deadly.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: I'll tell you one thing, if I were to chooſe
A Husband to mine own mind, I ſhould think
One of your Mothers making would content me,
For o' my Conſcience ſhe makes good ones.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Lady,
I'll leave you to your commendations:
I am in again, The Divel take their tongues.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: You ſhall not goe.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I will: yet thus far Livia,
Your Sorrow may induce me to forgive you,
But never love again; if I ſtay longer,
I have loſt two hundred pound.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Good Sir, but thus much—

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Turn if thou beeſt a Man.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: But one kiſs of you;
One parting kiſs, and I am gone too.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Come,
I ſhall kiſs fifty pound away at this clap:
We'll have one more, and then farewel.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Farewel.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Well, go thy wayes, thou bear'ſt a kind heart with thee.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: H'as made a ſtand.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: A noble, brave young fellow
Worthy a Wench indeed.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I will: I will not. Exit Rowland.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: He's gone: but ſhot agen; play you but your part,
And I will keep my promiſe: forty Angels
In fair gold, Lady: wipe your eyes: he's yours
If I have any wit.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I'll pay the forfeit.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Come then, let's ſee your ſiſter, how ſhe fares now,
After her skirmiſh: and be ſure, Moroſo
Be kept in good hand; then all's perfect, Livia.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: O Jaques, Jaques, What becomes of us?
Oh my ſweet Maſter.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Run for a Phyſitian,
And a whole peck of Pothecaries, Pedro.
He will die, didle, didle die: if they come not quickly,
And bring all People that are skilful
In Lungs and Livers: raiſe the neighbours,
And all the Aquavite-bottles extant;
And, O the Parſon, Pedro; O the Parſon,
A little of his comfort, never ſo little;
Twenty to one you find him at the Buſh,
There's the beſt Ale.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I fly. Exit Pedro.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Out with the Trunks, ho:
Why are you idle? Sirha, up to th' Chamber,
And take the Hangings down, and ſee the Linnen
Packt up, and ſent away within this half hour.
What, Are the Carts come yet? ſome honeſt body
Help down the Cheſts of Plate, and ſome the Wardrobe,
Alaſs, we are undone elſe.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Pray forſooth;
And I beſeech ye, tell me, is he dead yet?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, but is drawing on: out with the Armour.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Then I'll go ſee him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thou art undone then Fellow: no Man that has
Been neer him come near me.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Why how now Lady, What means this?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Now daughter, How does my Son?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Save all you can for Heavens ſake.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Be of good comfort, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: O my Casket.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How do's thy Husband Woman?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Get you gon, if you mean to ſave your lives: the Sickneſs.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Stand further off, I prethee.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Is i'th houſe Sir,
My Husband has it now;
Alas he is infected, and raves extreamly:
Give me ſome Counſel friends.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Why lock the doors up,
And ſend him in a Woman to attend him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I have beſpoke two Women; and the City
Hath ſent a Watch by this time: Meat nor Money
He ſhall not want, nor Prayers.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How long is't
Since it firſt took him?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: But within this three hours.
I am frighted from my wits: — O here's the Watch;
Pray doe your Office, lock the doors up Friends,
And patience be his Angel.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: This comes unlook'd for:

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I'll to the lodge; ſome that are kind and love me,
I know will viſit me. Petruchio within.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Doe you hear my Maſters: ho, you that lock the doors up.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: 'Tis his voice.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Hold, and let's hear him.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Will ye ſtarve me here: am I a Traytor, or an Heretick.
Or am I grown infectious?

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Pray ſir, pray.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I am as well as you are, goodman puppy.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Pray have patience.
You ſhall want nothing Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I want a cudgel,
And thee, thou wickedneſs.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: He ſpeaks well enough.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Had ever a ſtrong heart Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Will ye hear me?
Firſt be pleas'd
To think I know ye all, and can diſtinguiſh
Ev'ry Mans ſeveral voice: you that ſpoke firſt,
I know my father in law; the other Tranio,
And I heard Sophocles; the laſt, pray mark me,
• s my dam'd Wife Maria:
If any Man miſdoubt me for infected,
There is mine Arme, let any Man look on't.

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: Save ye Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: O welcome Doctor,
Ye come in happy time; pray your opinion,
What think you of his pulſe?

sp.speaker: Doct.
sp.l: It beats with buſieſt,
And ſhews a general inflammation.
Which is the ſymptome of a peſtilent Feaver,
Take twenty ounces from him.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Take a Fool;
Take an ounce from mine arme, and Doctor Deuz-ace,
I'll make a cloſe-ſtoole of your Velvet Coſtard.
—Gentlemen, doe ye make a may-game on me?
I tell ye once again, I am as ſound,
As well, as wholſome, and as ſenſible,
As any of ye all: Let me out quickly,
Or as I am a Man, I'll beat the walls down,
And the firſt thing I light upon ſhall pay for't.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Nay, we'll go with you Doctor.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: 'Tis the ſafeſt;
I ſaw the Tokens Sir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Then there is but one way.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Will it pleaſe you open?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: His fit grows ſtronger ſtill.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let's ſave our ſelves Sir,
He's paſt all worldly cure.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Friends do your office.
And what he wants, if Money, Love, or Labor,
Or any way may win it, let him have it.
Farewell, and pray my honeſt Friends— Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why Raſcals,
Friends, Gentlemen, thou beaſtly Wife, Jaques;
None hear me? Who at the door there?

sp.speaker: 1 Watch.
sp.l: Think I pray Sir,
Whether you are going, and prepare your ſelf.

sp.speaker: 2 Watch.
sp.l: Theſe idle thoughts diſturb you, the good Gentlewoman
Your Wife has taken care you ſhall want nothing.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Shall I come out in quiet? anſwer me,
Or ſhall I charge a Fowling-Piece, and make
Mine own way; two of ye I cannot miſs,
If I miſs three; ye come here to aſſault me.
I am as excellent well, I thank Heaven for't,
And have as good a ſtomach at this inſtant—

sp.speaker: 2 Watch.
sp.l: That's an ill ſign.

sp.speaker: 1 Watch.
sp.l: He draws on; he's a dead Man.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And ſleep as ſoundly; Will ye look upon me?

sp.speaker: 1 Watch.
sp.l: Do you want Pen and Ink? while you have ſenſe ſir,
Settle your ſtate.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Sirs, I am well, as you are;
Or any Raſcal living.

sp.speaker: 2 Watch.
sp.l: Would you were Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Look to your ſelves, and if you love your lives,
Open the door, and fly me, for I ſhoot elſe;
—I'll ſhoot, and preſently, chain-bullets;
And under four I will not kill.

sp.speaker: 1 Watch.
sp.l: Let's quit him,
It may be it is a trick: he's dangerous.

sp.speaker: 2 Watch.
sp.l: The Devil take the hinmoſt, I cry.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Have among ye;
The door ſhall open too, I'll have a fair ſhoot;
Are ye all gone? tricks in my old dayes, crackers
Put now upon me? and, by Lady Green-ſleeves?
Am I grown ſo tame after all my triumphs?
But that I ſhould be thought mad, if I rail'd,
As much as they deſerve, againſt theſe Women,
I would now rip up, from the primitive Cuckold,
All their arch-villanies, and all their doubles,
Which are more than a hunted Hare ere thought on:
When a Man has the faireſt, and the ſweeteſt
Of all their Sex, and as he thinks the nobleſt,
What has he then? and I'll ſpeak modeſtly,
He has a Quartern-ague, that ſhall ſhake
All his eſtate to nothing; never cur'd,
Nor never dying; He'as a ſhip to venture
His fame, and credit in, which if he Man not
With more continual labour than a Gally
To make her tith, either ſhe grows a Tumbrel,
Not worth the Cloth ſhe wears; or ſprings more leakes
Than all the fame of his poſterity
Can ever ſtop again: I could raile twenty dayes;
Out on 'em, Hedge-hogs,
He that ſhall touch 'em, has a thouſand thorns
Runs through his fingers: If I were unmarried,
I would do any thing below repentance,
Any baſe dunghill ſlavery; be a Hang-man,
Ere I would be a Husband: O the thouſand,
Thouſand, ten thouſand wayes they have to kill us!
Some fall with two much ſtringing of the Fiddles,
And thoſe are fools; ſome, that they are not ſuffer'd,
And thoſe are Maudlin-lovers: ſome, like Scorpions,
They poyſon with their tails, and thoſe are Martyrs;
Some dye with doing good, thoſe Benefactors,
And leave 'em land to leap away: ſome few,
For thoſe are rareſt, they are ſaid to kill
With kindneſs, and fair uſage; but what they are
My Catalogue diſcovers not: only 'tis thought
They are buried in old Walls, with their heels upward.
I could raile twenty dayes together now.
I'll ſeek 'em out, and if I have not reaſon,
And very ſenſible, why this was done,
I'll go a birding yet, and ſome ſhall ſmart for't. Exit

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: That I do love her, is without all queſtion,
And moſt extremely, dearly, moſt exactly;
And that I would ev'n now, this preſent Monday,
Before all others, Maids, Wives, Women, Widows,
Of what degree, or calling, Marry her,
As certain too; but to be made a Whim-wham,
A Jib-crack, and a Gentleman o'th firſt houſe
For all my kindneſs to her.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: How you take it?
Thou get a Wench, thou get a dozen night-caps?
Wouldſt have her come, and lick thee like a Calfe,
And blow thy noſe, and buſs thee?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Not ſo neither.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: What wouldſt thou have her do?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Do as ſhe would do;
Put on a clean Smock, and to Church, and Marry,
And then to Bed a Gods name, this is fair play,
And keeps the Kings peace; let her leave her bobs,
I have had too many of them, and her quillets,
She is as nimble that way as an Eeel;
But in the way ſhe ought to me eſpecially,
A ſow of Lead is ſwifter.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Quoat your griefs down.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Give fair quarter, I am old and craſie,
And ſubject to much fumbling, I confeſs it;
Yet ſomething I would have that's warme, to hatch me:
But underſtand me I would have it ſo,
••• y not more repentance in the bargain
Than the ware's worth I have; if you allow me
Worthy your Son-in-Law, and your allowance,
Do it a way of credit; let me ſhow ſo,
And not be troubled in my viſitations,
With blows, and bitterneſs, and down-right railings,
As if we were to couple like two Cats,
With clawing, and loud clamour:

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Thou fond Man.
• aſt thou forgot the Ballad, crabbed age,
Can May and January match together,
And nev'r a ſtorm between 'em? ſay ſhe abuſe thee,
〈◊〉 caſe ſhe doe.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Nay, believe ſhe do's.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I do believe ſhe do's.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: And div'liſhly:
Art thou a whit the worſe?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: That's not the matter,
I know, being old, tis fit I am abus'd;
I know 'tis hanſome, and I know moreover
I am to love her for't.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Now you come to me.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Nay more than this; I find too, and find certain,
What Gold I have, Pearle, Bracelets, Rings, or Owches,
Or what ſhe can deſire, Gowns, Petticotes,
Waſtcotes, Enbroydered-ſtockings, Scarffs, Cals, Feathers,
〈◊〉 , five pound Garters, Muffs, Masks, Ruffs, and Ribands,
I am to give her for't.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: 'Tis right, you are ſo.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: But when I have done all this, and think it duty,
• 't requiſit an other bore my noſtrils?
• iddle me that.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: Go get you gone, and dreame
• t's thine within theſe two dayes, for ſhe is ſo;
The Boy's beſide the ſaddle: get warm broths,
And feed a pace; think not of worldly buſineſs,
〈◊〉 cools the blood; leave off your tricks, they are hateful,
And meere fore-runners of the ancient meaſures;
Contrive your beard o'th top cut like Verdugoes:
It ſhows you would be wiſe, and burn your night-cap,
It looks like half a winding-ſheet, and urges
From a young Wench nothing but cold repentance:
You may eate Onyons, ſo you'l not be laviſh.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I am glad of that.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: They purge the blood, and quicken,
But after 'em, conceive me, ſweep your mouth,
And where there wants a tooth, ſtick in a clove.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Shall I hope once again, ſay't.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: You ſhall Sir:
And you ſhall have your hope.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Why there's a match then.

sp.speaker: Byan.
sp.l: You ſhall not find me wanting, get you gone.
Here's the old Man, he'l think you are plotting elſe
Something againſt his new Son. Exit Tranio.

sp.speaker: Moro.
sp.l: Fare ye well Sir. Exit Moroſo.

l.hi: And ev'ry Buck had his Doe,
And ev'ry Cuckold a Bell at his Toe:
Oh what ſport ſhould we have then, then Boyes then,
Oh what ſport ſhould we have then?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: This is the ſpirit, that inſpires 'em all.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Give you good ev'n.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: A word with you Sweet Lady.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I am very haſty, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: So you were ever.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Well, What's your will?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Was not your skilful hand
In this laſt ſtratagem? Were not your miſchiefs
Eeking the matter on?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: In's ſhutting up?
Is that it?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Doe.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: And truly.
Good old Man, I do grieve exceeding much,
I fear too much.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I am ſorry for your heavineſs.
Belike you can repent then?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: There you are wide too.
Not that the thing was done (conceive me rightly)
Do's any way moleſt me.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: What then Lady?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: But that I was not in't, there's my ſorrow, there
Now you underſtand me, for I'll tell you,
It was ſo ſound a piece, and ſo well carried,
And if you mark the way, ſo hanſomely,
Of ſuch a heighth, and excellence, and art
I have not known a bravery; for conceive me,
When the groſs fool her Husband would be ſick—

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Pray ſtay.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Nay, good, your patience: and no ſence for't,
Then ſtept your daughter in.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: By your appointment.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I would it had, on that condition
I had but one half ſmock, I like it ſo well;
And like an excellent cunning Woman, cur'd me
One madneſs with another, which was rare,
And to our weak beliefs, a wonder.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Hang ye,
For ſurely, if your husband look not to ye,
I know what will.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I humbly thank your worſhip.
And ſo I take my leave.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: You have a hand I hear too.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I have two Sir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: In my young daughters buſineſs.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: You will find there
A fitter hand than mine, to reach her frets,
And play down diddle to her.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I ſhall watch ye.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Do.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: And I ſhall have Juſtice.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: That's all one;
I ſhall be with you at a turne hence forward.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Get you a Poſſet too; and ſo good ev'n Sir.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And as I told your worſhip, all the hangings,
Braſs, Pewter, Plate, ev'n to the very looking-glaſſes.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And that that hung for our defence, the Armor,
And the March Beere was going too: Oh Jaques
What a ſad ſight was that?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Even the two Rundlets,
The two that was our hope, of Muskadel,
(Better nev'r tongue tript over) thoſe two Cannons,
To batter brawn withal at Chriſtmaſs, Sir,
Ev'n thoſe two lovely Twyns, the Enemy
Had almoſt cut off clean.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Goe trim the Houſe up.
And put the things in order as they were.
I ſhall find time for all this: could I find her
But conſtant any way, I had done my buſineſs;
Were ſhe a Whore directly, or a Scold,
An unthrift, or a Woman made to hate me,
I had my wiſh, and knew which way to rayne her:
But while ſhe ſhews all theſe, and all their loſſes,
A kind of linſey woolſey, mingled miſchief
Not to be gheſt at, and whether true, or borrowed,
Not certain neither, What a hap had I,
And what a tydie fortune, when my fate
Flung me upon this Bear-whelp? here ſhe comes,
Now, if ſhe have a colour, for the fault is
A cleanly one, upon my Conſcience
I ſhall forgive her yet, and find a ſomething
Certain, I Married for: her wit: I'll marke her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Not let his Wife come near him in his ſickneſs?
Not come to comfort him? ſhe that all Laws
Of heaven, and Nations have ordain'd his ſecond,
Is ſhe refus'd? and two old Paradoxes,
Pieces of five and fifty, without faith
Clapt in upon him? h'as a little pet,
That all young Wives muſt follow neceſſary,
Having their Maiden-heads—

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: This is an Axiome
I never heard before.

sp.speaker: Mar
sp.l: Or ſay Rebellion,
If we durſt be ſo foul, which two fair words
Alas win us from, in an hour, an inſtant,
We are ſo eaſie, make him ſo forgetful
Both of his reaſon, honeſty, and credit,
As to deny his Wife a viſitation?
His Wife, that (though ſhe was a little fooliſh,)
Lov'd him, Oh Heaven forgive her for't! nay doted,
Nay had run mad, had ſhe not married him.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Though I do know this falſer than the Devil,
I cannot chooſe but love it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What do I know
But thoſe that came to keep him, might have kill'd him,
In what a caſe had I been then? I dare not
Believe him ſuch a baſe, deboſh'd companion,
That one refuſal of a tender Maid.
Would make him faign this Sickneſs out of need,
And take a Keeper to him of Fourſcore
To play at Billiards; one that mew'd content
