And all her teeth together; not come near him?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: This Woman would have made a moſt rare Jeſuite
She can prevaricate on any thing:
There was not to be thought a way to ſave her
In all imagination, beſide this.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: His unkind dealing, which was worſt of all,
In ſending, who knowes whether, all the plate,
And all the houſhold-ſtuffe, had I not croſt it,
By a great providence, and my friends aſſiſtance
Which he will thank me one day for: alas,
I could have watch'd as well as they, have ſerv'd him
In any uſe, better, and willinger.
The Law commands me to do it, love commands me,
And my own duty charges me.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Heav'n bleſs me.
And now I have ſaid my Prayers, I'll go to her:
Are you a Wife for any Man?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For you Sir.
If I were worſe, I were better; That you are well,
At leaſt, that you appear ſo, I thank Heaven,
Long may it hold, and that you are here, I am glad too;
But that you have abus'd me wretchedly,
And ſuch a way that ſhames the name of Husband,
Such a malicious mangy way, ſo mingled,
(Never look ſtrangely on me, I dare tell you)
With breach of honeſty, care, kindneſs, manners.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Holla, you kick too faſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Was I a ſtranger?
Or had I vow'd perdition to your perſon?
Am I not Married to you, tell me that?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I would I could not tell you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Is my preſence,
The ſtock I come of, which is worſhipful,
If I ſhould ſay Right worſhipful, I ly'd not,
My Grandſire was a Knight.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: O'the Shire?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A Soldier,
Which none of all thy Family e're heard of,
But one conductor of thy name, a Graſier
That ran away with pay: or am I grown
Becauſe I have been a little peeviſh to you,
Onely to try your temper) ſuch a dogge-leech
I could not be admitted to your preſence?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: If I endure this, hang me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And two deaths heads,
Two Harry Groats, that had their faces worn,
Almoſt their names away too.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now hear me.
For I will ſtay no longer.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: This you ſhall:
How ever you ſhall think to flatter me,
For this offence, which no ſubmiſſion
Can ever mediate for, you'l find it ſo,
What ever you ſhall do by interceſſion,
What you can offer, what your Land can purchaſe,
What all your friends, or families can win,
Shall be but this, not to forſwear your knowledge,
But ever to forbear it: now your will Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Thou art the ſubtleſt Woman I think living,
I am ſure the lewdeſt; now be ſtill, and mark me;
Were I but any way addided to the Devil,
I ſhould now think I had met a play-fellow
To profit by, and that way the moſt learned
That ever taught to murmur. Tell me thou,
Thou moſt poor, paltry ſpiteful Whore: Do you cry?
I'll make you roare, before I leave.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Was it not ſin enough, thou Fruiterer,
Full of the fall thou eat'ſt: thou Devils Broker,
Thou Seminary of all ſedition,
Thou Sword of veng'ance, with a thred hung o're us,
Was it not ſin enough, and wickedneſs
In full abundance? Was it not vexation
At all points, cap a pe? nay, I ſhall pinch you,
Thus like a rotten Raſcal to abuſe
The name of Heaven, the tye of Marriage,
The honour of thy Friends; the expectation
Of all that thought thee virtuous, with Rebellion,
Childiſh and baſe Rebellion, but continuing
After forgiveneſs too, and worſe, your miſchief,
And againſt him; ſetting the hope of Heaven by,
And the dear reſervation of his honor
Nothing above ground could have won to hate thee:
Well, goe thy wayes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You ſhall hear me out firſt:
What puniſhment may'ſt thou deſerve, thou thing,
Thou Idle thing of nothing, thou pull'd Primroſe,
That two hours after, art a Weed, and wither'd,
For this laſt flouriſh on me? am I one
Selected out of all the Husbands living,
To be ſo ridden by a Tit of ten pence,
Am I ſo blind and Bed-rid? I was mad,
And had the Plague, and no Man muſt come near me,
I muſt be ſhut up, and my ſubſtance bezel'd,
And an old Woman watch me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Well Sir, well,
You may well glory in't.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And when it comes to opening, 'tis my plot,
I muſt undoe my ſelf forſooth: do'ſt hear me?
If I ſhould beat thee now, as much may be,
Do'ſt thou not well deſerve it, o' thy Conſcience,
Do'ſt thou not cry, come beat me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I defie you.
And my laſt loving tears farewell: the firſt ſtroke,
The very firſt you give me, if you dare ſtrike,
Try me, and you ſhall find it ſo, for ever,
Never to be recall'd: I know you love me,
Mad till you have enjoy'd me; I do turne
Utterly from you, and what Man I meet firſt
That has but ſpirit to deſerve a favour,
Let him bear any ſhape, the worſe the better.
• all kill you, and enjoy me; what I have ſaid
About your fooliſh ſickneſs, e're you have me
As you would have me, you ſhall ſwear, is certain,
And challenge any Man, that dares deny it;
And in all companies approve my actions,
And ſo farewell for this time. Ex. Mar.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Grief goe with thee,
If there be any witchcrafts, herbes, or potions,
Saying my Prayers backward, Fiends, or Fayries
That can again unlove me, I am made. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Miſtreſs, you muſt do it.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Are the Writings ready I told you of?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes they are ready, but to what uſe I know not.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Y'are an Aſs, you muſt have all things conſtru'd,

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes, and pierc'd too,
Or I find little pleaſure.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Now you are knaviſh,
Goe too, fetch Rowland hither preſently,
Your Twenty pounds lies bleeding elſe: ſhe is married
Within theſe twelve hours, if we croſs it not,
And ſee the Papers of one ſize.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I have ye.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: And for diſpoſing of 'em.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: If I fail you
Now I have found the way, uſe Marſhal Law
And cut my head off with a hand Saw:

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Well Sir.
Petronius and Moroſo I'll ſee ſent for,
About your buſineſs; goe.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I am gone. Ex. Tra.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Ho Livia.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: A friend of yours, Lord how you look now,
As if you had loſt a Carrack.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: O Byancha.
I am the moſt undone, unhappy Woman.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Be quiet Wench, thou ſhalt be done, and done,
And done, and double done, or all ſhall ſplit for't,
No more of theſe minc'd paſſions, they are mangy,
And eaſe thee of nothing, but a little Wind,
An Apple will do more: thou fear'ſt Moroſo.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Even as I fear the Gallowes.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Keep thee there ſtill.
And you love Rowland? ſay.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: If I ſay not,
I am ſure I lye.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: What wouldſt thou give that Woman,
In ſpight of all his anger, and thy fear,
And all thy Fathers policy, that could
Clap ye within theſe two nights quietly
Into a Bed together?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Why fairly,
At half ſword man and wiſe: now the red blood comes,
I marry now the matters chang'd.

sp.speaker: Liv.

l.hi: Byancha,

sp.l: Methinks you ſhould not mock me.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Mock a pudding.
I ſpeak good honeſt Engliſh, and good meaning.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I ſhould not be ungrateful to that Woman.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: I know thou would'ſt not, follow but my Councel,
And if thou haſt him not, deſpite of fortune
Let me nev'r know a good night more; you muſt
Be very ſick o'th inſtant.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Well, what follows?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: And in that ſickneſs ſend for all your friends,
Your Father, and your feaver old Moroſo,
And Rowland ſhall be there too.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: What of theſe?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Do you not twitter yet? of this ſhall follow
That which ſhall make thy heart leap, and thy lips
Venture as many kiſſes, as the Merchants
Doe Dollars to the Eaſt-Indies: you ſhall know all,
But firſt walke in, and practiſe, pray be ſick.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: I do believe you: and I am ſick.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Doe,
To bed then, come, I'll ſend away your Servants
Poſt for your Fool, and Father; and good fortune,
As we meane honeſty, now ſtrike an up-ſhot. Exunt

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Nay, on my conſcience, I have loſt my Money,
But that's all one: I'll never more perſwade you,
I ſee you are reſolute, and I commend you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: But did ſhe ſend for me?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You dare believe me.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I cannot tell, you have your wayes for profit
Allow'd you Tranio, as well as I
Have to avoid 'em.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No, on my word, Sir,
I deale directly with you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: How now fellow,
Whither Poſt you ſo faſt?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: O ſir my Maſter,
Pray did you ſee my Maſter?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Why your Maſter?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sir his Jewel.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: With the gilded Button?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: My pretty Miſtreſs Livia.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What of her?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Is falen ſick o'th ſuddain.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: How o'th ſullens?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: O'th ſuddain Sir, I ſay, very ſick:

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: It ſeems ſhe hath got the toothach with raw Apples.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: It ſeemes you have got the headach, fare you well Sir.
You did not ſee my Maſter?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Who told you ſo.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: No, no, he did not ſee him.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewell Blew-bottle. Ex. Servant.
What ſhould her ſickneſs be?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: For you it may be.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes, when my braines are out, I may believe it,
Never before I am ſure: Yet I may ſee her;
'Twill be a point of honeſty:

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: It will ſo.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: It may be not too: you would fain be fing'ring
This old ſin-offring of two hundred, Tranio,
How daintily, and cunningly you drive me
Up like a Deer to'th toyle, yet I may leap it,
And what's the Woodman then?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A loſer by you.
Speak, Will you go or not? to me 'tis equal.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Come, What goes leſs?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Nay, not a penny Rowland.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Shall I have liberty of conſcience,
Which, by interpretation, is ten kiſſes?
Hang me if I affect her: yet it may be,
This whorſon manners will require a ſtrugling,
Of two and twenty, or by'r-Lady thirty.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: By'r-Lady I'll require my wager then,
For if you kiſs ſo often, and no kindneſs,
I have loſt my ſpeculation, I'll allow you—

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Speak like a Gamſter now.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: It may be two.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Under a dozen Tranio, there's no ſetting,
You ſhall have forty ſhillings, winck at ſmall faults.
Say I take twenty, come, by all that's honeſt
I do it but to vex her.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I'll no by-blowes.
If you can love her, doe, if you can, hate her,
Or any elſe that loves you —

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Prethee Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Why farewell twenty pound, 'twill not undoe me;
You have my reſolution.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And your Money,
Which ſince you are ſo ſtubborn, if I forfeit,
Make me a Jack o' Lent, and break my ſhins
For untag'd Points and Compters: I'll goe with you,
But if thou gett'ſt a penny by the bargain;
A parting kiſs is lawful?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I allow it.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Knock out my brains with Apples; yet a bargain:

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I tell you, I'll no bargains; win, and wear it.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thou art the ſtrangeſt fellow.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That's all one.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Along then, twenty pound more if thou dar'ſt,
I give her not a good word.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Not a Penny. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Prethee, entreat her come, I will not trouble her
Above a word or two; ere I endure Exit Pedro.
This life, and with a Woman, and a vow'd one
To all the miſchiefs ſhe can lay upon me,
I'll go to Plough, and eate Leeke Porridge;
Begging's a pleaſure to't, not to be number'd:
No there be other Countries Jaques for me, and other people, yea, and other women.
If I have need, here's Money, there's your ware,
Which is faire dealing, and the Sun, they ſay.
Shines as warme there, as here, and till I have loſt
Either my ſelf, or her, I care not whether
Nor which firſt.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Will your worſhip hear me?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And utterly outworne the memory
Of ſuch a curſe as this, none of my Nation
Shall ever know me more.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Out alas Sir.
What a ſtrange way doe you run?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Any way,
So I out-run this Raſcal.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Me thinks now,
If your good worſhip could but have the patience.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: The patience, why the patience?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Why I'll tell you,
Could you but have the patience.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Well the patience.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: To laugh at all ſhe do's, or when ſhe railes,
To have a Drum beaten o'th top o'th houſe,
To give the neighbors warning of her Larme,
As I do when my Wife rebels.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Thy Wife?
Thy Wife's a Pigeon to her, a meere ſlumber,
The dead of night's not ſtiller.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Nor an Iron Mill.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: But thy Wife is certain.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: That's falſe Doctrine,
You never read of a certain Woman.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt her way.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I ſhould doe, I am ſure.
I have ridden it night, and day, this twenty year.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: But mine is ſuch a drench of Balderdaſh,
Such a ſtrange carded cunningneſs, the Rayne-bow
When ſhe hangs bent in Heaven, ſheds not her colours
Quicker, and more, than this deceitful Woman.
Weaves in her dye's of wickedneſs: what ſayes ſhe?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Nay not a word ſir, but ſhe pointed to me,
As though ſhe meant to follow; pray ſir bear it
Ev'n as you may, I need not teach your worſhip,
The beſt men have their croſſes, we are all mortal.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What ailes the fellow?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And no doubt ſhe may Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What may ſhe, or what do's ſhe, or what is ſhe
Speak and be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: She's mad Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Heaven continue it.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Amen if't be his pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: How mad is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: As mad as heart can wiſh Sir: ſhe has dreſt her ſel •
(Saving your worſhips reverence) juſt i'th 'cut
Of one of thoſe that multiply i'th Suburbs
For ſingle Money, and as durtily:
If any ſpeak to her, firſt ſhe whiſtles,
And then begins her compaſs with her fingers,
And points to what ſhe would have,

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What new way's this?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: There came in Maſter Sophocles,

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: And what
Did Maſter Sophocles when he came in?
Get my Truncks ready, ſirha, I'll be gone ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: He's here to tell you
She's horne mad Jaques.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Call ye this a Woman?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Yes ſir, ſhe is a Woman,

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Sir, I doubt it.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I had thought you had made experience,

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes, I did ſo.
And almoſt with my life.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You rid too faſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Pray be not miſtaken: by this hand
Your wife's as chaſte, and honeſt as a Virgin,
For any thing I know: 'tis true ſhe gave me
A Ring.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: For rutting.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: You are much deceiv'd ſtill,
Believe me, I never kiſt her ſince, and now
Co • ing in viſitation, like a friend,
I think ſhe is mad, Sir, ſuddainly ſhe ſtarted,
And ſnatch'd the Ring away, and drew her knife out,
To what intent I know not.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Is this certain?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: As I am here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I believe you honeſt.
And pray continue ſo.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: She comes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now Damſel,
What will your beauty do if I forſake you?
Do you deal by ſigns and tokens? as I gheſs then,
You'll walk abroad, this Summer, and catch Captains,
Or hire a piece of holy ground i'th' Suburbs,
And keep a Neſt of Nuns?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Oh do not ſtir her!
You ſee in what a caſe ſhe is?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: She is dogged,
And in a beaſtly caſe I am ſure: I'll make her,
If ſhe have any tongue, yet tattle. Sophocles,
Prethee obſerve this woman ſeriouſly,
And eye her well, and when thou haſt done, but tell me
(For thou haſt underſtanding) in what caſe
My ſenſe was, when I choſe this thing,

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I'll tell you
I have ſeen a ſweeter—

sp.speaker: Petru,
sp.l: An hundred times cry Oiſters.
There's a poor Begger-wench about Black-Fryers
Runs on her breech, may be an Empreſs to her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Nay, now you are too bitter.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Nev'r a whit Sir:
I'll tell thee woman; for now I have day to ſee thee,
And all my wits about me, and I ſpeak
Not out of paſſion neither (leave your mumping)
I know you're well enough: Now would I give
A million but to vex her: when I choſe thee
To make a Bedfellow, I took more trouble,
Than twenty Terms can come to, ſuch a cauſe,
Of ſuch a title, and ſo everlaſting
That Adams Genealogie may be ended
E'r any Law find thee: I took a Leproſie,
Nay worſe, the plague, nay worſe yet, a poſſeſſion
And had the devil with thee, if not more:
And yet worſe, was a beaſt, and like a beaſt
Had my reward, a Jade to fling my fortunes;
For who that had but reaſon to diſtinguiſh
The light from darkneſs, wine from water, hunger
From full ſatiety, and Fox from Fern-buſh
That would have married thee?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: She is not ſo ill.

sp.speaker: Petru,
sp.l: She's worſe than I dare think of: ſhe's ſo lewd;
No Court is ſtrong enough to bear her cauſe,
She hath neither manners, honeſty, behaviour,
Wife-hood, nor woman-hood, nor any mortal
Can force me think ſhe had a mother: no
I do believe her ſtedfaſtly, and know her
To be a Woman-wolfe by tranſmigration,
Her firſt forme was a Ferrets under-ground,
She kils the memories of men: not yet?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Do you think ſhe's ſenſible of this?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I care not,
• e what ſhe will: the pleaſure I take in her,
Thus I blow off; the care I took to love her,
Like this point, I untie, and thus I looſe it;
The husband I am to her, thus I ſever;
My vanity farewel: yet, for you have been
So near me, as to bear the name of wife,
My unquench'd charity ſhall tell you thus much,
(Though you deſerve it well) you ſhall not beg,
What I ordain'd your Joynture, honeſtly
You ſhall have ſetled on you: and half my houſe,
The other half ſhall be imploy'd in prayers,
(That meritorious charge I'll be at alſo
Yet to confirm you Chriſtian) your apparel,
And what belongs to build up ſuch a folly,
Keep I beſeech you, it infects our uſes,
And now I am for travel.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now I love you,
And now I ſee you are a man, I'll talke to you,
And I forget your bitterneſs.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: How now man?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Oh Pliny, if thou wilt be ever famous
Make but this woman all thy wonders.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sure Sir
You have hit upon a happy courſe, a bleſſed,
And what will make you virtuous?

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: She'll ſhip me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: A way of underſtanding I long wiſh'd for,
And now 'tis come, take heed you fly not back Sir,
Methinks you look a new man to me now,
A man of excellence, and now I ſee
Some great deſign ſet in you: you may think now
(And ſo may moſt that know me) 'twere my part
Weakly to weep your loſs, and to reſiſt you,
Nay, hang about your neck, and like a dotard
Urge my ſtrong tie upon you: but I love you,
And all the world ſhall know it, beyond woman;
And more prefer the honor of your Countrey,
Which chiefly you are born for, and may perfect,
The uſes you may make of other Nations,
The ripening of your knowledge, converſation,
The full ability, and ſtrength of judgement.
Than any private love, or wanton kiſſes.
Go worthy man, and bring home underſtanding.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: This were an excellent woman to breed School-men.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For if the Merchant through unknown Seas plough
To get his wealth, then dear Sir, what muſt you
To gather wiſdom? go and go alone,
Only your noble mind for your companion,
And if a woman may win credit with you,
Go far, too far you cannot: ſtill the farther
The more experience finds you: and go ſparing,
One meal a week will ſerve you, and one ſute,
Through all your travels: for you'll find it certain,
The poorer and the baſer you appear,
The more you look through ſtill.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Doſt hear her?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What would this woman do if ſhe were ſuffer'd.
Upon a new Religion?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Make us Pagans,
I wonder that ſhe writes not.

sp.speaker: Mar,
sp.l: Then when time,
And fulneſs of occaſion have new made you,
And ſquar'd you from a Sot into a Signior,
Or nearer, from a Jade into a Courſer;
Come home an aged man, as did Ʋlyſſes,
And I your glad Penelope.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: That muſt have
As many Lovers as I Languages.
And what ſhe does with one i'th' day, i'th' night
Undoe it with another.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Much that way, Sir;
For in your abſence it muſt be my honor,
That, that muſt make me ſpoken of hereafter,
To have temptations, and not little ones
Daily and hourly offered me, and ſtrongly,
Almoſt believed againſt me, to ſet off
The faith, and loyalty of her that loves you.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: What ſhould I do?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Why by my—I would travel,
Did not you mean ſo?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Alas no, nothing leſs man:
I did it but to try, Sir, ſhe's the Devil,
And now I find it, for ſhe drives me; I muſt go:
Are my trunks down there, and my horſes ready?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir, for your houſe, and if you pleaſe to truſt me
With that you leave behind.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Bring down the money.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: As I am able, and to my poor fortunes,
I'll govern as a widow: I ſhall long
To hear of your well-doing, and your profit:
And when I hear not from you once a quarter,
I'll wiſh you in the Indies, or Catayna,
Thoſe are the climes muſt make you.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: How's the wind?
She'll wiſh me out o' th' world anon.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: For France.
'Tis very fair; get you aboard to night, Sir,
And looſe no time, you know the tide ſtaies no man,
I have cold meats ready for you.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Fare thee well,
Thou haſt fool'd me out o'th' Kingdom with a vengeance,
And thou canſt fool me in again,

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Not I Sir,
I love you better, take your time, and pleaſure.
I'll ſee you hors'd.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I think thou wouldſt ſee me hanged too,
Were I but half as willing.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Any thing
That you think well of, I dare look upon.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You'll bear me to the Lands end, Sophocles,
And other of my friends I hope.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Nev'r doubt, Sir,
You cannot want companions for your good:
I am ſure you'll kiſs me e'r I go; I have buſineſs,
And ſtay long here I muſt not.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Get thee going.
For i • thou tarrieſt but another Dialogue
I'll kick thee to thy Chamber.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Fare you well, Sir,
And bear your ſelf, I do beſeech you, once more,
Since you have undertaken doing wiſely,
Manly, and worthily, 'tis for my credit,
And for thoſe flying fames here of your follies,
Your gambols, and ill breeding of your youth,
For which I underſtand you take this travel,
Nothing ſhould make me leave you elſe, I'll deal,
So like a wiſe that loves your reputation,
And the moſt large addition of your credit,
That thoſe ſhall die: if you want Limon-waters,
Or any thing to take the edge o' th' Sea off,
Pray ſpeak, and be provided.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Now the Devil,
That was your firſt good Maſter, ſhowre his bleſſing
Upon ye all: Into whoſe cuſtody —

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do commit your Reformation,

And ſo I leave you to your Stilo novo.
Exit Maria.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: I will go: yet I will not: once more Sophocles
I'll put her to the teſt.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: You had better go.

sp.speaker: Petru
sp.l: I will go then: let's ſeek my Father out,
And all my friends, to ſee me fair aboard:
Then women if there be a ſtorm at Sea,
Worſe than your tongues can make, and waves more broken,
Than your diſſembling faiths are, let me feel
Nothing but tempeſts, till they crack my Keel. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Petronius, and Byancha, with four pap • rs.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: NOw whether I deſerve that blame you gave me,
Let all the world diſcern, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: If this motion,
(I mean this fair repentance of my Daughter)
Spring from your good perſwaſion, as it ſeems ſo,
I muſt confeſs I have ſpoke too boldly of you,
And I repent,

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: The firſt touch was her own,
Taken no doubt from diſobeying you,
The ſecond I put to her, when I told her
How good, and gentle yet, with free contrition
Again you might be purchas'd: loving woman,
She heard me, and I thank her, thought me worthy
Obſerving in this point: yet all my counſel,
And comfort in this caſe, could not ſo heal her
But that grief got his ſhare too, and ſhe ſick'ned.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I am ſorry ſhe's ſo ill, yet glad her ſickneſs
Has got ſo good a ground.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Here comes Moroſo.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Oh, you are very welcome,
Now you ſhall know your happineſs.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I am glad on't.
What makes this Lady here?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: A diſh for you, Sir
You'll thank me for hereafter.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: True Moroſo,
Go get you in, and ſee your Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: She is ſick, Sir,
But you may kiſs her whole.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: How.

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: Comfort her.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Why am I ſent for, Sir?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Will you in, and ſee?

sp.speaker: By.
sp.l: May be ſhe needs confeſſion.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: By St. Mary,
She ſhall have abſolution then, and pennance,
But not above her carriage.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Get you in fool. Exit Mo •

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Here comes the other too.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Now Tranio.
Good ev'n to you too, and you are welcome.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I have a certain Daughter.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Would you had, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: No doubt you know her well.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Nor never ſhall, Sir.
She is a woman, and the waies unto her
Are like the finding of a certain path
After a deep fall'n Snow.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Well, that's by th' by ſtill.
This Daughter that I tell you of, is fall'n
A little crop ſick, with the dangerous ſurfeit
She took of your affection.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Mine Sir?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Yes Sir.
Or rather, as it ſeems, repenting.
And there ſhe lies within, debating on't,

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: I think 'twere well you would ſee her.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: If you pleaſe, Sir;
I am not ſqueamiſh of my viſitation.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: But, this I'll tell you, ſhe is alter'd much,
You'll find her now another Livia.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I have enough o' th' old, Sir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: No more fool,
To look gay babies in your eyes young Rowland,
And hang about your pretty neck.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am glad on't,
And thank my Fates I have ſcap'd ſuch execution.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: And buſs you till you bluſh again.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: That's hard, Sir;
She muſt kiſs ſhamefully e're I bluſh at it,
I never was ſo boyiſh; well, what follows?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: She's mine now, as I pleaſe to ſettle her
At my command, and where I pleaſe to plant her:
Only ſhe would take a kind of farewel of you,
And give you back a wandring vow or two,
You left in pawn; and two or three ſlight oaths
She lent you too, ſhe looks for.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: She ſhall have 'em
With all my heart, Sir;, and if you like it better,
A free releaſe in writing.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: That's the matter,
And you from her, ſhall have another Rowland,
And then turn tail to tail, and peace be with you.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: So be it: Your twenty pound ſweats Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: 'Twill not undoe me Rowland, do your worſt.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Come, ſhall we ſee her, Sir?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: What e'er ſhe ſaies
You muſt bear manly Rowland, for her ſickneſs
Has made her ſomewhat pettiſh

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Let her talk
Till her tongue ake, I care not: by this hand
Thou haſt a handſome face wench, and a body
Daintily mounted; now do I feel an hundred
Running directly from me, as I piſt it.

div.stage: Enter Livia diſcovered abed, and Moroſo by her.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Pray draw 'em ſoftly, the leaſt hurry, Sir,
Puts her to much impatience.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: How is't daughter?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Oh very ſick, very ſick, yet ſomewhat
Better I hope; a little lightſomer,
Becauſe this good man has forgiven me;
Pray ſet me higher; oh my head:

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Well done wench.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Father, and all good people that ſhall hear me,
I have abus'd this man perniciouſly; was never old man humbled ſo;
I have ſcorn'd him, and call'd him naſty names,
I have ſpit at him,
Fl • ng Candles ends in's beard, and call'd him harrow,
That muſt be drawn to all he does; contemn'd him,
For methought then, he was a beaſtly fellow.
(Oh my ſide) a very beaſtly fellow:
And gave it out, his Caſſock was a Barge-cloth,
Pawn'd to his predeceſſor by a Sculler,
The man yet living: I gave him purging comfits
At a great Chriſtning once,
That ſpoil'd his Chamblet breeches; and one night
I ſtrew'd the ſtairs with peaſe, as he paſt down;
And the good Gentleman (woe worth me for't)
Ev'n with this reverend head, this head of wiſdom,
Told two and twenty ſtairs, good and true;
• ſiſt not a ſtep, and as we ſay, verbatim
Fell to the bottom, broke his caſting Bottle,
Loſt a fair Toad-ſtone, of ſome eighteen ſhillings,
J • mbled his Joynts together, had two ſtools,
And was tranſlated. All this villany
Did I: I Livia, I alone, untaught.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: And I unask'd, forgive it.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Where's Byancha?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Here Coſin.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Give me drink,

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Who's that?

l.hi: Rowland.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Oh my diſſembler, you and I muſt part.
Come nearer, Sir.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I am ſorry for your ſickneſs.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Be ſorry for your ſelf, Sir, you have wrong'd me,
But I forgive you; are the Papers ready?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: I have 'em here: wilt pleaſe you view 'em?

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Shew 'em the young man too, I know he's willing
To ſhift his ſails too: 'tis for his more advancement;
Alas, we might have begger'd one another;
We are young both, and a world of children
Might have been left behind to curſe our follies:
We had been undone Byancha, had we married,
Undone for ever, I confeſs I lov'd him,
I care not who ſhall know it, moſt intirely;
And once, upon my conſcience, he lov'd me;
But farewel that, we muſt be wiſer, coſin,
Love muſt not leave us to the world: have you done?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes, and am ready to ſubſcribe.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Pray ſtay then:
Give me the papers, and let me peruſe 'em,
And ſo much time, as may afford a tear
At our laſt parting.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Pray retire, and leave her,
I'll call ye preſently.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen, the ſhowre muſt fall.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Would I had never ſeen her. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Thou haſt done bravely wench.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Pray Heaven it prove ſo.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: There are the other papers: when they come
Begin you firſt, and let the reſt ſubſcribe
Hard by your ſide; give 'em as little light
As Drapers do their Wares.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Didſt mark Moroſo,
In what an agony he was, and how he cry'd moſt
When I abus'd him moſt?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: That was but reaſon.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Oh what a ſtinking thief is this?
Though I was but to counterfeit, he made me
Directly ſick indeed. Thames-ſtreet to him
Is a meer Pomander.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Let him be hang'd.

l.hi: Amen.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: And lie you ſtill;
And once more to your buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Call 'em in.
Now if there be a power that pities Lovers,
Help now, and hear my prayers.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Is ſhe ready?

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: She has done her lamentations: pray go to her.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Rowland, come near me, and before you ſeal,
Give me your hand: take it again; now kiſs me.
This is the laſt acquaintance we muſt have;
I wiſh you ever happy: there's the paper.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Pray ſtay a little

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Let me never live more
But I do begin to pity this young fellow;
How heartily he weeps!

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: There's Pen and Ink, Sir.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Ev'n here I pray you. 'Tis a little Emblem
How near you have been to me.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Your hands too,
As witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: By any means
To th' Book ſon.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: You muſt deliver it.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: There Livia, and a better love light on thee,
I can no more.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: To this you muſt be witneſs too.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: We will.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Do you deliver it now.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Pray ſet me up;
There Rowland, all thy old love back: and may
A new to come, exceed mine, and be happy.
I muſt no more.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Farewel:

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: A long farewel. Exit Row.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Leave her by any means, till this wild paſſion
Be off her head: draw all the Curtains cloſe,
A day hence you may ſee her, 'twill be better,
She is now for little company.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Pray tend her.
I muſt to horſe ſtraight, you muſt needs along too,
To ſee my ſon aboard: were but his wife
As fit for pity, as this wench, I were happy.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Time muſt do that too: fare ye well: to morrow
You ſhall receive a wife to quit your ſorrow. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Jaques, Pedro, and Porters, with Cheſt and Hampers.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Bring 'em away Sirs.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Muſt the great Trunks go too?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes, and the Hampers; nay, be ſpeedy Maſters;
He'll be at Sea before us elſe.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Oh Jaques,
What a moſt bleſſed turn haſt thou?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I hope ſo

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: To have the Sea between thee and this woman,
Nothing can drown her tongue but a ſtorm.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: By your leave,
We'll get us up to Paris with all ſpeed;
For on my ſoul, as far as Amiens
She'll carry blank, away to Lyon-key
And ſhip 'em preſently, we'll follow ye.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Now could I wiſh her in that Trunk:

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: God ſhield man,
I had rather have a Bear in't.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Yes, I'll tell ye:
For in the paſſage, if a Tempeſt take ye,
As many doe, and you lie beating for it,
Then, if it pleas'd the fates, I would have the Maſter,
Out of a powerful providence, to cry,
Lighten the ſhip of all hands, or we periſh;
Then this for one, as beſt ſpar'd, ſhould by all means,
Over-board preſently.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: O' that condition,
So we were certain to be rid of her,
I would wiſh her with us, but believe me Pedro,
She would ſpoil the fiſhing on this coaſt for ever.
For none would keep her company but Dog-fiſh,
As curriſh as her ſelf; or Porpiſces,
Made to all fatal uſes: The two Fiſh-ſtreets
Were ſhe but once arriv'd amongſt the Whitings,
Would ſing a woful miſereri Pedro,
And mourn in Poor John, till her memory
Were caſt o' ſhore agen, with a ſtrong Sea-breach:
She would make god Neptune, and his Fire-fork,
And all his demi-gods, and goddeſſes,
As weary of the Flemmiſh Channel, Pedro,
As ever boy was of the School, 'tis certain,
If ſhe but meet him fair, and were well angred,
She would break his god-head.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Oh her tongue, her tongue.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Rather her many tongues.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Or rather ſtrange tongues.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Her lying tongue.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Her liſping tongue.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Her long tongue.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Her lawleſs tongue.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Her loud tongue.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And her liquoriſh —

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Many other tongues, and many ſtranger tongues
Than ever Babel had to tell his ruines,
Were Women rais'd withal; but never a true one.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Home with your ſtuff agen, the journey's ended.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: What does your worſhip mean?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Your Maſter, Oh Petruchio, oh poor fellows.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Oh Jaques, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Oh your Maſter's dead,
His body coming back, his wife, his devil;
The grief of—her

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Has kill'd him?

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Kill'd him, kill'd him.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Is there no Law to hang her.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Get ye in,
And let her know her miſery, I dare not
For fear impatience ſeize me, ſee her more,
I muſt away agen: Bid her for wife-hood,
For honeſty, if ſhe have any in her,
Even to avoid the ſhame that follows her.
Cry if ſhe can, your weeping cannot mend it.
The body will be here within this hour, ſo tell her;
And all his friends to curſe her. Farewel fellows.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Oh Jaques, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Oh my worthy Maſter.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Oh my moſt beaſtly Miſtriſs, hang her.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Split her.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Drown her directly.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Starve her.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Stink upon her.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Stone her to death: may all ſhe eat be Eggs.
Till ſhe run kicking mad for men.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And he,
That man, that gives her remedy, pray Heav'n
He may ev'n ipſo facto, loſe his Fadding

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Let's go diſcharge our ſelves, and he that ſerves her,
Or ſpeaks a good word of her from this hour,
A Sedgly curſe light on him, which is, Pedro;
The Fiend ride through him booted, and ſpurr'd, with a Sythe at's back. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Rowland, and Tranio ſtealing behind him.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: What a dull aſs was I to let her go thus?
Upon my life ſhe loves me ſtill: well Paper,
Thou only monument of what I have had,
Thou all the love now left me, and now loſt,
Let me yet kiſs her hand, yet take my leave
Of what I muſt leave ever: Farewel Livia.
Oh bitter words, I'll read ye once again,
And then for ever ſtudy to forget ye.
How's this? let me look better on't: A Contract?
—A Contract, ſeal' d, and ratified,
Her Fathers hand ſet to it, and Moroſo's:
I do not dream ſure, let me read again,
The ſame ſtill, 'tis a Contract

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo Rowland;
And by the virtue of the ſame▪ you pay me
An hundred pound to morrow.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Art ſure Tranio,
We are both alive now?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Wonder not, ye have loſt.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: If this be true, I grant it.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt certain,
There's a Ring for you too, you know it.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: When ſhall I have my money?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Stay ye, ſtay ye,
When ſhall I marry her?
To night.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Take heed now
You do not trifle me; if you do,
You'll find more payment, than your money comes to:
Come ſwear; I know I am a man, and find
I may deceive my ſelf: ſwear faithfully,
Swear me directly, am I Rowland?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Am I awake?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Ye are.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Am I in health?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: As far as I conceive.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Was I with Livia?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: You were, and had this Contract.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: And ſhall I enjoy her?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Yes, if ye dare.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Swear to all theſe.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: As thou art honeſt, as thou haſt a conſcience,
As that may wring thee if thou lieſt; all theſe
To be no viſion, but a truth, and ſerious.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Then by my honeſty, and faith, and conſcience;
All this is certain.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Let's remove our places.
Swear it again.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: By—'tis true.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I have loſt then, and Heaven knows I am glad on't.
Let's goe, and tell me all, and tell me how,
For yet I am a Pagan in it.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I have a Prieſt too,
And all ſhall come as even as two Teſters. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Petronius, Sophocles, Moroſo, and Petruchio born in a Coffin.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Set down the body, and one call her out.
sp.stage: Enter Maria in black, and Jaques.
sp.l: You are welcome to the laſt caſt of your fortunes;
There lies your Husband; there, your loving Husband,
There he that was Petruchio, too good for ye;
Your ſtubborn and unworthy way has kill'd him
〈◊〉 he could reach the Sea; if ye can weep,
• o • ye have cauſe begin, and after death
Doe ſomething yet to th' world, to think ye honeſt.
〈◊〉 many tears had ſav'd him, ſhed in time;
And as they are (ſo a good mind go with 'em)
Yet they may move compaſſion.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Pray ye all hear me,
And judge me as I am, not as you covet,
For that would make me yet more miſerable:
Tis true, I have cauſe to grieve, and mighty cauſe;
• d truly and unfeinedly I weep it.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I ſee there's ſome good nature yet left in her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: But what's the cauſe? miſtake me not, not this man,
〈◊〉 he is dead, I weep for; Heaven defend it,
• ver was ſo childiſh: but his life,
〈◊〉 poor unmanly, wretched, fooliſh life,
〈◊〉 that my full eyes pity, there's my mourning.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Doſt thou not ſhame?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I doe, and even to water,
• o what this man was, to think how ſimple,
〈◊〉 far below a man, how far from reaſon,
〈◊〉 common underſtanding, and all Gentry,
While he was living here he walk'd amongſt us.
He had a happy turn he dyed; I'll tell ye,
Theſe are the wants I weep for, not his perſon:
The memory of this man, had he liv'd
But two years longer, had begot more follies,
Than wealthy Autumn Flies. But let him reſt,
He was a fool, and farewel he; not pitied,
I mean in way of life, or action
By any underſtanding man that's honeſt;
But only in's poſterity, which I,
Out of the fear his ruines might out-live him,
In ſome bad iſſue, like a careful woman,
Like one indeed, born only to preſerve him,
Deny'd him means to raiſe.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Unbutton me,
— I die indeed elſe? Oh Maria,
Oh my unhappineſs, my miſery.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Goe to him whore;—if he periſh,
I'll ſee thee hang'd my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Why, why Maria?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I have done my worſt, and have my end, forgive me;
From this hour make me what you pleaſe: I have tam'd ye,
And now am vow'd your ſervant: Look not ſtrangely,
Not fear what I ſay to you. Dare you kiſs me?
Thus I begin my new love.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Once again?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Once again Maria,
Oh Gentlemen, I know not where I am.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: Get ye to bed then: there you'll quickly know Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Never no more your old tricks?

sp.speaker: Mar,
sp.l: Never Sir.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: You ſhall not need, for as I have a faith
No cauſe ſhall give occaſion.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Ask I am honeſt,
And as I am a maid yet, all my life
From this hour, ſince ye make ſo free profeſſion,
I dedicate in ſervice to your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Soph.
sp.l: I marry, this goes roundly off.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Goe Jaques,
Get all the beſt meat may be bought for money,
And let the hogſheads blood, I am born again:
Well little England, when I ſee a Husband
Of any other Nation, ſtern or jealous,
I'll wiſh him but a woman of thy breeding;
And if he have not butter to his bread,
Till his teeth bleed, I'll never truſt my travel.

div.stage: Enter Rowland, Livia, Byancha, and Tranio.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: What have we here?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: Another Morris, Sir.
That you muſt pipe too.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A poor married couple
Deſire an offering, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Never frown at it,
You cannot mend it now: there's your own hand;
And yours Moroſo, to confirm the bargain.

sp.speaker: Petron.
sp.l: My hand?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Or mine;

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: You'll find it ſo.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: A trick,
By — a trick.

sp.speaker: Bya.
sp.l: Yes Sir, we trickt ye.

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Father.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Haſt thou lain with him? ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Liv.
sp.l: Yes truly Sir.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: And haſt thou done the deed, boy?

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I have, Sir,
That, that will ſerve the turn, I think.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: A match then,
I'll be the maker up of this: Moroſo,
There's now no remedy you ſee, be willing;
Mor be, or be not, he muſt have the wench.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Since I am over-reach'd, let's into dinner,
And if I can, I'll drink't away.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That's well ſaid.

sp.speaker: Petro.
sp.l: Well ſirrah, you have plaid a trick, look to't,
And let me be a Grandſire within's twelve-month,
Or by this hand, I'll curtail half your fortunes.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: There ſhall not want my labour, Sir: your money;
Here's one has undertaken.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Well, I'll truſt her,
And glad I have ſo good a pawn.

sp.speaker: Row.
sp.l: I'll watch ye.

sp.speaker: Petru.
sp.l: Let's in, and drink of all hands, and be jovial:
I have my Colt again, and now ſhe carries;
And Gentlemen, whoever marries next,
Let him be ſure he keep him to his Text. Exeunt.

div.head: EPILOGUE.
div.l: THe Tamer's tam'd, but ſo, as nor the men
Can find one juſt cauſe to complain of, when
They fitly do conſider in their lives,
They ſhould not reign as Tyrants o'er their wives.
Nor can the Women from this preſident
Inſult, or triumph; it being aptly meant,
To teach both Sexes due equality;
And as they ſtand bound, to love mutually.
If this effect ariſing from a cauſe
Well laid, and grounded, may deſerve applauſe,
We ſomething more than hope, our honeſt ends
Will keep the Men, and Women too, our friends.

div.head: The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Governor of Terna, an Iſsand. An ill man,
Ruy Dias, a Captain of Portugal, alſo ſuitor to the Prin.
Piniero, Nephew to Ruy Dias, a merry Captain.
Armuſia, a noble daring Portugueze, in love with the Princeſs.

list.head: companions to Armuſia, and his valiant followers.
Women.
list.item: Quiſara, the Iſland Princeſs, Siſter to the King of Sidore.
Quiſa • a, Aunt to the Princeſs.
Panura, Waiting-woman to the Princeſs Quiſara.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Pymero.
sp.l: OPen the Ports, and ſee the Watch reliev'd,
And let the guards be careful of their buſineſs,
Their vigilant eyes fixt on theſe Iſlanders,
They are falſe and deſperate people, when they find.
The leaſt occaſion open to encouragement,
Cruel, and crafty ſouls, believe me Gentlemen,
Their late attempt, which is too freſh amongſt us,
In which, againſt all arms and honeſty,
The Governor of Ternata made ſurprize.
Of our Confederate, the King of Tidore,
As for his recreation he was rowing
Between both Lands, bids us be wiſe and circumſpect.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: It was a miſchief ſuddenly imagin'd,
And as ſoon done; that Governor's a fierce knave,
Unfaithful as he is fierce too, there's no-truſting;
But I wonder much, how ſuch poor and baſe pleaſures,
As tugging at an Oar, or skill in Steerage,
Should become Princes.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Baſe breedings, love baſe pleaſure;
They take as much delight in a Baratto,
A little ſcurvy boat to row her tightly,
And have the Art to turn and wind her nimbly,
Think it as noble too, though it be ſlaviſh,
And a dull labour that declines a Gentleman:
As we Portugals, or the Spaniards do in riding,
In managing a great horſe, which is princely:
The French in Courtſhip, or the dancing Engliſh,
In carrying a fair preſence.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: He was ſtrangely taken;
But where no faith is, there's no truſt: he has paid for't
His Siſter yet the fair and great Quiſara,
Has ſhew'd a noble mind, and much love in't
To her afflicted brother, and the nobler ſtill it appears,
And ſeaſons of more tenderneſs, becauſe his ruin ſtiles her abſolute
And his impriſonment adds to her profit.
Feeling all this, which makes all men admire her,
The warm beams of this fortune that fall on her,
Yet has ſhe made divers and noble Treaties,
And propoſitions for her brothers freedom,
If wealth or honor—.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Peace, peace, you are fool'd, Sir;
Things of theſe natures have ſtrange outſides Pedro,
And cunning ſhadows, ſet'em far from us,
Draw 'em but near, they are groſs, and they abuſe us;
They that obſerve her cloſe, ſhall find her nature,
Which I doubt mainly will not prove ſo excellent;
She is a Princeſs, and ſhe muſt be fair,
That's the prerogative of being Royal:
Let her want eyes and noſe, ſhe muſt be beauteous,
And ſhe muſt know it too, and the uſe of it,
And people muſt believe it, they are damn'd elſe:
Why, all our neighbor Princes are mad for her,

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: Is ſhe not fair then?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: But her hopes are fairer,
And there's a haughty Maſter, the King of Bakan,
That lofty Sir, that ſpeaks far more, and louder
In his own commendations, than a Cannon:
He is ſtrucken dumb with her.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Beſhrew me ſhe is a ſweet one.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: And there's that hopeful man of Syana,
That ſprightly fellow, he that's wiſe and temperate,
He is a Lover too.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: Wou'd I were worth her looking
For; by my life I hold her a compleat one,
The very Sun, I think affects her ſweetneſs,
And dares not, as he does to all elſe, dye it
Into his tauny Livery.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: She dares not ſee him,
But keeps her ſelf at diſtance from his kiſſes,
And her complexion in a Caſe; let him but like it
A week, or two, or three, ſhe would look like a Lion;
But the main ſport on't is, or rather wonder
The Governor of Ternata, her mortal enemy,
He that has catcht her brother King, is ſtruck too,
And is arriv'd under ſafe conduct alſo,
And hoſtages of worth delivered for him;
And he brought a Letter from his priſoner,
Whether compell'd, or willingly delivered
From the poor King, or what elſe dare be in't,

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: So it be honourable, any thing, 'tis all one
For I dare think ſhe'll do the beſt.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: 'Tis certain
He has admittance, and ſollicites hourly,
Now if he have the trick —

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: What trick?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: The true one,
To take her too, if he be but skill'd in Bat-fowling,
And lime his buſh right.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: I'll be hang'd when that hits,
For 'tis not a compell'd, or forc'd affection
That muſt take her, I gueſs her ſtout and virtuous,
But where's your Uncle, Sir, our valiant Captain,
The brave Ruy Dias all this while?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I marry.
He is amongſt 'em too.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: A Lover.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Nay,
I know not that, but ſince he ſtands in favour,
Or would ſtand ſtifly, he is no Portugal elſe.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: The voice ſays in good favour, in the liſt too
Of the privy wooers, how cunningly of late
I have obſerv'd him, and how privately
He has ſtolen at all hours from us, and how readily
He has feign'd a buſineſs to bid the Fort farewel
For five or ſix days, or a month together,
Sure there is ſomething —

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Yes, yes, there is a thing in't,
A thing would make the beſt on's all dance after it;
A dainty thing; Lord how this Uncle of mine
Has read to me, and rated me for wenching.
And told me in what deſperate caſe 'twould leave me,
And how 'twould ſtew my bones.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: You car'd not for it.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I'faith not much, I ventur'd on ſtill eaſily,
And took my chance, danger is a Soldiers honor;
But that this man, this herb of Grace, Ruy Dias,
This father of our faculties ſhould ſlip thus,
For ſure he is a ferriting, that he
That would drink nothing, to depreſs the ſpirit,
But milk and water, eat nothing but thin air
To make his bloud obedient, that his youth,
In ſpight of all his temperance, ſhould tickle,
And have a love mange on him.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: 'Tis in him, Sir,
But honourable courtſhip, and becomes his rank too.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: In me 'twere abominable Leachery, or would be,
For when our thoughts are on't, and miſs their level,
We muſt hit ſomething.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Well, he's a noble Gentleman,
And if he be a ſuitor, may he ſpeed in't.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Let him alone, our family ne'r fail'd yet.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: Our mad Lieutenant ſtill, merry Pyniero,
Thus wou'd he do, if the Surgeon were ſearching of him.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Eſpecially if a warm wench had ſhot him.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: But hark Chriſtophero; come hither Pedro;
When ſaw you our brave Countrey-man Armuſia?
He that's arriv'd here lately, and his gallants?
A goodly fellow, and a brave companion
Methinks he is, and no doubt, truly valiant,
For he that dares come hither, dares fight any where.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: I ſaw him not of late, a ſober Gentleman
I am ſure he is, and no doubt bravely ſprung,
And promiſes much nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I love him,
And by my troth wou'd fain be inward with him;
Pray let's go ſeek him.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: We'll attend you Sir.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: By that time we ſhall hear the burſt of buſineſs,

div.stage: Enter Ruy Dias, Quiſara, Quiſana; and Panura.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Aunt, I much thank you for your courteſie,
And the fair liberty you ſtill allow me,
Both of your houſe and ſervice, though I be
A Princeſs, and by that Prerogative ſtand free
From the poor malice of opinion,
And no ways bound to render up my actions,
Becauſe no power above me can examine me;
Yet my dear brother being ſtill a priſoner,
And many wandring eyes upon my ways,
Being left alone a Sea-mark, it behoves me
To uſe a little caution, and be circumſpect.

sp.speaker: Quiſan.
sp.l: You're wiſe and noble Lady.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Often Aunt
I reſort hither, and privately to ſee you,
It may be to converſe with ſome I favour;
• wou'd not have it known as oft, nor conſtru'd,
〈◊〉 ſtands not with my care.

sp.speaker: Quiſan.
sp.l: You ſpeak moſt fairly,
For even our pure devotions are examin'd.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: So mad are mens minds now.

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: Or rather monſtrous;
They are thick dreams, bred in fogs that know no fairneſs.

sp.speaker: Quiſan.
sp.l: Madam, the Houſe is yours, I am yours, pray uſe me,
And at your ſervice all I have lies proſtrate;
My care ſhall ever be to yield ye honor,
And when your fame falls here, 'tis my fault Lady;
A poor and ſimple banquet I have provided,
Which if you pleaſe to honor with your preſence —

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: I thank ye Aunt, I ſhall be with you inſtantly,
A few words with this Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Quiſan.
sp.l: I'll leave ye, Exeunt Quiſ. & Pan.
And when you pleaſe retire, I'll wait upon you.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Why, how now Captain, what afraid to ſpeak to me?
A man of Armes, and danted with a Lady?
Commanders have the power to parle with Princes.

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: Madam, the favors you have ſtill ſhowr'd on me,
Which are ſo high above my means of merit,
• o infinite, that nought can value 'em
•• t their own goodneſs, no eyes look up to 'em
But thoſe that are of equal light, and luſtre,
Strike me thus mute, you are my royal Miſtriſs,
And all my ſervices that aime at honor,
Take life from you, the Saint of my devotions;
Pardon my wiſh, it is a fair ambition,
And well becomes the Man that honors you;
I wou'd I were of worth, of ſomething near you,
Of ſuch a royal piece, a King I wou'd be,
A mighty King that might command affection,
And bring a youth upon me might bewitch ye,
And you a ſweet ſould Chriſtian.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Now you talk Sir;
You Portugals, though you be rugged Soldiers,
Yet when you liſt to flatter, you are plain Courtiers;
• d could you wiſh me Chriſtian, brave Ruy Dias?

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: At all the danger of my life great Lady,
At all my hopes, at all—

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Pray ye ſtay a little,
• o what end runs your wiſh?

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: O glorious Lady,
That I might— but I dare not ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: I dare then,
That you might hope to marry me; nay bluſh not,
〈◊〉 honorable end needs no excuſe;
•• d would you love me then?

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: My ſoul not dearer.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Do ſome brave thing that may entice me that way,
• omething of ſuch a meritorious goodneſs,
Of ſuch an unmatcht nobleneſs, that I may know
• ou have a power beyond ours that preſerves you:
Tis not the perſon, nor the royal title,
Not wealth, nor glory, that I look upon,
That inward man I love that's lin'd with virtue,
That well deſerving ſoul works out a favor;
〈◊〉 have many Princes ſuiters, many great ones,
Yet above theſe I love you, you are valiant,
〈◊〉 active man, able to build a fortune;
〈◊〉 do not ſay I dote, nor meane to marry,
Only the hope is, ſomething may be done,
That may compel my faith, and ask my freedome,
And leave opinion fair.

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: Command dear Lady,
And let the danger be as deep as Hell,
As direful to attempt —

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Y'are too ſudden,
〈◊〉 m • ſt be rul'd by you, find out a fortune
• iſely, and hanſomely, examine time,
•• d court occaſion that ſhe may be ready;
A thouſand uſes for your forward ſpirit
〈◊〉 may find daily, be ſure ye take a good one,
A brave and worthy one that may advance ye,
Forc'd ſmiles reward poor dangers; you are a Soldier,
I wou'd not talke ſo elſe, and I love a Soldier,
And that that ſpeaks him true, and great, his valor;
Yet for all theſe which are but Womens follies,
You may do what you pleaſe, I ſhall ſtill know ye,
And though ye weare no Sword.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: Excellent Lady,
When I grow ſo cold, and diſgrace my Nation,
That from their hardy nurſes ſuck adventures,
'Twere fit I wore a Tombſtone; you have read to me
The ſtory of your favor, if I miſtake it,
Or grow a truant in the ſtudy of it,
A great correction Lady—

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Let's toth' banquet,
And have ſome merrier talk, and then to Court,
Where I give audience to my general Suiters;
Pray heaven my womans wit hold; there brave Captain,
You may perchance meet ſomething that may ſtartle ye;
I'll ſay no more, come be not ſad—
I love ye. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Pyniero, Armuſia, Soza, Chriſtophero, and Emanuel.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: You are wellcome Gentlemen, moſt worthy welcom,
And know there's nothing in our power may ſerve ye,
But you may freely challenge.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Sir we thank ye,
And reſt your ſervants too.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Ye are worthy Portugals,
You ſhew the bravery of your minds and ſpirits;
The nature of our Country too, that brings forth
Stirring, unwearied ſoules to ſeek adventures;
Minds never ſatisfied with ſearch of honor
Where time is, and the Sun gives light, brave Countrymen,
Our names are known, new worlds diſcloſe their riches,
Their beauties, and their prides to our embraces;
And we the firſt of Nations find theſe wonders.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Theſe noble thoughts, Sir, have intic'd us forward,
And minds unapt for eaſe to ſee theſe miracles,
In which we find report a poor relater;
We are arriv'd among the bleſſed Iſlands,
Where every wind that riſes blows perfumes,
And every breath of air is like an Incence:
The treaſure of the Sun dwells here, each Tree
As if it envied the old Paradice,
Strives to bring forth immortal fruit; the Spices
Renewing nature, though not deifying,
And when that falls by time, ſcorning the earth,
The ſullen earth ſhould taint or ſuck their beauties,
But as we dreamt, for ever ſo preſerve us:
Nothing we ſee, but breeds an admiration;
The very rivers as we float along,
Throw up their pearls, and curle their heads to court us;
The bowels of the earth ſwell with the births
Of thouſand unknown gemms, and thouſand riches;
Nothing that bears a life, but brings a treaſure;
The people they ſhew brave too, civil manner'd,
Proportioned like the Maſters of great minds,
The Women which I wonder at—

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Ye ſpeak well.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Of delicate aſpects, fair, clearly beauteous,
And to that admiration, ſweet and courteous.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: And is not that a good thing? brave Armuſia
You never ſaw the Court before?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: No certain,
But that I ſee a wonder too, all excellent,
The Government exact.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: Ye ſhall ſee anon,
That that will make ye ſtart indeed, ſuch beauties,
Such riches, and ſuch form.

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: We are fire already;
The wealthy Magazine of nature ſure
Inhabits here.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Theſe ſure are all Ilanders.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Yes. and great Princes too, and luſty lovers.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: They are goodly perſons; What might he be Signior
That bears ſo proud a ſtate?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: King of Bakam,
A fellow that ſarts terror,

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.l: He looks highly.
Sure he was begot o'th' top of a Steeple.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: It may well be,
For you ſhall hear him ring anon.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: That is Syana,
And a brave temper'd fellow, and more valiant.

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: What rugged face is that?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: That's the great Governor,
The man ſurpriz'd our Friend, I told ye of him.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: 'Has dangerous eyes.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: A perilous Thief, and ſubtile.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: And to that ſubtilty a heart of Iron.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Yet the young Lady makes it melt.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: They ſtart all,
And thunder in the eyes.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Away ye poor ones,
Am I in competition with ſuch bubbles?
My virtue, and my name rank'd with ſuch trifles?

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Ye ſpeak loud.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Young-man, I will ſpeak louder;
Can any man but I deſerve her favor,
You petty Princes.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: He will put 'em all in's pocket.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Thou proud mad thing be not ſo full of glory,
So full of vanity.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: How? I contemn thee,
And that ſort-keeping fellow.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: How the Dog looks,
The bandog Governor?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Ha, Why?

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Away thing,
And keep your rank with thoſe that fit your royalty;
Call out the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Doſt thou know me bladder,
Thou inſolent impoſtume?

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: I deſpiſe thee;

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Art thou acquainted with my nature baby?
With my revenge for Injuries? darſt thou hold me
So far behind thy file, I cannot reach thee?
What canſt thou merit?

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Merit? I am above it;
I am equal with all honors, all atchievements,
And what is great and worthy; the beſt doer
I keep at my command, fortune's my ſervant,
'Tis in my power now to deſpiſe ſuch wretches,
To look upon ye ſlightly, and neglect ye,
And but ſhe daines at ſome hours to remember ye,
And people have beſtowed ſome Titles on ye,
I ſhould forget your names—

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: Mercy of me;
What a blown fool has ſelf affection
Made of this fellow? did not the Queen your Mother
Long for bellows, and bagpipes, when ſhe was great with ye,
She brought forth ſuch a windy birth?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: 'Tis ten to one
She eat a Drum, and was deliver'd of alarum,
Or elſe he was ſwadled in an old ſaile when he was young.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: He ſwells too mainly with his meditations;
Faith, talk a little handſomer, ride ſoftly
That we may be able to hold way with ye, we are Princes,
But thoſe are but poor things to you; talk wiſer,
'Twill well become your mightineſs; talk leſs,
That men may think ye can do more.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Talk truth,
That men may think ye are honeſt, and believe ye,
Or talk your ſelf aſleep, for I am weary of you.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Why? I can talk and do.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: That wou'd do excellent.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: And tell you, only I deſerve the Princeſs,
And make good only I, if you dare, you ſir,
Or you Syanas Prince.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Heres a ſtorm toward,
Methinks it ſings already, to him Governor.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Here lies my proof. Draw •

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: And mine.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I'll be ſhort with ye,
For theſe long arguments I was never good at.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: How white the boaſter looks?

div.stage: Enter Ruy Dias, Quiſara, Quiſana, Panura.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I ſee he lacks faith.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: For ſhame forbear great Princes, rule your angers
You violate the freedom of this place,
The ſtate and Royalty—

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: He's well contented
It ſeems, and ſo I have done.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Is this ſhe Signior?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: This is the Princeſs Sir.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: She is ſweet and goodly,
An admirable form, they have cauſe to juſtle.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Ye wrong me and my court, ye forward Prince •
Comes your Love wrapt in Violence to ſeek us?
Is't fit though you be great, my preſence ſhould be
Stain'd, and polluted with your bloody rages?
My privacies affrighted with your Swords?
He that loves me, loves my command; be temper'd,
Or be no more what ye profeſs, my Servants.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: We are calme as peace.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: What command ſhe carries?
And what a ſparkling Majeſty flies from her?

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Is it ye love to do? ye ſhall find danger,
And danger that ſhall ſtart your reſolutions,
But not this way; 'tis not contention,
Who loves me to my face beſt, or who can flatter moſt
Can carry me, he that deſerves my favor,
And will enjoy what I bring, love and Majeſty,
Muſt win me with his worth; muſt travel for me;
Muſt put his haſty rage off, and put on
A well confirmed, a temperate, and true valor.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: But ſhew the way.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: And will, and then ſhew you
A will to tread the way, I'll ſay ye are worthy.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: What task now
Will ſhe turn 'em to? theſe hot youths,
I fear will find a cooling card, I read in her eyes
Something that has ſome ſwinge muſt flye amongſt 'em;
By this hand I love her a little now.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: 'Tis not unknown to you
I had a royal Brother, now miſerable,
And Priſoner to that Man; if I were ambitious,
Gap'd for that glory was n're born with me,
There he ſhould lie his miſeries upon him:
If I were covetous, and my heart ſet
On riches, and thoſe baſe effects that follow
On pleaſures uncontrol'd, or ſafe revenges,
There he ſhould die, his death will give me all theſe;
For then ſtood I up abſolute to do all;
Yet all theſe flattering ſhews of dignity,
Theſe golden dreams of greatneſs cannot force
To forget nature and my fair affection.
Therefore that Man that would be known my lover,
Muſt be known his redeemer, and muſt bring him
Either alive or dead to my embraces.
For even his bones I ſcorn ſhall feel ſuch ſlavery,
Or ſeek another Miſtriſs, 'twill be hard
To do this, wondrous hard, a great adventure,
Fit for a ſpirit of an equal greatneſs;
But being done, the reward is worthy of it,

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: How they ſtand gaping all?

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Ruy Dias cold?
Not flye like fire into it? may be you doubt me,
He that ſhall do this is my husband Prince;
By the bright heavens he is, by whoſe juſtice
I openly proclaim it; if I lye,
Or ſeek to ſet you on with me, and reward my falſhood.
No ſtirring yet, no ſtart into a bravery?

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: Madam, it may be, but being a main danger,
Your grace muſt give me leave to look about me,
And take a little time, the cauſe will ask it.
Great Acts require great counſels.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Take your pleaſure,
I fear the Portugal.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: I'll raiſe an Army
That ſhall bring back this Iſland, Fort and all,
And fix it here.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: How long will this be doing?
You ſhould have begun in your Grandfather's days.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: What may be,
And what my power can promiſe nobleſt Lady,
My will I am ſure ſtands fair.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Faire be your fortune,
Few promiſes are beſt, and fair performance.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Theſe cannot doe,
Their power and arts are weak ones.
'Tis in my will, I have this King your brother,
He is my priſoner, I accept your proffer,
And bleſs the fair occaſion that atchiev'd him:
I love ye, and I honor ye, but ſpeak;
Whether alive or dead he ſhall be rendred,
And ſee how readily, how in an inſtant,
Quick as your wiſhes Lady—

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: No, I ſcorn ye,
You and your courteſie; I hate your love Sir;
And ere I would ſo baſely win his liberty,
I would ſtudy to forget he was my brother;
By force he was taken; he that ſhall enjoy me,
Shall fetch him back by force, or never know me.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: As I live, a rare Wench,

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: She has a noble ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: By force?

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Yes Sir, by force, and make you glad too
To let him goe.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: How? you may look nobler on me,
And think me no ſuch Boy; by force he muſt not,
For your love much may be.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Put up your paſſion,
And pack ye home, I ſay, by force, and ſuddenly.
He lies there till he rots elſe, although I love him
• oſt tenderly and dearly, as a brother,
And out of theſe reſpects would joy to ſee him;
•• t to receive him as thy courteſie,
With all the honor thou couldſt add unto him
From his hands that moſt hate him, I had rather,
Though no condition were propounded for him,
• ee him far ſunke i'th earth, and there forget him.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Your hopes are gelt good Governor.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: A rare Woman.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Lady,
〈◊〉 pull this pride, I'll quench this bravery,
And turne your glorious ſcorn to tears and howlings;
〈◊〉 will proud Princeſs; this neglect of me
• all make thy brother King moſt miſerable;
• all turn him into curſes 'gainſt thy cruelty:
〈◊〉 where before I us'd him like a King,
• d did thoſe Royal Offices unto him:
Now he ſhall lie a ſad lump in a dungeon,
• den with chains and fetters, colds and hunger,
• rkneſs, and lingring death for his companions;
And let me ſee who dare attempt his reſcue,
What deſperate fool? • ook toward it; farewel,
And when thou know'ſt him thus, lament thy follies,
Nay I will make thee kneel to take my offer:
Once more farewel, and put thy truſt in puppits. Exit.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: If none dare undertake it, I'll live a mourner.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: You cannot want.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: You muſt not.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt dangerous,
And wiſe men wou'd proceed with care and counſel,
Yet ſome way would I knew—
Walke with me Gentlemen— Exeunt. Manent, Arm. and his Comp.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: How do you like her ſpirit?

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: 'Tis a clear one,
Clog'd with no dirty ſtuff, ſhe is all pure honor.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.l: The braveſt Wench I ever look'd upon,
And of the ſtrongeſt parts, ſhe is moſt fair,
Yet her mind ſuch a mirrour —

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: What an action
Wou'd this be to put forward on, what a glory,
And what an everlaſting wealth to end it?
Methinks my ſoul is ſtrangely rais'd.

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: To ſtep into it,
Iuſt while they think, and ere they have determin'd
To bring the King off.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Things have been done as dangerous.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.l: And proſper'd beſt when they were leaſt conſider'd.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Bleſs me my hopes,
And you my friends aſſiſt me.
None but our companions.

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: You deale wiſely,
And if we ſhrink the name of ſlaves dye with us.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.l: Stay not for ſecond thoughts.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I am determin'd;
And though I loſe, it ſhall be ſung, I was valiant,
And my brave offer ſhall be turn'd to ſtory,
Worthy the Princeſs tongue. A Boat, that's all
That's unprovided, and habits like to Merchants,
The reſt wee'l councel as we goe.

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: A way then,
Fortune looks fair on thoſe, make haſte to win her.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Kee.
sp.l: I Have kept many a Man, and many a great one,
Yet I confeſs, I nere ſaw before
A Man of ſuch a ſufferance; he lies now
Where I would not lay my dog, for ſure 'twould kill him.
Where neither light or comfort can come near him;
Nor air, nor earth that's wholſome; it grieves me
To ſee a mighty King with all his glory,
Sunk o'th' ſudden to the bottome of a dungeon.
Whether ſhould we deſcend that are poor Raſcals
If we had our deſerts?

sp.speaker: 1. Mo.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſtrange wonder.
Load him with Irons, oppreſs him with contempts,
Which are the Governors commands, give him nothing,
Or ſo little, to ſuſtain life, 'tis next nothing;
They ſtir not him, he ſmiles upon his miſeries,
And beares 'em with ſuch ſtrength, as if his nature
Had been nurs'd up, and foſter'd with calamities.
He gives no ill words, curſes, nor repines not,
Blames nothing, hopes in nothing, we can hear of;
And in the midſt of all theſe frights, fears nothing.

sp.speaker: Kee.
sp.l: I'll be ſworne
He fears not, for even when I ſhake for him,
As many times my pitty will compell me,
When other ſouls, that bear not half his burthen,
Shrink in their powers, and burſt with their oppreſſions;
Then will he Sing, wooe his afflictions,
And court 'em in ſad airs, as if he wo • 'd wed 'em.
That's more than we have heard yet, we are only
Appointed for his Guard, but not ſo near him,
If we could hear that wonder—

sp.speaker: Kee.
sp.l: Many times
I fear the Governor ſhould come to know it;
For his voice ſo affects me, ſo delights me,
That when I find his hour, I have Muſick ready,
And it ſtirs me infinitely, be but ſtill and private,
And you may chance to hear.

div.stage: King appears loden with chains, his head, and armes only above.

sp.l: We will not ſtir, Sir;
This is a ſudden change, but who dares blame it.

sp.speaker: Kee.
sp.l: Now hark and melt, for I am ſure I ſhall;
Stand ſilent, what ſtubborn weight of chains—
Yet he looks temperately.
His eyes not ſunk, and his complexion firm ſtill,
No wildneſs, no diſtemper'd touch upon him,
How conſtantly he ſmiles, and how undanted?
With what a Majeſty he heaves his head up? Muſick.

sp.speaker: Kee.
sp.l: Now marke, I know he will ſing; do not diſturb him.
Your allowance from the Governor, wou'd it were more ſir,
Or in my power to make it hanſomer.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Do not tranſgreſs thy charge, I take his bounty,
And fortune, whilſt I bear a mind contented
Not leaven'd with the glory I am falen from,
Nor hang upon vain hopes, that may corrupt me.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Thou art my ſlave, and I appear above thee.

sp.speaker: Kee.
sp.l: The Governor himſelf.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: What, at your banquet?
And in ſuch ſtate, and with ſuch change of ſervice?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Nature's no glutton, Sir, a little ſerves her.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: This diet's holſome then.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: I beg no better.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: A calm contented mind, give him leſs next;
Theſe full meals will oppreſs his health, his Grace
Is of a tender, and pure conſtitution,
And ſuch repletions—

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Mock, mock, it moves not me ſir,
Thy mirths, as do thy miſchiefs, flie behind me.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Ye carry it handſomely, but tell me patience,
Do not you curſe the brave and royal Lady
Your gracious ſiſter? do not you damn her pitty,
Damn twenty times a day, and damn it ſeriouſly?
Do not you ſwear aloud too, cry and kick?
The very ſoul ſweat in thee with the agony
Of her contempt of me? Couldſt not thou eat her
For being ſo injurious to thy fortune,
Thy fair and happy fortune? Couldſt not thou wiſh her
A Baſtard, or a Whore, fame might proclame her;
Black ugly fame, or that thou hadſt had no ſiſter?
Spitting the general name out, and the nature;
Blaſpheming heaven for making ſuch a miſchief;
For giving power to pride, and will to Woman?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: No Tyrant, no, I bleſs and love her for it;
And though her ſcorn of thee, had laid up for me
As many plagues as the corrupted air breeds,
As many miſchiefs as the hours have minutes,
As many formes of Death, as doubt can figure;
Yet I ſhould love more ſtill, and more honor her;
All thou canſt lay upon me, cannot bend me,
No not the ſtroke of death, that I deſpiſe too:
For if fear could poſſeſs me, thou hadſt won me;
As little from this hour I prize thy flatteries,
And leſs than thoſe thy prayers, though thou wouldſt kneel to me;
And if ſhe be not Miſtriſs of this nature,
She is none of mine, no kin, and I contemne her.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Are you ſo • iant ſir?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Yes, and ſo fortunate;
For he that holds his conſtancy ſtill conquers;
Hadſt thou preſerv'd me as a noble enemy,
And as at firſt, made my reſtraint ſeem to me
But only as the ſhadow of captivity,
I had ſtill ſpoke thee noble, ſtill declar'd thee
A valiant, great, and worthy man, ſtill lov'd thee,
And ſtill prefer'd thy fair love to my ſiſter;
But to compell this from me with a miſery,
A moſt inhumane, and unhandſome ſlavery —

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You will relent for all this talk I fear not,
And put your wits a work agen.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: You are cozen'd;
Or if I were ſo weak to be wrought to it,
So fearful to give way to ſo much poverty,
How I ſhould curſe her heart if ſhe conſented?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You ſhall write, and entreat, or—

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Do thy utmoſt,
And e'en in all thy tortures I'll laugh at thee,
I'll think thee no more valiant, but a villain;
Nothing thou haſt done brave, but like a thief,
Atchiev'd by craft, and kept by cruelty;
Nothing thou canſt deſerve, thou art unhoneſt;
Nor no way live to build a Name, thou art barbarous.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Down with him low enough, there let him murmur,
And ſee his diet be ſo light and little,
He grow not thus high hearted on't, I will coole ye,
And make ye cry for mercy, and be ready
To work my ends, and willingly; and your ſiſter taken down,
Your ſcornful, cruel ſiſter ſhall repent too,
And ſue to me for grace.
Give him no liberty,
But let his bands be doubled, his eaſe leſſened;
Nothing his heart deſires, but vex and torture him:
Let him not ſleep, nothing that's dear to nature
Keep him as near death, and as willing to embrace it,
But ſee he arrive not at it; I will humble him.
And her ſtout heart that ſtands on ſuch defiance;
And let me ſee her champions that dare venture
Her high and mighty wooers, keep your guards cloſe,
And as you love your lives be diligent.
And what I charge, obſerve.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: We ſhall be dutiful. Exit. Gov.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I'll pull your courage King, and all your bravery.
Moſt certain he is reſolved nothing can ſtir him;
For if he had but any part about him
Gave way to fear or hope, he durſt not talk thus,
