There will be ſome lett ſtill, yet I muſt have ye,
Have ye of my faith too, and ſo enjoy ye.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Now I contemn ye, and I hate my ſelf
For looking on that face laſciviouſly,
And it looks ugly now me thinks.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: How Portugal?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: It looks like death it ſelf, to which 'twou'd lead me;
Your eyes reſemble pale diſpair, they fright me,
And in their rounds, a thouſand horrid ruins,
Methinks I ſee, and in your tongue hear fearfully
The hideous murmurs of weak ſouls have ſuffer'd;
Get from me, I deſpiſe ye; and know woman,
That for all this trap you have laid to catch my life in,
To catch my immortal life, I hate and curſe ye,
Contemn your Deities, ſpurn at their powers,
And where I meet your Mahumet gods, I'll ſwing 'em
Thus o'r my head, and kick 'em into puddles,
Nay, I will out of vengeance ſearch your Temples.
And with thoſe hearts that ſerve my God, demoliſh
Your ſhambles of wild worſhips.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Now, now you hear Sir.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: I will have my faith, ſince you are ſo crafty,
The glorious croſs, although I love your brother;
Let him frown too, I will have my devotion,
And let your whole State ſtorm.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Enter and take him;
I am ſorry friend that I am forc'd to do this.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Be ſure you bind him faſt.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: But uſe him nobly.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Had it to me been done, I had forgiven it,
And ſtill preſerv'd you fair, but to our gods Sir—

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Methinks I hate 'em now.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: To our Religion,
To theſe to be thus ſtubborn, thus rebellious
To threaten them.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Uſe all your violence,
I ask no mercy, nor repent my words:
I ſpit at your beſt powers; I ſerve one,
Will give me ſtrength to ſcourge your gods.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Away with him.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: To grind 'em into baſe duſt, and diſperſe 'em,
That never more their bloudy memories—

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Clap him cloſe up.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Good friend be cooler.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Never;
Your painted Siſter I deſpiſe too.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Softly.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: And all her deviliſh Arts laugh and ſcorn at,
Mock her blind purpoſes.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: You muſt be temperate;
Offer him no violence, I command you ſtrictly.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Now thou art up, I ſhall have time to ſpeak too.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Oh how I love this man, how truly honor him.

div.head: Seaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Chriſtophero, and Pedro (at one door) Emanuel, and Soza, (at another)

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: DO you know the news Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.l: Wou'd we knew as well, Sir,
How to prevent it.

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: Is this the love they bear us,
For our late benefit? taken ſo maliciouſly,
And clapt up cloſe? is that the thanks they render?

sp.speaker: Ch.
sp.l: It muſt not be put up thus, ſmother'd ſlightly,
'Tis ſuch a baſe unnatural wrong.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I know,
They may think to doe wonders, aim at all,
And to blow us with a vengeance, out o' th' Iſlands:
But if we be our ſelves, honeſt and reſolute,
And continue but Maſters of our antient courages,
Stick cloſe, and give no vantage to their villanies—

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: Nay, if we ſaint or fall apieces now,
We are fools, and worthy to be markt for miſery;
Begin to ſtrike at him, they are all bound too?
To cancel his deſerts? what muſt we look for
If they can carry this?

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.l: I'll carry coals then;
I have but one life, and one fortune, Gentlemen,
But I'll ſo husband it to vex theſe raſcals,
Theſe barbarous ſlaves.

sp.speaker: Ch.
sp.l: Shall we go charge 'em preſently?

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: No, that will be too weak, and too fool-hardy,
We muſt have grounds, that promiſe ſafety, friends,
And ſure offence, we loſe our angers elſe,
And worſe than that, venture our lives too lightly.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Did you ſee mine Uncle? plague o' theſe Barbarians,
How the rogues ſtick in my teeth, I know ye are angry,
So I am too, monſtrous angry, Gentlemen,
I am angry, that I choak agen.
You hear Armuſia's up, honeſt Arm:
Clapt up in priſon, friends, the brave Arm:
Here are fine boys.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.l: We hope he ſhall not ſtay there.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Stay, no, he muſt not ſtay, no talk of ſtaying,
Theſe are no times to ſtay; are not theſe raſcals?
Speak, I beſeech ye ſpeak, are they not Rogues?
Think ſome abominable names are they not devils?
But the devil's a great deal too good for 'em—fuſty villains.

sp.speaker: Ch.
sp.l: They are a kind of hounds.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Hounds were their fathers;
Old blear-ey'd bob-tail'd hounds—Lord, where's my Uncle?

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: But what ſhall be done, Sir?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Done?

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: Yes, to relieve him;
If it be not ſudden they may take his life too.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: They dare as ſoon take fire and ſwallow it,
Take ſtakes and thruſt into their tails for gliſters:
His life, why 'tis a thing worth all the Iſlands,
And they know will be rated at that value;
His very impriſonment will make the Town ſtink,
And ſhake and ſtink, I have phyſick in my hand for 'em
Shall give the goblins ſuch a purge—

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Your Uncle,

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: I hear ſtrange news, and have been ſeeking ye;
They ſay Armuſia's priſoner.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: 'Tis moſt certain.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: Upon what cauſe?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: He has deſerv'd too much, Sir;
The old heathen policie has light upon him.
And paid him home.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: A moſt unnoble dealing.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: You are the next, if you can carry it tamely,
He has deſerved of all.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs it,
Of me ſo nobly too.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I am glad to hear it,
You have a time now to make good your confeſſion,
Your faith will ſhew but cold elſe, and for faſhion,
Now to redeem all, now to thank his courteſie,
Now to make thoſe believe that held you backward,
And an ill inſtrument, you are a Gentleman,
An honeſt man, and you dare love your Nations,
Dare ſtick to virtue, though ſhe be oppreſt,
And for her own fair ſake, ſtep to her reſcue:
If you live ages, Sir, and loſe this hour,
Not now redeem, and vindicate your honor
Your life will be a murmure, and no man in't.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: I thank ye nephew, come along with me Gentlemen,
We'll make 'em dancing ſport immediately:
We are Maſters of the Fort yet, we ſhall ſee
What that can do.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Let it but ſpit fire ſinely,
And play their turrets, and their painted Palaces,
A frisking round or two, that they may trip it,
And caper in the air.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: Come, we'll do ſomething
Shall make 'em look about, we'll ſend 'em plums,
If they be not too hard for their teeth.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: And fine Potatoes
Roſted in Gunpowder, ſuch a Banquet, Sir
Will prepare their unmannerly ſtomachs.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: They ſhall ſee
There is no ſafe retreat in villany;
Come, be high-hearted all.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: We are all on fire, Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I am ungrateful, and a wretch, perſwade me not,
Forgetful of the mercy he ſhew'd me,
The timely noble pity—why ſhould I
See him faſt bound and fetter'd, whoſe true courteſie,
Whoſe manhood, and whoſe mighty hand ſet me free?
Why ſhould it come from me? why I command this?
Shall not all tongues and truths call me unthankful?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Had the offence been thrown on you, 'tis certain
It had been in your power, and your diſcretion
To have turn'd it into mercy, and forgiven it,
And then it had ſhew'd a virtuous point of gratitude,
Timely, and nobly taken; but ſince the cauſe
Concerns the honor of our gods, and their Title,
And ſo tranſcends your power, and your compaſſion,
A little your own ſafety, if you ſaw it too,
If your too fond indulgence did not dazle you,
It cannot now admit a private pitty;
'Tis in their Wills, their Mercies, or Revenges,
And theſe revolts in you, ſhew mere rebellions.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: They are mild and pittiful.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: To thoſe repent.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Their nature's ſoft and tender.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: To true hearts.
That feel compunction for their treſpaſſes:
This man defies 'em ſtill, threatens deſtruction
And demolition of their Arms and Worſhip,
Spits at their powers; take heed ye be not found, Sir,
And mark'd a favourer of their diſhonor;
They uſe no common juſtice.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What ſhall I do
To deſerve of this man—

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: If ye more bemoan him,
Or mitigate your power to preſerve him,
I'll curſe ye from the gods, call up their vengeance.
sp.stage: Enter Quiſara with her hands bound, Quiſana, Panura.
sp.l: And fling it on your Land and you, I have charge
I hope to wrack you all.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What ails my Siſter?
Why, is ſhe bound? why looks ſhe ſo diſtractedly?
Who does do this?

sp.speaker: Quiſan.
sp.l: We did it, pardon Sir,
And for her preſervation—She is grown wild,
And raving on the ſtrangers love and honor,
Sometimes crying out help, help, they will torture him,
They will take his life, they will murder him preſently,
If we had not prevented violently
Have laid hands on her own life.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Theſe are tokens,
The gods diſpleaſure is gone out, be quick,
And e'r it fall, doe ſomething to appeaſe 'em.
You know the ſacrifice—I am glad it works thus.

sp.speaker: Quiſa.
sp.l: How low and baſe thou lookſt now, that wert noble?
No figure of a King, methinks ſhews on you.
No face of Majeſty, foul, ſwarth ingratitude
Has taken off thy ſweetneſs, baſe forgetfulneſs
Of mighty benefits, has turned thee Devil:
Thou haſt perſecuted goodneſs, innocence;
And laid a hard and violent hand on virtue,
On that fair virtue that ſhould teach and guide us;
Thou haſt wrong'd thine own preſerver, whoſe leaſt merit,
Pois'd with thy main Eſtate, thou canſt not ſatisfie,
Nay, put thy life in too, 'twill be too light ſtill:
What haſt thou done?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Goe for him preſently,
And once more we'll try if we can win him fairly:
If not, let nothing ſhe ſays hinder ye, or ſtir ye;
She ſpeaks diſtractedly — Do that the gods command ye,
Do you know what ye ſay Lady?

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: I could curſe thee too,
Religion and ſeverity has ſteel'd thee,
Has turn'd thy heart to ſtone; thou haſt made the gods hard too,
Againſt their ſweet and patient natures, cruel:
None of ye feel what bravery ye tread on?
What innocence? what beauty?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Pray be patient.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: What honourable things ye caſt behind?
What monuments of man?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Once more Armuſia,
Becauſe I love ye tenderly and dearly,
And would be glad to win ye mine, I wiſh ye,
Even from my heart I wiſh and wooe ye—

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: What Sir,
Take heed how ye perſwade me falſly, then ye hate me:
Take heed how ye intrap me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I adviſe ye,
And tenderly and truly I adviſe ye,
Both for your ſouls health, and your ſafety.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Stay,
And name my ſoul no more, ſhe is too precious,
Too glorious for you flatteries, too ſecure too.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Conſider the reward, Sir, and the honor
That is prepared, the glory you ſhall grow to.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: They are not to be conſider'd in theſe caſes,
Not to be nam'd when ſouls are queſtion'd;
They are vain and flying vapors—touch my life,
'Tis ready for ye, put it to what teſt
It ſhall pleaſe ye, I am patient; but for the reſt
You may remove Rocks with your little fingers,
Or blow a Mountain out o' th' way, with bellows,
As ſoon as ſtir my faith; uſe no more arguments.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: We muſt uſe tortures then.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Your worſt and painfull'ſt
I am joyful to accept.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: You muſt the ſharpeſt,
For ſuch has been your hate againſt our Deities
Delivered openly, your theats and ſcornings,
And either your repentance muſt be mighty,
Which is your free converſion to our cuſtoms,
Or equal puniſhment which is your life, Sir.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: I am glad I have it for ye, take it Prieſt,
And all the miſeries that ſhall attend it:
Let the gods gl • t themſelves with Chriſtian bloud,
It will be ask'd again, and ſo far followed,
So far reveng'd, and with ſuch holy juſtice,
Your gods of gold ſhall melt and ſink before it;
Your Altars and your Temples ſhake to nothing;
And you falſe worſhipers, blind fools of ceremony,
Shall ſeek for holes to hide your heads, and fears in,
For ſeas to ſwallow you from this deſtruction,
Darkneſs to dwell about ye, and conceal ye;
Your mothers womb agen—

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Make the fires ready,
And bring the ſeveral tortures out.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Stand faſt, Sir,
And fear 'em not, you that have ſtept ſo nobly
Into this pious Trial, ſtart not now,
Keep on your way, a Virgin will aſſiſt ye,
A Virgin won by your fair conſtancy,
And glorying that ſhe is won ſo, will dye by ye:
I have touch'd ye every way, tried ye moſt honeſt,
Perfect, and good, chaſte, bluſhing chaſte, and temperate,
Valiant, without vain-glory, modeſt, ſtayed,
No rage, or light affection ruling in you:
Indeed, the perfect ſchool of worth I find ye,
The temple of true honor.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Whether will ſhe?
What do you infer by this fair argument, Lady?

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Your Faith, and your Religion muſt be like ye,
They that can ſhew you theſe, muſt be pure mirrors,
When the ſtreams ſlow clear and fair, what are the fountains?
I do embrace your faith, Sir, and your fortune;
Go on, I will aſſiſt ye, I feel a ſparkle here,
A lively ſpark that kindles my affection,
And tells me it will riſe to flames of glory:
Let 'em put on their angers, ſuffer nobly,
Shew me the way, and when I faint, inſtruct me;
And if I follow not—

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Oh bleſſed Lady,
Since thou art won, let me begin my triumph,
Come clap your terrors on.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: All your ſell tortures.
For there is nothing he ſhall ſuffer, brother,
I ſwear by a new faith, which is moſt ſacred,
And I will keep it ſo, but I will follow in,
And follow to a ſcruple of affliction,
In ſpight of all your gods without prevention.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Death! ſhe amazes me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What ſhall be done now?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: They muſt dye both,
And ſuddenly, they will corrupt all elſe;
This woman makes me weary of my miſchief,
She ſhakes me, and ſhe ſtraggers me, go in Sir,
I'll ſee the execution.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Not ſo ſuddain:
If they go, all my Friends and Siſters periſh.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Wou'd I were ſafe at home agen.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Arm, arm, Sir,
Seek for defence, the Caſtle plays and thunders,
The Town Rocks, and the houſes fly i' th' air,
The people dye for fear—Captain Ruy Dias,
Has made an oath he will not leave a ſtone here;
No, not the memory, here has ſtood a City,
Unleſs Armuſia be deliver'd fairly.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I have my fears: what can our gods do now for us?

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Be patient, but keep him ſtill: he is a cure, Sir,
Againſt both Rage and Cannon: goe and fortifie,
Call in the Princeſs, make the Palace ſure,
And let 'em know you are a King: look nobly;
And take you courage to ye; keep cloſe the priſoner,
And under command, we are betraid elſe.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: How joyfully I goe?

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Take my heart with thee.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I hold a Wolf by the car now:
Fortune free me. Exeunt.
Heaven bleſs us,
What a thund'ring's here? what fire-ſpitting?
We cannot drink, but our Cans are mauld amongſt us.
I wou'd they would mall our ſcores too:
Shame o'their Guns, I thought they had been bird-pots,
Or great Candle-caſes, how deviliſhly they bounce,
And how the Bullets borrow a piece of a houſe here,
There another, and mend thoſe up agen
With another Pariſh; here flies a poudring-tub,
The meat ready roſted, and there a barrel piſſing vinegar,
And they two over-taking the top of a high Steeple,
Newly ſlic'd off for a Sallet.
A vengeance fire 'em.
Nay, they fire faſt enough;
You need not help 'em.
Are theſe the Portugal Bulls—
How loud they bellow
Their horns are plaguy ſtrong, they puſh down Palaces
They toſs our little habitations like whelps,
Like grindle-tails, with their heels upward;
All the windows i'th Town dance a new Trenchmore,
'Tis like to prove a bleſſed age for Glaſiers,
I met a hand, and a Letter in't, in great haſte,
And by and by, a ſingle leg running after it,
As if the arm had forgot part of his errand,
Heads ſlie like Foot-balls every where.
What ſhall we do?
I care not, my ſhop's cancell'd,
And all the Pots, and earthen Pans in't vaniſh't:
There was a ſingle Bullet, and they together by the ears;
You would have thought Tom Tumbler had been there,
And all his troop of devils.
Let's to the King,
And get this Gentleman deliver'd handſomly:
By this hand, there's no walking above ground elſe.
By this leg — let me ſwear nimbly by it,
For I know not how long I ſhall owe it,
If I were out o'th' Town once, if I came in agen to
Fetch my breakfaſt, I will give 'em leave to cramm me
With a Portugal Pudding: Come; let's doe any thing
To appeaſe this thunder. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Art ſure it was that blind Prieſt?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Yes moſt certain,
He has provok'd all this; the King is merciful,
And wond'rous loving; but he fires him on ſtill,
And when he cools, enrages him, I know it:
Threatens new vengeance, and the gods ſierce juſtice
When he but looks with fair eyes on Armuſia,
Will lend him no time to relent; my royal Miſtriſs,
She has entertain'd a Chriſtian hope,

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Speak truly.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis moſt true, but Lord! how he lies at her,
And threatens her, and flatters her, and damns her,
And I fear, if not ſpeedily prevented,
If ſhe continue ſtout, both ſhall be executed,

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I'll kiſs thee for this news, nay more Panura,
If thou wilt give me leave I'll get thee with Chriſtian,
The beſt way to convert thee.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Make me believe ſo?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I will y' faith. But which way cam'ſt thou hither?
The Pallace is cloſe guarded, and barricado'd.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I came through a private vault, which few there know of,
It riſes in a Temple not far hence,
Cloſe by the Caſtle here.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: How—To what end?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: A good one:
To give ye knowledge of my new-born Miſtriſs;
And in what doubt Armuſia ſtands,
Think any preſent means, or hope to ſtop 'em
From their fell ends: the Princes are come in too,
And they are harden'd alſo.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: The damn'd Prieſt—

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Sure he's a cruel man, methinks Religion
Should teach more temperate Leſſons.

sp.speaker: Py,
sp.l: He the fire-brand?
He dare to touch at ſuch fair lives as theirs are?
Well Prophet, I ſhall propheſie, I ſhall catch ye,
When all your Prophecies will not redeem ye?
Wilt thou do one thing bravely?

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: Any good I am able.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: And by thine own white hand, I'll ſwear thou art virtuous,
And a brave wench, durſt thou but guide me preſently,
Through the ſame vault thou cam'ſt, into the Pallace
And thoſe I ſhall appoint, ſuch as I think ſit.

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: Yes I will do it, and ſuddainly, and truly.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I wou'd fain behold this Prophet,

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: Now I have ye:
And ſhall bring ye where ye ſhall behold him,
Alone too, and unfurniſh'd of defences:
That ſhall be my care; but you muſt not betray me.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Doſt thou think we are ſo baſe, ſuch ſlaves, rogues?

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: I do not:
And you ſhall ſee how fairly I'll work for ye.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I muſt needs ſteal that Prieſt,
Steal him, and hang him.

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: Do any thing to remove his miſchief, ſtrangle him—

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Come prethee love.

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: You'll offer me no foul play?
The Vault is dark.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: 'Twas well remember'd.

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: And ye may—
But I hold ye honeſt,

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Honeſt enough I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: I am but a poor weak wench, and what with the place
And your perſwaſions Sir—but I hope you will not;
You know we are often cozen'd.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: If thou doſt fear me,
Why doſt thou put me in mind?

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: To let you know Sir,
Though it be in your power, and things fitting to it,
Yet a true Gent—

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I know what he'll do:
Come and remember me, and I'll anſwer thee,
I'll anſwer thee to the full; we'll call at th' Caſtle,
And then my good guide, do thy Will; ſha't find me
A very tractable man.

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.l: I hope I ſhall Sir. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Bak.
sp.l: Let my men guard the Gates.

sp.speaker: Syan.
sp.l: And mine the Temple,
For fear the honor of our gods ſhould ſuffer,
And on your lives be watchful.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: And be valiant;
And let's ſee, if theſe Portugals dare enter;
What their high hearts dare do: Let's ſee how readily,
The great Ruy Dias will redeem his Countrey-men;
He ſpeaks proud words, and threatens.

sp.speaker: Sy.
sp.l: He is approv'd, Sir,
And will put fair for what he promiſes;
I could wiſh friendlier terms,
Yet for our liberties and for our gods,
We are bound in our beſt ſervice
Even in the hazard of our lives.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Come up Princes,
And give your counſels, and your helps: the Fort ſtill
Plays fearfully upon us, beats our buildings,
And turns our people wild with fears.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Send for the priſoner,
And give us leave to argue. Exit Ba. and Sy. then,

div.stage: Enter Ruy Dias, Emanuel, Chriſtoph. Pedro, with Sold.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: Come on nobly,
And let the Fort play ſtill, we are
Strong enough to look upon 'em,
And return at pleaſure; it may
Be on our view they will return him.

sp.speaker: Chr.
sp.l: We will return 'em ſuch thanks elſe,
Shall make 'em ſcratch where it itches not.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.l: How the people ſtare,
And ſome cry, ſome pray, and ſome curſe heartily:
But it is the King —

div.stage: Enter Syana, Bakam, Quiſara, Armuſia, with Soldiers above.

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: I cannot blame their wiſdoms.
They are all above, Armuſia chain'd and bound too?
Oh, theſe are thakful Squires.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.l: Hear us Ruy Dios,
Be wiſe and hear us, and give ſpeedy anſwer,
Command thy Cannon preſently to ceaſe,
No more to trouble the afflicted people,
Or ſuddainly Armuſia's head goes off;
As ſuddainly as ſaid.

sp.speaker: Em.
sp.l: Stay Sir, be moderate.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Do nothing that's diſhonourable Ruy Dyas
Let not the fear of me, maſter thy valour;
Purſue 'em ſtill, they are baſe malicious people.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Friend, be not deſperate.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I ſcorn your courteſies;
Strike when you dare, a fair arm guide the Gunner,
And may he let flie ſtill with fortune: friend,
Do me the honor of a Soldiers funerals,
The laſt fair Chriſtian right, ſee me i'th' ground,
And let the Palace burn firſt, then the Temples,
And on their ſcorn'd gods, erect my monument:
Touch not the Princeſs, as you are a Soldier.

sp.speaker: Quiſar.
sp.l: Which way you goe, Sir,
I muſt follow neceſſary.
One life, and one death.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Will you take a truce yet?

div.stage: Enter Pyniero, Soza, and Soldiers, with the Governor.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: No, no, go on:
Look here, your god, your prophet.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How came he taken?

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: I conjur'd for him, King.
I am a ſure Curr at an old blind Prophet.
I'll haunt ye ſuch a falſe knave admirably,
A terrier I; I eartht him, and then ſnapt him;

sp.speaker: Soz.
sp.l: Saving the reverence of your grace, we ſtole him,
E'en out of the next chamber to ye.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: Come, come, begin King,
Begin this bloudy matter when you dare;
And yet I ſcorn my ſword ſhould touch the raſcal,
I'll tear him thus before ye. Ha?
What art thou? Pulls his Beard and hair off.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How's this!
Art thou a Prophet?

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: Come down Princes.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: We are abus'd—
Oh my moſt dear Armuſia—
Off with his chains. And now my noble Siſter,
Rejoyce with me, I know ye are pleas'd as I am.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: This is a precious Prophet. Why Don Governor,
What make you here, how long have you taken Orders?

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: Why what a wretch
Art thou to work this miſchief?
To aſſume this holy ſhape to ruine honor,
Honor and chaſtity;

div.stage: Enter King, and all from above.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: I had paid you all,
But fortune plaid the ſlut. Come,
Give me my doom.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I cannot ſpeak for wonder.

sp.speaker: Gov.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis I Sir,
And here I ſtay your ſentence.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Take her friend,
You have half perſwaded me to be a Chriſtian,
And with her all the joyes, and all the bleſſings.
Why what dream have we dwelt in?

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.l: All peace to ye,
And all the happineſs of heart dwell with ye,
Children as ſweet and noble as their Parents.

sp.speaker: Py.
sp.l: And Kings at leaſt.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Good Sir, forget my raſhneſs.
And noble Princeſſes, for I was once angry,
And out of that, might utter ſome diſtemper,
Think not 'tis my nature.

sp.speaker: Sya.
sp.l: Your joy is ours, Sir.
And nothing we find in ye, but moſt noble.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: To priſon with this dog, there let him houl,
And if he can repent, ſigh out his villanies:
His Iſland we ſhall ſeize into our hands,
His Father and himſelf have both uſurp'd it,
And kept it by oppreſſion; the Town and Caſtle,
In which I lay my ſelf moſt miſerable,
Till my moſt honourable friend redeem'd me,
Signior Pyniero, I beſtow on you,
The reſt of next command upon theſe Gentlemen,
Upon ye, all my love.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Oh brave Ruy Dias,
You have ſtarted now beyond me. I muſt thank ye,
And thank ye for my life, my wife and honor.

sp.speaker: Ruy.
sp.l: I am glad I had her for you, Sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Come Princes,
Come Friends and Lovers all, come noble Gentlemen,
No more Guns now, nor hates, but joyes and triumphs,
An univerſal gladneſs fly about us:
And know however ſubtle men dare caſt,
And promiſe wrack, the gods give peace at laſt,

div.head: The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Monſieur Marine, the Noble Gent. but none of the wiſeſt.
Jaques, an old ſervant to Marine's family,
Clerimont, a Gull, Coſin to Monſieur Marine.
A Gentleman, Servant to Marine's wife.

list.head: two Courtiers that plot to abuſe Marine.

list.item: Shattillion, a Lord, mad for Love.

list.head: Women.
list.item: Clerimont's Wife, a ſimple countrey Gentlewoman,

div.head: PROLOGUE.
div.l: WIT is become an Antick, and puts on
As many ſhapes of variation,
To court the times applauſe, as the times dare,
Change ſeveral faſhions, nothing is thought rare
Which is not new, and follow'd, yet we know
That what was worn ſome twenty years agoe,
Comes into grace again, and we purſue
That cuſtom, by preſenting to your view
A Play in faſhion then, not doubting now
But 'twill appear the ſame, if you allow
Worth to their noble memory, whoſe name,
Beyond all power of death, live in their fame.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: WHat happineſs waits on the life at Court,
What dear content, greatneſs, delight and eaſe?
What ever-ſpringing hopes, what tides of honor?
That raiſe their fortunes to the height of wiſhes?
What can be more in man, what more in nature,
Than to be great and fear'd? A Courtier,
A noble Courtier, 'Tis a name that draws
Wonder and duty from all eyes and knees.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And ſo your Worſhips Land within the Walls,
Where you ſhall have it all inclos'd, and ſure.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Peace knave; dull creature, bred of ſweat and ſmoke,
Theſe myſteries are far above thy faith:
But thou ſhalt ſee—

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And then I ſhall believe;
Your fair revenues, turn'd into fair ſuits;
I ſhall believe your Tenant's bruis'd and rent
Under the weight of Coaches, all your ſtate
Drawn through the ſtreets in triumph, ſuits for places
•• ed with a Mine of Gold, and being got
• ed with a great ſtream. I ſhall believe all this.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: You ſhall believe, and know me glorious.
Coſin, good day and health.

sp.speaker: Coſin.
sp.l: The ſame to you, Sir,
And more, without my wiſhes, could you know
What calm content dwels in a private houſe:
Yet look into your ſelf, retire: this place
Of promiſes, and proteſtations, fits
• ſ • nds only bent to ruin, you ſhould know this,
You have their language perfect, you have tutors
• do not doubt, ſufficient: but beware.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: You are merry Coſin:

sp.speaker: Coſin.
sp.l: Yet your patience,
You ſhall learn that too, but not like it ſelf,
Where it is held a virtue; tell me Sir,
Have you caſt up your State, rated your Land,
And find it able to endure the change
Of time and faſhion? is it always harveſt?
Always vintage? have you Ships at Sea,
To bring you Gold and Stone from rich Peru,
Monthly returning Treaſure? doth the King
Open his large Exchequer to your hands
And bid ye be a great man? can your wife
Coin off her beauty? or the week allow
•• uits to each day? and know no ebb in honor?
• f theſe be poſſible, and can hold out,
Then be a Courtier ſtill, and ſtill be waſting,

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Coſin, pray give me leave:

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I have done.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I could requite your gall, and in a ſtrain
• s bitter, and as full of Rubarb, preach
• gainſt your Countrey life, but 'tis below me
And only ſubject to my pitty, know
The eminent Court, to them that can be wiſe,
• nd faſten on her bleſſings, is a Sun
That draws men up from courſe and earthly Being,
• mean theſe men of merit that have power
• nd reaſon to make good her benefits,
• earns them a manly boldneſs, gives their tongues
• weetneſs of Language, makes them apt to pleaſe;
•• les of all rudeneſs, and uncivil haviour,
• hews them as neat in carriage, as in cloaths;
Coſin, have you ever ſeen the Court?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: No Sir,
Nor am I yet in travel with that longing.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Oh the ſtate and greatneſs of that place
Where men are found
Only to give the firſt creation glory!
Thoſe are the models of the antient world
• eft like the Roman Statues to ſtir up
Our following hopes, the place it ſelf puts on
The brow of Majeſty, and flings her luſtre
• ike the air newly light'ned; Form, and Order,
• re only there themſelves, unforc'd, and ſound,
As they were firſt created to this place.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: You nobly came, but will goe from thence baſe.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: 'Twas very pretty, and a good conceit;
You have a wit good Coſin, I do joy in't,
Keep it for Court: but to my ſelf again,
When I have view'd theſe pieces, turn'd theſe eyes,
• nd with ſome taſte of ſuperſtition,
• ook'd on the wealth of Nature, the fair dames,
• eauties, that light the Court, and make it ſhew
• ike a fair heaven, in a froſty night:
• nd 'mongſt theſe mine, not pooreſt, 'tis for tongues
Of bleſſed Poets, ſuch as Orpheus was,
To give their worth and praiſes; Oh dear Coſin:
You have a wife, and fair, bring her hither,
Let her not live to be the Miſtriſs of a Farmers heir
And be confin'd ever to a ſearge,
Far courſer than my horſe-cloth.
Let her have Velvets, Tiffinies, Jewels, Pearls,
A Coach, an Uſher, and her two Lacquies,
And I will ſend my wife to give her rules,
And read the rudiments of Court to her.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Sir, I had rather ſend her to Virginia
To help to propagate the Engliſh Nation.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Sirrah, how ſlept your Miſtriſs, and what viſitants Are to pay ſervice?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: As I came out,
Two Counts were newly ent'red.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: This is greatneſs,
But few ſuch ſervants wait a Countrey beauty.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: They are the more to thank their modeſty,
God keep my Wife, and all my Iſſue Female
From ſuch upriſings.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: What? my learned Doctor?
You will be welcome, give her health and youth
And I will give you gold. Exit Doctor.
Coſin, how favors this? is it not ſweet
And very great, taſts it not of Nobleneſs?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Faith Sir, my pallat is too dull and lazie
I cannot taſte it, 'tis not for my reliſh,
But be ſo ſtill.
Since your own miſery muſt firſt reclaim ye,
To which I leave you, Sir,
If you will, yet be happy, leave the humor
And baſe ſubjection to your Wife, be wiſe,
And let her know with ſpeed, you are her Husband,
I ſhall be glad to hear it.
My horſe is ſent for, Exit.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Even ſuch another countrey thing as this
Was I, ſuch a piece of dirt, ſo heavy,
So provident to heap up ignorance,
And be an aſs: ſuch muſty cloaths wore I,
So old and thred-bare, I do yet remember
Divers young Gallants lighting at my Gate,
To ſee my honoured Wife, have offered pence,
And bid me walk their horſes, ſuch a ſlave
Was I in ſhew then: but my eyes are open'd.
Many ſweet morrows to my worthy Wife.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: 'Tis well, and aptly given, as much for you,
But to my preſent buſineſs, which is money—

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Lady, I have none left.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I hope you dare not ſay ſo, nor imagine ſo baſe and low,
A thought: I have none left?
Are theſe words fitting for a man of worth,
And one of your full credit? Do you know
The place you live in? me? and what I labour
For, you? and your advancement?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Yes my deareſt.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: And do you pop me off with this ſlight anſwer,
In troth I have none left? in troth you muſt have;
Nay ſtare not, 'tis moſt true, ſend ſpeedily
To all that love you, let your people flye
Like thunder, through the City,
And not return under five thouſand Crowns-
Try all, take all, let not a worthy Merchant be untempted
Or any one that hath the name of Money,
Take up at any Uſe, give Band, or Land,
Or mighty Statutes, able by their ſtrength,
To tye up Sampſon, were he now alive,
There muſt be money gotten; for be perſwaded,
If we fall now, or be but ſeen to ſhrink,
Under our fair beginnings, 'tis our ruin,
And then good night to all, (but our diſgrace)
Farewel the hope of coming happineſs,
And all the aims we levied at ſo long.
Are ye not mov'd at this? no ſenſe of want,
Towards your ſelf yet breeding? be old,
And common; jaded to the eyes
Of Grooms, and Pages, Chamber-maids, and Guarders,
And when you have done, put your poor houſe in order
And hang your ſelf, for ſuch muſt be the end
Of him that willingly forſakes his hopes
And hath a joy to tumble to his ruin.
All that I ſay is certain, if ye fail
Do not upbraid me with it, I am clear.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Now heaven forbid I ſhould do wrong to you
My deareſt Wife, and Madam; yet give leave
To your poor creature to unfold himſelf.
You know my debts are many more than means,
My bands not taken in, my friends at home
Drawn dry with theſe expences, my poor Tenants
More full of want than we, then what new courſe
Can I beget, to raiſe thoſe crowns by? ſpeak,
And I ſhall execute.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Pray tell me true,
Have you not Land in the Countrey?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Pardon me, I had forgot it.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Sir, you muſt remember it,
There is no remedy, this Land muſt be,
In Paris e'r to morrow night.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: It ſhall, let me conſider, ſome 300 acres
Will ſerve the turn.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: 'Twill furniſh at all points,
Now you ſpeak like your ſelf, and know like him,
That means to be a man, ſuſpect no leſs
For the return will give ye five for one,
You ſhall be great to morrow, I have ſaid it.
Farewel, and ſee this buſineſs be a-foot,
With expedition. Exit Wife.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Health, all joy, and honor
Wait on my lovely Wife. What? Juques, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Sir, did you call?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I did ſo, hie thee Jaques.
Down to the Bank, and there to ſome good Merchant
(Conceive me well, good Jaques, and be private)
Offer 300 acres of my Land:
Say it is choice and fertile, ask upon it
Five thouſand Crowns, this is the buſineſs
I muſt employ thee in, be wiſe and ſpeedy.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Sir, do not do this.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Knave, I muſt have money,

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: If you have money thus, your knave muſt tell ye
You will not have a foot of Land left, be more wary,
And more friend to your ſelf, this honeſt Land
Your Worſhip has diſcarded, has been true,
And done you loyal ſervice.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Gentle Jaques,
You have a merry wit, employ it well
About the buſineſs you have now in hand.
When ye come back, enquire me in the Preſence,
If not in the Tennis-Court, or at my houſe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: If this vain hold, I know where to enquire ye.
Five thouſand Crowns! this, with good husbandry,
May hold a month out, then 5000 more,
And more Land a bleeding for't, as many more,
And more Land laid aſide. God and St. Dennis
Keep honeſt minded young men batchelors.
'Tis ſtrange, my Maſter ſhould be yet ſo young
A puppy, that he cannot ſee his fall
And got ſo near the Sun. I'll to his Coſin.
And once more tell him on't, if he fail,
Then to my Mortgage, next unto my ſale. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Longovile, Bewford, and the Servant.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Gentlemen, hold on diſcourſe a while,
I ſhall return with knowledge how and where
We ſhall have beſt acceſs unto my Miſtriſs
To tender your devotions.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Be it ſo: Exit.
Now to our firſt diſcourſe.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: I prethee peace;
Thou canſt not be ſo bad, or make me know
Such things are living, do not give thy ſelf
So common and ſo idle, ſo open vile,
So great a wronger of thy worth, ſo low,
I cannot, nor I muſt not credit thee.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Now by this light I am a whoremaſter,
An open, and an excellent whormaſter,
And take a ſpecial glory that I am ſo:
I thank my Stars I am a whoremaſter,
And ſuch a one as dare be known and ſeen,
And pointed at to be a noble wencher.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Do not let all ears hear this, hark he Sir,
I am my ſelf a whoremaſter, I am
Believe it Sir (in private be it ſpoken)
I love a whore directly, moſt men are wenchers,
And have profeſt the Science, few men
That look upon ye now, but whoremaſters,
Or have a full deſire to be ſo.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: This is noble.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: It is without all queſtion, being private,
And held as needful as intelligence,
But being once diſcover'd, blown abroad,
And known to common ſenſes, 'tis no more
Than geometrical rules in Carpenters,
That only know ſome meaſure of an Art,,
But are not grounded: be no more deceived,
I have a conſcience to reclaim you, Sir.
Miſtake me not: I do not bid you leave your whore
Or leſs to love her; forbid it,
I ſhould be ſuch a villain to my friend,
Or ſo unnatural: 'twas never harbor'd here,
Learn to be ſecret firſt, then ſtrike your Deer.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Your fair inſtructions, Mouſieur, I ſhall learn.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: And you ſhall have them; I deſire your care.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: They are your ſervants.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: You muſt not love.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: How Sir?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: I mean a Lady, there's danger.
She hath an Uſher and a Waiting Gentlewoman,
A Page, a Coach-man, theſe are fee'd and fee'd
And yet for all that will be prating.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: You underſtand me Sir, they will diſcover't,
And there is a loſs of credit, Table-talk
Will be the end of this, or worſe, than that;
Will this be worthy of a Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Proceed good Sir.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Next leave your City Dame;
The beſt of that Tribe, are moſt meerly coy,
Or moſt extreamly fooliſh, both which vices
Are no great ſtirrers up, unleſs in Husbands
That owe this Cattle, fearing her that's coy
To be but ſeeming, her that's fool too forward.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: This is the rareſt fellow, and the ſoundeſt,
I mean in knowledge, that e'r wore a Codpiece,
H'as found out that will paſs all Italy,
All France and England; to their ſhames I ſpeak,
And to the griefs of all their Gentlemen,
The noble Theory of Luxury.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Your patience,
And I will lay before your eyes a courſe
That I my ſelf found out, 'tis excellent,
Eaſie, and full of freedome.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: O good Sir,
You rack me till I know it.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: This it is,
When your deſire is up, your blood well heated
And apt for ſweet encounter, chuſe the night,
And with the night your Wench, the ſtreets have ſtore,
There ſeize upon her, get her to your chamber,
Give her a cardecew, 'tis royal payment;
When ye are dull, diſmiſs her, no man knows,
Nor ſhe her ſelf, who hath encountred her.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: O but their faces.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Nere talke of faces:
The night allows her equal with a Dutcheſs,
Imagination doth all think her fair,
And great, clapt in Velvet, ſhe is ſo,
Sir, I have tryed thoſe, and do find it certain
It never failes me, 'tis but twelve nights ſince
My laſt experience.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: O my meiching Varlet, I'll fit ye as I live.
'Tis excellent, I'll be your Scholar Sir.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: You are fairly welcome both: troth Gentlemen
You have been ſtrangers, I could chide you for't,
And taxe ye with unkindneſs, What's the news?
The Town was never empty of ſome novelty;
Servant, What's your intelligence?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Faith nothing.
I have not heard of any worth relating.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Nor I ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Then give me attention,
Monſieur Shattillion's mad.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Mad?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Mad as May-butter,
And which is more, mad for a Wench.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange, and full of pity.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: All that comes near him
He thinks are come of purpoſe to betray him,
Being full of ſtrange conceit: the wench he loved
Stood very near the Crown.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Alaſs good Monſieur;
A' was a proper man, and fair demean'd,
A perſon worthy of a better temper.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: He is ſtrong opinion'd that the Wench he lov'd
Remains cloſe priſoner by the Kings command:
Fearing her title, when the poor grieved Gentlewoman
Follows him much lamenting, and much loving
• n hope to make him well, he knows her not,
Nor any elſe that comes to viſit him.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Let's walk in Gentlemen, and there diſcourſe
His further miſeries, you ſhall ſtay dinner,
As truth you muſt obey.

sp.speaker: Om.
sp.l: We are your ſervants. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: There's no good to be done, no cure to be wrought
Upon my deſperate Kinſman: I'll to horſe
And leave him to the fools whip, miſery.
I ſhall recover twenty miles this night,
My horſe ſtands ready, I'll away with ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Sir, may I crave your name?

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: Yes Sir you may:
My name is Cleremont.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: 'Tis well, your faction?
What party knit you with?

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: I Know no parties,
• or no Factions, Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Then weare this Croſs of white:
And where you ſee the like they are my friends,
Obſerve them well, the time is dangerous,

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: Sir keep your croſs, I'll weare none, ſure this fellow
Is much beſide himſelf, grown mad.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: A word Sir;
You can pick nothing out of this, this croſs
Is nothing but a croſs, a very croſs,
Plain, without ſpell, or witchcraft, ſearch it,
You may ſuſpect, and well, there's poyſon in't,
Powder, or wild-fire, but 'tis nothing ſo.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: I do believe you, Sir, 'tis a plain croſs.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Then do your worſt, I care not, tell the King,
Let him know all this, as I am ſure he ſhall;
When you have ſpit your venome, then will I
Stand up a faithful, and a loyal Subject,
And ſo God ſave His Grace, this is no Treaſon.

sp.speaker: Couſ.
sp.l: He is March mad, farewell Monſieur. Exit Couzen.

sp.speaker: Shat
sp.l: Farewel;
I ſhall be here attending, 'tis my life
They aime at, there's no way to ſave it, well
Let 'em ſpread all their nets: they ſhall not draw me
Into any open Treaſon, I can ſee,
And can beware, I have my wits about me,
I thank heaven for't.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: There he goes,
That was the faireſt hope the French Court bred,
The worthieſt and the ſweeteſt, temper'd ſpirit,
The trueſt, and the valianteſt, the beſt of judgment,
Till moſt unhappy I: ſever'd thoſe virtues,
And turn'd his wit wild with a coy denial,
Which heaven forgive me, and be pleas'd, O heaven
To give again his ſenſes: that my love
May ſtrike off all my follies.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Lady.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: I Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Your will with me ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Sir, I come.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: From the dread fovereign King, I know it Lady,
He is a gracious Prince, long may he live,
Pertain you to his chamber?

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: No indeed Sir,
That place is not for women, Do you know me?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Yes, I do know you.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: What's my name? pray you ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: That's all one, I do know you and your buſineſs,
You are diſcover'd Lady, I am wary,
It ſtands upon my life; pray excuſe me,
The beſt man of this Kingdom ſent you hither,
To dive into me, have I toucht you? ha?

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: You are deceiv'd Sir, I come from your love,
That ſends you fair commends, and many kiſſes.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Alaſs, poor ſoul, How does ſhe? Is ſhe living?
Keeps ſhe her bed ſtill?

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Still Sir, She is living,
And well, and ſhall do ſo,

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Are ye in counſel?

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: No Sir, nor any of my ſex.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Why ſo,
If you had been in counſel, you would know,
Her time to be but ſlender; ſhe muſt die.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: I do believe it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: And ſuddenly,
She ſtands too near a fortune.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo,
There is no jeſting with a Princes Title,
Would we had both been born of common parents,
And liv'd a private and retir'd life,
In homely cottage, we had then enjoyed,
Our loves, and our embraces theſe are things,
That cannot tend to Treaſon —

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: I am wretched.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: O I pray as often for the King as any,
And with as true a heart, for's continuance,
And do moreover pray his heirs may live;
And their fair iſſues, then as I am bound
For all the ſtates and commons: if theſe prayers
Be any wayes ambitious, I ſubmit,
And lay my head down, let 'em take it off;
You may informe againſt me, but withall
Remember my obedience to the Crown,
And ſervice to the State.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Good Sir, I love ye.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Then love the gracious King, and ſay with me

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Heaven ſave his Grace.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: This is ſtrange—
A woman ſhould be ſent to undermine me,
And buz love into me to try my ſpirit;
Offer me kiſſes, and enticing follies,
To make me open, and betray my ſelf;
It was a ſubtile and a dangerous plot,
And very ſoundly followed, ſarewel Lady,
Let me have equal hearing, and relate
I am an honeſt Man. Heaven ſave the King. Exit.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: I'll never leave him, till, by art or prayer,
I have reſtor'd his ſenſes, If I make
Him perfect Man again, he's mine, till when,
I here abjure all loves of other men. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jaques.
sp.l: Nay, good Sir be perſwaded, go but back,
And tell him hee's undone, ſay nothing elſe;
And you ſhall ſee how things will work upon't.

sp.speaker: Cozen.
sp.l: Not ſo good Jaques, I am held an aſſe,
A Countrey Fool, good to converſe with dirt,
And eate courſe bread, weare the worſt Wooll,
Know nothing but the high-way to Paris,
And wouldſt thou have me bring theſe ſtains,
And imperfections to the riſing view
Of the right worſhipful thy worthy Maſter?
They muſt be bright, and ſhine, their cloaths
Soft Velvet, and the Tyrian Purple
Like the Arabian gums, hung like the Sun,
Their golden beames on all ſides;
Such as theſe may come and know
Thy Maſter, I am baſe, and dare not ſpeak unto him,
Hee's above me.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: If ever you did love him, or his ſtate,
His name, his iſſue, or your ſelf, go back:
'Twill be an honeſt and a noble part
Worthy a Kinſman; ſave 300 Acres
From preſent execution; they have had ſentence,
And cannot be repriev'd, be merciful.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Have I not urg'd already all the reaſons,
I had to draw him from his will? his ruin?
But all in vain, no counſel will prevail;
H'as ſixt himſelf, there's no removing, Jaques,
'Twill prove but breath and labor ſpent in vain,
I'll to my horſe, farewell.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: For Gods ſake, Sir,
As ever you have hope of joy, turn back;
I'll be your ſlave for ever, do but go,
And I will lay ſuch fair directions to you
That if he be not doting on his fall,
He ſhall recover ſight, and ſee his danger,
And ye ſhall tell him of his Wives abuſes,
I fear, too foul againſt him; how ſhe plots,
With our young Mounſiers, to milk-dry her husband,
And lay it on their backs; the next her pride;
Then what his debts are, and how infinite
The curſes of his Tenants, this will work
I'll pawn my life and head, he cries away,
I'll to my houſe in the Countrey.

sp.speaker: Co.
sp.l: Come, I'll go, and once more try him,
If he yield not, ſo,
The next that tryes him ſhall be want and woe. Exe ••• .

l.hi: Jaques.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Sir. Within.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Riſe Jaques 'tis grown day,
The Country life is beſt, where quietly,
Free from the clamor of the troubled Court,
We may enjoy our own green ſhadowed walks,
And keep a moderate diet without art.
Why did I leave my houſe, and bring my Wife,
To know the manner of this ſubtile place?
I would, when firſt the luſt to fame and honor,
Poſſeſt me, I had met with any evil,
But that; had I been tied to ſtay at home,
And earn the bread for the whole family,
With my own hand, happy had I been.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Sir, this is from your wonted courſe at home,
When did ye there keep ſuch inordinate hours?
Goe to bed late? ſtart thrice? and call on me?
Would you were from this place; our Countrey ſleeps,
Although they were but of that moderate length
That might maintain us in our daily work,
Yet were they ſound and ſweet.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I Jaques, there we dreamt not of our Wives, we lay together;
And needed not; now at length my Cozens words,
So truly meant, mixt with thy timely prayers
So often urged, to keep me at my home,
Condemn me quite.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: 'Twas not your fathers courſe:
He liv'd and dy'd in Orleance, where he had
His Vines as fruitful as experience
(Which is the art of Husbandry) could make;
He had his preſſes for 'em, and his wines
Were held the beſt, and out-ſold other Mens,
His corn and cattel ſerv'd the neighbor Town •
With plentiful proviſion, yet his thrift
Could miſs one Beaſt amongſt the heard;
He rul'd more where he liv'd, than ever you will here.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis true, why ſhould my Wife then, 'gainſt my good,
Perſwade me to continue in this courſe?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Why did you bring her hither at the firſt,
Before you warm'd her blood with new delights?
Our Countrey ſports could have contented her;
When you firſt married her a puppet-play
Pleas'd her as well as now the tilting doth.
She thought her ſelf brave in a bugle chain,
Where Orient pearl will ſcarce content her now.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Sure Jaques, ſhe ſees ſomething for my good
More than I do; ſhe oft will talk to me
Of Offices, and that ſhe ſhortly hopes,
By her acquaintance with the friends ſhe hath,
To get a place ſhall many times outweigh
Our great expences, and if this be ſo—

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Think better of her words, ſhe doth deceive you,
And only for her vain and ſenſual ends
Perſwade ye thus. Let me be ſet to dwell
For ever naked in the bareſt ſoil,
So you will dwell from hence.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I ſee my folly,
Pack up my ſtuffe, I will away this morne.
Haſte—haſte.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I, now I ſee your Father's honors
Trebling upon you, and the many prayers
The Countrey ſpent for him, which almoſt now
Begun to turn to curſes, turning back,
And falling like a mighty ſhower
Upon ye.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Goe, call my Wife.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: But ſhall ſhe not prevail,
And ſway you, as ſhe oft hath done before?

sp.speaker: Gent
sp.l: I will not hear her, but raile on her,
Till I be ten miles off.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: If you be forty,
'Twill not be worſe Sir:

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Call her up,

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I will Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Why what an Aſs was I that ſuch a thing
As a Wife is could rule me?
Know not I that woman was created for the man,
That her deſires, nay all her thoughts ſhould be
As his are? is my ſenſe reſtor'd at length?
Now ſhe ſhall know, that which ſhe ſhould deſire,
She hath a husband that can govern her,
If her deſires leads me againſt my will;
Are you come?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: What ſad unwonted courſe
Makes you raiſe me ſo ſoon, that went to bed
So late laſt-night.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: O you ſhall goe to bed ſooner hereafter,
And be rais'd again at thriſty hours:
In Summer time wee'l walk
An hour after our Supper, and to bed,
In Winter you ſhall have a ſet at Cards,
And ſet your Maids to work.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I will no more of your new tricks, your honors,
Your Offices, and all your large preferments,
Which ſtill you beat into my ears, hang o'er me,
I'll leave behind for others, the great ſway
Which I ſhall bear at Court: my living here
With countenance of your honoured friends,
I'll be content to loſe: for you ſpeak this
Only that you may ſtill continue here
In wanton eaſe: and draw me to conſume,
In cloaths and other things idle for ſhew,
That which my Father got with honeſt thrift.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Why, who hath been with you Sir,
That you talk thus out of Frame.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: You make a fool of me:
You provide one to bid me forth to ſupper,
And make me promiſe; then muſt ſome one or other
Invite you forth, if you have born your ſelf
Looſely to any Gentleman in my ſight
At home, you ask me how I like the carriage,
Whether it were not rarely for my good,
And open'd not a way to my preferment?
Come, I perceive all: talk not, we'll away.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Why Sir, you'll ſtay till the next triumph Day be paſt?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I, you have kept me here triumphing
This ſeven years, and I have ridden through the ſtreets,
And bought embroyder'd hoſe and foot-cloths too,
To ſhew a ſubjects zeal, I rode before
In this moſt gorgeous habit, and ſaluted
All the acquaintance I could eſpie
From any window, theſe are wayes ye told me
To raiſe me; I ſee all: make you ready ſtraight,
And in that Gown which you came firſt to Town in,
Your ſafe-guard, cloak, and your hood ſutable:
Thus on a double gelding ſhall you amble,
And my man Jaques ſhall be ſet before you.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: But will you goe?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: And ſhall I too?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: And you ſhall too.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: But ſhall I by this light?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Why by this light you ſhall.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Then by this light
You have no care of your Eſtate, and mine.
Have we been ſeven years venturing in a Ship,
And now upon return, with a fair wind,
And a calm Sea, full fraught with our own wiſhes,
Laden with wealth and honor to the brim,
And ſhall we flye away and not receive it?
Have we been tilling, ſowing, labouring,
With pain and charge a long and tedious winter,
And when we ſee the corn above the ground,
Youthful as is the Morn and the full eare,
That promiſes to ſtuffe our ſpacious garners,
Shall we then let it rot, and never reap it?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Wife talke no more, your Rhetorick comes too late,
I am inflixible; and how dare you
Adventure to direct my courſe of life?
Was not the husband made to rule the Wife?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: 'Tis true: but where the man doth miſs his way,
It is the Womans part to ſet him right;
So Fathers have a power to guide their Sons
In all their courſes, yet you oft have ſeen
Poor little children, that have both their eyes,
Lead their blind Fathers.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: She has a plaguy wit,
I ſay you'r but a little piece of man.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: But ſuch a piece, as being t • ne away,
Man cannot laſt: the faireſt and talleſt ſhip,
That ever ſail'd, is by a little piece of the ſame
Wood, ſteer'd right, and turn'd about.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: 'Tis true ſhe ſayes, her anſwers ſtand with reaſon.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: But Sir, your Cozin put this in your head,
Who is an enemy to your preferment,
Becauſe I ſhould not take place of his wife;
Come, by this kiſs, thou ſhalt not go ſweet heart.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Come, by this kiſs I will go Sweet-heart,
On with your riding ſtuffe; I k • ow your tricks,
And if preferment fall ere you • e ready,
'Tis welcome, elſe adieu the Ci • y life.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Well, Sir, I will obey.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: About it then,

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: To pleaſe your humor I would dreſs my ſelf,
In the moſt loathſome habit you could name,
Or travel any whether o're the World,
If you command me, it ſhall ne'r be ſaid,
The frailty of a woman, whoſe weak mind,
Is often ſet on looſe delights, and ſhews,
Hath drawn her husband to conſume his ſtate,
In the vain hope of that which never fell.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: About it then, women are pleaſant creatures,
When once a man begins to know himſelf.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: But hark you Sir, becauſe I will be ſure,
You ſhall have no excuſe, no word to ſay
In your defence hereafter; when you ſee
What honors were prepar'd for you and me,
Which you thus willingly have thrown away,
I tell you I did look for preſent honor,
This morning for you, which I know had come:
But if they do not come ere I am ready
(Which I will be the ſooner leaſt they ſhould)
When I am once ſet in a countrey life,
Not all the power of earth ſhall alter me,
Not all your prayers or threats ſhall make me ſpeak
The leaſt words to my honorable friends,
To do you any grace.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I will not wiſh it.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: And never more hope to be honorable,

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: My hopes are lower.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: As I live you ſhall not,
You ſhall be ſo far from the name of noble
That you ſhall never ſee a Lord again;
You ſhall not ſee a Maske, or Barriers,
Or Tilting, or a ſolemn Chriſtning,
Or a great Marriage, or new Fire-works,
Or any bravery; but you ſhall live
At home, beſpotted with your own lov'd durt,
In ſcurvy cloaths, as you were wont to doe,
And to content you, I will live ſo too.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Tis all I wiſh, make haſte, the day draws on,
It ſhall be my care to ſee your Stuffe packt up.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: It ſhall be my care to gull you: you ſhall ſtay. Ex. Gen.
And more than ſo, intreat me humbly too,
You ſhall have honors preſently; Maria.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Bring hither, pen, ink, and paper.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: 'Tis here.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Your Maſter will not ſtay,
Unleſs preferment come within an hour.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let him command one of the City gates,
In time of mutiny, or you may provide him,
To be one of the counſel for invading,
Some ſavage Countrey to plant Chriſtian faith.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: No, no, I have it for him, call my page;
Now, my dear husband, there it is will fit you. Ex. Maria.
And when the world ſhall ſee what I have done,
Let it not move the ſpleen of any Wife,
To make an Aſs of her beloved husband,
Without good ground, but if they will be drawn
To any reaſon by you, do not gull them;
But if they grow conceited of themſelves,
And be fine Gentlemen, have no mercy,
Publiſh them to the World, 'twill do them good
When they ſhall ſee their follies underſtood,
Go bear theſe Letters to my ſervant,
And bid him make haſte, I will dreſs my ſelf,
• n all the Journey-Cloaths I us'd before,
Not to ride, but to make the Laughter more. Exit.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Is all packt up?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: All, all Sir, there is no tumbler
Runs through his hoop with more dexterity,
Then I about this buſineſs: 'Tis a day,
That I have long long'd to ſee.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Come, Where's my Spurs?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Here, Sir, and now 'tis come.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I, Jaques, now,
I thank my fates, I can command my Wife.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I am glad to ſee it, Sir,

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I do not love alwayes,
To be made a puppie, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: But, yet me thinks your Worſhip does not look,
Right like a Countrey Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I will, give me my t'other hat.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Here.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: So, my Jerkin.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: On with it Jaques, thou and I
Will live ſo finely in the Countrey, Jaques,
And have ſuch pleaſant walks into the Woods
A mornings, and then bring home riding-rods,
And walking ſtaves—

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: And I will bear them, Sir,
And Skurdge-ſticks for the children.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: So thou ſhalt,
And thou ſhalt do all, over-ſee my Work-folkes,
And at the weeks end pay them all their wages,

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I will, Sir, ſo your Worſhip give me Money.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt receive all too: give me my Drawers.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: They are ready, Sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: And I will make thy Miſtriſs,
My wife, look to her landrie, and her dairy,
That we may have our linnen clean on Sundayes.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: And Holy-dayes.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I, and ere we walk about the Grounds
Provide our break-faſt,
Or ſhe ſhall ſmoke, I'll have her a good huſwife;
She ſhall not make a voyage to her Siſters,
But ſhe ſhall live at home,
And feed her pullen fat, and ſee her Maides
In bed before her, and lock all the doors.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Why that will be a life for Kings and Queens.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Give me my Scarfe with the great Button quickly.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: 'Tis done, Sir.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Now my Mittens,

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Here they are, Sir,

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: 'Tis well: now my great dagger.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: There.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Why ſo; thus it ſhould be, now my riding rod.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: There's nothing wanting, Sir.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Another, man, to ſtick under my girdle.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: There it is.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: All is well.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Why now methinks your Worſhip looks
Like to your ſelf, a Man of means and credit,
So did your grave and famous Anceſtors,
Ride up and down to Fairs, and cheapen cattel.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Goe, haſten your Miſtriſs, Sirra.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: It ſhall be done. Ex. Jaques.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Who's that? who's that Boy?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: I think it be my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Who, he that walkes in gray, whisking his riding rod?

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, 'tis he.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis he indeed; he is prepar'd
For his new journey; when I wink upon you,
Run out and tell the Gentleman 'tis time—
Monſieur good day.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Monſieur, your Miſtriſs is within, but yet not ready.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: My buſineſs is with you, Sir; 'tis reported,
I know not whether by ſome enemy
Maliciouſly, that envies your great hopes,
And would be ready to ſow diſcontents
Betwixt his Majeſty, and you, or truely,
Which on my faith I would be ſorry for,
That you intend to leave the Court in haſte.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Faith, Sir, within this half hour. Jaques?

sp.speaker: Jaques within:
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Is my VVife ready?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Preſently.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: But Sir,
I needs muſt tell you, as I am your friend,
You ſhould have ta'en your journey privater,
For 'tis already blaz'd about the Court.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: VVhy Sir, I hope it is no Treaſon, is it?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis true, Sir, but 'tis grown the common talk,
There's no diſcovery elſe held, and in the preſence
All the Nobility and Gentry,
Have nothing in their mouths but only this,
Monſieur Marine, that noble Gentleman,
Is now departing hence: every Mans face
Looks ghaſtly on his fellows; ſuch a ſadneſs
(Before this day) I ne'er beheld in Court,
Mens hearts begin to fail them when they hear it,
In expectation of the great event
That needs muſt follow it, pray Heaven it be good!

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: VVhy, I had rather all their hearts ſhould fail,
Than I ſtay here until my purſe fail me.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: But yet you are a Subject, and beware,
I charge you by the love I bear to you,
How you do venture raſhly on a courſe,
To make your Sovereign jealous of your deeds,
For Princes jealouſies, where they love moſt,
Are eaſily found, but they be hardly loſt.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Come, theſe are tricks, I ſmell 'em, I will goe.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Have I not ſtill profeſt my ſelf your friend?

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Yes, but you never ſhewd it to me yet.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: But now I will, becauſe I ſee you wiſe,
And give ye thus much light into a buſineſs,
That came to me but now, be reſolute,
Stand ſtifly to it that you will depart,
And preſently.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Why ſo I mean to doe.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: And by this light you may be what you will;
Will you be ſecret, Sir?

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Why? What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: The King does fear you.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: How?
And is now in Counſel;

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: About me?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: About you, and you be wiſe,
You'll find he's in Counſel about you:
His Counſellors have told him all the truth.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: What truth?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why, that which now he knows too well.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: What is't?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: That you have followed him ſeven years,
With a great train: and though he have not grac't you,
Yet you have div'd into the hearts of thouſands,
With liberality and noble carriage;
And if you ſhould depart home unprefer'd,
All diſcontented, and ſeditious ſpirits
Would flock to you, and thruſt you into action:
With whoſe help, and your Tenants, who doth not know
(If you were ſo diſpos'd:)
How great a part of this yet fertile peaceful Realm of France
• ou might make deſolate? but when the King
Heard this—

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: What ſaid he?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Nothing, but ſhook,
• s never Chriſtian Prince did ſhake before.
• ad to be ſhort, you may be what you will?
〈◊〉 be not ambitious Sir, ſit down
With moderate honors, leaſt you make your ſelf
• ore fear'd.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I know, Sir, what I have to doe
• mine own buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Where's Monſieur Mount Marine.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why there he ſtands, will you ought with him?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Yes: Good day Monſieur Marine.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Good day to you.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: His Majeſty doth commend himſelf,
• oſt kindly to you Sir, and hath, by me,
• ent you this favor: kneel down, riſe a Knight.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I thank his Majeſty.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: And he doth further requeſt you,
• ot to leave the Court ſo ſoon,
• or though your former merits have been ſlighted,
• fter this time there ſhall no Office fall;
Worthy your ſpirit, as he doth confeſs
• here's none ſo great, but you ſhall ſurely have it.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Do you hear? if you yield yet you are an aſs.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I'll ſhew my ſervice to his Majeſty
• greater things than theſe, but for this ſmall one
• muſt intreat his Highneſs to excuſe me.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I'll bear your Knightly words unto the King,
•• d bring his Princely anſwer back again. Exit Long.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Well ſaid, be reſolute a while, I know
• here is a tide of honors coming on.
• warrant you.
Where is this new made Knight?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Let me enfold you in my arms,
Then call you Lord, the King will have it ſo,
Who doth entreat your Lordſhip to remember
His Meſſage ſent to you by Longavile.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: If ye be durty, and dare not mount aloft;
You may yield now, I know what I would do.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Peace, I will fit him; tell his Majeſty
I am a Subject, and I do confeſs
I ſerve a gracious Prince, that thus hath heapt
Honors on me without deſert, but yet
As for the Meſſage, buſineſs urgeth me,
I muſt be gone, and he muſt pardon me,
Were he ten thouſand Kings and Emperors.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: I'll tell him ſo.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why, this was like your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: As he hath wrought him, 'tis the fineſt fellow
That e're was Chriſtmaſs Lord, he carries it
So truely to the life, as though he were
One of the plot to gull himſelf. Exit Bewf.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why ſo, you ſent the wiſeſt and the ſhrewdeſt anſwer
Unto the King, I ſwear, my honored friend,
That ever any Subject ſent his Liege.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Nay now I know I have him on the hip,
I'll follow it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: My honorable Lord,
Give me your noble hand right courteous Peer,
And from henceforth be a courtly Earl;
The King ſo wills, and Subjects muſt obey:
Only he doth deſire you to conſider
Of his requeſt.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why faith you'r well my Lord, yield to him.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Yield? why 'twas my plot.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Nay, 'twas your Wives plot.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: To get preferment by it,
And thinks he now to pop me i'th' mouth
But with an Earldome? I'll be one ſtep higher.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis the fineſt Lord, I am afraid anon
He will ſtand upon't to ſhare the Kingdom with him.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Where's this Courtly Earl?
His Majeſty commends his love unto you;
And will you but now grant to his requeſt,
He bids you be a Duke, and chuſe of whence.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Why if you yield not now, you are undone,
What can you wiſh to have more, but the Kingdom?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: So pleaſe his Majeſty, I would be D. of Burgundy,
Becauſe I like the place.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: I know the King is pleas'd.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Then will I ſtay and kils his Highneſs hand.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: His Majeſty will be a glad man when he hears it.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: But how ſhall we keep this from the world's ear,
That ſome one tell him not, he is no Duke?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: VVee'l think of that anon.
Why Gentlemen, Is this a gracious habit for a Duke?
Each gentle body ſet a finger to
To pluck the clouds of this his riding weeds
From off the orient Sun of his beſt cloaths;
I'll pluck one Boot and ſpur off.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I another.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: I'll pluck his Jerkin off.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sit down my Lord;
Both his ſpurs off at once good Longavile,
And Bewford, take that Scarfe off, and that Hat,
Doth not become his largely ſprouting fore-head.
Now ſet your gracious foot to this of mine,
One pluck will do it, ſo, off with the other.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Loe, thus your ſervant Long avile doth pluck
The trophy of your former gentry off.
Off with his Jerkin Bewford.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Didſt thou never ſee
A nimble footed Taylor ſtand ſo in his ſtockings,
Whilſt ſome friend help'd to pluck his Jerkin off,
To dance a Jigg?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Here's his man Jaques come,
Booted and ready ſtill.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: My Miſtriſs ſtayes;
Why how now Sir? What do's your Worſhip mean,
To pluck your grave and thrifty habit off.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: My ſlippers, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: O thou mighty Duke,
Pardon this Man,
That thus hath treſpaſſed in ignorance.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I pardon him.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: His Graces ſlippers, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Why what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Foot-man, he's a Duke:
The King hath rais'd him above all his Land.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I'll to his Cozen preſently, and tell him ſo;
O what a dung-hill Countrey rogue was I. Exit Jaques.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: See, ſee, my Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Let's obſ • rve their greeting.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Unto your will, as every good Wife ought,
I have turn'd all my thoughts, and now am ready.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: O Wife, I am not worthy to kiſs the leaſt
Of all thy toes, much leſs thy Thumb,
Which yet I would be bold with; all thy counſel
Hath been to me Angelical, but mine to thee
Hath been moſt dirty, like my mind:
Dear Ducheſs I muſt ſtay.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: VVhat are you mad, to make me
Dreſs, and undreſs, turn and wind me,
• ecauſe you find me plyant? ſaid I not
The whole world ſhould not alter me, if once
were reſolv'd? and now you call me Ducheſs:
VVhy what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Loe a Knight doth kneel.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: A Knight?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: A Lord.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: A Fool.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: I ſ • y doth kneel an Earl, a Duke.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: In Drawers.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: VVithout ſhoes.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Sure you lunatick.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: No, honoured Ducheſs,
If you dare but believe your ſervants truth,
I know he is a Duke.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: God ſave his Grace.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I ask your Graces pardon.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Then I riſe,
And here, in token that all ſtrife ſhall end,
'Twixt thee and me, I let my drawers fall,
And to thy hands I do deliver them:
Which ſignifies, that in all acts and ſpeeches,
From this time forth, my Wife ſhall wear the breeches.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: An honorable compoſition. Exeunt omnes.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: SHall I believe thee, Jaques?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Sir you may.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: Didſt thou not dreame?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I did not,

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: Nor imagine?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Neither of both: I ſaw him great and mighty,
I ſaw the Monſieurs bow, and heard them cry,
Good health and fortune to my Lord the Duke.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: A Duke art ſure? a Duke?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I am ſure a Duke,
And ſo ſure, as I know my ſelf for Jaques.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: Yet the Sun may dazel; Jaques, Was it not
Some leane Commander of an angry Block-houſe
To keep the Fleemiſh Eele-boats from invaſion,
Or ſome bold Baron able to diſpend
His fifty pounds a year, and meet the foe
Upon the Kings command, in gilded canvas,
And do his deeds of worth? or was it not
Some place of gain, as Clerk to the great Band
Of maribones, that people call the Switzers?
Men made of Beufe and Sarcenet?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Is a Duke his chamber hung with Nobles like a preſence?

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: I am ſomething wavering in my faith;
Would you would ſettle me, and ſwear 'tis ſo,
Is he a Duke indeed?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I ſwear he is.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: I am ſatisfied, he is my Kinſman. Jaques,
And I his poor unworthy Cozen.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: True, Sir.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: I might have been a Duke too, I had means,
A wife as fair as his, and as wiſe as his;
And could have brookt the Court as well as his,
And laid about her for her husbands honor:
O Jaques, had I ever dreamt of this,
I had prevented him.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Faith Sir it came
Above our expectation, we were wiſe
Only in ſeeking to undoe this honor,
Which ſhewed our dung-hill breeding and our durt.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: But tell me Jaques,
Why could we not perceive? what dull Divel
Wrought us to croſs this noble courſe, perſwading
'Twould be his overthrow? 'fore me a Courtier
Is he that knows all, Jaques, and does all,
'Tis as his noble Grace hath often ſaid,
And very wiſely, Jaques, we are fools,
And underſtand juſt nothing.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I, as we were, I confeſs it.
But riſing with our great Maſter,
We ſhall be call'd to knowledge with our places,
'Tis nothing to be wiſe, not thus much there,
There's not the leaſt of the billet dealers,
Nor any of the Paſtry, or the Kitchin,
But have it in meaſure delicate.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: Methinks this greatneſs of the Dukes my Cozens,
(I ask you mercy, Jaques, that near name
Is too familiar for me) ſhould give promiſe
Of ſome great benefits to his attendants.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I have a ſuit my ſelf, and it is ſure,
Or I miſtake my ends much.

sp.speaker: Coz.
sp.l: What is't Jaques,
May I not crave the place?

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, you ſhall,
'Tis to be but his Graces Secretary,
Which is my little all, and my ambition,
Till my known worth ſhall take me by the hand,
And ſet me higher; how the fates may do
In this poor thread of life, is yet uncertain;
I was not born I take it for a Trencher,
Nor to eſpouſe my Miſtriſs Dairy-maid.

sp.speaker: Couz.
sp.l: I'll furniſh her, that is a ſpeeding cour • e,
And cannot chuſe but breed a mighty fortune;
What a fine youth was I, to let him ſtart,
And get the riſe before me? I'll diſpatch,
And put my ſelf in Moneys.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Maſs 'tis true,
And now you talke of Money; Sir, my buſineſs
For taking thoſe Crowns muſt be diſpatcht:
This little plot in the Countrey lies moſt fit
To do his Grace ſuch ſerviceable uſes,
I muſt about it.

sp.speaker: Couz.
sp.l: Yet, before you goe,
Give me your hand, and bear my humble ſervice
To the great Duke your Maſter, and his Ducheſs,
And live your ſelf in favor: ſay my Wife
Shall there attend them ſhortly, ſo farewell.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: I'll ſee you mounted, Sir,

sp.speaker: Couz.
sp.l: It may not be,
Your place is far above it, ſpare your ſelf,
And know I am your ſervant, fare ye well. Exit Couzen.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Sir I ſhall reſt to be commanded by you,
This place of Secretary will not content me,
I muſt be more and greater: let me ſee;
To be a Baron is no ſuch great matter
As people take it: for ſay I were a Count,
I am ſtill an under-perſon to this Duke,
Which methinks ſounds but harſhly: but a Duke?
O I am ſtrangely taken, 'tis a Duke
Or nothing, I'll adviſe upon't, and ſee
What may be done by wit and induſtry. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: It muſt be carried cloſely with a care
That no man ſpeak unto him, or come near him,
Without our private knowledge, or be made
Afore-hand to our practice:
My good husband,
• ſhall entreat you now to ſtay a while,
• ad prove a noble coxcomb.
Gentlemen,
• our counſel and advice about this carriage.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Alas good man, I do begin to mourn.
His dire Maſſacre: what a perſecution
• s pouring down upon him? ſure he is ſinful.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Let him be kept in's chamber under ſhew
Of ſtate and dignity, and no man ſuffer'd
To ſee his noble face, or have acceſs,
But we that are Conſpirators.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Or elſe down with him into the Countrey amongſt his Tenants,
There he may live far longer in his greatneſs,
And play the fool in pomp amongſt his fellows.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: No, he ſhall play the fool in the City, and ſtay,
• will not loſe the greatneſs of this jeſt,
That ſhall be given to my wit, for the whole Revenues.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Then thus wee'll have a guard about his perſon,
That no man come too near him, and our ſelves
Alwayes in company; have him into the City
To ſee his face ſwell; whilſt, in divers corners,
• ome of our own appointing ſhall be ready
To cry heaven bleſs your Grace, long live your Grace.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Servant, your counſel's excellent good,
