• nd ſhall be follow'd, 'twill be rarely ſtrange
To ſee him ſtated thus, as though he went
• ſhroving through the City, or intended
To ſet up ſome new Wake:
I ſhall not hold
From open laughter, when I hear him cry,
Come hither my ſweet Ducheſs: let me kiſs
Thy gracious lips: for this will be his phraſes?
I fear me nothing but his legs will break
Under his mighty weight of ſuch a greatneſs.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Now me thinks deareſt Lady you are too cruel;
His very heart will freeze in knowing this.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: No, no, the man was never of ſuch deepneſs,
To make conceit his Maſter: Sir, I'll aſſure ye
He will out-live twenty ſuch pageants.
Were he but my Cozen, or my Brother.
And ſuch a deſperate killer of his fortune,
In this belief he ſhould dye, though it coſt me
A thouſand Crowns a day to hold it up;
Or were I not known his wife, and ſo to have
An equal feeling of this ill he ſuffers,
He ſhould be thus till all the Boyes i'th' Town
Made ſute to weare his badges in their hats,
And walk before his Grace with ſticks and noſe-gayes,
We Married Women hold —

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: 'Tis well, no more.
The Duke is entring, ſet you faces right,
And bow like Countrey Prologues: here he comes.
Make room afore, the Duke is entring.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: The choiſeſt fortunes wait upon our Duke,

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: And give him all content and happineſs.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Let his great name live to the end of time.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We thank you, and are pleas'd to give you notice
We ſhall at fitter times wait on your Loves,
Till when, be near Us.

sp.speaker: Longv.
sp.l: 'Tis a valiant purge, and works extreamly;
'T has delivered him
Of all Right worſhipful and gentle humors,
And left his belly full of nobleneſs.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: It pleaſed the King my Maſter,
For ſundry vertues not unknown to him,
And the all-ſeeing ſtate, to lend his hand,
And raiſe me to this Eminence, how this
May ſeem to other Men, or ſtir the minds
Of ſuch as are my fellow Peers, I know not,
I would deſire their loves in juſt deſigns.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Now by my faith he does well, very well:
Beſhrew my heart I have not ſeen a better,
Of a raw fellow, that before this day
Never rehearſt his ſtate: 'tis marvellous well.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Is he not Duke indeed, ſee how he looks
As if his ſpirit were a laſt, or two
Above his veins, and ſtretcht his noble hide.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Hee's high-brac't like a Drum, pray God he break not

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Why let him break, there's but a Calves-skin loſt.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: May it pleaſe your Grace to ſee the City,
'Twill be to the minds and much contentment
Of the doubtful people,

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I am determin'd ſo, till my return
I leave my honour'd Dutcheſs to her chamber.
Be careful of your health, I pray you be ſo.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Your Grace ſhall ſuffer us your humble ſervants
To give attendance, fit ſo great a perſon
Upon your body.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I am pleaſed ſo.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Away good Bewford, raiſe a guard ſufficient
To keep him from the reach of Tongues, be quick;
And do you hear, remember how the ſtreets
Muſt be diſpos'd with, for cries, and ſalutations.
Your Grace determines not to ſee the King —

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Not yet, I ſhall be ready ten dayes hence
To kiſs his Highneſs hand, and give him thanks,
As it is fit I ſhould for his great bounty.
Set forward Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.l: Room for the Duke there. Exeunt Duke and Train.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: 'Tis fit he ſhould have room to ſhew his mightineſs,
He ſwells ſo with his poyſon,
'Tis better to reclaim ye thus, than make
A ſheeps-head of you, It had been but your due;
But I have mercy Sir, and mean to reclaim you
By a directer courſe.
That Woman is not worthy of a Soul
That has the ſovereign power to rule her husband,
And gives her title up, ſo long provided
As there be fair play, and his ſtate not wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Shat
sp.l: I would be glad to know whence this new Duke ſprings,
The people buz abroad; or by what title
He receiv'd his dignity, 'tis very ſtrange
There ſhould be ſuch cloſe jugling in the State,
But I am ty'd to ſilence, yet a day
May come, and ſoon to perfect all theſe doubts.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: It is the mad Shattillion by my Soul,
I ſuffer much for this poor Gentleman;
I'll ſpeak to him, may be he yet knows me.

l.hi: Monſieur Shattilion.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Can you give me reaſon from whence
This great Duke ſprang that walks abroad?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Even from the King himſelf.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: As you are a Woman, I think you may be cover'd?
Yet your prayer would do no harm good Woman.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: God preſerve him.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I ſay Amen, and ſo ſay all good Subjects.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Lady, as ever you have lov'd, or ſhall,
As you have hope of heaven lend your hand,
And wit, to draw this poor diſtracted man
Under your roofe, from the broad eyes of people,
And wonder of the ſtreets.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: With all my heart;
My feeling of his grief and loſs is much.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Sir, now you are come ſo near the priſon, will ye
Goe in, and viſit your fair Love: poor ſoul
She would be glad to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: This ſame Duke is but
Apocryphal, there's no creation
That can ſtand where titles are not right.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: 'Tis true, Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: This is another draught upon my life;
Let me examine well the words I ſpake.
The words I ſpake were, that this novel Duke
Is not o'th' true making, 'tis to me moſt certain.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: You are as right, Sir, as you went by line.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: And to the grief of many thouſands more.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: If there be any ſuch, God comfort them.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Whoſe mouths may open when the time ſhall pleaſe;
I'm betray'd, commend me to the King,
And tell him I am ſound, and crave but juſtice;
You ſhall not need to have your guard upon me,
Which I am ſure are plac'd for my attachment;
Lead on; I'm obedient to my bonds.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Good Sir be not diſpleaſed with us;
We are but ſervants to his Highneſs will,
To make that good.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I do forgive you even with my heart;
Shall I entreat a favor?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Any thing.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: To ſee my love before that fatal ſtroak,
And publiſh to the world my chriſtian death,
And true obedience to the Crown of France.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: I hope it ſhall not need Sir, for there is mercy
As well as Juſtice in his Royal heart. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Every man take his corner, here am I,
You there, and you in that place, ſo be perfect,
Have a great care your cries be loud; and faces
Full of dejected fear and humbleneſs.
He comes.

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Fye, how theſe ſtreets are charg'd and ſwell'd
With theſe ſame raſcally people? give more room,
Or I ſhall have occaſion to diſtribute
A martial almes amongſt you; as I am a Gentleman
I have not ſeen ſuch rude diſorder,
They follow him like a prize, there's no true gaper
Like to your Citizen, he will be ſure
The Beares ſhall not paſs by his door in peace,
But he and all his family will follow.
Room there afore: Sound:

sp.speaker: Ja.
sp.l: Give room, and keep your places,
And you may ſee enough; keep your places.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Theſe people are too far unmanner'd, thus
To ſtop your Graces way with multitudes.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Rebuke them not, good Monſieur, 'tis their loves
Which I will anſwer, if it pleaſe my ſtars
To ſpare me life and health.

sp.speaker: 2 Gen.
sp.l: Bleſs your Grace.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And you with all my heart.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Now heaven preſerve your happy dayes:

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I thank you too.

sp.speaker: 3. Gen.
sp.l: Now Heaven ſave your Grace;

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I thank you all.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: On there before.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Stand Gentlemen, ſtay yet a while.
For I am minded to impart my love
To theſe good people, and my friends,
Whoſe love and prayers for my greatneſs,
Are equal in abundance, note me well,
And with my words; my heart? for as the Tree—

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Your Grace had beſt beware, 'twill be inform'd
Your greatneſs with the people.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I had more,
My honeſt, and ingenious people.—But
The weight of buſineſs hath prevented me.
I am call'd from you: but this tree I ſpake of
Shall bring forth fruit, I hope, to your content,
And ſo I ſhare my bowels amongſt you all.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: A noble Duke, a very noble Duke.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Afore there Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: You'r faithfully met good Monſieur Mount Marine.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Be advis'd, the time is alter'd.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Is he not the ſame man he was afore?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Still the ſame man to you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: You have received mighty Grace, be thankful.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Let me not dye in ignorance;

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: You ſhall not.
Then know, the King out of his love, hath pleaſ'd
To ſtile him Duke of Burgundy.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: O great Duke,
Thus low, I plead for pardon, and deſire
To be enrol'd amongſt your pooreſt ſlaves.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Sir, you have mercy, and withal my hand,
From henceforth let me call you one of mine.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Make room afore there, and diſmiſs the people.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Every Man to his houſe in peace and quiet.

sp.speaker: Peop.
sp.l: Now heaven preſerve the Duke, heaven bleſs the Duke

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: This Letter came this morn from my Coſin
To the great Lady, high and mighty Ducheſs
Of burgundy, be theſe delivered. Oh,
For a ſtronger lace to keep my breath
That I may laugh the nine days till the wonder
Fall to an ebb: the high and mighty Ducheſs?
The high and mighty God? what a ſtile is this?
Methinks it goes like a Duchy lope-man,
A ladder of 100 rounds will fail
To reach the top on't: well my gentle Coſin
I know by theſe contents, your itch of honor;
You muſt to the Court you ſay, and very ſhortly:
You ſhall be welcome; and if your wife have wit
I'll put her in a thriving courſe, if not
Her own ſin on her own head not a blot
Shall ſtain my reputation, only this
I muſt for healths ſake ſometimes make an aſs
Of the tame moil my Husband; 'twill do him good,
And give him freſher brains, Me freſher bloud.
Now for the noble Duke, I hear him coming.
Your Grace is well return'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: As well as may be:
Never in younger health, never more able:
I mean to be your bed-fellow this night,
Let me have good encounter,

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Bleſs me heaven
What a hot meat this greatneſs is?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: It may be ſo,
For I'll be ſworn he hath not got a ſnap
This two months on my knowledge, or her woman
Is damn'd for ſwearing it

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I thank you Gentlemen for your attendance
And alſo your great pains, pray know my Lodgings
Petter and oftner, do ſo Gentlemen.
Now by my honor, as I am a Prince,
I ſpeak ſincerely, know my lodgings better,
And be not ſtrangers, I ſhall ſee your ſervice
And your deſervings, when you leaſt expect.

sp.speaker: Om.
sp.l: We humbly thank your grace for this great favor.

l.hi: Jaques?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Your Grace.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Be ready for the Countrey,
And let my Tenants know the Kings great love:
Say I would ſee them, but the weight at Court
Lies heavy on my ſhoulders: let them know
I do expect their duties in attendance
Againſt the next feaſt, wait for my coming
To take up Poſt-horſe, and be full of ſpeed. Exit Jaq.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I would deſire your Grace—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: You ſhall deſire, and have your
F • ll deſire: ſweet Ducheſs ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: To have ſome conference with a Gentleman
That ſeems not altogether void of reaſon.
He talks of Titles, and things near the Crown,
And knowing none ſo fit as your Grace,
To give the difference in ſuch points of State—

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: What is he? if he be noble, or have any part
That's worthy our converſe, we do accept him.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I can aſſure your Grace, his ſtrain is noble,
But he's very ſubtle.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Let him be ſo.
Let him have all the brains, I ſhall demonſtrate
How this moſt Chriſtian Crown of France can bear
No other ſhew of Title than the Kings.
• will go in and meditate for half an hour,
• nd then be ready for him preſently,
• will convert him quickly, or confound him.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Is mad Shattillion here?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Is here, and's Lady,
I prethee ſervant fetch him hither.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Why, what do you mean to put him to?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: To chat with the mad lad my Husband;
'Twill be brave to hear them ſpeak, babble,
Stare, and prate.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: But what ſhall be the end of all this, Lady?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Leave that to me, now for the grand diſpute,
For ſee, here comes Shattillion: as I live, methi • ks
All France ſhould bear part of his grieſs.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I'll fetch my Lord the Duke.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Where am I now, or whether will you lead me?
To my death? I crave my priviledge,
I muſt not dye, but by juſt courſe of Law.

sp.speaker: Serv,
sp.l: His Majeſty hath ſent by me your pardon,
He meant not you ſhould dye; but would intreat you
To la • the full ſtate of your Title open,
Unto a grave and Noble Gentleman.
The Duke of Burgundy who here doth come,
Who, either by his wiſdom will confute you,
Or elſe inform and ſatisfie the King.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: May't pleaſe your grace, this is the Gen • leman,

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is this he that chops Logick with my Liege?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: D'ye mock me? you are great, the time will come,
When you ſhall be as much contemn'd as I,
Where are the antient compliments of France,
The upſtarts brave the Princes of the bloud?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Your Title Sir, in ſhort.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: He muſt Sir,
Be a better Stateſ-man than your ſelf, that can
Trip me in any thing, I will not ſpeak
Before theſe witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Depart the room, for none ſhall ſtay,
No, not my deareſt Ducheſs.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: We'll ſtand behind the Arras and hear all. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: In that chair take your place, I in this,
Diſcourſe your Title now.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Sir, you ſhall know,
My Loves true Title, mine by Marriage,
Setting aſide the firſt race of French Kings,
Which will not here concern us, as Pharamond,
With Clodian, Meroveus, and Chilperick,
And to come down unto the ſecond Race,
Which we will likewiſe ſlip—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But take me with you.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I pray you give me leave, of Martel Charles,
The Father of King Pippin, who was, Sire
To Charles the Great, and famous Charlemain.
And to come to the third Race of French Kings,
Which will not be greatly pertinent in this cauſe,
Betwixt the King and me, of which you know
HƲGH CAPET was the firſt,
Next his Son Robert, Henry then, and Philip
With Lewis, and his Son a Lewis too,
And of that name the Seventh, but all this
Springs from a Female, as it ſhall appear.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Now give me leave, I grant you this your Title
At the firſt ſight, carries ſome ſhew of truth;
But if ye weigh it well, ye ſhall find light.
Is not his Majeſty poſſeſt in peace,
And juſtice executed in his name,
And can you think the moſt Chriſtian King
Would do this if he ſaw not reaſon for it?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: But had not the Tenth Lewis a ſole Daughter?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I cannot tell.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: But anſwer me directly.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: It is a moſt ſeditious queſtion.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Is this your juſtice?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I ſtand for my King.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Was ever Heir-apparant thus abus'd?
I'll have your head for this.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why, do your worſt.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Will no one ſtir to apprehend this Traitor?
A guard about my perſon, will none come?
Muſt my own royal hands perform the deed?
Then thus I do arreſt you.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Treaſon, help.

div.stage: Enter Wife, Long. Bew. and Serv.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Help, help, my Lord and Husband.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Help the Duke.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Forbear his grace's perſon.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Forbear you to touch him that
Your Heir-apparent weds,
But by this hand, I will have all your heads. Exit.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: How doth your Grace?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why? well.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: How do you find his Title?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: 'Tis a dangerous one,
As can come by a female.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: I, 'tis true,
But the Law Salique cuts him off from all.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I do beſeech your Grace, how ſtands his Title?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Pew, nothing; the Law Salique cuts him off from all.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: My gracious Husband, you muſt now prepare,
In all your Graces pomp to entertain
Your Coſin, who is now a convertite,
And follows here, this night he will be here.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Be ready all in haſte, I do intend,
To ſhew before my Coſin's wondring face,
The greatneſs of my pomp, and of my place.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: SIrrah, is all things carried to the Tailor?
The meaſure, and the faſhion of the Gown,
With the beſt trim?
Yes Sir, and 'twill be ready within this two days.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: For my ſelf I care not,
I have a ſuit or two of antient Velvet;
Which with ſome ſmall correcting and addition,
May ſteal into the preſence.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Would my Gown were ready; Husband, I'll lay my life,
To make you ſomething e'r to morrow night.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: It muſt not be
Before we ſee the Duke, and have advice,
How to behave our ſelves: lets in the while,
And keep our ſelves from knowledge, till time ſhall call us.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I much admire the fierce maſculine ſpirit,
Of this dread Amazon.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: This following night I'll have a wench in ſolace.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Sir, I hear you,
And will be with you if I live, no more.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: My Lady would intreat your preſence, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: We will obey your Lady, ſhe is worthy.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: You, light alone, a word, or two.

sp.speaker: M a.
sp.l: Your Will, Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Hark in your ear; wilt thou be married? ſpeak, wilt thou marry?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Married? to whom Sir?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: To a proper fellow, landed, and able bodied,

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Why do you flout me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I ſwear I do not; I love thee for thy Ladies ſake, be free?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: If I could meet ſuch matches as you ſpeak of,
I were a very child to loſe my time, Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: What ſaiſt thou to Monſieur Bewford?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Sir, I ſay he's a proper Gentleman, and far
Above my means to look at.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Doſt thou like him?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and ever did.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: He is thine own.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: You are too great in promiſes.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Be rul'd, and follow my advice, he ſhall be thine

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Would you would make it good, Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Do but thus,
Get thee a cuſhion underneath thy cloaths,
And leave the reſt to me.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I'll be your ſcholar,
I cannot loſe much by the venture ſure,

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Thou wilt loſe a pretty maidenhead, my rogue,
Or I am much o'th' bow hand, you'll remember
If all this take effect, who did it for you?
And what I may deſerve for ſuch a kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Yours Sir. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Save ye Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Save the King.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I pray you Sir, which is the neareſt way.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Save the King, this is the neareſt way.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Which is the neareſt way to the Poſt-houſe?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: God ſave the King and his Poſt-houſe.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I pray Sir, direct me to the houſe;

sp.speaker: Shyt.
sp.l: Heaven ſave the King, you cannot catch me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I do not underſtand you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: You do not, I ſay you cannot catch me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Not catch you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: No Sir, nor can the King,
With all his ſtratagems, and his forced tricks,
Although he put his Nobles in diſguiſe;
Never ſo oft to ſift into my words,
By courſe of Law, lay hold upon my life.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: It is buſineſs that my Lord the Duke
Is by the King imployed in, and he thinks
I am acquainted with it.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I ſhall not need to rip the cauſe up,
From the firſt, to you,
But if his Majeſty had ſuffer'd me
To marry her, though ſhe be after him,
The right heir general to the Crown of France.
I would not have convey'd her into Spain,
As it was thought, nor would I e'er have joyn'd,
With the reformed Churches, to make them,
Stand for my cauſe.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I do not think you would.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I thank you Sir,
And ſince I ſee you are a favourer
Of virtues, kept in bondage;
Tell directly to my ſoveraign King,
For ſo I will acknowledge him for ever,
How you have found my ſtaid affections
Setled for peace, and for the preſent ſtate.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: And good Sir, tell him further this,
That notwithſtanding all ſuggeſtions
Brought to him againſt me, and all his ſuſpitions,
Which are innumerable to my treaſons,
If he will warrant me but publique trial,
I'll freely yeild my ſelf into his hands;
Can he have more than this?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: No by my troth.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I would his Majeſty would hear but reaſon,
As well as you.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: But Sir, you do miſtake me,
For I never ſaw the King.
In all my life but once, therefore good Sir,
May it pleaſe you to ſhew me which is the Poſt-houſe.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: I cry you mercy, Sir, then you are my friend.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: And ſuch men are very rare with me,
The Poſt-houſe is hard by, farewel;

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I thank you, Sir, I muſt ride hard to night,
And it is dark already.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: I am cruel, to ſend this man directly to his death
That is my friend, and I might eaſily ſave him,
He ſhall not dye, come back, my friend, come back.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: What is your Will?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Do you not know?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Not I.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: And do you gather nothing by my face?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Virtue is ever innocent,
Lay not the fault on me, I grieve for you,
And wiſh that all my tears might win your ſafety.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Alas good friend you are undone,
The more ill fortune, mine to be the means
Of your ſad overthrow, you know not me.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: No truly Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Would you had never ſeen me,
I am a man purſu'd by the whole ſtate
And ſure ſome one hath ſeen me talk with you.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Yes, divers Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Why then your head is gone.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I'll out of town.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Would it were ſoon enough,
Stay if you love your life, or elſe you are taken.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: What ſhall I do?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: I'll venture deeply for him,
Rather than to caſt away an innocent,
Take courage friend, I will preſerve thy life,
With hazard of mine own.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I thank you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: This night thou ſhalt be lodg'd within my doors,
Which ſhall be all lock'd faſt, and in the morn
I'll ſo provide, you ſhall have free acceſs,
To the Sea-ſide, and ſo be ſhipt away,
• 'r any know it.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Good Sir, ſuddainly, I am afraid to dye.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Then follow me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: This way he went, and there's the houſe, I hope,
His better Angel hath directed him,
To leave the wandring ſtreets, poor Gentleman.
Would I were able with as free a heart,
To ſet his ſoul right, as I am to grieve,
The ruine of his fame, which God forgive me;
Sir, if you be within, I pray Sir ſpeak to me.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: I am within, and will be; what are you?

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: A friend.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: No Sir, you muſt pardon me,
I am acquainted with none ſuch: be ſpeedy,
• riend, there is no other remedy.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: A word Sir, I ſay, I am your friend.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: You cannot ſcape by any other means,
Be not fearful, God ſave the King,
What's your buſinéſs, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: To ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Speak out then?

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Shall I not come up?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not: flie if thou be'ſt thine own friend,
There lies the ſuit and all the furniture
Belonging to the head, on with it friend.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Sir do you hear?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: I do, God bleſs the King,
It was a habit I had laid aſide,
For my own perſon, if the ſtate had forced me.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Good Sir, unlock your door.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Be full of ſpeed, I ſee ſome 20 Muſquetiers in ambuſh
Whate'r thou art, know I am here and will be,
Seeſt thou this bloody ſword that cries revenge?
Shake not my friend, through millions of theſe foes
I'll be thy guard, and ſet thee ſafe aboard.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Dare you not truſt me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: My good ſword before me,
And my allegeance to the King I tell thee
Captain (for ſo I gheſs thee by thy Arms)
And the looſe ſlanks of Halberdiers about thee,
Thou art too weak, and fooliſh to attempt me.
If you be ready, follow me, and hark you
Upon your life ſpeak to no living wight,
Except my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Love
sp.l: Monſieur Shattillion?

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt not call agen; thus with my ſword,
And the ſtrong faith I bear unto the King;
Whom God preſerve, I will defend my chamber,
And cut thy throat, I ſwear I'll cut thy throat,
Steal after me and live.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: I will not ſtay.
The fury of a man ſo far diſtracted. Exit Love.
Where's the Officer that dares not enter,
To intrap the life of my diſtreſſed friend?
I, have you hid your ſelf? you muſt be found,
What do you fear? is not authority on your ſide
Nay, I know the Kings command
Will be your warrant, why then fear you? ſpeak
What ſtrange deſigns are theſe? Shattillion,
Be reſolute and bear thy ſelf upright.
Though the whole world deſpiſe thee: ſoft, methinks.
I heard a ruſhing which was like the ſhake
Of a diſcovered Officer, I'll ſearch
The whole ſtreet over, but I'll find thee out. Exit.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: How my joynts do ſhake, where had I been
But for this worthy Gentleman, that
Hath ſome touch of my infortunes; would I were
Safe under hatches once, for Callicut,
Farewel the pomp of Court, I never more
Can hope to be a Duke or any thing,
I never more ſhall ſee the glorious face
Of my fair ſpreading Lord that lov'd me well.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Fly you ſo faſt? I had a ſight of you,
But would not follow you; I was too wiſe,
You ſhall not lead me with a cunning trick;
Where you may catch me; poor Shattillion;
Hath the Kings anger left thee never a friend?
No, all mens loves move by the breath of Kings.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: It is the Gentleman that ſav'd my life, Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Bleſs Shattillion, another plot.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: No Sir, 'tis I.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Why, who are you?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Your friend whom you preſerv'd.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Whom I preſerv'd?
My friend? I have no woman friend but one,
Who is too cloſe in priſon to be here;
Come near, let me look on you.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: 'Tis I.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: You ſhould not be a woman by your ſtature.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I am none, Sir.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I know it, then keep off,
Strange men and times! how I am ſtill preſerv'd?
Here they have ſent a yeoman of the guard,
Diſguis'd in womans clothes, to work on me,
To make love to me; and to trap my words,
And ſo inſnare my life, I know you, Sir,
Stand back, upon your peril, can this be
In Chriſtian Common-weals, from this time forth
I'll cut off all the means to work on me,
I'll ne'er ſtir from my houſe: and keep my doors
Lockt day and night, and cheapen meat and drink
At the next ſhops by Signs, out of my window,
And having bought it, draw it up in my garters.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Sir, will you help me?

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Do not follow me,
I'll take a courſe to live, deſpight of men. Exit Shat.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: He dares not venture for me, wretched Jaques!
Thou art undone for ever and for ever,
Never to riſe again? what ſhall I do?
Where ſhall I hide me? here's one to take me,
I muſt ſtand cloſe, and not ſpeak for my life.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: This is the time of night, and this the haunt,
In which I uſe to catch my Waſtcoatiers,
It is not very dark, no, I ſhall ſpie 'em,
I have walk't out in ſuch a pitchy night.
I could not ſee my fingers this far off,
And yet have brought home veniſon by the ſmell,
I hope they have not left their old walk, ah?
Have I ſpied you ſitting by this light?
To me there's no ſuch fine ſight in the world,
As a white apron 'twixt twelve and one;
See how it gliſters? do you think to ſcape?
So now I have you faſt; come, and do not ſtrive,
It takes away the edge of appetite;
Come, I'll be liberal every way. Exeunt.
Take heed you make no noiſe, for waking of the Watch,

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Now the bleſſing of ſome happy guide,
To bring us to the Duke, and we are ready.
Come forward, ſee the door is open'd,
And two of his Gent. I'll ſpeak to them,
And mark how I behave my ſelf, God ſave ye;
For leſs I cannot wiſh to men of ſort, and of your ſeeming:
Are you of the Dukes?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: We are, Sir, and your ſervants, your ſalutes,
We give you back again with many thanks.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: When did you hear ſuch words before Wife? peace,
Do you not dare to anſwer yet; is't fit
So mean a Gentleman as my ſelf ſhould crave,
The preſence of the great Duke your Maſter?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Sir you may.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Shall we deſire your name, and buſineſs, Sir?
And we will preſently inform him of you,

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: My name is Cleremont.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: You are his Graces kinſman,
Or I am much miſtaken?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: You are right,
Some of his noble bloud runs through theſe veins,
Though far unworthy of his graces knowledge.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Sir, we muſt all be yours; his graces kinſman,
And we ſo much forgetful? 'twas a rudeneſs,
And muſt attend your pardon, thus I crave it:
Firſt to this beauteous Lady, whom I take
To be your Wife, Sir, next your mercy.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: You have it, Sir, I do not like this kiſſing,
It lies ſo open to a world of wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: This is the merry fellow; this is he
That muſt be noble too.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: And ſo he ſhall.
If all the Art I have can make him noble,
I'll dub him with a Knight-hood; if his wife
Will be but forward, and joyn iſſue,
I like her above excellent.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Wil't pleaſe you
To walk a turn or two, whilſt to the Duke
We make your comming known? Exit Serv. and Long

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I ſhall attend, Sir.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Theſe Gentlemen are very proper men,
And kiſs the beſt that e'er I taſted.
For goodneſs-ſake husband, let us never more
Come near the Countrey, whatſoe'er betide us;
I am in malice with the memory
Of that ſame ſtinking dung-hil.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Why now you are my chicken and my dear,
Love where I love, hate where I hate: now
You ſhall have twenty Gowns, and twenty Chains,
See, the door is opening.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.l: Room afore there, the Duke is entring.

div.stage: Enter Duke, Wife, Long. Servant, Maria.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: 'Tis the Duke, even he himſelf, be merry,
This is the golden age the Poet ſpeaks on.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I pray it be not brazen'd by their faces,
And yet methinks they are the neateſt Pieces
For ſhape, and cutting that e'er I beheld.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Moſt gracious Duke, my poor Spouſe and my ſelf,
Do kiſs your mighty foot, and next to that
The great hand of your Dutcheſs, ever wiſhing
Your honors ever ſpringing, and your years.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Coſin?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Your Graces vaſſal, far unworthy
The nearneſs of your blood.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Correct me not, I know the word I ſpeak,
And know the perſon.
Though I be ſomething higher than the place
Where common men have motion, and deſcending
Down with my eye, their forms are leſſened to me;
Yet from this pitch can I behold my own,
From millions of thoſe men that have no mark,
And in my fearful ſtoop, can make them ſtand,
When others feel my feet, and periſh: Coſin,
Be comforted, you are very welcome, ſo
Is your fair Wife: the charge of whom I give
To my own deareſt, and beſt beloved.
Tell me, you have reſolv'd your ſelf for Court,
And utterly renounc'd the ſlaviſh Countrey,
With all the cares thereof?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I have, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Have you diſmiſt your eating houſhold,
Sold your hangings of Nebuchadnezar, for ſuch they were,
As I remember, with the Furnitures
Belonging to your Beds and Chambers?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Have you moſt carefully ta'en off the Lead,
From you roof, weak with age, and ſo prevented
The ruin of your houſe, and clapt him
In a ſummer ſuit of thatch to keep him cool

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: All this I have perform'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Then lend me all your hands, I will embrace my Coſin
Who is an underſtanding Gentleman,
And with a zeal mighty, as is my name,
Once more I bid you welcome to the Court;
My ſtate again.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: As I was telling you, your Husband
Muſt be no more Commander, look to that,
Be ſeveral at meat, and lodging, let him have
Board-wages, and Diet, 'mongſt his men i' th' Town
For pleaſure, if he be given to't, let him have it,
Elſe as your own fancy ſhall direct you.
Coſin, you ſee this mighty man here: he was an aſs
When he came firſt to Town: indeed he was
Juſt ſuch another coxcomb as your Husband,
God bleſs the mark, and every good mans child!
This muſt not ſtir you Coſin.

sp.speaker: Wif.
sp.l: Heaven forbid?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Sweet Maria; provide the cuſhion ready for it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: It ſhall be done.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Receive all your advices from our ſelf,
Be once a day with us, and ſo farewel
For this time, my fair Coſin, Gentlemen
Conduct him to his Lodging.

sp.speaker: Duch.
sp.l: Farewel, and think upon my words.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I ſhall obſerve them. Exit Duke and Ducheſs.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Health, and the Kings continual love, attend you.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Oh for a private place to eaſe my Lungs!
Heaven give me patience, ſuch a pair of jades
Were never better ridden to this hour,
Pray heaven they hold out to the journeys end.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Twitch him aſide good Monſieur, whilſt I break
Upon the body of his ſtrength, his wife,
I have a conſtant promiſe: ſhe is my own.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Ply her to wind-ward Monſieur, you have taken
The moſt compendious way to raiſe your ſelf,
That could have been delivered by a Counſel.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I have ſome certain aims, Sir: but my wife—

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Your wife, you muſt not let that trouble you.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: It will Sir, to ſee her in a ſtrangers arms.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: What mean you? let her alone, be wiſe, ſtir not a foot
For if you do, all your hopes are buried:
I ſwear you are a loſt man if you ſtir.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I thank you Sir, I will be more advis'd.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: But what great Office do you level at?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Sir, they are kiſſing

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Let them kiſs,
And much may do their good hearts; they muſt kiſs
And kiſs, and double kiſs, and kiſs again,
Or you may kiſs the poſt for any riſing:
Had your noble kinſman ever mounted
To theſe high Spheres of honor, now he moves in,
But for the kiſſes of his wife?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I know not

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Then I do; credit me, he had been loſt,
A fellow of no mark, and no repute.
Had not his wife kiſt ſoon, and very ſweetly:
She was an excellent woman, and diſpatcht him
To his full being, in a moment, Sir— Exit. Long. and Wife.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: But yet methinks he would not take her, Sir,
Into a private room.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Now ſtand and flouriſh,
You are a mads man for ever.
• do envy you if you ſtand your fortunes up,
You are the happieſt man, but your great Coſin,
This day in Court: well, I will marry ſurely,
And not let every man out-run me thus.
'Tis time to be mine own friend, I live
•• town here, and direct the readieſt way,
To other men, and be a ſlave my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Nay, good Sir be not mov'd, I am your ſervant,
And will not be ungrateful for this knowledge.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Will you be walking home?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I would deſire to have my wife along.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: You are too raw,
Begone, and take no notice where you left her,
Let her return at leaſure. if ſhe ſtay
A month, 'twill be the better, underſtand me
This Gentleman can do't. Exit Coſin.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I will Sir, and wife remember me, a Duke, a Duke wife.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Aboard her Longaveile, ſhe's thine own,
To me the fooling of this fool is venery. Exit Servant.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Come, prethee come, have I not crowns? behold
• ad follow me, here; not a word, go in
Grope by the walls, and you ſhall find a bed,
Lie down there, ſee, ſee, a turn or two, to give
My blood ſome heats, and I am preſently
For action: darkneſs, by thy leave, I come. Exit Bew.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I am perfect in my leſſon, be my ſpeed,
Thou god of marriage, this is the door, I'll knock.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: within. Whoſe there, I cannot come yet.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Monſieur Bewford?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Stay till I light a candle, who are ye?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Sir? a poor Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Oh come in, I'll find a time for you too, be not loud.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Sir, you have found that time already, ſhame
On my ſoul therefore.

sp.speaker: Bew
sp.l: Why? what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Do you not ſee, Sir, is your light ſo dim?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Do you not wait on the Lady Mount Marine?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: I do Sir, but my love on you.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Poor ſoul! how cam'ſt thou by this big belly?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: By your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: By heaven I ne'er touch'd your body.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Yes, unſwear that oath again, I'll tell you all;
Theſe two years I have lov'd you, but the means
How to enjoy you, I did never know
Till Twelf-night laſt, when hearing of your game
To take up wenches private in the night,
I apprehended ſtraight this courſe to make
My ſelf as one of them, and wait your coming;
I did ſo, and enjoyed you, and now this child
That now is quick within me, hide my ſhame,
And marry me, or elſe I muſt be forc'd—
Long. within. Monſieur Bewford, Monſieur Bewford.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Whoſe that calls?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Are you a bed?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: No Sir, the hangings.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Nay Monſieur, I'll forbid that, we'll have fair play,
Lend me your candle, are you taken Bewford?
A lecher of your practice, and cloſe carriage
To be diſcovered thus? I am aſham'd
So great a maſter in his art ſhould fail,
And ſtagger in his grounds.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: You're wide,
This woman and my ſelf are man and wife,
And have been ſo this half year,
Where are you now? have I been diſcover'd?
You cannot break ſo eaſily on me, Sir,
I am too wary to be open'd by you.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: But theſe are but illuſions. to give colour
To your moſt myſtick leachery, but Sir,
The belly hath betraid you all, it muſt out.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Good Longaveil believe me on my faith,
I am her husband.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: On my faith I cannot, unleſs I ſaw
Your hands faſt, and your hearts.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Why Longavile, when did I give that to your ears,
That was not truth? by all the world ſhe's mine,
She is my wife, and to confirm you better
I give my ſelf again, here take my hand
And I yours, we are once more married,
Will this content you?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Yes I am believing, and God give you joy.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: My loving wife, I will not wrong thee,
Since I am thine and only loved of thee
From this hour I vow my ſelf a new man,
Be not jealous: for though I had a purpoſe,
To have ſpent an hour or two in ſolace otherwiſe,
And was provided for it, yet my love
Shall put a better temper to my blood,
Come out thou woman of unwholſome life,
Be ſorry for thy ſins, and learn to mend,
Nay, never hide your face, you ſhall be ſeen.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Jaques, why Jaques, art thou that Jaques,
The very ſtaffe, and right hand of our Duke?
Speak, thou bearded Venus.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I am he, by miracle preſerv'd to be that Jaques,
Within this two hours Gentlemen, poor Jaques
Was but as coarſe in grave: a man of wiſdom,
That of my conſcience, if he had his right
Should have a pretty State, but that's all one
That Noble Gentleman did ſave this life,
I keep it for him, 'tis his own.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Oh Bacchus! is all the world drunk? come we'll to the Duke
And give thanks for this delivery.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: NOt gone unto my Tenants to relate
My Grace and Honor; the mightineſs
Of my new name, which would have ſtruck a terror
Through their courſe doublets, to their very hearts?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Alas, great Lord and Maſter, I could ſcarce
With ſafety of my life return again
Unto your graces houſe, and but for one
That had ſome mercy, I had ſure been hang'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: My houſe?

sp.speaker: Jrq.
sp.l: Yes Sir, this houſe, your houſe i'th' Town.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Jaques we are diſpleas'd, hath it no name?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: What name?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Dull rogue; what hath the King beſtow'd
So many honors, open'd all his ſprings,
And ſhow'red his graces down upon my head,
And has my houſe no name? no title yet?
Burgundy houſe you aſs.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Your graces mercy,
And when I was come off, and had recover'd
Burgundy houſe, I durſt not yet be ſeen,
But lay all night for fear of purſevants
In Burgundy privie houſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Oh Sir, 'tis well,
Can you remember now? but Jaques know
Since thy intended journey is ſo croſt,
I will go down my ſelf this morning.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Have I not ſaid this morning?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: But conſider,
That nothing is prepared yet for your journey,
Your graces teams not here to draw your cloaths;
And not a Carrier yet in town to ſend by.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I ſay once more go about it,
You're a wiſe man, you'd have me linger time,
Till I have worn theſe cloaths out: will ye go? Ex. Jaq.
Make ye ready Wife

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: I am ſo, mighty Duke.

sp.speaker: Duke,
sp.l: Nay, for the Countrey.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: How? for the Countrey?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes I am reſolv'd to ſee my Tenants in this bravery,
Make them a ſumptuous feaſt, with a ſlight ſhew,
Of Dives and Lazarus, and a ſquib or two,
And ſo return.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Why Sir? you are not mad?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How many Dukes have ye known mad? I pray ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: You are the firſt, Sir, and I hope the laſt,
But you are ſtark horn-mad.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Forbear good wife.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: As I have faith you're mad: your horns
Have been too heavy for you, and have broke
Your skull in pieces: If you be in earneſt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Well, you ſhall know my skull and wits are whole
E'r I have done, and yet I am in earneſt.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Why, do you think I'll go?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I know you ſhall.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: I ſhall? by what authority ſhall I?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I am your Husband.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: True, I confeſs it,
And by that name, the world hath given you
A power to ſway me; but Sir, you ſhall know
There is a greater bond that ties me here,
Allegeance to the King, has he not heapt
Thoſe honors on you to no other end,
But to ſtay you here, and ſhall I have a hand
In the offending ſuch a gracious Prince?
Beſides, our own undoings lies upon't,
Were there no other cauſe, I do not ſee,
Why you ſhould go: If I ſhould ſay you ſhould not.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Do you think ſo?

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Yes faith.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Now good wife make me underſtand that point.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Why that you ſhall, did I not bring you hither?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: And were not all theſe honors wrought out of the fire by me?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: By you?

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: By me? how ſtrange you make it?
When you came firſt, did you not walk the Town,
In a long Cloak half compaſs? an old Hat,
Lin'd with Vellure, and on it for a band,
A skein of crimſon Cruil?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I confeſs it.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: And took baſe courſes?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Baſe?

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Baſe, by this light, extream baſe, and ſcurvie, monſtrous baſe.

sp.speaker: Duſte.
sp.l: What were theſe courſes, wife?

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Why, you ſhall know,
Did you not thus attir'd, trot up and down,
Plotting for vild and lowſie Offices,
And agreed with the Sergeant of the Bears,
To buy his place? deny this, if you can.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why it is true.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: And was not that monſtrous baſe?

sp.speaker: Duke,
sp.l: Be advis'd wife, a Bear's a Princely beaſt.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: A Bear?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes wife, and one ſide veniſon.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: You're more than one ſide fool, I am ſure of that.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But ſince you have vext me wife, know you ſhall go
Or you ſhall never have penny from me.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Nay, I have done, and though I know 'twill be
Your overthrow, I'll not forſake you now.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Be ready then. Exit Duke

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: I will.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: What are you married Bewford?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: I, as faſt as words, and hearts, and hands, and Prie • can make u •

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Oh Gentlemen, we are undone.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: This Gentleman, the Lord of Lorgue, my Husband
Will be gone down to ſhew his play-fellows
Where he is gay.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: What, down into Countrey?

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Yes faith, was ever fool but he ſo croſs?
I would as fain be gracious to him,
As he could wiſh me, but he will not let me;
Speak faithfully, will he deſerve my mercy?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: According to his merits he ſhould wear,
A guarded coat, and a great wooden dagger.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: If there be any woman that doth know,
The duties 'twixt a Husband and his wife,
Will ſpeak but one word for him, he ſhall ſcape;
Is not that reaſonable? but there's none,
Be ready therefore, to purſue the plot
We had againſt a pinch, for he muſt ſtay.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Wait you here for him, whilſt I goe
And make the King acquainted with your ſport,
For fear he be incens'd for our attempting
Places of ſo great honor. Exit Long.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Go, be ſpeedy.

div.stage: Enter Duke, Coſin, Wife, Jaques, Man.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come let me ſee how all things are diſpos'd of.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: One Cart will ſerve for all your furniture,
With room enough behind to eaſe the Footman,
A capcaſe for you linnen, and your plate,
With a ſtrange lo • k that opens with Amen,
For my young Lord, becauſe of eaſie portage,
A quiver of your graces lin'd with Cunney,
Made to be hang'd about the Nurſes neck,
Thus, with a Scarfe or Towel.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Very good.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Nay, 'tis well, but had you ſtaid another week,
I would have had you furniſht, in ſuch pomp,
As never Duke of Burgundy was furniſht,
You ſhould have had a Sumpter, though 't had coſt me
The laying on my ſelf, where now you are fain,
To hire a Rippers mare, and buy new doſſers,
But I have got them painted with your Arms,
With a fair darnex Carpet of my own
• aid croſs for the more ſtate.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Jaques I thank you: your Carpet ſhall be bruſht
• nd ſent you home; what, are you ready wife?

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: An hour ago.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I cannot chuſe but kiſs thy royal Lips,
Dear Ducheſs mine, thou art ſo good a woman.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Youl'd ſay ſo if you knew all, goodman Duckling.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: This was the happieſt fortune could beſal me
Now in his abſence will I follow cloſe
• ine own preferment, and I hope e'r long,
• o make my mean and humble name ſo ſtrong,
• s my great Coſins, when the world ſhall know,
• bear too hot a ſpirit to live low.
The next Spring will I down, my wife and houſhold,
• have my Uſhers, and my four Lacquies,
• rſpare Caroches too, but mum, no more,
• hat I intend to do, I'll keep in ſtore.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Mountey, mountey, Jaques, be our Querry.

sp.speaker: Groom.
sp.l: To horſe there Gentlemen, and fall in couples.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come honoured Ducheſs.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Stand thou proud man.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Thieves, Jaques, raiſe the people.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: No, raiſe no people, 'tis the Kings command,
Which bids thee once more ſtand, thou haughty man,
Thou art a monſter, for thou art ungrateful,
•• d like a fellow of a rebel nature,
• aſt flung from his embraces: and for
• s honors given thee, haſt not return'd
• o much as thanks, and to oppoſe his Will,
• eſolv'd to leave the Court, and ſet the Realm
•• re, in diſcontent, and open action:
• herefore he bids thee ſtand, thou proud man,
Whilſt with the whisking of my ſword about,
• take thy honors off: this firſt ſad whisk
• akes off thy Dukedom, thou art but an Earl.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: You are miſtaken, Longavile.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Oh would I were: this ſecond whisk divides
• hy Earldom from thee, thou art yet a Baron.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No more whisks if you love me Longavile.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Two whisks are paſt, and two are yet behind,
Yet all muſt come, but not to linger time.
With theſe two whisks I end, now mount Marine,
For thou art now no more, ſo ſays the King,
And I have done his Highneſs Will with grief.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Degraded from my honors?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: 'Tis too certain.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I am no Traitor ſure, that I know of;
Speak Jaques, haſt thou ever heard me utter word
Tending to Treaſon, or to bring in the enemy?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Alas Sir, I know nothing,
Why ſhould your Worſhip bring me in to hang me?
I never medled
But with the bruſhing of his cloaths, or f • tching
In water in a morning for his hands.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Are the • e the honors of this place? Anthony
Help me to ta • e her Gown off quickly,
Or I'll ſo ſwinge ye • or't —

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Why H • sband? Sir?

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: I'll • ot looſe a penny by this town.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Why what do you mean, Sir, have her to her lodging,
And there undre • s her, I will wait upon her.

sp.speaker: Coſ.
sp.l: Indeed you ſhall not, your month is out I take it,
Get you out before me wife;
Coſin farewel, I told you long agoe,
That pride begins with pleaſure, ends with woe.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Goe thy way ſentences, 'twill be thy fortune,
To live and dye a Cucko'd, and Churchwarden.
Oh my poor Husband! what a heavy fortune
Is fallen upon him?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Methinks 'tis ſtrange,
That heaven fore-warning great men of their falls,
With ſuch plain tokens, they ſhould not avoid 'em?
For the laſt night betwixt eleven and twelve,
Two great and hideous blazing ſtars were ſeen
To fight a long hour by the clock, the one
Dreſt like a Duke, the other like a King;
Till at the laſt the crowned Star o'er-came.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Why do ye ſtand ſo dead, Monſieur Marine?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: So Caeſar fell, when in the Capitol
They gave his body two and thirty wounds.
Be warned all ye Peers, and by my fall,
Hereafter learn to let your wives rule all.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Monſieur Marine, pray let me ſpeak with you;
Sir, I muſt wave you to conceal this party,
It ſtands upon my utter overthrow;
Seem not diſcontented, nor do not ſtir afoot,
For if you do, you and your hope —
I ſwear you are a loſt man if you ſtir.
And have an eye to Bewford, he'll tempt you.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Come, come, for ſhame go down;
Were I Marine, I would go down:
And being there, I would rattle him ſuch an anſwer
Should make him ſmoke.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Good Monſieur Bewford, peace
Leave theſe rebellious words,
Or by the honors which I once enjoyed,
And yet may ſwear by,
I'll tell the King of your proceedings;
I am ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: You talkt of going down when 'twas not fit,
But now let's ſee your ſpirit,
A thouſand and a thouſand will expect it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why wife, are ye mad?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: No, nor drunk, but I'd have you know your own ſtrength.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: You talke like a moſt fooliſh woman, wife;
I tell you I will ſtay, yet I have a
Crotchet troubles me,

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: More crotchets yet?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Follow me Jaques, I muſt have thy counſel,
I will return again, ſtay you there wife.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I fear this loſs of honor will give him ſome few ſtools.

sp.speaker: Wif.
sp.l: No, no, he is reſolv'd, he will not
Stir a foot, I'll lay my life.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: I, but he's diſcontented, how ſhall we reſolve that,
And make him ſtay with comfort?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Faith Bewford we muſt even let nature work,
For he's the ſweeteſt temper'd man for that
As one can wiſh, for let men but go about to fool him,
And he'll have his finger as deep in't as the beſt;
But ſee where he comes frowning, bleſs us all!

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Off with your hats, for here doth come
The high and mighty Duke of Burgundy.
What ever you may think, I have thought
And thought, and thought upon't, and I find it plain,
The King cannot take back what he has given,
Unleſs I forfeit it by courſe of Law.
Not all the water in the River Seine,
Can waſh the blood out of theſe Princely veins.

sp.speaker: Wife,
sp.l: God-a-mercy Husband, thou art the beſt
To work out a thing at a pinch in France.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I will aſcend my State again,
Ducheſs, take your place,
And let our Champion enter.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Has he his Champion? that's excellent.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And let loud Muſick ſound before his entrance.
Sound Trumpet.

div.stage: Enter Jaques in Armor, one carrying a Scutcheon before him, and a two-handed Sword.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: How well our Champion doth demean himſelf,
As if he had been made for ſuch an action?
Methinks his ſturdy truncheon he doth weild,
Like Mars approaching to a bloody field.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I think there's no man ſo deſperate
To dare encounter with our Champion,
But truſt me, Jaques, thou haſt pleas'd us well;
Once more our warlike Muſick, then proceed.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: What wondrous age is this? what cloſe proceedings?
I hear the clang of Trumpets in this houſe,
To what intent do not our Stateſ-men ſearch?
Oh no, they look not into ſimple truth;
For I am true, and they regard not me,
A man in Armor too: God ſave the King,
The world will end, there's nought but treachery.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: I Jaques, ſervant to the high and mighty Godfrey, Duke of Burgundy, do come hither to prove by natural ſtrength, and activity of my body, without the help of ſorcery, inchantment, or negromancy, that the ſaid Godfrey, late of Mount Marine, and now of Burgundy, hath perfect right thereto, notwithſtanding the Kings command to the contrary, and no other perſon whatſoever: and in token that I will be ready to make good the ſame: I throw down my gage, which is my honor, pronounced the 37 of Feb. Stilo novo, God ſave the Duke.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Of all the plots the King hath laid for me
This was the ſhrewdeſt, 'tis my life they ſeek
And they ſhall have it: if I ſhould refuſe
To accept the challenge in the Kings behalf,
They have ſome cauſe to take away my life,
And if I do accept it, who can tell,
But I may fall by doubtful chance of War?
'Twas ſhrew'd, but I muſt take the leaſt of evils,
I take thy gauntlet up, thou treacherous man,
That ſtands in armed Coat againſt the King.
Whom God preſerve, and with my ſingle ſword,
Will juſtifie whatever he commands;
I'll watch him for catching of my words.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Jaques go on, defend our Princely Title.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Why ſhrink'ſt thou back? thou haſt an evil cauſe;
Come forward man, I have a rock about me,
I fight for my true Liege.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Go forward Jaques.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I do beſeech your Grace to pardon me,
I will not fight with him, with any elſe
I'll ſhew my reſolution ſpeedily.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Come, do thy worſt, for the King ſhall ſee
All is not true, that is reported of me.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I may not fight with him by Law of Arms.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What? ſhall my Title fall? wilt thou not fight?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Never with him that once hath ſav'd my life

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Dar'ſt thou not fight? behold then, I do go
Strong with the zeal I bear my Sovereign,
And ſeize upon that haughty man himſelf.
Deſcend the ſteps (that thou haſt thus uſurp'd
Againſt the King and State,) down to the ground,
And if thou do utter but a ſyllable
To croſs the Kings intent, thou art but dead;
There, lye upon the earth, and pine, and dye.
Did ever any man wade through ſuch ſtorms
To ſave his life, as poor Shattillion?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I fear this challenge hath ſpoil'd all.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Ne'er fear it, he'll work it out again, ſervant.
See where Shattillion's Love, poor Lady, comes.

l.hi: Jaques.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Lie ſtill, Sir, if you love your life, I'll whiſtle when he's go ••

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Oh Gentlemen, I charge you by the Love
Which you bear to women, take ſome pitty
On this diſtreſſed man, help to reſtore
That precious Jewel to him he hath loſt.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Lady, what ever power doth lie in us
By Art, or Prayer, or danger, we are yours,

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: A ſtrange conceit hath wrought this malady,
Conceits again muſt bring him to himſelf,
My ſtrict denial to his Will wrought this:
And if you could but draw his wilder thoughts
To know me, he would ſure recover ſenſe.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: That charge I'll undertake.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Look Jaques, look, for Gods ſake let me riſe,
This greatneſs is a jade, I cannot ſit it.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: His ſword is up, and yet he watcheth you.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I'll down again, pray for thy Maſter, Jaques.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Now the King may ſee all the ſuggeſtions are not tr •
He hath receiv'd againſt my loyalty;
When all men elſe refuſe, I fight his battels,
And thruſt my body into dangers mouth;
I am become his Champion, and this ſword
Has taught his enemies to know themſelves;
Oh that he would no more be jealous of me!

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Monſieur Shattillion, the King aſſures you,
That for this valiant loyal act of yours,
He hath forgot all jealouſies and fears,
And never more will tempt you into danger.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: But how ſhall I believe this, what new token
Of reconcilement will he ſhew me?
Let him releaſe my poor Love from her torment,
From her hard fare, and ſtrict impriſonment.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: He hath don • this to win your after-love,
And ſee your Lady ſent you from the King
By theſe two Gentlemen: be thankful for her.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: She lives, ſhe lives, I know her by the power
Shoots from her eyes.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Riſe dear Shattillion.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I know my duty,
Next unto my King, I am to kneel to you.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: I'll have you riſe, fetch me a chair, ſit down Shat.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: I am commanded, and faith tell me Miſtriſs,
What uſage have you had? pray be plain?

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Oh my moſt lov'd Shattillion, pain enough,
But now I am free, thanks to my God and King.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: His eyes grow very heavy, not a word,
That his weak ſenſes may come ſweetly home.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: The King is honourable.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: When do you whiſtle Jaques?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: By and by.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Come hither Monſieur, canſt thou laugh a little?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: So thou ſhalt then. Bewford, how doſt thou?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Why well.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I'm glad on't, and how does thy wife?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Why, you may ſee her, Sir, ſhe ſtands behind you.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: By the maſs ſhe's there indeed, but where's her belly?

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Belly?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Her great belly, man; what haſt thou ſent thee?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: A Boy, I'll lay my life, it tumbled ſo.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Catcht by this light.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I'll be a Goſſip Bewford.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: And I.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I have an odd Apoſtle ſpoon.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: S'foot, catcht.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: He's married to your woman.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: And I not know it?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: 'Twas a venial ſin.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Gall, gall, gall.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Forgive her, Monſieur Bewford, 'twas her love.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: You may riſe if you pleaſe, I muſt endure it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: See how my great Lord lies upon the ground
• nd dare not ſtir yet?
• aques whiſtles?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Jaques, Jaques, is the Kings Champion gon yet?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: No, but he's aſleep.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is he aſleep art ſure?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: I am ſure he is, I hear him ſnore.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Then by your favours Gentlemen I riſe,
• nd know I am a Duke ſtill.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: And I am his Champion.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Hold thee there, and all France cannot mend thee.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: I am a Prince as great within my thoughts
• s when the whole ſtate did adorn my perſon;
What trial can be made to try a Prince?
• will appoſe this noble corps of mine
To any danger that may end the doubt.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: Great Duke, and Husband, there is but one way
To ſatisfie the world of our true right,
• nd it is dangerous.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What may it be?
Were it to bring the great Turk bound in chains
Through France in triumph: or to couple up
The Sophie, and great Preſtor John together,
• would attempt it Ducheſs, tell the courſe.

sp.speaker: Duc.
sp.l: There is a ſtrong opinion through the world,
• nd no doubt, grounded on experience,
That Lions will not touch a lawful Prince,
• f you be confident then of your right,
• mongſt the Lions bear your naked body,
And if you come off clear, and never winch,
The world will ſay you are a perfect Prince.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I thank you Ducheſs, for your kind advice,
But now we do not affect thoſe ravenous beaſts.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: A Lion is a beaſt to try a King;
But for the trial of ſuch a ſtate like this
Pliny reports a maſtive dog will ſerve.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We will not deal with dogs at all, but men.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: You ſhall not need to deal with them at all,
Hark you Sir, the King doth know you are a Duke:

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No, does he?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Yes, and is content you ſhall be, but with this caution,
That none know it but your ſelf:
For if ye do, he'll take it away by Act of Parliament.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Here's my hand, and whilſt I live or breath,
No living wight ſhall know I am a Duke.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Mark me directly, Sir, your wife may know it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: May not Jaques.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Yes, he may.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: May not my Countrey Coſin?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: By no means, Sir, if you love your life and ſtate.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Well then, know all, I am no Duke.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: No, I'll ſwear it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: See, he wakes.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Where am I, or where have I been all this while?
Sleep hath not ſate ſo ſound upon mine eyes
But I remember well that face;
Oh thou too cruel, leave at length to ſcorn
Him that but looking on thy beauty, dies,
Either receive me, or put out my eyes.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Deareſt Shattillion, ſee upon my knees,
I offer up my love, forget my wrongs.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Art thou mine own?

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: By heaven I am.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Then all the world is mine.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: I have ſtronger things to tell thee, my deareſt love.

sp.speaker: Shat.
sp.l: Tell nothing, but that thou art mine own:
I do not car • to know where I have been,

Or how I 〈◊〉
• li • 'd, or any thing,
But that t • ou a • t my own.

sp.speaker: Bew.
sp.l: Well wi • e, though 'twere a trick that made us wed,
We'll make o • r ſelves merry ſoon in bed.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Know all, I am no Duke.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: What ſay'e?

l.hi: Jaques?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke
sp.l: I am a Duke.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.l: Are ye?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes faith, yes faith.
But it muſt only run among our ſelves,
And Jaques, thou ſhalt be my Secretary ſtill.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Kind Gentlemen, lead in Shattillion,
For he muſt needs be weak and ſickly yet.
Now all my labours have a perfect end, as I could wiſh,
Let all young ſprightly wives that have
Dull fooliſh coxcombs to their Husbands,
Learn by me their duties, what to do,
Which is, to make 'em fools, and pleaſe 'em too.

div.head: EPILOGUE.
div.l: THe Monuments of virtue, and deſert,
Appear more goodly, when the gloſs of Art
〈◊〉 eaten off by time, than when at firſt
They were ſet up, not cenſur'd at the worſt.
We'ave done our beſt, for your contents to fit,
With new pains, this old monument of wit.

div.head: The Perſons repreſented in the Play.
PROLOGUE.
div.l: SInce 'tis become the Title of our Play,
A woman once in a Corporation day
With pardon, ſpeak the Prologue, give as free
A welcome to the Theatre, as he
That with a little Beard, a long black Cloak,
With a ſtarch'd face, and ſupple leg hath ſpoke
Before the Plays the twelvemonth, let me then
Preſent a welcome to theſe Gentlemen,
If you be kind, and noble, you will not
Think the worſe of me for my Petticote:
But to the Play, the Poet had me tell
His fears firſt in the Title, leſt in ſwell
Some thoughts with expectation of a ſtrain,
That but once could be ſeen in a Kings Reign,
This Coronation, he hopes you may
See often, while the genius of his Play,
Doth propheſie, the Conduits may run Wine,
When the days triumph's ended, and divine
Brisk Nectar ſwell his Temple to a rage,
With ſomething of more price t' inveſt the Stage.
There reſts but to prepare you, that although
It be a Coronation, there doth flow
No undermirth, ſuch as doth lard the Scene
For courſe delight the language here is clean.
And confident, our Poet bade me ſay,
He'll bate you but the folly of a Play.
For which, although dull ſouls his Pen deſpiſe,
Who thinks it yet too early to be wiſe.
The nobler will thank his Muſe, at leaſt
Excuſe him, cauſe his thought aim'd at the beſt,
But we conclude not, it does reſt in you.
To cenſure Poet, Play, and Prologue too?
But what have I omitted? is there not
A bluſh upon my cheeks that I forgot
The Ladies, and a Femal Prologue too?
Your pardon noble Gentlewomen, you
Were firſt within my thoughts, I know you ſit
As free, and high Commiſſioners of wit,
Have clear, and active ſouls, nay, though the men
Were loſt in your eyes, they'll be found agen,
You are the bright intelligences move,
And make a harmony this ſphere of Love,
Be you propitious then, our Poet ſays,
Our wreath from you, is worth their grove of Bayes:

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: MAke way for my Lord Protector.

sp.speaker: Liſan.
sp.l: Your graces ſervants.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I like your diligent waiting, where's Liſimachus?

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: I wait upon you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: The Queen looks pleaſant
This morning, does ſhe not?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I ever found
Her gracious ſmiles on me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: She does conſult
Her ſafety in't, for I muſt tell thee boy,
But in the aſſurance of her love to thee,
I ſhould advance thy hopes another way,
And uſe the power I have in Epire, to
Settle our own, and uncontrouled greatneſs;
But ſince ſhe carries her ſelf ſo fairly,
I am content to expect, and by her marriage
Secure thy fortune, that's all my ambition
Now, be ſtill careful in thy applications
To her, I muſt attend other affairs,
Return, and uſe what Art thou canſt to ſay
More charms of love upon her.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I preſume
She always ſpeaks the language of her heart,
And I can be ambitious for no more
Happineſs on earth, than ſhe encourages
Me to expect.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: It was an act becoming
The wiſdom of her Father to engage
A tye between our Families, and ſhe
Hath play'd her beſt diſcretion to allow it;
But we loſe time in conference, wait on her,
And be what thou wert born for, King of Epire,
I muſt away. Exit.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Succeſs ever attend you.
Is not the Queen yet coming forth?

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Your ſervant,
You may command our duties;
This is the Court Star, Philocles.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: The Star that we muſt ſail by.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: All muſt borrow
A light from him, the young Queen directs all
Her favours that way.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: He's a noble Gentleman,
And worthy of his expectations:
Too good to be the ſon of ſuch a Father.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Peace, remember he is Lord Protector.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: We have more need of Heavens Protection
I'th' mean time, I wonder the old King
Did in his life, deſign him for the office.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: He might expect his faith, I have heard when
The King, Who was no Epirote, advanc'd
His claim, Caſſander, our Protector now,
Young then, oppos'd him toughly with his faction,
But forc'd to yield, had fair conditions,
And was declar'd by the whole State, next heir;
If the King wanted iſſue, our hopes only
Thriv'd in this daughter.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Whom but for her ſmiles
And hope of marriage with Liſimachus,
His Father, by ſome cunning, had remov'd
E'r this.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Take heed, the Arras may have ears
I ſhould not weep much if his grace would hence
Remove to Heaven.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I prethee what ſhould he do there?

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Some Offices will fall.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: And the Skie too, e'r I get one ſtair higher
While he's in place.

sp.speaker: Ant.

l.hi: Liſander, Philocles,

sp.l: How looks the day upon us? where's the Queen?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: In her bed-chamber.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Who was with her?

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: None but the young Lord Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis no treaſon
If a man wiſh himſelf a Courtier
Of ſuch a poſſibility: he has
The mounting fate.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I would his Father were
• ounted to th' gallows.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: He has a path fair enough,
• f he ſurvive by title of his Father.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: The Queen will haſten his aſcent.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Would I were Queen,

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thou wou'dſt become rarely the petticoat,
What wou'dſt thou do?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Why, I wou'd marry
My Gentleman uſher, and truſt all the ſtrength
And burden of my State upon his legs,
Rather than be call'd wife by any ſon
Of ſuch a Father.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Come, let's leave this ſubject,
We may find more ſecure diſcourſe; when ſaw
You young Arcadius, Lord Macarius's Nephew?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: There's a ſpark, a youth moulded for a Favourite,
The Queen might do him honor.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Favourite, 'tis too cheap a name, there were a match
Now for her Virgin blood.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Muſt every man
That has a handſome face or leg, feed ſuch
Ambition: I confeſs I honor him,
He has a nimble ſoul, and gives great hope
To be no woman-hater, dances handſomly,
Can court a Lady powerfully, but more goes
To th' making of a Prince? he's here
And's Uncle.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Save you Gentlemen, who can direct me
To find my Lord Protector?

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: He was here
Within this half hour, young Liſimachus
His Son is with the Queen.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: There let him compliment,
I have other buſineſs, ha, Arcadius! Exit.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Obſerv'd you, with what eyes Arcadius
And he ſaluted, their two families
Will hardly reconcile.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Seleucus carries
Himſelf too roughly; with what pride and ſcorn
He paſt by 'em?

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Th'other with leſs ſhew
Of anger, carries pride enough in's ſoul,
I wiſh 'em all at peace, Macarius looks
Are without civil war, a good old man,
The old King lov'd him well, Seleucus Father
Was as dear to him, and maintain'd the character
Of an honeſt Lord through Epire: that two men
So lov'd of others, ſhould be ſo unwelcome
To one another.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: The Queen was not wont to ſend for me.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: The reaſon's to her ſelf,
It will become your duty to attend her.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Save you Gentlemen, what novelty
Does the Court breathe to day?

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: None Sir, the news
That took the laſt impreſſion is, that you
Purpoſe to leave the Kingdom, and thoſe men,
That honor you, take no delight to hear it.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I have ambition to ſee the difference
Of Courts, and this may ſpare; the delights
At home do ſurfet, and the Miſtriſs, whom
We all do ſerve, is fixt upon one object,
Her beams are too much pointed, but no Countrey
Shall make me loſe your memories.

l.hi: Arcadius.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Your Lordſhip honor'd me,
I have no bleſſing in his abſence.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: 'Tis done like a pious Uncle.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We muſt not
Give any licence.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: If your Majeſty
Would pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We are not pleas'd, it had become your duty,
To have firſt acquainted us, e'r you declar'd
Your reſolution publick, is our Court
Not worth your ſtay?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I humbly beg your pardon.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Where's Lyſimachus?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Your humble ſervant, Madam.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We ſhall find
Employment at home for you, do not loſe us.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Madam, I then write my ſelf bleſt on earth
When I may do you ſervice.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We would be private, Macarius.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Madam, you have bleſt me,
Nothing but your command could interpoſe to
Stay him.

sp.speaker: Qu.

l.hi: Liſimachus,

sp.l: You muſt not leave us.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Nothing but Liſimachus? has ſhe not
Ta'en a philter?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Nay, pray be cover'd, Ceremony from you,
Muſt be excus'd.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: It will become my duty.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Not your love?
I know you would not have me look upon
Your perſon as a Courtier, not as Favorite;
That Title were too narrow to expreſs
How we eſteem you.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: The leaſt of all
Theſe names from you, Madam, is grace enough.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Yet here you wou'd not reſt?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Not if you pleaſe:
To ſay there is a happineſs beyond,
And teach my ambition how to make it mine,
Although the honors you already have
Let fall upon your ſervant, exceed all
My merit; I have a heart is ſtudious
To reach it with deſert, and make it poſſible
Your ſavor's mine by juſtice, with your pardon.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We are confident this needs no pardon, Sir,
But a reward to cheriſh your opinion,
And that you may keep warm your paſſion,
Know we reſolve for marriage, and if
I had another gift, beſide my ſelf,
Greater, in that you ſhould diſcern, how much
My heart is fixt.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Let me digeſt my bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: But I cannot reſolve when this ſhall be,

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: How Madam? do not make me dream of Heaven,
And wake me into miſery, if your purpoſe
Be, to immortalize your humble ſervant,
Your power on earth's divine, Princes are here
The copies of Eternity, and create,
When they but will our happineſs.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I ſhall
Believe you mock me in this argument,
I have no power.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: How, no power?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Not as a Queen.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I underſtand you not.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I muſt obey, your Father's my Protector.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: When I am abſolute, Liſimachus,
Our power and Titles meet, before, we are but
A ſhadow, and to give you that were nothing.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Excellent Queen,
My love took no original from State,
Or the deſire of other greatneſs,
Above what my birth may challenge modeſtly,
I love your virtues; mercenary ſouls
Are taken with advancement, you've an Empire
Within you, better than the worlds, to that
Looks my ambition.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: T'other is not, Sir,
To be deſpis'd, Coſmography allows
Epire, a place i'th' Map, and know till I
Poſſeſs what I was born to, and alone
Do grasp the Kingdoms Scepter, I account
My ſelf divided, he that marries me
Shall take an obſolute Queen to his warm boſom,
My temples yet are naked, until then
Our Loves can be but compliments, and wiſhes,
Yet very hearty ones.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I apprehend.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Your Father.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Madam, a Gentleman has an humble ſuit,

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: 'Tis in your power to grant, you are Protector,
I am not yet a Queen.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I ſhall expound her meaning.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Why kneel you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Madam, to reconcile two families
That may unite, both Counſels and their blood
To ſerve your Crown.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Macarius, and Eubulus
That beare inveterate malice to each other.
It grew, as I have heard, upon the queſtion
Which ſome of either family had made
Which of their Fathers was the beſt Commander:
If we believe our ſtories, they have both
Deſerved well of our ſtate, and yet this quarrel
Has coſt too many lives, a ſevere faction.

sp.speaker: Sel
sp.l: But I'll propound a way to plant a quiet
And peace in both our houſes, which are torn
With their diſſentions, and loſe the glory
Of their great names, my blood ſpeaks my relation
To Eubulus, and I wiſh my veins were emptied
To appeaſe their war.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Thou haſt a noble ſoul,
This is a charity above thy youth,
And it flows bravely from thee, name the way.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: In ſuch a deſperate cauſe, a little ſtream
Of blood might purge the foulneſs of their hearts
If you'll prevent a deluge.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Be particular.

sp.speaker: Sel.
