sp.l: Let but your Majeſty conſent that two
May with their perſonal valour, undertake
The honor of their family, and determine
Their difference.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: This rather will inlarge
Their hate, and be a means to call more blood
Into the ſtream.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Not if both families
Agree, and ſwear—

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: And who ſhall be the Champions?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I beg the honor, for Eubulus cauſe
To be ingag'd, if any for Macarius,
Worthy to wager heart with mine, accept it,
I am confident, Arcadius,
For honor would direct me to his ſword,
Will not deny, to ſtake againſt my life
His own, if you vouchſafe us priviledge.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: You are the expectation, and top boughs
Of both your houſes, it would ſeem injuſtice,
To allow a civil war to cut you off,
And your ſelves the inſtruments, beſides
You appear a ſoldier; Arcadius
Hath no acquaintance yet with rugged war,
More fit to drill a Lady, than expoſe
His body to ſuch dangers: a ſmall wound
I'th' head, may ſpoil the method of his hair,
Whoſe curioſity exacts more time,
Than his devotion, and who knows but he
May loſe his ribond by it in his lock,
Dear as his Saint, with whom he would exchange
His head, for her gay colours; then his band
May he diſorder'd, and transform'd from Lace
To Cutwork, his rich cloaths be diſcomplexioned
With bloud, beſide the infaſhionable ſlaſhes:
And at the next Feſtival take Phyſick,
Or put on black, and mourn for his ſlain breeches:
His hands cas'd up in gloves all night, and ſweet
P •• atum: the next day may be endangerd'd
To bliſters with a ſword, how can he ſtand
Upon his guard, who hath Fidlers in his head,
To which, his feet muſt ever be a dancing?
Beſide a falſify may ſpoil his cringe,
Or making of a leg, in which conſiſts
Much of his Court-perfection.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Is this Character
Beſtow'd on him?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: It ſomething may concern the Gentleman,
Whom if you pleaſe to challenge
To Dance, play on the Lute, or Sing.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Some Ketch?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: He ſhall not want thoſe will maintain him
For any ſum.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: You are my Sovereign,
I dare not think, yet I muſt ſpeak ſomewhat,
I ſhall burſt elſe, I have no skill in Jiggs,
Nor Tumbling.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: How Sir?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Nor was I born a Minſtrel, and in this you have
So infinitely diſgrac'd Arcadius.
But that I have heard another Character,
And with your royal Licence do believe it,
I ſhould not think him worth my killing,

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Your killing?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Does ſhe not jeer me;
I ſhall talk treaſon preſently, I find it
At my tongues end already, this is an
Affront, I'll leave her.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Come back, do you know Arcadius?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I ha' chang'd but little breath with him; our perſons
Admit no familiarity; we were
Born to live both at diſtance, yet I ha' ſeen him
Fight, and fight bravely.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: When the ſpirit of Wine
Made his brain valiant, he fought bravely.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Although he be my enemy, ſhould any
Of the gay flies that buzze about the Court,
Sit to catch trouts i'th' ſummer, tell me ſo,
• durſt in any preſence but your own.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Tell him he were not honeſt.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I ſee Selecus, thou art reſolute,
And I but wrong'd Arcadius, your firſt
Requeſt is granted, you ſhall fight, and he
That conquers be rewarded, to confirm
Firſt place and honor to his Family:
Is it not this you plead for?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: You are gracious.

l.hi: Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: She has granted then

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: With much ado.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I wiſh thy ſword may open
His wanton veins, Macarius is too popular,
And has taught him to inſinuate.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: It ſhall
But haſte the confirmation of our loves,

And ripen the delights of marriage, Seleucus.
Exit cum Sel.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: As I gueſt,
It cannot be too ſoon.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: To morrow then we crown her, and inveſt
My Son with Majeſty, 'tis to my wiſhes,
• eget a race of Princes, my Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Firſt, let us marry, Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Thy brow was made
To wear a golden circle, I'm tranſported,
Thou ſhalt rule her, and I will govern thee.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Although you be my Father, that will not
Concern my obedience, as I take it.
Gentlemen,
Prepare your ſelves for a ſolemnity
Will turn the Kingdom into triumph, Epire
Look freſh to morrow, 'twill become your duties
In all your glory, to attend the Queen
At her Coronation, ſhe is pleaſed to make
The next day happy in our Calendar,
My office doth expire, and my old blood
Renews with thought on't.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Crown'd to morrow.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: And he ſo joyful to reſign his Regency,
There's ſome trick in't, I do not like theſe haſty
Proceedings, and whirls of ſtate, they have common •
As ſtrange and violent effects; well, heaven ſave the Queen.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Heaven ſave the Queen, ſay I, and ſend her a ſprightly
Bed-fellow, for the Protector, let him pray for
Himſelf, he is like to have no benefit of my devotion.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: But this doth quicken my old heart, Liſimachus,
There is not any ſtep into her throne,
But is the ſame degree of thy own ſtate;
Come Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: We attend your grace.

l.hi: Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: What heretofore could happen to mankind
Was with much pain to climb to heaven, but in
Sophias marriage of all Queens the beſt,
Heaven will come down to earth, to make me bleſt. Exe.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: INdeed you ſhall not go.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Whither?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: To travel,
I know you ſee me, but to take your leave,
But I muſt never yield to ſuch an abſence.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I prethee leave thy fears, I am commanded
To th' contrary, I wonot leave thee now.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Commanded? by whom?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: The Queen.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I am very glad, for truſt me, I could think
Of thy departure with no comfort, thou
Art all the joy I have, half of my ſoul,
But I muſt thank the Queen now for thy company,
I prethee, what could make thee ſo deſirous
To be abroad?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Only to get an appetite
To thee Polidora.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Then you muſt provoke it.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Nay, prethee do not ſo miſtake thy ſervant.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Perhaps yea ſurfeit with my Love.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Thy love?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Although I have ho beauty to compare
With the beſt faces, I have a heart above
All competition.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Thou art jealous now,
Come let me take the kiſs I gave thee laſt,
I am ſo confident of thee, no Lip
Has raviſht it from thine; I prethee come
To Court.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: There is the throne for beauty.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: 'Tis ſafer dwelling here.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: There's none will hurt,
Or dare but think an ill to Polydora,
The greateſt will be proud to honor thee.
Thy luſter wants the admiration here:
There thou wot ſhine indeed, and ſtrike a reverence
Into the gazer.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: You can flatter too.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: No praiſe of thee can be thought ſo, thy virtue
Will deſerve all, I muſt confeſs, we Courtiers
Do oftentimes commend to ſhew our Art,
There is neceſſity ſometimes to ſay,
This Madam breaths Arabian Gumms,
Amber and Caſſia; though while we are praiſing,
We wiſh we had no noſtrils to take in
Th' offenſive ſteam of her corrupted Lungs.
Nay, ſome will ſwear they love their. Miſtriſs,
Would hazard lives and fortunes, to preſerve
One of her hairs brighter than Berinices;
Or young Apollo's, and yet after this,
A favour from another toy would tempt him
To laugh, while the officious hangman whips
Her head off.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Fine men.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I am none of theſe,
Nay, there are women Polidora, too
That can do pretty well at flatteries;
Make men believe they dote, will languiſh for 'em,
Can kiſs a Jewel out of one, and dally
A carcanet of Diamonds from another,
Weep into th' boſome, of a third, and make
Him drop as many Pearls; they count it nothing
To talk a reaſonable heir within ten days
Out of his whole Eſtate, and make him mad
He has no more wealth to conſume.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: You'll teach me
To think I may be flattered in your promiſes,
Since you live where this Art is moſt profeſt.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I dare not be ſo wicked Polidora,
The Infant errors of the Court I may
Be guilty of, but never to abuſe
So rare a goodneſs, nor indeed did ever
Converſe with any of thoſe ſhames of Court,
To practiſe for baſe ends; be confident
My heart is full of thine, and I ſo deeply
Carry the figure of my Polydora,
It is not in the power of time or diſtance
To cancel it, by all that's bleſt I love thee:
Love thee above all women, dare invoke
A curſe when I forſake thee.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Let it be ſome
Gentle one.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Teach me an oath I prethee,
One ſtrong enough to bind, if thou doſt find
Any ſuſpition of my faith, or elſe
Direct me in ſome horrid imprecation:
When I forſake thee for the love of other
Women, may heaven reward my apoſtacy
To blaſt my greateſt happineſs on earth,
And make all joys abortive.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Revoke theſe haſty ſyllables, they carry
Too great a penalty for breach of Love
To me, I am not worth thy ſuffering,
You do not know, what beauty may invite
Your change, what happineſs may tempt your eye
And heart together.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Should all the graces of your ſex conſpire
In one, and ſhe ſhould court, with a Dowry,
Able to buy a Kingdom, when I give
My heart from Polidora.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I ſuſpect not,
And to requite thy conſtancy, I ſwear.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: 'Twere ſin to let thee waſte thy breath
I have aſſurance of thy noble thoughts.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: My Lord, your Uncle hath been every where
I'th' Court inquiring for you, his looks ſpeak
Some earneſt cauſe.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I am more acquainted with
Thy virtue, than to imagine thou wilt not
Excuſe me now, one kiſs diſmiſſes him
Whoſe heart ſhall wait on Polidora, prethee
Let me not wiſh for thy return too often,
My Father.

sp.speaker: Neſ.
sp.l: I met Arcadius in ſtrange haſte, he told me
He had been with thee.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Some affair too ſoon
Raviſh'd him hence, his Uncle ſent for him
You came now from Court: how looks the Queen
This golden morning?

sp.speaker: Neſ.
sp.l: Like a Bride, her ſoul
Is all on mirth, her eyes have quick'ning fires,
Able to ſtrike a ſpring into the earth,
In winter.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Then Liſimachus can have
No roſt in's blood, that lives ſo near her beams.

sp.speaker: Neſ.
sp.l: His politick father the Protector ſmiles too,
Reſolve to ſee the ceremony of the Queen
'Twill be a day of ſtate.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I am not well.

sp.speaker: Neſ.
sp.l: How! not well? retire then, I muſt return
My attendance is expected, Polidora,
Be careful of thy health.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: It will concern me.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: You amaze me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Dear Nephew, if thou reſpect thy ſafety
My honor, or my age, remove thy ſelf,
Thy life's in danger.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Mine? who's my enemy?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Take horſe, and inſtantly forſake the City,
Or elſe within ſome unſuſpected dwelling,
Obſcure thy ſelf, ſtay not to know the reaſon.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Sir, I beſeech your pardon, which i'th' number
Of my offences unto any, ſhould
Provoke this diſhonourable flight?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: I would, when I petition'd for thy ſtay,
I had pleaded for thy baniſhment, thou knowſt not
What threatens thee.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I would deſire to know it,
I am in no conſpiracy of treaſon,
Have raviſh'd no mans Miſtriſs, not ſo much
As given the lye to any, what ſhould mean
Your ſtrange and violent fears, I will hot ſtir
Until you make me ſenſible I have loſt
My innocence.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: I muſt not live to ſee
Thy body full of wounds, it were leſs ſin
To rip thy Fathers Marble, and fetch from
The reverend vault, his aſhes, and diſperſe them
By ſome rude winds, where none ſhould ever find
The ſacred duſt: it was his Legacy,
The breath he mingled with his prayers to Heaven
I would preſerve Arcadius, whoſe fate
He propheſied in death, would need protection,
Thou wot diſturb his ghoſt, and call it to
Affright my dreams, if thou refuſe to obey me.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: You more inflame me, to enquire the cauſe
Of your diſtraction, and you'll arm me better
Than any coward flight by acquainting me
Whoſe malice aims to kill me, good Sir tell me,

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Then prayers and tears aſſiſt me.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Mac.

l.hi: Arcadius,

sp.l: Thou art a raſh young man, witneſs the ſpirit
Of him that truſted me ſo much, I bleed,
Till I prevent this miſchief. Exit.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Ha. keep off.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: What mean you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: We are your friends.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I know your faces, but
Am not ſecure, I would not be betraid.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: You wrong our hearts, who truly honor you.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: They ſay I muſt be kill'd.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: By whom?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I know not, nor wou'd I part with life ſo tamely.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: We dare engage ours in your quarrel, hide
Your ſword, it may beget ſuſpition,
It's enough to queſtion you.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I am conſident;
Pray pardon me, come, I deſpiſe all danger:
Yet a dear friend of mine, my Uncle told me
He would not ſee my body full of wounds.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Your Uncle, this is ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Yes, my honeſt Uncle,
If my unlucky Stars have pointed me
So dire a fate.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: There is ſome ſtrange miſtake in't.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Arcadius, the Queen would ſpeak with you,
You muſt make haſte.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Though to my death. I flie
Upon her ſummons I give up my breath
Then willingly, if ſhe command it from me.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: This does a little trouble me.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I know not
What to imagine, ſomething is the ground
Of this perplexity, but I hope there is not
Any ſuch danger as he apprehends.

div.stage: Enter Queen, Liſimachus, Macarius, Eubulus, Seleucus Arcadius, Ladies, Attendants and Gent.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We have already granted to Seleucus
And they ſhall try their valour, if Arcadius Have ſpirit in him to accept the challenge, Our Royal word is paſt.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: This is ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Madam, my ſon knew not what he ask'd,
And you were cruel to conſent ſo ſoon.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Wherein have I offended, to be rob'd
At once, of all the wealth I have, Arcadius
Is part of me.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Seleucus's life and mine
Are twiſted on one thred, both ſtand or fall
Together, hath the ſervice for my Countrey
Deſerved but this reward, to be ſont weeping
To my eternal home? Was't not enough
When I was young, to loſe my bloud in wars,
But the poor remnant that is ſcarcely warm
And faintly creeping through my wither'd veins
Muſt be let out to make you ſport.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: How can
We, that ſhall this morn ſee the ſacred oyl,
Fall on your Virgin treſſes, hope for any
Protection hereafter, when this day
Too ſacrifice the blood of them that pray for you.
Arcadius, I prethee ſpeak thy ſelfe,
It is for thee I plead.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Seleucus. kneel
And ſay thou haſt repented thy raſh ſuit;
If e'er I ſee thee fight, I be thus wounded,
How will the leaſt drop forc'd from thy veins,
Afflict my heart.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Why, that's good;
Arcadius, ſpeak to h • r; hear him Madam.

sp.speaker: Arc,
sp.l: If you call back this honor you have done me
I ſhall repent I live, doe not perſwade me:
Seleucus, thou ar • a noble enemy,
And I will love thy ſoul, though I deſpair
Our bodies friendly converſation:
I would we were to tugg upon ſome cliffe,
Or like two prodigies i'th' air, our conflict
Might generally be gaz'd at, and our bloud
Appeaſe our grandfires Aſhes.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: I am undone.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Madam, my father ſays I have offended,
If ſo, I beg your pardon, but beſeech you
For your own glory, call not back your word.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: They are both mad.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: No more, we have reſolv'd,
And ſince their courage is ſo nobly ſlam'd,
This morning we'll behold the Champions
Within the Liſt, be not afraid, their ſtrife
Will ſtretch ſo far as death, ſo ſoon as we
Are Crown'd, prepare your ſelves, Seleucus. Kiſſes her hand.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I have receiv'd another life in this high favour,
And may loſe what nature gave me.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Arcadius, to encourage thy young valour,
We give thee our Fathers ſword.
Command it from our Armory; Liſimachus,
To our Coronation. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I'll forfeit
My head for a rebellion, than ſuffer it. Exit.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I am circled with confuſions, I'll do ſomewhat
My brains and friends aſſiſt me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: But do you think they'll fight indeed?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Perhaps
Her Majeſty will ſee a bout or two.
And yet 'tis wondrous ſtrange, ſuch ſpectacles
Are rare i'th' Court, and they were to skirmiſh naked
Before her, then there might be ſcome excuſe.
There is gimcracks in't, the Queen is wiſe
Above her years.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Macarius is perplex'd.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I cannot blame him, but my Lord Eubulus
Returns, they are both troubled, 'las good men,
But our duties are expected, we forget. Ex. Phil. Liſ.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: I muſt reſolve, and yet things are not ripe,
My brains upon the torture.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: This may quit
The hazard of his perſon, whoſe leaſt drop
Of blood, is worth more than our families.
My Lord Eubulus, I have thought a way
I ſtay the young mens deſperate proceedings,
It is our cauſe they fight, let us beſeech
The Queen, to grant us two the priviledge
Of Duel, rather than expoſe their lives
To eithers fury; it were pity they
Should run upon ſo black a deſtiny,
We are both old, and may be ſpar'd, a pair
Of fruitleſs trees, moſſie, and wither'd trunks,
That fill up too much room.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Moſt willingly,
And I will praiſe her charity to allow it;
I have not yet forget to uſe a ſword,
Let's loſe no time, by this act, ſhe will licence
Our ſouls to leave our bodies but a day,
Perhaps an hour the ſooner; they may live
To do her better ſervice, and be friends
When we are dead, and yet I have no hope
This will be granted, curſe upon our faction.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: If fine deny us—

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: I wou'd do ſomewhat —

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: There's ſomething o'th' ſuddain ſtruck upon
My imagination that may ſecure us.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Name it, if no diſhonor wait upon't
To preſerve them, I'll accept any danger,

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: There is no other way, and yet my heart
Would be excus'd, but 'tis to ſave his life.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Speak it Eubulus.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: In your ear I ſhall,
It ſha'not make a noiſe if you refuſe it.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Hum? though it ſtir my bloud, I'll meet Arcadius,
If this preſerve thee not, I muſt unſeal
Another miſtery. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Queen, Liſimachus, Caſſander, Charilla, Liſander, Philocles, Antigonus.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We owe to all your loves, and will deſerve
At leaſt by our endeavours, that none may
This day repent their prayers, my Lord Protector.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Madam, I have no
Such Title now, and am bleſt to loſe
That name ſo happily: I was but truſted
With a glorious burden.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: You have prov'd
Your ſelf our faithful Counſellor, and muſt ſtill
Protect our growing ſtate: a Kingdoms Scepter
Weighs down a womans arm, this Crown ſits heavy
Upon my brow already, and we know
There's ſomething more than mettal in this wreath,
Of ſhining glory, but your faith, and counſel,
That are familiar with myſteries,
And depths of ſtate, have power to make us fit
For ſuch a bearing, in which both you ſhall
Doe loyal ſervice, and reward your Duties.

sp.speaker: Caſ
sp.l: Heaven preſerve your Highneſs.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: But yet my Lords and Gentlemen, let none
Miſtake me, that becauſe I urge your wiſdoms,
I ſhall grow careleſs, and impoſe on you
The managing of this great Province, no,
We will be active too, and as we are
In dignity above your perſons, ſo,
The greateſt portion of the difficulties
We all to us, you in your ſeveral places
Relieving us with your experience,
Obſerving in your beſt directions
All modeſty, and diſtance; for although
We are but young, no action ſhall forfeit
Our royal priviledge, or encourage any
Too unreverent boldneſs; as it will become
Our honor to conſult, e'r we determine
Of the moſt neceſſary things of ſtate,
So we are ſenſible of a check,
But in a brow, that ſaucily controuls
Our action, preſuming on our years
As few, or frailty of our ſex; that head
Is not ſecure, that dares our power or juſtice.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: She has a brave ſpirit, look how the Protector
Grows pale already.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: But I ſpeak to you
Are perfect in obedience, and may ſpare
This Theme, yet 'twas no immatrial
Part of our character, ſince I deſire
All ſhould take notice, I have ſtudied
The knowledge of my ſelf, by which I ſhall
Better diſtinguiſh of your worth and perſons
In your relations to us.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: This language
Is but a threatening to ſome body.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: But we miſs ſome, that uſe not to abſent
Their duties from us, where's Macarius?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Retir'd to grieve, your Majeſty hath given
Conſent, Arcadius ſhould enter the Liſt
To day with young Seleucus.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We purpoſe.
They ſhall proceed, what's he?

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.l: A Gentleman belonging to Seleucus, that gives notice
He is prepar'd, and waits your royal pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: He was compos'd for action, give notice
To Ar • adius, and admit the challenger:
Let other Princes boaſt their gaudy tilting,
And mockery of battles, but our triumph
Is celebrated with true noble valour.
sp.stage: Enter Seleucus, Arcadius, at ſeveral doors, their Pages before them, bearing their Targets.
sp.l: Two young men ſpirited enough to have
Two kingdoms ſtaked upon their ſwords, Liſimachus
Do not they excellently become their arms?
'Twere pity but they ſhould do ſomething more
Then wave their plumes. A ſhout within.
What noiſe is that?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: The peoples joy to know us reconcil'd,
Is added to the jubile of the day,
We have no more a faction but one heart,
Peace flow in every boſom.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Throw away
Theſe inſtruments of death, and like two friends
Embrace by our example.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: This unfein'd?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: By our duties to your ſelf, dear Madam
Command them not advance, our houſes from
This minute are incorporated; happy day
Our eyes at which before revenge look'd forth,
May clear ſuſpition, oh my Arcadius!

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: We have found a nearer way to friendſhip, Madam
Than by expoſing them to fight for us.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: If this be faithful, our deſires are bleſt.
We had no thought to waſte, but reconcile
Your bloud this way, and we did propheſie
This happy chance, ſpring into eithers boſom,
Arcadius and Seleucus, what can now
Be added to this days felicity?
Yes, there is ſomething, is there not my Lord?
While we are Virgin queen.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Ha, that ſtring
Doth promiſe Muſick.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I am yet my Lords
Your ſingle joy, and when I look upon,
What I have took, to manage the great care
Of this moſt flouriſhing kingdom, I incline
To think I ſhall do juſtice to my ſelf,
If I chooſe one, whoſe ſtrength and virtue may
Aſſiſt my undertaking, think you Lords,
A Husband would not help?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: No queſtion, Madam,
And he that purpoſe to make you ſo bleſt
Muſt needs be worthy of our humbleſt duty,
It is the general vote.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We will not then
Trouble Ambaſſadors to treat with any
Princes abroad; within our own dominion,
Fruitful in honor, we ſhall make our choice;
And that we may not keep you over long
In tho imagination, from this circle, we
• ave purpoſe to elect one, whom I ſhall
•• ote a King and Husband.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Now my Lord Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Nor ſhall we in this action be accus'd
Of raſhneſs, ſince the man we ſhall declare
Deſerving our affection, hath been early
• our opinion, which had reaſon firſt
To guide it, and his known nobility
• ong marry'd to our thoughts, will juſtifie
Our fair election.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Liſimachus bluſhes.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Direct our duties, Madam, to pray for him.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Arcadius, you ſee from whence we come,
Pray lead us back, you may aſcend.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: How's this? o're-reach'd?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Madam, be charitable to your humbleſt creature,
Doe not reward the heart, that falls in duty
Beneath your feet, with making me the burden
Of the Court-mirth, a mockery for Pages,
Twere Treaſon in me but to think you meane thus.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Arcadius, you muſt refuſe my love,
• r ſhame this Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Is the wind in that corner?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I ſhall run mad Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: Sir, contain your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Is this to be believ'd?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: What dream is this?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: He kiſſes her, now by this day I am glad on't,

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Mark the Protector.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let him fret his heart-ſtrings.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Is the day cloudy on the ſudden?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Gentlemen,
• was not my ambition, I durſt never
• ſpire ſo high in thought, but ſince her Majeſty
• ath pleas'd to call me to this honor, I
Will ſtudy to be worthy of her grace,
• y whom I live.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: The Church to morrow ſhall
Confirme our marriage, noble Liſimachus;
We'll find out other wayes to recompence
Your love to us, ſet forward, come Arcadius.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: It muſt be ſo, and yet let me conſider,

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: He inſults already; policy aſſiſt me.
To break his neck.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: Who would truſt Woman?
Loſt in a pair of minutes, loſt, how bright
• morning roſe, but now, 'tis night? Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: OH where ſhall Virgins look for faith hereafter?
If he prove falſe, after ſo many vowes?
• nd yet if I conſider, he was tempted
Above the ſtrength of a young Lover, two
•• ch glorious courting his acceptance, were
Able to make diſloyalty no ſin,
At leaſt not ſeem a fault, a Lady firſt,
Whoſe very looks would thaw a man more frozen
Than the Alps, quicken a ſoulmore dead than Winter,
Add to her beauty and perfection,
That ſhe's a Queen, and brings with her a Kingdom
• ble to make a great mind forfeit Heaven.
What could the frailty of Arcadius
•• ggeſt, to unſpirit him ſo much, as not
To fly to her embraces, you were preſent
When ſhe declar'd her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Yes Madam.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Tell me,
Did not he make a pauſe, when the fair Queen
A full temptation ſtood him?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Very little
My judgment could diſtinguiſh, ſhe did no ſooner
Propound, but he accepted.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: That was ill,
He might with honor ſtand one or two minutes,
Me thinks it ſhould have ſtartled him a little,
To have rememberd me, I have deſerv'd
At leaſt a cold thought, well, pray give it him.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: When?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Inſtantly.
Pol, Not ſo,
But take a time when his joy ſwels him moſt,
When his delights are high and raviſhing,
When you perceive his Soul dance in his eyes,
When ſhe that muſt be his, hath dreſt her beauty,
With all her pride, and ſends a thouſand Cupids
To call him to the taſting of her lip;
Then give him this, and tell him, while I live,
I'll pray for him.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I ſhall. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: There is no way but death.
That's black, and horrid,
Conſider, Sir, it was her ſin, not his;
I cannot accuſe him, what man could carry
A heart ſo frozen, not to melt at ſuch
A glorious flame? Who could not fly to ſuch
A happineſs?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Have you ambition
To be a tame fool? ſee ſo vaſt an injury
And not revenge it make me not ſuſpect
Thy Mother for this ſufferance, my Son.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Pray hear me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Hear a patient gull,
A property, thou haſt no blood of mine,
If this affront provoke thee not, how canſt
Be charitable to thy ſelf, and let him live
To glory in thy ſhame? Nor is he innocent;
He had before crept ſlily into her boſome,
And practiſed thy diſhonor.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: You begin to ſtir me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: How elſe could ſhe be guilty
Of ſuch contempt of thee? and in the eye
Of all the Kingdom, they conſpir'd this ſtain,
When they had cunning meetings, ſhall thy love
And blooming hopes be ſcatter'd thus, and Liſimachus
Stand idle gazer?

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: What, Sir, will his death
Advantage us; if ſhe be falſe to me?
So irreligious, and to touch her perſon—
Pauſe, we may be obſerved.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: 'Tis the Protector
And his ſon.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Alas, poor Gentleman, I pitty
His neglect, but am not ſorry for his Father.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſtrange turne.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: The whirligigs of Women.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Your Graces ſervant.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I am yours Gentlemen,
And ſhould be happy, to deſerve your loves.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Now he can flatter.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: In't Sir, to inlarge your ſufferings, I have
A heart doth wiſh
The Qeeen had known better to reward
Your love and merit.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: If you would expreſs
Your love to me, pray do not mention it,
I muſt obey my fate.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: She will be married
To t'other Gentleman for certain then?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I hope you'll wiſh 'em joy.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Indeed I will, Sir.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Your Graces ſervant. Exit.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: We are grown
Ridiculous, the paſtime of the Court:
Here comes another.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Where's your Son, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Like a neglected ſervant of his Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I would ask him a queſtion.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Whether the Queen,
As 'tis reported, lov'd him, he can tell
Whether ſhe promis'd what they talke of, marriage,

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I can reſolve you that, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: She did promiſe?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Then ſhee's a Woman, and your Son;

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Not worthy his blood, and expectation,
If he be calme.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: There's no oppoſing deſtiny.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I would cut the Throat.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Whoſe throat?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: The deſtinies, that's all, your pardon, Sir,
I am Seleucus ſtill, a poor ſhadow
Oth' World, a walking picture, it concerns
Not me, I am forgotten by my ſtars.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: The Queen, with more diſcretion, might ha choſen
Thee.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Whom?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Thee, Seleucus.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Me? I cannot dance, and frisk with due activity,
My body is lead, I have too much phlegme, what ſhould
I do with a Kingdome? no, Arcadius
Becomes the cuſhion, and can pleaſe, yet ſetting
Aſide the trick that Ladies of Blood look at,
Another Man might make a ſhift to weare
Rich Clothes, ſit in the chair of ſtate, and nod,
Dare venture on diſcourſe, that does not trench
On compliment, and think the ſtudy of Armes
And Arts, more commendable in a Gentleman,
Than any Galliard.

sp.speaker: Caſ.

l.hi: Arcadius,

sp.l: And you, were reconcil'd.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: We? yes, oh yes,
But 'tis not manners now to ſay we are friends,
At our equality there had been reaſon,
But now, ſubjection is the word.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: They are not
Yet married.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I'll make no Oath upon't,
My Lord Liſimachus,
A word, you'll not be angry if I love you,
May not a Batchellor be made a Cuckold?

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: How, Sir?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Liſimachus, this Gentleman
Is worth our embrace, hee's ſpirited,
And may be uſeful.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Hark you, can you tell
Where's the beſt Dancing-maſter? and you mean
To riſe at Court, practiſe to caper, farewel
The noble ſcience, that makes work for cutlers,
It will be out of faſhion to weare ſwords,
Maſques, and devices welcome, I ſalute you,
Is it not pitty any diviſion
Should be heard out of Muſick? Oh 'twill be
An excellent age of crotchets; and of Canters.
Buy Captains, that like fools will ſpend your blood
Out of your Country, you will be of leſs
Uſe than your feathers, if you return unman'd
You ſhall be beaten ſoon to a new march,
When you ſhall think it a diſcretion
To ſell your glorious buffes to buy fine pumps,
And pantables, this is I hope no treaſon.

div.stage: Enter Arcadius leading the Queen, Charia, Eubulus, Liſander, Philocles, Polidora, ſervant.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Wot ſtay Liſimachus?

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: Yes, Sir,
And ſhew a patience above her injury.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: This honor is too much, Madam, aſſume
Your place, and let Arcadius waite ſtill:
'Tis happineſs enough to be your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Now he diſſembles.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Sir, you muſt ſit.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I am Obedient.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: This is not Muſick
Sprightly enough, it feeds the ſoul with melancholy.
How ſayes Arcadius?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Give me leave to think
There is no harmony but in your voice,
And not an accent of your heavenly tongue,
But ſtrikes me into rapture, I incline
To think, the tale of Orpheus no fable,
'Tis poſſible he might inchant the Rocks,
And charme the Forreſt, ſoften hell, hell it ſelf,
With his commanding Lute, it is no miracle
To what you work, whoſe very breath conveyes
The hearer into Heaven, how at your lips,
Day-winds gather Perfumes, proudly glide away,
To diſperſe ſweetneſs round about the world.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Fine ſtuff.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: You cannot flatter.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Not, if I ſhould ſay,
Nature had plac'd you here the creatures wonder,
And her own ſpring, from which all excellence
On Earth's deriv'd, and copyed forth and when
The character of fair, and good in others
Is quite worne out, and loſt, looking on you
It is ſupply'd, and you alone made mortal
To feed, and keep alive all beauty.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Ha, ha, Can you indure it Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: What do you meane?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Nay, ask him what he meanes, mine is a down
Right laugh.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Well, Sir, proceed.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: At ſuch bright eyes the ſtars do light themſelves,
At ſuch a forehead Swans renew their white,
From ſuch a lip the morning gathers bluſhes.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: The morning is more modeſt than thy praiſes,
VVhat a thing does he make her?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: And when you flie to Heaven and leave this work
No longer maintenance of goodneſs from you:
Then Poetry ſhall loſe all uſe with us,
And be no more, ſince nothing in your abſence
Is left, that can be worthy of a Verſe.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: VVhoſe that?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: 'Twas I, Madam.

l.hi: Seleucus?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Yes, Sir, 'twas I that laugh'd.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: At what?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: At nothing.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Contain your ſelf, Seleucus.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Are you mad?

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Have you ambition to be puniſh'd, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I need not, 'twas puniſhment
Enough to hear him make an Idol of you, he left
Out the commendation of your patience, I was a little
Mov'd in my nature, to hear his Rodomontados, and
Make a monſter of his Miſtreſs, which I pitty'd firſt,
But ſeeing him proceed, I gueſt he brought you
Mirth with his inventions, and ſo made bold to laugh at it.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: You are ſawcy,
We'll place you where you ſha'not be ſo merry,
Take him away.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Submit your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Let me plead for his pardon.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I wo'd not owe my life ſo poorly, beg thy own,
When you are King you cannot bribe your deſtiny.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Good Madam hear me, I fear he is d ſtracted,
Brave boy, thou ſhould'ſt be Maſter of a ſoul
Like his: thy honors more concern'd.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: 'Tis charity,
Away wo' mee, 'boy Madam?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: He has a daring ſpirit. Ex Sel. Eub. Caſ.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Theſe, and a thouſand more affronts I muſt
Expect: your favors draw them all upon me;
In my firſt ſtate I had no enemies,
I was ſecure, while I did grow beneath
This expectation; humble valleys thrive with
Their boſomes full of flowers, when the Hills melt
With lightning, and rough anger of the clouds,
Let we retire.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: And can Arcadius
At ſuch a breath be mov'd, I had opinion
Your courage durſt have ſtood a tempeſt for
Our love, can you for this incline to leave
What other Princes ſhould in vain have ſued for?
How many Lovers are in Epire now
Would throw themſelves on danger, not expect
One enemy, but empty their own veins,
And think the loſs of all their blood rewarded,
To have one ſmile of us when they are dying?
And ſhall this murmur ſhake you?

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Not dear Madam,
My life is ſuch a poor deſpiſed thing,
In value your leaſt graces, that
To loſe it were to make my ſelf a victory,
It is not for my ſelf, I fear: the envy
Of others cannot faſten wound in me
Greater, than that your goodneſs ſhould be check'd
So daringly.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Let not thoſe thoughts afflict thee,
While we have power to correct the offences,
Arcadius be mine, this ſhall confirm it.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I ſhall forget,
And loſe my way to heaven, that touch had been
Enough to have reſtor'd me, and infus'd
A ſpirit of a more celeſtial nature,
After the tedious abſence of my ſoul,
Oh bleſs me not too much one ſmile a day
Would ſtretch my life to mortality;
Poets that wrap divinity in tales,
Look here, and give your coppies forth of angels,
What bleſſing can remain?

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Our Marriage.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Place then ſome horrors in the way
For me, not you, to paſs, the journeys end
Holds out ſuch glories to me, I ſhould think
Hell but a poor degree of ſuffering for it,
What's that, ſome petition? a Letter to me.
sp.stage: You had a Polidora, ha, that's all.
sp.l: Ith' minure when my veſſels new • anch'd forth,
With all my pride, and ſilken wings about me
I ſtrike upon a Rock: What power can ſave me?
You had a Polidora; there's a name
Kill'd with grief, I can ſo ſoon forget her.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: She did impoſe on me this ſervice, Sir,
And while ſhe lives ſhe ſayes, ſhee'll pray for you.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: She lives,
That's well, and yet 'twere better, for my ſame,
And honor, ſhe were dead; What fate hath plac'd me
Upon this fearful precipice?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: He's troubled.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: I muſt reſolve, my faith is violated
Already, yet poor loving Polidora
Will pray for me, ſhe ſayes, to think ſhe can
Render me hated to my ſelf, and every
Thought's a tormentor, let me then be juſt.

l.hi: Arcadius.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: That voice prevailes agen, oh Polidora,
Thou muſt forgive Arcadius, I dare not
Turn rebel to a Princeſs, I ſhall love
Thy vertue, but a Kingdom has a charme
To excuſe our failty, deareſt Madam.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Now ſet forward.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: To perfect all our joyes.

div.stage: Enter Macarius, and a Biſhop, Caſander.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: I'll fright their glories.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: By what means?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Obſerve.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Our good Unckle, welcome.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: My Lord Macarius, we did want your perſon,
There's ſomething in our joyes wherein you ſhare.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: This you intend your highneſs wedding day.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: We are going.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Save you labor
I have brought a Prieſt to meet you.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Reverend Father.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Meet us, Why?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: To tell you, that you muſt not Marry.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Didſt thou hear that, Liſimachus?

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: And wonder what will follow.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: We muſt not marry.

sp.speaker: Biſh.
sp.l: Madam, 'tis a rule
Firſt made in heaven, and I muſt needs declare
You and Arcadius muſt tie no knot
Of Man and Wife.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Is my Unckle mad?

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: Joy has tranſported him,
Or age has made him dote, Macarius
Provoke us not too much, you will preſume
Above our mercy.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: I'll diſcharge my duty,
Could your frown ſtrike me dead, my Lord, you know
Whoſe character this is.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: It is Theodoſius,
Your graces Father.

sp.speaker: Biſ.
sp.l: I am ſubſcrib'd a witneſs.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Upon my life 'tis his.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Fear not, I'll croſs this Match.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I'll bleſs thee for't.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Unckle, d'ee know what you do, or what we are
Going to finiſh? you will not break the neck of my glorious
Fortune, now my foots ith' ſtirrup, and mounting,
Throw me over the ſaddle? I hope you'll let one
Be a King, Madam, 'tis as you ſay,
My Unckle is ſomething craz'd, there's a worm
In's brain, but I beſeech you pardon him, he is
Not the firſt of your counſel, that has talk'd
Idly, d'ee hear my Lord Biſhop, I hope
You have more Religion than to joyn with him
To undoe me.

sp.speaker: Biſ.
sp.l: Not I Sir, but I am commanded by oath,
And conſcience to ſpeak truth.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: If your truth ſhould do me any harm, I ſhall never
Be in charity with a Croziers ſtaffe, look too't.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: My youngeſt Brother,

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Worſe and worſe, my brains. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Deliver to me an Infant with this writing,
To which this reverend Father is a witneſs.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: This he whom we ſo long thought dead, a childe?

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: But what ſhould make my Father to truſt him
To your concealment? give abroad his death, and bury
An empty coffin?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: A jealouſie he had
Upon Caſſander, whoſe ambitious brain
He fear'd would make no conſcience to depoſe
His ſon, to make Liſimachus King of Epire.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.l: He made no ſcruple to expoſe me then
To any danger?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: He ſecur'd you, Madam,
By an early Engagement of your affection
To Liſimachus, exempt this teſtimony,
Had he been Arcadius, and my Nephew,
I needed not obtrude him on the ſtate,
Your love and marriage had made him King.
Without my trouble, and ſav'd that ambition,
There was neceſſity to open now
His birth, and title.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Demetrius alive.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: What riddles are theſe, Whom do they talk of?

sp.speaker: Omn.
sp.l: Congratulate your return to life, and honor,
And as becomes us, with one voice ſalute you,
Demetrius King of Epire.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: I am no Uncle, Sir, this is your Siſter,
I ſhould have ſuffer'd inceſt to have kept you
Longer ith' dark: love, and be happy both,
My truſt is now diſcharg'd.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: And we rejoyce.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: But do not mock me, Gentlemen,
May I be bold upon your words to ſay
I am Prince Theodoſius Son?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: The King.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: You'll juſtifie it?
Siſter, I am very glad to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: I am to find a brother, and reſign my glory,
My triumph is my ſhame. Exit.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Thine ear Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: Gentlemen I owe
Unto your loves, as large acknowledgment
As to my birth, for this great honor, and
My ſtudy ſhall be equal to be thought
Worthy of both.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Thou art turn'd Marble.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: There will be the leſs charge for my Monument.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: This muſt not be, ſit faſt young King. Exit.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Your ſiſter, Sir, is gone.

sp.speaker: Arc.
sp.l: My ſiſter ſhould have been my Bride, that name
Puts me in mind of Polidora, ha?
Liſander, Philocles, Gentlemen,
If you will have me think your hearts allow me
Theodoſius ſon, oh quickly ſnatch ſome wings,
Expreſs it in your haſte to Polidora,
Tell her what title is new dropt from heaven
To make her rich; onely created for me:
Give her the ceremony of my Queen,
With all the ſtate that may become our Bride,
Attend her to this throne; Are you not there?
Yet ſtay, 'tis too much pride to ſend for her,
Wee'll go our ſelf, no honor is enough
For Polidora, to redeem our fault,
Salute her gently from me, and, upon
Your knee, preſent her with this Diadem,
'Tis our firſt gift, tell her Demetrius follows
To be her gueſt, and give himſelf a ſervant
To her chaſt boſome, bid her ſtretch her heart
To meet me, I am loſt in joy and wonder. Exceunt Omnes.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: WHere's the Captain of the Caſtle?

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.l: Hee'll attend your honors preſently.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Give him knowledge we expect him.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.l: I ſhall, my Lord. Exit.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: He is my creature, fear not,
And ſhall run any courſe that we propound.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: My Lord, I like the ſubſtance of your plot,
'Tis promiſing, but matters of this conſequence
Are not ſo eaſily perfect, and it does
Concern our heads to build upon ſecure
Principles, though Seleucus, I confeſs,
Carry a high, and daring ſpirit in him,
'Tis hard to thruſt upon the ſtate new ſetled
Any impoſtor, and we know not yet
Whether hee'll undertake to play the Prince;
Or if he ſhould accept it, with what cunning
He can behave himſelf.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: My Lord, affairs
Of ſuch a glorious nature, are half finiſh'd,
When they begin with confidence.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Admit
He want no art, or courage, it muſt reſt
Upon the people to receive his title,
And with what danger their uncertain breath
May flatter ours, Demetrius ſcarcely warm
In the Kings ſeat, I may ſuſpect.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: That reaſon
Makes for our part, for if it be ſo probable,
That young Demetrius ſhould be living, Why
May not we work them to believe, Lenatus,
The eldeſt ſon was, by ſome trick, preſerv'd,
And now would claim his own: there were two ſons,
Who in their Fathers life we ſuppoſed dead,
May not we find a circumſtance to make
This ſeem as clear as t'other, let the vulgar
Be once poſſeſt, wee'll carry Epire from
Demetrius, and the World.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: I could be pleas'd
To ſee my Son a King.
The Captain's here.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I waite your Lordſhips pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: We come to viſit your late priſoner:
I will not doubt, but you intreat him fairly,
He will deſerve it for himſelf, and you
Be fortunate in any occaſion,
To have expreſt your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Sir, the knowledge
Of my honorable Lord his Father, will
Inſtruct me to behave my ſelf with all
Reſpects becoming me, to ſuch a ſon.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Theſe things will leaſt
Oblige you, but how bears he his reſtraint?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: As one whoſe ſoul's above it.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Patiently?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: With contempt rather of the great command
Which made him priſone • , he will talke ſometimes
So ſtrangely to himſelf.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Hee's here.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Why was I born to be a ſubject? 'tis
Soon anſwer'd, ſure my Father was no Prince,
That's all: the ſame ingredients uſe to make
A Man, as active, though not royal blood
Went to my compoſition, and I
Was gotten with as good a will perhaps,
And my birth coſt my Mother as much ſorrow,
As I had been born an Emperor.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: While I look
Upon him, ſomething in his face preſents
A King indeed.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: He does reſemble much
Theodoſius too.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Whoſe ſon we would pretend him,
This will advance our plot,

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: 'Tis but a name,
And mere opinion, that prefers one man
Above another, I'll imagine then
I am a Prince, or ſome brave thing on Earth,
And ſee what follows: but it muſt not be,
My ſingle voice will carry it the name
Of King muſt be attended with a troop
Of acclamations, on whoſe ayrie wings
He mounts, and once exalted, threatens Heaven,
And all the ſtars: how to acquire this noiſe,
And be the thing I talke of men have riſe
From a more cheap nobility to Empires,
From dark originals, and ſordid blood,
Nay ſome that had no fathers, ſons of the earth,
And flying people, have aſpir'd to Kingdoms,
Made nations tremble, and have practis'd frowns
To awe the world, their memory is glorious,
And I would hug them in their ſhades, but what's
All this to me, that am I know not what,
And leſs in expectation?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Are you ſerious?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Will you aſſiſt, and run a fate with us.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Command my life, I owe it to your favor.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Arcadius was once as far from being
As I, and had we not ſo cunningly
Been reconcil'd, or one, or both had gone
To ſeek our fortunes in another world;
What's the device now? If my death be next,
The ſummons ſhall not make me once look pale.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Chide your too vain ſuſpitions, we bring
• life, and liberty, with what elſe can make
Thy ambition happy, th'aſt a glorious flame,
We come to advance it.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Have but a will,
And be what thy own thoughts dare prompt thee to,
A King.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: You do not mock me Gentlemen?
You are my Father, Sir.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: This minute ſhall
Declare it, my Seleucus, our hearts ſwell'd
With joy, with duty rather, oh my boy!

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: What's the miſtery?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: You muſt be a King.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Seleucus, ſtay, thou art too incredulous,
Let not our faith, and ſtudy to exalt thee,
• e ſo rewarded.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: I pronounce thee King,
Unleſs thy ſpirit be turn'd coward, and
Thou ſaint to accept it.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: King of what?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Of Epire.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Although the Queen, ſince ſhe ſent me hither,
Were gone to Heaven I know not how,
That title could devolve to me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: We have
No Queen, ſince he that ſhould have married her,
Is prov'd her youngeſt brother, and now King
In his own title.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Thank you Gentlemen,
There's hope for me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Why, you dare fight with him
And need be, for the Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: With Arcadius?
If you'll make ſtakes, my life againſt his crown,
I'll fight with him, and you, and your fine Son,
And all the Courtiers one after another.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: 'Two'not come to that.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I am of your Lordſhips mind, ſo fare you well.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Yet ſtay and hear —

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: What? that you have betray'd me:
Do, tell your King, my life is grown a burden,
And I'll confeſs, and make your ſouls look pale,
To ſee how nimble mine ſhall leap this battlement
Of fleſh, and dying, laugh at your poor malice.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: No more, long live Leonatus King of Epire.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Leonatus, Who's that?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Be bold, and be a King, our brains have been
Working to raiſe you to this height, here are
None but friends, dare von but call your ſelf
Leonatus, and but juſtifie with confidence
What we'll proclaime you, if we do not bring
The Crown to your head, we 'ill forfeit ours.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: The ſtate is in diſtraction, Arcadius
Is prov'd a King, there was an elder brother,
If you dare but pronounce, you are the ſame,
Forget you are my ſon.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Theſe are no trifles, Sir, all is plotted,
To aſſure your greatneſs; if you will be wiſe,
And take the faire occaſion that's preſented.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Arcadius, you ſay, is lawful King,
And now to depoſe him, you would make me
An elder brother, is't not ſo?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Moſt right.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Nay, right or wrong, if this be your true meaning.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: Upon our lives.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: I'll venture mine, but with your pardon,
Whoſe brain was this? from whom took this plot life?

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: My Lord Caſſander.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: And you are of his mind? and you? and think
This may he done?

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: The deſtinies ſhall not cro • s us, if you have
Spirit to undertake it.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Undertake it?
I am not us'd to compliment, I'll owe
My life to you, my fortunes to your Lordſhip,
Compoſe me as you pleaſe, and when y'ave made
Me what you promiſe, you ſhall both divide
Me equally: one word, my Lord, I had rather
Live in the priſon ſtill, than be a prope •• y
To advance his politick ends.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Have no ſuſpition.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: So, ſo, I ſee Demetrius heels already
Trip'd up, and I'll diſpatch him out oth' way,
Which gone, I can depoſe this at my leaſure,
Being an Impoſtor, then my Son ſtands fair,
And may piece with the Princeſs, we loſe time,
What think you, if we firſt ſurprize the Court?
While you command the Caſtle, we ſhall curbe
All oppoſition.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Let's proclaim him firſt.
I have ſome faction, the people love me,
They gain'd to us, wee'll fall upon the Court.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Unleſs Demetrius yield himſelf, he bleeds.

sp.speaker: Sel.
sp.l: Who dares call treaſon ſin, when it ſucceeds?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Madam, you are too paſſionate, and loſe
The greatneſs of your ſoul, with the expence
Of too much grief, for that which providence
Hath eas'd you of, the burden of a ſtate
Above your tender bearing,

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Thour't a fool,
And canſt not reach the ſpirit of a Lady,
Born great as I was, and made onely leſs
By a too cruel deſtiny, above
Our tender bearing: What goes richer to
The compoſition of Man, than ours?
Our ſoul as free, and ſpatious; our heart's
As great, our will as large, each thought as active,
And in this onely Man more proud than we,
That would have us leſs capable of Empire,
But ſearch the ſtories, and the name of Queen
Shines bright with glory, and ſome precedents
Above Mans imitation.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: I grant it.
For the honor of our ſex, nor have you, Madam,
By any weakneſs, ſorfeited command,
He that ſucceeds, in juſtice, was before you,
And you have gain'd more, in a royal brother,
Than you could loſe by your reſign of Epire.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: This I allow Charilla, I ha done;
'Tis not the thought I am depos'd afflicts me,
At the ſame time I feel a joy to know
My Brother living: no, there is another
Wound in me above cure.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Virtue forbid.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Canſt find me out a Surgeon for that?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: My bleeding fame.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Oh do not injure
Your own clear innocence.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Do not flatter me,
I have been guilty of an act, will make
All love in women queſtion'd, is not that
A blot upon a Virgins name? my birth
Cannot ext • nuate my ſhame, I am
Become the ſtain of Epire.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: 'Tis but
Your own opinion, Madam, which preſents
Something to fright your ſelf, which cannot
Be in the ſame ſhape ſo horrid to our ſenſe,

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Thou wod'ſt, but canſt not appear ignorant:
Did not the Court, nay, the whole Kingdom, take
Notice, I lov'd Liſimachus?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: True, Madam.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: No, I was falſe,
Though counſel'd by my Father to affect him,
I had my politick ends upon Caſſander,
To be abſolute Queen, flattering his ſon with hopes
Of love and marriage, when that very day
I bluſh to think I wrong'd Liſimachus,
That noble Gentleman, but heaven puniſh'd me;
For though to know Demetrius was a bleſſing,
Yet who will not impute it my diſhonor.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Madam, you yet may recompence Liſimachus,
If you affect him now, you were not falſe
To him, whom then you lov'd not, if you can
Find any gentle paſſion in your ſoul
To entertain his thought, no doubt his heart,
Though ſad, retains a noble will to meet it,
His love was firm to you, and cannot be
Unrooted with one ſtorme.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: He will not ſure
Truſt any language from her tongue that mock'd him,
Although my ſoul doth weep ſor't, and is puniſh'd
To love him above the world.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Hee's here
As fate would have him reconcil'd, be free,
And ſpeak your thoughts.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: If, Madam, I appear
Too bold, your charity will ſign my pardon:
I heard you were not well, which made me haſte
To pay the duty of an humble viſit.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: You do not mock me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: I am confident
You think me not ſo loſt to manners, in
The knowledge of your perſon, to bring with me
Such rudeneſs, I have nothing to preſent,
But a heart full of wiſhes for your health,
And what elſe may be added to your happineſs.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: I thought you had been ſenſible.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: How Madam?

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: A man of underſtanding, can you ſpend
One prayer for me, remembring the diſhonor
I have done Liſimachus?

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: Nothing can deface that part of my
Religion in me, not to pray for you.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: It is not then impoſſible you may
Forgive me too, indeed I have a ſoul
Is full of penitence, and ſomething elſe,
If bluſhing would allow to give't a name.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: What Madam?

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Love, a love that ſhould redeem
My paſt offence, and make me white again.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: I hope no ſadneſs can poſſeſs your thoughts
For me, I am not worthy of this ſorrow,
But if you mean it any ſatisfaction
For what your will hath made me ſuffer, 'tis
But a ſtrange overflow of Charity,
To keep me ſtill alive, be your ſelf Madam,
And let no cauſe of mine, be guilty of
This rape upon your eyes, my name's not worth
The leaſt of all your tears.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: You think 'em counterfeit.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: Although I may
Suſpect a Womans ſmile hereafter, yet
I would believe their wet eyes, and if this
Be what you promiſe, for my ſake, I have
But one reply.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: I waite it.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: I have now
Another Miſtreſs.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Stay.

sp.speaker: Liſi.
sp.l: To whom I have made
Since your revolt from me, a new chaſte vow,
Which not the ſecond malice of my fate
Shall violate, and ſhe deſerves it, Madam,
Even for that wherein you are excellent,
Beauty, in which ſhe ſhines equal to you.
Her vertue, if ſhe but maintain what now
She is Miſtreſs of, beyond all competition,
So rich it cannot know to be improv'd,
At leaſt in my eſteem, I may offend,
But truth ſhall juſtifie, I have not flatter'd her,
I beg your pardon, and to leave my duty
Upon your hand, all that is good flow in you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Did he not ſay, Charilla, that he had
Another Miſtreſs?

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Such a ſound, methought,
Came from him.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Let's remove, here's too much ayre,
The ſad note multiplies.

sp.speaker: Cha.
sp.l: Take courage, Madam,
And my advice, he has another Miſtreſs,
If he have twenty, be you wiſe, and croſs him
With entertaining twice as many ſervants,
And when he ſees your humor he'll return.
And ſue for any Livery, grieve for this,

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: It muſt be ſhe, 'tis Polidora has
Taken his heart, ſhe live my rival,
How does the thought inflame me?

l.hi: Polidora?

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: And yet ſhe does but juſtly, and he too;
• would have rob'd her of Arcadius heart,
And they will both have this revenge on me,
But ſomething will rebel. Exit.

sp.speaker: De.
sp.l: The houſe is deſolate, none comes forth to meet us,
• hee's ſlow to entertain us: Philocles,
• prethee tell me, did ſhe weare no cloud
Upon her brow, was't freely that ſhe ſaid
We ſhould be welcome.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: To my apprehenſion,
Yet 'tis my wonder ſhe appears not.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: She, nor any other,
Sure there's ſome conceit
To excuſe it.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Stay, Who's this? obſerve what follows?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Fortune? ſome maske to entertain you, Sir.

div.stage: Enter Fortune crown'd, attended with Youth, Health, and Pleaſure.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: Not yet? What ſilence doth inhabit here?
No preparation to bid Fortune welcome!
Fortune, the genious of the World, have we
Deſcended from our pride, and ſtate to come,
So far attended with our darlings, Youth,
Pleaſure, and Health, to be neglected thus?
Sure this is not the place? call hither Fame.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: What would great Fortune?

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: Know.
Who dwells here.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Once more I report great Queen,
This is the houſe of Love.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: It cannot be,
This place has too much ſhade, and looks as if
• t had been quite forgotten of the Spring,
And Sun-beames Love affect ſociety,
And heat, here all is cold as the hairs of Winter,
No harmony, to catch the buſie eare
Of paſſengers, no object of delight,
To take the wandring eyes, no ſong, no grone
Of Lovers, no complaint of Wiliow garlands,
Love has a Beacon upon his palace top,
Of flaming hearts, to call the weary pilgrime
To reſt, and dwell with him, I ſee no fire
To threaten, or to warme: Can Love dwell here?

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: If there be noble love upon the World,
Truſt Fame, and find it here.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: Make good your boaſt,
And bring him to us.

sp.speaker: De.
sp.l: What does mean all this?

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I told you, Sir, we ſhould have ſome device.
There's Cupid now, that little Gentleman,
Has troubled every Maſque at Court this ſeven year.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: No more.

sp.speaker: Love.
sp.l: Welcome to Love, how much you honor me!
I • had become me, that, upon your ſummons,
I ſhould have waited upon mighty Fortune,
But ſince you have vouchſafed to viſit me;
All the delights Love can invent, ſhall flow
To entertain you, Muſick through the ayre
Shoot your inticing harmony.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: We came to dance and revel with you.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: I am poor
In my ambition, and want thought to reach
How much you honor Love. Dance.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: What intruſion's this?
Whom do you ſeek here.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: 'Tis honor.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: He my ſervant.

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: Fortune is come to viſit us.

sp.speaker: Hon.
sp.l: And has
Corrupted Love: Is this thy faith to her,
On whom we both waite, to betray her thus
To Fortunes triumph? take her giddy wheel,
And be no more companion to honor;
I bluſh to know thee, Who'll believe there can
Be truth in Love hereafter?

sp.speaker: Lov.
sp.l: I have found
My eyes, and ſee my ſhame, and with it, this
Proud ſorcereſs, from whom, and all her charmes,
I flye agen to Honor, be my guard,
Without thee I am loſt, and cannot boaſt,
The merit of a name.
Deſpis'd? I ſhall
Remember this affront.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: What Moral's this? Exeunt.
sp.stage: Enter Honor with the Crown upon a mourning Cuſhion.
sp.l: What melancholly object ſtrikes a ſudden
Chillneſs through all my veines; and turns me Ice?
It is the ſame I ſent, the very ſame,
As the firſt pledge of her inſuing greatneſs:
Why in this mourning livery, if ſhe live
To whom I ſent it? ha, What ſhape of ſorrow?
It is not Polidora, ſhe was faire
Enough, and wanted not the ſetting off
With ſuch a black: if thou beeſt Polidora,
Why mournes my love? it neither does become
Thy fortune, nor my joyes.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: But it becomes
My griefs, this habit fits a funeral,
And it were ſin, my Lord, not to lament
A friend new dead.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And I yet living? can
A ſorrow enter but upon thy Garment,
Or diſcomplexion thy attire, whilſt I
Enjoy a life for thee? Who can deſerve,
Weigh'd with thy living comforts, but a piece
Of all this Ceremony? give him a name.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: He was Arcadius.

l.hi: Arcadius?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: A Gentleman that lov'd me dearly once,
And does compel theſe poor, and fruitleſs drops,
Which willingly would fall upon his hearſe,
To imbalme him twice.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And are you ſure hee's dead?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: As ſure as you'r living, Sir, and yet
I did not cloſe his eyes, but he is dead,
And I ſhall never ſee the ſame Arcadius:
He was a Man ſo rich in all that's good,
At leaſt I thought him ſo, ſo perfect in
The rules of honor, whom alone to imitate
Were glory in a Prince, Nature her ſelf,
Till his creation, wrought imperfectly,
As ſhe had made but tryal of the reſt,
To mould him excellent.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And is he dead?
Come, ſhame him not with praiſes, recollect
Thy ſcatter'd hopes, and let me tell my beſt,
And deareſt Polidora, that he lives,
Still lives to honor thee.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Lives, Where?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Look here.
Am not I worth your knowledge?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: And my duty,
You are Demetrius, King of Epire, Sir.
I could not eaſily miſtake him ſo,
To whom I gave my heart.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Mine is not chang'd,
But ſtill hath ſed upon thy memory,
Theſe honors, and additions of ſtate
Are lent me for thy ſake, be not ſo ſtrange,
Let me not loſe my entertainment, now
I am improv'd, and rais'd unto the height,
Beneath which, I did bluſh to ask thy love.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Give me your pardon, Sir, Arcadius,
At our laſt meeting, without argument,
To move him more than his affection to me,
Vow'd he did love me; love me above all Women,
And to confirm his heart, was truely mine,
He wiſh'd, I tremble to remember it,
When he forſook his Polidora's love,
That Heaven might kill his happineſs on Earth:
Was not this nobly ſaid? did not this promiſe
A truth to ſhame the Turtles?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: And his heart
I • ſtill the ſame, and I thy conſtant Lover.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Give me your leave, I pray, I would not ſay,
Arcadius was perjur'd, but the ſame day
Forgetting all his promiſes, and oathes,
While yet they hung upon his lips, forſook me,
D'ee not remember this too, gave his faith
From me, tranſported with the noiſe of greatneſs,
And would be married to a Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: But Heaven permitted not I ſhould diſpoſe
What was ordain'd for thee.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: It was not virtue
In • im, for ſure he found no check, no ſting
In his own boſome, but gave freely all
The reines to blind ambition.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I am wounded,
The thought of thee ith' throng of all my joyes,
Like poyſon powr'd in Nectar, turnes me frantick:
Dear, if Arcadius have made a fault,
Let not Demetrius be puniſh'd for't,
He pleads that ever will be conſtant to thee.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Shall I believe Mans flatteries agen,
Loſe my ſweet reſt, and peace of thought agen,
Be drawn by you, from the ſtreight paths of virtue,
Into the maze of Love.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I ſee compaſſion in thy eye, that chides me,
If I have either ſoul, but what's contain'd
Within theſe words, or if one ſyllable
Of their full force, be not made good by me,
May all relenting thoughts in you take end,
And thy diſdain be doubled from thy pardon,
I'll count my Coronation; and that hour
Fix with a rubrick in my Calendar,
As an auſpicious time, to entertain
Affairs of weight with Princes; think who now
Intreats thy mercy, come, thou ſha't be kind,
And divide Titles with me.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Hear me, Sir,
I lov'd you once for virtue, and have not
A thought ſo much unguarded, as to be won
From my truth, and innocence with any
Motives of ſtate to affect you,
Your bright temptation mourns while it ſtayes here;
Nor can the triumph of glory, which made you
Forget me, ſo court my opinion back,
Were you no King, I ſhould be ſooner drawn
Again to love you, but 'tis now too late,
A low obedience ſhall become me beſt:
May all the joyes I want
Still wait on you, if time hereafter tell you,
That ſorrow for your fault hath ſtruck me dead,
May one ſoft tear drop from your eye, in pitty
Bedew my hearſe, and I ſhall ſleep ſecurely:
I have but one word more for goodneſs ſake,
For your own honor, Sir, correct your paſſion,
To her you ſhall love next, and I forgive you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Her heart is frozen up, nor can warm prayers
Thaw it to any ſoftneſs.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I'll fetch her, Sir, again.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Perſwade her not.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: You give your paſſion too much leave to triumph.
Seek in another what ſhe denies.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Where's the King? oh, Sir, you are undone,
A dangerous treaſon is a foot.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: What Treaſon?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Caſſander, and Eubulus have proclaim'd
Another King, whom they pretend to be
Leonatus your elder Brother, he that was,
But this morning priſoner in the Caſtle.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: The eaſie Epirotes
Gather in multitudes to advance his Title,
They have ſeiſed upon the Court, ſecure your perſon,
Whilſt we raiſe power to curbe this Inſurrection.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Loſe no time then.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: We will not Arme one Man,
Speak it agen, have I a brother living?
And muſt be no King.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: What means your Grace?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: This newes doth ſpeak me happy, it exalts
My heart, and makes me capable of more
Than twenty Kingdoms.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Will you not, Sir, ſtand
Upon your guard?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I'll ſtand upon my honor,
Mercy relieves me.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: Will you loſe the Kingdom?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: The World's too poor to bribe me: leave
Me all, leſt you extenuate my fame, and I
Be thought to have redeem'd it by your counſel,
Titles may ſet a gloſs upon our Name,
But Virtue onely is the ſoul of Fame.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: He's ſtrangely poſſeſt Gentlemen. Exeunt Omnes.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: HEres a ſtrange turne, Liſander.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: 'Tis a Kingdom
Eaſily purchas'd, who will truſt the faith
Of multitudes?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: It was his fault, that would
So tamely give his Title to their Mercy,
The new King has poſſeſſion.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: And is like
To keep't, we are alone, what doſt think of
This innovation? Is't not a fine Jigge?
A precious cunning in the late Protector
To ſhuffle a new Prince into the ſtate.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: I know not how they have ſhuffled, but my head on't,
A falſe card is turn'd up trump, but fates look to't.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Does he not carry it bravely?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Excellently.

l.hi: Philocles, Liſander.

sp.speaker: Phi. Liſ.
sp.l: Your Lordſhips ſervants,
Are we not bound to heaven, for multiplying
Theſe bleſſings on the Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Heaven alone
Works miracles, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Liſa.
sp.l: I think your Lordſhip
Had as little hope once to ſee theſe Princes Revive.

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Here we muſt place our thanks,
Next providence, for preſerving
So dear a pledge.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: The King.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: It is our pleaſure
The number of our guard be doubled, give
A Largeſs to the Soldiers; but diſmiſs not
The Troops till we command.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: May it pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: It will not pleaſe us otherwiſe, my Lord,
We have try'd your faith.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Does he not ſpeak with confidence?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: My Lords and Gentlemen, to whoſe faith we muſt
O • e next to Heaven our fortune, and our ſafety,
After a tedious eclipſe, the day
• bright, and we inveſted in thoſe honors,
Our bloud, and birth did challenge.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: May no time
• e regiſtred in our annals, that ſhall mention
•• e that had life to oppoſe your ſacred perſon,

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Let them, whoſe Titles forg'd and flaw'd, ſuſpect
Their ſtates ſecurity, our right to Epire,
• eaven is oblig'd to proſper, treaſon has
• o face ſo black to fright it, all my cares
• evel to this, that I may worthily
• anage the province, and advance the honor
• f our dear Countrey, and be confident,
• an expence of bloud, may give addition
• f any happineſs to you, I ſhall
• ffer my heart the ſacrifice, and rejoyce
• o make my ſelf a ghoſt, to have inſcrib'd
• pon my marble, but whoſe cauſe I died for.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: May Heaven avert ſuch danger.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Excellent Prince,
• whom we ſee the Copy of his Father,
• one but the Son of Theodoſius,
• ould have ſpoke thus.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We are pleas'd to interpret well,
• et give me leave to ſay in my own juſtice,
• have but expreſt the promptneſs of my ſoul
• o ſerve you all, but 'tis not empty wiſhes
• an ſatisfie our mighty charge, a weight
• ould make an Atlas double, a Kings name
•• th ſound harmoniouſly to men at diſtance;
•• d thoſe who cannot penetrate beyond
• he bark, and out-skin of a Common-wealth,
• ſtate, have eyes, but raviſh'd with the Ceremony
•• at muſt attend a Prince, and underſtand not
• hat cares allay the glories of a Crown,
• good Kings find and feel the contrary,
•• have try'd, my Lord, the burden, and can tell
• ould require a Pilot of more years
• o ſteer this Kingdom, now impos'd on me,
By juſtice of my birth.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I wiſh not life,
But to partake thoſe happy days, which muſt
Succeed theſe fair proceedings, we are bleſt,
But Sir, be ſparing to your ſelf, we ſhall
Hazard our joyes in you too ſoon, the burden
Of ſtate affairs, impoſe upon your counſel.
'Tis fitter that we waſte our lives than you,
Call age too ſoon upon you with the trouble,
And cares that threaten ſuch an undertaking,
Preſerve your youth.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And chooſe you our Proteſtor,
Is't that you would conclude my Lord? We will
Deſerve our ſubjects faith for our own ſake,
Not ſit an idle gazer at the helm

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: How obſerv'd you that,
Mark how Caſſander's Planet ſtruck.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.l: He might have look'd more calmly for all that,
I begin to fear; but do not yet ſeem troubled.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: With what news travels his haſte? I muſt ſecure
My ſelf betimes, not be a King in jeſt,
And wear my Crown a Tenant to their breath.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Demetrius, Sir, your brother,
With other Traitors that oppoſe your claims,
Are fled to the Caſtle of Neſtorius,
And fortifie.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: I ſaid not ſo my Lord.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I'll have it thought ſo, hence. Exit Meſſen.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Plant forces to batter
The walls, and in their ruin bring us work
They live not.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Good Sir hear me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Let it work,
Were Demetrius dead, we eaſily might uncrown
This ſwoln Impoſtor, and my Son be fair
To piece with young Sophia, who I hear
Repents her late affront.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Their lives may do
You ſervice, let not blood ſtain your beginnings
The people not yet warm in their allegeance,
May think it worth their tumult to revenge it
With hazard of your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Who dares but think it?
Yet offer firſt our mercy, if they yield,
Demetrius muſt not live, my Lord your counſel,
What if he were in heaven?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: You have my conſent,
You ſha'not ſtay long after him.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Sophia is
Not my Siſter,
To prevent all that may indanger us, we'll marry her;
That done, no matter though we ſtand diſcover'd,
For in her Title then we are King of Epire,
Without diſpute,

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Hum; in my judgement, Sir,
That wonot do ſo well.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What's your opinion?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: He countermines my plot: are you ſo cunning

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: What's that you mutter; Sir?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I mutter, Sir?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Beſt ſay I am no King, but ſome impoſtor
Rais'd up to gull the ſtate.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Very fine to have ſaid within
Few hours you'd been no King, nor like to be,
Was not in the compaſs of High Treaſon
I take it.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Reſtrein your anger, the Kings mov'd, ſpeak not.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I will ſpeak louder; do I not know him?
That ſelf-ſame hand that rais'd him to the throne
Shall pluck him from it, is this my reward?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Our guard, to priſon with him,

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Me to priſon?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Off with his head.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: My head?

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Vouchſafe to hear me, great Sir.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: How dares he be ſo inſolent?
I ha' wrought my ſelf into a fine condition,
Do'e know me Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Phi.
sp.l: Very well my Lord;
How are we bound to heaven for multiplying
Theſe bleſſings on the Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: We allow it.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Counſel did never blaſt a Princes ear.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Convey him to the ſanctuary of Rebels,
N • ſtorius houſe, where our proud brother has
Enſcons'd himſelf, they'll entertain him lovingly,
He will be a good addition to the Traitors,
Obey me, or you dye for't, what are Kings
When ſubjects dare affront 'em?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I ſhall vex
Thy ſoul for this.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Away with him: when Kings
Frown, let offenders tremble, this flows not
From any cruelty in my nature, but
The fate of an Uſurper: he that will
Be confirm'd great without juſt title to't,
Muſt loſe compaſſion, know what's good, not do't.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Madam, the Princeſs Sophia.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I attend her Highneſs.
How much your grace honors your humble ſervant

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: I hope my brother's well.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I hope ſo too, Madam.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Do you but hope? he came to be your gueſt.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: We are all his, whilſt he is pleas'd to honor
This poor roof with his royal preſence, Madam.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: I came to ask your pardon Polidora.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: You never, Madam, treſpaſs'd upon me,
Wrong not your goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: I can be but penitent,
Unleſs you point me out ſome other way
To ſatisfie.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Dear Madam, do not mock me.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: There's no injury like that to love,
I find it now in my own ſufferings:
But though I would have rob'd thee of Arcadius
Heaven knew a way to reconcile your hearts,
And puniſh me in thoſe joys you have found:
I read the ſtory of my loſs of honor,
Yet can rejoyce, and heartily, that you
Have met your own agen.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Whom do you mean?

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: My brother.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: He is found to himſelf and honor,
He is my King, and though I muſt acknowledge
He was the glory of my thoughts, and I
Lov'd him, as you did, Madam, with deſire
To be made his, reaſon, and duty ſince,
Form'd me to other knowledge, and I now
Look on him without any wiſh of more
Than to be call'd his ſubject.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Has he made
Himſelf leſs capable by being King?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Of what?

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Of your affection.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: With your pardon, Madam.
Love in that ſenſe you mean, loſt Polidora
When he forſook Arcadius, I diſclaim
