All ties between us, more than what a name
Of King muſt challenge from my obedience.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: This does confirm my jealouſie, my heart,
For my ſake, Madam, has he loſt his value?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Let me beſeech your grace, I may have leave
To anſwer in ſome other cauſe, or perſon:
This argument but opens a ſad wound
To make it bleed afreſh; we may change this
Diſcourſe: I would elect ſome ſubject, whoſe
Praiſes may more delight your ear than this
Can mine; let's talk of young Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Ha! my preſaging fears.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: How does your grace?

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Well, you were talking of Liſimachus,
Pray give me your opinion of him.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Mine?
It will be much ſhort of his worth: I think him
A gentleman ſo perfect in all goodneſs,
That if there be one in the world deſerves
The beſt of women, heaven created him,
To make her happy.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: You have, in a little, Madam,
Expreſt a volume of mankind, a miracle;
But all have not the ſame degree of faith,
He is but young.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: What Miſtriſs would deſire
Her ſervant old? he has both Spring to pleaſe
Her eye, and Summer to return a harveſt.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: He is black.

sp.speaker: Pil.
sp.l: He ſets a beauty off more rich,
And ſhe that's fair will love him; faint complexions
Betray effeminate minds, and love of change:
Two beauties in a bed, compound few men;
He's not ſo fair to counterfeit a woman,
Nor yet ſo black, but bluſhes may betray
His modeſty.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: His proportion exceeds not.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: That praiſes him, and a well compacted frame
Speaks temper, and ſweet flow of elements:
Vaſt buildings are more oft for ſhew than uſe:
I would not have my eyes put to the travel
Of many acres, e'r I could examine
A man from head to foot; he has no great,
But he may boaſt, an elegant compoſition.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: I'll hear no more, you have ſo far out-done
My injuries to you, that I call back
My penitence, and muſt tell Polidora,
This revenge ill becomes her. Am I thought
So loſt in ſoul to hear, and forgive this?
In what ſhade do I live? or ſhall I think
I have not, at the loweſt, enough merit,
Setting aſide my birth, to poize with yours:
Forgive my modeſt thoughts, if I riſe up
In my own defence, and tell this unjuſt Lady
So great a winter hath not frozen yet
My cheek, but there's ſomething nature planted,
That carries as much bloom, and ſpring upon't,
As yours. What flame is in your eye, but may
Find competition here? (forgive agen
My Virgin honor, what is in your lip
To tice the enamour'd ſoul, to dwell with more
Ambition, than the yet unwither'd bluſh
That ſpeaks the innocence of mine?
Oh brother?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I'll talk with you anon, my Polidora,
Allow thy patience till my breath recover,
Which now comes laden with the richeſt news
Thy ear was ever bleſt with.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Both your looks,
And voice expreſs ſome welcome accident.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Gueſs what in wiſh could make me fortunate
And heaven hath dropt that on Demetrius.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: What means this extaſie?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: 'Twere ſin to buſie
Thy thoughts upon't, I'll tell thee that I could
Retein ſome part; 'tis too wide a joy
To be expreſt ſo ſoon, and yet it falls
In a few ſyllables, thou wot ſcarce believe me,
I am no King.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: How's that!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Good Heaven forbid.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Forbid? Heaven has reliev'd me with a mercy
I knew not how to ask, I have, they ſay,
An elder brother living, crown'd already,
I only keep my name Demetrius,
Without deſire of more addition,
Than to return thy ſervant.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: You amaze me,
Can you rejoyce to be depoſed:

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: It but
Tranſlates me to a fairer and better Kingdom
In Polidora.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Me?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Did you not ſay,
Were I no King, you could be drawn to love
Me agen, that was conſented to in Heaven:
A Kingdom firſt betraid my ambitious ſoul
To forget thee, that, and the flattering glories,
How willingly Demetrius does reſign,
The Angels know: thus naked without Titles
• throw me on thy charity, and ſhall
Boaſt greater Empire to be thine agen, than
To wear the triumphs of the world upon me.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Be not ſo careleſs of your ſelf, the people
Gather in multitudes to your protection
Offering their lives and fortunes, if they may
But ſee you Sir, and hear you ſpeak to 'em,
Accept their duties, and in time prevent
• our ruin.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Be not deſperate, 'tis counſel.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: You trouble me with noiſe, ſpeak Polidora

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: For your own ſake preſerve your ſelf,
My fears diſtract my reaſon.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Lord Liſimachus,
With ſomething that concerns your ſafety, is
• led hither, and deſires a preſent hearing.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: His ſoul is honeſt, be not, Sir, a mad man,
• nd for a Lady, give up all our freedoms. Exit.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I'll ſay any thing here, Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Dear brother hear him.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Sir, I come to yield
My ſelf your priſoner, if my father have
• ais'd an Impoſtor to ſupplant your Title
Which I ſuſpect, and inwardly do bleed for,
• ſhall not only, by the tender of
My ſelf, declare my innocence, but either,
• y my unworthy life, ſecure your perſon,
Or by what death you ſhall impoſe, reward
The unexpected Treaſon.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Brave young man,
Did you not hear him Brother?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I am not minded.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Be witneſs Madam, I reſign my heart
• never was anothers, you declare
• oo great a ſatisfaction, I hope
This will deſtroy your jealouſie,
Remember now your danger.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: I deſpiſe it,
What fate dares injure me?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Yet hear me Sir.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Forgive me Polidora, you are happy,
My hopes are remov'd farther, I had thought
Liſimachus had meant you for his Miſtriſs,
'Tis miſery to feed, and not know where
To place my jealouſie.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: Now 'tis too late,
You may be deafe, until the Cannon make,
You find your ſenſe, we are ſhut up now by
A troop of Horſe, thank your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: They will
Admit conditions.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: And allow us quarter. A ſhout within.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: We are all loſt.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Be comforted.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: News my Lord Caſſander ſent by the new King.
To bear us company.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Not as priſoner?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It does appear no otherwiſe, the ſoldiers
Declare how much they love him, by their noiſe
Of ſcorn, and joy to ſee him ſo rewarded.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: It cannot be.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You'll find it preſently,
He curſes the new King, talks treaſon 'gainſt him
As nimble as he were in's ſhirt, he's here.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Oh let me beg untill my knees take root
I'th'earth, Sir, can you pardon me?

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: For what?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: For Treaſon, deſperate, moſt malicious Treaſon:
I have undone you Sir.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: It does appear
You had a Will.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I'll make you all the recompence I can,
But e'r you kill me, hear me, know the man,
Whom I to ſerve my unjuſt ends, advanc'd
To your throne, is an impoſtor, a mere counterfeit,
Eubulus' Son. Etxi Anti

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: It is not then our brother?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: An inſolent uſurper, proud, and bloudy;
Seleucus, is no leproſie upon me?
There is not puniſhment enough in nature
To quit my horrid act, I have not in
My ſtock of blood, to ſatisfie with weeping,
Nor could my ſoul, though melted to a flood
Within me, guſh out tears to waſh my ſtain off.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: How? an Impoſtor, what will become on's now?
We are at his mercy:

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Sir, the peoples hearts
Will come to their own dwelling, when they ſee
I dare accuſe my ſelf, and ſuffer for it,
Have courage then young King, thy fate cannot
Be long compell'd.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Riſe, our misfortune
Carries this good, although it loſe our hopes,
It makes you friend with virtue, we'll expect
What providence will do.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: You are too merciful.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Our duties ſhall beg heaven ſtill to preſerve you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Our enemy deſires ſome parley, Sir,

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: 'Tis not amiſs to hear their propoſition.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I'll wait upon you.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Thou art my Angel, and canſt beſt inſtruct me,
Boldly preſent our ſelves, you'll with Caſſander.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: And in death be bleſt
To find our charity, Exit.

l.hi: Liſimachus.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: They will not miſs your preſence, the ſmall time
Is ſpent in asking of a queſtion.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: I wait your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Sir, I have a ſuit to you.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: To me? it muſt be granted.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: If you have
Cancell'd your kind opinion of me,
Deny me not to know, who hath ſucceeded
Sophia in your heart, I beg the name
Of your new Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: You ſhall know her, Madam,
If but theſe tumults ceaſe, and fate allow us
To ſee the Court agen, I hope you'll bring
No mutiny againſt her, but this is
No time to talk of Love, let me attend you.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: I muſt expect, till you are pleas'd to ſatisfie
My poor requeſt, conduct me at your pleaſure. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Leonatus, Eubulus, Biſhop, Liſander, and Philocles.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: They are too ſlow, diſpatch new meſſengers,
To intreat 'em fairly hither, I am extaſi'd,
Were you witneſs for me too? is it poſſible
I am what this affirms, true Leonatus,
And were you not my Father, was I given
In truſt to you an Infant?

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: 'Tis a truth,
Our ſoul's bound to acknowledge, you ſupply'd
The abſence and opinion of my Son.
Who died, but to make you my greater care
I know not of Demetrius, but ſuppos'd
Him dead indeed, as Epire thought you were,
Your Fathers character doth want no teſtimony,
Which but compar'd with what concerns Demetrius
Will prove it ſelf King Theodoſius act,
Your Royal Father.

sp.speaker: Biſh.
sp.l: I am ſubſcrib'd to both his Legacies
By oath oblig'd to ſecreſie, until
Thus fairly ſummon'd to reveal the truſt.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: Caſſander had no thought you would prove thus,
To whoſe policie I gave this aim, although
He wrought you up to ſerve but as his Engine
To batter young Demetrius, for it was
Your Fathers prudent jealouſie, that made him
Give out your early deaths, as if his ſoul
Prophecy'd his own firſt, and fear'd to leave
Either of you, to the unſafe protection,
Of one, whoſe ſtudy would be to ſupplant
Your right, and make himſelf the King of Epire.

sp.speaker: Biſh.
sp.l: Your Siſter, fair Sophia, in your Fathers
Life, was deſign'd to marry with Liſimachus
That guarded her; although ſhe us'd ſome Art
To quit her pupillage, and being abſolute,
Declar'd love to Demetrius, which enforc'd
Macarius to diſcover firſt your brother.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: No more, leſt you deſtroy agen Leonatus
With wonder of his fate, are they not come yet?
Something it was, I felt within my envy
Of young Demetrius's fortune, there were ſeeds
Scattered upon my heart, that made it ſwell
With thought of Empire, Princes I ſee cannot
Be totally eclips'd, but wherefore ſtays
Demetrius and Sophia, at whoſe names
A gentle ſpirit walk'd upon my blood

div.stage: Enter Demetrius, Polidora, Sophia, Macarius, Caſſander, Liſima.

sp.speaker: Eub.
sp.l: They are here,

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Then thus I flie into their boſoms,
Nature has rectifi'd in me, Demetrius,
The wandrings of ambition, our dear Siſter
You are amaz'd, I did expect it, read
Aſſurance there, the day is big with wonder,

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: What means all this?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Liſimachus, be dear to us,
Caſſander, you are welcome too.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Not I,
I do not look for't, all this ſha'not bribe
My conſcience to your faction, and make
Me falſe agen, Seleucus is no ſon
Of Theodoſius, my dear Countrey-men
Correct your erring duties, and to that,
Your lawful King, proſtrate your ſelves, Demetrius
Doth challenge all your knees.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: All Love and Duty,
Flow from me to my Royal King, and Brother
I am confirm'd.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: You are two credulous,
What can betray your faith ſo much?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Sophia, you appear ſad, as if your Will
Gave no conſent to this days happineſs.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: No joy exceeds Sophia's for your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: With your pardon, Sir, I apprehend
A cauſe that makes her troubled, ſhe deſires
To know, what other Miſtriſs, ſince her late
Unkindneſs, I have choſen to direct
My faith and ſervice.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Another Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: And does our Siſter love Liſimachus?

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: Here's ſomething would confeſs.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: He muſt not dare
To affront Sophia.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: How my ſhame confounds me,
I beg your juſtice, without pity on
My age.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Your pennance ſhall be, to be faithful
To our ſtate hereafter,

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: May you live long and happy,
Leonatus, King of Epire.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: But where's your other Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Liſ.
sp.l: Even here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Our Siſter? is this another Miſtriſs, Sir?

sp.speaker: Siſ.
sp.l: It holds
To prove my thoughts were ſo when ſhe began
Her ſorrow for neglecting me, that ſweetneſs
Deſerv'd, I ſhould eſteem her another Miſtriſs,
Then when ſhe cruelly forſook Liſimachus,
Your pardon Madam, and receive a heart
Proud with my firſt devotions to ſerve you.

sp.speaker: Sop.
sp.l: In this I am crown'd agen, now mine for ever.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: You have deceiv'd her happily,
Joy to you both.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: We are ripe for the ſame wiſhes,
Polidora's part of me.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: He all my bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Heaven pour full joys upon you.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.l: We are all bleſt,
There wants but one to fill your arms.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: My Miſtriſs,
And Wife ſhall be my Countrey, to which I
Was in my birth contracted, your love ſince
Hath plaid the Prieſt to perfect what was ceremony
Though Kingdoms by juſt Titles prove our own,
The ſubjects hearts do beſt ſecure a Crown.

div.head: EPILOGUE.
div.l: THere is no Coronation to day,
Ʋnleſs your gentle votes do crown our Play;
If ſmiles appear within each Ladies eye,
Which are the leading Stars in this fair skie,
Our ſolemn day ſets glorious, for then
We hope by their ſad influence, the men
Will grace what they firſt ſhin'd on, make't appear,
(Both) how we pleaſe, and bleſs our covetous ear
With your applauſe, more welcome than the Bells
Ʋpon a triumph, Bonfires, or what elſe
Can ſpeak a Coronation. And though I
Were late depos'd, and ſpoil'd of Majeſty,
By the kind aid of your hands, Gentlemen,
I quickly may be Crown'd a Queen agen.

div.head: The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Ricardo, a young Gentleman, in love with Viola.

list.head: three merry Gentlemen, friends to Ricardo,

div.head: PROLOGUE.
div.l: THis Comedy long forgot, by ſome thought dead,
By us preſerv'd, once more doth raiſe her head.
And to your noble cenſures does preſent,
Her outward form, and inward ornament.
Nor let this ſmell of arrogance, ſince 'tis known,
The makers that confeſt it for their own
Were this way skilful, and without the crime
Of flatteries I may ſay did pleaſe the time;
The work it ſelf too, when it firſt came forth,
In the opinion of men of worth,
Was well receiv'd and favour'd, though ſome rude
And harſh among th' ignorant multitude,
(That reliſh groſs food, better than a diſh,
That's cook'd with care, and ſerv'd into the wiſh,
Of curious pallats) wanting wit and ſtrength,
Truly to judge, condemn'd it for the length,
That fault's reform'd, and now 'tis to be try'd
Before ſuch Judges 'twill not be deny'd
A free and noble hearing: nor fear I,
But 'twill deſerve to have free liberty,
And give you cauſe (and with content) to ſay,
Their care was good, that did revive this Play.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: LEt us make uſe of this ſtolen privacy,
And not looſe time in proteſtation, Miſtriſs,
For 'twere in me a kind of breach of faith,
To ſay again I love you.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Sweet, ſpeak ſoftly
For though the venture of your love to me,
Meets with a willing, and a full return:
Should it arrive unto my Fathers knowledge;
This were our laſt diſcourſe.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: How ſhall he know it?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: His watching cares are ſuch, for my advancement,
That every where his eye is fix'd upon me:
This night that does afford us ſome ſmall freedom,
At the requeſt and much intreaty of
The Miſtriſs of the Houſe, was hardly given me:
For I am never ſuffer'd to ſtir out,
But he hath ſpies upon me: yet I know not
You have ſo won upon me, that could I think
You would love faithfully (though to entertain
Another thought of you, would be my death)
I ſhould adventure on his utmoſt anger.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Why do you think I can be falſe?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: No faith,
You'ave an honeſt face, but if you ſhould —

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Let all the ſtor'd vengeance of heaven's juſtice—

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: No more, I do believe you, the dance ended,
Which this free womans gheſts have vow d to have
E'r they depart, I will make home, and ſtore me
With all the Jewels, Chains, and Gold are truſted
Unto my cuſtody, and at the next corner,
To my Fathers houſe, before one at the fartheſt,
Be ready to receive me.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: I deſire
No bond beyond your promiſe, let's go in,
To talk thus much, before the door, may breed Suſpition.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Here are company too.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Away,
Thoſe powers that proſper true and honeſt loves
Will bleſs our undertakings.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: 'Tis my wiſh, Sir. Exit Rich. and Viol.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Nay, Sir, excuſe me, I have drawn you to
Too much expence already in my travel:
And you have been too forward in your love;
To make my wants your own, allow me manners
Which you muſt grant I want, ſhould I increaſe,
The bond in which your courteſies have ti'd me:
By ſtill conſuming you, give me leave
To take mine own ways now, and I ſhall often,
With willingneſs, come to viſit you, and then thank you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: By this hand I could be angry, what do you think me?
Muſt we that have ſo long time been as one
Seen Cities, Countreys, Kingdoms, and their wonders;
Been bedfellows, and in our various journey
Mixt all our obſervations, part (as if
We were two Carriers at two ſeveral ways,
And as the fore-horſe guides, cry God be with you)
Without or compliment, or ceremony?
In Travellers, that know tranſalpine garbs,
Though our deſigns are nee'r ſo ſerious, friend,
• t were a capital crime, it muſt not be:
Nay, what is more, you ſhall not; you e'r long,
• hall ſee my houſe, and find what I call mine
Is wholly at your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: 'Tis this tires me,
Sir, I were eaſily woo'd, if nothing elſe
But my Will lay in the choice: but 'tis not ſo,
My friends and kindred that have part of me,
And ſuch on whom my chiefeſt hopes depend,
Juſtly expect the tender of my love
After my travel: then mine own honeſty
Tells me 'tis poor, having indifferent means
To keep me in my quality and rank,
At my return, to tire anothers bounty,
And let mine own grow luſty, pardon me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I will not, cannot, to conclude, I dare not:
Can any thing conferr'd upon my friend
Be burthenſome to me? for this excuſe
Had I no reaſon elſe, you ſhould not leave me,
By a travellers faith you ſhould not, I have ſaid,
And then you know my humor, there's no contending.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Is there no way to 'ſcape this Inundation?
I ſhall be drown'd with folly if I go:
And after nine days, men may take me up,
With my gall broken.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Are you yet reſolv'd?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Wou'd you would ſpare me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: By this light I cannot
By all that may be ſworn by.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Patience help me,
And heaven grant his folly be not catching:
If it be, the Town's undone, I now would give
A reaſonable ſum of gold to any Sheriff,
That would but lay an execution on me,
And free me from his company; while he was abroad,
His want of wit and language kept him dumb?
But Balaam's Aſſe will ſpeak now, without ſpurring.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Speak, have I won you?—

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: You are not to be reſiſted.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Be ready I intreat you, the dance done,
Beſides a liberal reward I have,
A bottle of Sherry in my power ſhall beget
New crotchets in your heads.

sp.speaker: Muſi.
sp.l: Tuſh, fear not us, we'll do our parts.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Go in.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I know this fellow.
Belong you to the houſe?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: I ſerve the Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Pretty, and ſhort, pray you Sir then inform her,
Two Gentlemen are covetous to be honor'd,
With her fair preſence.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: She ſhall know ſo much,
This is a merry night with us, and forbid not
Welcome to any that looks like a man:
I'll guide you the way.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Nay, follow, I have a trick in't. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Uberto, Silvio, Richardo, Maria, Pedro. Portia, Viola, with others.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.l: Come, where's this Masque? faireſt, for our chear,
Our thanks and ſervice, may you long ſurvive,
To joy in many of theſe nights.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I thank you.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.l: We muſt have Muſick too, or elſe you give us,
But half a welcome.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Pray you Sir, excuſe me.

sp.speaker: Silv.
sp.l: By no means, Lady.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.l: We'll crown our liberal feaſt,
With ſome delightful ſtrain ſitting your love:
And this good company.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Since you enforce it,
I will not plead the excuſe of want of skill
Or be, or nice, or curious, every year
I celebrate my marriage night; and will
Till I ſee my abſent Husband.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.l: 'Tis fit freedom,

sp.speaker: Silv.
sp.l: Richardo thou art dull—

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: I ſhall be lighter,
When I have had a heat.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now Sir, the news?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Miſtriſs, there are two Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Complimenting who ſhould firſt enter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What are they?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Heaven knows, but for their ſtrangeneſs, have you never ſeen a Cat waſh her face?

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Juſt ſuch a ſtir they keep, if you make but haſte,
You may ſee 'em yet before they enter.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Let 'em be what they we'll, I'll keep them fair
Entertain, and gentle welcome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It ſhall be ſo.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Then let it be your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Lets ſtand aſide, and you ſhall ſee us have
Fine ſport anon.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: A fair ſociety, do you know theſe Gentlewomen?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: What are they?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: The ſecond is a neighbors Daughter, her name is Viola. There is my kinſmans wife, Portia her name, and a Friend too.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Let her—what's ſhe that leads the dance?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: A Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I ſee that.

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: Indeed?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: A Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Udsfoot, good Sir, what's ſhe that leads the dance?

sp.speaker: 2 Serv.
sp.l: My Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: What elſe?

sp.speaker: 2 Serv.
sp.l: My Miſtriſs, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Your Miſtriſs? a pox on you,
sp.p: What a fry of fools are here? I ſee 'tis treaſon to underſtand in this houſe: if nature were not better to them, than they can be to themſelves, they would ſcant hit their mouths my Miſtriſs? is there any one with ſo much wit in's head, that can tell me at the firſt ſight, what Gentlewoman that is that leads the dance?
sp.l: 'Tis my wife.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Hum.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How doſt thou like her?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Well, a pretty Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Prethee be quiet.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I would I could
Let never any hereafter that's a man,
That has affections in him, and free paſſions,
Receive the leaſt tye from ſuch a fool as this is,
That holds ſo ſweet a wife, 'tis lamentable to conſider truly
What right he robs himſelf of, and what wrong
He doth the youth of ſuch a Gentlewoman?
That knows her beauty, is no longer hers,
Than men will pleaſe to make it ſo, and uſe it
Neither of which lies freely in a Husband,
Oh what have I done, what have I done, Coxcomb?
If I had never ſeen, or never taſted
The goodneſs of this kix, I had been a made man,
But now to make a Cuckold is a ſin
Againſt all forgiveneſs, worſe than a murther;
I have a Wolf by the ears, and am bitten both ways.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How now friend, what are you thinking of?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Nothing concerning you, I muſt be gone.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Pardon me, I'll have no going, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Then good Sir, give me leave to go to bed,
I am very weary, and ill-temper'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You ſhall preſently, the dance is done.

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: Miſtriſs, theſe are the Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: My Husband's welcome home, dear Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: She's fair ſtill, oh that I were a knave, or durſt be one,
For thy ſake coxcomb; he that invented honeſty, undid me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I thought you had not known me, y'are merry 'tis well
And how iſt with theſe worthy Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Ʋb. & Sil.
sp.l: We are glad to ſee you here again.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Oh Gent, what ha' you loſt? but get you into travels, thought,
There you may learn, I cannot ſay what hidden virtues.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Hidden from you I am ſure,
My blood boils like a furnace,
She's a fair one.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Pray entertain this Gent. with all the courteſ • e,
Fitting my moſt eſpecial friend.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What this poor houſe may yield,
To make you welcome, dear Sir, command
Without more compliment.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I thank you:
She's wiſe, and ſpeaks well too, oh what a bleſſing
Is gone by me, ne'er to be recovered?
sp.p: Well, 'twas an old ſhame the Devil laid up for me, and now has hit me home; if there be any ways to be diſhoneſt, and ſave my ſelf yet,— No, it muſt not be, why ſhould I be a fool too—Yet thoſe eyes would tempt another Adam, how they call to me, and tell me—S'foot, they ſhall not tell me any thing, Sir, will you walk in?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How is't, Signior?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Crazie a little.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: What all you, Sir?
What's in my power, pray make uſe of, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: 'Tis that muſt do me good, ſhe does not mock me ſure?
And 't pleaſe you nothing, my diſeaſe is only wearineſs.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p: Come Gentlemen, we, ll not keep you from your beds too long.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: I ha' ſome buſineſs, and 'tis late, and you far from your lodging.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Well. Exit manent, Ant. Mar and Mer.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Come my dear Mercury, I'll bring you to your chamber, and then I am for you Maria, thou art a new wife to me now, and thou ſhalt find it e'r I ſleep.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: And I, an old aſs to my ſelf, mine own rod whips me,—good Sir, no more of this, 'tis tedious, you are the beſt guide in your own houſe—go Sir— Exit Ant and Mer.
sp.l: This fool and his fair Wife have made me frantick
From two ſuch Phyſicks for the ſoul, deliver me. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Richardo, Uberto, Pedro, and Silvio.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.l: Well you muſt have this wench then.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: I hope ſo, I am much o'th' bow-hand elſe.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Wou'd I were hang'd, 'tis a good loving little fool, that dares venture her ſelf upon a coaſt ſhe never knew yet, but theſe women, when they are once thirteen, god ſpeed the plough.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Faith they'll venture further for their lading, than a Merchant, and through as many ſtorms, but they'll be fraughted, they are mad like Carrecks, only ſtrength and ſtorage.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: Come, come, you talk, you talk.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: We do ſo, but tell me Richardo, wot thou marry her? her?

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: Marry her? why, what ſhould I do with her?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Pox, I thought we ſhould have all ſhares in her, like lawful prize.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: No by my faith, Sir, you ſhall pardon me, I lanch'd her at my own charge, without partners, and ſo I'll keep her.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.l: What's the hour?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Twelve.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.l: What ſhall we do the while? 'tis yet ſcarce eleven.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: There's no ſtanding here, is not this the place?

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: And to go back unto her fathers houſe, may breed •• ſpition,
Let's ſlip into a Tavern, for an hour, 'tis very cold.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p:
Content, there is one hard by, a quart of burnt • ack will recover us, I am as cold as Chriſtmas, this ſteal
• ng fleſh in the froſty weather, may be ſweet i'th' eating, • ut ſure the Woodmen have no great catch on't; Shall's • o?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Thou art the ſtrangeſt lover of a Tavern, What • hall we do there now? loſe the hour and our ſelves • oo.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p: Loſe a pudding; What do'ſt thou talk of the • our; Will one quart muzle us? have we not ears to • ear, and tongues to ask the Drawers, but we muſt ſtand • ere like bawds to watch the minutes?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Prethee content thy ſelf, we ſhall ſcout here, as • hough we went a haying, and have ſome mangey prentice, • hat cannot ſleep for ſcratching, over-hear us; Come, Will • ou go Sirs? when your love fury is a little frozen, you'll • ome to us.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: Will you drink but one quart then?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: No more I'faith.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Content.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l:
Why then, have with you, but lets be very watch
• .

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p: As watchful as the Belman, come, I'll lead, becauſe • hate good manners, they are too tedious. Exeunt.
sp.stage: Enter Viola with a Key, and a little Casket.
sp.l: The night is terrible, and I enclos'd
• ith that my vertue and my ſelf hate moſt,
• arkneſs; yet muſt I fear that which I wiſh,
•• me company, and every ſtep I take
•• nds louder in my fearful ears to night
• han ever did, the ſhrill and ſacred bell
• hat rang me to my prayers; the houſe will riſe
• hen I unlock the dore, were it by day
• am bold enough, but then a thouſand eyes
• arne me from going, might not heaven have made
〈◊〉 time for envious prying folk to ſleep,
• hilſt lovers met, and yet the Sun have ſhone?
• et I was bold enough, to ſteal this key
• t of my fathers Chamber, and dare yet
• e • ture upon mine enemy, the night,
• rm'd only with my love, to meet my friend.
• las how valiant, and how fraid at once
• ove makes a Virgin? I will throw this key
• ack through a window, I had wealth enough
• Jewels with me, if I hold his love
• ſteal e'm for; farewell my place of birth,
• never make account to look on thee again;
• nd if there be, as I have heard men ſay,
• heſe houſhold gods, I do beſeech them look
• o this my charge, bleſs it from theeves and fire,
• nd keep, till happily my love I win,
• e from thy door, and hold my Father in. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Richardo, Pedro, Uberto, Silvio, and Drawer with a Candle.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: No more for Gods ſake, how is the night boy?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: Faith Sir, 'tis very late.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p: Faith, Sir, you lie, is this your jack i'th' clock-houſe? • ill you ſtrike, Sir? gi's ſome more ſack, you varlet.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: Nay, if you love me, good Ʋberto goe,
• m monſtrous hot with Wine.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p: Quench it again with love, Gentlemen, I will drink •• e health more, and then if my legs ſay me not ſhamefully • y, I will go with you, give me a ſingular quart.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: Of what Wine Sir?

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: Of Sack, you that ſpeak confuſion at the bar, of Sack, I ſay, and every one his quart, what a Devil lets be merry.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: You ſhall, Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: We will, Sir, and a dryed tongue.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: And an Olive, boy, and a whole bunch of fidlers, my head ſwims plaguely, 'uds pretious I ſhall be clawd.

div.stage: Enter Drawer with four quarts of wine.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: Pray go, I can drink no more, think on your promiſe, 'tis midnight Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p: O that it were dum midnight now, not a word more, every man on's knees, and betake himſelf to his ſaint, here's to your wench, ſeignior, all this, and then away.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: I cannot drink it.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: 'Tis a toy, a toy, away wo't.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: Now dare I ſpeak any thing, to any body living, come, Where's the fault? off with it.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: I have broke my wind, Call you this Sack? — I wonder who made it? he was a ſure workman, for 'tis plaguy ſtrong work, Is it gone round?

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p: 'Tis at the laſt, out of my way, good boy, Is the Moon up yet?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.l: Where is ſhe boy?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: There, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.l: We ſhall have rain and thunder, boy.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: When Sir?

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.l: I cannot tell, but ſure we ſhall, boy.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: The Gentleman is Wine-wiſe.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.l: Drawer?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: Here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.l: Can you procure?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: What Sir?

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.l: A Whore, or two or three, as need ſhall ſerve, boy?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I, a good Whore were worth money, boy.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.l: I proteſt Sir, we are all together unprovided.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: The mor's the pitty, boy, Can you not 'vize us where my Child?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Why where were you brought up, boy? no inckling of a Whore? no aym my boy?

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: It cannot ſink in my head now, that thou ſhouldſt marry, Why ſhouldſt thou marry, tell me?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: I marry? I'll be hang'd firſt: ſome more wine boy.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Is ſhe not a Whore tranſlated? and ſhe be, lets repair to her.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: I cannot tell, ſhe may be an offender; but ſignior Silvio, I ſhall ſcratch your head, indeed I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Judge me, I do but jeſt with thee, what an ſhe were inverted with her heeles upward, like a traitor's Coat? what care I.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p: I, hang her, Shall we fall out for her?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: I am a little angry, but theſe wenches, Did you not talke of wenches?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Boy, lend me your Candle.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: To ſet fire to your rotten feeling, you'll keep no Whores, Rogue, no good members.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: Whores, Sir.

sp.speaker: Silv.
sp.p: I, Whores Sir, Do you think we come to lye with your hogsheads?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: I muſt beat the watch, I have long'd for't any time this three weeks.

sp.speaker: Silv.
sp.p: Wee'll beat the Town too, and thou wilt, we are proof boy; Shall ſhe kill any body?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: No, but wee'll hurt 'em dangerouſly.

sp.speaker: Ʋber. Silv.
sp.p: Now muſt I kill one, I cannot avoid it, boy, eaſily afore there with your candle; Where's your Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: A bed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: With whom?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: With my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: You lye Boy, ſhee's better brought up than to lye with her husband, Has he not caſt his head yet? next year he will be a velvet-headed Cuckold. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: You are a merry Gentleman, there Sir, take hold.

sp.speaker: Viola.
sp.l: This is the place, I have out-told the Clock,
For haſte, he is not here. Richardo? no;
Now every power that loves and is belov'd:
Keep me from ſhame to night, for all you know
Each thought of mine is innocent, and pure,
As fleſh and blood can hold: I cannot back;
I threw the Kywi thin, and ere I raiſe
My Father up, to ſee his daughters ſhame,
I'll ſet me down, and tell the Northern Wind,
That it is gentler than the curling Weſt;
If it will blow me dead, but he will come;
I'ſaith 'tis cold; if he deceive me thus,
A woman will not eaſily truſt a Man. Hark, What's that?

sp.speaker: Sil. within.
sp.p: Th'art over long at thy pot, tom, tom, thou art over long at the pot tom.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Bleſs me! Whoſe that?

sp.speaker: Pedro within.
sp.l: Whoo!

sp.speaker: Ʋber within.
sp.l: There Boyes.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Darkneſs be thou my cover, I muſt fly,
To thee I haſte for help—

div.stage: Enter Richardo, Pedro, Uberto, Drawer with a Torch.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: They have a light,
Wind, if thou lov'ſt a Virgin, blow it out,
And I will never ſhut a window more,
To keep thee from me.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Boy?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: Sir.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Why Boy?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: What ſay you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Why Boy? Art thou drunk Boy?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: What would you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Why very good, Where are we?

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: I, that's the point.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: Why Sir, you will be at your Lodging preſently.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: I'll go to no lodging Boy.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: Whither will you go then, Sir?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: I'll go no farther.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: For Gods ſake, Sir, do not ſtay here all night.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: No more I will not, Boy, lay me down, and rowle me to a Whore.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: And me.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: There ſpoke an—

sp.speaker: Silvio.
sp.p: Then ſet your foot to my foot, and up tailes all.

sp.speaker: Viola.
sp.p: That is Richardo, what a noiſe they make?
'Tis ill done on 'em: here, Sirs, Richardo?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: What's that Boy?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: 'Tis a Wench, Sir, pray Gentlemen come away.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: O my dear love! How doeſt thou?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Faith ſweet heart? even as thou ſeeſt.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Where's thy Wench?

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: Where's this bed worme?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: Speak ſoftly for the love of heaven.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: Miſtriſs, get you gone, and do not entice the Gentlemen, now you ſee they'r drunk, or I'll call the Watch, and lay you faſt enough.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Alas, What are you? or, What do you mean?
Sweet love, Where's the place?

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: Marry ſweet love, e'en here, lye down, I'll feeſe thee.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Good God! What mean you?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: I'll have the Wench.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: If you can get her.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: No, I'll lye with the Wench to night, and ſhe ſhall be yours to morrow.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Let go the Wench.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Let you go the Wench.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: O Gentlemen, as you had mothers!

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: They had no mothers; they are the Sons of bitches.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: Let that be maintain'd.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Marry then.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: Oh bleſs me heaven!

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: How many is there on's?

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: About five.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: Why then lets fight three to three.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Content, Draw and fall down.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: The Watch? the watch? the watch? Where are you? Exit.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: Where are theſe Cowards? Exit.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: There's the Wore.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: I never ſaw a drunken man before,
But theſe I think are ſo.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: I miſt you narrowly there.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: My ſtate is ſuch, I know not how to think,
A prayer fit for me, only I could move,
That never Maiden more might be in love. Exit.

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: Where are they, Boy?

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: Make no ſuch haſte, Sir, they are no runners.

sp.speaker: Ʋb.
sp.p: I am hurt, but that's all one, I ſhall light upon ſome of ye.
Pedro, thou art a tall Gentleman, let me kiſs thee.

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: My friend.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: Your friend? you lie.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.p: Stand further off, the watch, you are full of fleas.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: Gentlemen, either be quiet, or we muſt make you quiet.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Nay, good Mr. Conſtable, be not ſo Rigorou s.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: Mr. Conſtable, lend me thy hand of Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: That I will Sir.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: Fy Mr. Conſtable, What golls you have? is Juſtice ſo blind
Y' cannot ſee to waſh your hands? I cry you Mercy, Sir;
Your gloves are on.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: Now you are up, Sir, Will you go to bed?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: I'll truckle here, Boy, give me another pillow.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: Will you ſtand up, and let me lay it on then?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Draw.
sp.p: There hold him two of ye, now they are up, be going Mr. Conſtable.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: And this way, and that way, tom.

sp.speaker: Ʋber.
sp.p: And here away, and there away, tom.

sp.speaker: Silv.
sp.p: This is the right way, the others the wrong.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Th' others the wrong.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Thou art over-long at the pot, tom, tom.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Lead valiantly, ſweet Conſtable, whoop! ha Boyes.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: This Wine hunts in their heads.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Give me the bill, for I'll be the Sergeant.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Look to him, Sirs.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Keep your Ranks, you Raſcalls,, keep your Ranks.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I Cannot ſleep for thinking of this Aſſes Wife, I'll be gon preſently, there's no ſtaying here, with this Devil about me? hoe, this is the houſe of ſleep hoe? again there, 'sfoot, the darkneſs, and this love together, will make me lunatick; ho?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Who calls there?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Pray take the pains to riſe and light a candle.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Preſently,

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Was ever man but I in ſuch a ſtocks? well, this ſhall be a warning to me, and a fair one too, how I betray my ſelf to ſuch a Dunce, by way of benefit.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Did you call?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Yes, pray do me the kindneſs, Sir, to let me out, and not enquire why, for I muſt needs be gone.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Not to night, I hope, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Good Sir to night, I would not have troubled you elſe, pray let it be ſo.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Alas, Sir, my Maſter will be offended.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: That I have buſineſs? no I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Good Sir take your reſt.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Pray my good friend let me appoint my own reſt.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Then ſhew me the way out, I'll conſider you.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Good Lord, Sir,

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: If I had not an excellent temper'd patience, now ſhould I break this fellows head, and make him underſtand 'twere neceſſary; the onely plague of this houſe is the unhandſome love of ſervants, that ne'er do their duty in the right place, but when they muſter before dinner, and ſweep the Table with a wodden dagger, and then they are troubleſome too, to all mens ſhoulders, the Woodcocks fleſht agen, now I ſhall have a new ſtir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why how now friend? What do you up ſo late? are you well? Do you want any thing? pray ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Onely the cauſe I riſe for.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What knaves are theſe? What do you want? why Sirrah?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Nothing i'th' World, but the keyes to let me out of dores; I muſt be gon, be not againſt it, for you cannot ſtay me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Be gon at this time? that were a merry jeſt.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: If there be any mirth in't, make you uſe on't, but I muſt go.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why for loves ſake?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: 'Twill benefit your underſtanding nothing to know the cauſe, pray go to bed, I'll trouble your Man only.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Nay, Sir, you have rais'd more, that has reaſon to curſe you, and you knew all, my Wifes up, and coming down too.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Alas, it will be a trouble, pray go up to her, and let me diſturbe no more, 'tis unmannerly.

div.stage: Enter Wife as out of her hed.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Shee's here already; ſweet heart: How ſay you by this Gentleman? he would away at midnight.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: That I am ſure he will not.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Indeed I muſt.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Good Sir let not your homely entertainment preſs you to leave your bed at midnight; if you want, what my houſe or our town may afford you, make it your own fault if you call not for it; pray go to bed again; let me compel you, I am ſure you have no power to deny a Woman; the ayr is piercing, and to a body beaten with long travel, 'twill prove an ill Phyſitian.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: If ſhe ſpeak longer I ſhall be a knave, as rank as ever ſweat for't; Sir, if you will ſend your Wife up preſently, I will either ſtay with you, d'ye mark me, or deliver you, ſo juſt a cauſe, that you your ſelf, ſhall thruſt me out of dores, both ſuddenly, and willingly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I would fain hear that 'faith, pray thee go up ſweet heart, I have half perſwaded him, beſides, he hath ſome private buſineſs with me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Good night, Sir, and what content you would have,
I wiſh with you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Could any man that had a back ask more! O me!
O me!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Now deal directly with me: Why ſhould you go?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: If you be wiſe do not enquire the cauſe, 'twill trouble you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why? prithee why?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: 'Faith I would not have you know it, let me go, 'twill be far better for you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Who's that, that knocks there? i'ſt not at the ſtreet door?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Who's there, cannot you ſpeak?

sp.speaker: Within Vio.
sp.p: A poor diſtreſſed Maid, for gods ſake let me in.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Let her in and me out together, 'tis but one labor, 'tis pity ſhe ſhould ſtand i'th' ſtreet, it ſeems ſhe knows you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: There ſhe ſhall ſtand for me, you are ignorant; this is a common cuſtome of the Rogues that lie about the looſe parts of the City.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: As how?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: To knock at doors in dead time of night, and uſe ſome feigned voice to raiſe compaſſion, and when the doors are open, in they ruſh, and cut the throats of all, and take the booty, we cannot be too careful.

sp.speaker: Within Vi.
sp.p: As ever you had pity let me in, I am undone elſe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Who are you?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: My name is Viola, a Gentlewoman, that ill chance hath diſtreſſed; you know my Father.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Alas of god we'll let her in, 'tis one of the Gentlewomen were here i'th' evening, I know her by her name, (poor ſoul) ſhee's cold I warrant her, let her have my warme Bed, and I'll take her fortune; come, pray come.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: It is not Viola, that's certain, ſhe went home to her Fathers, I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Will not you be ſo good to let me in?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I'll be ſo good to have you whipt away if you ſtay a little longer: Shee's gone I warrant her, now let me know your cauſe, for I will hear it, and not repent the knowing.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Since you are ſo importunate, I'll tell you, I love your Wife extreamly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: And ſo well that I dare not ſtay.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: For wronging you, I know I am fleſh and blood, and you have done me friendſhips infinite and often, that muſt require me honeſt, and a true Man, and I will be ſo, o • I'll break my heart.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why, you may ſtay for all this, methinks.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: No, though I wood be good, I am no ſaint, nor is it ſafe to try me, I deal plainly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Come, I dare try you, do the beſt you can.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: You ſhall not, when I am right agen, I'll come and ſee you, till when, I'll uſe all Countryes, and all means, but I will loſe this folly, 'tis a Divel.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Is there no way to ſtay you?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: No, unleſs you will have me ſuch a villain to you, as all men ſhall ſpit at me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Do's ſhe know you love her?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: No, I hope not, that were recompence fit for a Rogue to render her.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: If ever any had a faithful friend, I am that Man, and I may glory in't, this is he, that ipſe, he that paſſes all Chriſtendome for goodneſs, he ſhall not over goe me in his friendſhip, 'twere recreant and baſe, and I'll be hang'd firſt, I am reſolv'd, go thy wayes, a Wife will never part us: I have conſider'd, and I find her nothing to ſuch a friend as thou art; I'll ſpeak a bold world, take your time and woe her, you have overcome me clearly, and do what's fitting with her, you conceive me, I am glad at heart you love her: by this light, ne're ſtare upon me, for I will not flye from it, if you had ſpoken ſooner, ſure you had been ſerv'd; Sir, you are not every Man, now to your taske, I give you free leave, and the ſin is mine if there be any in it.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: He will be hang'd before he makes this good, he cannot be ſo innocent a Coxcombe, he can tell ten ſure, if I had never known you as I have done, I might be one, as others perhaps ſooner, but now 'tis impoſſible, there's too much good between us.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Well, thou art e'en the beſt man— I can ſay no more, I am, ſo over-joy'd, you muſt ſtay this night, and in the morning go as early as you pleaſe, I have a toy for you.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I thought this pill would make you ſick.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: But where you mean to be I muſt have notice,
And it muſt be hard by too, do you mark me?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Why, What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: There is a thing in hand.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Why? What thing?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: A ſound one, if it take right, and you be not peeviſh. We two will be— you would little think it; as famous for our friendſhip—

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: If Heaven pleaſe, as ever Damon was, and Pytheas; or Pylades, and Oreſtes, or any two that ever were: do you conceive me yet?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: No, by my troth, Sir; he will not help me up ſure.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You ſhall anon, and for our names, I think they ſhall live after us, and be remember'd while there is a ſtory; or I'll loſe my aime.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: What a vengeance ailes he? How do you?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Yes faith, we two will be ſuch friends, as the world ſhall ring of.
And why is all this?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You ſhall enjoy my wife.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Away, away.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: The wonder muſt begin, ſo I have caſt it, 'twill be ſcurvy elſe, you ſhall not ſtir a foot in't, pray be quiet till I have made it perfect.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: What ſhall a Man do with this wretched fellow? there is no mercy to be uſed towards him, he is not capable of any pitty, he will in ſpight of courſe be a Cuckold, And who can help it? muſt it begin ſo needs Sir? — think agen.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Yes marry muſt it, and I my ſelf will woe this woman for you, Do you perceive it now? ha?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Yes, now I have a little ſight ith' matter; O that thy head ſhould be ſo monſtrous, that all thy Servants hats may hang upon't! but do you meane to do this?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Yes certain, I will woe her, and for you, ſtrive not againſt it, 'tis the overthrow of the beſt plot that ever was then.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Nay, I'll aſſure you, Sir, I'll do no harm, you have too much about you of your own.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Have you thought of a place yet?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: A place?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I a place where you will bide, prethee no more of this modeſty, 'tis fooliſh, and we were not determin'd to be abſolute friends indeed, 'twere tolerable.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I have thought, and you ſhall hear from me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why, this will gain me everlaſting glory; I have the better of him, that's my comfort, good night. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Good night, well go thy wayes, thou art the tydieſt wittall this day I think above ground, and yet thy end for all this muſt be mottly. Exit.

div.stage: Enter a Tinker with a Cord, and Dorothy.

sp.speaker: Tink.
sp.p: 'Tis better cold; a plague upon theſe Rogues, how wary they are grown? not a door open now, but double barr'd; not a Window, but up with a caſe of wood like a ſpice box, and their locks unpickable, the very Smiths that were half ventures, drink penitent, ſingle Ale, this is the Iron age, the Ballad ſings of; well, I ſhall meet with ſome of our looſe Linnen yet, good fellows muſt not ſtarve; here's he ſhall ſhew God a mighties dog bolts, if this hold.

sp.speaker: Dorothy.
sp.p: Faith thou art but too merciful, that's thy fault, thou art as ſweet a Thief, that ſin excepted, as ever ſuffer'd, that's a proud word, and I'll maintain it.

sp.speaker: Tinck.
sp.p: Come, prethee let's ſhogg off, and browze an hour or two, there's Ale will make a Cat ſpeak, at the harrow, we ſhall get nothing now, without we batter, 'tis grown too near morning, the Rogues ſleep ſober, and are watchful.

sp.speaker: Dorit.
sp.p: We want a Boy extreamly for this function, kept under for a year, with milk, and knot-graſs; in my time I have ſeen a boy do wonders Bobbin the red Tinker had a Boy, Reſt his Soul, he ſuffer'd this time 4 years, for two Spoons, and a Pewter Candleſtick, that ſweet Man had a Boy, as I am Curſtend Whore, would have run through a Cat hole, he would have boulted ſuch a piece of Linen in an evening —

sp.speaker: Tinck.
sp.p: Well, we will have a Boy, prethee lets go, I am vengeance cold I tell thee.

sp.speaker: Dorothy.
sp.p: I'll be hang'd before I ſtir without ſome purchaſe, by theſe ten bones, I'll turn ſhe-ape, and untile a houſe, but I'll have it, it may be I have a humor to be hang'd, I cannot tell.

sp.speaker: Tinck.
sp.p: Peace, you flead Whore, thou haſt a mouth like a Bloodhound, here comes a night-ſhade.

sp.speaker: Dorit.
sp.p: A Gentlewoman Whore, by this darkneſs I'll caſe her to the skin.

sp.speaker: Tinck.
sp.p: Peace, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Viola,
sp.l: What fear have I endur'd this diſmal night?
And what diſgrace, if I were ſeen and known?
In which this darkneſs onely is my friend,
That onely has undone me; a thouſand curſes
Light on my eaſie, fooliſh, childiſh love,
That durſt ſo lightly lay a confidence
Upon a Man, ſo many being falſe;
My wearineſs, and weeping, makes me ſleepy, I muſt lie down.

sp.speaker: Tinck.
sp.p: What's this? a Prayer, or a Homily, or a Ballad of good councel? ſhe has a Gown, I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: Knock out her brains, and then ſhee'll nee'r bite.

sp.speaker: Tinck.
sp.p: Yes, I will knock her, but not yet, you? woman?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: For Gods ſake what are you?

sp.speaker: Tinck.
sp.p: One of the groomes of your wardrobe, come, uncaſe, uncaſe; byr Lady a good Kerſey.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Pray do not hurt me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: Let's have no pitty, for if you do, here's that ſhall cut your whiſtle.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: Alas, what would you have? I am as miſerable as you can make me any way.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: That ſhall be try'd.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Here, take my Gown, if that will do you pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Tink.
sp.p: Yes marry will it, look in the Pockets Doll, there may be birds.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: They are flown, a pox go with them, I'll have this Hat, and this Ruffe too, I like it, now will I flouriſh like a Lady, brave, I faith boy.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Y'are ſo gentle people to my ſeeming,
That by my truth I could live with you.

sp.speaker: Tin.
sp.p: Could you ſo? a pretty young round wench, well bloudded, I am for her, Theeves.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: But by this I am not, coole your Codpiece, Rogue, or I'll clap a ſpell upon't, ſhall take your edge off with a very vengeance.

sp.speaker: Tin.
sp.p: Peace, horſe-fleſh, peace, I'll caſt off my Amazon, ſhe has walk'd too long, and is indeed notorious, ſhee'll fight and ſcould, and drink like one of the worthies.

sp.speaker: Dort.
sp.p: Uds, pretious you young contagious Whore, muſt you be ticing? and, Is your fleſh ſo wranck, Sir, that two may live upon't? I am glad to hear your Cortalls grown ſo luſty; he was dry founder'd t'other day, wehee my pamper'd Jade of Aſia.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Good Woman do not hurt me, I am ſorry that I have given any cauſe of anger.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p:
Either bind her quickly, and come away, or by this
ſteel I'll tell thee, though I truſs for company; now could I eate her broyl'd, or any way, without Vinegar, I muſt have her Noſe.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: By any thing you love beſt, good Sir, good Woman.

sp.speaker: Tin.
sp.p: Why her Noſe, Dorothy?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: If I have it not, and preſently warm, I loſe that I go withal.

sp.speaker: Tin.
sp.p: Wood the Devil had that thou goeſt withall, and thee together, for ſure he got thy whelps if thou haſt any, ſhees thy deere dad, Whore! put up your cutpurſe; an I take my ſwitch up, 'twill be a black time with you elſe, ſheth your bung Whore.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: Will you bind her? we ſhall ſtand here prating, and be hang'd both.

sp.speaker: Tin.
sp.p: Come, I muſt bind you, not a word, no crying.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Do what you will, indeed I will not cry.

sp.speaker: Tin.
sp.p: Hurt her not, if thou doſt, by Ale and Beer, I'll clout thy old bald brain pan, with a piece of Braſs, you Bitch incarnate. Exeunt Tinker and Dorothy.

sp.speaker: Viola.
sp.l: O Heaven, to what am I reſerv'd, that knew not
Through all my childiſh hours and actions,
More ſin, than poor imagination,
And too much loving of a faithleſs Man?
For which I'm paid, and ſo, that not the day
That now is riſing to protect the harmleſs,
And give the innocent a ſanctuary
From theeves and ſpoilers, can deliver me
From ſhame, at lea • t ſuſpition—

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Sirrah, lead down the horſes eaſily, I'll walke a foot till I be down the hill, 'tis very early, I ſhall reach home betimes. How now, whoſe there?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Night, that was ever friend to Lovers, yet
Has rais'd ſome weary Soul, that hates his bed,
To come and ſee me bluſh, and then laugh at me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: H'ad a rude heart that did this.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Gentle Sir,
If you have that which honeſt men call pitty,
And be as far from evil as you ſhew;
Help a poor Maid, that this night by bad fortune
Has been thus us'd by Robbers,

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: A pox upon his heart that would not help thee, this Thief was half a Lawyer by his bands, How long have you been tyed here?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: Alas, this hour, and with cold and fear am almoſt periſht.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Where were the watch the while? good ſober Gent. • hey were like careful members of the City, drawing in diligent Ale, and ſinging catches, while Mr. Conſtable contriv'd the Toſts: theſe fellows would be more ſeverely puniſht than wandring Gipſies, that every ſtatute whips; for • f they had every one two eyes a piece more, three pots would put them out.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: I cannot tell, I found no Chriſtian to give me ſuccor.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p:
When they take a Thief, I'll take Oſtend agen; the • horſons drink Opium in their Ale, and then they ſleep like • ops; as for their bills, they only ſerve to reach down Ba
• on to make Raſhers on; now let me know whom I have • one this courteſie too, that I may thank my early riſing for it?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: Sir, All I am, you ſee.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: You have a name I'm ſure, and a kindred, a Father, • riend, or ſomething that muſt own you; ſhee's a handſome • oung Wench; What Rogues were theſe to Rob • er?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Sir, you ſee all I dare reveale,
And as you are a Gentleman preſs me no further;
For there begins a grief, whoſe bitterneſs
Will break a ſtronger heart than I have in me,
• nd 'twill but make you heavy with the hearing,
For your own goodneſs ſake deſire it not.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: If you would not have me enquire that, How do you live then?

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: How I have liv'd, is ſtill one queſtion,
Which muſt not be reſolv'd —
How I deſire to live, is in your liking,
So worthy an opinion I have of you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Is in my liking? How I pray thee? tell me, i'faith I'll do you any good lies in my power; ſhe has an eye would raiſe a bedrid man; come, leave your fear, and tell me, that's a good Wench.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: Sir, I would ſerve—

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Who would'ſt thou ſerve? do not weep and tell me,

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: Faith, Sir, even ſome good woman, and ſuch a wife if you be married, I do imagine yours.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Alas! thou art young and tender, let me ſee thy hand, this was ne'er made to waſh, or wind up water, beat cloaths, or rub a floor, by this light, for one uſe that ſhall be nameleſs, 'tis the beſt wanton hand that e're I lookt on.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Dare you accept me, Sir, my heart is honeſt,
Among your vertuous charitable deeds,
This will not be the leaſt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Thou canſt in a Chamber?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: In a Chamber, Sir?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I mean wait there upon a Gentlewoman,
How quick ſhe is, I like that mainly too;
I'll have her, though I keep her with main ſtrength like a beſieged Town, for I know I ſhall have the Enemy afore me within a week.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.l: Sir, I can ſow too, and make pretty laces,
Dreſs a head handſome, teach young Gentlewomen,
For in all theſe I have a little knowledge.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: 'Tis well, no doubt I ſhall encreaſe that knowledge; I like her better ſtill, how ſhe provokes me; pritty young Maid, you ſhall ſerve a good Gentlewoman, though I ſay't, that will not be unwilling you ſhould pleaſe me, nor I forgetful if you do.

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: I am the happier.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: My man ſhall make ſome ſhift to carry you behind him, Can you ride well?

sp.speaker: Viola.
sp.p: But I'll hold faſt for catching of a fall.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: That's the next way to pull another on you, I'll work her as I go, I know ſhee's wax, now, now, at this time could I beget a Worthy on this Wench,

sp.speaker: Viol.
sp.p: Sir, for this Gentleneſs, may Heaven requite you tenfold.

sp.speaker: Val
sp.p: 'Tis a good Wench, however others uſe thee, be ſure I'll be a loving Maſter to thee, come. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Antonio like an Iriſh Footman, with a Letter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I hope I am wild enough, for being known, I have writ a Letter here, and in it have abus'd my ſelf moſt bitterly, yet all my fear is not enough, for that muſt do it, that muſt lay it on, I'll win her out i'th' flint, 'twill be more famous, now for my language.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Now, Sir, Who would you ſpeak with?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where be thy Maſtres Man? I would ſpeak with her,
I have a Letter.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Cannot I deliver it?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: No, by my trot, and fait, can'ſt thou not Man.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Well, Sir, I'll call her to you, pray ſhake your ears without a little. Exit Servingman.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Cran a Cree do it quickly; this rebbel tonge ſticks in my teeth worſe than a tough Hen, ſure it was ne'er known at Babel, for they ſould no Apples, and this was made for certain at the firſt planting of Orchards, 'tis ſo crabbed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: What's he wood ſpeak with me?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: A kill kenny ring, there he ſtands Madam.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: What would you have with me, friend?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: He has a Letter for other Women, Wilt thou read it.
From whence?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: De Croſſe creeſt from my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Who is your Maſter?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I pray do you look.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Do you know this fellow?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: No Maddam, not I; more than an Iriſh Footman, ſtand further friend, I do not like your roperunners, What ſtallion Rogues are theſe, to weare ſuch dowſetts, the very Cotton may commit adultery.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I cannot find whoſe hand this ſhould be, I'll read, To the beauteous wi • e of Don Antonio, ſure this is ſome blind ſcribe — well now, What follows?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Pray God it take, I have given her that, will ſtir her conſcience, how it works with her; hope, if it be thy will, let the fleſh have it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: This is the moſt abhor'd, intollerable knavery, that ever ſlave entertain'd, ſure there is more than thine own head in this villany, it goes like practic'd miſchiefe; diſabled in his body? O good God, as I live he lies fearfully, and baſely, ha? I ſhould know that Jewel, 'tis my husband, come hither ſhat, Are you an Iriſh Man?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Sweete Woman a Cree I am an Iriſh man?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Now I know it perfectly; is this your trick, Sir? I'll trick you for it; How long have you ſerv'd this Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ant
sp.p: Pleaſe thee a little day, O my Mac dermond put me to my Maſtree, 'tis don I know.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: By my faith he ſpeaks as well as if he had been louſy for the language a year or two; well, Sir, you had been better have kept your own ſhape as I will uſe you, What have I done that ſhould deſerve this tryal? I never made him Cuckold, to my knowledge, Sirrah come hither.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Now will ſhe ſend ſome Jewel, or ſome Letter, I know her mind as well; I ſhall be famous.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Take this Iriſh bawde here.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: And kick him till his breeches and breech be of one colour, a bright blew both.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I may be well ſwing'd thus, for I dare not reveale my ſelf, I hope ſhe does not mean it, O hone, O hone, O St. Patricke, O a Cree, O ſweet Woman.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: No, turn him, and kick him o' t'other ſide, that's well.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: O good waiting Man, I beſeech thee good waiting man, a pox fyre your Legs.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: You Rogue, you enemy to all, but little breeches,
How dar'ſt thou come to me with ſuch a Letter?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Prethee pitty the poor Iriſhman, all this makes for me, if I win her yet, I am ſtill more glorious.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Now could I weep at what I have done, but I'll harden my heart agen, go ſhut him up, 'till my husband comes home, yet thus much ere ye go, ſirrah thach'd head, Would'ſt not thou be whipt, and think it Juſtice? well Aquavitae Barrel, I will bounce you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I pray do, I beſeech you be not angry.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: O you hobby headed Raſcal, I'll have you flead, and troſſers made of thy skin to tumble in, go a way with him, let him ſee no fun, till my husband come home, Sir, I ſhall meet with you for your knavery, I fear it not.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Wilt thou not let me go? I do not like this.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Away with him.

sp.speaker: Servingman.
sp.p: Come, I'll lead you in by your Jack a lent hair, go quietly, or I'll make your crupper crack.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: And do you hear me, Sirrah? and when you have done, make my Coach ready.

sp.speaker: Serving.
sp.p: Yes forſooth. Exit Servingman with Antonio.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Lock him up ſafe enough, I'll to this Gentleman,
I know the reaſon of all this buſineſs, for I do ſuſpect it,
If he have this plot, I'll ring him ſuch a peal, ſhall make his eares deaf for a month at leaſt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: Am I not mad? Can this weak temper'd head,
That will be mad with drink, endure the wrong
That I have done a Virgin, and my Love?
Be mad, for ſo thou ought'ſt, or I will beate
The walls and trees, down with thee, and will let
Either thy memory out, or madneſs in;
But ſure I never lov'd fair Viola,
I never lov'd my Father, nor my Mother,
Or any thing but drink; had I had love;
Nay, had I known ſo much charity,
As would have ſav'd an Infant from the fire,
I had been naked, raving in the ſtreet;
With halfe a face, gaſhing my ſelf with knives,
Two houres ere this time.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Good morrow Sir.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Good morrow Gentlemen, ſhall we go drink agen?
I have my wits.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: So have I, but they are unſetled ones, would I had ſome porrige.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: The Tavern boy was here this morning with me
And told me, that there was a Gentlewoman,
Which he took for a Whore, that hung on me:
For whom we quarrel'd, and I know not what.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I faith nor I.

sp.speaker: Ʋbe.
sp.l: I have a glimmering of ſome ſuch thing.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Was it you, Silvio,
That made me drink ſo much? 'twas you or Pedro.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I know not who.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: We are all apt enough.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: But I will lay the fault on none but me,
That I would be ſo entreated, come Silvio,
Shall we go drink agen, come Gentlemen,
Why do you ſtay, let's never leave off now,
Whil'ſt we have Wine, and Throats, I'll practiſe it,
Till I have made it my beſt quality;
For what is beſt for me to do but that?
For Heaven ſake come and drink; when I am nam'd,
Men ſhall make anſwer, VVhich Richardo mean you?
The excellent drinker? I will have it ſo,
VVill you go drink?

sp.speaker: Silv.
sp.l: VVe drunk too much too lately.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: VVhy there is then the leſs behind to drink,
Let's end it all, diſpatch that, wee'l ſend abroad,
And purchaſe all the VVine the world can yield,
And then drink it off, then take the fruits o'th' earth,
Diſtil the Juice from them, and drink that off;
Wee'l catch the rain before it fall to ground,
And drink off that that never more may grow;
Wee'l ſet our mouths to Springs, and drink them off,
And all this while wee'l never think of thoſe
That love us beſt, more than we did laſt night.
We will not give unto the poor a drop
Of all this drink, but when we ſee them weep,
Wee'l run to them, and drink their tears off too,
Wee'l never leave whilſt there is heat or moiſture,
In this large globe, but ſuck it cold and dry,
Till we have made it Elemental earth;
Merely by drinking.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Is't flattery to tell you, you are mad?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: If it be falſe,
There's no ſuch way to bind me to a Man;
He that will have me, lay my goods and lands,
My life down for him, need no more, but ſay,
Richardo thou art mad, and then all theſe
Are at his ſervice, then he pleaſes me,
And makes me think that I had vertue in me,
That I had love, and tenderneſs of heart,
That though I have committed ſuch a fault,
As never creature did, yet running mad,
As honeſt men ſhould do for ſuch a crime,
I have expreſt ſome worth, though it be late:
But I alas have none of theſe in me,
But keep my wits ſtill like a frozen Man,
That had no fire within him.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Nay, good Richardo leave this wild talk, and ſend a letter to her, I'll deliver it.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: 'Tis to no purpoſe; perhaps ſhe's loſt laſt night,
Or ſhe got home agen, ſhe's now ſo ſtrictly
Look'd to, the wind can ſcarce come to her, or admit
She were her ſelf; if ſhe would hear from me,
From me unworthy, that have us'd her thus,
She were ſo fooliſh, that ſhe were no more
To be belov'd.

div.stage: Enter Andrugio and Servant with a Night-gown.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Sir, we have found this night-gown ſhe took with her.

sp.speaker: Ricb.
sp.p: Where? where? ſpeak quickly.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Searching in the Suburbs, we found a Tinker and his Whore that had it in a Tap-houſe, whom we apprehended, and they confeſt they ſtole it from her.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: And murthered her?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: What aile you man?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Why all this doth not make me mad.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: It does, you would not offer this elſe, good Pedro look to his ſword.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: They do deny the killing of her, but ſwore they left her tyed to a Tree, in the fields, next thoſe Suburbs that • re without our Ladies gate, near day, and by the Rode, ſo • hat ſome paſſinger muſt needs unty her quickly.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p:
The will of Heaven be done? Sir, I will only en
• reat you this, that as you were the greateſt occaſion of her •• ſs, that you will be pleaſed to urge your friends, and be • our ſelf earneſt in the ſearch of her; if ſhe be found, ſhe 〈◊〉 yours, if ſhe pleaſe, I my ſelf only, ſee theſe people bet
• er examin'd, and after follow ſome way in ſearch, God • eep you Gentlemen. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Alas good man!

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: What think you now of me, I think this lump
• s nothing but a piece of fleagme congeal'd
Without a ſoul, for where there's ſo much ſpirit
As would but warm a flea, thoſe faults of mine
Would make it glow, and flame in this dull heart,
• nd run like molten gold through every ſin,
Till it could burſt theſe walls, and fly away.
• hall I intreat you all to take your horſes,
And ſearch this innocent?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: With all our hearts.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: Do not divide your ſelves till you come there,
Where they ſay ſhe was ty'd, I'll follow too,
But never to return till ſhe be found.
Give me my ſword good Pedro, I will do
No harm, believe me, with it, I am now
Farr better temper'd; if I were not ſo,
〈◊〉 have enow beſides, God keep you all,
And ſend us good ſucceſs. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: WHo is it? can you tell?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: By my troth, Sir, I know not, but 'tis a Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: A Gentleman, I'll lay my life, you puppy, h'as ſent his Wife to me: if he have, fling up the bed.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Here ſhe is, Sir.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: I am glad I found you Sir, there, take your Letter, and keep it till you have ano • her friend to wrong, 'tis too malicious falſe to make me ſin, you have provoked me to be that I love not, a talker, and you ſhall hear me.
sp.l: Why ſhould you dare to imagine me
So light a huſwife, that from four hours knowledge
You might preſume to offer to my credit
This rude and ruffian tryal, I am ſure
I never courted you, nor gave you tokens,
That might concern aſſurance, you are a fool.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I cannot blame you now, I ſee this letter,
Though you be angry, yet with me you muſt not,
Unleſs you'l make me guilty of a wrong,
My worſt affections hate—

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Did not you ſend it?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: No, upon my faith, which is more, I underſtand it not; the hand is as far from my knowledge, as the malice.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: This is ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: It is ſo, and had been ſtranger, and indeed more hateful,
Had I, that have receiv'd ſuch courteſies, and owe ſo many
Thanks, done this baſe office.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Your name is at it.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Yes, but not my nature, and I ſhall hate my name worſe than the manner, for this baſe broking; you are wiſe and vertuous, remove this fault from me; for on the love I bear to truth and goodneſs, this Letter dare not name me for the author.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Now I perceive my husbands knavery, if any man can but find where he has been, I will goe with this Gentleman whatſoever comes on't: and as I mean to carry it, both he and all the World ſhall think it fit, and thank me for it.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I muſt confeſs I loved you, at firſt, however this made me leave your houſe unmannerly, that might provoke me to do ſomething ill, both to your honor and my faith, and not to write this Letter, which I hold ſo truly wicked, that I will not think on't.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I do believe you, and ſince I ſee you are free, my words were not meant to you, but this is not the half of my affliction.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: 'Tis pitty you ſhould know more vexation; may I enquire?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Faith, Sir, I fear I have loſt my husband.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Your husband? it cannot be: I pitty her, how ſhe's vext?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: How now? What news? nay ſpeak, for we muſt know.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Faith I have found at length, by chance, where he has been.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: In a blind out-houſe in the Suburbs, pray God all be well with him.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: There are his cloaths, but, What's become of him,
I cannot yet enquire.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I am glad of this; ſure they have murther'd him,
What ſhall I do?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Be not ſo grieved, before you know the truth, you have time enough to weep, this is the ſodain'ſt miſchief; Did you not bring an Officer to ſearch there, where you ſay you found his cloaths.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Yes, and we ſearcht it, and charg'd the fellow with him: but he, like a Rogue, ſtubborn Rogue, made anſwer, he knew not where he was; he had been there, but where he was now, he could not tell: I tell you true, I fear h m.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Are all my hopes and longings to enjoy him,
After this 3 years travel, come to this?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: It is the rankeſt houſe in all the City, the moſt curſed roguy Bawdy-houſe. Hell fire it.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: This is the worſt I heard yet; Will you go home? I'll bear you company, and give you the beſt help I may: this being here will wrong you.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: As you are a Gentleman, and as you lov'd your dead friend, let me not go home, that will but heap one ſorrow on another.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Why propoſe any thing and I'll perform't; I am at my wits end too.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: So am I, O my dear Maſter!

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Peace you great fool.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Then good Sir carry me to ſome retir'd place, far from the ſight of this unhappy City, whether you will indeed, ſo it be far enough.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: If I might Councel you, I think 'twere better to go home,
And try what may be done yet, he may be at home afore you, Who can tell?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: O no, I know he's dead, I know he's murder'd; tell me not of going home, you murder me too.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Well, ſince it pleaſes you to have it ſo, I will no more perſwade you to go home, I'll be your guide in the Countrey, as your grief doth command me, I have a Mother dwelling from this place ſome 20 miles: the houſe though homely, yet able to ſhew ſomething like a welcome; thither I'll ſee you ſafe with all your ſorrows.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: With all the ſpeed that may be thought upon; I have a Coach here ready, good Sir quickly; I'll fit you my fine husband.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: It ſhall be ſo; if this fellow be dead, I ſee no band of any other Man, to tye me from my will, and I will follow her with ſuch careful ſervice, that ſhe ſhall either be my Love, or Wiſe; Will you walk in?
