sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I thank you, Sir, but one word with my Man, and I am ready; keep the Iriſh fellow ſafe, as you love your life, for he I fear has a deep hand in this, then ſearch agen, and get out warrants for that naughty man, that keeps the bad houſe, that he may anſwer it, if you find the body, give it due burial; farewel. You ſhall hear from me, keep all ſafe. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: O my ſweet Maſter!

sp.speaker: Ant. within.
sp.p: Man-a-cree, the Devil take thee, Wilt thou kill me here? I prethee now let me goe ſeek my Maſter, I ſhall be very cheel elſe.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Do you hear man-a-cree, I'll cree your coxcombe, and you keep not ſtill, down you rogue.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Good ſweet fact ſerving-man, let me out I beſeech de, and by my trot I will give dye VVorſhip 2 ſhillings in good argott, to buy dy Worſhip pippines.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: This rogue thinks all the worth of man conſiſts in Peepins; by this light I'll beat rebellion out of you for ever.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: VVilt thou not hear me Man? is fet; I'll give thee all I have about me.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: I thank you, Sir, ſo I may have picking work,

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Here is five ſhillings Man.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Here is a cudgel, a very good one.

sp.speaker: 2. Ser.
sp.p: How now, VVhat's the matter? VVhere's the Iriſhman.

sp.speaker: 1. Ser.
sp.p: There, a wyth take him, he makes more noiſe alone there, than ten Lawyers can do with double, and a ſcurvy Caſe.

sp.speaker: 2. Ser.
sp.p: Let him out, I muſt talk with him.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Wilt thou give me ſome drink, O hone? I am very dry Man.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: You ſhall have that ſhall quench your thirſt, my friend.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Fate doſt thou mean man.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: Even a good tough halter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: A halter? O hone!

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: Sirrah, you are a miſchievous Rogue, that's the truth.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: No, fet I am not.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: Shall I knock out his brains? I have kill'd dogs have been worth three of him for all uſes.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: Sirrah, the truth on't is, you muſt with me to a Juſtice. O Roger, Roger.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: Why, what's the matter William?

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: Heavy news Roger, heavy newes; god comfort us.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: What is't Man?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What's the matter now? I am e'en weary of this way, would I were out on't.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: My Maſter ſure is murder'd, Roger, and this curſed rogue
I fear, has had a hand in't.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: No fet not.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: Stand away, I'll kickt out of him: come, ſirrha, mount, I'll make you dance, you Raſcal, kill my Maſter? If thy breech were cannon proof, having this good cauſe on my ſide, I would encounter it; hold fair, Shamrocke.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why how now Sirs? you will not murder me indeed.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: Bleſs us Roger!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Nay, I am no ſpirit.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: How do you Sir, this is my very Maſter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why well enough yet, but you have a heavy foot of your own; Where's my Wife.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: Alas poor ſorrowful Gentlewoman, ſhe thinks you are dead, and has given o're houſe-keeping.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Whether is ſhe gone then?

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: Into the Countrey with the Gentleman your
Friend Sir, to ſee if ſhe can wear her ſorrows out there; ſhe weeps and takes on too too—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: This falls out pat; I ſhall be everlaſting for a name: Doe you hear? upon your lives and faiths to me, not one word I am living, but let the ſame report paſs along, that I am murther'd ſtill; I am made for ever.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: VVhy Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I have a Cauſe Sir, that's enough for you; well, i • I be not famous, I am wrong'd much; for any thing I know I will not trouble him this week at leaſt, no, let them take their way one of another.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: Sir, VVill you be ſtill an Iriſh-man?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Yes a while.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: But your VVorſhip will be beaten no more?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: No, I thank you William.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: In truth, Sir, if it muſt be ſo, I'll do it better than a ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Goe, you are Knaves both, but I forgive you, I am almoſt mad with the apprehenſion of what I ſhall be, no • a word I charge you. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Come, pretty ſoul, we now are near our home,
And whilſt our horſes are walkt down the hill,
Let thou and I walke here over this Cloſe:
The foot-way is more pleaſant, 'tis a time
My pretty one, not to be wept away,
For every living thing is full of love;
Art not thou ſo too? ha?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Nay, there are living things empty of love,
Or I had not been here but for my ſelf,
Alas, I have too much.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: It cannot be, that ſo much beauty, ſo much youth and grace ſhould have too much of love.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Pray what is love? for I am full of that I do not know.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Why, love fair Maid is an extream deſire,
That's not to be examin'd, but fulfill'd,
To ask the reaſon why thou art in love,
Or what might be the nobleſt end in love,
Would overthrow that kindly riſing warmth,
That many times ſlides gently o'r the heart,
'Twould make thee grave and ſtaid, thy thoughts would be,
Like a thrice married Widow, full of ends,
And void of all compaſſion, and to fright thee
From ſuch enquiry, whereas thou art now
Living in ignorance, mild, freſh, and ſweet,
And but ſixteen; the knowing what love is,
Would make thee ſix and forty.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Would it would make me nothing, I have heard
Scholars affirm, the world's upheld by Love,
But I believe, women maintain all this,
For there's no love in men.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Yes, in ſome men.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I know them not.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Why, there is love in me.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: There's charity I am ſure towards me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And love; which I will now expreſs, my pretty maid,
I dare not bring thee home, my wife is foul,
And therefore envious, ſhe is very old,
And therefore jealous: thou art fair and young.
A ſubject fit for her unlucky vices
To work upon, ſhe never will endure thee,

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: She may endure
• f ſhe be ought, but Devil, all the friendſhip
That I will hold with you; can ſhe endure
I ſhould be thankful to you? may I pray
For you and her, will ſhe be brought to think.
That all the honeſt induſtry I have,
Deſerves brown bread? if this may be endur'd
• he'll pick a quarrel with a ſleeping child,
E'r ſhe fall out with me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: But truſt me, ſhe does hate all handſomneſs.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: How fell you in love with ſuch a creature?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I never lov'd her.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: And yet married her?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: She was a rich one.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: And you ſwore I warrant you, ſhe was a fair one then too.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Or believe me, I think I had not had her.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Are you men all ſuch? wou'd you wou'd wall us in a place
Where all we women that are innocent,
• ight live together.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Do not weep at this,
Although I dare not for ſome weighty reaſon
Diſpleaſe my Wife, yet I forget not thee.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: What will you do with me?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt be plac'd
• t my mans houſe, and have ſuch food and raiment
• s can be bought with money: theſe white hands
•• all never learn to work, but they ſhall play
As thou ſay'ſt they were wont, teaching the ſtrings
To move in order, or what elſe thou wilt.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I thank you, Sir, but pray you cloath me poorly,
And let my labor get me means to live.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: But fair one, you, I know do ſo much hate
A foul ingratitude, you will not look

〈◊〉
• ould do this for nothing.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I will work as much out as I can, and take as little,
That you ſhall have as duely paid to you
• s ever ſervant did.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: But give me now a trial on't, I may believe
We are alone, ſhew me how thou wilt kiſs
And hug me hard, when I have ſtolen away
From my too clamorous wife that watches me,
To ſpend a bleſſed hour or too with thee.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Is this the love you mean? you would have that
Is not in me to give, you would have luſt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Not to diſſemble, or to mince the word,
'Tis Luſt I wiſh indeed.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: And by my tro • h I have it not: for heavens ſake uſe me kindly.
sp.l: Though I be good, and ſhew perhaps a monſter,
As this world goes.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I do
But ſpeak to thee, thy anſwers are thy own,
I compel none, but if refuſe this motion,
Thou art not then for me, alas good ſoul;
What profit can thy work bring me?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: But I fear, I pray goe, for l • ſt they ſay, will grow
Outragious, being deni'd, I give you thanks
For all your courteſies, and there's a Jewel
That's worth the taking, that I did preſerve
Safe from the robbers, pray you leave me here
Juſt as you found me, a poor innocent,
And Heaven will bleſs you for it.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Pretty maid, I am no Robber, nor no Raviſher,
I pray thee keep thy Jewel, I have done
No wrong to thee▪ though thou beeſt virtuous
And in extremity, I do not know,
That I am boun • to keep thee.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: No Sir, for gods ſake, if you know an honeſt man in all theſe Countreys, give me ſome directions to find him out.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: More honeſt than my ſelf, good ſooth I do not know; I would have lain with thee, with thy conſent, and who would not in all theſe parts, is paſt my memory, I am ſorry for thee, farewel gentle maid, God keep thee ſafe. Exit.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I thank you Sir, and you;
Woman they ſay, was only made of man,
Methinks 'tis ſtrange they ſhould be ſo unlike,
It may be all the beſt was cut away
To make the woman, and the naught was left
Behind with him, I'll ſit me down and weep,
All things have caſt me from 'em but the earth;
The evening comes, and every little flower
Droops now, as well as I.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Good Madge lets reſt a little, by my troth I am weary, this new pail is a plaguy heavy one, would Tom were hang'd for chooſing it, 'tis the untoward'ſt fool in a Countrey.

sp.speaker: Madg.
sp.p: With all my heart, and I thank you too, Nan.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: What true contented happineſs dwels here,
More than in Cities? wou'd to God my Father
Had liv'd like one of theſe, and bred me up
To milk: and do as they do: methinks
'Tis a life that I wou'd chooſe, if I were now
To tell my time agen, above a Princes; maids, for charity
Give a poor wench one draught of Milk,
That wearineſs and hunger have nigh famiſh'd.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: If I had but one Cows Milk in all the world, you ſhould have ſome on't; there, drink more, the Cheeſe ſhall pay for it, alas poor heart, ſhe's drie.

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: Do you dwell here abouts?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: No, would I did.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Madge, if ſhe does not looke like my coſin Sue o'th'
Moor lane, as one thing can look like another—

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: Nay, Sue has a hazle eye, I know Sue well, and by your leave, not ſo trim a body neither, this is a feat bodied thing I tell you.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: She laces cloſe by the maſs I warrant you, and ſo does Sue too.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I thank you for your gentleneſs, fair maids.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Drink agen pray thee.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I am ſatisfied, and heaven reward thee for't, yet thus far I will compell you to accept theſe trifles, toys onlythat expreſs my thanks, for greater worth, I'm ſure they have not in them; indeed you ſhall, I found 'em as I came.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Madge, look you here Madge.

sp.speaker: Madg
sp.p: Nay, I have as fine a one as you, mine's all gold, and painted, and a precious ſtone in't; I warrant it coſt a crown wench.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: But mine is the moſt ſumptuous one, that e'r I ſaw.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: One favour you muſt do me more, for you are well acquainted here.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Indeed we'll do you any kindneſs, Siſter.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Only to ſend me to ſome honeſt place, where I may find a ſervice.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Uds me, our Dorothy went away but laſt week, and I know my Miſtriſs want's a maid, and why may ſhe not be plac'd there? this is a likely wench, I tell you truly, and a good wench I warrant her.

sp.speaker: Madg.
sp.p: And 'tis a hard caſe if we that have ſerv'd four years apiece, cannot bring in one ſervant, we will prefer her, hark you ſiſter, pray what's your name?

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: A feat name i'ſaith; and can you milk a Cow? and make a merry-buſh? that's nothing.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I ſhall learn quickly,

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: And dreſs a houſe with flowers? and ſerve a pig? this you muſt do, for we deal in the Dary, and make a bed or two?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I hope I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: But be ſure to keep the men out, they will mar all that you make elſe, I know that by my ſelf; for I have been ſo touz'd among 'em in my days, come you ſhall e'en home with us, and be our fellow, our houſe is ſo honeſt, and we ſerve a very good woman, and a Gentlewoman, and we live as merrily, and dance a good daies after even-ſong: our Wake ſhall be on Sunday; do you know what a Wake is? we have mighty cheer then, and ſuch a coil, 'twould bleſs ye; you muſt not be ſo baſhful, you'll ſpoil all.

sp.speaker: Madg.
sp.p: Let's home for Gods ſake, my Miſtriſs thinks by this time we are loſt, come, we'll have a care of you, I warrant you; but you muſt tell my Miſtriſs where you were born, and every thing that belongs to you, and the ſtrangeſt things you can deviſe, for ſhe loves thoſe extreamly, 'tis no matter whether they be true or no, ſhe's not ſo ſcrupulous; you muſt be our Siſter, and love us beſt, and tell us every thing, and when cold weather comes, we'll lye together, will you do this?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Then home again o'gods name, can you go apace.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I warrant you. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: HOw now, any good news yet?

sp.speaker: Silvio.
sp.p: Faith not any yet.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: This comes o' tipling; would 'twere treaſon and't pleaſe God, to drink more than three draughts at a meal.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: When did you ſee Richardo?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: I croſt him twice to day.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: You have heard of a young wench that was ſeen laſt

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Has Richard heard of this?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Yes, and I think he's ridden after, farewel, I'll have another round.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: If you hear any thing, pray ſpare no horſe-fleſh,
I'll do the like.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Do. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Sir, I did think 'twas you by all deſcriptions.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo,
I took her up indeed, the manner how
You have heard already, and what ſhe had about her,
As Jewels, Gold, and other trifling things:
And what my end was, which becauſe ſhe ſlighted,
I left her there i'th' fields.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Left i'th' fields? could any but a Rogue
That had deſpis'd humanity and goodneſs,
Heavens law and credit; and had ſet himſelf
To loſe his nobleſt part, and be a beaſt,
Have left ſo innocent unmatch'd a virtue,
To the rude mercy of a wilderneſs?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Sir, if you come to rail, pray quit my houſe,
I do not uſe to have ſuch language given
Within my doors to me; for your wench,
You may go ſeek her with more patience,
She's tame enough, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Pray forgive me.
I do confeſs my much forgetfulneſs;
And weigh my words no farther, I beſeech you,
Then a mere madneſs, for ſuch a grief has ſeiz'd me
So ſtrong and deadly, as a puniſhment,
And a juſt one too,
That 'tis a greater wonder I am living,
Than any thing I utter; yet let me tell you thus much,
'Twas a fault for leaving her
So in the fields.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Sir, I will think ſo now, and credit me,
You have ſo wrought me with your grief, that I
Do both forgive and pity you:
And if you'll pleaſe to take a bed this night here;
To morrow I'll bring you where I left her.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: I thank you, now ſhall I be ſo unworthy:
To think upon a bed, or eaſe, or comfort,
And have my heart ſtray from me, God knows where,
Cold and forſaken, deſtitute of friends,
And all good comforts elſe, unleſs ſome tree
Whoſe ſpeechleſs charity muſt better ours,
With which the bitter eaſt winds made their ſport
And ſung through hourly, hath invited her
To keep off half a day? ſhall ſhe be thus,
And I draw in ſoft ſlumbers? God forbid.
No, night and bitter coldneſs, I provoke thee,
And all the dews that hang upon thy locks,
Showrs, Hails, Snows, Froſts, and two edged Winds that pri ••
The maiden bloſſoms, I provoke you all,
And dare expoſe this body to your ſharpneſs,
Till I be made a Land-mark.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Will you then ſtay and eat with me?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Y'are angry with me, I know y'are angry,
You would not bid me eat elſe; my poor Miſtriſs,
For ought I know thou'rt famiſh'd, for what elſe
Can the fields yield thee, and the ſtubborn ſeaſon,
That yet holds in the fruit? good gentle Sir,
Think not ill manners in me for denying
Your offer'd meat, for ſure I cannot eat
While I do think ſhe wants; well I'm a raſcal;
A villain, ſlave, that only was begotten,
To murder women, and of them the beſt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: This is a ſtrange affliction.
If you'll accept no greater courteſie, yet drink Sir.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: Now I am ſure you hate me, and you knew
What kind of man I am, as indeed 'tis fit,
That every man ſhould know me to avoid me.
• f you have peace within you, Sir, or goodneſs
Name that abhord word Drink, no more unto me,
You had ſafer ſtrike me.
〈◊〉 pray you do not, if you love me do not.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Sir, I mean no ill by it.

sp.speaker: Ric.
sp.l: It may be ſo,
Nor let me ſee
None Sir, if you love heaven;
You know not what offence it is unto me,
Nor good now do not ask me why:
And I warn you once again, let no man elſe ſpeak of't,
I fear your ſervants will be prating to me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Why Sir, what ail you?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: I hate drink, there's the end on't,
And that man that drinks with meat is damn'd
Without an age of prayers and repentance,
And there's a hazard too; good Sir, no more
• f you will do me a free courteſie;
That I ſhall know for one: go take your horſe,
And bring me to the place where you left her:

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Since you are ſo impotunate, I will;
But I will wiſh Sir, you had ſtaid to night
Upon my credit you ſhall ſee no drink.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Be gone, the hearing of it makes me giddy,
• ir, will you be intreated to forbear it,
〈◊〉 ſhall be mad elſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I pray no more of that, I am quiet,
〈◊〉 but walk in, and away ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Now I thank you,
•• t what you do, do in a twinkling, Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: As ſoon as may be. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Mother, Viola, and two Milk-maids.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Is this the wench you have brought me? ſome catch warrant.
• ow daringly ſhe looks upon the matter?

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: Yes forſooth, this is the maiden.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Come hither, wou'd you ſerve?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: If it ſhall pleaſe you to accept my ſervice, I hope I •• ll do ſomething that ſhall like you, though it be but •• th, and often praying for you.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: You are very curious of your hand methinks,
〈◊〉 preſerve it ſo with gloves, let me ſee it;
•• arry, here's a hand of march-pane, wenches,
•• is pretty palme never knew ſorrow yet;
• ow ſoft it is I warrant you, and ſupple:
〈◊〉 my word, this is fitter for a pocket to filch withal
•• an to work withal, I fear me little one,
•• u are no better than you ſhould be; goe to.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: My Conſcience yet is but one witneſs to me,
•• d that heaven knows, is of mine innocence,
〈◊〉 is true, I muſt confeſs with ſhame enough,
•• e time that I have led, yet never taught me
That 'twas to break a ſleep, or to be weary.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
You can ſay well: if you be mine, wench, you muſt • e well too, for words are but ſlow workers, yet ſo much •• pe I have of you, that I'll take you, ſo you'll be dili
•• nt, and do your duty: how now?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: There is a meſſenger come from your ſon,
•• at brings you word he is return'd from travel,
•• d will be here this night.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: Now joy upon thee for it, thou art ever
• bringer of good tidings, there, drink that:
• troth thou haſt much contented me, my Son?
•• d how thou haſt pleas'd me, ſhall I ſee my Son
•• e'r I dye? take care my houſe be handſome,
•• d the new ſtools ſet out, and boughs and ruſhes,
And flowers for the window, and the Turky Carpet,
And the great parcel Salt, Nan, with the Cruets,
And prethee Alexander goe to the Cook,
And bid him ſpare for nothing, my ſon's come home,
Who's come with him?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: I hear of none yet, but a Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: A Gentlewoman? what Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: I know not, but ſuch a one there is, he ſays.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: Pray God he have not caſt away himſelf
Upon ſome ſnout-fair piece, I do not like it.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: No ſure, my Maſter has more diſcretion.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: We'll be it how it will, he ſhall be welcome.
Sirs to your tasks, and ſhew this little novice
How to beſtir her ſelf, I'll ſort out things. Exit.

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: We will forſooth, I can tell you, my Miſtriſs is a ſtirring woman.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Lord how ſhe'll talk ſometimes? 'tis the maddeſt cricket—

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Methinks ſhe talks well, and ſhews a great deal of good huſwivery, pray let me deck the chambers, ſhall I?

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Yes, you ſhall, but do not ſcorn to be advis'd, Siſter, for there belongs more to that, than you are aware on; why ſhould you venture ſo fondly upon the ſtrowings? there's mighty matters in them I'll aſſure you, and in the ſpreading of a bough-pot, you may miſs, if you were ten years elder, if you take not a ſpecial care before you.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I will learn willingly, if that be all.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Sirrah where is't they ſay my young Maſter hath been?

sp.speaker: Madg.
sp.p: Faith I know not, beyond the Sea, where they are born without noſes.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Bleſs us! without noſes? how do they do for handkerchiefs?

sp.speaker: Madg.
sp.p: So Richard ſays, and ſirrah, their feet ſtand in their foreheads.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: That's fine by my troth, theſe men have peſtilent running heads then; do they ſpeak as we do?

sp.speaker: Mag.
sp.p: No, they never ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Are they curſend?

sp.speaker: Mag.
sp.p: No, they call them Infidels, I know not what they are.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Sirrah, we ſhall have fine courting now my young maſter is come home, were you never courted Siſter?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Alas, I know it not.

sp.speaker: Mag.
sp.p: What is that courting, ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: I can tell, for I was once courted in the matted chamber, you know the party Madge, faith he courted finely.

sp.speaker: Madg.
sp.p: Pray thee what is't?

sp.speaker: Nay.
sp.p: Faith, nothing but he was ſomewhat figent with me, faith 'tis fine ſport, this courting.

sp.speaker: Alex. within.
sp.p: Where be the Maids there?

sp.speaker: Madg.
sp.p: We ſhall be hang'd anon, away good wenches, and have a care you dight things handſomly, I will look over you. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: If your ſorrow will give you ſo far leave, pray think your ſelf moſt welcome to this place, for ſo upon my life you are, and for your own fair ſake, take truce awhile with theſe immoderate mournings.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I thank you Sir, I ſhall doe what I may;
Pray lead me to a chamber.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Preſently,
Before your bleſſing Mother, I intreat ye
To know this Gentlewoman, and bid her welcome,
The virtuous wife of him that was my ſelf
In all my travels.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: Indeed ſhe is moſt welcome, ſo are you ſon kneel.
Now all my bleſſing on thee; thou haſt made me
Younger by 20 years, than I was yeſterday,
Will you walk in? what ails this Gentlewoman?
Alas, I fear ſhe is not well, good Genlewoman.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: You fear right.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: She has faſted over long,
You ſhall have ſupper preſently o'th' board.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: She will not eat; I can aſſure you Mother,
For Gods ſake let your Maid conduct her up
Into ſome fair becoming Chamber
Fit for a woman of her Being, and
As ſoon as may be,
I know ſhe's very ill, and wou'd have reſt.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: There is one ready for her, the blew chamber.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: 'Tis well, I'll lead you to your chamber door
And there I'll leave you to your quiet, Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: I thank you, Sir, good reſt to every one,
You'll ſee me once again to night, I hope. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: When you ſhall pleaſe, I'll wait upon you, Lady.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p:
Where are theſe maids, attend upon the Gentlewoman, and ſee ſhe want no good thing in the houſe? goodnight with all my heart forſooth, good Lord how you are grown, is he not Alexander
〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Yes truly, he's ſhot up finely, God be thanked.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: An ill weed, Mother, will do ſo.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: You ſay true, Sir, an ill weed grows apace.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Alexander the ſharp, you take very quickly.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Nay, I can tell you, Alexander will do it, do you read madcap ſtill?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Sometimes forſooth.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: But faith Son, what Countreys have you travell'd?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Why many, Mother, as they lay before me, France, Spain, Italy and Germany, and other Provinces that I am ſure, you are not better'd by, when you hear of them.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: And can you theſe tongues perfectly?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Of ſome a little, Mother.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Pray ſpout ſome French Son.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: You underſtand it not, and to your ears 'twill goe like an unſhod cart upon the ſtones, only a rough unhandſome ſound.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: I would fain hear ſome French.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Good Sir, ſpeak ſome French to my Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: At your intreaty Alexander, I will, who ſhall I ſpeak to?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: If your worſhip will do me the favour Sir, to me.

p.hi: Mounſeir, Poultron, Coukew, Cullione, Beſay, Man cur.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, this fine indeed, gods bleſſing on thy heart Son, by my troth thou art grown a proper Gentleman, cullen and pullen, good god what awkeward words they uſe beyond the ſeas, ha, ha, ha?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Did not I anſwer right.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Yes good Alexander, if you had done ſo too,
But good Mother, I am very hungry, and have rid far to day, and am faſting.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: You ſhall have your ſupper preſently, my ſweet Son.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: As ſoon as you pleaſe, which once ended,
I'll go and viſit you ſick Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Come then. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Antonio like a Poſt, with a Letter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I have ridden like a fury, to make up this work, and I will do it bravely, e'r I leave it; this is the houſe I am ſure.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Who wou'd you ſpeak with, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Marry Sir, I would ſpeak with a Gentlewoman, came this night late here from the City, I have ſome Letters of importance to her, I am a Poſt Sir, and would be diſpach'd in haſte.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Sir, cannot I deliver 'em? for the truth is, ſhe's ill, and in her chamber.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Pray pardon me, I muſt needs ſpeak with her, my buſineſs is ſo weighty.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: I'll tell her ſo, and bring you preſent word.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Pray do ſo, and I'll attend her, pray god the grief of my imagined death, ſpoil not what I intend, I hope it will not.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Though ſhe be very ill, and deſires no trouble,
Yet if your buſineſs be ſo urgent, you may come up and ſpeak with her.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I thank you Sir, I follow you. Exit Alex

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: What ſhould this fellow be i'th' name of Heaven that comes with ſuch poſt buſineſs? ſure my Husband hath reveal'd himſelf, and in this haſte ſent after me, are you the Poſt my friend?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Yes forſooth Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: What good news haſt thou brought me gentle Poſt?
For I have woe and grief too much already.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I would you had leſs, Miſtriſs, I could wiſh it, beſhrew my heart ſhe moves me cruelly.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Have I found you once more Jugler? well Jewel, thou haſt only virtue in thee, of all I read of yet; what ears has this aſs to betray him with? well, what's you • buſineſs then?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I have brought a Letter from your ſervant, Miſtriſs in haſte.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Pray give it me, I hope the beſt ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: This is the upſhot, and I know I have hit it,
Well, if the ſpirits of the dead do walk, I ſhall
Hear more of this one hundred years hence.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: By any means you muſt have ſpecial care, for no • the City is poſſeſt for certain, my Maſter is made away which for ought I know is truth indeed; good Miſtriſs leav • your grief, and ſee your danger, and let that wiſe and noble Gentleman with whom you are, be your right hand i • all things.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Now do I know I have the better on't, by the la ••
guiſhing of her eye at this near inſtant, 'tis ſtill ſimming i • her blood, in coyning ſomewhat to turn Mercury, I kno • it.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: He is my Husband, and 'tis reaſonable he ſhoul • command in all things, ſince he will be an aſs againſt th • hair, at his own peril be it, in the morn you ſhall have pacquet, till when, I muſt intreat you ſtay, you ſhall not lo • by it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I do not doubt it, Miſtriſs; I'll leave you to you • reſt, and wait your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Do, and ſeek out the Gentleman of the houſe, b •• him come to me preſently.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Who, Mr. Mercury?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Do you know him, Poſt?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p:
Only by ſight forſooth, now I remember your ſe •
vant will'd me to let you know he is the only man, you a •• and your fortunes, are now to reſt upon.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Prethee no more, I know all this already.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I'll take my leave now, I am made for ever. Ex ••

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Good night, I am provided for you, my fine yout •

div.stage: Enter Mother, beating Viola, Alexander with a broken Glaſs.

sp.speaker: Mother.
sp.p: I'll make thee have more care.

sp.speaker: Viola.
sp.p: Good Miſtriſs pardon me

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Thou'lt ne'r be good I warrant thee, can your fi • fingers hold no faſter?

sp.speaker: Viola.
sp.p: Indeed it was againſt my will.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Alexander, let's ſee the glaſs, as I am true kirſome woman, it is one of the chryſtal glaſſes my Coſin ſent me, and the baggage hath broke it where it cannot be mended, Alexander, can Humphrey mend this think you?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: No truly, this will ne'er be mended.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Truly I meant but to waſh it for the Gentlewoman that is ſick above, and ſhaking out the water, knockt it againſt the pail ſide.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Did you ſo? be ſure I'll ſtop it, 'twill make a good gap in your quarters wages, I can tell you.

sp.speaker: Viola.
sp.p: I pray forgive me, and let me have no wages this firſt quarter.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Go whimling, and fetch two or three grating loaves out of the Kitching, to make Ginger-bread of, 'tis ſuch an untoward thing. Exit Viola.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: She's ſomewhat ſimple indeed, ſhe knew not what a kimnel was, ſhe wants good nurture mightily.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: My Son tells me, Alexander, that this young widow means to ſojourn here, ſhe offers largely for her board, I may offer her good cheer, prethee make a ſtep i'th' morning down to the Parſonage for ſome Pigeons? what are you mad there? what noiſe is that? are you at bowls within? why do you whine?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I have done another fault, I beſeech you ſweet Miſtriſs forgive me.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: What's the matter.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: As I was reaching for the bread that lay upon the ſhelf, I have thrown down the minc'd meat, that ſhould have made the pies to morrow.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Get thee out of my houſe, thou filthy deſtroying
Harlot, thou, I'll not keep thee an hour longer.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Good Miſtriſs, beat me rather for my fault, as much as it deſerves, I do not know whither to go.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: No I warrant thee, out of my doors.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Indeed I'll mend, I pray ſpeak you for me.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: If thou hadſt hurl'd down any thing but the Piemeat, I would have ſpoke for thee, but I cannot find in my heart now.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Art thou here yet? I think I muſt have an Officer to thruſt thee out of my doors, muſt I?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Why, you may ſtop this in my wages too,
For God's ſake do, I'll find my ſelf this year;
And let me ſtay.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Thou't ſpoil ten times as much, I'll cudgel thee out of my doors.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I am aſſur'd you are more merciful,
Than thus to beat me and diſcharge me too.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Doſt thou diſpute with me, Alexander carry the prating hilding forth.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Good Miſtriſs hear me, I have here a Jewel,
My Mother left me, and 'tis ſomething worth:
Receive it, and when all my faults together
Come to the worth of that, then turn me forth,
Till then I pray you keep me.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: What giggombob have we here? pray god you have not pilfred this ſomewhere, th'art ſuch a puling thing, wipe your eyes, and riſe, go your ways, Alexander, bid the Cook mince ſome more meat, come, and get you to bed quickly, that you may up betime i'th' morning a milking, or you and I ſhall fall out worſe yet. Exit Moth. and Alex.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: She has hurt my arm; I am afraid ſhe is a very angry woman, but bleſs him heaven that did me the moſt wrong, I am afraid Antonio's wife ſhould ſee me, ſhe will know me.

l.hi: Melvia.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I am coming, ſhe's not angry agen I hope. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Now what am I the better for enjoying
This woman that I lov'd ſo? all I find,
That I before imagined to be happy:
Now I have done, it turns to nothing elſe
But a poor pitied, and a baſe repentance,
Udsfoot, I am monſtrous angry with my ſelf:
Why ſhould a man that has diſcourſe and reaſon,
And knows how near he loſes all in theſe things,
Covet to have his wiſhes ſatisfied;
Which when they are, are nothing but the ſhame
I do begin to loath this woman ſtrangely,
And I think juſtly too that durſt adventure,
Flinging away her modeſty to take
A ſtranger to her bed, her Husbands body
Being ſcarce cold in the earth for her content,
It was no more to take my ſenſes with
Than if I had an idle dream in ſleep
Yet I have made her promiſes: which grieves me,
And I muſt keep 'em too, I think ſhe hunts me:
The devil cannot keep theſe women off,
When they are fletched once.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: To bed for gods ſake Sir, why do you ſtay here?
Some are up i'th' houſe, I heard the wife,
Good dear ſweet-heart to bed.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Why, I am going? why do you follow me?
You would not have it known I hope, pray get you
Back to your chamber, the doors hard by for me,
Let me alone, I warrant you this it is
To threſh well, I have got a cuſtomer,
Will you go to bed?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Will you?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Yes, I am going.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Then remember your promiſe you made to marry me.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I will, but it was your fault, that it came
To this pinch now, that it muſt need remembrance:
For out of honeſty I offer'd you
To marry you firſt, why did you ſlack that offer?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Alas I told you the inconvenience of it,
And what wrong it would appear to the world
If I had married in ſuch poſt-haſte
After his death: beſide, the fooliſh people
Would have been bold to have thought we had lain together in his time, and like enough imagin'd
We two had murther'd him.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I love her tongue yet,
If I were a Saint
A gilded Saint, and ſuch a thing as this
Should prate thus wittily and feelingly
Unto my Holineſs, I cannot tell,
But I fear ſhrewdly I ſhould do ſomething
That would quite ſcratch me out o'th' Kalender,
And if I ſtay longer talking with her,
Though I am mad at what I have done already,
Yet I ſhall forget my ſelf again;
I feel the Devil
Ready to hold my ſtirrop; pray to bed, good night.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: This kiſs, good night ſweet Love,
And peace goe with thee: thou haſt prov'd thy ſelf
The honeſteſt man that ever was entic'd
To that ſweet ſin as people pleaſe to call it,
Of lying with anothers wife, and I,
I think the honeſteſt woman without bluſhing,
That ever lay with another man, I ſent my Husband
Into a Cellar, poſt, fearing, and juſtly
He ſhould have known him, which I did not purpoſe
Till I had had my end.
Well, now this plot is perfect, let him brag on't.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Juſtice and Curio with a Paper.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: BIrlady Sir, you have rid hard that you have.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: They that have buſineſs, muſt do ſo, I take it.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: You ſay true, when ſet you out my friend?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: About ten a clock, and I have rid all night.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: By the maſs you are tough indeed, I have ſeen the day, I would have rid too with the proudeſt of them, and fling dirt in their faces, and I have don't with this fooliſh boy, Sir, many a time; but what can laſt always? 'tis done, 'tis done now, Sir, age, care, and office, brings us to our footcloaths, the more the pity.

sp.speaker: Curio.
sp.l: I believe that, Sir, but will it pleaſe you to read the buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: My friend, I can read, and I can tell you when.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Would I could too Sir, for my haſte requires it.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: Whence comes it do you ſay?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Sir from the City.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: Oh from the City, 'tis a reverent place.

sp.speaker: Curio.
sp.l: And his juſtice be as ſhort as his memory,
A Dudgion Dagger will ſerve him to mow down ſin withal,
What clod-pole Commiſſioner is this?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: And by my faith, govern'd by worthy members,
Diſcreet and upright.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Sir, they are beholding to you, you have given ſome of them a commendations, they were not worthy of this twenty years.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: Go to, go to, you have a merry meaning, I have found you Sir, i' faith, you are a wag, away, fie now I'll read Your Letter.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Pray do Sir; what a miſery 'tis
To have an urgent buſineſs wait the Juſtice
Of ſuch an old Tuff-taffata that knows not,
Nor can be brought to underſtand more ſence,
Than how to reſtore ſuppreſt Alehouſes,
And have his man compound ſmall treſpaſſes,
For ten groats.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: Sir, it ſeems here your buſineſs is of a deeper circumſtance than I conceiv'd it for; what do you mean, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: 'Tis for mine own eaſe I'll aſſure your Worſhip.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: It ſhall not be i'faith friend, here I have it,
That one Antonio a Gentleman, I take it ſo,
Yes, it is ſo, a Gentleman is lately thought to
Have been made away, and by my faith, upon a
Pearls ground too, if you conſider; well, there's
Knavery in't, I ſee that without ſpectacles.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Sure this fellow deals in revelation, he's ſo hidden,
Goe thy ways, thou wilt ſtick a bench ſpit as formally,
And ſhew thy Agot, and hatch'd chain
As well as the beſt of them.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: And now I have conſider'd, I believe it.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: What Sir?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: That he was murdered,

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Did you know him?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Nor how it is ſuppos'd.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: No, nor I care not two-pence, thoſe are toys and yet I verily believe he was murdered, as ſure as I believe thou art a man, I never fail'd in theſe things yet, w'are a man that's beaten to theſe matters, experience is a certain conceal'd thing that fails not: pray let me ask you one thing, why do you come to me?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Becauſe the Letter is addreſt to you, being the neareſt Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: The neareſt? is that all?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: I think it be Sir, I would be loth you ſhould be the wiſeſt.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Well Sir, as it is, I will endeavour in it; yet if it had come to me by name, I know not, but I think it had been as ſoon diſpatcht as by another, and with as round a wiſdom, I, and as happily, but that's all one: I have born this place this thirty years, and upwards, and with ſufficient credit, and they may when they pleaſe, know me better; to the neareſt? well.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Sir, it is not my fault, for had I known you ſooner—

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: I thank you Sir, I know it.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: I'll be ſworn you ſhould have plaid for any buſineſs now.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: And further, they have ſpecified unto me, his Wife is forely ſuſpected in this matter, as a main cauſe,

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: I think ſhe be Sir, for no other cauſe can be yet found.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: And one Mercury a traveller, with whom they ſay directly ſhe is run away, and as they think this way.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: I knew all this before.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Well Sir, this Mercury I know, and his breeding, a neighbors child hard by, you have been happy, Sir, in coming hither.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Then you know where to have him, Sir?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: I do Sir, he dwells near me.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: I doubt your Worſhip dwels near a knave then.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: I think ſo; pray put on: but 'tis a wonder
To ſee how graceleſs people are now given,
And how baſe virtue is accounted with them
That ſhould be all in all, as ſays a wiſe man.
sp.p: I tell you Sir, and it is true, that there have been ſuch murthers, and of late days, as 'twould make your very heart bleed in you, and ſome of them as I ſhall be enabled, I will tell you, it fell out of late days.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: It may be ſo, but will it pleaſe you to proceed in this?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: An honeſt Weaver, and as good a workman, a e'er ſhot ſhuttle, and as cloſe: but every man muſt dye; this honeſt Weaver being a little mellow in his Ale, that was the evidence verbatim, Sir, God bleſs the mark, ſprung his neck juſt in this place: well Jarvis, thou hadſt wrongs, and if I live ſome of the beſt ſhall ſweat for't, then a wench—

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: But Sir, you have forgot my buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: A ſober pretty maid about 17. they ſay, certainly,
howſoever 'tis ſhuffled, ſhe burſt her ſelf, and fondly, if it be ſo, with Furmety at a Churching, but I think the Devil had another agent in't: either of which, if I can catch, ſhall ſtretch for't.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: This is a mad Juſtice that will hang the Devil; but I would you would be ſhort in this, before that other notice can be given.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Sir, I will doe diſcreetly what is fitting; what, Antonio?

sp.speaker: Ant. within.
sp.p: Your Worſhip.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Put on your beſt coat, and let your fellow Mark goe to the Conſtable, and bid him and me with all the ſpeed he can, and all the power, and provide Pen and Ink to take their confeſſions, and my long ſword: I cannot tell what danger we may meet with; you'll go with us?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Yes, what elſe? I came to that end to accuſe both parties.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: May I crave what you are?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Faith Sir, one that to be known would not profit you, more than a near kinſman of the dead Antonio's.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: 'Tis well, I am ſorry for my neighbor, truly, that he had no more grace, 'twill kill his Mother; ſhe's a good old woman, will you walk in? I'll but put my cloak on, and my chain off, and a clean band, and have my ſhooes blackt over, and ſhift my Jerkin, and we'll to our buſineſs, and you ſhall ſee how I can bolt theſe matters.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: As ſoon as't pleaſe you, Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: This is the place; here did I leave the Maid
Alone laſt night, drying her tender eyes,
Uncertain what to do, and yet deſirous
To have me gone.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: How rude are all we men;
That take the name of Civil to our ſelves?
If ſhe had ſet her foot upon an earth
Where people live that we call barbarous;
Though they had had no houſe to bring her to,
They would have ſpoil'd the glory, that the ſpring
Has deckt the trees in, and with willing hands
Have torn their branches down, and every man
Would have become a builder for her ſake.
What time left you her there?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I left her, when the Sun had ſo much to ſett,
As he is now got from his place of riſe.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: So near the night ſhe could not wander far;
Fair Viola!

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: It is in vain to call; ſhe ſought a houſe
Without all queſtion.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Peace, fair Viola?
Fair Viola? who ſhould have left her here
On ſuch a ground? if you had meant to loſe her,
You might have found there were no ecchos here
To take her name, and carry it about,
When her true Lover came to mourn for her,
Till all the neighboring valleys and the hills,
Reſounded Viola,—
And ſuch a place,
You ſhould have choſe—
You pity us becauſe
The dew a little wets our feet,
Unworthy far to ſeek her in the wet;
And what becomes of her? where wandred ſhe,
With two ſhowers raining on her, from her eyes
Continually, abundantly, from which
There's neither tree nor houſe to ſhelter her;
Will you go with me to travel?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Whither?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Over all the world.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: No by my faith, I'll make a ſhorter journey
When I do travel.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: But there's no hope
To gain my end in any ſhorter way.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Why, what's your end?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: It is to ſearch the earth,
Till we have found two in the ſhapes of men,
As wicked as our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: 'Twere not ſo hard to find out thoſe.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Why, if we find them out,
It were the better, for what brave villany,
Might we four do? we wou'd not keep together:
For every one has treachery enough
For twenty countreys, one ſhould trouble Aſia,
Another ſhould ſow ſtrife in Africa;
But you ſhould play the knave, in at home in Europe,
And for America let me alone.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Sir, I am honeſter,
Than you know how to be, and can no more
Be wrong'd, but I ſhall find my ſelf aright.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: If you had any ſpark of honeſty,
You would not think that honeſter than I,
Were a praiſe high enough to ſerve your turn:
If men were commonly ſo bad as I,
Thieves would be put in Calendars for Saints;
And bones of murderers would work miracles.
I am a kind of knave, of knave ſo much
There is betwixt me, and the vileſt elſe—
But the next place of all to mine is yours.

div.stage: Enter two Milk-maids and Viola with pails,

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: That laſt is ſhe, 'tis ſhe.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Let us away, we ſhall infect her, let her have the wind,
And we will kneel down here.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Wenches away, for here are men.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Fair maid, I pray you ſtay.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Alas, agen?

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Why do you lay hold on her? I pray heartily let her go.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: With all my heart, I do not mean to hurt her.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: But ſtand away then for the pureſt bodies
Will ſooneſt take infection, ſtand away,
But for infecting her my ſelf, by heaven,
I would come there, and beat thee further off.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I know that voice and face.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: You are finely mad, goodbwy Sir, now you are here together, I'll leave oou ſo, god ſend you good luck, both; when you are ſoberer, you'll give me thanks. Exit.

sp.speaker: Madg.
sp.p: Wilt thou go milk? come.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Why doſt not come?

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: She nods, ſhe's aſleep.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: What wert up ſo early?

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: I think you man's mad to kneel there, nay come come away, uds body, Nan, help, ſhe looks black i'th face, She's in a found.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: And you be a man, come hither, and help a woman.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.p: Come thither? you are a fool.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: And you a knave and a beaſt that you are.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Come hither,'twas my being now ſo near,
That made her her ſwound, and you are wicked people,
Or you wou'd do ſo too; my venom eyes
Strike innocency dead at ſuch a diſtance,
Here I'll kneel, for this is out of diſtance.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: Th'art a prating aſs, there's no goodneſs in thee,
I warrant, how doſt thou?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Why? well.

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: Art thou able to go?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: No, pray go you and milk, if I be able to come
I'll follow you, if not, I'll ſit here,
Till you come back.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: I am loth to leave thee here with yon wild fool.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I know him well, I warrant thee he will not hurt me.

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: Come then Nan. Exeunt Maids.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: How do you? be not fearfull, for I hold my hands
Before my mouth, and ſpeak, and ſo
My breath can never blaſt you.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: 'Twas enough to uſe me ill, though you had never ſought me to mock me, why kneel you ſo far off, were not that geſture better us'd in prayer, had I dealt ſo with you, I ſhould not ſleep, till heaven and you had both forgiven me.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: I do not mock, nor lives there ſuch a villain
That can do any thing contemptible
To you, but I do kneel, becauſe it is
An action very fit and reverent,
In preſence of ſo pure a creature,
And ſo far off, as fearful to offend,
One too much wrong'd already.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: You confeſs you did the fault, yet ſcorn to come,
So far as hither, to ask pardon for't;
Which I could willingly afford to come,
To you to grant, good Sir if you have
A better love, may you be bleſt together.
She ſhall not with you better than I will,
I but offend you, there are all the Jewels
I ſtole, and all the love I ever had,
I leave behind with you, I'll carry none
To give another may the next maid you try
Love you no worſe, nor be no worſe than I.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Do not leave me yet for all my fault,
Search out the next things to impoſſible,
And put me on them when they are effected,
I may with better modeſty receive
Forgiveneſs from you.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I will ſet no pennance,
To gain the great forgiveneſs you deſire:
But to come hither and take me and it,
Or elſe I'll come and beg, ſo you will grant,
That you will be content to be forgiven.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Nay, I will come ſince you'll have it ſo,
And ſince you pleaſe to pardon me I hope
Free from infection, here I am by you;
A careleſs man, a breaker of my faith,
A lothſome drunkard; and in that wild fury:
A hunter after whores: I do beſeech you,
To pardon all theſe faults, and take me up
An honeſt, ſober, and a faithful man.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: For heavens ſake, urge your faults no more, but mend,
All the forgiveneſs I can make you, is,
To love you, which I will do, and deſire
Nothing but love again, which if I have not
Yet I will love you ſtill.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Oh Women, that ſome one of you will take,
An everlaſting pen into your hands:
And grave in paper which the writ ſhall make,
More laſting than the marble Monuments,
Your matchleſs virtues to poſterities:
Which the defective race of envious man,
Strive to conceal.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Methinks I would not now for any thing,
But you had miſt me, I have made a ſtory,
Will ſerve to waſte many a winters fire
When we are old, I'll my daughters then,
The miſeries their Mother had in love:
And ſay, my girls be wiſer, yet I would not
Have had more wit my ſelf, take up thoſe Jewels,
For I think I hear my fellows coming.

div.stage: Enter the Milk-maids with their pails.

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: How doſt thou now?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Why, very well I thank you, 'tis late, ſhall I haſte home?

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: I prethee we ſhall be ſhent ſoundly.

sp.speaker: Madge.
sp.p: Why does that railing man goe with us?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I prethee ſpeak well of him, on my word,
He's an honeſt man.

sp.speaker: Nan.
sp.p: There was never any ſo one's complexion, a Gentleman?
I'de be aſham'd to have ſuch a foul mouth. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Mother, Alexander, Andrugio, and his man Rowland.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: How now Alexander, what Gentleman is this?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Indeed forſooth I know not, I found him at the market full of woe, crying a loſt daughter, and telling all her tokens to the people; and what you wot? by all ſubſcription in the world, it ſhould be our new Maid Melvia, one would little think it, therefore I was bold to tell him of her Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Melvia? It cannot be, fool, alas you know ſhe is a poor wench, and I took her in upon mere charity.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: So ſeem'd my daughter when ſhe went away, as ſhe had made her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: What ſtature was your child of, Sir?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Not high, and of a brown complexion,
Her Hair aborn, a round face, which ſome friends that flattered me, would ſay 'twould be a good one.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: This is ſtill Melvia, Miſtriſs, that's the truth on't.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: It may be ſo, I'll promiſe you.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Well, goe thy ways, the flower of our Town, for a hand and a foot, I ſhall never ſee thy fellow.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: But had ſhe not ſuch toyes, as Bracelets, Rings, and Jewels?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: She was ſomething bold indeed to take ſuch things that night ſhe left me.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Then belike ſhe run away?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Though ſhe be one I love, I dare not lye, ſhe did indeed.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: What think you of this Jewel?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Yes, this was one of them, and this was mine, you have made me a new man, I thank you for it.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Nay, and ſhe be given to filching, there is your Jewel, I am clear on't: but by your leave, Sir, you ſhall anſwer me for what is loſt ſince ſhe came hither, I can tell you, there lye things ſcattering in every place about the houſe.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: As I am virtuous, I have the lyingſt old Gentlewoman to my Miſtriſs, and the moſt malicious, the devil a good word will ſhe give a ſervant, that's her old rule; and God be thanked, they'll give her as few, there is perfect love on both ſides, it yearns my heart to ſee the wench miſconſtrued, a careful ſoul ſhe is, I'll be ſworn for her, and when ſhe's gone, let them ſay what they will, they may caſt their caps at ſuch another.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.l: What you have loſt by her, with all my heart
I'll ſee you double paid for, you have ſav'd
With your kind pity, two that muſt not live
Unleſs it be to thank you; take this Jewel,
This ſtrikes off none of her offences, Miſtriſs,
Would I might ſee her.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Alexander, run, and bid her make haſte home, ſhe's at the milking Cloſe; but tell her not by any means who's here, I know ſhe'll be too fearful.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Well, we'll have a poſſet yet at parting, that's my comfort, and one round, or elſe I'll loſe my Will.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: You ſhall find Silvio, Ʋberto, and Pedro enquiring for the Wench at the next Town, tell them ſhe is found, and where I am, and with the favor of this Gentlewoman, deſire them to come hither.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: I pray do, they ſhall be all welcome. Exit. S • r.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: By your leave forſooth, you ſhall ſee me find the parties by a ſlight,

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Who's that, Mr. Juſtice? how do you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Why, very well, and buſie, where's your Son?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: He's within, Sir.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Hum, and how does the young woman my Coſin, that came down with him.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: She's above, as a woman in her caſe may be.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: You have confeſt it? then ſirrah call in the Officers: ſhe's no Coſin of mine; a mere trick to diſcover all.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: To diſcover? what?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: You ſhall know that anon: I think I have overreached you; oh welcome, enter the houſe, and by virtue of my warrant which you have there, ſeize upon the bodily perſons of thoſe whoſe names are there written, to wit, one Mercury, and the wife of one Antonio.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: For what.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Away I ſay,
This Gentleman ſhall certifie you for what. Ex. Officer.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: He can accuſe my Son of nothing, he came from travel but within theſe two days?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: There hangs a tale.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: I ſhould be ſorry this ſhould fall out at any time but eſpecially now Sir; will you favour me ſo much, a • to let me know of what you accuſe him?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Upon ſuſpition of murther.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Murther? I defie thee.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: I pray God he may prove himſelf innocent.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Fie, ſay not ſo, you ſhew your ſelf to be no good Common-wealths man: for the more are hang'd the better 'tis for the Common-wealth.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: By this rule you were beſt hang your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: I forgive your honeſt mirth ever: Oh welcome, welcome Mark.
sp.stage: Enter Mark and Officers, with Mercury and the Wife.
sp.p: Your Pen, Ink, and Paper, to take their examinations.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Why do you pull me ſo? I'll go alone.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Let them ſtand, let them ſtand quietly, whilſt they are examin'd?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: What will you examine us of.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Of Antonio's murther.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Why, he was my friend.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: He was my Husband.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: The more ſhame for you both; Mark, your Pen and Ink.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Pray God all be well, I never knew any of theſe travellers come to good; I beſeech you, Sir, be favourable to my Son.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Gentlewoman, hold you content, I would it were come to that?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: For gods ſake mother, why kneel you to ſuch a pigbrib'd fellow? he has ſurfeited of Geeſe, and they have put him into a fit of Juſtice; let him do his worſt.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Is your paper ready?

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: I am ready, Sir.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Accuſe them, Sir, I command thee to lay down accuſations againſt theſe perſons, in behalf of the State, and firſt look upon the parties to be accus'd, and deliver your name.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: My name is Curio, my murthered kinſman
If he were living now, I ſhould not know him,
'Tis ſo long ſince we ſaw one another.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: My Coſin Curio?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: But thus much from the mouths of his ſervants, and others, whoſe examinations I have in writing about me, I can accuſe them of; this Mercury, the laſt night, but this laſt, lay in Antonio's houſe, and in the night he roſe, raiſing Antonio, where privately they were in talk an hour, to what end I know not: but of likelyhood, finding Antonio's houſe not a fit place to murder him in, he ſuffered him to go to bed again, but in the morning early, he train'd him I think forth, after which time he never ſaw his home; his cloaths were found near the place where Mercury was, and the people at firſt denyed they ſaw him: but at laſt he made a frivilous tale, that there he ſhifted himſelf into a Footmans habit: but in ſhort, the next hour this woman went to Mercury, and in her Coach they poſted hither; true accuſations, I have no more, and I will make none.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: No more? we need no more, ſirrah, be drawing their Mittimus before we hear their anſwer. What ſay you Sir? are you guilty of this murther?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: No Sir.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Whether you are or no, confeſs, it will be the better for you.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: If I were guilty, your Rhetorick could not fetch it forth: but though I am innocent, I confeſs, that if I were a ſtander by, theſe circmſtances urg'd, which are true, would make me doubtleſs believe the accuſed parties, to be guilty.

sp.speaker: Juſt,
sp.p: Write down, that he being a ſtander by; for ſo you ſee he is, doth doubtleſly believe the accuſed parties, which is himſelf to be guilty.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I ſay no ſuch thing.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Write it down I ſay, we'll try that.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I care not what you write, pray God you did not kill him for my love, though I am free from this, we both deſerve—

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Govern your tongue I pray you, all is well, my Husband lives, I know it, and I ſee him.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: They whiſper, ſever them quickly I ſay, Officers, why do you let them prompt one another, Gentlewoman, what ſay you to this, are not you guilty?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: No, as I hope for mercy.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: But are not thoſe circumſtances true, that this Gentleman hath ſo ſhortly and methodically deliver'd?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: They are, and what you do with me, I care not, Since he is dead, in whom was all my care:
You knew him not.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: No, an't been better for you too, and you had never known him.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Why then you did not know the worlds chief joy,
His face ſo manly as it had been made,
To fright the world, yet he ſo ſweetly temper'd;
That he would make himſelf a natural fool,
To do a noble kindeſs for a friend.
He was a man whoſe name I'll not out-live,
Longer than heaven, whoſe Will muſt be obey'd;
Will have me do.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And I will quit thy kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Before me, ſhe has made the tears ſtand in mine eyes, but I muſt be auſtere, Gentlewoman; you muſt confeſs this murder.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: I cannot, Sir, I did it not, but I deſire to ſee thoſe examinations which this Gentleman acknowledges to have about him, for but late laſt night I receiv'd Letters from the City, yet I heard of no confeſſion, then.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: You ſhall ſee them time enough I warrant you, but Letters you ſay you had, where are thoſe Letters?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Sir, they are gone.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Gone? whither are they gone?
How have you diſpos'd of 'em?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Why Sir, they are for womens matters, and ſo I uſe 'em.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Who writ 'em?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: A man of mine.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Who brought 'em?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: A Poſt.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: A Poſt? there is ſome great haſte ſure, aha, where is that Poſt?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Sir, there he ſtands.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Does he ſo? bring hither that Poſt, I am afraid that Poſt will prove a knave; come hither Poſt, what? what can you ſay concerning the murder of Antonio?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What's that to you?

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Oh Poſt, you have no anſwer ready, have you? I'll have one from you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You ſhall have no more from me than you have; you examine an honeſt Gentleman and Gentlemoman here, 'tis pitty ſuch fools as you ſhould be i'th Commiſſion.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Say you ſo Poſt, take away that Poſt, whip him and bring him again quickly, I'll hamper you Poſt.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: 'Tis Antonio, I know him now as well; what an irregular fool is this?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Whip me? hold off.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Oh good Sir whip him, by his murmuring he ſhould know ſomething of my Husbands death; that may quit me, for gods ſake fetch't out.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Whip him I ſay.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Who is't dares whip me now?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.p: Oh my lov'd Husband.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: My moſt worthy friend? where have you been ſo long?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I cannot ſpeak for joy.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Why, what's the matter now, and ſhall not Law then have her courſe?

sp.speaker: Andra.
sp.p: It ſhall heve no other courſe than it has I think.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: It ſhall have other courſe before I go, or I'll beat my brains, and I ſay it was not honeſtly done of him to diſcover himſelf before the parties accus'd were executed, that Law might have had her courſe, for then the kingdom flouriſhes.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: But ſuch a wife as thou, had never any man, and ſuch a friend as he, believe me wife, ſhall never be good wife, love my friend, friend love my wife, hark friend.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.p: Mark, if we can have nothing to do, you ſhall ſwear the peace of ſome body.

sp.speaker: Mark.
sp.p: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: By my troth I am ſorry my wife is ſo obſtinate, ſooth, if I could yet do thee any good, I wou'd, faith I wou'd.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I thank you Sir, I have loſt that paſſion.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Coſin Curio, you and I muſt be better acquainted.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: It is my wiſh, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I ſhould not have known you neither, 'tis ſo long ſince we ſaw, we were but children then: but you have ſhew'd your ſelf an honeſt man to me.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: I would be ever ſo.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: Look you, who's there.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.l: Say nothing to me, for thy peace is made.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Sir, I can nothing ſay,
But that you are her Father, you can both
Not only pardon, when you have a wrong,
But love where you have moſt injury.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: I think I ſhall hear of no hanging this year, there's
A Tinker and a Whore yet, the Cryer ſaid, that rob'd her, and are in priſon, I hope they ſhall be hang'd.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.l: No truly Sir, they have broke priſon.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: 'Tis no matter, then rhe Jaylor ſhall be hang'd.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: You are deceiv'd in that too, Sir 'twas known to be againſt his will, and he hath got his pardon, I think for nothing, but if it doth coſt him any thing, I'll pay it.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: Mark, up with your papers, away.

sp.speaker: Mer!
sp.p: Oh you ſhall ſtay dinner, I have a couple of brawling neighbors, that I'll aſſure you will not agree, and you ſhall have the hearing of their matter.

sp.speaker: Juſt.
sp.l: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Go, Gentlemen, go in.

sp.speaker: Rich.
sp.l: Oh Viola, that no ſucceeding age,
Might looſe the memory of what thou wert,
But ſuch an overſwayed Sex is yours,
That all the virtuous actions you can do,
Are but as men will call them; and I ſwear,
'Tis my belief, that women want but ways;
To praiſe their deeds, but men want deeds to praiſe.

div.head: EPILOGUE.
div.l: 'TIs ended, but my hopes and fears begin,
Nor can it be imputed as a ſin
In me to wiſh it favour, if this night,
To the Judicious it hath giv'n delight.
I have my ends, and may ſuch for their grace,
Vouchſaf'd to this, find theirs in every place.

div.head: The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Albert, a French Pirat, in love with Aminta.
Tibalt du Pont, a merry Gentleman, friend to Albert.
Maſter of the Ship, an honeſt merry man.
Sebaſtian, a noble Gentleman of Portugal, Husband to Roſellia.
Nicuſa, Nephew to Sebaſtian, both caſt upon a deſart Iſland.

list.head: Women.
list.item: Aminta, Miſtriſs to Albert, a noble French Virgin.
Roſellia, Governeſs of the Amazonian Portugals.
Clarinda, Daughter to Roſellia, in love with Albert.

list.head: three Ladies, Members of the Female Common-wealth.

p.hi: The Scene, Firſt at Sea, then in the deſart Iſlands.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: A Tempeſt, Thunder and Lightning. Enter Maſter and two Sailors.

sp.speaker: Maſter.
sp.l: LAy her aloof, the Sea grows dangerous,
How it ſpits againſt the clouds, how it capers,
And how the fiery Element frights it back
There be Devils dancing in the air I think
I ſaw a Dolphin hang i'th horns o'th' moon
•• at from a wave, hey day, hey day,
•• w ſhe kicks and yerks?
Down with the Main Maſt,, lay her at hull,
Farle up all her Linnens, and let her ride it out.

sp.speaker: 1 Sailor.
sp.l: She'll never brook it Maſter.
She's ſo deep laden that ſhe'll bulge;

sp.speaker: Maſter.
sp.l: Hang her.
Can ſhe not buffet with a ſtorm a little?
How it toſſes her, ſhe reels like a Drunkard.

sp.speaker: 2. Sail.
sp.l: We have diſcover'd the Land, Sir,
Pray let's make in, ſhe's ſo drunk elſe,
She may chance to caſt up all her Lading.

sp.speaker: 1 Sail.
sp.l: Sland in, ſland in, we are all loſt elſe, loſt and periſh'd

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Steer her a Star-board there.

sp.speaker: 2 Sail.
sp.l: Bear in with all the ſail we can, ſee Maſter
See, what a clap of Thunder there is,
What a face of heaven, how dreadfully it looks?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Thou raſcal, thou fearful rogue, thou haſt been praying;
I ſee't in thy face, thou haſt been mumbling,
When we are ſplit you ſlave; is this a time,
To diſcourage our friends with your cold orizons?
Call up the Boatſwain; how it ſtorms; holla.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: What ſhall we do Maſter?
Caſt over all her lading? ſhe will not ſwim
An hour elſe;

div.stage: Enter Albert, Franvile, La-mure, Tibalt de pont. Morillat

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: The ſtorm is loud,
We cannot hear one another,
What's the coaſt?

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: We know not ye; ſhall we make in?

sp.speaker: Albert.
sp.l: What comfort Sailors?
I never ſaw, ſince I have known the Sea,
(which has been this twenty years) ſo rude a tempeſt:
In what State are we?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Dangerous enough Captain,
We have ſprung five leaks, and no little ones;
Still rage; beſides, her ribs are open;
Her rudder almoſt ſpent; prepare your ſelves;
And have good courages, death comes but once,
And let him come in all his frights.

sp.speaker: Albert.
sp.l: Is't not poſſible,
To make in to th' Land? 'tis here before us.

sp.speaker: Morill.
sp.l: Here hard by Sir.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Death is nearer, Gentlemen.
Yet do not cry, let's dye like in men.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Shall's hoiſe the Boat out,
And goe all at one caſt? the more the merrier.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: You are too haſty Mounſieur,
Do ye long to be i'th' Fiſh-market before your time?
Hold her up there.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Oh miſerable fortune,
Nothing but horror ſounding in mine ears,
No minute to promiſe to my frighted ſoul,

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Peace woman,
We ha ſtorms enough already; no more howling.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Gentle Maſter.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Clap this woman under hatches.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Prethe ſpeak mildly to her.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Can no help?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: None that I know.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: No promiſe from your goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Am I a God? for heavens ſake ſtow this

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Go: take your gilt Prayer-Book woman;
And to your buſineſs; wink and die,
There's an old Haddock ſtaies for ye.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Muſt I die here in all the frights and terrors,
The thouſand ſeveral ſhapes death triumphs in?
No friend to counſel me?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Have peace ſweet Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: No kindreds tears upon me? oh! my countrey?
No gentle hand to cloſe mine eyes?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Be comforted, heaven has the ſame
Power ſtill, and the ſame mercy.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Oh, that wave will devour me.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Carry her down Captain;
Or by theſe hands I'll give no more direction,
Let the Ship ſink or ſwim, we ha ne'er better luck,
When we ha ſuch ſtowage as theſe trinkets with us;
Theſe ſweet ſin-breeders: how can heaven ſmile on us,
When ſuch a burthen of iniquity
Lies tumbling like a potion in our ſhip's belly? Exit.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Away with her, and if ſhe have a Prayer,
That's fit for ſuch an hour, let her ſay't quickly,
And ſeriouſly. Exit.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Come, I ſee it clear Lady, come in,
And take ſome comfort. I'll ſtay with ye.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Where ſhould I ſtay? to what end ſhould I hope,
Am not I circled round with miſery?
Confuſions in their full heights dwell about me:
Oh Mounſieur Albert, How am I bound to curſe ye,
If curſes could redeem me? how to hate ye?
You forc'd me from my quiet, from my friends;
Even from their Arms, that were as dear to me,
As day-light is, or comfort to the wretched;
You forc'd my friends from their peaceful reſt,
Some your relentleſs ſword gave their laſt groans;
Would I had there been numbred;
And to fortunes never ſatisfied afflictions,
• e turn'd my Brother; and thoſe few friends I'd left,
Like deſperate creatures, to their own fears
And the world's ſtubborn pitties: Oh mercileſs!

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Sweet Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: And whither they are wandred to avoid ye,
Or whither dead, and no kind earth to cover 'em;
Was this a Lovers part? but heaven has found ye,
〈◊〉 in his loudeſt voice, his voice of thunder,
And in the mutiny of his deep wonders,
• e tells ye now, ye weep too late:

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Let theſe tears tell how I honor ye;
Ye know dear Lady, ſince ye are mine,
How truly I have lov'd ye, how ſanctimoniouſly
Obſerv'd your honor; not one laſcivious word,
Not one touch Lady; no, not a hope that might not render me
The unpolluted ſervant of your chaſtity;
For you I put to ſea, to ſeek your Brother;
Your Captain, yet your ſlave, that his redemption,
If he be living, where the Sun has circuit,
May expiate your rigor, and my raſhneſs.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: The ſtorm grows greater, what ſhall we do?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Let's in:
And ask heavens mercy; my ſtrong mind yet preſages,
Through all theſe dangers, we ſhall ſee a day yet
Shall crown your pious hopes, and my fair wiſhes. Exit

div.stage: Enter Maſter, Sailors, Gentlemen, and Boatſwain.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: It muſt all over-board.

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: It clears to Sea-ward Maſt.
Fling o'er the Lading there, and let's lighten her;
All the meat, and the Cakes, we are all gone elſe;
That we may find her Leaks, and hold her up;
Yet ſave ſome little Bisket for the Lady,
Till we come to the Land.

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Muſt my Goods over too?
Why honeſt Maſter? here lies all my money;
The Money I ha wrackt by uſury,
To buy new Lands and Lordſhips in new Countreys,
'Cauſe I was baniſh'd from mine own
I ha been this twenty years a raiſing it.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Out with it:
The devils are got together by the ears, who ſhall have it;
And here they quarrel in the clouds.

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: I am undone Sir:

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: And be undone, 'tis better than we

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Oh ſave one Cheſt of Plate.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Away with it luſtily, Sailors;
It was ſome pawn that he has got unjuſtly;
Down with it low enough, and let Crabs breed in't;

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Over with the Trunks too.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Take mine and ſpare not.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We muſt over with all.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Will ye throw away my Lordſhip
That I ſold, put it into cloaths and neceſſaries,
To goe to ſea with?

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Over with it; I love to ſee a Lordſhip ſink;
Sir, you left no wood upon't, to buoy it up;
You might ha' ſav'd it elſe.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: I am undone for ever;

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Why we are all undone; would you be only happy?

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Sir, you may looſe too.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Thou lieſt; I ha' nothing but my skin,
And my cloaths; my ſword here, and my ſelf;
Two Crowns in my pocket; two pair of Cards;
And three falſe Dice: I can ſwim like a fiſh
Raſcal, nothing to hinder me.

sp.speaker: Boatſw.
sp.l: In with her of all hands.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen, come Captain, ye muſt help all;
My life now for the Land,
'Tis high, and rocky, and full of perils;

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.l: However let's attempt it.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Then cheer luſtily my hearts. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Yes, 'tis a Ship, I ſee it now, a tall Ship;
She has wrought luſtily for her deliverance;
Heavens mercy, what a wretched day has here been?

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: To ſtill and quiet minds that knew no miſery,
It may ſeem wretched, but with us 'tis ordinary;
Heaven has no ſtorm in ſtore, nor earth no terror,
That can ſeem new to us.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: 'Tis true Nicuſa, if fortune were determin'd
To be wanton, and would wipe out the ſtories
Of mens miſeries: yet we two living,
We could croſs her purpoſe; for 'tis impoſſible
She could cure us, we are ſo excellent in our afflictions;
It would be more than glory to her blindneſs,
And ſtile her power beyond her pride, to quit us.

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: Do they live ſtill?

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Yes, and make to harbor:

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: Moſt miſerable men; I grieve their fortunes.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: How happy had they been, had the Sea cover'd em?
They leap from one calamity to another;
Had they been drown'd, they had ended all their ſorrows.
What ſhouts of joy they make?

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: Alas poor wretches, had they but once experience
Of this Iſland, they'd turn their tunes to wailings;

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Nay, to curſes.
That ever they ſet foot on ſuch calamities;
Here's nothing but Rocks and barrenneſs,
Hunger, and cold to eat; here's no Vineyards
To cheer the heart of man, no Chriſtal Rivers,
After his labour, to refreſh his body,
If he be feeble; nothing to reſtore him,
But heavenly hopes, nature that made thoſe remedies,
Dares not come here, nor look on our diſtreſſes,
For fear ſhe turn wild, like the place, and barren.

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: Oh Uncle, yet a little memory of what we were,
'Twill be a little comfort in our calamities;
When we were ſeated in our bleſſed homes,
How happy in our kindreds, in our families,
In all our fortunes?

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Curſe on thoſe French Pirats, that diſplanted us;
That flung us from that happineſs we found there;
Conſtrain'd us to Sea, to ſave our lives, honors, and our riches,
With all we had, our kinſmen, and our jewels,
In hope to find ſome place free from ſuch robbers,
Where a mighty ſtorm ſever'd our Barks,
That, where my Wife, my Daughter
And my noble Ladies that went with her,
Virgins and loving ſouls, to ſcape thoſe Pirats.

sp.speaker: Nicuſ.
sp.l: They are yet living; ſuch goodneſs cannot periſh.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: But never to me Coſin;
Never to me again; what bears their Flag-ſtaves?

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: The Arms of France ſure;
Nay, doe not ſtart, we cannot be more miſerable;
Death is a cordial, now, come when it will.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: They get to ſhore apace, they'll flie as faſt
When once they find the place; what's that which ſwims there?

sp.speaker: Ni.
