sp.l: A ſtrong young man, Sir, with a handſom woman.
Hanging about his neck.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: That ſhews ſome honor;
May thy brave charity, what e'er thou art,
Be ſpoken in a place that may renown thee,
And not dye here.

sp.speaker: Nicuſ.
sp.l: The Boat it ſeems turn'd over,
So forced to their ſhifts; yet all are landed:
They're Pirates on my life.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: They will not rob us;
For none will take out miſery for riches:
Come Coſin, let's deſcend, and try their pities;
If we get off, a little hope walks with us;
If not, we ſhall but load this wretched Iſland
With the ſame ſhadows ſtill, that muſt grow ſhorter. Ex.

div.stage: Enter Albert, Aminta, Tibalt, Morillat, La-mure, Maſter, Franvile, Surgeon, Sailors.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Wet come aſhore my mates, we are ſafe arrived yet.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Thanks to heavens goodneſs, no man loſt;
The Ship rides fair too, and her leaks in good plight.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: The weathers turn'd more courteous;
How does my Dear?
Alas, how weak ſhe is, and wet?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I am glad yet, I ſcap'd with life;
Which certain, noble Captain, next to heavens goodneſs,
I muſt thank you for, and which is more,
Acknowledge your dear tenderneſs, your firm love
To your unworthy Miſtriſs, and recant too
(Indeed I muſt) thoſe harſh opinions,
Thoſe cruel unkind thoughts, I heapt upon ye;
Farther than that, I muſt forget your injuries.
So far I am ti'd, and fet'red to your ſervice,
Believe me, I will learn to love.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: I thank ye Madam,
And it ſhall be my practiſe to ſerve.
What cheer companions?

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: No great cheer Sir, a piece of ſouc'd Bisket
And halfe a hard egg; for the Sea has taken order;
Being young and ſtrong, we ſhall not ſurfet Captain.
For mine own part, I'll dance till I'm dry;
Come Surgeon, out with your Cliſter-pipe,
And ſtrike a Galliard.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: What a brave day again?
And what fair weather, after ſo foul a ſtorm?

sp.speaker: La mure.
sp.l: I, an't pleas'd the Maſter he might ha ſeen
This weather, and ha' ſav'd our goods.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Never think on 'em, we have our lives and healths.

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: I muſt think on 'em, and think
'Twas moſt maliciouſly done to undoe me.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: And me too, I loſt all;
I ha'n't another ſhirt to put upon me, nor cloaths
But theſe poor rags; I had fifteen fair ſuits,
The worſt was cut upon Taffaty.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I am glad you ha' loſt, give me thy hand,
Is thy skin whole? art thou not purl'd with ſcabs?
No antient monuments of Madam Venus?
Thou haſt a ſuit then will poſe the cunning'ſt Tailor,
That will never turn faſhion, nor forſake thee,
Till thy executors the Worms, uncaſe thee,
They take off glorious ſutes Franvile: thou art happy,
Thou art deliver'd of 'em; here are no Brokers;
No Alchymiſts to turn 'em into Mettal;
Nor leather'd Captains, with Ladies to adore 'em;
Wilt thou ſee a Dog-fiſh riſe in one of thy brave doublets,
And tumble like a tub to make thee merry,
Or an old Haddock riſe with thy hatch'd ſword
Thou paid'ſt a hundred Crowns for?
A Mermaid in a Mantle of your Worſhips,
Or a Dolphin in your double Ruffe?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Ye are merry, but if I take it thus,
If I be foiſted and jeer'd out of my goods.

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Nor I, I vow thee.
Nor Maſter, nor Mate, I ſee your cunning,

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Oh be not angry Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Moril.
sp.l: Yes Sir, we have reaſon.
And ſome friends I can make.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: What I did Gentlemen, was for the general ſafety.
If ye aim at me, I am not ſo tame.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Pray take my counſel Gallants.
Fight not till the Surgeon be well,
He's damnable ſea-ſick, and may ſpoil all;
Beſides he has loſt his Fiddleſtick, and the beſt
Box of Bores-greaſe; why do you make ſuch faces,
And hand your ſwords?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Who would ye fight with Gentlemen?
Who has done ye wrong? for ſhame be better temper'd.
No ſooner come to give thanks for our ſafeties,
But we muſt raiſe new civil broils amongſt us
Inſlame thoſe angry powers, to ſhower new vengeance on us?
What can we expect for theſe unmanly murmurs,
Theſe ſtrong temptations of their holy pitties,
But plagues in another kind, a fuller, ſo dreadful,
That the ſinging ſtorms are ſlumbers to it?

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Be men, and rule your minds;
If you will needs fight, Gentlemen,
And think to raiſe new riches by your valours,
Have at ye, I have little elſe to do now
I have ſaid my prayers; you ſay you have loſt,
And make your loſs your quarrel.
And grumble at my Captain here, and the Maſter
Two worthy perſons, indeed too worthy for ſuch raſcals,
Thou Galloon gallant, and Mammon you
That build on golden Mountains, thou Money-Maggot;
Come all, draw your ſwords, ye ſay ye are miſerable.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Nay, hold good Tibalt

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Captain, let me correct 'em;
I'll make ye ten times worſe, I will not leave 'em;
For look ye, fighting is as nouriſhing to me as eating,
I was born quarrelling.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Pray Sir.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I will not leave 'em skins to cover 'em;
Do ye grumble, when ye are well, ye rogues?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Noble Du-pont.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Ye have cloaths now: and ye prate.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Pray Gentlemen, for my ſake be at peace.
Let it become me to make all friends.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: You have ſtopt our angers Lady.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: This ſhews noble.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: 'Tis well: 'tis very well: there's half a Bisket,
Break't amongſt ye all, and thank my bounty.
This is Cloaths and Plate too; come no more quarrelling.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: But ha! what things are theſe,
Are they humane creatures?

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I have heard of Sea-Calves.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: They are no ſhadows ſure, they have Legs and Arms.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: They hang but lightly on though.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: How they look, are they mens faces?

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: They have horſe-tails growing to 'em.
Goodly long manes.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Alas what ſunk eyes they have!
How they are crept in, as if they had been frighted!
Sure they are wretched men.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Where are their Wardrobes?
Look ye Franvile, here are a couple of Courtiers.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: They kneel, alas poor ſouls.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: What are ye? ſpeak; are ye alive,
Or wandring ſ • adows, that find no peace on earth,
Till ye reveal ſome hidden ſecret?

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: We are men as you are;
Only our miſeries make us ſeem monſters,
If ever pitty dwelt in noble hearts;

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: We underſtand 'em too: pray mark'em t Gentlemen

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Or that heaven is pleas'd with human echarity;
If ever ye have heard the name of friendſhip?
Or ſuffered in your ſelves, the leaſt afflictions,
Have gentle Fathers that have bred ye tenderly,
And Mothers that have wept for your misfortunes,
Have mercy on our miſeries.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Stand up wretches;
Speak boldly, and have releaſe;

sp.speaker: Nicuſ.
sp.l: If ye be Chriſtians,
And by that bleſſed name, bound to relieve us,
Convey us from this Iſland.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Speak; what are ye?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: As you are, Gentle born; to tell ye more,
Were but to number up our own calamities,
And turn your eyes wild with perpetual weepings;
Theſe many years in this moſt wretched Iſland
We two have liv'd: the ſcorn and game of fortune;
Bleſs your ſelves from it Noble Gentlemen;
The greateſt plagues that humane nature ſuffers,
Are ſeated here, wildneſs, and wants innumerable,

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: How came ye hither?

sp.speaker: Nicuſ.
sp.l: In a ſhip as you do, and you might have been.
Had not Heaven preſerv'd ye for ſome more noble uſe;
Wrackt deſperately; our men, and all conſum'd,
But we two; that ſtill live, and ſpin out
The thin and ragged threds of our misfortunes.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Is there no meat above?

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Nor meat nor quiet;
No ſummer here, to promiſe any thing;
Nor Autumn, to make full the reapers hands;
The earth obdurate to the tears of heaven,
Lets nothing ſhoot but poiſon'd weeds.
No Rivers, nor no pleaſant Groves, no Beaſts;
All that were made for man's uſe, ſlie this deſart;
No airy Fowl dares make his flight over it,
It is ſo ominous.
Serpents, and ugly things, the ſhames of nature,
Roots of malignant taſts, foul ſtanding waters;
Sometimes we find a fulſome Sea-root,
And that's a delicate? a Rat ſometimes,
And that we hunt like Princes in their pleaſure;
And when we take a Toad, we make a Banquet.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: For heavens ſake let's aboard.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: D'ye know no farther?

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: Yes, we have ſometimes ſeen the ſhadow of a place inhabited;
And heard the noiſe of hunters;
And have attempted ro find it, to far as a River,
Deep, ſlow, and dangerous, fenced with high Rocks,
We have gone; but not able to atchieve that hazard,
Return to our old miſeries.
If this ſad ſtory may deſerve your pities.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Ye ſhall aboard with us, we will relieve your miſeries:

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Nor will we be unthankful for this benefit,
No Gentlemen, we'll pay for our deliverance;
Look ye that plough the Seas for wealth and pleaſures,
That out-run day and night with your ambitions,
Look on thoſe heaps, they ſeem hard ragged quarries;
Remove 'em, and view 'em fully.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Oh heaven, they are Gold and Jewels.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Be not too haſty, here lies another heap.

sp.speaker: Moril.
sp.l: And here another,
All perfect Gold.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Stand farther off, you muſt not be your own carvers;

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: We have ſhares, and deep ones;

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Yes Sir, we'll maintain't: ho fellow Sailors,

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Stand all to your freedoms;
I'll have all this.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: And I this.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: You ſhall be hang'd firſt,

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: My loſſes ſhall be made good.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: So ſhall mine, or with my ſword I'll do't;
All that will ſhare with us, aſſiſt us.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Captain, let's ſet in.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: This money will undo us, undo us all:

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: This Gold was the overthrow of my happineſs
I had command too, when I landed here,
And lead young, high, and noble ſpirits under me,
This curſed Gold enticing 'em, they ſet upon their Captain,
On me that own'd this wealth, and this poor Gentleman,
Gave us no few wounds, forc'd us from our own;
And then their civil ſwords, who ſhould be owners,
And who Lords over all, turn'd againſt their own lives,
Firſt their rage, conſum'd the Ship,
That poor part of the Ship that ſcap'd the firſt wrack,
Next their lives by heaps; Oh be you wiſe and careful:

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: We'll ha'more: ſirrah, come ſhew it.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Or ten times worſe afflictions than thou ſpeak'ſt of.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Nay, and ye will be dogs. Beats 'em out.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Let me come, Captain:
This Golden age muſt have an Iron ending.
Have at the bunch. He beats 'em off. Exit.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Oh Albert; Oh Gentlemen, Oh Friends. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Come noble Nephew, if we ſtay here, we dye,
Here rides their Ship, yet all are gone to th' ſpoil,
Let's make a quick uſe.

sp.speaker: Nicuſ.
sp.l: Away dear Uncle.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: This Gold was our overthrow. Exit.

sp.speaker: Nicuſ.
sp.l: It may now be our happineſs.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: You ſhall have Gold: yes, I'll cram it int'ye;
You ſhall be your own carvers; yes, I'll carve ye,

sp.speaker: Morill.
sp.l: I am ſore, I pray hear reaſon:

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I'll hear none.
Covetous baſe minds have no reaſon;
I am hurt my ſelf; but whilſt I have a leg left,
I will ſo haunt your gilded ſouls; how d'ye Captain?
Ye bleed apace, curſe on the cauſers on't;
Ye do not faint?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: No, no; I am not ſo happy.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: D'ye howl, nay, ye deſerve it:
•• ſe greedy rogues; come, ſhall we make an end of'em?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: They are our Countrey-men, for heavens ſake ſpare 'em.
Alas, they are hurt enough, and they relent now.

sp.speaker: Aminta.
sp.l: Oh Captain, Captain.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Whoſe voice is that?

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: The Ladies.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Look Captain, look; ye are undone: poor Captain,
We are all undone, all, all: we are all miſerable,
• ad wilful men; ye are undone, your Ship, your Ship.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: What of her?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: She's under ſail, and floating;
See where ſhe flies: ſee to your ſhames, you wretches:
Theſe poor ſtarv'd things that ſhew'd you Gold.

div.stage: La-m. and Franvile goes up to ſee the Ship,

sp.speaker: 1 Sail.
sp.l: They have cut the Cables,
And got her out; the Tide too has befriended 'em.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Where are the Sailors that kept her?

sp.speaker: Boatſ.
sp.l: Here, here in in the mutiny, to take up money,
And left no creature, left the Boat aſhore too;
This Gold, this damn'd enticing Gold.

sp.speaker: 2 Sail,
sp.l: How the wind drives her,
As if it vied to force her from our furies?

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Come back good old men:

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Good honeſt men, come back.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: The wind's againſt ye, ſpeak louder;

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have all your Gold again: they ſee us.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Hold up your hands, and kneel,
And howl ye block-heads; they'll have compaſſion on ye;
Yes, yes, 'tis very likely, ye have deſerv'd it,
D'ye look like dogs now?
Are your mighty courages abated?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: I bleed apace Tibalt:

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Retire Sir: and make the beſt uſe of our miſeries.
They but begin now.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Are ye alive ſtill?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Yes ſweet.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Help him off Lady;
And wrap him warm in your arms,
Here's ſomething that's comfortable; off with him handſomely,
I'll come to ye ſtraight; but vex theſe raſcals a little.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Oh, I am hungry, and hurt, and I am weary.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Here's a Peſtle of a Portigue, Sir;
'Tis excellent meat, with four ſauce;
And here's two Chains, ſuppoſe 'em Sauſages;
Then there wants Muſtard;
But the fearful Surgeon will ſupply ye preſently:

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Oh for that Surgeon, I ſhall die elſe.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Faith there he lies in the ſame pickle too,

sp.speaker: Surg.
sp.l: My Salves, and all my Inſtruments are loſt;
And I am hurt and ſtarv'd;
Good Sir, ſeek for ſome herbs.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Here's Herb-graceleſs, will that ſerve?
Gentlemen will ye go to ſupper?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Where's the meat?

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Where's the meat? what a Veal voice is there?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Would we had it Sir, or any thing elſe;

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I would now cut your throat you dog,
But that I wo'not doe you ſuch a courteſie;
To take you from the benefit of ſtarving,
Oh! what a comfort will your worſhip have ſome three days hence?
Ye things beneath pitty, Famine ſhall be your harbinger;
You muſt not look for Down-beds here,
Nor Hangings; though I could wiſh ye ſtrong ones;
Yet there be many lightſome cool Star-chambers,
Open to every ſweet air, I'll aſſure ye,
Ready provided for ye, and ſo I'll leave ye;
Your firſt courſe is ſerv'd, expect the ſecond. Exit.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: A vengeance on theſe Jewels.

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Oh! this curſed Gold. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: ALas dear ſoul ye faint.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: You ſpeak the language
Which I ſhould uſe to you, heaven knows, my weakneſs
Is not for what I ſuffer in my ſelf,
But to imagine what you endure, and to what fate
Your cruel Stars reſerve ye.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Do not add to my afflictions
By your tender pitties; ſure we have chang'd Sexes;
You bear calamity with a fortitade
Would become a man; I like a weak girl, ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Oh, but your wounds,
How fearfully they gape? and every one
To me is a Sepulchre: if I lov'd truly,
(Wiſe men affirm, that true love can do no wonders,)
Theſe bath'd in my warm tears, would ſoon be cur'd,
And leave no oriſice behind; pray give me leave.
To play the Surgeon, and bind 'em up;
The raw air rankles 'em.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Sweet, we want means.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Love can ſupply all wants.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: What have ye done, Sweet?
Oh ſacriledge to beauty: there's no hair
Of theſe pure locks, by which the greateſt King
Would not be gladly bound, and love his Fetters.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Oh Albert, I offer this ſacrifice of ſervice
To the Altar of your ſtaid temperance, and ſtill adore it,
When with a violent hand you made me yours,
I curs'd the doer: but now I conſider,
How long I was in your power: and with what honor;
You entertain'd me, it being ſeldom ſeen,
That youth, and heat of bloud, could e'r preſcribe
Laws to it ſelf; your goodneſs is the Lethe,
In which I drown your injuries, and now live
Truly to ſerve ye: how do you Sir?
Receive you the leaſt eaſe from my ſervice?
If you do, I am largely recompenc'd.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: You good Angels,
That are ingag'd, when mans ability fails,
To reward goodneſs: look upon this Lady
Though hunger gripes my croaking entrails,
Yet when I kiſs theſe Rubies, methinks
I'm at a Banquet, a refreſhing Banquet;
Speak my bleſs'd one, art not hungry?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Indeed I could eat, to bear you company.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Bluſh unkind nature,
If thou haſt power: or being to hear
Thy ſelf, and by ſuch innocence accus'd;
Muſt print a thouſand kinds of ſhame, upon
Thy various face: canſt thou ſupply a drunkard,
And with a prodigal hand reach choice of Wines,
Till he caſt up thy bleſſings? or a glutton,,
That robs the Elements, to ſooth his palat,
And only eats to beget appetite,
Not to be ſatisfied? and ſuffer here
A Virgin which the Saints would make their gueſt,
To pine for hunger? ha, if my ſence Horns within.
Deceive me not, theſe Notes take Being
From the breath of men; confirm me my Aminta;
Again, this way the gentle wind conveys it to us,
Hear you nothing?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Yes, it ſeems free hunters Muſick;

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Still 'tis louder; and I remember the Portugals
Inform'd us, they had often heard ſuch ſounds,
But ne'r could touch the ſhore from whence it came;
Follow me, my Aminta: my good genius,
Shew me the way ſtill; ſtill we are directed;
When we gain the top of this near riſing hill,
We ſhall know further. Exit. And Enter above.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Courteous Zephyrus,
On his dewy wings, carries perſumes to cheer us;
The air clears too;
And now, we may diſcern another Iſland,
And queſtionleſs, the ſeat of fortunate men:
Oh that we could arrive there.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: No Albert, 'tis not to be hop'd;
This envious Torrent's cruelly interpos'd;
We have no veſſel that may tranſport us;
Nor hath nature given us wings to flie.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Better try all hazards,
Than periſh here remedileſs; I feel
New vigor in me, and a ſpirit that dares
More than a man, to ſerve my fair Aminta;
Theſe Arms ſhall be my oars, with which I'll ſwim;
And my zeal to ſave thy innocent ſelf,
Like w •• gs, ſhall bear me up above the brackiſh waves.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Will ye then leave me?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Till now I ne'er was wretched.
My beſt Aminta, I ſwear by goodneſs
'Tis nor hope, nor fear, of my ſelf that invites me
To this extream; 'tis to ſupply thy wants and believe me
Though pleaſure met me in moſt raviſhing forms,
And happineſs courted me to entertain her,
I would nor eat nor ſleep, till I return'd
And crown'd thee with my fortunes.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Oh but your abſence.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Suppoſe it but a dream, and as you may,
Endeavour to take reſt; and when that ſleep
Deceives your hunger with imagin'd food,
Think you have ſent me for diſcovery
Of ſome moſt fortunate Continent, yet unknown,
Which you are to be Queen of.
And now ye Powers, that e'er heard Lovers Prayers,
Or cheriſht pure affection; look on him
That is your Votary, and make it known
Againſt all ſtops, you can defend your own. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: How did we loſe Clarinda?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: When we believ'd the Stag was ſpent, and would take ſoil,
The ſight of the black lake which we ſuppos'd
He choſe for his laſt refuge, frighted him more
Than we that did purſue him.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: That's uſual; for, death it ſelf is not ſo terrible
To any beaſt of chaſe.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Since we liv'd here, we ne'er could force one to it.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo dreadful,
Birds that with their pinions cleave the air
Dare not flie over it: when the Stag turn'd head,
And we, even tir'd with labor, Clarinda, as if
She were made of Air and Fire,
And had no part of earth in her, eagerly purſu'd him;
Nor need we fear her ſafety, this place yields not
Fawns nor Satyrs, or more luſtful men;
Here we live ſecure,
And have among our ſelves a Common-wealth,
Which in our ſelves begun, with us muſt end.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I, there's the miſery.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: But being alone,
Allow me freedom but to ſpeak my thoughts;
The ſtrictneſs of our Governeſs, that forbids us,
On pain of death, the ſight and uſe of men,
Is more than tyranny: for her ſelf, ſhe's paſt
Thoſe youthful heats, and feels not the want
Of that which young maids long for: and her daughter
The fair Clarinda, though in few years
Improv'd in height and large proportion,
Came here ſo young,
That ſcarce remembring that ſhe had a father,
She never dreams of man; and ſhould ſhe ſee one,
In my opinion, a would appear a ſtrange beaſt to her.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis not ſo with us.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: For my part, I confeſs it, I was not made
For this ſingle life; nor do I love hunting ſo,
But that I had rather be the chace my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: By Venus (out upon me) I ſhould have ſworn
By Diana, I am of thy mind too wench;
And though I have ta'en an oath, not alone
To deteſt, but never to think of man,
Every hour ſomething tels me I am forſworn;
For I confeſs, imagination helps me ſometimes,
And that's all is left for us to feed on,
We might ſtarve elſe, for if I have any pleaſure
In this life, but when I ſleep, I am a Pagan;
Then from the Courtier to the Countrey-clown,
I have ſtrange viſions.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Viſions Crocale?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Yes, and ſine viſions too;
And viſions I hope in dreams are harmleſs,
And not forbid by our Canons; the laſt night
(Troth 'tis a fooliſh one, but I muſt tell it)
As I lay in my Cabin, betwixt ſleeping and waking.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Upon your back?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: How ſhould a young Maid lie, fool,
When ſhe would be intranc'd?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: We are inſtructed; forward I prethee.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Methought a ſweet young man
In years ſome twenty, with a downy chin,
Promiſing a future beard, and yet no red one,
Stole ſlylie to my Cabin all unbrac'd,
Took me in his arms, and kiſs'd me twenty times,
Yet ſtill I ſlept.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Fie; thy lips run over Crocale.
〈◊〉 to the reſt.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Lord, What a man is this thought I,
To do this to a Maid!
• et then for my life I could not wake.
The youth, a little danted, with a trembling hand
Heav'd up the clothes.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Yet ſtill you ſlept?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Y'faith I did; and when, methoughts, he was warm by my ſide,
Thinking to catch him, I ſtretcht out both mine armes;
And when I felt him not, I ſhreekt out,
And wak'd for anger.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: 'Twas a pretty dream.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: I, if it had been a true one.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: But ſtay, What's here caſt o'th' ſhore?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: 'Tis a man;
Shall I ſhoot him?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: No, no, 'tis a handſome beaſt;
Would we had more o'th' breed; ſtand cloſe wenches,
And let's hear if he can ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Do I yet live?
Sure it is ayr I breathe; What place is this?
Sure ſomething more than humane keeps reſidence here,
For I have paſt the Stygian gulph,
And touch upon the bleſſed ſhore? 'tis ſo;
This is the Elizian ſhade; theſe happy ſpirits,
That here enjoy all pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: He makes towards us.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Stand, or I'll ſhoot.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Hold, he makes no reſiſtance.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Be not offended Goddeſſes, that I fall
Thus proſtrate at your feet: or if not ſuch,
〈◊〉 Nymphs of Dian's train, that range theſe groves,
Which you forbid to men; vouchſafe to know
• am a man, a wicked ſinful man; and yet not ſold
• o far to impudence, as to preſume
To preſs upon your privacies, or provoke
• our Heavenly angers; 'tis not for my ſelf
〈◊〉 beg thus poorly, for I am already wounded,
Wounded to death, and faint; my laſt breath
〈◊〉 for a Virgin, comes as near your ſelves
〈◊〉 all perfection, as what's mortal may
• eſemble things divine. O pitty her,
And let your charity free her from that deſart,
〈◊〉 Heavenly charity can reach to Hell,
• or ſure that place comes near it: and where ere
• y gho • t ſhall find abode,
• ernally I ſhall powre bleſſings on ye.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: By my life I cannot hurt him.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Though I loſe my head for it, nor I.
muſt pitty him, and will.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: But ſtay, Clarinda?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What new game have ye found here, ha!
What beaſt is this lies wallowing in his gore?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Keep off.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Wherefore, I pray? I ne'er turn'd
• rom a fell Lioneſs rob'd of her whelps,
• nd, Shall I fear dead carrion?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: O but.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But, What is't?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: It is infectious.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Has it not a name?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Yes, but ſuch a name from which
• s from the Devil your Mother commands us me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Is't a man?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: It is.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What a brave ſhape it has in death;
How excellent would it appear had it life!
Why ſhould it be infectious? I have heard
My Mother ſay, I had a Father
And was not he a Man?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Queſtionleſs Madam.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Your fathers too were Men?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Without doubt Lady.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And without ſuch it is impoſſible
We could have been.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: A ſin againſt nature to deny it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nor can you or I have any hope to be a Mother,
Without the help of Men.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Which of you then moſt barbarous, that knew
You from a man had Being, and owe to it
The name of parent, durſt preſume to kill
The likeneſs of that thing by which you are?
Whoſe Arrowes made theſe wounds? ſpeak, or by Dian
Without diſtinction I'll let ſly at ye all.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Not mine.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Nor mine.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange to ſee her mov'd thus.
Reſtrain your fury Madam; had we kill'd him,
We had but perform'd your Mothers command.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But it ſhe command unjuſt and cruel things,
We are not to obey it.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: We are innocent; ſome ſtorm did caſt
Him ſhipwrackt on the ſhore, as you ſee wounded:
Nor durſt we be Surgeons to ſuch
Your Mother doth appoint for death.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Weak excuſe; Where's pity?
Where's ſoft compaſſion? cruel, and ungrateful
Did providence offer to your charity
But one poor Subject to expreſs it on,
And in't to ſhew our wants too; and could you
So careleſly neglect it?

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: For ought I know, he's living yet;
And you may tempt your Mother, by giving him ſuccor.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ha, come near I charge ye.
So, bend his body ſoftly; rub his temples;
Nay, that ſhall be my office: how the red
Steales into his pale lips! run and fetch the ſimples
With which my Mother heal'd my arme
When laſt I was wounded by the Bore.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Doe: but remember her to come after ye,
That ſhe may behold her daughters charity.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Now he breathes; Exit Hippolita.
The ayr paſſing through the Arabian groves
Yields not ſo ſweet an odour: prethee taſte it;
Taſte it good Crocale; yet I envy thee ſo great a bleſſing;
'Tis not ſin to touch theſe Rubies, is it?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Not, I think.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Or thus to live Camelion like?
I could reſign my eſſence to live ever thus.
O welcome; raiſe him up Gently. Some ſoft hand
Bound up theſe wounds; a womans hair. What fury
For which my ignorance does not know a name,
Is crept into my boſome? But I forget
My pious work. Now if this juyce hath power,
Let it appear; his eyelids ope: Prodigious!
Two Suns break from theſe Orbes.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Ha, Where am I? What new viſion's this?
To what Goddeſs do I owe this ſecond life?
Sure thou art more than mortal:
And any Sacrifice of thanks or duty
In poor and wetched man to pay, comes ſhort
Of your immortal bounty: but to ſhew
I am not unthankful; this in humility
I kiſs the happy ground you have made ſacred,
By bearing of your weight.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: No Goddeſs, friend: but made
Of that ſame brittle mould as you are;
One too acquainted with calamities,
And from that apt to pity. Charity ever
Finds in the act reward, and needs no Trumpet
In the receiver. O forbear this duty;
I have a hand to meet with yours,
And lips to bid yours welcome.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: I ſee, that by inſtinct,
Though a young Maid hath never ſeen a Man,
Touches have titillations, and inform her.
But here's our Governeſs;
Now I expect a ſtorme.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Child of my fleſh,
And not of my fair unſpotted mind,
Un-hand this Monſter.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Monſter, Mother?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes; and every word he ſpeaks, a Syrens note,
To drown the careleſs hearer. Have I not taught thee
The falſhood and the perjuries of Men?
On whom, but for a woman to ſhew pity,
Is to be cruel to her ſelf; the Soveraignty
Proud and imperious men uſurp upon us,
We conferr on our ſelves, and love thoſe fetters
We faſten to our freedomes. Have we, Clarinda,
Since thy fathers wrack, ſought liberty,
To loſe it un-compel'd? Did fortune guide,
Or rather deſtiny, our Barke, to which
We could appoint no Port, to this bleſt place,
Inhabited heretofore by warlike women,
That kept men in ſubjection? Did we then,
By their example, after we had loſt
All we could love in man, here plant our ſelves,
With execrable oaths never to look
On man, but as a Monſter? and, Wilt thou
Be the firſt preſident to infringe thoſe vows
We made to Heaven?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Hear me; and hear me with juſtice.
And as ye are delighted in the name
Of Mother, hear a daughter that would be like you.
Should all Women uſe this obſtinate abſtinence,
You would force upon us; in a few years
The whole World would be peopled
Onely with Beaſts.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: We muſt, and will have Men.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: I, or wee'll ſhake off all obedience.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Are ye mad?
Can no perſwaſion alter ye? ſuppoſe
You had my ſuffrage to your ſute;
Can this Shipwrackt wretch ſupply them all?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Hear me great Lady?
I have fellowes in my miſery, not far hence,
Divided o • ly by this helliſh River,
There live a company of wretched Men,
Such as your charity may make your ſlaves;
Imagine all the miſeries mankind
May ſuffer under: and they groan beneath 'em.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But are they like to you?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Speak they your Language?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Are they able, luſty men?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: They were good, Ladies;
And in their May of youth of gentle blood,
And ſuch as may deſerve ye; now cold and hunger
Hath leſſen'd their perfection: but reſtor'd
To what they were, I doubt not they'll appear
Worthy your favors.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: This is a bleſſing
We durſt not hope for.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Dear Mother, be not obdurate.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Hear then my reſolution: and labor not
To add to what I'll grant, for 'twill be fruitleſs,
You ſhall appear as good Angels to theſe wretched Men;
In a ſmall Boat wee'll paſs o'er to 'em;
And bring 'em comfort: if you like their perſons,
And they approve of yours: for wee'll force nothing;
And ſince we want ceremonies,
Each one ſhall chooſe a husband, and injoy
His company a Month, but that expir'd,
You ſhall no more come near 'em; if you prove fruitful,
The Males ye ſhall return to them, the Females
We will reſerve our ſelves: this is the utmoſt,
Ye ſhall e'er obtain: as ye think fit;
Ye may diſmiſs this ſtranger,
And prepare to morrow for the journey. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Come, Sir, Will ye walk?
We will ſhew ye our pleaſant Bowers,
And ſomething ye ſhall find to cheer your heart.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Excellent Lady;
Though 'twill appear a wonder one near ſtarv'd
Should refuſe reſt and meat, I muſt not take
Your noble offer: I left in yonder deſart
A Virgin almoſt pin'd.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Shee's not your Wife?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: No Lady, but my Siſter ('tis now dangerous
To ſpeak truth) To her I deeply vow'd
Not to taſt food, or reſt, if fortune brought it me,
Till I bleſs'd her with my return: now if you pleaſe
To afford me an eaſie paſſage to her,
And ſome meat for her recovery,
I ſhall live your ſlave: and thankfully
She ſhall ever acknowledge her life at your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You plead ſo well, I can deny ye nothing;
I my ſelf will ſee you furniſht;
And with the next Sun viſit and relieve thee.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Ye are all goodneſs— Exit

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: OH! What a tempeſt have I in my ſtomach?
How my empty guts cry out? my wounds ake,
Would they would bleed again, that I might get
Something to quench my thirſt.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: O Lamure, the happineſs my dogs had
When I kept houſe at home! they had a ſtorehouſe,
A ſtorehouſe of moſt bleſſed bones and cruſts,
Happy cruſts: Oh! how ſharp hunger pinches me?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: O my importunate belly, I have nothing
To ſatisfie thee; I have ſought,
As far as my weak legs would carry me,
Yet can find nothing: neither meat nor water;
Nor any thing that's nouriſhing,
My bellies grown together like an empty ſachel.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How now, What news?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Haſt any meat yet?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Not a bit that I can ſee;
Here be goodly quarries, but they be cruel hard
To gnaw: I ha got ſome mud, we'll eat it with ſpoons,
Very good thick mud: but it ſtinks damnably;
There's old rotten trunks of Trees too,
But not a leafe nor bloſſome in all the Iſland.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How it looks?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: It ſtinks too.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: It may be poyſon.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Let it be any thing;
So I can get it down: Why Man,
Poyſon's a Princely diſh.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Haſt thou no Bisket?
No crumbs left in thy pocket: here's my dublet,
Give me but three ſmall crumbes.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Not for three Kingdoms,
If I were maſter of 'em: Oh Lamure,
But one poor joynt of Mutton: we ha ſcorn'd (Man)

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Thou ſpeak'ſt of Paradiſe
Or but the ſnuffes of thoſe healths,
We have lewdly at midnight flang away.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Ah! but to lick the Glaſſes.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Here comes the Surgeon: What
Haſt thou diſcover'd? ſmile, ſmile, and comfort us.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: I am expiring;
Smile they that can: I can find nothing Gentlemen,
Here's nothing can be meat, without a miracle.
Oh that I had my boxes, and my lints now,
My ſtupes, my tents, and thoſe ſweet helps of nature,
What dainty diſhes could I make of 'em.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Haſt ne'er an old ſuppoſitory?

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Oh would I had Sir.
Or, but the paper where ſuch a Cordial
Potion, or Pills hath been entomb'd.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Or the beſt bladder where a cooling-gliſter.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Haſt thou no ſearcloths left?
Nor any old pulteſſes?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: We care not to what it hath been miniſtred.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Sure I have none of theſe dainties Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Where's the great Wen
Thou cut'ſt from Hugh the ſaylers ſhoulder?
That would ſerve now for a moſt Princely banquet.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: I, if we had it Gentlemen.
I flung it over-board, ſlave that I was.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: A moſt unprovident villain.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: If I had any thing that were but ſupple now!
I could make Sallads of your ſhoos Gentlemen,
And rare ones: any thing unctions.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I, and then we might fry the ſoals i'th' Sun.
The ſoals would make a ſecond diſh.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Or, ſouce 'em in the ſalt-water,
An inner ſoal well ſouc'd.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Here comes the Woman;
It may be ſhe has meat, and may relieve us,
Let's withdraw, and mark, and then be ready,
She'll hide her ſtore elſe, and ſo cozen us.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: How weary, and how hungry am I,
How feeble, and how faint is all my body?
Mine eyes like ſpent Lamps glowing out, grow heavy,
My ſight forſaking me, and all my ſpirits,
As if they heard my paſſing bell go for me,
Pull in their powers, and give me up to deſtiny,
Oh! for a little water: a little, little meat,
A little to relieve me ere I periſh:
I had whole floods of tears awhile that nouriſht me,
But they are all conſum'd for thee dear Albert;
For thee they are ſpent, for thou art dead;
Mercileſs fate has ſwallow'd thee.
Oh — I grow heavy: ſleep is a ſalve for miſery;
Heaven look on me, and either take my life,
Or make me once more happy.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Shee's faſt aſleep already,
Why ſhould ſhe have this bleſſing, and we wake ſtill,
Wake to our wants?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: This thing hath been our overthrow,
And all theſe biting miſchiefs that fall on us
Are come through her means.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: True, we were bound ye all know,
For happy places, and moſt fertile Iſlands,
Where we had conſtant promiſes of all things,
She turn'd the Captains mind,
And muſt have him go in ſearch, I know not of who,
Nor to what end: of ſuch a fool her brother,
And ſuch a coxcomb her kinſman, and we muſt put in every where,
She has put us in now yſaith.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Why ſhould we conſume thus, and ſtarve,
Have nothing to relieve us;
And ſhe live there that bred all our miſeries.
Unroſted, or unſod?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I have read in ſtories.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Of ſuch reſtoring meates,
We have examples;
Thouſand examples, and allow'd for excellent;
Women that have eate their Children,
Men their ſlaves, nay their brothers: but theſe are nothing;
Husbands devoured their Wives:
(thye are their Chattels,)
And of a Schoolma • ter, that i • a time of famine,
Powdered up all his Scholars.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Shee's young and tydie,
In my conſcience ſhe'll eat delicately;
• uſt like young Pork a little lean,
Your opinion Surgeon.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: I think ſhe may be made good meat,
But look we ſhall want Salt.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Tuſh, ſhe needs no powdering,

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: I grant ye;
But to ſuck out the humorous parts: by all means,
Lets kill her in a chaſe, ſhe'll eat the ſweeter.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Let's kill her any way: and kill her quickly,
That we might be at our meat.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: How if the Captain?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Ta • k not of him, he's dead, and the reſt famiſh'd.
Wake her Surgeon, and cut her throat,
And then divide her, every Man his ſhare.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: She wakes her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Holy and good things keep me!
What cruel dreams have I had! Who are theſe?
O they are my friends; for heavens ſake Gentlemen
A little to relieve me: I may bleſs ye;
For weak and wretched, ready to periſh,
Even now I die.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: You'll ſave a labor then,
You bred theſe miſeries, and you ſhall pay for't;
We have no meat, nor where to have we know not,
Nor how to pull our ſelves from theſe afflictions,
We are ſtarv'd too, famiſht, all our hopes deluded,
Yet ere we die thus, wee'll have one dainty meal.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Shall I be with ye Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Yes mary ſhall ye: in our bellies Lady.
We love you well—

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: What ſaid you Sir?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Mary wee'll eat your Ladiſhip.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: You that have buried us in this baſe Iſland,
Wee'll bury ye in a more noble Monument.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Will ye ſay your prayers, that I may perform Lady?
We are wondrous ſharp ſet; come Gentlemen,
Who are for the hinder parts?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: I.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: And I.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Be patient;
They will not fall to every Man's ſhare.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: O hear me;
Hear me ye barbarous men.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Be ſhort and pithy,
Our ſtomachs cannot ſtay a long diſcourſe.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: And be not fearful,
For I'll kill ye daintily.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Are ye not Chriſtians?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Why, do not Chriſtians eat Women?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Eat one another? 'tis moſt impious.

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: Come, come.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Oh, help, help, help.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: The Ladies voice! ſtand off ſlaves,
What do you intend villains?
I have ſtrength enough left me, if you abuſe this ſoul,
To—

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: They would have raviſht her upon my life,
Speak, how was it Lady?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Forgive 'em, 'twas their hungers.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Ha, their hungers!

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: They would have eaten her.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: O dam'd villains; ſpeak, Is it true?

sp.speaker: Sur.
sp.l: I confeſs an appetite.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: An appetite, I'll fit ye for an appetite.
Are ye ſo ſharp ſet, that her fleſh muſt ſerve you?
Murther's a main good ſervice with your Worſhips;
Since ye would be ſuch Devils,
Why did you not begin with one another handſomly,
And ſpare the Woman to beget more food on?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Good Sir.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: You ſhall grow mummy raſcals;
I'll make you fall to your brawns, and your buttocks,
And worry one another like keen bandogs.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Good Sir be merciful.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: You ſhall know what 'tis to be damn'd Canibals.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: O my beſt friend!

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Alas poor heart! here,
Here's ſome meat and ſovereign drink to eaſe you,
Sit down gentle Sweet.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I am bleſt to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Stir not within forty ſoot of this food,
If you do dogs!
Oh, Captain, Captain, Captain.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have meat all of you.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Captain, hear me firſt: hark,
'Tis ſo inhumane! I would not ha the air corrupted with it.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: O barbarous men! ſit down Dupont,
Good Maſter, and honeſt Saylors.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: But ſtand you off,
And waite upon our charity; I'll wait on you elſe;
And touch nothing but what's flung ye; as if you were dogs;
If you do, I'll cut your fingers; friends,
I'll ſpoil your carving.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: There wretches, there.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Eat your meat handſomely now,
• nd give Heaven thanks.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: There's more bread.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: See, they ſnarle like dogs;
Eat quietly you Raſcals, eat quietly.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: There is drink too.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Come, come, I'll fill you each your cups,
Ye ſhall not ſurfet.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: And what have you diſcover'd?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Sweet, a paradiſe,
A paradiſe inhabited with Angels,
Such as you are: their pitties make in Angels,
They gave me theſe viands, and ſupply'd me
With theſe pretious drinks.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Shall not we ſee 'em?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Yes, they will ſee you
Out of their charities, having heard our ſtory,
They will come, and comfort us, come preſently;
We ſhall no more know wants nor miſeries.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Are they all women?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: All, and all in love with us.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: How!

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Do not miſtake: in love with our misfortunes,
They will cheriſh and relieve our men.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Do you ſhrug now,
And pull up your noſes? you ſmell comfort,
See they ſtretch out their Legs like Dottrels,
Each like a new Saint Dennis.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Dear Miſtris,
When you would name me, and the women hear,
Call me your brother, you I'll call my ſiſter,
And pray obſerve this all—
Why do you change color ſweet.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Eating too much meat.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Sawc't with jealouſie;
Fie, fie, dear ſaint, yfaith ye are too blame,
Are ye not here? here ſixt in my heart?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Hark, hark;

div.stage: Enter Roſella, Clarinda, Crocale, Hipollitta, Juletta.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: They are come, ſtand ready, and look nobly,
And with all humble reverence receive 'em,
Our lives depend upon their gentle pitties,
And death waits on their anger.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Sure they are Fairies.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Be they Devils: Devils of fleſh and blood;
After ſo long a Lent, and tedious voyage,
To me they are Angels.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: O for ſome Eringoes!

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Potatoes, or Cantharides.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Peace you Rogues, that buy abilities of your 'pothecaries,
Had I but took the diet of green Cheeſe,
And Onions for a month, I could do wonders.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Are theſe the Jewels you run mad for?
What can you ſee in one of theſe,
To whom you would vouchſafe a gentle touch?
Can nothing perſwade you
To love your ſelves, and place your happineſs
In cold and chaſt embraces of each other.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: This is from the purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: We had your grant to have them as they were.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: 'Tis a beauteous Creature,
And to my ſelf, I do appear deform'd,
When I conſider her, and yet ſhe is
The ſtrangers ſiſter; Why then ſhould I fear?
She cannot prove my rival.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: When you repent,
That you refus'd my counſel, may it add
To your afflictions, that you were forward,
Yet leap'd into the Gulfe of your misfortunes,
But have your wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Now ſhe makes to us.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I am in •• ructed, but take heed Albert,
You prove not falſe;

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Ye are your own aſſurance,
And ſo acquainted with your own perfections,
That weak doubts cannot reach you; therefore fear not.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: That you are poor and miſerable men,
My eyes inform me: that without our ſuccors,
Hope cannot flatter you to dream of ſafety;
The preſent plight you are in, can reſolve you
That to be merciful, is to draw near
The Heavenly eſſence: whether you will be
Thankful, I do not queſtion; nor demand
What country bred you, what names, what maners;
To us it is ſufficient we relieve
Such as have ſhapes of men: and I command you,
As we are not ambitious to know
Farther of you, that on pain of death
You preſume not to enquire what we are,
Or whence deriv'd.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: In all things we obey you,
And thankfully we ever ſhall confeſs
Our ſelves your creatures.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: You ſpeak as becomes you;
Firſt then, and willingly, deliver up
Thoſe weapons we could force from you.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: We lay 'em down
Moſt gladly at your feet.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I have had many a combat with a tall wench;
But never was diſarm'd before.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: And now hear comfort,
Your wants ſhall be ſupply'd, and though it be
A debt women may challenge to be ſued to,
Eſpecially from ſuch they may command;
We give up to you that power, and therefore
Freely each make his choice.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Then here I fix.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Nay, ſhe is mine: I eyed her firſt.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: This mine.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Stay good raſcals;
You are too forward, ſir Gallant,
You are not giving order to a Taylor
For the faſhion of a new ſuit;
Nor are you in your warehouſe, maſter Merchant,
Stand back, and give your betters leave: your betters;
And grumble not: if ye do, as I love meat
I will ſo ſwinge the ſalt itch out on you.
Captain, Maſter, and the reſt of us,
That are brothers, and good fellows: we have been
Too late by the ears: and yet ſmart for our follies;
To end therefore all future emulation: if you pleaſe,
To truſt to my election, you ſhall ſay,
I am not partial to my ſelf; I doubt not
Give content to all.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Agreed, agreed.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Then but obſerve, how learned and diſcreetly,
I will proceed, and as a skilful Doctor
In all the quirks belonging to the game;
Read over your complexions: for you Captain
Being firſt in place, and therefore firſt to be ſerv'd,
I give my judgment thus, for your aſpect,
Y'are much inclin'd to melancholy: and that tells me,
The fullen Saturne had predominance
At your nativity, a malignant Planet,
And if not qualified by a ſweet conjunction
Of a ſoft and ruddy wench, born under Venus,
It may prove fatal: therefore to your armes,
I give this roſe-cheekt Virgin.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: To my wiſh;
Till now I never was happy.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Nor I accurs'd.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Maſter, you are old;
Yet love the game, that I perceive too,
And if not well ſpurr'd up, you may prove ruſty;
Therefore to help ye here's a Bradamanta,
Or I am coſen'd in my calculation.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: A poor old man alloted to my ſhare.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: Thou wouldſt have two;
Nay, I think twenty: but fear not wench,
Though he be old he's tough: look on's making,
Hee'll not fail I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: A merry fellow,
And were not man a creature I deteſt,
I could indure his company.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: Here's a fair heard of Does before me,
And now for a barren one:
For, though I like the ſport: I do not love
To Father children: like the Grand Signior,
Thus I walk in my Seraglio,
And view 'em as I paſs: then draw I forth
My handkercher, and having made my choice,
I thus beſtow it.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: On me.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: On you: now my choice is made;
To it you hungry Raſcals.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: As I love goodneſs,
It makes me ſmile i'th' height of all my fears.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What a ſtrong contention you may behold
Between my Mothers mirth and anger.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Nay, no coyneſs: be Miſtriſs of your word,
I muſt, and will enjoy you.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Be advis'd fool: alas I am old;
How canſt thou hope content from one that's fifty.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: Never talk on't;
I have known good ones at threeſcore and upwards;
Beſides the weathers hot: and men
That have experience, fear Fevers:
A temperate diet is the onely Phyſick,
Your Julips, nor Guajacum prunello's,
Camphire pills, nor Goord-water,
Come not near your old Woman;
Youthful ſtomachs are ſtill craving,
Though there be nothing left to ſtop their mouths with;
And believe me I am no frequent giver of thoſe bounties:
Laugh on: laugh on: good Gentlemen do,
I ſhall make holiday and ſleep, when you
Dig in the mines till your hearts ake.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: A mad fellow;

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Well, Sir, I'll give you hearing: and as I like
Your wooing, and diſcourſe: but I muſt tell ye Sir,
That rich Widows look for great ſums in preſent,
Or aſſurances of ample Joynters.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: That to me is eaſie,
For inſtantly I'll do it, hear me comrades.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: What ſay'ſt thou Tibalt?

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Why, that to woo a Wench with empty hands
Is no good Heraldry, therefore let's to the gold,
And ſhare it equally: 'twill ſpeak for us
More than a thouſand complements or cringes,
Ditties ſtolen from Petrarch, or Diſcourſe from Ovid,
Beſides, 'twill beget us reſpect,
And if ever fortune friend us with a Barque,
Largely ſupply us with all proviſion.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Well advis'd, defer it not.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: Are ye all contented.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We are?

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: Lets away then,
Strait wee'll return, Exit.
And you ſhall ſee our riches.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Since I knew what wonder and amazement was,
I nee'r was ſo tranſported.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Why weep ye gentle Maid?
There is no danger here to ſuch as you;
Baniſh fear: for with us I dare promiſe,
You ſhall meet all courteous entertainment.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: We eſteem our ſelves moſt happy in you.
And bleſs fortune that brought you hither.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Hark in your ear;
I love you as a friend already,
Ere long you ſhall call me by a nearer name,
I wiſh your brother well: I know you apprehend me.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I, to my grief I do;
Alas good Ladies, there is nothing left me,
But thanks, to pay ye with.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: That's more,
Than yet you ſtand ingag'd for.

div.stage: Enter Albert, Tibalt, and the reſt with treaſure.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: So ſoon return'd!

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Here: ſee the Idol of the Lapidary.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: Theſe Pearls, for which the ſlaviſh Negro
Dives to the bottom of the Sea.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: To get which the induſtrious Merchant
Touches at either pole.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: The never-fayling purchaſe
Of Lordſhips, and of honors.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: The Worlds Miſtriſs,
That can give every thing to the poſſeſſors.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: For which the Saylors ſcorn tempeſtuous Winds,
And ſpit defiance in the Sea.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: Speak Lady: Look we not lovely now?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yes, yes, O my Stars,
Be now for ever bleſt, that have brought
To my revenge theſe Robbers; take your arrowes,
And nayl theſe Monſters to the earth.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: What mean ye Lady?
• n what have we offended?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: O my daughter!
And you companions with me in all fortunes,
Look on theſe Caskets, and theſe Jewels,
Theſe were our own, when firſt we put to Sea
With good Sebaſtian: and theſe the Pyrats
That not alone depriv'd him of this treaſure,
But alſo took his life.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Part of my preſent
I will remember was mine own.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: And theſe were mine.

sp.speaker: Ju.
sp.l: Sure, I have worn this Jewel.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Wherefore do ye ſtay then,
And not perform my command?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: O Heaven!
What cruel fate purſues us.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: I am well enough ſerv'd,
That muſt be off'ring Joyntures, Jewels,
And precious ſtones, more than I brought with me.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Why ſhoot ye not?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Hear me dear Mother;
A •• when the greateſt cruelty, is Juſtice,
Do not ſhew mercy: death to theſe ſtarv'd wretches
Is a reward, not puniſhment: let 'em live
To undergoe the full weight of your diſpleaſure.
And that they may have ſence to feel the torments
They have deſerv'd: allow 'em ſome ſmall pittance,
To linger out their tortures.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: 'Tis well counſell'd.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: And wee'll follow it;

sp.speaker: Alb
sp.l: Hear us ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Peace dogs.
Bind 'em faſt: when fury hath given way to reaſon,
I will determine of their ſufferings,
Which ſhall be horrid. Vengeance, though ſlow pac'd,
At length o'rtakes the guilty; and the wrath
Of the incenſed powers, will fall moſt ſure
On wicked men, when they are moſt ſecure. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: 1. Sayl.
sp.l: HEre's nothing, Sir, but poverty and hunger;
No promiſe of inhabitance; neither track of Beaſt,
Nor foot of Man: we have ſearcht
All this Rocky deſart, yet cannot diſcover any aſſurance
Here is, or hath been ſuch men.

sp.speaker: 2. Sayl.
sp.l: Not a relique of any thing they wore;
Nor mark left by 'em, either to find relief,
Or to warn others from the like misfortune.
Believe it, theſe fellows are both falſe,
And, to get a little ſuccor in their miſery,
Have fram'd this cunning Tale.

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: The Ship, I know, is French, and own'd by Pirats,
If not by Albert my arch enemy.
You told me too there was a woman with 'em.
A young and handſome Woman.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: There was ſo Sir.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: And ſuch, and ſuch young gallants.

sp.speaker: Nic.
sp.l: We told you true, Sir,
That they had no means to quit this Iſland.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: And that amidſt their mutiny to ſave your lives,
You got their Ship.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: All is moſt certain, Sir.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: Where are they then? Where are theſe Men
Or Woman? we are landed where your faiths
Did aſſure us, we could not miſs their fights.
For this news we took ye to our mercy,
Reliev'd ye, when the furious Sea, and Famine
Strove, which ſhould firſt devour ye;
Cloath'd, and cheriſht ye; us'd ye as thoſe ye ſay ye are.
Fair Gentlemen, now keep your words,
Theſe men ye left in miſery; the Woman.
Men of thoſe noble breedings you pretend to
Should ſcorn to lie, or get their food with falſhood;
Come, direct us.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Alaſs, Sir, they are gone,
But by what means, or providence, we know not.

sp.speaker: 2. Sayl.
sp.l: Was not the Captain
A fellow of a fiery, yet brave nature,
A middle ſtature, and of brown complexion?

sp.speaker: Nic.
sp.l: He was, Sir.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: 'Twas Albert,
And my poor wretched ſiſter.

sp.speaker: 1. Sayl.
sp.l: 'Twas he certain,
I ha been at Sea with him; many times at Sea.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: Come, ſhew us theſe Men;
Shew us preſently, and do not dally with us.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: We left 'em here; What ſhould we ſay, Sir?
Here, in this place.

sp.speaker: 2. Sayl.
sp.l: The earth cannot ſwallow 'em;
They have no wings, they cannot fly ſure.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: You told us too
Of heaps of treaſure, and of ſums conceal'd,
That ſet their heart a fire; we ſee no ſuch thing,
No ſuch ſign; What can ye ſay to purge ye?
What have ye done with theſe men?

sp.speaker: Nic.
sp.l: We, Sir?

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: You Sir;
For certain I believe ye ſaw ſuch people.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: By all that's good,
By all that's pure and honeſt,
By all that's holy.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: I dare not credit ye,
Ye have ſo abus'd my hope, that now I hate ye.

sp.speaker: 1. Sayl.
sp.l: Let's put 'em in their ragged clothes again Captain,
For certain they are knaves, lets e'en deliver 'em
To their old fruitful Farm; here let 'em walk the Iſland.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: If ye do ſo, we ſhall curſe your mercies.

sp.speaker: Nic.
sp.l: Rather put us to Sea again.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: Not ſo.
Yet this I'll do, becauſe ye ſay ye are Chriſtians,
Though I hardly credit it: bring in the boat,
And all aboard again, but theſe two wretches;
Yet leave 'em four dayes meat. If in that time,
(For I will ſearch all nookes of this ſtrange Iſland)
I can diſcover any tract of theſe men,
Alive or dead, I'll bear ye off, and honor ye;
If not, ye have found your Graves; ſo farewell. Exit.

sp.speaker: Nic.
sp.l: That goodneſs dwells above, and knows us innocent,
Comfort our lives, and at his pleaſure quit us.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Come Couſin, come; old time will end our ſtory:
But no time (if we end well) ends our glory. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Roſella, Clarinda, Crocale, Hippolita, Juletta.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Uſe 'em with all the auſterity that may be,
They are our ſlaves; turn all thoſe pitties,
Thoſe tender reluctations that ſhould become your ſex,
To ſtern anger; and when ye look upon 'em,
Look with thoſe eyes that wept thoſe bitter ſorrows,
Thoſe cruelties ye ſuffer'd by their Rapines.
Some five dayes hence that bleſſed hour comes
Moſt happy to me, that knit this hand to my dear husbands,
And both our hearts in mutual bands.
That hour Ladies.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What of that hour?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Why, on that hour daughter,
And in the height of all our celebrations,
Our dear remembrances of that dear Man,
And thoſe that ſuffer'd with him, our fair kinſmen,
Their lives ſhall fall a ſacrifice to vengeance,
Their lives that ruin'd his; 'tis a full juſtice.
I will look glorious in their bloods;
And the moſt Noble ſpirit of Sebaſtian,
That periſht by the pride of theſe French Pirates,
Sha • l ſmile in Heaven, and bleſs the hand that kill'd 'em.
Look ſtrictly all unto your priſoners;
For he that makes a ſcape beyond my vengeance,
Or entertains a hope by your fair uſage;
Take heed, I ſay, ſhe that deceives my truſt,
Again take heed: her life, and that's but light neither;
Her life in all the tortures my ſpirit can put on.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We ſhall be careful.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Do ſo. Ex. Roſſella.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You are angry Mother, and ye are old too,
Forgetting what men are: but we ſhall temper ye.
How fare your priſoners, Ladies? in what formes
Do they appear in their afflictions?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Mine fare but poorly;
For ſo I am commanded: 'tis none of their fault.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Of what ſort are they?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: They ſay they are Gentlemen.
But they ſhew Mungrels.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: How do they ſuffer?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Faith like boyes;
They are fearful in all fortunes; when I ſmile
They kneel, and beg to have that face continued;
And like poor ſlaves, adore the ground I go on.
When I frown, they hang their moſt dejected heads,
Like fearful ſheephounds; ſhew 'em a cruſt of bread
They'll Saint me preſently, and skip like Apes
For a ſup of Wine. I'll whip 'em like hackneys,
Saddle 'em, ride 'em, do what I will with 'em.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Tuſh, theſe are poor things.
Have they names like Chriſtians?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Very fair names: Franvile, Lamure, and Morillat;
And brag of great kindreds too. They offer very handſomely,
But that I am a fool, and dare not venture.
They are ſound too o'my conſcience,
Or very near upon't.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Fy, away fool.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: They tell me,
If they might be brought before you,
They would reveale things of ſtrange conſequence.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Their baſe poor fears.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: I, that makes me hate 'em too;
For if they were but manly to their ſufferance,
• ure I ſhould ſtrain a point or two.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: An hour hence I'll take a view of e'm,
And hear their buſineſs. Are your Men thus too?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Mine? No, gentle Madam, mine were not caſt
• n ſuch baſe molds; afflictions, tortures,
Are names and natures of delight, to my men;
All ſorts of cruelties they meet like pleaſures.
• have but two; the one they call Du-pont,
• ibalt Du-pont; the other the Ship-maſter.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Have they not lives, and fears?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Lives they have Madam;
• ut thoſe lives never linkt to ſuch companions
• s fears or doubts.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Uſe 'em Nobly;
And where you find fit ſubjects for your pitties
• et it become ye to be courteous;
My Mother will not alwayes be thus rigorous.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Mine are Saylors Madam,
• ut they ſleep ſoundly, and ſeldom trouble me, unleſs it be when
They dream ſometimes of ſights and tempeſts;
Then they rore and whiſtle for Cans of Wine,
• nd down they ſling me; and in that rage,
(For they are violent fellows) they play ſuch reaks.
If they have meat, they thank me;
If none, they heartily deſire to be hang'd quickly.
And this is all they care.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Look to 'em diligently, and where your pitties tells ye
They may deſerve, give comfort.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: We will. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Come hither, be not frighted;
Think not ye ſteal this liberty, for we give it,
Your tender innocence aſſures me, Virgin,
Ye had no ſhare in thoſe wrongs theſe men did us;
I find ye are not hardned in ſuch miſchiefs.
Your brother was miſ-led ſure,
Foully miſ-led.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: How much I fear theſe pities!

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Certain he was, ſo much I pity him;
And for your ſake, whoſe eyes plead for him;
Nay, for his own ſake.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Ha!

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: For I ſee about him
Women have ſubtill eyes, and look narrowly;
Or I am much abus'd: many fair promiſes;
Nay beyond thoſe, two many ſhadowed virtues.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I think he is good.

sp.speaker: Cla
sp.l: I aſſure my ſelf he will be;
And out of that aſſurance take this comfort,
For I perceive your fear hath much dejected ye.
I love your brother.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay, do not take it for a dreamt of favor,
That comforts in the ſleep, and awake vaniſhes;
Indeed I love him.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Do ye indeed?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You doubt ſtill, becauſe ye fear his ſafety;
Indeed he is the ſweeteſt man I ere ſaw;
I think the beſt. Ye may hear without bluſhes,
And give me thanks, if ye pleaſe, for my curteſie.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Madam, I ever muſt;
Yet witneſs Heaven, they are hard pull'd from me.
Believe me, Madam, ſo many imperfections I could find,
(Forgive me Grace for lying) and ſuch wants,
('Tis to an honeſt uſe) ſuch poverties,
Both in his main proportion, and his mind too;
There are a hundred handſomer; (I lie l • udly)
Your noble uſage, Madam, hath ſo bound me to ye,
That I muſt tell ye.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Come, tell your worſt.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: He is no husband for ye.
I think ye mean in that fair way.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ye have hit it.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I am ſure ye have hit my heart.
You will find him dangerous, Madam;
As ſickle as the flying ayr, proud, jealous,
Soon glutted in your ſweets, and ſoon forgetful;
I could ſay more, and tell ye I have a brother,
Another brother, that ſo far excells this,
Both in the ornaments of Man, and making.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If you were not his ſiſter, I ſhould doubt ye mainly,
Doubt ye for his love, ye deal ſo cunningly.
Do not abuſe me, I have truſted ye with more than life,
With my firſt love; be careful of me.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: In what uſe, Madam?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: In this Lady,
Speak to him for me, you have power upon him;
Tell him I love him, tell him I dote on him:
It will become your tongue.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Become my grave.
O fortune, O curſed fortune!

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Tell him his liberty,
And all thoſe with him; all our wealth and Jewels.
Good ſiſter, for I'll call ye ſo.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I ſhall Lady,
Even die, I hope.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Here's Meat and Wine, pray take it,
And there he lies; give him what liberty you pleaſe;
But ſtill conceal'd. What pleaſure you ſhall pleaſe, Siſter.
He ſhall ne'er want again. Nay, ſee an you'l take it;
Why do you ſtudy thus?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: To avoid miſchiefs, if they ſhould happen.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Goe, and be happy for me.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: O blind fortune;
Yet happy thus far, I ſhall live to ſee him,
In what ſtrange deſolation lives he here now?
Sure this Curtai • , will reveale.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Who's that? ha!
Some gentle hand, I hope, to bring me comfort.
Or if it be my death, 'tis ſweetly ſhadowed.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Have ye forgot me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: My Aminta?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: She Sir,
That walks here up and down an empty ſhadow,
One, that for ſome few hours
But wanders here, carrying her own ſad Coffin,
Seeking ſome Deſart place to lodge her griefs in.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Sweet ſorrow welcome, welcome noble grief;
How got you this fair liberty to ſee me?
For ſorrows in your ſhape are ſtrangers to me.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I come to counſel ye.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Ye are ſtill more welcome;
For good friends in afflictions give good Councels.
Pray then proceed.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Pray eat firſt, ye ſhew faint;
Here's Wine to refreſh ye too.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: I thank ye dear.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Drink again.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Here's to our loves.
How, turn and weep!
Pray pledge it: this happineſs we have yet left,
Our hearts are free. Not pledge it? Why?
And though beneath the Axe this health were holy,
Why do ye weep thus?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I come to woo ye.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: To woo me Sweet? I am woo'd and won already,
You know I am yours. This pretty way becomes ye.
But you would deceive my ſorrows; that's your intent.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I would I could, I ſhould not weep, but ſmile.
Do ye like your Meat and Wine?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Like it?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Do you like your liberty?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: All theſe I well may like.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Then pray like her that ſent 'em.
Do ye like wealth, and moſt unequal'd beauty?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Peace, indeed you'l make me angry.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Would I were dead that ask it,
Then ye might freely like, and I forgive ye.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: What like, and who? add not more miſery
To a man that's fruitful in afflictions.
Who is't you would have me like?
Who ſent theſe comforts?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I muſt tell.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Be bold.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: But be you temperate.
If you be bold I die. The young fair Virgin;
(Sorrow hath made me old.) O hearken,
And wiſely hark, the Governeſs daughter:
That Star that ſtrikes this Iſland full of wonder,
That blooming ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: What of her?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: She ſent it: and with it,
It muſt be out, ſhe dotes on ye,
And muſt enjoy ye: elſe no joy muſt find ye.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: And have you the patience to deliver this?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: A ſiſter may ſay much, and modeſtly.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: A ſiſter?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Yes, that name undid ye;
Undid us both: had ye nam'd Wife, ſhe had fear'd ye;
And fear'd the ſin ſhe follow'd; She had ſhun'd, yea
Her Virgin modeſty had not touch'd at ye.
But thinking you were free, hath kindled a fire,
I fear will hardly be extinguiſht.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Indeed I played the • ool.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: O my beſt Sir, take heed,
Take heed of lies. Truth, though it trouble ſome minds,
Some wicked minds, that are both dark and dangerous:
Yet it preſerves it ſelf, comes off pure, innocent,
And like the Sun, though never ſo eclips'd,
Muſt break in glory. O Sir, lie no more.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Ye have read me a fair Lecture,
And put a ſpell upon my tongue for fayning.
But how will you counſel now?

sp.speaker: Amin
sp.l: Ye muſt ſtudy to forget me.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Be patient.
Be wiſe and patient, it concens ye highly.
Can ye lay by our loves? But why ſhould I doubt it?
Ye are a man, and man may ſhift affections,
'Tis held no ſin. To come to the point,
Ye muſt loſe me; many and mighty reaſons.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Hear me Aminta,
Have you a man that loves you too, that feeds ye,
That ſends ye liberty? Has this great Governeſs
A noble ſon too, young, and apt to catch ye?
Am I, becauſe I am in bonds, and miſerable,
My health decay'd, my youth and ſtrength half blaſted,
My fortune like my waining ſelf, for this deſpis'd?
Am I for this forſaken? a new love choſen,
And my affections, like my fortunes, wanderers?
Take heed of lying, you that chid me for it;
And ſhew'd how deep a ſin it was, and dangerous.
Take heed, your ſelf, you ſwore you lov'd me dearly;
No few, nor little oathes you ſwore Aminta,
Thoſe ſeal'd with no ſmall faith, I then aſſur'd my ſelf.
O ſeek no new wayes to cozen truth,

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: I do not.
By love it ſelf I love thee,
And ever muſt, nor can all deaths diſſolve it.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Why do you urge me thus then?

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: For your ſafety,
To preſerve your life.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: My life, I do confeſs, is hers,
She gives it,
And let her take it back, I yield it.
My loves intirely thine, none ſhall touch at it;
None, my Aminta, none.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Ye have made me happy,
And now I know ye are mine. Fortune, I ſcorn thee.
Goe to your reſt, and I'll ſit by ye;
Whilſt I have time I'll be your mate, and comfort ye,
For only I am truſted: you ſhall want nothing,
Not a liberty that I can ſteal ye.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: May we not celebrate our loves Aminta?
And where our wiſhes cannot meet.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: You are wanton,
But with cold kiſſes I'll allay that fever;
Look for no more, and that in private too.
Believe me, I ſhall bluſh elſe.
But, let's conſider, we are both loſt elſe.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Let's in, and prevent fate. Exeun •

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: You do well to ayr us, Ladies, we ſhall be m • ſty elſe
What are your wiſe wills now?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: You are very crank ſtill.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: As crank as a holy Fryer, fed with hail-ſtones.
But do ye bring us out to bait, like Bulls?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Or are you weary of the charge ye are at?
Turn us abroad again, let's jog Ladies;
We are groſs, and courſe, unſit for your ſweet pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Knock off our ſhooes, and turn's to graſs.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: You are determined
Still to be ſtubborn then: it well becomes ye.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: An humour Lady that contents a priſoner.
A ſullen ſit ſometimes ſerves for a ſecond courſe.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Ye may as well be kind,
And gain our favours; gain meat and drink,
And lodging to reſt your bones.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: My bones have bore me thus long,
And had their ſhare of pains and recreations;
If they fail now, they are no fair companions.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Are ye thus harſh to all our Sex?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We cannot be merry without a Fidler,
Pray ſtrike up your Tabors, Ladies.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: The fools deſpiſe us.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: We know ye are very hungry now.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Yes 'tis very wholſom, Ladies;
For we that have groſs bodies, muſt be careful
Have ye no piercing air to ſtir our ſtomachs?
We are beholding to ye for our Ordinary.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Why ſlaves, 'tis in our power to hang ye.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Very likely.
'Tis in our powers then to be hang'd, and ſcorn ye.
Hanging's as ſweet to us, as dreaming to you.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Come, be more courteous.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Do, and then ye ſhall be pleas'd, and have all neceſſaries.

sp.speaker: Tib..
sp.l: Give me ſome Ratsbane then.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: And why Ratsbane, Mounſieur?

sp.speaker: Tib
sp.l: We live like vermine here, and eat up your cheeſe,
Your mouldy cheeſe, that none but Rats would bite at;
Therefore 'tis juſt that Ratsbane ſhould reward us.
We are unprofitable, and our Ploughs are broken;
There is no hope of Harveſt this year, Ladies.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Ye ſhall have all content
I, and we'll ſerve your uſes.
I had rather ſerve hogs, there's more delight in't;
Your greedy appetites are never ſatisfied;
Juſt like hungry Camels, ſleeping or waking
You chew the cud ſtill.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: By this hand we'll ſtarve ye.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: 'Tis a noble courteſie.
I had as lief ye ſhould famiſh me, as founder me:
To be jaded to death, is only fit for a hackney.
Here be certain Tarts of Tarr about me,
And parcels of potargo in my Jerkin,
As long as theſe laſt.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Which will not laſt ever.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Then we'll eat one another like good fellows.
A ſhoulder of his for a haunch of mine.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: 'Tis excellent.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: 'Twill be as we'll dreſs it Ladies.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Why ſure ye are not men?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Ye had beſt come ſearch us,
A Seaman is ſeldom without a ſalt Eele.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I am bad enough,
And in my nature a notorious wencher;
And yet ye make me bluſh at your immodeſty.
Tell me good Maſter, didſt ever ſee ſuch things?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: I could like 'em, though they were lewdly given,
If they could ſay no;

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Well, ye may hang, or ſtarve us;
But your commanding impudence ſhall never fear us.
Had ye by bluſhing ſigns, ſoft cunings, crept into us,
And ſhew'd us your neceſſities: we had met your purpoſes,
Supply'd your wants. We are no Saints Ladies;
I love a good wench, as I love my life,
And with my life I will maintain my love:
But ſuch a ſordid impudence I'll ſpit at.
Let's to our dens again. Come noble Maſter.
You know our minds Lad • es:
This is the faith in which we'll die. Exit Tib. and Maſt.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: I do admire 'em

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: They are noble f •• lows,
And they ſhall not want, • o • this.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: But ſee, Clarinda comes.
Farewel, I'll to my charge.
〈◊〉 out thoſe priſoners now,
And 〈…〉 , a • d hear their buſineſs.
〈◊〉 Madam. Exit.
〈…〉 hath prevail'd upon her brother.

〈…〉
• ongue, and can deſcribe the happineſs
〈…〉 ready to fling on him.

〈◊〉 ſu • e he m •
〈◊〉 glad for certain, wonder,
• nd bl • ſs the hou • that brought him to this Iſland.
• long to hear t • e •• ll joy that he labours with.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Bleſs thy Divine Beauty.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Mirror of ſweetneſs.

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Ever-ſpringing brightneſs.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Nay, S • and up Gentlemen, and leave your flatteries.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: She calls us Gentl • men, ſure we ſhall have ſome meat now.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I am a mortal creature,
Worſhip Heaven, and give theſe at • ributes
To their Divinities. Methinks ye • ook but thin.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Oh we are ſtarv'd, immortal beauty.

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: We are all poor ſtarv'd knaves.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Neither liberty nor meat, Lady

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: We were handſome men, and Gentlemen, and ſweet men,
And were once gracious in the eyes of beauties,
But now we look like Rogues;
Like poor ſtarv'd rogues.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What would ye do if ye were to die now?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Alas, we were prepar'd. If you will hang us,
Let's have a good meal or two to die with,
To put's in heart.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Or if you'll drown us,
Let's be drunk firſt, that we may die merrily,
And bleſs the founders.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Ye ſhall not die ſo haſtily.
What dare ye do to deſerve my favour?

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: Put us to any ſervice,

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Any bondage,
Let's but live.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: We'll get a world of children,
For we know ye are hainouſly unprovided that way;
And ye ſhall beat us when we offend ye;
Beat us abundantly, and take our meat from us.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Theſe are weak abject things, that ſhew ye poor ones.
What's the great ſervice ye ſo oft have threatned,
If ye might ſee me, and win my favour?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: That buſineſs of diſcovery.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Oh, Ill tell ye Lady.

sp.speaker: La-m.
sp.l: And ſo will I.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: And I,
Pray let me ſpeak firſt.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Good, no confuſion.
We are before a Lady that knows manners;
And by the next meat I ſhall eat, 'tis certain,
This little Gentlewoman that was taken with us.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Your Captains Siſter, ſhe you mean.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I, I, ſhe's the buſineſs that we would open to ye.
You are couſened in her.

sp.speaker: Lam,
sp.l: How, what is't you would open?

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: She is no Siſter.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Good Sirs how quick you are.
She is no Siſter, Madam.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: She is his.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Peace I ſay.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Faith, ſweet Lady,
She is, as a man would ſay, his.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: His Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: Or, as ſome new Tranſlators read, his.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Oh me!

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: And why he ſhould delude you thus,
