Unleſs he meant ſome villany? theſe ten weeks
He has had her at Sea, for his own proper appetite.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: His Cabin-mate I'll aſſure ye.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: No Siſter, ſay ye?

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: No more than I am brother to your beauty.
I know not why he ſhould juggle thus.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Do not lie to me.

sp.speaker: Mor.
sp.l: If ye find me lie, Lady, hang me empty.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: How am I fool'd!
Away with 'em Juletta, and feed 'em
But hark ye, with ſuch food as they have given me.
New miſery!

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.l: Nor meat nor thanks for all this. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Make 'em more wretched.
Oh I could burſt! curſe and kill now,
Kill any thing I meet, Juletta, follow me,
And call the reſt along.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: We follow, Madam. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: I muſt be gone now, elſe ſhe may ſuſpect me;
How ſhall I anſwer her?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Tell her directly.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: That were too ſuddain, too improvident;
Fires of this nature muſt be put out cunningly,
They'll waſte all come near 'em elſe.
Farewel once more.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Farewel,
And keep my love entire.
Nay, kiſs me once again, me thinks we ſhould not part.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Oh be wiſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Nay, one kiſs more.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Indeed you're wanton;
We may be taken too.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Out thou baſe woman.
I'll ſhoot 'em both.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Nay ſtay, brave Lady, hold;
A ſuddain death cuts off a Nobler vengeance.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Am I made Bawd to your laſcivious meetings?
Are ye grown ſo wiſe in ſin?
Shut up that villany: and ſirrah,
Now expect my utmoſt anger.
Let him there ſtarve.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: I mock at your miſchiefs. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Tie that falſe witch unto that Tree,
There let that ſavage beaſts
Gnaw off her ſweetneſs, and Snakes
Embrace her beauties; tie her, and watch
That none relieve her.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: We could wiſh ye better fortune, Lady,
But dare not help ye.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Be your own friends, I thank ye.
Now only my laſt audit, and my greateſt,
Oh Heaven, be kind unto me,
And if it be thy Will, preſerve.

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: Who is this?
Sure 'tis a woman, I have trode this place,
And found much footing; now I know 'tis peopl'd.
Ha, let me ſee! 'tis her face.
Oh Heaven! turn this way Maid.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Oh Raymond, oh Brother.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: Her tongue too: 'tis my Siſter; what rude hand!
Nay kiſs me firſt, Oh joy!

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Fly, fly dear brother,
You are loſt elſe.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: A man, a man, a new man.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: What are theſe?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: An enemy, an enemy.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Diſpatch him,
Take him off, ſhoot him ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Raym.
sp.l: I dare not uſe my ſword, Ladies,
Againſt ſuch comely foes.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Oh brother, brother!

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Away with 'em, and in dark priſons bind 'em.
One word reply'd, ye die both.
Now brave • other, follow thy noble anger,
And •• l help thee. Exeun •

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Roſſella, Clarinda, Crocale, Juletta, Hippolita.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I Am deaf to all your intreaties: ſhe that moves me
For pity or compaſſion to theſe Pirats,
Digs up her Fathers, or her Brothers Tomb,
And ſpurns about their aſhes.
Couldſt thou remember what a Father thou hadſt once,
'Twould ſteel thy heart againſt all fooliſh pity.
By his memory'and the remembrance of his dear embraces,
I am taught, that in a Noble cauſe revenge is Noble;
And they ſhall fall the ſacrifices to appeaſe
His wandring Ghoſt, and my incenſed fury.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: The new come priſoner too!

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: He too yet that we may learn
Whether they are the ſame, or near ally'd
To thoſe that forc'd me to this cruel courſe,
Better their poor allowance, and permit 'em
To meet together and confer,
Within the diſtance of your ear; perhaps
They may diſcover ſomething that may kill
Deſpair in me, and be a means to ſave 'em
From certain ruine.

sp.speaker: Ceo.
sp.l: That ſhall be my charge.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Yet to prevent
All hope of reſcue: for this new-come Captain
Hath both a Ship and Men not far from us,
Though ignorant to find the only Port,
That can yield entrance to our happy Iſland,
Guard the place ſtrongly, and e'r the next Sun
Ends his diurnal progreſs, I will be
Happy in my revenge, or ſet 'em free. Exteunt.

div.stage: Enter Crocale, Juletta, Hippolita. A Table furniſh'd.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: So ſerve it plentifully,
And loſe not time to enquire the cauſe;
There is a main deſign that hangs upon this bounty.
See the Table furniſht with Wine too,
That diſcovers ſecrets which tortures cannot open:
Open the doors too of the ſeveral priſons,
And give all free entrance into this room.
Undiſcover'd I can here mark all.
Here's Captain careleſs, and the tough Ship-maſter,
The ſlaves are nos'd like Vultures
How wild they look.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Ha, the miſtery of this,
• ome good Hobgoblin riſe and reveal.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: I'm amazed at it: nor can I ſound the intent.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Is not this bread,
• ubſtantial bread, not painted?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: But take heed,
You may be poiſoned.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I am ſure I am famiſh'd;
And famine, as the wiſe man ſays,
Gripes the guts as much as any Mineral.
This may be Treacle ſent to preſerve me
After a long Faſt: or be it Vipers ſpittle,
• 'll run the hazard.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: We are paſt all fear, I'll take part with ye.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Do: and now i'faith, how d'ye feel your ſelf?
find great eaſe in't. What's here;
Vine, and it be thy Will;
• trong luſty Wine. Well, fools may talk
Of Mythridate, Cordials, and Elixirs.
But from my youth this was my only Phyſick.
Here's a colour, what Ladies cheek,
Though cerus'd over, comes near it?
• t ſparkles too: hangs out Diamonds.
Oh my ſweet-heart, how I will hug thee,
Again, and again! They are poor drunkards,
And not worth thy favors,
That number thy moiſt kiſſes in theſe Cryſtals.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: But Mounſieur,
• ere are Suckets, and ſweet diſhes.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Tuſh, boys meat,
• am paſt it; here's ſtrong food fit for men:
Nectar, old lad. Miſtriſs of merry hearts,
Once more I am bold with you.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Take heed (man)
Too much will breed diſtemper.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Haſt thou liv'd at Sea
The moſt part of thy life, where to be ſober
While we have Wine aboard, is capital Treaſon;
And doſt thou preach ſobriety?

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: Prethee forbear,
We may offend in it; we know not for whom
• t was provided.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I am ſure for me: therefore footra,
When I am full, let 'em hang me, I care not.

div.stage: Enter Albert, Aminta, Raymond, Lamure, Morrillat, Franvile, ſeverally.

sp.speaker: Maſt.
sp.l: This has been his temper ever.
•• e, provoking diſhes; candid Eringoes,
• nd Potatoes.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: I'll not touch 'em, I will drink;
But not a bit on a march, I'll be an Eunuch rather.

sp.speaker: Maſt
sp.l: Who are theſe?

sp.speaker: Tib,
sp.l: Marry, who you will;
• keep my Text here.

l.hi: Raymond!
Albert!

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Away, I'll be drunk alone;
Keep off Rogues, or I'll belch ye into air;
• ot a drop here.

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Dear brother, put not in your eyes ſuch anger;
Thoſe looks poiſon'd with fury, ſhot at him,
• ef • ect on me. Oh brother, look milder, or
The Cryſtal of his temperance
Will turn 'em on your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Sir, I have ſought ye long
To find your pardon: you have plough'd the Ocean
To wreak your vengeance on me, for the rape
Of this fair Virgin. Now our fortune guides us
To meet on ſuch hard terms, that we need rather
• mutual pitty of our preſent ſtate,
Than to expoſtulate of breaches paſt,
Which cannot be made up. And though it be
Far from your power, to force me to confeſs,
That I have done ye wrong, or ſuch ſubmiſſion
Failing to make my peace, to vent your anger;
You being your ſelf ſlav'd, as I to others:
Yet for you Siſters ſake, her bleſſed ſake,
In part of recompence of what ſhe has ſuffer'd
For my raſh folly; the contagion
Of my black actions, catching hold upon
Her purer innocence, I crave your mercy;
And wiſh however ſeveral motives kept us
From being friends, while we had hope to live,
Let death which we expect, and cannot fly from,
End all contention.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Drink upon't, 'tis a good motion;
Ratifie it in Wine, and 'tis authentical.

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: When I conſider
The ground of our long difference, and look on
Our not to be avoided miſeries,
It doth beget in me I know not how
A ſoft Religious tenderneſs; which tells me,
Though we have many faults to anſwer for
Upon our own account, our Fathers crimes
Are in us puniſh'd. Oh Albert, the courſe
They took to leave us rich, was not honeſt,
Nor can that friendſhip laſt, which virtue joyns not.
When firſt they forc'd the induſtrious Portugals,
From their Plantations in the Happy Iſlands.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: This is that I watch for.

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: And did omit no tyranny, which men,
Inured to ſpoil, and miſchief could inflict,
On the griex'd ſufferers; when by lawleſs rapine
They reap'd the harveſt, which their Labourer; ſow'd;
And not content to force 'em from their dwelling,
But laid for 'em at Sea, to raviſh from 'em
The laſt remainder of their wealth: then, then,
After a long purſuit, each doubting other,
As guilty of the Portugals eſcape,
They did begin to quarrel, like in men;
(Forgive me piety, that I call 'em ſo)
No longer love, or correſpondence holds,
Than it is cimented with prey or profit:
Then did they turn theſe ſwords they oft had bloodi'd
With innocent gore, upon their wretched ſelves,
And paid the forfeit of their cruelty
Shewn to Sebaſtian, and his Colonie,
By being fatal enemies to each other.
Thence grew Amintas rape, and my deſire
To be reveng'd. And now obſerve the iſſue:
As they for ſpoil ever forgot compaſſion
To women, (who ſhould be exempted
From the extremities of a lawful War)
We now, young able men, are fall'n into
The hands of Women; that, againſt the ſoft
Tenderneſs familiar to their Sex,
Will ſhew no mercy.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: None, unleſs you ſhew us
Our long loſt Husbands.
We are thoſe Portugals you talk'd of.

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: Stay,
I met upon the Sea in a tall Ship
Two Portugals, famiſh'd almoſt to death.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Our Ship by this Wine.
And thoſe the rogues that ſtole her,
Leſt us to famiſh in the barren Iſlands.

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: Some ſuch tale they told me,
And ſomething of a Woman, which I find,
To be my Siſter.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Where are theſe men?

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: I left 'em,
Suppoſing they had deluded me with forg'd tales,
In the Iſland, where they ſaid
They had liv'd many years the wretched owners
Of a huge maſs of treaſure.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: The ſame men: and that the fatal muck
We quarrell'd for.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: They were Portugals you ſay.

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: So they profeſs'd.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: They may prove ſuch men as may ſave your lives,
And ſo much I am taken with fair hope,
That I will hazard life to be reſolv'd on't:
How came you hither?

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: My ſhip lies by the Rivers mouth,
That can convey ye to theſe wretched men,
Which you deſire to ſee.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Back to your priſons,
And pray for the ſucceſs: if they be thoſe
Which I deſire to find, you are ſafe;
If not, prepare to die to morrow:
For the world cannot redeem ye.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: However, we are arm'd
For either fortune. Exit.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: What muſt become of me now
That I am not diſmiſs'd?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Oh Sir, I purpoſe
To have your company.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: Take heed wicked woman,
I am apt to miſchief now.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: You cannot be ſo unkind,
To her that gives you liberty.

sp.speaker: Ti.
sp.l: No, I ſhall be too kind, that's the devil on't;
I have had ſtore of good wine: and when I am drunk,
Joan is a Lady to me, and I ſhall
Lay about me like a Lord: I feel ſtrange motions:
Avoid me temptation.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Come Sir, I'll help ye in. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: What may that be
That moves upon the Lake?

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Still it draws nearer,
And now I plainly can diſcern it.
'Tis the French Ship.

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: In it a woman,
Who ſeems to invite us to her,

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Still ſhe calls with ſigns of Love to haſten to her;
So lovely hope doth ſtill appear:
I feel nor age, nor weakneſs.

sp.speaker: Nicu.
sp.l: Though it bring death,
To us 'tis comfort: and deſerves a meeting.
Or elſe fortune tyr'd with what we have ſuffer'd,
And in it overcome, as it may be,
Now ſets a period to our miſery. Exeunt. Horid Muſick.

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: What dreadful ſounds are theſe?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: Infernal Muſick,
Fit for a bloody Feaſt.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: It ſeems prepar'd
To kill our courages e'r they divorce
Our ſouls and bodies.

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: But they that fearleſs fall,
Deprive them of their triumph.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: See the furies,
• n their full trym of cruelty,

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: 'Tis the laſt
Duty that I can pay to my dead Lord,
Set out the Altar, I my ſelf will be
The Prieſt, and boldly do thoſe horrid Rites
You ſhake to think on, lead theſe Captains nearer,
For they ſhall have the honor to fall firſt
To my Sebaſtian's aſhes: and now wretches,
As I am taught already, that you are,
And lately by your free confeſſion,
French Pirats, and the ſons of thoſe I hate,
Even equal with the devil; hear with horror,
What 'tis invites me to this cruel courſe,
And what you are to ſuffer, no Amazons we,
But women of Portugal that muſt have from you
Sebaſtian and Nicuſa; we are they
That groan'd beneath your fathers wrongs:
We are thoſe wretched women,
Their injuries purſu'd, and overtook;
And from the ſad remembrance of our loſſes
We are taught to be cruel; when we were forc'd
From that ſweet air we breathed in, by their rapine,
And ſought a place of being; as the Seas
And Winds conſpir'd with their ill purpoſes,
To load us with afflictions in a ſtorm
That fell upon us; the two ſhips that brought us,
To ſeek new fortunes in an unknown world
Were ſevered: the one bore all the able men,
Our Treaſure and our Jewels: in the other,
We Women were embarqu'd: and fell upon,
After long toſſing in the troubled main,
This pleaſant Iſland: but in few months,
The men that did conduct us hither, died,
We long before had given our Husbands loſt:
Remembring what we had ſuff'red by the French
We took a ſolemn Oath, never to admit
The curs'd ſociety of men: neceſſity
Taught us thoſe Arts, not uſual to our Sex,
And the fertile Earth yielding abundance to us,
We did reſolve, thus ſhap'd like Amazons
To end our lives; but when you arriv'd here,
And brought as preſents to us, our own Jewels;
Thoſe which were boorn in the other Ship,
How can ye hope to ſcape our vengeance?

sp.speaker: Amint.
sp.l: It boots not then to ſwear our innocence?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Or that we never forc'd it from the owners?

sp.speaker: Ray.
sp.l: Or that there are a remnant of that wrack,
And not far off?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: All you affirm, I know,
Is but to win time; therefore prepare your throats,
The world ſhall not redeem ye: and that your cries
May find no entrance to our ears,
To move pity in any: bid loud Muſick ſound
Their fatal knells; if ye have prayers uſe 'em quickly,
To any power will own ye; but ha!
Who are theſe? what ſpectacles of misfortune?
Why are their looks
So full of Joy and Wonder?

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: Oh! lay by
Theſe inſtruments of death, and welcome
To your arms, what you durſt never hope to imbrace:
This is Sebaſtian, this Nicuſa, Madam:
Preſerv'd by miracle: look up dear Sir,
And know your own Roſſella: be not loſt
In wonder and amazement; or if nature
Can by inſtinct, inſtruct you what it is,
To be bleſſed with the name of Father,
Freely enjoy it in this fair Virgin.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Though my miſeries,
And many years of wants I have endur'd,
May well deprive me of the memory
Of all joys paſt; yet looking on this building,
This ruin'd building of a heavenly form
In my Roſilla; I muſt remember, I am Sebaſtian.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Oh my joyes!

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: And here,
I ſee a perfect model of thy ſelf,
As thou wert when thy choice firſt made thee mine:
Theſe cheeks and fronts, though wrinkled now with time
Which Art cannot reſtore: had equal pureneſs,
Of natural white and red, and as much raviſhing:
Which by fair order and ſucceſſion,
I ſee deſcend on her: and may thy virtues
Wind into her form, and make her a perfect dower:
No part of thy ſweet goodneſs wanting to her.
I will not now Roſilla, ask thy fortunes,
Nor trouble thee with hearing mine;
Thoſe ſhall hereafter ſerve to make glad hours
In their relation: All paſt wrongs forgot;
I'm glad to ſee you Gentlemen; but moſt,
That is in my power to ſave your lives;
You ſav'd ours, when we were near ſtarv'd a • Sea,
And I deſpair not, for if ſhe be mine,
Roſilla can deny Sebaſtian nothing.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: She does give up her ſelf,
Her power and joys, and all, to you,
Welcome in any ſhape.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Sir, in your looks,
I read your ſute of my Clarinda: ſhe is yours:
And Lady, if it be in me to confirm
Your hopes in this brave Gentleman,
Preſume I am your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: We thank you Sir.

sp.speaker: Amin.
sp.l: Oh happy hour!

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: O my dear Aminta;
Now all our fears are ended.

sp.speaker: Tib.
sp.l: Here I fix: ſhe's mettle,
Steel to the back: and will cut my leaden dagger,
If not us'd with diſcretion.

sp.speaker: Cro.
sp.l: You are ſtill no changling.

sp.speaker: Sebaſt.
sp.l: Nay,
All look chearfully, for none ſhall be
Deny'd their lawful wiſhes; when a while
We have here refreſh'd our ſelves; we'll return
To our ſeveral homes; and well that voyage ends,
That makes of deadly enemies, faithful friends.

div.head: Wit at ſeveral weapons. A COMEDY.
The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Sir Perfidious Oldcraft, an old Knight, a great admirer of Wit.
Witty-pate Oldcraft, his Fathers own Son.
Sir Gregory Fopp, a witleſs Lord of Land.
Cunningham, a diſcreet Gen. Sir Gregories comrade and ſupplanter.

list.head: Two ſharking companions.
list.item: Sir Ruinous Gentry, a decaid Knight,
Pompey Doodle, a clown, Sir Gregories man, a piece of puff-paſte, like his Maſter.
Mr. Credulous, Nephew to Sir Perfidions, a ſhallow-brain'd Scholar.

list.head: Women.
list.item: Neece to Sir Perfidious, a rich and witty Heir,
Lady Ruinous, Wife to Sir Ruinous.
Guardianeſs, to Sir Perfidious his Neece, an old doting Croane.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Sir Perfidious Old-craft an old Knight, and Witty-pate his Son.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: SIR, I'm no boy, I'm deep in one and twenty,
The ſecond years approaching,

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: A fine time
For a youth to live by his wits then I ſhould think,
If e'er he mean to make account of any.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Wits, Sir?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I Wits Sir, if it be ſo ſtrange to thee,
I'm ſorry I ſpent that time to get a Fool,
I might have imploy'd my pains a great deal better;
Thou knowſt all that I have, I ha' got by my wits,
And yet to ſee how urgent thou art too;
It grieves me thou art ſo degenerate
To trouble me for means, I never offer'd it
My Parents from a School-boy, paſt nineteen once.
See what theſe times are grown to, before twenty
I ruſh'd into the world, which is indeed
Much like the Art of ſwiming, he that will attain to't
Muſt fall plump, and duck himſelf at firſt,
And that will make him hardy and advent'rous,
And not ſtand putting in one foot, and ſhiver,
And then draw t'other after, like a quake-buttock;
Well he may make a padler i'th' world,
From hand to mouth, • ut never a brave Swimmer,
Born up by th' chi ••• , as I bore up myſelf,
With my ſtrong induſtry that never fail'd me;
For he that lies born up with Patrimonies,
Looks like a long great Aſs that ſwims with bladders,
Come but one prick of adverſe fortune to him
He ſinks, becauſe he never try'd to ſwim
When Wit plaies with the billows that choak'd him.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Why is it not a faſhion for a Father, Sir,
Out of his yearly thouſands to allow
His only Son, a competent brace of hundreds;
Or ſuch a toy?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Yes, if he mean to ſpoil him,
Or mar his wits he may, but never I,
This is my humor, Sir, which you'll find conſtant;
I love Wit ſo well, becauſe I liv'd by't,
That I'll give no man power out of my means to hurt it,
And that's a kind of gratitude to my raiſer,
Which great ones oſt forget; I admire much
This Ages dulneſs, when I ſcarce writ man,
The firſt degree that e'er I took in thriving,
I lay intelligencer cloſe for wenching,
Could give this Lord or Knight a true Certificate
Of all the Maiden-heads extant,, how many lay
'Mongſt Chamber-maids, how many 'mongſt Exchange
Though never many there I muſt confeſs
They have a trick to utter Ware ſo faſt;
I knew which Lady had a mind to fall,
Which Gentlewoman new divorc'd, which Tradeſman breaking,
The price of every ſinner to a hair,
And where to raiſe each price; which were the Tearmers,
That would give Velvet Petticoats, Tiſſue Gowns,
Which Pieces, Angels, Suppers, and Half Crowns;
I knew how to match, and make my market.
Could give intelligence where the Pox lay leidger,
And then to ſee the Letchers ſhift a point,
'Twas ſport and profit too; how they would ſhun
Their ador'd Miſtriſs chambers, and run fearfully,
Like Rats from burning houſes, ſo brought I
My Clyents the game ſtill ſafe together,
And noble gameſters lov'd me, and I felt it.
Give me a man that lives by his wits, ſay I,
And's never left a Groat, there's the true Gallant.
When I grew ſomewhat purſie, I grew then
In mens opinions too, and confidences,
They put things call'd Executorſhips upon me,
The charge of Orphans, little ſenſleſs creatures,
Whom in their Childhoods I bound forth to Felt-makers,
To make 'em loſe, and work away their Gentry,
Diſguiſe their tender natures with hard cuſtom,
So wrought 'em out in time there riſe ungently,
Nor do I fear to diſcourſe this unto thee,
I'm arm'd at all points againſt treachery,
I hold my humor firm, if I can ſee thee thrive by
Thy wits while I live, I ſhall have the more courage
To truſt thee with my Lands when I dye; if not,
The next beſt wit I can hear of, carries 'em:
For ſince in my time and knowledge, ſo many rich children
Of the City, conclude in beggery, I'de rather
Make a wiſe ſtranger my Executor, then a fooliſh
• on my Heir, and to have my Lands call'd after my
Wit, than after my name; and that's my nature.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſtrange harſh one, muſt I ſtill ſhift then?
• come brave Cheats, once to my trade agen.
And I'll ply't harder now than e'er I did for't,
You'll part with nothing then, Sir?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Not a jot, Sir.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: If I ſhould ask you bleſſing e'r I goe, Sir,
• think you would not give't me.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Let me but hear thou liv'ſt by thy wits once
Thou ſhalt have any thing, thou'rt none of mine elſe,
Then why ſhould I take care for thee?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: 'Thank your bounty. Exit.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: So wealth love me, and long life, I beſeech it,
As I do love the man that lives by his wits,
He comes ſo near my nature; I'm grown old now,
And even arriv'd at my laſt cheat I fear me,
•• t 'twill make ſhift to bury me, by day-light too,
And diſcharge all my Legacies, 'tis ſo wealthy,
And never trouble any Intereſt money:
• 've yet a Neece to wed, over whoſe ſteps
• have plac'd a truſty watchful Guardianeſs,
For fear ſome poor Earl ſteal her, 't has been threat'ned,
To redeem mortgag'd Land, but he ſhall miſs on't;
To prevent which, I have ſought out a match for her,
• op of Fop-Hall, he writes himſelf, I take it,
The antient'ſt Fop in England, with whom I've privately
Compounded for the third part of her portion.
sp.stage: Enter Sir Gregory Fop, and Cuningham.
sp.l: And ſhe ſeems pleas'd, ſo two parts reſt with me,
He's come; Sir Gregory, welcome, what's he Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Young Cuningham, a N • rfolk Gentleman,
One that has liv'd upon the Feps, my kindred,
Ever ſince my remembrance; he's a wit indeed,
And we all ſtrive to have him, nay, 'tis certain
Some of our name has gone to I aw for him;
Now 'tis my turn to keep him, and indeed
He's plaguy chargeable, as all your wits are,
But I will give him over when I liſt,
I ha' us'd wits ſo before.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I hope when y'are married Sir, you'll ſhake him off.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Why what do you take me to be, old Father-i'Law that ſhall be, do you think I'll have any of the Wits hang upon me, after I am married once? none of my kindred ever had before me; but where's this Neece? is't a faſhion in London, to marry a woman and never ſee her?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Excuſe the niceneſs, Sir, that care's your friend's,
Perhaps had ſhe been ſeen, you had never ſeen her;
There's many a ſpent thing call'd, and't like your honor,
That lies in wait for her, at firſt ſnap ſhe's a Counteſs,
Drawn with ſix Mares through Fleetſtreet, and a Coachman,
Sitting bare-headed to their Flanders buttocks,
This whets him on.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Pray let's clap up the buſineſs, Sir,
I long to ſee her, are you ſure you have her,
Is ſhe not there already, Hark? Hark, oh hark.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: How now, what's that Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Every Caroach goes by,
Goes ev'n to th' heart of me-

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I'll have that doubt eas'd, Sir,
Inſtantly eas'd, Sir Gregory, and now I think on't
A toy comes i' my mind, ſeeing your friend there,
We'll have a little ſport, give you but way to't,
And put a trick upon her, I love Wit pretiouſly,
You ſhall not be ſeen yet, we'll ſtale your friend firſt,
If 't pleaſe but him to ſtand for the Anti-mask.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Puh, he ſhall ſtand for any thing, why his ſupper
Lies i'my breeches here, I'll make him faſt elſe.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Then come you forth more unexpectedly
The Mask it ſelf, a thouſand a year joynture,
The cloud (your friend) will be then drawn away,
And only you the beauty of the Play.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: For Red and Black, I'll put down all your Fallers,
Let but your Neece bring White, and we have three colours.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I'm given to underſtand you are a Wit, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cuning.
sp.l: I'm one that Fortune ſhews ſmall favour to, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Why there you conclude it, whether you will or no, Sir;
sp.l: To tell you truth, I'm taken with a Wit.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: Fowlers catch Woodcocks ſo, let not them know ſo much,

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: A peſtilence mazard, a Duke Humphrey ſpark
Had rather loſe his dinner than his jeſt,
I ſay I love a Wit the beſt of all things.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Always except your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Has giv'n't me twice now.
All with a breath, I thank him; but that I love a Wit
I ſhould be heartily angry; cuds, my Neece,
You know the buſineſs with her,

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: With a Woman?
'Tis ev'n the very ſame it was I'm ſure
Five thouſand years ago, no fool can miſs it.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: This is the Gentleman I promis'd Neece,
To preſent to your affection.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: W'are that Arrow.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Deliver me the truth now of your liking.

sp.speaker: Cun
sp.l: I'm ſpoil'd already, that ſuch poor lean Game
Should be found out as I am.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Go ſet to her Sir—ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: How noble is this virtue in you, Lady?
Your eye may ſeem to commit a thouſand ſlaughters
On your dull ſervants which truly taſted
Conclude all in comforts.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Puh.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: It rather ſhews what a true worth can make,
Such as yours is.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: And that's not worth a groat,
How like you him Neece?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: It ſhall appear how well, Sir,
I humbly thank you for him.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Hah? ha, good gullery, he does it well i'faith,
Light, as if he meant to purchaſe Lip-land there:
Hold, hold, bear off I ſay, ſlid your part hangs too long.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: My joys are mockeries.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Y'have both expreſt a worthy care and love, Sir,
Had mine-own eye been ſet at liberty,
To make a publick choice (believe my truth, Sir)
It could not ha' done better for my heart
Than your good providence has.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: You will ſay ſo then,
Alas ſweet Neece, all this is but the ſcabbard,
Now I draw forth the weapon.

sp.speaker: Neece?
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Sir Gregory,
Approach thou lad of thouſands.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Who calls me?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: What motion's this, the Model of Ninivie?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Accoſt her daintily now, let me adviſe thee,

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: I was advis'd to beſtow dainty coſt on you.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: You were ill advis'd, back, and take better counſel;
You may have good for an Angel, the leaſt coſt
You can beſtow upon a woman, Sir
Trebles ten Counſellors Fees in Lady-ware,
Y'are over head and ears, e'r you be aware,
Faith keep a batchelor ſtill, and go to Bowls, Sir,
Follow your Miſtriſs there, and prick and ſave, Sir;
For other Miſtreſſes will make you a ſlave, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: So, ſo, I have my lerrepoop already.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Why how now Neece, this is the man I tell you.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: He, hang him, Sir, I know you do but mock,
This is the man you would ſay.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: The Devil rides I think.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I muſt uſe cunning here.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Make me not mad, uſe him with all reſpect,
This is the man I ſwear.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Would you could perſwade me to that;
Alaſs, you cannot go beyond me Uncle,
You carry a Jeſt well, I muſt confeſs,
For a man of your years, but—

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I'm wrought beſide my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I never beheld comlineſs till this minute.

sp.speaker: Guar.
sp.l: Oh good ſweet Sir, pray offer not theſe words
To an old Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Away fifteen,
Here's Fifty one exceeds thee.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: What's the buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Give me theſe motherly creatures, come, ne'er ſmother it,
I know you are a teeming woman yet.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Troth a young Gent. might do much I think, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Go too then.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: And I ſhould play my part, or I were ingrateful.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Can you ſo ſoon neglect me!

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Hence I'm buſie.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: This croſs point came in luckily, impudent baggage.
Hang from the Gentleman, art thou not aſham'd
To be a Widows hind'rance?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Are you angry, Sir?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: You're welcome, pray court on, I ſhall deſire
Your honeſt wiſe acquaintance; vex me not
After my care and pains to find a match for thee,
Leſt I confine thy life to ſome out-chamber,
Where thou ſhalt waſte the ſweetneſs of thy youth,
Like a conſuming Light in her own ſocket,
And not allow'd a male creature about thee;
A very Monky, thy neceſſity
Shall prize at a thouſand pound, a Chimney-s;weeper
At Fifteen hundred.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: But are you ſerious, Uncle?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Serious.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Pray let me look upon the Gentleman
With more heed; then I did but hum him over
In haſte, good faith, as Lawyers Chancery ſheets;
Beſhrew my blood, a tollerable man,
Now I diſtinctly read him.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Hum, hum, hum.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Say he be black, he's of a very good pitch,
Well ankled, two good confident calves, they look
As if they would not ſhrink at the ninth child;
The redneſs i'th face, why that's in faſhion,
Moſt of your high bloods have it, ſign of greatneſs marry;
'Tis to be taken down too with May-butter,
I'll ſend to my Lady Spend-tail for her Medicine.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Lum te dum, dum, dum, de dum.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: He's qualified too, believe me.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Lum te dum, de dum, de dum.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Where was my judgement?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Lum te dum, dum, dum, te dum, te dum.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Perfections cover'd meſs.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Lum te dum, te dum, te dum.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: It ſmoaks apparantly, pardon ſweet Sir,
The error of my Sex.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Why, well ſaid Neece,
Upon ſubmiſſion you muſt pardon her now, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: I'll do't by courſe, do you think I'm an aſs, Knight?
Here's firſt my hand, now't goes to the Seal-Office.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Formally finiſht, how goes this Suit forward?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I'm taking meaſure of the Widows mind, Sir,
I hope to fit her heart.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Who would have dreamt
Of a young morſel now? things come in minutes.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Truſt him not Widow, he's a younger brother,
He'll ſwear and lie; believe me he's worth nothing.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: He brings more content to a woman with that nothing,
Than he that brings his thouſands without any thing,
We have preſidents for that amongſt great Ladies.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Come, come, no language now ſhall be in faſhion,
But your Love-phraſe, the bell to procreation. Exeunt

div.stage: Enter Sir Ruinous Gentry, Witty-pate, and Priſcian.

sp.speaker: Witty-
sp.p: Pox, there's nothing puts me beſides my wits but this fourth,
sp.l: This laſt illiterate ſhare, there's no conſcience in't.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Sir, it has ever been ſo, where I have practis'd and muſt be.
Still where I am, nor has it been undeſerv'd at the year
End, and ſhuff • le the Almanack together, vacations and
Term-times, one with another, though I ſay't, my wife is •
Woman of a good ſpirit, then it is no lay-ſhare.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Faith for this five year, Ego poſſum probare, I have had
A hungry penurious ſhare with 'em, and ſhe has had as muc •
As I always.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Preſent, or not preſent;

l.hi: Reſidens aut non reſidens, per fidem.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p:
And what preſident's this for me? becauſe you Hic & hac, Turpis and Qui mihi diſcipulus brains (that never
got any thing but by accidence and uncertainty) did al
• ow it, therefore I muſt, that have grounded concluſions of • it, hereditary rules from my Father to get by—

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p:
Sir, be compendious, either take or refuſe, I will • ate no token of my wives ſhare, make even the laſt reckon
• ags, and either ſo unite, or here divide company.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.p: A good reſolution, profecto, let every man beg his own way, and happy man be his dole.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Well, here's your double ſhare, and ſingle brains P • l, aedipol, here's toward, a Caſtor ecaſtor for you, I will endure it a fortnight longer, but by theſe juſt five ends.—

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.p: Take heed, five's odd, put both hands together, or ſeverally, they are all odd unjuſt ends.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Medius filius, hold your tongue, I depoſe you from half a ſhare preſently elſe, I will make you a participle, and decline you, now you underſtand me, be you a quiet Conjunction amongſt the undeclined; you and your Latine ends ſhall go ſhift, Solus cum ſolo together elſe, and then if ever they get ends of Gold and Silver, enough to ſerve that Gerundine maw of yours, that without Do will end in Di and Dum inſtantly.

div.stage: Enter Old Knight and Sir Gregory.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: Enough, enough, here comes company, we loſe five ſhares in wrangling about one.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p:
My Father, put on Priſcian he has Latine frag
• ments too, but I fear him not, I'll caſe my face with a little more hair and relieve.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Tuſh Nephew (I'll call you ſo) for if there be
No other obſtacles than thoſe you ſpeak of
They are but Powder-charges without pellets,
You may ſafely front 'em; and warrant your own danger.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p:
No other that I can perceive i'faith, Sir, for I • ut her to't, and felt her as far as I could, and the ſtrong
• ſt repulſe was, ſhe ſaid, ſhe would have a little Soldier in • e, that (if need were) ſhould defend her reputation.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: And ſurely, Sir, that is a principle Amongſt your principal Ladies, they require • alour, either in a friend or a Husband.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: And I allow their requeſts i'faith, as well as any • omans heart can deſire, if I knew where to get vaour, I would as willingly entertain it as any man that blows.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Breaths, breaths Sir, that's the ſweeter phraſe.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: Blows for a Soldier, i'ſaith Sir, and I'm in • ractiſe that way.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: For a Soldier, I grant it.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: 'Slid, I'll ſwallow ſome bullets, and good round • es too, but I'll have a little Soldier in me,

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: Will you on and beg, or ſteal and be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: And ſome Scholar ſhe would have me beſides, • uſh, that ſhall be no bar, 'tis a quality in a Gentleman, but of the leaſt queſtion.

l.hi: Salvete Domini benigniſſimi, munificentiſſimi.

sp.speaker: Old K.

l.hi: Salvete dicis ad nos? jubeo te ſalvere,

sp.l: Nay, Sir, we have Latine, and other metall in us too.
•• r, you ſhall ſee me talk with this fellow now,

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: I could find in my heart to talk with him too,
• f I could underſtand him.

l.hi: Chariſſimi, Doctiſſimique, Domini, ex abundantia.
•• aritatis veſtrae eſtote propitii in me jejunum
•• iſerum, pauperem, & omni conſolatione exulem.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: A pretty Scholar by my faith, Sir, but I'll to him agen.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Does he beg or ſteal in this Language, can you tell Sir?
• e may take away my good name from me, and I ne'er • he wiſer.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: He begs, he begs, Sir.

l.hi:
Ecce, ecce, in occulis lachrymarum flumen, in ore • omes ſitiſ
que ignis in vultu, pudor & impudentia, 〈◊〉 omni parte neceſſitas & indigentia.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Audi tu bonus ſocius, tu es Scholaſticus, ſic intelligo, •• faciam argumentum, mark now Sir, now I fetch Him up.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: I have been fetcht up a hundred times for this,
Yet I could never learn half ſo much.

sp.speaker: Old K.

l.hi: Audi, & reſpon • e, hoc eſt Argumentu •• , nomen eſt
Nomen, ergo, quod eſt tibi nomen? Reſponde nunc,

sp.l: Reſponde argumentum m • um. Have I not put him to't, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Step in, the raſcal is put out of his pen'd Speech,
And he can go no farther.

l.hi: Cur non reſpondes?
Oh Domine, tanta mea eſt miſeria.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: So, he's almoſt in agen.

l.hi: Ʋt nocte mecum pernectat egeſtas, luce quotidie Paupertas habitat.
Sed quod eſt tibi nomen: & quis dedit? Reſponde Argumentum.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Hem, hem,

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: He's dry he hems, on quickly.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: Courteous Gentlemen, if the brow of a Military face may not be offenſive to your generous eye-balls, let his wounds ſpeak better than his words, for ſome branch or ſmall ſprig of charity to be planted upon this poor barren ſoil of a Soldier.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: How now, what Arms and Arts both go a begging?

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: Such is the Poſt-progreſs of cold charity now a-days, who (for heat to her frigid Limbs) paſſes in ſo ſwift a motion, that two at the leaſt had need be to ſtay her.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: Sir, lets reward um I pray you, and be gone. If any quarrel ſhould ariſe amongſt us, I am able to anſwer neither of them, his Iron and Steel tongue is as hard as the t'others Latine one.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Stay, ſtay Sir I will talk a little with him firſt,
Let me alone with both, I will try whether they
Live by their wits or no; for ſuch a man I love,
And what? you both beg together then;

l.hi: Conjunctis manibus, profecto, Domine.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: With equal fortunes, equal diſtribution, there's not the breadth of a ſwords point uneven in our diviſion.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: What two qualities are here caſt away upon two poor fellows, if a man had um that could maintain um? what a double man were that, if theſe two fellows might be bought and ſodden, and boil'd to a jelly, and eaten faſting every morning, I do not think but a man ſhould find ſtrange things in his ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Come Sir, joyn your charity with mine, and we'll make up a couple of pence bewixt us.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: If a man could have a pennyworth for his penny,
I would beſtow more money with 'em.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Save you Gentlemen, how now? what are you encount'red here? what fellows are theſe?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Faith Sir, here's Mars and Mercury, a pair of poor Planets it ſeems, that Jupiter has turn'd out to live by their wits, and we are e'en about a little ſpark of charity to kindle um a new fire.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Stay, pray you ſtay Sir, you may abuſe your charity, nay, make that goodneſs in you no better than a vice; ſo many deceivers walk in theſe ſhadows now a days; that certainly your bounties were better ſpilt than reſerv'd to ſo lewd and vicious uſes; which is he that profeſſes the Soldier?

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: He that profeſſes his own profeſſion, Sir, and the dangerous life he hath led in it, this pair of half ſcore years.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: In what ſervices have you been, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: The firſt that fleſht me a Soldier, Sir, was that great battel at Alcazar in Barbary, where the noble Engliſh Stukely fell, and where that royal Portugal Sebaſtian ended his untimely days.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Are you ſure Sebaſtian died there?

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p:
Faith Sir, there was ſome other rumour hop't amongſt us, that he, wounded, eſcap'd, and toucht on his Native ſhore agen, where finding his Countrey at home more diſtreſt by the invaſion of the Spaniard, than his loſs abroad, forſook it, ſtill ſupporting a miſerable and unfortunate
fortunate life, which (where he ended) is yet uncertain.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: By my faith Sir, he ſpeaks the neareſt fame of truth in this.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: Since Sir, I ſerv'd in France, the Low Countreys, Laſtly, at that memorable skirmiſh at Newport, where the forward and bold Scot there ſpent his life ſo freely, that from every ſingle heart that there fell, came home from his reſolution, a double honor to his Countrey.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: This ſhould be no counterfeit, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: I do not think he is, Sir.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: But Sir, me thinks you do not ſhew the marks of a Soldier, could you ſo freely ſcape, that you brought home no ſcarrs to be your chronicle?

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: Sir, I have wounds, and many, but in thoſe parts where nature and humanity bids me ſhame to publiſh.

sp.speaker: Witty,
sp.p: A good Soldier cannot want thoſe badges.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Now am not I of your mind in that, for I hold him the beſt ſoldier that ſcapes beſt, alwaies at a Cock-fencing I give him the beſt that has the feweſt knocks.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Nay, I'll have a bout with your Scholar too,
To ask you why you ſhould be poor (yet richly learn'd)
Were no queſtion, at leaſt, you can eaſily
Anſwer it; but whether you have learning enough,
To deſerve to be poor or no (ſince poverty is
Commonly the meed of Learning) is yet to be tryed;
You have the Languages, I mean the chief,
As the Hebrew, Syriack, Greek, Latine, &c.

l.hi: Aliquantulum, non totaliter, Domine,

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: The Latine I have ſufficiently tried him in,
And I promiſe you Sir, he is very well grounded.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: I will prove him in ſome of the reſt.

l.hi: Toia miois fatherois iſte Cock-ſcomboy?
Kay yonkeron nigitton oy fouleroi Aſiniſoy.
Cheateron ton biton?
Tous pollous ſtrikerous, Angelo to peeſo.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Certainly Sir, a very excellent Scholar in the Greek.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I do note a wondrous readineſs in him.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: I do wonder how the Trojans could hold out ten years ſiege (as 'tis reported againſt the Greeks, if Achilles ſpoke but this tongue? I do not think but he might have ſhaken down the Walls in a ſeven-night, and ne'er troubled the wooden horſe.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: I will try him ſo far as I can in the Syriack.

l.hi: Kircom bragmen, ſhag a dou ma dell mathou.
Haſhagath rabgaboſh ſhobos onoriadka.
Colpack Rubaſca, gnawerthem ſhigſhag.
Napſhamothem Ribſie bongomoſh laſhemech nagothi.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Gentlemen I have done, any man that can go farther,
I confeſs my ſelf at a Nonplus.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Faith not I, Sir, I was at my fartheſt in my natural language, I was never double-tongu'd, I thank my hard fortune.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Well Gentlemen, 'tis pity, (walk farther off a little my friends) I ſay, 'tis pity ſuch fellows ſo endow'd, ſo qualified with the gifts of Nature and Arts, yet ſhould have ſuch a ſcarcity of fortune's benefits, we muſt blame our Iron-hearted age for it.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: 'Tis pity indeed, and our pity ſhall ſpeak a little, for 'em;
Come Sir, here's my groat.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: A Groat Sir? oh ſie, give nothing rather, 'twere better you rail'd on 'em for begging, and ſo quit your ſelf, I am a poor Gentleman, that have but little but my wits to live on.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Troth and I love you the better, Sir.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Yet I'll begin a better example than ſo, here fellows, there's between you, take Purſe and all, and I would it were here heavier for your ſakes, there's a pair of Angels to guide you to your lodgings, a poor Gentleman's good Will.

l.hi: Gratias, maximas gratias, benigniſſime Domine.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: This is an ill example for us, Sir, I would this bountiful Gentleman had not come this way to day.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: Pox, we muſt not ſhame our ſelves now, Sir, I'll give as much as that Gentleman, though I never be Soldier or Scholar while I live; here friends, there's a piece, that if he were divided, would make a pair of Angels for me too, in the love I bear to the Sword and the Tongues.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: My largeſs ſhall be equal too, and much good do you, this bounty is a little abatement of my wit, though I feel that.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: May ſoldiers ever defend ſuch charities.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.p: And Scholars pray for their increaſe.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Fare you well, Sir, theſe fellows may pray for you, you have made the Scholars Commons exceed to day, and a word with you, Sir, you ſaid you liv'd by your wits, if you uſe this bounty, you'll begger your wits, believe it.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Oh Sir, I hope to encreaſe 'em by it, this ſeed never wants his harveſt, fare you well, Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: I think a man were as good meet with a reaſonable Thief, as an unreaſonable Begger ſometimes, I could find in my heart to beg half mine back agen, can you change my piece my friends?

l.hi: Tempora mutantur, & nos mutamur in illis.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: My Gold is turn'd into Latine.
Look you good fellows, here's one round
Shilling more that lay conceal'd.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Sir, away, we ſhall be drawn farther into damage elſe.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: A pox of the Fool, he live by his wits? if his wits leave him any money, but what he begs or ſteals very ſhortly, I'll be hang'd for him.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: This breakfaſt parcel was well fetcht off i'faith.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Tuſh, a by-blow for mirth, we muſt have better purchaſe, we want a fourth for another project that I have ripen'd.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.p: My wife ſhe ſhares, and can deſerve it.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: She can change her ſhape, and be maſculine.

sp.speaker: Ruin,
sp.p: 'Tis one of the free'ſt conditions, ſhe fears not the crack of a Piſtol, ſhe dares ſay Stand to a Grazier.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Good, then you Sir Bacchus, Apollo ſhall be diſpatcht with her ſhare, and ſome contents to meet us to morrow (at a certain place and time appointed) i • the Maſculine Gender, my Father has a Nephew, and • an own Coſin coming up from the Univerſity, whom he loves moſt indulgently, eaſie Maſter Credulous Oldcraft (for you know what your meer Academique is) your Carrier never miſſes his hour, he muſt not be rob'd (becauſe he has but little to loſe) but he muſt joyn with •• in a deviſe that I have, that ſhall rob my Father of a hundred pieces, and thank me to be rid on't, for there's the ambition of my wit, to live upon his profeſt wit, that has turn'd me out to live by my wits.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: And to confirm your ſelf in me renate,
I hope you'll find my wits legitimate. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: NAy Lady.
Lady. Put me not in mind on't, prethee,
You cannot do a greater wrong to Women,
For in our wants, 'tis the moſt chief affliction
To have that name remembred; 'tis a Title
That miſery mocks us by, and the worlds malice,
Scorn and contempt has not wherewith to work
On humble Callings; they are ſafe, and lye
Level with pitty ſtill, and pale diſtreſs
Is no great ſtranger to 'em; but when fortune
Looks with a ſtormy face on our conditions,
We find affliction work, and envy paſtime,
And our worſt enemy than that, moſt abuſes us,
Is that we are call'd by, Lady, Oh my ſpirit,
Will nothing make thee humble? I am well methinks,
And can live quiet with my fate ſometimes,
Until I look into the world agen,
Then I begin to rave at my Stars bitterneſs,
To ſee how many muckhils plac'd above me;
Peaſants and Droyls, Caroches full of Dunghils,
Whoſe very birth ſtinks in a generous noſtril,
Gliſtring by night like Glow-worms through the High ſtreets
H • rried by Torch-light in the Foot-mans hands
That ſhew like running Fire-drakes through the City,
And I put to my ſhifts and wits to live,
Nay ſometimes danger too; on Foot, on Horſeback,
And earn my ſupper manfully e'r I get it,
Many a meal I have purchas'd at that rate,
Fed with a wound upon me, ſtampt at midnight.
Hah, what are you?

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Now you may tell your ſelf, Lady. Pulls off's beard.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Oh Mr. Priſcian, what's the project,
For you ne'r come without one.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Firſt, your Husband,
Sir Ruinous Gentry greets you with beſt wiſhes,
And here has ſent you your full ſhare by me
In five Cheats and two Robberies.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: And what comes it too?

sp.speaker: Priſc.
sp.l: Near upon thirteen pound.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: A goodly ſhare,
'Twill put a Lady ſcarce in Philip and Cheyney,
With three ſmall Bugle Laces, like a Chamber-maid,
Here's precious liſting.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: 'Las you muſt conſider, Lady,
'Tis but young Term, Attornies ha ſmall doings yet,
Then Highway Lawyers, they muſt needs ha little,
We'ave had no great good luck to ſpeak troth, Beauty,
Since your ſtout Ladyſhip parted from's at Highgate,
But there's a fair hope now for a pr • ſent hunder'd,
Here's mans Apparel, your Horſe ſtands at door.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: And what's the virtuous plot now?

sp.speaker: Priſc.
sp.l: Marry Lady,
You, like a brave young Gallant muſt be robb'd.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: I robb'd?

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Nay then—

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Well, well, go on, let's hear Sir.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Here's a ſeal'd bag of a Hunder'd, which indeed
Are Counters all, only ſome ſixteen Groats
Of white money i'th' mouth on't.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: So, what Saddle have I?

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Monſieur Laroon's the Frenchmans.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: That agen,
You know ſo well it is not for my ſtride,
How oft have I complain'd on't?

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: You may have Jocke's then, the little Scotch one,
You muſt diſpatch. Exit Priſ.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: I'll ſoon be ready, Sir,
Before you ha ſhifted Saddles, many Women
Have their wealth flow to 'em, I was made I ſee
To help my fortune, not my fortune me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: My ways are Goblin-led, and the night-Elf
Still draws me from my home, yet I follow,
Sure, 'tis not altogether fabulous,
Such Haggs do get dominion of our tongues
So ſoon as we ſpeak, the Inchantment binds;
I have diſſembled ſuch a trouble on me,
As my beſt wits can hardly clear agen;
Piping through this old reed, the Guardianeſs,
With purpoſe that my harmony ſhall reach
And pleaſe the Ladies ear, ſhe ſtops below,
And ecchoes back my Love unto my Lips,
Perſwaded by moſt violent arguments
Of ſelf-love in her ſelf; I am ſo ſelf-fool,
To doat upon her hunder'd wrinkl'd face;
I could beggar her to accept the gifts
She would throw upon me; 'twere charity,
But for pities ſake I will be a niggard
And undo her, refuſing to take from her;
I'm haunted agen, if it take not now
I'll break the Spell.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Sweet Cuningam, welcome;
What? a whole day abſent? Birds that build Neſts
Have care to keep 'em.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: That's granted,
But not continually to ſit upon 'em;
Leſs in the youngling ſeaſon, elſe they deſire
To fly abroad, and recreate their labours,
Then they return with freſher appetite
To work agen.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Well, well, you have built a Neſt
That will ſtand all ſtorms, you need not miſtruſt
A weather-wrack, and one day it may be
The youngling ſeaſon too, then I hope
You'll ne'er fly out of ſight.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: There will be pains,
I ſee to ſhake this Burr off, and ſweeteſt,
Prethee how fares thy charge? has my good friend
Sir Gregory, the countenance of a Lover?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: No by my troth, not in my mind, methinks
(Setting his Worſhip aſide) he looks like a fool.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Nay i'faith, ne'r divide his Worſhip from him for that
Small matter; Fool and Worſhip are no ſuch
Strangers now adaies, but my meaning is,
Has he thy Ladies countenance of Love?
Looks ſhe like a welcome on him? plainly,
Have they as good hope of one another,
As Cupid bleſs us, we have?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Troth I know not,
I can perceive no forwardneſs in my charge,
But I proteſt I wiſh the Knight better
For your ſake, Bird.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why thanks ſweet Bird, and with my heart I wiſh,
That he had as ſtrong and likely hope of her
As thou haſt of me.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Well, he's like to ſpeed
Ne'er the worſe for that good wiſh, and I'll tell you
Bird (for ſecrets are not to be kept betwixt us two)
My charge thinks well of you.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Of me? for what?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: For my ſake' I mean ſo, I have heard her
A hundred times, ſince her Uncle gave her
The firſt bob about you, that ſhe'd doe ſomewhat
For my ſake, if things went well together,
We have ſpoke of doors and bolts, and things and things,
Go too, I'll tell you all, but you'll find
Some advancement, for my ſake, I do believe.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Faith be not ſparing, tell me.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: By my Lady
You ſhall pardon me for that, 'twere a ſhame
If men ſhould hear all that women ſpeak behind
Their backs ſometimes.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You muſt give me leave yet,
At leaſt to give her thanks.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Nor that neither,
She muſt not take notice of my blabbing,
It is ſufficient you ſhall give me thanks,
For 'tis for my ſake if ſhe be bountiful,
She loves me, and loves you too for my ſake.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: How ſhall I, knowing this, but be ingrate,
Not to repay her with my deareſt duty.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: I, but you muſt not know it, if you tell
All that I open to you; you'll ſhame us both;
A far off you may kiſs your hand, bluſh or ſo,
But I'll allow no nearer conference.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Whoop! you'll be jealous I perceive now.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Jealous? why there's no true love without it, Bird,
I muſt be jealous of thee, but for her,
(Were it within my duty to my Maſter)
I durſt truſt her with the ſtrongeſt temper,
And I dare ſwear her now as pure a Virgin
If thoughts may be untainted, hers are ſo.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And where's the cauſe of your fear then?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Well, well;
When things are paſt, and the wedding Torches
Lighted at Matches, to kindle better fire,
Then I'll tell you more.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Come, come, I ſee farther,
That if we were married, you'd be jealous.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: I proteſt I ſhould a little, but not of her
It is the married woman (if you mark it)
And not the Maid that longs, the appetite
Follows the firſt taſte, when we have reliſht
We wiſh cloying, the taſte once pleas'd before,
Then our deſire is whetted on to more,
But I reveal too much to you, i'faith Bird.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Not a whit i'faith, Bird, betwixt you and I,
I am beholding for bettering of my knowledg.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Nay, you ſhall know more of me, if you'll, be rul'd
But make not things common.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Ud' ſo, your Lady?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: I, 'tis no matter, ſhe'll like well of this,
Our familiarity is her content.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: This preſent from Sir Gregery?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: From my Maſter, the Worſhipful, right Sir Gregery Fop.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: A Ruffe? and what might be his high conceit
In ſending of a Ruff?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I think he had two conceits in it forſooth, too high too Low, Ruff high, becauſe as the Ruff does embrace your neck all day, ſo does he deſire to throw his Knightly Arms.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: But then I leave him off a-nights.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Why then he is ruffe low, a ruffian, a bold adventurous errand to do any rough ſervice for his Lady.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: A witty and unhappy conceit. does he mean (Toward Cuning.
As he ſeems to ſay unto that reverence?
He does wooe her ſure.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: To tell you you truth, Lady, his conceit was far better than I have blaz'd it yet.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: Do you think ſo, Sir?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Nay, I know it forſooth, for it was two days, e'r he compaſs'd it, to find a ſitting preſent for your Ladyſhip, he was ſending once a very fine Puppy to you.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: And that he would have brought himſelf.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: So he would indeed, but then he alter'd his device, and ſent this Ruffe; requeſting with all, that whenſoever it is foul, you (with your own hands) would beſtow the ſtarching of it.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: And what was the reaſon for that, Sir? Toward Cun.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: There lies his main conceit, Lady, for ſays he, in ſo doing ſhe cannot chuſe but in the ſtarching, to clap it often between her hands, and ſo ſhe gives a great liking and applauſe to my Preſent, whereas, if I ſhould ſend a Puppy, ſhe ever calls it to her with hiſt, hiſs, hiſs, which is a fearful diſgrace, he drew the device from a Play, at the Bull tother day.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: I marry Sir, this was a rich conceit indeed.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: And far fetch'd, therefore good for you, Lady.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: How now? which way look you, Bird?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: At the Fool Bird, ſhall I not look at the Fool?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: At the Fool and I here? what need that? pray look this way.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: I'll fit him aptly, either I'll awake
His wits (if he have any,) or force him
To appear (as yet I cannot think him)
Without any. Sirrah, tell me one thing true
That I ſhall aske you now, Was this device
Your Maſters own? I doubt his wit in it;
He's not ſo ingenuous.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: His own I aſſure you, Madam.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: Nay, you muſt not lye.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Not with a Lady, I'd rather lye with you, than lie with my Maſter, by your leave in ſuch a caſe as this.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: Yet agen your eye?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: The fool makes mirth i'faith,
I would hear ſome.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: Come, you ſhall hear none but me.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Come hither, friend, nay, come nearer me; did
Thy Maſter ſend thee to me? he may be wiſe,
But did not ſhew it much in that; men ſometimes
May wrong themſelves unawares, when they leaſt think on't,
Was Vulcan ever ſo unwiſe to ſend Mars
To be his ſpokeſman, when he went a wooing?
Send thee? hey-ho, a pretty rowling eye.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I can turn vp the white and the black too, and need be forſooth.

sp.speaker: Neec.
sp.p: Why, here's an amorus noſe.
You ſee the worſt of my noſe, forſooth

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: A cheek, how I could put it now in dalliance,
A pair of Lips, oh that we were uney'd,
I could ſuck Sugar from 'em, what a beard's here?
When will the Knight thy Maſter have ſuch a
Stamp of man-hood on his face? nay, do not bluſh.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: 'Tis nothing but my fleſh and blood that riſes ſo.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Death, ſhe courts the fool.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Away, away, 'tis ſport, do not mind it.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Give me thy hand, come, be familiar;
Here's a promiſing palm; what a ſoft
Handful of pleaſure's here, here's Down compar'd
With Flocks and quilted Straw, thy Knights fingers
Are lean mattrice rubbers to theſe Feathers,
I prethee let me lean my cheek upon't.
What a ſoft pillow's here?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Hum, umh, hu, hum.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Why there's a courage in that lively paſſion,
Meaſure thee all o'r, there's not a limb
But has his full proportion, it is my voice,
There's no compare betwixt the Knight and thee,
The goodlier man behalf, at once now
I ſee thee all over.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p:
If you had ſeen me ſwim t'other day on my back, you would have ſed you had ſeen, there was two Chambermaids that ſaw me, and my legs by chance were tangled in the flags, and when they ſaw how I was hang'd,
they cryed out, Oh help the man for fear he be drown'd.

sp.speaker: Neec.
sp.p: They could do no leſs in pity, come thine arm, we'll walk together.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: Blindneſs of Love and Women, why ſhe dotes upon the fool.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: What's that to you, mind her not.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Away you Burr.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: How's that?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Hang of Fleſhook, faſten thine itchy claſpe
On ſome dry Toad-ſtool that will kindle with thee,
And burn together.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Oh abominable,
Why do you not love me?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: No, never did;
I took thee down a little way to
Enforce a Vomit from my offended ſtomach,
Now thou'rt up agen, I loath thee filthily.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Oh villain.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why doſt thou not ſee a ſight.
Would make a man abiure the ſight of Women.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha,, he's vext; ha, ha, ha,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Why doſt thou laugh?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Becauſe thou laugh'ſt, nothing elſe i'faith.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: She has but mockt my folly, elſe ſhe finds not
The boſome of my purpoſe, ſome other way,
Muſt make me know; I'll try her, and may chance quit
The fine dexterity of her Lady-wit. Exit.

sp.speaker: Neec.
sp.l: Yes introth, I laught to think of thy Maſter,
Now, what he would think if he knew this?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: By my troth I laugh at him too, faith ſirrah, he's but a fool to ſay the truth, though I ſay't, that ſhould not ſay't.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Yes, thou ſhouldſt ſay truth, and I believe thee;
Well, for this time we'll part, you perceive ſomething,
Our tongues betray our hearts, there's our weakneſs,
But pray be ſilent.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: As Mouſe in Cheeſe, or Gooſe in Hay i'faith.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Look, we are cut off, there's my hand where my Lips would be.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I'll wink, and think 'em thy Lips, farewel. Exit.

sp.speaker: Neece,
sp.l: Now Guardianeſs, I need not ask where you have been.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Oh Lady, never was woman ſo abus'd.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Doſt thou hear Lady, ſweet-heart, I had forgot to tell thee, if you will, I will come back in the evening.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.p: By no means, come not till I ſend for you.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: If there be any need, you may think of things when I am gone, I may be convey'd into your chamber, I'll lye under the bed while midnight, or ſo, or you ſhall put me up in one of your little boxes, I can creep in at a ſmall hole.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.p: Theſe are things I dare not venture, I charge you on my love, never come till I ſend for you.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Verbum inſapienti, 'tis enough to the wiſe, nor I think it is not fit the Knight ſhould know any thing yet.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.p: By no means, pray you go now, we are ſuſpected.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: For the things that are paſt, let us uſe our ſecrets.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Now I'll make a firm trial of your love,
As you love me, not a word more at this time,
Not a ſyllable, 'tis the ſeal of love, take heed.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Hum, hum, hum, hum—.
He humhs loath to depart. Exit Clown.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: So, this pleaſant trouble's gone, now Guardianeſs,
What? your eyes eaſing your heart, the cauſe woman?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: The cauſe is falſe man, Madam, oh Lady,
I have been gull'd in a ſhining Carbuncle,
A very Glo-worm, that I thought had fire in't,
And 'tis as cold as Ice.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: And juſtly ſerv'd,
Wouldſt thou once think that ſuch an early ſpring
Would dote upon thine Autumn?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Oh, had you heard him but proteſt.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: I would not have believ'd him,
Thou might'ſt have perceiv'd how I mock'd thy folly.
In wanton imitation with the Fool,
Go weep the ſin of thy credulity,
Not of thy loſs, for it was never thine,
And it is gain to miſs it; wert thou ſo dull?
Nay, yet thou'rt ſtupid and uncapable,
Why, thou wert but the bait to fiſh with, not
The prey, the ſtale to catch another Bird with.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Indeed he call'd me Bird.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Yet thou perceiv'ſt not,
It is your Neece he loves, wouldſt thou be made
A ſtalking Jade? 'tis ſhe examine it,
I'll hurry all awry, and tread my path
Over unbeaten grounds, go level to the mark,
Not by circular bouts, rare things are pleaſing,
And rare's but ſeldom in the ſimple ſence,
But has her Emphaſis with eminence. Exit.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: My Neece? ſhe the rival of my abuſe?
My fleſh and blood wrong me? I'll Aunt her for't;
Oh opportunity, thou bleſſeſt me
Now Gentlewoman are you parted ſo ſoon?
Where's your friend I pray? your Cuningam?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What ſay you Aunt?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Come, come, your Cuningame?
I am not blind with age yet, nor deaf.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Dumb I am ſure you are not, what all you Aunt?
Are you not well?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: No, nor ſick, nor mad, nor in my wits, nor ſleeping, nor waking, nor nothing, nor any thing; I know not what I am, nor what I am not,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Mercy cover us, what do you mean, Aunt?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: I mean to be reveng'd.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: On whom?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: On thee Baggage.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Revenge ſhould follow injury,
Which never reacht ſo far as thought in me
Towards you Aunt,

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Your cunning, minion.
Nor your Cuningame; can either blind me,
The gentle Beggar loves you.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Beſeech you,
Let me ſtay your error, I begin to hear,
And ſhake off my amazement; if you think
That ever any paſſage treating love
Hath been betwixt us yet commenc'd, any
Silent eye-glance that might but ſparkle fire,
So much as Brother and Siſter might meet with,
The Lip-ſalute, ſo much as ſtrangers might
Take a farewel with, the commixed hands,
Nay, but the leaſt thought of the leaſt of theſe;
In troth you wrong your boſom, by that truth
(Which I think yet you durſt be bail for in me,
If it were offer'd ye) I am as free
As all this proteſtation.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: May I believe this?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: If ever you'll believe truth: why, I thought he had ſpoke love to you, and if his heart prompted his tongue, ſure I did hear ſo much.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Oh falſeſt man, Ixion's plague fell on me,
Never by woman (ſuch a maſculine cloud)
So airy and ſo ſubtle was embrac'd.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: By no cauſe in me, by my life dear Aunt.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: I believe you, then help in my revenge,
And you ſhall do't, or loſe my love for ever,
I'll have him quitted at his equal weapon,
Thou art young, follow him, bait his deſires
With all the Engines of a womans wit,
Stretch modeſty even to the higheſt pitch;
He cannot freeze at ſuch a flaming beauty;
And when thou haſt him by th' amorous gills,
Think on my vengeance, choak up his deſires,
Then let his banquetings be Tantaliſme,
Let thy diſdain ſpurn the diſſembler out;
Oh I ſhould climb my Stars, and ſit above,
To ſee him burn to aſhes in his love.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: This will be a ſtrange taſte, Aunt, and an
Unwilling labour, yet in your injunction
I am a ſervant to't.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Thou'lt undertak't?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, let the ſucceſs commend it ſelf hereafter.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Effect it Girl, my ſubſtance is thy ſtore,
Nothing but want of Will makes woman poor. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Why Pompey, thou art not ſtark mad, art thou?
Wilt thou not tell me how my Lady does?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Your Lady.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Did ſhe receive the thing that I ſent her kindly, or no:

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: The thing that you ſent her, Knight, by the thing that you ſent, was for the things ſake that was ſent to carry the thing that you ſent, very kindly receiv'd; firſt, there is your Indenture, now go ſeek you a ſervant: ſecondly, you are a Knight: thirdly and laſtly, I am mine own man: and fourthly, fare you well.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Why Pompey? prethee let me ſpeak with thee,
I'll lay my life ſome hare has croſt him.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Knight, if you be a Knight, ſo keep you; as for the Lady, who ſhall ſay that ſhe is not a fair Lady, a ſweet Lady, an honeſt and a virtuous Lady, I will ſay he is a baſe fellow, a blab of his tongue, and I will make him eat theſe fingers ends.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Why, here's no body ſays ſo Pompey.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Whatſoever things have paſt between the Lady and the other party, whom I will not name at this time, I ſay ſhe is virtuous and honeſt, and I will maintain it, as long as I can maintain my ſelf with bread and water.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Why I know no body thinks otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Any man that does but think it in my hearing, I will make him think on't while he has a thought in his boſom; ſhall we ſay that kindneſſes from Ladies are common? or that favours and proteſtations are things of no moment betwixt parties and parties? I ſay ſtill, whatſoever has been betwixt the Lady and the party, which I will not name, that ſhe is honeſt, and ſhall be honeſt, whatſoever ſhe does by day or by night, by light or by darkneſs, with cut and long tail.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Why I ſay ſhe is honeſt.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Is ſhe honeſt? in what ſenſe do you ſay ſhe is honeſt, Knight?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: If I could not find in my heart to throw my dagger at thy head, hilts and all, I'm an aſs, and no Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Throw your Dagger at me! do not Knight, I give you fair warning, 'tis but caſt away if you do, for you ſhall have no other words of me, the Lady is an honeſt Lady, whatſoever reports may go of ſports and toys, and thoughts, and words, and deeds, betwixt her and the party which I will not name; this I give you to underſtand, That another man may have as good an eye, as amorous a noſe, as fair a ſtampt beard, and be as proper a man as a Knight, (I name no parties) a Servingman may be as good as a Sir, a Pompey as a Gregory, a Doodle as a Fop; ſo Servingman Pompey Doodle, may be reſpected as well with Ladies (though I name no parties) as Sir Gregory Fop; ſo farewell: Exit.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: If the fellow be not out of his wits, then will I never have any more wit while I live; either the ſight of the Lady has gaſter'd him, or elſe he's drunk, or elſe he walks in his ſleep, or elſe's a fool, or a knave, or both, one of the three, I'm ſure 'tis; yet now I think on't, ſhe has not us'd me ſo kindly as her Uncle promis'd me ſhe ſhould, but that's all one, he ſays I ſhall have her, and I dare take his word for the beſt worſe I have, and that's a weightier thing than a Lady, I'm ſure on't. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Lady Ruinous (as a man) Witty-Pate, Sir Ruinous, Priſcian, and Maſter Credulous (binding and robbing her, and in Scarfs) Credulous finds the bag.

sp.speaker: Lady Ruin.
sp.l: Nay, I am your own, 'tis in your pleaſure
How you'll deal with me; yet I would intreat,
You will not make that which is bad enough,
Worſe than it need be, by a ſecond ill,
When it can render you no ſecond profit;
If it be coin you ſeek, you have your prey,
All my ſtore I vow, (and it weighs a hundred)
My life, or any hurt you give my body,
Can inrich you no more.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: You may purſue.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: As I am a Gentleman; I never will,
Only we'll bind you to quiet behaviour
Till you call out for Bail, and on th' other
Side of the hedge leave you; but keep the peace
Till we be out of hearing, for by that
We ſhall be out of danger, if we come back,
We come with a miſchief.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: You need not fear me.

sp.speaker: Priſe.
sp.l: Come, we'll beſtow you then.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.p: Why law you Sir, is not this a ſwifter Reven •• than, Sic probas, ergo's & igitur's can bring in? why is not this one of your Syllogiſmes in Barbara? Omne utile eſt boneſtum.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: Well Sir, a little more of this acquaintance,
Will make me know you fully, I proteſt.
You have (at firſt ſight) made me conſcious
Of ſuch a deed my dreams ne'er prompted, yet
I could almoſt have wiſh'd rather ye'ad rob'd me
Of my Cloak, (for my Purſe 'tis a Scholars)
Than to have made me a robber.
I had rather have anſwered three difficult queſtions,
Than this one, as eaſie, as yet it ſeems.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Tuſh, you ſhall never come to farther anſwer for't;
Can you confeſs your penurious Uncle,
In his full face of love, to be ſo ſtrict
A Nigard to your Commons, that you are fain
To ſize your belly out with Shoulder Fees?
With Rumps and Kidneys, and Cues of ſingle Beer,
And yet make Daymy to feed more daintily,
At this eaſier rate? ſie Maſter Credulous,
I bluſh for you.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: This is a truth undeniable.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Why go to then, I hope I know your Uncle,
How does he uſe his Son, nearer than you?

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: Faith, like his Jade, upon the bare Commons,
Turn'd out to pick his living as he can get it;
He would have been glad to have ſhar'd in ſuch
A purchaſe, and thank'd his good fortune too.
But mum no more—is all ſafe, Bullies?

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Secure, the Gentleman thinks him moſt happy in his loſs,
With his ſafe life and limbs, and redoubles
His firſt vow, as he is a Gentleman,
Never to purſue us.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Well away then,
Diſperſe you with Maſter Credulous, who ſtill
Shall bear the purchaſe, Priſcian and I,
Will take ſome other courſe: You know our meeting
At the Three Cups in St Gile's, with this proviſo,
(For 'tis a Law with us) that nothing be open'd
Till all be preſent, the looſer ſaies a hundred,
And it can weigh no leſs.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Come, Sir, we'll be your guide.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: My honeſty, which till now was never forfeited,
All ſhall be cloſe till our meeting. Exit Cred. and Ruin.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Tuſh, I believ't,
And then all ſhall out; where's the thief that's robb'd?

sp.speaker: L. Rui.
sp.l: Here Maſter Oldcraft, all follows now.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: 'Twas neatly done, wench, now to turn that bag
Of counterfeits to current pieces, & actum eſt.

sp.speaker: L. Rui.
sp.l: You are the Chymiſt, we'll blow the fire ſtill,
If you can mingle the ingredients.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: I will not miſs a cauſe, a quantity, a dram,
You know the place.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: I have told her that, Sir.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Good, turn Ruinous to be a Conſtable, I'm ſure
We want not beards of all ſorts, from the
Worſhipful Magiſtrate to the under Watchman;
Becauſe we muſt have no danger of life,
But a cleanly cheat, attach Credulous,
The cauſe is plain, the theft found about him;
Then fall I in his own Coſins ſhape
By mere accident, where finding him diſtreſt,
I with ſome difficulty muſt fetch him off,
With promiſe that his Uncle ſhall ſhut up all
With double reſtitution: Maſter Conſtable, Ruinous
His mouth ſhall be ſtopt; you, Miſtriſs rob-thief,
Shall have your ſhare of what we can gull my Father of;
Is't plain enough?

sp.speaker: L. Rui.
sp.l: As plain a cozenage as can be, faith.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Father, I come again, and again when this is
Paſt too, Father, one will beget another;
I'd be loath to leave your poſterity barren,
You were beſt come to compoſition Father,
Two hundred pieces yearly allow me yet,
It will be the cheaper (Father) than my wit,
For I will cheat none but you, dear Father.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Old Knight, and Sir Gregory.

sp.speaker: Old. K.
sp.l: WHy now you take the courſe Sir Gregory Fop:
I could enforce her, and I liſt but love
That's gently won, is a man's own for ever,
Have you prepar'd good Muſick?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: As fine a noiſe, Uncle, as heart can wiſh.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Why that's done like a Suitor,
They muſt be woo'd a hundred ſeveral ways,
Before you obtain the right way in a woman,
'Tis an odd creature, full of creeks and windings.
The Serpent has not more; for ſh'as all his,
And then her own beſide came in by her mother.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: A fearful portion for a man to venture on.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: But the way found once by the wits of men,
There is no creature lies ſo tame agen.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: I promiſe you, not a houſe-Rabbit, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: No ſucker on 'em all.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: What a thing's that?
They're pretty fools I warrant, when they'r tame
As a man can lay his lips too.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: How were you bred, Sir?
Did you never make a fool of a Tenants daughter?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Never i'faith, they ha' made ſome fools for me,
And brought 'em many a time under their aprons.

sp.speaker: Old R.
sp.l: They could not ſhew you the way plainlier, I think,
To make a fool again.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: There's fools enough, Sir,
'Leſs they were wiſer.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: This is wondrous rare,
Come you to London with a Maiden-head, Knight?
A Gentleman of your rank ride with a Cloak-bag?
Never an Hoſteſs by the way to leave it with?
Nor Tapſters Siſter? nor head-Oſtlers Wife?
What no body?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Well mock'd old Wit-monger,
I keep it for your Neece.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Do not ſay ſo for ſhame, ſhe'll laugh at thee,
A wife ne'er looks for't, 'tis a batchelors penny,
He may giv't to a begger-wench, i'th' progreſs time, Ex.
And ne'er be call'd to account for't.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Would I had known ſo much,
