I could ha' ſtopt a beggers mouth by th' way.
That rail'd upon me, 'cauſe I'd give her nothing—
What, are they come?

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.l: And plac'd directly, Sir,
Under her window.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: What may I call you, Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A poor ſervant to the Viol, I'm the Voice, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: In good time Maſter Voice.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Indeed good time does get the maſtery.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: What Countreyman, Maſter Voice?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Sir, born at Ely, we all ſet up in Ela
But our houſe commonly breaks in Rutland-ſhire.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: A ſhrewd place by my faith, it may well break your voice,
It breaks many a mans back; come, ſet to your buſineſs.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: FAin would I wake you, Sweet, but fear
I ſhould invite you to worſe chear;
In your dreams you cannot fare
Meaner than Muſick; no compare;
None of your ſlumbers are compil'd
Ʋnder the pleaſure makes a Child;
Your day-delights, ſo well compact,
That what you think, turns all to act:
I'd wiſh my life no better play,
Your dream by night, your thought by day.
Wake gently, wake,
Part ſoftly from your dreams;
The morning flies
To your fair eyes,
To take her ſpecial beams:

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: I hear her up, here Maſter Voice,
Pay you the Inſtruments, ſave what you can.
To keep you when you're crackt. Exit Boy.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Who ſhould this be?
That I'm ſo much beholding to, for ſweetneſs?
Pray Heaven it happens right.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Good morrow, Miſtriſs.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: An ill day and a thouſand come upon thee,

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: 'Light, that's ſix hundred more than any Almanack has.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Comes it from thee? it is the mangieſt Muſick
That ever woman heard.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Nay, ſay not ſo, Lady,
There's not an itch about 'em.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: I could curſe
My attentive powers, for giving entrance to't;
There is no boldneſs like the impudence
That's lockt in a fools bloud, how durſt you do this?
In conſcience I abus'd you as ſufficiently
As woman could a man; inſatiate Coxcomb,
The mocks and ſpiteful language I have given thee,
Would o' my life ha? ſerv'd ten reaſonable men,
And riſe contented too, and left enough for their friends.
Thou glutton at abuſes, never ſatisfied?
I am perſwaded thou devour'ſt more flouts
Than all thy body's worth, and ſtill a hungred!
A miſchief of that maw, prethee ſeek elſewhere,
Introth I am weary of abuſing thee;
Get thee a freſh Miſtriſs, thou'ſt make work enough;
I do not think there's ſcorn enough in Town
To ſerve thy turn, take the Court-Ladies in,
And all their Women to 'em, that exceed 'em.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Is this in earneſt, Lady?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Oh unſatiable!
Doſt thou count all this but an earneſt yet?
I'd thought I'd paid thee all the whole ſum, truſt me;
Thou'lt begger my deriſion utterly
If thou ſtay'ſt longer, I ſhall want a laugh:
If I knew where to borrow a contempt
Would hold thee tack, ſtay and be hang'd, thou ſhouldſt then:
But thou'ſt no conſcience now to extort hate from me,
When one has ſpent all ſhe can make upon thee;
Muſt I begin to pay thee hire again?
After I have rid thee twice? faith 'tis unreaſonable.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Say you ſo? I'll know that preſently. Exit.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Now he runs
To fetch my Uncle to this muſty bargain,
But I have better ware always at hand.
And lay by this ſtill, when he comes to cheapen.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I met the Muſick now, yet cannot learn
What entertainment he receiv'd from her

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: There's ſome body ſet already, I muſt to't, I ſee,
Well, well, Sir Gregory?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Hah, Sir Gregory?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Where e'er you come, you may well boaſt your conqueſt.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: She's loſt y'ſaith, enough, has fortune then
Remembred her great boy? ſhe ſeldom fails 'em.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: H' was the unlikelieſt man at firſt, methought,
To have my love, we never met but wrangled,

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: A pox upon that wrangling, ſay I ſtill,
I never knew it ſail yet, where e'er't came;
It never comes but like a ſtorm of hail,
'Tis ſure to bring fine weather at the tail on't,
There's not one match 'mongſt twenty made without it,
It fights i' th' tongue, but ſure to agree i' th' haunches.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: That man that ſhould ha' told me when time was.
I ſhould ha' had him, had been laught at piteouſly,
But ſee how things will change?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Here's a heart feels it—Oh the deceitful promiſes of love!
What truſt ſhould a man put i' th' lip of woman?
She kiſt me with that ſtrength, as if ſh'ad meant
To ha' ſet the fair print of her ſoul upon me.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: I would ha' ſworn 'twould ne'er ha been a match once.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I'll hear no more, I'm mad to hear ſo much,
Why ſhould I aim my thoughts at better fortunes
Than younger brothers have? that's a Maid with nothing.
Or ſome old Soap-boilers Widow, without Teeth,
There waits my fortune for me; ſeek no farther. Ex. Cun.

div.stage: Enter Old Knight, and Sir Gregory

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: You tell me things, Sir Gregory, that cannot be.
She will not, nor ſhe dares not.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Would I were whipt then.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: I'll make as little ſhew of love, Sir Gregory.
As ever Woman did, you ſhall not know
You have my heart a good while.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Heard you that?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Man will inſult ſo ſoon, 'tis his condition,
'Tis good to keep him off as long as we can,
I've much ado, I ſwear; and love i' th' end
Will have his courſe, let Maids do what they can,
They are but frail things till they end in man.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: What ſay you to this, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: This is ſomewhat handſome.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: And by that little wrangling that I fain'd,
Now I ſhall try how conſtant his love is,
Although't went ſore againſt my heart to chide him.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Alas poor Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Old K,
sp.l: Now y'are ſure of truth,
You hear her own thoughts ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: They ſpeak indeed.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Go, you're a brainleſs Coax; a Toy, a Fop,
I'll go no farther than your name, Sir Gr.
I'll right my ſelf there; were you from this place,
You ſhould perceive I'm heartily angry with you,
Offer to ſow ſtrife 'twixt my Neece and I?
Good morrow Neece, good morrow.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Many fair one to you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Go, you're a Coxcomb. How doſt Neece this morning?
An idle ſhallo • fool: ſleep'ſt thou well, Girl?
Fortune may very well provide thee Lordſhips,
For honeſty has left thee little manners.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: How am I • ang' do' both ſides?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Abuſe kindneſſe? Will't take the air to day Neece?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: When you pleaſe, Sir,
There ſtands the Heir behind you I muſt take,
(Which I'd as liaeve take, as take him I ſwear.)

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: La' you; do you hear't continued to your teeth now?
A pox of all ſuch Gregories; what a hand Neece le • s fa • her Scarfe.
Have I with you?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: No more y'ſeck, I ha' done, Sir:
Lady, your Scarf's fal'n down.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: 'Tis but your luck, Sir,
And does preſage the Miſtriſs muſt fall ſhortly,
You may wear it, and you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: There's a trick for you,
You're parlouſly belov'd, you ſhould complain.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Yes, when I complain, Sir,
Then do your worſt, there I'll deceive you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: You are a Dolt, and ſo I leave you, Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Ah ſirrah, Miſtriſs were you caught, i'faith?
We overheard you all; I muſt not know
I have your heart, take heed o' that, I pray,
I knew ſome Scarf would come.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: He's quite gone, ſure:
Ah you baſe Coxcomb, couldſt thou come again?
And ſo abus'd as thou waſt?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: 'Twould ha' kill'd
A ſenſible man, he would ha' gone to his chamber,
And broke his heart by this time.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Thank you heartily.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Or ſixt a naked Rapier in a Wall,
Like him that earn'd his Knighthood, e'r he had it,
And then refus'd upon't, ran up to th' hilts.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Yes, let him run for me, I was never brought up to 't,
I never profeſt running i' my life.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: What art thou made on? thou tough villanous vermin.
Will nothing deſtroy thee?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Yes, yes, aſſure your ſelf
Unkind words may do much.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Why, doſt thou want 'em?
I've e'en conſum'd my ſpleen to help thee to 'em:
Tell me what ſort of words they be would ſpeed thee?
I'll ſee what I can do yet.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: I'm much beholding to you,
You're willing to beſtow huge pains upon me.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: I ſhould account nothing too much to rid thee.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: I wonder you'd not offer to deſtroy me,
All the while your Uncle was here.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Why there thou betray'ſt thy houſe; we of the Old-Crafts.
Were born to more wit than ſo.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I wear your favor here.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Would it might rot thy arme off: if thou knewſt
With what contempt thou haſt it, what hearts bitterneſs,
How many cunning curſes came along with it,
Thoud'ſt quake to handle it.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: A pox, tak't again then;
Who'd be thus plagu'd of all hands?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: No, wear't ſtill,
But long I hope thou ſhalt not, 'tis but caſt
Upon thee, purpoſely to ſerve another
That has more right to't, as in ſome Countries they convey
Their treaſure upon Aſſes to their friends;
If mine be but ſo wiſe, and apprehenſive,
As my opinion gives him to my heart,
It ſtayes not long on thy deſertleſs arme;
I'll make thee e'er I ha' done, not dare to wear
Anything of mine, although I give't thee freely;
Kiſs it you may, and make what ſhew you can,
But ſure you carry't to a worthier Man,
And ſo good morrow to you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Hu hum, ha hum;
I han't the ſpirit now to daſh my brains out,
Nor the audacity to kill my ſelf,
But I could cry my heart out, that's as good,
For ſo't be out, no matter which way it comes,
If I can dye with a ſillip, or depart
At hot-cockles, What's that to any man?
If there be ſo much death that ſerves my turn there.
Every one knows the ſtate of his own body,
No Carrion kills a Kite, but then agen
There's Cheeſe will choak a Daw; time I were dead I'faith,
If I knew which way without hurt or danger.
I am a Maiden-Knight, and cannot look
Upon a naked weapon with any modeſty,
Elſe 'twould go hard with me, and to complain
To Sir Perſidious the old Knight agen,
Were to be more abus'd; perhaps he would beat me well,
But ne'er believe me.
And few Men dye o' beating, that were loſt too:
Oh, here's my friend, I'll make my moan to him.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I cannot tear her memory from my heart,
That treads mine down, was ever man ſo fool'd
That profeſt wit?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: O Cuningame?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Sir Gregory?
The choice, the Victor, the Towns happy Man?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: 'Snigs, What do'ſt mean? come I to thee for comfort, and do'ſt abuſe me too?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Abuſe you? How Sir?
With juſtifying your fortune, and your joyes?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Pray hold your hand, Sir, I've been bob'd enough,
You come with a new way now; ſtrike me merrily,
But when a man's ſore beaten o' both ſides already,
Then the leaſt tap in jeſt goes to the guts on him;
Wilt ha the truth? I'm made the rankeſt aſs
That e'er was born to Lordſhips.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: What? No Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I had not thought my body could a yielded
All thoſe foul ſcurvie names that ſhe has call'd me,
I wonder whence ſhe fetcht 'em?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Is this credible?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: She pin'd this Scarf upon me before her Unckle,
But his back turn'd, ſhe cur'ſt me ſo for wearing on't,
The very brawn of mine arme has ak'd ever ſince,
Yet in a manner forc't me to wear't ſtill,
But hop't I ſhould not long; if good luck ſerve
I ſhould meet one that has more wit and worth
Should take it from me, 'twas but lent to me,
And ſent to him for a token.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I conceit it, I know the Man
That lies in wait for't, part with't by all means,
In any caſe, you are way-laid about it.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: How Sir? way-laid?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Pox of a Scarf, ſay I,
I prize my friends life 'bove a million on 'em,
You ſhall be rul'd, Sir, I know more than you.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: If you know more than I, let me be rid on't,
'Laſs, 'tis not for my wearing, ſo ſhe told me.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: No, no, give me't, the knave ſhall miſs his purpoſe,
And you ſhall live.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I would, as long as I could, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: No more replyes, you ſhall, I'll prevent this,
Pompey ſhall ma • ch without it.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: What, is't he?
My Man that was?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Call him your deadly Enemy;
You give him too fair a name, you deal too nobly,
He bears a bloody mind, a cruel foe, Sir,
I care not if he heard me.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: But, Do you hear, Sir?
Can't found with reaſon ſhe ſhould affect him?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Do you talk of reaſon? I never thought to have heard
Such a word come from you; reaſon in love?
Would you give that, no Doctor could e'er give?
Has not a Deputy married his Cook-maid?
An Aldermans Widow, one that was her turn-broach?
Nay, Has not a great Lady brought her Stable
Into her Chamber: lay with her Horſe-keeper?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Did ever love play ſuch Jades tricks, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Oh thouſands, thouſands: Beware a ſturdy Clown e're while you live, Sir;
'Tis like a huſwifery in moſt Shires about us;
You ſhall ha' Farmers Widows wed thin Gentlemen,
Much like your ſelf, but put 'em to no ſtreſs;
What work can they do, with ſmall trap-ſtick legs?
They keep Clowns to ſtop gaps, and drive in pegs,
A drudgery fit for Hindes, e'en back agen, Sir,
Your're ſafeſt at returning.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Think you ſo, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: But, How came this Clown to be call'd Pompey firſt?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Puſh, one good-man Caeſar, a Pump-maker kerſen'd him;
Pompey he writes himſelf, but his right name's Pumpey,
And ſtunk too when I had him, now he's crank.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I'm glad I know ſo much to quell his pride, Sir,
Walk you ſtill that way, I'll make uſe of this,
To reſolve all my doubts, and place this favor
On ſome new Miſtriſs, only for a try,
And if it meet my thoughts, I'll ſwear 'tis I. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Is Pompey grown ſo malepert? ſo ſrampel?
The onely cutter about Ladies honors?
And his blade ſooneſt out?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Now, What's the news, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Gre.
sp.l: I dare not ſay but good; oh excellent good, Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: I hope now you're reſolv'd ſhe loves you, Knight?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Cuds me, What elſe Sir? that's not to do now.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: You would not think how deſperately you anger'd me,
When you bely'd her goodneſs; oh you vext me,
Even to a Palſey.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: What a thing was that Sir?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: 'Tis, that 'tis; as I have hope of ſweetneſs, the Scarfe's gone;
Worthy wiſe friend, I doat upon thy cunning,
We two ſhall be well matcht, our Iſſue-male, ſure
Will be born Counſellors; is't poſſible?
Thou ſhalt have another token out of hand for't;
Nay, ſince the way's found, pitty thou ſhouldſt want, y'faith,
O my beſt joy, and deareſt.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Well ſaid, Neece,
So violent 'fore your Uncle? What will you do
In ſecret then?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Marry call me ſlave, and raſcal.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Your Scarfe—the Scarfe I gave you—

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Maſs that's true Neece,
I ne'er thought upon that; the Scarfe ſhe gave you—Sir?
What dumb? No anſwer from you? the Scarfe?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I was way-laid about it, my life threatned;
Life's life, Scarfe's but a Scarfe, and ſo I parted from't.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Unfortunate woman! my firſt favor too?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Will you be ſtill an aſs? no reconcilement
'Twixt you and wit? Are you ſo far fallen out,
You'l never come together? I tell you true,
I'm very Iowſily aſham'd on you,
That's the worſt ſhame that can be;
Thus bayting on him: now his heart's hook't in,
I'll make him, e'er I ha' done, take her with nothing,
I love a man that lives by his wits alife;
Nay leave, ſweet Neece, 'tis but a Scarfe, let it go.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: The going of it never grieves me, Sir.
It is the manner, the manner—

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: O diſſembling Marmaſet! If I durſt ſpeak,
Or could be believ'd when I ſpeak,
What a tale could I tell, to make hair ſtand upright now?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Nay, Sir, at your requeſt you ſhall perceive,
Uncle,
With what renewing love I forgive this?
Here's a fair Diamond, Sir, I'll try how long
You can keep that?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Not very long, you know't too,
Like a cunning witch as you are.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Y'are beſt let him ha' that too.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: So I were, I think, there were no living elſe,
I thank you, as you have handled the matter.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Why this is muſical now, and Tueſday next
Shall tune your Inſtruments, that's the day ſet.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: A match, good Uncle.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Sir, you hear me too?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Oh very well, I'm for you.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: What e'er you hear, you know my mind.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: I, a— on't, too well, if I do not wonder how we two ſhall come together, I'm a Bear whelp? he talks of Tueſday next, as familiarly, as if we lov'd one another, but 'tis as unlikely to me, as 'twas ſeven year before I ſaw her; I ſhall try his cunning, it may be he has a way was never yet thought on, and it had need to be ſuch a one, for all that I can think on will never do't; I look to have this Diamond taken from me very ſpeedily, therefore I'll take it off o' my finger, for if it be ſeen, I ſhall be way-laid for that too.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: OH torture! torture! thou carrieſt a ſting i'thy tail,
Thou never brought'ſt good news i'thy life yet,
And that's an ill quality, leave it when thou wilt.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Why you receive a bleſſing the wrong way, Sir,
Call you not this good newes? to ſave at once Sir
Your credit and your kinſmans life together;
Would it not vex your peace, and gaule your worth?
T'have one of your name hang'd?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Peace, no ſuch words, boy.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Be thankful for the bleſſing of prevention then.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Le' me ſee, there was none hang'd out of our ho • ſe ſince Brute,
I ha' ſearch't both Stow, and Hollinſhead.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: O Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: I'll ſee what Polychronicon ſayes anon too.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: 'Twas a miraculous fortune that I heard on't

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: I would thou'dſt never heard on't,

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: That's true too,
So it had ne'er been done; to ſee the luck on't,
He was ev'n brought to Juſtice Aurums threſhold,
There had ſlew'n forth a Mittimus ſtraight for Newgate;
And note the fortune too, Seſſions a Thurſday,
Jury cull'd out a Friday, Judgment a Saturday,
Dungeon a Sunday, Tyburne a Munday,
Miſeries quotidian ague, when't begins once,
Every day pulls him, till he pull his laſt.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: No more, I ſay, 'tis an ill theam: where left you him?

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: He's i'th' Conſtables hands below i'th' Hall, Sir,
Poor Gentleman, and his accuſer with him.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: What's he?

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: A Judges Son 'tis thought, ſo much the worſe too,
He'l hang his enemy, an't ſhall coſt him nothing,
That's a great priviledge.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Within there?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Call up the folks i'th' Hall. I had ſuch hope on him,
For a Scholar too, a thing thou ne'er waſt ſit for
Therefore erected all my joyes in him;
Got a Welch Benefice in reverſion for him,
Dean of Cardigan, has his grace already,
He can marry and bury, yet ne'er a hair on's face;
sp.stage: Enter Credulous, Sir Ruinous (as a Conſtable,) and Lady Gentry (as a Man.)
sp.l: Like a French Vicar, and, Does he bring ſuch fruits to Town with him?
A Thief at his firſt lighting? Oh good den to you.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Nay, ſweet Sir, you'r ſo vext now, you'l grie • e him,
And hurt your ſelf.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Away, I'll hear no counſel;
Come you but once in ſeven year to your Uncle,
And at that time muſt you be brought home too?
And by a Conſtable?

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Oh ſpeak low, Sir,
Remember your own credit, you profeſs
You love a Man o'wit, begin at home, Sir,
Expreſs it i'your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Nay, Maſter Conſtable,
Shew your ſelf a wiſe man, 'gainſt your nature too.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Sir, no Diſh-porridgment, we have brought home
As good men as ye.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Out, a North-Brittain Conſtable, that tongue
Will publiſh all, it ſpeaks ſo broad already;
Are you the Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: The unfortunate one, Sir,
That fell into the power of mercileſs Thieves,
Whereof this fellow, whom I'd call your kinſman,
As little as I could (for the fair reverence
I owe to fame and years) was the prime villain.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: A wicked prime.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Nay, not ſo loud, ſweet father.

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.l: The reſt are fled, but I ſhall meet with 'em,
Hang one of 'em I will certain, I ha' ſwore it,
And 'twas my luck to light upon this firſt.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: A Cambridge man for this? theſe your degrees, Sir?
Nine years at Univerſity for this fellowſhip?

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Take your voice lower, dear Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: What's your loſs, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: That which offends me to repeat, the Money's whole, Sir,
'Tis i'th' Conſtables hands there, a ſeal'd hundred,
But I will not receive it.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: No? Not the Money, Sir,
Having confeſt 'tis all?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: 'Tis all the Money, Sir,
But 'tis not all I loſt, for when they bound me,
They took a Diamond hung at my ſhirt ſtring,
Which fear of life made me forget to hide;
It being the ſparkling witneſs of a Contract,
'Twixt a great Lawyers daughter and my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: I told you what he was; What does the Diamond
Concern my Cozen, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: No more did the Money,
But he ſhall anſwer all now.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: There's your conſcience,
It ſhewes from whence you ſprung.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Sprung? I had leapt a Thief,
Had I leapt ſome of your alliance.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Slave!

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: You prevent me ſtill.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: 'Slid, Son, Are you mad?

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Come, come, I'll take a legal courſe.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Will you undo us all? What's your demand, Sir?
Now we're in's danger too.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: A hundred Mark, Sir,
I will not bate a doit.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: A hundred Raſcals.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Sir, find 'em out in your own blood, and take 'em.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Go take your courſe, follow the Law, and ſpare not.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Does fury make you drunk? know you what you ſay?

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: A hundred dogs dungs, do your worſt.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: You do I'm ſure; Whoſe loud now?

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: What his own asking?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Not in ſuch a caſe?

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: You ſhall have but threeſcore pound; ſpite a your teeth,
I'll ſee you hang'd firſt.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: And what's ſeven pound more man?
That all this coyle's about? ſtay, I ſay, he ſhall ha't.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: It is your own, you may do what you pleaſe with it;
Pardon my zeal, I would ha' ſav'd you money;
Give him all his own asking?

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: What's that to you, Sir?
Be ſparing of your own, teach me to pinch
In ſuch a caſe as this? go, go, live by your wits, go.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: I practiſe all I can.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Follow you me, Sir,
And, Maſter Conſtable, come from the knave,
And be a witneſs of a full recompence.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Pray ſtop the Conſtables mouth, what ere you do Sir.

sp.speaker: O. K.
sp.l: Yet agen? as if I meant not to do that my ſelf,
Without your counſel? As for you, precious kinſman,
Your firſt years • ruits in Wales ſhall go to rack for this,
You lie not in my houſe, I'll pack you out,
And pay for your lodging rather.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Oh ſie Cozen,
The • e are ill courſes, you a Scholar too?
• was drawn into't moſt unfortunately,
By 〈…〉 bo •• t company.
' 〈…〉 the ſpoil of all our youth in England.
〈…〉 they Gentlemen?
Faith ſo like ſome on 'em,
They were ev'n the worſe agen.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Hum.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: Great Tobacco whiffers,
They would go near to rob with a pipe in their mouths.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: What, no?

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: Faith leave it Cozen, becauſe my Raſcals uſe it,

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: So they do meat and drink, muſt worthy Gentlemen.
Refrain their food for that? an honeſt man
May eat of the ſame Pig ſome Parſon dines with,
A Lawyer and a fool feed of one Woodcock,
Yet one ne'er the ſimpler, t'other ne'er the wiſer;
'Tis not meat, drink, or ſmoak, diſh, cup, or pipe,
Co-operates to the making of a Knave,
'Tis the condition makes a ſlave, a ſlave,
There's London Philoſophy for you; I tell you Cozen,
You cannot be too cautelous, nice, or dainty,
In your ſociety here, eſpecially
When you come raw from the Univerſity,
Before the World has hard'ned you a little,
For as a butter'd loaf is a Scholars breakfaſt there,
So a poach't Scholar is a cheaters dinner here,
I ha' known ſeven of 'em ſupt up at a Meale.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: Why a poacht Scholar?

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: 'Cauſe he powres himſelf forth,
And all his ſecrets, at the firſt acquaintance,
Never ſo crafty to be eaten i'th' ſhell,
But is outſtript of all he has at firſt,
And goes down glib, he's ſwallowed with ſharp wit,
Stead of Wine Vinegar.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: I ſhall think, Cozen,
O' your poach't Scholar, while I live.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Maſter Credulous,
Your Uncle wills you to forbear the Houſe,
You muſt with me, I'm charg'd to ſee you plac'd
In ſome new lodging about Theeving Lane,
What the conceit's, I know not, but commands you
To be ſeen here no more, till you hear further.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: Here's a ſtrange welcome, Sir.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: This is the World, Cozen;
When a Man's fame's once poyſon'd, fare thee well Lad.
This is the happieſt cheat I e'er claim'd ſhare in,
It has a two-fold fortune, gets me coyne,
And puts him out of grace, that ſtood between me,
My fathers Cambridge Jewel, much ſuſpected
To be his Heir, now there's a bar in's hopes.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: It chinks, make haſte.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: The Goat at Smithfield Pens.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Zo, zo, zufficient. Maſter Cunningame?
I never have ill luck when I meet a wit.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: A Wit's better to meet, than to follow then,
For I ha' none ſo good I can commend yet,
But commonly men unfortunate to themſelves,
Are luckieſt to their friends, and ſo may I be.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: I run o'er ſo much worth, going but in haſte from you,
All my deliberate friendſhip cannot equal.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Tis but to ſhew, that you can place ſometimes,
Your modeſty a top of all your virtues. Exit Wit.
This Gentleman may pleaſure me yet agen;
I am ſo haunted with this broad-brim'd hat,
Of the laſt progreſs block, with the young hat-band,
Made for a ſucking Devil of two years old,
I know not where to turn my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: More torture?
'Tis rumor'd that you love me.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: A my troth Gentlewoman,
Rumor's as falſe a knave as ever piſt then,
Pray tell him ſo from me; I cannot fain
With a ſweet Gentlewoman, I muſt deal down right.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I heard, though you diſſembled with my Aunt, Sir,
And that makes me more confident.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: There's no falſhood,
But payes us our own ſome way, I confeſs
I Fain'd with her, 'twas for a weightier purpoſe,
But not with thee, I ſwear.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Nor I with you then,
Although my Aunt enjoyn'd me to diſſemble,
To right her ſplene, I love you faithfully.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Light, this is worſe than 'twas.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I find ſuch worth in you,
I cannot, nay I dare not dally with you,
For fear the flame conſume me.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Here's freſh trouble,
This drives me to my conſcience, for 'tis ſoul
To injure one that deals directly with me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I crave but ſuch a truth from your love, Sir,
As mine brings you, and that's proportionable.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: A good Geometrician, 'ſhrew my heart;
Why are you out o'your wits, pretty plump Gentlewoman,
You talk ſo deſperately? 'tis a great happineſs,
Love has made one on's wiſer than another,
We ſhould be both caſt away elſe;
Yet I love gratitude, I muſt requite you,
I ſhall be ſick elſe, but to give you me,
A thing you muſt not take, if you mean to live,
For a' my troth I hardly can my ſelf;
No wiſe Phyſitian will preſcribe me for you.
Alaſs, your ſtate is weak, you had need of Cordials,
Some rich Electuary, made of a Son an Heir,
An elder brother, in a Culliſſe, whole,
'Tmuſt be ſome wealthy Gregory, boyl'd to a Jelly,
That muſt reſtore you to the ſtate of new Gowns,
French Ruſſs, and mutable head-tires,

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: But, Where is he, Sir?
One that's ſo rich will ne'er wed me with nothing.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Then ſee thy Conſcience, and thy wit together,
Would'ſt thou have me then, that has nothing neither?
What ſay you to Fop Gregory the firſt, yonder?
Will you acknowledge your time amply recompenc'd?
Full ſatisfaction upon loves record?
Without any more ſuit, if I combine you?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, by this honeſt kiſs.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You're a wiſe Clyent,
To pay your ſee before-hand, but all do ſo,
You know the worſt already, that's the beſt too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I know he's a fool,

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You'r ſhrewdly hurt then;
This is your comfort, your great wiſeſt Women
Pick their firſt Husband ſtill out of that houſe,
And ſome will have 'em to chuſe, if they bury twenty.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I'm of their minds, that like him for a Husband,
To run youths race with, 'tis very pleaſant,
But when I'm old, I'd alwayes wiſh for a wiſer.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You may have me by that time:
For this firſt buſineſs,
Reſt upon my performance.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: With all thankfulneſs.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I have a project you muſt aid me in too.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: You bind me to all lawful action, Sir,

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Pray wear this Scarf about you;

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I conjecture now—

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: There's a Court Principle for't, one office muſt help another;
As for example, for your caſt o' Manchits out o'th' Pantry,
I'll allow you a Gooſe out o'th' Kitchin.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: 'Tis very ſociably done, Sir, farewel performance,
I ſhall be bold to call you ſo.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Do, ſweet confidence,
If I can match my two broad brim'd hats;
'Tis he, I know the Maggot by his head;
Now ſhall I learn newes of him, my precious chief.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I have been ſeeking for you i'th' bowling-Green,
Enquir'd at Net • letons, and Anthonies Ordinary,
T'ha's vext me to the heart, look, I've a Diamond here,
And it cannot find a Maſter.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: No? That's hard y'faith.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: It does belong to ſome body, a—on him,
I would he had it, do's but trouble me,
And ſhe that ſent it, is ſo waſpiſh too,
There's no returning to her till't be gone.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Oh, ho, ah ſirrah, are you come?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: What's that friend?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Do you note that corner ſparkle?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Which? which? which Sir?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: At the Weſt end o'th' Coller.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Oh I ſee't now.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Tis an apparent mark; this is the ſtone, Sir,
That ſo much blood is threatned to be ſned for.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I pray.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: A tun at leaſt.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: They muſt not find't i'me then, they muſt
Goe where 'tis to be had.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Tis well it came to my hands firſt, Sir Gregory,
I know where this muſt go.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Am I diſcharg'd on't?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: My life for yours now.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: What now?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Tis diſcretion, Sir,
I'll ſtand upon my Guard all the while I ha't.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: 'Troth thou tak'ſt too much danger on thee ſtill,
To preſerve me alive.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Tis a friends duty, Sir,
Nay, by a toy that I have late thought upon,
I'll unndertake to get your Miſtriſs for you.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Thou wilt not? Wilt?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Contract her by a trick, Sir,
When ſhe leaſt thinks on't.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: There's the right way to't,
For if ſhe think on't once, ſhee'l never do't.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: She does abuſe you ſtill then?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: A —damnably,
Every time worſe than other; yet her Uncle
Thinks the day holds a Tueſday; ſay it did, Sir,
She's ſo familiarly us'd to call me Raſcal,
She'll quite forget to wed me by my own name,
And then that Marriage cannot hold in Law, you know.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Will you leave all to me?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Who ſhould I leave it to?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Tis our luck to love Neeces; I love a Neece too.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I would you did y'faith.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: But mine's a kind wretch.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I marry Sir, I would mine were ſo too.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: No raſcal comes in her mouth.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Troth, and mine has little elſe in hers.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Mine ſends me tokens,
All the World knows not on.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Mine gives me tokens too, very ſine tokens,
But I dare • not wear 'em.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Mine's kind in ſecret.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: And there mine's a hell-cat.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: We have a day ſet too.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: 'Slid, ſo have we man,
But there's no ſign of ever coming together.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I'll tell thee who 'tis, the old womans Neece.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Is't ſhe?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I would your luck had been no worſe for mildneſs;
But mum, no more words on't to your Lady.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Foh!

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: No blabbing, as you love me.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: None of our blood
Were ever bablers

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Prethee convey this Letter to her,
But at any hand let not your Miſtriſs ſee't.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Yet agen Sir?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: There's a Jewel in't,
The very art would make her doat upon't.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Say you ſo?
And ſhe ſhall ſee't for that trick only.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Remember but your Miſtriſs, and all's well.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg
sp.l: Nay, if I do not, hang me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I believe you;
This is the onely way to return a token,
I know he will do't now, 'cauſe he's charg'd to'th' contrary.
He's the neareſt kin to a Woman, of a thing
Made without ſubſtance, that a man can find agen,
Some Petticoat begot him, I'll be whipt elſe,
Engendring with an old pair of paund hoſe,
Lying in ſome hot chamber o'er the Kitchin:
Very ſteame bred him,
He never came where Rem in Re e'er grew;
The generation of a hundred ſuch
Cannot make a man ſtand in a white ſheet,
For 'tis no act in Law, nor can a Conſtable
Pick out a bawdy buſineſs for Bridewell in't;
A lamentable caſe, he's got with a Mans Urine, like a Mandrake.
How now? hah? What prodigious bravery's this?
A moſt prepoſterous Gallant, the Doublet ſits
As if it mock't the breeches.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Save you, Sir,

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: H'as put his tongue in the fine ſuit of words too.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: How does the party?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Takes me for a Scrivener. Which of the parties?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Hum, ſimplicity betide thee—
I would fain hear of the party; I would be loath to go
Farther with her; honor is not a thing to be dallied withall,
No more is reputation, no nor fame, I take it, I muſt not
Have her wrong'd when I'm abroad; my party is not
To be compell'd with any party in an oblique way;
'Tis very dangerous to deal with Women;
May prove a Lady too, but ſhall be nameleſs,
I'l bite my tongue out, e'er it prove a Traitor.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Upon my life I know her.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Not by me,
Know what you can, talk a whole day with me,
Y'are ne'er the wiſer, ſhe comes not from theſe lips.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: The old Knights Neece.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: 'Slid he has got her, pox of his heart that told him,
Can nothing be kept ſecret? let me entreat you
To uſe her name as little as you can, though.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Twill be ſmall pleaſure, Sir, to uſe her name.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I had intelligence in my ſolemn walks,
'Twixt Paddington and Pan • ridge, of a Scarfe,
Sent for a token, and a Jewel follow'd,
But I acknowledge not the receipt of any,
How e'er 'tis carried, believe me, Sir,
Upon my reputation I receiv'd none.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: What, neither Scarfe nor Jewel?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: 'Twould be ſeen
Some where about me, you may well think that,
I have an arme for a Scarfe, as others have,
An Ear, to hang a Jewel too, and that's more
Then ſome men have, my betters a great deal,
I muſt have reſtitution, where e'er it lights.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And reaſon good.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: For all theſe tokens, Sir,
Paſs i' my name.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: It cannot otherwiſe be.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Sent to a worthy friend.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I, that's to thee.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I'm wrong'd under that title.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I dare ſware thou art,
'Tis nothing but Sir Gregories circumvention,
His envious ſpite, when thou'rt at Paddington,
He meets the gifts at Pan • ridge.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Ah falſe Knight?
Falſe both to honor, and the Law of Arms?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: What wilt thou ſay if I be reveng'd for thee?
Thou ſit as Witneſs?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I ſhould laugh in ſtate then.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I'll fob him, here's my hand.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I ſhall be as glad as any Man alive, to ſee him well fob'd, Sir; but now you talk of fobbing, I wonder the Lady ſends not for me according to promiſe? I ha' kept out o' Town theſe two dayes, a purpoſe to be ſent for; I am almoſt ſtarv'd with walking.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Walking gets men a ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: 'Tis moſt true, Sir, I may ſpeak it by experience, for I ha' got a ſtomach ſix times, and loſt it agen, as often as a traveller from Chelſy ſhall loſe the ſight of Pauls, and get it agen.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Go to her, Man.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Not for a Million, enfringe my oath? there's a toy call'd a Vow, has paſt between us, a poor trifle, Sir; Pray do me the part and office of a Gentleman, if you chance to meet a Footman by the way, in Orange tawny ribbands, running before an empty Coach, with a Buzard i'th' Poop on't, direct him and his horſes toward the new River by Iſlington, there they ſhall have me looking upon the Pipes, and whiſtling. Exit. Clow.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: A very good note; this love makes us all Monkeyes,
sp.p: But to my work: 'Scarfe firſt? and now a Diamond? theſe ſhould be ſure ſigns of her affections truth; Exit.
sp.l: Yet I'll go forward with my ſurer proof. Exit.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Nay, here's his Letter too, there's a fine Jewel in't,
Therefore I brought it to you.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: You tedious Mongril! Is't not enough
To grace thee, to receive this from thy hand,
A thing which makes me almoſt ſick to do,
But you muſt talk too?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I ha' done.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Fall back,
Yet backer, backer yet, you unmannerly puppy,
Do you not ſee I'm going about to read it?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Nay, theſe are golden dayes, now I ſtay by't,
She was wont not to endure me in her ſight at all,
The World mends, I ſee that.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: What an ambiguous Superſcription's here?

sp.speaker: To the beſt of Neeces.
sp.l: Why that title may be mine,
And more than her's:
Sure I much wrong the neatneſs of his art;
'Tis certain ſent to me, and to requite
My cunning in the carriage of my Tokens,
Us'd the ſame Fop for his.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: She nodded now to me, 'twill come in time.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: What's here? an entire Rubye, cut into a heart,
And this the word, Iſtud Amoris opus?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Yes, yes, I have heard him ſay, that love is the beſt ſtone-cutter.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Why thou ſawcy iſſue of ſome travelling. Sowgelder.
What makes love in thy mouth? Is it a thing
That ever will concern thee? I do wonder
How thou dar'ſt think on't? haſt thou ever hope
To come i' the ſame roome where lovers are;
And ſcape unbrain'd with one of their velvet ſlippers?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Love tricks break out I ſee, and you talk of ſlippers once,
'Tis not far off to bed time.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Is it poſſible thou canſt laugh yet?
I would ha' undertook to ha' kill'd a ſpider
With leſs venome far, than I have ſpit at thee.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: You muſt conceive,
A Knight's another manner a piece of fleſh.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Back, Owles-face.

sp.speaker: Within.
sp.l: O. K. Do, do.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: 'Tis my Unckles voice, that.
Why keep you ſo far off, Sir Gregory?
Are you afraid, Sir, to come near your Miſtriſs?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Is the proud heart come down? I lookt for this ſtill.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: He comes not this way yet: Away, you dog-whelp,
Would you offer to come near me, though I ſaid ſo?
I'll make you underſtand my mind in time;
You run in greedily, like a hound to his breakfaſt,
That chops in head and all to beguile his fellows;
I'm to be eaten, Sir, with Grace and leiſure,
Behaviour and diſcourſe, things that ne'er trouble you;
After I have pelted you ſufficiently,
I tro you will learn more manners.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I'm wondring ſtill when we two ſhall come together?
Tueſday's at hand, but I'm as far off, as I was at firſt, I ſwear.

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Now Cuningame, I'll be reveng'd at large:
Lady, what was but all this while ſuſpition,
Is truth, full blown now, my Neece wears your Scarfe.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Hah?

sp.speaker: Gard.
sp.l: Do but follow me, I'll place you inſtantly
Where you ſhall ſee her courted by Cuningame.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: I go with greedineſs; we long for things
That break our hearts ſometimes, there's pleaſures miſery,

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Where are thoſe gad-flies going? to ſome Junket now;
That ſome old bumble-bee toles the young one forth
To ſweet meats after kind, let 'em look to't,
The thing you wot on be not miſt or gone,
I bring a Maiden-head, and I look for one.

l.hi: Which is only a Papper ſo dreſt.

div.stage: Enter Cunningame (in diſcourſe with a Mack't Gentlewoman in a broad hat, and ſcarf'd,) Neece at another door.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Too manifeſt now, the Scarfe and all.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: It cannot be, you're ſuch a fearful ſoul.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: I'll give her cauſe of fear e'er I part from her.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Will you ſay ſo? Is't not your Aunts deſire too?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: What a diſſembling croane's that? ſhe'l ſorſwear't now.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I ſee my project takes, yonder's the grace on't.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Who would put confidence in wit again,
I'm plagu'd for my ambition, to deſire
A wi • e Man for a husband, and I ſee
Fate will not have us go beyond our ſtint,
We are allow'd but one diſh, and that's Woodcock,
It keeps up wit to make us friends and ſervants of,
And thinks any thing's good enough to make us husbands;
Oh that Whores hat o' thine, o' the riding block,
A ſhade for lecherous kiſſes.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Make you doubt on't?
Is not my love of force?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Yes, me it forces
To tear that ſorcerous ſtrumpet from th' imbraces.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Lady?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Oh thou haſt wrong'd the exquiſit'ſt love—

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: What mean you, Lady?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Mine, you'l anſwer for't.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Alas, What ſeek you?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Sir, mine own with loſs.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: You ſhall.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: I never made ſo hard a bargain.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Sweet Lady?

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Unjuſt man, let my wrath reach her,
As you owe virtue duty;

sp.speaker: Cun.

l.hi: falls on purpoſe.

sp.l: Your cauſe trips you,
Now Minion, you ſhall feel what loves rage is,
Before you taſte the pleaſure; ſmile you falſe, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: How can I chuſe? to ſee what pains you take,
Upon a thing will never thank you for't.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: See what things you women be, Lady,
When cloaths are taken for the beſt part of you?
This was to ſhow you, when you think I love you not,
How y'are deceiv'd ſtill, there the Moral lies,
'Twas a trap ſet to catch you, and the only bait
To take a Lady nibling, is fine clothes;
Now I dare boldly thank you for your love,
I'm pretty well reſolv'd in't by this fit,
For a jealous ague alwayes uſhers it.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Now bleſſings ſtill maintain this wit of thine,
And I have an excellent fortune coming in thee,
Bring nothing elſe I charge thee.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Not a groat I warrant ye.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt be worthily welcome, take my faith for't,
Next opportunity ſhall make us.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: The old Gentlewoman has fool'd her revenge ſweetly.

sp.speaker: Neece.
sp.l: 'Laſs, 'tis her part, ſhe knows her place ſo well yonder;
Alwayes when Women jumpe upon threeſcore,
Love ſhoves e'm from the chamber to the door.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Thou art a precious ſhe-wit. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Cunningame (at one door) Witty-Pate, Ruinous, L. Ruinous, and Priſcian (at the other.)

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: FRiend, met in the harveſt of our deſigns,
Not a thought but's buſie.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: I knew it Man,
And that made me provide theſe needful Reapers,
Hooks, Rakers, Gleaners; we'll ſing it home
With a melodious Horne-pipe; this is the Bond,
That as we further in your great affair,
You'l ſuffer us to glean, pick up for crums,
And if we ſnatch a handful from thē ſheaf,
You will not look a churle on's.
Friend, we'll ſhare
The ſheaves of gold, only the Love Aker
Shall be peculiar.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Much good do you, Sir,
Away, you know your way, and your ſtay; get you
The Muſick ready, while we prepare the dancers.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: We are a conſort of our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: And can ſtrike up luſtily.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: You muſt bring Sir Fop.

sp.speaker: Cun,
sp.l: That's perfect enough.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Bring all the Fops you can, the more, the better fare
So the proverb runs backwards. Exeunt Ruin. and Priſ.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: I'll bring the Ladies. Exit.

sp.speaker: Wit.
sp.l: Do ſo firſt, and then the Fops will follow;
I muſt to my Father, he muſt make one. Exit.

div.stage: Enter two Servants with a Banquet.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: While I diſpatch a buſineſs with the Knight,
And I go with you. Well ſed, I thank you,
This ſmall Banquet will furniſh our few Gueſts
With taſte and ſtate enough; one reach my Gown.
The action craves it rather than the weather.

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: There's one ſtayes to ſpeak with you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: What is he?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: Faith I know not what, Sir, a Fool, I think,
That ſome Brokers ſhop has made half a Gentleman;
Has the name of a Worthy too.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Pompey? Is't not?

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.l: That's he, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Alas, poor fellow, prethee enter him, he will need too.
sp.stage: Enter ſecond Servant with a Gown.
sp.l: He ſhall ſerve for a Witneſs. Oh Gramercy:
• f my friend Sir Gregory comes, you know him,
Entertain him kindly. Oh Maſter Pompey, How is't man?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: 'Snails, I'm almoſt ſtarv'd with Love, and cold, and one thing or other;
Has not my Lady ſent for me yet?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Not that I hear, ſure ſome unfriendly Meſſenger • s imploy'd betwixt you,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I was ne'er ſo cold in my life, in my Conſcience I • ave been ſeven mile in length, along the New River; I • ave ſeen a hundred ſtickle bags; I do not think but there's • udgeons too; 'twill ne'er he a true water.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why think you ſo?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I warrant you, I told a thouſand Millers thumbs in it,
I'll make a little bold with your Sweet-meats.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And welcome Pompey.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: 'Tis a ſtrange thing, I have no taſte in any thing.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Oh, that's Love, that diſtaſts any thing but it ſelf.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: 'Tis worſe than Cheeſe in that point, may not a Man break his word with a Lady? I could find in my heart and my hoſe too.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: By no means, Sir, that breaks all the Laws of Love.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Well, I'll ne'er paſs my word without my deed to
A Lady, while I live agen, I would fain recover my taſte.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Well, I have news to tell you.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Good news, Sir?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Happy news, I help you away with a Rival your
Maſter beſtow'd.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Where, for this Plumbs ſake —

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Nay, liſten me.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I warrant you, Sir, I have two ears to one mouth,
I hear more than I eat, I'de ne'er row by Queen Hive
While I liv'd elſe.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I have a Wife for him, and thou ſhalt witneſs the Contract.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: The old one I hope, 'tis not the Lady?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Choak him firſt, 'tis one which thou ſhalt ſee,
See him, ſee him deceiv'd, ſee the deceit, only
The injunction is, you ſhall ſmile with modeſty.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I'll ſimper I'faith, as cold as I am yet, the old one
I hope.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Sir, here's Sir Gregory.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: U'd ſo, ſhelter, ſhelter, if you be ſeen,
All's ravell'd out again; ſtand there private,
And you'll find the very opportunity
To call you forth, and place you at the Table.
You are welcome, Sir, this Banquet will ſerve,
When it is crown'd with ſuch a dainty as you
Expect, and muſt have.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: 'Tuſh, theſe ſweet-meats are but ſauce to that,
Well, if there be any honeſty, or true word in a dream,
She's mine own, nay, and chang'd extreamly,
Not the ſame Woman.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Who, not the Lady?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: No, not to me, the edge of her tongue iS taken off,
Gives me very good words, turn'd up-ſide-down to me,
And we live as quietly as two Tortoiſes, if ſhe hold on,
As ſhe began in my dream. Soft Muſick.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Nay, if Love ſend forth ſuch Predictions,
You are bound to believe 'em, there's the watch-word
Of her coming; to your practis'd part now,
If you hit it, Aequus Cupido nobis.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: I will warrant you, Sir, I will give armes to
Your Gentry, look you forward to your buſineſs,
I am an eye behind you, place her in that Chair,
And let me alone to grope her out.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Silence, Lady, your ſweet preſence illuſtrates
This homely roof, and, as courſe entertainment;
But where affections are both Hoſt and Gueſt,
They cannot meet unkindly; pleaſe you ſit,
Your ſomething long ſtay made me unmannerly,
To place before you, you know this friend here,
He's my Gueſt, and more eſpecially,
That this our meeting might not be too ſingle,
Without a witneſs to't.

sp.speaker: Mirab.
sp.l: I came not unreſolv'd, Sir,
And when our hands are claſp'd in that firm faith
Which I expect from you; ſame ſhall be bold
'To ſpeak the loudeſt on't: oh you graſp me
Somewhat too hard friend.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: That's Loves eager will,
I'll touch it gentlier. Kiſſes her hand.

sp.speaker: Mirab.
sp.l: That's too low in you,
Leſs it be doubly recompenc'd in me. She kiſſes his hand.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: • Puh, I muſt ſtop my mouth, I ſhall be choakt elſe.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Come, we'll not play and trifle with delayes,
We met to joyn theſe hands, and willingly
I cannot leave it till confirmation.

sp.speaker: Mirab.
sp.p: One word firſt, how does your friend, kind Sir Gregory?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why do you mention him? you love him not?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I ſhall love you the leſs if you ſay ſo, Sir,
In troth I love him, but 'tis you deceive him,
This flattering hand of yours does rob him now,
Now you ſteal his right from him, and I know
I ſhall have hate for't, his hate extreamly.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why I thought you had not come ſo weakly arm'd,
Upon my life the Knight will love you for't,
Exceedingly love you, for ever love you.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I, you'll perſwade me ſo.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Why he's my friend,
And wiſhes me a fortune equal with him,
I know, and dare ſpeak it for him.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Oh, this hand betrayes him, you might remember him in ſome courteſie yet at leaſt.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: I thank your help in't, here's to his health Where e'er he be.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: I'll pledge it, were it againſt my health.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Oh, oh, my heart hops after twelve mile a day, upon a good return, now could I walk three hundred mile a foot, and laugh forwards and backwards.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: You'll take the Knights health, Sir,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Yes, yes forſooth, oh my ſides! ſuch a Banquet once a week, would make me grow fat in a fortnight.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Well, now to cloſe our meeting, with the cloſe
Of mutual hands and hearts, thus I begin,
Here in Heavens eye, and all loves ſacred powers,
(Which in my Prayers ſtand propitious)
I knit this holy hand faſt, and with this hand
The heart that owes this hand, ever binding
By force of this initiating Contract
Both heart and hand in love, faith, loyalty,
Eſtate, or what to them belongs, in all the dues,
Rights and honors of a faithful husband,
And this firm vow, henceforth till death, to ſtand
Irrevocable, ſeal'd both with heart and hand.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Which thus I ſecond, but oh, Sir Gregory.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Agen? this interpoſition's ill, believe me.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Here, in Heavens eye, and all Loves ſacred powers,
I knit this holy hand faſt, and with this hand
The heart that owes this hand, ever binding
Both heart and hand in love, honor, loyalty,
Eſtate, or what to them belongs in all the dues,
Rights, and duties of a true faithful Wife;
And this firm Vow, henceforth till death, to ſtand,
Irrevocable, ſeal'd both with heart and hand.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: A full agreement on both parts.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I, here's witneſs of that.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: Nay, I have over-reacht you Lady, and that's much,
For any Knight in England to over-reach a Lady.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: I rejoyce in my deceit, I am a Lady
Now, I thank you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Good morrow Lady Fop.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: 'Snails, I'm gull'd, made a worſhipful aſs, this is not my Lady.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: But it is Sir, and true as your dream told you,
That your Lady was become another Woman.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: I'll have another Lady, Sir, if there were no more Ladies in London, blind-man buff is an unlawful Game.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Come, down on your knees firſt, and thank your
Stars.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.l: A fire of my ſtars, I may thank you, I think.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: So you may pray for me, and honor me,
That have preſerv'd you from a laſting torment,
For a perpetual comfort; Did you call me friend?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: I pray pardon me for that, I did miſcall you, I confeſs.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: And ſhould I, receiving ſuch a thankful name,
Abuſe it in the act? Should I ſee my friend
Baffed, diſgrac'd, without any reverence
To your title, to be call'd ſlave, raſcal?
Nay curſt to your face, fool'd, ſcorn'd, beaten down
With a womans peeviſh hate, yet I ſhould ſtand
And ſuffer you to be loſt, caſt away?
I would have ſeen you buried quick firſt,
Your ſpurs of Knighthood to have wanted rowels,
And to be kickt from your heels; ſlave, raſcall?
Hear this Tongue?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: My deareſt Love, ſweet Knight, my Lord, my Husband.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: So, this is not ſlave, and raſcall then.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: What ſhall your eye command, but ſhall be done,
In all the duties of a loyal Wife?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Good, good, are not curſes fitter for you? wer't not better
Your head were broke with the handle of a fan,
Or your noſe bor'd with a ſilver bodkin?

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Why, I will be a ſervant in your Lady.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: 'Pox, but you ſhall not, ſhe's too good for you,
This contract ſhall be a nullity, I'll break't off,
And ſee you better beſtow'd.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: 'Slid, but you ſhall not, Sir, ſhe's mine own, and I am hers, and we are one anothers lawfully, and let me ſee him that will take her away by the Civil Law: if you be my friend, keep you ſo, if you have done me a good turn, do not hit me i'th' teeth with't, that's not the part of a friend.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: If you be content —.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Content? I was never in better content on it my life.
sp.l: I'll not change her for both the Exchanges, New or the Old.
Come, kiſs me boldly.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Give you joy, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Oh Sir, I thank you as much as though I did, you are belov'd of Ladies, you ſee we are glad of underwomen.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Ladies? let not Ladies be diſgrac'd, you are as it were a Married Man, and have a family, and for the parties ſake that was unnam'd before, being Peſe-cod time, I am appeas'd, yet I would wiſh you make a Ruler of your Tongue.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Nay, no diſſention here, I muſt bar that,
And this (friend) I entreat you, and be advis'd,
Let this private contract be yet conceal'd,
And ſtill ſupport a ſeeming face of love
Unto the Lady; mark how it availes you,
And quits all her ſcorns, her Unckle is now hot
In purſuit of the match, and will enforce her,
Bend her proud ſtomach, that ſhe ſhall proffer
Her ſelf to you, which when you have flouted,
And laught your fill at, you ſhall ſcorn her off,
With all your diſgraces trebled upon her,
For there the pride of all her heart will bow,
When you ſhall foot her from you, not ſhe you.

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: Good I'faith; I'll continue it, I'd fain laugh a • the old fellow too, for he has abus'd me as ſcurvily as hi • Neece, my Knight-hoods upon the ſpur, we'll go to Bed, and then to Church as faſt as we can.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I do wonder I do not hear of the Lady yet.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: The good minute may come ſooner than you are aware of,
I do not think but 'twill e'r night yet, as near as 'tis.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Well, I will go walk by the New River, in that meditation, I am o'er ſhooes, I'm ſure upon the drie bank, this gullery of my Maſter will keep me company this two hours too, if love were not an enemy to laughter, I ſhould drive away the time well enough; you know my walk, Sir, if ſhe ſends, I ſhall be found angling, for I will try what I can catch for luck ſake, I will fiſh fair for't,
Oh Knight, that thou ſhouldſt be gull'd ſo; ha, ha, it does me good at heart,
But oh Lady, thou tak'ſt down my merry part. Exit.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Friend.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Here friend.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Alls afoot, and will goe ſmooth away,
The woman has conquer'd the women, they are gone,
Which I have already complain'd to my Father,
Suggeſting that Sir Gregory is fall'n off
From his charge, for neglects and ill uſage,
And that he is moſt violently bent
On Gentries wiſe (whom I have call'd a widow)
And that without moſt ſudden prevention
He will be married to her.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: All this is wrong,
sp.p: This wings his purſuit, and will be before me; I am loſt for ever.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: No, ſtay, you ſhall not go
But with my Father, on my wit let it lie,
You ſhall appear a friendly aſſiſtant,
To help in all affairs, and in execution
Help your ſelf only.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Would my belief
Were ſtrong in this aſſurance.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: You ſhall credit it,
And my wit ſhall be your ſlave, if it deceive you.
My Father —

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Oh Sir? you are well met, where's the Knight your friend?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Sir, I think your Son has told you.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Shall I ſtand to tell't agen? I tell you he loves,
But not my Kinſwoman, her baſe uſage,
And your ſlack performance which he accuſes moſt
Indeed, has turn'd the Knights heart upſide down.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I'll curb her for't, can he be but recover'd,
He ſhall have her, and ſhe ſhall be dutiful,
And love him as a Wife too.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: With that condition, Sir,
I dare recall him where he enter'd the Church,
So much intereſt of love I aſſure in him.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Sir, it ſhall be no loſs to you if you do.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: I, but theſe are words ſtill, will not the deeds
Be wanting at the recovery, if it ſhould be agen;

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Why here fool, I am provided, five hunder'd in earneſt,
Of the thouſands in her Dower, but were they married once,
• 'd cut him ſhort enough, that's my agreement.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: I, now I perceive ſome purpoſe in you, Father..

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: But wherefore is ſhe then ſtol'n out of doors to him?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: To him? oh ſie upon your error, ſhe has another object, believe it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I never could perceive it.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I did Sir, and to her ſhame I ſhould ſpeak it,
To my own ſorrow I ſaw it, dalliance,
Nay, dotage with a very Clown, a Fool.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Wit and wantons? nothing elſe? nothing elſe?
She love a fool? ſhe'll ſooner make a Fool
Of a wiſe man.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I, my friend complains ſo,
Sir Gregory ſays flatly, ſhe makes a fool of him,
And theſe hold circumſtances are approv'd:
Favours have been ſent by him, yet he ignorant
Whither to carry 'em; they have been underſtood,
And taken from him, certain, Sir, there is
An unſuſpected fellow lies conceal'd,
What, or where e'er he is, theſe ſlight neglects
Could not be of a Knight elſe.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Well Sir, you have promis'd (if we recover him Unmarried) to ſalve all theſe old bruiſes?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I'll do my beſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I ſhall thank you, coſtly Sir, and kindly too.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Will you talk away the time here, Sir, and come behind all your purpoſes?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Away good Sir.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Then ſtay a little, good Sir, for my advice,
Why, Father are you broke? your wit beggar'd,
Or are you at your wits end? or out of
Love with wit? no trick of wit to ſurprize
Thoſe deſigns, but with open Hue and Cry,
For all the world to talk on, this is ſtrange,
You were not wont to ſlubber a project ſo.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Can you help at a pinch now? ſhew your ſelf?
My Son, go too, I leave this to your wit,
Becauſe I'll make a proof on't.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: 'Tis thus then,
I have had late intelligence, they are now
Buckſom as Bacchus Froes, revelling, dancing,
Telling the Muſicks numbers with their feet,
Awaiting the meeting of permoniſh'd friends,
That's queſtionleſs, little dreading you,
Now Sir, with a dexterous trick indeed, ſuddain
And ſufficient were well, to enter on um
As ſomething like the abſtract of a Masque;
What though few perſons? if beſt for our purpoſe
That commends the project.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: This takes up time.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Not at all, I can preſently furniſh
With looſe diſguiſes that ſhall fit that Scene.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Why what wants then?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Nothing but charge of Muſick,
That muſt be paid, you know.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: That ſhall be my charges, I'll pay the Muſick.
What e'er it coſt.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: And that ſhall be all your charge,
Now on, I like it, there will be wit in't Father.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: I will neither diſtruſt his wit nor friendſhip,
Yet if his Maſter brain ſhould be o'er-thrown
My reſolution now ſhall ſeize mine own. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Neece, Lady Ruinous, Guardianeſs, Ruinous, Priſcian, (with inſtruments masqu'd.)

sp.speaker: L. Rui.
sp.l: Nay, let's have Muſick, let that ſweet breath at leaſt
Give us her airy welcome, 'twill be the beſt
I fear this ruin'd receptacle will yield,
But that moſt freely.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: My welcome follows me,
Elſe I am ill, come hither, you aſſure me
Still Mr. Cunningame will be here, and that it was
His kind entreaty that wiſh'd me meet him.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: Elſe let me be that ſhame unto my Sex,
That all belief may flie um.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Continue ſtill
The Knights name unto my Guardianeſs,
She expects no other.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: He will, he will, aſſure you
Lady, Sir Gregory will be here, and ſuddainly
This Muſick fore-ran him, is't not ſo conſorts?

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Yes Lady, he ſtays on ſome device to bring along
Such a labour he was buſie in, ſome witty device.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: 'Till belong e'r he comes then, for wits a great
Labour to him.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Well, well, you'll agree better one day.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Scarce two I think.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Such a mock-beggar ſuit of cloaths as led me
Into the fools pair-of-Dice, with Dewze Ace,
He that would make me Miſtriſs Cun, Cun, Cunnie,
He's quite out of my mind, but I ſhall ne'er
Forget him, while I have a hole in my head;
Such a one I think would pleaſe you better,
Though he did abuſe you.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Fye, ſpeak well of him now,
Your Neece has quitted him.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: I hope ſhe has,
Elſe ſhe loſes me for ever; but for Sir Gregory.
Would he were come, I ſhall ill anſwer this
Unto your Uncle elſe.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: You know 'tis his pleaſure
I ſhould keep him company.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: I, and ſhould be your own
If you did well too: Lord, I do wonder
At the niceneſs of you Ladies now a days,
They muſt have Husbands with ſo much wit forſooth.
Worſhip and wealth were both wont to be
In better requeſt I'm ſure, I cannot tell,
But they get ne'er the wiſer children that I ſee.

sp.speaker: La. Ruin.
sp.l: La, la, la, la, Sol, this Muſick breaths in vain;
Methinks 'tis dull to let it move alone,
Let's have a female motion, 'tis in private,
And we'll grace't our ſelves, however it deſerves.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: What ſay you Guardianeſs?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: 'Las I'm weary with the walk,
My jaunting days are done.

sp.speaker: L. Ru.
sp.l: Come, come, we'll fetch her in by courſe, or elſe
She ſhall pay the Muſick.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Nay, I'll have a little for my money then.

div.stage: They Dance, a Cornet is winded.

sp.speaker: L. Ru.
sp.l: Hark? upon my life the Knight; 'tis your friend,
This was the warning-piece of his approach.

div.stage: Enter Old Knight, Witty-pate, Cunningame, Masqu'd, and take them to Dance.

sp.speaker: L. Ru.
sp.l: Ha? no words but mum? well then,
We ſhall need no counſel-keeping

l.hi: Cunningam?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Yes, fear nothing.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Fear? why do you tell me of it?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Your Uncles here.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Aye me.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Peace.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: We have caught 'em.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Thank my wit Father.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Which is the Knight think you?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: I know not, he will be found when he ſpeaks,
No Masque can diſguiſe his tongue.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Are you charg'd?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Are you awake?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: I'm anſwer'd in a queſtion.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: Next change we meet, we loſe our hands no more.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Are you prepar'd to tye 'em?

sp.speaker: Cun,
sp.l: Yes,
You muſt go with me.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: Whither Sir? not from my charge believe me.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: She goes along.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Will you venture and my Uncle here?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: His ſtay's prepar'd for.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.l: 'Tis the Knight ſure, I'll follow.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: How now, the Muſick tir'd before us?

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: Yes Sir, we muſt be paid now.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Oh that's my charge, Father.

sp.speaker: Old. K.
sp.l: But ſtay, where are our wanton Ladies gone?
Son, where are they?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Only chang'd the room in a change, that's all ſure.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I'll make 'em all ſure elſe, and then return to you.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: You muſt pay for your Muſick firſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Muſt? are there muſty Fidlers? are Beggars chooſers now?
Ha? why Witty-pate, Son, where am I?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: You were dancing e'en now, in good meaſure, Sir,
Is your health miſcarried ſince? what all you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Death, I may be gull'd to my face, where's my Neece?
What are you?

sp.speaker: L. Ru.
sp.l: None of your Neece, Sir?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: How now? have you loud inſtruments too? I'll hear
No more, I thank you; what have I done tro
To bring theſe fears about me? Son, where am I?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Not where you ſhould be, Sir, you ſhall be paying
For your Muſick, and you are in a maze.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Oh, is't ſo, put up, put up, I pray you,
Here's a crown for you.

sp.speaker: L. Ruin.
sp.l: Piſh, a crown?

sp.speaker: Ruin. Priſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, a crown?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Which way do you laugh? I have ſeen a crown
Has made a Conſort laugh heartily.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Father,
To tell you truth, theſe are no ordinary
Muſicians, they expect a bounty
Above their punctual deſert.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: A— on your Punks, and their deſerts too.
Am I not cheated all this while think you?
Is not your pate in this?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: If you be cheated,
You are not to be indicted for your own goods,
Here you trifle time to market your bounty
And make it baſe, when it muſt needs be free
For ought I can perceive.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Will you know the loweſt price, Sir?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: That I will Sir, with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Unleſs I was diſcover'd, and they now fled
Home agen for fear, I am abſolutely beguil'd,
That's the beſt can be hop'd for.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Faith 'tis ſomewhat too dear yet, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ruin.
sp.l: There's not a Denier to be bated, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Now Sir, how dear is it?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Bate but the t'other ten pound?

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Not a Bawbee, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: How? bate ten pound? what's the whole ſum then?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Faith Sir, a hundred pound, with much adoe,
I got fifty bated, and faith Father, to ſay truth,
'Tis reaſonable for men of their faſhion.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: La, la, la, down, a hunder'd pound? la, la, la,
You are a Conſort of Thieves, are you not?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: No Muſicians, Sir, I told you before.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Fiddle faddle, is it not a robbery? a plain robbery.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: No, no, no, by no means Father, you have receiv'd
For your money, nay and that you cannot give back,
'Tis ſomewhat dear I confeſs, but who can help it?
If they had been agreed with before-hand,
'Twas ill forgotten.

sp.speaker: Old C.
sp.l: And how many ſnares have you in this? I ſee my force,
Caſe up your inſtruments, I yield, here, as robb'd and
Taken from me, I deliver it.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: No Sir, you have perform'd your promiſe now,
Which was, to pay the charge of Muſick, that's all.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: I have heard no Muſick, I have receiv'd none, Sir,
There's none to be found in me, nor about me.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Why Sir, here's witneſs againſt you, you have danc'd,
And he that dances, acknowledges a receipt of Muſick.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: I denie that, Sir, look you, I can dance without Muſick, do you ſee, Sir? and I can ſing without it too; you are a Conſort of Thieves, do you hear what I do?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Pray you take heed, Sir, if you do move the Muſick agen, it may coſt you as much more.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Hold, hold, I'll depart quietly, I need not bid you farewel, I think now, ſo long as that hundred pound laſts with you.
Ha, ha, am I ſnapt i'faith?

sp.speaker: Guar.
sp.p: Oh, Sir, Perſidious,

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: I, I, ſome howling another while, Muſick's too damnable dear.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: Oh Sir, my heart-ſtrings are broke, if I can but live to tell you the tale, I care not, your Neece my charge is—

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: What, is ſhe ſick?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: No, no Sir, ſhe's luſtily well married.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: To whom?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: Oh, to that cunning diſſembler, Cuningam.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: I'll hang the Prieſt, firſt, what was he?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: Your kinſman, Sir, that has the Welch Benefice.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: I ſav'd him from the Gallows to that end, good: is there any more?

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: And Sir Gregory is married too.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: To my Neece too, I hope, and then I may hang her.

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: No Sir, to my Neece, thank Cupid; and that's all that's likely to recover me, ſhe's Lady Fop now, and I am One of her Aunts, I thank my promotion.

div.stage: Enter Credulous, Cuningam, Neece, Sir Gregory, and Mirabel.

sp.speaker: Gred.
sp.l: I have perform'd your beſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: What have you perform'd, Sir?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Faith Sir I muſt excuſe my Coſin in this act,
If you can excuſe your ſelf for making him
A Prieſt, there's the moſt difficult anſwer.
I put this practiſe on him, as from your deſire,
A truth, a truth; Father.

sp.speaker: Cred,
sp.p: I proteſt, Sir, he tells you truth, he mov'd me to't in your namh.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: I proteſt, Sir, he told you a lye in my name, and were you ſo eaſie, Mr. Credulous, to believe him?

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.p: If a man ſhould not believe his Coſin; Sir, whom ſhould he believe?

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Good'en to you, good Mr. Coſin Cuningam,
And your fair Bride, my Coſin Cuningam too,
And how do you Sir Gregory, with your fair Lady?

sp.speaker: Sir Greg.
sp.p: A little better than you would have had me, I thank you Sir, the days of Puppy, and Slave, and Raſcal, are pretty well blown over now, I know Crabs from Verjuyce, I have tryed both, and thou'dſt give me thy Neece for nothing, I'd not have her.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: I think ſo Sir Gregory, for my ſake you would not.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: I wou'd thou hadſt ſcap'd her too, and then ſhe had died of the Green ſickneſs: know this, that I did marry in ſpight, and I will kiſs my Lady in ſpight, and love her in ſpight, and beget children of her in ſpight, and when I dye, they ſhall have my Lands in ſpight; this was my reſolution, and now 'tis out.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: How ſpightful are you now, Sir Gregory?
Why look you, I can love my deareſt Husband,
With all the honors, duties, ſweet embraces,
That can be thrown upon a loving man,

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: —This is afore your Uncles face, but behind his back, in private, you'll ſhew him another tale—

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: You ſee, Sir, now the irrecoverable ſtate of all theſe things before you: come out of your muſe, they have been but Wit-weapons, you were wont to love the Play.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.p: Let me alone in my muſe a little, Sir, I will wa to you anon.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: U'd ſo, your friend Pompey, how will you anſwer him?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: Very well, if you' • but ſecond it, and help me.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I do hear ſtrange ſtories, are Ladies things obnoxious?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: Oh, the diſſembling falſeſt wretch is come.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: How now Lady?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Let me come to him, and inſtead of love
Let me have revenge.

sp.speaker: Witty,
sp.p: Pray you now, will you firſt examine, whether he be guilty or no.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: He cannot be excus'd,
How many Meſſengers (thou perjur'd man)
Haſt thou return'd with Vows and Oaths, that thou
Wouldſt follow, and never till this unhappy hour
Could I ſet eye of thee, ſince thy falſe eye
Drew my heart to it? oh I could tear thee now,
Inſtead of ſoft embraces, pray give me leave —

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Faith this was ill done of you Sir, if you promis'd otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: By this hand, never any Meſſenger came at me, ſince the firſt time I came into her company; that a man ſhould be wrong'd thus?

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Did not I ſend thee Scarfs and Diamonds?
And thou return'dſt me Letters, one with a falſe heart in't.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Oh fie, to receive favours, return falſhoods, and hold a Lady in hand —

sp.speaker: Claw.
sp.p: Will you believe me, Sir? if ever I receiv'd Diamonds, or Scarf, or ſent any Letter to her, would this ſword might ne'er go through me.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Some bad Meſſengers have gone between you then.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Take him from my ſight if I ſhall ſee to morrow.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Pray you forbear the place, this diſcontent may impair her health much.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: 'Foot, if a man had been in any fault, 'twould ne'er a griev'd him, Sir, if you'll believe.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Nay, nay, proteſt no more, I do believe you,
But you ſee how the Lady is wrong'd by't;
She has caſt away her ſelf, it is to be fear'd,
Againſt her Uncles Will, nay, any conſent,
But out of a mere negl ••• and ſpigh • to her ſelf,
Married ſuddainly without any advice.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p:
Why, who can help it? if ſhe be caſt aw ••
〈…〉 thank her ſelf, ſhe might have gone •• rther an •
〈◊〉 worſe; I could do no more than I 〈◊〉 for 'twas 〈◊〉 own pleaſure to command me, that I ſhould not come, till I was ſent for, I had been with her every minute of a • hour elſe.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Truly I believe you.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Night and day ſhe might have commanded me, and that ſhe knew well enough; I ſaid as much to her between her and I; yet I proteſt, ſhe's as honeſt a Lady for my part, that I'd ſay, if ſhe would ſee me hang'd: if ſhe be caſt away I cannot help it, ſhe might have ſtay'd to have ſpoke with a man.

sp.speaker: Witty.
