sp.p: Well, 'twas a hard miſs on both parts.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: So 'twas, I was within one of her, for all this croſs luck, I was ſure I was between the Knight and home.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: Not gone yet? oh my heart! none regard my health?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: Good Sir, forbear her ſight awhile, you hear how ill ſhe brooks it.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p:
Fooliſh woman, to overthrow her fortunes ſo; I ſhall think the worſe of a Ladies wit, while I live for't— I could almoſt cry for anger, if ſhe ſhould miſcarry now, 'twould touch my conſcience a little, and who knows
what love and conceit may do? what would people ſay, as I go along? there goes he that the Lady died for love on, I am ſure to hear on't i'th' ſtreets, I ſhall weep before hand; fooliſh woman, I do grieve more for thee now, than I did love thee before; well, go thy ways, wouldſt thou ſpare thy Husbands head, and break thine own heart? if thou hadſt any wit, I would ſome other had been the cauſe of thy undoing, I ſhall be twitted i'th' teeth with it, I'm ſure of that, fooliſh Lady. Exit.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: So, ſo, this trouble's well ſhook off, Uncle, how d'ye there's a Dowrie due, Sir.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.l: We have agreed it ſweeteſt,
And find your Uncle fully recover'd, kind to both of us.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: To all the reſt I hope;

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Never to thee, nor thee, eaſie coſin Credulous,
Was your wit ſo raw?

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: Faith yours Sir, ſo long ſeaſon'd
Has been faulty too, and very much to blame,
Speaking it with reverence, Uncle.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: Yes faith, Sir, you have paid as dear for your time, as any man here.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.p: I Sir, and I'll reckon it to him. Imprimis, The firſt preface cheat of a pair of pieces to the Beggars, you remember that I was the example to your bounty there, I ſpake Greek and Syriack, Sir, you underſtand me now. Next, the Robbery put upon your indulgent Coſin, which indeed was no Robbery, no Conſtable, no Juſtice, no Thief, but all Cheaters; there was a hunder'd Mark, mark you that: Laſtly, this memorable 100 pounds worth of Muſick, this was both cheats and wit too, and for the aſſiſtance of this Gentleman to my Coſin (for which I am to have a Fee) that was a little practice of my wit too, Father; will you come to compoſition yet, Father?

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: Yes faith Sir, do, two hundr'd a year will be eaſier than ſo much weekly, I do not think he's barren if he ſhould be put to't agen.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Why this was the day I look'd for, thou ſhalt have't,
And the next cheat makes it up three hundr'd;
Live thou upon thy ten pound Vicarage,
Thou get'ſt not a penny more, here's thy full
Hire now.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.l: I thank you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Why there was the ſum of all my Wit, Father,
To ſhuve him out of your favour, which I fear'd
Would have diſinherited me.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Moſt certain it had,
Had not thy wit recover'd it; is there any here
That had a hand with thee?

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Yes, all theſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Nephew, part a hundr'd pound amongſt 'em,
I'll repay it; wealth, love me as I love wit;
When I die,
I'll build an Alms-houſe for decay'd wits.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.p: I'll entertain one in my life time; Scholar, you ſhall be my Chaplain, I have the gift of twenty Benefices, ſimple as I am here.

sp.speaker: Priſ.
sp.l: Thanks my great Patron.

sp.speaker: Cun.
sp.p: Sir your Gentry and your name ſhall both be rais'd as high as my fortunes can reach 'em, for your friend • ſake.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Something will be in my preſent power, the future more,
You ſhall ſnare with me.

sp.speaker: Ruin and Wife.
sp.l: Thanks worthy Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.l: Sir, I would beg one thing of you?

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: You can beg nothing of me.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Oh Sir, if ſhe begs, there's your power over her.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: She has begg'd me for a fool already, but 'tis no matter.
I have begg'd her for a Lady, that ſhe might have been,
That's one for another.

sp.speaker: Witty.
sp.l: Nay, but if ſhe beg—

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Let her beg agen then.

sp.speaker: Nee.
sp.p: That your man Pompey's Coat may come over his ears back agen, I would not he ſhould be loſt for my ſake.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Well, 'tis granted, for mine own ſake.

sp.speaker: Mirab.
sp.l: I'll intreat it Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Gr.
sp.l: Why then 'tis granted for your ſake.

sp.speaker: Old K.
sp.l: Come, come, down with all weapons now, 'tis Muſick time,
So it be purchas'd at an eaſie rate;
Some have receiv'd the knocks, ſome giv'n the hits,
And all concludes in love, there's happy wits.

div.head: The Epilogue at the reviving of this Play.
div.l: WE need not tell you Gallants, that this night
The Wits have jumpt, or that the Scenes hit right
'Twould be but labor loſt for to excuſe
What Fletcher had to do in: his brisk Muſe
Was ſo Mercurial, that if he but writ
An Act, or two, the whole Play roſe up wit.
We'll not appeal unto thoſe Gentlemen
Judge by their Cloaths, if they ſit right, nor when
The Ladies ſmile, and with their Fanns delight
To whisk a clinch aſide, then all goes right:
'Twas well receiv'd before, and we dare ſay,
You now are welcome to no vulgar Play.

div.head: The Fair Maid of the Inn. A TRAGI-COMEDY.
The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Ceſario, a young Gentleman of a fiery nature, Son to Alberto.
Albertus, Father to Ceſario, Admiral of Florence.
Baptiſta, a brave Sea-Commander, antient friend to Albertus, and Father to Mentivole and Biancha.
Mentiuole, Son to Baptiſta, Lover of Clariſſa.
Proſpero, a noble friend to Baptiſta.
Hoſt, the ſuppoſed Father to Biancha.
Clown, the Mountebanks man, and ſetter

list.head: Four fools and knaves, who pretend love to Biancha, the Fair Maid of the Inn.
Women.
list.item: Mariana, Wife to Albertus, a virtuous Lady.
Clariſſa, Mariana's Daughter, in love with Mentiuole.
Juliana, Neece to the Duke of Genoa, Baptiſta's ſecond wife.
Biancha, the Fair Maid of the Inn, beloved of Ceſario, and Daughter to Baptiſta and Juliana.
Hoſteſs, the ſuppoſed Mother of Biancha.

div.head: PROLOGUE.
div.l: PLays have their fates, not as in their true ſence
They're underſtood, but as the influence
Of idle cuſtom, madly works upon
The droſs of many tongu'd opinion.
A worthy ſtory, howſoever writ
For Language, modest Mirth, Conceit or Wit,
Meets oftentimes with the ſweet commendation
Of hang't, 'tis ſcurvy, when for approbation
A Jigg ſhall be clapt at, and every rhime
Prais'd and applauded by a clamorous chime.
Let ignorance and laughter dwell together,
They are beneath the Muſes pity. Hither
Come nobler Judgements, and to thoſe the ſtrain
Of our invention is not bent in vain,
The Fair Maid of the Inn to you commends
Her hopes and welcomes, and withal intends
In th' Entertains to which ſhe doth invite ye,
All things to pleaſe, and ſome things to delight ye.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Ceſario.
sp.l: INterpret not Clariſſa, my true zeal
In giving you counſel, to tranſcend the bounds
That ſhould confine a brother; 'tis your honor,
And peace of mind (which honor laſt will leave you)
I labor to preſerve, and though you yet are
Pure and untainted, and reſolve to be ſo:
Having a Fathers eye, and Mothers care
In all your ways to keep you fair, and upright.
In which reſpects my beſt advices muſt
Appear ſuperfluous; yet ſince love, dear Siſter
Will ſometimes tender things unneceſſary,
Miſconſtrue not my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: Sir, I dare not:
But ſtill receive it as a large addition,
To the much that I already ſtand ingag'd for,
Yet pardon me, though I profeſs upon
A true examination of my ſelf,
Even to my private thoughts I cannot find
(Having ſuch ſtrong ſupporters to uphold me)
On what ſlight ground the leaſt doubt can be rais'd
To render me ſuſpected, I can fall,
Or from my Fame or Virtue.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Far be it from me,
To nouriſh ſuch a thought; and yet excuſe me,
As you would do a Lapidary, whoſe whole fortunes
Depend upon the ſafety of one Jewel,
• f he think no caſe precious enough
To keep it in full l • ſtre, nor no locks,
•• ough lending ſtrength to Iron doors ſufficient
• o guard it, and ſecure him; you to me are
A Gemm of more eſteem, and priz'd higher
• han •••• ers do their Muck, or great men Title
〈◊〉 any ſ •• w (which heaven avert) in you,
〈◊〉 reputation like a Diamond
Cut newly from the rock, women with envie,
And men with covetous deſires look up at)
By prying ei • s diſcovered in a moment
Would r • nder what the braveries of Florence
For want o • counterpoize, forbear to cheapen,
Of ••• e or no value,
I ſee brother
The mark you ſhoot at, and much thank your love;
• ut for my Virgin Jewel which is brought
In compariſon with your Diamond, reſt aſſur'd
• t ſhall not fall in ſuch a workmans hands
Whoſe ignorance or malice ſhall have power
To caſt one cloud upon it, but ſtill keep
Her native ſplendor.

sp.speaker: Ceſa.
sp.l: 'Tis well, I commend you;
And ſtudy your advancement with that care
As I would do a Siſters, whom I love
With more than common order.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: That from me,
I hope's return'd to you.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I do confeſs it,
Yet let me tell you, (but ſtill with that love,
I wiſh to increaſe between us) that you are
Obſerv'd againſt the gravity long maintain'd
• n Italy (where to ſee a maid unmasqu'd
Is held a blemiſh) to be over-frequent
In giving or receiving viſits.

sp.speaker: Clari.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Whereas the cuſtom is here to wooe by Picture,
And never ſee the ſubſtance: you are fair,
And beauty draws temptations on; You know it,
I wou • d not live to ſee a willing grant
•• m • ou, to one unworthy of your birth,
• e • ture or fortune; yet there have been Ladies
Of rank, proportion, and of means beyond you,
That have prov'd this no miracle.
One unworthy?
Why, pray you gentle brother, who are they
That I vouchſafe theſe bounties to? I hope
In your ſtrict Criticiſme of me, and my manners,
That you will not deny they are your equals.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Angry?

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: I have reaſon, but in cold blood tell me,
Had we not one Father?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Yes, and Mother too.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: And he a Soldier.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: True;

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: If I then borrow
A little of the boldneſs of his temper.
Imparting it to ſuch as may deſerve it;
(However indulgent to your ſelves, you brothers
Allow no part of freedom to your Siſters)
I hope 'twill not paſs for a crime in me,
To grant acceſs and ſpeech to noble ſuitors;
And you eſcape for innocent, that deſcend
To a thing ſo far beneath you. Are you touch'd?
Why did you think that you had Giges Ring,
Or the Herb that gives inviſibility?
Or that Biancha's name had ne'er been mention'd;
The fair Maid of the grand Oſteria, brother,

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: No more.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: A little, brother. Your night walks,
And offer'd preſents; which coy ſhe, contemn'd,
Your combats in diſguiſes with your Rivals,
Brave Muletiers. Scullions perfum'd with greaſe,
And ſuch as want meat for Cats muſt be remembred;
And all this pother for a common trull,
A tempting ſign, and curiouſly ſet forth,
To draw in riotous gueſts, a thing expos'd
To every Ruſſians rude aſſault; and ſubject
For a poor ſalary, to a rich mans luſt,
Though made up of diſeaſes.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Will you end yet?

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: And this a Miſtriſs for Albertus Son,
One that I ſhould call Siſter?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Part not with
Your modeſty in this violent heat; the truth is,
(For you ſhall be my Confeſſor) I love her,
But virtuouſly; report that gives her out
Only for fair, and adds not ſhe is chaſte,
Detracts much from her: for indeed ſhe is,
Though of a low condition; compos'd
Of all thoſe graces, dames of higheſt birth,
Though rich in natures bounties, ſhould be proud of;
But leave her, and to you my neareſt care,
My deareſt beſt Clariſſa. Do not think
(For then you wrong me) I wiſh you ſhould live
A barren Virgin life; I rather aim at
A noble Husband, that may make you mother
Of many children, one that when I know him
Worth your embraces, I may ſerve, and ſue too:
And therefore ſcorn not to acquaint me with
That man, that happy man; you pleaſe to favour.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: I ever purpos'd it, for I will like
With your allowance:

sp.speaker: Ceſa.
sp.l: As a pawn of this;
Receive this Ring, but e'r you part with it
On any terms, be certain of your choice,
And make it known to me.

div.stage: Enter Servants with Lights, Alberto, Baptiſta, Mariana, Mentivole.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: You have my hand ſor't;

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Which were it not my Siſters, I ſhould kiſs:
With too much heat.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: My Father and his gueſts, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Oh my old friend, my tri'd friend, my Bapties:
Theſe days of reſt and feaſting, ſute not with
Our tougher natures, thoſe were golden ones,
Which were enjoy'd at Sea; that's our true Mother:
The Land's to us a ſtep-dame; there we ſought
Honor, and wealth through dangers: yet thoſe dangers
Delighted more than their rewards, though great ones,
And worth the undertakers: here we ſtudy
The Kitchin Arts, to ſharpen appetite,
Dull'd with abundance; and diſpute with Heaven;
If that the leaſt puff of the rough North-wind,
Blaſt our times burthen, rendring to our Palats
The charming juice leſs pleaſing; whereas there
If we had Bisket, powder'd fleſh, freſh water,
We thought them Perſian delicates, and for Muſick
If a ſtrong gale but made the main yard crack,
We danc'd to the loud Minſtrel.

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.l: And fear'd leſs,
(So far we were in love with noble action)
A tempeſt than a calm.

sp.speaker: Alber,
sp.l: 'Tis true Baptiſta;
There, there, from mutual aids lent to each other,
And virtuous emulation to exceed
In manly daring, the true School of friendſhip,
We learnt thoſe principles, which confirm'd us friends
Never to be forgot.

sp.speaker: Baptiſt.
sp.l: Never I hope.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: We were married there, for bells the roaring Canon,
A loud proclaim'd it lawful, and a prize
Then newly ta'en, and equally divided,
Serv'd as a dowry to you, then ſtil'd my wife;
And did enable me to be a Husband,
Fit to encounter ſo much wealth, though got
With bloud and horror.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: If ſo got, 'tis fit Sir
Now you poſſeſs it, that you ſhould enjoy it
In peace, and quiet; I, your Son, and Daughter
That reap the harveſt of your winters labour,
Though debtors for it yet have often trembled,
When, in way of diſcourſe, you have related
How you came by it.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Trembled? how the ſoftneſs
Of your ſex may excuſe you, I'll not argue,
But to the world, howe'er I hold thee noble
I ſhould proclaim this boy ſome cowards baſtard,
And not the Image of Albertus youth,
If when ſome wiſh'd occaſion calls him forth,
To a brave trial, one weak artery
Of his, ſhould ſhow a fever, though grim death
Put on a thouſand dreadful ſhapes to fright him;
The Elements, the Sea, and all the Winds
We number on our compaſs, then conſpiring
To make the Scaene more ghaſtly; I muſt have thee
Sirrah, I muſt, • f once you grapple with
An enemies ſhip, to board her, though you ſee
The deſperate Gunner ready to give fire,
And blow the deck u • , or like Caeſar's Soldier
Thy hands like his cut off, hang by the teeth,
And die undaunted.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: I even die to hear you:
My ſon, my lov'd Ceſario run ſuch hazards?
Bleſs'd Saints forbid it: you have done enough
Already for one family, that rude way;
I'll keep him ſafe at home, and train him up
A compleat Courtier: may I live to ſee him,
By ſweet diſcourſe, and gracious demeanor,
Winn, and bring home a fair Wife and a rich;
'Tis all I reſt ambitious of.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: A Wife!
As if there were a courſe to purchaſe one
Prevailing more than honourable action?
Or any Interceſſors move ſo far,
To take a Miſtriſs of a noble ſpirit,
As the true fame of glorious victories,
Atchiev'd by ſweat and bloud! Oh the brave dames
Of warlike Genoua! they had eyes to ſee
The inward man, and only from his worth,
Courage, and conqueſts: the blind Archer knew
To head his ſhafts, or light his quenched Torch,
They were proof againſt them elſe.
No Carpet Knight
That ſpent his youth in Groves, or pleaſant Bowers;
Or ſtretching on a Couch his lazy limbs,
Sung to his Lute ſuch ſoft and melting Notes,
As Ovid, nor Anacreon ever knew,
Could work on them, nor once bewitch'd their ſenſe;
Though he came ſo perfund as he had robb'd
Sabea, or Arabia, of their wealth;
And ſtor'd it in one ſute:
• ſtill remember,
And ſtill remember it with joy, Baptiſta,
When from the reſcue of the Genoua Fleet,
Almoſt ſurpriz'd by the Venetian Gallies,
Thou didſt return, and wert receiv'd in triumph.
How lovely in thy honor'd wounds and ſcars
Thou didſt appear what worlds of amorous glances
The beauties of the City (where they ſtood,
Fix'd like ſo many of the faireſt ſtars)
Shot from their windows at thee? how it fir'd
Their blouds to ſee the enemies captive ſtream
Born through the ſtreets? nor could chaſte Juliana
The Duke's fair Neece, though guarded with her greatneſs
Reſiſt this gallant charge, but laying by
Deſparity of fortune from the object,
Yielded her ſelf thy priſoner.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Pray you chuſe ſome other theme.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Can there be one more pleaſing?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: That triumph drew on me a greater torture,
And 'tis in the remembrance little leſs
Than ever Captive ſuffer'd.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: How? to gain the ſavour of ſo great a Lady?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Yes, ſince it prov'd fatal, t'have been happy, Madam,
Adds to calamity, and the heavy loſs
Of her I durſt not hope for, once enjoy'd,
Turns what you think a bleſſing to a curſe,
Which grief would have forgotten.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: I am ſorry I touch'd upon it.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: I burn rather, Sir,
With a deſire to hear the ſtory of
Your loves, and ſhall receive it as a favour,
Which you may grant.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: You muſt not be deny'd,
Yet with all brevity I muſt report it;
'Tis true, fair Juliana (Genoua's pride)
Enamour'd of my actions, lik'd my perſon;
Nor could I but with joy meet her affection;
Since it was lawful, for my firſt wife dead;
We were cloſely married, and for ſome few months
Taſted the fruits of't; but malicious fate,
Envying our too much happineſs, wrought upon
A faithleſs ſervant, privy to our plot,
And Cabinet-Counſelor to Juliana,
Who either for hope, or reward, or fear,
Diſcover'd us to the incenſed Duke:
Whoſe rage made her cloſe priſoner, and pronounc'd
On me perpetual baniſhment: ſome three years
I wander'd on the Seas, ſince entertain'd
By the great Duke of Florence; but what ſate
Attended her? or Proſpero my friend,
That ſtaid at Genoua, to expect the iſſue,
Is yet uncertain.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: From the Duke:

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: He's welcome, to end my forc'd relation.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Signior Baptiſta;
The Great Dukes Will commands your preſent care,

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: It points indeed at both of you;

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I wait it.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: In Mariana, to your reſt.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Nay leave us, we muſt be private,

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Stay not long Ceſario:

sp.speaker: Mentivo.
sp.l: So theſe old men vaniſh'd, 'tis allow'd
That we may ſpeak, and howſoe'r they take
Delight in the diſcourſe of former dangers,
It cannot hinder us to treat a little
Of preſent pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Ceſario,
sp.l: Which if well injoy'd,
Will not alone continue, but increaſe
In us their friendſhip.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: How ſhall we ſpend the night?
To ſnore it out like drunken Dutchmen, would
Sort ill with us Italians. We are made
Of other metall, fiery, quick, and active;
Shall we take our fortune? and while our cold fathers
(In whom long ſince their youthful heats were dead,)
Talk much of Mars, ſerve under Venus Enſigns,
And ſeek a Miſtriſs,

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: That's a game dear friend,
That does admit no rival in chaſe of it.
And either to be undertook alone,
Or not to be attempted.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I'll not preſs you;
What other ſports to entertain the time with
The following morning?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Any that may become us.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Is the Neopolitan horſe the Viceroy ſent you,
In a fit plight to run?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: So my Groom tells me.
I can boaſt little of my horſemanſhip;
Yet upon his aſſurance, I dare wager
A thouſand Crowns, 'gainſt any horſe in Florence,
For an eight mile courſe,

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I would not win of you,
In reſpect you are impatient of loſs:
Elſe I durſt match him with my Barbary
For twice the ſum.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: You do well to excuſe it, being certain to be beaten

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Tuſh. You know the contrary.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: To end the controverſie
Put it to trial, by my life I'll meet you.
With the next riſing Sun.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: A match. But here
Appears a Cynthia, that ſcorns to borrow
A beam of light from the great eye of Heaven,
She being her ſelf all brightneſs; how I envy
Thoſe amorous ſmiles, thoſe kiſſes, but ſure chaſte ones
Which ſhe vouchſafes her brother?

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: You are wanton:
Pray you think me not Biancha, leave I pray you;
My Mother will not ſleep before ſhe ſee you,
And ſince you know her tenderneſs, nay fondneſs;
In every circumſtance that concerns your ſafety,
You are not equal to her.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I muſt leave you, but will not fail to meet you

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Soft ſleeps to you.

l.hi: Ceſario.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: You are call'd again.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Some Sons
Complain of too much rigor in their Mothers;
I of too much indulgence; you will follow.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Clariſ
sp.l: You are her firſt care, therefore lead the way.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: She ſtaies: bleſt opportunity, ſhe ſtaies:
As ſhe invited conference, ſhe was ever
Noble, and free: but thus to tempt my frailty,
Argues a yielding in her; or contempt
Of all that I dare offer; ſtand I now
Conſulting? No, I'll put it home.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: Who waits there? more Lights.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You need them not, they are as uſeleſs,
As at noon-day; can there be darkneſs, where
Nature then wiſely liberal, vouchſaf'd
To lend two Suns.

l.hi: Hyperboles:

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: No, truths:
Truths beauteous Virgin, ſo my love-ſick heart
Aſſures me, and my underſtanding tells me
I muſt approach them wiſely, ſhould I raſhly
Preſs near their ſcorching beams, they would conſume me
And on the contrary, ſhould your diſdain
Keep me at too much diſtance, and I want
Their comfortable heat, the froſt of death
Would ſeize on all my faculties.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Pray you pauſe, Sir.
This vehemency of diſcourſe muſt elſe needs tire you.
Theſe gay words take not me, 'tis ſimple faith
Honeſt integrity, and lawful flames
I am delighted with:

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Such I bring with me, and therefore Lady,

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: But that you took me off
E're I came to a period; I had added
A long experience muſt be requir'd
Both of his faith and truſt, with whom a Virgin
Trafficks for, what's deareſt in this life,
Her liberty, and honor; I confeſs
I oft have view'd you with an eye of favour,
And with your generous parts the many tenders
Of doing me all fair offices, have won
A good opinion from me.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Oh ſpeak ever, I never heard ſuch Muſick;

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: A plain tune, Sir:
But 'tis a hearty one; when I perceive
By evident proofs, your aims are truly noble,
And that you bring the Engines of fair Love,
Not of foul Luſt, to ſhake and undermine
My Maiden-fortreſs: I may then make good
What now I dare not promiſe.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You already
In taking notice of my poor deſervings,
Have been magnificent, and 'twill appear
A frontleſs impudence to ask beyond this
Yet qualifie, though not excuſe my error,
Though now I am ambitious to deſire
A confirmation of it.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: So it wrong not my modeſty to grant it,

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: 'Tis far from me,
I only am a ſuitor, you would grace me
With ſome toy, but made rich in that you wore it,
To warrant to the world that I uſurp not
When I preſume to ſtile my ſelf your ſervant,
A ribond from your ſhooe:

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: You are too humble,
I'll think upon't; and ſomething of more value
Shall witneſs how I prize you, it grows late,
I'll bring you to the door,

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You ſtill more bind me.— Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Duke of Florence, Alberto, Baptiſta, Magiſtrates, and Attendants.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: You find by this aſſur'd intelligence
The preparation of the Turks againſt us.
We have met him oft and beat him; now to fear him
Would argue want of courage, and I hold it.
A ſafer policie for us and our ſigniories
To charge him in his paſſage o'er the Sea,
Than to expect him here.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: May it pleaſe your Highneſs
Since you vouchſafe to think me worthy of
This great imployment, if I may deliver
My judgement freely, 'tis not flattery
Though I ſay my opinion waits on you,
Nor would I give my ſuffrage and conſent
To what you have propos'd, but that I know it
Worth the great ſpeaker, though that the denial
Call'd on your heavy anger. For my ſelf
I do profeſs thus much, if a blunt Soldier,
May borrow ſo much from the oyl'd tongu'd Courtier,
(That ecchoes whatſoe'er the Prince allows of)
All that my long experience hath taught me
That have ſpent three parts of my life at Sea,
(Let it not taſte of arrogance that I ſay it)
Could not have added reaſons of more weight
To fortifie your affections' than ſuch
As your grace out of obſervation meerly
Already have propounded.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: With the honor to give the daring enemy an affront
In being the firſt oppoſer it will teach
Your Soldiers boldneſs: and ſtrike fear in them
That durſt attempt you.

sp.speaker: 1 Magi.
sp.l: Victuals and Ammunition,
And Money too, the ſinews of the War, are ſtor'd up in the Magazine.

sp.speaker: 2 Magi.
sp.l: And the Gallies new rig'd and train'd up,
And at two dayes warning fit for the ſervice.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We commend your care,
Nor will we e'er be wanting in Our counſels,
As we doubt not your action; you Baptiſta
Shall ſtay with us; that Merchant is not wiſe,
That ventures his whole fortunes in one bottom.
Be our Admiral, ſpare your thanks,
'Tis Merit in you that invites this honor,
Preſerve it ſuch; ere long you ſhall hear more,
Things raſhly undertaken end as ill,
But great acts thrive when reaſon guides the will.
No queſtion 'twas not well done in Caeſario,
To croſs the horſe of young Mentivole
• n the midſt of this courſe.
That was not all, the ſwitching him dull'd him.
Would that both the jades
Had broke their necks, when they firſt ſtarted; 'Slight,
We ſtand here prating, give them leave to whiſper,
And when they have cut one anothers throats
Make in to part 'em.
There is no ſuch hazard,
Their Fathers friendſhip, and their love forbid it;
• ee where they come!
With fury in their looks.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You have the wager, with what foul play got
• ll not diſpute:

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Foul play?

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I cannot ſpeak it
• n a fairer language, and if ſome reſpects
• amiliar to my ſelf chain'd not my tongue,
• ſhould ſay no more. I ſhould, but I'll ſit down,
With this diſgrace; how e'er preſs me no farther.
• or if once more provok'd, you'll underſtand
• dare no more ſuffer an Injury,
Than I dare do one.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Why Sir are you injur'd
• n that I take my right which I would force,
Should you detain it?

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Put it to judgment.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: No; my will in this ſhall carry it.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Your will? nay, farewell ſoftneſs then.
This I foreſaw.
Hold, hold.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: I am hurt.
Shift for your ſelf, 'tis death.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: As you reſpect me, bear him off with care,
• f he miſcarry ſince he did the wrong,
• 'll ſtand the ſhock of't.
Gently, he will faint elſe—

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: And ſpeedily, I beſeech you; my rage over,
That pour'd upon my reaſon clouds of error,
• ſee my folly, and at what dear loſs
• have exchang'd a real innocence,
To gain a meer fantaſtical report,
Tranſported only by vain popular wind,
To be a daring, nay, fool-hardy Man.
But could I ſatisfie my ſelf within here,
How ſhould I bear my fathers frown? They meet me,
My guilt conjures him hither.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Sirrah:

sp.speaker: Mentiv.
sp.l: Sir:

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I have met the trophies of your ruſſian ſword:
Was there no other Anvile to make triall
How far thou durſt be wicked, but the boſome
Of him, which under the adulterate name
Of friendſhip, thou haſt murder'd.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Murder'd Sir?
My dreams abhor ſo baſe a fact; true valour
Imploy'd to keep my reputation fair
From the auſtereſt Judge, can never merit
To be branded with that title; you begot me
A man, no coward; and but call your youth
To memory, when injur'd, you could never
Boaſt of the Aſſes fortitude, ſlave-like patience:
And you might juſtly doubt I were your ſon,
If I ſhould entertain it; if Caeſario
Recover, as I hope his wound's not mortal,
A ſecond tryal of what I dare doe
In a juſt cauſe, ſhall give ſtrong witneſs for me
I am the true heir to Baptiſta's courage,
As to his other fortunes.

sp.speaker: Baptiſt.
sp.l: Boy, to neither:
But on this ſtrict condition, which intreaties
From Saints, nay Angels, ſhall not make me alter.
A friendſhip ſo began, and ſo continu'd
Between me and Alberto my beſt friend,
Your brawls ſhall not diſſolve; it is my will,
And as I am thy Father, I command thee,
That inſtantly, on any termes, how poor
So e'er, it skills not, thou deſire his pardon,
And bring aſſurance to me, he has ſign'd it,
Or by my Fathers ſoul I'll never know thee:
But as a ſtranger to my blood; perform it,
And ſuddenly, without reply, I have ſaid it.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: And in it given a heavier ſentence on me
Than the moſt cruel death; you are my father
And your will to be ſerv'd, and not diſputed
By me, that am your Son: But I'll obey,
And though my heart-ſtrings crack for't, make it known,
When you command, my faculties are your own. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Alberto, Phyſitian, and a Chirurgion.

sp.speaker: Phyſ.
sp.l: HAve patience, Noble Sir; your ſon Caeſario
Will recover without queſtion.

sp.speaker: Surgeon.
sp.l: A ſlight wound.
Though it pierc't his body, it hath miſs'd the vitals.

sp.speaker: Phyſ.
sp.p: My life for't, he ſhall take the air again within theſe ten dayes.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: O but from a friend,
To receive this bloody meaſure from a friend!
If that a man ſhould meet a violent death,
In a place where he had taken ſanctuary,
Would it not grieve him? ſuch all Florence held
Their friendſhip, and 'tis that which multiplies
The injury.

sp.speaker: Phyſi.
sp.l: Have patience worthy Signior.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: I do proteſt, as I am Man and Soldier,
If I had buried him in a wave at Sea,
(Loſt in ſome honorable action)
I would not, to the ſaltneſs of his grave,
Have added the leaſt tear; but theſe quarrels
Bred out of game and wine, I had as live
He ſhould have died of a Surfet.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Oh what comfort? How is it with our Son Sir?

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: His Work-maſters
Bear me in hand here, as my Lawyer does,
When I have a crackt Title, or bad Sute in Law,
All ſhall go well.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: I pray you Gentlemen, what think you of his wound.

sp.speaker: Phyſi.
sp.l: 'Tis but a ſcratch, nothing to danger.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: But he receiv'd it from a friend,
And the unkindneſs ta'en at that, may kill him.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Let me ſee him:

sp.speaker: Phyſi.
sp.l: By no means, he ſlumbers.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Then I cannot believe you,
When you tell me there's hope of him.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Yet many Ladies
Do give more ſaith to their Phyſitian
Than to their Confeſſor.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: O my poor loſt brother,
And friend more dear than Brother.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: More loud inſtruments
To diſturb his ſlumbers! goe, goe, take Caroch:
And as you love me, you and the Girle retire
To our Summer houſe, i'th' Country; I'll be with you
Within theſe two days.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: I am yours in all things,
Though with much ſorrow to leave him.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: I pray you Gentlemen,
With beſt obſervance tend your Patient;
The loſs of my heir-male, lies now a bleeding.
And think what payment his recovery
Shall ſhow'r upon you,
Of all men breathing;
Wherefore do you arrive here? Are you mad?
My injury begins to bleed afreſh
At ſight of you; why this affront of yours
I receive more malitious than the other.
Your hurt was only danger to my ſon:
But your ſight to me is death; Why come you hither?
Do you come to view the wounds, which you have made?
And glory in them?

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: Rather worthy Sir, to pour Oyl into them.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: I am a Soldier Sir,
Leaſt part of a Courtier, and underſtand
By your ſmooth Oyl,
Your preſent flattery.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: Sir, for my Fathers ſake acknowledge me
To be born a Gentleman, no ſlave; I ever
Held flatterers of that breed; do not miſconſtrue
In your diſtaſte of me, the true intent
Of my coming hither, for I do proteſt
I do not come to tell you I am ſorry
For your ſons hurt.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Not ſorry?

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: No not ſorry; I have to the loweſt ebbo, loſt all my fury:
But I muſt not loſe my honeſty; 'twas he
Gave heat unto the injury, which return'd
(Like a Petar, ill lighted, into 'th' boſome
Of him, gave fire to't) yet I hope his hurt,
Is not ſo dangerous, but he may recover;
When if it pleaſe him, call me to account,
For the loſs of ſo much blood, I ſhall be ready
To do him noble reaſon.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: You are arm'd me thinks with wondrous confidence.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: O with the beſt Sir;
For I bring penitence, and ſatisfaction.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Satisfaction? Why I heard you ſay but now,
You were not ſorry for his wounds.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: Nor am I: the ſatisfaction which I bring Sir, is to you;
You are a Gentleman ne'er injur'd me;
One ever lov'd my Father, the right way,
And moſt approv'd of noble amity.
Yet I have run my ſword quite through your heart,
And ſlightly hurt your ſon, for't may be ſcar'd,
A grief ta'en at theſe years for your ſons loſs,
May hazard yours: And therefore I am ſent
By him that has moſt intereſt in your ſorrow;
Who having chid me almoſt to the ruin
Of a diſheritance, for violating
So continued and ſo ſacred a friendſhip
Of 50 Winters ſtanding: ſuch a friendſhip,
That ever did continue like the ſpring;
Ne'er ſaw the fall o'th' leaf; by him I am ſent
To ſay the wrong I have done Sir, is to you:
And that I have quite loſt him for a Father,
Until I find your pardon; nay there follows
A weightier deprivation; his Eſtate
I could with a leſs number of ſighs part with.
Fortune might attend my youth, and my deſervings
In any Climate: but a Fathers bleſſing,
To ſettle and confirm that fortune, no where;
But only here. Your pardon, give me that;
And when you have done, kill me; for 'tis that
Takes from me the effect of excommunication;
A Fathers heavy curſe.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Nay, may that curſe
Light on himſelf, for ſending thee in this minute:
When I am grown as deaf to all compaſſion,
As the cruelleſt Sea-fight, or moſt horrid tempeſt.
That I had drown'd i'th' Sea a thouſand duckets,
Thou hadſt not made this viſit: raſh young man,
Thou tak'ſt me in an ill Planet, and haſt cauſe
To curſe thy Father; for I do proteſt,
If I had met thee in any part o'th' World,
But under my own roofe, I would have kill'd thee.
sp.stage: Within there.—Enter Phyſitian, Chirurgion, and Servants.
sp.l: Look you!
Here's a triumph ſent for the death of your young Maſter.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Shall we kill him?

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: No, I'll not be ſo unhoſpitable; but Sir,
By my life, I vow to take aſſurance from you,
That right hand never more ſhall ſtrike my ſon.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: That will be eaſily proteſted.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Not eaſily, when it muſt be exacted, and a bloody ſeal to't.
Bind him, and cut off's right hand preſently:
Fair words ſhall never ſatisfie foul deeds.
Chop's hand off.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: You cannot be ſo unrighteous, to your own honor.

sp.speaker: Phy.
sp.l: O Sir, collect your ſelf;
And recall your bloody purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: My intents of this nature, do ever come to action.

sp.speaker: Chirur.
sp.l: Then I muſt fetch another ſtickler.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Yet I do grieve at heart;
And I do curſe thy Father heartily,
That's the cauſe of my diſhonor; ſending thee
In ſuch an hour, when I am apt for miſchief:
Apt, as a Dutch-man after a Sea-fight,
When his enemy kneels afore him; come diſpatch.

sp.speaker: Phyſ.
sp.l: Intreat him, Noble Sir;

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: You ſhall excuſe me;
Whatſoever he dares do, that I dare ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Oh Sir, for honors ſake ſtay your foul purpoſe,
For if you do proceed thus cruelly,
There is no queſtion in the wound you give him,
I ſhall bleed to death for't.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Thou art not of my temper,
What I purpoſe, cannot be alter'd.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Sir; the Duke
With all ſpeed expects you. You muſt inſtantly
Ship all your followers, and to ſea.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: My bleſſing ſtay with thee upon this condition,
Take away his uſe of fighting; as thou hop'ſt
To be accounted for my ſon, perform't — Exit.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: You hear what I am injoyn'd to.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: Pray thee take it,
Only this ring, this beſt eſteem'd Jewel:
I will not give't to'th' hangman chops it off;
It is too dear a relique. I'll remove it nearer my heart.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Ha, that Rings my Siſters.
The Ring I injoyn'd her never part withal
Without my knowledge; come, Sir, we are friends:
Pardon my fathers heat, and melancholy;
Two violent Fevers which he caught at Sea,
And cannot yet ſhake off: only one promiſe
I muſt injoyn you to, and ſeriouſly.
Hereafter you ſhall never draw a Sword
To the prejudice of my life.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: By my beſt hopes I ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: I pray deliver me your ſword
On that condition.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: I ſhall Sir, may it hereafter
Ever fight on your part.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Noble Sir, I thank you;
But for performance of your vow, I intreat
Some gage from you.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: Any Sir.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Deliver me that ring.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: Ha, this Ring? indeed this Jewel binds me,
If you knew the vertue of it, never more
To draw my ſword againſt you.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Therefore I will have it.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: You may not.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Come: you muſt.
I that by violence could take your hand,
Can inforce this from you; this is a token Sir,
That we may prove friends hereafter. Fare you well.

sp.speaker: Phyſ.
sp.l: Why did you ceiſe his Sword Sir?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: To perform what my Father bade me,
I have for the preſent ta'en away his
Uſe of fighting.

sp.speaker: Phyſ.
sp.l: Better ſo,
Than take that which your Father meant.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: Was ever the like uſage? O that Ring!
Dearer than life, Whither is honor fled?

sp.speaker: Ceſario.
sp.l: Thou art unmanly in each part,
To ſeize my ſword firſt, and then ſplit my heart. Exit.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Thy Maſter that lodges here in my Oſteria,
Is a rare man of art, they ſay he's a Witch.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: A Witch? Nay, he's one ſtep of the Ladder to preferment higher, he is a Conjurer?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Is that his higher title?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Yes, I aſſure you, for a Conjurer is the Devils Maſter, and commands him; whereas a Witch is the Devils Prentice, and obeys him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Bound Prentice to the Devil!

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Bound and inroll'd I aſſure you, he cannot ſtart; and therefore I would never wiſh any Gentleman to turn Witch.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Why Man?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Oh he loſes his Gentility by it, the Devil in this caſe cannot help him, he muſt go to the Herald for new Armes believe it.

sp.l: As I am true Inkeeper, yet a Gentleman born,
I'll ne'er turn Witch for that trick;
And thou haſt been a great Traveller?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: No indeed, not I Sir;

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Come, you are modeſt.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No, I am not modeſt, for I told you a lye, that you might the better underſtand I have been a Traveller,

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: So Sir, they ſay your Maſter is a great Phyſitian too.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: He was no fool told you that, I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: And you have been in England? but they ſay, Ladies in England take a great deal of Phyſick.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Both wayes on my reputation.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: So 'tis to be underſtood:
But they ſay, Ladies there take Phyſick for faſhion.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and many times dye to keep faſhion.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: How? dye to keep faſhion!

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Yes, I have known a Lady ſick of the ſmall Pocks, onely to keep her face from Pitholes, take cold, ſtrike them in again, kick up the heels, and vaniſh.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: There was kicking up the heels with a witneſs.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No Sir; I confeſs a good face has many times been the motive to the kicking up of the heels with a witnſs: but this was not.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Here comes my wife and daughter.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: You have a prety commodity of this night-worm?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Why Man?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: She is a pretty lure to draw cuſtom to your ordinary.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Do'ſt think I keep her to that purpoſe?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: When a Dove-houſe is empty, there is cuminſeed uſed to purloine from the reſt of the neighbors; In England you have ſeveral Adamants, to draw in ſpurs and rapiers; one keeps ſilk-worms in a Gallery: A Milliner has choice of Monkies, and Paraketoes; another ſhewes bawdy Eaſt-Indian Pictures, worſe than ever were Aretines: a Goldſmith keeps his Wife wedged into his ſhop like a Mermaid, nothing of her to be ſeen (thats Woman) but her upper part?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Nothing but her upper part?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Nothing but her upper bodies, and he lives at the more hearts eaſe.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: What's the reaſon?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Becauſe her nether part can give no temptation; by your leave, Sir, I'll tend my Maſter, and inſtantly be with you for a cup of Cherally this hot weather.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: A nimble pated Raſcal, come hither Daughter,
When was Ceſario here?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Sir, not this fortnight.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I do not like his viſits, commonly
He comes by Owl-light, both the time and manner
Is ſuſpitious; I do not like it.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Sir, the Gentleman
Is every way ſo noble, that you need not
Queſtion his intent of coming, though you did;
Pray Sir preſerve that good opinion of me,
That though the cuſtome of the place I was born in,
Makes me familiar to every gueſt,
I ſhall in all things keep my ſelf a ſtranger
To the vices they bring with them.

sp.speaker: Hoſtis.
sp.l: Right my daughter:
She has the right ſtrain of her Mother.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Of her Mother?
And I would ſpeak, I know from whence ſhe took it;
When I was as young, I was as honeſt.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Leave your prating.
sp.p: And ſtudy to be drunk; and abuſe your gueſts over and over.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Peace Wife. My honorable gueſt.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: My indear'd Landlord?
And the reſt o'th' complements o'th' houſe.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Breakfaſt is ready Sir;
It waites only the tide of your ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: And mine gapes for't like a ſtale Oyſter.
Ere you go to bed, fail not of that I pray.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: We will inſtantly be with you;
Now we are all fellows.
Nine a Clock, and no Clyents come
Yet, ſure thou do'ſt not ſet up bills enough.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I have ſet up bills in abundance.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: What Bills?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Marry for curing of all diſeaſes,
Recovery of ſtoln goods,
And a thouſand ſuch impoſſibilities.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: The place is unlucky.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No certain, 'tis ſcarcity of mony; do not you hear the Lawyers complain of it? Men have as much Malice as ever they had to wrangle, but they have no Mony: Whither ſhould this Mony be travell'd?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: To the Devil I think.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: 'Tis with his Cofferer I am certain, that's the Uſurer.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Our cheating does not proſper ſo well as it was wont to do.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No ſure, why in England we coo'd cozen 'em as familiarly, as if we had travell'd with a Brief, or a Lottery.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: I'th' Low-countries we did pretty well.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: So ſo: as long as we kept the Mop-headed butter-boxes ſober; marry when they were drunk, then they grew buzards: You ſhould have them reel their heads together, and deliberate; your Dutchman indeed, when he is foxt, is like a Fox; for when he's ſunk in drink, quite earth to a Mans thinking, 'tis full Exchange time with him, then he's ſubtleſt; but your Switzer, 'twas nothing to cheat him.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Nothing?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No, nor conſcience to be made of it; for ſince nature afore-hand cozen'd him of his wit, 'twas the leſs ſin for us to cozen him of his Mony.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: But theſe Italians are more nimble-pated; we muſt have ſome new trick for them; I proteſt but that our Hoſteſs's daughter is a ſweet Laſs, and draws great reſort to'th' houſe, we were as good draw teeth a horſeback.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I told 'em in the Market-place you could conjure, and no body would believe me: but ere long I will make 'em believe you can conjure with ſuch a figuary.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: What language ſhall's conjure in? high Dutch I think, that's full i'th' mouth.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No, no, Spaniſh, that roars beſt; and will appear more dreadful.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Prethee tell me thy conceit thou haſt to gull them.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No, no, I will not ſtael it; but my dear Jewstrump, for thou art but my inſtrument, I am the plotter, and when we have cozen'd 'em moſt titely, thou ſhalt ſteal away the Inn-keepers daughter, I'll provide my ſelf of another moveable: and we will moſt purely retire our ſelves to Geneva.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Thou art the compaſs I ſail by.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Was ever expectation of ſo Noble
A requital anſwered with ſuch contumely!
A wild Numidian that had ſuck'd a Tigreſs,
Would not have been ſo barbarous; Did he threat
To cut thy hand off?

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and his ſlaves were ready to perform't.

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.l: What hind'red it?

sp.speaker: Meut.
sp.l: Only his ſons intreaty.

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.l: Noble youth,
I wiſh thou wert not of his blood; thy pitty
Gives me a hope thou art not.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You miſtake Sir,
The injury that followed from the ſon,
Was worſe than the fathers; he did firſt diſarme
And took from me a Jewel, which I prize
Above my hand or life.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Take thy ſword from thee?
He ſtole it like a Thief rather, he could not
I'th' Field deprive thee of it.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: He took it from me,
And ſent me forth ſo thin, and ſo unmade up,
As if I had been a Foot-boy.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: O my fury!
I muſt now ask thee forgiveneſs, that my raſhneſs,
Bred out of too much friendſhip, did expoſe thee
To ſo eminent a danger; which I vow
I will revenge on the whole Family:
All the calamities of my whole life,
My baniſhment from Genoa, my wifes loſs
Compar'd to this indignity, is nothing;
Their Family ſhall repair't; it ſhall be to them
Like a plague, when the Dog-ſtar reigns moſt hot:
An Italian's revenge may pauſe, but's ne'er forgot. Exit.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I would I had conceal'd this from my Father,
For my intereſt in Clariſſa; my care now
Muſt be to untangle this diviſion,
That our moſt equal flames may be united;
And from theſe various and perturbed ſtreames,
Riſe, like a ſweet Morn, after terrible dreams.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Brother, I am happy in your recovery,

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: And I Siſter, am ever beſt pleaſed in your happineſs:
But I miſs a toy ſhould be on your finger.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: My Ring; this morning when I waſh't
I put it off, 'tis in my Window.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Where's your Looking-glaſs?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: 'Tis a fair one.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Tis pure Chryſtal.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Can a Diamond cut in Cryſtal? let me ſee,
I'll grave my name in't.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Oh, you'll ſpoyl my glaſs.
Would you not have your brother in your eye?

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: I had thought he had been Planted in your heart,
Look you, the Diamond cuts quaintly, you are cozen'd,
Your Chryſtal is too britle.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: 'Tis the Ring
I gave unto Mentivole, ſure the ſame.
You put me to amazement Sir, and horror;
How came you by that Ring?

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Does the blood riſe?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Pray Sir reſolve me, O for pitty do;
And take from me a trembling at the heart,
That elſe will kill me: for I too much fear
Nothing but Death could raviſh it from his hand
That wore it.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Was it given to Mentivola on that condition?

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Tell me of his health firſt.
And then I'll tell you any thing.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: By my life he's well,
In better health than I am.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Then it was Sir.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Then ſhall I ever hate thee, Oh thou falſe one;
Haſt thou a Faith to give unto a friend,
And break it to a brother? Did I not,
By all the tyes of blood importune thee
Never to part with it without my knowledge?
Thou might'ſt have given it to a Muliter,
And made a contract with him in a ſtable,
At as cheap a price of my vengeance: never more
Shall a Womans truſt beguile me; You are all
Like Relicks: you may well be look't upon,
But come a Man to'th' handling of you once,
You fall in pieces.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Dear Sir, I have no way
Look't either beneath reaſon, or my ſelf,
In my election; there's parity in our blood,
And in our fortunes, antient amity
Betwixt our parents: to which wants nothing,
But the Fruit of bleſt Marriage between us,
To add to their poſterities: nor does now
Any impeachment riſe, except the ſad
And unexpected quarrel, which divided
So noble, and ſo excellent a friendſhip,
Which as I ne'er had Magick to foreſee,
So I could not prevent.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Well, you muſt give me leave
To have a hand in your diſpoſing, I ſhall,
In the abſence of my Father, be your Guardian;
His Suit muſt paſs through my office. Mentivole,
He has too much of my blood already; he has,
And he get's no more of't—
Wherefore weep you Mother?

sp.speaker: Marian.
sp.l: 'Tis occaſion'd by a ſorrow,
Wherein you have a Child's part, and the maineſt,
Your Father's dead.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Dead?

sp.speaker: Marian.
sp.l: There's one can relate the reſt.

sp.speaker: Sailor.
sp.l: I can Sir, your Father's drown'd,
Moſt unfortunately drown'd.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: How? In a tempeſt?

sp.speaker: Sailor.
sp.l: No Sir, in a calm,
Calm as this evening; the Gunner being drunk,
Forgot to faſten the Ordnance to their ports,
When came a ſudden guſt, which tumbled them
All to the Starboord ſide, o'erturn'd the Ship,
And ſunk her in a moment, ſome ſix men
That were upon the deck were ſav'd: the reſt
Periſh'd with your Father.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: O my deareſt Father—

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I pray thee leave us.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: I have a ſorrow of another nature, equal to the former.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: And moſt commonly they come together.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: The Family of the Baptiſti
Are grown to faction, and upon diſtaſt
Of the injury late offer'd in my houſe,
Have vow'd a moſt ſevere, and fell revenge
'Gainſt all our family, but eſpecially
'Gainſt you my dear Caeſario.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Let them threat, I am prepar'd to oppoſe them.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: And is your loſs then
Of ſo eaſie an eſtimation? What comfort
Have I but in your life, and your late danger
Preſents afore me what I am to ſuffer,
Should you miſcarry; therefore I'll adviſe you
When the Funeral is over, you would travel,
Both to prevent their fury, and wear out th' injury.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: No Mother, I will not travel,
So in my abſence he may marry my Siſter,
I will not travel certain.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: O my Ceſario,
Whom I reſpect and love 'bove my own life,
Indeed with a kind of dotage, he ſhall never
Go forth o' doors, but the contrary faction
Will indanger's life, and then am I moſt wretched.
I am thinking of a ſtrange prevention,
Which I ſhall witneſs with a bleeding eye,
Fondneſs ſometimes is worſe than cruelty.— Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: HAunted, my houſe is haunted with goblins. I ſhall be frighted out of my wits, and ſet up a ſign only to invite Carriers and Foot-poſts; ſcar-crows to keep off the Cavalry, and Gentry of the beſt rank. I will nail up my doors, and wall up my Girle (wife) like an Anchoreſs; or ſhe will be raviſht before our faces, by raſcalls and cacafugo's (wife) cacafugo's.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.p: Theſe are your In-comes, remember your own proverb, the ſavor of every gain ſmelt ſweet; thank no body but your ſelf for this trouble.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: No gauling (dear Spouſe) no gauling, every days new vexation abates me two inches in the waſte, terrible pennance for an Hoſt, Girle, girle, girle, Which of all this gally-maufry of Mans fleſh appears tolerable to thy choice, ſpeak ſhortly, and ſpeak truely: I muſt and will know, muſt and will; Hear ye that?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Sir, be not jealous of my care and duty;
I am ſo far from entertaining thoughts
Of liberty, that much more excellent objects
Than any of ſuch courſe contents as theſe are,
Could not betray mine eye to force my heart;
Conceive a wiſh of any dearer happineſs
Than your direction warrant's. I am yours Sir.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.p: What thinks the Man now? Is not this ſtrange at 13.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Very good words, there's a tang in e'm, and a ſweet one, 'tis muſick (wife) and now I come t'ee. Let us a little examine the ſeveral conditions of our Paragraphiſtical ſuitors. The firſt, a travelling Tailor, who by the myſtery of his Needle and Thimble, hath ſurvey'd the faſhions of the French, and Engliſh; this Signior Ginger-bread, ſtitcht up in the ſhreds of a gudy outſide, ſows Linings with his croſs-leg'd complement, like an Ape doing tricks over a ſtaffe, cringes, and crouches, and kiſſes his forefinger.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.p: Out upon him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: A ſecond, a lavolteteere, a ſaltatory, a dancer with a Kit at his Bum, one that, by teaching great Madonnas to foot it, has miraculouſly purchaſt a ribanded Waſtcote, and four clean pair of ſocks; a fellow that skips as he walkes, and inſtead of ſenſible diſcourſe, vents the curious conceit of ſome new tune ſtolen from a Mask, or a bawdy dittie, elevated for the Pole Artick of a Ladies chamber, in that file ſtands another of your inamoratoes.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.p: Hang him and his Fiddle together, he never fidles any child of ours.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: The third, a Mongrel, got by a Switzer on an Italian; this puppy, being left well eſtated, comes to Florence, that the world may take notice, how impoſſible it is for experience to alter the courſe of nature; a fool (wife) and indeed, a Clown turn'd Gallant, ſeldom or never proves other than a gallant fool, this toy prates to little purpoſe other than What's a Clock? Shall's go drink? De'e forſooth? and thank ye heartily; I fear no art in him to catch thee, and yet we muſt be tormented with this buzard amongſt the reſt.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.p: 'Tis your own folly, forbid him the Houſe.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: The fourth, a Mule-driver, a ſtubborn and a harſh knave: the fifth a School-Maſter, a very amorous Pedant, run almoſt mad with ſtudy of Sonnets, and Complements out of old Play-ends, the laſt an Advocates Clerk, that ſpeaks pure Fuſtian in Law-terms: excellent Courtiers all, and all as neate as a Magnifio's poſt new painted, at his entrance to an office; thou ſhalt have none of 'em. Laugh at 'em, do. I ſay thou ſhalt have none of 'em.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Still your command to me ſhall ſtand a Law.

Now they throng like ſo many horſe-courſers at a • air, in cluſters about the Man of Art, for Love-powders, i • gredients, potions, counſels, poſtures, complements, philt • rs: the Devil and the—How now? Tumults? Batteries, Noiſe? ha, get from my ſight. Clown cries within.

div.stage: Enter Foroboſco, and Clown, his head bloody.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Murther me, do, pound me to Mummy, do; ſee what will come on't.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Dog, leave thy ſnarling, or I'll cut thy tongue out,
Thou un ickt Bear, dar'ſt thou yet ſtand my fury,
My generous rage? yet! by the ſulpherous damps
That feed the hungry and inceſſant darkneſs,
Which curles around the grim Alaſtors back,
Mutter again, and with one powerful word,
Ill call an Hoſt up from the Stygian Lakes,
Shall waſt thee to the Acherontick fens;
Where choak't with Miſts as black as thy impoſtures,
Thou ſhalt live ſtill a dying.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Conjure me to the Devil and you can, I live in Hell upon earth already, and you had any mercy, you would not practice upon a kind heart thus.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: You have drawn blood from him Signior, Is his offence unpardonable?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A lump of ignorance, pray ſpeak not for him,
A drowſie groſsneſs, in all Chriſtian Kingdoms,
The mention of my art, my name, my practiſe,
Merit and Glory hath begot at once
Delight and wonder; I'll not be entreated;
Spare interceſſion for him,— O thou ſcorn
Of learning, ſhame of duty; muſt thy ſloth
Draw my juſt ſame in queſtion? I diſcharge thee
From my ſervice; ſee me no more henceforth.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Diſcharge me! Is that my years wages?
I'll not be ſo anſwer'd.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Not Camel? Sirrah I am liberal to thee;
Thou haſt thy life, be gone.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Vengeance, ſweet vengeance.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: D • 'e mumble?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I'll be reveng'd, monſtrouſly, ſuddenly, and inſatiably; my bulk begins to ſwell.

l.hi: Homotolenton, Pragmatophoros, Helioſtycorax.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Call up your Spirits, I defie 'em; well, I'll have Law for my broken pate, twelve ounces of pure blood; Troy-weight. In deſpight of thee my Maſter, and thy Maſter the grand Devil himſelf, vindicta, vindicta.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Signior, you are exceeding mov'd.
Mercy upon us, What terrible words thou talk'ſt?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A ſlave, a curr—but be not you afrighted
Young Virgin, 'twere an injury to ſweetneſs:
Should any rough found draw from your cheeks,
The pretious tincture which makes nature proud
Of her own workmanſhip.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Wiſe, Mark, mark that Wife.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Shake then your anger off Sir;

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: You command it
Fair one, mine Hoſt and Hoſteſs, with your leaves
I have a motion joyntly to you all.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: An honeſt one I hope.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Well put in Wife.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A very neceſſary one, the Meſs
And half of ſuitors, that attend to uſher
Their Loves ſir-reverence to your daughter, wait
With one conſent, which can beſt pleaſe her eye;
In offering at a Dance, I have provided
Muſick. And, 'twill be ſomething I dare promiſe
Worthy your laughter, Shall they have admittance?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: By any means, for I am perſwaded the manner will be ſo
Ridiculous, that it will confirm the aſſurance of their
Miſerable fooleries, but no longer trouble with 'em here,
Than they are in theſe May-games.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: So I am reſolv'd.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſs.
sp.l: Nor any wiſe word of ſenceleſs love.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Not any; I have charm'd them, Did you ſee
How they prepar'd themſelves? how they ſtroak up
Their foretops, how they juſtle for the Looking-laſs,
To ſet their faces by it; See they Muſter.
You would look for ſome moſt impoſſible antick.

div.stage: Enter Tailor, Dancer, Mule-driver, School-Maſter, Clark: (all with ſeveral papers, and preſent 'em to Foroboſco.)

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: So, ſo, ſo, ſo, here flutter the neſt of Hornets, the hotch-potch of raſcallity; now, now, now, now, the dunghill of corruption hath yawn'd forth the burthen of abhomination. I am vext, vext to the ſoul, will rid my houſe of this unchriſten'd fry, and never open my doors again.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Some other time, I'll give no anſwer now,
But have preſerred your ſuits, here ſhew your cunning.
Firſt, every one in order do his honor
To the fair mark you ſhoot at; courtly, courtly,
Convey your ſeveral loves in lively meaſure:
Come, let us take our ſeates, ſome ſprightly Muſick.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Dance all and part, 'tis a very neceſſary farewell.

div.stage: Enter Caeſario, They all make ridiculous conges to Bianca: rank themſelves, and dance in ſeveral poſtures: during the dance, Enter Caeſario, and ſtands off.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Well done my luſty bloods, preciſely well done,
One luſty rouſe of Wine, and take leave on all ſides.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Thanks for your Revels Gentlemen; accept
This Gold, and drink as freely as you danc'd.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: My noble Lord Ceſario, clear the rooms Sirs.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Away. Attend your anſwers.

div.stage: — Exeunt Foro, and thoſe that d • ne'd.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.p: With your favor Rolando, I would change a word or two with your fair daughter.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: At your Lordſhips pleaſure, come Wife, no muttering, have a care Girle, my love, ſervice, and duty to you good Lordſhip. —Exeunt and Wife.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: My often viſits (ſweet Bianca) cannot
But conſtantly inform thy judgment, wherein
Thy happineſs conſiſts, for to ſteal minutes
From great imployments, to converſe with beauty,
Lodg'd in ſo mean a fortune, to lay by
Conſideration of the unequal diſtance
Between my blood and thine, to ſhun occaſions
Of courtſhip with the Ladies of the time:
Noble, and fair, only for love to thee,
Muſt of neceſſity invite a tenderneſs;
As low as nature could have ſtampt a Bondwomans.
To entertain quick motions of rare gratitude
For my uncommon favors.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: 'Deed my Lord, as far as my ſimplicity can lead me,
I freely thank your curteſies.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: To thank them, is to reward them pretty one.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Then teach me
How I may give them back again; in truth
I never yet receiv'd a pair of Gloves:
A trifling Ring from any that expected
An equall ſatisfaction, but as willingly
I parted with the guift unto the owner, as he beſtow'd it.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: But I pour before thee
Such plenties, as it lies not in the ability
Of thy whole kindred, to return proportionable
One for a thouſand.
You my Lord conclude
For my inſtruction, to ingage a debt
Beyond a poſſibility of paiment,
I ever thought a ſin; and therefore juſtly
Without conceit of ſcorn, or curious rudeneſs,
I muſt refuſe your bounty.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Canſt thou love?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Love! Is there ſuch a word in any Language
That carries honeſt ſence?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Never dwelt ignorance
In ſo ſweet-ſhap't a building: love, Bianca,
Is that firm knot which ties two hearts in one:
Shall ours be tied ſo?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Uſe a plainer word,
My Lord. In ſtead of tyes, ſay marries hearts,
Then I may underſtand.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Their hearts are married
Whoſe enterchange of pleaſures, and embraces,
Soft kiſſes, and the privacies of ſweets,
Keeps conſtant league together, when temptation
Of great mens oathes and gifts, ſhall urge contempt,
Rather than batter reſolution, novelty
Of ſights, or taſte of new delights in wantonneſs,
Breeds ſurfeit more than appetite in any
Reſerv'd to noble vowes; my excellent Maid,
Live thou but true to me, and my contents,
Mine only, that no partner may partake
The treaſure of thoſe ſweets thy youth yet glories in,
And I will raiſe thy lowneſs to abundance
Of all varieties, and more triumph
In ſuch a Miſtris, than great Princes doating
On truth-betraying Wives.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Thus to yield up then
The cottage of my virtue, to be ſwallow'd
By ſome hard-neighbouring Landlord, ſuch as you are,
Is in effect to love, a Lord ſo vicious!
O where ſhall innocence find ſome poor dwelling,
Free from temptations tyranny.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Nay prethee.

sp.speaker: Byan.
sp.l: Gay clothes, high feeding, eaſie beds of luſt,
Change of unſeemly ſights; with baſe diſcourſe,
Draw curſes on your Pallaces; for my part,
This I will be confirm'd in, I will eate
The bread of labour, know no other reſt
Than what is earn'd from honeſt pains, ere once more
Lend ear to your vile toyles; Sir, would you were
As noble in deſires, as I could be in knowing virtue.
Pray do not afflict a poor ſoul thus.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I ſwear — to me? — Bianca ſteales off,

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: The Duke my Lord commands your ſpeedy preſence
For anſwering agrievances lately urg'd
Againſt you by your Mother?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: By my Mother.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: The Court is near on ſitting.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I wait on it Sir, — Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Duke, Magiſtrate, Secretary, Baptiſta, Attendants, Mentivole: (they ſit) Mentivole ſtands by.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What waſte of blood, what tumults, what diviſions,
What outrages, what uprores in a State,
Factions, though iſſuing from mean ſprings at firſt,
Have (not reſtrain'd) ſtowed to, the ſad example
At Rome, between the Ʋrſins and Columni's:
Nay, here at home, in Florence, 'twixt the Neers
And the Bianchi, can too mainly witneſs.
I ſit not at the Helm (my Lords) of Sovereignty
Deputed Pilot for the Common-wealth,
To ſleep while others ſteere (as their wild fancies
Shall counſel) by the compaſs of diſorders.
Baptiſta, This ſhort Preface is directed
Chiefly to you, the petty brawls and quarrels
Late urg'd betwixt th' Alberti and your family;
Muſt, yes, and ſhall, like tender unknit joynts,
Faſten again together of themſelves:
Or like an •• gry Chyrurgion, we will uſe
The ro • ghneſs of our juſtice, to cut off
• be ſtubborn • ancour of the limbes offending.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Moſt gracious Florence.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Our comman • was ſignified,
• hat neither of the followers of each party
Sho • l • appe • r here with weapons.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: 'Tis obey'd Sir, on my ſide.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We muſt leave the general cauſe
Of State employments, to give • ar to brawls
Of ſome particular grudges, pollitick government
For tutor'd Princes, but no more henceforth.
sp.stage: Enter Mariana, and Clariſſa at one door, Ceſario at the other.
sp.l: Our frown ſhall check preſumption, not our clemency.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: All bleſſings due to unpartial Princes,
Crown Florence with eternity of happineſs.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: If double Prayers can double bleſſings (great Sir)
Mine joyn for your proſperity with my Mothers.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Riſe both; now briefly (Lady) without circumſtance
Deliver thoſe agrievances, which lately
Your importunity poſſeſt our Counſel,
Were fit for audience, wherein you petition'd,
You might be heard without an Advocate,
Which boon you find is granted.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Though divided.
I ſtand between the Laws of truth and modeſty,
Yet let my griefs have vent: Yet the clearneſs
Of ſtrange neceſſity requires obedience
To nature and your Mercy, in my weeds
Of mourning, emblems of too dear misfortunes,
Badges of griefs, and Widdowhood, the burthe •
Of my charg'd ſoul, muſt be laid down before you;
Wherein, if ſtrict opinion cancel ſhame,
My frailty is my plea;
Stand forth young Man,
And hear a ſtory that will ſtrike all reaſon
Into amazement.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I attend.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Alberto (peace dwell upon his aſhes) ſtill the husband
Of my remembrance and unchanging vowes,
Has, by his death, left to his heir poſſeſſion
Of fair revenew, which this young man claimes
As his inheritance. I urg'd him gently,
Friendly, and privately, to grant a partage
Of this eſtate to her who ownes it all,
This his ſuppoſed Siſter.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: How ſuppoſed?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Pray Madam recollect your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: The reliſh
Of a ſtrange truth begins to work like Phyſick
Already: I have bitterneſs to mingle
With theſe preparatives, ſo deadly loathſome;
It will quite choak digeſtion; ſhortly hear it
Ceſario, for I dare not rob unjuſtly
The poor ſoul of his name; this, this Ceſario
Neither for Father had Alberto, me
For Mother, nor Clariſſa for his Siſter.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: Mother, O Mother.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I am in a Dream ſure.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No interruptions. Lady on.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Miſtake not,
Great Duke of Tuſcany, or the beginning
Or proceſs of this novelty; my husband
The now deceas'd Alberto, from his youth
In-ur'd to an impatiency, and roughneſs
Of diſpoſition, when not many months
After our Marriage were worn out, repin'd
At the unfritful barrenneſs of youth,
Which, as he pleas'd to terme it, cut our hopes off
From bleſſing of ſome iſſue; to prevent it
I grew ambitious of no fairer honor
Than to preſerve his love, and as occaſions
Still call'd him from me, ſtudied in his abſence
How I might frame his welcome home with comfort.
At laſt I fain'd my ſelf with Child; the Meſſage
Of freedome, or relief, to one half ſtarv'd
In priſon, is not utter'd with ſuch greedineſs
Of expectation, and delight, as this was
To my much affected Lord; his care, his goodneſs;
(Pardon me that I uſe the word) exceeded
All former fears, the hour of my deliverance
As I pretended, drawing near, I faſhion'd
My birth-rights at a Country Garden-houſe,
Where then my Faulk'ners Wife was brought a bed
Of this Ceſario; him I own'd for mine;
Preſented him unto a joyful Father.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Can • ou prove this true?

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Proof, I have moſt evident;
But oh the curſe of my impatiency; ſhortly,
E'r three new Moons had ſpent their borrow'd Lights,
I grew with Child indeed, ſo juſt is Heaven,
The iſſue of which burthen was this Daughter;
Judge now moſt gracious Prince, my Lords and you,
What combats then, and ſince, I have indur'd,
Between a Mothers piety, and weakneſs
Of a Soul trembling Wife; to have reveal'd
This ſecret to Alberto, had been danger
Of ruin to my fame, beſides the conflict
Of his diſtractions; now to have ſuppreſt it,
Were to defeat my Child, my only Child,
Of her moſt lawful honors, and inheritance.
Caeſario, th'art a Man ſtill, Education
Hath moulded thee a Gentleman, continue ſo;
Let not this fall from greatneſs ſink thee lower
Than worthy thoughts may warrant, yet diſclaim
All intereſt in Alberto's blood, thou haſt not
One drop of his or mine.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Produce your witneſs.

sp.speaker: Marian.
sp.l: The Faulconers Wife his Mother,
And ſuch women as waited then upon me,
Sworn to the privacy of this great ſecret.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Give them all their Oaths.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: O let me crave forbearance, gracious Sir,
Vouchſafe me hearing.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Speak Caeſario.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Thus long
I have ſtood ſilent, and with no unwillingneſs,
Attended the relation of my fall,
From a fair expectation; what I fear'd
(Since the firſt ſyllable this Lady utter'd
Of my not being hers) benevolent Fates
Have eas'd me off; for to be baſely born,
If not baſe-born, detracts not from the bounty
Of natures freedom, or an honeſt birth.
Nobility claim'd by the right of blood,
Shewes chiefly, that our Anceſtors deſir'd
What we inherit; but that Man whoſe actions
Purchaſe a real merit to himſelf,
And rancks him in the file of praiſe and honor,
Creates his own advancement; let me want
The fuel which beſt feeds the fires of greatneſs,
Lordly poſſeſſions, yet ſhall ſtill my gratitude
By ſome attempts, of mention not unworthy,
Endeavour to return a fit acquittance
To that large debt I owe your favours (Madam)
And great Alberto's memory and goodneſs;
O that I could as gently ſhake off paſſion
For the loſs of that great brave Man, as I can ſhake off
Remembrace of that once I was reputed;
I have not much to ſay, this Princely preſence
Needs not too ſtrictly to examine farther
The truth of this acknowledgment; a Mother
Dares never diſavow her only ſon,
And any woman muſt come ſhort of Piety,
That can, or diſ-inherit her own iſſue,
Or fears the voice of rumor for a ſtranger.
Madam, you have confeſt, my Father was
A ſervant to your Lord and you: by intereſt
Of being his ſon, I cannot but claim juſtly
The honor of continuing ſtill my ſervice
To you and yours; which granted, I beg leave
I may for this time be diſmiſt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Bold ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I love thee now with pitty;

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Go not yet —
A ſudden tempeſt that might ſhake a rock,
Yet he ſtands firm againſt it; much it moves me,
He, not Alberto's ſon, and ſhe a Widdow,
And ſhe a Widdow, — Lords your ear.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: Your pleaſure.— Whiſpers.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: So, Lady, what you have avouch'd is truth.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: Truth only, gracious Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Hear then our Sentence.
Since from his cradle you have fed and foſter'd
Caeſario as your Son, and train'd him up
To hopes of greatneſs; which now in a moment
You utterly again have ruin'd, this way
We with our Counſel are reſolv'd, you being
A Widdow, ſhall accept him for a husband.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Husband to me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: 'Tis in us to raiſe him
To honors, and his vertues will deſerve 'em.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: But Sir, 'tis in no Prince, nor his Prerogative,
To force a Womans choice againſt her heart.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: True, if then you appeale to higher Juſtice,
Our Doom includes this clauſe upon refuſal,
Out of your Lords revenues ſhall Caeſario
Aſſure to any, whom he takes for Wife,
The inheritance of three parts; the leſs remainer
Is dowry large enough to marry a daughter;
And we, by our Prerogative, which you queſtion,
Will publickly adopt him into th'name
Of your deceas'd Alberto, that the memory
Of ſo approv'd a Peer may live in him
That can preſerve his memory; 'leſs you find out
Some other means, which may as amply ſatisfie
His wrong, our Sentence ſtands irrevocable:
What think you Lords?

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: The Duke is juſt and honorable.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Let me embrace Caeſario, henceforth ever
I vow a conſtant friendſhip.

sp.speaker: Mentivole.
sp.l: I remit all former difference.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I am too poor
In words to thank this Juſtice. Madam, alwayes
My ſtudies ſhall be love to you, and duty.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Replies we admit none. Caeſario wait on us.

div.stage: Exeunt. Manent, Mentivole, Bap. Mari. Clariſ.

l.hi: Mentivole.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Look on Clariſſa, ſhe's noble, rich, young, fair.

sp.speaker: Mentivole.
sp.l: My Lord, and virtuous.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Mentivole and virtuous.—Madam.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Tyranny of Juſtice, I ſhall live reports deriſion,
That am compell'd to exchange a graceful Widdow-hood
For a continual Martyrdome in Marriage,
With one ſo much beneath me.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I'll plead for ye
Boldly and conſtantly, let your daughter only
Admit my ſon her ſervant, at next viſit,
Madam, I'll be a meſſenger of comfort.
Mentivole, be confident and earneſt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Married again, to him too! better 'thad been
The young Man ſhould have ſtill retain'd the honors
Of old Albertos ſon, than I the ſhame
Of making him ſucceſſor of his bed; I was too blame.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Indeed without offence,
Madam I think you were,

sp.speaker: Claris.
sp.l: You urge it fairly, and like a worthy friend.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Can you ſay any thing
In commendation of a Muſhroom withered
Aſſoon as ſtarted up?

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You ſcorn an Innocent
Of noble growth, for whiles your husband liv'd
I have heard you boaſt Ceſario in all actions
Gave matter of report of Imitation,
Wonder and envy; let not diſcontinuance
Of ſome few days eſtrange a ſweet opinion
Of virtue, cheifly when, in ſuch extremity,
Your pitty not contempt will argue goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: O Sir.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: If you would uſe a thriving courtſhip,
You cannot utter a more powerfull language
That I ſhall liſten to with greater greedineſs
Than th'argument you proſecute; this ſpeaks you
A man compleat and excellent.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I ſpeak not, they are his own deſerts.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Good Sir forbear,
I am now fully ſenſible of running
Into a violent Lethargy, whoſe deadlineſs
Locks up all reaſon, I ſhall never henceforth
Remember my paſt happineſs.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Theſe clouds may be diſperſt.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: I fear continuall night
Will over-ſhroud me, yet poor youth his treſpaſs
Lies in his fortune, not the cruelty
Of the Duke's ſentence.

sp.speaker: Cla,
sp.l: I dare think it does.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: If all fail I will learn thee to conquer
Adverſity with ſufferance.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: You reſolve Nobly. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Let any friend have entrance.

sp.speaker: Servant.
sp.l: Sir a'ſhall.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Any, I except none.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: We know, your mind Sir —Exit.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Pleaſures admit no bounds.
I am pitcht ſo high
To ſuch a growth of full proſperities
That to conceal my fortunes were an injury
To gratefulneſs, and thoſe more liberall favours
By whom my glories proſper. He that flowes
In gracious and ſwolne tydes of beſt abundance,
Yet will be Ignorant of his own fortunes,
Deſerves to live contemn'd, and dye forgotten;
The harveſt of my hopes is now already
Ripen'd and gather'd, I can fatten youth
With choice of plenty, and ſupplies of comforts,
My fate ſprings in my own hand, and I'll uſe it.
'Tis my place,
Yours? here fair one, I'll aquaint my Lord.
He's here, go to him boldly.
Pleaſe you to let him underſtand how readily
I waited on your errand?
Saucy fellow, you muſt excuſe his breeding.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: What's the matter?
Biancha, my Biancha, to your offices. Exit Ser.
This viſit (Sweet) from thee (my pretty dear)
By how much more 'twas unexpected, comes
So much the more timely: witneſs this free welcome,
What ere occaſion led thee.
You muſt gueſs Sir,
Yet indeed 'tis a rare one.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Prethee ſpeak it, my honeſt virtuous maid.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Sir I have heard
Of your misfortunes, and I cannot tell you
