Whether I have more cauſe of joy o • ſadneſs,
To • now they are a truth.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: What truth Biancha? misfortunes, how, wherein?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: You are diſclaym'd
For being the Lord Alberto's Son, and publickly
Acknowledg'd of as mean a birth as mine is,
It cannot chuſe but greive ye.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Greive me? ha ha ha ha? is this all?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: This all?

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Thou art ſorry for't
I warrant thee: alas good ſoul, Biancha,
That which thou call'ſt misfortune is my happineſs,
My happineſs Bian • ha.

sp.speaker: Bian
sp.l: If you love me, it may prove mine too.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: May it? I will love thee.
My good, good maid,
If that can make thee happy,
Better and better love thee,

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Without breach then
Of modeſty I come to claime the Intereſt
Your proteſtations, both by vows and letters,
Have made me owner of: from the firſt hour
I ſaw you, I confeſs I wiſht I ha • been
Or not ſo much below your rank and greatneſs,
Or not ſo much above thoſe humble flames
That ſhould have warm'd my boſome with a temperate
Equality of deſires in equal fortunes.
Still as you utter'd Language of affection,
I courted time to paſs more ſlowly on
That I might turn more fool to lend attention
To what I durſt not credit, nor yet hope for:
Yet ſtill as more I heard, I wiſht to hear more.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Didſt thou introth wench?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Willingly betraid
My ſelf to hopeleſs bondage.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: A good girl,
I thought I ſhould not miſs
What ere thy anſwer wa • .

sp.speaker: Biancha.
sp.l: But as I am a maid Sir, and l'faith
You may believe me, for I am a maid,
So dearly I reſpected both your ſame
And quality, that I would firſt have periſht
In my ſick thoughts than ere have given conſent
To have undone your fortunes by inviting
A marriage with ſo mean an one as I am.
I ſhould have dyed ſure, and no creature known
The ſickneſs that had kill'd me.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Pretty heart, good Soul, alas, alas.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Now ſince I know
There is no difference 'twixt your birth and mine,
Not much 'twixt our eſtates, if any be,
The advantage is on my ſide, I come willingly
To tender you the firſt fruits of my heart,
And am content t'accept you for my husband,
Now when you are at loweſt.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: For a husband?
Speak ſadly, doſt thou mean ſ • ?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: In good deed Sir,
'Tis pure love makes this proffer.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: I believe thee,
What counſail urg'd thee on, tell me, thy Father
My worſhipfull ſmug Hoſt? waſt not he wench?
Or mother Hoſteſs? ha?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: D'ee mock my parentage?
I doe not ſcorn yours.
Mean folks are as worthy
To be well ſpoken of if they deſerve well,
As ſome whoſe onely fame lies in their blood,
O y'are a proud poor man: all your oaths falſhood,
Your vows deceit, your letters forg'd, and wicked.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Thou'dſt be my wife, I dare ſwear.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Had your heart,
Your hand and tongue been twins, you had reputed
This courteſy a benefit.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Simplicity,
How prettily thou mov'ſt me? why Biancha,
Report has coz'ned thee, I am not fallen
From my expected honors, or poſſeſſions,
Though from the hope of birthright.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Are you not?
You'll grant it if you be a good man.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Any thing,

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Pray doe not talk of ought what I have ſaid t'ee.

sp.speaker: Ceſ,
sp.l: As I wiſh health I will not.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Pitty me, but never love me more.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Nay now y'are cruell,
Why an theſe tears?—Thou ſhalt not go.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: I'll pray for ye
That you may have a virtuous wife, a fair one,
And when I am dead—

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Fy, fy.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Think on me ſometimes,
With mercy for this treſpaſs.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Let us kiſs
At parting as at coming.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: This I have
As a free dower to a virgins grave,
All goodneſs dwell with ye.— Exit.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Harmeleſs Biancha! unskill'd;
What hanſome toyes are maids to play with?
How innocent? but I have other thoughts
Of nobler meditation.—my felicity,
Thou commeſt as I could wiſh, lend me a lip
Soft as melting as when old Alberto
After his firſt nights triall taking farewell
Of thy youth's conqueſt taſted.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: You are uncivill.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: I will be Lord of my own pleaſures, Madam
Y'are mine, mine freely,
Come, no whimpering henceforth
New con the leſſons of loves beſt experience,
That our delights may meet in equal meaſure
Of reſolutions and deſires; this ſulleneſs
Is ſcurvy, I like it not,

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Be modeſt.
And do not learn Ceſario how to proſtitute
The riot of thy hopes to common folly;
Take a ſad womans word, how ere thou doat'ſt
Upon the preſent graces of thy greatnes.
Yea I am not ſalen ſo below my conſtancy
To virtue, nor the care which I once tend'red
For thy behoof that I prefer a ſentence
Of cruelty before my honor.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Honor!

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Hear me, thou ſeeſt this girl! now the comfort
Of my laſt days. She is the onely pledge
Of a bed truely noble: ſhee had a father
(I • eed not ſpeak him more than thou remembreſt)
Whom to diſhonor by a meaner choice,
Were injury and infamy.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: To goodnes,
To time and virtuous mention.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I have vow'd,
Obſerve me now Ceſario, that how ere
I may be forc'd to marry, yet no tyranny,
Perſuaſions, flattery, guifts, intreats, or tortures,
Shall draw me to a ſecond bed.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Tis juſt too.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Yes and 'tis juſt Clariſsa. I allow
The Duke's late ſentence, am reſolv'd young man
To be thy wife, but when the ceremony
Of marriage is perform'd in life I will be,
Though not in name, a widdow.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Pray a word t'ee,
Shall I in earneſt never be your bedfellow?

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Never, O never; and 'tis for your good too.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Prove that.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Alas too many years are numbred
In my account to entertain the benefit
Which youth in thee Ceſario, and ability
Might hope for and require, it were Injuſtice
To rob a gentleman deſerving memory
Of Iſſue to preſerve it.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: No more herein,
You are an excellent pattern of true piety,
Let me now turn your advocate. Pray look into
The order of the Duke. Injoyn'd, admit
I ſatisfie the ſentence without mariage
With you, how then?

l.hi: Ceſario.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: If I know
How to acquit your fears, yet keep th'injunction
In every clauſe whole and entire, your charity
Will call me ſtill your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Still my ſon.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Right Madam, now you have it, ſtill your ſon,
The Genius of your bleſſings hath inſtructed
Your tongue oraculouſly, we will forget
How once I and Clariſsa enterchang'd
The tyes of brother and of ſiſter, henceforth
New ſtile us man and wife.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: By what authority?

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Heavens great appointment, yet in all my dotage
On thy perfections, when I thought Clariſsa
We had been pledges of one womb, no loſe
No wanton heat of youth, deſir'd to claime
Priority in thy affections, other
Than nature might commend. Chaſtly I tend'red
Thy welfare as a brother ought; but ſince
Our bloods are ſtrangers, let our hearts contract
A long life-laſting unity, for this way
The ſentence is to be obſerv'd or no way.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Then no way.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: I expected other anſwer Madam from you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, every age ſhall curſe me,
The monſter, and the prodigie of nature,
Horrors beyond extremity.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Pray mother confine the violence of greif.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Yes mother, pray do.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thus ſome catch at a matrons honor
By flying luſt to plot Inceſtuous witchcrafts.
More terrible than whoredomes; cruell mercy!
When to preſerve the body from a death
The ſoul is ſtrangled.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: This is more than paſſion,
It comes near to diſtraction.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am quieted.
Ceſario, thou mayeſt tell the Duke ſecurely
Alberto's titles, honors and revenues,
The Duke may give away, enjoy them thou.
Clariſſas birthright, Marianas dower
Thou ſhalt be Lord of; turn us to the world
Vnpittied and unfriended, yet my bed
Thou never ſleep'ſt in; as for her; ſhe hears me,
If ſhe as much as in a thought conſent;
That thou may'ſt call her wife, a Mothers curſe
Shall never leave her.

sp.speaker: Clar,
sp.l: As a brother once
I lov'd you, as a noble friend yet honor ye,
But for a husband ſir, I dare not own you,
My faith is given already.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: To a Villain, I'll cut his throat.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why this is more than paſſion?
It comes near a diſtraction.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: Call to mind Sir.
How much you have abated of that goodneſs
Which once reign'd in ye, they appear'd ſo lovely
That ſuch as friendſhip led to obſervation
Courted the great example.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Left, and flatter'd into a broad deriſion?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why d'ee think ſo?
My Lord Baptiſta, is your Son grown cold
In haſting on the marriage, which his vows
Have ſeal'd to my wrong'd daughter?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: We come Lady, to conſummate the contra • t.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: With Mentivole? is he the man?

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Clariſſas, troth and mine,
Ceſario, are recorded in a character
So plain and certain, that except the hand
Of heaven, which writ it firſt, would blo • it out again,
No humane power can raze it.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: But ſay you ſo too young Lady?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I ſhould elſe betray
My heart to falſhood, and my tongue to perjury.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Madam, you know the ſentence.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: From the Duke,
I have particular comforts which require
A private care.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I ſhall approve it gladly
We are reſolv'd Ceſario.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Be not inſolent upon a Princes favor.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Looſe no glory,
Your younger years have purchaſt.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: And deſerved too, y'have many worthy freinds.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Preſerve and uſe them. Exeunt: Man • t C • ſar.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Good, very good, why here's a complement
Of mirth in deſperation, I could curſe
My fate: O with what ſpeed men tumble down
From hopes that ſoar too high. Biancha now
May ſcorn me juſtly too, Clariſſa married,
Albertos widdow reſolute, Biancha
Refus'd, and I forſaken: let me ſtudy,
I can but die a Batchelor that's the worſt on't. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Hoſt, Taylor, Muliter, Dancer, Pedant, Coxcombe.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen,
This is the day that our great artiſt hath
Promis'd to give all your ſeverall ſuits ſaisfaction.

sp.speaker: Dancer.
sp.l: Is he ſtirring?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: He hath been at his book theſe to hours.

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.l: He's a rare Phyſitian.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Why I'll tell you,
Were Paracelſus the German now
Living, he'd take up his ſingle rapier againſt his
Terrible long ſword, he makes it a matter of nothing
To cure the gout, fore eyes he takes out as familiarly,
Waſhes them, and puts them in again,
As you'd blanch almonds.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: They ſay he can make gold.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I, I, he learnt it of Kelly in Germanny.
There's not a Chymiſt
In chriſtendome can goe beyond him for multiplying.

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.l: Take heed then;
He get not up your daughters belly my Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: You are a merry Gentleman
And the man of art will love you the better.

sp.speaker: Dancer.
sp.l: Does he love mirth and crotchets?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: O he's the moſt courteous • hyſitian,
You may drink or drab in's company freely,
The better he knows how yo • r diſeaſe grows,
The better he knows how to cure it.

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: But I wonder my Hoſt
He has no more reſort of Ladyes to him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Dan.
sp.l: O divers of them have great beleif in conjurers:
Lechery is a great help to the quality.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: He's ſcarce known to be in town yet,
Ere long we ſhall have 'em come
Hurrying hither in Fetherbeds.

sp.speaker: Dan.
sp.l: How? b • dridden?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: No ſir, in fetherbeds that move upon 4 wheels in
Spaniſh caroche • .

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Pray accquaint him we give attendance.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: I ſhall • en • lemen; I would fain be rid
Of theſe raſcalls, but that they ra • ſe profit
To my wine • e • ar.
When I have made uſe of them ſuffici • ntly,
I will intreat the conjurer to tye crackers to their tails,
And ſend them packing.

div.stage: Enter Forob • ſ • o as in his Study. (A paper)

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Come hither mine Hoſt, look here,

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: What's that?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A challenge from my man.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: For breaking's pate?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: He writes here •• I meet him not
I'th' Feild within this half hour,
I ſhall hear more from him.
O ſ • r, minde your profit,
Ne'er think of the ra • call, here are the gentlemen.
'Morrow my worthy clients,
That I may give my reſolution upon them?
We are Sir.

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.l: And have brought our mo • y.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Each then in order,
And differ not for pre •• d • ncy.

sp.speaker: Dan.
sp.l: I am buying of an o ••• Sir,
And to that purpoſe I would • a • learn
To diſſemble cunningly.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Doe you come to me for that? you ſhould rather
Have gone to a cunning woman.

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: I ſir but their Inſtru • tions are but like woman,
Pretty well but not to the depth, as I'd have it:
You are a conjurer, the devils Maſter,
And I would learn it from you ſo exactly.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: That the devill himſelf
Might not go beyond you.

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: You are i'th' right Sir.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: And ſo your mony for your purchaſe
Might come in again within a 12 month.

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: I would be a Graduate ſir, no freſhman.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Here's my hand ſir,
I will make you diſſemble ſo methodically,
As if the divell ſhould be ſent from the great Turk,
In the ſhape of an Embaſſador
To ſet all the chriſtian princes at variance.

sp.speaker: Danc.
sp.l: I cannot with any modeſty deſire any more.
There's your mony ſir.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: For the art of diſſembling.

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: My ſuit ſir will be news to you when I tell it.

sp.speaker: Foro,
sp.l: Pray on.

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: I would ſet up a preſs here in Italy,
To write all the Corantos for Chriſtendome.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: That's news indeed,
And how would you imploy me in't?
Marry ſir, from you
I would gain my intelligence.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: I conceive you, you would have me furniſh you
With a ſpirit to informe you.

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: But as quiet a Divell as the woman,
The firſt day and a half after ſhe's married,
I can by no means indure a terrible one.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: No, no, I'll qualifie him,
He ſhall not fright you,
• t ſhall be the ghoſt of ſome lying Stationer,
sp.p: A Spirit ſhall look as if butter would not melt in his mouth. A new Mercurius Gallo-belgicus.

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: O there was a captain was rare at it.
Ne'er thinke of him,
Though that captain writ a full hand gallop,
And waſted indeed more harmeleſs paper than
Ever did laxative Phyſick,
Yet will I make you to out-ſcribble him,
And ſet down what you pleaſe,
The world ſhall better believe you.

sp.speaker: Cox.
sp.l: Worthy ſir I thank you, there's mony.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A new office
For writing pragmaticall Curranto's
I am a ſchool-maſter ſir,
• nd would fain conferre with you
A • o •• erecting 4 new ſects of religion at Amſterdam.
What the Divell ſhould
〈…〉 or religion doe there?

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.l: I aſſure you I would get
A great deal of money by it.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: And what are the 4 new ſects
Of religion you would plant there?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Why that's it I come about ſir,
'Tis a Divel of your raiſing muſt invent 'em,
I con • eſs I am too weak to compaſs it.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: So ſir, then you make it a matter of no difficulty
To have them tolerated.

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.l: Trouble not your ſelf for that,
Let but your Divel ſet them a foot once.
I have Weavers, and Ginger-bread makers,
And mighty Aquavitae-men, ſhall ſet them a going.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: This is ſomewhat difficult,
And will a • ke ſome conference with the divell.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Take your own leaſure ſir,
I have another buſineſs too, becauſe I mean
To leave Italy, and bury my ſelf in thoſe neather parts
Of the low countries.
What's that ſir.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Marry I would fain make 9 dayes to the week, for the more ample benefit of the captain.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: You have a ſhrewd pate ſir.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: But how this might be compaſs'd?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Compaſs'd eaſily; tis but making
A new Almanack, and dividing the compaſs
Of the year into larger penny-worths,
As a Chandler with his compaſs makes
A Geom trick proportion of the Holland cheeſe
He retailes by ſtivers.
But for getting of it licenc'd?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Trouble not your ſelf with that ſir,
There's your mony,

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: For four new ſects of religions,
And 9 dayes to the week.
To be brought in at general pay-dayes,
Write I beſeech you.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: At generall pay-dayes.

sp.speaker: Taylor.
sp.l: I am by profeſſion a Taylor,
You have h • ard of me.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Yes ſir, and will not ſteal from you
The leaſt part of that commendation I have heard utter'd.

sp.speaker: Taylor.
sp.l: I take meaſure of your worth ſir,
And becauſe I will not afflict you with any large bill
Of circumſtances, I will ſnip off particulars.
I would fain invent ſome ſtrange
And exquiſite new faſhions.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Are you not travel'd ſir.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Yes ſir, but have obſerv'd all we can ſee
Or invent, are but old ones with new names to'em,
Now I would ſome way or other grow more curious.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Let me ſee; to deviſe new faſhions—
Were you never in the Moon?

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: In the Moon tavern! yes ſir, often.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: No, I do mean in the new world,
In the world that's in the Moon yonder.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: How? a new world 'ith' moon?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Yes I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: And peopled?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: O moſt fantaſtically peopled.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Nay certain then there's work for taylors?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: That there is I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Yet I have talked with a Scotch taylor
That never diſcover'd ſo much to me,
Though he has travell'd far, and was a pedlar in Poland.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: That was out of his way,
This lies beyond China:
You would ſtudy new faſhions you ſay?
Take my councell, make a voyage,
And diſcover that new world.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Shall I be a moon-man?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: I am of opinion, the people of that world
(If they be like the nature of that climate they live in)
Do vary the faſhion of their cloaths oftener than any
Quick-ſilver'd nation in Europe.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Not unlikely, but what ſhould that be we call
The man in the moon then?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Why 'tis nothing but an Engliſhman
That ſtands there ſtark naked,
With a pair of ſheers in one hand,
And a great bundle of broad cloath in the other
(Which reſembles the buſh of thorns)
Cutting out of new faſhions.

sp.speaker: Taylor.
sp.l: I have heard ſomewhat like this,
But how ſhall I get thither?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: I'll make a new compaſs ſhall direct you.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: Certain?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Count me elſe for no man of direction.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.l: There's 20 duckats in hand, at my return
I'll give you a 100.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: A new voyage to diſcover new faſhions.

sp.speaker: Mul.
sp.l: I have been a traveller too ſir,
That have ſhewed ſtrange beaſts in Chriſtendome,
And got money by them, but I find the trade to decay.
Your Camelion, or Eaſt-Indian hedg-hog
Gets very little mony, and your Elephant devours
So much bread, brings in ſo little profit,
His keeper were better every morning
Cram 15 Taylors with white manchet:
I would have ſome new ſpectacle,
And one that might be more attractive.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Let me ſee, were you ever in Spain?

sp.speaker: Mule.
sp.l: Not yet Sir.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: I would have you go to Madrill, and againſt ſome great feſtivall, when the court lies there, provide a great and ſpacious Engilſh Oxe, and roſt him whole, with a pudding in's bely; that would be the eighth wonder of the world in thoſe parts I aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Mule.
sp.p: A rare project without queſtion.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Goe beyond all their garlike olle padridoes, though you ſod one in Garguentuas couldron, bring in more money, then all the monſters of Affrick.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Good Sir do your beſt for him; he's of my acquaintance, and one if ye knew him—

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: What is he?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: He was once a man of infinite letters.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: A Scholar?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: No ſir, a packet carrier, which is alwaies a man of many letters, you know: then he was Mule-driver, now he's a gentleman, and feeds monſters.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: A moſt ungratefull calling.

sp.speaker: Mule.
sp.p: There's money for your direction; the price of the Oxe Sir?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p:
A hundred French crowns, for it muſt be a Lincolneſhire
Oxe, and a prime one:
For a rare and monſtrous ſpectacle, to be ſeen at Madrill.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſ.
sp.p: Pray forbear ſir, we ſhall have a new quarrell.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: You durſt not meet me 'ith field, I am therefore come to ſpoyl your market.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: What's the newes with you ſir.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Gentlemen, you that come hither to be moſt abominably cheated, liſten, and be as wiſe as your planet will ſuffer you, keep your mony, be not gul'd, be not laught at.

sp.speaker: Pedant.
sp.p: What means this? would I had my mony again in my pocket.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: The fellow is full of malice, do not mind him.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: This profeſt cheating rogue was my maſter, and I confeſs my ſelf a more preternotorious rogue than himſelf, in ſo long keeping his villainous counſell.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Come, come, I will not hear you.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No couz'ner, thou wouldeſt not hear me, I do but dare thee to ſuffer me to ſpeak, and then thou and all thy divells ſpit fire, and ſpout Aqua fortis.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Speak on, I freely permit thee.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Why then know all you ſimple animals, you whoſe parſes are ready to caſt the calf; if they have not caſt it already, if you give any credit to this jugling raſcal, you are worſe than ſimple widgins, and will be drawn into the net by this decoy duck, this tame cheater.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, pray mark him

sp.speaker: Clow
sp.p: He does profeſs Phyſicke, and counjuring; for his Phyſick.; he has but two medicines for all manner of diſeaſes; when he was i'th' low countreys, he us'd nothing but butter'd beer, colour'd with Allegant, for all kind of maladies, and that he called his catholick med'cine; ſure the Dutch ſmelt out it was butter'd beer, elſe they would never have endur'd it for the names ſake: then does he miniſter a grated Dogs turd inſtead of Rubarb, many times of Unicornes horn, which working ſtrongly with the conceit of the Patient, would make them beſcummer to the height of a mighty purgation.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: The rogue has ſtudied this invective.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Now for his conjuring, the witches of Lapland are the divells chare-women to him, for they will ſell a man a wind to ſome purpoſe; he ſells wind, and tells you fortie lyes over and over.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſſ.
sp.p: I thought what we ſhould find of him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Hold your prating, be not you an heretick.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Conjure! I'll tell you, all the divells names he calls upon are but fuſtion names, gather'd out of welch heraldry; in breif, he is a rogue of ſix reprieves, four pardons of courſe, thrice pilloried, twice ſung Lacrymae to the Virginalls of a carts tail, h'as five times been in the Gallies, and will never truely run himſelf out of breath, till he comes to the gallowes.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: You have heard worthy gentlemen, what this lying, detracting raſcall has vomited.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.p: Yes certain, but we have a better truſt in you, for you have ta'en our money.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: I have ſo, truth is he was my ſervant, and for ſome chaſtiſement I gave him, he does practiſe thus upon me; ſpeak truely ſirra, are you certain I cannot conjure?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Conjure! ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Nay, nay, but be very ſure of it.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Sure of it? why I'll make a bargain with thee, before all theſe gentlemen, uſe all thy art, all thy roguery, and make me do any thing before al this company I have not a mind to, I'll firſt give thee leave to claime me for thy bond ſlave, and when thou haſt done hang me.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: 'Tis a match, ſirra, I'll make you caper i'th' air preſently.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I have too ſolid a body, and my belief is like a Puritans on Good-Friday, too high fed with capon.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: I will firſt ſend thee to Green-land for a haunch of veniſon, juſt of the thickneſs of thine own tallow.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, I'll not ſtir an inch for thee.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Thence to Amboyna i'th' Eaſt Jndies, for pepper to bake it.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: To Amboyna? ſo I might be pepper'd.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Then will I conveigh thee ſtark naked to Develing to beg a pair of brogs, to hide thy mountainous buttocks.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: And no doublet to 'em?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: No ſir, I intend to ſend you of a ſleeveleſs errand, but before you vaniſh, in regard you ſay I cannot conjure, and are ſo ſtupid, and opinionated a ſlave, that nei • er • nor my art can compell you to do any thing that's beyond your own pleaſure, the gentlemen ſhall have ſome ſport, you cannot endure a cat • rra?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: What's that to thee Iugler?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Nor you'll do nothing at my entreaty?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I'll be hang'd firſt.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Sit Gentlemen, and whatſoever you ſee, be not frighted,

sp.speaker: Hoſteſſ:
sp.p: Alas I can endure no conjuring.

sp.speaker: Hoſt:
sp.p: Stir not wife.

sp.speaker: Bian:
sp.p: Pray let me go ſir, I am not ſit for theſe fooleryes.

sp.speaker: Hoſt:
sp.p: Move not daughter,

sp.speaker: For:
sp.p: I wil make you dance a new dance call'd leap-fro

sp.speaker: Clow:
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: For:
sp.p: And as naked as a frog.

sp.speaker: Clow:
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha, I defie thee.

div.stage: Foroboſco looks in a book, • trik • with his wand, Muſick playes.
Enter 4. Boyes ſhap'd like Frogs, and dance.

sp.speaker: Padant:
sp.p: Sprits of the water in the likeneſs of frogs.

sp.speaker: Tay:
sp.p: He has fiſht fa •• believe me.

sp.speaker: Mule:
sp.p: See, ſee, he ſweats and trembles.

sp.speaker: Foro:
sp.p: Are you come to your quavers?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Oh, ho, ho.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p:
I'll make you run diviſion on that o'r ere I leave you, looke you, here are the playfellowes that are 〈◊〉
• ndear'd to you; come ſir, firſt uncaſe, and then dance, nay I'll make him dance ſtark naked.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Oh let him have his ſhirt on and his Mogols breeches here are Women ith' houſe.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Well for their ſakes he ſhall.

div.stage: Clown teares off his doublet, making ſtrange faces as if compel'd to it, falls into the Dance.

sp.speaker: Tay.
sp.p: He dances, what a lying rogue was this to ſayth gentleman could not conjure?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: He does prettily well, but 'tis voluntary, I aſſure you, I have no hand in't.

sp.speaker: Clow,
sp.p: As you are a Counjurer, and a rare Artiſt, free me from theſe couplets; of all creatures I cannot endure a Frog.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: But your dancing is voluntary, I can compell you to nothing.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſ.
sp.p: O me, daughter, lets take heed of this fellow, he'll make us dance naked, an' we vex him.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Now cut capers ſirra, I'll plague that chine of yours

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Ho, ho, ho, my kidneys are roſted. I drop awa • like a pound of butter roſted.

sp.speaker: Tayl,
sp.p: He will dance himſelf to death.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: No matter I'll ſell his fat to the Pothecaries, and repair my injury that way.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Enough in conſcience.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Well, at your entreaty vaniſh. And now I wil only make him break his neck in doing a ſommerſ • t, and that's all the revenge I mean to take of him.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: O gentlemen, what a rogue was I to belye ſo a • approved Maſter in the noble dark ſcience? you can witneſs, this I did only to ſpoyle his practiſe and deprive you of the happyneſs of injoying his worthy labors; rogue that I was to do it, pray ſir forgive me.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: With what face canſt thou ask it?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: With ſuch a face as I deſerve, with a hanging look, as all here can teſtifie.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Well gentlemen, that you may perceive the goodneſs o • my temper, I will e • tertain th s rogue againe in hope of amendment, for ſhould I turn him off, he would be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: You may read that in this ſoul coppy.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Only with this promiſe, you ſhall never cozen any of my patients.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Never.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: And remember hence forward, that though I cannot conjure, I can make you dance ſirra, go get your ſelf into the cottage again.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I will never more dance leap-Frog: now I have got you into credit, hold it up, and cozen them in abundance.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Oh rare raſcall. — Exit Clown.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.p: How now, a Frankford mart here, a Mountebank, and his worſhipfull auditory?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: They are my gueſts Sir.

sp.speaker: C ſar.
sp.p: A — upon them, ſhew your jugling tricks in ſome other room.

sp.speaker: H ſt.
sp.p: And why not here Sir?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.p: Hence, or ſirra I ſhall ſpoil your figure flinging, and all their radicall queſtions.

sp.speaker: Omnes
sp.p: Sir we vaniſh.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Signior Ceſario, you make bold with me,
And ſomewhat I muſt tell you to a degree
Of ill manners: they are my gueſts, and men I live by,
And I would know by what authority
You command thus far.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: By my intereſt in your daughter.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Intereſt do you call't? as I remember I never put her out to Vſury on that condition.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Pray thee be not angry.
I am come to make thee happy, and her happy:
She's here; alas my pretty ſoul, I am come
To give aſſurance that's beyond thy hope,
Or thy beleif, I bring repentance 'bout me,
And ſatisfaction, I will marry thee.

sp.speaker: Bianca.
sp.l: Ha?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: As I live I will, but do not entertain 't
With too • uick an apprehenſion of joy,
For that may hurt thee, I have heard ſome dye of 't,

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Do not fear me.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Then thou think'ſt I feign
This proteſtation, I will inſtantly
Before theſe teſtifie my new alliance,
Contract my ſelf unto thee, then I hope
We may be more private.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: But thou ſhalt not ſir,
For ſo has many a maiden-head been loſt, and many a baſtard gotten,

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Then to give you the beſt of any aſſurance in the world,
Entreat thy father to go fetch a Preiſt
Wee will inſtantly to bed, and there be married.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Pride hath not yet forſaken you I ſee,
Though proſperity has.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Sir you are too conſident
To faſhion to your ſelf a dream of purchaſe
When you are a begger.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: You are bold with me.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſ.
sp.l: Doe we not know your value is cried down
Fourſcore i'th' hundred.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Oh ſir I did love you
With ſuch a fixed heart, that in that minute
Wherein you ſlighted, or contemn'd me rather,
I took a vow to obey your laſt decree,
And never more look up at any hope
Should bring me comfort that way: and though ſince
Your Foſter-mother, and the fair Clariſſa
Have in the way of marriage deſpis'd you,
That hath not any way bred my revenge,
But compaſſion rather. I have found
So much ſorrow in the way to a chaſte wedlock
That here I will ſet down, and never wiſh
To come to'th' journies end. Your ſuit to mee
Henceforth be ever ſilenc'd.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: My Bianca.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſ.
sp.l: Henceforward pray forbear her and my ho • ſe:
She's a poor virtuous wench, yet her eſtate
May weigh with yours in a gold balance.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Yes, and her birth in any Heralds office in Chriſtendom.

sp.speaker: Hoſteſ.
sp.l: It may prove ſo:
When you'll ſay, you have leapt a Whiting. Exit

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: How far am I grown behind hand with fortune?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Here's Ceſario!
My ſon Sir, is to morrow to be married
Unto the fair Clariſſa.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: So.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Wee hope you'll be a gueſt there.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: No I will not grace your triumph ſo much.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I will not tax your breeding.
But it alters not your birth Sir, fare you well.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Oh Sir, doe not greive him,
He has too much affliction already. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Every way ſcorn'd and loſt,
Shame follow you
For I am grown moſt miſerable.

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: Sir do you know a Ladies ſon in town here
They cal Ceſario?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: There's none ſuch I aſſure thee;

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: I was told you were the man.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: What's that to thee?

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: A — on't. You are melancholy, will you drink Sir?

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: With whom?

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.p: With me Sir; deſpiſe not this pitch'd Canvas; the time was we have known them lin'd with Spaniſh Duckets; I have news for you:

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: For me!

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: Not unleſs you'll drink;
We are like our Sea proviſion, once out of pickle,
We require abundance of drink; I have news to tell you,
That were you Prince,
Would make you ſend your mandate
To have a thouſand bonfires made i'th' City
And piſt out agen with nothing but Greek wine.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Come, I will drink with thee howſoever,

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: And upon theſe terms I will utter my mind to you.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Alberto, Proſporo, Juliana and Sailors.

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: SHall we bring your neceſſaries aſhore my Lord?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Do what you pleaſe, I am land-ſick, worſe by far
Than ere I was at ſea,

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Collect your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: O my moſt worthy Proſpero, my beſt friend,
The noble favor I receiv'd from thee
In freeing me from the Turks I now accompt
Worſe than my death; for I ſhall never live
To make requitall; what do you attend for?

sp.speaker: Sail.
sp.l: To underſtand your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: They do mock me;
I do proteſt I have no kind of pleaſure
In any thing i'th' world, but in thy friendſhip,
I muſt ever except that.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Pray leave him, leave him.— Exeunt Sailors.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: The news I heard related ſince my landing
Of the diviſion of my Family,
How is it poſſible for any man
To bear't with a ſet patience?

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: You have ſuffer'd
Since your impriſonment more waighty ſorrows.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: I, then I was man of fleſh and blood,
Now I am made up of fire, to the full height
Of a deadly Calenture; O theſe vild women
That are ſo ill preſervers of mens honors,
They cannot govern their own honeſties.
That I ſhould thirty and odd winters feed
My expectation of a noble heir,
And by a womans falſhood find him now
A fiction, a mere dream of what he was;
And yet I love him ſtill.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: In my opinion
The ſentence (on this tryall) from the Duke
Was noble, to repair Ceſario's loſs
With the marriage of your wife, had you been dead.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: By your favor but it was not, I conceive
T'was diſparagement to my name, to have my widdow
Match with a Faulkeiners ſon, and yet beli've't
I love the youth ſtill, and much pitty him.
I do remember at my going to Sea,
Upon a quarrel, and a hurt receiv'd
From young Mentivole, my rage ſo far
Oretopt my nobler temper, I gave charge
To have his hand cut off, which ſince I heard,
And to my comfort, brave Ceſario,
Worthyly prevented.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: And 'twas nobly done.

sp.speaker: Albert.
sp.l: Yet the revenge, for this intent of mine
Hath bred much ſlaughter in our families,
And yet my wife (which infinitely moans me)
Intends to marry my ſole heir Clariſsa
To the head branch of the other faction.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: 'Tis the mean to work reconcilement.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Between whom?

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Your ſelf and the worthy Baptiſta.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Never.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: O you have been of a noble and remarkable friendſhip,
And by this match 'tis generally in Florence
Hop'd, 'twill fully be reconcil'd; to me
'Twould be abſolute content.

sp.speaker: Iulia.
sp.l: And to my ſelf, I have main intereſt in it.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Noble Sir, you may command my heart to break for you
But never to bend that way; poor Ceſario,
When thou put'ſt on thy mournfull willow-garland,
Thy enemy ſhall be ſuted (I do vow)
In the ſame livery, my Ceſario
Loved as my foſter child, though not my Son,
Which in ſome countryes formerly were barbarous,
Was a name held moſt affectionate; thou art loſt,
Vnfortunate young man, not only ſlighted
Where thou received'ſt thy breeding, but ſince ſcorn'd
I th' way of marriage, by the poor Bianca
The In-keepers daughter.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: I have heard of that too;
But let not that afflict you: for this Lady
May happily deliver at more leaſure
A circumſtance may draw a fair event,
Better than you can hope for.
For this preſent we muſt leave you,
And ſhall viſit you again within theſe two hours.

sp.speaker: Albert.
sp.l: Ever to me moſt welcome, — O my Ceſario.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I am none of yours Sir, ſo 'tis proteſted;
And I humbly beg,
Since 'tis not in your power to preſerve me
Any longer in a noble courſe of life,
Give me a worthy death.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: The youth is mad.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Nay Sir, I will inſtruct you in a way
To kill me honorably.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: That were moſt ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: I am turning Pirate, You may be imployed
By the Duke to ſetch me in; and in a Sea-fight
Give me a noble grave.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Queſtionleſs he's mad: I would give any Doctor
A thouſand crowns to free him from this ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Here's the Phyſitian.—Shewes a Poniard.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Hold Sir, I did ſay
To free you from the ſorrow, not from life.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: Why life and ſorrow are unſeparable.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Be comforted Ceſario, Mentivole
Shall not marry Clariſsa.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: No Sir, ere he ſhall, I'll kill him.

sp.speaker: Albar.
sp.l: But you forſeit your own life then.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: That's worth nothing.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l:
Ceſario, be thy ſelf, be mi ••
Ceſario:
Make not thy ſelf uncapable of that portion
I have full purpoſe to confer upon thee?
By falling into madneſs: bear th • wrongs
With noble patience, the affi • ted's fri nd
Which ever in all actions crowns the •• d.

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: You well awak'd me; nay recover'd me
Both to ſence and full life, O moſt noble ſir,
Though I have loſt my fortune, and loſt you
For a worthy Father: yet I will not loſe
My former virtue, my integrity
Shall not yet forſake me; but as the wild Ivy,
Spreads and thrives better in ſome pittious ruin
Of tower, or defac'd Temple, than it does
Planted by a new building; ſo ſhall I
Make my adverſity my inſtrument
To winde me up into a full content.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: 'Tis worthily reſolv'd; our firſt adventure
Is to ſtop the marriage; for thy other loſſes,
Practis'd by a womans malice, but account them
Like conjurers winds rais'd to a fearfull blaſt,
And do ſome miſcheif, but do never laſt. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Now ſir, will you not acknowledge that I have mightily advanc'd your practice?

sp.speaker: Foroboſ.
sp.l: 'Tis confeſt, and I will make thee a great man ſor't.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I take a courſe to do that my ſelf, for I drink ſack in abundance.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: O my rare raſcall! We muſt remove.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Whither?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Any whither: Europe is too little to be coz'ned by us, I am ambitious to go to the Eaſt-Indies, thou and I to ride on our brace of Elephants.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: And for my part I long to be in England agen; you will never get ſo much as in England, we have ſnifted many countryes, and many names: but trance the world over you ſhall never purſe up ſo much gold as when you were in England, and call'd your ſelf Doctor Lambe-ſtones.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: 'Twas an atractive name I confeſs, women were then my only admirers.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: And all their viſits was either to further their luſt, or revenge injuries.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: You ſhould have ſorty in a morning beleaguer my cloſet, and ſtrive who ſhould be cozen'd firſt, am ng ſt ſourſcore love-ſick waiting women that has come to me in a morning to learn what fortune ſhould betide them in their firſt marriage, I have found above 94 to have loſt their maidenheads,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: By their own confeſſion, but I was fain to be your male midwife, and work it out of them by circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Thou waſt, and yet for all this frequent reſort of women and thy handing of their urinals and their caſes, thou art not given to lechery, what ſhould be the reaſon of it? thou haſt wholſome fleſh enough about thee; me thinks the divell ſhould tempt thee to't.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: What need he do that, when he makes me his inſtrument to tempt others.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Thou canſt not chuſe but utter thy rare good parts; thou waſt an excellent baud I acknowledge.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Well, and what I have done that way, I will ſpare to ſpeak of all you and I have done ſir, and though we ſhould—

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: We will for England, that's for certain.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: We ſhall never want there.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Want? their Court of Wards ſhall want money firſt: for I profeſs my ſelf Lord Paramount over fools and madolkes.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Do but ſtore your ſelf with lyes enough againſt • ou come thither.

sp.speaker: Foro.
Clow.
sp.p: What is it my moſt worſhipful Doctor Lamb- • ones?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: There is a Captain come lately from Sea,
They call Proſper, I ſaw him this morning
Through a chink of wainſcote that divides my lodging,
sp.p: And the Hoſt of the houſe, withdraw my Hoſt, and Hoſteſs, the fair Biancha, and an antient gentlewoman into their bedchamber; I could not overhear their conference, but I ſaw ſuch a maſs of gold & Iewels, & when he had done he lock't it up into a casket; great joy there was amongſt them, & forth they are gone into the city, and my Hoſt told me at his going forth he thought he ſhould not return till after ſupper: now Sir, in their abſence will we fall to our picklocks, enter the chamber, ſeize the Iewels, make an eſcape from Florence, and we are made for ever.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: But if they ſhould go to a true conjurer, and fetch us back in a whirle-wind?

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Do not believe there is any ſuch fetch in Aſtrology, and this may be a means to make us live honeſt hereafter.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: 'Tis but an ill road to't that lyes through the high way of theeving.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: For indeed I am weary of this trade of fortune-telling; and mean to give all over, when I come into England, for it is a very tickliſh quality,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: And i'th' end will hang by a twine thred.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Beſides the Iſland has too many of the profeſſion, they hinder on anothers market.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: No, no, the pillory hinders their market.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: You know there the jugling captain.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I there's a ſure card.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Only the fore-man of their jury is dead, but he dyed like a Roman.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Elſe 'tis thought he had made work for the hangman.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: And the very Ball, of your falſe prophets, he's quaſht too.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: He did meaſure the ſtars with a falſe yard, and may now travail to Rome, with a morter on's head to ſee if he can recover his money that way.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Come, come, lets fiſh for this casket, and to Sea preſently.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: We ſhall never reach London, I fear;
My mind runs ſo much of hanging, landing at Wapping.
This well may be a day of joy long wiſh'd for
To my Clariſſa, ſhe is innocent.
Nor can her youth but with an open boſome
Meet Hymens pleaſing bounties, but to me
That am inviron'd with black guilt and horror
It does appear a funeral though promiſing much
In the conception were hard to mannage
But ſad in event, it was not hate
But fond indulgence in me to preſerve
Ceſario's threatn'd life in open court
Then forc'd me to diſclaime him, chooſing rather
To rob him of his birth-right, and honor
Than ſuffer him to run the hazard of
Inrag'd Baptiſta's fury, while he lives;
I know I have a Son, and the Dukes ſentence
A while deluded, and this tempeſt over,
When he aſſures himſelf deſpair hath ſeiz'd him,
I can relieve and raiſe him—ſpeak, who is it
That preſſes on my privacies? Sir your pardon.
You cannot come unwelcome, though it were
To read my ſecret thoughts.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Lady to you
Mine ſhall be ever open; Lady ſaid I,
That name keeps too much diſtance, ſiſter rather
I ſhould have ſtil'd you, and I now may claime it,
Since our divided families are made one
By this bleſſed marriage; to whoſe honor comes
The Duke in perſon, waited on by all
The braveries of his Court, to witneſs it,
And then to be our gheſts, is the bride ready
To meet and entertain him?

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: She attends the comming of your Son.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Pray you bring her forth.
The Duke's at hand—Muſick, in her loud voyce,
Speaks his arrivall.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: She's prepar'd to meet it. —Exit.

div.stage: Enter Mariana, Clariſſa, led by two Maids: at the other door, Baptiſta meets with Mentivole, led by two Couriers, the Duke, Biſhop; divers Attendants: (A Song) whilſt they ſalute.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: It were impertinent to wiſh you joy,
Since all joyes dwell about you, Hymens torch
Was never lighted with a luckier Omen.
Nor burnt with ſo much ſplendor, to defer
With fruitleſs compliment, the means to make
Your certain pleaſures lawful to the world;
Since in the union of your hearts they are
Confirm'd already: would but argue us
A boaſter of our favours; to the Temple,
And there the ſacred knot once ti'd, all triumphs
Our Dukedom can afford, ſhall grace your Nuptials.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: On there.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: I hope it is not in the power
Of any to croſs us now.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: But in the breath
Of a wrong'd Father I forbid the Banes.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: What, do you ſtand at gaze?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Riſen from the dead!

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Although the Sea had vomited up the Figure
In which thy better part liv'd long impriſon'd,
True love deſpiſing fear, runs thus to meet it.

sp.speaker: Clariſ.
sp.l: In duty I kneel to it.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Hence vile wretches,
To you I am a ſubſtance incorporeal,
And not to be prophan'd, with your vile touch?
That could ſo ſoon forget me, but ſuch things
Are neither worth my Anger, nor reproof.
To you great Sir, I turn my ſelf and theſe
Immediate Miniſters of your Government,
And if in my rude language I trangreſs;
Aſcribe it to the cold remembrance of
My ſervices, and not my rugged temper.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Speak freely, be thy language ne'er ſo bitter,
To ſee thee ſafe Alberto, ſignes thy pardon.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: My pardon? I can need none, if it be not
Receiv'd for an offence. I tamely bear
Wrongs, which a ſlave-born Muſcovite would check at.
Why if for Treaſon I had been deliver'd
Up to the Hangmans Axe, and this dead trunk
Unworthy of a Chriſtian Sepulchre;
Expos'd a prey to feed the ravenous Vulture,
The memory of the much I oft did for you,
Had you but any touch of gratitude,
Or thought of my deſervings, would have ſtopp'd you
From theſe unjuſt proceedings.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Hear the motives that did induce us.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: I have heard them all,
Your Highneſs ſentence, the whole Court abus'd,
By the perjuries and practice of this woman.
(Wepeſt thou Crocodile) my hopeful ſon,
Whom I dare ſwear mine own, degraded of
The honors that deſcend to him from me:
And from that, in his love ſcorn'd by a creature
Whoſe baſe birth, though made eminent by her beauty,
Might well have mark'd her out Ceſario's ſervant,
All this I could have pardon'd and forgot;
But that my daughter with my whole Eſtate
So hardly purchas'd, is aſſign'd a Dower;
To one whoſe Father, and whoſe Family
I ſo deteſt; that I would loſe my eſſence
And be transformed to a Baſiliske
To look them dead, to me's an injury
Admits no ſatisfaction.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: There's none offer'd.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Nor would not be accepted,
Though upon thy knees 'twere tender'd,

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Now the ſtorm grows high.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: But that I thought thee dead, and in thy death
The brinie Ocean had entomb'd thy name;
I would have ſought a Wife in a Bordello
For my Mentivole, and gladly hugg'd
Her ſpurious iſſue as my lawful Nephews,
Before his bloud ſhould e'er have mix'd with thine;
So much I ſcorn it.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: I'll not bandy words, but thus diſſolve the contract.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: There I meet thee, and ſeize on what's mine own.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: For all my ſervice,
Great Sir, grant me the combat with this wretch,
That I may ſcourge his inſolence.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I kneel for it.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: And to approve my ſelf Alberto's Son,
I'll be his ſecond upon any odds,
'Gainſt him that dare moſt of Baptiſta's race.

sp.speaker: Menti.
sp.l: Already upon honourable terms,
In me thou haſt met thy better, for her ſake
I'll add no more.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Sir, let our ſwords decide it.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Oh ſtay Sir, and as you would hold the Title
Of a juſt Prince, e'r you grant licence to
Theſe mad-mens fury, lend your private ear
To the moſt diſtreſs'd of Women.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Speak, 'tis granted. He takes Mariana aſide.

sp.speaker: Clar.
sp.l: In the meantime, let not Clariſſa be
A patient looker on, though as yet doubtful,
To whom to bend her knee firſt, yet to all
I ſtoop thus low in duty, and would waſh
The duſt of fury with my Virgin tears,
From his bleſs'd feet, and make them beautiful
That would move to conditions of peace,
Though with a ſnail-like pace, they all are wing'd
To bear you to deſtruction: reverend Sirs,
Think on your antient friendſhip cemented
With ſo much bloud, but ſhed in noble action,
Divided now in paſſion for a brawl;
The Makers bluſh to own, much lov'd Ceſario.
Brother, or friend, (each Title may prevail,)
Remember with what tenderneſs from our childhood
We lov'd together, you preferring me
Before your ſelf, and I ſo fond of you
That it begot ſuſpition in ill minds
That our affection was inceſtuous.
Think of that happy time, in which I know
That with your deareſt bloud you had prevented
This ſhower of tears from me; Mentivole,
My Husband, regiſtred in that bright ſtar-chamber,
Though now on earth made ſtrangers, be the example
And offer in one hand the peaceful Olive
Of concord, or if that can be denied
By powerful interceſſion in the other
Carry the Hermian rod, and force attonement,
Now we will not be all marble. Death's the worſt then
And he ſhall be my Bridegroom. Offers to kill her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ment.
sp.l: Hold Clariſſa, his loving violence needs muſt
Offer in ſpite of honor—

div.stage: He ſnatches away her knife, and ſets it to his own breaſt, ſhe ſtaies his hand.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Was it to that end then on your Religion?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: And my hope in Heaven, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We then will leave intreaties, and make uſe
Of our authority, muſt I cry ai-me
To this unheard of inſolence? in my preſence
To draw your ſwords, and as all reverence
That's due to Majeſty were forfeited,
Cheriſh this wildeneſs! ſheath them inſtantly,
And ſhew an alteration in your looks, or by my power

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: Cut off my head.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: And mine, rather than hear of peace with this bad man.
I'll not alone, give up my throat, but ſuffer
Your rage to reach my family.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: And my name to be no more remembred.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What are theſe?

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.p: Biancha, 'tis Biancha, ſtill Biancha: but ſtrangely alter'd.

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.l: If that thirteen years
Of abſence could raze from my memory
The figure of my friend, I might forget thee;
But if thy Image be graven on my heart,
Thou art my Proſpero.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Thou my Baptiſta?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: A ſuddain change!

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I dare not ask, dear friend
If Juliana live! for that's a bleſſing
I am unworthy of, but yet denie not
To let me know the place ſhe hath made happy
By having there her Sepulchre.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: If your Highneſs pleaſe to vouchſafe a patient
Ear, we ſhall make a true relation of a ſtory
That ſhall call on your wonder.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Speak, we hear you.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Baptiſta's fortune in the Genoua Court,
His baniſhment, with his fair Wife's reſtraint
You are acquainted with; what ſince hath follow'd
I faithfully will deliver. E'r eight Moons
After Baptiſta's abſence were compleat,
Fair Juliana found the pleaſures, that
They had injoy'd together, were not barren,
And bluſhing at the burthen of her womb,
No father near to own it, it drew on
A violent ſickneſs, which call'd down compaſſion
From the angry Duke, then careful of her health.
Phyſitians were enquir'd of, and their judgment
Preſcrib'd the Baths of Luca as a means
For her recovery; to my charge it pleas'd her
To be committed; but as on the way
We journey'd, thoſe throws only known to Women
Came thick upon her, in a private Village.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: She died?

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Have patience, ſhe brought to the world
A hopeful Daughter; for her bodies ſickneſs
It ſoon decay'd, but the grief of her mind
Hourly increas'd, and life grew tedious to her,
And deſperate e'er to ſee you; ſhe injoyn'd me
To place her in a Greekiſh Monaſtery,
And to my care gave up her pretty Daughter.

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.l: What Monaſtery? as a Pilgrim bare-foot,
I'll ſearch it out.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: Pray you interrupt me not,
Now to my fortunes; the girl well diſpos'd of
With a faithful friend of mine, my cruel fate
Made me a priſoner to the Turkiſh Gallies,
Where for 12 years, theſe hands tugg'd at the Oar,
But fortune tyr'd at length with my afflictions,
Some Ships of Maltha met the Ottoman Fleet,
Charg'd them, and boarded them, and gave me freedom.
With my deliverers I ſerv'd, and got
Such reputation with the great Maſter
That he gave me command over a tall
And luſty ſhip, where my firſt happy ſervice
Was to redeem Alberto rumour'd dead,
But was like me ſurpriz'd by Cortugogly.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: I would I had died there.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: And from him learning
Baptiſta liv'd, and their diſſolv'd friendſhip,
I hois'd up ſails for Greece, found Juliana
A votary at her Beads; having made known
Both that you liv'd, and where you were: ſhe borrow'd
So much from her devotion, as to wiſh me
To bring her to you; if the object pleaſe you,
With joy receive her.

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.l: Rage and fury leave me. Throws away his ſword.
I am ſo full of happineſs, there's no room left
To entertain you, oh my long loſt Jewel,
Light of mine eyes, my ſouls ſtrength.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.l: My beſt Lord, having embrac'd you thus,
Death cannot fright me.

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.l: Live long to do ſo, though I ſhould ſix here.
Pardon me Proſpero, though I enquire my daughters fortune.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: That your happineſs
May be at all parts perfect, here ſhe is!

sp.speaker: Ceſ.
sp.l: Biancha, daughter to a Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: True with my faithful Hoſt I left her,
And with him till now ſhe hath reſided,
Ignorant both of her birth and greatneſs.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Oh my bleſt one. Joy upon joy o'erwhelms me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Above wonder.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: I do begin to melt too, this ſtrange ſtory
Works much upon me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Since it hath pleas'd heaven
To grace us with this miracle, I that am
Heavens inſtrument here, determine thus; Alberto
Be not unthankful for the bleſſings ſhown you,
Nor you Baptiſta; diſcord was yet never
A welcome ſacrifice; therefore rage laid by,
Embrace as friends, and let paſs'd difference
Be as a dream forgotten.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: 'Tis to me.

sp.speaker: Alber.
sp.l: And me, and thus confirm it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And to tye it
In bonds not to be broken, with the marriage
Of young Mentivole, and fair Clariſſa,
So you conſent great Lady, your Biancha
Shall call Caeſario Husband.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.l: 'Tis a motion I gladly yield to.

sp.speaker: Ceſar.
sp.l: One in which you make a ſad man happy.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Kneel not, all forgiven.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: With the Duke your Uncle I will make attonement, and will have no denial.

div.stage: Enter Hoſt, Foroboſco, Clown and Officers.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let this day be ſtill held ſacred.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Now if you can conjure, let the Devil unbind you.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: We are both undone.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Already we feel it.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Juſtice Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What are they?

sp.speaker: Proſ.
sp.l: I can reſolve you, ſlaves freed from the Gallies
By the Viceroy of Sicilia.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What's their offence?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: The robbing me of all my Plate and Jewels,
I mean the attempting of it.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Pleaſe your Grace I will now diſcover this Varlet in earneſt, this honeſt peſtilent rogue, profeſt the Art of Conjuring, but all the skill that ever he had in the black Art, was in making a Seacole fire; only with wearing ſtrange ſhapes, he begot admiration amongſt Fools and Women.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.l: Wilt thou peach thou varlet?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why does he goggle with his eyes, and ſtalke ſo?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: This is one of his Magical raptures.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: I do vilifie your cenſure, you demand if I am guilty, whir ſays my cloak by a trick of Legerdemain, now I am not guilty, I am guarded with innocence, pure Silver Lace • aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Thus have I read to you your virtues, which notwithſtanding I would not have you proud of.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: Out thou concealment of Tallow, and counterfeit Mummia.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: To the Gallies with them both.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: The only Sea-phyſick for a knave, is to be baſted in a Gally, with the oil of a Bulls Peeſel.

sp.speaker: Foro.
sp.p: And will not you make a ſour face at the ſame ſauce, ſirrah? I hope to find thee ſo lean in one fortnight, thou mayſt be drawn by the ears through the hoop of a a firkin.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Divide them, and away with them to th' Gallies.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: This will take down your pride, Jugler.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: This day that hath given birth to bleſſings beyond hope, admits no criminal ſentence: to the Temple, and there with humbleneſs, praiſe heavens bounties;
sp.l: For bleſſings ne'er deſcend from thence, but when
A ſacrifice in thanks aſcends from men. Exeunt omnes

div.head: The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Leontius, the old Duke of Lycia.
Nilo, ſent in Commiſſion to pull down Cupid's Image.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Agenor.
sp.p: TRuſt me my Lord Dorialus, I had miſt of this, if you had not call'd me; I thought the Princeſſes birth-day had been to morrow.

sp.speaker: Niſus.
sp.p: Why, did your Lordſhip ſleep out the day.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: I marvel what the Duke meant to make ſuch an idle vow.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.p: Idle, why?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: Is't not idle, to ſwear to grant his Daughter any thing ſhe ſhall ask on her birth-day? ſhe may ask an impoſſible thing: and I pray heaven ſhe do not ask an unfit thing at one time or other; 'tis dangerous truſting a mans vow upon the diſcretion on's Daughter.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.p: I wonder moſt at the Marquiſs her Brother, who is always vehemently forward to have her deſires granted.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: He's acquainted with 'em before.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.p: She's doubtleſs very chaſte and virtuous

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: So is Leucippus her brother.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: She's twenty year old, I wonder
She aske not a Husband.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: That were a folly in her; having refus'd all the Great Princes in one part of the world; She'll die a Maid.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: She may ask but one, may ſhe?

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: A hundred times this day if ſhe will;
And indeed, every day is ſuch a day, for though
The Duke has vow'd it only on this day,
He keeps it every day: he can deny
Her nothing.

div.stage: Enter Hidaſpes, Leucippus, Leontius, Timantas, Tellamon.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Come fair Hidaspes, thou art
Ducheſs to day,
Art thou prepar'd to aske, thou knoweſt
My oath will force performance.
And Leucippus, if ſhe now ask ought that ſhall,
Or would have performance
After my death, when by the help of heaven,
This Land is thine, accurſed be thy race,
May every one forget thou art my Son,
And ſo their own obedience.

sp.speaker: Leucip.
sp.l: Mighty Sir,
I do not wiſh to know that fatal hour,
That is to make me King, but if I do,
I ſhall moſt haſtily, (and like a Son)
Perform your grant to all, chiefly to her:
Remember that you aske what we
Agreed upon.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Are you prepar'd? then ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: Moſt Royal Sir, I am prepar'd,
Nor ſhall my Will exceed a Virgins bounds,
What I requeſt ſhall both at once bring
Me a full content.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: So it ever does:
Thou only comfort of my feeble age,
Make known thy good deſire,
For I dare ſwear thou lov'ſt me.

sp.speaker: Hidas.
sp.l: This is it I beg,
And on my knees. The people of your Land,
The Lycians, are through all the Nations
That know their name, noted to have in uſe
A vain and fruitleſs ſuperſtition;
So much more hateful, that it bears the ſhew
Of true Religion, and is nothing elſe
But a falſe-pleaſing bold laſciviouſneſs.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: What is it?

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: Many ages before this,
When every man got to himſelf a Trade,
And was laborious in that choſen courſe,
Hating an idle life, far worſe than death:
Some one that gave himſelf to Wine and Sloth,
Which breed laſcivious thoughts;
And found himſelf conjoyn'd
For that by every painful man,
To take his ſtain away, fram'd to himſelf
A god, whom he pretended to obey,
In being thus diſhoneſt, for a name
He call'd him Cupid. This created god,
Mans nature being ever credulous
Of any vice that takes part with his blood,
Had ready followers enow: and ſince
In every age they grew, eſpecially
Amongſt your Subjects, who do yet remain
Adorers of that drowſie Deitie:
Which drink invented: and the winged Boy,
(For ſo they call him) has his ſacrifices.
Theſe looſe naked ſtatues through the Land,
And in every Village, nay the palace
Is not free from 'em. This is my requeſt,
That theſe erect obſcene Images
May be pluckt down and burnt: and every man
That offers to 'em any ſacrifice, may loſe his life.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: But be advis'd my faireſt daughter, if he be
A god, he will expreſs it upon thee my child:
Which heaven avert.

sp.speaker: Leucip.
sp.l: There is no ſuch power:
But the opinion of him fills the Land
With luſtful ſins: every young man and maid
That feel the leaſt deſire to one another,
Dare not ſuppreſs it, for they think it is
Blind Cupid's motion: and he is a god.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: This makes our youth unchaſte. I am reſolv'd:
Nephew Iſmenus, break the Statues down
Here in the Palace, and command the City
Do the like, let proclamations
Be drawn, and haſtily ſent through the Land
To the ſame purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Iſmen.
sp.l: Sir, I will break down none my ſelf,
But I will deliver your command:
Hand I will have none in't, for I like it not.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Goe and command it. Pleaſure of my life,
Wouldſt thou ought elſe? make many thouſand ſuits.
They muſt and ſhall be granted.

sp.speaker: Hid.
sp.l: Nothing elſe. Exit Iſmenus.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: But go and meditate on other ſuits,
Some ſix days hence I'll give thee Audience again,
And by a new oath, bind my ſelf to keep it:
Ask largely for thy ſelf, dearer than life
In whom I may be bold to call my ſelf,
More fortunate than any in my age,
I will deny thee nothing.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: 'Twas well done, Siſter.

div.stage: Exeunt all but theſe three Lords.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: How like you this requeſt my Lord?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I know not yet, I am ſo full of wonder,
We ſhall be gods our ſelves ſhortly,
And we pull 'em out of Heaven o' this faſhion.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: We ſhall have wenches now when we can
Catch 'em, and we tranſgreſs thus.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: And we abuſe the gods once, 'tis a Juſtice
We ſhould be he • d at hard meat: for my part,
I'll e'en make ready for mine own affection.
I know the god incenſt muſt ſend a hardneſs
Through all good Womens hearts, and then we have
Brought our Eggs and Muskadine to a fair Market:
Would I had giv'n an 100 l. for a tolleration,
That I might but uſe my conſcience in mine
Own houſe,

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: The Duke he's old and paſt it, he would
Never have brought ſuch a plague upon the Land elſe,
'Tis worſe than Sword and Famine:
Yet to ſay truth, we have deſerv'd it, we have liv'd
So wickedly, every man at his Livery, and wou'd that
Wou'd have ſuffic'd us: we murmur'd at this
Bleſſing, that was nothing; and cry'd out to the
God for endleſs pleaſures, he heard us,
And ſuppied us, and our Women were new ſtill
As we need 'em: yet we like beaſts ſtill cry'd,
Poor men can number their woers, give us
Abundance: we had it, and this curſe withal.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: Berlady we are like to have a long Lent on't,
Fleſh ſhall be fleſh: now Gentlemen I had rather
Have anger'd all the gods, than that blind Gunner,
I remember once the people did but ſlight him
In a ſacrifice: and what followed?
Women kept their houſes, grew good huſwives
Honeſt forſooth? was not that fine?
Wore their own faces,
Though they wear gay cloaths without ſurveying,
And which was moſt lamentable,
They lov'd their Husbands.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: I do remember it to my grieſ,
Young Maids were as cold as Cowcumbers
And much of that complexion:
Bawds were aboliſht: and, to which miſery
It muſt come again,
There were no Cuckolds,
Well, we had need pray to keep theſe
Divels from us,
The times grow miſchievous.
There he goes, Lord!
This is a ſacriledge I have not heard of:
Would I were gelt, that I might not
Feel what follows.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: And I too. You ſhall ſee within theſe
Few years, a fine confuſion i'the Countrey: mark it:
Nay, and we grow for to depoſe the Powers,
And ſet up Chaſtity again, well, I have done.
A fine new goddeſs certainly, whoſe bleſſings
Are hunger and hard beds.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: This comes of fulneſs, a ſin too frequent with us
I believe now we ſhall find ſhorter commons.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Would I were married, ſomewhat has ſome ſavour;
The race of Gentry will quite run out now,
'Tis only left to Husbands, if younger Siſters
Take not the greater charity, 'tis lawful.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: Well, let come what will come,
I am but one, and as the plague ſalls,
I'll ſhape my ſelf: If Women will be honeſt, I'll be found.
If the god be not too unmerciful,
I'll take a little ſtill, where I can get it,
And thank him, and ſay nothing.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: This ill wind yet may blow the City good,
And let them, (if they can) get their own children,
sp.p: They have hung long enough in doubt, but howſoever, the old way was the ſurer, then they had 'em.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: Farewel my Lords, I'll e'en take up what Rent I can before the day, I fear the year will fall out ill.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: We'll with you Sir: And love ſo favour us,
As we are ſtill thy ſervants. Come my Lords;
Let's to the Duke, and tell him to what folly
His doting now has brought him. Exeunt.

body.head: Prieſt of Cupid, with four young men. and Maids.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Come my children, let your feet,
In an even meaſure meet:
And your chearful voices riſe.
For to preſent this Sacrifice;
Lo great Cupid, in whoſe name,
I his Prieſt begin the ſame.
Young men take your Loves and kiſs,
Thus our Cupid honour'd is
Kiſs again, and in your kiſſing,
Let no promiſes be miſſing:
Nor let any Maiden here,
Dare to turn away her ear,
Unto the whisper of her Love,
But give Bracelet, Ring or Glove,
As a token to her ſweeting,
Of an after ſecret meeting:
Now boy ſing to ſtick our hearts
Fuller of great Cupids darts.

lg.l: LOvers rejoyce, your pains ſhall be rewarded,
The god of Love himſelf grieves at your crying:
No more ſhall frozen honor be regarded,
Nor the coy faces of a Maids denying.
No more ſhall Virgins ſigh, and ſay we dare not,
For men are falſe, and what they do they care not,
All ſhall be well again, then do not grieve,
Men ſhall be true, and Women ſhall believe.
Lovers rejoyce, what you ſhall ſay henceforth,
When you have caught your Sweet-hearts in your arms,
It ſhall be accounted Oracle, and Worth:
No more faint-hearted Girls ſhall dream of harms.
And cry they are too young, the god hath ſaid,
Fifteen ſhall make a Mother of a Maid:
Then wiſe men, pull your Roſes yet unblown,
Love hates the too ripe fruit that falls alone.

div.stage: After the Meaſure, Enter Nilo and others.

sp.speaker: Nilo.
sp.l: No more of this: here break your Rights for ever,
The Duke commands it ſo; Prieſt do not ſtare,
I muſt deface your Temple, though unwilling,
And your god Cupid here muſt make a Scare-crow
For any thing I know, or at the beſt,
Adorn a Chimney-piece.

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Oh Sacriledge unheard of?

sp.speaker: Nilo,
sp.l: This will not help it, take down the Image
And away with 'em.
Prieſt, change your coat you had beſt, all ſervice now
Is given to men: Prayers above their hearing
Will prove but bablings: learn to lye and thrive,
'Twill prove your beſt profeſſion: for the gods,
He that lives by 'em now, muſt be a beggar.
There's better holineſs on earth they ſay,
Pray God it ask not greater ſacrifice. Go home,
And if our god be not deaf as well as blind,
He will ſome ſmoak for it.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Sir—

sp.speaker: Nilo.
sp.l: Gentlemen, there is no talking,
This muſt be done and ſpeedily;
I have commiſſion that I muſt not break.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: We are gone, to wonder what ſhall follow.

sp.speaker: Nilo.
sp.l: On to the next Temple. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cupid.
sp.l: Am I then ſcorn'd? is my all-doing Will
And Power, that knows no limit, nor admits none,
Now look'd into by leſs than gods? and weak'ned
Am I, whoſe Bow ſtruck terror through the earth,
No leſs than Thunder, and in this, exceeding
Even gods themſelves, whoſe knees before my Altars
Now ſhook off; and contemn'd by ſuch, whoſe lives
Are but my recreation! anger riſe
My ſufferance and my ſelf are made the ſubject
Of ſins againſt us. Go thou out diſpleaſure,
Diſpleaſure of a great god, flying thy ſelf
Through all this Kingdom: ſow what ever evils
Proud fleſh is taking off, amongſt theſe Rebels:
And on the firſt heart that deſpiſe my Greatneſs,
Lay a ſtrange miſery, that all may know
Cupid's revenge is mighty; with his Arrow
Hotter than plagues or mine own anger, will I
Now nobly right my ſelf: nor ſhall the prayers
Nor ſmoaks on my Altars hold my hand,
Till I have left this a moſt wretched Land, Exit.

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: Cleophila, what was he that went hence?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: What means your Grace now?

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: I mean that handſome man.
That ſomething more than man I met at door.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Here was no handſome man.

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: Come, he's ſome one
You would preſerve in private, but you want
Cunning to do it, and my eyes are ſharper
Than yours, and can with one neglecting glance,
See all the graces of a man. Who was't?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: That went hence now?

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: That went hence now, I, he

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Faith here was no ſuch one as your Grace thinks.
Zoylous your Brothers Dwarf went out but now.

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: I think 'twas he: how bravely he paſt by:
Is he not grown a goodly Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: A goodly Gentleman, Madam?
He is the moſt deformed fellow i'the Land.

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: Oh blaſphemy: he may perhaps to thee
Appear deform'd, for he is indeed
Unlike a man: his ſhape and colours are
Beyond the Art of Painting; he is like
Nothing that we have ſeen, yet doth reſemble
Apollo, as I oft have fancied him,
When riſing from his bed, he ſtirs himſelf
And ſhakes day from his hair.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: He reſembles Apollo's Recorder.

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: Cleophila, go ſend a Page for him,
And thou ſhalt ſee thy error, and repent. Exit Cleo.
Alas, what do I feel, my bloud rebells,
And I am one of thoſe I us'd to ſcorn,
My Maiden-thoughts are fled againſt my ſelf?
I harbor Traitors in my Virginity,
That from my Childhood kept me company,
Is heavier than I can endure to bear:
Forgive me Cupid, for thou art a god,
And I a wretched creature; I have ſinn'd,
But be thou merciful, and grant that yet
I may enjoy what thou wilt have me, Love.

div.l: Zoylous is here Madam.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: He's there indeed.
Now be thine own Judge; ſee thou worſe than mad,
Is he deformed? look upon thoſe eyes,
That let all pleaſure out into the world,
Unhappy that they cannot ſee themſelves;
Look on his hair, that like ſo many beams,
Streaking the Eaſt, ſhoot light o'er half the world,
Look on him altogether, who is made
As if two Natures had contention
About their skill, and one had brought forth him.

sp.speaker: Zoy.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha: Madam, though Nature
Hath not given me ſo much
As others in my outward ſhew;
I bear a heart as loyal unto you
In this unſightly body (which you pleaſe
To make your mirth) as many others do
That are far more befriended in their births;
Yet I could wiſh my ſelf much more deformed
Than yet I am, ſo I might make your Grace
More merry than you are, ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: Beſhrew me then if I be merry;
But I'm content whilſt thou art with me:
Thou that art my Saint:
By hope of whoſe mild favour I do live
To tell thee ſo: I pray thee ſcorn me not;
Alas what can it add unto thy worth
To triumph over me, that am a Maid,
Without deceit? whoſe heart doth guide her tongue,
Drown'd in my paſſions; yet I will take leave
To call it reaſon that I dote on thee.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: The Princeſs is beſides her Grace I think.
To talk thus with a fellow that will hardly
Serve i'th' dark when one is drunk.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: What anſwer wilt thou give me?

sp.speaker: Zoy.
sp.l: If it pleaſe your Grace to jeſt on, I can abide it.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: If it be jeſt, not to eſteem my life,
Compar'd with thee: If it be jeſt in me,
To hang a thouſand kiſſes in an hour
Upon thoſe Lips, and take 'em off again:
If it be jeſt for me to marry thee,
And take obedience on me whilſt I live:
Then all I ſay is jeſt:
For every part of this, I ſwear by thoſe
That ſee my thoughts, I am reſolv'd to do,
And I beſeech thee, by thine own white hand,
(Which pardon me, that I am bold to kiſs
With ſo unworthy Lips) that thou wilt ſwear
To marry me, as I do here to thee,
Before the face of heaven.

sp.speaker: Zoy.
sp.l: Marry you? ha, ha, ha,

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: Kill me or grant, wilt thou not ſpeak at all?

sp.speaker: Zoy.
sp.l: Why I will do your Will for ever.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: I ask no more: but let me kiſs that mouth
That is ſo merciful; that is my will:
Next go with me before the King in haſte,
That is my Will; where I will make our Peers
Know, that thou art their better.

sp.speaker: Zoy.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, that is fine, ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Madam, what means your Grace?
Conſider for the love of Heaven to what
You run madly; will you take this Viper
Into your bed?

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: Away, hold off thy hands:
Strike her ſweet Zoylus, for it is my Will,
Which thou haſt ſworn to doe.

sp.speaker: Zoy.
sp.l: Away for ſhame.
Know you no manners: ha, ha, ha. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt none I fear,
This is juſt Cupid's Anger, Venus look down mildly on us:
sp.p: And command thy Son to ſpare this Lady once, and let me be in love withal: and none in love with me. Exit.

sp.speaker: Timan.
sp.l: Is your Lordſhip for the Wars this Summer?

sp.speaker: Iſmen.
sp.l: Timantus, wilt thou go with me?

sp.speaker: Timan.
sp.l: If I had a Company, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Iſmen.
sp.l: Of Fidlers: Thou a company?
No, no, keep thy Company at home, and cauſe cuckolds:
The Wars will hurt thy face, there's no Semſters,
Shoomakers, nor Taylors, nor Almond-milk i'th' morning,
Nor poach'd Egs to keep your worſhip ſoluble,
No man to warm your Shirt, and blow your Roſes:
Nor none to reverence your round lace Breeches:
If thou wilt needs goe, and goe thus,
Get a Caſe for thy Captainſhip, a ſhower will ſpoil thee elſe.
Thus much for thee.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Your Lordſhip's wondrous witty, very pleaſant believe't. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Telamon, Dorialus, Agenor, Niſus, Leonti.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: No news yet of my Son?

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.l: Sir, there be divers out in ſearch:
No doubt they'll bring the truth where he is,
Or the occaſion that led him hence.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: They have good eyes then.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: The gods goe with them:
Who be thoſe that wait there?

sp.speaker: Tele.
sp.l: The Lord Iſmenus, your General, for his diſpatch.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Oh Nephew: we have no uſe to imploy your
Virtue in our War: now the Province is well ſetled.
Hear you ought of the Marquis?

sp.speaker: Iſmen.
sp.l: No Sir?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: 'Tis ſtrange he ſhould be gone thus:
Theſe five days he was not ſeen,

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: I'll hold my hold, I could bolt him in an hour:

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Where's my Daughter?

sp.speaker: Dori.
