sp.l: About the purging of the Temples, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: She's chaſte and virtuous; fetch her to me,
And tell her I am pleas'd to grant her now
Her laſt requeſt, without repenting me. Exit Niſ.
Be it what it will: ſhe is wiſe, Dorialus
And will not preſs me farther than a Father.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I pray the beſt may follow; yet if your Grace
Had taken the opinions of your people,
At leaſt of ſuch, whoſe wiſdoms ever wake
About your ſafety, I may ſay it, Sir,
Under your noble pardon: that this change
Either had been more honor to the gods,
Or I think not at all. Sir, the Princeſs.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Oh my Daughter, my health!
And did I ſay my ſoul, I ly'd not;
Thou art ſo near me, ſpeak, and have whatever
Thy wiſe Will leads thee too: had I a Heaven,
It were too poor a place for ſuch a goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: What's here?

sp.speaker: Agen.
sp.l: An Apes skin ſtuft I think, 'tis ſo plump.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: Sir, you have paſt your word,
Still be a Prince, and hold you to it.
Wonder not I preſs you, my life lies in your word:
If you break that, you have broke my heart, I muſt ask
That's my ſhame, and your Will muſt not deny me:
Now for Heaven be not forſworn.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: By the gods I will not,
I cannot, were there no other power,
Than my love call'd to a witneſs of it.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: They have much reaſon to truſt,
You have forſworn one of 'em out o'th' countrey already.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: Then this is my requeſt: This Gent.
Be not aſhamed, Sir:
You are worth a Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: In what?

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: In the way of marriage.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: In the way of marriage, it muſt be ſo,
Your oath is ti'd to Heaven: as my love to him.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I know thou doſt but try my age,
Come ask again.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: If I ſhould ask all my life-time, this is all ſtill.
Sir, I am ſerious, I muſt have this worthy man without enquiring why; and ſuddenly, and freely:
Doe not look for reaſon or obedience in my words: my
Love admits no wiſdom:
Only haſte, and hope hangs on my fury,
Speak Sir, ſpeak, but not as a Father,
I am deaf and dull to counſel: inflamed blood
Hears nothing but my Will;
For Gods ſake ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Here's a brave alteration.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: This comes of Chaſtity.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: Will not you ſpeak Sir?

sp.speaker: Agen.
sp.p: The god begins his vengeance; what a ſweet youth he has ſent us here, with a pudding in's belly?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Oh let me never ſpeak,
Or with my words let me ſpeak out my life;
sp.p: Thou power abus'd: great Love, whoſe vengeance now we feel and fear, have mercy on this Land.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: How does your Grace?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Sick, very ſick I hope.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Gods comfort you.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: Will not you ſpeak? is this your Royal word?
Do not pull perjurie upon your ſoul.
Sir, you are old, and near your puniſhment; remember.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Away baſe woman.

sp.speaker: Hidaſ.
sp.l: Then be no more my Father, but a plague,
I am bound to pray againſt: be any ſin
May force me to deſpair, and hang my ſelf,
Be thy name never more remembred King
But in example of a broken faith,
And curſt even to forgetfulneſs:
May thy Land bring forth ſuch Monſters as thy Daughter is?
I am weary of my rage. I pray forgive me,
And let me have him, will you Noble Sir?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Mercy, mercy heaven:
Thou heir of all diſhonor, ſhameſt thou not to draw
This little moiſture leſt for life, thus rudely from me?
Carry that ſlave to death.

sp.speaker: Zoy.
sp.l: For heavens ſake Sir, it is no fault of mine,
That ſhe will love me.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: To death with him, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: Then make haſte Tyrant, or I'll be for him:
This is the way to Hell.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Hold faſt, I charge you away with him.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: Alas old man, Death hath more doors than one,
And I will meet him. Exit Hida.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Dorialus, Pray ſee her in her chamber,
And lay a guard about her:
The greateſt curſe the gods lay on our frailties,
Is Will and Diſobedience in our Iſſues,
Which we beget as well as them to plague us,
With our fond loves; Beaſts you are only bleſt
That have that happy dulneſs to forget
What you have made, your young ones grieve not you
They wander where they liſt, and have their ways
Without diſhonor to you; and their ends,
Fall on 'em without ſorrow of their Parents,
Or after ill remembrance: Oh this Woman
Would I had made my ſelf a Sepulcher,
When I made her: Nephew, where is the Prince?
Pray God he have not more part of her baſeneſs
Than of her bloud about him.
Gentlemen: where is he?

sp.speaker: Iſin.
sp.l: I know not Sir.
H'as his ways by himſelf, is too wiſe for my company.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I do not like this hiding of himſelf,
From ſuch ſociety as his perſon
Some of it ye needs muſt know.

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: I am ſure not I: nor have known twice this ten days, which if I were as proud as ſome of 'em, I ſhould take ſcurvily, but he is a young man.
sp.l: Let him have this ſwinge, 'twill make him.
There's ſome good matter now in hand:
How the ſlave jeers and grins; the Duke is pleas'd,
There's a new pair of Scarlet Hoſe now, and as much
sp.p: Money to ſpare, as will fetch the old from pawn, a Hat and a Cloak to goe out to morrow:
sp.l: Garters and Stockings come by nature.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Be ſure of this.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.l: I durſt not ſpeak elſe, Sir.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Cupid.
sp.l: LEucippus thou art ſhot through with a ſhaft
That will not rankle long, yet ſharp enough
To ſow a world of helpleſs miſery—
In this unhappy Kingdom, doſt thou think
Becauſe thou art a Prince, to make a part
Againſt my power, but it is all the fault
Of thy old Father, who believes • his age
Is cold enough to quench my burning Darts,
But he ſhall know e'r long, that my ſmart looſe,
Can thaw Ice, and inflame the wither'd heart
Of Neſtor, thou thy ſelf art lightly ſtruck,
But his mad love, ſhall publiſh that the rage
Of Cupid, has the power to conquer Age. Exit.
sp.stage: Enter Bacha, and Leucippus, Bacha, a Handkerchief.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Have you got the ſpoil
You thirſted for? Oh tyrannie of men!

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I pray thee leave,

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Your envy is, Heaven knows,
Beyond the reach of all our feeble ſex:
What pain alas, could it have been to you,
If I had kept mine honor? you might ſtill
Have been a Prince, and ſtill this Countreys Heir,
That innocent Guard which I till now had kept,
For my defence, my virtue, did it ſeem
So dangerous in a State, that your ſelf came to ſuppreſs it?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Drie thine eyes again, I'll kiſs thy tears away,
This is but folly, 'tis paſt all help.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Now you have won the treaſure,
'Tis my requeſt that you would leave me thus:
And never ſee theſe empty Walls again,
I know you will do ſo, and well you may:
For there is nothing in 'em that's worth
A glance, I loath my ſelf, and am become
Another Woman; One methinks with whom
I want acquaintance.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: If I do offend thee, I can be gone,
sp.p: And though I love thy ſight, ſo highly do I prize thine own content, that I will leave thee.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Nay, you may ſtay now;
You ſhould have gone before: I know not now
Why I ſhould fear you: All I ſhould have kept
Is ſtol'n: Nor is it in the power of man
To rob me farther: if you can invent,
Spare not; No naked man fears robbing leſs
Than I doe: now you may for ever ſtay

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Why, I could do thee farther wrong.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: You have a deeper reach in evill than I:
'Tis paſt my thoughts.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: And paſt my will to act: but truſt me I could do it.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Good Sir do, that I may know there is a wrong beyond what you have done me.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I could tell all the world what thou haſt done.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Yes you may tell the world
And do you think I am ſo vain to hope
You will not? you can tell the world but this,
That I am a widow, full of tears in ſhew,
My Husband dead: And one that lov'd me ſo,
Hardly a week, forgot my modeſtie,
And caught with youth and greatneſs,
Gave my ſelf to live in ſin with you;
This you may tell: And this I do deſerve.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Why doſt thou think me ſo baſe to tell!
Theſe limbs of mine ſhall part
From one another on a wrack,
Ere I diſcloſe; But thou doſt utter words
That much afflict me: you did ſeem as ready
Sweet Bacha, as my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: You are right a man: when they have 'witcht us into miſerie, poor innocent ſouls,
sp.l: They lay the fault on us:
But be it ſo; for Prince Leucippus ſake
I will bear any thing.

sp.speaker: Leucip.
sp.l: Come weep no more,
I wrought thee to it, it was my fault:
Nay, ſee if thou wilt leave? Here, take this pearl,
Kiſs me ſweet Bacha, and receive this purſe.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.p: What ſhould I do with theſe? they will not deck my mind.

sp.speaker: Leucip.
sp.l: Why keep 'em to remember me.
I muſt be gone, I have been abſent long:
I know the Duke my Father is in rage,
But I will ſee thee ſuddenly again.
Farewell my Bacha.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Gods keep you,
Do you here Sir: pray give me a point to wear.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: Alas good Bacha, take on, I pray thee where thou wilt.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Coming from you. This Point is of as high Eſteem with me, as all pearl and gold: nothing but good be ever with or near you.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Fare thee well mine own good Bacha;
I will make all haſte. Exit.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Juſt as you are a Doſen I ſteem you:
No more, does he think I would proſtitute
My ſelf for love? it was the love of theſe pearls
And gold that won me, I confeſs
I luſt more after him than any other,
And would at any rate if I had ſtore,
Purchaſe his fellowſhip: but being poor,
I'll both enjoy his bodie and his purſe,
And he a Prince, nere think my ſelf the worſe.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Nay, you muſt back and ſhew us what it is,
That 'witches you out of your Honor thus.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.l: Look there Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon,
sp.l: Lady, never flye you are betray'd.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Leave me my tears a while,
And to my Juſt rage give a little place:
What ſaucy man are you, that without leave,
Enter upon a Widows mournfull houſe?
You hinder a dead man from many tears.
Who did deſerve more than the world can ſhed,
Though they ſhould weep themſelves to Images.
If not for love of me, yet of your ſelf
Away, for you can bring no comforts to me.
But you may carry hence, you know not what.
Nay ſorrow is infectious.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Thou thy ſelf
Art grown infectious: wouldſt thou know my name?
I am the Duke, father to this young-man
Whom thou corrupt'ſt?

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Has he than told him all?

sp.speaker: Leue.
sp.l: You do her wrong Sir.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: O he has not told. Sir I beſeech you pardon
My wild tongue, directed by a weak diſtemper'd head
Madded with • rief: Alas I did not know
You were my Sovereign; but now you may
Command my poor unworthy life,
Which w • ll be none I hop • ere long.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: All thy diſſembling will never hide thy ſhame:
And wer't not more reſpecting Woman-hood in
General, than any thing in thee, thou ſhouldſt
Be made ſuch an example, that poſteritie,
When they would ſpeak moſt bitterly, ſhould ſay,

l.hi: Thou art as imp • dent as Bacha was.

sp.speaker: Bacha
sp.l: Sir, though you be my King, whom I will
Serve in all juſt cauſes: yet when wrongfully
You ſeek to take my Honor, I will riſe
Thus, and defie you; for it is a Jewell
Dearer than you can give, which whilſt I keep,
(Though in this lowly houſe) I ſhall eſteem
My ſelf above the Princes of the earth
That are without it. If the Prince your ſon,
Whom you accuſe me with know how to ſpeak
Diſhonor of me, if he do not do it,
The plagues of hell light on him, may he never
Govern this Kingdome: here I chalenge him
Before the face of heaven, my Liege, and theſe,
To ſpeak the worſt he can: if he will lye,
To loſe a womans fame, I'll ſay he is
Like you (I think I cannot call him worſe.)
He's dead, that with his life would have defended
My reputation and I forct to play
(That which I am) the fooliſh woman,
And uſe my liberal tongue.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Is't poſſible! we men are children in our
Carriages, compar'd with women: 'wake thy ſelf
For ſhame, and leave not her whoſe honor thou
Shou'dſt keep ſafe as thine own, alone to free her ſelf:
But I am preſt I know not how, with guilt,
And feel my conſcience (never us'd to lye)
Loth to allow my tongue to add a lye
To that too much I did: but it is lawfull
To defend her, that only for my Love lov'd evill.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Tell me, why did you Leucip: ſtay here ſo long?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: If I can urge ought from me but a truth, hell Take me.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: What's the matter, why ſpeak you not?

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.l: Alas good Sir, forbear
To urge the Prince, you ſee his ſhamefaſtneſs.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: What does he ſay Sir? if thou be a Prince
Shew it, and tell the truth.

sp.speaker: Iſmen.
sp.l: If you have lain with her tell your Father
No doubt but he has done as ill before now:
The Gentlewoman will be proud on't.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: For God's ſake ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Have you done prating yet?

sp.speaker: Iſmen.
sp.l: Who prates?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt I do not ſpeak to thee Iſmenus:
But what ſaid you Tima; concerning my ſhamefaſtneſs?

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.l: Nothing I hope that might diſpleaſe your Highneſs.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: If any of thy great, Great-grandmothers
This thouſand years, had been as chaſt as ſhe,
It would have made thee honeſter, I ſtay'd
To here what you wou'd ſay: ſhe is by heaven
Of the moſt ſtrict and blameleſs chaſtitie
That ever woman was: (good gods forgive me)
Had Tarquin, met with her, ſhe had been kil'd
With a Slave by her ere ſhe had agreed:
• lye with her! wou'd I might periſh then.
Our Mothers, whom we all muſt reverence,
Could nere exceed her for her chaſtitie,
Upon my ſoul: for by this light ſhe's
A moſt obſtinate modeſt creature.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: What did you with her then ſo long Leucippus?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I'll tell you Sir: You ſee ſhe's beautifull.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I ſee it well.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Mov'd by her face,
I came with luſtful thoughts,
Which was a fault in me:
But telling truth, ſomething more pardonable,
(And for the world I will not lye to you:)
Proud of my ſelf, I thought a Princes name
Had power to blow 'em down flat of their backs;
But here I found a Rock not to be ſhook:
For as I hope for good Sir, all the battery
That I could lay to her, or of my perſon,
My greatneſs, or gold, could nothing move her.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: 'Tis very ſtrange, being ſo young and fair.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: She's almoſt thirty Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: How do you know her age ſo juſt?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: She told it me her ſelf
Once when ſhe went about to ſhew by reaſon
I ſhould leave wooing her.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: She ſtains the ripeſt Virgins of her age.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: If I had ſin'd with her, I would be loth
To publiſh her diſgrace: but by my life
I would have told it you, becauſe I think
You would have pardon'd me the rather:
And I will tell you father: By this light Sir,
(But that I never will beſtow my ſelf
But to your liking) if ſhe now would have me,
I now would marry her.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: How's that Leucippus!

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Sir, will you pardon me one fault, which yet
I have not done, but had a will to do, and I will tell it?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Be't what it will I pardon thee.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I offered marriage to her.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Did ſhe refuſe it?

sp.speaker: Leucip.
sp.l: With that earneſtnſs, and almoſt ſcorn
To think of any other after her loſt Mate, that ſhe
Made me think my ſelf unworthy of her.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: You have ſtay'd too long Leucippus

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Yes Sir, forgive me Heaven, what multitude
Of oaths have I beſtow'd on lies, and yet they were
Officious lyes, there was no malice in 'em.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: She is the faireſt creature that ever I beheld;
And then ſo chaſte, 'tis wonderfull: the more I look
On her, the more I am amaz'd.
I have long thought of a wife, and one I would have
Had, but that I was afraid to meet a woman
That might abuſe my age: but here ſhe is
Whom I may truſt to; of a chaſtitie
Impregnable, and approved ſo by my ſon:
The meaneſs of her birth will ſtill preſerve her
In due obedience; and her beauty is
Of force enough to pull me back to youth.
My ſon once ſent away, whoſe rivall-ſhip
I have juſt cauſe to fear, if power, of gold,
Or wit, can win her to me, ſhe is mine.
Nephew Iſmenus, I have new intelligence,
Your Province is unquiet ſtill.

sp.speaker: Iſmen.
sp.l: I am glad on't.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: And ſo dangerouſly, that I muſt ſend the
Prince in perſon with you.

sp.speaker: Iſmen.
sp.l: I am glad of that too: Sir, will you diſpatch
Us we ſhall wither here for ever.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: You ſhall be diſpatcht within this hour:
Leucippus. never wonder, nor ask, it muſt be thus.
Lady I ask your pardon, whoſe virtue I have
Slubberd with my tongue, and you ſhall ever be
Chaſt in my memory hereafter;
But we old men often doat: to make amends for
My great fault, receive that Ring:
I'm ſorry for your grief, may it ſoon leave you:
Come my Lords lets begon. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs your Grace.
One that had but ſo much modeſtie left, as to bluſh,
Or ſhrink a little at his firſt encounter,
Had been undone; where I come off with honor,
And gain too: they that never wou'd be tract
In any courſe, by the moſt ſubtle ſenſe
Muſt bear it through with frontleſs impudence.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: Gentlemen this is a ſtrange peece of Juſtice,
To put the wretched Dwarf to death becauſe
She doated on him; Is ſhe not a woman, and
Subject to thoſe mad figaries her whole Sex
Is infected with? Had ſhe lov'd you, or you, or I,
Or all on's (as indeed the more the merryer ſtill
With them) muſt we therefore have our heads par'd
With a Hatchet? So ſhe may love all the Nobility
Out o'th Dukedome in a month, and let the raskals in.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: You will not, or you do not ſee the need
That makes this juſt to the world?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: I cannot tell, I would be loth to feel it:
But the beſt is, ſhe loves not proper men, we three
Were in wiſe caſes elſe: but make me know this need.

sp.speaker: Eiſ.
sp.p: Why yes: He being taken away, this baſe incontinence dyes preſently, and ſhe muſt ſee her ſhame and ſorrow for it.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: Pray God ſhe do: but was the Sprat beheaded, Or did they ſwing him about like a chickin, and ſo break his neck?

sp.speaker: Agen.
sp.p: Yes, he was beheaded, and a ſolemn Juſtice made of it.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: That might have been deducted.

sp.speaker: Agenor.
sp.p: Why how would you have had him dyed?

sp.speaker: Dori.
sp.p: Faith I would have had him roſted like a warden in a brown paper, and no more talk on't: or a feather ſtuck in's head, like a Quail: or a hanged him in a Dog-coller: what ſhould he be beheaded? we ſhall have it grow ſo baſe ſhortly, Gentlemen will be out of love with it.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.p: I wonder from whence this of the Dwarf's firſt ſprung?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: From an old leacherous pair of breeches that lay upon a wench to keep her warm: for certainly they are no mans work: and I am ſure a Monkey would get one of the guard to this fellow, he was no bigger than a ſmall Portmanteu, and much about that making if'tad legs.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.p: But Gentlemen, what ſay you to the Prince?

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.p: I, concerning his being ſent I know not whither.

sp.speaker: Dorialus.
sp.p: Why then he will come home I know not when: you ſhall pardon me, I'll talk no more of this ſubject, but ſay, gods be with him where ere he is, and ſend him well home again: For why, he is gone, or when he will return, let them know that directed him: Only this, there's mad Moriſco's in the ſtate; but what they are, I'll tell you when I know. Come, let's go, hear all, and ſay nothing.

sp.speaker: Agen.
sp.p: Content. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.p: Timantus, is the Duke ready yet?

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: Almoſt.

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.p: What ails him?

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: Faith I know not, I think he has dreamt he's but eighteen: has been worſs ſince he ſent you forth for the frizling iron.

sp.speaker: Tel.
sp.p:
That cannot be, he lay in Gloves all night, and this morning I brought him a new Periwig, with a lock
at it, and knockt up a ſwing in's chamber.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: O but ſince, his Taylor came, and they have fallen out about the faſhion on's cloaths: and yonders a fellow come, has board a hole in's ear; and he has beſpoke a Vaulting-horſe, you ſhall ſee him come forth preſently: he looks like Winter, ſtuck here and there with freſh flowers.

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.p: Will he not Tilt think you?

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: I think he will.

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.p: What does he mean to doe?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: I know not: but by this light I think he is in love; he wou'd ha' bin ſhav'd but for me.

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.p: In love with whom?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: I could gueſs, but you ſhall pardon me: he will take me along with him ſome-whither,

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.p: I over-heard him ask your opinion of ſome bodies beauty.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: Yes, there it goes, that makes him ſo youthfull, and has layd by his Crutch, and halts now with a leading ſtaff.

div.stage: Enter Leontine with a ſtaff and a looking glaſs.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: This Feather is not large enough.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: Yes faith, 'tis ſuch an one as the reſt of the young Gallants wear.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Telamon, does it doe well?

sp.speaker: Tela:
sp.p: Sir, it becomes you, or you become it, tho rarelieſt—

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: A way, doſt think ſo?

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.p: Think Sir, I know it. Sir, the Princeſs, is paſt all hope of life ſince the Dwarf was put to death.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Let her be ſo, I have other matters in hand: but this ſame Taylor angers me, he has made my doublet ſo wide: and ſee, the knave has put no points at my arme.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: Thoſe will be put to quickly Sir, upon any occaſion.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Telamon, have you bid this Dancer come a mornings?

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.p: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Temantus, let me ſee the glaſs again: look you how careleſs you are grown, is this tooth well put in?

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: Which Sir?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: This Sir.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: It ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Telam.
sp.p: Me thinks that tooth ſhould put him in mind on's years: and Timantus, ſtands as if (ſeeing the Duke, in ſuch a youthfull habit) he were looking in's mouth how old he were.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: So, ſo.

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.p: Will you have your Gown ſir?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: My Gown? why, am I ſick? bring me my Sword.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Let a couple of the great horſes be brought out for us

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: He'll kill himſelf. Why, will you ride Sir:

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Ride? Doſt thou think I cannot ride?

sp.speaker: Timan.
sp.p: O yes Sir, I know it: but as I conceive your journey, you wou'd have it private; and then you were better take a Coach.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Theſe Coaches make me ſick: yet 'tis no matter, let it be ſo.

sp.speaker: Tel.
sp.p: Sir, here's your ſword.

sp.speaker: Leon,
sp.p: O well ſed: let me ſee it, I could me thinks Why Telamon, bring me another: what, thinkſt thou I will wear a ſword in vain?

sp.speaker: Tela.
sp.l: He has not ſtrength enough to draw it,
A yoak of Fleas ty'd to a hair would have drawn it.
'Tis out ſir now, the Scabbard is broke.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: O put it up again, and on with it; me thinks I am not dreſt till I feel my ſword on.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Telamon, if any of my counſell aske for me,
Say I am gone to take the air.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: He has not been dreſt this twenty years then, If this vain hold but a week, he will learn to play o'th baſe violl and ſing to't: He's poetical alreadie;
For I have ſpide a Sonnet on's making lye by's beds ſide, I'll be ſo unmannerly to read it. Exit.
He's dead, he's dead, and I am following.

div.stage: Enter Hidaſpes, Cleophila, and Hero, Hidaſpes in a Bed.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Ask Cupid mercie Madam.

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: O my heart.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Help!

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Stir her:

sp.speaker: Hida.
sp.l: O, O!

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: She's going, wretched woman that we are:
Look to her, and I'll pray the while.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Why Madam? Shee kneels.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Cupid, pardon what is paſt,
And forgive our ſins at laſt,
Then we will be coy no more,
But thy Deity Adore,
Troths at fifteen we will plight,
And will tread a Dance at night.
In the fields, or by the Fire,
With the youths that have deſire.

l.hi: (How does ſhe yet?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: O ill:

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Given Ear-rings we will wear,
Bracelets of our Lovers hair,
Which they on our Arms ſhall twiſt,
With their Names carv'd on our wriſt:
All the money that we owe,
We in Tokens will beſtow:
And learn to write, that when 'tis ſent,
Onely our Loves know what it meant:
O then pardon what is paſt,
And forgive our Sins at laſt.

l.hi: (What, Mends ſhe?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Nothing, you do it not wantonly, you ſhou'd ſing.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Leave, leave, 'tis now too late.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Why?
Shee is dead:

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Her laſt is breathed.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: What ſhall we doe.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Go run,
And tell the Duke; And whilſt I'll cloſe her eyes.
Thus I ſhut thy faded light,
And put it in eternall night.
Where is ſhe can boldly ſay
Though ſhe be as freſh as May:
She ſhall not by this Corps be laid,
Ere to morrows light doe fade.
Let us all now living be,
Warn'd by thy ſtrict Chaſtitie;
And marry all faſt as we can,
Till then we keep a piece of man,
Wrongfully from them that owe it
Soon may every Maid beſtow it. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Who is it?

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Forſooth there's gallant Coach at the dore,
And the brave old man in't, that you ſaid was the Duke.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Cupid, grant he may be taken. Away:

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.p: He is coming up, and looks the ſwaggeringſt, and has ſuch glorious cloaths.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Let all the houſe ſee me ſad, and ſee all handſome.

stage.hi: Enter Leontius, and Timantus, a Jewell and a Ring.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Nay widow flie not back, we come not now to chide, ſtand up and bid me welcome.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: To a poor widows houſe that knows no en • of her ill fortune: your Highneſs is moſt welcome.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Come kiſs me then, this is but manners widow: Nere fling your head aſide, I have more cauſe of grief than you: my Daughters dead: but what? 'Tis nothing. Is the rough French horſe brought to the dore?
They ſay he is a high goer, I ſhall ſoon try his mettle.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: He will be Sir, and the gray Barbary, they are fiery both.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: They are the better: Before the gods I am lightſome, very lightſome: How doeſt thou like me widow?

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: As a perſon in whom all graces are.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Come, come, ye flatter: I'll clap your cheek for that, and you ſhall not be angry.
Haſt no Muſick: Now could I cut three times with eaſe, and do a croſs point, ſhould ſhame all your gallants.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: I do believe you, and your ſelf too:
Lord what a fine old Zany my Love has made him?
'Is mine, I am ſure: Heaven make me thankful for him.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: Tell me how old thou art, my pretty ſweet heart?

sp.speaker: Timantus.
sp.p: Your Grace will not buy her, ſhe may trip Sir?

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.p: My ſorrow ſhowes me elder then I am by many years?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Thou art ſo witty I muſt kiſs agen.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: Indeed her Age lyes not in her mouth: nere look it there Sir, ſhe has a better Regiſter, if it be not burnt.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I will kiſs thee, I am a fire Timantus.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: Can you chuſe Sir, having ſuch heavenly fire before you?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Widow, gueſs why I come, I prethee do,

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.p: I cannot Sir, unleſs you be pleas'd to make a mirth out of my rudeneſs: and that I hope your pity will not let ye, the ſubject is ſo Barren: Bite King, Bite, I'll let you play a while.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Now as I am an honeſt man, I'll tell thee truely, how many foot did I Jump yeſterday Timantus?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: Fourteen of your own, and ſome three fingers.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.p: This fellow lyes as lightly, as if hee were in cut Taffata.
Alas good Almanack get thee to Bed, and tell what weather we ſhall have to morrow.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Widow I am come in ſhort to be a Suiter.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.p: For whom?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Why by my troth, I come to wooe thee wench:
And win thee for my ſelf: Nay, look upon me:
I have about me that will do it.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Now Heaven defend me, your Whore ſhall never: I thank the Gods, I have a little left me to keep me warm, and honeſt: if your grace take not that, I ſeek no more.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I am ſo far from taking any thing, I'll add unto thee.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.l: Such Additions may be for your eaſe Sir,
sp.p: Not my honeſtie: I am well in being ſingle, good Sir ſeek another, I am no meat for money.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Shall I fight for thee?
This ſword ſhall cut his throat, that dars lay claim
But to a Finger of thee, but to a look, I would
See ſuch a fellow.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: It would be but a cold ſight to you:
This is the father of S. George a foot-back,
Can ſuch dry mumming talk.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Before the gods, your grace lookes like Aeneas.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: He looks like his old father upon his back,
Crying to get A boord.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: How ſhall I win thy love, I pray thee tell me? I'll marry thee if thou deſireſt that: That is an honeſt Courſe, I am in good earneſt, and preſently within this hour, am mad for thee: prethee deny me not, For as I live I'll pine thee, but I'll have thee

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Now he's in the Toyl, I'll hold him faſt.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: You do not know what 'tis to be a Queen, Go too you Maid, elſe what the old man falls ſhort of, there's others can eech out, when you pleaſe to call on 'em.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: I underſtand you not, Love I adore thee, Sir, on my knees I give you hearty thanks, for ſo much Honoring your humble Hand-mayd above her birth:
Far more her weak deſervings, I dare not truſt the Envious tongues of all that muſt repine at my unworthy riſing.
Beſide, you have many fair ones in your Kingdome
Porn to ſuch worth: O turn your ſelf about
And make a Noble choice.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: If I do, let me famiſh: I will have thee,
Or break up houſe, and boord here.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Sir, you may command an unwilling woman to obey ye: but heaven knows—

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: No more: theſe half a dozen kiſſes, and this Jewell, and every thing I have, and away with me, and clap it up; and have a boy by morning. Timantus let one be ſent poſt for my ſon again: and for Iſmenus, they are ſcarce twenty miles on their way yet, by that time we'll be married.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.l: There ſhall Sir. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Niſus.
sp.p: Is not this a fine marriage?

sp.speaker: Agenor.
sp.p: Yes, yes, let it alone.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: I, I, the King may marry whom's liſt, let's talk of other matters.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.p: Is the Prince coming home certainly?

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: Yes, yes, he was ſent poſt for yeſterday, lets make haſte we'll ſee how his new Mother-in-law will entertain him.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.p: Why well I warrant you: did you not mark how humbly ſhe carried her ſelf to us on her marriage day, acknowledging her own unworthineſs, and that ſhe would be our ſervant.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: But mark what's done.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.p: Regard not ſhew.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.p: O God! I knew her when I have been off'red her to be brought to my bed for five pounds: whether it could have been perform'd or no, I know not.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.p: Her Daughters a pretty Lady.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: Yes: and having had but mean bringing up, it talks the pretileſt and innocentlieſt, the Queen will be ſo angry to hear her betray her breeding by her language: but I am perſwaded ſh • ' • well diſpos'd.

sp.speaker: Agenor.
sp.p: I think better than her Mother.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.p: Come, we ſtay too long. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: How now man, ſtrook dead with a tale?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: No, but with a truth.

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: Stand off your ſelf: can you endure blows, and ſhrink at words?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: Thou knowſt I have told thee all.

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: But that all's nothing to make you thus: your Siſters dead.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: That's much, but not the moſt.

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: Why, for the other let her marry and hang, 'tis no purpos'd fault of yours: and if your Father will needs • ave your caſt Whore, you ſhall ſhew the duty of a child better in being contented, and bidding much good doe his good old heart with her, than in repining thus at it; let her go: what, there are more wenches man, we'll have another.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: O thou art vain, thou knowſt I doe not love her:
What ſhall I doe? I would my tongue had led me
To any other thing, but blaſphemy,
So I had miſt commending of this woman,
Whom I muſt reverence now: ſhe is my Mother,
My ſin Iſmenus has wrought all this ill:
And I beſeech thee, to be warn'd by me,
And doe not lye, if any man ſhould aske thee
But How thou doſt, or What a clock 'tis now.
Be ſure thou doe not lye, make no excuſe
For him that is moſt near thee: never let
The moſt officious falſehood ſcape thy tongue,
For they above (that are intirely truth)
Will make that ſeed, which thou haſt ſown
Of lyes, • ield miſeries a thouſand fold
Upon thine head, as they have done on mine.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: Sir, your Highneſs is welcome home, the Duke and Queen will preſently come forth to you.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: I'll wait on them.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: Worthy Iſmenus, I pray you, have you ſped in your wars?

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: This Rogue mocks me. Well Timantus, Pray how have you ſped here at whom at ſhovelboord?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: Faith reaſonable. How many Towns have you taken in this Summer?

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: How many Stags have you been at the death of this graſs?

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.p: A number: 'Pray how is the Province ſettled?

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: Prethee how does the dun Nag?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: I think you mock me my Lord.

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: Mock thee? Yes by my troth doe I: why what wouldſt thou have me doe with thee; Art good for any thing elſe?

div.stage: Enter Leontius, Bacha, Dorialus, Agenor, Niſus, Telamon.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: My good Iſmenus, hold me by the wriſt:
And if thou ſee'ſt me fainting, wring me hard,
For I ſhall ſwoon again elſe— Kneels.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Welcome my ſon; riſe, I did ſend for thee
Back from the province, by thy Mothers counſell,
Thy good Mother here, who loves thee well:
She would not let me venture all my joy
Amongſt my enemies: I thank thee for her,
And none but thee. I took her on thy word.

sp.speaker: Leucip.
sp.l: Pinch harder.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: And ſhe ſhall bid thee welcome: I have now
Some near affairs, but I will drink a Health
To thee anon: Come Telamon, I am grown
Luſtier, I thank thee for't, ſince I marryed;
I can ſtand now alone, why Telamon,
And never ſtagger.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Welcome moſt noble Sir, whoſe fame is come
Hither before you: out alas you ſcorn me,
And teach me what to doe.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: No, you are my Mother.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Far unworthy of that name God knows:
But truſt me, here before theſe Lords,
I am no more but Nurſe unto the Duke;
Nor will I breed a faction in the State,
It is too much for me that I am rais'd
Unto his bed, and will remain the ſervant
Of you that did it.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Madam I will ſerve you
As ſhall become me. O diſſembling woman!
Whom I muſt reverence though. Take from thy
Quiver • ure-aim'd Apollo, one of thy ſwift darts,
Headed with thy conſuming golden beams,
And let it melt this body into miſt,
That none may find it.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Shall I beg my Lords
This Room in private for the Prince and me?

div.stage: Exeunt all but Leu. and Bach.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: What will ſhe ſay now?

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.l: I muſt ſtill enjoy him:
Yet there is ſtill left in me a ſpark of woman,
That wiſhes he ſhould move it, bu • he ſtands,
As if he grew there with his eyes on earth,
Sir, you and I when we were laſt together
Kept not this diſtance as we were afraid
Of blaſting by our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Madam 'tis true, Heaven pardon it.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.l: Amen Sir.
You may think that I have done you wrong in this ſtrange marriage.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: 'Tis paſt now.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.l: But it was no fault of mine:
The world had call'd me mad, had I refus'd
The King: nor layd I any train to catch him,
It was your own Oaths did it.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: 'Tis a truth: that takes my ſleep away, but
Would to Heaven, if it had ſo been pleas'd, you had
Refus'd him, though I had gratifi'd that courteſie
With having you my ſelf: But ſince 'tis thus,
I doe beſeech you that you will be honeſt
From henceforth; and not abuſe his credulous Age,
Which you may eaſily doe. As for my ſelf
What I can ſay, you know alas too well
Is ty'd within me, here it will ſit like lead,
But ſhall offend no other, it will pluck me
Back from my ent'rance into any mirth,
As if a ſervant came, and whiſper'd with me
Of ſome friends death, but I will bear my ſelf,
To you, with all the due obedience
A ſon owes to a Mother: more than this,
Is not in me, but I muſt leave the reſt to the
Juſt gods: who in their bleſſed time,
When they have given me puniſhment enough,
For my raſh Sin, will mercifully find
As unexpected means to eaſe my grief
As they did now to bring it.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Grown ſo godly? this muſt not be.
And I will be to you, no other than a natural Mother ought;
And for my honeſty, ſo you will ſwear
Never to urge me, I ſhall keep it ſafe from any other.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Bleſs me I ſhould urge you?

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Nay but ſwear then that I may be at peace,
For I doe feel a weakneſs in my ſelf,
That can denie you nothing, if you tempt me,
I ſhall embrace Sin as it were a friend, and run to meet it.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: If you knew how far
It were from me, you would not urge an Oath.
But for your ſatisfaction, when I tempt you

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Swear not: I cannot move him, this ſad talk
Of things paſt help, does not become us well.
Shall I ſend one for my Muſicians, and we'll dance?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Dance Madam?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Yes, Alaualta.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I cannot dance Madam.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Then lets be merry.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I am as my Fortunes bid me.
Do not you ſee me ſowr?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Yes.
And why think you I ſmile?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I am ſo far from any joy my ſelf,
I cannot fancie a cauſe of mirth.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I'll tell you, we are alone:

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Alone?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: 'Tis true: what then?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: What then? you make my ſmiling now
Break into laughter: what think you is to be done then?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: We ſhou'd pray to Heaven for mercy.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Pray? that were a way indeed
To paſs the time: but I will make you bluſh,
To ſee a baſhfull woman teach a man
What we ſhould doe alone try again
If you can find it out.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I dare not think I underſtand you.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I muſt teach you then; Come, kiſs me.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Kiſs you?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Yes, be not aſham'd:
You did it not your ſelf, I will forgive you.

sp.speaker: Leue.
sp.l: Keep you diſpleas'd gods, the due reſpect
I ought to bear unto this wicked woman,
As ſhe is now my Mother, Haſte within me,
Leſt I add ſins to ſins, till no repentance will cure me.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Leave theſe melancholly moods,
That I may ſwear thee welcome on thy Lipps
A thouſand times.

sp.speaker: Leue.
sp.l: Pray leave this wicked talk,
You doe not know to what my Fathers wrong
May urge me.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I'm careleſs, and doe weigh
The world, my life, and all my after hopes
Nothing without thy Love, miſtake me not:
Thy Love, as I have had it, free and open
As wedlock is, within it ſelf, what ſay you?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Pitty me, behold a Ducheſs
Kneels for thy mercie, and I ſwear to you
Though I ſhould lye with you, it is no Luſt,
For it deſires no change, I could with you
Content my ſelf; what anſwer will you give?

sp.speaker: Leue.
sp.l: They that can anſwer muſt be leſs amaz'd,
Than I am now: you ſee my tears deliver
My meaning to you.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Shall I be contem'd? thou art a beaſt, worſe than a ſavage beaſt,
To let a Lady kneel, to beg that thing
Which a right man would offer.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: 'Tis your will Heaven: but let me hear me like
My ſelf, how ever ſhe does.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Were you made an Eunuch, ſince you went hence?
Yet they have more deſire than I can find in you:
How ſond was I to beg thy love? I'll force thee to my will.
Doſt thou not know that I can make the King
Dote as my liſt? yield quickly, or by Heaven
I'll have thee kept in priſon for my purpoſe,
Where I will make thee ſerve my turn, and have thee fed
With ſuch meats as beſt ſhall ſit my ends
And not thy health, why doſt not ſpeak to me?
And when thou doſt diſpleaſe me, and art grown
Leſs able to perform; then I will have thee
Kill'd and forgotten: Are you ſtriken dumb?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: All you have nam'd but making of me ſin
With you, you may command, but never that;
Say what you will, I'll hear you as becomes me,
If you ſpeak, I will not follow your counſell,
Neither will I tell the world to your diſgrace,
But give you the juſt honor
That is due from me to my Father's wife.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Lord how full of wiſe formality you'r grown
Of late: but you were telling me
You could have wiſht that I had marry'd you,
If you will ſwear ſo yet, I'll make away the King.

sp.speaker: Leue.
sp.l: You are a ſtrumpet.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Nay, I care not
For all your Railings: They will Batter walls
And take in Towns, as ſoon as trouble me:
Tell him, I care not, I ſhall undoe you only, which is no matter.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I appeal to you ſtill, and for ever, that are
And cannot be other, Madam, I ſee 'tis in your power
To work your will on him: And I deſire you
To lay what trains you will for my wiſh'd death,
But ſuffer him to find his quiet grave
In peace, Alas he never did you wrong,
And farther I beſeech you pardon me,
For the ill word I gave you, for how ever
You may deſerve, it became not me
To call you ſo, but paſſion urges me
I know not whither: my heart break now, & eaſe me ever

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Pray yo • g • t you hence
With your goodly humor, I am weary of you extreamely:

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Truſt me, ſo am I of my ſelf too:
Madam, I'll take my leave; gods ſet all right.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Amen, Sir, get you gon;
Am I deny'd? it does not trouble me
That I have mov'd, but that I am refus'd:
I have loſt my patience: I will make him know
Luſt is not Love, for Luſt will find a mate
While there are men, and ſo will I: and more.
Than one, or twenty: yonder is Timantus,
A fellow void of any worth, to raiſe himſelf,
And therefore like to catch at any evil
That will but pluck him up: him will I make
Mine own: Timantus, Timantus. Madam?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt well
Thou wert by chance, a means of this my raiſing:
Brought the Duke to me, and though 'twere but chance
I muſt reward thee.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: I ſhall bend my ſervice unto your Highneſs.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: But do it then entirely, and in everything,
And tell me, couldſt thou now think that thing
Thou wouldſt not do for me?

sp.speaker: Timant.
sp.l: No by my ſoul Madam.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Then thou art right.
Go to my Lodging, and I'll follow thee.
With my inſtruction I do ſee already,
This Prince that did but now contemn me, dead:
Yet will I never ſpeak an evil word
Unto his Father of him, till I have won
A belief, I love him, but I'll make
His virtues his undoing, and my praiſes
Shall be ſo many ſwords againſt his breaſt,
Which once perform'd, I'll make Ʋrania
My Daughter, the Kings heir, and plant my iſſue
In this large Throne: nor ſhall it be withſtood,
They that begin in Luſt, muſt end in Blood. Exit.

sp.speaker: Doria.
sp.l: We live to know a fine time, Gentl.

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: And a fine Duke, that through his doting age
Suffers him to be a child again
Under his Wives tuition.

sp.speaker: Agen.
sp.l: All the Land holds in that tenor too: in womans ſervice? ſure we ſhall learn to ſpinn.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.l: No, that's too honeſt: we ſhall have other
Liberal Sciences taught us too ſoon;
Lying, and flattering, thoſe are the ſtudies now:
And Murther ſhortly I know, will be humanity, Gent.
If we live here we muſt be knaves, believe it.

sp.speaker: Niſus.
sp.l: I cannot tell my Lord Dorialus, though my
Own nature hate it, if all determine to be knaves,
I'll try what I can do upon my ſelf: that's certain,
I will not have my throat cut for my goodneſs,
The virtue will not quit the pain.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: But pray you tell me,
Why is the Prince now ripe and full experient,
Not made a dore in the State?

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.l: Becauſe he is honeſt.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: Goodneſs attend your Honors.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: You muſt not be amongſt us then.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: The Dutcheſs, whoſe humble ſervant I am proud to be, would ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.p: Sir, we are pleas'd to wait: when is it?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: An hour hence my good Lords, and ſo I leave my ſervice.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: This is one of her Ferrets that ſhe bolts buſineſs out withall: this fellow, if he were well ript, has all the linings of a knave within him: how ſlye he looks?

sp.speaker: Niſ.
sp.p: Have we nothing about our cloaths that he may catch at?

sp.speaker: Agenor.
sp.p: O my conſcience, there's no treaſon in my dublet, it there be, my elbows will diſcover it, they are out.

sp.speaker: Dor.
sp.p: Faith, and all the harm that I can find in mine is, that they are not pay'd for; let him make what he can of that, ſo he diſcharge that. Come, let's go.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: And you ſhall find Sir what bleſſing heaven gave you in ſuch a ſon.

sp.speaker: Le.
sp.p: Pray gods, I may, Let's walk & change our ſubject.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: O Sir, can anything come ſweeter to you, or ſtrike a deeper joy into your heart than your ſon's virtue?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I allow his virtues: but 'tis not handſome thus to feed my ſelf with ſuch moderate praiſes of mine own.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: The ſubject of our comendations is it ſelf grown ſo infinite in goodneſs, that all the glory we can lay upon it, though we ſhould open volumes of his praiſes, is a mere modeſty in his expreſſion, and ſhews him lame ſtill, like an ill wrought peece wanting proportion.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: Yet ſtill he is a man, and ſubject ſtill to more inordinate vices, than our love can give him bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.p: Elſe he were a god. yet ſo near as he is, he comes to heaven, that we may ſee ſo far as fleſh can point us things only worthy them, and only theſe in all his actions.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: This is too much my Queen.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: Had the gods, lov'd me; that my unworthy womb had bred this brave man.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Still you run wrong.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: I would have liv'd upon the comfort of him, fed on his growing hopes.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: This touches me.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: I know no friends, nor Being, but his virtues.

sp.speaker: Le.
sp.p: You have laid out words enough upon a ſubject.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: But words cannot expreſs him Sir: why what a ſhape Heaven has conceiv'd him in, oh Nature made him up!

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I wonder Dutcheſs.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: So you muſt: for leſs than admiration loſes this god-like man.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Have you done with him?

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: Done with? O good gods, what frailties thus paſs by us without reverence?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I ſee no ſuch perfection.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: O dear Sir: you are a father, and thoſe joys
To you, ſpeak in your heart, not in your tongue.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: This leaves a taſt behind it worſe than phyſick.

sp.speaker: Baca.
sp.l: Then for all his wiſdome, valour,
Good fortune, and all thoſe friends of honor,
They are in him as free and natural, as paſſions
In a Woman.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: You make me bluſh at all theſe years
To ſee how blindly you have flung your praiſes
Upon a Boy, a very child, and worthleſs,
Whilſt I live, of theſe Honors.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I would not have my love Sir, make my tongue
Shew me ſo much a woman: as to praiſe
Or diſpraiſe, where my will is, without reaſon,
Or generall allowance of the people.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Allowance of the people, what allow they!

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: All, I have ſed for truth, and they muſt do it,
And do at upon him: love him, and admire him.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: How's that?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: For in this youth and noble forwardneſs
All things are bound together that are kingly,
A fitneſs to bear rule:

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: No more.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: And Sovereignty not made to know command.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I have ſed, no more.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I have done Sir, though unwilling, and pardon me.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I do, not a word more.

sp.speaker: Baca.
sp.l: I have gi'n thee poyſon
Of more infection than the Dragons tooth,
Or the groſs Air o'er heated.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Timantus when ſaw you the Prince?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: I left him now Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Tell me truely, out of your free opinion without courting. How you like him.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: How I like him?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Yes: for you in converſation may ſee more Than a Father.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: It works.

sp.speaker: Timantus.
sp.l: Your Grace has choſen out an ill obſerver.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Yes, I mean of his ill: you talk rightly.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: But you take me wrong; All I know by him
I dare deliver boldly: He is the ſtore-houſe
And head of virtue; your great ſelf excepted,
That feeds the Kingdome.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Theſe are flatteries: ſpeak me his vices, there you do a ſervice worth a Fathers thanks.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: Sir, I cannot. If there be any, ſure they are the times which I could wiſh leſs dangerous.
But pardon me, I am too bold.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: You are not, forward and open what theſe dangers are.

sp.speaker: Timan.
sp.p: Nay, good Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Nay, fall not off again, I will have all.

sp.speaker: Timan.
sp.l: Alas Sir, what am I, you ſhould believe
My eyes or ears, ſo ſubtle to obſerve
Faults in a State: all my main buſineſs
Is ſervice to your Grace, and neceſſaries
For my poor life.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Do not diſpleaſe me Sirrah,
But that you know tell me, and preſently.

sp.speaker: Timan.
sp.l: Since your Grace will have it
I'll ſpeak it freely: Alwayes my obedience
And love preſerv'd unto the Prince.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Prethee to the matter.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: For Sir, if you conſider
How like a Sun in all his great employments,
How full of heat.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Make me underſtand what I deſire.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: And then at his return.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Do not anger me.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Then thus Sir: All miſlike ye,
As they would do the gods, if they did dwell with 'em.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Talke and prate, as their ignorant rages
Leads 'em without Alleageance or Religion.
For Heavens ſake have a care of your own perſon:
I cannot tell, their wickedneſs may lead
Farther than I dare think yet.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: O baſe people.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Yet the Prince, for whom this is pretended may
Perſuade 'em, and no doubt will: virtue is ever watchfull,
But be you ſtill ſecur'd and comforted.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Heaven how have I offended, that this rod
So heavy and unnaturall, ſhould fall upon me
When I am old and helpleſs.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Brave Gentl. that ſuch a madding love ſhould follow thee, to rob thee of a Father:
All the Court is full of dangerous whiſpers.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I perceive it, and 'ſpight of all their ſtrengths will make my ſafety: I'll cut him ſhorter.
sp.l: I'll cut him ſhorter firſt, then let him rule.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: What a foul Age is this, when Virtue is made a ſword to ſmite the virtuous? Alas, alas:

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I'll teach him to fly lower.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: By no means Sir, rather, make more your love,
And hold your favor to him: for 'tis now
Impoſſible to yoke him, if his thoughts,
As I muſt ne'er believe, run with their rages,
He never was ſo innocent, but what reaſon
His Grace has to withdraw his love from me,
And other good men that are near your perſon,
I cannot yet find out: I know my duty
Has ever been attending.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: 'Tis too plain: He means to play the villain,
I'll prevent him, not a word more of this, be private.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Madam 'tis done.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: He cannot eſcape me. Have you ſpoken with the noble men?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Yes Madam they are here: I wait a farther ſervice.

sp.speaker: Bac,
sp.l: Till yet be the Prince, you need no more inſtructions.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: No, I have it. Exit Timantus.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: That fool that willingly provoks a woman,
Has made himſelf another evill Angell,
And a new Hell, to which all other torments
Are but mere paſtime: Now my noble Lords,
You muſt excuſe me, that unmannerly
We have broke your private buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Agen.
sp.l: Your good Grace may command us, and that.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Faith my Lord Agenor: 'Tis ſo good a cauſe
I am confident, you cannot looſe by it.

sp.speaker: Dorialus.
sp.l: Which way does ſhe fiſh now?
The devill is but a fool to a right woman.

sp.speaker: Niſus.
sp.p: Madam, we muſt needs win in doing ſervice to ſuch a gracious Lady.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I thank you, and will let you know the buſineſs:
So I may have your helps, never be doubtfull,
For 'tis ſo juſt a cauſe, and will to you
Upon the knowledge ſeem ſo honorable,
That I aſſure my ſelf your willing hearts
Will ſtrait be for me in it.

sp.speaker: Age.
sp.l: If ſhe ſhould prove good now, what wer't like?

sp.speaker: Dorial.
sp.l: Thunder in Ianuarie, or a good woman,
That's ſtranger than all Affrick.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: It ſhall not need your wonder, this it is:
The Duke you know is old, and rather ſubject
To eaſe and prayers now, than all thoſe troubles,
Cares, and continuall watchings, that attend
A • Kingdomes ſafety, therefore to prevent
The fall of ſuch a flouriſhing Eſtate
As this has been, and to put off
The murmure of the people that encreaſe
Againſt my government, which the gods knows
I onely feel the trouble of: I preſent
The Prince unto your loves, a Gent.
In whom all Excellencies are knit together,
All peeces of a true man, let your prayers
Win from the Duke half his Vexation,
That he may undertake it, whoſe diſcretion
I muſt confeſs, though it be from the Father,
Yet now is ſtronger, and more apt to govern.
'Tis not my own deſire, but all the Lands,
I know the weakeneſs of it.

sp.speaker: Niſus.
sp.l: Madam, this noble care and love has won us
For ever to your lives, we'll to the King,
And ſince your Grace has put it in our mouths,
We'll win him with the cunning'ſt words we can.

sp.speaker: Dorial.
sp.l: I was never couſen'd in a woman before:
For commonly they are like Apples: If once they bruiſe
sp.p: They will grow rotten thorow, and ſerve for nothing but to aſſwage ſwellings.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Good Lords delay no time, ſince 'tis your good
Pleaſures to think my counſell good, and by no means
Let the Prince know it, whoſe affections
Will ſtir mainly againſt it: beſides his Father
May hold him dangerous, if it be not carried
So that his forward will appear not in it,
Go, and be happy.

sp.speaker: Dorial.
sp.l: Well, I would not be Chronicl'd as thou
Wilt be for a good woman, for all the world.

sp.speaker: Niſus.
sp.l: Madam, we kiſs your hand, and ſo inſpire.
Nothing but happineſs can crown our prayers. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: ANd thus ſhe has us'd me, is't not a good mother?

sp.speaker: Iſmenus.
sp.l: Why kill'd you her not?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: The gods forbid it.

sp.speaker: Iſmenus.
sp.l: S'light, if all the women i'th' world were barren, ſhee had dy'd.

sp.speaker: Leuc.
sp.l: But 'tis not reaſon directs thee thus.

sp.speaker: Iſmen.
sp.l: Then have I none at all, for all I have in me
Directs me: Your Father's in a pretty rage.

sp.speaker: Leucippus.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Iſmenus.
sp.p: Nay, 'tis well, if he know himſelf, but ſome of the Nobility have deliver'd a petition to him: what's in't, I know not, but it has put him to his trumps: he has taken a months time to anſwer it, and chafes like himſelf.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: He's here Iſmenus..

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Set me down Tellamon. Leucippus.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: Nay good Sir, be at peace, I dare ſwear he knows not of it.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: You are fooliſh: peace.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.p: All will go ill, deny it boldly Sir, truſt me he cannot prove it by you.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.l: You'll make all worſe too with your facing it.

sp.speaker: Leuc.
sp.l: What is the matter?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Know'ſt thou that petition?
Look on it well: wouldſt thou be joyn'd with me
(Unnaturall child to be weary of me)
E'r Fate eſteem me ſit for other worlds.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: May be he knows not of it.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Oh ſtrange carriages!
Sir, as I have hope that there is any thing
To reward doing well, my uſages
Which have been (but 'tis no matter what)
Have put me ſo far from the thought of Greatneſs,
That I ſhould welcome it like a diſeaſe
That grew upon me, and I could not cure.
They are my enemies that gave you this,
And yet they call me friend, and are themſelves
I fear abus'd. I am weary of my life,
For Gods ſake take it from me: it creates
More miſchief in the State than it is worth,
The uſage I have had, I know would make
Wiſdom her ſelf run frantick through the ſtreets,
And Patience quarrel with her ſhadow.
Sir, this ſword—

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Alas! help for the love of Heaven,
Make way through me firſt, for he is your Father.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: What, would he kill me?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: No Sir, no.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Thou always makes mak'ſt the beſt on't, but I ſear—

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Why do you uſe me thus? who is't can think
That I would kill my Father, that can yet
Forbear to kill you? Here Sir, is my ſword;
I dare not touch it, leſt ſhe ſay again
I would have kill'd you: let me not have mercy
When I moſt need it, if I would not change
Place with my meaneſt ſervant. Let theſe faults
Be mended Madam: if you ſaw how ill
They did become you, you would part with them.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: I told the Duke as much before.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: What? what did you tell him?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: That it was only an ambition,
Nurſt in you by your youth, provok'd you thus,
Which age would take away.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: It was his doing then? come hither Love.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: No indeed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: How am I made, that I can bear all this?
If any one had us'd a friend of mine ne'r this,
My hand had carried death about it.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Lead me hence Tellamon: come my dear
Bacha, I ſhall find time for this.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Madam, you know I dare not ſpeak before
The King; but you know well, if not, I'll tell you,
You are the moſt wicked'ſt, and moſt murderous
Strumpet, that ever was call'd Woman.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: My Lord, what can I do for him? he ſhall command me.

sp.speaker: Leon,
sp.l: I know thou art too kind; away I ſay.

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.l: Sir, I am ſure we dream, this cannot be.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Oh that we did, my wickedneſs has brought
All this to paſs, elſe I ſhould bear my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Iſme.
sp.p: Look, doe you ſee who's there? your virtuous Mothers iſſue: kill her, yet take ſome little pidling revenge.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: Away, the whole Court calls her virtuous; for they ſay, ſhe is unlike her Mother, and if ſo, ſhe can have no vice.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I'll truſt none of 'em that come of ſuch a breed.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: But I have found
A kind of love in her to me: alas,
Think of her death! I dare be ſworn for her,
She is as free from any hate to me
As her bad Mother's full. She was brought up
I'th' Countrey, as her tongue will let you know.
If you but talk with her, with a poor Uncle,
Such as her Mother had.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: She's come again.

sp.speaker: Ʋra.
sp.p: I would • ene ſpeak to the good Marqueſs my brother, if I but thought he could abaid me.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Siſter, how do you?

sp.speaker: Ʋra.
sp.l: Very well I thank you.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: How does your good Mother?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: Fie, fie, Iſmenus for ſhame, mock ſuch an innocent ſoul as this.

sp.speaker: Ʋra.
sp.l: Feth a ſhe be no good, god may her ſo.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: I know you wiſh it with your heart dear Siſter, but ſhe is good I hope.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Are you ſo ſimple, to make ſo much of this?
Do you not know,
That all her wicked Mother labours for, is but to raiſe
Her to your right, and leave her this Dukedom?

sp.speaker: Ʋra.
sp.l: I, but ne'r Sir be afred,
For though ſhe take th' ungain'ſt weas ſhe can,
I'll ne'er ha't fro' you.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I ſhould hate my ſelf Iſmenus;
If I ſhould think of her ſimplicity,
Ought but extreamly well.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Nay, as you will

sp.speaker: Ʋra.
sp.l: And though ſhe be my Mother,
If ſhe take any caurſe to do you wrong,
If I can ſee't, youſt quickly hear on't Sir:
And ſo I'll take my leave.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Farewel good Siſter, I thank you.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: You believe all this.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Yes.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: A good faith doth well, but methinks
It were no hard matter now, for her Mother to ſend her
Yonder's one you may truſt if you will too.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: So I wi • l, if he can ſhew me as apparent ſigns
Of truth as ſhe did; Does he weep Iſmenus?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.p: Yes, I think ſo: ſome good's happen'd I warrant: Do you hear, you? What honeſt man has ſcap'd miſery, that thou art crying thus?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Noble Iſmenus, where's the Prince?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Why there? haſt wept thine eyes out?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Sir, I beſeech you hear me.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Well, ſpeak on.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Why, will you hear him?

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Yes Iſmenus, why?

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: I would hear blaſphemy as willingly.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: You are too blame.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: No Sir: he is not to blame:
If I were as I was.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Nor as thou art, yſaith awhit too blame,

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: What's your buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Faith Sir, I am aſhamed to ſpeak before you,
My conſcience tells me I have injur'd you,
And by the earneſt inſtigation
Of others, have not done you to the King
Always the beſt and friendlieſt oſtices;
Which pardon me, or I will never ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Never pardon him and ſilence a knave.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: I pardon thee.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Your Mother ſure is naught.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Why ſhouldſt thou think ſo?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Oh noble, Sir, your honeſt eyes perceive not
The dangers you are led to; ſhame upon her,
And what fell miſeries the gods can think on
Shower down upon her wicked head, ſhe has plotted
I know too well your death: would my poor life
Or thouſand ſuch as mine is, might be offer'd
Like ſacrifices up for your preſerving,
What free oblations would ſhe have to glut her,
But ſhe is mercileſs, and bent to ruin;
If heaven and good men ſtep not to your reſcue,
And timely, very timely: Oh this Dukedom!
I weep, I weep for the poor Orphans i'th' Countrey
Left with but Friends or Parents.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Now Iſmenus, what think you of this fellow?
This was a lying knave, a flatterer,
Does not this Love ſtill ſhew him ſo.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: This Love? this Halter: if he prove not yet
The cunning'ſt rankeſt rogue that ever Canted,
I'll never ſee man again: I know him to bring,
And can interpret every new face he makes;
Look how he wrings like a good ſtool for a tear:
Take heed, Children and Fools
Firſt feel the ſmart, Then weep.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Away, away, ſuch an unkind diſtruſt,
Is worſe than a diſſembling, if it be one,
And ſooner leads to miſchief, I believe it,
And him an honeſt man: he could not carry
Under an evil cauſe, ſo true a ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Take heed, this is your Mothers ſcorpion,
That carries ſtings even in his tears,
Whoſe ſoul is a rank poiſon through: Touch
Not at him, if you do, you are gone, if you had twenty
Lives: I knew him for a Roguiſh boy, when
He would poiſon Dogs, and keep tame Toads,
He lay with his Mother, and infected her, and now
She begs i'th' Hoſpital, with a patch of Velvet,
Where her Noſe ſtood: like the Queen of Spades.
And all her teeth in her purſe, the Devil and this
Fellow are ſo near, 'Tis not yet known which is the eviler Angel.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Nay, then I ſee 'tis ſpite: Come hither friend.
sp.p: Haſt thou not heard the cauſe yet that incens'd my Mother to my death, for I proteſt I feel none in my ſelf?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Her Will Sir, and Ambition, as I think,
Are the provokers of it, as in Women,
Thoſe two are ever powerful to deſtruction,
Beſide a hate of your ſtill growing virtues,
She being only wicked.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Heavens defend me as I am innocent,
And ever have been from all immoderate thoughts and
Actions, that carry ſuch rewards along with 'em.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Sir, all I know, my duty muſt reveal,
My Countrey and my Love command it from me,
For whom I'll lay my life down: this night coming,
A Counſel is appointed by the Duke,
To ſit about your apprehenſion:
If you dare truſt my faith: which by all good things
Shall ever watch about you: goe along,
And to a place I'll guide you: where no word
Shall ſcape without your hearing, nor no plot.
sp.p: Without diſcovering to you, which once known, you have your anſwers and prevention.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.p: You are not ſo mad to goe; ſhift off this fellow, you ſhall be rul'd once by a wiſe man: Ratsbane get you gone, or—

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: Peace, peace for ſhame, thy love is too ſuſpitious, 'tis a way offer'd to preſerve my life, and I will take it: be my Guide Timantus, and do not mind this angry man, thou know'ſt him: I may live to requite thee.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.p: Sir, this ſervice is done for virtues ſake, not for reward, however he may hold me.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.p: The great pox on you: but thou haſt that curſe ſo much, 'twill grow a bleſſing in thee ſhortly. Sir, for wiſdoms ſake court not your death, I am your friend and ſubject, and I ſhall loſe in both: if I lov'd you not, I would laugh at you, and ſee you run your neck into the nooſe, and cry a Woodcock.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.p: So much of man, and ſo much fearful; • ie, prethee have peace within thee: I ſhall live yet many a golden day to hold thee here deareſt and neareſt to me: Go on Timantus, I charge you by your love • o •• re, • o more.

sp.speaker: Iſm.
sp.l: Goe, and let your own rod whip you:
I pity you. And dog, if he miſcarry thou ſhalt pay for't,
I'll ſtudy for thy puniſhment, and it ſhall laſt
Longer and ſharper than a tedious Winter,
Till thou blaſ • hem'ſt, and then thou dieſt and damn'ſt.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I wonder the Dutcheſs comes not.

sp.speaker: Tel.
sp.l: She has heard, Sir, your Will to ſpeak with her:
But there is ſomething leaden at her heart;
(Pray God it be not mortal) that even keeps her
From converſation with her ſelf.

sp.speaker: B.
sp.l: Oh whither will you my croſs affections pull me?
Fortune, Fate, and you whoſe powers direct our actions,
And dwell within us: you that are Angels
Guiding to virtue, wherefore have you given
So ſtrong a hand to evil? wherefore ſuffer'd
A Temple of your own, you Deities
Where your fair ſelves dwelt only, and your goodneſs
Thus to be ſoyl'd with ſin?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Heaven bleſs us all.
From whence comes this diſtemper? ſpeak my fair one.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: And have you none, Love and Obedience,
You ever faithful Servants to imploy
In this ſtrange ſtory of impiety,
But me a Mother; Muſt I be your ſtrumpet?
To lay black Treaſon upon, and in him,
In whom all ſweetneſs was: in whom my love
Was prov'd to have a Being, in whom Juſtice,
And all the gods for our imaginations
Can work into a man, were more than virtues,
Ambition down to hell, where thou wert foſter'd,
Thou haſt poiſon'd the beſt ſoul, the pureſt, whiteſt,
And meereſt innocent'ſt it ſelf that ever
Mens greedy hopes gave life to.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: This is ſtill ſtranger: lay this treaſon
Open to my correction.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Oh what a combat duty and affection
Breeds in my blood!

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: If thou conceal'ſt him, may,
Beſide my death, the curſes of the Countrey,
Troubles of conſcience, and a wretched end,
Bring thee unto a poor forgotten grave.

sp.speaker: Bach.
sp.l: My Being▪ for another tongue to tell it,
Ceaſe, a Mother! ſome good man that dares
Speak for his King and Countrey: I am full
Of too much womans pity: yet oh Heaven,
Since it concerns the ſafety of my Sovereign,
Let it not be a cruelty in me,
Nor draw a Mothers name in queſtion,
Amongſt unborn people, to give up that man
To Law and Juſtice, that unrighteouſly
Has ſought his Fathers death: be deaf: be deaf Sir,
Your Son is the offender: Now have you all,
Would I might never ſpeak again.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: My Son! Heaven help me.
No more! I thought it, and ſince
His life is grown ſo dangerous: Let them that
Gave him, take him: he ſhall dye,
And with him all my fears.

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Oh uſe your mercy: you have a brave ſubject
To beſtow it on. I'll forgive him, Sir; and for his
Wrong to me, I'll be before ye.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Durſt his villany extend to thee?

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: Nothing but heats of youth, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Upon my life he ſought my bed.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: I muſt confeſs he loved me
Somewhat beyond a Son: and ſtill purſu'd it
With ſuch a Luſt, I will not ſay Ambition:
That clean forgetting all obedience,
And only following his firſt heat unto me,
He hotly ſought your death, and me in Marriage.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Oh Villain!

sp.speaker: Bac.
sp.l: But I forget all: and am half aſham'd
To preſs a man ſo far.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Where is the Duke? for Gods ſake bring me to him:

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Here I am: each corner of the Dukedom
Sends new affrights forth: what wouldſt thou? ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: I cannot Sir, my fear ties up my tongue:

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter? Take thy courage
To thee, and boldly ſpeak, where are the Guard?
In the gods name, out with it:

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Treaſon, treaſon.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: In whom?

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Double the Guard.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: There is a fellow, Sir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Leave ſhaking man.

sp.speaker: Timan.
sp.l: 'Tis not for fear, but wonder.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Well.

sp.speaker: Timan.
sp.l: There is a fellow, Sir, cloſe i'th' Lobby:
You o'the Guard, look to the door there.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: But let me know the buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Tima.
sp.l: Oh that the hearts of men ſhould be ſo hard'ned
Againſt ſo good a Duke, for Gods ſake, Sir,
Seek means to ſave your ſelf; This wretched ſlave
Has his ſword in his hand, I know his heart:
Oh it hath almoſt kill'd me with the thought of it.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Where is he?

div.stage: Enter the Guard, and bring him in.

sp.speaker: Timan.
sp.l: I'th' Lobby Sir, cloſe in a corner:
Look to your ſelves for Heavens ſake,
Me thinks he is here already.
Fellows of the Guard be valiant.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Goe Sirs, and apprehend him; Treaſon ſhall
Never dare me in mine own Gates.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: 'Tis done.

div.stage: There they bring the Prince in.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: And thou ſhalt find it to thy beſt content.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Are theſe the comforts of my age?
They're happy that end their daies contented
With a little, and live aloof from dangers, to a King
Every content doth a new peril bring.
Oh let me live no longer, ſhame of Nature,
Baſtard to Honor: Traytor, Murderer,
Devil in a humane ſhape. Away with him,
He ſhall not breathe, his hot affection here.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Sir, hear me.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Am I or he your Duke? away with him
To a cloſe priſon: your Highneſs now ſhall know,
Such branches muſt be cropt before they grow.

sp.speaker: Leu.
sp.l: Whatever fortune comes, I bid it welcome,
My innocency is my Armor: gods preſerve you.

sp.speaker: Bacha.
sp.l: Fare thee well, I ſhall never ſee ſo brave a Gent.
Would I could weep out his offences.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Or I could weep out mine eyes.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Come Gentlemen, we'll determine preſently
About his death: we cannot be too forward in our
Safety: I am very ſick, lead me unto my bed. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.l: Sir. ah, goe fetch my Fox from the Cutlers:
sp.p: There's money for the ſcowring: Tell him I ſtop a groat ſ • nce the laſt great Muſter: he had in ſtone Pitch for the bruiſe: he took with the recoyling of his Gun.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: And do you hear? when you come, Take down my Buckler, and ſweep the Cobwebs oſt: and grind the pick out, and fetch a Nail or two: and ta • k on bracers: your Miſtriſs made a pot-lid ont't,
I thank her, at her Mans Wedding, and burnt off the Handle.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I will Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Cit.
sp.p: Who's within here, hoe Neighbor, not ſtir • ng yet?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Oh, good morrow, good morrow: what news, what news?

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: It holds, he dies this morning.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Then happy man be his fortune, I am reſolv'd.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: And ſo am I, and forty more good fellows,
That will not give their heads for the wa • hing, I • a • e it.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: 'S •• ot man, who would not hang in ſuch good company, and ſuch a cauſe? A Fire, a Wife and Children; 'Tis ſuch a jeſt that men ſhould look b • hind 'em to the world: and let their honors, their honors neighbor ſlip.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: I'll give thee a pint of Baſtard and a Roll for that bare word.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: They ſay, that we Tailors, are things that • ay one another, and our Geeſe hatch us: I'll make ſome of'em feel they are Geeſe o'th' game then.
sp.l: I'ſack, take down my Bill, 'tis ten to one I uſe it. Take a good heart man, all the low ward is ours, with a wet finger.
An lay my • ut-ſing'red Gautlet ready for me,
That, that I us'd to work in, when the Gentl • were
Up againſt us, and beaten out of Town, and almoſt out o'
Debt too: for a plague on 'em they never paid we • l ſince:
And take heed ſirrah, your Miſtriſs hears not of this
Buſineſs, ſhe's near her time: yet if ſhe do,
I care not, ſhe may long for Rebellion,
For ſhe has a deviliſh ſpirit.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Come, let's call up the new • remonger, he's as tough as ſteel, and has a ſine wit in theſe reſurrections; Are you ſtirring neighbor?

sp.speaker: 3. Within.
sp.l: Oh, Good morrow neighbors,
I'll come to you preſently.
Goe to, this is his Mothers doing; ſhe's a P • lecat.
As any is in the world.

sp.p: Then ſay, I have hit it, and a vengeance on her, let her be what ſhe will.
Amen ſay I, ſhe has brought things to a fine paſs with her wiſdom: do you mark it?

One thing I am ſure ſhe has, the good old Duke, ſhe gives him pap again they ſay, and dandles him, and hangs a corral and bells about his neck, and makes him believe his teeth will come agen; which if they did, and I he, I would worry her as never Curr was worried: I would neighbor, till my teeth met I know where, but that's counſel.
Good morrow neighbors: hear you the ſad news?
Yes, would we knew as well how to prevent it.
I cannot tell, methinks 'twere no great matter, if men were men: but—
You do not twit me with my calling neighbo • ?
No ſurely: for I know your ſpirit to be tall; pray be not vext.
Pray forward with your counſel:
I am what I am, and they that prove me ſhall find me to their coſt: do you mark me neighbor, to their coſt I ſay.
Nay, look how ſoon you are angry?
They ſhall neighbors: yes, I ſay they ſhall.
I do believe they ſhall.
I know they ſhall.

sp.l: Whether you do or no I care not two pence,
I am no beaſt, I know mine own ſtrength neighbors;
God bleſs the King, your companies is fair.

sp.p: Nay neighbor, now ye erre, now I muſt tell you ſo, and ye are twenty Neighbors.
You had beſt goe peach, doe, peach.
Peach; I ſcorn the motion.
Doe, and ſee what follows: I'll ſpend an hundred pound, and be two I care not: but I'll undoe thee.
Peach, Oh diſgrace! Peach in thy face, and doe the worſt thou canſt: I am a true-man, and a free-man: peach!
Nay, look, you will ſpoil all.
Peach!
Whilſt you two brawl together, the Prince will loſe his life.
Come, give me your hand, I love you well, are you for the action?
Yes: but Peach provokes me, 'tis a cold fruit, I feel it cold in my ſtomach ſtill.
No more, I'll give you Cake to diſgeſt it.

Shut up my ſho • , and be ready at a call boys, and one of you run over my old tuck with a few aſhes, 'tis grown odious with toſting Cheeſe: and burn a little Juniper in my Murrin, the Maid made it her Chamber-pot: an hour hence I'll come again; and as you hear from me, ſend me a clean ſhirt.
The Chandler by thy Wharf, and it be thy Will.
Goſſip, good morrow.
Oh good morrow Goſſip: good morrow all, I ſee ye of one mind you cleave ſo cloſe together: come 'tis time, I have prepared an hundred if they ſtand.
'Tis well done: ſhall we ſever, and about it?
Firſt, let's to the Tavern, and a pint a piece will make us Dragons.
