May periſh in this miſchief, who moves ſlow to't.
Shall add unto the flame.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: What mean you? give me your private hearing.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Perſwaſion is a partner in the crime,
I will renounce my claim unto a mother,
If you make offer on't.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: E'er a Torch can take flame, I will produce
The author of the fact.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Withdraw but for your Lights.

sp.speaker: Memb.
sp.l: Oh my too true ſuſpition.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Speak, where's the Engine to this horrid act?

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Here you do behold her; upon whom make good
Your cauſeleſs rage; the deed was done by my incitement,
Not yet repented.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Whether did nature ſtart, when you conceiv'd?
A birth ſo unlike woman? ſay, what part
Did not conſent to make a ſon of him,
Reſerv'd it ſelf within you to his ruine.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Ha, ha, a ſon of mine! doe not diſſever
Thy fathers duſt, ſhaking his quiet urn,
To which my breath would ſend ſo foul an iſſue.
My Son, thy Brother?

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Was not Theodoret my brother, or is thy tongue
Confederate with thy heart, to ſpeak and do
Only things monſtrous?

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Hear me and thou ſhalt make thine own belief,
Thy, ſtill with ſorrow mention'd, father liv'd
Three careful years, in hope of wiſhed heirs,
When I conceiv'd, being from his jealous fear
Injoyn'd to quiet home, one fatal day
Tranſported with my pleaſure to the chaſe,
I forc'd command, and in purſuit of game
Fell from my horſe, loſt both my child and hopes.
Deſpair which only in his love ſaw life
Worthy of being, from a Gard'ners Arms
Snatcht this unlucky brat, and call'd it mine,
When the next year repaid my loſs with thee:
But in thy wrongs preſerv'd my miſery,
Which that I might diminiſh, though not end,
My ſighs, and wet eies from thy Fathers Will,
Bequeath this largeſt part of his Dominions
Of France unto thee, and only left
Auſtracia unto that changling, whoſe life affords
Too much of ill 'gainſt me to prove my words,
And call him ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Come, doe not weep, I muſt, nay do believe you.
And in my fathers ſatisfaction count it
Merit, not wrong, or loſs:

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: You doe but flatter, there's anger yet flames
In your eyes.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: See, I will quench it, and confeſs that you
Have ſuffer'd double travel for me.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: You will not fire the houſe then?

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Rather reward the author who gave cauſe
Of knowing ſuch a ſecret, my oath and duty
Shall be aſſurance on't.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Protaldye, riſe good faithful ſervant, heaven knows.
How hardly he was drawn to this attempt.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Protaldye? he had a Gard'ners face I'll ſwear:
Tell by thy hand, Sir, we doe owe unto you for this ſervice.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Why lookeſt thou ſo dejected?

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.l: I want a little ſhift, Lady, nothing elſe.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: The fires are ready, pleaſe it your grace withdraw,
Whilſt we perform your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Reſerve them for the body; ſince he had the fate
To live and die a Prince, he ſhall not loſe
The Title in his Funeral. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: His fate to live a Prince,
Thou old impiety, made up by luſt and miſchief,
Take up the body. Exeunt with the body of Theod.

sp.speaker: Lecu.
sp.l: Doſt think Leforte's ſure enough?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: As bonds can make him, I have turn'd his eyes to the Eaſt; and left him gaping after the Morning ſtar, his head is a meer Aſtrolobe, his eyes ſtand for the Poles, the gag in his mouth being the Coachman, his five teeth have the neareſt reſemblance to Charles Wain.

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.p: Thou haſt caſt a figure which ſhall raiſe thee, direct my hair a little: and in my likeneſs to him, read a fortune ſuiting thy largeſt hopes.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: You are ſo far'bove likeneſs, you are the ſame,
If you love mirth, perſwade him from himſelf.
'Tis but an Aſtronomer out of the way,
And lying, will bear the better place for't

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: I have profitable uſe in hand, haſte to the Queen
And tell her how you left me chang'd.
Who would not ſerve this virtuous active Queen?
She that loves miſchief'bove the man that does it,
And him above her pleaſure, yet knows no heaven elſe.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: How well this loans ſuits the Art I ſeek,
Diſcovering ſecret, and ſucceeding Fate,
Knowledge that puts all lower happineſs on,
With a remiſs and careleſs hand,
Fair peace unto your meditations, father.

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: The ſame to you, you bring, Sir.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Drawn by your much fam'd skill. I come to know
Whether the man who owes his character,
Shall e'er have iſſue.

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: A reſolution falling with moſt eaſe,
Of any doubt you could have nam'd, he is a Prince
Whoſe fortune you enquire.

sp.speaker: Thie.
sp.l: He is nobly born.

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: He had a Dukedom lately fall'n unto him,
By one, call'd Brother, who has left a Daughter.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: The queſtion is, of Heirs, not Lands.

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: Heirs, yes, he ſhall have Heirs.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Begotten of his body, why look'ſt thou p • le?
Thou canſt not ſuffer in his want.

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: Nor thou, I neither can nor will
Give farther knowledge to thee.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Thou muſt, I am the man my ſelf,
Thy Sovereign, who muſt owe unto thy wiſdom
In the concealing of my barren ſhame.

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: Your Grace doth wrong your Stars; if this be yours,
You may have children.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Speak it again.

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: You may have fruitful iſſue.

sp.speaker: Thie.
sp.l: By whom? when? how?

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: It was the fatal means firſt ſtruck my bloud
With the cold hand of wonder, when I read it
Printed upon your birth.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Can there be any way unſmooth, has end
So fair and good?

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: We that behold the ſad aſpects of Heaven,
Leading ſence blinded, men feel grief enough
To know, though not to ſpeak their miſeries.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Sorrow muſt loſe a name, where mine finds life;
If not in thee, at leaſt eaſe pain with ſpeed,
Which muſt know no cure elſe.

sp.speaker: Lecure.
sp.l: Then thus,
The firſt of Females which your eye ſhall meet
Before the Sun next riſe, coming from out
The Temple of Diana, being ſlain, you live
Father of many ſons.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Call'ſt thou this ſadneſs, can I beget a Son?
Deſerving leſs than to give recompence
Unto ſo poor a loſs? what e'er thou art,
Reſt peaceable bleſt creature, born to be
Mother of Princes, whoſe grave ſhall be more fruitful
Than others marriage beds: methinks his Art
Should give her form and happy figure to me,
I long to ſee my happineſs, he is gone,
As I remember, he nam'd my brothers Daughter,
Were it my Mother, 'twere a gainful death
Could give Ordella's virtue living breath. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: YOur Grace is early ſtirring.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: How can he ſleep,
Whoſe happineſs is laid up in an hour.
He knows comes ſtealing towards, him Oh Martel!
Is't poſſible the longing Bride, whoſe wiſhes
Out-runs her fears, can on that day ſhe is married
Conſume in ſlumbers; or his Arms ruſt in eaſe,
That hears the charge, and ſees the honor'd purchaſe
Ready to gil'd his valour? Mine is more,
A power above theſe paſſions; this day France,
France that in want of iſſue withers with us;
And like an aged River, runs his head
Into forgotten ways, again I ranſome,
And his fair courſe turn right: this day, Thierry,
The Son of France, whoſe manly powers like priſoners
Have been tied up, and fetter'd; by one death
Give life to thouſand ages; this day beauty
The envy of the world, Pleaſure the glory,
Content above the world, deſire beyond it
Are made mine own, and uſeful.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Happy Woman
That dies to do theſe things.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: But ten times happier
That lives to do the greater; oh Martel,
The gods have heard me now, and thoſe that ſcorn'd me,
Mothers of many children, and bleſt fathers
That ſee their iſſues like the Stars un-number'd,,
Their comfort more than them, ſhall in my praiſes
Now teach their Infants ſongs; and tell their ages
From ſuch a Son of mine, or ſuch a Queen,
That chaſte Ordella brings me: bleſſed marriage
The chain that links two Holy Loves together
And in the marriage, more than bleſt Ordella,
That comes ſo near the Sacrament it ſelf,
The Prieſts doubt, whether purer.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Sir, y'are loſt.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: I prethee let me be ſo.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: The day • ears,
And thoſe that have been offering early prayers,
Are now retiring homeward.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Stand and mark then.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Is it the firſt muſt ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: The firſt Woman.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: What hand ſhall do it, Sir?

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: This hand Martell,
For who leſs dare preſume to give the gods
An incenſe of this offering?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Would I were ſhe,
For ſuch away to die, and ſuch a bleſſing
Can never crown my parting.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: What are thoſe?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Men, men, Sir, men.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: The plagues of men light on 'em,
They croſs my hopes like Hares, who's that?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: A Prieſt, Sir.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Would he were gelt.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: May not theſe raſcals ſerve, Sir,
Well hang'd and quarter'd?

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Nov

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Here comes a woman.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Stand and behold her then.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I think a fair one.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Move not whilſt I prepare her: may her peace
Like his whoſe innocence the gods are pleas'd with,
And offering at their Altars, gives his ſoul
Far purer than thoſe fires; pull heaven upon her
You holy powers, no humane ſpot dwell in her,
No love of any thing, but you and goodneſs,
Tie her to earth; fear be a ſtranger to her,
And all weak blouds affections, but thy hope
Let her bequeath to Women: hear me heaven,
Give her a ſpirit maſculine, and noble,
Fit for your ſelves to ask, and me to offer.
Oh let her meet my blow, doat on her death;
And as a wanton Vine bows to the pruner,
That by his cutting off, more may increaſe,
So let her fall to raiſe me fruit; hail woman.
The happieſt, and the beſt (if the dull Will
Do not abuſe thy fortune) France e'er found yet.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Sh'is more than dull, Sir, leſs, and worſe than Woman,
That may inherit ſuch an infinite
As you propound, a greatneſs ſo near goodneſs;
And brings a Will to rob her.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Tell me this then,
Was there e'er woman yet, or may be found,
That for fair Fame, unſpotted memory,
For virtues ſake, and only for it ſelf ſake
Has, or dare make a ſtory?

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Many dead Sir,
Living I thing as many.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Say, the kingdom
May from a womans Will receive a bleſſing,
The King and kingdom, not a private ſafety.
A general bleſſing, Lady.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: A general curſe
Light on her heart, denies it.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Full of honor;
And ſuch examples as the former ages
Were but dim ſhadows of, and empty figures.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: You ſtrangely ſtir me, Sir, and were my weakneſs
In any other fleſh but modeſt womans,
You ſhould not ask more queſtions, may I do it?

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: You may, and which is more, you muſt.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I joy in't,
Above a moderate gladneſs, Sir, you promiſe
It ſhall be honeſt.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: As ever time diſcover'd.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Let it be what it may then, what it dare,
I have a mind will hazard it.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: But hark ye,
What may that woman merit, makes this bleſſing!

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Only her duty, Sir.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: 'Tis terrible.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo much the more noble.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: 'Tis full of fearful ſhadows.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: So is ſleep, Sir.
Or any thing that's meerly ours, and mortal,
We were begotten gods elſe; but thoſe fears
Feeling but once the fires of nobler thoughts.
Flie, like the ſhapes of clouds we form, to nothing.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Suppoſe it death.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I do.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: And endleſs parting
With all we can call ours, with all our ſweetneſs,
With youth, ſtrength, pleaſure, people, time, nay reaſon:
For in the ſilent grave, no converſation,
No joyful tread of friends, no voice of Lovers,
Nor nothing is, but all oblivion,
Duſt and an endleſs darkneſs; and dare you woman
Deſire this place?

sp.speaker: Ordeel.
sp.l: 'Tis of all ſleeps the ſweeteſt,
Children begin it to us, ſtrong men ſeek it,
And Kings from heighth of all their painted glories
Fall like ſpent exhalations, to this centre:
And thoſe are fools that fear it, or imagine
A few unhandſome pleaſures, or lifes profits
Can recompence this place; and mad that ſtaies it,
Till age blow out their lights, or rotten humors.
Bring them diſpers'd to th' earth.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Then you can ſuffer?

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: As willingly as ſay it.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Martell, a wonder,
Here's a woman that dares die, yet tell me,
Are you a Wife?

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I am Sir.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: And have children?
She ſighs and weeps.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Oh none Sir.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Dare you venture
For a poor barren praiſe you ne'er ſhall hear,
To part with theſe ſweet hopes?

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: With all but Heaven,
And yet die full of children; he that reads me
When I am aſhes, is my Son in wiſhes,
And thoſe chaſte dames that keep my memory,
Singing my yearly requiems, are my Daughters.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Then there is nothing wanting but my knowledg.
And what I muſt doe, Lady?

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: You are the King, Sir,
And what you do I'll ſuffer, and that bleſſing
That you deſire, the gods ſhowr on the Kingdom.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Thus much before I ſtrike then, for I muſt kill you,
The gods have will'd it ſo they're made the bleſſing
Muſt make France young again, and me a man,
Keep up your ſtrength ſtill nobly.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Fear me not.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: And meet death like a meaſure.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I am ſtedfaſt.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt be ſainted woman, and thy Tomb
Cut out in Chryſtal, pure and good as thou art;
And on it ſhall be graven every age,
Succeeding Peers of France that riſe by thy fall,
Tell thou lieſt there like old and fruitful nature.
Dareſt thou behold thy happineſs?

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I dare Sir.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Ha? Puls off her veil, lets fall his ſword.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh Sir, you muſt not doe it.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: No, I dare not.
There is an Angel keeps that Paradice,
A fiery Angel friend; oh virtue, virtue,
Ever and endleſs virtue.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Strike, Sir, ſtrike;
And if in my poor death fair France may merit,
Give me a thouſand blows, be killing me
A thouſand days.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Firſt let the earth be barren,
And man no more remembred, riſe Ordella,
The neareſt to thy maker, and the pureſt
That ever dull fleſh ſhewed us,— oh my heart-ſtrings Exit.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I ſee you full of wonder, therefore nobleſt,
And trueſt amongſt Women, I will tell you
The end of this ſtrange accident.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Amazement
Has ſo much wove upon my heart, that truly
I feel my ſelf unfit to hear, oh Sir,
My Lord has ſlighted me.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Oh no ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Robb'd me of ſuch a glory by his pity,
And moſt unprovident reſpect.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Dear Lady,
It was not meant to you.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Elſe where the day is,
And hours diſtinguiſh time, time runs to ages,
And ages end the world, I had been ſpoken.
I'll tell you what it was, if but your patience
Will give me hearing.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: If I have tranſgreſt,
Forgive me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Your noble Lord was counſel'd,
Grieving the barrenneſs between you both,
And all the Kingdom with him, to ſeek out
A man that knew the ſecrets of the gods,
He went, found ſuch an one, and had this anſwer,
That if he wou'd have iſſue, on this morning,
For this hour was prefixt him, he ſhould kill
The firſt he met, being Female, from the Temple;
And then he ſhould have children, the miſtake
Is now too perfect, Lady.

sp.speaker: Ordel,
sp.l: Still 'tis I, Sir,
For may this work be done by common women?
Durſt any but my ſelf that knew the bleſſing,
And felt the benefit, aſſume this thing
In any other, 't'ad been loſt, and nothing,
A curſe and not a bleſſing; I was figur'd;
And ſhall a little fondneſs barr my purchaſe?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Where ſhould he then ſeek children?

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Where they are
In wombs ordain'd for iſſues, in thoſe beauties
That bleſs a marriage-bed, and makes it proceed
With kiſſes that conceive, and fruitful pleaſures;
Mine like a grave, buries thoſe loyal hopes,
And to a grave it covets.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: You are too good,
Too excellent, too honeſt; rob not us
And thoſe that ſhall hereafter ſeek example,
Of ſuch ineſtimable worthies in woman,
Your Lord of ſuch obedience, all of honor
In coveting a cruelty is not yours,
A Will ſhort of your Wiſdom; make not error
A Tomb-ſtone of your virtues, whoſe fair life
Deſerves a conſtellation: your Lord dare not;
He cannot, ought not, muſt not run this hazard,
He makes a ſeparation, nature ſhakes at,
The gods deny, and everlaſting juſtice
Shrinks back, and ſheaths her ſword at.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: All's but talk, Sir,
I find to what I am reſerv'd, and needful,
And though my Lord's compaſſion makes me poor,
And leaves me in my beſt uſe, yet a ſtrength
Above mine own, or his dull fondneſs finds me;
The gods have given it to me. Draws a knife.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Self-deſtruction!
Now all good Angels bleſs thee, oh ſweet Lady,
You are abus'd, this is a way to ſhame you,
And with you all that knows you, all that loves you,
To ruin all you build, would you be famous?
Is that your end?

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I would be what I ſhould be.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Live and confirm the gods then, live and be loaden
With more than Olive-bear, or fruitful Autumn;
This way you kill your merit, kill your cauſe,
And him you would raiſe life to, where, or how
Got you theſe bloudy thoughts? what Devil durſt
Look on that Angel face, and tempt? doe you know
What is't to die thus how you ſtrike the Stars,
And all good things above, do you feel
What follows a ſelf-bloud, whether you venture,
And to what puniſhment? excellent Lady,
Be not thus cozen'd, do not fool your ſelf,
The Prieſt was never his own ſacrifice,
But he that thought his hell here.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I am counſell'd,

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: And I am glad on't, lie, I know you dare not.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I never have done yet.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Pray take my comfort,
Was this a ſoul to loſe? two more ſuch women
Would ſave their ſex; ſee, ſhe repents and prayes,
Oh hear her, hear her, if there be a faith
Able to reach your mercies, ſhe hath ſent it.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Now good Martel confirm me.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I will Lady,
And every hour adviſe you, for I doubt
Whether this plot be heavens, or hells; your mother,
And I will find it, if it be in mankind
To ſearch the center of it: in the mean time
I'll give you out for dead, and by your ſelf,
And ſhew the inſtrument, ſo ſhall I find
A joy that will betray her.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Do what's fitteſt;
And I will follow you.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Then ever live
Both able to engroſs all love, and give. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: I'm in labour
To be deliver'd of that burthenous project
I have ſo long gone with; ha, here's the Midwife,
Or life, or death.

sp.speaker: Lecu.
sp.l: If in the ſuppoſition
Of her death in whoſe life you die, you ask me,
I think you are ſafe.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Is ſhe dead?

sp.speaker: Lecu.
sp.l: I have us'd
All means to make her ſo, I ſaw him waiting
At the Temple door, and us'd ſuch Art within,
That only ſhe of all her Sex was firſt
Giv'n up unto his fury.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Which if love
Or fear made him forbear to execute
The vengeance he determin'd, his fond pity
Shall draw it on himſelf, for were there left
Not any man but he, to ſerve my pleaſures,
Or from me to receive commands, which are
The joyes for which I love life, he ſhould be
Remov'd, and I alone left to be Queen
O'er any part of goodneſs that's left in me.

sp.speaker: Lecu.
sp.l: If you are ſo reſolv'd, I have provided
A means to ſhip him hence: look upon this,
But touch it ſparingly, for this once us'd.
Say but to dry a tear, will keep the eye-lid
From cloſing, until death perform that office.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Give't me, I may have uſe of it, and on you
I'll make the firſt experiment: if one ſigh
Or heavy look beget the leaſt ſuſpition,
Childiſh compaſſion can thaw the Ice
Of your ſo long congeal'd and flinty hardneſs.
Slight, go on conſtant, or I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.l: Beſt Lady,
We have no faculties which are not yours.

sp.speaker: Lecu.
sp.l: Nor will be any thing without you.

sp.speaker: Baun.
sp.l: Be ſo, and we will ſtand or fall together, for
Since we have gone ſo far, that death muſt ſtay
The journey, which we wiſh ſhould never end;
And innocent, or guilty, we muſt die,
When we do ſo, let's know the reaſon why.

sp.speaker: Lecu.
sp.l: The King.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: We'll be alone.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.l: I would I had
A Convoy too, to bring me ſafe off.
For rage although it be allai'd with ſorrow,
Appears ſo dreadful in him, that I ſtake
To look upon 't.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Coward I will meet it,
And know from whence 't has birth: Son, kingly Thierry.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Is cheating grown ſo common among men?
And thrives ſo well here, that the gods endeavour
To practiſe it above?

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Your Mother.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Ha!. or are they only careful to revenge,
Not to reward? or when, for your offences
We ſtudy ſatisfaction, muſt the cure
Be worſe than the diſeaſe?

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Will you not hear me?

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: To loſe th' ability to perform thoſe duties
For which I entertain'd the name of Husband,
Ask'd more than common ſorrow; but t'impoſe
For the redreſs of that defect, a torture
In marking her to death, for whom alone
I felt that weakneſs as a want, requires
More than the making the head bald: or falling
Thus flat upon the earth, or curſing that way,
Or praying this, oh ſuch a Scene of grief,
And ſo ſet down, (the world the ſtage to act on)
May challenge a Tragedian better practis'd
Than I am to expreſs it; for my cauſe
Of paſſion is ſo ſtrong, and my performance
So weak, that though the part be good, I fear
Th'ill acting of it, will defraud it of
The poor reward it may deſerve, mens pity.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: I have given you way thus long, a King, and what
Is more, my Son, and yet a ſlave to that
Which only triumphs over cowards ſorrow,
For ſhame look up.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Is't you, look down on me:
And if that you are capable to receive it,
Let that return to you, that have brought forth
One mark'd out only for it: what are theſe?
Come they upon your privilege to tread on
The Tomb of my afflictions?

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.l: No, not we Sir.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: How dare you then omit the ceremony
Due to the funeral of all my hopes.
Or come unto the marriage of my ſorrows,
But in ſuch colours as may ſort with them.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.l: Alas; we will wear any thing.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: This is madneſs
Take but my counſel.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Yours? dare you again
Though arm'd with th' authority of a mother,
Attempt the danger that will fall on you
If ſuch another ſyllable awake it?
Goe, and with yours be ſafe, I have ſuch cauſe
Of grief, nay more, to love it, that I will not
Have ſuch as theſe be ſharers in it.

sp.speaker: Lecu.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.l: Another time were better.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Do not ſtirr,
For I muſt be reſolv'd, and will, be ſtatues.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: I, thou art welcome, and upon my ſoul
Thou art an honeſt man, do you ſee, he has tears
To lend to him whom prodigal expence
Of ſorrow, has made bankrupt of ſuch treaſure,
Nay, thou doſt well.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I would it might excuſe.
The ill I bring along.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Thou mak'ſt me ſmile
I the heighth of my calamities, as if
There could be the addition of an Atome,
To the gyant-body of my miſeries
But try, for I will hear thee, all ſit down, 'tis death
To any that ſhall dare to interrupt him
In look, geſture, or word.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: And ſuch attention
As is due to the laſt, and the beſt ſtory
That ever was deliver'd, will become you,
The griev'd Ordella, (for all other titles
But take away from that) having from me
Prompted by your laſt parting groan, enquir'd,
What drew it from you, and the cauſe ſoon learn'd:
For ſhe whom barbariſm could deny nothing,
With ſuch prevailing earneſtneſs deſir'd it,
'Twas not in me, though it had been my death,
To hide it from her, ſhe I ſay, in whom
All was, that Athens, Rome, or warlike Sparta,
Have regiſtred for good in their beſt Women:
But nothing of their ill; knowing her ſelf
Mark'd out, (I know not by what power, but ſure
A cruel one) to dye, to give you children;
Having firſt with a ſetled countenance
Look'd up to Heaven, and then upon her ſelf,
(It being the next beſt object) and then ſmil'd,
As if her joy in death to do you ſervice,
Would break forth, in deſpight of the much ſorrow
She ſhew'd ſhe had to leave you: and then taking
Me by the hand, this hand which I muſt ever
Love better than I have done, ſince ſhe touch'd it,
Go ſaid ſhe, to my Lord, (and to goe to him
Is ſuch a happineſs I muſt not hope for)
And tell him that he too much priz'd a trifle
Made only worthy in his love, and her
Thankful acceptance, for her ſake to rob
The Orphan Kingdom of ſuch guardians, as
Muſt of neceſſity deſcend from from him;
And therefore in ſome part of recompence
Of his much love, and to ſhew to the world
That 'twas not her fault only, but her fate,
That did deny to let her be the mother
Of ſuch moſt certain bleſſings: yet for proof,
She did not envy her, that happy her,
That is appointed to them, her guick end
Should make way for her, which no ſooner ſpoke,
But in a moment this too ready engine
Made ſuch a battery in the choiſeſt Caſtle
That ever nature made to defend life,
That ſtrait it ſhook, and ſunk.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Stay, dares any
Preſume to ſhed a tear before me? or
Aſcribe that worth unto themſelves to merit:
To do ſo for her? I have done, now on.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Fall'n thus, once more ſhe ſmil'd, as if that death
For her had ſtudied a new way to ſever
The ſoul and body, without ſenſe of pain;
And then tell him (quoth ſhe) what you have ſeen,
And with what willingneſs 'twas done: for which
My laſt requeſt unto him is, that he
Would inſtantly make choice of one (moſt happy
In being ſo choſen) to ſupply my place,
By whom if heaven bleſs him with a daughter,
In my remembrance let it bear my name
Which ſaid ſhe dy'd.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: I hear this, and yet live;
Heart! art thou thunder proof, will nothing break thee?
She's dead, and what her entertainment may be
In th'other world without me is uncertain,
And dare I ſtay here unreſolv'd?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Oh Sir!

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Dear ſon.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.l: Great King.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Unhand me, am I fall'n
So low, that I have loſt the power to be
Diſpoſer of my own life?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Be but pleas'd
To borrow ſo much time of ſorrow, as
To call to mind her laſt requeſt, for whom
(I muſt confeſs a loſs beyond expreſſion)
You turn your hand upon your ſelf, 'twas hers
And dying hers, that you ſhould live and happy
In ſeeing little models of your ſelf,
By matching with another, and will you
Leave any thing that ſhe deſir'd ungranted?
And ſuffer ſuch a life that was laid down
For your ſake only to be fruitleſs?

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Oh thou doſt throw charms upon me, againſt which
I cannot ſtop my ears, bear witneſs heaven
That not deſire of life, nor love of pleaſure
Nor any future comforts, but to give
Peace to her bleſſed ſpirit in ſatisfying
Her laſt demand, makes me defer our meeting,
Which in my choice, and ſuddain choice ſhall be
To all apparent,

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: How? doe I remove one miſchief
To draw upon my head a greater?

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Go, thou only good man, to whom for her ſelf
Goodneſs is dear, and prepare to interr it
In her that was; oh my heart! my Ordella,
A monument worthy to be the casket
Of ſuch a jewel.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Your command that makes way
Unto my abſence is a welcome one,
For but your ſelf there's nothing here Martel,
Can take delight to look on; yet ſome comfort
Goes back with me to her, who though ſhe want it
Deſerves all bleſſings. Exit.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: So ſoon to forget
The loſs of ſuch a wife, believe it will
Be cenſur'd in the world.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Pray you no more,
There is no argment you can uſe to croſs it,
But does increaſe in me ſuch a ſuſpition
I would not cheriſh — who's that?

sp.speaker: Memb.
sp.l: One, no guard
Can put back from acceſs, whoſe tongue no threats
Nor praiſes can ſilence, a bold ſuitor, and
For that which if you are your ſelf, a King,
You were made ſo to grant it, Juſtice, Juſtice.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: With what aſſurance dare you hope for that
Which is deny'd to me? or how can I
Stand bound to be juſt, unto ſuch as are
Beneath me, that find none from thoſe that are
Above me?

sp.speaker: Memb.
sp.l: There is juſtice, 'twere unfit
That any thing but vengeance ſhould fall on him,
That by his giving way to more than murther,
(For my dear fathers death was parricide)
Makes it his own.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: I charge you hear her not.

sp.speaker: Memb.
sp.l: Hell cannot ſtop juſt prayers from ent'ring heaven,
I muſt and will be heard Sir; but remember
That he that by her plot fell, was your brother,
And the place where, your Palace, againſt all
Th'inviolable rites of hoſpitality,
Your word, a Kings word, given up for his ſafety,
His innocence, his protection, and the gods
Bound to revenge the impious breach of ſuch
So great and ſacred bonds; and can you wonder,
(That in not puniſhing ſuch a horrid murther
You did it) that heavens favour is gone from you?
Which never will return, until his bloud
Be waſh'd away in hers.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Drag hence the wretch.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Forbear, with what variety
Of torments do I meet? oh thou haſt open'd
A Book, in which writ down in bloudy Letters,
My conſcience finds that I am worthy of
More than I undergoe, but I'll begin
For my Ordella's ſake, and for thine own
To make leſs heavens great anger: thou haſt loſt
A father, I to thee am ſo; the hope
Of a good Husband, in me have one; nor
Be fearful I am ſtill no man, already
That weakneſs is gone from me.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: That it might Aſide.
Have ever grown inſeparably upon thee,
What will you do? Is ſuch a thing as this
Worthy the lov'd Ordella's place, the daughter
Of a poor Gardener?

sp.speaker: Memb.
sp.l: Your Son.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: The power
To take away that lowneſs is in me.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Stay yet, for rather than thou ſhalt add
Inceſt unto thy other ſins, I will
With hazard of my own life, utter all,
Theodoret was thy Brother.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: You deny'd it.
Upon your oath, nor will I now believe you,
Your Protean turnings cannot change my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Memb.
sp.l: And for me, be aſſur'd the means to be
Reveng'd on thee, vile hag, admits no thought,
But what tends to it.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Is it come to that?
Then have at the laſt refuge: art thou grown
Inſenſible in all, that thou goeſt on
Without the leaſt compunction? there, take that
To witneſs, that thou hadſt a mother, which
Foreſaw thy cauſe of grief, and ſad repentance,
That ſo ſoon after bleſt Ordella's death
Without a tear thou canſt imbrace another,
Forgetful man.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Mine eyes when ſhe is nam'd
Cannot forget their tribute, and your gift
Is not unuſeful now

sp.speaker: Lecu.
sp.l: He's paſt all cure, that only touch is death.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: This night I'll keep it,
To morrow I will ſend it you, and full of my affliction.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Is the poiſon mortal?

sp.speaker: Lecu.
sp.l: Above the help of Phyſick.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: To my wiſh,
Now for our own ſecurity, you Protaldye
Shall this night poſt towards Auſtracia,
With Letters to Theodorets baſtard ſon,
In which we will make known what for his riſing
We have done to Thierry: no denial,
Nor no excuſe in ſuch acts muſt be thought of,
Which all diſlike, and all again commend
When they are brought unto a happy end. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Devi.
sp.p: NO War, no Money, no Maſter; baniſh'd the Court, not truſted in the City, whipt out of the Countrey, in what a triangle runs our miſery? let me hear which of you has the beſt voice to beg in, for other hopes or fortunes I ſee you have not; be not nice, nature provided you with tones for the purpoſe, the peoples charity was your heritage, and I would ſee which of you deſerves his birth-right.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: We underſtand you not Captain.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: You ſee this cardicue, the laſt, and the only quinteſſence of 50 Crowns, diſtill'd in the limbeck of your gardage, of which happy piece thou ſhalt be treaſurer: now he that can ſooneſt perſwade him to part with't, enjoyes it, poſſeſſes it, and with it, me and my future countenance.
If they want Art to perſwade it, I'll keep it my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: So you be not a partial judge in your own cauſe, you ſhall.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: A match.

I'll begin to you, brave Sir; be proud to make him happy by your liberality, whoſe tongue vouchſafes now to petition, was never heard before leſs than to command. I am a Soldier by profeſſion, a Gentleman by birth, and an Officer by place, whoſe poverty bluſhes to be the cauſe, that ſo high a virtue ſhould deſcend to the pity of your charity.
In any caſe keep your high ſtile, it is not charity to ſhame any man, much leſs a virtue of your eminence, wherefore preſerve your worth, and I'll preſerve my money.

You perſwade? you are ſhallow, give way to merit: ah by the bread of a good man, thou haſt a bonny countenance and a blith, promiſing mickle good to a ſicker womb, that has trode a long and a fore ground to meet with friends, that will owe much to thy reverence, when they ſhall hear of thy courteſie to their wandring countreyman.
You that will uſe your friends ſo hardly to bring them in debt, Sir, will deſerve worſe of a ſtranger, wherefore pead on, pead on, I ſay.

It is the Welch muſt do't I ſee, comrade man of urſhip, St. Tavy be her Patron, the gods of the mountains keep her cow and her cupboard; may ſhe never want the green of the Leek, and the fat of the Onion, if ſhe part with her bounties to him, that is a great deal away from her cozines, and has two big ſuits in law to recover her heritage.

Pardon me Sir, I will have nothing to do with your ſuits, it comes within the ſtatute of maintenance: home to your cozines, and ſome garlick and hempſeed, the one will ſtop your hunger; the other end your ſuits, gammawaſh comrade, gammawaſh.
'Foot he'll hoord all for himſelf.

sp.speaker: Vitry.
sp.p: Yes, let him; now comes my turn, I'll ſee if he can anſwer me: ſave you Sir, they ſay, you have that I want, Money.
And that you are like to want, for ought I perceive yet.

sp.speaker: Vitry.
sp.p: Stand, deliver.
'Foot what mean you, you will not rob the Exchequer?

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.p: Do you prate?
Hold, hold, here Captain.
Why I could have done this before you?
And I.
And I.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.p: You have done this, brave man be proud to make him happy, by the bread of God man, thou haſt a bonny countenance, comrade man of urſhip, St. Tavy be her patron, out upon you, you uncurried colts, walking cans that have no ſouls in you, but a little Roſin to keep your ribs ſweet, and hold in liquor.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Why, what would you have us to do Captain?

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Beg, beg, and keep Conſtables waking, wear out ſtocks and whipcord, maunder for butter-milk, dye of the Jaundice, yet have the cure about you, Lice, large Lice, begot of your own duſt, and the heat of the Brick-kills, may you ſtarve, and fear of the gallows, which is a gentle conſumption to't, only preferr it, or may you fall upon your fear, and be hanged for ſelling thoſe purſes to keep you from famine, whoſe monies my valour empties, and be caſt without other evidence; here is my Fort, my Caſtle of defence, who comes by ſhall pay me toll, the firſt purſe is your mitimus ſlaves.
The purſe, 'foot we'll ſhare in the money Captain, if any come within a furlong of our fingers.
Did you doubt but we could ſteal as well as your ſelf, did not I ſpeak Welſh?
We are thieves from our cradles, and will dye ſo.

sp.speaker: Vit.
sp.p: Then you will not beg again.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Yes, as you did, ſtand, and deliver.
Hark, here comes handſel, 'tis a Trade quickly ſet up and as ſoon caſt down.

sp.speaker: Vitry.
sp.p: Have goodneſs in your minds varlets, and to't like men; he that has more money than we, cannot be our friend, and I hope there is no law for ſpoiling the enemy.
You need not inſtruct us farther, your example pleads enough.

sp.speaker: Devitry.
sp.p: Diſperſe your ſelves, and as their company is, fall on.
Come, there are a band of 'em, I'll charge ſingle.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: 'Tis wonderful dark, I have loſt my man, and dare not call for him, leſt I ſhould have more followers than I would pay wages to; what throws am I in, in this travel? theſe be honourable adventures; had I that honeſt bloud in my veins again Queen, that your feats and theſe frights have drain'd from me, honor ſhould pull hard, e'r it drew me into theſe brakes.

sp.speaker: Devitry.
sp.p: Who goes there?

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: Hey ho, here's a pang of preferment.

sp.speaker: Devi.
sp.p: 'Heart, who goes there?

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: He that has no heart to your acquaintance, what ſhall I do with my Jewels and my Letter, my codpiece that's too looſe; good, my boots, who is't that ſpoke to me? here's a friend.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: We ſhall find that preſently, ſtand, as you love your ſafety, ſtand.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: That unlucky word of ſtanding, has brought me to all this, hold, or I ſhall never ſtand you.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: I ſhould know that voice, deliver.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: All that I have is at your ſervice Gentlemen, and much good may it do you.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Zones down with him, do you prate?

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: Keep your firſt word as you are Gentlemen, and let me ſtand, alas, what do you mean?
To tye you to us Sir, bind you in the knot of friendſhip.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: Alas Sir, all the phyſick in Europe cannot bind me.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: You ſhould have jewels about you, ſtones, precious ſtones.
Captain away, there's company within hearing, if you ſtay longer, we are ſurpriz'd.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Let the Devil come, I'll pillage this Fregat a little better yet.
'Foot we are loſt, they are upon us.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p:
Ha, upon us, make the leaſt noiſe, 'tis thy part
• ng gaſpe.
Which way ſhall we make Sir?

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Every man his own; do you hear, only bind me, bind me before you goe, and when the company's paſt, make to this place again, this karvel ſhould have better lading in him, you are ſlow, why do you not tye harder?
You are ſure enough I warrant you Sir.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Darkneſs befriend you, away. Exit Soldiers.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: What tyrants have I met with, they leave me alone in the dark, yet would not have me cry. I ſhall grow won drous melancholly if I ſtay long here without company; I was wont to get a nap with ſaying my prayers, I'll ſee if they will work upon me now; but then, if I ſhould talk in my ſleep, and they hear me, they would make a Recorder of my windpipe, ſlit my throat: heaven be prais'd, I hear ſome noiſe, it may be new purchaſe, and then I ſhall have fellows.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: They are gone paſt hearing, now to taske Devitry, help, help, as you are men help; ſome charitable hand, relieve a poor diſtreſſed miſerable wretch, thieves, wicked thieves have robb'd me; bound me.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: 'Foot, would they had gagg'd you top, your noiſe will betray us, and fetch them again.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: What bleſſed tongue ſpake to me, where, where where are you Sir?

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: A plague of your bawling throat, we are well enough if you have the grace to be thankful for't, do but ſnore to me, and 'tis as much as I deſire, to paſs away time with, till morning, then talk as loud as you pleaſe Sir, I am bound not to ſtir, therefore lie ſtill and ſnore I ſay.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Then you have met with thieves too I ſee.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: And deſire to meet with no more of them.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Alas, what can we ſuffer more? they are far enough by this time; have they not all, all that we have Sir?

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: No by my faith have they not Sir; I gave them one trick to boot for their learning, my Boots Sir, my Boots, I have ••• 'd my ſtock, and my jewels in them, and therefore deſire to hear no more of them.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Now bleſſing on your wit, Sir, what a dull ſlave was I? dreamt not of your conveyance, help to unbind me Sir, and I'll undoe you, my life for yours, no worſe thief than my ſelf meets you again this night.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: Reach me thy hands,

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Here Sir, here, I could beat my brains out, that could not think of boots, boots Sir, wide top • boots, I ſhall love them the better whilſt I live; but are you fare your Jewels are here Sir?

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: Sure ſayſt thou? ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: So ho, illo ho. Wabin Soldiers.
Here Captain. here.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: 'Foot what do you mean Sir?

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: A trick to boot, ſay you; here you dull ſlaves, purchaſe, purchaſe the ſoul of the Rock, Diamonds, ſparkling Diamonds.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: I'm betraid, loſt, paſt recovery, loſt, as you are men

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Nay rook, ſince you will be prating, we'll ſ • are your carrion with you, have you any other conveyance now Sir?
'Foot hereare Letters, Epiſtles, familiar Epiſtles, we'll ſee what treaſure is in them, they are ſeal'd ſure.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: Gentlemen, as you are Gentlemen ſpare my Letters, and take all willingly, all: I'll give you a releaſe, a general releaſe, and meet you here to morrow with as much more.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Nay, ſince you have your tricks, and your conveyances, we will not leave a wrinkle of you unſeare • t.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: Hark, there comes company, you will be betraid, as you love your ſafeties, beat out my brains, I ſhall betray you elſe.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Treaſon, unheard of Treaſon, monſtrous, monſtrous villanies.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: I confeſs my ſelf a Traitor, ſhew your ſelves good ſubjects, and hang me up for't.
If it be treaſon, the diſcovery will get our pardon, Captain.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Would we were all loſt, hang'd, quarter'd, to ſave this one, one innocent Prince; Thierry's poiſon'd, by his mother poiſon'd, the Miſtriſs to this ſtallion, who by that poiſon ne'er ſhall ſleep again.
'Foot let us mince him by piece-meals, till he eat himſelf up.
Let us dig out his heart with needles, and half broil him, like a Muſſel.

sp.speaker: Prot.
sp.p: Such another and I prevent you, my bloud's ſetled already.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: Here's that ſhall remove it, road, viper, drag him unto Martel, unnatural paricide, cruel, bloudy woman.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: On you dogfiſh, leech, caterpillar.

sp.speaker: Devit.
sp.p: A longer ſight of him will make my rage turn pity, and with his ſuddain end, prevent revenge and torture, wicked, wicked Brunhalt. Exit.
Not ſleep at all, no means.
No Art can do it.

sp.speaker: Bawdb.
sp.l: I will aſſure you, he can ſleep no more
Than a hooded Hawks, a centinel to him,
Or one of the City Conſtables are tops.
How came he ſo?

sp.speaker: Bawdb.
sp.l: They are too wiſe that dare know,
Something's amiſs, heaven help all.
What cure has he?

sp.speaker: Bawdb.
sp.l: Armies of thoſe we call
Phyſitians, ſome with gliſters,
Some with Lettice-caps, ſome poſſet-drinks, ſome Pills,
Twenty conſulting here about a drench,
The bringing in of Leonor the baſtard
Son to your murther'd brother, her Phyſitian
By this time is attacht to that damn'd devil.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: 'Tis like he will be ſo, for e'er we came
Fearing an equal juſtice for his miſchiefs,
He drencht himſelf.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: He did like one of mine then.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Muſt I ſtill ſee theſe miſeries, no night
To hide me from their horrors, that Protaldy
See juſtice fall upon.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Now I could ſleep too.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: I'll give you yet more Poppy, bring the Lady
And heaven in her embraces; gives him quiet,
Madam, unveil your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I do forgive you,
And though you ſought my bloud, yet I'll pray for you.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: Art thou alive?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Now could you ſleep?

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: For ever.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Go carry her without wink of ſleep, or quiet,
Where her ſtrong knave Protaldye's broke o'th' wheel,
And let his cries and roars be muſick to her,
I mean to waken her.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Do her no wrong.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Nor right, as you love juſtice.

sp.speaker: Brun.
sp.l: I will think,
And if there be new curſes in old nature,
I have a ſoul dare ſend them.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Keep her waking. Exit Brunhalt.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: What's that appears ſo ſweetly? there's that face.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Be moderate, Lady.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: That Angels face.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Goe nearer.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Martel. I cannot laſt long, ſee the ſoul,
I ſee it perfectly of my Ordella,
The heavenly figure of her ſweetneſs there,
Forgive me gods, it comes, Divineſt ſubſtance,
Kneel, kneel, kneel every one, Saint of thy Sex,
If it be for my cruelty thou comeſt,
Do ye ſee her hoe?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Yes Sir, and you ſhall know her.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Down, down again, to be reveng'd for bloud,
Sweet Spirit I am ready, ſhe ſmiles on me,
O bleſſed ſign of Peace.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Goe nearer Lady.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: I came to make you happy.

sp.speaker: Thier,
sp.l: Hear you that, Sir?
She comes to crown my ſoul away, get ſacrifice
Whilſt I with holy Honors.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: She's alive, Sir.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: In everlaſting life, I know it friend,
Oh happy, happy ſoul.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Alas, I live Sir,
A mortal woman ſtill.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Can ſpirits weep too?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: She's no ſpirit Sir, pray kiſs her, Lady,
Be very gentle to him.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Stay, ſhe is warm,
And by my life the ſame lips tell me brightneſs,
Are you the ſame Ordella ſtill?

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: The ſame, Sir.
Whom heavens and my good Angel ſtaid from ruin.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Kiſs me again.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: The ſame ſtill, ſtill your ſervant.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe, I know her now Martel; ſit down ſweet.
Oh bleſt and happieſt woman, a dead ſlumber
Begins to creep upon me, oh my jewel!

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Oh ſleep my Lord.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: My joyes are too much for me.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: Brunhalt impatient of her conſtraint to ſee
Protaldye tortur'd, has choak'd her ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: No more, her ſins go with her.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Love, I muſt die, I faint, cloſe up my glaſſes.

sp.speaker: 1 Doct.
sp.l: The Queen faints too, and deadly.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: One dying kiſs.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: My laſt Sir, and my deareſt, and now
Cloſe my eyes too.

sp.speaker: Thier.
sp.l: Thou perfect woman.
Martel, the Kingdom's yours, take Memberge to you,
And keep my line alive; nay, weep not, Lady,
Take me, I go.

sp.speaker: Ordel.
sp.l: Take me too, farewel honour Die both.

sp.speaker: 2 Doct.
sp.l: They are gone for ever.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: The peace of happy ſouls go after them,
Bear them to their laſt beds, whilſt I ſtudy
A Tomb to ſpeak their loves; whilſt old time laſteh
I am your King in ſorrows.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: We your ſubjects.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Devitry, for your ſervice, be near us,
Whip out theſe inſtruments of this mad mother
From Court, and all good people; and becauſe
She was born Noble, let that Title find her
A private grave, but neither tongue nor honor:
And now lead on, they that ſhall read this ſtory,
Shall find that Virtue lives in Good, not Glory.

div.head: PROLOGUE.
div.p: GEntlemen, Inductions are out of date, and a Prologue in Verſe, is as ſtale as a black Velvet Cloak, and a Bay Garland: therefore you ſhall have it plain Proſe, thus: If there be any amongſt you, that come to hear laſcivious Scenes, let them depart: for I do pronounce this, to the utter diſcomfort of all two-penny Gallery men, you ſhall have no bawdery in it: or if there be any lurking amongſt you in corners, with Table-books, who have ſome hope to find fit matter to feed his —malice on, let them claspe them up, and ſlink away, or ſtay and be converted. For he that made this Play, means to pleaſe Auditors ſo, as he may be an Auditor himſelf hereafter, and not purchaſe them with the dearneſs of his cares: I dare not call it Comedy or Tragedy; 'tis perfectly neither: A Play it is, which was meant to make you laugh, how it would pleaſe you, is not written in my Part: for though you ſhould like it to day, perhaps your ſelves know not how you ſhould digest it to morrow: Some things in it you may meet with, which are out of the common road: a Duke there is, and the Scaene lies in Italy, as thoſe two things lightly we never miſs. But you ſhall not find in it the ordinary and over-worn Trade of jeſting at • ords and Courtiers, and Citizens, without taxation of any particular or new vice by them found out, but at the perſons of them: ſuch, he, that made this, thinks vile, and for his own part vows; That he did never think but that a Lord, Lord born might be a wiſe man, and a Courtier an honest man.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke of Millain, Arrigo, Lucio, and two Courtiers.
div.l: TIs now the ſweeteſt time for ſleep, the night is ſcarce ſpent, Arrigo, what's a clock?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: Paſt four.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is it ſo much, and yet the morn not up?
See yonder where the ſhamefac'd Maiden comes
Into our ſight how gently doth ſhe ſlide,
Hiding her chaſte cheeks, like a modeſt Bride,
With a red veil of bluſhes; as if ſhe,
Even ſuch all modeſt virtuous Women be.
Why thinks your Lordſhip I am up ſo ſoon?

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.l: About ſome weighty State plot.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And what thinks your knighthood of it?

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: I do think to cure ſome ſtrange corruptions in the Common-wealth.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Y'are well conceited of your ſelves to think
I chuſe you out to bear me company
In ſuch affairs and buſineſs of ſtate:
For am not I a pattern for all Princes,
That break my ſoft ſleep for my ſubjects good?
Am I not careful? very provident?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Your Grace is careful.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: Very provident.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Nay, knew you how my ſerious working plots,
Concern the whole Eſtates of all my ſubjects,
I, and their lives; then Lucio thou wouldſt ſwear,
I were a loving Prince.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I think your Grace intends to walk the publick ſtreets diſguis'd, to ſee the ſtreets diſorders.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: It is not ſo

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: You ſecretly will croſs ſome other ſtates, that do conſpire againſt you.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Weightier far:
You are my friends, and you ſhall have the cauſe;
I break my ſleeps thus ſoon to ſee a wench.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Y'are wond'rous careful for your ſubjects good.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: You are a very loving Prince indeed.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: This care I take for them, when their dull eyes,
Are clos'd with heavy ſlumbers.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: Then you riſe to ſee your wenches?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: What Milan beauty hath the power, to charme her Sovereign eyes, and break his ſleeps:

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Siſter to Count Valore, ſhe's a Maid
Would make a Prince forget his throne, and ſta • e,
And lowly kneel to her: the general fate
Of all mortality, is hers to give;
As ſhe diſpoſeth, ſo we die and live.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My Lord, the day grows clear, the Court will riſe.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: We ſtay too long, is the Ʋmbrances head as we commanded, ſent to the ſad Gondarino, our General?

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: 'Tis ſent.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But ſtay, where ſhines that light?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: 'Tis in the chamber of Lazarello.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Lazarillo? what is he?

sp.p: A Courtier my Lord, and one that I wonder your Grace knows not: for he hath followed your Court, and your laſt predeceſſors, from place to place, any time this ſeven years, as faithfully as your Spits and your Drippingpans have done, and almoſt as greaſily.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Oh we know him, as we have heard, he keeps a Kalender of all the diſhes of meat, that have been in the Court, ever ſince our great Grandfathers time; and when he can thruſt in at no Table, he makes his meat of that.

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.p: The very ſame my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: A Courtier call'ſt thou him?
B • lieve me Lucio, there be many ſuch
About our Court, reſpected, as they think,
Even by our ſelf; with thee I will be plain:
sp.p: We Princes do uſe, to preferre many for nothing, and to take particular and free knowledg, almoſt in the nature of acquaintance of many; whom we do uſe only for our pleaſures, and to give largely to numbers; more out of policy • o be thought liberal, and by that means to make the people ſtrive to deſerve our Love; than to reward any particular deſert of theirs, to whom we give: and do ſuffer our ſ • lves to hear flatterers, more for recreation
sp.l: Than • or love of it, though we ſeldom hate it:
And yet we know all theſe, and when we pleaſe,
Can touch the wheel, and turn their names about.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I wonder they that know their ſtates ſo well, ſhould • ancy ſuch baſe ſlaves.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Thou wond'reſt Lucio,
Doſt not thou think, if thou wert Duke of Milan,
Thou ſhould'ſt be flattered?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I know my Lord, I would not.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Why ſo, I thought till I was Duke, I thought I ſhould have left me no more flatterers, than there are now Plain-dealers; and yet for all this my reſolution, I am moſt palpably flattered: the poor man may loath covetouſneſs and flattery, but fortune will alter the mind when the wind turns: there may be well a little conflict, but it will drive the billows before it.
sp.l: Arrigo it grows late, for ſee, fair Thetis hath undone the barrs
To Phebus team; and his unrival'd light,
Hath chac'd the mornings modeſt bluſh away:
Now muſt we to our love, bright Paphian Queen;
Thou Cytberean goddeſs, that delights
In ſtirring glances, and art ſtill thy ſelf,
More toying than thy team of Sparrows be;
Thou laughing Errecina, oh inſpire
Her heart with love, or leſſen my deſire. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Go run, ſearch, pry in every nook and angle of the Kitchins, Larders, and Paſteries, know what meat's boil'd, bak'd, roſt, ſtew'd, fri'd, or ſous'd, at this dinner to be ſerv'd directly, or indirectly. to every ſeveral Table in the Court, be gone.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I run, but not ſo faſt as your mouth will do upon the ſtroke of Eleven. Exit Boy.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: What an excellent thing did God beſtow upon man, when he gave him a good ſtomach? what unbounded graces there are pour'd upon them that have the continual command of the very beſt of theſe bleſſings? 'tis an excellent thing to be a Prince; he is ſerv'd with ſuch admirable variety of Fare; ſuch innumerable choice of Delicates; his Tables are full fraught with moſt nouriſhing food, and his Cubbards heavy laden with rich Wines; his Court is ſtill filled with moſt pleaſant variety: In the Summer, his Palace is full of Green Geeſe; and in Winter it ſwarmeth with Woodcocks,
sp.l: Oh thou goddeſs of Plenty
Fill me this day with ſome rare delicates
And I will every year moſt conſtantly,
As this day celebrate a ſumptuous Feaſt,
If thou wilt ſend me victuals in thine honor?
And to it ſhall be bidden for thy ſake,
Even all the valiant ſtomachs in the Court:
All ſhort-cloak'd Knights, and all croſs-garter'd Gentlemen,
All pump and pantoſle, foot-cloth riders;
With all the ſwarming generation
Of long ſtocks, ſhort pain'd hoſe, and huge ſtuff'd doublets:
All theſe ſhall eat, and which is more than yet
Hath e'er been ſeen, they ſhall be ſatisfied
I wonder my Ambaſſador returns not?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Here I am Maſter.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: And welcome:
Never did that ſweet Virgin in her ſmock,
Fair-cheek'd Andromeda, when to the rock
Her Ivorie limbs were chain'd, and ſtraight before
A huge Sea-monſter, tumbling to the ſhore,
To have devour'd her, with more longing ſight
Expect the coming of ſome hardy Knight,
That might have quell'd his pride, and ſet her free,
Than I with longing ſight have look'd for thee.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Your Perſeus is come Maſter, that will deſtroy him,
The very comfort of whoſe preſence ſhuts
The monſter hunger from your yelping guts

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Brief boy, brief, diſcourſe the ſervice of each ſeveral Table compendiouſly.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Here's a Bill of all Sir.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Give it me, a Bill of all the ſeveral ſervices this day appointed for every Table in the Court,
sp.l: I, this is it on which my hopes relye,
Within this paper all my joyes are clos'd:
Boy, open it, and read it with reverence.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: For the Captain of the Guards Table, three chines of Beef, and two joals of Sturgeon.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: A portly ſervice, but groſs, groſs, proceed to the
Dukes own Table, dear boy, to the Dukes own Table,

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: For the Dukes own Table, the head of an Ʋmbrana.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Is't poſſible? can Heaven be ſo propitious to the Duke?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Yes, I'll aſſure you Sir, 'tis poſſible, Heaven is ſo propitious to him.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: Why then he is the richeſt Prince alive:
He were the wealthieſt Monarch in all Europe,
Had he no other Territories, Dominions, Provinces, Seats,,
Not Palaces, but only that Ʋmbrana's head.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: 'Tis very freſh and ſweet, Sir, the fiſh was taken but this night, and the head, as a rare novelty, appointed by ſpecial commandement for the Dukes own Table, this dinner.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: If poor unworthy I may come to eat
Of this moſt ſacred diſh, I here do vow
(If that blind Huſwife, Fortune will beſtow
But means on me) to keep a ſumptuous houſe,
sp.p: A board groaning under the heavy burden of the beaſts that cheweth the cudd, and the Fowl that cutteth the Air: I ſhall not like the Table of a countrey Juſtice, beſprinkled over with all manner of cheap Sallads, ſliced Beef, Giblets, and Petitoes, to fill up room, nor ſhould there ſtand any great, cumberſom, un-cut-up pies, at the nether end fill'd with moſs and ſtones, partly to make a ſhew with and partly to keep the lower Meſs from eating, nor ſhall my meat come in ſheaking, like the City ſervice, one diſh a quarter of an hour after another, and gone, as if they had appointed to meet there, and had miſtook the hour, nor ſhould it, like the new Court ſervice, come in in haſte, as if it fain would be gone again, all courſes at once, like a hunting breakfaſt, but I would have my ſeveral courſes, and my diſhes well fill'd, my firſt courſe ſhould be brought in after the antient manner, by a ſcore of old bleer-ey'd Serving-men, in long blew coats, (marry they ſhall buy Silk, Facing, and Buttons themſelves) but that's by the way.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Maſter the time calls on, will you be walking?

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: Follow boy, follow, my guts were half an hour ſince in the privy Kitchin.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Count, and his Siſter Oriana.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Faith brother, I muſt needs go yonder.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: And faith Siſter what will you do yonder?

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I know the Lady Honoria will be glad to ſee me.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Glad to ſee you? faith the Lady Honoria cares for you as ſhe doth for all other young Ladies, ſhe's glad to ſee you, and will ſhew you the Privy Garden, and tell you how many Gowns the Ducheſs had; Marry if you have ever an old Uncle, that would be a Lord, or ever a kinſman that hath done a murther, or committed a robbery, and will give good ſtore of Money to procure his pardon, then the Lady Honoria will be glad to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I, but they ſay one ſhall ſee fine fights at the Court.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I'll tell you what you ſhall ſee, you ſhall ſee many faces of mans making, for you ſhall find very few as God left them: and you ſhall ſee many legs too; amongſt the reſt you ſhall behold one pair, the feet of which, were in times paſt, ſockleſs, but are now through the change of time (that alters all things) very ſtrangely become the legs of a Knight and a Courtier; another pair you ſhall ſee, that were heir apparent legs to a Glover, theſe legs hope ſhortly to be honourable; when they paſs by they will bow, and the mouth to theſe legs, will ſeem to offer you ſome Courtſhip; it will not ſwear, but it it will lye, hear it not.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Why, and are not theſe fine ſights?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Siſter, in ſeriouſneſs you yet are young
And fair, a fair young Maid, and apt.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Apt?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Exceeding apt to be drawn to.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: To what?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: To that you ſhould not be, 'tis no diſpraiſe,
She is not bad that hath deſire to ill,
But ſhe that hath no power to rule that Will:
For there you ſhall be wooed in other kinds
Than yet your years have known, the chiefeſt men
Will ſeem to throw themſelves
As vaſſals at your voice, kiſs your hand,
Prepare your Banquets, Masques, Shews, all inticements
That Wit and Luſt together can deviſe,
To draw a Lady from the ſtate of Grace
To an old Lady widdows Gallery;
And they will praiſe your virtues, beware that,
The only way to turn a Woman whore,
Is to commend her chaſtity: you'll goe?

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I would go, if it were but only to ſhew you, that
I could be there, and be mov'd with none of theſe tricks.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Your ſervants are ready!

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: An hour ſince.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Well, if you come off clear from this hot ſervice,
Your praiſe ſhall be the greater. Farewel Siſter.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Farewel Brother.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Once more, if you ſtay in the preſence till candle-light, keep on the foreſide o'th' Curtain; and do you hear, take heed of the old Bawd, in the cloth of Tiſſue ſleeves, and the knit Mittines. Farewel Siſter. Exit Oria.

Now am I idle, I would I had been a Scholar, that I might a ſtudied now: the puniſhment of meaner men is, they have too much to do; our only miſery is, that without company we know not what to do; I muſt take ſome of the common courſes of our Nobility; which is thus: if I can find no company that likes me, pluck off my Hatband, throw an old Cloak over my face, and as if I would not be known, walk haſtily through the ſtreets, till I be diſcovered; then there goes Count ſuch a one, ſays one; there goes Count ſuch a one, ſays another: Look how faſt he goes, ſays a third; there's ſome great matters in hand queſtionleſs, ſays a fourth; when all my buſineſs is to hav • them ſay ſo: this hath been uſed; or if I can find any company, I'll after dinner to the Stage, to ſee a Play; where, when I firſt enter, you ſhall have a m • rmure in the houſe, every one that does not know cries, What Nobleman is that? all the Gallants on the Stage riſe, vail to me, kiſs their hand, offer me their places: then I pick out ſome one, whom I pleaſe to grace among the reſt, take his ſeat, uſe it, throw my cloak over my face, and laugh at him: the poor Gentleman imagines himſelf moſt highly grac'd, thinks all the Auditors eſteem him one of my boſom friends; and in right ſpecial regard with me. But here comes a Gentleman, that I hope will make me better ſport, than either ſtreet and ſtage fooleries.

This man loves to eat good meat, always provided, he do not pay for it himſelf, he goes by the name of the Hungry Courtier, marry, becauſe I think that name will not ſufficiently diſtinguiſh him, for no doubt he hath more fellows there, his name is Lazarello, he is none of theſe ordinary eaters, that will devour three breakfaſts, and as many dinners, without any prejudi • e to their Beavers, Drinkings, or Suppers; but he hath a more courtly kind of hunger, and doth hunt more after novelty, than plenty, I'll over-hear him.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: Oh thou moſt itching kindly appetite,
Which every creature in his ſtomach feels;
Oh leave, leave yet at laſt thus to torment me.
Three ſeveral Sallads have I ſacrific'd,
Bedew'd with precious oil and vinegar
Already to appeaſe thy greedy wrath. Boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: Will the Count ſpeak with me?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: One of his Gentlemen is gone to inform him of your coming, Sir.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: There is no way left for me to compaſs the Fiſh-head, but by being preſently made known to the Duke.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: That will be hard Sir.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: When I have taſted of this ſacred diſh,
Then ſhall my bones reſt in my Fathers tomb
In peace; then ſhall I dye moſt willingly,
And as a diſh be ſerv'd to ſatisfie,
Deaths hunger, and I will be buried thus:
My Bier ſhall be a charger born by four,
The Coſſin where I lye, a powd'ring-tub,
Beſtrew'd with Lettice, and cool Sallad herbs,
My Winding-ſheet of Tanſies, the black Guard
Shall be my ſolemn Mourners, and inſtead
Of ceremonies, wholſom burial Prayers:
A printed dirge in rhyme, ſhall bury me.
Inſtead of tears, let them pour Capon ſauce upon my h • arſe,
And ſalt inſtead of duſt, Manchets for ſtones, for other glorious ſhields
Give me a Voider; and above my Hearſe
For a Trutch ſword, my naked knife ſtuck up.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Maſter, the Count's here.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: Where? my Lord I do beſeech you.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Y'are very welcome Sir, I pray you ſtand up, you ſhall dine with me.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: I do beſeech your Lordſhip by the love
I ſtill have born to your honourable houſe.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Sir, what need all this? you ſhall dine with me, I pray riſe.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Perhaps your Lordſhip takes me for one of theſe ſame fellows, that do as it were reſpect victuals.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Oh Sir by no means.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip has often promiſed, that whenſoever I ſhould affect greatneſs, your own hand ſhould help to raiſe me.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: And ſo much ſtill aſſure your ſelf of.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: And though I muſt confeſs, I have ever ſhun'd popularity, by the example of others, yet I do now feel my ſelf a little ambitious, your Lordſhip is great, and though young, yet a Privy Counſellor.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I pray you Sir leap into the matter, what would
You have me do for you?

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: I would intreat your Lordſhip to make me known to the Duke.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: When Sir?

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Suddainly my Lord, I would have you preſent me unto him this morning.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: It ſhall be done, but for what virtues, would you have him take notice of you?

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip ſhall know that preſently.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: 'Tis pity of this fellow, he is of good wit, and ſufficient underſtanding, when he is not troubled with this greedy worm.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: 'Faith, you may intreat him to take notice of me for any thing; for being an excellent Farrier, for playing well at Span-counter, or ſticking knives in walls, for being impudent, or for nothing; why may not I be a Favorite on the ſuddain? I ſee nothing againſt it.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Not ſo Sir, I know you have not the face to be a
Favourite on the ſuddain.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Why then you ſhall preſent me as a Gentleman well qualified, or one extraordinary ſeen in divers ſtrange myſteries.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: In what Sir? as how?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Marry as thus.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Yonder's my old Spirit, that hath haunted me daily, ever ſince I was a privy Counſellor, I muſt be rid of him, I pray you ſtay there, I am a little buſie, I will ſpeak with you preſently.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: You ſhall bring me in, and after a little other talk taking me by the hand, you ſhall utter theſe words to the Duke: May it pleaſe your grace, to take note of a Gentleman, well read, deeply learned, and throughly grounded in the hidden knowledge of all Sallads and Pot-herbs whatſoever.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: 'Twill be rare if you will walk before, Sir, I will overtake you inſtantly.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Your Lordſhips ever.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: This fellow is a kind of an informer, one that lives in Alehouſes and Taverns, and becauſe he perceives ſome worthy men in this Land, with much labour and great expence, to have diſcovered things dangerouſly hanging over the State; he thinks to diſcover as much out of the talk of drunkards in Tap-houſes: he brings me informations, pick'd out of broken words, in mens common talk, which, with his malicious miſ-application, he hopes will ſeem dangerous, he doth beſides, bring me the names of all the young Gentlemen in the City, that uſe Ordinaries, or Taverns, talking (to my thinking) only as the freedom of their youth teach them, without any further ends; for dangerous and ſeditious ſpirits; he is beſides, an arrant whoremaſter, as any is in Milan, of a Lay-man; I will not meddle with the Clergy: he is parcel Lawyer, and in my conſcience much of their religion, I muſt put upon him ſome piece of ſervice; come hither Sir, what have you to do with me?

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Little my Lord, I only come to know how your Lordſhip would employ me.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Obſerved you that Gentleman, that parted from me but now?

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: I ſaw him now my Lord.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I was ſending for you, I have talked with this man, and I do find him dangerous.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Is your Lordſhip in good earneſt?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Hark you Sir, there may perhaps be ſome within ear-ſhots.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Sirrah, will you venture your life, the Duke hath ſent the Fiſh-head to my Lord?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir if he have not, kill me, do what you will with me.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: How uncertain is the ſtate of all mortal things? I have theſe croſſes from my Cradle, from my very Cradle, inſomuch that I do begin to grow deſperate: Fortune I do deſpiſe thee, do thy worſt; yet when I do better gather my ſelf together, I do find it is rather the part of a wiſe man, to prevent the ſtorms of Fortune by ſtirring, than to ſuffer them by ſtanding ſtill, to pour themſelves upon his naked body, I will about it.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Who's within there?

Let this Gentleman out at the back door, forget not my inſtructions, if you find any thing dangerous; trouble not your ſelf to find out me, but carry your informations to the Lord Lucio, he is a man grave, and well experienced in theſe buſineſſes.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Your Lordſhips Servant.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Your Lordſhips ſervant.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Will it pleaſe your Lordſhip to walk?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Sir I was coming, I will overtake you.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I will attend you over againſt the Lord Gonderinoes houſe.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: You ſhall not attend there long.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Thither muſt I to ſee my Loves face, the chaſte
Virgin head
Of a dear Fiſh, yet pure and undeflowred,
Not known of man no rough bred countrey hand,
Hath once toucht thee, no Pandars withered paw,
Nor an un-napkin'd Lawyers greaſie fiſt,
Hath once ſlubbered thee: no Ladies ſupple hand,
Waſh'd o'er with Urine, hath yet ſeiz'd on thee
With her two nimble talents: no Court hand,
Whom his own natural filth, or change of air,
Hath bedeck'd with ſcabs, hath marr'd thy whiter grace:
Oh let it be thought lawful then for me,
To crop the flower of thy Virginity.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: This day I am for fools, I am all theirs,
Though like to our young wanton cocker'd heirs,
Who do affect thoſe men above the reſt,
In whoſe baſe company they ſtill are beſt:
I do not with much labour ſtrive to be
The wiſeſt ever in the company:
But for a fool, our wiſdom oft amends,
As enemies do teach us more than friends.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: MY Lord:

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Ha!

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Here's one hath brought you a preſent,

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: From whom? from a woman? if it be from a woman, bid him carrie it back, and tell her ſhe's a whore; what is it?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: A Fiſh head my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: What Fiſh head?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: I did not aske that my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Whence comes it?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: From the Court.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: O 'tis a Cods-head.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: No my Lord, 'tis ſome ſtrange head, it comes from the Duke.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Let it be carried to my Mercer, I doe owe him money for ſilks, ſtop his mouth with that.
Was there ever any man that hated his wife after death but I? and for her ſake all women, women that were created only for the preſervation of little dogs.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: My Lord the Count's ſiſter being overtaken in the ſtreets, with a great hail-ſtorm, is light at your gate, and deſires Rome till the ſtorm be overpaſt.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Is ſhe a woman?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: I my Lord I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I have none for her then: bid her get her gone, tell her ſhe is not welcome.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: My Lord, ſhe is now comming up.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: She ſhall not come up, tell her any thing; tell her I have but one great room in my houſe, and I am now in it at the cloſe ſtool.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: She's here my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: O impudence of women: I can keep dogs out of my houſe, or I can defend my houſe againſt theeves, but I cannot keep out women.
sp.stage: Enter Oriana, a waiting woman, and a Page.
sp.p: Now Madam, what hath your Ladyſhip to ſay to me?

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: My Lord, I was bold to crave the help of your houſe againſt the ſtorm.

sp.speaker: Gond,
sp.p: Your Ladyſhips boldneſs in coming will be impudence in ſtaying; for you are moſt unwelcome.

sp.speaker: Oriana.
sp.p: Oh my Lord!

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Doe you laugh? by the hate I bear to you, 'tis true.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Y'are merry my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Let me laugh to death if I be, or can be whilſt thou art here, or liveſt; or any of thy ſex.

sp.speaker: Oriana.
sp.p: I commend your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Gond,
sp.p: Doe you commend me? why doe you commend • e? I give you no ſuch cauſe: thou art a ſilthy impudent whore; a woman, a very woman.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Begot when thy father was drunk.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip hath a good wit.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: How? what have I a good wit?

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p:
Come my Lord, I have heard before of your Lord
• hip merry vain in jeſting againſt our Sex, which I being • eſirous to hear, made me rather chooſe your Lordſhips • ouſe, than any other, but I know I am welcome.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Let me not live if you be: me thinks it doth not • ecome you, to come to my houſe being a ſtranger to you, I have no woman in my houſe, to entertain you, nor to ſhew you your chamber; why ſhould you come to me? I have no Galleries, nor banqueting houſes, nor bawdy pictures to ſhew your Ladyſhip.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Believe me this your Lordſhips plaineſs makes me think my ſelf more welcome, than if you had ſworn by all the pretty Court oaths that are, I had been welcomer than your ſoul to your body.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Now ſhe's in, talking treaſon will get her out, I durſt ſooner undertake to talk an Intelligencer out of the room, and ſpeak more than he durſt hear, than talk a woman out of my company.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: My Lord the Duke being in the ſtreets, and the ſtorm continuing, is entred your gate, and now coming up.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: The Duke! now I know your Errand Madam; you have plots and private meetings in hand: why doe you chooſe my houſe? are you aſham'd to goe to't in the old coupling place, though it be leſs ſuſpicious here; for no Chriſtian will ſuſpect a woman to be in my houſe? yet you may do it cleanlyer there, for there is a care had of thoſe buſineſſes; and whereſoever you remove, your great maintainer and you ſhall have your lodgings directly oppoſite, it is but putting on your night-gown, and your ſhippers; Madam, you underſtand me?

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Before I would not underſtand him, but now he ſpeaks riddles to me indeed.

div.stage: Enter the Duke, Arrigo, and Lucio.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: 'Twas a ſtrange hail-ſtorm.

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.p: 'Twas exceeding ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Good morrow to your grace.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Good morrow Gonderino.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Juſtice great Prince.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Why ſhould you beg for juſtice, I never did you wrong; What's the offendor?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: A woman.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: I know your ancient quarrell againſt that Sex; but what hainous crime hath ſhe committed?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: She hath gone abroad.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What? it cannot be.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: She hath done it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: How? I never heard of any woman that did ſo before.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: If ſhe have not laid by that modeſty
That ſhould attend a Virgin, and, quite void
Of ſhame, hath left the houſe where ſhe was born,
As they ſhould never doe; let me endure
The pains that ſhe ſhould ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Hath ſhe ſo? Which is the woman?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: This, this.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How! Arrigo: Lucio:

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: I then it is a plot, no Prince alive
Shall force me make my houſe a Brothell houſe;
Not for the ſins, but for the womans ſake,
I will not have her in my doors ſo long:
Will they make my houſe as bawdy as their own are?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is it not Oriana?

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.l: 'Tis.
