sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Siſter to Count Valero?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: The very ſame.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: She that I love?

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.l: She that you love.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I do ſuſpect

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.l: So doe I.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: This fellow to be but a counterfeit,
One that doth ſeem to loath all woman-kind,
To hate himſelf, becauſe he hath ſome part
Of woman in him; ſeems not to endure
To ſee, or to be ſeen of any woman,
Only, becauſe he knows it is their nature
To wiſh to taſt that which is moſt forbidden:
And with this ſhew he may the better compaſs
(And with far leſs ſuſpition) his baſe ends.

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.l: Upon my life 'tis ſo.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And I doe know,
Before his ſlain wife gave him that offence,
He was the greateſt ſervant to that Sex
That ever was: what doth this Lady here
With him alone? why ſhould he rail at her to me?

sp.speaker: Lucio.
sp.l: Becauſe your grace might not ſuſpect.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: 'Twas ſo: I doe love her ſtrangely:
I would fain know the truth: counſell me.

div.stage: Enter Count, Lazarello, and his boy.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: It falls out better than we could expect Sir, that we ſhould find the Duke and my Lord Gondarino together; both which you deſire to be acquainted with.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: 'Twas very happy: Boy, goe down into the kitchen, and ſee if you can ſpy that ſame; I am now in ſome hope: I have me thinks a kind of fever upon me. Exit Boy.

A certain gloomineſs within me, doubting as it were, betwixt two paſſions: there is no young maid upon her wedding night, when her husband ſets firſt foot in the bed, bluſhes, and looks pale again, oftner than I doe now. There is no Poet acquainted with more ſhakings and quakings, towards the latter end of this new play, when he's in that caſe, that he ſtands peeping betwixt Curtains, ſo fearfully that a Bottle of Ale cannot be opened, but he thinks ſome body hiſſes, than I am at this inſtant.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Are they in conſultation? If they be, either my young Duke hath gotten ſome Baſtard, and is perſuading my Knight yonder to father the child, and marry the wench, or elſe ſome Cock-pit is to be built.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: My Lord! what Nobleman's that?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: His name is Lucio, 'tis he that was made a Lord at the requeſt of ſome of his friends for his wives ſake: he affects to be a great States-man, and thinks it conſiſts in night-caps and jewells, and tooth-picks?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: And what's that other?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: A Knight Sir, that pleaſeth the Duke to favour, and to raiſe to ſome extraordinary fortunes, he can make as good men as himſelf, every day in the week, and doth—

sp.speaker: Laz:
sp.p: For what was he raiſed?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Truely Sir, I am not able to ſay directly, for what; But for wearing of red breeches as I take it; he's a brave man, he will ſpend three Knighthoods at a Supper without Trumpets.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: My Lord I'll talk with him, for I have a friend, that would gladly receive the humor.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: If he have the itch of Knighthood upon him, let him repair to that Phyſitian, he'll cure him: but I will give you a note; is your friend fat or lean?

sp.speaker: Laz,
sp.p: Something fat.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: 'Twill be the worſe for him.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: I hope that's not material.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Very much, for there is an impoſt ſet upon Knighthoods, & your friend ſhall pay a Noble in the pound.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I doe not like examinations,
We ſhall find out the truth more eaſily,
Some other way leſs noted, and that courſe,
Should not be us'd, till we be ſure to prove
Some thing directly, for when they perceive
Themſelves ſuſpected, they will then provide
More warily to anſwer.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Doth ſhe know your Grace doth love her?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: She hath never heard it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Then thus my Lord. They whiſper again

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: What's he that walks alone ſo ſadly with his hands behind him?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: The Lord of the houſe, he that you deſire to be acquainted with, he doth hate women for the ſame cauſe that I love them.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: For that which Apes want: you perceive me Sir?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: And is he ſad? Can he be ſad that hath ſo rich a gem under his roof, as that which I doe follow.
What young Lady's that?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Which? Have I mine eye-ſight perfect, 'tis my ſiſter: did I ſay the Duke had a Baſtard? What ſhould ſhe make here with him and his Councell? She hath no papers in her hand to petition to them, ſhe hath never a husband in priſon, whoſe releaſe ſhe might ſue for: That's a fine trick for a wench; to get her husband clapt up, that ſhe may more freely, and with leſs ſuſpition, viſit the private ſtudies of men in authority. Now I doe diſcover their conſultation, you fellow is a Pander without all ſalvation: But let me not condemn her too raſhly without weighing the matter, ſhe's a young Lady, ſhe went forth early this morning with a waiting woman, and a Page, or ſo: This is no garden houſe, in my conſcience ſhe went forth with no diſhoneſt intent: for ſhe did not pretend going to any Sermon in the further end of the City: Neither went ſhe to ſee any odd old Gentlewoman, that mourns for the death of her husband, or the loſs of her friend, and muſt have young Ladys come to comfort her: thoſe are the damnable Bawds: 'Twas no ſet meeting certainly; for there was no wafer-woman with her theſe three days on my knowledge: I'll talk with her; Good morrow my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Y'are welcome Sir: here's her brother come now to doe a kind office for his ſiſter; is it not ſtrange?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I am glad to meet you here ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: I thank you good brother: and if you doubt of the cauſe of my coming I can ſatisfie you.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: No faith, I dare truſt thee, I doe ſuſpect thou art honeſt; for it is ſo rare a thing to be honeſt amongſt you, that ſome one man in an age, may perhaps ſuſpect ſome two women to be honeſt, but never believe it verily.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.p: Let your return be ſuddain.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: Unſuſpected by them.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: It ſhall; ſo ſhall I beſt perceive their Love, if there be any; Farewell.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Let me entreat your grace to ſtay a little,
To know a gentleman, to whom your ſelf
Is much beholding; he hath made the ſport
For your whole Court theſe eight years, on my knowledge.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: His name?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: I heard of him this morning, which is he?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Lazarello, pluck up thy ſpirits, thy Fortune is now raiſing, the Duke calls for thee, and thou ſhalt be acquainted with him.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: He's going away, and I muſt of neceſſity ſtay here upon buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: 'Tis all one, thou ſhalt know him firſt.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Stay a little, if he ſhould offer to take me away with him, and by that means I ſhould looſe that I ſeek for; but if he ſhould I will not goe with him.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Lazarello, the Duke ſtayes, wilt thou loſe this opportunity?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: How muſt I ſpeak to him?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: 'Twas well thought of: you muſt not talk to him as you doe to an ordinary man, honeſt plain ſence, but you muſt wind about him: for example, if he ſhould aske you what a clock, it is, you muſt not ſay; If it pleaſe your grace 'tis nine; but thus; thrice three a clock, ſo pleaſe my Sovereign: or thus;
sp.l: Look how many Muſes there doth dwell
Upon the ſweet banks of the learned Well;
And juſt ſo many ſtroaks the clock hath ſtruck,
And ſo forth; And you muſt now and then enter into a deſcription.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: I hope I ſhall doe it.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Come: May it pleaſe your grace to take note of a Gentleman, wel ſeen, deeply read, and throughly grounded in the hidden knowledge of all ſallets and potherbs whatſoever.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: I ſhall deſire to know him more inwardly.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I kiſs the Oxe-hide of your graces foot.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Very well: will your grace queſtion him a little?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: How old are you?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Full eight and twenty ſeveral Almanacks
Have been compiled, all for ſeveral years
Since firſt I drew this breath, four prentiſhips
Have I moſt truely ſerved in this world:
And eight and twenty times hath Phoebus Car
Run out his yearly courſe ſince—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: I underſtand you Sir.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.p: How like an ignorant Poet he talks.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: You are eight and twenty years old? what time of the day doe you hold it to be?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: About the time that mortals whet their knives
On threſholds, on their ſhooe ſols, and on ſtairs,
New bread is grating, and the teſty Cook
Hath much to doe now, now the Tables all.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: 'Tis almoſt dinner time?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Your grace doth apprehend me very rightly.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Your grace ſhall find him in your further conference
Grave, wiſe, courtly, and ſcholar like, underſtandingly read
In the neceſſities of the life of man.
He knows that man is mortal by his birth;
He knows that man muſt dye, and therefore live;
He knows that muſt live, and therefore eat,
sp.p: And if it ſhall pleaſe your grace, to accompany your ſelf with him, I doubt not, but that he will, at the leaſt, make good my commendations.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Attend us Lazarello, we doe want
Men of ſuch Action, as we have received you
Reported from your honorable friend.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Good my Lord ſtand betwixt me and my overthrow, you know I 'm ti'd here, and may not depart, my gracious Lord, ſo waightie are the buſineſses of mine own, which at this time do call upon me, that I will rather chuſe to die, than to neglect them.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Nay you ſhall perceive, beſides the virtues that I have alreadie inform'd you of, he hath a ſtomach which will ſtoop to no Prince alive.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Sir at your beſt leiſure, I ſhall thirſt to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: And I ſhall hunger for it.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Till then farewell all.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Count. Long life attend your Grace.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I doe not taſt this ſport, Arrigo Lucio.

sp.speaker: Arrigo.
sp.l: Luci. We doe attend.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: His grace is gone, and hath left his
sp.p: Hellen with me, I 'm no pander for him, neither can I be won with the hope of gain, or the itching deſire of taſting my Lords lecherie to him, to keep her at (my houſe) or bring her in diſguiſe, to his bed Chamber.
sp.l: The twyns of Adders, and of Scorpions
About my naked breſt, will ſeem to me
More tickling than thoſe claſpes, which men adore;
The luſtfull, dull, ill ſpirited embraces
Of women; The much prayſed Amazones,
Knowing their own infirmities ſo well,
Made of themſelves a people, and what men
They take amongſt them, they condemne to die,
Perceiving that their folly made them fit
To live no longer that would willingly
Come in the worthleſs preſence of a woman.
I will attend, and ſee what my young Lord will doe with his ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: My Lord; The fiſh head is gone again.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Wither?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I know whither my Lord.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Keep it from Lazarillo: Siſter ſhall I confer with you in private, to know the cauſe of the Dukes coming hither, I know he makes you acquainted with his buſineſs of State.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: I'll ſatisfie you brother, for I ſee you are jealous of me.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Now there ſhall be ſome courſe taken for her conveiance.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Lazarillo, thou art happy, thy carriage hath begot love, and that love hath brought forth fruits; thou art here in the company of a man honorable, that will help thee to taſt of the bounties of the Sea, and when thou haſt ſo done thou ſhalt retire thy ſelf unto the court, and there taſt of the delicates of the earth, and be great in the eyes of thy Sovereign: now no more ſhalt thou need to ſcramble for thy meat, nor remove thy ſtomach with the Court; But thy credit ſhall command thy hearts deſire, and all novelties ſhall be ſent as p • eſents unto thee.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Good Siſter, when you ſee your own time, wil you return home.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Yes brother, and not before.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: I will grow popu • ar in this State, and overthrow the fortunes of a number, that live by extortion.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Laz • rello, beſtirr thy ſelf nimbly and ſodainly, and hear me with patience to • ear.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Let me not fall from my ſelf; Speak I 'm bound.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: So art thou to revenge, when thou ſhalt hear the fiſh head is gone, and we know not whither.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: I will not curſe, nor ſwear, nor rage, nor rail,
Nor with contemptuous tongue, accuſe my Fate;
Though I might juſtly doe it, nor will I
Wiſh my ſelf uncreated for this evil:
Shall I entreat your Lordſhip to be ſeen
A little longer in the company
Of a man croſs'd by Fortune?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: I hate to leave my friend in his extremities.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: 'Tis noble in you, then I take your hand,
And doe proteſt, I doe not follow this
For any malice or for private ends,
But with a love, as gentle and as chaſt,
As that a brother to his ſiſter bears:
And if I ſee this fiſh head yet unknown;
The laſt words that my dying father ſpake,
Before his eye ſtrings brake, ſhall not of me
So often be remembred, as our meeting:
Fortune attend me, as my ends are juſt,
Full of pure love, and free from ſervile luſt.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Farwell my Lord, I was entreated to invite your
Lordſhip to a Lady's upſiting.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: O my ears, why Madam, will not you follow your brother? you are waited for by great men, heel bring you to him.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: I'm very well my Lord, you doe miſtake me, if you think I affect greater company than your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: What madneſs poſſeſſeth thee, that thou canſt imagine me a ſit man to entertain Lady's; I tell thee, I doe uſe to tear their hair, to kick them, and twindge their noſes, if they be not carefull in avoiding me.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip may diſcant upon your own behavior as pleaſe you, but I proteſt, ſo ſweet and courtly it appeares in my eye, that I mean not to leave you yet.

sp.speaker: Crnd.
sp.p: I ſhall grow rough,

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: A rough carriage is beſt in a man,
I'll dine with you my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Why I will ſtarve thee, thou ſhalt have nothing.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: I have heard of your Lordſhips nothing, I'll put that to the venture.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Well thou ſhalt have meat, I'll ſend it to thee.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I'll keep no ſtate my Lord, neither doe I mourn,
I'll dine with you.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Is ſuch a think as this allowed to live?
What power hath let the looſe upon the earth
To plague us for our Sins? Out of my doors.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I would your Lordſhip did but ſee how well
This fury doth become you, it doth ſhew
So neer the life, as it were natural.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: O thou damn'd woman, I will flie the vengeance
That hangs above thee, follow if thou dar'ſt. Exit Gondarino.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I muſt not leave this fellow, I will torment him to madneſs,
To teach his paſſions againſt kind to move,
The more he hates, the more I'll ſeem to love.

l.hi: Exeunt Oriana and Maid.

stage.hi: Enter Pandar and Mercer a citizen.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.l: Sir, what may be done by art ſhall be done,
I wear nor this black cloak for nothing.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Perform this, help me to this great heir by learning, and you ſhall want no black cloaks; taffaties, ſilkgrograns, ſattins and velvets are mine, they ſhall be yours; perform what you have promis'd, and you ſhall make me a lover of Sciences, I will ſtudy the learned languages, and keep my ſhop-book in Latine.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Trouble me not now, I will not fail you within this hour at your ſhop.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Let Art have her courſe.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: 'Tis well ſpoken, Madona.

sp.speaker: Mad.
sp.p: Haſt thou brought me any cuſtomers.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: What the devil do'ſt thou in black?

sp.speaker: Pa.
sp.p: As all ſolemn profeſſors of ſetled courſes, doe, cover my knavery with it: will you marry a citizen; Reaſonably rich, and unreaſonably fooliſh, ſilks in his ſhop, mony in his purſe, and no wit in his head?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Out upon him, I could have otherwiſe than ſo, there was a Knight ſwore he would have had me, if I would have lent him but forty ſhillings to have redeem'd his cloak, to goe to Church in.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Then your waſtcote wayter ſhall have him, call her in?

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.p: Anon?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.l: Get you to the Church, and ſhrive your ſelf,
For you ſhall be richly marryed anon.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: And get you after her, I will work upon my citizen whilſt he is warm, I muſt not ſuffer him to conſult with his neighbours, the openeſt fools are hardly couſened, if they once grow jealous. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: SAve me ye better powers, let me not fall
Between the loſe embracements of a woman:
Heaven, if my Sins be ripe grown to a head,
And muſt attend your vengeance: I beg not to divert my fate,
Or to reprive a while thy puniſhment
Only I crave, and hear me equall heavens,
Let not your furious rod, that muſt afflict me
Be that imperfect peece of nature,
That art makes up, woman, unſatiate woman.
Had we not knowing fouls, at firſt infus'd
To teach a difference, 'twixt extremes and goods?
Were we not made our ſelves, free, unconfin'd
Commanders of our own affections?
And can it be, that this moſt perfect creature,
This image of his maker, well ſquar'd man,
Should leave the handfaſt, that he had of grace,
To fall into a womans eaſie armes.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Now Venus, be my ſpeed, inſpire me with all the ſeverall ſubtil temptations, that thou haſt already given, or haſt in ſtore heareafter to beſtow upon our Sex: grant that I may apply that Phyſick that is moſt apt to work upon him: whether he will ſooneſt be mov'd with wantonneſs, ſinging, dancing; or being paſſionate, with ſcorn; or with ſad and ſerious looks, cunningly mingled with fighs, with ſmiling, liſping, kiſſing the hand, and making ſhort curt'ſies, Or with whatſoever other nimble power, he may be caught, doe thou infuſe into me, and when I have him, I will ſacrifice him up to thee.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: It comes again; New apparitions,
And tempting ſpirits: Stand and reveal thy ſelf,
Tell why thou followeſt me? I fear thee
As I fear the place thou cam'ſt from: Hell.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: My Lord, I 'm a woman, and ſuch a one—

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: That I hate truely, thou hadſt better bin a devill,

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Why my unpatient Lord?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Devils were once good, there they excell'd you woman.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Can ye be ſo uneaſie, can ye freeze, and
Such a ſummers heat ſo ready
To diſſolve? nay gentle Lord, turn not away in ſcorn,
Nor hold me leſs fair than I am: look on theſe cheeks,
They have yet enough of nature, true complexion,
If to be red and white, a forehead high,
An eaſie melting lip, a ſpeaking eye,
And ſuch a tongue, whoſe language takes the ear
Of ſtrict religion, and men moſt auſtere:
If theſe may hope to pleaſe, look here.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: This woman with entreaty wo'd ſhow all,
Lady there lies your way, I pray ye farewell.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Y'are yet too harſh, too diſſonant,
There's no true muſick in your words, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: What ſhall I give thee to be gone?
sp.p: Here's ta, and tha wants lodging, take my houſe, 'tis big enough, 'tis thine own, 'twill hold five leacherous Lords, and their lackies without diſcovery: there's ſtoves and bathing tubs.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Dear Lord: y'are too wild.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Shalt have a Doctor too, thou ſhat, 'bout ſix and twentie, 'tis a pleaſing age; Or I can help thee to a handſome Vſher: or if thou lack'ſt a page, I'll give thee one, preethee keep houſe, and leave me.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I doe confeſs I 'm too eaſie, too much woman,
Not coy enough to take affection,
Yet I can frown and nip a paſſion,
Even in the bud: I can ſay
Men pleaſe their preſent heats; Then pleaſe to leave us.
I can hold off, and, by my Chymick power,
Draw Sonnets from the melting lovers brain;
Ayme's and Elegies: yet to you my Lord
My Love, my better ſelf, I put theſe off,
Doing that office, not befits our ſex,
Entreat a man to love;
Are ye not yet relenting? ha'ye blood and Spirit
In thoſe veins? ye are no image, though ye be as hard
As marble: ſure ye have no liver, if ye had,
'Twould ſend a lively and deſiring heat
To every member; Is not this miſerable?
A thing ſo truely form'd, ſhapt out by Symetry,
Has all the organs that belong to man,
And working too, yet to ſhew all theſe
Like dead motions moving upon wyers?
Then good my Lord, leave off what you have been,
And freely be what you were firſt intended for, a man.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Thou art a precious peece of ſlie damnation,
I will be deaf, I will lock up my ears,
Tempt me not, I will not love; If I doe.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Then I'll hate you.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Let me be 'nointed with hony, and turn'd into the Sun,
To be ſtung to death with horſe-flies,
Hear'ſt thou, thou breeder, here I'll ſit,
And, in deſpight of thee, I will ſay nothing.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Let me with your fair patience, ſit beſide you.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Madam, Lady, tempter, tongue, woman, ayr.
Look to me, I ſhall kick; I ſay again,
Look to me I ſhall kick.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: I cannot think your better knowledg can uſe a woman ſo uncivilly.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: I cannot think, I ſhall become a coxcombe,
To ha'my hair curl'd, by an idle finger,
My cheeks turn Tabers, and be plaid upon,
Mine eyes lookt babies in, and my noſe blowd to my hand,
I ſay again I ſhall kick, ſure I ſhall.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: 'Tis but your outſide that you ſhew, I know your mind
Never was guilty of ſo great a weakneſs,
Or could the tougues of all men joyn'd together.
Poſſeſs me with a thought of your diſlike
My weakneſs were above a womans, to fall off
From my affection, for one crack of thunder,
O wo'd you could love, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I wo'd thou wouldſt ſit ſtill, and ſay nothing: what mad-man let thee loſe to do more miſchief than a douſen whirlwinds, keep thy hands in thy muff, and warm the idle worms in thy fingers ends: will ye be doing ſtill? will no entreating ſerve ye? no lawfull warning? I muſt remove and leave your Ladyſhip; Nay never hope to ſtay me, for I will run, from that Smooth, Smiling, Witching, Couſening, Tempting, Damning face of thine, as far as I can find any land, where I will put my ſelf into a daily courſe of Curſes for thee, and all thy Familie.

sp.speaker: Oria,
sp.l: Nay good my Lord ſit ſtill, I'll promiſe peace
And fold mine Armes up, let but mine eye diſcourſe;
Or let my voyce, ſet to ſome pleaſing cord, found out
The ſullen ſtrains of my neglected love.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Sing till thou crack thy treble-ſtring in peeces,
And when thou haſt done, put up thy pipes and walk,
Doe any thing, ſit ſtill and tempt me not.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: I had rather ſing at doors for bread, than ſing to this fellow, but for hate: if this ſhould be told in the Court, that I begin to woe Lords, what a troop of the untruſt nobilitie ſhould I have at my lodging to morrow morning?

body.head: SONG.
body.l: Come ſleep, and with the ſweet deceiving,
Look me in delight a while,
Let ſome pleaſing Dreams beguile
All my fancies; That from thence,
I may feel an influence,
All my powers of care bereaving.
Though but a ſhadow, but a ſliding,
Let me know ſome little Ioy,
We that ſuffer long anoy
Are contented with a thought
Through an idle fancie wrought
O let my joyes, have ſome abiding.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Have you done your waſſayl? 'tis a handſome drowſie dittie I'll aſſure ye, now I had as leave hear a Cat cry, when her tail is cut off, as hear theſe lamentations, theſe lowſie love-layes, theſe bewailements: you think you have caught me Lady, you think I melt now, like a diſh of May butter, and run, all into brine, and paſſion? yes, yes, I 'm taken, look how I croſs my arms, look pale, and dwyndle, and wo'd cry, but for ſpoyling my face; we muſt part, nay we'll avoyd all Ceremony, no kiſſing Lady, I deſire to know your Ladiſhip no more; death of my ſoul the Duke!

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: God keep your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Gond,
sp.l: From thee and all thy ſex.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I'll be the Clark, and crie, Amen,
Your Lordſhips ever aſſured enemie Oriana.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: ALL the days good, attend your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: We thank you Gondarino, is it poſſible?
Can belief lay hold on ſuch a miracle,
To ſee thee, one that hath cloyſt'red up all paſſion,
sp.p: Turn'd wilfull votary, and forſworn converſe with women, in company and fair diſcourſe, with the beſt beauty of Millain?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: 'Tis true, and if your Grace that hath the ſway
Of the whole State, will ſuffer this lude ſex,
Theſe women: to purſue us to our homes,
Not to be prayd, not to be rail'd away,
But they will woe, and dance, and ſing,
And, in a manner, looſer than they are
By nature (which ſhould ſeem impoſſible)
To throw their armes, on our unwilling necks.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: No more, I can ſee through your viſlore, diſſemble it no more.
Doe not I know thou haſt us'd all Art,
To work upon the poor ſimplicitie
Of this yong Maid, that yet hath known none ill?
Thinkeſt that damnation will fright thoſe that wo • e
From oaths, and lies? But yet I think her chaſt,
And will from thee, before thou ſhalt apply
Stronger temptations, bear her hence with me.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: My Lord, I ſpeak not this to gain new grace,
But howſoever you eſteeme my words,
My love and dutie will not ſuffer me
To ſee you favour ſuch a proſtitute,
And I ſtand by dumb; Without Rack, Torture,
Or Strappado, I unrip my ſelf:
sp.p: I doe confeſs I was in company with that pleaſing peece of frailtie, that we call woman; I doe confeſs after along and tedious ſeige, I yielded.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Forward.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Faith my Lord to come quickly to the point, the woman you ſaw with me is a whore; An arrant whore.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Was ſhe not Count Valores, Siſter?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Yes, that Count Valores Siſter is naught.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Thou dar'ſt not ſay ſo.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Not if it be diſtaſting to your Lordſhip, but give me freedome, and I dare maintain, ſhe ha's imbrac'd this body, and grown to it as cloſe, as the hot youthfull vine to the elme.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Twice have I ſeen her with thee, twice my thoughts were prompted by mine eye, to hold thy ſtrictneſs falſe and impoſterous: Is this your mewing up, your ſtrict retirement, your bitterneſs and gaul againſt that ſex? Have I not heard thee ſay, thou wouldſt ſooner meet the Baſilisks, dead doing eye, than meet a woman for an object? Look it be true you tell me, or by our countries Saint your head goes off: if thou prove a whore, no womans face ſhall ever move me more.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: So, ſo, 'tis as 't ſhould be, are women grown ſo mankind? Muſt they be wooing, I have a plot ſhall blow her up, ſhe flyes, ſhe mounts; I'll teach her Ladyſhip to dare my fury, I will be known, and fear'd, and more truely nated of women than an Eunuch.
She's here again, good gaul be patient, for I muſt diſſemble.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Now my cold, froſty Lord, my woman-Hater, you that have ſworn an everlaſting hate to all our ſex: by my troth good Lord, and as I'm yet a maid, my thought 'twas excellent ſport to hear your honor ſwear out an Alphabet, chafe nobly like a Generall, kick like a reſty Jade, and make ill faces: Did your good Honor think I was in love? where did I firſt begin to take that heat? From thoſe two radiant eyes, that piercing ſight? oh they were lovely, if the balls ſtood right; and there's a leg made out of a dainty ſtaff, Where, the Gods be thanked, there is calf enough.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Pardon him Lady, that is now a convert.
Your beauty, like a Saint hath wrought this wonder.

sp.speaker: Oriana.
sp.p: Alaſs, ha's it been prick'd at the heart? is the ſtomach come down? will it rail no more at women, and tall 'em Divells, ſhe Cats, and Goblins?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: He that ſhall marry thee, had better ſpend the poor remainder of his days in a dung-barge, for two pence a week, and find him ſelf.

Down again Spleen, I prethee down again, ſhall I find favour Lady? ſhall at length my true unfeigned penitence get pardon for my harſh unſeaſoned follies? I'm no more an Atheiſt, no I doe acknowledge, that dread powerfull Deity, and his all quic'kning heats burn in my breaſt: oh be not as I was, hard unrelenting; but as I'm, be partner of my fires.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Sure we have ſtore of Larks, the Skies will not hold up long, I ſhould have look'd as ſoon for Froſt in the dog days, or another Inundation, as hop'd this ſtrange converſion above miracle: let me look upon your Lordſhip; is your name Gondarino? are you Millains Generall, that great Bug-bear bloody-bones, at whoſe name all women, from the Lady to the Landreſs, ſhake like a cold fit?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Good patience help me, this Fever will inrage my blood again: Madam I'm that man; I'm even he that once did owe unreconcil'd hate to you, and all that bear the name of woman: I'm the man that wrong'd your Honor to the Duke: I'm the man that ſaid you were unchaſt, and proſtitute, yet I'm he that dare deny all this.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Your big Nobility is very merry.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Lady 'tis true that I have wrong'd you thus,
And my contrition is as true as that,
Yet have I found a means to make all good again,
I doe beſeech your beautie, not for my ſelf,
My merits are yet in conception,
But for your honors ſafety and my zeal
Retire a while, while I unſay my ſelf unto the Duke,
And caſt out that ill Spirit I have poſſeſt him with,
I have a houſe conveniently private.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.p: Lord, thou haſt wrong'd my innocence, but thy confeſſion hath gain'd thee faith.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: By the true honeſt ſervice, that I owe theſe eyes ſtrangely,
My meaning is as ſpotleſs as my faith.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: The Duke doubt mine honor? a may judge
'Twill not be long, before I'll be enlarg'd again.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: A day or two.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Mine own ſervants ſhall attend me.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Your Ladyſhips command is good.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Look you be true. Exit Oriana.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Elſe let me loſe the hopes my ſoul aſpires to: I will be a ſcourge to all females in my life, and after my death, the name of Gondarino, ſhall be terrible to the mighty women of the earth; They ſhall ſhake at my name, and at the ſound of it, their knees ſhall knock together; And they ſhall run into Nunneries, for they and I are beyond all hope irreconcilable: for if I could endure an ear with a hole in't, or a pleated lock, or a bare headed Coachman, that ſits like a ſign where great Ladys are to be ſold within; agreement betwixt us, were not to be diſpaired of; if I could be but brought to endure to ſee women, I would have them come all once a week, and kiſs me, as Witches doe the devill, in token of homage: I muſt not live here; I will to the Court, and there purſue my plot; when it hath took, women ſhall ſtand in awe, but of my look. Exit

div.head: Actus Tertius.
Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter two Intelligencers, diſcovering treaſon in the Courtiers words.

sp.speaker: 1. Intel.
sp.p: THere take your ſtanding, be cloſe and vigilant, here will I ſet my ſelf, and let him look to his language, a ſhall know the Duke has more ears in Court than two.

sp.speaker: 2. Int.
sp.p: I'll quote him to a tittle, let him ſpeak wiſely, and plainly, and as hidden as a can, or I ſhall cruſh him, a ſhall not ſcape charracters, though a ſpeak Babel, I ſhall cruſh him: we have a Fortune by this ſervice hanging over us, that within this year or two, I hope we ſhall be called to be examiners, wear politick gowns garded with copper lace, making great faces full of fear and office, our labors may deſerve this.

sp.speaker: 1. Int.
sp.p: I hope it ſhall: why has not many men been raiſed from this worming trade, firſt to gain good acceſs to great men, then to have commiſſions out for ſearch, and laſtly, to be worthily nam'd at a great Arraignment: yes, and why not we? They that endeavor well deſerve their Fee.
Cloſe, cloſe, a comes: mark well, and all goes well.

div.stage: Enter Count, Lazarello, and his Boy.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Farewell my hopes, my Anchor now is broken,
Farewell my quondam joys, of which no token
Is now remaining, ſuch is the ſad miſchance,
Where Lady Fortune leads the ſlipp'ry dance.
Yet at the length, let me this favour have,
Give me my wiſhes, or a wiſhed grave.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: The gods defend ſo brave and valiant maw,
Should ſlip into the never ſatiate jaw
Of black Deſpair; no, thou ſhalt live and know
Thy full deſires, hunger thy ancient foe,
Shall be ſubdued; thoſe guts that daily tumble
Through ayr and appetite, ſhall ceaſe to rumble:
And thou ſhalt now at length obtain thy diſh,
That noble part, the ſweet head of a fiſh.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Then am I greater than the Duke.

sp.speaker: 2. Int.
sp.l: There, there's a notable peece of treaſon, greater than the Duke, mark that.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: But how, or where, or when this ſhall be compas'd, is yet out of my reach.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: I am ſo truely miſerable, that might
I be now knockt oth' head, with all my heart
I would forgive a dog-killer.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Yet doe I ſee through this confuſedneſs ſome little comfort.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: The plot my Lord, as er'e you came of a woman, diſcover.

sp.speaker: 1. Int.
sp.p: Plots, dangerous plots, I will deſerve by this moſt liberally.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: 'Tis from my head again.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: O that it would ſtand me, that I might fight, or have ſome venture for it, that I might be turn'd looſe, to try my fortune amongſt the whole frie in a Colledge, or an Inn of Court; or ſcramble with the priſoners in the dungeon; nay were it ſet down in the outward court, And all the Guard about it in a ring,
sp.l: With their knives drawn, which were a diſmall ſight,
And after twenty leiſurely were told,
I to be let looſe only in my ſhirt,
To trie the valour, how much of the ſpoyl,
I would recover from the enemies mouths:
Upon country people in progreſs time, and
Wilt thou loſe this opinion, for the cold head of a Fiſh?
I ſay, let it goe: I'll help thee to as good a diſh of meat.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: God let me not live, if I doe not wonder,
Men ſhould talk ſo propanely:
But it is not in the power of looſe words,
Of any vain or misbeleeving man,
To make me dare to wrong thy purity.
Shew me but any Lady in the Court,
That hath ſo full an eye, ſo ſweet a breath,
So ſoft and white a fleſh: this doth not lie
In almond gloves, nor ever hath bin waſht
In artificiall baths: no traveller
That hath brought doctor home with him, hath dar'd
With all his waters, powders, Fucuſſes,
To make thy lovely corps ſophiſticate.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: I have it, 'tis now infus'd, be comforted.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Can there be that little hope yet left in nature? ſhall I once more erect up Trophies? Shall I enjoy the ſight of my dear Saint, and bleſs my pallate with the beſt of creatures, ah good my Lord, by whom I breathe again, ſhall I receive this Being?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Sir I have found by certain calculation, and ſetled revolution of the ſtars, the Fiſh is ſent by the Lord Gondarino to his Mercer, now 'tis a growing hope to know where 'tis.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: O'tis far above the good of women, the Pathick cannot yield more pleaſing titilation.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: But how to compaſs it ſearch, caſt about, and bang your brains, Lazarello, thou art too dull and heavy to deſerve a bleſſing.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: My Lord, I will not be idle; now Lazarello, think, think, think,

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Yonder's my informer
And his fellow with table books, they nod at me
Upon my life, they have poor Lazarello, that beats
His brains about no ſuch waighty matter, in for
Treaſon before this—

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: My Lord, what doe you think, if I ſhould ſhave my ſelf,
Put on midwives apparell, come in with a hand-kercher,
And beg a piece for a great bellied woman, or a ſick child?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Good, very good.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Or corrupt the waiting prentiſe to betray the reverſion.

sp.speaker: 1. Inte.
sp.p: There's another point in's plot, corrupted with money; to betray: ſure 'tis ſome Fort a means: mark, have a care.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: And 'twere the bare vinegar 'tis eaten with, it would in ſome ſort ſatisfie nature: but might I once attain the diſh it ſelf, though I cut out my means through ſword and fire, through poiſon, through any thing that may make good my hopes.

sp.speaker: 2. Int.
sp.p: Thanks to the gods, and our officiouſneſs, the plots diſcover'd, fire, ſteel, and poiſon, burn the Palace, kill the Duke and poiſon his privie Councell.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: To the mercers, let me ſee: how, if before we can attain the means, to make up our acquaintance, the fiſh be eaten?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: If it be eaten, here he ſtands, that is the moſt dejected, moſt unfortunate, miſerable, accurſed, forſaken ſlave this Province yields: I will not ſure outlive it, no I will dye bravely, and like a Roman; and after death, amidſt the Elizian ſhades, I'll meet my love again.

sp.speaker: 1. In.
sp.p: I will dye bravely, like a Roman: have a care, mark that, when he hath done all, he will kill himſelf.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Will nothing eaſe your appetite but this?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: No could the Sea throw up his vaſtneſs,
And offer free his beſt inhabitants: 'twere not ſo much as a bare temptation to me.

sp.speaker: Count,
sp.l: If you could be drawn to affect Beef, Veniſon, or Fowl, 'twould be far the better.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: I doe beſeech your Lordſhips patience,
I doe confeſs that in this heat of blood,
I have contemn'd all dull and groſſer meats,
But I proteſt I doe honor a Chine of Beef,
I doe reverence a loyn of Veal,
But good my Lord, give me leave a little to adore this:
But my good Lord, would your Lordſhip, under color of taking up ſome ſilks, goe to the Mercers, I would in all humilitie attend your honor, where we may be invited, if Fortune ſtand propitious.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Sir you ſhall work me as you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Let it be ſuddenly, I doe beſeech your Lordſhip, 'tis now upon the point of dinner time.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I am all yours.

sp.speaker: 1. In.
sp.l: Come let us confer,
sp.p: Imprimis he ſaith, like a blaſphemous villain, he 's greater than the Duke, this peppers him, and there were nothing elſe.

sp.speaker: 2. In.
sp.p: Then he was naming plots; did you not hear?

sp.speaker: 1. In.
sp.p: Yes but he fell from that unto diſcovery, to corrupt by money, and ſo attain.

sp.speaker: 2. In.
sp.p: I, I, he meant ſome Fort, or Cyttadell the Duke hath, his very face betraid his meaning, O he is very ſubtile and a dangerous knave, but if he deal a Gods name, we ſhall worm him

sp.speaker: 1. In.
sp.p: But now comes the Stroak, the fatall blow, Fire, Sword and Poyſon, O Canibal, thou bloody Canibal.

sp.speaker: 2. In.
sp.p: What had become of this poor ſtate, had we not been?

sp.speaker: 1. In.
sp.p: Faith it had lyen buried in his own aſhes; had not a greater hand been in't.

sp.speaker: 2. In.
sp.p: But note the raſcalls reſolution, after th'acts done, becauſe he wo'd avoid all fear of torture, and couſen the Law, he wo'd kill himſelf; was there ever the like danger brought to light in this age? ſure we ſhall merit much, we ſhall be able to keep two men a peece, and a two hand-ſword between us, we will live in favour of the State, betray our ten or twelve treaſons a week, and the people ſhall fear us: come, to the Lord Lucio, the Sun ſhall not goe down till he be hang'd. Exeunt.

div.head: Actus Tertius.
Scaena quarta.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: LOok to my ſhop, and if there come ever a Scholar in black, let him ſpeak with me; we that are ſhopkeepers in good trade, are ſo peſter'd, that we can ſcarce pick out an hour for our mornings meditation: and howſoever we are all accounted dull, and common jeſting ſtocks for your gallants; There are ſome of us doe not deſerve it: for, for my own part, I doe begin to be given to my book, I love a ſcholar with my heart, for queſtionleſs there are merveilous things to be done by Art: why Sir, ſome of them will tell you what is become of horſes, and ſilver ſpoons, and will make wenches dance naked to their beds: I am yet unmarried, and becauſe ſome of our neighbours are ſaid to be Cuckolds, I will never be married without the conſent of ſome of theſe ſcholars, that know what will come of it.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Are you buſie Sir?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Never to you Sir, nor to any of your coat.
Sir is there any thing to be done by Art, concerning the great heir we talk'd on?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Will ſhe, nill ſhe: ſhe ſhall come running into my houſe at the farther corner, in Sa. Marks ſtreet, betwixt three and four.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Betwixt three and four? ſhe's brave in cloaths, is ſhe not?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p:
O rich! rich! where ſhould I get cloaths to dreſs her in? Help me invention: Sir, that her running through the
ſtreet may be leſs noted, my Art more ſhown, and your fear to ſpeak with her leſs, ſhe ſhall come in a white waſtcoat, And—

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: What ſhall ſhe?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: And perhaps torn ſtockings, ſhe hath leſt her old wont elſe.

sp.speaker: Pren.
sp.p: Sir my Lord Gond. hath ſent you a rare fiſh head.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: It comes right, all things ſute right with me ſince I began to love ſcholars, you ſhall have it home with you againſt ſhe come: carrie it to this Gentleman's houſe.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: The fair white houſe at the farther corner at S. Marks ſtreet, make haſte, I muſt leave you too Sir, I have two hours to ſtudy; buy a new Accedence, and ply your book, and you ſhall want nothing that all the ſcholars in the Town can doe for you. Exit Pander.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Heaven proſper both our ſtudies, what a dull ſlave was I before I fell in love with this learning? not worthy to tread upon the earth, & what freſh hopes it hath put in to me? I doe hope within this twelve-month to be able by Art to ſerve the Court with ſilks, and not undoe my ſelf; to truſt Knights, and yet get in my money again; to keep my wife brave, and yet ſhe keep no body elſe ſo.
Your Lordſhip is moſt honourably welcome in regard of your Nobility; but moſt eſpecialy in regard of your ſcholarſhip: did your Lordſhip come openly?

sp.speaker: Count,
sp.p: Sir this cloak keeps me private, beſides no man will ſuſpect me to be in the company of this Gentleman, with whom, I will deſire you to be acquainted, he may prove a good cuſtomer to you.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: For plain ſilks and velvets.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Are you ſcholaſticall?

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Something addicted to the Muſes.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I hope they will not diſpute.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: You have no skill in the black Art.

sp.speaker: Pren.
sp.p: Sir yonder's a Gentleman enquires haſtily for Count Valore,

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: For me? what is he?

sp.speaker: Pren.
sp.p: One of your followers my Lord I think.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Let him come in.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Shall I talk with you in private Sir?

div.stage: Enter a Maſſenger with a Letter to the Count, he reads.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Count, come to the Court your buſineſs calls you thither, I will goe, farewell Sir, I will ſee your ſilks ſome other time: Farewell Lazarillo.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Will not your Lordſhip take a peice of Beef with me?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Sir I have greater buſineſs than eating; I will leave this Gentleman with you.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: No, no, no, no: now doe I feel that ſtrain'd ſtrugling within me, that I think I could propheſie.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: The Gentleman is meditating.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Hunger, valour, love, ambition are alike pleaſing, and let our Philoſophers ſay what they will, are one kind of heat, only hunger is the ſafeſt: ambition is apt to fall; love and valour are not free from dangers; only hunger, begotten of ſome old limber Courtier, in pan'de hoſe, and nurs'd by an Attourneys wife; now ſo thriven, that he need not fear to be of the great Turks guard: is ſo free from all quarrels and dangers, ſo full of hopes, joyes, and ticklings, that my life is not ſo dear to me as his acquaintance.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir the Fiſh head is gone.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.l: Then be thou henceforth dumb, with thy ill-boding voice.
Farewell Millain, farewell Noble Duke,
Farewell my fellow Courtiers all, with whom,
I have of yore made many a ſcrambling meal
In corners, behind Araſſes, on ſtairs;
And in the action oftentimes have ſpoil'd,
Our Doublets and our Hoſe with liquid ſtuff:
Farewell you luſty Archers of the Guard,
To whom I now doe give the bucklers up,
And never more with any of your coat
Will eat for wagers, now you happy be,
When this ſhall light upon you, think on me:
You ſewers, carvers, uſhers of the court
Sirnamed gentle for your fair demean,
Here I doe take of you my laſt farewell,
May you ſtand ſtifly in your proper places, and execute your offices aright.
Farewell you Maidens, with your mother eke,
Farewell you courtly Chaplains that be there
All good attend you, may you never more
Marry your Patrons Ladys wayting-woman,
But may you raised be by this my fall
May Lazarillo ſuffer for you all.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.p: Sir I was hearkning to you.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I will hear nothing, I will break my knife, the Enſign of my former happy ſtate, knock out my teeth, have them hung at a Barbers, and enter into Religion.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Why Sir, I think I know whither it is gone.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: See the raſhneſs of man in his nature, whither? I do unſay all that I have ſaid, go on, go on: Boy, I humble my ſelf and follow thee; Farewell Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Not ſo Sir, you ſhall take a piece of Beef with me.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I cannot ſtay.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: By my ſay but you ſhall Sir, in regard of your love to learning, and your kill in the black Art.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I do hate learning, and I have no skill in black Art; I would I had.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Why your deſire is ſufficient to me, you ſhall ſtay.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: The moſt horrible and deteſted curſes that can be imagined, light upon all the profeſſors of that Art; may they be drunk, and when they goe to conjure, and reel in the Circle, may the ſpirits by them rais'd, tear 'em in pieces, and hang their quarters on old broken walls and Steeple tops.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: This ſpeech of yours, ſhews you to have ſome skill in the Science, wherefore in civilitie, I may not ſuffer you to depart empty.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: My ſtomach is up, I cannot endure it, I will fight in this quarrell as ſoon as for my Prince.
Room, make way:
Hunger commands, my valour muſt obey.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: IS the Duke private?

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.p: He is alone, but I think your Lordſhip may enter. Exit Count

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Who's with the Duke?

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.p:
The Count is new gone in, but the Duke will come
forth, before you can be weary of waiting.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I will attend him here.

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.p: I muſt wait without the door. Exit Arrigo.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Doth he hope to clear his Siſter? ſhe will come no more to my houſe, to laugh at me: I have ſent her to a habitation, where when ſhe ſhall be ſeen, it will ſet a gloſs upon her name; yet upon my ſoul I have beſtow'd her amongſt the pureſt hearted creatures of her ſex, and the freeſt from diſſimulation; for their deeds are all alike, only they dare ſpeak, what the reſt think: the women of this age, if there be any degrees of compariſon amongſt their ſex, are worſe than thoſe of former times; for I have read of women, of that truth, ſpirit, and conſtancy; that were they now living, I ſhould endure to ſee them: but I fear the writers of the time belied them, for how familiar a thing is it with the Poets of our age, to extoll their whores, which they call Miſtreſſes, with heavenly praiſes? but I thank their furies, and their craz'd brains, beyond belief: nay, how many that would fain ſeem ſerious, have dedicated grave Works to Ladies, toothleſs, hollow-ey'd, their hair ſhedding, purple fac'd, their nails apparently coming off; and the bridges of their noſes broken down, and have call'd them the choice handy works of nature, the patterns of perfection, and the wonderment of Women. Our Women begin to ſwarm like Bees in the Summer: as I came hither, there was no pair of ſtairs, no entry, no lobby, but was peſtred with them: methinks there might be ſome courſe taken to deſtroy them.

div.stage: Enter Arrigo, and an old deaf countrey Gentlewoman ſuitor to the Duke.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: I do accept your money, walk here, and when the Duke comes out, you ſhall have ſit opportunity to deliver your petition to him.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: I thank you heartily, I pray you who's he that walks there?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: A Lord, and a Soldier, one in good favour with the Duke; if you could get him to deliver your Petition —

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: What do you ſay, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: If you could get him to deliver your petition for you, or to ſecond you, 'twere ſure.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: I hope I ſhall live to requite your kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: You have already. Exit Arri.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: May it pleaſe your Lordſhip—

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: To conſider the eſtate—

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Of a poor oppreſſed countrey Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: No, it doth not pleaſe my Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Firſt and formoſt, I have had great injury, then I have been brought up to the Town three times.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: A pox on him, that brought thee to the Town.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: I thank your good Lordſhip heartily; though I cannot hear well, I know it grieves you; and here we have been delaid, and ſent down again, and fetch'd up again, and ſent down again, to my great charge: and now at laſt they have fetch'd me up, and five of my daughters —

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Enough to damn five worlds.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Handſome young women, though I ſay it, they are all without, if it pleaſe your Lordſhip I'll call them in.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Five Women! how many of my ſences ſhould I have left me then? call in five Devils firſt.
No, I will rather walk with thee alone,
And hear thy tedious tale of injury,
And give thee anſwers; whiſper in thine ear,
And make thee underſtand through thy French hood:
And all this with tame patience.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: I ſee your Lordſhip does believe, that they are without, and I perceive you are much mov'd at our injury: here's a paper will tell you more.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Away.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: It may be you had rather hear me tell it viva voce, as they ſay.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Oh no, no, no, no, I have heard it before.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Then you have heard of enough injury, for a poor Gentlewoman to receive.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Never, never, but that it troubles my conſcience, to wiſh any good to theſe woman; I could afford them to be valiant, and able, that it might be no diſgrace for a Soldier to beat them.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: I hope your Lordſhip will deliver my petition to his grace, and you may tell him withal—

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: What? I will deliver any thing againſt my ſelf, to be rid on thee.
That yeſterday about three a clock in the after noon, I met my adverſary.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Give me thy paper, he can abide no long tales.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: 'Tis very ſhort my Lord, and I demanding of him—

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I'll tell him that ſhall ſerve thy turn.

sp.speaker: Gentlew,
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I'll tell him that ſhall ſerve thy turn, begone: man never doth remember how great his offences are, till he do meet with one of you, that plagues him for them: why ſhould Women, above all other creatures that were created for the benefit of man, have the uſe of ſpeech? or why ſhould any deed of theirs, done by their fleſhly appetites, be diſgraceful to their owners? nay, why ſhould not an act done by any beaſt I keep, againſt my conſent, diſparage me as much as that of theirs?

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Here's ſome few Angels for your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Again? yet more torments?

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Indeed you ſhall have them.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Keep off.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: A ſmall gratuity for your kindneſs.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Hold away.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Why then I thank your Lordſhip, I'll gather them up again, and I'll be ſworn, it is the firſt money that was refus'd ſince I came to the Court.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: What can ſhe deviſe to ſay more?

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Truly I would have willingly parted with them to your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I believe it, I believe it.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: But ſince it is thus—

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: More yet.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: I will attend without, and expect an anſwer.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Do, begone, and thou ſhalt expect, and have any thing, thou ſhalt have thy anſwer from him; and he were beſt to give thee a good one at firſt, for thy deaf importunity, will conquer him too, in the end.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: God bleſs your Lordſhip, and all thar favour a poor diſtreſſed countrey Gentlewoman. Exit Gentlew.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: All the diſeaſes of man light upon them that doe, and upon me when I do. A week of ſuch days, would either make me ſtark mad or tame me: yonder other woman that I have ſure enough, ſhall anſwer for thy ſins: dare they incenſe me ſtill, I will make them fear as much to be ignorant of me and my moods, as men are to be ignorant of the law they live under. Who's there? My bloud grew cold, I began to fear my Suiters return; 'tis the Duke.

div.stage: Enter the Duke and the Count.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: I know her chaſte, though ſhe be young and free,
And is not of that forc'd behaviour
That many others are, and that this Lord,
Out of the boundleſs malice to the ſex,
Hath thrown this ſcandal on her.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Fortune befriended me againſt my Will, with this good old countrey gentlewoman; I beſeech your grace, to view favourably the petition of a wronged Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What Gondarino, are you become a petitioner for your enemies?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p:
My Lord, they are no enemies of mine, I confeſs, the better to recover my deeds, which ſometimes were looſe
enough, I pretended it, as it is wiſdom, to keep cloſe our incontinence, but ſince you have diſcover'd me, I will no more put on that vizard, but will as freely open all my thoughts to you, as to my Confeſſor.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What ſay you to this?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: He that confeſſes he did once diſſemble,
I'll never truſt his words: can you imagine
A Maid, whoſe beauty could not ſuffer her
To live thus long untempted, by the nobleſt,
Richeſt, and cunningſt Maſters in that Art
And yet hath ever held a fair repute;
Could in one morning, and by him be brought,
To forget all her virtue, and turn whore?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: I would I had ſome other talk in hand,
Than to accuſe a Siſter to her Brother:
Nor do I mean it for a publick ſcandal,
Unleſs by urging me you make it ſo.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I will read this at better leiſure:

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Where is the Lady?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: At his houſe.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: No, ſhe is departed thence,

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Whither?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Urge it not thus, or let me be excus'd,
If what I ſpeak betray her chaſtity,
And both increaſe my ſorrow, and your own?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Fear me not ſo, if ſhe deſerve the fame
Which ſhe hath gotten, I would have it publiſht,
Brand her my ſelf, and whip her through the City:
I wiſh thoſe of my bloud that doe offend,
Should be more ſtrictly puniſh, than my foes.
Let it be prov'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Gondarino, thou ſhalt prove it, or ſuffer worſe than ſhe ſhould do.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Then pardon me, if I betray the faults
Of one, I love more dearly than my ſelf,
Since opening hers, I ſhall betray mine own:
But I will bring you where ſhe now intends
Not to be virtuous, pride and wantonneſs,
That are true friends indeed, though not in ſhew,
Have entr'd on her heart, there ſhe doth bathe,
And ſleek her hair, and practiſe cunning looks
To entertain me with; and hath her thoughts
As full of luſt, as ever you did think
Them full of modeſty.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Gondarino, lead on, we'll follow thee.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: HEre hope I to meet my Citizen, and hopes he to meet his Scholar; I am ſure I am grave enough, to his eyes, and knave enough to deceive him: I am believ'd to conjure, raiſe ſtorms, and devils, by whoſe power I can do wonders; let him believe ſo ſtill, belief hurts no man; I have an honeſt black cloak, for my knavery, and a general pardon for his foolery, from this preſent day, till the day of his breaking. Is't not a miſery, and the greateſt of our age, to ſee a handſome, young, fair enough, and well mounted wench, humble her ſelf, in an old ſtammel petticoat, ſtanding poſſeſt of no more fringe, than the ſtreet can allow her: her upper parts ſo poor and wanting, that ye may ſee her bones through her bodies: ſhooes ſhe would have, if our Captain were come over, and is content the while to devote her ſelf to antient ſlippers. Theſe premiſſes well conſidered, Gentlemen, will move, they make me melt I promiſe ye, they ſtirr me much: and wer't not for my ſmooth, ſoft, ſilken Citizen, I would quit this tranſitory Trade, get me an everlaſting Robe, ſear up my conſcience, and turn Serjeant. But here he comes, is mine as good as prize: Sir Pandarus be my ſpeed, ye are moſt fitly met Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: And you as well encount'red, what of this heir? hath your Books been propitious?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Sir, 'tis done, ſhe's come, ſhe's in my houſe, make your ſelf apt for Courtſhip, ſtroke up your ſtockings, looſe not an inch of your legs goodneſs; I am ſure ye wear ſocks.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: There your Books ſail ye Sir, in truth I wear no ſocks.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: I would you had, Sir, it were the ſweeter grace for your legs; get on your Gloves, are they perfum'd.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: A pretty waſh I'll aſſure you.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: 'Twill ſerve: your offers muſt be full of bounty, Velvets to furniſh a Gown, Silks for Peticoats, and Foreparts Shag for lining; forget not ſome pretty Jewel to faſten, after ſome little compliment? if ſhe deny this courteſie, double your bounties, be not wanting in abundance, fulneſs of gifts, link'd with a pleaſing tongue, will win an Anchorite. Sir, ye are my friend, and friend to all that profeſſes good Letters; I muſt not uſe this office elſe, it fits not for a Scholar, and a Gentleman: thoſe ſtockins are of Naples, they are ſilk.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Ye are again beſide your Text, Sir, they're of the beſt of Wooll, and the clipped Jerſey.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Sure they are very dear.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Nine ſhillings, by my love to learning.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Pardon my judgement, we Scholars uſe no other objects, but our Books.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: There is one thing entomb'd in that grave breaſt, that makes me equally admire it with your Scholarſhip.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Sir, but that in modeſty I am bound not to affect mine own commendation, I would enquire it of you.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.p: Sure you are very honeſt; and yet ye have a kind of modeſt fear to ſhew it: do not deny it, that face of yours is a worthy, learned modeſt face.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Sir, I can bluſh.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Virtue and grace are always pair'd together: but I will leave to ſtirr your bloud Sir, and now to our buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Forget not my inſtructions.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I apprehend ye Sir, I will gather my ſelf together with my beſt phraſes, and ſo I ſhall diſcourſe in ſome ſort takingly.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: This was well worded Sir, and like a Scholar.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: The Muſes favour me as my intents are virtuous; Sir, ye ſhall be my Tutor, 'tis never too late Sir, to love Learning.
When I can once ſpeak true Latine—

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: What do you intend Sir?

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Marry I will then begger all your bawdy Writers, and undertake, at the peril of my own invention, all Pageants, Poeſies, for Chimneys, Speeches for the Dukes enterrainment, whenſoever and whatſoever; nay I will build, at mine own charge, an Hoſpital, to which ſhall retire all diſeaſed opinions, all broken Poets, all Proſe-men that are fall'n from ſmall ſence, to meer Letters; and it ſhall be lawful for a Lawyer, if he be a civil man, though he have undone others and himſelf by the language, to retire to this poor life, and learn to be honeſt.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Sir, ye are very good, and very charitable: ye are a true pattern for the City Sir.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.p: Sir, I doe know ſufficiently, their Shop-books cannot ſave them, there is a farther end—

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Oh Sir, much may be done by manuſcript.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I do confeſs it Sir, provided ſtill they be Canonical, and I have ſome worthy hands ſet to 'em for probation: but we forget our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Sir, enter when you pleaſe, and all good language tip your tongue.

sp.speaker: Merc.
sp.p: All that love Learning pray for my good ſucceſs.

div.head: Actus Quartus.
Scaena Tertia.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: WHereabouts are we?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir, by all tokens this is the houſe, bawdy I am ſure, becauſe of the broken windows, the Fiſh head is within; if ye dareventure, here you may ſurprize it.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: The miſery of man may fitly be compar'd to a Didapper, who when ſhe is under water, paſt our ſight, and indeed can ſeem no more to us, riſes again; ſhakes but her ſelf, and is the ſame ſhe was, ſo is it ſtill with tranſitory man, this day: oh but an hour ſince, and I was mighty, mighty in knowledge, mighty in my hopes, mighty in bleſſed means, and was ſo truly happy, that I durſt have ſaid, live Lazarello., and be ſatisfied: but now—

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir, ye are yet afloat, and may recover, be not your own wreck, here lies the harbor, goe in and ride at eaſe.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Boy, I am receiv'd to be a Gentleman, a Courtier, and a man of action, modeſt, and wiſe, and be it ſpoken with thy reverence, Child, abounding virtuous; and wouldſt thou have a man of theſe choiſe habits, covet the cover of a bawdy-houſe? yet if I goe not in, I am but—

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: But what Sir?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Duſt boy, but duſt, and my ſoul unſatisfied, ſhall haunt the keepers of my bleſſed Saint, and I will appear.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: An aſs to all men; Sir, theſe are no means to ſtay your appetite, you muſt reſolve to enter.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Were not the houſe ſubject to Martial Law—

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: If that be all, Sir, ye may enter, for ye can know nothing here that the Court is ignorant of, only the more eyes ſhall look upon you, for there they wink one at anothers faults.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: If I doe not.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Then ye muſt beat fairly back, again fall to your phyſical meſs of porridge, and the twice ſack'd carkaſs of a Capon: Fortune may favour you ſo much, to ſend the bread to it: but it's a meet venture, and money may be put out upon it.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I will go in and live; pretend ſome love to the Gentlewoman, ſcrew my ſelf in affection, and ſo be ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: This Fly is caught, is maſh'd already, I will ſuck him, and lay him by.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Muffle your ſelf in your cloak by any means, 'tis a receiv'd thing among gallants, to walk to their leachery, as though they had the rheum, 'twas well you brought not your horſe.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Why Boy?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Faith Sir. 'tis the faſhion of our Gentry, to have their horſes wait at door like men, while the beaſts their Maſters, are within at rack and manger, 'twould have diſcover'd much.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I will lay by theſe habits, forms, and grave reſpects of what I am, and be my ſelf; only my appetite, my fire, my ſoul, my being, my dear appetite ſhall go along with me, arm'd with whoſe ſtrength, I fearleſs will attempt the greateſt danger dare oppoſe my fury: I am reſolv'd where ever that thou art, moſt ſacred diſh, hid from unhallow'd eyes, to find thee out.
sp.l: Be'ſt thou in Hell, rap't by Proſerpina,
To be a rival in black Pluto's love;
Or mov'ſt thou in the heavens, a form Divine:
Laſhing the lazie Sphear,
Or if thou be'ſt return'd to thy firſt Being,
Thy mother Sea, then will I ſeek thee forth.
Earth, Air, nor Fire,
Nor the black ſhades below ſhall bar my ſight
So daring is my powerful appetite.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir, you may ſave this long voyage, and take a ſhorter cut: you have forgot your ſelf, the fiſh head's here, your own imaginations have made you mad.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Term it a jealous ſury, good my boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Faith Sir term it what you will, you muſt uſe other terms before you can get it.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: The looks of my ſweet love are fair,
Freſh and feeding as the air.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sir, you forget your ſelf.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Was never ſeen ſo rare a head,
Of any Fiſh alive or dead.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Good Sir remember: this is the houſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Curſed be he that dare not venture.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Pity your ſelf, Sir, and leave this fury

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: For ſuch a prize, and ſo I enter.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Dun's i'th' mire, get out again how he can:
My honeſt gallant, I'll ſhew you one trick more
Than e'er the fool your father dream'd of yet.

l.hi: Madona Julia?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: What news my ſweet rogue, my dear ſins-broker, what good news?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: There is a kind of ignorant thing,
Much like a Courtier, now gone in.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Is he gallant?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: He ſhines not very gloriouſly, nor does he wear one skin perfum'd to keep the other ſweet; his coat is not in Or, nor does the world run yet on wheels with him; he's rich enough, and has a ſmall thing follows him, like to a boat tyed to a tall ſhips tail: give him entertainment, be light, and flaſhing like a Meteor, hug him about the neck, give him a kiſs, and liſping cry, good Sir; and he's thine own, as faſt as he were tied to thine arms by Indenture.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: I dare doe more than this, if he be o'th' true Court cut; I'll take him out a leſſon worth the Learning: but we are but their Apes; what's he worth?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Be he rich, or poor; if he will take thee with him, thou maiſt uſe thy trade from Conſtables, and Marſhals: who hath been here ſince I went out?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: There is a Gentlewoman ſent hither by a Lord, ſhe's a piece of dainty ſtuff my rogue, ſmooth and ſoft, as new Sattin; ſhe was never gumm'd yet boy, nor fretted.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Where lies ſhe?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: She lies above, towards the ſtreet, not to be ſpoke with, but by my Lord that ſent her, or ſome from him, we have in charge from his ſervants.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Peace, he comes out again upon diſcovery; up with all your Canvas, hale him in; and when thou haſt done, clap him aboard bravely, my valiant Pinnace.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Begone, I ſhall doe reaſon with him.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Are you the ſpecial beauty of this houſe?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Sir, you have given it a more ſpecial regard by your good language, than theſe black brows can merit,

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Lady, you are fair

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Fair Sir: I thank ye? all the poor means I have left to be thought grateful, is but a kiſs, and ye ſhall have it Sir.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Ye have a very moving lip.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Prove it again Sir, it may be your ſenſe was ſet too high, and ſo over-wrought it ſelf.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: 'Tis ſtill the ſame; how far may ye hold the time to be ſpent Lady?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Four a clock, Sir.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I have not eat to day.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: You will have the better ſtomach to your ſupper; in the mean time I'll feed you with delight.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: 'Tis not ſo good upon an empty ſtomach: if it might be without the trouble of your houſe, I would eat?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Sir, we can have a Capon ready,

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: The day?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: 'Tis Friday, Sir.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I do eat little fleſh upon theſe days.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Come ſweet, ye ſhall not think on meat; I'll drown it with a better appetite.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I feel it work more ſtrangely, I muſt eat.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: 'Tis now too late to ſend; I ſay ye ſhall not think on meat: if ye do, by this kiſs I'll be angry.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I could be far more ſprightful, had I eaten, and more laſting.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: What will you have Sir? name but the Fiſh, my Maid ſhall bring it, if it may be got,

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Methinks your houſe ſhould not be ſo unfurniſh'd, as not to have ſome pretty modicum.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: It is now: but cou'd ye ſtay till ſupper?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Sure I have offended highly, and much, and my afflictions makes it manifeſt, I will retire henceforth, and keep my chamber, live privately, and dye forgotten.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Sir, I muſt crave your pardon, I had forgot my ſelf; I have a diſh of meat within, and it is fiſh; I think this Dukedom holds not a daintier: 'tis an Ʋmbranoes head.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: This kiſs is yours, and this.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Hoe within there? cover the board, and ſet the Fiſh head on it.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Now am I ſo truly happy, ſo much above all fate and fortune, that I ſhould deſpiſe that man, durſt ſay, remember Lazarello, thou art mortal.

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: This is the villain, lay hold on him.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Gentlemen, why am I thus intreated? what is the nature of my crime?

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: Sir, though you have carried it a great while privately, and (as you think) well; yet we have ſeen you Sir, and we do know thee Lazarello, for a Traitor.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: The gods defend our Duke,

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: Amen, Sir, Sir, this cannot ſave that ſtiff neck from the halter.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Gentlemen, I am glad you have diſcover'd him, he ſhould not have eaten under my roof for twenty pounds; and ſurely I did not like him, when he call'd for Fiſh,

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: My friends, will ye let me have that little favour—

sp.speaker: 1 Int.
sp.p: Sir, ye ſhall have Law, and nothing elſe.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: To let me ſtay the eating of a bit or two, for I proteſt I am yet faſting.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: I'll have no Traitor come within my houſe.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Now could I wiſh my ſelf I had been a Traitor, I have ſtrength enough for to endure it, had I but patience: Man thou art but graſs, thou art a bubble, and thou muſt periſh.
sp.l: Then lead along, I am prepar'd for all:
Since I have loſt my hopes, welcome my fall.

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.l: Away Sir.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: As thou haſt hope of man, ſtay but this diſh this two hours, I doubt not but I ſhall be diſcharged: by this light I will marry thee.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: You ſhall marry me firſt then.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I do contract my ſelf unto thee now, before theſe Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: I'll preſerve it till you be hang'd or quitted.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Thanks, thanks.

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: Away, away, you ſhall thank her at the gallows.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Adieu, adieu.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: If he live I'll have him, if he be hang'd, there's no loſs in it. Exit.

div.stage: Enter Oriana and her waiting woman, looking out at a window.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Haſt thou provided one to bear my Letter to my brother?

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: I have enquir'd, but they of the houſe will ſuffer no Letter nor meſſage to be carried from you, but ſuch as the Lord Gondarino ſhall be acquainted with: truly Madam I ſuſpect the houſe to be no better than it ſhould be.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.p: What doſt thou doubt?

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: Faith I am loth to tell it, Madam.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.p: Out with it, 'tis not true modeſty to fear to ſpeak that thou doſt think.

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: I think it to be one of theſe Bawdy houſes.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.p: 'Tis no matter wench, we are warm in it, keep thou thy mind pure, and upon my word, that name will do thee no hurt: I cannot force my ſelf yet to fear any thing; when I do get out, I'll another encounter with my Woman-Hater. Here will I ſit. I may get ſight of ſome of my friends, it muſt needs be a comfort to them to ſee me here.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Are we all ſufficiently diſguis'd? for this houſe where ſhe attends me, is not to be viſited in our own ſhapes.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: We are not our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.p: I know the houſe to be ſinful enough, yet I have been heretofore, and durſt now, but for diſcovering of you, appear here in my own likeneſs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Where's Lucio?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: My Lord, he ſaid the affairs of the Common-wealth would not ſuffer him to attend always.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Some great ones queſtionleſs that he will handle.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Come, let us enter.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: See how Fortune ſtrives to revenge my quarrel upon theſe women, ſhe's in the window, were it not to undoe her, I ſhould not look upon her.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Lead us Gondarino.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Stay; ſince you force me to diſplay my ſhame,
Look there, and you my Lord, know you that face?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Is't ſhe?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: It is.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: 'Tis ſhe, whoſe greateſt virtue ever was
Diſſimulation; ſhe that ſtill hath ſtrove
More to ſin cunningly, than to avoid it:
She that hath ever ſought to be accounted
Moſt virtuous, when ſhe did deſerve moſt ſcandal:
'Tis ſhe that itches now, and in the height
Of her intemperate thoughts, with greedy eyes
Expects my coming to allay her Luſt:
Leave her; forget ſhe's thy ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Stay, ſtay.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I am as full of this, as thou canſt be,
The memory of this will eaſily
Hereafter ſtay my looſe and wandring thought
From any Woman.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: This will not down with me, I dare not truſt this fellow.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Leave her here, that only ſhall be her puniſhment, never to be fetcht from hence; but let her uſe her trade to get her living.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Stay good my Lord, I do believe all this, as great men as I, have had known whores to their Siſters, and have laught at it: I would fain hear how ſhe talks, ſince ſhe grew thus light: will your grace make him ſhew himſelf to her, as if he were now come to ſatisfie her longing! whilſt we, unſeen of her, over-hear her wantonneſs, let's make our beſt of it now, we ſhall have good mirth.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Do it Gondarino.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I muſt; fortune aſſiſt me but this once.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Here we ſhall ſtand unſeen, and near enough.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Madam, Oriana.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Who's that? oh! my Lord?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Shall I come up?

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Oh you are merry, ſhall I come down?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: It is better there.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: What is the confeſſion of the lye you made to the Duke, which I ſcarce believe, yet you had impudence enough to do? did it not gain you ſo much faith with me, as that I was willing to be at your Lordſhips beſtowing, till you had recover'd my credit, and confeſt your ſelf a lyar, as you pretended to do? I confeſs I began to fear you, and deſir'd to be out of your houſe, but your own followers forc'd me hither.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: 'Tis well ſuſpected, diſſemble ſtill, for there are ſome may hear us.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: More tricks yet, my Lord? what houſe this is I know not, I only know my ſelf: it were a great conqueſt, if you could faſten a ſcandal upon me: 'ſaith my Lord, give me leave to write to my brother?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come down.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Come down.

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: If it pleaſe your Grace, there's a back door.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: Come meet us there then.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: It ſeems you are acquainted with the houſe.

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: I have been in it.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: She ſaw you and diſſembled.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Sir, we ſhall know that better,

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Bring me unto her, if I prove her not
To be a ſtrumpet, let me be contemn'd
Of all her ſex. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: NOw whilſt the young Duke follows his delights,
We that do mean to practiſe in the State,
Muſt pick our times, and ſet our faces in,
And nod our heads as it may prove moſt fit
For the main good of the dear Common-wealth:
Who's within there?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: My Lord?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Secretary, fetch the Gown I uſe to read Petitions in, and the Standiſh I anſwer French Letters with: and call in the Gentleman that attends: Exit Serv.
sp.l: Little know they that do not deal in State,
How many things there are to be obſerv'd,
Which ſeem but little; yet by one of us
(Whoſe brains do wind about the Common-wealth)
Neglected, cracks our credits utterly.
sp.p: Sir, but that I do preſume upon your ſecreſie, I would not have appear'd to you thus ignorantly attir'd without a tooth-pick in a ribbond, or a Ring in my bandſtring.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip ſend for me?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I did: Sir, your long practice in the State, under a great man, hath led you to much experience.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Luc.
