sp.p: Suffer not your modeſty to excuſe it: in ſhort, and in private, I deſire your direction, I take my ſtudy already to be furniſht after a grave and wiſe method.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: What will this Lord do?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: My Book-ſtrings are ſutable, and of a reaching colour.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: How's this?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: My Standiſh of Wood, ſtrange and ſweet, and my ſore-flap hangs in the right place, and as near Machiavel's, as can be gathered by tradition.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Are there ſuch men as will ſay nothing abroad, and play the fools in their Lodgings? this Lord muſt be followed: and hath your Lordſhip ſome new made words to ſcatter in your ſpeeches in publick, to gain note, that the hearers may carry them away, and diſpute of them at dinner?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I have Sir: and beſides, my ſeveral Gowns and Caps agreeable to my ſeveral occaſions.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: 'Tis well, and you have learn'd to write a bad hand, that the Readers may take pains for it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Yes Sir, and I give out I have the palſie.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Good, 'twere better though, if you had it: your Lordſhip hath a Secretary, that can write fair, when you purpoſe to be underſtood.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: 'Faith Sir I have one, there he ſtands, he hath been my Secretary theſe ſeven years, but he hath forgotten to write.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.p: If he can make a writing face, it is not amiſs, ſo he keep his own counſel: your Lordſhip hath no hope of the Gout?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Uh, little Sir, ſince the pain in my right foot left me.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: 'Twill be ſome ſcandal to your wiſdom, though I ſee your Lordſhip knows enough in publick buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I am not imploy'd (though to my deſert) in occaſions forreign, nor frequented for matters domeſtical.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Not frequented? what courſe takes your Lordſhip?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: The readieſt way, my door ſtands wind, my Sectetary knows I am not denied to any.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: In this (give me leave) your Lordſhip is out of the way: make a back door to let out Intelligencers; ſeem to be ever buſie, and put your door under keepers, and you ſhall have a troop of Clients ſweating to come at you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I have a back door already, I will henceforth be buſie, Secretary, run and keep the door. Exit Secretary.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: This will fetch 'um?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I hope ſo.

sp.speaker: Secr.
sp.p: My Lord, there are ſome require acceſs to you, about weighty affairs of State.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Already?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: I told you ſo.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: How weighty is the buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Secr.
sp.p: Treaſon my Lord.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Sir, my debts to you for this are great.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: I will leave your Lordſhip now.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Sir, my death muſt be ſuddain, if I requite you not: at the back door good Sir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: I will be your Lordſhips Intelligencer for once.

sp.speaker: Secr.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Let 'em in, and ſay I am at my ſtudy.

div.stage: Enter Lazarello, and two Intelligencers, Lucio being at his ſtudy.

sp.speaker: 1 Int.
sp.p: Where is your Lord?

sp.speaker: Secr.
sp.p: At his ſtudy, but he will have you brought in.

sp.speaker: Laza.
sp.p: Why Gentlemen, what will you charge me withal?

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: Treaſon, horrible treaſon, I Hope to have the leading of thee to priſon, and prick thee on i'th' arſe with a Halbert: to have him hang'd that ſalutes thee, and call all thoſe in queſtion that ſpit not upon thee.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p:
My thred is ſpun, yet might I but call for this diſh
of meat at the gallows, inſtead of a Pſalm, it were to be endur'd: the Curtain opens, now my end draws on.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Gentlemen, I am not empty of weighty occaſions at this time; I pray you your buſineſs.

sp.speaker: 1 Int.
sp.p: My Lord, I think we have diſcover'd one of the moſt bloudy Traitors, that ever the world held.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Signior Lazarillo, I am glad ye are one of this diſcovery, give me your hand.

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: My Lord, that is the Traitor.

sp.speaker: Luc,
sp.p: Keep him off, I would not for my whole eſtate have touchd him.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Peace Sir, I know the devil is at your tongue's end, to furniſh you with ſpeeches: what are the particulars you charge him with?

div.stage: They deliver a paper to Lucio, who reads.

sp.speaker: Both Int.
sp.p: We conferr'd our Notes, and have extracted that, which we will juſtifie upon our oaths.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: That he would be greater than the Duke, that he had caſt plots for this, and meant to corrupt ſome to betray him, that he would burn the City, kill the Duke, and poiſon the Privy Council; and laſtly kill himſelf. Though thou deſerv'ſt juſtly to be hang'd, with ſilence yet I allow thee to ſpeak, be ſhort.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: My Lord, ſo may my greateſt wiſh ſucceed,
So may I live, and compaſs what I ſeek,
As I had never treaſon in my thoughts,
Nor ever did conſpire the overthrow
Of any creatures but of brutiſh beaſts,
Fowls, Fiſhes, and ſuch other humane food,
As is provided for the good of man.
If ſtealing Cuſtards, Tarts, and Florentines
By ſome late Statute be created Treaſon;
How many fellow-Courtiers can I bring,
Whoſe long attendance and experience,
Hath made them deeper in the plot than I?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Peace, ſuch hath ever been the clemency of my gracious Maſter the Duke, in all his proceedings, that I had thought, and thought I had thought rightly; that malice would long e'r this have hid her ſelf in her Den, ahd have turn'd her own ſting againſt her own heart: but I well perceive, that ſo froward is the diſpoſition of a deprav'd nature, that it doth not only ſeek revenge, where it hath receiv'd injury, but many times thirſt after their deſtruction, where it hath met with benefits.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: But my good Lord —

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: Let's gagg him.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Peace again, but many times thirſt after deſtruction, where it hath met with benefits; there I left: Such, and no better are the buſineſs that we have now in hand.

sp.speaker: 1 Int.
sp.p: He's excellently ſpoken.

sp.speaker: 1 Int.
sp.p: He'll wind a Traitor I warrant him,

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: But ſurely methinks, ſetting aſide the touch of conſcience, and all inward convulſions.

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: He'll be hang'd, I know by that word.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip may conſider—

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Hold thy peace: thou canſt not anſwer this ſpeech: no Traitor can anſwer it: but becauſe you cannot anſwer this ſpeech, I take it you have confeſs'd the Treaſon.

sp.speaker: 1 Int.
sp.p: The Count Valore was the firſt that diſcover'd him, and can witneſs it; but he left the matter to your Lordſhip's grave conſideration.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I thank his Lordſhip, carry him away ſpeedily to the Duke.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: Now Lazarillo thou art tumbl'd down
The hill of fortune, with a violent arm;
All plagues that can be, Famine, and the Sword
Will light upon thee, black deſpair will boil
In thy deſpairing breaſt, no comfort by,
Thy friends far off, thy enemies are nigh.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Away with him, I'll follow you, look you pinion him, and take his money from him, leſt he ſwallow a ſhilling, and kill himſelf.

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: Get thou on before. Exeunt.

div.head: Actus Quintus.
Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter the Duke, the Count, Gondarino, and Arrigo.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: NOw Gondarino, what can you put on now
That may deceive us?
Have ye more ſtrange illuſions, yet more miſts,
Through which, the weak eye may be led to error:
What can ye ſay that may do ſatisfaction
Both for her wrong'd honor, and your ill?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: All I can ſay, or may, is ſaid already:
She is unchaſte, or elſe I have no knowledge,
I do not breathe, nor have the uſe of ſenſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Dare ye be yet ſo wilful, ignorant of your own nakedneſs? did not your ſervants
sp.l: In mine own hearing confeſs
They brought her to that houſe we found her in,
Almoſt by force: and with a great diſtruſt
Of ſome enſuing hazard?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: He that hath begun ſo worthily,
It fits not with his reſolution
sp.p: To leave off thus, my Lord, I know theſe are but idle proofs.
sp.l: What ſays your Lordſhip to them?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Count, I dare yet pronounce again, thy Siſter is not honeſt.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: You are your ſelf my Lord, I like your ſetledneſs.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Count, thou art young, and unexperienc'd in the dark, hidden ways of Women: Thou dar'ſt affirm with confidence, a Lady of fifteen may be a Maid.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Sir, if it were not ſo, I have a Siſter would ſet near my heart.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Let her ſit near her ſhame, it better fits her: call back the bloud that made our ſtream in nearneſs, and turn the Current to a better uſe; 'tis too much mudded, I do grieve to know it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Dar'ſt thou make up again, dar'ſt thou turn face, knowing we know thee, haſt thou not been diſcover'd openly? did not our ears hear her deny thy courtings? did we not ſee her bluſh with modeſt anger, to be ſo overtaken by a trick; can ye deny this Lord?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Had not your Grace, and her kind brother
Been within level of her eye,
You ſhould have had a hotter volley from her,
More full of bloud and fire, ready to leap the window where ſhe ſtood.
So truly ſenſual is her appetite.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Sir, Sir, theſe are but words and tricks, give me the proof.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.l: What need a better proof than your Lordſhip?
I am ſure ye have lain with her my Lord.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: I have confeſt it Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I dare not give thee credit without witneſs.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p:
Does your grace think we carry ſeconds with us, to ſearch us, and ſee fair play: your Grace hath been ill tutor'd in the buſineſs; but if you hope to try her truly, and ſatisfy your ſelf what frailty is, give her the Teſt: do not remember Count ſhe is your Siſter; nor let my Lord the Duke believe ſhe is fair; but put her to it without hope or pity, then ye ſhall ſee that golden form flie off, that all eyes wonder at for pure and fixt, and under't baſe bluſhing Copper; metall not worth the
meaneſt honor: you ſhall behold her then my Lord tranſparent, look through her heart, and view the ſpirits how they leap, and tell me then I did belie the Lady.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: It ſhall be done: come Gondarino bear us company,
We do believe thee: ſhe ſhall die, and thou ſhalt ſee it.
sp.stage: Enter Lazarello, two Intelligencers, and Guard.
sp.l: How now my friends, who have you guarded hither?

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: So pleaſe your Grace we have diſcover'd a villain and a Traitor: the Lord Lucio hath examin'd him, and ſent him to your Grace for Judgement.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: My Lord, I dare abſolve him from all ſin o • Treaſon: I know his moſt ambition is but a diſh of meat; which he hath hunted with ſo true a ſcent, that he deſerveth the Collar not the Halter.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Why do they bring him thus bound up? the poor man had more need have ſome warm meat, to comfort his cold ſtomach.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Your Grace ſhall have the cauſe hereafter, when you ſhall laugh more freely:
But theſe are call'd Informers: men that live by Treaſon, as Rat-catchers do by poiſon.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Would there were no heavier prodigies hung over us, than this poor fellow, I durſt redeem all perils ready to pour themſelves upon this State, with a cold Cuſtard.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Your Grace might do it without danger to your perſon.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: My Lord, if ever I intended treaſon againſt your Perſon, or the State, unleſs it were by wiſhing from your Table ſome diſh of meat, which I muſt needs confeſs, was not a ſubjects part: or coveting by ſtealth, ſups from thoſe noble bottles, that no mouth, keeping allegiance true, ſhould dare to taſte: I muſt confeſs, with more than covetous eye, I have beheld thoſe dear conceal'd diſhes, that have been brought in by cunning equipage, to wait upon your Graces pallat: I do confeſſe, out of this preſent heat, I have had Stratagems and Ambuſcado's; but God be thank'd they have never took.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Count, this buſineſs is your own; when you have done, repair to us. Exit Duke.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I will attend your Grace: Lazarello, you are at liberty, be your own man again; and if you can be maſter of your wiſhes, I wiſh it may be ſo.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I humbly thank your Lordſhip: I muſt be unmannerly, I have ſome preſent buſineſs, once more I heartily thank your Lordſhip. Exit Lazarillo.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Now even a word or two to you, and ſo farewell; you think you have deſerv'd much of this State by this diſcovery: y'are a ſlaviſh people, grown ſubject to the common courſe of all men. How much unhappy were that noble ſpirit, could work by ſuch baſer gains? what miſery would not a knowing man put on with willingneſs, e'r he ſee himſelf grown fat and full fed, by fall of thoſe you riſe by? I do diſcharge ye my attendance; our healthful State needs no ſuch Leeches to ſuck out her bloud.

sp.speaker: 1 Int.
sp.p: I do beſeech your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: 2 Int.
sp.p: Good my Lord.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Go learn to be more honeſt, what I ſee you work your means from honeſt induſtry,
sp.l: I will be willing to accept your labours:
Till then I will keep back my promis'd favours:
Here comes another remnant of folly:
sp.p: I muſt diſpatch him too. Now Lord Lucio, what buſineſs brings you hither?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Faith Sir, I am diſcovering what will become of that notable piece of treaſon, intended by that Varlet Lazarillo; I have ſent him to the Duke for judgement.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Sir, you have perform'd the part of a moſt careful Stateſman, and let me ſay it to your face, Sir, of a Father to this State: I would wiſh you to retire, and inſconce your ſelf in ſtudy: for ſuch is your daily labour, and our fear, that our loſs of an hour may breed our overthrow.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Sir, I will be commanded by your judgement, and though I find it a trouble ſcant to be waded through, by theſe weak years: yet for the dear care of the Common-wealth, I will bruiſe my brains, and confine my ſelf to much vexation.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Go, and maiſt thou knock down Treaſon like an Ox.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Amen. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Have I ſpoke thus much in the honor of Learning? learn'd the names of the ſeven liberal Sciences, before my marriage; and ſince, have in haſte written Epiſtles congratulatory, to the Nine Muſes, and is ſhe prov'd a Whore and a Begger?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: 'Tis true, you are not now to be taught, that no man can be learn'd of a ſuddain; let not your firſt project diſcourage you, what you have loſt in this, you may get again in Alchumie.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Fear not Husband, I hope to make as good a wife, as the beſt of your neighbors, have, and as honeſt.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: I will goe home; good Sir, do not publiſh this, as long as it runs amongſt our ſelves; 'tis good honeſt mirth: you'll come home to ſupper; I mean to have all her friends, and mine, as ill as it goes.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Do wiſely Sir, and bid your own friends, your whole wealth will ſcarce feaſt all hers, neither is it for your credit, to walk the ſtreets with a woman ſo noted; get you home and provide her cloaths: let her come an hour hence with an Hand-basket, and ſhift her ſelf, ſhe'll ſerve to ſit at the upper end of the Table, and drink to your cuſtomers.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: Art is juſt, and will make me amends.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: No doubt Sir.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: The chief note of a Scholar you ſay, is to govern his paſſions; wherefore I do take all patiently; in ſign of which, my dear Wife, I do kiſs thee, make haſte home after me, I ſhall be in my ſtudy. Exit Mercer.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: Go, avaunt, my new City Dame, ſend me what you promis'd me for conſideration; and may'ſt thou prove, a Lady.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt have it, his Silks ſhall flie for it.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: How ſweet is a Calm after a Tempeſt, what is there now that can ſtand betwixt me and felicity? I have gone through all my croſſes conſtantly; have confounded my enemies, and know where to have my longing ſatisfied: I have my way before me, there's the door, and I may freely walk into my delights: knock boy.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Who's there? Within.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Madona, my Love, not guilty, not guilty, open the door.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Art thou come ſweet-heart?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Yes, to my ſoft embraces, and the reſt of my overflowing bliſſes; come, let us in and ſwim in our delights: a ſhort Grace as we go, and ſo to meat.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: Nay my dear Love, you muſt bear with me in this; we'll to the Church firſt.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: Shall I be ſure of it then?

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.p: By my love you ſhall.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I am content, for I do now wiſh to hold off longer, to whet my appetite, and do deſire to meet with more troubles, ſo I might conquer them:
sp.l: And as a holy Lover that hath ſpent
The tedious night with many a ſigh and tears;
Whilſt he purſu'd his wench: and hath obſerv'd
The ſmiles, and frowns, not daring to diſpleaſe
When at laſt, hath with his ſervice won
Her yielding heart; that ſhe begins to dote
Upon him, and can hold no longer out,
But hangs about his neck, and wooes him more
Than ever he deſir'd her love before:
Then begins to flatter his deſert,
And growing wanton, needs will caſt her off;
Try her, pick quarrels, to breed freſh delight,
And to increaſe his pleaſing appetite.

sp.speaker: Jul.
sp.l: Come Mouſe will you walk?

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.p: I pray thee let me be deliver'd of the joy I am ſo big with, I do feel that high heat within me, that I begin to doubt whether I be mortal:
sp.l: How I contemn my fellows in the Court,
With whom I did but yeſterday converſe?
And in a lower, and an humbler key
Did walk and meditate on groſſer meats?
There are they ſtill poor rogues, ſhaking their chops,
And ſneaking after Cheeſes, and do run
Headlong in chace, of every Jack of Beer
That croſſeth them, in hope of ſome repaſt,
That it will bring them to, whilſt I am here,
The happieſt wight that ever ſet his tooth
To a dear novelty: approach my love,
Come, let's go to knit the True Loves knot,
That never can be broken.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: That is to marry a whore.

sp.speaker: Laz.
sp.l: When that is done, then will we taſte the gift,
Which Fates have ſent my Fortunes up to lift.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: When that is done, you'll begin to repent upon a full ſtomach; but I ſee, 'tis but a form in deſtiny, not to be alter'd.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Sir, what may be the current of your buſineſs, that thus you ſingle out your time and place?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: Madam, the buſineſs now impos'd upon me, concerns you nearly, I wiſh ſome worſer man might finiſh it.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: Why are ye chang'd ſo? are ye not well Sir?

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: Yes Madam, I am well, wo'd you were ſo.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Why Sir, I feel my ſelf in perfect health.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: And yet ye cannot live long, Madam.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Why good Arrigo?

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: Why? ye muſt dye.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: I know I muſt, but yet my fate calls not upon me.

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: It does; this hand the Duke commands ſhall give you death.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.l: Heaven, and the powers Divine, guard well the innocent.

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: Lady, your Prayers may do your ſoul ſome good.
That ſure your body cannot merit by'em:
You muſt prepare to die.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: What's my offence? what have theſe years committed,
That may be dangerous to the Duke, or State?
Have I conſpir'd by poiſon, have I giv'n up,
My honor to ſome looſe unſetl'd bloud
That may give action to my plots?
Dear Sir, let me not dye ignorant of my faults?

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: Ye ſhall not.
Then Lady, you muſt know, you 're held unhoneſt;
The Duke, your Brother, and your friends in Court,
With too much grief condemn ye: though to me,
The fault deſerves not to be paid with death.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Who's my accuſer?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: Lord Gondarino.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Arrigo, take theſe words, and bear them to the Duke,
It is the laſt petition I ſhall ask thee:
Tell him the child this preſent hour brought forth
To ſee the world has not a ſoul more pure, more white,
sp.p: More Virgin than I have; Tell him Lord Gondarino's Plot, I ſuffer for, and willingly: tell him it had been a greater honor, to have ſav'd than kill'd: but I have done: ſtrike, I am arm'd for heaven. Why, ſtay you? is there any hope?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: I would not ſtrike.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Have you the power to ſave?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: With hazard of my life, if it ſhould be known.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: You will not venture that?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: I will Lady: there is that means yet to eſcape your death, if you can wiſely apprehend.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Ye dare not be ſo kind?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: I dare, and will, if you dare but deſerve't.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.l: If I ſhould ſlight my life, I were too blame.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: Then Madam, this is the means, or elſe you die:
I love you.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: I ſhall believe it, if you ſave my life.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: And you muſt lie with me.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: I dare not buy my life ſo.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: Come, ye muſt reſolve, ſay yea or no.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: Then no; nay, look not ruggedly upon me, I am made up too ſtrong to fear ſuch looks:
sp.p: Come, do your Butchers part: before I would wiſh life, with the dear loſs of honour, I dare find means to free my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.l: Speak, will ye yield?

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Villain, I will not; Murtherer, do thy worſt, thy baſe unnoble thoughts dare prompt thee to; I am above thee ſlave.

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: Wilt thou not be drawn to yield by fair perſwaſions?

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: No, nor by —

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: Peace, know your doom then; your Ladyſhip muſt remember, you are not now at home, where you dare feaſt all that come about you: but you are fallen under my mercy, which ſhall be but ſmall; if thou refuſe to yield: hear what I have ſworn unto my ſelf; I will enjoy thee, though it be between the parting of thy ſoul and body; yield yet and live.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: I'll guard the one, let Heaven guard the other,

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.l: Are you ſo reſolute then?
Hold, hold I ſay.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.l: What I? yet more terror to my tragedy?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: Lady, the Scene of bloud is done; ye are now as free from ſcandal, as from death.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Thou Woman which wert born to teach men virtue,
Fair, ſweet, and modeſt Maid, forgive my thoughts,
My treſpaſs was my love.
Seize Gondarino, let him wait our dooms.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I do begin a little to love this woman; I could endure her already twelve miles off.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Siſter, I am glad you have brought your honor off ſo fairly, without loſs: you have done a work above your ſex, the Duke admires it: give him fair encounter.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Beſt of all comforts, may I take this hand, and call it mine?

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.p: I am your Graces handmaid.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Would ye had ſed my ſelf: might it not be ſo Lady?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Siſter, ſay I, I know you can afford it.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.p: My Lord, I am your ſubject, you may command me, provided ſtill, your thoughts be fair and good.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Here I am yours, and when I ceaſe to be ſo,
Let heaven forget me: thus I make it good.

sp.speaker: Ori.
sp.p: My Lord, I am no more mine own.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: So, this bargain was well driven.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Duke, thou haſt ſold away thy ſelf to all perdition; thou art this preſent hour becomming Cuckold: methinks I ſee thy gaul grate through thy veins, and jealouſie ſeize thee with her talons: I know that womans noſe muſt be cut off, ſhe cannot ſcape it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Sir, we have puniſhment for you.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: I do beſeech your Lordſhip, for the wrongs this man hath done me, let me pronounce his puniſhment.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Lady, I give't to you, he is your own.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I do beſeech your Grace, let me be baniſht with all the ſpeed that may be.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Stay ſtill, you ſhall attend her ſentence.

sp.speaker: Orian.
sp.p: Lord Gondarino, you have wrong'd me highly; yet ſince it ſprung from no peculiar hate to me, but from a general diſlike unto all women, you ſhall thus ſuffer for it; Arrigo, call in ſome Ladies to aſſiſt us; will your Grace make your State?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: My Lord, I do beſeech your Grace for any puniſhment ſaving this woman, let me be ſent upon diſcovery of ſome Iſland; I do deſire but a ſmall Gondela, with ten Holland Cheeſes, and I'll undertake it.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Sir, ye muſt be content, will ye ſit down? nay, do it willingly: Arrigo, tie his Arms cloſe to the chair, I dare not truſt his patience.

sp.speaker: Cond.
sp.p: Mayſt thou be quickly old and painted; mayſt thou dote upon ſome ſturdy Yeoman of the Wood-yard, and he be honeſt; mayſt thou be barr'd the lawful lechery of thy Coach, for want of inſtruments; and laſt, be thy womb unopen'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: This fellow hath a pretty gaul.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: My Lord, I hope to ſee him purg'd e'r he part,

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Your Ladyſhips are welcome:
I muſt deſire your helps, though you are no Phyſitians, to do a ſtrange cure upon this Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ladies.
sp.p: In what we can aſſiſt you Madam, ye may command us.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Now do I ſit like a Conjurer within my circle, and theſe the Devils that are rais'd about me, I will pray that they may have no power upon me.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Ladies, fall off in couples, then with a ſoft ſtill march, with low demeanors, charge this Gentleman, I'll be your Leader.

sp.speaker: Gond,
sp.p: Let me be quarter'd Duke quickly, I can endure it: theſe women long for Mans fleſh, let them have it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Count, have you ever ſeen ſo ſtrange a paſſion? what would this fellow do; if he ſhould find himſelf in bed with a young Lady?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: 'Faith my Lord, if he could get a knife, ſure he wou'd cut her throat, or elſe he wou'd do as Hercules did by Lycas, ſwing out her ſoul: h'as the true hate of a woman in him.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Low with your Curſies Ladies.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Come not too near me, I have a breath will poiſon ye, my lungs are rotten, and my ſtomach is raw: I am given much to belching: hold off, as you love ſweet airs; Ladies, by your firſt nights pleaſure, I conjure you, as you wou'd have your Husbands proper men, ſtrong backs, and little legs, as you would have 'em hate your Waiting-women.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Sir, we muſt court ye, till we have obtain'd ſome little favour from thoſe gracious eyes, 'tis but a kiſs a piece.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I pronounce perdition to ye all; ye are a parcel of that damned crew that fell down with Lucifer, and here ye ſtaid on earth to plague poor men; vaniſh, avaunt, I am fortified againſt your charms; heaven grant me breath and patience.

sp.speaker: 1 Lady.
sp.p: Shall we not kiſs then?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: No fear my lips with hot irons firſt, or ſtitch them up like a Ferrets: oh that this brunt were over!

sp.speaker: 2 Lady.
sp.p: Come, come, little rogue, thou art too maidenly by my troth, I think I muſt box thee till thou be'ſt bolder; the more bold, the more welcome: I prethee kiſs me, be not afraid. She ſits on his knee.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: If there be any here, that yet have ſo much of the fool left in them, as to love their mothers, let them on her, and loath them too.

sp.speaker: 2. Lady.
sp.p: What a ſlovenly little villain art thou, why doſt thou not ſtroke up thy hair? I think thou ne'er comb'ſt it: I muſt have it lie in better order; ſo, ſo, ſo, let me ſee thy hands, are they waſh'd?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I would thy were looſe for thy ſake.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: She tortures him admirably.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: The beſt that ever was.

sp.speaker: 2 Lady.
sp.p: Alas, how cold they are, poor golls, why doſt thee not get thee a Muff?

sp.speaker: Arri.
sp.p: Madam, here's an old Countrey Gentlewoman at the door, that came nodding up for juſtice, ſhe was with the Lord Gondarino to day, and would now again come to the ſpeech of him, ſhe ſays.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Let her in, for ſports ſake, let her in.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Mercy, oh Duke, I do appeal to thee: plant Canons there, and diſcharge them againſt my breaſt rather: nay, firſt let this ſhe-fury ſit ſtill where ſhe does, and with her nimble fingers ſtroke my hair, play with my fingers ends, or any thing, until my panting heart have broke my breaſt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: You muſt abide her cenſure.

div.stage: The Lady riſes from his knee.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: I ſee her come, unbutton me, for ſhe will ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Where is he Sir?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Save me, I hear her.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: There he is in ſtate to give you audience

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: How does your Lordſhip?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Sick of the ſpleen.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: Sick.

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.p: Will you chew a Nutmeg, you ſhall not refuſe it, it is very comfortable.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.l: Nay, now thou art come, I know it
Is the Devils Jubile, Hell is broke looſe:
My Lord, if ever I have done you ſervice,
Or have deſerv'd a favour of your Grace,
Let me be turn'd upon ſome preſent action,
Where I may ſooner die, than languiſh thus;
Your Grace hath her petition, grant it her, and eaſe me now at laſt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: No Sir, you muſt endure,

sp.speaker: Gentlew.
sp.l: For my petition, I hope your
Lordſhip hath remembred me.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: 'Faith I begin to pity him, Arrigo, take her off, bear her away, ſay her petition is granted.

sp.speaker: Centlew.
sp.p: Whither do you draw me Sir? I know it is not my Lords pleaſure I ſhould be thus uſed, before my buſineſs be diſpatched?

sp.speaker: Arr.
sp.p: You ſhall know more of that without.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: Unbind him Ladies, but before he go, this he ſhall promiſe; for the love I bear to our own ſex, I would have them ſtill hated by thee, and injoyn thee as a puniſhment, never hereafter willingly to come in the preſence, or ſight of any woman, nor never to ſeek wrongfully, the publick diſgrace of any.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: 'Tis that I would have ſworn, and do: when I meditate with them, for their good, or their bad; may Time call back this day again, and when I come in their companies, may I catch the pox, by their breath, and have no other pleaſure for it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Ye are moſt merciful.

sp.speaker: Oria.
sp.p: My Lord, I ſhew'd my ſex the better.

sp.speaker: Gond.
sp.p: All is over-blown Siſter: y'are like to have a fair night of it, and a Prince in your Arms: let's goe my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Thus through the doubtful ſtreams of joy and grief,
True Love doth wade, and finds at laſt relief.

div.head: The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Shamont his Favourite, a ſuperſtitious lover of reputation.
A paſſionate Lord, the Duke's diſtracted kinſman.
Lapet, the cowardly Monſieur of Nice Valour.
A Gallant of the ſame Temper.
Two Brothers to the Lady, affecting the paſſionate Lord
Galoſhio, a Clown, ſuch another try'd piece of Man's fleſh.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Lady, Siſter to the Duke, Shamont's beloved.
A Lady, perſonating Cupid, Miſtriſs to the mad Lord.

div.head: The PROLOGUE at the reviving of this Play.
div.l: IT's grown in faſhion of late in theſe days,
To come and beg a ſuffrage to our Plays
Faith Gentlemen, our Poet ever writ
Language ſo good, mixt with ſuch ſprightly wit,
He made the Theatre ſo Sovereign
With his rare Scaenes, he ſcorn'd this crouching vein:
We ſtabb'd him with keen daggers when we pray'd
Him write a Preface to a Play well made.
He could not write theſe toyes, 'twos eaſier far,
To bring a Felon to appear at th' Barr
So much he hated baſeneſs; which this day,
His Scaenes will beſt convince you of in's Play.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Shamount, and four Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: SHamount, welcome; we have miſt thee long,
Though abſent but two days: I hope your ſports
Anſwer your time and wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Very nobly Sir;
We found game, worthy your delight my Lord,
It was ſo royal.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I've enough to hear on't.
Prethee beſtow't upon me in diſcourſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: What is this Gentleman, Coz? you are a Courtier,
Therefore know all their inſides.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: No farther than the Taſſaty goes, good Coz.
For the moſt part, which is indeed the beſt part
Of the moſt general inſide; marry thus far
I can with boldneſs ſpeak this one mans character,
And upon honor, paſs it for a true one;
He has that ſtrength of manly merit in him,
That it exceeds his Sovereigns power of gracing;
He's faithfully true to valour, that he hates
The man from Caeſar's time, or farther off,
That ever took diſgrace unreveng'd:
And if he chance to read his abject ſtory,
He tears his memory out; and holds it virtuous,
Not to let ſhame have ſo much life amongſt us;
There is not ſuch a curious piece of courage
Amongſt mans fellowſhip, or one ſo jealous
Of honors loſs, or repuations glory:
There's ſo much perfect of his growing ſtory.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Twould make one dote on virtue as you tell it.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: I have told it to much loſs, believe it Coz.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: How the Duke graces him? what is he brother?

sp.speaker: 4 Gent.
sp.l: Do you not yet know him? a vain-glorious coxcomb,
As proud as he that fell for't:
Set but aſide his valour; no virtue;
Which is indeed, not fit for any Courtier;
And we his fellows are as good as he,
Perhaps as capable of favour too,
For one thing or another, if 'twere look'd into:
Give me a man, were I a Sovereign now
Has a good ſtroke of Tennis, and a ſtiff one,
Can play at AEquinoctium with the Line,
As even, as the thirteenth of September,
When day and night lie in a ſcale together:
Or may I thrive, as I deſerve at Billiards;
No otherwiſe at Cheſſe, or at Primero:
Theſe are the parts requir'd, why not advanc'd?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Truſt me, it was no leſs than excellent pleaſure,
And I'm right glad 'twas thine. How fares our kinſman?
Who can reſolve us beſt?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I can my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: There, if I had a pity without bounds,
It might be all beſtowed—A man ſo loſt
In the wild ways of paſſion, that he's ſenſible
Of nought, but what torments him?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: True my Lord,
He runs through all the Paſſions of mankind,
And ſhifts 'em ſtrangely too: one while in love,
And that ſo violent, that for want of buſineſs,
He'll court the very Prentice of a Laundreſs,
Though ſhe have kib'd heels: and in's melancholly agen,
He will not brook an Empreſs though thrice fairer
Than ever Maud was; or higher ſpirited
Than Cleopatra, or your Engliſh Counteſs:
Then on a ſuddain he's ſo merry again,
Out laughs a Waiting-woman before her firſt Child:
And turning of a hand, ſo angry—
Has almoſt beat the Northern fellow blind;
That is for that uſe only; if that mood hold my Lord,
Had need of a freſh man; I'll undertake,
He ſhall bruiſe three a month.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I pity him dearly:
And let it be your charge, with his kind brother
To ſee his moods obſerv'd; let every paſſion
Be fed ev'n to a ſurfet, which in time
May breed a loathing: let him have enough
Of every object, that his ſence is wrapt with;
And being once glutted, then the taſte of folly
Will come into his relliſh. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I ſhall ſee
Your charge my Lord, moſt faithfuly effected:
And how does noble Shamount?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Never ill man
Until I hear of baſeneſs, then I ſicken:
I am the healthfull'ſt man i'th' kingdom elſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Be arm'd then for a fit,
Here comes a fellow
Will make you ſick at heart, if baſeneſs do't.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Let me be gone: what is he?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Let me tell you firſt,
It can be but a qualm: pray ſtay it out Sir,
Come, y'ave born more than this.

sp.speaker: Sha.
sp.l: Born? never any thing
That was injurious.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Ha, I am far from that.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: He looks as like a man as I have ſeen one:
What would you ſpeak of him? ſpeak well I prethee,
Even for humanities cauſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You'd have it truth though?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: What elſe Sir? I have no reaſon to wrong heav'n
To favour nature; let her bear her own ſhame
If ſhe be faulty.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Monſtrous faulty there Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I'm ill at eaſe already.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Pray bear up Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I prethee let me take him down with ſpeed then;
Like a wild object that I would not look upon.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Then thus: he's one that will endure as much
As can be laid upon him.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: That may be noble:
I'm kept too long from his acquaintance.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Oh Sir,
Take heed of raſh repentance, y'are too forward
To find out virtue where it never ſetl'd:
Take the particulars firſt, of what he endures;
Videlicet, Baſtinadoes by the great.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: How!

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Thumps by the dozen, and your kicks by wholeſale.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: No more of him.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: The twinges by the noſtril he ſnuffs up,
And holds it the beſt remedy for ſneezing.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Away.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: H'as been thrice ſwitch'd from 7 a clock till 9.
Yet with a Cart-Horſe ſtomach, fell to breakfaſt;
Forgetful of his ſmart.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Nay, the diſgrace on't;
There's no ſmart but that: baſe things are felt
More by their ſhames than hurts, Sir. I know you not.
But that you live an injury to nature:
I'm heartily angry with you.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Pray give your blow or kick and begone then:
For I ne'er ſaw you before; and indeed,
Have nothing to ſay to you, for I know you not.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Why wouldſt thou take a blow?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I would not Sir,
Unleſs 'twere offer'd me; and if from an enemy?
I'd be loth to deny it from a ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: What, a blow?
Endure a blow? and ſhall he live that gives it?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Many a fair year—why not Sir?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Let me wonder!
As full a man to ſee to, and as perfect—
I prethee live not long—

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Let me intreat it:
Thou doſt not know what wrong thou doſt mankind,
To walk ſo long here; not to dye betimes.
Let me adviſe thee, while thou haſt to live here,
Ev'n for man's honour ſake, take not a blow more.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: You ſhould adviſe them not to ſtrike me then Sir,
For I'll take none I aſſure you, 'leſs they are given.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: How fain would I preſerve mans form from ſhame
And cannot get it done? however Sir,
I charge thee live not long.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: This is worſe than beating.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Of what profeſſion art thou, tell me Sir,
Beſides a Tailor? for I'll know the truth.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: A Tailor? I'm as good a Gentleman—
Can ſhew my Arms and all,

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: How black and blew they are?
Is that your manifeſtation? upon pain
Of pounding thee to duſt, aſſume not wrongfully
The name of Gentleman, becauſe I'm one,
That muſt not let thee live.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I have done, I have done Sir.
If there be any harm, beſhrew the Herald,
I'm ſure I ha' not been ſo long a Gentleman,
To make this anger: I have nothing no where,
But what I dearly pay for. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Groom begone;
I never was ſo heart-ſick yet of man.

div.stage: Enter Lady, the Duke's Siſter, Lapet's wife.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Here comes a cordial, Sir, from th'other ſex,
Able to make a dying face look chearful.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: The bleſſedneſs of Ladies —

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Y'are well met Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: The ſight of you has put an evil from me,
Whoſe breath was able to make virtue ſicken,

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: I'm glad I came ſo fortunately. What was't Sir?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: A thing that takes a blow, lives, and eats after it,
In very good health; you ha' not ſeen the like, Madam,
A Monſter worth your ſixpence, lovely worth,
Speak low Sir; by all likely-hoods 'tis her Husband, 〈◊〉 ,
That now beſtow'd a viſitation on me. Farewel Sir. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Husband? is't poſſible that he has a wiſe?
Would any creature have him? 'tis ſome forc'd match,
If he were not kick'd to th'Church o' th'wedding day,
I'll never come at Court. Can be no otherwiſe:
Perhaps he was rich, ſpeak miſtriſs Lapet, was't not ſo?

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Nay, that's without all queſtion.

sp.speaker: Sh.
sp.l: O ho, he would not want kickers enow then;
If you are wiſe, I much ſuſpect your honeſty;
For wiſdom never faſtens conſtantly,
But upon merit: if you incline to fool,
You are alike unfit for his ſociety;
Nay, if it were not boldneſs in the man
That honors you, to adviſe you, troth his company
Should not be frequent with you.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: 'Tis good counſel Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh, I am ſo careful where I reverence,
So juſt to goodneſs, and her precious purity,
I'm as equally jealous, and as fearful,
That any undeſerved ſtain might fall
Upon her ſanctified whiteneſs, as of the ſin
That comes by wilfulneſs.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: Sir, I love your thoughts,
And honor you for your counſel and your care.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: We are your ſervants.

sp.speaker: Wife.
sp.l: He's but a Gentleman o'th' chamber; he might have kiſt me:
Faith, where ſhall one find leſs courteſie, than at Court?
Say I have an undeſerver to my Husband:
That's ne'er the worſe for him: well ſtrange lip'd men,
'Tis but a kiſs loſt, there'll more come agen. Exit,

div.stage: Enter the paſſionate Lord, the Dukes kinſman, makes a congie or two to nothing.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Look, who comes here Sir, his love-fit's upon him:
I know it, by that ſett ſmile, and thoſe congies.
How courteous he's to nothing? which indeed,
Is the next kin to woman; only ſhadow
The elder Siſter of the twain, becauſe 'tis ſeen too.
See how it kiſſes the fore-finger ſtill;
Which is the laſt edition, and being come
So near the thumb, every Cobler has got it.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: What a ridiculous piece, humanity
Here makes it ſelf?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Nay good give leave a little, Sir,
Y'are ſo preciſe a manhood—

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: It afflicts me
When I behold unſeemlineſs in an Image
So near the Godhead, 'tis an injury
To glorious Eternity.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Pray uſe patience, Sir.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I do confeſs it freely, precious Lady,
And loves ſuit is ſo, the longer it hangs
The worſe it is; better cut off, ſweet Madam;
Oh, that ſame drawing in your neather Lip there,
Fore ſhews no goodneſs, Lady; make you queſtion on't?
Shame on me, but I love you.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Who is't Sir,
You are at all this pains for? may I know her?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: For thee thou faireſt, yet the falſeſt woman,
That ever broke man's heart-ſtrings.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: How? how's this Sir?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: What the old trick of Ladies? man's apparel,
Will't ne'er be left amongſt you? ſteal from Court in't?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I ſee the Fit grows ſtronger.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Pray le • ' • talk a little.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I can endure no more.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Good, let's alone a little:
You are ſo exa •• a work: love light things ſomewhat, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Th'a • e 〈◊〉 but ſhames.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: What 〈◊〉 yo • 'd ſay to me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l:
Can you 〈◊〉
• orgetful to enquire it Lady?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Yes truely, Sir.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: The more I admire your ſlintineſs:
What cauſe have I given you, 〈◊〉 Madam,
To play this ſtrange part with 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Cauſe enough,
Do but look back Sir, into your memory,
Your love to other women, oh lewd man:
'Tas almoſt kill'd my heart, you ſee I'm chang'd with it,
I ha' loſt the faſhion of my Sex with grief on t,
When I have ſeen you courting of a Dowdie;
Compar'd with me, and kiſſing your fore-finger
To one o'th' Black-Guards Miſtreſſes: would not this
Crack a poor Ladies heart, that believ'd love,
And waited for the comfort? but 'twas ſaid, Sir,
A Lady of my hair cannot want pittying:
The Countrey's coming up, farewel to you Sir.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Whither intend you, Sir?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: A long journey, Sir:
The truth is, I'm with child, and goe to travel.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: With child? I never got it.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I heard you were buſie
At the ſame time, Sir, and was loth to trouble you.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Why, are not you a whore then, excellent Madam?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Oh by no means, 'twas done Sir in the ſtate
Of my belief in you, and that quits me;
It lies upon your falſhood.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Does it ſo?
You ſhall not carry her though Sir, ſhe's my contract.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I prethee, thou four Elements ill brued,
Torment none but thy ſelf; away I ſay
Thou beaſt of paſſion, as the drunkard is
The beaſt of Wine; diſhonor to thy making,
Thou man in fragments.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Hear me, precious Madam.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Kn •• l for thy wits to Heaven.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Lady, I'll father it,
Who e'er begot it: 'tis the courſe of greatneſs.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: How virtue groans at this?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I'll raiſe the Court, but I'll ſtay your flight.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: How wretched is that piece? Ex. Paſ. Lord.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: He's the Dukes kinſman, Si • .

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: That cannot take a paſſion away, Sir,
Nor cut a Fit, but one poor hour ſhorter,
He muſt endure as much as the pooreſt begger,
That cannot change his money; there's th' equality
In our impartial Eſſence:
What's the news now?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: Your worthy brother, Sir, 'has left his charge,
And come to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh the nobleſt welcome
That ever came from man, meet thy deſervings:
Methinks I've all joyes treaſure in mine arms now,

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: You are ſo fortunate in prevention, brother,
You always leave the anſwerer barren, Sir,
You comprehend in few words ſo much worth—

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: 'Tis all too little for thee: come th'art welcome
So I include all: take eſpecial knowledge pray,
Of this dear Gentleman, my abſolute friend,
That loves a Soldier far above a Miſtriſs,
Thou excellently faithful to 'em both.
But love to manhood, owns the purer troth. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Shamont's brother, a Soldier and a Lady, the Dukes Siſter.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: THere ſhould be in this Gallery—oh th'are here,
Pray ſit down, believe me Sir, I'm weary.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: It well becomes a Lady to complain a little
Of what ſhe never feels: your walk was ſhort, Madam,
You can be but afraid of wearineſs;
Which well employs the ſoftneſs of your Sex,
As for the thing it ſelf, you never came to't.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: You're wond'rouſly well read in Ladies, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Shall I think ſuch a creature as you Madam,
Was ever born to feel pain, but in Travel?
There's your full portion,
Beſides a little tooth-ach in the breeding,
Which a kind Husband too, takes from you, Madam.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: But where do Ladies, Sir, find ſuch kind Husbands?
Perhaps you have heard
The Rheumatick ſtory of ſome loving Chandler now,
Or ſome ſuch melting fellow that you talk
So prodigal of mens kindneſs: I confeſs Sir,
Many of thoſe wives are happy, their ambition
Does reach no higher, than to Love and Ignorance,
Which makes an excellent Husband, and a fond one:
Now Sir, your great ones aim at height, and cunning,
And ſo are oft deceiv'd, yet they muſt venture it;
For 'tis a Ladies contumely, Sir,
To have a Lord an Ignorant; then the worlds voice
Will deem her for a wanton, e'r ſhe taſte on't:
But to deceive a wiſe man, to whoſe circumſpection,
The world reſigns it ſelf, with all his envy;
'Tis leſs diſhonor to us, than to fall,
Becauſe his believ'd wiſdom keeps out all.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Would I were the man, Lady, that ſhould venture
His wiſdom to your goodneſs.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: You might fail
In the return, as many men have done, Sir:
I dare not juſtifie what is to come of me,
Becauſe I know it not, though I hope virtuouſly;
Marry what's paſt, or preſent, I durſt put
Into a good mans hand, which if he take
Upon my word for good, it ſhall not cozen him.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.l: No, nor hereafter?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: It may hap ſo too, Sir:
A womans goodneſs, when ſhe is a wife,
Lies much upon a mans deſert, believe it Sir,
If there be fault in her, I'll pawn my life on't,
'Tis firſt in him, if ſhe were ever good,
That makes one; knowing not a Husband yet,
Or what he may be: I promiſe no more virtues,
Than I may well perform, for that were cozenage.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.l: Happy were he that had you with all fears,
That's my opinion, Lady.

div.stage: Enter Shamount and a ſervant liſt'ning.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: What ſay you now, Sir?
Dare you give confidence to your own eyes?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Not yet I dare not.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: No?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Scarce yet, or yet:
Although I ſee 'tis he. Why can a thing,
That's but my ſelf divided, be ſo falſe?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: Nay, do but mark how the chair plays hie part too:
How amoroeſly 'tis bent.

sp.speaker: Shvm.
sp.l: Hell take thy bad thoughts,
For they are ſtrange ones. Never take delight
To make a torment worſe. Look on 'em heaven,
For that's a brother: ſend me a fair enemy,
And take him; for a fouler Fiend there breathes not:
I will not ſin to think there's ill in her,
But what's of his producing.
Yet goodneſs, whoſe incloſure is but fleſh,
Holds out oft times but ſorrily. But as black Sir,
As ever kindred was: I hate mine own bloud,
Becauſe is is ſo near thine. Live without honeſty,
And mayſt thou dye with an unmoiſt'ned eye,
And no tear follow thee. Ex. Shamont, Servant.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Y'are wond'rous merry Sir; I would your Brother heard you.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Oh my Siſter,
I would not out o'th' way, let fall my words Lady,
For the preciſeſt humor.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Yea, ſo cloſe.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Th'are merry, that's the worſt you can report on 'em:
Th'are neither dangerous, nor immodeſt.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: So Sir,
Shall I believe you, think you?

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Who's this, Lady?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Oh the Dukes Coſin, he came late from travel, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Reſpect belongs to him.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: For as I ſaid, Lady,
Th'are merry, that's the worſt you can report of 'em:
Th'are neither dangerous, nor immodeſt.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: How's this?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: And there I think I left.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Abuſes me.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Now to proceed, Lady; perhaps I ſwore I lov'd you,
If you believe me not, y'are much the wiſer.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: He ſpeaks ſtill in my perſon, and derides me.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: For I can cog with you.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: You can all do ſo:
We make no queſtion of mens promptneſs that way.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: And ſmile, and wave a chair with comely grace too,
Play with our Taſtle gently, and do fine things,
That catch a Lady ſooner than a virtue.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: I never us'd to let man live ſo long
That wrong'd me.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Talk of Battalions, wooe you in a skirmiſh;
Divine my mind to you Lady; and being ſharp ſet,
Can court you at Half pike: or name your weapon,
We cannot fail you Lady.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Now he dies:
Were all ſucceeding hopes ſtor'd up wichin him.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Oh fie, i'th' Court, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: I moſt dearly thank you; Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis rage ill ſpent upon a paſſionate mad man.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: That ſhall not priviledge him for ever, Sir:
A mad man call you him? I have ſound too much reaſon
Sound in his injury to me, to believe him ſo.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: If ever truth from mans lips may be held
In reputation with you, give this confidence;
And this his Love-fit, which we obſerve ſtill,
By's flattering and his fineneſs: at ſome other time,
He'll go as ſlovenly as heart can wiſh.
The love and pity that his Highneſs ſhews to him,
Makes every man the more reſpectful of him:
Has never a paſſion, but is well provided for,
As this of Love, he is full fed in all
His ſwinge, as I may tearm it: have but patience,
And ye ſhall witneſs ſomewhat.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Still he mocks me:
Look you, in action, in behaviour, Sir;
Hold ſtill the chair, with a grand miſchief to you,
Or I'll let ſo much ſtrength upon your heart, Sir—

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I feel ſome power has reſtrain'd me Lady:
If it be ſent from Love, ſay, I obey it,
And ever keep a voice to welcome it.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: THou Deity, ſwift winged Love,
Sometimes below, ſometimes above,
Little in ſhape, but great in power,
Thou that mak'ſt a heart thy Tower,
And thy loop-holes Ladies eyes,
From whence thou ſtrik'ſt the fond and wiſe.
Did all the Shafts in thy fair Quiver
Stick faſt in my ambitious Liver;
Yet thy power would I adore.
And call upon thee to ſhoot more,
Shoot more, ſhoot more.

div.stage: Enter one like a Cupid, offering to ſhoot at him.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I prethee hold though, ſweet Celeſtial boy;
I'm not requited yet with love enough,
For the firſt Arrow that I have within me;
And if thou be an equal Archer Cupid,
Shoot this Lady, and twenty more for me.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Me Sir?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis nothing but device, fear it not Lady;
You may be as good a Maid after that ſhaft, Madam,
As e'er your mother was at twelve and a half:
'Tis like the boy that draws it, 'tas no ſting yet.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: 'Tis like the miſerable Maid that draws it— Aſide.
That ſees no comfort yet, ſeeing him ſo paſſionate,

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Strike me the Ducheſs of Valois in love with me,
With all the ſpeed thou canſt, and two of her Women.

sp.speaker: Cu.
sp.l: You ſhall have more. Exit.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Tell 'em I tarry for 'em.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Who would be angry with that walking trouble now?
That hurts none but it ſelf?

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: I am better quieted.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I'll have all women-kind ſtruck in time for me
After thirteen once:
I ſee this Cupid will not let me want,
And let him ſpend his forty ſhafts an hour,
They ſhall be all found from the Dukes Exchequer;
He's come already.

div.stage: Enter again the ſame Cupid, two Brothers, ſix Women, Maskers, Cupid's Bow bent all the way towards them, the firſt woman ſinging and playing, a Prieſt.

body.head: SONG.
body.l: OH turn thy bow,
Thy power we feel and know,
Fair Cupid turn away thy Bow:
They be thoſe golden Arrows,
Bring Ladies all their ſorrows,
And till there be more truth in men,
Never ſhoot at Maid agen.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: What a felicity of whores are here?
And all my Concubines ſtruck bleeding new:
A man can in his life time, make but one woman,
But he may make his fifty Queans a month.

sp.speaker: Cu.
sp.l: Have you remembred a Prieſt, honeſt brothers?

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Yes Siſter, and this is the young Gentleman,
Make you no queſtion of our faithfulneſs.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: His growing ſhame, Siſter, provokes our care:

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: He muſt be taken in this fit of Love, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: What elſe Sir, he ſhall do't.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: Enough.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Be chearful wench. A dance. Cupid leading.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Now by the ſtroke of pleaſure, a deep oath,
Nimbly hopt Ladies all; what height they bear too?
A ſtory higher than your common ſtatures;
A little man muſt go up ſtairs to kiſs 'em:
What a great ſpace there is
Betwixt Loves Dining Chamber, and his Garret?
I'll try the utmoſt height — the Garret ſtoops methinks;
The rooms are made all bending, I ſee that,
And not ſo high as a man takes 'em for.

sp.speaker: Cu.
sp.l: Now if you'll follow me Sir, I've that power,
To make them follow you.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Are they all ſhot?

sp.speaker: Cu.
sp.l: All, all Sir, every mothers daughter of 'em.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Then there's no fear of following; if they be once ſhot
They'll follow a man to th' devil—As for you, Sir—
sp.stage: Ex. with the Lady and the Maſquers.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Me Sir?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Nay ſweet Sir.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: A noiſe, a threatening, did you not hear it Sir?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Without regard, Sir, ſo would I hear you

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: This muſt come to ſomething, never talk of that Sir.
You never ſaw it otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Nay dear merit—

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Me above all men?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Troth you wrong your anger.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: I will be arm'd, my honourable Letcher.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Oh fie ſweet Sir.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: That devours womens honeſties by lumps,
And never chaw'ſt thy pleaſure:

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: What do you mean, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: What does he mean t'ingroſs all to himſelf?
There's others love a whore as well as he Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Oh, if that be part o'th' fury, we have a City
Is very well provided for that caſe;
Let him alone with her, Sir, we have Women
Are very charitable to proper men,
And to a Soldier that has all his limbs;
Marry the ſick and lame gets not a penny:
Right womens charity, and the Husbands follow't too:
Here comes his Highneſs Sir.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: I'll walk to cool my ſelf. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Who's that?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: The brother of Shamont.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: He's Brother then
To all the Courts love, they that love diſcreetly,
And place their friendlineſs upon deſert:
As for the reſt, that with a double face
Look upon merit much like fortunes viſage,
That looks two ways, both to life's calms and ſtorms,
I'll ſo provide for him, chiefly for him,
He ſhall not wiſh their loves, nor dread their envies.
And here comes my Shamont.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: That Ladies virtues are my only joyes,
And he to offer to lay ſiege to them?

l.hi: Shamont.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Her goodneſs is my pride: in all diſcourſes,
As often as I hear raſh tongu'd gallants,
Speak rudely of a woman, preſently
I give in but her name, and th'are all ſilent:
Oh who would looſe this benefit?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come hither Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: 'Tis like the Gift of Healing, but Diviner;
For that but cures diſeaſes in the body,
This works a cure on Fame, on Reputation:
The nobleſt piece of Surgery upon earth.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Shamont; he minds me not.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: A Brother do't?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Shamont I ſay.

div.stage: Gives him a touch with his ſwitch.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Ha?
If he be mortal, by this hand he periſhes; Draws.
Unleſs it be a ſtroke from heaven, he dies for't.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why, how now Sir? 'twas I.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: The more's my miſery.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter prethee?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Can you ask it, Sir?
No man elſe ſhould; ſtood ſorty lives before him,
By this I would have op'd my way to him;
It could not be you Sir, excuſe him not,
What e'er he be, as y'are dear to honor,
That I may find my peace agen.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Forbear I ſay,
Upon my love to truth, 'twas none but I.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Still miſerable?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come, come, what ails you Sir?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Never ſate ſhame cooling ſo long upon me,
Without a ſatisfaction in revenge,
And heaven has made it here a ſin to wiſh it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Hark you Sir?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh y'ave undone me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Cruelly undone me;
I have loſt my peace and reputation by you:
Sir, pardon me, I can never love you more. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What language call you this Sirs?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Truth my Lord, I've ſeldom heard a ſtranger—

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: He is a man of a moſt curious valour,
Wondrous preciſe, and punctual in that virtue.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: But why to me ſo punctual? my laſt thought
Was moſt intirely fixt on his advancement •
Why, I came now to put him in poſſeſſion
Of his fair fortunes: what a miſ-conceiver 'tis?
And from a Gentleman of our Chamber meerly,
Made him Vice-Admiral: I was ſetled in't.
I love him next to health: call him Gentlemen;
Why would not you, or you, ha' taken as much,
And never murmur'd? Exit 1 Gent.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Troth, I think we ſhould, my Lord,
And there's a follow walks about the Court,
Would take a hundred of 'em.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I hate you all for't.,
And rather praiſe his high pitch'd fortitude,
Though in extreams for niceneſs: now I think on't,
I would I had never done't—Now Sir, where is he?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: His ſute is only Sir, to be excus'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: He ſhall not be excus'd, I love him dearlier:
Say we intreat him; goe, he muſt not leave us
So virtue bleſs me, I ne'er knew him paralell'd;
Why, he's more precious to me now, than ever.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: With much fair language w'ave brought him?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Thanks — Where is he?

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Yonder Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come forward man.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Pray pardon me, I'm aſham'd to be ſeen Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Was ever ſuch a touchie man heard of?
Prethee come nearer.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: More into the light?
Put not ſuch cruelty into your requeſts my Lord,
Firſt to diſgrace me publickly, and then draw me
Into mens eye-ſight, with the ſhame yet hot
Upon my reputation.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What diſgrace, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: What?
Such as there can be no forgiveneſs for,
That I can find in honour.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: That's moſt ſtrange, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Yet I have ſearch'd my boſom to find one,
And wreſtled with my inclination,
But 'twill not be would you had kill'd me Sir.
With what an eaſe had I forgiven you then?
But to endure a ſtroke from any hand
Under a puniſhing Angel, which is juſtice,
Honor diſclaim that man, for my part chiefly:
Had it been yet the malice of your ſword.
Though it had cleft me, 't had been noble to me;
You ſhould have found my thanks paid in a ſmile
If I had fell unworded; but to ſhame me,
With the correction that your horſe ſhould have,
Were you ten thouſand times my royal Lord,
I cannot love you never, nor deſire to ſerve you more.
If your drum call me, I am vowed to valour,
But peace ſhall never know me yours agen,
Becauſe I've loſt mine own, I ſpeak to dye Sir;
Would you were gracious that way to take off ſhame,
With the ſame ſwiftneſs as you pour it on:
And ſince it is not in the power of Monarchs
To make a Gentleman, which is a ſubſtance
Only begot of merit, they ſhould be careful
Not to deſtroy the worth of one ſo rare,
Which neither they can make; nor loſt, repair. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Y'ave ſet a fair light Sir before my judgement,
Which burns with wondrous clearneſs; I acknowledge it,
And your worth with it: but then Sir, my love,
My love — what gone agen?

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: And full of ſcorn, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: That language will undoe the man that keeps it.
Who knows no diff'rence, 'twixt contempt and manhood.
Upon your love to goodneſs, Gentlemen,
Let me not loſe him long: how now?

sp.speaker: Huntſ.
sp.l: The game's at height my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Confound both thee and it: hence break it off;
He hates me, brings me news of any pleaſure:
I felt not ſuch a conflict ſince I cou'd;
Diſtinguiſh betwixt worthineſs and bloud. Ex.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter the two Brothers, 1 Gentleman, with thoſe that were the Maſquers, and the Cupid.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I Heartily commend your project, Gentlemen,
'Twas wiſe and virtuous.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: 'Twas for the ſafety
Of precious honour Sir, which near bloud binds us to:
He promis'd the poor eaſie fool there, marriage,
There was a good Maiden-head loſt i'th' belief on't,
Beſhrew her haſty confidence.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Oh no more, Sir,
You make her weep agen; alas poor Cupid:
Shall ſhe not ſhift her ſelf?

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Oh by no means Sir:
We dare not have her ſeen yet, all the while
She keeps this ſhape, 'tis but thought device,
And ſhe may follow him ſo without ſuſpition,
To ſee if ſhe can draw all his wild paſſions,
To one point only, and that's love, the main point:
So far his Highneſs grants, and gave at firſt,
Large approbation to the quick conceit,
Which then was quick indeed.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You make her bluſh inſooth.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: I fear 'tis more the flag of ſhame, than grace Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: They both give but one kind of colour, Sir:
If it be baſhfulneſs in that kind taken,
It is the ſame with grace; and there ſhe weeps agen.
In truth y'are too hard, much, much too bitter Sir,
Unleſs you mean to have her weep her eyes out,
To play a Cupid truly.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Come ha' done then:
We ſhould all fear to ſin firſt; for 'tis certain,
When 'tis once lodg'd, though entertain'd in mirth,
It muſt be wept out, if it e'er come forth.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Now 'tis ſo well, I'll leave you.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Faithfully welcome, Sir,
Go Cupid to your charge; he's your own now;
If he want love, none will be blam'd but you.

sp.speaker: Cu.
sp.l: The ſtrangeſt marriage, and unfortunat'ſt Bride
That ever humane memory contain'd;
I cannot be my ſelf for't. Exit.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Oh Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: How now, Sir, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: His melancholly paſſion is half ſpent already,
Then comes his angry fit at the very tail on't,
Then comes in my pain, gentlemen; h'as beat me e'en to a
Cullis. I am nothing; right worſhipful, but very pap,
And jelly: I have no bones, my body's all one buſineſs,
They talk of ribs and chines moſt freely abroad i'th' world,
Why, I have no ſuch thing; who ever lives to ſee me dead,
Gentlemen, ſhall find me all mummie good to fill Gallipots,
And long dildo glaſſes: I ſhall not have a bone to throw
At a dog.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.l: Alas poor vaſſal; how he goes?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Oh Gentlemen,
I am unjoynted, do but think o' that:
My breaſt is beat into my maw, that what I eat,
I am fain to take't in all at mouth with ſpoons;
A lamentable hearing; and 'tis well known, my belly
Is driven into my back.
I earn'd four Crowns a month moſt dearly Gentlemen,
And one he muſt have when the fit's upon him,
The Privy-purſe allows it, and 'tis thriftineſs,
He would break elſe ſame forty pounds in Caſements,
And in five hundred years undo the Kingdom:
I have caſt it up to a quarrel.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: There's a fellow kickt about Court, I would
He had his place, brother, but for one fit of his indignation.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: And ſuddainly I have thought upon a means for't.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: I prethee how?

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: 'Tis but preferring, Brother
This ſtockfiſh to his ſervice, with a Letter
Of commendations, the ſame way he wiſhes it,
And then you win his heart: for o' my knowledge
He has laid wait this half year for a fellow
That will be beaten, and with a ſafe conſcience
We may commend the carriage of this man in't;
Now ſervants he has kept, luſty tall feeders,
But they have beat him, and turn'd themſelves away:
Now one that would endure, is like to ſtay,
And get good wages of him; and the ſervice too
Is ten times milder, Brother, I would not wiſh it elſe.
I ſee the fellow has a ſore cruſh'd body,
And the more need he has to be kick'd at eaſe.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I ſweet Gentlemen, a kick of eaſe, ſend me to ſuch a Maſter.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: No more I ſay, we have one for thee, a ſoft footed Maſter,
One that wears wooll in's toes.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Oh Gentlemen, ſoft garments may you wear,
Soft skins may you wed,
But as plump as pillows, both for white and red.
And now will I reveal a ſecret to you,
Since you provide for my poor fleſh ſo tenderly,
Has hir'd meer rogues out of his chamber window,
To beat the Soldier, Monſieur Shamont's Brother:

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: That nothing concerns us, Sir.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: For no c •• ſe, Gentlemen,
Unleſs • be for w •• ring Shoulder-points,
With longer taggs than his.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro,
sp.l: Is not that ſomewhat?
Birlakin Sir, the difference of long tag • s,
• as co •• many a mans li • e, and advanc'd other ſome,

Com •
• o • ow me.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: See what a gull am I:
Oh every man in his profeſſion;
I know a thump now as judiciouſly,
As the proudeſt he that walks, I'll except none;
Come to a tagg, how ſhort I fall? I'm gone. Exeunt

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I have been ruminating with my ſelf,
What honor a man loſes by a kick:
Why; what's a kick? the fury of a foot,
Whoſe indignation commonly is ſtampt
Upon the hinder quarter of a man:
Which is a place very unfit for honor,
The world will confeſs ſo much:
Then what diſgrace I pray, does thot part ſuffer
Where honor never comes, I'de • ain know that?
This being well forc'd, and urg'd, may have the power
To move moſt Gallants to take kicks in time,
And ſpurn out the duelloes out o'th' kingdom,
For they that ſtand upon their honor moſt,
When they conceive there is no honor loſt,
As by a Table that I have invented
For that purpoſe alone, ſhall appear plainly,
Which ſhews the vanity of all blows at large.
And with what eaſe they may be took of all ſides,
Numbring but twice o'er the Letters patience
From C. P. to E. I. doubt not but in ſmall time
To ſee a diſſolution of all bloud-ſhed,
If the reform'd Kick do but once get up:
For what a lamentable folly 'tis,
If we obſerve't, for every little juſtle,
Which is but the ninth part of a ſound thump,
In our meek computation, we muſt fight forſooth, yes,
If I kill, I'm hang'd; if I be kill'd my ſelf,
I dye for't alſo: is not this trim wiſdom?
Now for the Con, a ma • may be well beaten,
Yet paſs away his fourſcore years ſmooth after:
I had a Father did it, and to my power
I will not be behind him.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh well met.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Now a fine punch or two, I look ſor't duly.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I've been to ſeek you.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Let me know your Lodging, Sir,
I'll come to you once a day, and uſe your pleaſure, Sir,

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I'm made the fitteſt man for thy ſociety:
I'll live and dye with thee, come ſhew me a chamber;
There is no houſe but thine, but only thine,
That's fit to cover me: I've took a blow, ſirrah.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I would you had indeed: why, you may ſee, Sir;
You'll all come to't in time, when my Book's out.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Since I did ſee thee laſt, I've took a blow.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Pha Sir, that's nothing: I ha' took forty ſince.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: What? and I charg'd thee thou ſhouldſt not?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I Sir, you might charge your pleaſure.
But they would give't me, whether I would or no.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh, I walk without my peace, I've no companion now;
Prethee reſolve me, for I cannot aske
A man more beaten to experience,
Than thou art in this kind, what manner of blow
• s held the moſt diſgraceful, or diſtaſteful?
For thou doſt only cenſure 'em by the hurt,
Not by the ſhame they do thee: yet having felt
Abuſes of all kinds, thou may'ſt deliver,
Though't be by chance, the moſt injurious one.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: You put me to't, Sir; but to tell you truth,
They're all as one with me, little exception.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: T • at little may do much, let's have it from you.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: With all the ſpeed I may, firſt then, and foremoſt, hold ſo reverently of the Baſtinado, Sir,
That if it were the deareſt friend i'th' world,
I'de put it into his hand.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Go too, I'll paſs that then.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Y'are the more happy, Sir,
Would I were paſt it too:
But being accuſtom'd to't. It is the better carried.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Will you forward? dowſt,

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Then there's your ſouce, your wherit and your
Tugs on the hair, your bob o'th' lips, a whelp on't,
• ne'er could find much difference: Now your thump,
• thing deriv'd firſt from your Hemp-beaters,
Takes a mans wind away, moſt ſpitefully:
There's nothing that deſtroys a Collick like it,
For't leaves no wind i'th' body.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: On Sir, on.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Pray give me leave, I'm out of breath with thinking on't.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: This is far off yet.
For the twinge by th' noſe,
'Tis certainly unſightly, ſo my Tables ſays,
But helps againſt the head-ach, wond'rous ſtrangely,

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Oh your cruſh'd noſtrils ſlakes your opilation,
And makes your pent powers fluſh to wholſome ſneezes.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I never thought there had been half that virtue
In a wrung noſe before.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Oh plenitude, Sir:
Now come we lower to our modern Kick,
Which has been mightily in uſe of late,
Since our young men drank Coltsfoot: and I grant you,
'Tis a moſt ſcornful wrong, cauſe the foot plays it;
But mark agen, how we that take't, requite it
With the like ſcorn, for we receive it backward;
And can there be a worſe diſgrace retorted?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: And is this all?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: All but a Lug by th' ear,
Or ſuch a trifle.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Happy ſufferer,
All this is nothing to the wrong I bear:
I ſee the worſt diſgrace, thou never felt'ſt yet;
It is ſo far from thee, thou canſt not think on't;
Nor dare I let thee know, it is ſo abject.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I would you would though, that I might prepare for't
For I ſhall ha't at one time or another:
If't be a thwack, I make account of that;
There's no new faſhion'd ſwap that e'er came up yet,
But I've the firſt on 'em, I thank 'em for't.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Haſt thou enquir'd?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: But can hear nothing, Madam.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: If there be but ſo much ſubſtance in thee
To make a ſhelter for a man diſgrac'd,
Hide my departure from that glorious woman
That comes with all perfection about her:
So noble, that I dare not be ſeen of her,
Since ſhame took hold of me: upon thy life
No mention of me.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I'll cut out my tongue firſt,
Before I'll looſe my life, there's more belongs to't.

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.l: See there's a Gentleman, enquire of him.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.l: For Monſieur Shamont, Madam?

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.l: For whom elſe, Sir?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: Why, this fellow dares not ſee him.

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: 1 Serv,
sp.l: Shamont, Madam?
His very name's worſe than a Feaver to him,
And when he cries, there's nothing ſtills him ſooner;
Madam, your Page of thirteen is too hard for him,
'Twas try'd i'th' wood-yard.

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.l: Alas poor grieved Merit!
What is become of him? if he once fail,
Virtue ſhall find ſmall friendſhip: farewel then
To Ladies worths, for any hope in men,
He lov'd for goodneſs, not for Wealth, or Luſt,
After the worlds foul dotage, he ne'er courted
The body, but the beauty of the mind,
A thing which common courtſhip never thinks on:
All his affections were ſo ſweet and fair,
There is no hope for fame if he deſpair,

div.stage: Enter the Clown. He kicks Lapet.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Good morrow to you agen moſt heartily, Sir,
Cry you mercy, I heard you not, I was ſomewhat buſie.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: He takes it as familiarly, as an Ave,
Or precious ſalutation: I was ſick till I had one,
Becauſe I am ſo us'd to't.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: However you deſerve, your friends and mine, here
Give you large commendations i'this Letter,
They ſay you will endure well.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I'de be loath
To prove 'em liers: I've endur'd as much
As mortal pen and ink can ſet me down for.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Say you me ſo?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I know and feel it ſo, Sir,
I have it under Black and White already;
I need no Pen to paint me out.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: He fits me,
And hits my wiſhes pat, pat: I was ne'er
In poſſibility to be better mann'd,
For he's half lame already, I ſee't plain,
But take no notice on't, for fear I make
The raſcal proud, and dear, to advance his wages;
Firſt, let me grow into particulars with you;
What have you endur'd of worth? let me hear.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Marry Sir, I'm almoſt beaten blind.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: That's pretty well for a beginning,
But many a Mill-horſe has endur'd as much.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Shame o'th' Millers heart for his unkindneſs then.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Well Sir, what then?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I've been twice thrown down ſtairs, juſt before ſupper.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Puh, ſo have I, that's nothing.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I but Sir,
Was yours pray before ſupper;

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: There thou poſeſt me.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I marry, that's it, 't had been leſs grief to me,
Had I but fill'd my belly, and then tumbled,
But to be flung down faſting, there's the dolour.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: It would have griev'd me, that indeed: proceed Sir.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: I have been pluck'd and tugg'd by th' hair o'th' head
About a Gallery, half an Acre long.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Yes, that's a good one, I muſt needs confeſs,
A principal good one that, an abſolute good one,
I have been trode upon, and ſpurn'd about,
But never tugg'd by th' hair, I thank my fates.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Oh 'tis a ſpiteful pain.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Peace, never ſpeak on't,
For putting men in mind on't.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: To conclude,
I'm burſten Sir: my belly will hold no meat.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: No? that makes amends for all.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Unleſs 't be puddings.
Or ſuch faſt food, any looſe thing beguiles me, I'm ne'er the better for't.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Sheeps-heads will ſtay with thee?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Yes Sir, or Chaldrons.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Very well ſir:
Your burſten fellows muſt take heed of ſurfets:
Strange things it ſeems, you have endur'd;

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Too true Sir.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: But now the queſtion is, what you will endure
Hereafter in my ſervice?

sp.speaker: Clo.
