sp.l: Any thing
That ſhall be reaſon Sir, for I'm but froth;
Much like a thing new calv'd, or come more nearer Sir,
Y'ave ſeen a cluſter of Frog-ſpawns in April,
E'en ſuch a ſtarch am I, as weak and tender
As a green woman yet.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Now I know this,
I will be very gently angry with thee,
And kick thee carefully.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Oh I, ſweet Sir.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Peace, when thou art offer'd well, left I begin now.
Your friends and mine have writ here for your truth,
They'll paſs their words themſelves, and I muſt meet 'em.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Then have you all: Exit.
As for my honeſty, there is no fear of that,
For I have ne'er a whole bone about me. Exit.

div.stage: Muſick, Enter the paſſionate Coſin, rudely, and careleſly apparrell'd, unbrac'd, and untruſs'd. The Cupid following.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: Think upon love, which makes all creatures handſome,
Seemly for eye-ſight; goe not ſo diffuſedly,
There are great Ladies purpoſe Sir to viſit you.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Grand plagues, ſhut in my eaſements, that the breaths
Of their Coach-mares reek not into my noſtrils;
Thoſe beaſts are but a kind of bawdy fore-runners.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: It is not well with you,
When you ſpeak ill of fair Ladies.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Fair miſchiefs, give me a neſt of Owls and take 'em;
Happy is he, ſay I, whoſe window opens
To a brown Bakers chimney, he ſhall be ſure there
To hear the Bird ſometimes after twilight:
What a fine thing 'tis methinks to have our garments
Sit looſe upon us thus, thus careleſly,
It is more manly, and more mortifying;
For we're ſo much the readier for our ſhrouds:
For how ridiculous wer't, to have death come,
And take a fellow, pinn'd up like a Miſtriſs?
About his neck a Ruff, like a pinch'd Lanthorn,
Which School-boys make in winter; and his doublet
So cloſe and pent, as if he fear'd one priſon
Would not be ſtrong enough, to keep his ſoul in;
But's Tailor makes another:
And truſt me; (for I know't when I lov'd Cupid,)
He does endure much pain, for the poor praiſe
Of a neat ſitting ſuit.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: One may be handſome, Sir,
And yet not pain'd, nor proud.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: There you lie Cupid,
As bad as Mercury: there is no handſomneſs,
But has a waſh of Pride and Luxury,
And you go there too Cupid. Away diſſembler,
Thou tak'ſt the deeds part, which befools us all;
Thy Arrow heads ſhoot out ſinners: hence away,
And after thee I'll ſend a powerful charm,
Shall baniſh thee for ever.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: Never, never,
I am too ſure thine own. Exit.

lg.l: HEnce all you vain Delights,
As ſhort as are the nights,
Wherein you ſpend your folly,
There's nought in this life ſweet,
If man w • re wiſe to ſee't,
But only mel • ncholly!
Oh ſweeteſt melancholly!
Welcome folded Arms, and fixed Eyes,
A ſigh that piercing mortifies,
A look that's faſt' need to the ground,
A tongue chain'd up without a ſound.
Fountain heads, and p • t bleſs Groves,
Places which pale paſſion loves:
Moon-light walks, when all the Fowl.
Are warmly hous'd, ſave Bats and Owls;
A mid-night Bell, a parting groan,
Theſe are the ſounds we feed upon;
Then ſtretch our bones in a ſtill gloomy valley,
Nothing's ſo dainty ſweet, as lovely melanch • lly.

div.stage: Enter at another door Lapet, the Cupid's Brothers watching his coming.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: So, ſo, the Woodcock's ginn'd;
Keep this door faſt brother.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: I'll warrant this.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: I'll got incenſe him inſtantly;
I know the way to't.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: Will't not be too ſoon think you,
And make two ſits break into one?

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Pah, no, no; the tail of his melancholy
Is always the head of his anger, and follows as cloſe,
As the Report follows the powder.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: This is the appointed place, and the hour ſtruck,
If I can get ſecurity for's truth,
I'll never mind his honeſty, poor worm,
I durſt lay him by my wife, which is a benefit
Which many Maſters ha' not: I ſhall ha' no Maid
Now got with child, but what I get my ſelf,
And that's no ſmall felicity: in moſt places
Th'are got by th' Men, and put upon the Maſters,
Nor ſhall I be reſiſted when I ſtrike,
For he can hardly ſtand; theſe are great bleſſings.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I want my food, deliver me a Varlet. Within.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: How now, from whence comes that?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I am allow'd a carkaſs to inſult on;
Where's the villain?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: He means not me I hope.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: My maintenance raſcals; my bulk, my exhibition.

sp.speaker: Dap.
sp.l: Bleſs us all,
What names are theſe? Would I were gone agen.

div.stage: The paſſionate man enters in fury with a Truncheon.

body.head: He Sings.
body.l: A Curſe upon thee for a ſlave,
Art thou here, and heardſt me rave?
Fly not ſparkles from mine eye,
To ſhew my indignation nigh?
Am I not all foam, and fire,
With voice as hoarſe as a Town-crier?
How my back opes and ſhuts together,
With fury, as old mens with weather?
Could'ſt thou not hear my teeth gnaſh hither?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: No truly, Sir, I thought 't had been a Squirrel,
Shaving a Hazel-nut.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Death; Hell, Fiends, and darkneſs.
I will thraſh thy maungy carkaſs.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Oh ſweet Sir.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: There cannot be too many tortures,
Spent upon thoſe louzie Quarters.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Hold, oh. Falls down for dead.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Thy bones ſhall rue, thy bones ſhall rue.

body.head: Sings again.
body.l: THou naſty, ſcurvy, mongril Toad,
Miſchief on thee;
Light upon thee,
All the plagues
That can confound thee
Or did ever raign abroad:
Better a thouſand lives it coſt,
Than have brave anger ſpilt or loſt. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lap,
sp.l: May I open mine eyes yet, and ſafely peep:
I'll try a groon firſt—oh—Nay then he's gone.
There was no other policy but to dy,
He would ha' made me elſe. Ribs are you ſore?
I was ne'er beaten to a tune before.

l.hi: Lapet.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Agen? Falls again.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Look, look, he's flat agen,
And ſtretched out like a Coarſe, a handful longer
Than he walks, truſt me brother. Why Lapet
I hold my life we ſhall not get him ſpeak now:
Monſieur Lapet; it muſt be a privy token,
If any thing fetch him, he's ſo far gone.
We come to paſs our words for your mans truth.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Oh Gentlemen y'are welcome: I have been thraſh'd i' faith.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: How? thraſh'd Sir?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Never was Shrove-tueſday Bird
So cudgell'd, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Pray how? by whom Sir?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Nay, that I know not.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Not who did this wrong?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Only a thing came like a Walking Song?

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: What beaten with a Song?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Never more tightly, Gentlemen:
Such crotchets happen now and then, methinks
He that endures well, of all waters drinks. Exeunt.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Shamont's Brother, the Soldier, and 1 Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: YEs, yes, this was a Madman, Sir, with you,
A paſſionate Mad-man.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Who would ha' lookt for this, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: And muſt be priviledg'd: a pox priviledge him:
I was never ſo dry beaten ſince I was born,
And by a litter of rogues, meer rogues, the whole twenty
Had not above elbows amongſt 'em all too:
And the moſt part of thoſe left-handed raſcals,
The very vomit, Sir, of Hoſpitals,
Bridewels, and Spittle-houſes; ſuch naſty ſmellers,
That if they'd been unfurniſh'd of Club-Truncheons,
They might have cudgell'd me with their very ſtinks,
It was ſo ſtrong, and ſturdy: and ſhall this,
This filthy injury, be ſet off with madneſs?

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Nay, take your own blouds counſel, Sir, hereafter,
I'll deal no further in't: if you remember,
It was not come to blows, when I advis'd you.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: No, but I ever ſaid, 'twould come to ſomething,
And 'tis upon me, thank him: were he kin
To all the mighty Emperors upon earth.
He has not now in life three hours to reckon;
I watch but a free time.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Your noble brother, Sir, I'll leave you now. Ex.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Soldier, I would I could perſwade my thoughts
From thinking thee a brother, as I can
My tongue from naming on't: thou haſt no friend here,
But fortune and thy own ſtrength truſt to them.
Treachery to virtue;
Thy treachery, thy faithleſs circumvention:
Has Honor ſo few daughters, never fewer,
And muſt thou aim thy treachery at the beſt?
The very front of virtue, that bleſt Lady? the Dukes Siſter?
Created more for admirations cauſe,
Than for loves ends; whoſe excellency ſparkles
More in Divinity, than mortal beauty;
And as much difference 'twixt her mind and body,
As 'twixt this earths poor centre, and the Sun:
And could'ſt thou be ſo injurious to fair goodneſs,
Once to attempt to court her down to frailty?
Or put her but in mind that there is weakneſs,
Sin, and deſire, which ſhe ſhould never hear of?
Wretch, thou'ſt committed worſe than Sacriledge,
In the attempting on't, and ought'ſt to dye for't.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: I rather ought to do my beſt, to live, Sir.
Provoke me not; for I've a wrong ſits on me,
That makes me apt for miſchief; I ſhall loſe
All reſpects ſuddainly of friendſhip, Brother-hood,
Or any ſound that way.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: But 'ware me moſt;
For I come with a two-edg'd injury;
Both my diſgrace, and thy apparent falſhood,
Which muſt he dangerous.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: I courted her, Sir;
Love ſtarve me with delays, when I confeſs it not.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: There's nothing then but death
Can be a pennance fit for that confeſſion.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: But far from any vitious taint.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh Sir,
Vice is a mighty ſtranger grown to courtſhip.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: Nay, then the fury of my wrong light on thee.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Forbear, the Duke's at hand,
Here, hard at hand, upon my reputation.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.l: I muſt do ſomething now. Ex. Sold.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I'll follow you cloſe Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: We muſt intreat you muſt not; for the Duke
Deſires ſome conference with you.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Let me go,
As y'are Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Faith we dare not Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Dare ye be falſe to honor, and yet dare not
Do a man juſtice? give me leave —

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Good ſweet Sir.
H'as ſent twice for you.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Is this brave, or manly?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I prethee be conform'd.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Death—

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: Peace, he's come in troth.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh have you betraid me to my ſhame afreſh?
How am I bound to loath you?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Shamont, welcome,
I ſent twice.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: But my Lord, he never heard on't.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Pray pardon him, for his falſeneſs, I did Sir,
Both times; I'd rather be found rude, than faithleſs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I love that bluntneſs dearly: h'as no vice,
But is more manly than ſome others virtue,
That lets it out only for ſhew or profit.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Will't pleaſe you quit me, Sir, I've urgent buſineſs?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Come, you're ſo haſty now, I ſent for you
To a better end.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: And if it be an end,
Better or worſe, I thank your goodneſs for't.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I've ever kept that bounty in condition,
And thankfulneſs in bloud, which well becomes
Both Prince and Subject, that where any wrong
Bears my impreſſion, or the haſty figure
Of my repented anger, I'm a Law
Ev'n to my ſelf, and doom my ſelf moſt ſtrictly
To Juſtice, and a noble ſatisfaction:
So that, what you, in tenderneſs of honor,
Conceive to be loſs to you, which is nothing
But curious opinion, I'll reſtore agen,
Although I give you the beſt part of Genoa,
And take to boot but thanks for your amends.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh miſerable ſatisfaction,
Ten times more wretched than the wrong it ſelf;
Never was ill better made good with worſe:
Shall it be ſaid, that my poſterity
Shall live the ſole heir of their fathers ſhame?
And raiſe their wealth and glory from my ſtripes?
You have provided nobly, bounteous Sir,
For my diſgrace, to make it live for ever,
Out-laſting Braſs or Marble:
This is my fears conſtruction, and a deep one,
Which neither argument nor time can alter:
Yet I dare ſwear, I wrong your goodneſs in't Sir,
And the moſt fair intent on't, which I reverence
With admiration, that in you a Prince,
Should be ſo ſweet and temperate a condition,
To offer to reſtore where you may ruine,
And do't with juſtice, and in me a ſervant,
So harſh a diſpoſition, that I cannot
Forgive where I ſhould honor, and am bound to't,
But I have ever had that curioſity
In bloud, and tenderneſs of reputation
Such an antipathy againſt a blow,
I cannot ſpeak the reſt: Good Sir diſcharge me,
It is not fit that I ſhould ſerve you more,
Nor come ſo near you; I'm made now for privacy,
And a retir'd condition, that's my ſuit:
To part from Court for ever, my laſt ſuit;
And as you profeſs bounty, grant me that Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I would deny thee nothing.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Health reward you, Sir Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: He's gone agen already, and takes hold
Of any opportunity: not riches
Can purchaſe him, nor honors, peaceably,
And force were brutiſh: what a great worth's gone with him,
And but a Gentleman? well, for his ſake,
I'll ne'er offend more, thoſe I cannot make,
They were his words, and ſhall be dear to memory.
Say I deſire to ſee him once agen;
Yet ſtay, he's ſo well forward of his peace,
'Twere pity to diſturb him: he would groan
Like a ſoul fetch'd agen; and that were injury,
And I've wrong'd his degree too much already.
Call forth the Gentleman of our chamber inſtantly.

sp.speaker: 1 Serv.
sp.l: I ſhall my Lord. Within.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I may forget agen,
And therefore will prevent: the ſtrain of this
Troubles me ſo, one would not hazard more.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Your Will my Lord?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yes; I diſcharge you all.

sp.speaker: 2 Gent.
sp.l: My Lord—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Your places ſhall be otherwiſe diſpos'd of.

sp.speaker: 4 Gent.
sp.l: Why Sir?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Reply not, I diſmiſs you all:
Y'are Gentlemen, your worths will find you fortunes;
Nor ſhall your farewell taxe me of ingratitude.
I'll give you all noble remembrances,
As teſtimonies 'gainſt reproach and malice,
That you departed lov'd.

sp.speaker: 3 Gen.
sp.l: This is moſt ſtrange, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: But how is your Grace furniſh'd, theſe diſmiſs'd?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Seek me out Grooms.
Men more inſenſible of reputation,
Leſs curious and preciſe in terms of honor,
That if my anger chance let fall a ſtroke,
As we are all ſubject to impetuous paſſions,
Yet it may paſs unmurmur'd, undiſputed,
And not with braver fury proſecuted. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: It ſhall be done, my Lord.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: Know you the cauſe, Sir?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Not I kind Gentlemen, but by conjectures,
And ſo much ſhall be yours when you pleaſe.
Thanks Sir.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: We ſhall i'th mean time think our ſelves guilty
Of ſome ſoul fault, through ignorance committed.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: No, 'tis not that, nor that way.

sp.speaker: 4 Gent.
sp.l: For my part,
I ſhall be diſ-inherited, I know ſo much.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Why Sir, for what?

sp.speaker: 4 Gent.
sp.l: My Sire's of a ſtrange humor,
He'll form faults for me, and then ſwear 'em mine,
And commonly the firſt begins with leachery,
He knows his own youths treſpaſs,

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Before you go,
I'll come and take my leave, and tell you all Sirs.

sp.speaker: 3 Gent.
sp.l: Thou wert ever juſt and kind. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: That's my poor virtue, Sir,
And parcel valiant; but it's hard to be perfect:
The chooſing of theſe fellows now will puzle me,
Horribly puzle me; and there's no judgement
Goes true upon mans outſide, there's the miſchief:
He muſt be touch'd, and try'd, for gold or droſs;
There is no other way for't, and that's dangerous too;
But ſince I'm put in truſt, and I will atttempt it:
The Duke ſhall keep one daring man about him.
Soft, who comes here? a pretty bravery this:
Every one goes ſo like a Gentleman,
'Tis hard to find a difference, but by th' touch.
I'll try your mettal ſure.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: Why what do you mean Sir?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Nay, and you underſtand it not, I do not.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: Yes, would you ſhould well know,
I underſtand it for a box o'th' ear Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: And o'my troth, that's all I gave it for.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: 'Twere beſt it be ſo.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: This is a brave Coward,
A jolly threat'ning Coward; he ſhall be Captain:
Sir, let me meet you an hour hence i'th' Lobby.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: Meet you? the world might laugh at you then i'faith.

sp.speaker: 1 Ge.
sp.l: Lay by your ſcorn and pride, they're ſcurvy qualities,
And meet me, or I'll box you while I have you,
And carry you gambril'd thither like a Mutton.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: Nay, and you be in earneſt, here's my hand
I will not fail you.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis for your own good.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: Away.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Too much for your own good, Sir, a pox on you.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: I prethee curſe me all day long ſo.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Hang you.

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: I'll make him mad: he's loth to curſe too much to me;
Indeed I never yet took box o'th' ear,
But it redounded, I muſt needs ſay ſo —

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Will you be gone?

sp.speaker: Gal.
sp.l: Curſe, curſe, and then I goe.
Look how he grins, I've anger'd him to th' kidneys. Ex.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Was ever ſuch a prigging coxcomb ſeen?
One might have beat him dumb now in this humor,
And he'd ha' grin'd it out ſtill:
Oh, here's one made to my hand,
Methinks looks like a Craven;
Leſs pains will ſerve his trial: ſome ſlight juſtle.

sp.speaker: Plain.
sp.l: How? take you that Sir:
And if that content you not—

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Yes very well, Sir, I deſire no more.

sp.speaker: Plain.
sp.l: I think you need not;
For you have not loſt by't. Exit.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: Who would ha' thought this would have prov'd a Gentleman?
I'll never truſt long chins and little legs agen,
I'll know 'em ſure for Gentlemen hereafter:
A griſtle but in ſhew, but gave his cuff
With ſuch a fetch, and reach of gentry,
As if h' had had his arms before the floud;
I have took a villanous hard taske upon me;
Now I begin to have a feeling on't.
sp.stage: Enter Lapet, and Clown his ſervant, and ſo habited.
sp.l: Oh, here comes a try'd piece, now, the reformed kick.
The millions of punches, ſpurns, and nips
That he has endur'd? his buttock's all black Lead,
He's half a Negro backward; he was paſt a Spaniard
In Eighty eight, and more Aegyptian like;
His Table and his Book come both out ſhortly,
And all the cowards in the Town expect it;
So, if I fail of my full number now,
I ſhall be ſure to find 'em at Church corners,
Where Dives, and the ſuff'ring Ballads hang.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Well, ſince thou art of ſo mild a temper,
Of ſo meek a ſpirit, thou mayſt live with me,
Till better times do ſmile on thy deſerts.
I am glad I am got home again.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I am happy in your ſervice, Sir,
You'll keep me from the Hoſpital.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: So, bring me the laſt proof, this is corrected.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I, y'are too full of your correction, Sir,

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Look I have perfect Books within this half hour.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Bid him put all the Thumps in Pica Roman.
And with great T's, (you vermin) as Thumps ſhould be.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Then in what Letter will you have your Kicks?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: All in Italica, your backward blows
All in Italica, you Hermophrodite:
When ſhall I teach you wit?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Oh let it alone,
Till you have ſome your ſelf, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: You mumble?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: The victuals are lockt up;
I'm kept from mumbling. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: He prints my blows upon Pot Paper too, the rogue,
Which had been proper for ſome drunken Pamphlet.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Monſieur Lapet? how the world rings of you, Sir?
Your name ſounds far and near.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: A good report it bears, for an enduring name—

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: What luck have you Sir?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Why, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I'm but thinking on't.
I've heard you wiſh theſe five years for a place.
Now there's one fall'n, and freely without money too;
And empty yet, and yet you cannot have't.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: No? what's the reaſon? I'll give money for't,
Rather than go without Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: That's not it Sir:
The troth is, there's no Gentleman muſt have it
Either for love or money, 'tis decreed ſo;
I was heartily ſorry when I thought upon you,
Had you not been a Gentleman, I had fitted you.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Who I a Gentleman? a pox I'm none, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: How? why did you ever think I was?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: What? not a Gentleman?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I would thou'dſt put it upon me i'faith;
Did not my Grand-father cry Cony-skins?
My Father Aquavitae? a hot Gentleman:
All this I ſpeak on, i' your time and memory too;
Only a rich Uncle dy'd, and left me chattels,
You know all this ſo well too —

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Pray excuſe me, Sir, ha' not you Arms?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Yes, a poor couple here,
That ſerve to thruſt in wild-Fowl.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Heralds Arms,
Symbols of Gentry, Sir: you know my meaning;
They've been ſhewn and ſeen.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: They have,

sp.speaker: 1 Gen.
sp.l: I fex have they.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Why I confeſs, at my wives inſtigation once,
(As Women love theſe Heralds kickſhawes naturally)
I bought 'em: but what are they think you? puffs.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Why, that's proper to your name being Lapet.
Which is La fart, after the Engliſh Letter.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: The Herald, Sir, had much adoe to find it.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: And can you blame him?
Why, 'tis the only thing that puzles the devil.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: At laſt he lookt upon my name agen,
And having well compar'd it, this he gave me,
The two Cholliques playing upon a wind Inſtrument.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: An excellent proper one; but I pray tell me,
How does he expreſs the Cholliques?
They are hard things.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: The Cholliques? with hot trenchers at their bellies,
There's nothing better, Sir, to blaze a Chollique.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: And are not you a Gentleman by this Sir?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: No, I diſclaim't: no belly-ake upon earth
Shall make me one: he ſhall not think
To put his gripes upon me.
And wring out gentry ſo, and ten pound firſt.
If the wind Inſtrument will make my wife one,
Let her enjoy't, for ſhe was a Harpers Grand-child:
But Sir, for my particular, I renounce it.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Or to be call'd ſo?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I Sir, or imagin'd.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: None fitter for the place: give me thy hand.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: A hundred thouſand thanks, beſide a Bribe, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Yov muſt take heed
Of thinking toward a Gentleman, now.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Piſh, I am not mad, I warrant you: nay, more Sir,
If one ſhould twit me i'th' teeth that I'm a Gentleman,
Twit me their worſt, I am but one ſince Lammas,
That I can prove, if they would ſee my heart out.

sp.speaker: 2 Gen.
sp.l: Marry, in any caſe keep me that evidence.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Here comes my ſervant; Sir. Galoſhio,
Has not his name for nought, he will be trode upon:
What ſays my Printer now?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Here's your laſt Proof, Sir.
You ſhall have perfect Books now in a twinkling.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Theſe marks are ugly.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: He ſays, Sir, they're proper:
Blows ſhould have marks, or elſe they are nothing worth.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: But why a Peel-crow here?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: I told 'em ſo Sir:
A ſcare-crow had been better.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: How ſlave? look you, Sir,
Did not I ſay, this Whirrit, and this Bob,
Should be both Pica Roman.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: So ſaid I, Sir, both Picked Romans,
And he has made 'em Welch Bills,
Indeed I know not what to make on 'em.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Hay-day; a Souſe, Italica?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Yes, that may hold, Sir,
Souſe is a bona roba, ſo is Flops too.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: But why ſtands Baſtinado ſo far off here?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Alas, you muſt allow him room to lay about him, Sir.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Why lies this Spurn lower than that Spurn, Sir?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Marry, this ſignifies one kick down ſtairs, Sir,
The other in a Gallery: I ask'd him all theſe queſtions.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Your Books name?
Prethee Lapet mind me, you never told me yet.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Marry but ſhall Sir: 'tis call'd the Upriſing of the kick;
And the downfall of the Duello

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Bring that to paſs, you'll prove a happy member,
And do your Countrey ſervice: your young blouds
Will thank you then, why they ſee fourſcore.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I hope
To ſave my hundred Gentlemen a month by't,
Which will be very good for the private houſe.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Look you, your Table's finiſh'd, Sir, already.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Why then behold my Maſter-piece: ſee, ſee, Sir,
Here's all your Blows, and Blow-men whatſoever;
Set in their lively colours, givers, and takers.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Troth wondrous fine, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Nay, but mark the poſtures,
The ſtanding of the takers, I admire more than the givers;
They ſtand ſcornfully, moſt contumeliouſly, I like not them,
Oh here's one caſt into a comely Figure.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: My Maſter means him there that's caſt down headlong

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: How ſweetly does this fellow take his Dowſt?
Stoops like a Cammel, that Heroick beaſt,
At a great load of Nutmegs; and how meekly
This other fellow here receives his Whirrit?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Oh Maſter, here's a fellow ſtands moſt gallantly,
Taking his kick in private, behind the hangings,
And raiſing up his hips to't. But oh, Sir,
How daintily this man lies trampled on?
Would I were in thy place, what e'er thou art:
How lovely he endures it?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: But will not theſe things, Sir, be hard to practiſe, think you?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Oh, eaſie, Sir: I'll teach 'em in a Dance.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: How? in a dance?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I'll loſe my new place elſe,
What e'er it be; I know not what 'tis yet.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: And now you put me in mind, I could employ it well,
For your grace, ſpecially: For the Dukes Coſin
Is by this time in's violent fit of mirth,
And a device muſt be ſought out for ſuddainly,
To over-cloy the paſſion.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Say no more, Sir,
I'll fit you with my Scholars, new practitioners,
Endurers of the time.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Whereof I am one Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You carry it away ſmooth; give me thy hand, Sir.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: HA, ha, ha. Within.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: Hark, hark, how loud his fit's grown.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Now let our Siſter loſe no time, but ply it
With all the power ſhe has.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: Her ſhame grows big, brother;
The Cupid's ſhape will hardly hold it longer,
'Twould take up half an Ell of China Damask more,
And all too little: it ſtruts per'louſly:
There is no tamp'ring with theſe Cupids longer,
The meer conceit with Woman-kind works ſtrong.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: The laugh comes nearer now,
'Twere good we were not ſeen yet. Ex. Bro.

div.stage: Enter Paſſion, and Baſe, his jeſter.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Ha. ha, ha,
And was he baſtinado'd to the life? ha, ha, ha.
I prethee ſay, Lord General, how did the raſcals
Entrench themſelves?

sp.speaker: Baſe.
sp.l: Moſt deeply, politickly, all in ditches.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: 'Tis thought he'll ne'r bear Arms in field agen,
Has much ado to lift 'em to his head, Sir.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I would he had.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: On either ſide round Truncheons plaid ſo thick.
That Shoulders, Chines, nay Flanks were paid to th' quick.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Well ſaid Lord-General: ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: But pray how grew the diff'rence firſt betwixt you?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: There was never any, Sir; there lies the jeſt man;
Only becauſe he was taller than his brother;
There's all my quarrel, to him; and me thought
He ſhould be beaten for't, my mind ſo gave me, Sir,
I could not ſleep for't: Ha, ha, ha, ha.
Another good jeſt quickly, while 'tis hot now;
Let me not laugh in vain: ply me, oh ply me,
As you will anſwer't to my coſin Duke.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Alas, who has a good jeſt?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I fall, I dwindle in't.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Ten Crowns for a god jeſt: ha' you a good jeſt, Sir?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: A pretty moral one,

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Let's ha't, what e'er it be.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.l: There comes a Cupid
Drawn by ſix fools.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: That's nothing.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Help it, help it then.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: I ha' known ſix hundred fools drawn by a Cupid.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: I that, that, that's the ſmarter Moral: ha, ha, ha.
Now I begin to be Song-ripe methinks.

sp.speaker: Baſ
sp.l: I'll ſing you a pleaſant Air Sir, before you ebb.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Oh how my Lungs do tickle? ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Oh how my Lungs do tickle? oh, oh, ho, ho.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Set a ſharp Jeſt
Againſt my breaſt,
Then how my Lungs do tickle?
As Nightingales,
And things in Cambrick rails,
Sing beſt againſt a prickle,
Ha, ha, ha. ha.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Ho, ho, ho, ho, ha.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Laugh.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Laugh.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Laugh.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Laugh.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Wide.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Loud,

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: And vary.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: A ſmile is for a ſimpering Novice.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: One that ne'er taſted Caveare,

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Nor knows the ſmack of dear Anchovis.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Ho, ho, ho, ho, ho.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: A gigling waiting wench for me,
That ſhews her teeth how white they be.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: A thing not fit for gravity,
For theirs are foul, and hardly three.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Ho, ho, ho.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Democritus, thou antient Fleerer,
How I miſs thy laugh, and ha' ſince.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: There you nam'd the famous Jeerer,
That ever jeer'd in Rome, or Athens.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Ho, ho, ho.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: How brave lives he that keeps a fool,
Although the rate be deeper?

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: But he that is his own fool, Sir,
Does live a great deal cheaper.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Sure I ſhall burſt, burſt, quite break, thou art ſo witty.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: 'Tis rare to break at Court, for that belongs to th' City.

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Ha, ha, my ſpleen is almoſt worn to the laſt laughter.

sp.speaker: Baſ.
sp.l: Oh keep a corner for a friend, a jeſt may come hereafter.

div.stage: Enter Lapet and Clown, and four other, like fools dancing, the Cupid leading, and bearing his Table, and holding it up to Lapet at every ſtrain, and acting the poſtures.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Twinge all now, twinge I ſay.
Souſe upon Souſe.
Douſes ſingle.
Juſtle ſides.
Knee Belly.
Kickſee Buttock.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Downderry.

div.stage: Enter Soldier, Shamont's brother; his ſword drawn.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.l: Not angry Law, nor doors of Braſs ſhall keep me,
From my wrongs expiation to thy Bowels,
I return my diſgrace; and after turn
My face to any death that can be ſentenc'd,

sp.speaker: Baſe.
sp.l: Murder, oh murder, ſtop the murderer there—

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: I am glad he's gone; h'as almoſt trode my guts out;
Follow him who liſt for me, I'll ha' no hand in't.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Oh 'twas your luck and mine to be ſquelch'd, Mr.
Has ſtamp'd my very Puddings into Pancakes.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: Oh brothers, oh, I fear 'tis mortal: help, oh help,
I'm made the wretchedſt woman by this accident,
That ever love beguil'd.

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: We are undone Brother,
Our ſhames are too apparent: Away receptacle
Of Luxury, and diſhonor, moſt unfortunate,
To make thy ſelf but lucky to thy ſpoil,
After thy Sexes manner. lift him up Brother;
He breaths not to our comfort, he's too waſted
Ever to cheer us more: A Chirurgeon ſpeedily;
Hence; the unhappieſt that e'er ſtept aſide,
She'll be a Mother, before ſhe's known a Bride.

sp.speaker: Cup.
sp.l: Thou hadſt a moſt unfortunate conception,
What e'er thou prov'ſt to be; in midſt of mirth
Comes ruine, for a welcome, to thy birth. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: This is a beautiful life now; privacy
The ſweetneſs and the benefit of Eſſence:
I ſee there is no man, but may make his Paradice;
And it is nothing but his love, and dotage
Upon the worlds foul joyes, that keeps him out on't:
For he that lives retir'd in mind, and ſpirit,
Is ſtill in Paradice, and has his innocence,
Partly allow'd for his companion too,
As much as ſtands with juſtice: here no eyes
Shoot their ſharp pointed ſcorns upon my ſhame;
They know no terms of reputation here,
No punctual limits, or preciſe dimenſions:
Plain down-right honeſty is all the beauty
And elegancy of life, found amongſt Shepheards;
For knowing nothing nicely, or deſiring it,
Quits many a vexation from the mind,
With which our quainter knowledge does abuſe us;
The name of envy is a ſtranger here,
That dries mens blouds abroad, robs Health and Reſt,
Why here's no ſuch fury thought on: no, nor falſhood,
That brotherly diſeaſe, fellow-like devil,
That plays within our boſom, and betrays us,

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Oh are you here?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: La Nove, 'tis ſtrange to ſee thee.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I ha' rid one horſe to death,
To find you out, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I am not to be found of any man
That ſaw my ſhame, nor ſeen long.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Good, your attention:
You ought to be ſeen now, and found out, Sir,
If ever you deſire before your ending
To perform one good office, nay, a dear one,
Mans time can hardly match it.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Be't as precious
As reputation; if it come from Court
I will not hear on't.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You muſt hear of this, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Muſt?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: You ſhall hear it.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I love thee, that thou'lt dye.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Twere nobler in me,
Than in you living: you will live a murderer,
If you deny this office.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Even to death, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Why then you'll kill your brother.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: Your Brother, Sir:
Bear witneſs heaven, this man deſtroys his Brother
When he may ſave him, his leaſt breath may ſave him:
Can there be wilfuller deſtruction?
He was forc'd to take a moſt unmanly wrong,
Above the ſuff'ring virtue of a Soldier,
Has kill'd his injurer, a work of honor;
For which, unleſs you ſave him, he dies ſpeedily
My conſcience is diſcharg'd, I'm but a friend,
A Brother ſhould go forward where I end. Exit.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Dyes?
Say he be naught, that's nothing to my goodneſs,
Which ought to ſhine through uſe, or elſe it loſes
The glorious name 'tis known by: he's my brother;
Yet peace is above bloud: Let him go; I,
But where's the nobleneſs of affection then?
That muſt be car'd for too, or I'm imperfect,
The ſame bloud that ſtood up in wrath againſt him,
Now in his miſery, runs all to pity;
I'd rather dye than ſpeak one ſyllable
To ſave my ſelf, but living as I am,
There's no avoiding on't, the worlds humanity
Expects it hourly from me: curſe of fortune,
I took my leave ſo well too: Let him dye,
'Tis but a brother loſt; ſo pleaſingly.
And ſwiftly I came off, 'twere more than irkſomneſs,
To tread that path agen; and I ſhall never
Depart ſo handſomely: but then where's poſterity?
The conſummation of our houſe and name?
I'm torn in pieces betwixt love and ſhame, Exit.

div.head: Scaena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Lapet, Clown, Poultrot, Moulbazon, and others, the new Court Officers.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Good morrow fellow Poltrot, and Moulbazon,
Good morrow fellows all.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Monſieur Lapet?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Look, I've remembred you, here's books apiece for you.

sp.speaker: Moul.
sp.l: Oh Sir, we dearly thank you.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: So you may:
There's two impreſſions gone already, Sirs.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: What no? in ſo ſhort a time?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: 'Tis as I tell you, Sir.
My Kick ſells gallantly, I thank my ſtars.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: So does your Table; you may thank the Moon too.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: 'Tis the Book ſells the Table.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: But 'tis the Bookſeller
That has the money for 'em, I'm ſure o' that.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: 'Twill much enrich the Company of Stationers,
'Tis thought 'twill prove a laſting benefit,
Like the Wiſe Maſters, and the Almanacks.
The hundred Novels, and the Book of Cookery,
For they begin already to engroſs it,
And make it a Stock-book, thinking indeed
'Twill prove too great a benefit, and help,
For one that's new ſet up: they know their way,
And make him Warden, e'r his beard be gray.

sp.speaker: Moul.
sp.l: Is't poſſible ſuch virtue ſhould lye hid,
And in ſo little Paper?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: How? why there was the Carpenter,
An unknown thing; an odoriferous Pamphlet,
Yet no more Paper, by all computation,
Than Ajax Telamon would uſe at once,
Your Herring prov'd the like, able to buy
Another Fiſhers Folly, and your Paſquil
Went not below the mad-caps of that time,
And ſhall my elaborate Kick come behind, think you?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Yes, it muſt come behind, 'tis in Italica too,
According to your humor.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Not in ſale, Varlet.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: In ſale, Sir? it ſhall ſail beyond 'em all I tro.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: What have you there now? oh Page 21.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: That Page is come to his years, he ſhould be a Serving man.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Mark how I ſnap up the Duello there:
One would not uſe a dog ſo,
I muſt needs ſay; but's for the common good.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Nay Sir, your Commons ſeldom fight at ſharp,
But buffet in a Warehouſe.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: This will ſave
Many a Gentleman of good bloud from bleeding, Sirs,
I have a curſe from many a Barber-Surgeon;
They'd give but too much money to call't in;
Turn to Page 45. ſee what you find there.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Oh, out upon him,
Page 45. that's an old thief indeed.

div.stage: Enter Duke, the Lady his Siſter, 1 Gent.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: The Duke, clap down your Books; away Galoſhio.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Indeed I am too ſoul to be i'th' preſence,
They uſe to ſhake me o • a • the chamber door ſtill. Ex.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Good my Lord, •• nt my ſuit: let me not riſe
Witho • t the comfort on't: I have not often
Been tedious in this ••• d.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Siſter, you wrong your ſelf,
And thoſe great virtues that your Fame i • ma • e of,
To waſte ſo much breath for a murderers life.

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.l: You cannot hate th' offence more than I do, Sir,
Nor the offendor, the reſpect I owe
Unto his abſent brother, makes me a ſuitor,
A moſt importunate Siſter, make me worthy
But of this one requeſt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I am deaf
To any importunacy, and ſorry
For your forgetfulneſs; you never injur'd
Your worth ſo much, you ought to be rebuk'd for't:
Purſue good ways, end as you did begin,
'Tis half the guilt to ſpeak for ſuch a ſin.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: This is loves beggery right, that now is ours,
When Ladies love, and cannot ſhew their powers. Ex.

l.hi: La Nove?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Are theſe our new Attendants?

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: We are my Lord, and will endure as much
As better men, my Lord, and more I truſt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What's he?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: My Lord, a decay'd Gentleman,
That will do any ſervice.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: A decay'd one?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: A renounc'd one indeed: for this place only.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We renounce him then; go, diſcharge him inſtantly.
He that diſclaims his gentry for meer gains,
That man's too baſe to make a vaſſal on.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: What ſays the Duke?

sp.speaker: 1 Duke.
sp.l: Faith little to your comfort, Sir,
You muſt be a Gentleman agen.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: There's no remedy.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: Marry, the fates foreſend: ne'r while I breathe, Sir,

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: The Duke will have it ſo, there's no reſiſting,
He ſpy'd it i' your forehead.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: My wife's doing.
She thought ſhe ſhould be put below her betters now,
And ſu'd to ha' me a Gentleman agen.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: And very likely, Sir,
Marry, I'll give you this comfort when all's done,
You'll never paſs but for a ſcurvy one,
That's all the help you have: come ſhew your pace.

sp.speaker: Lap.
sp.l: The heavieſt Gentleman that e'er loſt place;
Bear witneſs, I am forc'd to't. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Though you have a courſer Title yet upon you,
Than thoſe that left your places, without blame,
'Tis in your power to make your ſelves the ſame:
I cannot make you Gentlemen, that's a work
Rais'd from your own deſervings, merit, manners,
And in-born virtue does it. Let your own goodneſs
Make you ſo great, my power ſhall make you greater;
And more t'encourage you, this I add agen,
There's many Grooms, now exact Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Methinks 'tis ſtrange to me to enter here:
Is there in nature ſuch an awful power,
To force me to this place? and make me do this?
Is mans affection ſtronger than his Will?
His reſolution? was I not reſolv'd
Never to ſee this place more? Do I bear
Within my breaſt one bloud that confounds th' other?
The bloud of Love, and Will, and the laſt weakeſt?
Had I ten Millions, I would give it all now,
I were but paſt it, or 'twould never come;
For I ſhall never do't, or not do't well,
But ſpoil it utterly betwixt two paſſions,
Yonder's the Duke himſelf, I will not do't now,
Had twenty lives their ſeveral ſufferings in him. Exit.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Who's that went out now?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I ſaw none my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Nor you?

sp.speaker: Moul.
sp.l: I ſaw the glimpſe of one my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What e'er it was, methought it pleas'd me ſtrangely
And ſuddenly my joy was ready for't.
Did you not mark it better?

sp.speaker: Pol. & Moul.
sp.l: Troth my Lord,
We gave no great heed to't.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: 'Twill not be anſwer'd,
It brings me hither ſtill; by main force hither:
Either I muſt give over to profeſs humanity,
Or I muſt ſpeak for him.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: 'Tis here agen:
No marvel 'twas ſo pleaſing, 'tis delight
And worth it ſelf, now it appears unclouded.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: My Lord—
He turns away from me: by this hand
I am ill-us'd of all ſides: 'tis a fault
That fortune ever had t'abuſe a goodneſs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Methought you were ſaying ſomewhat.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Mark the Language,
As coy as fate; I ſee 'twill ne'er be granted.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We little look'd in troth to ſee you here yet.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Not till the day after my brother's death, I think.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Sure ſome great buſineſs drew you.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: No inſooth, Sir,
Only to come to ſee a brother dye, Sir,
That I may learn to go too; and if he deceive me not,
I think he will do well in't of a ſoldier,
Manly, and honeſtly: and if he weep then,
I ſhall not think the worſe on's manhood for't,
Becauſe he's leaving of that part that has it.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Has ſlain a noble Gentleman, think on't, Sir,

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I would I could not, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Our kinſman too.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: All this is but worſe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: When 'tis at worſt,
Yet ſeeing thee, he lives.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: My Lord—

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: He lives,
Believe it as thy bliſs, he dies not for't:
Will this make ſatisfaction for things paſt?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh my Lord —

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Will it? ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: With greater ſhame to my unworthineſs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Riſe then, we're even: I never found it harder
To keep juſt with a man: my great work's ended.
I knew your brother's pardon was your ſuit, Sir.
However your nice modeſty held it back.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: I take a joy now, to confeſs, it, Sir.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: My Lord —

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Hear me firſt, Sir, what e'er your news be:
Set free the Soldier inſtantly.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: 'Tis done, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: In effect: 'twas part of my news too,
There's fair hope of your noble kinſman's life, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What ſayſt thou?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: And the moſt admired change
That living fleſh e'r had; he's not the man my Lord;
Death cannot be more free from paſſions, Sir,
Than he is at this inſtant: he's ſo meek now,
He makes thoſe ſeem paſſionate, was never thought of:
And for he fears his moods have oft diſturb'd you, Sir,
He's only haſty now for his forgiveneſs,
And here behold him, Sir.

div.stage: Enter Paſſion, the Cupid, and two Brothers.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Let me give thanks firſt: our worthy Coſin —

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Your unworthy trouble, Sir;
For which, with all acknowledg'd reverence,
I ask your pardon; and for injury
More known and wilful, I have choſe a wife,
Without your counſel, or conſent, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: A wife? where is ſhe, Sir?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: This noble Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: How?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Whoſe honor my forgetful times much wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: He's madder than he was.

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: I would ha' ſworn for him.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: The Cupid, Coſin?

sp.speaker: Paſ.
sp.l: Yes, this worthy Lady, Sir.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Still worſe and worſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Bro.
sp.l: Our Siſter under pardon, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: 2 Bro.
sp.l: Which ſhape Love taught her to aſſume.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Is't truth then?

sp.speaker: 1 Gent.
sp.l: It appears plainly now, below the waſte, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Shamont, didſt ever read of a She-Cupid?

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Never in fiction yet: but it might hold, Sir;
For deſire is of both Genders.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Make that good here: He joyns Shamont's band and his Siſters.
I take thee at thy word, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: Oh my Lord,
Love would appear too bold, and rude from me,
Honour and admiration are her rights,
Her goodneſs is my Saint, my Lord,

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I ſee,
Y'are both too modeſt to beſtow your ſelves:
I'll ſave that virtue ſtill, 'tis but my pains: come,
It ſhall be ſo.

sp.speaker: Sham.
sp.l: This gift does but ſet forth my poverty.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Sir, that which you complain of, is my riches.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Soldier, now every noiſe ſounds peace, th'art welcome.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.l: Sir, my repentance ſues for your bleſt favour,
Which once obtain'd, no injury ſhall loſe it;
I'll ſuffer mightier wrongs.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Riſe, lov'd and pardon'd:
For where Hope fail'd, nay Art it ſelf reſign'd,
Thou'ſt wrought that cure, which skill could never find;
Nor did there ceaſe, but to our peace extend;
Never could wrongs boaſt of a nobler end.

div.head: EPILOGUE.
div.l: OƲr Poet bid us ſay for his own part,
He cannot lay too much forth of his Art:
But fears our over-acting paſſions may,
As not adorn, deface his labour'd Play,
Yet ſtill he's reſolute, for what is writ.
Of Nicer valour, and aſſumes the wit:
But for the Love-Scaenes which he ever meant,
Cupid in's Peticoat ſhould repreſent,
He'll ſtand no ſhock of cenſure; the Play's good,
He ſays he knows it, (if well underſtood.)
But we (blind god) beg, if thou art Divine.
Thou'lt ſhoot thy Arrows round, this Play was thine.

div.head: Mr. Francis Beaumonts Letter to Ben. Johnſon, written before he and Mr. Fletcher came to London, with two of the precedent Comedies then not finiſh'd, which deferr'd their merry meetings at the Mermaid.
div.l: THe Sun which doth the greateſt comfort bring
To abſent friends, becauſe the ſelf-ſame thing
They know they ſee however abſent, is,
Here our beſt Hay-makers forgive me this,
It is our Countreys ſtile. In this warm ſhine,
I l • e and dream of your full Mermaid Wine.
Oh we have water mixt with Claret Lees,
Drink apt to bring in dryer Hereſies
Than Beer, good only for the Sonnets ſtrain,
With ſuſtian Metaphors to ſtuff the brain,
So mixt, that given to the thirſtieſt one,
'Twill not prove Alms, unleſs he have the ſtone:
I think with one draught mans invention fades,
Two Cups had quite ſpoil'd Homers Illiads;
'Tis Liquor that will find out Sutcliff s wit,
Lye where he will, and make him write worſe yet;
Fil'd with ſuch moiſture in moſt grievous qualms;
Did Rob. Wiſdom write his Singing Pſalms;
And ſo muſt I do this, and yet I think
It is a potion ſent us down to drink,
By ſpecial Providence keeps us from fights,
Makes us not laugh, when we make legs to knights
'Tis this that keeps our minds fit for our States,
A Medicine to obey our Magiſtrates:
For we do live more free than you, no hate,
No envy at one anothers State
Moves us, we are all equal every whit:
Of Land that God gives men here is their wit:
If we conſider fully, for our beſt,
And graveſt men will with his main houſe jeſt,
Scarce pleaſe you; we want ſubtilty to do
The City tricks, lye, hate, and flatter too:
Here are none that can bear a painted ſhow,
Strike when you winch, and then lament the blow:
Who like Mills ſet the right way for to grind,
Can make their gains alike with every wind:
Only ſome fellows with the ſubtil'ſt pate
Amongſt us, may perchance equivocate
At ſelling of a Horſe, and that's the moſt.
Methinks the little wit I had is loſt
Since I ſaw you, for Wit is like a Reſt
Held up at Tennis, which men do the beſt,
With the beſt gameſters: what things have we ſeen,
Done at the Mermaid! heard words that have been
So nimble, and ſo full of ſubtil flame,
As if that every one from whence they came,
Had meant to put his whole wit in a jeſt,
And had reſolv'd to live a fool, the reſt
Of his dull life; then when there hath been thrown
Wit able enough to juſtifie the Town
For three days paſt, wit that might warrant be
For the whole City to talk fooliſhly
Till that were cancell'd, and when that was gone,
We left an Air behind us, which alone,
Was able to make the two next Companies
Right witty; though but downright fools, more wiſe.
When I remember this, and ſee that now
The Countrey Gentlemen begin to allow
My wit for dry bobs, then I needs muſt cry,
I ſee my days of Ballating grow nigh;
I can already Riddle, and can Sing
Ketches, ſell bargains, and I fear ſhall bring
My ſelf to ſpeak the hardeſt words I find,
Over, as oft as any, with one wind,
That takes no medicines: But one thought of thee
Makes me remember all theſe things to be
The wit of our young men, fellows that ſhow
No part of good, yet utter all they kno ••
Who like trees of the Guard, have growing ſouls.
Only ſtrong deſtiny, which all controuls,
I hope hath left a better fate in ſtore,
For me thy friend, than to live ever poor,
Baniſht unto this home; fate once again
Bring me to thee, who canſt make ſmooth and plain
The way of Knowledge for me, and then I,
Who have no good but in thy company,
Proteſt it will my greateſt comfort be
To acknowledge all I have to flow from thee.
Ben. when theſe Scaenes are perfect, we'll taſte wine;
I'll drink thy Muſes health, thou ſhalt quaff mine,

div.head: The Honeſt Man's Fortune. A TRAGI-COMEDY.
The Perſons repreſented in the Play.

list.item: Duke of Orleans, a ſpleenful detracting Lord, Brother-in-law to Orleans, a noble
Earl of Amiens, accompliſh'd Gentleman, ſervant to Lamira.
Voramer, the loving and loyal Page of Mountague.

list.head: WOMEN.
list.item: Ducheſs of Orleans, a virtuous Lady, and chaste, (but ſuſpected) wife to the Duke.
Lamira, a modeſt Virgin, and a Lady, rich and noble.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter the Duke of Orleance, and the Earl of Amiens, at ſeveral doors.

sp.speaker: Amiens.
sp.p: MOrrow, my Lord of Orleans.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: You ſalute me like a ſtranger; brother Orleance were to me a Title more belonging, whom you call the Husband of your Siſter.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: Would the circumſtances of your brotherhood, had never offer'd cauſe to make our converſation leſs familiar: I meet you like a hindrance in your way: your great Law-ſuit is now upon the tongue, and ready for a judgement.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: Came you from the Hall now?

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: Without ſtay, the Court is full, and ſuch a preſs of people does attend the iſſue, as if ſome great man were brought to his arraignment.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: Every mothers ſon of all that multitude of hearers, went to be a witneſs of the miſery your Siſters fortunes muſt have come to, if my adverſary who did love her firſt, had been her Husband.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: The ſucceſs may draw a teſtimony from them, to confirm the ſame opinion, but they went prepar'd with no ſuch hope or purpoſ • .

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: And did you intreat the number of them, that are come with no ſuch hope or purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: Tuſh, your own experience of my heart can anſwer ye.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: This doubtful, makes me clearly underſtand your diſpoſition.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: If your cauſe be juſt,
I wiſh you a concluſion like your cauſe.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: I can have any common charity to ſuch a Prayer
From a friend I would expect a love to proſper in;
Without exceptions ſuch a love as might
Make all my undertakings thankful to't;
Preciſely juſt is ſeldom faithful in our wiſhes
To another mans deſires: Farewel. Exit Orl.

div.stage: Enter Montague having a Purſe, Duboys, Longueville, and Voramer the Page, with two Caskets.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Here comes your adverſarie's brother-in-law.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: The Lord of Amiens.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: From the Hall I think.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: I did ſo: ſave your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.l: That's a wiſh my Lord, as courteous to my preſent ſtate,
As ever honeſt mind was thankful for;
For now my ſafety muſt expoſe it ſelf
To queſtion: yet to look for any free
Or hearty ſalutation (Sir) from you
Would be unreaſonable in me.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Your Siſter is my adverſarie's wife;
That nearneſs needs muſt conſequently draw
Your inclination to him.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: I will grant
Him all the nearneſs his alliance claims,
And yet be nothing leſs impartial,
My Lord of Montague.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Lord of Montague yet:
• ut (Sir) how long the dignity or ſtate
Belonging to it will continue, ſtands
Upon rhe dangerous paſſage of this hour.
Either for evermore to be confirm'd,
Or like the time wherein 'twas pleaded, gone:
Gone with it, never to be call'd again.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: Juſtice direct your proceſs to the end;
To both your perſons my reſpect ſhall ſtill
Be equal; but the righteous cauſe is that
Which bears my wiſhes to the ſide it holds,
Where-ever may it proſper. Exit Amiens.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Then my thanks
Are proper to you, if a man may raiſe
A conſidence upon a lawful ground
I have no reaſon to be once perplex'd
With any doubtful motion, Longuezille,
That Lord of Amiens, (didſt obſerve him?) has
A worthy nature in him.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Either 'tis his nature or his cunning.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: That's the vizard of moſt mens actions,
Whoſe diſſembled lives
Do carry only the ſimilitude
Of goodneſs on 'em: but for him
Honeſt behaviour makes a true report,
What diſpoſition does inhabit him,
Eſſential virtue.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Then 'tis pity that
Injurious Orleans is his brother.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: He is but his brother-in-law.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Law? that's as bad.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: How is your Law as bad? I rather wiſh
The hangman thy Executor than that
Equivocation ſhould be ominous.

div.stage: Enter two Lawyers, and two Creditors.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Some of your Lawyers—

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: What is ominous?

sp.speaker: 2 Law.
sp.l: Let no diſtruſt trouble your Lordſhips thought.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: The evidences of your queſtion'd Land
Ha' not ſo much as any literal
Advantage in 'em to be made againſt
Your Title.

sp.speaker: 2 Law.
sp.l: And your Council underſtands
The buſineſs fully.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: Th'are induſtrious, juſt.

sp.speaker: 2 Law.
sp.l: And very confident.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: Your ſtate endures
A voluntary trial; like a man
Whoſe honors are maliciouſly accus'd.

sp.speaker: 2 Law.
sp.l: The accuſation ſerves to clear his cauſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: And to approve his truth more.

sp.speaker: 2 Law.
sp.l: So ſhall all
Your adverſarie's pleadings ſtrengthen your
Poſſeſſion.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: And be ſet upon record
To witneſs the hereditary right
Of you and yours.

sp.speaker: 2 Law.
sp.l: Courage, you have the law.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: And you the profits.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: If diſcouragement
Could work upon me, your aſſurances
Would put me ſtrongly into heart again;
But I was never fearful: and let ſate
Deceive my expectation, yet I am
Prepared againſt dejection.

sp.speaker: 1 Cre.
sp.l: So are we.

sp.speaker: 2 Cre.
sp.l: We have received a comfortable hope
That all will ſpeed well.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: What is he Duboys?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: A Creditor.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I thought ſo, for he ſpeaks
As if he were a partner in his ſtate.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Sir, I am largely indebted to your loves,

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: More to their purſes.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Which you ſhall not loſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.l: Your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Dub,
sp.l: That's another creditor.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.l: Has intereſt in me.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: You have more of him.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.l: And I have had ſo many promiſes
From theſe, and all your learned Counſellors;
How certainly your cauſe will proſper: that —

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: You brought no Serjeants with you?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: To attend his ill ſucceſs.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Good Sir, I will not be
Unthankful either to their induſtries
Or your affections.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: All your Land (my Lord)
Is at the barr now, give me but ten Crowns
I'll ſave you harmleſs.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Take him at his word;
If he does loſe, you're ſav'd by miracle,
For I never knew a Lawyer yet undone.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: Then now you ſhall, Sir, if this proſpers not.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Sir, I beſeech you do not force your voice
To ſuch a loudneſs, but be thrifty now;
Preſerve it till you come to plead at bar
It will be much more profitable in
The ſatisfaction than the promiſe.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: Is not this a ſatisfaction to engage
My ſelf for this aſſurance, if he

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: No Sir, my ruin never ſhall import
Anothers loſs, if not by accident,
And that my purpoſe is not guilty of:
You're engag'd in nothing but your care. Ex. Law.
Attend the Procurator to the Court,
Obſerve how things incline, and bring me word.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I dare not, Sir, if I be taken there,
Mine ears will be in danger.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Why? haſt thou
Committed ſomething that deſerves thine ears?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: No, but I fear the noiſe; my hearing will be
Periſhed by the noiſe; 'tis as good 't want
A member, as to looſe the uſe—
A member as to loſe the uſe—

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: The ornament is excepted.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Well my Lord
I'll put 'em to the hazard. Exit Long.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.l: Your deſires be proſperous to you.

sp.speaker: 2 Cred.
sp.l: Our beſt Prayers wait
Upon your fortune. Exeunt Cred.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: For your ſelves, not him.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Thou canſt not blame 'em: I am in their debts.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: But had your large expence (a part whereof
You owe 'em) for unprofitable Silks
And Laces, been beſtowed among the poor,
That would have prayed the right way for you:
Not upon you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: For unprofitable Silks
And Laces? now believe me honeſt boy
Th'aſt hit upon a reprehenſion that belongs
Unto me.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: By — my Lord,
I had not ſo unmannerly a thought,
To reprehend you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Why I love thee ſor't.
Mine own acknowledgement confirms thy words:
For once I do remember, comming from
The Mercers, where my Purſe had ſpent it ſelf
On thoſe unprofitable toys thou ſpeak'ſt of,
A man half naked with his poverty
Did meet me, and requeſted my relief:
I wanted whence to give it, yet his eyes
Spoke for him, thoſe I could have ſatisfied
With ſome unfruitful ſorrow, (if my tears
Would not have added rather to his grief,
Than eas'd it) but the true compaſſion that
I ſhould have given I had not: this began
To make me think how many ſuch mens wants
The vain ſuperfluous coſt I wore upon
My outſide, would have clothed, and left my ſelf
A habit as becomming: to increaſe
This new conſideration there came one
Clad in a garment plain and thrifty, yet
As decent as theſe fair dear follies; made
As if it were of purpoſe to deſpiſe
The vanity of ſhew: his purſe had ſtill
The power to do a charitable deed,
And did it.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Yet your inclination, Sir,
Deſerv'd no leſs to be commended, than his action.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Prethee do not flatter me;
He that intends well, yet deprives himſelf
Of means, to put his good thoughts into deed,
Deceives his purpoſe of the due reward
That goodneſs merits: oh antiquity
Thy great examples of Nobility
Are out of imitation, or at leaſt
So lamely follow'd, that thou art as much
Before this age in virtue, as in time,

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Sir, it muſt needs be lamely followed, when
The chiefeſt men love to follow it
Are for the moſt part cripples.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Who are they?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Soldiers, my Lord, ſoldiers.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: 'Tis true Duboys: but if the law diſables me no more
For Noble actions, than good purpoſes,
I'll practice how to exerciſe the worth
Commended to us by our anceſtors;
The poor neglected ſoldier ſhall command
Me from a Ladies Courtſhip, and the form
I'll ſtudy ſhall no more be taught me by
The Taylor, but the Scholar; that expence
Which hitherto has been to entertain
Th' intemperate pride and pleaſure of the taſte
Shall fill my Table more to ſatisfie,
And leſs to ſurfeit.
What an honeſt work it would be; when we find
A Virgin in her poverty, and youth
Inclining to be tempted, to imploy
As much perſwaſion, and as much expence
To keep her upright, as men uſe to do upon her falling.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: 'Tis charity that many Maids will be unthankful for,
And ſome will rather take it for a wrong,
To buy 'em out of their inheritance,
The thing that they were born to.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Longueville, thou bringſt a chearful promiſe in thy face.
There ſtands no pale report upon thy cheek,
To give me fear or knowledge of my loſs, 'tis red and lively.
How proceeds my ſuit?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: That's with leave, Sir, a labour that to thoſe of Hercules,
May add another; or (at leaſt) be call'd
An imitation of his burning ſhirt:
For 'twas a pain of that merciful
Perplexity, to ſhoulder through the throng
Of people, that attended your ſucceſs:
My ſweaty linnen ſixt upon my skin,
Still as they pull'd me, took that with it; 'twas
A fear I ſhould have left my fleſh among 'em:
Yet I was patient, for (methought) the to • l
Might be an emblem of the difficult
And weary paſſage to get out of Law.
And to make up the dear ſimilitude,
When I was forth ſeeking my handkerchief
To wipe my ſweat off, I did find a cauſe
To make me ſweat more, for my Purſe was loſt
Among their fingers.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: There 'twas rather ſound.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: By them.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: I mean ſo.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Well, I will reſtore
Thy damage to thee: how proceeds my ſuit?

sp.speaker: Lang.
sp.l: Like one at Brokers; I think forfeited.
Your promiſing Counſel at the firſt
Put ſtrongly forward with a labour d ſpeed,
And ſuch a violence of pleading, that
His Fee in Sugar-candy ſcarce will make
His throat a ſatisfaction for the hurt
He did it, and he carried the whole cauſe
Before him, with ſo clear a paſſage, that
The people in the ſavour of your ſide
Cried Montague, Montague: in the ſpight of him
That cryed out ſilence, and began to laugh
Your adverſaries advocate to ſcorn:
Who like a cunning Footman ſet me forth
With ſuch a temperate eaſie kind of courſe
To put him into exerciſe of ſtrength,
And follow'd his advantages ſo cloſe,
That when your hot mouth'd pleader thought h' had won,
Before he reacht it, he was out of breath,
And then the other ſtript him.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: So all is loſt.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: But how I know not; for, (methought) I ſtood
Confounded with the clamour of the Court,
Like one embark'd upon a ſtorm at Sea,
Where the tempeſtuous noiſe of Thunder mixt
With roaring of the billows, and the thick,
Imperfect language of the Sea men, takes
His underſtanding and his ſafety both
Together from him.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Thou doſt bring ill news

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Of what I was unwilling to have been
The firſt reporter.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Didſt obſerve no more?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: At leaſt no better

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Then th'art not inform'd
So well as I am; I can tell thee that
Will pleaſe thee, for when all elſe left my cauſe,
My very adverſaries took my part.

sp.speaker: Long
sp.l: — Whoſoever told you that, abuſed you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Credit me, he took my part
When all forſook me.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Took it from you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Yes I mean ſo, and I think he had juſt cauſe
To take it. when the verdict gave it him.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: His Spirit would ha' ſunk him, e'r he could
Have carried an ill fortune of this weight ſo lightly.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Nothing is a miſery, unleſs our weakneſs apprehend it ſo;
We cannot be more faithful to our ſelves
In any thing that's manly, than to make
Ill fortune as contemptible to us
As it makes us to others.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Here come they
Whoſe very countenances will tell you how
Contemptible it is to others.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Sir?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: The Sir of Knighthood may be given him, e'r
They hear you now?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Good Sir but a word.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: How ſoon the loſs of wealth makes any man
Grow out of knowledge.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Let me ſee, I pray, Sir,
Never ſtood you upon the Pillory?

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: The Pillory?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Oh now I know you did not.
Y'ave ears, I thought ye had loſt 'em; pray obſerve,
Here's one that once was gracious in your eyes.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: Oh my Lord, have an eye upon him.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: But ha' you ne'er a Counſel to redeem
His Land yet from the judgement?

sp.speaker: 2 Law.
sp.p: None but this, a Writ of error to remove the cauſe.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: No more of error, we have been in that too much already.

sp.speaker: 2 Law.
sp.p: If you will reverſe the judgement, you muſt truſt to that delay.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Delay? indeed he's like to truſt to that,
With you has any dealing-

sp.speaker: 2 Law.
sp.l: E'r the Law proceeds to an Habere facias poſſeſſionem.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: That's a language Sir, I underſtand not.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Th'art a very ſtrange unthankful fellow to have taken Fees of ſuch a liberal meaſure, and then give a man hard words for's money.

sp.speaker: 1 Law.
sp.l: If men will hazard their ſalvations,
What ſhould I ſay; I've other buſineſs.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Y'are i'th' right;
That's it you ſhould ſay, now proſperity has left me.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.l: Have an eye upon him; if
We loſe him now, he's gone for ever; ſtay
And dog him: I'll go fetch the Officers.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Dog him you Bloud-hound: by this point thou ſhalt more ſafely dog an angry Lion, than attempt him.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: What's the matter:

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Do but ſtir to fetch a Serjeant; and beſides your loſs
Of labour, I'll have you beaten, till
Thoſe eaſement in your faces be falſe lights.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Falſer than thoſe you ſell by.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Who gave you Commiſſion to abuſe my friends thus?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Sir, are thoſe your friends that would betray you?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: 'Tis to ſave themſelves rather than betray me.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.l: Your Lordſhip makes a juſt conſtruction of it.

sp.speaker: 2 Cred.
sp.l: All our deſire is but to get our own.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Your wives deſires and yours do differ then.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: So far as my ability will go
You ſhall have ſatisfaction Longeville.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: And leave your ſelf neglected; every man
Is firſt a debtor to his own demands, being honeſt.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: As I take it, Sir, I did
Not entertain you for my Counſelor.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Counſel's the office of a ſervant,
When the maſter falls upon a danger; as
Defence is; never threaten with your eyes,
They are no cockatrices; do you hear?
Talk with the Girdler, or the Mill'ner,
He can inform you of a kind of men
That firſt undid the profit of thoſe trades
By bringing up the form of carrying
Their Morglays in their hands: with ſome of thoſe
A man may make himſelf a priviledge
To ask a queſtion at the priſon gates
Without your good permiſſion.

sp.speaker: 2 Cred.
sp.l: By your leave.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Stay Sir, what one example ſince the time
That firſt you put your hat off to me, have
You noted in me to encourage you
To this preſumption? by the juſtice now
Of thine own rule, I ſhould begin with thee,
I ſhould turn thee away ungratified
For all thy former kindneſs, forget
Thou ever didſt me any ſervice: 'tis not fear
Of being arreſted, makes me thus incline
To ſatisfy you; for you ſee by him,
I loſt not all defences with my ſtate;
The curſes of a man to whom I am
Beholding, terrify me more, than all
The violence he can purſue me with.
Duboys, I did prepare me for the worſt;
Theſe two ſmall Cabinets do comprehend
The ſum of all the wealth that it hath pleaſed
Adverſity to leave me, one as rich
As th'other, both in Jewels; take thou this,
And as the Order put within it, ſhall
Direct thee, diſtribute it half between
Thoſe Creditors, and th' other half among
My ſervants: for (Sir) they are my Creditors
As well as you are, they have truſted me
With their advancement: if the value ſail,
To pleaſe you all, my firſt increaſe of means
Shall offer you a fuller payment; be content
To leave me ſomething, and imagine that
You put a new beginner into credit.

sp.speaker: Cred.
sp.p: So proſper our own bleſſings, as we wiſh you to your merit.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Are you ſilences of diſcontent, or of ſorrow?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Sir, we would not leave you.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Do but ſuffer us to follow you, and what our preſent means, or induſtries hereafter can provide, ſhall ſerve you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Oh deſire me not to live
To ſuch a baſeneſs, as to be maintained
By thoſe that ſerve me; pray begone, I will
Defend your honeſties to any man
That ſhall report, you have forſaken me;
I pray begone. Exeunt Servants and Creditors.
Why, doſt thou weep my boy,
Becauſe I do not bid thee go to?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: No, I weep (my Lord) becauſe I would not go;
I fear you will command me.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: No my child,
I will not; that would diſcommend th' intent
Of all my other actions: thou art yet
Unable to adviſe thy ſelf a courſe,
Should I put thee to ſeek it; after that
I muſt excuſe, or at the leaſt forgive
Any charitable deed that can be done againſt my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Every day (my Lord) I tarry with you, I'll account
A day of bleſſing to me; for I ſhall
Have ſo much leſs time left me of my life
When I am from you: and if miſery
Befall you (which I hope ſo good a man
Was never born to) I will take my part,
And make my willingneſs increaſe my ſtrength
To bear it. In the Winter I will ſpare
Mine own cloths from my ſelf to cover you;
And in the Summer, carry ſome of yours
To eaſe you: I'll doe any thing I can.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Why, thou art able to make miſery
Aſhamed of hurting, when thy weakneſs can
Both bear it, and deſpiſe it: Come my boy
I will provide ſome better way for thee
Than this thou ſpeakſt of: 'tis the comfort that
I'll fortune has undone me into the faſhion:
For now in this age moſt men do begin,
To keep but one boy, that kept many men. Exeunt.

div.stage: Enter Orleans, a Servant, his Lady following.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Where is ſhe? call her.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: I attend you Sir.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Your friend ſweet Madam.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: What friend, good my Lord?

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Your Montague, Madam, he will ſhortly want
Thoſe Courtly graces that you love him for;
The means wherewith he purchaſed this, and this;
And all his own proviſions to the leaſt
Proportion of his feeding, or his clothes,
Came out of that inheritance of land
Which he unjuſtly lived on: but the law
Has given me right in't, and poſſeſſion; now
Thou ſhalt perceive his bravery vaniſh, as
This Jewell does from thee now, and theſe Pearls
To him that owes 'em.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Ye are the owner Sir of every thing that does belong to me.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: No, not of him, ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: O good Heaven!

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: But in a while your mind will change, and be
As ready to diſclaim him; when his wants
And miſeries have periſh'd his good face,
And taken off the ſweetneſs that has made
Him pleaſing in a womans underſtanding.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: O Heaven, how gratious had Creation been
To women, who are born without defence,
If to our hearts there had been doors through which
Our husbands might have lookt into our thoughts,
And made themſelves undoubtfull.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Made 'em mad.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: With honeſt women.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Thou doſt ſtill pretend
A title to that virtue: prethee let
Thy honeſty ſpeak freelie to me now.
Thou know'ſt that Montague, of whoſe Land
I'm the maſter, did affect thee firſt,
And ſhould have had thee, if the ſtrength of friends
Had not prevail'd above thine own conſent.
I have undone him; tell me how thou doſt
Conſider his ill fortune and my good.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I'll tell you juſtly his undoing is
An argument for pity and for tears
In all their diſpoſitions that have known
The honor and the goodneſs of his life:
Yet that addition of proſperity,
Which you have got by't, no indifferent man
Will malice or repine at, if the Law
Be not abuſed in't; howſoever ſince
You have the upper fortune of him, 'twill
Be ſome diſhonor to you to bear your ſelf
With any pride or glory over him.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: This may be truely ſpoken, but in thee
It is not honeſt.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Yes, ſo honeſt, that I care not if the chaſt Penelope
Were now alive to hear me.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Who comes there?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: My brother.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Save ye.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Now Sir, you have heard of proſperous Montague,

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: No Sir, I have heard of Montague,
But of your proſperity.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Is he diſtracted.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: He does bear his loſs with ſuch a noble ſtrength
Of patience that,
Had fortune eyes to ſee him, ſhe would weep
For having hurt him, and pretending that
Shee did it but for triall of his worth:
Hereafter ever love him.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: I perceive you love him, and becauſe (I muſt confeſs)
He does d ••• rve that though for ſome reſpects,
I have not • n him that acknowledgement,
Yet in mine honor I did ſtill conclude to uſe him nobly.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.p: Sir, that will become your reputation and make me grow proud of your alliance.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: I did reſerve the doing of this friendſhip till I had
His fortunes at my mercy, that the world
May tell him 'tis a willing courteſie.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: This change will make me happy.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: 'Tis a change; thou ſhalt behold it: then obſerve me when
That Montague, had poſſeſſion of my Land,
I was his rivall, and at laſt obtain'd
This Lady who, by promiſe of her own
Affection to him, ſhould ha' bin his wife;
I had her, and withheld her like a pawn,
Till now my Land is rend'red to me again,
And ſince it is ſo, you ſhall ſee I have
The conſcience not to keep her—give him her— draws
For by the faithfull temper of my ſword, ſhe ſhall not tarry with me.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Give me way— draws.
Thou moſt unworthy man —give me way;
Or by the wrong he does the Innocent,
I'll end thy miſery and his wickedneſs, together.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Stay and let me juſtifie
My husband in that, I have wrong'd his bed. Exeunt Am: Orl:
sp.stage: Enter Orleans in amazement, the ſervants following him.
sp.l: Never—all ſhames that can afflict me fall
Upon me if I ever wrong'd you;

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Didſt thou not confeſs it;

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: 'Twas to ſave your blood from ſhedding, that has
Turn'd my brothers edge;
He that beholds our thoughts as plainely as
Our faces, knowes it, I did never hurt
My honeſty but by accuſing it.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Womens conſents are ſooner credited
Than their denials: and I'll never truſt
Her body that prefers any defence
Before the ſafety of her honor—here
Show forth that ſtranger — give me not a word
Thou ſeeſt a danger readie to be tempted.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Caſt that upon me rather than my ſhame,
And as I am now dying I will vow—
That I am honeſt.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Put her out of dores; but that I fear my land
May go again to Montague, I would kill thee, I am loth,
To make a beggar of him that way; or elſe—
Go now you have the liberty of fleſh,
And you may put it to a double uſe,
One for your pleaſure, th'other to maintain
Your well beloved, he will want. Exit Lady.
In ſuch a charitable exerciſe
The virtue will excuſe you for the vice. Exit Orleans.

div.stage: Enter Amiens drawn, Montague, Veramor meeting.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: What means your Lordſhip?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: For the love of Heaven.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Thou haſt advantage of me, caſt away this buckler.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: So he is Sir, for he lives
With one that is undone — avoyd us boy.

sp.speaker: Ʋer.
sp.l: I'll firſt avoid my ſafety,
