sp.p: Your Rapier ſhall be button'd with my head, before it touch my Maſter.

l.hi: Montague?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Sir.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: You know my ſiſter?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Yes Sir.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: For a whore?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: You lye, and ſhall lie lower if you dare abuſe her honor.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I am honeſt.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: Honeſt!

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Upon my faith I am.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: What did then parſuade thee to condemn thy ſelf?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Your ſafety.

sp.speaker: Am.
sp.l: I had rather be expos'd
To danger, than diſhonor; th'aſt betray'd
The reputation of my familie
More baſely by the falſeneſs of that word,
Than if thou hadſt delivered me aſleep
Into the hands of baſe enemies.
Relief will never make thee ſenſible
Of thy diſgraces; let thy wants compell thee to it.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: O I am a miſerable woman.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Why Madam? are you utterly without means to relieve you?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I have nothing Sir, unleſs by changing of theſe cloaths for worſe, and then at laſt the worſt for nakedneſs.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Stand off boy, nakedneſs would be a change
To pleaſe us Madam, to delight us both.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: What nakedneſs Sir?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Why the nakedneſs of body Madam, we were Lovers once.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Never diſhoneſt Lovers.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Honeſtie has no allowance now to give our ſelves.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Nor you allowance againſt honeſtie.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: I'll ſend my Boy hence, opportunitie
Shall be our ſervant, come and meet me firſt
With kiſſes like a ſtranger at the door,
And then invite me nearer to receive
A more familiar inward wellcome; where,
Inſtead of tapers made of Virgins wax
Th'increaſing flames of our deſires ſhall light
Us to a banquet: and before the taſte
Be dull with ſatisfaction, I'll prepare
A nouriſhment compos'd of every thing
That bears a naturall friendſhip to the blood,
And that ſhall ſet another edge upon 't,
Or elſe between the courſes of the feaſt
We'll dallie out an exerciſe of time,
That ever as one appetite expires another may ſucceed it.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: O my Lord, how has your nature loſt her worthineſs?
When our affections had their liberty,
Our kiſſes met as temperatelie as
The hands of ſiſters, or of brothers, that
Our bloods were then as moving; then you were
So noble, that I durſt have truſted your
Embraces in an opportunity
Silent enough to ſerve a raviſher,
And yet come from you—undiſhonor'd—how
You think me altered, that you promiſe your
Attempt ſucceſs I know not; but were all
The ſweet temptations that deceive us ſet
On this ſide, and one that ſide all the waiters,
Theſe neither ſhould parſuade me, nor theſe force.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Then miſery may waſte your body.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Yes, but luſt ſhall never.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: I have found you ſtill as uncorupted as I left you firſt
Continue ſo; and I will ſerve you with
As much devotion as my word, my hand
Or purſe can ſhow you; and to juſtifie
That promiſe, here is half the wealth I have,
Take it, you owe me nothing, till you fall
From virtue, which the better to protect
I have bethought me of a preſent means:
Give me the Letter; this commends my Boy
Into the ſervice of a Lady, whoſe
Free goodneſs you have bin acquainted with, Lamira.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Sir I know her.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Then believe her entertainment will be noble to you?
My boy ſhall bring you thither: and relate
Your manner of misfortune if your own
Report needs any witneſs: ſo I kiſs your hand good Lady.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Sir, I know not how to promiſe, but I cannot be unthankfull.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: All that you can implore in thankfulneſs
Be yours, to make you the more proſperous.
Farwell my boy,—I am not yet oppreſs'd. Exit Lady
Having the power to helpe one that's diſtreſs'd. Ʋere.

div.head: Scaena Prima.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: WHat ſhall we do now: ſwords are out of uſe,
And words are out of credit.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: We muſt ſerve.

sp.speaker: Leng.
sp.l: The means to get a ſervice will firſt ſpend
Our purſes; and except we can allow
Our ſelves an entertainment, ſervice will
Neglect us; now 'tis grown into a doubt
Whether the Mr. or the ſervants gives the countenance.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Then fall in with Miſtreſſes.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: They keep more ſervants now (indeed) than men,
But yet the age is grown ſo populous
Of thoſe attendants, that the women are
Grown full too.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: What ſhall we propound our ſelves?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I'll think on't.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Do; Old occupations have too many ſetters up to proſper, ſome uncommon trade would thrive now.

sp.speaker: Long,
sp.l: Wee'll e'en make up ſome half a dozen proper men.
And ſhould not we get more
Than all your female ſinners?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: If the houſe be ſeated as it ſhould be privately.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I, but that would make a multitude of witches.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Witches? how prethee?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Thus the bands would all turn witches to revenge
Themſelves upon us, and the women that
Come to us, for diſguiſes muſt wear beards,
And that's they ſay, a token of a witch.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: What ſhall we then do;

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: We muſt ſtudy on't
With more conſideration; ſtay Duboyes
Are not the Lord of Orleans and the Lord
Of Amiens enemies?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Yes, what of that.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Methinks the factions of two ſuch great men.
Should give a promiſe of advancement now
To us that want it.

sp.speaker: Dub,
sp.p: Let the plot be thine, and in the enterprize I'll ſecond thee.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I have it we will firſt ſet down our ſelves
The Method of a quarrell; and make choyce
Of ſome frequented Tavern; or ſuch a place
Of common notice, to perform it in
By way of undertaking to maintain
The ſeverall honors of thoſe enemies.
Thou for the Lord of Orleans; I for Amiens.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: I like the project, and I think 'twill take
The better, ſince their difference firſt did riſe
From his occaſion whom we followed once.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: We cannot hope leſs after the report,
Than entertainment or gratuity,
Yet thoſe are ends, I do not aim at moſt;
Great ſpirits that are needy, and will thrive,
Muſt labour whiles ſuch troubles are alive. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Slander is ſharper than the ſword. I have fed this three dayes upon leaf Tobacco, for want of other Victuals.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: You have liv'd the honeſter Captain; but be not ſo dejected, but hold up thy head, and meat will ſooner fall i'thy mouth.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: I care not ſo much for meat, ſo I had but good liquor, for which my guts croak like ſo many Frogs for rain.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: It ſeems, you are troubled with the wind-Collick, Captain, ſwallow a bullet: 'tis preſent remedy I'll aſſure you.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: A bullet? I'll tell you Sir, my panch is nothing but a pile of bullets; when I was in any ſervice I ſtood between my Generall and the ſhot, like a mud-wall; I am all lead, from the crown of the head to the ſoal of the foot, not a ſound bone about me.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: It ſeems you have bin in terrible hot ſervice Captain.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: It has ever bin the fate of the low Country wars to ſpoil many a man, I ha' not bin the firſt nor ſhall not be the laſt: but I'll tell you Sir, (hunger has brought it in to mind) I ſerved once at the Siege of Braſte, 'tis memorable to this day, where we were in great diſtreſs for victuals, whole troops fainted more for want of food then for blood, and died, yet we were reſolved to ſtand it out; I my ſelf was but then Gentleman of a Company, and had as much need as any man, and indeed I had periſhed had not a miraculous providence preſerved me.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: As how good Captain?

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Marry Sir, e'en as I was fainting and falling down for want of ſuſtenance, the enemy made a ſhot at me, and ſtruck me full ith' paunch with a penny loaf.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Inſtead of a bullet!

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: In ſtead of a bullet.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: That was miraculous indeed; and that loaf ſuſtained you.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Nouriſhed me or I had famiſhed with the reſt.

sp.speaker: Lav,
sp.p: You have done worthy acts being a ſoldier, and now you ſhall give me leave to requite your tale, and to acquaint you with the moſt notorious deeds that I have done being a Courtier. I proteſt Captain I will lie no more than you have done.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: I can indure no lies.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: I know you cannot Captain, therefore I'll only tell you of ſtrange things: I did once a deed of charity for it ſelf; I aſſiſted a poor widow in a ſute, and obtained it, yet I proteſt I took not a penny for my labor.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: 'Tis no ſuch ſtrange thing.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: By Mars Captain, but it is, and a very ſtrange thing too in a Courtier, it may take the upper hand of your penny loaf for a miracle. I could ha' told you how many Ladyes have languiſhed for my love, and how I was once ſollicited by the mother, the daughter, and grand-mother; out of the leaſt of which I might have digg'd my ſelf a fortune; they were all great Ladyes, for two of them were ſo big I could hardly embrace them: but I was ſluggiſh in my riſing courſes, and therefore let them paſs; what means I had is ſpent upon ſuch as had the wit to cheat me; That wealth being gone, I have only bought experience with it, with a ſtrong hope to cheat others; but ſee here comes the much declined Montague, who had all the Manor houſes, which were the body of his eſtate, overthrowen by a great wind.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: How by a great wind? was he not overthrown by law?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Yes, marry was he: but there was terrible puffing and blowing before he was overthrown, if you obſerv'd, and believe it Captain, there's no wind ſo dangerous to a building as a lawyers breath.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: What's he with him?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: An eminent Citizen. Mounſier Mallicorne, let's ſtand a ſide and liſten their deſign.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Sir, profit is the Crown of labor, it is the life, the ſoul of the induſtrious Merchant, in it he makes his paradiſe, and for it neglects Wife, Children, Friends, Parents, nay all the world, and delivers up himſelf to the violence of ſtorms, and to be tos'd into unknown ayrs; as there is no faculty ſo perillous, ſo there's none ſo worthy profitable.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Sir, I am very well poſſeſt of it, and what of my poore fortunes remaines, I would gladly hazard upon the Sea: it cannot deal worſe with me than the Land, though it ſink or throw it in the hands of Pirats. I have yet five hundred pounds left, and your honeſt and worthy acquaintance may make me a young Merchant; th'one moity of what I have I would gladly adventure.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: How adventure? you ſhall hazard nothing: you ſhall only joyn with me in certain commodities that are ſafe arrived unto the Key; you ſhall neither be in doubt of danger nor dammage; But ſo much money disburſt, ſo much receive; Sir, I would have you conceive I purſue it not for any good your money will do me, but meerly out of mine own freeneſs and courteſie to pleaſure you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: I can believe no leſs, and you expreſs a noble nature, ſeeking to build up a man ſo ruin'd as my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p:
Captain here is ſubject for us to work upon if we have wit; you hear that there is money yet left, and it is going to be layd out in Rattels, Bels, Hobby-Horſes, brown paper, or ſome ſuch like ſale commodities; now it would do better in our purſes, upon our backs in good Gold-lace, and Scarlat, and then we might purſue our projects, and our devices towards my Lady Annabella; go to, there's a conceit newly landed; heark I ſtand in good reputation with him, and there • ore may
the better cheat him: Captain, take a few inſtructions from me.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: What monies I have is at your diſpoſing, and upon twelve I will meet you at the Pallace with it.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: I will there expect you, and ſo I take my leave. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: You apprehend me?

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Why do ye think I am a dunce?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Not a dunce Captain, but you might give me leave to miſdoubt that pregnancy in a Soldier, which is proper and hereditary to a Courtier; but proſecute it, I will both ſecond, and give credit to it. Good Mounſier Montague, I would your whole revenues lay within the circuit of mine armes, that I might as eaſily beſtow, or reſtore it unto you as my curteſie.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: My zealous wiſhes Sir, do accompany his for your good fortunes.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Believe it Sir, our affection towards you is a ſtrong band of friendſhip.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: To which I ſhall moſt willingly ſeal. But believe me Gentlemen in a broken eſtate, the bond of friendſhip oft is forfeited, but that it is your free and ingenuous nature to renew it.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Sir, I will amply extend my ſelf to your uſe, and am very zealouſly afflicted as not one of your leaſt friends for your crooked fate; But let it not ſeiſe you with any dejection, you have as I hear a ſufficient competency left, which well diſpoſed may erect you as high in the worlds account as ever.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: I cannot live to hope it, much leſs injoy it, nor is it any part of my endeavor; my ſtudy is to render every man his own, and to contain my ſelf within the limits of a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: I have the grant of an Office given me by ſome noble favorites of mine in Court, there ſtands but a ſmall matter between me and it, if your ability be ſuch to lay down the preſent ſumm, out of the love I bear you, before any other man, it ſhall be confirmed yours.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: I have heard you often ſpeak of ſuch a thing; If it be aſſur'd to you I will gladly deal in it: that portion I have, I would not hazard upon one courſe, for I ſee the moſt certain is incertain.

sp.speaker: La-p,
sp.p: Having money Sir, you could not light upon men that could give better direction; there is at this time a friend of mine upon the Seas; to be plain with you, he is a pyrate, that hath wrote to me to work his fredom, and by this Gentlemans means, whoſe acquaintance is not ſmall at Court; we have the word of a worthy man for it, only there is ſome money to be ſuddainly disburſt, and if your happineſs be ſuch to make it up you ſhall receive treble gain by it, and good aſſurance for it.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Gentlemen, out of the weakneſs of my eſtate you ſeem (to have ſome knowledge of my breſt) that wou'd if it were poſſible advance my declined fortunes, to ſatisfie all men of whom I have had credit, and I know no way better than theſe which you propoſe; I have ſome money ready under my command, ſome part of it is already promis'd, but the remainder is yours to ſuch uſes as are propounded.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Appoint ſome certain place of meeting, for theſe affaires require expedition.

sp.speaker: Mount.
sp.p: I will make it my preſent buſineſs: at twelve, I am to meet Mallicorne, the Marchant at the Pallace, you know him Sir, about ſome negotiation of the ſame nature, there I will be ready to tender you that money, upon ſuch conditions as we ſhall conclude of.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: The care of it be yours, ſo much as the affair concerns you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Your caution is effectuall, and till then I take my leave.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Good Mr Montague.

div.stage: Whithin a clamor, down with their weapons.
Enter Longavile, and Dubois, their ſwords drawn, ſervants and others between them.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Nay Gentlemen what mean you? pray be quiet, have ſome reſpect unto the houſe.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: A treacherous ſlave.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Thou doſt revile thy ſelf baſe Longavile.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: I ſay thou art a villain and a corrupt one, that haſt ſome ſeven years ſed on thy maſters trencher, yet never bredſt good blood towards him: for if thou hadſt, thou'dſt have a ſounder heart.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: So Sir, you can uſe your tongue ſomething nimbler than your ſword.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Wou'd you cou'd uſe your tongue well of your Maſter, friend you might have better imployment for your ſword.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: I ſay again, and I will ſpeak it loud and often, that Orleans, is a noble Gentleman with whom Amiens is too light to poyſe the ſcale.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: He is the weaker for taking of a prayſe out of thy mouth.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: This hand ſhall ſeal his merit at thy heart.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Part them my maſters, part them.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Part them Sir, why do you not part them, you ſtand by with your ſword in your hand, and cry part 'em.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Why you muſt know my friend my cloaths are better than yours, and in a good ſuit, I do never uſe to part any body.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: And it is diſcretion.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: I marry is it Captain.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Dubois though this place priviledge thee, know where next we meet, the blood which at thy heart flows drops at thy feet.

div.stage: Enter Amience in haſte, his ſword drawn.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: I would not ſpend it better than in this quarrell, and on ſuch a hazard.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: What uprore's this, muſt my name here be queſtion'd in Tavern brawls, and by affected Ruffins?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Not we indeed Sir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Fear cannot make me ſhrink out of your fury, though you were greater than your name doth make you, I am one, and the oppoſer; if your ſwoln rage have ought in malice to inforce expreſs it.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: I ſeek thee not, nor ſhalt thou ever gain
That credit, which a blow from me wou'd give thee,
By my—I more deteſt that fellow
Which took my part than thee, that he durſt offer
To take my honor in his feeble armes,
And ſpend it in a drinking room; which way went he?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: That way Sir, I wou'd you wou'd after; for I do fear we ſhall have ſome more ſcuffling.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: I'll follow him, and if my ſpeed o'er take him,
I ſhall ill thank him, for his forwardneſs. Exit.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: I am glad he's gone, for I doe not love to ſee a ſword drawn in the hand of a man that lookes ſo furious, there's no jeſting with edge tooles, how ſay you Captain?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: I ſay 'tis better jeſting than to be in earneſt with them.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: How now? what's the difference? they ſay there have bin ſwords drawn, and in my quarrell: let me know that man, whoſe love is ſo ſincere to ſpend his blood for my ſake, I will bounteouſly requite him.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: We were all of your ſide, but there he ſtands begun it.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: What's thy name?

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: Give me thy hand, haſt received no hurt?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Not any, nor were this body ſtuck full of wounds, I ſhould not count them hurts, being taken in ſo honorable a cauſe as the defence of my moſt worthy Lord.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: The dedication of thy love to me requires my ample bounty, thou art mine, for I do find thee made unto my purpoſes: Mounſieur Laverdine, pardon my neglect I not obſerved you, and how runs rumour?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Why, it runs my Lord like a foot-man without a cloak, to ſhow that what's once rumour'd it cannot be hid.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: And what ſay the rable, am not I the ſubject of their talk?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Troth my Lord the common mouth ſpeaks foul words.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: Of me, for turning away my wife, do they not?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Faith the men do a little murmure at it and ſay, 'tis an ill preſident in ſo great a man; marry the women; they rayl out right.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: Out upon them rampallions. I'll keep my ſelf ſafe enough out of their fingers, but what ſay my pritty jolly compoſed gallants that cenſure every thing more deſperate than it is dangerous; what ſay they?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Marry they are laying wagers, what death you ſhall die; one offers to lay five hundred pounds; And yet he had but a groat about him, & that was in two two-pences too to, any man that wou'd make it up a ſhilling; that you were kil'd with a Piſtoll charg'd with white Powder; another offerd to pawn his ſoul for five ſhillings, and yet no body wou'd take him, that you were ſtab'd to death, and ſhou'd die with more wounds than Ceſar.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: And who ſhou'd be the Butchers that ſhou'd do it? Montague and his aſſociates?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: So 'tis conjectured.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: And believe it, ſweet Prince, it is to be feared, and therefore prevented.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: By turning his purpoſe on himſelf, were not that the way?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: The moſt direct path for your ſafety. For where doth danger ſit more furious than in a deſperate man?

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: And being you have declined his means, you have increaſt his malice.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Beſides the generall report that ſteems in every mans breath, and ſtains you all over with infamy, that Time the devourer of all things cannot eat out.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: I, for that former familiarity, which he had with your Lady.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Men ſpeak it as boldly as words of compliment; good morrow, good even, or ſave you Sir, are not more uſuall; if the word cuckold had been written upon your forehead in great Capitall Letters, it could not have been dilated with more confidence.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: He ſhall not ſleep another night, I will have his blood, though it be required at my hands again.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip may, and without hazarding your own perſon; here's a Gentleman in whoſe looks I ſee a reſolution to perform it.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Let his Lordſhip give me but his honorable word for my life, I'll kill him as he walks.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Or piſtoll him as he ſits at meat.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Or at game.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Or as he is drinking.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Any way.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: Wou't thou? call what is mine thine own, thy reputation ſhall not be brought in queſtion for it, much leſs thy life; it ſhall be nam'd a deed of valour in thee, not murder: Farewell.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p:
I need no more 'encouragement, it is 〈◊〉
• k I will perſuade my ſelf that I was born to.

sp.speaker: Laver.
sp.p: And you may perſuade your ſelf too that you ſhall be ſav'd by it, being that it is for his honorable Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: But you muſt yield me means, how, when and where.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.l: That ſhall be our tasks;
Nay more, we will be agents with thee:
This hour we are to meet him, on the receipt of certain moneys,
Which indeed we purpoſe honeſtly to cheat him of,
And that's the main cauſe I wou'd have him ſlain,
Who works with ſafety makes a double gain.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: Stay Sir, I have took ſome pains to overtake you.
—Your name is Longaville.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: I have the word of many honeſt men for't, I crave your Lordſhips pardon, your ſudden apprehenſion on my ſteps made me to frame an anſwer unwitting and unworthy your reſpect.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: Doe you know me?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Yes, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: I know not you; nor am I well pleaſed to make this time, as the affair now ſtands, the induction of your acquaintance; you are a fighting fellow.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: How my Lord?

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: I think I too much grace you; rather you are a fellow dares not fight, but ſpit and pufte and make a noyſe, whilſt your trembling hand draws out your Sword, to lay it upon andirons, ſtools or tables, rather than on a man,

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Your honor may beſt ſpeak this; yet — with little ſafety, if I thought it ſerious.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: Come, you are a verie braggart, and you have given me cauſe to tell you ſo: what weakneſs have you ever ſeen in me to prompt your ſelf, that I could need your help; or what other reaſon could induce you to it? you never yet had a meals meat from my Table, nor as I remember from my Wardrop any caſt Suit.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: 'Tis true, I never durſt yet have ſuch a ſervile ſpirit, to be the minion of a full ſwoln Lord; but alwaies did deteſt ſuch ſlavery: a meals meat, or a caſt Suit? I wou'd firſt eat the ſtones, and from ſuch rags the dunghils doe afford, pick me a garment.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: I have miſtook the man, his reſolute ſpirit
Proclaimes him generous, he has a noble heart
As free to utter good deeds as to act them;
For had he not been right, and of one piece,
He would have crumpled, curled, and ſtruck himſelf
Out of the ſhape of man into a ſhaddow.
But prethee tell me, if no ſuch fawning hope
Did lead thee on to hazard life for my ſake;
What was it that incited thee?
Tell me; ſpeak it without the imputation of a Sycophant.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Your own deſert, and with it was joyn'd the unfained friendſhip that I judged you ever held unto my former Lord.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.p: The noble Montague?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Yes, the noble and much injured Montague.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: To ſuch a man as thou art, my heart ſhall be
A Casket: I will lock thee up there,
And eſteem thee as a faithfull friend,
The richeſt Jewell that a man enjoyes;
And in thy thou didſt follow once my friend,
And in thy heart ſtill doſt not with his fortunes caſting him off,
Thou ſhalt go hand in hand with me, and ſhare
As well in my ability as love; 'tis not my end
To gain men for my uſe, but a true friend.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: There's no ſuch thriving way to live in grace,
As to have no ſence of it; his back nor belly
Shall not want warming that can practiſe me miſchief;
I walk now with a full purſe, grow high and wanton,
Prune and briske my ſelf in the bright ſhine
Of his good Lordſhips favours; and for what virtue?
For faſhioning my ſelf a murderer.
O noble Montague, to whom I owe my heart,
With all my beſt thoughts, though my tongue have promis'd
To exceed the malice of thy deſtiny,
Never in time of all my ſervice knew I
Such a ſin tempt thy bounty; thoſe that did feed
Upon thy charge had merit or elſe need.

div.stage: Enter Laverdine, and La-poope, with diſguiſes.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Duboys, moſt proſperouſly met.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: How now? will he come this way?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: This way, immediately; therefore thy aſſiſtance, dear Duboys.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: What have you cheated him of the money you ſpoke of?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Fough, as eaſily as a ſilly Countrey wench of her maydenhead; we had it in a twinkling.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: 'Tis well Captain, let me help you, you muſt be our leader in this action.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Tut, fear not, I'll warrant you if my Sword hold, we'll make no ſweating ſickneſs of it.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Why that's well ſaid, but let's retire a little, that we may come on the more bravely; this way, this way.

div.stage: Enter Montague in the hands of three Officers, and three Creditors.

sp.speaker: 1 Cre.
sp.p: Officers look to him, and be ſure you take good ſecurity before he part from you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Why but my friends, you take a ſtrange courſe with me; the ſums I owe you are rather forgetfulneſs, they are ſo ſlight, than want of will or honeſty to pay you.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.p: I Sir, it may be ſo; but we muſt be paid, and we will be paid before you ſcape: we have wife and children, and a charge, and you are going down the wind, as a man may ſay; and therefore it behooves us to look to't in time.

sp.speaker: 2 Cred.
sp.p: Your cloak here wou'd ſatisfie me, mine's not above a three pound matter, beſides the arreſt.

sp.speaker: 3 Cred.
sp.p: 'Faith and mine is much about that matter too; your Girdle and Hangers, and your Beaver, ſhall be ſufficient bail ſor't.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.p: If you have ever a plain black ſute at home, this Silken one, with your Silke-ſtockings, Garters, and Roſes ſhall pacifie me too; for I take no delight, if I have a ſufficient pawn, to caſt any Gentleman in priſon; therefore 'tis but an untruſſing matter: and you are free, we are no unreaſonable creatures you ſee; for mine own part, I proteſt I am loth to put you to any trouble for ſecurity.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Is there no more of you? he wou'd next demand my skin,

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.p: No Sir, here's no more of us, nor do any of us demand your skin, we know not what to do with it: but it may be if you ow'd your Glover any money, he knew what uſe to make of it.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Ye dregs of baſeneſs, vultures amongſt men,
That tyre upon the hearts of generous ſpirits.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.p: You do us wrong Sir, we tyre no generous ſpirits, we tyre nothing but our hackneys.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: But here comes one made of another piece;
A man well meriting that free born name
Of Citizen; welcome my deliverer, I am falen
Into the hands of blood-hounds, that for a ſum
Leſſer than their honeſties, which is nothing,
Wou'd tear me out of my skin.

sp.speaker: Mol.
sp.p: Why Sir, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: 1 Cre.
sp.p: Why Sir the matter is, that we muſt have our money, which if we cannot have, we'll ſatisfie our ſelves with his carcaſs, and be payd that wayes: you had as good Sir, not have been ſo peremptory. Officer, hold faſt.

sp.speaker: 1 Offi.
sp.p: The ſtrenuous fiſt of vengeance now is clutcht; therefore fear nothing.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: What may be the debt in groſs?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Some forty Crowns, nay rather not ſo much, 'tis quickly caſt.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: 'Tis ſtrange to me, that your eſtate ſhou'd have ſo low an ebb, to ſtick at ſuch ſleight ſums: why my friends, you are too ſtrict in your accounts, and call too ſudden on this Gentleman, he has hopes left yet to pay you all.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.p: Hopes? I marry; bid him pay his friends with hopes, and pay us with currant Coyn: I knew a gallant once that fed his creditors ſtill with hopes, and bid 'em they ſhou'd fear nothing, for he had 'em tyed in a ſtring; and truſt me ſo he had indeed, for at laſt he and all his hopes hopt in a halter.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Good Sir, with what ſpeed you may, free me out of the company of theſe ſlaves, that have nothing but their names to ſhow 'em men.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: What wou'd you wiſh me do Sir? I proteſt I ha' not the preſent ſum (ſmall as it is) to lay down for you; and for giving my word, my friends no later than yeſter-night made me take bread and eat it, that I ſhou'd not do it for any man breathing i'th' world; therefore I pray hold me excuſed.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: You do not ſpeak this ſeriouſly?

sp.speaker: Mal,
sp.p: As ever I ſaid my prayers, I proteſt to you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: What may I think of this?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Troth Sir thought is free for any man; we abuſe our betters in it, I have done it my ſelf.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Truſt me, this ſpeech of yours doth much amaze me; pray leave this language, and out of that ſame ſum you lately did receive of me, lay down as much as may diſcharge me.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: You are a merry man Sir, and I am glad you take your croſſes ſo temperately; fare you well Sir, and yet I have ſomething more to ſay to ye, a word in your ear I pray; to be plain with you I did lay this plot to arreſt you to enjoy this money I have of yours, with the more ſafety. I am a fool to tell you this now; but in good faith I could not keep it in. And the money wou'd a done me little good elſe. An honeſt Citizen cannot wholly enjoy his own wife for you, they grow old before they have true uſe of them, which is a lamentable thing, and truely much hardens the hearts of us Citizens againſt you: I can ſay no more, but am heartily ſorry for your heavineſs, and ſo I take my leave.

sp.speaker: 1 Cred.
sp.p: Officers take hold on him again, for Mounſier Mallycorne will do nothing for him I perceive.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Nay come my maſters, leave dancing of the old meaſures, and let's aſſault him bravely.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: By no means; for it goes againſt my ſtomach to kill a roan in an unjuſt quarrell.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: It muſt needs be a clog to a mans conſcience all his life time.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: It muſt indeed Captain: beſides doe ye not ſee he has gotten a guard of friends about him, as if he had ſome knowledge of our purpoſe?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Had he a guard of Devils, as I think them little better, my Sword ſhould doe the meſſage that it came for.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: If you will be ſo deſperate, the blood lie upon your own neck, for we'll not meddle in't.

div.stage: Duboys runs upon Montague, and ſtrugling yields him his Sword; the Officers draw, Laverdine and La-poope in the ſcuffing retire, Montague chaſeth them off the Stage, himſelf wounded.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: I am your friend and ſervant.
Struggle with me and take my Sword;
Noble Sir, make your way, you have ſlain an Officer.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Some one of them has certainly
Requited me; for I doe loſe much blood.

sp.speaker: 1 Offic.
sp.p: Udſprecious, we have loſt a brother, purſue the Gentleman,

sp.speaker: 2 Offic.
sp.p: I'll not meddle with him: you ſee what comes on't; beſides I know he will be hang'd ere he be taken.

sp.speaker: 1 Offic.
sp.p: I tell thee yeoman he muſt be taken ere he be hanged; he is hurt in the guts, run afore therefore and know how his wife will rate his Sawſages a pound.

sp.speaker: 3 Offic.
sp.p: Stay brother, I may live, for ſurely I find I'm but hurt in the leg, a dangerous kick on the ſhin-bone.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Madam Lamira, Madam le Orleans, Veramour.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: YOU ſee Lady
What harmleſs ſports ous Countrey life affords;
And though you meet not here with City dainties,
Or Courtly entertainment, what you have
Is free and hearty.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: Madam, I find here
What is a ſtranger to the Court, content,
And receive curteſies done for themſelves,
Without an expectation of return,
Which binds me to your ſervice.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Oh your love;
My homely houſe built more for uſe than ſhew
Obſerves the Golden mean equally diſtant
From glittering pomp, and ſordid avarice;
For Maskes, we will obſerve the works of nature,
And in the place of viſitation, read:
Our Phyſick ſhall be wholſome walks, our viands,
Nouriſhing, not provoking: for I find
Pleaſures are tortures that leave ſtings behind.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: You have a great eſtate.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: A competency
Sufficient to maintain me and my rank,
Nor am I, I thank Heaven, ſo Courtly bred
As to imploy the utmoſt of my Rents
In paying Tailors for phantaſtick Robes;
Or rather than be ſecond in the faſhion,
Eat out my Officers and my Revenues
With grating uſury; my back ſhall not
Be the baſe on which your ſoothing Citizen
Erects his Summer-houſes; nor on th' other ſide
Will I be ſo penuriouſly wife,
As to make money (that's my ſlave) my Idoll,
Which yet to wrong, merits as much reproof,
As to abuſe our ſervant.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: Yet with your pardon
I think you want the Crown of all contentment.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: In what good Madam?

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: In a worthy husband.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: — It is ſtrange the galley-ſlave ſhould praiſe
His Oar, or ſtroaks; or you, that have made ſhipwrack
Of all delight upon this Rock, cal'd marriage,
Should ſing Encomions ou't.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: Madam, though one fall
From his horſe and break his neck, will you
Conclude from that it is unfit to ride?
Or muſt it follow, becauſe Orleans
My Lord's pleaſed to make his paſſionate triall
Of my ſuſpected patience, that my brother,
(Were he not ſo, I might ſay, worthy Amiens)
Will imitate his ills, that cannot fancy
What's truely Noble in him?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: I muſt grant
There's as much worth in him as can be lookt for
From a young Lord, but not enough to make
Me change my golden liberty and conſent
To be a ſervant to it, as wives are
To the Imperious humors of their Lords:
Me thinks I'm well, I riſe and goe to bed
When I think fit, eat what my appetite
Deſires without controle, my ſervants ſtudy
Is my contentment, and to make me merry
Their fartheſt ayms; my ſleeps are enquired after,
My riſing up ſaluted with reſpect:
Command and liberty now wait upon
My Virgin ſtate; what would I more; change all,
And for a husband? no; theſe freedoms die,
In which they live with my Virginity;
'Tis in their choice that's rich to be a wife,
But not being yoakt to chuſe the ſingle life.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Madam.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: How like you the Countrey?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: I like the ayr of it well Madam, and the rather becauſe, as on Iriſh Timber your Spider will not make his web, ſo for ought I ſee yet your Cheater, Pander, and Informer being in their diſpoſitions too ſoggy for this piercing climate, ſhun it, and choſe rather to walk in miſts in the City.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.p: Who did you ſerve firſt boy?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: A rich Merchants widow, and was by her preferred to a young Court-Lady.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.p: And what difference found you in their ſervice?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Very much: for look how much my old City Madam gave to her young viſitants, ſo much my Lady received from her hoary Court-ſervants.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.p: And what made you to leave her?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: My father (Madam) had a deſire to have me a tall-man, took me from thence.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.p: Well, I perceive you inherit the wag, from your father.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Doves beget Doves; and Eagles, Eagles, Madam: A Citizen here, tho left never ſo rich, ſeldome at the beſt proves a Gentleman: the ſon of an Advocate, tho dub'd like his father, will ſhew a reliſh of his deſcent, and the fathers thriving practice, as I have heard: ſhe that of a Chambermayd is metamorphoſed into a Madam, will yet remember how oft her daughter by her mother ventured to lie upon the ruſhes before ſhe could get in that which makes many Ladyes.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.p: But what think you of your late Maſter?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Oh Madam— Sighs.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.p: Why doe you ſigh? you are ſorry that you leſt him,
He made a wanton of you.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Not for that:
Or if he did, for that my youth muſt love him.
Oh pardon me, if I ſay liberty
Is bondage, if compar'd with his kind ſervice;
And but to have power now to ſpeak his worth
To its deſert; I ſhould be well content
To be an old man when his praiſe were ended:
And yet, if at this inſtant you were pleaſed,
I ſhould begin, the livery of age
Would take his lodging upon this head
Ere I ſhould bring it to a period.
• n brief he is a man (for Heaven forbid
That I ſhould ever live to ſay he was)
Of ſuch a ſhape as would make one beloved,
That never had good thought; and to his body
He hath a mind of ſuch a conſtant temper
In which virtues throng to have a room:
Yet 'gainſt this noble Gentleman, this Montague,
For in that name I comprehend all goodneſs,
Wrong, and the wreſted law, falſe witneſſes,
And envy ſent from hell, have roſe in Armes,
And though not pierc'd, batter'd his honor'd ſhield.
What ſhall I ſay? I hope you will forgive me,
That if you were but pleas'd to love,
I know no Juno worthy ſuch a Jove.

sp.speaker: Lam,
sp.l: 'Tis well yet that I have the ſecond place
In your affection: From whence?

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: From the Lord Amiens, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Tis wellcome, though it bear his uſual language:
I thought ſo much, his love-ſuit ſpeaks his health.
What's he that brought it?

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: A Gentleman of good rank, it ſeems.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Where is he?

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Receiving entertainment in your houſe
Sorting with his degree.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: 'Tis well.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: He waits your Ladyſhips pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: He ſhall not wait long:
I'll leave you for a while; nay ſtay you boy,
Attend the Lady. Exeunt Lam. Charl.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Would I might live once
To wait on my poor Maſter.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: That's a good boy:
This thankfulneſs looks lovely on thy forehead,
And in it, as a book, me thinks I read
Inſtructions for my ſelf, that am his debtor,
And wou'd do much that I might be ſo happy
To repair that which to our grief is ruin'd.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: It were a work a King might glory in,
If he ſaw with my eyes: If you pleaſe Madam,
For ſure to me you ſeem unapt to walk,
To ſit, although the churliſh Birds deny
To give us muſick in this grove, where they
Are prodigall to others: I'll ſtrain my voyce
For a ſad Song, the place is ſafe and private.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: 'Twas my deſire; begin good Viramour.

div.stage: Muſick, a Song, at the end of it enter Montague, fainting, his Sword drawn.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: What's he Viramour?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: A goodly perſonage.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Am I yet ſafe? or is my ſlight a dream;
My wounds and hunger tell me that I wake:
Whither have my fears born me? no matter where,
Who hath no place to goe to, cannot err:
What ſhall I do? cunning calamity!
That others groſs wits uſes to refine,
When I moſt need it duls the edg of mine.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: Is not this Montagues voyce?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: My Maſters? ſie.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: What ſound was that, 'piſh,
Fear makes the wretch think every leaf oth' Jury:
What courſe to live, 'beg? better men have done it,
But in another kind: ſteal? Alexander
Though ſtil'd a Conqueror, was a proud thief,
Though he rob'd with an Army; ſie how idle
Theſe meditations are: though thou art worſe
Than ſorrows tongue can ſpeak thee, thou art ſtill,
Or ſhouldſt be, honeſt Montague.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: 'Tis too true.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: 'Tis he: what villains hands did this? oh that my fleſh
Were Balm; in faith Sir, I would pluck it off
As readily as this; pray you accept
My will to do you ſervice: I have heard
The Mouſe once ſav'd the Lyon in his need,
As the poor S • arab ſpild the Eagles ſeed.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: How do you?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: As a forſaken man.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: Do not ſay ſo, take comfort,
For your misfortunes have been kind in this,
To caſt you on a hoſpitable ſh •
Where dwels a Lady—

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: She to whom, good Maſter,
You prefer'd me.

sp.speaker: L, Orl.
sp.l: In whoſe houſe, whatſoere
Your dangers are, I'll undertake your ſafety.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: I fear that I am purſued, and doubt that I,
In my defence have kild an Officer.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Is that all? there's no law under the Sun
But will I hope confeſs, one drop of blood
Shed from this arme is recompence enough
Though you had cut the throats of all the Catchpoles
In France, nay in the world.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: I would be loth
To be a burthen, or feed like a drone
On the induſtrious labor of a Bee,
And baſer far I hold it to owe for
The bread I eat, what's not in me to pay;
Then ſince my full fortunes are declin'd,
To their low ebb I'll faſhion my high mind.
It was no ſhame to Hecuba, to ſerve
When Troy was fir'd: if't be in your power
To be a means to make her entertainment,
And far from that I was; but to ſupply
My want with habit fit for him that ſerves,
I ſhall owe much to you.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: Leave that care to me.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.p: Good Sir, lean on my ſhoulder; help good Madam: oh that I were a horſe for half an hour, that I might carry you home on my back: I hope you will love me ſtill?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Thou doſt deſerve it boy, that I ſhould live
To be thus troubleſome.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: Good Sir, 'tis none.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.l: Trouble? moſt willingly I would be chang'd
Like Apuleius, weare his Aſſes ears,
Provided I might ſtill this burthen bear.

sp.speaker: L. Orl.
sp.l: 'Tis a kind boy.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: I find true proof of it.

div.stage: Enter Amiens, and Longeville, with a Paper.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: You'll carry it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: As I live although my packet were like Bellerophon's, what have you ſeen in me or my behavior ſince your favors ſo plentifully ſhowr'd upon my wants, that may beget diſtruſt of my preformance?

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: Nay, be not angry, if I entertained
But the leaſt ſcruple of your love, or courage,
I would make choyce of one which my eſtate
Should do me right in this, nor can you blame me
If in a matter of ſuch conſequence
I am ſo importunate.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Good my Lord let me prevent your farther conjurations
To rayſe my ſpirit, I know this is a challenge
To be delivered unto Orleane hand,
And that my undertaking ends not there,
But I muſt be your ſecond, and in that
Not alone ſearch your enemy, meaſure weapons,
But ſtand in all your hazards, as our blouds
Ran in the ſelf-ſame veins, in which if I
Better not your opinion, as a limb
That's putrifi'd and uſeleſs, cut me off,
And underneath the Gallows bury it.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: At full you underſtand me, and in this
Bind me, and what's mine to you and yours,
I will not ſo much wrong you as to add
One ſyllable more, let it ſuffice I leave
My honor to your guard: and in that prove,
You hold the firſt place in my heart and love. Ex. Ami.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: The firſt place in a Lords affection? very good; and how long doth that laſt? perhaps the changing of ſome three ſhirts in the Tennis-Court; well, it were very neceſſary that an order were taken (if it were poſſible,) that younger brothers might have more wit, or more money: for now, however the fool hath long been put upon him that inherits, his revenue hath bought him a ſpunge, and wip't off the imputation, and for the underſtanding of the younger, let him get as much Rhetorick as he can, to grace his language.
They will ſee, he ſhall have gloſs little enough to ſet out his Bark; ſtand Dubois, look about, 's all ſafe?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Approach not near me but with reverence
Lawrel and adorations, I have done more than deſerves, a hundred thanks.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: How now, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: With this hand, only aided by this brain,
Without an Orpheus Harp redeem'd from Hells
Three headed Porter, our Euridice.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Nay, prethee ſpeak ſence, this is like the ſtale bragart in a Play.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Then in plain Proſe thus, and with as little action as thou canſt deſire, the three headed Porter, were three unexorable Catch-poles, out of whoſe jaws without the help of Orpheus Harp, bait or bribe; for thoſe two ſtrings make the Muſick, that molifies thoſe flinty furies, I reſcued our Euridice, I mean my old Maſter Montague.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: And is this all? a poor reſcue; I thought thou hadſt revers'd the judgement for his overthrow in his ſute, or wrought upon his adverſary Orleance, taken the ſhape of a Ghoſt, frighted his mind into diſtraction, and for the appeaſing of his conſcience, forc'd him to make reſtitution of Montague's Lands, or ſuch like reſcue; S'light I would have hired Acrocheture for two Cardekues, to have done ſo much with his whip.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: You wood Sir, and yet 'tis more than three on their foot-cloaths, durſt do for a ſworn Brother, in a Coach.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Beſides, what proof's of it? for ought I know, this may be a trick, I had rather have him a priſoner, where I might viſit him, and do him ſervice, than not at all, or I know not where.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Well Sir, the end will ſhew it, what's that, a challenge?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Yes, where's Orleance? though we fight in jeſt, he muſt meet with Amiens in earneſt, — fall off, we are diſcovered; my horſe garſon; ha!

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Were it not in a houſe, and in his preſence,
To whom I owe all duty —

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: What would it do? prate as it does? but be as far from ſtriking, as he that owes it Orleance.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I think thou art his Porter,
Set here to anſwer creditors, that his Lordſhip
Is not within, or takes the diet: I am ſent,
And will grow here until I have an anſwer,
Not to demand a debt of money, but
To call him to a ſtrict account for wrong
Done to the honors of a Gentleman,
Which nothing but his heart-bloud ſhall waſh off.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Shall I hear this?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: And more, that if I may not
Have acceſs to him, I will fix this here
To his diſgrace and thine.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: And thy life with it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Then have the copies of it p • ſted on poſts,
Have his diſgrace talk for Tobacco-ſhops,
His picture baffled.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: All reſpect away, wer't in a Church— draw bath.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: This is the • ook I pray with.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.p: • or 〈…〉 your lives.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: 〈◊〉 are you 〈◊〉 I hope your Lordſhip can read (thought 〈◊〉 not his 〈…〉 Scholar-ſhip) doth it not pleaſe you 〈…〉 muſter up the reſt of your attendance, which 〈…〉 Cook, a Pander, Coach-man, and a Footm • n, in t ••• e day, a great 〈◊〉 Lords train, pretending I •• unworthy to bring you a • hallenge, inſtead of anſwering it have me 〈◊〉

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: If he does, tho • deſerv'ſt it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: I dare you all to touch me, I'll not ſtand ſtill,
What anſwer?

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: That thou haſt done to Ami • as
The office of a faithful friend, whi • h
Would cheriſh in thee, were he not my • oe,
How ever ſince on honourable terms
He calls me forth, ſay I will meet with him,
And by Dubois e'r Sun-ſet make him know
The time and place, my ſwords length, and what ever
Scruple of circumſtance he can expect.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: This anſwer comes unlookt for, fare you well,
Finding your temper thus, wou'd I had ſaid leſs. Exit.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Now comes thy love to the teſt.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: My Lord, 'twill hold,
And in all dangers prove it ſelf true Gold. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I will acquaint my Lady with your coming.
Pleaſe you repoſe your ſelves here.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: There's a Teſter, nay, now I am a wooer, I muſt be bountiful.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p:
If you would have two three-pences for it Sir, To give ſome of your kindred as you • ide, I'll ſ • e •• I can get them; we uſe not (tho ſervants) to take 〈◊〉
Ex.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Then thou art unfit to be in office, either in Court or City.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Indeed, corruption is a Tree, whoſe branches are of an unmeaſurable length, they ſpread every where, and the dew, that drops from thence, hath infected ſome chairs and ſtools of authority.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Ah Captain! lay not all the fault upon Officers, you know you can ſhark, tho you be out of action, witneſs Montague.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Hang him, he's ſafe enough; you had a hand in it too, and have gained by him; but I wonder you Citizens, that keep ſo many books, and take ſuch ſtrict accounts for every farthing due to you from others, reſerve not ſo much as a memorandum for the courteſies you receive.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Would you have a Citizen book thoſe? thankfulneſs is a thing, we are not ſworn to in our Indentures: you may as well urge conſcience.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Talk no more of ſuch vanities, Mountague is it recoverably ſunk, I would we had twenty more to ſend after him; the Snake that would be a Dragon, and have wings, muſt eat; and what implies that, but this, that in this Cannibal age, he that would have the ſute of wealth, muſt not care—whom he feeds on? and as I have heard, no fleſh battens better, then that of a profeſt friend; and he that would mount to honor, muſt not make dainty to uſe the head of his mother, back of his Father, or neck of his Brother, for ladders to his preferment; for, but obſerve, and you ſhall find for the moſt part, cunning villany ſit at a Feaſt as principal gueſt, and innocent honeſty wait as a contemn'd ſervant with a trencher.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: The Ladies.

div.stage: Enter Montague bare-headed, Lamira, Lady Orleance, Charlotte and Voramour,

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Do ye ſmell nothing?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Not I Sir.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: The carrion of knaves is very ſtrong in my noſtrils

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.l: we came to admire, and find Fame was a niggard,
Which we thought prodigal in our report
Before we ſaw you.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: • uſh Sir, this Courtſhip's old.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.l: I'll ſight for thee, ſweet wench,
This is my tongue, and woes for me.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Good man of War,
Hands off; if you take me, it muſt be by ſiege,
Not by an onſet; and for your valour, I
Think that I have derſeved few enemies,
And therefore need it not.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Thou need'ſt nothing, ſweet Lady, but an obſequious husband, and where wilt thou find him, if not in the City? We are true Muſcovites to our Wives, and are never better pleaſed, than when they uſe us as ſlaves, bridle and Saddle us; Have me, thou ſhalt command all my wealth as thine own, thou ſhalt ſit like a Queen in my Ware-houſe; And my Factors at the return with my ſhips, ſhall pay thee tribute of all the rarities of the earth, thou ſhalt wear gold, feed on delicates, the firſt Peaſcods, Strawberries, Grapes, Cherries ſhall—

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Be mine? I apprehend what you would ſay,
Thoſe dainties which the City pays ſo dear for,
The Countrey yields for nothing, and as early;
And, credit me, your far-fet viands pleaſe not
My appetite better than thoſe that are near hand.
Then for your promis'd ſervice and ſubjection
To all my humors, when I am your wife,
Which is as it ſeems, is frequent in the City,
I cannot find what pleaſure they receive
In uſing their fond Husbands like their Maids;
But of this, more hereafter: I accept
Your proffer kindly, and yours; my houſe ſtands open
To entertain you, take your pleaſure in it,
And eaſe after your journey.

sp.speaker: La. Orl.
sp.l: Do you note the boldneſs of the fellows?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Alas Madam, a Virgin muſt in this be like a Lawyer,
And as he takes all Fees; ſhe muſt hear all ſuitors; the
One for gain, the other for her mirth; ſtay with the
Gentlemen, we'll to the Orchards.

div.stage: Exeunt Lamira, Lady Orleance, Vera. and Charl.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.l: — What art thou?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: An honeſt man, though poor;
And look they like to monſters, are they ſo rare?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.l: Roſe from the dead.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Do you hear Monſieur Serviture, didſt thou never hear of one Montague, a prodigal gull, that lives about Paris?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: So Sir.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: One that after the loſs of his main eſtate in a Law-ſute, bought an Office in the Court.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: And ſhould have Letters of Mart, to have the Spaniſh treaſure as it came from the Indies; were not thou and he twins? put off thy Hat, let me ſee thy Fore-head.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Though you take priviledge to uſe your tongue,
I pray you hold your fingers,
'Twas your baſe cozenages made me as I am:
And were you ſomewhere elſe, I would take off
This proud film from your eyes, that will not let you,
Know I am Montague.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.p: I will obſerve this better.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: And art thou he? I will do thee grace; give me thy hand: I am glad thou haſt taken ſo good a courſe; ſerve God, and pleaſe thy Miſtriſs; if I prove to be thy Maſter, as I am very likely, I will do for thee.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Faith the fellow's well made for a Serving-man, and will no doubt, carry a chine of Beef with a good grace.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Prethee be careful of me in my chamber, I will remember thee at my departure.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: All this I can endure under this roof,
And ſo much owe I her, whoſe now I am,
That no wrong ſhall incenſe me to moleſt,
Her quiet houſe, while you continue here,
I will not be aſhamed to do you ſervice
More than to her, becauſe ſuch is her pleaſure.
But you that have broke thrice, and fourteen times
Compounded for two ſhillings in the pound,
Know I dare kick you in your ſhop; do you hear?
If ever I ſee Paris, though an Army
Of muſty Murrions, ruſty brown Bills and Clubs,
Stand for your guard — I have heard of your tricks,
And you that ſmell of Amber at my charge,
And triumph in your cheat; well, I may live
To meet thee, be it among a troop of ſuch
That are upon the fair face of the Court
Like running Ulcers, and before thy whore
Trampel upon thee.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.l: This a language for a Livery? take heed, I am a Captain.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: A Coxcomb are you not? that thou and I,
To give proof, which of us dares moſt, were now
In midſt of a rough Sea, upon a piece
Of a ſplit Ship, where only one might ride,
I would — but fooliſh anger makes me talk
Like a Player.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Indeed you act a part
Doth ill become you my ſervant; is this your duty?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: I crave your pardon, and will hereafter be more circumſpect.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Oh the power of a Womans tongue: it hath done more than we three with our ſwords durſt undertake; put a mad man to ſilence.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Why ſirrah, theſe are none of your comrades
To drink with in the Cellar; one of them
For ought you know, may live to be your Maſter.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.l: There's ſome comfort yet.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Here's choice of three, a wealthy Merchant.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Hem, ſhe's taken, ſhe hath ſpy'd my good Calf,
And many Ladies chuſe their Husbands by that.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: A Courtier that's in grace, a valiant Captain,
And are theſe mates for you, away, be gone.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: I humbly pray you will be pleaſed to pardon,
And to give ſatisfaction to you Madam,
(Although I break my heart) I will confeſs
That I have wrong'd them too, and make ſubmiſſion.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: No I'll ſpare that; go bid the Cook haſte ſupper.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Oh brave Lady, thou art worthy to have ſervants, to be commandreſs of a Family, that knoweſt how to uſe and govern it.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: You ſhall have many Miſtreſſes that will ſo miſtake, as to take their Horſe-keepers, and Footmen inſtead of their Husbands, thou art none of thoſe.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: But ſhe that can make diſtinction of men, and knows when ſhe hath gallants, and fellows of rank and quality in her houſe —.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Gallants indeed, if it be the Gallants faſhion
To triumph in the miſeries of a man,
Of which they are the cauſe: one that tranſcends
(In ſpight of all that fortune hath, or can be done)
A million of ſuch things as you, my doors
Stand open to receive all ſuch as wear
The ſhape of Gentlemen, and my gentler nature
(I might ſay weaker) weighs not the expence
Of entertainment; think you I'll forget yet
What's due unto my ſelf? do not I know,
That you have dealt with poor Montague, but like
Needy Commanders, cheating Citizens,
And perjur'd Courtiers? I am much mov'd, elſe uſe not
To ſay ſo much, if you will bear your ſelves
As fits ſuch, you would make me think you are,
You may ſtay; if not, the way lies before you. Exit.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: What think you of this Captain?

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: That this is a bawdy-houſe, with Pinacles and Turrets, in which this diſguiſed Montague goes to Rut gratis, and that this is a landed pandreſs, and makes her houſe a brothel for charity.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Come, that's no miracle; but from whence derive you the ſuppoſition?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Obſerve but the circumſtance; you all know that in the height of Mountagues proſperity, he did affect, and had his love return'd by this Lady Orleans; ſince her divorcement, and his decay of eſtate, it is known they have met, not ſo much as his boy but is wanting; and that this can be any thing elſe than a meer plot for their night-work, is above my imagination to conceive.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Nay, it carries probability, let us obſerve it better, but yet with ſuch caution, as our prying be not diſcovered: here's all things to be had without coſt, and therefore good ſtaying here.

sp.speaker: La-p.
sp.p: Nay, that's true, I would we might wooe her twenty years, like Penelopes ſutors; come Laverdine.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: I follow inſtantly, yonder he is.
The thought of this boy hath much cool'd my affection to his Lady, and by all conjectures, this is a diſguiſed whore; I will try if I can ſearch this Mine, Page —

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Your pleaſure, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Thou art a pretty boy.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: And you a brave man; now I am out of your debt.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Nay, prethee ſtay.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: I am in haſte, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: By the faith of a Courtier.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Take heed what you ſay, you have taken a ſtrange oath.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: I have not ſeen a youth that hath pleaſed me better; I would thou couldſt lie me, ſo far as to leave thy Lady and wait on me, I would maintain thee in the braveſt cloaths.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Though you took them up on truſt, or bought 'em at the Brokers.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Or any way: then thy imployments ſhould be ſo neat and cleanly, thou ſhouldſt not touch a pair of pantables in a month, and thy lodging —

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Should be in a brothel.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: No, but in mine arms.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: That my be the circle of a Bawdy-houſe, or worſe.

sp.speaker: Lev.
sp.p: I mean thou ſhould'ſt lye with me.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Lie with you? I had rather lye with my Ladies Monkey; 'twas never a good world, ſince our French Lords learned of the Neapolitans, to make their Pages their Bed-fellows, doth more heart to the Suburb Ladies, than twenty dead vacations; 'Tis ſupper time, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: I thought ſo, I know by that 'tis a woman, for becauſe, peradventure ſhe hath made trial of the Monkey, ſhe prefers him before me, as one unknown; well, theſe are ſtanding creatures, and have ſtrange deſires; and men muſt uſe ſtrange means to quenceh ſtrange fires.

div.head: Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Montague alone in mean habit.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: NOw Montague, who diſcerns thy ſpirit now?
Thy breeding, or thy bloud? here's a poor cloud
Eclipſeth all thy ſplendor; who can read
In thy pale face, dead eye, or lenten ſhute,
The liberty thy ever-giving hand
Hath bought for others, manacling it ſelf
In gyves of parchment indiſſoluble?
The greateſt hearted man ſupplyed with means,
Nobility of birth and gentleſt parts,
I, thought the right hand of his Sovereign,
If virtue quit her ſeat in his high ſoul,
Glitters but like a Palace ſet on fire,
Whoſe glory whilſt it ſhines, but ruins him,
And his bright ſhow each hour to aſhes tending
Shall at the laſt be rak'd up like a ſparkle,
Unleſs mens lives and fortunes feed the ſlame.
Not for my own wants, though blame I my Stars,
But ſuffering others to caſt love on me,
When I can neither take, nor thankful be.
My Ladies woman, fair and virtuous
Young as the preſent month, ſollicites me
For love and marriage now being nothing worth —

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Oh! Maſter, I have ſought you a long hour,
Good faith, I never joy'd out of your ſight;
For Heavens ſake, Sir, be merry, or elſe bear
The buffets of your fortunes with more ſcorn;
Do but begin to rail, teach me the way,
And I'll ſit down, and help your anger forth:
I have known you wear a ſuit; full worth a Lordſhip,
Give to a man whoſe need ne'er frighted you
From calling of him friend, five hundred Crowns
E'er ſleep had left your ſences to conſider
Your own important preſent uſes; yet
Since I have ſeen you with a tencher wait,
Void of all ſcorn, therefore I'll wait on you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Would Heaven thou wert leſs honeſt.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Would to Heaven you were leſs worthy: I am ev'n w'e Sir.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Is not thy Maſter ſtrangely fall'n, when thou
Serveſt for no wages, but for charity?
Thou doſt ſurcharge me with thy plenteous love:
The goodneſs of thy virtue ſhown to me,
More opens ſtill my diſability
To quit thy pains: credit me loving boy,
A free and honeſt nature may be oppreſt,
Tir'd with courteſies from a liberal ſpirit,
When they exceed his means of gratitude.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: But 'tis a due in him that to that end
Extends his love or duty,

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Little world
Of virtue, why doſt love and follow me?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: I will follow you through all Countreys,
I'll run (faſt as I can) by your horſe ſide,
I'll hold your ſtirrop when you do alight,
And without grudging, wait till you return:
I'll quit offer'd means, and expoſe my ſelf
To cold and hunger, ſtill to be with you;
Fearleſs I'll travel through a wilderneſs,
And when you are weary, I will lay me down
That in my boſom you may reſt your head,
Where whilſt you ſleep, I'll watch, that no wild beaſt
Shall hurt or trouble you: and thus we'll breed a ſtory
To make every hearer weep,
When they diſcourſe our fortunes and our loves,

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Oh what a ſcoff might men of women make,
If they did know this boy? but my deſire
Is, that thou wouldeſt not (as thou uſeſt ſtill:
When like a ſervant, I'mong ſervants ſit)
Wait on my Trencher, fill my cups with Wine:
Why ſhould'ſt thou do this boy? prethee conſider,
I am not what I was.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Curſt be the day when I forget that Montague was
Thy Lord, or not remember him my Maſter ſtill.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Rather curſe me, with whom thy youth hath ſpent,
So many hours, and yet untaught to live
By any worldly quality.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: Indeed you never taught me how to handle Cards
To cheat and cozen men with oaths and lies:
Thoſe are the worldly qualities to live:
Some of our ſcarlet Gallants teach their boys
Theſe worldly qualities.
Since ſtumbling fortune then leaves virtue thus
Let me leave fortune, e'r be vicious.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: Oh lad, thy love will kill me.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.l: In truth, I think in conſcience I ſhall dye for you:
Good Maſter weep not, do you want aught, Sir?
Will you have any money, here's ſome Silver;
And here's a little Gold, 'twill ſerve to play,
And put more troubleſome thoughts out of your mind:
I pray Sir take it, I'll get more with ſinging.
And then I'll bring it you, my Lady ga't me,
And—it was not covetouſneſs,
But I forgot to tell you ſooner on't.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Alas boy, thou art not bound to tell it me,
And leſs to give it, buy thee Scarfs and Garters,
And when I have money, I will give thee a ſword:
Nature made thee a beauteous Cabinet
To lock up all all the goodneſs of the earth.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: I have loſt my voice with the very ſight of this Gentlewoman? good Sir ſteal away, you were wont to be a curious avoider of womens company.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Why boy, thou dar'ſt truſt me any where, dar'ſt thou not?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: I had rather truſt you by a roaring Lion, than a ravening woman.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: Why boy?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Why truly ſhe devours more mans fleſh—

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: I, but ſhe roars not boy.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: No Sir, why ſhe is never ſilent but when her mouth is full.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.p: Monſieur Montague.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: My ſweet fellow, ſince you pleaſe to call me ſo,

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Ah my conſcience, ſhe wou'd be pleas'd well enough to call you bed-fellow: oh Maſter, do not hold her by the hand ſo: a woman is a Lime-buſh, that catcheth all ſhe toucheth.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.p: I do moſt dangerouſly ſuſpect this boy to be a wench; art thou not one? come hither, let me feel thee.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.p: Why doſt thou pull off thy Glove?

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Why, to feel whether you be a boy, or no.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.p: Fie boy, go too. I'll not look your head, nor comb your locks any more, if you talk thus.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Why, I'll ſing to you no more then.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.p: Fie upon't, how ſad you are? a young Gentleman that was the very Sun of France.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: But I am in the eclipſe now.

sp.speaker: Chal.
sp.p: Suffer himſelf to be over-run with a Lethargy of melancholy and diſcontent! rouze up thy ſpirit, man, and ſhake it off: A Noble Soul is like a Ship at Sea,
sp.l: That ſleeps at Anchor when the Ocean's calm;
But when ſhe rages, and the wind blows high,
He cuts his way with skill and Majeſty.
sp.p: I would turn a Fool, or Poet, or any thing, or marry, to make you merry; prethee let's walk: good Veramour, leave thy Maſter and me, I have earneſt buſineſs with him.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Pray do you leave my Maſter, and me: we were very merry before you came, he does not covet womens company.
sp.l: What have you to do with him? come Sir will you go?
And I'll ſing to you again:
sp.p: I'faith his mind is ſtronger than to credit Womens vows, and too pure to be capable of their loves.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.p: The boy is jealous, ſweet lad leave us: my Lady call'd for you I ſwear: that's a good child, there's a piece of Gold for thee, go buy a Feather.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: There's two pieces for you, do you go and buy one, or what you will, or nothing, ſo you go. Nay then I ſee you would have me go. Sir; why, i'faith I will, now I perceive you love her better than you do me; but Heaven bleſs you whatever you do, or intend, I know you are a very honeſt man. Exit.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Still will I wooe thee, whilſt thy ears reply
I cannot, or I will not marry thee?
Why haſt thou drawn the bloud out of my cheeks,
And given a quicker motion to my heart?
Oh thou haſt bred a Feaver in my veins
Call'd love, which no Phyſitian can cure;
Have mercy on a Maid, whoſe ſimple youth—

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: How your example, faireſt, teacheth me
A ceremonious Idolatry! Kneels.
By all the joy of love, I love thee better,
Than I or any man can tell another;
And will expreſs the mercy which thou crav'ſt,
I will forbear to marry thee: conſider
Thou art Natures heir in feature, and thy parents,
In fair Inheritances; riſe with theſe thoughts,
And look on me; but with a womans eye,
A decaid fellow, void of means and ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Of ſpirit?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Yes, could I tamely live,
Forget my Fathers bloud, wait, and make legs,
Stain my beſt breeches, with the ſervile drops
That fall from others draughts.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: This vizard wherewith thou wouldſt hide thy ſpirit,
Is perſpective, to ſhew it plainlier.
This undervalue of thy life, is but
Becauſe I ſhould not buy thee, what more ſpeaks
Greatneſs of man, than valiant patience,
That ſhrinks not under his fates ſtrongeſt ſtrokes?
Theſe Roman deaths, as falling on a ſword,
Opening of veins, with poiſon quenching thirſt,
(Which we erroneouſly do ſtile the deeds
Of the heroick and magnanimous man)
Was dead-ey'd cowardize, and white-cheek'd fear,
Who doubting tyranny; and fainting under
Fortunes falſe Lottery, deſperately run
To death, for dread of death; that ſoul's moſt ſtout,
That bearing all miſchance, dares laſt it out;
Will you perform your word, and marry me,
When I ſhall call you to't?

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: I'faith I will.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Who's this alights here?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: With leave, fair creature, are you the Lady Miſtriſs of the houſe?

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Her ſervant, Sir.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I pray then favour me, to inform your Lady, and Duke Orleans wife,
A buſineſs of import awaits 'em here,
And craves for ſpeedy anſwer.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: Are you in poſt, Sir?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: No, I am in Satin; Lady; I would you would be in poſt.

sp.speaker: Charl.
sp.l: I will return, Sweet. Exit.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Honeſt friend, do you belong to the houſe? I pray be covered.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Yes Sir, I do.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Ha, dream'ſt thou Longaville? ſure 'tis not he: Sir I ſhould know you.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: So ſhould I you, but that I am aſham'd.
But though thou know'ſt me, prethee Longaville,
Mock not my poverty, pray remember your ſelf;
Shows it not ſtrangely for thy cloaths to ſtand
Without a Hat to mine? mock me no more.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: The—embroider me all over, Sir,
If ever I began to mock you yet.
The—on me, why ſhould I wear Velvet
And Silver Lace?—I will tear it off.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Why Mad-man?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Put on my Hat? yes, when I am hang'd I will:
—I could break my head.
For holding eyes that knew not you at firſt:
But time and fortune run your courſes with him,
He'll laugh and ſtorm you, when you ſhew moſt hate.

div.stage: Enter Lamira, Orlean's Lady, Laverdine, La Poop, Malycorn, Veramour, Charlot.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: You're a fair Mounſieur.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Do you mock me, Lady?

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Your buſineſs, Sir, I mean.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Regard your ſelf good Mounſieur Longueville.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: You are too negligent of your ſelf and place,
Cover your head ſweet Mounſieur.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Miſtake me not fair Ladies,
'Tis not to you, nor you, that I ſtand bare.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.l: Nay ſweet dear Mounſieur, let it not be to us then.

sp.speaker: La Poop.
sp.l: —A compliment.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: And—of manners.
Pray hide your head, your gallants uſe to do't.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: And you your foreheads, why you needful acceſſary raſcals,
That cannot live without your mutual knaveries,
More than a Bawd, a Pandor, or a Whore
From one another; how dare you ſuſpect
That I ſtand bare to you? what make you here?
Shift your houſe, Lady of 'em, for I know 'em,
They come to ſteal Napkins, and your Spoons;
Look to your Silver-bodkin, (Gentlewoman)
'Tis a dead Ʋtenſil, and Page 'ware your pockets;
My reverence is unto this man, my Maſter,
Whom you, with proteſtations, and oaths
As high as Heaven, as deep as Hell, which would
Deceive the wiſeſt man of honeſt nature,
Have cozen'd and abus'd; but I may meet you,
And beat you one with th' other.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.l: Peace, no more.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Not a word, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.l: I am ſomething thick of hearing; what ſaid he?

sp.speaker: La poop.
sp.l: I hear him, but regard him not.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Nor I, I am never angry faſting.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: My love keeps back my duty, nobleſt Lady;
If Husband or brother merit love from you,
Prevent their dangers, this hour brings to trial
Their hereto ſleeping hates; by this time each
Within a yard is of the others heart,
And met to prove their cauſes and their ſpirits
With their impartial ſwords points; haſte and ſave,
Or never meet them more, but at the grave.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Oh my diſtracted heart, that my wrackt honor
Should for a Brothers, or a Husbands life, through thy undoing, die.

sp.speaker: Lam.
sp.l: Amiens engag'd; if he miſcarry all my hopes and joys,
I now confeſs it loudly, are undone:
Caroch, and haſte, one minute may betray
A life more worth than all time can repay.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Hump: Monſieur Laverdine purſues this boy extreamly, Captain, what will you do?

sp.speaker: La p.
sp.p: Any thing but follow to this Land-ſervice; I am a Sea-Captain you know, and to offer to part 'em, without we could do't like Watermen with long ſtave, a quarter of a mile off, might be dangerous.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Why then let's retire and pray for 'em, I am reſolv'd to ſtop your intent; abus'd more than we have been we cannot be, without they fall to flat beating on's.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: And that were unkindly done i' • aith.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: But you are the trouleſomeſt Aſs that e'er I met with; retire, you ſmell like a womans chamber, that's newly up, before ſhe have pinſht her vapours in with her cloaths.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: I will haunt thee like thy Grandames Ghoſt, thou ſhalt never reſt for me.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Well, I perceive 'tis vain to conceal a ſecret from you: believe it Sir, indeed I am a woman.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: Why la; I knew't, this Propheti • al tongue o • mine never ſail'd me; my mother was half a wi •• h, never any thing that ſhe foreſpake, but came to paſs: a woman? how happy am I? now we may lawfully come together without fear of hanging; ſweet wench, be gracious, in honourable ſort I woe, no otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: Faith, the truth is, I have loved you long.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: See, ſee.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: But durſt not open it.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.p: — I think ſo.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: But briefly, when you bring it to the teſt, if there be not one Gentleman in this houſe, w •• l ch • llenge more intereſt in me, than you can, I am at your di • poſure.

sp.speaker: Lav.
sp.l: Oh Fortunatus, I envy thee not
For Cap, or pouch, this day I'll prove my Fortune,

In which your Lady doth ele ••
•• r Husband,
Who will he Amiens, 'twill ſave my wedding dinner,
Povera, La Poop, and Malicor • : if all ſail,
I will turn Citizen, a beauteous wife
Is the Horn-book to the richeſt Tradeſmans life.

div.stage: Enter Duboys, Orleans, Longueville, Amiens, two Lacques, a Page with two Piſtols.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: Here's a good even piece of ground my Lords:
Will you fix here?

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Yes, any where; Lacquey, take off my ſpurs;
Upon a bridge, a rail, but my ſwords breadth upon a battlement.
I'll fight this quarrel.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: O' the Ropes, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Upon a Line.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: So all our Countrey Duels are carried, like a firework on a thred.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Go now, ſtay with the horſes, and, do you hear?
Upon your lives, till ſome of us come to you,
Dare not to look this way.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: Except you ſee ſtrangers or others that by chance or purpoſe are like to interrupt us.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Then give warning.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Who takes a ſword? the advantage is ſo ſmall,
As he that doubts, hath the free leave to chooſe.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Come, give me any, and ſearch me; 'tis not
The ground, weapon, or ſeconds that can make
Odds in thoſe fatal trials: but the cauſe.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: Moſt true, and, but it is no time to wiſh
When men are come to do, I would deſire
The cauſe 'twixt us were other than it is;
But where the right is, there prevail our Swords.
And if my Siſter have out-liv'd her honor,
I do not pray I may out-live her ſhame.

sp.speaker: Orl.
sp.l: Your Siſter Amiens, is a whore, at once.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: You oft have ſpoke that ſence to me before,
But never in ths language Orleance;
And when you ſpoke it fair, and firſt, I told you
That it was poſſible you might be abus'd:
B • t now, ſince you forget your manners, you ſhall find,
If I tranſgreſs my cuſtom, you do lye,
And are a villain, which I had rather yet
My ſword had prov'd, than I been forc'd to ſpeak:
Nay, give us leave, and ſince you ſtand ſo haughtily
And highly on your cauſe, let you and I,
Without engaging theſe two Gentlemen, ſingly determine it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: My Lord, you'll pardon us.

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.l: I truſt your Lordſhips may not do us that affront.

sp.speaker: Ami.
sp.l: As how?

sp.speaker: Dub.
sp.p: We kiſs your Lordſhips hand, and come to ſerve you here with ſwords.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: My Lord, we underſtand our ſelves.

sp.speaker: Dub.
